# Developmental Biology, Organization, and Function of , the Synovial Joints

### KEY POINTS

### Classification of Joints

The joints are essential for skeletal motion, function, and quality of life. They display a broad spectrum of shapes, sizes, tissue composition, and overall organization, with each combination uniquely fitted to anatomic location and to the specific type and range of motion and mechanical function needed for the performance of adjacent skeletal elements. In consideration of such structural and functional diversity, several classification systems have been developed over the years to describe, distinguish, and characterize the joints. Most often, joints are classified based on their main histologic component, namely fibrous, cartilaginous,

or synovial, as well as degree and type of movement, with these two main classification systems correlating with and instructing each other (Table 1.1).2,

Fibrous joints are characterized by a dense connecting tissue bridging and joining the adjacent bone structures. These joints permit minimal if any movement, have no joint cavity, and are also known as synarthroses (Table 1.1). One typical example of fibrous joints are the sutures of the growing skull that are minimally flexible at birth, permit and sustain the enlargement of cranial vault to accommodate the growing brain, and eventually ossify by the end of skull growth. Another example is the gomphoses in which the periodontal fibrous tissue connects the tooth to its underlying bone socket. Syndesmoses are constituted by ligament-like connective tissue that bridges two neighboring bones such as the ulna and radius, creating a slightly moveable joint structure in between.

Cartilaginous joints bridge bones through hyaline cartilage or fibrocartilage, eliciting some degree of flexibility and motion, known also as amphiarthroses (Table 1.1). Examples of these joints include the joint between the first rib and sternum and the epiphyseal growth plate and are referred to as primary cartilaginous joints or synchondroses. Additional examples are the pubic symphysis and intervertebral disks that have a fibrocartilaginous character and are also called secondary cartilaginous joints.

Synovial joints are characterized by a synovial cavity delimited by synovial lining and filled with a lubricating synovial fluid composed of water, plasma filtrate, and joint lubricants including hyaluronic acid, the glycoprotein lubricin, and phospholipids (Fig. 1.1). The joints are fully enclosed and separated from the body environment by a fibrous tissue-rich capsule. The opposing articulating ends of the flanking bones are covered by articular cartilage that is a resilient, zonal, and long-lasting tissue and provides critical mechanical and biologic function. These joints are characterized by nearly frictionless motion and a broad spectrum of range and degree of motion, represent the major functional joints in the skeleton, and are also known as diarthroses (Table 1.1). Synovial joints are classified by the number of axes of motion they allow, specifically uniaxial (i.e., humeroulnar), biaxial (wrist), and multiaxial (shoulder). They are also distinguished based on the type and architecture of the anatomic connection they mediate, including

ball and socket (i.e., hip), hinge (elbow), saddle (first carpometacarpal), and plane (patellofemoral). These various designs permit flexion, extension, abduction, adduction, or rotation of skeletal elements. Because of their preponderance, critical nature, and susceptibility to common diseases including all forms of arthritis,5 this chapter mainly focuses on the developmental biology, character, and functioning of limb synovial joints, referring to other joints as appropriate and relevant. Studying fetal development and embryonic processes in humans is exceedingly difficult for many

reasons. This chapter thus relies on studies carried out with experimental animals and relates data and insights to analogous human developmental processes whenever possible.

### Developmental Biology of Limb Diarthrodial Joints and Skeletal Elements

### Onset of Limb Skeletogenesis

The developing limb in mammalian and avian embryos has for over a century represented a common and experimentally approachable system to probe and decipher the basic cellular and morphogenetic mechanisms by which onset and progression of skeletal development are brought about. Original chick-quail tissue transplantation studies and more recent genetic cell lineage tracing mouse studies have established that the limb skeleton and neighboring connective tissues including the tissues of the synovial joint derive from early progenitor cells initially located in the lateral mesoderm,7 migrating into the incipient limb bud along with pioneer nerves and blood vessels. The limb skeletal muscles instead derive from progenitors originating in the somites.9, As the limb bud elongates along its main proximal-distal axis, the mesodermal cells begin to aggregate with each other by production of adhesion proteins including N-Cadherin and N-Cam (neural cell adhesion molecule), giving rise to dense, blood vesselfree, mesenchymal condensations that broadly pre-figure the future limb skeleton (Fig. 1.2A). Hox genes have been demonstrated to be essential in providing the mesenchymal condensations with skeletal element identity instructions, enabling them to eventually generate stylopod skeletal elements (humerus or femur), zeugopod elements (radius/ulna or tibia/fibula), and autopod elements (carpals/tarsals and digits). Hox10, Hox11, and Hox13 paralogous genes are respectively expressed in the stylopod, zeugopod, or autopod regions of the early limbs, in turn dictating the future development of region-specific skeletal elements. For example, transgenic ablation of all Hox11 genes (Hoxa11, Hoxcl1 and Hoxd1 1) in mice prevents the development of the radius/ulna and tibia/fibula in the zeugopod, without affecting the development of elements in the stylopod and autopod regions.

As they become configured and instructed under the guidance of Hox genes, the closely associated vessel-free mesenchymal condensations become concurrently committed to chondrogenesis, acquiring the ability to transition from a mesenchymal character to a differentiated cartilage phenotype (Fig. 1.2B). It was originally

shown that the vessel-free character of the condensations is required for chondrogenic commitment and differentiation,14 and several subsequent studies have demonstrated that chondrogenesis does require, and is stimulated by, hypoxia. A number of genes encoding transcription factors and signaling proteins are engaged in, and coordinate, chondrogenic cell differentiation within the mesenchymal condensations.16, A primary role is played by Sox transcription factors, in particular Sox9 together with its transcriptional partners Sox5 and Sox6 (the so-called Sox trio), and genetic ablation of Sox9 prevents limb chondrogenesis and skeletal development. The incipient cartilaginous tissue emerging from these critical differentiation steps is highly cellular but relatively poor in collagen II and aggrecan extra-cellular matrix. However, its cells are endowed not only with skeletal element identity as indicated but also morphometric information needed for skeletal primordia growth and elongation along the proximo-distal axis. Mechanisms including planar cell polarity in coordination with apical ectoderm ridge-derived fibroblast growth factors appear to play a preponderant role in aligning the condensing progenitors along that axis and facilitating growth and growth rates along it. As it is described below, the newly differentiated chondrocytes constituting the cartilaginous primordia in turn begin a complex and still unclear process by which they become distinguished in epiphyseal and diaphyseal cells and set about to organizing the growth plates and primary and secondary ossification centers.

### Determination of Joint Site and Interzone Formation

The initial primitive cartilaginous skeletal framework in the limb does not display overt signs of joint formation (Figs. 1.2B and 1.3A). Indeed, embryologists realized long ago that the initial limb skeletal framework, established by the mesenchymal cell condensations first and the cartilaginous tissue thereafter, is continuous and uninterrupted and does not contain obvious demarcations of where the joints will eventually form.6, An example is the Y-shaped cartilaginous anlagen representing the single prospective stylopod element (humerus or femur) proximally and continuing and branching into two prospective zeugopod elements (radius and ulna or tibia and fibula) distally (Fig. 1.2B). Considering

those morphologic findings, studies suggested that the exact anatomic location of the joints (elbow and knee in the example above) is determined by the boundaries and intersection points among the expression patterns of Hox genes (Figs. 1.3A-B).21, One group carried out a detailed stereological analysis in chick limbs and found that expression patterns of Hoxa genes were related to positional signaling and segmentation processes within the preskeletal condensations along the proximo-distal axis, whereas Hoxd gene expression patterns were also related to bifurcation and branching in the antero-posterior axis. They proposed that the biaxial intersection points of such Hox expression patterns would determine the joint sites. These notions have not been further tested or verified since, and there is still no clear understanding on how the anatomic sites of joint development are established.

Morphologically, however, embryologists discovered that joint initiation was revealed by the appearance of an "interzone" at each expected joint location, so named because it interrupted an otherwise continuous cartilaginous structure (Figs. 1.2C and 1.3C). Earlier investigators had used the terms "articular disk" or "zwisch- >>24 These original and perceptive studies and numerous enmasse. subsequent studies have established that the interzone is initially composed of mesenchymal cells, which are bound to each other even more closely than the cells constituting the flanking preskeletal condensations and are linked to each other by tight junctions and connexin 32 and 43, in particular. The interzone displays a degree of hypoxia higher than that of adjacent blood vesselfree condensations and it strongly expresses the major transcriptional hypoxia regulator Hif1α whose genetic ablation prevents joint development. Within a short time following its initial emergence, the interzone develops into a typical trilayer tissue with two compacted cell layers each associated with the epiphyseal ends of flanking long bone cartilaginous anlagen and one central and more dispersed cell layer. The trilayer configuration is clear in avian limbs in which the interzone is conspicuous and highly cellular but is more subtle in mammalian limbs where the interzone is fairly thin.27, In addition to Hif1α and Gdf5, the interzone specifically expresses several additional genes including Noggin, c-Jun, Lgr5, Wnt9a, Wnt4, Wnt16, β-catenin, Fgf9, and Creb5 but their respective functions are not entirely clear.29, However, genes such as Noggin and β-catenin are needed to maintain the

mesenchymal phenotype of the interzone given their strong antichondrogenic potency; their ablation prevents joint formation and the flanking cartilaginous elements remain fused.31, Fusion also occurs following coablation of Gdf5 and Gdf6.33 Creb5 has recently been shown to regulate the expression of Wnt9a, Wnt4, and Gdf5, and a dominant-negative form of this transcription factor blocks joint development.

### Interzone Roles and Regulation

The identification of the interzone in developing joints several decades ago was not immediately followed by studies unraveling its roles. Thus it remained long unclear whether the interzone represented a key but passive signpost demarcating the site where a joint needs to form or whether interzone cells and their progenies themselves would actively and directly take part in the formation of the joint and its tissues. Holder was the first to tackle this fundamental puzzle. Using stage 24 to 26 chick embryos in ovo (about 4.5 days old), this investigator resected microsurgically a large portion of interzone tissues from the developing right elbow site, monitoring the consequences over time by anatomic analysis and comparing the phenotype to the normal unoperated contralateral joint on the left limb. In operated limbs, the elbow joint failed to form and the

cartilaginous epiphyses of humerus, radius, and ulna remained continuous and fused, with a phenotypic penetrance of nearly 100%. Cartilaginous continuity and fusion were reported in a subsequent study in which a more precise microsurgical procedure was used to remove approximately a 150 µm-thick tissue slice from the prospective elbow joint interzone in stage 27 chick embryos. Together, these studies revealed and established that the interzone is not a passive component but is needed for synovial joint development and that its absence cannot be compensated for by cells in flanking long bone cartilaginous anlagen nor those in surrounding limb mesoderm tissues. The know-how nature of interzone cells was also unearthed by two studies using wholly different approaches carried out in the 1950s.37, Tissue masses containing the entire prospective knee region were dissected out from stage 20 to 22 chick limbs and transplanted onto the chorioallantoic membrane of host embryos. Both studies found that a phenotypically normal joint formed over time, resembling a native knee. Perceptively, the authors proposed that the transplanted tissues had acted autonomously and possessed all the determination mechanisms and morphogenetic information needed to create a joint. This is very much in line with the conclusions reached in the microsurgical interzone removal studies previously mentioned,35,36 a conclusion reiterated by others subsequently and now widely recognized and acknowledged.30,

Notwithstanding their elegance and importance, these studies still provided little if any information of exactly what interzone cells do during joint development and what specific contributions they may make. The advent of genetic cell lineage tracing/tracking provided the tool to probe and answer these fundamental questions. One group first discovered that the transforming growth factor-β superfamily member Gdf5 is specifically expressed by interzone cells in mouse and chick embryo limbs.41, The laboratory subsequently created a transgenic Gdf5-Cre mouse line that was also used to genetically label and track the Gdf5-expressing cells over time after mating with inducible R26R-LacZ reporter mice. Reporter-positive cells were found to persist at the joint sites when examined at a subsequent time point, were present in articular cartilage and other joint tissues, and did not contribute much to formation of adjacent long bone cartilaginous shafts or surrounding tissues. One group carried out collaborative follow-up studies with that group, using a similar transgenic approach but systematically monitoring the distribution and fate of LacZ-positive cells and their progenies (termed Gdf5+ cells) during embryogenesis and postnatal life up to about 2 months of age.44, The data revealed that over prenatal life, Gdf5+ cells generated not only incipient articular cartilage but also intrajoint ligaments, meniscus, synovial lining, and inner capsule in joints including hip, knee, elbow, and carpal/tarsal elements and digits. The Gdf5+ cells remained restricted to joint tissues postnatally and contributed little if any to formation of surrounding tissues and structures, though occasional Gdf5+ cells were seen in underlying cartilaginous shafts. The data agreed well with concurrent genetic cell lineage tracing studies in developing mouse embryo knees carried out by others indicating that Col2+ articular chondrocytes arise as a population distinct from Matrillin-1+ chondrocytes, which constitute the bulk of the long bone cartilaginous elements.

Recent cell lineage tracing studies have provided further insights 47,48The studies made into the biology and roles of the interzone. use of Gfd5-CreER transgenic mice mated with R26tdTomato mice in which reporter activity was activated by tamoxifen injection at different time points, allowing monitoring of Gdf5+ reporterpositive cells starting at different stages of joint development. The data verified that the initial interzone is made of cells previously part of the continuous cartilaginous anlagen, undergoing a phenotypic change from chondrocytic back to mesenchymal.49-51 The data also revealed that additional cells are then recruited into the interzone from its immediate vicinity,52 expanding the interzone laterally and in turn accommodating the growing epiphyseal ends. Such successive cohorts of interzone cells were found to make differential contributions to joint development based on their history and positional cues, with the initial central cohorts mainly contributing to articular cartilage and ligaments and later cohorts contributing more to synovial lining and capsule. These important data and insights bear directly into a critical, lingering question in this field and specifically whether the Gdf5+ interzone cells constitute a uniform progenitor cell population able to diversify and produce different tissues over time, whether they are composed from the start of different subsets of progenitors already committed to distinct developmental programs, and what in either scenario regulates their contributions to the development of different joint tissues. At present, this very challenging question is being approached by single-cell RNAseq, a current and very powerful analytical tool by which progenitor cell populations can be interrogated for phenotypic composition, developmental trajectories, and fate mechanisms. 53,

In a first-of-a-kind scRNAseq study in joint development, one group analyzed Gdf5+ cells isolated from the presumptive knee region of embryonic day 12.5 (E12.5), E13.5, E14.5, and E15.5 mouse embryo limbs, with E12.5 corresponding to onset of interzone formation and E15.5 corresponding to onset of joint cavitation (see below). The resulting single-cell transcriptional profiles generated three large cell clusters, one of which mostly represented the E12.5 cells (termed SC1) and the other two represented E13.5 to E15.5 cells (SC2 and SC3). Gene and developmental trajectory analyses indicated that the SC1 Gdf5+ cells were already subdivided into fibrogenic versus interzone/chondrogenic lineages at E12.5, and this trend was amplified over the next 3 days with developmental diversification and commitment toward other joint tissue phenotypes, including synovial lining and ligaments.

A second scRNAseq study focused on Lgr5+ interzone progenitors and found that they constituted a centrally located subset within the Gdf5+ interzone-wide population in E13.5 mouse embryo knees, were distinguishable based on markers such as Cilp and Col22a1, and mainly contributed to the formation of articular cartilage and cruciate ligaments over time. Taken together, interzone cells diversify early and contribute differentially to the genesis of joint tissues.

### Cavitation

The synovial cavity and its fluid are essential for frictionless motion and function of the limb joints (Fig. 1.1) and thus there has been continuous interest in understanding how the developing joints undergo cavitation (Fig. 1.3D). Because the cavity physically separates the opposing epiphyseal ends of the adjacent long bone anlagen, it was originally proposed that interzone cells located along the prospective joint cavity demarcation line would undergo cell death, thus breaking the tissue continuity and facilitating separation. .20, These data were not confirmed,58 and it is agreed now that cell death is not involved in cavitation.1, Because the opposing ends do need to separate and the cavity needs to enlarge and create a physical distance between the opposing ends (Fig. 1.3D), the process would likely be active and complex.

Tellingly, production of hyaluronic acid (HA) and its cell surface receptor Cd44 was found to accompany cavitation.59, HA has anti-adhesive properties and can attract and imbibe water and thus has swelling capacity. These mechanisms are thought to play an important role in loosening interzone cellcell contacts along the prospective cavitation line while at the same time expanding the water volume of the incipient cavity. This is in line with the finding that conditional ablation of HA synthase Has2, the main enzyme responsible for HA production, delays cavitation. Soon after, the cavitating interzone cells initiate the production of the additional synovial fluid component lubricin, which is encoded by Prg4 and has important anti-adhesive and cytokine-like activities.63, It appears then that cavitation is a stepwise process in which the initial separation of cells along the prescribed cavity line is followed by distancing of the opposing epiphyseal ends by water/HA/lubricin buildup and by establishment of an incipient synovial fluid eventually including also phospholipids (Fig. 1.3E). Studies have shown that muscle-driven skeletal movement is also important for cavitation, and mouse embryos receiving neuromuscular paralyzing drugs or lacking muscles exhibit a significant delay in cavitation.65, Skeletal flexion and elongation may work in concert with skeletal motion to promote cavitation. These developmental studies on cavitation relate well to the clinical fact that joints in adults are negatively affected by physical inactivity

and skeletal immobilization,68 a clear example of the intimate and mutually beneficial links between biologic and mechanical mechanisms in the normal functioning of the joints and their durability.

### Articular Cartilage Genesis, Morphogenesis, and Endurance

As indicated above, Gdf5 + progenitors are responsible for the generation of articular cartilage. However, the tissue emerging from this important embryonic process is a far cry from the functional tissue present in an adult joint. In mouse limbs, neonatal knee articular cartilage is thin, highly cellular, and extra-cellular matrix poor (Fig. 1.4A). The tissue rapidly grows in thickness over the following 2 to 3 weeks and accumulates a matrix rich in typical hyaline cartilage components including collagens II and VI, aggrecan, and HA. The chondrocytes slightly enlarge in average cell volume and remain dispersed throughout much of the tissue as also seen in human juvenile knee cartilage (Fig. 1.4B). A mature tissue eventually forms around 8 weeks of age in mice (corresponding to about 18 to 20 years in humans) and exhibits a stereotypic functional organization consisting of (Fig. 1.4C): (1) a top superficial zone abutting the synovial space that is made of flat and elongated cells producing synovial fluid lubricants; (2) a thick transition/deep zone that contains large chondrocytes in columns orthogonal to the tissue surface (Figs. 1.4C and 1.5) and embedded in an abundant and anisotropic matrix with collagen II fibrils and aggrecan-HA-link protein complexes providing tensile strength and elasticity, respectively; and (3) a bottom mineralized zone with large chondrocytes that is closely linked to subchondral bone, providing physical continuity and stabilization. The tidemark separates the unmineralized zones from the mineralized zone (Figs. 1.4C and 1.5B, arrowheads), subdividing articular cartilage into its upper mechanically resilient portion from its stiffer bottom zone anchoring it to bone. The above intricate zonal organization of mature articular cartilage is widely thought to be essential for the tissue to withstand routine compression and shear mechanical cycles from daily activities while also providing a frictionless lubricating function. These essential organizational features are regrettably deranged after acute joint injuries, natural aging, or chronic pathologies such as osteoarthritis (OA).5, Repositioning

of the tidemark can also occur in OA as well and is considered a manifestation and possible culprit of disease progression. The changes associated with joint disease remain a formidable clinical challenge because effective treatment modalities and tools are still largely lacking, despite major and ongoing biomedical research efforts over the last decades. 73,

One reason for current lack of effective remedies for cartilage damage is that we still know little about how articular cartilage undergoes the above process of morphogenesis during postnatal life to eventually produce a mature zonal tissue, thus hampering progress in reproducing and incorporating it into the design of potential therapeutic strategies. Thus it remains unclear how the various zones of articular cartilage become defined and how their diverse zonal cell phenotypes and relative zonal thickness become determined and established. For instance, the maximal thickness of articular cartilage in the tibial plateau is more than two-fold greater than the thickness of the opposing distal femoral articular cartilage (Fig. 1.5A),75 and differences in thickness occur on the opposite articulating sides of the hip as well. As indicated, the cells constituting the superficial zone are flat and elongated along the main axis of joint motion, are closely associated with each other, and produce lubricants but are otherwise separated by scanty cartilage matrix. In contrast, chondrocytes in the underlying zones are round and much larger, deposit matrix components in specific territorial manners and modulate matrix production in response to normal use or physical demand (Fig. 1.5B).1, Despite the increase in volume, the articular chondrocytes do not become fully hypertrophic (terminally differentiated) as it occurs in the lower zone of the growth plate. Thus articular chondrocytes avoid progression to terminal differentiation followed by apoptosis or transition to bone, subsisting in this intermediate differentiated state throughout adult life. These and many other traits of articular cartilage are not explained by current knowledge and will require much effort to be deciphered mechanistically.

The origin of the columnar arrangement of chondrocytes has attracted particular attention as it is deemed to be important for overall tissue function69,77 and may also aid the tissue to respond and adjust to mechanical stimuli via primary cilia on the chondrocyte surface.78, One model accounting for chondrocyte columnar arrangement was originally proposed following the

identification of progenitor/stemlike cells in the superficial zone of bovine articular cartilage expressing genes such as NOTCH1.80 Notionally cells would proliferate over time and produce vertical columns of overlapping daughter chondrocytes spanning the entire tissue thickness from superficial to deep zone. The zonal structure would thus be established by a mechanism of cell apposition. A similar appositional process was invoked in a more recent genetic lineage tracing/tracking study in which the authors monitored the behavior of developing joint cells in Prg4-CreER mice mated with inducible LacZ reporter mice. LacZ-positive cells were first observed only in a single top layer of incipient tibia articular cartilage in E17.5 mouse embryos and were then detected in columns forming over postnatal life and spanning the entirety of cartilage. However, Prg4 is normally expressed throughout the thickness of incipient articular cartilage in E17.5 tibia and not just in the very first top layer. A different and more effective Prg4- CreER line was used in conjunction with Confetti reporter mice in which cell progenies express reporter proteins of different fluorescent colors, allowing for discrimination of mother—daughter cell relationships. Each chondrocyte column in adult tibia articular cartilage was made of cells expressing different reporter proteins and thus did not arise from apposition of daughter cells. Though the exact mechanism of column formation remains unclear, it is likely that the columns come about by a process of repositioning and overlapping of neighboring chondrocytes, possibly aided by mechanisms such as convergent extension. This is a mechanism by which tissues grow in length by repositioning their cells into stacks, without cell proliferation. It is important to note that cells with a progenitor/stem character and expressing markers such as Cd90 and Stro-1 have also been identified in human articular cartilage84 and are found to increase and become activated during OA and injury. However, because articular cartilage has very poor repair capacity after injury or during OA, the roles, potentials, and effectiveness of these progenitors remain unresolved.

Once finally established and organized in definitive zones, adult articular cartilage needs to persist and function throughout life. The chondrocytes remain mitotically inactive,47 the main fibrillar matrix component, collagen II, is exceedingly stable and long lived,86 and aggrecan exhibits low turnover as well. Thus the tissue needs to rely on phenotypic stabilizers so that it can remain viable, metabolically active, and biomechanically functional throughout decades of life. One such important phenotypic regulator is the chondrogenic master gene Sox9 that has been shown to maintain and stabilize the adult articular cartilage phenotype and prevent progression to chondrocyte hypertrophy, as seen in cartilage degeneration in OA. Recent studies have shown that transcription factors Runxl and Runx3 are also key regulators of articular cartilage homeostasis, orchestrating signaling by Wnt, Yap, and Tgfβ and preventing expression of catabolic proteases.88, The ubiquitin ligase Wwp2 has similarly been shown to maintain articular cartilage homeostasis by regulating expression of the key catabolic protein Adamts5 via Runx2.90 In addition, the focal adhesion protein Kindlin-2 has roles in articular cartilage phenotypic stability and prevention of OA,91 likely acting through interactions with the cytoplasmic domain of β-integrins that are well known for their importance in mediating matrix-articular chondrocyte interactions. Together, the recent advances provide further support for the important notion that articular cartilage requires the intervention and cooperation among several regulatory mechanisms to function and endure through life and that defects in any of these basic mechanisms can have severe consequences on its health and on joints' long-term function.

### Growth Plates and Ossification Centers

The growth plates are the key engines of skeletal development, elongation, and morphogenesis during prenatal and early postnatal life and are composed of a top resting zone followed by

maturation zones of proliferating prehypertrophic and hypertrophic chondrocytes arranged in columns (Fig. 1.5C). The hypertrophic chondrocytes at the base of the growth plate mineralize their matrix and permit the transition from hypertrophic cartilage to new bone deposition in the process of endochondral ossification by which the bulk of the skeleton is built (except for the calvaria, mandible, and portions of the clavicle). Previous and recent studies have indicated that some of the mineralized hypertrophic chondrocytes persist and transdifferentiate into bone cells, 87,93,94 with the rest being eliminated by cell death. Skeletal elements such as tibia or femur contain one growth plate in each of their metaphyseal regions, with each growth plate flanked by a primary ossification center in the diaphysis and a secondary ossification center in the epiphysis (Fig. 1.1). The growth plates undergo involution and close at the end of puberty when skeletal growth is complete. But when do growth plates first appear during fetal development and how do they come about?

While the joints are forming from interzone progenitors in the early embryo limbs, the underlying immature, small, and largely homogenous chondrocytes constituting the entire long bone anlagen initiate a process of maturation and phenotypic diversification. The first sign of this process is appreciable in the emerging diaphyseal region of the anlagen in which the local chondrocytes change in shape and begin to express the signaling protein Indian hedgehog (Ihh). Ihh induces expression of parathyroid hormone—related protein (PthrP) in most epiphyseal cells located in proximity to the developing joints. This establishes a critical and fundamental Ihh-PthrP signaling loop that proceeds to regulate chondrocyte proliferation, maturation rates, and phenotypic expression, thus creating a primitive growth plate extending from epiphysis to diaphysis. The diaphyseal chondrocytes are in turn the first to progress to hypertrophy and transition to endochondral ossification, processes that are promoted by multiple mechanisms including such transcription factors as Runx2, Mef2c, FoxA2, and FoxA397-99 and signaling pathways elicited by Wnt/β-catenin and epidermal growth factor receptor. 100, Blood vessels and marrow progenitors from surrounding tissues invade the diaphyseal hypertrophic cartilage through the action by matrix metalloproteases and angiogenic cues such as vascular endothelium growth factors, 102,103 creating the primary ossification center and eliciting the first deposition of endochondral bone (Fig. 1.2D). At these early stages of skeletogenesis, Ihh has an additional function and induces formation of a so-called bone collar, surrounding the diaphyseal region and deriving from the direct differentiation of osteoprogenitors into bone by intramembranous ossification.96, Overall growth plate activity and rates of skeletal element elongation are fine-tuned by negative regulators. These include (1) histone deacetylase 4 (Hdac4), which is expressed in prehypertrophic chondrocytes and represses Runx2 and Mef2 activity,106 and (2) fibroblast growth factor receptor 3 (Fgfr3), which is expressed in upper growth plate zones, acts through the Statl and Mapk signaling pathways, and represses chondrocyte proliferation. Indeed, gain-of-function FGFR3 mutations in patients dramatically reduce chondrocyte proliferation and cause achondroplasia, the most severe form of human dwarfism.

The epiphyseal region of the long bone anlagen remains cartilaginous and rich in proliferative chondrocytes throughout embryogenesis and early postnatal life. In mice, it is around 1 week of age that a metaphyseal border begins to be established by the creation of a line of cells expressing PthrP, as a striking study has revealed recently. In this way, the epiphyseal region further develops into a secondary ossification center (Figs. 1.1

and 1.3E) and the underlying and newly established metaphyseal region comes to contain a more definitive growth plate flanked by diaphyseal bone and the secondary ossification center itself (eventually developing into endochondral bone). The PthrPexpressing cells have now been demonstrated to exhibit traits and behave like stem/progenitor cells,110 and their functioning is also regulated by mechanisms including FoxA2 and Wnt inhibitory 111, These stemlike cells are found to divide symmetrically cues. to maintain themselves or asymmetrically, with one cell remaining stem in character while the other commits to chondrocyte differentiation and produces all chondrocytes in each growth plate column. This process ensures the maintenance and functioning of the growth plate and continuously replenishes it with new cells that replace those undergoing hypertrophy and replacement by endochondral bone, allowing for growth of the long bones. The growth plates undergo involution during the end of puberty and disappear, a process regulated by complex interplays and involving estrogens and other hormones.

### Organization and Physiology of the Mature Joint

In the adult, the structural, cellular, and biochemical components of diarthrodial joints are organized into an organ structure that is uniquely equipped to support movement and bear mechanical loads throughout our lifetime. Mature diarthrodial joints are complex and dynamic structures, influenced by their unique anatomic environments and mechanical demands. The shoulder joint, which demands an enormous range of motion, is stabilized primarily by muscles, whereas the hip, which requires motion and antigravity stability, has an intrinsically stable ball-and-socket configuration. The components of the "typical" synovial joint are the synovium, muscles, tendons, ligaments, bursae, articular cartilage, and subchondral bone. Additionally, fibrocartilaginous structures such as the menisci of the knee and the labrae of the hip and shoulder contribute to joint function, stability, and health in important ways. The anatomy and physiology of muscles are described in detail in Chapter 5. Here we discuss the other joint tissues and structures and how they contribute to both joint homeostasis and disease, starting with the synovium.

### Synovium

The synovium is the lining of the joint cavity and is a thin connective tissue that covers the fibrous joint capsule and extends to the bone—cartilage interface without encroaching on articular cartilage (Chapter 2). It is divided into two functional compartments: the lining region (synovial intima) and the sublining (subintima) (Fig. 1.6). The synovial intima or lining is the superficial layer that faces the synovial cavity. It is the major site of production of synovial fluid that provides the nutrition for the articular cartilage and lubricates the cartilage surfaces. The synovial lining is loosely attached to the subintima, which contains the blood vessels, lymphatics, and nerves and represents the principal neurovascular supply for the joint. Each compartment has distinct functions and collectively is often referred to as the synovial membrane. But, unlike epithelial-derived "barrier" membranes in the body, the lining layer and sublining compartments are not separated by a distinct basement membrane. Instead, they are separated by more loosely organized matrix, although this matrix contains many of the molecular components normally found in basement membranes (i.e., perlecan,

fibronectin, laminin), as well as membrane peptidases, which control the diffusion of regulatory factors between compartments. This lack of a structured basement membrane makes the lining semipermeable to many molecular species, allowing for selective filtration of plasma components that comprise a portion of the synovial fluid that bathes the articular cartilage.

Far from being a homogeneous tissue throughout the joint, synovium is highly heterogeneous in appearance and structure. Three basic patterns are often described: areolar, fibrous, and fatty. Areolar synovium is characterized by loose subintimal connective tissue and is highly vascular; fibrous synovium is denser and poorly vascularized and fatty synovium has a higher proportion of adipocytes in the sublining compartment. Distribution of the vasculature of the subintima varies as well. Vascularity is high at the enthesis where synovium, ligament, and cartilage coalesce.

In the normal joint, the synovium provides functions critical to the maintenance of joint health throughout our lifespan, and this tissue is central to maintaining health of the avascular cartilage. Synovial functions include regulation of nutrient and metabolite trafficking into and out of the joint space, production of synovial fluid that bathes and lubricates the joint, maintenance of a cellular barrier between the tissue vasculature and the joint space, and limitation of pathologic inflammation in the synovial tissue. In many rheumatic and musculoskeletal diseases (RMDs), the function of synovium and its ability to maintain the health of the joint are compromised. For example, in rheumatoid arthritis (RA) the synovial lining of diarthrodial joints is the site of the initial inflammatory process 115- (see Chapter 71).

### Synovial Lining (Intima)

In normal synovium, the lining layer is one to three cells deep, although intraarticular fat pads are usually covered by only a single layer of synovial cells, and ligaments and tendons are covered by synovial cells that are sometimes widely separated. Cells of the intima (synoviocytes) are responsible for production of synovial fluid that provides nutrition for the articular cartilage and

lubricates the articular surfaces. In addition, intimal cells protect the joint from inflammatory damage by providing a barrier that prevents cellular extravasation and by clearing debris.

There are two main types of cells (synoviocytes) that comprise the intimal layer: type A synoviocytes are macrophages of hematopoietic origin and type B synoviocytes are fibroblasts of mesenchymal origin (Fig. 1.6). Type A synoviocytes contain vacuoles, a prominent Golgi apparatus, and filopodia, but they have little rough endoplasmic reticulum. In contrast, type B synoviocytes contain abundant rough endoplasmic reticulum, suggesting an important function in protein synthesis and secretion. 115, Type A cells express cell-surface markers typical of macrophages, including nonspecific esterase and CD68, while type B cells express high levels of uridine diphosphoglucose dehydrogenase (UDPGD; an enzyme involved in HA synthesis) and CD55. In the normal, healthy state, type B (fibroblast-like) cells predominate while type A cells make up about 10 to 20% of the lining cells (Fig. 1.6).115,

Several groups have now demonstrated that type B fibroblastlike synoviocytes develop early during embryogenesis from the same mesenchymal interzone precursor cells that give rise to other joint tissues including cartilage, bone, meniscus, and liga- 47, These cells, identified by expression of GDF-5, ments. condense to form a lining layer during cavitation. This is facilitated by expression of cadherin-11, a key adhesion molecule that mediates adherens junction formation and regulates the creation of the synovial lining during development. 120, Cadherin-11 is also upregulated in fibroblast-like cells at the pannuscartilage interface in rheumatoid synovium, where it plays a role in the invasive properties of the synovial fibroblasts 122 and treatment with a cadherin-l1 antibody or a cadherin-l1 fusion protein reduces synovial inflammation and cartilage erosion in an animal model of arthritis.

In the mature joint, fibroblast-like synoviocytes of the lining produce synovial extra-cellular matrix components including collagen type 1, fibronectin, and proteoglycans. These cells also bear

abundant membrane peptidases on their surface that can degrade a wide range of regulatory peptides, such as substance P and angiotensin II. In addition, type B lining cells express UDPGD, hyaluronate synthetase 1 (HAS1), and proteoglycan 4 (PRG4), which encodes the molecule lubricin. Thus they are the main producers of synovial fluid lubricin and HA, which together provide boundary lubrication of cartilage and shock absorption, 123,124 allowing friction-free motion of the joint during activity.

In addition to supporting synovial fluid production, type B synoviocytes also possess immunomodulatory capabilities. They have some phagocytic capacity and the ability to present antigens via the major histocompatibility complex (MHC) and thus are poised to activate immune responses when needed. However, they also express decay-accelerating factor (CD55),125 which inactivates intermediates of the complement cascade, suggesting an immunoregulatory function in homeostasis. In inflammatory conditions, however, these cells can contribute to pathology by producing large amounts of metalloproteinases and inflammatory cytokines and by driving activation of osteoclasts (via RANKL). Using cell sorting, mass cytometry, and single-cell RNA Seq, 126 a lining fibroblast population has been characterized by expression of podoplanin but not CD34 or CD90, which also expressed matrix metalloproteinases involved in cartilage matrix disruption in addition to typical type B synoviocyte products PRG4 and HAS1. Subsequently, CD90synovial lining fibroblasts were shown to express FAPα (fibroblast activation protein-α) and, through adoptive transfer, these cells mediated bone and cartilage destruction in a murine model of inflammatory arthritis. Whether these subsets are the same or represent distinct or overlapping populations of fibroblasts remains to be determined. However, epigenetic changes to synovial fibroblasts during chronic inflammation have been implicated in modulating a change from an immunoregulatory role in health, to an active pathogenic role in chronic arthritis.

Synovial intimal macrophages (type A synoviocytes) express numerous cell surface markers of the monocyte-macrophage lineage, including CD16, CD45, CD11b/CD18, CD68, CD14, and the immunoglobulin (Ig)G Fc receptor FcγRIIIa.115, The op/op osteopetrotic mouse, which is deficient in macrophages because of an absence of macrophage colony-stimulating factor, also lacks synovial lining macrophages,129suggesting that type A lining cells share a common lineage with other tissue macrophages. In addition, the cells express high levels of the fractalkine receptor CX3CR1130 and scavenger receptors such as CD163 and MERTK,131 which contribute to their phagocytic capacity. This feature allows them to participate in clearing debris and dying cells from the joint space to maintain joint health throughout our lifespan. Although macrophages represent only a small percentage of the cells in the normal synovium, macrophage content of the lining layer increases in several arthritic conditions as cells can be recruited into the lining and sublining from the circulation during synovial inflammation.

The synovial lining is not a true epithelial barrier, but type A macrophages may have unique features that allow them to establish and maintain a barrier between the joint space and the sublining capillaries. They attach to neighboring cells through desmosomes and tight junctions,130 allowing the lining to maintain the joint space as an immune-privileged site in the healthy state by limiting cellular movement into the joint. In joint disease, this barrier function can become compromised, allowing an influx of inflammatory leukocytes into the synovial fluid that compromises the integrity of other joint tissues.

### Synovial Sublining (Subintima)

The synovial intima and subintima both contain resident macrophage populations that are critical to maintaining joint health. For many years it was assumed that both lining and sublining macrophages were derived from monocyte precursors from the bone marrow (BM) and were replenished from the circulation throughout adulthood. However, in 2019 two reports demonstrated that CX3CR1+ embryonic macrophages begin to populate the developing synovium in the mouse before the BM has been established, between day E12.5 and E15.130, In contrast, BM-derived synovial macrophages, characterized by expression of CD11b and Ly6c, were not observed until after day 19. Using a series of BM chimeras, one group132 showed that most synovial resident macrophages in the adult are of embryonic origin and express the cytokines IL-4 and IL-10 consistent with an immune regulatory role, while BM-derived synovial macrophages preferentially express M1 pro-inflammatory-type cytokines such as interleukin (IL)-1β and TNF. Distinctions between lining and sublining macrophages were not made in this study. Using parabiosis experiments and fate-mapping, CX3CR1+ resident macrophages of the lining (type A synoviocytes) were shown to be continuously replenished throughout adulthood from a pool of proliferating MHCII+ sublining resident macrophages, and not from circulating BMderived monocytes. The same MHCII+ sublining precursors that give rise to the lining macrophages (type A synoviocytes) also give rise to a population of CX3CR1resident sublining macrophages. These resident macrophages express resistin-like molecule-α and CD163, associated with alternatively activated macrophages that may limit inflammation. These reports and others133 demonstrate that the origin of synovial macrophages is relevant to both joint health and disease and that the function of synovial macrophages is influenced both by their origin (embryonic vs. bone-marrow/ circulation) and their spatial location within the synovium (lining vs. sublining).

The sublining stroma is a highly variable loose connective tissue characterized by a sparse collagenous matrix and is populated by fibroblasts that produce the matrix. Although type B lining synoviocytes share a common mesenchymal origin with sublining fibroblasts, in the adult several populations of synovial fibroblasts that vary with respect to phenotype and function have been described. One group b126identified three distinct populations of human synovial fibroblasts, using cell-surface markers and transcriptomics. In addition to the CD90-CD34lining fibroblasts previously described, they found a population of sublining CD90+CD34fibroblasts that surround blood vessels and capillaries. This population highly expressed RANKL and promoted osteoclastogenesis in vitro, suggesting a role in synovial bone erosion; this subset of fibroblasts was increased in RA compared with OA patients. A third CD34+ fibroblast subset was found to be distributed in the lining and sublining and, in contrast to CD34cells, secreted IL-6, CXCL12, and CCL2 in response to TNF. Thus this population may promote cellular recruitment driving synovitis in pathologic states. Distinct populations of synovial fibroblasts have relevance to the low-grade synovitis that occurs in OA as well, as OA lining fibroblasts (CD90-CD34-) correlated with synovial macrophage content, and sublining (CD90+CD34+) fibroblasts correlated with synovial T-cell content. Lining and sublining fibroblasts are functionally distinct. FAPα+ CD90lining cells mediated destructive effects on bone and cartilage in a murine model of RA, while FAPα+THY1+ sublining fibroblasts supported synovial inflammatory cell infiltration but had less effect on bone

and cartilage pathology. Both NOTCH and Wnt/β-catenin signaling 135,136 are important in regulating the phenotypic heterogeneity of synovial fibroblasts, and single-cell sequencing has demonstrated a continuum of fibroblast phenotypes between the synovial sublining and lining, potentially arising from a Dpp4+ mesenchymal progenitor population in the sublining.

Consistent with the common origin of synovium and other joint tissues,48,119 the synovial subintima is a rich source of mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs), which can give rise to different cell lineages, including chondrocytes, osteoblasts, and adipocytes. Whether there is a relationship between these cells and the fibroblast progenitors remains to be determined. However, synovialderived MSCs have a high chondrogenic potential compared with other tissue sources of MSCs, consistent with older reports of the importance of synovium in cartilage repair. There is a PRG4 expressing synovial MSC population in the prenatal mouse that is exquisitely responsive to cartilage injury, pointing to the therapeutic potential of these cells. But, in addition to their ability to repair joint tissues, these cells may also help maintain immunologic homeostasis in the joint. BMand adipose-derived MSCs have been shown to have potent immunosuppressive effects in vitro on T-lymphocyte responses and augment regulatory T cell development. t38 MSs in synovium increase in arthritis139,140 and in animal models of joint tissue injury, due to both infiltration from BM sources and local proliferation of resident populations. MSCs expanded in arthritis may become pathogenic and lose their immunosuppressive functions. 139, Whether the immunomodulatory function of synovial MSCs can be harnessed for cell-based arthritis therapeutics is under investigation by several groups (reviewed in ref. 143).

The synovial subintimal contains a rich network of vessels and lymphatics that allows for movement of molecules, nutrients, and metabolites into and out of the joint to maintain the health of the avascular articular cartilage. The avascular articular cartilage depends on nutrition in the synovial fluid, derived from the synovial vasculature. The distribution of synovial vessels, which were formed largely as a result of vasculogenesis during development of the joint, displays considerable plasticity. Angiogenic factors such as vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), acting via VEGF receptors 1 and 2 (Flt1 and Flk2), and basic FGF promote proliferation and migration of endothelial cells, a process that is facilitated by matrix-degrading enzymes and adhesion molecules such as integrin αvβ3 and E-selectin, expressed by activated endothelial cells. Vessel maturation is facilitated by angiopoietin-1 acting via the Tie-2 receptor. The angiogenic molecules are restricted to the capillary epithelium in normal synovium, but their levels are elevated in inflamed synovium in perivascular sites and areas remote from vessels.144,

The vasculature of the synovial sublining is most dense closest to the lining layer and contains highly fenestrated capillaries and arterioles, whereas venules are located closer to the joint .118, Arterial and venous networks of the synovium are capsule. complex and are characterized by arteriovenous anastomoses that communicate freely with blood vessels in periosteum and periarticular bone. In healthy joints, low-molecular-weight substances diffuse across their concentration gradients. Plasma components and nutrients diffuse through fenestrated capillaries and into the synovial fluid, while low-molecular-weight metabolites produced within the joint are taken up by sublining venules and cleared. Larger-molecular-weight substances such as HA in the synovial fluid are generally retained in the joint space or cleared much more slowly by the synovial lymphatics. In addition, synovial

lymphatics are an important conduit to clear cells from the synovial tissue and fluid that accumulate during chronic inflammation.

Both vascularization of the subintima and clearance of substances from the joint space can be altered in arthritic diseases. Synovial vascularization can be increased in synovium in patients with arthritis. Increased synovial Doppler signal by ultrasound, a surrogate marker of increased blood flow, is more common in active RA where it is a predictor of disease activity. Despite increased synovial lymphatic vessels,149 lymphatic clearance was shown to be decreased in both OA and RA. An interesting recent report showed that synovial lymphatic function may be targetable for treatment in a murine model of OA. Whether interventions designed to modulate synovial vascularity or lymphatic function will translate to effective treatments for human disease characterized by synovial inflammation remains to be seen.

### Synovial Innervation

Dissection studies have shown that each joint has a dual nerve supply consisting of specific articular nerves that penetrate the capsule as independent branches of adjacent peripheral nerves and articular branches arising from related muscle nerves. The definition of joint position and the detection of joint motion are monitored separately and by a combination of multiple inputs from different receptors in varied systems. Nerve endings in muscle and skin and in the joint capsule mediate sensation of joint position and movement. Normal joints have afferent (sensory) and efferent (motor) innervations consisting of both unmyelinated and sensory thick myelinated A fibers in ligaments, fibrous capsule, menisci, and adjacent periosteum, where they are thought to function primarily as sensors for pressure and movements. Sensory A and C fibers terminate as free nerve endings in the fibrous capsule, synovium, adipose tissue, ligaments, menisci, and the adjacent periosteum, where they are thought to act as nociceptors and contribute to the regulation of synovial microvascular function.

In normal synovium, a dense network of fine unmyelinated nerve fibers follows the courses of blood vessels and extends into the synovial lining layers. These nerve fibers are largely unmyelinated and are slow-conducting fibers; they may transmit diffuse, burning, or aching pain sensation. Sympathetic nerve fibers surround blood vessels, particularly in the deeper regions of synovium, and contain and release classic neurotransmitters, such as norepinephrine, and neuropeptides that are markers of sensory nerves including substance P, calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP), neuropeptide Y, and vasoactive intestinal peptide. 152-154 Substance P and CGRP, in particular, have been implicated in modulating inflammation and the pain pathway in OA. In addition, substance P is released from peripheral nerve terminals into the joint, and specific, G proteincoupled receptors for substance P are localized to microvascular endothelium in normal synovium. Abnormalities in neuropeptide release in arthritis may contribute to changes in vascular permeability and the failure of synovial inflammation to resolve. The expression of substance P and CGRP are upregulated by nerve growth factor (NGF), which belongs to a family of neurotrophins that regulate neuronal growth during embryonic development. In addition to promoting nerve growth and mediating pain perception, NGF can act together with VEGF to promote blood vessel formation. Angiogenesis and nerve growth thus are linked by common pathways involving NGF, VEGF, and neuropeptides such as CGRP, neuropeptide Y, and semaphorins. 153,

Afferent nerve fibers from the joint play an important role in the reflex inhibition of muscle contraction. Trophic factors generated

by motor neurons, such as the neuropeptide CGRP, are important in maintaining muscle bulk and a functional neuromuscular junction. Decreases in motor neuron trophic support during articular inflammation probably contribute to muscle wasting in arthritic conditions. Inflammation and excessive local neuropeptide release may result in the loss of nerve fibers, and synovial tissue proliferation without concomitant growth of new nerve fibers may lead to an apparent partial denervation of synovium in arthritis. However, there is also evidence from humans and pre-clinical arthritis models of sprouting of sensory nerves in synovium and ingrowth of neurovascular channels at the osteochondral junction. 153, Overall, aberrant innervation of synovium and other joint structures during arthritis development may contribute to changes in synovial joint homeostasis, motor neuron trophic support, and pain.

Mechanisms of joint pain have been reviewed in detail.162-164 In a noninflamed joint, most sensory nerve fibers do not respond to movement within the normal range; these fibers are referred to as silent nociceptors. In an inflamed joint, however, these nerve fibers become sensitized by mediators such as bradykinin, neurokinin 1, NGF, and prostaglandins, and the resulting peripheral sensitization leads to pain during normal joint movement, a characteristic symptom of arthritis.155, Pain sensation is upregulated or downregulated further in the central nervous system, at the level of the spinal cord and in the brain, by central sensitization and "gating" of nociceptive input. A poor correlation often exists between the severity of apparent joint disease damage and perceived pain in people with chronic arthritis, and sensitization either at the peripheral or central levels may contribute to this discrepancy.

### Synovial Fluid

The volume and composition of synovial fluid are maintained by the synovium and its vasculature. A normal joint contains a small quantity of fluid (≤2.5 mL in the knee), sufficient to coat the synovial and cartilage surfaces. Tendon sheath fluid and synovial fluid are biochemically similar. Both are essential for the nutrition and lubrication of adjacent avascular structures, including tendons and articular cartilage, and for limiting adhesion formation and maintaining friction-free movement. Characterization and measurement of synovial fluid constituents have proven useful for the identification of locally generated regulatory factors, markers of cartilage turnover, and the metabolic status of the joint, as well as for the assessment of the effects of therapy on cartilage homeostasis. However, interpretation of such data requires an understanding of the generation and clearance of synovial fluid and its various components.

### Generation and Clearance of Synovial Fluid

Synovial fluid concentrations of a protein represent the net contributions of synovial blood flow, plasma concentration, microvascular permeability, lymphatic removal, and its production and consumption within the joint space. Synovial fluid is a mixture of a protein-rich ultrafiltrate of plasma and carbohydrates (i.e., hyaluronan) and glycoproteins (i.e., lubricin) synthesized by synoviocytes. Generation of this ultrafiltrate depends on the differences between intracapillary and intraarticular hydrostatic pressures and between osmotic pressures of capillary plasma and synovial tissue fluid. Fenestrations (i.e., small pores covered by a thin membrane) in the synovial capillaries and the macromolecular sieve of collagen and HA in the synovial matrix facilitate rapid exchange of

small molecules, such as glucose and lactate, assisted in the case of glucose by an active transport system. Proteins are present in synovial fluid at concentrations inversely proportional to molecular size, with synovial fluid albumin concentration being about 45% of that in plasma. Concentrations of electrolytes and small molecules are equivalent to those in plasma. Synovial fluid is cleared through a combination of diffusion into the vasculature and lymphatic assisted by joint movement. In contrast to ultrafiltration, lymphatic clearance of solutes is independent of molecule size. Low-molecular-weight metabolites and regulatory peptides may diffuse along concentration gradients into plasma. The kinetics of delivery and removal of a protein must be determined (e.g., using albumin as a reference solute) to assess the significance of its concentration in the joint.

HA synthesized by type B synovial lining cells appears in high concentrations in synovial fluid (around 3 g/L), compared with plasma (30 µg/L). Lubricin, a glycoprotein that assists articular lubrication, is another constituent of synovial fluid that is generated by the lining cells. It is now believed that hyaluronan functions in fluid-film lubrication, whereas lubricin is the boundary lubricant in synovial fluid. Because the volume of synovial fluid is determined by the amount of hyaluronan, water retention seems to be the major function of this large molecule. Lubricin also prevents pathologic deposition of protein onto the surface of articular cartilage.

Despite the absence of a basement membrane, synovial fluid does not mix freely with extra-cellular synovial tissue fluid. Hyaluronan may trap molecules within the synovial cavity by acting as a filtration screen on the surface of the synovial lining, resisting the movement of synovial fluid out from the joint space. Synovial fluid proteins have a rapid turnover time (around 1 hour in normal knees), and equilibrium is not usually reached among all parts of the joint. However, the turnover time for hyaluronan in the normal joint (13 hours) is an order of magnitude slower than that of small solutes and proteins, so association with hyaluronan may result in trapping of solutes within synovial fluid. Tissue fluid around fenestrated endothelium reflects plasma ultrafiltrate most closely, with a low content of hyaluronate compared with synovial fluid. Locally generated or released peptides within the tissue, such as endothelin and substance P, may attain much higher perivascular concentrations than those measured in synovial fluid.

In normal joints, intraarticular pressures are slightly subatmospheric at rest (0 to -5 mm Hg). During exercise, hydrostatic pressure in the normal joint may decrease further. Repeated abnormal mechanical stresses can interrupt synovial perfusion during joint movement, particularly in the presence of a synovial effusion. Resting intraarticular pressures in rheumatoid joints are around 20 mm Hg, whereas during isometric exercise, they may increase to greater than 100 mm Hg, well above capillary perfusion pressure and, at times, above arterial pressure. 168,169

### Synovial Fluid as an Indicator of Joint Health and Disease

In the absence of a basement membrane separating synovium or cartilage from synovial fluid, measurements of synovial fluid may reflect the activity of these tissues. A wide range of regulatory factors and products of synoviocyte metabolism and cartilage breakdown may be generated locally within the joint, resulting in marked differences between the composition of synovial fluid and plasma ultrafiltrate. Because little capacity exists for the selective concentration of solutes in synovial fluid, solutes that are present at higher concentrations than in plasma are probably synthesized locally. It is necessary, however, to know the local clearance rate to

determine whether the solutes present in synovial fluid at lower concentrations than in plasma are generated locally. , Because clearance rates from synovial fluid may be slower than those from plasma, synovial fluid levels of drugs or urate may remain elevated after plasma levels have declined.

Plasma proteins are less effectively filtered by inflamed synovium, perhaps because of increased size of endothelial cell fenestrations or because interstitial hyaluronate-protein complexes are fragmented by enzymes associated with the inflammatory process. Concentrations of larger plasma proteins, such as α2 macroglobulin (the principal proteinase inhibitor of plasma), fibrinogen, and IgM, are elevated in synovial fluid from patients with arthritis (Fig. 1.7A) as are associated protein-bound cations. In inflammatory arthritis, fibrin deposits may additionally retard flow between the tissue and the liquid phase.

Investigators171 analyzed synovial fluids and sera from a small series of patients with OA and RA using mass spectrometry and multiplex bead-based immunoassays. They identified more than a hundred proteins that were increased in the synovial fluid of patients with both OA and RA compared with healthy subjects. Of interest, they found that more than one-third of these were plasma proteins, suggesting that the normal synovial barrier to these proteins was disrupted. They speculated that the elevation of these plasma proteins in the synovial fluid could be related to alterations in the endothelial barrier or the lining barrier associated with local inflammation in the synovial tissue.

Synovial fluid alterations in joint disease may also reflect local aberrant production by cells within the joint. In a study using high-throughput proteomic analysis to define expression profiles of synovial fluid proteins,172 18 high-abundance proteins were significantly and differentially expressed in OA versus healthy controls. Although all 18 proteins were present in blood

and could enter the joint through alterations in vascular permeability, these molecules were also products of synovial cells and chondrocytes. Other studies further clarified that some of the OA proteome resulted from local production, by comparing the synovial fluid protein composition with mRNA expression profiles of joint tissues. This analysis demonstrated that many of the proteins elevated in synovial fluid were derived from synovium or cartilage, providing direct evidence that cells within the joint were a source of the synovial fluid products. Proteins associated with oxidative damage, activation of mitogenactivated protein kinases, and complement components were among the high-abundance molecules in the OA synovial fluids. Of interest, these molecules have been implicated in the pathophysiology of both OA and RA.

The barrier function of the synovial lining cells prevents extravasation of immune cells from the subintimal vasculature into the synovial fluid, so that in the normal healthy joint synovial fluid cell numbers are very low (generally below 200 cells per mm3). In the normal joint, mononuclear cells dominate with over 50% of cells being monocyte/macrophages, whereas neutrophils represent <10% of normal synovial fluid cells. In arthritis the synovial barrier is compromised, and cell concentrations are elevated. Joint aspiration with subsequent synovial fluid cellular analysis is an important clinical tool in the evaluation of patients with arthritis, as the range of cell concentrations observed can guide clinical diagnosis (Fig. 1.7B). Although cell concentrations are elevated in most forms of arthritis, concentrations in the range of 200 to 2000 are more typical of OA or traumatic joint injury and cell concentrations above 2000 suggest the presence of more inflammatory forms of arthritis. Synovial fluid cell concentrations above 50,000 cell/mm³ should always prompt further workup for infectious/septic arthritis.

### Lubrication and Nutrition of the Articular Cartilage

Synovial fluid serves as a lubricant for articular cartilage and a source of nutrition for the chondrocytes. Lubrication is essential for protecting cartilage and other joint structures from friction and shear stresses associated with movement under loading. There are two basic categories of joint lubrication. In fluid-film lubrication, cartilage surfaces are separated by an incompressible fluid film, and hyaluronan primarily provides this function. In boundary lubrication, specialized molecules attached to the cartilage surface permit surface-to-surface contact while decreasing the coefficient of friction. During loading, a noncompressible fluid film is trapped between opposing cartilage surfaces and prevents the surfaces from touching. Irregularities in the cartilage surface and its deformation during compression may augment this trapping of fluid. This stable film is approximately 0.1-µm thick in the normal human hip joint, but it can be much thinner in the presence of inflammatory synovial fluid or with increased cartilage porosity.

Lubricin (also called superficial zone protein or proteoglycan 4 [PRG4]) participates in boundary lubrication in the human joint. Lubricin is a glycoprotein synthesized primarily by type B synovial cells and superficial zone chondrocytes. It has a molecular weight of 225,000, a length of 200 nm, and a diameter of 1 to 2 nm. Dipalmitoyl phosphatidylcholine, which constitutes 45% of the lipid in normal synovial fluid, acts together with lubricin as a boundary lubricant. In boundary lubrication, lubricin functions as a phospholipid carrier via a mechanism that is common to all tissues and protects the cartilage by reducing pathologic deposition of proteins at the cartilage surface. Lubricin is enriched on the surface of articular cartilage and, although mechanisms that maintain its surface localization for boundary lubrication are unknown, recent work suggests that both noncovalent and covalent bonding with cartilage oligomeric matrix protein may be important. People with loss-of-function mutations in the lubricin gene (PRG4) have camptodactyly arthropathy-coxa vara-pericarditis syndrome, which is associated with the development of severe premature OA. Of interest, long-term overexpression of lubricin in animal models of OA protects against both age-related and posttraumatic OA through inhibition of transcriptional programs that promote cartilage catabolism and chondrocyte hypertrophy.

As observed by Hunter in 1743,178 normal adult articular cartilage contains no blood vessels, which is essential to maintain its mechanical properties. If vascularized, blood flow in cartilage would be repeatedly occluded during weight bearing and exercise, with reactive oxygen species generated during reperfusion, resulting in repeated damage to cartilage matrix and chondrocytes. Chondrocytes synthesize specific inhibitors of angiogenesis that maintain articular cartilage as an avascular tissue.179-181 As a result, chondrocytes normally live in a hypoxic and acidotic environment, with extra-cellular fluid pH values around 7.1 to 7.2, 182 and use anaerobic glycolysis for energy production. High lactate levels in normal synovial fluid, compared with paired plasma measurements, partially reflect this anaerobic metabolism. The two sources of nutrients for articular cartilage are the synovial fluid and subchondral blood vessels.

The synovial fluid and, indirectly, the synovial lining through which synovial fluid is generated, are the major sources of nutrients for articular cartilage. Nutrients may enter cartilage from synovial fluid either by diffusion or mass transport during com- .184,185Molecules as large as hemoglobin pression—relaxation cycles. (65 kDa) can diffuse through normal articular cartilage, and the solutes needed for cellular metabolism are much smaller. Diffusion of uncharged small solutes, such as glucose, is not impaired

in matrices containing large amounts of glycosaminoglycans, and diffusivity of small molecules through hyaluronate is enhanced.

Intermittent compression may serve as a pump mechanism for solute exchange in cartilage. The concept has arisen from observations that joint immobilization or dislocation leads to degenerative change, while exercise increases solute penetration into cartilage in experimental systems. During weight bearing, fluid escapes from the load-bearing region by flowing to other cartilage sites. When the load is removed, cartilage reexpands and draws back fluid, exchanging nutrients with waste materials.

In a growing child, the deeper layers of cartilage are vascularized, such that blood vessels penetrate between columns of chondrocytes in the growth plate. It is likely that nutrients diffuse from these tiny end capillaries through the matrix to chondrocytes. Diffusion from subchondral blood vessels is not considered a major route for the nutrition of normal adult articular cartilage because of the barrier provided by its densely calcified lower layer. Nonetheless, partial defects may normally exist in this barrier,187 and neovascularization of the deeper layers of articular cartilage in arthritis may contribute both to cartilage nutrition and to entry of inflammatory cells and cytokines. 161,188,189

### Mature Articular Cartilage

Articular cartilage is a specialized connective tissue that covers the weight-bearing surfaces of diarthrodial joints. The principal functions of cartilage layers covering bone ends are to permit lowfriction, high-velocity movement between bones, to absorb the transmitted forces associated with locomotion, and to contribute to joint stability. Lubrication by synovial fluid components provides frictionless movement of the articulating cartilage surfaces. Chondrocytes are the single cellular component of adult hyaline articular cartilage and are responsible for synthesizing and maintaining the highly specialized cartilage matrix macromolecules. The cartilage extra-cellular matrix is composed of an extensive network of collagen fibrils, which confers tensile strength, and an interlocking mesh of proteoglycans, which provides compressive stiffness through the ability to absorb and extrude water. Numerous other noncollagenous proteins also contribute to the unique properties of cartilage (Table 1.2). Histologically, the tissue appears homogeneous and clearly distinguished from the calcified cartilage and underlying subchondral bone (Fig. 1.5). However, significant topographic and regional differences exist in the molecular organization and composition of the articular cartilage, as described earlier in this chapter and in detail in Chapter 3. The resilience of articular cartilage is evident in its ability to absorb and transmit loads throughout our lifespan and maintain the articular matrix under these loads. However, several stimuli (including mechanical and inflammatory injury) can damage the articular matrix and disrupt the ability of the chondrocytes to repair the damage, propagating damage in the setting of various types of arthritis.

### Subchondral Bone

Subchondral bone (the layer of bone directly underlying the cartilage surface) is not a homogeneous tissue, and it consists of a layer of compact cortical bone and an underlying system of cancellous bone organized into a trabecular network. The subchondral bone is separated from the overlying articular cartilage by a thin zone of calcified cartilage. This complex biocomposite of bone and calcified cartilage provides an optimal system for distributing loads that are transmitted from the weight-bearing surfaces lined by hyaline articular cartilage. The so-called tidemark defines the

transition zone between the articular and calcified cartilage (Fig. 1.5). Although the tidemark was originally believed to form a barrier to fluid flow, evidence shows that biologically active molecules can transit this zone, providing a mechanism by which products produced by chondrocytes and bone cells can influence the activity of the other cell types. 191, In addition, further communication is provided via products released from vascular elements in channels that penetrate the calcified cartilage from the adjacent 161 Under physiologic conditions, the composition marrow space. and structural organization of the subchondral bone and calcified cartilage are optimally adapted to transfer loads, but several conditions can lead to changes in structural and functional properties of these tissues.

The subchondral bone undergoes continuous structural reorganization throughout postnatal life. These alterations are mediated by the coordinated activity of bone-resorbing osteoclasts and bone-forming osteoblasts that remodel and adapt the bone in response to local biomechanical and biologic signals. Osteocytes are the bone cell type that regulates the bone remodeling process.194, Osteocytes are distributed throughout the mineralized bone matrix, forming an interconnected network that is ideally positioned to sense and respond to local and systemic stimuli. These effects are mediated via both cell-cell interactions with osteoclasts and osteoblasts but also via signaling through the release of soluble mediators. These products include RANKL, the essential regulator of osteoclast differentiation and activity, and its inhibitor osteoprotegerin (OPG),196,197 as well as additional mediators, including prostanoids, nitric oxide, nucleotides, and a broad spectrum of growth factors and cytokines. In addition to these factors, osteocytes also produce sclerostin and Dickkopfrelated protein 1 (DKK-1), which are potent inhibitors of the Wnt/β-catenin pathway that regulates osteoblast-mediated bone formation. . The release of RANKL, OPG, and Wnt pathway regulators (DKK-1 and sclerostin) plays a major role in controlling the adaptation of the subchondral bone to alterations in mechanical loading in both physiologic and pathologic conditions.

The maintenance of the structural and functional integrity of articular cartilage and subchondral bone under physiologic loading is evidence of the unique and intimate interaction of these tissues, but controversy remains with regard to the relationship between them in the pathogenesis of OA.
