The age-related decline in chondrocyte autophagy could be related to decreased levels of forkhead-box class O (FOXO) transcription factors. FOXO1, FOXO3, and FOXO4 are found in articular chondrocytes, but with aging there is a reduction in FOXO1 and FOX3 levels associated with decreased autophagy. FOXOs regulate the expression of autophagy genes, as well as

antioxidants, including superoxide dismutase (SOD)-2 and catalase. Loss of FOXO activity results in reduced autophagy and increased susceptibility to oxidative stress, both of which would contribute to age-related OA.

Also compromised during aging is the unfolded protein response (UPR), which is a nonlysosomal pathway for ubiquitin/ proteasome degradation of unfolded proteins eliminated from the ER. The UPR enables chondrocyte survival in response to ER stress during growth plate development,196 but also during inflammatory, mechanical, and oxidative stress in articular cartilage via CCAAT enhancer-binding protein (C/EBP) homologous protein (CHOP) and X-box protein 1 (XBP1). Also related to autophagy are the classic cell survival signals PI-3K and its downstream target, AKT, a serine-threonine kinase. In addition, the impairment of chondrocyte mitochondrial function has emerged as a mechanism involved in impaired autophagy and deregulated bioenergetics during aging and OA development.

### Markers of Cartilage Matrix Degradation and Turnover

With increasing knowledge of the composition of the cartilage matrix, molecular markers in synovial fluid and body fluids such as urine, plasma, and serum have been identified for monitoring changes in cartilage metabolism and for assessing joint damage in arthritis.198, Molecules originating from articular cartilage ECM, including aggrecan fragments containing chondroitin sulfate and keratan sulfate, type II collagen fragments, collagen pyridinoline cross-links, and COMP, usually are released as degradation products as a result of catabolic processes. Specific monoclonal antibodies have been developed for analyzing OA and RA body fluids for products of proteoglycan or collagen degradation (catabolic neoepitopes) or synthesis of newly synthesized matrix components (anabolic neoepitopes), which represent attempts to repair the damaged matrix. Different monoclonal antibodies can distinguish subtle biochemical differences in chondroitin sulfate or keratan sulfate chains that result from degraded versus newly synthesized proteoglycans. Such epitopes can be detected in the synovial fluids and sera of patients with OA and RA, and the synovial fluid-to-serum ratio has been suggested as a potential diagnostic indicator. The degradation of aggrecan in cartilage has been characterized using antibodies 846, 3B3(), and 7D4, which detect chondroitin sulfate neoepitopes; 5D4, which detects keratan sulfate epitopes; and the VIDIPEN and NITEGE antibodies, which recognize aggrecanase and MMP cleavage sites within the interglobular G1 domain of aggrecan (Chapter 8).145,

Because collagens are the most abundant proteins in articular cartilage and type II collagen makes up approximately 50% of the cartilage ECM, many biomarker assays are designed to detect type II collagen breakdown products. It is possible to monitor the synthesis of type II collagen by measuring serum and synovial fluid levels of the carboxyl-terminal propeptide (CPII), and urinary excretion of hydroxylysyl pyridinoline cross-links or a cross-linked fragment of type II collagen (CTXII) may indicate collagen degradation. Specific antibodies that recognize epitopes on denatured type II collagen at the collagenase cleavage site are promising diagnostic reagents. These include the C12C antibody (previously known as Col2-3/4C Long mono) that has been used to detect specific cleavage of the triple helix of type II collagen in experimental models and in OA and RA cartilage. The ratios of these markers to the synthetic marker, CPII, are associated with a greater likelihood of radiologic progression in OA patients. These

biomarker assays have been used as research tools and are currently being developed and validated as diagnostic tools for monitoring cartilage degradation or repair in OA and RA patient populations and for assessment of treatment efficacy. 198,199

### Repair of Articular Cartilage

Articular cartilage has a poor capacity for regeneration, and pharmacologic enhancement of cartilage repair would have considerable potential in the treatment of arthritides and intra-articular fractures. The extent of intrinsic repair of a cartilage defect depends on the depth of the lesion and whether the defect penetrates the subchondral bone plate. Owing to the avascularity of cartilage, it differs from most other tissues in its response to injury. The vascular-dependent inflammatory and reparative phases of the classic healing response are unavailable. Partial defects generally do not regenerate because resident chondrocytes cannot migrate into the defect, and there is no vascular access for progenitor cells. Deep cartilage defects with disruption of the subchondral bone plate initiate vascular responses, however, including bleeding, fibrin clot formation, and inflammation, which permit cell invasion from the blood or underlying bone marrow. These defects can be filled by fibrocartilage produced by progenitor cells found in the bone marrow including MSCs. Current procedures for cartilage repair include joint lavage, tissue debridement, microfracture of the subchondral bone, and transplantation of autologous or allogeneic osteochondral grafts, in addition to the ultimate therapy of total joint replacement. These procedures may lead to the formation of fibrous tissue, chondrocyte death, and further cartilage degeneration, and they have variable success rates.

Transplantation of cultured autologous chondrocytes has been used successfully to repair small, full-thickness lesions in knee cartilage in young adults with sports injuries. Evidence of successful repair has been shown by turnover and remodeling of the initial fibrocartilaginous matrix formed by transplanted chondrocytes as the result of enzyme degradation and new synthesis of type II collagen. The donor site, although not load bearing, may undergo significant morbidity and osteoarthritic changes. Such procedures, however, show little difference in efficacy compared with microfracture of subchondral bone.

Major challenges for cartilage repair include restoration of the three-dimensional collagen structure and integration of the newly synthesized matrix with resident tissue. Novel approaches using autologous chondrocytes, which have been genetically engineered ex vivo to express anabolic factors, have been explored to promote differentiation before implantation in the defect. Because IGF-1 and TGF-β/BMP and FGF family members have roles in chondrogenesis and articular cartilage maintenance, they have been used as additive factors in tissue engineering strategies. Procedures for introducing these factors into joints directly or by in vivo or ex vivo gene delivery or via injectable or implantable carriers have been investigated for the repair of small defects in animal models. Gene transfer of combinations of anabolic factors and inhibitory cytokines combined with cartilage engineering approaches may be a long-term goal for repair of extensive defects in RA or late OA patients and for prevention of further damage.

Recent investigations have focused on scaffolds with the mechanical and material properties of the osteochondral unit that will integrate with the host tissue and attract migration of chondrocytes or osteochondral progenitors from the subchondral bone. . Although these are promising strategies for the future based on in vitro and in vivo studies, many challenges remain, especially for

cell-mediated cartilage repair. Among the cell sources are MSCs, which can be obtained from autologous adipose tissue, bone marrow, synovium, or muscle and expanded ex vivo in conditions that promote chondrogenesis; incorporated into scaffolds; and/or used as gene delivery vehicles to the site of cartilage damage. Although adult articular chondrocytes have little intrinsic repair capacity, the potential of a small population of cartilage-derived stem or progenitor cells to be stimulated in situ is the subject of current investigations.

### Conclusion

As the single cellular component in adult articular cartilage, chondrocytes are responsible for maintaining the ECM components in a low-turnover state. The composition and organization of ECM macromolecules, unique to this tissue, are determined during chondrocyte differentiation in embryonic and postnatal development of cartilage. Adult chondrocytes are spatially isolated and exist in a hypoxic environment within articular cartilage. They exhibit low metabolic activity, in part as a result of the absence of blood vessels and nerves, and display a rounded morphology that reflects their quiescent state, particularly in the middle and deep zones of cartilage. Chondrocytes interact with specific ECM components via cell surface receptors, including integrins, annexins, syndecans, DDR2, and CD44.

Studies in vitro and in vivo have shown that adult articular chondrocytes are capable of responding to biologic and mechanical stimuli that are anabolic or catabolic. Anabolic factors include members of the TGF-β/BMP and FGF families and IGF-I. Catabolic factors include proinflammatory cytokines, chemokines, DAMPs/alarmins, and adipokines, many of which stimulate the synthesis of matrix-degrading proteinases, such as MMPs and aggrecanases, by chondrocytes and increase intra-cellular events associated with inflammatory, mechanical, and oxidative stress processes. Many of the signaling pathways and transcription factors that mediate the responses of chondrocytes to these factors have been elucidated, but how they orchestrate specific chondrocyte functions is complex and is not fully understood. Under physiologic conditions, the adult articular chondrocyte maintains a stable equilibrium of low-turnover replacement of matrix components. Adult chondrocytes have a poor capacity for mediating effective repair of extensive cartilage lesions, and this capacity declines with age. Age-related changes in chondrocyte function decrease the ability of cells to maintain the tissue. There is decreased responsiveness to anabolic growth factors and increased production of proinflammatory factors due to cell senescence. Further understanding of how the adult articular chondrocyte functions within its unique environment and how this cell type undergoes metabolic reprogramming in a proinflammatory microenvironment would aid in the development of rational strategies for maintaining homeostasis and protecting against cartilage damage.

# Development and Biology of Bone

### KEY POINTS

Intramembranous or endochondral ossification generates bone tissue. Bones consist of a dense cortical shell and sponge-like trabecular network.

Bone formation depends on metabolically active osteoblasts synthesizing matrix proteins.

The immune system, in particular T lymphocytes, influences bone remodeling.

Neuroendocrine loops exert systemic control on bone remodeling.

### Structure and Composition of Bone

Bone is a specialized connective tissue that assists in (1) locomotion by providing the insertion site of the muscles; (2) protection of the internal organs; (3) bone marrow possession; and (4) metabolic functions, such as calcium and phosphate storage. Bone consists of four cell types: (1) osteoblasts, (2) bone-lining cells, (3) osteocytes, and (4) osteoclasts in addition to an extra-cellular matrix, which is composed of type I collagen fibers and a number of noncollagenous proteins including glutamic acid (Gla)-containing proteins, glycoproteins, and proteoglycans. The specific composition of the bone matrix allows for its mineralization, which is a specific feature of bone.

The two major types of bones are (1) flat bones, which develop through intramembranous ossification, and (2) long bones, which emerge from endochondral ossification. Intramembranous bone formation is based on the condensation of mesenchymal stem cells that directly differentiate into bone-forming osteoblasts. In contrast, during endochondral ossification of the long bones, the mesenchymal stem cells first differentiate into chondrocytes making a cartilage intermediate followed by differentiation of osteoblasts producing bone. Long bones consist of the following: (1) epiphyses, which are protrusions at the ends of the long bones; (2) diaphysis, constituting the bone's shaft; and (3) metaphyses, which are located between the epiphysis and the diaphysis (Fig. 4.1). The metaphysis is separated from the epiphysis by the growth plate, a proliferative cartilage layer that is essential for the longitudinal

growth of bones. After the growth is completed, this cartilage layer is entirely remodeled into bone.

The external shape of bones is formed by a dense cortical shell (cortical or compact bone), which is particularly strong along the diaphysis, where the bone marrow is located. The outer and inner surfaces of cortical bone are covered by layers of osteogenic cells, termed the periosteum and the endosteum, which are involved in the growth of width by bone apposition at the periosteal sites and bone resorption at the endosteal sites. The cortical bone shell becomes progressively thinner toward the metaphyses and epiphyses, where most of the trabecular bone is located. Trabecular bone (also called cancellous bone) is a sponge-like network consisting of a myriad of highly interconnected bony trabeculae. The metaphysis transfers load from the weight-bearing joint to the diaphysis of the bone and is critical for maintaining bone strength.

Although cortical and trabecular bone are composed of the same cells and the same matrix components, there is a substantial difference between these two forms of skeletal tissue. Cortical bone almost exclusively consists of mineralized tissue (up to 90%), allowing it to fulfill its mechanical requirements. In contrast, only 20% of trabecular bone is mineralized tissue, with the bone marrow, blood vessels, and a network of mesenchymal stem cells constituting the remainder of the bone. As a consequence, trabecular bone shares a vast surface with the nonmineralized tissue, which is the basis for the metabolic function of bone, necessitating a high level of communication between the bone surface and the nonmineralized tissue.

### Bone Vasculature

The metabolic function of bone is dependent on access to requisite nutrients, oxygen, hormones, growth factors, and neurotransmitters. Bone marrow resident cells and mesenchymal stem cells respond to bone mediators but can also produce metabolic factors that are relevant for body homeostasis.1, The exchange of such mediators into and out of the bone is mediated by a complex vascular system.

Oxygen is supplied by nutrient arteries; these enter the bone mainly at the metaphysis, run longitudinally along the bone shaft, and ramify toward the inner surface of the cortical bone, the endosteum (Fig. 4.2). At this interface, the arteries form loops and interconnect with sinusoidal capillaries. This fenestrated venous vessel type allows a fast exchange of metabolites between the blood circulation and bone marrow tissue. The sinusoids form a dense,

irregular network that converges into a large central sinus in the middle of the bone marrow tissue. This central sinus exits the bone shaft and connects the bone marrow with the general blood circulation.3,

In addition to bone marrow vascularization, mineralized bone also exhibits a dense vascular system, which is termed the Haversian—Volkmann system. This vascular network contains both arterial and venous vessels that ensure nutrient supply and metabolic exchange of calcified bone tissues. Its structural organization is complex and includes transcortical vessels (TCVs), which directly connect the bone marrow vascularization with the periosteum and the general circulation. Next to this, TCVs can show bifurcated or complex rope ladder—like morphologies. Although their diameters are much smaller than those of nutrient arteries and central sinus exits, numbers of TCVs are drastically higher. Based on their multitude, they facilitate the major blood transport through the bone.5,

At the endosteum, the vessels feed into the sinusoidal-arterial transition zones. These so-called type H vessels are also formed at the vascular transition zones of the metaphysis and exhibit specific metabolic profiles. Based on differences in tissue oxygenation and metabolic activity, they influence the growth potential and metabolism of hematopoietic stem cells, as well as bone remodeling cells. Thus the vascular supply of nutrients and oxygen is not only relevant for bone marrow metabolism but also for the formation and destruction of the mineralized bone matrix.

### Bone Matrix

The key protein component of bone is type I collagen. Collagen fibers follow specific directions, forming the basis for the lamellar structure of bone. This lamellar structure, which can be visualized when examining bone under polarized light, allows dense packaging, resulting in optimal resistance to mechanical load. The lamellar collagen structures can be assembled in parallel (e.g., along the cortical bone surfaces and inside the bony trabeculae) or concentrically around blood vessels embedded in the Haversian channels of the cortical bone. Upon rapid deposition of new bone, such as during fracture healing, this lamellar structure is missing, and the bone is then called woven bone. Woven bone is consecutively remodeled into lamellar bone, which is also considered "mature' D> bone. The composition of the collagen backbone also assists in the deposition of spindleor plate-shaped hydroxyapatite crystals, which contain calcium phosphate, thus allowing the calcification of the bone matrix.

In addition to type I collagen, noncollagenous proteins also exist in bone. Some of them, such as osteocalcin, osteopontin, and fetuin, are mineralization inhibitors, which serve to balance the degree of bone mineralization. Aside from their intrinsic function in bone, noncollagenous proteins also exert important metabolic functions, such as the control of energy metabolism by osteocalcin.

### Bone Cells

### Osteoblasts

Osteoblasts are the bone-forming cells that derive from mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs). MSCs also form chondrocytes, myocytes, and adipocytes. Osteoblasts are cuboid-shaped cells that form clusters covering the bone surface. They are metabolically highly active, synthesizing the collagenous and noncollagenous bone matrix proteins that are excreted and then deposited between the osteoblasts and the bone surface. This newly built matrix, which is not yet calcified, is termed the osteoid. The lag phase between osteoid deposition and its mineralization is approximately 10 days. Osteoblast differentiation depends on the expression of two key transcription factors: runt domain transcription factor 2 (Runx2) and its target osterix-1. These transcription factors confer MSC differentiation into osteoblasts in response to external stimuli. Prostaglandin E2 (PGE2), insulin-like growth factor (IGF)- 1, parathyroid hormone (PTH), bone morphogenic proteins (BMPs), and Wingless (Wnt) and Int-1 proteins are key stimuli for osteoblast differentiation. For instance, PGE2 is an important anabolic factor for bone and induces the expression of bone sialoprotein and alkaline phosphatase in MSCs. BMPs and transforming growth factor (TGF)-β foster osteoblast differentiation by activating intra-cellular Smad proteins. Finally, Wnt proteins, a family of highly conserved signaling molecules, are potent stimulators of osteoblast differentiation. Wnt proteins bind to surface receptors, including frizzled and low-density lipoprotein receptorrelated protein (LRP)5 on MSC, thereby eliciting activation and nuclear translocation of the transcription factor β-catenin, leading to transcription of genes involved in osteoblast differentiation. + Wnt proteins act in close synergy with BMPs and crosstalk with the receptor activator of nuclear factor-kB ligand (RANKL)— osteoprotegerin (OPG) system involved in the differentiation and function of bone-resorbing osteoclasts.

During aging, bone marrow adipocytes, derived from bone marrow MSCs, accumulate, and this accumulation correlates with osteoporosis. Activation of the nuclear receptor peroxisome

proliferator-activated receptor gamma (PPARγ) promotes adipocyte differentiation. In contrast, activation of the Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway stimulates MSCs to differentiate into osteoblasts and inhibit adipogenesis. Bone marrow adipocytes are metabolically active cells that play an active role in energy storage, endocrine function, and bone metabolism.

### Osteocytes

Osteocytes account for 90% to 95% of cells within bone. One cubic millimeter of bone contains up to 25,000 osteocytes that are well connected with each other and the bone surface by small tubes termed canaliculi. This large and dense communication network inside the bone shares similarities to the dendritic processes within the nervous system. Osteocytes reside in lacunae and connect to other osteocytes and bone lining cells by interconnecting filaments. Modeling suggests that this extensive network forms a total of 23 trillion connections; estimates place the total length of all osteocytic processes connected end-to-end at 175,000 km in the human body. Osteocytes are derived from osteoblasts, which are subsequently entrapped in the bone matrix. Upon terminal differentiation, osteocytes express specific genes not found in osteoblasts, including sclerostin, a secreted molecule that binds LRPs and blocks Wnt-stimulated bone formation. Consistent with its function as an inhibitor of bone formation, overexpression of sclerostin leads to low bone mass, whereas deletion of sclerostin leads to increased bone density and strength. This effect has been harnessed as a therapeutic strategy to increase bone mass by targeting and inhibiting sclerostin with a monoclonal antibody. Several local and systemic factors have been suggested

as possible regulators of sclerostin expression by osteocytes. For instance, intermittent administration of PTH, which is associated with strong anabolic effects on the bone, potently inhibits sclerostin expression.

Recent genetic studies in mice have revealed that osteocytes provide the majority of RANKL that controls osteoclast formation in trabecular bone. Thus, osteocytes are the master regulators of bone remodeling by secreting RANKL to stimulate osteoclastmediated bone resorption and secreting sclerostin to regulate osteoblastogenesis. Of note, osteocyte death is strongly linked to the pathogenesis of osteonecrosis, a condition that occurs when excessive death of bone tissue and absence of bone regeneration result in the collapse of necrotic bone.

### Osteoclasts

Osteoclasts are multinucleated cells that contain up to 20 nuclei and are unique in their ability to resorb bone. They are directly attached to the bone surface and build resorption lacunae (Howship lacunae). Apart from their multiple nuclei, another characteristic of the osteoclast is the ruffled border, a highly folded plasma membrane facing the bone matrix and designed to secrete and resorb proteins and ions into the space between the osteoclast and bone surface (Fig. 4.3). The space between this ruffled border and the bone surface is the place where bone resorption occurs. It is sealed by a ring of contractible proteins and tight junctions because it represents one of the few regions of the human body where a highly acidic milieu is found. Bone degradation by osteoclasts consists of two major steps: (1) demineralization of inorganic bone components and (2) removal of organic bone

matrix. To demineralize bone, osteoclasts secrete hydrochloric acid through proton pumps into the resorption lacunae. This proton pump requires energy that is provided by an adenosine triphosphatase (ATPase), allowing the enrichment of protons in the resorption compartment, which, in fact, represents an extracellular lysosome. In addition to protons and chloride, osteoclasts release matrix-degrading enzymes, including tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase (TRAP), lysosomal cathepsin K, and other cathepsins. Cathepsin K can effectively degrade collagens and other bone matrix proteins. Consequently, inhibitors of cathepsin K block osteoclast function and slow down bone resorption.

Osteoclasts originate from hematopoietic myeloid precursor cells and, upon the influence of specific signals, undergo a series of differentiation steps to become mature osteoclasts. Essential signals for osteoclast differentiation are macrophage colony-stimulating factor (M-CSF), produced by osteoblasts and MSCs, and RANKL, produced by osteocytes, preosteoblasts and stromal cells. During this differentiation and maturation process, osteoclasts acquire specific markers such as TRAP expression, fuse to become multinucleated giant cells, and polarize on contact to bone. Osteoclastogenesis depends on an adequate microenvironment, which provides essential signals such as M-CSF and RANKL and certain cytokines such as TNF, interleukin (IL)-6, and IL-17 that further enhance osteoclast differentiation. Osteoblasts express RANKL and M-CSF, highlighting the close interaction between bone formation and bone resorption.

RANKL, a TNF superfamily member, is a surface molecule expressed by osteocytes, preosteoblasts, and activated T and B cells. Under steady-state conditions, its expression is induced in cells of the osteoblastic lineage in response to osteotrophic factors such as vitamin D, PTH, and prostaglandins, whereby the nuclear factor peroxisome PPARβ represents an essential checkpoint in the regulation of RANKL expression. Moreover, inflammatory

cytokines such as TNF, IL-1, and IL-17 can induce RANKL expression. RANKL is essential for the final differentiation steps of osteoclasts, as well as for their bone-resorbing capacity, by engaging its receptor RANK on myeloid osteoclast-precursor cells. The interaction of RANKL with its receptor RANK is modulated by osteoprotegrin (OPG), a secreted glycoprotein, which is identified as a soluble RANK receptor that strongly suppresses osteoclast differentiation both in vitro and in vivo. Interestingly, OPG expression is induced by estrogens and quickly declines during menopause, explaining the rapid increase in osteoclast numbers and enhanced bone resorption during menopause. Accordingly, RANKL-deficient mice display severe osteopetrosis because of the lack of osteoclasts. Anti-RANKL antibody has proven effective in osteoporosis treatment in which it strongly inhibits osteoclast activity for 6 months. Beyond RANKL- RANK interactions, other important pro-osteoclastogenic signaling pathways are based on the triggering receptor expressed on myeloid cells-2 (TREM2), which interacts with the tyrosine kinase DAP12 and the osteoclast-associated immunoglobulinlike receptor (OSCAR). Both molecules are strong enhancers of osteoclastogenesis.

### Bone Remodeling

Developmental bone growth, postdevelopmental maintenance and repair of bone, and provision of calcium from the bone depend on a dynamic process called bone remodeling (Fig. 4.4). Osteocytes are the main mechano-sensing cells within bone and initiate bone remodeling at specific sites via a variety of mechanisms. Osteocyte apoptosis is one initiating event that leads to a decrease in osteoblast inhibitor, sclerostin, allowing osteoblast precursors to develop in the bone-remodeling unit. These cells recruit preosteoclasts to the area, resulting in differentiation of

osteoclasts and creation of a resorption lacuna. The naked bone surface inside this lacuna is subsequently populated by MSCs immigrating from the neighboring bone surface; the cells differentiate into osteoblasts and produce osteoid. The osteoid then mineralizes, trapping osteoblasts within the bone that differentiate into osteocytes, and the bone then returns to its resting state. This entire bone remodeling process takes about 3 to 6 months. Adults continuously remodel their skeleton, and this process occurs even faster during childhood and adolescence. In adults, the entire skeleton is remodeled every 7 to 10 years. Most of the bone remodeling happens in the trabecular bone, which promotes the building of an optimal inner microstructure adapted to individual mechanical demands. Trabecular bone is the leading structure in the vertebral bodies, contributing up to two-thirds of bone content, and in long bones such as the femurs contributes to 50% of bone structure.

### Fracture Repair

Healing of long bones requires multiple stages with production of a callus with a cartilaginous component followed by osteoblastmediated replacement with bone. Numerous cell types coordinate to achieve fracture union. The initial phase occurs with the formation of a fibrin-filled hematoma full of inflammatory cells including T and B cells, mast cells, macrophages, and neutrophils. Neutrophils and macrophages debride the injured and devitalized tissues, helping to prepare for tissue healing and new blood vessel formation. As inflammation resolves, macrophages differentiate into alternatively activated macrophages promoting angiogenesis and remodeling collagenase, as well as osteoclasts to resorb broken bone. The fibrovascular phase follows and involves the recruitment of endothelial cells to support angiogenesis, neovascularization, and MSCs, which produce chondrocytes and osteoblasts. At the fracture site, CXCR4-expressing MSCs are recruited

from periosteum and bone marrow by stromal cell-derived factor1 (SDF1), also known as CXCL12, that is upregulated in hypoxic tissue.

MSCs recruited into the fibrovascular tissue then undergo differentiation into either chondrocyte or osteoblasts via the transcriptional regulation of Sox9, required for chondrogenesis but suppressed during osteoblastogenesis. Mechanical forces, oxygen tension, Wnt growth factors, and BMPs are some of the cell-extrinsic microenvironmental factors that promote cell fate decisions within the callus. In fully stabilized defects, osteoblasts may form directly leading to intramembranous ossification. In areas with more movement, chondrogenesis is favored to create a dense cartilage in the callus. The chondrocytes become hypertrophic and eventually begin to express genes related to osteogenesis including osteopontin, osteocalcin, osterix, and alkaline phosphatase. Coupled with continued angiogenesis, the cartilage then begins to calcify, leading to bone formation. The last stage of fracture healing occurs with callus remodeling by osteoclasts. Thus full callus repair requires the recruitment of hematopoietic cells and inflammation followed by MSCs that differentiate into chondrocyte and osteoblasts, then angiogenesis and bone remodeling by osteoclasts.

### Regulation of Bone Remodeling

Normal physiologic circumstances ensure a balance between bone formation and bone resorption to maintain skeletal homeostasis. This bone remodeling process requires a tight mutual regulation of bone resorption by osteoclasts and bone formation by osteoblasts, a phenomenon called coupling. Coupling is regulated on at least three different levels: (1) by a direct interaction between osteoblasts and osteoclasts, (2) by systemic neuroendocrine control of bone metabolism, and (3) by local interactions between the immune system and bone cells.

### Direct Interactions Between Osteoblasts and Osteoclasts

A proper coupling between bone formation and bone destruction is essential to maintain bone integrity (Fig. 4.5). This coupling process involves two main mechanisms; the first is the expression of the essential pro-osteoclastogenic cytokines by the osteoblast lineage, and the second involves the ephrin ligand/ephrin receptor bidirectional signaling.23, Preosteoblasts are the main pro-osteoclastogenic cells in normal physiologic conditions and provide the first level of coupling between bone formation and bone resorption. In response to Wnt signaling, osteoblasts slowly lose their supportive activity for osteoclasts when they mature toward more mineralizing cells and then become the bone-embedded osteocytes. They then secrete anti-osteoclastogenic molecules such as OPG and Wnt inhibitors sclerostin, dickkopf-1 (DKK1), and secreted frizzled-related protein 1 (SFRP1), which either block osteoclast differentiation (OPG) or inhibit the further differentiation of osteoblasts. A second level of coupling involves the expression of ephrin ligands on the surface of osteoclast progenitors that can bind to ephrin receptors and activate their tyrosine kinase activity. Two ephrin ligands regulate bone remodeling. The first, ephrin-B2, binds to the receptor EphB4 on osteoblast progenitors, increasing their differentiation and stimulating bone formation. The second, ephrin-A2, acts in an autocrine manner by binding to the EphA2 receptor on the osteoclasts, which promotes their differentiation, and in a paracrine manner on the osteoblasts, thus inhibiting their differentiation.

### Systemic Control of Bone Remodeling by Neuroendocrine Mechanisms

Bone remodeling is regulated not only locally but also by various systemic hormonal pathways, including the sex hormone and

the growth hormone (GH)/IGF axes. In addition, two major systemic neuroendocrine regulators of bone homeostasis co-regulate bone, fat, and energy metabolism. The two central players of this systemic loop are osteocalcin and leptin. Osteocalcin is a hormone produced by mature osteoblasts and acts on the β cells of the pancreas to stimulate proliferation and thus insulin production in response to leptin. In addition, osteocalcin can directly stimulate adipocytes to regulate insulin sensitivity. Leptin is a peptide hormone produced by adipocytes of the white adipose tissues. Leptin deficiency causes obesity and increased bone mass. Although the increased fat mass is certainly linked to the role of leptin in controlling appetite, the effect of leptin on bone and fat can be dissociated. Indeed, bone formation is negatively regulated by leptin through a hypothalamic pathway, the β-adrenergic sympathetic nervous system that mediates decreased osteoblast proliferation via the induction of clock genes in osteoblasts. The question of how leptin regulates bone formation is debated. However, two potential hypothalamic relays have been identified. The first relay is neuropeptide Y, a repressor of bone formation, which is silenced by leptin. The second downstream modulator of leptin is neuromedin U, which inhibits clock gene expression and increases osteoblast proliferation. These observations suggest that disturbance of the metabolic loops linking adipogenesis, osteogenesis, and insulin production have profound consequences on bone homeostasis.

### Interactions of Immune System and Bone Cells: Osteoimmunology

Aside from the reciprocal regulation of osteoblasts and osteoclasts, bone remodeling is also controlled by the immune system. Insights into the control of bone by the immune system have

led to a new research field known as osteoimmunology, which has defined new pathways involved in immune regulation of postmenopausal osteoporosis and bone loss during inflammatory diseases. Importantly, T cells influence the differentiation of osteoclasts by producing RANKL, IL-17, IL-1, IL-6, and TNF (Fig. 4.6). RANKL is expressed by various subsets of proliferative T cells (CD8 and CD4 and Th1 and Th2), as well as on FoxP3expressing regulatory T cells (Tregs). Despite consistent expression of RANKL on various T cell lineages, individual T cells exert substantially different functions on the osteoclast, allowing a fine regulation of bone remodeling by the immune system. For instance, Th17 cells stimulate osteoclast differentiation via the production of IL-17 that induces upregulation of RANK on preosteoclasts, leading to increased osteoclastogenesis. Moreover, a subset of T cells expressing the IL-23 cytokine receptor is involved in bone remodeling, specifically at the insertion sites of the tendons. In contrast, other T cell lineages express strong inhibitors of osteoclastogenesis, such as interferon (IFN)-γ by Th1 cells, IL-4 by Th2 cells, or cytotoxic T lymphocyte—associated antigen-4 (CTLA-4) in the case of regulatory T cells, and thereby provide protection from bone loss.

### Osteoimmunology in Rheumatoid Arthritis

Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is associated with dysfunction of the close interaction between the immune system and bone and manifests as chronic inflammation disrupting the physiologic balance favoring bone resorption over bone formation. Bone loss is an early and common feature of RA and occurs in three forms during the course of the disease (see Chapter 72):

Localized bone loss in the form of articular bone erosions

Periarticular osteopenia adjacent to inflamed joints

Generalized bone loss involving the axial and appendicular skeleton

Bone Resorption in Rheumatoid Arthritis: Osteoclasts. Osteoclasts are bone tissue resident macrophages capable of bone resorption. The critical role of osteoclasts in pathogenesis of bone erosions in inflammatory arthritis has been elucidated in studies using genetically modified osteoclast-deficient RANKL and c-Fos knockout mice that are completely protected from bone erosions despite having significant joint inflammation. Increased bone resorption in RA results from an increase in osteoclast activation, lifespan, and numbers due to enhanced recruitment of osteoclast precursors and increased differentiation of osteoclasts from their precursor cells. Osteoclast differentiation is controlled by cytokines, M-CSF, and RANKL. During the process of physiologic bone remodeling, RANKL is mainly released by preosteoblasts and osteocytes; however, in arthritic joints, RANKL is dramatically increased due to production by synovial fibroblasts and infiltrating immune cells, including activated T cells. Under physiologic conditions, osteoclast activity is balanced by the expression of anti-osteoclastogenic OPG by stromal cells and RANKL by osteocytes, but this ratio is skewed toward RANKL in active RA (Fig. 4.6). A higher RANKL:OPG ratio predicts long-term radiologic damage progression in RA patients. Similarly, the therapeutic inhibition of RANKL holds potential to prevent bone erosions in patients with RA, without affecting inflammation status. A placebo-controlled phase 3 clinical study demonstrated that denosumab (a monoclonal antibody targeting RANKL) significantly reduced the progression of joint destruction and induced increases in bone mineral density (BMD) in RA patients receiving concomitant conventional disease-modifying antirheumatic drug (DMARD) therapy.

Bone Resorption in Rheumatoid Arthritis: B Cells. B cells are significantly involved in the development of bone erosions in RA, in large part due to effects of autoreactive anti-citrullinated protein antibodies (ACPA) and rheumatoid factor (RF). High serum levels of ACPA and RF correlate with more pronounced bone erosions in RA. ACPA antibodies bind citrullinated vimentin on osteoclast progenitor cells and synoviocytes, stimulating the production of TNF and RANKL, resulting in enhanced osteoclast differentiation (Fig. 4.6). The importance of these findings is supported through the observation that treatment of RA with the B cell depletion reduces synovial RANKL levels.

Bone Resorption in Rheumatoid Arthritis: T Cells. Activated T cells, in particular Th17 and Treg cells, have emerged as primary players in the pathogenesis of bone loss in RA. Th17 cells drive osteoclastogenesis by producing IL-17, which in turn induces RANKL expression by synovial fibroblasts, as well as RANK expression on osteoclast precursors. Additionally, IL-17 promotes osteoclastogenesis and bone resorption by inducing TNF and IL-1 production by synovial macrophages, IL-6 by fibroblasts, and suppressing anti-osteoclastogenic factors including IL-4.

Inhibition of Bone Formation in Rheumatoid Arthritis. Abnormal bone remodeling in RA is due not only to increased bone resorption but also to active suppression of new bone formation. Osteoblasts, bone-forming cells, are regulated by Wnt signaling via the LRP5/6 receptors. Sclerostin and dickkopf1 (DKK1) inhibit Wnt signaling and suppress bone formation. DKK1 is significantly upregulated in RA compared with healthy controls and correlates with disease activity. Drugs that activate Wnt signaling, such as Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitors, increase osteoblast function and can induce repair of articular bone erosions in RA patients.

### Osteoimmunology in Psoriatic Arthritis

Psoriatic arthritis (PsA) is unique in its presentation of synovial inflammation with bone destruction accompanied by juxtaarticular new bone formation resulting in osteophytes and enthesophytes. TNF and the IL-23/IL-17 axis are involved in PsA pathogenesis. Potential osteogenic pathways in PsA include the Wnt, TGF-β, BMPs, and PGE2 pathways. New bone formation, a hallmark of PsA, is mediated by IL-17 and IL-22 targeting MSCs and PGE2, activating osteoblast differentiation.

IL-23 binding to its receptor, IL-23R, on lymphocytes and myeloid cells activates the JAK/signal transducer and activator of transcription (STAT) pathway to induce inflammation in PsA. IL-23 promotes T cell differentiation into Th17 cells secreting IL-22 and IL-17A that stimulate RANK expression on osteoclast precursors driving osteoclastogenesis. Osteoclasts, synovial fibroblasts, lymphocytes, monocytes, and keratinocytes bind IL-17A via IL-17RA receptor and become activated promoting inflammation and tissue damage. IL-17A coupled with TNF drives the production of matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) in synovial fluid, leading to cartilage breakdown. IL-17A also drives RANKL expression in preosteoblasts leading to bone erosions. Inhibiting IL-17A in PsA inhibits the radiographic progression of bone erosions.

Similar to RA, both genetic and environmental factors contribute to PsA disease progression. Genetic factors include variants in genes coding for IL-12, IL-23R, IL-23A, TLR2, and STAT3, just to name a few. A variety of epigenetic alterations, including DNA methylation, post-translational histone modifications, and noncoding RNAs, are associated with PsA. The gut microbiome also plays a significant role in PsA with increased numbers

of Th17 cells and decreased Treg cells observed in the intestinal lamina propria. Additionally, gut microbiota alters microRNA expression, which appears to modulate gut permeability, leading to further increases in inflammation. Further studies are needed to determine the role of altering the microbiome to improve PsA outcomes.

### Osteoimmunology in Post-menopausal Osteoporosis

Cessation of ovarian function at menopause causes sharp declines in estrogen levels, leading to immune system activation, which affects bone homeostasis and drives the development of postmenopausal osteoporosis. Prior to menopause, estrogen increases OPG production, which serves to maintain the OPG/RANKL ratio and inhibit osteoclastogenesis. In the setting of estrogen deficiency, bone resorption is uncoupled from bone formation due to increased osteoclast numbers, while bone formation only marginally increases, leading to net loss of bone density. These findings suggest that post-menopausal osteoporosis is a high-bone-turnover disease with a shift in the remodeling balance in favor of resorption. By contrast, senile osteoporosis is often described as a low-bone-turnover disease.

Estrogen deficiency leads to chronic activation of the immune system producing low-grade inflammation with altered circulating

proinflammatory cytokines and immune cell profiles. Estrogen loss results in a significant expansion of T and B lymphocytes, as well as increases in inflammatory cytokines including IL-1, IL-6, and TNF. Estrogen deficiency also leads to increased differentiation of Th17 cells with increased IL-17 production. This in turn induces bone loss by increasing pro-osteoclastogenic cytokines including TNF, IL-6, and RANKL from osteoblasts. Mast cells may also have a role in post-menopausal osteoporosis. Mature mast cells have a large number of secretory granules with pre-formed mediators and are also capable of de novo synthesis and release of mediators, including IL-6, TNF, and vascular endothelial growth factor. Mast cell numbers are increased in the bone marrow of post-menopausal patients. For several mast cell mediators, osteo-catabolic or osteo-anabolic effects are described, suggesting a possible role of mast cells in the regulation of bone turnover.

### Conclusion

Bone is continuously remodeled by bone-resorbing osteoclasts and bone-forming osteoblasts. This remodeling process allows the optimal adaptation of the bone architecture to individual demands and tight control of calcium homeostasis. Local factors control the bone remodeling process on the basis of osteoclast-osteoblast interactions, as well as by systemic immune and neuroendocrine factors controlling the bone-resorbing and bone-forming cells.

# Muscle Anatomy, Physiology, and Biochemistry

### KEY POINTS

The smallest functional unit of muscle is the sarcomere, which is composed of a variety of important proteins, but actin and myosin are the key elements that contribute to active contraction. The organization of skeletal muscle, or its architecture, describes the serial and parallel arrangement of sarcomeres within a muscle and is an excellent predictor of muscle function. Muscles are attached to the skeleton through tendons, which vary in length and extend well into the muscle belly. Skeletal muscle activity is controlled by the nervous system; central neurons project from the motor cortex to the spinal cord, and peripheral alpha-motor neurons project from the ventral horn of the spinal cord to the neuromuscular junctions of each muscle cell. Sensory feedback from the muscle (e.g., muscle spindle or Golgi tendon organ) is required for normal muscle activation and ultimately movement. Skeletal muscle is highly "plastic," in that its structure and function changes rapidly in response to increased or decreased use.

### Introduction

Skeletal muscle is a large organ system, constituting approximately 40% of body mass. In fact, there are roughly 640 distinct skeletal muscles (depending on how muscle bellies are counted). The primary function of skeletal muscle is to generate active and passive forces in coordination with the nervous system, thereby allowing movement and stability. Each muscle has a complex and specialized origin (typically a proximal attachment) and a discrete insertion, both of which typically involve tendons that extend well into the muscle belly (a site of muscle fiber connections) and cross one or more joints to insert onto bone. This is important because muscles produce tension between these tendons, which in turn generates torque about a given joint. Here, we focus on the organization of skeletal muscles across size scales (molecules to the whole organ) and the molecular and biology of contraction, which ultimately dictates function. Importantly, muscle is highly plastic; it rapidly adapts its biochemistry and structure to increased and decreased use so as to accommodate the wide range of mechanical loads that it is placed under and ultimately to ensure that the functional requirements across a diverse range of activity levels are met.

### Structure

### Sarcomere

The smallest functional unit of skeletal muscle is the sarcomere. Sarcomeres are generally defined by the exquisitely organized actin and myosin filament lattice and associated protein machinery, which has been very well defined, that regulates structural stability and contraction. In short, actin filaments extend from Z-lines on each side of a sarcomere toward the middle, and polymerized myosin molecules make a filament that extends from the middle of the sarcomere toward the Z-lines on each side (Fig. 5.1). Activation of the sarcomere occurs via excitation—contraction coupling, which ends with calcium release into the cell, and allows for a couple major events to occur: (1) tropomyosin changes its structural configuration, which allows actin and myosin to interact, and (2) myosin (and its intrinsic adenosine triphosphatase [ATPase] activity) and adenosine triphosphate (ATP) produce a cycle of actin and myosin interactions that, under ideal circumstances, pulls the Z-lines toward the center of the sarcomere (e.g., contraction).

Although actin and myosin are key players in the contractile apparatus, tropomyosin and troponin are pivotally important in the regulation of actin and myosin interactions via their location on the actin filaments. Similarly, titin and nebulin have key functions in the assembly and maintenance of sarcomere structure. Titin is a massive protein (~3000 kDa) that anchors the thick filament in the center of the sarcomere by extending from the middle of the myosin filament to the Z-line.1, Nebulin is also a large protein (~800 kDa) and helps anchor thin filaments to the Z-line.3, The cytoskeleton of muscle fibers also contains cytoplasmic actin, microtubules, and intermediate filaments, all of which play important roles in structural organization and sensitivity to mechanical loads.

### Myotendinous Junction

Muscle forces generated by the contractile lattice (actin and myosin) are transmitted to the skeleton via the tendons. Although the identity and function of mechanical connections between the contractile lattice and the distal ends of the tendons are a topic of current research, there is certainly linear transmission of forces to the terminal ends of the fiber (or cell). If there were simply CC 'spot welds" between the end of the fiber and the tendon, this would be a region of very high stress, so the muscle has created

invaginations of sarcolemma (cell membrane) at its ends, filled with long bundles of collagen arising from the tendon. These membrane folds increase the surface area for bearing the mechanical load by approximately 30-fold, almost as if the fiber was terminating inside of a sock as opposed to terminating at a spot weld. These invaginations are rich in matrix and adherence proteins like α-actinin, vinculin, talin, and integrin, which provide a strong web of mechanical connectivity between the contractile apparatus inside the cell and the force-transmitting tendons at the ends of the muscle.

### Muscle Spindle

Muscle spindles are complex organs embedded between muscle fibers within the larger skeletal muscle organ. They comprise a connective tissue capsule, infrafusal (within the spindle) muscle fibers, and sensory organelles. The purpose of the infrafusal fibers is control of the length of the spindle in parallel with the larger skeletal muscle (extrafusal fibers), and there are special motor neurons called gamma motoneurons that innervate them. The sensory portion of the spindle is activated by length and velocity changes of the muscle, and this information is transmitted to the spinal cord and the supraspinal centers like the cerebellum that controls proprioception (i.e., the position or movement of the body). Because of the length and velocity sensitivity of these organs and their direct connection to the alpha motoneuron pool in the spinal cord, they are directly responsible for stretch reflexes (e.g., patellar tendon tap). They are also involved in pathology. For example, spasticity after stroke involves hyperactivity of the stretch reflex pathways, although this involves lack of descending inhibition of this circuitry more than hyperactivity of the spindle itself.

### Golgi Tendon Organ

The Golgi tendon organ (GTO) lies at the musculotendinous junction and is primarily involved in sensing tension generated by skeletal muscles. Each sensory organ lies in series with muscle fibers and tendon, and its sensory endings interdigitate with

collagen fibrils that ultimately become tendon. Compression of these sensory organelles results in its tension-sensing abilities. The most commonly discussed function of the GTO is to inhibit muscle force production when loads become too high for the musculotendinous junction, similar to a circuit breaker. However, the GTO is capable of both facilitating and inhibiting contraction via its influence on the alpha motoneuron pool in the spinal cord and its afferent projections to supraspinal control centers.

### Peripheral Nerves and Neurons

Peripheral nerves are composite tissues that are critical to the contraction of muscle fibers. Nerves provide an electrical signal for muscles to depolarize via the neuromuscular junction. They also communicate sensory feedback from muscle back to the CNS (consisting of the spinal cord and brain). Neurons ("nerve fibers") are the primary functional component of nerves. Neurons extend long axonal projections that span from their cell bodies, which are located in the spinal cord or its flanking ganglia, to their motor or sensory endings in the periphery. Individual neurons may be ensheathed by myelinating Schwann cells (glial cells in the peripheral nervous system [PNS]), allowing increased conduction velocity. Along the length of nerve fibers, saltatory conduction is enabled through gaps in myelination known as nodes of Ranvier. Neurons may alternatively be unmyelinated, resulting in slower conduction velocity. Within a nerve, bundles of neurons vary in size and identity, and this is linked to the type of motor units they comprise, as discussed later, and the muscle fibers that they innervate.5,6

### Motor and Sensory Neurons

Several varieties of neurons are fundamental in muscle function. Efferent (i.e., moving away from the brain) neurons communicate electrochemical signals from the motor cortex in the brain to the spinal cord and from the spinal cord to muscle. Alpha motor neurons have their cell bodies in the ventral horn of the spinal cord and innervate extrafusal muscle fibers, which are responsible for generating contractile force. Gamma motor neurons innervate intrafusal muscle fibers within muscle spindles and thus influence muscle length and tone without contributing to contractile force. Beta motor neurons are less well understood but innervate both intrafusal and extrafusal fibers. In the opposite direction, afferent (i.e., toward the brain) sensory neurons communicate feedback from muscle fibers back to the central nervous system. Such sensory information could include signals of pain via type A-delta or type C nociceptive neurons10 or proprioceptive feedback from GTOs (A-alpha/type IB neurons) or muscle spindles (A-alpha/type IA neurons or A-beta/type II neurons). Interneurons, which are neither motor nor sensory neurons, connect sensory and motor neurons in the spinal cord. They integrate sensory information and either send information back to the brain for additional processing or result in reflexive muscle movement.

### Neuromuscular Junctions

The neuromuscular junction (NMJ), also called the motor endplate, is the physical site of efferent peripheral neuronal signaling to a muscle fiber (Fig. 5.2). Here, a pre-synaptic motor neuron communicates with a specialized region of the muscle fiber called the postsynaptic junction. In vertebrates, most (though not all) muscle fibers have a single NMJ13 approximately midway along

the length of a fiber. This configuration allows unique control of a given fiber by a single neuron. To maximize the contact area between the preand postsynaptic junction, the structure of the NMJ is highly arborized, with healthy pre-synaptic termini aligned perfectly upon the postsynaptic endplate, across a synaptic cleft of ~20 nm in width.

The neuron is unmyelinated as it approaches the NMJ, but surrounding the NMJ are a specialized class of Schwann cells known as peri-synaptic Schwann cells. Recent evidence suggests that these cells play an important role in the structural and functional stability of NMJ. Loss of NMJ organization and structural integrity has significant implications for muscle function because of impaired neuromuscular transmission.

### Muscle Architecture

Muscle is a hierarchical structure (Fig. 5.3). For example, actin and myosin molecules are assembled into filaments (1 to 2 µm in length), which are key elements of a highly organized sarcomere (the functional unit of the muscle, which is 2 to 4 µm in length). Sarcomeres are packed in series to form myofibrils (~1 µm in diameter), which are then packed together to form myocytes (~50 µm in diameter). Myocytes are packed together to form muscle fascicles (~1 to 2 mm in diameter), which are in turn packed together to form whole muscles (several cm in diameter).

Muscle architecture refers to the arrangement of the functional units of muscle (sarcomeres) in series and in parallel in a muscle, and these features are highly predictive of whole muscle function. Whereas muscle fiber size (which is directly proportional to force generation) is relatively consistent among muscles of different sizes, architectural differences between muscles are much more variable and much more strongly affect function. Therefore understanding these structural features is of great practical importance for understanding the anatomic and physiologic basis for force production and movement and also for understanding pathology.

There are two general classes of muscle fiber architecture. Muscles composed of fibers that extend parallel to the muscle's forcegenerating axis are described as having a parallel or longitudinal architecture. Muscles with fbers that are oriented at an angle relative to the force-generating axis are described as having pennate architecture. The angle between the fiber and the force-generating axis (i.e., the pennation angle) has been measured at resting length in different mammalian muscles and varies from about 0° to 30°. It becomes obvious when performing muscle dissections that most human muscles are multipennate in structure because they have fibers that are oriented at several different angles relative to the axis of force generation. Because fibers may not be oriented along the anatomic (tendon—tendon) axis, force generation is not simply transmitted between two distinct tendons. This changes the directionality and stability of a muscle given contraction. Multiple pennation angles within a muscle also mean that measurement of muscle architecture features is impossible from a single biopsy or imaging modality (e.g., MRI, CT, or ultrasonography), because these methods cannot account for the variations in fiber length and orientation that occur along the muscle length.

Quantitative studies of muscle architecture were pioneered by a previous study17 that developed the methodology for defining muscle architecture based on microdissection of whole muscles. The parameters usually included in an architectural analysis are muscle length, fiber or fascicle length, pennation angle (i.e., the fiber angle relative to the axis of force-generation), and physiologic cross-sectional area (PCSA). Typically, muscles are chemically fixed in formalin to maintain fiber integrity during dissection. For the purposes of this chapter, two key architectural features will be described: (1) muscle fiber length and (2) PCSA.

Fiber length represents the total length spanned by sarcomeres in series, and experimental evidence suggests that muscle fiber length is proportional to both contraction velocity and whole muscle force—length properties. Essentially, this parameter is important because it will determine how sensitive to length and velocity a muscle will be during contraction. Muscle fiber length can only be determined by microdissection of individual fibers or fiber bundles (5 to 50 fibers). The important step in measuring fiber length is normalizing a grossly measured fiber/bundle length by the sarcomere length within the isolated fibers. This is necessary to compensate for differences in muscle length that occur during fixation. In other words, to conclude that a muscle has "long fibers," one must ensure that it was not merely fixed in highly stretched position corresponding to a long sarcomere length. Similarly, muscles with "short fibers" must be further investigated to ensure that they were not simply fixed at a short sarcomere length. To permit such conclusions, fiber length measurements should be normalized to an optimal sarcomere length (2.7 µm in humans)— the sarcomere length at which the sarcomere generates maximum force.

PCSA represents the sum of the cross-sectional areas of all the muscle fibers within the muscle, and thus, it is the only

architectural parameter that is directly proportional to the maximum isometric tension generated by the muscle. The PCSA is almost never the same as the cross-sectional area of the muscle measured in any of the traditional anatomic planes, as would be obtained using a noninvasive imaging method such as MRI, CT, or ultrasonography. It is calculated as muscle volume divided by fiber length and has units of area. Because fibers may be oriented

at a pennation angle relative to the axis of force generation, not all of the fiber tensile force is transmitted to the tendons. Therefore only a component of muscle fiber force [X • cos(θ)] will actually be transmitted along the muscle axis. Thus the volume/length is often multiplied by cos(θ) (pennation angle) to yield PCSA. Importantly, the architecture of human muscles in the upper20 and lower extremities21 has been defined, and these values have

been incorporated into musculoskeletal models22 to more deeply understand normal and abnormal human movement.

### Physiology

### Motor Control

### Motor Units

One study23 described the concept that individual motor neurons branch such that a single neuron can innervate multiple muscle fibers. Thus a motor unit is defined as a motor neuron and all of its targeted muscle fibers. Small motor units allow high levels of independent muscle control, but low strength (examples of this include the finger and eye [or extraocular] muscles). In contrast, large motor units allow low independent control of muscle, but high coordination and strength (e.g., biceps, quadriceps muscles).

### Size Principles of Motor Control

Two size principles govern neuronal activity as related to the control of muscle function. First, building on principles from a 1951 study,24 it is well established that the diameter of a neuron dictates is conduction velocity—the larger a neuron, the faster its conduction. Myelin sheath thickness also correlates with fiber diameter, so larger fibers are also "more myelinated." However, the G-ratio, or the ratio of the axon diameter (inner radius of the myelinating sheath) to the total nerve fiber diameter (outer radius of the myelinating sheath), is conserved. Second, another study26 proposed another size principle related to orderly motor unit recruitment: as additional muscle contractile force is required, motor units are recruited from small (low force output) to large (high force output). As with many nuances of muscle physiology, the size principle of this study26 is not without controversy, with interesting questions surrounding the limits of its application, as well as neuromuscular control systems that may perturb the generalized principle.

### Physiology of the Neuromuscular Junction

Action potentials propagate along the motor neuron toward the pre-synaptic terminal. Depolarization of the neuronal terminal results in the rapid influx of extracellular calcium into the cell via voltage-gated calcium channels. This calcium then initiates the docking and exocytosis of synaptic vesicles; as NMJs are cholinergic synapses, synaptic vesicles release acetylcholine (ACh) into the synaptic cleft. ACh diffuses across the cleft and binds to nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (AChRs) organized on the postsynaptic muscle. Receptor binding locally depolarizes the postsynaptic muscle fiber, a signal that is amplified through the opening of voltagegated sodium channels. This process initiates an action potential along the plasma membrane of the muscle fiber.

### Excitation-Contraction Coupling

The amplitude and frequency of neuronal input to muscle dictates the frequency and persistence of muscle contractility before intrinsic muscle regulation takes over. Stimulus rate can be so infrequent as to elicit single muscle twitches, such as those that occur with the monosynaptic stretch reflex involving patellar tendon stretch and quadriceps activation. Conversely, at higher frequencies, the contributions of individual twitches fuse and superpose, creating a tetanic contraction, or a continuous muscle contraction that generates forces several times higher than those generated by a single twitch. Within the muscle, a network of membranous tubules provides an electrically conductive network that transmits incoming signals at the NMJ throughout an entire muscle fiber. This transverse tubule (T-tubule) network pervades the fiber at regular intervals, coinciding with sarcomere boundaries along the length of the muscle, and surrounds the contractile apparatus with connected longitudinal and lateral segments. A specialized type of endoplasmic reticulum forms an entirely intracellular membrane system termed the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR). Prevalent structures containing a T-tubule flanked by two terminal cisternae of the SR to form junctional complexes are termed triads (Fig. 5.4).

### Length-Tension

Skeletal muscle is length sensitive. From the prior discussion of sarcomere structure, the key issue is overlap of actin and myosin filaments. At an optimal sarcomere length (2.7 µm in humans), there is maximum overlap between these proteins, and therefore a maximum number of cross-bridge interactions. At longer (descending limb) and shorter (ascending limb) sarcomere lengths, fewer cross-bridges interactions occur and force is lower. These regions and their corresponding isometric (no change in length) force-generating capacities are well described. This relationship

has been studied and described in detail39 and has resulted in the classic forcelength curve of sarcomeres (Fig. 5.6). Moreover, this relationship has been extrapolated to whole muscle by understanding muscle fiber length (or serial sarcomere number). Importantly, sarcomereand whole-muscle force—length curves, when presented in detail, note that passive tension is generated in muscle as it moves onto the descending limb (longer than optimal lengths). The shape and steepness of the passive tension curve is not well predicted by the architecture of muscle. It scales nonlinearly between the single cell (fiber) and the whole muscle, suggesting that the extracellular matrix structure, organization, and 40 biochemistry may be important.

### Force-Velocity

Skeletal muscle is also velocity sensitive. The velocity sensitivity of the muscle is related to the ability of actin and myosin (cross-bridges) to form and produce force while the filaments are sliding past one another. The net effect is a nonlinear reduction in force during active shortening of muscle (clinically called concentric contraction) and increases in force-generating capacity during active lengthening (clinically termed eccentric contraction) and as relative to peak isometric contraction force. Again, this phenomenon has been studied and described in detail,41 but the clinical and functional impacts are profound. First, muscle force declines rapidly when the muscle is actively shortening but can generate tremendous forces during lengthening (Fig. 5.7). Although debated in the literature, the rationale for elevated forces during lengthening contraction are rooted in the concept that cross-bridges are mechanically pulled apart instead of biochemically released through ATP and other substrates binding to the myosin head. This concept is also consistent with the fact that lengthening contractions

are more energy efficient than active shortening or isometric 42-44 contractions.

Plasticity, discussed later in the chapter, is also related to force— velocity and force—length properties in muscle. For example, if a clinical goal is to increase the size and strength of a muscle (hypertrophy), muscles are often overloaded via lengthening contractions through a wide range of length including the descending limb of the length tension curve. Thus the muscle fibers will begin to develop microdamage because of the elevated forces, and this damage is more likely to occur at long muscle lengths.

The microdamage becomes an anabolic stimulus for muscle fiber hypertrophy and subsequent increases in strength. The practical term for this form of exercise is "negative reps," which refers to the fact that very high loads are typically handled by controlled lowering of the weight that exceeds the capacity of the user to lift against gravity.

### Force Transmission

Force transmission (communication of forces generated by the sarcomere to the outside world) in skeletal muscle is a topic of current research. There are two general categories of force transmission: (1) lateral and (2) longitudinal. The muscle cell is anchored to the basal lamina though the length of the muscle fiber. Along this length, the actin filament complex, including the Z-line, is anchored through the intermediate filament system (e.g., vinculin, desmin, talin, and an integrin system) to laminin and on to a collagen networks that encases each fiber (endomysium), each fascicle (perimysium), and the whole muscle (epimysium). These connective tissue layers are, in turn, confluent with tendon, which allows muscle forces to be transmitted laterally out of the cell in addition to longitudinally along the fiber (cell). Defects or mutations in these force-transmitting proteins are the cause of a number of muscular dystrophies. The most widely recognized dystrophies are Becker and Duchenne muscular dystrophies, which are related to mutations or deletions in the dystrophin protein, which links the cytoskeleton to cell membrane in muscle, which allows for force transmission and contributes to membrane strength. When these force transmission proteins are absent or abnormal, force transmission, not necessarily generation, declines impairing function, and muscle cells begin to degenerate through elevated internal forces, membrane fragility, or both.

### Energy a and Biochemistry

A basic function of skeletal muscle is to produce movement via muscle contraction. This is achieved through excitation-contraction coupling, as discussed earlier, and the splitting of an ATP molecule by the enzyme, myosin ATPase: ATP → ADP + inorganic Pi + energy. In fact, ATP is the only molecule that is used by skeletal muscle to contract, and thus ATP is often referred to as the energy currency of skeletal muscle. In skeletal muscle, there is only enough ATP (5 mmol/kg of wet muscle) to sustain a maximal effort for several seconds. Thus the replenishment of ATP concentration within the cytoplasm of muscle is critical to sustaining skeletal muscle contraction and force production. To this point, while the use of ATP in resting skeletal muscle is quite low, during muscle contraction the use of ATP can increase by as much as two orders of magnitude and occurs with only a very minor decrease in ATP concentration. To meet the range of energy needs of skeletal muscle contraction and movement, there are three broad energy systems that replenish ATP: (1) the ATP-phosphocreatine (PCr) energy system, which is responsible for the "immediate" replenishment of ATP; (2) the glycolytic energy system, which provides "short-term" replenishment of ATP; and (3) the aerobic energy system, which provides "long-term" and sustained replenishment of ATP (Fig. 5.8). While there are examples of activities that specifically (and almost exclusively) use these energy systems (e.g., immediate: javelin throw, high jump; short-term: 200-m or 400-m sprint; long-term: marathon), most activities use a combination of these systems during an event. For example, in a soccer match, there is an underlying use of the

long-term system that is interspersed with contributions from the immediate and short-term systems.

### ATP-Phosphocreatine Energy System

In skeletal muscle, PCr is an important buffer for immediately replenishing ATP levels (by the rephosphorylation of ADP) through the actions of the enzyme, creatine kinase (also referred to as creatine phosphokinase or myokinase): PCr + ADP → ATP + Cr. Creatine kinase is located within the M line of the sarcomere and between the inner and outer membranes of the mitochondria, which gives it close proximity to ADP generated by contraction. Another important way to immediately generate ATP is through the actions of adenylate kinase (also known as myokinase, in muscle), which catalyzes the transfer of a phosphate group between two ADP molecules: ADP + ADP → ATP + adenosine monophosphate (AMP). Because a build-up of AMP can limit the ability to generate ATP through the adenylate kinase reaction, AMP is further metabolized to inosine monophosphate (IMP) by adenylate deaminase. Overall, these reactions are often referred to as anaerobic metabolism, as ATP is generated without oxygen.

### Glycolytic Energy System

In the glycolytic energy system, ATP is generated through the enzymatic breakdown of glucose to pyruvate: glucose + 2ADP + 2Pi → 2pyruvate + 2ATP. Thus the breakdown of one glucose molecule provides two ATP molecules. The glucose for glycolysis comes from two main sources: blood glucose (which primarily originates from the liver) and muscle glycogen, which is the storage form of glucose. At high to extreme exercise intensities, there is an increased reliance on ATP production from glycolysis, which occurs without the presence of oxygen and, as such, is also referred to as anaerobic glycolysis. Importantly, for the glycolytic energy system to continue to function during high effort exercise, the common coenzyme, nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+), is needed. This occurs by the conversion of pyruvate to lactate by

the enzyme, lactate dehydrogenase: pyruvate + NADH (nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide + hydrogen) → lactate + NAD+. The lactate generated by this reaction can be shuttled within muscle and between muscle and other tissues and serve as an important signaling molecule or be used as an energy source.' 47 For example, 47 the lactate generated by skeletal muscle can be transported to the liver through the blood and, in turn, converted back to glucose in a process referred to as the Cori cycle.

### Aerobic Energy System

Only a limited amount of ATP, over a limited period of time, can be generated by the immediate and short-term energy systems. The aerobic energy system, which refers to the generation of ATP through the use of oxygen, provides a sustained source of ATP for skeletal muscle. ATP from the aerobic energy system is generated in mitochondria, which are often referred to as the powerhouse of the cell, through the process of oxidative phosphorylation. Skeletal muscles are highly enriched in mitochondria, with type I (or slow) muscle fibers generally having the most mitochondria. Within the muscle, an intermyofibrillar subpopulation of mitochondria is a key source of ATP for contraction, with this subpopulation being dispersed throughout the contractile network.
