### Fatigue

Skeletal muscle fatigue can be defined as a reduced ability to maintain the desired force or power output during an activity. Generally, fatigue is experienced during higher-intensity exercise or heightened contractile activity, but it could apply in any setting. The underlying reason for contraction-related fatigue can be difficult to determine. This is because skeletal muscle fatigue can occur at any step of excitation—contraction coupling. For example, during extremely intense

exercise, fatigue arises at the level of NMJ fatigue, whereas during moderate-to-intense exercise, fatigue can result from a depletion of glycogen in the muscle. At the cellular level, a number of factors can contribute to muscle fatigue. During exercise that invokes a high production of lactate (or lactic acid), such as very intensive exercise, the H+ ions that are generated by lactate production and the subsequent drop in the intracellular pH can affect metabolic enzyme function (and, thus, ATP production), as well as cross-bridge cycling.

### Plasticity

The size, strength, and endurance of a muscle and its nervous system controllers are altered almost immediately after changes in use. The effects of these adaptive responses are relevant to many clinical situations and directly affect the long-term quality of life of the individual.

### Atrophy and Hypertrophy

Alterations in the magnitude of loading (e.g., immobilization or weightlifting) induce a series of stereotypic neuromuscular responses. For example, resistance exercise quickly (within days or weeks) improves the efficiency and synchrony of neuromuscular recruitment. Hence one can measure very acute increases in strength from a sedentary state. In the medium term, resistance exercise induces an anabolic response, which ultimately increases the size of existing fibers without inducing hyperplasia. This hypertrophy is driven primarily by increases in actin and myosin and associated proteins. However, intracellular components (e.g., mitochondria) are also increased. When activity is reduced (e.g., bed rest or immobilization), a catabolic response is initiated that reduces the size of existing fibers, which causes muscle weakness. Importantly, reduced activity in the presence of other systemic disease can result in a 3% to 5% loss of muscle protein content per week.49, This is a staggering figure that is difficult to recover from and is a key indicator for early physical activity interventions—even in the intensive care setting.

### Denervation

Denervation may be described as damage to a peripheral nerve, including through events such as a traumatic injury to a nerve, such that it is no longer capable of providing neural input to the muscle. Conversely, denervation also results in a lack of feedback from the muscle to the nervous system. Beyond the obvious inability of a muscle to contract following denervation, there are a number of downstream consequences. There is rapid and apparent disuse muscle atrophy, such as that described above. In addition, there is fragmentation of NMJ and, over time, the withdrawal of pre-synaptic neuronal termini and the dispersion of post-synaptic AChR, in a neuromuscular manifestation of "use it or lose it." A consequence of these changes, coupled with Wallerian degeneration that occurs in the distal stump of an injured nerve, is the progressively increasing barrier to reinnervation at the NMJ. Based on these events, typical guidelines for reinnervation after peripheral nerve injury are to perform nerve repairs within 3 to 6 months at the latest, with earlier repairs resulting in superior regenerative outcomes. An additional consequence of these events is the emergence of endplate maintenance after denervation as a major unmet clinical challenge. 52

### Fatigue Resistance

The resistance of skeletal muscle to fatigue, which is commonly referred to as endurance, is an important predictor of overall

functional capacity and performance. Similar to how skeletal muscle size is sensitive to use and disuse, the fatigability of skeletal muscle is highly pliable. Training, as defined by repeated bouts of contractile work over a period of time, is an excellent way to increase the endurance of skeletal muscle. In fact, the metabolic stress (as measured by changes in intracellular ADP, AMP, Pi, pH) in skeletal muscle to a controlled bout of exercise can be reduced by as little as 5 days of exercise training. In addition, exercise training results in other important adaptations in muscle, such as an increase in the density of capillaries in the muscle (which helps increase blood flow and oxygen and substrate delivery to the exercising muscle),54 an increase in the number of metabolic enzymes that metabolize fatty acids and glucose (including those in the TCA cycle and β-oxidation),55 and an increase in the number and size of mitochondria (which helps to meet ATP demand by utilizing the oxygen that is being delivered).55, Collectively, these changes reduce the fatigability of skeletal muscle. In contrast, a decrease in contractile activity (e.g., disuse through injury or sickness) will see a decrease in muscle endurance. In general, this reduction in endurance (at the level of skeletal muscle) is due, in part, to a decrease in the number and function of mitochondria and a decrease in metabolic enzymes and number of muscle capillaries. 57,58

### Aging

Generally speaking, skeletal muscle mass and function decreases with aging, with this process commonly referred to as sarcopenia. Because skeletal muscle mass and functional capacity are intimately linked to health and well-being, sarcopenia during aging is an important contributor to decreased quality of life; this is due, at least in part, to a reduced (or loss of) capacity to undertake everyday activities. Moreover, sarcopenia is associated with a greater risk of cardiometabolic disease, falls and/or fractures, and premature death. Importantly, maintaining an active lifestyle can help prevent the effects of age on skeletal muscle contractile function and, to some extent, muscle quality and mass. To this point, it was long thought that aging resulted in intrinsic changes in skeletal muscle that resulted in a reduced ability of the muscle to reduce force, separate from an overt decrease in muscle mass. However, a major issue when comparing aged and young individuals are differences in activity and sedentary time; this makes it difficult to determine whether the decrease in muscle contractile function with age is due to age itself or a secondary effect related to a decrease in overall activity and muscle use. Addressing this point, studies in individual muscle fibers from aged subjects that were very closely matched for activity and sedentary behavior to young subjects found that the ability of these muscle fibers to produce force and power was not different from their young counterparts. Thus the primary reason for the decrease in skeletal muscle force with age appears more related to an overall decrease in muscle mass (and the number of muscle fibers) than a loss of the ability of a given fiber to function. Relating to tissue plasticity, muscle responds robustly to training, even in nonagenarians,60 and is an excellent way to maintain or improve skeletal muscle health and functionality across the lifespan.

### Conclusion

Skeletal muscle is a classic example of a structure—function relationship in anatomy and physiology. The complex functional

capacity of muscle is largely dictated by the organizational structure of the muscle and nervous systems. Initiation of coordinated muscle contractions requires activation of motor control centers in the brain, coordinated and graded excitation of alpha motoneurons in the spinal cord, neuromuscular communication across the NMJ, Ca2+ release into the cytoplasm, and precise control of regulatory proteins and actin-myosin interactions at the level of the sarcomere. A robust set of biochemical reactions provides immediate, short-term, and long-term supplies of ATP to power this energy-intensive system of motors. Ultimately, the system yields exquisitely controlled and coordinated movements, or stability, and is highly plastic to changes in use patterns. Although the system is highly plastic and accommodating to an increase in use patterns (e.g., exercise), it is also susceptible to the reduced activity that is common with aging, disease, joint pain, and in compromised metabolic, hormonal, or nutritional conditions. Hence, the plasticity of skeletal muscle influences the clinical course of many diseases and, by extension, the quality of life of the individual.

# Biomechanics

### KEY POINTS

### Introduction

Biomechanics combines the field of engineering mechanics with the fields of biology and physiology. Biomechanics applies mechanical principles to the human body to understand the mechanical influences on bone and joint health. Forces that load the joints and tissues are generated by muscles and transmitted by tendons. Bones must withstand these forces and adapt to them. Developments in the field of biomechanics have improved our understanding of normal and pathologic gait, mechanics of neuromuscular control, and mechanics of growth and form. This knowledge contributed to the development of medical diagnostic and treatment procedures; it provided the basis for the design and manufacture of medical implants and orthotic devices and enhanced rehabilitation therapy practices. Biomechanics is also used to improve human performance in the workplace and in athletic competition.

Mechanics is a branch of physics that is concerned with the motion and deformation of bodies that are acted on by mechanical forces. Mechanics is one of the oldest physical sciences, dating back to Aristotle (384322 Bc), who conducted an organized analysis of animal movement. Leonardo da Vinci (14521519) investigated the mechanics of the human body; his detailed anatomic sketches represent the birth of anatomy as a discipline, and

of mechanics as the science governing human motion. Although da Vinci wrote extensively on body mechanics, the man generally credited to be the father of modern biomechanics is Giovanni Alphonso Borelli (16081679). His book De Motu Animalian provided a quantitative graphical solution to a musculoskeletal biomechanics problem (Fig. 6.1).

Engineering mechanics is the discipline devoted to the solution of mechanical problems through the integrated application of mathematical, scientific, and engineering principles. Engineering mechanics is an applied mechanics branch of the physical sciences. The broad field of applied mechanics can be further divided into three main parts: rigid body mechanics, deformable body mechanics, and fluid mechanics. In general, a material can be characterized as either a solid or a fluid. Solid materials can be considered to be rigid or deformable. A rigid body is one that cannot be deformed. In reality, every object undergoes deformation to some extent when acted upon by external forces. However, this is a definition of convenience that is used to simplify complex problems. For example, during the study of movement in gait analysis, the bones are considered to be rigid bodies compared with the soft tissues joining the bones. External loads applied to a rigid body result in internal loads, stresses, and deformations. The mechanics of deformable bodies deals with the relationships between externally applied loads and their internal effects, spanning the scale from cell to whole body. The mechanics of deformable bodies has strong ties with the field of materials science and are more complex compared with the analyses required in rigid body mechanics. The purpose of this chapter is to introduce the field of biomechanics. We focus on rigid body mechanics.

Basic biomechanics relies heavily on Newtonian mechanics. These laws were introduced by Sir Isaac Newton (16421727). The laws are:

1. Law of Inertia: A body in motion will stay in motion, and a body at rest will stay at rest, unless acted upon by a force.

2. Law of Acceleration: A force applied to a body will produce an acceleration of the body with a magnitude proportional to the force, in the direction of the force, and inversely proportional to the mass of the body. In other words, force equals mass multiplied by acceleration, or F = ma.

3. Law of Action and Reaction: For every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction.

These laws form the basis for analyses in statics and dynamics. Statics analyzes the forces that occur in rigid bodies that are in static equilibrium, that is, at rest (i.e., not moving) or moving with a constant velocity. Dynamics is the study of bodies in motion. The general field of dynamics consists of two major areas: kinematics and kinetics. Broadly speaking, kinematics is the study of motion,

and kinetics focuses on the forces that generate that motion. Knowledge of biomechanical principles can provide a fundamental understanding of the musculoskeletal system—both when the system is functioning well and when there is dysfunction.

### Kinematics

Kinematics is the study of motion without analyzing the forces causing the motion. Motion can be described as translation or rotation. In translation, all parts of the object move the same distance at the same time. This translation can be rectilinear (if the path is a straight line) or curvilinear (if the paths are curved lines). The direction of translation is typically described by the axis "along" which the object translates or the plane "in" which it translates. In rotation, all parts of the object rotate through the same angle and direction at the same time. The center of rotation (i.e., pivot point or axis) is the single point where there is no rotation of the object. Rotation is named by the axis "around" or "about" which it rotates or the plane "in" which it rotates. In the human body, most motion is a combination of translation and rotation, sometimes referred to as general motion.

Kinematic analysis is used to relate position, displacement, velocity, acceleration, and time. Kinematics can be analyzed in two-dimensional (2-D) or three-dimensional (3-D) space. When all points of a rigid body move parallel to a plane, the motion is referred to as planar motion, which can be thought of as 2-D motion. While true planar motion rarely happens in the human body, one often simplifies analyses as if movements are in two dimensions only. 3-D motion is the more general type of rigid body motion, where the body can move in all directions; that is, the body can translate along and rotate about the three axes, resulting in six degrees of freedom. Similar to how degrees of freedom are

defined in statistics, degrees of freedom are the number of independent coordinates required to completely specify the position (or motion) of an object.

Position is the location of a rigid body in space. As a rigid body in space has a maximum of six degrees of freedom, three translations (expressed by linear coordinates) and three rotations (expressed by angular coordinates) are necessary to fully characterize its position. They are defined relative to a specified origin or reference frame. Similar to indicating north on a compass, the reference frame is essential to establish a common orientation. Typically, this is done by denoting the positive directions of mutually perpendicular coordinate axes (e.g., x, y, and z), and denoting counterclockwise rotation as positive. For the human body, we can think of these in terms of three planes (sagittal, frontal, and transverse) and axes perpendicular to those planes (medial/lateral, anterior/posterior, and vertical).

Displacement is the change in position without regard to the time it takes to make that change. The general movement of an object is defined by a vector quantity that is a combination of both the linear and the angular displacement. For many joints in the human body, we simplify this to reflect only the angular displacement and describe the motion with terms such as flexion/extension, adduction/abduction, and internal/external rotation.

Velocity is the change of position (i.e., the displacement) with respect to time. Linear velocity is expressed in units of length per time (e.g., m/sec). Angular velocity is expressed in units of angular measure per time (e.g., radians/sec or degrees/sec). Because velocities reflect vector quantities, both magnitude and direction must be specified. This is in contrast to speed, which is a scalar quantity, and is the distance covered by the object per time without regard for direction.

Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity with respect to time. Linear acceleration is expressed in units of length per time squared (e.g., m/sec2). Angular acceleration is expressed in units of angular measure per time squared (e.g., radians/sec2 or degrees/ sec2). Similar to velocity, accelerations are also vector quantities, and both magnitude and direction must be specified.

Jerk is the rate of change in acceleration with respect to time, and thus has been used as a measure of smoothness of a movement. Linear jerk is expressed in units of length per time cubed (e.g., m/sec3). Angular jerk is expressed in units of angular measure per time cubed (e.g., radians/sec3 or degrees/sec3). Jerk quantifies the rate at which acceleration changes; acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, which is the rate of change of position. Thus initiating a movement to change position requires changes in velocity, acceleration, and jerk.

In addition to the above kinematic measures, there are common spatiotemporal parameters recorded during tasks such as walking. These measures capture either distance or time, and sometimes are converted to percentages. For example, step length is the distance between the heel of one foot when it contacts the ground and the heel of the contralateral foot when it contacts the ground; stride length is the distance between where one foot contacts the ground and where the same (ipsilateral) foot contacts the ground again. As such, one stride contains two steps and is considered a complete gait cycle. Step time and stride time would refer to the duration of time for each of these. Similarly, the time (and percentage of a gait cycle) spent with both feet on the ground is double limb support, and the time with only one foot on the ground is single limb support. Alterations in these parameters, either within an individual side-to-side or over time, or between individuals, can suggest impairments in function.

Kinematic techniques have been used to study movements in both 2-D and 3-D space. Independent of the technology used to capture the movement, the human body is typically modeled as a number of interconnected rigid body segments (Fig. 6.2). Each rigid body segment has a coordinate system defined for it to establish an anatomic coordinate system. Segment position is typically defined by the orientation of the segment coordinate system relative to a global (or lab) coordinate system that is external to the body. For example, the position and motion of the pelvis is often described without reference to the body segments above or below. This is in contrast to joint position and motion, which is typically described as the relative motion of the distal body segment with respect to the proximal body segment. For example, knee motion is described as the motion of the shank relative to the thigh, and hip motion is the motion of the thigh relative to the pelvis. While each body segment has six degrees of freedom, most joints are assumed to undergo primarily angular displacement (i.e., rotation) during human movement. However, more complex analyses may also quantify the linear displacement (i.e., translation) that limb segments or joints may undergo.

These measures of segment and joint angles have been used extensively to describe human walking and other activities of daily living.4-8 For example, during walking, knee motion primarily occurs in the sagittal plane about a mediolateral axis and can be characterized throughout the gait cycle (Fig. 6.3). At initial contact, the knee is near full extension (in about five degrees of knee flexion). As the limb is loaded, the knee flexes to about 15 degrees and then moves back into extension by the middle of stance. At 50% of the gait cycle, the contralateral (i.e., opposite) foot contacts the ground. As the weight is shifted to the opposite limb, the knee begins to flex again. The foot leaves the ground around 60%

of the gait cycle, ending the stance phase. During the swing phase, the knee continues to flex, with peak knee flexion occurring during the early portion of the swing phase. The knee then returns to near full extension before initial contact, and the cycle repeats. Thus the knee has two phases of flexion and extension motion, one during stance and one during swing. Each starts with the knee in relative extension, progresses into flexion, and then returns to extension. The first flexion phase, or stance phase knee flexion, acts as a shock absorber to aid weight acceptance. This curve peaks in early stance when the opposite foot leaves the ground.

The mechanical source for this shock absorber is the eccentrically contracting quadriceps muscles; that is, the quadriceps muscles are resisting the knee flexion. The second flexion phase is necessary for the foot to clear the ground in the early swing phase. The knee rapidly flexes beginning just after the heel comes off the ground to a maximum in the swing phase as the swinging foot passes the opposite (stance) limb. While the motion at the knee during gait primarily occurs in the sagittal plane, other joints may exhibit motion in multiple planes.

The complexity of kinematic analysis increases substantially when one moves from simplified planar analysis to 3-D analysis. While 3-D joint movement is described as motion of the distal segment relative to the proximal segment, in the same way it is done for 2-D, the sequence of rotations is extremely important and must be specified for a unique description of 3-D joint motion. For the exact same rotations, different final orientations will result from different sequences of rotation (Fig. 6.4). Investigators in orthopedic biomechanics have adopted the concept of Euler angles to unify the definition of finite spatial rotation. In this definition, one axis is fixed to the proximal segment (e.g., knee flexion-extension is defined about an axis through the medial and lateral femoral epicondyles), and one axis is fixed to the distal segment (e.g., internal/external rotation of the knee is defined about the long axis of the tibia) (Fig. 6.5). The final "floating axis" is defined as orthogonal to the other two axes (e.g., knee abduction/ adduction is defined about an axis that is at a 90-degree angle relative both to the flexion/extension axis and to the internal/external rotation axis). Using a specified sequence of rotations allows for the joint motion to be related to anatomic structures.

Human movement is often measured within a motion-capture laboratory using an optical motion capture system. The specific technology differs between systems but, generally, cameras around the room record the position of markers placed in pre-specified locations on the individual (Fig. 6.2). These markers may be passive (meaning that they reflect light back to the cameras) or active

(meaning that the marker is the light source). Markers are typically placed over specific bony landmarks to help define joint locations and axes. Markers are also placed at other locations on the segment to track its location in space. Initially, a marker at the end of a wand was used5 but, more recently, multiple markers either directly on the skin or as a rigid cluster are used to track segment position.

While the accuracy of the camera systems can be quite good, the ability of markers placed on a wand, or even directly on the skin, to accurately reflect the movement of the bones underlying the skin and soft tissue is less well accepted or standardized. Skin-motion artifact is a well-documented challenge, and one

that substantially affects the quality of the data in situations of increased adiposity. Markers used to define axes of rotation can be difficult to place accurately and reliably for some joints such as the hip. Thus movements can be used instead of markers to infer joint axes. This is commonly referred to as a "functional joint." Regression equations have also been used to predict joint locations. The joint locations predicted by equations are affected not only by the position of the markers but also by variation in anatomy between individuals. Inaccurate definitions of joint axes can lead to "kinematic crosstalk," where motion in one plane is interpreted as if it were in another plane. Additionally, transverse plane motion of the extremities (e.g., internal [medial] and external [lateral] rotation) is less accurate than sagittal and frontal plane motion. This is, in part, due to the shorter distance between the axis of rotation and the marker on the segment. The challenge of detecting rotation from markers near the axis of rotation is one argument for continuing to use markers placed on a wand. Although transverse plane motion is often of interest for clinical questions, it is frequently omitted from analysis due to this challenge.

A complete analysis of total joint movement (i.e., capturing all six degrees of freedom) is less common. Data for these analyses has been obtained using markers embedded in the bone.13, These data can be obtained using imaging techniques such as dual fluoroscopic imaging.15-17 This general unconstrained movement in 3-D space requires the specification of three translations and three rotations to fully describe joint motion (e.g., at the knee: lateral tibial translation, anterior tibial translation, knee joint distraction, flexion, adduction, and external rotation) and can also be represented by a helical (screw) axis.18,

Newer technologies provide alternative methods for measuring spatiotemporal gait parameters and kinematics. "Markerless" motion capture utilizes standard or high-speed video cameras to record motion without the need for markers placed by experienced personnel. These videos are often processed using software that employs deep learning, a type of machine learning that does not require human input to select important features from the data. Deep learning algorithms estimate the pose (body segment positions) in each frame of video data, from which joint angles can be calculated. The quality of data from both markered (optical) and markerless motion-capture systems is dependent on factors such as the number of cameras and their resolution. Compared with markered motion capture, markerless motion capture removes user error related to marker placement and improves data collection speed. However, the software is crucially important for the quality of the processed data and requires greater computing resources to run. Data quality can be affected by the number of key points identified per body segment and the quality of the training data used to develop the software, as well as the match between the training data and the new data (e.g., similar movements, participant/patient demographics, etc.). The use of software, rather than markers placed by individuals, to identify key points on body segments also means that raw video data can be reprocessed following any future software updates to improve data quality. Thus understanding the limitations of software versions is important in making comparisons with this type of data.

Wearable technology (e.g., accelerometers, gyroscopes, magnetometers, inertial measurement units attached to the body) has also been explored as a method for measuring kinematics due to its ease of use and potential to be used both in and outside of a laboratory or clinical environment.21-23 These small sensors are typically attached to one or more body segments to measure segment acceleration, angular velocity, and/or other parameters.

Multiple sensors placed on different body segments typically produce the most accurate estimation of joint kinematics; however, single sensors can also be used to capture clinically relevant parameters, such as varus thrust. Each type of sensor comes with its own limitations. For example, gyroscopes measure angular velocity well but can experience problems with signal drift over time. Data quality can also be affected by surrounding equipment; magnetometers, for example, can be affected by nearby ferromagnetic objects. These limitations can sometimes be mitigated by combining different types of sensors; however, this technology is rapidly changing, and users should be aware of the capabilities and limitations of the specific technologies they are working with. Combining wearable technologies with electronic health records, mobile health applications, and so on (called digital bealth) has been suggested as a way to improve health care delivery in rheumatology.

### Kinetics

Kinetics is the study of the forces that cause motion of an object. A force is a push or a pull on an object. Forces are vectors: they have magnitude and direction. The magnitude represents how strong the force is and is commonly expressed in Newtons or pounds. The direction of the vector can be resolved into the individual components, usually along specified, mutually perpendicular coordinate axes. Conversely, force components can be summed using vector addition to obtain the resultant force, which is the overall total or net force.

Forces have a point of application: the location along the body at which the force is applied. Forces can be contact forces (as when bodies touch each other) or field forces (as when bodies are separated by a distance, such as gravitational, electric, or magnetic forces).

Forces can generally be classified as being external or internal. External forces are those produced outside the body; this includes actions of objects contacting the body, gravitation force, and forces due to inertia of the body. Internal forces are those produced within the body and include muscle, capsulo-ligamentous structures, and joint contact forces.

When a force is applied at some distance from the axis of rotation, the force has a rotational effect called a moment. A moment represents the turning or twisting effect of a force and, mathematically, is defined as the cross product of the force vector and the distance vector to the axis of rotation. Moments are commonly expressed in Newton-meters (Nm) or foot pounds (ft-lb). Like a force, a moment is also a vector, and thus has both magnitude and direction. The magnitude of the moment is equal to the force multiplied by the perpendicular (or shortest) distance between the line of action of the force and the axis of rotation (Fig. 6.6). The direction of the moment is about the axis of rotation (or potential rotation) and, thus, perpendicular to the plane in which the rotating force is applied. Two different terms are commonly used to describe the distance between the force and the axis of rotation. Although inconsistent in the literature, moment arm is often used to describe the perpendicular (or shortest) distance from the force action line to the actual or potential pivot point of the system, as used above to calculate the moment. Lever arm is used to describe the distance along the lever (i.e., rigid segment) between the force action line and the actual or potential pivot point of the system. When the force is perpendicular to the segment, the moment arm and lever arm will be equivalent; otherwise, the moment arm will be shorter than the lever arm.

When evaluating the rotational capacity of a muscle, a change in a segment's position can change the moment arm of a force. A change in the segment's shape (e.g., osteotomy) or location of muscle insertion (e.g., tendon transfer) would change the lever arm in all positions and the moment arm for a given position.

While the terms "moment" and "torque" are often used interchangeably, a distinction is sometimes made to specify torque as a type of moment that results when a pair of forces acting on a body are equal in magnitude, have parallel lines of action, and act in opposite directions (Fig. 6.7). This is sometimes referred to as a force couple. The magnitude of the torque is the force multiplied by the distance—in this case, the distance is the perpendicular distance between the lines of action of the two forces. The resultant force on the body is zero because the two forces are equal and oppose each other; however, they create an axis of rotation between them.

When applying these terms to human movement, multiple simplifications are made for the ease of analysis and interpretation. The bones are modeled as rigid bodies that do not deform under load. Joints are often modeled as hinges. Unlike a true mechanical hinge, the axis of rotation may not be a single fixed point; instead, it may change throughout the movement and may also be impacted by pathology. The joint is assumed to be frictionless; this too can be affected by pathology (e.g., osteoarthritis [OA]). The

muscles are thought of as force vectors applied where the muscle attaches to the bone. These muscle forces can produce a moment (i.e., rotation) because a constraining force is applied at the joint to create the axis of rotation. This constraining force, also referred to as the joint contact force, is provided by both passive and active structures (e.g., the articular surface, capsulo-ligamentous structures, and muscles) and is in response to all other forces acting on the system. As most muscles insert close to the joint, the moment arm for a muscle is often quite small relative to the moment arm for an external force acting farther from the axis of rotation (e.g., biceps tendon insertion near the elbow vs. weight held in the hand). This smaller mechanical advantage of the internal (muscle) force relative to the external force necessitates large muscle and tendon forces, and subsequently large forces at the joint when performing any activity. For example, during natural walking, the total force at the hip (including the force generated by the surrounding muscles) has been measured at four times the body weight. If not considering the force on the joint exerted by the muscles, this joint force would be much lower. While the terminology, again, is inconsistent, with terms including "joint reaction force," "joint bone-to-bone force," and "joint contact force," the important distinction is whether the force includes the contribution from muscles and ligaments crossing the joint30 or if it simply reflects the forces from the adjacent segment (i.e., intersegmental force). Although the intersegmental force is important for calculations, the forces that the joint experiences, here referred to as joint contact force, are often of more interest for the clinician.

Just as forces can be classified as external or internal, so can moments. External forces create external moments; internal forces create internal moments, which are also called muscle moments. When interpreting data and the literature, it is critical to understand this distinction. For example, the external knee adduction moment implicated in the progression of knee OA31,32 is an external moment generated by the ground reaction force (GRF) passing medial to the knee axis of rotation. If the external moment were the only one acting on the knee, the distal tibia would rotate inward, creating knee adduction. However, in response to the external knee adduction moment, the knee generates an internal abduction moment to oppose the external knee adduction moment.

### Statics

Statics is the study of forces acting on a body at rest; that is, a body that is not accelerating. When performing a force analysis, the body or part of a body at equilibrium may be isolated from

the environment. The environment is then replaced by forces acting on the system, resulting in what is called a free-body diagram. For the body to be at rest (i.e., acceleration equal to zero), both the forces and the moments acting on the body must sum to zero in each of the three orthogonal (i.e., perpendicular) directions of the chosen reference system. Specifically, based on Newton's First Law:

∑F = 0 ∑M = 0

where ∑F is the sum of forces in each of three orthogonal directions and ΣM is the sum of moments about each of the three orthogonal axes.

For example, consider a person standing quietly (Fig. 6.8). The person's weight (force of gravity) tends to pull the person toward the ground (Fig. 6.8A). The person does not move downward through the ground, however, because the ground is also pushing up on the person with a total force equal in magnitude (and opposite in direction) to the individual's weight (Newton's Third Law). If the person has their weight distributed symmetrically, then their weight is evenly shared by each lower extremity (Fig. 6.8A). The load under each foot can be represented by resultant GRF vectors,

with one-half of the body weight supported by each foot. The base of support is the area between the feet, including the contact area under the feet. With one-half of body weight supported by each foot, the point of application of the resultant GRF passes approximately midway between the individual's two feet (Fig. 6.8B). No motion occurs because the external forces (i.e., body weight and the GRF) are balanced—they are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction. When the person leans to one side (Fig. 6.8C), the GRF location shifts in the direction that the person leans, which maintains this balance of forces. Thus overall body posture can affect the GRF location. If the person were to pick up one foot, they would become unstable; that is, the downward body weight vector would no longer be over the base of support, which now is only the single foot on the ground, but instead would be medial to it. To remain in static equilibrium, the individual would need to shift their body weight over the stance foot (Fig. 6.8D).

This example also highlights the force needed from the hip abductors to maintain a level pelvis in single limb stance (Fig. 6.9). The GRF passes medial to the hip joint axis of rotation, creating an external hip adduction moment. To maintain static equilibrium, the hip abductor muscles generate an internal moment that is equal in magnitude and opposite in direction; that is, the hip muscles must generate a hip abduction moment. If the muscles

### B: NEGATIVE

do not generate an adequate moment to counterbalance the external adduction moment, the pelvis will rotate such that the side farthest from the stance leg will be lower than the side closest to the stance leg. Most commonly, this is called contralateral pelvic drop, or simply pelvic drop, and is the motion noted during Trendelenburg gait. If the hip abductor muscles generate an internal moment equal to the external moment, the individual remains in static equilibrium with the pelvis level.

The hip abductor muscle force necessary to generate this moment is dependent on the moment arm for the muscles. The smaller the muscle moment arm, the larger the force needed to generate the same moment. For example, in a hip with coxa valga, the moment arm for the hip abductors is often smaller than in one with coxa vara; thus the hip abductors will need more force to generate the same moment (Fig. 6.10). As much of the force experienced by the hip joint is due to muscle force, a hip with coxa valga will likely experience a higher joint contact force than a hip with coxa vara.

Taking this one step further, coxa valga commonly co-occurs with acetabular dysplasia, which is reduced coverage from the acetabulum over the femoral head. The reduced coverage decreases the area of the acetabulum in contact with the femoral head. As stress is force divided by contact area, a hip with coxa valga and acetabular dysplasia could experience increased stress because of the increased muscle force needed to generate

the internal moment and the reduced contact area over which that force is dispersed. To reduce this stress, individuals may lean their trunk toward the stance leg farther than typical. During gait, this is sometimes referred to as compensated Trendelenburg. This lateral trunk motion moves the center of mass closer to the hip joint axis, reducing the external moment arm and thereby the external moment. The internal moment that the hip needs to generate is now smaller, and therefore the muscle force is smaller. This modification reduces the joint contact force and thereby joint stress.

### Dynamics

Dynamics is the study of forces accelerating a body. This occurs when unbalanced forces or moments are acting on a rigid body; the body is under a nonequilibrium, or dynamic, condition, resulting in motion. Based on Newton's Second Law, the acceleration of the body will be proportional to the ratio between the force and the mass. Whereas the sum of forces and of moments was equal to zero in the static condition, these are now equal to the mass multiplied by acceleration for forces and the moment of inertia multiplied by the angular acceleration for moments. Specifically, based on Newton's Second Law:

∑F = ma

∑M = Iα

where ∑F is the sum of forces in each of three orthogonal directions, ΣM is the sum of moments about each of the three orthogonal axes, m is the mass of the body, a is the linear acceleration of the body, I is the moment of inertia of the body, and α is the angular acceleration of the body. Newton's Second Law makes it possible to calculate the forces acting on the musculoskeletal system from measurements of segment motion and mass. During normal ambulation, vertical and medial GRF components balance the body weight and lateral inertial force. Using a process called inverse dynamics, the joint forces and moments at the proximal joint of each segment can be calculated using the segment mass and inertial properties, segment motion, and either GRF (for the most distal segment, often the foot or forefoot) or joint forces and moments at the distal segment (for all other segments) (Fig. 6.11). To conceptualize how the GRF results in knee joint loading, we can observe that the vertical GRF component generally passes lateral to the body's center of mass during gait (Fig. 6.12A). The resultant GRF (combined medial and vertical) passes medial to the knee joint center, creating an external knee adduction moment and resulting in a load imbalance in the medial and

lateral compartments of the knee; the medial compartment carries more load than the lateral compartment (Fig. 6.12B). The higher load in the medial side may contribute to the higher degree of OA, which typically develops in the medial compartment. Medial tibiofemoral OA is the most common form of OA, and it is apparent that knee OA is, at least partially, mechanically driven. Research scientists have implicated the external knee adduction moment in the progression of radiographic OA31,32; they identify this measure as a marker of disease severity. 33,34

### Joint Mechanics

Diarthrodial joints connect long bones to allow force transmission and joint rotation. The type of joint articulating motion depends on the shape of the joint surfaces. For example, the hip is modeled as a ball-and-socket joint, the elbow as a hinge joint, the knee and proximal interphalangeal joint as bicondylar joints, and the carpometacarpal joint of the thumb as a saddle joint. In general, the joint articulating motion can be described in terms of spinning, rolling, and sliding or gliding (Fig. 6.13). This relative motion between the articular surfaces is often referred to as artbrokinematics, whereas the physiologic motion observed (e.g., flexion/extension) is referred to as osteokinematics. Spinning and sliding/gliding motions involve the relative translation of one articulating surface against the other. Rolling has the least relative motion between articulating surfaces.

There are general expectations for the interaction between arthrokinematic motion and the osteokinematic motion. For example, at the hip, where the convex femoral head articulates with the concave acetabulum, the osteokinematic motion of hip flexion would typically be accompanied by the arthrokinematic motion of the femoral head rolling anteriorly and gliding

posteriorly on the acetabulum to maintain a stationary axis of rotation within the acetabulum. However, these arthrokinematic movements are not automatic; instead, they need to be facilitated by forces from active and passive tissues including muscles and joint structures. Alterations in arthrokinematics can lead to less precise movement, altered axes of rotation, and potentially joint injury.

Although diarthrodial joints experience a substantial amount of loading and motion, the cartilage surfaces typically undergo little or no damage during normal conditions because of the special lubrication qualities of synovial fluid and the biphasic structure of the cartilage. Synovial fluid, which is secreted by the synovium into the joint space, contains mainly hyaluronate. Biomechanically, hyaluronate is a highly viscous liquid, with the shear stress depending on the rate of shear strain applied. As the shear rate increases, the viscosity of synovial fluid decreases. However, this system may be diminished in the presence of pathology. For example, in rheumatoid arthritis, because of enzymatic degradation of the hyaluronate molecules, the viscosity of the rheumatoid synovial fluid does not have a normal shear rate dependency and is believed to be less effective in lubrication.

### Joint Constraint and Stability

All joints, in theory, have six degrees of freedom; that is, they can translate along and rotate about three independent axes. The actual amount of motion available for each of those degrees of freedom depends on the anatomic structures of the particular joint. As form follows function, it could also be said that the mobility and stability of a joint depends on how it is used. A common example is the difference between the shoulder joint (specifically the glenohumeral joint) and the hip joint. Both are

ball-and-socket joints, but the shoulder has far more mobility to move the arm around in space while the hip is far more stable to support the weight and motion of the body during functional tasks such as walking.

Because of the variations in anatomic structures of the joints, various limbs have different movement characteristics and load transmissions. Adequate joint stability that balances motion and loads is necessary for a joint to function properly. Chronic disease or traumatic injury may cause damage to joint tissue, thus compromising the constraints and stability of the joint. To improve the diagnosis and treatment of such joint disorders, it is essential to understand the basic joint constraint mechanics that provide stability. The anatomic structures responsible for joint constraint can be divided into passive and active elements. Passive elements, consisting of the capsulo-ligamentous structures and bony articulating surfaces, provide static constraints of the joint. The active elements include muscle-tendon units, which provide dynamic constraints of the joint.

The contribution of capsulo-ligamentous structures to joint stability and constraint are determined by the change in length, the line of action, and the tissue material properties (Fig. 6.14). For a given loading and displacement of the joint, the greater the elongation of the soft tissue (i.e., stretch), the higher the passive tension generated by that tissue. Intra-articular joint effusion can also stretch the capsulo-ligamentous structures, increasing

the passive tension in the tissue. The specific contribution of such passive tension to joint constraint further depends on the relative line of action of the capsulo-ligament structures. Therefore the relative locations of the origins and insertions of the ligaments in any given joint position may determine the contribution of the ligamentous tension in resisting joint displacement in three orthogonal directions. Surgical alterations of the soft tissue attachment to the bone would therefore change the joint constraints.

Lengthening and shortening of the capsulo-ligament structures during joint loading and movement determine the tissue deformation. The tissue material properties, along with the amount of deformation, will determine the structure passive tension. For the same amount of deformation, the stiffer the tissue is, the higher the tension will be; likewise, the more compliant the tissue is, the lower the tension will be. Alterations of the material properties due to physiologic and pathologic conditions definitely alter the joint constraint and the articulation. For example, the tight posterior capsule of a baseball pitcher limits the range of physiologic motion. On the other hand, the relaxation of capsulo-ligamentous structures during pregnancy and in people with rheumatologic diseases could potentially lead to abnormal motion and contact stress on the joint surface. These alterations of soft tissue material properties must be considered as potentially critical factors in initiating early joint cartilage

degeneration and may lead to the vicious cycle that perpetuates arthritis.

Experimentally, researchers have assessed the significance of various passive anatomic structures to joint stability by using two methods: the stiffness test and the laxity test. Stiffness, in the most general sense, is resistance to deformation. The stiffness test is commonly used to determine the relative contributions of individual anatomic elements to joint constraint. The laxity test demonstrates the outcome of joint instability when one or more constraining units are compromised. In the stiffness test, the joint is displaced under controlled testing conditions and the corresponding load is monitored. Based on the joint load-displacement curves, it is obvious that the load required to displace the joint is higher when all the ligaments are intact than when a ligament is lacerated. The difference in the constraining load between these two curves at the same joint displacement represents the contribution of that particular sectioned ligament to the joint constraint. Because the capsulo-ligamentous structures are passive tissues, as long as the joint displacement is controlled and experimentally reproduced, the relative contributions of individual tissues will not be dependent on the order in which the soft tissue is removed. Contrary to the stiffness test, during which displacement is varied and load is measured, in the laxity test a specific load is applied to the joint and the extent of joint displacement is measured. Joint laxity is documented with changes in displacement as anatomic elements are removed. The joint laxity as observed and measured provides more of a clinical scenario of the joint instability experienced by a patient who has sustained a similar soft tissue injury; however, it fails to capture the role of muscle in providing additional stability.

In addition to soft tissue constraints, the joint articulating surface is an element that provides joint constraint and stability. Theoretically, its significance to joint stability is determined by both the geometric shapes of the joint surfaces and the amount of compressive force encountered between those two surfaces (Fig. 6.15A). When two curved surfaces articulate, a vertically applied force will induce either a transverse displacement or a transverse constraining force. The greater the congruency between the curved articulating surfaces, the greater the induced horizontal joint constraint force. This mechanism is sometimes referred to as concavity-compression. In the shoulder joint, for example, the relative translations between the glenoid and humeral head and the forces resisting translation were recorded. The stability ratio, defined as the peak translational force divided by the applied compressive force, was higher in the hanging-arm position than in glenohumeral abduction (Fig. 6.15A). The highest stability ratio was detected in the inferior and superior directions, and the anterior direction was associated with

the lowest stability ratio. Resection of the glenoid labrum resulted in an average decrease in the stability ratio of 10%. In the treatment of traumatic recurrent anterior shoulder instability, patients with a large osseous glenoid defect are at risk for recurrent instability after arthroscopic Bankart repair. Bone grafting performed in shoulders with a large osseous glenoid defect to restore the articulating surface provides excellent clinical outcomes.

To benefit from the concavity-compression joint constraint, a compressive or oppositional force across the joint surface is required. This joint compressive force is usually generated by muscle contraction. The relative location and direction of the resultant joint force to the available articulating surfaces will determine the

potential stability of the joint. For example, in the glenohumeral joint, if the resultant force is well located at the center of the glenoid articulating surface, the joint is considered stable. When the resultant force is directed outside the available joint surfaces, joint dislocation is most likely. However, when the resultant force is located within the joint surfaces but more toward the rim of the glenoid surface, the potential exists for joint subluxation. The interaction of muscle force resulting in a resultant joint constraint force is illustrated later.

Intra-articular or intracapsular pressure is the other component of passive and static joint constraint (Fig. 6.16). The joint is usually surrounded by a capsule and sealed with synovial tissue. When the capsule is intact, any distraction force stretches and deforms the capsulo-ligamentous structure and will generate negative intra-articular pressure. This negative intra-articular pressure will counteract further displacement. When the joint capsule is compromised, either by deterioration, injury, or surgery, such negative pressure can no longer develop and cannot constrain the joint. Negative intracapsular pressure is, therefore, a constraint of

all joints and is especially important for joints under gravitational distraction such as the shoulder joint.

Active muscle contraction is also important for joint stability. Proper coordination of muscle contraction provides dynamic joint constraint. On the other hand, deficiency of muscle innervation or a tendon defect can result in unfavorable joint constraint and lead to joint instability. Importantly, muscle force can act as either a joint stabilizer or a joint dislocator. The contribution of muscles to joint constraint is similar to that of passive capsulo-ligamentous tension. It is determined by the line of action of the passive and active tension of the muscle. Based on the relative position of the bony structure and the direction of the joint displacement, the same muscle-tendon structure can contribute differently to joint constraint. When the joint is spanned by multiple muscles, the coordination of muscle contraction will ultimately determine the dynamic joint stability. For example, the contributions of muscle contractions to the articulating surfaces of the shoulder can be described in terms of the normal and shear directions (Fig. 6.17). The shear component has direct

influence on the transverse translation of the bony element at the joint. In contrast, the normal force component of the muscle provides the compressive force to bring the surfaces together. A glenohumeral joint with a lax capsule and loose ligaments might be dynamically stabilized if the glenoid concavity is maintained and the functions of the external and internal rotators, which are efficient stabilizers, are enhanced. On the other hand, in a patient with a rotator cuff tear, the pull of the major movers, such as deltoids during arm elevation or forward rotation, will result in a resultant joint force in the superior and anterior directions; this could result in superior impingement or anterior instability.

In general, muscle contraction will generate moments about all three axes of rotation for a given joint. However, when the constraints from other periarticular soft tissues are not available, the muscle will also be responsible for maintaining stability during the joint's rotation. If a muscle crosses multiple joints, the effect of muscle activation depends on the moment arms of all the joints it spans. The concept of biarticular muscle is of clinical importance. For example, when considering rehabilitation after reconstructive surgery of the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL), the goal is to strengthen the muscles without excessive tension being placed on the ligament. Quadriceps loading, especially with the knee in a near extended position, would result in an anterior joint shear force and anterior displacement of the tibia with respect to the femur. It has been suggested that this shear force would induce tension in the ACL, driving investigators to recommend closed kinetic-chain exercises. During closed kinetic-chain exercises, such as the squat and the leg press, the foot is fixed and knee motion is accompanied by motion at the hip and ankle joints. The GRF causes external flexion moments at both the knee and hip joints. The antagonistic muscle action of hamstrings at the knee joint is recruited to balance the hip flexion moment. Cocontraction of quadriceps and hamstrings at the knee joint reduces the anterior joint shear force and the tension in the ACL37 but can increase the compressive load as well. More recently, the avoidance of open kinetic-chain exercises following ACL reconstruction has been called into question, with ACL strain during walking being higher than during open kinetic-chain exercises. 38-40

### Mechanical Loading on Tendon

Tendons transmit muscle contraction force to bone to cause movement. The force transmitted is primarily tensile force. Tendons are composed primarily of water along with collagen, elastin, and proteoglycans. At rest, the collagen fibers have a crimped appearance, and initial loading on the tendon straightens the crimped collagen fibrils. As further load is applied, the straightened fibers are lengthened. This lengthening requires greater load than the straightening phase, thus tendons are considered to be "nonlinearly elastic." Specific portions of tendons also experience compression and shear force. Compression can occur when the tendon path is altered around a bony structure. As a tendon is subjected to compression in a specific area, the mechanical loading does not distribute evenly within the tendon, which can result in shear force inside the tendon. The contact surfaces of the tendon can also experience shear force as the tendon glides against surrounding tissues.

Loading on the tendon has been measured through both direct and noninvasive methods. Direct measurement of tendon

loading can be achieved using implanted sensors, such as strain gauges. While this approach provides a direct measurement of loading, it is not designed for long-term use and has limited clinical utility due to the need for surgical implantation. Radiographic measurement of implanted tantalum beads (e.g., through plain radiography, dual-plane fluoroscopy, or computed tomography scanning) has also been used to measure mechanical properties of tendon in vivo. Shear wave elastography,43,44 a a technique that uses ultrasound, can be used to measure the elasticity of tendon through noninvasive means. Shear wave tensiometry45 is another method to estimate tendon loading noninvasively. It uses accelerometers and a small "tapping device" to measure wave propagation along the tendon and has been shown to be reliable during different isometric contractions. Tendon length measurements 47 are also of interest as they are used in musculoskeletal models to help define moment arm lengths. Tendons respond differently to active versus passive loading. In a rehabilitation context, this could apply to active versus passive treatments, where the patient actively moves the knee through muscle contraction, putting load on the patellar tendon versus manual manipulation, where a physical therapist moves the knee through a specific range of motion, resulting in different load on the tendon despite similar joint angles. Some of these measurement methods may be more suited to capture active or passive loading and thus should be chosen accordingly to suit the situation at hand.

The three modes of mechanical loading (namely, tension, compression, and shear/gliding) can be demonstrated by three scenarios at the shoulder joint (Fig. 6.18). The short head of the biceps brachii tendon is an example of the first scenario, in which the tendon mainly experiences tension alone. The second scenario, in which the tendon encounters tension and compression together, occurs internally at the bone insertion site of the supraspinatus tendon. The insertional area of the tendon encounters tensile force and compression resulting from the transverse contact of the tendon with the attached bone. The third scenario occurs when the tendon is simultaneously subjected to tension, compression, and gliding. The long head of the biceps brachii tendon, where it passes through the bicipital groove, demonstrates an example of the third scenario. The supraspinatus tendon also fits the scenario and the second scenario. Subacromial impingement of the supraspinatus tendon generates high compressive stress that varies along the supraspinatus tendon, depending on humeroscapular elevation. The mode of mechanical tendon loading is potentially correlated to the incidence of tendon degeneration. The tendons in the first scenario rarely experience degenerative tendinopathy. Tendons commonly affected with tendinopathy are represented in the other two scenarios, in which the affected areas normally sustain compression and shear force with or without gliding in addition to tensile force.

### Mechanical Loading on Bursae

Bursae are fluid-filled sacs that act to reduce friction between bone and surrounding soft tissues (e.g., muscles, tendon, skin). Loading applied to the bursae is primarily compressive and/or shear force. Compression occurs when surrounding tissues press on the bursae and shear occurs when surrounding tissues slide past the bursae. Inflammation of a bursa (i.e., bursitis) can cause increased fluid within the bursa and thus increased pressure in the bursa, which can limit joint motion. Chronic bursitis can cause further swelling

and thickening of the bursa, sometimes without associated further increases in pain. While bursitis can be crystal induced (e.g., gouty bursitis, tophaceous gout) or induced by inflammatory arthritis (e.g., rheumatoid arthritis, spondyloarthritis), it can also be caused by prolonged loading or overuse.

Limited measurement of loading on bursae exists in the literature; however, retrocalcaneal bursa pressure has been measured with the use of a commercially available blood pressure measurement system.48, Despite the lack of bursae loading measurements, a general understanding of loading on the bursae is important in clinical applications such as greater trochanter pain syndrome. The etiology of this condition can be multifactorial, including trochanteric bursitis and/or tendinopathy of the gluteus medius or minimus tendons, or conditions affecting the back, core musculature, or contralateral limb. Patients often have pain during hip extension and lying on the affected side, which load the bursa. Conditions causing abnormal gait may also put increased load on the bursa. Thus rehabilitation and treatment should reduce or avoid these postures and movements that compress the bursa. Where possible, joint protection (e.g., kneeling pads for bursitis of the knee) can be used to reduce load on the bursae.

### Conclusion

Biomechanics is a powerful tool for understanding musculoskeletal function and the forces necessary to produce and control movement. Knowledge of biomechanical principles can help explain many commonly encountered situations in the musculoskeletal system, provide insight into mechanisms of injury, and inform intervention programs.

# Regenerative Medicine and Tissue Engineering

### KEY POINTS

Genetic factors, age, and comorbidities contribute to tissue repair and regeneration.

Cell-based therapeutics are safe and efficacious with longterm follow-up but are burdened by high costs and complex manufacturing.

The increased understanding of molecular signals governing native joint-resident progenitor cell function is leading to pharmacologic interventions that trigger intrinsic repair mechanisms.

### Introduction

Cartilage and bone damage, resulting from trauma or the destructive outcome of chronic rheumatic and musculoskeletal diseases, is very common. Chondral defects are detected in 61% of all arthroscopic procedures1,2 of which 35% are painful. Osteoarthritis affects approximately 10% to 12% of all individuals, and costs to society are 1.5% to 2% of the gross domestic product in Western countries. Inflammation is also a driver of cartilage loss: patients with inflammatory arthritis often develop cartilage and bone damage, which causes pain and disability even when the inflammation is controlled by pharmacologic interventions. Therefore in all these cases, regeneration of the joint structures— mainly cartilage and the underlying bone, but also menisci and ligaments—is essential for patients to return to a good, pain-free quality of life.

Regenerative medicine and tissue engineering (TE) seek to regenerate damaged tissues and organs, regardless of the cause of the damage, ideally without scar tissue formation, thereby restoring both the structure and function of the damaged tissues/organs. Postnatal tissue healing utilizes processes involved in tissue formation during embryonic development. Advances in developmental biology during the past three decades provide the knowledge platform underpinning novel regenerative approaches in postnatal life. These advances include not only our understanding of the mechanisms of organogenesis, but also progress in stem cell biology, including stem cell niches, lineage specification and cell differentiation, the regulation of stemness and reprogramming, and the molecular pathways driving these processes.

In this chapter we review the approaches that seek to repair damaged and diseased synovial joints and their structures (Fig. 7.1).

When we aim to repair tissues, three approaches are possible (Fig. 7.2). The first, traditional tissue engineering, consists of the implantation in the injury site of culture-expanded cells or tissue constructs generated in vitro by combining cells and biomaterials. In the second, cell preparations are implanted in the site of injury and allowed to differentiate in situ. The third relies on the presence of tissue-resident stem and progenitor cells and the ability to recruit them to the injury site and activate intrinsic repair mechanisms by using signaling molecules or chemicals targeting morphogenetic pathways (Fig. 7.2). Some tissue engineering approaches, such as autologous chondrocyte implantation, have demonstrated that cartilage repair can be reliably achieved and maintained long term, but the manufacturing of cell products is expensive, cumbersome, and sometimes unreliable. The advantage of the pharmacologic approach is the avoidance of ex vivo manipulation and culture of cells and availability of potentially affordable drugs with an established, consistent composition of matter and reliable potency and side effects.

### Extrinsic Repair: Current t Therapeutic Interventions

Cell-based therapies and TE for joint surface repair using expanded articular chondrocytes have entered clinical practice with longterm follow-up data. The use of adult stem/progenitor cells such as the mesenchymal stromal/stem cells (MSCs) has shown promising pre-clinical and early clinical safety and efficacy data, but it is at an earlier stage of clinical development. Cellular therapies and combination products contribute to tissue repair with multiple mechanisms, including not only direct engraftment, proliferation, and differentiation to tissue-specific cell types, but also paracrine actions such as the secretion of growth and differentiation factors that enhance the local tissue response. In addition, MSCs have immunomodulatory properties, which have been clinically explored in graft-versus-host disease and autoimmune diseases.

### Joint Surface Defects

A variety of articular cartilage repair techniques have been developed, typically for the treatment of focal joint surface defects. Such defects are often associated with excessive joint loading, either as a result of high-impact trauma or cumulative lowimpact repetitive overload. Joint surface lesions can extend to

the subchondral bone (osteochondral defects) or be limited to the cartilage (chondral defects). Most chondral defects do not reach bone (partial thickness), and only about 5% are full thickness1; nevertheless, because most partial-thickness lesions are either asymptomatic or debrided at the time of surgery to full

thickness, including the removal of the calcified layer (Fig. 7.3), repair strategies focus on the treatment of full-thickness defects. The best-established cell-based technology for the treatment of these lesions is autologous chondrocyte implantation and variations thereof.

### Autologous Chondrocyte Implantation

Regeneration or repair of symptomatic articular cartilage defects has been at the forefront of regenerative medicine since 1994 when one group8 reported a remarkably good clinical and structural outcome using a procedure called autologous chondrocyte transplantation/implantation (ACI). Briefly, cell populations were prepared by enzymatic release from a biopsy specimen of articular cartilage taken from an unloaded area in the symptomatic joint. The chondrocytes were subsequently expanded in vitro, and, after six to eight population doublings, they were reimplanted in the joint surface defect under a periosteal flap taken from the tibia from the same patient. This procedure was then followed by a long rehabilitation period to reach its optimal outcome at 18 to 24 months. This high-profile publication attracted considerable interest and triggered a wave of basic, translational, and clinical research activities in the field. It also evolved quite quickly in 1997 in the marketing of Carticel, an autologous cell product for the repair of symptomatic condylar defects of the knee, by Genzyme Corporation (Cambridge, MA).

Progress has been made since then, with studies aiming to improve and standardize the autologous chondrocyte preparation (the cell product), the development of other delivery systems for the chondrocytes, and the replacement of the periosteal flap with a membrane of diverse composition, and a series of clinical studies. After a number of mostly open-label studies with diverse outcomes (for a review, see ref. 9-11), one study12,13—the first multicenter, prospective, randomized trial—failed to demonstrate that ACI was superior to microfracture, a technique mostly considered to be the standard of care for small (<2 to 3 cm2) symptomatic joint surface defects. Microfracture is a bone marrow stimulation procedure and is based on the puncturing of the subchondral bone plate into the bone marrow, the generation of a blood clot containing precursor cell populations derived from the subchondral bone marrow, and the spontaneous transformation of the repair clot into a fibrocartilaginous repair tissue. Microfracture is clearly associated with a clinical benefit and a filling of the joint surface defect with repair tissue, but it is generally accepted that this repair is not durable, resulting in a decline in clinical outcome over the long term. 15-17

Subsequently, progress was made by improving the manufacturing process of the chondrocyte preparation. In Europe,

an autologous chondrocyte cell product called ChondroCelect (TiGenix, Leuven, Belgium) was developed, and it obtained the first cellular product central registration by the European Medicines Agency under the new advanced therapy medicinal product regulation. In a prospective randomized multicenter study, ChondroCelect, defined and characterized as a cell population capable of making stable cartilage in a surrogate in vivo model and quality controlled through the use of biomarkers, resulted in structurally superior repair tissue at 12 months after implantation compared with microfracture, with a superior clinical outcome at 3 years, but noninferiority in the overall population at 5 years. The 5-year data demonstrated a clinically relevant superior outcome in the subpopulation of patients with relatively recent lesions (<3 years). This prospective clinical trial supports the concept that an improved understanding of the underlying biology and the consequent optimization of the manufacturing process can lead to improved structural and clinical outcomes.

The surgical delivery of these therapies is another important factor that requires standardization. In this regard, ACI evolved into a more easily controllable arthroscopic procedure. A study that used an arthroscopic approach reported a statistically better clinical outcome for matrix-applied autologous chondrocytes after 2 years compared with microfracture.

Results from up to 20 years follow-up have demonstrated that ACI is an effective and durable treatment of large cartilage defects in the knee.9, Positive predictors of good outcome include the age of the patient, the location of the defect, early intervention (<3 years after becoming symptomatic), good quality of chondrocytes, well-trained surgeons, adherence to rehabilitation protocols, and no radiographical signs of osteoarthritis (OA). Stratification of patients will also have a major impact on the potential for regenerative therapies to move forward successfully to clinical use in daily practice. Cost-effectiveness will improve if the treatment also prevents the progression toward OA, but these data are not yet available.

Other cell sources, such as nasal chondrocytes, have been explored. Chondrocytes derived from the nasal septum, with known capacity to generate hyaline-like cartilage, were safe and successful for knee cartilage defect repair in 10 patients22

and in two patients with advanced OA (Kellgren and Lawrence grades 3 and 4). However, large controlled trials with longterm follow-up are warranted to assess efficacy.

### Stem Cell-Based Approaches

The next wave of development is the use of progenitor cell populations, or so-called MSCs, in particular via an allogeneic approach. MSCs are easy to isolate, expandable in culture, and chondrogenic; thus they are attractive alternatives to chondrocytes in an ACI procedure. These properties of MSCs would allow upscaling and generation of large quality-controlled batches, thus circumventing the limitations and patient-topatient variability of autologous cell protocols. For these reasons, the use of MSCs for joint surface repair is intensively sought and has been explored in humans.6, Several studies have shown promising results, with cartilage formation and endochondral bone formation restoring the bone front. However, uplift of the bone front at the expense of the articular cartilage has been commonly observed26 and has its clinical equivalent in intralesional osteophyte formation in patients after microfracture.15, This "side effect" appears to be less frequent in patients treated with ACI,28 suggesting that the phenotypic stability of articular chondrocytes could preserve the normal thickness of the repair cartilage and limit the advancement of the bone front. This finding points to a need, when using MSCs, for strategies to enhance stable cartilage properties and reduce fibrous tissue and hypertrophic cartilage formation.

Another important area of investigation is the tissue source of MSCs. Adult bone marrow MSCs are leading candidates for use in the repair of cartilage defects and other skeletal tissues such as bone defects. However, MSCs from bone marrow appear to have a high propensity to cartilage hypertrophy and bone formation30,31 and may not be the ideal chondroprogenitors for the repair of articular cartilage. Adipose-derived MSCs are attractive due to their easy harvest but they are poorly chondrogenic.32, Instead, superiority of MSCs from synovial membrane for cartilage formation in vitro compared with MSCs from other tissue sources, including bone marrow and periosteum, has been reported.34-37 Promising data using synovium-derived progenitors have been reported in pre-clinical and clinical studies. 38-40

The differences in chondrogenic potency of MSC populations could find their origins in the distinctive molecular programs of embryonic formation of their native tissues because lineage tracing studies in mice demonstrated a common developmental origin of articular cartilage and synovial membrane from the Gdf5-positive cells of the embryonic joint interzone. 41-43

The solution to the challenge of stable-cartilage formation, displaying also the very specific articular cartilage characteristics, may come from the use of chondroprogenitors isolated from the articular cartilage itself, which display the ability to maintain chondrogenic potency upon extensive culture expansion. A proof-of-principle pilot study in a goat model in vivo demonstrated the apparent noninferiority of these chondroprogenitors to form a cartilage-like repair tissue in a chondral defect compared with full-depth chondrocytes.

The use of MSCs in joint resurfacing in animal models and humans reveals a variable structural outcome, ranging from hyaline-like cartilage to fibrous tissue. This finding has prompted interventions to support tissue maturation by using cartilagepromoting growth factors along with smart biomaterials.46, However, the combination of cells, biomaterials, and morphogens

would make the assessment of efficacy and toxicity more complex and the path from animal experimentation to clinical application arduous.

The use of allogeneic MSCs has shown a satisfactory safety profile in clinical studies. There is a potential risk that the acquired differentiated phenotype of the implanted progenitor cells may result in the loss of the immunologic privilege, with consequent rejection of the cells.48, However, in a mouse study, it was shown that the implanted MSCs in vivo enhanced intrinsic joint surface repair primarily via paracrine mechanisms, through the release of factors that recruit locally resident chondroprogenitors, rather than through their differentiation into mature chondrocytes. The use of allogeneic cells would allow manufacturing of large batches of cell products with specific off-the-shelf clinical indications. Such an approach would increase consistency and decrease costs of cell therapies, potentially accelerating the translational process toward routine clinical application.

Human studies will be needed to demonstrate noninferiority of MSCs or any other stem/progenitor cell populations in clinical and structural outcomes compared with the gold-standard articular cartilage—derived chondrocytes in ACI-like procedures.
