MMP-2 processes monocyte chemoattractant protein (MCP)-3 into an MCP-3 fragment, deleting the N-terminal four amino acids, which can bind to CC-chemokine receptors and act as a general chemokine antagonist.

Stromelysins (MMP-3 and 10). The subgroup of stromelysins consists of MMP-3 (stromelysin-1) and MMP-10 (stromelysin-2). They share 78% identity in amino acid sequence and have similar enzymatic properties. The enzymes hydrolyze numerous ECM macromolecules, including aggrecan, fibronectin, laminin, and collagen IV (see Table 8.2). Types III, IX, and X collagen and telopeptides of types I, II, and XI collagen are also digested by MMP-3. In addition to the ECM components, MMP-3 is active on IGF-BP-3, IL-1β, heparin-binding epidermal growth factor (HB-EGF), CTGF, E-cadherin, α1 anti-chymotrypsin, and α1 proteinase inhibitor (see Table 8.2). MMP-3 also activates many proMMPs. A similar activator function has been identified for MMP-10.

Matrilysins (MMP-7 and 26). Matrilysins include MMP-7 (matrilysin-1) and MMP-26 (matrilysin-2), which are the smallest of the MMPs, having only the prodomain and catalytic domains. The substrate specificity of MMP-7 is similar to that of stromelysins, digesting numerous ECM components, including aggrecan; gelatins; fibronectin; laminin; elastin; entactin; types III, IV, V, IX, X, and XI collagen; fibrin/fibrinogen; vitronectin; tenascin; and link protein (see Table 8.2). Although these substrates overlap with the substrates of other MMPs, the specific activity of MMP-7 to most substrates is highest among the MMPs. Non-ECM molecules such as α-defensin, Fas ligand, β4 integrin, E-cadherin, plasminogen, TNF, and CTGF are also the substrates for MMP-7 (see Table 8.2). MMP-26 degrades gelatin, type IV collagen, fibronectin, fibrinogen, and αl proteinase inhibitor, but information about other substrates is still limited.

Furin-Activated Matrix Metalloproteinases (MMP-11 and 28). MMP-11 (stromelysin-3) and MMP-28 (epilysin) contain an RKRR sequence at the end of the prodomain, which is a unique motif for intra-cellular processing of proproteins to mature molecules by furin and other proprotein convertases. ProMMP-11 was activated during secretion by furin. MMP-11 shows only weak proteolytic activity against gelatin, laminin, fibronectin, and aggrecan, but it has respectable catalytic action in digesting α1 proteinase inhibitor, α2 macroglobulin, and IGF-BP-1 (see Table 8.2). MMP-28 can degrade casein, but its natural substrates are unknown.

Other soluble MMP enzymes (MMP-12, 19, 20, 21, 23, and 27). MMP-12 (metalloelastase), MMP-19 (RASI-1), MMP-20 (enamelysin), MMP-21, and MMP-27 have structural characteristics similar to those of collagenases and stromelysins. These MMPs are not classified into the previously mentioned subgroups because their substrates and other biochemical characters have not been fully examined to date. MMP-12, also called metalloelastase, digests elastin, fibronectin, collagen V, osteonectin, and plasminogen (see Table 8.2). MMP-19, initially reported as MMP-18 but

renamed MMP-19, cleaves type IV collagen, laminin, fibronectin, gelatin, tenascin, entactin, fibrin/fibrinogen, aggrecan, and cartilage oligomeric matrix protein (COMP; see Table 8.2). MMP- 20 also degrades amelogenin, aggrecan, and COMP. Substrates of MMP-21 and 27 are unknown, however.

MMP-23 (cysteine array-MMP) is unique among MMP enzymes as it is synthesized as a type II transmembrane protein but becomes a soluble enzyme upon activation. MMP-23 can degrade gelatin, but no information about other substrates is available (see Table 8.2). A unique aspect of MMP-23 is that this MMP is expressed in only the reproductive organs of both males and females, such as the endometrium, ovary, testis, and prostate. However, its biologic functions are not understood.

Membrane-Type Matrix Metalloproteinases (MMP-14, 15, 16, 17, 24, and 25 or MT1-, MT2-, MT3-, MT4-, MT5-, and MT6- MMP). There are two types of MT-MMPs, type I transmembranetype and GPI-anchored-type, and these MT-MMPs are unique in that they are expressed on the cell surface in their active form and function on the cell surface. Type I transmembrane type includes MMP-14 (MT1-MMP), MMP-15 (MT2-MMP), MMP-16 (MT3-MMP), and MMP-24 (MT5-MMP). All of these MT-MMPs activate proMMP-2, but MT1-MMP is considered an in vivo activator of proMMP-2 in various tissues (see later discussion). MT1-MMP also degrades fibrillar collagen on the cell surface. Like other collagen-degrading MMP enzymes (MMP-1, 2, 8, and 13), it cleaves the triple helical part of collagen at approximately three-fourths of the distance from the N-terminus. MT1-MMP also degrades other ECM components, including fibronectin, laminin, aggrecan, and gelatin (see Table 8.2). MT2-MMP digests fibronectin, tenascin, nidogen, aggrecan, perlecan, and laminin. MT3-MMP cleaves type III collagen, fibronectin, and gelatins. MMP-17 (MT4-MMP) and MMP-25 (MT6-MMP) are GPI-anchored MMPs.17, MT4and MT6-MMP can digest gelatin and fibrin/fibrinogen (see Table 8.2).

### ADAM and ADAMTS Families

Two ADAM (a disintegrin and metalloproteinase) gene families exist: enzymes with a transmembrane domain (ADAM) and those that are secreted, ADAM with thrombospondin motifs (ADAMTS; see Fig. 8.1). The active sites in the catalytic domains of most members of both gene families contain a common sequence of HEXGHXXGXXHD with the "Met-turn," which is also present in MMP members. The ADAMTS family includes 19 members. Although information about substrates and biologic functions is still limited, ADAMTS1 to 5, 8 to 9, 14 to 16, 18, and 20 are all ECM-degrading proteinases (see Table 8.3). ADAMTS1, 4, 5, 9, and 15 can preferentially cleave aggrecan at the five Glu-X bonds, including the Glu373-Ala374 bond (the aggrecanase site). Since ADAMTS4 and ADAMTS5 were the first two aggrecanases characterized, they are also named aggrecanase-1 and aggrecanase-2, respectively.19, These proteinases also digest versican, 21 and brevican is cleaved by ADAMTS4 (see Table 8.3). The C-terminus-truncated ADAMTS4 also degrades fibromodulin and decorin. ADAMTS16, 18, and 20 also appear to have weak aggrecanase activity. ADAMTS2 and 3 process the N-terminal prodomain of type I and II collagens and are named procollagen N-proteinase. ADAMTD14 is also known to exhibit the activity of procollagen N-proteinase. ADAMTS13 is a von Willebrand factor-cleaving proteinase, and its mutation causes thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura.

Proteinase activities of other ADAMTS species are still unknown. The human genome contains 25 ADAM genes, including four pseudogenes; thus the human ADAM family is composed of 21 members (Table 8.4). Among the ADAMs, ADAM8-10, 12, 15, 17, 19 to 21, 28, 30, and 33 and ADAM-like decysin 1 (ADAMDEC1) exhibit proteolytic activity (i.e., they are proteinase-type ADAMs; see Table 8.4). Although ADAM10, 12, and 15 degrade type IV collagen, the primary substrates of these ADAMs are considered to be various membrane proteins, which include precursors of cytokines and growth factors such as TNF, HB-EGF and neuregulin, IGF-BPs, receptors such as p75 TNF receptor, IL-1 receptor II, and other membrane proteins related to development such as NOTCH ligand and ephrin (see Table 8.4).24-29 According to these data, a major function of ADAM proteinases is membrane protein shedding. ADAM17 processes proTNF (type II transmembrane molecule), releasing soluble TNF. Thus it is also called a TNF-converting enzyme (TACE). ADAM17 also releases L-selectin, TGF-α, and p75 TNF receptor. ADAM9, 12, and 17 can shed HB-EGF from its precursor. ADAM12 and 28 cleave IGF-BP-3 and 5.29, ADAM8, 15, and 28 shed CD23.31 Other functions of ADAMs include binding to integrins, cellcell interaction, cell migration, and signal transduction (see Table 8.4).

### Regulation of Proteinase Activity

The activities of ECM-degrading proteinases in tissues are regulated by different means, including their gene expression, activation of their zymogen forms, and inhibition by their endogenous inhibitors. Some of these enzymes are also regulated by cell surface binding, endocytosis, and recycling.

### Gene Expression

### Matrix Metalloproteinases

Under physiologic conditions, cells express only limited levels of MMPs or TIMPs in tissues. However, under inflammatory conditions, the expression of the genes encoding these enzymes is stimulated by cytokines and other factors. Neutrophils synthesize MMP-8 and 9 during their differentiation and store these enzymes within their granules. Macrophages upon treatment with lipopolysaccharide or phorbol myristate acetate (PMA; 12-O-tetradecanoylphorbol-13-acetate) express MMP-1 and 9, MT1-MMP, and TIMP-1. Tumor cells express many MMPs, such as MMP-1, 7, 9, 10, and 14 (MT1-MMP), and TIMP-1, driven predominantly by oncogenic stimuli. Numerous factors, including cytokines, growth factors, and chemical and physical stimuli, regulate gene expression of MMPs and TIMPs in tissue cells. Much information is available for regulators of MMP-1 and 3, which are coordinately expressed in many cell types upon stimulation with cytokines and growth factors, factors acting at the cell surface, and chemical agents (Table 8.5). Retinoic acid, TGF-β, and glucocorticoid suppress the upregulated production of MMP-1 and 3. Similar factors regulate gene expression of MMP-7 and 9, but the regulation is stricter, and fewer factors modulate their expression (see Table 8.5). MMP-14 expression is upregulated by PMA, concanavalin A, fibrillar collagen, basic fibroblast growth factor, and TNF, and glucocorticoids downregulate it in various cells. TNF and IL-1α stimulate osteoarthritic

chondrocytes to express the MMP-14 gene. In contrast to these MMPs, MMP-2 and TIMP-2 are unique in that factors capable of enhancing the production of MMP-1 and 3 and TIMP-1 are inactive. TIMP-1 expression is enhanced or suppressed in response to many factors, including cytokines, growth factors, and oncogenic transformation (see Table 8.5). Effects of these stimulatory factors are common to the gene expression of MMPs, but they are regulated independently. TGF-β, retinoic acid, progesterone, and estrogen enhance TIMP-1 expression in fibroblasts, but they suppress the expression of MMP-1 and 3. Although information about stimulatory and suppressive factors of TIMP-1, 2, and 3 is available (see Table 8.5), factors controlling the gene expression of TIMP-4 are not well known. Previous studies have identified the elements in the promoters of MMPs and TIMPs, which are related to or responsible for the stimulation or suppression of gene expression with various factors. The structural characteristics of the promoters generally explain the regulation of their gene expression.

### Serine Proteinases

Neutrophil elastase, cathepsin G, chymase, and tryptase are stored within the secretory granules and secreted into the extra-cellular milieu after activation of neutrophils and mast cells. The expression of these serine proteinases is controlled mainly by cellular differentiation. Precursors of plasmin and plasma kallikrein are constitutively synthesized predominantly in the liver, circulate in the blood as zymogens (i.e., plasminogen and prokallikrein), and reach the inflamed tissues by being released from blood vessels. Plasminogen concentration in the plasma is roughly 200 µg/mL, and the activities in the tissues are controlled mainly through the activation of the proenzymes by activators. The uPA and tPA molecules, plasminogen activators, are synthesized by tissue cells, and their gene expression is regulated by many factors (Table 8.6). uPA synthesis is upregulated in many normal cell types and transformed cells by agents that increase intra-cellular cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) levels (e.g., calcitonin, vasopressin, cholera toxin, and cAMP analogs), growth factors (e.g., EGF, platelet-derived growth factor, and vascular endothelial growth factor), cytokines (IL-1 and TNF), and phorbol esters, whereas glucocorticoid decreases the expression. Similar factors regulate the expression of tPA (see Table 8.6). In endothelial cells, proteinases are enhancers; thrombin and plasmin stimulate the production of tPA. PAI-1 and 2 are also regulated by common factors, many of which also enhance the production of uPA and tPA (see Table 8.6). Most serpins are constitutively produced in the liver and secreted to plasma.

### Lysosomal Cysteine and Aspartic Proteinases

The expression of lysosomal cysteine proteinases, cathepsins B, L, and K, is generally constitutive, but malignant transformation is often associated with increased synthesis of cathepsins B and L. Cathepsin B transcription varies with cell type and the state of differentiation of tumor cells; it is increased in chondrocytes by IL-1. Malignant transformation, tumor promoters, and growth factors stimulate the synthesis of cathepsin L. Cathepsin K gene expression in monocyte-macrophage lineage depends on the cellular differentiation to osteoclasts. Still, all-trans retinoic acid upregulates the expression in rabbit osteoclasts. Lysosomal aspartic proteinase, cathepsin D, is

constitutively expressed in almost all cells, although estradiol, calcitriol, and retinoic acid can regulate the expression.

### Inhibition of Proteinases by Endogenous Inhibitors

Endogenous proteinase inhibitors control the activities of proteinases in vivo. The inhibitors are derived from plasma or cells in the local tissues. Plasma contains several proteinase inhibitors, with about 10% of all plasma proteins being proteinase inhibitors. Many of these are proteinase class specific, but α2 macroglobulin inhibits the activities of proteinases from all classes. Major endogenous inhibitors of the ECM degrading proteinases are listed in Table 8.7.

### α2 Macroglobulin

α2 macroglobulin (α2M) is a large glycoprotein of 725 kDa that consists of four identical subunits of 185 kDa that are linked in pairs by disulfide bonds. Regardless of the proteinase classes, almost all active proteinases cleave a stretch within the molecule, the so-called bait region, located near the center of the subunits. Upon cleavage of the bait region, a conformational change in α2M occurs and physically traps the proteinase within a molecular cage, resulting in a proteinase—α2M complex. Although the active site of the proteinase in the complex is free and remains active, the enzyme is trapped by the arms of α2M and is prevented from interacting and degrading large macromolecules. Besides its function as a proteinase inhibitor, α2M may also act as a carrier protein because it binds to numerous growth factors and cytokines such as platelet-derived growth factor, basic fibroblast growth factor, TGF-β, insulin, and IL-1β. α2M is synthesized mainly in the liver but also locally by macrophages, fibroblasts, and adrenocortical cells. The concentration of the inhibitor in plasma is 250 mg/dL. Because of its large molecular weight, it is not present in noninflammatory synovial fluid. However, during synovial inflammation, α2M penetrates the joint cavity. Rheumatoid synovial fluid has about the same concentration of the inhibitor as plasma.

### Inhibitors of Serine Proteinases

The primary inhibitors of serine proteinases include the members of the serpin (serine proteinase inhibitor) gene family, Kunitz-type inhibitors, and others (see Table 8.7). The serpins are 50 to 100 kDa glycoproteins and share homology with human αl proteinase inhibitor. The major serpins involved in the regulation of ECM-degrading serine proteinases are αl proteinase inhibitor, αl anti-chymotrypsin, α2 anti-plasmin, plasminogen activator inhibitors (PAI-1 and 2), protein C inhibitor (PAI-3), C1-inhibitor, kallistatin, and proteinase nexin-1 (PN-1). The main proteinases inhibited by these molecules are listed in Table 8.5. Although PAI-1 and 2 inhibit tPA and uPA, the inhibition by PAI-1 is more effective against tPA, and that of PAI-2 is more efficient against uPA. Kunitz-type inhibitors include aprotinin, trypstatin, and PN-2, identical to a β-amyloid protein precursor. Secretory leukocyte proteinase inhibitor, which inhibits neutrophil elastase and cathepsin G, is present in many secretory and inflammatory fluids and cartilage. Elafin is a serine proteinase inhibitor with 38% identity with the second domain of secretory leukocyte proteinase inhibitor; it inhibits neutrophil elastase and proteinase 3.

### Inhibitors of Cysteine Proteinases

The members of the cystatin superfamily and calpastatin belong to the family of inhibitors of ECM-degrading cysteine proteinases (see Table 8.7). Cystatins that inhibit lysosomal cysteine proteinases consist of three groups. Subgroup 1 comprises stefins A and B. Each has a molecular mass of 11 kDa, and the stefins reside within cells. Subgroup 2 contains cystatin C and S, each with a molecular mass of 13 kDa. They occur at relatively high concentrations in cerebrospinal fluid and saliva. Subgroup 3 comprises the kininogens. Kininogens that participate in blood coagulation and inflammation are also inhibitors of cysteine proteinases. Calpains are not inhibited by cystatins but are inhibited by calpastatin (120 kDa), which is a cytosolic-specific inhibitor of calpain.

### Tissue Inhibitors of Metalloproteinases

TIMPs are a gene family consisting of four members with approximately 40% to 50% sequence identity (i.e., TIMP-1, 2, 3, and 4) and molecular masses ranging from 21 to 28 kDa in humans. TIMPs inhibit the activities of MMPs by binding in a 1:1 molar ratio forming tight, noncovalent complexes. The exception is TIMP-1 that does not efficiently inhibit transmembrane-type MT-MMPs that include MT1-, MT2-, MT3and MT5-MMPs (MMP-14, 15, 16, and 24). TIMPs contain 12 highly conserved cysteine residues that form six intrachain disulfide bonds, which are essential for maintaining the correct structure of the molecule and stable inhibitory activity.

TIMP molecules have two structurally distinct subdomains: an N-terminal subdomain that consists of loops 1 through 3 and a C-terminal subdomain that consists of loops 4 through 6. The N-terminal subdomain of each TIMP molecule contains the inhibitory activity for MMPs. The crystal structures of the MMP/TIMP complexes show that the wedge-shaped TIMPs bind with their edge into the entire length of the active-site cleft of their cognate MMPs. The efficient inhibitory activity of TIMP-2 to MMP-14 (MT1-MMP) is explained by the additional interaction between a quite long hairpin loop of TIMP-2 and a loop over the rim of the active-site cleft of MMP-14.36 TIMP-1 and 2 are unique in that they make the complexes with proMMP-9 and 2 through their C-terminal subdomain and hemopexin domain of proMMP-9 and 2, respectively (i.e., the proMMP-9-TIMP-1 and proMMP-2-TIMP-2 complexes). A similar complex formation is also reported between TIMP-4 and proMMP-2. Since the MMP inhibitory site of TIMPs in these complexes is not occupied, these proMMP-TIMP complexes can inhibit other MMPs.

Interestingly, the proMMP-2TIMP-2 complex is necessary for the efficient activation of proMMP-2 by MT1-MMP on the cell surface. MT1-MMP forms a homodimer on the cell surface through its hemopexin and transmembrane domains. TIMP-2 binds to one of the MT1-MMP molecules in the dimer through its inhibitory domain and MMP-2 through its C-terminal subdomain, forming an (MT1-MMP)2-TIMP-2proMMP-2 complex on the cell surface (see later discussion). Thus TIMP-2 allows proMMP-2 to interact with MT1-MMP, which is essential for proMMP-2 activation. In addition to MMP inhibition, TIMP-3 inhibits ADAM10, 12, 17, 28, and 33 but not ADAM8, 9, and 19. TIMP-3 also inhibits ADAMTS4 and 5. The N-terminal inhibitory subdomain of TIMP-3 is critical for inhibiting both MMPs and ADAM

members, but the inhibitory mechanism seems slightly different. The major interactions of TIMPs with MMP involve two sections of the polypeptide chain of the TIMP around the Cys to Cys70 disulfide bond. Blocking the N-terminal α-amino group or the addition of an extra residue inactivates the MMP inhibitory activity of TIMPs. However, such modification of TIMP-3 does not influence ADAM17 inhibition.

Besides inhibiting MMP/ADAM/ADAMTS enzymes, TIMPs also possess growth factor activity, anti-angiogenic activity, and regulatory activity of apoptosis. Another MMP inhibitor is RECK (reversion-inducing, cysteine-rich protein with Kazal motifs). RECK is a GPI-anchored glycoprotein harboring three inhibitor-like domains and inhibited at least MMP-2, 9, 14, and ADAM10.40, Although this inhibitor seems to play a key role in the angiogenic processes in vivo, 39 the inhibitory mechanism of these enzymes and its functions in pathologic conditions such as arthritides remain to be further investigated.

### Activation Mechanisms sof Matrix Metalloproteinase Zymogens

All MMPs are synthesized as inactive zymogens (proMMPs), which are kept inactive through an interaction between a cysteine-sulfhydryl group in their conserved sequence PRCGXPD and the zinc ion at their catalytic site, preventing the interaction of a water molecule with the catalytic zinc that is essential for the enzymatic reaction. Activation occurs by proteolytic removal of the prodomain that exposes the catalytic site. There are three pathways of proMMP activation dependent on the enzymes: extra-cellular activation, intra-cellular activation, and cell surface activation (Fig. 8.2).

### Extra-cellular Activation

Many soluble MMPs (e.g., proMMP-1, 3, 7, 8 to 10, 12, and 13) are secreted in a zymogen form and need to be activated extra-cellularly. In vitro, this activation can be initiated by treatment with nonproteolytic agents that disturb the interaction of the Cys within the PRCGVPD motif in the prodomain with the catalytic zinc.6, Such agents include thiol-modifying reagents, hypochlorous acid, sodium dodecyl sulfate, chaotropic agents, and physical factors (heat and acid exposure). Among these, 4-amino phenylmercuric acetate (APMA) has been used for investigations into the activation mechanism of proMMPs. Upon APMA treatment, APMA disturbs the interaction of Cys in the PRCGVPD motif and causes proMMP molecules to undergo autolytic processing at the upstream region of PRCGVPD to remove a portion of the prodomain. Since the Cys no longer interacts with the catalytic zinc, the intermediate form possesses partial activity and processes the rest of the prodomain intramolecularly to generate a fully active form. This activation mode is designated as the stepwise activation mechanism. In the case of proMMP-9, APMA treatment only results in the cleavage of the Ala74-Met75 bond upstream of the conserved sequence retaining the PRCGVPD sequence, but this intermediate form was found to be fully active. ### Intra-cellular Activation

Some MMPs have a basic motif consisting of an RX(K/R)R sequence (where X can be any amino acids) at the end of the prodomain that is recognized and cleaved by proprotein convertases (PCs) such as furin, a processing enzyme in the trans- Golgi apparatus. PCs activate these MMPs, which include proMMP-11, 23, and 28 and proMT-MMPs, during secretion (see Fig. 8.2). Intra-cellular activation of proMMP-11 and 14 (proMT1-MMP) by furin has been reported.48, After the activation, active MMP-11 is secreted to the extra-cellular milieu, and active MMP-14 (MT1-MMP) is expressed on the cell surface. Because other proMT-MMPs, proMMP-23 and 28, also have the motif, PCs are responsible for the intra-cellular activation of these proMMPs. ADAM and ADAMTS family enzymes are also activated in this way since they have the same basic amino acid motif at the end of the prodomain.

### Cell Surface Activation

ProMMP-2 is unique because it is activated on the cell surface by MMP-14/MT1-MMP. The activation mechanism of proMMP-2 by MT1-MMP has been extensively investigated since it is considered a crucial step for cancer invasion and angiogenesis. The most accepted model for proMMP-2 activation by MT1-MMP is depicted in Fig. 8.2.

MT1-MMP forms a homodimeric complex on the cell surface through its Hpx and the transmembrane domains.50, Next, one of the MT1-MMP components of the dimer is bound to and inhibited by TIMP-2. Since the C-terminal subdomain of TIMP-2, which has a high affinity for the Hpx domain of proMMP-2, is available for interaction, the complex of (MT1- MMP)2-TIMP-2 acts as a proMMP-2 activation receptor. Upon forming the (MT1-MMP)2-TIMP-2-proMMP-2 complex, the other MT1-MMP, free from TIMP-2 in this complex, cleaves the proMMP-2 prodomain at Asn37-Leu38 to generate an intermediate form of MMP-2.

Finally, autolytic action by another intermediate form of MMP-2 removes a residual portion of the prodomain to generate a fully active enzyme. Interestingly, activated MMP-2 can be released to the extra-cellular milieu or function on the cell surface by associating with TIMP-2 at the Hpx domain.

Other transmembrane types of MT-MMPs—including MT2-MMP (MMP-15), MT3-MMP (MMP-16), and MT5- MMP (MMP-24)—also activated proMMP-2,54-57 but the

in vivo role of proMMP-2 activation by these enzymes and its mechanism of activation are not clear. GPI-anchored MT4- MMP (MMP-17) does not activate proMMP-2. Another GPI-anchored MT6-MMP (MMP-25) activated proMMP-2. However, it was subsequently shown that the full-length enzyme cannot activate proMMP-2 on the cell surface, although the isolated recombinant catalytic domain of MT6-MMP can activate proMMP-2 in vitro. MT1-MMP (MMP-14) also activates proMMP-13 on the cell surface,58 and this activation requires the hemopexin domain of MMP-13 but does not seem to require TIMP-2.58, It was also reported that proMMP-7 is also activated on the cell surface. This was discovered through screening proMMP-7-binding molecules in a yeast two-hybrid screen. ProMMP-7 is captured on the cell membrane by an interaction of the proMMP-7 prodomain with the C-terminal extra-cellular loop of CD151, a member of the transmembrane 4 superfamily, and is activated. This cell surface activation of proMMP-7 requires a substrate of MMP-7. Since α chains of α3β1 and α6β4 integrins interact with CD151, these integrins may also be involved in the activation. Although the precise molecular mechanisms of this activation and the activator itself are still unclear, proMMP-7 and CD151 are overexpressed in osteoarthritic chondrocytes, and proMMP-7 is activated by the interaction with CD151 in articular cartilage of OA.

### Endocytosis of ECM-Degrading Metalloproteinases

For MT-MMPs, endocytosis is crucial for their regulation. Some soluble enzymes are also known to be endocytosed via interaction

with membrane proteins. In general, endocytosis is considered a step of downregulation, but in some cases, it is necessary for the enzyme to express its biologic function. It has been shown that MT1-MMP is endocytosed via both clathrin and caveolae-dependent pathways.62, The clathrin-dependent pathway is faster than the caveolae-dependent pathway, but it was also demonstrated that clathrin-dependent endocytosis is required for MT1-MMP to promote cellular migration and invasion. In the cytoplasmic domain of MT1-MMP, there is an LLY573 motif recognized by adaptor protein 2, a subunit of clathrin, and it is crucial for the enzyme to be endocytosed through this mechanism. Just downstream of LLY573, there is a Cys574 that is post-translationally palmitoylated. Interestingly, this palmitoylation is crucial for the enzyme to be endocytosed via a clathrin-dependent mechanism and for its cell migration-promoting effect. MT1-, MT3-, and MT5-MMP are endocytosed and recycled back to the cell surface, and three amino acid motifs of DKV582 (MT1-MMP), EWV607 (MT3-MMP), and EWV645 (MT5-MMP) at the C-terminus were identified as recycling motifs.65,

Endocytosis is not only the regulatory mechanism of MT- MMPs but also for soluble enzymes. It was discovered that several ECM-degrading metalloproteinases and inhibitors are endocytosed via low-density lipoprotein receptor—related protein 1 (LRP- 1). LRP-1 is synthesized as a 600 kDa precursor processed by proprotein convertases during secretion to the cell surface, resulting in a 515 kDa alpha-chain and 85 kDa beta-chain that are associated noncovalently. The alpha chain contains four extra-cellular binding regions for various molecules. It binds to extra-cellular molecules, rapidly endocytosed through clathrin-dependent mechanisms, and molecules bound to LRP-1 are degraded in the lysosome. LRP-1 is widely expressed in different cell types and controls extra-cellular levels of numerous biologically active molecules to maintain tissue homeostasis. Currently, more than 50 ligands have been characterized, including lipoproteins, ECM proteins, growth factors, cell surface receptors, proteinases, proteinase inhibitors, and secreted intra-cellular proteins. In cartilage, it was shown that LRP-1 controls the Wnt/b-catenin signaling pathway by interacting with Frizzled-168 and connective tissue growth factor (CCN2), and both regulate endochondral ossification and articular cartilage regeneration. It has been shown that LRP-1 is also responsible for clearing extra-cellular MMP-2, 9, and 13; ADAMTS5; and TIMP-1 and 3.70-73 LRP-1 also endocytoses tPA, PAI-1, and uPA, and cathepsin D also bound to the LRP-1 ectodomain. Endocytic regulation of ECM degrading enzymes in arthritic tissues is becoming an important area that directly influences disease progression, and further investigation is required.

### Joint Tissue Destruction in Arthritis

Articular cartilage is the primary organ that supports joint function by providing smooth joint movement and a shock-absorbing function. Cartilage is a unique tissue composed of a large volume of ECM and a small number of chondrocytes. The major cartilage ECM components are type II collagen and a large proteoglycan called aggrecan (about 45% each). These components play crucial roles in cartilage function: aggrecan provides compressive resistance, and collagen provides structure for the architecture of cartilage. Thus the degradation of these components severely compromises joint function. The major aggrecan-degrading enzymes are thought to be ADAMTSs, but MMPs also serve this function; collagen degradation is carried out by collagen-degrading MMPs.

### Cartilage Destruction in Rheumatoid Arthritis

RA is characterized by chronic proliferative synovitis, a combination of hyperplasia of the synovial lining cells, inflammatory cell infiltration, and angiogenesis in the sublining cell layer (Fig. 8.4). Hyperplastic synovial lining cells are invasive and overproduce MMP-1, 3,

9, and 14; ADAMTS4; and TIMP-1 and 3. Sublining fibroblasts produce MMP-2 and TIMP-2. Polymorphonuclear leukocytes infiltrated in the synovium and joint cavity store MMP-8 in the specific granules and MMP-9 and neutrophil elastase, cathepsin G, and proteinase 3 in the azurophil granules. These are released from cells during phagocytosis of tissue debris and immune complexes. Other inflammatory cells in the synovium include macrophages, lymphocytes, and mast cells. Macrophages produce MMP-1 and 9, MT1-MMP, TIMP-1 and 2, and uPA and cathepsins B, L, and D are also secreted from activated macrophages. T lymphocytes in the synovium synthesize MMP-9. Chymase and tryptase are degranulated from mast cells in response to activation by immune complexes. Endothelial cells express many MMPs, including MMP-1 to 3 and 9 and MT1-MMP; tPA; and their inhibitors (Fig. 8.4). However, these proteinases produced by endothelial cells may be involved in tissue remodeling during angiogenesis in the synovium rather than cartilage destruction.

All of the soluble proteinases and inhibitors produced by synovial tissue cells and inflammatory cells are likely to be secreted into the synovial fluid and contribute to the degradation of articular cartilage when active proteinases overwhelm inhibitors. MMP-1 to 3, 8, and 9, ADAMTS4, and TIMP-1 and 2 are detectable in

rheumatoid synovial fluids, and the molar balance of MMPs to TIMPs in this compartment seems to favor MMP activity as proteolytic activities are detectable in rheumatoid synovial fluids. In the early stage of RA, cartilage surfaces exposed to synovial fluid show surface irregularity (fbrillation) and proteoglycan depletion without being covered by pannus tissue. This cartilage degradation may be caused by the action of the proteinases present in synovial fluid (see Fig. 8.5). Among the MMPs detected in synovial fluids, MMP-3 has the highest concentration, and the serum MMP-3 level can be used to monitor the activity of rheumatoid 78-80 Articular cartilage in contact with synovial tissue is synovitis. progressively degraded even in the early stage of the disease. This part of the synovial tissue becomes the pannus that further invades and destroys cartilage tissue, a major pathway of cartilage erosion in RA. It has been shown that MT1-MMP expressed in synovial fibroblasts is responsible for the invasion of the pannus into the cartilage (Fig. 8.5).81, Analyses of RA joint specimens indicate that MT1-MMP is notably overexpressed in the fibroblasts at the pannus-cartilage junction where they invade. This unique expression pattern of MT1-MMP cannot be explained by inflammatory cytokines-driven gene expression.

It was reported that the upregulation of MT1-MMP is due to the recognition of cartilage collagen by synovial fibroblasts through

collagen receptor tyrosine kinase, discoidin domain receptor 2 (DDR2). Collagen signaling through DDR2 upregulated MT1- MMP gene expression and function to degrade cartilage collagen matrix for invasion in synovial fibroblasts. Interestingly, DDR2 is not activated by healthy intact cartilage but instead by partially damaged, aggrecan-depleted cartilage, suggesting that aggrecan degradation precedes activation of the pannus invasion program. MMPs and ADAMTSs are thought to play a role in aggrecan degradation, but ADAMTSs are thought to play a major role in the early stages of arthritis. ADAMTS-1, 4, 5, 8, 9, 15, 16, and 18 can degrade aggrecan, but ADAMTS-5 is considered a major aggrecanase because it possesses the strongest aggrecanase activity, 85,86 and ADAMTS-5 null mice are protected from cartilage degradation in antigen-induced arthritis. Furthermore, knock-in mutant mice harboring a mutation in the ADAMTS cleavage site in the interglobular domain of aggrecan are also protected from cartilage degradation in the antigen-induced arthritis model. These observations suggest that aggrecan degradation is necessary for cartilage degradation to progress in inflammatory arthritis.

In addition to cells in inflamed synovial tissue, chondrocytes within cartilage tissue also produce cartilage-degrading proteinases upon proinflammatory stimulations (Fig. 8.4). Various inflammatory cytokines stimulate chondrocytes to produce MMP-1

to 3, 7 to 9, 13, 14, and 16; ADAM9, 10, and 17; ADAMTS4 and ADAMTS5; and other classes of proteinases. In rheumatoid arthritic cartilage, MMP-1 to 3, 7, 9, 13, and 14 are expressed in chondrocytes in the proteoglycan-depleted zone. When large areas of the cartilage surface are ulcerated after degradation of the cartilage ECM, death of chondrocytes occurs, leading to further progressive cartilage destruction.

Since MMPs play a central role in the degradation of ECM molecules in RA and cancers, many MMP inhibitors have been developed and subjected to clinical trials.84,89-91 1 However, all have failed due to a lack of efficacy. Consequently, MMP inhibitors for treating patients with RA and OA have been withdrawn from phase III trials. Moreover, in clinical trials for patients with cancer, most of the inhibitors had no definite benefit, and prolonged or high-dose treatment with broad-spectrum MMP inhibitors caused unexpected symptoms in the musculoskeletal system, such as inflammatory polyarthritis,92 designated the "musculoskeletal syndrome." Their failure is thought to be because of the nature of active site-directed broad-spectrum inhibitors. In humans, there are 62 metalloproteinases, and many of these enzymes are essential for normal tissue homeostasis. These small molecule inhibitors broadly inhibit most of these enzymes, causing unexpected side effects. Going forward, if this becomes a viable therapeutic alternative, it will be crucial to identify the responsible enzymes for specific diseases and identify highly selective inhibitors.

There are two potential MMPs that can be targeted in a selective manner and have shown efficacy, at least in an animal model of arthritis. The first is MMP-13, produced by rheumatoid synovial fibroblasts and chondrocytes upon stimulation with various inflammatory stimuli, including IL-1, TNF, IL-17, and myeloidrelated proteins (S100A8/S100A9) and oncostatin M.93-96 High levels of MMP-13 are found in the synovial pannus at the cartilage junction. There is a small molecule inhibitor highly selective against MMP-13, and administration of this inhibitor blocked the development of arthritis in several inflammatory arthritis models, including the SCID mouse co-implantation model and collageninduced arthritis model.

Another target is MT1-MMP (MMP-14). MT1-MMP is upregulated in rheumatoid synovial tissue99-101 and is highly expressed in synovial fibroblasts at the pannus-cartilage junction. Selective MT1-MMP inhibition by expressing a dominant negative form of MT1-MMP81 or knocking down MT1-MMP82 inhibited RASF invasion into cartilage in vitro. Also, the highly selective MT1-MMP inhibitory antibody DX2400 inhibited cartilage erosion in mice with collagen-induced arthritis. These findings suggest that MT1-MMP is the enzyme that mediates synovial pannus invasion and cartilage erosion. As described earlier, a selective MMP-13 inhibitor also inhibits cartilage erosion in an animal model of arthritis. Interestingly, silencing MMP-13 did not affect RASF invasion into cartilage in vitro. Therefore both MMP-13 and MT1-MMP are involved in cartilage invasion, but their roles may differ; while MT1-MMP directly promotes RASF invasion by degrading cartilage collagen, the mechanism through which MMP-13 promotes invasion is unclear. MT1-MMP, as a cellular collagenase, also plays an essential role in angiogenesis 103 and monocyte endothelial transmigration 104,105 and thus may also promote disease through other mechanisms.

### Bone Resorption in Rheumatoid Arthritis

Bone composition consists of 40% organic and 60% inorganic components. Ninety percent of the organic component in mature

bone is an insoluble, highly cross-linked type I collagen, although type III and V collagens are also present. Other minor components in the bone matrix are leucine-rich repeat proteoglycans (decorin and biglycan) and glycoproteins such as osteopontin, osteonectin (SPARC), osteocalcin (bone Gla-protein), and thrombospondin.

Bone is resorbed by osteoclasts, and this is commonly observed at the bare zone, where pannus-like granulation tissue invades the bone marrow and destroys subchondral bone. Activated osteoclasts attach to only mineralized bone matrix. This cellmatrix contact is carried out by αvβ3 integrin of osteoclasts binding to the Arg-Gly Asp (RGD) sequence of osteopontin in the bone matrix. ECM degradation of the mineralized bone can occur only after demineralization of the bone matrix because proteinases cannot permeate the matrix components in the mineralized tissues. Matrix degradation by osteoclasts is performed in the subosteoclastic compartments, which have acidic (pH 4 to 5) and hypercalcemic (40 to 50 mM Ca2+) conditions. Under these conditions, a collagenolytic cysteine proteinase, cathepsin K, is thought to be responsible for bone resorption because of its collagenolytic activity with a broad pH optimum and selective expression in osteoclasts and giant cells of giant cell tumors. Mutations of human cathepsin K are responsible for pyknodysostosis, an autosomal recessive osteochondrodysplasia characterized by osteopetrosis and short stature. Cathepsin Kdeficient mice have a similar phenotype. Despite the importance of cathepsin K in bone resorption, osteoclastic bone resorption cannot be completely inhibited by cysteine proteinase inhibitors; it is inhibited similarly by MMP inhibitors. . MMP-9 is highly expressed in osteoclasts in normal and rheumatoid bones108 and giant cells of giant cell tumors. MMP-9 has telopeptidase activity against soluble and insoluble type I collagen and strong gelatinolytic activity.' 45,

ProMMP-9 can be activated by acid exposure and, when activated, it is proteolytically active under acidic and hypercalcemic conditions. MMP-9-deficient mice show a transient disturbance of growth plate development. Cathepsin K and MMP-9 may thus be involved in bone resorption in persons with RA. Although MT1-MMP is also expressed in osteoclasts in RA,100 evidence for its direct involvement in osteoclastic bone resorption is limited. MMP-7 may be involved in the solubilization of receptor activator of nuclear factor-kB ligand (RANKL) in the murine prostate cancer—induced osteolysis model,109 but no data are available regarding the osteoclastic bone resorption in RA.

For the treatment of osteoporosis and destructive bone diseases, bisphosphonates that reduce bone turnover by inhibiting the boneresorbing activity of mature osteoclasts are commonly utilized. Denosumab, a human monoclonal antibody against RANKL, has been approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration and used to treat osteoporosis in patients with RA. Cathepsin K inhibitors were considered promising drugs for the treatment of post-menopausal osteoporosis because the reduction of osteoclast-stimulated bone formation is less compared with antibone resorptive drugs such as bisphosphonates. These inhibitors were also expected to be useful for treating osteoporosis in persons with RA. The drug went to phase III clinical trial and effectively increased bone densities. However, it also increased the risk of stroke, and the development of this inhibitor was discontinued. A detailed mechanism of increased incidence of stroke upon cathepsin K inhibition is not clear, but it is likely to be due to other roles of cathepsin K.

### Cartilage Degradation in Osteoarthritis

In osteoarthritis, the major cell type that produces cartilagedegrading enzymes is thought to be chondrocytes. In the early

stage of the disease, aggrecan degradation proceeds before collagen degradation, which is considered crucial for the disease to develop further. A number of MMPs, including MMP-1, 11 2,112,113 3, 114 7,115 8,111 9,113 and 1312,111and MT1-MMP, 0112 are expressed in osteoarthritic cartilage. MMP-3 and 7 and MT1-MMP are localized to chondrocytes in the proteoglycan-depleted zone of osteoarthritic cartilage, and the levels of their staining correlate directly with the histologic Mankin score.112, Among the collagenolytic MMPs, MMP-13 is considered the key enzyme in the degradation of cartilage collagen, as no cartilage collagen degradation was observed in the mice lacking MMP-13 in the DMM (surgical destabilization of the medial meniscus) OA model. Since MT1- MMP activates proMMP-13 on the cell surface, MT1-MMP may play a key role in cartilage collagen degradation through the activation of proMMP-13.

Recently it has been suggested that neutrophils in syno- 117-120 In addivial fluid may contribute to OA pathogenesis. tion, it was found that neutrophil elastase efficiently activates proMMP-13, which in turn inactivates alpha-1 anti-trypsin. As already described, MMP-13 is thought to be a major cartilage collagen-degrading enzyme in OA, and neutrophil elastase-mediated proMMP-13 activation becomes an additional pathway that leads to cartilage collagen degradation.

Besides neutrophil elastase, a type-II transmembrane serine proteinase, matriptase, played a role in the progression of OA.121, Matriptase was upregulated in OA cartilage. Matriptase does not degrade cartilage ECM components by itself, but the addition of

recombinant matriptase to human cartilage induced collagen degradation via activation of protease-activated receptor 2 (PAR2). Matriptase-activated PAR2 signaling induced MMP-1, 3, and 13 expression in chondrocytes and caused collagen release from cartilage in an MMP-dependent manner. Furthermore, matriptase activated proMMP-1 and 3.122 Thus matriptase may be an initiator of cartilage degradation in OA.

The major aggrecan-degrading proteinases include MMPs and ADAMTSs, but ADAMTSs, especially ADAMTS5, is believed to play a crucial role. ADAMTS5 null mice, but not ADAMTS4 null mice, were resistant to aggrecan degradation in the DMM model. Without ADAMTS5-dependent aggrecan degradation, cartilage tissue was completely protected. Thus aggrecan degradation needs to occur before further cartilage destruction can occur, and ADAMTS5 is likely the key enzyme during the early stage of cartilage degradation in OA. The biochemical property of ADAMTS5 also supports this notion. Full-length ADAMTS5 possesses 33-fold more potent aggrecanase activity than full-length ADAMTS4 and 600-fold higher activity compared with truncated ADAMTS4.85, In human osteoarthritic cartilage, ADAMTS4 can be induced by IL-1 and TNF, whereas ADAMTS5 expression is constitutive. It has been found that constitutively expressed ADAMTS5, together with MMP-13, is constantly downregulated by low-density LRP-1-mediated endocytosis in normal cartilage, which explains the reason why ADAMTS5 protein is difficult to detect in normal tissue (Fig. 8.6). In human OA cartilage, LRP-1 is shed by MT1-MMP and ADAM17, which are highly

upregulated in chondrocytes, causing a deficit in endocytic regulation of ADAMTS5 and MMP-13 (Fig. 8.6). Inhibition of LRP-1 shedding by highly selective inhibitors of MT1-MMP and ADAM17 in OA cartilage was found to reverse both aggrecan and cartilage degradation in the tissue,125 suggesting that ADAMTS5mediated aggrecan degradation is due to LRP-1 shedding, and local inhibition of MT1-MMP and ADAM17 may be an attractive potential therapeutic strategy. In the murine OA model, matriptase also played a role in LRP-1 shedding, resulting in increased aggrecan release. Together with the effect of matriptase in indirect cartilage collagen release, matriptase may be considered a potential therapeutic target.

### Conclusion

ECM molecules are crucial structural components for all organs. They fill the gaps between cells, provide th e structure, separate cellular compartments, provide survival signals, act as scaffolding and cues for migrating and differentiating cells, and act as a pool of growth factors. Proteinases play crucial roles in the degradation of ECM components, as described in this chapter. Excess activities of these proteinases cause ECM degradation, leading to tissue destruction and organ malfunction. RA and OA are diseases with joint tissue malfunction, and thus inhibition of these proteolytic enzymes may prevent joint damage. However, because of their physiologic roles, careful consideration of the consequence of proteinase inhibition is essential. In the 1990s, it was presumed that MMPs would be good therapeutic targets for cancer and arthritis. Many pharmaceutical companies developed broad-spectrum, active site-targeting small molecular inhibitors. However, all clinical trials failed due to lack of efficacy and/or significant side effects, designated "musculoskeletal syndrome."89, Th ese MMP inhibitors inhibit most of the 62 metalloendopeptidases in humans, and it is believed that the broad-spectrum nature of the inhibitors is the culprit of the failure. Thus it appears crucial that for clinical efficacy and acceptable toxicity, it will be essential to identify appropriate target enzymes and develop highly selective inhibitors.89, Further understanding of the biochemical properties, regulatory mechanisms, and pathophysiological roles of these proteolytic enzymes is thus important not only to deepen our knowledge but also for the development of novel therapeutic strategies in the future.

# Dendritic Cells

### KEY POINTS

### Introduction

In 1973 Ralph Steinman and Zanvil Cohn identified a new cell type in murine splenic cultures. They described these as adherent nucleated cells with multiple pseudopods. Owing to their unique morphology, they named them dendritic cells (DCs). A decade later, in 1983, Steinman led another study demonstrating that DC depletion completely ablated the stimulatory capacity in murine mixed lymphocyte reactions. Further research revealed that DCs are specialized in acquiring and presenting antigens to T cells and have superior capacity over other antigen-presenting cells (APCs) in activating cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs).3, Moreover, a

small number of DCs can directly or indirectly activate a large number of T cells, B cells, natural killer (NK) cells, and NK T cells, thus improving the efficiency of the immune response.5-7 Furthermore, DCs express a plethora of activating and co-stimulatory receptors and ligands. As such it is no surprise that DCs are often referred to as "nature's adjuvants."

Under normal circumstances DCs exist in an immature form, populating practically every tissue in the body. DCs are activated upon encountering pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) or danger-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs), which leads to a process of "maturation" that involves changes in the DC phenotype, antigen acquisition capacity, migration, and an ability to traffic to draining lymph nodes, where they prime cellular and humoral adaptive immune responses. Upon maturation, DCs process antigens (self and non-self) and then present them to antigen-specific adaptive immune cells (T cells and B cells) to induce immune responses to contain diseases such as cancer or infections but also to maintain tolerance to self-antigens. This chapter provides our current understanding of DC ontogeny and function, as well as DCs' potential in clinical applications as immunotherapeutic agents.

### Dendritic Cell Subsets and Development

DCs have been classified into subsets based on their location, function, and origin. It is currently believed that all DC subsets undergo four stages of development, namely hematopoietic precursors, DC precursors (pre-DC), immature DCs, and mature DCs. Pre-DCs are continuously produced at a steady rate in a pathogen-independent manner from CD34+ hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) within the bone marrow. Fms-like tyrosine kinase-3 ligand (Flt-3-L) and granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF) represent key DC growth and differentiation factors. The development of stromal cell culture systems comprised of co-cultures of cord blood isolated CD34+ HSCs and murine bone marrow stromal cells (OP9 cells) in the presence of factors such as stem cell factor (SCF), GM-CSF, and Flt3L have led to the identification of definitive pre-DCs that give rise to DC subsets found in the blood.10, In humans, all DCs originate from granulocyte monocyte dendritic cell precursors (GMDPs). Emerging evidence suggests that based on IRF8 expression levels, GMDPs may give rise to hitherto undefined distinct lineages. IRF8high GMDPs differentiate into common dendritic cell progenitor (CDP), while IRF8low cells lead to pre-DC3 and common monocyte precursors (CmoP), although it should be noted that

the validity of DC3 as a unique DC subset is still not completely established. The CDPs differentiate into pre-DCs that migrate out of the bone marrow and give rise to two classical DC subsets, the conventional DCs (cDCs) and plasmacytoid DCs (pDCs), pre- DC3s give rise to the DC3 subset, whereas the CmoPs differentiate into monocytes and eventually inflammatory DCs (iDCs), found in blood (Fig. 9.1).11,

For ex vivo studies and phenotyping in humans, DCs are identified as cells lacking the expression of lineage markers CD3 (T cell marker), CD19, and CD20 (B cell markers), CD14 (monocytic marker), and CD56 (NK cell marker) and as being positive for human leukocyte antigen, DR subregion (HLA-DR). Terminally differentiated DCs are now broadly classified into four subsets, namely cDCs, pDCs, DC3, and iDCs. Notably most scholars now agree that Langerhans cells (LCs) no longer classify as bona fide DCs, falling into the tissue macrophage category instead.13,15

### Conventional Dendritic Cells

cDCs comprise two subsets in humans and mice: cDCl and cDC2 (see Fig. 9.1). In humans, cDC1s are commonly phenotyped by surface expression of CD11c, HLA-DR, CD26, XCR1, Clec9A, CADM1, CD141, and BTLA4 (Fig. 9.2), while murine cDC1s express CD8a and/or CD103. The cDC2 cells in humans are typically CD1c+, HLA-DR, CD135, Dec205, Clec10a, and FCER1A, and they express high CD11c, CD11b, and CD172a (see Fig. 9.2), while in mice they are CD4+ and CD11b+. Although both cDC1 and cDC2 can activate CD4+ and CD8+ T cells, several key differences distinguish cDC1s from cDC2s. For instance, cDC1s are considered more adept at antigen crosspresentation and at CD8+ T cell activation than any other APCs, including cDC2s. Cross-presentation is a unique antigen-presentation pathway that allows APCs to present exogenous antigens on major histocompatibility complex class I (MHC-I) molecules;

this pathway is described in detail later. Second, although cDC1 can be found in blood and tissues in small numbers, these cells are thought to primarily reside in the lymph node, while the cDC2s are migratory cells, outnumbering cDC1s in peripheral tissues by several fold.

A key difference between DCs is the array of pattern recognition receptors (PRRs) expressed by each subset. PRRs are an important class of receptors that recognize PAMPs (expressed by microorganisms) or DAMPs (secreted by damaged cells). PRRs include secreted receptors such as MBL, CRP, SAP, LBP; cellsurface receptors like Toll-like receptors (TLRs1/2/4/5/6), CD14, MMR, MSR, MARCO, and intra-cellular receptors such as TLRs3/7/8/9, RIG-I, MDA5, STING, DAI, AIM2, and NOD receptors. cDC1s primarily express TLR3 and TLR8 and in response to their stimulation secrete interleukin (IL)-12, as well as type III interferons. By contrast, cDC2s express and respond to a wider range of TLRs.18,

The cDC1 and cDC2 cells exert distinct transcriptional programs. cDC1s express interferon response element-8 (IRF8), Batf3, Bcl16, and Flt3, whereas the cDC2s express IRF4, Csl, and Klf4.9, NOTCH signaling is a unique cell-to-cell signaling pathway that controls development of several immune cells including DCs. Stimulation of transmembrane NOTCH receptors by Delta-like ligands (DLL) 1, 3, and 4, or Jagged ligands (Jagged 1 and 2), leads to γ-secretase—driven NOTCH receptor cleavage. This event is followed by nuclear translocation of NOTCH intracellular domain and interaction with the transcription factor Csl (or RBPJ in mice). Overall, this pathway facilitates cellular development, maintenance, and differentiation programs. The role of NOTCH signaling in DC differentiation has remained controversial with different research models yielding conflicting reports. However, two independent groups confirmed the importance of NOTCH signaling in DC programming. Using the OP9 feeder culture system, NOTCH-2 signaling was shown to regulate pDC versus cDC differentiation from the precursor cells in both mice and humans.10, Specifically, in the context of human cells, one study demonstrated that expanding CD34+ cells (from either human cord blood or peripheral blood mononuclear cells [PBMCs]) with Flt3L, S-CSF, IL-7, and thrombopoietin (TPO) for 7 days followed by co-culture with OP9 cells yielded a high number of pDCs but not many cDC1s. However, co-culturing CD34+ cells with a mixture of OP9 and OP9_DLL1 cells (OP9 cells expressing NOTCH ligand DLL1) remarkably increased the yield of cDC1s while moderately inhibiting the yield of pDCs.

These NOTCH-dependent cDC1 cells were functionally and transcriptionally similar to cDC1s found in blood, suggesting the significance of NOTCH signaling for cDC1 differentiation in vivo. Other studies in murine models have emphasized the role of NOTCH signaling in cDC2 development, particularly in context of T follicular cell activation and induction of B cell response during infection.

Due to their phenotypic similarity with monocytes and cDC2s, such as CD14 and CD1c expression, respectively, DC3 cells initially were not conferred bona fide DC status.12, In 2020 two groups displayed that while DC3 subset could be differentiated in culture systems from precursor stem cells, they could not be derived from another DC subset, including DC2s. Further, using single-cell sequencing, they defined discreet DC3 ontogeny, originating in a distinct IRF8low, CD123low, and Cleacl2A+ GMPDs. In our current understanding, DC3s are phenotypically defined by presence of CD1c, CD163, and absence of CD5. Further DC3s could express CD14 or not depending on their differentiation status. Functionally, DC3s can activate T cells like other DC subsets, but there is no evidence yet ascribing a "specialized" function to DC3s.

### Plasmacytoid Dendritic Cells

pDCs are distinguished by expression of CD123, CD303, CD304, and lack of CD11c (see Fig. 9.2) and functionally characterized by type I interferon production upon viral stimulation. This response is primarily enabled by high expression of TLR7 and TLR9 on pDCs and their ability to rapidly present intra-cellular antigens, like those derived from viruses, to CD8+ T cells.27, The geospatial distribution of pDCs is more restricted than cDCs. Although small numbers of pDCs can been found in blood and tissues such as nasal mucosa and tonsils, pDCs primarily populate T cell areas of lymphoid tissues.

Interestingly, upon activation, pDCs differentiate into cells bearing similar characteristics to activated cDCs (such as high expression of MHC class II molecules and the capacity to prime naive T cells) but express low levels of CD1 1c and lack the typical myeloid markers.30, All of these studies highlight the complexity and plasticity of DC development. Furthermore, based on findings drawn from recent lineage tracing studies and in depth functional analysis, researchers are now suggesting that pDCs are in fact not DCs and should be reclassification as innate lymphocytes.

### Inflammatory Dendritic Cells

iDCs arise from monocytic precursors during infection and inflammation in blood and migrate to the site of inflammation. iDCs are characterized by surface expression of CD1c; high expression of CD11c, CD11b, CD172a, CD14, and CD1c (see Fig. 9.2); and MCSFR and ZBTB46 as transcription factors. iDCs can process and present antigens to both CD4+ and CD8+ T cells; however, their exact functional profile in vivo remains undetermined. It is postulated that the monocyte-derived dendritic cells (Fig. 9.3), used in most DC-based cell therapy vaccines, closely resemble the in vivo iDCs. Monocyte-derived DCs (moDCs) are generated from monocytes isolated from patient blood, and ex vivo differentiated into immature DCs under the influence of granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF) and IL-4.34

### Summary of Developments in Dendritic Cell Classification

### Emergence of DC3 Subset

With the growing use of high-throughput single-cell sequencing, several groups have characterized DC subgroups found in blood and tissue. One such early study24 using single-cell RNA sequencing analyzed blood DCs with unbiased gene clustering and identified six DC subsets (DC1 to DC6). Among these, the DC1 and DC6 subsets were found to correspond with predefined cDC1 and pDC subsets. The DC4 subset, negative for both CD141 and CD1c, was found enriched for CD16 and in genes involved in type I interferon secretion and response to virus. The DC2 (CD1c+_A) and DC3 (CD1c+_B) subsets were identified as two unique clusters under the cDC2 subset. Both subsets expressed CD1c, CD11b, and CD11c, but unlike DC2, the DC3 subset was found enriched for CD14 and acute and chronic inflammatory gene set. Recently, using in vitro culture systems, the distinct ontogeny of DC3 subset was established12,25,26 justifying a bona fide DC subclass status for DC3s. However, the exact functions of these cells in health and disease in vivo is not yet known. In future detailed and direct comparisons of these subsets will reveal whether DC3 may maintain its bona fide DC subset status.

### Transitional AS-DC Subset

In the single-cell RNA sequencing analysis,24 a novel but small subset, DC5, was also identified that did not cluster with any other blood DC subset and could be identified by the expression of Axl and Siglec6, earning the name AS-DC. Despite sharing many markers with pDCs, AS-DCs were functionally, phenotypically, and morphologically distinct from pDCs. Using time of flight mass cytometry (CyToF), the presence

of AS-DCs was corroborated in humans and mice by another group, although the murine AS-DC functional counterparts did not express Axl.35, However, ontogeny of AS-DCs has not been confirmed. Further, AS-DCs differentiate into cDC2s in culture, indicating that these cells may represent a transient cell 12,14 state.

### Legitimacy of pDCs

Based on findings drawn from recent lineage tracing studies and in-depth functional analysis, researchers are now suggesting that pDCs are in fact not DCs and should be reclassified as innate lymphocytes.

### Removal of LCs From DC Classification

LCs, characterized by Langerin and Birbeck granules, were initially classified as DCs due to their function as APCs and their capacity for migrating to lymph nodes and inducing T cell activation. However, recent developments in fate-mapping studies suggest that LCs originate from the yolk sac progenitors and the fetal liver and differentiate into specialized tissue resident macrophages. 37,

In addition to subsets mentioned previously, other groups, over the years, have described atypical DC subsets that do not identify with any classical DC subset. These include a small pool of migratory precursor cells that originate from the CDPs in the bone marrow and can only differentiate into either CDlc+ or CD141+ cDCs. A group of CD103+ DCs in the intestinal LNs induces expression of gut homing receptor, CCR9 on T cell and B cells through a retinoic acid receptor—dependent mechanism. Furthermore, intestinal CD103 DCs have been shown to process dietary vitamin A into retinoic acid to support the differentiation of gut-homing FoxP3+ regulatory T cells (Tregs).40,41

### Dendritic Cell Maturation and Activation

DC maturation is a complex process that relies on key functional properties, such as activation by environmental sensing, antigen uptake, processing and presentation, migration, and T cell stimulation. The DC process of maturation is related to their environment and is therefore heterogeneous. It confers specific and distinctive functional properties to different DC subsets.

DC maturation can be prompted by several activating cues such as pathogenor non-pathogen-derived factors, cellular debris, stress signals, receptorligand interaction, and so on and so forth. In the steady state, cDCs are in a quiescent state that is characterized by low surface expression of MHC molecules and co-stimulatory molecules. Immunogenic conditioning of cDCs induces expression of class I and II MHCs; T cell co-stimulatory molecules, such as CD80 and CD86; cytokines (e.g., TNF, IL-12, IL-18); and chemokines (e.g., RANTES, MIP-1α, IP-10). Additional changes include induction of CCR7, CCL19, and CCL21; migration to follicular T cell—enriched zones in lymphoid organs; and downregulation of receptors that serve to retain DCs at the site of activation (such as receptors for CCL3, CCL4 and CCL5). Upon antigen uptake, the DCs are programmed to dampen antigen acquisition and promote antigen processing and presentation. DCs acquire the ability to induce clonal expansion and differentiation of antigen-specific naive T cells into effector T cells.

The activation and maturation event also polarizes the DCs toward a tolerogenic or immunogenic phenotype. Based on their environmental conditioning, DCs regulate the adaptation of T cell polarization to the specific nature of the stimuli. For example, activation of DCs in the absence of help from CD4+ T cells,

activation with suboptimal or prolonged innate stimuli, or maturation in response to stimuli like thymic stromal lymphopoietin (TSLP), which leads to induction of co-stimulatory molecules but does not induce an inflammatory cytokine response, can all lead to tolerogenic DCs. In the steady state, tolerogenic DCs are thought to present self-antigen and promote peripheral tolerance. However, in events of tumorigenesis or infection, tolerogenic DCs promote tumor evasion and inhibit pathogen clearance, respectively. Indeed, tolerogenic DCs have often been observed in cases of chronic activation such as in cancer. Moreover, several pathogens have developed specific mechanisms of immune evasion via induction of tolerogenic DCs.

Activation allows immature DCs to acquire a diverse array of antigens from pathogens, exosomes, or apoptotic cells, etc. Pathways of antigen acquisition include, micropinocytosis, macropinocytosis, receptor-mediated endocytosis, and phagocytosis. Activation and maturation via PRRs is a key initial step in antigen acquisition, processing, and presentation.

### Pattern-Recognition Receptors and Dendritic Cell Maturation

DCs sense their environment through a broad panel of PRRs. PRRs are highly conserved innate immune receptors that detect PAMPs or endogenous DAMPs. PRRs are extremely diverse, detecting a wide range of molecular patterns, including proteins, lipids, carbohydrates, nucleic acids, and mineral crystals. PRRs include the Toll-like receptors (TLRs), the C-type lectin receptors (CLRs), the Nod-like receptors (NLRs), the retinoic acidinducible gene (RIG)-Ilike receptors (RLRs), the scavenger receptors (SRs), the integrins, and others such as the Ig Fc receptors (FcRs). Triggering of PRRs such as TLRs or C-type lectins on DCs is thought to be critical for their functional maturation and the priming of T cell responses to infection, therefore coupling innate and adaptive immunity.

### RLRs and Intra-cellular DNA Sensors

RIG-I and MDA5 RNA helicases are intra-cellularly expressed PRRs involved in the recognition of intra-cellular RNA upon viral infection,46 while cGAS and AIM2 receptors recognize intracellular DNA.

### TLRS

TLRs are a prominent class of PRRs that respond to PAMPs such as peptidoglycan, lipopolysaccharide (LPS), and flagellin and regulate DC functions. TLRs can be grouped into two subfamilies based on their subcellular localization: the TLRs expressed on the cell surface (in humans and mice, TLR1, TLR2, TLR5, and TLR6, restricted to humans, TLR10 [a pseudogene in mice] and restricted to mice, TLR11, TLR12, and TLR13) and those localized to specialized endosomal compartments (TLR3, TLR7, TLR8, and TLR9). Finally, TLR4 can localize both sites. Each DC subset expresses distinct panels of TLRs, which modulate their functional specialization. Notably, TLR10 is a cell surface receptor expressed on human cDCs. However, it lacks intra-cellular signaling mechanisms, and its ligands and exact functions are yet unknown. Human pDCs express high levels of nucleic acid-specific TLRs such as TLR7 and TLR9. TLR7 and TLR9 detect single-stranded RNA (ssRNA) and unmethylated cytosine—phosphatidyl—guanine (CpG) DNA, respectively, which are motifs usually found in both bacteria

and viruses. TLR8 also recognizes bacterial ssRNA. Human cDC2s express mostly TLR1 through TLR8, whereas the CD141+ cDCs express TLR3 and TLR7/8 and low levels of TLR1 and TLR2. Activation of DCs in response to binding of TLR agonists is controlled by signaling through the Toll/IL-1 receptor (TIR) domain present in the cytoplasmic domain of TLRs. TLR stimulation by self and non-self antigens can regulate cytokines such as TNF, IL-12, IL-6, IL-23, and IL-17, which have important roles in the polarization of T helper cell subsets during priming by DCs and thus the functional consequences of DC activation. 16,26,48

### NLRs

Another important inflammatory signaling circuit governed by PRRs is the inflammasome pathway. The inflammasome is a multiprotein complex that can be activated through NLRs like NLRP3, NLRC4, or NLRP1 through PAMPs (such as pore-forming toxins, RNA and DNA, flagellin, β-glucans, and zymosan) or DAMPs (such as adenosine triphosphate [ATP], uric acid crystals, amyloid β, alum, silica, and asbestos). Inflammasome activation induces the activation of key inflammatory cytokines, such as IL-1β and IL-18, and regulates an inflammatory cell death pathway known as pyroptosis. Each NLR regulates a unique inflammasome activation cascade. NLRP3 inflammasome is activated in a two-step process. The frst step requires TLR2or TLR4-driven upregulation of key inflammasome components, namely NLRP3, ASC, pro-IL-1β, and pro- IL-18. The second step involves NLRP3 activation, assembly of the inflammasome complex, caspase-1 cleavage, and subsequent release of cytokines and possibly the induction of pyroptosis. Notably human cDC1s do not express many NLRs and lack Caspase-1, a key mediator of inflammasome pathway. 16,50

### CLRs

C-type lectins are another family of PRRs that recognize sugar motifs in a calcium-dependent manner through their carbohydrate recognition functional domain. The repertoire of CLR expression varies among the different DC subsets and is tightly regulated by the interactions with the environment. CLRs are involved in endocytosis, phagocytosis, antigen processing, and presentation through regular class II MHC or by class I MHC cross-presentation. Several CLRs, such as DEC205, mannose receptor (MR), and DC immunoreceptor (DCIR), have been shown to contribute to the cross-presentation of endocytosed antigens. DC-SIGN, a CLR expressed on many DCs, is well known for interacting with pathogens like HIV-1 and 2, simian immunodeficiency virus (SIV), etc. BDCA-2 expressed by pDCs shares similar immunomodulatory properties as DEC-205 and has been targeted by recombinant antigens bound to antibodies in order to modulate DC function. This is accomplished by inducing antigen-specific tolerance or immune stimulation with the addition of a maturation signal. Finally, many CLRs recognize ligands expressed by apoptotic or necrotic cells and participate in the uptake of these dead cells by DCs, although most of the clearing process is mediated by neutrophils and macrophages. DNRG1 (CLEC9a), the expression of which is restricted to CD141+ DC in humans, recognizes F-actin, which is expressed at the surface of necrotic cells. This interaction induces immunogenic responses and promotes the cross-presentation of processed necrotic antigens on class I MHC. Indeed, CLEC9a has been shown to engage ligands derived from dead cells and initiate a signaling cascade

that results in rupture of phagosomes containing dead cell debris, thus promoting cross-presentation of exogenous antigens. Further, CLEC9a is implicated in dampening inflammation through controlling neutrophil infiltration52 In the same way, macrophageinducible C-type lectin (MINCLE), which is another CLR that recognizes necrotic cell, can induce inflammatory responses.

### Fc Receptors

FcRs, expressed by many immune cells, are important in regulation of immune responses to immune complexes composed of antigen bound to antibody and sometimes to components of the complement system. DCs express activating receptors FcγRI, FcγRIIA, FcγRIIIA, and inhibitory receptor FcγRIIB. Infected cells or pathogens coated with IgG activate FcγRmediated clearance by antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity (ADCC) or phagocytosis and/or indirectly through the release of cytokines.

In addition to the receptors mentioned above, SRs like CD36, CD-205, and LOX-1, to name a few, promote DC activation and maturation. These receptors also regulate multiple cellular functions like pathogen and apoptotic cell clearance. For example, CD36 on DCs detects phospholipid phosphatidylserine on apoptotic cells and facilitates apoptotic cell clearance. LOX-1 promotes DC activation by oxidized low-density lipoprotein (LDL) and contributes to artheroscelorosis. Complement receptors on DCs regulate opsonization of pathogens and dying cells. DCs also express receptors that specifically bind pathogens like CD4, CCR5, and CXCR4 that bind HIV. Other receptors aid in activating atypical immune cells. For example, the CD1 family of receptors allow DCs to present antigens such as sphingolipids, sulfatides, and glycosphingolipids to activate γδT cells and NK T cells. Hence, many distinct families of receptors adorn and regulate DC function.

Over the past decade, it has become evident that DC activation, especially through TLRs, significantly influences not just antigen acquisition but also the process of antigen presentation. TLR-induced DC activation induces an innate immune response conducive to micropinocytic antigen uptake but only transiently, followed by a near cessation of antigen uptake. Stimulation of TLR4 on DCs by LPS is also a mechanism through which DCs select the most immunogenic antigen for presentation.57-59 The role of TLRs in antigen presentation and processing is discussed below.

### Antigen Processing and Presentation

DCs are specialized in antigen processing and can efficiently present endogenous and exogenous antigens in both class I and II MHC contexts. This activity is influenced by the maturation and activation status of the DC, which promotes phagolysosome maturation, peptide processing, peptide macropinocytosis, and DC metabolism to promote antigen processing and presentation of antigens by class I MHC and class II MHC, as well as lipid presentation by CD1 molecules.

### Major Histocompatibility Complex Class I Antigen Presentation

DCs express MHC-I molecules on their cell surface bearing selfor non-self peptides derived from the cytosol. These peptides are predominantly generated from ubiquitinated nascent,

misfolded, and neosynthesized defective self-proteins or defective ribosomal products (DRiPs). In the cytoplasm, the cytosolic proteasome, comprised of interferon regulated PA28 proteasome activator and leucine aminopeptidase, cleaves these proteins into peptides of appropriate length for presentation on MHC class I molecules.60, Interestingly, DC maturation has been shown to enhance antigen processing through upregulation of such immune proteosomes. After being processed in the cytoplasm, the trimmed peptides are translocated to the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) through the transporter associated with antigen processing (TAP) and further shortened to 8to 9-mer peptides, an optimal length for loading onto MHC-I (Fig. 9.4). This shortening of peptides in the ER is performed by ER aminopeptidase-1 (ERAP-1). Once a stable MHC-Iantigen complex is formed, it is routed to the cell surface.

### Cross-Presentation

DCs have the unique capacity to acquire antigens exogenously, internalize them, and process them for presentation on MHC-I molecules. This property is atypical because, in most cells, class I MHC molecules exclusively present endogenous proteins. Although the precise mechanism of cross-presentation remains controversial, it is well established that DCs use this process to activate CD8+ T cells. DCs acquire antigens by endocytosis in the form of apoptotic cells, necrotic cells, antibody-opsonized cells, immune complexes, heat shock proteins, and exosomes and even by nibbling of live cells. 62, Two main intra-cellular pathways, the cytosolic and the vacuolar pathways, traffic exogenous antigens from phagolysosomal compartments to the ER for cross-presentation (seeFig. 9.4).

In the cytosolic pathway (also referred to as the endosome-tocytosol pathway), antigens are transferred to the cytoplasm from the endosomal compartment and processed by the cytosolic proteasome. Thereafter the peptides are transported back into the endosome or to the ER, where they are loaded onto MHC-I molecules. The shuttling of antigenic peptides is facilitated by TAP. MHC-I molecules, however, need to be present in the ER or endosomes to be available for antigen loading. For this, either newly assembled MHC-I molecules are transported into the ER, also aided by TAP,66 or cell surface—expressed MHC-I complexes are recycled back into the endosome for reloadinge . (see Fig. 9.4). This pathway is sensitive to proteasome inhibitors, suggesting that antigenic proteins access the cytosol and are degraded by proteasomes. However, whether the peptide loading occurs via the classical MHC-I pathway described previously or in endocytic compartments remains to be fully determined.

Antigen processing and loading through the vacuolar pathway is believed to occur in the endocytic compartments. This conclusion stems from the observations that inhibition of lysosomal proteolysis inhibits antigen presentation via this pathway, whereas inhibition of cytosolic proteasomes has no effect (see Fig. 9.4). While some evidence suggests that cytosolic pathway may be the predominant antigen processing mechanism here, there is no clear indication as to the relative contribution of the cytosolic pathway over the vacuolar pathway. Data from several groups indicate that DCs in general and specific DC subsets such as the CD8α+ DCs in mice and DC1s in humans are more specialized for cross-presentation than other APCs. Recently, progress has been made in better understanding the cross-talk between the different cellular compartments

and the role of TLRs in regulating cross-presentation. One group67 identified an important role in DCs for communication between the endosomal recycling compartment (ERC), which is a key reservoir of class I MHC molecules, and the phagosome in cross-presentation. Trafficking from the ERC to phagosomes is controlled by the TLR-MyD88-IKK2 pathway, which stabilizes membrane interactions between the phagosome and the ERC, ensuring that ERC-deployed class I MHCs are specifically routed to phagosomes engaged in TLR signaling. On the other hand, the class I MHC peptide-loading complex (PLC) is recruited from another subcellular compartment, the ER and Golgi intermediate compartment (ERGIC), in a TLR-independent manner. The highly coordinated trafficking from ERC and ERGIC delivers essential components for crosspresentation to phagosomes during infection, and control of the ERC pathway by TLR signals favors phagosomes that contain microbial proteins for cross-presentation in the context of TLR-primed T cell co-stimulation.

Interestingly, DCs have been documented to acquire complete functional MHC-Iantigen complex from a donor cell and decorate on their own (recipient) cell surface. This mode of antigen presentation has been coined "cross-dressing" and is postulated to boost a memory-like response in previously primed CD8+ T cells.

### Major Histocompatibility Class II Antigen Presentation

While all nucleated cells express MHC-I, only APCs express MHC-II. MHC-II presents short peptides to activate CD4+ T cells. Class II MHCa/β heterodimers rely on a specialized type II transmembrane chaperone protein, the invariant chain (Ii), for stable assembly in the ER. Assembled class II MHC molecules are transported and concentrated in multivesicular and multilamellar late endosomal compartments called class II MHC-containing compartments (MIICs). Antigens for MHC-II loading are acquired by APCs through macropinocytosis, receptor-mediated endocytosis, phagocytosis, and autophagy. Antigens are retained within late endosomes or phagosomes before fusing with lysosomes to form phagolysosomes.
