Much less is known regarding the plasticity of the other subsets of recruited macrophages during inflammation/infection, and hence their fate upon return to tissue homeostasis. Further fate-mapping studies are required to determine whether these die to make room for the expanding resident macrophage population or if these can also convert into a resident phenotype (Fig. 10.2).

### Studying Mononuclear Phagocyte Heterogeneity at Single-Cell Resolution

Now that we know there are likely many subsets of macrophages present, especially in the inflamed, infected, or injured tissue, how can we better understand them? Named Method of the Year in 2013 by Nature Methods,58 single-cell technologies, including scRNA-seq, 59,60 cellular indexing of transcriptomes and epitopes by sequencing (CITE-seq),61,62 cytometry by time of flight mass spectrometry (CyTOF),63 single-cell assay for transposase-accessible chromatin using sequencing (ATAC-seq),64 and the more recent spatial transcriptomics and spatial multiplex proteomics technologies65 are allowing the distinct subsets to be distinguished and insights into the functional heterogeneity of these cells to be obtained (Fig. 10.3). There are many distinct scRNA-seq methods including plate-based and droplet-based options (reviewed in refs 59, 60). These methods allow for the unbiased profiling of individual cells at the level of the transcriptome, enabling the discovery of new cell subsets or activation states. This profiling is at the level of the transcriptome, but, of course, mRNA and protein expression do not always align. Therefore any potential subsets and functions identified still must be validated at the protein level. This can be done using conventional flow cytometry (now capable of measuring ~30 parameters simultaneously) or using spectral flow cytometry or CyTOF methods, which enable more parameters to be profiled simultaneously. The downside of CyTOF approaches is that the cells are destroyed in the process, preventing any downstream sorting of the cells and functional studies. This is not the case with either spectral or conventional flow cytometry, making these the preferred methods to also allow biologic assessment of the subsets identified after fluorescence-activated cell sorting.

Regardless of which method is chosen, however, the first step is to predict from the transcriptomic data which mRNAs encode surface proteins that can be used to identify the cells and which antibodies against these epitopes are most likely to work (Fig. 10.3). As one can imagine, this can be an expensive and time-consuming endeavor. This is where performing CITE-seq instead of traditional scRNA-seq can be advantageous.61, This technology, also called REAP-seq, allows the simultaneous profiling of transcriptomes and epitopes using barcoded antibodies. These are the same antibodies that would be used for flow cytometry or CyTOF, except, instead of being labeled with fluorescent tags (flow cytometry) or heavy metals (CyTOF), they are labeled with barcodes. This prevents any issues with compensation, meaning multiple antibodies (>200) can be combined in one experiment, providing an unprecedented insight into the best antibodies to distinguish between subsets identified using the transcriptome data or a combination of the protein and transcript data when using algorithms such as TotalVI66 to analyze the data simultaneously. A recent study employing CITE-seq in the murine and human liver has, in one step, been able to identify the distinct subsets of cells present and provide gating strategies to isolate each of them. Moreover, these strategies were subsequently validated with conventional flow cytometry, demonstrating the power of this technology.

As for scRNA-seq approaches, being able to assess the chromatin state of cells at single-cell resolution using scATAC-seq is also enabling a clearer picture of cellular heterogeneity in any given tissue. This also allows an assessment of how these changes are controlled through prediction of the transcription factors regulating the gene expression profiles. Moreover, multiome assays have recently been developed allowing the simultaneous profiling of the transcriptome (scRNA-seq) and chromatin state (scATACseq). Note that, in these assays, RNA is isolated only from nuclei, which may have an effect on the transcripts isolated, as recently described for the liver. However, working with nuclei simplifies the process due to the ability to work with frozen tissue. It is also worth noting that many new kits are currently in development that aim to allow scRNA-seq to be performed on fixed tissues, which will allow the libraries of legacy clinical material to finally be profiled.

These approaches all make use of single-cell or single-nuclei suspensions. This means that the tissue must be disrupted prior to the analysis. As such, this prevents any assessment of spatial patterns the identified cell types may follow, which may also limit our ability to accurately define cell types/states. To overcome this issue, recently spatial transcriptomics methods have been applied. These technologies allow the transcriptome to be assessed in situ on tissue sections, meaning tissue architecture and hence spatial arrangement can be assessed (Fig. 10.3). There are many options ranging from unbiased whole transcriptome profiling (not yet at single-cell resolution) to single-cell approaches where only a selected number of transcripts (currently up to approximately 300) are detected. It is, however, important to mention that currently the bottleneck in these technologies (aside from price) is in data analysis, primarily cell segmentation. mRNA detection is punctate, so the question becomes how to decide to which cell the mRNA expression belongs. Approaches currently taken include assigning the mRNA to the nearest nuclei or generating in silico cells based on a given radius around the nuclei. While such approaches work for homogeneous round cells like T cells, this is not easy to do with macrophages, which are often elongated instead of round and extend many processes in different directions. One way to overcome this is to use surface markers for the cells to be able to segment the cells correctly. The combination of mRNA and protein measurements, however, remains tricky with the methods used to preserve mRNA often destroying epitopes, while methods used to preserve epitopes do not preserve mRNA. Therefore this represents a key area of study in the field.

To avoid this issue, such spatial profiling can also be done at the proteomic level, again highlighting the benefits of CITE-seq as if the specific proteins of interest are already known, which can dramatically speed up the process. There are multiple methods to do this, including traditional confocal microscopy approaches, which remain limited in terms of the number of antibodies that can be imaged simultaneously. Alternatively, approaches using barcoded antibodies or cyclical staining and bleaching or cleavage techniques are now becoming popular. The latter approach involves repeated rounds of staining and imaging, whereby a group of antibodies are added and imaged then the fluorescence is bleached or the fluorescent tag is cleaved and another round of antibodies are applied and the process continued. Of course, the limitation with these proteomic methods is the availability of antibodies to distinguish between the cell types of interest, which can be tricky if one is considering subtle differences between different activation states of the same macrophage population. However, despite these current limitations, these technologies are rapidly developing and

crucially allow spatially relevant cellcell interactions to be profiled for the first time, hence providing further insight into functional relevance of distinct cell types in specific settings.

### Mononuclear Phagocytes in Rheumatoid Arthritis

For decades, synovial tissue macrophages (STMs) have been recognized as key contributors to RA pathogenesis, and multiple clinical observations suggest a positive correlation between the abundance of STMs and the magnitude of synovial damage. In line with that, STMs are believed to be the main producer of TNF and interleukin 6 (IL-6), two key pro-inflammatory cytokines in RA69 supporting the putative pathogenic role of STMs. However, the specific roles of tissue-resident and recruited STMs in RA, as well as the different phenotypes that these macrophages might possess, have only recently begun to be unraveled.

### Synovial Macrophages in the Mouse

In the healthy mouse synovium, all tissue-resident STMs express the typical macrophage markers CD11b, CD64 and F4/80.70 Recently fate-mapping and scRNA-seq experiments have identified the existence of at least two populations of tissue-resident STMs, which coexist in the healthy synovium and can be identified thanks to their differential expression of specific markers . (Fig. 10.4). First, a population of macrophages, characterized by the expression of the CX3 motif chemokine receptor 1 (CX3CR1) and triggering receptor expressed on myeloid cells 2 (TREM2), reside in the uppermost cellular layer of the synovium, where they form a protective lining layer regulated by their expression of tightand gap-junction proteins. This population of STMs is already present at E15.5, suggesting they are generated during embryogenesis, similar to other TRM populations. However, no clear proliferation was observed in this population in adulthood, raising the question as to whether these cells are capable of self-renewal like other TRMs. Interestingly, while these cells are maintained independently of BM monocytes, using fate-mapping studies, it has been proposed that the macrophages themselves do not self-renew but rather are maintained by a local pool of CSF1R+CX3CR1-MHCII+ precursors, having a half-life of approximately 5 weeks.

Second, a population of tissue-resident CX3CR1- STMs that specifically express the resistin-like molecule alpha (RELMα) have been identified in the synovial sublining layer. Like the CX3CR1+TREM2+ STMs, the interstitial CX3CR1-RELM-α+ STMs are also proposed to be generated locally from the CSF1R+CX3CR1-MHCII+ progenitors. Importantly, these two subsets of tissue-resident STMs are discrete subsets as fate mapping either CX3CR1+ cells or RELMα+ cells identified very few pre-labeled CX3CR1+TREM2+ macrophages in the sublining layer or pre-labeled RELMα+ macrophages in the lining layer, respectively.

Using the K/BxN serum transfer arthritis (STA) model,71 analysis of the macrophage populations found that during the onset of inflammation, CX3CR1+TREM2+ STMs rapidly change their morphology with the appearance of pseudopods that protrude into the synovial cavity. In addition, these cells abrogate their reciprocal cellcell contacts, leading to the disruption of the protective lining layer formed by these cells. Despite these changes, the CX3CR1+TREM2+ STMs did not

dramatically alter their transcriptomic profile,20 suggesting a limited plasticity of these cells, fitting with their relatively slow turnover. Importantly, depletion of CX3CR1+TREM2+ STMs in the STA model worsened the onset of RA, highlighting the importance of these cells and the protective barrier. While the CX3CR1+TREM2+ STMs appear to play important roles in RA, little is known about the behavior of the RELMα+ tissue-resident STMs. Preliminary results suggest that these cells actively proliferate during inflammation;20 however, further studies are required to better understand their role(s) during the progression of RA.

Active RA is also characterized by a massive influx of BMderived STMs that accumulate in the inflamed synovial membrane. In the STA model of RA, these STMs are proposed to originate from recruited Ly6Cmonocytes. While the precise nature of these cells requires further study, these recruited STMs express high levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines, including interleukin 1 beta (IL1β). These cells play important roles in the onset of inflammatory arthritis as depleting all monocytes and macrophages with clodronate liposomes and subsequently adoptively transferring only Ly6Cmonocytes was sufficient to drive disease, whereas mice only treated with clodronate liposomes were protected from developing inflammatory arthritis. Whether similar macrophage populations are also recruited in other models of RA remains to be studied. As stated previously, it is known that the precursors of the recruited macrophages differ from model to model with the Ly6Cmono- cytes contributing in the STA model52 and the Ly6Chi monocytes differentiating into recruited macrophages in the collagen-induced arthritis (CIA) model.54, This of course raises the question of whether the macrophages generated from these distinct precursors would be the same. Perhaps suggesting this may not be the case,

BM-derived STMs have been proposed to differentiate into osteoclasts, driving bone erosion in the CIA model. Notably, regardless of their precise fates, which require further study, most studies to date agree that these recruited STMs drive pathology in models of RA.20,72,73

### Synovial Macrophages in the Human

The recent development of minimally invasive biopsy techniques coupled with the advances in single cell technologies has allowed a significant collection of human synovial tissue, both healthy and inflamed, to be profiled. This has revolutionized our understanding of the functional heterogeneity within mononuclear phagocytes in both the healthy and inflamed joint.4, In general, the healthy human synovium comprises a population of tissue-resident STMs characterized by expression of the pan-macrophage markers CD64, CD11b, and CD68 together with the specific expression of the proto-oncogene tyrosine-protein kinase MER (MerTK) and the C-type lectin mannose receptor (CD206). scRNA-seq has revealed that these human tissue-resident STMs can be further subdivided into at least two distinct populations (Fig. 10.4). First, a population of MerTK+CD206+ macrophages that express TREM2 and folate receptor 2 (FOLR2) form a protective lining layer in the uppermost part of the synovium. These are likely to be the human counterpart of the murine CX3CR1+TREM2+- resident STMs already discussed (Fig. 10.4). Second, a population of MerTK+CD206+ macrophages express the Lymphatic vessel endothelial hyaluronan receptor 1 (LYVE-1) and FOLR2, which mainly reside in the synovial sublining layer and hence likely represents the human equivalent of the mouse RELMα+-resident STMs (Fig. 10.4).

Recently the presence of tissue-resident LYVE-1+ macrophages has been reported in many tissues. These cells possess crucial roles in maintaining blood vessel integrity under steady-state condi- .75, Although the specific role of MerTK+CD206+LYVE-1+ tions. STMs remains to be investigated, the expression of LYVE-1 coupled with their specific location in the sublining synovial layer, which is highly vascularized, also suggests that these tissue-resident STMs may play important roles in preserving perivascular homeostasis.

While the embryonic origin of mouse tissue-resident STMs has been demonstrated, the origin of human tissue-resident STMs is unclear. Moreover, it remains to be seen if the human STMs are also maintained through the input of local precursors as observed in the mouse. A cluster of human tissue-resident STMs expressing high levels of CSF1 R and DNA-binding protein inhibitor ID-2 (ID2), which is a transcription factor that has been implicated in the process of cellular self-renewal, has been recently identified and suggested to be the human counterpart of the embryonically derived mouse STM precursors. .4, However, these findings have not yet been confirmed experimentally.

In the healthy human joint, both tissue-resident STM populations possess important regulatory functions and hence are proposed to contribute to synovial tissue homeostasis. As observed in the mouse, human MerTK+CD206+TREM2+ STMs express high levels of tight junction proteins, enabling the generation of a protective barrier against pathogens and debris. In addition, analysis of the transcriptomic profiles of these TRMs predict that they might play crucial roles in maintaining tissue homeostasis through the removal of dead cells and debris and in preventing inflammation through their expression of defensins and complement proteins. The sublining layer STMs are also predicted to have a regulatory function. Specifically, the transcriptome of these macrophages suggests they play roles in the phagocytosis of erythrocytes and iron recirculation, in the regulation of collagen deposition by synovial fibroblasts, and in controlling blood vessel permeability. 44, Importantly, however, most of these functions remain only as predictions based on the transcriptomic data and further experiments are required to validate them.

Mirroring the observations made in experimental animal models of RA,20,52 human arthritis is also accompanied by changes in the behavior of tissue-resident MerTK+CD206+ macrophages. Interestingly, unlike in mice, this is proposed to be linked with significant changes in their transcriptomic profiles. Specifically, human studies in early arthritis suggest a switch of MerTK+CD206+TREM2+ macrophages toward a TREM2o phe- 44 Moreover, a subset of LYVE-1+ macrophages expressnotype. ing ICAM1 has also been reported44 (Fig. 10.4). Whether these represent novel subsets of STMs or an altered profile of the existing macrophage subpopulations remains to be validated experimentally. MerTK+CD206+TREM2lo STMs also downregulate important immune regulatory pathways while upregulating their expression of pro-inflammatory mediators such as alarmins and osteopontin (encoded by Spp1). This altered phenotype, together with the disruption of the lining layer formed by the MerTK+CD206+TREM2+ TRMs, might represent the very first step in the initiation of joint inflammation. While a role for these tissue-resident STMs during RA onset has been proposed, additional studies are now required to fully elucidate how these macrophages behave during the progression of the disease and if this altered gene expression profile is maintained throughout the duration of the disease or in resolution.

Alongside these differences in the phenotype and profiles of MerTK+CD206+ STM populations, the inflamed synovium is also characterized by the presence of a significant population of MerTK-CD206macrophages.44, These are the predominant macrophage populations in RA in active disease (Fig. 10.4). Drawing parallels with the mouse, it is assumed that these macrophages would likely originate from recruited BM-derived monocytes. These MerTK-CD206- STMs can be further subdivided into different clusters based on their differential gene expression profiles.44, Specifically, four clusters of MerTK-CD206- STMs have been identified in human synovium in active RA, all of which express the marker CD48. This includes an S100A12+ (encoding for S100 calcium-binding protein A12) cluster, an SPP1+ cluster (perhaps representing the equivalent of murine BM-derived STMs in RA; Box 10.2), an ISG15+ cluster with a strong interferon (IFN) signature, and an HLA+CLEC10A+ cluster with antigenpresenting features. Whether this last cluster (HLA+CLEC10A+) represents bona fide STMs; an activated subset of cDC2s77; or a distinct population of DCs, recently referred to as DC3s,78-80 is unclear (Fig. 10.4). Indeed, the definition of genuine DC3s is also causing some confusion in the field, further complicating this assessment.

Together, these infiltrating cells are the main producers of the pro-inflammatory cytokines TNF and IL-6 and hence, given the clinical therapeutic validation of their pathogenetic importance, are proposed to be the main drivers of RA synovitis. In addition to the broad production of pro-inflammatory cytokines, each cluster of infiltrating macrophages (or macrophages and DCs) expresses a unique transcriptomic signature, which might reflect different and specific functions in the pathogenesis of RA. While additional research is required to decipher differences in function between these mononuclear phagocyte subsets, preliminary results obtained in vitro suggest that recruited MerTK-CD206- STMs, but not tissue-resident MerTK+CD206+ STMs, can trigger synovial fibroblast activation, which may drive the progression of RA. Aside from their largely unknown functions, another important question remaining is where these distinct subsets are located. Perhaps this information may also shed light on their specific roles in the pathogenesis of RA. Spatial transcriptomic approaches, as discussed, will provide additional information in this regard.

### Human Synovial Macrophages During Rheumatoid Arthritis Remission and Relapse

Although a definitive cure for RA does not exist, many treatments can drive RA remission, which is characterized by the resolution of synovial inflammation. Unfortunately, this remission is just temporary, and one-third of patients affected by RA will display alternating periods of remission and relapse. While the underlying mechanisms of this relapsing—remitting phenomenon remain largely unknown, recent studies have started to correlate the presence of different STM populations with the likelihood of remission or relapse, suggesting that STMs may hold a key in this process. Specifically, recent evidence suggests that tissue-resident MerTK+CD206+ STMs may be critical for RA remission.

In contrast to active RA, where the synovium of patients is filled with pro-inflammatory-recruited MerTK-CD206- STMs, the remission phase is characterized by a contraction of the MerTK-CD206- STM pool and restoration of the homeostatic and anti-inflammatory pool of both MerTK+CD206+ STMs encompassing both the TREM2+ and LYVE-1+ subpopulations. Interestingly, these macrophages are not identical to those present

in the healthy joint as they upregulate a number of genes alongside their surface expression of CD163.44 This of course raises the question as to whether these cells are the original tissue-resident STMs that expand in remission or if they represent monocyte-derived STMs (InfResMacs) that are recruited prior to or upon remission. Moreover, while in the past it has been difficult to predict which patients will flare when in remission, it has recently been suggested that the prevalence of MerTK+CD206+-resident STMs may be a good predictor of this, with patients maintaining remission having higher numbers of these macrophages than those who relapsed. While the exact mechanism of this phenomenon remains unclear, the regulatory nature of tissue-resident STMs, together with their ability to produce anti-inflammatory mediators, might drive the resolution of inflammation and continued RA remission. In addition to MerTK+CD206+ STMs, MerTK-CD206- STMs are also suggested to play an important role in RA relapse. Specifically, the persistence of the MerTK-CD206-CD48+S100A12+ STM cluster, which is particularly enriched in the expression of proinflammatory alarmins such as S100A8, S100A10, and S100A12, has been suggested to predict RA flare. .

### Human Macrophage Heterogeneity: Where Do We Go From Here?

For decades, synovial macrophages have been broadly considered to be a homogeneous and pro-inflammatory population implicated in the progression of RA. Recent studies, however, have brought this concept into question, demonstrating the existence of different subsets of synovial macrophages with different functions and origins. We now appreciate that tissue-resident STMs, far from being pathogenic, likely fulfill crucial roles in homeostasis and RA remission, whereas recruited STMs may represent a more pathogenic and heterogeneous population.55, In the future, this important finding might allow more precise therapeutic strategies to be designed that specifically target each of these STM populations individually. For instance, given the proposed regulatory nature of tissue-resident STMs, new therapeutic strategies might aim to boost their differentiation and survival. On the contrary, better inhibition of the STMs predominating in active RA may be beneficial, as these STMs appear to be pro-inflammatory. Such an approach would provide much more resolution than the current approaches, which aim to generally inhibit macrophage functions or development. Moreover, such approaches may even be relevant in other inflammatory diseases as some signatures of recruited STMs may be conserved with recruited macrophages in other inflamed tissues (Box 10.2). It is clear that we still need a better understanding of the precise roles played by the distinct subsets that have now been identified in order to further guide the development of specific therapies to counterbalance synovial inflammation.

In conclusion, the role of the myeloid lineages in the pathogenesis of immune-mediated inflammatory diseases ( IMID) i s paramount. The next frontier is to extend the detailed studies performed in RA to other IMIDs with a view to understanding common activities across the range of subsets thus far identified and to confirm that they are indeed consistent lineages. In this respect the advances in RA could presage a much broader revolution in the treatment of RMDs.

### KEY POINTS

### Introduction

Neutrophils (polymorphonuclear neutrophils) are a key part of the innate immune response and the first line of defense against invading microorganisms. They belong to the family of haematopoietically derived leukocytes that share the features of a multilobulated nucleus (thus polymorphonuclear) and characteristic intracytoplasmic granules (hence termed granulocytes). Based on the cytochemical staining properties of their respective granules, three classes of polymorphonuclear leukocytes can be identified: neutrophils, eosinophils, and basophils. Whereas neutrophil granules stain with neutral dyes, eosinophil granules stain with acidic dyes such as eosin, and basophil granules stain with basic dyes. In a standard polychromatic Wright stain of a peripheral blood smear, the cytoplasm of neutrophils appears blue-pink, and this helps to differentiate them from the other granulocytes.

Neutrophils are the most abundant type of white blood cell in humans, typically constituting greater than 50% of all circulating leukocytes. They are a major cell type involved in acute and some forms of chronic inflammation. The importance of neutrophils in bacterial defense is illustrated by patients who have hereditary defects in neutrophil numbers or function and are prone to repeated and often life-threatening infections. In contrast, tissue concentrations of neutrophils during periods of homeostasis are

low but increase in response to infection or other triggers. Over the past decade, neutrophils have reemerged as presumed culprits in various aspects of pathogenesis of rheumatologic diseases. Neutrophils develop and terminally differentiate in the bone marrow and are then released into the circulation, where they patrol and sense danger signals. Under conditions of homeostasis, neutrophils are also found in the lung, spleen, and liver, and they follow tightly regulated circadian rhythms that allow for disarming strategies prior to their migration to various tissues. Neutrophils use a complex armamentarium of strategies to immobilize and kill microbes, including phagocytosis and bacterial degradation through synthesis of reactive oxygen species (ROS); release of anti-microbial peptides from granules; and the synthesis of neutrophil extra-cellular traps (NETs), which are lattices of chromatin bound to granule peptides that have the ability to immobilize and potentially kill various microorganisms. In this chapter, we review neutrophil development, structure, and function; the role of neutrophils in protecting against infection; and the role and impact of neutrophils in the pathogenesis and pathophysiology of immune deficiency and autoimmune and autoinflammatory diseases.

### Neutrophils: Basic Principles

### Development and Clearance

Neutrophils originate in the bone marrow from the hematopoietic stem cells. A majority, nearly 60%, of the bone marrow is dedicated to neutrophil production. Every day approximately 1 x 1011 neutrophils are released into the bloodstream. Stem cells fated to become neutrophils differentiate into myeloblasts, then neutrophilic myelocyte, metamyelocyte, and band cells, and then mature neutrophils. The whole process takes about 14 days. At the metamyelocyte stage, neutrophil mitosis ceases, while neutrophil development and granule organization continues. Mature neutrophils are characterized by multilobed nucleus. On release from the marrow, neutrophils are terminally differentiated cells and neither divide nor, generally, alter their gross phenotype.

Although the mechanisms regulating neutrophil differentiation remain incompletely understood, various transcription factors and cytokines direct the early cells toward neutrophil development. Several myeloid factors like lymphoid enhancer binding factor 1 (LEF-1), CCAAT enhancer binding proteins α, β, and ε (C/EBP- α, -β, and -ε), and growth factor independent 1 (GFI1) are necessary for the transcriptional regulation of neutrophils. In contrast to other myeloid cells, lack of expression of the transcription factor GATA-1 also contributes to committed development of neutrophils.3, Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF) is the

key cytokine regulating granulopoiesis. G-CSF causes myeloid differentiation, proliferation of granulocyte precursors, and release of mature neutrophils from the marrow. G-CSF signals through its receptor (G-CSFR or CD1 14), a member of the class I cytokine receptor family. Other cytokines that may contribute to granulopoiesis include granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor [GM-CSF], interleukin 6 (IL-6), and IL-3.

Upon maturation, neutrophils pass through the sinusoidal endothelium of the bone marrow to enter the circulation, in a process known as transcellular migration. Neutrophils released from the marrow typically have a short bloodstream half-life of approximately 1 to 8 hours; however, some reports suggest longer lifespan of over 5 days, especially once the cells become activated.7-10 Clearance of circulating neutrophils appears to depend on the SDF-1/CXC chemokine receptor 4 (CXCR4) signaling system. CXCR4 is a G-protein coupled receptor that is expressed at low levels in the mature neutrophil. Aging neutrophils alter their phenotype and upregulate CXCR4. Increased expression of this chemokine receptor supports their homing back to the bone marrow via the chemoattractant stromal-derived factor 1 (SDF-1 or CXCL12). Here, senescent neutrophils are phagocytosed by stromal macrophages. Aging or apoptotic circulating neutrophils are also cleared by macrophages in the liver and spleen. Upregulation of the adhesion molecule P-selectin on Kupffer cells appears to be relevant for this form of clearance.

Neutrophil cycling in circulation and in tissues is tightly controlled by the circadian rhythm where, in general, more transcellular migration occurs during morning (or awake) hours and more neutrophils migrate back to the bone marrow for phagocytosis at the end of the day (or sleep) hours.12-14 Cell-intrinsic factors control this process, including clock genes, and external factors like glucocorticoid and bacterial metabolites are also involved. There may be evolutionary benefits of this circadian regulation as it ensures that the innate immune system is more responsive during the awake part of the day, when there is higher likelihood of encountering microbes. What happens to the neutrophils that have migrated to the tissues is still unclear—whether they are

cleared by local macrophages, pass back to the lymphatic drainage, or return to the bloodstream. It is also unclear what constitutes a tissue-resident neutrophil versus a neutrophil that has temporarily migrated from circulation.

### Morphology and Contents

The multilobed nature of the neutrophil nucleus reflects the condensation of chromatin, and it was believed that mature neutrophils may be incapable of transcription. However, recent evidence demonstrates that neutrophils retain the capacity for both constitutive and stimulated RNA and protein synthesis. On exposure to microbial agents, human neutrophils rapidly change their chromatin folding with subsequent changes to nuclear architecture and activation of proinflammatory genes. These changes are unique to the stimuli faced with the closed chromatin opening up in one of three mechanisms where the accessible chromatin occurs only in the promoter region or only in the distal sites or at the promoter and distal sites. This plastic transcriptional expression takes place under an intricate accessible chromatin regulation. Perturbation in this tight regulation can lead to susceptibility to autoimmune and inflammatory diseases. Variants associated with binding of myeloid master regulator PU. in primary neutrophils across 100 volunteers showed genetically driven differences in cell count and immune disease susceptibility.

Neutrophil granules have been classified into three types: azurophilic (primary) granules, specific (secondary) granules, and gelatinase (tertiary) granules (Fig. 11.1 and Fig. 11.2). Anti-microbial proteins contained in these granules are a cornerstone of innate immune responses. In addition to their direct anti-microbial effects, granular contents play important roles in amplifying or dampening innate and adaptive immune responses.

### Primary Granules

Azurophilic or primary granules form first in myeloblasts and promyelocytes and appear to be functionally equivalent to the lysosomes found in other cells. Primary granules contain

### Secondary Granules

Secondary or specific granules possess a vast array of membraneassociated proteins including cytochromes, signaling molecules, and receptors. Secondary granules have a reservoir of proteins that eventually migrate to the external surfaces of phagocytic vacuoles and the plasma membrane (see Table 11.1).2, An important family of proteinases found in these granules are the matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs), including neutrophil collagenase-2 (MMP-8), gelatinase-B (MMP-9), stromelysin (MMP-3), and leukolysin (MMP-25). Within the secondary granules, MMPs

are stored as inactive proenzymes upon fusion with the phagocytic vacuole and subsequent interaction with the contents of primary granule, and they undergo proteolytic activation. 18, Activated MMPs can alter and degrade membrane components of microbe in the phagocytic vacuole. MMPs are also important for neutrophil extravasation and diapedesis (see below). Lactoferrin, another protein found in specific granules, deprives microorganisms of iron and has anti-viral and anti-bacterial effects.

### Tertiary Granules: Gelatinase and Secretory Vesicles

Two additional classes of vesicles were identified using special techniques. Gelatinase granules are similar to secondary granules in size as well in some shared proteins. They are distinguished by their high concentrations of gelatinase, a latent enzyme with the capacity for tissue destruction. Gelatinase B amplifies neutrophil influx and inflammation by truncating and increasing release of the potent chemoattractant IL-8 and converting latent IL-1β into its active form.27, In contrast, secretory vesicles are smaller and lighter than the other classes and contain many membraneassociated proteins, including receptors otherwise identified in the plasma membrane, suggesting that they may serve as a reservoir of membrane proteins (see Table 11.1).

### Neutrophil Functions

The process of neutrophils responding to foreign targets in the periphery and tissue is called neutrophil activation (Fig. 11.3). Since there is high potential of tissue destruction, neutrophil activation is a carefully regulated process. Bloodstream neutrophils

on sensing foreign targets through chemoattractant like leukotriene B4 (LTB4), platelet-activating factor, formylated peptides or IL-8 can attach to the activated endothelium of blood vessels using adhesion molecules and their receptors through rolling and adhesion. Neutrophils then pass through the endothelium of the vessels by diapedesis and migrate to the source of signal through chemotaxis. Once they encounter the target, using distinct processes of either degranulation, phagocytoses or NET formation, they can neutralize the microbe. Below are details of each step of neutrophil activation (Fig. 11.3).

### Adhesion

An early and key feature of the inflammatory response is ability of neutrophils in the bloodstream to adhere to the vascular

endothelium before moving through the blood vessels into the tissues. Activated neutrophils also have the ability for homotypic aggregation or adhering to each other. Interaction between several adhesion molecules, like selectins, integrins, intercellular adhesion molecules (ICAMs), and sialylated glycoproteins, expressed on neutrophils and endothelial cells make this process possible.

The selectin class of proteins includes three related molecules: L-selectin found on leukocytes, E-selectin on endothelial cells, and P-selectin on activated platelets and endothelial cells. Each of these selectins have their respective specific target sialylated glycoprotein on the surface of its interacting cell. E-selectin binds to the sialyl LewisX antigen on neutrophils, P-selectin binds to P-selectin glycoprotein-1 (PSGL-1) on neutrophils, and L-selectin to PSGL-1 and GlyCAM-1 on the endothelium. These selectin/sialylated glycoprotein bindings are of low affinity and are

transient, leading to repetitive bindings and release of leukocytes on the endothelial surface. This leads to a rolling, tumbleweedlike motion where a pool of neutrophils in the bloodstream, at a given time, are loosely adherent to and slowly moving along the vascular endothelium (marginated). These neutrophils are usually not sampled during routine blood tests; however, exposure to certain stimuli (like corticosteroids) can lead to shedding of selectins with subsequent release of these neutrophils (demargination) and increase in measured peripheral blood neutrophil count.

The integrins are another large family of transmembrane cellsurface adhesion receptors involved in neutrophil adhesion. Neutrophils express four types of β2 integrins that are constructed from a common β2 chain (CD18) and a distinct α subcomponent (CD11a, CD11b, CD11c, and CD11d). Each integrin binds to its respective ICAMs. Binding of CD11a/CD18 to PSGL-1 is necessary for neutrophil adhesion and migration.31-33 This interaction causes activation and arrest during the rolling of neutrophils on inflamed endothelium, a critical first step before transmigration through the vascular endothelium. Integrin CD11b/Cd18 is important for neutrophil/endothelial and neutrophil/neutrophil interactions, specifically allowing the cells to crawl over the endothelium to identify possible location for diapedesis. Stimulation of neutrophils and endothelial cells triggers upregulation of respective receptor/ligands, leading to their tight adhesion to the vessel wall with subsequent movement into the tissues. This engagement also sends signals to the cells that results in regulation of various functions like cytoskeletal reorganization, oxidant production, degranulation, phagocytosis, and neutrophil-dependent adhesion in immune complex-mediated vascular inflammation. 34,35

### Diapedesis

The process of neutrophils passing through blood vessels is called diapedesis. The exact mechanism of diapedesis is still not completely understood. While many believe that it occurs by disruption of cellcell junctions between endothelial cells,7 some evidence has also shown that neutrophils can pass directly through the endothelial cells by generation of pores in them (Fig. 11.4).36, Interactions between adhesion molecules called platelet-endothelial cell adhesion molecules found on both neutrophils and endothelial cells is critical for diapedesis. Neutrophils also upregulate a6b1, an integrin that mediates binding to laminin, which is a key component of perivascular basement membrane. Other proteins that are also upregulated during transmigration of neutrophils through the endothelium include CD47, also known as integrin-associated protein and CD99. After passing through the endothelium, neutrophils then go through the basement membrane through transient disruption of the patency of this membrane.

### Chemotaxis

The directional motion of neutrophils across a molecular gradient is called chemotaxis. This is achieved by formation of membrane ruffles, known as lamellipodia, followed by anchoring of these extensions to the substrate and withdrawal of the trailing edge. This movement is accomplished through rearrangement of the actin cytoskeleton after sensing of chemotactic gradients that signal through G protein—coupled receptors and phosphoinositide 3-kinases. Chemoattractant receptors concentrate at the leading edge, the so-called "headlight phenomenon." As the cell moves forward, receptors on the formerly leading edge are swept to the tail and internalized.

### Degranulation

The process of mobilization of granules in neutrophils is called degranulation. Degranulation helps kill pathogens and modulate immune response in infectious and noninfectious diseases. Release of granular proteins can be extra-cellular when the vesicles fuse to the plasma membrane or intra-cellular when the vesicles fuse to the phagosome (detailed in the "Phagocytosis" section) to kill extra-cellular and intra-cellular microbes, respectively. For extra-cellular degranulation, there is a hierarchy by which vesicles fuse to the plasma membrane and spill their contents. Secretory vesicles mobilize first, followed by gelatinase granules, specific granules, and azurophil granules.

### Phagocytosis

Phagocytosis is one of the mechanisms used by neutrophils to eliminate infectious organisms, dead cells, and other particles.' 42 It requires direct contact and is activated by recognition of pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs), small molecule motifs found on/in bacteria or viruses. PAMPs are recognized by extra-cellular or intra-cellular Toll-like receptors (TLRs) and other pattern recognition receptors, which get activated and stimulate phagocytosis by stimulating structural and conformational changes.43, Another process that greatly enhances phagocytosis is opsonization, where the surface of the target is decorated with immunoglobulin, complement components, or both, resulting in modification and better recognition.

Phagocytosis involves extension of the neutrophil membrane called filopodia, lamellipodia formation around the target, and, at the same time, invagination of the neutrophil at the locus of the target (Fig. 11.5).45, Engagement of the FcγR and complement receptors on the neutrophils results in activation of various signaling pathways that play key roles in the process. Engagement of

CR3 (CD11b/CD18) results in actin stress fiber formation and invagination. FcyRII engagement results in extensions of membranes out from and around the target to form the phagocytic vacuole.

Intra-cellular degranulation then leads to fusion of vesicles with the phagocytic vacuole to form phagolysosome. There is preferential fusion of azurophilic granules in this process that leads to delivery of proteolytic proenzymes, MPO, and anti-bacterial proteins to the site of an ingested bacterium. This phagolysosome fuses with the specific granules that deliver collagenase, activation of azurophilic granule enzymes and nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADPH) oxidase. This closely regulated process maintains toxic agents in inactive forms until required near target pathogens and minimizes neutrophil self-destruction and host tissue damage. However, in certain cases known as frustrated phagocytosis, when the target is large, toxic granular proteins may spill over into the extra-cellular space, causing local tissue damage.
