### Neutrophil Extra-cellular Traps

Neutrophil extra-cellular traps (NETs) are typically generated and released through a distinct programmed inflammatory cell death process, although mechanisms of NET formation that do not result in cell death have been described. NETs are structures composed of externalized, concentrated nuclear and granule contents that contain many potent anti-microbial molecules that can trap, immobilize, inactivate, and kill microorganisms. They also have the ability to stimulate other neutrophils and immune cells. NET formation can be triggered by various stimuli including microorganisms and their products, cytokines, autoantibodies, immune complexes, crystals, chemicals/drugs, and platelets.54-57

While the exact mechanism that leads to NET formations continues to be refined, the process usually depends on ROS production, either through NADPH oxidase machinery and/or mitochondria. ROS can prevent actin polymerization and cause the release of many proteases (MPO and neutrophil elastase) that cleave histones and other structural proteins, including the poreforming gasdermin D, which subsequently leads to a decrease in membrane stability and an increase in the concentration of calcium in the cytoplasm.58-61 Once initiated, there is disassembly of the neutrophil cytoskeleton, assembly of granular proteins on both genomic and mitochondrial DNA, and post-translational modification of histones, including citrullination by the peptidyl arginine deiminase (PAD) family of enzymes, particularly PAD4.62-64 These modifications can disrupt the electrostatic interactions of DNA and histones that lead to changes in the chromatin structure and promote decondensation of nuclear material.

This is followed by degradation of cell membrane and extrusion of NETs in the extra-cellular space (Fig. 11.6 and Video 11.1). Post-translationally modified (citrullinated and carbamylated) proteins found in NETs have direct pathogenic action on target cells and can modify immunogenicity and vasculopathic effects compared with unmodified versions, suggesting their key role in the pathogenesis and generation of autoantigens and promotion of autoimmune response in predisposed individuals.

### Heterogeneity

Recent studies show that circulating neutrophils are not as homogenous as previously considered. Using single-cell RNA sequencing, neutrophils in peripheral blood can broadly be classified in four subsets based on their gene expression profile.66, The majority of neutrophils express genes associated with maturity. Nearly 20% are relatively immature, and another subset shows minimal transcriptional activity. Of note, there is a neutrophil subset that expresses a higher level of type I interferon (IFN) stimulated genes compared with other subsets. Women appear to have an IFNregulated neutrophil subset that respond more to this group of cytokines than the male subset, indicating that female neutrophils may have a more active intra-cellular machinery due to differences in maturation. This subset is also expanded in patients with severe COVID-19 and can be decreased by steroid treatment. Although the role of this IFN-responsive neutrophil subset in health and disease remains to be determined, it is possible that these neutrophils are primed cells that patrol the blood and may be readily available to fight off infections. Similarly, in those genetically predisposed or in the presence of other priming factors (like sex hormones), some individuals may have more activated neutrophils. This could explain sex differences in many systemic autoimmune diseases as well as robust response to many infectious diseases by females. Indeed, human neutrophils from young adult women are more mature and activated than those from young adult men, with an increased tendency to form NETs. These sex differences in neutrophils are likely driven by sex hormones as they are not present in pre-pubescent children or individuals with Klinefelter syndrome (47, XXY).

A subset of proinflammatory neutrophils described in inflammatory conditions, based on its density during separation of

blood components, is called low-density granulocyte (LDG). These neutrophils are pathogenic and differ from normal-density neutrophils in several phenotypic and functional parameters. For example, LDGs produce higher levels of proinflammatory cytokines like IFNs and are primed for increased NET formation. Presence of LDGs correlates with several clinical phenotypes including renal disease and vasculopathy. A recent closer look at LDGs using bulk and single-cell RNA sequencing and flow cytometry has shown that this group of cells, described by density gradient, is a mix of cells in various transcriptional states with differences in maturation and functions,7 72 although the majority are intermediate mature cells with proinflammatory features. The role of LDGs in various autoimmune diseases is discussed in more detail below.

Other neutrophil subsets like myeloid-derived suppressor cells have also been reported in cancer and sepsis but are beyond the scope of this chapter.73, LDGs do not display myeloid-derived suppressor cell activity despite expressing some of the markers associated to those suppressive phenotypes.

### Role of Neutrophils, Low-Density Granulocytes, and Neutrophil Extra-cellular Traps in Rheumatic Diseases

### Systemic Lupus Erythematosus

Evidence over the past decade has established that the innate immune system, specifically the neutrophils, play a crucial role in the initiation and propagation of aberrant immune responses, including organ damage and vasculopathy, seen in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) (Fig. 11.7). Patients with SLE show altered neutrophil populations and association of neutrophil-specific genes with more active disease. A multitude of abnormalities in phenotype and function, including increased cell death, impaired ability to phagocytose, and aberrant oxidative activity, have been reported in neutrophils from patients with SLE.57, In the bone marrow, neutrophils contribute to synthesis of type I IFNs and B cell dysregulation through B-cell activating factor (BAFF)—mediated effects.

Lupus patients have increased circulating levels of LDGs, which have been associated with distinct clinical manifestations, including skin and renal involvement, vasculopathy, arterial inflammation, and coronary artery disease.71,79,80" Lupus LDGs have distinct transcriptomic, epigenetic, and functional attributes compared with normal dense neutrophils from lupus or healthy controls. 70, They differ in protein content and have distinctive modulation of their cytoskeleton, which leads to differences in biochemical properties, potentially making them predisposed to getting trapped in organs like lungs and causing tissue damage. They are also key drivers of the type I IFN gene signature characteristic of SLE and contribute to the synthesis of type I IFNs and other proinflammatory cytokines. Recent evidence suggests that LDGs from SLE patients are not as homogenous as previously thought and there are at least two main subpopulations of intermediate-mature and immature neutrophils with differences in transcriptional, epigenetic, and functional readouts, like phagocytosis, response to type I IFNs, NET formation, and chemotaxis.

Neutrophils (particularly LDGs) from SLE patients, compared with those from healthy controls, exhibit increased propensity to form NETs that can cause direct tissue damage.57, NETs released from LDGs are more proinflammatory and immunostimulatory due to a higher abundance of modified self-antigens,

including oxidized nucleic acids and immunogenic molecules like LL37 and MMP-9. Increased NETs (through an imbalance between NET formation and NET degradation) have been implicated in the pathogenesis of lupus nephritis, in part through the promotion of endothelial dysfunction by inducing vascular leakage and endothelial-mesenchymal transition through their ability to degrade vascular endothelial cadherin and activate b-catenin signaling. NETs activate the NLRP3 inflammasome in macrophages, promoting increased release of IL-1 and IL-18 that can perpetuate tissue damage in lupus.83,

Several genetic polymorphisms associated with increased risk of SLE can also enhance NET formation. Mutations in TNFAIP3,

encoding A20, disrupts the proteins' deubiquitinase domain, promoting protein citrullination and NET formation through increased PAD activity. Increased NET complexes have also been reported in SLE patients with STAT4 risk allele. In another study, neutrophils from healthy individuals homozygous for IRF5, a major SLE risk haplotype, showed increased spontaneous NET formation, suggesting the role of neutrophil dysregulation in preclinical lupus.

Aberrant NET formation/degradation plays a number of key pathogenic roles in SLE. In genetically predisposed individuals, oxidized nucleic acids and post-translationally modified proteins that are externalized during NET formation may promote

enhanced immunogenicity. Both genomic and mitochondrial DNA become oxidized during NET formation. Oxidation of nucleic acid increases its half-life by making it more resistant to degradation by nucleases, thereby effectively engaging with intra-cellular DNA sensors that promote type I IFN responses, including the cGAS/STING pathway, making it more interferogenic. LDG NETs also display higher levels of oxidized nucleic acids than NETs purified from other sources, with subsequent increased induction of type I IFN response in target cells. NETs from LDGs also have increased presence of ubiquitinated proteins that increase activation of proinflammatory responses in SLE macrophages.

In addition to increased NET formation seen in SLE, a subset of patients also show impaired clearance of NET complexes, leading to increased half-life of immunostimulatory, modified self-antigens. Normally, enzymes DNAsel and DNAselL3 degrade DNA in circulation and in tissues. Several groups have now shown decreased levels and/or function of these nucleases in a sizable portion of SLE patients, which could explain the impaired NET degradation. Blocking antibodies against DNAses or genetic polymorphisms in DNAse can explain some of the effects, which are associated with kidney involvement and vascular damage. 90, Other possible mechanisms that could prevent NETs from clearance include complement activation within NETs, nucleic acid oxidation, and anti-NET antibodies. 88,

LDGs and NETs may also have a potential role in higher reported risk for acute coronary syndrome seen in SLE patients. A circulating number of LDGs and their gene signatures were associated with increased coronary plaque and aortic wall inflammation, independent of other vascular risk factors, in SLE patients. NETs oxidize high-density lipoprotein and diminish its atheroprotective role by modifying its ability to remove cholesterol from macrophages. NETs also induce endothelial cell death through an MMP-9/MMP-2 axis that is specially enhanced in NETs from lupus LDGs.

Overall, the presence of LDGs and dysregulated NET formation and clearance appears to be operational in vivo in SLE and can also be seen at tissue levels where neutrophils and NETs are increased in lupus skin, vessels, kidneys, and placenta in association with inflammation and organ damage. 76,95,96

### Anti-neutrophilic Cytoplasmic Antibody— Associated Vasculitis

In patients with anti-neutrophilic cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA)— associated vasculitis (AAV), antibodies against granular proteins in cytoplasm of neutrophils like MPO and PR3 serve as serologic biomarkers of diagnosis and severity.97, These antibodies may also activate neutrophils that have already been primed by proinflammatory stimuli, like TNF, G-CSF, lipopolysaccharide, or C5a, leading to degranulation and production of oxygen radicals that promote destructive necrotizing vascular and extravascular inflammation.99-104 This triggers an inflammatory amplification loop in the vessel wall that further attracts and activates neutrophils. Neutrophils from AAV patients also have enhanced NET formation in vitro. Studies suggest increased NET formation may be associated with ANCA generation, as several ANCA targets are part of the DNA-granular protein complexes that form NETs.105, NET remnants, like MPO-DNA complexes, and neutrophil granule proteins, such as calprotectin, have been found in increased levels in sera from AAV patients. Levels of NET remnants correlated with disease activity and neutrophil counts.

Furthermore, NETs and NET structures have also been detected on immunostaining of several affected tissues like vascular thrombi and kidneys from patients with AAV.108, As in SLE, increased LDGs and their transcriptional signature is seen in AAV. Moreover, LDG signature in peripheral blood is associated with disease severity and decreased treatment responses to agents like rituximab and cyclophosphamide.

### Rheumatoid Arthritis

Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is characterized by the presence of highly specific autoantibodies that target post-translationally modified proteins like anti-citrullinated protein antibodies (ACPAs) and anti-carbamylated protein (anti-CarP) antibodies. Immune complexes of citrullinated antigens and ACPAs display increased immunogenicity and arthritogenicity. Neutrophils are abundant in the inflamed joints of patients with RA, especially in synovial effusions in early stages of disease. Patients with RA have increased levels of NET complexes in circulation, which correlates with ACPA levels and systemic inflammatory markers. 113,114 4 In the tissue, increased NET formation is also seen in synovial fluid neutrophils, synovial tissue, rheumatoid nodules, and skin. An interesting finding is the presence of NETs in sputum and their association with IgA and IgG ACPA responses in relatives of RA patients and in individuals at high risk of developing RA. Reduced endocytic capacity of sputum macrophages and association of NET remnants and IgA ACPA with inflammatory cytokines like IL-1, IL-6, and TNF was also found in subjects at risk of developing RA. These findings suggest a potential mechanism for ACPA generation in the mucosa and the role for dysregulated neutrophil responses in the lung in early RA.115,

Neutrophils may also play a role in the presence of extracellular citrullinated autoantigens found in the joints of patients with RA and the subsequent generation of ACPAs. Many citrullinated autoantigens are part of the chromatin complex that is extruded from neutrophils during NET formation, forming a source of extra-cellular citrullinated proteins. NET formation also releases active peptidyl arginine deiminase (PAD) isoforms that could citrullinate extra-cellular histones and fibrinogen. Indeed, neutrophils overexpress PAD2 and PAD4 and these enzymes are seen in close association with neutrophil infiltrated in the synovium of patients with RA.

Moreover, NETs activate RA synovial fibroblast-like synoviocytes (FLS) that results in release of proinflammatory cytokines, chemokines, and adhesion molecules. 113, NET products can be internalized by FLS, with subsequent upregulation of class II major histocompatibility complex (MHC) molecules and presentation of NET-derived peptides by FLS to CD4 T cells, leading to antigen-specific T cell responses, ACPA responses, and joint damage. NET-derived elastase can also directly damage cartilage matrix, leading to release of membrane-bound PAD-2 by FLS. The cartilage fragments thus generated are subsequently citrullinated, taken up by FLS and then presented to antigen-specific CD4+ T cells. Immune complexes containing citrullinated cartilage components can activate macrophages to release proinflammatory cytokines. Thus, in a genetically predisposed individual, increased NET formation can lead to generation of key autoantibodies and disruption in adaptive immunity that leads to a vicious cycle, further promoting NET formation and amplification of inflammatory responses in joint and other tissues.

NETs also externalize carbamylated (car-P) antigens (like car-histones and car-LL37) that correlate with their respective

anti-CarP antibodies in RA patients and are associated with more aggressive erosive RA. Carbamylated proteins bound to NETs are internalized by FLS and loaded on class II MHC for T-cell presentation. Anti-CarP histone—IgG immune complexes promote osteoclast differentiation and osteoclast-mediated matrix resorption. 65,

There are also reports of circulating LDGs in RA patients with correlation with disease activity.122, However, in contrast to SLE, LDGs seen in RA patients do not seem to have increased levels of induced NET formation. They also express lower levels of TNF receptors, with decreased responsiveness to TNF. These findings suggest a functional heterogeneity of these cells, with much still to understand about the role of LDGs in RA.

### Antiphospholipid Antibody Syndrome

Neutrophils from patients with antiphospholipid antibody syndrome (APLS) have an activated, proinflammatory phenotype. There is increased expression of interferon stimulated genes and of surface adhesion proteins like P-selectin glycoprotein ligand 1 (PSGL1, aka SELPLG or CD162) that promotes the formation of vascular thrombi by enhanced binding of neutrophils to the endothelial cells of the vascular wall.124, Neutrophils from APLS patients form spontaneous NETs ex vivo. NETs are integral components of thrombi and are important activators of the coagulation cascade. Patients with primary APLS have elevated levels of both cell-free DNA and NET remnants in circulation and in affected tissues. Sera and IgG from patients with APLS can also stimulate NET formation from control neutrophils, which is considered to be ROSand TLR4-dependent. Sera from patients with APLS also has decreased ability to degrade NETs, likely due to presence of antibodies against NETs and neutrophil remnants. LDGs have also been reported in APLS; however, their role in its pathogenesis remains to be determined.129,130

### Idiopathic Inflammatory Myositis

Recent reports show the role of neutrophils in the pathogenesis of various idiopathic inflammatory myositis (IIMs). Neutrophilspecific molecules, like neutrophil elastase, PRTN3, and serine proteases, were found to be elevated in circulation as well as in tissues.131, Neutrophil gene signature was present in the muscle tissues of patients with IIM and associated with the IFN gene signature as well as extent of muscle damage. Affected tissues from IIM patients show increased neutrophil infiltration with NET formation. In some patients with IIM, increased levels of circulating NETs were associated with specific disease manifestations and disease severity. Similar to SLE, and likely due to presence of serum antibodies to DNASE1, NET degradation is also impaired in those with IIM. Patients also have increased levels of LDGs with increased NET formation ability. Additionally, myositisspecific autoantibodies like MDA5 can also directly induce NET formation in vitro. These NETs, in a manner dependent on citrullinated histones, can interfere with the biology of myoblasts and myotubes, leading to an impairment in the function of these cells in striated muscles.

### Psoriasis

Neutrophil infiltration is a hallmark of the initiation phase of psoriatic lesions. Neutrophil-derived MMP-9 likely induces cutaneous vasodilation and hyperpermeability by activating cutaneous

vascular endothelial cells, facilitating psoriatic lesion development. LDGs have also been found to be elevated in psoriasis and associated with skin disease severity. They associated with noncalcified coronary plaque burden and included endothelial cell damage in vitro. Interestingly, platelet-associated biologic pathways were upregulated in psoriasis LDGs along with colocalization of platelets with LDGs in circulation. This LDG-platelet interaction associated more strongly with noncalcified coronary plaque burden than LDGs alone, suggesting a role of activated platelets as potential stimuli for increased NET formation in LDGs from patients with psoriasis.

### Gout

Acute gouty arthritis, caused by deposition of monosodium urate (MSU) crystals in the joints, is characterized by presence of numerous neutrophils in the affected synovial fluid.138, In an acute episode, neutrophils may lead to direct damage of joint structures through discharge of intra-cellular lysosomal contents directly into the joint fluid during attempted phagocytoses of MSU crystals. MSU crystals are also potent inducers of NADPH oxidasemediated NET formation. Interestingly, recent studies show that MSU-induced NET formation can also help in the resolution of acute inflammation by creation of granuloma and NET aggregates that can degrade inflammatory cytokines like IL-1b.140,141

### Other Diseases

Deficiency of adenosine deaminase 2 (DADA2) is a rare, recessively inherited monogenic autoinflammatory vasculitis due to a biallelic mutation in the ADA2 gene that encodes for adenosine deaminase 2, an enzyme that breaks down extra-cellular adenosine and is mainly expressed by myeloid cells. The clinical presentation of DADA2 is broad, and manifestations include early-onset systemic inflammation, vasculitis, early-onset stroke, cytopenias, and immunodeficiency. Mutation in ADA2 leads to decreased enzyme activity, resulting in increased levels of extra-cellular adenosine that binds to A1 and A3 adenosine receptors on the neutrophils to trigger NET formation. Patients also have increased LDGs in circulation that are predisposed to form NETs. These NETs activate macrophages that subsequently produce proinflammatory cytokines like TNF. NETs have also been found in affected organs from patients with DADA2, further reinforcing the dysregulation of neutrophils in this disease.

Pyogenic arthritis, pyoderma gangrenosum, and acne syndrome (PAPA syndrome) is a rare autosomal-dominant, autoinflammatory disease caused by mutations in the PSTPIP1 gene that encodes proline-serine-threonine phosphatase-interacting protein 1.145, Patients with PAPA syndrome have variable presentation that includes neutrophil-predominant arthritis. Mutations in PSTPIP1 alter its interaction with pyrin and the inflammasome, leading to increased serum levels of IL-1b and other neutrophil-associated proteins, such as MMPs. PAPA patients show increased NET formation and reduced NET clearance, increasing their half-life. Additionally, NET remnants were also found in skin biopsies from PAPA patients. These neutrophils are more responsive to IL-1b and inhibition of IL-1b (with anakinra, an IL-1 receptor antagonist) can block NET formation. These observations suggest a link between IL-1b and neutrophil responses.

Vacuoles, E1 enzyme, X-linked, autoinflammatory, somatic syndrome (VEXAS) is a recently described monogenic, adult-onset, X-linked disease caused by somatic mutation in the UBA1 gene

that encodes ubiquitin-like modifier activating enzyme 1 and is expressed on cells of myeloid lineage. Patients with VEXAS are usually older men that present with treatment-refractory severe systemic inflammation and pronounced neutrophilic infiltrates in tissues with clinical features of vasculitis, polychondritis, and/ or myelodysplasia. The mutation inactivates E1 ubiquitin ligase activity of the enzyme, which is important for protein homeostasis through promotion of proteasomal degradation of damaged or unwanted proteins in a cell. Inactivation of UBA1 results in disruption of intra-cellular architecture in neutrophils that can often be visualized as cytoplasmic vacuoles. Neutrophils in this disease maintain their phagocytic activity; however, they have increased NET formation. Our understanding of this disease is still evolving, and further research may help untangle the role of ubiquitylation and other-post-translational modifications in neutrophil functions.

Several drugs have been attributed to induce autoimmunity. Recent evidence suggests a role of NET formation in some drug-induced vasculitis. Vasculitis purpura with neutropenia and ANCAs is seen in some active illicit users of cocaine contaminated with levamisole. This phenomenon is likely due to levamisole as it induces formation of NETs through engagement of muscarinic subtype 3 receptor. Patients actively using levamisole-adulterated cocaine have autoantibodies against NET components in sera. Additionally, NETs were found to be present in skin biopsies of areas with vasculitis in these patients.

Other studies have shown a role of neutrophil activation and increased NET formation in vasculitis induced by drugs like propylthiouracil (PTU), 108 procainamide, and hydralazine. Interestingly, the NETs generated by these drugs differ. For example, NETs generated by exposure of neutrophils to PTU are relatively resistant to digestion by DNase 1, whereas those generated by exposure to hydralazine require PAD4 activation and do not interfere with DNase 1 degradation. These variations in types of NETs could possibly explain the differences in phenotypes because these drugs.

### Targeting Neutrophils and Neutrophil Extracellular Traps in Systemic Autoimmune Diseases

Given the key role that neutrophils and NETs play in the pathogenesis of wide-ranging systemic autoimmune diseases, there is increasing interest in targeting them for therapeutic purposes. Drugs that can decrease formation, half-life, or release of NETs could be beneficial. Since ROS production is key in NET formation, inhibitors of NADPH oxidase or mitochondrial ROS production or ROS scavengers, like N-acetylcysteine (NAC), have been explored in vitro and in vivo with mixed results in murine models and SLE patients.57, Inhibition of various granule protein functions, like MPO, in mouse models of immune complex-mediated vasculitis decreased neutrophil recruitment, NET formation, and inflammatory cytokine formation and is a potential target. TLR inhibition may also have similar effects, with in vitro studies on human neutrophils showing TLR4 inhibition resulted in decreased NET formation and ROS production. Another protein of interest are the PAD enzymes, as targeting them has shown a decrease in NET formation and autoantibodies and protection from organ and vascular damage in mice models of lupus.64,

Degrading already formed NETs to help improve their removal is another potential approach. DNaselL3 is an enzyme involved in degradation of extra-cellular DNA, like in NETs. Humans and mice with genetic defects in this enzyme have lupus features with autoantibody production, suggesting a possible use of this enzyme in systemic autoimmune disease patients with high levels of NETs. Other drugs that can destabilize NET structures by affecting the actin cytoskeleton could also decrease the half-life of NETs.

Blocking IL-17 can decrease neutrophil trafficking and NET formation and may diminish lupus nephritis.162, Interruption of interactions between endothelial ligands and neutrophilexpressed kindlin-3 and B2 integrin could lead to a decrease in neutrophil recruitment and NET release in tissues. Similarly, blocking various chemokines may limit pathogenic tissue infiltration of neutrophils. Reduction of circulating NETs and improvement in lupus biomarkers was also seen by reducing autoantibodies and immune complexes by a combination of monoclonal antibodies targeting CD20 (rituximab) and BLyS/ BAFF (belimumab).

Neutrophils with elevated IFN signature are primed for NET formation. Blocking of IFN signaling through use of mAb (anifrolumab) targeting the type I IFN receptor (IFNAR1) has shown promising results in two lupus trials and is now approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration. Anifrolumab also decreased NET formation in SLE subjects compared with placebo. Similarly, anti-malarials like hydroxychloroquine are weak type I IFN inhibitors and can decrease NET formation in vitro. Also, inhibitors of Janus kinases (JAKs), signaling molecules for several proinflammatory cytokines like IFNs, can directly modulate neutrophil biology. Tofacitinib, a pan-JAK inhibitor, reduced NET formation in vitro and in vivo and decreased disease manifestations in lupusprone mice. In a phase Ia/IIb clinical trial of tofacitinib in SLE patients, LDGs and NETs were significantly decreased.

### Conclusion

Neutrophils play a key role as the first l ine o f d efense a gainst foreign organisms. Through chemotaxis, phagocytosis, oxidative burst, or NET formation, neutrophils protect our bodies from many forms of infection and also send signals to help develop more directed responses. However, growing evidence over the past decade has shown that dysregulated neutrophil responses are responsible for several autoimmune and autoinflammatory conditions. Rogue neutrophil responses can lead to direct tissue injury, create an inflammatory milieu, and generate autoantigens. Recent studies have also recognized the diverse and functionally distinct subsets of neutrophils. Targeting pathogenic neutrophil subsets or dysregulated neutrophil functions, like NET formation, are areas of exciting research with hopes of development of novel therapeutic strategies.

### 12 T Lymphocytes

### KEY POINTS

### Introduction

The establishment and maintenance of adaptive immune responses and memory depends to a large extent on T lymphocytes. T cells provide more than merely protection from infection and are involved in tumor surveillance, as well as tissue homeostasis. The generation of an enormous number of T cell receptors during T cell development is a random stochastic process that is agnostic to the host's self-antigens. T cells thus confront the dilemma of generating receptors that can recognize a broad array of antigens from foreign pathogens, tumors, and normal tissues without provoking an autoimmune response to the host. The price for generating an enormously varied population of antigen receptors needed

to recognize a wide spectrum of pathogens is the progressive risk of producing self-reactive lymphocytes. T lymphocytes are thus subjected to a rigorous selection process during development in the thymus to delete self-reactive T cells (central tolerance). In addition, premature activation of mature peripheral T cells is prevented by requiring two signals for activation (peripheral tolerance). Finally, the expansion of T cells that occurs during either homeostatic proliferation in peripheral lymphoid tissues or in response to an infection is resolved by the active induction of cell death. Autoimmune disorders (many discussed in other chapters of this text) have been described resulting from inefficient removal of T lymphocytes at any one of these junctures.

The activation of T lymphocytes yields a variety of effector functions that are pivotal to combating infections. Cytolytic T cells can kill infected cells through the release of granules containing perforin and granzymes that induce holes in cell membranes and cleave cellular substrates, respectively, or expression of ligands for death receptors such as Fas (cluster of differentiation 95 [CD95]) or TNF receptor 1. Production of T cell cytokines such as interferon-γ (IFNγ) by T helper type 1 (Th1) cells (see below) can inhibit viral replication, whereas other cytokines such as IL-4, IL-5, and IL-21 by T cell helper type 2 (Th2) cells are critical for optimal B cell growth and immunoglobulin production. However, this same armamentarium, if not tightly regulated, can also precipitate damage to host tissues and provoke autoimmune responses, such as in the synovium of inflammatory arthritides, pancreatic islets in type 1 diabetes, and the central nervous system in multiple sclerosis. Damage in these cases need not be directly the result of recognition of target tissues by the T cells. T cells may be activated elsewhere and then migrate to the tissue and damage innocent bystander cells. T cells may also promote autoimmunity through the augmentation of B cell responses. The following sections detail these events.

### T Cell Development

T lymphocytes originate from bone marrow progenitors that migrate to the thymus for maturation, selection, and subsequent export to the periphery. T cells must traverse two stringent hurdles during their development. First, they must successfully rearrange the genes encoding the two chains of the T cell antigen receptor (TCR). Second, T cells must survive thymic selection, during which T cells bearing a TCR that interacts strongly with selfmajor histocompatibility complex (MHC)/peptides are eliminated (called negative selection). This minimizes the chances of autoreactive T cells escaping to the periphery and is known as central tolerance. In addition, developing thymocytes must also make

moderate interactions with self-MHC/peptides to survive (called positive selection), as those T cells making no meaningful contact are also eliminated. The result of this "Goldilocks" concept of nottoo-strong, not-too-weak TCR-MHC/peptide interactions is that less than 3% of developing thymocytes actually leave the thymus. This amounts to about 107 naive T cells per day released from the human thymus,2 resulting in approximately 4 x 1011 circulating T cells in the adult human body.

The TCR is an 80 to 90 kDa disulfide-linked heterodimer composed of a 48 to 54 kDa α-chain and a 37 to 42 kDa β-chain. An alternate TCR composed of γand δ-chains is expressed on 2% to 3% of peripheral blood T cells and is discussed below. The TCR-αβ has an extracellular ligand-binding pocket for MHC/ peptide and a short cytoplasmic tail that by itself cannot signal. Consequently, it is noncovalently associated with as many as five invariant chains of the CD3 complex, which relay information to the intracellular signaling machinery via immunoreceptor tyrosine activation motifs (ITAMs) (see below). The structure of the TCR gene locus is, not surprisingly, similar to immunoglobulin genes in B cells (see details in Chapter 13). To economically package up to theoretically 1015 TCR specificities4 within a genome of fewer than 30,000 genes, the process of gene rearrangement and splicing evolved using machinery similar to what already existed to promote gene translocations. The βand δ-chain genes of the TCR contain four segments known as the V (variable), D (diversity), J (joining), and C (constant) regions. The αand γ-chains are similar but lack the J component. Each of the segments has a range of family members (approximately 50 to 100 V, D, 6 to 60 J, and 1 to 2 C members). An orderly process occurs during TCR gene rearrangement in which a D segment is spliced adjacent to a J segment, which is subsequently spliced to a V segment. Following transcription, the VDJ sequence is spliced to a C segment to produce a mature TCR messenger RNA. Arithmetically, this random rearrangement of a single chain of the TCR locus can give rise to minimally 50V x 15D x 6J x 2C or about 9000 possible combinations. At each of the splice sites, which must occur in-frame to be functional, additional nucleotides not encoded by the genome (so-called N-region nucleotides) can be incorporated, adding further diversity to the rearranging gene. The combinations from the two TCR chains, plus N-region diversity, yield at least 10 million theoretical possible combinations. The cutting, rearranging, and splicing are directed by specific enzymes. Mutations in the genes for these processes can result in an arrest in lymphocyte development. For example, mutation in the gene encoding a DNA-dependent protein kinase (DNA-PK) required for receptor gene recombination abrogates T cell development and results in a severe-combined immunodeficiency known as SCID.

Since the developing T cell has two copies of each chromosome, there are two chances to successfully rearrange each of the two TCR chains. As soon as successful rearrangement occurs, further β-chain rearrangements on either the same or the other chromosome are suppressed, a process known as allelic exclusion. This limits the chance of dual TCR expression by an individual T cell. The high percentage of T cells that contain rearrangements of both β-chain genes attests to the inefficiency of this complex event. Rearrangement of the α-chain occurs later in thymocyte development in a similar fashion, although without apparent allelic exclusion. This can result in dual TCR expression by a single T cell.

Development of T cells occurs within a microenvironment provided by the thymic epithelial stroma. The thymic anlage is formed from embryonic ectoderm and endoderm and is then

colonized by hematopoietic cells, which give rise to dendritic cells, macrophages, and developing T cells. The hematopoietic and epithelial components combine to form two histologically defined compartments: (1) the cortex, which contains immature thymocytes, and (2) the medulla, which contains mature thymocytes (Fig. 12.1A). As few as 50 to 100 bone marrow—derived stem cells enter the thymus daily.

The stages of thymocyte development can be defined by the status of TCR gene expression and the expression of CD4 and CD8, proceeding in an orderly fashion from CD4-8- → CD4+8+ → CD4+8or CD4-8+ (Fig. 12.1B). CD4 and CD8 define, respectively, the helper and cytolytic subsets of mature T cells.

CD4-8thymocytes can be further subdivided based on their expression of CD25 (the high-affinity IL-2 receptor α-chain) and CD44 (the hyaluronate receptor). Development proceeds in the order: CD25-CD44+ → CD25+CD44+ → CD25+CD44- → CD25-CD44- (Fig. 12.1A). These subpopulations correspond to discrete stages of thymocyte differentiation. CD25-44+ cells contain TCR genes in germline (unrearranged) configuration. These cells upregulate CD25 to give rise to CD25+CD44+ thymocytes, which now express surface CD2 and low levels of CD3ε. At the next stage (CD25+CD44-), there is a brief burst of proliferation followed by upregulation of the recombination-activating enzymes, RAG-1 and RAG-2, and the concomitant rearrangement of the genes of the TCR β-chain. A small subpopulation of T cells rearranges and expresses a second pair of TCR genes known as γ and δ. Productive TCR β-chain rearrangement results in a second proliferative burst, yielding CD25-CD44thymocytes.

The TCR β-chain cannot be stably expressed without an α-chain. Since the TCR α-chain has not yet rearranged, a surrogate invariant TCR pre-α-chain is initially disulfide linked to the β-chain. When associated with components of the CD3 complex, this allows a low-level surface expression of a pre-TCR and progression to the next developmental stage. Failure to successfully rearrange the TCR β-chain results in a developmental arrest at the transition from CD25+CD44to CD25-CD44with subsequent deletion of the T cells that failed to develop. This occurs in mice and humans who lack the enzymes critical for rearrangement of the genes encoding the TCR.

CD25-CD44cells upregulate expression of CD4 and CD8 to become CD4+8+, at which point the α-chain of the TCR rearranges. Unlike the β-chain, allelic exclusion of the α-chain is not apparent. Rearrangement of the α-chain can occur simultaneously on both chromosomes, and if one attempt is unsuccessful, repeat

rearrangements to other Vα segments are possible. Reports exist of dual TCR expression by as many as 30% of mature T cells in which the same T cell expresses different α-chains paired with the same β-chain. However, in most cases of dual TCR α-chains, one is downregulated during positive selection by Lck and Cbl, through ubiquitination, endocytosis, and degradation.

Although the structure of immunoglobulin and TCR are quite similar, they recognize fundamentally different forms of antigens. Immunoglobulins recognize intact antigens in isolation, either soluble or membrane bound, and are often sensitive to the tertiary structure. The TCR-αβ recognizes linear stretches of antigen peptide fragments bound within the grooves of either MHC class I or II molecules (Fig. 12.3A). Thymic selection molds the repertoire of emerging TCRs so that they recognize peptides within the groove of self-MHC molecules, ensuring the self-MHC restriction of T cell responses. The MHC structure is described in detail in Chapter 20. Pockets within the MHC groove bind particular residues along the peptide sequence of 7 to 9 amino acids for MHC class I and 9 to 15 amino acids for MHC class II molecules. As a result, certain amino acids make strong contact with the MHC groove, while others are exposed to contact the TCR.

The contact between the TCR and MHC/peptide has been revealed by crystal structure to be remarkably flat, rather than a deep lock and key structure as one might imagine. The TCR axis is tipped about 30° to the long axis of the MHC class I molecule and is slightly more skewed for MHC class II. The affinity of the TCR for MHC/peptide is in the micromolar range. This is a lower affinity than many antibody—antigen affinities and several logs less than many enzyme-substrate affinities. This has led to the notion that TCR interactions with MHC/peptide are brief, and successful activation of the T cell requires multiple interactions, resulting in a cumulative signal.

Once the T cell has successfully rearranged and expressed a TCR in association with the CD3 complex, it encounters the second major hurdle in T cell development: thymic selection. Selection has two phases, positive and negative, and the outcome is based largely upon the intensity of TCR signaling in response to interactions with self-MHC/peptides expressed on thymic epithelium and dendritic cells. TCR signals that are either too weak (death by neglect) or too intense (negative selection) result in elimination by apoptosis, whereas those with intermediate signaling intensity survive (positive selection) (Fig. 12.3B). Successful positive selection at the CD4+8+ stage is coincident with upregulation of

surface TCR, the activation markers CD5 and CD69, and the survival factor Bcl-2. T cells bearing a TCR that recognizes MHC class I maintain CD8 expression, downregulate CD4, and become CD4-8+. T cells expressing a TCR that recognizes MHC class II become CD4+8-.

An enigma for thymic selection has been how to present the myriad self-proteins to developing thymocytes so that self-reactive thymocytes are effectively eliminated by negative selection. This includes particularly those antigens with tissue or developmentally restricted expression. A solution was found with the discovery of the autoimmune regulator (AIRE) gene. AIRE is a transcriptional regulator expressed by the medullary epithelium of the thymus that induces transcription of a wide array of organ-specific genes, such as insulin, that might otherwise be sequestered from developing thymocytes. This effectively creates a self-transcriptome within the thymus against which autoreactive T cells can be deleted. Gene knockout mice of AIRE and humans bearing AIRE mutations manifest various autoimmune sequelae in a syndrome known as autoimmune polyendocrinopathy—candidiasis—ectodermal dystrophy (APECED).

Not surprisingly, a variety of signaling molecules activated by TCR engagement are important to thymic selection. These include Lck, the Ras → Raf-1 → MEK1 → extracellular signalregulated kinase (ERK) kinase cascade, the kinase ZAP-70, and the phosphatases CD45 and calcineurin, which are involved with positive selection. Among these, the Ras → ERK pathway is particularly important, as dominant-negative variants of these molecules can disrupt positive selection. Conversely, an activator of Ras known as GRP1 assists the positive selection of thymocytes expressing weakly selecting signals. These molecules are discussed in more detail in the section on TCR signaling. By contrast, although a number of molecules may promote negative selection, among them the mitogen-activated protein (MAP) kinases c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK) and p38, there appears to be sufficient redundancy so that only rarely does elimination of any one of these molecules alter the efficient deletion of thymocytes. The few exceptions include CD40, CD40L, CD30, or the proapoptotic Bcl-2 family member, Bim, in which preservation of at least some thymocytes bearing self-reactive TCR could be observed in mice deficient in these molecules.

The survivors of these stringent processes of TCR gene rearrangement and thymic selection represent less than 3% of total immature thymocytes. This is reflected by the presence of a high rate of cell death among developing thymocytes. This can be visualized by the measurement of DNA degradation, a hallmark of apoptosis, as shown in Fig. 12.4. The survivors become either CD4+ helper or CD8+ cytolytic T cells and reside in the thymic medulla for 12 to 14 days before emigrating to the periphery. The decision to become a CD4+ versus CD8+ T cell involves the observation that long TCR interactions are required for CD4 progression, whereas shorter TCR engagement favors CD8 progression.

### Immunodeficiencies Resulting From Defects in T Cell Development

Given the vast number of events in T cell development, it is not surprising that multiple causes can underlie human T cell immunodeficiencies. The influence of the thymic stroma on thymocyte ontogeny is underscored in the DiGeorge anomaly, in which development of the pharyngeal pouches is disrupted and the thymic rudiment fails to form. This results in the failure of normal T cell development. Less severe T cell deficiencies are associated with a failure to express MHC

class I and/or class II (the "bare lymphocyte syndrome"), which are directly involved with interactions required to induce the positive selection of, respectively, CD8+ and CD4+ mature T cells.

Metabolic disorders can affect thymocytes more directly. The absence of functional adenosine deaminase (ADA) and purine nucleoside phosphorylase (PNP) results in the buildup of metabolic by-products that are toxic to developing T and B lymphocytes. This ultimately produces forms of SCID.

### Peripheral Migration and Homeostatic Proliferation ofT Cells

In early life, the majority of T cells are newly emerged from the thymus and naive. With age, memory T cells are generated from exposure to foreign antigens or self-antigens during homeostatic proliferation. This may parallel a shift in function toward tumor surveillance and tissue homeostasis. With recurrent stimulation, immunosenescence occurs with a decline in T cell function, which can result in immunodysregulation and inflammation.17, The migration of naive T cells to peripheral lymphoid structures or their infiltration into other tissues requires the coordinate regulation of an array of cell adhesion molecules. Entry from the circulation into tissues occurs via two main anatomic sites: (1) the flat endothelium of the blood vessels and (2) specialized postcapillary venules known as high endothelial venules (HEVs). A three-step model has been described for lymphocyte migration: (1) rolling, (2) adhesion, and (3) migration. L-selectin expressed by naive T cells binds via lectin domains to carbohydrate moieties of GlyCAM-1 and CD34 (collectively known as peripheral node addressin), which are expressed on endothelial cells, particularly HEVs. The weak binding of CD62L to its ligand mediates a weak adhesion to the vessel wall, which, combined with the force of blood flow, results in rolling of the T cell along the endothelium. This increased cell contact facilitates the interaction of a second adhesion molecule on lymphocytes, the integrin LFA-1 (CD11a/CD18) with its ligands, intercellular adhesion molecule (ICAM)-1 (CD54) and ICAM-2 (CD102). This results in the arrest of rolling and firm attachment. Migration into the extracellular matrix of tissues involves additional lymphocyte cell surface molecules such as the hyaluronate receptor (CD44) or the integrin α4β7 (CD49d/β7), which binds the mucosal addressin cell adhesion molecule-1 (MAdCAM-1) on the endothelium of Peyer's patches and other endothelial cells.

Additional mediators known as chemokines contribute to lymphocyte homing. Chemokines are structurally and functionally related to proteins bearing an affinity for heparan sulfate proteoglycan and promote migration of various cell types. The chemokines regulated on activation, T cell expressed and secreted (RANTES), macrophage inflammatory protein (MIP)-1α, MIP- 1β, membrane cofactor protein (MCP)-1, and IL-8 are produced by a number of cell types, including endothelium, activated T cells, and monocytes, and are present at inflammatory sites such as rheumatoid synovium (see Chapter 71).

Once mature T cells have reached the peripheral lymphoid tissues of lymph node and spleen, they undergo a slow rate of proliferation known as homeostatic proliferation in response to self- MHC/peptide complexes, and the cytokines IL-7 and IL-15.22 This serves to maintain the number of peripheral T cells and can become enhanced in response to lymphopenia, such as following chemotherapy or HIV infection. Since homeostatic proliferation is driven by self-MHC/peptides and is thus inherently autoimmune, its acceleration could precipitate an autoimmune diathesis. In this regard, it is of interest that one of the standard murine models of autoimmunity is day 3 thymectomy, which results in the lymphopenia and autoimmunity of various organs. In addition, nonobese diabetic (NOD) diabetic mice have chronic lymphopenia that contributes to their diabetes,25 and evidence of augmented homeostatic proliferation has been suggested to occur in rheumatoid arthritis. Homeostatic proliferation is also regulated by the death receptor Fas (CD95). In the absence of Fas in mice or humans, T cells accumulate that express a gene profile that includes upregulation of cytolytic and proinflammatory molecules such as Fas-ligand, granzyme B, and IFNγ, as well as the immunoinhibitory molecules PD-1 and LAG3.28 This might serve to explain the clinical immunology paradox of sudden autoinflammatory features in immunodeficient individuals, such as the development of sudden psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis in HIV-infected individuals.

### Activation of T Cells

### Metabolic Switch

T cell activation initiates an intracellular signaling cascade that ultimately results in proliferation, effector function, or death,

depending on the intensity of the TCR signal and associated signals. This requires a dramatic change in metabolism from largely oxidative phosphorylation to glycolysis, in order to provide the synthetic machinery for proliferation and production of effector molecules. To guard against premature or excessive activation, T cells have a requirement of two independent signals for full activation. Signal 1 is an antigen-specific signal provided by the binding of the TCR to antigenic peptide complexed with MHC. Signal 2 is mediated by either cytokines or the engagement of costimulatory molecules such as B7.1 (CD80) and B7.2 (CD86) on antigen presenting cells (APCs). Receiving only Signal 1 without co-stimulation results in T cell unresponsiveness or anergy, a process known as peripheral tolerance.

### TCR Signal Regulation

TCR αβ and γδ have very short cytoplasmic domains and by themselves are unable to transduce signals. The molecules of the noncovalently associated CD3 complex couple the TCR to intracellular signaling machinery (Fig. 12.4). The CD3 complex contains nonpolymorphic members known as CD3ε, CD3γ, and CD3δ, as well as the ζ chain, which is a separate gene not genetically linked to the CD3 complex. Although the functional stoichiometry of the TCR complex is not completely defined, current data indicate that each TCR heterodimer is associated with three dimers: (1) CD3 εγ, (2) CD3εδ, and (3) ZZ. CD3 ε, γ, and δ have an immunoglobulin-like extracellular domain, a transmembrane region, and a modest cytoplasmic domain, whereas ζ contains a longer cytoplasmic tail. The transmembrane domains of ζ and the CD3 chains contain a negatively charged residue that interacts with positively charged amino acids in the transmembrane

domains of the TCR stabilizing the TCR/CD3 complex, allowing its cell-surface expression.

None of the proteins in the TCR/CD3 complex has intrinsic enzymatic activity. Instead, the cytoplasmic domains of the invariant CD3 chains contain conserved activation domains that are required for coupling the TCR to intracellular signaling molecules. These ITAMs contain a minimal functional consensus sequence of paired tyrosines (Y) and leucines (L): (D/E) XXYXXL(X)6-8YXXL. ITAMs are substrates for cytoplasmic protein tyrosine kinases (PTKs), and upon phosphorylation they recruit additional molecules to the TCR complex. Each ζ chain contains three ITAMs, whereas there is one in each of the CD3 ε, γ, and δ chains. Thus each TCR/CD3 complex can contain as many as 10 ITAMs.

Activation of PTKs is one of the earliest signaling events following TCR stimulation. Four families of PTKs are known to be involved in TCR signaling: (1) Src, (2) Csk, (3) Tec, and (4) Syk. The Src family members Lck and FynT have a central role in TCR signaling and are expressed exclusively in lymphoid cells. Src PTKs contain multiple structural domains including: (1) N-terminal myristylation and palmitoylation sites that allow association with the plasma membrane, (2) an Src homology (SH) 3 domain that associates with proline-rich sequences, (3) an SH2 domain that binds phosphotyrosine-containing proteins, and (4) a carboxyl-terminal negative regulatory site. Their catalytic activity is regulated by the balance between the actions of kinases and phosphatases. Activity is repressed by phosphorylation of a conserved carboxy-terminal tyrosine, and thus its dephosphorylation by the phosphatase CD45 is critical for the initiation of TCR-mediated signal transduction. In addition, autophosphorylation of other tyrosines within the kinase domain enhances catalytic activity. Lck is physically and functionally associated with CD4 and CD8. Of total Lck molecules, 50% to 90% are associated with CD4, and 10% to 25% are associated with CD8. CD4 and CD8 physically associate with the TCR/CD3 complex during antigen stimulation as a result of their interaction with MHC class II and class I molecules, respectively, and thus enhance TCR-mediated signals by recruiting Lck to the TCR complex. Lck phosphorylates the CD3 chains, TCRZ, ZAP-70, phospholipase C-γ1 (PLC-γ1), Vav, and Shc. Fyn binds TCRZ and CD3ε, and, although its substrates are less well defined, T cells lacking Fyn have diminished responses to TCR signals. In addition, the SH2 and SH3 domains of Src PTKs can mediate their association with, respectively, phosphotyrosineand proline-containing molecules.

Somewhat less is known about the Csk and Tec PTKs. Csk negatively regulates TCR signaling by phosphorylating the carboxyl-terminal tyrosine of Lck and Fyn. Dephosphorylation of this negative regulatory tyrosine is mediated by the transmembrane tyrosine phosphatase CD45. CD45 activity is essential for TCR signaling as CD45-deficient T cells fail to activate by TCR stimulation. The Tec family member Itk is preferentially expressed in T cells and regulates PLC-γ. T cells from Itk-deficient mice have diminished responses to TCR stimulation.

Phosphorylation of the ITAM motifs on the CD3 complex recruits the Syk kinase family member ZAP-70 by its tandem SH2 domains. ZAP-70 is expressed in developing B cells, natural killer cells, and T cells and plays a key signaling role in these lineages. Following TCR stimulation, ZAP-70 is activated by phosphorylation of tyrosine 493 by Lck. Loss-of-function hypomorphic alleles of ZAP-70 result in reduced TCR signaling and a propensity for autoimmune phenomena.

### Adaptor Proteins

Phosphorylation of tyrosine residues in ITAMs and PTKs following TCR stimulation creates docking sites for adaptor proteins. Adaptor proteins contain no known enzymatic or transcriptional activities but mediate protein-protein interactions or protein— lipid interactions. They function to bring proteins in proximity to their substrates and regulators and sequester signaling molecules to specific subcellular locations. The protein complexes formed can function as either positive or negative regulators of TCR signaling, depending on the molecules they contain.

Two critical adaptor proteins for linking proximal and distal TCR signaling events are (1) SH2 domaincontaining leukocyte protein of 76 kDa (SLP-76) and (2) linker for activation of T cells (LAT) (Fig. 12.4). Loss of these adaptor proteins has profound consequences for T cell development. Mice deficient for LAT or SLP-76 manifest a block in T cell development at the CD4-8- CD25+CD44+ stage. LAT is constitutively localized to lipid rafts and, following TCR stimulation, is phosphorylated on tyrosine residues by ZAP-70. Phosphorylated LAT then recruits SH2 domain-containing proteins including PLCγ1, the p85 subunit of phosphoinositide 3-kinase, IL-2inducible kinase (Itk), and the adaptors Grb2 and Gads. Since the SH3 domain of Gads is constitutively associated with SLP-76, this brings SLP-76 to the complex, where it is phosphorylated by ZAP-70. SLP-76 contains three protein-binding motifs: (1) tyrosine phosphorylation sites, (2) a proline-rich region, and (3) an SH2 domain. The N terminus of SLP-76 contains tyrosine residues that associate with the SH2 domains of Vav, the adaptor Nck, and Itk. Vav is a 95 kDa protein that acts as guanine nucleotide exchange factor for the Rho/Rac/ cdc42 family of small G-proteins, critical for cytoskeletal organization. The complex of LAT, SLP-76/Gads, PLCγ1, and associated molecules results in the full activation of PLCy 1 and activation of Ras/Rho GTPases and the actin cytoskeleton.

In addition to acting as positive regulators for TCR signaling, adaptors can also mediate negative regulation. As described previously, the activity of the Src family kinases is regulated by the interaction of kinases (Csk) and phosphatases (CD45) specific for inhibitory C-terminal phosphotyrosine, and this is determined by the subcellular localization of these regulatory molecules. A second mechanism by which adaptor proteins can negatively regulate TCR stability is through regulation of protein stability. Proteins can be targeted for degradation by the conjugation of ubiquitin to lysine residues via a series of enzymatic reactions by E1, E2, and E3 ubiquitin ligases. Cbl-b, c-Cbl, ITCH, and GRAIL are E3 ligases, and mice lacking these proteins manifest T cell hyperproliferation and autoimmune phenotypes. For example, Cbl-b binds and ubiquitinates ZAP70, resulting in its degradation and reduced TCR signaling.

### Downstream TCR Signaling

The previously described signaling events couple TCR stimulation to downstream pathways that culminate in changes in gene transcription that are required for proliferation and effector function (Fig. 12.4). One of the best-characterized genes induced following T cell activation is the T cell growth factor IL-2. Transcription of the IL-2 gene is regulated in part by the transcription factors AP-1, nuclear factor of activated T cells (NFAT), and nuclear factor (NF)-kB, all of which are activated following TCR stimulation. Proximal signaling events lead to the activation of Ras and PLCγ. Ras initiates a cascade of kinases

including Raf-1, MEK1, and the MAP kinase ERK, which leads to the production of the transcription factor Fos. Ligation of the co-stimulatory molecule CD28 results in the activation of another member of the MAP kinase family, JNK, and phosphorylation of the transcription factor c-Jun. c-Jun and Fos associate to form AP-1. PLCγ hydrolyzes membrane inositol phospholipids to generate phosphoinositide second messengers including inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate (IP3) and diacylglycerol. IP3 stimulates the mobilization of calcium from intracellular stores. Diacylglycerol activates protein kinase C (especially PCKθ in T cells) and, along with CARMA, Bcl-10, and MALT1, connects with the NF-κB pathway.

Increased intracellular calcium is central to many forms of cellular activation. Calcium activates the calcium/calmodulindependent serine phosphatase, calcineurin, which dephosphorylates NFAT. Dephosphorylated NFAT translocates to the nucleus and, together with AP-1 and NF-kB, activates the IL-2 gene. The immunosuppressive agents cyclosporin A and FK-506 specifically inhibit the calcium-dependent activation of calcineurin, thereby blocking activation of NFAT and the transcription of NFAT-dependent cytokines such as IL-2, IL-3, IL-4, and granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF). Differences in the amplitude and duration of calcium signals mediate different functional outcomes. Although high spikes of calcium are easily measured in lymphocytes during the first 10 minutes following antigen stimulation, sustained low-level calcium spikes over a few hours are necessary for full activation. These latter, more subtle calcium fluxes are controlled by cyclic ADP-ribose and ryanodine receptors. Selective inhibitors exist for these molecules, opening the potential for new specific blockers of T cell activation.

### Co-stimulation

Signal 2 is mediated either by growth factor cytokines or through a co-stimulatory molecule, of which the prototype is CD28 on T cells interacting with CD80 (B7-1) or (CD86) (B7-2) on APCs. CD28 is a disulfide-linked homodimer constitutively expressed on the surface of T cells. Virtually all murine T cells express CD28, while, in human T cells, nearly all CD4+ and 50% of CD8+ cells express CD28. The CD28subset of T cells appears to represent a population that has undergone chronic activation and can manifest suppressive activity. Increased levels of CD28- T cells have been reported in several inflammatory and infectious conditions, including granulomatosis with polyangiitis, rheumatoid arthritis, and certain viral infections such as cytomegalovirus (CMV) and mononucleosis.40-42 The cytoplasmic domain of CD28 has no known enzymatic activity but does contain two SH3-binding sites and one SH2-binding site. CD28 interacts with phosphoinositide 3-kinase and GRB2 and promotes JNK activation. CD28 ligation alone does not transmit a proliferative response to T cells but, in conjunction with TCR engagement, augments the production of several cytokines, including IL-2, IL-4, IL-5, IL-13, IFNγ, and TNF, as well as the chemokines IL-8 and RANTES at the level of both transcription and translation.

The ligands for CD28, CD80 (B7-1), and CD86 (B7-2) are expressed in a restricted distribution on B cells, dendritic cells, and monocytes. CD80 and CD86 have similar structures but share only 25% amino acid homology. They each contain rather short cytoplasmic tails that may signal directly and bind to CD28 with different avidities. Increased levels of soluble co-stimulatory

molecules CTLA-4, CD28, CD80, and CD86 have been reported in SLE patients and correlate disease activity.

### Immunologic Synapse

Antigen-specific interaction between the T cell and APC results in the formation of a specialized contact region called the immunologic synapse, or supramolecular activation cluster (SMAC) (Fig. 12.5). Synapse formation is an active, dynamic process that requires specific antigen and MHC. The synapse also overcomes the obstacles resulting from interactions of tall molecules (ICAM-1, LFA-1, CD45) to promote T cell/APC contact that is mediated by short molecules (e.g., TCR, MHC, CD4, CD8). Two stages of assembly have been described: (1) the nascent stage and (2) the memory stage. During the nascent stage, cell adhesion molecules such as ICAM-1 on APC and LFA-1 on T cells make contact in a central zone, surrounded by an annulus of close contact between the MHC and the TCR. Within minutes, the engaged TCR migrates to the central area, resulting in a mature synapse in which the initial relationships are reversed—the central area (cSMAC) now contains TCR, CD2, CD28, and CD4 and is enriched for Lck, Fyn, and protein kinase C (PKC)-θ. Surrounding the central domain is a peripheral ring (pSMAC) that contains CD45, LFA-1, and associated talin. T cell activation also leads to compartmentalization of TCR signaling molecules to plasma membrane microdomains called rafts. Rafts are composed primarily of glycosphingolipids and cholesterol and are enriched in signaling molecules, actin, and actin-binding proteins. Src family kinases, Ras-like G proteins, LAT, and phosphatidylinositolanchored membrane proteins all localize to raft domains. An example of a defect in immune synapse formation is illustrated in Wiskott—Aldrich syndrome (WAS). This is an X-linked severe primary immunodeficiency characterized by eczema and thrombocytopenia, caused by mutations in the Wiskott—Aldrich syndrome protein (WASp), a scaffold that promotes actin polymerization and links TCR stimulation to T cell activation and formation of the immune synapse. Absence or mutations in WASp affects intercellular APC-T cell communications by interfering with multiple mechanisms on both sides of the immune synapse.

Full T cell activation requires engagement of a minimum of approximately 100 to 200 MHC/peptide molecules on an APC, which can serially stimulate 2000 to 8000 TCRs. It has been estimated that naive T cells also require a sustained signal for 15 to 20 hours to commit to proliferation. T cells face a number of obstacles to achieving full activation, including the small physical size of the TCR and MHC molecules compared with other cell surface molecules, the low affinity of TCR for MHC/peptide complex, and the limited percentage of MHC molecules present on the APC that contain the antigenic peptide appropriate for the specific TCR. The immunologic synapse helps provide a mechanism for overcoming these barriers and achieving the duration of It has been shown that co-stimulatory signals may contribute to synapse formation by initiating the transport of membrane rafts containing the kinases and adaptor molecules required for TCR signaling to the site of contact.

### Tolerance and Control of Autoreactive T Cells

The immune system is continually confronted by the dilemma of how to ensure that T cells are activated only under conditions in which there is a true need for a response to a foreign pathogen

and not merely a self-component. As with many biologic filters, thymic negative selection is not 100% efficient, and not all selfreactive T cells are eliminated. Hence, a variety of additional mechanisms are engaged to suppress the ability of these errant T cells to undergo inappropriate clonal expansion. This is partly regulated by the requirement of two distinct signals from separate molecules (TCR and CD28) to be coordinately triggered in order for T cell activation and proliferation to proceed. If only the TCR signals is received, the T cell will not proliferate and will actually enter a nonresponsive state known as anergy.

The anergy that results from the absence of a CD28 co-stimulatory signal manifests as a failure to fully couple the TCR signal to Ras/MAP kinase pathway and consequent AP-1 transcriptional activity. An additional method of provoking an incomplete TCR signal and unresponsiveness is to make amino acid substitutions in the recognized peptide antigen. These so called altered peptide ligands cause a suboptimal phosphorylation of TCRZ and consequent inefficient recruitment of ZAP-70.

Additional members of the CD28 family serve as inhibitory molecules, many of which have been targeted for therapeutic intervention of autoimmune disorders. Cytolytic T lymphocyteassociated protein 4 (CTLA-4) also binds to CD80 and CD86 with 20-fold higher affinity than CD28. Unlike CD28, CTLA-4 is expressed only transiently following T cell activation and confers an inhibitory signal for T cell proliferation. In this capacity, CTLA-4 functions to limit T cell clonal expansion induced by

CD28. The consequences of the loss of CTLA-4 negative regulation are striking. The genetic deletion of the ctla-4 gene in mice results in enormous uncontrolled T cell expansion and an autoimmune syndrome. Ctla4 was also identified as a genetic risk factor in rheumatoid arthritis. CTLA4-Ig (Abatacept), which functions to interfere with CD28 binding to its ligands hence abrogating its ability to provide the key second signal, is licensed for treatment of rheumatoid arthritis and psoriatic arthritis.

Programmed cell death 1 (PD-1) is another member of the CD28 family that possesses an immunoreceptor tyrosine-based inhibiting motif (ITIM) within its cytoplasmic tail that associates with the tyrosine phosphatase SHP-2.51 PD-1 does not bind the CD28/CTLA-4 ligands, CD80 or CD86, but rather to PD-L1 and PD-L2. PD-L1 is expressed by both lymphoid tissues (e.g., regulatory CD4+CD25+ T cells, inflammatory macrophages) and nonlymphoid tissues (e.g., heart, placenta, lung, pancreas, and certain tumors). PD-L2 expression is more confined to macrophages and dendritic cells. Ligation of PD-1 on T cells leads to cell cycle arrest. Treatment of mice with a blocking antibody to PD-L1 caused virus-specific CD8+ T cells to undergo marked expansion. 51, The fact that many tumors also express PD-L1 explains the striking success in promoting anti-tumor responses with blocking antibodies to PD-1 or PD-L1 seen in clinical practice. The fact that PD-1-deficient mice develop lupus-like arthritis and glomerulonephritis enhances interest in manipulating PD-1 for therapeutic purposes. The converse is also true, of course,

and the use of antiPD-1 and anti—PD-L1 immunotherapy for a variety of tumors is coupled with concern for potential autoimmune side effects (see Chapter 130).

Chronic exposure to certain inflammatory cytokines, most notably TNF, can also induce anergy. It has been appreciated for some time that T cells from rheumatoid synovium manifest profound deficiencies of proliferation and cytokine production,54 and TNF is one of the major cytokines detectable in rheumatoid synovial fluid. Further studies demonstrated that chronic exposure of T cell clones to TNF for 10 to 12 days suppressed proliferative and cytokine responses to antigen by as much as 70%. Furthermore, a single administration of anti-TNF receptor monoclonal antibody to patients with rheumatoid arthritis rapidly restored the response of peripheral T cells to mitogens and recall antigens. Similar observations have been made in TCR transgenic mice following TNF exposure.

An additional negative regulator for T cells is the B lymphocyte—induced maturation protein 1 (Blimp-1) that was initially identified in B lymphocytes. Blimp-1deficient mice manifest augmented levels of peripheral effector T cells and develop severe colitis as early as 6 weeks of age. Blimp-1 mRNA expression in T cells increases with TCR stimulation, and Blimp-1-deficient T cells manifested enhanced proliferation and produced more IL-2 and IFNγ following activation.

### Regulatory T Cells

Another layer of cellular regulation occurs via a phenotypically defined subpopulation of CD4+CD25+ FoxP3+ regulatory T cells (Treg) that has the ability to inhibit antigen-induced proliferation. This subset represents 5% to 15% of peripheral blood CD4 T cells and is at least partly thymic-dependent. The absence of regulatory T cells following day 3 thymectomy likely contributes to the development of autoimmune disease in these animals. Diminished levels of CD4+CD25+ FoxP3+ regulatory T cells have been observed in other autoimmune syndromes, and the transfer of Treg to autoimmune mice has shown some alleviation of symptoms. The production of TGFβ and IL-10 and expression of CTLA-4 appear to be critical to the suppressive activity of Treg. This is a very active area of research because of the potential therapeutic implications for autoimmune diseases and their possible role in generating IL-17-producing CD4+ T cells, T helper type 17 (Th17) cells (see below). In this regard, studies to treat type 1 diabetes by increasing Treg number and function using anti-CD3 antibody or IL-2 are promising. In addition, a genetic analysis of risk loci for rheumatoid arthritis identified the greatest enrichment of trimethylation of histone H3 at lysine 4 of rheumatoid arthritis risk factors in Tregs out of 34 cell types studied, further supporting a role for Tregs in the pathogenesis of rheumatoid arthritis.

Tregs also have important functions in tissue homeostasis, particularly in skin, fat, and muscle. Whereas Tregs represent about 5% to 15% of CD4+ T cells in peripheral blood, they account for 60% to 80% of CD4+ T cells in adipose tissue, where they respond to IL-33 and are critical for adipocyte formation and insulin sensitivity.

In the skin, Tregs are located around hair follicles and are required for hair growth in a NOTCH-dependent manner. They also accumulate in injured muscle and are important for the switch of infiltrating macrophages from inflammatory M1 phenotype to noninflammatory M2 macrophages. Tregs also accumulate in the muscles of patients with muscular dystrophy. This underscores

the growing realization that certain T cell subsets are also involved with tissue homeostasis.

### T Cell Subsets

### CD4+ Helper and CD8+ Cytolytic T Cells

αβ T cells can be subdivided into two main subsets based on their recognition of peptides presented by MHC class I or II molecules and their respective expression of CD4 or CD8. CD4+ and CD8+ T cells have different functions and recognize antigens derived from different cellular compartments. The peptides presented by MHC class I molecules are produced by the proteasome67 and can be derived from either self-proteins or intracellular foreign proteins, as might occur during viral infection. MHC class IIbound peptides are derived largely from extracellular infectious agents or self cell-surface proteins that have been engulfed and degraded in the lysosomal complex.

CD8+ T cells, often referred to as cytolytic T cells (CTLs), are very efficient killers of pathogen-infected cells. Given the ubiquitous expression of MHC class I molecules, mature CD8+ CTLs can recognize infections in a wide array of cells, in distinction to the more restricted distribution of class II molecules. CTLs use three primary systems by which to kill target cells. The first is the release of two types of cytolytic granules: (1) perforin and (2) granzymes. Perforin, as the name implies, forms holes in the membrane of the target cell, similar to complement. This allows the granzymes contained in the granules to enter the target cell. Granzymes are serine proteases that cleave proteins within the target cell, ultimately leading to cell death. The cytolytic granules are released in the direction of the target cells to avoid collateral damage of bystander cells. The second pathway is secretion of interferon-γ, which has anti-microbial effects. The third pathway of CD8+ CTL is by production of TNF and Fas ligand (FasL), which bind their respective receptors on target cells and induce apoptosis through activation of a caspase cascade. CD8 manifests an affinity for MHC class I molecules and binds Lck by its cytoplasmic tail to enhance TCR signaling.

CD4+ T cells express a variety of cytokines and cell surface molecules that are important to B cell proliferation and immunoglobulin production, as well as to CD8+ T cell function. Following antigen stimulation, CD4+ T cells differentiate into different classes of effector T cells identified by their cytokine profiles, including Th1, Th2, Th17, T follicular helper (Tfh) cells (described below), and Treg cells (described previously) (Fig. 12.6). The CD4 molecule is structurally related to immunoglobulins and has an affinity for nonpolymorphic residues on the MHC class II molecule, similar to the affinity of CD8 for MHC class I. In this capacity, CD4 presumably increases the efficiency with which CD4+ T cells recognize antigen in the context of MHC class II molecules, the expression of which is restricted to B cells, macrophages, dendritic cells, and a few other tissues during states of inflammation. In addition, the cytoplasmic tail of CD4 binds to Lck and promotes signaling by the TCR as described earlier. However, ligation of CD4 prior to engagement of the TCR can render T cells susceptible to apoptosis upon subsequent engagement of the TCR. This is clinically important in HIV infections in which the gp120 molecule of HIV binds to CD4 and primes the T cell to undergo cell death when later triggered by the TCR. Accelerated apoptosis of CD4+ T cells has been demonstrated in AIDS patients.

### CD4 T Helper Subsets

CD4 T cells can be further subdivided based upon their cytokine profiles (Fig. 12.6). Th1 cells produce IL-2, TNF, and IFNγ and participate in cell-mediated inflammatory reactions and the activation of macrophages. Th2 cells, by contrast, produce IL-4, IL-5, IL-6, and IL-10. IL-4 and IL-5 are important B cell growth factors. In addition, IL-4 promotes B cell secretion of IgG1 and IgE, whereas IFN-γ drives IgG2a production. A third group of cytokine-producing T cells are Th17 cells, important for driving many aspects of autoimmune inflammation. Both IFN-γ and the type 2 cytokine locus shared by IL5, IL13, and IL4 are present only in vertebrates, whereas IL-17 is considerably more ancient in evolution, with orthologs in invertebrates; the sea urchin has 30 IL-17-like genes.

These Th cytokine patterns have been best characterized during chronic infections. In general, a Thl response helps eradicate intracellular microorganisms, such as Leishmania major and Brucella abortus,72 whereas a Th2 cell response can better control extracellular pathogens, such as the helminth, Nippostrongylus braciliensis. The cytokine profiles of Th1 and Th2 cells are mutually inhibitory, such that the Th1 cytokine IFN-γ, or IL-12 from APC, suppresses Th2 responses and augments Th1 cytokine gene expression, whereas the Th2 cytokine IL-4, or IL-6 from APC, promotes the opposite pattern. Polarization of the cytokine environment also occurs at the sites of inflammation in many autoimmune

syndromes. Th2 skewing has been observed in models of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), in which increased levels of immunoglobulins and autoantibodies are typical, as well as in chronic allergic conditions such as asthma. In a variety of autoimmune disorders, the infiltrating lymphocytes exhibit a bias toward Th1 cytokines. This occurs with brain-infiltrating lymphocytes in multiple sclerosis and its animal model experimental allergic encephalomyelitis (EAE),75 in β islet lymphocytes in diabetes,76 and in synovial lymphocytes in inflammatory arthritides. Unlike the beneficial effects of Th1 responses during infections, these same cytokines can be quite deleterious in autoimmune disorders. Thus therapies based on inhibition of certain Th1 cytokines have been of considerable interest and often ameliorative, such as anti-TNF treatment of in rheumatoid arthritis. Several cytokines can have pleotropic effects, and predicting the effects of modulating their levels can be complex. For example, despite the tendency of IL-6 to promote a Th2 cytokine profile, blocking IL-6 is beneficial in rheumatoid arthritis.

A subset of IL-17-producing CD4+ T cells (Th17) is critical for promoting a variety of autoimmune disorders. Th17 cells are regulated by the transcription factor RORyt and can be broadly divided into two groups: (1) host protective cells that express both IL-17 and IL-10 and are activated by TGFβ and IL-6 and (2) a highly inflammatory population that expresses IL-17, IL-22, and IFN-γ that are activated by IL-23 and IL-1β.80, IL-22 has important functions at mucosal surfaces in host defense, as well

as in wound repair.
