Chemokines are essential for normal homeostasis of the immune system by ensuring lymphocyte progenitors migrate to appropriate regions within primary lymphoid organs and that mature, naïve cells populate their correct niche within SLOs.55, Following activation in SLOs, chemokines also play a key role in directing effector cells to the appropriate tissues where they can exert their protective functions. There are four subfamilies of chemokines grouped as CXC, CC, CX3C, and XC based upon structural similarities within each category. The different receptors respond to their cognate chemokines and activate signaling pathways that direct migration of target cells and, in some circumstances, activate target cells. One example of coordinated lymphocyte movements directed by chemokine—receptor pairs is that of CCR7 and CXCR5. High CCR7 expression on naïve T cells (and activated APCs) directs these cells to the T cell zone where their ligand is present,68 whereas cells in the splenic B cell zone elaborate chemokines that bind CXCR5 expressed by naive B cells, resulting in their migration to the follicle. Once activated, B cells downregulate CXCR5 and upregulate CCR7, thus allowing for their transient movement to the TB interphase, in which they can be further activated. Conversely, a small population of T cells upregulate CXCR5 and downregulate CCR7, which causes them to move into the B cell follicle where they support B cell responses.

B and T cells that find their cognate antigen and are activated in the spleen leave the organ via the portal circulation. As part of their activation program, their chemokine receptors and adhesion molecules (see later) are altered, ultimately directing the cells to the tissues. Those B and T cells that fail to be activated in the spleen also reenter the circulation but, instead of homing to tissues, remain in the circulation, where they can reenter other SLOs in search of an antigenic signal.

### Lymphatics

Lymphocytes are unique cells in the body because they circulate through two parallel circulations: the blood and lymphatic vessels. Lymphatics are an open vascular network that serves to

drain tissue spaces, as well as the SLOs, and carry lymphocytes and fluids (known collectively as lymph) to the heart, where the lymph is admixed with blood. One important function of the lymphatic system is to ensure that fluids leaving the bloodstream

capillaries to bathe the tissues are returned to the circulation. It is estimated that approximately 3 liters of such fluid is generated each day. Failure of the lymphatics to maintain fluid homeostasis results in lymphedema, a condition that can become a debilitating disorder. Lymphatics draining the tissues also play a critical role in delivering activated APCs (with the antigens they present) to regional lymph nodes, thereby concentrating antigen in sites accessible to patrolling T cells. Lymphatics are also key to directing lymphocytes from SLOs back into the circulation as the network of lymphatic vessels end in the thoracic duct, which itself empties into the superior vena cava and subsequently the heart. Using the combined blood and lymphatic circulatory networks allows for continued migration of lymphocytes into the SLOs, where antigen encounters occur, but also allows for activated lymphocytes to leave the lymphoid system and home to the tissues where their effector functions may be needed. How lymphatics develop is an area of considerable investigation, with a number of recent discoveries describing their formation and maintenance. This work will certainly provide additional insights into the regulation of lymphocyte circulation, as well as clues for new approaches for the treatment of lymphatic disruption.

### Lymph Nodes and Mucosal Lymphoid Tissue

Lymph nodes are the SLOs found at the intersection of blood and lymphatic vessels.71,72 "True" lymph nodes are encapsulated organs, strategically located throughout the body to drain the various tissues. Mucosal lymphoid tissues do not have a capsule, but, in virtually all other regards, they are similar to lymph nodes and hence are grouped together in this description.

The lymph node capsule covers the cortex, which, in turn, surrounds the paracortex and then the medulla. Lymph nodes are vascularized by lymphatics originating in the tissues that deliver APCs that have been activated in the periphery (typically by danger signals associated with pathogen encounters) and are able to present antigen to arriving T cells. Afferent lymphatics enter the lymph node through the capsule and empty into the marginal sinus (Fig. 20.3A). Lymph bathes the node, allowing APCs to find their niche, largely through chemokine/chemokine receptor interactions. Lymph then collects in the efferent lymphatics, which leaves the lymph node and eventually makes its way to the thoracic duct, the heart, and the blood vessel circulation. Lymphocytes enter the lymph node through the blood circulation, flowing into the lymph node stroma via post-capillary venules designated high endothelial venules. Similar to the spleen, the lymph node architecture allows for spatial discrimination between T cell (parafollicular cortex) and B cell (follicular and germinal center) zones that are populated with the appropriate stromal elements, APCs, and support cells for the distinct lymphocyte populations (Fig. 20.3B and C). Lymphocytes dwell in the lymph node long enough to survey the environment for cognate antigen and then leave the lymph node via the efferent lymphatics to reenter the blood circulation. As in the spleen, should a productive encounter with antigen occur, cells emigrating from the lymph node alter expression of key receptors that will ultimately direct them to the tissues. Nonactivated cells maintain their naive phenotype and recirculate from the bloodstream back to SLOs.

Lymph nodes are the location for the expansion of B and T cells responding to an antigenic challenge. The extensive cell division is manifest as clinical lymphadenopathy. Under normal circumstances, following removal of the pathogen that incited expansion of these immune cells, lymph nodes are also

the site of the subsequent contraction phase eliminating the vast majority of the activated cells. Failure of this contraction to occur may result in persistent lymphadenopathy and survival of autoreactive cells, a hallmark of a number of rheumatic diseases.

The largest collections of lymphoid tissues in the body are found associated with mucosal surfaces. This makes a great deal of immunologic sense as these surfaces represent the barrier between the host and the outside world replete with potential pathogens. Hence, there are significant collections of B and T cells in the tonsils, adenoids, and along the respiratory mucosa, throughout the gut, and surrounding the urogenital tracts. These lymphoid collections are not encapsulated and are not considered by some investigators as true SLOs. However, they function in many of the same ways, have a similar architecture, and support B and T cell recirculation, activation, and tolerance induction as do encapsulated lymph nodes. Although there are many anatomic and functional similarities, mucosal-associated lymphoid structures also have unique properties related to the types of antigenic challenges that predominate in their particular locations. For example, Peyer's patches in the gut express specialized chemokines to attract particular classes of lymphocytes and are the most important site of IgA production. Similarly, intestinal and respiratory collections of lymphoid tissue are important locations for cytokine production that drive a particular subset of CD4+ T cells known as Th2 cells74 that are responsive to helminth infections, given the importance of these barrier surfaces to protect against ingested or inhaled parasites.

### Tertiary Lymphoid Structures

Tertiary lymphoid structures, also known as ectopic lymphoid follicles, are organized collections of lymphocytes and stromal elements that occur outside of the normal SLOs. While these structures resemble SLOs in many ways, they are distinguished from SLOs by the fact that they occur in organs not typically associated with lymphoid development or where a primary adaptive immune response (stimulation of naive cells to become effectors) takes place. The distinction between tertiary lymphoid structures and SLOs is debated as some investigators consider mucosal-associated lymphoid structures a part of the normal SLO network, while others consider all lymphocyte collections that lack a defined capsule as being part of the tertiary lymphoid structures system. Tertiary lymphoid structures often appear in response to chronic inflammatory conditions and are another hallmark of several autoimmune disorders. Such examples include collections of organized lymphoid collections in the synovium of patients with rheumatoid arthritis76 or in salivary glands of individuals with Sjögren's syndrome.77, It is thought that immune activation in these sites potentiates disease through continued stimulation of potentially self-reactive lymphocytes.

### Trafficking of Adaptive Immune Cells

### Egress From the Thymus and Lymph Nodes

For lymphocytes to exert their functions, they must enter and leave the circulation at various times. For example, maturing thymocytes remain resident in the thymus throughout their development but then leave to begin their surveillance in the SLOs. Similar to residency time in the thymus, T cells must remain in the SLOs long enough to encounter representative APCs to

allow for activation to occur. However, the likelihood that such an encounter will occur at any point in time is low, so there must be a mechanism for T cells to leave a lymph node, reenter the circulation, and then enter another lymph node where an APC with the appropriate antigen can be found. Recent work has shown that control of lymphocyte egress from primary and SLOs relies on the dynamic expression of a subclass of receptors for sphinogosine 1 phosphate (S1P1).79-81 Binding of S1P1 receptor type 1 by S1P1 is critical for lymphocytes to exit into the circulation and travel to the next set of SLOs for sampling of antigens or to tissues in the case of T cells that have been activated in the SLOs. Understanding the biology of lymphocyte egress has been exploited for therapeutic benefit with the introduction of FTY720, an agent that when modified in the body acts to internalize the S1P1 receptor, preventing T cell egress from both the thymus and lymph nodes. Use of FTY720 to sequester potentially autoreactive T cells and prevent their migration to peripheral organs has proven an effective strategy for multiple sclerosis. Studies are ongoing to determine use of this agent in other immune-mediated disorders.83-85

### Lymphocyte e Migration and Circulation to SLOs and Peripheral Tissues

There are multiple mechanisms that govern the appropriate migration of progenitor T and B cells into their generative organs, then for mature cells to travel through the circulation, transit through SLOs, and eventually reach their target tissues.55, These mostly rely on cell surface receptors expressed on the lymphocytes that drive directional chemotaxis of these cells (chemokine receptors) and other receptors on their surfaces that promote adhesion when the cells traffic to the appropriate location (integrins). T cells and B cells express different family members of these receptors that direct homing to appropriate locations in the body. Of note, expression of chemokine receptors is not static, but changes as cells undergo developmental progression and activation. Hence, for example, naive cells express a suite of chemokine receptors that direct these cells to SLOs and their appropriate APCs. Once activated, however, a different set of such receptors is expressed to direct the effector lymphocytes away from the SLOs and, instead, to the peripheral tissues. Beyond this, sublineages of lymphocytes also express characteristic chemokine receptors that are, in turn, responsive to tissue-specific ligands that are often expressed preferentially after contact with particular classes of antigens. This differential expression of chemokines and their receptors helps ensure the trafficking of the appropriate effector cells to the areas of greatest need.

In addition to chemokines and their receptors, integrins and their ligands are critical for lymphocyte trafficking. Unlike chemokines, which are soluble mediators that initiate leukocyte chemotaxis, integrin ligands are found on cell surfaces. The interaction between integrins and their ligands is important at a number of steps during lymphocyte circulation, as they enter and then migrate to appropriate regions within SLOs, as they leave these organs, and then as they extravasate into tissues and travel through the endothelial layers and parenchmya. Elegant studies have unraveled the multistep process by which integrins function to facilitate leukocyte migration through the bloodstream and then into tissues. A key first step for T and B cells to leave the high-flow, turbulent circulation is for these cells to be captured by the vascular endothelium at the entry point into the SLOs or tissues. This initial capture is accomplished by interactions between integrins on the adaptive immune cells and their ligands. For naive T cells, the integrin/receptor pair that is most critical is L-selectin (CD62L) on the lymphocyte that

interacts with one of the members of the peripheral node addressin (PNAd) family, glycosylation-dependent cell adhesion molecule 1 (GlyCAM 1) or CD34 on lymph node high endothelial venules, or mucosal vascular addressin cell adhesion molecule 1 (MAdCAM 1) in Peyer's patches. These interactions are not high affinity, and the lymphocytes arrest for only a short period of time. However, other signals, for example those delivered by chemokines, alter the integrins themselves on the T cells, increasing the affinity of the interactions between the integrins and their ligands. This process, known as inside-out signaling, in which second messengers activated by other receptors signal to integrins and change their characteristic,89 allows naive T cells to arrest firmly on the endothelial surface and then crawl between endothelial cell junctions into the lymph node parenchyma. From there, the lymphocytes follow chemokine gradients and populate their appropriate niche.

Productive interactions between lymphocytes and their antigens in the SLOs stimulate a number of intra-cellular signals. One consequence of these activation events is increased expression of integrins and increased integrin affinity for their ligands. These changes allow for more efficient arrest of the activated lymphocytes on endothelial surfaces in the region of inflamed tissues, once the activated lymphocytes leave the SLOs and survey the tissues through the bloodstream. For example, activated T cells express high levels of CD44, VLA-4, and VLA-5, molecules that bind tissue matrix components (such as hyaluronic acid, fibrin, and fibronectin) that increase with inflammation. Hence, as activated T cells pass near such regions, their integrins will bind avidly to their cognate ligands, arrest along the endothelium, and facilitate entry of the cells into the tissues. Collectively, the response to chemokines and increased function of integrins brings activated lymphocytes to the regions where they are most needed, areas of tissue damage and active inflammation (Fig. 20.4).

### Cell-to-Cell Interactions That Support Development t of an Immune Response

T cells and B cells do not function in isolation but are highly dependent on cooperation with cells of the innate immune system for their function (Fig. 20.5). The most obvious example of this is that naive T cells only become activated after encountering APCs with the appropriate peptide antigen displayed by the correct (for that TCR) MHC molecules. Importantly, however, APCs provide other cell surface structures that are critical for activating and shaping the adaptive immune response. One of the most important discoveries related to T cell biology stemmed from the observation that stimulation of T cells via a peptide—MHC combination on APCs (known as signal 1) is not sufficient to elicit a T cell response, and in fact, stimulating T cells solely through this mechanism results in T cells becoming unresponsive (anergic). Hence, activation of T cells requires stimulation of the TCR in combination with engagement of other T cell surface receptors by ligands present on APCs. These other receptors are known collectively as co-stimulatory receptors, and the signal delivered by their engagement has been designated signal 2. The chance that this required second signal will be delivered is augmented through stabilizing the interaction between T cells and APCs. Stabilization is accomplished, in part, by inside-out signaling from the TCR, which, like signals from chemokines, increases affinity of integrins, such as lymphocyte function associate antigen-1 (LFA-1) on T cells which then binds more tightly to its ligand, intercellular adhesion molecule-1 (ICAM-1) on the APC.

The most potent and best studied signal 2 is delivered by the co-stimulatory receptor CD28. In addition to CD28,92 there are a number of other co-stimulatory receptors that serve to reinforce or prolong T cell activation, including adhesion proteins that stabilize the interaction of T cells and the APC, other members of the CD28 superfamily93 such as inducible T cell co-stimulator (ICOS), as well as several members of the TNF and TNF receptor family of co-stimulatory proteins such as OX40 and 4-1BB. Much work is being done to better understand the biology of these receptors and their ligands, which are often upregulated on activated cells of the innate immune system.

Of equal importance to those signals that co-stimulate T cells are those that function to dampen their responses. Inhibitory receptors, such as programmed cell death 1 (PD-1) and cytotoxic T-lymphocyte—associated protein 4 (CTLA-4) begin to be expressed on activated T cells as a way to regulate the magnitude of their response. Signaling through these receptors can directly interfere with the positive signal provided by co-stimulatory receptors. Additionally, because CTLA-4 binds to the same ligands (B7.1 and B7.2) as CD28, CTLA-4 can directly interfere with CD28 engagement. Given the powerful impact of both co-stimulatory and inhibitory signals on T cell activation, it is no surprise that enhancing or limiting engagement of these types of receptors is actively being pursued as means to treat immune-mediated disorders and modulate the immune response to malignancy.95,

In addition to signals delivered through direct cellcell contact, innate immune cells elaborate a large number of cytokines, such as interleukin (IL)-12, and other soluble mediators that bind to receptors on T cells. These cytokines, often described as signal 3, have a profound influence on the magnitude as well as the type of T cell effector response that will be manifest. As with the co-stimulatory versus inhibitory signals described previously, cytokines from innate immune cells do not always promote immune responses. There are many inhibitory cytokines, IL-1098 and transforming growth factor (TGF)-β99 being classic among this group, that suppress the activation of adaptive immune cells. Moreover, just as the cytokine microenvironment generated by innate cells directs the differentiation of T cells, T cellderived cytokines can affect innate cell function. One example is macrophage differentiation into inflammatory versus suppressive subtypes. This process is dependent in part on T cells in the vicinity and on the type of cytokines they produce. Despite the complex nature of cytokines and their cellular functions, many have become attractive pharmacologic targets, with inhibition of TNF or its receptors being the most successful to date for the treatment of immune-mediated rheumatologic conditions.

T cells are the major source of help for B cells, providing both cell-to-cell interactions and soluble factors required for B cell activation. B cells that have taken up antigen via their BCR can process that antigen and present it as peptide—class II MHC complexes to CD4+ T cells. In turn, CD4+ helper T cells provide stimulatory signals, of which CD40 ligand (CD40L) is perhaps the best described. Ligation of CD40 on B cells induces a host of B cells functions, including proliferation, immunoglobulin class-switching, and somatic hypermutation within the variable regions of the BCR to increase antibody affinity within germinal centers. CD40L expression is also accompanied by secretion of one of a number of T cellderived cytokines (such as IL-4, a potent B cell proliferation factor), which direct B cells to classswitch their immunoglobulins to specific isotypes best suited to combat the infection at hand. In addition to providing stimulation for B cells, CD40 ligation on innate immune cells is also

critical for generating a robust immune response. Macrophages require CD40 ligation for full activation and upregulation of their anti-microbial activity, and ligation of CD40 on dendritic cells is a potent signal for their final maturation.

Innate immune cells also modulate the B cell response through altering the cytokine microenvironment. For example, innate cell production of type I interferons can render B cells more sensitive to BCR stimulation,103 thus enhancing their activation, a property that may significantly affect the severity of a number of rheumatologic disorders. As another example, within the bone marrow, eosinophils provide plasma cells with critical cytokines (APRIL and IL-6) to sustain their long-term survival and thus support "immunologic memory. "104

### Consequences of Failed Development or Activation of the Adaptive Immune System

Defects in the development or function of adaptive immune cells can have serious consequences for the host. Such outcomes have been shown in both experimental animal models and strikingly in patients with genetic or acquired abnormalities of the B and/ or T cell compartments. Understanding the molecular underpinnings of these disorders has provided important insights into the fundamental biology of the immune system and disease pathogenesis and has also given rise to potential targets for pharmaceutical agents that have proven extremely effective in many rheumatic (and other) disease states.

### B Cell Deficiency and Hyperactivity

X-linked (Bruton's) agammaglobulinemia was described in 1952 as an immunodeficiency affecting young boys. This disorder, the first immunodeficiency identified in human patients, is characterized by the lack of circulating antibody resulting in frequent, severe bacterial infections that may be life threatening. Subsequent studies revealed that the lack of antibody is due to the absence of mature B lymphocytes in these patients. Since the description of this disease, decades of investigation have provided insights into the molecular events critical for B cell development and subsequent B cell activation. Among these discoveries was the identification of key enzymes that coordinate B cell function following engagement of the BCR by antigen. One of these enzymes is a protein tyrosine kinase essential for a B cell activation signal to occur. This kinase, now known as Bruton's tyrosine kinase (BTK), functions to couple engagement of the stimulated BCR to the downstream biochemical events critical for B cell maturation and division. The absence of BTK in patients with Bruton's agammaglobulinemia abrogates the ability of the BCR to "signal," hence arresting B cell development at an early stage in the bone 106,107 marrow.

While it was long known that the absence of circulating antibody in patients with Bruton's agammaglobulinemia could be remedied by regular infusions of intravenous gamma globulin, identification of the molecular basis for this disease provides new opportunities not only for treatment of this particular disease but also, more widely, for therapeutic interventions. In the case of Bruton's agammaglobulinemia, understanding the molecular underpinnings of this disorder sets the stage for eventual cure by gene replacement therapy. Although this is not currently an approved mode of therapy, it is likely that advances in the field will result in ex vivo correction of the gene in patient-derived stem

cells with subsequent infusion into patients for reconstitution of corrected, autologous hematopoietic progenitor cells. Beyond this, however, the discovery of BTK and its essential role in B cell proliferation has already provided a new avenue for treatment of patients with B cell leukemias and lymphomas. 109-111 Drugs that interfere with BTK function, in clinical use since 2013, are now firmly established as an effective immunotherapy and have dramatically altered the course of disease in a subset of patients. Numerous studies are in progress evaluating the use of BTK inhibition in rheumatic diseases, in particular rheumatoid arthritis, with results expected to be forthcoming.

For many years, B cell biologists sought discovery of cell surface markers that would uniquely identify B cells for their studies. The cell surface antigen, CD20, emerged as one such marker, and the development of reagents directed against this protein added greatly to the fundamental study of B cell function. Given the importance of B cells and antibodies in disease pathogenesis, investigators quickly realized that anti-CD20 antibodies had the potential not only to identify B cells but also to target them for immune destruction and therapeutic advantage. It has now been more than 20 years that anti-CD20 antibodies have been available for the elimination of B cells in the setting of B cell malignancies. Since that time, indications for the use of anti-CD20 antibodies have expanded to include immune-mediated diseases that are triggered or perpetuated by overexuberant B cell function, including rheumatoid arthritis, microscopic polyangiitis, and granulomatosis with polyangiitis. Interestingly, one adverse effect that may occur with anti-CD20 therapy is hypogammaglobulinemia, the condition that in many ways heralded our understanding of the role of B cells as a critically important immune lineage.

### T Cell Deficiency and Hyperactivity

That the thymus and thymus-derived T cells play an essential, nonredundant role in host defense was not appreciated until the 1960s. Studies in mice by Jacques Miller in 1961 showed that neonatal thymectomy resulted in loss of T cells and coincident immune deficiency. These findings were extended to human patients in the mid-1960s with the identification of DiGeorge syndrome, a disorder that includes among its manifestations the congenital lack of the thymus with consequent absence of circulating T cells. DiGeorge patients suffer from serious infections, particularly due to intra-cellular pathogens. These findings were extended in nude mice, an important animal model of thymic deficiency. Experiments in murine model systems and further evaluation of patients with T cell defects established that the thymus is not a vestigial organ but instead plays a critical role in host defense as the generative organ for T cells.

As an appreciation developed for the central role played by T cells in host defense, patients with T cell defects were described. Some of these individuals had abnormalities restricted to the T cell compartment, while others manifested dysfunction in multiple immune lineages. s. This range of consequences underscored both some of the common features of immune cell development, as well as the functional interdependence of cells of the immune system. For example, loss of T cells precludes T cells from providing help to B cells and is manifested by diminished antibody production and near absence of class-switched antibodies. As our understanding of T cell biology became more sophisticated, an understanding of different T cell effector subsets grew. This work both led and was enhanced by the discovery of patients with selective defects in T cell compartments. A key example of such discoveries includes the identification

of patients harboring mutations in FOXP3, a gene required for the development of regulatory T cells, a T cell subset that functions to inhibit responses of other effector T cells. Loss of regulatory T cells was found to be causal for the wide range of devastating autoimmunity afflicting patients with immunodysregulation polyendocrinopathy enteropathy X-linked (IPEX) syndrome.

Discoveries related to the biology of T cells and the unique properties of T cell activation have led to numerous approaches to either augment or diminish T cell function in vivo to ameliorate disease. For example, understanding the requirement of costimulation for activation of T cells led to reagents that block the interaction between CD28 on T cells and its ligand on APCs. This blockade diminishes T cell reactivity and has become an established treatment for rheumatoid arthritis. Recent years have also seen remarkable success in treating cancer with so-called checkpoint blockade reagents. Instead of preventing stimulation of activating coreceptors, these drugs interfere with the "break" on T cell activation by blocking engagement of inhibitory receptors on T cells by their ligands on APCs or cancer cells, in the case of malignancies. Antibody-mediated blockade of the T cell inhibitory receptor, PD-1, or its ligand, PD-L1, functions in this way to restore expansion and functional properties of exhausted CD8+ T cells such that they reengage their anti-tumor properties. As would be expected, one of the adverse events seen with immunotherapeutic checkpoint blockade is the emergence of autoimmunity, underscoring the precarious balance the immune system must maintain to eliminate dangers from the host, while ensuring the health of self-tissues.

### Conclusion

Adaptive immunity is an essential component of the finely orchestrated immune system network that provides for defense of the host. T and B cells play nonredundant roles that function collaboratively with cells of the innate immune system and collectively protect individuals from a range of challenges, from external pathogens to mutation and damage of one's own cells. While the innate immune system is pre-wired to detect molecular patterns that signal danger, the adaptive immune system evolved to be highly specific and able to detect minute changes signaling "foreignness." Beyond its specificity and diversity, the adaptive immune system possesses memory so that subsequent encounters with pathogens are dealt with more quickly and efficiently. The flip side of the potential of the adaptive immune system to recognize foreign antigens is the risk for autoimmunity requiring multiple mechanisms to achieve and maintain tolerance to self.

Understanding the fundamental biology of adaptive immune cells has led to a greater appreciation for how these processes may go awry, leading to immune-mediated tissue destruction, a hallmark of many rheumatic disorders. New knowledge that we have gained about adaptive immune cell function has also given important insights into novel approaches to pharmacologically modulate immune function. This has led to remarkable therapeutic advances for important diseases and has put us on the threshold of continued progress in designing new therapies and personalizing those that are now available to the best advantage of our patients. However, understanding the "on-target" and the less well explained adverse effects of many of these novel agents will require further investigation into the fundamental biology of cells of the adaptive immune system.

# Tolerance and Immune Autoimmunity

### KEY POINTS

### Introduction

Autoimmune diseases represent a significant and increasing health burden for 3% to 9% of the general population, and rheumatology, perhaps more than any medical subspecialty, encompasses a broad array of such diseases that affect a wide range of organ systems (Table 21.1).1-5 Consequently, rheumatologists have a great interest in defining the causes and pathophysiology of autoimmunity and in applying this information in the clinic.

The immune system must effectively defend against a diverse universe of pathogens while simultaneously maintaining tolerance to self-antigens. Recent advances have begun to clarify how this equilibrium is established and sustained and, importantly, have identified many critical factors and processes involved in the pathogenesis of autoimmune diseases. This chapter provides a general overview of autoimmunity, covering the definition of the term, general tolerance mechanisms for T and B lymphocytes, theories of how tolerance can be breached, and ways in which genetic and environmental factors have been implicated in breaking tolerance and producing disease. Emphasis is placed on manifestations and mechanisms related to rheumatologic diseases.

### Definition and Classification of Pathogenic Autoimmunity

Autoimmunity—that is, the immune response against self— evokes the specter of "horror autotoxicus," a term coined by Paul Ehrlich at the turn of the 20th century to anticipate the disastrous consequences of this condition. In fact, autoreactivity is more nuanced, ranging from a low "physiologic" level of self-reactivity essential for lymphocyte selection and maintenance of normal immune system homeostasis, to an intermediate level of autoimmunity that manifests as circulating autoantibodies and tissue infiltrates that are not associated with clinical consequences, to pathogenic autoimmunity associated with immune-mediated dysfunction or injury. From the clinical perspective, it is the transformation to pathogenic autoimmunity that demarcates significant from insignificant self-reactivity.

The diagnosis of an autoimmune disease is generally based on the presence of adaptive immune system—mediated disease caused by self-reactive antibodies, T cells, or both. For many common autoimmune diseases, more definitive evidence for an autoimmune cause has come from studies showing transfer of disease by autoantibodies or self-reactive T cells and from animal models exhibiting congruent characteristics. However, no universally accepted criteria exist, and some less well-characterized diseases currently considered to be autoimmune may turn out to have other causes.

An example of disorders that exhibit some characteristics of autoimmunity but are distinct in their pathogenesis are the autoinflammatory diseases.8-16 These diseases are predominantly rare monogenic disorders typified by intermittent bouts of fever, rash, serositis, and arthritis caused by a widening spectrum of defects in the control of basic inflammatory pathways. Included in this category are familial Mediterranean fever, the cryopyrinopathies, hyperimmunoglobulinemia D with recurrent fever, familial cold urticaria, Blau syndrome, and others. These syndromes can be viewed broadly along with autoimmune disease as disorders in which autoreactivity causes tissue damage: the autoinflammatory diseases mediated entirely through the innate arm of the immune system comprise one end of the autoreactive spectrum, while at the other end are the autoimmune diseases that require both the innate and adaptive responses. Indeed, the possibility of a less stringent

demarcation has been suggested by disorders such as Behcet's disease, systemic juvenile rheumatoid arthritis, and Crohn's disease, which appear to manifest various degrees of both autoinflammatory and autoimmune features. Similarly, the interferonopathies, a subset of the autoinflammatory diseases caused by mutations that alter the processing or sensing of cytoplasmic nucleic acids, are associated with high levels of type I interferons, interferonassociated pathology, and lupus-like manifestations. 17,

Autoimmune diseases can be classified as systemic or organspecific depending on the extent of their clinical pathology (Table 21.2). The systemic category includes systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), rheumatoid arthritis (RA), scleroderma, antiphospholipid syndrome, primary Sjögren's syndrome, dermatomyositis, and systemic vasculitides. In systemic disease, autoimmunity targets ubiquitously expressed self-antigens. End organ injury is typically mediated by autoantibodies and, less commonly, by T cells. In contrast, in organ-specific diseases, the self-antigens are typically cellor tissue-specific in location or accessibility, and end organ damage or dysfunction can be mediated by antibodies and/ or T cells. Some of the more notable examples of the latter group,

which span virtually all organ systems, include Hashimoto's thyroiditis, Graves' disease, multiple sclerosis (MS), neuromyelitis optica, type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM), pemphigus vulgaris, autoimmune hemolytic anemia, idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura, and myasthenia gravis. It should be emphasized, however, that although the distinction of systemic and organ-specific disorders provides a conceptual framework, individual pathophysiologies are more diverse than is implied by this classification. Autoimmune diseases are also classified by a hypersensitivity reaction type based on the mechanism of adaptive immune system mediated injury,19 a topic that is discussed later in the chapter.

### Animal Models of Autoimmunity

Much of what is known about the immune system and autoimmunity has been derived from studies in animals, particularly the mouse, which has an immune system and genome composition like that of humans. Many well-characterized autoimmune models exist in which investigators can manipulate genomes and immune systems, test interventions, and modify environments, including the microbiome, diet, and exposure to microbial agents and toxins. Animal models of autoimmune disease can be divided into three main types based on their derivation: (1) spontaneous, (2) genetically modified, and (3) induced. Some of the more commonly studied models and those illustrative of prominent autoimmune pathogenetic pathways are listed in Table 21.3.

Within the spontaneous group are models of SLE, RA, and T1DM. The lupus-prone strains commonly develop anti-DNA and immune complex-mediated kidney damage, but they also possess unique phenotypic characteristics and differ in the genes underpinning susceptibility. For example, the BXD2 strain develops both lupus-like glomerulonephritis and inflammatory erosive peripheral arthritis. The SKG arthritis model is a spontaneous, inflammatory, and erosive arthritis caused by a ZAP70 mutation that, like RA, is associated with rheumatoid factor (RF) and antibodies to citrullinated proteins. T1DM develops in nonobese (NOD) mice as a result of T cell-mediated destruction of β-islet cells dependent on a unique major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class II, I-Ag7.23

The genetically modified group, encompassing transgenic, sitedirected genetic replacement (gene knockout or knockin), and N-ethyl N-nitrosourea—mutagenized mice, is by far the largest, with more than 100 different models of lupus and many models of organspecific diseases, particularly T1DM and MS.20, The lupus models, primarily single-gene knockout, knockin, or transgenic mice, have provided a wealth of information related to immune tolerance and disease pathogenesis. Some examples are (1) confirmation of human SLE gene associations and elucidation of mechanisms, such as C1q and Fc gamma receptor IIb (FcγRIIb) knockout mice, PTPN22 R620W,25 and gain-of-function TLR7 mutations26; (2) confirmation that molecules influencing B cell antigen receptor signaling (e.g., Lyn27) can regulate autoantibody formation; (3) discovery of novel mechanisms such as altered messenger RNA (mRNA) regulation in San Roque and miR-17-92 transgenic mice; and (4) identification of new pathways relevant to therapy, such as the B cell-activating factor (BAFF) of the TNF family transgenic.

An example of an autoimmune arthritis model created by genetic modification is the K/BxN mouse, a B6xNOD hybrid expressing a transgenic T cell receptor (TCR), named KRN, that recognizes a bovine ribonuclease peptide on H-2K. An acute severe inflammatory arthritis develops in these mice that is caused by antibodies to glucose-6-phosphate isomerase (GPI), an

antigen that, although intra-cellularly and ubiquitously expressed, is mainly accessible to antibodies in joints. Although there is no evidence that antibodies to GPI cause RA or other arthritides in humans, the model has nevertheless been useful for investigating

inflammatory mechanisms in arthritis. Other genetically modified murine models of spontaneous arthritis include the human T-lymphotropic virus-1 tax transgenic, the TNF transgenic, the interleukin (IL)-1 receptor antagonist transgenic, and a

The induced models encompass a wide variety of both systemic and organ-specific diseases. More commonly studied models of systemic disease include tetramethypentadecane (TMPD; also called pristane)-induced autoimmunity, mercury-induced autoimmunity, and chronic graft-versus-host disease.43-46 All models bear similarities to human SLE in that they feature anti-nuclear antibodies and immune complex deposits, but they differ in pathophysiology and strain susceptibility. For the induced models of organ-specific diseases, a common approach is to immunize rodents with a self-antigen or closely related peptide or foreign antigen, plus a strong adjuvant, usually complete Freund's. This approach makes it possible to induce autoimmunity in virtually all organ systems and to produce diseases mediated by cellular and humoral mechanisms. Some of the more commonly studied organ-specific models developed by this approach include collagen-induced arthritis, collagen antibody—induced arthritis, proteoglycan-induced arthritis, and experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE), but many others exist that are directed to the thyroid, eye, gonad, nerve, neuromuscular junction (acetylcholine receptor), muscle, heart, adrenal gland, bladder, stomach, liver, inner ear, kidney, and prostate tissues. ### Tolerance Mechanisms

Immunity must be sufficiently robust and diverse to recognize and protect the metazoan host from the vast universe of microbial pathogens. Simultaneously, the immune system must avoid excess or misdirected activation to avoid injury to the host. Tolerance is the immune system property whereby reactivity with potentially tissue-damaging infections or tumors is maintained while reactivity to host molecules and normal tissue is actively restrained.

Observations of immunologic tolerance preceded elucidation of its cellular and molecular underpinnings. In 1945 Owen observed that shared blood supply between fraternal bovine twins in utero resulted in adult tolerance of genetically foreign blood cells. Billingham and Medawar showed that in utero inoculation with foreign tissue resulted in adult animal ability to accept foreign skin grafts, advancing the concept of actively acquired immune tolerance. Burnet and Medawar then advanced the critical concept that tolerance was imposed by clonal deletion of selfreactive lymphocytes during early development, that is, central tolerance. The subsequent discovery that mature B cells undergo somatic hypermutation in the periphery led to the hypothesis by

Bretscher and Cohn that the production of autoantibodies might be impeded by the need for both B and T cell compartments to breach tolerance. In 1975 while studying allogeneic responses, Lafferty and Cunningham posited that activation ofT cells involved transduction of a second signal that need not be antigen related, thereby implicating co-stimulation from antigen-presenting cells (APCs) as a critical factor in lymphocyte activation. In 1987 the nature of the co-stimulation, or two-signal, requirement was further defined when Jenkins and Schwartz showed that engagement of antigen receptor alone without a second signal resulted in inactivation of T cells. An elegant mechanism for selfnonself discrimination was then advanced by Janeway in 1989 when he hypothesized that APCs remain quiescent unless activated by the engagement of pattern recognition receptors (PRRs) by microbial products. This concept was further extended by Matzinger in 1994 to a "danger model" that includes activation of the immune system by both foreign and endogenous factors associated with tissue stress and damage. These early insights laid the theoretical foundation for the current, more complex view of self—nonself discrimination in which tolerance is imposed by both innate and adaptive immune systems through layers of mechanisms occurring at various stages, called "self-tolerance checkpoints," throughout lymphocyte development and activation (Table 21.4).

### Clone-Specific Self/Nonself Recognition

In contrast to innate immune cells, which are activated primarily by hardwired germline-encoded microbial pattern recognition receptors that recognize broad classes of pathogen-associated structures (viral nucleic acids, microbial cell wall components, bacterial metabolic products), rearranged lymphocyte antigen receptors confer capacity for much more individualized and specific antigen binding. In T and B lymphocytes, capacity for self— nonself discrimination is generated at the clonal level. To control potentially damaging consequences of self-recognition, T and B cells utilize three general mechanistic strategies. First, lymphocyte developmental stage determines the outcome of antigen receptor signal transduction. Immature lymphocytes respond to strong antigen receptor stimulation by undergoing apoptotic cell death, whereas similar-strength signals in mature cells lead to activation. Antigen receptor signaling—induced cell death thus eliminates most self-reactive immature T clones before cells can join the mature cell repertoire with potential to cause tissue injury. For the limited self-reactive clones that do survive immaturity, a second controlling strategy is utilized: co-stimulatory signaling. Productive T cell activation of mature lymphocytes requires, in addition to antigen receptor engagement, a second co-stimulatory signal, the absence of which results in anergy or cell death. For the most part, this requirement limits activation of self-reactive T cells because co-stimulatory signals are largely provided by cells of the innate immune system. In the absence of activating signals (such as infection or inflammation) to the innate immune system, expression of co-stimulatory molecules on innate immune system cells is limited. Thus, when quiescent, resting innate immune cells interact with T cells bearing self-reactive receptors, the isolated TCR signal induces cellular unresponsiveness (anergy). Third, both T and B lymphocytes are fine-tuned in various ways by an extensive list of modulating factors necessary for controlling selfreactive clones.55-57 In B cells, but not T cells, the fine-tuning is also evidenced by an inverse correlation between antigen receptor (membrane immunoglobulin [Ig]M) self-reactivity and ability to induce calcium flux.

A broad range of signal transduction pathways are known to influence the consequences of self-reactivity by regulating lymphocyte survival. Signaling from both receptors that promote survival (IL-7R, BAFF receptor [BAFFR], and IL-2R) and receptors that promote death (TNF receptors, Fas ligand [FasL], and TNF-related apoptosis-inducing ligand [TRAIL]) may induce tissue damage from self-reactivity when dysregulated. Moreover, a diverse group of co-stimulatory lymphocyte receptors (CD28, CD40, and Toll-like receptors [TLRs]), differentiating (IL- 12R, IL-4R, interferon [IFN]-γ receptor, IL-23R, retinoic acid

receptor, transforming growth factor [TGF]-β receptors, signaling lymphocyte activation molecule [SLAM]/SLAM-associated protein [SAP] family members, OX40, and inducible co-stimulator [ICOS]/ICOS ligand), inhibitory (FcγRIIb, CD22, cytotoxic T lymphocyte-associated antigen-4 [CTLA-4], programmed cell death protein 1 [PD-1], lymphocyte activating gene-3 [LAG3], T cell Ig and mucin domain [TIM]-3, and T cell immunoreceptor with Ig and immunoreceptor tyrosine-based inhibitory motif domains [TIGIT]), antigen receptor signal modulating (CD19 and CD45), activating (SAP/SLAM family members), and others

have all been shown to influence the development of autoimmunity.20, Collectively, these selfnonself recognition mechanisms provide the means for the innate and adaptive immune systems to enforce T and B cell clonotypic tolerance to self-antigens and confer resistance to host autoimmune disease.

### The Innate System and Tolerance

It is not surprising that the innate immune system strongly influences both tolerance and proclivity toward autoimmunity, given its vital role in initiating and modulating adaptive immune responses. Several ways in which self-tolerance is influenced by the innate arm have been defined.

First, activation of the innate immune system under normal circumstances typically requires engagement of microbial PRRs, germline-encoded receptors that are normally only triggered by nonself or foreign antigens. PPRs recognize common structures on pathogens (pathogen-associated molecular patterns) and also a few self-molecules, such as certain damage-associated molecular patterns—for example, heat shock proteins61—which are released during cellular stress, injury, or death. PPRs can be classified by their location into the following types: secreted (e.g., collectins, pentraxins, and ficolins), plasma transmembrane (e.g., TLRs, certain C-type lectin receptors, and N-formyl methionine receptors), endosomal (e.g., TLRs), and cytosolic (e.g., retinoic acid inducible gene Ilike receptors, NOD-like receptors, and DNA receptors: IFI16, AIM2, and the cyclic guanosine monophosphate—adenosine monophosphate synthase [cGAS]-stimulator of IFN genes [STING] pathway).62-64 PRR subcellular location is likely important for control of self-ligand-induced PRR signaling that may in turn promote activation of autoreactive lymphocytes. TLR7 and TLR9 are examples of PRR that equally sense nucleic acids from both self and foreign sources. When TLR7 is overexpressed, by transgenesis or gene duplication, systemic autoimmunity results. A hypothesized mechanism for the regulation of autoimmunity by the TLR7 expression level is that signaling induced by normal substimulatory amounts of self RNA via endosome-localized TLR7 may be greatly increased by the overexpressed receptor. The usual requirement for microbial-originated RNA within endosomes to productively stimulate TLR7 is bypassed, and the immune cell activation threshold is effectively lowered. In support of the notion that threshold modulation in PRR signaling can drive autoimmunity, a mutation in TLR7 that increases signaling in response to normally subthreshold single-stranded RNA stimuli causes SLE in both humans and mice.

Second, some cells of the innate immune system actively suppress adaptive immune system activation. For example, both immature and mature dendritic cells (DCs) have been shown to promote tolerance by modulating CD4+ T regulatory (Treg) cell function and other mechanisms.66,

Third, failure of the rapid noninflammatory clearance of apoptotic cells, another critical function of the innate immune sys- 68,69 can result in secondary necrosis, leading to an increased tem, supply of self-derived material including nucleic acids that can be recognized by autoreactive lymphocytes, and to release of pro-inflammatory factors, leading to systemic autoimmunity. Accordingly, deficiencies in molecules required for noninflammatory apoptotic cell clearance are associated with autoimmunity, including (1) the Tyro3-Axl-Mer receptors on phagocytes that bind, through Gas6 or protein S, the exposed phosphotidylserine (PS) characteristic of apoptotic cell membranes,71 (2) the milk fat globule-epidermal growth factor 8 protein that bridges the αvβ3

integrin on phagocytes and PS on apoptotic cells,72,73 (3) Tim4 expressed on the surface of resident macrophages that binds PS74 (4) the 12/15 lipoxygenase that controls which macrophage subpopulations phagocytize apoptotic cells,75 and (5) natural IgM, C1q, or C1q receptor (SCARF1) that bind to, and enhance clearance of, apoptotic cells.76-79

Fourth, several complement cascade components have been directly implicated in the control of autoimmunity. For example, SLE is associated with deficiencies of proximal components of the classical pathway, including C1q, C4, and C2. Although the mechanism for this association is uncertain, defects in complement-dependent clearance of apoptotic material/immune complexes, or a shift in the activation threshold of lymphocytes, have been suggested. In the chronic graft-versus-host disease model of lupus, C1q also restrains autoimmunity by interacting with the protein p32/gC1qR to alter mitochondrial metabolism and dampen CD8+ T cell responses to viral infection and selfantigens. Deficiency of the cell surface protein and complement cascade-restricting CD55 (or decay-accelerating factor) is associated with enhanced T cell responses and exacerbation of neuroinflammation and lupus in animal models.82,

Fifth, innate immune cells could be a major source of selfantigenic material. For example, neutrophil extra-cellular traps (NETs), the nuclear material-containing weblike structure extruded by neutrophils in the setting of certain stimuli including bacterial infection, contain a number of modified autoantigens. However, understanding of the impact of NETs on SLE and on other human autoimmune syndromes is incomplete.

### T Cell Tolerance

T cells are critical mediators in not only achieving but also fine tuning self-antigen tolerance to a high degree of specificity. Mechanisms whereby the tissue-damaging potential of autoreactive T cells are thought to be controlled may be broadly categorized into three main areas: central tolerance, wherein T cells first acquire their antigen receptor; peripheral tolerance, in which T cells encounter self-antigens not present in the thymus; and postactivation regulation, which occurs when activated and expanded T cell clones undergo apoptosis or are induced into functional quiescence. Central tolerance, as alluded to earlier, is established in the T cell compartment during thymocyte development, primarily through deletion of T cell clones bearing receptors with high affinity for self, but also through anergy induction and potential editing of the TCR α-chain.85, Thymus-dependent tolerizing processes are highly effective but incompletely efficient in generating a mature T cell repertoire capable of both robust responses to foreign antigens and of muted response to self-peptides. Clearly, T cells exhibiting autoreactivity—primarily those bearing TCR with intermediate or low antigen affinity—or T cells that recognize self-antigens poorly expressed in the thymus are permitted to mature and emigrate from the thymus to the peripheral tissues in significant numbers. This "leakiness" is probably necessary to generate a broad repertoire, but the resultant vulnerability to autoimmunity necessitates additional mechanisms to maintain tolerance of mature peripheral T cells.

In the periphery, multiple mechanisms for limiting potentially tissue-injurious autoreactive T cells have been identified. One is that segregation of self-antigen away from T cells bearing cognate self-reactive TCR may effectively maintain tolerance, such that most self-antigens cannot trigger responses of mature autoreactive T cells by virtue of their subcellular or tissue antigen location or

their low abundance. This mechanism is supported by experimental findings that transgenic TCR-bearing cells with capacity to recognize tissue-specific antigens are neither deleted or activated; nor do they cause autoimmune disease. Yet these so-called "ignorant" T cells are fully functional and respond to self-antigen when presented in a conventional context.35, For a few self-antigens, such as those expressed in the anterior chamber of the eye, central nervous system (CNS), gonads, or other so-called immune privileged sites—as originally defined by their ability to accept allograft transplants—suppression of self-reactivity arises partly from anatomic sequestration caused by limited access of blood-borne cells and the absence of conventional lymphatic drainage,88 although the latter is not universally accepted.89, Nevertheless, other anatomic structures that enable separation of immune cells from the brain such as endothelial, epithelial, and glial cell barriers that establish compartments within the CNS have been identified with higher-resolution imaging. Sequestration is important because T cells are typically first activated in secondary lymphoid organs and subsequently migrate to target organs where reactivation by local APCs and the production of pro-inflammatory factors lead to tissue damage. Anatomic barriers alone, however, is not sufficient for tissues to support immunologic "privilege" and, as is discussed later, such sites employ additional local mechanisms.92,

Another peripheral mechanism depends on regulation of the requirement for both TCR engagement and a co-stimulatory signal usually provided by T cellexpressed CD28 to engender full T cell activation. High-level surface expression of CD28 ligands CD80 and CD86 on professional APC is typically induced only under activated conditions. When co-stimulatory ligands are expressed at low levels, as is observed on quiescent APC, such cells may present self-antigen to T cells without providing a costimulatory signal. Functionally, such APC-T cell interaction can induce tolerance. Experimental support for this mechanism comes from observations that immature DCs constitutively presenting low doses of self-antigen on MHCs can cause cell death or induce anergy of the corresponding T cells.

Peripheral tolerance is also maintained by active suppression exerted by immunoregulatory cells, among which CD4+ regulatory T cells (Tregs), are the best characterized. Treg comprise a distinct CD4+ αβ-T cell lineage that expresses the transcription factor forkhead boxP3 (FOXP3) and that function to continuously suppress inflammation and autoimmunity. Treg develop in the thymus as an alternative lineage fate to conventional CD4+ T cells, when they receive distinctly timed agonist TCR and TGFβ signals. Treg may also differentiate from CD4+ precursors extrathymically (peripheral or pTreg) at barrier sites like the 98-100 where they enforce tolerance to food antigens and intestine, microbiota. Treg typically express high levels of CTLA-4 and the IL-2 receptor component IL-2Rα (CD25) and require IL-2 for survival. Tregs are activated alongside conventional T cells in all adaptive immune responses and are critical for maintaining a level of immune response proportional to the size and strength of infectious challenge. Treg-mediated suppression relies on both cell-cell interactions and on secretion of soluble factors. As an example of the former, Tregs suppress DC function through engagement of DC CD80/CD86 by Treg-expressed CTLA-4. Treg also inhibit activation of conventional T cells by competing with them for IL-2, by production of immunosuppressive cytokines (such as TGF-β, IL-10, and IL-35), and by expression of inhibitory surface molecules (CD39, CD73, LAG3, and TIGIT). The net effect of Treg cellcell interactions and secreted products is global suppression of immune and inflammatory cells in close proximity.

Conventional T cell suppression occurs regardless of Treg TCR specificity,101 although Treg sharing autoantigen specificity with conventional effector T cells is more potent, in part because it s. Treg can deny access of effector cells to stimulatory antigens. cells exhibit functional diversity represented by subsets (Th1, Th2, Th17, Tfr)103 that share differentiation features with conventional effector CD4+ T cells. Generally, Tregs are a highly stable lineage, but under certain conditions. Treg capacity for conversion to conventional CD4+ T cells has been described.104-106 Tissue-resident subsets of Tregs in adipose tissue, muscle, lung, gut, and skin, in addition to their immunosuppressive function, have been shown to express tissue-specific transcription factors and elaborate mediators that promote homeostasis and healing.103, Other T cells occupy regulatory niches in regulating autoimmunity, including Tr1, CD8+ Treg, Qa-1/human leukocyte antigen (HLA)- E-restricted CD8+ T cells, and γδ T cells, but their key functions (e.g., IL-10 secretion by Tr1 cells) cannot compensate for loss of those functions by FOXP3+ Treg in most immunosuppressive scenarios. The ability of Tregs to target specific organs or cell types, including antigen-specific lymphocytes, has generated considerable interest in harnessing them for the management of autoimmune diseases. 111-113

Tissues that contain or are surveilled by T lymphocytes employ mechanisms that locally suppress self-reactivity and that also contribute to the establishment of immune privilege.92, These tissues fall into three general groups. First, certain tissues are decorated with cell surface inhibitory molecules—such as the proapoptotic FasL and TRAIL, lymphocyte inhibitory and Treg-promoting PD-L2, and complement regulatory proteins CD55 and CD46— that can potentially eliminate or impede the activation of autoreactive T cells. Second, soluble inhibitors of inflammation and immune activation are secreted by particular tissues. Notably, in the aqueous humor of the eye, there is a broad spectrum of such factors that include TGF-β, α-melanocyte-stimulating hormone, vasointestinal peptide, calcitonin gene-related protein, somatostatin, macrophage inhibitory factor, and complement inhibitors. Third, resident stromal cells and lymphatic endothelial cells that express MHC antigens and surface inhibitory molecules in lymph nodes have been shown to induce tolerance of CD8+ T cells that recognize peripheral tissue-restricted self-antigens. 117-119 Thus, it has been proposed that stromal cells in lymph node and tissues provide a means to eliminate T cells that bind to tissue-restricted antigens not expressed in the thymus. In addition to these general mechanisms, the anterior chamber of the eye elicits a uniquely altered immune response through a complex multistep process termed "anterior chamber-associated immune deviation" (ACAID) that leads to a dampened, less tissue-destructive response. 92, Although ACAID was long thought to be important for tolerance, it has been argued that its primary function may be to modulate the immune response so the eye can respond to infection without endangering ocular integrity.

Immune deviation, wherein modulation of cytokine signaling skews mature CD4+ T cell subset differentiation, constitutes another possible mechanism to limit tissue damage from autoreactivity. Some T celldriven autoimmune tissue pathology depends on the polarization of autoreactive clones toward a Th1 cytokine secretion profile. Altering the balance of differentiation statepromoting cytokines may result in, for example, skewing of pathogenic T cells away from Th1 and toward a protective, Th2 cytokine secretion profile. In experimental autoimmune uveitis, activation of natural killer T cells with α-GalCer, which induces IFN-γ production, is associated with dampening of the adaptive

Th1 and Th17 effector responses and protection from experimental autoimmune uveitis. In these models, autoreactive T cells are activated but do not produce the pro-inflammatory factors necessary for tissue damage.

In addition to establishing central and peripheral tolerance in the resting state, the host has capacity to limit the risk of autoimmune tissue injury posed by broad-based T cell activation and expansion occurring during appropriate protective responses. Dynamic regulation of activated T cells is achieved through upregulation of inhibitory receptors such as CTLA4 and PD-1,124 expression of proapoptotic receptors such as CD95, synthesis of metabolic regulators such as indoleamine-2,3-dioxygenase (IDO), 125 and action of intra-cellular proapoptotic factors such as Bim. Deficiencies of such mediators that control the magnitude of T cell responses are associated with expansion of T lymphocyte populations and with autoimmunity in varying degrees.

### B Cell Tolerance

The importance of B cells for the progression of clinical autoimmunity has been powerfully supported by observed therapeutic effects of specific B celldepleting therapies such as rituximab on human inflammatory arthropathies, anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody-associated vasculitis, SLE,127 and other rheumatologic autoimmune diseases. Moreover, B cell depletion has shown promise even in autoimmune states considered to be largely mediated by T cells such as T1DM128 and MS. Therefore, substantial interest in defining both mechanisms of B cell tolerance and its specific role in autoimmune disease has developed. Cellintrinsic functions of B cells relevant to autoimmunity include, most obviously, production of autoantibody, but also the capacities to present antigen to T cells, to stimulate follicular DC, and to exert regulatory function. 131,

In parallel with T cells, tolerance in B cells is established through complementary central and peripheral mechanisms. Autoreactivity in B lymphocytes is controlled principally through interactions of such factors as B cell antigen receptor (BCR) signal strength and context, location and nature of antigen, and developmental stage. In contrast to T cell tolerance, the process of antigen receptor—mediated apoptosis (deletion) is comparatively less important than receptor editing mechanisms for developing and maintaining the B cell repertoire. Several signaling and developmental checkpoints considered important for controlling autoreactive B cells and maintaining self-tolerance have been identified.

Central tolerance of B cells is established in the bone marrow during pre-B to immature B cell transition as cells begin to express rearranged Ig antigen receptors. In response to ligation by bone marrow stromal membrane-bound self-antigen, many cells bearing BCR with high affinity to membrane-bound self-antigen undergo receptor editing, wherein immunoglobulin light [L] chain sequence is altered followed by surface Ig reappearance. To a lesser extent, self-antigens induce B cell clonal deletion. In contrast to membrane-bound antigens, soluble self-antigens induce both BCR receptor editing and anergy.134, Anergic B cells are detectable in the periphery as an IgD+IgMpopulation136 or in mice as splenic transitional 3 (T3) B cells. Anergic B cells are short-lived, potentially caused by their downregulated expression of survival signal-transducing BAFFR. Moreover, anergic cells are less able to enter B cell follicles, putting them at a competitive disadvantage with other immature B cells.

Among peripheral B cells, the earliest tolerance checkpoint occurs at the T1 B stage over a 2-day interval, prior to maturation

to T2 and later naive B cell developmental stages.133, T1 B cells are the immediate bone marrow emigrant population and are dependent on BAFF for survival. Importantly, autoreactive T1 B cells undergo apoptosis rather than activation when stimulated, which results in deletion of B cells that recognize peripheral self-antigens that are not expressed in the bone marrow compartment. This periphery-located mechanism, which is unique to B cells but which forms a parallel to autoimmune regulator (AIRE)— dependent deletion of thymocytes reactive with nonthymic tissue-specific antigens, essentially represents an extension of central tolerance. Self-reactive mature B cells can also downmodulate surface IgM,58 which allows them to escape deletion and affords the host a broader repertoire despite the risk of autoimmunity.

Maintenance of peripheral B cell anergy depends partly on regulation of signaling through receptors that cooperate with BCR to drive cell activation, particularly pattern recognition receptors. Notably, TLR7 signaling is central to the development of a subset of B cells originally named age-associated B cells (ABCs), now known to represent a mixed population of memory B cells that are expanded in older adult females and certain infections but also in autoimmune diseases.141, Most ABCs exhibit a similar phenotype (Tbet+, CD11c+, IgD-, CD21-, CD27-, MHC-II+, CD80+), require unique activation and survival factors, and can promote autoimmunity by autoantibody production, cytokine secretion, and antigen presentation. In SLE, ABCs, called double negative (DN; IgD-, CD21-) B cells, produce pathogenic autoantibodies and appear to arise within the extrafollicular compartment from naive B cells that undergo activation, class-switch recombination, and somatic hypermutation. 143,

B cell peripheral tolerance mechanisms differ from those of T cells qualitatively because of differences in required modes of antigen recognition by B cells and T cells. BCRs can bind to virtually all tertiary structures, whereas TCRs are restricted to recognizing self-MHC/peptide complexes on host cell surfaces. Accordingly B cells can be ignorant of their corresponding self-antigen because of insufficient quantity or access36 or can undergo anergy and ultimately cell death when engagement of the BCR occurs without co-stimulation.

Another B cell tolerance regulatory checkpoint occurs during T-dependent immune responses as B cells undergo affinity maturation in germinal centers (GCs). The process of somatic hypermutation results in new surface-expressed BCR specificities exhibiting varying degrees of self-reactivity. Loss of tolerance at this juncture is often apparent in autoimmune diseases because most autoantibodies have acquired autoreactivity through somatic hypermutation and are class-switched,146-148 processes that are indicative of GC maturation. The manner in which tolerance among class-switched autoreactive B cells is achieved is still incompletely defined. The strongest evidence suggests that (1) autoreactive B cells compete poorly for the cognate T cell help essential for GC B cell survival because the autoreactive BCR would bind less well to the original antigen, resulting in less internalization of antigen for processing and presentation to T cells,149-151 and (2) B cells that acquire BCRs with reactivity to high-density membrane self-antigens can be deleted by a Fas-dependent mechanism. 152,153

### Theories of Autoimmunity

Development of autoimmune diseases is influenced by genetic and, to varying degrees, environmental, sex, and other factors, with current evidence supporting a model in which genetic predisposition is required (Fig. 21.1). Therefore theories of

autoimmunity and loss of tolerance are closely intertwined with genetic influences. In addition, such theories must also explain how tolerance is breached when autoimmunity is induced in otherwise healthy animals. Broadly, theories of autoimmune disease development can be consolidated into two major mechanistic concepts representing opposite ends of a continuum. On one end, loss of tolerance and consequent autoimmune disease is caused by genetically imposed defects in central and/or peripheral tolerance mechanisms. On the other end of the spectrum, autoimmunity springs from the conventional immune response to self-antigens to which tolerance is normally incompletely established (Table 21.5). In general, most systemic autoimmune diseases are caused by tolerance defects, whereas organ-specific diseases can be mediated by either mechanism.

### Defective Tolerance

Although it can be inferred that loss of tolerance underlies autoimmunity, the specific defects in tolerance establishment and maintenance that underlie common autoimmune diseases have been difficult to delineate, most likely because disease most often occurs because of multiple partial defects operating at diverse cellular and molecular pathway checkpoints. Nevertheless, studies of monogenic human diseases featuring autoimmune phenomena, and of both spontaneous and induced animal models of autoimmune disease, have identified a wide range of defects within the manifold layers of central and peripheral lymphocyte tolerance that raise risk of real-world multigenic autoimmune disease. Such defects are caused by diverse genetic abnormalities and are mediated by a variety of lymphoid and nonlymphoid cell types. A few representative examples are discussed.

The importance of thymus-dependent central tolerance for the establishment of immune homeostasis and prevention of autoimmunity has been illustrated after discovery that loss-of-function mutations in the gene encoding the transcription factor, AIRE is the cause of autoimmune polyglandular syndrome 1 (also called autoimmune polyendocrinopathy-candidiasis-ectodermal dystrophy [APECED]). APECED is a rare inherited disease featuring T cell-mediated damage or destruction of multiple endocrine organs. 154-156 Aire-deficient mice and patients harboring AIRE

mutations develop similar autoimmune syndromes. Disease in both humans and rodents is caused by the reduced thymic stromal expression of thousands of genes with limited, mostly extrathymic (e.g., pancreatic beta cell-specific) tissue expression profiles, the protein gene products of which are termed tissue-specific antigens (TSA). Reduced transcription of AIRE-dependent genes results in diminished expression of MHC complexes bound to TSA protein-derived peptides expressed on thymic medullary epithelium. The resulting failure to eliminate T cells recognizing such peptides by clonal deletion in the thymus results in maturation and migration to the periphery of CD4+ T cells bearing high-affinity TCR reactive with self-antigens. Within thymic medullary epithelium, AIRE likely functions by binding repressive transcriptional regulatory complexes such as MBD1-ATF7ip that target specific methylated cytosine-phosphatidyl-guanine (CpG) dinucleotides in genetic regions encoding tissue-specific antigens. AIRE also promotes positive selection of perinatal thymic generation of CD4+ FOXP3+ regulatory T cells (Tregs, discussed later) that express peripheral TSA-reactive specificities. AIRE exhibits sex hormone—biased thymic expression, and females display lower expression of peripheral tissue-specific genes, consistent with observed higher female prevalence of disease. Recently several additional transcription factors, FEZF2 and PRDM1, were also shown to regulate expression of peripheral tissue-specific antigens in thymic medullary cells and to be important for suppressing autoimmune phenomena in mice. 159,

Autoimmune disease observed in animals bearing mutations in genes that modulate TCR strength highlights the importance of TCR signaling for selection of a tolerant T cell repertoire. A prime example is the SKG arthritis model. Here, a function-impairing mutation in the C-terminal SH2 domain of ZAP70, a cytosolic Syk family tyrosine kinase activated by the TCR complex Z-chain, reduces TCR signal strength. The resultant altered thymocyte selection results in a shifted TCR repertoire among developing conventional T cells and Tregs, and seemingly enhanced positive selection of autoreactive T cells. Interestingly, using several ZAP70 mutants, it was shown that susceptibility to arthritis was altered by only slight differences in ZAP70-mediated signaling strength. 162,

For B cells, major defects in central tolerance leading to autoimmunity have been more difficult to demonstrate. No AIRElike equivalent regulating TSA expression has been discovered, presumably because immature B cells continue to undergo negative selection after egress from the bone marrow, allowing developing B cells direct exposure to TSA. A tolerance regulatory role for lymphocyte-expressed microRNA (miRNA) was suggested in experiments wherein overexpressed miRNA-148a causes escape from BCR-induced central deletion. MiRNA-148a promotes cell survival by suppressing multiple autoimmune and tumor suppressors, as well as proapoptotic genes in immature B cells. High miRNA-148a expression facilitates lethal autoimmunity in a mouse model of lupus. Defective central tolerance of B cells in human autoimmunity has been suggested by the findings of a higher frequency of naive mature B cells with self-reactivity in human autoimmune syndromes, including SLE and RA.165-167 Whether epigenetic mechanisms contribute to such augmented B cell autoreactivity is unknown.

In the periphery, FAS (also known as CD95) deficiency provides an example of defective peripheral tolerance promoting 168 FAS is a surface receptor that plays a critical autoimmunity. role in maintaining immune homeostasis by mediating lymphocyte programmed cell death (apoptosis). Defects in FAS cause

autoimmune lymphoproliferative syndrome (ALPS; also called Canale-Smith syndrome) and, in mice, lymphoproliferative (lpr) disease. ALPS patients and lpr mice exhibit massive enlargement of secondary lymphoid organs caused by the accumulation of T cells lacking both CD4+ and CD8+ coreceptors, which normally are rarely found in peripheral circulation, along with a variety of autoimmune manifestations. Lpr mice are also defective in eliminating B cells that acquire self-reactivity in the periphery, a process that typically occurs in the GC during somatic hypermutation. Similar abnormalities are found in humans and mice with defects in the ligand for FAS (FASLG, CD95L, CD178).

Peripheral tolerance is also breached by overexpression of the co-stimulatory molecule ICOS on T follicular helper (Tfh) cells in San Roque mice. These mice have a point mutation in Roquin-1 (Rc3h1 gene), a RING-type ubiquitin ligase that impairs its ability to interact with components of the mRNA deadenylation and decapping machinery and to degrade ICOS mRNA. Increased expression of ICOS promotes the expansion of Tfh cells and GCs, production of IL-21, and autoimmunity. A similar autoimmune phenotype was recently reported with deletion of Regnase-1, an mRNA endonuclease that forms a complex with Roquin-1.172

An example of a lymphocyte-extrinsic cause for loss of tolerance and autoimmunity is deficiency in the 3' repair exonuclease 1 (TREX1; deoxyribonuclease [DNase] III). Loss-of-function mutations in TREX1 have been implicated in Aicardi-Goutières syndrome, a rare progressive encephalopathy associated with elevated IFN-α levels in the cerebral spinal fluid, and chilblain lupus, a rare form of SLE characterized by painful bluish-red inflammatory skin lesions typically affecting areas exposed to cold .173, Autoimmunity is thought to be caused by temperatures. the intra-cellular accumulation of single-stranded DNA reportedly derived from endogenous retro-elements normally degraded by TREX1, resulting in the activation of the intra-cellular DNA sensor STING and consequent overproduction of IFN-α.175-177 Intriguingly, oxidized DNA, which is abundant in NETs and in ultraviolet-induced skin lesions, is resistant to TREX1 degradation and can promote STING activation and type I IFN production, 178 suggesting that the TREX1 pathway may play a more general role in SLE pathogenesis. The importance of DNA disposal in lupus has been further illustrated by the association of Dnase I and DnaselL3 deficiencies with development of SLE in humans and mice. 179-182 Curiously, deletion of cGAS or

STING in spontaneous (MRL-lpr) and induced (pristane) lupus models does not inhibit, but unexpectedly slightly exacerbates, disease.
