The mechanism might be related to differences in pro-inflammatory and anti-inflammatory activities of nucleic acid sensors, altered clearance of nucleic acids, or tissue-specific 183 responses.

Defective regulation can also result in loss of tolerance and autoimmune disease, as illustrated by the absence of Tregs. 184, In humans, monogenic deficiency of the FOXP3 gene, which is required for Treg development, is associated with the immune dysregulation, polyendocrinopathy, enteropathy X-linked (IPEX) syndrome, a severe systemic autoimmune disease associated with diarrhea, eczematous dermatitis, and endocrinopathy that is usually fatal within the first year of life. T1DM, autoimmune cytopenias, and nephritis are among other, less common autoimmune manifestations of this syndrome. Similar findings are observed in scurfy mice, which have a spontaneous function-impairing mutation of Foxp3.

### Autoimmunity Caused by Activation of − Nontolerant or Partially Tolerant T Cells

The other main theory is that autoimmunity develops through the conventional activation of self-reactive T cells that have not been deleted in the thymus and that remain oblivious to the corresponding self-antigen after emigration. Such ignorant T cells, commonly found in the periphery of both healthy humans and animals, can be activated by antigen presented by professional APCs in the context of an innate inflammatory milieu. Once activated, T cells are able to gain access to virtually all tissues and, when activated again locally, can elaborate pro-inflammatory factors, causing tissue damage. Breach of tolerance by this mechanism is most often associated with organ-specific diseases, presumably because TSA that are candidate activators for ignorant self-reactive T cells are less likely to be expressed in the thymus. This theory is supported by the finding that T1DM is prevented in BB rats and NOD mice by intrathymic transplantation of pancreatic islets.186, Similarly, EAE can be prevented by intrathymic administration of either the immunizing antigen, myelin basic protein, or its major encephalitogenic epitope, 188 and autoantibody production can be delayed in lupus-prone mice following intrathymic injections of polynucleosomes. Taken together, these data support the concept that autoimmunity can be caused by the activation of lymphocytes, which are not susceptible to central tolerance by virtue of the tissue-specific self-antigens that they recognize. Notably, this theory does not imply the presence of a defect in central tolerance, such as would be operative in the APECED syndrome caused by AIRE deficiency.

Breach of tolerance by ignorant lymphocytes has been shown to depend on many factors, including the (1) nature of the selfantigen, (2) extent of exposure to antigen, (3) antigen receptor affinity, (4) frequency of autoreactive lymphocytes, (5) types and levels of co-stimulatory molecule expression, (6) cytokine and chemokine profiles, and (7) presence of inflammation.35, It should also be emphasized that despite the well-documented presence of autoreactive T cells in humans and rodents, earlierdescribed peripheral tolerance mechanisms are difficult to overcome. Consequently, supraphysiologic amounts of self-antigen, strong adjuvant, specific MHC haplotypes, and a susceptible background are all typically required to reveal the functional presence of peripheral autoreactive T cells and to break tolerance. These findings are consistent with the fact that autoimmunity does not

develop in most humans or animals despite the presence of autoreactive T cells, and they speak to the robustness of peripheral tolerance. Although it is difficult to prove which of these theoretical mechanisms are operable in patients, they provide frameworks for understanding how autoimmunity can develop along with guidance in devising interventions.

As with conventional protective immune responses, key factors for the initiation of autoimmunity are innate inflammatory and co-stimulatory factors that promote the initial activation and expansion of resting autoreactive lymphocytes. Release of self-antigens after cell damage or death, increased MHC/peptide expression, upregulation of co-stimulatory factors, and activation of professional APCs all may contribute to both conventional and autoimmune responses. 191, Indeed, moderate to severe tissue necrosis is often associated with some evidence of autoreactivity, although this condition rarely progresses to clinical disease. 198, In autoimmune diseases, chronic cell and tissue injury is associated with a continual release of self-antigens under conditions favorable for antigen presentation; co-stimulatory signaling promotes epitope spreading and the activation of an expanding repertoire of lymphocytes that recognize autoantigens beyond the initiating autoantigen.20, This process is thought to at least partially account for the often-progressive course of autoimmunity. Overall, these and other findings support the theory that, under certain conditions such as infection or trauma, self-antigens are released. When coupled with the presence of inflammatory factors and an activated innate immune system, such self-antigen release may trigger activation and expansion of previously ignorant autoreactive lymphocytes and progress to clinically evident disease.

In addition to the release of sequestered self-antigens, the initial activation of naive autoreactive lymphocytes has been postulated to occur in several other ways. Some investigators have suggested that the initial response may be directed toward certain determi- s202,203 based on the concept of "crypticity," wherein a hiernants archy of dominant and cryptic epitopes can be established for a given protein based on differences in peptide binding affinity to the MHC, protein processing, preference for presentation by different APCs, and the constitutive prevalence of epitope-specific T cells.201, It is therefore posited that during thymic selection, T cells that engage the few dominant epitopes are eliminated by clonal deletion, whereas those recognizing the less antigenic, but more abundant, cryptic epitopes are spared. The latter T cells then emigrate to the periphery, where they can be activated by the corresponding cryptic epitope under certain inflammatory conditions.

Another mechanism by which self-antigens can activate nontolerant lymphocytes is through the production of neo self-antigens after post-translational or chemical modifications. A prominent example is the formation of citrullinated proteins generated by the deimination of arginine residues by peptidylarginine deminase (PADI) enzymes. Serum autoantibodies against citrullinated vimentin, collagen II, enolase, and other citrullinated proteins are not only present in, and predictive markers of destructive joint disease for, a majority of RA patients, but they may play significant roles in driving or restraining disease.205-207 Deficiency of L-isoaspartate O-methyltransferase, which catalyzes the repair of isoAsp proteins formed by the spontaneous conversion of aspartic acid to its isoaspartyl derivative, has also been shown to result in accumulation of isoAsp proteins and development of lupus in a mouse model. Furthermore, in the PL/J model of EAE, acetylation of the encephalitogenic Ac1-11 peptide of myelin basic protein (MBP) is required for T cell activation even though unmodified peptide binds to MHC. These and other studies suggest that

protein modifications can generate new epitopes either directly by creating new structures such as citrulline or indirectly by altering MHC binding or modifying sites of peptide processing to reveal new and/or self-peptides.

Neo self-antigens can also arise from conformation changes conferred by protein-protein associations. RFs, defined as antibodies reactive with the Fc portion of complexed IgG, occur due to immunogenicity of IgG-containing immune complexes that are multimers of nonantigenic monomeric IgG.211, Likewise, in Goodpasture's disease, a configuration change in type IV collagen due to sulfilimine bonds produces a neotarget for pathogenic autoantibodies, a mechanism termed conformeropathy.

Another potential mechanism for triggering autoimmunity in susceptible hosts is lymphopenia-induced homeostatic proliferation (LIP) of T cells.214, Lymphopenia-induced expansion occurs because of greater availability of survival-promoting cytokines (IL-7, IL-15) to fewer competing lymphocytes. Combined with low-affinity engagement of the TCR to self-peptide/MHC, such cytokines induce low-grade lymphocyte proliferation without causing cellular activation. Since self-reactivity is required for LIP, repeated rounds of lymphopenia could theoretically result in the preferential expansion of autoreactive T cells and, consequently, √. This hypothesis is supported by observations of autoimmunity. (1) repeated lymphopenia in persons with autoimmune disease including SLE and RA, (2) autoimmune manifestations in some primary immunodeficiencies with lymphopenia, and (3) LIPassociated disease in several experimental autoimmune models.

Foreign antigens with sufficient sequence or structural similarity to self-derived proteins can cross-activate nontolerant self-recognizing T (and B) lymphocytes, a mechanism termed molecular mimicry. For T cells, several features of antigen receptor signaling give credence to the notion that cross-reactivity could happen: (1) TCR recognition of MHCpeptide complexes is highly degenerate and depends on only a few key amino acid residues, and it is possible to have mimotopes with no identical amino acids at any position217,218; (2) a single T cell, despite requiring anchor residues to bind the HLA, can react with an estimated 104 and 108 different peptides219; and (3) cross-reactivity requires only short peptide lengths of 8 to 15 amino acids. T cells capable of cross-reacting to microbial and self-peptides have been detected in autoimmune states. In mice, infection with a modified Theiler's virus expressing a foreign cross-reactive peptide (Haemophilus influenzae protease IV protein that shares only 6 out of 13 amino acids) can activate T cells reactive with a myelin protein, proteolipid protein, resulting in autoimmune CNS disease. In humans, MBP-specific T cells cloned from patients with MS can be stimulated by diverse microbial peptides. 221,

A model of spontaneously occurring myocarditis provides a rare example of T celldependent molecular mimicry causing autoimmune pathology. Lethal disease in these mice depends on expansion of cardiac Th17 cells. The pathologic T cells recognize cardiac myosin but cross-react and proliferate to mimicking peptides derived from a gut commensal Bacteroides species. Notably, human myocarditis patients exhibit high Bacteroides-specific CD4+ T cell and B cell responses. These results suggest that mimic peptides from commensal bacteria can promote autoimmune cardiomyopathy in a predisposed host.

Molecular mimicry provides the basis for cross-activation of self-reactive B cells observed in several autoimmune diseases. The best examples include cross-reactivity of (1) bacterial adhesin FimH with lysosomal membrane protein 2 in anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA)-positive pauci-immune focal

necrotizing glomerulonephritis,224 (2) group A streptococcal carbohydrate epitope, N-acetyl glucosamine with M protein with cardiac myosin in rheumatic fever,225 and (3) Campylobacter jejuni lipo-oligosaccharide with ganglioside GM1 on peripheral nerves in the acute motor axonal neuropathy subtype of Guillain-Barré syndrome with an identical neuron-expressed determinant, Gal β13 GalNAc β14 (NeuAc α2-3) Galβ.226, Overall, however, supportive evidence for most autoimmune diseases is lacking. Whether the lack of evidence for causality is due to technical issues that impede detection of cross-reactive lymphocytes, such as multiple mimotopes from diverse sources, diverse HLA haplotypes, and the considerable plasticity of the T cell receptor, or whether mimicry is an uncommon cause of autoimmune disease remain open questions.

Depression of suppressive, tolerizing signals that normally keep peripheral autoreactive T cells in check can reveal potential autoreactivity. This mechanism is highlighted by observations of immune-related adverse events (IRAE) in diverse tissues occurring in patients treated with immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) for cancer. ICI therapy targets include surface proteins CTLA4 and the ligand pair PD1/PDL1, which exert suppressive effects on immune cells including effector T cells, Treg, and dendritic cells. Within a tumor microenvironment, CTLA4 and PD1/PDL1 can suppress immunity via diverse mechanisms, including suppression of tumor-reactive CD4+ and CD8+ T cell activation and proliferation, promotion of T cell apoptosis, enhancement of Treg function, release of suppressive cytokines TGF-β and IL-10, and suppression of antigen presentation and activation by antigen presenting cells. Suppressive functions of CTL4, PD-1, or PDL1 are blocked after treatment with monoclonal antibodies targeting these proteins. The resulting rapid and robust potentiation of effector T cell function promotes robust anti-tumor activity. However, in addition to driving anti-tumor effects, ICI therapy frequently stimulates inflammatory reactions within diverse tissues. Investigation of ICI-induced myocarditis has produced evidence supporting a key causative role for CD8+ T cells in IRAE. Cardiac infiltrates from Pdcd1-/-Ctla4+/- mice that model ICI cardiotoxicity comprise numerous effector CD8+ T cells bearing TCR specific for the myocardium-restricted protein α-myosin. Immune cells extracted from mice with myocarditis can transfer fatal, CD8+-dependent disease. Moreover, blood and myocardium from patients with ICI-induced myocarditis contain T cells reactive with α-myosin peptides, strongly suggesting that α-myosin is a key autoantigen. The contributions of immune cells other than CD8+ effectors remain to be defined, but these studies strongly suggest that a break in CD8+ T cell self-tolerance may drive inflammatory reactions observed in IRAE.

### Immunological Mechanisms of Tissue Inflammation and Dysfunction

The same effector mechanisms used by the immune system to neutralize pathogens are utilized in autoimmunity to inflict a wide range of deleterious effects on self-molecules, cells, and tissues. These mechanisms, initially classified by Gell and Coombs in the 1960s, were broadly grouped into hypersensitivity types II to IV, which encompass antibody-, immune complex-, and T cellmediated processes, respectively (see Table 21.2).

In type II reactions, pathologic autoantibodies bind to self-antigens primarily located on cell surfaces or in tissues and mediate autoimmune disease by three general mechanisms: (1) altering the

function of the target antigen, (2) promoting cell injury or death, and (3) inducing inflammation. Blocking or enhancing self-molecule function represents a special kind of type II hypersensitivity response in which autoantibodies alone are causal in generating pathologic function effects. Examples include the agonist anti-thyroid stimulating hormone receptor antibodies in Graves' disease that stimulate thyrocyte growth and production of thyroid hormone, the anti-acetylcholine receptor antibodies that block neuromuscular transmission in myasthenia gravis, and anti-β2-glycoprotein I antibodies in antiphospholipid antibody syndrome that alter the regulation of anticoagulant activity. Cell injury or death in type II hypersensitivity is mediated by the binding of IgM or IgG to surface antigens, leading to cell lysis directly by complement activation or to phagocytosis via interaction of deposited C3 fragments with CR1 and CR3 receptors. Bound IgG also promotes phagocytosis through its interaction with Fc receptors. Examples include autoimmune hemolytic anemia, idiopathic thrombocytopenia, and autoimmune neutropenia. Finally, antibodies bound to tissue antigens promote inflammation by activating complement, which generates the chemoattractant C5a and leukocyte-activating C3 fragments, and by FcγR binding, which activates immigrating leukocytes such as neutrophils and macrophages, as well as tissue-resident mast cells and basophils. These cells produce pro-inflammatory factors that further expand the inflammatory response by recruiting and then activating additional circulating leukocytes.

Type III responses are caused by abnormal deposition of immune complexes of IgG antibody and soluble antigen in tissues. Such complexes, which also contain bound C3 complement fragments, are normally cleared from the circulation by complement receptors on red blood cells (RBCs) and by complement receptors and FcγRs on mononuclear phagocytes and platelets. However, this clearance can be overwhelmed under certain conditions such as overabundant production or immune complexes composed of excess antigen wherein less antibody coverage reduces complement deposition and aggregation of Fc regions, leading to less efficient clearance. Once deposited in tissues, immune complexes initiate through complement activation and FcγR binding, the same inflammatory cascades as type II responses.

Type IV hypersensitivity encompasses cell and tissue injury mediated by activated T cells. Apart from direct evidence of this mechanism in animal models using approaches that are not feasible in human studies, indirect evidence supporting this mechanism includes a higher frequency of autoreactive T cells with effector function in patients with autoimmune diseases, immunopathologic findings similar to T cellmediated autoimmune models, and inhibition of disease with T cellblocking agents such as cyclosporin A. T1DM and MS are examples of pathologic type IV reactions.

It should be mentioned that these classifications are generalized and, for some diseases, the underlying effector mechanism may be more complex. In RA, for example, the mechanism responsible for injury or dysfunction probably involves more than one hypersensitivity type, whereas in others, such as SLE, different clinical manifestations are mediated by different mechanisms; for example, anti-neuronal antibody-mediated CNS disease is a type II process whereas glomerulonephritis has features of type III.235-238

### Pathophysiology of Autoimmune Rheumatic Diseases

Although the general principles underlying loss of tolerance and autoimmunity discussed previously provide a useful conceptual

foundation for understanding pathogenesis of autoimmune phenomena underpinning common rheumatic diseases, pathophysiology observed in patients reflects multicomponent immune dysregulation that is disease state specific. The generation of anti-nuclear antibody production in SLE and the progression of destructive joint disease in RA are notable examples of multiphasic processes that are briefly discussed in the context of their broader significance to autoimmune diseases.

Several findings provide mechanistic insight into the question of why anti-nuclear antibodies are virtually always present in SLE despite substantial genetic and clinical heterogeneity. 65, First, autoreactive B cells are activated when self-reactive BCRs bind to nucleic acidcontaining antigens (nucleosomes, oxidized mitochondrial DNA,240 or ribonucleoprotein). BCR-antigen complexes are endocytosed, and nucleic acids engage TLR7 and TLR9 within lysosomes. Combined BCR and PRR signaling drive a gene expression program that includes upregulation of MHC Class II and T cell co-stimulatory ligands CD80/CD86. The resulting activated B cells act as potent APCs for T lymphocytes but are also induced to undergo class-switch recombination and produce IgG autoantibodies. Plasmacytoid DCs (pDCs) and DCs are then activated following uptake of autoantibody-nucleic acid-containing complexes by FcγRIIA (FcγRIII in mice). Elaboration of lupuspromoting cytokines such as type I IFN and BAFF by pDCs and DCs as well as enhanced antigen presentation are thought to further drive loss of tolerance, activation of autoreactive B cells, and higher-affinity autoantibody production, thereby resulting in an amplification loop. Thus in persons susceptible to SLE, confinement of nucleic acidbinding TLRs to endolysosomes is not sufficient to block cellular activation by normally substimulatory amounts of self-nucleic acids. This mechanism provides an explanation for the high prevalence of autoantibodies in SLE that bind to nucleic acids such as DNA and to antigens physically associated with nucleic acids such as histones, ribonucleoproteins, myeloperoxidase (ANCA), and surface molecules derived from many cell types including platelets, lymphocytes, neutrophils, and even RBCs. Autoantibodies to cell surface epitopes are likely induced by apoptotic bodies containing nucleic acids. Importantly, this model suggests the possibility that other autoimmune diseases might also be mediated by specific PRRs.242,

Autoimmune pathophysiology of joint disease in RA is best understood for the HLA-DR1*401 (DR4)- and anti-cyclic citrullinated protein antibody (ACPA)-positive patient subset, in which common and specific pathways together underpin disease progression through three clinical phases. 244-246 An initial preclinical phase is thought to be characterized by activation of T cells and B cells at extraarticular sites including gut, respiratory, and oral epithelium. Driven by local inflammatory responses to microbes at these sites, increased citrullination of both bacteria and host proteins occurs via activity of peptidylarginine deiminase released from apoptosing granulocytes and monocytes. The HLA-DRB1 shared epitope, which has been shown to specifically bind and present citrullinated self-peptides, is thought to enhance likelihood of productive antigen presentation to T cells reactive with cyclic citrullinated peptides. Isotype-switched IgA and IgG autoantibodies that react with citrullinated peptides fibrinogen, vimentin, α-enolase, and other host proteins (ACPA) then appear.

The specific triggers of anti-citrullinated peptide-specific T and B cells leading to a loss of tolerance, proliferation, and activation observed in RA patients at high risk of erosive joint disease have been the subject of intense study. Accumulating evidence points strongly toward the oral, respiratory, and gastrointestinal epithelia

as sites where activated innate immune cells instigate breaches in T and B cell tolerance, generating a limited ACPA response prior to joint involvement. Activating stimuli at these sites may likely include inflammation, such as occurs in periodontal disease (PD), 247 toxins such as cigarette smoke,248 and autoreactive T cellinducing intestinal microbiota249 (discussed further below). Multiple lines of evidence support a triggering role for periodontal disease, which features chronic inflammatory injury to gingival mucosa. PD is more common in RA, especially in ACPA-positive patients250 and in patients with active, treatment-refractory inflammatory joint disease. RA patients with PD experience frequent bacteremia with oral cavity-derived organisms, coincident with increased circulating inflammatory monocytes and with clinical disease flares. The oral cavity bacteria repeatedly found in RA patient blood exhibit extensive citrullination and are recognized by hypermutated ACPA produced by blood-borne plasmablasts. These findings strongly suggest that repeated translocation of mouth-originated citrullinated bacteria may be foundational to both triggering innate immunity, and for initiation and expansion of adaptive immune responses, in RA.

The pre-clinical phase characterized by detectable ACPA and RFs typically lasts for years, and higher titers of ACPA increase likelihood of progression. The next, early "clinically evident" arthritis phase is characterized by inflammation (featuring edema, cellular infiltrates, hypervascularity) occurring in synovial tissue. Within joints, immune complexes and activated T cells engender Fc receptorand cytokine-mediated stimulation of macrophages, synovial fibroblasts, endothelial cells, mast cells, osteoclasts, and platelets, 252 and FcR-induced activation concurrent with the eventual production of pro-inflammatory factors including TNF, IL-1, IFN-γ, IL-17A, IL-23, chemokines, matrix metalloproteinases, and osteopontin that contribute to synovitis, pannus formation, bone erosion, and cartilage destruction. Indeed, unique populations of PD-1 hiCXCR5- CD4+ T cells in RA synovium and peripheral blood have been identified that express factors promoting B cell help and that likely contribute to this process.

The combined innate and adaptive immune activation at the synovium leads to a third chronic "established" RA phase that is characterized by increased numbers of activated fibroblast-like synoviocytes (FLS). FLS produce a wide array of pro-inflammatory mediators that promote recruitment and activation of circulating and resident cells. The aggressive and invasive properties of FLS are independent of B and T cells indicative of appreciable remodeling by epigenetic or other mechanisms. Trafficking to joints and proliferation of such activated fibroblast-like synovial cells may underlie the progressive, additive joint disease observed clinically in RA. Treatments that target the receptor tyrosine phosphatase sigma that is specifically upregulated on FLS in diseased synovium can synergize with low-dose TNF inhibition and suppress experimental inflammatory arthritis,257 strongly suggesting a requirement for FLS in destructive synovitis. Molecular and cellular connections between neoantigen (citrullinated peptide)—driven autoimmunity and the advent of the nonimmune FLS-dominated destructive joint disease phase in RA remain under study.

### Genetics of Autoimmune Diseases

During the past three decades, substantial insight into genetic autoimmune disease susceptibility factors has emerged from both human and animal studies. Progress has been greatly facilitated by major technical advances such as increasingly inexpensive and rapid high-throughput DNA sequencing, but also the emergence

of large databases containing annotated whole genome data, improved definition of genetic variations and haplotype frequencies in human populations, and consortia that coordinated participation of large numbers of autoimmune disease patients and healthy persons.258, Since the early years of the 21st century, the field of genetic investigation progressed from testing a few specific candidate susceptibility polymorphisms to genome-wide family analyses of hundreds of cases, and even larger-scale genome-wide association studies (GWAS) involving thousands of partici- 260, These experiments permitted not only verification of pants. long known genetic associations (e.g., HLA associations with RA and SLE), but also identified many novel disease-predisposing variants (typically single-nucleotide polymorphisms [SNPs]) with modest effect sizes. GWAS have identified more than 100 candidate genes or loci in SLE and RA (metaanalyses and multiple GWAS reviewed in ref 262) and numerous susceptibility loci in other rheumatologic diseases such as systemic sclerosis, Kawasaki's disease, Behcet's disease, spondyloarthropathies, and ANCAassociated vasculitis (reviewed in references,263-276 http://www. genome.gov/gwastudies). Many autoimmune disease susceptibility alleles have known or suspected cellular biologic functions within innate and adaptive immune systems. For example, in SLE, candidate genes are involved in antigen presentation (HLA-DR3), clearance of self-antigens (C1Q, C2, and C4), B and T cell receptor signaling (PTPN22, BANK1, and BLK), CD4+ T helper cell regulation (OX40L, TNFSF4, and CTLA4), T cellmediated regulation (PDCD1), cytokine signaling (STAT4), IFN and TLR7/9 signaling (PTPN22, IRF5, TNFAIP3, IRAK1, IRF7, and TYK2), Fc receptor function (FCGR2A), neutrophil function (ITGAM), and clearance of intracytoplasmic DNA (TREX1). Several susceptibility loci contain genes with no known connection to the immune system or lupus. Together, these candidates provide clues to pathogenetic pathways involved in human SLE, which indeed has dovetailed well with findings from genetic studies in mice.

From GWAS and other studies, including those in animal models, several general conclusions can be made about genetic susceptibility in autoimmune disease. First, autoimmune diseases are associated with many susceptibility genes that have been shown to have an impact on a wide range of immunologic, cellular, and end organ functions in ways that enhance, modify, or even suppress relevant pathophysiologic processes.

Second, considerable genetic heterogeneity exists at both the individual and population levels regardless of whether the phenotype is relatively uniform, as in RA, or diverse, as in SLE. Thus although there are many predisposing genes, inheritance of only a subset of these genes is generally sufficient for disease development. Whether this heterogeneity is caused by variants affecting a few common pathways or altering function in numerous unique pathways remains unclear.

Third, the vast majority of candidate genes or loci have only modest effect sizes, with most odds ratios less than 1.5. Low effect sizes comport well with the notion that genetic susceptibility to most common autoimmune disease is polygenic, resulting from concerted function of several, perhaps dozens, of predisposing loci. Overall, however, for most candidate variants, low effect size predicts difficulty in defining a clear-cut cellular or molecular mechanism of variant autoimmune disease—predisposing action.

Fourth, some SNPs and associated markers are shared among autoimmune diseases, suggesting the presence of common underlying mechanisms. Noteworthy examples are the association of PTPN22 with a range of autoimmune diseases, including T1DM, RA, SLE, juvenile idiopathic arthritis, Graves' disease, systemic

sclerosis, myasthenia gravis, generalized vitiligo, and ANCAassociated vasculitis, but not psoriasis or MS,278 and the association of STAT4 with RA, SLE, systemic sclerosis, and Sjögren's syndrome. 279, This finding supports a role for such broadly predisposing genetic factors in the known occurrence of multiple different autoimmune diseases in some families.

Fifth, common SNP-defined variants in aggregate account for only a portion of overall heritability in autoimmune diseases, that is, approximately 20% to 60%,258,259,281 of which the HLA region by itself typically accounts for a substantial part of overall disease association. Several explanations for inability to account for missing heritability to date have been proposed. First, failed detection because of inadequate SNP coverage or the presence of diseasepromoting non-SNP genomic variations such as copy number variants. Second, a large number of common variants with modest to marginal effects (odds ratio <1.1-1.2) that are undetectable despite large study sizes given that the statistical power is reduced by both smaller effect size and lower variant frequency in the population. Indeed, for many traits, common single-nucleotide variations with small effect sizes below what is detectable by GWAS are suspected to account for the majority of missing heritability. And third, uncommon variants (1% to 5%) or rare disease-associated risk alleles (<1% frequency) are missed even in large GWAS. It is estimated that 25,000 cases plus a replication set would be required for detection of a genetic signal due to a causative rare variant in a well-powered genome-wide study,283 illustrating the technical hurdles that impede further progress using the GWAS approach. These observations pose significant challenges to further defining genetic susceptibility and to incorporating gene variant—specific diagnostic or therapeutic interventions into patient 284 care.

Sixth, most common SNP variants associated with autoimmune diseases do not occur within coding regions. This observation increases the difficulty of determining whether the disease-associated SNP variant sequence itself modulates biologic function and drives disease susceptibility or, alternatively, the associated variant is in linkage disequilibrium with nearby biologic functionchanging sequence. A subset of disease-associated variants occurs within regulatory regions called superenhancers or stretch enhancers. Such regions can function as lineage-determining master transcription factors that regulate cell identity. An example is the association of SNPs in the superenhancer region of BACH2, a regulator of T cell activation, with several autoimmune diseases including RA, Crohn's disease, MS, and T1DM. Furthermore, the Janus kinase inhibitor tofacitinib approved for the treatment of RA was shown to alter the expression of RA risk genes within predicted superenhancer regulatory nodes. Thus finer characterization of the noncoding enhancer and superenhancer regions for different immune cell types and other autoimmune diseases could yield new insights into pathways central to pathogenesis and that have therapeutic potential.

Seventh, the more recent application of transcriptomics, the high-throughput profiling of virtually all RNAs derived from patient cells or tissues, is a powerful approach that complements genome mapping studies and has led to the identification of therapeutic targets such as type I IFN, IL-1, and IL-17 for autoimmune 286, The ability to rapidly assess gene expression profiles diseases. associated with clinical phenotypesdisease state/diagnosis, disease activity status, and response to treatment has great potential for both advancing understanding of basic pathogenesis and for improving many areas of clinical practice including diagnosis, risk patient stratification, and monitoring.

Finally, information gleaned from genetic studies to date has not translated into the clinic with assays for risk stratification or other personalized medicine purposes, largely because of the small effect sizes of risk alleles and the relatively high frequency of known risk alleles combined with incomplete coverage of heritability. Nevertheless, these data and newer technology-driven approaches have helped define disease-relevant pathways, and within that context have provided clues and support for developing therapeutic strategies.

### Sex and Autoimmunity

A significant female bias in autoimmunity has been observed for as long as the disease states were clinically described. The female predilection for many autoimmune syndromes was considered an important clue to disease pathogenesis. The strength of this predilection varies among autoimmune disorders, with female prevalence in the 80% to 95% range for thyroiditis, SLE, Sjögren's syndrome, and antiphospholipid syndrome; in the 60% to 75% range for RA, scleroderma, myasthenia gravis, and MS; and close to 50% for T1DM and autoimmune myocarditis. Why some autoimmune diseases are affected more by sex than others is not known, but the lack of common or distinguishing characteristics in those diseases with female predominance suggests the possibility of multiple mechanisms.

Indeed, to differing extents depending on the disease, both sex hormones and sex chromosomes have been implicated in greater prevalence of autoimmune disease among women. 290-294 Substantial evidence from in vitro, animal, and clinical studies supports a role for both female and male sex steroids in modifying the incidence and severity of autoimmunity. In persons with SLE, both estrogens and prolactin have been shown to exacerbate disease. In animal studies, sex steroids promote loss of tolerance and expansion of B cell populations, which, for estrogens, was also shown to be associated with greater expression of anti-apoptotic factor B cell lymphoma 2 and enhanced cellular survival. Importantly, studies of lupus-prone mice involving combinations of castration and hormone replacement convincingly demonstrated a disease-promoting effect of female hormones on spontaneous autoimmunity.

Evidence also supports a role for sex chromosome dosage in autoimmune disease susceptibility. Persons with Klinefelter's syndrome (XXY) have a higher-than-expected incidence of SLE, whereas there is underrepresentation of SLE in Turner's syndrome (XO).297, Furthermore, using genetic and gonad manipulation in mice that allowed direct comparison of the effects of one or two X chromosomes on autoimmunity, susceptibility to both EAE in SJL mice and TMPD-induced lupus was shown to be more severe in mice with XX.299, Another potential contributing factor is the biallelic expression of the X chromosome TLR7 gene in some B cells, monocytes, and pDCs due to incomplete X chromosome inactivation at the single cell level in females. Biallelic expression in B cells correlates with more TLR7 protein, greater response to TLR7 ligands, and a propensity to class switch, findings that support an increased predisposition to lupus. T cells from SLE patients and from lupus mice also demonstrate incomplete X chromosome inactivation—associated impaired epigenetic controls and consequent upregulation of numerous X chromosome— encoded genes. Thus disruption of epigenetic processes such as Xist-mediated maintenance of X chromosome inactivation could lead to augmented lymphocyte signaling and function in SLE. The influence of sex on the immune response to the microbiome

and other environmental factors has also been implicated in autoimmune disease susceptibility.292, Together, these findings suggest that actions of several sex hormones, the number or extent of inactivation of X chromosomes, and environmental influences likely each contribute to observed sex bias in SLE.

### Microbial and Other Environmental Triggers −

As alluded to previously, considerable evidence indicates that environmental factors exert major, yet variable, influence on the development of common autoimmune diseases. A major pathogenetic role for the environment is strongly suggested by the low concordance rate (20% to 50%) among monozygotic twins for common autoimmune diseases. Nevertheless, the nature of environmental factors and the extent to which they contribute to disease induction and exacerbation remain poorly understood for most autoimmune disorders. The reasons for this lack of knowledge are likely manifold and, depending on the disease, may include requirements for additive or multiplicative effects of environmental factors that individually contribute only small portions of the overall effect, a highly variable or prolonged interval between exposure and disease onset, and a low incidence of autoimmune disease after exposure to a candidate trigger. Another impediment is that commonly employed epidemiologic approaches to identifying autoimmune disease triggers can document association with, but not establish causation by, candidate factors. Because of these difficulties, animal studies have been invaluable in allowing controlled experimentation to test putative roles of disease-triggering environmental triggers.

Investigative limitations notwithstanding, a broad range of environmental factors have been implicated in autoimmune disease causation or susceptibility. The most prominently cited candidate factors are infection and exposure to microbial products, which are suggested by epidemiologic and animal studies to either enhance or inhibit autoimmunity depending on the type of exposure and disease.305, Rheumatologic disease examples of suspected causative links between infection and disease include reactive arthritis after genitourinary or enteric infections, chronic Lyme arthritis resulting from infection with Borrelia burgdorferi, and the association of oral Porphyromonas gingivalis (which expresses a peptidylarginine deiminase that can citrullinate proteins) with RA. Several mechanisms by which microbes are postulated to induce or exacerbate autoimmunity include (1) molecular mimicry,225 as discussed earlier; (2) bystander activation of autoreactive T cells, potentially occasioned by breaches in gut, respiratory, or mucosal epithelial barriers that normally limit hostpathogen interactions, by pathogen-activated APC247,307- 309; (3) inflammation of the target tissue and the release of immunologically hidden self-antigens310; (4) enhanced production of disease-promoting cytokines, such as IFN-α,65,311" by infectionresponsive cells; (5) expansion of pathogenic immune cells including Th17 T cells and plasmacytoid DCs307,312-314, ; and (6) release of metabolites that affect the frequencies of autoreactive and regulatory T cells or inflammation.315,

Clearly, microbes impinge on susceptibility to autoimmune disease. Gut microbiota, specifically commensal bacteria, are critical for immune homeostasis in adult metazoan hosts. Tonic signaling engendered by GM through innate immune receptors TLR and NOD1 is needed for maturation of both gut barrier and maintenance of gut-associated lymphoid tissues. Observations of inverse correlations between microbial exposure burden in early life and incidence of atopic diseases, asthma, and even

autoimmune diseases such as T1D and MS gave rise to the "hygiene hypothesis" in the late 1980s. This concept has since been supported by additional epidemiologic and experimental data, although individual microbial pathogens or commensals and type of exposure required for effects remain uncertain. 318, Alterations in the localization, abundance, and function of gut microbiota may drive loss of tolerance and tissue damage. Disrupted signaling through innate sensors and gut translocation by commensal bacteria leads to colitis and T celldependent autoimmune diabetes. 321-323 T1DM incidence increases in NOD mice housed under "clean" laboratory conditions and lessens with exposure to microbial products. Thus alterations in gut microbiota, which can interact with and modulate the host immune and inflammatory apparatus, could account for major environmental effects on disease susceptibility and even influence female sex bias.324-327 Disease-inducing effects have occasionally been attributed to individual microbes (see below), but most mechanisms appear to be rooted in dysbiosis or imbalance between the types of organisms comprising the microflora in aggregate. Additionally, in some animal models, autoimmune disease develops under germ-free conditions, thereby excluding an absolute requirement for microbial environment or infection. In such cases, the suspected autoimmune trigger is provided by self-derived antigens, most likely produced by cell damage. Examples include T1DM in NOD mice and BB rats, APECED in Aire-deficient mice, IPEX in the presence of Foxp3 deficiency, and lupus in MRL-lpr mice.328- 332 Interestingly, in MRL-lpr mice, the addition of a filtered diet containing fewer pathogen-associated molecular patterns reduces disease severity. This finding suggests that microbial products at least partially affect disease susceptibility in this model and points to the difficulty of completely excluding a role for microflora.

Striking relationships between the gut microbiome, altered immune system homeostasis, and autoimmune diseases have been demonstrated.309,333 3Interactions between commensal microbiota, metabolic intermediaries, and diet components can influence likelihood of autoimmunity. One mechanism whereby gut microbiome can drive or restrain autoimmunity is through metabolism of dietary elements. In the breast-fed infant, bacteria capable of utilizing human milk oligosaccharides are key for production of indole 3 lactic acid, which induces galectin-1 expression in intestinal T cells. Galectin-1 promotes cytokine-mediated skewing toward Th1 and regulatory phenotypes, and away from intestinal inflammation-associated Th17 and Th2 fates, likely reducing proclivity for autoimmune disease. Germ-free NOD mice develop T1DM as a consequence of dietary gluten, but gluten-dependent disease requires gut bacteria expression of proteases that can break down gluten. Bacterial digestion of gluten generates T cell—activating gluten peptides and enhanced innate immune cell reactivity to lipopolysaccharides, which are required for disease expression. Dysbiotic microbiota have been observed in mice bearing multiple lupus susceptibility genes. When microbiota taken from diseased lupus mice is transferred into healthy animals, autoantibody production and immune cell activation results. Transferable autoimmunity in this case depends on altered tryptophan metabolites in dysbiotic feces. A diet low in tryptophan prevents autoimmunity in the animals, whereas a high tryptophan diet promotes it. These findings illustrate potential for interplay between microbial dysbiosis, gut microbial metabolism, and genetic susceptibility to lupus.

Another mechanism of microbiome action in autoimmune pathogenesis is disruption of the intestinal barrier that normally sequesters microbes away from autoreactive lymphocytes.

Pathogenic effects of dysbiosis can trigger SLE. The gut pathobiont Enterococcus gallinarum is capable of inducing SLE in animals featuring autoantibody production and tissue infiltrates. E. gallinarum promotes leakiness of the gut mucosal barrier, leading to colonization of extraintestinal organs and SLE. Impressively, lupus was prevented in mice by treatment with antibiotics or vaccination against E. gallinarum. In another study, a five-fold greater representation of Ruminococcus gnavus was detected in large SLE patient cohorts; presence of the bacterium correlated with reduced taxonomic complexity of the microbiome, antibodies to R. gnavus, increased disease activity, and greater severity.

A third mechanism whereby microbiome may impinge on autoimmune pathogenesis is through recruitment/expansion of T cells reactive with post-translational modified antigens, such as cyclic citrullinated peptides. A commensal bacterium, Ruminococcaceae Subdoligranulum, was identified in RA patient feces by virtue of its binding to ACPA. Germ-free mice colonized with a single R. Subdoligranulum strain exhibit autoantibody production and expansion of splenic Th17 cells. Colonized animals also develop swollen joints and display Ig and complement deposition in synovium; these features require CD4+ T cells and B cells. Together, these findings suggest that specific bacterial species can both stimulate gut-based humoral and T cell responses and trigger joint disease.

The COVID-19 pandemic has highlighted the potential for viral infection to drive humoral autoimmunity. Multiple novel autoantibodies against a range of self-antigens, including IFNα, prothrombotic proteins, and G proteincoupled receptors, commonly arise in SARS-CoV2-infected patients.338-340 Interestingly, high-titer autoantibodies against these antigens correlate with worse COVID-19 disease severity and complications like thromboembolism, whereas infection-driven autoantibodies against chemokines associate with better outcomes and protection against post-acute coronavirus syndrome. Although an array of autoimmune disorders has sporadically been reported following vaccination against SARS-CoV2, it is notable that vaccination, unlike natural infection, does not drive pre-existing autoantibody titers higher. 342

Nonmicrobial environmental factors also may play roles in the development of systemic autoimmunity. These include (1) drugs, such as procainamide, gold salts, and IFNs, that typically cause mild autoimmunity that resolves after discontinuation; (2) trauma, exemplified by sympathetic ophthalmia caused by penetrating injury to the eye globe; and (3) diverse environmental agents such as adulterated oil (which caused toxic oil syndrome), ultraviolet radiation (which exacerbates systemic autoimmunity), iodine (which causes autoimmune thyroiditis), silica (which is associated with RA, SLE, and systemic sclerosis), and tobacco smoke (which is associated with APA and HLA-DR4+ RA).304,343

### Conclusion

Since 1904, when Donath and Landsteiner reported the first evidence of self-reactivity in paroxysmal hemaglobinuria,344 the field of autoimmunity has progressed tremendously at both the clinical and basic science levels. Notably, substantial progress has been made since the previous edition of this book in environmental factors, particularly within understanding of how microbiome and host—pathogen interactions may promote systemic autoimmunity and pathophysiology and with the continued refinement of the many pathways that connect cause with immunopathology. Recent advances suggest how the innate response plays key roles in both initiating autoimmunity and determining the nature of

adaptive autoimmune response and disease phenotype. Genetic studies have progressed to larger GWAS projects and with larger focus on identifying and characterizing causative variants underlying mechanisms. Advances in the understanding of disease pathogenesis primarily in more common rheumatologic diseases have further solidified and extended existing frameworks on which researchers can build on to identify critical pathways and molecules. Of importance to patient care has been the successful bench-to-bedside translation approach that has resulted in the introduction of new therapies to the clinic. However, the highly sought-after objective of specifically reestablishing tolerance in patients has remained elusive despite considerable effort, and currently used therapies are only partially effective and are frequently associated with significant side effects. Consequently, the critical needs for investigation of the basic processes that underpin autoimmune disease, and for leveraging resulting knowledge for development of safer and more effective therapies, remain.

# 22 Pre-clinical Autoimmunity

### KEY POINTS

Autoimmune diseases start with a prolonged pre-classification period that may include few or no symptoms, autoantibodies, elevation of cytokines and chemokines, and immune cell changes.

Type 1 diabetes investigators have described stages for the preclassification period and have successfully treated individuals to delay the onset of clinical disease. This may be a paradigm for other autoimmune diseases.

Autoantibody and soluble mediator production and immune cell changes precede the diagnosis by several years.

Staging of pre-classification autoimmune diseases is paramount to propel research and medication prevention studies going forward.

### Introduction

In many fields of medicine, the concept of a prolonged, clinically silent phase is well known and often a target of disease modification or prevention. Atherosclerotic changes in the coronary or cerebral circulations are typically present for decades before a clinical event such as a myocardial infarction or cerebrovascular accident. Cellular dysplasia is present years before the transformation to invasive cervical or colon carcinoma. Screening strategies such as blood pressure monitoring, measurement of serum cholesterol, and colonoscopy are widely accepted strategies to minimize morbidity and mortality.

Over the past several decades, similar constructs have been developed for systemic autoimmune and rheumatic diseases. The risk factors for conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis (RA) and systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) have been identified, and specific alterations in the immune systems of people at risk have been documented by researchers in the field. This has led to the concept that early and widespread screening of populations can identify those persons most at risk of developing systemic autoimmune disease and, potentially, intervention to either extend the clinically silent stage or prevent autoimmune disease entirely. At this time, such strategies are not available for most autoimmune diseases— the exception being type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM). This chapter will review the concept of "pre-classification" autoimmune and rheumatic disease and discuss the strategies for intervention.

A general schema for the progression of individuals through the stages of autoimmunity is shown in Fig. 22.1. The majority of the population has low risk for the development of autoimmune disease. Various genetic, demographic, and exposure factors discussed below place a fraction of the population at risk for the development of autoimmunity. A portion of the at-risk population

then develops detectable features of autoimmunity (stage 1). The most obvious features of autoimmunity are autoantibodies, but increasing evidence exists for activation of pro-inflammatory gene expression of multiple chemokines and cytokines. This stage of autoimmunity can be relatively plastic, with the possibility of progression to one or more defined autoimmune conditions (stages 2 and 3) or to an undifferentiated state of few clinical features that are insufficient for classification of any one disease. Alternatively, the individual may stay in a state with no clinical features—e.g., the healthy patient with a positive anti-nuclear antibody (ANA) for life. The key gaps in our understanding reflect uncertainty in the triggers that move individuals from a pre-classification state to the accumulation of clinical features, whether movement to one disease or another is based on patient-specific exposures or chance and, importantly, whether and how progression is prevented or reversed.

### Defining Pre-classification Autoimmunity: More Than Just Semantics

One issue facing investigators, medical providers, and patients is the lack of a precise definition of pre-classification or pre-clinical autoimmunity. For some, the use of terms such as incomplete lupus spark controversy as they may label people who do not have progressive disease needing treatment.1, Different terms have been used to apply to similar clinical situations (e.g., incomplete lupus, pre-clinical lupus, and undifferentiated connective tissue disease [UCTD]) by different investigators making comparison among studies difficult.3, Alternatively, these early disease states may be thought of as the early stages of their respective diseases, or preclassification. This is most clear when the biomarkers or clinical features have high specificity and progression to clinically evident disease is clear. For example, children who are first-degree relatives (FDRs) of patients with T1DM and who have two or three diabetes-associated antibodies have an 84% chance of developing the disease.5, Thus they are considered to have early T1DM, even though their insulin secretion is normal. Patients with anticitrullinated protein antibodies (ACPAs) and synovitis on MRI have an approximately 39% to 65% chance of developing RA over the next 3 years. They can be thought of as having the earliest stages of RA. This distinction—defining the early stages of disease to include the asymptomatic phase—is important in order to obtain regulatory approval for interventions and to convince these individuals to take immunomodulatory therapies. These definitions of the early stages of each autoimmune disease are not likely to come from retrospective studies but will require

prospective research into their epidemiology. Only then will widespread screening efforts and therapeutic interventions be generally accepted.

### Population Epidemiology of Autoimmunity

There is an indistinct line differentiating the majority of healthy persons with laboratory evidence of autoimmunity (e.g., ANA or ACPA) and those who are in the earliest phases of systemic disease. Placing patients in stages is both a theoretical and practical construct to define those who need monitoring and consideration for interventions. To enter into the earliest stage, a person will have a biomarker or set of biomarkers with high sensitivity and specificity for the particular autoimmune condition. It is tempting to use autoantibodies as screening biomarkers due to their ease of measurement, but their lack of specificity makes them poor choices by themselves. For example, anti-nuclear antibodies have been reported in up to 27% of the general population depending on the titer and are thus inappropriate as standalone screening tests. 9-12 Rheumatoid factor (RF) is found in approximately 3% to 10% of the population, rising with age,9,13 and ACPA is found in under 4%.9, Thyroid antibodies, including anti-thyroglobulin and anti-thyroid peroxidase, are found in the United States population at a rate of 7.7% and 11.7%, respectively, also rising with age. Further complicating the use of disease-associated antibodies as specific biomarkers is the fact that FDRs of patients with SLE and RA have antibodies of the opposite condition, as well as thyroid and antiphospholipid antibodies. Further, one-third of patients with T1DM have thyroid antibodies. Thus most autoantibodies are general markers of autoreactivity, with only the potential for immune dysregulation, but not useful by themselves for the staging.

Often referred to as benign autoimmunity, the implications of patients remaining in the asymptomatic autoimmunity stage are unknown. ANAs have been studied in population-based cohorts and after a 9-year median follow-up were associated with all-cause mortality (hazard ratio [HR] per 1 SD of log [ANA]: 1.27; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.10 to 1.46; P = .0008), cardiovascular death (HR, 1.42; 95% CI, 1.13 to 1.77; P = .002), and atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD; HR, 1.17; 95% CI, 1.01 to 1.35; P = .04) after adjusting for age, sex, race, and CVD risk factors. Additional cohorts in Finland18 and Italy19 and two

United States studies (NHANES10 and Rochester Epidemiology Project²) have shown mixed results of ANA predicting all-cause mortality, CVD death, and cancer.9, Longitudinal cohorts and advanced biomarker research will help clarify the risks associated with this stage.

### Type 1 Diabetes Paradigm for as a Pre-classification Autoimmunity −

T1DM results in loss of insulin secretion due to immune-mediated destruction of pancreatic beta cells. Genetic risk for T1DM includes human leukocyte antigen (HLA) DR and DQ alleles and genes related to metabolism and immune regulation. Environmental risk factors for developing T1DM include physical inactivity, stress, low vitamin D, obesity, and infections. Several autoantibodies have been described in the early stages, including those targeting insulin, insulinoma-associated antigen-2, glutamic acid decarboxylase, zinc-transporter 8, and islet cell antibodies. Other biomarkers in early stage include the proinsulin to C-peptide ratio and pancreatic volume. The pre-classification period in T1DM has been rigorously studied in prospective, longitudinal studies and has been standardized into several stages21 (Fig. 22.2A). Based on the presence of two or more highly specific antibodies, stage 1 characterizes 5% of the general population, largely FDRs of T1DM patients. The 10-year risk of progression to stage 3 is 70%. Stage 2 includes patients with both antibodies and early evidence of dysglycemia. Their lifetime risk of advancing to stage 3, which is incident diabetes with typical clinical features, is nearly 100%. Given the opportunity to identify those at higher risk, there have been several investigations of therapies targeting multiple mechanisms in early stage disease, aiming to delay or prevent the development of T1DM.5, A recent study using a specific anti-CD3 monoclonal antibody, teplizumab, delayed the progression of symptomatic T1DM in FDRs of those with T1DM (Fig. 22.2B).22, In November 2022 the United States Food and Drug Administration approved teplizumab for adults and children in stage 2 of T1DM, that is, individuals with at least two islet autoantibodies and an abnormal oral glucose tolerance test, without fasting hyperglycemia. T1DM is an organ-specific disease, and the long-term consequence of this therapy is not yet known. However, this paradigm suggests that by precisely defining

a disease stage susceptible to modification and developing effective interventions, it may successfully delay or prevent systemic autoimmune diseases.

### Pre-classification nSystemic Autoimmune Disease

### Rheumatoid Arthritis

The nomenclature for the time period in RA before classification has included pre-RA, pre-clinical RA, at risk, and early RA, each of which emphasizes the expected development of RA.24, However, these terms are limited in that not all patients who have risk factors go on to develop clinically apparent or classifiable disease. Similar to T1DM, efforts to standardize the nomenclature have described specific phases that patients may progress through based on genetic/environmental risk factors, systemic autoimmunity, symptoms without clinical arthritis, and, finally, RA.

Pre-classification cohorts have helped bring about a better understanding of RA disease progression. These include the Rochester Epidemiology Project in Minnesota, Epidemiological Investigation of RA in Sweden, the Nurses' Health Studies in the United States, Studies of the Etiology of RA (SERA) in the United States, and early arthritis clinics located in Europe. They have been influential in defining phases of disease and linking the epidemiologic data with observed immunobiology.

In the right genetic framework, risk factors impart an additive risk for developing RA and encompass the microbiome at mucosal surfaces; infectious agents; and environmental, occupational, and lifestyle factors.25, Periodontitis is a risk factor for developing RA. Porphyromonas gingivalis causes periodontitis and produces peptidyl arginine deiminase (PAD) enzymes leading to citrullination of bacterial and host proteins. Antibodies to this bacteria are found not only in 11% to 23% of patients with RA but also in FDRs with RA-associated antibodies (4.89 ± 1 vs. 4.59 ± 0.88; P = .01) compared with antibody-negative FDRs.28, The gut microbiome is also under investigation. Prevotella copri enrichment has been shown in patients with positive autoantibodies compared with antibody-negative FDRs32 and in new-onset untreated RA. To date, only animal data suggest that interventions such as treating gingivitis or altering gut microbiota can disrupt disease progression in the pre-classification period.34,

Smokers have higher levels of citrullinated peptides compared with those who do not smoke (57% vs 7%; P < .05) and increased expression of PAD2 enzymes (smokers: median, 86%; range, 65% to 94% vs nonsmokers: 63%; range, 40% to 89%; P < .001) in the alveolar compartment. RA-related autoantibodies are detectable in the sputum of 39% at-risk patients. In several cohorts of patients with positive ACPA and no inflammatory arthritis, more than three-quarters had airway disease or interstitial lung disease and approximately 10% developed inflammatory arthritis in the 2-year follow-up period.38-40

Knowing which antibodies and their isotypes prior to diagnosis has spearheaded research into the pathogenesis and prediction models of RA (see Antibodies in RA section). Studies have shown that once initial tolerance is broken by the creation of autoantibodies targeting post-translationally modified proteins, months to years may go by before signs of damage start occurring in the joint. A serologic analysis of stored serum samples from United States military personnel who developed RA was performed to look for antibodies to specific citrullinated peptide antigens commonly

seen in RA synovium. All 81 subjects developed autoantibodies prior to onset of RA, and over 25% were noted to have antibodies to citrullinated histone, vimentin, enolase, and fibrinogen peptide antigen as early as 10 years prior to the diagnosis.42, Several international cohorts—Swedish, Dutch,15 and American46 —have analyzed stored serum obtained prior to diagnosis. They found immunoglobulin (Ig)A-RF or IgM-RF and IgG-ACPA ranging from 2.5 to 17 years prior to diagnosis, followed by IgG-RF and IgA-ACPA closer to diagnosis. 15, Risk factors for developing antibodies and length of time present prior to diagnosis include smoking and age.45, More recently, antibodies to PAD-4, an enzyme responsible for citrullination of arginine, have been shown in 18% of patients to precede the diagnosis of RA by 4.6 years. Beyond traditional ACPA antibodies, there are additional post-translational modifications leading to a new class of autoantibodies termed anti-modified protein antibodies or AMPA. Thus far, these antibodies tend to be present in ACPA-positive subjects, and there is cross-reactivity with ACPA. Examples include antimalondialdehyde-acetaldehyde,53 anti-acetylated antibodies, 52 and anti-carbamylated protein antibodies.

Cytokine upregulation and inflammatory cell changes accompany autoantibody formation. As the number of ACPA subtypes expand, 10% to 50% of subjects subsequently develop elevated cytokine levels 2 to 3 years prior to the RA diagnosis. These inflammatory cytokines include TNF, interleukin (IL)-6, IL-2, IL-4, IL-15, IL-12p70, IL-1β, IL-10, IL-17, interferon (IFN)-γ, granulocyte-macrophage (GM) colony-stimulating factor (CSF), G-CSF, monocyte chemoattractant protein (MCP)1, MIP1α, and high sensitivity C-reaction protein.42,49,55Following antibody development, CD4+ T cells affect the progression to inflammatory arthritis. A study of CD4+ T cells in 158 subjects found in 37% of those who progressed to RA had lower numbers of naive and regulatory CD4 T cells and higher inflammation-related cells. ACPA-positive patients having at least two of these parameters had an odds ratio (OR) of 4.95 to progress,56 whereas ACPA negative subjects had an OR of 2.46.56

In order to define stages of RA to target with prevention strategies, it is necessary to further characterize patients at the highest risk for progression to disease.47, The SERA prospective cohort followed seropositive FDRs for a median of 4 years and found approximately 15% of subjects progressed to RA, with ACPA being the strongest risk factor (HR, 3.95; P < .01). Preclassification retrospective and prospective cohorts have shown that ACPA, particularly at higher titers, increases the risk of RA in 3 to 5 years.58, A study assessing asymptomatic individuals used a model including family history of RA or SLE in FDRs; serology status; epidemiologic factors including age, smoking, alcohol, BMI, parity, and education; and genetic risk score using 39 RA risk alleles. To predict incident RÅ for seropositive patients with positive family history, the area under the curve (AUC) was 0.82 (95% CI, 0.74 to 0.90). Antibody-negative RA models performed slightly less well at AUC 0.70 (95% CI, 0.65 to 0.75). Another study found that a biomarker profile using the autoantibodies targeting citrullinated enolase, fibrinogen, and vimentin, as well as cytokines IL-12(p70), IL-1β, IL-5, IL-7, LIF, and TNF-β predicted imminent RA in 2 years with an AUC of 0.79.42

The use of imaging to evaluate the joints before clinical synovitis can be detected is another tool to quantify risk of developing RA. However, caution must be employed in interpretation of findings as some features consistent with RA can be found in healthy individuals or at least in individuals in whom no evidence of active autoimmune disease is present. A contrast-enhanced MRI study of

symptom-free individuals aged 19 to 89 years found mostly lowgrade erosions, bone marrow edema, and tenosynovitis in regions typical of inflammatory arthritis, such as metacarpophalangeal and metatarsophalangeal joints, wrists, and ulna in a majority (72%) of individuals. Ultrasound evaluation of the digit flexors and extensor carpi ulnaris tendons in healthy subjects aged 18 to 80 years noted that 15% of patients had features of tenosynovial inflammation including power Doppler signals, tendon hypertrophy, or effusions over the hand.

The term clinically suspect arthralgia (CSA) has been employed to identify patients at risk for developing RA who have joint discomfort but do not have synovitis. Several studies using ultrasound or MRI found that tenosynovitis was the strongest predictor of who would progress to inflammatory arthritis.64-67 One study assessing CSA patients with MRI noted 15% progressed, and MCP-extensor tenosynovitis was predictive with a HR 4.38 (2.07 to 9.25). While autoantibody status, particularly ACPA, can be additive, not all patients with imaging signals progress to inflammatory arthritis.7, In a multicohort of ACPA-positive patients with arthralgia, just over 30% had subclinical synovitis by MRI at baseline, and yet 35% to 61% of those patients with subclinical synovitis did not develop inflammatory arthritis after a 3-year follow-up. Future models that measure autoantibodies, inflammatory and regulatory cytokines, and cellular defects and imaging will help us get closer to staging patients to aid in prevention trials and prognosis. As in T1DM, serial measurements will be necessary.

RA prevention trials have aimed to capture patients in the different stages of the pre-classification period, including those patients with or without CSA, positive biomarkers, and suggestive imaging findings with mixed results in outcomes. Table 22.1 describes several trials in the pre-classification phase of RA. A recent study in the earliest stage of the pre-classification period, StopRA, was halted as interim analysis showed no benefit of

hydroxychloroquine for preventing RA. However, we anticipate biomarker analysis to help guide future research and treatment. Encouragingly, the PRAIRI study investigated later-stage seropositive subjects with arthralgia and found delayed onset of inflammatory arthritis with one dose of rituximab. The ARIAA study looked at seropositive subjects with arthralgia and positive MRI findings and showed not only delayed onset but also preliminary data suggesting prevention of inflammatory arthritis with 6 months of abatacept. There have also been trials in very early inflammatory arthritis or undifferentiated arthritis suggesting that intervention may delay the onset of disease. 72-74

Recruitment for prevention trials has been challenging. People who are asymptomatic or have mild symptoms perceive that benefits may not outweigh the risks of treatment and the burden of clinical trials.8, Despite pre-classification symptoms of arthralgia, fatigue, functional limitations, work absence, and early bone loss, a patient's willingness to take medications or change lifestyle behaviors prior to the onset of disease is limited.8, More studies are needed to determine whether patient choices change if presented with a delay or reduced severity of disease rather than prevention. Modifying risk factors, such as diet, sleep, stress, and activity levels, is paramount to addressing societal health and possibly affecting the course of autoimmune disease. Recommendations for managing patients with risk factors for developing RA include smoking cessation, exercise, maintaining healthy body weight, and consuming a Mediterranean-style diet. The PRE-RA study found that patients at risk for RA who were made aware of their genetic/biomarker risk factors were more likely to change the risk behaviors. Data on recovery from systemic inflammation when these factors are modified are needed.

Research in RA is making strides toward identifying the most robust, predictive biomarkers that will guide the staging of preclassification patients with RA. In a few short years, we have seen trials with various degrees of success depending on the stage of

RA. Longitudinal sampling will be necessary as will engaging the public in the importance of investigating pre-classification autoimmune diseases.

### Systemic Lupus Erythematosus

Experienced rheumatologists are not likely to miss a case of active SLE. However, patients are often referred for evaluation from primary care or specialty clinics, and unfortunately, organ damage may occur while a patient is waiting for rheumatologic evaluation. Having better screening tools or a compilation of tests that provide better sensitivity and specificity is essential to prevent morbidity and mortality.

Similar to the stages in T1DM, SLE has been divided into phases: (1) genetic risk, (2) asymptomatic autoimmunity, and (3) early symptoms of SLE. This model is simplistic, for two reasons. The phase of asymptomatic autoimmunity is typically identified by the presence of one or more autoantibodies, usually including an ANA. Such individuals may go on to develop SLE, but this phase may also precede other conditions such as Sjögren's disease, systemic sclerosis, or inflammatory myositis. Second, SLE is a heterogeneous disease, with various individuals exhibiting mainly hematologic, cutaneous, musculoskeletal, or renal manifestations. The risk factors, including genetics, environmental exposures, and immune dysregulation, as well as the rates of progression for each of these manifestations may be different.

The clearest demonstration of asymptomatic autoimmunity was the initial study of stored serum samples from the United States Department of Defense (DoD) biorepository. In the original study, sequential stored serum samples from 130 individuals who had subsequently developed SLE and matched controls were analyzed for ANA and a panel of other autoantibodies frequently found in SLE patients. The majority of SLE patients (88%) had autoantibodies a mean of 3.4 years before diagnosis. Some patients had autoantibodies detected over 9 years before diagnosis. There was a temporal pattern with ANA, anti-Ro, anti-La, and antiphospholipid antibodies appearing a mean of 3.4 years before diagnosis, followed by anti-Smith and anti-RNP a mean of 1.2 years before diagnosis (P = .005). Anti-DNA was noted 2.7 years prior to diagnosis.

Subsequent analyses of the DoD cohort have quantified cytokine, chemokines, and other soluble mediators of inflammation, as well as symptoms onset, in the subjects who developed SLE compared with controls. In the 2 years prior to the onset of SLE, 44% of patients developed elevated IFN-α activity, and 75% had increased type II interferon at the time of disease classification. IFN-α and upregulation of BLyS was preceded by autoantibody development and type II IFN activity. The median onset of clinical symptoms was 1.5 years before the diagnosis.

The cytokine changes in patients prior to diagnosis differ from those who do not go on to develop disease. Cytokine up-regulation includes interplay with type I interferon, enhanced T and B cell proliferation and longevity, increased type II interferon expression, and upregulation of BLyS. Interestingly, type II interferon upregulation, specifically IFN-γ, CXCL10, and MCP-3 levels, precedes the rise of IFN-α and autoantibodies.81, Other mediators described include IFN-γ, IL-12p70, monokine induced by gamma (MIG), IL-4, IL-5, and IL-6.4, Assays measuring complement activation on cell surfaces (cell-bound C4d) predict progression to classifiable SLE, although the sensitivity of this assay is such that it, too, is insufficient as a screening tool.4,

Investigators studying the pre-classification phase of SLE have coined the term incomplete lupus erythematosus (ILE) to describe a subset of patients who do not meet SLE classification criteria or the clinical diagnosis of SLE.1, The term was coined86 to mean people who meet two or three ACR criteria for the classification of SLE. Since then, many other studies have used the term (a 2020 review87 discusses these studies) to mean someone with an ANA and one to two SLE criteria. Not unexpectedly, this has defined a very heterogeneous cohort of patients. Prospective studies have noted that up to 57% of ILE patients meet SLE classification criteria at a median of 5.3 years of follow-up. Predictors of the ILE to SLE progression vary among studies as well. They include female sex, high titers of ANA, overall autoantibody burden, oral ulcers, anti-DNA, active urinary sediment, photosensitivity, anti-DNA, and hypocomplementemia.89-91 Patients whose only disease manifestation is cutaneous lupus erythematosus (CLE) also meet these definitions of ILE. Of 77 CLE patients, 13 developed criteria for SLE over a mean of 8 years, with 38% developing moderate to severe systemic disease.

Several techniques have been used to characterize the immune response in people with ILE versus SLE. Using techniques to quantify IgM and IgG antibodies to over 100 known autoantigens, investigators demonstrated that ILE patients had a higher ratio of IgM to IgG for most antigens, and the burden of IgG antibodies rose as the disease progressed from healthy to SLE. IgG clusters included RNA/DNA-related antigens, histones, and collagens. ILE patients were also found to exhibit an increased type 1 interferon signature compared with controls and lower IFI27, anti-C1q, IP10, MCP-1, MIPIα, TNF, and IL-9 compared with SLE.94, Levels of BLyS, are intermediate in ILE patients compared with healthy controls and SLE patients. Thus ILE is an immunologically progressive condition with features that can both be used to predict progression, as well as potential targets for therapy.

FDRs of SLE patients also represent an at-risk population due to shared genetic and environmental exposures. Some of these FDRs also meet the definition of ILE. In a study of 409 unaffected FDRs of lupus patients, 45 developed criteria for SLE over a mean follow-up time of 6.4 years. Features that characterized those who developed lupus included elevated ANA levels; higher burden of autoantibodies; worse scores on patient reported outcomes; increased plasma levels of BLyS, stem cell factor, and interferonregulated chemokines; and reduced levels of the regulation mediators transforming growth factor (TGF)-β and IL-10.

Anti-nuclear antibodies are often the first test chosen to determine whether a patient has SLE or other autoimmune conditions. As noted above, the high sensitivity of the ANA makes this reasonable, while the low specificity precludes its use as a screening test. Additional testing may identify the few ANA-positive individuals who go on to develop SLE. A study of 84 asymptomatic ANApositive individuals included 14 who progressed with features of systemic autoimmune disease over a 2-year period. Only IgG anti-Ro52 antibody was associated with progression to symptoms with a positive predictive value of 46% and a negative predictive value of 89%.

In the early stage pre-classification time frame, asymptomatic ANA-positive individuals have demonstrated alterations in both cellular and humoral immunity.99, ANA-positive individuals have increased T follicular helper cells and Th2 cells and decreased NK and NKT cells.99, Immune regulation is altered in asymptomatic ANA-positive patients with increased T regulatory cell populations and higher levels of plasma TGF-β. Thus a strategy

of performing a secondary screen of ANA-positive individuals for features of increased risk of progression to disease is necessary, although cost and access to specialized testing may limit feasibility.

A case-control study of innate and adaptive immune pathway soluble mediators compared 170 controls to 246 patients who developed classifiable SLE and found that autoantibody development occurred after immune dysregulation. The authors used random forest models to predict at different time points those going on to develop classifiable SLE. At 0.9 to 3.5 years prior to classification, cases with a positive ANA could be distinguished from controls with 92% (±0.52%) accuracy by elevated levels of MIG, IFN-γ—induced chemokine, and IL-12. Across the entire pre-classification period, ANA positivity, IL-5, IL-6, and MIG predicted SLE with 92% (±1.78%) accuracy.
