A recently published paper evaluating the Nurses' Health Study used a complex risk model to predict SLE in a predominately White population, with an AUC of 0.76 (95% CI, 0.72 to 0.81). This model was based on a weighted genetic risk score composed of 86 single nucleotide polymorphisms and 10 HLA alleles; family history of RA or SLE; and lifestyle and environmental risk factors, including age, race/ethnicity, smoking, alcohol use, body mass index, sleep, socioeconomic status, U.S. region, menarche age, oral contraceptive use, and menopausal status/postmenopausal hormone use.

Assuming that a suitable combination of patient features and biomarkers can be developed to identify persons at high risk of developing SLE, the next appropriate question is whether the disease onset can be slowed or prevented. Lupus prevention trials have lagged compared with RA. A retrospective study of 130 individuals in the DoD cohort documented that those who were given hydroxychloroquine (HCQ) or prednisone before classification had a slower time to progression from their first clinical ACR criteria to the classification of SLE (HCQ median time 1.08 vs 0.29 years; P = .018). Further, patients who were treated were less likely to develop leukopenia and proteinuria before classification. Patients who were not treated developed more autoantibodies and more specificities of autoantibodies. Based on this research, a placebo-controlled, randomized trial, the Study of Anti-Malarials in Incomplete Lupus Erythematosus (SMILE), was undertaken testing the effect of HCQ in ILE. Trial results are anticipated in 2024. Another large, randomized, double-blind, placebocontrolled trial investigating the impact of vitamin D and fish oil found that vitamin D supplementation reduced the incidence of developing autoimmune disease, although there were not enough data to assess for SLE specifically.4, For patients at risk for SLE, current recommendations are to modify at-risk behaviors, including stopping smoking, exercising regularly, monitoring environmental exposures, maintaining a healthy weight, and practicing good sleep hygiene.

Staging pre-classification SLE will be more challenging. Within asymptomatic autoimmunity, patients may not progress or may move on to different diseases in the autoimmune spectrum. Studying asymptomatic autoimmunity may also prove to be resource intensive; however, ILE presents a distinct opportunity for engagement.

### Systemic Sclerosis

Pre-classification systemic sclerosis (SSc) or scleroderma also has several names, including UCTD-risk-SSc, early SSc, and prescleroderma. These terms encompass a patient exhibiting various combinations of features, such as Raynaud's phenomenon,

characteristic nailfold capillary abnormalities, and autoantibodies. These serum biomarkers include ANA, anti-centromere, anti-topoisomerase I, anti-RNA polymerase III, anti-Th/To, and anti-Pm-Scl.

The strongest risk factor for developing systemic sclerosis is having a family member affected. Genetic risk factors for developing SSc overlap with other autoimmune conditions, or "shared autoimmunity," and include interferon and T cell signaling genes, including IRF5, STAT4, and CD247.106 Additional factors such as DNA methylation, histone modifications, and microRNA contribute to risk.

In the earliest phase of scleroderma, there is an increase in type 1 interferon, which with further study may help identify those who progress over time. Several small studies have assessed patients in early stages of pre-classification scleroderma who, according to criteria established in 2001,108 do not have fibrotic features of scleroderma and are at higher risk of progression, These patients had higher levels of CCL2, sICAM-1, CXCL8, IL-13, very high IL-33, TNFR2, CHI3L1, CXCL10, and CXCL11, with the latter two being predictive of progression. 109, Peripheral blood cell gene expression found increased interferon signaling and decreased transcription of markers for erythropoiesis, cytotoxic/NK cell, and lymphoid lineage expression, with persistent down-regulation of NK cell expression in those who progressed. Early disease clinics and studying relatives will be critical for risk prediction in this rare disorder.

### Sjögren's Disease

In Sjögren's disease, autoantibodies have been found in serum samples in patients up to 20 years (median, 4.3 to 5.1 years) prior to diagnosis. These autoantibodies include ANA, RF, anti-Ro 60/SSA, anti-Ro 52/SSA, and anti-La/SS-B. Patients less than 40 years of age had a greater prevalence of autoantibodies, higher titers, and more antibody specificities. Salivary proteomic biomarkers were investigated in anti-Ro/SSA asymptomatic patients and revealed that 57 of 166 proteins were differentially expressed compared with healthy controls. Inflammatory innate and humoral immunity-related and typical acinar proteins (MUC5B, PIP, CST4, and lipocalin 1) were identified. Ongoing research into salivary biomarkers may help aid in differentiating early Sjögren's disease from healthy.

### Axial Spondyloarthritis

Early disease recognition of axial spondyloarthritis (formerly ankylosing spondylitis) (axSpA) has been challenging given the lack of autoantibodies and inflammatory biomarkers. HLA-B27 is a strong genetic risk factor, as are IL23R and ERAP1113; however, broad population screening is not feasible. Early research in the bone morphogenic protein signaling pathway and wnt/β-catenin is ongoing. Imaging has been a useful tool; however, many of the findings suggesting inflammatory arthritis can also be seen in the healthy population, patients with osteoarthritis or malignancy, and in asymptomatic individuals with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). Further, entities such as nonradiographic axial spondyloarthritis are not felt to be early axSpA, given the lack of progression in many cases.

As in other conditions, FDRs of axSpA patients have been studied.114, Greater than 50% of FDRs had back pain, and roughly 22% had inflammatory back pain at baseline. Further, 16% to 20% of patients had MRI evidence of inflammation in the

sacroiliac joints, 114,115 and 22% of subjects had IBD-associated antibodies.

In IBD, risk factors for Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis (UC) often have diverging impacts for developing disease. Factors such as smoking, statin use, and appendectomy history increase risk for one but not the other.116,117 7 Dysbiosis in luminal microbiota increases the risk for IBD, as do enteric infections and dietary factors such as fiber, life stressors, and antibiotic usage. Patient serum from the DoD was analyzed 5 years prior to diagnosis. Panels of candidate biomarkers, including C-reactive protein (CRP), serum amyloid P, complement factors, proteinase-3, several interleukins, and the antimicrobial marker anti-Saccharomyces cerevisiae antibodies (ASCA)-IgA, were found to aid in the prediction of Crohn's disease. For UC, the most specific marker was pANCA. Given the spectrum of overlap in axSpA and IBD and strong genetic risk, long-term follow-up of FDRs will be needed to develop and refine prediction algorithms.

### Multiple Sclerosis

Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a demyelinating, inflammatory disorder of the central nervous system with a female predominance. Genetic risk factors are similar to other autoimmune diseases, with a strong risk factor from HLA-DRB1 alleles, as well as gene expression for cytokine and cytokine receptors.20, Environmental triggers include cigarette smoking, vitamin D deficiency, obesity, Epstein—Barr virus infection, and low sun exposure. 20, To date, no autoantibodies have been discovered to be predictive; however, the neuro-imaging biomarker radiologically isolated syndrome (RIS) and the serum protein neurofilament light chain (sNfl) are used to characterize pre-classification MS. In RIS, imaging of the CNS finds MS-like lesions, but no symptoms 20, Long-term follow-up suggests that 50% of RIS are present. patients will progress to MS within a 10-year span. sNfl can be considered a biomarker of neuraxonal degeneration, which can be seen a median of 6 years prior to the diagnosis.20, Following the diabetes early-stage paradigm, the phase 4 CELLO study investigating ocrelizumab, an anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody, is . Dimethyl fumarate reduces the risk of a first clinical enrolling. event (unadjusted HR, 0.18; 95% CI, . to .63; P = .007) in patients with RIS. MS, like T1DM, has described the high-risk population and found benefit in treating patients in early-stage disease.

### Conclusion

In this chapter, we have reviewed the research in pre-classification autoimmune and rheumatic disease and described how these diseases may fit into stages. Autoimmunity, defined primarily by the detection of autoantibodies, is common; however, plasticity of the stages and patient calculations of risks and benefits affect research and costs. T1DM and multiple sclerosis can be used as a paradigm with defined disease stages that are susceptible to modification and interventions. Combinations of blood biomarkers, imaging, genetic risk models, and patient exposures will be necessary to build impactful prediction tools to aid research and pre-classification clinical trials. The areas of opportunity for advancement in research and therapy are broad.

# The Microbiome in Rheumatic Diseases

### KEY POINTS

### Introduction

Whipple's disease was first discovered to be an infectious disease by Relman and colleagues. Tropheryma whippleii is a gut pathogen that can also reside in the small intestine of healthy subjects, suggesting that Whipple's disease is one of the first chronic rheumatic diseases causally linked to a gut microorganism. Associations of oral or gut microorganisms with rheumatic diseases, however, are long-standing. Over a century ago, rheumatoid arthritis (RA) had been associated with microorganisms and microbially driven inflammatory disease at barrier sites, in particular the mouth. In the late 19th and early 20th century, RA was described to co-occur with periodontitis (PD), and periodontal treatment improved disease activity when evaluated months later. The incidence of RA was linked with the spread of sugar trade, which promoted the development of PD. More recent studies have associated specific periodontal pathogens with RA, which are described in more detail below.

Other inflammatory triggers on mucosal barriers such as the gut and the lungs were also recognized more recently in patients with RA. The overall concept of mucosal sites participating in the pathogenesis of RA was coined the mucosal origins hypothesis. The hygiene hypothesis connects epidemiologically the decline in pathogen infections due to increased hygiene with the rapidly rising incidence of immune-mediated diseases over the last decades. The central theme of this hypothesis is that modern living conditions provide too little microbial stimuli for the hosts' immune systems to develop properly and that may lead to allergic and autoimmune diseases in genetically prone individuals. Besides RA, other rheumatic diseases, particularly spondyloarthritides (SpA), a cluster of diseases characterized by shared clinical features and genetic predisposition such as human leukocyte antigen (HLA)-B27, have historically been associated with mucosal inflammation and dysbiosis. Dysbiosis is an ill-defined term for a deviation of the normal composition of the microbiota (the collection of all microbes colonizing a host).

The first evidence for subclinical gut involvement in the SpA spectrum of diseases was provided in the mid-1980s by a histologic study in patients with HLA-B27-positive reactive arthritis (ReA) presenting with oligoarthritis with or without axial involvement. In this small study of 12 patients, all had signs of microscopic inflammation in the terminal ileum that was clinically asymptomatic in the majority of cases. It was suggested to be a subclinical form of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). In the following years, similar findings were observed in larger groups of ReA and SpA patients with or without peripheral arthritis irrespective of the HLA-B27 status. In 1987, one group found signs of ileitis, colitis, or ileocolitis in 62% of ReA/SpA patients.8, The authors described two histologic patterns of gut inflammation: acute and chronic. The acute type of inflammation resembled infectious enterocolitis characterized by infiltration of the epithelium with neutrophils and eosinophils, crypt abscess formation, and infiltration of the lamina propria with polymorphonuclear cells. The normal mucosal structure was, however, preserved. The chronic type of inflammation was histologically indistinguishable from early Crohn's disease and characterized by a disturbed mucosal architecture, crypt distortion, villous blunting and fusion, increased mixed lamina propria cellularity, and the presence of basal lymphoid

aggregates. Repeat ileocolonoscopy in a subgroup of SpA patients showed that gut and joint inflammation generally evolve in parallel. Gut inflammation disappeared in patients reaching articular remission, while it was persistent in patients with ongoing active joint disease. Gut inflammation was persistent especially in patients with chronic gut inflammation; this phenotype was later identified as carrying the highest risk for evolution toward Crohn's disease (6.5% over 5 years). Crohn's disease—associated SpA is the most obvious historical connection with the gut microbiome. The associations of gut microbial dysbiosis with other rheumatic diseases developed later and are described further below.

### Microbiome by Location

### The Gut Microbiome

The human gut microbiota, the collection of all organisms residing inside the gastrointestinal (GI) tract, is highly abundant compared with other microbiotas in the human body. It is estimated that about as many commensal microorganisms colonize humans as human cells are in the body. The human gut microbiome, the collection of all genes within the microbiota, is thought to be at least 150-fold larger than the human genome. The small intestine is anatomically and functionally different from the large intestine and carries different gut bacteria and metabolites (Fig. 23.1). The mucus

layer is thicker, and more commensal microorganisms colonize this part of the GI tract, whereas dietary antigens reach the highest concentrations in the small intestine where immunologic tolerance is established to food and other environmental factors (Fig. 23.2). In the colon, on the other hand, the gut microbiota ferment fibers to short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) that have immunoregulatory effects on immune cells and gut barrier strengthening properties.

Insight into the composition of the intestinal mucosal barrier is crucial for understanding the immunologic linkage between gut and joint inflammation. Under physiologic circumstances, the gut mucosal immune system remains tolerant to the large number of commensal bacteria but induces an immune response against pathogenic microorganisms. To preserve gut homeostasis, the intestinal barrier comprises different components: a single layer of epithelial cells connected through tight junctions, a mucus layer covering the epithelial cell layer, and a (sub)epithelial gut immune system (Fig. 23.3). The latter largely consists of CD8+ intraepithelial lymphocytes anchored to the epithelium through the αEβ7/Ecadherin connection. The lamina propria underlying the intestinal epithelial layer contains macrophages, dendritic cells, and plasma cells but also highly specialized innate-like T cells such as mucosal-associated invariant T cells, invariant natural killer T cells and γδ-T cells. These cells have immunomodulatory properties and can produce a range of Th1 (interferon [IFN]γ and TNF)-, Th2 (interleukin [IL]-4)-, or Th17 (IL-22 and IL-17)-related cytokines

in a T cell receptor-dependent or -independent manner. These innate-like cells act as a bridge between innate and adaptive immunity.

The mucosal lymphoid tissue is organized in Peyer's patches (lymphoid follicles), which can be found between the crypts. The gut barrier function is crucial in preventing bacteria to translocate that can otherwise instigate inflammatory diseases in host tissues, which is influenced by various genetic, environmental, and host factors (Fig. 23.4).17, In addition, gut bacteria can express cross-reactive antigens and trigger systemic immune responses in genetically prone hosts. This was shown

in rheumatic and other autoimmune diseases (reviewed in refs. and 19). Other mechanisms of gut commensal-induced autoimmune phenomena are still poorly defined in rheumatic diseases but may include innate immune stimulation, T helper cell skewing, and B cell activation that lead to autoantibodies against citrullinated and other post-translationally modified antigens. 19-21 These processes are not mutually exclusive and can be instigated by the same gut microorganisms or by different gut microorganisms acting in concert within the same host. Further details are described in the sections on individual rheumatic diseases and are summarized in Fig. 23.5.

### The Oral Microbiome

The oral cavity is a barrier site maintaining an important crosstalk between oral bacteria and the host immune system. Unlike in the GI tract, where microorganisms are compartmentalized within the mucosal layers, the oral cavity is distinct where bacteria may form biofilms on the surfaces of the teeth. The mucosal barrier may be broken by bacteria during infection when pathogenic strains penetrate the underlying soft tissue, for example, when invading the periodontal epithelium around the teeth. Like the GI mucosal immune system, antimicrobial peptides, immunoglobulin (Ig)A, and mucins provide a barrier-sealing function against infection. However, mouth epithelia are multilayered and vary in their permeability and function.22, They include both keratinized and nonkeratinized epithelia, which differ substantially from intestinal epithelia. These epithelia provide added protection against invasive pathogens and also promote oral health by sustaining immune tolerance. Various interactions between the oral microbiota and the host immune system have been suggested to underlie numerous disease states such as RA or IBD, metabolic (type 2 diabetes), cardiovascular, and even neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's disease.27,35a Moreover, there seems to be an intermucosal connection between oral and gut inflammation (gut-mouth axis), both through translocation of pathobionts (directly) and generation of pathogenic Th17 cells (indirectly).35b These observations suggest that the oral microbiota may influence inflammatory responses both locally and systemically, but causal links are largely missing.

### The Lung Microbiome

Compared with the gut and oral microbiomes, much less is known about the role of the lung microbiome in health and disease, in part due to the difficulty studying the microbiota composition or function in the respiratory tract. Importantly, the tracheobronchial tree maintains environmental gradients that influence the colonizing microbiota based on oxygen tension, blood perfusion, and pH. In cystic fibrosis, the three-dimensional microbiome revealed various genera in distinct areas of the human lung. In rheumatic diseases, such sophisticated studies have not yet been performed but could shed light on the biogeography of the lung microbiota in RA-interstitial lung disease (ILD), for instance.

Airway inflammation and autoimmunity have been linked in cystic fibrosis and RA with citrullination as a post-translational modification of autoantigens. Smoking, a well-established risk factor for developing RA, has been put forth as one mechanism of citrullination of autoantigens. Whether smoking affects the lung microbiota in RA, and thereby its pathogenesis, is unknown, but cigarette smoking has demonstrable effects on intestinal inflammation and the gut microbiota. Mechanisms of how the lung microbiota contributes to diseases are best understood in animal models. Mouse models have revealed that the lung microbiota is influenced by distal microbial signals from the gut microbiota. In fact, a gut-lung axis is well established and influences airway inflammation, autoimmunity,41 and host resistance. It may also explain how smoking contributes to the pathogenesis in RA. The murine lung microbiome has recently been demonstrated to also modulate brain autoimmunity,43 suggesting a broader role of pulmonary microbiota in distant organ inflammation than previously appreciated. If and how the lung microbiome contributes to RA and other rheumatic diseases with pulmonary involvement such as polymyositis, scleroderma, or sarcoidosis remains to be determined. Similarly, genetic polymorphisms such as those in mucin genes (MUC5B) associated with pulmonary fibrosis and RA-ILD44,45 that affect the human lung microbiota composition and thereby disease pathogenesis are obvious areas to investigate in this understudied field of respiratory microbiota—host interactions in autoimmune diseases.6,18

### The Skin Microbiome

The skin microbiota colonizing a barrier site frequently inflamed in rheumatic diseases is an active area of basic and translational research that was recently summarized.18, The skin microbial biomass is much less than in the gut microbiome, which poses technical challenges and leaves skin microbiome studies prone to experimental and environmental biases. The human skin microbiome, however, is more stable than the gut microbiome,47 which facilitates longitudinal studies besides the ease of access of this barrier surface compared with the small intestinal or colonic surfaces. On the other hand, obvious topographic differences across the human skin support different bacterial and fungal microbiota based on the specific conditions within each niche (such as moist vs. dry sites). Overall, the human skin microbiome is complex to study and requires body site—matched sampling in both patients and control subjects.

Skin immunity is influenced by the microbiota and, vice versa, the cutaneous microbiome is regulated by various components of the host immune system, in particular by antimicrobial peptides and type-17 immunity (reviewed in ref. 49). Dysregulation in the

skin microbiota composition or in cutaneous immunity may lead to chronic inflammatory states. Skin microbiota—immune interactions have been shown to contribute to atopic dermatitis that is characterized by a dysfunctional epithelial barrier. Skin pathobionts, especially Staphylococcus aureus, grow out during flares51 and were shown to be mechanistically involved in the pathogenesis of skin inflammation in animal models.52, S. aureus was also shown to be expanded in cutaneous lupus lesions,54 suggesting it is more broadly a skin pathobiont that promotes cutaneous inflammation and systemic inflammation based on a murine model. More specific pathobionts in cutaneous lupus are Ro60 ortholog-expression commensal bacteria,56 as summarized in more detail in the section on systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).

The skin and gut microbiome in psoriasis has also been surveyed in patient cohorts (reviewed in ref. 57), but if and how the microbiota contributes to psoriatic arthritis still remains illdefined. Overall, the role of the skin microbiota in rheumatic diseases needs to be explored in more depth, as recently summarized.18, Given the profound role of the skin microbiota in host immunity,49 a role in dermatomyositis, cutaneous sarcoidosis, or cutaneous vasculitis is plausible.

### Microbiome Analyses

### Sequencing and Omics Approaches

Human bacterial microbiomes can be surveyed by unbiased sequencing approaches or culture-based approaches, respectively. Sequencing has been traditionally performed using the variation of the 16S ribosomal gene in bacteria, the so-called 16S ribosomal DNA (rDNA) sequencing. Some variable regions are more suitable for certain niches, for instance, the V3-V4 16S rDNA region for fecal microbiome sequencing and the V1-V3 16S rDNA region for skin microbiome sequencing. Many caveats must be considered when sampling and sequencing human or murine microbiomes besides the variable regions chosen within the 16S rDNA (reviewed in refs. 59-61). Technical variations and confounder effects are to be considered (Fig. 23.6)60 besides many host variables that may skew sequencing results, with some of the strongest being alcohol intake and proton pump inhibitor use.62,

With costs for sequencing falling over the years, metagenomic sequencing of all genes within microbiomes has become more feasible. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing allows one to determine

the breadth of genes within a given microbiome, which provides insights into the functional potential besides taxonomy.

Untargeted metabolomics remains expensive and renders many undefined metabolites that first require chemical definition and further characterization before any biologic relevance can be inferred. Targeted metabolomics that refers to the selected measurements of known metabolites is more economically feasible but requires a hypothesis-driven approach. One of the most commonly studied gut-derived metabolites in this context are SCFAs. Acetate, butyrate, and propionate can be measured in the stool and blood of patients, which has been insightful in various immunologic diseases given its known effects on host immunity. .

More sophisticated sequencing approaches of human microbiomes involve the sorting of gut bacteria that are tagged by IgA (or other immunoglobulin isotipes). This approach, originally called IgA-seq, rendered new pathobionts in IBD66 and was instrumental in identifying an IgA-coated Escherichia coli strain in Crohn's disease—associated spondyloarthritis that promotes Th17 responses in a gnotobiotic animal model. It has been less fruitful in antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) than a hypothesis-driven approach,68 likely because gut inflammation is not an overt clinical feature in APS.

Advanced bioinformatic approaches allow inferring host protein interactions with bacterial proteins (reviewed in ref. 69). Ongoing progress in bioinformatics and sequencing will likely lead to new insights into the otherwise descriptive approaches of microbiome sequencing. In addition, new species will be identified by deeper sequencing approaches that reveal the so-called "dark matter" within microbiomes.70, Lastly, while a major focus remains on the bacterial microbiomes, sequencing of fungal or viral microbiomes is improving rapidly and will certainly provide

further insights into interkingdom interactions that may be relevant for immune-mediated diseases. 72,73

### Culture-Based Approaches

Culture-based approaches are not as unbiased as sequencingbased approaches to the human microbiome but have the obvious advantage of recovering viable bacteria. Isolating bacterial strains for downstream mechanistic in vitro and in vivo studies is a crucial step to understand host—microbiota interactions that go beyond association studies. Aerobic cultures are more prone to contamination than anaerobic cultures that require an anaerobic chamber and significant microbiologic expertise. One downside of attempting to culture gut microbiota is that they are adapted to the GI environment and are often difficult to recover in conventional culture media. In addition, some species such as Actinomyces spp. are slow-growing and require longer than usual culture periods. Using rich, gut microbiota—adapted culture media and developing clonally arrayed culture collections allowed for culturing most human gut bacteria. Similar culture-based approaches linked to whole-genome sequencing and computational modeling defined new isolates of previously unculturable bacteria75 and revealed eco-evolutionary dynamics within individuals.

Studying viable murine or human gut bacteria isolated from healthy subjects, patients or disease models can be advantageous for many reasons. First, some pathogenic aspects such as expression of cross-reactive proteins are only evident at a certain growth state. Second, cultured isolates can be used for gavage into germfree mice. Utilizing susceptible animal models, gnotobiotic in vivo studies can support the pathogenic role in rheumatic diseases such

as lupus, spondyloarthritis, or RA.67, Lastly, culture-based approaches allow for identification of low-abundance strains in largely sterile tissues of internal organs that would otherwise be missed or difficult to discern from contaminating microbial DNA. Culturing translocated microbiota has led to the identification of pathobionts in extraintestinal organ-specific and systemic autoimmune diseases.77,79,80

### Gnotobiotics

As pointed out in the previous section, culturing bacteria from human or murine microbiomes is useful for mechanistic in-vivo studies. A highly reductionist approach to studying the role of the microbiota in rheumatic diseases is using germ-free animals that are devoid of any microorganisms. These can be achieved by germ-free rederivation of genetic disease models or by acquiring commercially available germ-free mice of common strains. Germfree animals can be gavaged with viable bacteria, either single bacteria—so-called monocolonizations—or multiple with a defined consortium. These approaches are called gnotobiotic and reduce the complexities of a full set of microbiota and have been useful in studying host—microbiota interactions in autoimmune diseases (reviewed in refs. 6, 18).

An alternative approach to reducing the complexity is the depletion of the resident gut microbiota with oral antibiotics, which has the advantage of a normal immune maturation after weaning of animals but the obvious downside of not completely removing all microbiota. Cohousing of mice with different microbiota is another functional manipulation that leads to transfer of microbiota via coprophagy from one host to another with either dominant or subordinate effects, depending on the presence of pathobionts and their interactions with other microbiota. So-called microorganism-phenotype triangulation may identify causal bacteria from complex microbial communities by studying diseased, healthy, and intermediate phenotypes. Finally, gut microbiota can also evolve within a host, changing their pathogenic potential over time. This concept of within-host evolution may explain the time-dependent penetrance of systemic autoimmune diseases in susceptible hosts, which would be difficult to study without gnotobiotic models.

### Emerging Technologies

Recent advances in studying host—microbiota interactions led to new insights in health and disease but have not yet been applied to rheumatic diseases. A few examples are given to illustrate which technologies and emerging approaches may enhance the study of the microbiota in rheumatology. For instance, organoids are increasingly used in the study of immunologic diseases (reviewed in ref. 84). Bacterial-organoid coculture systems allow for mechanistic dissection of host—microbiota interactions as done with pathobionts identified in primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC).

Organs on-a-chip are increasingly tested for disease-related research. Addition of gut bacteria is particularly challenging given the anaerobic culture conditions often needed. The development of an anaerobic intestine on a chip85 may serve as a future discovery tool to test host—microbiota interactions and therapeutic interventions.

A murine 3D-gut culture system enables the ex-vivo study of microbiota-immune interactions in the context of the nervous system and other cell types normally lacking in in vitro systems. This unique experimental setup enables the study of human

microbiota from multiple sclerosis patients and its metabolites in the pathogenesis of this chronic, neuroinflammatory disease. Infusing human microbiota from rheumatic disease patients in a 3D-intestine ex vivo should equally allow for new insights into host—microbiota interactions in the field of rheumatology.

### The Microbiota in Rheumatic c Diseases

### Spondyloarthritis

Gut and Joints Are Interconnected in Spondyloarthritides The close relationship between gut and joint inflammation in SpA has been recognized for decades. The association between SpA and IBD is not only based on clinical observations but also arises from a genetic, immunologic, and therapeutic point of view.

As for the genetic linkage, SpA and IBD share several susceptibility loci such as IL23R, IL12B, STAT3, CARD9, and TNFSF15. Another example are polymorphisms in the CARD15 (NOD2) gene. Individuals that are homozygous or compound heterozygous for mutations in CARD15 carry a 20to 40-fold increased risk of developing IBD. CARD15 codes for a protein that acts as an intracellular pattern-recognition receptor. Upon binding to bacterial components, it activates nuclear factor kappa B, a key transcriptional regulator controlling the expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines, adhesion molecules, and growth factors. One group found an association between CARD15 and isolated sacroiliitis, although the association with ankylosing spondylitis (AS) could not be confirmed in other studies.89, On the other hand, another study found a similarly high frequency of CARD15 mutation carriers in SpA patients with chronic gut inflammation (38%) and in patients with Crohn's disease (49%). These proportions were significantly different from SpA patients without gut inflammation or a control population without SpA, suggesting a genetic link between intestinal and joint inflammation. Another study analyzing mucosal gene expression found similar transcriptomic profiles in the intestine of SpA patients (especially those with chronic subclinical gut inflammation) and patients with Crohn's disease.

Several lines of immunologic evidence support the link between gut and joint inflammation. First, upregulation of the adhesion molecule E-cadherin has been demonstrated in IBD and in SpA patients with subclinical gut inflammation.92a Its ligand αEβ7 integrin was also upregulated on mucosal T cells from AS patients in the absence of histologic signs of inflammation.92b Interestingly, an enrichment of T cells carrying αEβ7 integrin has also been identified in inflamed synovial tissue of SpA patients, suggesting an intestinal origin.92c More recently, loss of the mucosal barrier integrity was described in patients with SpA, with marked changes in zonulin expression in the intestinal epithelium. These findings mirror the emerging picture that loss of barrier integrity represents a key step in the development of intestinal inflammation in SpA. This concept is not restricted to SpA but is also emerging in other rheumatic diseases such as lupus (discussed below)18 and RA.94-96 Second, in ReA, identical clonally expanded T cells have been identified in the intestine and the joint. However, only a few expanded T cell clones were shared by both compartments. Third, simultaneous upregulation of a macrophage subpopulation expressing scavenger receptor CD163 was observed in the synovium and intestine (including noninflamed areas) of SpA patients, illustrating that not only T cells but also antigenpresenting cells account for the relationship between joint and gut inflammation.97a In addition, not only macrophages but also activated lymphocytes isolated from the human intestinal lamina

propria are able to bind vessels from inflamed synovial tissue in vitro via various adhesion molecules.97b Fourth, gut-associated IL-17and IL-22-positive innate lymphoid cells were found in the peripheral blood and synovial fluid of patients with AS.

In addition, there is emerging evidence of translocation of lipopolysaccharide throughout the bowel wall in spondyloarthritis. This is in line with earlier studies on the presence of bacterial DNA in synovial tissues from SpA patients.

Finally, chronic TNF overproduction, which occurs in the TNFΔARE mouse model, is sufficient to lead to combined gut and joint inflammation and tissue damage through TNFRI signaling in synovial fibroblasts and intestinal myofibroblasts (reviewed in ref. 16). Experimental evidence using pre-clinical mouse models and ex vivo analyses suggest immune cell trafficking from the gut to the joint, although this has not been firmly established in humans. Other pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-23 may also induce combined gut and joint inflammation. However, although IL-23 induces peripheral joint inflammation in an animal model, only very limited signs of sacroiliitis are seen compared to the TNF-overproducing model. This finding mirrors the failure of IL-23 blockade in treatment of patients with AS.

### Microscopic Gut Inflammation and Its Implications

Besides the link between SpA and clinically overt IBD, the causal or contributing role of subclinical gut inflammation in

SpA-related joint inflammation has been a long-standing area of investigation. Over recent years, much emphasis has been placed on identifying SpA patients at an earlier stage, which resulted in new classification criteria with an increased importance of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). To this end, the results of microscopic gut inflammation were confirmed in a cohort of newly diagnosed SpA patients, based on the Assessment of SpondyloArthritis International Society classification criteria, and showed that approximately 50% of them exhibit microscopic signs of gut inflammation in the absence of abdominal discomfort (Fig. 23.7). Importantly, the presence of microscopic gut inflammation correlates with disease activity in axial SpA patients, measured through objective parameters like bone marrow edema of the sacroiliac joints on MRI and subjective evaluations like patient-reported outcomes.

Studying intestinal tissue samples from SpA patients revealed insights in the gut-joint axis with relevance for disease pathogenesis. In ileal samples of IBD-related SpA patients, the gut barrier integrity was impaired with epithelial damage (as evidenced by increased serum levels of intestinal fatty acid binding protein) and downregulation of tight junction proteins (occluding, claudin-1/-4), allowing microbial translocation and innate immune activation (e.g., increased lipopolysaccharide and soluble CD14 levels). Similar observations were made in ileal tissue samples of patients with AS.

### Intestinal Dysbiosis in Spondyloarthritis

Many factors may influence the gut microbial composition, such as sex, comorbidities, diet, immunity, infections, antibiotic use, route of delivery, hygiene, and stress, among others. 104-106 Gut dysbiosis, in particular a restricted diversity of the gut microbiota, is emerging as a common alteration among systemic inflammatory diseases. Several research groups have reported decreased bacterial richness and diversity in SpA patients. Some taxa such as Ruminococcus gnavus in fecal samples and Dialister spp. in mucosal biopsies are more abundant in SpA and correlate with disease activity in these patients.108-110 In another study, AS patients demonstrated increased Prevotella copri and Bifidobacterium, while Bacteroides spp. were decreased. Also, in patients with psoriatic arthritis and skin psoriasis, decreased microbial diversity was observed compared with healthy controls. Patients with psoriatic arthritis have a lower relative abundance of multiple intestinal bacteria, especially reportedly beneficial taxa. Interestingly, the host genetic background seems to drive dysbiosis. In healthy subjects without AS, significant differences were observed in microbiota composition between HLA-B27-positive and -negative individuals. . Studies in HLA-B27-transgenic rats similarly showed significant differences in the gut microbiota between transgenic animals and wild type animals, with an increase in Prevotella spp. and a decrease in Rikenellaceae. Furthermore, it was shown in animal models of SpA that the effect of HLA-B27 on dysbiosis depends on the interplay between the host genetic background and the environment, although immune dysregulation involving IL-23/IL-17, TNF, and IL-1 pathways also plays into it. An ecological model of dysbiosis was put forth with the effects of multiple microorganisms contributing to the aberrant immune response rather than a single pathobiont or a small number of microorganisms driving the pathogenesis.

Evidence for the pivotal role of the gut microbiota in arthritis initiation comes from the HLA-B27-transgenic rat model that spontaneously develops similar manifestations as SpA patients, namely colitis, peripheral arthritis, sacroiliitis, and spondylitis, respectively. When rederived in germ-free conditions, these rats were completely protected from colitis and arthritis while recolonization with commensal microbiota was sufficient to trigger gut and joint inflammation.116, In humans, the role of gut dysbiosis in modulating the local and systemic immune responses leading to SpA-related manifestations is not yet fully understood. One study revealed a unique role for the bacterial genus Dialister, which appeared to be more abundant in microbiota from SpA patients with microscopic gut inflammation compared with those without. In addition, bacteria such as Akkermansia and Prevotella can contribute to intestinal barrier disruption through their mucolytic capacities. On the other hand, dysbiosis may equally affect distant immune functions. A study in patients with AS demonstrated an association between gut dysbiosis, impaired mucosal barrier function, and epithelial release of zonulin. This tight junction molecule, as well as bacterial products, induced a proinflammatory M2 phenotype in circulating monocytes. Mucosal antigens derived from commensal microorganisms consequently trigger a systemic pathogenic immune response following bacterial translocation. For example, lipopolysaccharide, a bacterial product that downregulates the expression of CD14 on circulating monocytes, could rescue these CD14-depleted cells from their anergic state when combined with soluble D14.93 This resulted in upregulation of IL-23, a pivotal cytokine in SpA pathogenesis, which promotes gut inflammation by inhibiting Th1 and Treg

cells and by promoting Th17 cells through upregulation of the Th17-related transcription factor RORγt. 100, Overexpression of IL-23 is thus a pivotal feature of subclinical gut inflammation in AS. However, upregulation of IL-17 was only observed in the gut of Crohn's disease but not in AS patients. Collectively, these data illustrate that unbalanced intestinal microbial communities directly or indirectly influence gut mucosal homeostasis. In turn, these events impact local (gut) and systemic immune functions, thereby contributing to the different manifestations of SpA.

More recently, research has focused not only on the potential pathogenic role of certain microbes but also on the role of perturbed metabolic pathways ("metabolome"). Rather than a single pathobiont, key pathogenic features might be due to metabolic functions of a microbial community. These may in turn depend on the gut microbial community structure and host genetic context. Thus some microorganisms are deemed commensals in a healthy state but can act as pathobionts under certain environmental and host genetic influences. Nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy revealed that fecal metabolites of patients with AS contain reduced levels of the SCFAs butyrate and propionate but increased tryptophan concentrations compared with healthy controls. This might be mechanistically important as administrating microbiota-derived metabolites such as propionate in the HLA-B27-transgenic rat model significantly reduced the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-1β, IL-17A, IFN-γ, and colonic inflammation. In an inducible model of experimental autoimmune uveitis, exogeneous administration of propionate attenuated uveitis through regulatory T cell induction and suppressed migration of effector T cells to gut or extraintestinal tissues.

Based on the accumulating evidence for a pathogenic role of dysbiosis in SpA, direct or indirect modulation of the gut microbiota might provide novel treatment options for these patients. Probiotics containing a cocktail of beneficial live bacteria and yeast, however, did not show significant benefit over placebo in improving disease activity and physical functioning of active axial SpA patients. This may just reflect the need for a better understanding of which microorganisms are beneficial in which context, likely requiring a personalized approach with knowledge of the pre-existing microbiota, which was not studied in this trial. Restoration of a healthy gut microbiota using fecal microbial transplant (FMT) is another, more disruptive option of microbiota manipulation. FMT is highly effective in treating refractory Clostridioides difficile infection, but results in SpA are discouraging so far. Given the complex and dynamic interactions between the gut microbiota, host background, and immune dysregulation, more data from human studies are needed before recommending therapeutic modulation of the microbiota in SpA.

### Rheumatoid Arthritis

An association between poor dental status and arthritis has long been known. This link has been corroborated more recently in 126-130Periodontal studies on periodontal disease in RA patients. diseases affect the gingiva, the supporting connective tissue, and the alveolar bone. Periodontitis (PD) is defined as the inflammation of the tooth-supportive tissues. It leads to loss of attachment and bone destruction. Because the oral cavity is colonized by many different microorganisms, with more than 700 species of oral bacteria being described in biofilms present in dental plaque,131 it has been postulated that this host—microbiota interplay may be instrumental in onset of PD. Several studies showed an association

between PD and three periodontal pathogens, Porphyromonas gingivalis (P. gingivalis), Tannerella forsythia (T. forsythia), and Treponema denticola (T. denticola), respectively. This has been recently extended to Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans (A. actinomycetemcomitans), Filifactor alocis (F. alocis), and other species belonging to the genera Peptostreptococcaceae, Desulfobulbus, and Synergistetes.132-134 Mechanistically, it has been suggested that these bacteria modulate the host immune responses, thereby contributing to the onset of PD. Interestingly, the pathogen P. gingivalis itself does not cause PD in mice lacking commensal bacteria, supporting this paradigm.

How oral microorganisms may promote RA has been explored in multiple studies including large metagenomic studies of oral and gut microbiomes. RA is characterized by a destructive, symmetric polyarthritis associated with autoantibodies directed against citrullinated proteins. Citrullination or deamination is a post-translational modification that converts a positively charged arginine into a neutral citrulline residue. This reaction is catalyzed by calcium ion-dependent enzymes called peptidylarginine deiminases (PADs). While citrullination of proteins is a physiologic process, in genetically predisposed individuals it may trigger the onset of autoimmunity against citrullinated antigens. Thus the interaction between RA-associated major histocompatibility complex-II polymorphisms, smoking, and PD has been linked to development of anti-citrullinated protein antibodies (ACPAs). Several citrullinated autoantigens have been described, among them against collagen type II, fibrinogen, vimentin, and .137-140 Smoking is considered a key environmental risk α-enolase. factor for RA and PD. It is unclear whether smoking promotes autoimmunity against citrullinated antigens directly or indirectly. Smoking itself may foster peptide citrullination by PAD2 and PAD4,141 but smoking also promotes the growth of bacteria in the oral cavity, which may worsen both PD and RA, respectively. Hence, an association with increased T. forsythia, Peptostreptococcus micros (P. micros), Fusobacterium nucleatum (F. nucleatum), and Campylobacter rectus (C. rectus) in subgingival dental plaque has been reported in smokers versus nonsmokers.

How such periodontal pathogens may modulate immune responses has been the subject of several studies and entails multiple mechanisms.143, For example, proteases secreted by T. forsythia, F. nucleatum, or P. gingivalis cleave proteins in the extracellular matrix, which results in tissue degradation. P. gingivalis peptidylarginine deiminase (PPAD) is secreted by this pathobiont and citrullinates C-terminal arginine residues of proteins and peptides, thereby generating new epitopes recognized by ACPAs. The activity of PPAD along with deiminases from other PD-promoting bacteria such as F. alocis and Cryptobacterium curtum results in an increased pH in the oral cavity. In contrast, A. actinomycetemcomitans secretes a toxin (leukotoxin A) that binds to lymphocytes, macrophages, and neutrophils and induces pyroptosis. Importantly, this toxin also induces hypercitrullination in neutrophils, thereby inducing the formation of neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) and promoting the production of ACPAs. NETs are in turn degraded by nucleases expressed by Prevotella intermedia, which leads to endogenous PAD release. In addition, F. nucleatum outer membrane vesicles were shown to translocate to the joints of RA patients and mediate local inflammatory responses via the virulence factor FadA.

Recently a paired analysis ofhuman and bacterial transcriptomics in longitudinal blood samples from RA patients was reported. Interestingly, patients with RA and periodontal disease experienced repeated oral bacteremias associated with transcriptional

signatures of ISG15+HLADRhi and CD48highS100A2+ monocytes. These monocyte subsets have previously been identified in inflamed synovia and blood of RA patients suffering from flares. The oral bacteria observed transiently in the blood were broadly citrullinated, and the in-situ citrullinated epitopes were recognized by extensively somatically hypermutated ACPAs encoded by blood plasmablasts from RA patients. These data are compatible with a scenario that PD results in repeated breaches of the oral mucosa leading to release of citrullinated oral bacteria in the circulation, which in turn activate inflammatory monocyte subsets and ACPA-producing B cells. This process promotes affinity maturation and epitope spreading to citrullinated antigens.

Another recent study used dual IgA and IgG family plasmablast-derived monoclonal autoantibodies obtained from the peripheral blood of individuals at risk for RA to identify crossreactivity between RA-relevant autoantigens and bacterial taxa in the closely related families Lachnospiraceae and Ruminococcaceae. Bacterial isolates from these families bound by the monoclonal autoantibodies revealed strains within the genus Subdoligranulum from the feces of an individual that activate CD4+ T cells from RA patients. Intriguingly, some Subdoligranulum isolates, but not all, stimulated Th17 cell expansion, serum RA-relevant IgG autoantibodies, and joint swelling reminiscent of early RA. Germ-free mice monocolonized with a Subdoligranulum strain developed signs of early RA in vivo with antibody deposition and complement activation in the affected joints (Fig. 23.8).

Another gut pathobiont that was originally identified in newonset RA patients and linked to Th17 responses in vivo in gno- 160,161It was later also associated with tobiotic models is P. copri. pre-RA in at-risk individuals162 that mount antibodies against P. copri antigens. Patients with RA carry anti-P. copri antibodies as well that correlate with RA-relevant autoantibodies in the serum 133, RA-derived P. copri was further shown of RA subsets. to harbor more pathogenic potential than P. copri isolated from healthy subjects, suggesting strain differences that are relevant to disease.

Collectively, these findings suggest a mechanism in the pathogenesis of RA by which a specific gut bacterial strain may drive systemic autoantibody generation and joint-centered antibody deposition and immune activation.

Taken together, multiple mechanisms may contribute to the pathogenesis of RA ranging from oral pathobionts citrullinating autoantigens, gut bacterial outer membrane vesicles translocating to the joints of RA patients, thereby promoting local inflammation, to gut pathobiont-induced systemic Th17 expansion and ACPA induction in early RA via yet to be determined molecular mechanisms.

### Systemic Lupus Erythematosus

Mechanistic studies in animal models and human association studies also support a role for the microbiota in SLE. Translocation of enterococci and lactobacilli from the small intestine to secondary lymphoid organs and the liver occurs in genetically or chemically predisposed lupus models with overactivation of the TLR7 pathway. Genetic overexpression of TLR7 leads to an impaired gut barrier, whereas genetic deficiency of TLR7 improves barrier tightness compared with wild type mice in vivo. The translocation of viable gut bacteria to secondary lymphoid organs without causing an infectious disease but autoimmunity was first shown in a hybrid autoimmune model, the NZW x BXSB F1 mice, that is characterized by a duplication of the TLR7 gene. A predominant

species that translocated across the leaky small intestinal gut barrier to mesenteric lymph nodes (MLNs), liver, and at later time points to the spleen was Enterococcus gallinarum, a gram-positive Enterococcus found in various hosts including chicken (hence the species name), mice, and humans. E. gallinarum instigates innate and adaptive immune cell activation that leads to Th17 and Tfh differentiation and systemic autoantibody production against nucleic acids, in particular double-stranded DNA (dsDNA) and RNA. Translocation to the liver was also associated with features of autoimmune hepatitis (AIH) and DNA from E. gallinarum was found in liver biopsies of both SLE and AIH patients, respectively. Another study from Japan identified human E. gallinarum together with two other pathobionts (Klebsiella pneumoniae and Proteus mirabilis) from the stool of patients with PSC to translocate to the MLN in a gnotobiotic model of PSC. These pathobionts also induced Th17 cell activation and liver inflammation. Overall, these data support that certain enterococci translocate to internal organs in autoimmune-prone hosts, thereby instigating different autoimmune diseases depending on the host genetic predisposition. A role in human SLE is supported by association studies between systemic immune reactivity to E. gallinarum RNA and human RNA and RNA-binding proteins.7,

A pathobiont first identified in SLE patients with lupus nephritis is Ruminococcus gnavus. Outgrowth of R. gnavus was strongly associated with lupus nephritis and linked to antibodies against a lipoglycan of R. gnavus with similar serum reactivity in two unrelated SLE cohorts. In gnotobiotic models, this pathobiont impaired the gut barrier function and translocated DNA was found in MLNs. As in humans, cell-wall lipoglycan antibodies were induced together with anti-dsDNA antibodies and increased serum zonulin levels, a marker of gut barrier dysfunction. Inhibition of zonulin with larazotide improved gut barrier leakiness in

mice. This study supports potential future treatment approaches in SLE targeting the gut barrier.

Besides E. gallinarum und R. gnavus, lactobacilli appear to be particularly prone to translocation and instigation of systemic autoimmunity. In TLR7 transgenic mice, Limosilactobacillus reuteri (L. reuteri) translocated across the gut barrier and led to systemic inflammatory responses with type I IFN signature aggravation and lupus nephritis. A diet rich in resistant starch (a certain type of starch resistant to digestion in the small intestine) improved gut barrier leakiness and reduced translocation of L. reuteri and systemic type-I IFN signatures and organ damage. This proof-ofconcept dietary study demonstrated that dietary interventions may be beneficial in subsets of SLE patients with the type I IFN signature. Low dietary fiber was also linked to accelerated lupus-like disease in the NZB/WF1 mouse model. This intervention led to increased white adipose tissue mass and inflammation, connecting metabolic disease with systemic inflammation,170 which was also apparent with a high-fat diet in another lupus model. An active compound of ginger, on the other hand, ameliorated disease in models of lupus. If and how the gut microbiota is involved is less clear, since the dietary compound was not given orally but injected intraperitoneally. An orally fed tryptophan-rich diet, however, was clearly shown to mediate host effects through the microbiota in the so-called triple congenic mice. In this lupus model with gut dysbiosis, lactobacilli grew out further after oral feeding of a diet high in tryptophan which worsened lupus pathology. Fecal transfer into germ-free mice induced similar autoimmune phenotypes, supporting that the diet-altered microbiota mediated the observed autoimmune phenomena and tissue damage.

Microbiota outside the gut also contribute to lupus pathogenesis. Cross-reactivity with oral, skin, and gut commensal bacteria that express orthologs of the Ro60 autoantigen were shown

to trigger human anti-Ro60 T and B cell responses. In germfree mice, one Ro60-ortholog-containing bacterium, Bacteroides thetaiotaomicron, triggered systemic human anti-Ro60 autoantibodies and, with additional innate stimuli via TLR7, immune complex depositions in the kidneys. The Ro60 skin commensal Pseudopropionibacterium propionicum was increased in skin lesions of SLE patients, suggesting outgrowth in lesions might perpetuate cutaneous lupus. Also, the oral Ro60 bacterium Actinomyces massiliensis was linked to Ro60+ SLE patients in this study56 and enriched in the stool of another SLE cohort supporting oral-togut relocation. Furthermore, T cell cross-reactivity with the lacrimal ductand skin-resident Ro60 bacterium Corynebacterium amycolatum (and several other commensal bacteria without orthologs) was already previously demonstrated in vitro using T cell hybridomas175 and linked to autoantibodies in the study focused on Ro60 orthologs. All these Ro60 bacteria are likely candidates to trigger sustained human anti-Ro60-directed autoimmune responses in subsets of SLE patients. Their phenotypes (sicca symptoms, skin rashes, cytopenias, nephritis) might be related to which type of Ro60 bacteria are colonizing which site, supporting the notion that future targeting of microbiota will require a highly personalized approach with prior identification of the targets in each subject and niche.

Geographic differences may also be important to consider in this context. In a Japanese SLE cohort, for instance, Streptococcus spp. and Streptococcus-derived genes were associated with SLE in a metagenome-wide study. A smaller 16S rDNA sequencing study from China found Streptococcus associated with disease as well. While this may suggest that microbiomes of Asian SLE patients are preferentially enriched in streptococci, a study in the United States also found Streptococcus to be enriched in the stool of SLE patients. Further studies are needed to determine which patient subsets or disease manifestations may be most closely related to these taxa and, importantly, what functional link can be established to confirm that these associations are not due to concomitant therapies or other environmental factors affecting the gut microbial community structures.

In summary, several pathobionts have been identified in lupus-like animal models and in human association studies that were combined with in vitro and in vivo work to strengthen a potential causal link (Fig. 23.9). New candidates emerge with larger cohorts and more sophisticated sequencing approaches but providing mechanistic links to SLE will remain crucial to ensure the candidate taxa from association studies are disease relevant. Those can potentially become future targets for personalized therapies for SLE patients. Vice versa, loss of beneficial bacteria needs to be explored more extensively in SLE to determine whether live biotherapeutics or provision of beneficial microbial products (such as SCFAs) may be a new therapeutic avenue for SLE in the future.

### Other Rheumatic c Diseases

The role of the microbiome in other rheumatic diseases than SpA, RA, and SLE is less studied. Given the clinical and pathogenetic relatedness of rheumatic diseases, similar microorganisms may contribute to different rheumatic diseases. In particular, the connective tissue diseases may share common microbial triggers. The above-mentioned SLE-associated Ro60 ortholog-expressing bacteria56 are likely to also play a role in Sjögren's syndrome (SjS) besides lupus. One of these taxa, Corynebacterium amycolatum, is physiologically found in lacrimal glands. The anatomic location

of this bacterium within a target organ of SjS suggests it could be a theoretical candidate for promoting sicca symptoms via Ro60cross-reactive immune responses. Using the unbiased approach of 16S rDNA sequencing, the human gut microbiome of SjS patients has been profiled together with studies in a corresponding animal model, which revealed reduced diversity of the gut microbiota in SjS compared with controls. Studies with a larger cohort of SjS confirmed gut dysbiosis, which was associated with disease activity. . The buccal microbiome in SjS is also dysbiotic but is influenced by the reduced salivary secretions. Mechanistic research is needed to define which taxa may be causally related to SjS as opposed to secondary effects such as salivary gland dysfunction or other host variables.

In APS, a hypothesis-driven study identified by systematic homology a common human gut bacterium, Roseburia intestinalis, as a cross-reactive trigger for the major autoantigen β2glycoprotein I. R. intestinalis gavage in a genetic model for SLE-related APS led to increased thrombotic disease, supporting a pathogenic role in APS for this otherwise beneficial commensal bacterium. A broader role of the microbiome in APS was recently reviewed and is likely given the long-standing role of infectious triggers in transiently inducing antiphospholipid antibodies.

The gut microbiota in systemic sclerosis (SSc) was explored in various association studies (reviewed in ref. 184). One study compared the SSc microbiome between patients with and without GI involvement, which revealed that GI disease is associated with more overt dysbiosis and certain taxa such as L. reuteri. Since L. reuteri translocation can aggravate the type I IFN signature (as discussed in the section on SLE),167 it is plausible that the dysbiotic SSc microbiome might also contribute to the type I IFN signature in SSc, which would be testable. A more in-depth metagenomic study of patients with SSc and IgG4-related disease demonstrated similar taxa and disease-associated pathways in both disease states. These results suggest similar processes in fibrosing autoimmune diseases, which warrant further studies. In addition, this study confirmed the enrichment of lactobacilli in SSc as seen in other association studies such as the one on GI tract involvement.

The involvement of the microbiota in vasculitides is little studied. A thorough analysis of temporal artery biopsies for microbial signals did not reveal a significant association with specific microbiota that may have migrated to these sites. An altered gut barrier and increased IgA production was, however, mechanistically linked to extraintestinal vasculitis in a Kawasaki disease model. If translocation of the gut microbiota as in lupus77,167 is involved in vascular inflammation of the vasculitides remains to be determined. Human microbiome studies in small-vessel vasculitides have recently been summarized189 and appear to be inconclusive besides an association between nasal Stapbylococcus species and granulomatosis with polyangiitis.

Little is also known about a contribution of the human gut microbiota to autoinflammatory diseases. A mouse model for STING-associated vasculopathy with onset in infancy revealed a protective gut commensal. Another murine study suggests a modulatory role in chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis. A genetic mouse model for this autoinflammatory disease was markedly protected by a high-fat diet and reductions in Prevotella spp. The protective effect was mediated by reductions in IL-1β in neutrophils, which was microbiota dependent. If these findings relate to human autoinflammatory disease and if other autoinflammatory monogenetic diseases with variable disease phenotypes may be influenced by the microbiota remain to be determined.

### Microbiota Therapies

The diagnosis and therapy of rheumatic diseases partly based on the microbiome is still in the distant future but can be envisioned given the rapid progress made in the field over the last two decades. The emerging field of pharmacomicrobiomics192 may allow some day to utilize gut microbial signatures to predict responsiveness or adverse events to certain medications. Targeting the microbiome may also become an adjunctive approach to treating or preventing rheumatic diseases. The strategies in development range from dietary interventions to live biotherapeutics to highly specific depletion of pathobionts by bacteriophages. While the latest proofof-concept studies with pathobiont targeting by a bacteriophage cocktail in IBD are promising,193 the most likely success in autoimmune diseases is a combinatorial approach of host immune and microbiota targeting. One can envision a personalized approach, which requires first identifying which disease subset to target

besides developing a therapeutic avenue that reliably depletes the disease-relevant pathobionts. For instance, ACPA-positive RA patients should be selected to address citrullinating pathobionts1 149 or Ro60-positive SLE patients to target Ro60 ortholog-expressing bacteria. Next, the presence of the pathobionts, not necessarily the overgrowth compared with control subjects, is needed before a microbiome-based therapy is tested. Once the microbial targets have been identified in barrier sites or with blood biomarkers, a depleting approach could be attempted together with reseeding the niche with innocuous microbiota that prevent recolonization. Importantly, additional host-targeted approaches may be needed concomitantly. For instance, strengthening the gut barrier with dietary and pharmacologic approaches may be beneficial to prevent translocation of microbiota products or viable strains that could concomitantly be targeted by vaccination or bacteriophage approaches (Fig. 23.10). In addition, suppressing key host pathways may still be needed that have already been reinforced in

chronic disease by trained immunity or tissue-resident memory cells.

### Conclusion

Several approaches are in development that may target the host barriers or the microbiota. Combinations of these treatment strategies with conventional immunosuppressives may someday put patients with rheumatic diseases into long-lasting remission or prevent the onset of autoimmune diseases in the first place. Although far from current practice, the progress made by hostmicrobiota research over the last decades has greatly enhanced our understanding of the multifactorial pathogenesis of rheumatic diseases and may also facilitate the development of new treatment strategies beyond conventionally targeting the immune system.

### KEY POINTS

New genomic techniques have led to the discovery of genetic polymorphisms, which can contribute to the rheumatic diseases.

In many cases, the genes and variants associated with disease have not yet been determined, although a locus of association has been identified.

Exploiting genetic data provides insights into important key risk pathways, the cell types responsible for disease, and potential targets for novel drug development.

Genetic testing has not translated into the clinical setting for most diseases—more work is required to identify signatures of drug response and prognosis.

### Introduction

Many of the musculoskeletal diseases seen by rheumatologists are thought to arise as a result of an environmental insult that triggers disease in a genetically susceptible individual. As such, they are called complex diseases because both genes and environment contribute to the risk of disease development. Genetic risk factors are easier to study than environmental risk factors because genetic variants are present from conception (and therefore must have been present before disease onset and could contribute to disease susceptibility and severity), are stable throughout life, and are easily measured. This contrasts with environmental risk factors, for which information is often collected after the patient has developed disease but the exposure could have occurred many years before disease onset, thereby introducing recall bias; or the exposure is measured after initial symptom onset, making it difficult to determine causality. Furthermore, environmental risk factors often cannot be reliably or consistently measured. Thus while research has identified a few environmental factors that predispose to disease, there has been an explosion of knowledge about the genetic contribution to many rheumatic diseases.

### Evidence for Genetic Component to a Rheumatic Diseases

To justify investigating the genetic basis of any disease, it is first necessary to have some evidence that genes play a role. This evidence comes from twin or family studies most commonly, although

adoption and migration studies can also support a genetic component. Classic twin studies compare the incidence of disease concordance in monozygotic (MZ) and dizygotic (DZ) twin pairs. Higher disease concordance in MZ twins provides support for a genetic etiology and can be used to estimate the heritability of disease. The percentage of concordance of disease in MZ twins at one point in time will underestimate the genetic contribution to risk in diseases of late age at onset, like many musculoskeletal disorders. This is because, as time progresses, the concordance rate in MZ twins is likely to increase as their age increases. Thus the concordance rate from one twin study of patients with rheumatoid arthritis in the United Kingdom found a rate of 15% in MZ twins and 4% in DZ twins, equating to a 60% heritability.

For less common rheumatic diseases, it may be impossible to collect enough data on twin pairs to interpret the data reliably. However, family studies can also indicate a genetic contribution to disease. The sibling recurrence risk ratio is defined as:

Diseases that show an increased prevalence in family members are likely to have a genetic component. Obtaining a reliable value of λs depends on having accurate estimates of disease prevalence in the two comparison groups. This is not a trivial matter. A firm diagnosis of rheumatic disease is difficult to make in large population surveys, with errors in both directions possible. Underestimation may occur because of the lack of reporting of disease that is no longer active. Overestimation may result from inadequate distinction between different forms of rheumatic disease. Table 24.1 shows the sibling recurrence risk ratios and heritability estimates for some of the rheumatic diseases; heritability estimates have not been calculated for all conditions because very large sample sizes are required for accurate estimates, and these large samples are not yet available for rarer conditions like juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA).

If genome-wide genotype data are available, it is now also possible to estimate heritability from the data itself using statistical methods that assume that patients with a disease are more genetically similar overall than controls, and several such methods are available. However, in some cases, the genetic data can suggest lower heritability than the original twin/family estimates; for example, an estimation of "callous-unemotional" behavior based on twin study methodology yielded a heritability estimate of 64%

compared with a genome-wide genetic study that yielded a heritability estimate of 7%.

### Study Design

There are a number of important considerations when designing a study to identify genetic variants contributing to disease. These include the use of linkage versus association approaches, case-control versus family-based studies, the choice of marker to be tested, and candidate gene versus whole-genome methods (Table 24.2). The choice may be driven by cost considerations, power, and/or the availability of samples. The differing approaches have been outlined in more detail in the following sections.

### Linkage Studies

Linkage methods depend on the ability to track polymorphic markers in families and to show that these genetic markers cosegregate with the disease phenotype in families in which there are multiple members affected. Thus multiplex families are required for linkage analysis. Statistical methods are based on examining the likelihood of a particular pattern of co-inheritance of marker and disease (linkage), compared with the likelihood that there is no linkage (the null hypothesis). A measure of this likelihood is referred to as the LOD score (log of the odds score), with an LOD score greater than 3 generally interpreted to indicate significant evidence of linkage when markers across the entire genome are examined.

For highly penetrant Mendelian disorders with a clear pattern of inheritance, classic linkage analysis is a powerful means of identifying the underlying molecular basis of disease. However, for complex diseases, alternative approaches based on the affected sibling pair (ASP) method are required. This method is based on a simple question: When two siblings are both affected with a disease, do they share alleles at particular genetic markers more frequently than would be expected by chance? Fig. 24.1 illustrates this basic approach. ASP linkage analysis has resulted in a few successes, most notably the identification of the NOD2 gene as a major risk factor for Crohn's disease.6, Furthermore, the presence of a linkage peak (LOD score > 3.5) on chromosome 2q in rheumatoid arthritis (RA) ASPs8 led to the identification of the STAT4

gene as a risk gene for RA, as well as systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). Thus, although challenging to carry out, linkage can occasionally be applied successfully to complex diseases.

### Population Association Studies

The most common way to establish whether a genetic variant (allele) confers risk for a disease is by performing a case-control study. In this type of study, subjects are initially identified according to whether they have the disease, and individuals without the disease are the controls. The risk of disease in those carrying a particular variant is described using the odds ratio (OR). An OR of 1 indicates that the genetic factor confers no risk for the disease. An OR less than 1 suggests that the genetic factor under study is negatively associated with the disease (i.e., it is protective). Traditionally, ORs are reported with respect to the less common genetic variant (minor allele), so an OR of less than 1 indicates that the major allele confers risk. Sometimes, however, the OR

with respect to the risk variant (whether the major or minor allele) is reported, and, in that case, the ORs are always greater than 1 if the result is statistically significant.

One of the potential drawbacks of case-control association studies is that spurious association can occur if the cases and controls are not sampled from the same population (population stratification). An example would be if all disease cases were samples from a Scottish population and all controls were from a Spanish population. The gene variant conferring red hair color is more prevalent in the Scottish population with or without disease. Therefore the red hair color gene would be associated with disease in such a study, but the association would be a false positive. In reality, if information is available on a large number of genetic variants across the genome or for variants known to differ across populations of different ancestry, methods exist to correct for population stratification in the analysis, but the best solution is to consider this potential confounder in the study design. While family-based association designs, such as the transmission disequilibrium test (TDT)10 (which calculates any deviation from the 50:50 random chance of passing a specific allele from a parent to an affected child [Fig. 24.2]), use parental control genotypes to eliminate the risk of population stratification, it is generally more expensive to collect and genotype trio families, so most studies use a casecontrol approach.

### Choice of Genetic Marker to Test

There has been an explosion in new genetic knowledge, and a number of initiatives have sequenced individuals of various ancestries to create a reference catalog of the common sequence variation across the human genome (e.g., https://www.genomicsengland.co.uk/initiatives/100000-genomes-project). The most common form of variation across the genome is where a single base change occurs, for example, from adenine (A) to guanine (G) in the DNA sequence. Such changes are called single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), and there are now more than 900 million variants referenced for Homo sapiens in dbSNP, an online SNP reference database (www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/SNP/).

In addition to SNPs, there are tens of thousands of variable numbers of tandem repeat (VNTR) variants and insertions and deletions 11 providing other sources of genetic variation that can be associated with human disease. For example, Huntington's disease is caused by variable number of repeats of a CAG triplet within the Huntingtin gene. Smaller insertions and deletions are also frequent, and the number of these genetic variants will grow substantially as more human genomes are fully sequenced.

### Candidate Gene Versus Genome-wide Association Studies

The first wave of genetic studies of complex diseases focused on candidate gene studies. The candidate genes investigated were selected based on biologic plausibility, because they were associated with another disease or based on animal model studies. However, the prior probability of detecting association to one gene among the at least 30,000 known protein-coding genes is very low, especially when only one or a few markers were tested at the genomic locus, as was generally the case in such candidate gene studies. Furthermore, few studies tested large sample sizes of cases and controls and so were underpowered to generate robust findings. Nonetheless, several genes of large effect sizes were consistently detected, notably the HLA and PTPN22 genetic associations observed with many complex diseases.

The acceleration in the knowledge of genetic variation across the genome, coupled with sweeping technologic advances, has meant that it is now possible to test SNP markers spanning the genome for evidence of association, so-called genome-wide association studies (GWASs). The era of SNP-based GWASs began in earnest in 2005, when the complement regulatory protein Factor H was identified as a significant risk factor for age-related macular degeneration. A major advance was made in 2007 with the realization that, for most complex diseases, effect sizes of individual variants on disease would be modest; hence large sample sizes would be required to robustly detect association.
