### Conclusions

Pain is a personal experience, caused and influenced by many factors. The associations found between pain severity and any single causal factor are often weak. Joint radiographs cannot indicate synovitis. MRI cannot measure peripheral sensitization. CNS processing modulates nociceptive signaling, often irrespective of pathology in the musculoskeletal system. This complexity p rovides opportunities for managing pain through multiple treatment modalities but poses challenges when assessing for the best interventions to be offered to the individual at the right time. Peripheral nociceptive mechanisms are key to understanding pain in rheumatic diseases. Blocking peripheral neurotransmission, for example using local anesthetics or neuroablation techniques or by suppressing inflammation or restructuring a deranged joint, each might relieve pain. Pain, however, has a homeostatic and protective function, and complete analgesia can itself limit normal protective reflexes and initiate joint damage. Furthermore, neurons have important efferent functions, and molecules involved in nociception might also have other important biologic functions on non-neuronal cells. Understanding the mechanisms of pain in peripheral tissues should pave the way to novel treatments that can more effectively and safely relieve musculoskeletal pain. At the very least, contemporary understanding can help explain the mysteries of pain and help those who suffer from rheumatic diseases to live fulfilling lives.

# Clinical Research Methods in the Rheumatic Diseases

### KEY POINTS

The first critical decision to make is clarifying the research question. The research methods, including choosing data sources, study design, analytic considerations, potential bias, and interpretation, follow.

Real-world data sources such as electronic health records, administrative claims data, registries, vital status data, patientreported data, wearables, and other digital data are growing and have unique methodologic considerations.

Prevalence is the only appropriate measure of occurrence or disease burden in cross-sectional data and is important for priority setting and resource allocation in public health. Given that prevalence is a function of getting the disease (incidence) and living with and surviving it, changes in prevalence do not necessarily reflect changes in incidence.

Incidence reflects new cases or events among a population at risk for the outcome being studied. Measures of association such as ratio and difference measures can be calculated from incidence and prevalence, as well as other measures such as odds and rates.

Study designs include not only the more familiar designs of crosssectional, cohort, and case control but many other alternatives including case-only designs to study gene—environment interaction, case-crossover for acute triggers, and many types of natural experiments. With the growing pool of data sources, some less traditional designs may be a good alternative.

Case-control studies sample on the basis of whether individuals have the outcome of interest (case) or not (control) and then examine the odds of exposure among cases versus controls (the odds ratio). Controls can be sampled in different ways, but importantly their sampling should not be related to the exposure of interest as the controls.

Randomized controlled trials are usually viewed as the gold standard for many research questions. There are several types of randomized controlled trials but note that there are some constraints (e.g., cost, ethics) and that even these designs may be subject to some of the same concerns for bias as observational studies.

Confounding, selection bias, and measurement error/misclassification are threats to internal validity. These can arise in many different study designs, including in prospective cohort studies. Directed acyclic graphs are a powerful visual tool that can facilitate identification of these biases and inform design and analytic choices.

### Data Sources for Research in Rheumatology

The ability to produce, store, and leverage large amounts of health data has been facilitated by the rapidly increasing use of computers, mobile devices, wearables, and other biosensors in health care settings. These data sources are useful for research in rheumatology to answer clinical and research questions, in addition to aiding patient care. Novel study designs and analytical capabilities (including artificial intelligence) have also been developed to analyze and apply the large volumes of multidimensional data generated by these devices. Real-world data (RWD) in medicine refers to data generated from patient health status and/or during routine health care delivery. Here, we highlight RWD sources such as electronic health records, administrative claims data, registries, vital status data, patient-reported data, wearables, and other digital data used for generating real-world evidence in rheumatology.

### Electronic Health Records

Electronic health records (EHRs) have evolved beyond their primary purpose of scheduling and billing patient encounters to serve a comprehensive range of uses, including clinical documentation and treatment planning, communication among health care team members and patients, patient safety and quality improvement, and clinical research and disease-surveillance activities.2, One key obstacle in using EHRs in understanding the evolution of chronic diseases such as cancers and rheumatic diseases are the gaps in the natural history before and after diagnosis, particularly in open health care systems or referral/specialty care settings. EHRs offer multidimensional data including demographics, diagnostic codes, vital signs, medications, procedures, symptomatology, laboratory tests, clinic notes, and comorbidities. Case ascertainment or combinations of these data elements can be created using computational algorithms, phenotypes, or cohorts of rheumatic diseases, with varying degrees of accuracy.

Due to the rarity of autoimmune rheumatic diseases such as systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and the nonspecificity of the initial symptoms of these diseases, creating inception cohorts from EHR may be often prohibitive. In recent years, novel findings such as the association between the Epstein-Barr virus and multiple sclerosis could only have been achieved through linkages of EHR data to biorepositories that collect longitudinal specimens

from patients across multiple years.5, In the future, machine learning techniques will likely explore disease progression and etiologies (e.g., discovering novel comorbidities), risk predictors, and prognostic factors for rheumatic diseases using routinely collected EHR data.

### Administrative Claims Databases

Administrative claims databases (ACDs) are obtained from reimbursement information or payment of bills and consist of some patient demographics, clinician billing claims, hospital discharge summaries, procedures, and prescription drug records. In general, data elements in ACDs necessary to establish payment/reimbursement tend to be more complete and have less missingness than other information reported on a claim. In the United States four major sources of administrative claims data for clinical research in rheumatology are IBM MarketScan Research Databases, Optum Insight, Medicaid, and Medicare.10-13 The strengths of ACDs such as Medicare lies in their volume, generalizability, long follow-up periods, and the possibility to link to other data sources including census, registries, surveys, and vital records. However, ACDs tied to private insurance may have shorter follow-up periods. Many ACDs may be population based (e.g., an estimated 98% of adults 65 years and older are enrolled in Medicare), making Medicare data one of the richest sources of clinical data in the United States.14,

There are a few broad limitations of ACDs. Like EHR data, case ascertainment requires algorithms, the record of care received may be inconsistent, and details on the duration, subtypes, and severity of disease may be limited. Unlike EHR, measures such as blood pressure, body mass index, and smoking status are not present. In addition, the timing of events may be difficult to ascertain, especially in hospitalization data where time from admission to a given event or timestamps for dates of service may not be found. The generalizability in ACDs depends on the specific data, the research question, and the study design. For example, employment-based or privatized systems such as MarketScan and Optum Insight may have limited generalizability and individuals may cycle in and out of enrollment. Follow-up in an ACD may be fragmented and not linkable. Nonetheless, ACDs are useful for treatment comparison studies, pharmacoepidemiology, health disparities research, and cost-effective studies in rheumatology. .16-19

### Registry Data

One common type of disease registry contains secondary data for tracking clinical care and outcomes of a defined patient population. Recently disease registry functionality is available as an add-on to many EHR systems. The Rheumatology Informatics System for Effectiveness (RISE) was developed by the American College of Rheumatology to help clinicians and researchers optimize patient outcomes. RISE is an EHR-enabled rheumatology registry in the United States, with more than 1000 clinicians and 2.4 million patients. Another registry, the Arthritis, Rheumatism and Aging Medical Information System (ARAMIS), is a National Institutes of Health (NIH)funded registry to collect medical records and patient reported outcomes for over 14,000 patients with rheumatoid arthritis and osteoarthritis. Case ascertainment in RISE and ARAMIS is based on classification criteria or clinician diagnosis, often requiring no validation. Disease subtypes are often well defined in registries; however, comparators are not available. Patient-reported outcomes and disease-specific

clinical data may be available in registries, including disease activity measures. Laboratory, imaging, procedures, and treatment data may also be available but might be restricted to disease-related measures or those captured within the rheumatology visit.

Other valuable registry data exist in several countries or regions, where population-based data are collected for a range of purposes. For example, several Scandinavian countries and Canada have registries that collect individual-level data for a myriad of resources including outpatient care visits, hospitalizations, births, pharmacy prescriptions, and disease-specific registries focusing on stroke and .23-25 In many of these regions, individual data can be linked cancer. by a third party to develop a population-based registry data linkage that can be used to answer a myriad of research questions. There are also registries that serve specific purposes such as postapproval surveillance of biologics and COVID-19 sequelae. 26-28

### Vital Statistics Data

In surveillance epidemiology, vital records are important for describing the health profiles of a population, priority setting for policymaking, and evaluating the impact of health interventions. Vital records data (birth and death records) can be linked to EHR, ACD, and registry data for epidemiologic inference. Death does not often result from a single cause. When death records are used without linkage to other sources, multiple causes of death data can be used to characterize important disease interactions and permits a wide-ranging approach to mortality surveillance. Multiple causes of death data can be used to explore associations between different diseases leading to death, thus giving some context to the overall morbidity process. For example, SLE is associated with several conditions resulting in an increased risk of death, mainly renal failure, cardiovascular disease, and infections. Care must be taken in using vital records alone as they may underestimate the burden of disease.

### Survey Data

In the United States, several national surveys collect information on the health and nutritional status of adults and children. The National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey annually collects interviews, physical examinations, and laboratory tests. 31, The National Health Interview Survey (NHIS) is an annual crosssectional household health survey using geographically clustered sampling techniques to select the sample of households for the 33, The sample is designed to collect data that are repsurvey. resentative of the U.S. civilian, noninstitutionalized population. The Medical Expenditures Panel Survey comprises half of the households sampled in each year's NHIS and provides nationally representative data on health care use, expenditures, health insurance coverage, and source of payment for medical care for the sample individual and household members. One disadvantage of survey data is the cross-sectional nature of the data collection, which precludes any causal interpretation.

### Wearables

The opportunities to capture sensor data continuously and passively in real-world settings with minimal burden are growing due to the ubiquity of mobile devices, wearable and other biosensors. Over 80% of adults in the United States own a smartphone; smartwatches and wearable activity trackers are also widely used to record physical activity, sleep, and physiology.36, For patients

with rheumatic diseases, passive and continuous collection of digital biomarkers can facilitate real-time monitoring between medical visits, enabling the extension of coverage and reach of 36, Digital biomarkers may reflect significant fluctuations care. in functional status, symptomatology, quality of life, and risk of adverse outcomes.36, Although the use of digital biomarkers for clinical research in rheumatology is still in its nascent stages, there is great potential to measure disease progression to advance the understanding of how rheumatic diseases and their treatment affect patients and improve outcomes.

### Measures of Occurrence

Most clinical research is concerned with the ability to quantify the occurrence of disease (or any other clinical outcome) in populations. There are four entities that need to be defined for measures of occurrence to be valid. First, in the previous sections, we discussed the contexts or settings. Second, we need to define what is meant by the case (e.g., a patient or individual in the context who has the condition or undergoes an event of interest such as pregnancy or death). Cases often compose the numerator. In epidemiologic inquiry, a case definition for a condition may not be the same as the clinical definition and may change depending on the context and research question. For example, a case definition for SLE in an EHR or ACD may include diagnostic codes and specific medications and a requirement for one or more diagnoses codes to be given in specialty care or in-patient settings. In a disease registry, case definition is often more aligned with clinical definition including classification criteria and well-defined subtypes. In survey data, case definitions are almost always self-reported. Third, there needs to be a clear definition of the denominator or the population where the cases originated. (The denominator is also called the population at risk.) Finally, the time under study needs to be clearly defined. In this section, we discuss prevalence and incidence, the two major measures of occurrence, with emphasis on how they relate to the clinical context, case definition, the population at risk and the time under study.

### Prevalence

Point prevalence is defined as the proportion of cases (new and old) in a population in a single time point and period prevalence is measured over some time. There might be some difficulty in defining the prevalence of rheumatic diseases. The general assumption in registries is that once an individual is diagnosed with a chronic disease, they represent a prevalent case until death. In a study using an ACD, this may be a problem when case definitions occur during a time of remission where if a patient has no doctor visits and no medication use, this case might be missed. Prevalence is the only appropriate measure of occurrence or disease burden in cross-sectional data. These data are important for priority setting and resource allocation in public health. If we see an association between a prevalent outcome and exposure, it may be that the exposure is associated with incident disease, the exposure is associated with survival with disease, or the disease is associated with the exposure.

### Incidence

Incidence is defined as the occurrence (and identification) of new cases in a population. Incident cases are defined as individuals who progress from nondisease—or from one disease state to

another—and are identified in a specific time interval. For example, in a study of incident cases of rheumatoid arthritis (RA) in 2022, only those who developed RA in that year are considered incident cases. When attempting to define the risk factors or antecedents of a disease or answer causal questions, prevalence is less useful than incidence (see the section on selection bias). Incidence may be difficult to estimate in EHR and ACD for different reasons. They are both right and left censored because the observation period starts when a patient is enrolled in a health plan or first seen in a health system and stops when the patient leaves the plan or health system. In EHR, the observation period is difficult to determine, while in claims data, the plan enrollment period defines who is under observation during a specific time interval. For these reasons, prevalence and incidence estimates from an EHR and ACD may not always align and pose significant consequences for clinical research.

### Measures of Association

Generally, there are three major ways to measure occurrence of an event or outcome (e.g., incidence, and to some extent, prevalence): odds, risk, and rate. Here, we present ways to measure associations based on these three entities.

### Risk-Based Measures

Risk is defined as the number of new cases of disease occurring in a defined population over a given time interval divided by the number of disease-free individuals in that population at the beginning of the time interval. Risk can also be conceptualized as the average probability that an individual will develop an outcome/ event during a time interval. It is important to specify the time under study when measuring risk because the value increases with longer follow-up duration. In clinical research, the survival experience of patients with a disease is often measured using risk. Thus the risk ratio, or relative risk, is calculated as a ratio comparing the survival experience of two groups on the multiplicative scale. The risk difference is calculated as an absolute difference comparing the survival experience of two groups on the additive scale (i.e., risk of the outcome among exposed minus the risk of the outcome among the unexposed).

### Odds-Based Measures

The odds of an event/outcome is the number of (new) cases of disease arising in a defined population divided in a given time interval divided by the number of individuals who remain disease-free during that time interval. Odds can also be defined as the ratio of the probability of getting a disease to the probability of not getting the disease during a time frame. The odds ratio is calculated as a ratio comparing the odds of a given event between two groups on the multiplicative scale.

### Rate-Based Measures

The assumption during the calculation of odds and risk is that there is complete follow-up for all individuals during the time interval under study. However, this scenario almost never occurs in clinical research, as most study populations are dynamic, and most individuals will not be followed up for the same length of time. For example, some individuals may only be observed after the study begins, and some may be lost to follow-up. Neither risk

nor odds takes the time under observation into consideration. In calculating rates, the numerator is the same as risk; however, the denominator is the total amount of person-time-at-risk contributed by individuals, measured in days, months, or years. Rate, or incidence rate, is also called the incidence density. The rate ratio is calculated as a ratio comparing the incidence rates of two groups on the multiplicative scale (i.e., rate in exposed divided by rate in the unexposed). The rate difference is calculated as an absolute difference comparing the incidence rates of two groups on the additive scale.

### Study Designs

### Observational Studies

Observational studies are defined as studies in which the researcher does not control the exposure or intervention, often in contrast to experimental studies. We describe the better-known observational designs (Fig. 31.1) and variations on these including case-only designs and briefly mention natural experiments.

Ecological studies use aggregate-level or grouped data to describe an association between two factors, often reported using a scatter plot to show how one factor varies by a second factor. These associations are observed at the population or group level and may not hold up when we look at the same association within individuals within a group. In other words, if you find the counties that sell more chocolate have higher rates of gout, this doesn't necessarily mean that the people consuming the chocolate are the ones being diagnosed with gout. This cross-level inference is often referred to as an ecological fallacy. While this is an important consideration when interpreting ecological study results, this design can be powerful when considering hypothesis-generating work.

If we think of ecological studies as snapshots of aggregated data, cross-sectional studies provide snapshots of individual-level data at one time point. Surveys are the most common way to collect cross-sectional data. In these designs, exposure and outcome are often measured at the same time, along with data on additional factors that may be important confounders or other study variables. These types of studies tend to capture prevalent outcomes or disease, in contrast to incident outcomes (see "Measures of Occurrence" section). Additionally, because of the emphasis on preva- 25 lence, temporality may be a problem and reverse causation should be considered (e.g., disease → exposure).

For many other study designs, some element of temporality is built into the data and data collection. Frequently studies are referred to as either prospective or retrospective, and how different researchers define these terms varies. In thinking about how bias may be introduced and inference affected, we define these terms as follows focusing on the collection of the data. Prospective studies are ones where the exposures are measured before the outcomes have occurred. Retrospective studies have exposure measurement/collection after the outcomes have occurred. This is helpful because the concern with retrospective designs is often that having information about the outcome influences the accuracy (and misclassification) of the exposure (e.g., recall bias). If the exposure data are measured before the outcome occurs, then it is unlikely that knowledge of the outcome by the investigator or the patient will lead to erroneous exposure data. When thinking about temporality and study design this way, one can conceive of prospective case-control studies, particularly if they are nested case-control studies (see below and Fig. 31.1).

Cohort studies are often the simplest transition from experimental studies, except that the exposure is not assigned by the investigator, unlike in a trial. A group of individuals is defined by some membership-defining factor (e.g., people with Sjögren's syndrome receiving care in 2005 in a specific clinic; individuals enrolled in a specific health insurance plan; all adults in a specific county). Their exposure status (which can be defined in a variety of ways: yes/no, quantity, duration, categorical variable) is identified, and their outcome status is also identified. Although the study doesn't have to be conducted in a longitudinal fashion where the investigator waits for the outcome to occur, there is time that has passed between the exposure and the outcome. For example, in a cohort study in an ACD, investigators could identify all individuals with psoriasis with a specific health plan using an established International Classification of Diseases code algorithm combined with other data to examine whether exposure increases the risk of developing psoriatic arthritis. Put simply, we want to estimate the effect of an exposure on the occurrence of a particular outcome during some period of observation. For rare outcomes the number of individuals in a cohort study will need to be large and the study period long. If this is not done using secondary data, this can be costly. However, one big benefit to the cohort design is that you can follow individuals in the study population for a range of outcomes, so these can be collected and accrued over time and yield data to answer a range of questions.

Cohorts may be described as closed versus open. In the closed cobort, once individuals satisfy the membership-defining criteria to be in the cohort, they are in it (e.g., graduating class of 2022) and followed over time. In an open cohort, individuals may come in and out of the cohort for a variety of reasons, the study population is dynamic and can change over time, such as with migration. Because this design is specifically designed to consider an incident outcome, individuals in the study population must be at risk for the outcome. If someone could never have the outcome that is being studied, they should be excluded because regardless of what their exposure is, they cannot get the outcome (i.e., they are not at risk for the outcome).

A word of caution: When exposure is a disease (e.g., studying whether patients with sarcoidosis have a higher risk of myocardial infarction), people sometimes refer to those with and without sarcoidosis as cases and controls, respectively. This often leads to incorrectly assuming that the study is a case-control design when actually it is a cohort study. As described in more detail below, if a study like this were to be conducted as a case-control study, then

individuals would be selected on the basis of whether they have an myocardial infarction or not (cases and controls), and then their history of sarcoidosis would be assessed as exposure.

The objective with a case-control study is similar, that is, estimating the effect of an exposure on some outcome; however, this design samples the study population differently. Individuals are selected based on whether they have (or have had) the outcome (cases) or not (controls) and their exposure information is collected. Although this may sound like a retrospective study, casecontrol studies do not have to be retrospective. Exposure can be assessed in a variety of ways, ranging from self-report to documentation, and then the odds of exposure in the cases is compared with the odds of exposure in the controls. Often it is helpful to think about a case-control being derived from a larger (potentially hypothetical) underlying cohort. When this hypothetical cohort is real, we refer to this as a nested case-control study.

Cases may be identified in a variety of ways, including in registers, using surveillance work, by self-report, or captured in administrative data. Controls, however, present a larger challenge. Their purpose is to provide a valid estimate of the distribution of exposure in the underlying base from which the cases arise. Therefore control selection should generally be independent of exposure. There are two primary sampling approaches: cumulative incidence sampling and risk set sampling. Cumulative incidence sampling selects controls from the population at the end of followup from the subset of individuals left at risk for the outcome. This may be more feasible depending on what data are available, but an important caveat to consider is that the group of individuals left at the end of the study period without having the event may be systematically different from the full "at-risk" population. For instance, those who are lost to follow-up or drop out are not eligible to be sampled as controls, and the attrition of the population may be informative. Risk set sampling (also called incidence density sampling) samples controls when a case becomes a case and, as such, requires longitudinal data where person-time can be enumerated. Because controls are sampled as a function of persontime, or sometimes described as matched on time, the probability of being selected is proportional to an individual's person-time in the study base. Additionally, in risk set sampling an individual who is selected as a control at one time can later be chosen as a control again for another case, as well as go on to become a case in the future (see Fig. 31.2).

Aside from the logistics of how controls are sampled, there are also considerations about the source of the controls. When cases and controls are sampled from a pre-existing cohort (i.e., a nested case-control study), this is more straightforward. Outside of this

some sources may include population registers, neighborhoods, friends and family, and health care settings such as hospitals. Keeping in mind two questions is often helpful to think about the controls: Would these individuals be captured as a case in my study if they were to develop the outcome of interest? and Is the sampling of these controls independent of exposure? One of the most common criticisms of case-control studies is that there may be recall bias (e.g., differential misclassification of exposure, see the section on information bias).

Because individuals are sampled on the basis of having the outcome or not, the case-control design is appropriate for studying one outcome, although data on multiple exposures can be assessed (although this may get complicated quickly because sampling of controls should be independent of exposure, and the more exposures considered, the more challenging it is to do this). When the outcome is rare, this design can be particularly efficient.

The case-cohort design can be thought of as another variant of a case-control study, but instead the controls (referred to as a subcohort) are randomly sampled at the start of follow-up from the entire study population. Everyone is followed up for the outcome, and the subcohort also has all of the exposure assessments. It is possible that individuals in the subcohort may go on to become cases, and different analytic approaches have been proposed to analyze these types of study designs. 42,

Some other, less commonly used designs, include a couple of case-only designs, such as those for studying gene—environment interactions and the case-crossover design. When conducting a case-only study to evaluate gene—environment interaction, investigators can estimate the association between environmental exposure and genotype but cannot assess the main effects of either the environmental exposure or the genotype. This approach assumes that these two are independent in the underlying source population and, by not including controls, are not subject to the concerns and corresponding biases and challenges of selecting controls. In a case-crossover study, each case serves as their own control, whereby for each case, different time periods are selected as control periods. This is a particularly useful design when studying potential triggers of acute events. The control periods can be selected a number of ways, and therefore correspond to different types of analysis. When using a pair-matched interval approach, a single time period is compared (perhaps the 24 hours before the onset of the event). It is also possible to use a multiple-intervals approach where several time periods are assessed before the onset of the event. Lastly, the usual frequency approach may gather data on patterns of exposure during a longer time period (the past month or past year).

Natural experiments often leverage unplanned events where some populations may be divided into exposed and unexposed subsets (or this could be based on the outcome). The 1854 Broad Street cholera outbreak in London, where the exposure to polluted water was not due to personal choice nor investigator control, is a classic example. When designing and analyzing natural experiments, there are several methodological approaches to choose from, some more familiar (like regression adjustment and propensity scores) and others more commonly seen in fields like economics (i.e., differences-in-differences and instrumental variables). A simple and intuitive approach may be comparing preand postmeasurements to examine how outcomes change before and after some intervention has been applied.

Differences-in-differences builds on this and compares whether there is a change in outcome among those who were newly exposed to some intervention with those who remain unexposed. Synthetic control designs identify and create a weighted comparator with similar trends where the intervention is not implemented to compare with a region where the intervention occurred.

### Clinical Trial Considerations

Clinical trial design and methodology warrants a separate in-depth discussion. Here we briefly touch on a few general principles and considerations. Often people first think of double-blinded randomized controlled trials, but this is just one type (with many subtypes). First, trials can be blinded or unblinded, meaning that the participant is or is not aware of the treatment to which they have been assigned. In the case of double-blinded, both the participant and the investigator are unaware of the treatment assignment. Second, trials can be randomized or not. In nonrandomized trials, participants or the investigators may assign or choose the treatment. In the setting of randomization, one of several randomization techniques can be used to randomly assign participants to one of the treatment arms, which theoretically should yield more comparable groups that do not systematically differ. As a result, there is less concern about potential bias due to confounding, for example.

Three types of trials are commonly seen in the literature, superiority, equivalence, and noninferiority, to examine how a treatment of interest compares to a control treatment (which may be placebo, standard of care, or something else). As their names imply, superiority trials assess whether the intervention or treatment of interest is better than the control; equivalence trials test whether the intervention or treatment is equivalent (i.e., neither better nor worse) than the control; and noninferiority trials assess whether the intervention is not worse than the specified control. How the null hypothesis is specified varies for each45 and, as described, answers different research questions. Considerations such as costs, drug availability, or side effects can influence why one approach may be chosen over another.

Clinical trials commonly compare at least two treatment arms. Defining the comparison (treatment intervention vs. control with two arms) is critical. Control arms often include either a placebo or standard of care. There is considerable discussion in the theory and ethics of trials about whether placebo-controlled trials are appropriate when there is an effective treatment available. Providing a placebo, in those settings, may be perceived as withholding treatment, and hence leads to important ethical discussions. Also, investigators must contend with whether it is valuable to know if something is better than nothing or if something is better than the current standard of care (such as methotrexate in

RA or allopurinol for gout), or another not-yet standard-of-care alternative. These critical discussions are outside the scope of this chapter but warrant careful consideration. Furthermore, many trials may allow for background standard-of-care treatment to continue, with some constraints. How this might influence the trial and what constraints to set around these needs to also be carefully considered so that poor response in one arm is not masked by background modification of corticosteroids, for example.

How individuals are identified and what is measured needs careful specification. Determining the study population—for example, what inclusion and exclusion criteria to employ, recruitment, and representativeness—is critical. Classification criteria for a range of rheumatologic conditions are frequently incorporated into the inclusion criteria. Contraindications of either treatment, stability of current disease, history of specific manifestation, concomitant medications, and more must all be factored into these decisions. They influence the risks, the variability of your study population, and your generalizability; this includes sufficient recruitment of participants of different sexes, ages, and race/ethnicities, for example. We and others have shown that the trial populations for a number of rheumatologic diseases do not reflect the demographic composition of the patient population.46, Outcomes measures in clinical trials may vary, but there is a strong preference (and in many cases, requirements) for validated endpoint measures (see Chapter 33) such as disease activity indices, ACR response measures, or serologic measures. Additional outcomes, sometimes considered as secondary, include patient-reported outcomes such as the NIH Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System (PROMIS®; www.nihpromis.org), which measures a range of health-related quality-of-life domains such as physical functioning, sleep, depression, and self-efficacy. 48,49

### Common Sources of Bias

### Selection Bias

Selection bias is simply defined as when the study population that one is analyzing and drawing inferences on does not represent the population one intended to analyze. Although there are some aspects of selection bias that people are more familiar with (e.g., healthy worker effect), there are other, less commonly known sources. Individuals who are healthier (or sicker, depending on the study) may be more likely to be studied or volunteer to participate. It is important to note that selection bias isn't only about how people are selected or included in the study but also can be a consequence of how they are retained (or even survive).

In cross-sectional studies nonparticipation among some subgroups may lead to selection bias. Also, prevalence/incidence bias, as discussed briefly, can result in selection bias. Given that being captured as a prevalent case of some disease is a function of getting the disease and living with and surviving it, one important consideration is incidence/prevalence bias. For example, if you find that exposure is associated with a higher prevalence of outcome it might be that this exposure is associated with getting the disease or being able to live with and survive the disease. In cohort studies, nonresponse and potentially unrepresentative groups can yield selection bias and attrition of the population. One well-known type of this bias is called the depletion of susceptibles, whereby individuals who are most susceptible to specific outcomes may be lost early. In case-control studies, both case and control selection can lead to selection bias. One common source of this bias in control selection is when conducting a matched case-control study where

it is common to match on something believed to be a confounder. We know that confounders are associated with the outcome and with the exposure and, as a result, when matching on a confounder, controls are not selected independent of the exposure. In essence, controls are selected with the same value of the matching factor/confounder as the case, and that also means that they are more similar with respect to the exposure of interest. This selection bias in control selection in the matching leads to bias toward the null because the cases and controls are forced to be more similar with respect to the exposure. If analyzed crudely, a bias toward the null will occur; however, stratifying by the matching factors will counter this bias.

A paper was published using directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) to illustrate a common structural relationship between factors that yield selection bias. In short, what the authors showed was that selection bias can also arise in the setting of collider stratification bias, where the collider is a consequence of exposure. A similar underlying DAG structure was common across several types of selection bias. For further reading, we recommend the following reference: 50. We provide a brief primer on DAGs later in the chapter (Fig. 31.3).

### Information Bias

Information bias is another frequently discussed source of bias, which many refer to when discussing either measurement error or misclassification. Measurement error is frequently used when discussing a continuous variable, and misclassification is used to refer to information bias in the setting of a categorical or binary variable. This type of error can occur at any phase of a study ranging from how an instrument is designed, poor execution of study

Furthermore, no variable is exempt from being at risk for this type of bias, whether it's the exposure, outcome, confounder, or another variable of interest. When conducting research, it is important to consider what sources of data may be available for different factors to strive to minimize misclassification and measurement error.

When discussing information bias, it is common to refer to it as differential or nondifferential. Differential, or systematic, misclassification means that the way in which the error is arising is not random and depends on some other parameter. A common type of differential misclassification that is discussed in the literature is recall bias, where the reliability of an individual's report of their exposure, for example, is related to whether they have the outcome.

Differential misclassification can bias in either direction (toward or away from the null). Nondifferential misclassification means that the measurement or classification is not related to other variables. Many people state that nondifferential misclassification of exposure or outcome biases associations toward the null, but it is important to note that this is not always true, particularly when you have nonbinary factors being studied. Numerous analytic techniques exist to address and attempt to correct analyses for misclassification using data from validation studies. Some advanced methods may leverage probabilistic bias analysis (discussed next).

Randomization tends to balance the characteristics of participants equally among the intervention arms, making the exposed and unexposed more similar and reducing potential bias produced by confounding. However, most clinical research is conducted using observational data owing to issues of feasibility and ethics, and thus there will be confounding, or a mixing of effects other than the effect we wish to study, among other biases. Therefore, it is important to assess for and manage confounding in observational data to isolate the effectiveness or harmful effects of interventions, behaviors, practices, or conditions.

Confounding is a source of bias in nonrandomized studies that distorts the perceived association between the exposure or predictor of interest and the outcome or disease due to the presence or absence of a third factor. To be considered a confounder, the variable must be independently associated with the exposure, a risk factor for the outcome, and cannot be on the causal pathway between the exposure and outcome (i.e., the variable cannot be an intermediate or an effect of the exposure).52,53

### Types of Confounding

Measured confounders should be identified a priori and measured in the collected data. If the measured confounder is improperly measured or not entirely representative of the confounding variable, then this will result in residual confounding. Most studies will have residual confounding because it is highly unlikely that variables will be perfectly measured. When the observed effect (i.e., the relative risk is close to 1, a null effect) is weak, residual confounding is most problematic as it may obscure an association or create a spurious association. Unmeasured confounding results from variables that are not measured, either because of feasibility issues in collecting the data ("known unknown") or knowledge gaps giving way to unknown confounders ("unknown unknown"). Unlike measured variables, we cannot adjust for unmeasured variables, although some approaches for addressing unmeasured confounding exist. It is common to have unmeasured confounding in studies that employ medical claims data because these data were collected for billing purposes initially and not for clinical research. This is particularly true for modifiable behavior variables such as smoking, alcohol consumption, or diet or variables capturing facets of a disease such as disease activity, severity, or particular phenotypes. Observational studies investigating the effect of therapeutics are prone to channeling bias, which occurs when physicians preferentially prescribe a treatment based on the patient's prognosis or patients of particular baseline characteristics opt to take a medication. In other words, there is "channeling" of interventions toward patients with similar underlying characteristics, such as patients with more advanced disease or shared comorbidities. Confounding by indication is a type of channeling bias that occurs when the indication for the intervention is associated with the outcome. Thus it is difficult to isolate the causal effect of an intervention because it becomes unclear what the effect of the intervention is on the outcome versus the effect of the indication on the outcome. For example, a late-entry drug is more likely to be prescribed to patients with intractable disease who have already tried other regimens; in turn, these patients have more severe disease and are therefore at higher risk for developing the outcome.

Patients with RA who have higher levels of disease activity and uncontrolled disease and/or high inflammation will be more likely to get started on tumor necrosis factor inhibitor (TNFi) therapy, which reduces inflammation. 59,60I Disease activity is a confounder

and represents an indication for which therapy is initiated (Fig. 31.4).

### Assessing for Confounding

Confounding may be present if the association of a treatment or exposure with an outcome is due to the effect of other factors on the outcome. The effect of confounding may distort the association and result in an overor underestimation of the causal effect. Therefore it is important when investigating a research question to establish plausibility for the causal association between the predictor(s) of interest and the outcome (e.g., Bradford-Hill criteria). In epidemiologic practice, identifying confounders relies on subject-matter expertise and checking to see if the definition of a confounder is met (or identifying a common cause in a DAG).

We describe some common approaches that are used; however, we caution individuals to consider selecting confounding variables a priori informed by subject-matter knowledge and using a DAG. This is because some other types of bias or factors in the data may lead to changes in the estimate that are unrelated to confounding (and may introduce bias). Comparisons of these approaches have been discussed in depth elsewhere.

Some statistical approaches that are used to determine whether there may be confounding rely on comparing adjusted and unadjusted estimates. The adjusted estimates of the association can be from a multivariable adjusted model or, if we stratify on levels of confounder variables, we could calculate a summary measure pooling the stratum-specific measures of association; this is another type of adjusted effect measure. The Cochran Mantel Haenszel procedure is one of the ways in which this summary measure may be obtained. While there is no statistical test for confounding, the rule of thumb is that a change-in-estimate or magnitude of confounding greater than or equal to 10% in crude effect measure compared with adjusted effect measure is indicative of confounding. As another example, comparing crude and adjusted effect measures from a study on serious infection risk after 1 year for patients with RA treated with rituximab or with a second TNFi, the adjusted hazard ratio (HR) versus the crude or unadjusted HR, shows little difference. However, we would still report the adjusted values since these confounders were specified a priori and on base knowledge.

Some rely on statistical methods such as automatic selection procedures like stepwise selection or regression, which will add or remove variables based on an improvement of fit that is statistically significant.62, These approaches may cultivate a set of explanatory variables that satisfy some statistical criteria, but these

are not necessarily confounders; moreover, this method is mired by biased estimates.

### Dealing With Confounding

Whether we have measured or unmeasured confounding (admittedly more challenging), there are various ways to limit or remove confounding at the design and analysis stage of a study.

Randomization is an aspect of design that attempts to minimize confounding through balancing confounders among the treatment and control group in a randomized control trial. Using blocked randomization, we can use the measured baseline characteristics of participants to block or group by particular characteristics to estimate a subgroup effect while randomizing at this level to control for confounding.

We can limit the confounding effect of measured variables in observational studies at the design stage through the use of restriction/specification or matching. Restriction limits the study to patients in some strata of the confounder, such as limiting a study to women or a specific age group. Restriction is generally limited to few variables, as a lot of restriction results in smaller sample size and consequently reduces power.51, Individuals can be sampled into a study population by matching on potential prespecified confounders. For example, cases that are age-matched to controls eliminate or reduce the effect of age on estimating the causal effect.51, Commonly, frequency matching, where multiple individuals are matched to one individual, is employed to preserve power. If matching is incomplete, this can lead to bias.

In the analysis phase, confounding can be dealt with through means of stratification, propensity scores, multivariable adjustment, instrumental variable(s), marginal structural models, or sensitivity analyses. Most commonly, analyses will either be stratified by the confounder or include the confounder(s) in multivariable adjusted regression models. Propensity scores, which are calculated using logistic regression to estimate how likely each individual is to be exposed based on the distribution of their baseline characteristics (suspected confounders) or prior information,51 can be incorporated a number of ways: models, matching, stratification, and weighting. Propensity score methods are useful for tackling bias from confounding by indication because they may control for characteristics related to disease activity, which confound the association between use of a therapy and disease outcome. A variety of studies parsing the effects of therapy in patients with rheumatic diseases have employed propensity score methods,70,71 and a review by one group72 enumerates the various applications of propensity score methods for rare diseases such as systemic sclerosis. Propensity scores may balance the measured covariates, but there is no guarantee that they will balance unmeasured or unadjusted factors (although they may to some extent depending on the correlation between the measured and unmeasured factors).51,

Marginal structural models are useful in longitudinal data as they can address time-varying confounders through use of inverse probability weighting methods, such as the time-varying use of anti-TNF treatment among patients with RA as shown in Fig. 31.4. Inverse probability of treatment weights (IPTW) are closely related to propensity scores, but instead of estimating how likely each individual is made known to the exposure of interest, IPTW are based on an estimate of how likely each individual is to be exposed to the exposure that they had. Although little discussed here, these types of methods are important to estimate associations in the presence of time-varying confounding where a confounder can also be an intermediate variable. Extending the simple confounding by indication DAG, one study used these methods to account for this complex confounding structure to estimate the

association between TNFi initiation in RA and infection. Disease activity and concomitant medications influence choice of medication, and whether medications are or are not initiated, disease activity (and possibly the need for additional therapeutics) changes. Over time this will influence the use of medication on the next visit, and so it goes. If disease activity and concomitant medications like corticosteroids are also associated with infection, then time-varying confounding arises. These types of models are no longer estimating the association between exposure and outcome on the basis of comparing the exposed to the unexposed, but instead use baseline characteristics, suspected confounders, and other factors to create a pseudostudy population where the model estimates what would have happened to the entire study population had they been exposed compared with what would have happened to the entire study population had they not been exposed (in other words, estimating the counterfactual).

With instrumental variable (IV) analysis the estimation of the exposure—outcome association shifts to studying the association between the instrument and the outcome. An IV, or instrument, is causally associated with the exposure, affects the outcome only through exposure, and is not associated with known or unknown confounders of the exposureoutcome association (Fig. 31.5). Through its effect on the exposure, it may be substituted for the study's main exposure (if the exposure is particularly difficult to capture) and achieve better control for confounding and result in less bias. Some instruments that you might be familiar with include policy or other ecologic parameters, randomized treatment assignment in a trial, or specific genotype in the setting of mendelian randomization. 78, Identifying an instrument can be challenging, and if a weak instrument is chosen then estimates may be biased.

Additional methods such as probabilistic bias analysis (PBA) can be used to address unmeasured confounding and imputation of incomplete data leading to missing data in a confounder.51, One study estimating the incidence of lung disease in patients with SLE employed PBA in a sensitivity analysis to account for potential unmeasured confounding by smoking 81 (Fig. 31.5).

Another tool, the application of a negative control, may be used to detect bias such as confounding. A negative control can be applied to the exposure or the outcome and, though more common in biologic sciences, it is gaining more attention in epidemiology. For example, when applying to an exposure, a negative control would be a variable that is not associated with the outcome of interest but may share common traits with the exposure, and thus it may be these shared traits that explain an apparent effect or lack of effect as opposed to the exposure alone. Sensitivity analyses can include quantifying the effect that a possible unmeasured confounder could have on the observed effect. The purpose is to investigate how sensitive the association between the exposure and outcome is to unmeasured confounding variables. Probabilistic bias analysis, already described briefly, is considered a type of sensitivity analysis that specifies parameters of bias and calculates the resulting adjusted effect measure associated with pre-specified assumed degrees of bias.51,84

### Effect Measure Modification, Interaction, and Heterogeneity

Effect modification and interaction are often used interchangeably, but the distinction is that effect modification represents asymmetry between the exposure and the effect modifier, meaning that the effect of one intervention or exposure varies across strata of the effect modifier. In contrast, interaction represents symmetry between the exposure and the third variable, meaning the two interventions or exposures have a joint effect in addition to a separate, individual effect on the outcome. As an example of biologic interaction, patients with RA that smoke tend to respond poorly to anti-TNF treatment, so it has been proposed that smoking may affect the bioavailability of anti-TNF treatment (i.e., the effect of smoking negatively interacts with the effect of the treatment). In contrast, sex may be an example of effect modification, where the effects of a drug may differ by sex.51, Unlike confounding, effect modification and interaction can be statistically measured. One of the ways for testing for effect modification is by way of the Breslow-day test for homogeneity, which assesses whether the differences in strata by a third variable are statistically different from each other. If effect modification is present, the appropriate way to display results is to stratify by the effect modifier.

### Surveillance and Screening

Public health surveillance, considered the cornerstone of public health, is the "...systematic, ongoing collection, management, analysis, and interpretation of data followed by the dissemination

of these data to public health programs to stimulate public health action."92 Since 2004, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has funded five population-based cohort studies of patients with SLE. The goal of the cohorts is to follow the natural and treated history of lupus. Each site uses similar active surveillance methods to estimate the incidence and prevalence of lupus. However, estimates of the burden of disease rely on accurate case definitions. In an EHR and ACD, case definitions or computational phenotypes for rheumatic diseases often combine diagnostic codes and prescriptions. One cannot study the effects of elements that comprise a particular phenotype. For example, if a rheumatic disease phenotype includes prescriptions, researchers may be limited in how they study the effect or trends of prescriptions using that phenotype. The gold standard used in case definitions is usually the judgment of clinicians based on the "synthesis of medical history details beyond. . .classification criteria. "94

Here, we describe measures used to determine which case definitions are most accurate in clinical research. These frequently arise in validation studies, which are important to ensure that we are capturing what we intend to capture when we define exposure, outcomes, or other factors of interest. Sensitivity refers to the proportion of people who truly have an identified outcome, whether it be due to a computational phenotype or self-report. For example, a computational phenotype with high sensitivity will have few false-negative results, thus fewer patients with the disease are missed. Specificity refers to the appropriate designation of a patient without the disease as negative. A computational phenotype with high specificity will have few false-positive results. The positive predictive value of a computational algorithm or test is the probability that a patient meeting the case definition or testing positive has the disease. The negative predictive value is the probability that a person who does not meet the case definition is disease-free. The goal is to identify a definition (whether it be a test, question, or computational algorithm) that provides the highest positive predictive value, highest sensitivity, and highest specificity to minimize false positives, exclude true negatives, and identify as many cases as possible.

### Conclusion

Epidemiology and clinical research methods offer a wide range of approaches to answer important clinical and public health questions. Identifying answerable research questions is the first important step, which dictates and informs a myriad of choices from appropriate design, type of data, outcome measures, anal-ysis, and interpretation. DAGs facilitate making assumptions more explicit and provide a visual tool to potential sources of bias, which can be used to consider both the design and analysis of data. Bias can arise from random and nonrandom sources, including how the study population is identified and retained over the study period, how factors are measured, what is miss-ing, and more. Many sophisticated analytic methods strive to address these problems, such as propensity scores, instrumen-tal variables, matching, and statistical adjustment, but some threats to validity can be effectively minimized in the design phase of a study as well. # Epidemiology and Impact of Rheumatic Diseases

### KEY POINTS

### Epidemiology of Arthritis and Other − Rheumatic Diseases

In public health surveillance, arthritis1 is defined as answering "yes" to the question, "Have you ever been told by a doctor or other

health professional that you have some form of arthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, gout, lupus, or fibromyalgia?" This standard question was designed in 2002 to incorporate key elements of the 1994 public health definition of arthritis developed by the National Arthritis Data Workgroup, which sought to capture conditions treated by rheumatologists and other health care providers. The primary focus of this chapter is on arthritis defined broadly, with a secondary focus on some of the individual rheumatic conditions including rheumatoid arthritis (RA), osteoarthritis (OA), lupus, and gout.

In the United States arthritis is a highly prevalent and widespread chronic condition impacting 58.5 million adults (24%) (Fig. 32.1).2, By 2040, it is projected to affect 78.4 million adults. Arthritis disproportionately impacts older adults, those who are disabled, and adults with chronic conditions. Additionally, over half (50.4%) of adults age 65 and older have arthritis, and about 3 in 10 adults age 45 to 64 report it. Over 27% of non-Hispanic White adults report arthritis, while only 14% of Hispanic adults have the condition. More than half of adults who report being disabled/unable to work have arthritis. The prevalence of arthritis is substantially higher among adults with heart disease (49%), diabetes (47%), or obesity (31%). Over 37% of adults who report fair/poor health have arthritis. Its prevalence compared with other common chronic conditions such as obesity, coronary heart disease, and diabetes among adults in the United States is shown in Fig. 32.1.

The U.S. prevalence of some notable types of arthritis has also been ascertained. OA is the most common type and impacts over 13% of U.S. adults (over 30 million) (Fig. 32.2). The prevalence of gout is estimated at 3.9% (9.2 million people)—5.2% [5.9 million] in men and 2.7% [3.3 million] in women (Fig. 32.2). Both conditions—OA and gout—are more common among obese adults.6, A recently published meta-analysis shows the prevalence of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is estimated to be at 72.8 per 100,000 person-years, impacting slightly over 200,000 adults (Fig. 32.2). SLE disproportionately impacts women (prevalence is nine times higher than men), particularly non-Hispanic Black and non-Hispanic American Indian/Alaska Native women (three to four times higher than non-Hispanic White women). The prevalence of RA in the

U.S. is unknown. The most credible RA estimate comes from a study from Rochester, Minnesota, which estimated a prevalence of 0.85% in 1995—1.06% in women and 0.61% in men. This estimate is extrapolated to determine a national estimate (Fig. 32.2). A summary of these prevalence estimates among adults in the United States for the more notable arthritis conditions are shown in Fig. 32.2.

### Risk Factors for Arthritis

Risk factors for arthritis can vary depending on the specific arthritis condition or location, and most have a genetic component. Some of the modifiable and nonmodifiable risk factors of arthritic conditions are discussed here. Some risk factors are modifiable, such as obesity and consumption of certain food products, but others are nonmodifiable, such as age and genetics.

### Osteoarthritis

Obesity has been shown to be a major risk factor for knee OA,10 whereas there is only moderate evidence of an association

between obesity and hip and hand OA.11, Other risk factors for OA include older age, being female, family history, lower socioeconomic status, Black race, joint injuries, metabolic factors (such as higher leptin levels), rural residence, and higher bone density. 13,14

### Gout

There are many risk factors for gout, including older age; being male; family history; high consumption (particularly for hard liquor and beer) of alcohol and sugar-sweetened beverages; consumption of high-fructose foods, red meat, and seafood that is high in purines; chronic conditions (e.g., obesity, heart disease, diabetes, hypertension, hyperuricemia, elevated cholesterol, renal disease); and use of diuretics.

### Systemic Lupus Erythematosus

Many of the risk factors for lupus are unknown but may be related to genetic, environmental, and hormonal factors. Major histocompatibility complex—encoded genes are associated with susceptibility to SLE. As mentioned, women are disproportionately impacted by SLE versus men. Black and American

Indian/Alaska Native women are at the highest risk of lupus in the U.S. population, and Hispanic women are more likely to have it than White women. SLE predominantly affects women of childbearing age.

### Rheumatoid Arthritis

Similar to SLE, many of the risk factors for RA have yet to be identified and are likely a combination of genetic and environmental factors, though more is known about the genetic contributions to the development of lupus. About 50% of RA cases appear to have a genetic link/familial risk contribution. Certain alleles that are grouped together, known as the "shared epitope," may predict about 40% of the risk of RA. These alleles encode amino acid sequences that predict structural similarities in the human leukocyte antigen peptide—binding groove. Other risk factors that have been consistently identified in the literature include being female (~ two-fold higher risk vs. men) and smoking.

### Arthritis and Physical Activity

The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS) recommends that adults take part in 150 minutes of moderate aerobic activity per week to receive substantial health benefits. The moderate to severe joint pain caused by arthritis can be a major barrier to physical activity and interfere with an individual's desire to be active. Adults with arthritis are significantly (p < 0.01) less likely to meet the recommended amount of aerobic physical activity compared with adults without arthritis (adults with arthritis: age-standardized prevalence = 41.9%; adults without arthritis: age-standardized prevalence = 52.2%). Moreover, almost one in three adults with arthritis is physically inactive (report 0 minutes of moderate-intensity leisure-time aerobic physical activity per week). Nonetheless, evidence-based physical activity and self-management interventions have been developed to help adults with arthritis engage in safe and effective physical activity, and thus improve their ability to meet DHHS recommendations.22, These interventions are discussed in greater detail later in the chapter.

### Arthritis Impact

This section illustrates some of the literature regarding arthritis and its impacts on critical measures of quality of life, employment, cost burden, health care burden, and morbidity and mortality.

### Disability

A disability is any condition of the body or mind resulting in diffculty performing certain activities and in participation restrictions. In the United States, arthritis is considered the most common cause of disability (defined as reporting specific activity difficulties, selected impairments, use of an assistive aid, household work limitations, and/ or paid work limitations), impacting 9.1 million adults or 19.2% of all adults who reported a disability in 2010.25 About 55% of adults with a disability (either activities of daily living [ADL] disability or instrumental activities of daily living [IADL] disability) report having arthritis. Among adults with arthritis, 11.1% and 5.7% report an IADL and an ADL disability, respectively (Fig. 32.3).

### Severe Joint Pain

Severe joint pain can be a debilitating condition for adults with arthritis that can limit physical function, result in poor mental health, and reduce social participation.26, In the United States, more than one in four adults with arthritis report severe joint pain in the last 30 days (Fig. 32.3).28, The trend in prevalence of severe joint pain among U.S. adults with arthritis has remained stable over the years; however, the number of adults with arthritis reporting severe joint pain has increased as the population size has risen over time.

### Physical Function

Poor physical function is a common outcome among adults with arthritis. 30, About one in four find stooping, bending, or kneeling very difficult (Fig. 32.3), and about 20% cannot or find it very difficult to walk three blocks or push/pull large objects. Adults with arthritis are more likely to have poorer mobility, limitations with ADL, and limitations with large-muscle tasks.2,31

### Mental Health

Poor mental health can impact all aspects of life. The link between arthritis and poor mental health is well established. 32, The

age-standardized prevalence of anxiety symptoms is almost twofold higher among adults with arthritis, and the age-standardized prevalence of depression symptoms is nearly 2.6 times higher for adults with arthritis. About 23% of adults with arthritis report anxiety symptoms and 12% report depression symptoms (Fig. 32.3). Among adults with arthritis, anxiety and depression symptoms are more common among younger adults, adults with chronic pain or comorbid chronic conditions, and those unable to work or who are disabled. Furthermore, about one in three adults age 45 and older reports having anxiety or depression, of whom only half sought help for their mental health condition in the past year.

### Employment

Working-age adults with arthritis have been shown to have lower employment rates (7.2% lower) compared with adults without arthritis in 2013.34, There are several factors that likely play a role in these lower employment rates, including mental health, physical function, and pain. A recent study showed that adults with arthritis who report symptoms of depression are half as likely to be employed compared with adults with arthritis who do not report symptoms of depression. Another recent study showed that the age-standardized prevalence of arthritis-attributable activity limitations (a potential marker of physical function and pain) was significantly higher (42% higher) among unemployed versus employed adults with arthritis.

### Opioid Use

The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) Guideline for Prescribing Opioids for Chronic Pain states that there are serious risks associated with long-term use of opioid therapy to treat chronic pain and recommends the use of other treatments (e.g., exercise therapy, weight loss, cognitive-behavioral therapy, certain interventional procedures, acetaminophen, and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs) for arthritis. Despite this, about 30% of adults with arthritis are prescribed an opioid in the United States (55% of all adults prescribed an opioid) to treat their pain.

### Joint Replacement

About 1.3 million joint replacements occur each year (3.6% of all inpatient procedures) with 95% of the joint replacements performed on the knees (723,000) or hips (494,000). Women are more likely to have a joint replacement than men (60% vs. 40%). About 98% of knee replacements are attributable to OA and 87% of total hip replacements are attributable to OA.

### Hospitalizations

Over 21% of all hospitalizations are associated with arthritis and other rheumatic conditions. Nearly half of the hospitalizations of those with arthritis and other rheumatic conditions are associated with OA (46%). About 59% were in women, and women made up 75% of hospitalizations for RA. Men made up 67% of hospitalizations with gout. Non-Hispanic Blacks were disproportionately impacted by hospitalizations due to gout, for which they comprised 18% of hospitalizations, compared with 12% of all hospitalizations associated with arthritis and other rheumatic conditions. OA is also the seventh leading hospital discharge diagnosis according to the Healthcare Cost and Utilization Project's National Ambulatory Medical Care Survey in 2020.41

### Falls

Falls are the leading cause of injury-related morbidity and mortality in older adults (age 65 and older). More than two in five nonfatal emergency department visits and more than five in six unintentional fall deaths occur in older adults.' 42 Major consequences of falls among older adults include hip fractures, brain injuries, decline in functional abilities, and reductions in social activities. Adults with arthritis are at risk for falls and fall injuries,4 potentially because of their reduced physical function (e.g., walking speed and balance). A CDC report showed that adults with arthritis (age 45 and older) are more than twice as likely to report an injury related to a fall and about twice as likely to report two or more falls in the past year. Moreover, several cohort studies have shown an increased risk of incident falls and fall injuries among adults with knee OA.45-47 A recent meta-analysis shows about a 35% increased risk of falls among adults with knee OA compared with adults without knee OÅ.

### Mortality

Systematic reviews and meta-analyses have been published that examine the association between individual rheumatic conditions and mortality.49-53 A meta-analysis of eight studies showed a standard mortality ratio (SMR) of 1.66 (95% CI: 1.44, 1.92) in women and an SMR of 1.39 (95% CI: 1.11, 1.73) in men when comparing those with RA to the general population. Gout has been linked to an elevated risk of allcause and cardiovascular disease (CVD) mortality in one systematic review (six studies) and to CVD mortality (HR: 1.29, 95% CI: 1.14-1.44) in a meta-analysis of four studies.50, A meta-analysis of seven studies showed an increased risk (HR: 1.21; 95% CI: 1.10, 1.34) of CVD mortality among those with OA. A meta-analysis of 12 studies showed a three-fold elevated risk for all-cause mortality and CVD mortality and an eight-fold increased risk of renal disease mortality among individuals with lupus versus the general population. A more recent study examining lupus and race/ethnicity showed that cardiovascular disease deaths were nearly four and six times higher for Asian and Hispanic individuals with lupus, respectively, compared with the general population. From these studies, it appears that although the risk of mortality is increased for adults with OA and gout, mortality is highest in individuals with lupus and RA.

### Arthritis-Attributable Costs

### Direct and Indirect Costs

In the United States, the total annual arthritis-attributable costs were estimated to be over $303 billion in 2013.54 The direct costs (arthritis-attributable medical care costs)—estimated for all adults (over age 18)—were $139.8 billion (range: $135.9157.5 billion). The indirect costs (arthritis-attributable earnings losses)—estimated for working-age adults (age 1864)—were $163.7 billion (range: $163.7-170.0 billion). Ambulatory care expenditures accounted for about half of arthritis-attributable medical expenditures. The large annual arthritis-attributable earning losses was a result of the annual employment rate being substantially lower among individuals with arthritis.

### Public Health Approaches to Arthritis Self- Management

This section discusses public health approaches to arthritis selfmanagement such as physical activity and education interventions.

### Physical Activity

Although medications can help treat arthritis sequela, nonpharmaceutical approaches such as physical activity can help as well. A meta-analysis of 33 studies showed that community-deliverable physical activity interventions were associated with decreases in pain and improvements in function, each by about 40%. In addition to reducing arthritis symptoms, physical activity programs can lower annual health care costs. Participation in EnhanceFitness (CDC-recognized, evidence-based physical activity intervention) was shown to reduce total health care costs by $945 per person,55 and produce improvements in function and self-reported health at follow-up at 8 months. Close to 70% of adults with arthritis are counseled by health care providers to be physically active (Fig. 32.4). Only 40% of primary care providers always assess and recommend physical activity to their patients with arthritis. Though the number of adults with arthritis who are encouraged by their health care providers to be physically active is robust, more providers need to encourage these patients to engage in physical activity to help bridge the differences in physical activity among adults with and without arthritis.

### Self-Management Interventions

Self-management education interventions are designed to improve an individual's confidence and skills to manage a condition. A meta-analysis of 23 studies showed that self-management

interventions for arthritis reduced pain, fatigue, and depression by 10 to 20%. However, in 2014 only 11% of adults with arthritis reported taking a self-management education course (Fig. 32.4). A more recent report using 2019 state-specific data showed an encouraging increase in self-management education course attendance (state-specific median = 15.7%; range:12.0% in Connecticut to 20.8% in Hawaii). However, only about 10% of adults with arthritis receive a health care provider recommendation to take a self-management education class (Fig. 32.4). A health care provider's recommendation to arthritis patients is essential, and significantly increases the chances of attendance in a self-management education program. In fact, 52% of adults with arthritis who receive a recommendation attend a self-management education class. Because of the relatively low rates of self-management education course attendance in the United States, this remains a major area in regard to arthritis management that can be targeted for exponential growth and impact.

### Conclusion

In conclusion, the public health burden of arthritis in the United States remains large for those who have it and the health care sys-tem that supports them. It continues to be a highly prevalent, widespread, expensive, and debilitating condition. The risk of arthritis can be mitigated by addressing modifiable risk factors such as obesity, though many of the risk factors are nonmodifi-able.
