Public health approaches to managing arthritis exist and are currently underutilized. These approaches should be encouraged as they are evidence based and have been shown to reduce pain and improve function in adults with arthritis.

# Assessment of Health Outcomes

JOSHUA F. BAKERa AND PATRICIA KATZ

### KEY POINTS

Health outcomes can serve many purposes including facilitating research, evaluating quality of care, and promoting shared decision making between patients and providers.

Health outcomes can be specific to a disease state or cover a single symptom or health domain.

A good" health outcome tool will (1) measure what it is meant to, (2) be reproducible, (3) change over time in response to interventions, (4) be feasible, (5) have categories of states and changes that are meaningful, and (6) capture the full range of possible e experiences.

### Introduction

Over the past few decades, a plethora of work has been done to develop, evaluate, and validate a number of quantitative health outcomes in rheumatic diseases. This work has provided the framework necessary for the field to perform key research trials to understand disease impact and to change the treatment landscape in a number of important diseases and inform management strategies. Further, in addition to clear benefits that these outcomes have provided for research, the formal assessment of health outcomes within clinical care may also promote more precise care and provide opportunities to monitor the quality of that care.

The aim of this chapter is to summarize and discuss health outcomes in the rheumatic diseases and evaluate their utility in both research and clinical contexts. Health outcomes may focus on a single construct such as fatigue, or combine multiple constructs that are important to patients with a particular disease to evaluate and quantify the overall impact of the disease (e.g., disease activity). Disease-specific outcomes are often useful for clinical research because they combine a number of different constructs related to the disease into a single, quantifiable measure and used to capture the overall impact of the disease and the effects of interventions to treat the disease. In other contexts, both clinical and research, it may be preferable to assess a construct within a single symptom or health domain in order to better understand the experience of the individual in a key area. A construct aimed at a single symptom or health domain (e.g., fatigue) can be assessed across many diseases,

while disease-specific outcomes are generally used for a specific disease or set of diseases.

It is also important to note that there are a variety of types of health outcomes that can be assessed. These can include patientreported outcomes (PROs) that use patient responses to quantify symptoms related to a specific disease's impact (e.g., disease activity) or related to a specific symptom construct (e.g., fatigue). Others health outcomes may be designed as composite outcomes and may include additional assessments such as physician/evaluator performed assessments (e.g., joint counts), biomarkers (e.g., inflammatory markers), and/or observed clinical assessments (e.g., test of physical function).

This chapter is meant to provide a brief overview of key concepts surrounding outcome development and evaluation. Further, the chapter will provide a review of some of the most common and important disease-specific measures, as well as measures that evaluate health domains that are highly relevant for patients with rheumatic diseases. Special attention is made to discuss the type of outcome, its strengths and weaknesses, and some of its common uses in clinical and research settings.

### Types of Outcomes

Health outcomes are often developed with different goals in mind. Perhaps the most obvious reason that health outcomes are defined is to be able to test the benefit of therapies or interventions for a condition. However, health outcomes in rheumatology are used for many additional purposes including aiding in clinical decision making (e.g., "treat-to-target"), as well as in following and evaluating the quality of care. Clarity about how one intends to use the scores from an instrument, or the purpose for measuring, is important for defining which attributes should be prioritized. One group describes three purposes: descriptive (measurement of a domain at a single point in time), predictive (using a current measure to predict another outcome in the future), and evaluative (helping to determine a change in status, such as the benefit or harm from a treatment) (Fig. 33.1). Each purpose requires slightly different evidence to support an argument that an instrument will work well in that setting. Evaluative purposes, for example, place a lot more emphasis on the elements around change, such as responsiveness. These are not as important for descriptive applications for which change is not the focus. Understanding how and why tools were developed can help understand their limitations in different applications. For example, an outcome

developed for testing the benefit of a treatment in a trial may not serve the purpose of a clinician who hopes to use the measure to inform clinical decision making or to predict who will suffer an adverse event.

### Evaluation and Endorsement of Outcomes

What makes a measure or instrument good? In order to facilitate an informed discussion some of the most commonly used measurements in rheumatology, it is necessary to introduce some of the terminology around the evaluation of these measures (Table 33.1). A perfect measure would (1) measure what it is meant to measure, (2) be easily reproducible, (3) have components/

pieces that are consistent with each other, (4) change over time in response to interventions, (5) be feasible to do in most settings, (6) have categories of states and changes that are meaningful to patients, and (7) capture the whole range of experiences for a population.

In a basic health outcome, one might ask a patient with rheumatoid arthritis (RA) to report the answer to a yes or no question: "Do your joints hurt today?" This may have some properties that are quite good, such as reproducibility and feasibility. However, this measure may poorly represent the activity of inflammatory arthritis (poor validity) and may show little change over time (poor responsiveness). In this section each of these aspects of evaluating the psychometric qualities of health outcome measures will be discussed in more detail to provide the reader with the important concepts and terminology.

### Validity

Validity is an expression of the extent to which an outcome assesses what it is intended to measure. The validity of an instrument is assessed in multiple ways. Some may be more appropriate than others for specific instruments. The method of validation will vary depending on whether other scales or measures of similar constructs are already available with which to compare the performance of the proposed instrument.

### Content Validity

This concept is often referred to as "face validity" and asks whether the instrument covers the concepts it is intended to measure. An instrument is built by understanding a concept (e.g., fatigue) and then identifying the items, responses, and scoring systems that seem to capture it. The goal is a score that represents the domain of interest in the patients and setting within which it will be used. Content validity can be assessed through a thorough review of the instrument and information on its administration by a clinical or research team with patient input. Patient partners

can be helpful by providing their opinion of the face validity of the measure, the clarity of the wording of the questions, and the comprehensiveness of the content (i.e., does it fully capture their experience).

### Construct Validity

If a measure is a good representation of the concept it is intended to cover, then the measure should correlate with the "gold standard" measure of the concept. This is termed criterion validity, and its assessment requires that a criterion (gold standard) exists against which a new measure can be compared; e.g., scores on a measure of depression might be compared with clinical diagnoses of depression. The sensitivity of a measure refers to the proportion of persons who have the condition (e.g., depression) that are correctly classified as having the condition based on the new instrument. Alternatively, the specificity refers to the proportion of persons who do not have the condition who are correctly classified by the measure. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves may be used to illustrate the tradeoff between sensitivity and specificity and to set ideal thresholds for the measure.

Where no gold standard criterion exists, other means are necessary to determine the validity of the construct. This can be done by showing that the measure correlates with other measures of the same concept/construct (convergent validity) or by showing that the measure correlates with other variables in a way that is consistent with what would be hypothesized; e.g., a score for depression correlates with a measure of poor sleep quality. Construct validity can also be supported by showing discriminant validity. An instrument that is a valid measure of a construct should not correlate with apparently unrelated constructs; e.g., a measure of depression should not correlate significantly with a measure of intelligence. Predictive validity is also a useful concept that asks whether a measure correlates with the event of a criterion measure in the future; e.g., does a measure of depression performed now predict a subsequent diagnosis of depression?

### Reliability and Reproducibility

In general, assessments of reliability and reproducibility indicate the consistency of scores over time or among different raters or the extent to which a response of score is free from random error (precision). Concepts of reliability and reproducibility can be assessed quantitatively using multiple approaches depending on whether the data are dichotomous or continuous in nature. Kappa coefficients may be used to express agreement between two dichotomous assessments, correcting for the amount of agreement that would be expected by chance. Kappa coefficients range from 0 to 1.0, but the ceiling is influenced by the sensitivity and specificity of the measure. Intraclass correlation (ICC) may be used to express agreement between raters on continuous measures. The ICC is conceptually similar to a correlation.

### Test/Retest Reliability

This is the concept of assessing the stability of scores from the measure from one administration to another. Test—retest reliability is usually measured over a short period of time, during which little or no change would be expected. If the results are variable between tests when there is no expectation of change, it suggests that measured changes occurring over time in this measure may suffer from variability simply due to poor reproducibility of the test.

### Intra-/Inter-rater Reliability

A reliable test will result in the same rating or judgment on repeated administrations on the same subject either by the same rater or by another rater. A measure with high intra-rater and inter-rater reliability can be trusted to not vary between administrations or administrators.

### Internal Consistency

When a scale is internally consistent, it is expected that the items that compose that scale measure the same underlying construct or theme. Internal consistency is usually reported as Cronbach's coefficient alpha (α), which can range from 0 to 1.0. It has been suggested that an α greater than 0.80 should be considered "good" and sufficient for tests used to compare groups.

### Responsiveness

Responsiveness is good for a measure if scores on the instrument change to reflect changes in the underlying construct. For example, a measure has poor responsiveness if it fails to change in a measurable way with effective treatment of the underlying disease. There are a number of measures of sensitivity or responsiveness. One of the most commonly used is the standardized response mean, calculated as the mean change in score divided by the standard deviation of the change scores. Standardized effect sizes may also be used to describe how sensitive instruments are to detecting change.

### Feasibility

Feasibility covers the practical aspects of using the instrument in its intended setting. Does it take too much time? Is it expensive to use? Does it require special equipment? Is it too burdensome for your patients (e.g., language, literacy, acceptability of questions, time of procedure, physical discomfort) or observers (training)? Is the protocol for performing the test clear? Are the results of the score easily interpretable? Feasibility is often one of the most important determinants of whether a candidate instrument is incorporated into a research study or practice.

### Meaningful States or Changes

### Thresholds of "States"

Clinicians want to know whether pain is at a tolerable level or whether a patient is in a low disease state (e.g., disease remission), which requires us to be able to understand and benchmark scores. Examples of this type of threshold include patient-acceptable symptom states (PASSs),7,8 for what patients deem to be tolerable levels of symptoms (e.g., pain level is less than 2 on a scale of 0 to 10), and estimates of states reflecting low disease activity scores (e.g., disease remission).9, These can be determined by evaluating associations with patient's own evaluation of their disease or how the scores affect clinical decision making or predict long-term outcomes. An important outcome for a clinical study may be the meeting of one of these thresholds. The achievement of a low disease activity state may be used to identify patients who are less likely to suffer from adverse long-term outcomes in clinical practice (i.e., radiographic damage in RA).

### Minimally Important Differences/Changes

Minimally important differences/changes are thresholds that define a change/difference in a score that represents an important

change/difference as reported by patients. These measures are particularly important in interpreting whether a change or difference measured in a study is actually important or meaningful. The minimal clinically important difference (MCID) was originally defined as the smallest difference in score that patients would perceive as beneficial. Minimal important difference/ change was introduced to remove the emphasis from clinical interpretations, to include both worsening and improvement, and to differentiate between cross-sectional and longitudinal comparisons.

### Minimal Detectable Change

Minimal detectable change is a statistical concept and is an estimate of the minimal amount of change needed to differentiate from random variation or measurement error.

### Floor and Ceiling Effects

Floor or ceiling effects occur when a large number of respondents have the lowest or highest scores, respectively. Floor/ceiling effects can reduce the ability of an instrument to detect change at the ends of the scoring range. This is a problem because it suggests that the measure does not fully capture the range of experiences within the population. Some have recommended that floor/ceiling effects are problematic if 15% or more of responses are at the lowest/highest score; others have suggested more stringent criteria.

### Outcome Measures in Rheumatology (OMERACT) and Other Organizations

It is unreasonable to expect most clinicians and researchers to understand the nuances of all outcome measures that are utilized in the field. Fortunately, there are organizations established with the aim of bringing information on outcomes and instruments together for people through the creation of what they consider suitable sets of outcomes: both what should be measured and how it should be measured. One such organization is Outcome Measures in Rheumatology (OMERACT), an international consensus-based group established in 1992 that works within the arthritis communities (i.e., clinicians, researchers, patients, payors, regulators, industry) to define domains and instruments of importance in different rheumatologic conditions. This organization examines core outcome sets for research. Another organization, the International Consortium for Health Outcome Measurement (ICHOM), looks at core outcomes for clinical practice and quality improvement. Both work on defining a small set of prioritized outcome domains and matching high-quality instruments that should be used across outcome assessments. There are also resources compiled specifically for rheumatology that provide information on specific outcome measures.

### Review of Disease-Specific Outcomes

The myriad health outcomes that have now been defined and are relevant to rheumatology would be impossible to cover in an all-inclusive manner. This chapter will review some of the most common health outcomes relevant for rheumatologists, some of their basic properties, and some of their typical uses. Fig. 33.1 illustrates the overlap in disease-specific measures, particularly in terms of overlapping symptoms such as pain and physical function (Fig. 33.2).

### Rheumatoid Arthritis and Peripheral Psoriatic Arthritis

The development of RA-specific outcomes has evolved over decades and has been discussed in detail in recent reviews and guidelines.14-19 Outcomes developed for RA have also been extensively used in trials and clinical research studies in other forms of peripheral inflammatory arthritis such as psoriatic arthritis (PsA). The discussion provided here is not exhaustive.

### American College of Rheumatology Response Criteria

The American College of Rheumatology (ACR) response criteria were developed as clinical trial outcomes and continue to be widely used. This dichotomous measure of response is defined by an improvement in swollen and tender joints, as well as a similar improvement in three of five additional assessments. These include patient global scores, physician global scores, patient assessments of pain, results of the Health Assessment Questionnaire (a measure of function and disability that is described below), and C-reactive protein (CRP) or erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR). Thus an improvement of 20% in each of these assessments would be considered an ACR20 response. This measure has shown excellent discrimination and construct validity for clinical trials. ACR responses also are associated with a meaningful response for patients. Therefore the United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has described the ACR20 as a well-validated composite end point for clinical trials and has encouraged its use in guidance to industry on the conduct of trials in patients with RA. The complexity of the measure, the fact that it is relative to some baseline measure (i.e., 20% improvement), and the lack of ability to define thresholds of states have made this a poor measure for use in clinical practice and in observational research studies.

### Disease Activity Score in 28 Joints

The Disease Activity Score in 28 Joints (DAS28) is a composite measure of disease activity that has been used widely for decades. This measure combines a count of tender and swollen joints, a patient global score, and a measure of systemic inflammation (either CRP or ESR). Each component is transformed and combined to create a score that ranges from 0 to 9.4. The DAS28 was developed by identifying factors that were associated with perceived high and low disease activity states and was a good predictor of physician decision making. The DAS28 also correlates with other measures of disease activity and of disability and can predict radiographic damage progression on x-rays, all of which suggests good construct validity. The DAS28 also has high internal consistency, high reliability, and excellent responsiveness. Thresholds of states have been defined for the DAS28: high, ≥5.1; moderate, 3.2 to 5.0; low, 2.6 to 3.1; and remission, <2.6. The DAS28 is somewhat feasible to perform in clinic and thus has been incorporated in "treat-totarget" studies aimed at goal-oriented therapy to achieve low disease activity or remission. In addition, MCIDs in the DAS28 have been defined.17, Limitations of the DAS28 include the incorporation of an inflammatory marker (which is not always available to clinicians) as well as the somewhat complex calculation (online calculators are available). It is important to note that the DAS28 demonstrates bias in certain clinical contexts (e.g., fibromyalgia, obesity, medications that affect inflammatory markers).23-25 Recently there has also been some concern that DAS28 remission may not be sufficiently strict, as some patients show progression of disease despite achieving this threshold state. Several modifications to the DAS28 have been proposed and are not discussed here. 27,28

### Simplified Disease Activity Index

The Simplified Disease Activity Index (SDAI) incorporates some of the same components as the DAS28, including tender and swollen joint counts, a patient global score, and a CRP level. Further, the SDAI includes a physician/provider visual analogue scale assessment of disease activity. The SDAI (range, 0 to 86) has a simplified approach to calculation compared with the DAS28 (the individual components are added together without transformation), which improves feasibility for use as a clinical measure. The SDAI is highly reliable and is strongly correlated with the DAS28, with similar prediction of radiographic damage progression. It is also highly responsive to change. Thresholds of states have been defined, and the minimal clinically important improvement has been defined. One study showed that some patients in DAS28 remission had active disease on ultrasound unless they were also in SDAI remission, suggesting that SDAI remission may be somewhat more strict. The SDAI is limited in many of the same ways as the DAS28, including the potential for bias related to comorbid conditions such as fibromyalgia and obesity.

### Clinical Disease Activity Index

The Clinical Disease Activity Index (CDAI) is similar to the SDAI, with the exception that it does not include an inflammatory marker (ESR or CRP), which means that it can be performed with clinical assessments only without the need to access laboratory results, improving feasibility. The continuous score represents the sum of the four component measures (range, 0 to 76). The components have good internal consistency (α = 0.87) and high reliability. The CDAI converges with other measures such as the DAS28 and shows moderate agreement to the DAS28 in terms of

categorization of disease states. The CDAI predicts radiographic damage progression. The CDAI definition of remission is somewhat more strict than the DAS28 and similar to that of the SDAI. The MCID for the CDAI has been defined. The CDAI is widely used in clinical research and practice given its high feasibility and is preferred when comparing treatments that may have direct effects on inflammatory markers (e.g., tocilizumab). The CDAI may be falsely elevated in the context of comorbid fibromyalgia or other chronic pain conditions.

### Routine Assessment of Patient Index Data

The Routine Assessment of Patient Index Data (RAPID3) is the most widely used of the RAPID measures and includes a patient global score, a pain assessment, and a functional assessment (Multi-dimensional Health Assessment Questionnaire [MDHAQ]; range, 0 to 30). The RAPID3 correlates moderately with DAS28, SDAI, and CDAI, and there is fair agreement in terms of disease categorization. The MCID for the RAPID3 has been defined. One study showed that sustained low RAPID3 scores were associated with reduced radiographic progression. . The high feasibility of this measure in certain circumstances is its primary strength (e.g., telemedicine), although there may be fees associated with use of this measure in electronic health systems. The primary limitation of the RAPID3 is the lower content and construct validity, with poorer correlation to other RA disease activity measures and somewhat lower responsiveness compared with other measures. The RAPID3 is likely influenced to an even greater extent by comorbid conditions such as fibromyalgia and chronic pain syndromes.

### Patient Activity Scale Systems

The Patient Activity Scale (PAS, PAS-II) systems are PROs that include similar elements to the RAPID3 but incorporate the HAQ or HAQ-II questionnaire, respectively, whereas the RAPID measures include the MD-HAQ. PAS-II contains fewer questions than the PAS. Not unexpectedly, the PAS correlates strongly with the RAPID3, and disease activity categorization agreement with DAS28 is only fair to moderate. The MCID for the PAS-II has been defined. Strengths and weaknesses of the PAS/PAS-II are similar to those of the RAPID measures, described above.

### Boolean Remission

Boolean remission is a strict definition of remission that requires the presence of all component assessments of disease activity to be very low (swollen and tender joints ≤ 1, patient global score ≤ 10 [range, 0 to 100], and CRP ≤ 1.0). This definition has excellent face validity. Patients who achieve this definition of remission have superior outcomes, suggesting prognostic validity. As a result, this definition is often included as an outcome in RA clinical trials. Rates of Boolean remission are lower than for other definitions, and in the real world and for many patients it is not possible to achieve due to false elevations in inflammatory markers as well as elevated patient global scores due to other comorbid conditions (e.g., obesity, fibromyalgia).25, Modifications to these criteria have been proposed but have not been studied in detail. While perhaps a useful measure for clinical trials, it is likely that such a definition would be overly strict for a typical clinical practice.

### Disease Activity in Psoriatic Arthritis

The Disease Activity in Psoriatic Arthritis (DAPSA) is meant to represent peripheral joint disease activity and is the summation of the tender and swollen joint counts, a patient arthritis global

score, a pain score (0 to 10 cm), and a CRP value. If the CRP value is not included, the measure is called the cDAPSA. Strong correlation with other joint measures suggests good validity, although the DAPSA does not adequately capture other domains of interest to patients with psoriasis, such as enthesitis and skin disease. Thresholds for disease states have been defined for both the DAPSA and cDAPSA, but clinically important differences have not. The DAPSA is responsive but may be less responsive than other measures.42, While DAPSA may be a valuable measure in clinic, it has not received as much attention as primary clinical trial outcomes.

Minimal Disease Activity. Minimal disease activity (MDA) is a target disease state for PsA that was developed in order to serve as useful target of treatment for both patients and physicians. In this definition a patient achieves MDA when five of the following seven criteria are met: tender joint count ≤ 1; swollen joint count ≤ 1; Psoriasis Area and Severity Index ≤ 1 or body surface area ≤ 3%; patient pain visual analogue score (VAS) ≤ 15; patient global disease activity VAS ≤ 20; Health Assessment Questionnaire (HAQ) disability index ≤ 0.5; and tender entheseal points ≤ 1. The MDA does not include acute-phase reactants or a measure of spondylitis activity. Although the MDA performs well in clinical trials in discriminating effective therapies, some have raised concern about the content validity for clinical use since many patients who have apparently low inflammatory disease have persistent pain, disability, and tenderness. While approximately 25% to 50% of participants in clinical trials achieve this threshold, there is concern that many patients in the real world will never be able to achieve this definition of minimal disease due to persistent symptoms that are unlikely to respond to immunomodulatory therapies.

### Axial Spondyloarthritis and Enthesitis

Clinical disease assessments developed for RA, a disease that involves primarily peripheral joints, are not ideally designed for inflammatory diseases of the axial spine and those that primarily manifest as enthesitis. As a result, disease activity measures have been developed for axial spondyloarthritis and for other features of seronegative spondyloarthritis and have been utilized in clinical trials.

### Bath Ankylosing Spondylitis Disease Activity Index

The Bath Ankylosing Spondylitis Disease Activity Index (BASDAI) is a commonly used patient-reported measure that aims to capture and quantify symptoms typical of ankylosing spondylitis. The measure comprises six questions that ask about back pain, peripheral joint pain, tender areas, fatigue, and morning stiffness, each on a scale of 1 to 10. This measure is easy to perform, reliable, and responsive.45-47 As a result, this measure is widely used in clinical trials and research. Active disease has been defined as a score of 4 or higher, and the minimal clinically important change and patient acceptable states have also been defined.47-49 As a result, this measure is widely used in clinical trials and research. It is important to note, however, that this measure is subject to the effects of noninflammatory causes of pain (e.g., fibromyalgia) and psychological comorbidities and thus should be used with this in mind as it pertains to decision making in clinical practice. 50,51

### Ankylosing Spondylitis Disease Activity Score

The Ankylosing Spondylitis Disease Activity Score (ASDAS) is now the most commonly used outcome in clinical trials for axial

SpA. This composite measure incorporates four patient-reported outcomes (three of which are taken from the BASDAI) and an acute phase reactant (ESR or CRP). The lowest possible score is O.6, but it has no upper limit. The score has good reliability. Thresholds have been defined for inactive, low, high, and very high disease activity, and clinically important changes have been defined.52, The outcome is reliable and correlates with other assessments of disease, suggesting good construct validity.45, A particular strength of the ASDAS is its responsiveness and ability to discriminate among therapies in the clinical trial setting. Bias from comorbidities such as fibromyalgia are still a concern for use in clinical care, although this bias may be to a lesser degree compared with the BASDAI.

### Leeds Enthesitis Index

Enthesitis is an important and unique feature of PsA and spondyloarthritis that is not captured by other disease activity assessments. For this reason, the Leeds Enthesitis Index (LEI) and other enthesitis scores have been developed.18, The LEI examines tenderness at six sites: the lateral epicondyles of the humerus, the medial condyles of the femur, and the insertion of the Achilles tendon. Patients can receive a score between O and 6 based on the number of tender locations. This measure has good reliability and improves with active therapy in clinical trials. No important differences or thresholds of states have been defined. Low content validity in particular subgroups is a concern, because validation is difficult with no reference standard and because scores can be particularly high in noninflammatory conditions such as fibromyalgia. Thus caution in overinterpreting tenderness in this and other contexts is needed.

### Systemic Lupus Erythematosus

Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a notoriously protean disease, and the development of a single quantity that encompasses disease activity has been a long-term challenge. Several indices have been developed to measure both disease activity and organ damage, but there is no universal consensus about which to use. These measures are used primarily in clinical trials and less frequently in clinical settings.

### Systemic Lupus Erythematosus Disease Activity Index

The Systemic Lupus Erythematosus Disease Activity Index (SLEDAI-2K)60 is completed by the physician, who assesses for the presence of disease manifestations in nine core domains including rash, alopecia, oral ulcers, and proteinuria. The score is then weighted to give a global score ranging from 0 to 105. Categories of disease states and MCID has been defined. The score is relatively easy to complete, although it does require review of medical records including laboratory assessments and physical exam findings. While widely used, a limitation of the SLEDAI is the inability of the score to capture gradation or severity within individual domains, thus limiting responsiveness. Modifications of the SLEDAI-2K include the Safety of Estrogens in Lupus National Assessment (SELENA)-SLEDAI, which permits assessment on ongoing disease activity,61 and the SLEDAI-2KG, which accounts for glucocorticoid use (SLEDAI-2KG).

### British Isles Lupus Assessment Group Index

The British Isles Lupus Assessment Group (BILAG) 2004 index63 is a disease activity index that assesses disease manifestations. It consists of 97 items across 9 organs/systems plus an additional 4

items to calculate the glomerular filtration rate. Each item is scored as not done or 0 to 4. Scores are converted to alphabetic scores for each system: A indicates severe disease activity, B indicates moderate disease activity, C indicates mild disease, D indicates inactive disease but previously affected, and E indicates that the system was never involved. Reliability, validity, and responsiveness have been demonstrated, and MCID has been defined. Scoring requires either a computerized system or training, so the administrative time burden is a consideration. However, the BILAG does capture partial improvements.

### Cutaneous Lupus Erythematosus Disease Area and − Severity Index

The Cutaneous Lupus Erythematosus Disease Area and Severity Index (CLASI) focuses specifically on cutaneous manifestations of both SLE and cutaneous lupus.64, The CLASI yields scores of both disease activity and damage. Definitions of mild, moderate, and severe disease have been established. The performance of the CLASI requires training in the cutaneous manifestations of SLE.

### Safety of Estrogens s in Lupus National Assessment- Systemic Lupus Erythematosus Disease Activity Index Flare Index

The Safety of Estrogens in Lupus National Assessment (SELENA)— SLEDAI Flare Index was developed to distinguish severe disease flares from moderate/mild flares.61, It includes changes in the SELENA-SLEDAI score, a physician global assessment, and treatment modifications. A modified version does not require completion of the SLEDAI. Both the original and modified versions have demonstrated acceptable reliability and validity.

### Systemic Lupus Erythematosus Responder Index

The Systemic Lupus Erythematosus Responder Index (SRI) and its modification, the SRI-4, are composite indices developed to be used in trials to assess response to treatment.67, The SRI requires scoring of the SLEDAI-2K, the BILAG, and a physician global assessment (PGA).

### British Isles Lupus Assessment Group-Based Composite Lupus Assessment

The BILAG-based Composite Lupus Assessment (BICLA) is another measure used to assess response to treatment. It also includes the BILAG, SLEDAI-2K, and a PGA, but scoring is driven primarily by the BILAG. Both the SRI and the BICLA provide comprehensive view of disease, but the time to complete the measures is a major caveat that may limit feasibility in some settings.

### Systemic Lupus International Collaborating g Clinics/ American College of Rheumatology Damage Index

The Systemic Lupus International Collaborating Clinics/American College of Rheumatology Damage Index (SDI) is the most widely used measure of disease damage accrual in SLE.69, It contains 41 items covering 12 systems. SDI scores range from 0 to 47, but scores greater than 10 are rare. A complete history and physical examination are required for completion. Reliability and validity have been demonstrated. By definition, scores do not decrease but tend to increase over time. The SDI is rarely used in clinical trials, but scores are associated with adverse outcomes including mortality. The need for a complete chart review may limit feasibility for patients with long-standing disease.

Patient-reported measures of both disease activity and damage have been developed. The Systemic Lupus Activity Questionnaire (SLAQ)71,72 was developed to correspond to the physician-completed Systemic Lupus Activity Measures (SLAM), which is now rarely used. The SLAQ consists of 24 items, rated as no problem, mild, moderate, or severe. Total scores range from 0 to 44. Also included are a flare report and a 0 to 10 global assessment of disease activity. While the SLAQ was validated against the SLAM, it demonstrates low correlations with other physician-completed measures of disease activity. The Brief Index of Lupus Damage (BILD) was developed as patient-completed proxy for the SLICC Damage Index.73, The BILD consists of 26 items and is scored from 0 to 31. Reliability and validity have been established. The BILD has a moderately high correlation with the SDI.

### Systemic Sclerosis

A number of outcomes have been developed to capture the manifestations of systemic sclerosis (SSc) and to facilitate the study of novel interventions. These measures range from assessing skin only to capturing overall disease activity and damage that includes other organ involvement. As with other disease states, the list and discussion here are not exhaustive. Further, a number of measures have aimed to address specific symptoms related to the disease and are too numerous to cover here but have been discussed elsewhere.

### European Scleroderma Study Group Activity Index

The European Scleroderma Study Group Activity Index (EScSG- AI) aims to capture disease activity in SSc by evaluating 10 variables including those that assess skin changes, the presence of arthritis, levels of inflammatory markers, and patient-reported assessments of cardiopulmonary function. The weighted score ranges from 0 to 10. The validity of this measure has been assessed through the demonstration of associations with physician assessments of disease activity and through the prediction of progression of visceral disease and functional disability.76, A small study suggested good responsiveness to change. Categories of disease have been defined, with a score greater than 3 indicating active disease. Revised indices have also been derived and validated.

### Medsger Disease Severity Scale

The Medsger Disease Severity Scale aims to capture the severity of SSc, with inclusion of both reversible and irreversible components and includes components from nine health domains that cover multiple organ systems affected by SSc. Each system is graded from 0 to 4 by an evaluator and summed to create a score that ranges from 0 to 36. Convergent validity has been established showing that the score correlates with disability and quality of life. Thresholds of disease states have not been defined. Further, partly because the score is meant to capture overall damage from the disease, the responsiveness to change is unclear, and thus the use of the score as an outcome in clinical trials has been limited.

### Scleroderma Clinical Trials Consortium Damage Index

The Scleroderma Clinical Trials Consortium Damage Index (SCTC-DI) is a physician-assessed measure that covers 23 items over 6 domains related to SSc and aims to quantify organ damage from the disease. The weighted summed score ranges from 0 to 55. Criterion and construct validity have been supported by associations with disease and with the prediction of worsening morbidity. 2 The observation of accrual of items over time supports

responsiveness in this context; however, the short-term responsiveness and utility in the context of clinical trials have not been established.

### Scleroderma Health Assessment Questionnaire

The Scleroderma Health Assessment Questionnaire (SHAQ) is a combination of the HAQ and six visual analogue scales specific to SSc. This is a patient-reported measure that has excellent reliability and internal consistency. Convergent validity has also been supported by strong associations with other measures of quality of life and disease severity. The SHAQ is responsive to change, and the MCIDs for improvement and worsening have been defined, although the thresholds of change have not. The SHAQ overlaps with other domains and is likely to be influenced by comorbid conditions that can influence physical function.

### Modified Rodnan Skin Score

The Modified Rodnan skin score is the most commonly used measure over many decades of quantifying of skin disease in SSc. This approach has been used in numerous clinical trials and clinical studies to quantify skin disease and follow changes over time. The measure is performed by a trained evaluator and is focused on capturing the severity of skin involvement by grading skin disease (normal to severe thickness) in multiple areas. The method has good reliability and reproducibility86 and has been validated by longitudinal correlations with other manifestation of the disease as well as skin biopsies. This measure is responsive to change and has been used in many clinical trials to evaluate the effects of treatment. This measure is limited in that it does not address other manifestations of the disease (which may be more important to measure over the long term) and does not include any assessment of the patient experience of their condition, which may not always correlate with the objective skin findings.

### Scleroderma Skin PRO

The Scleroderma Skin PRO (SSPRO) is an 18-item patientreported outcome that asks patients to report on four domains related to quality of life related to skin involvement. These domains cover physical, emotional, and social aspects of the impact of the skin disease. The reliability and internal consistency of the measure is very good, and the validity is supported by correlations with other patient-reported outcome and associations with physician-reported assessments of skin involvement. Responsiveness to change has not been well defined. This patient-reported outcome is infrequently used in clinical studies compared with the Rodnan skin score.

### Vasculitis

A number of outcomes have been defined in different types of vasculitis in order to study the impact of the disease and the effect of interventions. As with outcome measures in other settings, some measures aim to quantify disease activity, and others aim to quantify the damage that has occurred from the disease. 89,90

### Birmingham Vasculitis Activity Score

The Birmingham Vasculitis Activity Score (BVAS) is the most widely used measure of disease activity in vasculitis. This physician-derived measure consists of 56 weighted items addressing symptoms in 9 organ systems. The measure is reliable, and the validity of the BVAS is supported by evidence that it identifies patients with physician-assessed active disease (versus remission),

as well as through correlations with quality of life, biomarkers, and other measures of disease activity.91, Categories of disease states have not been defined other than "active" (score > 0) versus "inactive" (score = 0). The score is sensitive to change; however, clinically important changes have not been defined. The limitations of the BVAS are that it was developed to be used in multiple different forms of vasculitis and that it relies on some judgment on the part of a physician evaluator as to what symptoms are related to damage versus active disease. Further, whether the measure can be used as a continuous measure to capture subtle differences in disease activity among those with active disease is unclear. The BVAS may not perform well among patients with large vessel vasculitis conditions, such as giant cell arteritis.

### Vasculitis Damage Index

The Vasculitis Damage Index (VDI) consists of 64 items and is commonly used to assess for irreversible damage related to the disease. The validity of the VDI has largely been based on the observation of correlation with damage scores for SLE and with preceding vasculitis disease activity. The score is also predictive of future mortality. The score is relatively easy to perform, although there is concern that it may miss important impacts of vasculitis. and additional questions have been proposed. Further, the measure is likely most useful in long-term studies in which morbidity from the disease is the primary interest.

### Gout

Formal and well-defined health outcomes are rarely utilized in clinic to assess gout. However, several have been recently developed primarily with the goal of assessing the impact or burden of gout over time in the clinical research or trial setting.

### Gout Assessment Questionnaire

The Gout Assessment Questionnaire (GAQ) is a PRO measure that was developed for use in clinical trials. This is a 31-item questionnaire that collects information about gout impact and assesses pain, well-being, productivity, and treatment satisfaction on a 5-point Likert scale. While this measure has good reliability, the internal consistency and construct validity have been questioned. The responsiveness is also low, overall, particularly among those without a high disease burden,99 although the measure was able to discriminate those that had gout flares from those who did not. There are no defined thresholds or clinically important differences. While this measure attempts to fill an important gap in terms of patient-reported gout outcomes, it is unclear what its role should be in clinical research given these limitations, and there is currently no evidence to support its use in routine clinical practice.

### Gout Activity Score

The Gout Activity Score (GAS) collects information on gout flares, serum urate levels, overall well-being, and tophi. These measures are combined and generate a weighted score through a freely available formula. While the reliability has not been well defined, the score demonstrated reasonable construct validity by discriminating those who were more likely to be recommended to escalate urate-lowering therapy, as well as the patients' perception that they were in remission. Thresholds correlating with remission have been defined. While this measure has not been widely used in clinical research to date, it may have value in this setting. Its role in clinical care remains unclear.

### Gout Flare

Gout is, by nature, a disease that presents with episodic symptoms, or flares. Thus work has been done to define and validate an outcome for acute episodes or flares of gout.102, This definition was highly correlated with the physician reference standard in one study (73% sensitive and 96% specific). This outcome is likely to be incorporated in clinical trials for gout, and it may also be helpful for clinical care since this definition may guide clinicians in terms of the appropriate questions to ask when a patient reports a gout flare over the phone.

### Knee and Hip Osteoarthritis

Knee and hip osteoarthritis (OA) are some of the most common joint conditions seen by rheumatologists. Several patient-reported outcomes have been developed, primarily for research purposes.

### Knee Osteoarthritis Outcome Score

The Knee Osteoarthritis Outcome Score (KOOS) is a PRO that is highly similar to the Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Arthritis Index (WOMAC) but is free to use. The KOOS covers five domains related to symptoms of knee OA including pain, other symptoms, function, participation in sports and recreation, and quality of life. The KOOS has demonstrated good reliability and construct validity and has excellent responsiveness in patients with OA as well as knee injury populations.104, Clinically meaningful changes have been defined, although thresholds of disease states have not. The KOOS is long (42 items) but is feasible to perform in most settings. The KOOS and WOMAC have been utilized in many clinical trials and other research studies. The main limitation to more widespread incorporation in clinical practices is the large number of questions, which can limit feasibility in a busy practice.

### Hip Osteoarthritis Outcome Score

The Hip Osteoarthritis Outcome Score (HOOS)109,110 is highly similar to the KOOS and incorporates 40 items over 5 subscales. The measure has good reliability, internal consistency, and construct validity.111, Like the KOOS, the HOOS is somewhat burdensome in terms of time (10 to 15 minutes). Minimally important differences and thresholds of states have been defined. Short forms of both the KOOS and HOOS are also available.

### Measures That Address s Symptoms and Individual Health Domains

Many symptoms are shared by patients who have different rheumatic diseases. Of these, perhaps the most relevant are pain, limitations in physical function, and fatigue. Mental health challenges, such as depression and anxiety, are also relatively common in people with rheumatic diseases. Measures commonly used to assess these symptoms and domains may be free-standing or may be part of the PROMIS suite of measures.

### PROMIS (Patient-Reported d Outcome Measurement Information System)

The National Institutes of Health Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System (PROMIS) initiative was undertaken to improve and standardize measurement of PROs.

The PROMIS measures cover physical, mental, and social health domains, including domains of particular importance in rheumatic conditions, such as pain, fatigue, and function. PROMIS measures may be administered as traditional static questionnaires (known as short forms) or through computer adaptive testing. All PROMIS scale scores can be transformed to T scores, with a mean of 50 and standard deviation of 10, allowing comparisons to the general population and across conditions. Both adult and pediatric measures are available (https://www.healthmeasures. net/search-view-measures); only the adult measures are addressed here. Short forms are available in multiple languages. PROMIS measures have been integrated into some electronic health record systems.

### Pain

The most commonly used measure of pain in rheumatic conditions is a simple rating of pain severity. This may be done as a visual analogue scale or as a numeric rating scale. In a visual analogue scale, a horizontal line is presented, usually 100 cm long, with verbal descriptors at each end (e.g., no pain and severe pain). Respondents are asked to mark the line at a point representing their severity of pain. In a numeric rating scale, respondents would be asked to rate their pain on a scale, typically from 0 to 10 or 0 to 100. Both forms have reasonable reliability, validity, and responsiveness; however, the VAS may be more difficult to implement in clinical settings.115, PROMIS includes several pain measures that have been used in rheumatic conditions. The PROMIS Pain Interference scale assesses the impact of pain on daily activities. It has been used in multiple rheumatic conditions and is reliable, valid, and responsive. 117-119

### Function

The Health Assessment Questionnaire (HAQ), also referred to as the HAQ-Disability Index (HAQ-DI), was the first widely used questionnaire to measure physical function in rheumatology. Published in 1980 for use in RA, its use has since expanded to other rheumatic conditions, either in the original form or slightly modified. Scoring of the HAQ is relatively complex as both ratings of difficulty on 20 items plus answers to an additional 21 items regarding use of assistive devices or help are required. HAQ scores range from 0 to 3, with higher scores indicating more functional impairment. While the HAQ is reliable, valid, and responsive, more recent use shows a proportion of 0 scores (floor effect),121 which limits responsiveness. Multiple variations of the HAQ have since been developed, with the Multidimensional Health Assessment Questionnaire (MDHAQ), currently in greatest use, likely due to its inclusion in the RAPID3.122 The MDHAQ consists of items rating difficulty in 10 daily activities. Scores range from 0 to 3. Despite improvements intended to improve assessment at the lower end of the scale, the MDHAQ has a skewed distribution that may affect responsiveness, specifically the ability to detect improvement among people with low scores (i.e., better function). The HAQ-II was developed to improve the psychometric qualities of the HAQ, specifically to correct floor effects. It includes 10 items with scores ranging from 0 to 3. While demonstrating adequate reliability and validity, the HAQ-II also shows floor effects that may affect its ability to detect improvement at the lower end of the scale. PROMIS includes multiple short forms assessing physical function. The most commonly used in rheumatology are the 4and 10-item versions. The 10-item PROMIS

Physical Function 10a, along with the MDHAQ and the HAQ-II, have been recommended by the American College of Rheumatology as functional status assessments for RA.

Function may also be assessed through performance measures, mostly commonly in rehabilitation settings. The Timed Up and Go (TUG) test measures the ability to rise from a chair, walk 3 meters, turn around, walk back, and sit down. A time longer than 14 seconds is associated with poor health outcomes. Timed walking tests, based either on the time to walk a specified distance (e.g., 400 meters) or the distance covered in a specified time (e.g., 6 minutes), are used primarily in studies of OA or joint replacement. Both measures appear to be reliable and valid in OA populations; use in other conditions is less common. Scores predictive of poor health outcomes (e.g., fast-paced walking test time slower than 1.0 meter/second127) have been established for many timed walking tests. The Osteoarthritis Research Society International (OARSI) has endorsed the TUG and a fast-paced walk (40 meters) as core outcome measures for adults with hip or knee OA. Both are often used to assess function after surgery. Space constraints may limit the use in clinical settings.

The Short Physical Performance Battery (SPPB) was originally developed for use as a measure of frailty in older populations. It consists of a test of balance, timed chair stands, and a 4-meter walk test. Scores range from 0 to 12. The SPPB is predictive of falls and other poor health outcomes; scores lower than 10 are predictive of all-cause mortality. Because of the potential impact of RA on hand function, grip strength, measured either with a full-grip dynamometer or as a "pinch grip" between thumb and forefinger, may be measured in either clinical trial or rehabilitation settings. Reference values are not agreed upon, so the best use of these measures would be to follow individuals over time for deterioration or improvement with treatment.

### Fatigue

While fatigue is a concern for many rheumatic conditions, there are no agreed-upon measures for assessing it. A 2020 review of fatigue outcome measures for rheumatology included almost 20 individual questionnaires. Some were designed for RA, the condition in which the most research on fatigue has been conducted (e.g., Bristol Rheumatoid Arthritis Fatigue scales133,134) ); others are generic (e.g., SF-36 Vitality135) or were developed for other conditions and are now used in rheumatology (e.g., the FACIT-F, which was developed for oncology136,137). Some provide a single score for fatigue, while others yield scores for different domains of fatigue (e.g., physical fatigue, cognitive fatigue, emotional fatigue). More recently, the PROMIS Fatigue measures are gaining popularity. There are multiple fatigue short forms, ranging from four to eight items, as well as the CAT version. The psychometric properties of the PROMIS Fatigue measures have been examined in multiple rheumatic conditions and demonstrated to be adequate.

### Depression and Anxiety

A variety of measures of depression or depressive symptoms have been used in rheumatic conditions. Historically, probably the most common was the Center for Epidemiological Studies-Depression scale (CESD). The CESD contains 20 items, with scores ranging from 0 to 60. Scores of 16 or higher are generally used as an indication for possible depression. Alternative (higher) cut points have been proposed for specific rheumatic conditions. More recently, the various forms of the Patient Health Questionnaire

(PHQ) are used. The longest version, the PHQ-9, was developed to correspond with the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual (DSM) criteria for major depression. Scores range from 0 to 27. PHQ-9 scores of 5, 10, 15, and 20 represent thresholds for mild, moderate, moderately severe, and severe depression, respectively. The PHQ-9 includes a question on suicidality, so if it is used, a realtime plan to follow-up on endorsement of suicidality is needed. The PHQ-8, which excludes the suicidality question, is often used in research settings where real-time follow-up is not feasible. A cut point of 10 or higher is used for defining depression. The psychometric properties of both instruments are strong, including good correspondence with clinical assessments of depression (criterion validity). The PHQ-2 is often used in clinical settings as a screening measure. Scores of 3 or higher yield acceptable correspondence with clinical diagnoses. pROMIS includes both short form and CAT measures for depression. These have been less commonly used but do appear to have acceptable psychometric appear to be reasonable thresholds for defining mild, moderate, moderately severe, and severe depression.

Anxiety has been less frequently studied in rheumatic conditions. The Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7 (GAD-7) is a measure developed to correspond to clinical diagnostic criteria for GAD. Scores range from 0 to 21. The seven-item scale has good reliability and validity, and a cut point of 10 has high correspondence with clinical GAD diagnosis. The two-item GAD-2 can be used 147 Scores of 3 or higher have acceptable as a screening measure. correspondence with clinical diagnoses. The PROMIS Anxiety measures have acceptable psychometric properties. T scores of 60 to 62 appear to correspond to the GAD-7 cut score of 10.148

### Imaging and Biomarker Outcomes

As technology has advanced and there has been improvement in molecular and imaging tests in many areas, these tools have often been used as biomarkers and outcomes in both interventional and observational studies. For example, the assessment and quantification of structural damage over the long term has been an important outcome for decades. Many studies have evaluated scoring systems using radiography, magnetic resonance imaging, computed tomography, and ultrasound to assess the activity and impact of a range of diseases. 149, Table 33.2 briefly summarizes some examples of the most common imaging outcomes that have been utilized in clinical research studies.150-160 Although none of these is discussed in detail in this chapter, it is important to note that each of these should undergo a similar process of validation as other clinical outcome measures.

Imaging and biomarker studies have primarily been performed as part of research studies. There is limited evidence at this time to suggest that these biomarkers are useful in routine clinical practice. There have been several examples of studies demonstrating no clear benefit of incorporating imaging outcomes into clinical care compared with using clinical assessments alone in the management of RA.161, Thus future study is needed to determine what value these outcomes will play in the care of patients with rheumatic diseases.

### Health Outcomes in Real-World Settings

Health outcomes, including patient-reported outcomes, may often be collected as part of clinical care and recorded in the health record. These can either be collected purposefully to facilitate

research and to monitor quality of care or may be derived from variables that are incidentally collected or extractable. Automated processes may provide this information directly to clinical providers through clinical dashboards or can be stored for later queries. For example, the collection of health outcomes in the medical record can then fuel real-world research through large registry studies such as the Rheumatology Informatics System for Effectiveness (RISE) registry managed by the American College of Rheumatology that combine data from numerous individual providers over multiple health systems.

### Conclusion

There has been an explosion of health outcomes in rheumatology over the past several decades. The utility of each of these health outcomes depends on the purpose for which it each is being used as well as its validity, reliability, feasibility, and responsiveness to change, among other qualities. It is important for clinicians and researchers to understand the strengths and weaknesses of health outcomes in order to more appropriately interpret research studies, as well as interpret clinical assessments performed with the goal of managing patients with disease.

### KEY POINTS

Biomarkers are objective measurements that can assist in the diagnosis (e.g., anti-citrullinated protein antibodies in rheumatoid arthritis [RA]), prognosis (e.g., copy number of human leukocyte antigen [HLA]-DR subregion shared epitope in RA), and monitoring activity of diseases (e.g., complement or double-strand DNA autoantibodies in systemic lupus erythematosus [SLE]).

Biomarkers are often used to aid development of therapeutics to assess effects on target pathway modulation, as surrogate endpoints for clinical efficacy, or as predictors of adverse events.

Discovery and development of biomarkers for clinical utility is a complex and challenging process requiring considerations of many factors that affect their reliability and reproducibility.

Co-development of companion diagnostics with therapeutics requires a high degree of coordination so that qualified and validated assays are in place in time for each phase of therapeutic development.

In osteoarthritis (OA), biomarkers to identify patients at high risk for cartilage loss as well as for predicting future cartilage loss will greatly aid development of disease-modifying OA drugs.

In RA, biomarkers to identify pre-RA patients at high risk of developing clinical RA, to identify patient subsets that have greater clinical benefit with targeted therapeutics, and to predict patients with greater bone and cartilage loss would advance disease understanding and development of therapeutics.

In SLE, biomarkers that predict disease activity and end organ involvement will greatly aid patient care.

### Biomarker Definitions and Applications

Biomarkers or biologic markers represent objective measurements of a patient at a given time. They are widely used in medicine for the diagnosis, prognosis, and monitoring of disease activity. In drug discovery and development, they are often used to predict the degree of pharmacologic activity by a therapeutic candidate and as surrogate endpoints for potential toxicities and clinical efficacy. Use of surrogate biomarkers to establish therapeutic efficacy in registrational trials is also an accepted route for accelerated regulatory approval for therapeutics.

The definition of biomarkers has evolved over the past decades. In 1993 the International Programme on Chemical Safety defined biomarker to include "any measurement reflecting an interaction between a biological system and a potential chemical, physical

or biological hazards (including) functional and physiological, biochemical at the cellular level, or a molecular interaction."2 In 2001, a Biomarkers Definitions Working Group commissioned by the National Institutes of Health (NIH) broadened its definition CC as "a characteristic that is objectively measured and evaluated as an indicator of normal biological processes, pathogenic processes, or pharmacologic responses to a therapeutic intervention."3 Biomarkers have evolved to be important tools that have significant potential to guide both clinical management and development of therapeutics. In 2016 the United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and NIH collaboratively published The Biomarkers, EndpointS, and other Tools (BEST) Resource glossary to promote the consistent use of biomarker terms and concepts. BEST defines a biomarker as "a defined characteristic that is measured as an indicator of normal biological processes, pathogenic processes, or responses to an exposure or intervention, including therapeutic interventions." They can aid in the diagnosis of disease (diagnostic), determine the potential for developing the disease (susceptibility/risk), assess the status of disease (monitoring), predict the future course of disease (prognostic), evaluate target engagement in response to a therapeutic (pharmacodynamic response), identify responders and nonresponders (predictive and complementary), and determine safety. Definitions of each biomarker category are listed in Table 34.1 and schematized in Fig. 34.1.

### Defining Patient Heterogeneity

A major challenge in biomarker discovery and translation into clinical practice is disease heterogeneity. Most rheumatic diseases, historically considered monotypic, actually comprise multiple molecularly driven pathogenic pathways, although they share a common clinical presentation. In contrast, inherited monogenic diseases, such as hemophilia A, have a common pathogenic cause due to factor VIII (fVIII) deficiency and can be uniformly diagnosed by measuring fVIII levels and treated with fVIII replacement. In addition, the concept that one biomarker can be predictive in defining a patient population in heterogeneous clinical syndromes may need to be replaced by an integrative approach that includes multiple biomarkers, possibly involving more than one technology platform. For example, rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a common rheumatic disease. That only approximately one-third of patients achieve improvement of their ACR50 scores (improvement of 50% in tender or swollen joints and in at

least three of the other five American College of Rheumatology [ACR] response criteria) with targeted therapies underscores the complex and multiple pathogenic causes of this disease. Accordingly, considerable research has focused on understanding patient disease heterogeneity and on identification of markers associated with patient subsets that may reflect their underlying disease pathogenesis and biomarkers that predict therapeutic responses. The ability to match therapy and patient, coined personalized or precision medicine, can have profound benefits for patients to provide them with the most effective therapy and avoid potential toxicities associated with ineffective therapies, as well as for the economics of health care. However, the discovery of such biomarkers and their transfer to clinical practice remains a significant challenge.

### Pitfalls in Translation From Biomarker − Discovery to Clinical Utility −

### Challenges With Biomarker Discovery and Qualification

Discovery and implementation of biomarkers in clinical practice require both analytical method validation and clinical qualification. Analytical method validation is the process of assessing the assay, its performance characteristics, and the optimal conditions that will ensure assay reproducibility and accuracy. Clinical qualification is the process of linking a biomarker with biologic processes and clinical endpoints. Progress in the introduction of new biomarkers into clinical practice has been slow and underscores the multiple challenges of discovery, analytical validation, and clinical qualification of biomarkers.

While there has been a myriad of proposed biomarkers, only a few useful biomarkers have been successfully validated for routine clinical practice. Contributing to the high failure rate is the poor clinical characteristics and qualification of the biomarkers of interest. A qualified biomarker must have adequate sensitivity (be able to correctly identify a high proportion of true positive rate) and specificity (be able to correctly identify a high proportion of true negative rate). Qualification not only requires appropriate bioanalytical methods but also sufficient sample size; statistical analysis; availability of appropriately age-, sex-, and ethnicitymatched samples; information on sample collection, processing, and storage; and detailed knowledge of disease duration, severity, and medications associated with each sample. Each of these parameters will be discussed later.

### Biomarker Assay Qualification and Validation

A critical component of biomarker development is the availability of reliable biomarker assays. Biomarker development often fails early in discovery not because of the underlying science but due to poor assay choice and inappropriate assay validation. Assay qualification/ validation is complex and depends on the context of use (COU) of the biomarker and requires a fit-for-purpose strategy. In addition, the level of biomarker assay validation/qualification can differ between predictive biomarkers intended for clinical decision making and those intended for investigative work to support drug development. While both qualification and validation of analytical methods are designed to prove that the method is suitable for its intended purpose, they differ in terms of the depth and robustness of the evaluation. Qualifications are often sufficient for methods used for investigative evaluations. However, if the biomarker is used for clinical decision making or as a diagnostic associated with a therapeutic (e.g., dosing decisions, safety evaluations, and/or patient selection as with diagnostic markers), the method also needs to be validated.

A number of factors can affect the quality of bioanalytical assays that contribute to the challenges of biomarker discovery and translation to the clinic. It is therefore essential that the assay qualification used includes assessment of the following parameters: (1) precision, which determines closeness in data from replicate determinations of the same sample under normal assay conditions; (2) analytical measurement range, which is the concentrations of analyte or assay values between the low and high limits of quantitation for which there are suitable levels of precision, accuracy, and linearity; (3) sensitivity, which is the smallest concentration of analyte that can be measured accurately and precisely; (4) parallelism, which includes assessment of the effects of dilution on quantitation of endogenous analyte(s) and confirmation of similar performance of calibrators and endogenous analyte in the assay; (5) selectivity/specificity, which is the ability to assess the target analyte in matrices (e.g., serum, plasma, synovial fluid, or urine) without interference from matrix components—a method that is selective for an analyte or group of analytes is said to be specific; (6) accuracy, which is the degree of closeness of the determined value to the nominal or known true value; and (7) stability of analytes and assay components to ensure shortand long-term reproducibility.

Biomarker qualification includes establishing that the analytical performance characteristics of a biomarker are acceptable for the proposed COU. This includes pre-analytical considerations including sample type, sample collection times, sample stability, study design, and biologic variability of the biomarker in the populations of interest. Research grade assays with well-characterized reagents are typically used in the biomarker discovery phase but often are expensive, time consuming, and typically not automated

to enable application in the clinical commercial setting. Commercial kits are an attractive option, but there are no currently harmonized qualification criteria for kit manufacturers.

### Sample Matrices and Assay Interference

Biomarkers are often measured in readily available matrix such as serum, plasma, and synovial fluid and hence have to be qualified for the disease-specific matrix rather than buffer or samples from healthy volunteers. Matrix interference is defined as "the effect of a substance present in the sample that alters the correct value of the result."8 These interferences are due to interactions between constituents in the sample with one or more reagent components and can be analyte-dependent (caused by matrix components) or analyte-independent (caused by assay components).

Analyte-dependent interference is often caused by endogenous substances including natural, polyreactive antibodies, autoantibodies (heterophiles) such as rheumatoid factor (RF) or human anti-animal antibodies (e.g., human anti-mouse antibodies

[HAMA]). These interferences can alter the measurable concentration of the analyte or alter antibody binding causing erroneous results.9-11 Using sera containing high titers of Fc-reactive heterophilic antibodies (HA), 21 of 170 immunoassay kits tested, including commercially available clinical assays covering 19 analytes, were susceptible to interference from heterophilic antibodies. The presence of RF or HA can augment (positive interference) or inhibit (negative interference) antigen detection by binding the capturing or detecting antibody (Fig. 34.2). RF interference has been reported in a multitude of immunoassay measurements, including tacrolimus, cytokines (interleukin [IL]-1β, IL-4, IL-6, and IL-8), thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), free thyroxine, mast cell tryptase, prostate specific antigen, and CA 19-9.11-14 HA interference can be reduced or eliminated through the use of HA inhibitors such as HeteroBlock, an immunoglobulin-inhibiting reagent to quench HA activity,12 or elimination of the Fc domain of capture or detection antibodies through use of F(ab')2 fragments15 or single-chain fragments (scFv).

Analyte-independent interference can also compromise biomarker assay integrity. As one recent example, biotin or vitamin B7 is a common dietary supplement that can exceed the daily recommended dose (30 µg) by more than 300-fold and is also given at a daily dose of 300 mg in clinical trials of the progressive form of multiple sclerosis. The presence of biotin can interfere with biotin-streptavidin—based diagnostic immunoassays. Biotin interference can result in either falsely high or falsely low results and confounds measurements of thyroid function tests (fT3, fT4, and TSH), estradiol, progesterone, amino-terminal prohormone of brain natriuretic peptide, digoxin, and troponin. The FDA recently released an FDA Safety Communication18 to raise awareness of this under-recognized analyte-independent interference complicating immunoassay performance.

### Impact of Patient Selection on Validation of Biomarkers

Following biomarker discovery, rigor in biomarker validation in a well-designed independent validation patient data set is requisite for success in the clinical setting. Factors to consider in choosing the validation patient population include ensuring a diverse population that reflects the intended use of the biomarker; a balanced population in regard to age, sex, and ethnicity; and consideration of variables including alcohol consumption, tobacco use, body mass index, physical activity, and use of medications. The impact of age and sex on erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and C-reactive protein (CRP) levels is well recognized in rheumatology. 19-21 These factors can have profound impact on the qualification and interpretation of the biomarker or when setting limits for diagnosis.

Biomarker profiles vary widely between ethnic groups, and the clinical significance and implications of these differences are currently poorly understood.22, There are now a number of examples of the impact of genetics on biomarker profiles and disease risk. For instance, Latin American and African populations have a higher risk of type 2 diabetes (T2D) compared with populations with European ancestries.3-5, This difference in risk has been hypothesized to be, at least in part due, to genetic, environmental, lifestyle, and biologic factors27,28 and should be taken into account as it can affect the qualification and interpretation of biomarkers as well as in setting diagnostic thresholds that can leading to inaccurate diagnosis and treatments.' 23 This challenge has recently been addressed by the FDA, which has issued a draft guidance expanding on the 2016 guidance on collection of race and ethnicity data in developing therapeutics in clinical trials. This guidance recommends that sponsors develop and submit a race and diversity plan to address inclusion of clinically relevant populations, increasing enrollment from historically under-represented racial and ethnic populations. This will increase evaluation of therapeutics and their success rate in a more diverse population.

### Pre-analytical Variables

Pre-analytical variables also need to be carefully controlled, especially in early phases of biomarker development. These include specimen collection, processing, storage, shipment, and handling, which can introduce inconsistency into assay results, either systematically or randomly, compromising reproducibility. A classic example involves the importance of temperature in sample handling, processing, and storage of blood samples when assessing complement function and levels. All of these parameters must be established, remain consistent during all phases of biomarker development, and be amenable to real-world practice.

### Surrogate Biomarkers

Primary endpoints are typically utilized to establish the clinical effectiveness of investigational therapies. In RA, primary efficacy endpoints in clinical response and physical function can be assessed by the ACR response criteria or Disease Activity Score 28 (DAS28) and Health AssessmentDisability Index (HAQ-DI), respectively. Additional endpoints include prevention of structural damage progression supported by radiographic evidence and clinical remission based on the durability of the remission response. In systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), the primary efficacy endpoints in clinical response to support development of therapeutics include reduction in disease activity using a disease activity index, complete clinical response/remission, reduction in flare or increase in time to flare, reduction in concomitant steroid use, and treatment of acute clinical manifestations.24, Many of these endpoints require prolonged clinical study. An alternative to these clinical endpoints is the use of "surrogate" endpoints. Surrogates are biomarkers that are indirect measures, including physical signs of disease and laboratory measurements and radiographic tests that are expected to predict clinical benefit or harm. There are numerous advantages for use of surrogate biomarker endpoints, including smaller sized or shorter duration clinical studies resulting in cost and time savings, as well as the more quantitative nature of many surrogate biomarkers, compared with clinical endpoints.

While surrogate biomarkers offer significant advantages, their ability to reliably predict clinical efficacy adds uncertainty in the regulatory process. Surrogate biomarkers that strongly correlate with clinical efficacy measures but are not in the disease causal pathway are fraught in their translation to clinical efficacy endpoints.
