So-called CD28null T cells are believed to have undergone reprogramming, leading to premature senescence. 19, Expansion of these senescent T cells among people with RA is associated with extraarticular inflammatory manifestations, including vasculitis, lung disease, and CAD.19, In the setting of heart disease, CD28null T cells are identified in atherosclerotic plaque, where they are believed to contribute to the inflammatory process by producing cytokines and by killing vascular smooth muscle cells. Interestingly, HLA-DRB1, the aforementioned RA-risk gene, also predisposes to expansion of CD28null T cells in RA and in CAD.

Premature senescence of T cells in RA appears to be caused by fundamental defects in the hematopoietic system. CD34+ hematopoietic progenitor cells have accelerated telomere erosion, a sign

of senescence. Naive T cells in people with RA also are prematurely aged, with increased fragility and damage of their DNA because of insufficient activity of basic DNA repair enzymes. Similarly, telomere shortening in hematopoietic progenitor cells correlates with myocardial dysfunction in people with CAD. The onset of both RA and CVD coincides with the loss of thymic emigration of naive T cells in the fifth decade, which suggests that T cell senescence may contribute to the pathogenesis of both of these age-associated conditions. In the foreseeable future, rejuvenation of senescent T cells with the use of new drugs, which restore genomic repair and integrity, has the potential to be an effective strategy for the prevention and treatment of CVD.

### Cardiovascular Morbidity and Mortality in Rheumatoid Arthritis and Systemic Lupus Erythematosus

### Rheumatoid Arthritis

### Ischemic Heart Disease in Rheumatoid Arthritis

Patients with RA are at increased risk of ischemic heart disease (IHD).3, Indeed a recent meta-analysis and systematic review of 2355 article once again confirmed an excess risk of cardiovascular events among persons with RA compared with those without (relative risk [RR], 1.55; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.18 to 2.02). Notably, data from the Rochester Epidemiology Project

have shown that in the 2-year period immediately preceding the fulfillment of the American College of Rheumatology (ACR) 1987 criteria, people with RA were more likely to experience hospitalization for MI (odds ratio [OR], 3.17; 95% CI, 1.16 to 8.68) and unrecognized ("silent") MI (OR, 5.86; 95% CI, 1.29 to 26.64) than ageand sex-matched control subjects. The increased risk of unrecognized MI persisted after the diagnosis of RA (hazard ratio [HR], 2.13; 95% CI, 1.13 to 4.03). One group31 failed to demonstrate a statistically significant elevated increase in MI, angina, or heart failure (HF) prior to the onset of symptoms in two large Swedish cohorts, although trends toward such elevation were reported. As in studies of mortality, these results suggest that accelerated atherosclerosis begins at the onset of RA symptoms, or even earlier, and not at the time of diagnosis or later in the disease course. In a recent study of 11,782 patients with RA and 57,973 ageand sex-matched general population controls, the risk for IHD was significantly higher among RA patients in comparison to controls, independent of traditional CV risk factors.

Patterns of clinical care and outcome after MI may vary in people with RA compared with the general population. Some evidence suggests that, although patients with RA receive MI care similar to that received by patients without RA, they experience higher rates of HF and death after sustaining an MI (Fig. 36.2).29, However, other investigators have reported that patients with RA who experience acute MI receive acute reperfusion and secondary prevention medications (e.g., β-blockers and lipid-lowering agents) less frequently than control subjects. Among patients with MI, those with RA were more likely to undergo thrombolysis and percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) but were less likely to Patients with RA may have an in-hospital survival advantage, particularly those undergoing medical therapy and PCI, although potential confounding could not be ruled out. A recent analysis of 1446 participants with CAD and RA compared with 205,575 participants with CAD without RA showed all-cause death and cardiac death, as well as congestive heart failure, to be significantly higher in CAD patients with coexisting RA compared with the control group of participants with CAD without RA. Notably, other outcomes including repeated revascularization and ischemic

events and even patients undergoing revascularization by PCI were similar in both groups.

### Heart Failure in Rheumatoid Arthritis

People with RA are at increased risk of developing HF compared with the general population.38, In the Rochester RA cohort, the cumulative incidence of HF (defined according to the Framingham criteria) at 30-year follow-up was 34%, compared with 25% in the non-RA cohort (Fig. 36.3). Even after adjustment for demographics, CV risk factors, and IHD, patients with RA had almost twice the risk of developing HF as subjects without RA (HR, 1.87; 95% CI, 1.47 to 2.39). This increased risk of HF appeared to be predominant in the subgroup of patients with rheumatoid factor (RF) who were RF+; the HR in RF+ patients was 2.59 with a 95% CI of 1.95 to 3.43, whereas the HR in RFpatients was 1.28 with a 95% CI of 0.93 to 1.78. These findings were confirmed in a large analysis of two contemporary cohorts of Swedish RA subjects that included 45,982 patients with established RA and 12,943 patients with new onset RA matched 1:10 to general population comparator subjects. A more recent study again confirmed an increased risk for HF among RA patients compared with patients without rheumatologic conditions. The excess risk was independent of traditional cardiovascular risk factors, including prevalent coronary artery disease. Of note, the magnitude of this risk, 21% (95% CI, 3% to 42%), was smaller than previously observed, and it has been hypothesized that this may be a result of more aggressive RA treatment, including the use of biologics, in more recent times.

Patients with RA are at an increased risk for HF that cannot be explained by their increased risk of IHD; this increased risk occurred early and was associated with RA severity. Disease activity and health assessment have been associated with reduced left ventricular systolic myocardial function in RA patients.

The clinical presentation of HF in patients with RA differs from that of HF in patients without RA. Patients with RA who have HF are less likely to be obese or hypertensive or have clinical IHD. Moreover, patients with RA who have HF are less likely to

have typical signs and symptoms. Importantly, the proportion of patients with HF who have preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) (EF >50%) is significantly higher among patients who have RA compared with patients who do not have RA (Fig. 36.4).

### Cardiovascular Mortality in Rheumatoid Arthritis

Mortality of patients with established RA is higher than that of the general population. A meta-analysis of 24 mortality studies in people with RA, which were published between 1970 and 2005, reported a weighted combined all-cause standardized mortality ratio (met-SMR) of 1.50 (95% CI, 1.39 to 1.61) with similar increases for IHD (met-SMR, 1.59; 95% CI, 1.46 to 1.73) and stroke (met-SMR, 1.52; 95% CI, 1.40 to 1.67) and for men (met- SMR, 1.45) and women (met-SMR, 1.58).44-46 Approximately 50% of all deaths in subjects with RA are attributable to CV causes, including IHD and stroke,47 and CVD appears to occur earlier in people with RA. A large community-based prospective cohort study that used UK Biobank data confirmed higher rates of CVDrelated mortality in multiple inflammatory conditions, including RA, and reported, once again, that these events can occur early in the disease course. The latter observation is consistent with the recent hypothesis of accelerated aging in people with RA. Moreover, people with RA frequently experience "silent" IHD and/or silent MI—that is, showing no symptoms at all before a sudden cardiac death. Sudden cardiac deaths are almost twice as common in patients with RA as in the general population (HR, 1.99; 95% CI, 1.06 to 3.55). One group recently demonstrated mortality due to CVD to be increased among Norwegian RA (and axSpA) patients compared with the general population.

The excess CVD mortality related to RA may be confined to, or at least be substantially higher in, subjects who are RF+.51-53

The link may be even stronger with anticitrullinated protein antibody (ACPA) positivity. As might be expected, the RR of CVD mortality is highest in younger age groups (i.e., people younger than 55 years of age) and in women, whereas the attributable risk is highest in the oldest age groups and in men.28,

Controversy persists regarding how soon after symptom onset the excess CVD mortality risk becomes apparent and/or whether there is a secular trend toward improving CVD mortality in people with RA (as is seen in the general population). This controversy may, in part, be explained by differences in the period of follow-up—that is, follow-up starting from the time of symptom onset, from a physician's diagnosis of RA, or from the date of fulfillment of ACR criteria or other diagnostic criteria. The latter may not occur until some years after the first symptoms appear. In the Norfolk Arthritis Register (NOAR), the excess CVD mortality is detectable beginning around 7 years after symptom onset. In a Dutch inception cohort of 1049 patients with RA recruited between 1985 and 2007, excess mortality became apparent at around 10 years after diagnosis (with all subjects having <1 year symptom duration). Emerging evidence indicates that mortality may be improving among people with RA, but CV mortality has also improved in the general population; thus the relative increase in CV mortality in patents with RA compared with the general population has not changed over time. A 2009 metaanalysis that included 17 studies (91,916 patients) also showed no trend toward improving CVD mortality with time. A follow-up analysis from the Mayo Clinic published in 2021 assessed trends in incidence of cardiovascular disease (CVD) and mortality following incident CVD events in patients with RA. On the other hand, importantly, this analysis59 showed that the incidence of major CVD events in RA has declined in recent decades and that the gap in CVD occurrence between patients with RA and the general population is closing.

### Systemic Lupus Erythematosus

### Ischemic Heart Disease in Systemic Lupus Erythematosus

Accelerated atherosclerosis and an increased risk of CAD are well established in SLE.60-65 The prevalence of atherosclerotic vascular events varies from 1.8% early in the course of the disease to more

than 27% later in the course of SLE. The majority of studies reported increased risk of MI ranging from twofold to greater than tenfold in various SLE patient groups compared with the general population.63, This increased RR of MI is particularly apparent in younger patients with SLE. The most striking example comes from the University of Pittsburgh lupus cohort, in which women with SLE aged 35 to 44 years were more than 50 times more likely to have an MI compared with women without SLE in the Framingham Offspring study (RR, 52.43; 95% CI, 21.6 to 98.5). Furthermore, the majority (67%) of women with SLE were younger than 55 years of age at the time of their first cardiac event. In addition, a more than twofold increased risk of hospitalizations for MI have been reported in young women with SLE between the ages of 18 and 44 years compared with people without SLE (OR, 2.27; 95% CI, 1.08 to 3.46).68, As in RA, it appears that the increased risk of CVD among people with SLE may begin before the diagnosis of SLE (OR, 3.7; 95% CI, 1.8 to 7.9). One report in a population-based study of 70 patients who had SLE compared with 2565 patients who did not have SLE supported similar findings. The risk of CVD and mortality also increased tenfold among women with SLE who had successful deliveries, despite the rarity of CVD among women of reproductive age.

More recently a large case-control study (5018 patients with SLE and 25,090 ageand sex-matched controls) was conducted in Israel examining the association between ischemic heart disease and SLE. Multivariate analysis demonstrated that SLE was strongly associated with IHD (OR, 3.77; 95% CI, 3.34 to 4.26), confirming that SLE patients (especially women) suffer from an excess risk of IHD and that SLE is an independent risk factor for IHD.

In a study of patients undergoing coronary revascularization procedures, no significant differences were found in the mean percentage of coronary stenosis and total occlusion in subjects with and without SLE. Except for the increased likelihood of lesions confined to the left anterior descending artery in subjects with SLE versus subjects without SLE (42% versus 19%; P = .003), the pattern of coronary involvement, including artery dominance and prevalence of multivessel disease, appeared similar in subjects with SLE versus subjects without SLE. However, the study reported significantly worse CV outcomes at 1 year after PCI in subjects with SLE versus subjects without SLE, including higher risk of MI (16% versus 5%; P = .01) and repeat PCI (31% versus 12%; P = .009) in people with SLE, even after adjustment for important covariates.68, Given the increased vulnerability of coronary atherosclerosis in people with SLE, which is associated with the risk of occlusive events irrespective of the size of the plaque, these findings suggest an increased risk of unfavorable CV events in people who had SLE compared with people who did not have SLE with a seemingly similar pattern of coronary involvement.

A large population-based study from 1996 to 2000 of patients hospitalized in California with acute MI showed that in-hospital mortality and length of stay were essentially similar in patients who had SLE compared with patients who did not have SLE; the study adjusted for age, race, ethnicity, type of medical insurance, and Charlson Index. In contrast, data from the 1993 to 2002 U.S. Nationwide Inpatient Sample showed significantly increased rates of in-hospital mortality (RR, 1.46; 95% CI, 1.31 to 1.61) and prolonged hospitalization (RR, 1.68; 95% CI, 1.43 to 2.04) for acute MI in people who had SLE compared with control subjects after adjusting for age, sex, race/ethnicity, income, and HF. Differences in methodology (e.g., a smaller sample size, older age

of patients and controls in the earlier study, potential ascertainment bias, and a shorter observation period in the later study) may partially explain these contrasting results. Considering the presence of myocardial involvement, chronic systemic inflammation, vasculitis, and hyperviscosity syndrome in SLE, worse outcomes after acute coronary events and associated interventions can be expected. Further CVD risk in other rheumatic diseases will also be briefly reviewed. Additional studies are warranted.

Given these well-documented excess risks, studies have called for research assessing the predictive ability of biomarkers, imaging techniques, and other monitoring tools to address the initial (potentially reversible) stages of atherosclerosis. Promising results have been reported for CV magnetic resonance (CMR) as a tool to detect subclinical cardiac involvement in SLE78; however, these findings have not been replicated.

### Heart Failure in Systemic Lupus Erythematosus

The risk of HF and related hospitalization in people with SLE appears to be substantially increased.68, In particular, young women with SLE between the ages of 18 and 44 years have more than a 2.5-fold increased risk of hospitalization for HF compared with people who do not have SLE, even after adjustment for age, race, insurance status, hospital characteristics, and the presence of hypertension (HT), diabetes mellitus (DM), and chronic renal failure. A recent large multicenter population-based study further elucidated risk factors for heart failure, identifying 523 (2.3%) HF cases among 1466 children, 2163 young adults, and 19,349 adults age 25 to 44 with SLE. In this cohort 50% or more of HF diagnoses in children and young adults presented near the time of initial SLE diagnosis, reminiscent of similar observations in RA. Also, several risk factors for the development of HF later in the disease course were identified, including baseline cardiac or renal involvement and antiphospholipid antibody syndrome, as well as modifiable CV risk factors such as HT. The study also reported significant racial disparities in HF risk and indicated that early antimalarial use may be associated with a decreased risk of HF.

The nature of HF in SLE is likely multifactorial and only partly attributable to atherosclerosis.81, The presentation of HF in people with SLE may vary from severe overt HF to insidious myocardial involvement. 81-85 Finally, mortality in patients with SLE who have HF is significantly higher than in patients without HF (18% versus 6%, P < .001) and approximates 3.5-fold compared with patients who have HF in the general population.

### Cardiovascular Mortality in Systemic Lupus Erythematosus

Mortality in SLE follows a bimodal pattern, with an early peak in mortality (within 1 year of diagnosis) and a later peak occurring more than 5 years after diagnosis. Reported survival in the first 5 years of SLE has improved considerably from about 50% in the 1950s to greater than 90% in the 1990s. However, this improvement may be due, at least in part, to earlier diagnosis and improved ascertainment of mild cases. In the Toronto lupus cohort of 1241 patients recruited between 1970 and 2005, the SMR improved from 13.84 (95% CI, 9.78 to 19.76) during 1970 to 1978 for those who entered the cohort in that decade to 3.81 (95% CI, 1.98 to 7.32) during 1997 to 2005 in people who entered the cohort in that period. The SMR during 1997 to 2005 was very similar for patients regardless of their disease duration; it ranged from 3.23 for those who had entered the cohort in 1970 to 1978 to 3.93 for those who had entered the cohort in 1988 to 1996. Similarly, evidence from Olmsted County showed

an SMR of 2.70 with significant improvement in survival in recent decades. In a study of 434 female patients with SLE from Seoul, Korea, who were followed up from 1992 to 2002, the SMR was 3.02 (95% CI, 1.45 to 5.55). A recent population-based cohort study of 70 patients with incident SLE in 1991 to 2008 reported nearly twofold increased mortality and increased CVD rates. In addition, increased mortality and CVD event rates were found perioperatively in women with SLE who were undergoing surgical procedures, even for low-risk procedures (OR, 1.54; 95% CI, 1.00 to 2.37). A community-based prospective cohort study from the United Kingdom showed increased CV-related mortality in SLE and emphasized the public health value of early screening and effective preventive strategies.

More recently a carefully conducted, 10-year case-control study from the Karolinska Institute showed that patients with mild SLE have a threeto fourfold increased risk of incident CV events and mortality compared with controls with the same levels of traditional risk factors and intima-media measures (by carotid ultrasound). These findings appear to be related to accumulated disease damage and antiphospholipid syndrome. Notably, the early observations of a bimodal pattern in mortality was not seen in this study. Rather the findings were more in line with longterm follow-up studies that revisited the concept of the bimodal pattern of mortality in SLE and showed the importance of both disease severity and moderate to severe atherosclerosis for death of any cause in patients with SLE after a prolonged duration of the disease.

### Risk Factors for Cardiovascular Disease

Evidence for the pivotal role of inflammation in driving increased CVD risk in people with RA is compelling, yet despite improved

control of inflammation, CVD risk among people with RA remains elevated. Moreover, the identification of clinically valuable biomarkers of CVD risk in people with RA remains elusive. In the next sections, we highlight recent evidence and discussions regarding the relative contribution of traditional and nontraditional risk factors (e.g., markers of inflammation and RA features) toward the excess CVD risk in people with RA and suggest directions for future research.

### Traditional Cardiovascular Risk Factors in Rheumatoid Arthritis: Occurrence and Impact

In the general population, five major CVDRFs (i.e., HT, elevated total cholesterol [TC] levels, smoking, obesity, and DM) account for 80% of the risk for MI95 and half of the CV mortality. Moreover, a recent meta-analysis found that these five major CVDRFs also increased the risk of CVD in patients with RA. One possible explanation for the increase in CVD in people with RA could be that the traditional CVDRFs are more common in people with RA or that they are as common but more deleterious. The five CVDRFs (i.e., HT, elevated TC, smoking, obesity, and DM) were comparable across patients with RA, ankylosing spondylitis (AS), and psoriatic arthritis (PsA), except for more HT and obesity in the older age categories. In addition, the excess CVD risk may also be explained by the adverse impact of the inflammatory and immune changes of RA on the vessel wall. It is most likely, however, that traditional risk factors and inflammation are intimately interconnected and perhaps act synergistically (Fig. 36.6). Indeed, one study showed that progression of a new CVD event in subjects with early RA may be predicted by traditional CVDRFs but precipitated by high disease activity.

### Disparities in Cardiovascular Risk

Currently, there are controversial results on the influence of sex in the risk of CV morbidity and mortality in patients with RA and other inflammatory joint diseases (IJDs). RA is more common in women, whereas AS is more frequent in men, and the sexes are equally represented in PsA. This different prevalence according to sex of the IJDs makes it difficult to conclude on the actual influence of sex on the risk of CVD and heart complications in these chronic inflammatory rheumatic diseases. Further studies addressing this specific issue are still needed.

A study on socioeconomic status on CV risk screening and management revealed that at least 25% of the patients with high CV risk did not follow the recommendation to contact their general practitioner for a follow-up. Higher education decreased the odds to follow recommendations for a follow-up. The diagnosis of SpA, AS, or PsA significantly increased the odds of having a consultation at general practice with a relevant action compared with RA patients. Sex, age, diagnosis, cohabitant status, and employment status did not influence whether the high-risk patients consulted their general practitioner.

### Smoking in People With Rheumatoid Arthritis

The link between tobacco smoking and CVD events is well known and is identified both in the general population and in patients with RA.97, Smoking is a known risk factor for the development of RA, in particular RF+ and ACPA+ RA. In a meta-analysis of four case-control studies of traditional CVDRFs in RA that included 1415 patients with RA, the prevalence of smoking was found to be significantly higher than in control subjects (OR, 1.56; 95% CI, 1.35 to 1.80). A known interaction exists between smoking, HLA-DR1 shared epitope (SE) alleles, and the production of ACPA105 and between smoking, ACPA, and the SE in premature CVD mortality in RA. There are some discrepancies regarding smokers with RA having higher disease activity. 107, In the A TransAtlantic Cardiovascular Consortium for Rheumatoid Arthritis patients (ATACC-RA) register, in which 3311 RA patients were followed for a median of 3.5 years, smoking cessation resulted in comparable disease activity as nonsmokers and having a significant lower disease activity compared with smokers. Furthermore, smoking cessation was a predictor of reduced CVD event rates in patients with RA.

### Hypertension in Rheumatoid Arthritis

HT is common in people with RA, but it remains unclear whether it is more common than in the general population. Whereas some studies have found HT to be an important risk factor for CVD in people with RA, 110 a recent meta-analysis of seven case-control studies (1053 patients with RA) found the prevalence of HT to be the same in people with RA as in control subjects (OR, 1.09; 95% CI, 0.91 to 1.31). However, evidence exists for underdiagnosis and undertreatment of HT in people with RA.111, Multiple other factors may influence blood pressure control in people with RA, including physical inactivity, obesity, specific genetic polymorphisms, smoking, and some anti-rheumatic medications, including nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), corticosteroids, leflunomide, and cyclosporine. In a recent systematic review from 2021, the conclusion was that overall, there is a paucity of research investigating factors associated with incident HT among RA patients in longitudinal studies. The findings indicated that regular exercise and methotrexate (MTX) may protect against HT, while corticosteroids and COX-2 inhibitors may increase risk of HT in RA patients. Physicians should consider these risks when prescribing anti-rheumatic medication to their patients.

### Blood Lipids in People With Rheumatoid Arthritis

There is a complex relationship between low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C), high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL- C), and risk of CVD, and this is nonlinear in RA patients and not different from non-RA people114 (Fig. 36.7A). RA patients have lower lipid levels related to disease activity/inflammation (Fig. 36.7B). Effective anti-rheumatic treatment, decreasing inflammation, has an "adverse" effect on lipids that manifests as the level increases (Fig. 36.7C). Knowing that high cholesterol level is a major risk factor for future CVD and is a major component in CVD risk calculators, this may make it difficult to predict the risk for future CVD in RA patients. Lower total and LDL-C levels are associated with higher CVD risk. In fact, despite lower total cholesterol levels in 1779 RA patients followed for approximately 8 years, they had an increased risk of both myocardial infarction and ischemic stroke compared with nearly 400,000 non-RA people in the AMORIS study.

Suppression of total and LDL-C levels during acute or chronic high-grade inflammation is well described, as is a proportionately greater suppression of HDL-C, which resulted in a disadvantageous TC: HDL-C ratio. This phenomenon may explain why hyperlipidemia (i.e., high TC or LDL-C) appears to be less common in people who have RA compared with subjects who do not.115, Indeed, even among patients who sustained a previous MI, those with RA had significantly lower levels of total and LDL-C than did those without. Dyslipidemia (i.e., alterations of individual lipid components and their ratios as defined by specific criteria) may affect up to half of all people with RA. A recent metaanalysis showed that RA is associated with an abnormal lipid pattern, principally low levels of HDL-C. An in vitro animal model and in vivo human studies clearly demonstrate that the interplay between inflammation and lipid components is far more complex than simple alterations of their serum levels (Fig. 36.8).

Inflammation-induced alterations of the structure and function of lipid molecules require further study, specifically in people with RA and in the context of disease control through nonbiologic and biologic disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs (DMARDs). Several studies suggest anti-rheumatic therapy effects on lipid levels, including glucocorticoids, hydroxychloroquine, gold, and cyclosporine, and the biologics, which include TNF inhibitors, rituximab, and tocilizumab, as well as the newer Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitors (see Table 36.1 for list of RA medications). 126, However, these studies are of short duration, and more research is needed. Multiple other factors are involved in lipid regulation and function, including physical activity, adiposity, diet, alcohol intake, and smoking. However, their effects have not been assessed in sufficient detail in people with RA. Similarly, the importance of genetic regulation of lipid metabolism, particularly in the context of gene—environment interactions, has not been addressed in the RA population. This factor may be particularly important because lipid alterations appear to predate the diagnosis of RA. Although the relationships between lipids and CVD in RA are complex, the value of primary lipid screening in people with RA is undisputed. Unfortunately, evidence suggests an unacceptably low rate of primary lipid screening and of statin use in people with RA.122, This has not improved over the years, as shown in a recent large international survey including RA patients from 19 countries between 2014 and 2019.132

### Diabetes Mellitus and Metabolic Syndrome in Rheumatoid Arthritis

The prevalence of DM has increased in patients with RA in comparison with control subjects. Likewise, patients with RA were

significantly more likely to have metabolic syndrome than were subjects who did not have RA.133, Abdominal obesity, antihypertensive medication, disease activity, and use of corticosteroids all affect glucose metabolism in RA. On the other hand, use of hydroxychloroquine reduces the risk of developing DM in people with RA by approximately 77%. Epidemiologic studies on RA and non-RA subjects indicate that RA patients and diabetics have twice the risk of CVD compared with nondiabetic, non- RA individuals, and that DM accounts for 3% to 10% of CVD events. 137-139

### Body Composition/Obesity in Rheumatoid Arthritis

High body mass index (BMI) signifies excess weight and is a surrogate marker for elevated adipose tissue. BMI ≥25 kg/m2 and ≥30 kg/m2 is the standard definition for overweight and obese, respectively. Globally, the World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that 650 million of the adult populations in 2016 were obese (13% of the worldwide population). Interestingly, there are profound differences across regions, as prevalence of obesity varies from 5% in South East Asian populations to 29% in the United States. IJD patients may be at increased risk of unwanted weight gain due to physical inactivity and prolonged use of corticosteroids. 142

One study143 reported a "paradoxical effect of BMI on survival in people with RA," demonstrating that as BMI declined, so did survival probability among study subjects with RA. Among people without RA, low BMI is not associated with increased risk of CV

death. However, among patients with RA, low BMI, which may indicate uncontrolled active systemic inflammation, is associated with a threefold increased risk of CV death144 even after adjustment for cardiac history, smoking, DM, HT, and malignancy.

Obesity is associated with the development of RA.145, Obesity is also associated with an increased frequency of traditional CV risk factors in patients with RA. In particular, abdominal fat is associated with insulin resistance and inflammatory load in patients with RA, and new evidence indicates that in such patients, abdominal fat is distributed differently between the visceral and subcutaneous compartments, with visceral fat more strongly associated with cardiometabolic risk.148, Adipose tissue is metabolically active and, through a network of adipocytokines, regulates not only energy intake and expenditure but also inflammation.

Regardless, attentive management of obesity in inflammatory rheumatic diseases is warranted because obesity increases the risk of developing other CVDRFs (e.g., HT, DM, and hypercholesterolemia) 150-152 and because it induces a pro-inflammatory state characterized by impaired anti-inflammatory treatment response. 153, Interventions to reverse cachexia and to control obesity in people with RA have been inadequately studied.

### Impact of Rheumatoid Arthritis Disease Activity on Cardiovascular Comorbidity

A number of studies have linked CVD risk with markers of RA disease activity, such as CRP and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR).27, In a study of 231 male veterans with RA, a

baseline disease activity score (DAS28) greater than or equal to 5.1 predicted CV events (HR, 1.3; 95% CI, 1.1 to 1.6). Markers of disease severity, such as RF, ACPA, physical disability, destructive changes on joint radiographs, rheumatoid nodules, vasculitis, and rheumatoid lung disease, are statistically significant and associated with increased risk of CV events and/or death even after adjustment for traditional CV risk factors.54, RA flares have been associated with an increased risk of CVD, whereas patients in remission were found to have CVD risks similar to subjects without RA (Fig. 36.9). A large international cohort of patients with RA demonstrated that 30% of CVD events were attributable to RA characteristics. Thus RA characteristics should play an important role in efforts to reduce CVD risk in RA.

### Medications and Cardiovascular Risk

Medications used for the treatment of rheumatic diseases may also affect CVD risk. Because of the common use of NSAIDs and concerns surrounding CVD risk with their use, this subject has been extensively studied. Although some evidence indicates that NSAID use is not associated with increased CVD risk in people with RA,163 a meta-analysis of 31 trials in 116,429 patients concluded that there was little evidence to suggest that any of the investigated drugs (i.e., naproxen, ibuprofen, diclofenac, celecoxib, etoricoxib, rofecoxib, or lumiracoxib) were not safe in relation to CVD. In contrast, use of DMARDs (methotrexate and hydroxychloroquine in particular) and/or biologic agents may decrease CVD risk.165-170 A recent large meta-analysis evaluating b-DMARDS on risk of CV event, including 55 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and 17 cohort studies in patients with RA, psoriasis, and SLE, found that b-DMARDS reduced CVD events. Although these results were mostly driven by the reduced events in RA patients,171 this outcome likely reflects effective long-term control of systemic inflammation. Although these findings are intriguing, they cannot be considered definitive evidence that these agents reduce CVD risk because of confounding by indication and/or contraindication. Reports of the effect of corticosteroids on CVD risk are conflicting, but low doses (<7.5 mg/day) may be beneficial, and high doses may be detrimental.172-174 A

study in an early RA, treatment-naive RCT cohort with no known CV history and maximum of one traditional risk factor (excluding diabetes) revealed that abnormal vascular stiffness (which predicts major CV events independently of traditional clinical risk scoring models in patients without known CVD) and evidence of diffuse myocardial fibrosis and reduced left ventricular mass. First-line etanercept with methotrexate or initial methotrexatetreat-to-target strategy improved vascular stiffness. However, RA treatment response and cumulative disease activity did not appear to add to this improvement in vascular stiffness. JAK inhibitors (consisting of tofacitinib, baricitinib, and upadacitinib) are a class of targeted synthetic DMARDs that are increasingly used for management of patients diagnosed with moderate to severely active RA.176, In an RCT comparing tofacitinib with a TNF inhibitor in a cardiovascular risk—enriched population, risks of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACEs) and cancers were higher with tofacitinib. Several adverse events were more common with tofacitinib. Concerns regarding venous thromboembolism related to JAK inhibitor treatments have been raised, but evidence is not conclusive. Consequently, in the longer term, large studies are needed to accurately quantify thromboembolic risks attributable to JAK inhibitors and other drugs used to treat RA and to differentiate these risks from those attributable to RA itself and its comorbidities.

During the past few decades, mounting evidence on CVD risk in RA has led to advances in CVD risk management in this patient modern DMARD medications versus placebo are not ethically sound and will never be done. However, several DMARDs, especially methotrexate, TNF inhibitors, and IL-6 inhibitors, seem to improve various biomarkers of CVD and are associated with reduced risk of CV events in observational studies among RA cohorts.

### Traditional and Nontraditional Cardiovascular − Risk Factors in Systemic Lupus Erythematosus S

While the traditional CV risk factors may not fully explain the increased CV risk observed in SLE patients, they are frequent and need to be addressed to prevent CV events.63, For instance, SLE patients have increased levels of elevated LDL cholesterol and triglycerides, as well as high prevalences of sedentary lifestyles, smoking, premature menopause, chronic renal impairment, HT, hyperhomocysteinemia, metabolic syndrome, and insulin resis- 182-187 Indeed, SLE patients with HT or dyslipidemias have tance. higher risk of experiencing an MI or stroke.18,189 g Since SLE is a relatively uncommon disease, scientific documentation of the effects of common CV preventive medication is scarce, and existing studies often have designs that are prone to confounding. Based on the scarce available evidence, the authors of the first European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology (EULAR) recommendation for CV risk management in SLE patients, published in 2022, advocates for a blood pressure (BP) target of <130/80 and that one should follow recommendations for the general population in dyslipidemia treatment.

The association between systemic inflammation and CV risk is well known and has been described in detail previously in this chapter. High cumulative disease activity appears to be an important cause of the high CV event rates reported in SLE patients. Although some studies have not found an association between recent assessments of SLE disease activity and future risk for CV events, 190,191 this is likely because SLE is a chronic

remitting-relapsing disease and because atherosclerotic CV disease takes years to develop. In fact, previous studies have shown that prolonged disease remission is associated with better CV outcomes, and in the EULAR recommendations for CV risk management in SLE, maintaining low disease activity is recommended to reduce the CV risk.181, Although no specific immunosuppressive medicine could be recommended due to limited scientific knowledge, the lowest possible glucocorticoid dose should be used to minimize adverse cardiometabolic effects.

### Cardiovascular Mortality, Morbidity, and Risk Factors in Other Rheumatic Diseases

### Ankylosing Spondylitis

The risk of CV disease in people with AS is less well defined than for RA. The available data point toward increased mortality rates in AS patients compared with the general population.50, It appears that increased frequencies of CVD is a main driver of the increased mortality in AS patients, although they seem to be at lower risk than RA patients. 197-199 Traditional CVD risk factors, including dyslipidemia and HT, are commonly found in AS patients, and there exists much room for improvement in terms of introducing and intensifying preventive measures to obtain lipid and blood pressure treatment goals.194,200

### Psoriasis and Psoriatic Arthritis

Increased rates of CVD morbidity in cutaneous psoriasis and PsA patients relative to the general population have been reported, although, as in AS patients, the documentation is less strong than for people with RA. While a great deal of heterogeneity exists in the studies in this field, two meta-analyses have reported a pooled odds ratio (95% CI) of MI and stroke of 1.19 (1.11 to 1.27) and 1.46 (1.26 to 1.69) in cutaneous psoriasis, while it was 1.68 (1.31 to 2.15) and 1.2 (1.05 to 1.41) in PsA.202, Several studies have reported a striking increase in the metabolic syndrome, meaning a co-occurrence of several traditional CVD risk factors including obesity, insulin resistance, dyslipidemia, and HT, in patients with cutaneous psoriasis and PsA. 204-208 While there is an unmet need for traditional CVD-preventive measures in PsA patients, the frequency of various CVD events remains high even after adjusting for traditional CVD risk variables. 209,

Interestingly, while there is a small but significant increase in CVD related mortality in patients with cutaneous psoriasis, there are now controversies regarding whether the rates of CVD mortality are raised in PsA patients compared with the general population.50, Although the underlying reasons for these rather surprising results have yet to be settled, it may be due to improved PsA therapies, and there may still be excess mortality due to CVD in patients with more aggressive disease.

### Giant Cell Arteritis, Takayasu's Arteritis, and Polymyalgia Rheumatica

Although there are some conflicting data on the risk of cardiovascular disease in giant cell arteritis (GCA),212-215 recent analyses indicate an increased mortality from CVD.216, The increased risk of vascular events is due to both direct and indirect effects of .218, For GCA, a relationship that can be complex to delineate. Takayasu's arteritis, a meta-analysis found the pooled prevalence

of stroke to be 8.9 and 3.4, respectively, suggesting up to a tenfold increase in severe cardiovascular events in this patient group. Traditional CV risk factors are also more common in patients with Takayasu's arteritis. Previous treatment recommendations for large vessel vasculitis (GCA and Takayasu's arteritis) have indicated that aspirin should be used for primary prevention in these diseases, but recent data have led to newer recommendations that treatment with platelet inhibitors should follow recommendations used in the general population.

A few studies have reported increased risks for CVD in patients with polymyalgia rheumatica, which are similar to the risk levels reported in other inflammatory diseases.22, However, two systematic reviews found the studies to be heterogenous, suggesting that more research is needed to definitively determine whether the risk of CVD is increased in polymyalgia rheumatica. 224,225

### Anti-neutrophil Cytoplasmic Antibodies (ANCA)- Associated Vasculitis

ANCA-associated vasculitis is a heterogenous group of diseases including granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA, previously termed Wegener's granulomatosis),226 microscopic polyangiitis (MPA),227 and eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA, previously termed Churg—Strauss syndrome). A population-based study demonstrated a threefold increased risk of CVD and an eightfold increased risk of cerebrovascular events in patients with ANCA-associated vasculitis without increased prevalence of CV risk factors compared with the general population. The increased risk for CVD has been confirmed in a number of studies. 230-236

### Dermatomyositis and Polymyositis

Cardiac involvement is well recognized as a clinically important manifestation of myositis. In a recent meta-analysis patients with dermatomyositis and polymyositis had a 2.4 times increased risk of CVD, particularly males diagnosed in the previous 5 years. One study found the incidence of cardiovascular events in a combined population of dermatomyositis and polymyositis to be comparable to that of patients with RA in the first 5 years after diagnosis. A report utilizing the Nationwide Inpatient Sample found that one-fifth of dermatomyositis hospitalizations in the United States were associated with an atherosclerotic CV diagnosis or procedure; the report also found that patients with dermatomyositis and CVD have twice the risk of in-hospital death compared with control subjects and patients who have dermatomyositis without CVD.

### Osteoarthritis

Although osteoarthritis is the most common rheumatic disease, little is known about the link between osteoarthritis and CVD. While the link between systemic inflammation and CVD is not as apparent in this degenerative disease as in the IJDs, excessive pro-inflammatory cytokine production also plays a role in the pathogenesis of osteoarthritis. Furthermore, genetic, metabolic, and neuroendocrine factors, as well as lifestyle factors, including sedentary lifestyles, are possible links between CV disease and osteoarthritis. Previous studies have found that patients with osteoarthritis have a high prevalence of CVD risk factors such as HT, dyslipidemia, BMI, and increased fasting glucose levels.242-244 Indeed, a previous meta-analysis reported significantly higher

CVD rates in osteoarthritis patients than in controls; perhaps most striking was the doubled risk of experiencing heart failure or ischemic heart disease. Whether this increased risk is simply a result of high burdens of CVD risk factors or whether osteoarthritis is also an independent risk factor for CVD remains unknown.

### Pediatric-Onset Rheumatologic c Diseases

CVD has been difficult to study in patients with pediatric-onset rheumatologic disease, such as juvenile idiopathic arthritis, pediatric-onset SLE, and juvenile dermatomyositis, as CV events are rare at young ages. However, traditional and disease-related CVD risk factors are evident in children with rheumatic diseases, with juvenile SLE, for example, being associated with premature atherosclerosis beginning in childhood, early myocardial infarction, and stroke.246, Data on hospitalizations in the United States showed juvenile dermatomyositis to be associated with significantly higher odds of cardiovascular and cerebrovascular comorbidities, with adolescents, girls, and racial/ethnic minorities being at highest risk.

Surrogate measures of CVD, such as flow-mediated dilation, carotid intima media thickness, and pulse wave velocity, have been used to explore CVD in children with pediatric-onset rheumatologic diseases. Studies of these measures of subclinical CVD and of lipids have shown increased levels among children with juvenile idiopathic arthritis, pediatric-onset SLE, and juvenile dermatomyositis.249-253 It is likely that these patients wil experience significant CVD morbidity and mortality in adulthood. More studies are needed to better define the increased risk of CVD among patients with pediatric-onset rheumatologic diseases, to design and test preventive strategies to circumvent this eventuality, and to improve the long-term outcomes of these patients. Although data on the increased risk of CVD among patients with less widely studied inflammatory rheumatic diseases are still emerging, CVD has been recognized as an important contribution to increased mortality and morbidity in this patient population and represents an area of ongoing research.

### Managing Cardiovascular Risk in Rheumatic Disease

### Coordinating Care: Cardiology and Rheumatology

Despite the large and growing body of knowledge showing increased risk of CVD in people with RA and other rheumatic diseases, even when controlling for traditional CV risk factors,6 63,254 little translation into clinical care has occurred. Inflammation and immune mechanisms underline the atherosclerotic process. Because traditional risk factors alone do not explain the elevated CVD risk in patients with rheumatic diseases, addressing the control of inflammation is essential to decrease the CVD risk.

Thus close collaboration between the rheumatologist and the cardiologist is vital.127, Not only does the rheumatologic condition need to be treated aggressively to decrease the inflammatory burden but the traditional CV risk factors must also be identified and appropriately treated. Specialized preventive cardiorheuma clinics that specifically address the needs of rheumatologic patients allow these patients to be followed up in a more rigorous fashion, with more uniform evaluation and longitudinal follow-up. Examples of such clinics include the Preventive Cardio-Rheuma

clinic at the Department of Rheumatology at Diakonhjemmet Hospital in Norway and the Cardio-Rheum clinic at the Division of Cardiovascular Diseases at the Mayo Clinic in Rochester, Minnesota. Both models represent deep and ongoing collaborations between the clinical disciplines of rheumatology and preventive cardiology. Integral to both models are (1) extensive patient and provider education regarding CVD risk in the unique setting of autoimmune diseases, such as RA; (2) comprehensive CVD risk assessment including history, physical examination, and use of relevant risk assessment scores, as well as noninvasive and (when indicated) invasive measurement techniques; and (3) development and monitoring of an aggressive plan for CVD risk reduction, considering not only traditional CVD risks but also tight control of systemic inflammation and RA disease management. Each program also includes a clinical research component aimed at continually evaluating and improving the preventive care paradigms.

### Cardiovascular Disease Risk Assessment

### Risk Calculators

As previously discussed, traditional CVD risk factors such as dyslipidemia, HT, and smoking are common inflammatory rheumatic disease entities. However, such traditional CV risk factors alone cannot account for the increased risk of CVD in these patients.63, Moreover, traditional CV risk factors appear to behave differently in patients with inflammatory rheumatic diseases compared with the general population, suggesting that risk scores based on traditional CV risk factors alone are unlikely to accurately estimate CVD risk in these patients. Indeed, risk calculators (e.g., the Framingham Risk Score [FRS]) have underestimated CVD risk twofold in patients with RA. The Systematic COronary Risk Evaluation (SCORE), QRISK II, and Reynolds Risk Score (RRS) CVD risk calculators also underestimate future CV events in patients with RA, except for those in the highest risk classes.254, For SLE patients, several studies have found that SCORE and FRS performs poorly,258,262 even after applying a multiplier of 2.263 More recently, the CVD risk prediction scores have also been tested on hard CVD endpoints in smaller cohorts of AS and PsA patients, with unsatisfying res ults. 187,

The 2012 European Society of Cardiology (ESC) guidelines for CVD prevention were the first to recognize immunologic diseases, such as RA, as CVD risk factors. Later, the presence of RA has also been implemented in CVD risk algorithms such as the United Kingdom CV risk calculators and the QRISK2 and 3, as well as in the Norwegian NORRISK2. 267-269

The EULAR recognizes that patients with IJDs have increased risk for CVD and make recommendations for management of The EULAR task force recommended a multiplication factor of 1.5 to the calculated CVD risk by SCORE for all patients with RA. This multiplier and other RAand SLE-specific risk calculators have generally underperformed or have a lack external documentation of improved prediction accuracy compared with risk calculators used in the general population.270-274 Attempts to apply the 1.5 EULAR RA multiplier in AS and SLE patients have also been disappointing. 263, Further development of accurate CVD risk calculators for patients with chronic inflammatory rheumatic diseases and external validation of previously developed calculators are needed to improve CVD risk prediction in these patients.

### Risk Scores and Risk Markers: Biomarkers and Tests for Subclinical Disease

One reason for underestimation of CVD risk in people with RA may be the high frequency of asymptomatic atherosclerosis, 275-278 which is easily visualized upon ultrasound of the carotid arteries. In addition, carotid artery plaques in patients with RA are predictors of a future acute coronary syndrome. RA-specific factors, such as disease duration and disease activity, have been associated with plaque size and vulnerability in patients with RA. Moreover, in the European guidelines on CVD prevention,280 the presence of carotid artery plaques is considered a CVD equivalent, which suggests that including ultrasound of carotid arteries in the CVD risk evaluation (class IIa, level of evidence: B, GRADE: strong) would increase the proportion of correct risk stratification. Due to the high pre-test probability for detection of carotid artery plaques by use of ultrasound in patients with RA and the clinical consequence of indication for statin treatment if a carotid plaque is present, this procedure could be of additional value for CVD risk evaluation. Ultrasound of the carotid arteries to identify atherosclerosis has reclassified a considerable proportion of patients with RA into a more appropriate CVD risk group in accordance with current guidelines.

Other tests for subclinical disease that might be useful for assessing CVD risk in patients with RA include aortic pulse wave velocity and lipoprotein(a). Soluble biomarkers are also appealing because they are typically less costly and have more widespread availability. However, they also may be more difficult to interpret in patients with rheumatic disease because of their dual association with CVD and rheumatic disease (Fig. 36.10). In conclusion, available CVD risk calculators developed for the general population inaccurately estimate CVD risk in patients with RA but currently represent the best utility for CVD risk evaluation in these patients.

### Managing CVD Risk in Patients With Rheumatic Disease

Patients with RA are significantly less likely to receive CVDpreventive measures compared with the general population. 283 A study showed that despite receiving similar treatment, patients with RA who had an MI experienced worse long-term outcomes than did patients with an MI who did not have RA. This deficiency in CVD risk management is amply confirmed in an investigation of CV risk factor control in 836 patients with RA by one study. Among the most striking observations is that in the 644 patients without established CVD or DM, inadequate blood pressure and lipid control were documented in 36% and 55% of the participants, respectively. Findings from a Preventive Cardio- Rheuma clinic revealed that 63% of the patients referred were in need of CVD-preventive medical intervention.

Statins have established effectiveness in the primary prevention of CV events in the general population and at-risk subpopulations (e.g., patients with DM). These agents have both lipid modifying and anti-inflammatory effects. There exists only one RCT in primary prevention, the TRACE-RA study,286 which compared atorvastatin with placebo. The primary outcome was MACE. Unfortunately, this trial was stopped prematurely due to lower event rate than expected, resulting in a short follow-up time (2.5 years) and only 2986 patients included, which ended in a nonsignificant effect of atorvastatin on MACE. Although, the effect size was 34% risk reduction of a CVD event. This magnitude of

risk reduction is highly significant in other placebo-controlled statin RCTs with longer observation time and a higher number of patients included, indicating that statin treatment in primary prevention in patients with RA is highly effective. Furthermore, there is a paucity in cardiovascular outcome trials concerning CVD prevention as lipid-lowering treatment in patients with RA having established atherosclerotic CVD (ASCVD). Results from a systematic meta-analysis involving 148,722 participants with immune-mediated inflammatory diseases from RCTs or observational studies found that statin use was associated with lower risk of mortality and MACE in such patients having established ASCVD. None of these were RCTs in chronic coronary syndrome patients, although there exist indications from post hoc analyses in the TNT and Incremental Decrease in Endpoints through Aggressive Lipid Lowering (IDEAL) trials that patients with IJDs have comparable lipid-lowering effect and reduction of CVD risk as those without IJDs. RA patients are still undertreated in terms of secondary CVD prevention. 112,

An important CV risk factor in the general population is lipid levels, although lipid levels may appear to be less important for patients with inflammatory rheumatic diseases. However, meta-analyses of RCTs have shown that patients in the general population benefit from lipid-lowering treatment regardless of baseline lipid levels. Clinical experience regarding use of CVDpreventive medications in IJDs is scarce. Results from a Preventive Cardio-Rheuma clinic for patients with IJDs revealed that lipid targets were attained using fewer than three consultations

in 90% of the patients without serious adverse events. These results indicate that treating patients who have RA with statins and achieving recommended lipid goals are safe. Prospective, longitudinal data are needed to demonstrate whether patients with RA need to achieve the same low lipid targets as people without RA or whether a relatively smaller or larger reduction in lipids will result in the same CVD protection as in people without RA.

Modern RA therapy and the multiple comorbidities lead to polypharmacy, thus increasing the possibility of drug to drug interactions with CVD-preventive medications, such as statins. Interaction between anti-rheumatic treatments, such as NSAIDs and synthetic or biologic DMARDs, with CVD-preventive medications is also an area of uncertainty. Neither inflammation (by CRP or ESR levels) nor anti-rheumatic medications, such as NSAIDS, prednisolone, or synthetic or biologic DMARDs, influenced the dose of statin needed to obtain lipid recommended targets. The influence of statins on clinical response and B cell depletion after rituximab treatment in people with RA is inconclusive.292, An increased CVD risk" associated with NSAID use is recognized in the general population,164,294 but in a recent Danish nationwide study, the CVD risk associated with use of NSAIDs in people with RA was modest and significantly lower than in people without RA. Furthermore, NSAIDs interfere with the thrombocyte inhibitory effect of aspirin, which complicates secondary CVD prevention. Observational studies have provided indications that use of synthetic and biologic DMARDs is associated with reduced CVD risk in people with RA.166, However, it is unknown whether this effect is related to the reduction in inflammation opposing the increased levels of atherogenic lipids that occur with biologic DMARDs and improvement of HDL function. Studies to clarify these issues are needed.

CVD prevention in patients with RA is fraught with concerns of drugand disease-related complexities. Therapies of rheumatic conditions have evolved enormously in the past two decades, as have CVD prevention strategies. The available literature suggests substantial underuse of CVD-preventive pharmacotherapy in the general population.298, More than half of all patients did not reach their LDL treatment goals in general practice. These findings are also supported by the Eurospire IV report, which indicates that clinical implementation of secondary prevention treatments remains suboptimal. Similar undertreatment and failure to obtain recommended lipid and blood pressure targets have been shown in patients with RA. Large international survey of risk factors (SURF) in various high CVD risk rheumatic patients are underway, and the SURF-RA demonstrated considerable geographic differences in estimated CVD risk and preventive treatment. Low goal attainment for lipid-lowering treatment was observed, and only half the patients obtained their blood pressure goals. Despite a high focus on the increased CVD risk in RA patients over the last decade, there is still substantial potential for improvement in CVD-preventive measures.

Efforts to address the high CVD risk in patients with rheumatic disease should be a focus in the cardiology community and among rheumatologists. It is hoped that such a focus will result in more patients with RA being evaluated for CVD risk and the institution of preventive measures when necessary.

There are several new medications for CVD prevention; the most promising are alirocumab/evolocumab (proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 [PCSK9] inhibitors), which are recommended for patients with primary hypercholesterolemia who do not achieve lipid goals with statins. 301 Recently it has been highlighted that since PCSK9 is lower in RA patients, it has been

hypothesized that there may be a greater expression of CD36 and its pro-inflammatory ligands. Further studies are needed to elucidate this in relation to the use of PCSK9 inhibitors in IJD patients. Caution should be taken if unexpected adverse effects are experienced in patients with RA treated with PCSK9 inhibitors.

### Patient Awareness of Cardiovascular Disease Risk

Communicating future risk and the need for preventive treatment is one of the most challenging aspects of the patient/health professional interaction. Individuals with RA at highest risk for CVD report low awareness and perceived risk of this comorbidity. This represents a knowledge gap in need of intervention but must be tailored to patients' needs. An understanding of the systemand individual-level barriers preventing CVD awareness is needed. Only then will approaches to improve CVD screening and management in RA be successful. Furthermore, although programs for assessing CVD risk in people with RA have been developed, it will take a great effort to fully disseminate them. These strategies include education of health care professionals, written material, and online and group education of patients and their families. Even starting with simple information and brochures as a precursor to implementing a full education program is a step forward. It is of the utmost importance for patients with rheumatic diseases to understand that effective CVD risk management comprises not only adequate treatment of conventional CV risk factors but also tight control of rheumatic disease activity.

### Conclusion

CVD remains a major problem for people with systemic inflammatory diseases. Systemic inflammation and its interplay with traditional and nontraditional CV risk factors appear to have a major role. Optimal control of traditional risk factors is imperative but insufficient to reduce CVD risk for people with rheumatic diseases. Tight control of systemic inflammation will be required for optimal results. Future work should focus on further delineating the underlying biologic mechanisms involved, developing and evaluating risk assessment tools and biomarkers, and above all developing prevention and treatment strategies specific to rheumatic disease populations. On might learn from CVD-preventive programs from other high-risk patient populations, such as those with diabetes mellitus.

### KEY POINTS

### Introduction

Systemic rheumatic diseases have been associated with an increased risk of development of malignancy. This increased risk is the result of fundamental underlying immunologic effects of autoimmunity on cancer risk and on the risk of cancers associated with drug treatments for rheumatic diseases.

Accelerated growth of cancer cells in immunodeficient mice and increased risk of cancer in heavily immunosuppressed transplant patients have shaped the perception of the immune system as a potent barrier against neoplasms. 1, It might be expected that immunosuppressive treatment would inevitably result in effects favoring malignant cell growth. However, emerging evidence supports the seemingly paradoxical notion, perhaps formulated first by Rudolph Virchow in 1863, that inflammation is a critical component of cancer initiation and progression and that reduction of systemic inflammation may reduce cancer risk in these conditions.

Assessment of cancer risk in rheumatic diseases must be weighed against the lifetime risk of developing cancer, which is approximately 20% in Western Europe and North America, with 5% of the general population having current cancer or a history of cancer. Approximately 1 in 10 women will develop breast cancer,

and as many as 1 in 8 men will develop prostate cancer. Overall, 1 in 25 patients with RA will develop colorectal cancer, 1 in 40 lung cancer, and approximately 1 in 100 lymphoma or other lymphoproliferative malignancy.

The combination of increased risk for some and decreased risk for other types of cancers in different rheumatic diseases may result in a neutral effect for malignancies in general, emphasizing why, from a clinical standpoint, it is important to identify risks pertaining to specific cancers, which may be uncommon. The statistical approach for capturing differences in sparse event data, particularly when malignancy is not a pre-specified study outcome, and assumptions of proportional hazards models and stable frequencies of events over time for a nonlinear risk such as cancer can lead to major errors in interpretation.

### Malignancy yin Autoimmune Rheumatic Diseases

Several rheumatic diseases appear to be associated with increased risk of malignancy, particularly lymphoproliferative disorders. A list of rheumatic diseases that have been associated with malignancy is provided in Table 37.1. A global assessment of susceptibility to Hodgkin lymphoma using population-based linked registry data from Sweden and Denmark identified significantly increased risks of Hodgkin lymphoma associated with a personal history of autoimmune disorders, including rheumatoid arthritis (odds ratio [0R], 2.7; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.9 to 4.0), systemic lupus erythematosus (OR, 5.8; 95% CI, 2.2 to 15.1), sarcoidosis (OR, 14.1; 95% CI, 5.4 to 36.8), and immune thrombocytopenic purpura (OR, ∞; p = .022). A statistically significant increase in the risk of Hodgkin lymphoma was associated with family histories of sarcoidosis (OR, 1.8; 95% CI, 1.01 to 3.1) and ulcerative colitis (OR, 1.6; 95% CI, 1.02 to 2.6).

The occurrence of cancer has a profound effect on the already compromised quality of life of patients with rheumatic diseases and may affect survivorship and influence treatment decisions. A population-based study of cancer survival in patients with inflammatory arthritis from Great Britain suggests decreased survival compared with the general population. Survivorship related to the occurrence of cancer in this population was unrelated to disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drug (DMARD) exposure.

### Rheumatoid Arthritis

### KEY POINTS

Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is associated with a greater than twofold increased risk of lymphoma. This risk is higher in patients with high disease activity and with more severe disease, including extra-articular involvement.

The risk of solid malignancies is variable, with an increased risk of lung cancer and likely melanoma and decreased risks of colorectal cancer and cancers of the urogenital tract in men and women.

A considerable body of evidence supports RA as a pathogenic factor in the development of lymphoma. A standardized incidence ratio (SIR) of 2.4 for lymphoma was described in a population of more than 20, Danish patients, as was a twofold increased risk in U.S. patients.7-9

In many studies, the risk of cancer is particularly increased early in the disease course, and cancer risk appears to be greater in patients who have persistently high disease activity, high cumulative disease activity, and more severe disease and in those who have positive rheumatoid factor (SIR, 3.6; 95% CI, 1.3 to 7.8).10, The unadjusted OR for average disease activity comparing highest versus lowest quartile was 71.3 (95% CI, 24.1 to 211.4), and the

OR for cumulative disease activity of the 10th decile versus the first decile was 61.6 (95% CI, 21.0 to 181.0) in a case-control registry study from Sweden.

Extra-articular disease of RA, particularly Felty syndrome and Sjögren's syndrome, confers a further increased risk of non-Hodgkin lymphoma; one study of 906 men with RA revealed a twofold increase in total cancer incidence among patients with RA who have Felty syndrome. Large granular T cell leukemia (T-LGL) may rarely occur in association with RA. T-LGL in RA is usually chronic and rarely becomes aggressive.

Contemporary studies continue to show that patients with RA are at higher risk for some cancers. A meta-analysis of 21 publications from 1990 to 2007 combined with an updated analysis of nine studies from 2008 through 2014 summarized the risk of malignancy in patients with RA. The risk of lymphoma was increased and is from almost a doubling (SIR 1.7) to 12-fold increase, with greater risks of Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin lymphoma. The total pooled SIR (95% CI) for all studies for this period was 2.08 (1.80 to 2.39) for malignant lymphoma, 3.29 (2.56 to 4.22) for Hodgkin disease, and 1.95 (1.70 to 2.24) for non-Hodgkin lymphoma. The risk of lung cancer was increased with an SIR of 1.64 (95% CI, 1.51 to 1.79), as was the risk of melanoma (SIR 1.23; 95% CI, 1.01 to 1.49). The risk of colorectal cancer was decreased (SIR, 0.78; 95% CI, 0.71 to 0.86), as was the risk of breast cancer (SIR, 0.86; 95% CI, 0.73 to 1.01). The

overall risk for malignancy is about 10% higher than the general population, SIR 1.09 (95% CI, 1.06 to 1.13). The lower risk of colorectal cancer may be attributable to the use of long-term nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory agents in patients with RA. The overall increased risk of cancer in patients with RA was largely driven by increased risks of lymphoproliferative cancers.

In summary, cancer is frequent in the general population and is at least as common among patients with RA. Following a diagnosis of RA at the typical age of 55 years, one in five patients will be diagnosed with cancer; however, in the great majority of patients, the cancer cannot be linked to RA or to its treatment but, rather, reflects the background cancer risk.

### Systemic Lupus Erythematosus

### KEY POINTS

The risk of at least certain malignancies appears to be increased in patients with SLE. A large multinational study across 30 centers including 16,409 patients observed for 121,283 (average 7.4) person-years reported 644 cancers. Overall, a small increased risk was estimated across all cancers (SIR, 1.14; 95% CI, 1.05, 1.23). The risk of hematologic malignancies was increased (SIR, 3.02; 95% CI, 2.48, 3.63), particularly non-Hodgkin lymphoma (SIR, 4.39; 95% CI, 3.46, 5.49) and leukemia. The risk is especially high for diffuse large B cell lymphoma, often of aggressive subtypes. In addition, increased risks of cancer of the vulva (SIR, 3.78; 95% CI 1.52, 7.78), lung (SIR, 1.30; 95% CI, 1.04, 1.60), thyroid (SIR, 1.76; 95% CI, 1.13, 2.61), and possibly liver (SIR, 1.87; 95% CI, 0.97, 3.27) were suggested. Cancer risk was lower for breast (SIR, 0.73; 95% CI, 0.610.88), endometrial (SIR, 0.44; 95% CI, 0.230.77), and possibly ovarian cancers (SIR, 0.64; 95% CI, 0.341.10).

Patients with SLE in a California statewide patient hospital discharge database from 1991 to 2001 were followed using Cancer Registry data to compare observed versus expected numbers of cancers based on age, sex, and specific incidence rates in the California population. A total of 30, SLE patients were observed for 157,969 person-years. There were a total of 1273 cancers for an overall significantly increased cancer risk (SIR, 1.14; 95% CI, 1.07 to 1.20). Patients with SLE had higher risks of vagina/vulva (SIR, 3.27; 95% CI, 2.41 to 4.31) and liver cancers (SIR, 2.70; 95% CI, 1.54 to 4.24). Also, elevated risks of lung, kidney, and thyroid cancers and hematopoietic malignancies were observed with lower rates of screenable cancers, including breast cancer, cervical cancer, and prostate cancer. Drug effects were not assessed.

The origin of any risk of the development of malignant disorders in SLE remains unclear, although it does not appear to be related to the use of immunosuppressive or cytotoxic agents; most cohorts are too small to allow detection of a statistically meaningful risk increase in rare events over short periods of observation. Race and ethnicity have not been identified as major factors in

cancer risk in SLE. Anti-malarial drug use does not appear to affect the relative risk of malignancy, as was postulated in early studies.

Risk factors for the development of hematologic malignancies may relate to inflammatory burden and disease activity, immunologic defects and overexpression of Bcl-2 oncogenes, and viruses, especially Epstein-Barr virus (EBV). A nested case-control study that included 6438 patients with SLE linked to the national cancer registry in Sweden found that leukopenia, independent of immunosuppressive treatment, was a risk factor for developing these leukemias. Bone marrow investigation was suggested for SLE patients with long-standing leukopenia and anemia. Disease characteristics predisposing to non-Hodgkin lymphoma include longer disease duration and increased disease activity with moderately severe end organ damage.

Women with SLE, likely out of concern for treatment side effects and effects of pregnancy on disease control, are less often exposed to oral contraceptives and are more likely to be nulliparous, which may affect their malignancy risk. On the other hand, the possibly increased breast cancer risk suggests that other, poorly understood factors may increase this risk in women with SLE, whereas at least one study suggested that patients with SLE are less likely than healthy women to undergo breast cancer screening. Patients with SLE also appear to be less likely to undergo routine Pap testing. Increased prevalence of human papillomavirus infection and immunosuppression have been implicated in the apparently increased prevalence of abnormal Pap smears and cervical dysplasia in patients with SLE. .

Women with SLE may be at higher risk of lung cancer, for which smoking is a predictor. Similar to RA, smoking is a risk factor for developing both SLE and lung cancer, reflecting a complex interplay of disease susceptibility factors.

### Systemic Sclerosis (Scleroderma)

### KEY POINTS

The risk of malignancy in patients with scleroderma appears to be increased in most reviews and reports, although at least one population-based study failed to detect increased risk.25, A metaanalysis of six population-based cohort studies reported a standardized incidence ratio of 1.41 (95% CI, 1.18, 1.68) for cancer overall, with no difference between limited and diffuse cutaneous scleroderma. The highest SIRs for individual cancers are those for lung cancer, with an incidence ratio of up to 7.8, and non- Hodgkin lymphoma, with an incidence rate ratio of 9.6.

A population-based disease registry and cancer registry retrospective cohort linkage study from Sweden following patients from 1965 to 1983 revealed an SIR of 1.5 for overall cancer, with the highest rates for lung cancer (SIR, 4.9), skin cancer (SIR, 4.2), hepatoma (SIR, 3.3), and hematopoietic malignancies (SIR, 2.3). A cohort study of patients followed from 1987 to 2002

revealed a similar magnitude of increased overall risk of malignancy (SIR, 1.55) with the observation of markedly increased risks of oropharyngeal cancer (SIR, 9.63; 95% CI, 2.97 to 16.3) and esophageal cancer (SIR, 15.9; 95% CI, 4.2 to 27.6). Esophageal disease related to systemic sclerosis is the likely reason for the increased incidence of Barrett's esophagus, which is present in 12.7% of patients with scleroderma.

A high rate of abnormal Pap tests in women with onset of scleroderma before the age of 50 has been reported, with a lifetime prevalence by self-report of 25.4% (95% CI, 20.9 to 30.4) compared with a self-reported prevalence of abnormal Pap tests in the general Canadian population of 13.8% (95% CI, 11.6 to 16.4). A significant relationship was found between self-reported abnormal Pap tests and diffuse disease and younger age at disease onset.

Lung cancer accounts for up to 30% of all cancers in patients with scleroderma; it is thought to be related to fibrosis. The relationship to smoking is uncertain and studies are contradictory, with some reporting a link and others failing to find a link to smoking. 26,

The mechanisms of malignancy in scleroderma are largely unexplored. Risk factors for development of malignancy in patients with scleroderma may be related to inflammation and fibrosis of affected organs. The link to smoking is controversial.27, As in some other autoimmune rheumatic diseases, the risk appears higher early in the disease, and patients who are older at the time of diagnosis may be at higher risk as well.28, Presence of anti- RNA polymerase III is associated with a twofold increased risk of cancer at scleroderma onset compared with anti-centromere antibodies. Some patients with scleroderma harbor autoantibodies to RPC1, an RNA polymerase subunit encoded by the POLR3A gene that may drive both cancer and the disease. In contrast to systemic sclerosis, localized scleroderma, including morphea and linear scleroderma, has not been associated with increased risk of 34 cancer.

### Idiopathic Inflammatory Myopathy

### KEY POINTS

Both dermatomyositis and polymyositis occurring in adults have been associated with malignancies. The link to malignancy in newly diagnosed patients with dermatomyositis is strongest, although in neither condition is the origin of the association well understood. The association between malignancy and polymyositis and inclusion body myositis is less strong.

The incidence of cancer occurring in patients with inflammatory myositis is approximately two to five times higher than in the general population. A meta-analysis of 20 publications reported a pooled relative risk of malignancy for patients with polymyositis

of 1.62 (95% CI, 1.19, 2.04); for dermatomyositis, 5.50 (4.31, 6.70); and for dermatomyositis/polymyositis (4.07 [3.02 to 5.12]). The prevalence of malignancy is about 25%; cancers are reported more frequently in dermatomyositis, occurring in 6 to 60% of patients, and in 0 to 28% of patients with polymyositis. In dermatomyositis, over 80% of patients with malignancy have autoantibodies specific for nuclear matrix protein 2 (NXP-2) or transcription intermediary factor lγ (TIF 1γ), which confers a 27-fold increased risk for cancer; however, a sizable proportion do not manifest cancer.

In most studies, cancers manifest within 2 years before or after the initial diagnosis of inflammatory myopathy.38, Inflammatory myopathies may initially manifest with the recurrence of a previously diagnosed cancer. A previously diagnosed but inactive inflammatory myopathy may become reactivated with occurrence of a cancer, supporting the hypothesis of autoantigens as drivers of the inflammatory disease.

The strength of the association between malignancy and inflammatory myositis varies. An older study done at the Mayo Clinic failed to reveal an increased risk of malignancy in patients with inflammatory myopathy, and a more recent registry study from Sweden of 788 patients diagnosed with dermatomyositis or polymyositis between 1963 and 1987 revealed that 15% of 392 patients with dermatomyositis had cancer diagnosed concurrently with or after the diagnosis of dermatomyositis, with a relative risk of cancer of 2.4 (95% CI, 1.6 to 3.6) for males and 3.4 (95% CI, 2.4 to 4.7) for females.38, Of 396 patients with polymyositis, 9% had cancer at or after the time of diagnosis, with the relative risk of 1.8 for development of cancer (95% CI, 1.1 to 2.7) in males and 1.7 (95% CI, 1.0 to 2.5) in females.
