A population-based retrospective cohort study from Victoria, Australia, of 537 patients with biopsy-proven dermatomyositis and polymyositis reported a relative risk for malignancy in dermatomyositis compared with polymyositis of 2.4 (95% CI, 1.3 to 4.2), with a higher SIR for dermatomyositis than polymyositis (6.2 vs. 2.0). Finally, ORs for association of cancer with dermatomyositis from a large meta-analysis were 4.4 and, for polymyositis, 2.1. .

A wide range of malignancies is associated with dermatomyositis and polymyositis. The most common malignancies in populations of Northern European descent are adenocarcinomas of the cervix, lungs, ovaries, pancreas, bladder, and stomach, which account for more than two-thirds of these cancers.36, In patients from Southeast Asia, a higher proportion of nasopharyngeal cancers are found, followed by lung cancer.

The association of cancer is less well understood for more unusual forms of inflammatory myopathies. Amyopathic dermatomyositis, a rare form of dermatomyositis with typical cutaneous but no muscle involvement, can be associated with the development of cancer, but the frequency of this condition is low, so that no stable estimates of cancer risk are available. Inclusion body myositis has not been well studied for the same reasons, although the overall risk of cancer of 2.4 suggests a possible link.

It is likely that relevant antigens are expressed in the underlying tumor and affected muscle. Myositis-specific antigens develop during the process of regeneration in patients who have myositis; these are the same antigens expressed in some cancers known to be associated with the development of inflammatory myopathies. This relationship is supported by the finding that antibodies to NXP-2 or TIF 1γ are present in most (83%) patients with cancer-associated dermatomyositis. A link between malignancy

and inflammatory myositis is further supported by observations that, in many cases, myositis improves after removal of the malignancy.

Clinical disease characteristics that may portend higher malignancy risk include active inflammatory disease with normal serum levels of creatine kinase, distal extremity weakness, pharyngeal and diaphragmatic involvement, and leukocytoclastic vasculitis.46, Other independent risk factors for the development of cancer in patients who have dermatomyositis in one study of 92 patients included age at diagnosis greater than 52 years (hazard ratio [HR], 7.24; 95% CI, 2.35 to 22.41), rapid onset of skin and/or muscle symptoms (HR, 3.11; 95% CI, 1.07 to 9.02), periungual erythema (HR, 3.93; 95% CI, 1.16 to 13.24), low baseline level of complement factor C4 (HR, 2.74; 95% CI, 1.11 to 6.75), and possibly topoisomerase I.48, A low baseline lymphocyte count was a protective factor for malignancy (HR, 0.33; 95% CI, 0.14 to 0.80), although the number of assessable patients was small.

### Sjögren's Syndrome

### KEY POINTS

The risk of lymphoproliferative cancers, especially various types of lymphoma, is at least sixfold increased in patients with primary Sjögren's syndrome.

Immunologic perturbations, including p53 mutations and B cell activation, and Helicobacter pylori are likely predisposing risk factors.

Patients with primary Sjögren's syndrome are at increased risk of lymphoproliferative diseases. A systematic review of 14 studies involving more than 14,523 patients with progressive systemic sclerosis reported significantly increased risks of overall cancer (pooled RR, 1.53; 95% CI, 1.17 to 1.88), non-Hodgkin lymphoma (pooled RR, 13.76; 95% CI, 8.53 to 18.99), and thyroid cancer (pooled RR, 2.58; 95% CI, 1.14, 4.03). Individual studies report that the relative risk for the development of lymphoproliferative disorders in these patients ranges from 6 to 44 in individual studies, and a meta-analysis of cohort studies reported a pooled SIR of 18.8.51 Lymphoproliferative disorders eventually occur in between 4% and 10% of patients with primary Sjögren's syndrome, with a lifetime risk of non-Hodgkin lymphoma of about 5%.8,

In addition to non-Hodgkin lymphoma, forms of lymphoproliferative disease seen in patients with Sjögren's syndrome include low-grade B cell lymphoma and diffuse large B cell lymphoma, including follicular center lymphoma. Less commonly seen lymphoproliferative diseases include lymphocytic leukemia, Waldenström's macroglobulinemia, and multiple myeloma. The risk of other cancers does not appear to be particularly high in patients with Sjögren's syndrome.53, The development of lymphoma and malignancy in patients with the condition does not appear to affect or cause mortality.8,

The pathoetiology of lymphoproliferative diseases occurring in patients with Sjögren's syndrome is unclear. It is likely that the B cell activation characteristic of this is a predisposing risk factor. Most lymphomas in Sjögren's syndrome appear to arise from lymphoepithelial sialadenitis or benign lymphoepithelial lesions, perhaps associated with p53 mutations. Infectious agents such as hepatitis C and EBV have been implicated, although the nature

of this relationship remains speculative. H. pylori is associated with mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue lymphoma in Sjögren's syndrome.

Appropriate evaluation in symptomatic patients should include diagnostic testing for H. pylori in this setting. The link of cancer in Sjögren's syndrome to the proto-oncogene Bcl-2 translocation is, as yet, not clearly defined but may be helpful for early detection of malignancy.

### Vasculitis

### KEY POINT

Some forms of systemic vasculitis, particularly ANCA-associated vasculitis, are associated with increased cancer risk. It is unclear whether the risk of cancer development is increased in vasculitis independent of drug treatment effects.

Vasculitis as a paraneoplastic syndrome may be present in about 8% of patients with malignancy. Not as well studied is the risk of primary malignancy in patients with vasculitis. Most cases appear to be related to treatment, although one study using the Danish Cancer Registry suggested an increased risk of nonmelanoma within 2 years of the vasculitis diagnosis in anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA)—associated vasculitis (AAV) (granulomatosis with polyangiitis [GPA]) (OR, 4.0; 95% CI, 1.4 to 12).

Current data do not support a link between AAV (GPA) and malignancy as a trigger for vasculitis, or the vasculitis itself as a trigger for malignancy, independent of treatment effects. However, data from several studies suggest a standardized incidence ratio of cancer in AAV of 1.6 to 2.0 compared with the general population and a possibly higher risk in GPA than in microscopic polyangitis.

The overall risk of malignancy among patients with giant cell arteritis was not increased in a population-based study of 204 patients with giant cell arteritis and 407 ageand sex-matched controls. A meta-analysis of six studies suggested that the risk of malignancy could be increased in the first 1 to 12 months of disease; the finding is negated by removal of one study with high risk of selection bias.

### Seronegative Spondyloarthritis

### KEY POINT

The overall risk of cancer does not appear to be increased in the seronegative spondyloarthropathies.

The risk of cancer among patients with spondyloarthropathies is not as well studied as that of patients with RA and other connective tissue diseases. A cohort study of 665 patients from Canada with psoriatic arthritis revealed an SIR for all cancers of 0.98 (95% CI, 0.77 to 1.24) without evidence of increase in cancer type—specific SIR for hematologic, lung, or breast cancer.

Most studies of patients with ankylosing spondylitis (AS) report no overall increased risk of cancer. These include a Swedish national cohort and population-based cohort study of patients with AS from Australia.65, In contrast, an increased rate of

cancer in Asians with AS was reported using national health insurance system data in Taiwan. Matching each of 5452 patients with four comparators, the SIR for all cancers was 1.15 (95% CI, 1.03 to 1.27).

SIR was highest for hematologic malignancy at 2.10 (1.32, 3.19). The cancer risk was higher in the first 3 years following diagnosis of ankylosing spondylitis. A U.S.-based administrative data set study of 1410 patients with AS also found no overall increased risk for cancer, although skin cancers (squamous cell, malignant melanoma, and basal cell) and head and neck cancers were increased compared with persons without AS.

### Cancer Risks Associated With Anti-rheumatic Drug Therapies

### KEY POINTS

Assessment of risk associated with both nonbiologic and biologic DMARDs is challenging because of the overall generally high burden of cancer in the population, the variable rheumatic disease—related cancer risk, and the potential risk of cancer associated with agents used to treat them. Disease severity may be a risk factor for developing cancer, introducing confounding or channeling bias if patients with severe disease are treated more intensively with immunomodulatory agents. The sequential and combined use of immunomodulatory agents further complicate the assessment of risk related to individual agents. A further concern, as with all immunosuppressive drugs, is the oncogenic potential of immunosuppressive therapies in patients who have a pre-existent or concurrent cancer, and whether such patients should be treated with DMARDs and, if so, which should be given. Major guidelines for management of rheumatic diseases lack recommendations for DMARD use in patients with pre-existing solid organ malignancies.69,

However, in several meta-analyses, the risk of recurrent or new nonskin cancers was not increased in patients with various forms inflammatory arthritis and a history of cancer who subsequently received biologic DMARDs (bDMARDs) compared with those not receiving bDMARDs or conventional DMARDs. 71,

NSAIDs and glucocorticosteroids do not appear to be associated with increased risk of malignancy in patients with RA or other rheumatic diseases. In a large population-based cohort study from Sweden, a total duration of oral corticosteroid treatment of less than 2 years was not associated with lymphoma risk (OR, 0.87; 95% CI, 0.51 to 1.5), whereas treatment lasting longer than 2 years was related to a lower lymphoma risk (OR, 0.43; 95% CI, 0.26 to 0.72). The duration of RA at initiation of oral corticosteroids did not affect lymphoma risk. Whether this

observed reduced lymphoma risk may be due to decreased disease activity, is a generic effect of corticosteroids, or is specific to RA is uncertain.

### Conventional (Traditional) Nonbiologic DMARD Therapy

### KEY POINTS

The risk of lymphoma, especially B cell lymphoma, may be increased with methotrexate. Some patients may experience regression with discontinuation of methotrexate.

Use of azathioprine is associated with increased risk of lymphoma, and alkylating agents are particularly related to increased risk of several types of malignancies, including bladder and lung cancer and leukemia in patients treated with cyclophosphamide.

The nonbiologic (nb-)DMARDs sulfasalazine and hydroxychloroquine and gold and penicillamine do not appear to be associated with increased risk of cancer. Radiation is no longer used for the treatment of rheumatic diseases and is not further addressed. Although no increase in cancer occurrence has been reported, a paucity of data is available regarding the long-term risks of malignancies occurring with leflunomide.

All of the anti-metabolites used in prevention of transplant rejection and treatment of cancer have tumorigenic potential and, in general, may, or do, confer an increased risk of malignancy. The risk of cancer is increased with chemotherapeutic nb-DMARDs, particularly cyclophosphamide, and the risk of certain cancers, particularly lymphoproliferative disorders, may be increased with the use of other nb-DMARDs, such as azathioprine, methotrexate, and cyclosporine, although data are relatively sparse. Data regarding cancer risk in rheumatic diseases in patients treated with mycophenolate mofetil are few, although cancers clearly do occur in patients treated with this drug.

Overall risk for cancer in patients with RA treated with nb- DMARDs was 28% higher compared with the general population in a review of 3771 patients from the British Society for Rheumatology Biologics Register. The cancer risk appears to be greatest in patients who have had the highest cumulative exposure to DMARDs, compared with patients with less than 1 year of exposure (SIR, 4.82). Administration of azathioprine, cyclosporine, or cyclophosphamide increased the relative risk for cancer 65% in the British study, although only 367 patients had taken one of these drugs.

### Methotrexate

The overall malignancy risk attributable to methotrexate treatment in patients with rheumatic diseases does not appear to be increased, although numerous studies suggest that the risk of lymphoproliferative disease may be increased.

Most cases of methotrexate-associated lymphomas reported in the literature are B cell lymphomas, often with extranodal involvement. Assays for EBV in one study revealed that 7 out of 17 patients (41%) were positive. Further evidence supporting a link between methotrexate use and the development of lymphoma

comes from observations of spontaneous remission of B cell lymphoma in 8 of 50 cases, including four that were positive for EBV. This suggests that methotrexate may potentiate persistent immunologic stimulation, clonal selection, and malignant transformation of B cells by direct oncogenic action, decreased apoptosis of infected B cells, and decreased natural killer cell activity.

### Azathioprine

The use of azathioprine may be associated with increased risk of lymphoproliferative disorders. Studies from a Canadian azathioprine registry revealed increased rates of lymphoproliferative disorders in patients with RA compared with the general population (SIR, 8.05). A study from Britain also revealed a markedly increased risk of development of lymphoma in RA patients treated with azathioprine, with an estimated one case of lymphoma per 1000 patient-years of azathioprine treatment. Risk was highest in patients on higher daily doses of azathioprine of up to 300 mg per day.

The risk of leukemia in patients with SLE treated with azathioprine has been generally reported as not increased, although one study revealed an increase in risk. In up to 24 years of longitudinal follow-up, 5.4% of patients treated with azathioprine developed malignancies, none of which were lymphomas, compared with 6.7% of patients who had never received azathioprine, three of whom developed lymphoma.

### Cyclosporine

Relatively few patients with rheumatic diseases treated with cyclosporine have been followed for protracted periods, making assessment of malignancy risk in these patients difficult. Similar to methotrexate, cyclosporine has been associated with the development of EBV-associated lymphomas in a few patients with RA. A retrospective study aggregating experience from clinical trials of more than 1000 patients with RA treated with cyclosporine failed to demonstrate an increased risk of malignancy, at least beyond that seen with other DMARDs.

### Alkylating Agents

The use of alkylating agents in patients with RA, SLE, and vasculitis has been associated with an increase in non-Hodgkin lymphoma, leukemia, skin cancer, bladder cancer, and solid malignancies.85, Considerably more experience with cyclophosphamide than chlorambucil has been documented in these diseases.

Cyclophosphamide use in rheumatic diseases is associated with an overall increased risk of developing malignancy of between 1.5 and 4.1, compared with controls. This risk is best studied in AAV (especially necrotizing GPA), in which risk is highest for bladder cancers (SIR, 4.8), leukemia (SIR, 5.7), and lymphoma (SIR, 4.2). Bladder cancer is a particular concern, and patients who have been treated with higher doses over longer periods and those who smoke appear to be at especially high risk. Bladder cancer related to cyclophosphamide use may occur within 1 year of initiation of therapy and up to 15 years or longer after discontinuation of cyclophosphamide treatment.

Increased risk of hemorrhagic cystitis of the urinary bladder or development of bladder cancer is due to cyclophosphamide metabolites, especially acrolein. For this reason, current recommendations are to attempt to restrict the use of cyclophosphamide to 6 months or less, and to use it only in life-threatening

or organ-threatening disease. The risk of bladder cancer, although probably not the overall malignancy risk, may be less with the use of pulse intravenous cyclophosphamide than with daily oral administration. Some authors advocate concurrent administration of mesna, which inactivates acrolein in the urine. Mesna may be administered intravenously at the time of pulse cyclophosphamide dosing, or by mouth daily, although this is rarely done because of its disagreeable taste.

### Biologic Response Modifiers

### KEY POINTS

The overall risk of a first or second cancer associated with biologics used in the treatment of RA or spondyloarthritis does not appear to be markedly increased from baseline cancer risk in these patients. The risk of skin cancer, especially nonmelanoma skin cancer, does appear to be somewhat increased by about 1.5-fold in patients treated with anti-TNF therapy.

Biologic response modifiers target specific pathways involved in the pathogenesis of some rheumatic diseases such as RA and spondyloarthritis. The term targeted should not imply absolute selectivity between physiologic and pathologic processes with these drugs. It is speculative that the risk of malignancy with use of biologics therapy may be related to the specific biologic mechanisms of the drug. However, an observational nationwide and population-based cohort study from Sweden of 69,308 patients with RA treated by TNF inhibitors (TNFi) or other biologics or targeted/synthetic (t/s) DMARDs compared with RA patients not treated with b/ tsDMARDs and matched to the general population did not show an increased overall relative risk of cancer with TNFi (HR = 1.0) or other b/tsDMARDs (HRs ranged from 1.0 to 1.2) other than abatacept. An important aspect of all randomized clinical trials of biologics is the exclusion of patients with a history of cancer, sometimes excepting nonmelanoma skin cancer (NMSC).

### Tumor Necrosis Factor Inhibitor Agents

Since their introduction, inhibitors of TNF have been studied over a wide range of indications. The concern regarding cancer arises from animal models of TNF action, in vitro studies, and studies in humans suggesting that TNF is important in cancer initiation and promotion; indeed, TNFi agents may even be beneficial for patients with cancers, although clinical evidence of such a benefit is lacking. An interesting observation of regression of non—small cell lung cancer in a patient receiving TNFi therapy has been reported, which adds to the biologic plausibility of a connection between TNFi therapies and malignancy in individual patients who may have particular susceptibility.

Cancer does not occur more frequently in patients on TNFi agents compared with patients on nb-DMARDs.90-94 Lymphoma also does not occur more frequently.91-95 NMSC does not occur more frequently,90,94,96,97 whereas melanoma may occur more frequently.9, Table 37.2 contains a list of meta-analyses and cohort studies undertaken to explore TNFi treatment and solid cancers, lymphoma NMSC, and melanoma in RA.

The possibly increased risk of cancer early after the start of TNFi therapy may be a factor in meta-analyses of randomized clinical trials, which have suggested a possibly increased risk of

cancer in patients with RA treated with these agents. One metaanalysis of nine randomized clinical trials including infliximab and adalimumab found an OR of 2.4 for developing any malignancy for patients receiving infliximab or adalimumab compared with patients receiving placebo. A meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) including 15,418 patients on TNFi agents and 7486 randomized to comparators could not refute or verify that individual TNFi therapies affect the short-term clinical emergence of cancer.

A pooled analysis of RCT using etanercept, infliximab, or adalimumab attempted to distinguish between the effects of recommended versus higher doses of TNFi on the development of malignancy, excluding NMSC. Exposure-adjusted analysis revealed ORs of 1.21 (95% CI, 0.79 to 4.28) and 3.04 (95% CI, 0.05 to 9.68) in patients treated with recommended and high doses of TNFi agents, respectively.

Results of larger observational studies have not replicated the increased risk of malignancy observed with meta-analytical approaches. In the Swedish Biologics Registry, overall cancer risk was similar in TNFi-treated patients with RA compared with three different control cohorts. In this database, no trend toward increased cancer incidence was noted with longer duration of TNF exposures. Studies from other databases including the German and British Biologic Registries and North American cohort and administrative databases have detected no significant safety signals with respect to overall cancer risk.92, A systematic database search including 14,245 patients with spondyloarthritis including psoriatic arthritis found no increase in risk of cancer in patients treated with biologics, majority TNFi therapy compared with those treated with nonbiologics.

Use of TNFi agents may be associated with increased risk of NMSC. An OR for NMSC of 1.5 (95% CI, 1.2 to 1.8) was reported from the U.S. National Databank of Rheumatic Diseases. A cohort study from this population suggested that the combination of TNFi plus methotrexate versus control was associated with a higher risk of NMSC (HR, 1.97; 95% CI, 1.51 to 2.58) compared with an HR of 1.24 (95% CI, 0.97 to 1.58) in patients receiving TNFi monotherapy versus controls, while a study using a large clinical database found no difference in risk of NMSC in patients on TNFi compared with those on metho- 102, The possible potentiating effects of combination trexate. therapies for the development of cancers is perhaps underlined by observations from a RCT of 180 patients with ANCA-associated GPA vasculitis. The occurrence of solid and skin malignancies in the group assigned to etanercept was increased above that expected from treatment with cyclophosphamide alone.

Discordant results regarding cancer risk are likely explained by different patient populations and differing drug exposures. Metaanalyses of clinical trials generally reflect relatively short-term effects but offer the advantage of randomization, which should largely neutralize the variability introduced by individual comorbidities and previous drug exposures; long-term observational studies place more emphasis on midand long-term results. In either case, if cancer events occur in a nonlinear fashion with early dropout of individuals at risk for cancer, a conclusive analysis, even after several years of follow-up, may be unable to capture such a signal.

A crucial clinical question is whether patients with pre-existent cancers should be exposed to TNFi or other immunomodulatory therapies. Patients with pre-existent malignancies are generally excluded from clinical trials and, in clinical practice, clinicians may be reluctant to treat such patients with TNFi therapy, resulting in channeling of treatment with these agents toward low-risk cohorts. Thus far, registry and population-based studies have failed

to detect an increased risk of recurrent or second cancer in patients treated with TNFi agents. .71, A recent meta-analysis involving 13,598 patients with RA and with prior cancer and 32,473 patient-years of follow up who were subsequently treated with bDMARDs (TNF inhibitors, rituximab and anakinra) showed no increased risk of developing cancer overall compared with similar RA patients treated with nb-DMARDs. Further studies exploring the risk of individual cancer development and timing of initiation of biologic therapy after cancer diagnosis and treatment are lacking at present.

### Rituximab

B cells appear to be involved in generation of anti-tumor responses and are important in maintaining inflammatory states, which promote carcinogenesis and tumor growth. The absence of B cells, for example, in hypogammaglobulinemia, has not been associated with increased susceptibility to cancers, and B cell depletion with rituximab slows the growth of solid nonhematopoietic murine 108 tumors.

Pooled analysis of safety data from patients with RA treated with rituximab in RCT with more than 5000 patient-years of exposure revealed an incidence of malignancy excluding NMSC of 0.84 per 1000 patient-years (SIR, 1.05; 95% CI, 0.76 to 1.42). The incidence appeared to be stable over multiple courses of rituximab, and no unusual pattern of malignancy type was observed.

### Abatacept

Abatacept is a fusion protein consisting of the extra-cellular domain of human cytotoxic T lymphocyte—associated antigen-4 (CTLA-4) linked to the Fc portion of human immunoglobulin. CTLA-4-mediated T cell suppression has been suggested to be important in the pathogenesis of several types of malignancies, especially malignant melanoma. Because abatacept blocks the same signal that new anti-cancer treatments based on this interaction are intended to enhance, theoretically a potentially increased risk of malignancies may be seen with the use of this biologic; however, data for the association between its use and malignancy is controversial. In a meta-analysis of observational studies, abatacept has been associated with a slightly increased overall cancer risk (pooled RR 1.13, 95% CI 1.02-1.24) relative to nb-DMARDs or TNFi in RA patients. However, in another large observational study using VigiBase, the World Health Organization's global database of individual case safety reports, the use of abatacept was not associated with an increased risk of reporting cancer overall (reporting OR 0.98, 95% CI 0.91, 1.05), except for melanoma (reporting OR 1.58, 95% CI 1.17, 2.08). Thus the question of association between abatacept and malignancy requires further long-term study.

### Tocilizumab

Tocilizumab is a humanized monoclonal antibody to the interleukin (IL)-6 receptor. IL-6 has an important role in inflammation and in the promotion of various types of malignancies, including suppression of apoptosis, promotion of angiogenesis, and induction of genes that mediate cell proliferation.

Data from studies of RA, the disease in which experience with this agent is most extensive, so far have not revealed any signals of an increased incidence of cancer.87, Labeling information for tocilizumab contains a general statement that "treatment with

immunosuppressants may result in an increased risk of cancer, 2 but no specific warnings are included.

### Anakinra

The IL-1 receptor antagonist anakinra has been best studied in RA. As is the case for most studies of biologic response modifiers, methotrexate has usually been administered concomitantly. The case rate for the development of malignant lymphoma with anakinra is 0.12 cases per 100 patient-years, with eight cases of lymphoma observed among 5300 patients with RA treated with this drug in clinical trials for a mean of 15 months. This represents a 3.6-fold higher than expected rate of lymphoma compared with the general population. The SIR for lymphoma in this study (3.71; 95% CI, 0.77 to 11.0) is consistent with ORs from other studies of patients with RA. A number of solid tumors have also been reported with this agent.

### Janus Kinase Inhibitors

The JAK family consists of JAK1, JAK2, JAK3, and tyrosine kinase (Tyk) 2, with each cell surface receptor requiring a pair of JAKs. Tofacitinib (JAK1/JAK3 inhibitor), baricitinib (selective inhibitor of JAK1/2), and upadacitinib (selective JAK1 inhibitor) are members of this class with approvals in RA and some other inflammatory diseases. To date, the most safety data exist for tofacitinib. Due to signals for increased incidence of cancer and lipid levels during drug development, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) required a prospective, randomized, noninferiority head-to-head safety endpoint trial comparing tofacitinib with TNF inhibitors—the Oral Surveillance Rheumatoid Arthritis Trial. This trial selected patients over the age of 50 with active RA with at least one cardiovascular risk factor, randomized to receive tofacitinib or a TNF inhibitor. Adjudicated co-primary endpoints were major adverse cardiac events (MACE) and cancers (excluding NMSC). The trial demonstrated that the risks of MACE (HR 1.33; 95% CI 0.91 to 1.94) and cancers (HR 1.48; 95% CI 1.04 to 2.09) were higher with tofacitinib and did not meet noninferiority criteria. There remains a paucity of long-term safety data for baricitinib and upadacitini, with most coming from integrated analysis and meta-analysis of clinical trials, and the malignancy risk of JAK inhibitors in other forms of inflammatory arthritis and other indications is not yet well studied. This drug class carries an FDA black box warning regarding the potential risk for malignancy and for increased rates of all-cause mortality, major adverse cardiovascular events, and thrombosis. Further longterm follow-up from observational studies is warranted to better delineate the association between JAKi and risk of cancer.

### Immune Checkpoint Inhibitors

Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) are monoclonal antibodies that block inhibitory signaling pathways in the immune system that then allow for unchecked activation of T cells and the subsequent development of anti-tumor immunity in a tumor-agnostic approach. Currently, ICIs targeting three different immune checkpoint receptors or ligands are approved for the treatment of a broad array of cancers. Given that ICIs are cancer therapeutics that promote anti-tumor responses driven by T cell activation and expansion, it is not expected that they would increase the risk of de novo or recurrent malignancy in the general population, or those with rheumatic disease, although long-term studies addressing

this specific question are not available. While ICI therapy has been shown to be a highly effective therapeutic approach for a broad variety of cancers, unopposed T cell activation has led to a wide array of inflammatory side effects termed immune-related adverse events (irAEs). It appears that patients with cancer who have been exposed to ICI treatment have a greater risk of autoimmune disease flare or new irAEs than for cancer-related ICI therapy. See Chapter 130 for a detailed discussion of rheumatic manifestations related to ICIs.

### Cancer Screening in Patients With Rheumatic Disease

Evidence of cancer risk in patients with rheumatic diseases forms the basis for clinically useful recommendations regarding cancer screening. First, with respect to management of inflammatory disease, it is imperative to achieve optimal disease control and the lowest level of clinical disease activity possible using the least intensive treatment regimen available. Second, patients for whom immunomodulatory therapy, including nonbiologic and biologic DMARDs, is being contemplated should undergo routine cancer screening that is appropriate to their age, sex, familial cancer burden, and risk factors such as smoking. Third, because cancers may develop at an accelerated rate in the first few months to the first year or so of treatment, patients should be seen at frequent intervals and closely questioned and examined for signs and symptoms of malignancy, especially during this initial treatment period and throughout the course of their disease.

Routine blood counts and differential blood cell counts should be performed at the initiation of treatment and as appropriate for the specific drug therapy used. Ageand sex-appropriate cancer screening for colorectal cancer, prostate cancer, breast cancer, and cervical cancer is advisable. In patients with particularly high cancer risk, such as dermatomyositis, assessment for tumor markers such as CA-125 and radiographic imaging of chest, abdomen, and pelvis may be appropriate yearly in the first year or two of the disease, and then as otherwise clinically indicated.

Patients taking alkylating agents such as cyclophosphamide may be at particularly high risk of cancer. These patients certainly should undergo routine cancer-screening Pap smears and urinalyses for at least 15 years from cyclophosphamide therapy. With these considerations, the morbidity and mortality experienced by patients with rheumatic disease can be favorably managed.

### Conclusion

Assessment of risk for malignancy in patients with rheumatic diseases is complex. Some rheumatic diseases such as dermatomyositis and Sjogren's syndrome appear to confer a particularly high risk of cancer, particularly lymphoproliferative disorders. Many of these diseases are relatively rare, so that large patient cohorts required for more precise assessment of risk are not available or must be studied over long periods of time to develop stable risk estimates.

Malignancy and perineoplastic syndrome should be considered when patients present with musculoskeletal symptoms caused by an underlying malignancy or noted as symptoms and signs associated with the presence of an underlying malignancy in a patient with a pre-existent autoimmune disease.

Most of the agents used in the treatment of these diseases are purposefully employed to modulate the immune response, and some, including the alkylating agents, are known carcinogens. Others may

modulate immune response to decrease tumor surveillance. Further complicating the assessment are the individual susceptibility host factors, including the presence of oncogenic genes such as Blc-2, and family history and environmental factors such as viruses, which may enhance the carcinogenic potential of the treatments.

Recommendations for treatment must include a general understanding of the disease and treatment-related malignancy and individualized discussion with the patient regarding risks and benefits of treatment as they relate to disease activity and severity and, most importantly, patient preference.

# Occupational Therapy, Physical Therapy, and Rehabilitation

### KEY POINTS

Occupational therapists and physical therapists are integral members of the interprofessional team in the management of rheumatic conditions.

Occupational therapists and physical therapists offer expertise in optimizing function and quality of life.

Key rehabilitation interventions include exercise and physical activity, functional training, self-management, joint protection, energy conservation, orthoses, and assistive technology.

### Introduction

Functional limitation, pain, fatigue, and poor quality of life are prevalent problems reported by individuals with rheumatic and musculoskeletal conditions despite great advances in pharmacologic management of rheumatic disease in the early 21st century. Members of the rehabilitation disciplines, particularly occupational and physical therapy, are specifically trained to address these impairments. Utilization of occupational and physical therapy varies widely among rheumatic and musculoskeletal conditions and has evolved over time. Yet the goal of these rehabilitation disciplines remains the same: optimize function and quality of life in the people they serve. In this chapter, we review the role of rehabilitation in rheumatology, specifically occupational therapy and physical therapy examination and treatment approaches, detailing the typical interventions provided.

### Role of Rehabilitation in Rheumatology

The role and understanding of rehabilitation and exercise in rheumatology has evolved over the last 50 years. Current evidence supports the use of rehabilitation and exercise as safe, beneficial, and often essential for individuals with rheumatic conditions. Before the advent of effective disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs and biologic therapies around the turn of the 21st century, the role and recommendations for rehabilitation and exercise for adults with rheumatic conditions were considerably different. Physical activity and exercise were generally viewed as detrimental to joint health

and a potential accelerant for joint destruction. While gentle exercise and resistance training were encouraged when disease activity was low, patients were encouraged to rest when in pain and avoid strenuous or high-impact activities to protect the body.1-3 Physical and occupational therapists at that time focused on providing palliative care to help patients manage pain, with approaches like thermal modalities (e.g., ultrasound, paraffin baths) and electrical stimulation. They also focused on compensatory strategies to help patients with impairments to function in their daily lives by introducing adaptive tools to execute tasks (e.g., opening a jar, cutting vegetables) and providing custom orthoses to improve joint positioning and protection for those experiencing severe joint impairment in their hands and wrists. As rheumatologic research and drug intervention progressed, the opportunities for occupational and physical therapy to improve the health and lives of people with rheumatic conditions have shifted. Currently pharmacologic strategies, like treat-to-target approaches and biologic therapies, reduce overall disease activity and increase the proportion of people managing rheumatic conditions with remission or low disease activity.5-9 For those with early and successful pharmacologic management, permanent damage, or joint destruction, is no longer a prevalent hallmark of rheumatic disease, yet functional limitation and disability remain common.5-7,

At the same time that pharmacologic care was advancing, new understanding of the role of physical activity and exercise was emerging. Evidence demonstrated that physical activity and exercise are not harmful11 and they actually help patients by reducing pain and increasing function.12-16 For rehabilitation professionals, this means that occupational and physical therapy is no longer limited to palliative and compensatory approaches to care. While these may still be necessary in advanced disease, early control of disease activity expands the occupational and physical therapy approaches to include restorative and preventive strategies in managing rheumatic disease. Restorative strategies serve to assist patients in regaining their prior level of function, whereas preventive strategies delay or prevent loss of function and onset and progression of disability. Palliative and compensatory approaches remain important for those who need it (e.g., advanced or aggressive disease). Taken together, occupational therapy and physical therapy help rheumatologists capitalize on the improved control

of disease activity that has resulted from drug advances to help patients reclaim and preserve function and quality of life at higher levels and for longer periods of time. Occupational and physical therapy are now integral components in the care of patients with rheumatic conditions as witnessed by the prevalence of treatment guidelines from multiple international rheumatology societies recommending the use of these therapies for patients with a variety of rheumatic diagnoses (Table 38.1).

Occupational and physical therapy share primary goals when approaching patients with rheumatic conditions: decrease pain, reduce fatigue, optimize function, and enhance self-management. Yet the lens through which occupational therapists and physical therapists view these goals differs, which results in complementary treatment approaches. Occupational therapists focus on addressing physical, cognitive, and environmental barriers to enable or optimize patients' engagement in activities of daily life. Physical therapists address functional limitations caused by movement dysfunction associated with disease or injury, primarily focusing on limitations in mobility and physical function. Table 38.2 provides examples to illustrate how occupational and physical therapists share common goals and interventions, while focusing on different aspects of an individual's life. Depending on needs and

goals, the patient may benefit from consultation with one or both professions.

### Components of Rehabilitation

Occupational and physical therapy episodes of care share a similar process and structure. An episode of care begins with an examination, which informs intervention approaches, and ends after reexamination indicates that goals are met or conditions have stabilized. The following sections describe the process of examination and intervention.

### Physical Examination

Assessment in occupational and physical therapy uses a holistic approach to understand the impact of disease-related impairments on a patient's functional performance, that is, the capacity to participate in meaningful, important tasks essential to everyday life. The structure of the initial examination is similar to a rheumatologist examination, as it consists of a combination of structured interviews (e.g., patient history), clinical observations (e.g., physical examination and clinical tests), and standardized assessments (e.g., patient-reported or performance-based outcome measures). However, the lens through which rheumatologists and rehabilitation providers approach this examination differs (Table 38.3). While rheumatologists use the examination process to assess the activity of the disease itself, rehabilitation providers focus on assessing the functional ramifications of the disease on the patient's activities and participation in life.

During the initial interview, therapists gather information on patients' history, medications, physical function, emotional status, and sociocultural backgrounds. Occupational therapists collect information on the physical, cognitive, and environmental demands of activities and occupations relevant to the patient. Data obtained during assessment allow the understanding of how occupations are impacted by rheumatic conditions and the elaboration of a therapeutic plan to enable occupational performance. Examination in occupational therapy considers the ergonomic aspects of an activity, such as body posture, joint movements, and the task's pacing, cognitive requirements, and concomitant demands (i.e., cooking while taking care of children, typing minutes during a business meeting). Physical therapists gather detailed information about the patient's mobility. This includes careful observation of movement patterns during common movements such as locomotion and rising from a sitting position. This movement analysis is combined with data from an extensive physical examination of the patient's musculoskeletal system, including strength, range of motion, and joint integrity assessed by standardized special tests, to provide an understanding of the patient's mobility barriers and to generate a plan to optimize mobility.

Occupational and physical therapists use standardized outcome measures to complement their interview, observations, and physical examination. Standardized outcome measures include patient-reported outcome measures (PROMS), such as the Disabilities of the Arm, Shoulder and Hand (DASH) questionnaire19 and the Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Arthritis Index (WOMAC),20 and performance measures such as the timed stair climb and the 6-minute walk test. These measures provide information on patients' functional level, satisfaction, and physical and emotional status and are repeated over the episode of care to evaluate response

to intervention. Some outcome measures (e.g., the Canadian Occupational Performance Measure and the Patient-Specific Functional Scale) are appropriate for a broad range of conditions and occupations, whereas others are task, body-region, or disease specific.

In summary, examination procedures by occupational and physical therapists classify a patient's functional performance within the context of the patient's unique background and demands. The therapist combines the picture of the patient's functional status with the data collected during the physical examination to develop a comprehensive patient-centered plan of care focused on meaningful goals. Positioning patients as active participants in their treatment is the most effective way to incorporate rehabilitation interventions in daily life; setting meaningful goals in a collaborative process helps to meet patients' demands while considering their physical, environmental, and sociocultural habits.22, The following section discusses the interventions typically provided by occupational and physical therapists to meet these goals.

### Interventions

Occupational and physical therapists use various interventions to help patients with rheumatic conditions progress toward selfmanagement of pain, fatigue, and functional limitation. These interventions fall into seven broad categories: functional and activities of daily living training, physical activity, exercise, joint protection and energy conservation training, orthoses, assistive and adaptive equipment, and adjunctive physical agents. Table 38.2 demonstrates that each of these intervention categories addresses

a primary treatment goal, while some categories address all three. We provide more detailed descriptions of these interventions in the following sections.

It is important to note that almost all of the interventions used by occupational and physical therapists are appropriate for patients across the lifespan. For example, physical activity and exercise are important for all ages, although certain accommodations may be necessary. In young children, physical activity and exercise may need to be incorporated into play activities. In older adults, comorbidities may influence the choice of activities and exercise as well as the dose and intensity. Regardless, these interventions can benefit patients of all ages.

### Self-Management

A central tenet of rehabilitation intervention is a progression to independent patient self-management. In other words, occupational and physical therapists strive to help patients learn to use therapist-provided interventions to manage their own disease and symptoms. Toward this goal, occupational and physical therapy interventions require active participation by the patient and are progressed with the overarching goal of self-management. Optimizing a patient's self-management skills is integral to all intervention strategies.

Self-management is the ability to regulate one's own behaviors, thoughts, and emotions to optimize a relevant outcome. Skills in self-management lead to a sense of self-efficacy, which is an individual's belief that they have the capacity to behave in ways necessary to produce specific performance attainments. Development of self-management skills and an improved sense of self-efficacy is an integral part of treatments provided by occupational and physical

therapists well versed in treating patients with chronic disease. Research shows that self-management training has positive effects on pain and function in individuals with osteoarthritis (OA) and rheumatoid arthritis (RA).24, Treatment guidelines from the American College of Rheumatology (ACR) recommend the use of self-management programs for patients with OA and RA26,27 and are likely to benefit any patient with a rheumatic disease.

While self-management education should be embedded in the treatments provided by occupational and physical therapists, specific standardized, evidence-based self-management programs are available to individuals with arthritis. Such programs are available in face-to-face small-group formats, online formats, and in mailed, hard-copy materials. Table 38.4 provides links for selfmanagement resources available for individuals with arthritis or with chronic health conditions. Optimizing a patient's self-management skills should be an integral part of the plan of care for any patient with a rheumatic disorder.

### Functional and Activities of Daily Living Training

A defining contribution of occupational and physical therapists is to enable individuals to perform meaningful and important activities of daily living (ADLs). ADLs are defined as the occupations, activities, and tasks performed during everyday life. Although commonly associated with measures of independence, ADLs have profound cultural and personal meaning, impacting the patient's autonomy and, consequently, perceived health and quality of life. ADLs can be categorized in three distinct groups: self-care, productivity, and leisure. Self-care includes activities whose primary objective is the care for one's body, such as eating, dressing, toileting, sleep, and sexual activities. Productivity encompasses

activities related to economic sustenance and self and community improvement, including work (paid or volunteer) and education. Lastly, leisure includes activities performed with the sole purpose of enjoyment. It is important to note that the classification of occupations and ADLs depends on the environment and setting where they are performed: cooking everyday meals can be considered self-care, while doing it on holidays can be a leisure activity—or work, as it happens with professional cooks and chefs.

Occupational therapists' primary focus is to enable patients to perform relevant ADLs, adapting the motor and cognitive strategies used by patients, as well as their environment. Alternating joint positioning during task performance promotes improved joint alignment, reducing pain and facilitating tasks such as buttoning a shirt. Carrying heavy objects with both hands distributes the load over larger body areas, reducing the stress applied over distal joints. Changing commonly used utensils as hairbrushes and cutlery for lighter ones with thicker handles facilitates grasp and reduces energy expenditure.

Physical therapists focus primarily on mobility issues that are associated with ADLs. For example, rising from a seated position is an essential element of toileting. Bending correctly is central to an individual's ability to lift a box or even do laundry. The physical therapist focuses on optimizing the bodily movements needed to perform ADLs by altering movement patterns, improving strength or flexibility, or by providing compensatory mechanisms to perform those tasks.

ADL and functional training should be a part of any patient's plan of care who reports difficulties performing everyday activities—from ordinary self-care tasks, to complex, highly specialized work-related activities.

### Physical Activity

Physical activity (PA) is defined as any volitional bodily movement that uses voluntary muscles and requires energy expenditure. PA includes all activities, at any intensity, performed at any time. It includes any daily activity and exercise, which is a special form of PA discussed in the next section. Examples of PA include walking, dancing, raking leaves, washing dishes, and gardening.

PA improves function and reduces pain and fatigue in people with most forms of arthritis. Abundant research exists demonstrating the benefits of PA in patients with OA. Research also supports its use in RA,26,32,33 juvenile arthritis (JA), 34 spondyloarthropathies,35 fibromyalgia,36 systemic sclerosis (SSc),37,38 and systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). Treatment guidelines from the ACR27 and from the European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology (EULAR)40 strongly recommend the use of PA by individuals with OA. Importantly, little evidence of adverse events from PA exists in the literature for any rheumatic disorder.

Patients often wonder how much PA is safe for them. Evidence suggests that people with arthritis can safely follow the PA guidelines established by the American College of Sports Medicine (ACSM) for healthy individuals (a minimum of 30 minutes of moderate aerobic activity 5 days per week and muscle-strengthening activities at least twice weekly). EULAR recommends that patients with inflammatory arthritis, including spondyloarthropathies and RA, or OA aim to exercise at the recommended ACSM levels for healthy adults. However, people with arthritis may need to begin activity more gently and progress the dosage and intensity more gradually. Instruction and supervision by a physical therapist may help an individual with arthritis in determining an appropriate PA regimen.

There are many evidence-based community resources available to assist patients as they begin to incorporate PA in their lives, many of which can be accessed through the Arthritis Foundation, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, and American Physical Therapy Association. Some programs are provided in person in

groups and others are provided online and are designed for individual use. Keeping a list of such programs available for patients will help the patient recognize the value of PA and also find community resources to initiate a PA program. The bottom line is that people with any form of rheumatic disease will benefit from PA. The rheumatologist provides a trusted and influential voice to encourage the patient to be physically active and by referring the patient who is having difficulty incorporating PA into their life to a knowledgeable physical therapist. Consistent PA helps to reduce pain and fatigue and increase function. It should be a part of every patient's plan of care.

### Exercise

Exercise is a special form of PA. Specifically, it is planned, structured, and repeated. Examples include strengthening exercises such as straight leg raises and minisquats to improve quadricep muscle function, range-of-motion exercises to improve flexibility, and walking to increase endurance. The main categories of exercise are strengthening (resistance), flexibility, and endurance. Like PA, these exercises have been shown to reduce pain and fatigue and increase function in individuals with arthritis, including OA, RA, JA, ankylosing spondylitis, SSc, and SLE.32-34, Treatment guidelines from the ACR strongly recommend the use of exercise by individuals with OA and RA.26, As in PA, there is little or no evidence of harm from any of these exercise types.

Flexibility exercises are designed to increase or maintain joint mobility. These exercises are particularly important to patients with arthritis. When a joint is inflamed, it tends to stiffen. Similarly, when a joint is not moved regularly, surrounding muscles and ligaments tend to adapt and shorten, reducing joint range of motion. Flexibility exercises are needed to avoid a loss of flexibility or range of motion in both cases. Flexibility exercises should be performed slowly and gently and can be performed safely on a daily basis.

Strengthening, or resistance, exercises increase muscle strength (the ability of a muscle to lift a load). These exercises are particularly

important for the large muscle groups of the shoulders, elbows, hips, knees, ankles, and trunk. They are typically performed two or three times weekly and must be sufficiently challenging to fatigue the muscles so that muscle adaptation can occur.

Aerobic, or endurance, exercises are long-duration exercises with little or no resistance. They increase heart and respiratory rates during exercise and are recommended to be performed for up to about 30 minutes several times weekly.

Two additional types of exercise are commonly offered to individuals with arthritis: balance exercises and neuromuscular exercises. Balance exercises are beneficial to many individuals with or without arthritis, including older adults.46, Examples of balance exercises include standing on one leg, standing on a soft or moving surface, or standing on two feet with the heel of one foot directly in front of the toes of the other foot. The challenge of the activity increases by performing the activity with the eyes closed. Improving balance decreases the risk of falls, a danger to older adults and to patients with arthritis.48,

Neuromuscular exercises are similar to some weight-bearing strengthening exercises. However, the focus of neuromuscular exercises is on the quality of the movement and less on the intensity of the dose. The goals of neuromuscular exercises are to improve sensorimotor control and dynamic joint stability. Examples include stepping up one step or coming to standing from a sitting position. Individuals beginning a neuromuscular exercise program require instruction from a physical therapist initially to ensure quality of exercise performance. Neuromuscular exercises improve function and decrease pain in individuals with knee OA.

There is insufficient evidence available to recommend one form of exercise over another in individuals with rheumatic conditions. However, the patient's disease activity and joint integrity may dictate which exercises are most tolerable to the patient. It is likely that most patients will benefit from an exercise program that incorporates flexibility, strengthening, and endurance exercises. Balance and neuromuscular exercises may also improve a patient's function and safety. Like PA, evidence suggests that patients with arthritis can safely participate in exercise at the dosage and intensity recommended by the ACSM for healthy individuals (Table 38.5). Data demonstrate that patients with OA and RA can safely exercise at moderate to vigorous levels of intensity. However, people with arthritis may need to start at a low dose and progress slowly to avoid any increase in joint symptoms. A knowledgeable physical therapist can help the patient to identify and modify exercises to avoid undue loads on involved joints and to optimize the exercise regimen to meet the patient's goal.

Regular exercise helps to reduce pain and fatigue and to increase function. Exercise for flexibility, strength, and endurance should be a part of every patient's plan of care.

### Joint Protection and Energy Conservation

Joint protection and energy conservation programs are interventions that use ergonomic principles to reduce pain, manage fatigue, and help preserve joint integrity during daily activities. Such interventions combine biomechanics, behavioral, and cognitive concepts to analyze and modify movement, posture, and pace during self-care, work, and leisure activities. The goals of joint protection and energy conservation interventions are to eliminate ineffective, automatic movement patterns and replace them with motor strategies that preserve joint alignment and reduce the risk of joint deformities, incorporating resting breaks, pacing, and time-management strategies to minimize fatigue, reduce pain,
