This procedure can be beneficial in cases of mild to moderate sensory carpal tunnel syndrome that do not respond to conservative therapies, such as splints. It can also be indicated when surgical release cannot be done because of long wait times or patient preference. The median nerve lies below the palmaris longus (PL) tendon, which can be used as a landmark for this procedure. The clinician can visualize the PL tendon by asking the patient to oppose the thumb and little finger. It is anatomically absent in 14% of the population.

Materials needed for the procedure are a 25-gauge needle, a 2-mL syringe, and a preparation of a longer-acting corticosteroid, such as triamcinolone acetonide, triamcinolone hexacetonide, methylprednisone (5 to 10 mg).

The procedure is as follows:

1. Place the patient's palm facing upward.

2. Insert the needle at an angle of approximately 45 degrees at the distal palmar crease and medial to the PL tendon, and advance the needle toward the index finger and below the PL tendon (Fig. 54.15). If the patient feels any paresthesia, withdraw the needle slightly and reposition it because this can be an indication of penetration of the median nerve.

For ultrasound-guided procedures, a transverse view of the median nerve should be obtained. Insert the needle from the ulnar side toward the median nerve. The clinician should be able

to visualize the whole length of the needle in real time. Be careful not to penetrate the nerve. Inject the corticosteroid close to the median nerve under the flexor retinaculum.

### De Quervain's Tendinopathy/Tenosynovitis

This procedure is indicated for treatment of inflammation of the abductor pollicis longus and the extensor pollicis brevis common sheath. This procedure is best performed under direct ultrasound guidance. We do not recommend triamcinolone due to its greater risk of skin related complications.

Materials needed for the procedure are a 25-gauge needle, a 2-mL syringe, and a preparation of a longer-acting corticosteroid such methylprednisolone (5 to 10 mg).

The procedure is as follows:

1. Locate and mark the tendons by asking the patient to extend and abduct the thumb. The tendon sheath can be swollen, which helps direct the position of the needle.

2. Insert the needle just distal to the radial styloid near the base of the thumb and advance it proximally along the line of the tendon sheath, directing it toward the radial styloid.

For ultrasound guidance, the approach is similar to the tendon sheath injection, which we described previously.

### Tennis Elbow Injection

This injection can be indicated for lateral epicondylitis (tendinopathy of the forearm of common extensor tendon origin) in

combination with or after failure of conservative management treatment, such as physiotherapy.

Materials needed are a 23-gauge needle, a 5-mL syringe, and a preparation of a longer-acting corticosteroid, such as triamcinolone acetonide, triamcinolone hexacetonide, or methylprednisone, 10 to 40 mg (±1 mL 1% lidocaine).

The procedure is as follows:

1. Place the patient in a supine position, with the elbow flexed to 90 degrees and placed over the chest.

2. Locate the most tender point at the level of the insertion of the common extensor tendons on the lateral epicondyle (Fig. 54.16). Insert the needle until the bone surface is reached, withdraw slightly, and then inject.

### Subacromial Bursa

This injection can be indicated for treatment of subacromial bursitis, impingement syndrome, rotator cuff tendinopathy, adhesive capsulitis, and calcific tendonitis. Both the anti-inflammatory effects of steroids and the hydrodistension of the capsule and bursa may have roles in relief of symptoms.

Materials needed for the procedure are a 21-gauge needle, a 5-mL syringe, and a preparation of a longer-acting corticosteroid, such as triamcinolone acetonide, triamcinolone hexacetonide, or methylprednisone, 20 to 40 mg (±3 mL 1% lidocaine).

The procedure is as follows:

1. While the patient's arm is in internal rotation, feel the depression below the acromial process posterior-laterally with your thumb.

2. Insert the needle, aiming to position it slightly anterior and inferior to the acromial process, directing it toward the coracoid process (Fig. 54.17). Little or no resistance should be encountered while injecting the plunger because the subacromial bursa has a potentially large space.

### Soft Tissue Injections: Lower Limbs

### Morton's Neuroma Injection

Morton's neuroma is a benign neuroma of an intermetatarsal plantar nerve. Patients are seen with a pain between the third and fourth toes (the most commonly affected area) and/or with a feeling similar to a pebble in the shoe. Morton's neuroma can be confirmed with a click sound on MTP squeeze (Mulder's sign) or by ultrasound examination.

Materials needed for the procedure are a 25-gauge needle, a 2-mL syringe, and a preparation of a longer-acting corticosteroid, such as methylprednisolone, 10 to 20 mg (±5 mL, 2% lidocaine).

The procedure is as follows:

1. Palpate and mark the place of entry, which should be halfway between the MTP heads and one-half inch proximal from the web space from the dorsal side (Fig. 54.18).

2. Insert the needle perpendicular to the skin and advance it through the resistance of the transverse tarsal ligament. A give sensation is felt when the needle passes through the ligament.

### Plantar Fascia Injection

Plantar fasciitis injections are indicated if conservative (physical) interventions fail (e.g., stretching exercises and insoles). The injection is usually very painful and may lead to fat pad atrophy, which reduces shock absorption. Rupture of plantar fascia is also a reported complication. For these reasons, we do not recommend frequent injections or injection of the fat pad directly at the foot base.

Materials needed for the procedure are a 23-gauge needle, a 5-mL syringe, and a preparation of a longer-acting corticosteroid, such as methylprednisolone, 20 to 40 mg (±2 mL, 1% lidocaine).

The procedure is as follows:

1. Place the patient in a lateral decubitus position on the affected side, with the lower leg extended and the upper leg flexed at the hip and knee.

2. Palpate the medial calcaneal tuberosity, and mark the maximum tender point. Insert the needle medially perpendicular to the skin and slightly distal to the medial calcaneal tuberosity (Fig. 54.19). Advance the needle until it touches the bony surface.

3. Aspirate and then slowly inject the syringe. Follow the postinjection care steps.

For an ultrasound-guided procedure, a transverse view of the plantar fascia at the area just distal to the calcaneal tuberosity should be obtained. Insert the needle from the medial aspect, where its whole length and the location of the injection can be visualized in real time. Proceed as described in the preceding text.

### Retrocalcaneal Bursa

This procedure is best performed under ultrasound guidance; however, it can still be done without imaging assistance if ultrasound is not available.

Materials needed for the procedure are a 23-gauge needle, a 5-mL syringe, and a preparation of methylprednisolone, 20 mg (±1 mL, 1% lidocaine).

The procedure is as follows:

1. Mark the spot in front of the skin overlying the Achilles tendon just proximal to the calcaneus.

2. Insert the needle from the medial or lateral side, perpendicular to the skin at the marked spot for approximately 1.5 cm (Fig. 54.20). Never inject against resistance.

For ultrasound-guided procedures, place the Achilles tendon in a transverse view at the area where the retrocalcaneal bursa can be visualized. Insert the needle from the medial or lateral aspects

where the whole length of the needle can be visualized and the location of injection can be seen in real time. Proceed as described in the preceding text.

### Tibialis Posterior and Peroneal Tendon Sheaths

This procedure is best done under ultrasound guidance. However, a blind procedure can be performed if swelling of the tendon sheaths is very visible, can be identified, and can be injected.

Materials needed for the procedure are a 25-gauge needle, a 2-mL syringe (an insulin syringe can be used as well), and a preparation of hydrocortisone (25 mg/mL) or methylprednisolone (10 to 20 mg).

The procedure is as follows:

Posterior tibialis tendon sheath

1. Palpate the medial malleolus and identify the pulsation of the posterior tibial artery. Mark the line of the posterior tibial artery to avoid it.

2. Insert the needle just posterior to the level of the distal end of the medial malleolus (Fig. 54.21). The tibialis posterior tendon is the first structure posterior to the medial malleolus (lateral malleoli for the peroneal tendon sheath injection). The needle needs to be directed proximally in a 45-degree angle on an artificial line, which extends from the big toe to the heel and follows the path of the tendon. Aspirate and then slowly withdraw the syringe. The tendon sheath may form a sausage-like swelling depending on the injection volume. Follow the postinjection care steps.

Peroneal tendon

1. Palpate the lateral malleolus. The peroneal tendon sheaths lie behind it and lie adjacent to each other. Do not inject the tendon sheath unless it is clearly swollen. Otherwise, you should request an ultrasound examination.

2. Insert the needle just posterior to the level of the distal end of the lateral malleolus using a similar technique to that of the medial ankle tendons. Aspirate and then slowly withdraw the syringe. The tendon sheath may form a sausage-like swelling depending on the injection volume. Follow the postinjection care steps.

### Tarsal Tunnel Syndrome Injection

This injection is indicated for tarsal tunnel syndrome, which is an entrapment of the posterior tibial nerve in the tarsal tunnel. Patients with tarsal tunnel syndrome can be seen with numbness and tingling in the medial third of the plantar area. Posterior tibial nerve

pathology can be confirmed with nerve conduction studies. In our practice, it is a relatively rare injection. Ultrasound guidance would help reduce the risk of damaging the neurovascular bundle.

Materials needed for the procedure are a 25-gauge needle, a 2-mL syringe (an insulin syringe can be used as well), and a preparation of hydrocortisone (25 mg/mL) or methylprednisolone (10 to 20 mg).

The procedure is as follows:

1. Palpate the medial malleoli and identify the pulsation of the posterior tibial artery. Mark the line of the posterior tibial artery to avoid it.

2. Insert the needle posterior to the medial malleoli and anterior to the posterior tibial artery (Fig. 54.22). The needle should be inserted parallel to the skin, directed distally in a 45-degree angle on an artificial line extending from the big toe to the heel. Aspirate and then slowly inject the syringe. Follow the general postinjection care steps.

### Trochanteric Bursa −

Trochanteric bursitis, now often referred to as greater trochanteric pain syndrome, is a common condition. Patients often describe hip pain over the greater trochanter area, which is related to severe tenderness when they lie (e.g., at night) on the affected side. It may be associated with tightness of the iliotibial band. Imaging evidence suggests the pain in this condition is multifactorial with tendinopathy of the gluteal tendons more common than bursitis. The greater trochanter can be identified as a bony prominence on palpation of the lateral aspect of the femur.

Materials needed for the procedure are a 23-gauge (long 2-inch) needle, a 5-mL syringe, and a preparation of a longer-acting corticosteroid like triamcinolone acetonide, triamcinolone hexacetonide, or methylprednisone, 40 mg (±2 mL, 1% lidocaine).

The procedure is as follows:

1. Ask the patient to lie on the side, with the affected side facing upward.

2. Palpate and mark the most tender point over the greater trochanter area.

3. Insert the needle perpendicular to the skin until it reaches the hard bony surface of the greater trochanter, withdraw the needle slightly, aspirate, and then inject. Follow the general postinjection care steps.

### Conclusion

Arthrocentesis and joint and soft tissue injections are a key part of rheumatology management with respect to diagnosis and treatment. These procedures can be safe and effective as long as certain key points are considered. The correct indication, knowledge of anatomy, right technique, and use of correct medications can all impact the outcome of the procedure. Appropriate documentation, patient education about potential complications, and postinjection care all help improve patient satisfaction and minimize complaints. In general, injections work better for conditions of an inflammatory cause, whereas in OA, the benefits are for 6 to 12 weeks if they work. For soft tissue problems, the role of injections is less proven and places the patient at a higher risk of local complications. It is therefore recommended that an exploration of conservative approaches be done first unless the patient requires a prompter resolution of symptoms; steroids may resolve symptoms quicker and in the short term, whereas physical therapies may be more helpful longer term.

As long as the technique that is used is safe and the operator is suitably trained, there is no one way to best perform an injection. In our practice, ultrasound is increasingly used to guide procedures, especially in joints that may be difficult to aspirate or inject using a conventional blind technique.

# Anti-nuclear Antibodies

### KEY POINTS

Among the rheumatic diseases, anti-nuclear antibodies (ANAs) are most characteristic of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), systemic sclerosis (SSc), idiopathic inflammatory myopathies (lIMs), and Sjögren's syndrome (SjS). Their presence is required for the diagnosis of some syndromes, such as drug-induced lupus or mixed connective tissue disease. ANA testing is an appropriate screening step when such diseases are suspected.

Key ANA specificities in SLE include anti-double-stranded DNA, which may correlate with renal disease and overall disease activity; anti-Sm and antiribosomal P; and anti-Ro and anti-La, which are associated with cutaneous and neonatal lupus.

Key ANA specificities in SSc include anti-centromere/kinetochore, which is associated with CREST (calcinosis, Raynaud's phenomenon, esophageal dysmotility, sclerodactyly, and telangiectasias) manifestations, and anti-Scl-70 (topoisomerase I) and anti-RNA polymerase II, which are associated with diffuse cutaneous disease and interstitial lung disease.

Key ANA specificities in lIM include anti-aminoacyl tRNA synthetases such as anti-Jo-1 (anti-histidyl-tRNA synthetase), which are associated with the poor prognosis anti-synthetase syndrome in polymyositis/dermatomyositis; and anti-HMGCR (3-hydroxy- 3-methylglutaryl coenzyme A reductase) and anti-SRP (signal recognition particle), which are associated with immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy.

Key ANA specificities in SjS include anti-Ro (including Ro52 and Ro60) and anti-La, which are also found in mothers of children with neonatal lupus and congenital heart block.

Many ANA specificities are generally considered disease or manifestation specific, but exceptions are notoriously common, confounded by the presence of many autoantibodies in other inflammatory conditions or healthy people.

Ideally, testing of individual ANA specificities should be performed only in the context of clinical signs that correlate with antibody—disease associations (e.g., anti-dsDNA in the setting of glomerulonephritis, suspecting lupus nephritis), but the growing availability and implementation of ANA panels in many clinical laboratories often result in the availability of specific ANA tests in settings of uncertain clinical significance. As a result, ANA and specific ANA testing are generally insufficient to establish or refute diagnoses; rather, they add weight to diagnostic considerations that rely heavily on other clinical information.

### Introduction

Despite the name, anti-nuclear antibodies (ANAs) include a wide diversity of autoantibodies directed against multiple cellular antigens, classically consisting of nuclear specificities such as DNA or

small nuclear ribonucleoproteins but also various other cell components including the mitotic spindle apparatus, cytosol, cytoplasmic organelles, and cell membranes.1, The "ANA diseases" 27 (Table 55.1) are characterized by a particularly high prevalence of ANAs, often screened for by the indirect immunofluorescence (IIF) ANA test: systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), systemic sclerosis (SSc), and mixed connective tissue disease (MCTD). The prevalence of ANAs in the idiopathic inflammatory myopathies (IIMs) and in Sjögren's syndrome (SjS) is somewhat lower than in the other ANA diseases, but these conditions are often grouped together because they share several target antigens and treatment approaches, and therefore presumably also share similar fundamental etiologies. For decades, ANA testing has been an important diagnostic and prognostic tool for these connective tissue diseases (CTDs), and it has become a routine assay in the evaluation of patients with suspected autoimmune disease by both specialists and primary care providers. However, ANAs also arise in a variety of infectious, inflammatory, and neoplastic diseases, as well as in healthy people, and thus some knowledge regarding their intricacies and the limitations of the assays is required for appropriate clinical utilization.

### History

### KEY POINT

ANAs are among the most common diagnostic aids for rheumatic and sometimes other autoimmune diseases. They have also played a significant role in the basic scientific understanding of their target antigens, which often play critical roles in cellular homeostasis.

The first formal report of an ANA-related phenomenon is attributed to the 1948 description of lupus erythematosus (LE) cells in SLE bone marrow. These cells were soon discovered to be polymorphonuclear leukocytes that had engulfed the denatured nucleus of a cell injured by anti-DNA autoantibodies and were often sought in the diagnosis of SLE and drug-induced lupus, as well as SjS and rheumatoid arthritis (RA). Assessment of LE cells was a cumbersome technique, however, and in 1957 fluorescent ANA testing was introduced as a more sensitive assay for SLE and related diseases. Finer distinction of autoantibody reactivities detected by IIF ANA testing led to the description of multiple specificities that continue to be well known today, such as Smith (Sm), nuclear ribonucleoprotein, and Ro and La specificities, which gained further biologic prominence with the

demonstration that their autoantigens play prominent roles in cellular homeostasis (Table 55.2).

### Methods of Detection

### KEY POINTS

The typical standard screening test for ANAs is the IIF ANA test. Positive is generally reported with any titer of 1:40 or higher, although a clinical positivity threshold of 1:80, 1:160, or higher may afford greater specificity in specific situations and should be guided by individual laboratory technique and experience.

Many antibody tests, including ANA screening in some laboratories, are performed via enzyme-linked immunosorbent or other solid-phase assays, affording high throughput; however, such techniques may result in lower diagnostic and/or prognostic accuracy.

Optimal clinical interpretation of ANA tests requires knowledge of the technique(s) used in each specific case.

### Immunofluorescence

IIF ANA testing provides a rapid yet highly sensitive screening method for ANA detection and remains an important standard for initial clinical testing. With this method, test sera at varying dilutions (typically serially increasing by twofold) are incubated with substrate cells, and bound antibodies are detected by fluorescein-conjugated anti-human immunoglobulin G, followed by visualization via a fluorescence microscope. Cultured HEp-2 cells have remained a standard substrate for this test because of their higher concentration of nuclear and cytoplasmic antigens and standardization of use, but some laboratories may still use alternative heterogeneous substrates, such as rodent liver or kidney tissues, which possess the advantage of eliminating interference from blood-group antibodies, heterophile antibodies, or passenger viruses, but may exhibit lower sensitivity of some cell cycle—dependent antigens such as Ro60. Some may also utilize or incorporate alternative HEp-2 substrates such as HEp-2000, which overexpresses Ro60.4 Regardless of the specific substrates, results are typically reported by two parameters: pattern and titer. In most laboratories, any pattern of reactivity at a titer of 1:40 or greater is generally considered positive.

### ANA Staining Patterns

Pattern includes one or more morphologic descriptors that presumably reflect the subcellular localization of the respective autoantigen(s) (Table 55.2; Figs. 55.155.3). As of 2023, an International Consensus on Antinuclear Antibody Patterns (ICAP) working group has identified 30 distinct HEp-2 patterns (detailed at ANApatterns.org), of which 14 should be reported by all "competent-level" laboratories, including various nuclear (e.g., homogeneous, speckled, dense fine speckled, discrete nuclear dots, nucleolar) and cytoplasmic (e.g., fibrillar, speckled, rods and rings) patterns. However, these recommendations have not yet been widely or formally implemented, resulting in laboratory-tolaboratory variances in the specificity of many pattern descriptions. Historically, ANA patterns have often been of great clinical interest, implicating particular ANA specificities with diagnostic and/or prognostic implications in the absence of specificity testing (e.g., centromere staining in limited SSc or speckled nuclear or nucleolar in diffuse SSc). However, none are disease specific or pathognomonic, and in current practice positive screening ANAs are typically further evaluated and confirmed by additional solidphase assays to identify specific, disease-associated antibodies. Thus the utility of ANA pattern in routine rheumatological decision making may be waning.

### ANA Titer

Titer is generally reported as the last dilution at which an ANA pattern is detectable; however, controversy remains regarding the ideal dilution cutoff for positivity. A cutoff of 1:40 was proposed by a large multicenter study based on the reduced sensitivity of higher dilutions for SLE, SSc, and SjS; however, 32% of healthy adults were also positive at this dilution, suggesting a high "falsepositive" rate with that threshold,7 and the prevalence of ANA positivity in healthy persons may only be increasing. More recent international expert recommendations suggest that clinical laboratories should identify a screening dilution that produces a positive result in 5% of healthy controls (which would correspond to 1:160 in the aforementioned study), but this practice has not been widely implemented. In comparison, a titer of 1:80 has been proposed for the inclusion of SLE patients in

clinical trials. Interpretation of the ANA titer therefore must account for the testing laboratory's technique and reference population.

### Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay

Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays (ELISAs) are solid-phase assays that provide highly sensitive and rapid techniques for specific ANA detection. They are commonly employed for the detection of many specificities associated with the ANA diseases—such as anti-DNA, anti-Sm, anti-U1 RNP, anti-Ro, or anti-La/SS-B— and are often performed in a "reflex" manner upon detection of a positive screening IIF ANA test.

With this technique, test sera are incubated in wells pre-coated with purified target antigen(s) or a mixture thereof, and bound antibodies are detected via an enzyme-conjugated anti-human immunoglobulin antibody, followed by color visualization with the appropriate enzyme substrate. The popularity of this technique has further resulted from the commercial availability of ELISA kits and the ability to perform these assays on a multiplex platform, enabling large numbers of clinical specimens to be processed quickly at reasonably low expenditure. These issues likely also account for the growing use of ELISA instead of IIF for ANA screening in some laboratory settings. Such an approach facilitates higher throughput and perhaps greater consistency than IIF, but may be less sensitive overall due to the inclusion of only a finite number of target antigens, typically only the 8 to 10 most

common specificities. At the same time, because the technique can also denature autoantigens, ELISAs may produce false-positive results (due to the detection of, e.g., single-stranded [ss] rather than double-stranded [ds] DNA), and confirmation may warrant further testing, which is not always routinely clinically available. Recognition of the local technique used for the detection of ANAs is therefore critical for their optimal clinical application in diagnosis and/or prognosis.

### Anti-DNA Antibody Tests

Anti-DNA autoantibodies warrant special consideration because of their long-recognized assay difficulties. They can be primarily divided into antibodies that react with denatured, ssDNA and those that react with various forms of native, dsDNA, the latter being of far greater clinical importance for diagnosis and/or management. ELISA is the most common methodology implemented by clinical laboratories, but its specificity may be limited by the tendency for dsDNA to at least partially denature to ssDNA in such assays, resulting in increased sensitivity but reduced specificity.

To compensate, some have proposed that the Crithidia luciliae IIF assay may be preferred, at least for diagnosis. This hemoflagellate's kinetoplast, a modified giant mitochondrion, contains a concentrated focus of stable, circularized dsDNA, without contaminating RNA or nuclear proteins, providing a sensitive and specific immunofluorescence substrate. Although this assay is semiquantitative like the IIF ANA, its accuracy appears comparable to

the Farr radioimmunoassay, which is based on the precipitation of radioactively labeled DNA—anti-DNA antibody complexes and has traditionally been regarded as the gold standard for anti-dsDNA testing but is no longer in widespread use because of the complexity associated with its use of radioactive DNA. Thus C. luciliae IIF may be preferred for the diagnosis of SLE, if available, but other quantitative methodologies may be preferred for longitudinal monitoring of disease activity, such as ELISA or Farr if available.

### Other Assays

Several additional assays for the determination of ANA specificity include the immunodiffusion and counterimmunoelectrophoresis

techniques, two relatively insensitive assays used in many historical clinical studies associating ANA specificities with disease manifestations and outcome; immunoprecipitation and immunoblot, two sensitive and specific assays predominantly confined to research settings; and enzyme inhibition assays, which include specialized techniques to characterize ANAs functionally in cases where the autoantigen is an enzyme (e.g., topoisomerase I). Such assays have not achieved widespread use in clinical diagnostic laboratories because of their relatively cumbersome and/or highly specialized natures and greater complexity in validation but are worth recognizing since they are often used by many clinical research studies, upon which many antibody-disease associations have been based.

# Relevance of Anti-nuclear Antibodies to Disease Pathogenesis

### KEY POINT

ANAs may contribute to disease pathogenesis by producing directly toxic or other pro-inflammatory effects upon binding to their autoantigens.

ANAs have long been debated to play a role in the pathogenesis of multiple diseases. The most well-studied specificities in this regard are anti-dsDNA antibodies, which have been suggested to promote inflammation in SLE, especially nephritis, via immune

complex deposition, direct binding to cross-reactive glomerular antigens, and/or intra-cellular penetration and induction of cellular toxicity. Indeed, in some patients, anti-dsDNA titers correlate with clinical disease activity, consistent with such a pathogenic role. Analogous roles have been proposed for multiple other specificities, including anti-Ro/La, anti-tRNA synthetases or anti-Mi-2, but in many if not most patients, ANAs do not correlate with disease activity, making their utility more useful for diagnosis rather than longitudinal follow-up.14, Multiple factors, both genetic and environmental, likely contribute to this heterogeneity, affecting the appearance of autoantigenic epitopes in target tissues, the functional activity of the autoantigens themselves, and/or the sensitivity of target tissues to autoantibodies.

### Diseases Primarily Associated With Anti-nuclear Antibodies

### Systemic Lupus Erythematosus

ANAs remain a hallmark of SLE: more than 99% of patients test positive via current methods at diagnosis, although many may later seroconvert to ANA negativity, attributed to the natural history of the disease and/or the effects of immunosuppressive agents. SLE often evokes autoantibodies against a wide range of antigens in many cellular locations, but the majority reside in the nucleus (Tables 55.2 and 55.3; Fig. 55.1).

### Anti-dsDNA

Anti-DNA antibodies have been described to bind to multiple forms of DNA, including ssDNA, Z-DNA, or cruciform DNA. Antibodies against the physiologic nucleosome or chromatin forms of DNA have been suggested to be most relevant to disease pathogenesis,18 but the vast majority of clinical literature and clinical laboratory capabilities remains focused on classic anti-dsDNA antibodies, which often associate with glomerulonephritis, may fluctuate in correlation with disease activity, and also continue to be included in the 2019 American College of Rheumatology (ACR)/European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology (EULAR) Classification Criteria for SLE.13, In such situations, anti-dsDNA is typically initially present in high titer and reflects a strong disease association with SLE, in contrast to lower titers that may be observed in other disorders or even healthy individuals. Anti-ssDNA antibodies are generally not clinically useful for diagnosis or monitoring because of their much broader prevalence and lack of correlation with disease activity. Anti-DNA antibodies have also been observed in drug-induced lupus (DIL); these are typically anti-ssDNA and associate with anti-histone antibodies (see below). As a result, the presence of anti-dsDNA activity should always prompt consideration of lupus and renal disease, but the presence of anti-dsDNA activities does not always indicate lupus, lupus nephritis, or vice versa. Indeed, in clinical settings inconsistent with SLE, anti-dsDNA antibodies likely have low diagnostic and predictive value.

### Anti-Small Nuclear Ribonucleoproteins: Anti-Sm and anti-U1 snRNP

Small nuclear ribonucleoprotein (snRNP) autoantibodies target the RNAs or proteins of the spliceosome, a complex of RNP particles involved in pre-messenger (m)RNA splicing. These particles include the U1, U2, U4/U6, U5, U7, U11, and U12 snRNPs, each of which consists of its own uridine-rich ("U") snRNA and a set of polypeptides, including a common core of "Sm" polypeptides (B/B', D1, D2, D3, E, F, and G) and particle-specific polypeptides.

The most commonly assessed snRNP specificities include anti- Sm and anti-U1 snRNP (anti-RNP or anti-U1 RNP).22, Anti- Sm antibodies target proteins of the Sm core, particularly the B/B' and D polypeptides and the Sm-like LSm4. They appear in only a minority of patients and are only inconsistently associated with disease activity or prognosis but are considered highly specific for SLE and also continue to be included in the 2019 ACR/EULAR Classification Criteria for SLE. In contrast, anti-U1 snRNP antibodies target the 70K, A, or C polypeptides specific to the U1 snRNP and are observed more frequently but are not specific for the disease and have also been only variably associated with specific disease manifestations. Some of these issues may be

confounded by variability in testing format, since some Sm or U1 snRNP ELISAs may not include all possible Sm or U1 snRNPspecific antigens for detection. The presence of anti-Sm can therefore be of particular importance during the diagnosis of SLE, but testing for both specificities may increase overall sensitivity and the findings should be interpreted within the context of the specific laboratory's assay format.

### Anti-Ro and Anti-La

This family of autoantibodies includes three distinct autoantigens: Ro60 (TROVE2; Telomerase, Ro, and Vault 2), which binds misfolded noncoding RNAs, pre-5S rRNA, and several small noncoding cytoplasmic RNAs known as Y RNA24; Ro52 (TRIM21; tripartite motif containing-21), an E3 ubiquitin ligase that regulates pathogen defense via immunoglobulin detection25; and La/ SS-B, which facilitates the production of RNA polymerase III transcripts such as tRNAs and the translation of some mRNAs.

Because of the primarily cytoplasmic localization of Ro52 and the potential loss of Ro60 during preparation of HEp-2 cells for immunofluorescent staining, the IIF ANA may be falsely negative when anti-Ro are the only autoantibodies present and may account for more than half of patients with "ANA-negative" SLE. In contrast, anti-La antibodies are routinely detected by IIF ANA and rarely occur in the absence of anti-Ro. In most commercial clinical laboratories today, "anti-Ro/SS-A" testing consists of a single test combining both Ro60 and Ro52 antigens, a practice that likely reduces the sensitivity for monospecific sera. Knowledge of the specific laboratory technique is therefore important for optimal interpretation of Ro autoantibody results.

Anti-Ro may be found in a wide range of autoimmune disorders, including SLE, SjS, SSc, IIM, MCTD, RA, and other primarily nonrheumatic diseases such as primary biliary cirrhosis and interstitial lung disease (ILD), and may be the first ANA specificity detected in asymptomatic individuals, preceding the development of SLE or SjS. In contrast, anti-La is generally specific to SLE and SjS but only when accompanied by anti-Ro; the clinical significance of anti-La in the absence of anti-Ro remains uncertain. Both specificities may be observed in mothers of children with neonatal lupus syndrome and/or congenital heart block.

Anti-Ro52/Ro60 with or without anti-La has been most strongly associated with SjS and the neonatal lupus syndrome, whereas anti-Ro52/Ro60 alone has been most strongly associated with cutaneous LE as well as "ANA-negative" or "preclinical" SLE or SjS. The prevalence of anti-Ro52 versus anti-Ro60 appear similar in SLE and SjS but appear to differ in other autoimmune diseases (e.g., with anti-Ro52 more prevalent than anti-Ro60 in IIM, SSc, and MCTD). In general, anti-Ro52 antibodies have been suggested to associate with more severe disease and/or interstitial lung disease.

Specific testing for anti-Ro and anti-La is therefore generally considered as a diagnostic tool in patients in whom SjS is suspected, regardless of ANA status, or in whom SLE is suspected despite a negative ANA. They are also a consideration for patients with SLE, SjS, or known ANA positivity who wish to become pregnant or for patients with a history of birthing a child with neonatal lupus syndrome or congenital heart block.

### Antiribosomal P

Antiribosomal P (anti-P), the most well-studied antiribosome antibodies in SLE, target the P0, P1, and P2 proteins of the large 60S ribosome subunit. Although they occur in only a minority of patients, they are considered highly specific for SLE. They have

been most commonly suggested to be associated with central nervous system, liver, kidney, and skin manifestations but studies have been conflicting. As a result, their primary utility may be in helping to establish the diagnosis of SLE, analogous to the presence of anti-dsDNA or anti-Sm. Specific testing for anti-P antibodies may be particularly helpful in the setting of a negative screening IIF ANA, where they may be negative due to their predominantly cytoplasmic localization.

### Anti-histone (Nucleosome)

Anti-histone antibodies target the protein components of nucleosomes, the DNA-protein complexes that form the substructure of transcriptionally inactive chromatin. They are relatively common in SLE but can be found in multiple other rheumatic and nonrheumatic diseases. They continue to be classically associated with DIL, although more recently implicated drugs appear to result in a lower frequency of anti-histone positivity. Histone subunit specificity testing has been suggested to help distinguish SLE from DIL, but these distinctions are not robust, and such testing is not routinely available. Testing for anti-histone antibodies is therefore probably best reserved when considering a diagnosis of DIL, although their presence is not required for the diagnosis.

### Anti-Ku

Anti-Ku antibodies target the Ku heterodimer (Ku70/Ku80), which participates in dsDNA break repair. They have been identified in multiple CTDs and have mostly been associated with PM/ SSc overlap. Clinical associations are confounded, though, in part due to assay complexity for this DNA-binding antigen.

### Other ANAs in Systemic Lupus Erythematosus

Several other specificities have been described in SLE, such as proliferating cell nuclear antigen, DEK proto-oncogene, RNA

polymerase 2 (RNAP2), other snRNPs (e.g., U2, U5, U7) or SR proteins, and other specificities described primarily in other CTDs, such as topoisomerase I or centromere. Clinical laboratory testing is not routinely performed or widely available for these specificities in SLE, and clinical context remains unclear.

### Systemic Sclerosis (Scleroderma)

ANAs against certain chromatin and nucleolar antigens characterize the autoantibody response in SSc; positive ANAs appear in approximately 95% of patients. Unlike in SLE, however, SSc sera typically, but not always, contain monospecific autoantibody specificities, targeting such structures as the centromere, topoisomerase I, or RNA polymerases (Tables 55.2 and 55.4; Fig. 55.2).32,33

### Anti-centromere (Kinetochore) and Anti-topoisomerase I (Scl70)

Anti-centromere/kinetochore antibodies target several components of the centromere/kinetochore macrocomplex. These antigens are notable in that they require mitotically active cells for robust detection, possibly accounting for some ANA-negative SSc findings. Anti-topoisomerase I (Scl70) antibodies predominantly target the catalytic region of the DNA helicase topoisomerase I, which does not require mitotic activity.

These two specificities together constitute major diagnostic tools in the subclassification of SSc. Centromere antibodies have been extensively studied and are heavily associated with Raynaud's phenomenon and CREST. In contrast, anti-topoisomerase I generally predicts diffuse cutaneous disease with proximal skin involvement and interstitial lung disease. Anti-centromere and anti-topoisomerase antibodies are included in the 2013 ACR/ EULAR Classification Criteria for Systemic Sclerosis,36 although they are each present in only a minority of patients with SSc

overall and are rarely both found in the same patient. Therefore they play critical roles in disease classification and prognosis but may not be used alone for definitive diagnosis.

### Anti-RNA Polymerase

Anti—RNA polymerase (RNAP) antibodies target the eukaryotic RNA polymerases 1 to 3. RNAP2 antibodies have been observed in other diseases, such as SLE or overlap syndromes, but RNAP1 and RNAP3 antibodies appear specific for SSc. RNAP3 antibodies in particular, including those directed against the RP11 and RP155 subunits, may be helpful for diagnosis and/or prognosis: they are included in the 2013 ACR/EULAR Classification Criteria for Systemic Sclerosis36 and may be associated with rapidly progressive skin disease and joint contractures, renal crisis, gastric antral vascular ectasia, and malignancy.

### Other SSc-Related ANAs

Other specificities less frequently assessed in SSc include antipolymyositis/scleroderma (anti-PM/Scl), anti-Th/To, and anti-U3 RNP/fibrillarin antibodies.

Anti-PM/Scl antibodies target the PM/Scl-75 and PM/ Scl-100 components of the exosome, an exoribonuclease complex that regulates rRNA. Responses against PM/Scl- 75 alone appear more common among patients with diffuse SSc, whereas overlap syndromes are typically associated with responses against both components. Its presence associates with features of myositis-SSc overlap, including features of anti-synthetase syndrome such as interstitial lung disease, without SLE.

Anti-Th/To antibodies are directed against a macromolecular complex that includes RNase P and RNase for mitochondrial RNA processing (RNase MRP). They have been most strongly associated with the development of pulmonary hypertension.

Anti-U3 RNP/fibrillarin antibodies are directed against the U3 RNP, primarily its fibrillarin subunit, which is involved in the processing of ribosomal RNA. Their presence is associated with diffuse disease, including internal

organ or skeletal muscle involvement, or pulmonary hypertension.

Several other specificities have been described in SSc, such as topoisomerase II, nuclear phosphoprotein B23, Sp1, TNF translational regulators, U11/U12, nucleolar organizer region 90 (human upstream binding factor), and other specificities described in other CTDs, such as Ku, Ro, snRNP, and tRNA. Clinical laboratory testing is not routinely performed or widely available for these specificities, and clinical relevance remains unclear.

### Idiopathic Inflammatory Myopathies

Of IIMs, PM and DM are the most often characterized as ANA positive, typically involving autoantibody responses against cytoplasmic antigens. Although up to 80% of patients with PM/DM have a positive ANA, this frequency is confounded by differing practices regarding the reporting of cytoplasmic and other nonnuclear specificities during ANA testing. Myositis autoantibodies are generally categorized into myositis-specific autoantibodies (MSAs), which are considered exclusive to inflammatory myositis, and myositis-associated autoantibodies (MAAs), which are observed in overlap and other rheumatic diseases (Tables 55.2 and 55.5; Fig. 55.1). Notably, MSAs typically occur in isolation, mutually exclusive of other MSAs, although they often coexist with MAAs.

### Myositis-Specific Autoantibodies

Anti-tRNA Synthetase. The most well-characterized MSAs include the anti-aminoacyl RNA synthetase antibodies, which target different specific aminoacyl tRNA synthetases. Some of these antibodies target the tRNA anti-codon loop, enabling them to inhibit enzymatic activity. The most common specificity, Jo-1, targets the histidyl tRNA synthetase and is the only MSA included in the 2017 ACR/EULAR Classification Criteria for IIM42; EJ, Ha/YRS, KS, OJ, PL-7, PL-12, and Zo correspond to the glycine, tyrosine, asparagine, isoleucine (multisynthetase complex43), threonine, alanine, and phenylalanine tRNA synthetases, respectively. Recently, anti-cysteinyland anti-valyl-tRNA synthetase antibodies have been identified.

In general, tRNA synthetase antibodies are most strongly associated with the "anti-synthetase" syndrome, which includes interstitial lung disease, Raynaud's phenomenon, arthritis, and mechanic's hands, and a relatively poor prognosis, although each varies with regard to the frequency of other IIM manifestations, particularly myositis; in fact, they have all also been observed in patients with ILD without evidence of myositis. Nonetheless, tRNA synthetase testing is often undertaken during the initial evaluation of PM/DM, helping to confirm the diagnosis and/or offer prognostic information.

Antibodies in Immune-Mediated Necrotizing Myopathy. Two autoantibody specificities have been strongly associated with immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy (IMNM): (1) anti- HMGCR antibodies, which target 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl coenzyme A reductase (HMGCR), a key enzyme in cholesterol synthesis, and (2) anti-SRP antibodies, which target the signal recognition particle involved in protein translocation.46, Both are associated with a necrotizing myopathy with minimal inflammation but rarely coexist within the same patient. Anti-HMGCR is often associated with statin use, whereas anti-SRP is related to more severe muscle weakness, including esophageal and cardiac involvement.

Other Myositis-Specific Antibodies. Other MSAs less frequently assessed in IIM include the following, all of which are dermatomyositis-specific antibodies:

Anti-MDA5 (CADM-140) antibodies target melanoma differentiation-associated gene 5 (MDA5), an RNA helicase associated with the innate type I interferon immune response to dsRNA. Patients with this autoantibody generally exhibit clinically amyopathic DM (CADM), often with a unique mucocutaneous phenotype including cutaneous and oral ulceration, painful palmar papules, alopecia, panniculitis and arthritis, and importantly, an elevated risk of rapidly progressive ILD and high mortality. 48,

Anti-Mi-2 antibodies target a helicase in the nucleosome remodeling-deacetylase complex involved in chromatin remodeling and transcription regulation. They are often associated with an acute onset of DM with more severe muscle weakness and classic shawl and V-signs but reduced incidence of other complications such as ILD and malignancy and good therapeutic responsiveness.

Anti-NXP-2 (MJ, pl40) antibodies target nuclear matrix protein-2 (NXP-2). They associate with juvenile or young-onset DM and increased risk of malignancy, generally with a distinct systemic phenotype including myalgia, proximal and distal weakness, dysphagia, peripheral edema, and calcinosis51,52 and have also been described in DM sine dermatitis.

Anti-SAE antibodies target the small ubiquitin-like modifier-1 activating enzyme (SAE). They are associated with dysphagia and cutaneous manifestations that precede clinical myopathy, often resulting in an initial diagnosis of CADM, and may also be predictive of malignancy.

Anti-TIF-1γ (p155/p140) antibodies target transcription intermediary factor 1γ (TIF-1γ, p155), often in association with antibodies against TIF-1α (p140). They are associated with a particular cutaneous phenotype including palmar hyperkeratotic papules, psoriasis-like lesions, and hypopigmented and telangiectatic ("red on white") patches, and an increased risk of malignancy.

### Myositis-Associated Autoantibodies

Several MAAs—antibody specificities found in other rheumatic diseases—have been observed in IIM.

Anti-cN1A antibodies, which target cytoplasmic 5'-nucleotidase 1A (cN1A), are commonly present in inclusion body myositis and have been proposed as a specific diagnostic tool. However, they may be occasionally observed in other rheumatic diseases, including PM/DM, SjS, and SLE, and do not appear to associate consistently with specific disease manifestations or prognosis.

Other MAAs include snRNP specificities (including U1, U2, and U3 RNP; Sm, Ro, and La), PM/Scl, and Ku. In general, their presence suggests an association or overlap with another systemic rheumatic disease (see sections above).

### Sjögren's S Syndrome

In individuals with SjS, reported frequencies of positive ANAs range widely, reflecting differences in study populations, disease criteria applied, and the inclusion/exclusion of secondary, CTD-related SjS, which increases the likelihood and amplitude of positive tests. Thus although ANA positivity as low as 40% has been reported, many studies report frequencies of greater than 95%, with a diverse range of autoantibodies, including both ubiquitous (Tables 55.2 and 55.6; Fig. 55.1) and tissuespecific reactivities, such as anti-thyroid, gastric parietal cell, and muscarinic receptor. Such issues hinder interpretation of disease associations and disease specificities of ANAs in primary or secondary SjS.

### Anti-Ro and Anti-La

In SjS, the most well-characterized and widely employed antibody specificities include Ro52, Ro60, and La (see "Anti-Ro and Anti-La," under SLE, above). They are collectively found in the majority of patients with SjS, and the presence of anti-Ro (with or without anti-La) is included in the 2016 ACR/EULAR Classification Criteria for Primary Sjögren's Syndrome. Specific disease associations with each antibody have not remained consistent across studies, however, perhaps in part due to technical variability in distinguishing Ro52 from Ro60 in prior studies. Recent studies, however, suggest that the presence of anti-Ro52, particularly in the presence of anti-Ro60, may associate with more severe disease.

### Other ANA Specificities in SjS

Several other ANA specificities have been described in SjS. Some have been proposed as at least somewhat specific to SjS, such as fodrin, NuMA, and p80 coilin; others have been more characteristically associated with other rheumatic diseases, such as centromere. These have not been consistently associated with diagnostic or prognostic specificity, limiting their routine use.

### Specific ANA Clinical Scenarios

### KEY POINTS

Positive screening ANA in the absence of clinically significant signs or symptoms of rheumatic disease is an increasingly common diagnostic scenario. Such situations may reflect pre-clinical rheumatic disease but also may reflect nonrheumatic autoimmune or inflammatory disease, or simply the normal autoantibody repertoire in an otherwise healthy individual.

Positive ANA specificity testing the absence of a positive screening ANA has been described for multiple autoantigens, particularly those poorly retained by most HEp-2 cells during processing and/or expressed in the cytoplasm, such as Ro or ribosomal P.

When a positive ANA screening result is suspected to be "false positive," dense fine speckle (DFS70) specificity testing, when available and clinically warranted, may help exclude significant underlying rheumatic disease.

### "False-Positive" ANA

A common clinical scenario involves a positive screening ANA test in a patient with no or undifferentiated rheumatic signs or symptoms. Many such patients will not develop an ANA-related disease but may harbor another inflammatory or autoimmune disease, sometimes nonrheumatic, that has been associated with ANA positivity, such as autoimmune thyroid, gastrointestinal or liver disease, infection, or malignancy. Nonetheless, ANA positivity may predate a diagnosed rheumatic disease by years or decades,60 while many patients who present with high-titer screening ANAs may continue for years or decades without diagnosable signs or symptoms. Greater likelihood of an ANA-related CTD has generally been thought to correlate with higher titers (e.g., 1:640 or higher), but no specific cutoff has proven reliable for the exclusion of significant rheumatic disease. Therefore in such scenarios, "false positive" may be an erroneous designation; the positive ANA may represent a true autoreactivity but may not necessarily associate with or predict a clinically significant, specific ANA-related disease (SLE, SSc, IIM, or SjS).

Indeed, there is growing recognition of specificities that comprise a nonpathogenic or natural autoantibody repertoire. In particular, the dense fine speckled (DFS70) ANA pattern, which can sometimes present with a high titer in a screening IIF ANA, has been found to reflect reactivity with lens epithelium-derived growth factor (p75; Fig. 55.3) and associates with the lack of systemic autoimmune rheumatic disease. In a clinical presentation otherwise inconsistent with rheumatic disease, a positive DFS70 test may therefore help exclude a significant underlying systemic rheumatic diagnosis, especially if the IIF ANA reports a dense fine

speckled pattern and no other ANA specificities are identified. This likely accounts for only a minority of ANA-positive healthy people, but its testing may prove cost-beneficial in some scenarios.

### "False-Negative" ANA

Conversely, some patients may present with a positive specific ANA test in the setting of a negative screening ANA. This scenario is becoming increasingly common as ANA panels, including both screening ANAs and multiple ANA specificities simultaneously, have become widely accessible. Most cases reflect monospecific reactivity against antigens such as Ro60, which may be lost from HEp-2 cells during membrane permeabilization, or Ro52 or ribosomal P, which are predominantly cytoplasmic in localization. In such situations, further diagnostic evaluation should consider the strength of correlation with disease diagnosis and/or prognosis— for instance, ribosomal P antibodies are generally highly specific

for SLE, so their presence, with or without a positive screening ANA, should usually warrant further evaluation.

### Overlap Rheumatic Syndromes

Overlap syndromes of CTD remain matters of nosologic debate, but virtually all investigators concur that ANAs are universal in these conditions. Indeed, the presence of anti-U1 snRNP has been consistently required for classification and/or diagnosis of MCTD, with associated ANA titers often exceeding 1:10,000.65 However, many such patients experience manifestations, both clinical and serologic, that allow the diagnosis of a defined CTD, hindering the accuracy of specific clinical associations of specific ANAs in "overlap" settings. Therefore in such instances, it seems most reasonable to base the importance of individual autoantibody specificities upon their primary associations with disease manifestations, despite the lack of definitive, well-codified evidence (e.g., anti-topoisomerase I as

predictive of diffuse SSc-like skin disease or ILD or anti-dsDNA as predictive of lupus-like glomerulonephritis).

### Other Conditions

ANA positivity continues to be described in an ever-growing number of rheumatic and nonrheumatic conditions. In addition to their role in the diagnosis of the traditional ANA-related diseases, ANA may contribute to the diagnosis of some nonrheumatic diseases, particularly autoimmune hepatitis and primary biliary cirrhosis (Fig. 55.3). Furthermore, ANA may be prognostic in some settings. In Raynaud's phenomenon, positivity increases the likelihood of the development of a systemic rheumatic disease, such as SLE, RA, and SSc,67 and in JIA, positivity predicts the development of uveitis (see Table 55.1). In most other scenarios, the clinical significance of a positive ANA remains indeterminate and may distract the clinician from a correct diagnosis or prognosis.

### Recommendations for Anti-nuclear Antibody Testing

Fig. 55.4 describes an algorithm for the rheumatologic evaluation of a patient for ANAs. In most clinical settings, the ANA serves as a screening test, with a positive result prompting "cascade" testing by the laboratory and/or prescribing physician for specific autoantibody specificities, such as anti-dsDNA, anti-Ro, anti-La/SS-B, anti-U1 snRNP, and anti-Sm.

A negative or low-titer ANA in the setting of a low clinical suspicion of rheumatic disease usually indicates the absence of significant ANAs and argues against the diagnosis of one of the ANA-related CTDs. In some situations, though, follow-up anti-DFS70 testing may be helpful to more confidently rule out systemic rheumatic disease, especially if a dense fine s peckled pattern is reported for the A NA a nd o ther testing confirms the absence of other ANA specificities. If the clinical picture strongly suggests CTD despite a negative or low-titer ANA, further investigation may involve specific assays for antigens that are sometimes ANA negative, such as ribosomal P, Ro, tRNA synthetases, or other myositis-specific antigens. Positive results in such assays may accordingly suggest further investigation for SLE, SjS, or an IIM.

Positive ANA results in the setting of strong clinical suspicion usually warrant follow-up with specialized assays. If SLE features are present, further testing may focus on anti-DNA, anti-Sm, anti-RNP/ U1 snRNP, and anti-Ro antibodies. Similarly, if MCTD, SjS, SSc, or IIM are suspected, further testing could include, respectively, anti-U1 snRNP; anti-Ro and anti-La; anti-topoisomerase I, anti-centromere, and anti-RNA polymerase III; or anti-tRNA synthetases and other myositis-specific antibodies, the latter potentially guided by the presence of specific c linical c haracteristics ( e.g., M DA5 f or s uspected CADM). If these tests are negative in the setting of high clinical suspicion, repeat testing at a later date may be warranted because titers of such autoantibodies can fluctuate over time.

Positive results in these more specialized assays do not alone signify specific d iseases b ut r ather a dd w eight t o d iagnoses t hat should throughout the evaluation rely heavily on other clinical information. Indeed, many clinical and research studies upon which antibodydisease associations have been developed often utilized highly refined reagents or methods unavailable in the routine, highthroughput clinical laboratory setting. Therefore t he r elevance o f many ANA results in clinical practice continues to require careful, individualized interpretation by the referring physician.

# Autoantibodies in Rheumatoid Arthritis

### KEY POINTS

### Introduction

Autoantibodies have proven to be very useful tools for diagnosis and prediction in autoimmune rheumatic diseases. Emerging data from several autoimmune diseases has demonstrated that the clinical evolution of disease from the pre-clinical phase to overt clinical disease is marked by a change in the specificity of the immune response, with autoantibodies directed against distinct antigenic targets at different disease phases. Whereas numerous autoimmune rheumatic diseases traditionally have been marked by highly phenotype-specific autoantibody responses (e.g., antidoublestranded DNA antibodies in systemic lupus erythematosus [SLE] and high-titer anti-topoisomerase-1 antibodies in diffuse scleroderma), the discovery of highly specific autoantibody markers of

rheumatoid arthritis (RA) lagged significantly behind these other diseases. During the past two decades, enormous progress has occurred in this area, largely fueled by the discovery that citrullinated proteins are specific targets of autoantibodies in RA. This finding has highlighted post-translational modifications (PTMs) as critical antigenic determinants targeted by autoantibodies in RA, which has led to the identification of novel autoantibody systems and pathogenic mechanisms in this disease.

It is now recognized that autoantibodies in RA target a large and diverse group of proteins (Table 56.1), which appear to reflect distinct pathogenic mechanisms and contribute to the marked clinical heterogeneity among patients with RA. In this chapter, we review the known autoantibodies in RA, with emphasis on discrete subgroups of autoantibodies that have distinct value for diagnosis, prognosis, and identifying pathogenic pathways. These subsets include citrullination-associated autoantibodies, antibodies to acetylated or chemically modified proteins, and autoantibodies to unmodified antigens that are shared with other autoimmune and inflammatory diseases. The implications of these specificities for diagnosis and prediction of disease outcome, as well as for understanding pathogenic events in the disease, are highlighted.

### Citrullination-Associated Autoantibodies

Citrulline residues in proteins are generated post-translationally through the deimination of arginine residues. This process, known as citrullination, is mediated by the peptidylarginine deiminase (PAD) enzymes (Fig. 56.1A). Patients with RA can develop antibodies to the products of citrullination (i.e., citrullinated proteins) and the PAD enzymes themselves (i.e., PAD2 and PAD4). Among autoantibodies found in RA patients, citrullination-associated antibodies have the highest specificity for RA, making them unique clinical tools for disease diagnosis. These antibodies also provide clues into disease mechanisms, suggesting that understanding the process of citrullination and factors that lead to the reversal of immunologic tolerance to these proteins may provide a foundation for understanding the etiology of RA.

### Anti-citrullinated Protein Antibodies

### Discovery of Citrullinated Proteins as Targets of Autoantibodies in Rheumatoid Arthritis

The discovery of a novel type of autoantibody by Nienhuis and Mandema in 1964 revolutionized the study of autoantibodies in

RA1 (Fig. 56.2). These investigators identified autoantibodies that stained keratohyalin granules surrounding the nucleus in cells of human buccal mucosa, which they called antiperinuclear factor (APF). APF antibodies were found in 49 to 91% of patients with RA,1-5 and had a reported disease specificity of 73 to 99%.1, The assay was difficult to standardize because of variability in the staining of buccal mucosal cells from different donors,8-11 and the assay did not find its way into routine clinical practice. However, the striking specificity of APF antibodies for RA suggested that the assay might be reporting on RA-specific pathogenic pathways. Another group subsequently demonstrated that RA-sera-recognized antigens in stratified squamous epithelia—a staining pattern they termed antikeratin antibodies (AKAs) (Fig. 56.2)12,13—had very good specificity properties but was of limited sensitivity1 14-17 and was not clinically useful. Nonetheless, these assays provided a framework for antigen discovery that would later lead to highly specific and convenient tools for RA diagnosis and classification.

Although early studies identified (pro)filaggrin as the potential target of APF in human buccal mucosa cells,3 different

approaches used to confirm this finding failed.3, Important insights to address this paradox came from other studies, which demonstrated that a 40 kDa neutral/acidic isoform of basic filaggrin was indeed the main target of AKAs in human epidermis19 and that APF and AKAs were the same autoantibody, collectively termed anti-filaggrin antibodies (AFAs) (Fig. 56.2). Filaggrin (filament-aggregating protein) is produced during the late stages of terminal differentiation of epithelial cells. The protein is synthesized as a large, heavily phosphorylated acidic precursor (profilaggrin), which is dephosphorylated, proteolytically cleaved and a significant proportion (~20%) of the arginine residues are citrullinated by PAD enzymes.21-23 These findings led to the proposal that the 40 kDa filaggrin isoform was most likely an intermediate in the processing from acidic profilaggrin to basic filaggrin, a cleavage product of profilaggrin, or the result of filaggrin citrullination.

In a landmark paper, it was demonstrated that RA sera that were positive in the APF/AKA/AFA assays specifically recognize citrulline residues within peptide sequences derived from

fillagrin,24 defining citrulline as the antigenic determinant recognized by APF/AKA/AFA in RA (Fig. 56.2). It was further recognized that although at least one citrulline residue within a polypeptide sequence is necessary for APF/AKA/AFA binding, this residue can only be targeted when it is found in the context of specific amino acids neighboring the citrulline. In particular, it was proposed that glycine in the -1 or +1 flanking position (i.e., glycine-citrulline, citrulline-glycine, respectively) is a constituent of the major epitopes targeted by APF/AKA/AFA and that these antibodies are probably largely cross-reactive with most of these epitopes. Similarly, these initial findings showed that RA sera has an important variability in the recognition of different citrullinated polypeptides, from one serum to another,24,25 illustrating that AKA/APF/AFA represents a pool of antibodies with slightly different specificities that recognized citrulline residues within the larger context of their surrounding amino acids. These early concepts were later confirmed by others. 26-31

Importantly, the epidermis is not a target of rheumatoid inflammation, and there is no evidence that (pro)filaggrin is expressed in articular tissues, indicating that filaggrin was unlikely to be the driver of the autoantibody response in the RA joint. This, together with the observations that antibodies reactive to citrullinated filaggrin were enriched in synovial tissue compared with the serum or synovial fluid32 and that these antibodies were synthesized locally by plasmacytes within the rheumatoid pannus,33 suggested that the primary citrullinated antigens recognized by these antibodies were enriched in the RA synovium. The relevance of filaggrin in RA is therefore largely historic and unlikely to be of pathogenic relevance. Instead, its conformation and high content of citrulline residues made it an excellent surrogate with which to detect antibodies against citrullinated molecules. Many other citrullinated autoantigens found in the rheumatoid joint that have been characterized are much more likely to be of pathogenic relevance (see the section "Detection of ACPAs Using Proteins/Peptides Derived

from Citrullinated Proteins"). The term anti-citrullinated protein autoantibodies (ACPAs) was then introduced to refer to a family of RA autoantibodies targeting protein epitopes including one or more citrulline residues.

### Assays for ACPA A Detection

The Anti-cyclic Citrullinated Peptide Antibody Assay. In the initial characterization of AKA/APF antibodies, a single C-terminal peptide derived from filaggrin (amino acids 306 to 324) was used to generate nine variants in which five arginine residues were changed to citrullines, either individually or in pairs, and these peptides were assayed by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA). Multiple different peptides were required for maximum reactivity, supporting that AKA/APF correspond to a pool of antibodies with different specificities against citrullinated sequences. Indeed, when data from all peptides were pooled, assay sensitivity for RA increased from 20 to 48% for single peptides to 76% for the pool.

To improve antibody detection, a cyclic citrullinated peptide of filaggrin (substituting the terminal serine residues with cysteines and cyclizing the peptide through the formation of a disulfide bond) was engineered to generate a β-turn conformation more likely to mimic the original antigenic determinant. Using this cyclic citrullinated peptide (later named CCP1) compared with its linear counterpart, it was demonstrated that the cyclic structure increased the sensitivity of the assay (68% vs. 49%, without affecting specificity). 24, In 2000, CCP1 became the antigen for the first generation of ELISAs designed to detect immunoglobulin G (IgG) antibodies against citrullinated autoantigens in the research setting (Fig. 56.2), leading to the term anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (anti-CCP) antibodies. .

As a single antigen, CCP1 was specific for RA but was less sensitive than assays using a combination of linear peptides (i.e., 76% vs. 68%). Since ACPAs comprise a family of antibodies with distinct specificity to epitopes containing citrulline, it was unlikely that a single peptide sequence would be sufficient to detect the majority of ACPA specificities. This prompted the development of libraries of cyclic citrullinated peptides that were used to construct the second-generation anti-CCP IgG assay (CCP2), which was introduced for aiding in the diagnosis of RA in 200337 and broadly adopted for clinical use.38, Later, a third generation anti-CCP IgG assay (CCP3) was made available for the laboratory diagnosis of RA. CCP3 recognizes additional citrullinated epitopes that are not identifiable with CCP2. Studies directly comparing secondand third-generation anti-CCP assays found them to perform very similarly, with a slightly increased sensitivity of CCP3 in one study (e.g., sensitivities of 82.9 vs. 78.6% for CCP2, with specificities in the 93 to 94% range) (Table 56.1).

Since anti-CCP IgA antibodies are also often found in patients with RA,42 simultaneous detection of anti-CCP IgA and IgG was thought to have advantages over the detection of anti-CCP IgG alone. This rationale led to the development of the CCP3.1 assay, which detects both the IgG and IgA isotypes of anti-CCP antibodies simultaneously. Although the anti-CCP3.1 assay is slightly more sensitive than the anti-CCP2 IgG assay, the specificity is markedly lower due to a higher false-positive rate.43- 45 Since patients with RA are rarely positive for anti-CCP IgA alone,42,45 the additive contribution of IgG and IgA in CCP3.1 likely increases the overall signal intensity, even for low-titer anti- CCP IgG positive samples, which are normally considered negative by the anti-CCP2 IgG assay. Indeed, using a higher cutoff,

the specificity of the anti-CCP3.1 assay increases and becomes comparable to the anti-CCP2 IgG assay. 43-45

Although CCPs are not the physiologic targets of ACPAs in RA, these peptides have proven to be excellent surrogates to detect the majority of ACPAs in patients with RA. Therefore anti-CCP antibodies are considered equivalent to ACPAs when referring to antibodies recognizing citrullinated antigens.

Detection of ACPAs Using Proteins/Peptides Derived From Citrullinated Proteins. The finding that autoantibodies in RA recognize peptide sequences containing citrulline residues and that filaggrin was unlikely to be the physiologic target of these antibodies prompted the search for the primary protein targets of the antibodies detected by the CCP assay. It was proposed that the identification of antibodies to specific citrullinated antigens might aid patient subtyping (compared with the general anti-CCP assay) and provide novel insights into disease etiology and pathogenesis.

Using protein extracts from rheumatoid synovial membranes and affinity purified anti-citrullinated filaggrin antibodies, one study showed that RA synovial tissue contains several citrullinated proteins and defined the α and β chains of fibrin(ogen) as the first local targets for ACPAs in RA synovial tissue (Fig. 56.2). Since circulating fibrinogen is not citrullinated, the presence of citrullinated fibrin in the rheumatoid synovium strongly suggested that citrullination occurs in situ after fibrin deposition through the activity of locally expressed PAD enzymes. This proposal (i.e., that the joint is a site at which autoantigen citrullination occurs in RA) has been further supported and extended to many other citrullinated RA autoantigens.

Using proteomic and high throughput approaches and the analysis of antigens from different RA sources (such as pannus and synovial fluid), more than 250 citrullinated proteins have been identified as potential targets of ACPAs.48-68 However, although some ACPAs may have a more antigen-specific reactivity to certain citrullinated proteins, it seems that most are multireactive (see the section "ACPA Development and Specificity"). Among citrullinated antigens in RA, those first discovered have had the best clinical and pathogenic characterization, including fibrin(ogen), vimentin, collagen type II, and α-enolase. ELISA-based assays have been developed using citrullinated proteins (e.g., fibrinogen) or citrullinated peptides (e.g., vimentin, collagen type II, and α-enolase) to detect ACPAs in RA. In the case of vimentin, the citrullinated sequence from a mutated isoform isolated from RA synovial fluid (named mutated citrullinated vimentin [MCV]) has been more commonly used in place of the native sequence. Although it was proposed that the detection of ACPAs targeting single antigens might provide additional diagnostic or prognostic information compared with the anti-CCP ELISA, studies addressing this question remain inconclusive.

Since detecting individual ACPAs appears to have limited clinical utility in RA, a multiplex assay was created to detect multiple ACPAs simultaneously (e.g., custom Bio-Plex bead-based autoantibody assays in which citrullinated peptides from different proteins are conjugated to spectrally distinct beads). This assay is slightly more sensitive than the CCP ELISA, detecting ACPAs in approximately 10% of patients negative for anti-CCP antibodies (representing 3.7% of the total patient cohort),71 a difference that might be explained by the array of peptides used on the assay. In addition, the bead-based multiplex assay has been useful for defining the epitope spreading of ACPAs in pre-clinical RA (see "Pre-clinical Detection of ACPAs and Anti-PAD Antibodies"). Although the multiplex assay provides additional information with regard to unique ACPA specificities, this information has not

yet demonstrated any significant clinical advantage over the CCP assay for RA diagnosis or prognosis. The use of anti-CCP therefore remains the most widely used clinical test for identifying the presence of ACPAs.

### Clinical Relevance of Antibodies to Citrullinated Proteins

The clinical importance of autoantibodies against citrullinated antigens in RA stems from the following favorable features:

1. Anti-CCP antibodies have high sensitivity and specificity for the diagnosis of RA. In systematic reviews and meta-analyses, anti- CCP antibody positivity has been shown to be as sensitive as, but more specific than, rheumatoid factor (RF) in distinguishing RA from other forms of inflammatory arthritis (see the section "Rheumatoid Factor").38,72,73

2. The presence of anti-CCP autoantibodies is an important predictor of RA development. In retrospective studies, increased anti- CCP positivity was observed in a period of 1 to 5 years prior to the onset of clinical RA, with increased antibody levels more strongly associated with an increased risk of progression to RA. In one study of patients with undifferentiated arthritis who tested positive for anti-CCP, RA developed within 3 years in more than 90% of patients, in contrast to only 25% of patients who tested negative for anti-CCP. 74-76

3. Anti-CCP positivity is associated with a more severe and destructive disease course. Some investigators have shown that both RF and anti-CCP antibodies are independent predictors of severity, whereas others have shown that anti-CCP antibodies rather than RF are the better predictor of radiographic progression, 77-84 particularly in patients who were seronegative for RF (see "Rheumatoid Factor").

4. Anti-CCP/ACPAs are associated with RA-related interstitial lung disease (ILD) and cardiovascular disease (CVD).85-91 ILD and CVD are extraarticular manifestations with high mortality in persons with RA. Although the mechanistic significance of these associations is still unclear, one possibility is that these antibodies are markers of systemic inflammation, which plays a role in mediating lung and cardiovascular damage. Alternatively, the observation that citrullination occurs in lung, myocardium, and atherosclerotic plaque92-95 has suggested that these antibodies may be directly pathogenic, targeting extraarticular tissues containing citrullinated antigens. The presence of anti-CCP antibodies in patients who have ILD but do not have RA is intriguing and has focused attention on the lung as a possible extraarticular site where RA may be initiated96,97 (see the section "Environmental Factors Linked to the Development of Citrullination-Associated Autoantibodies").

The early and accurate diagnosis of RA, together with effective treatment with disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs (DMARDs), decreases accrual of joint damage in RA. Because anti-CCP/ACPAs are markers of disease severity and are detectable early in the disease course, they are powerful tools to classify patients with early-stage inflammatory arthritis who will benefit from treatment. 98-100

### Citrullination Is Dysregulated in Rheumatoid Arthritis

Peptidylarginine Deiminase Activity and Regulation. Since citrulline is not a classical amino acid encoded by a codon during protein translation, citrulline residues need to be generated post-translationally once the protein has been synthesized. This process, termed deimination or citrullination, is mediated by the calcium-dependent PAD enzymes. PADs target arginine residues in proteins and mediate hydrolysis of the arginine guanidinium

side chain, resulting in the generation of citrulline residues and ammonia (Fig. 56.1A). The enzymes are specific for peptidylarginine (i.e., they cannot citrullinate free L-arginine) and can only modify residues within polypeptide chains but not at their termini (i.e., they are endodeiminases). 101,

Five PAD enzymes have been identified in mammals, and the PADI genes are located in a single cluster on chromosome 1p36.1.23, For historical reasons, these isozymes have been designated PAD1 to PAD4 and PAD6. Human PAD4 was initially named PAD5104 but was later renamed PAD4 to reflect the fact that it is a true ortholog of mouse PAD4. PAD13 are classically viewed as cytosolic enzymes, with PAD4 primarily expressed in the nucleus. However, recent evidence suggests a more complex picture, with surface expression of PAD4105 and nuclear or secreted PAD2 reported in certain cell types.105, The PADs are highly conserved and share 50 to 55% sequence identity107 but exhibit distinct substrate preferences and tissue expression. The calcium binding residues are highly conserved among PADs,107-111 except for PAD6,107 which lacks some of these sites; the catalytic cysteine is also different in PAD6. Consistent with these observations, PAD6 is the only PAD member with no demonstrable citrullination activity. Among the PAD enzymes, evidence suggests that PAD2 and PAD4 are the predominant PAD enzymes responsible for the generation of citrullinated autoantigens in RA.47, These PAD isoforms are found in the tissue and fluid of inflamed RA joints, and both enzymes have been shown to citrullinate proteins that are targeted by ACPAs.51,

Unlike many other enzymatic PTMs, such as phosphorylation, ubiquitination, methylation, and others, citrullination appears to be an irreversible process.117, The mechanisms involved in the clearance or turnover of citrullinated proteins in cells also remain unknown. Because citrullination reduces the net charge of proteins by neutralizing one positive charge per arginine residue modified, it can increase protein hydrophobicity, lead to protein unfolding, and alter intraand intermolecular interactions. These structural changes can lead to alterations in protein activity, most commonly a loss of function.119-124 Given that citrullinated proteins are prominent targets of autoantibodies in RA, the mechanisms that control excessive citrullination of physiologic targets or citrullination of nonphysiologic substrates are important to define.

The activity of the PAD enzymes and generation of citrullinated proteins can be regulated at multiple levels. One regulatory component is calcium.102, The binding of calcium ions to PADs induces a conformational change that generates active forms of the enzymes. 107-111 While this requires millimolar amounts of 102, PAD activation in cells is observed under calcium in vitro, physiologic nanomolar calcium concentrations. 106, This suggests that physiologic calcium conditions are suboptimal but may select for high-efficiency substrates and limit aberrant citrullination events.
