Another important regulatory component of PAD activity is the oxidative environment.102, Reducing conditions, like those present in the cytoplasm, are necessary to maintain PAD activity due to the presence of free thiol cysteine in the active site required for catalysis. Because the extra-cellular environment is oxidizing,135 this may protect against aberrant extracellular citrullination by inactivating PADs that may leak from activated or dying cells. Indeed, PAD activity is not detected in extra-cellular fluids in vitro unless reducing agents are exogenously added. Citrullinated extra-cellular proteins, however, can be detected in healthy human serum and synovial fluid at low levels, which are significantly enhanced in RA,65 suggesting that additional mechanisms are involved in controlling extra-cellular PAD

activity and that such mechanisms are altered in RA. Similarly, reactive oxygen species (ROS) generated by nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADPH) oxidase inhibits the catalytic activity of PAD2 and PAD4 and, conversely, PAD4-mediated citrullination blocks ROS production by targeting components of the phagocyte NADPH oxidase (p47phox and p67phox). 136, The activity of the PADs may also be negatively regulated through autocitrullination, since the enzymes can citrullinate themselves as well as substrates. 138, While there are multiple natural mechanisms that inhibit PAD activity, the accumulation of citrullinated proteins in the RA joint demonstrates that these regulatory mechanisms are incompletely effective in patients with RA (see the section "Mechanisms for Citrullination-Associated Autoantigen Production in the Rheumatoid Joint").

The Citrullinome in Rheumatoid Arthritis. Citrullination is a normal process. A recent study identified 209 proteins as targets of citrullination across 26 of 30 human tissues, which together constitute the healthy citrullinome. The levels of citrullinated proteins differ markedly across healthy tissues, with the brain and lung containing the highest levels and the largest spectrum of citrullinated proteins (~60 proteins per tissue). In contrast, fewer than 10 proteins were identified as targets of citrullination in more than half of the other body sites. Interestingly, the majority of proteins were only found to be citrullinated in a single tissue, implying that citrullination of unique proteins is organ specific, that citrullination under steady-state conditions is tightly regulated, and that protein citrullination may regulate or be regulated by distinct factors in different tissues. Functionally, the majority of citrullinated proteins across normal tissues are associated with broad categories of cytoskeleton organization and protein synthesis.140,

This collection of citrullinated proteins importantly contrasts with the inflamed rheumatoid joint, in which both the type and the magnitude of citrullinated proteins are significantly amplified, a characteristic that has been termed hypercitrullination.62, More than 250 citrullinated proteins have been identified in the RA joint,61-65 which collectively comprise the RA citrullinome. The identity of citrullinated proteins in the RA joint includes proteins found across healthy tissues, although the vast majority are proteins not detected in the healthy citrullinome. The spectrum of citrullinated proteins in RA reflects hypercitrullination of cellular and soluble components enriched in the distinct inflammatory compartments in the rheumatoid joint. For instance, RA synovial fluid contains high levels of citrullinated extra-cellular proteins, such as components of the complement and coagulation cascades.61, Cells in synovial fluid (mainly neutrophils) and the synovium (containing synovial and inflammatory cells) are the source of intra-cellular citrullinated proteins, ,61-63,65which are associated with categories of cytoskeleton organization and cellular stress. In particular, it is intriguing that citrullination in RA, but not in the healthy citrullinome, targets proteins found in metabolic pathways, 65,141 suggesting that these proteins became accessible to citrullination under inflammatory conditions.

The unparalleled amount and variety of citrullinated proteins in the RA joint, not found in any other healthy tissue or organ,62,141 likely creates the perfect immunogenic environment for ACPA production and immune complex formation in RA. Importantly, there is no evidence that a single citrullinated protein is the primary target of ACPAs or a candidate toward which immunologic tolerance is initially lost in RA. Instead, given the significant variability in the recognition of distinct citrullinated polypeptides by different RA sera,24,25 it suggests that the ACPA

response among individual patients with RA is not initiated by a single antigen but by different citrullinated proteins, most likely with common citrullinated motifs.

### Autoantibodies to Peptidylarginine Deiminase Enzymes

In addition to their prominent enzymatic role in the generation of citrullinated autoantigens, PAD2 and PAD4 are targeted by auto- .142-144Although antibodies in unique subsets of patients with RA. PADs can citrullinate themselves, 138,139 antibodies to the PADs are distinct from ACPAs in that antibody recognition is independent of citrullination status. The sensitivity of PAD4 antibodies for RA is in the 23 to 45% range, with a specificity of greater than 95% (Table 56.1).146, PAD4 autoantibodies are strongly associated with anti-CCP antibodies and are independently associated with the presence of radiographic joint damage in multiple studies. Recent studies have shown that anti-PAD4 antibodies of various isotypes and IgG subclasses are present in patients and can delineate unique disease features. 148-i50 Despite the association with severe joint disease, the relationship between anti-PAD4 antibodies and treatment response are less clear. One small openlabel study reported an association of anti-PAD4 antibodies with the progression of erosive disease despite treatment with TNF inhibitors, 151,152 while a more recent retrospective analysis of sera from a randomized controlled trial showed that anti-PAD4 antibodies predict a more favorable response to treatment escalation in patients who failed first-line DMARD therapy.

A subset of anti-PAD4 antibodies that cross-react with the PAD3 isoenzyme has been identified in 10 to 12% of patients with RA (Table 56.1).153-156 These antibodies also have the unique ability to enhance PAD4 enzyme activity upon binding, which may play a novel role in the pathogenesis of RA (see the section "Anti-PAD4 Antibodies: Origin and Pathogenicity"). Anti-PAD3/ PAD4 cross-reactive antibodies were most strongly associated with severe progressive joint damage and the highest risk of RA-associated ILD.154,

PAD2 has recently been identified as a target of autoantibodies in 18.5% of RA patients a single cohort study (Table 56.1). In contrast to anti-PAD4 or anti-PAD3/PAD4 antibodies, anti- PAD2 were found in patients with milder disease, including fewer swollen joints over time, less risk of RA-associated ILD, and a lower likelihood of progressive radiographic joint damage. These antibodies were not associated with other RA serologies such as ACPA, RF, or anti-PAD3/PAD4 antibodies. Although antibodies to the PAD enzymes are not yet used in the clinical setting, this study suggested that, when used together, anti-PAD2 and anti-PAD3/4 antibodies may provide prognostic value in predicting patients who will progress in their erosive joint disease over time. 144

### Etiology and Pathogenesis of Citrullination- Associated Autoantibodies

While the etiology of RA remains to be defined, the presence of citrullination-associated autoantibodies in the pre-clinical phase of the disease suggests that dysregulated citrullination is an important event during disease initiation. This notion has sparked the idea that environmental factors that dysregulate citrullination, especially at mucosal surfaces, may promote the breech of tolerance to citrullination-associated antigens and promote the development of autoantibodies in genetically susceptible hosts

(Fig. 56.3). There is evidence that this leads to the establishment of feed-forward loops of disease propagation in the joint, in which ongoing immune responses drive the continued generation and release of PAD enzymes and citrullinated autoantigens (Fig. 56.4).

### Pre-clinical Detection of ACPAs and Anti-PAD Antibodies

Several studies have demonstrated that autoantibodies may precede the onset of clinical disease in both tissue-specific and systemic autoimmune diseases, including RA. 158-165 Analysis of stored preclinical blood samples has established that autoantibodies precede RA diagnosis in many persons in whom seropositive RA subsequently develops, often by 2 to 6 years.164-167 In several studies, 20 to 60% of patients with RA were RF positive prior to diagnosis, and 30 to 60% of patients were positive for anti-CCP.164-167 With one exception, 167 the prevalence of anti-CCP prior to diagnosis was almost twice as high as RF. Interestingly, whereas RF positivity was constant, anti-CCP could vary over time, even disappearing in some individuals. In one study, pre-clinical anti-CCP positivity was strongly associated with the presence of radiographic erosions at or after RA diagnosis, whereas RF was not. As has been observed for anti-CCP, anti-PAD4 antibodies are present in a subset of individuals pre-clinically, prior to the onset of any disease symptoms, and mostly develop after ACPAs.

The evolution of autoantibody epitope spreading in pre-clinical RA has been addressed using a multiplex assay to detect ACPAs to multiple protein antigens. This study confirmed that ACPA positivity predicts progression to RA in asymptomatic individuals and showed that the number of ACPA specificities accumulate over time during the pre-clinical phase of the disease. Moreover, the expansion of the ACPA response precedes the elevation of many inflammatory cytokines, including TNF, interleukin (IL)-6, IL- 12p70, and interferon-γ, suggesting that ACPAs may be involved in driving the inflammatory process in RA. Analyses of unaffected first-degree relatives of patients with RA have also shown an increased prevalence of ACPA positivity compared with healthy controls.168-170 Moreover, reactivity to multiple ACPAs and the presence of an increasing number of ACPAs in this group at risk for RA is more likely associated with signs of joint inflammation and progression to RA.168-170 Together, these data highlight that the development of autoimmunity against citrullination-associated antigens is often asymptomatic and generally precedes the onset of clinical disease. This pre-clinical phase is potentially of great importance because it may identify persons in whom important precursor conditions for the subsequent development of RA have been satisfied and could represent a unique therapeutic opportunity. The subsequent events that convert this RA precursor into a chronic, self-sustaining process are not yet known, but defining them is of great importance.

### Genetic Factors Linked to the Development t of Citrullination-Associated Autoantibodies

Although the association of specific human leukocyte antigen— DR (HLA-DR) alleles (which encode for class II antigen-presenting molecules) and RA has been known for decades,171the relationship between genetics and the development of RA autoantibodies is just beginning to be elucidated. A subset of HLA- DRβ1 alleles, termed the "shared epitope" (SE) alleles, includes HLA-DRβ1*0101, *0102, *0401, *0404, *0405, *0408, *0410, *1001, and *1402. SE alleles are so named because they encode

A. Genetic factors

a similar amino acid sequence (QRRAA, QKRAA, or RRRAA) at position 70 to 74 in the peptide-binding groove. Although early studies identified SE alleles as inherited risk factors for RA development, the discovery of ACPAs revealed that SE was most strongly associated with ACPA-positive RA (Fig. 56.3). This is supported mechanistically by studies, which have shown that SE-containing HLA molecules preferentially bind some citrullinated peptides over their arginine-containing counterparts and

B. Environmental factors

that global structural changes induced by citrullination lead to an altered peptide repertoire, including the generation of unmodified peptides with higher affinity to SE alleles. 174-176

Furthermore, there appears to be a gene dosage effect on the relative risk of anti-CCP development with an odds ratio (OR) of 3.3 to 4.7 for patients with one SE allele and an OR of 11.8 to 13.3 for patients with two SE alleles.74, Together, the combination of anti-CCPs and SE carriage is strongly associated

with future onset of RA. Interestingly, smoking has been shown to modulate the genetic association of SE alleles with anti-CCP development (see the section "Environmental Factors Linked to the Development of Citrullination-Associated Autoantibodies"). Beyond the SE model, recent genome-wide association studies have suggested that unique polymorphisms that encode key amino acids in the peptide binding grooves of HLA-DRβ1 (at positions 11, 71, and 74), HLA-B (at position 9) and HLA-DPβ1 (at position 9), may explain most of the association between the HLA locus and anti-CCP-positive RA.

In addition to HLA alleles, a single-nucleotide polymorphism in the PTPN22 gene (1858C/T) is also associated with anti-CCP antibodies with an OR of 3.80 (Fig. 56.3). PTPN22 encodes for lymphoid protein tyrosine phosphatase and has been shown to be associated with several autoimmune disorders, including RA. The combination of PTPN22 1858C/T genotype and anti- CCP antibodies is 100% specific for RA and confers a relative risk of 130.03. The 1858C/T polymorphism is not associated with RF isotypes and appeared to act independently of SE alleles. Genetic factors such as the SE and PTPN22 may therefore play

a role in the pre-clinical phase of RA, predisposing individuals to the generation of anti-CCP antibodies and susceptibility to the overt disease phenotype.

Polymorphisms in the genes encoding PAD2 and PAD4 (PADI2 and PADI4, respectively) are independently associated with RA development, particularly in Asian populations. 183-186 Two common haplotypes of the PADI4 gene were initially identified183 and designated "susceptible" or "nonsusceptible" based on their relative frequency in patients with RA versus control subjects. Although the susceptible haplotype generates a PAD4 molecule containing three amino acid substitutions in the N-terminal region (i.e., Gly55-Ser, Val82-Ala, and Gly112-Ala), current evidence suggests that these changes increase PADI4 messenger RNA stability but have no effect on the global level or function of the tible gene appears to contribute to the development and progression of RA regardless of ACPA status, 188,189 supporting the notion that the susceptible variant may also drive RA susceptibility as a consequence of its immunogenicity, rather than just its enzyme activity. Consistent with this hypothesis, the susceptible PAD4

haplotype was strikingly associated with anti-PAD4 autoantibodies in a cohort of Caucasian RA patients, even though the association of the susceptible haplotype with RA development has not been observed in Caucasians. While this association was not observed in a cohort of RA patients from Mexico, an association between the susceptible haplotype and anti-CCP and anti-MCV antibodies was found. Thus, the role for the PADI4-susceptible haplotype in RA risk remains unclear and may involve alternations in PAD4 immunogenicity as well in its ability to generate immunogenic citrullinated products.

### Environmental Factors Linked to the Development of Citrullination-Associated Autoantibodies

Although hypercitrullination is found in the RA joint once disease is established (see the section "The Citrullinome in Rheumatoid Arthritis"), it is unknown whether abnormal citrullination precedes the onset of clinical RA, a requisite to explain the presence of ACPAs long before the onset of clinical disease. Although such evidence will be very challenging to obtain, a body of data suggests that the joint is not the only possible site of hypercitrullination that might initiate the RA-specific immune responses to citrullination-associated autoantigens. There is growing support for the hypothesis that aberrant protein citrullination and breach of immunologic tolerance to citrullinated antigens initially occurs at mucosal sites such as the oral mucosa, lung, and gastrointestinal 191-193 In support of this hypothesis, anti-CCP antibodies of tract. the IgA class (an isotype associated with mucosal immunity) are found in about one-third of patients with recent-onset RA194; and anti-CCP antibodies can be detected in the sputum of individuals at risk of developing RA (e.g., RA-free first-degree relatives). If the lung is an initial site of ACPA production, it is postulated that joints only become targeted secondarily after the immune response is initiated as a consequence of an inflammatory event triggered by a common environmental exposure, such as infection, inflammation, or smoking (Fig. 56.3).191-193 Interestingly, PAD4-activating anti-PAD3/PAD4 IgA was identified in the induced sputum from a subset of patients with established RA, but not at-risk individuals, suggesting that these antibodies may arise later in the disease process and play an active role in lung disease.

Smoking is the most widely studied environmental factor linked to RA and ACPA development. A history of smoking in patients with SE alleles (see "Genetic Factors Linked to the Development of Citrullination-Associated Autoantibodies") has been linked to the development of ACPA-positive RA in some populations, 179,197-199 but there is growing appreciation that this relationship is nuanced. Whereas HLA-DRB1*04 alleles have been primarily associated with ACPA production in the general RA population,200-202 in smokers, HLA-DRB1*0101, *0102, and *1001 alleles demonstrate the strongest association with anti-CCP antibodies. In addition, it has been shown that certain ACPA fine specificities and specific anti-CCP isotypes may be responsible for driving this association.203, Anti-CCP antibodies can also be found in patients with ILD who do not have RA,96,97 further suggesting that smoking may play a role in generating or sustaining autoantibodies to citrullinated proteins. In this regard, a study of smokers without RA has shown that cigarette smoking increased expression of PAD2 with a modest increase in protein citrullination in the lungs.

Despite the strong relationship between ACPAs and anti- PAD4 antibodies, and increased risk for ILD in anti-PAD3/

PAD4-positive patients who were past or present cigarette smokers,156 a history of cigarette smoking is not associated with the development of anti-PAD4 or anti-PAD3/4 antibodies. This suggests a two-hit model of lung damage in which anti-PAD3/ PAD4 antibodies may synergize with smoking to induce more severe lung disease. In addition, this data suggests a role for other environmental factors, which have not yet been identified, in the development of anti-PAD immune responses.

Infection, particularly at mucosal sites, may represent another factor associated with autoantibody development in RA. Tantalizing similarities and epidemiologic associations exist between periodontitis and RA, including the presence of bone erosions, association with similar SE alleles and smoking, and enrichment of severe periodontal disease in patients with RA. 192, These connections have focused attention on the study of oral pathogens as potential triggers of autoimmunity in RA. The identification that Porphyromonas gingivalis (P. gingivalis) produces and secretes a PAD enzyme (termed PPAD) led to the initial hypothesis that infection with this periodontal pathogen may be etiologically linked to RA.210, Unlike mammalian PADs, however, PPAD citrullinates free L-arginine in addition to peptidylarginine and does not require calcium or any other metal ion for activity. Importantly, PPAD has preference for (and is potentially restricted to) citrullination of carboxy-terminal arginines (C-terminal exodeiminase).210, Although some studies have supported the idea that PPAD can citrullinate autoantigens targeted by ACPAs,213 the pattern of citrullination induced by this enzyme (i.e., C-terminal citrulline residues) is not characteristic in proteins recognized by ACPAs, which target citrulline residues within protein sequences (i.e., endocitrullination). Indeed, there is evidence supporting that the presence of amino acid residues on the C-terminal side of citrulline are essential for ACPA reactivity.

An alternative mechanism that has been proposed for the involvement of PPAD in RA pathogenesis is by citrullinating its own bacterial products, which may act as the inciting citrullinated antigens. Although initial studies suggested that autocitrullination of PPAD may be relevant in this regard,214 further studies by mass spectrometry and crystal structure analysis of PPAD isolated from P. gingivalis have not supported this hypothesis.212, In addition, one study showed that proteins from a mutant strain of P. gingivalis lacking PPAD activity were recognized similarly to the wild-type strain by both ACPA-positive and -negative sera, suggesting that autocitrullinated P. gingivalis are not a major target of ACPAs. The recent finding of a P. gingivalis strain encoding a mutant PPAD with endodeiminase activity, however, has renewed interest in unique P. gingivalis strains that could play a role in RA pathogenesis.

The periodontal microenvironment in patients with periodontitis is highly enriched in citrullinated proteins, mimicking patterns of hypercitrullination generated by PADs in the RA joint. This has suggested that the citrullinome in periodontitis is generated by the abnormal activation of host, rather than bacterial, PAD enzymes. Among different microbial species associated with severe periodontitis, Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans (Aa) was identified as the only pathogen that could reproduce the citrullinome found in periodontitis and RA. However, in contrast to P. gingivalis in which citrullination is attributed to its own PAD, Aa does not encode a PAD enzyme. Instead, the bacterium secretes a pore-forming toxin (leukotoxin A) that targets neutrophils, inducing prominent calcium influx, osmotic lysis, and hyperactivation of PAD enzymes in a process termed leukotoxic bypercitrullination (LTH).219, This dysregulated PAD activation was shown

to induce global citrullination of a wide range of proteins in the neutrophil, mirroring hypercitrullination found in periodontitis and the RA joint. 62,

Mechanistically, LTH induced by bacterial toxins is similar to that induced by host immune-effector pathways in the RA joint (see the section "Mechanisms for Citrullination-Associated Autoantigen Production in the Rheumatoid Joint").62, If tolerance is broken to the citrullinated products of Aa-induced hypercitrullination, this process may initiate the subsequent production of ACPAs.117, Moreover, a recent study found that oral bacteria targeted by ACPAs are citrullinated in the mouth by extra-cellular host PADs,223 supporting a role of PADs released from dying cells, such as LTH, in the production of citrullinated bacteria targeted by ACPAs in periodontitis. Importantly, as other bacterial species also produce pore-forming toxins,224 it is possible that a similar mechanism may also be relevant to other pathogens at various mucosal sites, including the lung and gut. 117,

Recent studies have shown that human cytomegalovirus (CMV) can induce overexpression and activation of PAD2 and PAD4 in infected cells, promoting hypercitrullination of both viral and host proteins as a mechanism of viral fitness.' 225 Interestingly, pathogens promote their survival by interfering with or hijacking host PTM pathways.226, Thus, similar to other PTMs, it appears that pathogens promote dysregulated or abnormal protein citrullination as a mechanism to subvert antimicrobial immune responses of the host and thereby maximize their progeny. During this process, pathogens can induce citrullination of unique proteins, which are not part of the normal citrullinome, generating novel patterns of citrullination and likely neoantigens. For instance, the citrullinomes induced by Aa and CMV comprise proteins described within the healthy citrullinome, as well as novel citrullinated proteins, many of which are found in the RA joint. The production of citrullinated neoantigens during infection and in response to environmental factors is an important mechanism that may explain the initiation of an antibody response to citrullinated proteins in susceptible individuals.

Although there is no clear evidence that Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) and human papillomavirus (HPV) are citrullinated during infection, it is interesting that a subset of ACPA-positive RA sera has been demonstrated to cross-react with synthetic citrullinated peptides from EBV EBNA-1 and HPV-47 E2345-362.2 228, Defining the kinetics of appearance of these antibodies during disease development, and demonstrating directly that these modified proteins are generated during natural infection, will be important to determine whether this cross-reactivity is relevant to RA pathogenesis.

These gene—environment interactions playing out in microenvironments outside the joint add important dimensions to the framework within which RA pathogenesis must be investigated and understood. The list of pathogens that are associated with the development of RA-associated autoantibodies and immune responses is growing, 230,231 some of which are arthritogenic in animal models. While pathogens may contribute to RA development, RA-associated immune responses may also be beneficial in controlling infection. Although it is possible that none of the mechanisms currently defined represent a unifying mechanism of RA pathogenesis, the broader view of potential immunizing environments and the search for a frequent worldwide environmental exposure is of great importance.

### Development, Specificity, and Pathogenesis s of Citrullination-Associated Antibodies: Lessons Learned From Monoclonal Antibodies Derived From Patients With Rheumatoid Arthritis

### ACPA Development and Specificity

Important insights into ACPA development, target specificity, and pathogenicity have been gained through the study of monoclonal ACPAs derived from single B cells/plasmablasts isolated from patients with RA.26, The first lesson has been that ACPAs are enriched in somatic mutations, 27,235,236,239-241 supporting the notion that ACPAs are produced by constant exposure to citrullinated autoantigens. The second is that individual ACPAs, even those cloned from seemingly antigen-specific B cells, are multire- 26, This feaactive to many citrullinated antigens. ture can be explained by recognition of consensus peptide motifs found across multiple citrullinated proteins (e.g., citrulline-glycine, glycine-citrulline, arginine-citrulline-aspartic acid), implying that ACPAs target consensus binding motifs rather than unique citrullinated proteins.26, This may explain why the clinical and pathogenic value of detecting ACPAs to "specific" citrullinated proteins is limited. The third lesson is that distinct patterns of mutations during affinity maturation of a single ACPA precursor can generate diverse antibodies recognizing different citrullinated 235, This means that, in theory, the entire polyclonal antigens. repertoire of ACPAs in a patient could be generated from a small number of B cell precursors through affinity maturation. The fourth lesson is that ACPAs are glycosylated in the variable domain, 243,244 an uncommon feature among antibodies,245 which results from the generation of N-linked glycosylation consensus sequences during the process of somatic hypermutation. While this modification appears to have no effect on antigen recognition, it has been proposed that N-glycosylation provides a selective advantage to ACPA-producing B cells to escape negative selection in germinal centers. The fifth and final lesson is that ACPAs are cross-reactive to other PTMs with a similar shape, charge, and hydrophobicity as citrulline, such as carbamylated lysine (homocitrulline) and acetylated lysine (Fig. 56.1).

### ACPAs in the Pathogenesis of Rheumatoid Arthritis

Initial in vitro evidence suggests that polyclonal ACPAs from RA serum can activate both the classical and alternative pathways of complement246 and that ACPA immune complexes drive macrophages to produced TNF via engagement of Fcγ receptors and Toll-like receptor 4 (Fig. 56.4).241, In addition, ACPAs purified from RA serum using MCV can induce differentiation of human osteoclast precursors into osteoclasts in vitro and promote osteopenia and osteoclastogenesis in lymphocyte-deficient Rag1-/- mice after intraperitoneal injection with lipopolysaccharide. More recently, mechanistic studies have been centered on the analysis of monoclonal antibodies. Interestingly, although monoclonal antibodies to citrullinated collagen type II generated by immunization in mice can cause arthritis by cross-reactivity to joint cartilage,251 monoclonal ACPAs derived from RA patients cannot alone induce arthritis in mice. In healthy mice, monoclonal ACPAs can induce arthralgia, tenosynovitis, or bone loss in the absence of joint edema or synovitis.252, In experimental arthritis, studies have found that monoclonal ACPAs can display different effects in vivo and can either enhance, ameliorate, or even inhibit arthritis in mice.236, Although initial studies suggested that cC "anti-inflammatory" ACPAs are specific for citrullinated histones

2A and 4254,257 (also known as anti-NET ACPAs), 258 subsequent studies showed that the antior pro-inflammatory effect of ACPAs was not related to the targeting of specific citrullinated .255, The mechanisms by which RA-derived monoproteins. clonal ACPAs modulate arthritis in mice is unclear, particularly because autoantigen citrullination is not a mechanism involved in the induction of experimental arthritis in mice. Therefore these data need to be taken with caution before translating into the human model. Nevertheless, the possibility that distinct ACPAs, likely defined by targeting unique sets of antigens with common citrullination motifs, may have different effects on modulating RA is interesting and could make an important change in the pathogenic paradigm of ACPAs in RA.

### Anti-PAD4 Antibodies: Origin and Pathogenicity

Anti-PAD4 monoclonal autoantibodies have been derived from PAD4-specific memory B cells isolated from patients with RA. Analysis of these antibodies has suggested that they arise from PAD4-reactive precursors, implying that defective checkpoints in B cell tolerance are likely involved in the initial production of these antibodies. Nevertheless, autoantibodies to PAD4 have evidence of somatic hypermutation, suggesting that in patients with RA, these antibodies have undergone antigendriven affinity maturation. Although ACPAs and anti-PAD4 autoantibodies appear to originate by different mechanisms, chronic exposure to immunogenic self-antigens appears to be a common driver.

Functional analysis of RA-derived monoclonal anti-PAD4 autoantibodies showed that, like polyclonal IgG from RA patients with anti-PAD3/PAD4 antibodies (see the section "Autoantibodies to Peptidylarginine Deiminase Enzymes"), 154,259 they were able to increase PAD4-citrullination activity at low calcium concentrations. Biochemical studies have revealed that this enhancement is mediated by an interaction with structural epitopes at calciumbinding sites at the interface between the Nand C-terminal domains. This suggests that anti-PAD4 antibodies could possess the unique ability to propagate the generation of citrullinated proteins in the RA joint (Fig. 56.4) (see "Mechanisms for Citrullination-Associated Autoantigen Production in the Rheumatoid Joint"), but further in vitro and in vivo characterization is needed to determine the full pathogenic potential of anti-PAD4 antibodies in patients with RA.

### Mechanisms for Citrullination-Associated Autoantigen Production in the Rheumatoid Joint

Once citrullinated-associated autoantibody responses are formed, the propagation of inflammation in the RA joint requires the continued generation of citrullinated antigens and presence of active PAD enzymes (Fig. 56.4). Analysis of synovial fluid and cells suggests that dysregulated PAD activation with ongoing protein citrullination occurs both intraand extra-cellularly in the RA joint.61-65, Several PAD-expressing cells (such as immune cells and synoviocytes) and distinct mechanisms of cell death (including autophagy, NETosis, necrosis, and cytolysis induced by pore-forming proteins) have been implicated in the production of citrullinated autoantigens in RA by inducing intra-cellular PAD activation and the release of PADs into the extra-cellular environ- 117, In this regard, recent studies have implicated neutroment. phils as a major source of intra-cellular citrullination and soluble PADs for extra-cellular citrullination.51, These cells represent one of the most abundant cell types in RA synovial fluid and constitutively express several PADs.

Two mechanisms have been proposed to drive the cellular generation of RA autoantigens in neutrophils: (1) formation of neutrophil extra-cellular traps (NETs),260 an anti-microbial form of cell death (also known as NETosis) in which granule proteins and chromatin are extruded from the cell and form extra-cellular fibers that bind pathogens, 262 and (2) membranolytic damage mediated by pore-forming proteins.62, NET formation is increased in the joints of patients with RA and may be a relevant source of inflammatory signals through the extra-cellular redistribution of intra-cellular antigens. While these may include citrullinated autoantigens, a growing body of data has demonstrated that the formation of NETs is a complex process resulting from the activation of different pathways that can be triggered by a broad range of stimuli, only some of which are associated with citrullination of a limited number of substrates, mainly histones.62, Hence, even though NETs in RA may be associated with PAD4 activation, the contribution of this process to generating the RA citrullinome is unclear. Thus, although citrullination and the formation of NETs may be increased in the RA joint, and NETs may contribute to RA pathogenesis,260 these processes may not necessarily be directly associated.

As described (see the section "Environmental Factors Linked to the Development of Citrullination-Associated Autoantibodies"), bacterial toxins have the capacity to activate PADs and induce hypercitrullination, which could initiate the production of ACPAs at extraarticular sites. Host pore-forming proteins, such as perforin and the membrane attack complex of complement, may then be responsible for sustaining the production of citrullinated autoantigens in the joints of patients with RA.62, These host effector pathways are active in the RA joint,265-269 and have been demonstrated to be potent activators of PADs and efficient inducers of the neutrophil hypercitrullination that mirrors the RA joint citrullinome. 62,

In addition to neutrophils, monocytes and fibroblast-like synoviocytes can also generate citrullinated autoantigens as a result of autophagy. However, this process does not lead to hypercitrullination but, rather, to the citrullination of α-enolase and vimentin. Interestingly, increased expression of autophagy markers correlates with ACPA titers, suggesting that autophagy may contribute to generation of these citrullinated antigens in patients with RA.

The discovery that fibrinogen is heavily citrullinated in the RA joint provided initial evidence that citrullination can also occur extra-cellularly. Soluble PAD2 and PAD4 have been detected in the synovial fluid from patients with RA,47,126 suggesting that these enzymes are released from activated or dying cells, most likely neutrophils. In this regard, a recent report showed that neutrophils constitutively secrete PAD2 and express a fraction of PAD4 on their cell surface, which can be upregulated following cell activation. Although regulatory mechanisms exist to limit aberrant PAD activity (see the section "Peptidylarginine Deiminase Activity and Regulation"), accumulation of PAD enzymes in the inflamed RA joint could overcome these inhibitory factors. For example, although the oxidizing extra-cellular environment is inhospitable to PAD activity, a continued supply of active PADs release from neutrophils infiltrating the inflamed RA joint could fuel the generation of citrullinated proteins. Autoantibodies to the PAD enzymes themselves may also support extracellular PAD activity by stabilizing the active conformation of PAD4. Human anti-PAD4 monoclonal and anti-PAD3/PAD4 cross-reactive autoantibodies were also shown to enhance PAD4 enzymatic activity by lowering the amount of calcium needed for .154, Thus, PAD4 released catalysis into the physiologic range.

during neutrophil activation or death may encounter anti-PAD4 antibodies in synovial fluid with the capacity to sustain enzymatic activity, contributing to extra-cellular citrullinated autoantigen generation in RA. Together, the presence of effector pathways that drive hypercitrullination and extra-cellular release of citrullinated antigens and PADs likely create a feed-forward loop that keeps a constant production of autoantigens for B cell stimulation, autoantibody production, immune complex formation, and tissue damage (Fig. 56.4).

### Antibodies s to Post-translational Modifications With Structural Similarity to − Citrulline

### Antibodies to Carbamylated Proteins

Carbamylation or homocitrullination is a nonenzymatic posttranslational process in which lysine residues are converted to homocitrulline. This process results from the reaction of cyanate or carbamyl phosphate with the primary amine of lysine residues (Fig. 56.1B).133, Cyanate is present in the body in equilibrium with urea and, therefore, carbamylation accumulates in conditions that enhance cyanate levels, such as uremia, inflammation, and cigarette smoking. Carbamyl phosphate is generated from ammonia and bicarbonate by the catalytic activity of carbamoyl phosphate synthases. Although homocitrulline is one methylene group longer than citrulline, these amino acids are similar in shape, charge, and hydrophobicity (Fig. 56.1B). Different than citrullination, however, carbamylation is generated in conditions associated with oxidative stress 274-278 and is considered in the group of PTM-derived products (PTMDPs).279, PTMDPs are irreversible, accumulate during life, and have critical influence on protein structure and biologic functions, especially in the context of aging, physiologic stress, and inflammation. 276,

The study of anti-carbamylated protein (anti-CarP) antibodies resulted from the search for PTMs that may explain the pathogenic role of citrullinated proteins in RA.281, Because attempts at using citrullinated proteins or antibodies targeting citrullinated peptides to induce experimental arthritis yielded modest or negative results, 283-285 it was postulated that other factors might be responsible for triggering arthritis. Since citrulline and homocitrulline are structurally similar, it was hypothesized that carbamylated proteins may be the "missing link" between citrullination and RA. 281, In support of this hypothesis, initial studies demonstrated that mice immunized with carbamylated peptides developed erosive arthritis. Moreover, these mice became susceptible to a more aggressive form of erosive arthritis following a subsequent intraarticular injection of citrullinated peptides. While the significance of these interesting findings has not been pursued experimentally, these observations sparked interest in defining whether patients with RA have antibodies to carbamylated proteins.

Using carbamylatedfetal calf serum and carbamylated-fibrinogen as surrogate antigens in ELISA assays, IgG and IgA anti-CarP antibodies were identified in more than 40% of patients with RA (Table 56.1). Although homocitrulline structurally resembles citrulline, the finding that anti-CarP IgG and IgA antibodies are present in approximately 35% of ACPA-negative patients and that these antibodies are predictive of a more severe disease course independent of ACPA status, initially suggested that these antibodies were not merely cross-reactive between the two PTMs.

However, the analysis of monoclonal antibodies has challenged this notion, suggesting the possibility that ACPAs and anti-CarP antibodies are cross-reactive antibodies (see the section "Implications of the Anti-Modified Protein Antibodies Concept"). Anti- CarP antibodies appear many years before the diagnosis of RA and predict the development of RA independently of anti-CCP antibodies in patients with arthralgia. 287-289

Although the mechanism by which carbamylated antigens are generated in RA is still unknown, it has been proposed that inflammation may be the trigger of enhanced carbamylation. Myeloperoxidase released from neutrophils in the RA joint may promote the conversion of thiocyanate to cyanate, further enhancing carbamylation.274, Nevertheless, despite the growing interest in anti-CarP antibodies, a major caveat is that their primary protein targets in RA are still unknown. Recently alpha-1-antitrypsin was found to be carbamylated in synovial fluid from an RA patient and was found to be recognized more strongly by RA patient sera compared with control sera. Additional studies are needed to define the specific set of carbamylated autoantigens targeted in RA and their presence in RA target tissue in order to better understand the clinical significance and pathogenic role of anti-CarP antibodies in RA.

### Anti-acetylated Protein Antibodies

Lysine acetylation is a reversible PTM consisting of the transfer of an acetyl group from acetyl-coenzyme A to the ε-amino group of lysine residues. Although acetylation can occur nonenzymatically,293 in the majority of cases, it is regulated by a balance between lysine acetyltransferases and lysine deacetylases (Fig. 56.1C). Several thousand proteins have been identified as targets of acetylation in different cell lines and tissues from humans and mice.294, Lysine acetylation is a dynamic process used in nearly all intra-cellular compartments to regulate the function and interactions of proteins involved in distinct cellular processes, such as epigenetic regulation, cellular proliferation, and mitochondrial function, among others.

The identification of anti-acetylated protein antibodies (AAPAs) followed the search for novel antibodies targeting PTMs with structural similarity to citrulline and/or homocitrulline. Since acetylated lysine (KAc) resembles homocitrulline (except for the side-chain terminal amine, which is replaced by a methyl group) (Fig. 56.1), it was hypothesized that this modification may also be recognized by antibodies in RA. However, in contrast to the discovery of ACPAs and anti-CarP antibodies, in which their detection was based on modified antigens with potential biologic relevance, AAPAs were initially detected using a peptide sequence that does not exist in proteins.

To investigate the presence of AAPAs, a 12 amino acid peptide sequence derived from MCV (used to detect ACPAs) was changed to include KAc instead of citrulline at position 7.296 The rationale of using this peptide to screen for AAPAs may have followed the idea that antigen recognition by these antibodies is only dependent on the presence of KAc and that ACPAs do not bind KAc. However, it is important to consider that efficient antigen binding by ACPAs is not only dependent on the modified residue but occurs only in the context of specific amino acids neighboring the citrulline.24-27, Therefore, using a peptide containing an ideal ACPA recognition motif in which citrulline was changed for a structurally similar residue (e.g., KAc or homocitrulline), it is likely to be recognized by subsets of ACPAs that tolerate this change in the antigen, rather than validating the existence of a

new subset of antibodies in RA. Indeed, when KAc is introduced at position 2 instead of position 7 into MCV (i.e., outside the ACPA recognition motif), antibody reactivity to this peptide was importantly reduced. Moreover, analysis of RA-derived monoclonal antibodies supports the notion of cross-reactivity of ACPA subsets with peptides/proteins containing KAc26,233,234,298 (see the section "Implications of the Anti-Modified Protein Antibodies Concept").

A similar approach has been used to detect AAPAs, but instead using acetylated ornithine (which is one methylene group shorter than KAc) rather than citrulline at position 7 within the MCV peptide. Similar to the MCV peptide containing KAc, ACPApositive sera reacted with the peptide containing the acetylated ornithine residue, 297-299 suggesting that binding to this peptide is also observed with some ACPAs. Importantly, since ornithine is not an amino acid present in proteins naturally, this modification is not relevant as a source of autoantigens in RA.

Although the initial data suggesting the existence of AAPAs in RA were ambiguous,296 further studies have pursued this modification in RA using peptides from proteins containing naturally occurring KAc sites (i.e., histones).297, In one study, reactivity to KAc-Histone 2B was almost exclusively detected in individuals with anti-CCP-positive RA,298 supporting cross-reactivity with ACPAs. Thus, whereas the detection of AAPAs may be useful as a surrogate to identify RA subsets and antibody-positive RA in 298,299rigorous evisome patients negative using the CCP assays, dence is lacking to confirm that AAPAs are an independent antibody specificity in RA, as initially suggested. 296

### Antibodies to Malondialdehyde- Acetaldehyde Adducts

Similar to carbamylation, the generation of malondialdehydeacetaldehyde adducts (MAAs) is nonenzymatic. During oxidative stress caused by a variety of stimuli, including inflammation and exposure to alcohol, ROS triggers peroxidation of membrane lipids, resulting in the formation of reactive malondialdehyde (MDA) and acetaldehyde (AA).300-303 These products can covalently modify proteins through carbonylation of amino acids carrying free amine groups (i.e., lysine, arginine, histidine) and, to a lesser extent, amino acids with amide groups (i.e., asparagine, glutamine), resulting in the formation of stable MDA-AA protein adducts, referred to as MAA (Fig. 56.1D).304, These adducts have been implicated in contributing to inflammation and cellular injury associated with cardiovascular and alcoholic liver disease. 300-302

Interestingly, RA synovial tissue, but not tissue from patients with osteoarthritis, is enriched in MAA-modified proteins, which co-localize with citrullinated proteins, leading to the search of anti-MAA antibodies in RA. Using MAA-modified albumin as a surrogate antigen, anti-MAA antibodies are found in up to 44% of patients with RA. Although anti-MAA antibodies are strongly associated with anti-CCP and RF, it is interesting that anti-MAA antibodies of the IgG isotype are found in 33% to 88% of patients (depending on the cohort) who are negative for anti-CCP antibodies, 8,306 suggesting that these may be useful biomarkers, particularly in people with ACPA-negative RA (Table 56.1). In addition, anti-MAA IgG and IgA are detected in pre-clinical RA but appear later than anti-CCP2 or RF, suggesting that anti-MAA antibodies may play a role in the transition from subclinical to clinical RA. MAA-modified proteins in

RA synovial tissue includes serum proteins (i.e., albumin, hemoglobin, IgG gamma chain, transferrin, and apolipoprotein A1), the acute-phase protein αl-glycoprotein-1, the enzyme carbonic anhydrase-1, and cytoskeletal proteins (actin and vimentin), 308 which are candidates targets of anti-MAA antibodies in RA.

Anti-MDA IgG levels significantly correlate with disease activity by DAS28-ESR, and with high serum levels of TNF, IL-6, and C-reactive protein. Moreover, using a large cohort of patients with RA to compare antibodies to different PTMs (i.e., CCP2, anti-CarP, AAPAs, and anti-MAA), patients with more active disease by DAS28 had higher levels of IgG anti-MAA antibodies, which was not observed for any other autoantibody or RF isotype tested. Nevertheless, compared with other autoantibodies, IgG anti-MAA antibodies were not significantly elevated in RA-risk individuals, suggesting that anti-MAA antibodies likely contribute to established and active disease. In addition to the RA joint, MAA is highly expressed in RA-ILD lung tissue, . and anti-MAA IgA and IgM antibodies have been associated with ILD in patients with RA. Together, these data suggest that MAAmodified proteins, which colocalize with citrullinated proteins in RA target tissues, likely enhance autoantibody-induced damage in RA. It is important to highlight that anti-MAA antibodies are not specific for RA but have also been found in patients with osteoarthritis, SLE, alcohol-induced liver disease, diabetes, and CVD.298, Therefore, these antibodies may not exclusively be markers of joint damage but may be generated as a result of comorbidities associated with RA.

In contrast to anti-CarP antibodies and AAPAs, current evidence supports that anti-MAA antibodies are not cross-reactive with ACPAs. MAA adducts have no structural similarity to citrulline residues (Fig. 56.1), and the shape and charge of MAA adducts are unlikely to fit into the ACPA paratope. Moreover, while anti-MAA antibodies are associated with ACPA positive disease, these antibodies are not directly related to anti-citrulline reactivity. More importantly, monoclonal ACPAs have no reactivity with MAA-modified proteins and, similarly, RA-derived monoclonal anti-MAA antibodies have no reactivity with citrullinated sequences. Interestingly, although anti-MAA monoclonal antibodies have not been characterized as extensively as ACPAs, current evidence suggests that, unlike ACPAs, anti-MDA/MAA antibodies primarily target the modified amino acid residue without the need of interacting with the neighboring amino acids, 308 resembling the immune response to a hapten.315-317 Haptens are small molecules that cannot induce an antibody response unless they are attached to a larger carrier. In this scenario, even though anti-MAA antibodies in RA were generated with and react against modified self-antigens, these antibodies may not represent autoantibodies per se but rather anti-hapten antibodies.

### Implications of the Anti-modified Protein Antibodies Concept

The concept of anti-modified protein antibodies (AMPAs) was introduced to unify three seemingly independent but crossreactive classes of autoantibodies targeting PTMs in RA: ACPAs, anti-CarP antibodies, and AAPAs.233, The definition of AMPAs offers some advantages for diagnosis and mechanisms in RA. Because a small proportion of ACPA-negative RA (detected by anti-CCP assays) is positive for anti-CarP antibodies and/or AAPAs, the model of AMPAs permits classifying a larger number of patients as seropositive RA regardless of the antibody

specificity. 233, Moreover, because these antibodies are highly cross-reactive among citrullinated, carbamylated, and acetylated peptides, their classification as AMPAs implies that these antibodies are mechanistically related and likely generated by common pathogenic mechanisms. Against the AMPA concept, however, is the lack of evidence supporting that ACPAs, anti-CarP antibodies and AAPAs are indeed independent antibodies, particularly for the AAPA group (see the section "Anti-Acetylated Protein Antibodies"). Rather, these distinct subsets of antibodies may correspond to heterogenous ACPAs, some of which can bind to PTMs with structural similarity to citrulline, mostly when the modified residue is found within an ACPA binding motif. In support of this notion, the study of RA-derived monoclonal antibodies has shown the existence of ACPA subsets with the additional capacity to efficiently bind carbamylated and acetylated sequences. 26, Since carbamylation is an immunogenic PTMDP, however, it cannot be excluded that this modification may play a role, via crossreactivity, in the initial induction of ACPAs in RA.

It is certain that by interacting with other protein modifications—for instance, carbamylated and acetylated proteins— ACPAs may extend their pathogenic effect in RA through 233, Similarly, using specific carbamylated and cross-reactivity. acetylated peptides may overcome potential limitations in the detection of some antibodies using CCPs and to identify ACPA subsets that may target unique cross-reactive epitopes. However, this nomenclature, while conceptually useful, does not necessarily imply the existence of etiologically distinct antibody subsets that cross-react with diverse antigen modifications in RA. This is particularly relevant since the initial definition of AMPAs was done to unify cross-reactive antibodies reactive to citrullinated, carbamylated, and acetylated antigens, and the further inclusion of anti-MAA antibodies as AMPAs,298,319 which do not recognize these three modifications, 308 may not be appropriate.

### Other RA Autoantibodies

### Rheumatoid Factor

RFs are autoantibodies that target the Fc region of IgG. Besides their potential relevance to autoimmune disease pathogenesis, RFs hold a special place in rheumatology because they were the first autoantibodies discovered in the autoimmune rheumatic diseases. In 1940, Erik Waaler found that sera from patients with RA inhibited the hemolysis of antibody-sensitized sheep erythrocytes and, instead, cause marked agglutination of these cells. He also noted that this effect was thermostable and associated with the globulin fraction of the serum, demonstrating that it was not dependent on complement activation. It was suggested that this process resulted from the existence of a factor ("the agglutination activating factor," later called rheumatoid factor), which was increased in patients with RA. Nevertheless, despite the high prevalence of a positive agglutination reaction in sera from patients with RA (35% positive), Waaler did not consider it of diagnostic value for RA because some patients with other diseases (such as cancer and infections) were also positive (~5%). Later, this phenomenon was rediscovered in 1948 by Rose and colleagues while performing complement fixation tests for rickettsialpox, and they suggested the potential of this test in the diagnosis of RA. These assays were later shown to be detecting IgM antibodies from patients with RA that recognized the Fc portion of IgG.322-325 Numerous modifications of the agglutination assay have evolved (called the Waaler-Rose agglutination test), which led to the use of

IgG-coated latex beads instead of sheep erythrocytes. 326, Subsequent developments established RF assays in radioimmunoassay, ELISA, and nephelometry formats, with increased convenience but similar performance in terms of sensitivity and specificity.

RFs are positive in ~70% of RA patients but have been shown to have lower specificity for RA compared with anti-CCP antibodies (85 vs. 95%, respectively) (Table 56.1). RFs may be positive in healthy control subjects (1% in younger persons and up to 5% in persons older than age 70) and in patients with numerous other non-RA diseases (including other rheumatic diseases such as Sjögren's syndrome and cryoglobulinemia), and chronic infections. 328-330 The pre-test probability of diagnosing RA therefore greatly influences the performance of the RF test, with sensitivities and specificities both in the 50 to 90% range, depending on the patient groups studied.331, The existence of IgG and IgA RFs and evidence of somatic hypermutation have suggested that some RFs in RA are T cell dependent. 333, Although some studies have suggested that IgG and IgA RFs increase the specificity of RFs for RA,35 a recent meta-analysis showed that assays of the different RF isotypes performed very similarly in terms of sensitivity and specificity to standard RF assays.

Importantly, patients with RA also vary in terms of timing of the appearance of RF, with RF preceding symptomatic disease in a significant subpopulation158,336-338a and following disease onset with variable kinetics in other patients. Indeed, earlier onset of RF in patients with RA has been associated with more severe disease, highlighting a possible contribution of these antibodies to disease amplification. The observation that RF only appears after disease onset in some patients suggests that it may mark distinct, sequential events in pathogenesis, which are very close together in the subgroup in whom RF occurs early, or are separated in time in patients in whom RF follows symptoms. The mechanisms that drive the production of RF in persons with RA are not fully understood. The presence of somatic hypermutation in RFs and the evidence that these antibodies are produced by plasma cells in the rheumatoid synovium have suggested that the RF response is driven locally by antigens.333,334I However, it is still unclear how IgG becomes a target of the autoimmune response in the rheumatoid joint. In contrast to other autoantigens in RA, there is no evidence that the IgG targeted by RFs requires modification (e.g., PTM) for antibody recognition. Nevertheless, it is still possible that the initial events that break tolerance to IgG may be initiated through an abnormally modified molecule, as occurs for other autoantigens in RA. The possible mechanisms whereby RF may play an amplifying role in RA are numerous and include formation of immune complexes as well as amplification of cellular antigen capture, signaling, and effector functions, among others (Fig. 56.4). More recently, in vitro studies have suggested that RFs increase the capacity of ACPA immune complexes to activate complement and stimulate pro-inflammatory cytokine production by macrophages.341-343 Thus, although RF may not be specific for RA, these autoantibodies may enhance the pathogenicity of RA-specific autoantibodies such as ACPAs.

### Anti-RA33 Autoantibodies

Anti-RA33 antibodies were discovered in 1989 as a novel autoantibody specificity recognizing a nuclear protein with an apparent molecular mass of 33 kDa. These autoantibodies were detected in 35% of patients with RA but were also detected in a small number of patients who had other autoimmune or degenerative rheumatic disorders (Table 56.1). In later studies, the RA33 antigen

was identified as the A2/B1 protein of the heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoprotein complex (hnRNP-A2/B1). Further characterization of this antibody showed that it was not specific for RA but was also found in approximately 20% of patients with SLE and in 40 to 60% of patients with mixed connective tissue disease (MCTD).346, However, in SLE and MCTD, anti-RA33 usually occurred together with antibodies to U1-small nuclear ribonucleoproteins (snRNPs) or Smith (Sm) antigen. Therefore anti-RA33 without concomitant anti—U1 snRNP autoantibodies were found to have specificity of 96% for RA. Additionally, anti-RA33 antibodies in RA, SLE, and MCTD are distinguished by their recognition of different conformation-dependent epitopes in hnRNP-A2/B1.348 Moreover, in the absence of RF and ACPAs, anti-RA33 antibodies in patients with very early arthritis (<3 months' duration) are associated with a relatively mild nonerosive disease course, potentially identifying patients with a good prognosis who will respond well to treatment with DMARDs. Stimulation assays using hnRNP-A2 showed proliferation of RA-derived T cells in almost 60% of patients with RA, but only 20% of the control subjects, with substantially stronger responses observed in patients with RA. Interestingly, immunohistochemical analyses have revealed pronounced overexpression of hnRNP-A2 in the synovial tissue of patients with RA, placing the antigen at sites of disease in RA.

An intriguing feature of RA33 is that this antigen is also citrullinated in the RA joint and is a target of ACPAs in RA. Thus, patients with RA can have antibodies to both the native and citrullinated forms of RA33. Moreover, four transcript variants encoded by the same gene have been identified in cells from RA synovial fluid (designated hnRNP-A2, B1, A2b, and B1b), with B1b being most strongly recognized. In a single cohort, antibodies against citrullinated hnRNPB1b were identified in 44% patients with RA, whereas antibodies against the native protein were detected in 10.7% of patients. Only 6% of patients with RA had both antibody specificities. The presence of autoantibodies against the same antigen in two different forms (i.e., native and citrullinated) may reflect an evolving immune response to structural immunogenic changes in autoantigens that occur during the development of the disease.

### Anti-glucose-6-Phosphate Isomerase Antibodies

Glucose-6-phosphate isomerase (G6PI) is another autoantigen of potential interest in RA, which is a glycolytic enzyme residing in the cytoplasm of all cells. Anti-G6PI antibodies were first discovered in the K/BxN mouse model of arthritis, in which pathogenic immunoglobulins that recognize G6PI are formed.351-353 These antibodies are directly pathogenic in mice, as passive transfer of anti-G6PI antibodies alone can transfer arthritis to healthy recipients. The pathogenic potential of this antibody prompted its study in human RA. However, although initial studies reported a high frequency of such antibodies in sera of patients with RA,355 these results have been the subject of debate.356-358 Overall, anti-G6PI antibodies are found in 12 to 29% of patients with RA in different cohorts and are more prevalent in patients with active disease (Table 56.1). Patients with psoriatic arthritis, undifferentiated arthritis, and spondylarthropathy also develop anti-G6PI antibodies at similar frequencies (12 to 25%), and similar titers are detected in a proportion (5 to 10%) of control subjects or patients with Crohn's disease or sarcoidosis. The potential relevance of these antibodies in RA is still uncertain.

### Conclusion

The autoantibody repertoire in patients with RA is diverse, and new antigen specificities continue to be discovered. Autoantibodies in RA are important tools for disease diagnosis and for identifying clinically informative patient subgroups. They are also serologic clues for understanding disease pathogenesis. Autoantibodies identified to date fall into four major categories: citrullination-associated autoantibodies; antibodies to PTMs with structural similarity to citrulline (i.e., homocitrulline and acetyl-lysine); anti-MAA antibodies; and those that recognize largely native proteins that are shared with other diseases. Understanding how autoantigens are generated and defining the genetic and environ-mental factors linked to autoantibody development offer valuable insights into disease mechanisms. To date, citrullination-associ-ated antibodies are the most specific for the diagnosis of RA, and specific genetic and environmental factors associated with their development have been defined. The discovery of these antibodies has identified dysregulated protein citrullination as a key patho-genic mechanism and potential therapeutic target in this disease. The finding that ACPAs are cross-reactive with carbamylated and acetylated proteins is intriguing and demands understanding of the significance of such crossreactivity. The possibility that anti-CarP antibodies and AAPAs are simply subsets of ACPAs requires major consideration. The analysis of RA autoantibodies and their target antigens at sites of disease initiation and propagation may enable the development of additional novel strategies for the treat-ment and prevention of RA.

# Acute Phase Reactants

### KEY POINTS

Inflammation comprises a complex and highly variable set of processes that represent a response to tissue damage from infection or injury. The acute phase response, a major accompaniment of inflammation, is induced by inflammation-associated cytokines and includes a reorchestration of acute phase protein synthesis by the liver. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), a commonly used clinical measure of inflammation, depends on numerous physical and chemical characteristics of blood, many of which are not related to inflammation. The quintessential acute phase protein, C-reactive protein (CRP), not only offers biomarker utility in the clinic but it also plays a role in host defense by recognition of biologic substrates, activation of the complement pathway, and by binding to leukocytes. Cytokines, chemokines, adhesion molecules, and other products of activated inflammatory cells are secreted during inflammation and play roles in the inflammatory response, but several problems limit the clinical usefulness of their quantitation for routine clinical purposes. CRP and ESR may reflect disease activity and correlate with disease prognosis in rheumatoid arthritis but generally are not helpful for differential diagnosis. Although CRP and ESR correlate with clinical activity in many inflammatory rheumatic diseases, the absent or modest CRP response seen in some patients with active systemic lupus erythematosus remains unexplained. Minor elevations of CRP, within the normal population reference range, are associated with increased risk of myocardial infarction but are nonspecific (especially in patients with rheumatic disease). Minor CRP elevation is associated with well-recognized risk factors for cardiovascular disease, which may explain its predictive value.

### Introduction

The inflammatory response provides a natural defense against unchecked tissue damage from infection or injury. It occurs during the acute phase of an inciting event and, if the stimulus is not eliminated, in a chronic, putatively healing stage. When excessive or uncontrolled, acute and chronic responses have the potential to cause significant harm to the host through autoimmune diseases, allergic reactions, or septic shock.

The concept of inflammation itself has evolved over millenia. Celsus first described the cardinal signs of redness, swelling, heat, and pain in the first century AD. The fifth sign, loss of function, is often attributed to Galen's work in the second century. Since that time, countless advances have been made in the understanding of inflammation, from histologic findings of inflammatory cells

within tissues, to the discovery of hematologic and soluble mediators such as cytokines and complement. The molecular signaling pathways that drive both its protective effects and the inappropriate injurious responses have been elucidated (see Chapters 19, 26, and 27).

With increasing insight into mechanisms of the inflammatory response has come an appreciation of its significant complexity. Molecular and microscopic processes are different during acute and chronic stages, and diverse responses are induced by various types of exogenous and endogenous stimuli (e.g., bacteria, viruses, parasites, crystals, allergens, and ischemia). More recently, the role of the milieu of the inflammatory response, especially at the level of the vascular endothelium, has taken on considerable importance. Furthermore, inherent redundancies of functions have been noted, as have interactions between the mediators of inflammation that allow for a broad, effective response, but these redundancies make it difficult to understand the pathways of inflammation in a linear fashion. These intricacies have resulted in a vague definition and on continued reliance on the final downstream macroscopic cardinal signs to tie together all of the ongoing processes. It is these same intricacies that have made evaluation of inflammation through laboratory tests imprecise.

Basic hematologic abnormalities may give clues to the presence of inflammation, but different patterns are often associated with underlying causes and are not universally found. Leukocytosis can be seen in infections, acute crystal diseases, and some autoimmune disorders such as adult Still's disease. Anemia is often associated with certain diseases that cause chronic inflammation, such as rheumatoid arthritis (RA). Reactive thrombocytosis occurs secondary to the release of cytokines after an inciting infectious or inflammatory event, and the role of platelets and platelet-derived mediators in stimulating inflammation has been described at the molecular level.

Laboratory tests most commonly used by physicians to obtain information about the extent of inflammation are those that measure the acute phase reaction. In response to injury, local inflammatory cells secrete cytokines that influence the liver to increase or decrease production of various proteins. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) has been the classic marker of inflammation, with serum C-reactive protein (CRP) taking on an increasingly prominent role. Other novel inflammatory markers such as procalcitonin have been recognized, but their clinical utility has yet to be fully determined.

CRP elevations, especially minor ones, have been noted in numerous conditions that traditionally have not been considered inflammatory, most significantly involving the cardiovascular system and in cancer. This has shed light on subclinical inflammation

as a possible factor in the pathogenesis of a number of nonrheumatologic diseases.

### Acute Phase Response

Within minutes of tissue injury, activation of the innate immune system induces cytokine production that results in a multisystem acute phase response involving the liver, vascular system, bone marrow, and central nervous system.4, Many elements of the reaction can be regarded as part of the innate response and are defensive or adaptive in nature. Murine studies suggest that as much as 7% of the regulatory gene pool undergoes significant changes in expression during inflammation and that induction of liver acute phase genes is mediated by the transcription factor signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 (STAT3).7-9

Although the acute phase response can trigger numerous neuroendocrine, hematopoietic, and metabolic effects, the changes in plasma proteins synthesized by hepatocytes are monitored as signs of underlying inflammation (Tables 57.1 and 57.2). An acute phase protein is one in which the plasma concentration changes from baseline by at least 25% during inflammation; responses vary in terms of concentration and kinetics (Fig. 57.1). CRP and serum amyloid A (SAA) levels increase more than 1000-fold during acute infection and peak at 2 to 3 days. Concentrations of other proteins peak at longer periods and can range from a 50% increase in complement and ceruloplasmin, to a several-fold amplification in haptoglobin, fibrinogen, α1-proteinase inhibitor, and α1-acid glycoprotein. Other proteins are negative acute phase proteins, the concentrations of which fall during the inflammatory response. These include anti-thrombin III, protein S, prealbumin, albumin, transferrin, and apolipoprotein A-I.4,

Hepatic stimulation of acute phase proteins is induced by cytokines released by activated monocytes, macrophages, neutrophils, natural killer cells, and endothelial cells acting at the front lines of the inflammatory response. The main cytokine influencing the liver is interleukin (IL)-6, once called the bepatocyte-stimulating factor. IL-6 regulates protein expression via the Janus kinase (JAK) and STAT3 pathways, as well as C/EBP family members and Rel proteins (nuclear factor-κB [NF-kB]).9, During initial stages, IL-1 and TNF synergize with IL-6 and trigger further IL-6 production, but their roles are limited. IL-6R is only expressed by hepatocytes, endothelial cells, and some leukocytes; however, via transsignaling, a process wherein IL-6 binds to a soluble IL-6R, can activate inflammatory pathways via ligation of the coreceptor gp130, effectively amplifying. IL-6 effects both locally and systemically. IL-6 also performs a protective role during disease, inducing the expression of an IL-1 receptor antagonist.

Acute phase protein levels are not uniform in their expression; this is likely related to the underlying pathophysiologic state and is regulated by different combinations and interactions of cytokines. The roles of the acute phase proteins themselves are discussed throughout the chapter but have been found to include direct involvement in host defense by activation of the complement, proteinase inhibition, and antioxidant activity. However, some of the described in vitro effects of proteins may not be relevant in vivo.

### Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate

Although ESR is an indirect screen for elevated concentrations of acute phase proteins, it has been the most widely used marker of inflammation for almost a century. Measurement of ESR is

performed when blood is placed in a vertical tube and the rate of fall of erythrocytes is measured. The ancient Greeks recognized increased red blood cell (RBC) sedimentation as a way to detect "bad bodily humors," but our modern understanding and use of RBC sedimentation as a test date back to the German scholar Fahraeus in 1918.16 He determined that certain plasma proteins,

especially fibrinogen, are able to lower the electrostatic charge on RBC surfaces so they can aggregate, form rouleaux, and fall faster.

Several factors are involved in acceleration of ESR. Asymmetric plasma proteins, such as fibrinogen and, to a lesser extent, alpha2, beta, and gamma globulins decrease the negative charge of erythrocytes (zeta potential) that prevents rouleaux formation. Red cell factors themselves play a role as changes in plasma ratios in anemic states also favor rouleaux. However, microcytosis, polycythemia, and abnormally shaped RBCs (e.g., sickle cells and spherocytes) hinder aggregation and lower the ESR. Conditions that elevate fibrinogen, even if they are not necessarily considered inflammatory, can raise ESR. These include pregnancy, diabetes, end-stage renal disease, and heart disease. Major increases in the concentration of a single molecular species, such as a monoclonal immunoglobulin in multiple myeloma, also increase sedimentation rates. The ESR is elevated in obesity, as is CRP, presumably as a result of IL-6 secretion by adipocytes. Factors such as glucocorticoids, cryoglobulinemia, hypofibrinogenemia, and hyperviscosity lower the value. The physiochemical dynamics that allow for sedimentation have been a continued source of debate, with disparate models presented to explain how proteins on cell surfaces interact to cause RBC aggregation.

Although novel and rapid tests for ESR have proven promising, the International Committee for Standardization in Hematology continues to recommend the Westergren technique of testing anticoagulated blood. .21-24 Reference ranges are established locally, but

the usual accepted upper limits of normal are 15 mm/hr for males and 20 mm/hr for females; however, the ESR increases with age and varies by race, which calls the reliability of the test into question. A simple formula for calculating the upper limit of normal ESR at any age has been used regularly: In men, age in years divided by two; in women, 10 plus age in years divided by two. Despite the ability to control for age, other limitations of the test have been noted and are listed in Table 57.3. The relative virtues of CRP determination have diminished some of the importance of ESR, but it remains an easy, inexpensive test with a wealth of background literature. Therefore the ESR continues to play a prominent role in clinical practice.

### C-Reactive Protein

CRP is an acute phase protein, the serum concentration of which reflects ongoing inflammation better than other tests in most, but not all, diseases. CRP was identified in 1930, when sera obtained from patients with Streptococcus pneumonia infection were found to contain a protein that could bind to the "C" polysaccharide of the bacterial cell wall. This protein circulates as a 115 kDa pentamer of noncovalently linked 23 kDa subunits, which has been highly conserved during hundreds of millions of years of evolution. In contrast to immunoglobulins and complement components, CRP deficiency in humans has not been described. Genome-wide associated studies performed recently have shown that at least seven distinct loci are involved in the basal expression of CRP,27-29 which is upregulated upon stimulation by the transcription factors C/EBP and Rel. It is present in trace concentrations in the plasma of all humans (roughly

1 mg/L, with higher concentrations in women and older adults). Plasma CRP is synthesized by hepatocytes, although other sites of local production and possibly minimal secretion have been suggested.

The precise function of CRP is unknown, but it exhibits defined recognition and activation capabilities and it binds to numerous ligands. CRP recognizes phosphocholine, phospholipids, fibronectin, chromatin, and histones, all of which are exposed at sites of tissue damage and by apoptotic cells; CRP may target them for clearance. CRP bridges the gap between innate and adaptive immunity by activating the classic complement pathway and interacting with cells of the immune system through binding of Fcγ receptors.33,34CRP induces inflammatory cytokines, tissue factors, and shedding of the IL-6 receptor, all of which result in a complement-dependent increase in tissue damage. Other CRP functions are anti-inflammatory, including promotion of the non-inflammatory clearance of apoptotic cells and prevention of neutrophil adhesion to the endothelium.34, Thus CRP may play many pathophysiologic roles during the course of the inflamma- 15,36 tory process.

After an acute inflammatory stimulus, CRP concentration increases rapidly and peaks at 2 to 3 days at levels that reflect the extent of tissue injury. If the stimulus has been removed, serum CRP levels drop rapidly, with a half-life of roughly 19 hours. Persistent elevations in CRP are seen in chronic inflammatory or infectious states such as active RA or pulmonary tuberculosis and may also be observed in extensive malignant disease.

Immunoassays and laser nephelometry are used at modest cost to quantify serum CRP levels. Most healthy adults have levels less than 0.3 mg/dL. The significance of minor elevations in CRP is a subject of debate and is discussed subsequently. However, usual methods of CRP determination are less precise at concentrations in the range of 0.3 to 1 mg/dL, so high-sensitivity (hs) CRP methods are used to accurately measure these levels. Generally, concentrations greater than 1 mg/dL reflect clinically significant inflammatory disease.10, Concentrations of 1 to 10 mg/dL can be considered to represent moderate increases, and concentrations greater than 10 mg/dL show marked increases. Most patients with extremely high levels (e.g., >15 mg/dL) have bacterial infection. One study found that in patients with CRP concentrations greater than 50 mg/dL, infection was present in 88% of participants. Clinical conditions associated with varying degrees of elevation of

CRP are listed in Table 57.4, and the range of CRP concentrations in many rheumatologic diseases is shown in Fig. 57.2.

Several limitations associated with the use of C-reactive protein measurement must be acknowledged.
