An overview of the use of glucocorticoids in the treatment of autoimmune rheumatic diseases includes evidence guiding appropriate doses of high-dose glucocorticoids as induction therapy, the emergence of glucocorticoid-sparing regimens, and evidence guiding long-term use of low-dose glucocorticoids. Finally, the chapter includes a detailed examination of glucocorticoid adverse effects.

### Structure and Classification of Steroid Hormones

Glucocorticoids are a type of steroid hormone, which are compounds derived from cholesterol that share a common backbone of 17 carbon atoms arranged in four rings (the cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene backbone) (Fig. 60.1). In humans, cortisol (called hydrocortisone when used as a medication) is the primary endogenous glucocorticoid and is produced in the adrenal cortex. The adrenal cortex also produces additional steroid hormones: dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA), which can subsequently be converted to the sex hormones testosterone and estrogen, and the mineralocorticoid aldosterone. The word steroid, in fact, refers to a large class of hormones that includes glucocorticoids and mineralocorticoids (collectively termed "corticosteroids"), sex hormones, and other hormones. While patients may be more familiar with the word steroids than glucocorticoids, steroid may sometimes lead to confusion with anabolic-androgenic steroids (synthetic versions of the sex hormone testosterone), which are misused by some weight lifters. The therapeutics used to treat autoimmune rheumatic diseases are most precisely termed glucocorticoids.

A number of synthetic glucocorticoids are used in the treatment of rheumatic diseases, with prednisone, prednisolone, methylprednisolone, and dexamethasone the most commonly used oral glucocorticoids. These compounds have small structural modifications compared with cortisol, as shown in Fig. 60.1, which affect solubility, half-life, glucocorticoid-receptor binding, and mineralocorticoid activity (see the "Pharmacology" section).

### Release of Endogenous Glucocorticoids

Release of the endogenous glucocorticoid cortisol from the adrenal cortex is regulated by the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis, with corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH) from the hypothalamus stimulating adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) release from the anterior pituitary, leading to cortisol and DHEA production. Cortisol and exogenous glucocorticoids exert

negative feedback at both the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary (Fig. 60.2). The total amount of cortisol typically released daily from the adrenal glands is approximately 10 mg, equivalent to approximately 2.5 mg/day of prednisone. During periods of stress, however, increased production of CRH and ACTH, triggered in part by inflammatory cytokines, lead to increased cortisol

release; cortisol levels may increase as much as sixfold during severe illness. Cortisol release is circadian, with the highest levels in the morning and lowest at night,5 and its release also fluctuates in ultradian rhythms, with pulses every 60 to 120 minutes——a pattern that is disrupted with exogenous glucocorticoid use with potential implications for side effects such as insomnia.

### Glucocorticoid Mechanisms of Action

### Genomic Mechanisms of Action

Endogenous cortisol and synthetic glucocorticoids act by binding the glucocorticoid receptor (GR) in the cytosol and translocating to the nucleus. The GR—glucocorticoid complex then regulates transcription by directly binding to DNA at multiple glucocorticoid response elements (GREs), leading to transactivation or transrepression (Fig. 60.3).4, Effects are dose-dependent, with different glucocorticoid concentrations needed for GR binding for different GREs. In addition, the GR-glucocorticoid complex further affects transcription through interference with other transcription factors such as nuclear factor-kB (NF-kB). Glucocorticoids have effects on the transcription of thousands of genes—an estimated 20% of the genome—affecting metabolism, inflammation, development, and other processes.12, Recent work has revealed that actions of glucocorticoids are highly cell-type specific, with the majority of glucocorticoid responsive genes differing across cell types. This cell-type-specific response is driven by differences in chromatin accessibility, expression of GR cofactors, and possibly by cell-type-specific GR isoforms and post-translational modification. 12, Through regulation of genes in different cell types, glucocorticoids have wide-ranging physiologic effects, including effects not only on hematopoetic cells of the innate and adaptive immune system but also on osteoblasts, chondrocytes, myoblasts, fibroblasts, endothelial cells, adipocytes, hepatocytes, and other cell types. 15-18 Effects on these other cell types may contribute to both therapeutic and adverse effects of glucocorticoids. The fact that glucocorticoids have effects on thousands of genes across multiple cellular targets has made it particularly challenging to identify and isolate the specific mechanisms driving therapeutic response in different rheumatic diseases.

### Nongenomic Mechanisms of Action

Glucocorticoids also have nongenomic physiologic effects at the cellular level that do not rely on effects on transcription and

protein synthesis. Although some genomic effects can be seen within 30 minutes of glucocorticoid exposure, nongenomic effects are even more rapid and may in part explain the very rapid onset of action of glucocorticoids compared with other therapeutics. For example, glucocorticoid binding to the GR leads to release of both the GR and Src kinase from the Hsp90 complex, leading to inhibition of epidermal growth factor receptor signaling. Other nongenomic mechanisms that have been described to date include signaling through a membrane-bound form of the GR, 16 effects on ion transport across membranes, GR interactions with components of mitogen-activated protein kinase pathways,18 and effects on the regulation of apoptosis.

Intravenous (IV) high-dose "pulse" glucocorticoids (e.g., 1 g of methylprednisolone daily for 3 days) were initially used in renal transplant but subsequently applied to a range of severe autoimmune rheumatic diseases. Doses above 100 mg are thought to saturate most GRs, with higher doses leading to more nongenomic effects of glucocorticoids. Several studies have examined whether lower glucocorticoid doses can lead to similar therapeutic effects with lower infection risk,22 but more studies are needed to identify optimal glucocorticoid doses in different conditions.

### Immunologic and Anti-inflammatory Effects of Glucocorticoids

Glucocorticoids are most commonly employed for their immunomodulatory and anti-inflammatory effects. These effects are thought to be primarily due to effects on immune cells and, indeed, glucocorticoids have varying effects on a wide range of adaptive and innate immune cells including T helper and cytotoxic T cells, B cells, mast cells, macrophages, neutrophils, basophils, eosinophils, natural killer cells, and dendritic cells (Table 60.1). In many but not all cases these effects involve downregulation of gene transcription (transrepression) within these cell types. For example, glucocorticoid effects have been shown to lead to an impairment in B cell receptor and Toll-like receptor signaling. Yet glucocorticoids have also been found to lead to upregulation of interleukin-10 expression in B cells and monocytes, an inhibitory cytokine. In addition, there is evidence from mouse models that some anti-inflammatory effects of glucocorticoids may also be mediated by effects on mesenchymal cells such as chondrocytes.

### Other Physiologic Effects of Glucocorticoids and Mechanisms Driving Adverse Effects

As discussed in the "Adverse Effects of Glucocorticoids" section, glucocorticoids are associated with a wide range of adverse effects. While the increased risk of infection is directly related to the immunologic effects of glucocorticoids, other adverse effects are driven by different mechanisms. The most studied mechanisms are glucocorticoid effects on glucose metabolism, bone, and muscle. Effects are complicated and again are mediated by effects on multiple cell types.

Glucocorticoid effects on glucose metabolism involve effects on adipocytes, hepatocytes, myocytes, and pancreatic beta cells. Glucocorticoids lead to insulin resistance in the liver, adipose tissue, and skeletal muscle, with glucocorticoid-induced diabetes having a mechanism similar to that of type 2 diabetes mellitus. Effects on hepatocytes also lead to increased gluconeogenesis in the liver. In addition, glucocorticoids may cause pancreatic beta cell dysfunction, limiting compensatory increases in insulin production to counteract insulin resistance.

In addition to notable effects on glucose metabolism in muscle, glucocorticoids can exert catabolic and anti-anabolic effects that can promote breakdown of muscle proteins and induce myocyte apoptosis, resulting in adverse changes to body composition. These effects are primarily observed at moderate to high doses. Glucocorticoids also inhibit amino acid transport and disrupt the insulin-like growth factor-1 pathways, which can reduce the ability to maintain muscle integrity and promote muscle growth. Glucocorticoids thus can lead to muscle wasting by reducing anabolic protein synthesis and increasing protein degradation. Muscle loss can be mirrored by changes in fat distribution, as glucocorticoids also have direct effects on adipose tissue metabolism and can promote fat redistribution toward greater accumulation in the visceral

compartment. Glucocorticoids increase the hydrolysis of circulating triglycerides and promote de-novo fatty acid synthesis in the liver. The result is an increase in fatty acids in circulation and the promotion of ectopic fat distribution. In addition to direct effects on fatty acid metabolism, glucocorticoids also have effects on adipocyte differentiation and hypertrophy and appetite.

In bone, glucocorticoids affect osteoblasts, osteoclasts, and osteocytes. Glucocorticoids inhibit osteoblast proliferation, increase osteoblast apoptosis and autophagy, and reduce the production of bone matrix proteins. Suppression of osteoprotegerin and an increase in the receptor activator of NF-kB ligand in osteoblasts increase osteoclast activation. Glucocorticoids also induce proteolytic enzymes such as collagenase 3 in osteoclasts. In osteocytes, glucocorticoids can cause apoptosis and increase the release of sclerostin.

Glucocorticoids such as cortisol and prednisone can also bind the mineralocorticoid receptor, affecting regulation of salt and water, although in normal physiologic circumstances the enzyme 1 1β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2 leads to inactivation of endogenous glucocorticoids in cells expressing the mineralocorticoid receptor. Mineralocorticoid effects of supraphysiologic doses of glucocorticoids, however, may lead to edema, increased blood pressure, heart failure exacerbations, or other adverse effects. Effects independent of mineralocorticoid activity, however, are also thought to contribute to the increased risk of hypertension with glucocorticoids.

As discussed below, glucocorticoids can also lead to other toxicity, including central nervous system, skin, ocular, gastric, and cardiovascular adverse effects. The mechanisms underlying these adverse effects are less well understood and remain active areas of investigation.

### Pharmacology of Glucocorticoids

### Pharmacokinetics

Because glucocorticoids in their free form are essentially insoluble in water, synthetic glucocorticoids are formulated as either organic esters or salts. Salts are more suitable for IV use while esters are suitable for oral or local use (e.g., intra-articular injection). The

pharmacokinetics of glucocorticoid formulations largely depend on the solubility of the drug and the mode of administration (Table 60.2). Orally administered glucocorticoids generally demonstrate excellent absorption whether in free form or as an ester or salt, although absorption can vary widely from person to person. 29,30

### Potency of Different Glucocorticoid Formulations and Factors Affecting Glucocorticoid Response

The therapeutic potency of glucocorticoids depends on their relative glucocorticoid activity. This difference in potency can also be stated in terms of equivalent glucocorticoid doses of different formulations. As shown in Table 60.2, the potency of prednisone 5 mg is equivalent to approximately 0.75 mg of dexamethasone, 4 mg of methylprednisolone, or 20 mg of hydrocortisone. Committing the numbers 0.75, 4, 5, and 20 to memory provides the equivalence of the most commonly used systemic glucocorticoids. Mineralocorticoid activity also varies between different glucocorticoids, with the least mineralocorticoid activity observed with dexamethasone.

Most glucocorticoid in circulation (~90%) is bound to plasma proteins, while only free, unbound drug is pharmacologically active. Thus it has often been raised as a concern that the effects of glucocorticoids may be affected by plasma protein concentrations and binding. For example, patients with liver disease and hypoalbuminemia might be hypothesized to benefit from reduced dosing of glucocorticoids in order to avoid toxicity. Differences in plasma protein binding may also affect central nervous system penetration, although whether these differences are relevant in the treatment of autoimmune rheumatic disease is unclear. The metabolism and regulation of glucocorticoids may also be disrupted in older adults, resulting in greater risk of toxicity. Some drug interactions can inhibit the breakdown of glucocorticoids (e.g., ketoconazole, diltiazem), although the clinical relevance of this is unclear. Other traits have been associated with variability in free-form glucocorticoid levels including biologic sex, body weight, and genetic polymorphisms.

Additionally, some glucocorticoids, such as cortisone and prednisone, are prohormones containing an 11-keto group, which must be reduced to their 11-hydroxyl forms (hydrocortisone and prednisolone) for activation. This activation occurs predominantly in the liver by the enzyme 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 1 (11β-HSD1). Rare patients with a deficiency in this enzyme do not respond to cortisol and prednisone.4, Hypothetically, patients with severe liver disease may be unable to convert prohormones to their active forms, and use of prednisolone rather than prednisone may be preferred.4, Interestingly, synovial tissue expresses 11β-HSD1 and can locally activate glucocorticoids, with increased activation shown in untreated patients with RA. This local activation may contribute to increased local effects of endogenous glucocorticoids and enhanced response to exogenous glucocorticoids.

Glucocorticoid resistance is also observed in some individuals and a number of mechanisms have been described that include variability in pharmacokinetics, genetic variants, local variation in cytokine concentrations, drug interactions, and protein modifications. Upregulation of cytochrome P450 isoenzymes and the resultant increase in metabolism of glucocorticoids can be a clinically significant cause of glucocorticoid resistance. Rifampin, for example, has been described as a cause of nonresponse to prednisone in rheumatic conditions, acting through this mechanism.

Variation in clinical responsiveness and susceptibility to glucocorticoid adverse events likely stems from differences in these factors, although prediction of clinical outcomes is challenging and dosing guidelines based on these factors do not currently exist. Attempts to lower risks of glucocorticoids have been considered, including alternative-day dosing regimens, the goal of which is to preserve normal pituitary-adrenal responsiveness. While some small studies have suggested benefits, there are no large trials to routinely support this approach.

### Modified-Release Prednisone

A formulation of prednisone was created that leads to delayed release approximately 4 hours after ingestion, such that taking this medication in the evening could lead to peak levels in the morning, more closely matching the natural circadian rhythm of cortisol and providing higher levels in the morning when inflammatory symptoms are worse. This modified-release prednisone has been studied for use in RA,40,41 with one study demonstrating a reduction in morning stiffness compared with taking immediaterelease prednisone in the morning 41 and another study demonstrating improved symptoms over placebo. This treatment is

substantially more expensive that other glucocorticoids, however, and is not widely used.

### Repository Corticotropin Injection

Repository corticotropin injection is an intramuscular injection that includes ACTH analogs and other pituitary peptides. This therapy increases endogenous cortisol release from the adrenal glands and also has other nonglucocorticoid effects that have not been fully elucidated. Although studied in several autoimmune rheumatic conditions,43,44 the expense of this therapy and a lack of studies directly comparing its effectiveness and safety to glucocorticoids limits widespread use at this time.

### Glucocorticoid Use in the Treatment of Autoimmune Rheumatic Diseases

Glucocorticoids are commonly used for the treatment of a wide range of autoimmune and inflammatory rheumatic conditions. In the interest of having consistent terminology, definitions for what is considered low, moderate, and higher doses have previously been published, although there are substantial differences in therapeutic and adverse effects even within these categories (Table 60.3).

Details on the use of glucocorticoids for individual autoimmune rheumatic diseases are discussed within chapters focusing on the treatment of these conditions. This section focuses on overall themes related to use of glucocorticoids, using data from several different autoimmune conditions as examples. Specifically, the continued debate around the role of glucocorticoids as a disease-modifying therapy and as bridging therapy in RA is discussed, as is the role of long-term use of low-dose glucocorticoids across autoimmune rheumatic diseases. The use of glucocorticoids as induction therapy in severe autoimmune rheumatic diseases and emerging data guiding specific glucocorticoid tapering regimens and movement toward glucocorticoid sparing regimens are also covered.

### Glucocorticoid Use in Rheumatoid Arthritis

RA was the first autoimmune rheumatic condition in which glucocorticoids were tested as a therapeutic,3 and more than 70 years later glucocorticoids continue to be commonly used.46-48 While more data exist evaluating the use of glucocorticoids in RA compared with other diseases, the specific indications for

glucocorticoid use remain controversial, with conflicting recommendations from professional societies and significant variability in use across providers. 47-50

### Glucocorticoids as Short-Term Bridging Therapy and Effects on Radiographic Progression in Patients With Rheumatoid Arthritis

Several clinical trials have examined the use of glucocorticoids as part of initial therapy of RA. The Combinatietherapie Bij Reumatoide Artritis (COBRA) trial found that combination therapy with sulfasalazine, low-dose methotrexate (7.5 mg/week, stopped at week 40), and prednisolone (60 mg tapered down to 7.5 mg over 6 weeks and stopped at week 28) led to improvements in disease activity over the first 28 weeks of the trial, although after discontinuation of prednisolone there were no significant differences in disease activity between groups. The combination therapy group, however, had less radiographic damage over the course of the trial and lower rates of radiographic progression in long-term follow-up over the next 5 years. The COBRA strategy was also compared with more commonly used current regimens in the BeSt trial. Starting with the COBRA regimen of sulfasalazine, low-dose methotrexate, and prednisolone led to similar clinical outcomes and similar rates of radiographic progression compared with initial combination methotrexate and infliximab. Compared with initial use of methotrexate with step-up combination therapy, starting with the COBRA regimen led to improved clinical outcomes at 6 months and lower rates of radiographic progression, although clinical differences were not apparent at 12 months and differences in radiographic progression were small. Lower doses of glucocorticoids have also been studied, with similar clinical outcomes with a "COBRA-light" strategy including weekly methotrexate titrated up to 25 mg/week in combination with prednisolone starting at 30 mg, tapered to 7.5 mg at week 9, and continued through week 28.54 A recent trial of lowor highdose glucocorticoids (10 mg or 60 mg) tapered over 12 weeks versus placebo as bridging therapy in patients initiating methotrexate found differences at disease activity at 26 weeks but not at 52 weeks, with no differences in radiographic progression.

Taken together, these and other studies demonstrate that initial use of glucocorticoids can lead to more rapid improvements in disease activity than conventional disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs) alone, although clinical improvements are not sustained once glucocorticoids are discontinued. While these studies suggest that glucocorticoids indeed have small impacts as disease-modifying therapies by reducing radiographic damage, short courses of glucocorticoids (e.g., 12 weeks) seem to have minimal effects on radiographic progression. Furthermore, the role of glucocorticoids as disease-modifying therapies may be less relevant in the current era of highly effective therapies, which limit radiographic progression in the majority of patients. The clinical benefits of glucocorticoids have justified their use as shortterm bridging therapy for some patients starting or switching DMARDs, especially those with high disease activity and substantial functional limitations. It is notable, however, that the onset of action of biologic and targeted synthetic DMARDs (i.e., Janus kinase [JAK] inhibitors) is more rapid than that of conventional therapies. For example, in the BeST trial there were no differences in disease activity at 3 months among those that received methotrexate and a TNF biologic compared with those that received high doses of prednisone. The use of glucocorticoids as a bridging therapy to provide short-term clinical disease activity benefits is endorsed by European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology

(EULAR) guidelines,50 although current guidelines from the American College of Rheumatology (ACR) conditionally recommend against using glucocorticoids as bridging therapy because of the difficulty tapering off of glucocorticoids for many patients. As with many therapies, a consideration of individual patient factors and patient preference is important when making decisions about glucocorticoid use as bridging therapy.

### Long-Term Use of Low-Dose Glucocorticoids in Patients With Rheumatoid Arthritis

Although both EULAR and ACR guidelines recommend against the use of glucocorticoids as a long-term treatment in most patients, 30% to 40% of patients with RA remain on low-dose glucocorticoids long term. 48, It is clear from a number of trials that low-dose glucocorticoids at doses described by some as "physiologic" (i.e., prednisone <10 mg/day) can provide clinical benefit for patients with RA. In the CAMERA-II (Computer Assisted Management in Early Rheumatoid Arthritis trial-II), the addition of prednisone 10 mg to methotrexate led to lower disease activity and disability and less need for additional therapies over a 2-year period. Similarly, in the BARFOT (Better Anti-Rheumatic PharmacOTherapy) trial, the addition of prednisolone 7.5 mg/ day to DMARD therapy increased the rate of disease remission at 2 years. More recently the 2-year GLORIA (Glucocorticoid LOw-dose in RheumatoId Arthritis) trial found that prednisolone 5 mg/day led to modestly lower disease activity compared with placebo. Additionally, the Steroid EliMination in Rheumatoid Arthritis (SEMIRA) trial demonstrated that low-dose glucocorticoids provide benefit to some patients receiving biologic therapy. In this trial, patients with low disease activity who were receiving tocilizumab and prednisone 5 mg/day were randomized to taper or continue prednisone; disease flares were more common in patients who discontinued prednisone, although two-thirds of patients were able to taper off of glucocorticoids without experiencing a disease flare.

Based on the SEMIRA trial, patients who have achieved low disease activity but remain on glucocorticoids should attempt glucocorticoid tapering, as many of these patients are able to discontinue them altogether. For patients who have worsening disease activity with glucocorticoid tapering, however, decisions on whether to change DMARD therapy or continue glucocorticoids requires weighing risks and benefits and considering patient preferences. Existing clinical trials are not powered to assess adverse effects, although the GLORIA trial did find an increase in the risk of nonserious infections in patients receiving glucocorticoids and a numerically higher rate of serious infections. These findings are in line with data from observational studies using claims databases demonstrating a modest increase in infection risk even with prednisone ≤5 mg/day, similar in magnitude to the risk of infection with biologic therapies. Impacts of low-dose glucocorticoids on long-term metabolic outcomes, osteoporosis, and cardiovascular disease remain uncertain. Some but not all studies have suggested cardiovascular risk even with doses ≤5 mg/day.61, These outcomes are discussed in more detail in the section "Adverse Effects of Glucocorticoids."

### Long-Term Use of Low-Dose Glucocorticoids in Other Autoimmune Rheumatic Diseases

Glucocorticoids are also commonly used at low doses in numerous other autoimmune rheumatic conditions. As has been observed in RA, low doses of glucocorticoids have demonstrated effectiveness

in maintaining disease control in many of these conditions. Longterm glucocorticoid use is even more frequent in patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) than in patients with RA, with more than half receiving them long term.63, EULAR guidelines for the treatment of SLE recommend that glucocorticoids should minimized to <7.5 mg/day and discontinued when possible. An open-label, randomized trial of patients with SLE with clinical quiescent disease for 1 year on a regimen including prednisone 5 mg found that patients were more likely to have a disease flare if they discontinued versus continued prednisone 5 mg, although, as in the SEMIRA trial for RA, about two-thirds of patients were able to discontinue prednisone without experiencing a flare. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of low-dose glucocorticoids for maintaining remission but also support EULAR recommendations to attempt glucocorticoid tapering in patients who are doing well. A similar glucocorticoid tapering trial (The Assessment of Prednisone In Remission Trial [TAPIR]) is currently underway for patients with granulomatosis with polyangiitis.

### How to Taper Low-Dose Glucocorticoids

As discussed previously, mounting evidence in different diseases suggests that a substantial number of patients on long-term lowdose glucocorticoids who have achieved disease control are able to discontinue them and maintain disease control, although some will have disease flares. Direct evidence on how to best taper glucocorticoids is limited. In the SEMIRA trial, patients on prednisone 5 mg reduced their dose by 1 mg every 4 weeks, with no episodes of adrenal insufficiency reported. This approach is commonly employed in practice and has the advantages of limiting the risk of adrenal insufficiency and allowing patients and clinicians to identify the lowest needed dose of glucocorticoids if disease activity increases during tapering. Patients who have been on glucocorticoids for shorter periods of time may be able to discontinue them more quickly.

### Glucocorticoids as Induction Therapy in Life- Threatening or Organ-Threatening Autoimmune Rheumatic Diseases

Glucocorticoids are used at high doses (e.g., prednisone ≥30 mg/ day) in a number of autoimmune rheumatic conditions with lifethreatening or organ-threatening manifestations, with the goal of rapidly controlling inflammation. Specific evidence to guide the optimal glucocorticoid doses in these conditions is limited, although an increasing number of studies have begun to compare glucocorticoid regimens or evaluate glucocorticoid sparing regimens.

High-dose IV glucocorticoids at doses 250 to 1000 mg/day are commonly used in patients with severe, organ-threatening manifestations of SLE, although the optimal initial glucocorticoid doses remain uncertain and it is possible that lower doses could achieve similar outcomes for many patients.20, After IV glucocorticoids are complete, oral glucocorticoids are frequently given at a starting dose of 1 mg/kg with tapering over several months. The recent AURORA-1 trial, which evaluated the addition of voclosporin to mycophenolate induction for lupus nephritis, employed a more rapid glucocorticoid taper compared with previous studies. In this trial, after initial IV doses, patients received prednisone 20 to 25 mg/day, which was tapered to 2.5 mg by week 16 (Table 60.4). Voclosporin was superior to placebo, suggesting that the addition of

voclosporin to mycophenolate may allow more rapid glucocorticoid tapering, although the trial did not directly compare different glucocorticoid tapering regimens. For comparison, the glucocorticoid tapering regimen for lupus nephritis from the BLISS-LN trial is also shown in Table 60.4. Studies that directly compare different glucocorticoid regimens and studies that further evaluate glucocorticoidsparing therapies are needed.

Giant cell arteritis (GCA) is typically treated with high-dose glucocorticoids as part of induction therapy. IV glucocorticoids are often used in cases with ocular involvement, although data to support this practice are limited. A recent trial examining the efficacy of tocilizumab in giant cell arteritis evaluated two different glucocorticoid tapering regimens in GCA. In this study, use of tocilizumab with a 26-week glucocorticoid taper led to fewer disease flares and lower cumulative glucocorticoid use compared with a standard 52-week glucocorticoid taper with placebo, demonstrating the steroid-sparing ability of tocilizumab in this condition. Among those that did not receive tocilizumab, rates of flare were higher in those receiving the 26-week versus 52-week taper. Thus the 26-week glucocorticoid taper described in this paper provides a guide that clinicians can follow to ensure that patients are not exposed to excessive glucocorticoids when tocilizumab is used, and the 52-week taper may be a guide for those treated without tocilizumab (Table 60.4). The need for IV glucocorticoids in cases of ocular involvement, optimal initial oral glucocorticoid dose, and the potential for using even more rapid glucocorticoid tapers in patients receiving tocilizumab or other glucocorticoidsparing therapies are important areas for future investigation.

The highest-quality direct data to date to guide glucocorticoid dosing for induction therapy comes from antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA)-associated vasculitis. The PEXIVAS trial evaluated plasma exchange but also two different glucocorticoid tapering regimens. A reduced-dose glucocorticoid regimen was found to be noninferior to a standard glucocorticoid taper in patients receiving initial IV glucocorticoids along with rituximab or cyclophosphamide, and current ACR guidelines conditionally recommend use of this reduced-dose glucocorticoid regimen (Table 60.4). A recent study also found that, in patients receiving induction therapy with rituximab or cyclophosphamide with initial IV glucocorticoids, the use of avacopan (with no additional glucocorticoids) led to a higher frequency of sustained remission compared with use of a more conventional 20-week glucocorticoid taper.

Together, these studies demonstrate accumulating data to guide initial glucocorticoid dosing and glucocorticoid tapers in severe autoimmune rheumatic diseases. Over time it is likely that an increasing number of reduced-dose or glucocorticoid-free induction regimens will be evaluated, assessing comparative effectiveness and just as critically comparative safety.

### Adverse Effects of Glucocorticoids

Glucocorticoids are associated with multiple adverse effects dependent on both glucocorticoid dose and duration of therapy, with an increased risk for infections, 8,22,23 metabolic side effects, 20,21 cardiovascular events, 24,25 and osteoporosis26 being of particular concern (Fig. 60.4).

### Infection Risk With Glucocorticoids

Infection risk is substantially increased by glucocorticoids, with an approximate doubling in the risk of serious infections with longterm glucocorticoid use at doses above 10 mg/day in prednisone

equivalents. 56, It is notable that this risk is substantially greater than that associated with biologic therapies and JAK inhibitors, 76,77 indicating the importance of glucocorticoid sparing therapies to improve long-term patient outcomes.

Glucocorticoid doses ≥20 mg/day also increase the risk for opportunistic infections such as Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP),78 and the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices recommends avoiding live vaccines in patients on these doses.' 79 There are no clear guidelines on when to initiate PJP prophylaxis with trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole or alternative prophylactic therapies, and risk depends on dose and duration of glucocorticoid use and comorbidities and other immunosuppression that

patients are using. One study that included patients with rheumatic diseases receiving ≥30 mg/day of prednisone for at least 4 weeks found a significantly lower risk of PJP with prophylaxis, with a number needed to treat of 52, suggesting that such patients should typically receive prophylaxis. Some experts suggest discontinuing prophylaxis when glucocorticoid doses are <15 mg depending on the presence of other PJP risk factors (e.g., vasculitis, use of other potent immunosuppression).

While infection risks are particularly increased with more longterm glucocorticoid use, studies have suggested that even short courses of glucocorticoids (i.e., 6 to 7 days) are associated with increased risk of sepsis and other infections, although absolute

risks are small over this time frame. Clinicians should be aware that risks exist even with short-term therapy, avoiding glucocorticoids in commonly used settings such as acute back pain where they have not been shown to be effective.

Risk of infection with lower-dose glucocorticoids has been more controversial, with clinical trials underpowered to assess serious infections and concerns that observational studies may suffer from confounding. Recent results from both clinical trials and observational data, however, have suggested a small but clinically meaningful increase in infection risk even with prednisone doses ≤5 mg/day.56, The absolute risk of infection depends substantially on the underlying risk in the population being treated but appears to be approximately one to two extra serious infections nitude similar to that observed with TNF inhibitors.

### Metabolic Side Effects With Glucocorticoids

Metabolic side effects are especially common with glucocorticoids, with one study demonstrating weight gain in more than half of patients receiving a mean of 15 mg/day of prednisone. In contrast, studies of low-dose glucocorticoids ≤7.5 mg/day have not demonstrated substantial effects on body weight in most patients.58, Changes in body composition including Cushingoid features (moon face, buffalo hump, central obesity) may develop with higher-dose glucocorticoids.15, Hyperglycemia and diabetes mellitus are common and are caused by both insulin resistance and increased gluconeogenesis in the liver as well as direct effects in muscle, bone, and adipose tissue.24, Effects on hepatocytes also contribute to lipogenesis and the development of fatty liver disease. Effects are smaller and may not be observed with

lower-dose glucocorticoids, although even low doses have been associated with insulin resistance and may increase the risk of incident diabetes, particularly among those with obesity, of older age, or with a family history of diabetes.

### Cardiovascular Risk With Glucocorticoids

As already discussed, high doses of glucocorticoids have a number of metabolic effects that are likely to contribute to a greater risk of premature heart disease. In addition to adverse effects on metabolism, glucocorticoids may have direct effects on the heart and the vasculature. It is perhaps not surprising, then, that high doses of glucocorticoids have been linked to a higher risk of cardiovascular events in several studies.61, The risks of low doses of prednisone are less clear, with some studies demonstrating a significant risk even for doses <5 mg/day and others showing no increase in risk with low doses.61, Because glucocorticoids are used in greater amounts during periods of more active and severe illness, there is a significant concern for confounding in epidemiologic studies. Clinical trials of low-dose prednisone have not demonstrated higher rates of cardiovascular events, although these studies are underpowered to detect small differences in risk.

### Effects of Glucocorticoids on Bone Health and Fracture Risk

The direct effects of glucocorticoids on bone have been well defined. Glucocorticoids have direct effects on osteoblasts, osteocytes, and osteoclast precursors and act to increase bone resorption and inhibit bone formation. Glucocorticoid use and resulting bone loss has also been defined as a clinical risk factor for osteoporotic

fracture in prior studies, even at low doses.57, These well-defined risks have led to guidelines aimed at prevention of osteoporosis and fracture among patients using glucocorticoids over the long term. In these guidelines, bone mineral density screening is recommended for patients over 40 years of age within 6 months of the initiation of glucocorticoids in order to facilitate more accurate risk prediction. These guidelines recommend using the FRAX™ calculator to determine 10-year risks of osteoporotic fractures. These estimates should be increased by 15 to 20% for prednisone doses >7.5 mg daily. FRAX thresholds for prophylaxis among glucocorticoid users are quite low compared with standard thresholds (10% for major osteoporotic fracture and 1% for hip fracture) such that older patients are often observed to meet the threshold for prophylaxis. Delays in initiating bisphosphonate therapy should be avoided since the greatest bone loss may occur early, particularly with the initiation of high doses of glucocorticoids. Unfortunately rates of adherence to these guidelines are low.

High-dose and prolonged use of glucocorticoids is also associated with osteonecrosis, although the mechanism has not been defined. Patients experiencing osteonecrosis often have additional risk factors. Osteonecrosis may be asymptomatic or can present with significant pain, primarily with weight bearing. Patients are at risk for progression and continued use of glucocorticoids may increase the risk of new lesions.

### Glucocorticoids and the Risk of Myopathy

Myopathy is underrecognized as a side effect of chronic glucocorticoid use. While myopathy is unusual at low doses (<10 mg/day prednisone equivalents), glucocorticoids can induce muscle weakness at high doses within weeks (although onset is highly variable). Myopathy is more common among older, physically inactive patients. Muscle weakness typically occurs gradually and preferentially in large, proximal muscle groups, sometimes resulting in functional limitations. There is no specific diagnostic testing, but symptoms generally begin to improve after 2 to 4 weeks with appropriate dose reduction.

### Other Glucocorticoid Side Effects

Glucocorticoids are associated with numerous other side effects that are dose-dependent, including sleep disturbance, psychiatric effects (irritability, insomnia, mood swings, and, in some cases, psychosis), skin changes (striae, ecchymoses, acne), glaucoma, and cataracts (Fig. 60.4). Poor wound healing is also observed in patients that have received chronic systemic glucocorticoids, particularly at high doses. The association between glucocorticoids and peptic ulcer disease is less clear based on conflicting reports, although some studies suggest up to a twofold increase in risk.102-104 Routine gastrointestinal (GI) prophylaxis with glucocorticoids, however, is not recommended. Given the higher risk among those that use both glucocorticoids and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, this combination should be used with caution and prompt consideration of the addition of a proton-pump inhibitor.

Among those taking lower doses of glucocorticoids, the most commonly described side effects include acne, skin ecchymoses, cataracts, and weight gain. Of these common side effects, weight gain was the most important to patients in one survey study. The GLORIA trial, evaluating the benefits and risks of low-dose prednisone in patients with RA, demonstrated a numerically higher risk of infection (28.9 vs. 21.9%), GI disorders (20.8 vs. 14.6%), and metabolic disorders (7.9 vs. 2.8%) and twice the risk of skin and subcutaneous disorders (17.4 vs. 8.4%).

### Capture and Measurement of Glucocorticoid Adverse Effects

A specific glucocorticoid adverse event measurement instrument called the Glucocorticoid Toxicity Index was developed by a committee of experts across a range of medical specialties for use in clinical trials (Table 60.5). This instrument includes 31 items across 9 domains, with weighting to account for differences in severity. Domains include weight (body mass index), glucose tolerance, blood pressure, lipids, bone density, steroid myopathy, skin toxicity, neuropsychiatric toxicity, and infection. A separate "specific list" of less common but severe adverse effects was also included for capture in trials. This tool is designed to allow quantification of multiple adverse effects in a single instrument, and not all adverse effects of glucocorticoids are included. A particularly notable omission is cardiovascular events, which were excluded because of the potential for confounding by comorbidities or disease severity.

The Outcome Measures in Rheumatology (OMERACT) Glucocorticoid Impact Working Group subsequently has identified a core domain set that they recommend should be captured in clinical trials to evaluate the adverse effects and benefits of glucocorticoids (Fig. 60.5). This core domain set was developed by incorporating data from literature review and patient surveys and through a Delphi process that included patients, clinicians, and researchers—the consideration of which glucocorticoid effects are most important to patients is a particularly important aspect of this work. In addition to effects of glucocorticoids on disease control, mandatory domains recommended to measure in all trials include infection, bone fragility, mood disturbance, hypertension, diabetes mellitus, weight, fatigue, and death. Additional domains that were considered important but were noted as optional because they are either rare or usually occur with high doses or long-term follow-up included osteonecrosis, eye problems, physical appearance, and sleep disturbance. Domains overall are similar to that in the Glucocorticoid Toxicity Index, although myopathy, lipid changes, and skin changes are not included in the OMERACT core domain set, and effects on fatigue and mortality are not included in the GTI. While these measures are intended to guide capture in clinical trials, they may also serve as a reminder of some of the most important adverse effects of glucocorticoids, although not all are included. Future work should include the identification of instruments that best characterize and quantify effects in each of the OMERACT domains both for use in trials and for use in clinical practice.

### Glucocorticoid Use in Pregnancy and Lactation

The use of nonfluorinated glucocorticoids is generally felt to be safe for the fetus in pregnancy, particularly at low doses because very little of the drug reaches the fetus (~1%). These nonfluorinated glucocorticoids include prednisone, prednisolone, and methylprednisolone. In fact, fluorinated glucocorticoids such as dexamethasone and betamethasone are specifically employed for fetal lung maturation in pre-term delivery because of the potential to cross the placenta.

While the risks of nonfluorinated glucocorticoids to the fetus are considered low, there is some evidence to support a modestly higher risk of low birth weight and cleft lip. Studies have also suggested that the HPA axis can be suppressed for the first weeks to months of life, though the long-term implications of this suppression are not clear. 110, Glucocorticoids may also increase the risk of gestational diabetes and gestational hypertension and may

increase the risk of pre-eclampsia,112 although the literature in this area may suffer from confounding by indication. Thus while generally considered safe, there is reason to ensure the use of the lowest effective glucocorticoid dose for the shortest possible period of time. In EULAR guidelines from 2016, most experts reported that they would not alter their approach to glucocorticoids in the context of pregnancy. Reproductive health guidelines from the ACR conditionally recommend continuing low-dose glucocorticoids ≤10 mg/ day prednisone equivalent, but strongly recommend that glucocorticoid dose be reduced to <20 mg, adding a pregnancy-compatible glucocorticoid sparing therapy, if needed.

Very little of synthetic glucocorticoids pass through breast milk, resulting in lower exposure to the breastfeeding infant (<1% of

maternal dose). Some have suggested waiting several hours after taking glucocorticoids before breastfeeding, although it is unclear whether this is likely to significantly lower exposure to the infant.115, ACR guidelines recommend that women delay breastfeeding or discard breast milk accumulated in the 4 hours after glucocorticoid administration with doses of prednisone ≥20 mg/day.

### Adrenal Insufficiency

As noted previously, exogenous glucocorticoids exert negative feedback on CRH and ACTH production in the hypothalamus and pituitary. This suppression of ACTH then can cause atrophy of the adrenal cortex, specifically the zona fasciculata where

cortisol is produced. Aldosterone production, however, is relatively unaffected. Atrophy of the zona fasciculata impairs production of endogenous cortisol even after exogenous glucocorticoids are withdrawn. Because the exogenous glucocorticoids have led to this state by impairing CRH (and ACTH) release, this type of adrenal insufficiency is termed tertiary adrenal insufficiency.

The dose and duration of glucocorticoids necessary to cause tertiary adrenal insufficiency is variable between individuals and is difficult to predict.117, In general, however, short-term use of glucocorticoids for less than 3 weeks is unlikely to cause significant tertiary adrenal insufficiency. Adrenocortical function can be assessed through use of an ACTH stimulation test; such testing is not necessary prior to glucocorticoid tapering as long as it is gradual, but may be employed when glucocorticoids are abruptly discontinued. In addition, for patients who have reduced their glucocorticoid dose to <5 mg/day (prednisone equivalent) in whom there are clinical concerns for potential adrenal insufficiency, ACTH simulation testing may provide helpful diagnostic information, although this testing is more helpful at ruling in than at ruling out the diagnosis.

Although inflammatory cytokines may lead to increased CRH and ACTH release, observations that patients with RA with active disease have lower cortisol/ACTH ratios have led to suggestions that these patients could have relative adrenal insufficiency, with cortisol production suppressed by high levels of inflammatory cytokines.

### "Stress-Dose" Glucocorticoids

During times of stress, including acute illness and surgical procedures, endogenous release of cortisol is increased. Patients with primary adrenal insufficiency require supraphysiologic doses of glucocorticoids in these situations. The need for supraphysiologic doses of glucocorticoids in patients with adrenal insufficiency due to chronic glucocorticoid use, however, remains unclear and controversial.

The routine practice of treating patients receiving chronic glucocorticoids who are undergoing surgery with supraphysiologic doses began with the deaths of two young patients with RA in the 1950s. In both patients, glucocorticoids were abruptly stopped

prior to orthopedic surgery, and adrenal insufficiency was considered a possible but not confirmed cause of death. .122,123Subsequent small trials, however, have not demonstrated a clear benefit from this practice, as long as the home dose of glucocorticoids is given on the day of surgery (as opposed to abrupt discontinuation).124-126 At the same time, there are concerns that increased glucocorticoids around the time of surgery may increase complications, as has been seen with chronic glucocorticoid use. 127, Somewhat reassuringly, a large placebo-controlled trial evaluating the use of 8 mg of IV dexamethasone intraoperatively to prevent post-operative nausea and vomiting found no differences in surgical site infections.

Guidelines from the ACR in combination with the American Association of Hip and Knee Surgeons conditionally recommend continuing home-dose glucocorticoids rather than using stress-dose glucocorticoids in patients treated with chronic glucocorticoids undergoing joint arthroplasty, with additional glucocorticoids reserved for patients who develop refractory hypotension perioperatively. Notably these guidelines do not apply to patients with primary adrenal insufficiency, who should receive additional glucocorticoids before surgery. Some experts recommend alternative approaches, however, such as use of stress-dose glucocorticoids in patients receiving >20 mg/day of prednisone or its equivalent and testing of the HPA axis in patients receiving 5 to 20 mg/day of glucocorticoids for at least 3 weeks.

### Conclusion

More than 70 years after their discovery, glucocorticoids remain a key therapy for the treatment of rheumatic diseases. The wideranging effects of glucocorticoids contribute to both their therapeutic benefit and adverse effects, and extricating beneficial effects from harms has thus far proved elusive. Consequently, clinicians are frequently faced with the challenge of balancing the risks and benefits of glucocorticoids, requiring an understanding of the dose-dependent risks of glucocorticoid therapy. Fortunately, accumulating evidence is providing more data-driven approaches for the use of glucocorticoids. While glucocorticoids will remain an important therapeutic tool for the foreseeable future, there are an increasing number of reduced-glucocorticoid

or glucocorticoid-free treatment regimens under study which aim to improve outcomes and reduce side effects for p atients with rheumatic diseases.

# Traditional DMARDS: Methotrexate, Leflunomide, Sulfasalazine, Hydroxychloroquine, and Therapies Combination

### KEY POINTS

Methotrexate is one of the most durable and frequently used diseasemodifying anti-rheumatic drugs (DMARDs), for use as monotherapy or as the cornerstone of combination therapy for rheumatoid arthritis (RA).

Leflunomide, sulfasalazine, and hydroxychloroquine are effective therapies in rheumatic disease and are commonly used in combination therapy.

Although the precise mechanisms of action of the traditional DMARDs are incompletely understood, most have both anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory actions.

The choice of DMARD therapy should be tailored to the individual patient, with attention given to age, fertility plans, concomitant medications, and comorbidities.

Toxicity from DMARD therapy can cause significant morbidity and rarely mortality; thus appropriate dosing and monitoring are essential.

Combination therapy in RA can be more effective than mono-DMARD therapy in groups of patients with early-stage and established RA.

Unfortunately, no data are available to guide in the selection of the best DMARD for each individual patient.

### Methotrexate

### KEY POINTS

An important mechanism of action for methotrexate (MTX) in addition to blocking dihydrofolate reductase is the increased release of adenosine, which is a potent inhibitor of inflammation.

MTX is polyglutamated in cells, and this is responsible for its long therapeutic effect.

The effects of MTX may be enhanced by splitting the dose (within a 12-hour window) when levels greater than 15 mg/week are used or by using a subcutaneous route of administration.

Although rare, MTX pneumonitis is a serious and potentially fatal complication of therapy.

It would be difficult to overstate the importance of methotrexate (MTX) in contemporary management of rheumatic disease, particularly rheumatoid arthritis (RA). Because of its anti-proliferative effects, MTX was introduced in the 1950s to treat malignancy. The first reports of its use in rheumatic diseases were in the 1960s for psoriasis and RA.1, With more experience in efficacy, dosing, and toxicity, MTX has become the disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drug (DMARD) of choice in the treatment of RA, and it is also used in many other rheumatic diseases.

### Chemical Structure

MTX is a structural analogue of folic acid and has substitutions in the pteridine group and para-aminobenzoic acid structure (Fig. 61.1). The structure of folic acid (pteroylglutamic acid) consists of three elements: a multiring pteridine group linked to a para-aminobenzoic acid, which is connected to a terminal glutamic acid residue.

### Actions of Methotrexate

Because MTX is a folate analogue, it enters cells via a reduced folate carrier (RFC). Leucovorin competes with MTX for uptake by using the same RFC; however, folic acid enters cells via another group of transmembrane receptors called folate receptors (FRs). FRs may be upregulated in cells with increased metabolic activity, including synovial macrophages, and serve as a second conduit for MTX influx.4, MTX efflux occurs via members of the adenosine triphosphate (ATP)binding cassette (ABC) family of transporters, specifically ABCC1-4 and ABCG2.6 Genetic polymorphisms may affect MTX transporter proteins (influx and efflux) and can result in a variable MTX response and toxicity profile. Furthermore, multidrug-resistance proteins have been identified that transport MTX, folic acid, and leucovorin out of cells, leading to MTX resistance.

Once inside the cell, naturally occurring folates as well as MTX undergo polyglutamation by the enzyme folyl-polyglutamyl synthetase. Polyglutamation of MTX (MTX-PG) is essential to prevent efflux of MTX, which easily occurs in the monoglutaminated state. MTX-PG has several key inhibitory effects on intra-cellular enzymes, which result in its postulated anti-inflammatory and anti-proliferative (immunosuppressive) mechanisms: (1) inhibition of aminoimidazole carboxamide ribonucleotide (AICAR) transformylase (ATIC) results in decreased purine and pyrimidine synthesis and increased intra-cellular and extra-cellular adenosine, (2) inhibition of thymidylate synthetase (TYMS) results in decreased pyrimidine synthesis, and (3) inhibition of dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR) results in inhibition of transmethylation reactions essential for cellular functioning and uncoupling of nitric oxide synthase leading to increased cellular sensitivity to apoptosis and NF-kB (nuclear factor kappa light chain enhancer of activated B cells) downregulation (Fig. 61.2).

Inhibition of ATIC by MTX-PG leads to accumulation of AICAR and, ultimately, to increased levels of adenosine. Three mechanisms are postulated and likely work in combination: (1) AICAR inhibition of adenosine monophosphate (AMP) deaminase (AMPDA) leads to excess production of adenosine from AMP, (2) AICAR inhibition of adenine deaminase (ADA) leads to decreased breakdown of adenosine to inosine, and (3) AICAR inhibition of AMPDA and ADA leads to the release of adenine nucleotides in the extra-cellular space where they are converted to adenosine by CD39 (ectonucleoside triphosphate dephosphorylase 1) and CD73 (ecto-5'-nucleotidase). 8-11

Evidence that the anti-inflammatory effects of MTX are mediated through adenosine has accumulated in in vitro and in animal studies. However, because of adenosine's short blood half-life of 2 seconds and MTX's long latent period for active metabolites that modulate adenosine, it has been difficult to demonstrate changes in blood adenosine levels directly related to MTX. Using forearm blood flow as a surrogate marker for adenosine release in patients with RA treated with MTX, it has been shown that MTX inhibits deamination of adenosine and potentiates adenosine-induced vasodilation. Demonstration of altered adenosine kinetics in patients treated with MTX coupled with adenosine's known antiinflammatory effects lends further credence to the hypothesis that MTX increases extra-cellular adenosine, which likely mediates some of the anti-inflammatory effects of MTX.

In addition to vasodilation, adenosine's cardiovascular effects include negative inotropic and chronotropic cardiac effects, inhibition of vascular smooth muscle cell proliferation, pre-synaptic inhibition of sympathetic neurotransmitter release, and inhibition of thrombocyte aggregation. It is well recognized that patients with RA have a higher incidence of cardiovascular disease than the general population. MTX has been suggested to have a preferentially beneficial effect on cardiovascular mortality compared with other DMARDs in RA, and this effect may partially occur via adenosine modulation.

The anti-inflammatory and anti-proliferative effects of MTX may be mediated through its inhibition of transmethylation reactions. Both MTX and MTX-PG inhibit DHFR, resulting in diminution of tetrahydrofolate (THF). THF acts as a proximal methyl donor for several reactions by donating the methyl group for the conversion of homocysteine to methionine. Methionine is then converted to S-adenosylmethionine (SAM), which acts as a methyl donor for methylation of RNA, DNA, amino acids, proteins, and phospholipids and synthesis of the polyamines spermidine and spermine. Upon demethylation of SAM to S-adenosylhomocysteine (SAH), SAH is converted to adenosine and homocysteine. Methylation products that are dependent on SAM, and thus indirectly on DHFR, to generate THF are required for cellular survival and function, although specific cellular dependence upon each varies.

In RA patients, polyamines (spermine and spermidine) accumulate in urine,30 in peripheral blood mononuclear cells,31 and in synovial fluid and tissue. Metabolism of polyamines by mononuclear cells gives rise to toxic agents, including ammonia and hydrogen peroxide, which may impair lymphocyte function.33,

Additionally, accumulation of polyamines in B cells is associated with enhanced production of rheumatoid factor (RF) in vitro, and incubation of these cells with MTX diminishes their ability to secrete both immunoglobulin and RF. These effects are seen with high in vitro concentrations of MTX and may not translate into the in vivo therapeutic effects of MTX in RA.

Inhibition of DHFR also leads to nitric oxide synthase uncoupling. DHFR catalyzes the reduction of dihydrobiopterin to tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4). BH4 is a cofactor for nitric oxide (NO) synthases, which catalyze the production of nitric oxide from L-arginine. Reductions in BH4 shunts the NO synthase to produce reactive oxygen species (ROS), activate the JUN N-terminal kinases, phosphorylate the transcription factor JUN and leads to transcription of the JUN-FOS heterodimer activator protein 1 (AP1). AP1 can inhibit NF-kB, induce cell cycle arrest, and sensitize the cell to apoptosis.

MTX also inhibits methylation of 2'-deoxyuridylate into 2'-deoxythymidylate by TYMS, resulting in a further mechanism for disruption of DNA synthesis and proliferation of inflammatory cells. This effect has been shown in vitro in human peripheral blood mononuclear cells incubated with low concentrations of MTX. Cell cycle disruption may lead to apoptosis of mononuclear cells via CD95 (APO-1/Fas) ligand-dependent36 and ligandindependent mechanisms.

In support of the proposed mechanism of action already mentioned, the anti-inflammatory and anti-proliferative effects of MTX occur differentially in the cells of the immune system. For example, anti-inflammatory effects in T cells are mediated by inhibition of transmethylation reactions, which lead to NO synthase uncoupling, ROS production, apoptosis sensitivity, and increased expression of cell cycle checkpoints. Downregulation of NF-kB activity also affects T cell function. Inhibition of ATIC at the fibroblast-like synoviocytes leads to adenosine release and receptor binding with downregulation of NF-kB. Disruption of DNA, RNA, amino acid, and phospholipid synthesis results affects rapidly dividing cells, such as the neutrophils and lymphocytes. Therefore its anti-inflammatory and anti-proliferative properties make it a potent inhibitor of the immune response that characterizes many rheumatic diseases. Indeed, MTX has become the cornerstone of therapy for RA and is efficacious in multiple other rheumatic diseases.

### Pharmacology

### Absorption and Bioavailability

At low doses, MTX can be administered either orally or parenterally (subcutaneous [SQ] or intramuscular [IM]) and absorption is rapid, peaking at 1 to 2 or 0.1 to 1 hour, respectively. The absorption of low-dose oral MTX (<15 mg/week) can be variable and, once the oral dose exceeds 15 mg/week, absorption diminishes by as much as 30%. Absorption is not reduced by concomitant food intake, except for milk, which may be inhibitory. MTX absorption may be reduced in the setting of intestinal pathology, such as inflammatory bowel disease or malabsorptive conditions.

Orally administered MTX is absorbed via the gastrointestinal (GI) tract and passes through the liver via the portal vein; parenterally administered MTX passes through the liver via the hepatic artery. Systemic levels are higher for parentally administered MTX compared with orally administered MTX at equal dosing intervals. Due to saturation of a membrane transporter mainly present in the upper small intestine,40 the bioavailability of single-dose daily oral MTX plateaus at doses of 15 mg/week,

whereas parenteral MTX has a linear increase in systemic levels with increasing dosages. These higher systemic levels have not been associated with any increase in toxicity.41, Although not prospectively studied in RA patients receiving long-term MTX treatment, the parenteral route should have diminished potential for hepatotoxicity. This effect has been seen in a retrospective study wherein more elevations in transaminases were noted when oral MTX was administered to the same individuals versus when given parenterally. With monotherapy, equivalent MTX doses showed improved efficacy in RA clinical endpoints for parenteral versus orally administered MTX. When used in the background of hydroxychloroquine therapy, the oral route was not inferior to the SQ route with respect to efficacy and tolerability.'

As previously discussed, absorption of orally administered MTX plateaus above certain doses. Forty-one RA patients who received 10 mg/m2 of oral MTX had a mean bioavailability of 70% with a range of 40 to 100%. The mean absorption time was 1.2 hours. Four hours after MTX administration, synovial fluid concentrations equaled serum levels. A study of high-dose oral MTX (median dose, 30 mg/week) has shown that mean bioavailability is improved by splitting the dose by 8 hours compared with one single dose (mean bioavailability of 0.9 and 0.76, respectively). The pharmacokinetics of SQ MTX are equivalent to those of IM MTX, with maximum serum concentration attained within 2 hours of injection by either route. Also, important for cost savings, the bioavailability is equivalent between tablets and orally administered parenteral solution.

### Distribution and Half-Life

MTX is 50 to 60% bound to plasma proteins and has a half-life of approximately 6 hours. An increase in free MTX caused by displacement from albumin by more highly protein-bound drugs, such as aspirin, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), and sulfonamides, can occur. This is generally of limited clinical significance with low MTX doses because the increase in free MTX is usually only modest.

MTX accumulates in third-space fluids, which can serve as a reservoir for redistribution into the circulation long after the last dose is administered. Caution should be used when administering MTX to patients with pleural effusions or ascites. Furthermore, unexpectedly high levels of MTX have been seen in patients with bladder cancer who have undergone ileal conduit surgery because of enhanced intestinal absorption through the newly fashioned conduit.

The biologically active form of MTX occurs after intra-cellular polyglutamation (MTX-PG). MTX undergoes up to five polyglutamations, and recent studies have looked at this aspect of MTX pharmacology. Once on a stable dose of MTX, the median time until 90% of the maximum steady-state concentration of MTX- PG was reached was found to be 27.5 weeks (range, 6.6 to 62.0 weeks).

### Elimination

Most MTX is excreted in the urine within the first 12 hours after administration, except for MTX-PG. MTX undergoes some hepatic metabolism by the enzyme aldehyde oxidase to the 7-hydroxymethotrexate metabolite; this metabolite has unknown significance in RA. MTX and metabolites are excreted by the kidney by glomerular filtration and proximal tubular secretion but also undergo distal tubular reabsorption. The estimated median half-life of elimination of MTX-PG is 3.1 weeks (range, 0.94 to 4.1 weeks), and MTX-PG is undetectable at 15 weeks. MTX-PG3 is

the most common subtype seen (30% of total MTX-PG) and has a median half-life elimination of 4.1 weeks.

### Indications

### Rheumatoid Arthritis

The efficacy of MTX in RA has been clearly established. Four well-designed, blinded, placebo-controlled trials52-55 published in 1984 and 1985 had a tremendous impact on the treatment of RA. These trials varied in design and duration, but they all showed MTX to be superior to placebo in the short-term treatment of RA. A meta-analysis of these trials by one study56 showed that MTX-treated patients had a 37% greater improvement in swollen joint and tender joint scores, a 39% greater improvement in joint pain, and a 46% greater improvement in morning stiffness. MTX was generally well tolerated in these trials; withdrawal rates ranged from 0 to 32% and were mostly related to minor toxicities (i.e., stomatitis and nausea). Taken together, the results of these trials firmly established MTX as an effective therapy for the treatment of RA.

Numerous trials have compared MTX with other DMARDs. A meta-analysis showed that MTX was superior to placebo, auranofin, and probably hydroxychloroquine (HCQ), and was comparable with penicillamine, sulfasalazine (SSZ), and IM gold. No trial has ever suggested that any other synthetic DMARD is superior to MTX.

Accumulating evidence suggests that the short-term benefit of most DMARDs is not sustained, and few patients continue to take these drugs after 3 years.58, MTX appears to have the best durability. Another study has shown that 60% of patients continued MTX at 5 years, compared with less than 25% for penicillamine, gold, HCQ, and azathioprine. Of all the DMARDs, MTX appears to have the best efficacy-to-toxicity ratio. However, despite all the favorable efficacy reports, MTX alone rarely induces sustained remissions of RA, and it has become the cornerstone of combinations of DMARD therapies, as discussed later.60,61

### Rheumatoid Arthritis-Related Conditions

MTX has been used successfully in treating Felty's syndrome62 and the large granular lymphocyte syndrome when it is found in patients with RA. Improvement in neutrophil count occurs within 4 to 8 weeks of MTX initiation in both cases. MTX has been used successfully in adult-onset Still's disease64 and for the cutaneous vasculitis of RA.

### Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis

MTX is efficacious in juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA). A definitive, randomized, placebo-controlled trial (RCT) demonstrated that MTX at a dose of 10.0 mg/m2 was superior to 5.0 mg/m2 or placebo. Sixty-three percent of children receiving the higher dose (10.0 mg/m2) of MTX improved, compared with 32% in the lower-dose group (5.0 mg/m2) and 36% in the placebo group.

### Psoriatic Arthritis

Numerous prospective and retrospective trials have showed a benefit for MTX in psoriatic arthritis (PsA). The largest double-blind randomized trial compared weekly oral MTX with placebo and showed statistically significant results only for physician global assessment of arthritis activity and the amount of affected skin surface area; however, this study was small and may have been underpowered to detect differences in joint count, pain,

and swelling. Despite the paucity of RCT data, MTX remains a commonly used systemic agent in the treatment of PsA.

### Systemic Lupus Erythematosus

MTX is efficacious in controlling cutaneous and/or articular manifestations of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), particularly in disease resistant to anti-malarials or requiring high doses of systemic steroids. Concomitant folic acid should be administered to abrogate the elevated levels of homocysteine that may be a side effect of MTX therapy and is considered a risk factor for cardiovascular disease in SLE. The role of MTX in treating more severe SLE involvement, including renal, hematologic, or central nervous system (CNS) disease, has not yet been established. Extreme caution should be used in patients with renal disease.

### Vasculitis

MTX in conjunction with corticosteroids is efficacious in treating early and non-life-threatening granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) and microscopic polyangiitis (MPA), including upper airway disease and mild renal disease.71-75 In addition to induction of remission, MTX can maintain remission in GPA and MPA, although physician vigilance for patient relapse is warranted.75, Despite a lack of well-designed studies, MTX has been efficacious in corticosteroid-resistant Takayasu's arteritis77,78 and in relapsing polychondritis. Recent guidelines also recommend the use of MTX plus corticosteroids80 in nonsevere polyarteritis nodosa to induce and maintain remission.

The use of MTX for polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR) and giant cell arteritis (GCA) has been controversial. RCTs of MTX in addition to corticosteroids in PMR and GCA have shown conflicting results.81-84 However, some advocate the use of MTX in GCA (and PMR) in an effort to more rapidly taper corticosteroid use in patients with intolerable side effects or when tocilizumab is not available or contraindicated. 78,85

### Inflammatory Myopathies

A review of the published reports of MTX and the inflammatory myopathies polymyositis and dermatomyositis shows overall positive results. However, despite the frequent use of MTX in the inflammatory myopathies, a recent Cochrane Database Review reveals a paucity of well-designed trials.

### Other Rheumatic Diseases

MTX has been used effectively in systemic sclerosis. One RCT looking at MTX use in early systemic sclerosis89 showed a trend in benefit for skin scores and pulmonary diffusion capacity and a significant benefit for physician global assessment; a second RCT in established systemic sclerosis90 showed significant benefit for skin scores and total creatinine clearance.

Prospective trials have shown that MTX is efficacious in the treatment of corticosteroid-resistant multisystem sarcoidosis91,92 and a RCT showed that, if initiated early in sarcoidosis, MTX is an effective steroid-sparing agent. MTX is also effective as primary treatment and as a corticosteroid-sparing agent in inflammatory ocular disease.94, Finally, MTX in combination with corticosteroids is effective in the treatment of multicentric reticulohistiocytosis.

MTX has been used in a dose-dependent manner to prevent the formation of anti-drug antibodies for the anti-TNF therapies adalimumab and infliximab. Furthermore, MTX at 15 mg per week reduced anti-drug antibodies to pegloticase, increasing the number of patients maintaining a therapeutic effect at 6 months.

### Dose and d Drug Administration

MTX is available as 2.5, 5, 7.5, 10, and 15 mg tablets and as a solution of 25 mg/mL for SQ or IM injection. Recently the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved singleand multiple-use, pre-filled auto-injection pens at various dosages.

In patients with normal renal function, the starting dose is usually 15 mg given as a single weekly dose, with a range of 5 to 25 mg weekly, and consideration should be given to initiation via the parenteral route for improved efficacy. More frequent administration is associated with a significantly increased risk of liver toxicity. If the oral dose of MTX exceeds 15 mg, consideration should be given to splitting the dose, with each half given 6 to 12 hours apart, for improved absorption and bioavailability. The dosage of MTX can be escalated, usually every 4 to 8 weeks to 25 mg/week to achieve the desired clinical response. MTX may be administered orally via tablet or parenteral solution; the latter may be less costly. Because its oral bioavailability is variable and decreases at higher doses, parenteral MTX is generally recommended if patients have active disease despite oral doses at approximately 20 mg weekly. In fact, recent data have shown that parenteral MTX is clinically superior to orally administered MTX and that this may be a preferred route of administration for initial therapy 100 or if oral MTX is not optimally effective.

MTX is not directly toxic to the kidneys but, as the main mechanism of elimination is via the kidneys, it is contraindicated in patients with a glomerular filtration rate (GFR) less than 30 mL/ minute. MTX may be used in patients with a GFR of 30 to 59 mL/minute, but it is prudent to initiate a lower dose and monitor carefully with subsequent dose escalations.

Because MTX works by interfering with folate-dependent pathways, a relative folate-deficient state can occur in individuals taking MTX. Concomitant administration of folic acid (1 to 3 mg/day) or folinic acid decreases the frequency of MTX side effects, including GI toxicity (nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain) and stomatitis. Supplementation of folic or folinic acid is protective against elevated transaminase concentrations, results in fewer toxicity-related withdrawals of MTX, and does not interfere with the efficacy of MTX. Folic acid administration also decreases hyperhomocysteinemia in patients on MTX, and this may be important to help decrease the already high cardiovascular risk of patients with RA. There is insufficient evidence to suggest that one form of folate has clinical advantages versus the other and, because folic acid is widely available and may be less expensive, it has become the preferred agent for most.

In the case of overdose leading to amino transferase elevations over three times the upper limits of normal and cytopenias, intravenous leucovorin should be given at a dose of 5 to 10 mg every 12 hours until the patient has recovered.

Measurement of MTX-PG levels is commercially available (MTXGlun). It would be valuable to have a marker to predict response and adverse events associated with MTX therapy, but mixed results have been obtained in the search for a trend in the dose—response relationship for MTXGlun levels and RA disease activity. A recent study showed no relationship between MTX- Glun concentration and reduced disease activity in RA. Furthermore, no relationship was identified between MTXGlun levels and adverse events. Disease activity was influenced by red blood cell folate level, and further study is warranted to determine whether this may serve as a marker for MTX efficacy.

### Geriatric Patients

Patients older than age 65 represent a special subset of patients receiving pharmacotherapy. Pharmacokinetic profiles, including drug distribution, are changed in older adults as the result of decreases in end organ blood flow and lean body mass, decreased hepatic drug metabolism, and decreased renal drug excretion. Furthermore, these patients are more likely to have multiple comorbidities, polypharmacy, nonadherence, increased risk for dosage errors, and limited access to medication for financial reasons.

In practice, recommended doses should be reduced when therapy is initiated and should be adjusted for renal function based on creatinine clearance (CrCl). The serum creatinine may be a misleading measure of renal function in older patients because of an overall reduction in lean muscle mass. Dosing recommendations are as follows: initial doses should be approximately 5 to 7.5 mg/week and should not exceed 20 mg/week without close monitoring. Dosage adjustments for CrCl are as follows: for a CrCl of 61 to 80 mL/min, reduce the dose by 25%; for a CrCl of 51 to 60 mL/min, reduce the dose by 30%; for a CrCl of 30 to 50 mL/ min, reduce the dose by 50 to 80%; and for a CrCl less than 30 mL/min, avoid use106 (Table 61.1).

### Pediatric Patients

MTX is commonly used in the pediatric population (see Table 61.1). It can be given orally or SQ. It is common to start at 0.3 mg/kg dosed once weekly and escalate to a dose of 25 mg/wk. It is suggested that at doses greater than 15 mg/week, parenteral application should be considered because of better bioavailability and tolerability. Guidelines for toxicity monitoring are similar to adult recommendations.

### Toxicity

Despite initial concerns, when given once a week in doses used for rheumatic diseases and monitored correctly, MTX is very well tolerated. Some of the toxicities of MTX (e.g., stomatitis, nausea, and bone marrow depression) are dose dependent, appear to be related to folate deficiency, and respond to folate replacement. Other toxicities (e.g., pneumonitis) appear to be idiosyncratic or allergic and, in most cases, require discontinuation of MTX. Still other toxicities, such as liver fibrosis and cirrhosis, appear to be multifactorial and may depend on the presence of concomitant risk factors, total dose, and frequency of administration.

### Gastrointestinal and Hepatic Side Effects

GI symptoms, including dyspepsia, nausea, and anorexia, are common, occurring in as many as 20 to 70% of patients within the first year of therapy. These symptoms may be attenuated by adding folic acid or by changing to a parenteral dosing regimen.

The risk of significant liver toxicity appears to be low when MTX is given once weekly to patients who abstain from alcohol and are monitored carefully and occurs in approximately one patient per 1000 after 5 years of use.
