IL-17 production by T helper 17 cells is also inhibited. Tofacitinib, along with all the other JAK inhibitors, do not block IL-1 or TNF signaling.

Additional JAK inhibitors have demonstrated in pre-clinical models to be more specific JAK1 inhibitors (upadacitinib/filgotinib).37, Peficitinib has been demonstrated in pre-clinical studies to inhibit JAK1/3 preferentially but regulatory authorities consider it to be a pan JAK inhibitor (Table 65.2). The assays evaluating specificity of the JAK inhibitors vary depending on the methodology, whether it be biochemical or cellular, which makes the comparative data difficult to interpret. Additionally, depending on the amount of ATP substrate utilized in the assay or degree of cytokine stimulation, results may vary. For example, at the doses used in the clinic, tofacitinib demonstrates substantial nanomolar inhibitory potency in enzymatic assays against all JAK family kinases except TYK2, but in cellular assays it shows functional greater specificity for JAK1 and JAK1/3 versus JAK2.41 Regulatory agencies now consider tofacitinib, baricitinib, and peficitinib to be pan-JAK inhibitors. Complicating the issue of JAK selectivity is whether the maximal concentration (Cmax) or the average drug concentration results in the major impact on JAK inhibition. For example, at Cmax, JAK selectivity may not exist, whereas at lower concentrations such as the average concentration, preferential JAK inhibition would be possible. Studies have demonstrated that clinical profiles of cytokine inhibition for a number of JAK inhibitors in RA are strikingly similar when efficacious doses are considered, suggesting possible limited potential for differentiation of these therapeutics based on their JAK pharmacology.' 41 One group did demonstrate differences in in-vitro pharmacologic profiles with tofacitinib, baricitinib, filgotinib, and upadacitinib in different cell types. The relevance of specific JAK inhibition in these assays to their clinical effectiveness remains unknown.

### JAK Inhibitors for Rheumatoid Arthritis

Multiple JAK inhibitors have been approved as treatment for RA and other IMIDs in patients failing conventional synthetic diseasemodifying anti-rheumatic drugs (csDMARDS) or biologic therapies (Table 65.3). Tofacitinib was approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in 2012, followed by baricitinib in 2017 and upadacitinib in 2019. These therapies are now approved worldwide. Peficitinib was approved in Japan and South Korea in 2019 and is not approved elsewhere. Filgotinib was approved by the European Medicines Agency (EMA) and outside of the United States in 2020. All of the approved JAK inhibitors were evaluated as combination therapy or monotherapy in similar development programs, including csDMARD incomplete responders, primarily methotrexate; biologic DMARD (bDMARD) incomplete responders; and in early RA patients compared with methotrexate.

### JAK Inhibitor Pharmacology

### Tofacitinib

Tofacitinib was approved by the FDA in 2012 and the EMA in 2017 for patients with active RA despite methotrexate treatment at a dose of 5 mg, twice daily, in combination with nonbiologic DMARDs or as monotherapy. .43-48 The delay in EMA approval was over safety concerns of a trend for greater risk of infection and malignancies with a 10 mg twice-daily (bid) dose in clinical trials. A post-marketing study in patients over age 50 with cardiovascular risk factors demonstrated a dose-dependent increase in venous thromboembolic disease, malignancies, and major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) in RA patients treated with tofacitinib 5 mg bid and 10 mg bid compared with TNF inhibitors, resulting in regulatory authorities limiting use to patients who have failed TNF inhibitors.

Tofacitinib was initially approved at a dose of 5 mg bid and an 11 mg XR (extended-release) once-daily formulation was approved in 2016, which is the most commonly used dose. This

formulation was approved by the FDA based on a pharmacokinetic study and not a clinical trial. Japan regulatory authorities have not approved the 11 mg XR formulation based on a small study in RA patients failing to demonstrate noninferiority to the 5 mg bid dose in change in disease activity as determined by the Disease Activity Score-28 with C-reactive protein (DAS28-CRP). Realworld experience has not demonstrated a significant difference in clinical response to that seen with the 5 mg bid dose, and postmarketing clinical trials have demonstrated benefit of the 11 mg XR formulation. The pharmacokinetic profile of tofacitinib 11 mg XR is characterized by rapid absorption (peak plasma concentrations are reached within 4 hours), rapid elimination (half-life of approximately 6 hours), and dose-proportional increases in systo 48 hours with minimal accumulation after twice-daily administration. Tofacitinib is eliminated through both hepatic (70%) and renal clearance (30%). The metabolism is primarily through cytochrome P450 3A4 (CYP3A4) and less so by CYP2C19. At the approved dosage, no extrinsic factors or drugs require dose modification based on pharmacokinetic evaluation in pre-clinical studies except for ketoconazole, which suppresses CYP3A4 activity, and rifampin, which enhances CYP3A4 activity. The pharmacodynamic effects of tofacitinib have been demonstrated to persist for 4 to 6 weeks after dosing, which includes a reduction in NK cells. Tofacitinib is a teratogen, as are all the JAK inhibitors in animal models, and pre-menopausal women should utilize contraception and avoid conception for 4 to 6 weeks after the last dose.

### Baricitinib

Baricitinib was approved by the EMA and several other countries in 2017 at 4 mg once daily for csDMARD incomplete responders and in 2018 was approved by the FDA at 2 mg daily in patients with active disease despite previous treatment with TNF inhibitors.53-56 The FDA expressed concerns over the benefit—risk profile of the 4 mg dose with a trend for increased rates of AEs. Outside

the United States, the 4 mg dose is widely utilized and real-world studies have not demonstrated safety issues with rates similar to those seen with other JAK inhibitors.

Baricitinib is rapidly absorbed with a time to maximum drug concentration (Tmax) of 1 hour and a half-life of 12.5 hours. It is eliminated primarily by renal excretion, and it is recommended to use the 2 mg dose in patients with renal insufficiency. Probenecid and other strong organic anion transporter 3 (OAT3) inhibitors reduce baricitinib clearance. Baricitinib undergoes minor metabolism by CYP3A4 but no dose modification is necessary with drugs that impact the CYP450 enzymes. Baricitinib is also associated with a decrease in NK cells, with a reduction of 40% to 50% over 24 weeks in phase III trials.

### Upadacitinib

Upadacitinib 15 mg XR was approved for use in RA as monotherapy or combination therapy in 2019 for csDMARD incomplete responders.60-64 The 30 mg dose was not approved due to doserelated toxicity without any improvement in observed efficacy in the clinical trials, although this dose has been approved for other IMIDs.65,

Upadacitinib is rapidly absorbed with Tmax of 2 to 3 hours and half-life of 10 to 12.5 hours. Elimination is primarily through hepatic metabolism through the CYP3A enzyme and, to a lesser degree, CYP2D6. Modification of the dose is necessary with ketoconazole and rifampin. Reduction in NK cells has been noted with upadacitinib.

### Filgotinib

Filgotinib was approved in 2020 by the EMA at 100 and 200 mg as monotherapy or combination therapy for RA patients with active disease despite csDMARD therapy. It has not been approved

by the FDA for reasons that remain unclear, as efficacy and safety in the clinical trials was similar to the other JAK inhibitors.67-70 Pre-clinical studies had demonstrated a negative impact on male spermatogenesis and studies in male patients with inflammatory arthritis and inflammatory bowel disease were conducted to evaluate impact on spermatogenesis, but to date that data has not been available. A press release did report that filgotinib had similar impact on sperm concentrations to placebo in these patients, and in November 2022 the EMA removed language from the package insert on filgotinib's impact on spermatogenesis based on the results of these studies.

Filgotinib is a prodrug rapidly metabolized to an active metabolite. Absorption is rapid with Tmax 2 to 3 hours and half-life of 4.9 to 5.7 hours, although the active metabolite has a half-life of 18 to 23 hours. Elimination is both hepatic by carboxyesterases and renal clearance. Limited impact on the CYP450 enzymes has been noted. Filgotinib monotherapy had no impact on NK cells in a 24-week phase II dose-ranging study.

### Peficitinib

Peficitinib 100 and 100 mg was approved in Japan in 2019 for treatment of RA patients as monotherapy and combination therapy with active disease despite csDMARDS.74, In vitro kinase assays show that peficitinib is a pan-JAK inhibitor, blocking JAK activity with half maximal inhibitory concentrations (IC50) of 3.9 nM (JAK1), 5.0 nM (JAK2), 0.7 nM (JAK3), and 4.8 nM (TYK2). Peficitinib inhibited IL-2-induced human T-cell proliferation (IC50 18 nM) and STAT5 phosphorylation (IC50 127 nM) in a concentration-dependent manner. Peficitinib is absorbed rapidly: after a single dose under fasting conditions, median Tmax was 1 to 1.8 hours. Peficitinib metabolism is mediated mainly by sulfotransferase 2A1, and nicotinamide N-methyltransferase was

1 to 1.8 hours. While peficitinib is mostly cleared by hepatic metabolism, peficitinib is also cleared by other mechanisms (renal and possibly biliary excretion).

### JAK Efficacy

The approved JAK inhibitors were evaluated in multiple clinical trials in RA patients, demonstrating statistically significant efficacy compared with placebo treated patients. Phase II clinical trials evaluated tofacitinib at doses of 1 to 30 mg bid as monotherapy or in combination with methotrexate.79, Consistent improvement in clinical outcomes were seen with doses of 5 mg twice daily or greater, but toxicity was greater at higher doses. Based on the efficacy and safety profile from the phase II clinical trials, tofacitinib 5 mg twice daily and 10 mg twice daily doses were progressed to phase III trials. Baricitinib was evaluated at doses of 1, 2, 4, and 8 mg once daily in phase II trials.81, Efficacy was similar at 2, 4, and 8 mg daily with a trend for more safety issues at 8 mg, resulting in the 2 and 4 mg doses progressing to phase III clinical trials. Upadacitinib was evaluated in immediate-release formulations of 6, 12, and 18 mg bid in phase1/2 trials, based on studies demonstrating similar pharmacokinetics to the 12 and 18 mg bid, and a 15 and 30 mg once daily formulation was evaluated in phase III clinical trials. Filgotinib was evaluated in phase I/II clinical trials at 30, 75, 150, 200, and 300 mg daily or 100 mg bid.84, Based on phase I/II efficacy and safety, the 100 and 200 mg once-daily doses were evaluated in phase III trials. Peficitinib was evaluated in phase II trials of RA patients at doses of 50, 100, and 150 mg daily. Based on results from phase II dose-ranging trials, the 100 mg and 150 mg daily doses were evaluated in phase III.86,

The phase III clinical trials program designs were similar for all of the approved JAK inhibitors. All of the trials were global programs, with the majority of patients enrolled outside of the United States. The development programs were large, with 2500 to 4000 patients enrolled.43-48, The clinical trials evaluated RA patients with active disease despite methotrexate or csDMARDs, patients with active disease despite receiving TNF inhibitors, and patients naive to methotrexate. All therapies were also evaluated as monotherapy in patients who had failed csDMARDS. The ability of these therapies to slow radiographic progression was evaluated over 12 months in RA patients receiving background methotrexate compared with an active comparatoradalimumab. Long-term extension studies to evaluate persistence of response and to monitor long-term safety issues were included in all of the development programs.

Tofacitinib (5 and 10 mg bid), baricitinib (4 mg daily), upadacitinib (15 and 30 mg daily), and peficitinib (100 and 150 mg) in combination with methotrexate or csDMARDs all demonstrated statistically significant improvement compared with placebo in signs and symptoms as measured by the American College of Rheumatology (ACR) response, the Clinical Disease Activity Index (CDAI), the Simple Disease Activity Index (SDAI) and change in disease activity as measured by DAS28. In RA patients on background methotrexate nonresponsive to TNF inhibitors tofacitinib (5 and 10 mg bid), baricitinib (2 and 4 mg), and upadacitinib (15 and 30 mg), filgotinib (100 and 200 mg daily) demonstrated significant improvement compared with placebo over 6 months.46, In RA patients naive to methotrexate, tofacitinib monotherapy at 5 and 10 mg bid daily was statistically superior to modest dosed oral methotrexate as determined by ACR70 response. Baricitinib 4 mg monotherapy and baricitinib 4 mg in combination with methotrexate was statistically superior

to methotrexate in a DMARD-naive population in improvement in disease activity as determined by ACR response or change in DAS28.54 In a DMARD-naive population, filgotinib 100/200 mg in combination with methotrexate was statistically superior to methotrexate, but filgotinib 200 mg monotherapy failed to achieve statistical superiority in ACR20 response. Upadacitinib 15 and 30 mg monotherapy was demonstrated to be superior to modest doses of oral methotrexate monotherapy in DMARD-naive RA patients by ACR50 response and change in DAS28-CRP <2.6.88

Data from two 52-week phase III trials of peficitinib 100/150 mg daily in RA patients with active disease despite methotrexate or csDMARDs demonstrated statistical superiority in improvement as measured by the ACR20/50/70 and change in DAS28 at week 12.74, In one study, open-label etanercept was included as an active comparator with numerically greater ACR responses than peficitinib and change in DAS28 and low disease activity state (LDAS)/remission, but no statistical comparison was conducted.

### JAK Inhibitors Versus Adalimumab

In the development program, tofacitinib was compared with adalimumab in the methotrexate incomplete responder populations with similar clinical benefit, but the study was not powered to evaluate statistical difference between the groups. In a phase IV study, tofacitinib 5 mg bid plus methotrexate was determined to be noninferior to adalimumab plus methotrexate in ACR50 response at 6 months. Although there was a good clinical response with tofacitinib monotherapy, noninferiority to adalimumab/methotrexate was not achieved in this study.

Baricitinib and upadacitinib were both compared with adalimumab in the methotrexate incomplete responder population.63, Baricitinib was statistically superior to adalimumab at week 12 for the ACR20/50/70 response and for the ACR20 and ACR70 response at week 24. Upadacitinib was statistically superior to adalimumab at week 12 in ACR50, DAS28-CRP, and LDAS. At week 26, more patients achieved LDAS or remission on upadacitinib than adalimumab. Filgotinib 200 mg was noninferior to adalimumab in RA patients on background methotrexate for DAS28-CRP <3.2.69

### Radiographic Outcomes

Radiographic outcomes were evaluated in the clinical trials for all the JAK inhibitors. Improvement in structural benefit as measured by the modified Total Sharp scores (mTSS) was observed at the 10 mg tofacitinib twice-daily dosage in the methotrexate incomplete responder population, but did not achieve statistical significance at the 5 mg twice-daily dosage. In the methotrexate-naive population, mean changes in the mTSS from baseline to month 6 were statistically significantly less in the tofacitinib groups than in the methotrexate group (0.2 in the 5 mg tofacitinib group and <0.1 in the 10 mg tofacitinib group, compared with a change of 0.8 in the methotrexate group [p < 0.00i for both comparisons]). Based on this trial, the FDA allowed the claim for slowing of radiographic progression for tofacitinib.

Baricitinib 4 mg in combination with methotrexate reduced radiographic progression compared with placebo, as did the active comparator adalimumab in a 52-week study (mTSS placebo 1.80; baricitinib 0.71; adalimumab 0.60). In the csDMARD-naive population, baricitinib 4 mg plus methotrexate inhibited radiographic progression compared with methotrexate at 52 weeks but

baricitinib monotherapy was not statistically different (methotrexate [MTX] -1.02; baricitinib -0.80; baricitinib/MTX -0.40).

Data from a 26-week phase III clinical trial of 15 mg upadacitinib in combination with methotrexate demonstrated statistically significant inhibition of radiographic progression (mTSS placebo -0.92; upadacitinib -0.24, p < 0.001). Similar findings were reported for peficitinib 100/150 mg daily in combination with methotrexate in a 28-week study (mTSS placebo 3.4; peficitinib 100 mg -1.6; peficitinib 150 mg -1.0, p < 0.001). Filgotinib 100 (mTSS -0.17) and 200 mg (mTSS -0.13) in combination with methotrexate slowed radiographic progression compared with patients continuing methotrexate at 52 weeks (mTSS -0.37), with similar slowing of radiographic progression in DMARDnaive patients.68,69

### Patient-Reported Outcomes

Patient-reported outcomes were evaluated in all of the development programs for the JAK inhibitors. These included the Health Assessment Questionnaire (HAQ), the 36-Item Short Form Health Survey (SF36), and measures of patient pain and fatigue. Significant improvements compared with placebo-treated patients in the HAQ were seen in all of the studies in early disease, methotrexate or csDMARD incomplete responders, and TNF or biologic incomplete responders exceeding the minimally clinically important difference of 0.22. In comparison to the combination of adalimumab/methotrexate, baricitinib/methotrexate and upadacitinib/methotrexate were statistically superior to adalimumab in improvement in HAQ scores at several timepoints during the 52-week studies.63, Filgotinib and peficitinib had similar improvements in HAQ scores to the active comparators adalimumab and etanercept, respectively.71, Improvements in the physical and mental component of the SF36 were noted and the changes were comparable for each of the JAK inhibitors. Similar improvements in pain and fatigue were also observed.

### Post-marketing Clinical Trials

Several clinical trials have been conducted in RA patients after approval. Tofacitinib 5 mg bid as monotherapy or in combination with methotrexate was compared with adalimumab plus methotrexate in patients with active disease despite methotrexate in the Oral Strategy study. This study was a 12-month noninferiority trial with the primary endpoint of ACR50 response at month 6. A total of 1146 patients were enrolled and ACR50 response was attained in 147 (38%) of 384 patients with tofacitinib monotherapy, 173 (46%) of 376 patients with tofacitinib and methotrexate, and 169 (44%) of 386 patients with adalimumab and methotrexate. The study demonstrated that tofacitinib plus methotrexate was noninferior to adalimumab plus methotrexate. Tofacitinib monotherapy failed to achieve noninferiority to adalimumab plus methotrexate even though the ACR50 response was robust.

A second study with tofacitinib evaluated the 11 mg XR formulation and the ability to withdraw methotrexate after achievement of LDAS at week 24 and maintenance of LDAS as monotherapy. The Oral Shift study enrolled RA patients with active disease despite methotrexate and patients received openlabel tofacitinib 1 1 mg XR once daily. At week 24 patients in LDA by CDAI (10 or less) were randomized to blinded withdrawal of methotrexate. The primary endpoint was the least squares mean change from Week 24 to 48 (∆) in DAS28-4-erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) (disease activity) in the double-blind phase full

analysis set. Noninferiority of tofacitinib monotherapy versus tofacitinib plus methotrexate was declared if the upper bound of the 95% confidence interval (CI) for the difference in ΔDAS28- 4-ESR between treatment arms was <0.6; 530/694 achieved LDA by CDAI at week 24 and noninferiority was demonstrated at week 48 (difference [95% CI] 0.30 [0.120.48]). This study confirmed the efficacy of the 11 mg XR formulation and supported the use of tofacitinib monotherapy as an appropriate treatment for RA patients.

The Select Choice study compared upadacitinib 15 mg daily to intravenous abatacept 10 mg/kg in patients with active disease despite previous biologic treatment. This was a 24-week noninferiority study with the primary endpoint the change in DAS28- CRP at week 12. A total of 303 patients received upadacitinib and 309 patients received abatacept. From baseline DAS28-CRP values of 5.70 in the upadacitinib group and 5.88 in the abatacept group, the mean change at week 12 was -2.52 and −2.00, respectively. Noninferiority of upadacitinib was achieved and superiority at week 12 was observed. Upadacitinib was also superior to abatacept at week 12 for DAS28-CRP remission (30% vs. 13%). This study demonstrated the rapid response of JAK inhibitors in RA. By week 24, the differences in clinical improvement were less pronounced.

### Real-World Experience

In the real-world setting, patients initiating tofacitinib tend to have longer disease duration and have been exposed to more bDMARDs, in comparison with patients initiating a bDMARD. A 5-year prospective observational study using the U.S. Corrona RA registry compared patients initiating tofacitinib with patients initiating a bDMARD or those initiating a csDMARD (and with no prior or current tofacitinib exposure). In this study, patients initiating tofacitinib had an average duration of disease of 13.7 years, versus 10.5 years for bDMARD initiators and 4.6 years for csDMARD initiators. The tofacitinib initiators also had exposure to more bDMARDs (mean 2.7) versus the bDMARD initiators (1.5) and the csDMARD initiators (0).

In real-world patients, tofacitinib also appears to be effective as monotherapy, as measured by patient adherence to therapy (i.e., filling prescriptions regularly) and persistence with therapy. One study analyzing tofacitinib use in clinical practice in two U.S. Health Care Claims Databases assessed a total of 455 patients and found that slightly over 50% of patients received monotherapy and over 75% of patients had prior biologic use. There was no significant difference in adherence to therapy and persistence with therapy or with all-cause or RA-related costs in monotherapy versus combination therapy. Another study assessed real-world experience with tofacitinib compared with adalimumab, etanercept, and abatacept in RA patients with one previous biologic DMARD, using data from a U.S. commercial database and a Medicare supplemental claims database. Findings showed that tofacitinib patients were older versus adalimumab patients, the 12-month pre-index use of bDMARDs was greater in tofacitinib patients (77.6%) versus bDMARD cohorts (47.6%59.6%), and tofacitinib patients were more likely to receive monotherapy (53.1% vs. 41.4%48.3% of bDMARD patients). Persistence and adherence to tofacitinib was similar compared with persistence and adherence to the bDMARDs assessed in this study.

The JAK-pot study evaluated the persistence on treatment of over 30, RA patients from 19 international registries in comparison to approved biologics from 2013 to 2021.96 Forty-one

percent of the JAK inhibitor treatment courses were baricitinib and 59% tofacitinib. There were no patients included in this the study period taking upadacitinib. Patients starting TNF inhibitors were younger, had a shorter disease duration, less previous b/tsDMARD experience, and were less often on monotherapy. JAK inhibitors and IL-6 inhibitors were more often given as monotherapy, and JAK inhibitors were more often prescribed after several treatment failures. Treatment groups were comparable for gender, seropositivity, and disease activity.

There were 31,846 treatment courses included in the observational database: 17, TNF inhibitors, 2775 abatacept, 3863 IL-6 inhibitors, and 7686 JAK inhibitors. Adjusted analyses of overall discontinuation were similar across all treatments. The main single reason of stopping treatment was ineffectiveness. Compared with TNF inhibitors, JAK inhibitors were less often discontinued for ineffectiveness (adjusted hazard ratio [aHR] 0.75, 95% CI 0.67 to 0.83), as was IL-6 inhibitors (aHR 0.76, 95% CI 0.67 to 0.85) and more often for AEs (aHR 1.16, 95% CI 1.03 to 1.33). Adjusted CDAI response rates at 1 year were similar between TNF inhibitors, JAK inhibitors, and IL-6 inhibitors and slightly lower for abatacept.

There have been no clinical trials evaluating efficacy of initiating a second JAK inhibitor after initial JAK inhibitor failure for lack of efficacy or intolerability. Data from observational studies in small numbers of patients have reported that initiating a second JAK inhibitor after initial failure can be associated with success regardless of the cause for treatment failure with the initial JAK inhibitor. An updated report from the JAK-pot collaborating registries demonstrated that patients switching from an initial JAK inhibitor to another JAK inhibitor had similar drug survival at 24 months to patients switching to a biologic, but an adjusted analysis showed that cycling to another JAK inhibitor was associated with higher drug retention (p = 0.04). However, when the initial JAK inhibitor was discontinued due to an AE, it was more likely that the second one would also be discontinued due to an AE.

### Safety

The nature of AEs associated with JAK inhibitors have been well characterized in the clinical trial programs and post-marketing clinical trials and real-world experience.99-103 The most common AEs were upper respiratory infections, headache, nasopharyngitis, and diarrhea, which were seen slightly more often in the patients on JAK inhibitors than in the placebo group. AEs associated with JAK inhibitors include serious infectious episodes, opportunistic infections, herpes zoster, gastrointestinal (GI) perforations, and possible increased risk of thromboembolic disease (Box 65.1). The type and frequency of AEs are similar to that seen with bDMARDS except for the increased incidence of herpes zoster.

Data from long-term safety databases is available for the approved JAK inhibitors. Safety data for tofacitinib has been reported on 7061 RA patients with 22,875 patient-years (pt yrs) of exposure to tofacitinib 5 or 10 mg bid.99, The median exposure was 3.1 years. The rate of serious adverse events (SAEs) with tofacitinib was 9.6/100 pt yrs for the 5 mg dose and 8.6 per 100 pt yrs, which was similar to that for adalimumab in the active comparator trial (9.76/100 pt yrs). The most common SAE was pneumonia. The incidence rate for serious infectious episodes (SIEs) was 2.5/100 pt yrs, similar to that seen with biologic therapies. The rate of SIEs remained stable over time in the long-term extension protocol through 6 years follow-up. The most common

At the time of FDA approval in the longterm extension trials, the rate of SIEs was 2.3/100 pt yrs for the 5 mg dose and 4.06/100 pt yrs for the 10 mg dose, which was statistically different because the CIs did not overlap. Nonserious or serious herpes zoster infection events were reported in 3.6/100 pt yrs, which is greater than that seen with csDMARDs or other bDMARDS. Those involving a single dermatome (90.2%) were considered serious in 7.3% of herpes zoster 107 The rate of herpes zoster did not increase over time. patients. A Cox regression analysis of risk factors demonstrated that the 10 mg dose, glucocorticoid usage, age, and being Asian increased the likelihood of developing herpes zoster. Increased herpes zoster risk has been reported with all the JAK inhibitors approved or in development for RA in clinical trials and in the real-world experience in clinic. If possible, RA patients should be vaccinated for herpes zoster before initiating JAK inhibitors.

Tuberculosis (TB) was reported in 36 patients(0.2/100 pt yrs). Incidence rates were similar for the 5 and 10 mg doses. Most of the cases were from areas endemic for TB. Cases of both pulmonary and extrapulmonary TB were reported. The incidence of TB in the randomized clinical trials was consistent with those reported for TNF inhibitors (0.02 [global] to 2.56 [South Korea]) and nonbiologic DMARDs (0.01 [global] to 0.28 [South Korea]). Screening for latent TB is indicated before initiating JAK inhibitors.

Excluding cases of TB, 61 patients experienced an opportunistic infection (0.3 events/100 pt yrs [95% CI, 0.20 to 0.4]).The cases included multidermatomal herpes zoster, esophageal candidiasis (several were incidental findings on endoscopies performed for other reasons), cytomegalovirus infection/viremia, cryptococcal infection (pneumonia, meningitis), Pneumocystis pneumonia, nontuberculous mycobacteria in the lung, and BK virus encephalitis. Opportunistic infections were more common in Asia and Latin America, in older patients, and with the 10 mg dosage.

The overall mortality rate of tofacitinib, malignancy risk, and lymphoma incidence in the phase II, III, and LTE studies was consistent with the published rates in RA clinical trials for TNF inhibitors and other bDMARDs (Box 65.1). Lymphomas reported were predominantly non-Hodgkin's B cell lymphomas.

Twenty-two GI perforations occurred in the development program on tofacitinib, and none in the placebo. These events occurred in patients on background corticosteroids and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). The incidence rate reported at the time of approval was 0.11/100 pt yrs, similar to what had been reported with TNF and IL-6 inhibitors. Use of this

therapy in patients with diverticulitis should probably be avoided, similar to the present standard of care with IL-6 inhibitors.

### Baricitinib

The baricitinib-integrated safety summary provided safety information on 3770 RA patients with 14,744 pt yrs of follow up with median duration of exposure 4.3 years. Serious infectious episodes were reported in 2.6 per 100 pt yrs, and the incidence rate for herpes zoster was 3.0 per 100 pt yrs. The incidence rate for these AEs were stable over the 3 years of follow-up. The most common serious infectious episodes were pneumonia, urinary tract infections, herpes zoster, cellulitis, and sepsis. Ninety-four percent of herpes zoster were nonserious and the incidence rate was greater in Asia as seen with tofacitinib.

The incidence rate of TB was 0.1 per 100 pt yrs and GI perforations was 0.06 per 100 pt yrs. MACE was seen in 0.5 per 100 pt yrs and malignancy in 0.9 per 100 pt yrs, with six patients developing lymphoma. Numerically for these AEs, incidence rates were higher for the 4 mg dose compared with the 2 mg dose, although confidence intervals overlapped.

During the placebo-controlled portion of the clinical trial program, an imbalance in the incidence rates of venous thromboembolism (VTE) and pulmonary embolism (PE) was seen: 4 mg baricitinib 1.7% (five events), 2 mg baricitinib 0% (zero events), and placebo 0% (zero events). No difference in arterial thrombotic events was reported. In the development program overall, the infection rate for venous thromboembolism was 0.5/100 pt yrs, similar to that reported in claims-based databases. Although deep vein thrombosis and PE have been reported in the development programs for the other JAK inhibitors, no imbalance in comparison to placebo-treated patients has been reported.

### Upadacitinib

Upadacitinib has reported safety data from the integrated safety analysis of the phase III trials in RA at both the 15 mg and 30 mg doses. A total of 3834 patients received one or more doses of upadacitinib 15 mg (n = 2630) or 30 mg (n = 1204), for a total of 4020.1 pt yrs of exposure. Upper respiratory tract infection, nasopharyngitis, and urinary tract infection were the most commonly reported AEs. Adverse events were reported as event rates. For the 15 mg approved dose, SIEs were reported in 3.8 per 100 pt yrs; opportunistic infections, 0.6 per 100 pt yrs; herpes zoster, 3.7 per 100 pt yrs; active/latent TB, 2.2 per 100 pt yrs; malignancies, 0.9 per 100 pt yrs; MACE, 0.6 per 100 pt yrs; VTE, 0.6 per 100 pt yrs; GI perforations, 0.2 per 100 pt yrs; hepatic disorders, 14.4 per 100 pt yrs; and creatine phosphokinase (CPK) elevation, 6.1/100 pt yrs. Rates of serious infection were similar between upadacitinib 15 mg and adalimumab but higher compared with methotrexate. Rates of herpes zoster and CPK elevations were higher in both upadacitinib groups versus methotrexate and adalimumab, as were rates of GI perforations. SIEs, opportunistic infections, herpes zoster, nonmelanoma skin cancer, and CPK elevations were reported more commonly with the 30 mg upadacitinib dose and approval in RA for this dose was not pursued. Upadacitinib has been approved for ulcerative colitis patients at the 30 mg dose.

### Filgotinib

The safety of filgotinib was evaluated in the clinical trials resulting in approval in RA patients in the European Union and Japan. A total of 3691 RA patients received filgotinib for 6080.7 pt yrs (median 1.6, maximum 5.6 years). Exposure adjusted incidence rates (EAIRs) for serious infection were 3.9, 3.3, and

2.4/100 pt yrs for filgotinib 200 mg, filgotinib 100 mg, and placebo; EAIRs for herpes zoster were 0.6, 1.1, and 1.1/100 pt yrs for filgotinib 200 mg, filgotinib 100 mg, and placebo. EAIRs for major adverse cardiovascular events were 0, 1.7 and 1.1/100 pt yrs for filgotinib 200 mg, filgotinib 100 mg, and placebo. EAIRs for deaths were 0.6/100 pt yrs for filgotinib 200 mg, filgotinib 100 mg, and placebo. No VTE occurred during the placebo-controlled period; long-term EAIRs were 0.2 and 0/100 pt yrs for filgotinib 200 mg and filgotinib 100 mg. Overall safety issues were similar for filgotinib compared with the other approved JAK inhibitors, although the reported rate of herpes zoster was lower than with other JAK inhibitors.

### Oral Surveillance Clinical Trial

The Oral Surveillance was an FDA-mandated post-approval study to evaluate the safety of the 5 and 10 mg bid doses of tofacitinib due to concerns of the long-term extension protocols from the development program, suggesting a dose-related increase in lung cancer and SIEs with the 10 mg dose. The trial was an open-label randomized study with a median follow-up of 4 years, involving 4362 RA patients who were taking methotrexate, were at least 50 years old, and had at least one risk factor for heart disease. The two doses of tofacitinib were compared with etanercept or adalimumab plus methotrexate. This was an event-driven trial with two primary endpoints—the incidence rates of malignancy and MACE—and the trial was a noninferiority study. Noninferiority of tofacitinib regimens to the TNF inhibitor control regimen was concluded if the upper confidence limits for both malignancy (Total Time Analysis) and MACE (On-Treatment Time Analysis) for the combined tofacitinib were less than 1.8. The results demonstrated a trend toward an increase in MACE with the combined tofacitinib cohorts (0.98 vs. 0.73 events per 100 pt yrs, HR 1.33, 95% CI 0.911.94), so noninferiority was not achieved. Similar findings were reported for the incidence rate of malignancy for both doses of tofacitinib 1.13 per 100 pt yrs compared with 0.77 per 100 pt yrs with HR of 1.48 (95% CI 1.042.09), with failure to achieve noninferiority (Fig. 65.4).

During the study, a statistically significant increase in rate of PE with the tofacitinib 10 mg dose was observed, with a trend for the 5 mg dose that was not statistically different from the TNF inhibitors. A numerical increase in deep venous thrombosis was also observed that did not achieve statistical difference. All-cause mortality and serious infectious episodes were increased with tofacitinib 10 mg bid compared with the TNF inhibitors. Based on these results, 5 years into the study patients on 10 mg were switched to 5 mg bid while the study continued for an additional 18 months, although AEs post-transition in dose continued to be attributed to the 10 mg dose for those patients.

Based on this study, the FDA in 2021 and, in October 2022 after additional review of data were available, the EMA PRAC recommended limiting the use of JAK inhibitors in IMID patients over 65 years of age, patients who are current or past smokers, patients with other cardiovascular risk factors, and patients with other malignancy risk factors to those who had failed TNF inhibitors or no other suitable alternative was available in patients.106, Initially in 2021 the EMA recommended against specific use of tofacitinib in this patient cohort unless no suitable treatment alternative was available but did not include the other JAKs. However, in 2022 the EMA expanded their recommendation to include all JAK inhibitors. The EMA PRAC also recommended using JAK inhibitors with caution in patients with risk factors for blood clots in the lungs and deep

veins (VTE). Furthermore, the doses should be reduced in some patient groups who may be at risk of VTE, cancer, or major cardiovascular problems. The FDA has added black box warnings for all JAK inhibitors about increased VTE/PE risk with JAK inhibitors. Studies in this high-risk population have not been conducted with upadacitinib, filgotinib, or peficitinib. A recent study using international observational registries and claimsbased data reported an increased risk of VTE with baricitinib compared with TNF inhibitor use in RA patients. A study from the Swedish Quality Registry evaluated the risk of VTE in patients on JAK inhibitors primarily baricitinib, compared with bDMARDs and reported an increased risk of VTE with the JAK inhibitors compared with patients initiating bDMARDs. In these real-world analyses, patients on JAK inhibitors were older, failed more therapies, and had greater comorbidities, which would increase VTE risk. An FDA-mandated phase IV clinical trial similar to the Oral Surveillance trial is ongoing, evaluating risk of VTE with baricitinib.

A post-marketing clinical trial called the Select Choice study compared upadacitinib to abatacept in combination with methotrexate in RA patients who had failed previous biologics over 24 weeks. More serious AEs were reported for upadacitinib (6.1%) compared with abatacept (3.1%), and more withdrawals due to AEs were reported for upadacitinib (4.6%) compared with abatacept (2.9%). Although rare, more serious infectious episodes (UPA 1.0%/ABA 0.3%) and opportunistic infections (1.3% UPA/0.3% ABA) were seen with upadacitinib, but no difference was reported for herpes zoster. Hepatic disorders, primarily liver function abnormalities, were observed with upadacitinib (UPA 7.6%/ABA 1.6%). One MACE and two VTEs were observed with upadacitinib, and none were observed on placebo.

### Laboratory

Based on their mechanism of action, certain laboratory abnormalities were expected (see Box 65.2). JAK1 facilitates signaling for IL-6, which results in neutrophil homeostasis. IL-6 inhibitors have been associated with reduction in neutrophil counts, and this is felt to be part of their mechanism of action in RA, so it would be expected that inhibiting JAK1, which facilitates signal transduction for IL-6, would be associated with a reduction in neutrophil counts. A modest reduction in neutrophil counts has been seen with all the JAK inhibitors, with rare grade 3/4 neutropenia noted. The reduction in neutrophil counts were infrequently associated with AEs and not associated with increased infection risk. JAK3 plays an integral role in lymphocyte survival/maturation and all of the JAK inhibitors have been associated with lowered lymphocyte counts with rare grade 4 lymphopenia. Monitoring complete blood cell and total lymphocyte counts on a regular basis is recommended by the regulatory agencies, as would be done for routine care. A boxed warning in the package inserts for both tofacitinib and baricitinib for lymphopenia and discontinuation of treatment is recommended for patients with persistent lymphocyte counts <500/μL due to increased risk of infection noted in the tofacitinib clinical trials. Upadacitinib and filgotinib have also rarely been associated with lymphopenia and neutropenia.

JAK2 facilitates signal transduction for erythropoietin and significant concern over the safety of JAK2 inhibitors was suggested in pre-clinical research. Concern over significant anemia was raised based on pre-clinical investigation, but clinically this has been unusual. Baricitinib blocks JAK2 greater than the other JAK inhibitors in enzymatic and biochemical assays, but significant anemia has been rare with any of the JAK inhibitors.

### BOX65.2 JAK Inhibitors: Laboratory Changes Observed

Liver function test abnormalities: More prevalent with combination therapy

Lipid: Increased highand low-density lipoprotein cholesterol; ratio generally unchanged

Hemoglobin: Reduced if JAK2 inhibited; rarely clinically significant

Neutrophils: Reduced; rarely <1000/mm3; presumed part of mechanism of action

Lymphocytes: Reduced; rarely <500/mm3; dose reduction or discontinuation indicated due to increased risk of SlEs

CPK: nonsignificant elevations

Serum creatinine: Small nonsignificant elevations seen

IL-6 plays a homeostatic role for hepatocytes and JAK1 inhibition reduces IL-6 signaling. Compared with placebo in the clinical trials, all of the JAK inhibitors have been associated with transaminase elevations. Liver function abnormalities have been more common when the JAK inhibitors were used in combination with methotrexate. No cases fulfilling Hy's Law were reported in the clinical trials and liver function abnormalities resolved with dose reduction or discontinuation. Monitoring of liver function tests every 4 to 6 weeks for the first 3 months, then every 3 months, is recommended for patients on JAK inhibitors.

Elevations in serum lipids have been seen in patients receiving biologic therapies, with the most significant increases seen with IL-6 inhibitors. Elevations in total cholesterol, high-density lipoprotein (HDL), and low-density lipoprotein (LDL) have been reported with all the JAK inhibitors in ~30% of patients. Generally, the elevations were in the range of 15% to 20%. Elevations have been noted by 12 weeks and are generally stable thereafter. In general, the mean HDL/LDL ratio remains unchanged. An association of MACE with lipid changes was not observed in the clinical trials. Atorvastatin treatment has been demonstrated to be effective in patients with elevations in cholesterol on tofacitinib. Monitoring of serum lipids is recommended 8 to 12 weeks after initiating therapy.

Small, clinically insignificant increases in serum creatinine and increased creatinine kinase were noted with all the JAK inhibitors and have not been associated with significant safety risks. Creatinine increases were in the 0.02 and 0.04 mg/dL range greater than placebo in the development program. The etiology of this minor change is unclear.

### JAK Inhibitors for Other Rheumatic Diseases −

### Psoriatic Arthritis

Tofacitinib was approved for use in the United States for treatment of psoriatic arthritis (PsA) in 2017. This was based largely on the data from two phase III studies, the Oral Psoriatic Arthritis trial (OPAL) Broaden, which assessed tofacitinib versus adalimumab versus placebo in patients with PsA who had previously failed csDMARDs, and the OPAL Beyond trial, which was a study of tofacitinib versus placebo in patients who previously failed TNF inhibitors. 118,

The OPAL Broaden trial enrolled 422 patients who had an inadequate response to at least one csDMARD and who were TNF naive. This was a 12-month, double-blind, active-controlled and placebo-controlled trial, which compared tofacitinib at 5 mg

or 10 mg twice-daily doses to adalimumab 40 mg every 2 weeks, or to placebo with a blinded switch at 3 months to either tofacitinib 5 mg or 10 mg. ACR20 response rates at month 3 were 50% in the 5 mg tofacitinib group and 61% in the 10 mg group, compared with 33% in the placebo group (p = 0.01 for the comparison of the 5 mg dose with placebo and p < 0.001 for the 10 mg dose). ACR20 was 52% in the adalimumab group. The active treatment arms also improved significantly in physical function compared with placebo. Researchers observed greater benefit with tofacitinib versus placebo by week 2 (ACR20 of 22% for the 5 mg group and 32% for the 10 mg group vs. 6% for patients receiving placebo). Minimal disease activity (MDA) at week 12 was observed in 26% of patients on tofacitinib (at 5 and 10 mg doses) and 25% of adalimumab patients, compared with only 7% on placebo.

Seventy-four percent of the patients had psoriasis affecting at least 3% of their body surface area and had Psoriasis Area and Severity Index 75 (PASI75) response assessed. Both 5 and 10 mg tofacitinib PASI75 response rates were statistically superior to placebo and similar to adalimumab at week 12. The improvement in the PASI75 persisted at 12 months. Sixty-six percent of the patients had enthesitis, and statistically significant improvement (determined by change in the Leeds Enthesitis index at week 12) was observed for the 10 mg dose but not for the 5 mg dose. Similar improvements in dactylitis were also seen, and improvements in enthesitis and dactylitis were maintained at 1 year.

Over a 12-month period, there were similar rates of SAEs with the tofacitinib 5 mg and 10 mg and with the adalimumab groups. The SAEs were similar to those reported in studies of tofacitinib in RA, including four cases of herpes zoster in patients who received tofacitinib continuously, versus none of the patients who received placebo or adalimumab. The most common AEs were nasopharyngitis, upper respiratory infection, and headache.

The OPAL Beyond trial was a phase III trial that enrolled 395 patients with a prior inadequate response to at least one TNF inhibitor. Patients had previously failed a mean 1.5 TNF inhibitors and 8% had received other biologics. This was a 6-month randomized, double-blind trial in which patients were assigned to treatment with tofacitinib (5 mg or 10 mg twice daily) or placebo with a switch at 3 months to either 5 mg or 10 mg of tofacitinib. At week 12, the rates of ACR20 response were 50% with the 5 mg tofacitinib dose and 47% with the 10 mg dose, compared with 24% with placebo (p < 0.001 for both). The mean changes from baseline in the HAQ and Disability Index score were -0.39 and -0.35 compared with -0.14 (p < 0.001 for both comparisons). As in the OPAL Broaden trial, ACR20 response was noted to be superior, as early as week 2 of the study, in patients receiving tofacitinib 5 mg or 10 mg versus placebo. Both tofacitinib doses were superior to placebo at 12 weeks for ACR50 but not ACR70 response rates. Statistically superior improvement in PASI75 was observed for the 10 mg dose but not the 5 mg dose. Similar improvements in enthesitis and dactylitis for the 5 and 10 mg doses were numerically greater than placebo but, due to hierarchical statistical testing, significance was not assessed.

SAEs over the 6-month trial period occurred at similar rates as in other tofacitinib trials (4% in patients who received 5 mg tofacitinib continuously and 6% in patients who received 10 mg continuously). Three cases of herpes zoster were reported in tofacitinib-treated patients. Numerically, more AEs and study discontinuations were reported for the 10 mg dose (8%) compared with the 5 mg dose (3%) and the placebo-treated patients (3%).

A third phase III trial, OPAL Balance, was a long-term openlabel extension study to evaluate the safety, tolerability, and efficacy

of tofacitinib in subjects who had previously participated in randomized studies of tofacitinib for PsA. In this study, long-term safety up to 48 months and long-term efficacy up to 36 months were found to be consistent with the previous phase III trials. A total of 686 patients were enrolled and 453 completed the longterm extension study or a substudy, which was a methotrexate withdrawal study. Efficacy of tofacitinib was sustained to month 36. SAEs were reported in 115 participants (17%), with the incidence of SAEs being 6 to 9 patients with events (95% CI 78.4) per 100 person-years. The incidence of specific AEs (in number of patients with events per 100 person-years) included 1.7 for herpes zoster, 1.0 for serious infections, 0.7 for malignancies (excluding nonmelanoma skin cancer), 0.2 for major adverse cardiac events, 0.1 for PE, and 0.4 for arterial thromboembolism.

Baricitinib has been studied in moderate to severe plaque psoriasis. A total of 271 patients were randomized to a 24-week doseranging study evaluating 2, 4, 8, and 10 mg daily. Statistically significant improvements in the PASI75 at week 12 were only seen for the 8 and 10 mg doses compared with placebo and baricitinib is not approved for the treatment of psoriasis. Baricitinib has not been evaluated in PsA. Peficitinib was evaluated in a phase II trial in psoriasis but has not been evaluated in PsA.

Upadacitinib was approved for PsA in December 2021, based on the results of two phase III clinical trials. The first study compared upadacitinib and adalimumab in biologic-naive patients with PsA123; 1704 patients were enrolled and randomized into one of four arms: upadacitinib 15 mg or 30 mg, placebo, or adalimumab. Both upadacitinib doses were noninferior to adalimumab for the primary endpoint, which was ACR20 response at week 12, and the 30 mg dose was superior. In addition, the percentage of patients with a PASI75 response was higher in the upadacitinib arms (62.6% and 62.4% in the upadacitinib 15 mg and 30 mg, respectively) versus adalimumab (53.1%) and placebo (21.3%). Similar impact on enthesopathy and dactylitis was seen.

A second study in biologic-refractory PsA patients compared upadacitinib 15 mg and 30 mg to placebo. Significantly more upadacitinib patients achieved the primary endpoint of ACR20, as well as minimal disease activity (MDA) at week 24, with MDA achieved by 25.1% of 15 mg patients and 28.9% of 30 mg patients, versus 2.8% of placebo (p < 0.001). Significant improvements in enthesitis, dactylitis, and fatigue were also seen.

Safety data from these two phase III trials was pooled for an integrated analysis of 2504.6 person years of exposure to upadacitinib and 549.7 person years of exposure to adalimumab. Rates of malignancies, adjudicated major adverse cardiovascular events, VTE events, and deaths were similar across treatment groups. However, rates of herpes zoster and opportunistic infections were higher with upadacitinib.

Tofacitinib was not approved by the FDA for the treatment of plaque psoriasis due to concerns about clinical efficacy and longterm safety for this indication. Upadacitinib has not been studied in psoriasis.

Early studies showed promising results for filgotinib in PsA, but the development program for this indication was terminated in 2020 after the FDA expressed concerns about the benefit—risk profile of filgotinib in RA.

Deucravacitinib is a TYK2 inhibitor that received FDA approval in 2022 for moderate to severe plaque psoriasis.23, The recommended dose is 6 mg daily. Deucravacitinib binds to the regulatory domain of TYK2, stabilizing an inhibitory interaction between the regulatory and the catalytic domains of the enzyme. This results in allosteric inhibition of receptor-mediated

activation of TYK2 and its downstream activation of STATs, as shown in cell-based assays. This mechanism is different from the other approved JAK inhibitors, which block the ATP binding site. TYK2 facilitates signal transduction for IL12/23 and type 1 interferons (Fig. 65.5).

In psoriasis, efficacy was seen compared with placebo as well as apremilast 30 mg bid. In the placebo-controlled trials, PASI75 was 53 to 58% at week 16 compared with placebo-treated patients (9%13%). PASI75 at week 16 for apremilast was 40%.

Overall safety was similar to other JAK inhibitors, with a numerical increase in herpes simplex and herpes zoster as would be expected with a type 1 interferon inhibitor. Periodic monitoring of liver function tests, CPK, and triglycerides is recommended based on the results of the clinical trials. A black box warning was not added as with other JAK inhibitors, but a statement on the risk for MACE/malignancy/VTE with other JAK inhibitors is included in the package insert.

Deucravacitinib 6 mg daily is in phase III trials for PsA in biologic-inexperienced and -experienced patients. 127, A doubleblind, phase II trial of 203 patients with PsA evaluated deucravacitinib 6 mg or 12 mg once a day or randomized 1:1:1 to placebo. The primary endpoint was ACR20 response at week 16.129 ACR20 response was significantly higher with deucravacitinib 6 mg once a day (52.9%, p = 0.0134) and 12 mg once a day (62.7%, p = 0.0004) versus placebo (31.8%) at week 16. PASI75 was achieved by 59.6% on 12 mg daily, 42.4% on 6 mg daily, and 20.4% on placebo. Safety issues were similar to other JAK inhibitors, with a numerical increase in overall infections for the higher 12 mg daily.

### Ankylosing Spondylitis

Tofacitinib was approved in the United States for treatment of ankylosing spondylitis (AS) in patients with inadequate response to or intolerance of TNF inhibitors in December 2021, based primarily on a phase III study in 269 patients who were randomized to tofacitinib 5 mg twice daily or placebo for 16 weeks. From week 17 to 48, all patients received open-label tofacitinib. The study population was approximately 80% bDMARD-naive and about 20% had prior exposure to bDMARDs, including up to two TNF inhibitors. The primary endpoint was Assessment in SpondyloArthritis International Society (ASAS) 20 at week 16, which was met by 56.4% of the tofacitinib group versus 12.5% of the placebo group (p < 0.0001). Improvement in the tofacitinib group was seen as early as 2 to 4 weeks, and the treatment response was sustained at 48 weeks. AEs were seen more frequently in the tofacitinib group, including 2.3% with adjudicated hepatic events, 2.3% with nonserious herpes zoster, and 0.8% with a serious infection. The safety profile was consistent with the established safety profile of tofacitinib 5 mg twice daily in the established clinical programs.

Prior to the phase III study, a phase II randomized, doubleblind, placebo-controlled, dose-ranging study of tofacitinib in patients with AS of 207 biologic-naive participants showed similar efficacy. A follow-up, post hoc analysis of this study assessed improvement in magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) findings of inflammation. Patients with available radiographic data for MRI of the sacroiliac (SI) joints and spine were assessed for minimally important changes (MIC) of the Spondyloarthritis Research Consortium of Canada MRI scores. A greater proportion of patients achieved MIC with tofacitinib 2, 5, and 10 mg twice a day versus placebo for SI joint and spine scores. In addition, a greater proportion of patients receiving tofacitinib versus placebo, who achieved

MIC for SI joint and spine scores, also achieved ASAS20 versus patients who did not achieve MIC, which indicates a correlation of radiographic response with clinical responses.

by ASAS. Efficacy was similar in patients who switched from placebo to upadacitinib versus patients who received continuous upadacitinib.

Upadacitinib was also assessed in a patient population of bDMARD nonresponders who had active AS with inadequate response to one or two of either TNF inhibitors or IL-17 inhibitors. In this phase III trial, 420 patients were randomized to upadacitinib or placebo, with significantly more patients in the treatment arm achieving the primary endpoint of ASAS40 at week 14 (45% vs. 18%, p < 0.0001). .

Upadacitinib has also been evaluated in patients with nraxSpA. In this phase III study, 314 biologic-naive patients were enrolled with active nr-axSpA based on objective signs of inflammation seen on MRI of the SI joints, or with elevated C-reactive protein (CRP) and an inadequate response to NSAIDs. A significantly higher proportion of the upadacitinib patients met the primary endpoint of ASAS40 at week 14 (45% vs. 23%, p < 0.0001). In these studies, AEs with upadacitinib in AS were consistent with prior studies in the clinical development program, and no new safety signals were reported.

Filgotinib has been studied in bDMARD-naive AS patients in a phase II trial. A total of 263 patients were enrolled and randomized to filgotinib or placebo, and significantly more patients in the treatment arm met the primary endpoint of change from baseline in ASDAS at week 12. Two phase III trials of filgotinib in AS were underway, but in November 2020 the filgotinib development program was halted in response to FDA concerns about possible AEs on sperm concentration.

### Systemic Lupus Erythematosus

### Pre-clinical Studies

Tofacitinib. Pre-clinical data suggest that tofacitinib may be of benefit in SLE. One study of experimental lupus nephritis assessed the efficacy of tofacitinib in NZB/NZWF1 mice, a murine model for lupus nephritis. Animals treated with tofacitinib showed significantly reduced proteinuria and improved renal function and histologic lesions of the kidney, including diminished C3 and immunoglobulin G (IgG) deposition in glomeruli.

In another pre-clinical study, NZB/NZWF1 mice were treated with tofacitinib and found to have reduced levels of anti-doublestranded DNA (dsDNA) antibodies, decreased proteinuria, and amelioration of nephritis compared with control animals. A third study found that in MLR/lpr lupus-prone mice, treatment with tofacitinib led to improvement in measures of disease activity, including nephritis, skin inflammation, and autoantibody production. The researchers observed that tofacitinib modulated factors associated with premature vascular damage in SLE, including endothelium-dependent vasorelaxation and endothelial differentiation.

There is one published phase I study of tofacitinib in SLE.142, This was a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study primarily designed to assess safety and tolerability in this patient population. Thirty subjects were randomized to tofacitinib 5 mg twice daily or placebo in a 2:1 ratio, and no new safety signals were noted. The secondary endpoints included mechanistic studies assessing cardiometabolic and immunologic parameters felt to be associated with premature atherosclerosis in SLE. Tofacitinib was shown to improve a number of these parameters, including HDL cholesterol levels and arterial stiffness. There are two small open-label studies currently enrolling patients with SLE and cutaneous lupus, and a third small open-label study in discoid lupus with or without SLE was terminated. 144,

Baricitinib. A report of a 24-week phase II, double-blind, placebo-controlled study of baricitinib demonstrated efficacy in patients with SLE receiving standard therapy. 46Participants were randomly assigned to receive either placebo or baricitinib 2 mg or 4 mg once daily along with continuation of background therapy, which is standard for lupus clinical trials. The primary endpoint was resolution of arthritis or rash, measured by the SLE Disease Activity Index (SLEDAI-2K) at 24 weeks. Of the 314 participants who were randomly assigned to treatment, 79, 82, and 83% completed 24 weeks of treatment with placebo, baricitinib 2 mg, and baricitinib 4 mg, respectively.

A significantly greater percentage of patients in the baricitinib 4 mg group compared with placebo achieved resolution of SLE- DAI-2K arthritis or rash (67% vs. 53%; p < 0.05) and had a SLE Responder Index-4 response (64% vs. 48%; p < 0.05) at 24 weeks compared with placebo. In addition, the percentage of patients achieving flare reduction, lupus LDAS, and tender joint count change from baseline were also more improved in the baricitinib 4 mg group compared with placebo.

SAEs were reported in 10 (10%) patients receiving baricitinib 4 mg, 11 (10%) receiving baricitinib 2 mg, and 5 (5%) receiving placebo; no deaths were reported. Serious infections were reported in six (6%) patients with baricitinib 4 mg, two (2%) with baricitinib 2 mg, and one (1%) with placebo.

The investigators concluded that the baricitinib 4 mg dose, but not the 2 mg dose, significantly improved the signs and symptoms of SLE. Based on these results, phase III studies of baricitinib in SLE were designed to assess response to baricitinib high dose, baricitinib low dose, or placebo. However, two phase III studies of baricitinib in SLE were terminated due to insufficient evidence to support a positive benefit—risk ratio.147, Reportedly, AEs in the study were consistent with previously published studies with baricitinib. Based on these results the pharmaceutical company decided not to pursue approval in SLE.

Upadacitinib. There are two studies assessing upadacitinib in SLE. The first is a phase II study to assess the safety and efficacy of upadacitinib and elsubrutinib, a BTK inhibitor, either alone or in combination. This study has completed enrollment, but results are not yet published. The second study is a long-term extension in patients who have completed the initial phase II trial; this study is currently enrolling.

Deucravacitinib. Deucravacitinib was evaluated in a 48-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase II trial. Eligible patients met the Systemic Lupus International Collaborating Clinics criteria, were seropositive (ANA/anti-dsDNA/anti- Smith), and had a SLEDAI-2K score ≥ 6 and ≥1 BILAG index A or >2 BILAG B manifestations from the musculoskeletal or mucocutaneous domain. Patients on standard background medications were randomized 1:1:1:1 to placebo or deucravacitinib (3 mg bid, 6 mg bid, or 12 mg once daily). Oral corticosteroid tapering to 7.5 mg/day was required from weeks 8 to 20; further tapering was optional from weeks 32 to 40. The primary endpoint was the proportion of patients achieving SLE responder index (SRI[4]) at week 32. A total of 363 patients were randomized, with baseline demographic and disease characteristics similar across treatment groups. Of randomized patients, 275 (76%) completed 48 weeks of treatment. The primary endpoint at week 32 was met, with significantly greater proportion of patients in deucravacitinib 3 mg bid and 6 mg bid groups versus placebo achieving SRI(4) responses (placebo: 34.4%; deucravacitinib 3 mg bid: 58.2%, p = 0.0006; deucravacitinib 6 mg bid: 49.5%, P = 0.021; deucravacitinib 12 mg once daily: 44.9%, p = 0.078). SRI(4) response was sustained across all deucravacitinib groups up to 48 weeks. At week 48, the deucravacitinib 3 mg bid group demonstrated statistical significance in the British Isles Lupus Assessment Group— Based Combined Lupus Assessment (BICLA), the Lupus Low Disease Activity State, the Cutaneous Lupus Erythematosus Disease Area and Severity Index, and active joint count, and the two other deucravacitinib groups demonstrated clinically meaningful differences versus placebo. Rates of AEs, serious AEs, and AEs of interest were similar between deucravacitinib and placebo groups.

Pharmacodynamic studies in a subset of patients demonstrated significant reduction in type 1 interferon at 2 weeks through week 48 and for gamma interferon from week 12 to week 48.152

### Juvenile Inflammatory Arthritis

Tofacitinib was approved for polyarticular juvenile inflammatory arthritis (JIA) in 2020. Approval was based on a clinical trial of JIA patients with active disease despite methotrexate or biologic therapy. A total of 225 patients received tofacitinib for 18

weeks based on weight (3.2 mg twice daily for body weight 10 kg to <20 kg, 4 mg twice daily for body weight 20 kg to <40 kg, and 5 mg twice daily for body weight ≥40 kg). At the end of this run-in phase, 142 patients with at least a 30% improvement in the ACR JIA response criteria (ACR30) were randomly assigned to tofacitinib or placebo and followed for an additional 24 weeks. The primary endpoint was the JIA flare rate by week 44 in Part 2 of the study in patients with polyarticular-course JIA. Flare was defined per Pediatric Rheumatology Collaborative Study Group and Paediatric Rheumatology International Trials Organisation criteria as a worsening of 30% or more in three or more variables, with one or none of the variables improving by 30% or more. Flare rate by week 44 was significantly lower with tofacitinib (21 [29%] of 72 patients) than with placebo (37 [53%] of 70 patients; HR 0.46, 95% CI 0.270.79; p = 0.0031). In Part 2 of the study, AEs occurred in 68 (77%) of 88 patients receiving tofacitinib and 63 (74%) of 85 in the placebo group. SAEs occurred in one (1%) receiving tofacitinib and two (2%) given placebo.

Baricitinib has been evaluated in clinical trials with similar design, and results have not been published. Data is available on FDA Clinicaltrials.gov reporting superiority for baricitinib 2 and 4 mg compared with placebo. Upadacitinib is in clinical trials for polyarticular JIA.

### Other Rheumatic c Diseases

Efficacy of tofacitinib was reported in a small placebo-controlled trial in progressive systemic sclerosis. Fifteen patients with early scleroderma were randomized to tofacitinib 5 mg bid or placebo. The primary endpoint was safety and tolerability through 24 weeks. Tofacitinib was well tolerated; no participants experienced grade 3 or higher AEs before or at week 24. Trends in efficacy outcome measures favored tofacitinib. Baseline gene expression in fibroblast and keratinocyte subpopulations indicated IFN-activated gene expression. Tofacitinib inhibited IFN-regulated gene expression in SFRP2/DPP4 fibroblasts (progenitors of myofibroblasts) and in MYOC/CCL19, representing adventitial fibroblasts (p < 0.05), as well as in the basal and keratinized layers of the epidermis. Gene expression in macrophages and dendritic cells indicated inhibition of STAT3 by tofacitinib (p < 0.05).

There have been a few reports of tofacitinib's benefit in refractory dermatomyositis, with greatest benefit reported for the cutaneous manifestations.157, A small open-label trial in 10 patients with refractory dermatomyositis receiving 11 mg XR tofacitinib were evaluated. The primary outcome measure was assessment of disease activity improvement based on the International Myositis Assessment and Clinical Studies group definition of improvement. At 12 weeks, the primary outcome was met in all the 10 subjects. Five (50%) of 10 subjects experienced moderate improvement in disease activity, and the other 50% experienced minimal improvement according to the 2016 ACR/European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology myositis response criteria. The secondary outcome of the mean change in the Cutaneous Dermatomyositis Disease Area and Severity Index activity score over 12 weeks was statistically significant (mean ± SD 28 ± 15.4 at baseline vs. 9.5 ± 8.5 at 12 weeks) (p = 0.0005). The mean ± SD level of creatine kinase in the 10 subjects at baseline was 82 ± 34.8 IU/liter, highlighting that disease activity was predominantly located in the skin.

A clinical trial evaluating the JAK1/Tyk2 inhibitor brepocitinib is being conducted in refractory dermatomyositis patients.

Brepocitinib inhibits type 1 interferon signaling, which is involved in the pathogenesis of dermatomyositis.

### Bruton's Tyrosine Kinase Inhibitors

Oral BTK inhibitors (ibrutinib) have been approved for treatment of patients with mantle cell lymphoma, Waldenstrom's macroglobulinemia, and chronic lymphocytic leukemia who have received at least one previous therapy. BTK inhibitors have been evaluated as potential treatments for RA, SLE, and Sjogren's syndrome. BTK plays a prominent role in BCR signal transduction and also has a role in Toll-like receptor and FcR signaling in myeloid cells. BTK is a member of the Tec family of cytoplasmic PTKs. In humans, mutations in BTK can result in the development of Bruton's agammaglobulinemia (known also as X-linked agammaglobulinemia), an immunodeficiency characterized by a defect in B cell development and resulting in a significant absence of circulating B cells. Upon ligand binding to the BCR, BTK is activated by upstream SRC-family kinases LYN, FYN, and SYK (Fig. 65.4). Activated BTK drives phosphorylation of PLCy and subsequent PKC activation, which in turn results in calcium flux and the activation of transcription factors, including NF-κB and NFAT, regulating the expression of downstream genes controlling proliferation, survival, and chemokines and cytokines (Fig. 65.6). B cells play multiple roles in the pathogenesis of RA and SLE, including antigen presentation, inflammatory cytokine production and rheumatoid factor, and cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody production. Rituximab, which depletes B cells, has demonstrated efficacy as treatment for patients with RA, and belimumab for SLE supports efforts to develop a small-molecule BTK inhibitor that impacts B cell activation. 163,

Animal models of arthritis suggest that BTK inhibition can result in blockage of B cell receptor-dependent cell proliferation and a reduction of inflammatory cytokine production from myeloid cells (including TNF, IL-1, and IL-6) by preventing signaling through the FCγRIII receptor. 165, Additionally, activated BTK has been demonstrated to be increased in peripheral blood B cells of patients with RA compared with controls. An in vitro study demonstrated that BTK inhibition decreased monocyte differentiation into M1 macrophages, which are inflammatory and skewed differentiation more to the M2 phenotype, which are anti-inflammatory. The BTK inhibitors fenebrutinib and evobrutinib were evaluated in two phase II clinical trials in RA and SLE. Pre-clinical models have demonstrated significant target engagement for these BTK inhibitors, with limited impact on other kinases. Fenebrutinib is a noncovalent BTK inhibitor and was evaluated in a phase II dose-ranging study in RA patients with active disease despite methotrexate. In the RA study, two cohorts were evaluated, with 480 patients receiving fenebrutinib (50 mg once daily, 150 mg once daily, 200 mg twice daily), 40 mg adalimumab every other week, or placebo and 98 patients with inadequate response to TNF inhibitors receiving fenebrutinib (200 mg twice daily) or placebo. Both cohorts continued methotrexate therapy. The ACR50 at week 12 was the primary endpoint. In cohort 1, ACR50 response at week 12 was similar for fenebrutinib 50 mg once daily and placebo and higher for fenebrutinib 150 mg once daily (28%) and 200 mg twice daily (35%) than placebo (15%) (p = 0.017; p = 0.0003). Fenebrutinib 200 mg twice daily and adalimumab (36%) were comparable (p = 0.81). In cohort 2, more patients achieved ACR50 with fenebrutinib 200 mg twice daily (25%) than placebo (12%) (p = 0.072). The most common AEs for fenebrutinib included nausea, headache, anemia, and upper respiratory tract infections. Fenebrutinib had significant

effects on myeloid and B cell biomarkers (CCL4 and rheumatoid factor). Fenebrutinib and adalimumab caused overlapping and distinct changes in B cell and myeloid biomarkers.

Fenebrutinib was evaluated in a lupus clinical trial with a negative outcome. A total of 260 patients who had moderate to severe SLE while receiving background standard therapy were randomized to receive placebo, fenebrutinib 150 mg once daily, or fenebrutinib 200 mg twice daily. The primary endpoint was the SLE Responder Index 4 (SRI-4) response at week 48. The SRI-4 response rates at week 48 were 51% for fenebrutinib 150 mg once daily (p = 0.37 vs. placebo), 52% for fenebrutinib 200 mg twice daily (p = 0.34 vs. placebo), and 44% for placebo. BICLA response rates at week 48 were 53% for fenebrutinib 150 mg once daily (p = 0.086 vs. placebo), 42% for fenebrutinib 200 mg twice daily (p = 0.879 vs. placebo), and 41% for placebo. Safety results were similar across all arms, although SAEs were more frequent with fenebrutinib 200 mg twice daily. By week 48, patients treated with fenebrutinib had reduced levels of a BTK-dependent plasmablast RNA signature, anti-dsDNA autoantibodies, total IgG, and IgM and increased complement C4 levels, all relative to placebo. Fenebrutinib has not moved forward in rheumatic diseases but is under evaluation for treatment of multiple sclerosis.

Evobrutinib is a highly selective BTK inhibitor and has been evaluated in RA, SLE, and multiple sclerosis. RA patients with active disease despite methotrexate were enrolled in a phase II clinical trial and were randomized 1:1:1:1 to oral evobrutinib 25 mg once daily, 75 mg once daily, 50 mg bid, or placebo. The primary endpoint was ACR20 response, assessed at week 12 using high-sensitivity CRP (hsCRP). Key secondary endpoints were ACR50 and ACR70 and DAS28-CRP < 3.2 and DAS28-CRP < 2.6. Other secondary endpoints included change from baseline in the Outcomes Measures in Rheumatology Rheumatoid Arthritis Magnetic Resonance Imaging Scoring System (RAMRIS) and the Rheumatoid Arthritis MRI Quantification (RAMRIQ) score for synovitis, osteitis, and erosion for patients in an MRI substudy.

A total of 390 patients were randomized. The primary endpoint of ACR20 response was not met. ACR20 response in the placebo group was 49.5% higher than normally observed in RA clinical trials. Evobrutinib at all doses was nominally significant

versus placebo on DAS28-CRP < 3.2 and DAS28-CRP < 2.6. HsCRP decreased in all evobrutinib arms. No dose response was observed. There were no significant differences in MRI scores between placebo and evobrutinib by either RAMRIS or RAM- RIQ. Evobrutinib was well tolerated at all doses. Minor reversible liver function test elevations were seen.

Evobrutinib was evaluated in SLE. Patients enrolled had a SLEDAI-2K total score ≥6 at screening; were autoantibody-positive; on stable SLE standard-of-care background therapy; and were randomized 1:1:1:1 to evobrutinib 25 mg or 75 mg once daily, 50 mg bid, or placebo. Active or severe central nervous system manifestations were exclusionary. The two primary endpoints were the SRI-4 at week 52 in all patients and the SRI-6 response at week 52 in the subgroup of patients with high disease activity (defined as SLEDAI-2K total score ≥10 at screening). Key secondary endpoints were SRI-4 response in the serologically active subgroup, defined as patients with positive anti-dsDNA antibodies and/or low complement levels at screening, and time to first new severe (BILAG A) flare during treatment. A total of 469 patients were randomized for the study's primary analysis. Age at baseline was 40.7 years ±12.3 (mean ±SD) and 95% were female. Baseline disease characteristics were generally balanced across treatment groups. Neither primary endpoints, SRI-4 response at week 52 or SRI-6 response in patients with high disease activity, were met. There was no clinically meaningful treatment difference for SRI-4 response in the serologically active subpopulation. SAEs were infrequently reported in all groups, 8.5% in placebo versus 9.4% in the evobrutinib groups combined. Infections and infestations were the most common treatment-emergent AE (TEAE), 42.7% for placebo versus 58.0% for evobrutinib groups combined. Overall, there was no dose effect in TEAEs or SAEs. This phase IIb dose-ranging study in SLE showed no treatment effect of evobrutinib versus placebo at any dose and is no longer in development for rheumatic diseases.

Branebrutinib is an oral, highly selective, irreversible covalent inhibitor of BTK that is being evaluated in clinical trials for RA and SLE. Data is not yet available. Remibrutinib is an oral, covalent, and highly specific inhibitor of Bruton's tyrosine kinase. A preliminary report of a clinical trial of remibrutinib in 73 patients with primary Sjogren's syndrome reported benefit.

Remibrutinib resulted in a statistically significant improvement in EULAR Sjögren's Syndrome Disease Activity Index score compared with placebo at week 24 (-2.86, p = 0.003 [two-sided; for both regimens combined]) with numerical improvement over placebo at all time points. No difference from placebo was reported for patient-reported outcomes.

There has been significant interest in a combination of JAK inhibitors with BTK inhibitors due to the impact on different intracellular kinases with potential for greater immune modulation. ABBV-599, a novel, orally administered combination of elsubrutinib 60 mg, a BTK inhibitor, and upadacitinib 15 mg was evaluated in a randomized, double-blind, phase II trial of RA adult patients with previous inadequate response or intolerance to bDMARDs. Patients were randomized 3:2:2:2:2:1 to receive daily ABBV-599; elsubrutinib 60 mg, 20 mg, or 5 mg; upadacitinib 15 mg; or placebo. The primary efficacy endpoint was change from baseline in DAS28- CRP at week 12. Two hundred forty-two patients were randomized to ABBV-599 (n = 62); elsubrutinib 60 mg (n = 41), 20 mg (n = 39), or 5 mg (n = 41); upadacitinib 15 mg (n = 40); and placebo (n = 19). At week 12, ABBV-599 demonstrated significantly greater change from baseline in DAS28-CRP versus placebo (-2.56 vs. -1.12; p < 0.001). ABBV-599 also showed significant improvement versus placebo in ACR50 improvement criteria (p < 0.05), DAS28-CRP score < 2.6 (p < 0.05), and change from baseline in clinical disease activity index score (p < 0.001). ABBV-599 also demonstrated superiority over each dose of elsubrutinib monotherapy (p < 0.001) but not upadacitinib monotherapy. No significant improvements versus placebo were detected with any elsubrutinib monotherapy dose for any efficacy endpoints despite adequate plasma exposure and target engagement. Treatment-emergent AE rates were similar for all treatment groups and placebo, indicating that ABBV-599 was well tolerated. This study failed to demonstrate additional benefit from adding a BTK inhibitor to a JAK inhibitor. A study of this combination is ongoing in SLE.

### MK2 Inhibitors

The p38α mitogen activated protein kinase (MAPK)/MAPK-activated protein kinase 2 (MK2) inflammatory signaling pathway plays a significant role in the expression of multiple cytokines, chemokines, matrix metalloproteases and other inflammatory signals including TNF, IL-1α and β, and IL-6). Although p38 MAPK inhibition failed in previous clinical trials for RA due to limited efficacy and safety signals of dermatitis, central nervous system dysfunction, and transaminitis, there has been a renewed interest in this pathway. Zunsemetinib is an orally available, small-molecule inhibitor that targets the high-affinity docking interaction between p38α MAPK and MK2. Upon binding to the interface created upon formation of this bimolecular complex, zunsemetinib blocks MK2 phosphorylation by p38MAPK, locks MK2 in an inactive conformation, and thereby inhibits the downstream MK2-mediated inflammatory drive. This inhibitor is being studied in RA, PsA, and hidradenitis suppurativa. 177-179 A proof-ofconcept study in 20 RA patients suggested benefit and acceptable safety and larger trials are ongoing in PsA. The phase II study with this compound did not confirm efficacy, although there might have been a very high placebo effect. Based on these results, further development of zunsemetinib was discontinued. Other Mk2 inhibitors are in early clinical trials in RA and axSpA. 181,182

### Sphingosine 1 Phosphate Modulators
