Sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P) is an abundant, biologically active lysophospholipid. In the immune system, changes in local

S1P concentrations and gradients can modify lymphocyte migration patterns, alter inflammatory cell responses, and affect the barrier function of endothelial cells. Interaction of S1P with its receptor results in inhibition of lymphocyte egress from primary and secondary lymphoid tissues, resulting in lymphocyte depletion in the peripheral blood. The major and irreversible route of S1P degradation is via S1P lyase (S1PL). Fingolimod, a sphingosine-1-phosphate receptor modulator, was approved in 2013 for relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis.

Pre-clinical studies demonstrated that reduced S1PL activity has a significant effect in reducing the inflammatory response in models of RA.183, LX3305, a small-molecule inhibitor of S1PL, was evaluated as a DMARD. Results of a placebo-controlled, dose-ranging, phase II randomized controlled trial of LX3305 in patients with RA with active disease despite methotrexate treatment has been reported. In the study, 208 patients received 70 mg, 110 mg, or 150 mg daily or placebo for 12 weeks, and the primary endpoint was ACR20 at week 12. Of patients receiving the 150 mg dose, 60% achieved an ACR20 response compared with 49% on placebo, which was not statistically different. Various subanalyses were conducted, suggesting potential benefits, and no significant safety issues were noted. Based on the results of this proof-of-concept study, development in RA was terminated. Fingolimod, a S1P receptor modulator, is approved for treatment of multiple sclerosis but to date has not moved forward in clinical trials for RA.

### Phosphodiesterase Inhibitors

Inhibition of type 4 phosphodiesterase (PDE) has been demonstrated to inhibit TNF production and other proinflammatory cytokines.187, Cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) is the principal second messenger responsible for immune response regulation. PDE4 is the main cAMP-degrading enzyme found in cells of the immune system and keratinocytes. It is the predominant isoenzyme expressed in macrophages, lymphocytes, and neutrophils. Elevation of intra-cellular cAMP inhibits TNF production through the protein kinase A pathway. Three PDE4 inhibitors have been approved to date for treatment of inflammatory diseases: roflumilast, approved for the treatment of severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and asthma symptoms in the European Union in 2010 and the U.S. in 201 1; crisaborole, a topical therapy approved for treatment of atopic dermatitis by the U.S. in 2016; and apremilast, which was approved by the FDA for treatment of PsA in March 2014, for treatment of plaque psoriasis in September 2014, and for oral ulcers associated with Behcet's syndrome in July 2019.

Apremilast inhibits production of the proinflammatory cytokines, IFN-γ, TNF, IL-12, and IL-23, and inducible nitric oxide synthase. Oral administration of apremilast has an absolute bioavailability of 73%, with peak concentration at 2.5 hours (Tmax). The half-life of apremilast is 6 to 9 hours, necessitating twicedaily dosing. Dosages of apremilast at 20 mg bid and 30 mg bid were evaluated in three multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials of 1493 patients with active PsA.190-192 Patients ranged in age from 18 to 83 years, with an overall median disease duration of 5 years. Patients were randomly assigned to receive either 20 mg bid or 30 mg bid. Patients with varied subtypes of PsA were enrolled across the three studies, including symmetric polyarthritis (62.0%), asymmetric oligoarthritis (27.0%), distal interphalangeal joint arthritis (6.0%), arthritis mutilans (3.0%), and predominant spondylitis (2.1%). Patients received concomitant therapy with at least one DMARD (65.0%), methotrexate (55.0%), sulfasalazine (9.0%), leflunomide (7.0%),

low-dose oral corticosteroids (14.0%), and NSAIDs (71.0%). Prior treatment with nonbiologic DMARDs only was reported in 76.0% of patients, and prior treatment with bDMARDs was reported in 22.0% of patients, which includes 9.0% who had not responded to prior bDMARD treatment. The primary endpoint in the trials was the percentage of patients achieving an ACR20 response at week 16.

ACR responses with apremilast, 30 mg twice daily, were statistically superior to placebo in all three studies (ACR20 response, apremilast, 32%41%; placebo, 18%19%; p < 0.05). ACR50 and ACR70 responses were numerically greater for apremilast but did not achieve statistical significance (Fig. 65.7). The PASI75 response was 21% for apremilast and 5% for the placebo group. The responses for both skin and arthritis are less robust than the responses generally seen with TNF inhibitors.

Long-term safety and efficacy data are available for apremilast in PsA and psoriasis patients.193, Diarrhea, headache, and nausea were the most commonly reported AEs. The most common AEs leading to discontinuation were nausea (1.8%), diarrhea (1.8%), and headache. The initial dose is titrated from 10 mg once daily to 30 mg twice daily during a period of 5 days to reduce the likelihood of GI AEs. The proportion of patients with PsA who discontinued treatment in the trials because of any adverse reaction was 4.6% for patients taking apremilast 30 mg bid and 1.2% for placebo-treated patients.

Warnings in the package insert include the possibility of weight loss and depression. Weight loss of 5 to 10 lb in the PsA clinical trials was reported in 10% of apremilast-treated patients and 3.3% of placebo patients. Depression was seen in a small number of patients, but slightly more frequently than in placebo patients.

Apremilast was evaluated in RA in 237 patients who were incomplete responders to methotrexate; they remained on a stable dose of methotrexate and were randomized to placebo or apremilast 20 mg bid or 30 mg bid. At week 16, similar proportions of patients in each group met ACR20 criteria. At week 52, no trends were seen for clinical endpoints by treatment group. Development was terminated in RA.

Apremilast 30 mg bid showed positive results in a 12-week phase II placebo-controlled clinical trial for Behcet's treat- 196 A phase III randomized clinical trial was conducted in ment. patients with Behcet's and active oral ulcers but no major

organ involvement. Patients were randomized to apremilast or placebo. The primary endpoint was area under the curve (AUC) for the total number of oral ulcers during the 12-week placebocontrolled study period, with lower numbers indicating fewer ulcers. The AUC for the number of oral ulcers was significantly lower in the apremilast group versus placebo (129.5 vs. 222.1, p < 0.001). Patients on apremilast also showed improvement in secondary endpoints including change from baseline in the Behcet's Disease Quality of Life score (-4.3 vs. -1.2 points). AEs were consistent with the phase II results, primarily diarrhea, nausea, and headache. A long-term open-label extension study to week 64 showed that patients on apremilast maintained improvements in number of oral ulcers through week 64.198 In addition, improvements in secondary endpoints of pain, complete/partial responses, disease activity, and quality of life were maintained through week 64. AEs included diarrhea, nausea, headache, and upper respiratory infection and were consistent with the known safety profile of apremilast. Apremilast is approved for Behcet's and has become the standard of care. A phase III study of apremilast in children with Behcet's syndrome is now underway. A recent preliminary study reported benefit for the cutaneous manifestations of dermatomyosisits.

### Conclusion

The unraveling of the intra-cellular pathways involved in signal transduction, resulting in T and B cell activation and inflammatory cytokine production, has resulted in the development of small-molecule inhibitors to these pathways that can abrogate inflammation i n i nflammatory di seases. Effi cacy simi lar to bDMARDs and overall acceptable safety profile in clinical trials and real-world data has been demonstrated. Safety issues in patients over age 65, smokers, and patients with cardiovascular, venous thromboembolic, or malignancy risk factors have been reported and risk mitigation strategies for use of JAK inhibitors should be followed. JAK inhibitors are now utilized widely for IMIDs in the clinic and evaluation of these therapies and other kinase inhibitors in diseases such as SLE and dermatomyositis are ongoing, which may expand the indications for these treatments.

# Urate-Lowering Therapy

### KEY POINTS

Urate-lowering therapy (ULT) is central to the management of hyperuricemia in gout.

The goal of ULT is to reduce or eliminate disease burden in gout posed by symptomatic flares, tophi, and progressive joint destruction. This goal can be achieved by lowering and maintaining serum urate (sUA) concentrations below 5 to 6 mg/dL.

Optimal ULT requires careful patient selection with attention to comorbid illness, ongoing education, adoption of a treat-to-target approach, and effective anti-inflammatory prophylaxis with treatment initiation.

### Introduction

The long-term management of gout is based primarily on the optimal use of urate-lowering therapy (ULT). Available ULT classes include (1) xanthine oxidase (XO) inhibitors (allopurinol and febuxostat); (2) uricosurics (probenecid, benzbromarone, and sulfinpyrazone); and (3) recombinant uricase (pegloticase) (Table 66.1). This chapter focuses primarily on the most common rheumatic indication for ULT: the treatment of hyperuricemia in gout.

### Nonpharmacologic Treatment in Hyperuricemia

The importance of education and lifestyle advice, including weight loss, select dietary restrictions, and reduced alcohol intake, is consistently outlined in gout management guidelines.1, Despite a growing list of dietary factors implicated in hyperuricemia (often defined as concentrations >6.8 mg/dL or >400 µmol/L) and gout, investigations of dietary interventions on health outcomes in gout are lacking. Furthermore, evidence suggests that such interventions in isolation yield modest results3 and suffer from a lack of widespread patient acceptance and long-term adherence. In addition to dietary modifications that include reducing the intake of dietary purines (particularly meats and seafood), fructose, beer, and liquor, weight loss represents an important goal for overweight gout patients. Although even modest amounts of weight loss can be important to overall health, resulting reductions in serum urate (sUA) are modest and insufficient in most patients with gout. A metanalysis of 20 studies with a total of 5233 patients examined the impact of bariatric surgery on sUA and the incidence of gout. Pooled results demonstrated a mean sUA decrease of 0.73 mg/ dL 3 months post-operatively with continued decreases until the

third post-operative year, with reductions in sUA proportionate to total weight loss.

### Patient Selection, Time of Treatment Initiation, and Asymptomatic Hyperuricemia

Hyperuricemia should be treated in patients with gout with recurrent and frequent flares (often defined as ≥2 flares annually), tophi, and/or radiographic changes consistent with gout.1, Although it has long been suggested that ULT should be initiated only after flare resolution (with the rationale that its earlier initiation could amplify the duration or magnitude of symptoms), this dogma has been challenged. In a randomized controlled study of 57 men with gout, allopurinol initiation during a flare resulted in no differences in pain or flare recurrence compared with placebo when administered with background anti-inflammatory prophylaxis. Since this 2012 study, two other randomized controlled trials, one using allopurinol7 and one using febuxostat,8 have shown similar results with no increase observed in daily pain or flare recurrence when ULT was initiated during flare. As a result, ULT initiation during gout flare is now conditionally recommended by the American College of Rheumatology (ACR) over delaying its initiation until after flare resolution. Results from a cost-effectiveness analysis in nontophaceous gout, involving a hypothetical patient cohort, suggest that the institution of allopurinol is cost-effective in patients seen with two or more gout flares within a 1-year period. Traditionally reserved for those with well-established disease, at least one recent study suggests that the initiation of ULT earlier in the disease course may yield substantial benefit. In a 2-year doubleblind, placebo-controlled study of 314 gout patients with a history of only one or two lifetime flares, the initiation and titration of febuxostat led to significant declines in flare incidence as well as reductions in synovitis detected by magnetic resonance imaging. European guidelines have endorsed earlier consideration of ULT, recommending that ULT be discussed with all patients once a diagnosis of gout is established.

In addition to its initiation earlier in the course of gout, there has been substantial speculation regarding the potential role of ULT in individuals with asymptomatic hyperuricemia, particularly given hypotheses of a protective benefit in cardiovascular disease (CVD) and chronic kidney disease (CKD). Recent studies of ULT in asymptomatic hyperuricemia, however, have yielded conflicting results. A 2018 randomized, double-blind, placebocontrolled trial involving 467 patients with stage 3 CKD demonstrated no benefit of febuxostat over placebo in preserving renal function over 2 years of follow-up. As part of a recent randomized controlled study, allopurinol administered in daily

doses of 100 to 300 mg showed no benefit over placebo in slowing declines in renal function among 369 nongout patients with a mean baseline sUA of 8.2 mg/dL and stage 3 or 4 CKD. In contrast, a 2022 multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebocontrolled trial enrolling 395 patients with stage 3 CKD found that febuxostat mitigated decline in these patients, specifically in the population without proteinuria,13 indicating febuxostat may be beneficial for select patients with CKD.

In addition to showing beneficial effects on endothelial func- , ULT has been proposed to yield protection against tion, adverse cardiovascular outcomes. In a placebo-controlled study of pediatric essential hypertension, allopurinol use resulted in significant, albeit modest, declines in blood pressure. A randomized open-label study of more than 1000 older individuals (>65 years) with asymptomatic hyperuricemia found that febuxostat therapy (vs. no therapy or allopurinol 100 mg/day) was associated with a 25% reduction (hazard ratio [HR] 0.75; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.590.95) in the composite endpoint of death from any cause, CVD, nonfatal coronary artery disease, heart failure, other arteriosclerotic disease, atrial fibrillation, or renal impairment. The benefit for ULT in this study appeared to be primarily driven by lower rates of renal impairment. Additional subgroup analysis from this trial found that febuxostat reduced the risk of the primary composite endpoint of cerebral, cardiovascular, and renal events and death, specifically in the secondary prevention setting. A randomized controlled trial of 5721 patients 60 years and older (all with ischemic heart disease but no history of gout) demonstrated no cardiovascular benefit of allopurinol titrated to daily doses as high as 600 mg compared with usual care. However, application of these findings to patients with hyperuricemia must be done with caution as mean sUA concentrations at enrollment were <6.0 mg/dL.

### Duration of Urate-Lowering Therapy

Understanding that gout flare can occur as a physiologic consequence of urate lowering, flare is not an indication to interrupt or discontinue ULT. In asymptomatic gout patients successfully treated with ULT, withdrawal of therapy often results in an abrupt increase in sUA, with recurrent attacks occurring in approximately one-third of patients within 2 years. Similarly, reductions from continuous ULT to an "intermittent" regimen in previously stable patients with gout lead to significantly higher flare rates,21 whereas ULT discontinuation in the setting of tophaceous gout leads to recurrent gout flares in a vast majority and recurrent tophi in nearly half. Taken together, these reports suggest that once initiated ULT should be "lifelong" in most patients.

### Target Serum Urate Goals

Lowering and maintaining serum urate (sUA) at concentrations less than 6.0 mg/dL (<360 µmol/L) leads to improved long-term outcomes in gout, a treat-to-target approach advocated for in rheumatology management guidelines.1, Current European recommendations advocate for an even lower target goal (<5.0 mg/ dL or <300 µmol/L) in patients with tophi. ULT reduces the long-term risk of recurrent flare by approximately 60% for each 1 mg/dL decrease in sUA. Additional evidence suggests that reaching and maintaining sUA concentrations less than 6.0 mg/ dL is important for the depletion of total body urate stores. It is important to recognize that these target goals often fall well below the upper limit of normal for sUA in clinical laboratories that

often define ranges based on population-based distributions. Currently, controversy exists regarding sUA concentrations that might be considered "too low." This notion is based on studies suggesting that uric acid may be protective against neurodegenerative conditions such as Parkinson's disease or Alzheimer's dementia, though the evidence is mixed, and further study is warranted.25-28 European guidance reflects this concern by recommending that sUA concentrations are maintained above 3.0 mg/dL while ACR guidelines have not defined a lower threshold in the absence of compelling data. 1,2

### Anti-inflammatory Prophylaxis With Urate-Lowering Therapy Administration

Rebound gout flare is the most common "complication" of ULT regardless of the agent used, rendering anti-inflammatory prophylaxis a key component of successful gout treatment.1, Gout flares complicating ULT are thought to be caused by reduced sUA concentrations that result in the mobilization of monosodium urate crystals from articular and periarticular deposits into joints. The frequency of treatment-related gout flares appears to be higher with more rapid and potent urate-lowering interventions and can be at least partially mitigated by initiating low-dose ULT with stepwise dose increases to achieve target sUA goal even in the absence of prophylaxis.29, Both colchicine and low-dose nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs; e.g., naproxen 250 mg twice/day) are effective in reducing gout flares during ULT initiation.31-33 Although low-dose glucocorticoids (e.g., prednisone ≤10 mg/day) are commonly used in this context, supporting data are limited. Results from one group 32 suggest that anti-inflammatory prophylaxis with low-dose oral colchicine (0.6 mg, twice/day) protects against rebound gout flares and may need to be continued for at least 6 months after ULT initiation. Of note, in a recent study comparing ULT agents, 91% of patients were administered colchicine as the prophylactic agent of choice (over naproxen or low-dose prednisone), suggesting a strong preference for this agent among gout investigators. Agents targeting interleukin (IL)-1 have demonstrated preliminary efficacy in the prevention of gout flare complicating ULT initiation, although their use is limited given expense and lack of patient access. 35,36

### Urate-Lowering Therapy Adherence

Suboptimal treatment compliance poses a major obstacle to effective ULT, with reports consistently demonstrating rates of medication adherence of 50% or less in gout.37, Treatment adherence in gout has been shown to be the lowest of seven different chronic conditions examined,37 emphasizing the importance of patient education in disease management. By supporting patient education, engagement, and shared decision making, nonphysician providers may play an important role in improving ULT adherence. Compared with usual care, implementation of a simple pharmacist-led intervention utilizing automated telephone technology improved both ULT adherence and goal sUA achievement (50% vs. 37% and 30% vs. 15%, respectively). Likewise, one group found that a nurse-led intervention incorporating treat-to-target ULT coupled with patient education and frequent follow-up was superior to usual care in sUA goal achievement, improving health-related quality of life, and reducing flares and tophi. Importantly, results from this randomized controlled trial found that patients receiving the nurse-led intervention had significantly greater ULT persistence (96%) after 2 years compared with usual care (56%).

### KEY POINTS

In addition to its established track record in gout management, allopurinol has several advantages over other available ULTs: (1) low cost, (2) once-daily oral administration, (3) effectiveness in patients who underexcrete and those who overproduce uric acid (UA), (4) favorable safety profile, and (5) potential effectiveness in patients with renal impairment. Although subject to limited study, incremental dose changes in allopurinol (e.g., 100 mg/day increase) may also afford more gradual sUA lowering than incremental changes in other forms of ULT such as febuxostat (e.g., 40 mg/day increase), an effect that could reduce the relative risk of flares complicating ULT initiation and titration. Allopurinol treatment results in significant declines in sUA,31,33,41 decreased ,31,33,41-47 and declines in tophus area. gout flare rates,3 31

### Role in Rheumatic Disease and Indications

Approved indications for allopurinol include (1) treatment of hyperuricemia in gout, (2) the management of hyperuricemia resulting from the treatment of malignancy (most often leukemia or lymphoma), and (3) the management of nephrolithiasis in the context of increased urinary UA excretion. As with other ULTs, allopurinol is not approved for the treatment of asymptomatic hyperuricemia in the absence of gout.

### Chemical Structure and Mechanism of Action

An anti-metabolite in simple organisms, allopurinol inhibits XO (Fig. 66.1), a key enzyme in purine catabolism, but does not inhibit the biosynthesis of purines in humans.

### Pharmacology

Pharmacologic characteristics of the ULTs are summarized in Table 66.2. Allopurinol is approximately 90% absorbed from the gastrointestinal (GI) tract and is metabolized into oxypurinol, its active metabolite. Peak serum concentrations for allopurinol and oxypurinol are achieved within approximately 1 to 2 hours and 4 to 5 hours, respectively. The plasma half-life of allopurinol is relatively brief (1 to 2 hours), although the half-life of oxypurinol is substantially longer (~15 hours or longer), allowing for once-daily dosing. Allopurinol is eliminated primarily via glomerular filtration, whereas oxypurinol undergoes some degree of renal tubular reabsorption. With renal mechanisms primarily responsible for drug elimination, the plasma half-life of allopurinol, and to a greater degree oxypurinol, are increased with renal insufficiency.

### Dose and Drug Administration

Allopurinol is available as 100 mg and 300 mg pills for oncedaily oral administration (see Table 66.2), with split dosing advocated in some instances for daily doses 600 mg or higher. Used in the treatment and/or prevention of tumor lysis syndrome, allopurinol is available intravenously. Approved at daily doses as high as 800 mg in the United States and 900 mg in Europe, allopurinol is often maintained at inappropriately low doses (e.g., ≤300 mg/day) in everyday clinical practice, 48 as higher doses are often required to appropriately manage the signs and symptoms of gout. It is well established that only a modest proportion of patients achieve a target sUA less than 6.0 mg/dL with allopurinol 300 mg/day, the most commonly used dose. With a target sUA threshold of less than 5.0 mg/ dL, investigators have shown that only one-fourth of patients with gout achieve this goal with 300 mg of daily allopurinol, a proportion that increased to 78% with a daily dose of 600 mg. The limitation of "standard" dose allopurinol has been demonstrated in randomized clinical trials comparing fixed daily doses of allopurinol 300 mg with febuxostat in various doses. In those studies, approximately 40% of allopurinol-treated patients with gout achieved a final sUA less than 6.0 mg/dL.31, Gout treatment guidelines recommend that allopurinol be started in low doses (e.g., 100 mg/day) and increased by 100 mg every 2 to 5 weeks as required to achieve the target.1,

Data from two studies suggest that each 100 mg increase in allopurinol leads to an additional decline in sUA approaching 1.0 mg/dL.44, Implementing a "start low and go slow" approach and other key elements of proposed "best practices,"1,2 95% of gout patients in a study examining a nurse-led intervention achieved target sUA concentrations after 2 years of treatment compared with just 30% of those receiving usual care. Importantly, those receiving the intervention after 2 years experienced fewer gout flares and had a lower number of tophi compared with gout patients subject to usual care. Among the intervention patients receiving allopurinol, the most commonly used ULT in the study, the mean daily dose achieved after 2 years was 460 mg. A more recent study examining treat-to-target ULT showed that a median daily allopurinol dose of 382 mg was needed to achieve SU goal.

There is general consensus that initial allopurinol dosing should be adjusted for diminished renal function,2,51,52 which prolongs the plasma half-life of oxypurinol. Commonly cited dosing algorithms suggest administering an initial daily dose of 100 mg or less for patients with a glomerular filtration rate below 20 mL/min, with even lower doses for those with more severe renal impairment. Whether existing dosing guidelines preclude the use of incremental dosing beyond these recommended renal thresholds has been the subject of debate. Renal dosing guidelines53 suggesting that maximum allopurinol doses be dictated by renal function are not evidence based and are founded largely on a single retrospective case series showing that patients in whom allopurinol hypersensitivity syndrome (AHS) developed were more likely to have renal insufficiency. Indeed, of patients with CKD in whom AHS developed, many received "appropriately" dosed allopurinol.54, In a review of 120 patients with gout receiving allopurinol, more than half (57%) required titration of daily doses higher than the "renal threshold" recommended by Hande,53 a strategy that was well tolerated in the vast majority of patients. In a large randomized comparative effectiveness study, allopurinol doses titrated as high as 800 mg/day using a treat-to-target strategy showed similar efficacy and tolerability as febuxostat in

patients with stage 3 CKD. In a large population-based cohort study, investigators observed no associations of allopurinol initiation or dose escalation with mortality risk in gout patients with CKD.

### Toxicity

AHS is an uncommon but potentially fatal treatment complication, with approximately 90% of cases occurring within 60 days of allopurinol initiation. AHS is characterized by the presence of an erythematous desquamating rash (similar to Stevens-Johnson syndrome), fever, eosinophilia, and end organ damage, including hepatitis and renal failure. AHS complicates as many as 0.1 to 0.4% of allopurinol treatment courses, although rates have been estimated to be as low as 1 in 56,000 allopurinol users. In addition to its association with higher initial allopurinol doses and impaired renal function.60, AHS is substantially more common in individuals positive for HLA-B*5801. In a small Taiwanese casecontrol study, all patients in whom AHS developed were positive for HLA-B*5801, compared with only 15% of allopurinol-treated patients without AHS. In the United States this risk allele has been estimated to be present in 0.7% of Whites and Hispanics, 7.4% of Asians, and 3.8% of African Americans. With genetic assays commercially available, testing for HLA-B*5801 has been proposed to be cost-effective and even cost-saving when implemented in intermediateor high-risk populations, 64,65 such as African Americans or Asians, respectively, particularly in the context of CKD64,65 and is currently recommended in these high-risk groups by the ACR (regardless of renal function). It has been estimated that the use of low starting doses, adjusted for renal function, may by itself reduce AHS risk by approximately 10-fold. Given the potential severity of AHS, patients should be educated about the remote possibility of this adverse event and cautioned to discontinue allopurinol if a rash develops, particularly if accompanied by fever or mucocutaneous lesions.

Recognizing the rare occurrence of AHS, allopurinol is generally well tolerated. Estimates suggest that less than 5% to 10% of those exposed are intolerant to the drug. Rebound flares are among the most common complication that accompanies allopurinol and all other ULT, an issue that is most prominent in the early phases of drug initiation and can be mitigated by anti-inflammatory prophylaxis. Isolated maculopapular skin rash can occur outside the context of AHS and is estimated to complicate approximately 1% to 3% of allopurinol treatment courses. Other common adverse events associated with allopurinol use are summarized in Table 66.1. Liver function abnormalities can be seen in approximately 6% to 7% of allopurinol users,41 although rates of severe liver injury appear to be exceedingly low. The role and recommended frequency for laboratory surveillance in toxicity monitoring has not been well defined.

### Fertility, Pregnancy, and Lactation

Recognizing that there have been no human studies of its use in pregnancy,67 allopurinol should be avoided in pregnancy; animal reproduction studies have shown adverse fetal effects. Both allopurinol and oxypurinol are expressed in breast milk and, because drug effects in the developing infant are largely unknown, it should be administered to a nursing mother with caution.

### Drug Interactions and Contraindications

Allopurinol drug interactions have been well characterized. Azathioprine and 6-mercaptopurine (6-MP) are metabolized by XO, hence co-administration of allopurinol leads to marked increases in circulating drug levels that can lead to bone marrow suppression. Theophylline is also metabolized by XO; therefore, coadministration of this agent with allopurinol can lead to increased theophylline levels and potentiate toxicity. The co-administration of allopurinol with ampicillin/amoxicillin has been associated with a higher incidence of drug-related rash. Thiazide diuretics may also reduce the renal excretion of allopurinol and oxypurinol, with suggestions that this could potentiate drug-related toxicity, including the risk of AHS. Uricosurics increase the renal excretion of oxypurinol, thus offsetting to some degree the urate-lowering effect of allopurinol. Allopurinol co-administration may increase drug levels of cyclosporine and warfarin, mandating close monitoring of drug levels and bleeding parameters, respectively. Other allopurinol-associated drug interactions are summarized in Table 66.1. Although regimens for desensitization have been described, allopurinol should be avoided in patients with known allergies to allopurinol, especially AHS.

### Febuxostat

### KEY POINTS

Febuxostat is a potent inhibitor of xanthine oxidase, with a chemical structure that is distinct from that of allopurinol.

Febuxostat represents an important alternative to patients for whom allopurinol is not effective, either because of intolerance or lack of efficacy.

### Role in Rheumatic Disease and Indications

Febuxostat is approved for the treatment of hyperuricemia in patients with gout. Similar to other ULTs, febuxostat is not currently indicated for the treatment of asymptomatic hyperuricemia. Given its unique structure, febuxostat represents an important

alternative means of XO inhibition, particularly in patients with gout who are intolerant to allopurinol.

### Chemical Structure and Mechanism of Action

In contrast to allopurinol, febuxostat is a nonpurine analog that reduces serum and urinary urate concentrations through selective XO inhibition (see Fig. 66.1). In contrast to allopurinol, which may inhibit other enzymes involved in purine and pyrimidine synthesis, febuxostat demonstrates significant enzymatic inhibition only for XO at therapeutic concentrations.

### Pharmacology

After oral administration, febuxostat is rapidly absorbed from the GI tract with approximately 50% absorption, reaching peak plasma concentrations within a few hours75 with near-complete plasma protein binding (see Table 66.1). Febuxostat displays linear pharmacokinetics undergoing primary hepatic metabolism through conjugation via uridine diphosphate glucuronosyltransferase and oxidation via cytochrome P450 (CYP) enzymes. Peak urate-lowering effects with febuxostat generally occur during the first 5 to 7 days of treatment. Drug elimination occurs via both hepatic and renal pathways. Although active metabolites are produced via oxidation, these are present in much lower plasma concentrations.

Metabolized primarily in the liver, febuxostat may not require renal dosing. This receives support from small short-term pharmacokinetic studies that included a limited number of patients with renal impairment.77, There are insufficient data from longer-term studies of febuxostat in patients with moderate renal impairment (serum creatinine of ~1.62.0 mg/dL) and even less data from patients with more severe renal dysfunction (serum creatinine >2.0 mg/dL). Available data, albeit limited, suggest that those with mild or moderate renal impairment (estimated creatinine clearance between 30 and 90 mL/min) experience similar efficacy and similar rates of toxicity compared with those with preserved renal function receiving the same doses of febuxostat.31,41,79

### Toxicity

Similar to other ULTs, rebound gout flares are the most common complication of febuxostat administration, underscoring the importance of anti-inflammatory prophylaxis. Other adverse reactions observed with febuxostat are summarized in Table 66.1, which appear to occur at similar rates to those observed with allopurinol.41, In initial studies comparing febuxostat with allopurinol, there was a slightly higher rate of cardiovascular events in patients receiving febuxostat (0.74 events per 100 patient-years; 95% CI, 0.361.37) compared with those randomly assigned to allopurinol (0.60 events per 100 patient-years; 95% CI, 0.161.53). In the large 6-month CONFIRMS trial, investigators found no differences in the rates of cardiovascular events between patients treated with febuxostat (40 mg and 80 mg/day) and allopurinol (200 mg to 300 mg/day). Although showing no difference in its primary endpoint (a composite of cardiovascular death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke, or unstable angina requiring revascularization), the large-scale, randomized Cardiovascular Safety of Febuxostat and Allopurinol in Patients with Gout and Cardiovascular Comorbidities (CARES) study showed febuxostat treatment to be associated with a 20% to 30% higher risk than allopurinol for the pre-specified secondary endpoints of all-cause and cardiovascular mortality in patients with gout. Recognizing important limitations including the absence of a placebo arm and a loss to follow-up approaching 50%,80 results of the CARES trial led to a U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) warning related to cardiovascular risk with febuxostat. The European Febuxostat versus Allopurinol Streamlined Trial (FAST) further explored the cardiovascular safety of febuxostat. In contrast to CARES, the FAST trial found no differences between febuxostat and allopurinol in the occurrence of cardiovascular events. Reassurance provided from the FAST study (which had a loss to follow-up rate of only 5.8%) has led some experts to ask the FDA to reconsider its warning.

Because of its unique structure and select XO inhibition, it has been suggested that febuxostat may represent a rational alternative for patients with gout with a history of AHS. Whether febuxostat can be effectively administered in such patients is not clear, given post-marketing reports of hypersensitivity in those given febuxostat. In a small retrospective study involving 13 patients with gout with a history of severe allopurinol-related adverse reactions, 12 were subsequently treated safely with febuxostat (10 achieved target sUA goals). A hypersensitivity vasculitis of the skin developed in a single patient.

### Fertility, Pregnancy, and Lactation

The effects of febuxostat on fertility are not known. Likewise, there have been no studies of febuxostat in pregnant women,

although results from animal studies have not suggested a significant risk of teratogenicity. However, in the absence of appropriate human studies, febuxostat should be avoided in pregnancy. It is not known whether the drug is excreted in human milk and febuxostat should be used only with caution in nursing women.

### Drug Interactions and Contraindications

Although formal drug-interaction studies have not been performed, febuxostat should not be used concomitantly with drugs that are metabolized by XO (azathioprine, 6-MP, theophylline) (see Table 66.1). Because of its hepatic metabolism, febuxostat should not be used in patients with moderate to severe liver impairment.

### Uricosurics

### KEY POINTS

Probenecid, sulfinpyrazone, and benzbromarone are the most common uricosuric agents used in gout treatment worldwide.

Sometimes requiring twoor three-times-per-day dosing, uricosurics are potentially effective in lowering sUA in patients who underexcrete UA, the most common pathologic defect leading to hyperuricemia.

Probenecid and sulfinpyrazone may have limited efficacy in the context of moderate to severe renal insufficiency.

Uricosurics represent the first drug class used to lower sUA in gout treatment. A complex system of renal handling of urate has been proposed that sequentially includes four components86. (1) near-complete glomerular filtration, (2) proximal reabsorption, (3) tubular urate secretion occurring more distally, and (4) reabsorption for a second time more distally. Available uricosurics diminish the post-secretory reabsorption of UA, therefore promoting its elimination and reducing sUA. Uricosurics address the most common physiologic defect in gout: UA underexcretion. In addition to promoting renal UA excretion, uricosurics may inhibit the tubular secretion of a number of other compounds, including penicillins. Although many agents display uricosuric properties, the most commonly used uricosurics in gout worldwide are probenecid, sulfinpyrazone, and benzbromarone. Probenecid is the most widely used uricosuric in gout treatment. Although approved in gout management to be used in combination with either allopurinol or febuxostat, lesinurad is no longer commercially available. Primarily because of concerns of treatment-related toxicity, sulfinpyrazone and benzbromarone are less widely available, and neither is available in the United States.

Although the focus of this section is on "primary" uricosu- 2 rics, there are several medications approved for the treatment of nongout conditions that exert uricosuric effects. "Secondary" uricosurics and their indications are summarized in Table 66.2.87-92 Salicylates exert a paradoxical effect on renal urate elimination, with the inhibition of active secretion with lower doses (e.g., <1 g/day) and a "uricosuric-like" inhibition of UA reabsorption at higher doses (>4 to 5 g/day). Along with salicylates, losartan has perhaps been most closely scrutinized for its hypouricemic properties, an effect that is mediated via inhibition of uric acid transporter (URAT) 1 and appears to be specific to this angiotensin receptor blocker. The magnitude of sUA lowering that can be achieved with these "secondary" hypouricemics is typically

modest. Losartan used at an anti-hypertensive dose of 50 mg/day resulted in mean sUA declines approaching 9%. It is important to recognize that the urate-lowering effect of losartan appears to be negated when co-administered with hydrochlorothiazide,93 a combination used in hypertension treatment. Additionally, dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers such as amlodipine have been found to have an sUA-lowering effect94 and were associated with a lower risk of gout in post hoc analysis of the ALLHAT trial, one of the largest randomized clinical trials conducted on hypertension to date. Sodium/glucose transporter-2 inhibitors also appear to reduce the risk of gout96 and have sUA-lowering effects, likely due to uric acid excretion stimulated by glycosuria.

### Role in Rheumatic Disease and Indications

Probenecid, sulfinpyrazone, and benzbromarone are used to treat hyperuricemia associated with gout and are indicated in patients with gout who underexcrete UA (24-hour urine UA, <700 mg). Probenecid is also approved as an adjuvant to penicillin therapy, increasing plasma concentrations and prolonging the terminal half-life of penicillin and other penicillin derivatives. Although potentially effective for a majority of patients with gout, uricosurics are much less commonly used than allopurinol and have been designated as second-line ULTs in gout management guidelines. In a population-based study from the United Kingdom, uricosuric therapy accounted for less than 5% of all ULT prescriptions.

### Mechanism of Action

Uricosurics work primarily through the inhibition of the renal tubular urate transporters: URAT1, glucose transporter 9, and organic anion transporter (OAT) 1, 3, and 4 (Fig. 66.2). Thus uricosurics reduce UA reabsorption, promote renal elimination, and decrease sUA.99-103

### Pharmacology

Administered orally, uricosurics undergo gastrointestinal absorption and are extensively protein bound in the serum. Half-lives of probenecid104 and sulfinpyrazone105 are relatively brief, ranging from approximately 3 to 12 hours (see Table 66.1). Although benzbromarone also has a relatively short half-life of approximately 3 hours, its active metabolite 6-hydroxybenzbromarone has a much longer half-life, allowing for effective once-daily administration. Elimination of the uricosurics is primarily via hepatic metabolism, followed by variable excretion of metabolites in the urine, bile, and/or feces. The metabolism of probenecid is limited to side-chain hydroxylation, N-depropylation, and glucuronic conjugation of its carboxyl group. Sulfinpyrazone and benzbromarone are metabolized via CYP, with CYP2C9 representing a principal mediator. 110, Warfarin is also metabolized primarily via CYP2C9, explaining its potential drug—drug interactions with these agents.

### Dose and Drug gAdministration

Usual probenecid dosing is 500 to 2000 mg daily in divided doses. Probenecid (500 mg) is also formulated with colchicine (0.5 mg) as a combination tablet (col-probenecid). In a 12-week randomized study involving patients with preserved renal function, probenecid 1500 mg/day was associated with a 32% reduction in plasma urate concentration, 112 with older studies documenting other qualitative benefits of therapy, including softening of tophi, functional improvement, and improved pain symptoms.46,1 bSulfinpyrazone is given in divided doses at an initial daily dose of 200 to 400 mg, increasing to 800 mg daily, if necessary, to achieve target sUA goals.

Although there is no level of renal function below which probenecid and sulfinpyrazone are known to completely lose efficacy,59 these drugs may lose effectiveness in patients with moderate to severe renal insufficiency. In a retrospective study of 57 patients with gout, probenecid yielded moderate efficacy as a ULT with baseline sUA, but not renal function per se, predicting treatment response. In contrast to common dogma, these results suggest that probenecid can be used effectively in select patients with mild to moderate CKD. Probenecid may also be used as an adjuvant to XO inhibition. Among patients failing allopurinol monotherapy (200 to 300 mg/day), 86% achieved a target sUA of less than 5 mg/dL after the addition of probenecid (1000 mg/day).

Benzbromarone is administered once daily and may be effective in patients with moderate renal impairment. Benzbromarone treatment in usual doses (50 to 200 mg/day) leads to between 25 and 50% reductions in sUA,117-120 in addition to decreases in gout flare rates and tophi.121-123 In a randomized controlled trial, benzbromarone maintained its hypouricemic effect even among patients with a creatinine clearance as low as 20 to 40 mL/min. Among patients intolerant to or experiencing treatment failure with allopurinol 300 mg/day, 92% of those administered benzbromarone (200 mg/day) achieved a sUA less than 5.0 mg/dL compared with 65% of those receiving probenecid (2000 mg/day).

### Toxicity

As with other ULTs, rebound gout flares represent a common complication of uricosurics. Because urinary UA acts as a potential nidus for stone formation, uricosuric therapy is associated with an increased risk of nephrolithiasis. In a longitudinal study including more than 780 patient-years of benzbromarone exposure, nephrolithiasis developed in approximately 10% (21 of 216 patients). Of the 21 patients with incident nephrolithiasis, oxalate stones developed in 7 patients, and stones composed of either UA or a combination of UA and calcium developed in 14 patients. In addition to limiting uricosurics to those who underexcrete UA, the risk of treatment-related nephrolithiasis can be mitigated by optimizing fluid intake and alkalinizing the urine with a goal of maintaining a urine pH higher than 6.0.125 Other adverse effects observed with uricosurics are summarized in Table 66.1. Rare adverse effects include anaphylaxis, anemia (including aplastic and hemolytic anemia), other cytopenias, fever, nephrotic syndrome, and back pain. Rare reports of severe liver injury led to the withdrawal of benzbromarone by its primary manufacturer in 2003, a decision challenged in systematic riskbenefit analysis of the drug. Because of its NSAID-like properties, sulfinpyrazone has been associated with an increased frequency of blood dyscrasia (rare) in addition to upper gastrointestinal disturbances including peptic ulcer disease.

### Fertility, Pregnancy, and Lactation

There are limited data regarding the impact of uricosurics on fertility, fetal development, and use with nursing infants; thus these agents should be used with caution in such patients only when the potential benefits of treatment outweigh its potential risks.

### Drug Interactions and Contraindications

With the knowledge that tubular secretion plays a central role in the renal clearance of numerous drugs, drug—drug interactions with the use of uricosurics, particularly probenecid, are well known. Inhibition of tubular drug secretion appears to be greater for probenecid and sulfinpyrazone than benzbromarone due to the specific inhibition of URAT1 attributed to the latter agent. Drug interactions observed with uricosurics are summarized in Table 66.1.

Because of the potential for cross-reactivity, sulfinpyrazone should be avoided in patients with allergies to phenylbutazone or other pyrazole compounds. Except under special circumstances, these agents should be avoided in patients with nephrolithiasis, evidence of UA overexcretion, and during cancer treatment including chemotherapy and/or radiation. Caution should also be used in patients with known blood dyscrasias, active peptic ulcer disease, and/or significant hepatic or renal disease.

### Uricases

### Pegloticase

### KEY POINTS

Anti-genicity and an immune response directed toward the drug are major limitations in the repeated dosing of pegloticase (a problem heralded by a rise in sUA to concentrations above 6.0 mg/dL), although anti-drug antibody formation can be mitigated through concomitant immunosuppression.

Pegloticase, a modified mammalian uricase, is a biologic parenterally administered agent. Unlike other mammalian species, humans have lost the ability to synthesize functional uricase that

converts UA into allantoin, the latter being 5 to 10 times more soluble. The use of alternative uricases (e.g., rasburicase, a recombinant uricase from Aspergillus flavus127) in the treatment of tumor lysis syndrome has been substantially limited by drug-related antigenicity and prohibitively high rates of anaphylaxis with repeat drug administration. In contrast to older-generation uricases, pegloticase appears to be less allergenic and can be administered successfully using repeated intravenous (IV) infusions.

### Role in Rheumatic Disease and Indications

Pegloticase is approved for the treatment of hyperuricemia in patients with treatment refractory gout. Approved with an orphan drug status in the United States, pegloticase is indicated in a small subset of patients with gout. Treatment-refractory disease is characterized by severe disabling gout, often accompanied by marked tophaceous deposition and significant comorbidity, in which conventional ULT is either contraindicated or ineffective. Pegloticase administration is associated with rapid and marked declines in sUA. In clinical trials, pegloticase use resulted in plasma concentrations as low as 0.5 to 1 mg/dL within 24 hours of an initial dose. As a consequence, pegloticase administration has been associated with dramatic regression of tophi130 and depletion of urate stores, raising speculation that pegloticase or other uricase formulations could play a role as an induction therapy in select patients with severe tophaceous gout and excessive total body urate stores (Fig. 66.3).

### Chemical Structure and Mechanism of Action

Pegloticase is a recombinant mammalian uricase linked to polyethylene glycol (PEG). Pegloticase facilitates the conversion of

UA into allantoin. The conversion of allantoin from UA generates hydrogen peroxide that is rapidly scavenged by erythrocytes.

### Pharmacology

The pharmacokinetics of pegloticase follows a one-compartment linear model. Maximum serum concentrations and the magnitude of urate-lowering effect after IV pegloticase administration increase in a dose-dependent fashion. Pegloticase pharmacokinetics are not affected by age, sex, weight, or underlying renal function. Variability in drug elimination and treatment durability appears to be related at least in part to the presence and concentration of circulating anti-pegloticase antibody (see below).

### Dose and Drug Administration −

Pegloticase is approved for IV infusion administered during a 2-hour period at a dose of 8 mg every 2 weeks (see Table 66.1). Regulatory approval of pegloticase is based on results from two 6-month replicate randomized placebo-controlled studies, 129 in addition to open-label follow-up extensions (n = 212). Patients in these clinical trials had pre-treatment sUA exceeding 8.0 mg/dL, symptomatic gout, and failed prior allopurinol therapy based on reported intolerance or ineffectiveness at a maximum medically appropriate dose. Patients received prophylaxis against infusion reactions (see Table 66.1) and against rebound gout flares (colchicine, NSAID, or glucocorticoid). The primary outcome for both randomized studies was a sUA of less than 6.0 mg/dL for 80% or more of the sampling period from month 3 to 6 of follow-up.

This outcome was met by 47% and 38% of patients who received pegloticase, 8 mg by IV every 2 weeks, in the two randomized studies. In pooled analyses, 40% of patients with baseline tophi who received pegloticase, 8 mg every 2 weeks (vs. 7% of patients receiving placebo), had complete resolution of tophi by the time of the final study visit.

Although nonresponders generally experienced plasma urate reductions equally as dramatic as responders after their initial pegloticase infusion, nonresponders usually lost the treatment effect within the first 3 months of therapy. Efficacy loss, defined as sUA rising higher than 6.0 mg/dL during treatment, appears to be strongly associated with the formation of anti-pegloticase antibodies (primarily immunoglobulin [Ig] M and IgG subtypes that bind the PEG portion of the drug). Clinically meaningful manifestations of anti-pegloticase antibody formation, including an increased risk of anaphylaxis and neutralization of drug effect, appear to be most striking at antibody titers exceeding 1:2430. It is recommended that sUA, rather than drug antibody titers, be monitored closely during treatment, with discontinuation of pegloticase if pre-infusion sUA increases higher than 6.0 mg/ dL.

### Toxicity

The most common serious adverse event observed with pegloticase therapy is anaphylaxis, observed in approximately 7% of participants in regulatory studies (see Table 66.1). Anti-pegloticase antibody can be detected in a vast majority of patients

(~90%) receiving treatment, although clinically meaningful antibody titers are encountered less often. In clinical studies, anaphylaxis occurred despite prophylaxis that included antihistamine and glucocorticoid therapy with an onset of symptoms typically seen within 2 hours of drug administration. Treatment-related anaphylaxis is far more common among patients with treatment failure; thus close sUA surveillance and discontinuation of pegloticase for patients with sUA higher than 6.0 mg/dL is an essential element in risk mitigation. Post hoc analysis of the replicate studies suggests that nearly all cases of anaphylaxis would have been prevented with the use of this strategy. The concomitant use of all other ULTs is contraindicated, as these agents can mask antibody-mediated increases in sUA.

Studies investigating immunosuppression as a possible means of reducing anti-pegloticase antibody formation and improving treatment durability have yielded promising results. A randomized controlled study examined the co-administration of methotrexate (15 mg weekly) vs. placebo in patients with gout receiving pegloticase (8 mg biweekly). At 6 months, a significantly higher proportion of methotrexate-treated patients maintained response to pegloticase (71%) compared with placebo (38.5%), with lower rates of infusion reaction observed in those randomized to methotrexate. In a phase II, proof-of-concept, randomized, placebocontrolled trial, concomitant use of mycophenolate mofetil (1000 mg twice daily) initiated 14 days prior to the first pegloticase infusion and extended through treatment allowed 15 of 22 patients to maintain sUA <6.0 mg/dL at 6 months, while only 3 of 10 patients were able to maintain sUA <6.0 mg/dL in the placebo 135 Results of these trials are encouraging and may outline arm. effective strategies that will allow for more prolonged use of a highly effective ULT, which, to date, has frequently been limited due to immunogenicity.

Recognizing overlap with symptoms of anaphylaxis, infusion reactions may occur in as many as 25% of patients receiving pegloticase, with manifestations that include urticaria, dyspnea, chest discomfort, pain, erythema, and pruritis. Infusion reactions can occur any time in the course of therapy, with rare reports of delayed hypersensitivity reactions.

As with other ULTs, rebound gout flare is common after the administration of pegloticase. Other adverse events observed are summarized in Table 66.1. In the clinical studies and in open-label follow-up, exacerbations of congestive heart failure were more common with pegloticase than placebo, although a causal association with active drug therapy has not been established.

### Fertility, Pregnancy, and Lactation

No studies have examined the impact of pegloticase on either fertility or pregnancy in humans, and it is unknown whether it is excreted in human milk. In the absence of appropriate human studies, pegloticase should be used only with caution in pregnancy and is not recommended for use in nursing mothers.

### Drug Interactions and Contraindications

Recognizing that anti-pegloticase antibodies bind the PEG portion of the agent, pegloticase should be used only with caution in patients receiving other PEG-containing therapies. Whether the formation of anti-pegloticase antibodies precludes or impacts future treatment with other PEGylated molecules is unknown. Pegloticase is contraindicated in patients with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency because of

an increased risk of hemolysis and methemoglobinemia. Patients with an increased risk for G6PD deficiency should be screened before initiation.

### Urate-Lowering Drugs in Development

The treatment armamentarium in chronic gout will likely grow in the future, with several novel ULTs under development.

A peroxisome proliferator—activated gamma modulator, arhalofenate (MBX-102) has been highlighted in studies as an agent demonstrating dual uricosuric and anti-inflammatory effects.136, In addition to inhibiting renal UA transporters (URAT1, OAT4), in vitro studies have shown that the agent effectively blocks monosodium urate—induced production of IL-1. In a five-arm, 12-week randomized controlled study, investigators compared the efficacy and safety of arhalofenate (600 mg or 800 mg/day), allopurinol (300 mg/day) with or without colchicine prophylaxis (0.6 mg/ day), and placebo. Arhalofenate led to 12.5% and 16.5% reductions in sUA, respectively, with the 800 mg dose yielding significantly fewer gout flares than placebo or allopurinol without colchicine. Among 16 hyperuricemic gout patients receiving the combination of arhalofenate 800 mg/day and febuxostat 80 mg/ day, all achieved a sUA target of <6.0 mg/dL and 93% achieved sUA lower than 5 mg/dL.

Verinurad (RDEA3170) is a highly selective URAT1 inhibitor currently in development. In phase II dose-ranging studies involving 375 total patients, verinurad administered as a monotherapy in daily doses of 2.5 mg to 15 mg led to dose-dependent reductions (17.5% to 55.8%) in sUA but was associated with more renal toxicity than either placebo or allopurinol. In parallel phase II studies, verinurad was examined in combination with XO inhibitors, allopurinol and febuxostat.139, In addition to demonstrating dose-dependent urate-lowering effects, verinurad was generally well tolerated and resulted in no meaningful changes in serum creatinine concentrations when used in combination. Of note, its co-administration with allopurinol led to decreased concentrations of oxypurinol, suggesting that the potential synergy of these two therapies may be at least partially reduced by this effect.

Tigulixostat, a novel nonpurine selective XO inhibitor, has undergone phase II trials. This medication has been shown to lower sUA levels in gout patients with hyperuricemia compared with placebo in a dose-dependent fashion (47%, 51%, and 67% reduction on 50, 100, and 200 mg, respectively). In preliminary trials, tigulixostat appeared to be generally well tolerated without serious adverse events.

There are additional compounds in the early stages of development. SEL-212, which combines pegsitcase (uricase enzyme also known as pegadricase) with synthetic vaccine particles containing rapamycin, was demonstrated in pre-clinical studies to attenuate the immunogenicity of pegsiticase. Dosed monthly as an IV infusion, SEL-212 is currently in phase II trials. ALLN-346 is a pH-stable oral recombinant uricase that degrades intestinal urate into allantoin, thus decreasing total urate burden. In a proof-ofconcept study, the oral administration of ALLN-346 yielded significant reductions in plasma and urine urate concentrations in an established animal model of hyperuricemia. AR-882 and ABP- 671, both selective inhibitors of URAT-1, have demonstrated effects of increased uric acid urinary excretion and are currently in phase II studies.144,145

### Introduction

Bisphosphonates (BPs) were first synthesized over 150 years ago, as inhibitors of insoluble calcium salt formation. Their principal application was industrial, as anti-scaling agents. Their initial use in humans was in toothpaste to prevent calcified tartar accumulation. BPs were explored in nonclinical and clinical studies as inhibitors of ectopic calcification and calcium-containing kidney stone formation and for targeting radionuclides to sites of bone mineralization. The 99mTc-methylene BP complex (99mTc-MDP) binds to hydroxyapatite on bone surfaces and has been the standard "bone scan" imaging agent since the 1970s. Efforts to treat and prevent heterotopic ossification with a BP met with very limited success. No beneficial effects of BPs on either vascular calcification or kidney stone disease have been established in human studies. Nonclinical studies of BPs identified a "side effect"—inhibition of osteoclast-mediated bone resorption3,4—that has been exploited for the treatment of osteoporosis and Paget's disease of bone and prevention of bone loss. While etidronate inhibits both resorption and mineralization, newer BPs selectively inhibit bone resorption at much lower doses than those that inhibit bone

mineralization. This chapter reviews the clinical pharmacology of BPs currently used for the treatment and prevention of osteoporosis and Paget's disease, the clinical trial data that support their use as treatments of these diseases, and a review of their potential adverse effects. The clinical pharmacology is also relevant to the use of BPs for the treatment of cancer metastatic to bone and hypercalcemia of malignancy.

### Clinical Pharmacology

BPs were developed to treat metabolic bone diseases characterized by abnormally high rates of bone resorption, the most common of which are osteoporosis and Paget's disease of bone. BPs also have a role in the treatment of cancer metastatic to bone including hypercalcemia of malignancy that may result from lysis of bone by enlarging skeletal metastases. While the clinically relevant objectives of treatment may differ by disease, the underlying clinical pharmacology resulting in inhibition of osteoclast-mediated bone resorption is common.

### Chemistry of Bisphosphonates

BPs are analogs of pyrophosphate in which the central oxygen of the P-O-P structure of pyrophosphate is a central carbon of the P-C-P structure of bisphosphonaten.

BPs retain a relatively high affinity for hydroxyapatite found in bone but are not hydrolyzed by phosphatases in humans or other vertebrates. Table 67.1 lists the generic names and structures of marketed BP products including the more common brand names used in the United States.

### Pharmacokinetics

### Absorption

The bioavailability of BPs after oral administration is generally low (i.e., <1%),6 when administered at least 2 hours prior to a meal. Food and beverages (other than water) reduce bioavailability by about 90% when BPs are dosed with a meal and reduced by about 50% if taken 30 to 60 minutes before food. One exception is enteric-coated risedronate 35 mg (Atelvia) that has a bioavailability when taken with food that is like that of regular risedronate 35 mg tablets taken fasting, 4 hours before a meal. Doses of BPs greater than 100 mg typically have higher bioavailability. The fractional bioavailability of ibandronate 100 mg is 30% greater and 150 mg 91% greater than the fractional bioavailability of

ibandronate 50 mg than that of a 50 mg tablet. The fractional bioavailability of etidronate 400 or 800 mg for Paget's disease is approximately 3%.

### Distribution and Metabolism

T 1/2

The kinetics of BPs in bone may be described by a threecompartment model: in bone extra-cellular fluid (ECF), on the bone surface, and within the bone matrix. The flow of BPs to bone is through afferent arteries and from bone to systemic ECF is through the efferent veins; there is no known diffusion of BPs from bone surfaces or matrix directly to or from the systemic ECF.

Due to the high affinity of BPs for hydroxyapatite on bone surfaces and very high bone surface area, the great majority (>99%) of BPs that flow into bone are initially retained on bone surfaces. Nonclinical studies demonstrated that [3H]alendronate was found almost exclusively on bone surfaces and was concentrated under active osteoclasts 4 hours after IV administration. However, 7 weeks later, very little [3H]alendronate remained on bone surfaces, and most was found within recently mineralized bone matrix. BPs trapped within mineralized bone remain there unless freed by new osteoclastic bone resorption. BPs are not metabolized and once resorbed and released into bone ECF they may (1) bind to another bone surface or (2) leave bone and reenter the systemic circulation. BPs recycled from bone into blood are either terminally eliminated in urine or reenter bone anywhere in the skeleton.

Elimination of BPs in urine occurs through both glomerular filtration and tubular secretion, the latter via a transport system shared by alendronate and etidronate. While the great majority of oral BPs pass through the gastrointestinal (GI) tract without being absorbed, less than 1% of IV alendronate is excreted through the GI tract.10,12
