### Mechanism of Action

Pregabalin and gabapentin are synthetic molecules that are structurally related to GABA. Both structures are derived by the addition of a cyclohexyl or branched-chain aliphatic carbohydrate moiety to the GABA backbone. However, the three-dimensional shapes of pregabalin and gabapentin are significantly different from GABA. The amine (NH2) and carboxyl groups (CO2H) are closer to each other than in the native GABA structure. It is proposed that this difference in the three-dimensional structure of pregabalin and gabapentin versus GABA accounts for their different pharmacologic activities.128,

Although the exact mechanism of action of gabapentin and pregabalin is unknown, results from animal models suggest that pregabalin modulates neuronal hyperexcitability, resulting in analgesic and anti-convulsant effects. Reduction of neurotransmitter release occurs because pregabalin selectively binds to the α2-δ of the N and P/Q subtypes of calcium channels of neurons in the brain and spinal cord, thereby modulating calcium influx into presynaptic cells. Therefore, there is less postsynaptic activation through the AMPA/kainite, NMDA, and neurokinin receptors. Unlike the opioids, which limit calcium influx via a G protein pathway, no tolerance is associated with pregabalin and gabapentin. Gabapentin and pregabalin do not have any effect on L-type calcium channels (e.g., verapamil); therefore there is no effect on blood pressure. New evidence suggests that gabapentin's site of action, unlike pregabalin, is at the locus coeruleus rather than the spinal dorsal horn. A recent study delivering gabapentin by the spinal route had no effect on pain. 30,131

### Pharmacology of Gabapentin and Pregabalin

### Gabapentin

Gabapentin has a nonlinear bioavailability with a reduction in absorption as the dose increases. This is the result of an active and saturable transport mechanism. Gabapentin in a 900-mg dose has 60% bioavailability, and a 3600-mg dose has only 33% bioavailability. More frequent delivery of smaller doses may improve bioavailability through the saturable transport mechanism. It is less than 3% protein bound, and because of its high lipid solubility, it readily penetrates the CNS. Gabapentin is not metabolized and is excreted unchanged in the urine. Therefore renal impairment will

significantly increase the drug half-life. Studies have shown efficacy at doses up to 1800 mg and 2400 mg; however, doses greater than 1800 mg/day do not appear to be more efficacious, and the current maximum FDA-approved dose to treat pain is 1800 mg/ day. Because of its nonlinear kinetics, titration of gabapentin to an effective dose can be prolonged with an average onset of 10 to 14 days after initiation.

### Pregabalin

Pregabalin is not dependent on active transport for absorption and therefore has linear kinetics with bioavailability of about 90%. Unlike gabapentin, pregabalin absorption is independent of dose. It has negligible protein binding and readily penetrates into the central nervous system. Pregabalin is not metabolized and is excreted unchanged in the urine; therefore renal impairment will significantly increase the drug half-life, and dose adjustments are required. The effective dose of pregabalin is between 150 and 300 mg/day. Owing to the linear kinetics and high bioavailability, the effective dose can be achieved in 2 to 3 days; therefore onset is faster than with gabapentin.

### Toxicity of Gabapentin and Pregabalin

Neither gabapentin nor pregabalin has any significant drug interactions, and protein binding is minimal. Because gabapentin and pregabalin have similar mechanisms of action, their side effect profiles are very similar. The most common side effects with at least more than twice the incidence of placebo in controlled trials were dizziness, somnolence, dry mouth, peripheral edema, blurred vision, weight gain, and thinking abnormalities. Dizziness and somnolence usually began shortly after initiation of therapy, and most cases resolved with continued dosing. Dizziness and somnolence are dose related and can be reduced with slow titration. This side effect can also be an advantage when administered at night in that it will improve sleep. Controlled studies with gabapentin and pregabalin have demonstrated improved sleep quality compared with placebo.1, Xerostomia (dry mouth) is dose dependent; however, it is usually mild, and few withdrawals from clinical trials have resulted from this side effect. Peripheral edema occurred in almost a third of subjects in clinical trials. It does not appear to be dose related, nor is it associated with any cardiovascular, renal, or hepatic abnormalities. It is more common with the concomitant use of a thiazolidinedione antidiabetic agent. Blurred vision is dose related and usually resolves with continued use. It is not associated with any ocular abnormalities. Weight gain is as high as 8% of baseline weight but is not associated with any cardiac, renal, or hepatic abnormalities. A mildly increased appetite was reported in epilepsy and fibromyalgia trials. There is no association with baseline body mass index (BMI), sex, or age. Weight gain appears to plateau and is mild. Thinking abnormalities are typical of anticonvulsants and are consistent with the calcium channel modulation mechanism of these agents. Thinking abnormalities tend to be mild but can be bothersome enough in some patients to lead to discontinuation.

Anti-convulsants, including gabapentin and pregabalin, have approximately twice the risk of suicidal ideation over placebo. This increased risk is not age related and appears to occur at between 1 and 24 weeks of therapy. Patients should be warned of this side effect and instructed to contact their health care provider immediately if it occurs.

Studies with pregabalin have shown a mild PR interval prolongation that was not associated with increased risk of secondor third-degree atrioventricular block. Pregabalin may result in a mildly decreased platelet count, which is not associated with an increase in bleeding-related adverse events. Pregabalin may also result in mild elevations in creatinine kinase, which are asymptomatic in most patients.

In controlled clinical trials of pregabalin, more patients reported euphoria compared with placebo. In a follow-up drug likability study in recreational drug users of sedative-hypnotics, pregabalin subjects reported a "good drug effect," "high," and "liking" to a

degree that was similar to 30 mg of diazepam. In addition, clinical studies showed withdrawal symptoms of insomnia, nausea, headache, and diarrhea. Therefore the FDA approved the drug with a category V controlled substance schedule. Although pregabalin is Schedule V, it has very low abuse potential. As with any anticonvulsant therapy, pregabalin and gabapentin should be withdrawn slowly over at least a week to avoid withdrawal symptoms (Fig. 68.3).

### Muscle Relaxants

Patients frequently describe muscular pain as "spasms," and clinicians clearly know that loss of range of motion is detrimental to their patients. It makes sense that a medicine that acts as a "muscle relaxant" would be of great value in treating patients with these complaints. Unfortunately, skeletal muscle relaxants do not have a primary role in the treatment of chronic pain because of limited true effects on muscles, significant side effect profiles, drug interactions, or addiction potential.

The list of medications classified as skeletal muscle relaxants is highly diverse (Fig. 68.4). Because each of the drugs in this class has a unique mechanism of action and side effect profile, each medication from this class must be examined separately. Adding to the difficulty of understanding these medications is the lack of consensus as to how or why they provide benefit. The two approved clinical indications are for treatment in upper motor neuron diseases that result in spasticity and in peripheral musculoskeletal disorders that cause pain and spasms. Each of these medications can thus be classified as an antispastic or antispasmodic agent. These medications should not be used as first-line medications and usually should be used in conjunction with other pain medications. In addition, most antispasmodic medications come with restriction of use to 2 to 3 weeks. Despite this, many skeletal muscle relaxants are prescribed on a long-term basis for chronic conditions.

Understanding the reflex arc in muscle is important in understanding where these agents act. The simplest reflex is monosynaptic. A muscle spindle transmits an efferent signal through the Ia afferent neuron; this enters the dorsal horn of the spinal cord and synapses on an alpha motoneuron. This neuron then exits the spinal cord through the ventral root and innervates the extrafusal fibers of the same muscle, causing a contraction in the muscle. The Ia afferent signal is also transmitted polysynaptically through interneurons that inhibit alpha motoneurons of antagonist muscles, causing them to relax. Gamma motoneurons located in the ventral horn adjust the sensitivity of the muscle spindles to stretch. They travel with the alpha motoneurons and receive input from cutaneous receptors and many supraspinal pathways, including the corticospinal and reticulospinal tracts. Polysynaptic spinal reflexes with supraspinal connections are much more abundant

than monosynaptic reflexes. These connections are both excitatory and inhibitory, providing improved control and feedback to set and fine-tune motor tone. The main tract that inhibits spinal reflexes is the dorsal reticulospinal tract, and the main excitatory pathway is the bulbopontine tegmentum.

Spasticity occurs in upper motoneuron disorders such as multiple sclerosis, spinal cord injuries, traumatic brain injuries, strokes, and cerebral palsy. These diseases cause loss of descending inhibition from the brain to the spinal cord, leading to muscular hypertonicity and increased resistance to stretch. This presentation, which is classically described as a "clasp-knife phenomenon,' D> tends to affect the flexors of the upper extremities and the extensors of the lower extremities more than other muscle groups. Medications approved for spasticity include baclofen (Lioresal), dantrolene (Dantrium), tizanidine (Zanaflex), and diazepam (valium).

The antispasmodic agents are used to treat muscle pain and spasms when hypertonicity, hyperreflexia, or other signs of upper motoneuron disorders are not present. This presentation is much more common than spasticity and would include syndromes such as fibromyalgia, tension headaches, myofascial pain disorders, and nonspecific back pain. Medications include cyclobenzaprine (Flexeril), carisoprodol (Soma), metaxalone (Skelaxin), chlorzoxazone (Parafon Forte), methocarbamol (Robaxin), and orphenadrine (Norflex). Tizanidine and benzodiazepines are approved for both spasticity and musculoskeletal disorders. How each of these drugs improves these conditions is not completely clear, but the nonspecific sedative effects may have greater importance than the effects on muscles or spinal reflexes.

### Antispasmodic Medications

### Baclofen

Baclofen blocks presynaptic and postsynaptic GABAB recep- 136,137 tors and disrupts polysynaptic and monosynaptic reflexes at the spinal cord level. Oral doses usually start at 5 mg three times/day with a maximum dose of 80 mg/day. This medication frequently can be used intrathecally for the same indication with a reduction in clinical side effects. Sedation, weakness, hypotension, nausea, depression, and constipation have been reported. Titrating slowly and adjusting for renal impairment can limit the development of the previously stated side effects. Withdrawal symptoms include hallucinations, seizures, and pruritus.

### Dantrolene

Dantrolene acts directly on the muscle by decreasing the release of calcium from skeletal muscle sarcoplasmic reticulum. It has a black box warning about hepatotoxicitiy. Its risk is much greater with patients taking 800 mg/day or more compared with doses of 400 mg/day. It is recommended to stop this medication after 45 days if no benefit is derived.

### Tizanidine

Tizanidine is a centrally acting agonist of the α2 receptor .141,142 that reduces the release of excitatory amino acids from the presynaptic terminal of spinal interneurons. This reduces tonic stretch reflexes and polysynaptic reflex activity. Doses start at 2 to 4 mg at night and increase by 2 to 4 mg three to four times/day with a maximum dose of 36 mg/day. Side effects include hypotension,

sedation, and dry mouth. Its major route of elimination is renal, and renal impairment can significantly decrease clearance. It is metabolized via CYP1A2, and concomitant use with ciprofloxacin or fluvoxamine is contraindicated. Elevated liver functions— three times the upper level of normal—have occurred in 5% of patients. Monitoring of liver function is recommended. Acute withdrawal can cause hypertension, tachycardia, and hypertonia. Use with alcohol should be warned against, and oral contraceptives will decrease clearance with doses as low as 4 mg/day.

### Diazepam

Diazepam works by central blockade of GABAA, 139,146 which is an inhibitory neurotransmitter in the central nervous system. It was the first drug used to treat spasticity and is often used to compare new agents in clinical trials. Efficacy for spasticity and muscle pain is believed to be similar to that of benzodiazepines as a clas. Clinical trials showing efficacy with benzodiazepines are based on tetrazepam, which currently is not available in the United States. It is not considered a first-line agent for spasticity or muscle pain because of its sedative effects, drug interactions, and significant abuse potential.

### Cyclobenzaprine

Cyclobenzaprine is structurally related to tricyclic anti-depressants and thus causes sedation through its anticholinergic effects. It acts primarily at the brainstem to reduce tonic somatic motor activity influencing both gamma and alpha motoneurons. Dosing at 5 mg three times/day has shown similar efficacy compared with 10 mg three times/day with reduced side effects. The maximum daily dose is 30 mg. This medication also comes in 15and 30-mg extended-release formulations. Concomitant use with MAO inhibitors is contraindicated. This drug should not be used during the acute recovery phase of myocardial infarction or in patients with arrhythmias, heart block, congestive heart failure, or hyperthyroidism. The risk of seizures with tramadol is increased if this medication is added. The risk of serotonin syndrome can be increased in patients taking selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors.

### Carisoprodal

Carisoprodal in animal studies has shown muscle relaxation through altered interneuronal activity in the spinal cord and in the descending reticular formation of the brain. It is metabolized in the liver to meprobamate, a Schedule IV medication with abuse potential.152" Meprobamate binds to GABAA receptors, which results in further sedation. Doses start at 250 mg up to four times/day with a maximum dose of 1400 mg/day. It is contraindicated in patients with a history of acute intermittent porphyria. CYP1C19 inhibitors such as omeprazole or fluvoxamine may increase carisoprodal levels and decrease meprobamate. CYP1C19 inducers such as rifampin or St. John's wort increase exposure to meprobamate.

### Methocarbamol

Methocarbamol, a carbamate derivative of guaifenesin, is a central nervous system depressant with no direct action on striated muscle, the motor end plate, or the nerve fiber. It comes in 500and 750-mg tablets and can be given up to four times/day with a maximum dose of 8 g/day. The parenteral form has been associated with skin sloughing and thrombophlebitis. It should be used with caution in patients with myasthenia gravis receiving anticholinesterase agents.

### Metaxalone

Metaxalone also has no direct actions on muscles. Its effects occur mainly through generalized central nervous system depression. It tends to cause much less sedation than other drugs in this class and has limited drug interactions. It is contraindicated in druginduced, hemolytic anemias and in significantly impaired renal or hepatic function. The dose most commonly used is 800 mg three or four times/day.

### Chlorzoxazone

Chlorzoxazone is a centrally acting agent that acts primarily at the level of the spinal cord and subcortical areas of the brain, where it inhibits multisynaptic reflex arcs. Doses are 250 to 500 mg three or four times/day. Hepatocellular toxicity has been reported with this drug.

### Orphenadrine

Orphenadrine is derived from diphenhydramine. It does not directly relax muscles and possesses greater anticholinergic properties than diphenhydramine. Its dosage recommendation is 100 mg twice a day. It is contraindicated in patients with glaucoma, pyloric or duodenal obstruction, stenosing peptic ulcers, prostatic hyperplasia or obstruction of the bladder neck, cardiospasm (megaesophagus), and myasthenia gravis.

### Efficacy

Clinical studies using these drugs are very limited, poorly controlled, and of short duration. One meta-analysis153 found fair evidence that tizanidine and baclofen are roughly equivalent and are similar to diazepam for the treatment of spasticity. Investigators go on to state that data on efficacy for muscle relaxants with musculoskeletal conditions are limited, but for treatment compared with placebo, cyclobenzaprine, tizanidine, carisoprodol, and orphenadrine showed a consistent trend favoring active treatment. Data demonstrating effectiveness for chlorzoxazone, methocarbamol, baclofen, and dantrolene are limited. Last, data for metaxalone are mixed.

### Emerging Targets

### Chemokine Receptor Blockers

Chemokines are small peptides that control the trafficking of leukocytes, especially monocytes, to targeted tissues. There are numerous chemokine receptors (CCRs) involved in this trafficking process leading to inflammation and pain. Some of these CCR subtypes are more specific to inflammation and pain than others (for example CCR2). Highly specific CCR blockers are currently in phase II clinical trial for knee osteoarthritis pain.

### Mixed d Ligand Receptor Agonists

The analgesic effects of highly selective MOR agonists are well established. However, greater awareness of adverse effects and worse outcomes have led to recommendations to limit use for chronic pain. There have been recent developments in using low-selectivity and multifunctional "mixed ligands" to maintain analgesic effects while reducing the side effect profiles. Cebranopadol is a centrally acting mixed ligand that combines nociception/orphanin FQ peptide (NOP) receptor and opioid receptor agonists. NOP receptor activation is effective against neuropathic, inflammatory, and visceral pain with a broad therapeutic index with a low risk of respiratory

depression and addiction. The combination of the NOP and MOR agonists results in broad analgesic activity with reduced risk of respiratory depression and addiction compared with "traditional" opioids. A phase II study of cebranopadol in knee osteoarthritis (207 participants) showed that 400 µg (but not 200 µg and 75 µg) was superior to placebo (NCT01357837). A second trial (619 participants) compared 200 to 800 µg daily compared with placebo and oxycodone. Improvements in the Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index (WOMAC) score, pain subscale, and physical functioning were reported for the 200 μg and 400 µg doses compared with placebo (NCT01709214)

### TRP Vanilloid Channel Agonists (TRPV1)

TRPV1 channels are localized in sensory neurons and can be activated by vanilloid molecules such as capsaicin. CNTX-4975 is a synthetic form of tans-capsaicin that activates the TRPV1 channel, leading to densensitization of the nerve lasting several months. A phase II study using intra-articular injections showed significant improvements out to 24 weeks. Resiniferatoxin (RTX) is a highly potent TRPV1 agonist that may irreversibly defunctionalize the TRPV1-expressing nociceptors leading to long-lasting pain relief. Preliminary results of a phase 1b intra-articular injection of RTX study in patient with moderate to severe osteoarthritis of the knee showed a significant reduction in pain compared with placebo at 12 weeks.

### Cannabinoid Agonists

Type 1 cannabinoid receptors (CB1s) are located at multiple locations in the peripheral and central nervous system, whereas CB2 receptors are located on inflammatory cells (monocytes, B/T cells, mast cells). CB2 activation results in a reduction in inflammatory mediator release, plasma extravasation, and sensory terminal sensitization. Activation of peripheral CB1 receptors results in a reduction in the release of proinflammatory terminal peptides and a reduction in terminal sensitivity. Activation of central CB1 receptors leads to reduced dorsal horn excitability and activates descending inhibitory pathways in the brain. The net result is a reduction in both pain and hyperalgesia. Inhaled cannabis has been extensively studied in various pain syndromes with mixed results. More recent well-controlled trials in neuropathic pain have shown promise. Stativex is a sublingual spray containing a mixture of tetrahydrocannabinol and cannabidiol that failed to reach the primary efficacy end point in a phase III cancer pain trial. Studies with cannabis in musculoskeletal pain are limited; however, it reduces the pain of rheumatoid arthritis and chronic pain of various other causes. 159,160

# Nutrition and Rheumatic Diseases

### KEY POINTS

In all rheumatic disorders, weight control through dieting is advised to aid symptom improvement.

Diets of exclusion are not recommended due to potential drawbacks. Healthy balanced diet similar to Mediterranean-style diet is a part of the global management of patients with rheumatic disorders.

### Introduction

Inflammatory arthritis, which includes rheumatoid arthritis (RA), ankylosing spondylitis (AS), and psoriatic arthritis (PsA), has undergone a therapeutic revolution over two decades with the use of targeted therapies that have profoundly changed their prognosis. However, the management of these patients should not be restricted to pharmacologic drugs and to the treat-to-target strategy, as nonpharmacologic treatments also play an important role.1-3 Moreover, the holistic patient-centered care approach, beyond articular outcomes, is now emphasized, giving an important place to nondrug therapy. Along this line, changes in lifestyle behaviors in inflammatory arthritis have a central position, especially with the wish to incorporate wellness practices to improve quality of life and health status. 4,

Among the lifestyle behaviors, improving dietary habits has a special place because patients may consider that it is a natural way to manage their diseases themselves. Health-care professionals (HCPs) are also increasingly interested by this aspect of care. Such growing interest on both sides is well illustrated by recent dedicated recommendations from scientific societies (French Society of Rheumatology [SFR] and European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology [EULAR]) (Table 69.1, Box 69.1).4,

Dietary behavior improvement may represent a way to target joint symptoms, which can be especially relevant for subjective persistent symptoms (e.g., residual joint pain or stiffness), without the need for medication changes. Dietary changes can also be critical for managing associated comorbidities, such as depression, cardiovascular diseases, and osteoporosis, and the risk of cancer.

From the patient education perspective, change in dietary behavior can allow patients to be actively involved in their own

care beyond medication adherence. Such patient involvement can enhance empowerment, self-efficacy, and coping ability.

However, nutritional advice in inflammatory arthritis is not a substitute for disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs (DMARDs). It is essential that patients understand that dietary approaches are adjunctive to disease-modifying therapies. Indeed, nutritional intervention studies often have a low level of evidence due to methodological drawbacks. Further, efficacy of nutrition interventions remains modest compared with those related to DMARD, and they tend to focus only on symptoms, with no demonstrated effect on the structural damage noted in RA. They are therefore primarily additional adjunctive measures to pharmacologic treatments that must not interfere with DMARDs.

### Rationale fort the Use of Diet to Modulate the Immune System

A large majority of our immune system resides in the digestive tract and is therefore in close contact with food antigens and metabolites. Furthermore, immune cells from the digestive tract can migrate to the periphery and notably to the joints. Thus a digestive "priming" could have quite direct consequences on articular immune cells. Diet affects the immune system in several ways, outlined below.

### Direct Effects

Various nutrients are required for proper functioning of the immune system, including vitamins A, C, and E, zinc, and selenium. Deficiencies in these nutrients can impair immune function, while adequate intake can support optimal immune function. For example, vitamin D decreases Toll-like receptors (TLRs), TNF, and interleukin-6 (IL-6), while increasing tolerogenic dendritic cells and regulatory T cells. Vitamin D prevents arthritis in mouse models. Salt promotes T helper cell (Th)17 differentiation,12 and salt restriction prevents arthritis development in mice. Furthermore, the nutritional landscape affects immunometabolism and immune cell polarization. Antioxidants, such as vitamin C, vitamin E, and β-carotene, can also help neutralize reactive oxygen species and modulate immune function.

### ACR:

ACR, American College of Rheumatology; EULAR, European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology.

### Gut Microbiota

The gut microbiota, which consists of trillions of microorganisms that reside in the intestinal tract, play a critical role in immune system function. Certain dietary components, such as fiber, can influence the composition of the gut microbiota. Commensal bacteria, recognized by TLRs, mediates development of the host immune system and plays a crucial role in the maintenance of intestinal epithelial homeostasis. Gut microbiota modulates the immune system:

By releasing food metabolites: digestion of fiber releases shortchain fatty acids (SCFAs) that induce regulatory T cells in the intestinal epithelium, while digestion on L-carnitine releases trimethylamine N-oxide (TMAO) that promotes inflammation and tryptophan metabolites regulation gut barrier.

By releasing extra-cellular vesicles (EVs): EVs derive from either plasma membrane or intra-cellular membranes and carry proteins, nucleic acids, and lipids. Pathogenic bacteria-derived EVs have proinflammatory effects of host immune cells, while probiotic-derived EVs mostly shape the immune response toward tolerance.

Through membrane contacts: Polysaccharide A (PSA) derived from Bacteroides fragilis membranes induces regulatory T cells in the intestinal epithelium.

The gut microbiota shapes the intestinal barrier. Patients with inflammatory arthritis have an increased gut permeability that may precede disease symptoms.9, Leaky gut allows the passage of bacterial antigens. Those antigens might promote Th17 cells that can migrate to the joints.9, The Th17 environment will also favor alteration of anti-citrullinated protein antibodies (ACPA) glycosylation patterns that precede RA symptoms. In addition to its impact on immune system, the gut microbiota may also influence pain through vagal tone and the gut—brain axis (Fig. 69.1).

### Patient Belief and Experience About Diet and Inflammatory Arthritis

Different dietary patterns occur in the general population from "prudent" to "processed" patterns. Exclusion diets or consumption of organic food are increasingly practiced with the aim to improve health state and also for other nonmedical purposes (e.g., ecology). Of note, the World Health Organization (WHO) states that all adults should aim for a healthy, balanced diet

containing fruits, vegetables, nuts, and whole grains and limited free sugar, fat, and salt.

In the case of inflammatory arthritis, diet behaviors represent for the patient a natural way to influence their disease symptoms. Practices can be diverse and varied, ranging from avoidance of specific foods to more comprehensive exclusion diets. For example, in a recent U.S. study of 217 patients with RA, ≈25% of patients reported an effect (beneficial or detrimental) of foods on their symptoms, and ≈25% avoided certain foods to control their symptoms. In another study investigating several inflammatory diseases (inflammatory arthritis, psoriasis, and inflammatory bowel diseases), 28% to 42% of patients (depending on the disease) had changed their dietary habits since their diagnosis. Of note, the impact of dietary changes was sometimes negative (e.g., more fatigue), while others did not experience any particular effect, suggesting that a response to dietary changes does not occur in everyone and may differ across populations according to sociocultural specificities.

One critical point is that those dietary experiences of patients with inflammatory arthritis have long been underestimated by rheumatologists since the majority of patients engage in dietary modifications on their own without having sought the advice of HCPs. Patients use multiple sources of information easily accessible (social networks, websites, and health books), but the content is not always valid. Patients can thus be exposed to fake news, which can lead to false beliefs and erroneous practices, especially restrictive or popular fad diets. HCPs should therefore warn patients about promotion of diets based either on no data, on scientific empiricism, or on experimental pre-clinical or in vitro data that have not been translated in humans.

### Challenges in Studying Dietary Effects

### Dietary Assessment

It is challenging to accurately measure dietary intake in clinical trials or observational cohort studies, particularly over extended periods of time. Different methods of dietary assessment, such as food frequency questionnaires, 24-hour dietary recalls, and diet records, can be used. However, the reliability is often limited by recall bias or important variations that can exist between different preparations of a dish, for example. eHealth solutions might solve some limitations related to questionnaires in the near future.

### Confounding g Factors

It is impossible to evaluate a nutrient or food item individually. In fact, eating behaviors are often global. As an example, it was shown that people avoiding gluten are 14 times more likely to have an overall healthy dietary pattern. Moreover, diet is often just one of many lifestyle factors that can influence health outcomes. Other factors, such as physical activity, smoking, and alcohol consumption, are important confounding factors that need to be considered.

### Adherence in Interventional Studies

In interventional studies, adherence with dietary interventions is critical. However, it can be challenging to ensure that participants follow the prescribed diet consistently. Adherence can be affected by various factors, such as taste preferences, cultural habits, and social support. Moreover, the accurate nutritional supervision implemented in clinical studies is not always easily applicable to routine care.

### Study Design and Placebo Effect

While double-blind randomized controlled trials are the gold standard for evaluating the efficacy of interventions, it is not always possible in dietary intervention clinical trials. In some supplementation studies (e.g., omega-3), a double-blind design with a placebo arm can be readily achieved, whereas in some dietary intervention trials (mainly exclusion diets), it is not feasible to use a placebo control group, and the design is most often open-label, raising the problem of the placebo effect. In the context of dietary intervention trials, the placebo effect can be a concern because participants may experience changes in health outcomes simply because they believe they are receiving a beneficial treatment, even if the treatment has no actual effect on their health.

### Effect of Diet on Disease Risk Must Be Distinguished From Effect on Disease Activity

It is very important to distinguish studies investigating association between diet or nutrients and the risk of inflammatory arthritis from those investigating the effect of diet on disease activity and symptoms in established inflammatory arthritis. There are numerous case-control and cohort studies reporting an association between diet or nutrients or food and the risk of developing inflammatory arthritis. Table 69.2 summarizes foods and diet that may influence the risk of developing RA. However, their applicability in the care of patients with established disease is less clear since patients are not in a disease risk setting. Moreover, it is inaccurate to consider that diet alone or one type of food can prevent inflammatory arthritis, but rather that a global nutritional intervention should be integrated into a holistic preventive approach (smoking cessation, promotion of physical activity, stress management, etc.).

### Absence or Paucity of Scientific Data Does Not Mean Absence of Effect of Diet

Patients are interested mostly in exclusion diets such as intermittent fasting or ketogenic diet despite absence of clinical data in the context of inflammatory arthritis. It is important to consider that giving nutritional advice based on results from basic research studies (e.g., experimental murine models or cell culture experiments) do not necessarily translate to clinical effects. Another challenge occurs in the case of available clinical data that is very low quality, as frequently occurs for dietary factors. In conclusion, dietary interventions in clinical trials face several methodological and scientific challenges that often limit the quality and interpretability of dietary studies, which complicates the explanations given to the patient in practice.

### Weight Loss

Weight management is an important focus since obesity is a frequent comorbidity in inflammatory arthritis. Further, obesity is a risk factor of RA (especially seronegative) and of PsA, may worsen disease outcomes, and makes clinical assessment difficult, leading to erroneous clinical evaluation. Interestingly, in RA, not only are systemic inflammatory features (e.g., C-reactive protein [CRP] or number of synovitis) worse with obesity but so are subjective symptoms such as pain. This may lead to excessive DMARD prescription, which will be less effective because obese patients also respond less well to DMARDs, particularly anti-TNF drugs. Weight gain can also occur with use of anti-TNF drugs. Moreover, overweight and obesity are known to increase the risk of cardiovascular diseases and depression. Surprisingly, obesity is associated with less radiographic structural progression in RA.

Encouraging weight loss is part of the holistic management of the patients with inflammatory arthritis.4, Weight loss provides symptom alleviation and further decreases disease activity when combined with TNF inhibitor initiation: in a study with 126 patients with PsA, following a hypocaloric diet versus a freely managed diet, minimal disease activity (MDA) was more often achieved with the hypocaloric than the free managed diet (hazard ratio [HR] = 1.85; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.02 to 3.35) with a dose effect noted between the importance of weight loss and clinical response. Psoriasis may also improve with weight loss. In RA, a proof-of-concept, 12-week, single-blind, randomized controlled trial of 40 obese RA patients (body mass index [BMI] ≥ 30) with the disease activity score on 28 joints (DAS28) ≥ 3.2 indicated that a diet intervention (hypocaloric diet of 1000 to 1500 kcal/day and high-protein meal replacements) induced an average loss of 9.5 kg and provided significant improvements for Routine Assessment of Patient Index Data 3 (RAPID3) and positive trends for DAS28 and health-assessment questionnaire (HAQ)-Disability Index compared with control (0.5 kg loss).

Weight loss can also be achieved by bariatric surgery, which leads to substantial weight loss. According to a retrospective cohort study, bariatric surgery decreased disease activity in RA and may be associated with less RA-related medication use.

In practice, weight loss is encouraged possibly with the supervision by a dietitian and/or nutritionist, who will also explore the potential complications of obesity and who will avoid any nutritional deficiency during the weight loss program. Of course, the effect of weight loss goes beyond articular outcomes since it has a favorable cardiovascular, metabolic, and psychological effect. There is no specific predefined weight loss goal in inflammatory arthritis.

The role of the rheumatologist is to document patient weight, calculate body mass index, and initiate a discussion about obesity and the need for weight loss: such a discussion is an important first step to induce dietary change behaviors.5, Some simple messages may be given to patients (e.g., intake of fruit, vegetables, and water; reducing unhealthy food/drinks; reducing portion sizes; and switching to lowcalorie food/drinks).

Some points of vigilance regarding weight loss in patients with inflammatory arthritis are (1) to explore unexplained weight loss or weight loss insufficiently explained by diet alone, as it may be a sign of another progressive condition; (2) weight loss must not be accompanied by muscle wasting and sarcopenia, especially in elderly patients with frailty; and (3) a long-term improvement in eating habits to maintain weight loss over time should be preferred rather than a strict hypocaloric diet that will not last over time. The pharmacologic management of obesity is currently evolving with the use of glucagon-like

peptide 1 (GLP-1) inhibitor, and thus weight loss management in the context of inflammatory arthritis will change soon.

### What Do We Know About Exclusion Diet in Inflammatory Arthritis?

In this section, we will present data exploring the effect of different exclusion diets on the risk of inflammatory arthritis development and on disease activity in established inflammatory arthritis. We will also discuss potential risk or disadvantages of each exclusion diet. The most popular diets will be addressed, that is the glutenfree and dairy-free diets, the vegetarian/vegan diet, fasting, and the ketogenic diet. Other diets, such as the paleo/Seignalet diet, the Kousmine diet, or a diet rich/poor/supplemented in starchy foods (bread, cereals, potatoes, pulses) or "acidic" foods (tomatoes, etc.), are practiced by some patients, but there are no data in the literature to be discussed.

### Gluten-Free Diet

A gluten-free diet is becoming very popular in the general population for its supposed beneficial effects on health, with around 10% of people without celiac disease avoiding gluten. This is also the case in patients affected by inflammatory arthritis. Among the patients with inflammatory arthritis who declared to have change their dietary habits, about 25% followed a gluten-free diet.

### Are Inflammatory Arthritis and Celiac Disease Linked?

Contrary to their specific HLA pre-disposition, RA and celiac disease share multiple non-HLA loci. A recent mendelian randomization study suggested that genetically predisposed RA increased the risk of celiac disease in individuals of European descent by 46%, while genetic predisposition to celiac disease was not associated with an increased risk of RA. In a small cohort of 45 patients with celiac disease, ACPA-specific auto-antibodies seemed to be overrepresented, as they were found in 35% of the patients. However, an association between RA and celiac disease remains very rare. Moreover, perceived gluten intolerance is reported with a prevalence similar in RA patients as in the general population. Mucosal reactivity to gluten is seen in a minor fraction of RA patients and is not related to the frequently perceived intolerance to these proteins.

### Does Gluten Increase the Risk of Inflammatory Arthritis?

No study supports the link between gluten consumption and the risk of developing inflammatory arthritis.

### Is a Gluten-Free Diet Effective in Decreasing Joint Symptoms?

Some patients report symptom improvement after eliminating gluten from their diets. No randomized study has evaluated the effects of a gluten-free diet alone. Three randomized controlled studies were performed involving a combined a gluten-free diet with a vegan diet,48,49 with or without prior fasting,50 or with meat and dairy product exclusion. The diet was followed for 1 year and for 3.5 (preceded by a 10-day fast) and 3 months, respectively. These small studies suffer from important methodological issues. While the outcomes were evaluated by an independent observer in the first study, the evaluation was open in the others. Moreover, a large proportion of the patients in the "intervention" group dropped out from the study before it ended (42% [16 of 38], 37% [10 of 27], and 30% [12 of 40], respectively), and in the first and last studies,

the effectiveness was only determined in the patients who completed the study (per protocol analysis), which greatly limits ability to make valid conclusions. In the subgroup of patients who finished the first study, DAS28 decreased significantly in the intervention group (from 5.3 to 4.3; P < .001) but not in the control group (from 5.3 to 5.0; P = .19). In the third study, DAS28 did not improve significantly; visual activity score decreased significantly after the exclusion diet (from 50 to 40; P = .003), while the decrease was not significant in the control group. No intergroup comparison was performed. In the second study, where an intention-to-treat analysis was done, the number of tender and swollen joints was less during the follow-up period in the intervention group. Nevertheless, it is important to note that patients in the intervention group still had on average 18 tender joints and 8 swollen joints, which is not anywhere near the current treatment target for RA. Also, structural progression was observed in both groups. In the first two studies, the patients in the intervention groups lost a significant amount of weight (mean ≈ 4.2 and 6 kg, respectively), contrary to patients in the control groups (mean ≈ 0.7 and 0 kg, respectively). This weight loss could at least partly explain the observed effect.

### What Are the Potential Disadvantages of a Gluten-Free Diet?

First, the cost of gluten-free products is two to three times that of the standard corresponding foods. Then, while gluten-free products are perceived as healthier than conventional products, they contain fewer proteins and more monounsaturated fatty acids, carbohydrates, and sugar. In addition, following a strict gluten-free diet may have impact on patients' lives socially. Moreover, two American cohorts suggest that, in the general population, the consumption of gluten may have cardiometabolism benefits. Using two U.S. longitudinal cohorts with 26 years follow-up, over 2.27 million patient-years, and 6529 coronary events, gluten consumption was associated with 15% decreased coronary risk after adjustments for cardiovascular risk factors and cereal consumption. Gluten consumption also decreased the risk of diabetes by 20%. Given that cardiovascular risk is increased in patients with inflammatory arthritis, this is important data to consider when assessing the benefit/risk balance of the glutenfree diet in inflammatory arthritis. Thus the French national rheumatology recommendation proposed that "A gluten-free diet should not be proposed as a means to control chronic inflammatory rheumatic disease activity, in the absence of confirmed celiac disease."6

### Dairy-Free Diet

### Do Dairy Products Increase the Risk of Inflammatory Arthritis?

As with gluten, the belief that dairy products have deleterious effects is widespread. Nevertheless, there are no studies supporting this hypothesis in inflammatory arthritis. Dairy consumption is not associated with the risk of RA.

### Is a Dairy-Free Diet Effective in Decreasing Joint Symptoms?

In a pre-clinical study, bovine milk—derived extra-cellular vesicles were beneficial, attenuating arthritis scores. As with gluten, the intestinal mucosa of RA patients is not hyper-reactive to cow's milk proteins, and there is no correlation between the intolerance experienced by the patient and the reactivity of the intestinal mucosa. In patients, the only data in the literature comes from a study in which the reintroduction of dairy products after the vegan period did not lead to a change in joint parameters. To our knowledge, no other controlled

human or animal studies have been conducted on the effect of dairy products, or their avoidance, in inflammatory arthritis.

### What Are the Potential Disadvantages of a Dairy-Free Diet?

Dairy products are the main dietary source of calcium. Patients with inflammatory arthritis are at increased risk of osteoporosis due to their disease and frequent and prolonged exposure to corticosteroids. A recent meta-analysis confirms the beneficial effect of calcium supplementation for 12 to 24 months on bone mineral density, especially in countries with low dietary calcium intake. Another cohort metaanalysis reported a protective effect of high dairy consumption on hip fracture risk, with a 13% risk reduction. This fracture risk reduction was observed with fermented dairy products (i.e., yogurts, cheese, and fermented milk) but not with milk. However, this work has been criticized because of the great variability from one study to another of the definitions of the consumption categories, leading to a possible classification bias, as well as the many possible confounding factors. Indeed, patients at higher risk of fracture may voluntarily consume more dairy products.

In addition, fermented dairy products also appear to decrease cardiovascular events (stroke, myocardial infarction, ischemic heart disease, and cardiovascular mortality) by 4%, the risk of type 2 diabetes by 27%, and the risk of metabolic syndrome by 20%. Whole milk consumption was also associated with a lower coronary calcification score at inclusion and less progression during follow-up after multiple adjustments. Thus the working group proposed following the recommendations issued for the general population, which are an intake of two dairy products per day for adults. Because fermented dairy products are more digestible and could have more marked extraarticular beneficial effects, they could potentially be a favored form of dairy intake.

### Fasting

Three controlled studies have been conducted on fasting in RA: one with a short-term evaluation of a 7-day fast involving 13 patients (cross-over study)63 and two with an evaluation of a 7to 10-day fast followed by a lacto-vegetarian diet for 9 weeks64 (n = 26) or a glutenfree vegan diet for 3.5 months followed by a lacto-vegetarian diet for 9 months (study described in the previous paragraph, n = 53). The first study showed a short-term beneficial effect of fasting but did not provide any information on the maintenance of joint effects after return to eating. The second study reported a beneficial effect of fasting in 5 of the 15 patients, but this was not maintained after the lacto-vegetarian diet period. In the third study, the beneficial effect on joints was obtained at the end of the fasting period, and the vegetarian diet maintained this effect without providing any additional benefit. However, the analysis was conducted on a per-protocol basis, without considering the numerous patients who discontinued the intervention (10 of 27 in the intervention group and 9 of 26 in the control group), which makes the results difficult to interpret. In conclusion, although a prolonged 7-day fast might have beneficial effects, these do not seem to be maintained after refeeding, which considerably limits its value. It is important to remember that prolonged fasting must be strictly medically supervised. No interventional study has explored alternative fasting of shorter duration.

### Vegan/Vegetarian

In addition to the studies mentioned above, two other studies in RA patients combined a vegetarian diet with either omega-3rich fish oil65 or lactobacillus-rich drinks. In the groups without omega-3 supplementation in the first study, only pain was improved by the vegetarian diet compared with the Western diet

(no effect on the number of painful or swollen joints or on the HAQ). The other study found no significant effect of vegetarian diet on RA activity parameters. Thus the data on the vegetarian or vegan diet do not support joint efficacy. In addition, meat consumption is not associated with the risk of RA.

### What Do We Know About Mediterranean Dietary Pattern and Omega-3 Fatty Acids?

### What Is the Mediterranean Dietary Pattern?

The Mediterranean dietary pattern is based on the traditional foods that people used to eat in countries bordering the Mediterranean Sea. It corresponds to a various and balanced diet and is characterized by high consumption of unprocessed cereals, fruits, legumes, vegetables, and olive oils and a low intake of animal products. The features of this diet are described in the Box 69.2. A benefit of this diet has been shown mainly on cardiovascular events and neurologic diseases.

### Do Mediterranean Diet and Omega-3 3 Fatty Acids Decrease the Risk of Inflammatory Arthritis?

In the American cohorts of nurses, NHS-I and NHS-II (3,511,050 person-years of follow-up and 913 incident cases of RA), a Mediterranean dietary pattern did not decrease the risk of RA in women.' 67 However, in the same cohorts, a healthy lifestyle, assessed on five modifiable components, i.e., smoking, alcohol consumption, body mass index, physical activity, and diet, was associated with a decreased risk of RA. In a French cohort of 62,629 women with 480 incident cases of RA, the Mediterranean diet adherence score was also not significantly associated with RA risk (HR = 0.86 [95% CI, 0.67 to 1.09] for high score versus low score; P = .09). However, among eversmokers, a higher score was associated with a decreased risk of RA (HR = 0.91 [95% CI, 0.84 to 0.99] for one-point increase in score; P = .03). Fish is probably the food most often considered protective. Fish consumption is associated with a decreased risk of RA. A 100-g/day increment in fish intake is associated with a 15% decreased risk of RA. Dose—response analysis shows a modest U-shaped association between fish consumption and incidence of RA, with the lowest risk at a fish intake of 20 to 30 g/day.

### Is a Mediterranean-Type Diet Effective in Decreasing Joint Symptoms?

Five randomized controlled studies on the joint effect of a Mediterranean diet in inflammatory arthritis have been conducted, including three in Scandinavian countries, one in England, and one in Mexico.70-74 Three were open-label studies, and two were studies with independent assessors. The quality of the studies was poor (Jadad score between 0 and 3). In two articles, no details were available on the proposed diet. For the others, regular consumption of fish (more than two times/week or three to four times/ week depending on the study), whole grains (several servings/day), fruits and vegetables (at least five servings/day), legumes (one to two or more than two/week depending on the study), nuts and oilseeds (daily), and low-fat dairy (limit other dairy) were recommended with limited meat consumption (red meat fewer than two times/week or any meat three times/week or fewer) and the use of vegetable fat (margarine, olive oil, or grape seed oil). No study encouraged alcohol consumption, but one study suggested regular

In addition to dietary modifications, one study proposed probiotics,70 and another suggested a program of sustained physical activity. Three studies showed a significant improvement in joint symptoms,71-73 one study showed no difference between the intervention and control arms, although both arms received a sustained physical activity program. Finally, the last study showed no significant improvement in the primary endpoint, but the DAS28-ESR (erythrocyte sedimentation rate) decreased significantly during the intervention periods compared with the control periods in unadjusted analysis (cross-over study). Thus although studies are few and of poor quality, there might be a favorable signal in favor of a beneficial symptomatic joint effect of the Mediterranean-type diet in RA.

In addition, the Spanish PREDIMED study, involving 7447 subjects at high cardiovascular risk in primary prevention, showed a reduction of approximately 30% in major cardiovascular events with a Mediterranean-type diet enriched with olive oil or nuts compared with a low-fat diet. In this study, the proposed Mediterranean diet included more than three servings of fruit/day, two servings of vegetables/day, three servings of fish/week, less than one serving of red or processed meat/day, and one serving of fat spread/day accompanied by an intake of olive oil (50 g/day or 4 tablespoons) or nuts/dry fruits (30 g/day with 15 g of walnuts, 7.5 g of almonds, and 7.5 g of hazelnuts). The Mediterranean-type diet should thus be recommended to patients with inflammatory arthritis primarily for its cardiometabolic effects and possibly for its symptomatic articular effects and is somewhat close to what is recommended in the general population by the WHO. EULAR does not specifically recommend this diet but advocates a healthy, balanced diet, which is in line with a Mediterranean-type diet. The 2022 American College of Rheumatology (ACR) Guideline for Exercise, Rehabilitation, Diet, and Additional Integrative Interventions for Rheumatoid Arthritis conditionally recommends the Mediterranean diet (in conjunction with DMARD therapy) over no formally defined diet and also conditionally recommends against any other formally defined diet.75a

### Are e Omega-3 Fatty Acids Effective in Decreasing Joint Symptoms?

Contrary to the other interventions, polyunsaturated fatty acid supplementation was evaluated in 43 randomized controlled trials against placebo, and several meta-analyses were performed. The vast majority of the studies involved patients with RA. Supplementation with polyunsaturated fatty acids significantly reduced all the clinical parameters studied, with a significant effect on activity visual analog scale (VAS); a moderate effect on pain VAS, DAS28, and HAQ; and a weak effect on morning stiffness. It also significantly reduced the sedimentation rate but not C-reactive protein.

Most of the studies involved supplementation for 3 to 6 months, a supplementation of at least 2 g/day of omega-3 of animal origin, with mainly fish oil and eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA)/docosahexaenoic acid (DHA). Analyses after 1 month did not show a significant effect, suggesting that supplementation should last at least 3 months. Most studies involved omega-3 supplementation and, less frequently, other polyunsaturated fatty acids (omega-6, omega-9). There are no structural data, and this supplementation can only be considered as a complement to medical treatment for inflammatory arthritis. Although the data are based on few studies and not definitive, a recent meta-analysis suggested a protective effect on the risk of cardiovascular events of polyunsaturated fatty acid supplementation only at doses of 2 g/day and greater.

Conversely to the EULAR recommendations, the French guidelines about diet in inflammatory arthritis advocated the possibility of a supplementation by capsule, with a preference for fish oils (essentially EPA and DHA) at dosages of 2 to 3 g/day for a period of 3 to 6 months, which should be re-evaluated according to the effects observed by the patient (Table 69.1, Box 69.2).4, It should be noted that supplementation at high doses or for very long periods of time could be associated with an increased risk of bleeding, and it is therefore preferable to respect these dosages and prescription periods. To date, there are no data on the prescription of repeated courses of treatment, and it is therefore difficult to propose a frequency or number of courses of treatment to be offered if the patient experiences beneficial effects. Importantly, no structural protection has been shown with omega-3 supplements, which may have only a symptomatic effect. Patients can also be encouraged to increase their dietary intake of essential polyunsaturated fatty acids, mainly omega-3, in particular by following a Mediterranean diet.

### Specific Dietary Supplements

Many dietary supplements have been proposed to control inflammatory arthritis activity. The most studied supplements are vitamins (A, B, C, D, E), probiotics, or trace elements (selenium or zinc).78, Overall, none of them have displayed relevant clinical efficacy and thus cannot be recommended to specifically alleviate joint symptoms. However, the usefulness of vitamin B9 (i.e., folic acid) and of vitamin D for methotrexate tolerance and bone health, respectively, is not questioned.

Concerning probiotics, such a strategy seems very attractive considering the role of gut dysbiosis in immune response. However, studies investigating probiotics have reported heterogenous results, and their interpretation is limited by the different strains of probiotics, heterogeneity across studies, and few or no replication studies. Overall, it is impossible to specially recommend one strain of probiotic to alleviate joint symptoms without eliminating a potential benefit from other strains. Some other supplements presented as encapsulated spices concentrates such as saffron, ginger, garlic, or sesamin have been sparsely evaluated with interesting results, but these results need replication in larger trials. The 2022 ACR guideline regarding integrative interventions for rheumatoid arthritis conditionally recommends following established dietary recommendations without dietary supplements over adding dietary supplements.75a

### How to Deal With Diet in Patients With Inflammatory Arthritis: Practical Aspects

In practice, we face two types of situations: patients who want or have started an exclusion diet and patients who want general

recommendations. In the first situation, it is essential to listen and remain pragmatic. Large-scale interventional studies are lacking, and small studies might suffer from interpatient variability. However, it is important to stay open-minded and listen to patients' feelings and experiences and to keep in mind that absence of data on one specific diet does not mean that it is not effective. We propose explaining possible deleterious effects of a gluten-free diet on cardiovascular risk and lack of evidence for efficacy on joints, as well as beneficial effects of fermented milk (on bone, the cardiovascular system, and metabolic syndrome) and lack of evidence of diary-free diet efficacy on inflammatory arthritis. If patients still wish to practice exclusion diets, we recommend proposing the advice of a dietician to avoid deficiencies with alternative source of calcium if dairy-free, of fiber if gluten-free, and of iron, B12, and zinc if vegan. We propose to insist on the "diagnostic" interest of the approach with no need to prolong the diet if it is not effective on symptoms and the importance of gradually reintroducing foods to achieve a balanced diet as much as possible.

In the second situation, we support overweight and obese individuals toward weight loss by referring patients to a nutritionist and encouraging a Mediterranean diet and a diet rich in omega-3 and olive oil. Omega-3 EPA/DHA supplementation of >2 g/day as complements may also be proposed. Addressing the problem of obesity as a comorbidity aggravating inflammatory arthritis outcome is critical.

More generally, beyond these two situations, the rheumatologist should inquire about patients' dietary habits and to ask whether they have tried some specific diet for their arthritis. This will be the first step to initiate discussion about dietary issues. Finally, the rheumatologist has to not forget the usefulness of some specific diets in specific medical settings such as diabetes, osteoporosis, gout, and sarcopenia.

### Diet and Other Types of Arthritis

### Osteoarthritis

In osteoarthritis (OA), the main issue is weight management in case of overweight or obesity since they are main risk factors for OA (especially on knee), and higher body weight is associated with greater pain. Many studies have shown clinical efficacy in knee OA of various dietary interventions leading to weight loss. Among all interventions, bariatric surgery induces the most important weight loss in OA patients.82, Addressing weight loss is central in the management of patients with knee OA and may involve dietitian or nutritionist for supervision, follow-up, medical management, screening for obesity complications, and bariatric surgery discussion. Beyond obesity and overweight management, patients should be educated that there are no specific diets shown in trials to be effective for OA. Cohort studies have shown that oral dietary fiber intake could decrease the risk of symptomatic knee OA and pain worsening. In a more global approach, analyses from the Osteoarthritis Initiative cohort indicated that higher adherence to Mediterranean diet is associated with a lower risk of knee OA incidence, less knee pain worsening, better knee function, and better quality of life.85, Two studies on probiotics (Lactobacillus casei or Streptococcus thermophilus) have not shown any relevant efficacy in knee OA.87,

Many oral supplements have been investigated in OA without identifying one of them unanimously as providing relevant clinical efficacy on OA-related symptoms. There is a particular interest in vitamin D, curcuma, and omega-3 fatty acids. Several well-conducted clinical trials indicated that vitamin D does not

provide any efficacy.1, Curcuma supplements have given interesting results, but the studies are very heterogeneous, especially in term of the nature of the curcuma formulation. In a randomized double-blinded placebo-controlled trial including 235 patients with knee OA, supplementation with high-dose omega-3 (4 g krill oil/day 4 g containing 0.60 g EPA/d, 0.28 g DHA/day, and 0.45 g astaxanthin/day) provided a statistically significant effect on pain over placebo (mixed vegetable oil), but with debatable clinical relevance. Finally, a well-balanced healthy diet in association with physical activity will be helpful for general health and certainly on osteoarthritis symptoms, especially in case of weight loss if appropriate.

### Systemic Lupus Erythematosus

In systemic lupus erythematosus, higher weight is associated with worse function, comorbidities, and mental health, justifying the inclusion of weight loss in the global management of the patients. Healthy lifestyle including physical activity and healthy diet is again advocated. A diet that addresses the adverse effects of glucocorticoids should be considered. There is no supplement that can be recommended, although omega-3 could improve some parameters. Again, a healthy diet is not viewed as an alternative to drug therapy but as a complementary strategy.

### Gout

Dietary factors in gout are reviewed in Chapter 97. Most studies to date have focused on the risk of developing gout. Overall, dietary factors have small effects on serum urate levels in people in the general population and in people with gout. Thus, uratelowering therapy is the foundational cornerstone to gout management. Nonetheless, avoidance of certain foods, such as animal sources of purines and alcohol of all types, is conditionally recommended by the 2020 ACR Guideline for the Management of Gout due to their associations with triggering gout flares, as well as avoidance of high-fructose corn syrup. However, the impact of diet on the long-term clinical course in gout, such as on tophi or radiographic damage, is uncertain. Weight loss is also conditionally recommended by the 2020 ACR Gout Guideline.

### Conclusion

Diet is an important factor for health in general since it interacts with gut microbiota and innate and adaptive immune response and subsequently modulates inflammation. Such interactions explain the close relationship with auto-immune process and influence on inflammatory arthritis.

The interest of rheumatologists for diet management in patients with inflammatory arthritis is recent and addresses patient expectations. Diet behavior improvement is a key objective of patient education and should be thus fully integrated in the holistic management of the patients for inflammatory arthritis outcomes, for comorbidities and for health status and disease copying. Such an approach must be combined with physical activity promotion but should not interfere with DMARD usage. It is important to acknowledge that the benefit of dietary changes remains modest and is primarily of low-quality evidence, especially considering the efficacy of DMARD.

In case of obesity, weight loss is recommended in all types of arthritis. A healthy balanced diet or the Mediterranean diet are generally advisable, and in fact, both are recommended by the WHO for the general population. There is no clear demonstration of

the usefulness of restrictive diets, but more high-quality trials are needed. Finally, it is essential that rheumatologists and nutritionists take up this subject in order to bring scientifically proven information to patients, who can be exposed to abundant fake news.

# Etiology of Rheumatoid Arthritis

70

### KEY POINTS

### Introduction

Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is one of the most common inflammatory arthritides, affecting from 0.5% to 1% of the general population worldwide. Although the prevalence is surprisingly constant across the globe, regardless of geographic location and race, there are some exceptions. For instance, the occurrence of RA is somewhat lower in China (~0.3%), whereas it is substantially higher in other groups, such as the Pima Indians in North America (~5%). Because of its prevalence and the ready accessibility of joint samples for laboratory investigation, RA has served as a useful model for the study of inflammatory and immune-mediated diseases. As

such, the information gleaned from these studies provides new unique insights into the mechanisms of normal immunity.

RA is primarily considered a disease of the joints, but abnormal systemic immune responses are evident throughout its course and can cause a variety of extra-articular manifestations, such as vasculitis, nodules, and accelerated atherosclerosis. These manifestations clearly show that RA has features of a systemic disease that can involve many organs. In some cases, autoantibody production with the formation of immune complexes that fix complement contribute to these extra-articular findings. One of the mysteries of RA is why the synovium is the primary target, although the unique structure of its vascular bed and the display of certain modified proteins (especially on solid surfaces like cartilage) provide an environment that is ideal for innate and adaptive immune responses.

Although the causes of RA remain uncertain, combinations of environmental and genetic influences clearly contribute. Clues have been provided by detailed immunogenetic research and observational studies demonstrating that asymptomatic autoimmunity (pre-RA) antedates the onset of arthritis by many years. Studies after the onset of clinical symptoms have implicated smallmolecule mediators of inflammation, autoantibodies, cytokines, growth factors, chemokines, adhesion molecules, epigenetics, aberrant signal transduction, and matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) in the pathogenesis of disease. Synovial mesenchymal cells display a variety of transcriptionally defined phenotypes, exhibit aggressive behavior, and can invade joint tissues. Irreversible loss of articular cartilage and bone can begin soon after the onset of RA; in some cases, bony abnormalities can be detected in the microarchitecture associated with progression to disease. Early treatment and very tight disease control through "treat-totarget" strategies improve long-term outcomes. Increased appreciation of how comorbidities, especially cardiovascular disease and accelerated atherosclerosis, affect mortality has also led to aggressive therapeutic paradigms to suppress synovial and systemic inflammation and improved long-term survival. Clinical trials in RA have also provided insights into the diversity of disease mechanisms, which can, in turn, help investigators translate clinical observations into a deeper understanding of disease etiology and pathogenesis (Video 70.1).

### How Rheumatoid Arthritis Begins F

The cause and pathogenesis of RA are complex and multifaceted. A variety of predetermined factors (genes) and stochastic factors (random events and environmental triggers) contribute to susceptibility and pathogenesis. A summary of how these mechanisms interact to create and perpetuate RA is shown in Fig. 70.1. Individual mechanisms are discussed in greater detail throughout the chapter.

The initiation of RA begins years before the onset of clinical symptoms. The onset involves certain polymorphisms in specific genes and inflammation at mucosal surfaces that can lead to modification of proteins, ultimately leading to production of antibodies against these neoepitopes. This process evolves through antigen spreading and ultimately helps break immunologic tolerance with concomitant autoreactivity. The earliest phases are marked by environmental stress, either through toxic exposures or activation of innate immunity (see Fig. 70.1). Cigarette smoke

is the best characterized, but some studies also implicate bacterial products, viral components, local infections on mucosal surfaces, and other environmental stimuli. These stresses induce enzymes that lead to the modification of normal peptides, most commonly through conversion of arginine to citrulline but possibly through other pathways like carbamylation or production of malonyldialdehyde—acetaldyde adducts.

Protein modification occurs often in healthy people, is selflimited, and has no obvious deleterious effects. Nevertheless, in people with certain genetic backgrounds, most notably the class II major histocompatibility complex (MHC) genes implicated in RA, citrullinated peptides bind very tightly into the antigenbinding groove and are presented to T cells more efficiently than the native unmodified protein. Because T cells are not exposed to the altered peptide during development, developing T cells with such specificity are not deleted in the thymus and, once present in the periphery, can respond, driving an adaptive immune response directed against these new epitopes.

These exposures often occur at mucosal surfaces, such as the gut and oral cavity, although the data are particularly compelling for the lung. Altered peptides are loaded onto dendritic cell (DC) MHC proteins. Antigen presentation can then occur in the synovial germinal centers or in central lymphoid organs after the loaded DCs migrate via the lymphatics. T cells are activated and can produce pathogenic cytokines at these sites and help B cells produce antibodies. These antibodies are most commonly directed against citrullinated peptides, but some recognize other altered peptides, such as through carbamylation. The anti-citrullinated protein antibodies (ACPAs), including IgA isotype at mucosal surfaces, are produced against a variety of proteins, including fibronectin, vimentin, α-enolase, histones, and many others.

Over a period of years, the titers of ACPAs increase many-fold, with expansion of the antigens recognized. Oligoclonal expansion of antigen-specific B cells is followed by affinity maturation that increases the avidity of the antibodies for their targets.3, There is no unique "RA-associated ACPA" but instead a general rise of many different antibodies that bind to a variety of modified proteins. These systemic changes do not lead to significant synovial pathology during pre-clinical stages of RA as shown in synovial biopsy studies, even if individuals have arthralgias.

The ACPAs themselves are not sufficient to initiate synovitis, and a "second hit" is necessary. The nature of the second signal is not well defined, but immune complexes can serve this purpose in animal models. These complexes do not have to be specific for altered peptides but can be directed at a myriad of antigens, such as those including viruses or other xenoantigens. They can engage Fc receptors in the synovium, especially on mast cells, which release vasoactive mediators and increase access of ACPAs to the joint. Once in the joint, if they encounter their antigen, they can fix complement and initiate a cascade of events, leading to recruitment of innate and adaptive immune cells, production of additional cytokines and chemokines, and activation of local fibroblast-like synoviocytes (FLS) and macrophages. As the cells are recruited and activated, clinical synovitis ensues.

Additional genetic associations beyond the MHC can amplify the adaptive response to modified proteins and autoreactivity against the native proteins. For example, polymorphisms in genes encoding key T cell signaling proteins (e.g., protein tyrosine phosphatase-22 [PTPN22]) can favor these events. Cytokine gene promoter polymorphisms, signal transduction gene polymorphisms, and other genetic markers also could provide positive feedback to enhance the response. Epigenetic changes that imprint synovial cells through DNA methylation, microRNA (miRNA) production, or histone modification can enhance local immune dysregulation.

Ultimately, a destructive phase ensues that has antigen-dependent and antigen-independent mechanisms and is mediated by mesenchymal elements such as fibroblasts that degrade cartilage and macrophage-derived cells like osteoclasts that erode into bone. Progressive epigenetic modifications occur during the evolution of disease that can alter the function of some synovial cells and enhance matrix damage. Although anti-inflammatory molecules such as soluble cytokine receptors (e.g., TNF receptors), suppressive cytokines (e.g., interleukin [IL]-10), cytokine-binding proteins (e.g., IL-18bp), protease inhibitors (e.g., tissue inhibitor of metalloproteinases [TIMPs]), lipoxins, antioxidants, anti-angiogenic factors, and natural cytokine antagonists may be present, they are not sufficient to arrest the inflammatory and destructive process. Suppressing the inflammatory response requires therapeutic interventions that either modulate pathogenic cells, neutralize the effector molecules produced by the rheumatoid process, or restore tolerance.

Highly targeted therapeutics to individual cytokines, mediators, or cell lineages demonstrate remarkably diverse clinical responses. Although overlap exists, the spectrum of responses demonstrates that some patients have cytokine-dependent disease, some have B celldependent disease, while others have T cell— dependent disease (and some have a more complex combination). These clinical observations suggest that RA is not a single pathogenic entity but is instead a spectrum of disorders that depends on the genetic makeup and environmental triggers for individual patients. By understanding the basic mechanisms of disease, we can begin to untangle which RA a particular person might have, determine how to individualize therapy, and eventually develop new disease taxonomies that focus on pathogenesis rather than clinical features.

### Genetic and Environmental Risk

### KEY POINTS

The interaction of environmental and genetic factors conspires to launch the complex process that leads to the initiation of rheumatoid synovitis. The most compelling evidence for a genetic component is in monozygotic twins, in whom the concordance rate is about 12% to 15% when one twin is affected, compared with 1% for the general population. Nevertheless, the fact that concordance is not higher suggests that other influences such as the environment or epigenetics are as important as the genetic component. The risk for a fraternal twin of a patient with RA is also high (~2% to 5%) but similar to the rate for other first-degree relatives.

Although the immunogenetics is not fully understood, one of the best-studied and perhaps most influential genetic risk factors is the class II MHC haplotype of an individual. Single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in PTPN22 and PADI4 increase risk in some (but not all) racial and ethnic groups. Genome-wide screens have implicated more than 100 genes, many of which are involved with immune function. Most genes, however, have a relatively modest contribution, and the susceptibility polymorphism confers only a 1.05to 1.2-fold increase. Combinations of genes can clearly interact with one another. For example, a 45-fold increase in risk is conferred by expression of a combination of the risk alleles of HLA-DR, PTPN22, and TRAF1-C5.6 Nevertheless, this combination is found in less than 1% of people with RA, and algorithms of other SNPs have not yet identified a critical

combination that can account for the disease. Additional progress in understanding the role of genes in RA, including rare variants that might be more important than some common polymorphisms, might clarify how individual alleles contribute to susceptibility, severity, and responses to targeted therapies.

### Role of Human Leukocyte Antigen-DR in Disease Susceptibility and Severity

The structure of class II MHC molecules on antigen-presenting cells is associated with increased susceptibility and severity of RA and accounts for about 40% of the genetic influence. A genetic link between HLA-DR and RA was initially described in the 1970s with the observation that HLA-DR4 occurred in 70% of patients with RA, compared with about 30% of control subjects, giving a relative risk of having RA to those with HLA-DR4 of approximately fourto fivefold.

The susceptibility to RA was originally ascribed to an association with the third hypervariable region of DRβ chains, from amino acids 70 through 74. The epitope is glutamine—leucine— arginine—alanine—alanine (QKRAA), a sequence found in DR4 and DR14, in addition to some DR1β chains. The "susceptibility epitope" (SE) on DR4β chains with the greatest association with RA are DRB*0401, DRB*0404, DRB*0101, and DRB*1402 (Table 70.1). Up to 96% of patients with RA exhibit the appropriate HLA-DR locus in some populations. In certain ethnic and racial groups, the association with QKRAA is not as prominent. The QKRAA epitope also predicts increased severity of established RA, with a greater prevalence of extra-articular disease and erosions in patients with two copies. Other HLA genes such as DRB*1301 contain the DERAA sequence and are associated with decreased susceptibility to RA. Microchimerism with transfer of maternal cells expressing the SE could potentially contribute to disease susceptibility in individuals lacking the classic MHC genes.

Many explanations have been offered as to how the region associated with RA exerts its effect.
