The QKRAA sequence primarily faces away from the antigen-binding cleft of the DR molecule, which makes a direct effect on antigen binding unlikely. QKRAA could serve as an autoantigen as a result of molecular mimicry in some situations because some xenoproteins such as gpl10 from the Epstein—Barr virus (EBV) also include this sequence.

However, the mechanism is probably related to linkage disequilibrium between the SE and the residues at sites 11 and 13,10 which lie in the antigen-binding groove of HLA-DR. A leucine or valine at amino acid 11 is associated with increased risk of developing disease, whereas serine at amino acid 13 confers decreased risk. Studies of antigen-binding affinities show that citrullinated vimentin peptides bind much more avidly to the RA-associated alleles than the unmodified protein. HLA-DR genes that are not associated with RA do not display this disparity. Functional studies show that these same RA-associated alleles present antigen more efficiently to T cells with higher amounts of cytokines such as IL-17 and interferon (IFN)-γ.11, A recent unbiased study isolated a panel of native and citrullinated peptides from HLA-DRpeptide complexes. Several of the endogenous peptides induce expression of CD40L on RA peripheral blood T cells and induce IFN-γ production. These data support the notion that the RAassociated alleles play a key role selecting and displaying pathogenic peptides.

Based on these observations, the MHC association likely represents an independent risk factor for RA as a marker for immunoreactivity to altered peptides that lead to ACPAs. Early in

this process, asymptomatic individuals might have circulating or mucosal (e.g., sputum) ACPAs, where the latter could potentially even have anti-inflammatory functions by helping to clear citrullinated proteins (CPs). Perhaps 30% to 50% of these healthy individuals with high levels of ACPAs will progress to RA.

### Additional Polymorphisms: s: Cytokines, Citrullinating g Enzymes, PTPN22, and Others −

The genetic influence on RA has also led to studies evaluating non-MHC genes. SNPs in promoter regions, coding regions, or areas with no known function have been extensively investigated in RA. Table 70.2 shows some of the disease-associated SNPs and microsatellites. The relative contribution for any individual allele is modest, and variations in technique, stage of disease, and patient populations likely contribute to disagreement among various reports.

Given the importance of cytokines in RA, it is not surprising that many studies have focused on genes encoding these mediators. The most intriguing evidence relates to TNF. This proinflammatory factor is a major cytokine in the pathogenesis of RA, and the TNF genes are located in the MHC locus on chromosome 6 in humans. Several polymorphisms of the TNF promoter, including positions -238 and -308, can alter gene transcription. Associations among the TNF polymorphisms and RA susceptibility and radiographic progression have been reported, although agreement

### TABLE Key Genetic Associations in Rheumatoid 70.2 Arthritis

among investigators is not uniform. In addition, certain polymorphisms in immunologically relevant genes, especially TNF or Fc receptors, have been associated with a differential response to therapy. For instance, substitution of a T for a C at position -857 in the TNF promoter might confer greater responsiveness to TNF inhibitors. IL-6 receptor polymorphisms that affect IL-6 function have also been associated with RA. Although many of these associations are statistically significant, they are not sensitive or specific enough to assist with clinical decision-making.

Among the many noncytokine and non-MHC genetic linkages described for RA, the ones associated with PADI and PTPN22 have the greatest impact on susceptibility. The PADI genes are responsible for the post-translational modification of arginine to citrulline and for creating the neo-antigens that bind so efficiently to RA-associated MHC proteins. PADIs also have other less-wellcharacterized functions, such as citrullination of histones that can then remodel chromatin. An extended PADI4 haplotype that can lead to increased levels of PADI4 protein as a result of enhanced messenger RNA (mRNA) stability and could increase peptide modification is associated with RA. In a Japanese cohort, a twofold increase in risk of RA was observed with PADI4 SNPs. Similar studies confirm the association in Asian populations, as well as a risk gene in North America.

An association at position 1858 in the PTPN22 gene confers a twofold increase in risk. The allele containing thymidine leading to an amino acid substitution (R620W) was present in 8.5% of control subjects but was found in nearly 15% of patients with seropositive RA. Other studies have demonstrated a similar association with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), type 1 diabetes, and several other autoimmune diseases. PTPN22 encodes a phosphatase that regulates the phosphorylation status of several kinases important to T cell activation, including Lck and ZAP70. The R620W allele surprisingly results in a gain of function that alters the threshold for T cell receptor (TCR) signaling. Because the PTPN22 allele is rare in Japan, other genes (e.g., PADI4) influence susceptibility in this population.

The genes associated with RA consistently involve immune regulation, and many are commonly shared with other immune-mediated

diseases such as SLE, type 1 diabetes, and celiac disease. Cytokine polymorphisms, such as for TNF and the IL-1 inhibitor, IL-1Ra, are not surprising. Genes that regulate adaptive immune responses in T cells, such as PTPN22 and the co-stimulation receptor cytotoxic T-lymphocyte-associated protein 4 (CTLA), have also been associated with RA. Other genes associated with B cell function and/or antigen presentation, such as BTLA (Band T-lymphocyte attenuator), Fc receptors, and CD40, have also been implicated. Polymorphisms have also been identified in signal transduction pathways that regulate immune function, such as TRAF1-C5 and signal transducer and activator of transcription (STAT) 4, cell migration (ELMO1), and fetal development (LBH). The consistent thread in this analysis is that most gene associations for RA cluster to innate immunity, adaptive immunity, matrix regulation, and inflammation. Aside from providing insight into the mechanisms of disease, they could also contribute to responses to targeted therapies.

### Epigenetics

Epigenetics describes phenotypic or gene expression properties caused by mechanisms other than changes in the underlying DNA sequence. Modification of cytosine—phosphatidyl-guanine (CpG) DNA sequences by methylation, for example, can suppress gene expression and plays a role in cell differentiation. Histone acetylation also alters accessibility of DNA for transcription factors and RNA polymerases. miRNAs can bind to DNA and suppress expression of key genes involved with the inflammatory process. Epigenetic information, such as DNA methylation, can be transferred from one generation to the next, thereby providing an alternative mechanism for rapidly altering disease susceptibility in a population as a result of the environment.

Most information on epigenetics in RA comes from studies of RA synovium or cultured synoviocytes, the fibroblast-like cells that form the lining of the joint. For example, candidate gene approaches have identified several genes, such as IL6, CXCL12, and ephrin-B1 (EFNB1), that are hypomethylated, and others, like HLA-DRB3, EBF2, and IRX1, that have increased methylation. Unbiased approaches suggest that the overall level of methylation in RA FLS is not different from osteoarthritis (OA) or normal cells. However, there are distinct patterns of differential methylation in RA, with some loci being hypermethylated, whereas others are hypomethylated. RA-specific methylation patterns in FLS are apparent in early RA but are somewhat different from longstanding RA. Epigenetic changes that distinguish early and late disease are involved in cell differentiation and proliferation pathways, perhaps indicating that the disease becomes more aggressive after it is established.

Detailed analysis of synoviocyte methylation patterns indicates that the differentially methylated genes are enriched in pathways such as cell adhesion, focal adhesion, matrix regulation, cytokine— cytokine receptor interactions, and other functions important to immune function. Some of these pathways could be activated due to the local cytokine milieu because IL-1 can suppress expression of DNA methyl transferases. However, the effect of cytokines is transient in culture, and the cells return to baseline after the cytokine is removed. Permanent FLS imprinting in RA could be due to a variety of additional influences, such as reactive oxygen or nitrogen, or they could be inherited.

The patterns of DNA methylation also demonstrate joint specificity in RA. Some of these changes are disease-independent (i.e., they occur in other diseases or in normal individuals) and are probably defined by the different functional needs of each joint. In addition, certain epigenetic marks are specific to RA and suggest that the

pathogenesis of disease in individual joints might vary. For example, RA hip and knee FLS have distinct transcriptomes and DNA methylation that show differences in pathways related to targeted therapies like IL-6 or Janus kinases (JAKs) (see Fig. 70.2). Distinct gene expression profiles could account for why some joints might respond to a particular agent, whereas others have less benefit.

Numerous candidate genes have been identified through the genome-wide methylation studies. For example, the limb bud heart development gene (LBH) has SNPs associated with multiple autoimmune diseases, including RA. Abnormal methylation in

an LBH enhancer regulates LBH expression and alters the growth patterns of RA FLS. The PTPN11 gene, which encodes the phosphatase SHP-2, has an abnormally methylated locus in an intron near a glucocorticoid receptor binding site and increases the invasive behavior of these cells. Blocking SHP-2 function decreases disease severity in a pre-clinical model and demonstrates how we can potentially translate the genome-wide epigenetics screens into new therapies.

Histone marks that regulate gene expression and repression are also characteristic of RA and may be important regulators of synovitis. For example, histone deacetylases are expressed in RA FLS, and histone deacetylase 1 (HDAC1) is overexpressed. The use of small interfering RNA to knock down HDAC1 or HDAC2 increases expression of the p53 tumor suppressor gene and TNF-induced expression of MMP-1.35 Cytokines such as TNF can increase HDAC1 expression in cultured FLS. SIRT1 also exhibits HDAC activity and is overexpressed in RA FLS and synovium. Blocking SIRT1 in FLS reduces IL-6 and IL-8 production. HDAC inhibitors are also effective in animal models of arthritis, including adjuvant arthritis in rats and collagen-induced arthritis in mice. These data indicate that histone marks can play a role in remodeling the chromatin to increase production of inflammatory mediators in RA.

More recently, the epigenomic landscape of RA FLS was mapped, including whole genome DNA methylation, histone marks, chromatin accessibility, and transcriptomics. Using novel computational tools, several patterns of epigenetic imprinting were identified, with most of the characteristic marks in RA involving active enhancers and promoters. Pathway analysis revealed several anticipated changes related to immune responses. Unexpected findings were also discovered, such as an overlap between the Huntington's disease pathway and RA pathways. Biologic validation showed that at least one member of the Huntington's disease gene, Huntington-interacting protein-1, regulates FLS cytoskeletal rearrangement, migration, and invasion. Mining these comprehensive data sets identified changes in the epigenetic landscape of genes related to nutrient transporters and metabolic pathways 38 and will hopefully provide more new insights into pathogenesis, as well as identify interesting therapeutic targets.

Several miRNAs, such as miRNA-124a, are decreased in RA FLS compared with OA cells. This particular miRNA can suppress cell cycling and chemokine genes. Increasing miRNA-124a levels in RA synoviocytes decreased the production of the chemokine macrophage chemoattractant (MCP)-1.39 Forced expression of miRNA-203 increases metalloproteinase and IL-6 expression by synoviocytes as well. miRNA-155 is especially interesting because it is overexpressed in RA synovial cells and peripheral blood cells. Knocking down this miRNA reduces MMP and cytokine expression in these cells. In vivo miRNA-155 deficiency has mixed effects in animal models, with decreased severity in collagen-induced arthritis and no effect in the passive K/BxN serum transfer model. miRNA-147 deficiency improves synovitis in the pristane-induced model of arthritis, and the mechanism is related to alterations of the zinc finger protein ZNF148.42 Several other miRNAs are differentially expressed in RA, including miRNA-16, -124a, -202, -134a, -23, -346, and -15a. miRNA- 34a in RA patients can also contribute to abnormal DC function by regulating the tyrosine kinase receptor AXL.

The enormous volume of accumulating data on the genetic and epigenetic influences that contribute to the initiation and perpetuation of RA is daunting. No single gene polymorphism or epigenetic mark can account for the disease. It is more likely that complex combinations incrementally increase risk and that the

full expression of RA requires one or many environmental triggers. The nature of these stochastic events is increasingly understood (see below), which creates opportunities to intervene and potentially prevent RA.

### Environment Influences on Rheumatoid Arthritis Risk

As noted above, environmental stress is a likely cofactor that can lead to progression from "at-risk" individuals with a genetic/epigenetic burden to the onset of clinically apparent synovitis. Smoking is the best-defined environmental risk factor through activation of innate immunity and PADI in the airway. Smoking induces PADI expression in the airway and increases protein citrullination, which could provide a stimulus for generation of local IgA or IgG ACPAs in susceptible individuals (Fig. 70.3). The local antibody response to modified antigens is also supported by the presence of ACPAs in the sputum of RA patients, as well as individuals at high risk for developing RA.46, Smoking-related ACPAs recognize a wide array of modified proteins, with no particular predominant antigen associated with smoking or the propensity to develop RA. Highresolution CT studies demonstrate associations between ACPA formation and bronchial thickening in the pre-RA stages, suggesting that the local inflammatory response could begin at this mucosal site. Smoking is only one example of how mucosal immunity in the airway could contribute to development of RA. In fact, a variety of respiratory diseases in registry studies and inhalation of silica are associated with increased risk, particularly in the presence of circulating ACPAs and rheumatoid factor (RF).

The interaction between HLA-DR and tobacco exposure is perhaps the best example of how genes and the environment interact to enhance risk. Although smoking and the SE alone modestly increase the likelihood of developing RA, the combination is synergistic. A person with a history of cigarette smoking and two copies of the SE increases the odds of developing RA by 20to 40-fold. The mechanism of the interaction probably relates to increased

protein citrullination in smokers and the ability of SE-containing HLA-DR molecules to present CPs. The extent of smoking is also predictive, with the greatest risk seen with at least 20 pack-years. The risk declines slowly with cessation of smoking, taking more than a decade to begin approaching the risk in nonsmokers.

The role of diet and vitamins in RA risk has been confirmed by meta-analyses demonstrating an association with low levels of vitamin D.51, A recent clinical trial suggests that supplementing the diet with vitamin D for several years substantially decreases risk. Long-term adherence to a healthier diet in women from the Nurses' Health Study was protective of younger-onset (≤55 years old) seropositive RA development (hazard ratio [HR], 0.60; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.51 to 0.88); specifically, lower red/processed meat and sodium consumption were associated with a significant decrease in RA risk. Interestingly, sodium interacts with smoking to increase RA incidence only in smokers (odds ratio [OR], 2.26; 95% CI, 1.06 to 4.81), particularly that of ACPA and/or HLA-SE-positive disease. A meta-analysis of obesity and risk recently showed that a higher BMI, for example an increase of 5 kg/m2, increased risk by 1.1to 1.2-fold. Obesity could potentially contribute to disease susceptibility through increased production of adipokines. Conversely, a Mediterranean diet decreases the odds developing RA in women who have smoked,58 while depression increases the risk in woman. Alcohol consumption decreases RA risk, demonstrating the complexity of the environment and human behavior on disease susceptibility.

Other environmental factors such as oral contraceptives appear to provide modest protection from RA, perhaps as a result of changes in the hormone milieu. A large Swedish study evaluating RA risk confirmed the small protective effect of the oral contraceptives but found no association between RA and breastfeeding.

### Sex

RA is one of many chronic autoimmune diseases that predominates in women. The ratio of female-to-male patients is 2:1 to 3:1, which

is not as high as Hashimoto's thyroiditis (25:1 to 50: 1) or SLE (9:1). The sex effect is often observed in some animal models of autoimmunity such as the NZB/NZW model of SLE, in which female mice have more severe disease. Estrogens are one obvious explanation, and some data support the concept that these hormones modulate immune function. For example, autoantibody-producing B cells exposed to estradiol are more resistant to apoptosis, suggesting that autoreactive B cell clones might escape tolerance. Estrogen receptors are expressed on FLS and increase production of metalloproteinases. In macrophage cell lines, estrogen can enhance production of TNF. Spontaneous arthritis occurs in mice with a specific mutation in the ZAP70 gene, which regulates T cell responses. Exogenous administration of estrogen ameliorates disease in this model, suggesting that the interactions between sex hormones and disease are complex. Nulliparity has also been suggested as a risk factor in early studies, but more recent reports do not support this notion. Thus the specific mechanisms responsible for the female preponderance of RA are not fully understood.

Pregnancy is often associated with remission of the disease in the last trimester. More than three-quarters of pregnant patients with RA improve in the first or second trimester, but 90% of these women experience a flare of disease associated with a rise in RF titers in the weeks or months after delivery. The mechanism of protection is not defined but might be due to the expression of suppressive cytokines such as IL-10 during pregnancy, production of α-fetoprotein, or alterations in cell-mediated immunity. One intriguing finding is that fetal DNA levels in the maternal peripheral blood correlate with the propensity for improved symptoms in pregnant women with RA. It is not certain whether the DNA itself contributes or whether it is a marker for increased leakage of fetal cells into the maternal circulation. Immune responses directed against paternal HLA antigens can occur and lead to the production of alloantibodies in the maternal circulation. Maternalfetal disparity in class II HLA phenotypes can correlate with pregnancy-induced remission. More than three-fourths of pregnant women with maternalfetal disparity of HLA-DRB1, DQA, and DQB haplotypes have significant improvement, whereas disparity is only observed in one-fourth of women whose pregnancy is characterized by continuous active arthritis. Therefore, suppression of maternal immune responses to paternal HLA haplotypes might be protective. This question remains unsettled because another study failed to find a correlation between the HLA disparity and clinical improvement during pregnancy.

### Autoimmunity and Innate Immunity

### KEY POINTS

The idea that aberrant immune responses are directed toward selfantigens in RA was recognized with the discovery of RF in the blood of patients with the disease. Initially described by Waaler and later by Rose, it was not until the mid-1950s that investigators firmly established that RF is an autoantibody. ACPAs have largely supplanted RFs as the most sensitive and specific antibody associated with RA. They reflect the underlying immune dysregulation in RA and, in addition to being a biomarker of disease, can also play an important role in the pathogenesis of inflammation in the joint and perhaps even in mucosal sites. Although ACPAs have largely supplanted RF as the most sensitive and specific test for diagnosing RA, the presence of combinations of antibody classes, like ACPÅ and other specificities, could increase specificity for RA and help identify very-high-risk populations for development of synovitis.

### Anti-citrullinated Protein Antibodies

Antibodies that bind to CPs are produced by patients with RA and have significant prognostic implications. The discovery originated with reports in the 1970s that antibodies directed against keratin were detected in rheumatoid serum and that the primary target antigen was filament-aggregating protein, filaggrin. These antibodies bind to epitopes on filaggrin that contain citrulline, which is derived from post-translational modification of arginine by PADI. Humans have four isoforms of PADI. PADI2 and PADI4 are especially abundant in synovium,68 and certain SNPs are associated with RA. The function of PADIs in normal immune responses is not certain, and citrullination of some chemokines can decrease their chemoattractant properties. Histones are also citrullinated by PADs, which can alter chromatin accessibility and gene expression and adds a significant gene regulatory component to citrullination as a stress response.

PADI induction and citrullination of peptides are not specific to RA and can occur in many inflammatory settings. Not only are other inflammatory arthropathies marked by CPs, but other organs such as the lungs in smokers also have significant PADI activity. The presence of CPs in the lungs of smokers or in other mucosal sites could provide the antigen exposure that can contribute to anti-CP antibody production and begin the long road to the development of RA. CPs are also present in most animal models of arthritis. Immunohistochemistry demonstrates CPs in RA synovial tissue infiltrating cells (Fig. 70.4), as well as in extra-cellular deposits that often colocalize with various isoforms of PADI, especially PADI2 and PADI4. Moreover, ACPAs are produced by the rheumatoid synovium, especially tissues with lymphoid aggregates.

NETosis, or cell death accompanied by the release of nuclear material to the extra-cellular space, can also release citrullinated peptides, and numerous modified proteins can be presented to T cells. Protein modification can occur by release of PADs into the microenvironment during release of DNA. This process can occur in joints but, perhaps more relevant to initiation of disease, also occurs in the airway where ACPAs are associated with sputum neutrophil extra-cellular traps; strikingly, this phenomenon also occurs in first-degree relatives of RA patients.72, A genetic component was confirmed in studies, demonstrating that the PTPN22 polymorphism associated with RA interferes with the interaction between the phosphatase and PAD4.74 By disrupting this regulatory mechanism, PAD4 can then citrullinate intra-cellular peptides and enhance NETosis. In addition, bacteria present in periodontal infection can produce toxins that activate citrullination in neutrophils and release modified peptides. The

mucosal immune reactivity could help explain the production of IgA ACPAs and IgA-producing plasmablasts in pre-RA and early RA, as well as fine specificity of ACPAs that are associated with specific pathogens like Prevotella intermedia and the association with smoking. 75-77

The specific proteins that are modified vary widely but include many normal constituents such as fibrinogen, vimentin, and fibronectin, as well as xenoproteins such as EBV-derived peptides. The pattern of protein citrullination or the specificity of antibodies to particular proteins does not have predictive value for the development of RA or the severity of disease. One interesting subset involves antibodies that recognize mutant citrullinated vimentin (MCV). These antigens have two modifications that render them more immunogenic: First, there are amino acid changes in the primary sequence such as glycine to arginine. Second, either the new amino acid or another arginine on the protein is citrullinated. These anti-MCV antibodies might be more specific for RA in established disease and predictive for radiographic progression.

ACPAs are present in the serum of 80% to 90% of patients with RA who have established disease using conventional assays. They are also more specific than RF for RA with a specificity approaching 90%. When custom-designed arrays are used, as many as 10% of patients negative for ACPA have other ACPA specificities. Perhaps most interesting, ACPA, like RF, are detected in mucosal fluids (e.g., sputum) or in the blood long before the onset of clinical arthritis. Sputum ACPAs can bind a variety of modified peptides including fibrinogen, vimentin, and apolipoprotein A1 with patterns that might enrich patients that transition to classifiable disease. Elevated serum cytokines are also associated with the impending transition from pre-RA to clinical arthritis. ACPAs serve as a marker for immune hyper-reactivity and subclinical inflammation, leading to protein citrullination in a variety

of tissues and potentially immune complexes with the modified peptides (Fig. 70.5). As the number of peptides recognized by various ACPAs increases, such as to vimentin, enolase, or various fragments of fibronectin, the more likely that RA will develop. 84

The pattern and timing of ACPAs and RF can be clues to the risk for developing RA in asymptomatic individuals. Longitudinal studies show that IgG ACPAs are present for about 18 years before onset of classifiable RA, while IgA and IgM appear later (14 and 7 years, respectively). For each isotype, there is a gradual increase in levels over time as transition to clinical disease becomes imminent. Combinations of high-titer ACPA and RF are associated with developing RA within 3 years, especially with concomitant increases in serum calprotectin. Even when ACPA is an isolated antibody, high levels (e.g., three times the upper limit of normal) doubles the risk of developing RA from 21.5% to 46%.87, About 20% of first-degree relatives of RA patients have serum ACPAs, which also identifies individuals with high risk of progression. Epigenetic changes can also influence susceptibility, and RA-related DNA methylation patterns in blood cells could be detected in ACPA-positive individuals. This raises the possibility of developing combinations of biomarkers like antibodies, epigenetic marks, genetic markers, and cytokines that might be used as prognostic tests in asymptomatic individuals.

Single-cell sequencing of circulating B cells and plasmablasts suggests that the cells producing ACPAs undergo antibody maturation driven by antigens.91, The germline genes utilized by these cells demonstrate oligoclonality and are consistent with expansion of individual specificities due to antigen exposure, including fibrinogen, α-enolase, and histone H2B (Fig. 70.6). Somatic hypermutations lead to epitope spreading and polyreactivity in circulating plasmablasts, especially IgA-producing cells, in patients with classifiable disease. Mutations induced during maturation also might contribute to pathogenic potential of ACPAs through

the production of new N-glycosylation sites. Increased glycosylation can alter affinity toward citrullinated peptides and increase the ability of ACPAs to activate osteoclasts. This process is, in part, regulated by the IL-23Th17 axis, which can then induce glycosylating enzymes in antibody-producing cells.

A genetic contribution to ACPA production was confirmed in the Native American population, in whom ACPAs are present in nearly 20% of unaffected first-degree relatives and in more than 10% of more distant relatives. ACPAs are also produced by synovial tissue B cells and can be detected in synovial fluid. Nevertheless, the fact that ACPAs, like RFs, can be detected years before the onset of arthritis and can be found in some normal relatives of patients with RA indicates that the antibodies alone cannot account for initiation of the disease.

Despite these caveats, ACPAs could have pathogenic potential. For instance, ACPAs can activate the classic and the alternative complement pathways. The antibodies have minimal effect when directly injected into mice, and they enhance the arthritogenic potential of anti—type II collagen antibodies in the collagen-induced arthritis model. Mice immunized with citrullinated fibronectin, but not native fibronectin, can develop inflammatory arthritis. Hence the autoreactivity and autoantibodies are not simply a marker of disease but can participate in the disease process. Citrullination can also increase T cell responses to some arthritogenic antigens. For instance, citrullination of albumin leads to the formation of antibodies that also cross-react with the unmodified protein. Citrullinated type II collagen and vimentin are more immunogenic than the native protein, most likely because of increased affinity in the binding groove of HLA-DR proteins that contain the SE. ACPAs can also bind to and enhance the activity of osteoclast precursors, suggesting that they can directly contribute to increased bone damage in ACPA+ patients.

### Antibodies to Other Modified Proteins

ACPAs are the best characterized antibodies directed against modified antigens in RA. Other antibody systems are also present and define additional subsets of disease. For example, some patients have antibodies that recognize carbamylated proteins. In this case lysine is converted to homocitrulline through a nonenzymatic reaction with isocyanic acid and creates neo-epitopes in much the same manner as conversion of arginine to citrulline. Both ACPAs and anti-carbamylated protein antibodies (ACarPs) are present in a subset of patients with RA. More intriguingly, up to 30% of ACPApatients have ACarPs, including IgG and IgA antibodies.

Like ACPAs, antibodies to modified proteins like carbamylated fibrinogen can occur before the onset of clinical disease in nearly 40% of patients with RA, and carbamylation of vimentin can be induced by exposure to cigarette smoke in pre-clinical models. 104, The antibodies are also associated with more severe disease and increased joint damage. They can participate in the inflammatory response, and mice immunized with carbamylated peptides can develop erosive arthritis. Like ACPAs, the antibodies alone do not cause synovitis. Nevertheless, lymphocytes from immunized animals can transfer disease to naive mice.

An additional antibody system directed against malondialdehyde—acetaldehyde (MAA) adducts was recently described. The modified peptides are present in RA synovial tissue and colocalize with B cells and CPs. Elevated levels of anti-MAA antibodies are also present in serum. Anti-MAA titers are higher in the joint than in the blood, suggesting local production.

These antibody systems, like ACPAs, can be detected in some healthy individuals that are at risk for developing RA. For example,

ACarPs are found in the pre-RA phase, often with ACPAs, and are associated with subsequent destructive disease. IgG and IgA antibodies that detect MAA also predict future RA. Another antibody system associated with pre-RA detect EBV early antigen, although the mechanisms and pathogenic significance are still uncertain.

### Rheumatoid Factor

The identification and characterization of RF as an autoantibody that binds to the Fc portion of IgG was the first direct evidence that autoimmunity might play a role in RA. Their utility as a diagnostic test for RA has largely been replaced by ACPAs, including the diagnostic test detecting antibodies to cyclic citrullinated peptides (CCPs). RF+ patients have more severe clinical disease and complications than do seronegative patients, including increased cardiovascular complications, although this outcome might be due to the association of RFs with ACPAs. RF can activate synovial fluid complement by the classic pathway. Large quantities of IgG RF and RF-containing complexes are produced by rheumatoid synovial tissue and detected in cartilage. B celltargeted therapies such as rituximab can deplete peripheral B lymphocytes and modestly decrease titers of RF. This effect does not correlate precisely with clinical responses, and synovial RF production is not significantly changed by B cell depletion. Nevertheless, RF levels often decrease in responders and increase again coincident with clinical relapses.

About three-quarters of RA patients have detectable IgM RF levels in their serum. Like ACPAs, first-degree relatives of RFpositive patients with RA are frequently seropositive, suggesting a genetic contribution. Although IgG and IgM RFs are the most abundant in RA, IgA and IgE RF have also been detected. IgE RF can potentially complex with aggregated IgG in synovial tissue, and the subsequent complexes could then degranulate synovial mast cells through activation of Fc receptors in the synovium.

RF is commonly found in individuals without RA, especially with increasing age. Most of these people will never manifest this disorder. This observation casts doubt on a direct role of RF in the pathogenesis of RA. However, it is become increasingly clear that the RFs produced in people with RA differ from those produced by healthy people or from patients with paraproteins. The avidity of RF for the Fc portion of IgG is much greater in RA than in Waldenström's macroglobulinemia or in cryoglobulins. Many RFs expressed by abnormal B cells (such as Waldenström's macroglobulinemia) and by normal B cells in human tonsils are derived from the germline. In contrast, RFs in RA are derived through rearrangements and somatic mutations of the germline genes. RF production can be quite high in rheumatoid synovium; IgM RF represents about 7% of the total IgM and 3% of the total IgG produced by synovial cell cultures.

RFs in RA primarily use the IgG variable heavy 3 (IGHV3) gene and a variety of variable light (VL) genes, whereas natural antibodies with RF activity use IGHV1 or IGHV4 and the IGKV3 genes. . The k light chain repertoire expressed in RF-producing cells isolated from one RA patient was enriched for two specific Vκ genes but contained many somatic mutations and non—germlineencoded nucleotides. Therefore the selection and production of these RFs, like ACPAs, were likely due to antigenic drive with somatic mutation rather than derived directly from the germline.

### Autoimmunity to Cartilage-Specific Antigens

The emerging picture of autoimmunity in RA implicates patterns of self-directed responses against articular and nonarticular

antigens that vary between individuals and different stages of disease.

### Type II Collagen

Immunization with type II collagen can cause arthritis in rodents, and the disease can be passively transferred by serum containing anti-collagen antibodies or by transfer of lymphocytes from affected animals. T cells are required for initiation of collageninduced arthritis, and a major immunogenic and arthritogenic epitope on type II collagen resides in a restricted area of the type II collagen chains. The disease is caused by anti-collagen antibodies that localize to the joint and activate complement.

Type II collagen antibody generation probably does not initiate RA but can amplify the inflammatory response (Table 70.3). Collagen immunoreactivity, like other native proteins, likely begins with antibodies that bind to citrullinated type II collagen, with epitope spread to include the unmodified or denatured protein. Of interest, T cell responses to type II collagen, especially a dominant epitope at amino acids 263 to 270, are much greater if the protein is glycosylated or citrullinated. Sera from patients with RA contain antibody titers to denatured bovine type II collagen that are significantly higher than those found in control sera. Anticollagen antibodies purified from the sera of patients with RA can activate complement, generating C5a when they bind to cartilage. In addition, isolated synovial tissue B lymphocytes actively secrete anti—type II collagen antibodies in almost all patients with seropositive RA, whereas articular cells from patients who do not have RA do not secrete these antibodies.

The presence of anti—type II collagen antibodies might have prognostic significance in RA. A Swedish cohort of patients with early RA was stratified based on the presence of these antibodies. High levels were associated with elevated acute phase reactants and greater disease severity, especially in patients with acute onset of disease. When patients were followed for up to 5 years, the presence of anti—type II collagen antibodies was associated with less disease activity and a favorable outcome in that study.

### gp39 and Other Cartilage-Specific Antigens

Several other cartilage components besides type II collagen also elicit immune responses in RA. Among the most interesting is cartilage glycoprotein gp39. Several gp39 peptides can bind to the HLA-DR*0401 molecule and stimulate proliferation of T cells from patients with RA. BALB/c mice, which are often resistant to experimental arthritis treatments, develop polyarticular inflammatory arthritis after immunization with gp39. Although anti-gp39 antibodies are detected in only a small percentage of patients, these antibodies are relatively specific for RA when present. Other cartilage components, including proteoglycans, aggrecan, cartilage-link protein, and other types of collagen, can also elicit autoantibody responses in RA. Proteomic analysis of RA serum using peptide arrays to detect multiple autoantibodies also identifies anti-gp39 antibodies in patients with early RA, which may be associated with less aggressive disease.

### Autoimmunity to Nonarticular Antigens

Autoimmune responses in RA can also involve antigens that are broadly expressed beyond the joint. These antigen-antibody systems comprise a pattern of autoimmune responses that can potentially lead to synovial inflammation.

### Glucose-6-Phosphoisomerase

Spontaneous inflammatory arthritis develops in K/BxN mice as a result of antigen-specific immunity against a seemingly irrelevant nonarticular antigen. Autoantibodies to the ubiquitous enzyme glucose-6-phosphate isomerase (GPI) cause the disease, and transient synovitis also develops in normal mice injected with the serum of the affected K/BxN mice or anti-GPI antibodies. Mice immunized with GPI also develop antibodies and then inflammatory arthritis. The passive arthritis model requires the alternate complement pathway, Fc receptors (especially FcRγIII), and mast cells, but not T or B cells. IL-1 is more important than TNF in this model, and the IL-1 knockout mice are almost completely protected from disease. Notably, this effect can be overcome by administration of a Toll-like receptor (TLR) ligand like lipopolysaccharide (LPS), which shares a downstream signaling pathway with IL-1. Other cytokines, such as IL-6, and signaling pathways, such as p38 MAPK, and upstream kinases, such as MKK3 and MKK6, are also required for full expression of the disease.

Immunohistochemical studies show that GPI adheres to the surface of cartilage, which permits local antibody binding and complement fixation. Initiation of synovial inflammation increases vascular permeability and provides access to the synovium and cartilage. This phase is followed by antibody-mediated complement fixation when serum proteins have access to GPI-decorated cartilage.

The display of GPI on the surface of cartilage suggests that the pathogenesis might be similar to arthritis models caused by "jointspecific" antigens. Anti-GPI antibodies are detected in a relatively small percentage of patients with RA and are not specific for the disease. Nevertheless, it might, along with several other antibody systems, contribute to local complement fixation by binding to GPI arrayed on cartilage.

### Heterogeneous Nuclear Ribonucleoprotein-A2 and Heavy-Chain Binding gProtein

Several other autoantigens that are expressed in synovium have been characterized in RA, although they are also produced in many other locations. For instance, antibodies directed against the heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoprotein-A2 (hnRNP-A2), sometimes called RA33, occur in about one-third of patients with RA, as well as

patients with other systemic autoimmune diseases. Anti-RA33 antibodies are also produced in the TNF transgenic mouse model of RA, suggesting that proinflammatory cytokines can independently lead to a breakdown of tolerance for this particular protein. Of interest, RA33+ patients with early RA (symptoms for less than 3 months) tend to have less destructive disease. Although not especially sensitive or specific for RA when used in isolation, an algorithm involving antiRNP-A2, RF, and ACPA can be used to predict which patients with early synovitis will progress to erosive RA.

Autoantibodies that bind to stress-protein Ig heavy-chain binding protein (BiP) have also been observed. About 60% of patients with RA have anti-BiP antibodies, and the specificity is reportedly more than 90%. In addition to humoral responses, RA T cells can proliferate in response to this protein.

### Heat Shock Proteins s (HSPs)

Immunity against HSPs contributes directly to synovitis and joint destruction in some pre-clinical models, including adjuvant arthritis in rats, in which T lymphocytes recognize mycobacterial HSP65. Some of these cells cross react with cartilage proteoglycan epitopes, perhaps explaining the targeting of joints.

Some patients with RA have elevated levels of antibodies to mycobacterial HSPs, especially in synovial fluid. The majority of T cell clones isolated from RA synovial fluid with specificity to mycobacterial components express the γδ-TCR and do not display CD4 or CD8 surface antigens. Freshly isolated synovial fluid T cells from patients with RA briskly proliferate in response to recombinant 65 kDa HSP, whereas the response to other recall antigens such as tetanus toxoid is not increased. Synovial fluid mononuclear cells activated by the 60 kDa mycobacterial HSP inhibit proteoglycan production by human cartilage explants.

Overall, the panoply of antibodies to native and modified antigens reflects immune dysregulation and the propensity for auto-reactivity. The precise role of these antibodies in disease etiology is uncertain, although it is more likely that most of them exacerbate rather than initiate synovitis. ACPAs, however, might play a more pivotal role than the other autoantibodies in seropositive RA as a marker that indicates high risk and can create proinflammatory immune complexes.

### T Cell Metabolism in Early RA

Compared with cells derived from individuals without disease, naive CD4+CD45RA+ T cells from RA patients have a decreased expression of the glycolysis-activating enzyme, 6-phosphofructo- 2-kinase/fructose-2,6-bisphosphatase 3 (PFKFB3), which results in a decrease of ATP levels and lactate and an activation of the pentose phosphate pathway (PPP) to generate NADPH and biosynthetic precursors to products to fuel T cell expansion and function. T cells from patients with RA also proliferate in part due to activation of the cell cycle kinase ATM, component of a redoxdependent signaling pathway, and a shortening of the G2/M phase of the cell cycle and commit these cells to the Th1 and Th17 cell lineage rather than Treg. RA T cells also have defective activation of the AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) pathway and aberrant activation of mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1), which are also critical for T cell differentiation.

### Innate Immunity: Toll-like Receptors and Inflammasome in the Joint

Infectious agents could contribute to the initiation or perpetuation of RA through a variety of mechanisms. Some arthrotropic

microorganisms could potentially infect the synovium and cause a local inflammatory response. The innate immune system could also indirectly lead to the onset of synovitis. Pathogen-associated molecular pattern receptors, especially the TLRs, are expressed by sentinel cells in the host that provide a first line of defense (see Chapter 19). These receptors recognize preserved structures in bacteria and other infectious agents and permit responses to pathogens.

Repeated engagement of TLRs in the synovium could potentially initiate or exacerbate inflammation. Even if pathogens are not detected or are not unique for RA, nonspecific TLR activation could increase vascular permeability and ingress of antibodies (e.g., ACPAs). Supporting this notion, several animal models of disease require TLR ligands for initiation, such as TLR9 in adjuvant arthritis. TLR2 is required for streptococcal cell wall arthritis, and the chronic T celldependent phase of that model requires TLR4. Mice lacking TLR4 have significantly less joint damage induced by IL-1 overexpression, even though synovial inflammation is stll robust. Thus, endogenous TLR ligands play a key role in matrix regulation independent of inflammatory responses. TLR2 stimulation also impairs activity of M2 macrophages, which normally produce a variety of anti-inflammatory factors that could suppress synovial inflammation.

As discussed in more detail in Chapter 95, the inflammasome also regulates innate immunity and involves the recognition of "danger signals" and products of pathogens such as muramyl dipeptides and uric acid. One central component is NALP3, which is linked to caspase 1 (IL-1 convertase) by adapter proteins. When the inflammasome is engaged, caspase 1 is activated, and IL-1 is processed and released. Mutations in this pathway, especially in cryopyrin, have been associated with autoinflammatory disorders such as MuckleWells syndrome and familial cold autoinflammatory disease. NALP3 is abundant in RA synovium and is constitutively expressed by FLS and macrophages. Other inflammasome components and related genes are highly expressed in RA peripheral blood cells, including apoptotic speck protein (ASC), Mediterranean fever (MEFV), and cryopyrin-NALP3.130 Expression in cultured FLS is markedly increased by TNF. In addition, a NALP3 SNP has been associated with increased risk of RA. Because the TNF-induced inflammasome activation can induce cytokine production after exposure to bacterial products and other danger signals, it could participate in synovial IL-1 and IL-18 regulation.

TNF also leads to mitochondrial (mt) DNA release and triggers a type I IFN response that is dependent on the cyclic guanosine monophosphate-AMP synthase (cGAS) stimulator of IFN genes (STING) pathway. Notably, an IFN gene signature is present in about half of early RA patients and is associated with decreased initial response to treatment.

### Infectious Agents and the Microbiome

### KEY POINTS

An etiologic link has not been established for a specific infectious agent with RA, although several pathogens such as viruses, retroviruses, bacteria, and mycoplasma have been associated with the disease.

While a single specific "RA pathogen" is unlikely, the microbiome at mucosal surfaces likely plays a key role through a variety of mechanisms, including the induction of ACPAs.

A role for infectious agents as the etiology of RA has been sought for decades (Table 70.4). A potential pathogen could initiate disease through a variety of mechanisms, including direct infection

of the synovium, activation of innate immunity by patternrecognition receptors that bind to components of the agent, or molecular mimicry that induces an autoreactive adaptive immune response. It seems unlikely that there is a single infectious trigger for RA. However, as noted below, there may well be circumstances in some patients in which microbial pathogens do play a role in disease pathogenesis or severity.

### Bacteria, Mycobacteria, Mycoplasma, and Their Components

Active infection of synovial tissue by pyogenic bacteria is an unlikely cause of RA, and extensive searches for a unique or specific organism in synovial tissue or joint effusions have been negative. Antibodies to certain organisms such as Proteus are reportedly elevated in the blood of patients with RA, but this finding could represent nonspecific B cell activation. Most patients with RA and reactive arthritis contain bacterial DNA sequences in their synovium. The bacteria identified are not unique and generally represent a cross-section of skin and mucosal bacteria, including Acinetobacter and Bacillus spp. The accumulation of bacterial products is probably due to phagocytosis by local macrophages.

Bacterial peptidoglycans are also abundant in RA synovial tissue. Antigen-presenting cells containing these products express TLRs that can be ligated and produce proinflammatory cytokines. Either the peptidoglycans could activate cells in situ, or phagocytic cells from other sites or the blood could engage the molecules and then migrate to the joint. In either case, it is not difficult to imagine how they can contribute to synovial inflammation.

Several animal models of arthritis are dependent on TLR2, TLR3, TLR4, or TLR9. For instance, rodents injected with streptococcal cell walls (TLR2 ligand) develop severe polyarticular arthritis. The initial phase of disease resolves and is then followed by a chronic T celldependent phase that resembles RA. The arthritogenicity of complete Freund's adjuvant in the rat adjuvant

arthritis model is dependent on mycobacterial DNA that binds to TLR9 and activates an adaptive immunity. Endogenous TLR4 ligands such as HSPs and fibrinogen also play a role in immune complex models such as passive K/BxN arthritis.

Mycoplasma-derived superantigens such as from Mycoplasma arthritidis can directly induce T cellindependent cytokine production by macrophages and exacerbate or trigger arthritis in mice immunized with type II collagen. Despite circumstantial evidence, most efforts to identify Mycoplasma and Chlamydia organisms or DNA in joint samples have been negative, and no direct evidence exists to support these organisms as etiologic agents.

### Epstein-Barr Virus, DnaJ Proteins, and Molecular Mimicry

EBV is a polyclonal B lymphocyte activator that increases the production of RF. Rheumatoid macrophages and T cells have defective suppression of EBV-induced proliferation of human B cells. Patients with RA have higher levels of EBV shedding in throat washings, an increased number of virus-infected B cells in the circulating blood, higher levels of antibodies to normal and citrullinated EBV antigens, and abnormal EBV-specific cytotoxic T cell responsiveness compared with control subjects. CD25+ B cells from patients with RA respond more briskly to EBV than do those from healthy people, with increased polyclonal IgG and IgM production.

Defective elimination of EBV-transformed lymphocytes in RA has fueled speculation that immune dysfunction contributes to initiation of disease, although anti-EBV (and anti-parvovirus B19) antibody titers might be lower in ACPA+ RA patients. Persistent EBV infection is also associated with lymphoproliferative disease in RA. Of interest, EBV DNA can also exacerbate collagen-induced arthritis in mice with increased IFN-γ and IL-17 production as an alternative mechanism to enhance synovial inflammation.

Sequence homology between the susceptibility cassette in HLA-DR proteins and the EBV glycoprotein gp110 is a tantalizing clue that molecular mimicry might be important. Like DRB*0401, gp110 contains the QKRAA motif, and patients with serologic evidence of a previous EBV infection have antibodies against this epitope. Hence T cell recognition of EBV epitopes in some patients with the SE might elicit an immune response directed at innocent bystander cells. RA T cells, especially synovial fluid T cells, have increased proliferative responses to gp1 10, perhaps supporting the molecular-mimicry link between a variety of QKRAA-containing proteins and arthritis.

gp1 10 is only one of many xenoproteins such as the Escherichia coli HSP DnaJ containing QKRAA, so this might be a more general mechanism. Of particular interest, responses directed against DnaJ protein also recognize human Hsp40 proteins DnaJA1 and DnaJ2. Therefore molecular mimicry is not limited to HLA-DR and can involve other cellular proteins.

### Parvovirus

Parvovirus B19 infection has been implicated in some patients with RA based on serologic evidence, including the nonstructural protein NS1. Only about 5% of patients have evidence of recently acquired parvovirus B19 infection at the time of disease onset. Of interest, 75% of RA synovium samples contain B19 DNA compared with about 20% of non-RA control subjects. Immunohistochemical evidence of the B19 protein VP-1 was detected in patients with RA but not in patients with other forms of arthritis.

Nevertheless, evidence of the B19 genome in RA joint samples was not found in other studies.

The mechanisms of B19-induced synovitis, when it does occur, could also involve alterations in FLS function. In a cell-culture model of synoviocyte invasion into cartilage, infection with the parvovirus significantly increased the migration of cells into the matrix. Mice that are transgenic for the B19 protein NS1 were more susceptible to collagen-induced arthritis and developed high titers of anti—type II collagen antibodies. These data suggest that the B19 genome might not cause arthritis but can enhance an arthritogenic response to other environmental stimuli. The observation that B19 VP-1—induced IFN-γ production by peripheral blood cells is low in B19+ RA patients supports the possibility that a possible RA-B19 link relates to immune dysregulation rather than direct infection.

### Other Viruses

COVID-19 could potentially activate or exacerbate autoimmune diseases, including RA. Several cases of ACPA-positive RA have been described after severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARSCoV-2) infection. One study carefully monitored the patient's autoantibodies from the beginning of their SARS— CoV-2 infection to the onset of clinical RA. Although ACPAs were already detectable when the patient tested positive for SARSCoV-2; by the time arthritis developed, ACPA titers had substantially increased. Increasing ACPA titers could indicate epitope spreading before clinical RA.

Because rubella virus and the rubella vaccine can cause arthritis in humans, the virus has attracted some attention as a possible triggering agent. Live rubella virus can be isolated from the synovial fluid of some patients with chronic inflammatory oligoarthritis or polyarthritis without clinical evidence of rubella. Nevertheless, most patients with rubella do not have the classic polyarticular involvement and display an oligoarthritis involving large joints. As with B19 infection, it is possible that a small subset of patients with chronic polyarthritis that is called RA actually have direct infection with wild-type or attenuated rubella virus.

Studies of synovial tissue in a variety of inflammatory and noninflammatory arthropathies have also demonstrated DNA of other viruses such as cytomegalovirus and herpes simplex, but not adenovirus or varicella-zoster. As with bacterial DNA, parvovirus, and EBV, the localization of viral DNA to the inflamed joint is probably related to the migration of inflammatory cells containing the viral genome or other nonspecific mechanisms rather than an active infection.

Retroviral infections could also contribute to the etiology of RA. However, endogenous retroviruses are abundant in both inflamed and normal synovium. In one study, higher levels of HERV-K10 gag protein from a common endogenous retrovirus were detected more often in RA compared with OA and normal peripheral blood mononuclear cells. In addition, the pX domain of one human retrovirus, human T lymphotropic virus-1 (HTLV-1), causes synovitis in transgenic mice, and synoviocytes from patients infected with HTLV-1 have increased cytokine production.

### Microbiome

The observation that airway inflammation might contribute to disease risk has led to various studies to evaluate contributions at other mucosal sites. Similar associations are observed in animal models of arthritis, in which arthritis susceptibility and severity

can be lower in rodents raised in a germ-free or defined bacteria environment. The most prominent association is with periodontitis, commonly caused by Porphyromonas gingivalis, which was confirmed in a Swedish cohort. This bacterium is one of the few that produces its own PADI, which could lead to local citrullination of proteins such as fibronectin. P. gingivalis can also act by stimulating TLR2, which increases IL-1 production and leads to production of pathogenic Th17 cells. It is not clear whether P. gingivalis is specific or causative in new onset RA because it is equally abundant in many control populations (78% and 83% for early RA and control, respectively). Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans was implicated in oral dysbiosis in RA. The organism produces a pore-forming toxin (leukotoxin A), which releases hypercitrullinated proteins from neutrophils and provides substrate for subsequent ACPA formation.

In the gut, expansion of Prevotella copri species occurs in patients with early-stage RA, with a concomitant decrease in Bacteroides (Fig. 70.7). These differences are not seen in longstanding RA, although increased immune reactivity to a 27 kDa P. copri protein and anti—P. copri antibodies were detected and associated with ACPA positivity. In other studies, distinct patterns of gut bacteria were observed in spondyloarthropathies, RA, and healthy controls, including confirmation of the P. copri observations and noting a new correlation between the degree of synovitis and Euryarchaeota organisms.148, The abnormal gut microbiome is not fixed, as treatment of patients with a TNF inhibitor modified the dysbiotic microbiome toward the healthy controls. Blood markers of the microbiome, much of which is obtained from mucosal surfaces, have similar findings and suggest that blood tests might be able to distinguish disease-specific patterns that can be altered with novel approaches like fecal transplantation. Certain gut bacterial taxa and their genes are associated with clinical response to drugs such as methotrexate.

The importance of the microbiome is also evident in murine models, in which an increasing segmented filamentous bacteria population is associated with increased follicular T helper (Th) activity and increased arthritis severity in the K/BxN model of arthritis.152, Antibiotic treatment to decrease the gut flora decreased arthritis severity. Of interest, oral administration of P. gingivalis exacerbates synovial inflammation in the mouse collagen arthritis model. Not only the dysbiosis but the intestinal barrier integrity plays a role in translating autoimmunity to inflammation. Increased levels of zonulin, a potent regulator for intestinal tight junctions, in serum were accompanied by a leaky intestinal barrier, dysbiosis, and inflammation. Treatment with the zonulin antagonist larazotide acetate, which specifically increases intestinal barrier integrity, effectively reduced arthritis onset in an animal model of arthritis. These emerging data on the critical role of the bacteria and intestinal barrier integrity creates opportunities to modulate the microbiome as a form of treatment or prevention.

### Changing Epidemiology

Currently the lifetime risk of developing RA is unexpectedly high—namely, 3.6% in women and 1.7% in men. Interestingly, however, the history of RA reveals the surprising observation that it is a relatively new disease in Europe and Northern Africa. Examination of ancient skeletal remains in Europe and Northern Africa fails to reveal convincing evidence of RA, even though other rheumatic diseases such as OA, ankylosing spondylitis, and gout are readily discernable. In contrast, typical marginal erosions and rheumatoid lesions are present in the skeletons

of Native Americans found in Tennessee, Alabama, and Central America from thousands of years ago. The first clear descriptions of RA in Europe appeared in the 17th century, and the disease was distinguished from gout and rheumatic fever by Garrod in the mid-19th century. Although the theory is still controversial, the disease might have migrated from the New World to the Old World coincident with opening of trade and exploration routes. Because genetic admixture was relatively limited, an undefined environmental exposure, in collaboration with risk-associated MHC genes, potentially caused RA in susceptible Europeans. The most obvious explanation, of course, would be that an infectious agent is responsible. However, other environmental influences

such as tobacco smoking were also introduced to the Old World at the same time and could play a role. Smoking-induced citrullination of proteins in the airway could be an especially intriguing clue to the introduction of RA in Europe.

The severity and incidence of RA appeared to decrease in the late 20th century (Fig. 70.8). In certain well-defined populations, including Native Americans, the incidence of RA has gradually declined by as much as 50% during the past half of the 20th century. Nevertheless, when the Olmsted County cohort was extended into the early 21st century, the trend reversed. The age-adjusted increase occurred in all age groups but mainly occurred in women. Because smoking has decreased in the United States, a change in tobacco use is probably not the explanation. Other influences such as hygiene and other lifestyle modifications related to industrialization might contribute, and an infectious agent might have variable prevalence as a result of these societal changes, as with many other infectious diseases.

# Pathogenesis of Rheumatoid Arthritis

### KEY POINTS

### Introduction

The pathogenesis of rheumatoid arthritis (RA) has been extensively studied for decades and has revealed an abundance of mechanisms that contribute to the perpetuation of synovitis and joint damage. These careful observations led to novel agents that target the inflammatory response that provide significant clinical benefit. In this chapter, the diversity of pro-inflammatory and destructive pathways that contribute to RA is described.

### Synovial Features, Cell Types, and Biology

### KEY POINTS

Although systemic autoimmunity is a hallmark in RA, the primary inflammatory site is the synovium. Infiltration of synovial tissue with mononuclear cells, especially T cells and macrophages, and synovial intimal lining hyperplasia are hallmarks of the disease (see Fig. 71.1 for an example of RA synovial histopathology).

### Synovial Histopathology in Rheumatoid Arthritis

The structure of synovium includes two layers, namely the synovial intimal lining and the sublining (see Chapter 2). The former comprises macrophageand fibroblast-like cells, and the latter is usually relatively acellular and with fibrous tissue, fat cells, and a relatively sparse vascular network. In RA, the synovium can assume diverse histologic patterns that can include infiltration of varying amounts of adaptive and innate immune cells (see Fig. 71.1). The tissue locally expands and invades cartilage, bone, and joint support structures. The invasive front of rheumatoid synovium, especially as it extends over cartilage and erodes bone, is sometimes called pannus.

T cells on average constitute 30% to 50% of cells in RA synovia, most of which are small CD4+ memory cells. About 5% of synovial cells are B lymphocytes or plasma cells, although in some tissues the percentage can be considerably higher. The B cells are often located within reactive lymphoid centers, whereas macrophages and plasma cells, primary producers of synovial immunoglobulins like anti-citrullinated protein antibodies (ACPAs) and rheumatoid factors (RFs), are more broadly distributed. CD4+

T cells in RA synovium can be in intimate contact with B lymphocytes, macrophages, and DCs and drive adaptive responses to modified proteins and autoantigens (see Chapter 70).

Synovial lymphoid aggregates are present in about 15% to 20% of RA synovia. Although originally considered specific for RA, it is now clear that they are equally prevalent in psoriatic arthritis and are even seen in some people with osteoarthritis (OA). Even though the cytokine and chemokine profile of RA synovium can support formation of these structures, progression to fully differentiated follicles are uncommon. The presence of aggregates correlates with higher production of ACPAs and RF in synovium but not necessarily with clinical disease activity. In fact, there is evidence of the differential involvement of cellular and molecular pathways involved in the pathogenesis of seropositive and seronegative RA subtypes, with an up-regulation of CCL13, CCL18, and matrix metalloproteinase (MMP)-3 in myeloid cell subsets of ACPA- RA compared with ACPA+ RA. Inflammatory histologic patterns may be associated with increased evidence of systemic inflammation, such as elevated C-reactive protein, but also without a clear correlation to clinical disease activity.'

The distribution of lymphocytes in the tissue varies from discrete lymphoid aggregates to diffuse sheets of mononuclear cells, with the most prominent location for T cells being the perivascular region. These collections consist of small, CD4+ memory T cells (CD45RO+) with scant cytoplasm. More recent studies identified a novel T cell subset of CD4+ PD-1+ CXCR5peripheral helper T cells (Tph) that have pathogenic potential (see Table 71.1). They are located in lymphoid aggregates adjacent to B cells and produce interleukin (IL)-21 to support B cell proliferation and differentiation into plasma cells. Tph cells are distinct from classical T helper follicular cells based on their transcriptome, including expression of chemokine receptors CCR2, CXCR1, and CCR5 to facilitate recruitment to inflamed synovium.

Scattered CD8+ T cells also accumulate in aggregates, although overall, substantially more CD4+ cells are present. CD8+ GZMK+ T cells were recently discovered in RA synovium, mainly in the sublining region (see Table 71.1). This unique population is a potential source of interferon (IFN)-γ that can drive adaptive articular immune responses.

Evaluation of fibroblasts in enzymatically dispersed RA synovium using single-cell transcriptomics indicates the presence of multiple mesenchymal cell, as well as other immune cell phenotypes (see Table 71.1 and Fig. 71.2).7, Among these for fibroblasts, the CD90+ fibroblast activation protein (FAP) α+ population is particularly noteworthy. These cells are found in

perivascular regions and are induced by endothelial cellderived NOTCH3.10 This phenotype is pro-inflammatory and could play a role perpetuating synovitis. Fibroblasts farther away from blood vessels and away from NOTCH3 influence generally assume the phenotype of intimal lining fibroblasts (CD90- FAPα+). Synovial tissue fibroblasts in RA also have enhanced metabolic activity that is, in part, regulated by intra-cellular complement protein C3 and type 1 receptor (MC1), synovial fibroblasts acquire a senescence phenotype characterized by arrested proliferation and metabolic reprogramming and leads to anti-arthritic effects in an animal model of arthritis associated with induction of senescence in the synovial tissue and cartilage protection.

Macrophages comprise about 20% of cells in the synovium. Evaluation of enzymatically disaggregated synovial tissue reveals several transcriptionally defined phenotypes. Based on expression of various surface markers, there appears to be a gradient of phenotypes from the perivascular regions to the intimal lining. This could represent differentiation of macrophages as they migrate toward the lining layer. More recently, two synovial subsets have been identified known as MerTK+ and MerTK-. The former is associated with production of anti-inflammatory mediators like resolvins and lipoxin (LX) and a low proportion of synovial MerTKpos macrophages. Consistent with this notion is the observation that a paucity of these cells in synovial tissue from patients in remission is associated with increased risk of disease flare after discontinuing treatment. MerTKcells, which are more prominent in RA tissues, produce cytokines like TNF and IL-6 that can drive synovitis. A third phenotype that expresses the chemokine receptor CXCR3 can be found in the lining, where it forms tight junctions and creates an immunologic barrier. Lastly, a subset referred to as HBEGF+ inflammatory macrophages is also enriched in RA tissues and is shaped by FLS and TNF. These macrophages promote fibroblast invasiveness in an epidermal growth factor receptor—dependent manner.

Rheumatoid synovium histopathology is highly diverse, not only between patients and between joints but also within an individual joint. As such, studies of synovial biopsies show that at least six samples from various locations in an individual joint need to be evaluated to decrease the coefficient of variation to less than 10% to 20%. In situations in which the synovial tissue from more than one joint in an individual patient is available, the same general histopathologic patterns are usually apparent in tissues from separate sites. These patterns have been associated with some systemic immune abnormalities, with a more intense

lymphocytic infiltration linked to anergic responses in peripheral blood. The use of histopathologic patterns and cell infiltration to predict response to therapy has generally been disappointing, including Janus kinase (JAK) inhibition, B cell depletion, and T cell co-stimulation.

A variety of classification methods have been used based on histopathology, such as abundance of lymphocytes or myeloid cells, although clinical correlations with symptoms or response to therapy have had limited success. More recently a new system based on single-cell transcriptomics could provide more precise ways to measure cell infiltration. Six broad "cell type abundance phenotype" (CTAP) patterns were described, including enrichment of T and B cells (CTAP-TB) and several patterns that include different mixtures of specific fibroblast, myeloid, and endothelial lineages but lack T or B cells (CTAP-EFM; Table 71.1). The transcriptionally defined patterns also correlate with histopathology and expression inflammatory genes like cytokines. The availability of new molecular signatures creates the potential to stratify patients based on their infiltrating cells and, possibly, their individualized mechanisms of disease. Such stratification will be an important advance for clinical investigation, as well as care of individual patients.

### Synovial Intimal Lining Cells: Macrophage-like and Fibroblast-like Synoviocytes

### Synovial Intimal Lining Phenotype and Function

The synovial intimal lining is a loosely organized collection of cells that form an interface between the synovium and the synovial fluid space. The intimal lining cells lack tight junctions and a defined basement membrane. The increase in cell number in RA can be substantial. In the normal joint, the lining is only one to two cell layers deep, whereas in RA it is often 4 to 10 cells deep. Two major cell types are found in the lining: macrophagelike synoviocytes (MLSs, also called type A synoviocytes) and FLS (also called type B synoviocytes). The former are derived from the bone marrow and express macrophage surface markers such as CD68, Fc receptors, and CD14, as well as abundant HLA-DR, whereas the latter express little if any class II major histocompatibility complex (MHC) antigens, are devoid of macrophage markers, and have a scant endoplasmic reticulum. FLS express some proteins that are unusual for mesenchymal cells, including vascular cell adhesion molecule-1 (VCAM-1), podoplanin (PDPN), CD55 (decay activating factor), cadherin-11, junctional adhesion molecule C (JAM-C), and the proteoglycan-synthesis enzyme uridine diphosphoglucose dehydrogenase. The relative numbers of MLS and FLS cells are usually similar in normal synovium. There is an absolute increase in both cell types in RA, although the percentage of increase in macrophage-like cells is often greater. In addition, the MLS synoviocytes tend to accumulate in the more superficial regions of the intimal lining.

Intimal lining synovial macrophages are terminally differentiated cells that do not appear to divide in the joint, and the accumulation of these cells in RA likely results from the ingress of new bone marrow-derived precursors. In contrast, mesenchymalderived FLS can divide locally in response to the growth factors generated by the activated immune response. Platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF), transforming growth factor (TGF)-β, TNF, and IL-1 produced by many different cells combine with products of arachidonic acid metabolism to induce proliferation of these cells. In addition, pluripotential mesenchymal stem cells that arise in the bone marrow and circulate through the blood can

migrate into the synovium and differentiate into FLS. Retention of macrophages in the intimal lining is probably due to expression of adhesion molecules such as VCAM-1 and JAM-C on FLS and is likely directed by chemotactic factors produced by FLS. For example, in micromass cultures composed of laminin and FLS, the FLS migrate to the surface of the micromasses and then can recruit macrophages in the interior to the "lining" (Fig. 71.3). Formation of this artificial intimal lining is dependent on the adhesion molecule cadherin-1 1.

Although local proliferation of cells in the intimal lining can occur, mitotic figures in rheumatoid synovium are rare, and thymidine uptake indicating DNA synthesis occurs in only a small percentage of synovial cells. Using a monoclonal antibody that recognizes dividing cells, an even lower rate of cell division (~0.05%) is apparent. A somewhat higher percentage of cells that express the cell cycle—specific antigen proliferating cell nuclear antigen are present in RA lining compared with OA.

The architecture of the synovial intimal lining is distinct from other lining layers in the body. In contrast to serosal surfaces, the intimal lining does not include epithelial cells and lacks a basement membrane. Rather than serving as a discrete barrier, it is a loose association of cells that is discontinuous in some locations. As noted above, recent data suggest that CXCR3+ macrophages in the lining can form tight junctions that create a less porous structure. However, the presence of desmosomes diminishes in inflamed synovium and allows freer exchange of molecules between the synovium and the synovial fluid space.

Cadherin-11, from a class of adhesion proteins that are ubiquitous in various tissues, serves as the major mediator of homotypic aggregation by FLS. Immunohistochemistry shows abundant expression of this protein in the intimal lining. Its importance in the synovial architecture was confirmed in cadherin-11 knockout mice, in which the intimal lining was virtually nonexistent. Blocking cadherin-11 with antibodies suppresses arthritis in the K/BxN murine serum transfer model and decreases cartilage damage but not bone damage.

The origin of the fibroblasts in the rheumatoid synovium is presumably from circulating mesenchymal stem cells that differentiate after arrival to the joint. A recently described circulating cell type called preinflammatory mesenchymal (PRIME) cells has been identified in the blood of RA patients. Normally present in very low abundance, the number increases preceding a disease flare. This unusual population represents a possible predictive biomarker, as well as an interesting potential therapeutic target for flare prevention.

When the enzymatically dispersed synovial adherent cells are cultured for several passages, mesenchymal cells survive and proliferate, while the macrophages ultimately die, resulting in a population of fibroblast-like cells. Therefore most published reports of cultured synoviocytes use this population of cells. This cell population is homogeneous; many are likely derived from the lining, but some might originate from the sublining. The cultured population represents the convergence of multiple fibroblast phenotypes; expresses varying levels of podoplanin, cadherin-11, VCAM-1, CD90, and FAPα; and generally lacks CD34. This population of synovial fibroblasts from RA are imprinted in vivo, possibly as a result of epigenetic changes like DNA methylation, and exhibit an invasive phenotype when cultured in vivo or when implanted into mice (see the "Aggressive Behavior of Rheumatoid Arthritis Fibroblast-like Synoviocytes" section).

RA FLS and synovium also display metabolic abnormalities, including choline metabolism with high expression of choline

kinase α and aberrant glutamine regulation.24, Choline kinase α inhibition decreases cell migration and decreases disease severity in the K/BxN murine serum transfer model, suggesting that metabolic modulation could be useful in RA. Glucose metabolism is also dysregulated in RA FLS, with a shift toward glycolysis in RA FLS compared with OA FLS. This leads to dysregulated glucose metabolism via hexokinase-2, which is the first step in glucose metabolism (Fig. 71.4) Evidence for the importance of this metabolic finding includes the observation that glycolytic and glutaminase inhibitors decrease cell invasion, proliferation, and cell migration. Other metabolic inhibitors targeting inducible enzymes in the glycolytic pathway, such as hexokinase-2, can also be effective agents in pre-clinical arthritis models.

FLS derived from very early RA biopsies differ from those obtained from late RA synovium because they lose their ability to inhibit cytokine-induced endothelial cell activation and lymphocyte recruitment. As the disease evolves, the FLS assume a more stimulatory phenotype and can activate vascular endothelium. These data are consistent with DNA methylation changes that occur during the evolution of disease and suggest that early interventions might prevent progression to more aggressive disease.

### Targeting Fibroblasts

Given the pathogenic function of FLS and sublining fibroblasts, a variety of interventions have been designed to target this lineage. One advantage of this approach is the potential to decrease
