synovitis without affecting adaptive immune responses. Cadherin-11 was a particularly attractive target due to its limited expression in other cell types and pre-clinical efficacy. However, anti-cadherin-11 antibody was ineffective in a phase II clinical trial. A second approach was to target the proliferative machinery in synovial fibroblasts with a small molecule seliciclib, which inhibits several cyclin-dependent kinases. The phase Ib portion of the TRAFIC clinical trial in RA showed that the compound was well tolerated with a signal of efficacy. These kinases are expressed by many other cell types and other potential targets, such as FAPα, and might be more specific for synovial fibroblasts in inflamed tissue.

The therapeutic potential for inhibitors of caspases has been problematic because they could potentially inhibit apoptosis. One isoform called caspase 8G (CASP8G) is relatively selective for fibroblasts and has nonenzymatic functions that regulate FLS invasion. Selective inhibition of CASP8G could have minimal effect on programmed cell death while still blocking the aggressive behavior of RA FLS.

### Aggressive Behavior of Rheumatoid Arthritis Fibroblast-like Synoviocytes

Tumor-like Properties. FLS typically require adherence to a substrate when grown in tissue culture, but RA synoviocytes, like transformed cells, can proliferate in an anchorage-independent manner. In addition, cultured RA synoviocytes exhibit defective

contact inhibition and express proto-oncogenes, such as c-Myc, which are typically abundant in tumor cells. Poorly regulated cell growth likely occurs in vivo as well, and studies examining crosslinked genes demonstrate oligoclonality in the synoviocyte population from RA, but not OA, synovium. Increased telomerase activity, another feature of transformed cells, is also present in RA synovium and is observed in fibroblast growth factor (FGF)—stimulated RA synoviocytes. Epigenetic analysis suggests that overexpression of certain microRNAs (miRNAs) or differential DNA methylation is associated with increased cytokine production or more aggressive behavior.

Matrix Invasion. The most compelling evidence suggesting that RA synovial fibroblasts are permanently altered is derived from studies in a severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID) mouse model in which synoviocytes and cartilage are co-implanted. The rheumatoid cells adhere to and invade into the cartilage matrix, unlike OA and skin fibroblasts33 (Fig. 71.5). Because this population is devoid of T cells and macrophages, there is no contribution from an immune response to murine antigens. The invading cells express VCAM-1, which could facilitate adhesion to cartilage or chondrocytes, as well as proteases that digest the cartilage matrix. If explants are introduced into two locations in the SCID mice, the rheumatoid FLS can migrate from one site to another, presumably via lymphatics and the bloodstream. This finding raises the intriguing possibility that imprinted, aggressive cells can

cC 'metastasize" from joint to joint and contribute to the polyarticular nature of RA.

Blocking IL-1 signaling in the SCID model with IL-1 receptor antagonist (IL-1Ra), a natural IL-1 antagonist, has no effect on synoviocyte invasion but decreases perichondrocyte matrix loss. In contrast, IL-10 or blocking membrane-type matrix metalloproteinases (MT-MMPs), Ras, or c-Myc expression decreases invasion. Surprisingly, overexpression of soluble TNF receptors has little effect in this model. These studies suggest that excessive production of IL-1 and underexpression of IL-10 contribute to the invasive properties of RA synoviocytes. In another study, transfecting normal synoviocytes with the human papillomavirus gene encoding E6, which inactivates p53, induced the rheumatoid phenotype. RA FLS also have prolonged and exaggerated responses to synovial cytokines. For example, TNF induces higher levels of chemokines and MMPs in RA FLS than in control FLS, perhaps because of prolonged activation of transcription factors like nuclear factor-κB (NF-κB). Overall, these studies suggest that imprinted RA FLS serve as effector cells that display unique aggressive properties in inflammatory synovitis.

Various cytokines and growth factors in the joint, most notably PDGF, enhance FLS migration and invasion into the matrix. The signaling molecules that regulate FLS movement could represent interesting therapeutic targets. Phosphoinositide 3 kinases (PI3Ks) are especially important. FLS express three isoforms (α,

β, and δ); whereas α is expressed by many cell lineages, δ is generally restricted to bone marrowderived cells. The δ isoform is unexpectedly expressed by FLS and is markedly induced by TNF. Functional studies and the use of relatively selective kinase inhibitors suggest that PI3Kδ is perhaps the most important isoform that regulates FLS movement and matrix invasion.

Phosphatases are also dysregulated in RA FLS and contribute to pathogenic fibroblast behavior. In addition to SHP-2, RPTPα and RPTPo regulate the rheumatoid aggressive phenotype. 37, The latter is regulated by binding to the proteoglycan syndecan-4, which can be disrupted by decoy protein to suppress disease severity in a murine model. This represents a potential FLS-directed therapy that can complement current immune-cell targeting.

### Synovial T Lymphocyte Phenotype and Function

T Cell Aggregate Formation in Rheumatoid Arthritis Synovium Chemokines play a central role in the organization of tissues into lymphoid structures such as aggregates and germinal centers. CXCL13 and CCL21 are especially important, and their expression in rheumatoid synovium correlates with the presence of this microarchitecture. The former, in particular, is produced by synovial follicular DCs (FDCs). Similarly, plasma cells expressing the chemokine receptor CXCR3 are present in the rheumatoid synovium. The CXCR3 ligand Mig/CXCL9 is highly expressed by intimal lining synoviocytes and sublining cells and attracts these cells toward T cell aggregates.

The architecture of lymphoid structures in rheumatoid synovium is regulated by members of the TNF superfamily. Lymphotoxin-α and -β (LTα and LTβ), as well as the lymphotoxin-related inducible ligand that competes for glycoprotein D binding to herpes virus entry mediator on T cells (LIGHT), form trimeric molecules in various combinations that can bind to distinct cell surfaces. Deletion of either LTα or LTβ impairs lymphoid development, whereas lymph nodes develop normally in LIGHT-deficient mice. In the SCID mouse model using RA tissue explants, depletion of CD8+ T cells led to loss of FDCs, depletion of LTα 1β2, and disintegration of the lymphoid follicles.

Although LTα levels are low in RA, other TNF superfamily members such as LTβ, TWEAK (TNF-like weak inducer of

apoptosis), and LIGHT are abundant. In addition to regulating lymphoid aggregate and germinal center formation, LTs can also stimulate FLS to produce chemokines such as CCL2 and CCL5 that attract T cells into the joint. LIGHT also enhances osteoclast differentiation and induces expression of MMP-9, TNF, IL-6, and IL-8 by macrophages. LTβ and LIGHT blockade using soluble receptors decreases the severity of collagen-induced arthritis. However, the inhibitor was not effective in the passive arthritis model in which the pathogenic antibodies were directly administered to mice. Hence LIGHT has a more important role in the early phases of disease when adaptive immunity to joint antigens is developing. TWEAK can also play a role in Th17 differentiation, and its inhibition suppresses disease severity in collageninduced arthritis.

### Synovial T Cell Co-stimulatory Molecules

Many RA synovial T lymphocytes exhibit an activated surface phenotype, with high expression of HLA-DR, CD69, and CD27. The co-stimulatory molecule CD28 is highly expressed by synovial T cells in RA. Its ligands, CD80 and CD86, are also displayed on antigen-presenting cells in the joint, thereby providing an excellent environment for T cell activation. The importance of the CD80/86CD28 interaction is supported by the observation that abatacept, which blocks CD80/86, is effective in RA. Other costimulatory molecule pairs such as CD40L on T cells and CD40 on antigen-presenting cells are also expressed in RA synovium.

### Synovial T Cell Adhesion Molecules

Synovial lymphocytes express adhesion molecules in the very late activation antigen (VLA) and lymphocyte function—associated antigen (LFA) integrin superfamily, which facilitates recruitment to and retention of lymphocytes in the synovium. The cytokine milieu of the joint induces adhesion molecules such as intercellular adhesion molecule-1 (ICAM-1), VCAM-1, and connecting segment-1 (CS-1) fibronectin on vascular endothelium. These, in conjunction with chemokines and other chemoattractants, attract cells that express the cognate adhesion molecule counter-receptors on their surface.

### Synovial T Cell Chemokine Receptors

Synovial T cells in RA express characteristic receptors to specific chemokines. The chemokine receptor CCR5 is the ligand for macrophage inhibitory proteins 1α and 1β and is highly expressed in the infiltrating RA T cells. This particular receptor, along with CXCR3, is preferentially found on Th1 cells, an observation that might explain accumulation of this phenotype in the rheumatoid synovium. Expression of nonfunctional CCR5 alleles (CCR5- d32) that protect from HIV infection has been associated with diminished disease severity in people with RA who carry the variant (although small molecule CCR5 antagonists have limited clinical efficacy). The chemotactic factor stromal cellderived factor-1 (SDF-1) is also produced by synovial tissue, and its specific receptor, CXCR4, is displayed by rheumatoid synovial T cells. Other T cell phenotypes recruited to the rheumatoid synovium include Th17 cells that express CCR2 or CCR6 and produce IL-17 and CD4+ CD25+ regulatory T (Treg) cells that can suppress immune responses (see the subsequent discussion of T cell subsets). Preferential recruitment of CCR6+ Th17 cells into the rheumatoid joint appears to be due to the local release of the chemokine CCL20.45

T Cell Receptors. Early studies of T cell receptors (TCRs) in RA suggested enrichment for Vβ3, Vβ14, and Vβ17, especially in synovial tissue. These Vβ genes are structurally related

and are susceptible to activation by superantigens. In addition to superantigens, commonality in TCRs could reflect rheumatoid "antigen(s)" that bind to these TCRs. However, many subsequent studies failed to observe restricted clonality of T cells in RA synovial fluid, synovial tissue, or blood or identified expansion of different Vβ or Vα genes. More recent studies identified inflammation-associated Treg clonotypes in the peripheral blood of patients similar to Tregs identified in joint samples. These inflammation-associated Tregs were fully functional and provide evidence of active exchange between peripheral and joint compartments for adaptive immune cells.

### Metabolic Mechanisms Contributing to T Cell Accumulation

The dominant mechanism for synovial T cell accumulation most likely results from antigen-independent processes that include cell recruitment and retention mediated by chemokines and adhesion molecules. A high level of telomerase activity is present in rheumatoid synovial lymphocytes, which reflects their proliferative activity and could indicate repeated cycles of cell division. In addition to limited antigen-driven cell growth, hyperproliferation of T cells due to metabolic derangements can also contribute to T cell accumulation in RA synovium. For example, RA T cells have defective glycolytic activity due to increased shunting to the pentose phosphate pathway and accumulation of NADPH.48, This decreases activation of ataxia telangiectasia mutated (ATM) and enhanced proliferation of pro-inflammatory Th1 and Th17 cells. Restoring redox potential and increasing reactive oxygen species to normal can potentially suppress synovial inflammation. Overexpression of the podosome scaffold protein TKS5 is also regulated by a metabolic state of RA synovial T cells marked by reduced glycolytic flux. The pathogenic potential of these T cells is diminished by restoring pyruvate production or by inhibition of fatty acid synthesis.

### Synovial T Cell Immunoreactivity and Activation

The histopathologic appearance of RA, with exuberant infiltration of the synovium with T lymphocytes, is characteristic of tissues with chronic antigen-specific responses. However, the synovium can only respond to inflammation in a limited number of ways, and many chronic immune-mediated arthropathies have similar histologic patterns. In fact, chronic arthritides that clearly are not mediated by T cells (e.g., chronic tophaceous gout) exhibit many of the same features.

There are ample opportunities in the rheumatoid synovial environment for exposure to antigens and T cell activation. For example, proteins modified through processes such as citrullination provide a rich source of antigenic stimulation by T cell clones that were not deleted during development. Resultant T cell cytokine production, perhaps in central lymphoid organs, can drive the subsequent adaptive immune responses. Animal models also suggest that breakdown of tolerance can be due to events that occur early in development of the adaptive immune system. For instance, mutations in ZAP70, which is involved with TCR signaling, can lead to spontaneous T celldependent inflammatory arthritis in mice. An abnormal ZAP70 gene leads to defective positive and negative selection in the thymus and allows autoreactive T cells to escape. As a result, mice produce autoantibodies (e.g., RF and anti-dsDNA) and develop a severe destructive arthritis. The disease can be transferred by thymocytes or peripheral CD4+ T cells into syngeneic mice with a normal ZAP70 gene, which suggests that resetting the immune rheostat in development or survival of pathogenic clones in the thymus can lead to synovitis and abnormal immune responses later in life.

These studies show that minor changes in the TCR signaling and lack of subsequent clonal deletion can alter T cell selection and induce arthritis. The finding is especially relevant in light of the association of a PTPN22 SNP with RA (see Chapter 70), because this gene is also involved with TCR signaling. Despite the clear T cell dependence of the model, the cytokines implicated are remarkably similar to autoantibody-dependent models of RA. Therefore the cytokine profile in RA may represent a final common pathway for a variety of immune-mediated mechanisms. This concept is supported by the diversity of responses to targeted therapies in RA and suggests that RA is not a single disease but instead is a group of mechanistically distinct entities with a shared phenotype.

Although synovial T cells display an activated phenotype, proliferation and cytokine responses are usually less than normal in peripheral blood cells or even autologous peripheral blood T cells from the same patient. Spontaneous and stimulated cytokine production, including Th1 factors such as IFN-γ and IL-2, are relatively low. Responses directed toward most recall antigens are also deficient, although RA synovial T cells can proliferate briskly to certain heat shock proteins. Th17 cells have been detected in both the blood and synovium, perhaps because of exposure to a cytokine milieu that includes IL-1, IL-6, and/or IL-23 that can promote differentiation toward production of IL-17 family members (especially IL-17A and F).

The mechanisms of decreased responsiveness in the synovial compartment likely include exposure to suppressive factors (e.g., TGF-β or IL-1Ra), abnormal redox potentials that suppress TCR signal transduction, the presence of Tregs, or induction of anergy. Another contributor to local anergy could be the relative lack of the co-stimulatory molecule CD80 on HLA-DR+ FLS, which could induce anergy. This phenomenon has been observed in cocultures of T cells with synoviocytes.

### Cell-Cell Contact-Mediated T Lymphocyte Activation

Even though evidence of local T cell activation is relatively modest in rheumatoid synovium, direct cellcell contact permits these cells to participate in synovial cytokine networks and matrix destruction. Membranes prepared from activated T cells can directly stimulate macrophages and FLS to produce cytokines and MMPs. The membrane constituents that regulate this process vary, depending on the culture conditions, but include adhesion molecules such as LFA-1 and membrane-bound TNF. Hence a T cell displaying these proteins can potentially contribute to macrophage and fibroblast activation in an antigen-independent fashion. One of the bestcharacterized consequences of this pathway is the ability of T cells to enhance synovial macrophage TNF production in a contactdependent manner after exposure to macrophage-derived IL-15.54

Because memory T cells accumulate into the joint due to a chemoattractant gradient, there is no requirement for a specific antigen through this mechanism. Instead, activation of innate immunity by nonspecific stimuli permits subsequent ingress of the correct T cell phenotype to engage resident synovial intimal lining cells, sublining fibroblasts, or macrophages. The combination of antigen-driven adaptive immune responses and antigenindependent stimulation could contribute to the diversity of individual responses to targeted therapy and the relative paucity of complete remissions.

### Re-establishing Immune Homeostasis

Restoring Tolerance. The role of synovial T cell responses and autoreactivity in the pathogenesis of RA has led to efforts to treat the disease by restoring tolerance. Early aggressive treatment of

early RA (within the first year of clinical disease) with methotrexate and a TNF inhibitor can, in some circumstances, lead to longlasting remissions. In some cases, therapy can be withdrawn after 1 year of treatment, and patients do not experience a flare for at least an additional year. However, most drug-tapering regimens result in disease flares, suggesting that even aggressive therapy and long-lasting remissions do not indicate a return to tolerance. Additional individualized therapies that enhance Treg function, alter co-stimulation, or delete pathogenic T cells are other ways to restore homeostasis and normal immune function.

### Treg Cells and Innate Lymphoid Cells

The role of classically defined inducible Tregs (CD4+ CD25+ CD127+) in RA remains uncertain. Deficiency of this subset, which produces IL-10 and TGF-β and regulates other T cells through cell contact, could contribute to autoimmunity. The number of Tregs is generally low in RA synovium, although some reports suggest that it is not that different from OA synovium. Interestingly, the number decreases after intra-articular injection with corticosteroids. Characteristic regulatory cells that express Foxp3 and CD39 can be found in RA lymphoid aggregates, especially adjacent to DCs. As noted previously, Tregs from the joint can freely circulate and can be detected in peripheral blood.

The transcription factor STAT3 regulates Treg differentiation in the RA joint. Activated STAT3 is abundant in the rheumatoid synovium and can enhance Th17 differentiation while suppressing production of Tregs, whereas STAT5 appears to have the opposite effect. Thus modulating the balance between STATs in RA T cells, such as through JAK inhibition, could change the balance between pathogenic and immunosuppressive lymphocytes. FMSlike tyrosine kinase 3 ligand (FLT3L) also appears to regulate Tregs in RA and increase their formation.

Studies of RA peripheral blood generally demonstrate normal numbers of Tregs, although the CD4+ CD25+ cells can accumulate in rheumatoid synovial effusions. However, peripheral blood Treg responses in vitro after stimulation with anti-CD3 and anti-CD28 antibody displayed an anergic phenotype and were unable to suppress T cell or monocyte cytokine production. This abnormality might be reversed when patients are treated with TNF inhibitors.

These data suggest that abnormal Treg function could also be secondary to cytokine imbalance in RA rather than a primary event. Treatment can have a significant effect on the number and function of Tregs, which makes evaluation of their role in patient samples difficult to interpret. Nevertheless, enhancing or restoring Treg activity as a therapeutic intervention has the potential to downregulate other T cells and cytokine production.

Enhancing the number or activity of Tregs has been evaluated in animal models of arthritis with encouraging results. Antigen-induced arthritis is exacerbated when CD4+ CD25+ cells are depleted and suppressed when they are passively transferred to affected animals. Treg function is low in some inflammation models. Methotrexate also increases Treg function in collageninduced arthritis. Administration of neuropeptides such as vasoactive intestinal peptide appears to suppress collagen-induced arthritis by enhancing the Treg function in synovium and lymph nodes. However, it is still difficult to ascribe efficacy of therapeutic agents in RA to increased numbers or function of Treg.

The role of tissue innate lymphoid cells (ILCs) is increasingly recognized in immune-mediated diseases. Like Tregs, type 2 ILCs can suppress inflammation during disease resolution. IL-9 is a particularly important cytokine that regulates type 2 ILC-mediated

Treg induction. In pre-clinical models, IL-9 deficiency leads to chronic inflammation and increased joint damage. Interesting therapeutic strategies focused on enhancing normal processes that resolve inflammation could take advantage of the ILCTreg axis. Type 3 ILCs that express the chemokine receptor CCR6 are also present in the rheumatoid joint and could increase inflammation through the production of IL-17 and IL-22.66

### Synovial B Cells

Synovial B cell and plasma cell hyper-reactivity are major participants in the initiation and perpetuation phases of RA. This notion is supported by development of spontaneous arthritis in mice, such as the K/BxN model, in which loss of tolerance leads to autoantibody production, activation of innate immunity, and chronic synovitis. Furthermore, B celldirected therapies such as anti-CD20 antibody are often effective in RA. The rheumatoid synovium contains a relatively small number of B cells (<5% of the total cell population), but they, along with synovial plasma cells, are major producers of ACPAs, RFs, and other antibodies that can form immune complexes and fix complement.

### Cytokine Regulation of Synovial B Cells

Although many rheumatoid synovial tissues exhibit a diffuse infiltration with mononuclear cells, a significant percentage also have discrete lymphoid follicles populated by B cells in the sublining region. FDCs, B cells, plasma cells, and T lymphocytes collect in these aggregates. The germinal centers are highly organized structures in which affinity maturation occurs. B cells are present in the aggregates and express the maturation marker CD20, as well as proliferation-associated antigens such as Ki67 (the protein encoded by the MKI67 gene). The formation of these structures is dependent on soluble and membrane-bound cytokines, including lymphotoxin. B cells accumulate in lymphoid aggregates in RA synovium under the influence of a variety of chemotactic factors, including CCL21 and CXCL13.

A member of the TNF superfamily of cytokines known as B lymphocyte stimulator (BLyS, also called BAFF) is a key molecule that regulates B cell differentiation. BLyS binds to transmembrane activator and CAML interactor (TACI), which is present on both B and T cells. If this system is blocked using recombinant TACI- Ig to absorb the cytokine and a related B cell differentiation factor called a proliferation-inducing ligand (APRIL), then the number of B cells is dramatically reduced, and antibody production is decreased. The same construct is effective as a therapeutic agent in collagen-induced arthritis, a model that depends on autoantibody production.

BLyS is produced in RA synovium, especially by macrophages and to a lesser extent by TNF-stimulated B cells. APRIL is localized mainly to DCs in synovial germinal centers. TACI-Ig disrupts the germinal centers and decreases Ig receptors in SCID mice implanted with rheumatoid synovium. However, results of clinical trials neutralizing BLyS were disappointing, indicating that targeting of this cytokine is not as effective as B cell depletion with anti-CD20 antibody. Although improved benefit might be possible with a biologic agent that blocks both APRIL and BLyS, TACI-Ig markedly decreases serum immunoglobulin concentrations but has limited efficacy in RA.

### Synovial B Cell Maturation and Clonality

B cells isolated directly from germinal centers of RA synovium demonstrate a heterogeneous pattern of V-gene usage and

rearrangement. The majority of VH genes are not mutated, suggesting that they are recent immigrants from the peripheral blood and are activated locally. For RF-producing cells, shared mutations containing an identical sequence throughout the variable domain of immunoglobulins have been identified in synovial tissue. Preferential utilization of a limited number of VH and DH gene segments and marked preference for a DH reading frame encoding particular hydrophilic residues have also been observed, consistent with antigen-related selection and maturation. Analysis of expressed heavychain variable domains supports the notion that the B cell response in RA synovium is oligoclonal. Recently a highly enriched synovial B cell population characterized by co-expression of a family of orphan nuclear receptors (NR4A) has been described. NR4A+ B cells coexpress lymphotoxins α and β and IL-6, supporting functions in ectopic lymphoid-like structures (ELS) promotion. Expanded and shared clones between synovial plasma cells and NR4A+ B cells suggest an in situ differentiation of this B cel population.

Analyses of gene usage on synovial B cells and plasma cells demonstrate oligoclonality. Most of the cells are class-switched and enriched for immunoglobulin heavy gene V4-34 and have longer CDR3 lengths compared with B cells analyzed from peripheral blood. Interestingly, these heavy chain genes are also associated with chronic lymphocytic leukemia and autoimmunity. 72, B cells in synovium that produce ACPAs also have abundant somatic mutations consistent with affinity maturation and antigen-driven selection. Of interest, studies of serial blood samples from individuals with ACPA+ RA found increasing numbers of IgG and especially IgA expressing plasmablasts that bind to citrullinated peptides over time with shared complementary-determining region 3 sequences. As the disease progressed, divergent somatic mutations provide evidence of expanding polyreactivity of citrullinated proteins. The resultant antibodies increasingly display the ability to form immune complexes and activate macrophages to produce cytokines like TNF. The data suggest that B cells go through repeated cycles of trafficking from mucosal sites through the blood to synovium, with antigen spread and increasing avidity for modified peptides.

Plasma cells in the synovium also have distinct rearrangements compared with the B lymphocytes. Although plasma cell rearrangements are not always similar to the B cells, groups of plasma cells use similar genes, albeit with distinct mutations. Therefore the plasma cells are likely either derived from antigen-driven synovial B cell clones in the joint or migrate to the synovium after affinity maturation.

B cell differentiation and survival depend on stromal cells and cells with nurse-like properties that support lymphocyte maturation in the thymus. The synovium of patients with RA also contains nurse-like cells, which can increase expression of CD40 and class II MHC proteins on B cells. B cell survival is supported by this population of cells, whereas autoreactive clones evade deletion and produce autoantibodies. A variety of cytokines including granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF), IL-6, and IL-8 are produced by RA nurse-like cells, and direct contact with B cells is critical for maximal proliferation and antibody production.

### Clinical Improvement After B Cell Depletion

Anti-CD20 antibody (rituximab) is effective in RA with benefit similar to other biologics. Response rates are higher in patients with antibody profiles that include RF and ACPA, and high levels of chemokines like CXCL13 that attract B cells to synovium might also serve as a biomarker associated with efficacy. Increasing

serum levels of CXCL13 also predict the return of B cells in the peripheral circulation and could be a useful marker for stratifying patients or planning additional courses of rituximab. Metabolomics studies in RA patients treated with rituximab suggest that some polar metabolites like choline and phenylalanine or lipid species at baseline were associated with subsequent clinical improvement. A variety of metabolic changes occurred after treatment, including alterations in polar and lipid compounds.

On the other hand, higher numbers of plasmablasts, identified by IgJ expression, in the blood are associated with poor response to B cell depletion by ocrelizumab and rituximab. Because anti- CD20depleting antibody does not affect plasma cells, which lack CD20, persistent disease could be related to the presence of plasmablasts in the blood or joint.

In RA, serial synovial biopsies demonstrate only partial B cell depletion after rituximab therapy despite the virtual absence of peripheral B cells. The clinical responses do not always correlate closely with the extent of synovial depletion, although some patients with the most impressive responses appear to have marked declines in the number of B cells in the post-treatment synovial specimens. Surprisingly, B cell depletion does not consistently decrease autoantibody production or cytokine production in the synovium, nor does a change in ACPA or RF levels predict a clinical response. Longer-term biopsy studies suggest that plasma cells are decreased in synovium 24 weeks after treatment with rituximab and that this outcome correlates with decreased symptoms. A large prospective clinical trial recently also failed to show a correlation between B cell infiltration in RA synovium and response to rituximab.

The synovial biopsy data on synovial autoantibody production suggest that B cells play a more complex role in the disease than simply producers of ACPAs or RF. B cells are potent antigen-presenting cells that could also contribute to disease in the inflamed synovium or in central lymphoid organs. In a SCID mouse model using rheumatoid synovial explants, for example, T cell activation, lymphangiogenic, and cytokine production depend on B cells. In the same model, treatment with TACI-Ig to inhibit APRIL and BLyS decreases synovial inflammation and IFN-γ production in tissues with germinal centers.

B cells can also contribute to rheumatoid synovitis by producing cytokines, including comparatively small amounts of LTα, TNF, and IL-6. Although macrophages and synoviocytes produce quantitatively greater amounts, B cells in strategic locations like lymphoid aggregates might help drive synovitis. Certain B cell subsets could play a role, such as the FcRL4+ B cell subset that produces TNF and RANKL in RA and synovial CD79a+ B cells that correlate with erosive disease in patients with long-standing RA. Alternatively, regulatory B cells, like Tregs, could decrease inflammatory responses in RA through the elaboration of suppressive cytokines like IL-10 and TGF-β.

### Dendritic Cells

DCs are potent antigen-presenting cells that populate synovial tissue and synovial effusions of patients with RA. In established RA, synovial DCs could present antigens in the joint to elicit a local immune response. DCs also produce type I IFNs, which have been implicated in numerous autoimmune diseases such as lupus and RA. Moreover, coordinated expression of genes that are regulated by IFNs, sometimes called the IFN signature, has been observed in the joint and blood of patients with RA.

Rheumatoid synovium in many ways functions like extralymphatic lymphoid tissues, with mature DCs expressing CD86,

CD83, and DC-LAMP localized in perivascular lymphocytic infiltrates and aggregates. Ultrastructural analysis of the synovium shows the DCs in contact with lymphocytes, where they can present antigens. The presence of DCs is not unique to RA and has been identified in other inflammatory arthritides, including gout and spondyloarthropathies.

DCs can express the chemokine receptor CCR7, which drives their migration to lymphoid tissue and orchestrates organization into the appropriate germinal centers. Synoviocytes in RA express two CCR7 ligands (CCL19 and CCL21), which provide a signal for the DCs to remain in the peripheral tissue. Immature DCs and plasmacytoid DCs are also scattered throughout the synovial sublining region. B cellenriched lymphoid follicles, which are usually organized around FDCs, are also found in RA joints. Cytokines in the rheumatoid synovium such as GM-CSF influence the proliferation and maturation of DCs. Increased numbers of DCs are found in the tissue and synovial effusions, where they can constitute up to 5% of mononuclear cells.

FDC-containing ectopic lymphoid structures in rheumatoid synovium also express high levels of activation-induced cytosine deaminase, a gene that participates in Ig class switching. ACPA+ plasma cells surround these aggregates, suggesting that the aggregates play a role in autoantibody production. The architecture and ACPA+ cells persist when tissue is transplanted into SCID mice. Therefore synovial DCs not only help organize the microarchitecture of synovial tissue but also participate in the development of high-affinity IgG autoantibodies.

In addition to FDCs, several other subsets are present in the rheumatoid joint. CD1c+ DCs in the synovium accumulate in inflamed synovium, are highly responsive to Toll-like receptor (TLR) 7/8 stimulation and have a distinctive transcriptome compared with their peripheral blood counterparts. Recently described CD141+ DCs, distinct from CD1c+ DCs, are associated with viral and tumor immune responses and are also enriched in inflammatory synovium. These DCs can activate CD4+ and CD8+ T cells and increase GM-CSF, TNF, and IFN-γ production. They can also increase the invasive potential of synoviocytes. Another population of DCs, namely CD209/CD14+, are derived from rheumatoid monocytes produce greater amounts of cytokines than the cells derived from health controls.

### Mast Cells

Mast cells are present in the synovial membranes of patients with RA and, in some patients, are located at sites of cartilage erosion. Rheumatoid synovial membranes contain more than 10 times as many mast cells than control synovial samples from patients undergoing surgery for meniscectomy. Mast cells and histamine are also found in a majority of synovial fluid specimens from inflammatory synovitis. A strong correlation exists between the number of mast cells in synovial tissue and the degree of lymphocyte infiltration, autoantibody positivity, and high disease activity. Mast cells from RA synovium express significantly higher amounts of the C5a receptor and express higher amounts of prostaglandin D2 (PGD2) compared with OA synovium.

Resident mast cells in synovium respond to cytokines that stimulate mast cell growth and chemotaxis. Extracts of mast cells can induce adherent rheumatoid synovial cells to increase production of prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) and collagenase, and immunostaining of RA synovial mast cells demonstrates tryptase and TNF. Mast cellderived heparin has significant effects on connective tissue. In particular, it can modulate the effects of hormones

on osseous cells and thereby alter the balance of bone synthesis toward degradation. Synovial mast cells also express Fcε receptors, as well as Fcγ receptor types I and II, but not type III. Immune complexes that ligate type I receptors release PGD2 and TNF, whereas type II receptor ligation releases histamine.

Mast cells have been implicated in the initiation of disease in the K/BxN serum transfer model,90 but some studies cast doubt on that conclusion. The role of mast cells in established disease is also uncertain, yet mast cell depletion in the pre-clinical phase of murine collagen-induced arthritis is protective.91, In RA, treatment of synovial tissue explant cultures with a c-Kit tyrosine kinase inhibitor blocks stem cell factor signaling and decreases production of TNF. These data suggest that mast cells might contribute to synovial cytokines. Mast cells might also contribute to the cytokine milieu of RA synovium because they contain pre-formed IL-17A granules. Furthermore, cultured mast cells release IL-17 when they are stimulated with TNF or immune complexes.

A clinical trial using the c-Kit (a receptor tyrosine kinase that facilitates mast cell growth and survival) inhibitor masitinib suggested clinical efficacy in RA, but a phase III study did not confirm benefit. In addition, a controlled trial of a histamine H4 receptor antagonist to block immunomodulatory effects of mastcell derived histamine did not show significant clinical benefit. Thus, there is no direct evidence that blocking mast cell function will be useful in RA.

### Polymorphonuclear Leukocytes

Neutrophils are common in RA synovial effusions, but very few infiltrate the synovium. Even though circulating neutrophils from patients with arthritis resemble those from healthy controls, neutrophils in joint fluid cells exhibit IFN-γ, as well as TNF, IL-6, and hypoxia gene signatures. Neutrophils are immunologically active and can also produce IL-17B and IL-1Ra. Synovial neutrophils also release extra-cellular traps (NETs), which are composed of extruded DNA. Synovial, synovial fluid, peripheral blood neutrophil, and even pulmonary NETosis are increased in RA. It can be further enhanced by RA serum (especially ACPA-containing serum), IL-17A, and TNF. The resultant extra-cellular DNA includes PADI4 and a variety of citrullinated peptides. The decorated NETs can then induce other cytokines, IL-6, IL-8, and chemokines. Citrullinated proteins bound to NETs or released from neutrophils due to bacterial products like leukotoxin A can also serve as antigens to drive ACPA production, cytokine release, or immune complex formation.

### Natural Killer Cells

NK cells are also present in RA synovium. A potential role in RA is suggested by an RA-associated gene variant of NKG2D, which is a C-lectin receptor present on NK cells (as well as some additional immune cell subsets). Cytotoxic NK cells contain large amounts of granzymes, which are serine proteases. One potentially important immunoregulatory role of NK cells is that they can stimulate B cells to produce RFs. A subset of NK cells that expresses large amounts of CD56 is abundant in RA synovial tissue and fluid. These cells produce cytokines like GM-CSF102 and enhance pro-inflammatory cytokine production by T lymphocytes and macrophages. IL-32 exacerbates arthritis and joint damage in collagen-induced arthritis, possibly by increasing the number of synovial NK cells. Less information is available on invariant NK T cells (iNKTs), which respond to lipid antigens.

However, blocking CD1d and iNKT function decreases the severity of collagen-induced arthritis in mice.

### Bone Marrow Cells

Subcortical bone and bone marrow likely contribute to synovial inflammatory responses in RA. Primitive bone marrow mesenchymal cells can traverse cortical bone through pores in murine collagen-induced arthritis before the onset of clinical disease, take up residence in the synovium, and produce mediators that enhance synovitis. The cell migration is TNF-dependent and is abrogated in mice that lack TNF receptors. CD34+ mesenchymal cells in rheumatoid bone marrow are more highly activated as judged by their NF-kB status and their ability to differentiate into fibroblast-like cells that produce MMPs and proangiogenic factors.

Bone marrow also can contribute other relevant cells, including macrophage lineage cells that migrate to the synovium and nurselike cells that support the survival of B cells. Just as the bone marrow can influence the synovium, the reverse is also true. Invasive pannus can rupture through cortical bone and invade the marrow space in some patients. When this occurs, B cell aggregates are especially prominent in the marrow and occur in an environment rich in B cell chemoattractants such as CCL21, and B cell survival factors such as BLyS B cells enriched in the subchondral and endosteal bone marrow areas were found adjacent to osteocalcin+ osteoblasts in two murine RA models and expressed high levels of osteoblast inhibitors CCL3 and TNF, inhibiting osteoblast differentiation by activating extra-cellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK) and NF-κB signaling pathways.

The bone marrow changes in RA could be either a result of synovitis or a primary event. The most common explanation for RA is that synovitis occurs first and expands into the marrow through soluble factors and direct extension (the "outsidein" hypothesis). The notion that bone marrow reactivity might be a primary event and that the activated cells migrate directly to the synovium through cortical bone or via the bloodstream has received increasing attention (the "inside-out" hypothesis). The bidirectional interactions between the synovium and the bone marrow suggest that both inside-out and outside-in mechanisms participate in RA.

### Synovial Biology at Various Stages of Rheumatoid Arthritis

The observation that autoantibody levels are elevated in patients with RA many years before the clinical arthritis manifests also supports the notion that a pre-clinical phase can precede symptomatic synovitis. In addition, profiling of cytokine and chemokine levels in stored serum samples of people in whom RA ultimately develops shows increased levels of chemokines and cytokines, especially in the ACPA+ patient population. This finding reinforces the concept that RA is a continuum that can progress to clinical synovitis. However, the environmental stimuli and stochastic events that cause progression are not known.

In murine models, synovial inflammation and transcription factor activation are present before clinical synovitis is apparent. In contrast, synovial biopsies from high-risk individuals with arthralgia but no evidence of arthritis are largely normal, even if they are ACPA+ and/or RF+ and progressed to bona fide RA within 2 years. There was a trend toward higher numbers of CD8+ T cells in the synovium but no other apparent increase in cellular infiltrate or cytokine production.

During the first few weeks of symptomatic RA, the synovium occasionally demonstrates a paucity of lymphocyte infiltration, endothelial cell injury, tissue edema, and neutrophil accumulation; in general, it has a histologic appearance similar to longstanding disease. The extent of lymphoid aggregation, T cell infiltration, and synovial-lining hyperplasia can resemble chronic disease even when symptoms have been present for a short period. The cytokine patterns of these biopsies as determined by immunohistochemical analysis indicated similar levels of T cell factors (such as IFN-γ) and nonT cell factors (such as IL-1 and TNF). The tumor suppressor gene p53 is also expressed in early-stage RA, likely as a result of intense oxidative stress.

Biopsy specimens of asymptomatic joints from patients with earlyor late-stage RA also show lymphocyte infiltration, cytokine production, and p53 expression. Although IFN-γ, IL-1, and TNF levels are increased compared with normal synovium, they are modestly lower than in clinically active joints. The levels of some cytokines such as IL-8 and the number of macrophages are higher in the painful joints. Macrophage and plasma cell infiltration in early RA might predict more erosive or severe disease. Pre-RA treatment with rituximab was evaluated in the PRAIRI study and modestly delayed transition to RA. However, it did not ultimately prevent disease. Recent data suggest that abatacept treatment in pre-RA might delay or even prevent the transition to classifiable RA. Behavior modification to eliminate risk factors like smoking in high-risk populations is another approach that might have an impact on evolution from pre-RA to early RA.

Understanding the distinct mucosal, systemic, and synovial mechanisms that contribute to risk for RA and are responsible for transitions will be a critical step for disease interception. Distinct mechanisms could be responsible for each stage and location. For example, epigenetic data suggest that cell imprinting, at least in FLS, is plastic and can change over time. This creates opportunities for "stage-specific" interventions that address pathogenic mechanisms characteristic for early versus long-standing disease. Ultimately biomarkers that serve as prognostic markers and stratify individuals based on patient-specific pathogenic pathways will be critical.

The amount of rheumatoid synovial transcriptome data that has accumulated in recent years is daunting and has contributed to enormous progress to understanding pathogenesis. Even now, however, the precise mechanisms of disease are not fully defined, and it is more likely that there are multiple pathogenic pathways leading to a common clinical phenotype. The role of immune responses to modified peptides at mucosal surfaces and the migration of this response to the synovium is a likely critical step in the transition from pre-RA to clinical disease. These adaptive immune responses by T cells and B cells are antigen specific, albeit to altered proteins in the initial stages, and set in motion a multistep process that requires additional "hit(s)" to initiate synovitis. Preventing protein modification or inducing tolerance is an attractive approach for disease prevention or treatment. Importantly, adaptive immunity does not work in isolation, and a robust innate response involving macrophage and fibroblast (and perhaps DC, mast cell, and NK cell) activation plays an integral role in disease perpetuation. Mechanisms are diverse and can depend on when in the pre-RA to RA continuum a patient happens to reside, which cells are most important at that time, and what antigens are the most important.

As tempting as it may be, reducing the RA biology and response to therapy to synovial histologic patterns and cell lineage infiltration has had limited capacity to predict outcomes

or clinical benefit to targeted agents to date. This might not be surprising, as mechanisms can vary between patients, between locations (mucosa versus blood versus synovium), over time, and even between joints. Stratification algorithms to determine for individualized treatments will likely require integrated approaches genomic, epigenomic, behavioral, and environmental influences.

### Synovial Fluid and the Synovial Fluid Cartilage Interface

### KEY POINTS

RA synovial effusions contain neutrophils and mononuclear cells, including T lymphocytes, B cells, and macrophages.

Immune complexes that contain autoantibodies such as RFs or ACPAs can fix complement, leading to the generation of chemoattractants that recruit inflammatory cells into the joint.

Small molecule mediators of inflammation such as prostaglandins and leukotrienes are present in RA synovial fluid.

Synovial effusions accumulate in the joints of most patients with active RA. An inverse relationship exists between the molecular weight of proteins and their concentrations in minimally inflamed synovial fluid. High-molecular-weight serum proteins gain access more easily to synovial fluid in inflamed joints, and the relatively high concentration of IgG in RA synovial fluid is good evidence for local synthesis of immunoglobulins. Markedly increased permeance of proteins in patients with rheumatoid disease is due to microvascular damage in rheumatoid synovitis. Assays for autoantibodies or assessments of exudate versus transudate in synovial fluid generally have little value; the concentration of serum proteins in effusions is usually about half to two-thirds the level in the blood.

Evaluation of the synovial fluid proteome in RA using mass spectroscopy provides some insights into the most important mediators. More than 400 proteins in RA effusions have been identified as potential biomarkers of disease activity, including C-reactive protein and six members of the S-100 family of calcium granule—binding proteins. Additional studies show higher levels of proteins related to complement activation, as well as MMPs and neutrophil-derived proteins. None of these is a particular surprise given the genes expressed by the synovial intimal lining and the abundance of neutrophils in RA fluid. Perhaps more interesting, the "citrullinome" of RA fluids—that is, the pattern of protein citrullination—showed about 3000 different citrullinated peptides, including multiple peptides from vimentin, fibrinogen, and α-enolase. In another study, immune-mediated membranolytic pathways mediated by perforin and the membrane attack complex of complement, both of which are hallmarks of RA effusions, markedly increased citrullination of neutrophils.

### Synovial Fluid Neutrophils

Large numbers of polymorphonuclear leukocytes (PMNs) accumulate in rheumatoid synovial effusions and enter via postcapillary venules in the synovium. Neutrophils adhere to activated synovial microvasculature as a result of their abundant surface expression of selectins and the β2 integrins. After adherence, chemotactic agents produced by endothelium and resident synovial cells facilitate exit from the intravascular space into the tissue.

Thus considering the survival time of PMNs in synovial fluid, an average rheumatoid effusion containing 25, PMNs per mm3 could exceed 1 billion cells each day. The ultimate fate of these cells is usually apoptosis or NETosis with release of DNA and citrullinated peptides. Neutrophil survival requires expression of the forkhead transcription factor gene FOXO3.116 Mice that lack this gene are resistant to inflammatory arthritis because of a shortened PMN life span.

High concentrations of chemotactic agents in the synovial fluid in RA recruit a large number of cells to the intra-articular cavity. Few PMNs are seen in the synovium itself; once in the tissue, they move rapidly to the synovial fluid, drawn by agents such as C5a that are generated as a result of complement activation, LTB4, platelet-activating factor, and chemokines. CXC chemokines including ENA-78 and IL-8 are especially abundant in synovial fluid and can attract neutrophils into the intra-articular space. RA PMNs can also release chemokines such as macrophage-inflammatory protein (MIP)-3α into the milieu that promote migration of additional cells into the joint space.

Once in the joint, neutrophils engage immune complexes through Fc receptors, especially FcRγI and FcRγIII, which activate spleen tyrosine kinase (Syk). Receptor ligation initiates a signaling cascade that includes the mitogen-activated protein kinases (MAPKs) and NF-kB, cytoskeletal reorganization, release of granule content, generation of reactive oxygen and nitrogen species, and enhanced phagocytosis. Many of the cells contain immune complexes within phagosomes that include IgG and IgM along with RF and complement proteins such as C1q, C3, and C4. PMNs from synovial fluid in RA release de novo synthesized proteins including matrix proteins such as fibronectin, neutral proteinases, and IL-1. Neutrophils also secrete IL-1Ra and oncostatin M, which is a member of the IL-6 family. Although the amount of IL-1Ra each neutrophil produces is low compared with macrophages, the sheer number of PMNs allows them to produce large amounts in synovial effusions.

Neutrophils also release numerous proteases that can adversely affect the lubricating properties of synovial fluid and the integrity of the cartilage, including elastase and trypsin. Neutrophil collagenase (MMP-8) can digest native collagen in cartilage, which then makes it susceptible to degradation by other MMPs, such as the stromelysins. Synoviocytes are generally considered major producers of the MMPs, but animal models of arthritis suggest that neutrophilderived proteases also play a significant role in cartilage damage.

### Synovial Fluid Mast Cells

Mast cells and mast cells mediators such as histamine and tryptase are present in RA synovial fluid (SF). The activation of mast cells can also induce NETs formation. Human synovial mast cells from RA patients produced greater amounts of PGD2 via the PTGS2miR-199a-3p axis compared with mast cells from OA patients.

### Synovial Fluid Lymphocytes

The lymphocyte subsets in synovial fluid differ from those of peripheral blood and synovial tissue. Even though synovial effusions contain an abundance of T cells, the CD4 to CD8 ratio is actually reversed compared with that of blood or synovial tissue, with an excess of CD8+ cells relative to CD4+ lymphocytes. In addition, synovial tissue is nearly devoid of neutrophils, which often constitute 50% to 75% of synovial fluid cells. The percentage of Tregs (CD4+ CD25+) is also higher in synovial fluid than in peripheral blood.

Synovial fluid T cells generally express high levels of surface HLA-DR antigens. Surface activation antigens are increased on synovial fluid lymphocytes, including VLA-1 and CD69. Of CD4+ cells in rheumatoid synovial fluid, most are memory cells and express CD45RO on their surface. Despite the activated phenotype, synovial fluid T cell function is usually less than peripheral blood cells. For instance, synovial fluid lymphocyte proliferation in response to mitogens or most recall antigens such as tetanus toxoid is significantly less than that of paired blood T lymphocytes. Mycobacterial antigens and the 60 kDa heat shock protein (HSP) are exceptions because proliferation is actually greater in synovial fluid cells, perhaps because they can also activate TLRs. Cytokine production by synovial fluid T cells in vitro is also low, including mitogen-induced expression of IFN-γ and IL-1.

Anti-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-1Ra and TGF-β contribute to the decreased responsiveness of synovial fluid T cells. Nonspecific components of joint effusions such as hyaluronic acid can indirectly suppress T cell activation. Diminished T cell activation also could be due to defective TCR signaling. Articular T cells have diminished tyrosine phosphorylation of proteins after stimulation, especially the key signal transduction pathway p38 MAPK. Furthermore, tyrosine phosphorylation of the TCR ζ chain, an early event in TCR signaling, is low compared with peripheral blood T cells. The hyporesponsiveness of synovial fluid T cells correlates with a significant decrease in the levels of the intra-cellular redox-regulating agent glutathione. Restoration of intra-cellular glutathione increases proliferation of RA synovial fluid T cells. Therefore oxidative stress in the inflamed environment can suppress antigen-specific T cell responses.

### Synovial Fluid Fibroblasts

Fibroblasts are present in RA SF and can be expanded in tissue culture. They have presumably been shed from the synovial intimal lining and might serve as surrogates for tissue disaggregation as they are easier to obtain. The cells that emerge are, like traditional cultured FLS, CD34-CD45-PDPN+ CD90+ and can produce pro-inflammatory cytokines like IL-1β and IL-6.118 Like traditional synovial tissue—derived FLS, they also can invade the matrix of cartilage explants in the SCID mouse model.

### Synovial Fluid Platelets and Platelet Microparticles

Platelets are a rich source of growth factors and cytokines, including PDGF. They are present in rheumatoid synovial effusions and can form microparticles that contain immune complexes and are present in high concentrations compared with OA effusions. Some of these particles can display citrullinated peptides, which can increase innate and adaptive responses and require collagen receptor glycoprotein VI. The microparticles activate cultured synoviocytes and, through an IL-1-dependent mechanism, stimulate cytokine secretion. Platelet depletion also suppresses arthritis severity in animal models.

### Intra-articular Immune Complexes and Complement Fixation

### Synovial Fluid Immune Complexes

Complexes containing Igs are abundant in the blood and synovial fluid of patients with RA, especially those containing IgM and

citrullinated proteins. The most prevalent antigens in these aggregates contain IgG bound to RF as a result of their ability to bind the Fc portion of Ig, as well as ACPAs and citrullinated peptide complexes. Use of more sensitive techniques has revealed that circulating immune complexes in RA contain up to 20 polypeptides, including albumin, Ig, complement, type II collagen, fibrinogen, and acute-phase reactants, as well as DNA. These complexes in synovium and also in the circulation or mucosal sites can potentially fix complement, releasing chemotactic peptides and factors that activate neutrophils and other inflammatory cells.

The aggregates of RF, immunoglobulin, ACPAs, and various peptides can embed into cartilage and other tissues that are in contact with synovial fluids. Electron microscopic studies demonstrate immunoglobulin complexes with damage to the cartilage matrix in the microenvironment. Immune complexes are absent under areas of cartilage invaded actively by synovial pannus, suggesting that phagocytic cells in the invasive synovium bind to and ingest the immune complexes. Rheumatoid cartilage contains more than 40-fold more IgM and more than 10-fold more IgG than healthy cartilage extracts. IgM RF is found in the majority of RA cartilage extracts but not in OA or healthy control subject extracts. In addition, more than 60% of the RA cartilage extracts are positive for native and denatured type II collagen antibody.

### Synovial Fluid Complement

The liver is the major source of complement synthesis in humans, and passive transfer of serum proteins into effusions accounts for many of the complement proteins found there. However, synovial tissue also actively produces many complement proteins, including C2 and C3. Macrophages and fibroblasts produce complement proteins under the influence of cytokines such as IFN-γ, IL-1, and TNF. Synovial tissue analysis shows that complement genes from the classic pathway are expressed in RA, as well as in healthy synovium.

Despite the local production of complement components, the levels of C4, C2, and C3 in rheumatoid synovial effusions are lower compared with synovial fluids from other arthritides. Although the most prominent evidence of activation implicates the classic pathway, cleavage products of the alternate pathway, including factor B and properdin, also occur in RA. IgM RF appears to be a more important determinant of complement activation than IgG RF in serum and synovial fluid, and accelerated catabolism of C4 in RA and the presence of C4 fragments in the plasma correlate with titers of IgM RF.

Neutrophil lysosomal lysates contain enzymes that cleave complement proteins and generate chemotactic activity, such as C5a from serum. C5a, in addition to being a principal chemotactic factor in inflammatory effusions, mediates lysosomal release from human PMNs and induces cytoskeletal rearrangement. The chemotactic anaphylatoxins C3a and C5a are often present in rheumatoid effusions, as are the terminal complement components that comprise the C5bC9 membrane attack complex.

### Targeting Complement

Inhibiting complement proteins has therapeutic potential in RA. Several pre-clinical models support this, such as intra-articular treatment in the rat antigen-induced arthritis model where soluble complement receptor (sCR1) inhibits joint swelling. C5-deficient mice have markedly decreased joint inflammation in collageninduced arthritis and the K/BxN serum transfer model. Absence of C3 or factor B also inhibits collagen-induced arthritis. Unlike the C5 knockout mice, which have normal antibody responses,

C3and factor Bnull animals have lower levels of anti—type II collagen antibodies in that model.

These data suggest that classic and alternative complement pathways participate in inflammatory arthritis. For instance, effective therapy of RA with either methotrexate or a TNF inhibitor decreases circulating levels of the terminal complement complex. However, an anti-C5 antibody demonstrated only modest evidence of clinical efficacy in a controlled RA clinical trial. Similarly, a C5a receptor antagonist did not decrease inflammation in a short-term placebo-controlled synovial biopsy study, even though the compound was effective in pre-clinical models. Recent approval of the C5a inhibitor avacopan in ANCA-associated arthritis might lead to further studies in other diseases or stimulate other approaches to complement inhibition for RA.

Arachidonic acid belongs to omega-6-PUFA, and its metabolites are produced in the inflamed joint via oxidation by cyclooxygenases (COXs) to prostaglandins and thromboxanes or by lipoxygenases (LOXs) to leukotrienes (LTs). COX inhibitors are clearly effective in RA, although the effect is modest and is due to combination of local synovial effects and spinal analgesic action. Animal models of arthritis are variably sensitive to prostaglandin; indomethacin almost completely prevents adjuvant arthritis in rats but has minimal benefit in collagen-induced arthritis in mice.

Stable prostaglandins, especially PGE2, produce vasodilation, increase vascular permeability, and are involved centrally in fever. Synovial fibroblast production of prostaglandins together with inflammatory factors drive HBEGF+ inflammatory macrophages that promote fibroblast invasiveness. They also display some antiinflammatory activities that could account for limited efficacy. For example, misoprostol, which is a prostaglandin analogue, has modest but significant anti-inflammatory or immunomodulatory effects. Physiologic concentrations of PGE2 inhibit IFN-γ production by T cells, HLA-DR expression by macrophages, and T cell proliferation.

Production of prostaglandins in RA depends on both COX-1 and COX-2 (see Chapter 27). The former is constitutively expressed and is responsible for the normal endogenous production of prostaglandins in the joint, as well as in other tissues. Cytokines such as IL-1 and TNF induce COX-2 gene expression by cultured synoviocytes and macrophages. COX-2 mRNA and protein are increased in RA synovium. Much of the antiinflammatory activity and analgesia in RA results from COX-2 inhibition. Targeting prostaglandin receptors such as E2 or E4 or prostaglandin E synthases is an alternative approach that might have less deleterious effects on the gastric mucosa and cardiovascular disease. The PGE receptor 4 (EP4) can also act on DCs and T cells to enhance production of Th1 and Th17 cells.

PGI2, like PGE2, can also contribute to synovial inflammation. For instance, mice lacking the PGI2 receptor have significantly decreased arthritis severity in the collagen-induced arthritis model compared with wild-type mice, even though they make similar amounts of anticollagen antibodies.

### Leukotrienes

LTBs are potent pro-inflammatories produced by neutrophils and chemotactic for neutrophils, eosinophils, and macrophages. They also promote neutrophil aggregation and adherence to endothelium. Peripheral blood PMNs from patients with rheumatoid disease have an enhanced capacity for LTB4 production compared with healthy

people. In murine collagen-induced arthritis, LTB4 antagonists decreased paw swelling and joint destruction, suggesting a pivotal role for this potent chemoattractant. Unfortunately, LTB4 blockade has limited minimal efficacy in RA, and this suggests that they might contribute but do not drive inflammation.

### Specialized Proresolving Mediators

Certain arachidonic acid metabolites such as 15-Deoxy-delta- 12,14-prostaglandin J2 (15d-PGJ2) activate peroxisome proliferator-activated receptors (PPARs) and inhibit cytokine production and inflammation in animal models of arthritis. Cyclopentenone prostaglandins can also inhibit NF-kB by blocking one of the enzymes that activates this pathway, namely IkB kinase-β (IKKβ). LXs and resolvins also represent a unique class of lipid mediators that help resolve inflammatory diseases. LXs have a trihydroxytetraene structure and are produced from arachidonic acid via the LOX pathways. LXA4 binds with high affinity to a G protein— coupled receptor denoted LXA4 receptor (ALXR). Activation of ALXR inhibits recruitment of neutrophils by attenuating chemotaxis, adhesion, and transmigration into tissues and by diminishing chemokine and cytokine production. LXA4 significantly decreased cytokine and MMP expression in FLS through an NF-kBdependent mechanism. Resolvins, omega-3-PUFA-derived metabolites, are increased in murine arthritic tissues and modulate T cell phenotype. Of interest, blood proresolving mediators are linked with synovial pathology and are predictive of disease-modifying antirheumatic drug (DMARD) responsiveness in RA.

### Peripheral Blood Lymphocytes

The number of CD4+ Th cells is mildly increased in the circulation of patients with RA, with a concomitant decrease in CD8+ lymphocytes. The surface phenotype of circulating T cells in RA is highly variable. For instance, an increased percentage of αβ and γδ TCR-bearing cells expressing HLA-DR and the adhesion protein VLA-4 (α4β1 integrin) has been observed. The latter is especially important because VLA-4 helps cells enter the synovium through interactions with VCAM-1 on endothelial cells. Other markers of activation are not always elevated on RA T cells in the circulation. Therefore peripheral-blood T cells express some, but not all, phenotypic characteristics of prior activation. It is not clear whether this occurs in the peripheral or central lymphoid organs or whether cells are activated in the synovium and re-enter the circulation via the synovial lymphatics

As noted for articular T cells, RA peripheral lymphocytes also have impaired responses to some antigens. For example, IFN-γ and IL-2 production is significantly suppressed in RA lymphocyte cultures. Epstein-Barr virus (EBV)—infected B lymphocyte growth is greater due to a defect in T cell function in RA. The abnormal T cell response correlates with disease activity, although the abnormality is present in T cells of some patients with inflammatory arthropathies other than RA.

T cell diversity and maturation are abnormal in RA. Whereas thymic output normally decreases with age, senescence appears to be accelerated in RA. The presence of TCR rearrangement excision circles (TRECs) is a measure of thymic release of mature T cells. Using this parameter, the thymic output in RA may decline prematurely. Some evidence points to RA T cell senescence, perhaps due to continued immune stimulation. Telomeres are shorter in RA T cells, perhaps due to repeated cell divisions. Premature aging has also been observed in antigen-unprimed naive T cells, suggesting alternative mechanisms might contribute.

In addition, DNA surveillance is defective in RA T cells and contributes to cellular aging. For example, deficiency of recombination 11 homolog A (MRE1 1A), which senses double-stranded DNA breaks and helps amplify DNA repair, occurs in RA T cells and allows DNA damage to accumulate. The observation is analogous to impaired DNA mechanisms previously described for RA FLS that, along with abnormalities in genes like ATM (see earlier), increase invasiveness and arthritogenic potential of T cells. Abnormal DNA methylation of peripheral blood T cells has also been observed, especially in the naive T cell population.

Of interest, DNA methylation patterns in peripheral blood T cells are quite different from T cells isolated from synovium of the same patient. The genes and pathways that are differentially marked primarily in synovium involve a variety of immune processes. This enrichment could result from preferential recruitment/retention of T cells with abnormal DNA methylation or local expansion of immunologically active cells in the joint. Treatment of RA with TNF inhibitors also alters the DNA methylation patterns, especially in pathways associated with T cell activation, and correlates with clinical response.

Activated B lymphocytes in peripheral blood appear to traffic between mucosa and synovium, with evidence of affinity maturation of RFs and ACPAs. The number of circulating B cells that spontaneously produce RF and other autoantibodies is significantly higher in people with RA compared with those without disease. B cells that are enriched in autoantibody production are characterized by a surface determinant CD5. This antigen is normally expressed by T cells but is also displayed by fetal B cells and a small number of immature B cells in adults. In addition, regulatory B cells that produce IL-10 are reduced in patients with RA. Treatment with TNF inhibitors increases the number of these cells in the peripheral circulation and decreases expression of the activation marker CD69 on B cells.136, Elevated IgAand IgG-producing plasmablasts are also increased in the blood of people at high risk of developing RA.

Patients with RA who have normal circulating numbers of lymphocytes show an abnormal k-to-λchain analysis compared with control subjects. Alterations in gene usage are consistent with oligoclonal B cell proliferation, which was confirmed by single-cell sequencing studies. As noted above, barcode-enabled sequencing of peripheral blood plasmablasts demonstrates that the antibodies produced by these cells bind to citrullinated proteins. Increased plasmablasts in blood can precede B cell repopulation and disease flare after treatment with anti-CD20 antibody.

### Role of T Cell Cytokines

### KEY POINTS

The cytokine milieu in RA is rich in factors produced by many cell lineages. Many factors produced by T lymphocytes are surprisingly low in RA, whereas those generated by macrophages and by synovial fibroblasts are markedly increased (Table 7 1.2). Although low, the T cell cytokines can have profound effects, especially in the synovial microenvironment. The production and contribution of T cellderived cytokines can be examined on the basis of functional lymphocyte subsets.

### Type 1 T Helper Cell Cytokines

Early investigation into the cytokine profile of RA suggested a bias toward the Th1 phenotype, cells characterized by the production of cytokines such as IL-2 and IFN-γ, and expression of the chemokine receptors CXCR3 and CCR5. Th cell differentiation might be driven, in part, by local production of IL-7 by stromal cells and macrophages, which supports the production of Th1 and Th17 cells. Unexpectedly, lower serum IL-7 levels in patients with early-stage inflammatory arthritis are associated with progression to RA. Many T cell clones derived from RA synovial tissue produce a Th1 cytokine pattern. Considerable data have accumulated on the relative abundance and function of the prototypic Th1 cytokine, IFN-γ, which is the most potent inducer of HLA-DR and enhances antigen presentation. IFN-γ also induces adhesion molecules on the surface of endothelial cells and can help recruit inflammatory cell accumulation at sites of injury. One important function of IFN-γ is its capacity to alter the balance of extra-cellular matrix synthesis and degradation by decreasing collagen synthesis and inhibiting MMP production by cytokine-stimulated cultured FLS.

Relatively low concentrations of IFN-γ are found in RA joints. Immunohistochemical analysis clearly demonstrates IFN-γ protein in RA synovial T cells, although the percentage of cells containing IFN-γ is less than in tonsils. However, the role of IFN-γ is quite complex because IFN-γ knockout mice or IFN-γ receptor deficiency exacerbates collagen-induced arthritis in mice. This serves as a reminder that the effects of cytokines are often context dependent.

Another major Th1 cytokine, IL-2, is a T cellderived cytokine that serves as an autocrine or paracrine T cell growth factor. IL-2 is detected in only a small percentage of RA synovial effusions and synovial tissues and, when present, is only found in low concentrations. The relative absence of IL-2 could be pro-inflammatory because of decreased numbers of CD25+ Tregs. TNF, GM-CSF, and IL-6 can be expressed by Th1 and Th2 cells and are abundant in synovial fluid and produced by RA synovial tissue. Some data suggest that T cells derived from disaggregated RA synovial tissue express TNF using single cell RNAseq. However, the primary sources of these cytokines in the rheumatoid joint are macrophages and fibroblasts.

### Type 2 T Helper Cell Cytokines

Th2 cytokine levels are often quite low in rheumatoid joints. For example, IL-4 and LTα are generally not detected in RA synovial fluid, and little or no IL-4 mRNA is expressed by RA synovial tissue. Using sensitive nested reverse-transcriptase polymerase chain reaction techniques, Th2 cytokines IL-4 and IL-13 are absent in RA, whereas both IFN-γ and IL-12 (a cytokine that directs T cell maturation toward the Th1 and Th17 phenotypes) are usually present. The Th2 cytokine IL-10, which has potent anti-inflammatory activities, is expressed in RA synovium; however, macrophages rather than T cells are the major producers in RA. Some data suggest that synovial fluids in early synovitis have

high concentrations of Th2 cytokines such as IL-4 and IL-13 and that this pattern distinguishes patients who progress to RA. As the disease evolves in these patients, the Th2 signature diminishes.

### Type 17 T Helper Cytokines

Th17 cells have been implicated in autoimmunity, especially psoriasis and spondyloarthritis, and are present in RA synovial effusions. Although IL-17 protein is present in some sublining T cells, mast cells appear to be an important alternative source. The pro-inflammatory cytokine produced by Th17 cells, IL-17, is encoded by six genes (IL-17A through F). IL-17A and, to a certain extent, IL-17F mimic and synergize with IL-1 and TNF effects on FLS, including induction of collagenase and cytokine production. IL-17A is present in modest but functionally relevant concentrations in RA synovial effusions. IL-17 receptors IL-17RA and IL-17RC are expressed by synoviocytes, activate the transcription factor NF-κB, and initiate an inflammatory cascade.

IL-21 is also produced by RA T cells, which can serve to further enhance Th17 cell numbers and IL-17 production and induce MMP production by FLS and activate osteoclasts. Similarly, IL-22 produced by Th17 cells is present in RA synovial effusions. Like IL- 17A, IL-22 activates FLS to produce osteoclast-activating factors such as RANKL. Animal models of arthritis demonstrate that IL-17 inhibition is anti-inflammatory and protects animals from bone and cartilage destruction. IL-1, IL-23, and/or TGF-β in the joint can potentially enhance Th17 cell differentiation in humans.

The contribution of the IL-17 family to inflammation is impressive in animal models of arthritis, in which blocking IL- 17A in particular has dramatic effects on inflammation and matrix destruction. The results in RA are less robust, and clinical trials with IL-17 blockers show only modest improvement compared with TNF inhibitors. This contrasts with psoriasis or psoriatic arthritis, in which anti—IL-17A antibody is more impressive. Alternative approaches that inhibit both IL-17A and F, such as soluble receptors, do not increase efficacy.

### Type 9 Helper T Cell and Innate Lymphoid Cell Cytokines

T cells differentiate to the Th9 phenotype under the influence of cytokines like IL-4 and TGB-β. The transcription factors STAT6, IFN regulatory factor 4 (IRF4), and GATA3 are required for this transition. The prototypical Th9 cytokine is IL-9, which is found in RA synovial fluid and synovial tissue, as well as in inflammatory bowel disease. This glycosylated polypeptide is part of the IL-7/IL-9 family and binds to receptors on a wide variety of cells, including T and B lymphocytes. RA T cells express IL-9 receptors, and exposure to the cytokine promotes T cell survival and proliferation.

In addition to Th9 cells, type 2 ILCs can produce IL-9 and can regulate the proliferation and activation of Tregs. In the absence of IL-9 in mice, chronic arthritis develops, and treatment with IL-9 facilitates ILC-dependent Treg proliferation. RA synovial tissue contains IL-9—expressing ILCs, especially in individuals whose disease is in remission.

### T Helper Cell Cytokine Imbalance

The presence of Th1, Th9, and Th17 cells, as well as the recently described Tph cell described above, in the rheumatoid synovium suggests that they play a role in the initiation and perpetuation of

RA or perhaps in response to tissue damage caused by the disease. Th2 cytokines and cellular responses that normally suppress Th1 activation are nearly absent, so this counter-regulatory mechanism cannot mediate disease resolution. This concept is supported by the observations that exogenous IL-10 or IL-4 suppresses synthesis of pro-inflammatory cytokines and MMPs by cultured RA synovial tissue explants and cells. In addition, IL-10 and IL-4 increase release of other anti-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-1Ra by synovial cells. Although IL-10 protein is present in RA synovial fluid and the gene is expressed by synovial tissue cells, in vitro studies of cultured synovial cells suggest that not enough IL-10 is produced to suppress the limited amounts of IFN-γ produced even further.

The notion that Th1 and Th17 cytokines initiate and perpetuate arthritis, in part as a result of the influence of IL-7, IL-9, IL-21, and IL-22, whereas Th2 cytokines are suppressive, is supported by studies in animal models. For instance, IL-4 and IL-10 administered individually have a modest affect in collagen-induced arthritis, but combination treatment was more impressive. 153 The complexity of cytokine networks in inflammatory arthritis is underscored by studies on the role of IL-12 in collagen-induced arthritis. In early-stage arthritis, IL-12 administration increases the incidence of collagen-induced arthritis, whereas anti—IL-12 is beneficial. However, in late-stage disease, IL-12 administration suppresses arthritis, and antiIL-12 causes an exacerbation.

Therapeutic approaches aimed at increasing Th2 cells or cytokines have thus far been unsuccessful. For example, a clinical trial using IL-10 in RA did not demonstrate significant clinical benefit or improvement in histologic evidence of synovial inflammation. It is possible that combinations of Th2 cytokines will be required to coordinate a maximum effect. Inhibitors of T cell cytokine signaling through JAK3 demonstrate efficacy in RA. However, many of these compounds also block JAK1, and synovial biopsy studies suggest that this is the most important JAK for treatment of RA. Notably, selective JAK1 inhibitors like upadacitinib are as effective as drugs that block multiple JAK isoforms.

The precise role of individual T cell subsets is not clear and could also vary with the stage of disease and vary between patients. Newer single-cell technology can potentially identify rare subsets and might provide clues to enable targeting of individual T cell populations.

### Macrophage and Fibroblast Cytokines
