### KEY POINTS

Macrophage and fibroblast pro-inflammatory mediators are abundant in the RA synovium, and many have been successfully targeted with biologic therapeutics. Macrophages, in particular, are vigorous producers of cytokines, and fibroblasts produce many of

the proteases. Studies that profile blood cytokines and chemokines indicate that these cytokines and chemokines increase many years before the onset of clinical disease.

### Pro-inflammatory Macrophage and Fibroblast Cytokines

### IL-1 Family

The IL-1 family is a ubiquitous group of polypeptides with a wide range of biologic activity; they include IL-1α, IL-1β, IL-1Ra (see below), IL-18, and IL-33. Abundant pre-clinical data indicate that IL-1 can serve as a key regulatory factor in inflammatory arthritis. For instance, recombinant IL-1β induces the accumulation of PMNs and mononuclear leukocytes in the joint space and the loss of proteoglycan from articular cartilage when injected directly into rabbit knee joints. Transgenic mice that overexpress IL-1 also develop inflammatory arthritis, whereas mice that lack the natural IL-1 antagonist IL-1Ra have increased susceptibility to collageninduced arthritis. In most cases, IL-1 blockade in animal models modestly decreases synovial inflammation and markedly diminishes bone and cartilage destruction.

Interleukin-1. Synovial macrophages are a prolific source of IL-1 in the rheumatoid joint, and nearly half of all macrophages in the RA synovium express IL-1β. IL-1 protein is highly expressed by synovial lining macrophages adjacent to FLS and in sublining macrophages near blood vessels. IL-1 in the lining can subsequently activate FLS to proliferate and secrete a variety of mediators. A broad range of stimuli induce IL-1 production by macrophages; for example, immunoglobulin Fc fragments and, to a lesser extent, immune complexes can generate IL-1 production by rheumatoid synovial macrophages. Collagen fragments can induce IL-1 production, and type IX collagen in articular cartilage is a potent inducer of IL-1 by monocytes.

Within the rheumatoid joint, IL-1 induces fibroblast proliferation; stimulates the synthesis of IL-6, IL-8, and GM-CSF by synovial cells; and enhances collagenase and prostaglandin production. It increases glycosaminoglycan release in human synovial fibroblast cultures, although the effect of IL-1 on the production of intact proteoglycan molecules by intact articular cartilage explants can be the opposite. IL-1 induces a number of adhesion molecules on FLS and endothelial cells, including VCAM-1 and ICAM-1, and enhances bone resorption.

IL-1 has been implicated in RA, but inhibition of this mediator using various IL-1-targeted biologic agents has only modest clinical benefit. Even combinations of IL-1 and TNF-directed therapy do not provide significant benefit beyond TNF blockade alone despite biologic effects on acute-phase reactants and rates of infection. In contrast, diseases with a well-defined role for IL-1, such as the autoinflammatory diseases, have remarkable efficacy.

One explanation for the relatively modest benefit of IL-1 in RA relates to its signaling mechanisms. IL-1 activates NF-kB through the kinase MyD88, which is the same pathway as TLRs. When IL-1 signaling is blocked, TLR ligands in the synovium, including exogenous ones such as peptidoglycan or endogenous ones such as HSPs, can potentially overcome IL-1 blockade. This concept was confirmed in the K/BxN serum transfer model, in which small amounts of the TLR4 ligand LPS can induce aggressive disease in mice that lack IL-1 receptors. Thus IL-1 blockade might not control RA synovitis as long as TLR signaling remains intact.

Interleukin-18. IL-18, which is another member of the IL-1 family, has also been implicated in RA. In collagen-induced arthritis, IL-18 inhibition significantly attenuates disease. Subsequent

studies showed that IL-18 induces GM-CSF, nitric oxide (NO) production, and TNF expression by synovial macrophages. IL-18 is expressed by RA synovial tissue, especially by synovial fibroblasts and macrophages, and its production is markedly increased by TNF and IL-1β. A natural inhibitor, IL-18 binding protein, could potentially be used as a therapeutic agent. However, other IL-18directed approaches, like anti-IL-1 therapeutics, have been disappointing in RA. For example, IL-1 convertase inhibitors have only a modest benefit, even though they block IL-18 processing required to produce the active cytokine.

Interleukin-33 and Other Alarmins. IL-33 signals through the ST2 surface receptor and is an "alarmin" that provides a danger signal as a result of tissue damage and necrosis with release of intra-cellular contents. Extra-cellular, but not intra-cellular, IL-33 signals primarily through the transcription factor NF-κB to increase transcription of the pro-inflammatory program. Blocking IL-33 decreases inflammation in several animal models of arthritis, including collagen-induced arthritis, antigen-induced arthritis, and ST2-deficient mice in the K/BxN model. IL-33 can also bias T cells toward the Th2 phenotype, but the relative lack of Th2 cells suggests that this is not important in the context of RA. TLR3 ligands like poly I:C increase IL-33 production by FLS, and exogenous IL-33 increases FLS RANKL and chemokine production.

High mobility box 1 (HMGB1) is also highly expressed in RA joints and can activate pro-inflammatory pathways similar to other alarmins. Blocking HMGB1 decreases damage and immune responses in a variety of autoimmune models. It might contribute to the aggressive RA FLS phenotype, and incubating OA FLS with HMGB1 can recapitulate this behavior. HMGB1 polymorphisms have been associated with RA in a Chinese Han population, suggesting that it can contribute to disease susceptibility.

### Tumor Necrosis Factor and the Tumor Necrosis Factor Superfamily

The TNF superfamily is a broad group of related genes that play a major role in inflammation, immune responses, cell survival, and apoptosis. At least 19 ligands in the family have been identified, with TNF identified as the eponymous member. Each cytokine has its own preference for cell surface receptor, although there is some overlap of receptor binding and functional overlap. The TNF superfamily members exhibit conserved amino acid sequences, suggesting a single ancestral gene. Many TNF superfamily members include type II membrane protein characteristics and can be released from cell surfaces after proteolytic cleavage. A C-terminal conserved domain called the TNF-homology domain is also shared by several superfamily members. The active forms of the proteins are homotrimers, except for LTα and LTβ, which can form either heterotrimers or homotrimers.

TNF is a pleiotropic cytokine that has been implicated as a key pro-inflammatory cytokine that is detected in rheumatoid synovial fluid and serum. It is produced as a membrane-bound protein, primarily by synovial macrophages in RA, which is released from the cell surface after proteolytic cleavage by TNF convertase, a membrane MMP. IL-1 and TNF have many similar activities, including the ability to enhance cytokine production, adhesionmolecule expression, proliferation, and MMP production by cultured synoviocytes. In some systems, the effects of these two agents are synergistic. Although they share many functions and signal transduction pathways, IL-1 and TNF use distinct surface receptors and intra-cellular signaling pathways.

TNF, like IL-1, stimulates collagenase and PGE2 production by synoviocytes, induces bone resorption, inhibits bone formation in vitro, and stimulates resorption of proteoglycan and inhibits its biosynthesis in explants of cartilage. Animal models have also supported the general role played by TNF in inflammatory arthritis. For instance, overexpression of TNF in transgenic mice leads to severe destructive synovitis. In fact, arthritis also spontaneously occurs in transgenic mice that express only a membrane-bound form of TNF on T cells. TNF blockade is an effective antiinflammatory agent in many animal models of arthritis, although the effects on bone and cartilage destruction are less prominent than with IL-1 inhibitors. Similarly, TNF inhibition in RA significantly decreases or prevents joint damage.

The efficacy of TNF inhibitors in RA confirms its role in many patients with the disease; however, diversity of responses to TNF inhibitors and other targeted agents also highlights the heterogeneity of disease mechanisms despite similar clinical features. Patients with an inadequate response to a TNF inhibitor can still respond to other targeted agents like rituximab or abatacept, which supports the notion that multiple independent pathways can contribute to the pathogenesis of RA and the heterogeneous nature of the disease. Early therapy with TNF inhibitors can induce long-term remissions in a limited number of patients even after therapy is withdrawn. Therefore interventions in the earliest stages of disease could potentially prevent the establishment of chronic synovitis and prevent the evolution of epigenetic imprinting or other factors that promote perpetuation.

Patterns of synovial gene expression are associated with a higher likelihood of a good response to a TNF inhibitor, but the predictive power is relatively minor and not useful for clinical decisions. Thus far, various algorithms that include autoantibodies, blood cytokine profiles, synovial tissue TNF levels and histologic patterns, and TNF promoter polymorphisms have limited capacity for predicting a clinical response to a TNF inhibitor. When a difference is noted, the magnitude has not enabled clinical decision-making yet. Surprisingly, patients with little or no clinical improvement still have significant delay or arrest of joint damage when treated with a TNF inhibitor, most likely due to inhibition of osteoclast differentiation and activation.

### Interleukin-6 Family

IL-6 is a complex cytokine produced by many cell types including T cells, monocytes, and FLS. A striking correlation between serum IL-6 activity and serum levels of acute-phase reactants such as C-reactive protein, α1-anti-trypsin, fibrinogen, and haptoglobin occurs in patients with RA. Very high levels of IL-6 are present in RA synovial fluid, and synovial cells in culture from diverse inflammatory arthropathies produce IL-6. In situ hybridization of synovial tissue also shows IL-6 mRNA in the intimal lining, and immunohistochemistry studies show IL-6 protein in the lining and sublining regions. Although many synovial macrophages express the IL-6 gene, much of the IL-6 in the joint is produced by synoviocytes in the intimal lining.

The pivotal role of IL-6 in RA was confirmed by efficacy of monoclonal antibodies that bind to IL-6R or to IL-6 itself. The clinical responses are similar to TNF inhibitors, including protective effects on bone and cartilage damage. IL-6R antibody is also effective in some patients who have not responded to TNF blockade. Therefore the cytokine network in RA is complex, without a clear hierarchy implicating a single cytokine like TNF at the apex for all, or even most, patients. Neutropenia, increased liver enzymes, and altered blood lipids have been observed with IL-6

inhibition, although the relative importance of these observations is still uncertain. JAK inhibitors have also demonstrated efficacy in RA, which decreases activation of STAT1 and STAT3 in FLS and mimics the effect of IL-6 blockade by decreasing IL-6 signaling.

Cytokines with structural similarity to IL-6 and that share receptor subunits have also been implicated in RA. Several of these cytokines—IL-11, leukemia inhibitory factor (LIF), and oncostatin M—are expressed by rheumatoid synovium and can be detected in synovial effusions. LIF is especially interesting because it could account for sustained STAT4 activation by RA FLS. The biologic effects of these factors are complex and can be either protective (e.g., by increasing expression of protease inhibitors such as tissue inhibitors of metalloproteinase [TIMP]) or pro-inflammatory (e.g., by increasing expression of chemokines or MMPs), depending on the culture conditions or the specific model evaluated. This dichotomy among the family members is demonstrated by the fact that IL-11 administration ameliorates collagen-induced arthritis, whereas antibodies to oncostatin M are protective.

### Interleukin-12 Family

The IL-12 family includes cytokines that play a role in the differentiation of T cells and inflammation. IL-12 is a heterodimeric cytokine with two subunits (e.g., p35 and p40) encoded on separate genes and produced by antigen-presenting cells. IL-23 and IL-27 have similar heterodimeric structures to IL-12, with p29/ p40 and p28/EB13 components, respectively. In the context of antigen presentation, IL-27 can bias T cell responses toward the Th1 phenotype. IL-23 plays a pivotal role in the production of Th17 cells in combination with IL-1 and TGF-β. The IL-12 family members are generally produced by macrophages in the rheumatoid joint in addition to other antigen-presenting cells such as DCs. Blocking IL-12 or IL-12/23 has limited benefit in RA, which is consistent with the modest effect of IL-17 blockers and contrasts with psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis.

### Interleukin-15

IL-15 is an IL-2like cytokine that regulates numerous immunologic functions relevant to RA, including T cell chemotaxis and proliferation, production of immunoglobulins by B cells, and the generation of NK cells. Although IL-15 can serve as an IL-2—independent mechanism for activating T cells, its role in RA may be related to its role in TNF regulation. Macrophages are the primary source of IL-15 in RA, and the cytokine is macrophage TNF production that requires contact with T cells. This network provides a potential mechanism whereby local IL-15 production in the synovium can lead to autocrine production of TNF in a T celldependent but antigen-independent fashion. IL-15 is expressed by RA synovial macrophage cells. The soluble IL-15 receptors can function as an inhibitor and decreases joint inflammation in collagen-induced arthritis when administered systemically. Clinical trials in RA using an antiIL-15 antibody showed benefit, although it was not enough to justify continued development.

### Interleukin-32

IL-32 activates NF-kB and induces the production of several proinflammatory cytokines and chemokines, including TNF, IL-1, IL-6, and IL-8. It is expressed by RA synovial tissue, especially in synovial-lining macrophage-like cells. The level of IL-32 expression correlates with the presence of other cytokines implicated in RA, including TNF, IL-1, and IL-18. Injection of IL-32 into the joints of naive mice causes a robust transient synovitis.

The synovial response could be partially abrogated by anti-TNF antibodies, suggesting that IL-32 induces this cytokine in vivo. These data suggest that IL-32 might be upstream from several proinflammatory mediators in RA and could represent a therapeutic target.

### Colony-Stimulating Factors

GM-CSF supports the differentiation of bone marrow precursor cells to mature granulocytes and macrophages and participates in immune responses. It is a potent neutrophil and macrophage activator. Its actions include the induction of HLA-DR expression, IL-1 secretion, intra-cellular parasite killing, and priming for enhanced release of TNF and PGE2.

RA synovial fluid and synovium contain GM-CSF. The major source is synovial macrophages, although IL-1or TNFstimulated FLS also express the CSF2 gene (which encodes GM-CSF). Its ability to induce HLA-DR gene expression on macrophages might be of particular importance in RA. GM-CSF, not IFN-γ, is the major DR-inducing cytokine in RA synovial effusions. Collagen-induced arthritis in mice is less severe in animals that lack a functional CSF2 gene or are treated with anti— GM-CSF antibody, which supports the hypothesis that CSF2 is an important pro-inflammatory mediator. Clinical trials demonstrate clinical benefit with antiGM-CSF antibodies in RA. Pulmonary alveolar proteinosis, which occurs in GM-CSFdeficient mice and in autoimmune diseases marked by antiGM-CSF antibodies, has not been a significant issue in RA patients treated with these agents.

Macrophage CSF (M-CSF, also called CSF-1) is also expressed by RA synovium and is present in synovial effusions. Its primary pathogenic role in RA probably relates to its osteoclast-differentiating capacity. This factor cooperates with RANKL to facilitate bone erosions. The M-CSF receptor also binds to a novel cytokine that is produced by FLS, namely IL-34. The cytokine is expressed in RA synovium and represents an alternative therapeutic target for M-CSF receptor-driven events in synovitis.

### Interferons

Type I IFNs, especially IFN-β, are expressed by RA synovium. The IFNs possess a range of biologic activities and can be immunostimulatory or inhibitory depending on the context. In murine models of arthritis, exogenous IFN-β has prominent anti-inflammatory activity. However, a similar benefit has not been observed in RA. One possible explanation relates to the mechanism of action in arthritis: In murine models, IFN-β acts by increasing IL-1Ra production. Although IL-1 is a therapeutic target in pre-clinical models, it is less important in RA. Exogenous IFN-β does increase synovial IL-1Ra production in patients with RA, but blocking IL-1 is not sufficient for robust clinical effects. Another IFN, IL-29, has been identified in RA synovium and can increase IL-6, IL-8, and MMP production by cultured FLS.

### Chemokines

Chemokines are a family of related chemoattractant peptides that, with the assistance of adhesion molecules, summon cells into inflammatory sites. Many chemokines are produced in the rheumatoid joint. IL-8, a CXC chemokine that was originally characterized as a neutrophil chemoattractant, along with immune complexes and other chemotactic peptides such as C5a, contribute to the large influx of PMNs into the joint. Immunohistochemical analysis of synovial tissue demonstrates IL-8 protein in sublining perivascular macrophages, as well as in scattered lining cells.

Cultured synovial tissue macrophages constitutively produce IL-8, and FLS express the same gene whether they are stimulated with IL-1 or TNF. IL-8 accounts for about 40% of the neutrophil chemoattractant activity in synovial fluid. In addition, IL-8 activates neutrophils through G protein—coupled receptors and is a potent angiogenesis factor. Macrophage-inhibitory protein-1α, macrophage-inhibitory protein-1β, MCP-1, and regulated on activation, normally T cell expressed and secreted (RANTES)—members of the CC subfamily—are also produced by RA synovium, as are many other CC chemokines.

CXCL16 and epithelial neutrophil-activating peptide-78 (ENA-78) are CXC chemokines and are particularly abundant. CXCL16 binds to CXCR6 on T cells and contributes to the recruitment of lymphocytes into the synovium. ENA-78 accounts for about 40% of the chemotactic activity for neutrophils in RA synovial fluid. Concentrations of these chemokines are higher in RA synovial effusions compared with non-inflammatory arthritides such as OA. Although the chemokines also can be detected in the blood, the levels are considerably lower than in the joint, thereby providing a gradient that signals cells to migrate into the synovium.

Lymphocyte-specific chemotactic factors contribute to the germinal center architecture of RA. The CXC factor B cell—activating chemokine-1 (BCA-1; CXCL13) binds to specific CXCR5 receptors on B cells. CXCL13 is expressed in the RA synovial tissues, especially by FDCs in germinal centers, and likely accounts for B cell migration to these regions. CCL21 and several other factors participate in the anatomic organization of germinal centers, marginal zones, and other regions of lymphoid follicles. Another chemokine, SDF-1, is expressed by synoviocytes and endothelial cells and serves as a chemoattractant for T cells in synovium via its receptor, CXCR4. Unlike other chemokine receptors that can bind multiple members of the family, CXCR4 is highly specific for SDF-1 and is expressed by memory CD4+ lymphocytes.

Chemokines have attracted considerable attention as therapeutic targets to prevent recruitment of immune cells into the synovium. Numerous pre-clinical models support the use of chemokine blockers. For instance, antibodies to fractalkine (CXC3L1) suppress murine collagen-induced arthritis, even though anti-type II collagen antibody production was not affected. Anti-CXCL16 antibody also decreases clinical arthritis in the same model. However, the system is highly redundant, and several different chemotactic proteins can bind to the same receptor. No clinical improvement in RA was observed in a study using antiMCP-1 antibody, perhaps because the antibody also altered the kinetics of MCP-1 metabolism. AntiIL-8 antibodies met with limited success in psoriasis. More promising results were observed with antibody to IP-10 (CXCL10), which demonstrated some efficacy in a phase II study in RA, but clinical development was discontinued. IP-10 also serves as a biomarker for JAK activation in RA, and blood levels decrease within hours after patients receive the pan-JAK inhibitor tofacitinib.

Chemokines bind to G protein-coupled receptors and could be targeted to block multiple factors. For instance, CCR1 antagonists, which block RANTES and MIP-1α, have been evaluated in clinical trials. Although one compound significantly decreased synovial infiltration by CCR1-expressing cells in a synovial biopsy study, no significant clinical improvement was observed. Chemokine receptor blockade has other levels of complexity such as CCR2-deficient mice, which develop more severe arthritis in some models. Several CCR2 antagonists, which block MCP-1, have not demonstrated significant efficacy in RA. These data suggest that

the chemokine system, including the receptors, is both redundant and complex.

Chemokines and other chemotactic factors (such as C5a and LTB4) can signal through a variety of mechanisms, although many pathways converge on PI3K. Of the several PI3K isoforms, PI3Kγ is relatively specific for chemokine signal transduction, which provides an opportunity to block multiple chemokine receptors simultaneously. PI3Kγ knockout mice have less synovial inflammation in passive and active collagen-induced arthritis than wildtype mice. . Therefore, targeting shared intra-cellular pathways could potentially overcome some of the limitations presented by the complex chemoattractant system. A combined PI3Kγ/δ inhibitor did not show efficacy in an RA clinical trial.

### Platelet-Derived Growth Factor and Fibroblast Growth Factor

PDGF is a potent growth factor that is a chemoattractant and a mitogen for fibroblasts and induces collagenase expression. It is the most potent stimulator of long-term growth of synovial cells in culture. PDGF is expressed in vascular endothelial cells, platelets, and other synovial sublining cells in rheumatoid synovium, compared with healthy tissue. Multiple isoforms of this molecule have been identified (PDGFs A through D), all of which have been detected in RA synovial membranes. PDGF D has been identified as an especially potent stimulator of MMP-1 expression in cultured synoviocytes. PDGF activates the PI3K pathway, which leads to Akt phosphorylation and supports synoviocyte survival through activation of the α and δ isoforms.

FGFs are a family of peptide growth factors with pleiotropic activities. In patients with rheumatoid disease, it is likely that heparin-binding growth factor, the precursor of acidic FGF, is a major mitogen for many cell types and stimulates angiogenesis. Interactions between FGF and proteoglycans are required for biologic activity. It is a potent angiogenic factor, inducing capillary endothelial cells to invade a three-dimensional collagen matrix and form capillaries. RANKL is also produced by FGFstimulated synoviocytes, thereby enhancing osteoclast activation and bone resorption. FGF is present in RA synovial fluid, and the genes are expressed by synovial cells. Synovial fibroblasts express FGF receptors and proliferate after exposure to the growth factor.

### Immunosuppressive Cytokines and Cytokine Antagonists

The pro-inflammatory cytokine network in RA is offset by a variety of suppressive and anti-inflammatory factors that attempt to re-establish homeostasis. Low production of suppressive cytokines could contribute to the perpetuation of the synovitis.

### Interleukin-1 Receptor Antagonist

IL-1Ra is a naturally occurring IL-1 inhibitor that binds directly to types I and II IL-1 receptors and competes with IL-1 for the ligand-binding site. Interaction of IL-1Ra with the IL-1 receptors does not result in signal transduction, and, in contrast to IL-1α or -β, the receptor-ligand complex is not internalized after it binds to the IL-1 receptor. Even though IL-1Ra has high affinity for the IL-1 receptor, it is a relatively weak inhibitor because IL-1 can activate cells, even if only a small percentage of IL-1 receptors are occupied. As a result, a substantial excess of the inhibitor is required to saturate the receptor and thereby block IL-1-mediated stimulation (usually 10to 100-fold excess of IL-1Ra).

IL-1Ra is present in rheumatoid synovial effusions; much of it is produced by neutrophils and macrophages. In RA synovium, IL-1Ra protein is found in perivascular mononuclear cells and in the synovial intimal lining. The IL-1Ra protein and mRNA can be detected in synovial macrophages and, to a lesser extent, in type B synoviocytes. The presence of IL-1Ra in synovium is not specific to RA because OA synovial tissue also contains IL-1Ra, albeit in lesser amounts. Normal synovium contains little, if any, IL-1Ra protein. Synovial cell culture experiments show that the amount of IL-1Ra in the rheumatoid joint is not sufficient to antagonize synovial IL-1.

### Interleukin-10

IL-10 protein is present in RA synovial fluid, and the gene is expressed by synovial tissue macrophages. Serial synovial biopsies in patients with RA who were treated with recombinant IL-10 did not show any significant histologic improvement, and significant clinical improvement was not observed.

### Transforming gGrowth Factor-β

TGF-β is a member of the TGF superfamily, which includes the bone morphogenic proteins (BMPs) that signal through intracellular signaling molecules known as SMAD. TGF-β is widely distributed in different tissues and is produced by many cells, including T cells, monocytes, and platelets. It suppresses the production of collagenase and induces the expression of TIMP. Substantial amounts of TGF-β are present in synovial fluid, although it is mainly present in an inactive, latent form, and the mRNA can be detected in RA synovial tissue.

In RA, TGF-β is one of the factors responsible for blunted responses of synovial fluid T cells. TGF-β also downregulates IL-1 receptor expression on some cell types, including chondrocytes. When it is injected directly into the knees of animals, fibrosis and synovial lining hyperplasia develop. In streptococcal cell wall arthritis, parenteral administration or systemic gene therapy with the TGF-β gene ameliorates the disease. However, intra-articular administration of anti-TGF-β antibody decreases arthritis in the injected joint but not in the contralateral joint in the same model. Although mainly considered antiinflammatory, TGF-β also can play a role in the development of autoimmunity through the differentiation of T cells into the Th17 phenotype.

### Soluble Cytokine Receptors and Binding F Proteins

Soluble cytokine receptors and binding proteins can absorb free cytokines and prevent them from engaging functional receptors on cells. For example, TNF receptors can be released from the cell surface after proteolytic cleavage. Soluble p55 and p75 TNF receptors are present in RA synovial fluid, sometimes in high concentrations. Based on studies with TNF inhibitors and soluble TNF receptor—Fc fusion proteins like etanercept, it is clear that the levels of soluble TNF receptors are not high enough to block TNF biologic activity.

Many other soluble receptors and binding proteins are produced in RA, albeit in concentrations too low to effectively suppress the pro-inflammatory cytokine milieu of the joint. For instance, the IL-1 type II receptor is present in RA synovial fluid, along with lesser amounts of the type I receptor. These soluble receptors can bind to IL-1 or IL-1Ra in synovial effusions. Soluble receptors to IL-15 and IL-17 that neutralize their respective ligands have been characterized, and an IL-18 binding protein also can inhibit cytokine activity.

### Perpetuating Synovitis Through Cytokine Networks

Mapping the cytokine profile in RA led to targeted biologic therapy to inhibit cytokines and supports the concept that cytokine networks play a key role. The network pathway is not autonomous, and except for certain patients with very early disease, discontinuation of anti-cytokine therapy often results in disease flares. Nevertheless, paracrine and autocrine cytokine networks in the synovial intimal lining contribute largely to inflammatory arthritis in RA (Fig. 71.6).

Several cytokines that have been identified in the synovium or synovial fluid can participate in this system and might explain lining cell hyperplasia, HLA-DR and adhesion-molecule induction, and synovial angiogenesis. The list of potential candidates in this highly redundant system is extensive. Several of these candidates, including IL-1, TNF, GM-CSF, and IL-6, now have well-defined roles. The first two, along with numerous other factors (e.g., IL-15, IL-18, and IL-32), are produced by synovial macrophages and stimulate synovial fibroblast proliferation and secretion of IL-6, GM-CSF, and chemokines, as well as effector molecules such as MMPs and prostaglandins. GM-CSF, which is produced by both synovial macrophages and IL-1βor TNF-stimulated synovial fibroblasts, can, in turn, induce IL-1 secretion, creating a positive feedback loop. GM-CSF, especially in combination with TNF, also increases HLA-DR expression on macrophages. Macrophage and fibroblast cytokines also could indirectly contribute to local T cell and B cell activation, including ACPA production. Alarmins can also contribute to the macrophage-fibroblast cytokine network such as IL-33 and HMGB1, by activating mast cells and other cell lineages.

The cytokines in the joint can recruit other immune and inflammatory cells into the synovium through the production of chemokines. Many of these chemokines are produced by macrophages and fibroblasts and attract neutrophils, macrophages, and subpopulations of T and B cells. The sublining chemokine profile, including CXCL13 and CCL20 produced by DCs, also

helps organize these newly infiltrated cells into organized lymphoid structures in some patients. IL-12 and IL-23 help differentiate CD4+ T cells into the Th1 phenotype to produce relatively small amounts of IFN-γ and other relevant cytokines. IL-1 and TGF-β produced mainly by the lining can, along with IL-23, support the production of Th17 or Th9 cells. All of this occurs in the presence of inhibitory factors, soluble receptors, and binding proteins that are overwhelmed by the inflammatory drive. Other cytokines, such as RANKL and M-CSF, activate osteoclasts that remodel bone.

Even though cytokines might not cause RA per se, they clearly help orchestrate and perpetuate rheumatoid synovitis. The pivotal cytokine or cytokines that must be blocked varies between patients and perhaps with the stage of disease.

### Signal Transduction and Transcription Factors

### KEY POINTS

Intra-cellular signal transduction systems transmit information from the environment to the interior of a cell, which can then respond appropriately to stress. The remarkable diversity of signaling pathways and transcription factors provides a selective mechanism for orchestrating activation and repression for appropriate genes. Many of the inflammatory responses observed in RA synovium, including the activation of cytokine, proteases, and adhesion-molecule genes, can be traced to specific transcription factors and signal transduction pathways. Although many targeted therapies directed at signal transduction have met with limited success, recent approvals of oral JAK inhibitors continue to expand the therapeutic armamentarium for RA.

### Janus Kinases and the Signal Transducers and Activators of Transcription

The JAK proteins transduce signals from a wide variety of cytokine and growth factor receptors that use the common γ chain in their receptors. Four JAKs have been identified (JAK1, JAK2, JAK3, and TYK1), and they can form heterodimers and homodimers. The JAK proteins phosphorylate the STATs, which then translocate to the nuclei and alter gene transcription. The JAKs are expressed in RA FLS, immune cells, and synovium, with immunohistochemistry studies localizing JAK3 mainly to sublining DCs.

JAKs have become a focus of interest because of the efficacy demonstrated by several JAK inhibitors in RA, including tofacitinib. The benefit and toxicity are similar to many biologic agents. However, longer-term studies are needed to assess effects

on host defense and possibly oncogenesis. The optimal isoform specificity also needs to be defined to maximize safety and efficacy, and the JAK1/2 selective baricitinib and JAK1 inhibitors like upadacitinib and filgotinib have demonstrated clinical efficacy.

Multiple STATs are expressed in rheumatoid synovium, and STAT1 activation correlates with disease activity in RA. Administration of STAT1 decoy oligonucleotides suppresses antigeninduced arthritis in mice. In addition, studies of rheumatoid tissue have an expression signature suggesting STAT1-regulated gene expression, including IFN-regulated genes.

A synovial biopsy study in patients receiving the JAK inhibitor tofacitinib showed a close correlation between clinical responses and a decrease in phospho-STAT1 and phospho-STAT3 (Fig. 71.7). These data suggest that JAK1 inhibition is especially important for clinical efficacy, most likely by blocking IL-6 and type I IFNs. Given the efficacy of selective JAK1 inhibitors and the results of the synovial biopsy study, it is likely that JAK inhibitors in RA act through the JAK1/STAT1/STAT3 pathway.

### Mitogen-Activated Protein n Kinases

MAPKs are signal transduction enzymes activated in response to cellular stress and are composed of parallel protein-kinase cascades that regulate cytokine and MMP gene expression. There are three main families of MAPKs known as c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK), p38, and ERK. MAPKs phosphorylate selected

intra-cellular proteins, including transcription factors, which subsequently regulate gene expression by transcriptional and posttranscriptional mechanisms.

The MAPKs are widely expressed in synovial tissue and are activated in rheumatoid synovium. Phosphorylated ERK, p38, and JNK can be detected by immunohistochemistry or Western blot analysis. All three kinases and their upstream regulators are constitutively expressed by cultured FLS and can be activated within minutes after exposure to cytokines. They regulate production of pro-inflammatory cytokines and MMPs.

p38 inhibitors are effective anti-inflammatory agents in murine collagen-induced arthritis and rat adjuvant arthritis, possibly by decreasing the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines. In addition, p38 inhibitors block TNF and IL-6 production by cultured macrophages and synoviocytes, as well as cultured synovial tissue cells. Spinal p38 also plays a major role in pain processing, and inhibitors have potential for both analgesic and anti-inflammatory action. Recent studies suggest that p38 in the CNS can regulate peripheral inflammation because intrathecal administration of a p38 inhibitor suppresses inflammation and joint destruction in rat adjuvant arthritis.

Given the putative role of p38 in RA, it is surprising that clinical efficacy of the selective p38 inhibitors is modest, at best. The likely cause of these disappointing results was delineated in the passive K/BxN serum transfer model, in which lack of p38α in macrophages paradoxically increased arthritis severity. This could be due to lower production of the anti-inflammatory cytokine IL-10 by p38-deficient macrophages. Expression of phosphatases that deactivate other MAPKs is also suppressed, resulting in markedly higher levels of phosphorylated JNK and ERK. Thus a compensatory increase in pro-inflammatory pathways abrogates the beneficial effect of p38 inhibition.

Instead of blocking p38 directly, upstream kinase or downstream might be targeted. MKK3 and MKK6, both of which regulate p38, are expressed and activated in the rheumatoid synovium. MKK3 knockout mice and MKK6 knockout mice have markedly decreased joint inflammation in the passive K/BxN model and collagen-induced arthritis. MK2 is downstream of p38 and also regulates TNF gene expression. Several compounds are currently being developed that target MK2 in order to avoid tachyphylaxis observed with direct p38 antagonists.

Two of the three JNK isoforms (JNK1 and JNK2) regulate a variety of genes in inflammation, including TNF and metalloproteinases. Using a JNK inhibitor, marked protection of bone destruction was observed in the adjuvant arthritis model, along with decreased synovial AP-1 activation and collagenase gene expression. No benefit was observed in the JNK1mice, and only modest cartilage protection was seen in the JNK2-/- animals, which has decreased the enthusiasm for targeting this pathway.

The ERK pathway regulates cell growth and some inflammatory mediators and can be targeted by inhibiting its upstream kinases MEK1 and MEK2. A variety of MEK inhibitors, including trametinib, binimetinib, selumetinib, and cobimetinib, are approved in the United States for use in cancer and could potentially be explored in inflammatory arthritis. However, a clinical trial with a small molecule inhibitor (ARRY-438162) found minimal benefit in RA.

### Nuclear Factor-κB

NF-kB is a ubiquitous transcription factor that plays a critical role in the expression of many genes central to RA, including

IL-1, TNF, IL-6, and IL-8. The signaling components of the NF-kB pathway, including the IkB kinases, are described in more detail elsewhere (see Chapter 18). It is abundant in rheumatoid synovium, and immunohistochemical analysis demonstrates p50 and p65 NF-kB proteins in the nuclei of cells in the synovial intimal lining indicate that the transcription factor is activated. NF-kB activation is much greater in RA than OA because phosphorylation and degradation of its inhibitor, IkB, is prominent in RA intimal lining cells.

Nuclear translocation of NF-κB in cultured FLS occurs rapidly after stimulation with many pro-inflammatory cytokines (e.g., IL-1, TNF, and IL-17) or TLR ligands (e.g., peptidoglycan and LPS). NF-kB is also a survival factor for cells and is responsible for resistance to apoptosis in some cell lineages after activation. This characteristic is especially important in intestinal inflammation, in which IKKβ deficiency actually increases mucosal damage because the lack of NF-kB can increase cell death in epithelium. Treatment of FLS with TNF for at least 3 days remodels the chromatin, leading to acetylation of histones and increased NF-κB recruitment to the CXCL10 promoter. These data suggest that persistent NF-kB activation in RA might be due, in part, to TNF sensitization by prolonged exposure to synovial cytokines.

NF-κB activation is required in numerous animal models of arthritis. In the pre-clinical phases of collagen-induced arthritis, synovial NF-kB is rapidly activated, often long before clinical arthritis is evident. Adjuvant arthritis in rats is ameliorated using intra-articular gene therapy with a dominant-negative IKKβ construct that blocks the IKK pathway, and streptococcal cell-wall arthritis is blocked with decoy oligonucleotides or a dominantnegative IkB adenovirus. NF-κB inhibition is associated with decreased synovial cellular infiltration, as well as increased apoptosis. Small molecule IKKβ inhibitors also suppress arthritis and joint destruction in murine collagen-induced arthritis. The translation of this science to humans has been difficult because of the pivotal role that NF-kB plays in host defense.

### Activator Protein-1

AP-1 regulates many genes implicated in RA, especially TNF and the MMPs, which have AP-1 binding motifs in their promoters. AP-1 activity can be induced by many signals including cytokines, growth factors, tumor promoters, and the Ras oncoprotein. AP-1 comprises heteroand homodimers that include various Jun and Fos family members. AP-1-driven gene expression is greatly enhanced when one of its components, such as c-Jun, is phosphorylated by the MAP kinase JNK.

AP-1 expression and nuclear binding are elevated in RA synovium, especially in the intimal lining layer. c-Jun and c-Fos proteins are also expressed in the sublining inflammatory infiltrate, albeit to a lesser degree. AP-1 activation in lining correlates with high expression of MMPs and various cytokines. AP-1 proteins are usually not detected in normal synovium, although modest amounts have been detected in OA.

Cytokines such as IL-1 and TNF and TLR ligands contribute to the activation of AP-1 in RA synovium. These factors are potent inducers of AP-1 nuclear binding in cultured FLS. IL-1 is particularly effective and can dramatically increase AP-1 binding at very low concentrations. The specific Jun family members that constitute AP-1 in synoviocytes have unique functions. For instance, c-Jun increases the production of pro-inflammatory mediators, whereas JunD suppresses cytokine and MMP production. AP-1 decoy oligonucleotides suppress collagen-induced arthritis and

inhibit cytokine production by synovial tissue. Therapeutic interventions that specifically block AP-1 have not been developed for RA. However, blocking the downstream sequelae, such as with MMP inhibitors, was evaluated, with several compounds showing limited clinical improvement.

### Interferon Regulation: IKK-Related Kinases and Interferon Regulatory Factors

IFN signatures have been noted in several autoimmune diseases, such as systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and RA. Type I IFNs are expressed in RA synovium, especially by synoviocytes in the intimal lining. Regulation of IFN production and the IFN response genes such as CCL5, CXCL10, and CCL2 involves a pathway that runs parallel to the canonical NF-kB pathway and includes two IKK-related kinases, known as IKKε and TANK binding kinase 1 (TBK1). Triggered when TLR3 is ligated by viral double-stranded RNA (dsRNA), IKKε and TBK1 phosphorylate the transcription factor IRF3 and induce production of an array of genes that orchestrate this response. IKKε and its substrate IRF3 are expressed and highly activated in RA synovium. Using a combination of IKKε-/- mice and genetic constructs that block endogenous IKKε and TBK1 activity, the role of IKK-related kinases as regulators of IFN-β, RANTES, and MMP expression in cultured FLS was observed. In contrast to DCs, in which IRF7 is the primary IRF that regulates IFN responses, IRF3 is a pivotal factor that is responsible for the IFN signature in FLS.

Some IRF3-driven genes, most notably IFN-β, could be beneficial in inflammatory arthritis. Mice with collagen-induced arthritis that are injected with IFN-β or transduced fibroblasts expressing IFN-β have less severe disease compared with control subjects, including decreased bone and cartilage destruction. However, a clinical trial of IFN-β in RA showed no benefit, possibly because IFN acts by increasing IL-1Ra, which is only modestly effective itself as a therapeutic agent. An alternative approach might be to inhibit IKK-related kinases to block the chemokines associated with the IFN response and concomitantly provide treatment with low levels of exogenous IFN-β.

### Spleen Tyrosine Kinase

Several other signaling molecules have been implicated in RA and are potential therapeutic targets. For example, Syk is involved in immunoreceptor signaling in a variety of cell types and plays a critical role in Fc receptor signaling in macrophages and mast cells. It also participates in B cell activation after ligation of the B cell receptor. A small molecule Syk inhibitor, fostamatinib, demonstrated efficacy in patients with RA in early clinical trials, although off-target effects were dose limiting, and the larger phase III showed less efficacy than early studies. Another more selective compound, MK-8457, also had evidence of efficacy but was complicated by increased infections.

### PI3 Kinases and Other Signaling Pathways

The PI3Ks, especially the δ and γ isoforms, are attractive therapeutic targets because of their role in innate immunity and cell recruitment, respectively. PI3Kγ is the convergence point for chemokine signaling and could permit targeting of several chemoattractants with a single compound. The δ isoform is notable because it not only regulates FLS invasion but is also required for B cell differentiation and activation. PI3Kδ or BTK inhibitors

represent B cell—targeted therapy and block activation of myeloid cells. A combined PI3K δ/γ was not effective in RA, and one BTK inhibitor, fenebrutinib, decreased disease severity in a phase II study. However, another BTK blocker did not show efficacy in RA. There is no shortage of targets, and many others, including upstream MAPK regulators, Ras, IL-1-associated kinases (IRAKs), and sphingosine kinase-1 (SK-1), could be evaluated for a variety of immune-mediated diseases. Combinations of signal inhibition at suboptimal dosage are also potential strategies to improve the risk—benefit ratio.

### Cell Survival and Death in Rheumatoid Synovium

### KEY POINTS

This section will discuss aberrant regulation of cell division, oxidative damage, programmed cell death, and permanent changes in the genome and how they contribute to RA.

### Reactive Oxygen and Nitrogen

Oxidative stress in the joints of patients with RA results from increased pressure in the synovial cavity, reduced capillary density, vascular changes, an increased metabolic rate of synovial tissue, and locally activated leukocytes. The generation of reactive oxygen species can also be facilitated by repetitive ischemia—reperfusion injury in the joint. Tissue injury releases iron and copper ions and heme proteins that are catalytic for free-radical reactions.

Increased reactive oxygen species occurs in patients with RA, which elevates lipid peroxidation products, degrades hyaluronic acid by free radicals, decreases ascorbic acid levels in serum and synovial fluid, and increases exhaled pentane. The levels of thioredoxin, a marker of oxidative stress, are also significantly higher in synovial fluid from patients with RA compared with other forms of arthritis. Peripheral blood lymphocyte DNA from patients with RA contains significantly increased levels of the mutagenic 8-oxohydrodeoxyguanosine, which is a product of oxidative damage to DNA and is a marker of the genotoxic effects of oxidative stress.

NO production is also high in rheumatoid synovial tissue. Low levels of NO are constitutively produced by endothelial or neuronal NO synthases, and enzyme levels are substantially increased by inducible NO synthase after stimulation by cytokines or bacterial products. Numerous proteins are nitrosylated in the rheumatoid joint, and nitrite levels in synovial fluid are elevated in patients, indicating local NO production. In addition, the urinary nitrateto-creatinine ratio is increased, and inducible NO synthase is present in the synovium.

### Apoptosis and Autophagy

Programmed cell death, or apoptosis, removes cells safely from living tissue and permits remodeling, or cell deletion, without causing an inflammatory response. Apoptosis is a normal process that is tightly regulated and can be initiated by withdrawal of hormones and growth factors. Autophagy represents an alternative adaptive mechanism for cell survival that breaks down some cellular components through lysosomes and maintains critical functions to ensure that the cell does not die.

### Genes Regulating Apoptosis

The accumulation of cells in RA results from a balance of cell recruitment, cell egress, local proliferation, and local death. Ultrastructural studies in RA synovial tissue show very few apoptotic nuclei. Macrophage apoptosis is probably low because macrophages express high levels of the caspase 8 inhibitor FLICE-like inhibitory protein (FLIP), which can inhibit Fas-mediated apoptosis. T cell apoptosis in RA synovial effusions, for instance, is significantly less than lymphocytes from crystal-induced arthropathy. High expression of the anti-apoptotic molecule Bcl-2 is found in lymphoid aggregates and protects synovial T cells from programmed cell death. Resistance to apoptosis in vitro increases if RA T cells are co-cultured with FLS. The specific adhesion molecules involved are not defined, although the integrin-binding RGD motif (arginine—glycine—asparagine) blocks the protective effects of synoviocytes.

Fas and its TNF superfamily counter-receptor Fas ligand regulate cell death for many cell types, including synovial T cells and synoviocytes. Fas is expressed by rheumatoid synovial fluid T cells, and the number of Fas+ cells in the peripheral blood of patients with RA is greater than in healthy control subjects. Ánti-Fas antibody, which cross-links Fas on cell surfaces, rapidly causes apoptosis in synovial fluid B and T lymphocytes in RA, although peripheral-blood T cells are more resistant. Another member of the TNF superfamily, TNF-related apoptosis-inducing ligand (TRAIL), binds to two receptors (DR4 or DR5) to induce caspase-dependent apoptosis. DR5 is expressed in RA FLS but not OA cells, and apoptosis can be induced by either TRAIL or agonistic anti-DR5 antibody.

It is comparatively difficult to induce apoptosis in synoviocytes by Fas ligation. p53, which typically induces cell-cycle arrest and either DNA repair or apoptosis, is also expressed in the synovial lining and sublining. However, expression of a key effector of p53-mediated apoptosis, p53 upregulated modulator of apoptosis (PUMA), is low in the synovium and cultured synoviocytes. Thus synoviocytes are resistant to p53-mediated apoptosis even when cells overexpress the protein by transfection with a p53 expression vector. Synoviocyte apoptosis can, however, occur after oxidative stresses such as hydrogen peroxide or nitrogen oxide.

The relative paucity of apoptotic cells in the affected tissues of RA patients may also be partially explained by patterns of gene expression that favor cell survival. The protease ADAM15 was implicated in FLS resistance induced by Fas ligand through activation of the focal adhesion kinase pathway. Many other genes in the same pathway are differentially methylated and could also increase resistance to cell death. Sentrin-1, a ubiquitin-like protein, regulates cell survival by modifying proteins involved in apoptosis. Sentrin-1 is expressed in RA synovium, especially at sites of cartilage invasion, and it protects cells from Fas-mediated death. A second protein, phosphatase and tensin homolog on chromosome 10 (PTEN), protects against tumorigenesis through

antagonism of PI3K, Akt, and many other proliferative pathways. Low PTEN in RA is a feature of the rheumatoid synovial intimal lining, as well as cultured FLS.

### Genes Regulating Autophagy

Genes associated with increased autophagy, such as those encoding LC3 and Beclin-1 and the miRNA miR-30a, are increased in the RA synovial intimal lining compared with OA synovium. These genes program cells for improved survival through autophagy rather than directing cell death through apoptosis. In RA FLS, induction of autophagy by inhibiting proteasome-mediated protein degradation protected against cell death, whereas endoplasmic reticulum stress increased apoptosis. Therefore the degree to which autophagy regulates cell survival is context specific.

### Ferroptosis and Pyroptosis

Ferroptosis is a nonapoptotic cell death process that requires cellular iron and the accumulation of lipid peroxides. This process is dysregulated in RA, which can have profound effects on the cell survival and response to therapeutics (Fig. 71.8). For instance, TNF regulates ferroptosis resistance by upregulating solute carrier family 7 member 11 (SLC7A11), glutamatecysteine ligase catalytic subunit (GCLM), and glutamate—cysteine ligase regulatory subunit (GCLC). This process promotes cystine uptake and the biosynthesis of cellular glutathione (GSH) that protects from oxidative stress. As a result, low concentrations of a ferroptosis inducer together with etanercept, a TNF inhibitor, induce ferroptosis in fibroblasts and attenuates arthritis progression in murine collagen-induced arthritis. The impact of this novel pathway on clinical outcomes is not yet fully understood but could potentially explain some of the variability in response to targeted therapies

Pyroptosis is a pathway to cell death mediated by gasdermins and the activation of caspases. Compared with cells from healthy controls, monocytes and synovial macrophages from RA patients showed increased expression of activated caspase 3 and gasdermin E, and gasdermin E deficiency effectively alleviated arthritis in a mouse model of collagen-induced arthritis. Another work described that myeloid cellspecific deletion of the RA susceptibility gene A20/Tnfaip3 in mice triggered a spontaneous erosive polyarthritis by enhancing inflammasome-mediated caspase-1 activation, pyroptosis, and IL-1β secretion. Although this mechanism was described in myeloid cells, it has also been involved in FLS aggressive phenotype.

### Interventions to Increase Apoptosis in Arthritis Models

Fas-induced death has been used successfully in murine collagen-induced arthritis using anti-Fas antibodies and adenovirus encoding for Fas ligand. Anti-Fas antibody also induces synovial cell death in RA synovial tissue explanted in SCID mice. In the SCID mouse model using RA synovial explants, anti-DR5 antibody decreased cartilage erosion. Similarly, adenoviral transfer of TRAIL in a rabbit model of arthritis decreases synovial inflammation. The importance of apoptosis as a regulator of inflammation was confirmed in murine collagen-induced arthritis, in which genetic DR5 deficiency exacerbated the disease. Blocking Foxo3a in PMNs is also an effective method of deleting these inflammatory cells and suppressing inflammatory arthritis in mice.

The Bcl-2 homology 3 (BH3) domain-only proteins are potent inducers of apoptosis. The challenge is how to get these proteins expressed in the target cell. One of these proteins, Bim, was engineered into a cell membrane—permeable protein

(TAT-Bim) and evaluated in the passive K/BxN model. The construct decreased arthritis severity in prophylactic and therapeutic treatment protocols and was associated with apoptosis of cells, mainly in the myeloid lineage. Therefore targeted cell death of individual lineages can potentially decrease inflammatory arthritis.

The relative resistance to apoptosis in FLS can be overcome by overexpressing PUMA in these cells. The approach was enabled through an optimized adenoviral vector designed to increase infectivity because FLS are resistant to adenoviruses. Perhaps more interesting, gene therapy approaches that deliver PUMA by injecting directly into the joint in rat adjuvant arthritis ameliorate arthritis and decrease joint damage. This raises the possibility of treating patients with proapoptotic agents that act as a "genetic synovectomy. D>

Other molecules that regulate apoptosis demonstrated utility in animal models. For instance, NF-kB blockade in streptococcal cell-wall arthritis induces synovial apoptosis and suppresses arthritis. ### Tumor Suppressor Genes

The p53 tumor suppressor is a key regulator of DNA repair and cell replication. p53 protein expression is significantly greater in the rheumatoid synovium compared with OA and normal tissue. p53 protein can also be detected in RA synovium from patients with very early disease. However, its expression is much lower in other inflammatory arthropathies such as reactive arthritis, which might reflect greater DNA damage and oxidative stress in RA.

TP53 somatic mutations in RA synovium could contribute to inadequate apoptosis in synovial tissue. Transition mutations, which are characteristic of damage induced by reactive oxygen or NO, account for more than 80% of the base changes. Some of the mutant TP53 genes are dominant negative and suppress the function of the wild-type allele. Microdissection studies identified mutant islands of cells with oligoclonal expansion, and the loss of p53 function in a region of RA synovium was associated with increased IL-6 gene expression in the same location. The data suggest that mutations do not cause RA but, instead, are the result of long-standing oxidative stress. The gene alterations can then potentially increase the aggressive nature of the synovium and alter the natural history of RA. TP53 also regulates T cell differentiation through a STAT-mediated mechanism.

Mutations in other genes have also been reported in RA. For instance, vimentin mutations occur, and the citrullinated abnormal protein can lead to anti-citrullinated mutated vimentin antibodies. Mutations are present in rheumatoid synoviocyte mitochondrial DNA, and synovial T cells in RA have an increased incidence of HPRT1 mutations. The latter serve as a marker for oxidative damage that occurs in the synovial milieu. Some of these mutant lymphocytes can also be detected in the peripheral blood, suggesting that articular T cells can migrate out of the joint.

### Synovial Vasculature

Blood vessels play an active role in inflammatory processes, not only as a means of selecting which cells should enter the tissue, but also as a determinant of tissue growth and nutrition through the proliferation of new capillaries. Understanding the structure and function of the microvasculature provides insights into how a highly catabolic tissue such as the rheumatoid synovium can flourish.

### Angiogenesis: Feeding the Starved Synovium

The importance of luxurious new capillary growth early in the development of synovitis has been recognized for many years (Chapter 28). The absolute number of blood vessels is increased in RA synovium (Fig. 71.9), with a rich network of sublining capillaries and postcapillary venules in histologic sections stained with endothelium-specific antibodies. These blood vessels are not normal, however, with a predominance of straight, branching morphologic features compared with tortuous vessels in psoriatic arthritis synovium. The vasculature in the inflamed synovium is less mature, probably as a result of increased DNA damage and decreased recruitment of pericytes. These immature blood vessels are selectively depleted by TNF inhibitors in RA.

### Hypoxia

O2

HIF-1α regulates a number of other pathways that can modify inflammation and blood vessel formation. For example, it induces the alarmin IL-33 in RA FLS, creating a novel regulatory circuit that connects hypoxia to innate immune responses. HIF-1α also activates STAT3, mimicking some of the sequelae of IL-6 stimulation. Blocking HIF-1α in rheumatoid synovial explants decreases production of IL-6, IL-8, and MMP-3. These data suggest that hypoxia not only drives blood vessel proliferation but also cytokine expression and matrix destruction.

### Angiogenic Factors

VEGF can bind to two receptors with tyrosine kinase domains: VEGF-R1/Flt-1 and VEGF-R2. VEGF-R1 regulates inflammatory responses in macrophages such as production of IL-6 and enhanced phagocytosis. Small-molecule VEGF-R inhibitors can suppress severity of acute models of inflammation. Therefore targeting this receptor with a small molecule might suppress the angiogenic and pro-inflammatory actions of VEGF.

In addition to the hypoxia-driven stimulus for blood vessel growth, the inflammatory cytokine milieu of the joint supports angiogenesis. Several pro-inflammatory factors expressed by the rheumatoid joint, including IL-8, FGF, and TNF, are angiogenic, and adiponectin increases VEGF in RA FLS through inhibition of miRNA-106a-5p. Many of these cytokines further enhance angiogenesis by increasing expression of angiopoietins (Ang-1 and Ang-2) by synoviocytes, which can then bind to their tyrosine kinase receptor, Tie-1, on RA capillary endothelial cells. Co-expression of Tie-1 and Ang-1 in early undifferentiated arthritis correlates with the progression to classifiable RA. IL-35 was identified as an anti-angiogenic factor that inhibits VEGF function by the Ang-2l Tie2 pathway. Additional angiogenesis factors derived from activated adhesion molecules on the surface of endothelial cells, such as soluble E-selectin and soluble VCAM, are released in RA synovium and contribute to vascular proliferation.

Vascular remodeling is an active process that involves the continuous creation and resorption of blood vessels. In RA, new capillaries that form under the influence of proangiogenic factors can be identified by the expression of integrins such as avβ3. Endothelial proliferation is especially prominent in synovial tissue regions containing VEGF. Synovial blood vessel involution with endothelial apoptosis also occurs. The ratio of proliferating and involuting blood vessels is significantly higher in RA than in OA or normal synovium.

### Lymphatic Vessels

The lymphatic system is strongly implicated in the onset of synovitis and disease progression in animal models of arthritis presumably by the removal of catabolic factors, cytokines, and inflammatory cells from the inflamed synovium. Persistent inflammation results in chronic damage to the lymphatic vessel, reduced lymphatic drainage, and ultimately severe synovitis and joint erosion. A recent study assessed the differences in lymphatic function of hands in patients with RA and active synovitis via near infrared-indocyanine green (NIR-ICG) imaging, and the lymphatic drainage in the hands of RA patients with active disease was reduced compared with controls, suggesting that targeting lymphatics represents an innovative strategy for therapeutic intervention for RA.

### Targeting Angiogenesis in Models of Arthritis

The importance of new blood-vessel formation in inflammatory arthritis was elegantly demonstrated in the rat collagen-induced arthritis model. The disease was markedly attenuated in animals pretreated with an angiostatic compound similar to fumagillin, which is derived from Aspergillus. This compound is cytotoxic to proliferating, but not resting, endothelial cells. In addition, established arthritis regressed if treatment was initiated well into the course of the disease. Hence angiogenesis is essential for the establishment and progression of inflammatory arthritis because of the need for blood vessels to recruit leukocytes and provide nutrients to the tissue.

Several other anti-angiogenesis approaches are effective in animal models of arthritis. Targeting HIF-1α with a small molecule inhibitor that blocks nuclear translocation and VEGF induction was effective in adjuvant arthritis. Other small molecule inhibitors of the VEGF-R1 with either antibodies or kinase inhibitors have been successfully tested in pre-clinical models of arthritis as well. One of these, vatalanib, decreased inflammatory knee arthritis in rabbits. Direct intra-articular administration of a cyclic RGD peptide that blocks αvβ3 integrin increased endothelial cell apoptosis and suppressed bone and cartilage destruction. A similar RGD peptide that binds to proliferating blood vessels was also used to direct a proapoptotic agent to synovial neovasculature in murine collageninduced arthritis. The potent angiogenesis inhibitor endostatin has been tested in the SCID mouse model, and it decreased synovial explant inflammatory cell infiltration and capillary density. Despite the compelling rationale for anti-angiogenic therapy, an anti-αv antibody showed minimal efficacy in an RA clinical trial.

Human studies designed to inhibit angiogenesis in RA have been limited. TNF inhibitors, such as etanercept and infliximab, rapidly deplete the synovium of inflammatory cells. Power Doppler ultrasound showed that blood flow also decreases within' 4 weeks. Oxygen tension rises despite the decreased perfusion, most likely because of immune cell depletion and decreased in metabolic activity in the joint. A synovial biopsy study in patients treated with the IL-6 inhibitor tocilizumab showed that microvascular density was significantly decreased compared with patients treated with a TNF inhibitor. Thus, the microvascular circulation can be modified by anti-cytokine therapy and returned to a more normal state.

### Adhesion Molecules and Their Regulation

Endothelial cells activated by cytokines and other mediators express adhesion molecules that bind to counter-receptors on mononuclear cells and neutrophils from the circulation and facilitate their recruitment from the blood (see Chapter 29). The Eand P-selectins are expressed by RA synovial endothelial cells, which can initiate the influx of blood cells into the joint. A second family is integrins, which are heterodimers that include α and β chains. The counter-receptors depend on the specific combination of these chains and are frequently proteins in the immunoglobulin supergene family or extra-cellular matrix proteins.

### Integrins and Their Ligands

Expression of integrins and their counter-receptors is increased in the RA synovium under the influence of the rich cytokine milieu. Immunohistochemical techniques localize ICAM-1 to sublining macrophages, macrophage-like synovial lining cells, fibroblasts, and blood vessels compared with normal tissue. Cultured FLS also constitutively express ICAM-1, which is markedly increased by TNF, IL-1, and IFN-γ. ICAM-1 and the other ICAM family members can bind to cells expressing the β2 integrins, especially neutrophils. Integrin α9 expressed by FLS binds to tenascin-C and regulates PDGF-induced proliferation and TNF-induced MMP production. Perhaps more interesting, downregulation of integrin α9 decreases cadherin-11 expression and prevents spontaneous aggregation into synovial lining structures in micromasses. This might be an opportunity for FLS-directed therapy.

Adhesion of α4β1(VLA-4)expressing mononuclear cells such as memory T cells or monocytes to cytokine-activated endothelial cells can be mediated by VCAM-1 or CS-1 fibronectin. A role for VLA-4 in arthritis has been suggested by a number of

experimental observations. In adjuvant arthritis in rats, anti-α4 antibody decreases lymphocyte accumulation in the joint but not in lymph nodes, suggesting that VLA-4 is more important in recruitment to inflamed sites than to non-inflamed sites. T lymphocytes isolated from the synovial fluid and synovial membrane of patients with RA exhibit increased VLA-4-mediated adherence to VCAM-1 relative to autologous peripheral blood lymphocytes. These studies also suggest that leukocytes expressing functionally activated VLA-4 are selectively recruited to inflammatory sites in RA. Natalizumab, an antiVLA-4 antibody that is effective in multiple sclerosis, has potential utility in RA, but the development pathway was limited due to effects on host defense observed with this agent.

Moderate amounts of VCAM-1 are expressed in RA synovial blood vessels. Surprisingly, the intimal lining is the location of the most intense staining with antiVCAM-1 antibodies on histologic sections in RA and normal synovium. Cultured FLS constitutively express small amounts of VCAM-1, and the level is increased by a variety of macrophage and T cellderived cytokines. VCAM-1 also contributes to T cell adhesion to high endothelial venules in frozen sections of RA synovium.

The integrin α4β7, which also binds to VCAM-1, is involved in lymphocyte homing to Peyer's patches. Most intraepithelial and lamina propria lymphocytes express α4β7; this molecule is rarely identified in other lymphoid tissues. α4β7 expression on peripheral blood lymphocytes in RA is similar to that in healthy individuals, but up to a quarter of synovial fluid CD8+ T lymphocytes express this adhesion molecule and support a link between arthritis and the gut. α2β1, which binds to native collagen, has also been implicated in Th17 cell differentiation in mice.

### Therapeutic Approaches to Blocking gAdhesion Molecules

The therapeutic potential for anti-adhesion therapy has been studied in a variety of pre-clinical models. In the SCID mouse model, human peripheral mononuclear cells were injected into engrafted mice, and migration into the tissue was examined. When the mice were treated with TNF, ICAM-1 expression and trafficking into synovium were significantly increased. Anti— ICAM-1 antibody also blocked leukocyte migration into the explant under these conditions. In another study, tonsil mononuclear cells also migrated into the RA synovial grafts in SCID mice. RA clinical trials using anti—ICAM-1 antibody or antisense ICAM-1 oligonucleotides were minimally effective. Surprisingly, mice lacking Eand P-selectin actually had accelerated disease in the collagen-induced arthritis model. This paradoxical result serves as a reminder of the complexity of the immune-mediated diseases and the interdependence of proand anti-inflammatory mechanisms.

### Cartilage and Bone Destruction

### KEY POINTS

A variety of enzymes and cell types contribute directly to destruction in cartilage and bone damage, as well as other support joint structures in RA. In this section, the proteolytic mediators and the cells that produce them will be described.

### Proteases: Mediators of Joint Destruction

### Matrix Metalloproteinases

The MMPs are a family of enzymes that participate in extra-cellular matrix degradation and remodeling (see Chapter 8). They are usually secreted as inactive proenzymes, and their proteolytic activity requires limited cleavage or denaturation to reveal a zinc cation at the core. Their activation can be mediated by other proteases, including trypsin, plasmin, or tryptase. The substrates for MMPs are varied but quite specific for individual members of the family. Many different families of proteinases are found in the joint (Table 71.3), but the MMPs are thought to play a pivotal role in joint destruction.

Regulation of Matrix Metalloproteinase Production. The cytokine milieu can induce the biosynthesis of MMPs by synovial cells and alter the balance between extra-cellular matrix production and degradation. IL-1 and TNF, in particular, induce MMP gene expression by many cells, especially FLS and chondrocytes. The two cytokines are additive or synergistic when used in combination. Many other cytokines and TLR ligands implicated in rheumatoid synovitis can also induce MMP expression, including IL-17, LIF, LPS, and peptidoglycans. Counter-regulatory mechanisms also inhibit MMP expression, such as miRNA-4423-3p, which targets MMP-13 in cultured FLS.

Culture medium from rheumatoid synovium stimulates cartilage degradation in vitro, mainly because IL-1 stimulates MMP production by synovial intimal lining cells. IL-6 does not generally induce MMP production by synovial cells but instead increases the production of TIMP-1, a naturally occurring inhibitor of MMPs. TGF-β inhibits collagenase synthesis and enhances the production of TIMP and collagen by fibroblasts and chondrocytes, thereby shifting the balance from destruction to matrix repair.

Although multiple upstream regulatory regions are involved in MMP gene transcription, the dominant element in the promoter is AP-1. Other regulatory sites such as an NF-kBlike region can also contribute to collagenase expression. AP-1 activity is markedly increased in FLS by pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-1, TNF, and IL-17, and its transcriptional activity is mediated by increased expression of components such as c-Jun. The MAPKs are especially important for this activity, and JNK is the most efficient upstream activator. Glucocorticoids markedly inhibit MMP gene expression by blocking AP-1. Cadherin-11 ligation on FLS can also increase MMP expression and is associated with increases in MAPK and NF-κB activation.

Collagenases and stromelysins have the capacity to degrade virtually all the important structural proteins in the extra-cellular tissues within joints. Collagenase-1 (MMP-1) cleaves through the triple-helical collagen molecule at a single glycine—isoleucine bond approximately three-quarters of the distance from the NH2 terminus. This enzyme degrades only the interstitial helical collagens (e.g., types I, II, III, and X). It has little or no activity against types IV, V, and IX and other nonhelical collagens or denatured collagen; the degradation of the latter is primarily accomplished by the gelatinases. MMP-1, however, is a relatively inefficient enzyme, whereas collagenase-3 (MMP-13) has more favorable kinetics. Neutrophil collagenase, or MMP-8, is constitutively stored in neutrophil granules and is released into the milieu after degranulation.

Matrix Metalloproteinase Expression in Synovium. Collagenase-1 and collagenase-3 (MMP-13) genes are produced by RA synovial tissue, and the latter is highly expressed by chondrocytes in cartilage. In situ hybridization studies show that the primary location of collagenase-1 gene expression in the synovium, like many other MMPs, is the intimal lining, especially in FLS. Subchondral bone is another region in which proteinase expression occurs in RA and could participate in bone resorption. Increased MMP gene expression is an early feature of RA and occurs during the first few weeks of clinically active disease. High expression of collagenase-1, as well as gelatinases such as MMP-2, early in the disease process correlates with rapidly progressive erosions. Similarly, increased blood levels of the proenzymes are also associated with more severe disease.

Stromelysin-1 (MMP-3) and the other members of the stromelysin family degrade type IV collagen, fibronectin, laminin, proteoglycan core protein, and type IX collagen. Stromelysin removes the NH2-terminal propeptides from type I procollagen and can activate procollagenase, creating a positive feedback loop that amplifies damage. Like collagenase, stromelysin gene expression occurs mainly in the synovial intimal lining (Fig. 71.10). Despite the presumed importance of this enzyme in matrix destruction, stromelysin knockout mice are susceptible to collagen-induced arthritis and develop as much joint destruction as mice with functional stromelysin.

MMP inhibitors suppress bone destruction and inflammatory synovitis in pre-clinical models of RA. In OA models, deletion of MMP genes such as stromelysin does not improve outcomes. Several clinical trials in RA using nonselective inhibitors have had minimal success and significant adverse effects, possibly related to decreased matrix turnover. TNF converting enzyme (TACE) inhibitors can unexpectedly increase disease severity in RA, perhaps as a result of higher levels of membrane-bound TNF. One of the most consistent adverse effects experienced by patients treated with MMP inhibitors is increased joint stiffness, which is thought to result from deposition of fibrous tissue without sufficient protease activity to permit removal of matrix proteins.

### Cysteine Proteases: Cathepsins

Cathepsins are a family of cysteine proteases that have broad proteolytic activity, including activity on types II, IX, and XI collagen and proteoglycans. Like MMPs, the cathepsins are regulated by cytokines and by proto-oncogenes such as Ras. IL-1 and TNF induce cathepsin L expression in cultured FLS. In situ hybridization studies demonstrate cathepsin B and L RNA transcripts in RA synovium, especially at sites of erosion. A ribozyme that cleaves cathepsin L decreases FLS invasion and cartilage destruction in the SCID mouse model with implanted cultured synoviocytes, which suggests that this protease has clinical relevance.

Cathepsin K has been implicated in bone resorption by osteoclasts. This protease is unique among the cathepsins because it can degrade native type I collagen. It is expressed in RA synovial tissue by both macrophages and fibroblasts and is present in significantly higher concentrations than in OA. Serum levels of cathepsin K correlate with the extent of radiographic damage. A potential role of cathepsins as mediators of bone destruction in arthritis was confirmed in studies in which cysteine protease inhibitors significantly decrease joint damage in the rodent arthritis models. In the TNF-transgenic mouse model, cathepsin K deficiency decreased, but did not eliminate, bone erosions.

Cathepsin K inhibition could potentially block bone erosions due to synovitis, as well as generalized bone loss that occurs in RA. One agent, MIV-711, was evaluated in OA and preserved femoral bone volume and reduced blood biomarkers of cartilage and bone degradation. Of note, the inhibitor did not improve pain, which would limit its utility in a disease like RA because pain is an important symptom. Another inhibitor, odanacatib, was tested in post-menopausal women with osteoporosis but was discontinued due to an increased incidence of stroke.

### Aggrecanases

Aggrecan is a major proteoglycan component of articular cartilage. Because of its large size and negative charge, it contains a considerable amount of water, which increases compressibility. Two proteolytic sites are available on aggrecan in its globular domain. One site is susceptible to MMP cleavage, whereas the other, located 32 amino acids toward the C terminus, is the site for cleavage by a family of enzymes known as aggrecanases. The two sites can be identified in tissues using monoclonal antibodies after cleavage when specific neoepitopes are revealed.

Normal cartilage contains a surprising amount of aggrecanase neoepitope, suggesting continuous matrix turnover. The level of aggrecanase cleavage product increases with age. Two aggrecanase genes, aggrecanase-1 and aggrecanase-2, have been cloned and are members of the "a disintegrin and metalloproteinase with thrombospondin motif" (ADAMTS) family of proteins (ADAMTS-4 and ADAMTS-5, respectively). They are expressed in OA and RA cartilage, and their proteolytic activity can be detected in synovial fluids. Especially high levels of the neoepitope are present in arthritic cartilage. IL-1 increases aggrecanase expression in cartilage explants, as well as cultured chondrocytes. Aggrecanase-1 and aggrecanase-2 are constitutively expressed by RA and OA FLS and synovial tissues. Aggrecanase-1, but not aggrecanse-2, is induced in synoviocytes by cytokines, especially TGF-β. Genetic deletion of aggrecanse-1 has no effect on a murine OA model, but loss of aggrecanase-2 prevents degenerative changes.

### Endogenous Protease Inhibitors

α2-Macroglobulin (α2M) accounts for more than 95% of collagenase inhibitory capacity in serum. The mechanism of inhibition by α2M involves hydrolysis by the proteinase of a susceptible region in one of the four polypeptide chains of α2M (sometimes called the bait), with subsequent trapping of the proteins within the interstices of the α2M. Ultimately, the protease is covalently linked to a portion of the α2M molecule.
