The serine protease inhibitors (SERPINs) are also abundant in synovial effusions and plasma and can serve a dual purpose of directly blocking serine protease function and indirectly decreasing MMP activity by preventing serine proteases from activating MMP proenzymes. One SERPIN, αl-anti-trypsin, has been well characterized in synovial fluid and is frequently inactivated after oxidation by reactive oxygen species. Fibronectin also inhibits aggrecanase-1 (ADAMTS-4). However, citrullinated fibronectin is much less efficient and increases aggrecanase activity, representing another potential pathogenic effect of protein citrullination in RA.

A family of proteins that specifically block MMP activity, called TIMPs, is probably the most important physiologic inhibitor in

the inflamed joint. The TIMP proteins block proteinase activity by binding directly to MMPs in a 1:1 molar ratio. The inhibitors bind to MMPs with extremely high avidity. Even though the interaction does not result in new covalent bonds; it is essentially irreversible.

TIMP proteins are present in RA synovial fluid in excess. It is, in fact, difficult to detect free active collagenase and stromelysin because they are quickly bound by the inhibitors after activation. Immunohistochemical and in situ hybridization studies localized TIMPs in hyperplastic synovial intimal lining cells in rheumatoid synovium, but not in the cells of normal synovium. TIMP gene expression is not directly affected by IL-1 or TNF but is increased by IL-6, oncostatin M, and TGF-β. Not all effects of TIMPs are beneficial in inflammation. For instance, TIMP-3 knockout mice have significantly more synovitis and TNF production in antigeninduced arthritis, perhaps because it is not available to inhibit TACE. In contrast, TIMP-1 or TIMP-3 gene transfer limits rheumatoid FLS invasion into cartilage in an SCID mouse model. The function of these genes can extend beyond protease inhibition and include a number of paracrine functions, as well as induction of apoptosis when present within cultured synoviocytes.

The relative balance between MMPs and TIMPs ultimately determines the fate of the extra-cellular matrix. The ratio in RA favors degradation, whereas OA has a lower MMP-to-TIMP ratio. The levels of TIMP gene expression are similar in the two diseases and may well be maximal, and the higher ratio in RA results from increased MMP production. The balance between protease and inhibitor can potentially be modified in vivo with drug therapy. For instance, methotrexate therapy decreases collagenase but not TIMP-1 mRNA, which could decrease joint damage in patients treated with this agent.

### Regulation of Cartilage Destruction

Macrophage-like and fibroblast-like cells migrate onto the surface of cartilage, and the FLS in particular penetrate into cartilage matrix. This invasive pannus is more commonly found in metatarsophalangeal joints, compared with hip and knee joints, perhaps explaining why erosions often occur around small joints.

FLS from the intimal lining are major effectors of cartilage destruction in RA. They produce prodigious amounts of proteases, bind to cartilage, and invade the extra-cellular matrix (see Fig. 71.11). The pivotal role of synoviocytes in cartilage destruction was demonstrated in arthritis models using cadherin-11 blockade to disrupt the intimal lining. Cartilage destruction is markedly attenuated, even though bone erosion progress.

Other cells in the joint, including macrophages and synovial fluid neutrophils, could also be responsible for cartilage damage, whereas osteoclasts are responsible for bone erosions. More primitive mesenchymal cells isolated directly from the cartilage—pannus junction express phenotypic and functional features of both synoviocytes and chondrocytes and have also been described in the synovium.

Cartilage is destroyed in RA by enzymatic and mechanical processes. The enzymes induced by factors such as IL-1, IL-17, TNF, phagocytosis of debris by synovial cells, and mechanical trauma degrade the matrix proteins. Early in synovitis, proteoglycans are depleted from the tissue, most likely as a result of the catabolic effect of cytokines such as IL-1 on chondrocytes with the production of MMPs and aggrecanases, and this depletion leads to mechanical weakening of cartilage.

As proteoglycans are depleted, cartilage loses elasticity and becomes susceptible to mechanical fragmentation and fibrillation. Eventually the tissue loses functional integrity concurrent with its dissolution by collagenases and stromelysins. Some of the MMPs responsible for this process are also derived from the chondrocytes themselves. Multiple MMPs, especially stromelysin (MMP-3) and collagenases (MMP-1 and MMP-13), are expressed in RA cartilage, and in situ hybridization studies confirm the presence of their RNA transcripts in chondrocytes. Hence the cartilage is under attack from a multitude of sources: It is bathed in protease-rich synovial fluid, under extrinsic attack from the invasive pannus, damaged from within by chondrocytes, and fragmented by mechanical forces.

Enzymes released by PMNs in synovial fluid, including neutrophil collagenase and multiple serine proteases, also contribute to cartilage loss. Immune complexes containing RFs are embedded in the superficial layers of cartilage and can attract and activate neutrophils. Electron microscopic examinations of articular cartilage in RA reveal evidence of breakdown of collagen and proteoglycan as a result of superficial activity of joint fluid enzymes.

Most animal studies suggest that IL-1 is a key regulator of matrix degradation in arthritis. For example, when IL-1 is injected directly into rabbit joints, proteoglycan depletion in cartilage occurs rapidly and correlates with MMP levels in synovial fluid.

Neutrophil depletion does not interfere with subsequent destruction of the extra-cellular matrix. Although TNF blockade has anti-inflammatory effects, chondroprotection is less prominent. The joint destruction observed in TNF-dependent models often requires IL-1. IL-17 and TLR ligands can also contribute to joint destruction directly or by synergizing with IL-1 and TNF.

The rate-limiting step in cartilage loss is collagen cleavage, even though proteoglycans are degraded soon after inflammation begins. MMPs, which are released into the extra-cellular space and are active at neutral pH, are probably responsible for most proteolysis of articular-cartilage proteins, but other classes of enzymes also contribute to joint destruction. Enzymes such as cathepsins B, D, G, K, L, and H may play a role inside and outside cells by degrading noncollagenous matrix proteins. Serine proteinases (e.g., elastase and plasmin) and aggrecanases also cause damage to the extra-cellular matrix.

### Regulation of Bone Destruction

Marginal erosions are the most characteristic location for bone damage in RA. These often occur in metacarpal phalangeal joints and proximal interphalangeal joints traditionally ascribed to a "bare area" where cartilage does not protect the underlying bone from invasive pannus. However, anatomic pathology and CT studies suggest that erosions actually occur near collateral ligaments in these small joints where microdamage was observed in cadaveric studies. It is possible that local factors related to stress are more important than the anatomic location of overlying cartilage.

Osteoclasts are the primary cells responsible for bone degradation in RA. It was recently described that osteoclasts in pannus originate from circulating bone marrow—derived cells and not from locally resident macrophages. Murine CX3CR1hiLy6CintF4/80+I- A+/I-E+ macrophages are the osteoclast precursor-containing population in the inflamed synovium and are regulated by FOXM1 (forkhead box protein M1). RANKL is perhaps the single most important factor that modulates bone resorption. Osteoclast development is complex and involves the differentiation of monocytes under the influence of cytokines such as M-CSF in combination with RANKL. RANKL is produced by many cell types, including activated T cells and FLS. The LTB4 receptor (BLT1) regulates osteoclast differentiation, with BLT1 deficiency

increasing the number of osteoclasts and sensitizing cells to the effects of RANKL.

Similar processes contribute to generalized bone loss in RA, beginning with periarticular osteopenia and progressing to diffuse osteoporosis. Osteoclast activation and osteopenia occurs in ACPA+ healthy individuals, with decreased cortical thickness and increased cortical porosity compared with controls. Polyclonal and some monoclonal ACPAs induce bone loss when injected into mice and confirm the importance of protein citrullination and pathogenic antibodies on osteoclast activation. The pathogenic effect of ACPA binding to osteoclasts or osteoclast precursors, especially in the presence of IL-8, is responsible for this effect. Extra-cellular miRNA-574-5p contained in microvesicles can also enhance osteoclast differentiation via TLR7/8.273

Abundant evidence implicates this powerful mechanism in bone destruction caused by inflammatory arthritis. For instance, administration of osteoprotegerin (OPG), a RANKL decoy receptor, to rats with adjuvant arthritis inhibits bone destruction but has almost no effect on inflammation or clinical signs of arthritis. RANKL-/- mice are also protected from bone erosions in the passive K/BxN model of arthritis, although cartilage destruction still occurs. Animal models of arthritis point to IL-17 as a mediator of osteoclast generation. Genetic deficiency of IL-17 or antiIL-17 antibodies has remarkable bone-sparing effects in these experiments.

RANK, RANKL, and OPG (as well as M-CSF and IL-17) have been detected in the synovium and synovial fluid of patients with RA. The ratio of RANKL to OPG is significantly higher in RA synovial effusions than in either OA or gout, which is consistent with the more destructive nature of RA. Osteoclasts expressing tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase (TRAP) are capable of forming resorption lacunae and can be generated from cultured RA synovial cells (Fig. 71.12). This activity is mediated by RANKL displayed by synovial T cells and FLS and is blocked by the addition of exogenous OPG.

The functional relevance of the RANK-RANKL system was confirmed by RA studies in which the anti-RANKL antibody denosumab decreased bone erosions. As predicted from animal

model studies, the antibody had no effect on inflammation or clinical signs of synovitis.

A second system that modulates bone remodeling involves the Wnt proteins, which regulate the balance between bone damage caused by osteoclasts and bone formation by osteoblasts. Several members of this family bind to receptors that regulate osteoblast differentiation through effects on β-catenin. A role of this system in inflammation and bone destruction was confirmed in TNF transgenic mice in which loss of Wnt9a ligand exacerbated disease severity. Wnt signaling is modulated by many other proteins, most notably the Dickkopf (DKK) family. DKK-1 in particular blocks binding of Wnts to its receptors. In TNF-transgenic mice with arthritis, bone erosions are blocked by inhibiting either TNF or DKK-1. With the latter, proliferative bone lesions such as osteophytes formed instead. Therefore, DKK-1 is a critical switch that determines the fate of bone in inflammatory lesions. When present, bone destruction is favored; when absent, bone formation occurs. Other factors can also stimulate osteoclastogenesis, such as IL-21, which increases bone damage in collagen-induced arthritis and increases protease production by FLS.

### Tissue Repair e

Extra-cellular matrix turnover in RA has been likened to wound healing as a result of the critical role of collagen production, proteases, and protease inhibitors. Remodeling the matrix by removing damaged proteins is a key element in early repair. Subsequently, the balance shifts to protease inhibition, production of cytokine inhibitors, removal of inflammatory cells through apoptosis, and release of anti-inflammatory eicosanoids such as LXs to suppress inflammation. Neutralization of oxidants via glutathione reductase or superoxide dismutase further limits tissue damage. Normalization of oxidant signaling can also reprogram the adaptive immune system and suppress arthritogenic T cells.

Tissue repair mechanisms then permit either a return to normal architecture or scar formation. TGF-β, in particular, plays a key role in that it increases collagen deposition, suppresses MMP expression, and enhances production of the TIMPs. Although TGF-β levels in the rheumatoid joint are substantial, they are mainly in the inactive latent form and are not sufficient to overcome the impressive array of pro-inflammatory cytokines that induce protease expression. Persistent antigen-driven T cell activation, continued antibody-driven complement fixation, or activation of other cell lineages like macrophages or FLS overwhelms the negative feedback loops that attempt to restore homeostasis. Strategies to shift from tissue damage by enhancing endogenous mechanisms could suppress symptoms and enhance appropriate remodeling of the matrix to restore homeostasis.

Because of invasive behavior by rheumatoid synovium, the possibility that the tissue contains immature cells or embryonic genes that regulate repair has been explored. The embryonic growth factors from the Wnt and Fz gene families are expressed by RA synovium. Normally, these proteins participate in bone marrow progenitor differentiation and limb bud mesenchyme. Wnt5a and Fz5, in particular, are markedly elevated in RA tissues and cultured synoviocytes. When normal fibroblasts are transfected with the WNT5A gene, cytokine expression, such as IL-6, increases significantly. Antisense WNT5A and dominant-negative WNT5A vectors diminish cytokine expression by synoviocytes.

These data raise the possibility that immature mesenchymal cells populate the synovium in RA, either as a primary event or as a repair or inflammatory mechanism. Primitive mesenchymal

cells circulate in the peripheral blood of both people with RA and healthy people. The former might decrease inflammation, while the latter might presage disease flares (e.g., PRIME cells [see above]). In pre-clinical models like collagen-induced arthritis, they infiltrate the synovium before synovial inflammation becomes clinically apparent. Treatment with either adiposeor bone marrow—derived mesenchymal stem cells has been proposed as a treatment modality. However, cell therapy remains primarily an experimental approach that is currently focused on degenerative diseases like OA and would need carefully controlled studies to avoid widespread and inappropriate use.

Tissue repair in RA is a complex process that also involves the ingress or dedifferentiation of mesenchymal cells that can remodel the matrix. These cells are modulated by TGF-β and the BMPs. The BMPs are members of the TGF-β superfamily, and like TGF-β, they signal through the SMAD pathway. Several members, including BMP-2 and BMP-7, are expressed in the joint and facilitate repair, although inappropriate release can also enhance joint damage or lead to ankylosis or enthesophyte formation. BMP function is also regulated by a family of inhibitors such as Noggin, which can limit cartilage damage when it is overexpressed in murine antigeninduced arthritis. Modulating the relative balance and timing of BMP expression ultimately could be used to modify the destructive influence of synovitis or to regenerate damaged tissues.

### Conclusion

The causes and pathogenesis of RA are complex and involve the interplay between environment and genes. Many years before clinical disease is apparent, evidence of immune dysregulation is observed, including antibody responses to modified peptides and increased production of cytokines and chemokines. A tipping point is ultimately reached, perhaps after a "second hit," when antibodies activate complement in the joint and attract other immune cells from the blood. The local synovial milieu is rich with cytokines, inflammatory cells, and proteases that can drive further adaptive immune responses and joint damage. Understanding the diverse pathogenic events involved in RA helps us understand the diversity of responses to targeted agents that block TNF and IL-6, interfere with T cell co-stimulation, deplete B cells, or inhibit cytokine signal transduction. As we gain additional information about the critical events prior to clinical disease, namely "pre-RA," approaches that prevent rather than treat RA might be feasible.

# Clinical Features of Rheumatoid Arthritis

### KEY POINTS

### Epidemiology and Disease e Burden

Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic, systemic autoimmune condition with protean manifestations. The primary expression of disease occurs in the synovial tissues and is characterized clinically by symmetric polyarticular inflammation, which can lead to progressive joint damage. As a result, RA can be associated with substantial functional disability, morbidity, and accelerated mortality, which pose a substantial societal burden.

### Disease Frequency

The prevalence of RA has been estimated at 0.5% to 1% in most developed countries, although epidemiologic estimates vary widely depending on geographic region and methodological approach. The Global Burden of Disease 2017 study conducted a rigorous systematic review and metaregression, estimating a global age-standardized prevalence of 0.25%. North America, Western

Europe, and the Caribbean (0.3% to 0.4%) exhibited the greatest regional prevalence of RA in contrast to Southeast Asia, Oceania, and Western Sub-Saharan Africa (0.1%). The highest rates of RA incidence are observed among individuals of Native American ancestry, with a reported disease prevalence approaching 5% to 7% in Pima and Chippewa Indians in the United States, respectively. There is a much lower prevalence in select African regions, thought to be the result of a lower population frequency of the human leukocyte antigen (HLA)-DRB1 shared epitope—containing allele,3 which is the single strongest known genetic risk factor for RA. A 40-year population-based study from Rochester, Minnesota (1955 to 1994), demonstrated an overall ageand sex-adjusted annual incidence of 44.6 cases per 100,000 personyears. In this study, incidence rates were approximately twofold higher in women than men, with peaks in disease onset observed at younger ages in women (55 to 64 years) compared with men (75 to 84 years). Notably, these authors reported marked temporal trends, including a 47% decline in overall RA incidence during the study period. A more recent cohort (1985 to 2014) from the same population suggested that the incidence of RA has been stable, but seropositive RA incidence rates have modestly decreased, while seronegative RA incidence rates have increased. These results underscore the potential impact of environmental exposures (e.g., cigarette smoking) in mediating risk, and the potential relevance of birth cohort effects. Based on this population, the lifetime risk for RA among U.S. adults has been estimated at 3.6% for women and 1.7% for men. Globally, the incidence of RA has increased by 8.2% with a 7.4% increase in prevalence from 1990 to 2017.1

### Pre-rheumatoid Arthritis

Substantial recent gains have been made in our understanding of the risk factors and mechanisms involved in early disease development. It is now well established that circulating autoantibodies (primarily rheumatoid factor [RF] and anti-citrullinated protein antibodies [ACPAs] but also anti-carbamylated protein antibodies, anti-peptidylarginine deiminase 4 antibodies, and antimalondialdehyde-acetaldehyde antibodies)7 can be detected in the serum before RA symptom onset, often by many years. The period of autoimmunity preceding the initial articular signs and symptoms of disease has been termed pre-RA (Fig. 72.1). In addition to detectable levels of serum autoantibody, pre-RA is often

characterized by the presence of subclinical inflammation that is reflected by increased serum levels of C-reactive protein (CRP) and other pro-inflammatory cytokines and chemokines. Several potentially relevant alterations in these serum biomarkers have been demonstrated that may herald imminent disease onset. Autoantibody changes include increased circulating concentrations, enhanced binding avidity and affinity, aberrant glycosylation (promoting complement activation and Fc receptor binding), and epitope spreading.

With the use of a multiplex antigen array and pre-clinical samples from the U.S. Department of Defense Serum Repository, investigators have demonstrated a time-dependent expansion of ACPA specificity, with an increasing number of positive ACPA subtypes through the pre-clinical period and peaking at the time of RA symptom onset. In this study, early ACPA expansion predicted subsequent increases in serum concentrations of inflammatory cytokines, including TNF, interleukin (IL)-6, IL-12p70, and interferon (IFN)-γ. Among patients in whom seropositive RA develops, the detection of these pre-clinical inflammatory cytokines and chemokines appears to predict a shorter time to disease onset. Furthermore, the concentration of these cytokines predicts disease onset in an age differential manner, with a longer pre-clinical period for older individuals (≥40 years) than younger individuals (<40 years).

Mounting evidence suggests that early inflammatory events leading to RA may occur at extra-articular locations, with mucosal sites predominant among these. Evidence supporting mucosal tissues as possible sites of initiation includes (1) the absence of demonstrable synovitis, histologically in seropositive individuals during the pre-clinical period11; (2) the predominant role of environmental exposures that are known to cause mucosal injury as independent RÅ risk factors (e.g., cigarette smoking, silicosis, and, possibly, periodontitis)12,13; (3) the robust metrics of immunoglobulin (Ig) A-ACPA in predicting future disease onset14; (4) the production

of RA-related autoantibodies in diseases characterized by mucosal inflammation, namely bronchiectasis15; and, perhaps most importantly, (5) evidence of demonstrable mucosal inflammation during the pre-clinical period. In a study of unaffected first-degree relatives (FDRs) of RA probands, individuals with high-risk autoantibody, defined by the presence of ACPA or two or more RF isotypes, were far more likely than seronegative FDRs to have detectable pulmonary airway abnormalities by high-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) (76% vs. 33%, P = 0.005),16 an association that was independent of cigarette smoking. The prevalence and type of airway abnormalities observed in these high-risk FDRs were similar to those observed in patients with early-stage RA.

In addition to the lungs, other potential mucosal sites of initiation could include the oral or intestinal mucosa,10 although evidence demonstrating inflammation from these sites in preclinical RA is limited. Periodontitis is increased in frequency, even among patients with early, treatment-naive RA, compared with controls. Infection with Porphyromonas gingivalis (among the only prokaryotic organisms with the ability to citrullinate protein antigen) has been associated with expression of disease-specific autoantibody in individuals at increased risk for RA.18, Antibodies against leukotoxic strains of Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans, indicative of periodontitis, have also been detected in RA patients and are associated with positivity for RF and ACPA. In addition, prior work evaluating the intestinal microbiome has shown an abundance of Prevotella copri in patients with new-onset untreated RA compared with controls,21 and human leukocyte antigen, DR subregion (HLA-DR)-presented peptide from this organism can induce T helper (Th)1 responses in peripheral blood mononuclear cells from early RA patients.

In many patients, arthralgias herald the end of pre-clinical disease and often precede the onset of synovitis detected by physical examination. Advanced imaging modalities, namely MRI and musculoskeletal ultrasound (MSUS), have shown promise in

detecting subclinical inflammation that predicts the transition to clinical RA. In a study of 136 ACPA-positive patients, of whom 42% subsequently developed RA over a median follow-up of 18 months, more than 95% of patients had gray-scale synovitis in at least one joint on MSUS, but only 33% had power Doppler findings present. Power Doppler was particularly informative of progression to inflammatory arthritis of the same joint, with a 10-fold higher risk if any power Doppler signal was detected. Similarly, MRI features of subclinical inflammation (synovitis, bone marrow edema, tenosynovitis, and intermetatarsal bursitis) of the metacarpophalangeal (MCP), wrist, and metatarsophalangeal (MTP) joints are frequently detected in patients with clinically suspect arthralgia and predict the development of inflammatory arthritis, independent of other clinical risk factors (such as age, joint involvement, CRP, and ACPA positivity).24, Notably, a prospective study of 149 patients with clinically suspect arthralgia demonstrated that the predictive ability of MRI inflammation is similar in magnitude to that of ACPA positivity (hazard ratio [HR] 5.07 for MRI inflammation and 6.43 for ACPA positivity). Much less is known about the transition to clinical RA in seronegative patients, in part because of typical definitions for pre- RA that require autoantibody positivity. During this transition to clinical RA, seronegative individuals appear to have less frequent lower extremity involvement, shorter time from symptom onset to presentation with arthralgias, more tender joints, and a longer time to development of arthritis than seropositive individuals.

### Clinical Presentations of Early Rheumatoid Arthritis

The early presentation of RA includes systemic and articular signs and symptoms. Extra-articular features are more commonly seen in later disease, although occasionally they may precede articular manifestations. Systemic findings include fatigue and, less commonly, weight loss or low-grade fever. Articular symptoms most often begin with stiffness, pain, and swelling involving the small joints of the hands and feet in a symmetric distribution, including the MCP, proximal interphalangeal (PIP), and MTP joints. Understanding that RA-related synovitis can involve almost any synovial joint in the body, the condition characteristically spares the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joints (affecting <10% of cases)28 and also spares the thoracic and lumbosacral spine. Joint activity in RA rarely remits completely in an involved joint when developing in another. This quality of arthritis distinguishes RA from conditions such as rheumatic fever, serum sickness, or palindromic rheumatism, which can be characterized by a true migratory arthritis pattern. With increasing efforts to diagnose and treat RA earlier, rheumatology consultations for inflammatory arthritis are occurring at earlier stages of disease, often before fulfilling classic disease criteria. Among patients with an early undifferentiated inflammatory arthritis, 30% to 40% will experience a spontaneous remission, whereas classifiable RA will eventually develop in approximately one in four. In addition to ACPA positivity, other features predictive of later RA classification in patients with early undifferentiated inflammatory arthritis include polyarthritis, symmetric joint involvement, and the presence of radiographic erosions.

### Patterns of Onset

RA onset typically follows one of several different temporal patterns, ranging from an acute or "explosive" polyarticular disease

onset to a far more insidious inflammatory arthritis that can be oligoarticular and additive during the initial course.

### Insidious Onset

Estimated to affect 55% to 65% of patients,30 an insidious disease onset represents the most common early presentation of RA. The small joints of the hands, wrists, and feet are most commonly affected. The joint pattern is often symmetric and is accompanied by morning stiffness, a cardinal sign of inflammatory arthritis that may last as long as several hours. Less commonly, onset is characterized by a slowly evolving monoarticular or oligoarticular presentation, with a predilection for larger joints, such as the elbows, knees, or hips. This presentation mimics a seronegative spondyloarthropathy, but, with time, most patients experience symptoms in additional joint areas, including the contralateral joint or other small joints, resulting in a pattern of involvement more typical of RA. In older patients (e.g., >65 years), an insidious onset can be dominated by systemic features, including fever, weight loss, fatigue, marked acute phase responses, and occasional proximal girdle involvement, which together parallel the signs and symptoms of polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR) or remitting seronegative symmetric synovitis with pitting edema (RS3PE). This type of presentation should also prompt consideration of an occult malignancy.

### Acute or Intermediate Onset

Estimated to affect between 8% to 15% of all cases, RA less frequently manifests as an explosive polyarticular arthritis that can be intensely inflammatory and may involve both small and large joints at presentation. With acute onset, the pain may be so limiting that the initial evaluation occurs in an urgent ambulatory setting. This dramatic, but uncommon, disease onset appears to have a predilection for the elderly and has been described as one of the characteristic presentations in "elderly onset" or "lateronset" RA. An intermediate disease onset, in which symptoms develop over days to weeks, affects approximately one in five incident cases.

### Atypical Onset

In a minority of patients with RA, the initial presentation involves a simple bursitis or tendonitis that may evolve into tenosynovitis. Such patients may also be seen with early carpal tunnel syndrome from wrist involvement and subsequent median nerve compression. As with insidious presentations, the disease in individuals with an atypical presentation often evolves over time to the more typical symmetric small joint findings of RA.

### Other Patterns of Onset

Palindromic Rheumatism. Palindromic rheumatism is an uncommon form of disease onset characterized by relatively brief but intense episodes of joint inflammation. Often, by the time patients are seen by a rheumatologist, they may already be asymptomatic because of the self-limited nature of palindromic flares, which can last from a few hours to a few days. Joint involvement with palindromic onset is often monoarticular, with maximal inflammation achieved within hours. Affecting almost any joint, this onset most commonly affects the patient's knees, fingers, or shoulders. Because of the highly inflammatory and often monoarticular presentation, palindromic RA can closely mimic crystalline arthropathy or septic arthritis. Serologic testing, including RF and/or ACPA, is often helpful in differentiating palindromic rheumatism from other inflammatory

arthritides. If followed over time, one-third to one-half of patients with initial palindromic rheumatism evolve to develop a daily pattern of joint involvement more typical of RA. This disease evolution appears to be more common among those with hand involvement and ACPA positivity. The disease in the remainder of patients tends to continue to be palindromic or to evolve into a definable crystal-related arthropathy (suggesting that early misclassification is common).

Arthritis Robustus. As with palindromic onset, arthritis robustus is a relatively uncommon RA subtype that was first described in 1973.35 The typical patient profile is an older man, with an occupational history notable for manual labor. Patients seen with arthritis robustus often have a markedly inflammatory arthritis, usually involving the hands and feet. Nevertheless, affected patients often have few if any symptoms, giving the impression in some cases of a patient who is "blissfully unaware" of the condition. The challenge in the care of these patients is they often do not communicate complaints, rendering the physical examination and laboratory assessments key components in physician management decisions.

Extra-articular Disease as Initial Presentation. Several reports have shown that extra-articular disease manifestations rarely represent the initial disease manifestation in RA. This relatively uncommon phenomenon has perhaps been most widely observed with the appearance of rheumatoid nodules preceding demonstrable synovitis. "Rheumatoid nodulosis" has been classically described by the combination of subcutaneous rheumatoid nodules, subchondral bone cysts, and recurrent joint symptoms, an entity with a favorable prognosis most often seen in the context of RF seropositivity. Other forms of extra-articular disease have also been observed to precede the development of synovitis in patients with RA, most notably lung disease. Retrospective studies of RA—associated interstitial lung disease (RA-ILD) cohorts have evaluated the onset of articular versus lung disease manifestations, finding the lung disease to predate articular disease in 10% to 20% of RA- ILD patients.39, One study examined 74 patients who were seen with respiratory symptoms (radiography demonstrating airway

and/or interstitial disease) and a positive ACPA but without evidence of RA or alternative connective tissue disease. Despite a median follow-up of only approximately 1.2 years, 3 of the 33 patients with high-titer ACPA developed articular manifestations of RA.

### Diagnosis

The characteristic patient with RA reports pain and swelling of the small joints of the hands, wrists, and feet, with prolonged morning stiffness, often lasting more than an hour. This typical articular presentation, the presence of any extra-articular manifestations, and laboratory and radiographic assessments are critical in differentiating RA from other inflammation-driven diseases. This is in comparison with osteoarthritis (OA), which is a far more prevalent "low-grade" inflammatory articular disease (Table 72.1). Early in the disease course, patients with RA may experience difficulty using their hands with routine activity and pain in the forefeet with weight bearing or walking. Patients commonly report a "gelling" phenomenon following periods of rest, which improves with activity. Systemic symptoms such as fatigue and low-grade fever may also be present, but polyarthritis accompanied by a high fever (e.g., >38.5° C) strongly suggests an alternative etiology. The joint examination often reveals swelling (or synovitis), tenderness, increased warmth, and limited range of motion. Other findings may include palmar erythema and subcutaneous nodules on extensor surfaces.

Adding to the complexity of early diagnosis, other rheumatic diseases included in the differential diagnosis of RA may share many of these findings. Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), primary Sjögren's syndrome, and viral diseases, such as hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and HIV, can be characterized by these typical joint findings and may be accompanied by RF positivity (Table 72.2). Owing to its superior specificity, detection of ACPA can help confirm RA in these settings. Other diseases in the differential diagnosis include gout, particularly with tophi mimicking the subcutaneous nodules of RA; calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate

deposition (CPPD) arthropathy, with a pseudo-RA presentation; and psoriatic arthritis, in a polyarticular pattern and prior to the development of psoriasis. In elderly patients, PMR and RS3PE should be considered, whereas in younger patients, the signs and symptoms from parvovirus B19 infection or a postinfectious reactive arthritis can closely parallel those of RA. Conditions included in the differential diagnosis of RA and distinguishing characteristics are summarized in Table 72.2. The differential diagnosis will guide subsequent laboratory, serologic, and radiographic assessments. In RA, the initial laboratory and radiographic testing often shows the following results:

Normal peripheral white blood cell (WBC) count and differential

Thrombocytosis, reflecting increased systemic inflammation

Mild normocytic anemia (anemia of chronic disease); less often microcytic

Normal urinalysis

Normal renal, hepatic, and other metabolic or endocrine testing

Increased erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR; typically <50 mm/hour) and elevated CRP of similar magnitude. Both may be normal in as many as one-third of patients when first evaluated

RF seropositivity in approximately 70% at the time of diagnosis; an additional 15% of patients may "seroconvert" from RFto RF+ status early in the disease course

ACPA seropositivity with a frequency approaching that observed with RF; in contrast to RF, ACPA positivity is highly specific (>95%)

Negative anti-nuclear antibody (ANA), although as many as 30% of patients may be positive, typically in a low to moderate titer without positive subserologies

Early in the disease process, radiographs are often normal, other than periarticular soft tissue swelling and evidence of effusions in some large joints

Arthrocentesis, if performed, typically demonstrates inflammatory synovial fluid with less than 50, WBC/mm3 with the proportion of polymorphonuclear (PMN) cells typically less than 90%. Higher WBC and PMN counts in synovial fluid are more indicative of an infectious or crystalline etiology. Most often, synovial fluid values range between 5000 to 25, WBCs/mm3 in RA, with 60% to 80% PMN neutrophils. Qualitative and nonspecific, the mucin clot test in RA classically demonstrates either no clot formation or an easily friable clot caused by a reduced concentration of synovial fluid hyaluronic acid in the context of inflammation. Both culture and crystal analyses are negative in RA. Although lacking disease specificity, synovial fluid ragocytes (also called rheumatoid cells or inclusion body cells) have been described in RA. Ragocytes are phagocytic cells with distinctive cytoplasmic granules composed of immune complexes. Other synovial fluid testing such as RF, ACPA, lactate, complement, and glucose are of little diagnostic utility in RA and thus are not indicated.

RA classification criteria have been developed for clinical trials and are based on components from the clinical history, physical examination, and laboratory and radiographic testing. Satisfaction of the 1987 American College of Rheumatology (ACR) RA classification criteria requires the presence of objective synovitis for 6 weeks or longer to exclude alternative self-limited forms of arthritis. Other components of these criteria are shown in Table 72.3. Because these criteria include findings more consistent with longstanding disease, such as the presence of radiographic damage and

subcutaneous nodules, the 1987 criteria lack sensitivity for the detection of early RA. Recognizing the importance of both early diagnosis and treatment, updated RA classification criteria were proposed as part of a joint ACR/European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology (EULAR) effort in 2010 (Table 72.4). The 2010 criteria place an emphasis on additional laboratory tests, including RF, as well as ACPA, ESR, and CRP. Articular involvement is qualified by joint swelling and/or tenderness. Application of these criteria provides a score of 0 to 10, with a score of 6 or higher being classified as definite RA. The 2010 criteria render an earlier diagnosis possible, even with a very low (or in some cases absent) number of tender and/or swollen joints, stressing the

aJoint involvement refers to any swollen or tender joint on examination or evidence of synovitis on MRl or ultrasonography. Distal interphalangeal joints, first carpometacarpal joint, and first metatarsophalangeal joint are excluded from assessment. Categories of joint distribution are classified according to the locations and numbers of involved joints, with p placement into the highest category possible based on the pattern of joint involvement.

importance of applying these in the appropriate setting (patients with at least one joint with synovitis not better explained by another disease). Although the 2010 criteria yield excellent sensitivity (97%) in identifying patients with RA, the specificity is

lower than that of the 1987 criteria (55% vs. 76%, respectively). By default, satisfaction of the 1987 criteria satisfies the 2010 criteria, the latter including provisions for the use of other imaging modalities (e.g., ultrasound or MRI) to document the presence of synovitis. Although useful for teaching and in clinical practice, it is important to recognize that both the 1987 and 2010 criteria were primarily developed with the goal of identifying homogeneous study populations for RA clinical trials and not for the diagnosis of individual patients.

Radiographic assessments are an important element in the evaluation of RA, often serving as a measure of treatment efficacy in therapeutic trials. Although radiographic assessments used in clinical trials focus primarily on quantitative measures of articular damage, including bony erosions and joint space narrowing, which is limited to the hands, wrists, and feet, it is well recognized that RA affects a number of other joints, with findings that can be highly characteristic and markedly destructive. Often accompanied by periarticular osteopenia, bony erosions in RA are distinctive in location, affecting the so-called bare area where synovium wraps back on itself and lays directly on the bone. This bare area is located periarticularly in the proximal and distal metaphyseal regions (Fig. 72.2). Radiographic progression tracks with clinical measures of disease activity, with few patients progressing once achieving sustained remission, although a latency period (prior disease activity levels, duration of remission) exists. Both ultrasound and MRI have superior sensitivity over conventional radiography for the detection of bony erosions in RA and for the identification of synovitis or juxta-articular inflammation (tenosynovitis, bursitis) when results from physical examination are equivocal. Bony ankyloses, confirmed radiographically, is rare in RA, is associated with increased duration and severity of disease, and is found in joints that have been immobilized by pain, inflammation, treatment, or any of these factors in combination. Because RA is characterized exclusively by bone loss, the presence of new periarticular bone formation on imaging suggests an alternative etiology, such as OA, psoriatic arthritis, other spondyloarthropathy, or crystalline disease.

### Course and Complications of Established Rheumatoid Arthritis

### Articular Manifestations

With its primary manifestation involving synovial tissues, the signs and symptoms of RA are primarily driven by active synovitis that results in joint swelling, stiffness, palpable warmth, and pain. The classic joint distribution in early disease includes the small joints of the hands and feet (MCP, PIP, and MTPs) (Fig. 72.3A). With time, intermediate (wrists, elbows, and ankles) and large (hips, shoulders, and cervical spine) joints may become involved. With more advanced and longer duration of disease, RA may also involve atypical joints, including the temporomandibular joint (TMJ), cricoarytenoid, and sternoclavicular joint. In contrast to OA, RA rarely affects the DIP joints and seldom targets the thoracic or lumbosacral spine.

### Hands and Wrists

The hands and wrists are often considered together because they form a single functional unit. For example, wrist involvement is strongly associated with the presence of ulnar deviation of the MCP joints. This may occur via weakening of the extensor carpi ulnaris muscle or tendon, either as a direct or indirect result of

inflammation, which leads to radial deviation of the wrist as the carpal bones rotate (the proximal row in an ulnar direction and the distal row in a radial direction). Subsequently, ulnar deviation of the MCP joints and the associated palmar subluxation may serve as compensatory mechanisms to maintain digital tendons in a normal line with the radius. Together, changes of the wrist and MCP joints result in a highly characteristic "zigzag" deformity (Fig. 72.3B and C). Although classically described as irreversible, reducible ulnar deviation of the MCP joints can result from bulky synovitis, tendon laxity occurring after the reduction of synovitis, tendon rupture, or muscle weakness in the hands. Nevertheless, reversible MCP deviation is more typical of nonerosive processes such as SLE or non-inflammatory neurologic conditions such as Parkinson's disease.

Proliferative synovium contains both the inflammatory and enzymatic machinery sufficient to destroy ligaments, tendons, and the articular regions distal to the ulnar head, resulting in joint subluxation, dislocation, and bony erosions. This inflammatory synovium may also invade and impinge normal tissue spaces, and lead to nerve entrapment syndromes, such as carpal tunnel syndrome (median nerve). The inflammatory and enzymatic degradation of tissue, coupled with naturally occurring forces, act together to impair the integrity of the radiocarpal, radioulnar, and midcarpal joints. The ulnar collateral ligament can become stretched or even destroyed by synovitis of the radioulnar joint. As a result, the ulnar head may "spring up" into dorsal prominence where it "floats" and can be easily depressed (the so-called piano key styloid) (Fig. 72.4). Severe disease progression in the wrist can lead to marked loss of joint space, bone erosions, and ankyloses; the latter is more common with wrist immobilization resulting from unremitting disease.

Perhaps the best recognized of the articular deformities observed in RA are swan neck and boutonnière deformities of the fingers (Fig. 72.5A and B). The swan neck deformity involves DIP flexion with simultaneous PIP hyperextension. This condition is thought to result from direct involvement of the PIP and/or MCP joints. Boutonnière deformities, PIP flexion, and DIP hyperextension are related to relaxation of the central slip, with buttonholing of the PIP joint between its lateral bands. Involvement of the thumb in RA also has unique characteristics. Several corresponding deformities are described and result from involvement of the first MCP, interphalangeal (IP), or carpal metacarpal (CMC) joints, either alone or in combination.

Predominant thumb deformities include a boutonnière-like deformity, which begins with synovitis of the first MCP joint,

results in weakening of the joint capsule and surrounding connective tissues, and culminates with the subluxation of the extensor pollicis longus (EPL) tendon in both volar and ulnar directions. As a result, the MCP joint is abnormally flexed, and the IP joint is secondarily hyperextended, forming a characteristic "Z-deformity" (Fig. 72.5C). The MCP joint may be partially reducible or fixed. Less commonly, RA patients develop a swan necklike deformity of the thumb, resulting from CMC synovitis and joint

subluxation at the base of the thumb. This ultimately leads to exaggerated adduction at the distal end of the MCP joint, markedly narrowing the first web space and effectively reducing the object size that a patient can grasp.

In a prospective cohort study of 183 early RA patients enrolled from 1985 to 1989, 59% of patients developed a hand deformity over 10 years of follow-up, with the majority of deformities occurring during the first 2 years (56%). Higher inflammatory markers and poorer functional status (markers of RA severity), as well as RF positivity, were associated with development of hand deformities. The most frequent hand deformities observed were ulnar deviation of the MCPs (74%), boutonnière (41%), and swan neck (40%), with many patients having multiple deformities. Estimates of hand deformities for patients more recently diagnosed during the "treat-to-target" era are lacking.

A common, and perhaps underappreciated, manifestation of RA in the hands and a major cause of hand weakness is tenosynovitis in the flexor tendon sheaths. Using MRI, tenosynovitis is detected in up to 80% of patients with early RA and, when present at the level of the wrist and MCP joints in early undifferentiated arthritis, is highly predictive of progression to clinical RA.49, Tenosynovitis at the wrist most frequently involves the common extensor and extensor carpi ulnaris tendons, whereas the flexor tendons are more frequently involved at the MCP joints. Along with wrist joint synovitis, flexor tenosynovitis occurring in close proximity to the median nerve may result in carpal tunnel syndrome through nerve impingement. Without concomitant and typical RA synovitis, this finding may pose a substantial diagnostic challenge. Nodular thickening may also develop in the tendon sheaths or the pulley system and cause the finger to "lock" in fixed flexion (known as stenosing tenosynovitis or trigger finger), resulting in significant pain. With chronic symptoms or frequent recurrence, stenosing tenosynovitis can be treated with tendon sheath injection or surgical intervention.

RA also represents the most common etiology of tendon ruptures involving the hand. RA can lead to attritional rupture of the digital extensor tendons, occurring at the ulnar head in the wrist, described by Vaughn-Jackson in 1958.51 Because surgical intervention can prevent extensor tendon rupture and subsequent loss of function, identifying patients most at risk for this complication is paramount. In extensor tendon rupture, the extensor digiti

minimi (EDM) usually ruptures first, a defect that may go unnoticed because the extensor digitorum communis (EDC) extends the second through fifth digits simultaneously. Thus testing for EDM function, via active independent extension of the little finger, may be valuable in identifying patients that could benefit from prophylactic extensor tendon repair52 (Fig. 72.6). Less frequently, RA may lead to rupture of the extensor pollicis longus in addition to attritional ruptures of the flexor pollicis longus and

the index finger flexor digitorum profundus tendons within the carpal tunnel.

Although more typical of severe psoriatic arthritis, the most serious consequence of RA involving the hand can be seen with marked bone resorption that begins with the articular cartilage and spreads along the diaphysis of involved phalanges. As a result, the digits can become grossly shortened, exposing excess skin folds, and the phalanges can be retracted (or telescoped) into one another and then pulled out into abnormally long extension, often without eliciting pain. Typically involving multiple digits, this rare arthropathy has been termed arthritis mutilans or the opera glass hand.

### Feet and Ankles

As with the hand and wrist, the foot and ankle may also be considered as a single functional unit. For example, hindfoot abnormalities that involve the ankle and/or subtalar joint directly affect forefoot pressures with loading and weight bearing. Thus optimal correction of an existing forefoot deformity is reliant upon simultaneous correction of any residual hindfoot defect. Ankle and foot involvement is common in RA, with forefoot involvement observed in as many as 90% of patients at some point in the disease process and serving as the initial disease manifestation in approximately 15% of patients. In addition to MTP synovitis, juxta-articular inflammation including intermetatarsal bursitis, submetatarsal bursitis, and tenosynovitis is increasingly recognized as a common manifestation in patients with early RA.54,

As a result of forefoot/MTP involvement, pain experienced during push-off in striding results in altered gait mechanics. Plantar subluxation of the metatarsal heads occurs soon after the MTP joints become involved, producing "cock-up" or "claw" toe deformities of the PIP joints. Cystic collections that represent outpouchings of flexor tendon sheaths often develop under the MTP joints. Pressure necrosis and callus formation on the plantar surfaces can develop in patients with subluxation of metatarsal heads, and claw deformities can lead to pressure ulcers on the dorsal surface of PIP joints (Fig. 72.7). Metatarsal subluxation leads to increased pressure on the MTP joints, with a sensation described by many patients as "walking on marbles." Concurrently, hallux valgus results in progressive overlap of the second and third toes on top of the great toe. With the development of fixed deformities, including a broadened forefoot, hallux valgus, and claw toes,

mechanical foot symptoms often persist in patients, even in the absence of active inflammation.

Involvement of the hindfoot, midfoot, and adjacent joints are also common in RA. Valgus deformity of the hindfoot may occur, likely related to pronation forces applied to weakened and inflamed talonavicular and subtalar joints (Fig. 72.8). Similarly, ankle instability may result from stretching and even erosion of ligamentous support tissues. With involvement of the subtalar joint, which provides the major axis for foot inversion and eversion, patients may report difficulty with ambulation on uneven ground. With midfoot involvement, inflammation of the talonavicular and naviculocuneiform joints can result in pes planus (flat foot) deformities. Pes planus can be further exacerbated through insufficiency of the posterior tibialis tendon and the plantar calcaneonavicular (spring) ligament and result in collapse of the longitudinal arch. Inflammation and subluxation of the tarsometatarsal joints may result in a "rocker-bottom" foot deformity, resembling that observed with Charcot's foot disease. Rheumatoid nodules can develop in the Achilles tendon, and spontaneous tendon

rupture can occur, in the context of granulomatous inflammation. Parallel to carpal tunnel syndrome in the wrist, tarsal tunnel syndrome can occur in the ankle and results in a compressive tibial neuralgia.

### Cervical Spine

Reported in as many as 80% of patients with RA, although estimates vary widely, cervical spine involvement appears to be most common in those with long-standing and poorly controlled disease. Reviewed by Joaquim and Appenzeller,58 risk factors for cervical spine involvement in RA include erosive disease, glucocorticoid use, treatment failure, and early age at disease onset. Importantly, the development of cervical spine involvement and its complications may be abrogated by intensive treatment. One study showed that patients treated aggressively with combination disease-modifying therapy were at lower risk for cervical spine disease than patients treated with less aggressive monotherapy.

Of the cervical spine findings observed in RA, the most serious clinical presentations relate to atlantoaxial (C1C2) subluxation, cranial settling, and subaxial subluxation. Of these, atlantoaxial subluxation is the most common radiologic abnormality of the cervical spine observed60 and may include:

The atlas (C1) moving anteriorly on the axis (C2) (prevalence 27%)

The atlas moving posteriorly, laterally, or rotary on the axis (prevalence 0.1% to 0.7%)

Subluxation of the atlas vertically in relation to the axis (prevalence 11%)

The earliest and most common symptom of atlantoaxial subluxation is pain radiating into the occiput. Two other serious but less common clinical patterns include (1) slowly progressive spastic quadriparesis with painless sensory loss in the hands and (2) transient episodes of medullary dysfunction associated with vertical penetration of the dens and probable vertebral artery compression. In the latter case, paresthesias may occur in the shoulders or arms during movement of the head. With vertical C1-C2 subluxation, patients may complain of facial pain with decreased sensation in the V1 and V2 distributions of the fifth cranial nerve. A recent meta-analysis suggests that the incidence of anterior atlantoaxial subluxations is decreasing over time, but rates of vertical subluxation, subaxial subluxation, and cervical myelopathy remain stable.

Neurologic symptoms resulting from spinal cord involvement often have little relationship to the degree of C1-C2 subluxation present. When present, symptoms range from simple paresthesias to altered consciousness, loss of sphincter tone, and other well-defined signs of cord compression. Signs of cord compression portend a poor prognosis, often heralding the rapid progression of myelopathy with an approximate 50% 1-year mortality rate. Risks are further magnified in the context of patient falls, whiplash injury, or the need for general anesthesia with intubation requiring cervical manipulation. The incidence of sustained neurologic deterioration following surgical correction of C1-C2 disease may be as high as 6%, suggesting that a conservative management strategy may be optimal for a substantial proportion of asymptomatic patients.

As with neurologic symptoms, physical examination findings are nonspecific and unreliable in detecting C1-C2 subluxation. Physical findings may include the loss of cervical lordosis, resistance to passive spine motion, or the abnormal protrusion of the axial arch felt with the examining finger on the posterior pharyngeal wall. In symptomatic patients, cervical spine films in flexion

should be taken only after radiographs have been taken to rule out odontoid fracture or high-grade atlantoaxial subluxation. Advanced imaging modalities, including CT and especially MRI, have proven to be particularly useful in defining pathology affecting this region in RA.

Although not lined by synovium, discovertebral joints of the cervical spine can be involved, leading to osteochondral tissue destruction and disk space narrowing that is visible on lateral radiographs. Patients with cervical spine involvement may report significant neck pain, although passive range of motion may be preserved in the absence of significant muscle spasm. At least two possible mechanisms have been proposed to explain the cervical spine involvement characteristic of RA: (1) extension of inflammation from adjacent synovial-lined neurocentral joints (the joints of Luschka) into the discovertebral area and (2) chronic cervical instability initiated by apophyseal joint destruction, leading to vertebral misalignment or frank subluxation.

### Intermediate and Large Peripheral Joints

Intermediate and large joint involvement is more indicative of long-standing and often poorly controlled disease. Elbow involvement is reported in approximately one-third to one-half of patients. The earliest clinical manifestation is extension loss, a finding that frequently goes unnoticed by the patient. Bilateral olecranon bursal swelling is observed in RA and may be encountered in gout or pseudogout, although typically unilaterally. Shoulder involvement affects not only the glenohumeral joint but also the subacromial (subdeltoid) bursa, the distal third of the clavicle (related to adjacent inflammatory bursitis), and rotator cuff tendons (Fig. 72.9A). In contrast to other joints, shoulder involvement is often quite painful, with symptoms referred to the deltoid region. Patients commonly complain of significantly disturbed sleep with painful awakenings in side sleeping positions. Rotator cuff dysfunction is common in RA and may relate to the proximity of proliferative synovium to the rotator cuff insertion on the greater tuberosity. Resulting in substantial morbidity, rotator cuff tears have been demonstrated to affect approximately 20% of patients with RA, with another one-fourth having evidence of frayed tendons. Because the rotator cuff acts as a downward stabilizer of the humerus in the glenoid, rotator cuff dysfunction can lead to superior migration of the humeral head from unopposed forces of the deltoid and resultant secondary degenerative arthritis of the glenohumeral joint.

Hip and knee involvement also results in substantial disability. In contrast to the hip, knee involvement in RA is usually readily identified on examination, with joint effusions that can be large and associated with increases in intra-articular pressures. As with the elbow, loss of full extension may be an early finding of knee involvement. Increased intra-articular pressure, particularly those accompanying flexion, can lead to an outpouching of the posterior components of the joint, resulting in a popliteal or Baker's cyst. In extreme circumstances, a popliteal cyst can rupture, and inflammatory fluid may dissect distally into the calf, resembling acute thrombophlebitis or deep vein thrombosis (Fig. 72.9B). A helpful but uncommon sign of popliteal cyst rupture is the presence of a crescentic hematoma inferior to either the lateral or medial malleolus. MRI and ultrasound are often used to identify a popliteal cyst and help differentiate this complication from other entities.

Unlike the knee, detecting involvement of the hip often poses a challenge. As with other forms of arthritis, including OA, hip involvement in RA is associated with pain most often localized

to the groin or occasionally the buttock. Similar to other forms of inflammatory arthritis involving the hip, RA leads to symmetric joint space narrowing and cartilage loss, leading to an axial migration of the femoral head. This is in contrast to OA of the hip, which is characterized by asymmetric joint space narrowing that is most evident in the superior aspect of the joint. In advanced cases of RA-related hip involvement, the femoral head can collapse and undergo resorption with remodeling and medial migration of the acetabulum, leading to protrusio acetabuli (Fig. 72.9C). Well recognized in RA, protrusio acetabuli may also be seen in other forms of inflammatory arthritis, including spondyloarthritis, and has been described in genetic, metabolic, and non-inflammatory connective tissue disorders, such as Stickler's syndrome.

### Temporomandibular, Cricoarytenoid, Sternoclavicular, and Manubriosternal Joints

Although not commonly thought of as synovial joints, both the TMJ and cricoarytenoid joints contain synovial tissue and can be affected in RA. Patients with TMJ involvement often complain of jaw pain, which can be confused with tooth or ear problems or jaw claudication in the elderly, in whom giant cell arteritis with PMR may be suspected. As in other joints, radiographic findings of the TMJ in RA can include both joint space narrowing and erosions. Symptoms of cricoarytenoid joint involvement are often more subtle. The cricoarytenoid joints are diarthrodial joints responsible for rotation of the vocal cords as they abduct and adduct. With cricoarytenoid joint involvement in RA, a patient may complain of new-onset hoarseness, sore throat, dysphagia, or pain with speech. In extreme cases, the vocal cords can become immobilized in an adducted midline position, resulting in inspiratory stridor. Laryngoscopy and CT scanning are the most sensitive methods to evaluate for cricoarytenoid arthritis. Finally, as synovial lined joints, both the sternoclavicular and manubriosternal joints can also be involved in RA, although this rarely causes symptoms due to their relative immobility. Overt involvement of the sternoclavicular joint should raise suspicion for possible septic arthritis.

### Extra-articular Manifestations

Recognizing that RA is a systemic inflammatory disease is requisite for optimal management. Inflammation in RA involves not only articular structures but also potentially extra-articular tissues, leading to the development of subcutaneous nodules and other mucocutaneous findings, as well as serositis and cardiopulmonary, neurologic, ocular, and hematologic complications. Extra-articular manifestations are observed in up to 50% of patients with RA and generally portend a poor prognosis, including increased morbidity and mortality.64, In a singlecenter series, mortality risk in patients with RA with extra-articular manifestations was more than twice that of patients without extra-articular disease (relative risk [RR], 2.49; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.43 to 4.03), and cardiovascular disease (CVD) accounted for 70% of all deaths in this group. A, Fortunately, clinically important extra-articular complications are decreasing, likely as a consequence of better treatment practices. Nevertheless, some of our treatments may further complicate assessments for extra-articular complications in RA, because disease-remitting therapies can lead to adverse effects that closely mimic extra-articular disease manifestations. For example, glucocorticoids exacerbate both osteoporosis and CVD risk, conditions already over-represented in patients with RA. The focus of this section will be on the "disease-specific" extra-articular manifestations of RA and not complications related to therapy, which are covered elsewhere in this textbook.

### Mucocutaneous

Rheumatoid nodules occur in up to 30% to 40% of RA patients, primarily in seropositive patients with active disease. A history of cigarette smoking appears to be a robust risk factor for the development of subcutaneous nodules in RA, particularly among 65B When present and histologically confirmed, rheumamen. toid nodules are pathognomonic for RA. In rare circumstances, nodules may precede arthritis and may herald the development of other extra-articular manifestations when present early in the disease course. Rheumatoid nodules develop most commonly on

extensor surfaces and pressure areas, including the forearm, Achilles and foot regions, and finger joints (Fig. 72.10). The appearance of nodules in unusual sites can pose a significant diagnostic dilemma, with reports of rheumatoid nodules involving areas overlying the sacrum, sole, and occiput (in bedridden patients), in addition to rare cases involving the heart, lungs (see the following discussion), sclera (rarely leading to perforation of the globe), and central nervous system (CNS). In the larynx, rheumatoid nodules on the vocal cords may cause progressive hoarseness and mimic cricoarytenoid arthritis.

On examination, rheumatoid nodules are typically subcutaneous and firm and may be either mobile or adherent to underlying structures. Because the physical findings are nonspecific and subcutaneous, nodules can be seen with other forms of inflammatory arthritis; biopsy may be needed to confirm the diagnosis in select circumstances. Other conditions that can result in inflammatory arthritis and nodules include rheumatic fever, tophaceous gout, SLE, and multicentric reticulohistiocytosis (Table 72.5). Histologically, rheumatoid nodules are characterized by a central area of necrosis rimmed by a corona of palisading fibroblasts, which are surrounded by a collagenous capsule with perivascular collections of inflammatory cells. These nodules grow by accumulating cells that expand centrifugally, leaving behind central necrosis of the connective tissue matrix. Inspection of early lesions suggests that the nodule is composed of smal, inflamed arterioles,67 suggesting that rheumatoid nodules are a form of small vessel vasculitis. This

fact may explain the relationship of this finding to other forms of extra-articular disease, such as CVD. Although rheumatoid nodules may regress either spontaneously or with disease-remitting therapy, increased nodulosis is an uncommon but well-recognized complication of methotrexate treatment that often paradoxically occurs in patients with well-controlled disease.

Amyloidosis may also complicate long-standing inflammatory disease. The purpura of amyloidosis may be confused with the skin fragility and "senile purpura" seen in patients who have been on long-standing glucocorticoid therapy. Renal disease, especially proteinuria, or diarrhea with malabsorption in a patient with long-standing RA should prompt investigation for secondary amyloidosis.

Vasculitis in RA may present with multiple skin findings, ranging from relatively benign nail-fold infarcts to a deep, erosive, scarring pyoderma gangrenosum (see the section on Vasculitis). The presence of livedo reticularis, with its characteristic lacey appearance (most prominent on the lower extremities), should raise a concern for a medium-vessel vasculitis or an associated connective tissue disease, such as SLE or antiphospholipid antibody syndrome (APS).

The prevalence of secondary Sjögren's syndrome (autoimmune exocrinopathy) in RA has been estimated at 17%,70 resulting in symptoms of keratoconjunctivitis sicca (dry eyes) or xerostomia (dry mouth). These symptoms are accompanied by objective evidence of lacrimal or salivary gland dysfunction.

### Ocular

In addition to keratoconjunctivitis sicca, episcleritis and scleritis complicate the disease course in less than 1% of patients with RA. Episcleritis typically presents as a painless red eye without vision loss or frank discharge, the latter more indicative of conjunctivitis. Inspection reveals engorged blood vessels that stop at the limbic border. Scleritis also results in scleral injection without discharge, but, in contrast to episcleritis, this is typically accompanied by boring pain that can be precipitated by palpation of the globe and areas of dusky discoloration. Manifesting with variable levels of involvement, scleritis can be localized and superficial or more generalized and can extend into deeper tissue layers. In severe cases, deeper involvement can be characterized by granulomatous scleral resorption leading to scleromalacia perforans (Fig. 72.11). Although episcleritis can usually be managed with topical antiinflammatory agents, scleritis requires prompt evaluation by an ophthalmologist, and treatment routinely requires systemic or intraocular immunomodulating therapy. In some cases, the sclera can become thinned, even in the absence of overt inflammation, and lead to scleromalacia.

Other forms of eye involvement in RA include chronic blepharitis or, rarely, peripheral ulcerative keratitis. This latter condition is caused by the deposition of cryoproteins (RF—IgG complexes), which can lead to perforation of the anterior chamber. Iritis and uveitis can occur in RA but are more commonly seen with other rheumatic conditions (e.g., spondyloarthritis, sarcoidosis, Behçet's disease, and juvenile idiopathic arthritis).

### Bone

In addition to periarticular bone loss and local erosions, RA is a well-recognized cause of systemic bone loss, placing patients at a substantially higher risk for the development of osteoporosis and fracture. This risk is further heightened in a dose-dependent fashion in the context of glucocorticoid therapy. In a prospective series of 395 patients with early RA, more than one-third experienced a fracture over just 5 years of follow-up. In addition to glucocorticoid use, risk factors for bone loss and fracture in RA included older age, disability, longer disease duration, decreased grip strength, low body mass, and increased inflammation. Systemic inflammation in RA results in the increased expression of growth factors, including macrophage colony-stimulating factor (M-CSF) and receptor for activation of nuclear factor-kB ligand (RANKL), and pro-inflammatory cytokines that promote osteoclast differentiation and ultimately bone resorption. More recently, antigen-specific ACPAs have been implicated as direct promoters of the osteoclastogenesis process and bone loss that characterizes, and occasionally precedes, RA. These findings are bolstered by animal work showing that immune responses to citrullinated self-antigen may serve as a trigger for declines in bone mineral density and bone quality.

### Muscle

Weakness is a common patient complaint in RA. Although this may be related to articular complaints such as joint pain and/ or instability, true muscle pathology, including sarcopenia, can also occur in RA as a result of deconditioning, inflammatory processes, or type II muscle atrophy complicating glucocorticoid use. Most typically with long-standing, active disease, loss of lean body mass, primarily muscle, signifies rheumatoid cachexia, which is strongly associated with functional disability and mortality risk (reflecting the appropriate naming by Paget nearly 150 years ago; the direct translation is "bad condition").75, There have also been reports of inflammatory myopathy accompanying RA presenting with muscle tenderness and increased muscle enzymes. Muscle biopsies demonstrate focal accumulations of lymphocytes and plasma cells in a condition referred to as nodular myositis. Necrotizing myositis has also been reported as a rare complication of RA.

### Hematologic

Thrombocytosis is frequent with active RA, with platelet counts serving as an indirect measure of systemic inflammation. Platelet counts are positively correlated with both clinical and laboratory parameters of disease activity in RA, including ESR, CRP, and several acute phase proteins. Thrombocytopenia, on the other hand, is rare in RA in the absence of treatment-related bone marrow suppression or Felty's syndrome. As with other rheumatic and autoimmune conditions, eosinophilia may accompany active RA.

Associated with the presence of the HLA-DRB1 *0401 allele, Felty's syndrome comprises an uncommon but severe disease subset, defined by the triad of RA, splenomegaly (present in >90% of cases), and leukopenia. The syndrome classically occurs in patients with long-standing disease, characterized by RF and ANA seropositivity and the presence of rheumatoid nodules and articular deformities, often in the context of minimal synovitis. In addition to rheumatoid nodules, these patients often have other extra-articular manifestations and are at an increased risk for bacterial infections and chronic nonhealing ulcers, leading to skin infections. The risk of bacterial infection is greatest in patients with more pronounced neutropenia (e.g., absolute neutrophil count [ANC] <100/mm3). Low serum complements may also be seen in Felty's

syndrome, with bone marrow biopsy typically yielding either normal or hyperplastic cell lines. In addition to associations with the HLA-DRB1 *0401 allele, Felty's syndrome is characterized by the presence of autoantibodies directed against citrullinated histones that bind to activated neutrophils and neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs).

Large granular lymphocyte (LGL) syndrome may also complicate the course of RA and may be related to Felty's syndrome. In addition to marked neutropenia, patients typically demonstrate expansion of LGL cells in both the blood and bone marrow, but splenomegaly is less common than in Felty's. LGL cells represent in vivo activated cytotoxic T cells (CTC) or natural killer (NK) cells, and they proportionally represent 85% (CTC) and 15% (NK) of LGL syndromes, respectively.81, LGL affects as many as 1% of patients with RA but is also seen in other inflammatory diseases (SLE, Sjögren's syndrome), viral infections, and hematologic malignancies (myelodysplastic syndrome). As opposed to aggressive and fatal subsets of LGL leukemia, the lymphocytosis associated with RA tends to follow an indolent course. In addition to rare malignant transformation (characterized by monoclonality), LGL places patients with RA at risk of infection. Although seemingly counterintuitive in the context of marked neutropenia, methotrexate remains the treatment of choice for both Felty's and LGL syndromes complicating RA. Other second-line therapies include cyclosporine, cyclophosphamide, glucocorticoids, and granulocyte colony-stimulating factor. Splenectomy is reserved for those patients with Felty's syndrome and documented splenomegaly who are recalcitrant to medical management.

### Malignancy

RA patients have a 10% higher risk of malignancy than the general population. The risk varies based on cancer type, with RA patients disproportionately afflicted by lymphoproliferative (particularly Hodgkin's disease and non-Hodgkin's lymphoma [NHL]), lung, and skin malignancies. As with assessing the etiology of other extra-articular manifestations, delineating the simultaneous contributions of underlying RA from the effect of immunosuppressive agents used to treat the disease is difficult. Lymphoma risk in RÅ appears to be closely associated with RA disease activity and severity, even in the absence of RA treatments. In a large case-control study involving more than 11,000 patients with RA (many of whom were treatment naive), those with higher levels of inflammation had a more pronounced risk of lymphoma, with an odds ratio of greater than 25 among those with the highest cumulative disease activity. Patients with Felty's syndrome had an approximate 12-fold risk for lymphoma compared with patients with RA without this extra-articular manifestation. In the absence of immunosuppressive therapy, RA results in the clonal expansion of CD5+ cells, decreases the number and function of T-suppressor lymphocytes and NK cells, and inhibits T-suppressor function directed against the prooncogenic Epstein— Barr virus (EBV), which are all potential contributing factors to an increased lymphoma risk in RA. These immunologic changes may also explain the general state of immunosuppression that characterizes RA even in the absence of immunomodulation therapy. Much less is understood regarding the mechanisms linking RA with other cancers, although higher serum cytokine expression was associated with an increased risk of lung and overall cancer incidence and mortality in a prospective RA cohort.86, Mounting evidence suggests that the immune system is closely involved with cancer neogenesis and progression through processes that

have been termed immunosurveillance and immunoediting; several cytokines well characterized in RA are also detected in the tumor microenvironment.

### Vasculitis

A smallto medium-vessel vasculitis can complicate the natural course of RA, a manifestation that is more common in men and associated with RF positivity (high titer), smoking, long-standing disease, and radiographic damage. Clinically, an important clue to the development of vasculitis is low serum complements with associated circulating immune complexes and cryoglobulins, along with the presence of other extra-articular manifestations, including subcutaneous nodules. Perhaps owing to improvements in treatment, the incidence of rheumatoid vasculitis has decreased substantially in recent years, with a study from a prospective vasculitis registry showing a greater than fivefold decline in incidence between 1990 and 2010.89

Rheumatoid vasculitis can present in a variety of ways, including:

Distal arteritis with splinter hemorrhages, nail-fold infarcts, and possible gangrene (Fig. 72.12)

Cutaneous ulceration, including pyoderma gangrenosum

Palpable epurpura

Peripheral neuropathy with either a mononeuritis multiplex or a sensory-related stocking-glove polyneuropathy

Coronary arteritis

Pulmonary capillaritis

Arteritis involving viscera, similar to polyarteritis nodosum (although lacking microaneurysms)

Rheumatoid pachymeningitis (rare), confined to the dura and pia matter

As with other forms of vasculitis, the signs and symptoms of systemic vasculitis in RA stem from vascular occlusion and resulting ischemic injury. Organ involvement is variable, with the skin and peripheral nervous system being the most frequently involved; involvement of the lungs, kidneys, gastrointestinal tract, and CNS is rare.
