Intestinal involvement typically manifests as abdominal pain with bowel infarction representing a surgical emergency. Digital gangrene, intestinal ischemia/infarction with bleeding or perforation, and mononeuritis multiplex are indicative of severe vasculitis and are associated with poor patient outcomes. With diagnostic biopsy or tissue resection, histopathology in rheumatoid vasculitis typically demonstrates a "panarteritis" with fibrinoid necrosis. Obliterative endarteritis can be seen with distal gangrene, with immune complex deposition in the involved vessels reported. As with other vasculitides, the treatment of rheumatoid vasculitis depends on the extent and severity of organ involvement. Conservative approaches, consisting of conventional disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs (DMARDs), can be used with splinter hemorrhage or palpable purpura in isolation, whereas more aggressive regimens, including high-dose glucocorticoids and cytotoxic therapies, should be reserved for organ-threatening involvement. Treatment success with biologic DMARDs, including TNF inhibitors and rituximab, has been reported. Prognosis remains relatively poor for rheumatoid vasculitis, with no improvement in survival over time and 5-year mortality in recent cohorts ranging from 26% to 50%.89,92

### Pulmonary

Pulmonary involvement in RA is relatively common, targeting the pleura, parenchyma, and airways. Although reported, pulmonary arterial hypertension appears to be relatively uncommon in RA.

Several risk factors are associated with pulmonary complications related to RA, but some of the most consistently identified include male sex, smoking, and autoantibody positivity.

Pleural Disease. Clinically apparent pleuritis affects approximately 5% of RA cases, whereas postmortem examination suggests this number is substantially higher, up to 70%. Pleural effusions can be large and result in symptomatic dyspnea. Pleural fluid analysis in RA typically reveals exudative fluid, with mixed cell counts (predominance of monocytes), high protein and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) levels, low glucose concentrations (resulting from a defect in the transport of glucose across the pleura), and low pH. Low pH and low fluid glucose (10 to 50 mg/dL) are highly characteristic of RA-related effusions, although these values can also be observed in infectious etiologies (particularly tuberculosis).

Interstitial Lung Disease. As the most over-represented cause of mortality in RA, interstitial lung disease (ILD) is perhaps the most serious form of pulmonary involvement in RA. Risk factors for the development of ILD include male sex, smoking, older age, autoantibody (ACPA and RF) positivity, and severe RA. The strongest genetic risk factor for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, a MUC5B promoter variant, was recently found to be highly associated with RA-ILD in a large, multiethnic study. Its frequency is highly variable across ethnic groups, but when present, it confers similar risk of developing ILD, and this is restricted to ILD in a usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP) pattern. ILD prevalence estimates vary widely across study populations with perhaps 10% of patients with RA having clinically apparent disease and

an additional 30% having subclinical parenchymal involvement. Variability in these prevalence estimates likely reflects important differences in methods of case ascertainment. The clinical course of ILD in RA is also highly variable, ranging from an asymptomatic and indolent course to rapidly progressive and life threatening in a minority of patients. On average, patients with RA complicated by ILD experience a 7-year reduction in median survival compared with RA patients without lung disease. In a cohort of 227 patients with RA-ILD, uncontrolled RA disease activity coupled with a forced vital capacity of <80% predicted was associated with an over fourfold increased risk of death. HRCT, more sensitive than chest radiography, typically demonstrates bibasilar reticular or reticulonodular patterns in both lung fields, with a characteristic honeycombing appearance and traction bronchiectasis in more advanced disease. Lung biopsy, which has traditionally been considered the gold standard for diagnosing ILD, is infrequently performed. This likely reflects the fact that HRCT findings correlate well with biopsy, HRCTs are less invasive, and immunomodulatory therapies are often initiated independent of the specific histopathology. UIP is the most common pattern seen on HRCT (Fig. 72.13), with biopsy results showing heterogenous fibrosis, fibroblastic foci, and lymphoid aggregates. This is in contrast to ILD encountered in the context of other connective tissue diseases, where nonspecific interstitial pneumonia (NSIP) is more frequent. NSIP, characterized on HRCT by ground-glass opacities without honeycombing, is the next most common pattern of ILD observed in RA. Even with limited disease, pulmonary function tests frequently reveal a decreased diffusion capacity with evidence of restrictive ventilator defects (e.g., diminished vital capacity) and lung volumes (e.g., total lung capacity) becoming evident with more extensive ILD.40,

Caplan's syndrome9 represents a rare complication of RA in which extra-articular ILD acts in concert with a pneumoconiosis (related to coal, silica, or asbestosis exposure) to produce a rapidly progressive obliterative granulomatous fibrotic syndrome. Lymphoid interstitial pneumonitis (LIP), a benign lymphoproliferative disorder of the lung, has been observed in patients with RA and Sjögren's syndrome. Characteristic HRCT findings of LIP include ground-glass changes accompanied by thickened bronchovascular bundles, small ill-defined pulmonary nodules, and scattered thin-walled cysts within the lung parenchyma in a perivascular or subpleural location. Consistent with a lymphoproliferative process, approximately 80% of patients with LIP have evidence of a polyclonal or monoclonal IgM gammopathy. Cryptogenic organizing pneumonia (COP; also known as idiopathic bronchiolitis obliterans with organizing pneumonia) is another rare pattern of ILD present in RA; it appears to be more responsive to immunosuppression than UIP. Complicating the evaluation of RA patients with parenchymal lung findings, most DMARDs used in the treatment of RA have been associated with drug-induced pneumonitis.

Obstructive Lung Disease. Although its links with restrictive lung disease have long been recognized, obstructive lung disease, and specifically chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), remains the leading cause of respiratory-related death in RA patients. In prior studies, obstructive lung diseases were over 50% more likely to develop in individuals with RA than in controls, even after adjusting for pertinent covariates, most importantly smoking. COPD is the most prevalent form of obstructive lung disease and was more closely linked with RA than asthma. Far less common than COPD and asthma, obliterative or constrictive bronchiolitis is an uncommon and severe

form of obstructive lung disease that results from inflammatory and fibrotic narrowing of the bronchioles, leading to respiratory failure and, in some cases, death. Pathologically, bronchiolitis is characterized by fibroblast proliferation, inflammatory infiltrates, concentric narrowing of the bronchial wall, and narrowing of the bronchiolar lumen.

Nodular Lung Disease. In addition to their appearance in subcutaneous tissues, rheumatoid nodules can develop in the pulmonary parenchyma, presenting either singly or in clusters, and may serve as a hallmark of Caplan's syndrome, as already detailed. Characterized by central necrosis, pulmonary nodules from RA can cavitate, leading to the formation of bronchopleural fistulas and rarely pneumothorax. Although a core needle biopsy can be used for evaluation, particularly in the context of a solitary pulmonary nodule, a more aggressive diagnostic strategy may be warranted when results are equivocal or the patient is otherwise deemed to be "high-risk," recognizing that pulmonary nodulosis and bronchogenic carcinoma coexist in RA. The importance of obtaining an adequate biopsy is emphasized by the fact that advanced imaging (positron emission tomography/ CT) may not accurately discriminate rheumatoid nodules from malignancy.

### Cardiovascular

Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is the leading cause of mortality in RA. In addition to associations with atherosclerosis and coronary artery disease, extra-articular cardiac manifestations also relate to cardiomyopathy, serositis, and valvulitis. CVD risk in RA patients appears to be beyond that explained by traditional CVD risk factors alone (such as hypertension, hyperlipidemia, diabetes) and results from the complex interaction of both traditional and RA-related risk factors (Fig. 72.14).106,

Atherosclerosis. Patients with RA are disproportionately affected by atherosclerotic CVD,105,108 including angina, myocardial infarction (MI), stroke, and the need for coronary revascularization. In a meta-analysis of observational studies including 41,490 patients, individuals with RA were found to be at a 48% higher risk of incident CVD events, with a pooled RR of 1.68 (95% CI, 1.40 to 2.03) specifically for MI and 1.41 (95% CI, 1.414 to 1.4) for cerebrovascular events. Additionally, a metaanalysis of 111,758 patients noted a 50% increase in CVD-related mortality, with a 52% increase in death from cerebrovascular disease as well as a 59% increase in death from ischemic heart disease among patients with RA compared with non-RA controls.

The premature atherosclerosis and resulting CVD risk observed appears to be a consequence of the systemic inflammatory burden posed by RA. Several studies have now demonstrated that greater levels of RA disease activity, including both ESR and CRP, are robust predictors of major adverse cardiovascular events. 109, These data underscore the importance of disease-remitting therapy not only to improve articular symptoms but to mitigate CVD risk through disease activity reduction, as well as potentially

beneficial direct pharmacologic effects that select therapies (e.g., methotrexate) may possess. 111-113 In addition to associations with higher acute phase responses, both RF114 and ACPA115 positivity are associated with increased CVD risk. Although mechanisms linking autoantibody status to CVD have not been well elucidated, recent data have shown that citrullinated autoantigens are expressed in atheromatous plaque. Moreover, ACPA targeting citrullinated forms of fibrinogen and vimentin are associated with aortic plaque burden in patients with RA. Beyond atherosclerotic plaque burden, coronary microvascular dysfunction (CMD) is an increasingly recognized cause of CVD morbidity in the general population and associated with higher levels of pro-inflammatory biomarkers including TNF, IL-6, and CRP. In a retrospective cohort of RA patients who underwent myocardial perfusion imaging, CMD was as prevalent in RA patients as diabetes and was associated with a more than twofold increased risk of all-cause and CVD-related mortality.

The relationship between dyslipidemia and CVD risk in RA is complex. Both quantitative and qualitative lipid changes have been characterized in the serum of RA patients. With active inflammation, low density lipoprotein (LDL) concentrations decline (the ratio of total cholesterol to LDL remains stable), perhaps explaining why lower LDL concentrations have been linked to higher CVD risk in RA, which has been termed the lipid paradox. Consequently, LDL concentrations may increase with improved disease control. Beyond serum concentrations, the functional capacity of HDL to regulate cholesterol efflux and serve as an antioxidant are impaired in the context of active RA and appears to improve with disease-modifying therapies. 119,

Heart Failure. A large, prospective study identified a twofold higher risk of heart failure (HF) among RA patients compared with individuals without RA. The heightened risk of HF in RA has been demonstrated independent of ischemic CVD and traditional CVD risk factors, implicating RA-related risk factors as mediators of HF in this population. 122, Indeed, higher RA disease activity and elevated measures of systemic inflammation were associated with increased risk of HF, in particular nonischemic HF, in two large RA cohorts.123, These findings are consistent with studies in non-RA populations supporting the role of systemic inflammation in the development of ventricular stiffening, diastolic dysfunction, and HF with preserved ejection fraction. In addition to a heightened risk of HF development, RA patients are at risk for poorer HF-related outcomes, including a nearly twofold increased risk of mortality in the year following a HF diagnosis.

Pericarditis. Pericarditis is the most common cardiac manifestation of RA and may be seen in as many as 50% of patients at autopsy. Clinically apparent disease is far less common, with cardiac tamponade serving as a rare consequence. With RA involvement, pericardial fluid demonstrates findings similar to that described with RA-related pleuritis; an exudative sample characterized by cellular infiltrate, high protein and LDH concentrations, and low glucose and low pH levels. Rarely, constrictive pericarditis can complicate the course of RA and may require pericardiectomy or pericardial stripping for definitive treatment.

Myocarditis. Myocarditis is rare but may be related to granulomatous disease or interstitial myocarditis. The granulomatous process, when present, pathologically resembles rheumatoid nodules and is highly specific for RA.

Conduction Defects. Atrioventricular (AV) block is an unusual complication of RA but if present is probably related to direct granulomatous involvement. Complete heart block has been described and is also more common in patients with seropositive nodular disease. Because RA is a chronic inflammatory process, patients with long-standing, poorly controlled disease are at risk for amyloidosis, which can result in both cardiomyopathy and conduction disturbances.

Endocardial Inflammation and Granulomatous Aortitis. Cross-sectional echocardiographic studies have demonstrated a high prevalence of aortic and mitral valve abnormalities in RA, including calcifications, thickening, and nodular involvement. 128, While the epidemiologic burden of valvular disease in RA has been infrequently studied, a 75% increased risk of valvular heart disease-related death was recently observed in a national RA cohort. In severe RA, granulomatous disease of the endocardium can spread to the base of the aorta, resulting in aortitis and valvular incompetency, which can rarely necessitate emergent valve replacement.

### Neurologic

Most commonly, neurologic disease in RA is a result of local compression, such as carpal tunnel syndrome and atlanto-axial instability with cervical myelopathy (see section on "Articular Manifestations"). Noncompressive involvement of the central and peripheral nervous system can develop, although rarely as a direct result of RA. In a case-control study examining the risk of inflammatory CNS events with prior exposure to TNF inhibitors, RA was associated with a higher risk for both demyelinating and nondemyelinating CNS events with TNF exposure compared with other autoimmune diseases including ankylosing spondylitis, psoriatic arthritis, psoriasis, and inflammatory bowel disease. Cases

of rheumatoid pachymeningitis have been described, presenting as an aseptic meningitis with plasma cells and rheumatoid nodules on meningeal biopsy. In addition, cognitive impairment and dementia are over-represented in patients with RA. Beyond traditionally recognized risk factors, such as hypertension, CVD, depression and anxiety, more active RA may additionally increase the risk of incident dementia.

### Disease Outcomes and Prognosis

### Disease Outcomes

Because of its systemic and polyarticular nature, RA can negatively affect physical functioning and health-related quality of life. Compared with individuals without arthritis, patients with RA in one study were 36% more likely to report fair or poor general health, twice as likely to report a health-related activity limitation, and almost 30% more likely to require assistance with personal care. Likely reflecting the strain that living with a chronic disease renders, impaired quality of life as a consequence of RA is not limited to physical health domains but also encompasses mental health domains. In a long-term study of RA patients with disease onset less than 1 year from enrollment, 39% were unable to work after just 10 years of follow-up. Rates of work disability were highest among older patients, those with lower education, manual laborers, and those reporting more baseline physical impairment. Altogether, with the prevalence of RA increasing in an aging population, disability-adjusted life-years related to RA have increased. Correspondingly, RA-related expenditures in the United States are staggering. In 2013 alone, related health care costs were estimated to have exceeded $10 billion, and societal costs approached $45 billion.137, In addition to detrimental effects on physical functioning and quality of life, RA portends an increased risk of premature mortality. In a meta-analysis of eight studies of RA patients within 2 years of disease onset at the start of follow-up, a pooled standardized mortality ratio (SMR) of 1.48 (95% CI, 1.19 to 1.83) was estimated.

### Prognosis

Several factors have been associated with poor outcomes in RA including reduced survival and increases in disability, related health care costs, the accrual in structural joint damage, and the need for total joint arthroplasty. Some of the factors that have been associated with poor outcomes include:

Autoantibody (RF and ACPA) status 140-142

Measures indicative of greater disease activity and poorer functional status at baseline 102,

Extra-articular disease 140

Disease duration 142

Diagnostic and treatment delays 143

HLA-DRB1 shared epitope status 144

Cigarette smoking and heavy alcohol use 140,

Occupational factors and socioeconomic status 136

Erosive disease 144

Comorbid illnesses, including depression, post-traumatic stress disorder, and others 140,

Altered body composition, namely sarcopenia and excess adiposity 76,

Older age 102

Select medication use (glucocorticoids worsened survival, and methotrexate improved survival) 102,

Past ACR treatment guidelines have "risk-stratified" patients based on characteristics such as RF or ACPA positivity or the

presence of radiographic erosions. It is important to recognize, however, that although these factors may be statistically correlated with select outcomes in RA, none of them (either alone or in combination) have been demonstrated to provide robust predictions of any outcome at the level of the individual patient.

### Temporal Trends in Outcomes

The landscape of RA has dramatically changed over the last three decades. With earlier diagnosis and treatment, aggressive treatment to a target of disease remission or minimal disease activity, and expanding therapeutic choices, many patient outcomes have dramatically improved. RA patients are more likely to achieve treatment targets (low disease activity or remission) and have improved functional status and quality of life. Occurrence of extra-articular disease manifestations and rates of joint replacement and hospitalization are declining. Despite these improvements and favorable trends in all-cause mortality, the gap in mortality rates for specific causes of death between RA patients and the general population has not been consistently narrowing. Patients with RA continue to experience a heightened risk of allcause, respiratory, and CVD-related mortality, with nearly 70% of excess deaths attributable to cardiopulmonary disease. Additional surveillance of RA patients with disease onset in the current era will be needed to determine whether improvements in mortality rates are on the horizon.

# Treatment of Rheumatoid Arthritis

BRYANT R. ENGLAND AND JAMES R. O'DELL

### KEY POINTS

### Introduction

The treatment of rheumatoid arthritis (RA) has evolved dramatically during the past 30 years, perhaps more so than for any of the other rheumatic diseases. The majority of patients newly diagnosed with RA who have access to health care and medications can expect to experience remission or low disease activity if they are treated early by a skilled rheumatologist. This expected

outcome is truly remarkable, and it is appropriate to take a step back and examine the reasons behind this sea change. Biologic agents, which became available in 1998, are very effective, and importantly, they have helped invigorate clinicians and patients alike, making both parties believe that higher expectations regarding control of RA are justified. However, it is critical to acknowledge all the other changes that occurred in roughly that same period and that have been universally embraced by rheumatologists (Table 73.1). It is difficult, if not impossible, to know which of these changes are most important. Early diagnosis aided by use of anti-citrullinated protein antibodies (ACPAs) and the recent American College of Rheumatology (ACR)/European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology (EULAR) RA classification criteria are critical. The universal acknowledgment that all patients with RA should be treated with a disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drug (DMARD)2,3 and the effective use of methotrexate (MTX) with folic acid have also played huge roles. In the mid- 1990s, the use of combination DMARDs became an accepted strategy. Together, the early diagnosis, effective use of MTX and combination DMARDs, and biologic agents are the tools that allow rheumatologists to successfully manage RA (Table 73.2). The development and periodic updating of evidence-based clinical practice guidelines by the ACR and EULAR over the past three decades has provided clinicians guidance on the use of these tools.2,

Treat to target (T2T) defines the scope of work and job of rheumatologists. T2T is arguably one of the most important factors in improved outcomes in RA. The Tight Intensive Control of RA (TICORA) trial (see later) was the seminal study that put T2T on the map because it dramatically illustrated the benefits of this approach. The TICORA trial demonstrated that if patients are treated aggressively to achieve remission or low disease activity, the outcomes improve significantly both clinically and radiographically, with or without the use of biologic agents. Similarly, in the Dutch Behandel-Strategieen (BeSt) study, the aggressive use of therapeutic adjustment (i.e., T2T) led to significant clinical improvement regardless of the initial choice of DMARDs, which included both biologic agents and conventional regimens. Therefore the most important tenet of successful RA therapy today is not which of the many DMARDs, conventional or biologic, are used (see Table 73.2), but that all patients are treated to meet the disease activity target. In short, this treatment strategy is more important than individual medication choices.

In this chapter the following topics are discussed: the overarching principles of treatment, the goals of RA therapy, the timing of different therapies, and the strategies of using all the tools in the toolbox for each unique patient. Most of the medications themselves are not covered in detail here; rather, this chapter focuses on strategies. Please refer to the many other excellent chapters in this book for specific information on therapeutic targeting of prostenoid (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs [NSAIDs]; Chapter 59), glucocorticoids (Chapter 60), traditional DMARDs (Chapter 61), MTX and combinations (Chapter 61), immunosuppressive drugs (Chapter 62), anti-cytokine therapies or biologic agents (Chapters 63 and 64), and Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitors (Chapter 65).

### Goal of Rheumatoid Arthritis Treatment

Many RA disease activity measures have been proposed, ,7-13all of which are composite measures that include information derived from some combination of joint examinations, patient and physician assessment of disease activity, patient function, and/or laboratory measures of inflammation (erythrocyte sedimentation rate [ESR] or C-reactive protein [CRP] levels). The ACR has endorsed a list of disease activity measures for regular use that possess the best psychometric properties and feasibility (see Table 73.3). Each of these measures has strengths and weaknesses; some rely only on data from the patient, some require complete joint counts by clinicians, and some require laboratory tests to measure inflammation. Busy clinicians rarely have time to document disease activity in more than 60 tender and swollen joints or wait for laboratory test results to make treatment decisions during a patient's visit. Therefore measures that simplify this process as much as possible are being embraced, including measures that limit the joints that are examined to 28, do not require laboratory tests, or are entirely dependent on patient-reported data. These measures frequently correlate, and treatment guided by different measures has produced largely comparable results. Thus, currently in the clinic it is very important that disease activity be regularly measured and far less important which of these measures is used. This sentiment is shared by health care payers, with regular RA disease activity assessment being a quality measure in the meritbased incentive payment system in the United States.

Because none of our therapies cure RA, it would seem obvious that the next best goal should be remission. However, the concept of remission as a goal for patients with RA is problematic. First, a definition of remission that is both relevant and practical has been elusive. To be relevant, remission should be highly predictive of the absence of disease progression over time, not just in the joints but systemically, including, but not limited to, vascular damage. To be practical for clinicians, a definition of remission should be easy to apply in real time to patients seen in the clinic. A provisional definition of remission for use in clinical trials was developed by a joint ACR/EULAR effort, rigorously tested against short-term radiologic outcomes in 1to 2-year randomized controlled trials (RCTs). This definition, termed Boolean 1.0, and proposed index-based definitions standardized remission and were a huge step forward for reporting and comparing results across clinical trials. However, the Boolean 1.0 definition was designed for clinical trials and not for clinical care, where rigorous counts of joints with disease activity are not always performed, the need to have CRP results in real time becomes a major problem for clinical workflow, and comorbid conditions such as osteoarthritis, fibromyalgia, and mental health disorders may influence components of these definitions (e.g., patient global assessment). Recognizing the latter, ACR/EULAR recently revised the definition by

increasing the threshold of patient global assessment from 1.0 to 2.0 cm on a 0 to 10 cm visual analogue scale. This Boolean 2.0 definition (Table 73.4) has improved agreement with endorsed index-based remission definitions (Clinical Disease Activity Index and Simplified Disease Activity Index) while retaining its performance predicting radiographic nonprogression and functional outcomes in RCTs.

Perhaps more problematic is that many people who believe that remission is defined by clinical data alone will always underestimate the amount of low-level disease activity that could be found if synovial biopsies or advanced imaging techniques such as ultrasound or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) were used. Significant data indicate that many, perhaps most patients with RA who meet the definitions of "remission" are found to have active disease when they are assessed by ultrasound or MRI.18- 20 For example, in a substudy of the Treatment of Early Aggressive Rheumatoid (TEAR) trial (discussed later), it was reported that all patients believed to be in clinical remission had evidence of joint inflammation on MRI scans of the wrist. Indeed, the ACR/EULAR definition allows for a swollen joint, which many people would argue is not really full clinical remission. Another major problem with the term remission is that, according to currently available data, it is not clear that remission, regardless of how it is defined, should be the treatment goal for all patients with RA. Many patients do very well despite having low levels of disease activity. The following important question remains unanswered in RA: Where is the tipping point between pushing the disease activity ever lower and the toxicity and cost of doing so? To further complicate matters, it is almost guaranteed that the tipping point will be different for each patient. The following issues need to be considered:

When do the risks and considerable expense of some of our RA therapies outweigh the benefits of escalating therapy?

Which patients who have improved dramatically but still have two tender or swollen joints need to switch to another medication? How should this decision differ when patients have been treated with one or two conventional DMARDs compared with multiple biologic agents?

Which patients with RA are most at risk for toxicities if we push too hard for remission?

In real-world treatment settings where RA patients are frequently multimorbid, how do we accurately identify the patients in low or moderate disease activity based on composite indices with treatment-amendable disease?

Finally, with current therapies, the vast majority of patients achieving remission require ongoing treatment with DMARDs, so the concept of drug-free remission—meaning one where no therapy is required—remains beyond our current reach.

Despite the problems in defining remission or low disease activity, it is clear that patients do better when clinicians have a goal. The Scottish TICORA study5 was the first to convincingly demonstrate this concept in a randomized fashion and, therefore, remains the standard over 15 years later. In this study, patients who had disease for fewer than 5 years were randomized to receive either routine care or intensive care. Both groups were treated with an algorithm of conventional DMARDs (Fig. 73.1A).

The routine care group had regular follow-up and monitoring, whereas the intensive group was seen monthly and underwent protocolized escalation of therapy if they had not achieved the goal of low disease activity (defined in this study as a Disease Activity Score [DAS] of ≤2.4). Both groups improved significantly, but the T2T group (i.e., the intensive group) did significantly better, with mean DASs (1.6) in the remission range at 18 months (Fig. 73.1B). In the intensive group, 71% of subjects achieved an ACR 70% composite improvement (ACR70) compared with 18% in the routine care group (p < 0.0001). Furthermore, this clinical improvement translated to significantly less radiographic progression of erosions compared with the routine care group (0.5 vs. 3.0 for median erosion score; p = 0.002). Importantly, this improved disease control was not associated with an increase in treatment-associated adverse events. Finally, although it entailed more frequent visits, intensive therapy resulted in a cost savings even in the short term. These results were particularly remarkable considering that they were obtained using conventional DMARDs alone (see Fig. 73.1A). Findings from other studies have corroborated these findings. 6, Furthermore, a meta-analysis of tight control strategies23 has suggested these strategies work best if they are performed according to a protocol, as occurred in the TICORA study.

Although the TICORA investigators selected low disease activity as the target, the target could have been remission, as was previously discussed. Most of the aforementioned measures of disease activity have defined levels that signify "remission" (see Table 73.3). Predictably, the harder clinicians push for remission with increasing numbers and higher doses of DMARDs, the more that the toxicity and expense (Table 73.5) become a concern. Both the ACR and EULAR guidelines,2,3 state that low disease activity or remission is the goal and leave the decision about which goal is most appropriate for each unique patient's situation to the clinician. Therefore until further data elucidate this question, clinicians will need to continue to practice both the art and the science of medicine when selecting the most appropriate target for each patient. This approach could be thought of as T2T witbin reason, not at all costs.

### Classes of Medications

### Disease-Modifying gAnti-rheumatic Drugs

DMARDs have the ability to change the course of RA for the better. The most rigorous application of this definition requires RCTs to show that a DMARD has the ability not only to change the clinical course of the disease but also to decrease or halt radiographic progression. By this definition, all of the nine conventional DMARDs, at least two JAK inhibitors approved for use, and the 10 biologic DMARDs listed in Table 73.2 qualify, with the possible exception of minocycline and hydroxychloroquine (HCQ), for which the few small studies that address this can only suggest radiographic benefits. When the DMARDs listed in Table 73.2 are used individually or in combinations of two, three, or four, as is often the case, 10,641 possible combinations exist for each individual patient, assuming that biologic and JAK agents are not used in combination. Obviously, this huge number of choices is both good and bad news; it is great to have all the options but impossible to keep them all straight or try them in individual patients. Therefore to use all these

medications effectively, the clinician must have goals, strategies, and an up-to-date knowledge of the medications and their interactions, toxicities, and unique niches.

### Conventional Disease-Modifying Anti-rheumatic Drugs

The most widely used conventional DMARDs—MTX, sulfasalazine (SSZ), HCQ, and leflunomide (LEF)—are discussed in detail in Chapter 61. Together, these four DMARDs, along with glucocorticoids (see Chapter 60), currently account for the vast majority of conventional DMARD use. New medications in this arena are tofacitinib, baricitinib, and upadacitinib, with several more on the way (see Chapter 65); their role in the treatment of RA is discussed later. Although less commonly used, azathioprine (AZA), cyclosporine (CSA), and the tetracyclines (minocycline and doxycycline) remain important as niche therapies. They are not covered elsewhere in this book and thus are discussed later in this chapter.

### Biologic Disease-Modifying Anti-rheumatic Drugs

The biologic DMARDs are discussed in detail in Chapters 63 and 64. Within this class of agents we now have the ability to inhibit multiple inflammatory cytokines, including TNF, which is inhibited with three monoclonal antibodies, infliximab, adalimumab, and golimumab; the TNF receptor protein, etanercept (ETAN); the pegylated Fab fragment certolizumab, which also binds TNF; interleukin (IL)-1, which is bound with the IL-1 receptor antagonist anakinra; and IL-6, which is inhibited by the monoclonal antibodies to the IL-6 receptor, tocilizumab or sarilumab. We also have the ability to kill or inhibit cell lines important in inflammation, including B cells (with rituximab) and T cells (with abatacept). Biologic agents are key advances that changed the landscape of RA therapy in terms of therapeutic expectations and the understanding of RA pathogenesis. Because of their often rapid onset of action, particularly with the TNF and IL-6 inhibitors, and their ability to retard radiographic progression of disease, they are increasingly used earlier and more often in people with RA. Arguably, all the biologic agents work better with concomitant use of MTX, and this phenomenon is particularly true of the TNF inhibitors. One reason for the increased efficacy of TNF inhibitors with concomitant use of MTX is the ability of MTX to prevent the formation of antidrug antibodies. The challenge for clinicians is to appropriately utilize conventional and biologic therapies—escalating to biologic agents when necessary but ensuring that much less expensive but very effective conventional therapies are first optimized.

### Glucocorticoids

Glucocorticoids, discussed in detail in Chapter 60, have a long and storied history in the treatment of RA. Several landmark studies have proven not only clinical efficacy24-28 but also the significant radiographic efficacy of glucocorticoids.26, The Combinatietherapie Bij Reumatoide Artritis (COBRA) trial25,26 and the COBRA arm of the BeSt study (discussed later6,22) again demonstrated the significant clinical and radiographic benefit that glucocorticoids can provide. However, despite their rapid onset and other positive benefits of glucocorticoids in RA, their toxicities are also abundant.

Currently glucocorticoids are most often used along with DMARDs as part of initial "induction" therapy to gain rapid control of RA, and then they are aggressively tapered as the sloweracting DMARD begins to take effect. While glucocorticoid-aided induction clearly hastens improvement, it may complicate the assessment of therapeutic response to other agents and whether

better disease-related outcomes such as disease activity and radiographic progression result over longer periods of follow-up (e.g., >12 months) remains unsettled.27, Historically, the belief has been that once a patient with RA began taking glucocorticoids, the patient would never be able to stop using them. This scenario is clearly no longer true with the effective DMARDs that are now available; successful tapering of glucocorticoids is now the rule.6, The inability to taper glucocorticoids successfully is a strong indication that the current DMARD regimen is not working and should be modified. Unfortunately, the optimal glucocorticoid tapering strategy is unknown and, in real-world settings tapering off them may take 2 to 5 years. Long-term use of glucocorticoids at doses of greater than 5 to 7.5 mg per day (prednisone equivalent) is a clear indication that DMARD therapy needs to be escalated, but emerging evidence suggests glucocorticoid risks also occur at prednisone doses <5 mg per day and with short-term 33, Importantly, glucocorticoids should almost never be use. used to treat RA without concomitant use of DMARDs, with the ultimate goal of maintaining patients in remission or low disease activity without glucocorticoids.

### Other Conventional Disease-Modifying Anti-rheumatic Drugs

Azathioprine. AZA, 50 to 200 mg/day, has been used to treat RA for more than 50 years. Although clearly it is not a first-line DMARD in contemporary RA treatment, AZA is most commonly used as a substitute for MTX when contraindications or intolerance to it exist. This situation most commonly arises in patients with the so-called "MTX flu," but other situations—including pregnancy, MTX nodulosis, and liver, pulmonary, or renal disease—may be indications for use of AZA in people with RA. A particularly problematic patient population is patients with RA, frequently male, who have RA-associated interstitial lung disease (ILD). Clinicians may be reluctant to use MTX and/or LEF, so AZA more frequently becomes the conventional DMARD of choice.

Neutropenia is the most common complication of AZA treatment. Neutropenia can be predicted with a genetic test for polymorphisms of the enzyme thiopurine methyltransferase. Patients who are homozygous for the mutant polymorphism that is nonfunctional (1 in 300 or 0.3% of patients) are very sensitive to bone marrow and other toxicities of AZA. Patients who are heterozygotes (≈10% of the population) may have milder neutropenia. Unfortunately, this test is expensive; in some centers it may cost more than $1000, and reimbursement is not always assured. Some clinicians elect to start with low doses of 50 mg/day, check complete blood cell counts at 2 weeks, and then increase the dose as needed if the white blood cell count is acceptable. It has been speculated that the subset of patients with the rare nonfunctional polymorphisms could be the patients who, when AZA was added to a stable MTX regimen, experienced an acute febrile toxic reaction characterized by fever, leukocytosis, and a cutaneous leukocytoclastic vasculitis.

Cyclosporine. In the 1990s, CSA, mostly used in transplantation to prevent allograft rejection, gained a foothold in the treatment of RA. Interest in CSA peaked when studies showed that the addition of CSA (2.5 to 5 mg/kg/day) to a stable dose of MTX provided substantial additive benefit compared with MTX alone (Fig. 73.2). Moreover, this therapy seemed to slow radiographic progression. Unfortunately, follow-up reports revealed that only 22% of patients continued taking this combination at 18 months, with the most common reason for discontinuation being hypertension or increased creatinine levels.

### Minocycline and Doxycycline

Tetracycline and its derivatives have a long and somewhat checkered history with regard to the treatment of RA and other arthritides.40, They are not mainstream therapy for RA but have a niche in patients for whom laboratory monitoring is not feasible, in those with frequent infections, or in patients who have concomitant periodontal disease. The mechanism of action (MOA) of tetracyclines in RA is poorly understood. Tetracyclines are, of course, antibiotics, but they also inhibit metalloproteinases, modulate immune responses, and have anti-inflammatory effects. Given in a dose of 100 mg twice daily, moderate, statistically significant improvement in clinical parameters of disease activity was found in patients with established RA who were treated with minocycline compared with placebo.42, Findings in the treatment of early-stage, seropositive RA have similarly demonstrated improvement in clinical measures and the ability to taper glucocorticoids.28, Although doxycycline is less frequently studied, a trial of patients with early RA found doxycycline plus MTX was superior to MTX alone. Potential adverse effects of tetracyclines include lightheadedness, vertigo, rare liver toxicity, lupus-like syndromes, and, with longer-term use, cutaneous hyperpigmentation.46, Hyperpigmentation may, but does not always, resolve with discontinuation of minocycline and occurs much less commonly, if at all, with doxycycline.

### Nonsteroidal Anti-inflammatory Drugs

NSAIDs, including salicylates, which are covered in detail in Chapter 59, have been a ubiquitous part of RA treatment for more than a century. During the past several decades, as toxicities (particularly gastrointestinal [GI],48,49 cardiovascular, 50,51 and renal52,53) have become apparent and our DMARDs have become more effective and abundant, the use of NSAIDs, fortunately, has been declining. The cardiovascular toxicities, which are now known to be strongly associated not only with the cyclooxygenase-2-specific NSAIDs but essentially with all NSAIDs, have been particularly concerning in RA patient populations in which the excess mortality is largely due to accelerated cardiovascular disease. As with glucocorticoids, NSAIDs should rarely be used without concomitant use of DMARDs, and the goal should be to taper their use as soon as possible to avoid GI and cardiovascular toxicities.

### Historical Treatments

Gold salts, used in the treatment of RA for more than a century, are an effective therapy, particularly if used intramuscularly, 54-56 but it is cumbersome to administer, has less efficacy than many other available agents, and has a narrow therapeutic window. Similarly, penicillamine is of historical interest but is rarely used. These therapies are not discussed further in this chapter.

### Treatment Approaches and Strategies

As previously detailed, the goal of treatment for all patients with RA is remission or at least low disease activity. Other than toxicity concerns and expense, clinicians should not focus on which DMARD or combination of DMARDs is used in an individual patient but should focus on getting patients to the disease activity target with whatever DMARDs achieve that goal. There is no evidence-based correct DMARD or combination of DMARDs that is right for all patients. Each patient presents a unique challenge and comes with unique expectations, biases, disease activity level, damage burden, comorbidities, and, in many countries, health care coverage issues. One of the most important areas of investigation in RA is to identify parameters that will predict which patient will respond to which therapy. Several studies have suggested that factors such as serologic status, 58 human leukocyte antigenDRB1 haplotypes,59 and a variety of findings in synovial tissue60-63 are statistically associated with responses to therapy. This is a highly active area of investigation, but no clear-cut answers that are applicable to routine clinical care have emerged yet.

Some investigators have suggested that treatment should be different for patients with RA who have a good prognosis versus poor prognosis. This concept is problematic because separating patients into those who have a good versus a poor prognosis is difficult. Although some data suggest that certain features are associated with worse prognosis (Table 73.6), unfortunately, no data exist that suggest that stratifying our therapies based on prognosis at the individual patient level yields better outcomes. These prognostic factors are primarily disease-centric, identifying patients most likely to have treatment nonresponse or radiographic progression. However, equally as important when selecting therapies are the therapy-related toxicity prognostic factors, such as the potentially disease-unrelated risk factors for infections (e.g., age, comorbidities, and vaccination status, among others). Most patients who meet the criteria for classification of RA in the clinic, and essentially all those included in clinical trials, have poor-prognosis RA, with several of the factors listed in Table 73.6. Regardless of the prognostic factors, the goal for each individual patient is to achieve at least a low level of disease activity. Until, or unless, predictive parameters are identified, rheumatologists will out of necessity continue to use their clinical judgment at the individual patient level.

Without parameters or biomarkers that differentially predict responses to DMARDs in terms of efficacy or toxicity, one approach to treatment decisions is illustrated in Fig. 73.3. Note that several "spins" of the wheel may be required when combinations are needed. Fig. 73.3 dramatically illustrates that we currently do not have these much-needed predictive parameters. The figure also emphasizes that if we hope to treat RA in a rational, scientific way, it is critical that we find these parameters, and it highlights and reinforces the need to include biobanks with all of our clinical trials, particularly comparative effectiveness trials. Treatment of RA in specific patient populations is discussed in the following sections.

### Treatment of the Disease-Modifying Anti-rheumatic Drug-Naive e Patient

The most important principle of treating RA effectively is to initiate and rapidly advance DMARD therapy as early as possible. Although this principle is universally accepted, a paucity

### TABLE Factors Associated With Poorer Prognosis in 73.6 Rheumatoid Arthritis

of rigorous data directly addresses this point. Few randomized, double-blind trials have been conducted in which patients are randomized to early treatment versus delayed treatment,64-68 and it is very unlikely, not to mention unethical, that any more will be forthcoming. Rather, we accept this foundational principle based on the common and firm belief that treating patients early prevents damage and deformity and preserves function.

Strong, credible evidence to support this central tenet comes from cohort studies of early versus delayed therapy,66 randomized studies of intensive therapy versus usual care, RCTs of combi- ,6,22,25,69-73and, finally, studies of prenation versus monotherapy, clinical RA. One cohort study of note reported on patients who

had recently received a diagnosis of RA. The first cohort received DMARD therapy early (a mean of 123 days after diagnosis), whereas the second cohort received DMARDs very early (a mean of 15 days after diagnosis). The cohort initiating treatment later had significantly more radiographic damage at 2 years and, importantly, continued to have radiographic progression, unlike the early treatment cohort. The findings of the TICORA trial (previously detailed) clearly show the advantages of better disease control with earlier treatment.

Multiple studies in early-stage RA have demonstrated that when groups of patients are compared, those that receive combinations of therapy fare better than those that receive monotherapy. 6, Some early examples of these studies are COBRA, with the combination of MTX, SSZ, and prednisolone versus SSZ alone26; the Finnish Rheumatoid Arthritis Combination Therapy (FIN-RACo) trial,71 with the combination of MTX, SSZ, HCQ, and prednisone versus SSZ; the BeSt study, with the multiple combinations compared with step-ups or switches6,22; the Anti-TNF Trial in Rheumatoid Arthritis with Concomitant Therapy (ATTRACT),70 with the combination of infliximab and MTX versus MTX alone; and the PREMIER study, with the combination of adalimumab and MTX versus each alone. In all these trials and many others, the combinations outperformed monotherapy. However, as discussed in a subsequent section of this chapter, it does not follow that all patients need combination therapy initially.

The new ACR/EULAR RA classification criteria,1 discussed in detail in Chapter 72, allow us to classify patients with RA earlier for clinical trials but also have supported earlier diagnosis and treatment. The previous absolute requirement that all patients must have certain features for a minimum of 6 weeks has been removed. The 6-week threshold still is acknowledged as important but is no longer required, and many patients (perhaps most patients), particularly with poor prognostic features, will fulfill criteria before 6 weeks. Importantly, the presence of ACPA, particularly in a higher titer, is weighed heavily in the new criteria.

### Initial Therapy: The First Disease-Modifying Anti-rheumatic Drug

Upon accepting the premise that DMARD therapy should be started as early as possible, we must then ask which DMARD should be initiated and whether we should begin with monotherapy or combination DMARD therapies. Although many of the previously cited studies have shown that combinations outperform monotherapy in RCTs, this does not mean that initial combination therapy should be the standard approach for all patients in the clinic. Most clinicians initially start with DMARD monotherapy; the evidence to support this approach is discussed in a subsequent section of this chapter and is strongly validated by the TEAR trial73 and the subanalysis of patients treated only with MTX from this trial. The decision of which DMARD to initiate at the individual patient level is complex, and at this time it is clear that no one right answer exists for all patients and all clinical situations (Fig. 73.3)—one size, or in this case one DMARD, clearly does not fit all. Many factors need to be considered, including but not limited to the patient's disease activity, comorbidities, and preference, the relative expense to the patient and to the health care system (weighing the benefits and including direct and indirect costs in our thinking), and importantly, when relevant, the desire of the patient (both female and male) to conceive. Until or unless parameters become available that accurately and reliably guide selection, this complicated decision will still require the clinician's best judgment.

Given all these factors, MTX should be the initial DMARD prescribed for the vast majority of patients. It is inexpensive (see Table 73.5), effective, well tolerated, improves longevity, 75,76 and, importantly, is the cornerstone of most successful combination therapies (see Fig. 73.2). MTX is perhaps our most effective therapy, and in head-to-head comparison it has been as effective or more effective than all conventional and biologic therapies. The possible exception to this is in trials where MTX was used suboptimally (maximal 20 mg/week and only administered orally) and optimal dosing of the JAK inhibitors has shown superior efficacy. Furthermore, anti-TNF therapy with all the currently available agents is much more effective with MTX on board in terms of clinical and radiographic outcomes (see Chapter 61 on MTX).70, MTX is usually administered orally at first, although subcutaneous (SC) dosing has more predictable bioavailability (Fig. 73.4) and is better tolerated. In most cases, the dose should be pushed to 25 mg/week, if necessary, to control disease unless contraindications or tolerance problems exist. Most studies have shown that maximum efficacy takes up to 6 months but that in most situations the response at 3 months predicts ultimate success.

The bioavailability of oral MTX starts to plateau at doses of 15 to 20 mg/week (see Fig. 73.4); therefore if acceptable efficacy has not been achieved with a single weekly dose of MTX, two options exist. The first option, splitting the weekly dose of MTX into two doses taken 4 to 12 hours apart on the day MTX is taken, improves efficacy, presumably because of better absorption. The best strategy is to switch to SC MTX. MTX bioavailability and clinical response clearly improve if MTX is given SC.80, Some investigators have suggested that SC MTX, 25 mg/week, be initiated in all patients, but this promising approach will require further study. No data are available to compare split oral dosing to SC MTX. If MTX is optimally used, approximately 60% of patients will have a good response and, according to consistent data from several trials where MTX was only used at a maximum of 20 mg/week orally, 30% will achieve low disease activity status5,6,73,83 and will not require additional therapy.

Unfortunately, MTX dosing is generally not optimized in the United States. A recent study that covered 272 million patients found 35,000 newly diagnosed RA patients in 2012 for which 2-year follow-up was available. In these newly diagnosed RA patients, 25% received biologics before being treated with MTX. When MTX was used, the mean dose of MTX before adding or switching to a biologic was 15.3 mg, and the median time to this change was less than 3 months. Furthermore, only 7% of patients

received SC MTX before a biologic. Rheumatologists need to rethink their therapeutic algorithms (see later) for the benefit of our patients and health care systems. The most recent ACR treatment guidelines provide recommendations on the administration of MTX that hopefully will aid clinicians and patients in optimizing the use of this anchor therapy. Key principles for optimizing initial treatment with MTX include:

Start MTX at doses of ≥15 mg/week, unless contraindications exist.

Quickly escalate MTX to doses of 20 to 25 mg/week if treatment target is not achieved.

Utilize SC administration or split oral dosing when needing MTX at doses of ≥17.5 mg/week.

Co-administer folic acid to increase tolerability and increase folic acid dose if MTX tolerance side effects are occurring.

### Initiating Treatment With a Single Disease-Modifying Anti-rheumatic Drug g Versus Combinations of Disease-Modifying Anti-rheumatic Drugs

Although most clinicians still favor starting treatment with monotherapy, combination DMARD therapy has clearly changed the treatment of RA forever. In the early 1990s, the treatment model called for individual DMARDs and then, when necessary, switching to a different DMARD. At that time, combinations of DMARDs were not used. Studies published in the mid-1990s showing the impressive efficacy and tolerability of various combinations of DMARDs dramatically changed the treatment paradigm.4, Now, the majority of patients with RA are treated with combinations of two, three, or more DMARDs. The study that put combination DMARD therapy on the map was the so-called triple therapy study by the RAIN group of investigators. This study clearly demonstrated that the triple combination of MTX, HCQ, and SSZ was significantly more effective than MTX alone or the combination of HCQ and SSZ. Importantly, this combination of DMARDs did not lead to an increase in toxicity. Multiple publications on this and other successful combinations of conventional DMARDs soon followed.23,

Today the important question of whether treatment of all patients should start with combinations of DMARDs that are then stepped down (i.e., tapered) or whether monotherapy should be used initially and then stepped up only if patients are not at target is an ongoing debate. Both approaches have their supporters, and data can be presented to support both sides. On the one hand, there is no doubt that if short-term responses are examined in groups of patients, combinations outperform monotherapy. This is true for combinations of conventional DMARDs25,69,71 and combinations of conventional DMARDs with a biologic agent. On the other hand, the strategy of initial monotherapy with step-ups only in the patients who need it was clearly effective in the TICORA study (as previously discussed5) and, importantly, in the BeSt6,22 and TEAR73,74 trials; although initial responses were better in both of the latter trials in the clinical parameters of patients initially treated with combination therapy, all groups in both the BeSt and TEAR trials had identical DAS or DAS28 scores at the end of 2 years. Clinicians do not treat groups of patients but individual patients, and if the results are similar at 2 years or beyond, effective treatment approaches that minimize the number of DMARDs and therefore their potential toxicities and expenses are desirable for patients and health care systems alike. Like other clinical situations in RA treatment, we need the precision medicine tools that can

guide patient selection for initiating monotherapy versus combination therapy.

### The BeSt Study

The BeSt study, now nearly two decades old, continues to be an important multicenter trial of 508 patients with early RA randomized to receive one of four treatment "strategies" in an openlabel study.6, The four arms of the study were as follows: group 1, sequential DMARD monotherapy; group 2, step-up combination therapy; group 3, initial combination therapy; and group 4, initial MTX and infliximab. Treatment adjustments were made every 3 months with the target of a DAS less than or equal to 2.4 (corresponding to low disease activity). The major results at 1 and 2 years are shown in Fig. 73.5; both combination groups (groups 3 and 4) improved more quickly than did groups 1 and 2, which was expected, with high-dose prednisone in group 3 and a high initial dose of MTX and also infliximab in group 4. At 1 year, DAS and other clinical outcomes were similar in all four groups and, importantly, at 2 years they were identical. Health Assessment Questionnaire (HAQ) scores improved more in the early combination groups (groups 3 and 4) at 1 year but were not different at 2 years, and radiographic progression at 2 years was greater in group 1 than in group 2 and greater in groups 1 and 2 than in the combination groups. Progression of the joint space narrowing score (the importance of which is discussed in a subsequent section), although numerically higher in group 1, was not statistically different among the four groups. Interpretation of these differences is complicated by the fact that despite having disease for only 6 months, group 2 had more radiographic progression at baseline.

The main conclusion of the BeSt study should be that all patients treated with a disease activity target will do well, even if they are receiving very different therapies. The type of therapy patients receive is not as important; it is only important that they are at low disease activity or in remission. Several important caveats must be noted:

The strategy of adding DMARDs, as in group 2, was more effective than the strategy of switching from one DMARD to another, at least for the DMARDs and their order of use in the BeSt trial. Although the clinical outcomes were similar at 2 years for these groups, radiographic progression was greater in group 1, more group 1 patients required infliximab, and many group 1 patients ended up taking combinations of medications anyway.

Initial therapy with combinations of conventional DMARDs (group 3) or combinations including biologic agents (group 4) works more quickly than step-up therapy (group 2). However, at 2 years, the clinical results were identical. There was a statistical advantage favoring the combination groups in terms of total radiographic progression (not reaching a threshold of clinical significance unless it continues at a similar rate for years), but no difference was noted in terms of joint space narrowing. When relevant, further treatment changes need to be made among the small group of patients (perhaps 10%) receiving only conventional therapy who may experience radiographic progression.

### The TEAR Trial

The TEAR trial was a landmark study of initial DMARD therapy in patients with early-stage (mean disease duration = 3.6 months),

poor prognosis (all had RF, ACPA, or erosions) RA.73, TEAR, a 2-year, investigator-initiated, randomized, double-blind study, addressed two critical questions: (1) Should treatment with combination therapy be used initially, or should patients be stepped up to combinations of DMARDs only after a trial of MTX monotherapy? and (2) Is combination therapy with MTX-ETAN superior to therapy with MTX-SSZ-HCQ (triple) therapy?

The 755 patients were randomized to four groups: (1) MTX- ETAN; (2) triple therapy (MTX-SSZ-HCQ); (3) MTX-only, step-up to MTX-ETAN; and (4) MTX-only, step-up to triple therapy. Patients randomized to the MTX-only groups were stepped up (72% of patients were stepped up) to their assigned combination at 6 months in a blinded fashion unless their DAS28 scores were less than 3.2.

The major clinical findings are illustrated in Fig. 73.6. All four groups had excellent improvement, with a mean reduction in the DAS28 of 2.8. For the primary endpoint of the study (mean DAS28 between weeks 48 and 102), all four groups were identical. At the 6-month time point, patients started on combination therapy (either triple or MTX-ETAN) had better results than patients started on MTX monotherapy. However, this difference disappeared within 12 weeks of the step-up, and the step-up group's DAS28 scores were identical to those of the other groups for the remainder of the study (see Fig. 73.6). Functional assessments and quality of life measures closely mirrored the DAS28

results. As shown in the cumulative probability plot in Fig. 73.7, the radiographic outcomes of all four groups were superimposable. Table 73.7 shows that there was no difference between the four groups in total Sharp score (TSS) progression. Many investigators had speculated that serious adverse events may be more common in the ETAN-treated group, whereas minor toxicities such as GI upset and others would be more common in the triple-treated patients, but no differences in adverse effects were observed.

Conclusions from the TEAR trial were:

Strategies that initially treat patients with MTX and step up to combination therapy only if they have not achieved their target at 6 months are as effective as initial combination therapy at 1 and 2 years, with no difference in clinical or radiographic outcomes. At the core of the debate about initial therapy—single DMARD versus combination—is the question of how soon is soon enough when considering control of RA. Is it important to control synovitis and radiographic progression in days or weeks, or is control by 3 to 6 months adequate? No clear long-term (>2-year) data exist to answer this important question. In both the TEAR trial and the BeSt study, as previously discussed, the groups treated with combination therapy early did better more quickly, but in both trials, the step-up groups looked identical to the early combination groups at 2 years in terms of clinical parameters. However, in both studies the early combination groups had very small but statistically significant

less radiographic progression at 2 years. In the TEAR trial, this difference was 0.5 TSS/year, and in the BeSt trial, it was 1.3 per year. Therefore central to this issue is the clinical relevance of small degrees of radiographic progression.

The strategy of using triple therapy was as effective as using the combination of MTX-ETAN. This observation is clearly important and should allow clinicians to be comfortable with this
