conventional therapy combination. Importantly, and somewhat sobering, the mean DAS28 scores of the four groups between 1 and 2 years of the trial was around 3.0, which means that almost half of the patients were not at target (DAS28 <3.2) regardless of treatment assignment. Therefore in clinical situations, usually after 6 months of therapy, these patients should be switched to other therapies to obtain better control of their disease. For

example, patients receiving triple therapy should be switched to or have ETAN added, and patients receiving MTX-ETAN should have HCQ and SSZ added. Trial data on patients who have failed to respond to triple therapy and are then treated with biologic agents or vice versa are discussed in a subsequent section, and both groups have the opportunity to do well.

### Treatment of Patients With Active Disease Despite Treatment With Methotrexate

As previously discussed, excellent data from clinical trials in which patients in general have high disease activity and poor prognostic features show that approximately 30% of patients will achieve a state of low disease activity or better if treated with modest doses of oral MTX. This figure is consistent across three major trials that documented this response.6, If MTX therapy is optimized by switching to SC delivery and pushing doses to at least 25 mg/ week, additional patients will experience disease control. Those who have still not achieved this level of control are candidates for treatment escalation, though hesitancy to make changes may occur among patients who experienced significant improvement with MTX. The first question to ask is: Should patients switch to another DMARD, or should other DMARDs be added to MTX? Data from multiple studies, including the previously discussed BeSt trial, strongly support adding conventional DMARDs or biologic agents to MTX rather than switching to another DMARD.6, A trial of 151 patients has addressed the question of stopping MTX versus continuing MTX in patients with active disease who start taking ETAN. The group randomized to continue to take MTX fared much better, with an ACR20 response rate of 86% versus 64%, and they experienced significantly less radiographic progression.

Excellent data now exist that support the efficacy of at least 16 different clinically available DMARDs or DMARD combinations when added to MTX in patients who have active disease despite treatment with MTX. This is true for all of the commonly used DMARDs, conventional, JAK inhibitors, and biologic agents alike. Fig. 73.2 highlights representative blinded clinical trials that have studied approved therapies in this patient popula- .23, The problem for the clinician is the marked paution. city of data with regard to comparing active therapies with each other in this critically important patient population. Knowing

that more than 16 different treatments are better than a placebo is of limited value because most clinicians do not use placebos to treat patients with RA. Fortunately, a growing body of comparative effectiveness trials has begun to shed light on patients with active disease despite treatment with MTX, as discussed in a subsequent section of this chapter.

The critical decision for clinicians is whether to add additional conventional therapies to MTX or to add a biologic agent or a JAK inhibitor. Compared with the number of therapies that we know work in patients with active disease despite treatment with MTX, far less data address this question. The open-labeled Swefot study in this population of patients with active disease despite treatment with MTX compared adding SSZ and HCQ (triple) with adding infliximab. At 6 months, both approaches appeared identical, with 25% of patients receiving triple therapy and 26% of patients receiving infliximab and MTX responding (EULAR good response); by 1 year, the results favored the biologic group (26% for triple therapy vs. 39% for infliximab), but this difference was no longer apparent at 2 years. Importantly, in the 2-year data from this trial, there was no advantage to using the biologic agents first with regard to work disability. 100,101

### The Rheumatoid Arthritis: Comparison of Active Therapies Trial

Rheumatoid Arthritis: Comparison of Active Therapies (RACAT)102 was a double-blind, randomized, controlled, noninferiority trial. RACAT was a multinational trial of 353 patients with RA who had active disease despite taking a mean of 19.6 mg per week of MTX. It was funded by the Veterans Administration, Canadian Institute of Health Research, and the National Institutes of Health. Of critical importance, this study was specifically designed to test the strategy of first adding conventional DMARDs (SSZ and HCQ) compared with a biologic agent (ETAN) to MTX (Fig. 73.8). Importantly, while maintaining blinding, both groups were switched to the other treatment if they had not improved in a clinically significant amount by 24 weeks. The primary endpoint was the improvement in DAS28 at 48 weeks (∆DAS28) based on the original group randomization.

During the RACAT trial, more patients in the triple therapy group experienced GI adverse effects (30% vs. 22%; p = 0.01), whereas more patients in the ETAN group had infections (37% vs. 25%; p = 0.02). Serious infections occurred in 12 patients in the ETAN group and in four patients in the triple therapy group.

Conclusions from the RACAT trial were:

The strategy of first adding SSZ and HCQ to MTX (triple therapy) is not inferior to first adding ETAN clinically or radiographically.

Switching to ETAN in patients with active disease who are receiving triple therapy provides additional benefit, as does switching to triple therapy in patients with active disease despite taking MTX and ETAN.

GI toxicities were more common in the patients receiving triple therapy, and infections were more common in the patients receiving ETAN.

Finally, the TEAR trial, as previously discussed,73,74 addressed the question of conventional combination versus biologic agent indirectly, but importantly, in a double-blind study. Although the TEAR trial was designed to evaluate initial therapy, half of patients were initially treated with MTX monotherapy and are relevant

to this discussion. Of patients treated with MTX monotherapy, 72% (n = 271) of patients did not achieve a DAS28 score of 3.2 or less and were treated with ETAN or the addition of HCQ/ SSZ (triple therapy) in a blinded fashion. As shown in Fig. 73.6, disease activity in both of these groups looked identical 12 weeks after stepping up therapy and continued to look identical as far as week 102, which was the end of the study. Importantly, with regard to radiographic progression, there was no difference in the radiographic progression of these MTX "failures" in the HCQ/ SSZ group versus those in the ETAN group (mean progression of 1.7 vs. 1.1, p = 0.57). Thus there was no "penalty" to starting with conventional combination therapy over adding a biologic.

Increasingly, demands are being made on rheumatologists to provide value-based care. This demand forces us to consider not only the clinical effectiveness and safety of our therapies but also their economic costs and consequences. Follow-up analysis of the Swefot trial did not show benefit of the biologic arm compared with the triple therapy arm for work loss, with numerically fewer work days lost in the triple therapy arm. 100Economic analyses of Swefot, TEAR, 104and RACAT105 have shown that the strategy of first using biologic agents rather than triple therapy in patients with active disease despite the use of MTX costs approximately $1 to $2 million per quality-adjusted life-year gained.

Until further data are available that guide clinicians in the selection of the best therapy for each patient based on the different MOAs of the many effective therapies, the aforementioned data dictate that conventional combinations should be tried first. When conventional combinations fail to help the patient achieve the disease activity target, data now show that TNF inhibition can provide additional benefit. When a biologic agent is needed, most clinicians favor a TNF inhibitor as the first biologic agent to use because of their long track record and the absence of convincing evidence of better efficacy and safety profiles with other biologic agents or JAK inhibitors. Reflecting the paucity of data, major RA treatment guidelines do not endorse a specific biologic or JAK agent.2,3

### Treatment of Patients With Active Disease Despite TNF Inhibition

Despite the effectiveness of conventional DMARD combinations and the TNF inhibitors, a subset of patients will continue to have unacceptable levels of disease activity. Estimates of the size of this subset range from 20% to 40% of patients with RA. The good news is that we still have multiple options with data to support them, which include switching to another TNF agent, 106-109 starting rituximab,110 starting abatacept,111inhibiting IL-6,112,113 or adding a JAK inhibitor. 114-116 Currently, data elucidating this choice are limited, as discussed next. Thus until markers or parameters are available that may help clinicians select a therapy potentially reflecting a patient's unique disease mechanisms, we will again be making this decision largely empirically (see Fig. 73.3).

The strategy of TNF inhibition has been in use the longest and, because of its efficacy and the comfort level of clinicians with its use, many clinicians would switch to a second TNF inhibitor before switching to a biologic agent with a different MOA or to a JAK inhibitor. A number of observational studies and one RCT support this approach.106-109 From the observational studies, a consistent theme has been that if the first TNF inhibitor was discontinued for toxicity or loss of efficacy, patients have a better chance of efficacy with the second TNF than if the first was discontinued because of primary inefficacy (hazard ratio [HR], 2.7; confidence interval [CI], 2.1 to 3.4). Discontinuation rates,

particularly as measured in observational studies, are not the same as efficacy and reflect many things, including other treatment options that are available at the time of the study. In the previously cited study published in 2008, golimumab, certolizumab, tocilizumab, sarilumab, and the JAK inhibitors were not options. In a RCT addressing the efficacy of switching to a second TNF inhibitor, golimumab was administered after failure of at least one anti-TNF agent, and 43% of subjects responded, compared with 17% in the placebo-treated group.

Again, the key question is not if switching to a second TNFi is better than placebo but which of the several available therapies has the best efficacy and safety in this clinical scenario. To address this question, a pragmatic, open-label trial in France randomized 300 TNFi inadequate responders to receive a second TNF inhibitor or a non-TNFi biologic (intravenous [IV] abatacept, IV rituximab, or IV tocilizumab). At 24 weeks, the majority of patients in both arms had a moderate or good EULAR response, though significantly more of the non-TNFi-treated patients responded (69% vs. 52%). This risk difference indicates that for every six patients treated with a non-TNFi rather than a TNFi, one additional patient would be expected to have a good response. Fig. 73.9 shows that DAS28-ESR improved to a greater degree in the non-TNFi treated (week 52 difference of -0.38; CI -0.69 to -0.08; p = 0.01), but HAQ scores were equivalent between treatment groups (p = 0.75 at week 52). Reassuringly, safety profiles were similar between treatment arms. The lack of blinding is an important limitation to this trial and, because of the high response rate in both arms, clinicians and patients can have reasonable confidence in either treatment option.

After initial TNFi failure, special consideration might be given to patients in whom antidrug antibodies have developed as a cause of secondary failure. After 3 years of treatment, antidrug antibodies developed in 28% of patients treated with adalimumab. In 67% of cases, these antibodies developed in the first 6 months. Development of antidrug antibodies was associated with lack of or loss of efficacy (HR, 3.0; CI, 1.6 to 5.5), and patients were less likely to achieve remission (HR, 7.1; 95% CI, 2.1 to 23.4). Importantly, 38% of patients with antidrug antibodies compared with 14% of those without antidrug antibodies discontinued therapy because of lack of efficacy (p = 0.001). Perhaps of more concern was a recent finding that the development of antiadalimumab

antibodies was associated with thromboembolic events (HR, 7.6; CI, 1.3 to 45.1; p = 0.25). These interesting findings raise the possibility that monitoring patients for development of antidrug antibodies, not only to adalimumab but also to other monoclonal antibodies, may be an important strategy to explain lack of efficacy but also to prevent toxicities such as thromboembolic events. While such studies have not been completed among only RA patients, therapeutic drug monitoring with infliximab treatment for immune-mediated diseases (e.g., RA, spondyloarthropathy, inflammatory bowel disease) showed promise for maintaining disease control but did not aid induction therapy in the Norwegian Drug Monitoring Trials (NOR-DRUM A and B).120,

Once the decision has been made to use a biologic agent with a different MOA, three choices are currently available: rituximab, abatacept, or IL-6 inhibition (tocilizumab or sarilumab). Few data are available to help differentiate among them. Based on strong suggestions in the literature that patients who are seronegative for ACPA and RF do not respond as well as seropositive patients when treated with rituximab, 122 most clinicians would opt for either abatacept or IL-6 inhibition in seronegative patients. However, seropositivity for ACPA and RF is a favorable predictor of response to all biologics. Randomized, placebo-controlled trials have shown the efficacy of all three MOAs in this patient population. .110-113 In these trials, patients taking MTX who have active disease or intolerance to at least one TNF inhibitor have had it stopped and are randomized to receive the intervention + MTX or MTX + placebo. ACR response rates in the three different trials for the active medication versus placebo were as follows: rituximab, 51% versus 18%110; abatacept, 50% versus 20%111; tocilizumab, 50% versus 10%112; and sarilumab, 58% versus 34%. All these responses, however, are less robust than in patients naive to biologic agents. Based on the strikingly similar response rates of 50% across these trials, there is little to guide treatment choice until predictors of responses or compelling comparative effectiveness trial data are available.

A limited number of randomized trials have compared biologic agents to each other, but those trials were not in patients who had failed to respond to a TNF inhibitor. In the ATTEST trial of patients with active disease despite MTX, adding abatacept was similar to adding infliximab for efficacy but had lower rates of

serious infections. In a head-to-head trial among MTX inadequate responders, the addition of either abatacept or adalimumab resulted in similar efficacy and safety outcomes. Finally, in a monotherapy trial (ADACTA), tocilizumab was superior to adalimumab in reducing disease activity. The later trial is of interest in patients who cannot take MTX. Increases in low-density lipoprotein cholesterol were observed with tocilizumab treatment in ADACTA, as noted in other tocilizumab trials. Reassuringly, the ENTRACT trial, which studied over 3000 RA patients with inadequate response to conventional DMARDs and had at least one cardiovascular disease risk factor, found tocilizumab treatment was noninferior to ETAN for the risk of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE). This large trial did highlight differential safety profiles between these therapies with more frequent serious infections and GI perforations occurring among tocilizumab-treated patients. A select number of trials have compared JAK inhibitors to biologic agents after MTX or TNFi failure and is discussed in a later section.

### The Role for JAK Inhibitors

The therapeutic role for tofacitinib, baricitinib, and upadacitinib is being elucidated (see Chapter 65 for a detailed discussion on JAK inhibitors). All three JAK inhibitors work well as monotherapy in early-stage disease, 127-129 when added to MTX in patients who have active disease despite use of MTX,95,115,116 and in patients who have failed to respond to a TNF inhibitor. 116, Unlike all other DMARDs, the efficacy of these JAK inhibitors is not increased substantially by MTX. The considerable efficacy of these medications is not in question, but their place in the treatment algorithm is largely being determined by their safety profile compared with biologics.

Unlike biologic versus biologic trials restricted to MTX-inadequate responders, comparative trials of JAK inhibitors versus biologic agents exist for both MTXand biologic-inadequate responders. Among MTX-inadequate responders, several trials suggested that their efficacy is similar to, or marginally exceeds, that of adalimumab.116, In a trial of RA patients with an inadequate response to, or intolerance of, a biologic agent, treatment with upadacitinib was reported as superior to abatacept. However, these findings appear to be driven by the unique influence of JAK inhibitors on CRP and slightly early responses observed at 12 weeks. Together, convincing evidence that JAK inhibitors are meaningfully superior to biologic agents is currently lacking.

Initial safety concerns emerged regarding thrombosis and the increased frequency of herpes zoster infections with JAK inhibitors. Furthermore, a mandatory post-marketing study was completed to evaluate the safety of tofacitinib with regard to cardiovascular and malignancy events. ORAL Surveillance was a randomized, open-label, noninferiority trial of patients with active RA despite MTX who were over 50 years of age and had at least one additional cardiovascular risk factor. The co-primary endpoints were MACE and malignancies, excluding nonmelanoma skin cancer. Patients were randomized to add tofacitinib at doses of 5 mg twice daily, 10 mg twice daily, or TNF inhibition (adalimumab or ETAN based on geographic region) to background MTX. During the trial, a higher risk of death and pulmonary embolism prompted switching all patients on the tofacitinib 10 mg dose to 5 mg. Among 4362 patients and over nearly 15,000 patient-years of follow-up, the incidence of MACE and malignancies in the tofacitinib-treated arms exceeded the noninferiority

margin (HR of 1.8) for comparisons to TNF inhibitors. Additionally, the pooled tofacitinib-treated arms had a 48% increased risk of malignancy, which was statistically significant. Post hoc analyses demonstrated the MACE risk related to tofacitinib was primarily observed among the patients with a history of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. Further illustrating the importance of considering the population under treatment, pharmacoepidemiologic studies using real-world evidence replicated trial findings among a population mirroring ORAL Surveillance eligibility criteria, but these findings did not generalize to the broader routine-care RA patients initiating these therapies. These concerning safety results have brought further uncertainty to the decision of when to utilize a JAK inhibitor in the treatment of RA, mandated rheumatologists to engage in discussions with patients about their risk profile, and raised important questions such as the generalizability of these findings to other JAK inhibitors.

### Treatment of Patients With "Refractory" Disease

As our expectations for our patients increase and the availability of different DMARDs expands, we push to control disease sooner and use biologic agents or JAK inhibitors earlier. As a result, RA is being labeled "refractory" by clinicians much earlier than ever before. When faced with "refractory" disease, a close inspection of previous treatments that "failed" is in order. It is common for patients to be treated initially with low doses of MTX (≤15 mg by mouth) for 3 months and then be started on a TNF inhibitor with or without MTX. When the patients still have active disease after a few months, they are inappropriately labeled as refractory. It is critical to assess whether MTX therapy has been optimized (see the previous discussion and Chapter 61); unless contraindications are present, most patients should have their dose of MTX pushed to 25 mg per week, and SC administration should be used. As previously discussed, data show that triple therapy is as effective as MTX-ETAN73,102 and can provide benefit in patients who failed to respond to MTX and ETAN. Thus, this combination should be considered before progressing too far down the biologic road. Some people have raised concern about treatment with a subsequent biologic agent after treatment with rituximab, which depresses B cell counts significantly for at least 6 to 12 months. Limited data from observational studies provide some reassurance because a significant increase in toxicities has not been reported.

The lack of a universal definition of "refractory" RA and of CC unacceptable" levels of disease activity in this population has hampered this discussion. With regard to levels of disease activity, it is clear and probably appropriate that clinicians are willing to tolerate more active disease in this "refractory" group before changing therapy, compared with patients who are naive to treatment or those treated with active disease despite use of MTX only. EULAR recently convened a task force to derive an initial definition for "refractory" RA, selecting the term "difficult-to-treat RA."138 This definition requires the following: (1) failure of ≥2 biologic agents or JAK inhibitors after conventional DMARD failure, (2) signs of active or progressive disease, and (3) management of signs and/or symptoms is perceived as problematic by rheumatologist and/or patient. Once fulfilling this definition, additional strategies proposed by the EULAR task force that may assist in management include139.

Reassessing the RA diagnosis

Assessing for comorbidities that mimic RA signs/symptoms or interfere with RA assessment

Assessing RA activity, including the use of advanced imaging if uncertain

Evaluating and optimizing treatment adherence

Increasing focus on nonpharmacologic treatments (e.g., education, exercise, self-management)

### Biosimilars: Why Have We Been Slow to Adopt?

Many have voiced large and mostly unfounded concerns for the introduction of biosimilars into the RA marketplace. We have of course been using biosimilars for years; every batch of any biologic is only biosimilar and never identical to the one before it. Simply put, biosimilars should be interchangeable140 and, with the advent of new and better production processes that decrease impurities, the challenge for the biosimilar developer is to not make them bio-better. Almost all approved biosimilars have quicker onset of action and lower injection site reactions than the innovator. Therefore the real question in the United States, where biosimilars have been approved for four bio-originators, is not should we be using them but how to overcome incentives that drive physicians to use the branded product. Biosimilars have been widely successful in Europe, with huge cost savings and no loss of efficacy. 140, Whether similar savings can be achieved in the United States given the differences in health care systems remains to be determined.

### Use of Combination Biologic Agents (and JAK Inhibitors)

Combinations of conventional DMARDs and combinations of conventional DMARDs, especially MTX, with biologic agents have played a critical role in the vast improvement in responses to treatments that we currently see. However, thus far efforts to combine biologic products have not met with success. To date, studies to combine ETAN with anakinra have shown no improvement in disease control, with an ACR50 score of 41% in the ETAN-only arm compared with 31% in the combination arm, and they have shown an increase in serious infections in the combination arm (7.4% vs. 0%). Similarly, in patients with active disease despite use of ETAN, patients were randomized to add abatacept or placebo; efficacy showed a nonstatistically significant trend toward improvement (ACR20 for combination, 48% vs. 31%; p = 0.07), but again, with an increased risk of serious adverse events in the combination group (17% vs. 3%) and serious infections (4% vs. 0%). Additionally, a small trial in which patients who had active disease despite use of MTX and either ETAN or adalimumab were treated with the addition of rituximab or placebo showed very modest improvement in efficacy (an ACR20 score of 30% vs. 17%). Again, serious adverse events including infections were numerically greater in the group treated with combination therapy.

Despite these less-than-encouraging results from biologic combination trials, it is likely that ultimately patients will be treated with combinations of biologic agents. What is critically needed are good ways to measure the degree of immune suppression we create with our interventions—a type of thermostat for TNF, IL-1, or IL-6.145 Currently, it is likely that suppression is inadequate in some patients, therefore not achieving optimal disease control, and that suppression in other patients is occurring at dangerous levels, leading to increased toxicity. When better immune system monitoring techniques are developed, not only will we be able to use the biologic agents we currently have in a more effective manner but it is likely that we will be able to safely and effectively combine biologic agents to improve outcomes in terms of both efficacy and safety.

### Managing Patients "At Target" Who Are Taking Disease-Modifying Anti-rheumatic Drugs

It is a powerful testament of how far therapy for patients with RA has come that this section has now become a regular part of this chapter. It is common practice for clinicians to ask whether and how to taper DMARDs in patients who are "at target." Unfortunately, few definitive data exist regarding what level of disease control is necessary before considering tapering, how to identify the optimal patients for tapering, and the specific DMARDs (and their order) to taper.

Because of their well-chronicled toxicities, the highest priority should be discontinuation of glucocorticoids and NSAIDs for all patients. A number of trials6,22,28 have shown that with effective DMARD therapy, glucocorticoid tapering not only is possible but should be expected. An excellent example of this is from the BeSt trial, in which 92% of group 3 (the group that received high-dose prednisone initially) had stopped taking all prednisone at 2 years. In this trial, prednisone was tapered only if the DAS was at or below 2.4 (a low level of disease activity). More recently in the SEMIRA trial, 65% of RA patients who achieved stable low disease activity with tocilizumab and prednisone were able to taper off prednisone over 16 weeks (5 mg to 0 mg by 1 mg every 4 weeks) and remain in low disease activity.

After a patient is off glucocorticoids and is still at target, it is more difficult to select which patients are candidates for tapering their DMARDs and a tapering approach. For many patients who cannot reach remission, low disease activity represents their ideal treatment "target." For these individuals, maintaining low disease activity is a reasonable goal when considering tapering,2 although their risk of flare is higher. A greater depth of disease control, not only remission but "deep" (i.e., Boolean) remission, is associated with lower risk of flares when tapering. Regardless of which disease activity state is chosen, a key determinant of tapering success is how long the patient has been at that disease activity state. While the exact amount of time needed at the disease activity target is uncertain, patients should generally be stable for at least 6 to 12 months, reflecting eligibility criteria of many tapering trials. Unfortunately, few additional predictors of tapering success have been elucidated, namely seronegativity147 (or attenuated autoantibody responses148) and the absence of synovitis and Doppler signal on ultrasound (Table 73.8). We do not currently have laboratory tests or clinical parameters that can accurately predict which patients can safely undergo tapering; their identification and validation is a high priority.
