If an appropriate DMARD tapering candidate is identified, clinicians must then decide on a general tapering strategy. Several trials have evaluated tapering strategies, sharing the common design elements of selecting patients with stable disease at target (low disease activity or remission) and randomizing them to continuation of DMARDs, tapering DMARDs, or stopping a/all DMARD(s).147, As a representation of these trials, Fig. 73.10 shows the results from the PRESERVE trial. This trial randomized 604 patients who achieved stable low disease activity with MTX and ETAN 50 mg/week to (1) continue MTX and ETAN 50 mg/week; (2) continue MTX and reduce ETAN to 25 mg/week; or (3) continue MTX and discontinue ETAN. The group that discontinued ETAN was significantly less likely to maintain disease control (proportion in remission/low disease activity, DASs) compared with either the continuation or reduced ETAN dose arms over the 52-week follow-up period (Fig. 73.10). Functional status and quality of

life measures were significantly better in the continuation or reduced ETAN dose arms. Radiograph outcomes also favored ETAN continuation or dose reduction, but limited radiographic progression occurred.

Conclusions that can be drawn from PRESERVE and other tapering trials include:

Discontinuation of all DMARDs has an unacceptably high rate of relapse.21, Thus drug-free remission might not be an attainable goal at this time, and patients should be counseled to remain on at least one DMARD.

The highest risk of disease worsening is with abrupt discontinuation of a DMARD. This is not the tapering approach that should be recommended to patients.

The lowest risk of disease worsening is with continuation of all DMARDs at current doses, but many patients (4080%) can remain under good disease control on reduced doses of DMARDs.

Patients who experience disease worsening while tapering DMARDs can rapidly regain disease control by returning to their prior DMARD dosing regimen.

Whether these trial conclusions support tapering DMARDs as long as patients remain on at least one is in the eye of the beholder. Is success maintaining the lowest DASs, utilizing the fewest DMARDs, or a balance of maintaining the treatment target with the necessary DMARD(s)? One limitation of the tapering approaches used in trials is they are required to follow a protocolized schedule. However, in clinic, the tapering approach can more easily be tailored to the patient. In our clinic, we slowly and gradually lengthen the interval between SC injections, and it is not uncommon for patients who are in remission to take 50 mg of ETAN every 2 to 4 weeks or 40 mg of adalimumab every 3 to 6 weeks. The most important task of the clinician engaging in tapering is to educate the patient not only on the risk of disease worsening, but the immediate action plan to follow should their disease symptoms worsen. The patient should quickly resume their prior effective DMARD dose and not wait until their next clinic visit. Of note, while the aforementioned trials have consistently studied TNFi, similar findings have been observed when tapering rituximab doses.

A common DMARD tapering situation is the patient who is receiving combination therapy with MTX and a biologic agent. Because of the expense and concerns for long-term toxicities, the approach tested in most tapering trials is to taper the biologic to the lowest dose possible by decreasing the dose or lengthening the .147,150-154Many of these patients interval between administrations. in practice may have started taking this combination initially or had the biologic added after receiving only a very short course of MTX (often with suboptimal use). We also know from early trials that biologic doses lower than those usually clinically prescribed can be very effective. For example, the ERA trial compared doses of ETAN of 10 mg and 25 mg given twice weekly156; although the data were slightly better for the higher dose, the low dose clearly had substantial efficacy nearly equal to "full-dose" ETAN, both as measured by clinical (ACR20) parameters and lack of radiographic progression. Therefore a significant percentage of current patients in remission may be overdosed.

Two trials have directly compared tapering or discontinuing conventional DMARDs versus TNFi. In the TARA trial, 57% patients who tapered TNFi maintained disease control compared with 67% tapering conventional DMARDs (p = 0.17). Tapering was highly successful in both arms, with 82% of those tapering TNFi being on half or less of the original dose at the end of the study. Importantly, there were no significant differences in DAS, functional status, quality of life, and radiographic progression between the arms. Substantially higher health care costs were incurred for those who continued TNFi (tapering conventional DMARDs) related to medication expenses. Productivity costs seem to offset this difference, though these estimates were based on costs in the Netherlands and are expected to differ in other countries and health care systems. In the SEAM-RA trial, RA patients in SDAI remission on MTX and ETAN were randomized to MTX and ETAN continuation, MTX discontinuation, or ETAN discontinuation. The proportion who remained in SDAI remission at 48 weeks without disease worsening was 52.9%, 49.5%, and 28.7% (p = 0.004 between discontinuation arms), respectively. What may initially seem a meaningful difference between discontinuation arms must be interpreted in the context of three key points: (1) ETAN was utilized at full dose (50 mg/week) compared with suboptimal use of MTX (mean dose of

16 mg/week), (2) >90% of patients were in low disease activity at week 48 with the use of strategies to recapture disease control, and (3) prior tapering studies have established that abrupt discontinuation is not an appropriate strategy for de-escalating DMARDs. Clearly, for those on conventional DMARDs and biologic agents, tapering of a therapy should be chosen over discontinuation; a substantial proportion of patients can maintain disease control without, or with a lower dose of, a biologic agent; and there do not appear to be significant consequences to attempting to taper biologic agents.

### Prevention Trials: A Step in the Right Direction

Many observations clearly show that the immune response that becomes RA starts years before most patients present with the classic symptom complex.160, Studies to elucidate this transition ,162,163 as are initial studies aiming to intervene with are ongoing, medications during this pre-RA period. These RA prevention trials have recruited individuals at risk of developing RA based on autoantibody positivity, arthralgias, genetic risk, elevated hsCRP, and/or subclinical joint inflammation on MRI or ultrasound. Among these at-risk populations, atorvastatin, dexamethasone, MTX, HCQ, abatacept, and rituximab have been compared with placebo.164-170 While none of these trials has demonstrated the ability to prevent RA, some have shown the potential to delay its onset and/or the benefit of early, or very early, treatment. In the PRAIRI trial, a single 1000 mg dose of rituximab delayed the onset of clinical arthritis by 12 months. In the TREAT EARLIER trial, 1 year of MTX treatment produced sustained improvements after treatment cessation in physical function, work outcomes, and MRI findings. Preliminary results from the ARIAA trial have similarly reported the ability to delay RA onset and improve subclinical joint inflammation with 6 months of weekly SC abatacept. . Two intramuscular doses of dexamethasone reduced autoantibody concentrations up to 6 months later. In contrast to these trials, neither HCQ nor atorvastatin prevented or delayed RA onset in their respective trials, both of which were terminated .164, Designing, recruiting for, and conducting these preearly. vention studies has been challenging, but these founding prevention trials will pave the way for future prevention efforts.

### Interpreting Radiographic Progression and the Use of Other Imaging Modalities

What is the clinical relevance of radiographic progression? How much progression is significant, and over what period? Are erosions important, or should we be concerned only with joint space narrowing? Finally, what role, if any, should ultrasound or MRI play in the management of RA?

In clinical trials, RA treatments are evaluated by clinical parameters (e.g., ACR20 responses and DAS) and radiographic progression (TSS or van der Heijde Sharp [VHS]). This form of evaluation is problematic for a number of reasons. Clinical and radiographic progression do not always parallel one another. Perhaps the most dramatic example of this phenomenon from an RCT is the PRE- MIER trial, where, in the monotherapy arms, MTX alone even at low doses was significantly better than adalimumab alone, while at the same time, adalimumab was better than MTX with regard to radiographic progression (Fig. 73.1172). So which treatment was

better? Some would say it is moot because the combination of the two outperformed either monotherapy arm in both measures. However, that misses the point about how to balance radiographic progression versus clinic parameters. Because patients do not come to the clinic complaining of radiographic progression or demanding that it be stopped, the question of how radiographic progression is related to factors that patients do care about—most importantly, physical function—is highly relevant.

Data exist that relate TSS or similarly total (VHS) progression to changes on HAQs (the gold standard for physical function in RA). These data suggest that a ΔTSS of 1 equals a change in HAQ of ~0.01.171 It is well accepted that a clinically significant ∆HAQ is ~0.22, so it follows that a ΔTSS of 22 is required for a radiographic change to be clinically relevant. This large change is never seen in clinical trials in which active therapies are compared and, with current therapies and treatment strategies, almost never seen in clinic. Thus although many RCTs have shown statistically significant radiographic progression differences, no contemporary active comparator trials have shown a clinically significant difference of any therapy versus any other therapy within the 1 to 2 years of the clinical trial. Additionally, recent data suggest that joint space narrowing correlates well with clinical progression but that erosions do not,172,173 so perhaps we should be less concerned with TSS compared with joint space narrowing. Additionally, over what duration should we be concerned about radiographic progression? If a trial shows that therapy A results in two less TSS points progression per year compared with therapy B, then it follows that if those same therapies are used for 11 years and the same rate of radiographic progression continues, then patients receiving therapy A will have a clinically significant clinical benefit—HAQ 0.22 less than patients receiving therapy B. This is the magnitude of difference (∆TSS of 1 to 2/year) that has been seen in trials and leads to claims of superiority. Two problems are readily apparent with this type of extrapolation:

1. Within clinical trials, patients are often randomized to a therapy and continue to receive that therapy for the duration of the trial regardless of how they are doing. This approach does not

reflect how patients are taken care of in the clinic; if patients are not doing well, therapy is or should be adjusted. Again, the PREMIER trial72 is an excellent example of this issue; patients were in their assigned groups for 2 years (Fig. 73.11B). Many patients were not having an optimal clinical response, and therapy would have been changed if this response had happened in a real-life clinical setting. These patients would not still be in the trial demonstrating their predictable radiographic progression, so in any RCT, radiographic progression that occurs after the time the therapy should have had maximal clinical benefit, and therefore the time that patients would have been switched to a new therapy, is not clinically relevant. In the PREMIER trial, the therapies should have had maximal benefit by 6 months, so if the data after that time point include patients who were not at target (at least at low disease activity), then it is not relevant to patients seen in the clinic.

2. The second point is similar; to extrapolate forward in the example of a ΔTSS of two per year to 11 years of therapy would only be relevant if all patients were doing well clinically. Patients who are not doing well clinically would have their therapies changed before the two TSS progressions per year had a chance to become clinically relevant.

Another major reason why radiographic progression is problematic for the clinician is that formal evaluation of radiographic progression is almost never performed outside of clinical trials; few patients have formal Sharp score assessment of radiographs. In this regard, routine yearly radiographs are not indicated in many patients with RA and only add to the expense of care. This is true for patients who are not doing well clinically. Those patients need a change of care regardless of what the radiographs show, and this is also true for patients who are unwilling or unable to change therapies. The small minority of patients who are at the clinical target but who are progressing radiographically are the ones for whom we hope to discover important information with serial radiographs.

Finally, the manner in which radiographic information is presented in clinical trials is problematic. Most commonly, the mean

TSS progression of group A is compared with group B, statistical analysis is performed, and we are told that therapy A is superior to therapy B because one or two fewer TSS progressions occur in that group. A much more informative way to examine radiographic outcomes is to look at cumulative probability plots for radiographic changes (Fig. 73.12) for the Trial of Etanercept and Methotrexate with Radiographic Patient Outcomes (TEMPO)77,78 and Fig. 73.7 for the TEAR trial. When data are looked at this way, it is readily appreciated that a small number of patients, perhaps 15% to 20% in the TEMPO trial and even fewer in many studies, are driving the radiographic outcome. In the TEAR trial, there are no differences across the four groups in the probability plot. With this epiphany, we must ask the following important questions: Who are these patients, and how do we focus on this small group that would benefit from a different therapy and not subject the other 80% to 95% to additional risks and expense? As previously mentioned, one study172 has called into question the relevance of erosions with regard to clinical correlations and have suggested that joint space narrowing correlates much more strongly with clinical progression; therefore going forward we need to ensure that we take this into account.

Finally, what is the place, if any, of "advanced" imaging techniques in evaluating patients with RA? Clearly, both ultrasound and MRI are powerful techniques to evaluate early erosions and to detect synovitis. One potential use of these obviously sensitive techniques, as previously suggested, may be to verify the true absence of synovitis in patients who are believed to be in remission on clinical grounds. However, trials have not found treatment guided by these advanced imaging modalities to outperform conventional T2T approaches. In a 24-month, open-label, randomized trial of 238 DMARD-naive patients with active RA, ultrasound-guided tight control did not improve clinical outcomes compared with conventional (DAS-guided) tight control. Similarly, a 2-year randomized trial of 200 RA patients in clinical remission found

equivalent remission and radiographic progression rates between MRI-guided and conventional T2T strategies. Ultrasound has shown promise in predicting which patients in clinical remission are most likely to experience flares while receiving stable ther- 174,177 and synovitis on Doppler ultrasound predicts which apy, patients are more likely to experience flares when their medication is tapered (Chapter 41). Even if, statistically, patients who are shown by ultrasound to have synovitis are more likely to have flares, the difference is of questionable clinical significance. More importantly, these advanced modalities and expertise to appropriately interpret these modalities is not widely available, which significantly limits their practical application.

### Adjuncts to Medications

### Patient Education

RA is a lifelong disease, so it not only makes sense that patients who are educated about their disease might do better, but good data exist to show that education is associated with better out- . Use of the Arthritis Self-Management Program leads comes. to less pain, decreased visits to physicians, and economic sav- .179, Chronic diseases such as RA affect the entire family, ings. and participation of spouses in educational group sessions leads to additional beneficial effects. Training in stress management is particularly effective in improving measures of helplessness, coping, pain, self-efficacy, and health status. Unfortunately, formal education level, a factor that we cannot readily modify, is associated with morbidity and mortality rates. Formal educational level is inversely proportional to these outcomes, and this finding cannot be explained by age, duration of disease, joint count, functional measures, or medications.

It is clearly important for patients to take an active role in the management of their chronic disease. The more patients understand their disease and medications, the more control they feel they have over this chronic condition. The bond that develops between patients and clinicians as they work together to control this lifelong disease is an important factor in outcome and the satisfaction level of both parties. The stronger the bond, the less likely patients will become frustrated and turn to alternative therapies that are not only expensive but may do more harm than good.

### Pain Control

If patients with RA are treated early and effectively with DMARDs and therapy is escalated to achieve excellent control of the active components of disease, the need for specific pain medications, particularly narcotics, can be minimized. If pain is a major problem, the first thing to do is review the DMARD regimen and modify it to achieve maximum control of any active synovitis. Unfortunately, some patients present later in the course of their disease after substantial joint damage has already occurred, and their pain needs to be addressed. Pain can be the factor that limits effective physical and occupational therapy. In addition to inhibiting function, pain is a major cause of depression in patients with polyarthritis. To maximize therapy in patients with early-stage RA or undifferentiated polyarthritis, pain must be controlled without altering consciousness or generating addiction. Treatment strategies of education, rest, exercise, and disease-modifying therapies are generally favored as an approach to pain control in people with arthritis, and strategies that rely on narcotic derivatives do not address control of active RA. In most medical centers, experts in

pain management are available for consultation by rheumatologists and primary care physicians (PCPs). Chapter 68 provides an excellent discussion of analgesics in rheumatic disease.

### Rest and/or Exercise and Activities of Daily Living

Education and supervision of a patient by trained professionals regarding the importance of finding the best balance of rest and exercise for inflamed joints are essential. This component of therapy can be started well before a definitive diagnosis is made. No matter the cause, finding this balance should ensure that a patient develops or retains sufficient strength to support joint function without exacerbating inflammation.

Details of physical and occupational therapy are outlined in Chapter 38. While rest and splints may be needed to immobilize the acutely and severely inflamed joints, even the most painful joints must be moved passively through a full range of motion each day to prevent flexion contractures. For moderately inflamed joints, isometric exercises with muscles contracted in a fixed position provide adequate muscle tone without exacerbating joint inflammation and pain. Patients with well-controlled arthritis will benefit from variable-resistance programs, high-intensity strength training, and aerobic exercise, which provide significant improvements in functional status, pain, and fatigue levels. Aquatic therapy offers benefits of both aerobic and resistance exercise while simultaneously avoiding excess mechanical loading on joints. Older patients with RA benefit from progressive resistance exercises, similar to younger patients. In a study of older patients given closely regulated workouts, maximal strength of all major exercised muscle groups was increased 75% without exacerbation of disease activity. Not only does prescribed sustained exercise increase muscle strength but also it helps the ability of patients to perform daily routines, improves global assessments and moods, and can decrease pain.

Most patients with RA should have one or more sessions with a licensed occupational therapist (OT) to learn how to preserve joint function and alignment while carrying out the necessary and enjoyable activities of daily living and to be introduced to available assistive devices. Ideally, this initially should occur early in the disease course and be utilized again, as needed, throughout the disease course. The basic concept is to avoid excessive force applied across non—weight-bearing joints and to avoid unnecessary impact loading on weight-bearing joints. A prospective and controlled Canadian trial demonstrated that home therapy by OTs produced a statistically significant and clinically important improvement in function in patients with RA.

### Comorbidities and the Interactions of Rheumatologists With Primary Care Physicians

The best possible outcomes for patients with RA can be achieved only with a carefully orchestrated collaboration between PCPs and rheumatologists. On the one hand, the ever-increasing complexity of RA management options, combination therapies, and possible toxicities of therapy has made it essential that all patients with RA be treated by rheumatologists. Good-quality evidence shows that patients with RA are more likely to be taking DMARDs, as well as combination DMARDs, and are happier with their care when

### TABLE Role of Primary Care Physicians in Treating 73.9 Rheumatoid Arthritis a

they are treated by rheumatologists. .187-189 On the other hand, the realization of the critical nature of the comorbidities associated with RA, especially cardiovascular disease, 190 make ongoing engagement of a PCP essential191 to produce optimal outcomes.

Despite the importance of the rheumatologist, the PCP needs to be closely engaged (Table 73.9). People with RA suffer from a high burden of multimorbidity, the presence of multiple chronic conditions. Conditions overrepresented in RA include premature atherosclerosis and congestive heart failure, ILD, cancer, mental health disorders, osteoporosis, fractures, and infections. RA is a significant risk factor for cardiovascular morbidity and mortality, approaching that of diabetes. In this regard, clinicians need to aggressively address traditional cardiovascular risk factors such as cigarette smoking, hypertension, and dyslipidemia in patients with RA. Smoking cessation has the added benefit of potentially making patients more responsive to therapies. Statins appear to reduce cardiovascular disease risk to a similar degree in RA patients as in the general population194 and in at least one RCT in humans, 195 modestly decreased RA activity. Given the unique influence of RA (e.g., "lipid paradox") and DMARDs (specifically IL-6 and JAK inhibition) on cholesterol values and the absence of cardiovascular risk scores that appropriately account for RA, ,190 collaboration between a PCP, rheumatologist, and cardiologist may be needed to guide cardiovascular disease risk stratification and prevention.

Because RA and particularly glucocorticoids are risk factors for osteoporosis, the PCP and rheumatologist need to address this issue. Screening for osteopenia and osteoporosis should regularly occur by obtaining dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry scans. Patients taking glucocorticoids should be receiving calcium and vitamin D3 supplementation. Bisphosphonates prevent steroidinduced osteoporosis, and their use should be strongly considered in patients taking steroids on a long-term basis unless contraindications exist (e.g., women of childbearing age). To inform these decisions, the ACR has developed guidelines for the prevention and management of glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis.

With the increased risk of infections experienced by patients with RA because of their disease and therapies, up-to-date immunizations, including influenza, pneumococcal, zoster, and now SARS-CoV-2 vaccines, are critical. Recently the ACR established guidelines on vaccinations in patients with rheumatic diseases. 197 These guidelines suggest that most DMARDs can be continued around the time of non—live-attenuated vaccinations, with the exception of MTX and rituximab. When disease activity allows, holding MTX for 2 weeks after influenza vaccination appears to improve serologic responses. It is similarly recommended to delay administering rituximab for at least 2 weeks after influenza and

other non—live-attenuated vaccinations. Because the PCP often sees the patient first during an illness, the PCP needs to be familiar with the common toxicities of RA medications, including concerns about MTX in the patient with decreasing renal function, MTX pneumonitis, and the need for heightened concern and aggressive workup of all potential infections, including opportunistic infections in immunosuppressed patients, particularly those taking biologic agents. Often the difference between life and death or at least between excellent outcomes and less-than-optimal results is the rapidity of response to the early warning signs for conditions as simple as cellulitis or a pulmonary infiltrate.

Clearly the best care is achieved when a team of a rheumatologist, a PCP, and an educated patient all work closely together. Timely consultation with physical and occupational therapists, orthopedic surgeons, and other clinicians also plays a role in optimal outcomes. Although the need for joint replacement surgery is thankfully decreasing, few interventions have been as successful in improving patient mobility and quality of life as having properly timed hip and knee replacements.

### Perioperative Management t of Rheumatoid Arthritis Medications

Not uncommonly, the question of what to do with RA medications around the time of surgery comes up. The ACR has worked with orthopedic surgeons to put together excellent guidelines, which were recently updated. Highlights of these guidelines include continuing all conventional DMARDs through the surgical period, holding all biologics prior to surgery for a length of time consistent with their individual functional half-lives, and holding JAK inhibitors for 3 days prior to surgery. These therapies can be resumed after the wound shows evidence of healing, typically around 14 days post-operatively.

### Patients With Rheumatoid Arthritis Are Doing Better

The prognosis for patients with RA has improved dramatically. Every rheumatologist fortunate enough to see the changes during the past few decades is only too happy to witness the improvements in care. The clinic days when wheelchairs were commonplace and symptomatic C1 cervical subluxations, chronic leg ulcers, constrictive pericarditis, and corneal melts were not uncommon are, we hope, gone forever. Despite this firmly held perception by clinicians, strong data to support this change have been slow to accumulate.

It may take up to 20 years for the results of a change in therapy or treatment approach to fully translate into improvement in long-term outcomes, such as joint replacements and mortality. However, emerging evidence suggests the therapeutic principles utilized in the past two decades are beginning to impact these long-term outcomes. Cohort studies from the Veterans Health Administration and Olmstead County have demonstrated improved longevity in RA over more recent time periods.199, In the same cohort of patients in Olmstead County, knee surgeries and hand surgeries substantially decreased. A 30% reduction in severe extra-articular manifestations of RA has occurred since the year 2000 among more than 35, U.S. veterans with RA. Data from California for the years 1983 to 2001 showed that hospitalizations for RA vasculitis or splenectomy for Felty's

syndrome decreased by 33% and 71%, respectively. Data from Sweden and Spain204 both show that DASs and health assessment scores have significantly improved during the past decade. Further evidence of improved long-term outcomes in RA is expected to follow these early reports.

### Conclusion

Despite the progress made, no cure exists for RA, and the vast majority of our patients require lifelong DMARD therapy. Thus plenty of opportunity remains for further progress. By the time the 13th edition of this book is published, we will most likely have new biologic agents and small-molecule DMARDs available for use in treatment regimens. Regardless of new therapies that expand our portfolio of choices, the two areas where we still need to see the most progress are profiling patients based on parameters that predict differential responses to different therapies and monitoring the types and intensity of immunologic modification that we are producing. When substantial progress is made in these areas, even without new therapies, we will be able to obtain vastly superior and more expeditious disease control.

# 74 Sjögren's Syndrome

### KEY POINTS

### Historical Perspective

In 1888, Johann von Mikulicz-Radecki described a case of bilateral painless swelling of the lacrimal, parotid, and submandibular glands,1 an entity that later bore his name. Reports soon followed showing that Mikulicz disease was not a distinct pathologic entity but rather a clinical potpourri of conditions caused by leukemia, lymphoma, and tuberculosis. Shortly thereafter, salivary gland disease became linked with dryness of the eyes and oral mucosa when Henri Gougerot, a well-known and successful French dermatologist, wrote in 1925 about three cases of salivary gland atrophy with dryness of the eyes, mouth, and vagina. The modern concept of Sjögren's syndrome became firmly rooted when Henrik Sjögren, a Swedish ophthalmologist, reported in 1933 a series of 19 cases of keratoconjunctivitis sicca, including two cases with swelling of the major salivary glands. During the next two decades, Sjögren and others published extensively on various facets of the disease that now carries his name (also called Gougerot-Sjögren disease), with most of these early contributions coming from European ophthalmologists.

In 1953, Morgan and Castleman published their detailed histopathologic findings from 18 patients with enlarged lacrimal and salivary glands. This pathologic treatise consisted of cases with clinical features resembling those of Mikulicz's disease and Sjögren's syndrome. Notably, 15 of the 18 patients were women with lacrimal and salivary gland swelling that developed in the

fifth and sixth decades of life. Morgan and Castleman found in the salivary gland tissue a consistent "lymphoid element" accompanied by a striking proliferation of myoepithelial and epithelial cells. The salivary gland pathology in these cases was similar to that of the patients described by Henrik Sjögren with keratoconjunctivitis sicca. Because Sjögren's cases occurred mostly in middle-aged women, Morgan and Castleman incorrectly reasoned that Mikulicz's disease was a subset of Sjögren's syndrome with incomplete clinical manifestations. This now classic paper had the effect of unifying Mikulicz's disease and Sjögren's syndrome into a single disease entity. This belief prevailed for decades until the discovery of IgG4-related disease, which is now considered to be the underlying cause of most reported cases of Mikulicz's disease and distinct from Sjögren's syndrome (see Chapter 126).

When Joseph J. Bunim delivered the Heberden Oration at the Wellcome Foundation in London on December 2, 1960, he described in elegant detail the clinical, pathologic, and laboratory findings of the 40 patients with Sjögren's syndrome evaluated by Kurt Bloch, Martin Wohl, Richard Oglesby, Irwin Ship, and himself at the Clinical Center of the U.S. National Institutes of Health (NIH). All patients in their series had at least two of the three following features: keratoconjunctivitis sicca, xerostomia (with or without enlargement of the salivary glands), and rheumatoid arthritis (RA). Bunim also knew from the work of others that keratoconjunctivitis sicca and xerostomia, or sicca complex, occurred in some patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), scleroderma, polymyositis, and polyarteritis nodosa. In his lecture, he made the point that the exocrinopathy extended beyond the lacrimal and salivary glands to affect the pharynx, larynx, and trachea, as well as the vagina. Many of the patients with Sjögren's syndrome in the NIH cohort also had extraglandular manifestations, such as Raynaud's phenomenon, purpura, pulmonary infiltrates, and peripheral neuropathy. Among the NIH cases, Talal and Bunim took note of three patients with reticulum cell sarcoma (an older term that includes non-Hodgkin's lymphoma [NHL]) and a fourth patient with Waldenström's macroglobulinemia, drawing attention for the first time to the increased risk for lymphoma in this disease. They speculated that a "chronic state of immunologic hyperactivity and the proliferation of immunologically competent cells producing abnormal tissue antibodies predisposes to the relatively frequent development of malignant lymphoma.' "6

The NIH group also characterized the serologic markers of Sjögren's syndrome. In 1965 they reported that 12 of their 16 patients (75%) with sicca symptoms without another connective tissue disease tested positive for serum anti-nuclear antibody (ANA) reactivity by indirect immunofluorescence on rat liver tissue. Applying the Ouchterlony plate method, they further

showed sera from 13 of 16 (81%) of these patients contained precipitating antibodies to SjD and SjT, self-antigens later named Ro (SS-A) and La (SS-B). Another group next set the stage for our modern classification criteria by subdividing their patients into primary and secondary Sjögren's syndrome. Secondary Sjögren's syndrome referred to patients with sicca symptoms in the setting of another connective tissue disease, such as RA, SLE, scleroderma, or dermatomyositis, whereas primary Sjögren's syndrome was designated for those patients with a sicca complex in the absence of another connective tissue disease.

In the late 1960s and early 1970s, labial salivary gland biopsy was investigated as a diagnostic test for Sjögren's syndrome, leading to the development of grading systems based on the extent of chronic inflammation in these tissue specimens. In 1968 Chisholm and Mason proposed a simple grading scale (0 to 4), in which grades 0, 1, and 2 represented absent, slight, and moderate mononuclear cell infiltrates, respectively, and grades 3 and 4 corresponded to focal inflammatory cell scores of one or more foci per 4 mm2 of tissue, in which a focus equated to an aggregate of 50 or more mononuclear cells. In this initial study, 9 of the 10 patients with Sjögren's syndrome were classified as grade 3 or grade 4. By comparison, biopsies with lower grades came from patients with other chronic inflammatory conditions, as well as controls. Although it was a small study by today's standards, this work inspired others to validate and refine these findings.

One group at the NIH subsequently developed a grading system incorporating scales quantifying the extent of inflammation in the salivary gland tissue and the amount of acinar gland destruction. As expected, they found that labial salivary gland biopsies from patients with the sicca complex alone had higher grades of cellular infiltrates and acinar destruction than those with sicca symptoms and RA or RA alone. However, grading acinar destruction did not add diagnostic value independent of the severity of the infiltrates. One study from the University of California at San Francisco later modified the Chisholm and Mason grading scale by analyzing labial salivary gland biopsies from 54 patients with definite or probable Sjögren's syndrome together with 21 controls. Their results reinforced the diagnostic relevance of the focus score, including its relationship to focus size, and highlighted the presence of germinal centers (GCs). Grade 4 biopsies (>1 focus per 4 mm2 of tissue) were primarily from patients with Sjögren's syndrome, with the highest focus scores occurring in those with the primary form. The focus score was expanded to range from 1 to 12, in which a score of 12 was arbitrarily assigned to specimens with confluent foci. It was thereafter adopted as the "gold standard" for quantifying chronic inflammation in labial salivary gland biopsies. It is also possible to more precisely and specifically quantify T and B cell infiltrates in tissue utilizing digital technology, whole slide scanning methods, and software-based image assessment.

### Definitions and Classification Criteria

The clinical hallmarks of Sjögren's syndrome are keratoconjunctivitis sicca and xerostomia, or the sicca complex. The term keratoconjunctivitis sicca is derived from Latin, and its translation is "dryness of the cornea and conjunctiva." Xerostomia is synonymous with a dry mouth. As already mentioned, Sjögren's syndrome is subdivided into primary and secondary forms. Secondary Sjögren's syndrome refers to patients with keratoconjunctivitis sicca, xerostomia, or both, in the setting of another connective tissue disease such as RA, SLE, inflammatory myopathy, systemic sclerosis,

or a systemic vasculitis such as granulomatosis with polyangiitis. Patients with primary Sjögren's syndrome, on the other hand, manifest signs and symptoms of keratoconjunctivitis sicca and xerostomia in the absence of another connective tissue disease, provided they also meet serologic and/or histopathologic criteria. Since primary Sjögren's syndrome is associated with extraglandular features that overlap with those of other connective tissue diseases, it may be difficult in some cases to distinguish primary from secondary forms.

Sjogren's syndrome is often referred to as an autoimmune exocrinopathy12 or autoimmune epithelitis. The term exocrinopathy highlights the glandular involvement in this disease, which affects not only the lacrimal and salivary glands but also the apocrine sweat glands of the skin and the submucosal glands of the nose, pharynx, larynx, large airways, and vagina. The term epithelitis stems from the understanding that epithelial cells are not simply bystanders in the pathogenesis of this disease but play important roles in driving the chronic inflammatory response.

The first widely accepted classification criteria for Sjögren's syndrome were proposed by the American-European Consensus Group (AECG) in 2002.14 It included six items:

I. Ocular symptoms

II. Oral symptoms

III. Ocular signs (Schirmer-I test ≤5 mm/5 min or Rose Bengal score ≥4 by the van Bijsterveld scoring system)

IV. Histopathologic features (focus score ≥1 on labial salivary gland biopsy)

V. Objective evidence of salivary gland involvement by at least one abnormal test (salivary scintigraphy, parotid sialography, or unstimulated salivary flow rate ≤1.5 mL/15 min)

VI. Positive test for anti-Ro/SS-A or anti-La/SS-B antibodies

By this method, patients could be classified with primary Sjögren's syndrome if they satisfied any four of these criteria, provided that item 4 (histopathology) or 6 (serology) was positive. Patients could also meet criteria if they fulfilled any three of the four objective criteria items (3, 4, 5, and 6). Secondary Sjögren's syndrome was defined by the presence of item 1 or 2 plus a positive result for any two of items 3, 4, and 5 in the context of another well-defined connective tissue disease. Exclusion criteria were the use of anticholinergic drugs, preexisting lymphoma, prior head and neck radiation, AIDS, hepatitis C infection, sarcoidosis, and graft-versus-host disease.

In 2012, new classification criteria were proposed by the Sjögren's International Collaborative Clinical Alliance Cohort (SICCAC) and provisionally accepted by the American College of Rheumatology (ACR). These criteria sought to classify patients with primary Sjögren's syndrome solely on the basis of objective tests. To meet these classification criteria, patients must have at least two of the following:

I. Positive test for serum anti-Ro/SS-A and/or anti-La/SS-B antibodies or a positive test for rheumatoid factor and an ANA titer of greater than or equal to 1:320

II. Labial salivary gland biopsy exhibiting focal lymphocytic sialadenitis with a focus greater than or equal to 1 per 4 mm2

III. Keratoconjunctivitis sicca with an ocular staining score greater than or equal to 3

These classification criteria had a sensitivity of 92.5% and a specificity of 95.4% and were simpler than the 2002 revised AECG criteria that relied on tests of salivary gland function unavailable in most clinical practices. However, the 2012 criteria were criticized as unduly invasive because they required a slit lamp exam and corneal staining and/or lip biopsy. Studies comparing the operating characteristics of the 2002 AECG and 2012

SICCAC/ACR criteria showed general agreement between these two classification systems, with the primary sources of discordance due to differences in the ocular staining score cut-offs (SICCAC/ ACR ≥3/12 vs. AECG ≥4/9) and the inclusion of a positive ANA and/or rheumatoid factor in the SICCAC/ACR criteria. 16,

In 2016, the ACR and the European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology (EULAR) proposed a new set of classification criteria endorsed by both organizations.18, This classification system was designed to apply to patients with ocular or oral dryness or systemic manifestations suggestive of Sjögren's syndrome and included the following items:

I. Histopathology showing focal lymphocytic sialadenitis with a focus score greater than or equal to 1 per 4 mm2

II. Presence of anti-Ro/SS-A antibodies

III. SICCA ocular staining score of greater than or equal to 5 using lissamine green or fluorescein dye (or Rose Bengal score ≥4 by the van Bijsterveld scoring system)

IV. Schirmer test of less than or equal to 5 mm per 5 minutes

V. Unstimulated whole salivary flow of less than or equal to 0.1 mL per minute

Each component is assigned a weighted score with a maximum score of 9 (Table 74.1). A patient may be classified as having primary Sjögren's syndrome if they have a score of 4 or greater. Similar to the 2002 AECG criteria, these criteria can only be met if they satisfy item 1 (histopathology) or 2 (serology). In a validation cohort, this set of criteria showed a sensitivity of 96% and a specificity of 95%.

The 2016 ACR/EULAR classification criteria differ from previously published criteria in their weighted scoring system, the removal of anti-La/SS-B antibodies as a serologic item, and the use of the Sjögren's International Collaborative Clinical Alliance (SICCA) ocular staining score. Anti-La/SS-B antibodies were excluded from these criteria because the SICCA research group and others found no difference in clinical features between patients with anti-La/SS-B antibodies alone and patients testing negative for anti-Ro/SS-A and anti-La/SS-B. The SICCA ocular staining score utilizes lissamine green or fluorescein dye instead of Rose Bengal dye, which can be painful and damaging to the cornea. The 2016 ACR/EULAR criteria have shown high concordance with previously published classification criteria. 22-24

### Epidemiology

Primary Sjögren's syndrome ranks among the most common of the autoimmune diseases, with a prevalence rate ranging from 0.06% to 1.5%.25-27 However, the epidemiologic data are confounded by variations in the ages of the study populations and differences in the classification criteria used for case identification. The prevalence of primary Sjögren's syndrome is much higher in women than in men (e.g., approximately 10:1), with a peak incidence in the fifth and sixth decades of life. Sex ratio, age distribution, and clinical features can vary depending on the ethnicity and geographic region of the study population.26,

Primary Sjögren's syndrome occurs infrequently in children, with onset as early as 5 years. Classification criteria may be less sensitive for identifying cases of primary Sjögren's syndrome in children than in adults because of differences between these two age groups in the clinical presentation of this disease.29,

The prevalence of secondary Sjögren's syndrome ranges between 4% and 31% in RA, 6 and 19% in SLE, and 14% and 21% in systemic sclerosis. To be classified with secondary Sjögren's syndrome, patients must have symptoms of keratoconjunctivitis sicca or xerostomia and objective evidence of decreased tear or salivary flow.

### Etiology and Pathogenesis

In primary Sjögren's syndrome, a common feature of disease pathogenesis is the presence of serum autoantibodies, indicative of a loss of immunologic tolerance to self-antigens. The appearance of autoantibodies may precede the onset of clinical disease, and thus the loss of immune tolerance appears to be permissive and insufficient alone to induce tissue inflammation and damage. T cells and B cells infiltrate the labial salivary glands of patients with primary Sjögren's syndrome. However, the evolution of these aberrant cellular responses in the secondary and tertiary lymphoid tissues and their role in inciting tissue inflammation remain incompletely understood. It is often assumed that a genetically predisposed innate and adaptive immune system increases disease susceptibility and that environmental and stochastic factors are involved in triggering the chronic inflammatory response.

Because a disproportionately high number of the cases of primary Sjögren's syndrome occur in women, the search for environmental triggers has included studies of abnormal regulation of estrogens and androgens. However, no major differences have been found between patients with primary Sjögren's syndrome and healthy controls in serum levels of sex steroid hormones. Another piece of evidence against the role of sex hormones in

the mechanisms of ongoing disease is that treatment with the hormone dehydroepiandrosterone, which acts on the androgen receptor, has shown no clinical efficacy in women with primary Sjogren's syndrome.

Among possible viral triggers, human herpesviruses such as Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) and cytomegalovirus have received the most attention because of their suppressive effects on T cell immunity, their ability to establish persistent infection, their tropism for salivary and lacrimal gland tissue, and the knowledge that lytic replication requires polyclonal B cell stimulation and plasma cell differentiation. In patients with primary Sjögren's syndrome, the EBV genome has been detected in autoantibody-producing plasma cells located in the periphery of ectopic lymphoid structures; in addition, high levels of EBV DNA are found in salivary glands from patients with this disease.34-35 Furthermore, patients with the primary type demonstrate higher positivity rates of serum antibodies against EBV early antigen that are positive for both anti-Ro/SSA and anti-La/SSB (48.7%) and anti-Ro/SSA alone (39.8%) compared with Ro/SSA and La/SSB negative cases (28.3%), implying a role for EBV in stimulating these autoantibody responses. Other studies have attempted to link primary Sjögren's syndrome to infection with human T-lymphotropic virus type 1, coxsackievirus, hepatitis B, and hepatitis C. A viral etiology for the primary type is further suggested by the presence of a type I interferon (IFN) signature, which is a hallmark of host defense against viral infection. Despite these tantalizing clues, the available evidence does not yet support a direct role for viral infection as a cause of this disease.

### Genetics and Epigenetics

It has been difficult to estimate the genetic risk for primary Sjogren's syndrome because of the absence of large twin studies. However, many large families have two or more members with 37 primary Sjögren's syndrome, attesting to a genetic component. The primary type is considered a complex genetic disorder, similar to the heritability of SLE and RA. In fact, the gene variants identified as risk factors in primary Sjögren's syndrome include many of the same gene variants identified as risk factors in other systemic autoimmune diseases. Also, the familial clustering of cases of primary Sjögren's syndrome with cases of SLE, RA, systemic sclerosis, and autoimmune thyroid disease implies common genetic risk factors across these autoimmune conditions.

The strongest genetic contributor to disease susceptibility in primary Sjögren's syndrome can be found in the human leukocyte antigen (HLA) locus on human chromosome 6, especially the HLA-class II alleles.39, In Caucasian populations, the most reproducible risk variants are within the DR2 and DR3 alleles in the DRB1 locus. The strongest associations are found between DRB1*03 and DQB1*02 alleles and the presence of anti-Ro/SSA and/or anti-La/SSB antibodies. In a meta-analysis of 1166 cases and 6470 controls of diverse ethnicity, the most significant risk variants were DRB1*03:01, DQA1*05:01, and DQB1*02:01.41

Efforts to identify disease susceptibility genes outside of the HLA locus in primary Sjogren's syndrome have been greatly aided by genome-wide association studies (GWASs). Results from these studies have shown the non-HLA risk alleles are much weaker in effect size than the HLA risk variants and are located in genes relating to type I IFN signaling, B cell development, and cellular immunity.42-51 Genes in the type I IFN pathway are of particular interest in primary Sjögren's syndrome, as they are highly

expressed in the peripheral blood and salivary glands of patients with this disease compared with controls. A summary of these initial genetic associations in primary Sjögren's syndrome and their potential pathologic relevance can be found in Table 74.2. A more recently published GWAS of patients with Sjögren's syndrome with European ancestry increased the total number of identified genetic risk loci from 12 to 22.52 In this study, a pathway analysis suggested these new risk variants are involved in regulating immune cell function, inflammatory signaling, cell survival and proliferation, and cell stress.

Epigenetics can also influence the type of immune response through the regulation of gene expression by mechanisms other than a change in DNA sequence of that gene. This type of heritable change in gene expression primarily occurs through the alteration of chromatin structure by DNA methylation and histone modification in conserved noncoding elements of genes, namely, promoters, enhancers, and silencers. These regions of DNA bind transcription factors, which in turn initiate and regulate transcription. Epigenetic modification via methylation and demethylation and histone modification affects the binding of transcription factors by altering DNA accessibility and chromatin structure. There is increasing evidence for the contribution of epigenetics to the development of autoimmune diseases.

Epigenetic modification may be cell type and tissue specific. Early studies of peripheral blood from patients with primary Sjögren's syndrome have shown that naive CD4 T cells from peripheral blood are hypomethylated in regulatory regions of several immune response genes, including lymphotoxin-α and several IFN-related genes, with more conspicuous differences in those patients with anti-Ro/SSA and/or anti-La/SSB antibodies. A genome-wide DNA methylation analysis of whole blood has found that IFN-related genes are also hypomethylated in B cells compared with controls, resulting in increased IFN gene expression. However, not much is known about the chromatin architecture in the salivary gland tissues of patients with Sjögren's syndrome and the limited data thus far lacks cellular granularity. Since many of the non-HLA risk loci associated with primary Sjogren's syndrome are located within gene regulatory networks that may drive the pathology of this disease in the salivary gland tissue, 53 a more thorough understanding of the functional implications of these risk loci will require analysis of specific cell types and tissues at single-cell resolution.

Some of the conserved noncoding elements also encode microRNAs (miRNAs), epigenetic modulators that also regulate mRNA expression without altering gene sequences. MiRNAs influence gene expression in both the innate and adaptive immune system and play key roles in late B cell differentiation and development and the establishment of B cell tolerance. Their transcription may too be regulated by DNA methylation and histone modification and RNA modification. Early studies have shown that miRNA expression patterns in salivary gland tissue can distinguish patients with Sjögren's syndrome from controls, suggesting a pathologic role for miRNAs in the regulation of the tissue chronic inflammatory response.

### Adaptive and Innate Immunity

Many insights have been gained about disease mechanisms in primary Sjögren's syndrome from studies of animal models and of humans with this disease. Experiments in model systems enable hypotheses to be examined in ways not possible in humans and have contributed to our understanding of the

immunoregulatory disturbances underlying the clinical phenotype (Table 74.3).55, While animal studies have shed light on possible disease mechanisms, human studies of salivary gland tissue have significantly advanced our understanding of disease pathogenesis. In labial salivary gland biopsies from patients with primary Sjögren's syndrome, approximately 90% of the infiltrating cells are CD4+ T lymphocytes and B lymphocytes, with the remainder consisting of an admixture of plasma cells, CD8+ T cells, FoxP3+ T regulatory cells, CD56+ natural killer cells, and macrophages, as well as myeloid and plasmacytoid dendritic cells (DCs) (Fig. 74.1). Most of the infiltrating T cells bear the memory phenotype (CD45RO) and display a restricted T cell receptor repertoire representing several different clonotypes across multiple Vβ families. The proportion of B cells in the infiltrate generally increases with the severity of the inflammatory lesion.

The infiltrating mononuclear cells tend to coalesce around ducts and blood vessels, and in more severe inflammatory lesions form aggregates organized into GC-like structures. The GC-like structures display well-circumscribed mononuclear cell infiltrates with B and T cell components, Ki-67+ proliferating cells, CD21/ CD35+ follicular DC networks, and CD31+ high endothelial venules (HEVs). The expression of chemokines like CXCL12, CXCL13, and CCL21 by epithelial cells and the formation of HEVs and GC-like structures foster a microenvironment capable of attracting and retaining B cells.59, Myeloid DCs and macrophages are mostly found in proximity to the ductal epithelium, where they secrete inflammatory cytokines like TNF, interleukin (IL)-6, IL-10, IL-12, and IL-18. Minor salivary glands also contain a small number of plasmacytoid DCs, the main producers of the type I IFNs. A robust type 1 IFN signature has been detected both in the salivary glands and peripheral blood of patients with

primary Sjögren's syndrome.61-63 The secretion of type 1 IFNs by plasmacytoid DCs is among the first lines of defense against viral infection and is partially dependent on signals through TLR7 and TLR9, providing a rationale for a link between this disease and a viral or retroviral trigger.

The analysis of T cell cytokines in labial salivary gland biopsies from patients with primary Sjögren's syndrome suggests a

predominantly Th1and Th17-driven response. Studies of the expression of cytokine messenger RNAs (mRNAs) in salivary gland tissue show mainly upregulation of IL-2 and IFN-γ, Th1specific cytokines, and lesser quantities of IL-4, IL-5, and IL-13, the Th2-specific cytokines. The salivary gland microenvironment in primary Sjögren's syndrome is also rich in transforming growth factor-β, IL-6, and IL-23, cytokines that are known to

promote the development of Th17 cells. This finding, along with increased levels of circulating IL-17 in primary Sjögren's syndrome, supports a role of Th17 cells in disease pathogenesis. In addition, the salivary gland contains FoxP3+ regulatory T cells. These cells typically show suppressive behavior, but as yet they have an uncertain role in regulating chronic inflammation in the salivary gland.

GC-like structures found in some of the salivary gland biopsies provide an opportune environment for the selection and differentiation of antigen-driven B cell responses. Evidence of immune system dysregulation is not limited to glandular tissue. The distribution of peripheral blood B cell subsets in primary Sjögren's syndrome differs from healthy controls, showing increased proportions of CD27- (naive) B cells and decreased proportions of CD27+ (memory) B cells. These changes in the peripheral blood could result from abnormal trafficking of CD27+ memory B cells to the target tissues, aberrations in B cell development, or both.

Several intrinsic B cell defects have also been found in patients with primary Sjögren's syndrome, including abnormal retention of pre-switch Ig transcripts in circulating post-switch CD27+ memory B cells69 and enhanced B cell signaling due to altered kinetics of B cell receptor translocation to lipid rafts. Moreover, studies in patients with primary Sjögren's syndrome have shown increased serum and salivary gland tissue levels of B cell—activating factor (BAFF), a prosurvival factor for B cells. BAFF is typically produced by monocytes, macrophages, and plasmacytoid DCs; however, in primary Sjögren's syndrome it is also produced by

T cells, B cells, and salivary epithelial cells. BAFF production is induced by type I IFN, and thus may provide a link between the innate and adaptive immune dysregulation in primary Sjögren's syndrome. Interest in BAFF as a therapeutic target has grown since belimumab, a monoclonal antibody against BAFF, was approved for the treatment of SLE.

Lymphotoxin (LT)-β, another B cell-related molecule, is upregulated in salivary gland tissue of patients with primary Sjögren's syndrome. LT-β is required for the formation of lymph nodes and GCs, whereas the heterodimer LT-α/LT-β can induce the development of ectopic GC-like structures. LT-α in soluble form stimulates the secretion of IFNs and chemokines, which are elevated in the diseased salivary gland tissue. IL-14, an important B cell growth factor, is also increased in the serum and saliva of patients with primary Sjögren's syndrome. IL-14 transgenic mice develop a Sjögren's-like phenotype in which the local tissue response is critically dependent on LT-α. Blocking LT-β receptor signaling in nonobese diabetic (NOD) mice ablates the lymphoid organization in the salivary glands and improves their function, further evidence that LTs may play a role in the pathogenesis of Sjögren's syndrome. Nevertheless, in a randomized, placebocontrolled, phase II clinical trial, treatment with baminercept, a LT-β receptor fusion protein, failed to significantly improve glandular and extraglandular disease in patients with primary Sjögren's syndrome.

### Autoantibodies

Anti-Ro/SS-A and anti-La/SS-B antibodies do not appear to have a pathogenic role in disease mechanisms despite their diagnostic and prognostic significance. The stimulating antigen(s) for these antibody responses is unknown. An aberrant response to self may be provoked by altered expression of autoantigens. Several models have been proposed to explain the altered expression of autoantigens, including differential expression of protein isoforms, post-translational modification, and abnormal autoantigen presentation via apoptotic blebs, exosomes, or heat shock proteinmediated cross-priming. Ro/SS-A and La/SS-B proteins do in fact show increased expression in the vicinity of immunopathologic lesions where they may induce local immune responses. Saliva from patients with primary Sjögren's syndrome contains anti-Ro/SS-A and anti-La/SS-B antibodies. Although this finding may be the result of local production of autoantibodies, it may also reflect extravasation of proteins from blood vessels into the inflamed tissues.
