However, the different assays for detecting serum anti-M3R antibodies in patients with primary Sjögren's syndrome have produced inconsistent results. For this reason, it has been difficult to determine the true prevalence of serum anti-M3R antibodies in the primary type and the possible relationship of these autoantibodies to glandular hypofunction.

Other autoantigens have been identified in patients with primary Sjögren's syndrome and include α-fodrin, poly(ADP)ribose polymerase, carbonic anhydrase, ICA69 protein, salivary protein 1 (SP1), parotid secretory protein (PSP), aquaporins, and calponin-3.81-83 Despite initial enthusiasm for the potential importance of α-fodrin as a stimulating autoantigen in primary Sjögren's syndrome, subsequent studies have shown that serum anti-αfodrin antibodies are not highly specific for this diagnosis. A recent evaluation of autoantibodies to SP1, carbonic anhydrase 6, and PSP found that at least one of these antibodies was present in 60.9% of patients with primary Sjögren's syndrome; however, they were also present in 50% of control patients with dry eyes.

### Glandular Epithelium

In primary Sjögren's syndrome, glandular epithelial cells may in part drive the abnormal immune response. As discussed previously, mononuclear cells preferentially congregate around the ductal epithelium in the diseased salivary gland tissue. The epithelial cells in the inflamed glands show upregulated expression of several cell surface markers, including class I and II HLA molecules, adhesion molecules such as intercellular adhesion molecule-1 (CD54), vascular cell adhesion molecule-1 (CD106), and E-selectin and costimulatory molecules such as CD40, CD80, and CD86. They also produce increased levels of proinflammatory cytokines, such as IL-1, IL-6, IL-12, IL-18, TNF, and BAFF.63, Salivary gland epithelial cells express functional Toll-like receptors (TLRs), including TLR3, TLR7, and TLR9, endowing them with a capability to sense pathogens and endogenous molecules produced by injured tissues. Activated epithelial cells are likely important drivers of the aberrant innate and adaptive immune responses, not only in the lacrimal and salivary glands but also in the lungs and kidneys and other extraglandular sites.

At least two models have been proposed to explain the glandular hypofunction in Sjögren's syndrome. In one model, it may be hypothesized the glandular tissue is destroyed by an immune onslaught perpetuated by persistent exposure to self-antigens or other environmental stimulants (e.g., viral infection), leading to apoptosis of acinar epithelial cells, fibrosis, and irreversible loss of salivary gland function (Fig. 74.2A). A weakness of this model is that studies suggest epithelial cells rarely undergo apoptosis in the salivary gland tissue despite the fact they increase expression of mediators of cell death such as Fas, Fas ligand, and Bax (B cell lymphoma 2—associated X protein). Ligand binding to CD40 expressed on epithelial cells in the salivary gland tissue may also lead to Fas-mediated cell death by downregulating cellular FLICE-like inhibitor protein, an inhibitor of Fas-mediated cell death. Because no studies have yet shown an imbalance truly exists between the rates of glandular proliferation and damage, the relevance of this model to glandular hypofunction is uncertain. It also does not explain why many patients with markedly diminished salivary flow retain substantial amounts of normalappearing acinar tissue in their salivary glands.

A second model assumes apoptosis is not a significant factor in the loss of acinar epithelium and instead posits that glandular function is inhibited (and not destroyed) by immune-mediated mechanisms (Fig. 74.2B). This model implies a reversibility component to the loss of salivary flow and a pathologic process interrupting M3R activation. Possible mechanisms for such inhibitory effects include a reduction in acetylcholine release, increased breakdown of acetylcholine in the epilemmal space (e.g., acetylcholine must diffuse 100 nm from its release point at the nerve ending to the receptor on the cell), increased cell stress, and blockade of M3R by antibodies. Relatively little direct evidence supports any of these mechanisms, except for the experiments showing that anti-M3R antibodies may block receptor function. Studies have also shown that salivary gland acinar cells from patients with Sjögren's syndrome have defects in Ca+2 signaling, impaired cell volume regulation, and reduced aquaporin 5 expression. Thus, it is possible the immune cell infiltration and cytokine milieu in the salivary gland microenvironment interferes in some way with acinar gland function, perhaps by altering molecular signaling pathways, inducing cell stress, or causing mitochondrial dysfunction. To this point, impairment of salivary gland secretion in the NOD mouse does not appear to be readily explained by the destruction of acinar glands. Regardless, the "immune-destructive" and "immune-inhibited" models are not mutually exclusive and both CC• mechanisms may contribute at different stages of disease to the observed glandular hypofunction.

### Clinical Features

### Keratoconjunctivitis Sicca

Chronic inflammation of the lacrimal glands diminishes secretion of aqueous tears, which, if severe, may destroy the conjunctival and bulbar epithelium. Aqueous tear deficiency produces dry eye, causing symptoms of grittiness or foreign body sensation, burning, photophobia, and eye fatigue. Routine eye examination usually reveals a reduction in the tear flow, as measured by the Schirmer-I test. Additional findings may include the absence of tears in the conjunctival sac and dilated bulbar conjunctival vessels. Thick mucus may also be seen in the inner canthus of the eye. Slit-lamp examination allows for more detailed visualization of the corneal and conjunctival surface. After instillation of lissamine green dye or fluorescein onto the ocular surface, slit-lamp examination may expose devitalized cells or epithelial defects, respectively, signs of corneal and conjunctival damage. Severe dryness may result in corneal abrasion or ulceration.

The anatomy of the tear film informs the differential diagnosis of dry eye (Table 74.4). The tear film consists of three major layers: the outer lipid layer, the middle aqueous layer, and the inner mucin layer. The middle aqueous layer is diminished in Sjögren's syndrome owing to reduced tear flow. Conditions associated with infiltration of the lacrimal glands (e.g., sarcoidosis) and the loss of tear flow from medications, aging, and estrogen deficiency may also cause dry eye. The lipid layer derives from the meibomian glands and traps the aqueous tear film on the eyeball and protects it from rapid evaporation. Meibomian gland dysfunction, or posterior blepharitis, produces dry eyes from rapid evaporation of tears; it often accompanies aqueous tear deficiency in Sjögren's syndrome and can be an aggravating factor in patients with keratoconjunctivitis sicca that requires additional therapy. Meibomian gland dysfunction is often associated with ocular rosacea and seborrheic dermatitis, two conditions that also lead to dry eye. Lipid

degradation resulting from meibomian gland inflammation leads to the production of free fatty acids, which irritate the ocular surface and in turn may cause punctate keratopathy. The mucin layer originates from the goblet cells of the conjunctiva and, if deficient, leads to an uneven distribution of the tear film over the surface of the eye. Vitamin A deficiency and Stevens-Johnson syndrome are examples of conditions associated with an abnormal mucin layer.

### Xerostomia

The changes in the quality and quantity of the saliva are responsible for the signs and symptoms of xerostomia. Although symptoms of dry mouth are relatively common in the general population, they are usually more severe in Sjögren's syndrome and cause perpetual difficulties with chewing and swallowing dry food, altered taste (metallic, salty, or bitter), and struggles with prolonged speaking. Patients with xerostomia may have problems wearing dentures. Despite complaints of a dry mouth and reduced salivary flow, many patients may appear to have a normal oral examination. Others with more severe hypofunction will manifest a dry, sticky, or erythematous oral mucosa.

Two complications of xerostomia are important in the care of patients, especially those with severe deficits in salivary flow. Dental complications include rampant caries, cracked teeth, and loose fillings. A predisposition to oral candidiasis, another frequent complication, typically manifests as the atrophic variant, which is characterized by erythema and atrophy of the oral mucosa and filiform papillae on the dorsum of the tongue, with angular cheilitis. Sometimes, a thin, white exudate may appear on the surface of the tongue. The "thrush-like" variant of oral candidiasis is seen much less frequently in patients with xerostomia except in the face of recent antibiotic therapy.

Approximately one-quarter of patients with primary Sjögren's syndrome suffer enlargement of the parotid or submandibular glands during the course of their disease. Chronic swelling is usually painless and may be unilateral or bilateral; it is often diffuse and firm by palpation (Fig. 74.3). Acute episodes of swelling are frequently painful and may intermittently punctuate the clinical course of primary Sjögren's syndrome. These acute episodes, which likely result from dried mucus transiently obstructing the major ducts, usually subside within a few days with conservative therapy. Rarely, bacterial infections may cause acute salivary gland swelling and should be considered as a possible etiology if the patient has a fever or other constitutional complaints. Asymmetric gland enlargement with palpable hard nodules that are increasing in size may indicate a neoplasm such as a lymphoma.

### Involvement of Other Exocrine Glands

Glandular hypofunction affects the nasal passages (meatal obstruction from dried mucus), larynx (hoarseness), trachea (cough), vagina (dyspareunia), and skin (pruritus), producing symptoms of dryness. Virtually any exocrine gland may be involved in this disease.

### Extraglandular Manifestations

Approximately half of the patients with primary Sjögren's syndrome manifest signs or symptoms of extraglandular disease, and this percentage is even higher if fatigue is considered as a systemic manifestation. Extraglandular involvement is more likely to occur in patients with positive serologies (serum anti-Ro/SS-A,

anti-La/SS-B antibodies, and rheumatoid factor) and hypergammaglobulinemia, cryoglobulinemia, and hypocomplementemia. Approximately 15% of patients with primary Sjögren's syndrome develop severe extraglandular disease.

### Fatigue

Fatigue, a complex and multifaceted phenomenon, occurs in approximately 70% of patients with primary Sjögren's syndrome. It is also a symptom of depression, chronic anxiety, fibromyalgia, and sleep deficit, as well as a side effect of certain medications. The United Kingdom Sjögren's Interest Group has developed an instrument called the Profile of Fatigue and DiscomfortSicca Symptoms Inventory that specifically measures both somatic (needing rest, poor starting, low stamina, weak muscles) and mental fatigue (poor concentration, poor memory) in this disease. In 547 patients with a confirmed diagnosis of primary Sjogren's syndrome, somatic fatigue was the dominant predictor of physical function and general health. The relative contribution of behavioral and cognitive variables to fatigue was studied in 94 patients with primary Sjogren's syndrome, finding that fatigue is common in patients without depression and only partially explained by psychosocial variables. The link between fatigue and "biologic disease activity" is not fully understood in primary Sjögren's syndrome. Increased serum cytokines such as IL-6 and type I IFNs and neuroendocrine and autonomic dysfunction are postulated to be contributing factors to the physical and mental aspects of fatigue in this setting.

### Raynaud's Syndrome

Raynaud's syndrome, reported in 13% to 33% of patients with primary Sjögren's syndrome, often precedes the onset of sicca symptoms by several years. Digital ulcers occur only rarely.

### Skin

Among the dermatologic manifestations of primary Sjögren's syndrome, the most common are xerosis, or dry skin, eyelid dermatitis, and angular cheilitis. In addition, many patients develop a variety of other cutaneous manifestations, including annular erythema, purpura, and cutaneous vasculitis.

Annular erythema has been described in three major types: a donut-ring-like erythema with an elevated border (type I); a subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus—like lesion with marginally scaled polycyclic erythema (type II); and a papular insect bite—like erythema (type III). Histopathologically, these lesions are characterized by a deep perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate without the epidermal changes associated with lupus. 1 In some cases, immunoglobulin and complement deposition is observed along the basement membrane with liquefaction degeneration in the basal layer of the involved skin. The type I lesion appears to be specific for primary Sjögren's syndrome, occurring predominantly in Asian as opposed to Western populations.

The most common form of cutaneous vasculitis in primary Sjögren's syndrome is palpable purpura, primarily of the lower extremities. Purpuric lesions in Sjögren's syndrome may cause pain but they rarely ulcerate or lead to severe ischemia. Other manifestations of cutaneous vasculitis in primary Sjögren's syndrome include erythematous papules, macules, and urticarial vasculitis. Patients with cutaneous vasculitis are more likely to experience other extraglandular manifestations of disease, such as arthritis, peripheral neuropathy, Raynaud's syndrome, and livedo reticularis. Likewise, cutaneous vasculitis is often associated with

abnormal laboratory findings such as anemia, elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, hypergammaglobulinemia, hypocomplementemia, an elevated serum rheumatoid factor, and positive tests for serum anti-Ro/SS-A and anti-La/SS-B antibodies. About half of cases with palpable purpura are associated with detectable serum cryoglobulins.

### Joints

Polyarthralgia occurs frequently in patients with primary Sjogren's syndrome. In a retrospective study, articular symptoms in the primary type had a prevalence rate of 45%. A subset of these patients show objective signs of synovitis, which is nonerosive, symmetric, and variable in intensity. Joint symptoms may precede the diagnosis of primary Sjögren's syndrome in as many as onethird of cases. In two separate studies, anti-citrullinated protein antibodies (ACPAs) were detected in serum from 7.5% and 9.9% of patients with primary Sjogren's syndrome. 105, However, in only one of these studies was their presence closely associated with synovitis, 106 and in neither study did it appear that serum ACPA positivity was associated with radiographic erosions or progression to RA.

### Lung

Involvement of the airways and lung parenchyma in primary Sjögren's syndrome may take several forms, including xerotrachea and xerobronchitis, nonspecific interstitial pneumonitis (NSIP), lymphocytic interstitial pneumonitis (LIP), usual interstitial pneumonitis (UIP), bronchiolitis, and lymphoma. The estimated prevalence of pulmonary involvement in primary Sjögren's syndrome varies depending on the thoroughness of the evaluation. In a study of 123 patients with the primary type, 11.4% showed pulmonary signs or symptoms and/or impaired pulmonary function with abnormal chest computed tomography (CT) findings at the time of evaluation.

Evidence of small-airway dysfunction is often found in asymptomatic patients with normal radiologic studies. In symptomatic patients, NSIP appears to be the predominant type of lung involvement. The diagnosis can often be made on the basis of clinical presentation, pulmonary function tests (PFTs), and abnormal chest CT findings. PFTs in patients with NSIP show a restrictive pattern with reduced diffusion capacity of lung carbon monoxide (DLCO). Chest CT scans reveal ground-glass opacities and a reticular nodular pattern. Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL), which is not usually required for diagnosis, shows evidence of alveolar inflammation, with elevated neutrophil or lymphocyte counts, or both. LIP, a subset of NSIP, is also associated with a restrictive pattern on PFTs. Chest CT findings are ground-glass opacities and thin-walled cysts, with centrilobular nodules, interlobular septal thickening, and bronchovascular bundle thickening (Fig. 74.4A). Microscopically, the lung biopsy from patients with LIP shows a diffuse interstitial infiltrate composed of lymphocytes, plasma cells, and histiocytes that expand the interlobular and alveolar spaces (Fig. 74.4B). PFTs in patients with UIP also show a restrictive pattern as in NSIP and LIP, but the presence of lower lobe fibrosis, honeycombing, and traction bronchiectasis on chest CT distinguishes it from these other two types. In patients with bronchiolitis, PFTs may show a restrictive or obstructive functional defect. The chest CT scan usually displays reticulonodular infiltrates, but it may be normal in mild cases. Follicular bronchiolitis is characterized by nodular opacities, which on biopsy are characterized by lymphocytic infiltrates with GC-like structures encircling respiratory bronchioles.

Lung biopsy can reveal evidence of NSIP, bronchiolitis, or other pathologic processes. One study evaluated 33 patients with primary Sjögren's syndrome that had biopsy-proven lung disease and found evidence of NSIP in 20 (61%), NHL in 4 (12%), diffuse bronchiolitis in 4 (12%), and amyloid in 2 (6%). . These patients' PFTs demonstrated restrictive changes in 19 (58%) and obstructive changes in 3 (9%). Analysis of BAL fluid from the 28 patients who had this procedure was uniformly abnormal, showing elevated lymphocyte counts in 18 (64%) and elevated neutrophil counts in 19 (68%). Chest CT findings revealed an NSIP pattern in 14 (45%) and a UIP pattern in 4 (13%); 3 patients (10%) showed a pattern of organizing pneumonia. There were no cases of LIP in this series. By comparison, one study evaluated 18 patients with biopsy-proven lung disease and found a

histopathologic pattern of NSIP in 5 (28%) patients, organizing pneumonia in 4 (22%), UIP in 3 (17%), LIP in 3 (17%), lymphoma in 2 (11%), and amyloid in 1 (6%). Pulmonary arterial hypertension is a rare complication of Sjögren's syndrome.

### Kidney

Clinically significant renal disease in primary Sjögren's syndrome is present in approximately 5% of patients and may manifest as tubular interstitial nephritis, type I renal tubular acidosis (RTA), glomerulonephritis, or nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.93, Tubular interstitial nephritis, which is characterized histopathologically by a peritubular lymphocytic infiltrate and fibrosis, may progress to end-stage renal disease (Fig. 74.5). A patient with primary Sjögren's syndrome has been described with the rare finding of tubular interstitial nephritis and acquired Gitelman's syndrome. Rarely, severe potassium wasting from type I RTA can lead to muscle paralysis. Glomerular disease in primary Sjögren's syndrome may take several forms, including membranous, membranoproliferative, mesangial proliferative, and focal crescentic glomerulonephritis. Glomerular disease is most often the result of immune complex deposition in the kidney and is more frequently associated with lymphoma than tubulointerstitial disease.

### Gastrointestinal

Patients with primary Sjögren's syndrome have an increased frequency of gastrointestinal symptoms compared with the general population. Dysphagia and heartburn are particularly common complaints that may result from impaired salivary flow or esophageal dysmotility, or both. Approximately one-third of patients with primary Sjögren's syndrome have varying degrees of esophageal dysfunction, although many studies have been unable to correlate symptoms of dysphagia with a functional abnormality. One study found that patients with the primary type do not have a primary disturbance of esophageal motility but, rather, defective clearance of esophageal acid that exposes the esophageal lining to excessive amounts of acid, which in turn produces morphologic changes and secondary dysmotility. Other results suggest parasympathetic dysfunction might be at the root of the esophageal abnormalities. A case has also been described of a patient with primary Sjögren's syndrome in whom esophageal achalasia developed in the setting of a sensory ataxic neuropathy, which damaged the myenteric plexus and was responsible for producing the esophageal dysfunction. In addition, chronic atrophic gastritis, which may cause dyspeptic symptoms, has been reported in a small number of cases of primary Sjogren's syndrome.

Liver enzyme abnormalities may develop in patients with the primary type for a variety of reasons, most often from an associated disorder such as hepatitis C virus infection, autoimmune hepatitis, primary biliary cirrhosis, celiac disease, or nonspecific hepatitis. Bowel symptoms such as abdominal pain and constipation occur more commonly in patients with primary Sjogren's syndrome than healthy controls, but their etiology is often obscure.

### Nervous System

Neurologic abnormalities are protean in primary Sjögren's syndrome, with varied patterns of peripheral and central nervous system (CNS) involvement. The prevalence of CNS involvement that can be directly attributed to primary Sjögren's syndrome is exceedingly low (approximately 1% to 2% of patients), although higher rates have been reported with more liberal case definitions. Higher prevalence rates are reported when minor cognitive and

mood disturbances are included in the definition of CNS involvement. Neuropsychiatric symptoms such as depression and minor cognitive disturbances occur in approximately one-third of patients with primary Sjögren's syndrome. However, these neuropsychiatric problems occur frequently in the general population and patients with chronic diseases in general. Rarely, cases have been described in which severe cognitive dysfunction develops in patients with primary Sjögren's syndrome. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) in these instances typically shows nonspecific T2-weighted, high-intensity signals in the white matter that have an uncertain relationship to the clinical CNS findings.

Although rare, there is an increasing recognition of the association between primary Sjögren's syndrome and neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD), an autoimmune disease of the CNS associated with serum anti—aquaporin-4 antibod- . The major clinical manifestations of NMOSD include ies. optic neuritis, longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis, and/or demyelinating lesions in the area postrema of the dorsal medulla, brainstem, diencephalon, and/or cerebrum. In some cases, NMOSD occurs prior to or simultaneous with the diagnosis of primary Sjögren's syndrome. Other rare CNS deficits in patients with the primary type include hemiparesis, movement disorders, cerebellar syndromes, recurrent transient ischemic attacks, transverse myelitis without associated anti—aquaporin-4 antibodies, and other myelopathies. 122_125

Peripheral nervous system involvement is among the most common of the extraglandular features of primary Sjögren's syndrome. In a cross-sectional study, peripheral neuropathy was diagnosed in 17 (27%) of 62 patients with the primary type on the basis of a conventional neurologic examination. However, only 34 (55%) of the patients with primary Sjogren's syndrome in this group had abnormal nerve conduction velocity studies,

including 19 (31%) with a motor neuropathy, 8 (13%) with a sensory neuropathy, and 7 (11%) with a sensorimotor neuropathy. In this study, two patients with normal nerve conduction velocity studies were diagnosed with a small-fiber neuropathy, which is characterized by the loss of nerve fibers less than 7 micrometers, and thus cannot be assessed by conventional nerve conduction studies. Small-fiber neuropathies are increasingly recognized in a large proportion of patients with primary Sjögren's syndrome, although the true prevalence is unknown. Typically, small-fiber neuropathies present with painful neuropathic symptoms and may be associated with autonomic dysfunction, such as vasomotor symptoms, hyperhidrosis, and orthostasis. The diagnosis of a small-fiber neuropathy requires a skin biopsy showing reduced intraepidermal nerve fiber density. Other peripheral neuropathies reported in patients with primary Sjögren's syndrome are cranial neuropathies, autonomic neuropathies, and multiple mononeuropathies. Most cases of peripheral neuropathy are dominated by sensory symptoms and typically do not progress to cause motor weakness.

### Vasculitis

Beyond lower-extremity purpura, systemic vasculitis appears to be a rare manifestation of primary Sjögren's syndrome. A small-vessel vasculitis and type II or III mixed cryoglobulinemia may develop in the absence of hepatitis C virus infection. A medium-sized vessel vasculitis may rarely occur with features ranging from mononeuritis multiplex to ischemic bowel.

### Cardiovascular Disease

Patients with primary Sjögren's syndrome have an increased risk for cerebrovascular events and myocardial infarction compared with healthy matched controls. 128, These higher risks may be

due to an increased prevalence of hypertension and hypercholesterolemia in patients with primary Sjögren's syndrome despite a lower prevalence of smoking, obesity, and diabetes mellitus. The reasons behind the increased burden of cardiovascular disease in the primary type are poorly understood at this time.

### Lymphoma

Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma (NHL) is a complication of primary Sjögren's syndrome with important prognostic significance. In a European study, the prevalence of NHL was determined to be 4.3%, with a median time of approximately 7.5 years from the diagnosis of primary Sjogren's syndrome to the development of NHL. The risk for NHL in patients with the primary type increases by at least fivefold in the presence of any of the following risk factors: neutropenia, cryoglobulinemia, splenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, or low C4 levels. 131

Several histopathologic types of NHL have been described in association with primary Sjögren's syndrome, including marginal zone B cell lymphoma, follicular cell lymphoma, diffuse large B cell lymphoma, and lymphoplasmacytoid lymphoma.

Mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) lymphoma, a member of the marginal zone B cell lymphoma family, is the most common subtype of NHL to occur in primary Sjögren's syndrome (Fig. 74.6). It develops at extranodal sites in relation to mucosal or glandular epithelium, such as the lacrimal and salivary glands, lung, gastrointestinal tract, and skin. The earliest histopathologic feature of MALT lymphoma is the finding of monocytoid B cells surrounding the epithelium. Immunochemical staining of these lesions demonstrates their clonality with monotypic infiltrates of either IgKor Igλ-light chains. With progression, these lesions show increasing proliferation of neoplastic cells, replacement of reactive follicles, and ductal dilation.

### Associated Diseases

Primary Sjögren's syndrome has been associated with a higher risk for other autoimmune diseases, including thyroid disease, autoimmune hepatitis, primary biliary cirrhosis, and celiac disease. In addition, women with the primary type are at risk for delivering

a child with neonatal lupus given the high prevalence of anti-Ro/ SS-A antibodies in this population.

### Diagnosis and Diagnostic Tests

### Keratoconjunctivitis Sicca and Xerostomia

A diagnostic suspicion of Sjögren's syndrome is initially raised by complaints of dry eye and dry mouth. However, many patients may not volunteer this information at first because they do not feel it is important enough to bring to the attention of the physician. Therefore it is essential for the physician to inquire about these symptoms if the patient does not mention them during the initial history taking. In patients with symptoms of dry eye and dry mouth, the next step is to further investigate these symptoms by objective testing. An easy method to evaluate aqueous tear flow is the Schirmer-I test, which is performed by inserting a sterile piece of filter paper in the middle to lateral third of the patient's lower eyelid and measuring the distance tears elute over 5 minutes. A distance of 5 mm or less is the usual cutoff for abnormally low tear production.

Although a Schirmer-I test has an approximately 20% falsenegative rate, normal tear flow in the face of ocular foreign body sensations suggests an alternative diagnosis such as blepharitis. Patients with moderate to severe symptoms of dry eyes are usually referred to an ophthalmologist for slit-lamp examination. With a slit-lamp, the ophthalmologist can examine the ocular surface for any signs of damage. Instillation of lissamine green or fluorescein dye onto the surface of the eye displays the integrity of the conjunctival and corneal surface. Lissamine green dye stains epithelial surfaces lacking mucin (Fig. 74.7), whereas the fluorescein dye targets areas of cellular disruption on the ocular surface. Fluorescein dye can also be used to measure tear break-up time. A rapid tear break-up time (less than 10 seconds) can result from a deficiency of the aqueous or lipid layers of the tear film, and thus cannot distinguish between lacrimal gland destruction and blepharitis. Lissamine green and fluorescein dye staining are used to determine the SICCA ocular staining score, which is a component of the 2016 ACR/EULAR classification for primary Sjögren's syndrome. Rose Bengal dye, which stains dead or degenerated cells,

is no longer preferred for evaluating the ocular surface because of its toxic effects on the cornea.

Several methods may be used for the objective assessment of dry mouth, or xerostomia. Not all patients with xerostomia show obvious signs of a dry mucosa by exam (e.g., absent sublingual salivary pool, thick and sticky saliva). Sialometry is a method for measuring salivary flow from individual glands (parotid, submandibular, or sublingual) or the mouth as a whole. An unstimulated whole salivary flow rate less than or equal to 1.5 mL/15 min meets the definition for xerostomia according to classification criteria. When performing this test, patients should keep their head tilted forward and then be asked to swallow once to clear the mouth of excess saliva. The 15-minute collection period is then initiated, and patients expectorate as needed, accumulating saliva into a preweighed, 50-cm3 cryovial. Samples are weighed on an analytic balance to determine the volume (1 g = 1 mL) of saliva.

Sialography, another technique for evaluating xerostomia, visualizes radiographic patterns of duct obstruction in the major salivary glands. It is most useful for differentiating an inflammatory process from a neoplasm. This technique calls for injection of radiographic contrast dye into the salivary duct, followed by serial radiographs to image the pattern of dye flow. A water-based contrast is strongly preferred to an oil-based contrast agent because the latter may damage the adjacent salivary gland tissue. Sialography is not routinely used in clinical practice because it is an invasive procedure with complications that include duct rupture, pain, and infection. Scintigraphy is a radionuclide technique for

measuring salivary gland function. After radiolabeled sodium pertechnetate technetium is injected into the blood, it is absorbed into the salivary gland and secreted into the mouth, allowing for determination of the salivary flow rate. The diagnostic sensitivity and specificity of salivary gland scintigraphy for the diagnosis of primary Sjögren's syndrome has been estimated to be 75% and 78%, respectively. Salivary scintigraphy is not widely available for routine testing.

### Ultrasound and Other Imaging Tests

The use of ultrasound as a diagnostic and prognostic tool in primary Sjögren's syndrome has steadily increased over the last decade. Ultrasound can detect abnormal parenchymal volume, echogenicity, inhomogeneity, and vascularity in salivary gland tissue of patients with the primary type (Fig. 74.8). Published reports vary widely in the methods by which these ultrasound parameters are used in the diagnosis of primary Sjögren's syndrome; however, most studies suggest that ultrasound has a comparable sensitivity and specificity to sialography and scintigraphy.

MRI of the major salivary glands has also been explored as a diagnostic tool in primary Sjögren's syndrome. In these scans, the degree of parotid gland inhomogeneity correlates with focus scores on salivary gland histopathology. Other studies have demonstrated potential utility of performing MRI on submandibular and sublingual salivary glands in addition to the parotids. Dedicated magnetic resonance sialography can also be performed to visualize ductal pathology noninvasively, thus avoiding the complications of conventional sialography described earlier.

### Salivary Gland d Biopsy

Labial salivary gland biopsy has long been considered the gold standard for diagnosing primary Sjögren's syndrome. However, in clinical practice, its use is often reserved for patients in whom the diagnosis remains unclear after a thorough clinical and laboratory evaluation. The biopsy is usually performed by an oral surgeon, otolaryngologist, or other appropriately trained individual. This minor procedure calls for removal of four or more salivary gland lobules through a small incision in the inner lip. A biopsy is considered to be positive if histopathologic analysis shows focal lymphocytic sialadenitis with a focus score of greater than or equal to 1 per 4 mm2 of tissue (a focus is defined as a cluster of 50 or more lymphocytes). With this cutoff, the sensitivity and specificity of labial salivary gland biopsy for the diagnosis of primary Sjögren's syndrome has been reported at 83.5% and 81.8%, respectively.136, The interpretation of labial salivary gland biopsies is subject to considerable interreader variability, depending on the experience of the reader. Therefore, it is recommended that the biopsy slides be read by an experienced pathologist or other specialist with an appreciation for the nuances of interpretation. The basic rules for interpreting biopsies were established by Daniels and Whitcher in 1994. They recommended that lymphocytic foci should contain only a small proportion of plasma cells and be located adjacent to normal-appearing acini in lobules without duct dilation or fibrosis. These rules are important to follow because many biopsy specimens, especially from older adults, show patterns of inflammation consistent with nonspecific chronic sialadenitis, namely mixed lymphocytic and plasma cell infiltrates in association with ductal dilation, acinar atrophy, and fibrosis. Chronic nonspecific sialadenitis should not be confused with Sjögren's syndrome. These rules were recently discussed and

modified by the EULAR Sjögren's Syndrome Study Group for the purpose of assessing patients in clinical trials. Among the points raised in this discussion was the counting of foci adjacent to areas of atrophy, duct dilation, and fibrosis. Once focal lymphocytic sialadenitis is confirmed to be present in the biopsy, the new guidance calls for inclusion of all foci in the specimen even if adjacent to abnormal acini or ducts.

### Laboratory Evaluation

Most patients with primary Sjögren's syndrome test positive for serum ANAs. In a large study from Spain, ANAs were detected in sera from 85% of patients with the primary type. Approximately one-half and one-third of patients with primary Sjögren's syndrome in this study tested positive for anti-Ro/SS-A and anti- La/SS-B antibodies, respectively, and approximately one-half tested positive for rheumatoid factor. There also appears to be a small subset of patients (<5%) with the primary type that lack serum anti-Ro/SS-A and/or anti-La/SS-B positivity and test positive for serum anti-centromere antibodies. In one study, patients with serum anti-centromere antibodies had a lower prevalence of dry eye, hypergammaglobulinemia, and anti-Ro/SS-A and anti- La/SS-B antibodies than other patients with primary Sjögren's syndrome and a higher prevalence of Raynaud's syndrome.

Approximately 5% to 10% of patients with primary Sjögren's syndrome have hypocomplementemia. For example, 9% of

the Spanish cohort mentioned earlier had low C3 or C4 levels. Approximately the same proportion of patients with primary Sjögren's syndrome have either type II or III cryoglobulinemia or a monoclonal gammopathy. Among patients with a type II cryoglobulinemia, patients of European descent typically have an IgMk monoclonal gammopathy with rheumatoid factor activity; patients of Japanese descent express a higher prevalence of IgA and IgG monoclonal gammopathies. Hematologic abnormalities are observed in approximately 5% to 15% of patients with primary Sjögren's syndrome and include neutropenia, lymphopenia, and thrombocytopenia.

### Approach to Diagnosis

The clinical diagnosis of primary Sjögren's syndrome is highly likely if a patient with symptoms of dry eye and dry mouth has objective evidence of keratoconjunctivitis sicca and/or xerostomia in conjunction with a positive test for serum anti-Ro/SS-A antibodies and shows no signs of another connective tissue disease. Patients with anti-La/SS-B antibodies in the absence of anti-Ro/ SS-A antibodies are clinically indistinguishable from patients lacking both antibodies, and thus the presence of anti-La/SS-B antibodies alone is not a diagnostic biomarker of primary Sjögren's syndrome.

It may not be necessary to obtain histopathologic evidence of salivary gland involvement if the other clinical and laboratory

features are consistent with this diagnosis. In some cases, a clinical diagnosis of primary Sjögren's syndrome may be made in the presence of a moderate or high titer positive test for ANAs, without serum anti-Ro/SS-A antibodies. Because approximately 25 to 50% of patients with the primary type test negative for anti-Ro/ SS-A antibodies, a positive test for ANAs may often be the only evidence of autoimmunity. Serum ANAs of low titer have relatively little diagnostic value in this setting unless they are accompanied by anti-Ro/SS-A antibodies.

Biopsy of the labial salivary glands may be warranted in cases in which signs and symptoms of keratoconjunctivitis sicca and xerostomia are extant in the absence of convincing serologic evidence of autoimmunity. In this case the labial salivary gland biopsy may be used to further investigate the diagnosis of primary Sjögren's syndrome while exploring possible alternative diagnoses, such as sarcoidosis or amyloidosis.

The diagnosis of primary Sjögren's syndrome in children and adolescents requires special consideration because younger patients do not generally present like adults with symptoms of dry eye and dry mouth. Compared with adults, children and adolescents more often present with recurrent parotitis, which is not a criterion in the current classification criteria. However, if recurrent parotitis is added to the AECG classification criteria, the sensitivity of this classification scheme for diagnosing primary Sjögren's syndrome in children and adolescents increases from 39% to 76%.

### Differential Diagnosis

The differential diagnosis of primary Sjögren's syndrome is broad because of the variety of conditions that also cause dry eye and dry mouth, salivary gland enlargement, and similar extraglandular manifestations (see Table 74.4). It is important to realize most patients diagnosed with keratoconjunctivitis sicca by an ophthalmologist do not have primary Sjögren's syndrome. The etiology of keratoconjunctivitis sicca in many of these cases is often obscure and presumably related to aging, hormonal changes, or other degenerative processes. Evaporative tear loss secondary to meibomian gland dysfunction is another common cause of dry eye. In addition, medications with anticholinergic effects may contribute to sicca complaints. Since approximately 25% of the general population has symptoms of dry mouth, it is not surprising that dry eye and dry mouth often may coexist in a person without having to invoke a systemic disease such as Sjogren's syndrome.

Chronic parotitis has several possible etiologies, including sarcoidosis. Sarcoidosis shares many clinical features with Sjögren's syndrome, such as dry eye, dry mouth, arthralgia, lymphadenopathy, and lung disease. Bilateral diffuse enlargement of the parotid glands may also result from sialadenosis, a noninflammatory process associated with diabetes mellitus, severe hypertriglyceridemia, chronic liver disease, and alcoholism.

Another clinical entity, termed IgG4-related disease, has emerged as an important consideration in the differential diagnosis of primary Sjogren's syndrome. IgG4-related disease is characterized in some cases by high serum levels of IgG4 and tissue biopsies showing a marked lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate, a high number of IgG4* plasma cells, and a storiform pattern of fibrosis. Compared with primary Sjögren's syndrome, IgG4-related disease does not show the same female predominance and is associated with a lower frequency of dry eye and mouth, arthralgia, and serum ANA positivity, as well as a higher rate of autoimmune pancreatitis.

### Treatment

The treatment of primary Sjögren's syndrome is primarily aimed at reducing the signs and symptoms of dry eye and dry mouth and controlling the systemic manifestations (Fig. 74.9). The Sjögren's Syndrome Foundation and the British Society for Rheumatology have proposed guidelines for the management of primary Sjögren's syndrome. 145, These guidelines can serve as a useful reference; however, they are largely based on expert opinion due to the paucity of high-quality, randomized controlled trials.

In general, sicca complaints may be lessened by withdrawal of medications with drying effects. For the treatment of dry eye, the patient is advised to avoid central heating and air conditioning and windy environments. Tear supplements are available over the counter in various formulations of different viscosities. Low-viscosity tears are administered more often than high-viscosity tear formulations; the latter are most useful at bedtime for sustained lubrication during the sleeping hours. Artificial tears are also available with and without preservatives. Preservative-based tears may worsen dry eye if they are instilled more than four times per day because preservatives may be toxic to the ocular surface. More frequent instillation of tears warrants use of formulations without preservatives.

Cyclosporine ophthalmic emulsion, 0.05% (Restasis), has been approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for the treatment of keratoconjunctivitis sicca. In clinical trials, its use reduced the signs and symptoms of dry eye and achieved a statistically significant improvement in tear flow as measured by the Schirmer-I test. Many patients have trouble tolerating ophthalmic cyclosporine because its instillation causes burning. An ophthalmic preparation of lifitegrast (Xiidra) reduces ocular inflammation through the inhibition of lymphocyte function— associated antigen-1 and has also been approved by the FDA for the treatment of dry eye disease. Treatment with ophthalmic lifitegrast improves symptoms of dry eye compared with placebo; however, it has not been directly compared with ophthalmic cyclosporine. Lifitegrast can cause ocular irritation when instilled in the eye, similar to ophthalmic cyclosporine. A nanomicellular, clear aqueous formulation of cyclosporine 0.09% (Cequa) has also been approved for the treatment of dry eye and has lower rates of instillation site pain and irritation compared with the cyclosporin ophthalmic emulsion and lifitegrast.

Tears may be conserved by blocking the nasolacrimal drainage channels with temporary or permanent occlusion, a relatively simple procedure performed by an ophthalmologist. This procedure may be performed in patients with persistent symptoms of dry eye despite use of artificial tears. Plugs are initially placed in the two inferior punctae because 90% of tears drain through these channels. Plugs may later be used to block the two superior punctae. Excessive tearing is the most frequent complication of punctual occlusion, which is the rationale for a trial of temporary blockade with dissolvable collagen plugs before undertaking permanent closure. Long-term punctual closure may be achieved using silicone plugs, which in some cases are poorly tolerated, or by cauterization or heat from a laser.

Blepharitis often complicates a dry eye state. Patients with blepharitis may benefit from warm compresses and lid scrubs with an eyelid detergent such as Johnson's Baby Shampoo mixed 1:1 with water. Some ophthalmologists recommend avoiding lid scrubs because they can be irritating. More refractory cases of blepharitis may be managed with chronic oral doxycycline therapy. Occasionally, the tear film may contain excessive mucous

debris, which can be dispersed by 10% acetylcysteine ophthalmic solution, a mucolytic agent.

Symptoms of dry mouth may be managed by replacing existing saliva or stimulating residual salivary flow. Various over-the-counter preparations of artificial saliva are available containing hypromellose or methylcellulose. However, they provide limited relief in most cases because of their short duration of action. More often, patients rely on sugarless candy or sugarless gum to stimulate salivary flow. Two oral secretagogues are available by prescription that stimulate saliva and tear flow: pilocarpine and cevimeline. Pilocarpine, which acts by stimulating the M3 muscarinic acetylcholine receptor (M3R), is given at a dose of 5 mg, three to four times daily, and, in controlled clinical trials, improved subjective and objective measures of both dry eye and dry mouth.150, Cevimeline also stimulates the M3R and in trials similarly improved subjective and objective measures of dry eye and mouth. Common side effects of these two secretagogues are sweating and flushing, which derive from their mechanism of action. Other possible side effects include visual disturbances, increased urination, nausea, abdominal pain, and diarrhea. Because of their pharmacologic properties, pilocarpine and cevimeline are contraindicated

in patients with iritis, narrow-angle glaucoma, and moderate to severe asthma. Varenicline solution (Tyrvaya) is a nasal spray indicated for the treatment of signs and symptoms of dry eye disease that activates the trigeminal parasympathetic pathway accessible within the nose, enhancing tear production.

Because xerostomia predisposes to dental carries and broken teeth, daily flossing, frequent dental visits, and regular fluoride applications are recommended for prevention of cavities. Oral candidiasis, another complication of xerostomia, may be treated for 10 to 14 days with a nystatin elixir, clotrimazole troches, or fluconazole. Clotrimazole cream is beneficial for the treatment of angular cheilitis, which typically accompanies oral candidiasis.

Patients with primary Sjöogren's syndrome also suffer from dryness of the lips, skin, and nasal passages. This problem may be ameliorated by the frequent application of moisturizers, lip balm, and nasal saline spray. The oily content of vitamin E softgel capsules may be used topically on the skin or the lips for its moisturizing effects. Vaginal dryness with dyspareunia is a frequent complaint of women with primary Sjögren's syndrome. This condition may respond to moisturizers, lubricants, and treatment with a topical estrogen cream.

Currently, the therapeutic armamentarium of primary Sjögren's syndrome lacks a proven disease-modifying drug. Clinical experience suggests that symptoms of fatigue, myalgia, and arthralgia/arthritis may respond favorably to treatment with hydroxychloroquine. However, a double-blind, parallel group, placebo-controlled trial showed that treatment with hydroxychloroquine was no better than placebo for reducing dryness, pain, or fatigue. A post hoc analysis of patients with arthralgia in this study also found that hydroxychloroquine therapy was not significantly beneficial for reducing joint pain, although insufficient numbers of patients with synovitis made it difficult to draw any reliable conclusions on this point. In patients taking hydroxychloroquine, care should be taken to avoid doses exceeding 5 mg/kg/day of actual body weight to minimize the risk of retinal toxicity. Annual ophthalmologic examinations are recommended to monitor for possible retinal complications.

Corticosteroids and other immunosuppressive drugs are employed for the treatment of organ-threatening extraglandular disease. NSIP and LIP are usually treated with high doses of corticosteroids and other immunosuppressive agents, such as azathioprine, mycophenolate mofetil, cyclophosphamide, or rituximab. Because virtually no controlled data are available to support the use of these agents for the treatment of NSIP or LIP, this approach is necessarily empiric and demands judicious monitoring and close follow-up. Bronchiolitis typically improves with high doses of corticosteroids alone, but close follow-up is mandatory for treatment of relapses. Asymptomatic patients whose PFTs show an isolated mild reduction in DLCO or evidence of small-airway disease may be carefully followed up without treatment. Consensus guidelines have been developed for the management of pulmonary involvement in this disease.

Conservative measures may be the only therapy for a sensory peripheral neuropathy, utilizing medications like gabapentin, pregabalin, and analgesics to control neuropathic symptoms. High doses of corticosteroids may produce transient improvement in the symptoms of a peripheral neuropathy, but it is unclear if this approach provides any long-term benefits that would justify the risks of corticosteroid use. Clinically demonstrable weakness due to a motor neuropathy calls for more aggressive treatment using corticosteroids and other immunosuppressive agents. Some patients with severe motor involvement may benefit from treatment with intravenous immunoglobulin.

In patients with lower-extremity purpura, the use of moderate to high doses of corticosteroids can bring symptomatic relief in most cases; however, subsequent tapering to low doses and withdrawal usually lead to recurrence of the purpura. Therefore it is best to avoid corticosteroids in the absence of severe and uncontrollable symptoms or progression to skin ulceration. Support stockings provide symptomatic relief in many cases and can be used in combination with analgesics, antihistamines, or nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs to manage painful symptoms. These patients are usually left with postinflammatory changes in the skin, which may be an acceptable outcome given the long-term side effects of corticosteroids.

Biologic therapies have been investigated recently for their clinical efficacy and safety in primary Sjögren's syndrome. Infliximab and etanercept, which are TNF inhibitors, have failed in small controlled clinical trials to demonstrate therapeutic benefit. 157, Rituximab had shown promise in several small trials, including evidence of improvement in fatigue, sicca symptoms, and systemic disease activity, although results across trials were frequently conflicting. 159-161However, two large randomized trials have recently failed to show significant benefit of rituximab

versus placebo.162, Currently, rituximab is reserved for treating systemic manifestations of primary Sjögren's syndrome, an approach supported by evidence only from case series suggesting acceptable tolerability and efficacy. Other biologics have also not shown efficacy for the treatment of primary Sjögren's syndrome in randomized, placebo-controlled clinical trials, including baminercept, abatacept, and tocilizumab.76, Additional targeted therapies are in the pipeline.

The EULAR Sjögren's Syndrome Disease Activity Index (ESSDAI) and EULAR Sjögren's Syndrome Patient Reported Index (ESSPRI) are validated measures to assess disease activity and patient-reported outcomes in primary Sjögren's syndrome. These indices are utilized in clinical trials as outcome measurements to assess systemic disease activity (ESSDAI) and symptoms of dryness, fatigue, and pain (ESSPRI).

### Outcome

Overall mortality is not increased in patients with primary Sjögren's syndrome compared with the general population, although subsets of patients with severe disease are subject to poor outcomes. In particular, patients with extraglandular involvement, vasculitis, hypocomplementemia, and cryoglobulinemia are at increased risk of mortality.

Although much can be done to ease the symptoms of Sjögren's syndrome, many patients still suffer significant morbidity as a result of their disease. An effective disease-modifying therapy for Sjögren's syndrome could substantially improve patient outcomes and represents a critical unmet need at this time. Given recent advances in our understanding of disease pathogenesis, classification, and diagnosis, this goal seems closer now than ever before. However, many important questions remain unanswered. What leads to glandular hypofunction in the early stages of disease before the accrual of significant glandular damage? Once salivary flow hypofunction occurs, can it be reversed? Which of the many cytokines, immune cells, and other mediators of disease are most integral to disease progression? What outcome measures should be used in trials to prove therapeutic efficacy? These questions remain an area of active investigation and will be key to the discovery of more effective therapies in the future.

The lack of success in identifying disease-modifying therapies for primary Sjögren's syndrome partly results from its clinical and serologic complexity and incomplete understanding of its pathogenesis. To address these challenges, recent research efforts have attempted to define molecular subsets of this disease that could be used in the future to guide targeted therapy. To this end, a multiomic analysis of blood from 382 patients with primary Sjögren's syndrome has characterized four molecular phenotypes, each with distinct patterns of immune dysregulation, i69which were similar to those previously described and shared across a diverse array of seven systemic autoimmune and chronic inflammatory diseases, including primary Sjögren's syndrome. These results will need to be validated in longitudinal cohorts to determine whether these molecular patterns remain stable throughout the disease course or reflect disease stages or disease activity. Nevertheless, such a paradigm could improve the selection of patients for clinical trials and increase the likelihood of developing effective therapies.

### Conclusion

Primary Sjögren's syndrome is second in prevalence only to RA among the autoimmune rheumatologic disorders. Many patients

with mild forms of primary Sjögren's syndrome probably never come to the attention of the rheumatologist, but rather are managed exclusively by primary care physicians, ophthalmologists, otolaryngologists, and dentists. Others may never be referred for a diagnosis because of the misperception that little can be done for patients with Sjögren's syndrome. This tendency toward n eglect could change with the discovery of a disease-modifying therapy. However, primary Sjögren's syndrome may result in more serious organ system involvement and lymphoma. While the rheumatologist is trained to accurately diagnose the primary type, management of serious organ system disease may require a multidisciplinary team of specialists to manage its systemic complications. While much can be done now to care for patients with primary Sjögren's syndrome, the discovery of novel therapeutics in the future holds promise for improving the lives of people with this disease.

# Classification and Epidemiology of Spondyloarthritis

### KEY POINTS

### Introduction

Spondyloarthritis (SpA) is an umbrella term referring to a heterogeneous group of related, yet distinct, inflammatory disorders: psoriatic arthritis (PsA), reactive arthritis (ReA), arthritis associated with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), and ankylosing spondylitis (AS). These inflammatory conditions share similar clinical characteristics, genetic features, and pathophysiological mechanisms and can cluster among families and even within the same individual. The shared clinical features include involvement of the spine, peripheral arthritis (typically asymmetric oligoarthritis), enthesitis, and an over-representation of three specific extramusculoskeletal manifestations: acute anterior uveitis, psoriasis, or IBD. The relationship among these conditions was further strengthened on the discovery of a shared association, of varying degrees, with human leukocyte antigen-B*27 (HLA-B*27). Experimental models supported this relationship, with HLA- B*27 transgenic rats developing clinical features seen in humans with SpA. This chapter outlines how classification criteria in SpA evolved and discusses the current epidemiologic data.

### Classification Criteria

The purpose of classification criteria is to provide a standardized definition of a condition, with the primary intention of creating well-defined homogeneous cohorts of affected individuals, which will allow clinical research to be performed. Such criteria should only be applied in scenarios where there is already an established diagnosis. They are not intended to capture all possible manifestations of a disease but rather the majority. This allows interpretation of findings and comparison between studies examining similar populations. By their nature, classification criteria are designed to be highly specific in order to limit the number of people without the disease who are wrongly classified as positive (i.e., false positives). The drawback of classification criteria is that with a clear yes or no result, there will invariably be individuals with the disease who do not fulfill the classification criteria. Therefore classification criteria can limit the extrapolation of the results of studies to real-life individuals with the diagnosis, as affected individuals may not share all aspects of the disease.

In contrast, diagnostic criteria are intended to be used to guide the care of individual patients.4, They provide clinicians with signs, symptoms, and diagnostic tests that can be used in a clinical setting to arrive at a diagnosis with a certain level of probability. If all patients with the disease are to be captured, they must be sufficiently broad, reflecting the variations that can present with all diseases. They are also more flexible, as they take negative findings and expert opinion into consideration. Rheumatology is faced with unique challenges in that many rheumatic conditions share features with other nonrheumatic conditions. Therefore diagnostic criteria can be challenging to develop, and as a result there are very few validated diagnostic criteria in rheumatology. Due to the difficulties associated with validating diagnostic criteria, the American College of Rheumatology (ACR) no longer endorses these criteria. More commonly, a physician's clinical acumen is employed to establish a diagnosis based on the interpretation of combinations of signs, symptoms, available diagnostic results, and current knowledge of the prevalence and epidemiology of conditions. However, in reality diagnostic and classification criteria represent opposite ends of a continuum.

### Moll and Wright Criteria: Seronegative Spondarthritides

The term seronegative spondarthritides was introduced in 1974 by one group to identify a group of nonrheumatoid diseases that shared clinical and familial features, with the prefix sponddenot- ing an association between each included condition and AS. Criteria to be included in Moll's "seronegative spondarthritis" group included being negative for rheumatoid factor, absence of rheumatoid nodules, inflammatory peripheral arthritis, sacroiliitis, presence of two or more specific clinical features, and familial aggregation. Knowledge and terminology have since evolved and spondyloarthritis is now the preferred term to describe this group of conditions.

### Ankylosing Spondylitis: The Prototypic Spondyloarthritis Condition

AS was the prototypic SpA condition and has several eponyms, including Bechterew's disease and Marie-Strumpell's disease. Pathologic changes of AS in skeletal remains have been described as far back as the Egyptian era,2 although it is likely that some of the skeletal changes reported as AS were more degenerative in nature. The first family study of AS was that of the Medicis, a famous Florentine family, and took place when their bodies were removed from the Medici chapel in 1945. At least two male members of this family, spanning the years 1389 to 1516, almost certainly had AS. Irish physician Bernard Connor gave the first clear description of AS in 1693, which was based on a skeleton with the disease: "all the bones. ..united to make but one bone without articulation.' "10, There was an early belief in the United States that AS represented a variation of rheumatoid arthritis (RA). However, in Europe, the opinion was that AS represented a disease entity independent to RA, a belief subsequently confirmed with the discovery of rheumatoid factor.

### Modified New York Criteria

In 1960, the first attempt at classification criteria for AS was made, following meetings at the National Institutes of Health in the United States and in Rome, Italy; these were subsequently amended at a third symposium in New York in 1966, removing thoracic pain because of low specificity and uveitis because of low sensitivity, culminating in the New York criteria. They were further amended in 1984, incorporating inflammatory back pain (IBP) instead of low back pain (LBP) as a clinical feature, and were referred to as the modified New York (mNY) criteria. To satisfy these criteria, individuals were required to fulfill radiologic criteria (bilateral grade 24 or unilateral grade 34 sacroilitis on plain radiographs of the pelvis), in addition to at least one clinical criteria (Table 75.1).

### Spondyloarthropathy Study Group Criteria for Spondyloarthropathy

A drawback of the mNY criteria was that they solely addressed AS, despite the recognition of a broader spectrum of SpA conditions. A need was identified for classification criteria, which would encompass the entire spectrum of SpA conditions, including individuals who had early disease but no radiograph changes. In 1990 one group15 published a set of classification criteria for the group of spondyloarthritides (Table 75.2). A year later, the European Spondyloarthropathy Study Group (ESSG) published different

### Assessment of SpondyloArthritis Society Criteria

Although the ESSG and Amor criteria were an improvement on the mNY criteria, they did not capture all forms of disease, particularly those with IBP but no radiograph changes. It was increasingly recognized that in many adults with AS, radiographic sacroiliitis could take many years to develop from the onset of IBP. The introduction of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) in the assessment of AS confirmed that individuals with IBP symptoms but without radiograph changes were experiencing inflammation in the sacroiliac (SI) joints and/or spine. In addition, the presence of inflammation of the SI joints on MRI at baseline was associated with 5-year SI joint damage. An examination of 416 individuals from the DESIR (acronym in French for recent-onset SpA) cohort demonstrated only 5% progressed from nonradiographic to radiographic sacroiliitis. One group demonstrated no overall progression of radiographic sacroiliitis over 6 years in an early SpA cohort,21 and another group showed a net progression of only 1.9% to sacroiliitis by mNY criteria over 4.4 years of follow-up. Furthermore, it was recognized that the presence or absence of radiographic sacroilitis did not primarily dictate burden of disease and quality of life. It was therefore concluded that the presence and absence of radiographic sacroiliitis represented a continuum of a single disease, rather than two separate disease entities, and that individuals with predominantly axial symptoms but no radiographic changes of the SI joints should be regarded as the same disease entity as AS individuals. Thus the Assessment of SpondyloArthritis Society (ASAS) developed new classification criteria to account for this, with two tracks depending on whether the prominent symptom is axial or peripheral.23,24

### Axial Spondyloarthritis

In 2009, the first ASAS criteria were published,23 and the term axial spondyloarthritis (axSpA) was introduced. AxSpA is intended as a broader term than AS, encompassing both disease before structural change is evident on radiographs, as well as disease with radiographic changes (see Chapter 76). Entry into these criteria includes chronic back pain of at least 3 months duration, with onset under 45 years of age. There are two arms by which a classification of axSpA can be made: an imaging arm (sacroiliitis by radiograph or MRI, plus at least one SpA feature) and a clinical arm (HLA-B*27 positive plus at least two SpA features) (Fig. 75.2). The term nonradiographic axSpA (nr-axSpA) refers to individuals without definite sacroiliitis on plain films23 (Fig. 75.3) and radiographic axSpA refers to individuals fulfilling mNY criteria. Sensitivity of the ASAS criteria for axSpA was 82.9% and specificity was 84.4%.

AxSpA is traditionally associated with IBP. Determining whether LBP represents IBP can be challenging. LBP is common in the general population, with a point prevalence globally of 9.4%, and is the condition with greatest contribution to global disability. However, the proportion of LBP cases involving IBP is low: the prevalence of IBP in a primary care population is estimated to be between 1.7% and 3.4% in the whole population and 22.4% among individuals who have ever consulted with back pain. Recognition of the features of IBP is additionally low among general practitioners. The Calin criteria (Table 75.3) were the first attempt to classify IBP and were used in the ESSG classification criteria. Subsequently, the Berlin criteria were published in 2006 (Table 75.3)29 and the ASAS criteria for IBP in 2009 (see Table 75.3). In a study of 759 individuals with LBP for more than 3 months, none of the three criteria was able to discriminate individuals with axSpA from those with other causes of LBP. It was decided that chronic back pain, rather than IBP, was the required entry point for the new ASAS classification criteria for axSpA (see Fig. 75.2). However, IBP is included in the criteria as an SpA feature.

### Peripheral Spondyloarthritis

ASAS criteria for peripheral SpA (pSpA) were developed in 201124 to account for individuals with predominant peripheral manifestations (Fig. 75.4). Entry requirements for these criteria are the presence of peripheral manifestations only: peripheral arthritis compatible with SpA, and/or enthesitis, and/or dactylitis. Additional SpA features are also required, divided into two separate sets, with individuals required to have one of set A or two of set B to fulfill the criteria (see Fig. 75.4). The arthritis in these criteria typically refers to predominantly lower limb and/or asymmetric arthritis.

In contrast to the axSpA criteria, an entry age cutoff was not applied to these criteria, as it was felt to not be as relevant in pSpA as axSpA. Sensitivity of these criteria was 77.8% and specificity was 82.2%. When combined with the axSpA criteria, sensitivity was 79.5%, and specificity was 83.3%. When the ASAS criteria were first published, there was strict separation between the axSpA and pSpA sets of criteria. Individuals could not have current back pain; if this was present, the axSpA criteria were instead applied.

### Undifferentiated Spondyloarthritis

Prior to the publication of the new ASAS classification criteria, individuals who had symptoms and/or signs of AS but did not fulfill the criteria were classified as undifferentiated spondyloarthritis (uSpA). Often over time, the eventual diagnosis of these individuals would become clear. However, as the ASAS criteria have been more widely adopted, the term uSpA has been phased out, as almost all individuals with SpA can instead be classified as either axSpA or pSpA.

### Psoriatic Arthritis

PsA was included as a separate disease entity in classification of rheumatic disease for the first time in 1964,33 under the heading "polyarthritis of unknown etiology." Prior to that, if an individual had both inflammatory arthritis and psoriasis, it was thought to represent RA with coincidental psoriasis. Moll and Wright34 introduced the original definition for PsA: presence of psoriasis, presence of inflammatory arthritis (peripheral arthritis and/or spondylitis), and usually negative serology for rheumatoid factor (see Chapter 78). Several other criteria were subsequently proposed. 16, However, validation of any of these criteria was less than ideal, which lead to the development of the CASPAR (ClASsification criteria for Psoriatic ARthritis) criteria from patientderived data published in 2006.40 These criteria were developed using 588 patients with PsA and 536 comparison patients (RA, n = 384; AS, n = 72; undifferentiated arthritis, n = 38; connective tissue disease, n = 14; others, n = 28) and sensitivity and specificity were compared with existing criteria. The CASPAR criteria are outlined in Table 75.4. If individuals displayed three or more of these features, they could be classified as PsA, with a specificity of 98.7% and sensitivity of 91.4% in the development cohort. These criteria had better specificity than the Vasey and Espinoza criteria37 but were less sensitive.

A limitation of these criteria is that individuals are required to have an inflammatory articular disease affecting either the joint, spine, or entheses to be eligible, which was not otherwise defined. In addition, the average duration of disease of the PsA development cohort was 12.5 years, with only 5.3% having disease duration of less than 12 months. This limits its applicability to individuals with early disease. One group41 went on to examine the sensitivity and specificity of these criteria in 111 individuals with early PsA (median disease duration 8 months) and found that using the same cutoff of three or more features led to a sensitivity of 87.4% and a specificity of 99.1%. Although this sensitivity was less than that found in the original criteria, the authors concluded that the CASPAR criteria were nonetheless valid in early PsA.

### Overlap Between Peripheral Spondyloarthritis and Other Subtypes, Particularly Psoriatic Arthritis

The application of pSpA classification criteria is limited by lack of data exploring their utility, the absence of biomarkers for pSpA and overlap with other SpA subtypes. Indeed, pSpA is often used interchangeably with ReA, PsA, and uSpA.2, There is a particular overlap between pSpA and PsA, especially when skin psoriasis is absent in PsA. However, there are some key differences, whereby pSpA has a male predominance, a higher prevalence of HLA-B*27, more enthesitis but less dactylitis, and involvement of the large joints of the lower limbs compared with those with PsA without psoriasis. Further research is required to better characterize pSpA as a disease.

### Reactive Arthritis

ReA is an inflammatory arthritis associated predominantly with certain infections of gastrointestinal or genitourinary origin (see Chapter 77). Several attempts have been made to develop diagnostic or classification criteria for ReA, but none have yet been validated. The earliest known attempt at defining the disease occurred in 1979,43 when the American Rheumatism Association (ARA) Diagnostic and Therapeutic Committee analyzed 249 case reports from seven centers, consisting of 83 typical patients and 166 disease controls with seronegative arthritis. They concluded that the presence of peripheral arthritis with urethritis and/or cervicitis could be considered clinically acceptable, with a characteristic episode lasting more than 1 month. Specificity of these criteria in this cohort was 98.2% and sensitivity was 84.3%. Adding eye involvement, HLA-B*27 positivity or other minor criteria (conjunctivitis, balanitis, mucous membrane, heel pain, fever, weight loss) did not improve performance of this definition. At that time, the condition was referred to as Reiter's syndrome. However, that eponym was associated with controversy, when it came to light that the German physician associated with the original description of the condition, Hans Reiter, was a leader of the Nazi party in World War II,44 leading to the retraction of the term Reiter's syndrome. The term reactive arthritis was instead adopted and is now preferred.

In 1995, the Third International Workshop on Reactive Arthritis took place in Berlin, Germany,46 and new diagnostic criteria for ReA were proposed: typical peripheral arthritis (predominantly lower limb asymmetric oligoarthritis) plus evidence of preceding infection. In a 1996 study of 46 individuals with ReA, 19 with Chlamydia-induced arthritis and 27 with ReA induced by enterobacteria, the combination of HLA-B*27 positivity,
