### Inflammatory Bowel Disease-Related Spondyloarthritis

IBD describes a chronic relapsing-remitting inflammatory condition of the bowel and includes Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis. It is well recognized that there is a link between IBD and arthritis and, more specifically, SpA. In 1964 the ARA included ulcerative colitis and regional ileitis as diseases with which arthritis is frequently associated. By 1974, Moll and Wright included arthritis associated with IBD as one of the SpA subgroups. However, formal classification criteria for IBD-related SpA don't yet exist. Indeed, the spectrum of SpA phenotypes associated with

IBD are varied and include peripheral and axial disease. IBD exists as a feature of SpA in the ASAS criteria.23, It has long been recognized that both peripheral arthritis and axial disease can occur in individuals with IBD-SpA. The Oxford IBD clinic in 1998 studied individuals attending their clinic with peripheral joint symptoms only (i.e., excluding those with axial disease) and proposed classifying individuals with IBD and peripheral arthritis into two types. This classification, however, has not been validated prospectively and has fallen out of favor. In the absence of a specific IBD-associated SpA classification system, the ASAS criteria (axial and peripheral)23,24 are often used. However, these criteria have not been assessed in enough detail in IBD-SpA to know if they accurately capture the spectrum of the disease.

### Epidemiology of Spondyloarthritis

In 2016, one group systematically summarized the global prevalence of SpA and its subtypes, reporting a worldwide prevalence of 0.55% (0.37 to 0.77), with the lowest prevalence in South East Asia (pooled prevalence 0.20%, 95% CI 0.00 to 0.66) and the highest in the northern Arctic communities (pooled prevalence 1.61%, 95% CI 1.27 to 2.00). The prevalence of SpA in Europe was 0.54% (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.36 to 0.78) and North America 1.35% (95% CI 0.44 to 2.79). The epidemiology of each subtype of SpA is varied, therefore the remainder of this section examines each type of SpA separately.

### Axial Spondyloarthritis

### Age of Presentation

axSpA typically presents in the second or third decade of life, and almost exclusively before age 45.57 A recent study of 2579 axSpA patients reported a median age of 26 years at onset of symptoms, with 92% reporting an age of onset prior to 45 years. AxSpA presents earlier in individuals who are HLA-B*27 positive by approximately 5 years.59, Delay to diagnosis of axSpA is a feature of the disease, with a mean delay of 6.7 years61 and median of 2 to 6 years62 reported in separate systematic reviews. The delay to diagnosis has been shown to be longer in women than in men: 8.8 versus 6.5 years. Lower education levels, younger age at onset of symptoms, and absence of extramusculoskeletal manifestations are associated with a longer delay to diagnosis.

### Prevalence

Variation in the methodology of studies used to estimate the prevalence and incidence of axSpA, particularly the change in classification criteria that occurred in 2009, has led to difficulties in accurately establishing epidemiologic estimates for axSpA. The global prevalence of axSpA was estimated as ranging from 0.36% to 0.70% in a systematic review in 2016,56 although this was based on point estimates from only two studies: one from France and one from the United States. The pooled prevalence of AS ranged from 0.20% in North America (95% CI 0.10 to 0.34) to 0.25% in Europe (95% CI 0.18 to 0.33). A systematic review of population-based studies estimated the prevalence of AS at 23.8 cases per 10,000 in Europe. A more recent study from England demonstrated an annual rise in the prevalence of axSpA until it peaked in 2020 at 0.113% (95% CI 0.773, 0.784). A 2018 Japanese study reported a very low prevalence: 0.0026% for AS and 0.0006% for nr-axSpA. It is feasible that the prevalence figures reported in these reviews underrepresented the true prevalence figures, due to a lack of true general population

studies and continued underrecognition and underdiagnosis of axSpA.

### Human Leukocyte Antigen-B*27

The wide variation in the global prevalence of axSpA is at least partly explained by differences in background HLA-B*27 prevalence. HLA-B*27 is a class I surface antigen encoded by the major histocompatibility complex (MHC) and is found in 74% to 89% of individuals with axSpA. The prevalence of HLA- B*27 is highest in the Pawaia tribe in Papua New Guinea (53%) and the Haida indigenous Americans on Queen Charlotte Islands in Western Canada (50%) and lowest in Arab countries (2%— 5%) and Japan (1%).70, In Europe, HLA-B*27 varies from 4% to 13% in the west and 15% to 25% in northern Scandinavia (Norway, Sweden, and Finland), with approximately 90% of individuals with AS HLA-B*27 positive. 70, HLA-B*27 is exceedingly rare in Japan and Arab countries75,76 and almost nonexistent in some populations such as the indigenous tribes of South America. In Black populations, HLA-B*27 occurs in less than 60% of cases of AS,77 and AS is almost nonexistent in South American Indians and Australian Aborigines. The association between HLA-B*27 and AS is weaker in the Middle East than in Europe.78,79

### Sex Differences

Historically, AS has been considered to have a male predominance, with striking male to female ratios of up 10:1 reported in early studies. More recently, that ratio has been revised down, closer to 3:1.80 In contrast, the distribution of nr-axSpA is virtually identical between males and females.59, Axial symptoms typically begin earlier in men compared with women (25 vs. years, p < 0.001), with definite regional differences; the biggest gender difference was noticed in Asia (age 23 in men vs. age 28 in women) and no significant gender differences in age of onset were noted in Europe or North America. A systematic review and meta-analysis published in 2017 examined the diagnostic delay in SpA and found a mean of 8.8 (7.410.1) years for females and 6.5 (5.67.4) years for males, a difference that was statistically significant. This may relate to the differences in presenting symptoms, with men more likely to report typical IBP symptoms and women more likely to report widespread pain, which made a delayed diagnosis twice as likely.

### Other Genetics of Ankylosing Spondylitis

Most pathogenesis studies to date have focused on AS rather than axSpA. Studies performed on monozygotic twins and familial aggregation studies suggest that AS has a heritability of above 90%.82, As already outlined, HLA-B*27 positivity is strongly linked with AS, occurring in only about 5% of the general population but up to 90% of individuals with AS. However, despite this strong association, HLA-B*27 contributes only 33% of the total heritability of AS.

Genome-wide association studies based on single-nucleotide polymorphisms have identified over 100 genetic variants associ ated with AS. Twenty percent of the genetic heritability was explained by MHC variants, which includes HLA-B*27, and 7% by non-MHC variants. Two other genetic loci have been identified as of potential interest: endoplasmic reticulum aminopeptidase (ERAP) and the interleukin (IL)-23 receptor. ERAP has a role in preparing peptides before MHC Class I presentation to immune effector cells. Also implicated are genes that affect the IL-23 receptor that cause activation of the

T-helper cells, which leads to the secretion of IL-17 and other pro-inflammatory cells.

### Psoriatic Arthritis

### Prevalence and Incidence

The prevalence and incidence of both PsA and psoriasis vary globally. A systematic review in 2018 reported a global estimate of the pooled prevalence of PsA as 0.13%. There was significant heterogeneity between the studies, in part due to differences in how PsA was defined between studies. When limited to PsA by CASPAR criteria only, the prevalence was 0.12%. In an English-based study, the prevalence of PsA increased every year from 2004 to 2019, peaking at 0.287% (95% CI 0.284, 0.291). The incidence of PsA in that same systematic review was 8.3 per 100,000 patient years. The highest prevalence rates of PsA are found in North America (158 every 100,000 subjects) and northern Europe (670 per 100,000 subjects), whereas much lower prevalence rates are reported in Asia (38 per 100,000 subjects) and southern Europe (28 per 100,000 subjects).

Although the prevalence of PsA in the general population is low, it is much higher in those with existing psoriasis. A systematic review analyzing 266 studies reported the prevalence of PsA in those with psoriasis as 19.7%, with significant global variation, ranging from 22.7% in Europe to 14.0% in Asia. Approximately 10% to 15% of individuals develop PsA prior to the onset of psoriasis. However, the majority of cases of PsA occur about a decade after the onset of psoriasis. Early-onset psoriasis (type 1) refers to an onset of disease before the age of 40 years, and lateonset psoriasis (type 2) occurs after the age of 40 years, with peak age of onset between 57 and 60 years; there is no clear consensus on a similar stratification for PsA. There is mounting evidence that the peak age of onset is shifting to an older age than was previously found.

PsA is thought to affect men and women almost equally. However, there may be a sex effect in the expression of the disease. Women tend to develop psoriasis earlier than men94; unfortunately, there is less literature available regarding the sex differences in PsA.

### Genetics and Psoriatic Arthritis

A positive family history of psoriasis or PsA is strongly associated with developing PsA. An individual's risk of developing PsA is 30 to 55 times higher if a first-degree relative is affected. Many different genes have been implicated in the pathogenesis of PsA, but the strongest link has been found between HLA and PsA. Approximately 20% of individuals with PsA are HLA-B*27 positive. HLA-B*39 and B*07 have also been associated with PsÅ. HLA- B*27 is more common in those with axial disease, whereas HLA- B*38 is more frequently found in those with peripheral arthritis. The association between HLA-B*27 and PsA is weaker than that in axSpA.

A strong association has been found between psoriasis and the MHC region, in particular with the HLA-C*06 allele. Although this gene is also increased in patients with PsA compared with the general population, the association is less strong than for psoriasis. The presence of the HLA-C*06 allele is associated with a later onset of disease in both psoriasis and PsA. The presence of HLA-B*27, HLA-B*08, and HLA-B*38 is all associated with an increased risk of developing PsA in those with psoriasis.

### Reactive Arthritis

ReA tends to affect individuals between the ages of 20 and 40 years. ReA typically has onset 1 to 3 weeks after an extra-articular infection. Microbes from the genitourinary tract (Chlamydia trachomatis, Neisseria gonorrhea, Mycoplasma genitalium, Ureaplasma urealyticum) and gastrointestinal tract (Yersinia, Salmonella, Campylobacter, and Shigella species) are the most common causes of triggering ReA. Both sexes are equally involved when ReA is secondary to gastrointestinal infections. The prevalence of ReA secondary to Chlamydia trachomatis, the most common organism to trigger genitourinary ReA, occurs more commonly in men.

The global prevalence of ReA is estimated to be 1/1000.99 However, there is significant global variation. A systematic review analyzed 17 studies and reported the prevalence of ReA to range from 0.03 to 0.21% in Europe. No cases were reported in a single study from India and the prevalence was only 0.001% in Zimbabwe. In contrast, the prevalence was much higher among northern Arctic indigenous people, ranging from 0.25% to 1%. No studies from North America were included in this systematic review. The incidence of ReA is estimated to range from 4.6 to 13 per 100,000 for genitourinary ReA and 5 to 14 per 100,000 for gastrointestinal ReA. There is a perception that ReA may be decreasing in frequency and severity, based on a study characterizing Canadian rheumatologists' perspectives.

The variations in global prevalence of ReA may be at least partially explained by the differing prevalence of HLA-B*27. There is a strong association between ReA and HLA-B*27, with the prevalence of ReA in HLA-B*27-positive individuals reportedly 5 to 10 times higher than the general population. A recent study reported a HLA-B*27 positivity rate of 81.8% in those with ReA. HLA-B*27 may have an influence on the phenotype of the disease, with positive individuals displaying more axial symptoms and those negative for HLA-B*27 more likely to display peripheral symptoms. Individuals with HLA-B*27 positivity are also at higher risk for progression to persistent SpA.

### Inflammatory Bowel Disease-Associated Spondyloarthritis

The National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) estimated the prevalence of IBD to be 1.3% in 2015.104 A systematic review estimated the prevalence of IBD- SpA from four studies, all European based, to range from 0.0% to 0.09%. The prevalence of axSpA in IBD is estimated to be 5% and of peripheral disease to be 16%. Peripheral arthritis is the most frequent manifestation of SpA in those with IBD (pooled prevalence 13%, 95% CI 12%15%), followed by sacroiliitis (pooled prevalence 10%, 95% CI 8%12%) and AS (pooled prevalence 3%, 95% CI 2%4%).

### Peripheral Spondyloarthritis

There is scant data available regarding the epidemiology of pSpA. Limited data investigating the prevalence and incidence of pSpA suggest a prevalence between 22.8% and 28.5% in those with SpA. The ASAS-Peripheral involvement in SpA (PerSpA) study aimed to characterize the peripheral musculoskeletal manifestations of individuals with subtypes of SpA. It found that pSpA was least prevalent in Latin America (8.1%) and most prevalent in the Middle East and North Africa (36.5%). An ancillary analysis

of the PerSpA study aimed to better characterize pSpA. Of the 4185 patients included in this ancillary analysis, 5.3% had a pure pSpA classification (i.e., fulfilled only ASAS pSpA criteria), and 6.4% had a pure diagnosis of pSpA (i.e., diagnosed with pSpA exclusively according to the treating rheumatologist). When pSpA was considered as the main disease, it was diagnosed in 10.3% of individuals. Of those with a combined form, the majority (65.5%) had an overlap with axSpA, rather than PsA (46.5%).

# Axial Spondyloarthritis

### KEY POINTS

### Introduction

Axial spondyloarthritis (axSpA) is a term introduced in 20041 to help describe patients with inflammatory arthritis of the sacroiliac (SI) joints and spine who did not have radiographic sacroiliitis.

Although such patients may have been diagnosed as having ankylosing spondylitis (AS) prior to 2004, AS was thought to be an unsatisfactory term because the 1984 modified New York criteria3 would not have classified such patients as AS. Therefore the term axial SpA more comprehensively covers the spectrum of inflammatory spine and SI arthritis from mild to severe disease and from early to late disease. Although such a move ignored the possibility of just changing the classification criteria rather than the name of the disease, the term axial SpA has become gradually more established, and now for the first time, it is a chapter title of the 12th edition of this textbook, where once ankylosing spondylitis served.4,

However, a significant focus of this chapter will still be on radiographic axial SpA, since a large amount of what is known about axial SpA comes from studies of radiographic axial SpA (that is, ankylosing spondylitis). Furthermore, other members of the SpA family will be discussed in other chapters, even though they may be considered forms of axial SpA and be classified as such. Psoriatic, enteropathic, and reactive SpA will not be discussed in detail here. This chapter focuses on AS. However, many aspects also apply to patients with axial SpA.

Inflammatory sacroiliitis is considered a hallmark of axial SpA and may be identified pathologically by various imaging techniques. Although inflammation of the SI joints and spine may eventually lead to bony ankylosis, spinal ankylosis tends to appear in late stages of the disease and does not occur in many patients with mild disease.

Many patients with AS have onset of back pain during the third decade of life. It takes, on average, 6 to 8 years from the onset of back pain until a clinician establishes a definite diagnosis of AS. This diagnostic delay in the majority of patients results mainly from the relatively late appearance of definite radiographic sacroiliitis on conventional plain radiographs.3, Active sacroiliitis on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) predicts the later appearance of sacroiliitis on radiographs. Thus many patients at an early stage of AS typically are seen with characteristic clinical features of AS, but definite sacroiliitis may not yet be detected on radiographs. Therefore they may not be classified with AS according to the modified New York criteria (see also Chapter 75). In such patients with suspected early stage AS, sacroiliitis may best be detected on MRI. Radiographic sacroiliitis (i.e., structural damage of SI joints observable on plain radiographs) may develop in a minority of such patients over time (approximately 20% to 25% over a period of 15 years, 5% to 10% over 5 years).3-8 In addition, modern treatment may have the potential for preventing

structural damage. All of this implies that a significant proportion of patients will never show radiographic changes, despite harboring inflammation of SI joints at least at some point in time but without incurring radiographically detectable damage during the subsequent years. Therefore to describe these patients correctly, the term early AS has been dropped in favor of the term nonradiographic axial spondyloarthritis (nr-axSpA). The term axial spondyloarthritis comprises both nr-axSpA and classic AS (patients who generally fulfill the modified New York criteria). The total prevalence of axial SpA has been estimated at two to four times that of AS.9-11 Contrary to the population of patients classified by the modified New York criteria, there is no male preponderance among patients with nr-axSpA. In population-based studies on axial SpA, human leukocyte antigen (HLA)-B27 prevalence varies widely (from 20% to 97%) depending on how patients were included.10, At the group level, nr-axSpA patients tend to respond less favorably to treatment with TNF inhibitors than AS patients defined by modified New York criteria.12, Patients classified as nr-axSpA who lack objective signs of SI or spinal inflammation, despite apparently active disease, do not typically respond to TNF inhibition. Such an observation raises questions about the accuracy of the diagnosis of such patients.

### Classification Criteria for Ankylosing Spondylitis and Axial Spondyloarthritis

Classification criteria are intended for clinical and epidemiologic studies and also for research on the etiopathogenesis of diseases. Such criteria should create homogeneous groups of patients who have already been diagnosed clinically. Inappropriate use of classification criteria as diagnostic criteria increases the likelihood of overdiagnosis due to inclusion of patients with false-positive diagnoses, especially if the criteria lack specificity and the prior probability of disease is low. Note that only about 5% of people with chronic back pain have axial SpA.

The diagnosis of axial SpA is based on the integration of clinical, laboratory, and imaging features in a specific context. In daily practice, a presumptive clinical diagnosis of axial SpA is usually supported by evidence of sacroiliitis on imaging. Although radiographic sacroiliitis is frequent in AS, it is by no means an early or obligate manifestation of the disease. Contrary to the New York criteria, radiographic evidence of sacroiliitis is not obligatory to fulfill the Rome criteria (Table 76.1). Both the Rome and New York criteria were primarily intended for use in epidemiologic studies. Lack of either sensitivity or specificity led to a modification of the New York criteria for AS3 (Table 76.1). Two criteria, limitation of lumbar spine motion and limitation of chest expansion, appear to reflect disease duration since they are usually not present in early disease. Therefore the modified New York criteria are not useful for inclusion of early cases of AS. MRI is useful to detect axial manifestations before the presence of radiographic sacroilitis.6, To encompass both nonradiographic AS and AS (according to the modified New York criteria), classification criteria (the Assessment of SpondyloArthritis [ASAS] criteria) have been proposed for the full spectrum of AS (see Chapter 75, Fig. 75.2). Full spectrum of AS and axial spondyloarthritis are essentially synonyms. These terms provide an umbrella for patients with predominantly axial involvement, regardless of the presence of structural damage on radiographs. According to the ASAS classification criteria,1 a patient with chronic back pain and age at onset younger than 45 years can be classified with axial SpA if sacroiliitis on imaging (radiographs or MRI) is present, plus at least one other SpA feature, or, in the

The sensitivity of ASAS criteria for axial SpA was 83%, and the specificity was 84%. In the ASAS study on these new criteria, 30% of all patients considered to have axial SpA had definite radiographic sacroiliitis and fulfilled the modified New York criteria for AS. Therefore two-thirds were classified with nr-axSpA. It should be noted that patients classified with axial SpA according to the ASAS criteria tend to be more heterogeneous than AS patients classified by modified New York criteria.1, Due to lack of specificity of the ASAS criteria, applying these classification criteria as a diagnostic tool creates a considerable risk of overdiagnosis and inappropriate management because the prevalence of axial SpA among chronic back pain patients is only about 5%. Applying the ASAS classification criteria diagnostically in that setting would create almost four false-positively labeled people for each true axial SpA patient. Clearly, classification criteria are not suited for diagnostic 19,20 purposes.

### Epidemiology

### Prevalence

Prevalence estimates of axial SpA vary among populations and are associated with the occurrence of the HLA-B27 allele in the

population but are also dependent on the disease (sub)category (SpA, axial SpA, AS, or nr-axSpA). The prevalence of AS closely parallels the frequency of HLA-B27. This holds true for those HLA-B27 subtypes that are associated with the disease, but it is not true for populations in which the HLA-B27*06 subtype, which lacks a strong association with AS, occurs frequently. 21-23

In the general population, AS is likely to develop in approximately 1% to 2% of HLA-B27-positive adults who have a diseaseassociated HLA-B27 subtype, although there may be regional or geographic differences.24, For example, in northern Norway, radiographic AS has been estimated to develop in 6.7% of HLA- B27-positive people.

The estimated prevalence of AS, as defined by the modified New York criteria, ranges from 0.07% in a population older than 20 years in the Netherlands, to 0.2% in the United States24,26 and from 0.02% (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.00% to 0.21%) in sub-Saharan Africa to 0.35% (95% CI, 0.24% to 0.48%) in Northern Arctic communities. The prevalence of SpA ranged from 0.20% (95% CI, 0.00% to 0.66%) in Southeast Asia to 1.61% (95% CI, 1.27% to 2.00%) in Northern Arctic communities. Although the population prevalence of axial SpA and especially nr-axSpA is not clearly defined,28 there is evidence to suggest that the prevalence of axial SpA could be two to four times the prevalence of radiographic AS.11,

The risk is considerably increased for first-degree relatives of patients with AS compared with individuals in the general population. This applies in particular to HLA-B27—positive relatives. Sex also affects the risk as axial SpA occurs more often among HLA- B27-positive children of mothers with AS (risk up to 41.4%) compared with HLA-B27-positive children of fathers with AS (risk up to 12.6%). Axial SpA is much more common among HLA-B27-positive first-degree relatives of HLA-B27-positive AS patients; up to 30% of them may have signs or symptoms of axial SpA.24, On the other hand, the risk for HLA-B27-negative relatives of AS probands to develop axial SpA is low (about 1%).24,33

### Incidence

AS and axial SpA prevalence and incidence may have increased in the United States between 2006 and 2014. Reasons are unknown but may include increased disease awareness leading to increased detection.

Clinical features, age of onset, and survival time have remained stable over time. A Scandinavian study revealed an overall ageand sex-adjusted incidence of 7.3 per 100,000 person-years, whereas an overall incidence of 3.1 per 100,000 person-years was observed in the United States.

### Sex Distribution

Clinically, AS is more common in males, with a reported male to female ratio of approximately 2:1 to 3:1.32, In contrast, studies of patients with nr-axSpA usually show female preponderance, but these women are more often negative for HLÁ-B27.32, One possible explanation for the male preponderance of AS could be that structural changes are less likely to develop in women. It has been shown that females with nr-axSpA demonstrate increased heterogeneity in disease manifestations and have lower polygenetic risk scores (less genetic predisposition) than males with nraxSpA or males and females with AS.

Disease expression of AS is thought to be different in males and females. A case-control study comparing 35 female patients with

70 male patients with AS showed no differences in spinal symptoms, chest expansion, peripheral arthritis, extra-articular manifestations, or functional outcome. However, males with AS more often had radiographic spinal changes and hip joint involvement than their female counterparts. There is still some controversy, but on average, the disease seems to be more severe in men.39,40

### Burden of Disease

Axial SpA is associated with a considerable burden to the patient and society. Apart from axial and peripheral articular manifestations, extra-articular manifestations, such as enthesitis and acute anterior uveitis (AAU), and associated comorbidities, such as inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) and psoriasis, contribute to the burden of disease. In addition, a large proportion of patients have spinal osteoporosis, leading to vertebral fractures and thoracic kyphosis. All of these features result in a decreased quality of life (QoL). Impaired physical functioning and disease activity correlate clearly with psychological scores for anxiety and depression. The prevalence of comorbid depression in axial SpA is high. The impact of AS can also be seen in various aspects of employment, ranging from required assistance at work to increased sick leave and withdrawal from the workforce.43, Socioeconomic factors including higher education levels are associated with a higher likelihood of patients maintaining employment. Uveitis, older age, reduced physical function, and higher disease activity predict long-term adverse work outcomes. Patients with AS render an important impact on health care and nonhealth care resource utilization, resulting in mean total costs (direct and productivity) of approximately $6700 to $9500 per year per patient. 47-49

The burden of illness increases with disease duration. Because the burden caused by AS reduces QoL, and because all types of costs associated with AS result from loss of function and disease activity, early diagnosis and treatment are necessary to prevent or reduce functional decline and improve long-term patient outcomes.

Although nonradiographic axial SpA may be associated with fewer inflammatory features and less spinal stiffness, the burden of disease appears to be similar to that of AS by modified New York criteria.51, Comorbidities in SpA adversely influence physical function, work ability, and QoL. The increased prevalence of cardiovascular disease among patients with AS contributes to the burden of disease.

### Genetics and Pathogenesis

### Genetics

Twin and family studies have shown that the risk for AS runs strongly in families and is largely genetically determined and that genetic factors also play major roles in determining disease activity and severity.55, Major progress has been made in recent years in defining the alleles (genetic variants) that underlie this genetic predisposition, with at least 116 known loci (genetic regions) associated with the disease, including different loci within the major histocompatibility complex (MHC) and in non-MHC regions.

### Major Histocompatibility Complex Associations With Ankylosing Spondylitis

The association of HLA-B27 with AS was first reported in the early 1970s, and since then increasing numbers of HLA-B27 subtypes have been identified, with nearly 400 subtypes defined by DNA sequence now known. The majority of these subtypes are too rare

for us to know whether they are disease associated. The ancestral HLA-B27 subtype is HLA-B*2705, from which the other subtypes have arisen largely by point mutation. AS has occurred in individuals with the following HLA-B27 subtypes: B*2702, B*2703, B*2704, B*2705, B*2706, B*2707, B*2708, B*2710, B*2714, B*2715, and B*2719. But two subtypes appear to show reduced or possibly absent association with AS: HLA-B*2706, which is found predominantly in Southeast Asia, and HLA-B*2709, which is found in Sardinia. The impact of subtype variation on AS risk has been a cornerstone of research into the mechanism by which HLA-B27 induces AS. HLA-B27 is found in 85% to 95% of cases of primary AS compared with a prevalence in most populations of European descent of approximately 8%. A lower prevalence of HLA-B27 (~60%) is found in AS associated with psoriasis or IBD.

HLA-B27 homozygotes have roughly double the risk of AS, compared with B27 heterozygotes. The odds ratio (OR) for AS for HLA-B27 (as defined by the tag single nucleotide polymorphism [SNP] rs116488202) heterozygotes is 62 and for homozygotes 105.58 HLA-B27 is widely used in clinical practice as a diagnostic aid in patients with chronic back pain, whereas the clinical arm of the ASAS axial SpA classification criteria requires the presence of HLA-B27 to classify the condition (see Chapter 75, Fig. 75.2). HLA-B27 typing is also of use in determining the risk of occurrence of AS in families, with the risk of occurrence extremely low in the absence of HLA-B27 (<1% chance). Because the prevalence of AS is quite low in the community, and because only approximately 5% of HLA-B27 positive individuals develop AS, population screening that uses HLA-B27 is not recommended. Disease develops in HLA-B27-negative individuals on average a decade later than HLA-B27-positive individuals, but their disease activity and severity of ankylosis is not different. There is some evidence to suggest that HLA-B27-negative individuals are less responsive to TNF inhibition; nonetheless, these agents are clearly effective overall in treating HLA-B27-negative AS. Whether other genetic loci influence responses to TNF inhibitors is unknown in AS, but given that large studies in rheumatoid arthritis (RA) have failed to show any convincing evidence of an association between individual genetic variants with response to TNF inhibition, it would appear unlikely that such an effect will be seen in AS. There are no data at this point regarding potential genetic determinants of response to interleukin (IL)-17A, or IL-17A/IL-17F inhibition.

The prevalence of AS worldwide roughly parallels the prevalence of HLA-B27. Regions with high HLA-B27 prevalence include Scandinavia and in some North American indigenous populations, and low prevalence is found through most of Africa and in Australian Aboriginals. This variation may be the result of population bottlenecks in human history or natural selection for HLA-B27 in some populations. It should be noted that HLA-B27 is protective for HIV infection in the general population. It has recently been suggested that HLA-B27 may influence survival, potentially through an effect on cardiovascular risk. This finding suggests another potential selective pressure on HLA-B27 prevalence.

HLA-B27 is not the only HLA-B allele associated with AS. Multiple studies have confirmed a role for HLA-B60 (also known as HLA-B40), which further increases AS risk by approximately 1.5-fold,61 with many other HLA-B, HLA-A, and HLA Class II alleles yielding modest effects on AS susceptibility.

### Non-major Histocompatibility Complex Associations of Ankylosing Spondylitis

Despite well-characterized associations between HLA-B27 with disease susceptibility, the majority of the genetic risk for AS is

thought to be determined by loci outside the MHC. To date over 110 non-MHC loci have been convincingly demonstrated to be associated with the disease, and these have cast new light on the disease pathogenesis (summarized in Table 76.2).

Aminopeptidase Genes and Ankylosing Spondylitis. Three genes in the aminopeptidase pathway are robustly associated with AS: ERAP1 and ERAP2 encoded at chromosome 5q15 and NPEPPS (puromycin-sensitive aminopeptidase) at chromosome 17q21. At least two associated haplotypes are present at ERAP1, with one driven by the noncoding SNP rs30187 and the second haplotype where the AS-protective SNP leads to splice-site variation, transcription of a different isoform, and ultimately to far less protein production and so reduced functional ERAP1.58, At ERAP2 the genetic association is very broad, but on the key disease-associated haplotype, one protective variant (rs2248374[G]) leads to a transcribed RNA product that undergoes nonsensemediated decay and thus no translated protein product. This variant is thus the major functional variant at ERAP2. This variant has recently been demonstrated to protect from Yersinia pestis infection (the "Black Death"), which is thought to have driven its high current prevalence.

Gene—gene interaction between ERAP1 and HLA-B27 is the first example of replicated, statistically significant gene—gene interaction in any human disease and indicates that the mechanism by which HLA-B27 induces AS likely involves aberrant peptide processing. ERAP1 also interacts with HLA-B40 in causing AS, and it is now also known that the same variants in ERAP1 are associated with psoriasis, and interaction is observed with HLA- Cw6, the major psoriasis class I HLA allele. Similarly, in Behçet's disease, there is ERAP1 association restricted to HLA-B51+ cases, the major Behçet's disease class I HLA risk allele. This suggests that HLA-B27, HLA-B40, HLA-Cw6, and HLA-B51 operate in these diseases through similar mechanisms.

Interleukin-23 Pathway Genes and Ankylosing Spondylitis. The genetic discovery of the association of IL23R with AS was the first demonstration of the involvement of this pathway in AS and has driven the repositioning of inhibitors of the IL-23 pathway for clinical use in AS. There are now multiple IL23R polymorphisms identified that are associated with AS, IBD, psoriasis, and other associated diseases. Several other IL-23 pathway genes have also now been associated with AS, including IL12B, TYK2, and JAK2, as well as other genes that interact with the IL-23 pathway such as IL1RL1, IL1RL2, IL6R, PTGER4, and CARD9 (Table 76.2). The molecular mechanisms underlying these associations largely await dissection, but these findings clearly demonstrate that this is a major pathway in AS pathogenesis. Consequently, it is a major target for development of therapies for AS. The association of IL23R is found in both HLA-B27-positive and HLA-B27-negative disease, and thus, the pathway is relevant to both AS subsets. Whether these genes play any role in controlling disease activity or severity of ankylosis is the subject of ongoing research. Association of IL23R variants with anterior uveitis, however, has been demonstrated, along with association with other AS-associated variants including HLA-B27 and SNPs in ERAP1 and chromosome 2p15, at genome-wide significant thresholds.

Lymphocyte Development and Activation Genes. The association of AS with multiple cytokines, cytokine receptors, and transcription factors involved in controlling lymphocyte development and activation points to the key involvement of the affected cell types in AS pathogenesis. Associated genes include EOMES, RUNX3, TBX21, ZMIZ1, IL7, and IL7R.58, The functional

significance of these findings is discussed in more detail in subsequent text.

### Polygenic Risk Scores

There is a clear need for improved approaches to enable earlier diagnosis of axial SpA and for better screening tools to identify early cases or people at high risk of the disease. Given the high heritability and low prevalence of axial SpA, genetic tests are an obvious candidate. Polygenic risk scores (PRS) are a method in which weighted scores of genetic variants carried by patients provide a measure of genetic load for particular diseases that are carried by individuals. PRS have been developed for both AS72 and the AS-related disease AAU72 and shown in different studies to have high discriminatory capacity in both patients of European and East Asian descent. A replication study performed in a 35-year follow-up study in Swiss AS patients, their family members, and unrelated healthy controls demonstrated the PRS had an area under the curve (AUC) in receiver operator characteristic analysis of 0.96, compared with an AUC of 0.91 for HLA-B27.73 This exceeds the discriminatory capacity for both MRI and C-reactive protein (CRP).

### Pathogenesis

Better understanding of the genetics of AS has advanced understanding of AS pathogenesis. Of the more than 1 10 loci associated with AS susceptibility, several fall into pathogenic "pathways" that may be important immunopathogenic drivers of AS: classic and nonclassic roles of HLA-B27; ERAP1 and other aminopeptidases involved in peptide trimming and antigen presentation; and IL-23

and IL-17 cytokines. Analysis of the overlap between AS-associated SNPs and epigenetic marks of gene activation in cell and tissue types has implicated, not surprisingly, the involvement of cells of the immune system (cluster of differentiation [CD]4+ and CD8+ T cells, T-regulatory cells) but also of the gastrointestinal mucosa, implicating a role of disordered gut immunity in disease pathogenesis.

### HLA-B27

Despite more than 40 years of research, the precise role of HLA- B27 in AS remains unclear. Current models for how HLA-B27 operates in AS can be divided into classic models of how class I alleles operate in antigen presentation versus nonclassic models associated with irregular properties of HLA-B27, including a slowfolding rate and cell-surface homodimer formation.

The dominant role of class I HLA molecules, such as HLA- B27, is in the presentation of antigens to CD8+ T lymphocytes. In the case of infected or transformed cells, presentation of foreign or tumor antigens provide danger signals to CD8+ T lymphocytes. The "arthritogenic peptide" model of AS pathogenesis suggests that in genetically predisposed individuals, aberrant presentation of self-peptides by HLA molecules results in recognition of innocuous self-antigens as harmful, inducing autoreactivity from CD8+ T cell responses. Self-reactive T cells have been isolated from synovium of AS patients, but these studies have not been convincingly replicated.75-77 This model is not well supported by studies in B27-transgenic rats, in which disease pathogenesis is independent of CD8+ T cells. One caveat to this model is that B27-transgenic rats express approximately 40 to 50 copies of HLA-B27 per cell compared with, at most, two copies in humans.

The effects of such overexpression of class I alleles in this animal model require cautious interpretation of data from such experiments because it is possible that an AS-like condition may arise from pathogenic mechanisms that may not be relevant to human disease.

During antigen processing and presentation, the highly polymorphic heavy chain of HLA-B27 noncovalently associates with β2-microglobulin, and that complex is loaded with a peptide before transport of this complex to the cell surface. The highly ordered process of HLA:peptide assembly, which occurs in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), happens more slowly for HLA-B27 than any other HLA molecule. The unfolded protein response (UPR) theory suggests that slow assembly of HLA-B27 complexes initiates ER stress pathways that lead to IL-23 secretion from macrophages. Support for the UPR theory is, again, strongest in B27-transgenic rats but has also been reported in the synovium of AS patients.80, However, studies of circulating cells from AS patients have found little evidence for ER stress.

Following transport to the cell surface, β2-microglobulin can dissociate from the heavy chain, leaving a free heavy chain. Free heavy chains can then dimerize to form cell surface heavy-chain homodimers. Recent reports have shown that subsets of T cells and natural killer (NK) cells recognize B27 homodimers through specific killer immunoglobulin receptors (KIRs). Recognition of cell surface B27 heavy-chain homodimers by KIR3DL2+ CD4+ T cells leads to IL-17 secretion by those T cells. However, studies of genetic variants of KIR that determine the circulating KIR profile in individuals have shown little evidence that these associate with disease. Further, the ability of HLA-B27 subtypes to form homodimers has been shown not to correlate with their association with AS, making this theory unlikely to be relevant in the mechanism by which HLA-B27 induces the disease.

The development of sequencing-based methods to profile T cell receptor (TCR) usage has provided strong evidence that the arthritogenic peptide hypothesis is involved in the mechanism by which HLA-B27 drives AS pathogenesis. CD4 and CD8 lymphocytes carry a TCR, which is a heterodimer made up of a TCRa and TCRb chain. The TCR recognizes antigenic peptide presented by HLA proteins on antigen presenting cells like dendritic cells. CD4 T cells recognize antigen presented by HLA Class II proteins like HLA-DRB1, and CD8 T cells typically recognize internally processed antigens presented by HLA Class I proteins, such as HLA-B27. The two TCR chains are highly variable between cells, with up to 1011 different TCRs theoretically possible in any individual. Expansion of a clone of T cells carrying the same TCR is strongly indicative of a common antigenic driver. Multiple studies have now demonstrated that particularly among CD8 T-lymphocytes from AS patients, there is expansion of T cell clones bearing a characteristic motif in the hypervariable CDR3 region of TCRb.87-91 This motif was found in 37 of 37 AS cases but in only 4 of 19 HLA-B27-positive healthy controls in one study88 and is overrepresented in cases of both European and East Asian ancestry. Collectively, these data implicate this TCRb motif in the pathogenesis of AS in different environments and likely in patients carrying different HLA-B27 subtypes. Notably, this motif has also been identified in patients with bacterial induced reactive arthritis,92 further supporting the theory that AS is driven by interactions between the gut microbiome and a genetically primed host immune system. This discovery raises the potential that, using the AS-associated T cells, the antigenic triggers for AS could be defined and that targeting this subset of CD8 T cells could be therapeutic and potentially preventive for AS.

### ERAP1 and Other Aminopeptidases

Outside the HLA locus, ERAP1 has the strongest association with AS susceptibility. ERAP1 is an aminopeptidase involved in trimming of peptides that have been processed through the proteasome from approximately 13 to 15 amino acids in length down to typically 9 amino acid peptides. ERAP1 is therefore considered to be a "molecular ruler," shaping peptides before loading onto class I MHC molecules. The association with AS has been described and validated in several studies.66, At least two AS-associated ERAP1 haplotypes have been described, tagged by the nonsynonymous SNPs rs30187 and rs10050860.58 These SNPs only show associations in HLA-B27—positive patients, thus demonstrating gene— gene interaction between ERAP1 and HLA-B27.66 Despite this knowledge, our understanding of the precise role of ERAP1 in AS pathogenesis remains limited.

ERAP1 exists in either a closed (enzymatically active) or open (enzymatically inactive) state. Radiograph crystallography revealed that the main AS-associated SNP rs30187 (K528R) in ERAP1 is located at the hinge region of the enzyme that controls the switch between open and closed conformations. Functional studies comparing the HLA-B27-bound peptidome from cell lines carrying ERAP1 variants show increased enzymatic activity conferred by carriage of the Lys528 variant that results from AS risk-associated polymorphism at rs30187.95 This increased ERAP1 activity results in increased peptide epitope destruction but also increases production of some peptides relative to the protective Arg528 variant. Altered HLA:peptide complexes may have a profound effect on cell surface stability of HLA-B27 with concomitant effects on self-reactive T cell and NK cell engagement.

It is now understood that ERAP1 associations can be partitioned into a primary SNP effect at rs30187 and a secondary independent association with rs10050860 that retains significance upon conditioning on the primary signal. While the AS-protective rs30187 allele leads to reduced ERAP1 enzymatic activity,97 the rs10050860 disease-protective haplotype leads to production of a differentially spliced ERAP1-mRNA and reduced ERAP1 protein production. HLA-B27-positive individuals homozygous for protective variants at both SNPs are afforded a three to four times lower disease risk than HLA-B27 carriers coinheriting the risk alleles. Remarkably, these associations do not prevail in HLA- B27/ HLA-B40-negative disease.

Controlling for the association of ERAP1, variants in two additional aminopeptidases falling within the chromosome 5q15 locus, ERAP2 and leucyl/cystinyl aminopeptidase (LNPEP), have also been identified. Association with the lead SNP in ERAP2 remains significant in HLA-B27-negative cases; whether LNPEP is independently associated with AS is unclear. The cytosolic aminopeptidase NPEPPS at chromosome 17q21 is the fourth aminopeptidase demonstrating an association with disease and is involved in peptide processing prior to transport of substrates into the ER. As with ERAP1, loss-of-function variants in ERAP2 are protective against AS. The protective allele at rs2248374 produces truncated ERAP2 transcripts that undergo nonsense-mediated decay, knocking down expression of the protein completely in homozygote individuals and by approximately 50% in heterozygotes. ERAP2 functions to break down peptides in the ER that are eight amino acids or shorter in length. Thus in combination with the known function of ERAP1 to break down antigenic peptides of greater than nine amino acids in length, it can be deduced that the peptides which are involved in AS pathogenesis must be nine amino acids in length. Further understanding of how each of these aminopeptidases functions in AS is warranted, but

inhibition of ERAP1 and ERAP2, at least, appears as a potentially attractive therapeutic strategy for AS.

### Interleukin-23 Signaling Pathway

IL-23 signals through a cell surface receptor composed of an IL-23specific subunit (IL-23R) and a subunit shared with IL- 12R (IL-12RB1). IL-23 signaling is necessary for the development of IL-17— and IL-22—secreting cells. As described previously, polymorphisms in IL23R and, more recently, downstream components of the IL-23 signaling pathway, JAK2 and TYK2, and the IL-23 subunit IL12B, have been associated with AS.58, Under normal physiologic conditions, IL-23, IL-17, and IL-22 regulate gut homeostasis. IL-23 expression is increased in spondyloarthritis synovial fluid,100 and serum IL-17 levels and the number of IL-23R expressing CDR T-lymphocytes are increased in AS patients.

Improved understanding of the cells involved in IL-23 signaling in AS has shone light on new immune cell subsets involved in pathogenesis. Until recently, CD4+ T cells were thought to be the dominant cell type involved in IL-23mediated immune responses. However, studies in IL-23R—green fluorescent protein (GFP) reporter mice revealed that CD4+ T cells are only a small component of the IL-23 signaling family. Several other cell types in these mice express high levels of IL-23R, including γδ T cells, macrophages, dendritic cells, and lymphoid tissue inducer-like (LTi) cells. In AS patients, several "noncanonical" IL-23responsive cells have been described, including γδ T cells, KIR3DL2+ CD4+ T cells, mast cells, and neutrophils.83, The precise hierarchy of these cell types remains unclear, but it is conceivable that each cell type may play tissue-specific roles in regulating IL-23 responses in AS. The prominent source of IL-23 in AS also remains unclear.

Whatever the source of IL-23 and IL-17, clinical trials of biologics that block these cytokines have shown divergent results. Phase III clinical trials of IL-17 blockade with the fully humanized monoclonal anti-IL-17, secukinumab, demonstrated clinical benefit, leading to this agent and other agents targeting IL-17 now being widely used in clinical practice for patients with AS. In contrast, inhibition of IL-12/IL-23 signaling, through blockade of the IL-12/23 shared subunit by the fully humanized monoclonal antibody ustekinumab, failed to reach primary endpoint measures in AS, although it did show beneficial effects in subsets of patients. This conclusion is supported by the suggestive evidence that ustekinumab-treated HLA-B27-positive psoriatic arthritis patients had greater reductions in neck/back/ hip pain than HLA-B27-negative patients. Thus, this agent is likely at least partially effective in AS. In contrast, inhibition of IL-23p19, the IL-23-specific subunit, showed no efficacy in well-designed studies. These unexpected findings remain unexplained.

### Mucosal Immunity and the Microbiome

Clinical overlap between AS and gut inflammation has been recognized for many years with 5% to 10% of AS patients developing IBD and a further 70% presenting with subclinical gut inflammation. Furthermore, patients with AS display increased intestinal permeability. Early genetic studies provided evidence of shared genetic susceptibilities between AS and IBD, but cross-disease genetic comparisons facilitated by the Immunochip project has demonstrated the extent of that genetic overlap. Of the overlapping genes identified, several lie in the IL-23 signaling pathway, including IL23R, IL12B, TYK2, JAK2, and IL27. Several other

genes are implicated in mucosal immunity, including TBX21, RUNX3, EOMES, NKX2-3, ZMIZ1, and ICOSLG, while others play roles in microbial sensing (GPR35, GPR37, and GPR65).

IL-23 is an important regulator of mucosal health, mediating anti-microbial responses and protection from extra-cellular bacteria. IL-23 is markedly increased in the terminal ileum of AS patients. It is hypothesized that IL-23 responses in AS are exaggerated as a result of altered intestinal microbiome. Examination of the microbiome in both mucosal biopsies and fecal samples from AS patients demonstrates unique compositions of the intestinal microflora. These findings have been replicated widely, including in patients of European and East Asian ancestry. 117, Histopathology studies have also shown increases in bacteria in the gut wall of AS patients compared with healthy controls and correlated this with evidence of inflammasome activation. 119, Alterations to the microbiome, however, do not necessarily indicate a pathogenic mechanism since an altered microbiome may be a consequence, rather than a driver, of disease. Nonetheless, in animal studies there is strong evidence for a causal role for the microbiome in disease pathogenesis. HLA-B27-transgenic rats express multiple copies of human HLA-B27 along with an invariant MHC light chain, β2-microglobulin. These animals develop SpA-like disease, but both intestinal inflammation and joint inflammation are reduced in a germ-free environment.121, Carriage of HLA-B27 has been demonstrated to influence the gut microbiota in HLA-B27-transgenic rats and AS patients.123, Additionally, studying healthy subjects, a significant effect of HLA-B27 was seen on the gut microbiome, indicating that the major risk factor gene for AS influences the microbiome in the absence of disease, favoring models in which the microbiome drives disease rather than the converse. However, the precise interplay between host genetics, immune responses, and microbiota is yet to be fully mapped in humans, and their collective influence on health and disease remains unclear. Trials of therapies targeting the microbiome such as fecal microbiome transplant therapy, or broad-spectrum antibiotic therapies, which are effective in IBD, are awaited in AS.

### Structural Remodeling and Ankylosis

A major distinguishing feature of seronegative from seropositive arthropathies is that although inflammation typically causes erosion during early stages of both groups of diseases, osteoproliferation occurs in later stages of seronegative disease. There is little direct evidence in humans about the processes involved in osteoproliferative disease because of the difficulty in obtaining suitable specimens for histopathologic examination. Therefore most of the information that is available comes from imaging studies or from studies of murine models of disease.

Inflammation is clearly a critical early step in the osteoproliferative process. Baseline CRP is the only robust predictor of future radiographic change that has been reported to date (reviewed in ref. 127), and there is increasing evidence that although TNF inhibition does not altogether prevent bone formation, it does significantly slow ankylosis. 128-130 This is particularly evident in patients achieving clinical remission of disease activity. It had been postulated that TNF inhibition releases Wnt pathway—driven bone formation as it reduces expression of the Wnt inhibitor DKK1.131 However, this would be expected to lead to accelerated ankylosis in TNF inhibitor—treated patients, when in fact the converse appears to be the case. This may reflect the suppressive effect of TNF inhibition on disease activity in early stages of inflammation prior to activation of bone-forming pathways.129,

IL-17A and IL-12/23p40 levels are elevated in sera and synovial fluid of patients with AS. IL-17A regulates expression of JAK2, which is highly expressed in bone tissue from AS patients, and this may promote osteoblastic activity. IL-17A expressing γδ T cells may promote osteoblast differentiation from mesenchymal stem cells. IL-17A enhances expression of proinflammatory cytokines, such as RANKL, and metalloproteinases by a variety of cell types. This dual role of IL-17A on bone formation and resorptive pathways may depend on the extra-cellular cytokine milieu and stage of differentiation of different cell types but suggests the possibility that IL-17 may be a target cytokine linking inflammation with new bone formation. IL-17 family contains several different cytokines (IL-17A to IL-17F), and it has been proposed that IL-17F has a greater role than IL-17A in osteoproliferative diseases. The development of IL-17F—specific inhibitors raises the potential to test this hypothesis.

Chronic nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) use, particularly in patients with elevated acute phase reactants, retarded new bone formation. This was thought possible because of the known association of AS with genetic variants in PTGER4,57 which encodes a receptor for prostaglandin E2 (PGE2). PGE2 is produced at entheses in response to physical stress, driving IL-23 production and bone formation. However, a subsequent study of chronic NSAID use compared with on-demand treatment and using a very similar study design failed to demonstrate any benefit in retarding new bone formation, even in patients with elevated acute phase reactants.

MRI studies of the spine and SI joints suggest that bone marrow fat metaplasia is an intermediate step prior to new bone formation and that once fat metaplasia has occurred, new bone formation .138, The cellular and molecular processes that are may develop. involved are not well understood, but animal model studies suggest involvement of the Wnt and bone morphogenetic protein (BMP) pathways, which are the major bone anabolic pathways in animals. These may prove useful targets for reducing the rate of ankylosis in AS, but medications that specifically target inflammation-induced bone formation may be required to avoid generalized osteoporosis as a therapeutic side effect.

### Clinical Manifestations

### Skeletal Manifestations

### Low Back Pain and Stiffness

Back pain is an extremely common symptom, occurring at some point in up to 80% of the general population. Therefore it is important to note that back pain in axial SpA may have inflammatory features that help differentiate it from mechanical back pain, 141

143 although these traditional clues to inflammatory disease have limited diagnostic performance with sensitives 74% to 81% and specificity 25% to 44% for axial SpA144 (Table 76.3). Back pain is the most common symptom of AS (Table 76.4). Estimates of the proportion of adults with chronic back pain having inflammatory back pain (IBP) vary between 2.3% to almost 25%. 145-147 However, at 10 years from the onset of IBP, the probability of having spondyloarthritis for patients with IBP was only 30%, while the resolution of IBP occurred in 43%. Those who progress to clinical axial SpA are predominantly HLA-B27-positive. Among relatives of AS patients, a clinical history of IBP at an early age failed to reliably predict axial SpA as long-term outcome. The most important predictors for progression of IBP to spondyloarthritis were uveitis, male sex, and family history of SpA.

Typically, the low back pain of axial SpA is initially felt primarily deep in the gluteal region, is dull in character, difficult to localize, and insidious in onset. Pain can be severe at this early phase of the disease; it localizes in the SI joints but is occasionally referred toward the iliac crest or greater trochanteric region or down the dorsal thigh. Radiation of buttock pain may suggest root compression of the sciatic nerve. Buttock pain in axial SpA typically alternates from side to side. Coughing, sneezing, or other maneuvers that cause a sudden twist of the back may accentuate pain. Although the pain is often unilateral or intermittent

at first, within a few months, it usually becomes persistent and bilateral, and the lower lumbar area becomes stiff and painful. The pain is associated with a feeling of low back stiffness that is worse in the morning and may awaken the patient from sleep, particularly during the second half of the night. Many patients do not differentiate between low back pain and stiffness. The morning stiffness may last up to 3 hours or longer. Both the stiffness and the pain tend to be eased by a hot shower, an exercise program, or physical activity; they do not improve with rest. Fatigue as a result of chronic back pain and stiffness may be an important problem and can be accentuated by sleep disturbances due to these symptoms.

### Chest Pain

With subsequent involvement of the thoracic spine (including costovertebral and costotransverse joints) and the occurrence of enthesitis at the costosternal and manubriosternal joints, patients may experience chest pain accentuated by coughing or sneezing, which is sometimes characterized as "pleuritic." Chest pain at the sternal region may also be an early manifestation of the disease and has important diagnostic value (sensitivity 72%; specificity 83%).33, Likewise, mild to moderate reductions of chest expansion may be detectable in an early stage of axial SpA. Chest pain occurs relatively often in HLA-B27-positive relatives, even in the absence of radiographic evidence of sacroiliitis.33,148

### Tenderness Due to Enthesitis

Extra-articular tenderness due to enthesitis is a prominent complaint in some patients. Common tender sites include the costosternal junctions, spinous processes, iliac crests, greater trochanters, ischial tuberosities, tibial tubercles, and heels (Achilles tendonitis or plantar fasciitis). Radiographically, bone spurs may develop at these sites.

### Extra-axial Joints

The girdle or "root" joints (hips and shoulders) are the most frequently involved extra-axial joints in AS, and pain in these areas is the presenting symptom in as many as 15% of patients. Shoulder involvement, 149 but especially hip involvement, may cause considerable physical disability. Co-existing disease in the lumbar spine often contributes significantly to disability of the lower extremities. Hips and shoulders are involved at some stage of disease in as many as 35% of patients with AS. Hip disease is relatively more common as a presenting manifestation if the disease starts in childhood (juvenile AS). In boys 8 to 10 years of age, hip disease as a manifestation of juvenile AS is the most frequent type of chronic arthritis. Children with hip disease in AS are mostly HLA-B27 positive and anti-nuclear antibody (ANA) negative. The knee joint may also be affected in AS, often presenting as an intermittent effusion. The temporomandibular joint is involved in approximately 10% of patients.

### Osteoporosis

Decreased bone mineral density (BMD) can already be seen in early stages of AS. It is reported in more than 50% of patients with less than 10 years disease duration. The overall prevalence of osteoporosis approaches 15%.150, Osteoporotic deformities of the thoracic spine contribute significantly to abnormal posture, particularly fixed hyperkyphosis. Disease-related damage to the cervical and lumbar spine, thoracic wedging, and disease activity are determinants of hyperkyphosis. An increased

occiput-to-wall distance is associated with vertebral fractures. Symptomatic osteoporotic spinal fractures are increased in AS.121, Fused osteoporotic segments may be particularly susceptible to fracture. Neurologic complications occur rather fre- a. Proper assessment of bone quently, even after minor trauma. density in the spine is difficult in the presence of syndesmophytes because they may give rise to falsely high BMD values on dual x-ray absorptiometry (DEXA).

### Extramusculoskeletal Manifestations

Constitutional symptoms such as fatigue, weight loss, and lowgrade fever occur frequently. Other extramusculoskeletal manifestations are more localized.

### Eye Disease

AAU or iridocyclitis is the most common extra-articular manifestation of AS, occurring in 25% to 30% of patients at some time during the course of the disease. Even rates of greater than 50% have been observed with very long disease duration. There is no clear relationship between activity of the articular disease and this extra-articular manifestation. The onset of eye inflammation is usually acute and typically unilateral but the attacks may alternate. With AAU, the eye is typically red and painful, often accompanied by visual impairment. Photophobia and increased lacrimation may be present. If the eye remains untreated or if treatment is delayed, posterior synechiae and glaucoma may develop. Most attacks subside in 4 to 8 weeks without sequelae if early treatment is provided. AAU is more common in HLA- B27-positive than HLA-B27-negative patients with AS. Relatives who have AAU are at higher risk for AS. The calculated incidence of AAU in a Swiss family study was 89 attacks per 1000 patient-years for AS patients, but only 8 attacks per 1000 to 70% of patients with HLA-B27-positive AAU have axial SpA by ASAS criteria. 159,160

### Cardiovascular Disease

Cardiac involvement may be clinically silent or may cause considerable problems. Manifestations of cardiac involvement include ascending aortitis, aortic valve incompetence, conduction abnormalities, cardiomegaly, and pericarditis. In rare situations, aortitis may precede other features of AS. Aortic incompetence was noted in 3.5% of patients who had the disease for 15 years and in 10% after 30 years. Inflammation and dilation of the aorta are the main causes of aortic valve incompetence. Cardiac conduction disturbances are seen with increasing frequency with the passage of time, occurring in 2.7% of those with disease of 15 years duration and in 8.5% after 30 years. Both aortic incompetence and cardiac conduction defects occur twice as often in patients with peripheral joint involvement. In one study, a history of prior myocardial infarction was significantly more common in patients with AS (4.4%) than compared with the general population (1.2%). Cases of AS with concurrent Takayasu arteritis have been reported.

### Pulmonary Disease

Lung involvement is a rare and typically late manifestation of AS. It is characterized by slowly progressive fibrosis of the upper lobes of the lungs, appearing, on average, two decades after the onset of AS. Patients may complain of cough, dyspnea, and

sometimes hemoptysis. High-resolution computed tomography (CT) may be helpful in detecting interstitial lung disease in patients with respiratory symptoms whose chest radiographs are 164, In appropriate clinical circumstances, especially normal. where TNF inhibitors (TNFi) are being used, pulmonary tuberculosis must also be considered as a potential cause of apical lung disease.

Pulmonary ventilation is usually well maintained; an increased diaphragmatic contribution helps compensate for chest wall rigidity, which is due to involvement of the thoracic joints in the inflammatory process. Vital capacity and total lung capacity may be moderately reduced as a consequence of the restricted chest wall movement, whereas residual volume and functional residual capacity are usually increased.

### Neurologic Involvement

Neurologic complications of AS can be caused by vertebral fracture, instability, compression, or inflammation. Traffic accidents or minor trauma can cause fractures of a vulnerable osteoporotic spine. The C5-C6 or C6-C7 level is the most commonly involved site.

As in rheumatoid arthritis, atlantoaxial joint subluxation, atlanto-occipital subluxation, and upward subluxation of the axis may occur in AS as a consequence of instability resulting from the inflammatory process. Spontaneous anterior atlantoaxial subluxation is a well-recognized complication occurring in approximately 2% of patients and manifests with or without signs of spinal cord compression. Nontraumatic causes of neurologic complications caused by compression include ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament (which may lead to compressive myelopathy), destructive intervertebral disk lesions, and spinal stenosis.

Cauda equina syndrome, affecting lumbosacral nerve roots, is a rare but serious complication of long-term AS. Most often characterized by pain and sensory loss, this complication is accompanied by gradual onset of urinary and fecal incontinence, impotence, saddle anesthesia, and occasionally the loss of ankle jerk reflexes. Motor symptoms, if present, are usually mild. CT and MRI allow the accurate noninvasive diagnosis of this complication. Arachnoiditis and arachnoid adhesions may be important in the pathogenesis.

### Renal Involvement

Renal complications, including immunoglobulin (Ig)A nephropathy, can be observed in AS. IgA nephropathy complicating AS may be accompanied an elevated IgA serum level (93%) and renal impairment (27%). Microscopic hematuria and proteinuria appear in as many as 35% of AS patients. The significance of these findings in terms of subsequent deterioration of renal function is unclear. Amyloidosis (secondary type) is a rare complication.

### Imaging

### Conventional Radiography

Characteristic radiographic damage is an obligatory criterion in the definition of AS and r-axSpA.3, Patients with these conditions must, according to the modified New York criteria, have at least grade 2 radiographic sacroiliitis bilaterally (small localized areas with erosion or sclerosis, with no alteration in joint width)

or at least grade 3 radiographic sacroiliitis unilaterally (moderate or advanced sacroiliitis with erosions, evidence of sclerosis, widening, narrowing, or partial ankylosis). The entire modified New York grading system and examples of the grades are given in Fig. 76.1.

Conventional radiography visualizes skeletal structures with a high resolution and shows cumulative joint damage. The advantages of radiography are that it is fast, accessible, relatively inexpensive, and reliable. It has the limitation of being a twodimensional (2D) method, which may lead to projectional superimposition when visualizing three-dimensional (3D) structures. Radiography remains the most commonly used imaging modality in SpA.

In patients with AS/r-axSpA, radiographic changes are primarily seen in the axial skeleton, most often with the earliest changes in the SI joints, characteristically bilaterally and symmetrically. The initial findings consist of blurring of the articular surface, followed by erosions and sclerosis of adjacent bone. Progression of subchondral bone erosions can lead to radiographic pseudowidening of the joint space (Fig. 76.1D). With time, the definition of the joint may gradually be lost with radiographic superimposition of erosion, sclerosis, and new bone formation, which fills in the erosions and the original cartilaginous "joint space," with ankylosis as the end stage (Fig. 76.1E).

In the axial SpA spine, radiographic manifestations may be seen in discovertebral, apophyseal, costovertebral, and costotransverse joints. The earliest radiographic manifestations are often vertebral corner focal sclerosis (the "shiny corner") or erosion (the "Romanus lesion") at the sites of attachment of the annulus fibrosis to the vertebral end plate caused by previous inflammation at the enthesis.177-179 Furthermore, periosteal proliferation of new bone may fill in the normal concavity of the vertebral bodies, causing the anterior borders of vertebrae to appear straight ("squaring") and also often contributed to by erosion at the anterosuperior and anteroinferior vertebral margins. Furthermore, gradual ossification of the outer fibers of the annulus fibrosus may occur, starting as thin vertical bone proliferations before forming "mature" syn- 22 desmophytes. Progressive growth of these syndesmophytes may lead to complete bone "bridging" between vertebrae (bridging syndesmophytes, ankylosis).

Concomitant ankylosis often occurs in the apophyseal joints, with ossification of the adjacent ligaments. In a number of patients, this may result in complete fusion of the spine ("bamboo spine"). The thin vertical syndesmophytes should be distinguished from other (more voluminous) types of bone formation occurring in other inflammatory and degenerative conditions, such as psoriatic arthritis, diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis (DISH), and degenerative disk disease/osteoarthritis.

The key radiographic feature of peripheral manifestations of SpA is the combination of osteodestructive and osteoproliferative changes. Bone erosions and radiographic osteitis ("whiskering") at sites of osseous attachment of tendons and ligaments are frequently seen, e.g., at the calcaneus, ischial tuberosities, iliac crest, femoral trochanters, and vertebral spinous processes. In axial SpA, the hips are frequently involved. Hip involvement may lead to concentric joint space narrowing, irregularity of the subchondral bone with subchondral sclerosis, osteophyte formation at the outer margin of the articular surface, and, ultimately, ankylosis. Proliferative changes in psoriatic arthritis are seen as ill-defined ossifications around the joint or "juxta-articular new bone formation." Other radiographic features include joint space narrowing

resulting from cartilage loss, as well as joint subluxations or interphalangeal ankylosis. 176,

Radiography of the spine is not included in the classification criteria but may be useful to follow structural disease progression in patients with spinal involvement. Several validated scoring methods are available to quantify structural damage in the spine in AS, including the Bath Ankylosing Spondylitis Radiology Index (BASRI, cervical and lumbar spine and potentially the SI joint), the Stoke Ankylosing Spondylitis Spine Score (SASSS; lumbar spine only), and the modified SASSS (anterior cervical and lumbar spine). The modified SASSS is the most sensitive to change. These scoring methods are primarily used in clinical trials and observational studies but rarely in clinical practice.

### Computed Tomography

CT is the gold standard imaging technique for detection of abnormalities such as sclerosis and erosion, which are detected sooner and in more detail than by conventional radiography. The use of CT is limited by radiation exposure and the minimal ability

to assess changes in soft tissues or bone marrow, where the earliest features of sacroiliitis occur. However, low-radiation CT techniques ("low-dose CT") have been developed for imaging of the SI joints and spine at radiation doses similar to that with conventional radiography. Subsequently, low-dose CT may increasingly replace conventional radiography, both for the identification of structural damage caused by sacroiliitis in SpA and for sensitive assessment of new bone formation/progression in the spine in clinical trials. 187-189

### Magnetic Resonance Imaging

MRI is, through its ability to detect inflammatory changes in bone and soft tissues, the most sensitive imaging modality for recognizing early spine and SI joint changes in axial SpA, including .190, Particularly, it has a key role the in the early diagnr-axSp nosis of axial SpA in clinical practice through the documentation of sacroiliitis in patients with suggestive signs and sympotoms.

MRI sequences that are generally used in routine practice include a water-sensitive sequence, such as short tau inversion recovery (STIR) or T2-weighted fat-suppressed sequences that

are sensitive in detecting bone marrow edema (BME; a frequent finding in AS/axial SpA [Fig. 76.2A and eFig. 76.1]). Routine scanning protocols also include a T1-weighted sequence, which is well suited for depiction of structural lesions (erosions, fat lesions, sclerosis, and ankylosis) (Fig. 76.2C-F and eFigs. 76.1-76.3). Diagnostic MRI (see below) should include both sequences, whereas injection of a contrast agent (gadolinium compound) does not appear to enhance diagnostic accuracy over conventional imaging of the spine or SI joints. 192, The recommended imaging planes are semicoronal/oblique coronal (parallel to the posterior surface of S2 vertebral body), potentially supplemented with semiaxial (perpendicular to semicoronal) views for the SI joints and sagittal views for the spine. 194, Juxta-articular BME is the MRI finding most indicative of active sacroiliitis, but capsulitis and enthesitis may also be seen (eFig. 76.2B). Structural changes include bone erosions, sclerosis, periarticular fat metaplasia (fat lesions), and ankylosis (Fig. 76.2C-F). Typical lesions of the spine, which indicate active disease, are inflammation at the insertion of the annulus fibrosis and anterior/posterior ligaments (anterior/posterior corner inflammation), inflammation along the vertebral end plate (spondylodiscitis) (Fig. 76.3), and arthritis of the facet, costovertebral, and costotransverse joints and the adjacent entheses (Fig. 76.3 and eFig. 76.4).197-199 Structural changes, such as bone erosions, focal fat infiltration, bone spurs, and/or ankylosis (eFigs. 76.4 and 76.5) frequently 198, Enthesitis is common and may affect the interspinal occur. and supraspinal ligaments and the interosseous ligaments in the ligamentous part of the SI joints.

Validated scoring systems for assessing SI joint inflammation include the SPARCC (Spondyloarthritis Research Consortium of Canada) and Berlin SI joint inflammation scores. 200, Both are highly sensitive to change, and SPARCC also allows for

assessments of structural damage progression (SPARCC SSS). It has been documented that the SPARCC SSS method can discriminate between active and placebo therapy after as little as 3 months, 203,204 illustrating its high discriminatory ability. Compared with the radiographic modified Stoke Ankylosing Spondylitis score (mSASSS) method, which requires 2 years to demonstrate a difference, this illustrates a major potential advantage of MRI as a measure of structural damage outcome for future clinical trials. Several MRI-based scoring systems of spinal inflammation (e.g., Berlin, SPARCC and Canada-Denmark) are sensitive to change and routinely used in clinical trials.206, In contrast to other methods, the CanadaDenmark method assesses various areas in both vertebral bodies and posterolateral areas (costovertebral joints, facet joints, and spinous and transverse processes) for both inflammation and damage; this is an advantage because different types of structures (e.g., entheses and synovial joints) may respond differently to different therapies.207, In clinical practice, serial MRI can objectively document treatment response (eFig. 76.6), although it is important to recognize that MRI scores for inflammation correlate well with CRP but only weakly with symptoms, including pain.

MRI-detected inflammation is associated with the future development of structural damage on radiography in both the SI joints and spine.6, Resolution of inflammation, seen with treatment with TNF and JAK inhibitors, is associated with the development of fat metaplasia in the spine. 211-213 To what extent the same is true with other mode-of-action agents is less well known. Resolution of inflammation in SI joints by TNF, IL-17, and JAK inhibitors has been associated with healing of erosions and development of new tissue in the joint space (fat metaplasia in an erosion cavity; also called backfill).214, The histopathology of backfill remains unclear, but MRI data indicate

it is important intermediary tissue associated with the development of ankylosis.214, It has been reported that inflammatory lesions in the spine with no signs of concomitant fat metaplasia may resolve completely without sequelae, provided effective antiinflammatory therapy is administered.211, On the other hand, inflammatory lesions that already demonstrate fat metaplasia may be at higher risk of developing into new bone formation, even if the inflammation resolves with treatment. Consequently, the concept of a window of opportunity for effective treatment with anti-inflammatory agents has been proposed.
