Patients may also have inflammatory (synovitis, tenosynovitis, BME, soft tissue inflammation, enthesitis) (eFig. 76.7) and/ or structural manifestations (bone erosion, new bone formation, cartilage damage) in peripheral joints and entheses.217, This can also be detected with high sensitivity by MRI, improving the diagnosis and monitoring of peripheral involvement in SpA, compared with clinical examination.175, T1-weighted images in two planes and water-sensitive images are mandatory, while optimal visualization of synovitis also requires T1-weighted images after intravenous gadolinium contrast 175, Most enthesitis studies have looked at the injection. heel region (i.e. insertions of Achilles tendon and/or plantar fascia).20, Whole-body MRI is an exciting, relatively new technique, in which axial and peripheral joints and entheses on the entire body can be assessed in one MRI session (eFig. 76.7).194, It is currently not used in clinical routine practice, but clinical trials and cohort studies have documented a high sensitivity to change. 222,223

### Ultrasound

Ultrasonography (US) is useful for examination of peripheral joints and entheses, whereas US is not suited for evaluation of the SI joints and spine in axial SpA. US can detect both peripheral inflammatory manifestations in soft tissues such as synovium, tendons, and entheses and structural changes in the bone surface (erosions). No contrast agent is required, and no ionizing radiation is given. Furthermore, US may be used to guide invasive procedures, such as joint aspiration and injections. Evaluation of several joint areas can be done in one session, limited only by the time needed for the examination. A major advantage of US in clinical practice is that it can be performed as an extension of the rheumatological examination, if a properly trained rheumatologist and high-end US equipment is available. US is limited by the fact that it cannot penetrate bone, resulting in a lower sensitivity for detecting erosions than CT and MRI,224 due to limited access to some joint areas, and lacking capacity to diagnose osteitis. Examinations are performed using B-mode, which evaluate morphologic changes, combined with color or power Doppler. Doppler is a modality that superimposes color information on the gray-scale image, derived by the US reflection of moving erythrocytes in the tissue, and gives information on vascularization.

US can detect inflammation both intra-articularly (synovitis, erosions) (eFig. 76.8) and extra-articularly (enthesitis, tendinitis, tenosynovitis) (eFigs. 76.8 and 76.9) with higher sensitivity than .226, US assessments of synovitis, tenosynoclinical examination. vitis, and enthesitis are sensitive to change during therapy. 175,

Many validated assessment systems, several developed through international consensus and validation in Outcome Measures in Rheumatology (OMERACT), are available for US monitoring of peripheral joints and entheses. 229,230

### Diagnosis

There are no validated diagnostic criteria for AS or axSpA. Clinical manifestations of AS usually appear in patients in early adulthood; only rarely do they first appear in adults older than 40 years. This presumably must also be the case for axial SpA, and age constitutes an important part of the ASAS Classification Criteria for axial SpA. However, the diagnosis of axial SpA remains challenging. The critical consideration when assigning a diagnosis of axial SpA is the belief that there is an inflammatory disease of the axial spine or SI joints or both. This can be pathologically confirmed by a positive plain radiograph or MRI. A raised CRP level is also supportive of an inflammatory process, although is not specific to inflammatory SI or spinal disease. Absence of these features is associated with nonresponse to TNF inhibition, suggesting that such patients may not have axial SpA.

A careful history combined with examination and appropriate imaging is also required. Back pain is a common symptom in the community. Those with back pain for longer than 3 months of insidious onset, without a precipitating event, especially those with associated features such as psoriasis or anterior uveitis, should be further evaluated for the possibility of axial SpA. A primary care study is illustrative of a possible approach: people with back pain for greater than 3 months, with an age of onset of less than 45 years, who did not have a current confirmed diagnosis of axial SpA, who then had at least one of (1) IBP, (2) HLA-B27, or (3) sacroiliitis on any modality of imaging were evaluated for axial SpA by rheumatologists. In this group 42% were ultimately given a diagnosis of axial SpA.

### History

The history should focus initially on back pain. While back pain was traditionally considered to be predominately of an inflammatory nature (Table 76.3), a large proportion of patients with axial SpA do not have IBP. The specificity of IBP in axial SpA is 25% to 44% with a sensitivity of 74% to 81%. Family history is relevant as a positive family history increases the pretest probability of r-axSpA from 0.1% for a person belonging to the general population to approximately 10% for any first-degree relative of an HLA-B27-positive radiographic axial SpA proband. The probability that a first-degree relative with a positive family history of r-axSpA will themselves have r-axSpA increases from 10% to nearly 50% if this relative also has IBP. In contrast, the likelihood for a person who has IBP (without any other inflammatory feature) and negative family history for r-axSpA, is increased from 0.1% to only 1%. The other important features to note are the presence of peripheral inflammatory arthritis, especially lower limb inflammatory arthritis and/or hip joint involvement in addition to anterior uveitis, skin psoriasis, IBD, and enthesitis. Less common features include dactylitis (which is usually seen in those with psoriasis or reactive arthritis), aortitis, and IgA nephropathy.

### Examination

The examination should focus on the spine and SI joints and associated features such as peripheral arthritis, psoriasis, and enthesitis.

Early in disease and in those in remission, the physical examination will often be normal.

### Spinal Mobility

To arrive at an early diagnosis of AS, the physician must perform a thorough physical examination, noting that patients with early axial SpA often have minimal or no abnormalities on exam. On examination of the spine, there may be some limitation of motion of the lumbar spine as elicited by forward flexion, extension, or lateral flexion. Early loss of the normal lumbar lordosis is often the first sign and is easily assessed on inspection.

The Schober test (or its modifications) is useful to detect any limitation of forward flexion of the lumbar spine, although it is typically normal in early disease. While the patient stands erect, one mark is placed with a pen on the skin overlying the fifth lumbar spinous process (usually at the level of the posterosuperior iliac spine or the "dimple of Venus"), and another mark is placed 10 cm above in the midline. The patient is then asked to bend forward maximally, without bending the knees. If the distance between both marks is less than 15 cm, this indicates reduced lumbar spine mobility. Lateral flexion may also be diminished, and spinal rotation may cause pain. Normal values for forward and lateral spinal flexion should be corrected for age and sex. 233,234

### Chest Expansion

Mild to moderate reduction of chest expansion may be detectable in early stages of AS. Normal values are ageand sex-dependent, and there is considerable overlap between normal values and those obtained from AS patients.235, Values less than 5 cm in young people with an insidious onset of chronic, inflammatory low back pain strongly suggests AS. Chest expansion should be measured on maximal inspiration after forced maximal expiration at the level of the fourth intercostal space in males and just below the breasts at the xiphisternal level in females.

### Enthesitis

Examination of the ischial tuberosities, greater trochanters, spinous processes, costochondral and manubriosternal junctions, supraspinatus insertion, and iliac crests can determine the presence of enthesitis. Heel pain, especially when getting out of bed, is a characteristic manifestation of Achilles tendon enthesitis and plantar fasciitis.

### Sacroiliitis

Direct pressure over the SI joints may elicit pain, as may special testing maneuvers (for example pelvis rock test; FABERE—Flexion, ABduction, External Rotation, Extension; and Gaenslen test), although these latter maneuvers lack specificity and sensitivity. These signs may also be absent in early disease or may become negative in late stages as inflammation is replaced by fibrosis or bony ankylosis.

### Posture

Over the course of the disease, the patient may lose normal posture. Involvement of the cervical spine is manifested by pain and limitation of neck movement. The physician can detect a forward slope of the neck by having the patient stand against a wall and try to position his or her occiput against it.

After many years of progression in patients with severe disease, the entire spine may become increasingly stiff, with loss of normal posture from gradual loss of lumbar lordosis and the development of thoracic kyphosis.152, The abdomen becomes protuberant;

breathing is primarily by diaphragmatic action. These typical deformities usually evolve after a disease duration of 10 years or more (see supplemental eFig. 76.10 on Elsevier eBooks+).

### Laboratory Tests

Axial SpA can be diagnosed on clinical and imaging grounds with a negative HLA-B27 test. This test often has no additional value in diagnosis but can be useful in screening procedures. Acute phase reactants such as CRP can be raised in axial SpA patients, but a substantial proportion of patients with early disease or nraxSpA have normal or near normal CRP. A substantial minority of patients with radiographic axial SpA (AS) also have a normal CRP. The clinician should not be discouraged from further evaluation by a normal CRP or a negative HLA-B27 in the right clinical context.

Generally, blood tests are not helpful for the diagnosis of AS. Elevated levels of fecal calprotectin may suggest associated IBD in the appropriate clinical context237 and have specificity and sensitivity exceeding 90%. A normal erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) or normal CRP level does not exclude active disease, although CRP does correlate with patient reported disease activity, and elevated CRP is associated with better treatment response. Neither ESR nor CRP is superior in assessing disease activity. A mild normochromic anemia may be present in up to 15% of patients. Elevation of serum alkaline phosphatase (derived primarily from bone) is seen in some patients but is unrelated to disease activity or duration. Elevations of serum IgA are frequent in AS and correlate with acute phase responses.

### Imaging

Imaging is often initiated with a plain radiograph of the pelvis, but this is commonly normal early in disease or in those with nr-axSpA. The complex anatomy of the SI joint and the fact that a radiograph is a 2D representation of a 3D anatomy and frequent overlying bowel gas and soft tissues make reliable detection of radiographic sacroiliitis difficult, even for experienced readers and after extensive training and calibration.241, Diagnosis was previously dependent on presence of bilateral moderate or unilateral severe radiographic sacroilitis, using the modified New York classification criteria incorrectly for diagnosing AS. This delayed the diagnosis by an average of 7 to 10 years.

MRI of the SI joints is a more useful option than radiography, particularly in early disease. The use of MRI has been endorsed by the European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology (EULAR) recommendations for the use of imaging in the diagnosis and management of SpA in clinical practice and by the European Society of Musculoskeletal Radiology (ESSR) Arthritis Subcommittee. 191, The introduction of MRI has resulted in a major improvements in the diagnosis and evaluation of patients with SpA. Now, through the ASAS (ASsessment of SpondyloArthitis) classification criteria for axial SpA, MRI has a key role in detection of axial SpA, as patients with "active sacroiliitis on MRI" plus one clinical feature (e.g., psoriasis, enthesitis, or uveitis) should be classified as axial SpA. A consensus-based definition of active sacroilitis on MRI, i.e., to fulfll the MRI criterion of the ASAS criteria ("ASAS-positive MRI"), includes both that SI BME should be "highly suggestive of axial SpA" and that BME should be present in at least two s.244,245Subsequent sites and/or in at least two consecutive slices. data have demonstrated that incorporating structural damage lesions (erosions) into the criteria could further improve the diagnostic utility of MRI.246-258 In contrast, SI joint fat lesions and/or

spine lesions have not been documented to improve the diagnostic utility of MRI.249, An update from the ASAS MRI working group emphasized that subtle BME changes should not be overinterpreted, that determining their importance should never be made in isolation of the clinical context, and that the presence or absence of structural changes, particularly erosions, should be taken into account in case of subtle BME. In accordance with this, separate reports have shown that BME that resembles milder degrees of inflammatory sacroiliitis can be observed in athletes and postpartum women. 251, It is characteristic that such falsepositive MRI findings are located in the anterior upper part of the joint and/or the posterior lower part, while the midportion is spared.251, In axial SpA, inflammation can also be observed in these same areas but is then generally also located in the midportion of the joint.253, Furthermore, patients with axial SpA will often also have other manifestations, such as fat metaplasia in the bone marrow (homogenous, intensely bright, sharply marginated), and bone erosion is common, often in close relation to areas of BME, which will markedly increase the likelihood of it being axial SpA.255, Simultaneous contextual interpretation of MRI that allows for visualizing features of inflammation as well as of structural damage is crucial for both diagnostic evaluation and application of the ASAS definition of a positive SI joint MRI for the purpose of disease classification. It must be remembered that the ASAS criteria are classification criteria, not diagnostic criteria, and that diagnosis should not be made on MRI alone but be made based on the combined information of the clinical context (signs and symptoms), laboratory tests (HLA-B27 and CRP), and imaging (MRI and potentially radiography). 245,

An important differential diagnosis is osteitis condensans ilii, which is most frequently, but not solely, seen in postpartum women; this is characterized by anterior iliac sclerosis and frequently anterior BME (Fig. 76.4).254, For juvenile inflammatory arthritis, MRI is much more reliable for diagnosis of sacroiliitis than radiography. Pediatric-specific definitions for sacroiliitis in children are needed, since normal variation frequently mimics BME261 with more than half of normal healthy children harboring findings that satisfy the criteria for an adult definition of erosion.

Spinal MRI is not recommended for routine diagnostic evaluation of axial SpA, unless the SI joint MRI is equivocal and the clinical suspicion of axial SpA is high.184, Vertebral corner lesions demonstrating BME and/or fat metaplasia may be observed at up to two to three spinal levels in healthy individuals, especially in patients with mechanical disorders. To assess all components of spinal involvement in axial SpA, it is essential that the sagittal images extend sufficiently laterally to cover all lateral spinal structures that could be inflamed, including the transverse processes. 191,

In 2012, ASAS proposed a definition of a positive MRI of the spine for classification of axial SpA, requiring the presence at least three inflammatory lesions in the vertebrae, and each of these lesions should be present on two or more consecutive sagittal slices. However, the addition of MRI of the spine as an imaging criterion to the ASAS axial SpA classification criteria only led to an increase of 1% to 2% in the percentage of patients classified with AS/axial SpA; it is not sufficiently specific and is therefore not recommended.191,

Conditions such as neoplasia, fracture, and infectious arthritis are also differential diagnoses but are rarely a major diagnostic challenge, although more chronic infections, such as tuberculosis or brucellosis, may pose challenges. MRI characteristics of infection are unilaterality, high volume and intensity of BME, and spread into surrounding soft tissues.

### Prognosis and Outcomes

More is known about outcomes of patients with AS than of patients with nr-axSpA. One study indicates that the burden of patient-reported outcomes, peripheral arthritis, and extraskeletal manifestations over time is similar between AS and nr-axSpA.

The course of AS is highly variable, characterized by spontaneous remissions and exacerbations. The disease may run a relatively mild or self-limited course or lead to severe spinal deformity, disability, and extra-articular disease, including aortitis. Men with AS may have greater progression to radiographic damage. Life expectancy is reduced, particularly after 10 years of disease. Three studies report higher standardized mortality rate (SMR) for females than for males.267-270 In a Swiss study, the mean number of life-years lost for female AS patients was 15.6 years compared with 4.7 years for male patients. A study from Finland indicates that the risk of dying for patients with AS is increased by 50% compared with controls matched for age and sex. Causes of death include complications of the disease such as amyloidosis and spinal fractures, as well as cardiovascular, gastrointestinal, and renal disease. No differences exist between familial and sporadic AS in terms of age at onset, age at diagnosis, or prevalence of peripheral arthritis and AAU.

Functional limitations increase with disease duration. Although structural damage seen on radiographs is clearly associated with impaired physical function and spinal mobility at the group level, individual patients with normal radiographs might exhibit a major reduction in spinal mobility, whereas those with severe radiographic abnormalities might function quite well in everyday tasks. .

In at least one study, sick leave was comparable in AS and nr-axSpA. Withdrawal from work in those with paid jobs varies from 10% after 20 years of disease duration to 30% after 10 years, depending on the characteristics of the patients included and the social security system considered.43-47, The ageand sex-adjusted withdrawal rate from labor-force participation was 3.1 times higher among Dutch patients compared with the general population. Older age at disease onset, manual work, lower educational level, and coping strategies characterized by the limitation and pacing of activities were associated with a higher risk for work disability. .43-47, Vocational counseling, job training, easy access to the workplace, and support of colleagues and management may reduce the probability of withdrawal from work.274, Sick leave in those with paid jobs has been linked to higher disease activity and presence of extraspinal disease manifes- .43-47, Patients with peripheral joint involvement tations. are more likely to take sick leave than are AS patients with axial manifestations only. Generally, poor QoL in patients with axial

SpA is associated with high disease activity, poor function, sleep disturbance, mood, and widespread pain.

Overall, the first 10 years of disease are particularly important with respect to subsequent outcome. Most of the loss of function among patients with AS occurs within this period and is associated with the presence of peripheral arthritis, spinal radiographic changes, and development of a so-called bamboo spine. 281, Although radiographic progression is highly variable among patients, radiographic evidence of spinal involvement, especially the presence of syndesmophytes, appears to be the primary factor that independently predicts further radiographic progression.

Increasing evidence supports the importance of inflammation in predisposition to radiographic progression (i.e., the progression of structural damage and inflammation are coupled in axial SpA). Clinical parameters of inflammation, notably the Ankylosing Spondylitis Disease Activity Score (ASDAS) and CRP levels, are associated with prognostic risk, especially early in the disease course, which is consistent with MRI data that evaluate prognostic risk of inflammatory lesions in the spine. 129, This is also consistent with data from an observational retrospective cohort study showing that the introduction of anti-TNF therapy early in the disease course may be associated with a lower risk for radiographic progression by reducing inflammatory activity. Smoking (increases radiographic progression) and NSAID utilization (reduces radiographic progression) influence prognostic risk, although it is unclear whether this is related to inflammation. 285-288 Biomarkers reflecting connective tissue remodeling (e.g., metalloproteinase 3 and citrullinated vimentin) and formation of bone (e.g., sclerostin and dickkopf-1) have been associated with radiographic progression. 288-291

Involvement of the hip joint may cause serious disability. After 30 years of disease duration, 12% to 25% of patients have at least one hip replaced. It is well known that only a minority of people with nr-axSpA eventually develop radiographic sacroiliitis after a mean follow up period of 10.6 years, although the longer the observation period, the higher the transition rate.7,31,293

### Monitoring and Management

### Standardized Assessment of Disease Activity and Treatment Response

Signs and symptoms such as spinal pain and limitation of motion might be due to current disease activity or the result of damage. Several tools are available to assess these dimensions. For example, there are many ways to measure limitation of motion of the

lumbar spine. New instruments have been developed to assess various aspects of the disease, including the Bath and Edmonton AS Metrology Indices, the Bath AS Global Index, the BASRI, the Bath AS Disease Activity Index, and the Dougados Functional Index.294-300 An international ASAS working group was formed with the aim of selecting, proposing, and testing core sets of measures for different settings. It was thought that a certain set of variables should be targeted to a specific task. For example, when assessing the efficacy of physical therapy, it would not be realistic to include measures of radiographic changes of the spine. Likewise, the set of measures for a drug's disease-modifying capabilities will differ from a set that measures analgesic effectiveness only. Instruments for four settings have been defined: disease-controlling anti-rheumatic therapy; symptom-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs, such as NSAIDs; physical therapy; and clinical record keeping in daily practice (Table 76.5). Composite criteria to assess the response of individual patients have also been developed and validated. The ASAS-20 improvement criteria are frequently used in clinical trials. In addition, more stringent improvement criteria—ASAS-40 and ASAS-5/6—have been proposed,302 as well as criteria to define partial remission. The three sets of improvement criteria and the partial remission criteria are presented in Table 76.6.302-304I In addition to the composite criteria above, the

AS Disease Activity Score (ASDAS) enables physicians to define disease activity states and to demonstrate improvement by applying cutoff values. MRI allows objective and sensitive monitoring of inflammation in the sacroiliac joints and spine.

A needs-based QoL instrument specific for AS has been developed. It is well accepted by patients and easy to perform and has shown good scaling, psychometric properties, and sensitivity to change. 303,

Another disease-specific instrument (Evaluation of Ankylosing Spondylitis Quality of Life; EASi-QoL) that scores in the domains of physical function, disease activity, emotional well-being, and social participation has also shown excellent psychometric properties and responsiveness in a clinical trial setting.

### General Management Considerations

Updated recommendations that emphasize the key evidencebased components of disease management have been compiled306-309 (Tables 76.7 and 76.8). Treatment objectives in axial SpA are to improve QoL, relieve pain, stiffness, and fatigue and to maintain good posture and physical and psychosocial functioning. Evidence is lacking that any of the conventional synthetic

aLoE/GoR 2b/B.

disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs (csDMARDs), including sulfasalazine and methotrexate (MTX), alter or inhibit the inflammation seen in the axial joints and entheses in AS.

Most patients do not experience significant extramusculoskeletal manifestations except for AAU, which occurs in approximately 25% to 50% of patients. The number of patients who have experienced uveitis increases with disease duration. Usually, eye disease can be well managed with eye drops that contain glucocorticoids to reduce inflammation and with pupil-dilating, mydriatic agents to prevent or diminish synechiae (when the iris adheres to the cornea or lens). At the outset, patients should be warned that AAU may occur at any time during the course of the disease, especially in those patients known to carry the HLA-B27 allele.

A full explanation of the disease, its course, possible complications (e.g., AAU), and its prognosis is very helpful to facilitate treatment adherence. Self-help groups can provide important information and social support. In addition, patient organizations may provide access to hydrotherapy and group physiotherapy. Exercise is a mainstay of treatment. Swimming and other extension-promoting exercises or sporting activities such as volleyball or cross-country skiing may be appropriate for individual patients. These activities counteract the kyphotic effects of pain and fatigue on posture and reduce stiffness. Patients should reconsider contact sports if the spine has become fused or osteoporotic because of susceptibility to fracture. Appliances such as driving mirrors may improve comfort and safety, especially if there is considerable cervical spine involvement.

When considering the treatment of axial SpA, it is helpful to stratify patients by active and stable disease. Despite the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and European Medicines Agency (EMA) having separate indications for r-axSpA and nraxSpA, these groups should generally be treated similarly.

### Osteoporosis

Osteoporosis occurs in particular in AS patients with longer disease duration and active disease. DEXA scans are appropriate, but

syndesmophytes of the lumbar spine can artifactually increase BMD readings. Lateral and volumetric DEXA images may improve the usefulness of lumbar DEXA for assessment. Once diagnosed with osteoporosis, patients should be screened for secondary causes or exacerbating factors. The combination of segmental spinal fusion and osteoporosis probably increases the risk of spinal fracture.

Currently, it is unclear whether antiosteoporotic drugs such as bisphosphonates or denosumab are effective in preventing spinal fractures. Reducing disease activity might be more promising in controlling osteoporosis of the vertebral spine. A meta-analysis showed significant improvement in BMD of both hip and lumbar spine, only after 2 years of treatment with TNF inhibition. Nevertheless, in a longitudinal cohort study from Swedish registries, a reduced fracture rate could not yet be shown. The authors suggest that the observation period was probably too short.

### Reproduction and Sexuality

Female patients with AS have normal fertility. Most patients (50% to 60%) do not experience major changes in disease activity during pregnancy, but an increase in morning stiffness and low back pain, particularly at night, may occur at approximately the 20th week of gestation and last for a few days to weeks. In approximately 50% of patients, an exacerbation of symptoms is seen within the first 6 months postpartum. Sacroiliitis including complete ankylosis of the SI joints does not constitute a contraindication for vaginal delivery. Epidural anesthesia is usually possible because most patients have a rather short duration of disease and do not have extensive spinal syndesmophytes. Every pregnancy in patients with axial SpA should be considered potentially high risk, and such pregnancies require close collaboration between rheumatologists and obstetricians. Pregnant women with axial SpA may have a higher risk of pregnancy complications (gestational diabetes, preeclampsia, infection, preterm premature rupture of membranes), small-for-gestational-age infants, and preterm deliveries.

In at least one study, active disease served as a predictor for preterm delivery (OR, 13.8; 95% CI, 1.33 to 143.94), while most patients had vaginal deliveries.

In addition to possible impact on birth outcomes, a questionnaire-based study that included 552 respondents with AS showed that 38% of patients reported that their sexual relationships were at least "moderately" affected by their condition. This negative impact appeared to be greatest among those reporting poor

physical functioning, depression, higher disease activity, unemployment, and poor self-efficacy.

### Pharmacologic c Therapy

The following section will review the evidence and recommendations for the use of pharmacologic therapy in axial SpA. For drug-specific mechanisms of action and adverse events, please also

refer to other excellent chapters in this book for information on NSAIDs (Chapter 59), glucocorticoids (Chapter 60), biologic agents (Chapters 63 and 64), and JAK inhibitors (Chapter 65).

### Nonsteroidal Anti-inflammatory Drugs

In patients with active axial SpA, first-line therapy is typically a full dose of an NSAID used continuously, although consideration of adverse effects is important, especially in patients with coexistent IBD, comorbid hypertension, or cardiovascular or renal disease. There is no particular NSAID that is preferred, and indirect evidence suggests that different NSAIDs yield similar efficacy. However, this evidence is based only on those NSAIDs that have been evaluated. In the authors' opinion, using an extended-release formulation is more helpful in patients with active disease as it allows a basal drug level through the night without the need for multiple-dosing per day. If a first NSAID does not result in adequate efficacy, a second NSAID should be tried. Typically, response to treatment is rapid, and a reassessment can be performed at 2 to 4 weeks after initiation.

In patients who attain a low disease activity state or inactive disease, should they maintain continuous or daily high-dose NSAID therapy? There are no withdrawal studies to address this question directly. The current recommendation in patients with stable disease is that they use on-demand dosing of NSAIDs. The caveat to this situation is that they may require daily or highdose NSAIDs to maintain this state. There is a single study using celecoxib in AS continuously versus on demand that suggested continuous use celecoxib resulted in less spinal radiographic progression at 2 years compared with on-demand use. However, more recently diclofenac was studied in the Effects of Non-Steroidal Anti-Inflammatory Drugs on RAdiographic Damage in Ankylosing Spondylitis (ENRADAS) trial with a primary endpoint of radiographic progression, and no benefit was observed in the continuous-use group compared with the on-demand group.

### Glucocorticoids

There is no evidence that systemic glucocorticoids (at low to moderate doses) work in axial SpA, and current guidelines strongly recommend against their use. Systemic oral glucocorticoids have been assessed in a 2-week placebo-controlled trial of daily 50 mg prednisolone, 20 mg prednisolone, or placebo. The study found no difference in primary endpoint (50% improvement in BASDAI) based on treatment group, although mean reductions in BASDAI were greater for those in the high-dose prednisolone group versus placebo (2.39 versus 0.66, respectively). Intra-articular injections for both the peripheral joint and SI joints can be considered. The authors' opinion is that SI joint injections work only temporarily and are associated with additional unnecessary radiation with fluoroscopic or CT-guided injection, although American College of Rheumatology (ACR)/Spondylitis Association of America (SAA)/Spondyloarthritis Research and Treatment Network (SPAR- TAN) guidance provides a conditional recommendation for intraarticular administration of glucocorticoids for isolated sacroiliitis. However, because axial SpA often affects the bilateral SI joints, a unilateral injection may not fully benefit the patient. Additionally, in the presence of unilateral sacroilitis, infection should be considered as one contemplates injection or other therapies.

### Conventional Synthetic Disease-Modifying Anti-rheumatic Drugs

Traditional csDMARDs have been studied without demonstration of benefit in axial disease. 320, In a subgroup of patients with

peripheral synovitis, there may be benefit on the peripheral arthritis, although if active axial disease exists, consideration should be made for the most effective and safest therapeutic options to cover both manifestations.

### Tumor Necrosis Factor Inhibitors

TNF inhibitors have revolutionized the treatment of axial SpA. Their introduction was based on the finding of TNF expression in SI joint biopsies of AS patients, the observation that overexpression of TNF leads to sacroiliitis in animal models, and earlier clinical trial data demonstrating the efficacy of one TNF inhibitor, infliximab, in Crohn's disease. Five TNF inhibitors are of proven benefit in AS according to pivotal phase III trials: infliximab, etanercept, adalimumab, certolizumab, and golimumab (subcutaneous and intravenous). In nr-axSpA, adalimumab, certolizumab, etanercept, and golimumab have been studied. Infliximab is an IgG1 chimeric monoclonal antibody, with the Fab portion derived from the mouse. It is given in a dose of 5 mg/kg every 6 to 8 weeks after loading at 0, 2, and 6 weeks. Etanercept is a recombinant TNF receptor IgG1 fusion protein that is self-administered by subcutaneous injection once weekly (50 mg). Adalimumab and golimumab are human monoclonal antibodies that are self-administered by subcutaneous injection on alternate weeks (40 mg) or every 4 weeks (50 mg), respectively. Certolizumab is a pegylated Fab fragment of a humanized anti-TNF monoclonal antibody that is given as a subcutaneous injection either as 200 mg every 2 weeks or 400 mg every 4 weeks after loading. None of these agents require concomitant therapy with MTX. The guidelines recommend these agents be used as monotherapy as there is not enough evidence that MTX is necessary for primary efficacy or prevention of anti-drug antibody formation. Infliximab is the most immunogenic of the TNF inhibitors, and consideration for low-dose MTX is reasonable, despite the absence of strong evidence.

When patients have inadequate response or are intolerant of NSAIDs, TNFi are recommended for the treatment of axial SpA, although the option to use an IL-17 inhibitor can also be considered, especially if there is a high burden of psoriasis. Countries have different requirements for therapeutic eligibility, with much of the world requiring a Bath Ankylosing Spondylitis Disease Activity Index (BASDAI) of ≥4 (at least moderate disease activity), although there is a shift to consider the ASDAS (≥2.1) as the threshold to initiate a biologic based on the 2022 updated ASAS— EULAR guidelines. The United States requires only the rheumatologist opinion for indication and an International Classification of Disease (ICD) diagnosis code. For the indication of nonradiographic disease specifically, the EMA has granted approval in the setting of objective signs of inflammation (MRI BME and/or an elevated CRP level) in addition to subjective disease activity. Similarly, the ASASEULAR guidelines recommend this as a requirement for nonradiographic disease. The United States currently does not require objective inflammation for initiation of immunomodulatory therapy. The FDA granted approval for the first indication in nonradiographic disease in 2019 for certolizumab pegol based on a Phase III, 52-week double-blind randomized controlled trial (RCT).

Consideration of Extramusculoskeletal Manifestations. There are special situations to consider when initiating treatment with a TNF inhibitor. If a patient also has IBD, then prescribing a TNF inhibitor that is a monoclonal antibody is recommended. Adalimumab, golimumab, and infliximab are approved for ulcerative colitis, while adalimumab, certolizumab pegol, and infliximab are approved for Crohn's disease. In patients with frequently

recurrent anterior uveitis, consideration for the use of a monoclonal antibody is also recommended. In this case the best evidence exists for adalimumab and infliximab. Golimumab and certolizumab have been studied in an uncontrolled manner, with a suggestion that their use might associate with less flares. 323,

Stable Disease on TNF Inhibitor Therapy. When a patient with axial SpA responds to TNF inhibition, should the NSAID be discontinued? The Study to Evaluate the NSAIDS Sparing Effect of Etanercept in Subjects with Axial Spondyloarthritis (SPARSE) trial addressed the NSAID-sparing effect of TNF inhibition in axial SpA patients, finding that 41% of patients exposed to etanercept were able to become NSAID-free compared with 14% of the placebo group (P = 0.013). When patients reach inactive disease, should the TNF inhibitor be withdrawn or dose-deescalated? Several trials have now been completed randomizing patients in remission on TNF inhibition to either remain on drug or withdraw. One study randomized patients with early axial SpA on certolizumab pegol to stay on drug, dose reduce or discontinue. This study showed patients on any dose of certolizumab did similarly well, compared with the placebo group, who almost all flared, suggesting we may be able to safely taper but not stop TNF inhibition when patients reach remission, especially when therapy is started at an earlier stage. Tapering can be considered per the ASASEULAR guidelines but is conditionally recommended against in the 2019 ACR/SAA/SPARTAN guideline. In nr-axSpA, withdrawal studies have also been completed. In ABILITY 3,327 patients with active nr-axSpA were initiated on adalimumab in an open-label fashion for 28 weeks. If inactive disease was reached, patients were randomized to maintain adalimumab versus discontinuing the agent, and all patients were followed for 40 weeks. As expected, more patients randomized to placebo flared, but 47% patients randomized to placebo did not flare through 40 weeks of follow-up. During the etanercept withdrawal trial with the same patient population, patients were treated with etanercept for 24 weeks and if attaining inactive disease (ASDAS <1.3), they were randomized to stay on drug or discontinue with up to 40 weeks of follow-up. Approximately 25% remained flare-free for the 40 weeks of follow-up, while the rest flared at various timepoints. Absence of MRI sacroiliitis and CRP concentrations of ≤3 mg/L at randomization predicted remaining in a flare-free state following treatment withdrawal. Unlike RA and psoriatic arthritis, for which RCT data show TNF inhibitors reduce radiographic progression, high-quality RCT data for inhibition of radiographic progression do not exist in axial SpA.

### Interleukin-17 Inhibitors

There are two IL-17A inhibitors approved in axial SpA, in both radiographic and nonradiographic disease based on phase III clinical trials.105, Additionally, bimekizumab, a dual IL-17A and IL- 17F inhibiting humanized monoclonal antibody is effective in both radiographic and nonradiographic axial SpA in Phase III trials. Bimekizumab is now approved for use in psoriatic arthritis and in axial spondyloarthritis. Secukinumab is given as a 150-mg subcutaneous injection every 4 weeks with or without a loading regimen of 150 mg weekly for 4 weeks. Ixekinumab is given as an 80-mg subcutaneous injection every 4 weeks. North American treatment recommendations recommend secukinumab or ixekinumab after inadequate response to TNF inhibition or where TNF inhibitors are contraindicated; however, the most recent 2019 guideline was published soon after the approval of only one IL-17A inhibitor, and the evidence base was small. The 2022 ASASEULAR

recommendations suggest IL-17A inhibitors be considered in a lateral position to TNF inhibition, with the exception of the presence of extramusculoskeletal manifestations, which might favor a specific targeted biologic (e.g., TNF inhibition in context of IBD).

### Janus Kinase (JAK) Inhibitors

Two different JAK inhibitors have Phase III data in AS, and one of them, upadacitinib (JAK1 inhibitor), has Phase III data in nraxSpA and an FDA indication for both radiographic and nonradiographic disease in the setting of inadequate response to TNF inhibition. Tofacitinib, a JAK 1,3 inhibitor, was studied in a Phase III 16-week trial, with significant improvement in the symptoms and signs. The tofacitinib Phase II trial additionally showed improvement in MRI inflammation. Upadacitinib was studied in three Phase III trials: two in radiographic disease (biologic naive and TNF inhibitor inadequate responder) and one in nr-axSpA. All trials met their primary endpoints with a difference in ASAS40 at 14 weeks. .333-335 What is not clear is whether the risk of cancer and major adverse cardiovascular events noted in patients with RA enrolled in the tofacitnib ORAL Surveillance study336 will translate to patients with axial SpA. However, until there is more direct evidence in this group to suggest otherwise, we should assume similar risk as observed in RA. As such the 2022 ASASEULAR guidelines recommend against JAK inhibition in patients with cardiovascular disease or risk or in patients 65 or older.

### Other Agents

A controlled dose-response (60 mg vs. mg) evaluation of a bisphosphonate, pamidronate, given intravenously on a monthly basis for 6 months, showed evidence of symptomatic efficacy, primarily in patients with only axial disease. In a 48-week open-label RCT, axial SpA patients assigned to pamidronate versus golimumab had no difference in pain or QoL, but the golimumab arm had significant suppression of inflammation detected both by CRP and MRI compared with the pamidronate-exposed patients. In general, side effects are significant and benefit is limited, such that these agents are not recommended for the primary treatment of AS.

Thalidomide has been used in three open-label studies in AS because of its known anti-TNF effect, through enhanced degradation of the TNF mRNA.339-341 In one study, improvement was reported in 80% of patients, with loss of efficacy 3 months after treatment discontinuation. Frequent side effects are drowsiness, constipation, and dizziness. Particular caution is required because of other major thalidomide-associated side effects, such as teratogenicity and peripheral neuropathy. Thalidomide is not recommended as a treatment for axial SpA.

### Failed Biologic Trials

Several biologic agents have been studied in up to Phase III trials with failed primary endpoints. Rituximab was studied in a phase II study with suggested efficacy in some patients but not in TNFiinadequate responders. 342, Abatacept did not demonstrate efficacy in AS. Tocilizumab, an IL-6 inhibitor, and sarilumab, an IL-6 receptor inhibitor, did not demonstrate efficacy, including no improvement in MRI BME.345, Despite ustekinumab's efficacy and approval for use in Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, psoriasis, and psoriatic arthritis, the phase III program was closed early, when the trial in biologic-naive AS patients did not meet the primary endpoint. The IL-23 inhibitor, risankizumab, did not meet its primary endpoint in AS, despite suggested efficacy in Crohn's disease, psoriasis, and psoriatic arthritis.

### Treat-to-Target

A treat-to-target pragmatic cluster-randomized controlled trial (TICOSPA) was performed in axial SpA. Centers were randomized to usual care (patients assessed every 12 weeks) or tight control (patients assessed every 4 weeks) with a treatment target of ASDAS <2.1 (low disease activity or less). Although a difference in the primary endpoint was not reached (the proportion of patients achieving a 30% improvement in the ASAS Health Index), the 2022 ASASEULAR guidelines recommend following the ASDAS for at least a clinically important improvement (change in ASDAS ≥1.1) to continue therapy.

### Nonpharmacologic cTherapy

### Physical Therapy

This therapeutic approach is important for patients with axial SpA. Patients feel better with exercise; improvement with exercise is one of the IBP criteria. The ASASEULAR guideline for axial SpA recommends exercise for all patients. Physical therapy improves outcomes in axial SpA patients.308, In addition to formal physical therapy, patients should perform back exercises and stretching. In an RCT, a program of supervised physiotherapy in groups was superior to individualized programs in improving thoracolumbar mobility and fitness. The program, which consisted of hydrotherapy, exercises, and sporting activities twice weekly for 3 hours per session, resulted in improved overall health and less stiffness, as reported by the patient. An intensive 3-week spa-exercise therapy program resulted in marked improvement in both subjective and objective assessments that lasted for as long as 9 months. Health resource use, in particular NSAID use and sick leave, was significantly reduced during this 9-month follow-up period. The clinical benefits of such treatments can be achieved at acceptable costs. 351, A Cochrane review concluded that a home exercise program is better than no intervention, supervised group physiotherapy is better than home exercises, and combined inpatient spa-exercise therapy followed by supervised outpatient weekly group physiotherapy is better than weekly group physiotherapy alone (level A evidence). The tendency toward positive effects of physiotherapy in the management of axial SpA calls for further research in this field. Moreover, the impact on physical functioning of physiotherapy in patients who respond well to biologics needs to be assessed.

Lying prone for 15 to 30 minutes once or several times a day is useful to reverse the tendency toward kyphosis, which is aggravated by pain and fatigue, as well as flexion contractures of the hip joints. Patients should sleep fully supine on a firm mattress with only a small neck-support pillow. In addition to formal physical therapy, patients should perform back exercises and stretching. 308 There is no evidence for an anti-inflammatory or gluten-free diet in axial SpA, although, in the authors' opinion, a diet free of processed food is generally a good principle for all patients, regardless of disease state.

### Surgery

The long-term results of total hip replacement in AS are satisfactory. The outcome of 138 total hip replacements and 12 revisions was good or very good in 86% of patients, and 63% of patients had no pain. Mobility was good or very good in 44% of patients. The mean follow-up was 7.5 years (range, 1 to 34 years). Altogether, 69% of the male total hip recipients younger than 60 years

were at work at the time of the survey. Ectopic bone formation may occur, with the rate of heterotopic ossification being 30%.353- 355 One large study of cemented implants with more than 10 years of follow-up showed 96% had low pain scores, and implant survival was excellent.356, In the United States, the majority of patients undergo cementless stem total hip replacement.

Vertebral osteotomy may be required in selected cases to correct marked flexion deformity when forward vision is severely impaired but note that the 2019 ACR/SAA/SPARTAN guideline conditionally recommends against vertebral osteotomy for severe kyphosis. Diaphragmatic herniation may result from the procedure.

In patients with r-axSpA, careful consideration of neck involvement is required pre-operatively, including imaging. General anesthesia needs to be planned well because it requires intubation that may involve neck manipulation. These movements may increase the risk of fracture through syndesmophytes or osteoporotic vertebrae. If there is extensive cervical spine disease, special positioning may be required because of kyphosis. Respiratory assessment is also important in established disease because lung function may be adversely affected.

### Treatment Summary

The therapeutic options for axial SpA remain limited after NSAIDs, with only two biologic classes (TNF and IL-17 inhibitors) and two JAK inhibitors approved in axial SpA. The advent of biologics and targeted small molecules has nevertheless revolutionized the therapeutic landscape of the disease. Despite the dramatic improvements, most patients do not reach an inactive disease state, possibly mediated by a still unacceptable delay to diagnosis and significant burden of damage at first recognition of disease. The treatment options are even more limited based on the differential treatment effects across the extramusculoskeletal manifestations. Treat-to-target trials have failed to show benefit, although treatment targets may still be important for the individual patient.

### Conclusion

The term axial spondyloarthritis has now largely replaced the traditional name of the disease, ankylosing spondylitis. nr-axSpA is more heterogeneous than radiographic AS. Uniform nomenclature will facilitate communication and reporting of study results. Therefore it has b een s uggested that the term axial SpA should be the preferred nomenclature. Inappropriate use of classification criteria for diagnostic purposes increases the risk of falsepositive labeling of individuals as having nr-axSpA. NSAIDs, physiotherapy, and patient education remain first-line therapy, but three new classes of drug treatment are available for NSAID nonresponders. Current evidence suggests that early suppression of inflammation with biologic treatment may decrease or retard the risk of new bone formation of the axial skeleton. Research is needed to more accurately identify those patients who will progress from nr-axSpA to r-axSpA and on how progression can be prevented or delayed by early treatment. Better understanding of gut mucosal immunology interactions may lead to novel treatment approaches.

# Reactive Arthritis

### KEY POINTS

Reactive arthritis is a form of spondyloarthritis triggered by any of several particular infections.

Reactive arthritis is often self-limiting, can become chronic, and can have both peripheral and axial features.

Diagnosis of reactive arthritis depends on symptoms and signs of spondyloarthritis, including various extra-articular disease aspects, as well as evidence of a preceding infection; chlamydial infections are often difficult to demonstrate, however.

Treatment of reactive arthritis is conservative in early self-limiting disease but more aggressive in chronic disease.

### Introduction and Historical Background

Reactive arthritis (ReA) is an inflammatory syndrome that by formal definition can result from certain gastrointestinal or genitourinary infections. The classic triad of symptoms comprising ReA includes acute inflammatory arthritis, inflammatory eye conditions (conjunctivitis), and dysuria. However, most patients who develop the arthritis do not present with this triad. Indeed many other clinical manifestations of ReA have been described.1, Interestingly and as developed next, acute inflammatory arthritis in concert with other possible clinical manifestations following specific gastrointestinal or genitourinary infections has been known for centuries. Importantly, ReA is one of the first systemic disease processes to be recognized as resulting from a classic host—pathogen interaction.

The term reactive arthritis was introduced in 1969 to describe this syndrome.1, However, considerable ambiguity exists in the literature in terms of the nomenclature of the condition, and many terms and eponyms have been utilized. Perhaps the most common eponym used until relatively recently was Reiter's syndrome. In 1942 two Harvard researchers, Bauer and Engelmann, recognized a case of ReA, and upon their review of the literature, they discovered that Dr. Hans Reiter had described the same syndrome in 1916.4, Reiter's patient, a German army officer, developed acute arthritis, nongonococcal urethritis, and conjunctivitis after an episode of dysentery. In recent years the designation Reiter's syndrome has become problematic, because after World War II Hans Reiter was arrested, tried, and convicted at Nuremburg for war crimes. It also has been suggested that health care providers too often have associated the term Reiter's syndrome exclusively

with the "classic triad" of symptoms, thereby resulting in under-/ misdiagnosis (see below). Currently, ReA is classified among the spondyloarthropathies, and it has been given several different clinical designations, including, originally, Reiter's disease or syndrome. More usually, however, the arthritis has been referred to simply as ReA. Some reports indicate that about half of all ReA cases are due to genital infection with Chlamydia trachomatis, and in such cases the disease is simply designated Chlamydia-induced arthritis. Interestingly, several reports have pointed out that some cases of ReA can be attributable to infection with the related respiratory pathogen Chlamydia pneumoniae.7,

The historical literature is replete with descriptions of patients with ReA. Importantly and more recently, recognition of the critical interplay between host and pathogen has become common in that literature. The earliest description of ReA may be that from circa 460 B.C., when Hippocrates wrote: "A youth does not suffer from gout until sexual intercourse"; at the time, the term gout was used indiscriminately to describe inflammatory arthritis of any origin. Several authors have speculated that Christopher Columbus may have had ReA in 1494, when he developed fever and severe arthritis of the lower extremities after a case of dysentery. Several others have described similar cases, including van Forest's description of a case of "secondary arthritis and urethritis" in 1507, Sydenham's association of arthritis with diarrhea in 1686, Stoll's documentation of arthritis following dysentery in 1776,13 and Yvan's description of a French captain who developed "ophthalmia" and inflammatory arthritis of the lower extremities after a venereal infection. Perhaps the earliest and most eloquent description of ReA in the modern clinical literature was penned by Brodie in 1818 when he described five patients with urethritis, arthritis, and conjunctivitis. In 1824, Cooper proposed a relationship between venereal infections and arthritis, particularly of the lower extremities, and in 1916 two French physicians (Feissinger and Leroy) described a clear case of ReA. In addition to the descriptions of ReA by both Reiter and the French physicians in the same year more than a century ago, the literature clearly includes description of cases of ReA many years before either Reiter or Feissinger and Leroy (for further discussion, see ref. 17).

The standard etiologic agents triggering ReA have been defined and include various species of gastrointestinal pathogens from the genera Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter, and Yersinia, as well as the genitourinary pathogen C. trachomatis. Importantly, many additional bacterial pathogens and several viral pathogens have been implicated recently as likely or potential triggers for ReA as well, as discussed below.

### Epidemiology

Despite extensive description over the centuries, as well as the clear realization that ReA results from a bacterial infection, epidemiologic studies of the disease remain problematic. As suggested above, significant ambiguity has long existed concerning the exact nomenclature for this clinical entity, and similar ambiguity occurs in terms of an apparent over-reliance on the so-called classic triad of ReA in diagnosis. Further, several studies have suggested a similar over-reliance on the presence of the HLA-B27 antigen to diagnose ReA. Because ReA represents the classic interplay between host and environment and because bacterial populations and genetics vary worldwide, the incidence and prevalence of the disease vary widely. The majority of ReA cases are transient in nature, adding to the difficulty in gathering epidemiologic data. In the case of Chlamydia-induced ReA specifically, emerging data strongly suggest that the initial infection can be clinically silent, rendering the ensuing diagnosis extremely difficult. The percentage of patients with ReA who develop peripheral arthritis versus axial arthritis versus a combination of both also remains poorly understood. Most importantly, no universally accepted sets of classification or diagnostic criteria exist at this point.

The first attempt to develop diagnostic criteria for ReA took place in 1979, when a group of experts met and analyzed 249 cases; however, they were unable to define universally accepted criteria. The American College of Rheumatology proposed diagnostic criteria for ReA in 1981, but these simply specified a seronegative arthritis that develops after an episode of urethritis, cervicitis, or diarrhea. The Third International Workshop on ReA convened in 1995, and one of its goals was to propose new diagnostic criteria. The criteria proposed were somewhat vague, but they did state that the patient must have the typical peripheral arthritis (asymmetric oligoarthritis predominately of the lower limbs), as well as evidence of a preceding infection (clinical diarrhea or urethritis within the preceding 4 weeks); in cases in which no clear clinical infection has been established, laboratory confirmation of infection is essential. It should be noted that the specification of 4 weeks was somewhat arbitrary, since some patients develop their arthritis 6 or more weeks after infection, but it was agreed that the extension of the time beyond 4 weeks would make the criteria less specific. The group recognized the weakening association of HLA- B27 with ReA even then and specifically stated that its determination should play no part in the diagnostic criteria. The Fourth International Workshop met in 1999, adding some clarity to the nomenclature and classification of ReA. Agreement was reached to use the term reactive arthritis; it was also agreed that clinicians should differentiate between acute and chronic ReA using a recommended cutoff of 6 months' duration.

Because the majority of individuals exposed to causative bacteria do not develop ReA, the concept of "attack rate" is important. The attack rate represents the percentage of people exposed to a specific bacterial infection who develop ReA. Attack rates can vary widely among the causative bacteria and in various populations, but it generally ranges from 1% to about 30%, depending on the study and causative organism in post-enteric ReA18,23,24; that of post-chlamydial ReA ranges from 4% to 8%.25-28 Because the prevalence of the bacterial triggers can also vary widely in populations and over time, especially with enteric organisms, the incidence and prevalence also vary accordingly.

The sex ratio for post-enteric ReA is nearly 1:1, but venereally acquired ReA is more often diagnosed in men. This is primarily a function of the requirement for confirmed genital infection,

and such infections are frequently subclinical in women. 1, Adults are more likely to develop ReA than children. In Scandinavia, an annual incidence of 10/100,000 to 30/100,000 has been reported.30, In one of those studies, incidence rates of postenteric ReA and post-chlamydial ReA were essentially equal at 5/100,000 and 4.6/100,000, respectively. In the United States, the estimated age-adjusted annual incidence of ReA in males younger than age 50 was 3.5/100,00032; however, no female cases were identified, strongly suggesting an underestimate. A German study indicated a prevalence of 10/100,000.33 ReA has become more common in Africa in the wake of the AIDS epidemic, without any association with B27, an allele that is rare in these populations. The expected number of cases of ReA compared with those actually diagnosed strongly argues that ReA is underdiagnosed overall; perhaps this is most true with post-chlamydial ReA. Because acute genital C. trachomatis infections are a reportable disease in the United States, the annual incidence of such infections is well described. An estimate of the incidence of Chlamydiainduced ReA in the United States using the known attack rate suggests significant misor underdiagnosis.

Initial reports suggested that 60% to 85% of patients who develop ReA secondary to Shigella, Yersinia, or C. trachomatis infection are HLA-B27 positive. However, other studies suggest a lower prevalence of B27 in Salmonella-induced ReA, and one study suggested no such association in Campylobacter-induced ReA.36-38 Several more recent community-based or commonsource epidemic studies demonstrate the prevalence of B27 in ReA to be less than 50%.39-44 Data regarding HLA-B27 in the setting of ReA, however, are convincing that this HLA antigen lends to disease chronicity. It also appears to render the host with more fulminant acute symptoms, and it more often predisposes to the classic triad of symptoms.45, It should be emphasized at this point that, in addition to the bacterial pathogens classically understood to be the etiologic agents for ReA, recent studies have associated a large and diverse array of infectious organisms with this clinical entity. Although many of these studies are case reports that include only small numbers of patients, we consider it important to provide some initial discussion of this emerging etiologic issue.

### Etiology and Triggering Organisms

Bacteria long-recognized to be definitive etiologic triggers of ReA include several species from the genera Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter, and Yersinia, as well as the genital pathogen C. trachomatis. However, many other infectious agents have been implicated as potential causes of ReA, including C. pneumoniae, Ureaplasma urealyticum, Helicobacter pylori, various intestinal parasites, Escherichia coli, Clostridioides difficile,49 and intravesicular Bacillus Calmette—Guerin (BCG). Further and as mentioned above, additional infectious organisms have been postulated to elicit ReA, including HIV, Cryptosporidium, Giardia lamblia, Cyclospora cayetanensis, Entamoeba hartmanni, Vibrio parahaemolyticus, Orientia tsutsugamushi, Rickettsia conorii, Staphylococcus aureus, Staphylococcus epidermidis, Staphylococcus haemolyticus, and importantly severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) (for detailed discussion of these organisms, see ref. 51). Again, many of these latter associations appeared only in one or a few case reports, with few patients described. More information will be required before these pathogens are established in the etiology of ReA, and if any are so established, some revision in the formal definition of this clinical entity will be required.

C. trachomatis is the most common etiologic agent causing ReA in the United States.1, Interestingly, the clinical features of ReA appear to be congruent whether the inciting infection is enteric or venereal. The post-dysentery form of ReA is always preceded by a symptomatic infection, and many studies suggest that the more severe the initial gastrointestinal infection, the more likely ReA is to develop.48, In contrast and as mentioned above, initial genital C. trachomatis infections are often asymptomatic, 1,18,27,54 especially in women, and data indicate these initial asymptomatic infections do indeed engender ReA.19,

The four enteric organisms known to cause ReA represent a large proportion of the cases of ReA as a group. Salmonella are gram-negative, rod-shaped, motile bacteria that are widespread in animals and environmental sources. Because Salmonella outbreaks are relatively common worldwide, these organisms are the most frequently studied enteric bacteria associated with ReA. The attack rate for Salmonella-induced ReA has ranged between 6% and 30% in different studies.55, All four Shigella species (S. flexneri, S. dysenteriae, S. sonnei, and S. boydii) can cause arthritis. The attack rate for Shigella-induced ReA has been estimated at 7% to 9%. Campylobacter spp. also are gram-negative motile bacteria, and they are an extremely common cause of enteric infections. In spite of high infection frequency, these organisms appear to be somewhat less arthritogenic, with an attack rate of 1% to 5%. Yersinia spp. have been estimated to have an attack rate of 12% to 23%, 46,58 but these organisms apparently have been a less frequent cause of ReA in recent years. 46,

C. trachomatis is an obligate intracellular gram-negative pathogen; this bacterial species is comprised of 14 strains/serovars (A, B, Ba, and C are ocular/trachoma serovars, D to K are genital serovars), plus 3 biovars of lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV; L1 to L3). Chlamydial infections are not usually clonal, and these organisms can and frequently do exchange DNA among strains, making the production of new substrains common. The attack rate for genital C. trachomatis in ReA is 4% to 8%. C. trachomatis has been demonstrated in about half of patients with a preceding symptomatic urogenital infection who developed ReA.60, Importantly, two previous studies with similar results demonstrated that asymptomatic initial infections can lead to ReA, perhaps in the majority of cases. 1, Historically, infection with LGV has been relatively uncommon in the United States and Europe, although these organisms have been identified increasingly in anal infections in men who have sex with men; some recent studies have implicated LGV as the source for ReA in patients with such infections. We again note that the related respiratory pathogen C. pneumonia has been implicated as a cause of ReA, although available data indicate that it does so at lower frequency than does C. trachomatis.1,

ReA has been described as a "sterile" arthritis that develops following infection by these known bacterial triggers, the apparent sterility due to the inability to grow the organisms by routine culture methods from the synovial fluid in patients with the arthritis. However, many studies have demonstrated that the causative chlamydiae in ReA can infect monocytic cells at the site of primary infection, and they are held intracellularly during dissemination from the genital tract to the synovium. The processes that allow the bacteria to remain intact within monocytic cells have yet to be elucidated, but it has been clearly demonstrated that in this context the organisms undergo a transcriptional arrest for certain genes governing cell division late in the intracellular developmental cycle.63-65 Analyses using polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and reverse transcriptase-PCR have shown that synovial chlamydiae

within their monocytic host cells are viable and metabolically active, albeit in an aberrant state termed persistence. These aberrant synovial chlamydiae have been detected by electron microslevels during a normal acute chlamydial infection are down-regulated strongly when the organisms are in the persistent state.63-65 Persistent chlamydiae have been demonstrated in other organ tissues and other disease states, suggesting that they may be involved in additional clinical entities. Several well-controlled studies of ReA have demonstrated consistently that the PCR positivity rate for chlamydiae DNA is significantly higher in ReA patients compared with controls. One surprising recent report indicated that synovium-based persistent chlamydiae uniquely belong to the ocular, not genital, serovars. This unusual observation has not yet been confirmed, but ocular chlamydial strains in the initial infectious material may explain in part two unusual features of Chlamydia-induced ReA. First, ocular serovars are included only rarely as part of the inoculum in genital infections (1% to 5% of the time), potentially explaining the attack rate. Second, patients with Chlamydia-induced ReA often develop ocular symptoms. Interestingly, recent studies have shown that increased tryptophan levels can reactivate persistent chlamydiae to the normal biphasic developmental cycle, and a significant difference is known to exist in the capacity of ocular and genital C. trachomatis serovars to counter tryptophan deprivation. Clues to the apparent arthritogenicity of the ocular chlamydial serovars may have been seen years ago. In the 1960s and early 1970s, "Bedsonia" (now know to be C. trachomatis) recovered from patients with ReA caused arthritis 100% of the time when injected into rabbits. Congruently, intraarticular injection of these same organisms often caused ocular involvement.69,

As with chlamydiae, extensive efforts have been made to detect the enteric pathogens in synovial tissue or fluid of patients with post-enteric ReA. Bacterial DNA or bacterial degradation products have been identified, but unlike the case for chlamydiae, viable organisms have not been demonstrated.71-73 The single possible exception to this was published in a study targeting Yersinia74; to our knowledge, this observation has not been replicated in another similar study. Whether these synovially based persistent organisms or bacterial fragments trigger an autoimmune response or whether they actually drive the inflammatory process remains to be determined.

In all established and possible etiologic contexts, ReA represents a classic interplay of host and environment. The environmental triggers outlined above play an undeniable role in disease genesis and possibly propagation. However, genetic susceptibility also plays a role. As mentioned, the role that HLA- B27 plays in the pathophysiology of ReA has been overstated. Certainly, B27-negative patients can and do develop ReA, but it is important to remember that HLA-B27 has multiple alleles that could influence host response and disease susceptibility. Few studies have analyzed the specific HLA-B27 alleles in the context of ReA. One recent such report, however, suggested that HLA-B*2705 is the most common allele observed in B27-positive ReA patients. Another study suggested that HLA-B*5703 increases the risk for the classic triad of symptoms of ReA in a specific population. Much remains to be learned about other HLA loci and non-HLA genes that may be important in the pathophysiology of ReA. A good deal of data exists that indicate that patients with HIV are at increased risk for ReA and that the symptoms can improve with anti-retroviral HIV therapy (ref. and see below).

### Clinical Features

In the context of ReA elicited by the classic enteric and venereal pathogens, the disease shares many clinical features in common with the other spondyloarthritides (SpAs). In spite of the fact that ReA has several distinct etiologic agents, as well as some differences in the pathophysiology depending on the classic triggering microbe, clinical features of ReA are quite congruent regardless of the initiating infection. The clinical syndrome that encompasses ReA can involve many different organ systems, although it has a predilection for the synovium, urethra, eye, and skin (Table 77.1). Symptoms typically become apparent within 1 to 4 weeks of the initial infection, but occasionally the delay can be longer. If a patient experiences symptoms of longer than 6 months' duration, they are diagnosed as having chronic disease. Traditionally, rheumatologists have felt that 90% or more of cases of ReA resolve spontaneously within weeks to months, but more recent observations suggest that a higher percentage of patients, although still a minority, proceed to develop chronic disease.37, Typically, patients have more significant symptoms during the acute phase of the disease, and these can include constitutional symptoms (malaise, fatigue) and fever. If symptoms persist, the long-term manifestations tend to be milder. In these chronic cases, it is not unusual for symptoms to wax and wane. In cases in which apparent ReA is elicited by a noncanonical organism, the initial clinical features can differ somewhat from those given above. For example, in the case of SARSCoV-2 infection, the arthritis may not manifest itself for as long as 3 weeks post-infection; involvement may be oligoarticular, as in enteric or venereal elicitation, and psoriatic lesions along with enthesitis may be present. Culture and molecular analyses targeting the virus in synovial fluid and related areas are negative in many cases.

Of all the SpAs, the phenotypic articular manifestations of ReA are most similar to psoriatic arthritis (PsA). These articular-based inflammatory features include synovitis, enthesitis, and dactylitis. While both ReA and PsA can present as peripheral or axial arthritis or a combination of both, the peripheral arthritis of ReA most typically involves the large joints of the lower extremities (Fig. 77.1). Epidemiologic data are not available by which to determine the frequency of peripheral arthritis vs. axial involvement alone vs. a combination of both, but many rheumatologists agree that peripheral involvement with an asymmetric oligoarticular distribution is the most common. Nearly all patients with ReA have peripheral symptoms at presentation, with about half showing axial symptoms.

Of those with peripheral involvement, some data suggest that enthesitis is more common than synovitis. Two different types of entheses (bony attachment of a tendon or ligament) are known in the human body, and both seem to be susceptible to inflammatory disease in ReA. Common sites of enthesitis include the Achilles tendon (Fig. 77.2), plantar insertion/fascia, and patellar tendon; this also appears in many cases of arthritis resulting from SARS— CoV-2.83 Some authors have argued that sacroilitis is, at least in part, a form of enthesitis. Evidence of enthesitis can often be seen on plain radiographs in patients with chronic ReA (Fig. 77.3).

Dactylitis is a relatively common finding in ReA, as it is in other types of SpA, especially PsA (Fig. 77.4). One series of studies suggested that it was present in 28% of patients presenting with ReA. The underlying pathophysiology has been difficult to define, but elements of synovitis, enthesitis, and tenosynovitis all have been recognized. Dactylitis also is helpful with the differential diagnosis, in that it is only seen in a few other conditions

(sarcoidosis, gout, sickle cell disease, and a variety of infections). Dactylitis can be refractory to treatment.

The most common extra-articular features of ReA are mucocutaneous and ocular in nature. Urethritis or cervicitis occurs rather frequently in post-chlamydial ReA, but these same symptoms are rarely seen in the post-enteric variety. However as noted above, the absence of these symptoms does not rule out Chlamydia-induced ReA. Typical skin lesions include keratoderma blenorrhagicum, circinate balanitis, and nail changes; more rarely, oral ulcers can occur. Keratoderma blenorrhagicum is clinically indistinct from palmoplantar pustular psoriasis (Fig. 77.5). Relatively little information is available to define how frequently this rash occurs in ReA, but early reports describe it in about 20% of cases. The same is true for circinate balanitis; estimates suggest it occurs in ~10% to 15% of cases86,87 (Fig. 77.6). Interestingly, the histologic features of circinate balanitis resemble pustular psoriasis,88 and chronic cases can look like plaque psoriasis. Nail changes include onycholysis and pitting, and these occur in about 10% of patients. The relationship between distal interphalangeal arthritis and nail involvement is well recognized in PsA89; the same also is likely to be true for ReA, but no definitive data exist in this regard. The most common form of ocular involvement includes conjunctivitis and anterior uveitis, but many other manifestations have been described. Ocular involvement is unilateral in about two-thirds of cases, and all ocular manifestations can become chronic and/or recurrent, requiring systemic therapy. The relatively limited available observations indicate that many of the extra-articular features elicited by noncanonical pathogens are not seen; for one example, in the case of ReA elicited by C. pneumoniae, no ocular features or skin lesions have been observed. Extant data for arthritis apparently due to other organisms is incomplete and requires further definition.

### Laboratory, Radiographic, and Advanced Imaging Findings

No diagnostic test for ReA is currently available. The diagnosis remains clinical despite the lack of validated/accepted diagnostic criteria. Every effort should be made to culture the triggering organism from genital or stool specimens in patients with acute ReA, but attempts to document the causative bacteria are often unsuccessful. Historically, this is particularly true in postchlamydial ReA. These triggering bacteria can be cultured from synovial fluid or tissue only rarely, but as detailed above these bacteria or bacterial products have been demonstrated in such synovial specimens using PCR. PCR has been suggested for analysis of urethral or cervical specimens in patients with suspected Chlamydia-induced ReA, but to date no data are available to know the sensitivity or specificity of such testing (see refs. and 92 for review). Because these bacteria traffic to synovial tissue in an apparently rapid manner, genital specimens may test negative even by PCR. Acute phase reactants (APRs) are often elevated in the acute phase.

In chronic ReA, stool and urogenital sampling to assess causative organisms has been analyzed, but many patients test negative, thus limiting the utility of this approach.93, No data are available to assess whether PCR analysis of urethral or cervical specimens in patients with chronic disease might be useful. PCR analysis of synovial specimens might be useful in chronic patients, but this approach currently is utilized only as a research tool. Further, serologic testing for antibodies to the causative organisms is unreliable. Some data also suggest that APRs normalize in

patients with chronic disease. Because more than half of affected patients are HLA-B27 negative, this genetic antigen should not be utilized as a diagnostic tool.

The plain radiographic appearance of ReA is congruent with those of PsA; however, the changes might not be as severe. In terms of peripheral disease, radiographic changes may be absent or

confined to juxta-articular osteoporosis in early disease. With longstanding disease, marginal erosions, joint space narrowing, and periostitis with reactive new bone formation are characteristic.
