Spurs at the insertion of the Achilles tendon and/or plantar fascia are common. Plain radiographic axial changes include sacroilitis and nonmarginal syndesmophytes (Figs 77.7 and 77.8). Advanced imaging,

in particular MRI, has been advocated recently to detect changes early in nonradiographic SpA. Bone marrow lesions, sclerosis, and erosions of the sacroiliac joints are frequently asymmetric and can be seen on MRI (Fig. 77.9). The "shiny corner sign" and nonmarginal syndesmophytes might also be evidence on spine MRI. These advanced imaging findings are similar to those of other SpAs.

### Diagnosis

As described above, universally accepted diagnostic or classification criteria are lacking for ReA of any etiology. Similarly and as indicated above, a generally accepted diagnostic test or set of tests does not exist, and standard laboratory analyses are typically unhelpful. Attempts to isolate the causative organism must be performed, but a negative test does not rule out ReA. Recognition of an underlying spondyloarthritis and potential identification of one of the triggering infections remain the most practical means of diagnosis of ReA until better diagnostic tests are widely available.

### Treatment

The role that triggering organisms play in the genesis of ReA is undisputed. However, whether these bacteria drive the inflammatory process or trigger a related but independent immune response remains to be resolved. Treatment for acute ReA is relatively straightforward, but the ambiguity that surrounds the pathophysiology is mirrored in the various treatment strategies for those who develop chronic disease.

Most cases of ReA are self-limiting, so the initial treatment is often conservative. As in other types of SpA, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs are effective for most cases as an initial treatment approach. Two randomized clinical trials have been performed demonstrating their efficacy. The first was a double-blind crossover study comparing azapropazone to indomethacin in patients with both PsA and ReA. Both medications were efficacious, with a trend favoring indomethacin. The second compared ketoprofen to indomethacin in 50 patients with ReA96; both were efficacious with no significant difference between the two. However, indomethacin does tend to have more side effects than other NSAIDs, so treatment with any NSAID is appropriate.

In those patients who do not respond to NSAIDs, corticosteroids have been utilized. Because ReA can present as a monoor oligoarthritis, intra-articular steroids are often quite effective. Enthesitis may benefit from intralesional glucocorticoids. It has been suggested that systemic corticosteroids are more effective for the peripheral symptoms rather than the axial manifestations.52, Topical corticosteroids are the initial treatment of many of the extra-articular features of ReA, including iritis/uveitis, keratoderma blenorrhagicum, and circinate balanitis.52, In patients with HIV infection and ReA, many of whom have severe skin lesions, the skin lesions in particular respond to antiretroviral therapy.

Data also demonstrate that prompt treatment of the triggering infections with antibiotics decreases the likelihood of the development of ReA. This is a likely explanation for the recent decrease

in incidence of ReA. Antibiotics have been studied as a potential treatment for ReA during the acute phase with mixed results. An early study suggested that lymecycline might decrease the disease duration of ReA, particularly in patients with Chlamydiainduced ReA98; however, subsequent studies failed to confirm this effect.99-103 We note that both post-enteric and post-venereal ReA patients were included in these trials.

In those with chronic ReA the most efficacious approach is less clear. Traditional disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs (DMARDs), anti-TNF therapy, and antibiotics have been studied. Although several traditional DMARDs are advocated as potential therapeutic agents for chronic ReA, only sulfasalazine has been formally evaluated in a prospective clinical trial. In that study, all patients had failed NSAIDs and were followed for 36 weeks duration. Researchers identified a trend favoring sulfasalazine over placebo in terms of overall response, but the difference was not statistically significant. Sulfasalazine was, however, significantly better than placebo in some of the secondary endpoints. One small case series suggested benefit with a Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitor. Methotrexate, azathioprine, apremilast, and cyclosporine can be used in chronic ReA, but data supporting their use are largely anecdotal. No randomized trials in ReA are available to accurately assess the efficacy of anti-TNF therapy, but several case reports and two small open label studies suggest clinical benefit with these drugs in the treatment of ReA.106-109 It should be noted that in vitro studies have demonstrated up-regulation of chlamydial replication when TNF levels are decreased,110 so this treatment approach should be used with caution in those with suspected Chlamydia-induced ReA. Some case reports suggest benefit with interleukin (IL)-6 and IL-17 inhibitors. 111,

As mentioned, a study from the early 1990s suggested benefit with lymecycline as a treatment for acute ReA. This led to several studies assessing the utility of long-term treatment with various antibiotics, including ciprofloxacin, azithromycin, and doxycycline, all of which produced negative results.99-103 These studies included both acute and chronic ReA patients, and little effort was made to separate post-chlamydial and post-enteric patients. More recent data have suggested that a prolonged course of combination

antibiotics, specifically doxycycline with rifampin or azithromycin with rifampin, represent an efficacious treatment specifically for chronic post-chlamydial ReA. In this study, all participants had to be PCR positive for C. trachomatis or C. pneumoniae in blood or synovial tissue at study entry. After 6 months of therapy with combination antibiotics, PCR clearance of these organisms mirrored clinical response.

### Conclusion

ReA is unique in that it is a systemic disease with known etiologic triggers. It represents the classic interplay between host and environment. Because the bacterial triggers usually cannot be detected with routine culture from synovial fluid, it has been referred to as a "sterile" inflammatory arthritis arising after such infections. However, recent advances in our understanding of the pathophysiology of ReA have called into question whether this is truly the case. Because acute ReA is often self-limiting, the initial treatment approach should be conservative, but more aggressive treatment is warranted in those with chronic disease. Importantly, much emphasis has been placed on understanding host genetics in the determination of disease susceptibility, but specific bacterial characteristics appear to be uniquely arthritogenic. Recent studies suggesting new etiologic organisms for the arthritis may require significant rethinking regarding the host and pathogen contributions to disease development.

# Psoriatic Arthritis

### KEY POINTS

Psoriatic arthritis (PsA) should be suspected in any patient with psoriasis and arthritis in an asymmetric joint distribution coinciding with additional clinical features, such as dactylitis, enthesitis, or inflammatory-type back pain. Classification criteria, the CIASsification of Psoriatic ARthritis (CASPAR) criteria, have been validated. PsA is a progressive disease. Erosions develop in 47% of patients within 2 years of diagnosis. Polyarticular disease and elevated acute phase reactants are markers of poor outcome. A core set of outcomes covering different domains and measured with different instruments are necessary for inclusion in clinical trials. Environmental factors such as microtrauma and the gut and skin microbiome have recently been implicated as initiators of disease. Studies of synovial tissue with novel single-cell technologies demonstrate new immune cell populations, which might help distinguish psoriatic from rheumatoid arthritis pathology. Change in mesenchymal and immune cell populations that infiltrate synovial tissue might be associated with clinical response to treatment. Prominent entheseal involvement with bone marrow edema at bone insertions on magnetic resonance imaging has prompted the hypothesis that PsA may originate at the enthesis. CD8+ T cells and the innate immune response are also thought to participate in disease pathogenesis. Novel targets and drugs with a variety of mechanisms of action have shown a dramatic amelioration in psoriatic skin outcomes. Improved clinical efficacy, albeit less profound, has also been demonstrated in PsA using the same medications.

### Introduction

Psoriatic arthritis (PsA) is a member of the spondyloarthritis disease spectrum and may be defined as an inflammatory arthropathy associated with psoriasis and usually negative for high-titer rheumatoid factor (RF) or anti-citrullinated protein antibodies. Until the 1950s, an inflammatory arthritis that occurred in the presence of psoriasis was thought to represent rheumatoid arthritis (RA) occurring coincidentally with psoriasis. Based primarily on clinical and radiologic grounds and with use of the RF, the distinction between RA and PsA was gradually accepted. However, it was not until 1964 that PsA was recognized by the American Association of Rheumatism as a distinct clinical entity and Moll and Wright published their original classification criteria in 1973.1,2

### Epidemiology

The reported prevalence of PsA in the general population ranges from 0.01% to 0.67%.3, A 2018 meta-analysis found a pooled prevalence of 0.13%, but very high levels of heterogeneity among studies exist,5 likely due to both differing definitions of PsA and geographic factors. While the prevalence in the United States is 0.25%,6 estimates within Europe are quite divergent (0.05% to 0.67%).7-11 Similarly, and although the affected population in Asia has generally been very low (e.g., less than 0.01%), this could be a reflection of underdiagnosis of PsA rather than true absence of disease.12, Importantly, the prevalence of PsA is on the rise, with increases seen worldwide, 14,15 although this may be due in part to increased awareness and consequent diagnosis of PsA.

There is no sex predilection and onset of PsA can occur at any age, although progression from skin psoriasis to synovio-entheseal involvement usually takes between 5 and 10 years. The vast majority of individuals with PsA develop skin psoriasis prior to the development of arthritis, while the rest either develop psoriasis and arthritis simultaneously or have arthritis prior to skin involvement, with the latter most commonly occurring in pediatric PsA. Importantly, the prevalence of synovio-entheseal involvement in patients with psoriasis is much higher than in the general population, ranging from 6% to 41%.13,

Despite the high prevalence within this psoriasis population, PsA remains underdiagnosed. One study found that 29% of patients with psoriasis attending a dermatology clinic with no known diagnosis of inflammatory arthritis had undiagnosed PsA. This has led to the development of screening questionnaires for PsA, including the Psoriatic Arthritis Screening Evaluation, the Psoriasis Epidemiology Screening Tool, and the Toronto Psoriatic Arthritis Screen. When compared head-to-head, all three tools had similar sensitivities (74%77%) but with low specificities (30%39%), ,20,21 complicating their use in clinical and research settings.

### Clinical Features

PsA is a complex and heterogenous disease that can involve multiple domains, including the skin and nails, peripheral joints, axial disease, entheses, and dactylitis.

Plaque psoriasis, or psoriasis vulgaris, is the most common skin phenotype in patients with PsA. Other patterns of skin involvement may be seen (Fig. 78.1). In a patient with the classic articular manifestations of PsA but without a history of psoriasis or the

presence of a rash, a careful nail and skin examination are warranted, which should include the scalp, ears, and umbilical and intergluteal regions, because psoriasis frequently occurs in such "occult" areas. Additionally, a family history of psoriasis should be obtained, as the diagnosis can also be made in the context of a first-degree relative with psoriasis. Although several studies suggested that the prevalence of PsA increases with skin severity,6 in clinical practice, a significant proportion of patients presenting with mild psoriasis can have associated PsA, and a weak relationship has been observed between severity of skin involvement and severity of arthritis.

Additionally, psoriatic nail changes, such as pitting, ridging, or onycholysis, are very common in patients with psoriasis. Pitting and nail dystrophy are risk factors for the development of PsA.22-24 One possible explanation is that nail dystrophy results from subclinical enthesitis at the level of the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joint. Examples of nail dystrophic changes are shown in Fig. 78.2.

Peripheral arthritis can begin at any joint; however, the anatomic involvement at presentation in early PsA predominantly involves small joints of the hands and feet and the knees (Fig. 78.3). In one of their seminal papers on PsA, Wright and Moll18 described five clinical patterns (Fig. 78.4):

1. Asymmetric oligoarthritis

2. Symmetric polyarthritis

3. . Predominant DIP joint involvement

4. Predominant spondyloarthritis

5. Destructive (mutilans) arthritis

While this clinically driven taxonomy is the most commonly cited, many alternative descriptions have been proposed. Variability in the definition of terms has led to differences in the reported frequency of PsA in the different studies. Furthermore, the pattern of joint involvement is not fixed.

The CASPAR (ClASsification for Psoriatic ARthritis) criteria have included a breakdown of disease-pattern subtypes. This multicenter study incorporated data on 588 PsA cases and 536 controls. In contrast to the original Moll and Wright paper, but similar to many subsequent publications, approximately 63% of patients had polyarticular joint involvement (often difficult to distinguish from RA), compared to 13% with oligoarticular disease. The other patterns of joint involvement described by Moll and Wright occurred much less commonly. Lone DIP disease was found in less than 5%, but DIP involvement can occur in any of the subtypes.

Predominant spondyloarthritis is also uncommon (occurring in less than 5%), although axial involvement, including sacroiliitis and syndesmophyte formation, may be found in 25% to 70% of PsA cases, depending on the definition used.29, Risk factors for spinal involvement include severe peripheral arthritis

and the presence of the human leukocyte antigen (HLA)-B*27.31 Differentiating between PsA with axial involvement and axial spondyloarthritis (AxSpA) can be difficult. (HLA)-B*27 is more common in patients with AxSpA, and peripheral arthritis is more frequent in those with axial PsA (AxPsA).32, Patients with AxSpA tend to have more severe radiographic findings, including higher-grade sacroiliitis, and are more likely to have complete sacroiliac joint ankylosis and bridging syndesmophytes.32" The predominant pattern of sacroilitis in both is symmetric rather than unilateral, but unilateral involvement is seen more commonly in AxPsA.32, Additionally, in AxSpA, syndesmophytes are more symmetrically distributed, progress caudal to cranial, and are primarily marginal; in AxPsA, syndesmophytes typically progress randomly and are equal in frequency of marginal and paramarginal. Despite these distinctions, individual patients may be difficult to classify and may simultaneously satisfy criteria for both AxPsA and AxSpA.

Finally, arthritis mutilans, a destructive form of arthritis associated with digital shortening, is rare. The Group for Research and Assessment of Psoriasis and Psoriatic Arthritis (GRAPPA) has developed a broad consensus on the features of arthritis mutilans. Clinical criteria include shortening digits, finger telescoping, and/ or flail joint not caused by subluxation. Radiographic findings include erosion involving entire articular surfaces on both sides of the joint and/or pencil-in-cup change; osteolysis is considered to be the defining feature.

Dactylitis is characterized by a sausage-shaped swelling of the fingers or toes (Fig. 78.4B) and may be found in up to a third of patients with PsA at first presentation; 48% may have an episode of dactylitis during follow-up. 36, Ultrasound and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) studies have shown that joint and tenosynovial inflammation are prominent in involved digits with dactylitis.38,

Enthesitis, inflammation at the site of tendon and ligament insertion into bone, is a feature of all of the spondyloarthropathies and may be a presenting feature in PsA. Overall, enthesitis is found in 38% of patients at presentation. The most common entheseal sites involved are the Achilles tendon and plantar fascia insertions. Other sites include the insertions of the quadriceps and patellar tendons, the iliac crest, the rotator cuff, and the epicondyles at the elbow. Patients have reported pain at these sites, with tenderness and swelling sometimes noted on examination. Entheseal involvement may be asymptomatic, and ultrasound is more sensitive than clinical palpation. Enthesophytes, new bone formation at the area of tendon and ligament insertion onto the bone, may be detected on radiograph but are not always associated with symptoms.

Other systemic features of inflammation are common in patients with PsA, including stiffness after rest and fatigue. Fatigue is reported by up to 78% of patients and is independently associated with worse physical function, quality of life, and work productivity.

There is a long-established relationship between the eye and psoriatic disease. PsA usually precedes the development of psoriatic eye complications, but this is not necessarily the case. The incidence of uveitis in patients with PsA is approximately 3.5 times higher than that of the general population. In PsA, uveitis usually affects the anterior chamber, but posterior uveitis and pan-uveitis can occur, and these may be more severe and threatening to vision. Other eye complications associated with psoriatic disease include conjunctivitis, keratoconjunctivitis sicca, and episcleritis.

Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is more common in patients with PsA than in either patients with psoriasis or the general population. Some studies have found an association between PsA and both Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis; others have found an association between PsA and Crohn's disease only.41, There is also a significantly increased prevalence of subclinical bowel inflammation in patients with PsA with axial disease.' 44-46

### Differential Diagnosis

The diverse clinical features of PsA can make the diagnosis challenging, which must be differentiated from RA, osteoarthritis

(OA), crystal disease, and other forms of spondyloarthritis (Tables 78.1 and 78.2). Certain articular features, if present, are useful in distinguishing PsA from RA, including dactylitis, DIP involvement, and inflammation at entheseal sites. Additionally, PsA tends to be oligoarticular and less symmetric than RA, especially early in the disease course. Inflammatory-type back pain or sacroilitis on plain radiograph or MRI should raise the suspicion of PsA because spinal involvement is uncommon in RA. The absence of rheumatoid nodules or other systemic features common to RA can be another useful differentiating feature.

Monoarticular involvement, and dactylitis in particular, may also be confused for crystal-associated arthropathies, especially in the toes. Adding to this, serum urate levels may be increased in patients with PsA, and synovial fluid crystal analysis is the best differentiator when possible. The differential for monoarticular involvement must also always include septic arthritis and soft tissue malignancy. Dactylitis can also be present in sarcoid and other spondyloarthropathies and, if involving multiple toes, may resemble pernio.

It may be particularly difficult to distinguish PsA from reactive arthritis (see Table 78.2), as both can be associated with joint pain, dactylitis, and skin involvement. The palmoplantar pustular rash seen in reactive arthritis (keratoderma blennorrhagicum) may be clinically and histologically indistinguishable from pustular psoriasis. In relation to spinal involvement, sacroiliitis may be unilateral, and the spinal changes on plain radiography may be more asymmetric in PsA than with classic ankylosing spondylitis/axial spondyloarthritis (AS). Additionally, PsA with predominant DIP involvement can sometimes be difficult to distinguish from OA. However, the presence of other clinical features described in the previous section should assist the clinician in making the correct diagnosis.

### Laboratory Features

There is currently no diagnostic laboratory test for PsA, and this remains an area of unmet need. Although the absence of RF is considered an important distinguishing feature from RA (i.e., included in the CASPAR classification criteria), low levels of RF may be found in some patients (5% to 13%) with typical PsA features. Anti-citrullinated protein antibodies were initially thought to be specific to RA but can also be seen in up to 12% of patients with PsA49 (even in relatively high titers), and its presence is associated with more joint involvement and erosive disease.50, Therefore, the clinical features described previously must be used

to help differentiate between PsA and RA with psoriasis. Work in genetics, proteomics, lipidomics, and newly discovered immune cell populations are all being studied in an attempt to identify biomarkers, although none of them have yet been validated for use in clinical practice.52-55

Acute-phase reactants, such as erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) or C-reactive protein (CRP), may be elevated in patients with PsA but less commonly and to a lesser degree than in those with RA. However, elevated ESR and CRP are associated with polyarthritis and ultrasound abnormalities and may act as markers of poor prognosis. 56-58

### Radiographic Features

Although substantial advances have been made in the application of both musculoskeletal ultrasound (MSKUS) and MRI in patients with arthritis, plain radiographic imaging remains the most widely utilized imaging modality for assessing bony changes in peripheral joints in PsA.

### Plain Radiography

PsA is characterized by the presence of both osteodestructive and osteoproliferative changes (Fig. 78.5). Radiographs of the peripheral joints can show co-occurrence of bony erosions and joint space narrowing with new bone formation, sometimes resulting in the classic "pencil-in-cup" deformity. New bone formation can be characterized by periostitis, bony ankylosis, and enthesophyte formation and is part of the CASPAR classification criteria (i.e., juxtaarticular new bone formation). Involvement is often asymmetric.

Radiographic progression in PsA is slow in early stages of the disorder, with a mean modified Sharp (to include DIP joints in the hands) erosion score increasing from 1.2 at presentation to 3.0 at 2 years. However, within this time period, up to 47% of patients with PsA develop erosive changes. In PsA clinical trials, radiographic progression is an important outcome measure; however, with the exception of the Ratingen score, no scoring system (including the Sharp-van der Heijde modified scoring method, which is the most frequently used in PsA trials) has been developed

specifically for PsA. Rather, they were designed and validated for use in RA and subsequently modified for use in PsA, often not including measures of bony proliferation. None of the existing radiographic measures are both sufficiently feasible and sensitive to change to be easily applied in large longitudinal observational studies.

### Musculoskeletal Ultrasound

MSKUS can be used to identify both structural changes and perturbations in perfusion of joints, entheses, and soft tissues (Fig. 78.6). MSKUS features at the entheses include entheseal thickening, hypoechoic change, increased vascularity as shown on power Doppler, tenosynovitis, and bony erosions or enthesophyte formation.61, MSKUS is more sensitive than clinical examination in detecting subclinical synovitis or entheseal abnormalities in early PsA. In one study, 47 out of 49 patients with PsA had at least one joint with subclinical synovitis. Furthermore, patients with psoriasis without a diagnosis of PsA demonstrate significantly more MSKUS abnormalities than healthy controls. MSKUS has also been used in objective monitoring of the response of synovitis to therapy. Finally, MSKUS guidance for small joint or entheseal aspiration or injection may have practical application in patients with PsA.

### Magnetic Resonance Imaging

MRI studies have been particularly useful in offering new insights into disease pathogenesis in PsA (Fig. 78.7). Based on the prominent entheseal-related bone marrow edema seen on MRI, investigators have proposed that PsA, in contrast to RA, is an entheseal-driven disease. MRI can be used to study all aspects of joint involvement, including the enthesis, but the role of MRI as a routine clinical tool in PsA has not been clarified. The application of MRI for imaging the spine or sacroiliac joints can be very helpful in PsA, especially in determining whether there is active axial disease. An MRI scoring system that measures peripheral articular inflammation and damage in patients with PsA has demonstrated promising initial results.69,70

### Other Imaging Modalities

Use of other imaging modalities, such as computed tomography (CT) or scintigraphy, has largely been superseded by MRI. However, micro-CT and high-resolution peripheral quantitative CT are an excellent imaging platform for detecting morphologic changes of juxtaarticular bone,71,72 but CT is usually reserved for patients for whom MRI is contraindicated or unavailable. Positron emission tomography (PET) has shown promise for the detection of early changes of PsA. In one study, PET/CT detected asymptomatic enthesitis in one-third of patients with psoriasis. Another exploratory study used high-resolution [18F] fluoride PET to explore the pattern of DIP joint bone metabolism in PsA compared with OA and healthy joints. There was a greater uptake of [18F] fluoride at the enthesis and periosteum and at the tufts of the distal phalange of PsA compared with OA. More recently, new PET tracers such as fibroblast activation protein inhibitors have been used to allow for identification of dynamic tissue responses to inflammation.

### Diagnosis and Classification Criteria

There are currently no diagnostic criteria, and there is no single diagnostic test for PsA. Nevertheless, in its simplest form, PsA can be considered as an arthritis occurring in the presence of psoriasis but in the absence of RF. While most patients with PsA meet this simple definition, in clinical practice, PsA can be much more

difficult to identify. For example, arthritis can be predominantly spinal, it may involve only entheseal sites, psoriasis may be absent, or low-titer positive RF may be found. Recognizing these difficulties, the CASPAR group published classification criteria based on an analysis of 588 patients with PsA and 536 controls (see Chapter 75, Table 75.4). These criteria have now been well validated in a number of studies, both prospective and retrospective, including early PsA patients. In the setting of clinical research, the CASPAR criteria have a specificity of 98.7% and a sensitivity of 91.4%. The CASPAR classification criteria should now be used as the reference standard to ensure uniformity of patients recruited to cohort studies or randomized controlled trials (RCTs).

### Clinical Course and Outcome

While the emergence of effective therapies has significantly impacted the clinical course of PsA, studies performed in the pre-targeted therapy era provide important information on the natural history of the disease. Five such early cohorts were studied27,36,77-79 in which the mean disease duration at enrollment was 6 to 12 months, the median patient age at onset of psoriasis was 27 to 31 years, and the median patient age at onset of arthritis was 38 to 52 years. Overall, little relationship was noted between skin disease severity and onset of PsA. The small joints of the hands and feet were most commonly involved; the DIP joints were involved in one-third of patients, usually in association with nail disease, which was present in two-thirds of patients; dactylitis

and enthesitis were present in one-third; spinal involvement only, without other articular involvement, was found in 2% to 4%, but spinal involvement was present in 20% overall. At follow-up, disease had continued to progress in most patients. Erosive disease developed in 47% of patients within 2 years. Markers for progression included polyarticular disease and an elevated ESR.

Studies examining mortality in PsA have generated conflicting results. While earlier studies showed higher mortality rates in patients with PsA compared with the general population, 80 more recent data did not show a significantly increased risk.81-83 These differing results may, at least partially, reflect the improvement in diagnosis and treatment of the disease over the past two decades. In fact, one cohort study reported a temporal improvement in survival for individuals with PsA over time, from 1978 to 2004.84

### Comorbidities in Psoriatic Arthritis

### Cardiovascular Disease

It is well established that both local and systemic inflammation play an important role in the development of atherosclerosis.

The "Psoriatic March" is a proposed concept whereby systemic inflammation results in insulin resistance, which in turn triggers endothelial cell dysfunction, leading to atherosclerosis and finally myocardial infarction or stroke. Consequently, individuals with PsA have a higher prevalence of cardiovascular disease compared with the general population and an increased risk of cardiovascular morbidity and mortality.87, A recent meta-analysis comprising over 30,000 patients with PsA found a 43% increased risk of cardiovascular disease compared with the general population. Specifically, the risk of myocardial infarction, cerebrovascular disease, and heart failure was increased by 68%, 22%, and 31%, respectively. In addition, traditional risk factors of cardiovascular disease, such as hypertension, hyperlipidemia, obesity, and diabetes, are all elevated in PsA.90-92

An increased inflammatory burden may also impact the risk of cardiovascular disease. Studies have shown that extent of psoriatic skin involvement is an independent risk factor for cardiovascular disease93,94 and, in one cohort study, disease activity as measured by number of dactylitic joints increased risk for major cardiovascular events. This is also seen when studying surrogate markers of atherosclerosis. One study assessing ultrasonic measurement of

carotid total plaque area (TPA) found a higher TPA in patients with PsA compared with participants with skin psoriasis alone. In those with PsA, a higher TPA was associated with duration of PsA, skin severity, and ESR. Additionally, the use of coronary CT angiography in individuals without any symptoms of coronary artery disease found that 76% of individuals with PsA versus 44% of controls demonstrated coronary plaques. Elevated CRP, high swollen joint count, and disease duration were all independent risk factors of increased coronary plaque burden in PsA. Furthermore, TNF inhibition (TNFi) in patients with psoriatic disease was associated with reduced carotid plaques in men and improvement in vascular inflammation in both men and women.

Highlighting the impact of inflammation, the American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association Guidelines on the Primary Prevention of Cardiovascular Disease now recognize chronic inflammatory conditions (such as psoriasis) as a "risk-enhancing factor."99 The European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology (EULAR) has published evidence-based guidelines for cardiovascular risk management in patients with inflammatory arthritis.

### Diabetes Mellitus and Metabolic Syndrome

Insulin resistance, obesity, metabolic syndrome, and type 2 diabetes mellitus are all more prevalent in patients with PsA.

In one cohort of 283 individuals with PsA, 44% had metabolic syndrome, and 16% had insulin resistance. A significant association was also noted between metabolic syndrome and more severe PsA (odds ratio [OR] 4.47; p < 0.001). In a study using a large UK general practice database, the Health Improvement Network, investigators found an increased risk of incident diabetes in PsA. The ageand sex-matched hazard ratio (HR) for diabetes was 1.72 (95% confidence interval [CI], 1.462.02) and remained significant even after adjusting for body mass index, smoking, alcohol, baseline glucocorticoid use, and comorbidities (HR 1.33, 95% CI, 1.09-1.61). Additionally, the risk of metabolic syndrome may be higher in PsA compared with other types of inflammatory arthritis. In one study of 109 PsA patients compared with 699 RA and 122 AS controls, the adjusted OR for the metabolic syndrome in PsA was 2.44 (95% CI, 1.484.01; p < 0.001) relative to RA or AS. The adjusted ORs for central obesity, impaired fasting glucose, and low high-density lipoprotein cholesterol were also significantly higher in patients with PsA.

### Other Comorbidities

The prevalence of nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) is increased in patients with psoriasis and further elevated in patients with PsA. In patients with psoriasis, an increased prevalence of NAFLD is associated with metabolic syndrome, hypercholesterolemia, obesity, and the presence of PsA. Liver disease can also result from medications used to treat PsA, particularly methotrexate and leflunomide, and the presence of liver disease can complicate treatment selection.

Depression and anxiety are closely associated with psoriatic disease, and the prevalence appears to be higher in PsA compared with psoriasis alone. In PsA, the prevalence of depression has been estimated between 9% and 36% and that of anxiety between 15% and 20%.105, Identification and management of mental health comorbidities are essential as depression has been shown to affect pain perception, quality of life, and ability to achieve remission. Presence of depression may also affect treatment choice. Apremilast, for example, contains a label warning regarding

emergence or worsening of depression, suicidal thoughts, or other mood changes.

Most studies of osteoporosis do not show higher prevalence 11,112; however, in PsA compared with the general population patients treated with long-term glucocorticoids may be at higher risk. Additionally, hyperuricemia and gout have an increased incidence in PsA,114 which is of particular importance as gouty arthropathy may be confused with PsA in certain circumstances.

### Outcome Domains and Instruments

The measurement of response to treatment of PsA in clinical trials is complicated by the heterogenous nature of the disease and its multiple domains (i.e., arthritis, psoriasis, enthesitis, dactylitis, nail and spinal involvement). An essential core set of domains to be included in PsA clinical trials has been proposed (Fig. 78.8). While instruments exist for many of these domains, others have yet to be developed and validated or have acknowledged limitations. 116,

In the setting of clinical trials, composite indices are one way of assessing all relevant clinical outcomes in a single instrument, measuring both disease activity and response to therapy. Ideally, a composite measure should combine feasibility with validity and clinical relevance. Many of the composite scores used (e.g., American College of Rheumatology [ACR]20, ACR50, ACR70; EULAR Disease Activity Score [DAS] response criteria) have been adapted from RA and are therefore solely focused on peripheral joints. However, PsA-focused measures have been developed, including the Disease Activity Index for Psoriatic Arthritis (DAPSA),118 which focuses on peripheral joint activity, and the Composite Psoriatic Disease Activity Index (CPDAI),119 the

Psoriatic Arthritis Disease Activity Score (PASDAS), 120 and the GRAPPA Composite Exercise Score (GRACE Index), which are more domain focused. All have been validated with their own intrinsic advantages and limitations (Table 78.3). In a comparison of composite measures using data from patients treated with TNFi, while all indices were able to discriminate treatment from placebo, the PASDAS and the GRACE Index were better at distinguishing treatment effect compared with CPDAI, DAPSA, or DAS28.

Additionally, a PsA-specific measure of health-related quality of life, the Psoriatic Arthritis Impact of Disease Questionnaire, has been developed and validated in two versions: a nine-item version used for clinical research and a 12-item version used in clinical practice. The items include pain, fatigue, skin problems, ability to work and participate in leisure activities, functional capacity, discomfort, sleep disturbance, coping, and anxiety. The domains of embarrassment and/or shame, social participation, and depression were added for the clinical practice questionnaire.

Minimal disease activity (MDA) criteria have also been developed as a clinically useful target of treatment by both the patient and physician, encompassing both remission and low disease activity, given current treatment possibilities and limitations. 123, It can also be used as a responder index. Patients with PsA are considered to have MDA when they meet five out of seven criteria (see Table 78.3). However, application of the MDA has limitations. For example, a patient with PsA could have ongoing severe psoriasis and potentially meet the criteria for MDA as there is no set threshold value for the two criteria that are not met. However, the criteria can be made stricter by mandating certain domains. "MDA joints and skin" requires that tender and swollen joint counts and skin body surface area (BSA) criteria are met along with two other criteria and very low disease activity (VLDA) is defined as meeting all seven criteria. A definition of remission criteria in PsA is currently being considered, but, as mentioned previously, the heterogenous nature of this disease makes the development of a broadly acceptable definition challenging. Further work on this topic is necessary.

### Pathogenesis

Many studies have explored key components of disease pathogenesis, including the contribution of genetic factors, the role of infection or trauma, studies of animal models or involved sites of disease, and the importance of components of the immune system, such as cytokines. Despite much progress in identifying factors that contribute to the development of PsA, overall the pathogenesis of the disease remains incompletely understood.

### Genetic Factors

Familial clustering of psoriasis and PsA is well described. Twin studies have shown a relatively high rate of concordance of psoriasis in monozygotic twins (up to one-third depending on the study),126 but a much lower concordance of PsA (i.e., 11%). The genetic basis for this clustering has been the subject of extensive investigations in psoriasis but has been less studied in PsA. Studies of PsA have often included patients as a subset of larger psoriasis cohorts, and the diversity of clinical phenotypes has not often been recognized. Earlier studies focused on the genetic contribution of the major histocompatibility complex (MHC) region located on chromosome 6, and a number of more recent genomewide association studies (GWAS) have revealed genetic contributions from non-MHC loci.

A strong association between psoriasis and the HLA-C region of the MHC has long been recognized. Whether this was HLA- C*06 itself, found in approximately 60% of individuals with psoriasis, or a region telomeric to HLA-C has been the subject of much controversy. Elder definitively showed that the HLA susceptibility region for psoriasis is HLA-C*06, which is often in linkage disequilibrium with other HLA-B alleles such as HLA- B*57, HLA-B*37, and HLA-B*13.128 The presence of HLA-C*06 is associated with an earlier patient age of onset of psoriasis (type 1 disease, <40 years old) and with more extensive and severe disease. Multiple studies have shown that in patients with PsA the frequency of HLA-C*06 was lower than that in patients with psoriasis (28.7% vs. 57.5%; p < 0.001).129, Additional associations in PsA have been found with HLA-B*08, HLA-B*27, HLA-B*38, and HLA-B*39. It was also observed that arthritis develops much closer to the appearance of psoriasis in the HLA-B*27:05:02 or B*39:01:01 subset than in the HLA-C*06:02 subset of patients with PsA. Overall, patients with HLA-B*27:05:02 had similar penetrance for musculoskeletal and skin disease, and they were roughly contemporaneous in onset; however, nearly a third of these patients actually had the onset of skin disease after the onset of musculoskeletal disease (i.e., psoriatic arthritis sine psoriasis). Conversely for HLA-C*06:02 patients, the interval between skin disease and musculoskeletal disease was more than a decade, and the HLA-C*06:02 gene appeared to specify an effect that included highly penetrant severe cutaneous disease and delayed milder musculoskeletal disease with greatly reduced penetrance.

In a further exploratory study, HLA-B*27:05 was also strongly associated with symmetric sacroiliitis, enthesitis, and dactylitis. In contrast, HLA-B*08:01 was associated with predominant asymmetric sacroiliitis, joint fusion, joint deformities, and dactylitis. HLA-C*06 was negatively associated with asymmetric sacroiliitis.

These findings have been interpreted to suggest that the MHC association with psoriasis lies close to the HLA-C region, whereas the MHC association with the articular manifestations more likely lies in or close to the HLA-B region. A study of a large cohort of

patients with PsA in the United Kingdom found HLA-C*06 to be in linkage disequilibrium with HLA-DRBI*07 and that possession of both alleles was associated with fewer involved or damaged joints (Pauline Ho, personal communication, 2007).

Other genes within the MHC region have been explored in psoriasis and PsA. TNF promoter polymorphisms or a gene in linkage disequilibrium with TNF may predispose the patient to, or increase susceptibility to, psoriasis and PsA. One study has found a further association between the TNF-308 A allele and disease progression in early PsA. Investigators have pointed to a class I MHC chain-related A (MICA)-A9 polymorphism that confers additional relative risk, in particular for polyarticular disease, in patients with psoriasis who carry HLA-C*06:02.133 MICA-A9 polymorphism was found in linkage disequilibrium with HLA-B alleles (B*57:01, B*38:01). These results suggest that the MICA gene or other nearby genes may be involved in the development of PsA.

Psoriasis whole-genome scans have identified additional non- MHC susceptibility regions, known as the PSORS regions on chromosomes 4, 6, and 17. To date, no candidate genes from these PSORS regions have been identified. GWAS studies have confirmed associations of PsA susceptibility with HLA-C and interleukin (IL)-12B. These efforts have identified another susceptibility region, TRAF3IP2 on chromosome 6p, which encodes a protein involved in IL-17 signaling and interacts with members of the Rel/nuclear factor-kB (NF-kB) transcription factor family. 134, Further studies have provided genome-wide significant evidence for the involvement of the REL locus in PsA susceptibility and confirmed the previously reported association with psoriasis vulgaris. A genome-wide significant association was found between PsA and a single-nucleotide polymorphism (rs13017599), detected at 2p16 near the REL locus encoding c-Rel (rs13017599; p = 1.18 x 10-8; OR, 1.27; 95% CI, 1.181.35). Multiple other PsA-specific susceptibility loci with functional and pathophysiologic repercussions have been found, including IL-23R (interleukin-23 receptor), TNFAIP3 (TNF alpha-induced protein 3; also known as A20), and PTPN22 (protein tyrosine phosphatase, nonreceptor type 22).137, TRAF3IP2, which encodes for Act1, an adapter protein critical for Th17-mediated inflammatory responses, has also been associated with PsA. Importantly, these and other newly discovered genetic signatures have been computationally integrated to provide robust risk assessment of PsA development in psoriasis patients.

### Environmental Factors

The role of environmental factors in triggering skin or joint disease in patients with psoriasis or PsA has been supported largely by clinical observations, although explanatory mechanisms remain poorly understood. A strong association between guttate psoriasis and preceding streptococcal infections in children has long been recognized,140 and the possibility of a streptococcal superantigen underlying this association has been proposed. One study found bacterial antigens in synovial tissue samples from PsA patients, but this may be no different from those in non-inflammatory control participants.

The microbiome—the collection of symbiotic, commensal, and pathogenic microorganisms (and their genomes) residing in the skin, mucosal surfaces, and other organs—is being extensively studied as a potential trigger for psoriatic spectrum disease. A perturbation of the microbial community equilibrium (i.e., dysbiosis) has been implicated in the initiation and perpetuation of several

immune-mediated inflammatory disorders, including psoriatic disease. In fact, studies in both animal models and humans have demonstrated a mechanistic link between the microbiome, gut inflammation, and both psoriasis and PsA. For example, multiple established susceptible murine models of psoriasiform disease and spondyolarthritis (SpA) features, do not demonstrate the phenotype under germ-free conditions but exhibit an IL-23/ IL-17-driven, SpA-like inflammatory process when exposed to (specific) microbes.143, These observations strengthen the hypothesis that intestinal dysbiosis is required to orchestrate synovio-entheseal and cutaneous inflammatory disease. In fact, multiple studies in humans have demonstrated perturbations in the intestinal (and skin) microbiota composition in psoriatic dis- ,146-150 as well as worsening pathology after fecal microbial ease, transplantation. In the currently prevailing hypothesis, this dysbiotic state leads to dysregulation of the gut (and/or perhaps skin) epithelial barrier and the stimulation of IL-23-producing resident immune cells. IL-23R+ mucosal innate cells are then activated and circulate away from the gut, migrating to the enthesis and synovial tissues to cause inflammatory responses. 153, Multiple groups are focusing efforts to further characterize the modulating effects of the microbiome and its by-products in psoriatic disease pathogenesis, including as a diagnostic and therapeutic target.

The Koebner phenomenon is the development of psoriasis along the site of skin trauma and has been reported in 20% to 25% of patients with psoriasis. While less understood, clinical observations indicate that mechanical stress may trigger episodes of joint inflammation, and the term deep Koebner phenomenon has been coined to describe this phenotypic manifestation. 23,

The association between smoking and psoriatic disease has been a matter of debate. In the general population, smoking has been linked to an increased risk of psoriasis and PsA.157-159 Paradoxically, however, some studies have shown smoking to be negatively associated with the development of PsA in patients with established psoriasis. 159, Further prospective studies are required to elucidate the exact role of smoking in the progression of psoriatic disease.

Finally, a link between stress and exacerbation of psoriasis has been proposed, supported largely by clinical observational studies. A similar association may exist in PsA, but this has not been systematically examined.

### Animal Models

Although spondyloarthropathy has been detected in a variety of primates, rodent models have proven helpful in deciphering pathogenic pathways. In HLA-B*27 transgenic rats, skin, nail, and joint features have been described that mimic select features of the human phenotype. HLA-B*27 transgenic rats raised in a germ-free environment seemed to be protected from joint disease. Mice genetically lacking class II MHC have developed skin and joint disease, but the disease is confined to the distal phalanges, with skin and nail disease also on the affected digits. Involvement of the distal phalanges and nails was reported in aging male DBA/1 mice from different litters that were caged together from 12 weeks. In these animals, dactylitis, periostitis, and ankylosing enthesitis were observed. The SKG mice harbors a point mutation in the ZAP-70 gene yielding reduced T cell receptor signaling that leads to multiorgan inflammation that mimics human SpA disease—characterized enthesitis and axial and peripheral arthritis along with extra-articular manifestations, including psoriasis,

uveitis, and ileitis.165, A20, the product of the TNFAIP3 gene, is a strong anti-inflammatory agent that regulates NF-kB transcription and restricts its activation to suppress inflammatory responses in normal homeostasis. Mice expressing distinct targeted mutations of A20 develop various phenotypic features characteristic of PsA, most notably axial arthritis, enthesitis, DIP erosions, and psoriasis.

Finally, the JunB protein is expressed in healthy and in clinically uninvolved psoriatic skin, but expression is considerably reduced in involved psoriatic lesions. Epidermal deletion of JunB and c-Jun in a mouse model results in skin and joint disease with 100% penetrance and a clinical and histologic phenotype highly consistent with human psoriasis and PsA. In further experiments, the same authors showed that the joint disease, but not the skin disease, required T and B cells and intact TNF receptor 1 signaling.

### Immunopathology

The key pathologic events in PsA occur in the skin, synovium, entheseal sites, cartilage, and bone. Pathobiologic features in the skin and synovium have been well described, and emerging studies have focused on the enthesis. In relation to cartilage and bone, studies have shown the presence of osteoclasts at the cartilage—pannus junction and high numbers of circulating osteoclast precursors in the circulation of PsA patients. Detailed studies, similar to those done in RA, on the synovial-cartilage-bone interface could possibly yield valuable information regarding joint destruction in PsA.

### Skin

Psoriasis is a complex immune-mediated disease in which keratinocyte hyperproliferation associates with aberrant activation of T lymphocytes, dendritic cells, and cytokines (primarily IL-23, IL-17, and TNF) that lead to characteristic cutaneous plaques. Involved psoriatic skin is characterized by epidermal hyperplasia, mononuclear leukocytes in the papillary dermis, neutrophils in the stratum corneum, and an increase in various subsets of dendritic cells, which are major producers of TNF, IL-12, and IL-23.169, CD8+ T cells are the predominant T cell subset chiefly found in the epidermis, whereas dermal T cells contain a mixture of CD4+ and CD8+. In response to IL-23, naive CD4+ T cells differentiate into Th17 and Type 17 cells, which in turn produce IL-17A synergizing with other cytokines (most notably TNF) to stimulate keratinocyte proliferation and production of anti-microbial peptides and other pro-inflammatory cytokines. Most T cells in skin lesions express addressin, a cutaneous lymphocyte antigen, in contrast to circulating T cells and T cells found in the inflamed synovium in PsA. Finally, vascular changes are prominent in psoriasis, with impressive growth and dilation of superficial blood vessels.

### Synovium

Many early studies of synovial pathology in PsA highlighted the presence of prominent and striking vascular changes. In the first study that compared PsA and RA synovial tissues, quantitative immunopathologic analysis confirmed these vascular changes and found that vessel number was significantly increased in PsA (see Chapter 28). Lining layer hyperplasia was less marked in PsA, and fewer macrophages were seen trafficking into the synovium and out to the lining layer. The numbers of T lymphocytes and their subsets and the number of B cells were similar to the

frequency found in RA. Although neutrophil infiltration was not assessed, this study examined adhesion molecule expression further in the two patient subgroups and found E-selectin expression to be considerably reduced in PsA. Many of these observations have been confirmed by other authors.

In one study, the synovial immunopathologic features in patients with SpA, including PsA, were compared with the features seen in RA. Using a semiquantitative scoring system, the authors identified many features characteristic of the SpA group as a whole and in the PsA subgroup alone. Increased vascularity, higher neutrophil numbers (also seen in involved psoriatic skin), and a higher number of infiltrating CD163+ macrophages, a marker of mature tissue macrophages, reliably distinguished spondyloarthropathy from RA. No significant differences were seen between oligoarticular versus polyarticular PsA.

The important role of the vasculature in PsA pathogenesis is perhaps most elegantly shown by the large numbers of tortuous and dilated blood vessels observed through an arthroscopic view of psoriatic joints. An interaction of key growth factors is thought to regulate closely the new vessel formation or angiogenic process. Growth factors—including TNF, transforming growth factor (TGF)-β, platelet-derived growth factor, angiopoietins (ANG-1, ANG-2), and vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF)—have been described in skin and synovial tissue.176, Because this expression is found at an early stage of inflammation, it may represent a primary event in PsA versus a reaction or response to hypoxia. One possibility is that a genetic predisposition exists to endothelial activation, which results in new vessel formation and increased cellular trafficking.

Of interest, two studies have identified a change in synovial CD3+ T cell infiltration as correlating with clinical response in .178, Changes in CD3+ patients commencing biologic therapies. T cell infiltration also correlated with changes in MRI assessment of synovitis. Changes in CD3+ T cell infiltration may well prove to be a useful tissue biomarker of treatment response. In another study, there was a reduction in the expression of CD4+ regulatory T cells (Tregs) in the synovium of PsA patients treated with abatacept.

Importantly, transcriptomic analyses comparing skin and joint biopsies demonstrated a predominant Th17 profile in psoriatic skin while PsA synovial tissues exhibited strong signals in TNF and angiogenic pathways. When the immunophenotype, molecular profile, and function of synovial cell populations were studied, a polyclonal subset of T resident memory cells were shown to be polyfunctional, high pro-inflammatory mediator producers and with increased CXCR6 expression.

### Enthesis

Structural entheseal lesions are known to occur in a substantial proportion of psoriasis patients, even before clinically evident inflammation develops, and they are also associated with an increased risk of PsA development. 183, These lesions develop extra-articularly where tendons and ligaments insert into the periosteum. Inflammatory events at these anatomic sites are led by PGE2, IL-17A, and IL-22, which activate mesenchymal cells to proliferate and differentiate into bone-forming osteoblasts -187 via expression of Wnt proteins and bone morphogenic proteins (BMPs).

One group described the immunopathologic features of the enthesis in patients undergoing joint replacement surgery with SpA, including PsA, and compared them with RA. The number of patients was small in this study, but a consistent increase in

CD8+ T cell expression was observed at the enthesis in patients with PsA compared with RA patients. These findings are consistent with the well-described association of PsA with class I HLA antigens. They are also consistent with the previously described dominance of activated and mature CD8+ T cells in PsA synovial fluid samples compared with RA. In contrast, another study of ultrasound-guided biopsies of five sites of acute enthesitis in early SpA showed an inflammatory response with increased vascularity and cellular, predominantly macrophage infiltration. These studies have conflicting findings with respect to the predominant infiltrating cell type and further work is needed in this area.

### Cytokines

Synovial explant tissues obtained from PsA joints produce higher levels of the T helper (Th) type 1 cytokines IL-2 and interferon-γ protein than explants similarly cultured from OA s. This Th1 lymphocyte profile has also been and RA patients. observed in psoriasis plaques. The cytokines IL-1β and TNF were released by psoriasis synovial explants in high concentrations. In contrast, IL-4 and IL-5 were not identified, but IL-10 was highly expressed in psoriatic synovium, although not in skin. A similar pattern of cytokine production in PsA synovium was shown by using immunohistochemical and gene expression techniques.194, Other innate cytokines, such as IL-18 and IL-15, are present in PsA synovial tissue and are downregulated by methotrexate therapy.

The role of Th17 cells has been explored, and an important immunomodulatory role has been better established in psoriasis than in PsA. Comparison of lesional skin gene expression in responders versus nonresponders to etanercept revealed rapid downmodulation of innate IL-1β and IL-8 sepsis cascade cytokines in both groups, but only responders downregulated IL-17 pathway genes to baseline levels. An increase in circulating Th17 cells has been found in PsA,197 and an increase in IL-17 has been found in skin, synovial tissue, and synovial fluid of PsA patients. One study demonstrated that IL-17+CD4- T cells (predominantly CD8+) are present at increased levels in PsA synovial fluid but not in RA synovial fluid. In addition, the frequency of these synovial fluid IL-17+CD4- T cells is correlated with serologic, clinical, and imaging measures of PsA disease activity and erosive disease sta- 199 Further supporting a key role for the Th17 pathway, genetic tus. polymorphisms in key cytokines involved in differentiation of T cells to Th1 and Th17 subtypes, IL-12, and IL-23 have been found to be associated with susceptibility to both psoriasis and PsA,200 and inhibition of the common p40 subunit of IL-12/IL-23 has led to clinical improvement in both skin and joint manifestations. Importantly, inhibition of the p19 subunit of IL-23 has demonstrated the most robust clinical improvement in the skin yet, with many patients achieving complete or near clearance of psoriasis.202, Further observations by investigators revealed a higher proportion of IL-17and IL-22-producing CD4+ cells within the peripheral blood of PsA and psoriasis patients compared with healthy controls. There was no difference in the frequency of IL-17+ and IL-22+ CD4+ T cells between patients with psoriasis alone and those with PsA. In addition to the genetic associations described previously, there are now substantial data implicating the IL17/IL-23 axis in mouse models of both psoriasis and SpA; investigators have shown that the anatomic sites that are inflamed in SpA are primed to rapidly react to IL-23 by the presence of a previously unidentified population of IL-23R+ resident cells. They also showed that in vivo exposure to IL-23 is sufficient to induce highly specific entheseal inflammation in the absence of Th17 cells

and with rapid kinetics. These observations strengthen the case for the central involvement of the IL17/IL-23 axis in both psoriasis and PsA, as demonstrated by the clinical success of targeting these pathways (see the "Treatment" section).

TNF levels are elevated in psoriatic skin, synovium, and synovial fluid of patients with PsA.192, Several lines of evidence support the concept that TNF is an important cytokine in the psoriatic joint. TNF transgenic mice exhibit extensive bone destruction similar to that observed in some PsA patients. In a study of 129 patients with early PsA, patients with erosions were significantly more likely to have the TNF-308 A allele, an allele associated with high TNF production. As mentioned earlier, immunohistochemical and gene expression studies have shown marked upregulation of TNF in the psoriatic synovial membrane. Histopathologic analysis of synovial specimens from eight SpA patients, four of whom had PsA, treated with the anti-TNF monoclonal antibody infliximab revealed decreased vascularity, synovial lining thickness, and mononuclear cell infiltration after therapy. 207, In another study examining the synovial membrane of patients with PsA, infliximab therapy induced a significant reduction in the quantity of infiltrating macrophages, the CD31+ vascular area, αvβ3+ neovessels/Ulex europaeus agglutinin+ vessels, VEGF and its receptor KDR/fk-1 (VEGFR-2), and SDF-1+ vessels. 209

### Matrix Metalloproteinases and Cartilage Destruction

Radiographs of psoriatic joints often reveal cartilage loss manifested as joint space narrowing. Similar to RA, matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) and tissue inhibitors of MMPs (TIMPs) were identified in PsA synovial lining and sublining layers. 210, In particular, immunohistochemical studies revealed that MMP-9 localized to blood vessel walls, whereas MMP-1, MMP-2, MMP- 3, TIMP-1, and TIMP-2 showed a cellular and interstitial staining pattern in the synovial lining. Serum levels of MMP-3 exhibited a marked and rapid decrease after successful anti-TNF therapy, raising the possibility that this molecule may serve as an informative biomarker in disease management. In another study, similar levels of MMP-1 and MMP-3 messenger RNA were detected in RA and PsA synovial tissues despite the fact that RA patients exhibited more erosions on plain radiographs. The elevated ratio of MMPs to TIMP-1 in synovial tissue favored cartilage degradation, although expression of MMPs was not significantly elevated at the cartilage—pannus junction compared with other sites. These reports indicate that MMPs are upregulated in PsA synovium, but their precise functions remain to be defined.

### Bone Remodeling

Radiographs of PsA joints can reveal markedly altered bone remodeling in the form of bone resorption (tuft resorption or osteolysis, large eccentric erosions, and pencil-in-cup deformities) and new bone formation (periostitis, spur or enthesophyte formation, bony ankylosis). PsA joint biopsy specimens show large multinucleated osteoclasts in deep resorption pits at the bone— pannus junction. These osteoclasts play an important role in bone resorption.

Osteoclastogenesis (differentiation of monocytes into osteoclasts) is a contact-dependent process directed by osteoblasts and stromal cells in the bone marrow. These cells release signals necessary for differentiation of an osteoclast precursor derived from the CD14+ monocyte population into an osteoclast. One of these signals is the receptor activator ofNF-kB ligand (RANKL), a member of the TNF superfamily that binds to receptor activator of NF-kB (RANK) on the surface of osteoclast precursors and osteoclasts.

This ligand-receptor interaction stimulates proliferation and differentiation of osteoclast precursors and activation of osteoclasts. It has been proposed that the relative expression of RANKL and of its natural antagonist osteoprotegerin (OPG) ultimately controls osteoclastogenesis. Marked upregulation of RANKL and low OPG expression were detected in the synovial lining layer of patients with PsA compared with patients with OA. Osteoclasts strongly expressing RANK were also noted in cutting cones traversing the subchondral bone, supporting a bidirectional attack on the bone in psoriatic joints. In addition, osteoclast precursors, derived from circulating CD14+ monocytes and known to express dendritic cell-specific transmembrane protein (DC-STAMP), were markedly elevated in the peripheral blood of patients with PsA compared with healthy controls. In the arthritis prone transgenic Tg(hTNF) mice, genetic ablation of DC-STAMP abrogated both bone resorption and inflammation. Treatment of patients with PsA with anti-TNF agents significantly decreased the level of circulating osteoclast precursors, supporting a central role for TNF in the generation of this precursor population.

The mechanisms responsible for new bone formation in the psoriatic joint are poorly understood. Higher circulating levels of bone formation markers, in particular bone alkaline phosphatase, in patients with PsA compared with patients with RA both before and after TNF inhibitor therapy have been demonstrated. TGF-β and VEGF may be pivotal in this process of new bone formation, given that TGF-β is strongly expressed in synovial tissues isolated from patients with AS and synergizes with VEGF to induce bone formation in animal models. Investigators showed that BMP-2 and BMP-7 are upregulated in regions of pathologic new bone formation. These investigators showed that expression of phosphorylated Smad1 and Smad5, important signaling molecules downstream of BMP, was markedly increased in regions of new bone formation taken from the calcaneus in a patient with Achilles tendinitis and periostitis. These studies provide evidence that BMP molecules and possibly VEGF and TGF-β are potential mediators of ankylosis and periostitis in the psoriatic enthesis and joint. Finally, the Wnt pathway and the balance between Wnt and the Wnt antagonist dickkopf-1, which binds to the Wnt receptor complex on the surfaces of osteoblast lineage cells, may well be of considerable importance in the disordered bone remodeling found in PsA.

### Transition From PsO to PsA

Cross-sectional studies have identified several risk factors associated with progression from skin psoriasis to PsA, including having a firstdegree relative with PsA, psoriasis phenotype, obesity, and other comorbidities. By using the Icelandic genealogy database, risk ratios (RRs) for the development of PsA in a sample that spanned five generations were estimated and results confirmed a strong and complex genetic component with a significant RR detectable for individuals with a positive family history extending to fourth-degree relatives of PsA patients. Additionally, a Canadian cohort found that the RR of developing PsA in an individual with psoriasis who has a first-degree relative with PsA compared with the risk in the general population was over 30.218 Intriguingly, both the extent and location of psoriasis may play a role in determining transition. When comparing patients with a PASI score of greater than 20 versus less than 10, one study found that severe psoriasis yielded a RR of 5.4 (95% CI, 1.621.7), a finding supported by other studies despite differing definitions of psoriasis severity.2, Additionally, nail involvement, scalp, and inverse psoriasis (involving the body

fold; i.e., armpits, groin, inframammary regions) have all been associated with increased risk of progression.22-24 Patients with comorbidities of uveitis, thyroid disease, depression, and obesity also have increased risk of progression. 23,221,222

### Pathogenesis Summary

A current and yet evolving model for disease pathogenesis in (and progression toward) PsA incorporates genetic susceptibility, the role of the environment including trauma and microbial antigens, downstream immunologic mechanisms (both resident and infiltrating

cells), and associated secreted cytokines, chemokines, and other pro-inflammatory as well as osteo-modulatory proteins (Fig. 78.9). The potential role of the effector cells and components of the innate immune response to mechanical and/or microbial elements continues to be under intense investigation. It is possible that the interaction of environmental factors, such as those derived from skin and gut microbiome or expressed after trauma in a genetically susceptible individual, may set in motion intraand intercellular signaling events that lead to cytokine release, immune activation, and release of destructive enzymes (Fig. 78.10). It remains a matter of debate whether PsA is primarily a disease of autoimmunity or autoinflammation.

### Treatment

In considering treatment strategies for PsA, the diverse nature of the clinical phenotype (peripheral arthritis, skin and nail disease, axial disease, dactylitis, and enthesitis) may complicate therapeutic decisions because not all treatments are effective for all features, and patients often display a mixture of all of the features simultaneously. EULAR, ACR, and GRAPPA have all published recommendations for the treatment of PsA.223-225 Fig. 78.11 shows the treatment schema developed by GRAPPA. Treatment choices may be driven by the disease feature or features considered most severe at the time of evaluation.

### Nonsteroidal Anti-inflammatory Drugs

Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) are commonly used as first-line agents in PsA, although few controlled trials demonstrating efficacy are available.226, Experts continue to recommend NSAIDs to relieve musculoskeletal symptoms, 223

particularly in axial disease. Although no studies have been completed specifically in PsA, studies in AS show that NSAID therapy may prevent or slow radiographic progression. 228, There is no evidence that they have any efficacy in skin psoriasis. Additionally, use of NSAIDs also needs to be balanced with potential for renal and cardiovascular disease risk.

### Glucocorticoids

The use of systemic glucocorticoids is not evidence based and no RCTs have been performed,230 although a recent systematic review found that up to 35% of patients with psoriatic disease were treated with oral glucocorticoids. Concerns have arisen suggesting that exacerbations of psoriasis may follow corticosteroid withdrawal.232, Systemic glucocorticoids, when prescribed, should be used for the shortest duration possible at the lowest effective dose.

No RCTs have examined intraarticular steroids in PsA or the use of local entheseal or dactylitis injections. Expert opinion

indicates that intraarticular steroids can be quite effective, especially in oligoarticular disease or where localized entheseal involvement is present, as in plantar fasciitis. 223,224

### Conventional Synthetic Disease-Modifying Antirheumatic Drugs

Based on limited evidence and expert opinion, nearly all conventional synthetic disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs (csD- MARDs) appear to have small to moderate beneficial effects on peripheral joints, enthesitis, and dactylitis.230, Axial features and nail disease, however, do not appear to respond to treatment with these agents.236, Good or moderate improvements in skin disease have been reported with some of the older systemic agents, such as methotrexate, cyclosporine, sulfasalazine, leflunomide, and acitretin.

Methotrexate remains for many rheumatologists the csDMARD choice for patients with PsA, but RCT evidence is limited. The Methotrexate in Psoriatic Arthritis (MIPA) study randomized 221 participants to methotrexate or placebo and found no difference in disease activity scores at 6 months in the treatment groups. However, this study had a high dropout rate and many participants in the methotrexate group did not reach the target dose of 15 mg/week. A small RCT of 35 patients with early PsA found that participants receiving NSAIDs and methotrexate had more improvement in joint counts and inflammatory markers than those receiving NSAIDs alone. The Study of Etanercept and Methotrexate in Subjects with Psoriatic Arthritis (SEAM-PsA) RCT examined response to treatment with methotrexate, etanercept, or combination therapy. This study found that 50.7% of participates receiving methotrexate alone, at a median dose of 20 mg weekly, achieved an ACR20 response at 24 weeks, although this was lower than those receiving etanercept alone or in combination with methotrexate. Those on methotrexate alone also had improvements in enthesitis (43.1% had resolution) and psoriasis was clear or almost clear in 66.3%. An open-label prospective trial of 73 patients on methotrexate (average dose 17.5 mg/week) found that at 9 months, MDA was achieved in 63% of patients242; however, this study and the SEAM-PsA trial did not include placebo arms. The discrepancy in results between these studies and the MIPA trial may be reflective of the methotrexate dose. Additionally, multiple observation cohort studies have also found methotrexate to be effective.230,

In a 24-week RCT of 190 patients, leflunomide was found to be superior to placebo in improvement in the Psoriatic Arthritis Response Criteria (PsARC) scoring system (59% vs. 30%). There were also significant, although small, improvements in individual parameters, including joint scores, Health Assessment Questionnaire results, PASI, and Dermatology Life Quality Index scores. Observational studies have also shown improvement with leflunomide.

Six RCTs have studied the use of sulfasalazine in PsA. The largest study included 221 patients. Using the PsARC scoring system, 59% of patients in one study achieved a therapeutic response but, consistent with other studies, a high therapeutic response (42.7%) was also noted in placebo-treated patients.

Cyclosporine has also been shown to be highly effective for skin psoriasis,238 but there are no RCTs comparing cyclosporine with placebo in PsA. In a 12-month RCT, 72 patients with PsA and an incomplete response to methotrexate were randomized to either continue methotrexate alone or to add cyclosporine. The combination group had significant improvements in synovitis detected by ultrasound and PASI score.

In contrast to other DMARDs, anti-malarial agents (i.e., hydroxychloroquine) have shown no evidence of treatment benefit; although exacerbation of psoriasis has been reported, and these agents are not recommended for the treatment of PsA.

### Biologic Disease-Modifying Anti-rheumatic Drugs

The approach to treatment in PsA has changed considerably with the introduction of biologic therapies in the early 2000s.

### TNFI Inhibitors

As a result of numerous large, well-conducted RCTs, accumulating evidence indicates that anti-TNF treatments are effective in controlling peripheral arthritis signs and symptoms, improving quality of life, and preventing radiographic progression. Approved anti-TNF agents include adalimumab, etanercept, infliximab, golimumab, and certolizumab pegol. Although the anti-TNF therapies have not been compared head-to-head, their efficacy on peripheral arthritis seems to be similar. In clinical trials, infliximab showed an ACR20 response rate of 59% (vs. 15% placebo), adalimumab 58% (vs. 14% placebo), certolizumab 58% (vs. 24% placebo), golimumab 51% (vs. 9% placebo), and infliximab 58% (vs. 11% placebo).247-251 Evidence indicates that anti-TNF therapies are also effective for other musculoskeletal disease features, such as enthesitis, dactylitis, and axial disease.115,

Anti-TNF therapy also improves both skin and nail disease. In patients on adalimumab, certolizumab, and infliximab, 59%, 62%, and 64% of patients, respectively, achieved an improvement in PASI-75 score compared with placebo rates of 1% to 3%.247, Etanercept was the least effective on skin (23% achieved PASI-75 vs. 3% placebo)250; however, better skin (but not articular) responses have been demonstrated in etanercept patients treated with 50 mg twice weekly compared with once weekly.

The past 5 years have seen the emergence of a number of TNFi biosimilar agents (bsDMARDs). These compounds clearly reduce health care costs and increase patient access to biologic therapy while maintaining the same benefits as the originator compounds. Two RCTs demonstrated noninferiority of biosimilars compared with their original counterparts (infliximab vs. CT-P13 and etanercept vs. CHS-0214).253, The safety profiles of these agents are also highly similar to the reference product.

Methotrexate is often prescribed as a comedication in TNFi treatment for PsA. Its role in this setting was evaluated using the Norwegian DMARDs registry. The study analyzed 440 patients, 170 on anti-TNF alone and 270 on combination therapy. Results showed that anti-TNF drug survival in the group receiving combination therapy was superior to those not on TNFi alone. The effect was mainly seen in those on infliximab, which leaves open the possibility of a role for methotrexate in inhibiting development of anti-drug antibodies when patients are treated with monoclonal antibodies. In contrast to these results, results from the SEAM- PsA study showed little additional benefit from treatment with combination methotrexate and etanercept compared with etanercept monotherapy at 24 weeks.

### IL-17 Blockers

There is accumulating evidence that IL-17 is central to the pathogenesis of psoriasis and PsA. Two treatments targeting IL-17 are currently U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-approved for treatment of PsA, secukinumab and ixekizumab. Secukinumab

Ixekizumab is another humanized monoclonal antibody that inhibits IL-17A and is approved for the treatment of PsA. Ixekizumab was tested against placebo and adalimumab in the phase 3 SPIRIT 1 open-label clinical trial. Ixekizumab had significantly higher ACR20 response compared with placebo (62.1% vs. 30.2%) but similar to active control adalimumab (57.4%). Ixekizumab also showed improvement in physical function measures and dactylitis and showed slowed progression of radiographic evidence of structural damage compared with placebo. For patients with baseline BSA ≥3, 75.3% achieved a PASI-75 response by week 12 and had improvement in nail involvement.

Despite effectiveness for psoriasis and PsA, trials for IL-17 blockers in IBD have either been unsuccessful or stopped early due to exacerbation of disease.259, While trials of IL-17 blockers in psoriasis and PsA have not been associated with increased incidence of IBD,261 several case reports describe this phenom- 262 Therefore, these agents are usually avoided in patients enon. with concomitant IBD.

### IL-23 Blockers

Agents targeting IL-23 have also been shown to be effective in psoriasis and PsA. Ustekinumab is a fully human IgGlk monoclonal antibody that binds to the common p40 subunit shared by IL-12 and -23. Using doses of 45 mg and 90 mg, 42.4% and 49.5% of participants achieved an ACR20 response (vs. 22.8% placebo). Åt 1 year, in those with BSA ≥3% at baseline, 69.1% of the ustekinumab-treated patients achieved at least a PASI-75 skin response and 49.5% had at least a 90% improvement in skin psoriasis. Patients also demonstrated improvement in physical function, dactylitis, and enthesitis and showed slowed radiographic progression of joint damage.263, Importantly, studies on ustekinumab in axial SpA did not meet their primary endpoints265; therefore these agents should not be selected for those with active axial disease.
