Guselkumab and risankizumab are IL-23 inhibitors that act via IL-23 p19 subunit binding. For guselkumab, at 24 weeks, 52% of participants achieved an ACR20 response (vs. 22% placebo) and 76% achieved a PASI-75 skin response. For risankizumab, 57% of participants achieved ACR20 response (vs. 33% placebo) and 52% achieved a PAS190 at 24 weeks. Participants on both guselkumab and rizankizumab also showed improvement in dactylitis, enthesitis, and physical function measures. 267,268

### T Cell Inhibitor

Abatacept is a human fusion protein that inhibits T cell activation through costimulatory blockade approved for the treatment of PsA. Abatacept showed a significantly increased ACR20 response versus placebo after 24 weeks (39.4% vs. 22.3%; p < 0.001). However, only 16.4% achieved a PASI-75 response (compared with 10.1% in placebo). Given its modest efficacy compared with other currently available biologics, this medication is rarely used in psoriatic disease.

### Small Molecules or Targeted Synthetic Disease- Modifying g Anti-rheumatic Drugs

There are a number of small molecules that have been developed for the treatment of PsA that have the advantage over biologic therapies of being available as oral preparations.

Two Janus kinase inhibitors are approved for the treatment of PsA. In a phase 3 trial of tofacitinib in patients who had an inadequate response to csDMARDs, those receiving tofacitinib had a significantly greater ACR20 response rate compared with placebo (50% vs. 33% placebo) and greater PASI-75 score (43% vs. 15%) after 3 months. In a different phase 3 trial of upadacitinib, 70.6% of participants treated with upadacitinib achieved an ACR20 response (vs. 36.2% for placebo) after 6 months. In this same study, 62.6% achieved a PASI-75 response (vs. 21.3% placebo).

### Treat to Target

In the TIght COntrol in Psoriatic Arthritis (TICOPA) study, 206 patients were randomly assigned to either tight control (step-up regimen aiming for MDA by using methotrexate, combination DMARDs, and anti-TNF) or to standard care. In the tight control group, 61.7% achieved ACR20 response at 48 weeks compared with 44.6% in the standard care group. However, there were more adverse events in the tight control group. This study highlights the possibility of adopting a treat-to-target approach in PsA and accepting MDA as a potential treatment target in the future.

### Future Therapy Strategies

The therapeutic options for PsA continue to expand, and the advent of biologic and small-molecule therapies mean that PsA patients are reaching levels of disease control previously not thought possible. However, it is noteworthy that while most patients meet primary clinical endpoints of ACR20 in clinical trials, this indicates at best a partial response. To date, less than 35% of patients meet clinically meaningful endpoints such as MDA. Additionally, a significant proportion of patients do not respond to biologics. Discordant responses in arthritis and skin outcomes are not uncommon, and some treatments may lose efficacy with time or patients may experience intolerable side effects. Therefore highly effective treatment strategies for PsA remain a significant unmet need and new strategies must be pursued including novel therapeutic targets, combination therapy, and prevention. 275,

New therapeutic targets are currently in development. Bimekizumab, a dual IL-17A and IL-17F inhibiting humanized monoclonal antibody, has been approved in Europe and Japan for the treatment of psoriasis and is awaiting evaluation for PsA. In a phase 2b clinical trial, 51% to 73% of bimekizumab patients (depending on dosing regimen) achieved an ACR20 response at 12 weeks, compared with 19% in the placebo group. Deucravacitinib, an oral, selective inhibitor of tyrosine kinase 2 (TYK2) acting via binding to the TYK2 regulatory domain, was FDA approved for

skin psoriasis. A phase II trial in PsA, showed improvement in ACR20 response at 16 weeks compared with placebo (52.9% [6 mg] vs. 62.7% [12 mg] vs. 31.8% [placebo]).

Another strategy for treatment may be a combination of targeted therapies. A bispecific TNFand IL-17A-targeted variable domain immunoglobulin (ABT-122) did not show any difference in ACR20 response compared with adalimumab, but ACR50/70 and PASI75 were higher for the ABT-122 group at several timepoints. Perhaps even more importantly, the safety profile was similar to that of adalimumab alone. Several case reports have reported improved efficacy with the use of combination TNFi and anti-IL-23 therapies. 280, The VEGA trial in ulcerative colitis examined guselkumab and golimumab in combination with preliminary results showing improvement in clinical response at 12 weeks without an increase in adverse events. A similar clinical trial is now underway in PsA.

Prevention may be a relevant strategy in PsA given that there is a readily apparent pre-clinical marker (skin psoriasis) that generally precedes synovio-entheseal involvement, creating a unique opportunity for intervention in a susceptible and readily identifiable population. Retrospective observational studies have sought to address the question of whether treatment with biologic agents has an impact on PsA development. However, these studies have reported disparate results and reached different conclusions. 284-288 Prospective RCTs are currently underway to address this question.

### Lifestyle Modifications

Lifestyle modifications, such as weight loss and exercise, may also be undertaken with the potential to lessen pain and improve function. Elevated body mass index has been associated with inadequate response to anti-TNF therapy290 while weight loss in conjunction with anti-TNF therapy has been associated with improvements in PsA assessed by different measures. 291, Exercise has also demonstrated improvement for disease activity, wellbeing, and associated comorbidities.

### Conclusion and Future Research Agenda

PsA is a chronic, complex immune-mediated inflammatory condition that affects multiple domains and organ systems. Although transformational efforts over the past 20 years have helped elucidate many aspects of pathogenesis and revolutionized therapeutics for both psoriasis and PsA, outcomes for synovio-entheseal inflammation have not achieved those seen in psoriatic skin disease. Targeted therapies against TNF, followed by antibodies that block the IL-23/IL-17 axis in addition to the availability of smallmolecule therapies, have dramatically improved the ability to treat psoriasis, with a significant number of patients now achieving total clearance of cutaneous disease.

However, this extraordinary degree of clinical response has yet to be attained in PsA, where up to half the patients do not experience clinically relevant improvement with blockade of the same pathways. Multiple groups are working toward uncovering yet unidentified targets, implementing combination therapy strategies with currently available modalities, and designing interventional strategies to halt PsA before it becomes clinically evident. These efforts include private—public, multicenter, and multipartner endeavors such as the National Institutes of Health—driven Accelerating Medicines Partnership Autoimmune and Immune Mediated Diseases and the European Innovative Medicines Initiative HIPPOCRATES.

These endeavors, combined with programs that tackle multitherapy interventional approaches (for a multidomain disease) and preventive strategies, promise to propel the field forward by studying the psoriasis-to-PsA continuum in an integrated and comprehensive (both molecularly and phenotypically) manner.

### KEY POINTS

Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD)—associated arthritis is a member of the spondyloarthritis (SpA) family of disorders.

Several hypotheses have been formed to explain how gut inflammation may be linked to joint inflammation: (1) dysbiosis in the gut may lead to systemic inflammation; (2) there may be shared genetics that could explain physiologic aberrations in differing tissues; (3) overexuberant Th17 pathway activation as a result of dysbiosis, genetic abnormalities, or another mechanism leading to inflammation in susceptible tissues; or (4) translocation of activated inflammatory cells from the gut to the joint.

Previous classification of IBD-associated arthritis includes "type I" and "type Il" categories, but it is better classified as axial or peripheral SpA. As such, Assessment of Spondyloarthritis International Society classification criteria for axial SpA and peripheral SpA can be helpful in guiding diagnosis.

IBD-associated arthritis has similar manifestations to other SpA family disorders and may include axial or peripheral disease including SpA features such as enthesitis and dactylitis. Uveitis and psoriasis can also occur.

The treatment of IBD-associated arthritis includes therapies typically used for SpA but depends on whether the patient has Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis.

Certain therapies often prescribed for SpA do not have effectiveness for IBD (e.g., etanercept) and some may worsen it (e.g., secukinumab). Similarly, some therapies with efficacy in IBD (e.g., ustekinumab) do not have efficacy for axial disease. Thus the activity of IBD and inflammatory arthritis, and other extra-articular and extraintestinal manifestations, must be considered in therapy selection, and these decisions should be made in collaboration with a gastroenterologist.

### Introduction

In recent years, there has been increasing recognition of the role of the gut in the pathophysiology of systemic diseases. In particular, a growing body of literature supports the association between

gut pathology and various rheumatic diseases, in particular joint disease. Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD)associated arthritis (sometimes referred to as enteropathic arthritis) is one such disease that exhibits a clear relationship between the gut and joints. In this chapter, we give an overview of IBD-associated arthritis and discuss the pathophysiology of the gut mucosa and the gut microbiome in relation to both spondyloarthritis (SpA) and IBD. This is followed by a discussion of the clinical manifestations and treatment of IBD-associated arthritis. We then address other arthropathies associated with gut pathology.

### Inflammatory Bowel Disease-Associated Arthritis

The spondyloarthritidies are a group of inflammatory arthritidies with shared clinical features such as axial spondylitis and sacroiliitis, peripheral inflammatory arthritis (often asymmetric but sometimes a symmetric, rheumatoid arthritis [RA]—like presentation), enthesitis, and dactylitis. The spondyloarthritidies include ankylosing spondylitis (AS), psoriatic arthritis (PsA), reactive arthritis (ReA), and IBD-associated arthritis. Additionally, synovitis, acne, pustulosis, hyperostosis, and osteitis (SAPHO) syndrome and Bechet's disease share some features with SpA.1-3

Peripheral arthritis in patients with IBD was first described in 1929 by investigators.4, They also described a propensity for arthritis to flare with exacerbations of colitis. For several decades, patients with this condition were often classified as having RA. Then, at the end of the 1950s multiple authors described sacroiliitis in patients with IBD.6-9 In 1964 the American Rheumatism Association classified arthritis associated with IBD as an independent clinical condition. In 1976 Wright and Moll included enteroarthritis as part of the SpA group of diseases.

Beyond the typical relationship between IBD and clinical syndromes that occur in SpA, asymptomatic gut inflammation is relatively common in these diseases. One cohort analysis of

65 patients with SpA found evidence of asymptomatic microscopic bowel inflammation in 46% of patients. Another study found that one-third of patients with AS and PsA have microscopic gut inflammation but no signs or symptoms of IBD. Similarly, among patients with IBD, asymptomatic sacroiliitis is frequently discovered on pelvis imaging performed for assessment of the patient's IBD. 13,

To date, relatively little is known about IBD-associated arthritis, and it remains an understudied disease entity. Additionally, there is widespread disagreement about how to classify IBD-associated arthritis and its place in the context of other enteropathic arthropathies. In this chapter, we provide an overview of what is known and where disagreement lies or where little data exist. We examine the pathophysiology of SpA and IBD and where these two diseases intersect. Additionally, we examine the current treatment modalities available and the contemporary clinical management approach.

### Pathophysiology of Spondyloarthritis and Inflammatory Bowel Disease: From Gut Mucosa and Microbiome to Joint Disease

### Overview of the Gut Environment in Health

The mucosal barrier of the gut serves to absorb dietary nutrients while balancing defense against potentially harmful environmental agents maintaining tolerance to normal microflora. The gut epithelium comprises epithelial cells connected by tight junctions regulating

permeability through the intraepithelial space, as well as mucin-producing goblet cells and anti-microbial peptide-secreting Paneth cells in the small intestine15 (Fig. 79.1). Subjacent to the tight junctions are intraepithelial lymphocytes, a subset of T cells that function as immune surveyors. Overlying the epithelial cells is a mucin layer that serves as a first layer of defense between pathogens and the gut epithelium. Beneath the epithelial cells lies the basement membrane, which separates the epithelial layer from the underlying lamina propria. The lamina propria, a key contributor to gut immunity, contains lymphocytes, dendritic cells, and macrophages.

The normal gut is also composed of a healthy microbiota. It has been estimated that trillions of microbes inhabit the human gut, most of which reside in the distal intestine. Our understanding of the complexity of the microbiome in health and disease is expanding rapidly. The microbiome plays a role in maintaining gut homeostasis. Functions of the microbiome include modulating host energy metabolism, maintaining intestinal immune homeostasis through modulation of both the innate and adaptive immune system, and immune defense through the inhibition of pathogenic colonization, among others. Fluctuations in microbial populations may either trigger or sustain inflammatory disease (within the gut and in other tissues throughout the body) and, likewise, subsequent immunosuppression may lead to alterations in the microbiome. Understanding this underlying premise makes it easier to understand why diseases of the gastrointestinal (GI) system, either infectious or inflammatory, may then lead to alterations in immunity throughout the body, particularly within the joints, as discussed more in this chapter.

### Maintaining Balance in the Gut

The mucosal barrier plays an important role in maintaining gut homeostasis. The mucous layer (secreted by goblet cells) provides a physical and chemical barrier. One of the critical roles of this barrier is to keep the gut microbes at a safe distance from intestinal epithelial cells (IECs). Within the mucus are anti-microbial peptides secreted by Paneth cells and immunoglobulin (Ig) A secreted by plasma cells to support homeostasis. Immune cells within the lamina propria aid in immunosurveillance. In a normal state, all of these components exist in harmony. In other words, there is a state of immune tolerance: epithelial cells secrete interleukin (IL)- 33, T-regulatory cells secrete IL-10, and retinoic acid receptorrelated orphan receptor-γt+ innate lymphoid cells (ILCs) secrete IL-22. ILCs play a particularly important role in maintaining this balance; lack or dysfunction of these cells leads to dysbiosis. Additionally, the balance between Th17 cells and T-regulatory cells also seems to be important for maintaining homeostasis.

### Barrier Disruption

The mucus layer of the gut is an important physical and chemical barrier. Disruption of the mucosal barrier or protein polymorphisms associated with perturbation of the mucous layer are associated with altered immune responses in the gut and stimulate more wide-reaching altered immunity. Dysregulated mucus production has been reported in the intestine of both Crohn's disease and SpA. When barrier injury occurs, microbes are given direct access to the cellular microenvironment, penetrating through the mucus layer. It remains unclear if injury to the layer must first occur or whether certain microbes or dysbiosis cause this injury; both are plausible pathways. Germ-free mice, however, do not develop microscopic or gross colonic inflammation; thus microbes are required for this process to occur. Exposed to microbes from the other side of the mucosal barrier, IECs then launch an inflammatory response, sending out a "danger signal" by secreting IL-1 and IL-6. Subsequently, dendritic cells secrete IL-12 and IL-23, stimulating Th1 and Th17 responses. This leads to the secretion of IL-17 and interferon (IFN) γ. B cells may also begin to secrete commensal specific IgG. Taken together, these factors may result in local tissue damage (i.e., IBD or subclinical gut inflammation).

### Dysbiosis in Inflammatory Bowel Disease and Spondyloarthritis

In IBD, there is a decrease in gut diversity and specifically a loss of microbes that may normally promote gut homeostasis. 17-19 Microbes that induce inflammation, such as Prevotellaceae, may be increased. Similar alterations in the gut microbiome have been observed in patients with SpA. Patients with axial SpA, compared with controls, have been found to have associated increases in numerous bacterial taxa, including Ruminococcus gnavus19 and the genus Dialister,20 that correlated with SpA disease activity in patients with bowel inflammation. Genetic risk such as human leukocyte antigen (HLA)-B27 may partly explain changes in bacterial diversity.

### From the Gut to the Joint

Why might inflammation or immune activation in the gut lead to synovitis and/or enthesitis? A number of potential mechanisms and several theories exist. First, there may simply be shared genetics with similar environmental triggers. Next, increased intestinal

permeability allows for exposure of microbial antigens to mucosal immune cells. This may then lead to accumulation of microbial antigens systemically, which then stimulate joint inflammation. Alternatively, exposure of the mucosal immune cells to microbial antigens may lead to a systemic inflammatory response that triggers inflammatory arthritis. Finally, another hypothesis is that immune activation leads to translocation of inflammatory cells from the gut to synovium, suggested by studies showing both shared macrophages and T cells in the gut and joint,17,22 increased affinity of mucosal T cells for synovial proteins,23 and expansion of T cells within the circulation, joint, and eye sharing receptors that potentially react with both bacterial and tissue peptide24 (Fig. 79.2 and Fig. 79.3).

### Shared Genetics

HLA-B27 positivity is present in 50% to 60% of patients with spondylitis associated with IBD. However, the association is not as strong with peripheral arthritis associated with IBD. The role of HLA-B27 has been postulated for many years to contribute to development of both gut inflammation and joint inflammation, in part because of the cell's dysfunction when encountering an intra-cellular pathogen. Instead of loading the protein for antigen presentation appropriately, the clunky HLA-B27 can form homodimers leading to an unfolded protein response and ultimately an inflammatory "danger" response (IL-1, IL-6, TNF, IL-23, and IL-17 production) or autophagy (resulting in a similar inflammatory cascade). Studies in HLA-B27 rat models suggest that microbes induce inflammatory changes similar to those observed in subjects with IBD. Additionally, in healthy patients, differences in microbiota between HLA-B27 positive and negative siblings have been observed, suggesting a role for genetic background on gut microbiota composition. Dysbiosis may occur as the result of infections (i.e., Campylobacter and other infections long associated with ReA) or antibiotics. Finally, recent data support a long-held hypothesis that HLA-B27 can present bacterial peptides that trigger T cell cross-reactivity with those in host tissues.

HLA-B27 is not the only genetic risk factor for AS or IBD. Endoplasmic reticulum aminopeptidase 1 (ERAP1) and 2 (ERAP2) are genetic loci that have been associated with both AS and IBD.26, They code for proteins that play a role in trimming proteins for presentation on major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class 1 molecules. This relationship is particularly relevant in HLA-B27-positive patients. Interaction between ERAP1, but not ERAP2, and HLA-B27 has been established. The association between ERAP and AS is stronger than with IBD, but association with IBD has been demonstrated. More about the pathogenesis related to HLA-B27 can be found in Chapter 76.

Beyond HLA-B27 and ERAP, there are other common genetic pathways in SpA and IBD. IL-23R polymorphisms have been demonstrated in both IBD and SpA with several shared susceptibility loci.25, These polymorphisms generally lead to increased Th17 cells and increased secretion of IL-17, IL-22, and IL-21. Caspase recruitment domain-containing protein 9 (CARD9) mutations have been associated with both IBD and AS. CARD9 may play an important protective role in maintaining gut homeostasis such that, when mutated, it leads to disease. The precise inflammatory mechanism remains unclear, however, as most ASassociated CARD9 polymorphisms are associated with decreased CARD9 expression.

CARD9 pathway proteins play a role in mediating signals from dectin-1 and dectin-2 receptors17 and recognize β-glucan

in bacterial and fungal cell walls. Exposure to β-glucan induces IL-23-dependent SpA phenotype in SKG mice (a mouse model that spontaneously develops chronic autoimmune arthritis) and exaggerated IL-23 responses in macrophages from AS patients. CARD9 mutations may also lead to activation of inflammasomes in response to some bacterial and fungal cell wall proteins. In CARD9 null mice, Citrobacter rodentium exposure leads to development of intestinal inflammation but, if raised in a germ-free environment, these mice do not develop intestinal inflammation, suggesting again that microbiota are necessary for disease.

The most consistent genetic susceptibility locus for IBD is on chromosome 16q12 at NOD2/CARD15. NOD2/CARD15 leads to enhanced immune activity and production of damage-associated molecular patterns (S100 proteins). This triggers an inflammatory cascade. Of note, calprotectin, commonly used in measuring and assessing the degree of intestinal inflammation (discussed later in the chapter), is a heterodimer of S100A8 and S100A9. To date, there is no clear link between NOD2/CARD15 and AS. However, there have been associations with the S100 proteins in PsA. Finally, there may still be other genetic links between AS and IBD. An exome-wide study of about 5000 patients with AS and 21,000 healthy controls identified three AS-associated variants, CDKAL1, C7orf72, and TLR10, that have previously been associated with IBD.

### The Th-17 Pathway and the Implications for Developing Spondyloarthritis

The Th17 pathway has been found to play an important role in the development and maintenance of SpA and IBD. Th17 responses are an important component of the normal immune response, particularly in protection against infections such as fungal and some bacterial infections. Th17 cells assist in

regulation of the mucosal border, and intestinal microbiota have been linked to homeostasis of this pathway at the level of the gut. Th17 cells can be sorted into those that are homeostatic and those that are inflammatory based on specific cellular markers and cytokines that are secreted. Homeostatic Th17 cells develop in the setting of IL-6 and transforming growth factor-β and produce IL-17A, IL-17F, IL-22, and IL-10 to maintain barrier homeostasis.

Inflammatory Th17 cells are typically activated by IL-23 to produce IL-17A, IL-17F, IFNγ, and granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor. IL-23 has been found to be overproduced in the bowel walls of patients with AS. Studies in wild-type mice demonstrated that when IL-23 levels are driven up (through a microcircle technique in which IL-23-containing microcircles injected intravenously lodge in the liver and release IL-23), these mice develop an SpA phenotype. One theory is that IL-23 produced at the level of the gut, possibly due to alterations in the microbiome or ongoing inflammation, could lead to development of SpA in a similar way. One of the problems with this theory is that IL-23 inhibitors have failed to demonstrate efficacy in AS. Increasing data support IL-23-independent pathways to activate Th17 immunity through innate lymphocyte populations including ILCs, MAIT (mucosal-associated invariant T cell), and γδ T cells.

### Role of Dysbiosis in Stimulating Joint Disease

Some studies have supposed that dysbiosis in the gut leads to increased intestinal permeability, local inflammation, and subsequently, systemic inflammation, particularly Th17 pathwaydriven inflammation. A Th17 response can be triggered by the intestinal microbiota. For example, differences in response to segmented filamentous bacteria, compared with noncommensal bacteria responses, and dysregulation of these responses is linked

to inflammation in the gut. Immune cells such as T cells, ILC3, MAIT, and monocytes then migrate in the circulation to the entheses; this has been demonstrated in animal models. These "tissue-resident cells," however, may have the capacity to travel. For example, NKp44+ ILC3 cells in patients with AS express intestinal homing receptor alpha-4-beta-7 in both the gut and the bone marrow, tissues where its ligand MAdCAM1 is also highly expressed. This suggests a migratory capacity of cells from the gut to synovium in humans.

### Clinical Manifestations and Diagnosis of Inflammatory Bowel Disease-Associated Arthritis

### Introduction

Inflammatory arthritis is the most common extraintestinal manifestation of IBD. IBD-associated arthritis occurs in both Crohn's disease (CD) and ulcerative colitis (UC).35, Overall, the

prevalence of inflammatory arthritis in IBD patients ranges widely, though generally from 13% to 33%.36-40 Patients with IBD-associated inflammatory arthritis share many of the features of SpA. Most epidemiologic studies have historically broken IBD-associated arthritis into peripheral and axial disease. For example, a meta-analysis found that in patients with IBD, the prevalence of AS, sacroilitis, and peripheral arthritis were 3%, 10%, and 13%, respectively. However, the prevalence of axial disease may be higher due to the presence of asymptomatic sacroiliitis, which is frequently not brought to the attention of the provider treating bowel disease. Conversely, among patients with SpA, the prevalence of IBD is lower. One large meta-analysis found that IBD occurs in approximately 6.8% of patients with AS.

Because both IBD and SpA often have an insidious onset, it can sometimes be difficult to determine which process started first. Given the overlap among these conditions, the nomenclature becomes challenging. Is it IBD-associated arthritis or SpA with IBD? Most use the term IBD-arthritis to refer to patients who first developed IBD or in whom the IBD drives therapy. Overall, the pathophysiology is currently presumed to be similar, and thus the terminology differences are likely not important or meaningful. Regardless of the term used, the two processes commonly coexist. In a study of the extraintestinal manifestations in the Swiss Inflammatory Bowel Disease Cohort, peripheral arthritis and axial disease were present prior to the diagnosis of IBD in 20% and 40% of patients, respectively. One population-based study found that in AS patients, the highest risk of developing IBD was within the first year of diagnosis. Certain characteristics of bowel inflammation are correlated with more active joint disease. For example, arthritis is more likely to occur in patients with large bowel disease and in patients with abscesses, pseudomembranous polyposis, and perianal disease.

### Clinical Manifestations

Joint disease in IBD-associated arthritis resembles that seen in other types of SpA and includes inflammatory arthritis (peripheral, axial, or both), enthesitis, and dactylitis. Any combination of these manifestations can be seen, as commonly occurs in other types of SpA. In addition, other extraintestinal manifestations of IBD and extra-articular manifestations of SpA, such as uveitis, erythema nodosum, and pyoderma gangrenosum, can be seen in affected patients.

Peripheral arthritis is among the more common manifestations of IBD-associated arthritis. The peripheral arthritis seen in patients with IBD was historically categorized into two phenotypes: type I and type II. This classification schema first arose from investigators at the Oxford IBD clinic. Published in 1998, their study was a review of case notes of all the patients with IBD seen in their clinic, including 976 patients with UC and 483 with CD. They noticed a pattern among their patients and categorized them as having either pauciarticular (type I) or polyarticular (type II) arthritis (Table 79.1). They then reviewed the natural history, joint distributions, and frequency of other complications to further characterize each type. This schema has since become the standard in discussions about IBD-associated peripheral arthritis, particularly among gastroenterologists, and as such is frequently cited in the literature. The distinction between type I and type II arthritis is relevant for an understanding of the literature, and therefore we describe the two types in more detail. However, it should be noted that this classification scheme is no longer used in rheumatology practice. A more practical and reliable way to

classify disease is with a method used for the SpA in general, such as the validated Assessment of SpondyloArthritis international Society (ASAS) criteria for axial SpA or those for peripheral SpA.45, ASAS and other classification systems for SpA are further discussed in Chapter 76.

Patients with a predominantly oligoarticular pattern of disease, historically referred to as type I arthritis, develop joint disease that is asymmetric, involving the large and small joints. Most frequently the lower extremities are involved, including the knees, ankles, and metatarsophalangeal joints. The arthritis can be migratory. It is typically less severe than predominantly polyarticular disease and is often self-limited and transient, resolving on its own without treatment. However, recurrence of disease is common. Erosive disease is rare. The arthritis seen in these patients occurs early in the course of bowel disease and may even occur up to several years prior to the development of bowel disease. Flares are often associated with active bowel disease, and arthritis and bowel disease relapses often occur simultaneously. One study reported that surgical removal of the colon in patients with UC had a curative effect on type I arthritis, further illustrating the link between bowel and joint disease activity. Patients with this pattern as the predominant feature of their joint disease often develop other extraintestinal manifestations seen in IBD patients, including erythema nodosum and uveitis.

Patients with a predominantly polyarticular pattern of disease, historically referred to as type II arthritis, develop a symmetric polyarthritis of the small joints, most commonly the metacarpophalangeal joints. This RA-like pattern disease rarely precedes bowel disease, and joint disease activity occurs independently of bowel disease activity. Synovitis in patients with this pattern of joint disease is typically more severe, can be erosive, and is not self-limiting. Per the initial description, this type of arthritis more frequently required treatment with immunosuppressive therapy. However, these categories are fluid and can change over time.

Axial disease seen in IBD-associated arthritis is similar to that seen in SpA in general. It can range from asymptomatic sacroiliitis,

to inflammatory low back pain with or without sacroiliitis, to true AS. Symptoms include inflammatory low back pain and buttock pain. Patients usually describe back pain that has an insidious onset. Morning stiffness is a prominent feature, and pain is usually worse with rest and relieved with movement. Symptoms can be intermittent. Patients may describe awakening toward the later portion of the night due to back pain. Other important features include the persistence of symptoms for greater than 3 months and onset before the age of 45. It has traditionally been thought that axial disease activity is not associated with bowel disease activity and that flares occur independently. However, some studies have suggested an association between AS clinical activity scores and the development of CD, as well as with disease activity scores in CD.48, Another study found that patients with IBD who develop axial SpA are more likely to have a chronic and active IBD disease course. Surgical bowel resection has no impact on axial disease.

Enthesitis and dactylitis are common and are signature features of SpA. Enthesitis can occur at the Achilles, plantar fascia, patellar tendon, lateral and medial epicondyles, and a variety of other enthesitis sites throughout the body. Enthesitis is clinically identified by putting pressure on the site of the tendon insertion and eliciting pain (these clinical measures may have moderate sensitivity but low specificity); enthesitis can also be measured using magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) or ultrasound. Erosions and/or new bone formation may occur at the site of enthesitis. Dactylitis is inflammatory swelling of fingers or toes caused by tenosynovitis and full-thickness inflammation of many of the tissues in the digits. Dactylitis and enthesitis occur less frequently in IBD-associated arthritis than other types of SpA, such as PsA. However, one study suggested dactylitis may be more common than previously thought in patients with IBD-associated arthritis, with a prevalence of 15% in one cohort. In this study, dactylitis was more common in IBD patients with CD and in those with peripheral arthritis.

SAPHO syndrome is another musculoskeletal disorder that is associated with IBD. SAPHO is sometimes thought of as part of the SpA family and there does seem to be an association with HLA-B27.1 One review found that IBD was present in 4.8% of patients with SAPHO, while SAPHO was present in 0.2% of patients with IBD. For a more detailed discussion of SAPHO, please refer to Chapter 104.

Finally, hypertrophic osteoarthropathy is another type of joint disease seen in IBD. Hypertrophic osteoarthropathy is an excessive proliferation of skin and bone at distal parts of the extremities. Periosteal proliferation and synovitis can occur in late stages. Patients can develop bulbous deformity at the tips of the digits. These deformities are a poor prognostic sign for bowel disease severity in IBD patients. Hypertrophic osteoarthropathy is similarly associated with uncoupling of osteoclast and osteoblast activity and new bone formation, both key features in AS.

While arthritis is the most common extraintestinal manifestation in IBD, there are several additional extraintestinal manifestations of IBD, described in Table 79.2.

### Diagnosis

IBD-associated arthritis should be suspected when a patient with IBD develops joint pain, stiffness, or symptoms of inflammatory back pain (see Table 79.3). Once this is suspected, the diagnosis of joint disease is similar to that for SpA in general. The history should focus on the distribution of joints involved, symptoms that

### Inflammatory Back Pain (IBP) Criteria

1. Age at onset < 40 years

2. Insidious onset

3. Improvement with exercise

4. No improvement with rest

5. Pain at night (with improvement upon getting up)

might suggest inflammatory joint pain (i.e., morning stiffness, swelling, improvement with activity), current IBD activity, and the relation of joint pain to bowel disease activity. A thorough physical examination should be undertaken in such patients, with careful attention paid to tender and swollen joints, dactylitis, enthesitis, axial spondylitis, and sacroiliitis, particularly in patients with symptoms of inflammatory back pain (see Chapter 76 for more

about the assessment of SpA). Other extraintestinal manifestations of IBD, such as erythema nodosum or inflammatory eye disease, should be ascertained. Laboratory testing to help support a diagnosis of inflammatory arthritis such as C-reactive protein (CRP) may be obtained, although CRP may also be elevated in the presence of active bowel disease. In monoor oligo-articular arthritis, an arthrocentesis should be considered to exclude infection and crystal disease and to document inflammatory fluid. To reduce confirmatory bias, clinicians should also consider mechanical pain and central sensitization or fibromyalgia55 in the differential diagnosis and investigate whether these conditions may be present.

There is no formal test to confirm IBD-associated arthritis. Rather, the diagnosis is made in a patient with confirmed IBD with features of inflammatory arthritis, as described previously. Since arthritis may develop first, rheumatologists should likewise follow patients with SpA for the development of signs or symptoms of IBD (e.g., new abdominal pain, diarrhea, bloody stools, or new anemia). Such patients should be referred to a gastroenterologist to be evaluated for IBD.

### Screening for Spondyloarthritis in Patients With Inflammatory B Bowel Disease

Because of the increasing recognition that earlier identification and treatment of SpA leads to improved outcomes, screening for SpA in patients with IBD has received increasing attention. A few screening tools have recently been developed. There are several questionnaires that have been developed that may be useful tools to assist in the early detection of inflammatory back pain and/or AxSpA in patients with IBD.56-59

### Assessment and Monitoring of Disease Activity

Activity levels ofboth joint and bowel disease should be monitored regularly and objectively in patients with IBD-associated arthritis.60, For the purpose of this discussion, we focus on monitoring joint disease. However, the level of bowel disease activity should always be considered when making decisions about treatment. Selecting the best therapy for these patients is often challenging, and partnership between a rheumatologist and gastroenterologist is critical.

In general, as in other types of SpA, monitoring should objectively record the patient's clinical status and this measure should be followed at each visit. Measures that are used in SpA in general are useful in measuring the activity of IBD-associated arthritis. Such measures include the Ankylosing Spondylitis Disease Activity Score (ASDAS), the Bath Ankylosing Spondylitis Disease Activity Index (BASDAI), and a more recently developed patient reported outcome measure, the ASAS Health Index (ASAS HI). Please refer to Chapter 76 for a more detailed description of measuring disease activity in patients with SpA. Patient-reported outcomes (such as BASDAI and ASAS HI) are also useful measures that can be monitored longitudinally and are often more practical in the clinical setting. The Routine Assessment of Patient Index Data (RAPID3) is a commonly used patient-reported outcome measure used across diseases in United States practices that was found to correlate well with BASDAI in the assessment of disease activity in patients with AS62and PsA.63-65

Recent studies have investigated additional methods that may help specifically monitor disease activity in patients with

IBD-associated arthritis, though these are not currently used in the clinical setting. The use of fecal biomarkers, such as calprotectin, are promising noninvasive tests for the evaluation of disease activity and mucosal healing in patients with IBD.66-68 They may also have a role in assessing arthritis and for predicting disease course. In one study, elevated fecal calprotectin accurately identified SpA patients with bowel inflammation and more joint inflammation on MRI, and patients with higher baseline levels had a better response of their arthritis to treatment with TNF inhibitors. However, available evidence is mixed. Some studies have shown calprotectin levels to be an independent marker for radiographic spinal progression in patients with AxSpA, whereas others have found no association between calprotectin level and measures of clinical disease activity in AS patients.

Capsule endoscopy (a procedure in which the patient swallows a tiny camera that records images of the entire length of the GI tract) was shown to be useful for the detection of both CD and subclinical small-bowel inflammation in patients with AS and may be more sensitive than traditional colonoscopy due to the ability to view areas not picked up by colonoscopy. However, it should be noted that we understand little about the role of subclinical bowel inflammation in AS patients, and many would argue there is little to be gained from detecting and monitoring subclinical disease until further evidence is available.

There are also other novel biomarkers under development such as sclerostin,71serum levels of beta-2-microglobulin,72a and more. However, these potential biomarkers are still in their infancy and require more study in patients with both IBD and various forms of inflammatory arthritis.

### Management

The management of IBD-associated arthritis should focus on the well-being of patients and their disease manifestations. Ideally there should be a multidisciplinary treatment team in which patients are co-managed by a rheumatologist and a gastroenterologist. Patients have shorter delays in diagnosis and better outcomes of both bowel and joint symptoms when this strategy is used.73, When deciding on a treatment strategy, it is important to consider the pattern of arthritis and the type of IBD (UC vs. CD) and its severity. Some treatments are useful for all of the various manifestations of IBD-associated arthritis, whereas others are effective for only specific aspects of the disease. Furthermore, the doses may be different for IBD as opposed to AxSpA or PsA.

In general, treatment modalities are similar to those used in SpA (Chapters 76 and 78). We walk through each of the therapies here and in Table 79.4. The use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) as a first step in treatment is controversial and is discussed in more detail in the next section. The introduction of small molecules/synthetic disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs may be used for peripheral arthritis (and sometimes dactylitis or enthesitis), whereas axial disease will require a TNF inhibitor if initial treatment with NSAIDs has been unsuccessful. Physical therapy is an important part of management and should be recommended to all patients with axial disease77 and may also be beneficial to those with peripheral disease.

### Nonsteroidal Anti-inflammatory Drugs

The use of NSAIDs in IBD-associated arthritis is a controversial topic. 67, NSAIDs have a known role in the treatment of SpÅ. However, reduced prostaglandin production due to

inhibition of cyclooxygenase (COX)-1 and COX-2 from NSAIDs has been implicated in clinical relapse of IBD. This thought process has led to a common fear among both rheumatologists and gastroenterologists that NSAIDs may induce exacerbation of IBD. However, the evidence evaluating this relationship is weak and conflicting. One review found that there is no causal relationship between NSAIDs and relapse of IBD. Another review, mostly based on case reports, concluded that exacerbations of IBD occur after NSAID administration. Yet another review, based on one randomized controlled trial (RCT), concluded that most patients with IBD tolerate NSAIDs; one in five patients may experience a relapse, and relapses are typically mild and do not require escalation of IBD therapy. A large meta-analysis did not find any association between NSAID use and exacerbation of UC or CD. Furthermore, a recent large cohort study raised concern that previous studies showing risk associated with NSAID use may have suffered from residual confounding because of protopathic bias. There has also been consideration given to the use of selective COX-2 inhibitors due to their reduced GI side effect profile. Some reviews have found that selective COX-2 inhibitors may have a lower risk of inducing relapse.83, However, while they may be safer in theory, current American College of Rheumatology (ACR) recommendations suggest there is not sufficient

evidence to support the use of selective COX-2 inhibitors over other NSAIDs in patients with IBD. The most recent recommendations for the treatment of AS, as well as a recent Italian expert panel on the management of patients with coexisting SpA and IBD, suggest that short courses of NSAIDs to treat arthritis are safe in patients with quiescent IBD.77, One challenge that may arise is if patients develop GI symptoms after initiation of NSAID use. It can be difficult for gastroenterologists to determine whether symptoms are related to NSAID use or active bowel disease. Therefore use of NSAIDs should be discussed with a patient's gastroenterologist prior to initiation whenever possible. Current gastroenterology-based guidelines recommend avoiding NSAIDs in CD and UC despite low levels of evidence.67, In summary, there are theoretical harmful effects, but evidence is lacking. Therefore short courses of NSAIDs are a reasonable option in patients with inactive IBD. If signs or symptoms of worsening bowel disease develop, use should be discontinued, and the patient should be evaluated by their gastroenterologist.

### Role of Glucocorticoids

The use and effectiveness of glucocorticoids in IBD-associated arthritis is similar to that in other forms of SpA, recognizing also

that glucocorticoids may be used for the management of IBD.67, The distribution of joint disease should dictate whether or not glucocorticoids are considered. Intra-articular glucocorticoids have a role in the treatment of oligoarticular peripheral arthritis. As in other types of SpA, systemic glucocorticoids may have a role in severe flares of peripheral arthritis. If used for this purpose, they should be given for the shortest possible course at the lowest possible dose to effectively treat the patient. Their use should be avoided for axial disease because of their lack of efficacy and risk for adverse effects.

Glucocorticoids are often required in the management of bowel disease in patients with CD and UC. Whenever possible, agents with limited systemic effects (such as budesonide or topical formulations) are used in mild UC or CD. Compared with oral prednisone, this formulation of glucocorticoid has less systemic side effects and less effect on bone mineral density.90, The efficacy of budesonide on inflammatory arthritis is less clear. One study suggested it may be as effective as prednisolone in RA, and another demonstrated benefit in treating arthralgias in patients with IBD.92,

For more severe bowel disease, oral prednisone or intravenous methylprednisolone is sometimes used for induction of remission. Patients receiving glucocorticoids for management of bowel disease and peripheral arthritis are at risk for high cumulative doses over time. In such patients, consider screening for osteoporosis, and refer to the ACR guidelines for bone health management in the setting of glucocorticoid use. In addition to the typical considerations in using glucocorticoids, particular caution should be considered in children, as glucocorticoids may lead to growth retardation in children with IBD.

### Oral Therapies

Traditional oral therapies have an important role in the management of IBD-associated arthritis. With regard to joint disease, they are most useful for the management of peripheral arthritis. As in other types of SpA, there is little evidence that they are effective in the management of axial disease.96,

Methotrexate is an immunosuppressant prescribed as both monoand combination-immunosuppression in CD. It is effective for maintenance therapy in CD. Conversely, the METEOR trial found that methotrexate did not improve maintenance of steroid-free remission in UC, although there was a trend toward increased levels of remission. No large RCTs of methotrexate specifically in patients with IBD and peripheral arthritis have been conducted. A small observational study found that methotrexate improved joint symptoms in patients with peripheral arthritis and UC. Methotrexate has a long history of use for peripheral arthritis in patients with SpA. However, there are mixed results for its efficacy in PsA.101-103

Sulfasalazine is sometimes used for the management of IBD.67, There is evidence supporting its use for active bowel disease in UC. The evidence is not as strong for its effectiveness in CD, but there is still occasionally a role for its use, particularly in mild disease. Sulfasalazine has been shown to be effective in the management of peripheral arthritis in patients with SpA. A study conducted by the Department of Veterans Affairs of over 600 patients with SpA found that patients with peripheral articular manifestations treated with sulfasalazine had a 59% response rate (tender/swollen joints) compared with 43% in the placebo group. Importantly, patients with axial disease treated with sulfasalazine had a similar response rate to the placebo group, and sulfasalazine is no longer recommended for treatment of axial SpA.107,

Azathioprine is used for maintaining remission in patients with IBD, both as monoand combination-immunosuppression. 109, Azathioprine is thought to have some effect on peripheral arthritis in rheumatic diseases, but it is uncommonly used in SpA and has not been extensively studied.

### TNFI Inhibitors

TNF inhibitors are widely used in the management of patients with IBD-associated arthritis. There is substantial evidence for their effectiveness in both IBD and SpA. Multiple large RCTs have demonstrated benefit in SpA patients with both axial and peripheral joint disease. Please see Chapters 76 and 78 for a more detailed discussion about TNF inhibitor use in SpA. Infliximab is effective in moderate-to-severe CD and UC, promoting fistula closure and mucosal healing and sparing the use of steroids. Adalimumab is also efficacious in inducing and maintaining remission in moderate-to-severe CD and UC. Etanercept, on the other hand, has been shown to be ineffective for CDi13 and has been associated with flares of IBD.114, One observational study evaluating etanercept in patients with IBD-associated arthritis found a positive effect on joint disease but none on bowel disease. This may be related to its differing structure as a fusion protein. Therefore given the presence of other TNF inhibitors that work for both inflammatory arthritis and IBD, etanercept is generally avoided in patients with IBD.77, Other TNF inhibitors have also been approved for use in both IBD and SpA. Certolizumab has been approved for the treatment of AS, PsA, and CD, whereas golimumab has been approved for the treatment of AS, PsA, and UC.81, Note that dosing of TNF inhibitors is frequently different for IBD compared with SpA.

Overall, few studies have evaluated treatment effects in patients with IBD-arthritis specifically. As such, most of the data informing treatment decisions are from trials in IBD and, separately, trials in PsA, AS, or peripheral SpA. One single-arm trial evaluated response to infliximab among 30 patients with CD and SpA over a 12-month period, with periodic evaluation by a rheumatologist and gastroenterologist. Joint and bowel disease activity scores significantly improved and were maintained over 12 months of follow-up. Patients also reported improvements in health-related quality of life scores. Another study analyzed pooled results of 11 clinical trials of adalimumab in CD that reported an effect on extraintestinal manifestations. Over 1200 patients with arthralgias or arthritis were included. Pooled analysis showed a significant and sustained reduction in arthralgias and arthritis.

Biosimilars are now commonly used in patients with both IBD and SpA in Europe and will increasingly be used as they have now become available in the United States. Multiple TNF biosimilars have been approved for use in AS, PsA, and IBD. Their use specifically in IBD-associated arthritis is extrapolated from these indications. Because of their similarity with the originator drug and the use under the same indications as the originator drugs, the etanercept-biosimilar should likewise be avoided in patients with IBD.

### Other Biologics and Targeted d Therapies

Over the last two decades, an increasing number of targeted therapies have become available for the treatment of immune-mediated diseases, including SpA and IBD. In this section we review some of the other non-TNF-targeted therapies relevant for the management of IBD-associated arthritis.

Ustekinumab is a human monoclonal antibody that binds to the p40 subunit of both IL-12 and IL-23. It has been shown to be effective for psoriasis and PsA. It is also effective for CD that is refractory to TNF therapy. Trials have also demonstrated efficacy of ustekinumab in UC. 125, Extrapolating from the data in PsA, this is an option for patients with IBD-associated arthritis. Importantly, ustekinumab was not effective for axial disease, so its use should be limited to those with peripheral arthritis. Additionally, note that the dose for IBD is higher than the dose used for PsA. The IL-23 inhibitors (IL-23i) guselkumab and risankizumab have also been approved for PsA and are being tested in CD127-129 and UC. Similarly, dosing is different for these therapies in IBD and, like ustekinumab, efficacy has not been demonstrated in axial SpA. Because of the relative safety of IL-23i, a UC trial recently tested the efficacy and safety of golimumab plus guselkumab compared with either therapy alone. While not yet part of standard care, more combination therapy trials are forthcoming, and this may be a treatment approach in the future.

The Janus kinase inhibitors, specifically tofacitinib and upadacitinib, also have a role in the management of IBD-associated arthritis. An additional benefit of these therapies is that they are also affective for axial SpA. The dose for both therapies is often higher in the first 8 to 12 weeks of therapy for IBD. Since their initial approval, concerns have been raised about the increased risk for cardiovascular disease and malignancy,132 particularly in patients over the age of 65, and may be avoided or used after other therapy options have been examined in this population.

Some biologics used in SpA are not effective in patients with IBD. Secukinumab and ixekizumab are human monoclonal antibodies that bind to IL-17a. Secukinumab was tested for the management of CD and was found to be ineffective. Furthermore, long-term extension studies from RCTs of IL-17 inhibitors, including the newest IL-17a and IL-17f inhibitor bimekizumab and IL-17 receptor blocker brodalumab, have identified several cases of new IBD or flares of previously quiescent IBD. Therefore IL-17 inhibitors should be avoided in patients with IBD. Abatacept, a CTLA-4 immunoglobulin that inhibits T-cell costimulation, did not demonstrate efficacy for the management of IBD. Tocilizumab, a humanized monoclonal antibody against IL-6, was not effective in SpA and has been associated with intestinal ulcers and perforation.

Vedolizumab, a monoclonal antibody against integrin α4β7, is unique among biologics used to treat IBD because it specifically targets the GI tract. It has demonstrated efficacy compared with placebo in both UC and CD. It was postulated that vedolizumab could improve articular symptoms by treating GI inflammation that may be driving the joint disease. Post-hoc analysis of the GEMINI trials, which showed the initial efficacy for UC and CD, showed mild improvement of joint symptoms. However, in clinical practice there is not felt to be any benefit of these drugs for treating inflammatory arthritis. Additionally, other studies have suggested the possibility for vedolizumab to trigger new cases of inflammatory arthritis,137 possibly in the setting of switching from a TNF inhibitor to vedolizumab, where the inflammatory arthritis was controlled on the TNF inhibitor and switching it off caused reoccurrence or emergence of the symptoms. Ultimately, given the limited evidence for its effectiveness and the concerns over triggering inflammatory arthritis, vedolizumab is not routinely used in the management of patients with IBD-associated arthritis. Natalizumab, a monoclonal antibody against integrin α4β1, is approved for use in CD and ozanimod, a sphingosine- 1-phosphate receptor modulator, is approved for use in CD and

UC. Neither of these therapies has data to support use in inflammatory arthritis.

### Probiotics

Probiotics are widely used among patients with IBD. However, while there is mild evidence for benefit in UC (particularly in patients with a J pouch and pouchitis), there is no evidence for their effectiveness in CD. Probiotics were not effective for SpA in one small study. There is currently no evidence to support their use in patients with IBD-associated arthritis. Likewise, there was a recent trial examining fecal transplant in PsA to reset the microbiome that was not found to be effective. 140,141

### Other Enteropathic Arthropathies

### Whipple's Disease

In 1907, George H. Whipple described a 36-year-old patient with "gradual loss of weight and strength, stools consisting chiefly of neutral fat and fatty acids, indefinite abdominal signs, and a peculiar multiple arthritis. This constellation of symptoms, now known as Whipple's disease, is caused by Tropheryma whipplei, a gram-positive bacillus related to Actinomycetes. T. whipplei is ubiquitous in the environment and is often associated with sewage systems. It is transmitted via oral-oral or oral-fecal route and is therefore more commonly found in areas with poor hygiene.

The cardinal features of Whipple's disease include arthralgias, weight loss, diarrhea, and abdominal pain. GI symptoms are often associated with malabsorption. Symptoms can present over years, and arthralgias are often the first to manifest. Patients can also present with fevers, as well as neurologic, cardiac, dermatologic, and other organ-specific manifestations. The most common articular symptoms are migratory arthralgias of the large joints. Effusion and joint damage are rare. Sacroiliitis has been described. Given the somewhat similar picture of joint distribution to SpA, an association between Whipple's disease and HLA-B27 positivity has been hypothesized. However, studies have not confirmed this relationship. The disease does seem to have a predilection for those with European ancestry, and an association between HLA alleles DRB1*13 and DQB1*06 and Whipple's disease has been demonstrated in a cohort of 122 European patients. Diagnosis usually involves exclusion of other, more common causes of diarrhea, followed by periodic acidSchiff staining and polymerase chain reaction testing for the T. whipplei organism from involved sites, such as the GI tract or synovial fluid. Initial approach to treatment includes intravenous ceftriaxone followed by maintenance therapy with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. Refractory cases have been treated with combination doxycycline and hydroxychloroquine.

### Brucellosis

Brucellosis is a zoonotic disease transmitted to humans by contact with fluids from infected animals or from animal-derived food products. The most common species in the Brucella genus to cause human infection is Brucella melitensis. Brucellosis due to B. melitensis is the most common zoonosis worldwide. Endemic areas include countries in the Mediterranean, Central Asia, China, Sub- Saharan Africa, and parts of Central and South America, although new foci of geographic distribution are constantly emerging. Acute brucellosis is a systemic febrile illness, and symptoms can

include malaise, arthralgia, myalgia, and headache. Focal infection occurs in about 30% of patients. Of those with localized infection, articular disease is the most common, occurring in about twothirds of cases.

Articular disease in brucellosis can present as either peripheral arthritis, sacroiliitis, and spondylitis. Affected children most commonly present with a monoarticular arthritis of the knee or hip, and adults have a predilection for both peripheral and axial disease. .149, Sacroiliitis can be extremely acute and painful. Complications of brucellar spondylitis, such as epidural abscess, can occur. Diagnosis is made either by culture of the organism from blood or other involved tissue or by serologic testing. Synovial fluid is not particularly helpful in the diagnosis of brucellosis and synovial fluid culture is rarely positive. Synovial fluid analysis may reveal an inflammatory fluid, but white blood cell count rarely exceeds 15,000.152 First-line treatment for noncomplicated brucellosis is doxycycline for 6 weeks, in combination with either streptomycin for 2 to 3 weeks or rifampin for 6 weeks. Patients with spondylitis require longer treatment and should receive at least 12 weeks of therapy. They also appear to respond better to the combination of doxycycline and streptomycin, compared with doxycycline and rifampin.

### Celiac Disease

Celiac disease is a chronic gluten-sensitive autoimmune disease of the small intestine that primarily affects genetically susceptible individuals. It is estimated that 0.5% to 1% of the world's population is affected by celiac disease. The disease is strongly associated with the HLA-DQ2 and DQ8 gene loci, and studies suggest that DQ2and DQ8-positive individuals have a rate of celiac disease of 1:7 compared with 1:2518 in patients without genetic susceptibility. Patients most commonly present with diarrhea and foul-smelling and floating stools related to steatorrhea and may develop signs of malabsorption.

There may be an association between celiac disease and the development of arthritis, though this remains unclear. One casecontrol study of 200 patients and 40 controls found that arthritis was present in 26% of patients compared with 7.5% of controls. Arthritis was peripheral in 19 patients, axial in 15, and an overlap of both in 18. There have also been case reports of arthritis as the presenting symptom of celiac disease. More studies are needed to better characterize this association. Importantly, patients with celiac disease are also more prone to metabolic bone disease than the general population. Osteoporosis can also be a manifesta- . Celiac disease is managed by tion of subclinical celiac disease. adhering to a gluten-free diet.

### Bowel-Associated Dermatosis-Arthritis Syndrome

Bowel-associated dermatosis-arthritis syndrome (BADAS) was first identified in the 1970s in patients who had undergone jejunoileal bypass surgery. At the time it was reported in up to 20% of patients who underwent the procedure. Initially called "bypass arthritis," it has since been renamed as it can be seen in patients who have undergone other types of abdominal surgery and in patients who have conditions causing abnormal gut function, such as IBD. BADAS is a neutrophilic dermatosis characterized by fever and/or flulike symptoms followed by arthralgias, myalgias, and inflammatory skin eruptions. The articular manifestations are typically an oligoarticular, asymmetric, episodic, and

nonerosive arthritis of the large and small joints. Tenosynovitis and enthesitis can also occur. The diagnosis is mainly a clinical one in patients with the typical cutaneous eruptions. Treatment includes reanastomosis in patients who have undergone bypass surgery; antibiotics including minocycline, neomycin, and metronidazole; and symptomatic relief with local or oral glucocorticoids.

### Other Conditions

There a re s everal o ther c onditions that a re r elevant to m ention in the context of enteropathic arthritis, but their connection between gut and joint pathology is not as clear. Microscopic colitis has been associated with various autoimmune conditions. Poncet's disease, an arthritis related to tuberculosis, is thought to have a possible association with HLA-B27. Enterovirus and the viral hepatidities affect various portions of the GI tract and can at times be associated with polyarthritis. Pseudomembranous colitis and specifically Clostridioides d ifficile hav e bee n ass ociated wit h ReA. Various parasites that infect the GI tract can be associated with arthritis.

# Etiology and Pathogenesis of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus

80

### KEY POINTS

### Introduction

Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is one of the most widely studied diseases in medicine. Predominantly a disease of young women in their childbearing years and with the potential to cause significant physical disfigurement, morbidity, and occasionally mortality, lupus is the focus of strong advocacy to support research that will generate insights into disease pathogenesis and improve patient outcomes. In fact, characterization of the immunologic contributors to lupus, the prototype systemic autoimmune disease, has been the focus of particularly intense study since the flowering of the discipline of immunology in the 1950s and 1960s. Efforts to define the genetic variations that underlie susceptibility to lupus have supported the central role of the immune system in disease pathogenesis but have extended the view of lupus pathology beyond the important role of autoantibodies and T cells to include a significant contribution of the innate immune system to disease. An underlying role for the vasculature as a target of the immune system and

its products has gained renewed interest as an important component of lupus pathogenesis. Together, these recent advances provide important insights into how the intersection of genetic diversity with environmental triggers amplifies immune system activation and target organ vulnerability to generate the classic manifestations of lupus and its clinically significant comorbidities. Fig. 80.1 provides an overview of many of the risk factors, potential triggers of immune activation, contributors to autoimmunity and inflammation, and target organs affected by the immune system mediators that are responsible for the clinical manifestations of disease.

### Historic View of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus Pathogenesis

Insights into the immunopathogenic mechanisms that account for development of autoimmunity in patients with SLE and the tissue damage that results in disease have developed over many decades. Progress has been informed by the scientific tools available at the time, along with the astute observations of clinicians and research scientists. Descriptions of the clinical manifestations of SLE have defined a multisystem disease that typically involves skin and joints, with renal, cardiac, and/or neurologic pathology often documented with histologic or imaging studies. Alterations of blood vessels in many organs were recognized as an important component of the disease process in early studies, with the pathognomonic "onion skin- ,> ning of splenic arterioles, cellular infiltration and damage to renal glomeruli, and vasculopathy in skin and brain expressed clinically by manifestations such as nephritis, livedo reticularis, and stroke. The lupus erythematosus (LE) cell, first described in 1948, suggested that engulfment of components of cell nuclei targeted by serum antibodies, a mechanism that remains an important concept in considerations of lupus pathogenesis, was active at sites of inflammation.

Characterization of antibodies specific for DNA and for nucleic acid-associated proteins (e.g., histones and components of the spliceosome) in the sera of patients with SLE directed the attention of researchers toward the immune system.4-6 Pathologic studies of kidneys from patients with lupus nephritis showing glomerular deposition of immunoglobulin and complement components, combined with the elution of anti-DNA autoantibodies from lupus kidneys, contributed to the concept that autoantibodies, particularly anti-DNA

antibodies, were pathogenic. Isolation from lupus sera of complexes of antibody with DNA, RNA, or DNAor RNA-binding proteins was an important factor in the classification of SLE as predominantly an immune complex-mediated autoimmune disease. Subsequent investigation identified virtually all immune cell components and many soluble immune system products as contributors to the immune system dysfunction that ultimately accounts for disease in SLE.

The development of the field of cellular immunology in the 1970s led to the implication of self-reactive T cells as important regulators of immune responses, as well as helpers for B cell differentiation to autoantibody-producing cells in the case of patients with SLE. Numerous deficiencies in T cell function were described, including altered production of typical T cell cytokines, such as interleukin (IL)-2, and studies of murine lupus models strongly supported the essential role that T cells play in lupus pathogenesis.7,

The discovery of Toll-like receptors (TLRs) in the 1990s, the recognition that those receptors recognize common determinants expressed by microbes, and the demonstration that TLRs mediate immune system activation together formed a major advance

that was one of several significant milestones that have advanced lupus research. Nucleic acids are the most relevant TLR ligands for amplification of immune system activation and autoimmunity in SLE. Additional sensors of DNA and RNA present in the cytosol have been defined in recent years. It is not yet clear to what extent the TLRs, the cytosolic receptors, or both contribute to initiation of innate immune system activation in SLE or augment immunologic activity that is initiated by other molecular pathways. The potential for both TLR and cytosolic sensors to signal new gene transcription and production of potentially pathogenic mediators, such as type I interferon (IFN), is well supported by abundant data.9,

In spite of these considerable gains in elucidating the pathogenesis of SLE, the environmental triggers that initiate autoimmunity in some individuals but not others are less well defined. Clinical observations have pointed to exposure to sunlight, microbial infection, and certain drugs as factors that can lead to initiation or exacerbation of lupus. Whether there is a common molecular change induced by these environmental triggers is not clear, but ultraviolet (UV) light—mediated DNA damage, modification of DNA methylation, and oxidation of mitochondrial DNA or other

cell components are among the processes that might render selfnucleic acid stimulatory to the immune system.

Consortia of investigators have cooperated to share biologic samples from large numbers of patients and control subjects to define the genetic variants with a statistical strong association with a diagnosis of SLE. These genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have helped identify lupus-associated genes that encode important components of molecular pathways that promote production of or response to type I IFN, alter the threshold for activation of lymphocytes, or generate immune stimuli. In addition, new concepts suggested by single-gene mutations that alter regulation of genome integrity and nucleic acid degradation, resulting in lupus-like clinical syndromes, point to the significance of endogenous nucleic acids as candidate disease triggers.13,

Together, these scientific advances have led to drug development programs, with several resulting in approval of therapeutic agents by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA). Belimumab, approved in 201 1, was the first new therapy to be approved for use in SLE since 1955. Others, including anifrolumab, FDA approved in 2021, also target mechanisms affecting lupus disease activity, with more in the pipeline. This chapter reviews recent studies that have illuminated the immunopathogenesis of SLE.

### Genetic Contributions to Systemic Lupus Erythematosus Pathogenesis

Current concepts in genetic studies of complex human diseases, including SLE, identify common variants with a small impact on risk of disease, as well as low-frequency mutations that can have a great impact on the risk for lupus or a lupus-like syndrome. Observations of the occurrence of several individuals with SLE within a family, along with a high frequency of concordance of SLE in identical twins, have pointed to a strong genetic contribution to SLE. Data from a national health registry in Taiwan suggest that the contribution of genetic heritability to occurrence of SLE is 44%, with identical twins having a relative risk (RR) of developing SLE of 316 and siblings a RR of 24 compared with unrelated individuals. More than 150 genetic variants, typically identified by statistical analysis of single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in association with a diagnosis of SLE, identify important molecular pathways implicated in lupus pathogenesis (Table 80.1). A study based on the Immunochip SNP platform identified more than 50 nonhuman leukocyte antigen (HLA) risk variants and indicated that some of the variants differ between Caucasians and African-Americans. Additional loci have been identified in studies that include Asian patients.16, The risk for development of SLE increases in a nonlinear manner with the number of risk loci, and genetic risk scores have been developed that are associated with early onset of disease, damage accrual, and increased mortality. 18,

While most lupus-associated variants are located in regulatory rather than coding regions of the genome, many are near genes encoding proteins implicated in immune system function, providing clues to important pathogenic mechanisms. In parallel to the requirements for immune system activation stimulated by foreign antigens, SLE-associated genes are involved in generation or impaired clearance of self-antigen, activation of the innate immune response, or activation of the adaptive immune response. Additional genetic variants may affect target organ vulnerability (Table 80.1). As is the case with many autoimmune diseases, alleles and specific SNPs in the major histocompatibility complex (MHC) have a large

impact on overall risk for development of SLE. A study of European and African ancestry patients supports a region of the MHC between DRB1 and DQA1 as having a strong association with SLE. The identified HLA risk haplotype is HLA-DRB1*03:01— HLA-DQA1*05:01—HLA-DQB1*02:01 (DR3) for European

ancestry and HLA-DRB1*15:03—HLA-DQA1*01:02—HLA- DQB1*06:02 (DR2) for those of African ancestry. The implications of the strong association of these alleles and loci with SLE are not yet understood. As preferential presentation of an antigenic peptide on MHC class II molecules encoded by risk alleles might be a reasonable mechanism to account for the observed associations, recent studies have suggested that a so-called superenhancer in the identified MHC region might augment expression of a number of genes, resulting in a more generalized level of immune system activation.2, The MHC 8.1 haplotype block associated with lupus susceptibility, encoding the alleles B8 and DR3, bears a short C4B gene and no C4A gene, whereas other nonrisk haplotypes carry either a longer C4B segment and/or one or more copies of C4A. In fact, the RR related to the C4A null allele, with C4 deficiency accounting for one of the most severe forms of clinical lupus, is twice that of either HLA-B8 or DR3, pointing to the significance of the C4 genes in disease risk and another significant region of the MHC beyond the class II region. 24-26

A large number of lupus-associated SNPs are in or near genes that encode proteins involved in induction of type I IFN or response to that family of cytokines.27-29 IFN regulatory factor 5 (IRF5) and IRF7 are cytoplasmic proteins that translocate to the nucleus after effective activation of the endosomal TLRs by DNA or RNA. IRF5 and IRF7 then act as transcription factors to initiate transcription of IFN-α and other pro-inflammatory mediators. TNFAIP3 encodes A20, a protein that regulates several proinflammatory cellular mechanisms, including signaling through endosomal TLRs and activation of nuclear factor κB (NF-kB). Genetic variants in IRF5, IRF7, TNFAIP3, TNIP1, and others can be mapped to molecular pathways responsible for induction or regulation of innate immune system activation or responsiveness to its products, particularly IFN-α. The risk alleles for IRF5 and IRF7 are associated with increased serum type I IFN activity in those patients who demonstrate autoantibodies targeting DNA or RNA-associated proteins, suggesting the interpretation that nucleic acidand autoantibody-containing immune complexes are important stimuli that act through endosomal TLRs such as TLR7 and TLR9, the TLRs that mediate cell signals through the IRF5 and IRF7 transcription factors.1, Notable support for the significance of the TLR7 pathway in lupus pathogenesis derives from a recent case report of clinical SLE in a patient with a gain-of-function TLR7 mutation.

Other lupus-associated gene variants contribute to adaptive immune system activation by altering thresholds for lymphocyte activation or efficiency of cell signaling in T and B lymphocytes. Variants in PTPN22 affect cell activation in both T and B lymphocytes, and BANK1, BLK, TNFAIP3, and others are expressed in B cells and are likely to modulate their activation either during B cell development, possibly affecting generation of the B cell repertoire, or in the setting of exposure to antigen. Table 80.1 identifies many lupus-associated variants that point to significant candidate mechanisms that may promote development of autoimmunity or inflammatory responses. Although additional functional genomics studies are required to fully understand the implications of these common variants conferring risk for disease development, the clues provided have supported the detailed investigation of the type I IFN pathway, as well as requirements for T and B cell activation and differentiation in SLE patients.

While coding mutations that alter the function of their gene products are rare, children diagnosed with SLE before the age of 10 may be most likely to bear single mutations leading to disease. Recent studies suggest that up to 10% of such children have

documented monogenic mutations.32, Monogenic deficiencies in complement pathway gene products, including C2, C4, and C1q, represent the highest risk for development of SLE and are thought to contribute to lupus pathogenesis by impairing clearance of cellular debris. Increased availability of nuclear debris can provide sufficient self-antigen for induction of self-reactive T cells or serve as an endogenous adjuvant for activation of the innate immune response. Deficiency of C1q, the recognition protein for the classical complement pathway, might contribute to disease on the basis of its important role in promoting clearance of apoptotic cell debris by mononuclear phagocytes.
