C1q plays an additional role in inhibition of IFN-α production by directing stimulatory immune complexes to monocytes rather than IFN-producing plasmacytoid dendritic cells (pDCs). Through this mechanism C1q deficiency can augment IFN-α and promote broad immune dysregulation. C-reactive protein (CRP), a member of the pentraxin family, also contributes to clearance of apoptotic debris. Polymorphisms in CRP have been associated with SLE and with decreased levels of CRP, but it remains unclear how much of the genetic contribution to basal CRP levels is caused by variations within the gene itself versus variations in other genes.

Characterization of patients with rare syndromes has demonstrated that mutations in genes that regulate the integrity or degradation of endogenous DNA or RNA can result in excess stimulatory nucleic acids, innate immune system activation, and excessive production of type I IFN. Two DNases, DNasel and DNasel-like 3, degrade DNA in neutrophil extra-cellular traps (NETs), and the absence of those enzymes is associated with vascular occlusions due to the accumulation of intravascular NET clots.36, Genetic variants in DNASE1 may contribute to SLE, and families with a frameshift mutation in the DNASE1L3 gene include patients with aggressive lupus and anti-DNA antibodies or hypocomplementemic urticarial vasculitis syndrome. Extra-cellular DNase1L3 degrades DNA associated with circulating microparticles. A recent report describes several individuals with biallelic mutations in DNASE2 and some features of SLE, including membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis, anti-DNA antibodies, and high levels of IFN-α. The gene product, DNase II, is typically responsible for digestion of DNA extruded from apoptotic cells and erythroid precursors.

Studies of families with a lupus-like disease, Aicardi-Goutières syndrome (AGS), have identified additional mutations implicated in control of nucleic acid integrity. AGS is characterized by skin lesions, autoantibodies, central nervous system (CNS) disease, and high levels of type I IFN, but unlike SLE it is typically diagnosed in young children. Mutations in the TREX1 gene, encoding a DNase that is required to degrade potentially stimulatory reverse-transcribed DNA, were identified in patients with AGS, and a functional connection between TREX1 and control of type I IFN production was demonstrated in a murine model in which TREX1 deficiency resulted in increased levels of IFN-β.41-43 An analysis of more than 8000 lupus patients found TREX1 mutations in approximately 0.5% of patients. In addition, a common variant in the TREX1 gene conferred an odds ratio for diagnosis of lupus of 1.73 compared with healthy controls. Mutations in SAMHD1, encoding an enzyme that removes phosphates from deoxyribonucleotide triphosphate (dNTPs), reducing available nucleotides for reverse transcription, have also been identified in AGS patients and are associated with triggering a DNA damage response and type I IFN production.

Mutations in members of the RNASEH2 family that remove ribonucleotides from RNADNA hybrids also activate an innate

immune response and are associated with a diagnosis of AGS. Parents of AGS patients who were heterozygous for the variant RNASEH2 demonstrated an intermediate autoimmune phenotype characterized by anti-nuclear antibodies and showed accumulation of ribonucleotides in their genomes, generation of DNA damage characterized by elevated cyclobutane pyrimidine dimer formation, and activation of the p53 pathway. ADAR, with mutations also reported in association with AGS, encodes an RNAspecific adenosine deaminase that converts adenosine to inosine in double-stranded RNAs (dsRNAs), particularly those enriched in Alu sequences, and typically functions as a suppressor of the cell intrinsic type I IFN response. Each of these gene products plays a role in control of the quality of endogenous nucleic acids, reduces the risk to the genome of production of endogenous virus-like transposons, and appears to be important for avoiding aberrant activation of an innate immune response characterized by IFN pathway activation. An additional form of AGS is associated with gain-of-function genetic variants of IFIH1, encoding the RNA sensor MDA5.48 In those patients recognition of Alu-rich dsRNAs by MDA5 drives amplified production of type I IFN. Similarly, gain-of-function mutations in DDX58, encoding RIG-I, have been reported and are associated with mitochondrial anti-viral signaling protein (MAVS) aggregation, activation of TBK1, and IFN production. Collectively, these syndromes have been termed interferonopathies and provide important clues to pathogenic mechanisms relevant to SLE.

A syndrome with some features consistent with the vasculopathy that characterizes many patients with SLE or systemic sclerosis develops in young children with mutations in TMEM173, encoding STING (stimulator of IFN genes), an essential component of the TLR-independent pathway of immune system activation that functions downstream of recognition of cytosolic DNA by cyclic GMPAMP synthase (cGAS). Skin rash, a livedo-like vascular pattern, distal extremity ulcerations, interstitial lung disease, markers of systemic inflammation, and low-titer autoantibodies are among the clinical characteristics of patients with STING gain-of-function genetic alterations. These patients show increased transcription of IFN-β and IFN-stimulated genes and constitutive phosphorylation of signal transducer and activator of transcription (STAT)1, a signaling component of the Janus kinase (JAK)STAT pathway that is activated downstream of IFNAR, the type I IFN receptor. In vitro studies that use a JAK inhibitor support targeting the effector arm of the IFN pathway in this syndrome. While a role for nucleic acid sensing in activation of innate immunity and induction of type I IFN is accepted as important in lupus pathogenesis, determining the contribution of the cGAS-STING pathway will require additional research.

Additional examples of monogenic lupus point to mutations in the DNMT3A gene, mediating DNA methylation, and Fas, mediating apoptosis. Mutations in protein kinase C delta (PRKCD) are reported, implementing apoptosis in the setting of DNA damage and as a component of the mitochondrial cell death pathway triggered by ionizing radiation and with a role in B cell tolerance. 13, Taken together, these recent demonstrations of the association of rare genetic variants encoding proteins that regulate access of nucleic acids to their sensors and efficiency of signaling of components of nucleic acidsensing pathways and mediators of cell death point to key mechanisms that can promote innate immune activation and lupus disease when sustained.

Another category of lupus-associated genetic variants defines determinants of target organ damage. Understanding of genetic determinants of target organ vulnerability to immune-mediated

or oxidative damage is less well developed than the role of genetic variants in altered immune system function in SLE. Recent studies have found an association between both lupus nephritis and IgA nephropathy and MTMR3, which encodes the phosphatase myotubularin-related protein 3, a regulator of autophagy. 54, HAS2, encoding hyaluronan synthase 2, and platelet-derived growth factor receptor alpha (PDGFRA), have also been associated with lupus nephritis. A link between alleles of APOL1, involved in cholesterol transport, and end-stage renal disease, is particularly notable in patients of African descent.57-59 Table 80.1 lists many of the genetic variants documented to have a statistical association with a diagnosis of SLE.

Subphenotype analysis amplifies the information that can be gleaned from patient and control genotyping. A study of anti— double-stranded DNA-positive (dsDNA+) and anti-dsDNA- SLE patients, along with healthy controls, identified HLA-DR3, STAT4, and ITGAM as significantly associated with the presence of anti-dsDNA antibodies. A case-only analysis additionally associated PTPN22, IRF5, and PTTG1 with anti-dsDNA antibodies. In contrast, a distinct group of lupus-associated genes showed comparable association between anti-dsDNA-positive and -negative patients, including FCGR2A, OX40L, IL10, PXK, UHRF1BP1, PRDM1, BLK, and IRAK1. Although it is possible that some of these variants are associated with distinct autoantibody specificities, it is more likely that they represent risks for general immune system activation, inflammation, or tissue damage. GWAS-derived genetic risk scores have been used to identify those patients with increased risk for severe disease or particular manifestations, such as lupus nephritis, and analysis of SNPs in patients of distinct ancestry have identified different molecular pathways that dominate in relation to those ancestries18, The recent large transancestral study using the Immunochip platform demonstrated a pattern of amplified risk of SLE as the number of risk variants increased, suggesting to the authors a cumulative hit hypothesis for disease susceptibility. Assaying numbers of risk variants from among a selected group of documented lupus-associated SNPs could be a promising approach to disease prediction. It should be noted that the SLE cohorts studied in GWAS derive predominantly from those of European ancestry. The data provided from subjects of African and Hispanic-Amerindian descent suggest both overlapping and unique risk variants, and extension of the data from those ancestral groups will likely provide important insights into the special risks that result in particularly severe disease in those groups.

### Female Predominance of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus

A discussion of genetic contributions to SLE pathogenesis should address the dramatic 9:1 female predominance of the disease. Of all characteristic clinical features of lupus, it is the extreme sex skewing that remains least understood. Hormonal contributions to immune system activation are likely to represent a component of the female predominance of the disease; estrogen can modulate lymphocyte and pDC activation, and prolactin is expressed at increased levels in lupus serum.64, In addition to the role of hormones, current concepts prioritize X chromosome—encoded genes and the potential for alterations in X chromosome inactivation in the female skewing of SLE. It is intriguing that Klinefelter's syndrome, characterized by a 47,XXY genotype, is increased 14-fold among men with SLE compared with men without SLE. These

data suggest an X chromosome gene dose effect as an important contributor to SLE pathogenesis. Identifying the X chromosome as a possible risk factor for SLE provides a basis for new hypotheses regarding disease susceptibility. While the nature of that risk remains undefined, the TLR7 gene may be an important contributor to the augmented risk for SLE in females.67, Murine studies support the impact of duplications of portions of the X chromosome that encode the TLR7 gene in activation of the innate immune system, production of type I IFN, and generation of autoimmunity, and a recent report of a gain-of-function variant of TLR7 in a young girl with SLE further supports the role of that gene and its protein product.31, Of note, data from study of a humanized mouse model support roles for both estrogen and X chromosome dosage in augmented pDC production of type I IFN in response to TLR7 ligation. The TLR7 gene is located on a region of the X chromosome in which escape from X chromosome inactivation has been documented, and a study using single-cell analysis indicates that biallelic expression of TLR7 variably occurs in B cells from healthy women and is associated with increased expression of TLR7 protein. In addition to TLR7, TASL and IRAK1, both encoding components of the TLR7 signaling pathway, are also X chromosome genes that may promote development of SLE in females.

A potential pathogenic role for the distinct events that occur in the ovary compared with those in the testes also deserves further study. The onset of SLE typically occurs in the childbearing years, after menarche and before menopause. A striking positive association between early menarche and SLE has been observed and might be consistent with molecular and cellular events related to ovulation. In addition, ovarian reserve is diminished in women with lupus irrespective of medical therapy. Although not yet fully understood, the carefully orchestrated demethylation and remethylation of DNA that occur during oocyte maturation, along with the expression of genomic retroelements, can mediate oocyte atresia and may provide a source of stimulatory nucleic acids that could drive immune activation.72, The challenge in pursuing such concepts is the obvious limitation on access to ovarian tissue for study, although murine models could be helpful.

### Environmental Triggers s of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus

The noted study from Taiwan indicates that heritability accounts for approximately 44% of the risk of developing SLE, supporting a strong genetic contribution but also allowing for both environmental factors and stochastic events (i.e., chance) in development of SLE in an individual. Although some environmental triggers of disease have been identified on the basis of clinical observation and epidemiologic studies, in general there is incomplete understanding of the range of factors that can induce disease and the mechanisms by which they do so.11, Socioeconomic factors have been demonstrated to contribute to poor outcomes in lupus patients.75-77 The distinct contributions of low socioeconomic status versus genetic factors that affect disease severity in certain ethnic groups are difficult to dissect, although a recent study suggests that ancestry-related genetic factors may be most important in determining lupus-related mortality.

Clinical manifestations that are often present at the time of diagnosis, including fatigue and arthralgias, have suggested that a virus might initiate the disease. In fact, epidemiologic studies demonstrating higher prevalence of antibodies specific for EpsteinBarr

virus (EBV) antigen in patients with SLE compared with the general population, as well as higher frequency of anti-EBV antibodies in a military cohort before diagnosis of lupus, support a possible role for that virus in disease pathogenesis. 79, In addition, SLE patients demonstrate increased EBV DNA in their blood.

Several potential mechanisms might account for a pathogenic role for EBV in SLE, including production of EBV-encoded RNAs that induce type I IFN, risk allele-specific binding of EBNA2 to genomic regulatory regions, utilization of B cell signaling pathways to promote B cell activation and differentiation, and generation of autoantibodies reactive with DNAor RNAbinding proteins through a molecular mimicry mechanism. 82, EBV-encoded small RNAs (EBERs) are expressed in cells latently infected with EBV. EBERs induce expression of type I IFN after binding to the dsRNA-dependent protein kinase (PKR) and activating signaling through a TLR-independent pathway. EBNA2, encoded in the EBV genome, can bind to genomic loci that have been statistically associated with a diagnosis of SLE in a risk allelespecific manner, thus regulating the expression of relevant genes that can alter immune system function.82, This phenomenon was also observed in relation to risk loci associated with other autoimmune diseases, such as multiple sclerosis and rheumatoid arthritis. A related mechanism implicates EBV transformation of B cells in activating the long terminal repeats of endogenous retroviruses, unleashing their capacity to serve as enhancers and promoters. Latent membrane protein 1, encoded by EBV, can act as a mimic of cluster of differentiation (CD)40 and promote B cell dysfunction and autoimmunity in lupus-susceptible mice. A recent study demonstrates that antibodies specific for the virus-encoded EBNA-1 protein can also react with dsDNA. The molecular basis of this apparent cross-reactivity is not known, although DNA can associate with EBNA-1 and might account for the described antibody reactivity. T cell responses specific for EBV have been studied in patients with lupus and were found to be deficient, perhaps contributing to the increased numbers of EBV-infected mononuclear cells and the increased copy number of EBV DNA found in SLE patients.

Although EBV may or may not be an important etiologic agent in SLE, recent studies of murine models of persistent infection with lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus provide a useful system for study of pathogenic mechanisms that appear highly relevant to the immunopathogenesis of SLE. Sustained production of type I IFN and a shift from expansion of T effector cells to expansion of T follicular helper cells accompanies the organ inflammation and damage that characterize those models of persistent virus infection. In mice with prolonged production of IFN, blockade of the type I IFN receptor abrogates tissue damage. Data from comparisons of immune system function in patients with HIV-1 infection to macaques infected with the related but less lethal simian version of the virus further support a view of chronic production of type I IFN as an important mechanism that promotes widespread inflammation similar to that seen in patients with lupus. These models of chronic viral infection provide a guide for further study of key mechanisms that sustain disease in patients with lupus.

There is also growing interest in a potential contribution of endogenous bacteria in initiating or exacerbating autoimmunity and SLE. Proposed roles for the microbiome in generating autoimmunity and inflammation relevant to SLE include T cell and antibody cross-reactivity/molecular mimicry between commensal bacteria expressing Ro-related epitopes and the human Ro antigen. Anti- Ro antibodies are characteristic of SLE although not specific for that disease. In a provocative study, translocation of commensal gut

bacteria to the liver in lupus-susceptible mice induced anti-DNA antibodies, an IFN signature, and tissue inflammation. Documentation of DNA specific for the implicated microbe, Enterococcus gallinarum, in liver samples from some patients with SLE or autoimmune hepatitis provides some support for the potential clinical relevance of the intriguing mouse findings. A study of ribosomal RNA sequences of bacteria present in fecal specimens from SLE patients demonstrated enrichment of Ruminococcus gnavus and an association of that microbe with disease activity and anti-DNA antibodies. Impaired mucosal barrier integrity may also contribute to systemic circulation of gut bacteria or their products.

Environmental toxins are of interest, yet their potential role in lupus pathogenesis has not been comprehensively explored. Data support current smoking as a risk factor for SLE, with a dose response relating pack-years of smoking to risk, and the relationship between smoking and anti-dsDNA+ SLE is particularly strong. 70,74,96 6 As is currently proposed with regard to pathogenesis of rheumatoid arthritis, smoking might provide an inflammatory stimulus to epithelial or mononuclear cells in the lungs, promoting protein modification or nonspecific inflammation. In contrast to cigarette smoking, moderate alcohol consumption is a negative risk factor for SLE. Data from the Nurses' Health Study identified early menarche (age 10 or younger), use of post-menopausal hormones, and use of oral contraceptives as associated with a significant RR of incident SLE (RR, 2.1, 1.9, and 1.5, respectively),70,97 although placebo-controlled trials showed that oral contraceptives did not increase the rate of lupus flare, and hormone replacement therapy in post-menopausal women did not increase the rate of severe flare over 12 months and only modestly increased risk of a mild or moderate disease flare.98, Data support residential pesticides as a contributor to SLE in African-American women, ,100and silica is also supported as a pathogenic factor in SLE on the basis of its known capacity to serve as an adjuvant. Data from analysis of the Black Women's Health Study additionally implicate obesity during teenage years with later diagnosis of SLE, 102 and interesting data from the study of relatives of lupus patients identified less than 7 hours/night of sleep as associated with transition to SLE.

Two well-described triggers of lupus, UV light and certain drugs, are likely to promote lupus pathogenesis through their effects on DNA. UV light induces DNA breaks that might alter gene expression or lead to apoptotic or necrotic cell death. Even in the absence of cell death, DNA breaks or prolonged maintenance of DNA-protein cross-links might provide an adjuvant or antigenic stimulus to the immune system. In that regard, recent data show UV-induced generation of cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers and induction of IFN-stimulated genes in cells from individuals heterozygous for mutations in RNASEH2 genes encoding enzymes that remove ribonucleotides from genomic DNA.46, Altered DNA methylation has been proposed as a likely mechanism of drug-induced lupus, as can be observed in the setting of treatment with procainamide or hydralazine. In the case of hydralazine, the drug inhibits extra-cellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK) pathway signaling, resulting in decreased expression of DNA methyltransferase (DNMT) 1 and DNMT3a, two enzymes that mediate DNA methylation. Modification of ERK signaling can be mediated by the effects of oxidizing agents on protein kinase C delta, an upstream regulator of ERK. Altered DNA methylation and other epigenetic modifications can alter gene expression or prime cells for increased reactivity to subsequent stimuli.107-109 Decreased DNA methylation can also generate nucleic acids enriched in endogenous retroelements with the potential to activate nucleic acid sensors, promoting immune

110 Table 80.2 lists candidate environmental system activation. triggers of SLE or lupus flare.

### Innate Immune System n Activation in Systemic Lupus Erythematosus

Arguably the most significant recent advance that has improved understanding of the pathogenesis of SLE and other autoimmune and inflammatory diseases is the discovery of the TLRs and, more generally, the elucidation of the central role of innate immune

system activation in regulation of the adaptive immune response, inflammation, and tissue repair. The TLRs are composed of an ectodomain with leucine-rich repeats, a transmembrane domain, and a cytoplasmic domain that associates with adaptor molecules that initiate signaling, resulting in activation of members of the IFN-regulatory factor family, NF-kB, and members of the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) family. TLR-independent innate immune activation can be initiated by intracytoplasmic RNA sensors, such as RIG-I and MDA5, that signal through a mitochondrial adaptor protein, MAVS, to activate TBK1.50 DNA sensors include IFI16, DAI, and the nucleotidyltransferase cGAS,

which generates a 2',5'-linked cyclic dinucleotide, cGAMP, that binds the endoplasmic reticulum protein STING, also resulting in activation of TBK1.112 Recognition of both RNA and DNA leads to activation of IRF3, as well as NF-kB, which serve as transcription factors that generate IFN-β and other pro-inflammatory mediators. Although these nucleic acid—sensing pathways likely evolved to detect infectious microbes, they can also be triggered by endogenous nucleic acids, of great relevance as a mechanism of induction of type I IFN and for the pathogenesis of SLE. While there is strong support for nucleic acid-containing immune complexes as relevant triggers for endosomal TLRs, the nature of triggers of TLR-independent pathways mediated by cytosolic sensors is not yet defined. Candidates include nucleic acids derived from endogenous retroelements such as long interspersed nuclear element 1 (LINE1) and oxidized mitochondrial DNA.114-116 Investigation of innate immune system activation by nucleic acids complements the demonstration of broad expression of type I IFN-inducible genes in peripheral blood cells of lupus patients, referred to as the IFN signature. 117-119 Fig. 80.2 depicts many of the key components of the TLR-dependent and TLR-independent immune system pathways that are important in activation and control of lupus immune responses.

The endosomal TLRs, particularly TLR7, reactive with singlestranded RNA, and TLR9, reactive with unmethylated cytosinephosphate-guanine (CpG)-rich DNA, have been associated with lupus pathogenesis on the basis of in vitro studies that demonstrate activation of those TLRs by immune complexes that gain access to their intracytoplasmic compartment with the help of Fc receptors that bind the Fc fragment of immunoglobulin in the complex. b.120, Clinical data demonstrating association of autoantibodies with specificity for RNA-binding proteins (such as Ro, La, Sm, and ribonucleoprotein [RNP]) with high expression of IFN-induced genes in patient peripheral blood cells point to a significant role for RNA-containing immune complexes in innate immune activation and IFN production.122, Lupus mice made deficient in one or another TLR have supported the role of TLR7 in generating type I IFN, autoantibodies specific for RNA-binding proteins, and disease. TLR9 activation can also generate IFN- α, but the findings from TLR9-deficient MRL/lpr (Fas-deficient) mice have demonstrated more severe disease, suggesting that the activation of TLR9 might be protective. In addition to demonstrating the important role of the endosomal TLRs in lupus pathogenesis, the data link TLR pathway activation with production of particular autoantibody specificities. These significant advances in characterization of the role of TLRs, type I IFN, and the innate immune response in lupus disease have led to the development and approval of anifrolumab, a monoclonal antibody specific for the type I IFN receptor, and have suggested additional therapeutic targets that are currently under development (Fig. 80.3).126,

Elucidation of the mechanisms of induction of type I IFN, with pDCs as the major producers, has promoted studies that identified roles for additional cell types in this pathway. Macrophages, particularly those with a M1 pro-inflammatory profile, show particularly strong expression of type I IFN-stimulated genes, and a recent analysis describes those cells as associated with lupus disease activity and lupus flares. Platelets, largely ignored in studies of SLE pathogenesis, promoted IFN production by pDCs through signals mediated by CD40 ligand (CD154) on activated platelets and CD40 on the pDCs. Keratinocytes in skin produce IFN- κ that can promote expression of IFN-stimulated gene products and contribute to recruitment of inflammatory cells, potentially important for the pathogenesis of cutaneous lupus. Access to

bone marrow from patients with SLE has supported the capacity of cells at that site to produce IFN-β,131 and the studies of patients with STING-associated vasculopathy with onset in infancy (SAVI), associated with gain-of-function mutations in TMEM173, encoding STING, suggest that epithelial cells and macrophages might be additional producers of type I IFN.

Studies from several groups have investigated the contribution of neutrophils and their products, including NETs, to IFN pathway activation and have documented low-density granulocytes in the circulation of lupus patients. NETs derive from a discrete cellular process, termed NETosis, in which aggregates of nuclear or mitochondria-derived DNA and its associated histones, HMGB1, LL37, elastase, and myeloperoxidase, are systematically extruded into the extra-cellular environment. Generation of NETs can be induced by interaction of neutrophils with vascular endothelial cells, activated platelets, or various cytokines. Data also implicate nucleosomes and RNA-containing immune complexes in the induction of NETosis.133, NETs have the capacity to induce production of type I IFN by pDCs, serve as a source of relevant self-antigens for presentation to T lymphocytes, and mediate vascular damage and thrombosis.

In addition to their strong expression of type I IFN-induced transcripts, monocytes are gaining attention as critical cells in the pathogenesis of lupus nephritis. Patrolling monocytes activated through endosomal TLRs travel to the kidneys and contribute to inflammation. Monocytes are also active producers of cytokines and other soluble mediators that promote B and T cell differentiation and support inflammatory responses, including B-lymphocyte stimulator (BLyS), IL-12, and TNF.

As described earlier, the elucidation of a significant role for the nucleic acidsensing TLRs in recent years has drawn attention to the important role of autoantigens in driving disease in lupus. The contribution of apoptotic debris, either through increased apoptosis and/or impaired clearance of apoptotic cells and assumed for a number of years to be at least one likely mechanism that drives immune system activation, focuses attention on nucleic acids and their associated proteins. Apoptotic blebs are enriched in the typical targets of autoantibodies, such as Ro and Sm. So-called microparticles, small membrane-enclosed particles released by activated and dying cells, are bound by some autoantibodies in lupus plasma. Increased generation of nuclear or mitochondrial material, perhaps modified by oxidative stress, together with impaired clearance may be an important mechanism of lupus immunopathogenesis. The role of C1q and complement components in the clearance of apoptotic debris has been suggested as an explanation for the strong association of C1q, C2, and C4 deficiencies with SLE.

### Adaptive Immune System Alterations in Systemic Lupus Erythematosus

T cell function has been extensively studied in SLE patients, and deficiencies or alterations in signaling and metabolic pathways, production of cytokines, cell proliferation, and regulatory functions have been documented. CD4+ T cells are viewed as a requirement for development of lupus on the basis of their essential role in providing helper signals and cytokines that drive differentiation of B cells to autoantibody-producing cells. The activation status and signaling mechanisms of lupus T cells are distinct from those of T cells from healthy individuals, with mTOR activation and altered mitochondrial oxidative pathways and hyperpolarization characteristic. T cells readily express CD40 ligand (CD154) after activation and maintain expression of that important costimulatory molecule longer than control T cells, leading to augmented help for activation and differentiation of B cells exposed to those T cells. Another long-standing observation is that lupus T cells produce less IL-2 than control T cells, perhaps one factor that contributes to impaired generation of IL-2dependent T regulatory cells (Tregs). The molecular basis of the altered T cell activation in lupus patients is complex, and one observation is substitution of the T cell receptor zeta chain with the common gamma chain that is a component of the Fc receptor signaling machinery.

Augmented calcium responses following T cell receptor ligation have been observed, and hyperpolarization of mitochondria in T cells is associated with T cell activation.

Studies of lupus T cells show epigenetic alterations to the lupus genome that affect autoimmunity. Lupus T cells studied ex vivo show hypomethylation of regulatory regions, particularly of type I IFN-stimulated genes, and a study of genome methylation in identical twins discordant for lupus demonstrated relatively less methylation of cells in the twin with active lupus. 109, Epigenetic modifications to the lupus genome are not necessarily accompanied by gene transcription but can represent a genome that is

CC 'primed" or "trained" and ready to respond to subsequent stimuli with exaggerated or sustained gene expression.

Generalized lymphopenia is typical of SLE, but expansions of specific T cell populations have been described. The T follicular helper population, characterized by expression of ICOS, CXCR5, and Bcl-6 and by production of IL-21, mediates important signals that promote differentiation of autoantigen-specific B cells. In recent studies a related T cell subset termed T peripheral helper cells (Tph), expressing high levels of PD-1, was identified early in the course of SLE and is active in driving B cell differentia- .145, The elevated levels of type I IFN in most SLE patients tion. are likely to contribute to the differentiation of Tph cells. Type I IFN also promotes altered mitochondrial function in an expanded population of CD8+ T cells. In addition, analysis of T cell populations in SLE patients participating in a therapeutic trial of rapamycin, an inhibitor of the serine/threonine kinase mTOR, identified relative depletion of CD8+ effector-memory T cells as a predictor of response, with those cells increasing over the course of treatment.

The regulation and function of Tregs, which have the capacity to suppress immune responses, and Th17 cells, which promote inflammation by production of IL-17, have been studied in recent years, although most data derive from murine models. Some studies of lupus patients do show a relative depletion of Tregs and increased Th17 cells and IL-17.151 The functional impact of those alterations in human lupus is still not clear, but it is presumed that augmenting Treg numbers and/or function could be beneficial in controlling clinical disease. Data are beginning to emerge from studies of low-dose IL-2, an approach that may augment Tregs and reduce disease activity. While secretion of IL-2 by lupus T cells is impaired, those cells produce cytokines that promote macrophage activation, such as IFN-gamma, and those that contribute to B cell differentiation, including IL-21.153,

Production of autoantibodies specific for nucleic acids or nucleic acidbinding proteins is a fundamental feature of lupus pathogenesis, although the efficient presentation of specific selfantigens to T cells and production of pro-inflammatory cytokines are additional functions of B cells that contribute to disease. Progress in investigation of the mechanisms that regulate activation and differentiation of autoantibody-producing cells has identified receptors, signaling pathways, and cytokines that drive those cells. BLyS produced by myeloid cells, IL-10, and IL-21 are among the candidate therapeutic targets that can modify the B cell differentiation program, as demonstrated by successful clinical studies of BLyS blockade by belimumab. In addition, efforts are underway to determine whether alterations in B cell tolerance mechanisms might contribute to autoimmunity in SLE.

The baseline activation status of lupus B cells, as well as their response to antigen stimulation, is altered compared with B cells from healthy individuals, with lupus-associated genetic variants in several kinases, phosphatases, and adaptor molecules such as BLK, BANK, and PTPN22 potential contributors to altered B cell function. Studies of the risk variant of PTPN22 in B cells from healthy participants point to the influence of that lupusassociated variant on impaired counterselection of self-reactive B cells. LYN deficiency in mice is associated with a lupus-like phenotype, and similar deficiencies in the LYN kinase have been described in lupus B cells. The gene encoding the inhibitory Fc receptor, FCGR2B, is polymorphic, and several variants have been associated with SLE. SLE B cells show decreased expression of this FcR, particularly on marginal zone B cells, supporting B cell hyperactivation. While studies are limited, there are some

data to support altered B cell tolerance mechanisms in lupus bone marrow, with production of type I IFN in neutrophils or mesenchymal stem cells impairing B cell tolerance. 131,

Current investigations of antibody-producing cells are defining several categories of B lineage cells that contribute to autoimmunity and disease. A recently described B cell population, the so-called age-associated B cells (ABCs), is dependent on the transcription factors T-bet and IRF5 and is enriched in patients with lupus and other autoimmune diseases. 160, Signaling through TLR7 is important for differentiation of those cells, extending the significant role of that TLR in lupus pathogenesis from induction of type I IFN in pDCs to an association with B cell function and autoimmunity, and IL-21 is also required. ABCs can differentiate into plasmablasts, producing anti-dsDNA autoantibodies, or plasma cells, more likely the producers of autoantibodies specific for RNA-binding proteins. Long-lived plasma cells that are maintained by chemokines and stromal cell products in protective niches in the bone marrow are proposed as sources of those lupus autoantibodies, such as anti-Smith (Sm) and anti-Ro that are chronically maintained at fairly constant levels. Those antibodies have been relatively refractory to modulation by immunosuppressive or B cell depletion therapy, although current trials of CD19-targeted chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells may be more successful164, In contrast, circulating pre-plasma cells or plasmablasts are sources of anti-dsDNA antibodies that fluctuate in some patients in association with variations in disease activity and are more amenable to anti—B cell therapy, such as belimumab, targeting BLyS.

The T and B cell alterations that have been described in studies of lupus immune function reflect multiple genetic variations that play out in altering the threshold for cell activation and efficiency of cell signaling. They are also the result of interactions among those lymphocytes, along with antigen-presenting cells and their products that, with time, amplify the overall level of immune activation. Increased production of type I IFN and presence of antinuclear antibodies in healthy family members of lupus patients may reflect the consequences of genetic variations that are among the factors that predispose to SLE. When the baseline setpoint of immune system activity encounters environmental triggers, conditions are in place to generate the characteristic T and B cell autoimmunity that is required for tissue damage and disease. The triggers, potentially viral, that generate the particular features of autoimmunity specific to SLE, the targeting of autoantibodies to nucleic acids, and their associated proteins are as yet not well defined.

### Autoantibodies in Systemic Lupus Erythematosus

Autoantibodies are traditionally viewed as essential mediators of pathology in SLE, particularly when they are in the form of immune complexes. Virtually all lupus patients demonstrate a positive anti-nuclear antibody test, and the majority of patients have one or more of the characteristic autoantibody specificities that have been associated with lupus (Table 80.3) (see also Chapter 55). Among those, anti-dsDNA and anti-Sm are most specific for SLE. Interestingly, those specificities have been linked functionally in murine studies that demonstrate that dsDNA can bind to a peptide comprising amino acids 83 to 119 of the SmD1 protein, and T cells specific for that peptide provide help for production of anti-dsDNA antibody.167, Microbial mimics of lupus-associated autoantigens have also been described, suggesting that the

microbiome might provide endogenous triggers of autoantibody specificities. Anti-Ro, anti-La, and anti-RNP antibodies are characteristic of SLE but are also seen in other systemic autoimmune diseases. Lupus autoantibodies can be categorized in relation to their targets, including DNA and DNA-binding proteins, typically aggregated in nucleosomes that contain histones; RNA and RNA-associated proteins, typically aggregated in cytoplasmic or nuclear RNP particles; phospholipids exposed in plasma membranes and associated proteins such as β2-glycoprotein I; and cell membrane proteins, typically those expressed in blood cells. Some of these self-antigens typically targeted by lupus autoantibodies are most likely accessed by antigen-presenting cells in the form of cell membrane—enclosed blebs derived from apoptotic cells or microparticles, small aggregates of cellular material derived from cells and generated after flipping of phosphatidylserine to the outer aspect of the cell membrane in the setting of cell activation or apoptosis. Although some patients who present with a clinical picture characteristic of SLE do not have significant titers of those autoantibodies, it is likely that those patients have undefined autoimmunity targeted at unspecified antigens.

It is not possible to identify the earliest step in the generation of pathogenic autoantibodies with certainty, and in fact it is probable that the generation of autoimmunity can begin in any number of ways. Presentation of self-antigen by an excessively activated antigen-presenting cell, stochastic activation of low-avidity selfreactive T cells that are present in healthy individuals but have the potential to expand and drive differentiation of B cells with broad specificity for self-antigens, or direct activation of self-reactive B cells in the presence of activating TLR ligands, such as those provided by demethylated CpG-rich DNA from bacteria or viruses or self-derived nuclear debris, might all be starting points for development of pathogenic autoimmunity. As noted earlier, microbial epitopes present on endogenous bacteria or virus-encoded proteins that associate with host particles might also represent an initiating point for generation of autoimmunity. The process might begin with production of type I IFN by a virus-infected cell or a cell with impaired degradation of intra-cellular nucleic acids, altering the threshold for activation of the immune system by subsequent exposures to self-antigens. Oxidative or UV-mediated DNA damage by environmental stressors might synergize with altered maintenance of genome integrity to jump start immune

activation. Less important than the precise starting point is the observation that autoimmunity develops and builds with time. The presence of autoantibodies can be observed more than 5 years before clinical manifestations of disease appear, and the scope of autoantibody specificities expands with time. Anti-Ro antibodies typically present earliest, anti-dsDNA antibodies appear several years later, and anti-Sm, the antibody specificity most specific for a diagnosis of SLE, appears approximately at the time of clinical diagnosis. This pattern, along with studies from murine models that demonstrated determinant spreading of autoantibody specificities not only to distinct proteins within a nucleic acid-protein particle but also to other self-antigen targets, provides clues to lupus pathogenesis that are not yet understood but hold promise for future breakthroughs in elucidating important pathogenic mechanisms.

A shift from a predominant polyclonal immunoglobulin (Ig) M picture toward polyclonal IgG, driven by T cell help and cytokines, occurs with time in most patients with lupus and with development of tissue pathology and damage. In fact, some IgM antibodies that have self-reactivity are viewed as protective, with the switch from IgM to IgG or IgA representing an important point of altered immune regulation that contributes to the immunopathogenesis of SLE.

In addition to immunoglobulin class, with class-switched antibodies better able to access extravascular spaces compared with IgM antibodies, the amino acid sequence and charge of the antigen-binding site can influence pathogenicity. Arginines in the CDR3 region of anti-dsDNA antibodies are characteristic and influence binding to their DNA target. Molecular mimicry is a concept that has been applied to reactivity of antibodies specific for a microbial protein that also react with self-antigens, but the concept can also be applied to those antibodies that unexpectedly bind to two distinct self-antigens. For example, some anti-dsDNA antibodies were found to bind to a peptide that is a feature of glutamate receptors on CNS neurons. Beyond features of Ig class and antigen-binding site that influence access to tissue and affinity of binding, glycosylation and complement-fixing capacity are important determinants of an antibody's capacity to bind to Fc receptors and promote complement activation, resulting in target cell death or inflammation.

The role of SLE autoantibodies in the pathogenesis of the disease has traditionally focused on the deposition of immune complexes in skin, renal glomerulus, and other sites of tissue injury, along with a potential contribution of direct targeting of antibodies to local or "planted" antigens. With the recognition that nucleic acid-containing immune complexes can directly induce cell signaling and new gene transcription after accessing endosomal TLRs, an additional important pathogenic role for autoantibodies as immune modulators has been defined.

Particular lupus autoantibody specificities have been associated with specific clinical manifestations of disease. Perhaps the bestdeveloped characterization of the mechanisms by which an autoantibody mediates disease is the role of maternal-derived anti-Ro antibody in neonatal lupus syndrome. After transplacental transfer of anti-Ro antibody, RNA-containing immune complexes are thought to form, activating the production of cytokines that contribute to fibrosis of the cardiac conduction system. . This scenario, similar to that which mediates production of type I IFN by pDCs, identifies nucleic acid—autoantibody immune complexes as regulators of cytokines that mediate tissue damage. Anti-Ro and anti-La antibodies, although common to several autoimmune diseases, are also characteristic in association with sicca symptoms,

subacute cutaneous lupus, and, as noted, in neonatal lupus. Anti- RNP antibodies are seen in both SLE and mixed connective tissue disease.

Antiphospholipid antibodies, with lupus anti-coagulant the most informative antibody profile, contribute to placental damage and vascular thrombosis, as well as thrombocytopenia in the antiphospholipid syndrome and in some patients with lupus. 176 Studies in a murine model and supported by data from patients indicate that tissue damage and thrombosis depend on inflammation promoted by activation of the complement system by the antiphospholipid antibodies. Similar mechanisms might be relevant in forms of lupus renal disease characterized by microangiopathy.

### Mechanisms of Target t Organ Damage

Clinical disease is ultimately a reflection of tissue damage mediated by the cells and soluble products of the immune system, along with an exaggerated or aberrant tissue repair response. The classic view of the mechanisms that result in tissue damage involves activation of the complement system by immune complexes deposited in tissue, as well as release of products of phagocytes, including enzymes released from neutrophil granules and reactive oxygen intermediates from macrophages. Recent studies in mouse and human systems involving extensive analysis of renal infiltrating cells and their transcriptomes at various points in the disease process have identified monocyte populations that mediate inflammation and contribute to sclerosis and organ dysfunction. Infiltrating T and B cells present in the kidney interstitium can also contribute to renal damage. Data from both murine lupus models and kidney tissue from patients with lupus nephritis demonstrate the cell-related transcriptomes associated with transition from acute to chronic nephritis, with a robust renal tubule transcriptome associated with resistance to development of chronic disease. .

The role of the vasculature as a significant target organ contributing to disease in lupus involves altered structure and function of both venous and arterial vessels. Periarteriolar concentric onion skinning is seen in the spleen, microangiopathy and associated microthrombi are observed in some organs, and endothelial dysfunction is associated with premature atherosclerosis in lupus patients. Recent studies have focused on the potential role of type I IFN on endothelial cells and endothelial cell progenitor cells and have postulated that increased production of IFN is at least one contributor to impaired vascular repair and cardiovascular disease in SLE. A contribution of type I IFN to vascular injury supplements the previously described role of complement activation products C3a and C5a and expression of endothelial cell surface adhesion molecules E-selectin, vascular cell adhesion molecule 1, and intercellular adhesion molecule 1 in lupus flares. A role for granulocytes and pro-inflammatory lipids has also been proposed. 181, Podocytes are specialized epithelial cells and components of the renal glomerulus that, when damaged, contribute to the proteinuria characteristic of lupus nephritis. Current studies are investigating the signaling pathways and podocyte products that might represent therapeutic targets for patients with lupus nephritis. Mechanisms of CNS lupus have extended the concept that autoantibodies with dual specificity for DNA and the NMDA receptor contribute to excitotoxic cell death to consider the contribution of cytokines to neuronal damage and clinical manifestations of CNS damage.

### Conclusion

Gains in understanding the mechanisms of lupus pathogenesis have established the knowledge base that will underlie future advances in development of targeted therapies to achieve improved patient outcomes. As technologies evolve, they will be used by investigators to gain deeper insights into lupus disease mechanisms and to identify additional therapeutic targets. Single-cell transcriptome and immune repertoire analysis, use of spatial transcriptomics to characterize cell distribution within involved tissues, and application of long-read sequencing for characterization of genomic regions harboring lupus-associated genetic variants can facilitate our understanding of mechanistic and effector contributions to disease. The recognition of a central role for innate immune system activation, including the role of type I IFN, in lupus pathogenesis is a major advance. Rapid progress in characterizing the genetic variants that are associated with a diagnosis of lupus has provided strong evidence that alterations in molecular pathways that regulate genome integrity, nucleic acid degradation, TLR-dependent and -independent innate immune signaling, and lymphocyte activation thresholds and signaling efficiency ar e im portant me chanisms th at de termine disease susceptibility. The products of the immune system, including autoantibodies and their immune complexes, cytokines, and complement components, along with pro-inflammatory mediators and reactive oxygen products released from neutrophils and macrophages, remain key mediators of tissue damage. However, an additional pathogenic role for nucleic acid-containing immune complexes as immune modulators through their important capacity to access and activate endosomal TLRs and insights into regulation of endogenous cytoplasmic nucleic acids are important concepts that can guide future therapeutic approaches. Defining and then targeting the components of the innate immune system involved in activation of the TLR and TLR-independent pathways, along with modulation of pathogenic T cell help for B cell differentiation to autoantibody-producing cells, is a rational therapeutic strategy given our current understanding of pathogenic mechanisms. It seems likely that no one therapeutic approach will be sufficient to control this disease, but rather therapies that target components of both innate and adaptive immune systems may be required to achieve improved patient outcomes. In the end, prevention of disease is an important goal. Efforts to apply the many lessons learned relevant to pathogenic mechanisms of SLE to assessment of patients at risk for disease development might result in design of preventive strategies.

# Clinical Features of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus

### KEY POINTS

Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a multisystem autoimmune disease that is characterized by a relapsing-remitting course and a highly variable prognosis. SLE is characterized by the production of a broad array of autoantibodies. Anti-nuclear antibodies have the greatest sensitivity for the diagnosis, and anti—double-stranded DNA and anti-Smith antibodies have the greatest specificity. Women of childbearing age and African ancestry, Asian, and Hispanic populations have the highest incidence and prevalence of disease. Constitutional symptoms, rash, mucosal ulcers, inflammatory polyarthritis, photosensitivity, and serositis are the most common clinical features of the disease. Lupus nephritis is the most common of the potentially life-threatening manifestations. Atherosclerosis, a complication of long-standing SLE, requires aggressive risk factor modification. It is important to consider the possibility of drug-induced systemic lupus or drug-induced subacute cutaneous lupus in a patient with a lupuslike syndrome who is taking a drug that is known to be associated with these syndromes.

### Introduction

Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is the prototypic systemic autoimmune disease, characterized by diverse multisystem involvement and the production of an array of autoantibodies. Clinical features in individual patients can be quite variable and range from mild joint and skin involvement to severe, life-threatening internal organ disease. Criteria for the classification of SLE were initially developed by the American College of Rheumatology (ACR) in 1971, revised in 1982, and revised for a second time in 19971,2 (Table 81.1). A person must fulfill 4 of 11 criteria to be classified as having SLE, all other reasonable diagnoses having been excluded. Each criterion is assigned an equal weight. A patient does not have to manifest all 4 criteria simultaneously; the required 4 of 11 criteria can be fulflled during a period of weeks or years. The ACR criteria were developed as a way to classify patients with SLE for the purpose of inclusion in clinical trials and epidemiologic studies. In clinical practice, these criteria are often

cited to support a diagnosis of SLE. Nevertheless, the fulfillment of these classification criteria is not a requirement for diagnosis. Rather, diagnosis rests on the judgment of an experienced clinician who recognizes a characteristic constellation of symptoms and signs in the setting of supportive serologic studies, after exclusion of alternative differential diagnostic possibilities.

In an effort to improve upon the ACR classification criteria, the Systemic Lupus International Collaborating Clinics (SLICC) developed revised classification criteria. These criteria were divided into "clinical" and "immunologic" categories, and the final criteria included 11 clinical categories and 6 immunologic categories. A patient is classified as having SLE if the individual (1) has biopsy-proven lupus nephritis with a positive anti-nuclear antibody (ANA) or antidouble-stranded DNA (dsDNA) antibody test result or (2) fulfills four of the criteria, including at least one clinical criterion and one immunologic criterion. The newly proposed criteria and the ACR 1997 criteria were validated using data from 690 additional SLE and control patients who had not been included in the derivation phase. In this validation phase, the SLICC criteria were more sensitive (97% vs. 83%) but less specific (84% vs. 96%) than the ACR criteria. The SLICC criteria are being increasingly used along with the ACR criteria as eligibility criteria in contemporary lupus clinical trials. Both sets of criteria are recognized by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration and the European Medicines Agency.

More recently, a working group composed of members of the ACR and the European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology (EULAR) completed the development of a new set of SLE classification criteria. Overarching aims of this joint effort were to develop criteria with similar specificity to those of the ACR in 1997 but with improved sensitivity and improved classification of early SLE. In contrast to previous classification criteria, this set uses weighted criteria. The final criteria consist of seven clinical domains and three immunologic domains, with criteria that are additive within a continuous scale. ANA positivity of ≥1:80 is also a requirement for classification4 (Table 81.2). A four-phase process was established to develop these criteria. The first phase, consisting of a systematic review of ANA sensitivity and specificity and item generation using three different approaches, resulted in the nomination of 144 candidate criteria. A unique aspect of this phase was the inclusion of the SLE patient perspective through

a cross-sectional patient survey asking about early symptoms of disease. The second phase used a nominal group technique to reduce the candidate criteria down to 40 items. In the third phase, an expert panel refined and weighted the candidate criteria using multicriteria decision analysis. In the fourth phase, the candidate criteria were tested in 500 SLE patients and 500 controls and were determined to have 98% sensitivity and 96% specificity for classification of SLE. In conjunction with the prior ACR and SLICC criteria, this ACR/EULAR effort reflects a continuation of efforts to continually refine and update classification criteria based on new clinical data and progress in understanding the disease. With the goal of identifying clinical and serologic features that are consistent with early SLE, a substudy was performed in which seven academic centers collected clinical and serologic data in patients with early SLE (presented within the previous 3 years; n = 389) and patients who presented with features of SLE but who were ultimately diagnosed with an alternative disease (n = 227). Features more consistent with SLE than an alternative diagnosis included unexplained fever, alopecia, weight loss, and ascites. Features more consistent with an alternative diagnosis included Raynaud's phenomenon, sicca symptoms, dysphagia, and fatigue. Of the serologic variables, ANA, anti-dsDNA, anti-ribonucleoprotein (RNP), and antiphospholipid (aPL) antibodies were more frequent in the SLE group.

### Epidemiology

Prevalence and incidence rates of SLE vary widely in the published literature. Reported prevalence frequencies range from 20 to 240 per 100,000 people, and reported incidence rates range from 1 to 10 per 100,000 person-years. This variation is partly the result of methodological differences between studies (e.g., different case definitions of SLE and methods of case ascertainment) and differing racial-ethnic compositions of the study populations. To determine more accurate and contemporary epidemiologic estimates for SLE in the United States, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention funded five population-based lupus registries to conduct extensive lupus surveillance in several counties in Georgia, Michigan, California, New York, and the Indian Health Service (IHS), totaling 6.5 million people.6-10 The Georgia and Michigan registries were composed primarily of White and African American patients, whereas the California and New York registries included substantial numbers of Asian and Hispanic patients. The IHS registry consisted of American Indians and Alaska Natives.6-10 A meta-analysis leveraging data from the four state-specific registries calculated a pooled prevalence of SLE of 72.8 per 100,000 person-years. The prevalence estimate was nine times higher among females than males (128.7 vs. 14.6 per 100,000), and highest among Black females (230.9 per 100,000), followed by Hispanic females (120.7 per 100,000), White females (84.7 per 100,000), and Asian/Pacific Islander females (84.4 per 100,000). In a separate analysis, the American Indian/Alaska Native female prevalence was 270.6 per 100,000. After applying sex/race stratified estimates to the 2018 U.S. Census population, an estimate of the number of SLE cases in 2018 was 204,295.11

Most patients with SLE are diagnosed between the ages of 15 and 64 years old. SLE tends to be more severe in men and in pediatric patients. Late-onset SLE (>50 years old) is characterized by a more insidious onset, with a higher occurrence of serositis and pulmonary involvement and a lower incidence of malar rash, photosensitivity, alopecia, Raynaud's phenomenon, neuropsychiatric disease, and nephritis.12,13

### Clinical Features

SLE has protean clinical manifestations that may differ dramatically from patient to patient. Just as the signs and symptoms of SLE vary widely among patients, so does the severity of disease. Some patients will have relatively mild disease that is no threat to a life-sustaining organ; other patients' disease will progress rapidly to life-threatening severity.

The great variability in the expression and severity of SLE constitutes a major challenge to accurate diagnosis. Although it is difficult to pinpoint their precise frequencies, it is clear that the most common presenting manifestations are constitutional symptoms (fever, fatigue, and/or weight loss), cutaneous manifestations (e.g., malar rash), and articular manifestations (arthritis and/or arthralgia). Each of these manifestations appears to be present in at least 50% of patients with SLE at the time of diagnosis. The other clinical features of SLE are much less likely to be presenting manifestations, although virtually any of them may be the first clue to the correct diagnosis. More commonly, these manifestations appear while the disease evolves. Taken together, various descriptive studies in the literature1 1,14-18 support a cumulative frequency of symptoms and signs, summarized in Table 81.3.

### Mucocutaneous Involvement

Mucocutaneous involvement is very common in SLE. Investigators have categorized cutaneous lupus erythematosus (LE) lesions as "lupus specific" or "lupus nonspecific" on the basis of the histopathologic finding of interface dermatitis19,20 (Table 81.4). In a patient with SLE, the presence of lupus-specific lesions confirms the diagnosis of cutaneous LE; lupus-nonspecific lesions can occur in diseases other than SLE. Lupus-specific lesions are further subdivided into acute cutaneous lupus erythematosus (ACLE), subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus (SCLE), and chronic cutaneous lupus erythematosus (CCLE) lesions, on the basis of additional chronologic, clinical, and histopathologic information. Discoid

lupus is the most common subtype of CCLE. SCLE and CCLE can occur as distinct isolated entities or as one of several manifestations of SLE. The risk of SLE varies with each cutaneous subset. One study of 161 patients with lupus-specific lesions showed that the classification criteria for SLE were present in 72% of patients with ACLE, 58% with SCLE, 28% with any form of discoid lupus, and 6% with localized discoid lupus confined to the head and neck. Many patients displayed more than one type of cutaneous lesion.

Cutaneous lupus lesions are frequently pruritic. One multinational study of patients with active cutaneous lupus lesions demonstrated that 77.1% of patients experienced pruritis, with ~50% reporting moderate to severe pruritis. The most common locations for pruritis were the scalp, face, and arms. A significant correlation was found between pruritis intensity and activity of the skin lesions but not with skin damage scores. Other sensations associated with pruritis were described as burning, superficial, and

like ants crawling. Of note, dermatomyositis lesions are generally more pruritic and less painful than lupus lesions.

### Acute Cutaneous Lupus Erythematosus

ACLE lesions can be localized or generalized. The hallmark feature of ACLE is observed in the malar region ("butterfly rash") and is characterized by confluent, macular, or papular erythema lasting days to weeks, appearing symmetrically on the cheeks and bridge of the nose. Unlike the lesions of dermatomyositis, ACLE lesions do not involve the nasolabial folds, which are sun-protected areas (Fig. 81.1). Induration and scaling may occur. Erythema also commonly occurs on the forehead, eyelids, chin, and neck. The malar rash of SLE can be mimicked by a variety of other facial rashes, including acne, rosacea, seborrheic dermatitis, perioral dermatitis, atopic dermatitis, and erysipelas. If the diagnosis remains uncertain after an extensive clinical and serologic evaluation, biopsy of the lesion can help distinguish cutaneous lupus from other dermatologic conditions. It is important to remember that other forms of lupus-specific skin lesions, such as discoid lupus, can also occur in the malar distribution.

The generalized form of ACLE refers to widespread macular or maculopapular erythema occurring in a photosensitive distribution on any area of the body. The palmar surfaces, dorsa of the hands, and extensor surfaces of the fingers are commonly involved. In contrast to Gottron's papules of dermatomyositis, the erythema of ACLE spares the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints and is typically located between the interphalangeal joints. In severe forms of ACLE, a widespread bullous eruption similar to toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN) can occur. This variant occurs when the interface changes at the dermoepidermal junction are severe enough to cause epidermal detachment from the dermis. ACLE lesions heal without scarring, although temporary postinflammatory hyperpigmentation may be observed.

### Subacute Cutaneous Lupus Erythematosus

SCLE is characterized by the presence of nonscarring, photosensitive lesions that can take one of two distinct forms: (1) papulosquamous lesions that resemble psoriasis or (2) annular-polycyclic lesions with peripheral scale and central clearing (Fig. 81.2). These two forms can occur concurrently in the same patient. SCLE has a predilection for the back, neck, shoulders, and extensor surfaces of the arms and usually spares the central face. The lesions typically last for weeks to months and heal without scarring. Rarely, a severe TEN-like eruption can evolve from SCLE lesions after sun exposure. SCLE, particularly the annular subtype, is strongly associated with the presence of the HLA-DR3 haplotype and anti- SSA/Ro antibody.24, Several drugs are known to induce SCLE; angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors, terbinafine, hydrochlorothiazide, and calcium channel blockers are common culprits. The time interval between exposure to the drug and development of skin lesions can vary from several days up to 6 years. Interestingly, the drugs that are implicated in drug-induced SCLE are distinct from those that cause drug-induced SLE. Finally, SCLE has been implicated as a paraneoplastic syndrome.

### Chronic Cutaneous Lupus Erythematosus

CCLE refers to a variety of subtypes of photosensitive lesions that can lead to skin atrophy and scarring and that may persist for several months or years. Discoid lupus (DLE) is the most common subtype of CCLE. DLE is subdivided into localized discoid lupus (limited to head and neck) and generalized discoid (occurring above and below the neck) (Figs. 81.3 and 81.4). The term "discoid" refers to the sharply demarcated disk-shaped appearance of the lesions, which are raised, erythematosus plaques with adherent scales that commonly occur on the patient's scalp, face, and neck. The cheeks, nose, ears, and upper lip are classic locations for lesions. Typically, a raised, erythematous border denotes the actively expanding component. Follicular plugging is a characteristic finding. Left untreated, DLE can result in permanent alopecia and disfigurement. Squamous cell carcinoma has been described as a sequela of long-standing DLE; thus active surveillance of known lesions and evaluation of changing lesions are critical. Other subtypes of DLE include mucosal DLE (described in a subsequent section) and hypertrophic LE. Hypertrophic LE consists

of chronic, indurated lesions that are covered by hyperkeratotic, multilayered scales. These lesions can be a source of diagnostic confusion because they may visually and histologically resemble squamous cell carcinoma.

Other forms of CCLE include lupus panniculitis/profundus, chilblain lupus, and lupus tumidus. Lupus panniculitis is a lobular panniculitis that has a predilection for the scalp, face, arms, buttocks, and thighs. The lesions can result in depressed, sunken

areas. When a cutaneous discoid lesion overlies the panniculitis, the entity is referred to as lupus profundus. Biopsy is often necessary to secure the diagnosis because reports have described cases of T cell lymphoma that mimic panniculitis. Nevertheless, biopsy should be performed carefully because the lesions have a tendency to break down. Lupus panniculitis is one of the few panniculitides that can occur above the waist. Lupus panniculitis is associated with a low risk of concomitant SLE. Chilblain lupus manifests as tender, erythematous, or violaceous papules or plaques occurring on acral areas, especially the fingers, toes, heels, nose, and ears. The lesions are brought on by cold, damp air. Chilblain lupus morphologically resembles idiopathic chilblain but is more likely than idiopathic chilblain to be present even in warm weather. Histopathology demonstrates a superficial and deep perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate. .

Lupus tumidus lesions are characterized by edematous, erythematous plaques with a smooth surface. These lesions are highly photosensitive and have a predilection for the zygomatic region of the face. The epidermis is not involved; thus there is a lack of overlying scale or follicular plugging. Lupus tumidus is also referred to as intermittent cutaneous LE.

### Other Systemic Lupus Erythematosus Skin Lesions

Lupus-nonspecific skin lesions such as cutaneous leukocytoclastic vasculitis, bullous lesions, periungual erythema, livedo reticularis, and livedo racemosa can develop in patients with SLE. Cutaneous leukocytoclastic vasculitis most commonly presents as palpable purpura on the lower extremities. Bullous lupus erythematosus is a rare cutaneous manifestation characterized by subepidermal vesiculobullous skin changes, manifested by a nonscarring bullous eruption31 (Fig. 81.5). Bullous lupus is associated with antibodies targeting Type VII collagen. The physical examination finding of periungual erythema represents dilation of the capillaries at the base of the nail. The physician can visualize these capillaries at the patient's bedside with a dermatoscope or ophthalmoscope. Other disorders associated with periungual erythema include

scleroderma and mixed connective tissue disease (MCTD). Unlike scleroderma and MCTD, SLE is not associated with capillary dropout. Livedo reticularis and livedo racemosa are characterized by erythematous to violaceous reticular or netlike patterns of the skin. In contrast to livedo reticularis, livedo racemosa is always pathologic and is characterized by an irregular reticular pattern with "broken" circles. Both lesions are highly associated with antiphospholipid syndrome (APS). Atrophie blanche, characterized by stellate, white plaques with central atrophy and peripheral hyperpigmentation, is also associated with APS.

### Photosensitivity

Photosensitivity occurs frequently in SLE. In one study, photo provocation testing caused an abnormal skin reaction to ultraviolet A, ultraviolet B, or visible light in more than 90% of patients with lupus. Most abnormal skin reactions occurred 1 to 2 weeks after exposure to light and persisted for weeks to months. Photosensitive patients may report worsening of their systemic disease symptoms, such as fatigue and joint pain, after sun exposure. During evaluation of a photosensitive patient, polymorphous light eruption (PMLE) and phototoxic medications are important diagnostic considerations. Accurate differentiation between PMLE and SLE is essential because PMLE is treated by ultraviolet radiation phototherapy, but this treatment makes SLE worse. PMLE can occur concomitantly in patients with known SLE.

### Alopecia

Alopecia is common in the setting of SLE and is typically categorized as lupus-specific, lupus-nonspecific, or non-lupus-related alopecia. Lupus-specific alopecia refers to ACLE, SCLE, or discoid LE lesions that occur on the scalp. These are active, inflammatory lesions that are associated with underlying erythema and scale. Scarring alopecia is a common complication of discoid LE as a result of inflammatory-mediated destruction of hair follicle ostia. Scalp discoid lesions most frequently occur on the vertex and parietal areas. Lupus-nonspecific alopecia includes

nonscarring lesions that can occur in settings other than SLE. Examples include "lupus hairs," diffuse areas of alopecia that fluctuate with SLE disease activity, and alopecia areata. "Lupus hairs" are characterized by coarse, irregularly sized hair with increased fragility at the frontal hairline and are associated with active systemic disease. The incidence of alopecia areata (discrete areas of hair loss) is believed to be increased in patients with SLE.

Non-lupus-related alopecia includes telogen effluvium secondary to metabolic stress or medications, androgenic alopecia, frontal fibrosing alopecia, tinea capitis, and traction alopecia.

### Mucosal Ulcers

Nasal or oral lesions that represent the mucosal counterparts of cutaneous lupus commonly develop in patients with SLE. Acute oral lupus lesions present as red macules, palatal erythema or petechiae, erosions, or ulcerations. These lesions are usually painless. Subacute oral lesions are rare and are characterized by welldemarcated, round, red patches. Oral discoid lesions present as painful, well-demarcated, round, red lesions with white radiating hyperkeratotic striae. The buccal mucosa is the most commonly involved site. When the lesions evolve, they may take on a honeycomb appearance. Oral discoid lupus frequently involves the patient's lip and spreads from the vermilion border to the skin of the lip. Mucosal discoid lesions can also occur on the conjunctiva and genital areas. In general, lupus oral ulcers have a gradual onset and can occur anywhere on the oral mucosa, with the most common locations being the hard palate, buccal mucosa, and vermilion border. These lesions are most commonly unilateral or asymmetric. The relationship between the presence of oral lesions and systemic disease activity remains unclear. Note that oral candidiasis and oral lichen planus can take on a similar appearance to SLE oral ulcers. The histopathology and immunopathology of mucosal lesions are similar to the alterations seen in the skin. Vasculitis is absent.

### Dermatopathology and Immunopathology

A skin biopsy is useful in the diagnosis of cutaneous lupus in the setting of an atypical clinical presentation. Immunofluorescence should always be performed, along with conventional histology. "Lupus-specific" skin lesions are characterized by an interface dermatitis consisting of a mononuclear cell infiltrate at the dermal epidermal junction. Other pathologic findings present in lupus skin lesions include basal layer vasculopathic degeneration of keratinocytes, perivascular and periadnexal inflammation, follicular plugging, mucin deposition, and hyperkeratosis. These findings occur to different degrees in various lupus-specific skin lesions; discoid lesions show the most profound changes. In contrast, early ACLE lesions may have minimal histopathologic findings and only a sparse lymphocytic infiltrate.

Immunofluorescence demonstrates granular deposition of immunoglobulin and complement components along the dermalepidermal junction. Immunoglobulin (Ig)G and IgM are the most common immunoglobulin subtypes deposited. Various complement components, including C3, C1q, and the membrane attack complex, have also been identified. Direct immunofluorescence (DIF) of nonlesional, sun-exposed skin is referred to as the "lupus band test." Although a positive lupus band test is often seen in patients with SLE, this may also be seen in patients with other rheumatic diseases and in healthy people. In one study, 20% of healthy young adults had a positive DIF in sun-exposed skin. It is important to note that serologic testing with ANA, anti-dsDNA, and anti-Smith (anti-Sm) has largely supplanted use

of the lupus band test in confirming the diagnosis of SLE. DIF of nonlesional, sun-protected skin is believed to be more specific for SLE.

### Musculoskeletal Involvement

### Arthritis

Arthritis and arthralgias are very common manifestations of SLE, present in as many as 90% of patients at some point during the course of their disease.41, Severity of involvement can range from mild joint pain to deforming arthritis. Although any joint can be involved, lupus arthritis is typically characterized by a symmetric, inflammatory arthritis that predominantly affects the knees, wrists, and small joints of the hands. Synovial effusions are usually small and not as inflammatory as those present in rheumatoid arthritis (RA). Importantly, ultrasound studies have demonstrated a high frequency of subclinical synovitis and tenosynovitis in SLE patients without clinically apparent joint swelling or warmth. Hand deformities can occur as a result of ligamental and/or joint capsule laxity, joint subluxation, and muscle imbalance. Characteristic findings include subluxations of the MCP joints, ulnar deviation, swan-neck deformities, and Z thumb deformities. This manifestation is referred to as Jaccoud's arthropathy because it resembles the arthropathy that develops in patients with rheumatic fever (Fig. 81.6). These deformities are typically reducible, although sometimes they can become fixed and are associated with disability. Jaccoud's arthropathy sometimes occurs in the foot.

One magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) study of the hands of 20 patients with SLE-associated Jaccoud's arthropathy demonstrated the presence of synovitis and tenosynovitis in all patients. Tenosynovitis occurred predominantly in the flexor tendons of the second, third, and fourth fingers. Although lupus arthritis is not classically associated with erosions on plain radiography, erosive disease has been described in a small subset of patients. Studies using more sensitive imaging techniques have shown a higher prevalence of erosive disease. In one ultrasound study of 108 patients with a history of musculoskeletal involvement, bone erosions were detected in 26% of patients. A contrast-enhanced

MRI study of 34 SLE patients with joint symptoms demonstrated bone erosions at the wrist in 93% of patients and at the MCP joints in 63% of patients. The presence of erosions was independent of anti-citrullinated protein antibodies (ACPA) or rheumatoid factor (RF) antibody status. In addition, MRI studies have shown occasional erosions in some patients with lupus arthritis. A subset of patients with SLE who also meet classification criteria for RA have historically been referred to as "rhupus." One study demonstrated the presence of marginal joint erosions on plain radiography in 60% of such patients. Erosive arthritis is commonly a feature of MCTD. In addition to arthritis, tendinitis or tenosynovitis is frequently observed in patients with SLE. Tendon rupture is a very uncommon occurrence.
