Unlike anti-Sm, anti-RNP is not specific for SLE. High titers of anti-RNP antibodies can be helpful in supporting the diagnosis of MCTD.

Numerous other autoantibodies can be found in patients with SLE. Antibodies to cytoplasmic antigens, such as Ro and La (SS-A and SS-B), can be found in some patients with SLE. Autoantibodies against the Ro antigens comprise autoantibodies targeting cellular proteins with molecular weights of 52 and 60 kD (Ro52 and Ro60). Ro60 is found in the nucleus and Ro60 is found in the cytoplasm. Although these autoantibodies lack both sensitivity and specificity for SLE, they are sometimes associated with distinct clinical syndromes. The best example of such a relationship involves the presence of anti-Ro antibodies in more than 90% of cases of neo- .189, Anti-Ro antibodies are also seen with increased natal lupus. frequency in patients with SCLE. Other autoantibodies may be directed against cell surface molecules or against circulating proteins. For example, antibodies to blood components can be responsible for hemolytic anemia, neutropenia, or thrombocytopenia, and antibodies to phospholipids and phospholipid binding proteins can be detected in some patients with SLE with or without APS. It

should be noted that RF (anti-IgG) can be found in 15% to 20% of people with SLE, whether or not joint disease is present. ACPA can also be present.

Complement consumption arising from immune complex disease may lead to hypocomplementemia in patients with SLE. 193, Because hypocomplementemia is rare in other rheumatic diseases, its presence in a patient with SLE can provide valuable supportive evidence for the diagnosis. Moreover, because hypocomplementemia most likely reflects complement activation by immune complexes, its presence is often a sign of active disease. Nevertheless, hereditary complement deficiencies may be found in patients with SLE (C1q, C2, C4), so absence of a particular complement component does not always reflect consumption. 195-197 For this reason, it is often necessary to measure more than one complement component (e.g., C3 and C4) before concluding that hypocomplementemia is the result of active disease.

The utility of serologic tests in assessing disease activity and predicting disease flares remains a topic of controversy. In the absence of a hereditary complement deficiency, hypocomplementemia is a reliable indicator that the disease is active, but normal complement levels do not rule out active disease. Titers of anti-dsDNA antibodies correlate with disease activity in some patients but not in others. One study attempted to resolve the long-standing debate about the prognostic value of changes in lupus serology. In this study, patients with clinically quiescent lupus underwent monthly monitoring for levels of anti-dsDNA, C3a, C3, C4, and CH50 to identify patients with serologically active, clinically quiescent disease. These patients were then randomly assigned to treatment with corticosteroids or placebo to determine whether treatment of serologically active disease could prevent impending clinical flares. The results were equivocal. Some patients with serologically active disease flared, and some flares were apparently prevented. Nevertheless, in most control subjects, serologic deterioration was not followed by a clinical flare, and most of the flares that occurred in the original patient population that had been monitored were not preceded by serologic deterioration. Thus there remains no substitute for knowledge of a particular patient's disease pattern or whether there is an association between clinical and serologic manifestations in that patient.

### Differential Diagnosis

Because of the involvement of multiple organ systems and the lack of specificity of symptoms and/or signs, many systemic diseases can mimic SLE. Thus before a diagnosis is established, a comprehensive search for infectious, malignant, and other autoimmune diseases must be undertaken.

Several viral infections can produce symptoms and signs that are present in SLE. In addition, many viral illnesses are associated with the production of autoantibodies. A careful patient history with serologic testing for the potential pathogen should help secure the correct diagnosis. Patients with classic parvovirus B19 can have fever, rash, symmetric inflammatory polyarthritis, and cytopenias. Furthermore, the presence of ANA, anti-dsDNA, and hypocomplementemia has been observed in a few cases. CMV and EBV can mimic SLE in that patients often experience fatigue, cytopenias, abdominal pain, and liver test abnormalities. Patients with acute HIV infection are typically seen with fever, diffuse lymphadenopathy, and oral ulcers. Inflammatory arthritis and positive autoantibodies can develop in patients with hepatitis B and C.

Malignancy, particularly non-Hodgkin's lymphoma, can manifest with constitutional symptoms, joint pain, cytopenias (including AIHA), lymphadenopathy, rash, and a positive ANA. Large granular lymphocytic leukemia is a clonal disorder of large granular lymphocytes that mimics SLE because of its association with cytopenias (most commonly neutropenia), fevers, splenomegaly, positive ANA, and positive RF. Physicians must be particularly alert to the possibility of malignancy in older patients seen with new lupus-like syndromes. It is important to ensure that patients undergo appropriate malignancy screening tests.

Other autoimmune diseases such as RA, dermatomyositis, and Still's disease often share similar clinical features with SLE. Differentiating between these disorders might be difficult in early phases of the disease. Patients with RA and SLE may develop a symmetric inflammatory arthritis with a predilection for the wrists and small joints of the hands. ANA and RF may be elevated in both disorders, although ACPA suggests RA, and anti-dsDNA or anti-Sm suggests SLE. The photosensitive, erythematous rashes of dermatomyositis and SLE can appear clinically and histopathologically identical. A careful patient history and supporting serologies will aid in making the correct diagnosis. Another distinguishing feature is that the malar rash of SLE spares the nasolabial folds, whereas the malar rash of dermatomyositis involves the nasolabial folds. Physicians must also consider MCTD when evaluating a patient for possible SLE. MCTD is a syndrome characterized by a high-titer anti-RNP antibody in conjunction with clinical features that are often present in SLE, scleroderma, and/or polymyositis. Patients are frequently seen with puffy, swollen hands and Raynaud's phenomenon. In contrast to SLE, an erosive arthritis that looks very similar to RA can develop in patients with MCTD.

Careful evaluation for drug-induced lupus should be undertaken in every new patient in whom the diagnosis of SLE is suspected. This is especially important in an older person who is seen with a lupus-like syndrome. Arthralgia, myalgia, fever, and serositis are common manifestations. A wide variety of drugs have been implicated in the development of drug-induced lupus; minocycline, procainamide, hydralazine, isoniazid, IFN-α, and TNF inhibitors are well-known culprits. Hydrochlorothiazide is associated with drug-induced SCLE. All of these drugs may cause a positive ANA. Minocycline is occasionally associated with anti-dsDNA antibodies and perinuclear-staining anti-neutrophil

cytoplasmic antibodies, and TNF inhibitors can cause positive anti-dsDNA antibodies. Anti-histone antibodies are present in more than 95% of cases of drug-induced lupus, with the exception of those cases caused by minocycline. Anti-histone antibodies, however, cannot be used to confirm a diagnosis of drug-induced lupus because up to 80% of idiopathic patients with SLE will also produce anti-histone antibodies.

### Neonatal Lupus

Neonatal lupus is a passively acquired autoimmune disease of neonates that results from transplacental passage of maternal anti-SS- A and/or anti-SS-B antibodies. It can occur in mothers with SLE or Sjögren's syndrome or in those in whom an autoimmune disease has not been diagnosed. Neonatal lupus can involve multiple organ systems, including the heart, skin, liver, and hematologic system; the most severe complications are congenital 199, The term neocomplete heart block and cardiomyopathy. natal lupus stems from early observations that the skin lesions in affected newborns were similar to the lesions of SCLE.

Congenital complete heart block is associated with a neonatal mortality rate as high as 20%, and most patients will eventually require a permanent pacemaker. This complication occurs in as many as 2% of babies born to mothers who are positive for anti- Ro/SS-A and/or anti-LA/SS-B antibodies. Thus maternal antibodies are essential but not sufficient to cause disease. Once a woman has given birth to a baby with complete heart block, the risk for recurrence in a subsequent pregnancy is approximately 17%. Once a woman has given birth to a baby with cutaneous features of neonatal lupus (without heart block), the risk for heart block in a subsequent pregnancy is 18%. Evidence from in vitro studies suggests that during fetal development, fetal cardiocytes undergo apoptosis that results in expression of Ro/SS-A and La/SS-B on the cell surface. Binding of anti-Ro/SS-A and/or anti-La/SS-B to fetal cardiocytes leads to inflammatory injury and subsequently to fibrosis of the atrioventricular node and surrounding tissue. The sinoatrial node may also be involved. Prospective studies have shown that the vulnerable period for the fetal heart is between 16 and 24 weeks of gestation. Thus it is recommended that mothers with anti-Ro/SS-A and/or anti-La/SS-B antibodies undergo monitoring with fetal echocardiography beginning at 16 weeks of gestation.

The hope has been that detection of early stages of heart block (first and second degree) might allow for treatment that would prevent progression to third-degree heart block. Currently, the treatment of choice is maternal administration of a fluorinated glucocorticoid such as dexamethasone. Fluorinated glucocorticoids are preferred because of their ability to cross the placenta and enter the fetal circulation. Nevertheless, treatment of incomplete fetal heart block remains controversial because the benefits have not been clearly delineated, and glucocorticoids have been associated with several fetal side effects such as intrauterine growth retardation, oligohydramnios, and adrenal suppression. Complete heart block is irreversible even with treatment, and firstor seconddegree heart block may or may not reverse with treatment. Complicating matters, complete heart block can occur in the absence of preceding firstor second-degree block. In addition to conduction blocks, structural cardiac abnormalities have been observed in the setting of neonatal lupus, including but not limited to patent ductus arteriosus, ventricular septal defect, atrial septal defect, and patent foramen ovale. Myocarditis and pericarditis have also been described.

Rash, a common manifestation of neonatal lupus, consists of erythematous, annular lesions that resemble the annular subtype of SCLE. The rash typically occurs on the scalp, face, trunk, and extremities with a predilection for the periorbital area; it often develops after exposure of the newborn to ultraviolet light. Lesions typically occur within the first 4 to 6 weeks of life but may be present at birth. The rash is self-limiting and does not necessitate treatment. Lesions tend to resolve by 6 months of age, at which time maternal anti-Ro/SS-A and/or anti-La/SS-B antibodies are no longer present in the baby's circulation. Lesions develop in approximately 25% of babies born to anti-SSA/SS-B-positive mothers. Less common manifestations of neonatal lupus include hepatic, hematologic, and neurologic involvement. Hepatic manifestations include asymptomatic elevation of liver function tests, hepatitis, hepatomegaly, cholestasis, and cirrhosis. Hematologic manifestations include thrombocytopenia, AIHA, and leukopenia. Neurologic complications, including myelopathy, seizures, and aseptic meningitis, have been reported.

# Treatment of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus

### KEY POINTS

### Clinical Course and General Treatment Strategy

### KEY POINTS

Treatment of moderate or severe systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) includes initial intensive induction immunosuppressive therapy followed by less intense maintenance therapy.

Only a small proportion of SLE patients achieve prolonged periods of disease quiescence.

Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) usually follows a relapsing-remitting course. Recent studies have shown that an equal number of patients have continuously active disease, and only a small proportion experience long periods of disease quiescence. 1-3 Despite improvements in overall survival (85% to 90% during

the first 10 years),4 patients with SLE are still at risk for premature death. Persistent inflammation results in irreversible major organ damage, which is linked to decreased quality of life and increased mortality.6, Accordingly, therapeutic strategies should aim at reducing overall burden of systemic inflammation. Achieving these goals requires (1) accurate assessment of disease activity and flares, (2) stratification of patients according to severity of target organ involvement, (3) use of safe and effective drugs to induce remission promptly and prevent flares, and (4) prevention and management of disease and treatment-related comorbidities.

In general, patients with mild lupus manifestations (skin, joint, and mucosal involvement) are treated with anti-malarials or disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs (DMARDs), alone or in combination with low-dose oral glucocorticoids (GCs). Severe SLE with major organ involvement typically requires an initial period of intensive immunosuppressive therapy to control aberrant immunologic activity and halt tissue injury, followed by a longer period of less intensive and less toxic maintenance therapy to consolidate remission and prevent flares. Immunosuppressive therapy helps reduce the use of GCs, thus reducing their deleterious effects.

### Patient and Physician n Preferences

Patients with SLE experience poor quality of life, which is only in part associated with disease activity and organ damage. Indeed, patients considered to be in "remission" by their treating physicians often report a considerable residual symptom burden; important contributors include fatigue, fibromyalgia, depression, and cognitive dysfunction. Treating physicians should regularly address these issues and engage symptomatic or remedial therapies, as indicated. The realization that a significant proportion of patients have diseaseand treatment-related comorbidities has shifted the attention of physicians to adjunct therapies and primary prevention strategies, such as infection and cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk reduction measures.

Health professionals are encouraged to involve patients in treatment decisions, recognizing them as experts with a unique knowledge of their own health and their preferences for treatments and outcomes. This approach may be particularly challenging in patients with severe lupus, who might benefit from cytotoxic therapy, which is associated with significant toxicity. Physicians should provide patients with balanced information to ensure accurate perception of the risks and benefits of prescribed medications.

# Drugs Used in the Treatment of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus

### KEY POINTS

For chronic maintenance treatment, GC dose should be minimized to less than 7.5 mg prednisone/day and, when possible, withdrawn. Use of pulses of intravenous methylprednisolone at initial treatment stages may facilitate glucocorticoid sparing. Hydroxychloroquine (HCQ) is recommended for all patients with SLE due to its multiple beneficial effects. Pulses of intravenous cyclophosphamide (CYC) are recommended for organor life-threatening SLE. Mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) is equally effective and has a better toxicity profile than CYC for moderately severe proliferative lupus nephritis (PLN). Calcineurin inhibitors can be used in refractory LN, usually in combination with MMF as part of a multitarget therapy. Belimumab is approved for moderately active SLE despite standard-ofcare therapy. Anifrolumab may be used as add-on to standard therapy in moderate to severe lupus. Rituximab has been tried in severe disease refractory to immunosuppressive treatment and as add-on in lupus nephritis. Approval of new drugs for lupus is challenging due to disease heterogeneity and challenges in clinical trial design.

### Glucocorticoids

GCs exert broad inhibitory effects on immune responses mediated by T and B cells, as well as on the effector functions of monocytes and neutrophils. On the basis of these effects and their rapid onset of action, GCs have been remarkably efficacious in managing acute SLE manifestations.

Low-dose GC therapy (≤10 mg prednisone equivalent per day) is generally used when initial therapies (mainly anti-malarials) are not tolerated or are inadequate to control disease activity. In moderate to severe disease, GCs are used preferably in combination with immunosuppressive agents, at doses of 0.5 to 0.7 mg/kg in a single dose, usually in the morning. When combined with immunosuppressive agents, the GC dose should rarely exceed 0.5 to 0.6 mg/kg due to concerns for infections and other toxicities. Tapering of GC dose may start after the first 4 weeks of therapy, targeting a maximum daily dose of 7.5 mg after 6 months. Concomitant use of immunosuppressive agents facilitates tapering and decreases cumulative GC toxicity.

In severe, rapidly progressing disease or when doses greater than 0.6 mg/kg/day prednisone equivalent are required to control disease activity, GC pulse therapy may be introduced. Intravenous (IV) pulses of methylprednisolone (MP) (250 to 1000 mg daily for 1 to 3 consecutive days) are used, as they allow for lower cumulative oral (per os [PO]) dose and less damage accrual without compromising efficacy. In addition to expediting remission, IV MP pulses may allow for the use of lower GC doses during the induction period.

GC toxicity may involve early (mood effects, acne, myalgias, infections), later (metabolic), and late-onset (osteoporosis, avascular bone necrosis, cataract, CVD) adverse events. Although confounded by increased systemic disease activity, most effects are considered to be dependent on the cumulative dose and duration. Chronic exposure to GC doses higher than 6 to 7 . mg/day of prednisone equivalent is clearly associated with an increased risk for irreversible organ damage. 14, Thus, the European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology (EULAR) recommendations for the management of SLE suggest

that the chronic maintenance dose of GC should be less than 7.5 mg/day prednisone equivalent, if GC cannot be totally withdrawn. Although minimization of exposure to GCs is a universal target of therapy, tapering should be done with caution and may take considerable time. Abrupt withdrawal of 5 mg/day prednisone in SLE clinically quiescent for more than 1 year increased the risk of subsequent flare (relative risk [RR] in patients maintained on 5 mg/day prednisone 0.2; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.1 to 0.7).

### Anti-malarial Drugs

Anti-malarial drugs, mainly HCQ, are considered as anchor drugs for the treatment of SLE due to their multifaceted beneficial effects. Importantly, prospective observational studies have reported an inverse association between use of HCQ and accrual of irreversible organ damage, as well as mortality.6, Additional effects, ranging from the prevention of congenital heart block to a more favorable metabolic profile and reduction of the risk of thrombosis in patients with antiphospholipid antibodies (aPLs), have also been described.21-23 In a randomized controlled trial (RCT) in stable active patients with SLE on HCQ treatment, those who achieved blood HCQ levels greater than or equal to 1000 ng/mL had a tendency for reduced SLE flares (20.5% vs. 35.1%) during a 7-month period.

HCQ is typically well tolerated, with low rates of mild gastrointestinal and skin adverse events. The major concern arising from its use is the risk for retinal toxicity. Advanced, more sensitive screening techniques for the detection of HCQ-induced retinopathy (10-2 visual fields and spectral domain-optical coherence tomography) suggest that the latter may be more prevalent than originally believed; the risk may reach 10% or more among longterm users (more than 10 years).25, A daily dose greater than 5 mg/kg real weight and a duration of use of more than 5 and, especially, more than 10 years, are particularly associated with heightened risk of retinal toxicity. Patients with chronic kidney disease, pre-existing retinal or macular abnormalities, or concomitant use of tamoxifen are at increased risk. Thus the daily dose should currently not exceed 5 mg/kg real body weight, although a recent study suggested that doses of ≤5 mg can be associated with increased risk for flares. Routine ophthalmologic evaluation is recommended at baseline, 5 years later, and yearly thereafter, if baseline examination is normal. More frequent monitoring is warranted in patients with pre-existing retinal abnormalities or other risk factors.

### Immunosuppressive and Cytotoxic c Drugs

### Methotrexate

Methotrexate (MTX) is a steroid-sparing treatment in mild to moderate SLE, particularly for articular and cutaneous manifestations. MTX is administered once weekly orally or parenterally. A systematic literature review reported significant reduction of the SLE Disease Activity Index (SLEDAI) among MTX-treated patients compared with controls (odds ratio [OR], 0.44), followed by significant reduction in the average dose of GC (OR, 0.34). Concomitant administration of folic acid (1 to 2 mg/day) is recommended to minimize toxicity (Table 82.1).

### Cyclophosphamide

Pharmacology and Route of Administration. CYC is an alkylating agent that depletes lymphocytes and reduces the production of autoantibodies in lupus (Table 82.2). Both oral and IV

administration of CYC result in similar plasma concentrations, and the serum half-life is approximately 6 hours. CYC is metabolized to various active metabolites by cytochrome P450 in the liver or other tissues. Drugs that induce hepatic microsomal enzymes (barbiturates, alcohol, phenytoin, rifampin) may accelerate the metabolism of CYC into its active metabolites and thus increase its pharmacologic and toxic effects. Conversely, drugs that inhibit the hepatic microsomal enzymes (anti-malarials, tricyclic anti-depressants, and allopurinol) may slow the conversion of CYC to active metabolites. Approximately 20% of the drug is excreted by the kidneys; therefore dose adjustment is necessary in cases of renal impairment.

The National Institutes of Health (NIH) trials demonstrated equivalent efficacy yet lower toxicity with monthly IV (0.5 to 1 g/m2) versus oral regimens, which led to the predominant use of IV CYC in clinical practice (Table 82.3). Reversible myelotoxicity is common and dose-related. After pulse therapy, the nadir of the patient's lymphocyte count occurs on days 7 to 10, and that of granulocyte count occurs on days 10 to 14. The dose should be adjusted to keep the patient's white blood cell count higher than 3000 cells/mm3. A prompt recovery from granulocytopenia usually occurs after 21 to 28 days. Reversible alopecia and nausea are common, whereas infections (especially herpes zoster) and malignancy (including bladder toxicity and carcinoma) are less frequent, although much more serious adverse events. Gonadal toxicity is the major concern with CYC therapy, and its occurrence depends mainly on cumulative dose and patient age. 31, Lower cumulative dose CYC regimens are associated with significantly less risk for premature ovarian failure.

Use in Lupus Nephritis. RCTs with long-term follow-up have shown that intermittent pulse IV CYC therapy is effective for moderate to severe proliferative lupus nephritis (PLN).34, CYC delays renal scarring, preserves renal function, and reduces the risk for progression to end-stage kidney disease (ESKD). Following induction therapy, a maintenance regimen is necessary to decrease

the risk of flares. A combination of pulse therapy with IV CYC and IV MP improves renal outcomes without increasing toxicity. Severe forms of proliferative LN (i.e., with acute reduction in glomerular filtration rate (GFR) and/or adverse renal biopsy findings) may be treated with seven monthly pulses of IV CYC (0.5 to 1 g/m2), followed by maintenance therapy (see later in the chapter). In most severe cases, monthly pulses of IV MP may be given during the induction period.

In the Euro-Lupus Nephritis Trial, which studied Caucasian patients with milder forms of LN, low-dose IV CYC (six fortnightly [every 2 weeks] pulses at a fixed dose of 500 mg each in combination with three daily doses of 750 mg of IV MP), followed by azathioprine (AZA) for maintenance, had comparable efficacy and less toxicity than high-dose IV CYC (eight pulses). Mean patient survival rate at 10 years was 92% for both groups; ESKD and doubling of serum creatinine (Cr) rates did not differ between the two groups. Therefore, low-dose IV CYC may be an alternative option for patients with moderately severe LN, as it has the additional benefit of less gonadotoxicity.

IV CYC has also been used in membranous lupus nephropathy, in an RCT comparing cyclosporin A (CsA), IV CYC (0.5 to 1 g/m2 x six bimonthly doses), and GC alone, in 42 patients. All patients received alternate-day oral prednisone (1 mg/kg every other day for 8 weeks, then tapered). At 1 year, the cumulative probability of remission was 27% with prednisone, 60% with IV CYC, and 83% with CsA. Rates of nephrotic syndrome relapse were 10 times higher in patients treated with CsA versus those treated with IV CYC.

Use in Extrarenal Disease. CYC has demonstrated efficacy in life-threatening or refractory extrarenal lupus manifestations such as severe thrombocytopenia (platelet count < 20,000/mm3), neurologic disease, severe cardiopulmonary manifestations, and extensive skin disease.42-44 Investigators45 have reported the superiority of IV CYC versus IV MP for severe nonthrombotic neurologic SLE (seizures, peripheral neuropathy, optic neuritis, transverse myelitis, brainstem disease, coma, internuclear ophthalmoplegia).

### Azathioprine

AZA inhibits the conversion of purine bases such as inosine to adenine and guanine ribonucleotides. AZA (2 to 2.5 mg/kg/day) is safe in the long term with no significant increase in the risk for infections; a study in patients with inflammatory bowel disease has linked AZA to an increased risk for cancer but with no evidence of causality. Gastrointestinal complaints are frequent, and mild liver enzyme elevation may occur, but severe liver injury is infrequent. Reversible, dose-related bone marrow toxicity is also common; leukopenia is encountered in 4.5% and thrombocytopenia in 2% (see Table 82.1) of patients, respectively. AZA toxicity has been associated with genetic polymorphisms, resulting in decreased thiopurine methyltransferase (TPMT) activity and impaired ability to detoxify intermediate metabolites. Genetic testing is available—although not widely—for TPMT variant alleles, so that the starting dosages of AZA can be adjusted accordingly. Concomitant use of allopurinol, which inhibits xanthine oxidase (the enzyme that metabolizes AZA), substantially increases toxicity and should be avoided.

Patients with manifestations of moderate severity, such as constitutional symptoms, thrombocytopenia with platelet count 30 to 50 x 103/mm3, and serositis may respond to AZA, usually in combination with moderate to high starting GC doses (see Table 82.2). AZA has also been used in a controlled study of European patients with proliferative LN who were randomly assigned to

receive pulse IV CYC plus prednisone versus IV MP plus AZA plus a tapering dose of prednisone. Both groups received maintenance therapy with AZA plus prednisone after the second year. Despite no significant differences between groups in rates of sustained doubling of Cr, ESKD, or mortality after a median of 9.6 years, renal relapses occurred more frequently in the AZA group (hazard ratio [HR], 4.5 compared with IV CYC). Repeat renal biopsies showed that progression of chronic lesions was more effectively halted by CYC than by AZA. Thus, AZA has been abandoned as a therapeutic option in the induction phase of LN unless other options are not available or are contraindicated, such as during pregnancy.

AZA can be used for maintenance of response in LN. Two RCTs have compared AZA versus MMF as maintenance regimens in PLN. In the MAINTAIN trial, which included European patients who received induction with low-dose IV CYC, both agents were equally efficacious in terms of time-to-renal flare, severe flares, renal remission, and doubling of Cr (median follow-up 110 months).51, Repeat kidney biopsies failed to reveal histologic differences between the two groups. In contrast, the Aspreva Lupus Management Study (ALMS), which included a larger number of patients with multiethnic backgrounds who received induction therapy with either IV CYC or MMF, reported increased renal flares in the AZA versus the MMF group (see also next section). To this end, both agents can be used after initial therapy (3 to 6 months)55 on the basis of availability, clinical experience, and potential for pregnancy, because MMF is associated with an increased risk of spontaneous abortion and fetal malformation.

### Mycophenolate Mofetil

Pharmacology. Mycophenolate is a prodrug of mycophenolic acid (MPA), a potent inhibitor of inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase that is indispensable for the de novo synthesis of guanosine nucleotides. It is orally administered either as MMF or as enteric-coated mycophenolate sodium (eMPS). A 720-mg dose of eMPS is roughly equivalent to a 1-g dose of MMF. The lack of any salvage nucleotide synthesis pathway in lymphocytes renders them a selective target for MMF. MMF has excellent oral bioavailability, with peak levels occurring within 1 to 2 hours after administration and a half-life of 17 hours. Although therapeutic drug monitoring to guide MMF dosing has been proposed in renal transplantation, validation of therapeutic MPA monitoring in LN is still required. MMF is strongly teratogenic and should not be administered during pregnancy.

Use in Lupus Nephritis. Several RCTs have demonstrated equal or even superior efficacy of MMF versus CYC in inducing renal response in PLN. Nevertheless, the ALMS, one of the largest and most racially diverse RCTs in LN, failed to demonstrate the superiority of MMF (2 to 3 g/day) versus monthly pulses of IV CYC (0.5 to 1 g/m2), both combined with oral prednisone (maximum starting dose, 60 mg/day). At 6 months, response rates were 56% for patients treated with MMF and 53% for patients treated with IV CYC. Post hoc analysis suggested superiority of MMF in black and Hispanic patients and noninferiority in the subgroup of patients with poor renal function at baseline.58, Meta-analyses of the previously mentioned and other RCTs have concluded that MMF is as effective as CYC for induction treatment of PLN and is associated with lower risks of leukopenia, amenorrhea, and alopecia but not infections.55, Based on these data, MMF is now considered as first-line treatment in PLN, especially when gonadal toxicity is an issue.

A pooled analysis of 84 patients with pure membranous LN (MLN) who participated in two RCTs has demonstrated comparable anti-proteinuric effects and nephrotic syndrome remission rates in MMFand IV CYC—treated patients. Due to more favorable toxicity profile compared with CYC, MMF is recommended as first-line treatment of MLN.

Meta-analysis of RCTs comparing MMF versus AZA as maintenance therapy in PLN showed comparable rates of renal remission, doubling of Cr, and renal remission during a 3-year period.55, However, treatment with AZA was associated with increased risk for renal relapses (RR, 1.45) and leukopenia (RR, 7.1) compared with MMF. Both MMF and AZA can be used for maintenance of response in PLN on the basis of availability and potential for pregnancy. Early (before 18 to 24 months) discontinuation of MMF or switching to other immunosuppressant is associated with increased risk for renal flare.

Use in Extrarenal Lupus. A randomized study compared mycophenolate (in the form of eMPS) and AZA, in combination with both GC (starting dose 20 to 30 mg/day) and anti-malarials, in 240 Caucasian SLE patients without renal involvement. Most patients had musculoskeletal and mucocutaneous manifestations, but almost 30% also had cardiorespiratory disease. The primary endpoint of the study was the rate of remission (measured by SLE- DAI-2K and BILAG) at 3 and 24 months, and the results were remarkably in favor of the mycophenolate arm; 71.2% of patients reached a clinical SLEDAI = 0 at 24 months compared with 48.3% in the AZA group. Mycophenolate also reduced the occurrence of flares more than AZA (71.7% vs. 50% for BILAG A or B flares) without excess toxicity. Post hoc analysis of the ALMS data showed that MMF was equally efficacious with IV CYC pulse therapy on controlling extrarenal disease activity, particularly in the general, mucocutaneous, musculoskeletal, and hematologic domains. In observational studies, MMF reduces disease activ- 65,66with mucocutaneous, ity, flare rate, and permits GC tapering, musculoskeletal, vasculitic, and cardiopulmonary manifestations showing the best responses.

### Calcineurin Inhibitors

### Cyclosporin A

Pharmacology. CsA is a calcineurin inhibitor (CNI) that deactivates T cells and reduces antigen presentation and autoantibody production by lupus B cells. After oral administration, peak serum concentration occurs within 1 to 8 hours. Drug concentration is measured in whole blood, but this is rarely necessary in autoimmune diseases, unless CsA is used in doses greater than or equal to 3 mg/kg/day. Clinical response occurs 1 to 2 months after treatment initiation. Numerous drugs interact with CsA, leading to reduced (rifampin, phenytoin, phenobarbital, nafcillin) or increased drug concentrations (erythromycin, clarithromycin, azoles, calcium channel blockers, amiodarone, allopurinol, colchicine). Other drugs may enhance nephrotoxic effects of CsA (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs [NSAIDs], aminoglycosides, quinolones, angiotensin-converting enzyme [ACE] inhibitors, amphotericin B). Common adverse effects include gastrointestinal complaints, hirsutism, gingival hyperplasia, and mild elevation in serum alkaline phosphatase levels. Tremor, paresthesias, electrolyte disturbances (hyperkalemia and hypomagnesemia), and hyperuricemia may also occur. Hypertension occurs in nearly 20% of patients receiving CsA and is controlled by either dose reduction or anti-hypertensive treatment. A significant adverse effect is nephrotoxicity, which is reversible after adjustment of the

dose or drug discontinuation. Physicians should avoid use of CsA in patients with impaired renal function (see Table 82.1).

Use in Lupus Nephritis. CsA, used in combination with GC, has demonstrated efficacy in PLN, including refractory cases. .67, In the CYCLOFA-LUNE trial, 40 patients with newly diagnosed PLN and mild renal insufficiency received sequential inductionmaintenance therapy with either CYC (oral boluses 10 mg/kg) or CsA (4 to 5 mg/kg/day, then tapered), both combined with oral GC. At 9 months, 76% of the CYC group and 68% of the CsA group achieved renal response; extended follow-up after median 7.7 years showed comparable rates of ESKD, adverse events, mean Cr, proteinuria, and Systemic Lupus International Collaborating Clinics (SLICC) damage score. Investigators have also demonstrated comparable efficacy of AZA versus CsA as maintenance therapies in patients with diffuse PLN and preserved renal function. Together, CsA may be used for the induction and maintenance treatment of proliferative LN but only as a second-line option due to its safety profile. In MLN, an older trial41 compared treatment with prednisone alone or in combination with CsA or pulses of IV CYC. Remission rates at 1 year were 27% for prednisone, 60% for IV CYC, and 83% for CsA. After treatment discontinuation, however, rates of nephrotic syndrome relapse were 10-fold higher in the CsA than in the IV CYC group, suggesting that, at a minimum, patients treated with CsA may require maintenance therapy to prevent relapses in MLN.

Use in Extrarenal Lupus. Uncontrolled studies have shown improvement in disease activity (clinical and serologic) and cytopenias with modest GC reduction in patients with SLE who received low-dose CsA.72-74 The British Isles Lupus Assessment Group (BILAG) group compared the steroid-sparing effect of CsA (2.5 to 3.5 mg/kg/day) versus AZA (2 to 2.5 mg/kg/day) in moderately severe lupus. Although nearly 50% of the patients failed to respond, the mean reduction in prednisolone dose at 12 months was 9.5 mg in the CsA group and 10.2 mg in the AZA group. The two groups performed similarly with regard to disease activity, response to treatment, flares, damage accrual, and qualityof-life measures. CsA may be used as an alternative steroid-sparing agent in patients with SLE, especially for hematologic manifestations, but with close monitoring of renal function and blood pressure.

### Tacrolimus

Pharmacology. Tacrolimus (TAC) is a 10 to 100 times more potent CNI than CsA. Dose-dependent reversible nephrotoxicity and blood pressure elevation are less frequent than with CsA. Other adverse effects include cardiomyopathy in children, anxiety, seizures, delirium and tremor, diabetes, and hyperlipidemia. Small uncontrolled studies have shown favorable responses to TAC in patients with autoimmune thrombocytopenia or minor lupus flare.76,

Use in Lupus Nephritis. Controlled studies and meta-analyses have demonstrated beneficial effects of TAC in proliferative and membranous LN including refractory disease. In Asian patients with LN with relatively preserved renal function, TAC exhibited fast anti-proteinuric action and at least equal efficacy with MMF or IV CYC in inducing renal response at 6 to 12 months.79-81 In Chinese patients with class III and IV (81%) or pure class V (19%) LN, prednisolone (0.6 mg/kg/day) was administered with either TAC (0.06 to 0.1 mg/kg/day) or MMF (2 to 3 g/day). At 6 months, complete renal response was achieved by 59% of patients in the MMF group and 62% of patients in the TAC group. During maintenance with AZA,

proteinuric and nephritic flares developed in 24% of patients and 18% of patients in the MMF group and in 35% and 27% in the TAC group, respectively. Long-term maintenance treatment with TAC has also been used, although hypertension and/ or metabolic adverse events may develop in a considerable proportion of patients. Validation of drug efficacy in non-Asian populations is pending.

Recent interest in TAC and generally in CNIs, has been fueled further by its combination with MMF to treat LN, as part of a socalled "multitarget" therapy.84, A recent large RCT in Chinese patients, including both phases of LN treatment (n = 362 and 206 in induction and maintenance phases, respectively) found the combination of TAC with MMF to be superior to IV CYC in the induction phase (overall response rate at 6 months: 83.5% vs. 63.0%, respectively, P < 0.001) and equal to AZA for maintenance (similar relapse rate at 18 months: 5.47% vs. 7.62%, respectively, with fewer adverse events in the multitarget arm). 86,

Voclosporin. Voclosporin is a novel CNI. Its predictable pharmacokinetics and milder inhibition of calcineurin eliminate the need for therapeutic drug level monitoring and also account for fewer side effects than "legacy" CNIs. In two clinical trials (one phase 2 and a larger phase 3), the addition of voclosporin (orally 23.7 mg bid) to standard-of-care therapy (MMF plus GCs) significantly improved complete renal response rate with a rapid reduction in proteinuria.89, This led to its approval by both U.S. and European authorities for the treatment of LN, in combination with MMF and GCs. As is the case with CsA and TAC, voclosporin may cause reduction in estimated GFR (eGFR) requiring dose modification. Regular monitoring of eGFR and blood pressure are required in clinical usage of voclosporin in patients with LN (Table 82.1).

### Intravenous Immunoglobulin

Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) exerts immunomodulatory effects by interaction with anti-idiotypic antibodies, interference with complement and cytokines, cytolysis of target cells, induction of apoptosis through Fc receptors, and modulation of costimulatory molecules. A systematic review of 13 studies concluded that treatment with IVIG resulted in significant reduction in the SLE disease activity scores and improvements in serum complement levels. Improvements in cytopenias, especially immune thrombocytopenia and hemolytic anemia, proteinuria, arthritis, fever, and mucocutaneous manifestations, have been reported. Common adverse events include fever, myalgia, headache, and arthralgia; less common are aseptic meningitis, nephropathy in patients who receive sucrose-containing preparations, and thromboembolic complications in older patients with atherosclerotic risk factors.

### Biologic Therapies

### Belimumab

Belimumab is a fully human monoclonal antibody against the B lymphocyte stimulator (BlyS) protein. Following successful RCTs, it is approved either for IV (10 mg/kg/month) or subcutaneous (200 mg/wk) administration.94-96 Enrolled patients in RCTs had moderately active SLE (average SLEDAI 9 to 10; severe renal or neuropsychiatric lupus was excluded) and were receiving combinations of HCQ and GC, with or without immunosuppressants. Belimumab treatment resulted in a modest yet statistically significant reduction in disease activity (difference in primary endpoint, the composite SLE responder index [SRI], ranging from

9% to 14.7% in the three studies, OR to attain SRI response at 52 weeks 1.31 for belimumab). Stronger effects were observed in the musculoskeletal (arthritis), mucocutaneous (alopecia, ulcers, malar rash) and immunologic domains, and skin vasculitis. Belimumab-treated patients exhibited significantly reduced risk for severe SLE flares (HR, 0.74), modest reductions in GC dose, and improvements in fatigue and health-related quality of life.99, Post hoc analysis showed that drug effectiveness was higher in patients with baseline SLEDAI scores of ≥10 or serologic activity (low C3/C4 and/or high antidouble-stranded DNA [dsDNA]]) or those who were on GCs upon enrollment. A series of observational studies have subsequently confirmed efficacy of the drug in real-life patient populations.102-104 Belimumab should be considered in extrarenal disease with inadequate control (ongoing disease activity or frequent flares) to first-line treatments (typically including combination of HCQ and prednisone with or without immunosuppressive agents) and the inability to taper GC daily dose to acceptable levels (i.e., maximum 7.5 mg/day). Long-term follow-up data (up to 7 years) suggest that belimumab is generally well tolerated, with no significant increase in risk for serious infections, although infusion reactions can be encountered, especially during the first three infusions. 105,

In addition to its use in extrarenal disease, belimumab was recently approved as an add-on to standard therapy in LN. In the BLISS-LN phase 3 RCT, 448 patients were randomized to receive standard-of-care (MMF or low-dose IV CYC) with either belimumab or placebo, together with GCs. At the end of the 104-week follow-up, significantly more patients in the belimumab group met the endpoint of primary efficacy renal response (defined as urine protein to creatinine ratio (UPCR) ≤0.7, eGFR ≥80% pre-flare value or ≥60 mL/min/1.73 m2, and no use of rescue therapy for treatment failure; met by 43% vs. 32%, respectively; OR, 1.6; 95% CI, 1.0 to 2.3). Adverse events were comparable between the two groups. In a post hoc analysis of this study, belimumab was also found to reduce the risk of renal flares by 55% (HR, 0.45; 95% CI, 0.28 to 0.72) and the rate of eGFR decline (eGFR slope difference, 3.61; 95% CI, 0.15 to 7.06), compared with placebo. Based on these findings, belimumab received approval as a therapeutic option for LN, in combination with either MMF or CYC.

### Rituximab

Rituximab (RTX) is a chimeric mouse-human monoclonal antibody against CD20 on B-cells. Controlled clinical trials both in extrarenal SLE and in LN have failed to show statistically significant clinical benefit, but multiple observational studies have provided evidence for drug efficacy. In extrarenal disease, uncontrolled studies including more than 1200 patients suggest the efficacy of RTX, which is mainly used as add-on therapy to GCs, other immunosuppressive (IS) agents, or both.109-111 Complete or partial responses are noted in 64% to 91% of patients within 3 to 9 months, particularly in the musculoskeletal (arthritis), hematology (autoimmune hemolytic anemia [AIHA], thrombocytopenia), and immunology domains. As a rule, more than one IS drug need to have failed before RTX administration, except in cases of severe autoimmune thrombocytopenia, due to the drug's demonstrated efficacy both in lupus and in isolated immune thrombocytopenia. In LN, observational data from 300 patients with active LN despite treatment with GCs plus immunosuppressives (CYC, MMF, or AZA) support RTX efficacy. After an average of 60 weeks, rates of complete and partial renal response were approximately 40% and 34%, respectively, with lower responses in mixed class V and III to IV or pure class V LN. In a nonrandomized study, patients with active

proliferative LN received induction treatment with GCs plus either RTX (1000 mg on days 0 and 14), MMF (2 to 2.5 g/day), or lowdose IV CYC (3 g), followed by maintenance with AZA, MMF, or CsA. Renal response rates at 12 months were comparable between the RTX, MMF, and IV CYC groups (71%, 53%, and 65%, respectively). In lupus membranous nephropathy, a retrospective multicenter study of RTX monotherapy in 15 patients reported a complete response (CR) rate of 58% at 12 months.

Prior to the COVID-19 pandemic, RTX was associated with a slightly increased risk for infections, most of which were mild, with no serious signal for serious or opportunistic infections. Nevertheless, during the pandemic, it became clear that treatment with RTX is accompanied by increased risk for hospitalization and other adverse sequelae, across a spectrum of rheumatic conditions, including SLE, due to its impact on the patient's capacity to produce neutralizing antibodies. This reality, combined with the drug's off-label status, suggests that RTX should currently be considered only after failure of other therapies in multidrug refractory SLE.

### Anifrolumab

Anifrolumab is a monoclonal antibody against the type I interferon receptor, thus inhibiting signaling from all type I interferons, which have a central role in SLE pathogenesis. Following a very successful phase 2 trial,117 the drug was tested on two large phase 3 trials (Treatment of Uncontrolled Lupus via the Interferon Pathway [TULIP]-1 and -2) in a large number of patients.118, Despite the fact that TULIP-1 did not meet its primary endpoint, SRI-4, in both studies a significantly higher number of SLE patients achieved a British Isles Lupus Assessment Group (BILAG)-based Composite Lupus Assessment (BICLA) response, and total TULIP data showed that anifrolumab reduced skin and joint disease activity, allowed better GC tapering, and reduced flares significantly more than placebo. Following these results, the drug was approved in 2021 for the treatment of moderate to severe extrarenal SLE.

Anifrolumab has also been tested in a phase 2 RCT in 147 patients with LN, using two different regimens (basic regimen, 300 mg/month; intensified regimen, 900 mg for 3 months and 300 mg thereafter) in combination with MMF and GCs versus placebo. Although the study did not meet its primary endpoint of proteinuria reduction in combined anifrolumab groups versus placebo, this was due to increased drug clearance and suboptimal exposure to anifrolumab in patients receiving the basic regimen. More patients in the anifrolumab intensified regimen achieved complete remission (~15% difference compared with placebo) and sustained GC reduction (~20% difference); currently, the drug is being tested in a larger phase 3 trial in LN.

Both in extrarenal SLE and in LN, anifrolumab seems to be associated with an increased risk of herpes zoster infection. Although most cases were mild or moderate, caution is needed for this particular type of infection in patients starting anifrolumab. ### Therapies in Development

### Janus Kinase Inhibition

Baricitinib is an oral selective Janus kinase (JAK)1 and JAK2 inhibitor approved for the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis (RA). In a recent randomized, 24-week phase 2 study in 314 patients with skin and joint disease, the 4 mg/day dose of baricitinib was accompanied by a marginally statistically significant difference in the proportion of patients achieving resolution of arthritis or rash, as defined by the SLEDAI (OR for resolution 1.8 against placebo, P = 0.04), and a safety profile consistent with previous baricitinib studies. Following this observation, two large identical phase 3 studies were launched (SLE-BRAVE-I and -II) in a total of more than 1500 SLE patients. The results were recently published and yielded discordant results in the primary endpoint, SRI-4 (positive results in BRAVE-I and negative in BRAVE-II).122, Moreover,

major secondary endpoints, like GC tapering and risk for flares, were not met in either study. Thus further development of baricitinib in SLE has been halted.

### B Cell Depletion Beyond d Rituximab

Obinutuzumab, a humanized anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody (type II) glycoengineered for greater affinity for the FcγRIII on effector cells to promote more potent B-cell depletion than RTX, was tested in the NOBILITY trial, a phase 2 RCT in 125 LN patients. Obinutuzumab was superior to placebo in achieving complete renal response at 52 and 104 weeks (35% vs. 23%; difference, 12%; 95% CI, -3.4% to 28%, which was statistically significant; and 41% vs 23%; difference, 19%; 95% CI, 2.7% to 35%, respectively) without any significant safety concerns. Following these promising results, the use of obinutuzumab in proliferative LN is currently being evaluated in a phase 3 study.

### Management of Specific Systemic Lupus Erythematosus Manifestations and Treatment Algorithms

### KEY POINTS

### Mucocutaneous and Joint Disease

For all forms of cutaneous involvement (including photosensitivity) in SLE, the use of sun protection measures (broad spectrum sunscreens and protective clothing) cannot be overemphasized. Smoking cessation is essential, as it also interferes with efficacy of anti-malarials in cutaneous lupus. Topical GCs reduce redness and scaling. Topical CNIs (TAC, pimecrolimus) are a useful alternative, especially for the face, because they cause fewer atrophic and rosacea-like effects than topical steroids.

First-line systemic treatment for skin disease consists of antimalarials, if not already prescribed, which can be used alone or in combination with oral GCs at moderate doses. HCQ is the anti-malarial of choice due to its additional beneficial effects in SLE; in cases of incomplete response or evidence of retinopathy, quinacrine may be used (in the former case, as add-on therapy to HCQ), although it is not available in all countries. Almost 40% of patients will not respond to this first-line treatment. In such cases, MTX can be added, as it has shown efficacy in refractory subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus (SCLE) and discoid

lupus erythematosus. Alternative choices for conventional synthetic drugs are retinoids, dapsone, and MMF.130-132 From biologic drugs, anifrolumab seems to have particular efficacy in skin disease, although formal real-life evidence is still pending. Belimumab and RTX have also shown efficacy in mucocutaneous manifestations, but reported studies did not use a validated assessment for response of skin lesions; RTX may be less efficacious in chronic cutaneous lupus.110, Finally, thalidomide should be reserved for severe recalcitrant CLE cases, because of its serious and potentially irreversible neurotoxicity (Fig. 82.2).134,

In mild lupus arthritis, anti-malarials will usually suffice. In persistent disease, utilization of DMARDs is advocated, particularly MTX. Patients with inadequate response to DMARDs may benefit from belimumab treatment, although the latter is less efficacious in cases of severe arthritis resembling RA. In such cases, or in SLERA overlap syndromes refractory to DMARDs, RTX can be used instead.

### Lupus Nephritis

Traditional therapeutic strategies in LN include an initial treatment period, aimed at substantially improving disease activity (or even attaining remission), followed by a maintenance phase, in which the goal is to maximize the therapeutic effect, consolidate the response and prevent relapses. MMF and IV CYC, both in combination with GCs, are considered equally effective for initial therapy; MMF or AZA is recommended for subsequent therapy (usually when MMF or IV CYC has been used for initial therapy, respectively). The recent advent of belimumab and voclosporin has challenged this sequential approach,136 suggesting that some—if not all—patients could be treated with upfront combination therapies from the beginning (i.e., multitarget therapy with voclosporin/TAC plus MMF, or belimumab plus MMF or CYC). While this is currently a matter of debate, patient risk stratification, according to renal pathology and demographic, clinical, and laboratory characteristics, can enable the identification of patients at risk poor prognosis who may benefit from more aggressive initial therapy (Table 82.4). Fig. 82.3 and Table 82.5 summarize a potential treatment algorithm for LN.

### Treatment of Renal Flares— Relapsing Disease

Approximately 30% to 50% of patients with moderate to severe PLN will relapse after achieving partial or complete remission. Nephritic flares are characterized by active urine sediment and reproducible increases of Cr (≥30% increase) and may adversely affect renal prognosis. In contrast, proteinuric flares without significant changes in renal function have a more benign prognosis. The risk factors for progression to ESKD after a nephritic flare are marked loss of renal function (Cr > 2 mg/dL) at the time of response, partial response to therapy, and high chronicity and activity indices at renal biopsy. A repeat renal biopsy at the time of renal flare should be considered, for the possibility of histologic class switch or presence of advanced chronicity.

Therapeutic options for relapsing disease include (1) switching between MMF and CYC,139 (2) CNIs (alone or as add-on to MMF), (3) addition of belimumab (if not used from baseline), or (4) RTX. For severe nephritic flares, aggressive cytotoxic therapy with monthly pulses of IV CYC (if not previously used) combined with IV MP is the authors' preferred approach.

Nephroprotective Therapies in Lupus Nephritis. In addition to immunosuppressive treatment, strategies and therapies aiming

at preserving kidney function and decelerating further nephron loss are of utmost importance. Salt intake should be minimized, while agents that inhibit the renin—angiotensin—aldosterone axis (ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers) are recommended for all patients with LN since they have potent antiproteinuric effects in addition to their blood pressure-lowering properties. More recently, the drug class of sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT-2i) has gained significant attention, as these drugs have been found to exert kidney and cardiac protective effects across a spectrum of diseases. Thus, since LN patients are by definition at increased risk for chronic kidney disease, they may be ideal candidates for this treatment. In support of this, increased SGLT-2 expression has been found by transcriptomic analysis in kidney samples from patients with LN, mainly in the tubulointerstitial space. Although a small case series showed significant reduction in proteinuria with empagliflozin in LN patients under stable immunosuppressive therapy, 142 a first exploratory phase I/II

trial in 38 SLE patients (17 with LN) did not show improvement of proteinuria. Overall, despite their promising nephroprotective potential, more data will be needed prior to universal recommendation of SGLT2-I in LN. Potential candidates could include patients with GFR less than 60 mL/min or proteinuria of at least 1+ by dipstick (albuminuria more than 30 mg/24 h or urinary albumin creatinine ratio [UACR] ≥ 30 mg/g).

### Central Nervous System n Disease

Neuropsychiatric SLE (NPSLE) represents a clinical challenge because of the often ambiguous attribution of neuropsychiatric syndromes to SLE per se and the paucity of controlled trials. Attribution of neuropsychiatric manifestations to SLE requires a multidisciplinary approach to rule out mimics (infections, malignancy, and others) and should consider the presence of risk ("favoring") factors (type and timing of manifestation, presence of generalized, nonneurologic disease

activity, abnormal neuroimaging and cerebrospinal fluid analysis, positive aPLs), as well as confounding factors favoring other diagnoses (Fig. 82.4). Immunosuppressive therapy (GCs alone or in combination with AZA for mild to moderate cases and IV CYC or RTX for severe cases) is advocated for neuropsychiatric events thought to reflect an immune/inflammatory process (e.g., acute confusional state, aseptic meningitis, myelitis, optic neuritis, refractory seizure disorder, peripheral neuropathies, or psychosis) or when they occur in the context of active generalized lupus. 146-148' Anti-coagulation therapy is recommended for events, especially thrombotic cerebrovascular disease, related to aPLs.149, If aPLs are absent, anti-platelet therapy can be used. The two pathophysiologic processes (inflammatory and thrombotic) may not be easy to distinguish or may coexist in a given patient. In these cases, a combination of immunosuppressive and anti-coagulant/anti-thrombotic therapy may be considered, as in the case of a cerebrovascular disease occurring in the presence of generalized disease activity.

### Hematologic Disease

Peripheral cytopenias are common but usually mild in SLE. A thorough clinical and laboratory evaluation is necessary

to exclude offending drugs or other secondary causes. Mild cytopenias require no specific therapy other than regular monitoring.

Hematologic manifestations frequently necessitating immunosuppressive treatment are thrombocytopenia and AIHA. Initial and subsequent management of significant lupus thrombocytopenia is outlined in Fig. 82.5.18 When treatment is indicated (thrombocytopenia: platelet count <20 to 30 x 103/mm3 or active bleeding, AIHA: Hb <8 to 9 mg/dL), GCs are the mainstay of treatment. Use of IV MP pulses during the immediate treatment phase and early initiation of GC-sparing agents (AZA, MMF, or CsA) is encouraged, in order to facilitate GC tapering. IV immunoglobulin may also be given in the acute phase, if the response to GC is not adequate. In patients with no response to GC (i.e., failure to reach a platelet count of >50,000/mm3) or relapses, RTX should be considered, while CYC has also been used. 112, Thrombopoietin (TPO) agonists or splenectomy should be considered when all other therapeutic options have failed. Treatment of AIHA follows the same principles, with the exception of TPO agonists.

### Antiphospholipid Syndrome

aPL (anti-cardiolipin [aCL], anti—β2-glycoprotein I [anti- β2GPI], and lupus anti-coagulant [LAC]) are encountered in 30% to 40% of SLE patients and confer increased risk for thrombotic events, adverse obstetric outcomes, and irreversible damage accrual.153, The combination of vascular thrombosis, obstetric morbidity, or both, and persistently positive aPL measured at least 12 weeks apart define the APS. Studies in APS have not distinguished between primary APS and SLE-APS patients; thus the principles of APS treatment (anti-platelet or anti-coagulation, target international normalized ratio [INR]]) do not differ between the two conditions and are described in detail in Chapter 83. The EULAR has also issued a recommendation set for the treatment of APS.

A distinct type of small-vessel vaso-occlusive nephropathy with histologic features of thrombotic microangiopathy and chronic vascular lesions, termed APS nephropathy, should be suspected in APA-positive patients with SLE with hypertension, proteinuria (usually subnephrotic range), hematuria, and renal impairment. These patients may benefit from anti-platelet or anti-thrombotic therapy, although development of ESKD is still common. Aberrant activation of the mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) pathway has been documented in APS nephropathy and APSrelated renal vascular lesions superimposed on inflammatory LN, suggesting that agents targeting this pathway may prove useful for these patients.

### Special Issues: Treat-to-Target, Refractory Disease and Lupus in Pregnancy

### KEY POINTS

### Treat-to-Target in Systemic Lupus Erythematosus

Similar to RA, the principle of treating to target has been proposed for SLE. Despite the phenotypic heterogeneity, certain goals of treatment may be applicable to all patients. These include (1) control of disease activity, (2) prevention of disease flares, (3) minimization of irreversible damage accrual, (4) avoidance of drug toxicity, and (5) improvement of patient quality of life (Fig. 82.6). These goals are tightly interdependent, and their accomplishment is best achieved through a strategic plan tailored to each patient rather than being a matter of individual drugs. This strategy has to take into consideration patient preferences, age, childbearing potential, safety, and cost of available drugs.

Regarding control of disease activity, the optimal target should be the absence of activity in all organ systems, accomplished with the lowest possible dose of GC and standard dose of immunosuppressive drugs. In 2021 the Definition of Remission in SLE (DORIS) Task

Force defined remission as clinical SLEDAI (i.e., excluding serologic items) = 0, physician global assessment (PGA) <0.5 (0 to 3), prednisone 5 mg/day or less, and stable anti-malarials, immunosuppressives, and biologic drugs. If remission cannot be achieved, the Lupus Low Disease Activity State (LLDAS), defined as a SLEDAI-2K ≤4 without major organ activity, no new disease activity, PGA ≤1 (0 to 3), prednisone ≤7.5 mg/day, and well-tolerated dosages of immunosuppressive drugs, has also been associated with lower damage accrual1 [163-165; to be prognostically significant, LLDAS should be present for a substantial period of time (i.e., at least 12 months).

### Pregnancy and Fertility in Systemic Lupus Erythematosus

Pregnancy may increase disease activity and precipitate the appearance of flares, which are usually mild; 35% to 50% of lupus

patients will have evident disease activity during pregnancy. Risk factors for adverse maternal and fetal outcomes (pre-eclampsia, pregnancy loss, and preterm birth, among others) are active disease during the last 6 months before conception, HCQ discontinuation, a history of LN, and the presence of APA, especially LAC. 168, The management of a pregnant woman with an SLE flare is challenging and should be dealt with on a multidisciplinary basis (Table 82.6).

Neonatal lupus is a rare occurrence in babies born to mothers with anti-SSA/Ro or anti-SSB/La antibodies. The most serious complication is neonatal complete heart block (CHB), which occurs in ~2% of such pregnancies and carries a 20% to 30% mortality risk. Importantly, the risk of recurrence in a mother who has already born a child with CHB approaches 20%. Therefore, all women with SLE should be screened for anti-Ro/La antibodies before a planned pregnancy. The most vulnerable period for the development of conduction disturbances is between weeks 18 and 26 of gestation, during which anti-Ro/La-positive patients should be evaluated with weekly or biweekly fetal Doppler echocardiography for the prompt identification of conduction anomalies, mainly PR interval prolongation. If CHB develops, no modality reverses it.

By contrast, first-degree block may potentially be reversed by fluorinated GCs such as dexamethasone (4 mg/day) initiated at the time of diagnosis and continued throughout pregnancy. Most importantly, use of HCQ has been associated with a 50% to 60% reduced risk for recurrences of cardiac neonatal lupus, ,21,172while recent data suggest that it is also associated with a significantly (60%) reduced risk for cutaneous manifestations of the syndrome.

Regarding breastfeeding, the American College of Rheumatology (ACR) recommends that nursing is permissible for women receiving GCs, but the interval between dose and nursing should be at least 4 hours if prednisone dosage is greater than 20 mg/day. Anti-malarials and AZA may be continued during lactation; cyclosporine is also considered compatible with breastfeeding, although data are limited. On the contrary, MTX, MMF, leflunomide, and CYC are contraindicated during lactation.

Premature ovarian failure is an ageand dose-dependent adverse effect of high-dose CYC therapy; cumulative dose >10 g and age >40 are associated with a particularly increased risk. Strategies to preserve fertility in post-pubertal SLE women include hormonal contraceptives, gonadotropin-releasing hormone antagonists (GnRHa), and embryo and oocyte cryopreservation. Individual patient preferences should be considered. In a meta-analysis of 218 female SLE patients, ovarian function was preserved in 125 of 132 (94.6%) of women who received GnRHa concurrently with CYC compared with 50 of 86 (58%) of women who did not receive GnRHa (OR, 10.3). The authors recommend this protocol in high-dose CYC-treated female patients (see Table 82.3).

Hormonal contraceptive methods are generally safe for most patients with SLE with stable, inactive disease. Two RCTs found no significant increase in flares in patients without severe disease activity at study entry, and a systematic review concluded

that the benefits of use outweigh the potential risks for most contraceptive methods. However, women with aPL should avoid combined hormonal methods because of increased risk for thrombosis. Similarly, in SLE patients around menopause, hormone replacement therapy can be used for the management of prominent vasomotor menopausal manifestations, provided a stable/inactive disease status and negative APA. On the other hand, when the latter are positive, the use of hormone replacement should be carefully weighed against the risk of thrombosis and CVD. EULAR has issued recommendations related to women's health in SLE.

Assisted reproduction techniques are generally safe in SLE patients with stable, quiescent disease, as suggested by observational studies. Efficacy in terms of pregnancy rate may exceed 40%, comparable to the general population. The occurrence of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome can be avoided by the application of milder hormonal stimulation or concomitant use of GnRH antagonists. In general, the protocol used for ovulation induction should be tailored to the individual patient, after balancing the safety and risks of the procedure. Similarly, for patients who wish to pursue oocyte cryopreservation for a future pregnancy, when disease activity allows, the procedure is considered safe. It can be safely undertaken even during periods when the patient is receiving teratogenic medications not allowed during pregnancy (MMF, CYC, etc.); oocytes can be cryopreserved and used in the future when such medications will no longer be needed.

### Comorbidities

### KEY POINTS

In a patient with SLE with possible infection, the clinical syndrome, history of epidemiologic exposures, and net state of immunosuppression should be considered.

Immunizations (including against severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 [SARS—CoV-2]) are safe, effective, and important in stable, inactive patients with SLE. Live vaccines are contraindicated in patients taking immunosuppressive drugs or high-dose glucocorticoids.

Hemodialysis may be preferred versus peritoneal dialysis in end-stage renal disease. Patients should be evaluated for renal transplantation.

Strict adherence to general population guidelines for primary prevention of cardiovascular disease is recommended.

### Infections and Immunizations

### Risk Factors and General Management

Infections account for 20% to 55% of all deaths in patients with SLE. The respiratory system, urinary tract, and CNS are the most commonly involved sites. Risk of infection in SLE is associated with both disease-related and treatment-related factors; high-dose GC therapy (each increase of 10 mg/day prednisone is associated with an 11-fold increased risk for serious infection), CYC, MMF,
