and RTX are all associated with an increased risk for infection. Additionally, high disease activity, severe leukopenia, and presence of kidney involvement also contribute independently. 181, Regarding COVID-19, patients with SLE warrant particular attention, due to their degree of immunosuppression, frequent use of moderate to high prednisone doses, and high comorbidity burden. A report from the COVID-19 Global Rheumatology Alliance found that use of GCs, active disease, and RTX use were associated with more severe COVID-19 outcomes (along with features similar to the general population like male sex, older age, and comorbidities). In general, protection against infections should be proactive, focusing both on primary prevention and on timely recognition and treatment.

The evaluation of a patient with lupus who receives immunosuppressive therapy and is seen with symptoms or signs suggestive of infection is complicated by the fact that infections can mimic a lupus flare. Findings that favor the diagnosis of infection include the presence of shaking chills, leukocytosis and/or neutrophilia (especially in the absence of steroid therapy), and high CRP. A high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hsCRP) value of >6 mg/dL has been associated with active infection in SLE (84% specificity), but this may not occasionally be the case in clinical practice. Similarly, elevated serum procalcitonin (PCT) levels may be useful to distinguish between infection and disease flare in SLE; a systematic literature review suggested that a PCT level of ≥0.5 µg/L should strongly suggest bacterial infection in the context of SLE. Pending microbiology results, empiric anti-microbial therapy (including broad-spectrum antibiotics in suspected nosocomial infection) may be instituted, based on the severity of clinical syndrome and the net state of immunosuppression (Fig. 82.7).

Early recognition of sepsis is of utmost importance; to this end, validated scores like the quick Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (qSOFA) may identify patients at risk for adverse outcome.

### Immunizations

Lupus patients should receive vaccinations according to the EULAR recommendations for vaccination of patients with autoimmune rheumatic diseases. Inactivated live vaccines (measles, mumps, rubella, polio, varicella-zoster virus [VZV], and vaccinia [smallpox]) are contraindicated in patients taking immunosuppressive drugs or prednisone at a dose greater than 20 mg/day. Vaccination against influenza and Streptococcus pneumoniae (both pneumococcal conjugate 13 and pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine 23) is mandatory, despite lower seroconversion/seroprotection rates in lupus versus healthy controls. All vaccines should preferentially be administered during disease quiescence. Vaccination against human papillomavirus (HPV) is also recommended in adolescent lupus patients, given its safety and the likelihood of persistent HPV infection and resulting squamous intraepithelial neoplasia in the context of SLE.

Herpes zoster vaccination, especially with the newer nonlive two-dose vaccine Shingrix, should also strongly be considered in all patients with lupus, as the latter are in significantly higher risk of shingles compared with the general population. Despite the fact that the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has recommended Shingrix in immunocompromised patients >18 years (including SLE) since 2021, frustratingly in many countries this is not covered by insurance for patients younger than 50 years. The older vaccine (Zostavax) is both live-attenuated and also less efficient (~65% vs. 90% protection from herpes zoster).

Finally, SARS-CoV2 vaccines are safe193 and strongly recommended for all lupus patients by both EULAR and the ACR, 194,195 although patients receiving immunosuppressive medication (especially RTX and/or MMF) may not be able to mount satisfactory antibody responses. mRNA vaccines are generally preferred over the Johnson and Johnson vaccine.

### Chronic Kidney Disease and End-Stage Kidney Disease

### Risk Factors and Dialysis

A systematic review and meta-analysis demonstrated decreased risks of LN-associated ESKD between the 1970s and 1990s (15-year risk from over 30% to 22%), which was followed by a plateau and then, surprisingly, by an increased risk in recent . Class IV LN confers the highest risk for ESKD develyears. opment. Another study showed that all-cause mortality due to LN-ESKD has decreased during the past 20 years, at least in the United States, where the mortality rate/100 patient-years declined from 11.1 in 1995 to 1999 to 6.7 in 2010 to 2014 (mortality hazard ratio, 0.51 to 0.68, depending on patient race). Infections and cardiovascular events constitute the main causes of death, although their incidence has declined accordingly.

Clinical predictors for ESKD include baseline-reduced GFR 199persistent isolated C3 and hypertension, diabetes mellitus, hypocomplementemia,200and failure to achieve renal remission, while the histologic presence of fibrinoid necrosis, fibrous crescents, and interstitial fibrosis with tubular atrophy are also associated with increased risk. In patients presenting with rapid

deterioration of renal function, immunosuppressive therapy (pulse of IV MP and IV CYC 0.4 to 0.5 g/m2, administered 8 to 10 hours before dialysis (so that the drug may be removed) may continue during dialysis.

The 5-year survival rate of patients with SLE on dialysis approximates 80% to 90%, comparable with that in non-SLE dialysis patients. Hemodialysis may be the first choice of renal replacement therapy, especially for patients who are still on

immunosuppressive therapy, due to increased rates of infectious complications (most commonly peritonitis) in patients on chronic ambulatory peritoneal dialysis, although the latter is generally considered safe in SLE. Discontinuation of cytotoxic therapy may be considered in patients with steadily rising Cr to ≥5 mg/ dL with inactive urine sediment, renal biopsy showing exclusively scarring and atrophy, or contracted renal size. Spending more than 2 years on dialysis before kidney transplantation may have a negative impact on survival. Nevertheless, a period of at least 3 months on dialysis may allow some patients to recover adequate renal function for significant time periods.

### Renal Transplantation

Renal transplantation is a viable alternative for lupus patients with ESKD. Graft and patient survival rates are generally comparable with those in other patient groups, although ethnic background may have an impact on long-term renal survival.205, Preemptive transplantation should be considered because it is associated with superior graft and patient outcomes.

There are no prospective studies comparing various immunosuppressive regimens after renal transplantation in SLE. CNIs are generally included in the induction phase (6 to 12 months) to prevent acute transplant rejection. Their use should be minimized during the maintenance phase, and other immunosuppressive agents (MMF, AZA) should preferentially be employed. Surveillance biopsy studies have shown that subclinical recurrence of LN (usually mild class I/II) in the renal allograft is not rare, but this is rarely a significant clinical problem. Risk factors for recurrence include black race, female sex, and living-donor transplantation. APS has been associated with post-transplant renal thrombosis and poor graft outcome and warrants anti-coagulation therapy.

### Cardiovascular Morbidity

SLE is an independent risk factor for CVD due to both traditional and disease-related risk factors, such as persistent disease activity, presence of aPL and use of GC. Biomarkers such as proinflammatory high-density lipoprotein (HDL) or hsCRP are elevated in lupus patients and have been correlated with carotid intima media thickness (CIMT), a surrogate marker for subclinical atherosclerosis. Mendelian randomization and network analysis show shared genetic association between lupus and coronary artery disease.

Tight control of traditional CVD risk factors is recommended for patients with SLE. Primary CVD prevention should follow the principles applied to the general population. In all lupus patients, the 10-year CVD risk should be calculated, using one of the validated prediction scores. Importantly, because many SLE patients are young, RR will give a more accurate prediction than absolute risk. The importance of smoking cessation cannot be overemphasized. Hypertension should be controlled below 130/80 mm Hg. For dyslipidemia, two RCTs in adult and pediatric SLE have failed to show benefits of atorvastatin in CIMT and coronary artery calcium.216, Accordingly, lipidlowering therapy in lupus should follow the guidelines for the general population. Low-dose aspirin reduces the risk for incident CVD in SLE (HR = 0.24 in one retrospective study),218 but its universal use for primary CVD prevention is discouraged by the recent studies in the general population, which showed the benefits of aspirin to be largely counterbalanced by a significantly larger bleeding hazard.

### Osteoporosis

Persistent disease activity, premature menopause caused by use of gonadotoxic drugs, vitamin D deficiency, and use of GCs all contribute to reduced BMD in SLE. Lifestyle modifications, such as exercise uptake and maintaining a normal body mass index, are important, as are smoking cessation and reduction of alcohol consumption. Vitamin D supplementation is recommended in cases of deficiency (<10 ng/mL) or insufficiency (<20 ng/mL), to maintain 25-OH vitamin D levels greater than 30 ng/mL.

For the prevention of GC-induced osteoporosis, the ACR guidelines for the general population include fracture risk stratification, including calculation of the FRAX score for patients over 40 years. If treatment is warranted, bisphosphonates are generally considered the drugs of first choice.

### Malignancy in Lupus

Patients with SLE have a slightly increased risk for overall cancer development with pooled RR of 1.18 (95% CI, 1.00 to 1.38) from 3694 events across >80,000 patients. Certain types of malignancies occur more commonly in patients with SLE, in particular non-Hodgkin's lymphoma (NHL) and cervical and lung cancer. Immunosuppressive therapy, viral exposures, and the disease per se have been implicated for this altered risk.

NHL is associated with SLE (systemic inflammatory response syndrome [SIRS], 3.6 to 4.3), even in pediatric-onset disease, 224-226 with diffuse large B cell lymphoma being the most common subtype. Hodgkin's lymphoma (HL) is also more frequent (SIRS, 3.2). Accordingly, a high index of suspicion is necessary for early detection of lymphoma, followed by aggressive investigation and a low threshold for lymph node biopsy.

Cervical dysplasia is increased in women with SLE (pooled OR, 8.7227) as a result of impaired clearance of HPV. Screening cervical cytology with HPV testing is recommended for all female patients with SLE; for women with detectable HPV DNA, subsequent screening with cervical cytology should be performed every 6 months. For the remaining patients, annual rescreening is sufficient. SLE patients under 25 years should receive vaccination against HPV, similar to the general population. Increased risk for lung cancer may be smaller than previously believed yet is higher in smokers (SIRS, 1.16 to 1.30).223, On the contrary, patients with lupus seem to have a slightly reduced risk of certain nonhematologic cancers (breast, ovarian, endometrial, and prostate: SIRS, 0.66 to 0.77). Based on the previously mentioned, preventive strategies to minimize malignancy risk are warranted in all lupus patients (disease control, judicious use of cytotoxic agents, smoking cessation, and HPV vaccination).

### Evidence and Expert-Based Recommendations sinS Systemic Lupus Erythematosus

Due to the systemic nature of SLE, multiple medical specialties are involved in the care of these patients, dictating a multidisciplinary approach. To this end, EULAR has developed recommendations covering the most important aspects of diagnosis, management, and monitoring.18, These recommendations are based on a combined evidence-based approach and expert opinion consensus. Similar sets of recommendations have also been published by

the ACR and the Pan American League of Associations for Rheumatology (PANLAR). 231,232

### Current Trends and Future Perspectives

This decade has witnessed major advances in defining risk factors and phenotypes, elucidating pathogenesis, and optimizing treatment in lupus. Studies have created novel pathogenesis and treatment paradigms that have benefited the entire fi eld of medical inflammation and autoimmunity. New classification criteria have allowed the earlier recognition for diagnosis and classification for clinical studies. Recognition of adjuvant-like factors that promote the production of type I interferon offers new targets for therapy in addition to those targeting B and T cells, cell metabolism, and various populations of effector cells. Similar to multiple sclerosis targeting of brain microglia through new drugs or drug repositioning may represent a therapeutic frontier in neuropsychiatric disease. Despite the frustrating results of the phase 3 baricitinib trials, the recent successful phase 2 study of deucravacitinib may gain a momentum for kinase inhibitors in lupus. Lupus nephritis is currently witnessing a major breakthrough, while neuropsychiatric lupus emerges as a major frontier in more recent cohorts. Fatigue is another frontier that needs to be better documented and treated. Exploration of the genetic and environmental factors (especially smoking) that determine susceptibility to disease may eventually lead to the identification of individuals at risk and elucidate the primary events that cause autoimmunity.

In contrast to monogenic diseases, the expansion of personalized medicine in lupus awaits a more complete description of predisposition. Genome-wide, next-generation sequencing efforts of single cells in target tissues now underway will provide within the next few years a more comprehensive description of the relations between genome sequence variation and clinical phenotypes.

### KEY POINTS

### Introduction

Antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) is a systemic autoimmune disease characterized by varied clinical manifestations, most commonly thrombosis or pregnancy morbidity, in the setting of persistent antiphospholipid antibodies (aPL), documented by a solid-phase serum assay (anti-cardiolipin antibody [aCL] or anti- β2-glycoprotein-I antibody [aβ2GPI] immunoglobulin [Ig]G or IgM), a coagulation assay (inhibitor of phospholipid-dependent clotting—the lupus anti-coagulant [LA] test), or both.

APS can occur as an isolated diagnosis (primary APS), or it can be associated with other systemic rheumatic diseases such as systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). Individuals with aPL positivity may present with heterogeneous disease manifestations, with varying aPL types and titers, and clinical manifestations ranging from arterial or venous thrombosis, microvascular disease, nonthrombotic manifestations such as thrombocytopenia, catastrophic antiphospholipid syndrome (CAPS), and severe placental insufficiency resulting in pregnancy morbidity.

The original Sapporo classification criteria for APS were developed in 19991 and revised in 2006.2 Given various limitations of the Revised Sapporo criteria, an international multidisciplinary effort to develop new APS classification criteria was completed in 2023, resulting in newly developed classification criteria approved by the American College of Rheumatology (ACR) and European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology (EULAR) to identify homogeneous cohorts of APS patients for research purposes.

### Epidemiology

Although the epidemiology of primary APS is still under investigation, based on a few international studies, the current estimated annual incidence is approximately 1 to 2 per 100,000 personyears, and prevalence is 50 per 100,000 person-years.4-7 However, due to significant study design limitations, an updated targeted literature review using applied methodology to derive a best available estimate noted a much higher incidence of APS in the United States of approximately 7.1 to 13.7 per 100,000 person-years. Population-based studies are needed to confirm these estimates.

Transient aPL positivity can be induced by drugs and infections. Low-titer, usually transient aCL occurs in up to 10% of normal blood donors4,7,10,11; however, persistent moderateto high-titer aCL/aβ2GPI or a positive LA test occurs in less than 1%. The prevalence of positive aPL tests increases with age, with an estimated mean age of 50 years for APS, although this requires further confirmation.4, The peak age of incidence may be lower in women (35 to 39 years) than in men (55 to 59 years); other studies report that APS incidence increases with age only in men, peaking at the age of 70 to 79 years. Although the distribution of APS by gender varies based on the cohorts studied and depends on exclusion of patients with concomitant SLE or obstetric APS, the female-to-male ratio appears to be close to 1:1.12, Prevalence of positive aPL is higher in specific disease-related subgroups. Up to 40% of SLE patients and approximately 20% of rheumatoid arthritis patients have positive aPL tests11,14; however, the incidence of APS is relatively low.

Based on a limited number of uncontrolled and non-risk-stratified studies, available data suggest an annual thrombosis incident rate ranging from 0% to 5.3% for aPL-positive patients, including those with another systemic autoimmune disease; however, in aPL-positive individuals with no other systemic autoimmune disease or thrombosis risk factors, the annual risk of first thrombosis is probably very low (<1%/year). 15, The aPL profile and patients' clinical characteristics (presence or absence of other acquired or genetic provoking thrombosis risk factors) influence the individual risk of thrombosis.

Although it is difficult to determine the association of the highrisk aPL profile in general-population patients (without concomitant autoimmune diseases) with aPL-related clinical outcomes due to the lack of robust data, systematic literature reviews and meta-analyses estimated the overall aPL frequency is 6% for pregnancy morbidity, 14% for all stroke, 17% for young (<50 years old) stroke, 11% for myocardial infarction (MI), and 10% for deep vein thrombosis (DVT).18, In the United States APS is estimated to cause approximately 50,000 pregnancy losses, 110,000 strokes, MIs, and 30, DVTs annually. CAPS, a lifethreatening condition characterized by the rapid development of systemic thromboses, is observed in less than 1% of APS cases.

### Etiology

Activation of vascular and immune cells by aPL is widely considered to be the driving force for pathologic outcomes in APS.21-23 Low levels of aPL may be present normally; one of the functions of normal aPL may be to participate in the physiologic removal of oxidized lipids. However, thrombotic events occur only occasionally in patients with persistently present aPL, and aPL are considered not only disease markers but also implicated in disease pathogenesis. However, aPL infusions in experimental models notably fail to induce thrombosis when given in isolation,24 suggesting that the antibodies are necessary but insufficient and that other factors may play an important role in the development of APS. Potential pathogenic pathways are illustrated in Fig. 83.1. The "two-hit" model of thrombosis associated with aPL proposes that an initiating "first hit" disrupts the endothelium and a "second hit" potentiates thrombosis25 in both animal models and in humans with an underlying genetic predisposition. Second hits or triggers for APS may include environmental factors (such as infection, estrogen-containing hormones), inflammation (from concomitant systemic autoimmune diseases), lifestyle and other traditional cardiovascular risk factors (smoking, obesity, hypertension, hypercholesterolemia), and prothrombotic factors (surgery, immobility, acute medical illness, pregnancy, active malignancy), although these remain to be confirmed.

Because high levels of aPL may persist for years in asymptomatic individuals, it is likely that vascular injury, endothelial cell activation, or both immediately precede the occurrence of thrombosis in those bearing the antibody. Of note, at least 50% of APS patients with vascular factors possess other acquired thrombosis risk factors at the time of their events.26, Additionally, familial studies support the concept of a genetic predisposition to APS, in part accounted for by the human leukocyte antigen (HLA) system, with the most consistent associations being HLA-DR4 and HLA-DRw53.28-30 Other genes may also play a role in APS pathogenesis, including encoding interferon regulatory factor 5 and encoding signal transducer and activator of transcription (STAT) 4.31

However, certain infection-induced aPLs (syphilitic and nonsyphilitic Treponema, Borrelia burgdorferi, HIV, Leptospira, or parasites) are thought to bind phospholipids directly. Potential links between APS and COVID-19 have been examined based on similar immunothrombotic features of both diseases; shared mechanisms such as molecular mimcry, neoepitope formation, and phosphatidylserine exposure are proposed to explain aPL development in CÓVID-19.41, While numerous studies have described high aPL titers in hospitalized patients with SARS-CoV-2 infection who experienced macrovascular thrombotic events, 43-47 substantial heterogeneity exists across studies of patients with COVID-19 in terms of overall aPL prevalence (up to 50%), use of anti-coagulation at time of LA testing, and variation in aPL type (ranging from IgG/IgM isotypes of aCL to various "noncriteria" aPL [including IgG/IgM isotypes of anti-phosphatidylserine/ prothrombin (aPS/PT) and IgA isotypes of aCL and aβ2GPI]). Further research is warranted to determine whether aPL induced by SARS-CoV-2 infection are transient, as reported in other viral infections, or persistent and more likely to be associated with long-term thrombotic risk.

Drugs (chlorpromazine, procainamide, quinidine, and phenytoin) and malignancies (lymphoproliferative disorders) can also induce β2GPI-independent aPL. Recent data debunks the belief that cofactor-independent aPL production is nonpathogenic and may increase thrombosis risk in vivo.48, Conversely, autoimmune aPL bind β2GPI or other phospholipid-binding plasma proteins, which in turn bind negatively charged phospholipids such as cardiolipin (β2GPI-dependent aPL). Variation in activation of certain intra-cellular signaling molecules may determine which genes are upregulated in response to aPL activity and, thus, which clinical phenotypes of APS will manifest.

### Target Receptors and Intra-cellular Signal Transduction

In animal models, infusion of aβ2GPI increases the protein expression of tissue factor, which leads to activation of the coagulation cascade. aPL binding to β2GPI on cellular surfaces upregulates the expression of prothrombotic cellular adhesion molecules such as E-selectin and tissue factor. Notably, people congenitally lacking β2GPI59 and β2GPI knockout mice appear normal.

The putative receptor of β2GPI binding protein that transduces signals from the cell membrane to the nucleus is not yet identified and may vary among cells. Many studies report the importance of aPL interaction with cell-surface TLR4, annexin A2, and apoER2 (a member of the low-density lipoprotein receptor superfamily, also known as lipoprotein receptor-related protein 8) in the activation of endothelial cells in APS.60-62 ApoER2 associates with

β2GPI at the cell membrane. Other candidate receptors have been suggested: TLR2, calreticulin, and nucleolin. Both nuclear factor kB and p38 mitogen-activated protein kinase play a role in the downstream intra-cellular signaling cascade.63, In addition, through downregulation of the STAT5, aPL inhibit the production of placental prolactin and insulin growth factor—binding protein-165 and adversely affect the formation of a trophoblast syncytium, trophoblast migration, invasion, and placental apoptosis—all processes that are required for normal placental development. Studies with human first-trimester extravillous trophoblasts demonstrate that β2GPI antibodies trigger production of pro-inflammatory cytokines (such as interleukin [IL]-1, IL-7, and IL-8) via TLR4.66 Other receptors may also be involved, but the exact mechanisms are not understood.

### Activation of Complement Cascade

aPL also initiate complement activation. aPLβ2GPI dimer binding to cell surfaces activates the classical complement cascade and thus initiates an intra-cellular signaling cascade, probably through the C5a and β2GPI surface receptors. Activated complement fragments recruit and activate inflammatory effector cells, including monocytes, neutrophils, and platelets, leading to the release of pro-inflammatory products (e.g., TNF, oxidants, proteases) and the induction of a prothrombotic phenotype.25,

Complement-mediated disruption of endothelial and trophoblast function partly explains pregnancy complications and microthrombosis associated with aPL. Around the time of a thrombotic event, patients with APS demonstrate increased complement activation and cell surface deposition of terminal complement C5b-9; additionally, rare germline mutations in complement regulatory genes that limit activation of the alternative pathway can be identified in patients with CAPS. Placental thrombosis and aPL interactions with decidual cells may also contribute to pregnancy complications.

In experimental animal models, aPL cause fetal resorption and increase the size and duration of trauma-induced venous and arterial thrombi.69, Inhibiting complement activation prevents experimental aPL-induced fetal death and angiogenic dysregulation—associated abnormal placental development and pre-eclampsia; C5 knockout mice carry pregnancies normally despite aPL, 71 implying that a complement-mediated effector mechanism is an absolute requirement for fetal death to occur. Complement activation triggers production of inflammatory mediators such as TNF and influences placental development and vascular remodeling. In addition, the reduction of heparin-binding epidermal growth factor—like expression mediated by aPL leads to defective placentation in APS. A role for complement in pathogenesis of pre-eclampsia associated with APS is supported by the presence of C4d, a complement fragment and a marker of classical complement pathway activation, in the placentae of women with SLE and/or APS and women with pre-eclampsia, whereas it is absent in healthy controls.74-76 Recent data from a large cohort of pregnant patients also suggest that circulating markers of complement activation, particularly the alternative pathway (Bb and C5b-9), contribute to adverse pregnancy outcomes in patients with SLE and/or aPL positivity.

The role of local thrombosis in pregnancy complications is less clear. Complement activation is also required for experimental thrombosis.71, Compared with control mice, mice deficient in complement factors C3, C5, and C6 demonstrate reduced thrombotic responses following aPL administration and vascular

injury. Complement activation in APS may be modulated by rivaroxaban, a direct factor Xa inhibitor, based on recent evidence that levels of activation markers C3a, C5a, SC5b-9, and Bb fragment were reduced in thrombotic APS patients after switching from warfarin to rivaroxaban treatment in the Rivaroxaban in Antiphospholipid Syndrome (RAPS) trial.80, In addition, heparin attenuates activation of complement.

### Activated Protein C Resistance

Although the most common antigens recognized by aPL are the phospholipid binding proteins β2GPI and prothrombin, the anticoagulant protein C pathway, which plays a central role in regulation of coagulation and maintenance of blood fluidity, may also be a key aPL target. Activated protein C resistance strongly predisposes to venous thromboembolism (VTE). In vitro, aPL induces activated protein C resistance; the autoantibodies compete with activated protein C for phospholipid binding, thereby limiting the access of protein C to its substrates. The effect in vivo is currently unknown. Thrombotic APS patients have greater resistance to both recombinant human-activated protein C and activation of endogenous protein C, suggesting that high-avidity anti—protein C antibodies, associated with greater activated protein C resistance, may provide a marker for a severe thrombotic phenotype. . Animal models are needed to investigate the role of aPL-induced activated protein C resistance in the development of VTE in APS patients.

### Other Mechanisms

Substantial research continues to unravel underlying mechanisms of aPL-induced thrombosis and targets for treatment. Other possible contributory mechanisms of aPL-mediated thrombosis include oxidative stress, impaired function of endothelial nitric oxide synthase, increased expression of glycoprotein IIb/IIIa, decreased tissue factor inhibitor activation on monocytes, reduction of fbrinolysis, and disruption of the annexin V anti-coagulant shield. Neutrophils may also be directly activated by aβ2GPI that recognize and bind to cell-surface β2GPI antigen, stimulating the formation of neutrophil extra-cellular traps (NETs) via the development of reactive oxygen species and TLR4.86 NETs—consisting of webs of nuclear DNA, histones, and microbicidal proteins extruded by activated neutrophils—may be major contributors to thromboinflammation in APS. NETs activate platelets and endothelial cells and form an important part of venous and arterial clots. 88-90 Increased NET formation and higher circulating low-density granulocytes in APS patients may lead to increased type 1 interferon86; NETs are also found infiltrating placental intervillous spaces, in association with inflammatory and vascular changes in individuals with SLE and with pre-eclampsia. Data from a single-center study demonstrates that some APS patients develop anti-NET antibodies (anti-NET Abs) that impair NET clearance and may amplify inflammatory responses. Although it remains to be determined whether anti-NET Abs can serve as biomarkers in addition to traditional aPL, recent data demonstrates high levels of anti-NET Abs in 45% of aPL-positive patients, suggesting a possible role in disease pathogenesis.

Gene expression studies elucidating immune-thrombosis mechanisms in APS are limited. Two studies provided data from RNA-sequencing of neutrophils and plasmacytoid dendritic cells in 9 and 10 patients with primary APS, respectively.94, Recent data aiming to identify gene signatures in thrombotic primary

APS patients show a potential role for upregulated type I and II interferon-regulated genes in peripheral blood to discriminate thrombotic primary APS from healthy controls. Further research is needed to investigate the roles for these mechanisms as potential therapeutic targets in APS.

Microvascular manifestations, such as vasculopathy in APS, may be explained in part by upregulation of the mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) on endothelial cells, a kinase that integrates a variety of signaling pathways to regulate cellular growth, proliferation, and survival.97, As demonstrated in patients with aPL-associated nephropathy, molecular markers consistent with activation of mTOR and downstream signaling were found in intrarenal vascular endothelium.

Prospective studies of novel measures of potential targets for thrombosis development, including antiDomain I and aPS/PT, may reveal mechanistic roles for these antibodies. For instance, some studies suggest that Domain Ispecific aβ2GPI are the aPL most likely to cause thrombosis and obstetric morbidity compared with antibodies directed against other regions of β2GPI. While some studies also suggest a predictive role for anti—Domain I antibody positivity for the first thrombotic event in aPL carriers, further research is needed to confirm these findings. 101, Additionally, measuring antibodies to prothrombin, detected using aPS/PT, may be useful in establishing thrombotic risk of patients with previous thrombosis and/or history of SLE, as well as in a subset of patients who test negative for the recommended criteria aPL tests. 103,104

### Clinical Features

Clinical manifestations in APS are heterogeneous. Patients with APS may present with a spectrum of often overlapping clinical phenotypes. While the principal manifestations of aPL are venous or arterial thromboses (thrombotic APS) and pregnancy events (obstetric APS), APS can range from asymptomatic aPL positivity to microvascular events (microvascular APS), to CAPS (multiple thromboses occurring over days). Symptomatic patients may experience a combination of the above findings and thus should not be evaluated and managed as if they have a single disease.

### Macrovascular Thrombosis

APS can affect all organ systems. DVT (with or without pulmonary embolism) and stroke are the most common clinical manifestations of APS and have strong positive associations with aPL. Except for the youth of affected patients, the unusual anatomic locations (e.g., Budd-Chiari syndrome, sagittal sinus and upperextremity thromboses), venous thromboses in APS do not differ clinically from thromboses attributable to other causes. Similarly, arterial thromboses differ from non-aPL-associated thromboses only by their recurrent nature, unusual locations, and occurrence in young patients. Thrombosis of renal vessels may lead to severe hypertension, 105 and occasionally peripheral artery thrombosis may occur.

### Microvascular Antiphospholipid d Syndrome (Without Catastrophic Antiphospholipid Syndrome Classification)

Ten to twenty percent of aPL-positive patients develop livedo, the most frequently associated cutaneous manifestation in patients

with APS. While most studies do not distinguish between livedo reticularis (uniform, reversible, unbroken, and symmetric discoloration) versus livedo racemosa (nonuniform, irreversible, broken, and asymmetric discoloration), "primary" livedo reticularis is typically considered physiologic or benign, whereas livedo racemosa is considered pathologic. Another relatively uncommon cutaneous finding linked to APS, known as livedoid vasculopathy, is characterized by purpuric macules and papules, cutaneous nodules, and/or painful ulcerations on the lower legs and feet, and is observed primarily in young to middle-age women with APS107,108 (Fig. 83.2).

Diffuse alveolar hemorrhage (DAH) is a rare microvascular manifestation of aPL, characterized by the red blood cell leak from alveolar capillaries into the intraalveolar space. While prevalence estimates range from 2% to 12% in APS patients, it may be difficult to calculate due to nonspecific clinical and radiographic findings and the inconsistent ability to perform invasive diagnostic testing (i.e., bronchoscopy). .109, Pulmonary capillaritis with or without microthrombosis has been detected in ~50% of the lung pathology specimens from aPL-positive patients with DAH.

Biopsy-proven aPL-associated nephropathy, which develops in ~3% of aPL-positive patients, can present as acute (thrombotic microangiopathy [TMA] in glomeruli or arterioles/arteries) or chronic (i.e., organized arterial or arteriolar microthrombi with or without recanalization, organized glomerular thrombi, fibrous and fibrocellular [arterial or arteriolar] occlusions, focal cortical atrophy with or without thyroidization, and fibrous intimal hyperplasia) lesions113 (Fig. 83.3). Chronic aPL nephropathy is typically characterized as slowly progressive kidney disease with proteinuria, microscopic hematuria, and/or hypertension.

Additionally, aPL-positive patients can rarely develop myocardial ischemia/infarction with nonobstructive coronary artery disease due to microvascular thrombosis, adrenal infarction/hemorrhage, or acute ischemic encephalopathy.

### Nonthrombotic Manifestations

Mild-to-moderate thrombocytopenia (≥50,000/mm3) develops in approximately 20% of aPL-positive patients and, once other etiologies are excluded, typically does not require further investigation. Cardiac valve disease (vegetations, thickening, or both) is a late manifestation. Vegetations (also known as Libman-Sacks endocarditis) are usually small (less than 4 mm) verrucae, which can be composed of sterile immune complexes, hematoxylin bodies, and/or platelet thrombi. Recent studies suggest that APS does

not add to the risk of atherosclerosis imparted by SLE. Pulmonary hypertension may develop owing to recurrent pulmonary embolism or small vessel thrombosis; rarely, aPL-positive patients may present with diffuse pulmonary hemorrhage. Although rare and controversial, nonfocal neurologic manifestations such as cognitive dysfunction (independent of cerebrovascular disease), characterized by lack of concentration, forgetfulness, dizzy spells, multiple sclerosislike syndrome, chorea, and seizures, have also been reported in aPL-positive patients. Multiple small, hyperintense lesions seen on magnetic resonance imaging, primarily in the periventricular white matter, do not correlate well with clinical symptoms. Rarely, high-affinity anti-prothrombin antibodies may cause hemorrhage by depleting prothrombin (LA hypoprothrombinemia syndrome).

### Catastrophic Antiphospholipid Syndrome

CAPS is a rare, abrupt, life-threatening complication. It consists of multiple thromboses (e.g., stroke; cardiac, hepatic, adrenal, renal, and intestinal infarction; and peripheral gangrene) occurring over a period of days and is commonly associated with microvascular disease with or without systemic TMA. In a review of 220 patients with CAPS, the main clinical manifestations included renal (70%), pulmonary (66%), cerebral (60%), cardiac (52%), and cutaneous involvement (47%). Acute adrenal failure due to adrenal hemorrhage may be the initial clinical event. Some

CAPS patients may have moderate thrombocytopenia and schistocytes as part of systemic TMA. CAPS can also overlap with other thrombotic microangiopathies such as sepsis or thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura. Renal failure and pulmonary hemorrhage may occur. Acute adrenal insufficiency is highly suggestive of CAPS in aPL-positive patients. Tissue biopsies may show noninflammatory vascular occlusion. Precipitating factors for CAPS may include infections, drugs, major/minor surgical procedures, and anti-coagulation withdrawal.

### Pregnancy Morbidity

Pregnancy losses in patients with aPL typically occur after 10 weeks' gestation (fetal loss) and are more specific when accompanied by signs of vascular insufficiency such as severe pre-eclampsia or severe placental insufficiency. Although recurrent early pregnancy losses (<10 weeks' gestation) are reported in aPL-positive patients, they are commonly due to chromosomal and other genetic defects. Pregnancy in those with APS is often normal until the second trimester, when fetal growth slows and amniotic fluid volume decreases. Intrauterine growth restriction due to placental insufficiency in APS patients is also elevated, ranging from 15% to 40%, although the definition of placental insufficiency remains controversial. APS patients may develop severe, early pre-eclampsia or placental insufficiency. In aPL-positive patients with HELLP (bemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, low platelets)

syndrome associated with pregnancy, the possibility of the evolving CAPS must be considered, particularly in patients with a history of thrombosis. 122,

In a prospective, multicenter study (PROMISSE), the primary predictor of adverse pregnancy outcome after 12 weeks gestation in aPL-associated pregnancies was positive LA test. Prior thrombosis and SLE were also risk factors of adverse pregnancy outcomes. Prior pregnancy loss did not predict outcomes, but previous studies suggested that prior late pregnancy losses predict future losses, independent of the aPL profile.

### Classification

### Antiphospholipid Syndrome

The revised Sapporo classification criteria for APS required clinical (thrombosis or pregnancy morbidity) and laboratory (LA, aCL IgG/M, and/or aβ2GPI IgG/M) items with at least two aPL tests performed at least 12 weeks apart. However, with advancements in our understanding of APS and given various limitations of the Sapporo criteria, such as the lack of evidence-based definitions (i.e., for items such as aPL positivity, microvascular disease, or pregnancy morbidity), risk stratification by aPL profile, better characterization of nonthrombotic aPL manifestations, and inclusion of a heterogenous group of "aPL-positive" patients with different risk profiles, an international effort, jointly supported by ACR and EULAR, resulted in the development of new classification criteria for APS using rigorous methodology for classification criteria development.3,

The new 2023 ACR/EULAR APS Classification Criteria aim to identify homogeneous cohorts of APS patients for research purposes and, in contrast to the Sapporo criteria, incorporates a hierarchical, weighted, additive system, assessing the individual probability of APS compared with a threshold above which APS is classified. The new classification criteria include entry criteria of at least one positive aPL test within 3 years of an aPL-associated clinical criterion followed by additive weighted criteria (each 1 to 7 points) clustered into six clinical (macrovascular VTE, macrovascular arterial thrombosis, microvascular, obstetric, cardiac valve, and hematologic) and two laboratory (LA functional coagulation assay and aCL and/or aβ2GPI IgG/M enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays) domains. Patients accumulating at least three points each from clinical and laboratory domains are classified as having APS. Validation of the new criteria versus the 2006 revised Sapporo classification criteria yielded a specificity of 99% versus 86% and a sensitivity of 84% versus 99%126 (Table 83.1).

The newly developed APS classification criteria incorporate novel features, including risk stratification of macrovascular thrombotic events by traditional thrombosis risk factors, welldefined microvascular domain items, redefined pregnancy morbidity definitions, and other clinical features such as cardiac valve disease and thrombocytopenia. Future studies will be needed to assess the performance of the new APS classification criteria in subpopulations such as aPL-positive lupus patients, non-White race/ethnicities, pediatric patients, and nonacademic cohorts.
