### Vascular Damage and Failure of Compensatory Vascular Repair

In medium-sized and larger vessels, a combination of intimal and medial hypertrophy and adventitial fibrosis occurs. Together with endothelial cell apoptosis and thrombosis, the process culminates in obliterative vasculopathy with the characteristic paucity of blood vessels seen by angiography in late-stage SSc. Loss of microvasculature results in reduced blood flow and chronic tissue hypoxia, which induces hypoxia-inducible factor-1 (HIF-1)α− dependent genes, such as VEGF and its receptors, and promotes myofibroblast transformation.

The balance between angiogenic and anti-angiogenic factors is fundamentally dysregulated in SSc. The plasma levels of the angiogenesis inhibitor endostatin, a degradation product of type XVIII collagen, are elevated. Other investigators found elevated levels of the angiogenic factors such as VEGF and its receptors, basic fibroblast growth factor, IL-8, CXCL-12, and PDGF in circulation and in tissue.72, It remains unclear why, in the face of tissue hypoxia and elevated angiogenic factors, there is a failure of compensatory angiogenesis or vasculogenesis in SSc. An intriguing possibility implicates alternate mRNA splicing of VEGF to generate an anti-angiogenic isoform called VEGF165b. The VEGF165b isoform is released by SSc platelets and is overexpressed in SSc skin, suggesting that an enzyme-mediated alternate mRNA splicing event causing a switch from angiogenic to anti-angiogenic VEGF isoform plays a crucial role in the failure to mount an appropriate compensatory response to hypoxia in SSc.

Vasculogenesis, or de novo blood vessel formation, is critically dependent on bone marrow-derived circulating endothelial progenitor cells (EPCs) and their differentiation into mature endothelial cells. A reduction in the number of CD34+ EPCs and their impaired differentiation into mature endothelial cells has been documented in patients with SSc.74-76 Because EPCs are required for physiologic vasculogenesis in ischemic tissues, defective progenitor cell mobilization or function might compromise vascular repair. Whether the reduction in circulating EPCs in SSc is due to diminished release from the bone marrow as a result of fibrosis or "exhaustion" or their destruction in the peripheral circulation remains unresolved.

### Hypoxia

The widespread microangiopathy and resultant capillary loss in SSc leads to diminished blood flow and consequent hypoxia of affected tissues. With the onset of fibrosis, excessive ECM accumulation increases diffusion distance from blood vessels to cells, further aggravating tissue hypoxia. Hypoxia is itself a potent inducer of the basic helix—loophelix transcription factors HIF-1α and HIF- 1β, which are undetectable under normoxic conditions, due to rapid proteasomal degradation mediated by the protein von HippelLindau (pVHL) tumor suppressor. In hypoxic cells, pVHL is unable to bind to its target, and therefore HIF-1α is protected from degradation and translocates into the nucleus, where it binds to hypoxia-responsive DNA elements and induces the transcription of VEGF and other hypoxia-regulated genes involved in erythropoiesis, angiogenesis, and glucose metabolism. Hypoxia is also a potent stimulus for upregulation of ECM genes, including collagens, prolyl hydroxylases, and lysyl oxidase, and directly stimulates epithelial myofibroblast differentiation.78, These and other hypoxia-induced profibrogenic responses are partially mediated by autocrine TGF-β. Compelling experimental support for the role of hypoxia in fibrosis

is provided by a recent study that shows increased fibrosis in mice with myeloid cell-specific deletion of VEGF.

A state of tissue hypoxia in SSc has been documented by noninvasive means, and cutaneous oxygen concentrations inversely correlate with skin thickness. With the use of an intradermal electrode, patients with SSc were found to have significantly reduced levels of pressure of oxygen (pO2) compared with control subjects (23.7 mm Hg vs. 33.6 mm Hg).

### Oxidative eStress and Reactive e Oxygen Species

Oxidative stress results when there is an imbalance between the generation of chemically reactive oxygen-derived molecules called ROS and anti-oxidant defense mechanisms. Substantial evidence indicates a role for elevated ROS generation with SSc.81, The endothelium generates ROS in response to episodes of ischemiaperfusion, while fibroblasts generate ROS in response to TGF- β, PDGF, angiotensin II, and ET-1, or stimulatory anti-PDGFR antibodies. Explanted SSc dermal fibroblasts and monocytes spontaneously produce ROS. Several cellular enzymes, as well as mitochondria, can generate ROS. In SSc, increased activity of the membrane-associated enzyme nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate oxidase (Nox 4) plays a predominant role. Hydrogen peroxide and other oxygen free radicals can stimulate collagen synthesis, myofibroblast differentiation, and secretion and activation of TGF-β and Wnt-βcatenin pathways, as well as induce cellular senescence. Alterations in cellular metabolism are increasingly recognized in SSc. These include an increase in glycolysis, generation of lactic acid and acidic microenvironment, and reduction in fatty acid oxidation. Similar to the process of biologic aging, SSc cells show evidence of mitochondrial stress and altered mitophagy. These mitochondrial changes contribute to metabolic reprogramming, cellular stress, genomic instability, and genotoxic damage.

### Inflammation and Immune Dysregulation in the Pathogenesis of Systemic Sclerosis

In early-stage disease, biopsies from lesional skin and lungs may show perivascular accumulation of mononuclear cells, macrophages, pDCs, mast cells, and innate lymphoid cells (ILCs). In the blood, the number of circulating monocytes is elevated, and T cells, B cells, monocytes, and DCs show evidence of activation and polarization. The "type I IFN signature" characteristic of SLE and other autoimmune diseases can also be seen in patients with SSc. Humoral autoimmunity manifested by highly specific and mutually exclusive autoantibodies can be detected even prior to clinical disease manifestations and is prominent throughout the course of the disease (Fig. 84.9). The striking genetic associations of SSc with the class II HLA locus, as well as numerous genes related to B and T cell function and innate immunity (see above), provide compelling support for an immunologic basis of disease risk. Results from recent therapeutic trials of global (myeloablative) and targeted immunomodulatory interventions in SSc provide further evidence that the immune system contributes to progressive disease.

### Cellular Effectors of Dysregulated Immunity

### T Cell Subsets and Activation

T cell activation is evident in both SSc lesional tissues, as well as in peripheral blood, and T cells play a direct role in tissue damage. In the early stage of the disease, activated CD4 and CD8

T lymphocytes, along with monocytes/macrophages, and B cells, eosinophils, mast cells, and natural killer cells, are observed in a perivascular distribution in the lesional skin, lungs, and other affected organs and can be detected before the appearance of fibrosis or even in clinically unaffected skin. In situ hybridization studies show that fibroblasts with prominent procollagen gene expression in early-stage SSc skin are adjacent to inflammatory cells, suggesting that they or their soluble products play a direct role in fibroblast activation.

In SSc, tissue-infiltrating T cells are predominantly CD4+, express markers of activation (CD69, CD45, HLA-DR, and IL-2 receptor [IL-2R]), and display restricted T cell receptor signatures, suggesting oligoclonal T cell expansion in response to an as-yet unidentified antigen. In the lungs, a predominance of CD8+ and γ/δ T cells is observed. Currently it is not known whether T cells in lesional tissue are activated nonspecifically (by cytokines or chemokines) or in response to antigen. Evidence of T cell activation in SSc is also detected in the peripheral blood, with elevated serum levels of IL-2 and IL-2R and chemokines receptors, spontaneous cytokine secretion, and increased expression of leukocyte function—associated antigen 1 (LFA-1) and α1 integrins, which enable T cells to adhere directly to endothelium and fibroblasts. At the same time, vascular endothelial cells express intercellular adhesion molecule-1 (ICAM- 1), E-selectin, and other adhesion molecules that facilitate leukocyte diapedesis. Peripheral blood lymphocytes show the "IFN signature' )> defined by the expression of type I IFN-inducible genes. 88-90

### T Helper 1/T Helper 2 Cytokine Balance and Polarized Immune Responses

A skewed balance between T helper (Th)1 and Th2 cytokines is a hallmark of several conditions associated with fibrosis. Th2 cells

secrete abundant IL-4, IL-5, and IL-13 but only low levels of the hallmark Th1 cytokine IFN-γ. Th2 cytokines directly stimulate collagen synthesis, myofibroblast transdifferentiation, and production of TGF-β, a potent stimulus for ECM accumulation, whereas IFN-γ blocks these responses and exerts anti-fibrotic effects. The Th2 skewing of the immune response thus creates a profibrotic environment. Support for the profibrotic role of a Th2-polarized immune response comes from animal studies, which show that in vitro Th2-polarized T cells induce fibrosis when they are passively transferred in mice. Moreover, in mice lacking the T-bet transcription factor, which directs Th1 differentiation, exaggerated skin fibrosis develops in response to bleomycin. 91,

Patients with SSc display an altered Th1/Th2 cytokine balance with a predominant Th2 profile. For example, IFN-γ serum levels and in vitro IFN-γ production by peripheral blood monocytes are reduced in SSc. Microarray analysis of SSc peripheral blood leukocytes showed elevated expression of GATA3, which controls Th2 polarization. Cloned CD4+ T cells from SSc skin biopsies secrete IL-4 but not IFN-γ. T cell lines generated from SSc skin biopsies or alveolar fluid produce high levels of Th2 cytokines, and the Th2 predominance predicts accelerated decline in lung function.94, Proteomic and DNA microarray transcriptome analysis also demonstrated a Th2 cytokine predominance in SSc bronchoalveolar lavage fluids and CD8+ lymphocytes. Furthermore, a longitudinal study of patients with SSc showed that skin improvement over time was associated with a decline in serum levels of Th2 cytokines and a concomitant increase in IL-12, a Th1 cytokine.

### Other T Cell Subsets in Systemic Sclerosis

Th17 lymphocytes are implicated in the pathogenesis of rheumatoid arthritis and other inflammatory diseases. Studies described

increased numbers of IL-17-producing CD4+ T cells in both peripheral blood and bronchoalveolar lavage fluid in SSc, but their direct roles in pathogenesis remain to be elucidated.

Suppressor Treg cells (Foxp3/CD25) are important in controlling autoimmunity and are implicated in SSc. Notably, the organs prominently affected in SSc, including the skin, gut, and lungs, harbor a majority of the body's pool of Tregs. One study found that although the frequency of peripheral blood Tregs was increased in patients with SSc, these Treg cells showed impaired suppressive capacity and defective secretion of TGF-β and IL-10.98 Other studies demonstrated reduced numbers of Foxp3+ CD4+ T cells in the lesional skin in SSc compared with other inflammatory skin diseases. Mice with transient genetic ablation of Tregs developed skin fibrosis. Enhanced Treg engraftment and an increase in the number of circulating Tregs correlates with clinical improvement in SSc patients undergoing autologous hematopoietic transplantation, further supporting an anti-fibrotic beneficial role of Tregs in SSc.

### Monocytes and Macrophages

Monocytes and macrophages originating from circulating or tissue-resident progenitors are emerging as key actors in tissue repair and fibrosis. Macrophages regulate both innate immunity and tissue repair by virtue of their ability to secrete paracrine regulators of cell function.

Bone marrow-derived monocytes are a major source of cytokines and chemokines, including IL-1, monocyte chemotactic protein-1 (MCP-1), PDGF, and TGF-β, each of which is important in inflammatory and fibroproliferative processes. Additionally, monocytes produce collagenases and other matrix-degrading enzymes and their inhibitors, as well as collagen-cross-linking enzymes such as transglutaminase 2, a potential therapeutic target in SSc. In early-stage SSc, macrophages are prominent in the lesional skin and express activation markers Siglec-1 and AIF-1. SSc skin and lung biopsies show a prominent gene signature of alternately activated macrophages.

In SSc patients, circulating monocytes express elevated levels of CCL18 and CD163, an alternatively activated monocyte/ macrophage marker, and their numbers are correlated with the severity of lung disease. The number of macrophages expressing CD163, CD204, MARCO, and other activation markers is also elevated in the lesional skin and lungs. Inflammatory monocytes characterized by surface expression of the scavenger macrophage receptor with collagenous structure (MARCO), CD206, and the NAD hydrolase ectoenzyme CD38 accumulate in affected organs and play a role in fibrosis. Selectively targeting monocytes or macrophages, or particular subsets of these cells, might represent a potential approach to therapy.

### Dendritic Cells

DCs bearing CDl1c surface markers are potent antigen-presenting cells that reside in skin and other tissues and bridge innate and adaptive immunity by modulating T cell, B cell, and monocyte/macrophage function (see Fig. 84.9). DCs are broadly classified as conventional (myeloid) and plasmacytoid (pDCs). Primarily known as the major source of type I IFN, pDCs play a fundamental role in innate anti-viral immunity. pDCs are generally absent from normal nonlymphoid tissue but under the influence of chemokines such as CCL19 and chemerin are recruited to sites of inflammation. They secrete inflammatory and profibrotic cytokines and chemokines including CXCL4

(also called PF4) and TGF-β, suggesting that they may participate in fibrogenesis independent of their T cell-stimulatory properties. pDC activation is mediated via TLR7 and TLR9, which recognize endogenous DNA and RNA in the form of immune complexes. Recent studies show that activated CD11c+ DCs accumulate in lesional tissue in animal models of fibrosis and in patients with SSc.60, Activated pDCs might directly or indirectly modulate activation of resident fibroblasts. However, their precise roles and mechanisms of action in SSc pathogenesis require further investigation.

### Mast Cells and Innate Lymphoid Cells

Mast cells accumulate in fibrotic tissue in SSc, as well as in animal models. Activated mast cells release fibrogenic cytokines including TGF-β, IL-4, and IL-13, as well as serine proteases such as tryptase that activate profibrotic receptors on fibroblasts. In a recently described transgenic mouse model, activated mast cells adhere to fibroblasts, and this heterotypic interaction resulted in fibroblast activation and fibrosis. ILCs are a recently identified cell type that represents the innate immune counterpart of polarized T helper cells. ILCs are elevated in lesional tissue, as well as in the circulation in SSc; appear to be skewed to an ILC2-polarized phenotype102; and are potential sources of fibrogenic cytokines such as IL-13. However, the precise role of ILCs in SSc pathogenesis remains to be defined.

### Humoral Autoimmunity and B Cells

### Autoantibodies in Systemic Sclerosis: Pathogenetic Considerations

Humoral autoimmunity, manifested by serum autoantibodies with multiple antigenic specificities, can be detected in virtually all SSc patients and can precede clinical disease manifestations by years. The presence of SSc autoantibodies aids in diagnosis and classification, as well as predicting organ-specific complications and clinical course. While a direct role of SSc autoantibodies in tissue damage has been proposed, to date this has not been conclusively established. There is some evidence that the levels of SSc autoantibodies, particularly anti-DNA topoisomerase I, correlate with the extent of skin and lung fibrosis and fluctuate with disease activity.

Various hypotheses exist to explain the generation of autoantibodies in SSc. Self-antigens such as DNA topoisomerase I might, in the presence of ROS, undergo proteolytic cleavage, exposing cryptic epitopes that break immune tolerance. Other potential mechanisms include molecular mimicry as a consequence of viral infection, chronic B cell hyperreactivity, and altered expression or subcellular localization of potential autoantigenic peptides. Additionally, SSc autoantibodies might be generated by B cells in response to endogenous TLR ligands such as nucleic acid-containing cellular debris.

Recent reports in SSc described a range of functional antibodies directed against a variety of ECM components, cell surface receptors, fibroblasts, and endothelial cells. These stimulatory autoantibodies can induce target cell activation or apoptosis 104, In one study, autoantibodies against PDGFRs were in vitro. detected in patients with SSc and shown to induce ROS generation and myofibroblast differentiation in cultured fibroblasts. It is not known whether these autoantibodies precede, or are consequent to, fibrosis, and their direct pathogenic role in SSc remains to be established.

### B Cells in Systemic Sclerosis

Recent reports and clues from genetic studies provide increasing evidence for a potential direct role for B cells in the pathogenesis of SSc. B cells have multiple immune regulatory functions in addition to the generation of antibodies, including antigen presentation, IL-6 and cytokine production, lymphoid organogenesis, and T cell differentiation. Candidate gene and GWA studies in SSc have implicated several B cell genes, including BANK1, BLK, CSK, and PTPN22, all of which are involved in regulating B cell signaling. Although increased B cells were found in the lungs in SSc-associated interstitial lung disease,106 they are not generally strictly in lesional skin and are found in surrounding blood vessels. Nevertheless, microarrays demonstrate molecular signatures indicative of B cell and plasma cell activation in SSc skin biopsy specimens, particularly in early-stage disease. Patients with SSc display intrinsic B cell abnormalities, with elevated numbers of naive B cells, reduced numbers of plasma cells, and increased expression of activation markers CD95 and CD86, as well as CD19, a cell surface receptor that regulates intrinsic and antigen receptorinduced B cell responses. Transgenic mice that overexpress CD19 develop spontaneous autoimmunity and high titers of anti-topoisomerase I antibodies. Chronic B cell activation in SSc also may contribute directly to fibrosis, because activated B cells secrete profibrotic TGF-β and IL-6. Levels of BAFF (B cell activating factor belonging to the TNF family) are elevated in the serum and in lesional skin in SSc patients, as is the expression of the BAFF receptor on B cells. BAFF specifically stimulates effector B cells and promotes fibrogenic cytokines. Depletion of B cells, or blocking BAFF, in the mouse attenuates scleroderma. Clinical trials of B cell depletion by targeting CD20 or CD19 have reported improvement in SSc, particularly in patients who show an elevated plasma cell gene signature in baseline skin biopsies.

### Type I Interferon Signature and Innate Immune Signaling: Parallels With Systemic Lupus Erythematosus

Stimulation of pDCs by ligands of TLR3, TLR7, and TLR9 results in robust secretion of type I IFN. Accordingly, the presence of IFN or IFN-dependent cellular responses suggests ongoing TLR-mediated innate immune signaling. Type I IFNs (α and β) are themselves potent modulators of innate immunity. Elevated expression of IFN-regulated genes (the "IFN signature") in peripheral blood cells, indicative of their exposure to IFN in the circulation or in the periphery, was first described in patients with SLE. Circulating immune complexes containing antibodies to nucleic acids serve as endogenous TLR ligands that stimulate type I IFN secretion by pDCs and macrophages. Similar to SLE, a prominent IFN signature is detected in leukocytes from patients with SSc. Indeed, a recent study reported that the most highly expressed genes in SSc peripheral blood leukocytes were IFNregulated. Moreover, incubation of leukocytes with SSc sera induced secretion of IFN, indicative of TLR activation by nucleic acidcontaining immune complexes in the serum. While these observations, along with immunogenetic studies, highlight parallels between SLE and SSc, the reasons why these two related autoimmune diseases display largely nonoverlapping clinical phenotypes remain elusive. Moreover, the pathogenetic role of type I IFN in SSc vasculopathy and fibrosis and the mechanisms responsible remain to be established.

### Fibrosis

Fibrosis is characterized by replacement of normal tissue architecture with rigid pauci-cellular connective tissue. Fibrosis in multiple organs is the distinguishing pathologic hallmark of SSc that results from a series of vascular and immune-mediated responses to injury and is perpetuated by self-amplifying cross-talk between stromal cells and the scar Fig. 84.10. .

### Extra-cellular Matrix

The connective tissue consists of a cellular compartment of resident fibroblasts, myofibroblasts and other stromal cell types, and infiltrating cells, all embedded in an ECM composed of collagens, proteoglycans, elastin, microfibrils, adhesive proteins, and other structural proteins. The ECM additionally serves as a reservoir for sequestering growth factors and matricellular proteins that control the differentiation, function, and survival of mesenchymal cells. To date, a comprehensive characterization of the fibrotic ECM, called the "matrisome" has not been achieved. Excessive ECM accumulation results from overproduction by stromal cells in response to autocrine and paracrine signals such as cytokines and chemokines; hypoxia and ROS; a variety of biologic, structural, and mechanical signals emanating from the surrounding ECM; or via cellcell interactions (Table 84.3). Impaired ECM degradation and turnover, as well as expansion of the tissue pool of ECMproducing mesenchymal cells, also play roles.

### Regulation of Collagen Synthesis

The collagens comprise a family of more than two dozen structural proteins with critical roles in organ development, growth, and differentiation. The skin, bones, and tendons are composed largely of type I collagen, the most abundant protein in mammals, with smaller amounts of associated type III collagen. Type II collagen is found mainly in articular cartilage, whereas type IV collagen is found in the basement membranes. The fibrillar collagens consist of three α chains wound into a characteristic triple helix. This structure is made possible by the presence of a glycine at every third residue of repeating Gly-X-Y sequence, where X is frequently proline and Y is frequently hydroxyproline. The cellular biogenesis of proline is regulated by PYCR1, which is upregulated in fibrosis. Fibrillar collagens undergo extensive enzymatic modifications inside the cell followed by additional extra-cellular maturation and assembly. Covalent cross-linking stabilizes the collagen fiber network in the extra-cellular space.

Environmental cues instruct fibroblasts to respond to dynamic tissue requirements during development and wound healing (Table 84.3). The genes encoding the various collagens harbor cis-acting regulatory elements recognized by DNA-binding transcription factors including cJun, Fra2, Gli1/2, EN1, IRF7, Sp1, Ets1, PU.1, Smad2/3, STAT3, Egr-1, and CCAAT-binding factor (CBF) that stimulate transcription, and Sp3, C/EBP, YB1, c-Krox, NR4A1, KLF5 and Fli-1 that suppress transcription. Relevant insights from single-cell RNA sequencing of SSc skin biopsies indicate that some of these transcription factors such as PU.1, Glil, or EN1 may even serve as markers for profibrotic subsets of fibroblasts. These DNA-binding transcription factors also interact with one another and with nonDNA-binding cofactors, scaffold proteins, chromatin-modifying enzymes such as p300/CBP, PCAF, and HDACs; their DNA-binding activities and protein— protein interactions and post-translational modifications such as

ubiquitination and acetylation are also controlled by extra-cellular cues. Alterations in the levels, activities, or interactions among the various transcription factors, cofactors, and chromatin-modifying enzymes contribute to persistent fibroblast activation in fibrosis.

### Effector Cells of Fibrosis: Fibroblasts

Fibroblasts are embryonic mesenchyme-derived stromal resident versatile cells capable of both ECM production and resorption. Although at homeostasis adult fibroblasts are biosynthetically quiescent, upon injury they are triggered to secrete ECM macromolecules and proteolytic enzymes, growth factors, cytokines, and chemokines; adhere to and contract connective tissue; transdifferentiate into apoptosis-resistant myofibroblasts; or undergo cellular senescence. Under normal conditions these biosynthetic, proinflammatory, adhesive, and prosurvival functions combine to enable fibroblasts to execute effective wound healing. In contrast to homeostatic ECM maintenance in which the fibroblast repair program is tightly regulated and self-limited, pathologic fibrosis is characterized by uncontrolled fibroblast activation that results in exaggerated, disorganized, and persistent ECM accumulation and remodeling. Fibroblasts derived from diverse anatomic locations retain their distinct gene expression profiles. The so-called "positional memory" of fibroblasts is governed by genetic imprinting by the homeobox (HOX) family transcription factors. Moreover,

recent studies using single-cell RNA sequencing of samples from different organs, in steady state as well as in perturbed states, identified fibroblast populations that are common across organs and fibroblast populations that are tissueor disease-specific. Some of the universal fibroblasts can serve as a reservoir for differentiation into specialized, tissueor context-specific fibroblast populations. Healthy human lungs appear to contain two major and one minor fibroblast population characterized by high expression of SPINT2 (serine peptidase inhibitor, Kunitz type 2), MFAP5 (microfibril-associated protein 5), and WIF1, respectively. Similarly, in the skin two major fibroblast subpopulations defined by the expression of SFRP2 (secreted frizzled-related protein 2)/DPP4 and FMO1 (flavin-containing dimethylaniline monooxygenase 1)/LSP1 (lymphocyte-specific protein 1), respectively, as well as five minor populations, each of them expressing distinctive genes (CRABP1 [cellular retinoic acid-binding protein 1), COL11A1, FMO2, PRG4 [proteoglycan 4], or C2ORF40 [augurin]), have been identified. Further work provided evidence that myofibroblasts in SSc arise from a fraction of SFRP2hi/DPP4-expressing fibroblasts that additionally expresses SFRP4 and FND1.1 114 Another study demonstrated numerical and functional perturbation of an LGR5-positive homeostatic fibroblast subpopulation in SSc skin. These LGR5-positive fibroblasts express several genes associated with ECM degradation (including MMP2, TIMP2, and the dipeptidyl peptidase IV [DPP4/CD26]), genes associated with vascular formation and remodeling, platelet aggregation and coagulation, and atypical receptors for the chemokines CXCL11 and CXCL12.115 Together, these emerging studies unravel a profound heterogeneity of fibroblasts and identify disease-specific populations that may open venues for specific targeting of these pathogenic populations as novel therapeutic approaches in SSc.

### Effector Cells of Fibrosis: Myofibroblasts, Pericytes, Endothelial Cells, and Cellular Plasticity

In fibrosis, the pool of activated resident mesenchymal cells is expanded not only by proliferation of fibroblasts but also by transdifferentiation of other stromal progenitor cell types, as well as by the influx of bone marrow-derived progenitor cells. Myofibroblasts are characterized by the incorporation of α—smooth muscle actin into cytoskeletal stress fibers. They are specialized contractile nonmuscle mesenchymal cells in the skin and other parenchymal organs that arise from resident fibroblasts, as well as epithelial, endothelial, and perivascular mural cells (pericytes) and preadipocytes. While no unique distinguishing surface markers have been identified to date, myofibroblasts display elevated levels of cadherin-11, integrins and receptors for PDGF (PDG- FRA), secrete fibronectin-EDA, matricellular proteins such as CCN2, collagens, tissue inhibitor of metalloproteinases (TIMPs), and other structural components of the ECM and are a major site of TGF-β activation during the fibrotic response. In normal wound healing, myofibroblasts transiently populate early granulation tissue, followed by their disappearance via apoptosis. Indeed, the ordered removal of activated myofibroblasts is a crucial step in normal wound repair. In contrast, failure of effective removal of myofibroblasts by apoptosis in pathologic fibrogenesis leads to their persistence in lesional tissue, contributing to the formation of a rigid and contracted ECM characteristic of a chronic scar. This may offer potential for therapeutic intervention. A recent

study provided evidence that mitochondria in activated myofibroblasts are primed by death signals, which creates a requirement for tonic expression of the anti-apoptotic proteins. In consequence, myofibroblasts were found to be particularly susceptible to apoptosis induced by "BH3 mimetic" drugs.

Residing within the walls of small blood vessels, pericytes (mural cells) are in intimate contact with the underlying endothelium that regulates vascular homeostasis. In patients with SSc, a marked increase in the microvascular pericyte compartment and increased expression of PDGFRs have been reported. Activated pericytes expressing CD248, ADAM12, or the hedgehog (HH) pathway transcriptional activator Gli1 can transdifferentiate into collagen-producing myofibroblasts in fibrosis. The pericyte-myofibroblast transition is thought to represent a link between microvascular injury and fibrosis.

Under certain conditions, epithelial cells can also undergo phenotypic transformation to fibroblasts. EMT plays a vital role during vertebrate embryonic development. Pathologic EMT is prominent in cancer and has also been implicated in renal fibrosis and idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, although its significance in SSc pathogenesis has not been established. Similar to epithelial cells, vascular endothelial cells, mesothelial cells, and intradermal adipocytes can also transition to myofibroblasts upon fibrotic injury. These processes have been demonstrated in various forms of experimental fibrosis and might also be implicated in SSc. Whether myofibroblasts originating from different progenitors show identical or distinct phenotypes and functions remains to be determined.

### Fibrocytes and Monocyte-Derived Mesenchymal Progenitor Cells

Fibrocytes are rare bone marrow—derived CD34+ circulating mesenchymal progenitor cells that can present antigen and synthesize collagen. They express CD14+ (a monocyte marker), as well as chemokine receptors (CCR3, CCR5, and CXCR4), which allows them to accumulate in specific tissues. The role for fibrocytes in fibrosis was established in animal models using neutralizing antibodies and in CXCR4-deficient mice. Mice with accelerated senescence have an increased number of circulating fibrocytes and show increased sensitivity to bleomycin-induced fibrosis. Other studies have identified monocyte-derived mesenchymal progenitor cells in peripheral blood. Despite these experimental observations, the pathogenic significance of bone marrow—derived progenitor cells in SSc remains unknown.

### Cellular Senescence and Fibrosis in Systemic Sclerosis

Cellular senescence, a hallmark of biologic aging, is a state of stable cell cycle arrest. Cells exposed to genomic, proteomic, oxidative, or metabolic stress stop dividing, which normally serves as a protective mechanism to limit transmission of deleterious mutations. However, as senescent cells progressively accumulate in tissues, due in part to inefficient immune clearance, their deleterious effects, including promotion of aberrant tissue remodeling, may come to predominate. Accumulation of senescent cells in many organs is a hallmark of aging. Detrimental effects of senescent myofibroblast accumulation in the skin and lung include depletion of the mitotically active progenitor cell pool and secretion of a senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) secretome,

composed of PAI-1, matrix-degrading metalloproteases, and prototypical inflammatory and profibrotic chemokines and cytokines including TGF-β, IL-6, MCP-1, and PDGF. While elevated expression of p16 and p21 and expression of β-galactosidase are commonly used as markers of senescent cells, precise identification of senescent cells remains problematic, as no unique markers have been determined to date. Recent studies indicate that organ fibrosis is accompanied by premature accumulation of senescent myofibroblasts that are characterized by expression of prosurvival and anti-apoptotic pathways (ephrins and Bcl-2), mitochondrial alterations, elevated expression of NAD-depleting enzymes CD38 and NNMT, and reduced activity of anti-aging HDAC enzymes (sirtuins). These senescent myofibroblasts also display evidence of genome and telomere damage, and the SASP secretome. While these findings support the view of fibrosis as an "accelerated aging phenotype," the importance of chronic cellular senescence in SSc pathogenesis and as a therapeutic target using "senolytic" strategies still remains to be determined.119,120

### Molecular Determinants of Fibrosis: Transforming Growth Factor-β

The expression of ECM genes is normally tightly controlled by paracrine/autocrine mediators, cellcell contact, hypoxia, and contact with the surrounding ECM. Of the multitude of cytokines implicated in SSc (see Table 84.3), TGF-β is considered to be the master regulator of both physiologic fibrogenesis (wound healing and tissue repair) and pathologic fibrosis.

A member of a large cytokine superfamily that also includes activin and bone morphogenetic proteins, TGF-β is secreted by platelets, monocytes/macrophages, DCs, and fibroblasts, and most cell types express surface receptors for TGF-β. TGF-β plays essential roles in tissue repair, angiogenesis, and immune regulation, and its dysregulation is implicated in cancer, fibrosis, and autoimmunity. TGF-β is generally secreted as a latent complex that is sequestered in an inactive form within the ECM. Upon injury, latent TGF-β is converted in situ to its biologically active form. Activation of latent TGF-β is controlled in part by fibrillin-1 and is mediated by cell membrane integrins, thrombospondins, αyβ6 integrin, and proteolytic enzymes. Because of its fundamental role in orchestrating fibrotic responses, TGF-β is considered a potential therapeutic target in SSc.

### Cellular Signaling by Transforming Growth Factor-β: Canonical Smad Pathways

The type of response elicited by TGF-β is specific for the target cell and is highly context dependent. In mesenchymal cells, TGF-β acts as a potent inducer of fibrillar collagen synthesis and fibroblast proliferation, migration, adhesion, and senescence, and it suppresses the production of matrix-degrading metalloproteinases (Tables 84.4 and 84.5). In endothelial and epithelial cells and adipocytes, TGF-β drives transdifferentiation into myofibroblasts. Binding of activated TGF-β to the type II TGF-β surface receptor triggers an intra-cellular signal transduction cascade that leads to target gene expression. The evolutionarily conserved canonical TGF-β signal transduction pathway involves the transmembrane type I TGF-β receptor, a serine—threonine kinase that in turn phosphorylates cytosolic Smads. Phosphorylated Smad2/3 form heterocomplexes with Smad4 and translocate into the nucleus, where they bind to consensus Smad-binding elements (SBEs)

and together with cofactors such as the histone acetylase p300/ CBP regulate transcription. Conserved SBE sequences are found in many TGF-βinducible genes, including type I collagens,

plasminogen activator inhibitor—1, α—smooth muscle actin, and connective tissue growth factor (CTGF). The strength and duration of TGF-β signaling through the Smad pathway is tightly controlled by endogenous inhibitors such as Smad7.

### Noncanonical Transforming Growth Factor-β Signaling in Fibrosis

Alternative non-Smad TGF-β signaling involves protein kinases (c-Abl, extra-cellular signal-regulated kinase [ERK]1/2, p38, and JNK, focal adhesion kinase [FAK], CDK5, and TGF-β activated kinase [TAK1]); the JAKSTAT pathways converging on STAT3; protein-tyrosine phosphatase PTP4A1; lipid kinases such as phosphatidylinositol 3'-kinase and its downstream target Akt; and noncoding RNAs such as miR29. A recent study found that IL-11, induced in response to TGF-β, mediated many of its profibrotic effects in fibroblasts in an autocrine, ERK-dependent manner, while pharmacologic inhibition of IL-11 activity protected mice from fibrosis. Notably, expression of IL-11 is markedly elevated in SSc fibroblasts in vitro, providing the rationale for targeting IL-11 as a potential therapy.

### Cytokines, Growth Factors, Chemokines, and Lipid Mediators

In addition to TGF-β, soluble mediators such as CTGF, PDGF, IL-4, IL-6, IL-11, IL-13, FGF9, adenosine, prostaglandin F2α, adipokines, and lysophosphatidic acid (LPA) are aberrantly expressed, contribute to SSc pathogenesis, and represent potential therapeutic targets.

### Connective Tissue Growth Factor/CCN2

CTGF (also called CCN2) is a cysteine-rich 40 kDa matricellular growth factor that is implicated in angiogenesis, wound healing, and development. Although it is undetectable in healthy adults, CTGF is markedly elevated in fibrotic tissues. In SSc patients,

serum CTGF levels correlate with the extent of skin and pulmonary fibrosis. The expression of CTGF can be induced by TGF-β, IL-4, and VEGF, whereas TNF and prostacyclins block stimulation. Transgenic mice overexpressing CTGF develop diffuse skin . While cellular receptors for fibrosis and microvascular disease. CTGF and the mechanism of action underlying CTGF profibrotic responses remain incompletely characterized, targeting CTGF with monoclonal antibodies represents a potential therapeutic strategy for controlling fibrosis.

### Platelet-Derived Growth Factor

PDGFs are disulfide-bonded heterodimeric proteins that act mainly on stromal cells and play key roles in wound healing. Originally isolated from platelets, PDGF isoforms are also secreted from macrophages, endothelial cells, fibroblasts, and senescent cells. By signaling via the α and β transmembrane PDGFRs, PDGF acts as a potent fibroblast mitogen and chemoattractant and induces ROS generation and synthesis of collagen, fibronectin, and proteoglycans, as well as the secretion of TGF-β1, MCP-1, and IL-6. Transgenic mice expressing a constitutively active PDGF-α receptor spontaneously develops skin and multiple organ fibrosis. 124, Lesional skin fibroblasts from patients with SSc show elevated PDGF and PDGF-β receptor expression, b126and PDGF levels are increased in SSc bronchoalveolar lavage fluid. Some patients with SSc appear to have functional circulating antibodies to the PDGFR that can induce fibroblast activation and ROS generation; however, such autoantibodies have also been detected in patients with graft-versus-host disease, and their significance in pathogenesis remains to be established.

### Developmental (Morphogen) Pathways: Wnt, Hedgehog, and NOTCH

The morphogens Wnt, HH, and NOTCH are involved in embryonic developmental pathways that appear to be deregulated in fibrosis and SSc. The Wnts comprise a family of poorly soluble glycoproteins with dual roles in cellcell adhesion and transcriptional regulation. While they play essential roles in morphogenesis, stem cell homeostasis, and cell fate determination, abnormal Wnt signaling is implicated in cancer, rheumatoid arthritis and osteoarthritis, osteoporosis, PAH, fibrosis, and aging. Intra-cellular Wnt signaling is mediated via both canonical (β-catenin) and noncanonical pathways, with extensive cross-talk with TGF-β signaling. Transgenic mice overexpressing Wnt10b or a constitutively active mutant β-catenin develop noninflammatory tissue fibrosis. Lungs from patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis show increased nuclear β-catenin accumulation at fibrotic foci. Genomewide transcriptome analysis of SSc skin biopsies shows elevated expression of Wnt ligands, receptors, and targets. Constitutive Wnt—β-catenin signaling in SSc is due, in part, to epigenetic silencing of endogenous Wnt inhibitors such as DKK1.

NOTCH, the transmembrane receptor for Jagged, has a fundamental role in embryonic development, wound healing, and tissue repair. NOTCH signaling via Snail, Twist, and Slug regulates endothelial cell and fibroblast responses, including myofibroblast differentiation. NOTCH signaling was markedly enhanced in the skin of SSc patients. Activity of ADAM17, a proteinase that initiates NOTCH signal transduction, is elevated in SSc skin biopsies. Inhibition of NOTCH signaling ameliorated fibroblast activation of experimental fibrosis in mice.129, HH signaling represents another essential developmental pathway involved in

tissue repair. Sonic hedgehog (SHH), the best characterized mammalian HH ligand, binds to its Patched receptor on a variety of cell types, and triggers an intra-cellular signaling pathway via Gli family transcription factors. Components of the HH pathways are elevated in SSc biopsies, and SHH elicits profibrotic responses in vitro. Besides this canonical activation, Gli transcription factors can also be induced by TGF-β to drive the expression of HH regulated genes. Remarkably, the activity of multiple morphogen developmental pathways is regulated by their localization in the primary cilium, potentially implicating altered cilia formation in aberrant HH and NOTCH signaling in fibrosis.

### Interleukins

Members of the IL-1 family are secreted from multiple cell types. A recent study showed that SSc epidermal keratinocytes secreted IL-1α, and their coculture with normal skin fibroblasts resulted in fibroblast activation and myofibroblast differentiation that was mediated by IL-1α. The Th2 cytokine IL-4 stimulates fibroblast proliferation, chemotaxis, collagen synthesis, and production of TGF-β, CTGF, and TIMP. Serum levels of IL-4 are elevated in SSc, and the number of IL-4-producing T cells is increased in both peripheral blood and skin. IL-6, which is produced by monocytes, B and T cells, fibroblasts, and endothelial cells, directly stimulates collagen and TIMP-1 synthesis in fibroblasts and promotes a Th2-polarized immune response. The biologic activities of IL-6 are mediated via the JAK—signal transducer and activator of transcription (STAT) intra-cellular signaling pathway that is shared with multiple other cytokines. Recent observations reveal evidence of JAK-STAT pathway activation associated with fibrosis in SSc and provide the rationale for therapeutically targeting JAK to attenuate fibrotic cellular responses. 132-134 Serum levels of IL-6 are elevated in SSc and correlate with the severity of skin involvement. Another Th2 cytokine, IL-13, is implicated in asthma and a variety of fibrotic conditions. IL-13 has profibrotic effects that are both indirect via stimulation of TGF-β production by macrophages and direct via stimulation of fibroblast proliferation and collagen synthesis. Serum levels of IL-13 are elevated in SSc.

### Chemokines

Chemokines represent a superfamily of more than 40 low-molecular-weight soluble mediators. Originally identified based on their chemotactic effects on leukocytes, chemokines have a broad range of cellular targets and biologic activities, including regulation of angiogenesis, wound healing, and fibrosis. The CC chemokine MCP-1 stimulates collagen production directly, as well as through induction of endogenous TGF-β. Serum and bronchoalveolar lavage fluid levels of MCP-1, along with those of macrophage inflammatory protein (MIP)1α, IL-8 (CXCL8), and CCL18, are elevated in SSc and correlate with the severity of skin fibrosis. Mononuclear cells and dermal fibroblasts from patients with SSc spontaneously produce these chemokines, and lesional SSc fibroblasts show constitutively high expression of the MCP-1 receptor CCR2. Because MCP-1 drives a Th2 response, the MCP-1- CCR2 axis is thought to play a major role in the pathogenesis of SSc by both amplifying collagen stimulation and promoting Th2 cytokine production. Significantly, MCP-1 null mice are resistant to the development of fibrosis induced by bleomycin. A global survey of chemokine expression in SSc skin revealed enhanced levels of MCP-1, CCL19, CXCL13, and MCP-3, particularly in early-stage disease.

Additional chemokines overexpressed in lesional tissue or serum in patients with SSc or in animal models of scleroderma include the CC chemokines regulated upon activation, normal T cell expressed and secreted (RANTES), pulmonary and activationregulated chemokine (PARC), CXCL4 (also called PF4), as well as MIP-2 and fractalkine (CXC chemokines). Insulin-like growth factor-binding protein-1 (IGFBP-1) stimulates collagen synthesis and fibroblast proliferation and induces TGF-β. Patients with SSc have elevated levels of IGF-1 in the bronchoalveolar lavage fluid. Expression of IGFBP-3 is markedly elevated in SSc fibroblasts. Adenovirus-mediated overexpression of IGFBP-5 caused chronic scleroderma-like fibrosis in mice.

### Angiotensin II

Angiotensin II is a vasoconstricting peptide hormone generated via proteolytic cleavage of angiotensin I by the angiotensin-converting enzyme. The renin—angiotensin system is implicated in pathologic fibrosis in the heart, liver, lung, and kidneys. Serum levels of angiotensin II are elevated in patients with diffuse SSc (dcSSc), functional antibodies targeting the angiotensin II type 1 receptor have been detected. Moreover, angiotensin II is elevated in SSc dermal fibroblasts. In cultured fibroblasts, angiotensin II promotes collagen synthesis and TGF-β production. Chronic subcutaneous administration of angiotensin II induces sclerodermalike skin fibrosis and inflammation in mice, whereas treatment with an inhibitor of the angiotensin II type I receptor ameliorates fibrosis.

### Bioactive Lipids

Bioactive lipids are potent modulators of fbroblast function and tissue repair. Although some prostanoids inhibit fibrotic responses, prostaglandin F (PGF2α) stimulates collagen production and fibroblast proliferation and is elevated in patients with pulmonary fibrosis. Mice with targeted deletion of the PGF receptor are protected from bleomycin-induced pulmonary fibrosis. Another lipid mediator capable of activating fibroblasts and inducing collagen release is LTA4.139 LPA, generated from membrane phospholipids via hydrolysis, exerts multiple biologic activities through G protein—coupled transmembrane receptors. LPA has profibrotic effects including stimulation of fibroblast chemotaxis and CTGF production. A recent study indicated that LPA induces αyβ6 integrin-mediated TGF-β activation in epithelial cells, contributing to sustained autocrine TGF-β signaling. LPA levels are elevated in the lungs of patients with pulmonary fibrosis. Moreover, mice lacking the LPA receptor are protected from bleomycin-induced skin and lung fibrosis.

### Regulation of Fibroblast Function via Innate Immune Signaling: : Toll-like Receptors, Endogenous Ligands, and Inflammasome

The prominent type I IFN signature in SSc leukocytes and genetic studies showing an association of innate immunity genes with SSc support the role of TLR-mediated innate immune responses in pathogenesis. All members of the TLR family are expressed by normal fibroblasts. Activation of TLR4 by its microbial ligand LPS plays a critical role in liver fibrosis, with sensitization to TGF-β as the underlying mechanism. In SSc, fibroblast TLRs are activated by endogenous TLR ligands. These so-called damageassociated molecular patterns (DAMPs) generated by tissue injury,

autoimmunity, and oxidative stress can be broadly grouped into three categories: ECM-derived molecules such as hyaluronan and its small-molecular-weight degradation products, tenascin C, alternatively spliced extra domain A (EDA) fibronectin (Fn-EDA), and biglycan; cellular stress proteins (alarmins) such as HMGB1 released by activated platelets and other injured or necrotic cell types; and nucleic acids and immune complexes. The levels of TLR3 and TLR4 are elevated in SSc skin and lung biopsies and correlate with disease progression. The damage-associated molecules Fn-EDA and tenascin-C are alternatively spliced isoforms of ECM proteins that are highly expressed during normal development but are largely absent in adult tissue at homeostasis. They are transiently generated during tissue injury but during fibrosis accumulate in lesional SSc skin and lung, where they are sensed by resident stromal cells as endogenous TLR4 ligands to elicit persistent profibrotic responses.

The cytosolic innate immune sensors NOD-like receptors (NLRs), retinoic acid inducible gene I (RIG-I), and NALP3 respond to cytosolic nucleic acids, damage-associated endogenous molecules, oxidative stress, and environmental signals such as silica, bleomycin, and gadolinium. Once activated, these sensors facilitate inflammasome assembly with activation of caspase-1 and secretion of proIL-1β and IL-18. NLRP1 has been identified as a susceptibility gene for SSc-associated pulmonary fibrosis. Inflammasome activation and IL-1β generation play an important role in experimental mouse fibrosis and might be involved in SSc as well.

### Matrix Regulation of Fibrosis via Mechanosensing and Mechanotransduction

The fibrotic scar itself plays a key role in maintaining persistent myofibroblast activity and impeding the resolution of fibrosis. Resident stromal mesenchymal cells sense structural and mechanical cues from their surrounding matrix via mechanosensing involving integrin receptors, as well as by recognizing matrixderived biochemical cues, such as tenascin-C, through TLRs and other pattern recognition receptors. A rigid fibrotic microenvironment triggers cellular mechanotransduction pathways involving focal adhesion kinases and Yes-associated protein (YAP), as well as STAT3, which translocate into the nucleus. Mechanotransduction pathways drive myofibroblast activation, while also blocking myofibroblast apoptosis by inducing expression of the prosurvival factor BCL-X. In addition to the stiffness of the matrix, fibroblasts also sense structural changes in collagen. It has been recently shown that increased alignment of collagen bundles in the fibrotic dermis, in contrast to random collagen orientation characteristic of a normal dermis, is sufficient to induce and maintain an activated fibroblast phenotype. Thus a fibrotic microenvironment is both a result and a driver of myofibroblast activation and is responsible for persistence of fibrosis. Pharmacologic targeting of mechanosensing and mechanotransduction to prevent persistent myofibroblast activity and survival are therefore emerging as therapeutic strategies for intractable fibrosis. 143-145

### Negative Regulation of Myofibroblast Activity and Matrix Accumulation

In addition to inhibitory cytokines such as IFN-γ and adiponectin, fibroblasts are equipped with a variety of endogenous molecules that repress ECM gene expression and TGF-β stimulation in order to prevent excessive scarring after injury. For example,

Smad7 blocks TGF-β signal transduction by accelerating ubiquitin-mediated TGF-β receptor degradation. Functional impairment of Smad7 was demonstrated in SSc fibroblasts. Other cell-intrinsic endogenous repressors of collagen synthesis potentially implicated in SSc pathogenesis include the transcription factors Sp3, Fli-1, p53, and Nrf2; the nuclear hormone receptor peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor-γ (PPAR-γ); the deacetylases SIRT1 and SIRT3; and miRNAs such as miR29a. Impaired expression or function of these endogenous inhibitors might contribute to the failure to limit fibroblast activation that underlies fibrosis in SSc.

### Interferon-γ

IFN-γ, the prototypical Th1 cytokine, is a negative regulator of fibroblast activation that abrogates stimulation of collagen gene expression, fibroblast-mediated matrix contraction, and myofibroblast transdifferentiation elicited by TGF-β. Some studies showed that SSc fibroblasts were relatively resistant to the inhibitory effects of IFN-γ. However, clinical trials of IFN-γ in SSc have demonstrated a modest and inconsistent improvement in skin fibrosis.

### Peroxisome Proliferator-Activated Receptor-γ

The nuclear receptor PPAR-γ modulates TGF-β signaling and mesenchymal cell plasticity and is functionally associated with fibrosis. Originally identified as a key regulator of adipogenesis, glucose homeostasis, and metabolism, PPAR-γ has a dual function as both a nuclear receptor and ligand-inducible transcription factor. Electrophilic lipid moieties and prostanoids such as 15d-prostaglandin J2 (15d-PGJ2) serve as endogenous ligands for PPAR-γ, while the thiazolidinedione class of insulin-sensitizing anti-diabetic drugs, including rosiglitazone and pioglitazone, are potent pharmacologic PPAR-γ agonists. PPAR-γ has profound effects on vascular and inflammatory processes, and abnormal PPAR-γ function is implicated in lipodystrophy, atherosclerosis, PAH, and inflammatory diseases. In fibroblasts, 15d-PGJ2 or pharmacologic PPAR-γ ligands abrogated TGF-β—induced collagen production, myofibroblast transdifferentiation, and other fibrotic responses, while treatment with PPAR agonists mitigated fibrosis in mice. Both the expression and the activity of PPAR-γ are impaired in patients with dcSSc. Of note, multiple SSc-associated pathogenic factors, including TGF-β, Wnt ligands, IL-13, hypoxia, LPA, and CTGF, inhibit PPAR-γ function. However, a recent clinical trial using a pan-PPAR agonist to treat SSc failed to reach its primary endpoint. 147,148

### Scleroderma Fibroblast

Fibroblasts explanted from SSc skin or lungs display an abnormal activated phenotype that persists during their serial passage in vitro, indicating intrinsic and durable cellular reprogramming. However, ex vivo cultured SSc fibroblasts do not fully recapitulate the altered profibrotic gene expression profile of SSc skin biopsies, suggesting that in SSc, fibrosis driven by activated fibroblasts represents a combination of cell-autonomous gene changes together with in vivo activation by extra-cellular cues, including biophysical and matrix ultrastructural guidance cues emanating from the microenvironment. The SSc fibroblast phenotype is characterized by enhanced ECM synthesis, constitutive secretion of profibrotic cytokines and chemokines, activation of FAK and consequent myofibroblast differentiation, insensitivity to inhibitory signals, mitochondrial and

energetic perturbations, generation of ROS, and resistance to apoptosis. Many of these features of SSc fibroblasts are reminiscent of the senescent cell phenotype, suggesting that targeting anti-apoptotic or senescence pathways could promote selective killing of SSc fibroblasts and enhance resolution of fibrosis

Numerous molecules involved in intra-cellular signal transduction are abnormally expressed, mislocalized, or constitutively activated in SSc fibroblasts. The list includes Smad3, STAT3, protein kinase C, FAK, Akt, Egr-1, p300, EN1, GLI proteins, AP1 family members, and sirtuins SIRT1 and SIRT3. Elevated expression of the prosurvival factors Bcl-2 and Akt in SSc fibroblasts potentially reflecting mechanotransduction from a rigid microenvironment may play a role in their resistance to apoptosis. Mitochondrial alterations and spontaneous ROS generation contribute to the sustained activation of SSc fibroblasts in a self-amplifying loop (Fig. 84.11). Because many of the phenotypic hallmarks of SSc fibroblasts can be induced in normal fibroblasts treated with TGF- β, the SSc phenotype could be in part ascribed to autocrine TGF- β signaling. The levels of TGF-β receptors are elevated on SSc fibroblasts, which might sensitize these cells to endogenously produced TGF-β or to low levels of environmental TGF-β. Furthermore, SSc fibroblasts express thrombospondin and αvβ3 integrins, which activate latent TGF-β at the cell surface. Consistent with the autocrine TGF-β hypothesis, SSc fibroblasts show constitutive TGF-β signaling with elevated Smad3 activation. Other studies demonstrate defective expression or function of endogenous suppressors of TGF-β signaling and ECM production such as Smad7, Fli1, adiponectin, and Nr4a1, suggesting that failure to terminate fibroblast activation may represent a fundamental defect in SSc.

Autocrine TGF-β activation cannot fully account for all of the phenotypic hallmarks of SSc fibroblasts, indicating that both Smad-independent TGF-β signaling mechanisms, as well as non TGF-β-mediated activation events, underlie the induction or maintenance of the SSc phenotype. The autonomous SSc phenotype could also result from abnormal integrin-mediated signaling from the surrounding ECM. Moreover, epigenetic alterations in SSc fibroblasts are associated with persistent and heritable fibroblast dysfunction. For example, silencing the FLI1 gene, an

important endogenous negative regulator of collagen gene expression, by DNA methylation or chromatin histone deacetylation in fibroblasts increases collagen synthesis.

### Conclusion

Insights from genetic association and whole-exome sequencing studies, genome-scale analysis of gene expression, and epigenetic modifications in bulk tissues and individual cell lineages have identified a very large number of alterations in immune, inflammatory, developmental, aging, and metabolic processes that arise from gene—environment interactions and underlie the clinical and pathologic manifestations of SSc. At the same time, these unbiased high-throughput studies also highlight the surprising degree of molecular heterogeneity and redundancy that are hallmarks of SSc and represent a considerable challenge in classification, prognostication, and treatment decisions. Of interest, the genes associated with increased risk in SSc are predominantly those that are involved in inflammation, innate immunity, and immune cell signaling and that show pervasive overlap with the genetic risk associated with SLE, psoriasis, rheumatoid arthritis, and other autoimmune conditions. These observations suggest that immune activation might have a primary role in determining SSc disease susceptibility.

Nonetheless, it remains unknown why distinct autoimmune diseases with shared genetic risk factors, such as SSc and SLE, show such diverse and nonoverlapping clinical and pathologic manifestations, natural histories, responses to immunomodulatory therapies, and disease outcomes. The roles of cellular aging, and environmental exposures in SSc and how they elicit cell type— specific durable epigenetic modifications that contribute to the persistence of inflammatory, autoimmune, and fibrotic processes, are beginning to be uncovered. These insights are likely to contribute identification of novel biomarkers of diseases activity and subtype and discovery and validation of novel therapeutic targets. An improved granular understanding of pathogenesis is opening the door for selective immunomodulatory, anti-fibrotic agents, and epigenetic modifiers that can be applied in a precision-targeted

approach for the treatment of SSc to the right patient at the right time, as evidenced by the recent approval of nintedanib and tocilizumab for the treatment of SSc-ILD.

# Clinical Features and Treatment of Scleroderma

### KEY POINTS

Systemic sclerosis is a multisystem connective tissue disease affecting the skin and internal organs. The disease process is characterized by early manifestations of inflammation resulting in variable degrees of collagen accumulation (fibrosis) in affected tissues and obliterative vasculopathy of the peripheral and visceral vasculature. Patients fall into different subtypes of disease characterized by distinct severity and type of internal organ involvement as well as pace of clinical progression. Morbidity and mortality are particularly higher when lungs, heart, gastrointestinal tract, and kidneys are involved. Early detection and assertive treatment of organ-specific disease manifestations are critical to effectively manage systemic sclerosis. While an overall disease modifying therapy is not available, novel drugs targeting specific pathways involved in systemic sclerosis are emerging.

In its more aggravated forms, diffuse scleroderma is one of the most terrible of all buman ills. Like Tithonus, to "whither slowly," and like bim to be "beaten down and marred and wasted" until one is literally a mummy, encased in an ever-shrinking, slowly contracting skin of steel, is a fate not pictured in any tragedy, ancient or modern.—Sir. William Osler1a

### Epidemiology

### Incidence and Prevalence

Scleroderma is a rare disease with an estimated incidence of approximately 18 to 20 cases per million population per year and a prevalence of 100 to 300 cases per million population. Reported rates vary based on the method of ascertainment, the population under study, and the definition of disease. Scleroderma is found in all races and in various geographic areas, but the prevalence and severity of disease vary among different racial-ethnic groups. The prevalence of scleroderma appears to be greater in the United States, where it has been estimated at 24.2 per 100,000, than in Europe. Studies conducted in Iceland, England, France, Poland, Norway, and Greece have estimated rates ranging from 7.1 to 15.8 per 100,000.1, In Australia, estimates are similar to those in the United States, whereas in Asia (i.e., Japan and Taiwan), a lower prevalence (3.8 to 5.6 per 100,000) has been reported.3, The highest scleroderma prevalence has been reported

among Choctaw Native Americans (469 per 100,000), in whom the disease appears to be more severe than in other populations. Several surveys in the United States show that African Americans have a higher age-specific incidence rate and experience more severe disease compared with subjects of European ancestry. Disease occurrence does not differ in urban and rural areas. Occasional reports have described unusually large numbers of cases of scleroderma clustered in restricted geographic regions, suggesting nonrandom distribution of the disease. For example, in a rural area in the province of Rome, a geographic cluster of scleroderma was reported with a prevalence 1000 times greater than expected. Likewise, a study in the United Kingdom found a higher scleroderma prevalence in three geographic locations close to airports compared with other areas.

The average age at onset is between 35 and 50 years, and the disease is more common among women (3 to 7:1 female-to-male ratio). Disease onset in older adults is well described; it is uncommon for the disease to become manifest before the age of 25 years. Older age at onset is associated with increased risk for multisystem disease and, in particular, for development of pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH). During the period from 1963 to 1982, in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, the highest rates of scleroderma were observed between the ages of 45 and 54 years in Black women and between the ages of 55 and 64 years in White women. Younger age at disease diagnosis among Black women compared with White women was reported in Detroit, Michigan. Interest in defining pre-clinical or early forms of scleroderma has led to the identification of patients with minimal manifestations and different risk of progression. The evolution to definite systemic sclerosis (SSc) is more frequent in patients presenting minimal manifestations of disease such as Raynaud's phenomenon (RP), nail-fold capillary changes, and scleroderma-related autoantibodies. 10,11

### Survival

Mortality among patients with scleroderma is higher than in ageand sex-matched healthy individuals, with most deaths (up to 11-14The 75%) being attributed directly to disease manifestations. standardized mortality rate (SMR) measures the ratio of observed death rate in a specific disease group to the death rate expected in the general population. A comprehensive review of 29 scleroderma cohort studies published between 1988 and 2019 reported pooled SMRs ranging from 2.72 to 3.64.15 While overall survival rates have improved in scleroderma patients over time, several studies indicate that the SMR has not changed.16-20

Survival in scleroderma is significantly influenced by disease subtype, degree of internal organ involvement, and comorbid conditions. Factors associated with poor prognosis include diffuse skin disease, the presence of pulmonary disease (particularly PAH), renal or cardiac involvement, severe gastrointestinal (GI) failure, multisystem disease, older age at disease onset, and the presence of anemia. Studies conducted on inception cohorts indicate that early mortality is predicted by male sex, older age at disease onset, diffuse disease subtype, development of PAH, renal crisis, and anti-SCL70 positivity. In particular, lung and cardiac involvement have been identified as the leading causes of scleroderma-related mortality. A population-based study conducted in Canada found 1-, 5-, and 10-year overall survival rates in scleroderma patients of 85.0, 64.5, and 44.9%, respectively, compared with 77.1, 44.4, and 22.0% in subjects affected by interstitial lung disease (ILD). Both presence of diastolic dysfunction and pulmonary hypertension (PH) secondary to heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (PH-HFpEF) have been independently associated with increased risk of death.22, Anti-Scl70 is associated with higher overall mortality as well as increased SMR. Anti-centromere antibody (ACA) predicts a normal expected mortality. Anti-RNA polymerase III antibody positivity is associated with diffuse skin disease and scleroderma renal crisis (SRC), but also with a lower frequency of ILD and survival rates, similar to those detected in patients with ACA. A more severe disease course with increased mortality has been reported in African American patients.24, A recent public database survey found the highest age-adjusted mortality rate among Blacks or African Americans at 5.703 per million (95% confidence interval [CI], 5.5215.885), followed by Native Americans or Alaska Natives at 5.047 (95% CI, 4.4285.667) and Whites at 3.766 (95% CI, 3.7133.819). Infection, malignancy, and cardiovascular events are expected causes of death in scleroderma patients not related to the underlying disease. However, recent studies indicate that scleroderma is independently associated with a higher risk of developing complications from macroscopic coronary artery or cerebrovascular involvement beyond what is expected in the general population. .27-29

Improved survival in recent years results from more assertive management and adoption of more effective treatments for specific organ-based complications. In particular, the natural history of SRC has changed with the use of angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors. Historically, patients with this complication had a 1-year survival rate of less than 15%. Recent case-control studies conducted after the introduction of ACE inhibitors suggest a 1-year survival rate greater than an 85%. Decreased mortality over the past few decades has been confirmed in several cohorts. In a large U.S. scleroderma center, the 10-year survival rate from the time of disease diagnosis improved from 54% in the 1972 to 1981 patient group to 66% in the 1982 to 1991 group. A meta-analysis of 43 studies (n = 13,529) reported survival rates from the time of diagnosis of 1 year, 86.5%; 5 years, 74.9%; 10 years, 62.5%; and 20 years, 41.8%. Comparing studies performed before and after 1990, the authors observed an improvement in 5-year survival from date of diagnosis (70.6% pre-1990 compared with 84.4% post-1990; p < 0.001) but not from the date of disease onset. A recent French incident cohort demonstrated a 5-year and 10-year survival rate of 85.9% and 71.7%, respectively. ### Environmental Influences

Geographic clustering, low concordance rates in identical twins, and case reports following exposures to toxins suggest that environmental factors may be responsible for triggering scleroderma, but definitive proof is still lacking. Evidence of geographic clustering has been reported in London boroughs located near international airports, in a rural community near Rome, in an area of high-density industry in Canada, in areas of mining in Montana, and in locations with increased density of industry and waste sites in Massachusetts. 37-39

The most compelling evidence for an environmental factor driving the disease has been the detection of typical manifestations of scleroderma among coal miners and workers exposed to silica. A meta-analysis including 15 case-control studies and four cohort studies of silica exposure showed an overall odds ratio (OR) of 2.81 (95% CI, 1.864.23; p < 0.001) and relative risk of 17.52 (95% CI, 5.9851.37; p < 0.001), respectively. Cases are more likely to be males manifesting diffuse skin involvement and ILD. Although occupational exposure to solvents (e.g., paint thinner or removers, mineral spirits, trichloroethylene, trichloroethane, perchloroethane, gasoline, aliphatic hydrocarbons, halogenated hydrocarbons, and solvents containing benzene, toluene, or xylene), heavy metals, or polyvinyl chloride is associated with scleroderma, the role of these agents in causing disease is controversial and remains unproven.

Case reports have suggested that the silicone present in certain breast implants may play a role in triggering scleroderma. A study evaluating long-term implant-related outcomes in women who received silicone implants indicates a scleroderma standardized incidence ratio (SIR) of 7.00 compared with the general population. In contrast, many other epidemiologic surveys have not found a greater incidence of scleroderma in women with breast implants or in those exposed to silicone. Epidemics of sclerodermalike illness after exposure to dietary (L-tryptophan or adulterated rapeseed oil), occupational (silica), or pharmacologic (e.g., bleomycin and gadolinium-based contrast media) toxins and exaggerated reactions to radiation support the idea that certain chemical and various agents can trigger a fibrotic disease. Drugs implicated as potentially causative for SSc-like illnesses include bleomycin, pentazocine, and cocaine. Interestingly, cigarette smoking is not associated with an increased risk for scleroderma. A survey of 3319 patients (23% ex-smokers, 11% current smokers) did not identify any major adverse effect of smoking on progression of

scleroderma-specific pulmonary or cutaneous manifestations.' 44 A semiquantitative analysis assessing cumulative exposure to toxic compounds in the work environment (i.e., crystalline silica, chlorinated solvents, aromatic solvents, hydrocarbons, epoxy resins, and welding fumes) and in nonwork lifestyle settings (i.e., smoking, gardening, painting, woodwork) established a dosedependent association between such exposures and decline over time of the forced vital capacity (FVC), independent of sex. A retrospective analysis conducted in Brazilian scleroderma patients found that myopathy was independently associated with previous exposure to organic solvents, silica, silicone, and pesticides (OR = 2.09; 95% CI, 1.153.82), especially silica exposure (OR = 3.09; 95% CI, 1.675.73.46

### Clinical Features

### Diagnostic Criteria

A subcommittee of the American College of Rheumatology (ACR) established the "preliminary" diagnostic criteria in 1980 based on expert consensus. The purpose of these criteria was to provide diagnostic certainty and consistency for research and other documentary exercises. Consequently, despite a high specificity, their sensitivity was poor, and patients with early-stage scleroderma and 20% of those with limited cutaneous disease did not meet these criteria. Since then, knowledge about the prognostic relevance of scleroderma-specific autoantibodies has significantly improved, and the use of nail-fold capillaroscopy has become a widely accepted, reliable diagnostic tool, supporting the recommendation by some experts to revise the 1980 classification criteria to be more inclusive of patients with early disease

manifestations.10, For this reason, the ACR and European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology (EULAR) established a joint committee to define new classification criteria, which were published in 2013 (see Table 85.1). The single finding of skin thickening proximal to the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints of the hands remains a criterion that alone is sufficient to classify a patient as having scleroderma. If skin thickening is found only distal to the MCP joints, then a point system is applied based on the presence of seven other specific manifestations. These manifestations include skin thickening of the fingers, fingertip lesions, telangiectasias, abnormal nail-fold capillaries, PAH and/or ILD, RP, and scleroderma-related autoantibodies. Patients with a combined score of nine or more points are classified as having scleroderma. The new criteria have a specificity of 0.91 and a sensitivity of 0.92, which overall represent a much better performance compared with previous criteria. Nonetheless, patients without skin thickening but with the presence of RP, abnormal nail-fold capillaries, and positive scleroderma-specific autoantibodies still do not meet the 2013 ACR/EULAR criteria. Large longitudinal surveys confirm that clinically manifested scleroderma develops within a 2to 4-year period of follow-up in a high percentage of patients with this "early" phenotype.10, Therefore, although classification criteria are useful in defining cases for research purposes, the clinician needs to consider subtle features of the disease to make an early diagnosis and institute prompt management. Most experts would accept the finding of three of the five features of the CREST syndrome (calcinosis, Raynaud's phenomenon, esophageal dysfunction, sclerodactyly, and telangiectasias) to make a clinical diagnosis of scleroderma. In clinical practice, one needs to recognize that although some patients have not experienced skin changes, they nonetheless have some features of systemic disease

(systemic sclerosis sine scleroderma) and that in many cases only partial expression of the disease (e.g., RP with nail-fold changes only) may be present, for some time before full-defined manifestations develop.

In 201 1, a multicenter Delphi exercise resulted in development of the preliminary criteria for the very early diagnosis of systemic sclerosis (VEDOSS). Based on these criteria, patients presenting with no skin fibrosis but RP, positive ANA, and puffy fingers should be further evaluated and, in the presence of abnormal nail-fold capillaries or positive SSc-specific autoantibodies (i.e., anti-centromere, anti-topoisomerase I or -SCL70, and anti-RNA polymerase III), or both, should be classified as manifesting very early SSc. Follow-up studies have shown that these early patients often progress to full expression of the disease.54, Many experts propose that subjects who present the VEDOSS phenotype should be considered to have a diagnosis of scleroderma and be evaluated and treated accordingly.

### Classification and Clinical Subsets

The scleroderma disease process is complex, and its clinical expression is heterogeneous, such that the disease is expressed in several distinct clinical phenotypes. Classifying patients into subtypes is useful both for investigative purposes and for clinical practice. A specific subtype can define increased risk for internal organ involvement and overall prognosis. The traditional way to classify patients is by the degree of skin thickening as determined by physical examination. The skin is scored by pinching a fold and deciding whether it is abnormally thickened because of the scleroderma process. A committee of experts decided by consensus that two major groups of patients can be identified based on the distribution of skin changes and associated clinical and laboratory outcomes (see Fig. 85.1). Patients are considered to have diffuse skin disease if skin changes are found proximal to the elbows and/ or knees or on the trunk, excluding the face. These patients tend to have higher risk of multisystem disease and poorer survival.

Patients are considered to have limited disease if skin changes occur distal to the elbows and/or knees and not on the trunk. Facial skin thickening can be present in the limited group. Some clinicians argue that the term CREST syndrome should be eliminated and that these patients should be classified in the limited skin group. Others believe that the CREST acronym identifies a unique subtype within the broader group of limited skin diseases with a distinct disease course.

Another less popular classification system divides patients into three groups based on skin changes: limited or type I (fingers only), intermediate or type II (skin up to the elbows or knees), and diffuse or type III (skin above the elbows and/or knees and/or trunk). Studies using this classification found that the intermediate group had distinct clinical outcomes, including an intermediate survival statistic between limited (best) and diffuse (worse) subsets. A subtype of disease with absence of skin fibrosis has been recognized and referred to as scleroderma sine scleroderma. Patients with early or partial expression of the disease (e.g., RP alone with nail-fold capillary loop abnormalities) are often diagnosed as having undifferentiated connective tissue disease (CTD). However, criteria for VEDOSS have been proposed including RP, positive ANA, puffy fingers together with abnormal nail-fold capillaries and scleroderma related autoantibodies, without skin thickening. Evidence shows that clear features of scleroderma frequently will develop in these patients, usually within 3 to 5 years of follow-up. 10,

Other classification systems are now being used including subtypes defined by the presence of specific serum autoantibodies that predict clinical features of the disease (see the "Natural History of Disease" section). Nail-fold capillary patterns and tissue gene expression signatures have also been proposed as innovative means of defining scleroderma subtypes. Classification by a composite score modeling clinical features and serology data is becoming more popular as it may better define overall outcome and management plans. Patients with scleroderma often exhibit features of other rheumatic or autoimmune diseases and are considered to

have an overlap syndrome. The most common overlap syndromes are with inflammatory polyarthritis, myositis, sicca complex, and hypothyroidism.
