Less frequently, scleroderma can be associated with primary biliary cholangitis (PBC), autoimmune hepatitis, vasculitis, rheumatoid arthritis (RA), and anti-neutrophil cytoplasm antibody (ANCA)—associated pauci-immune glomerulonephritis. Mixed CTD is an overlap syndrome manifesting features of scleroderma, polymyositis, lupus-like rashes, and rheumatoidlike polyarthritis.

### Autoantibodies

Scleroderma-specific autoantibodies are established as strong predictors of the pattern of organ complications and disease outcome (see Table 85.2). The three most frequently observed types of autoantibodies in scleroderma are anti-centromere, anti-SCL70, and anti-RNA polymerase III antibodies.

Anti-centromere antibodies have a high specificity for patients with limited scleroderma but can be found in about 5% of those with diffuse disease. Patients with anti-centromere antibodies tend to be older White women presenting with skin disease limited to the fingers and indolent clinical course. Often the diagnosis in these subjects is delayed until anti-centromere antibodies are discovered or late organ disease becomes evident. Patients frequently have features of the CREST syndrome. Subcutaneous calcinosis is a late manifestation, commonly manifesting as small clusters present on the fingers or along the forearm and anterior lower leg. In the anti-centromere-positive group, RP can become more severe with increased risk for macrovascular disease. This can lead to digital gangrene and amputation. ILD is less common, but progressive pulmonary vascular disease with PAH and right heart failure occurs in a significant proportion of these patients. Overall, epidemiologic studies indicate that anti-centromere antibodies generally are predictors of a favorable prognosis. A recent survey reported a lower risk for cancer than expected in the general population. Anti-centromere antibodies directed against different epitopes than those targeted in scleroderma can also be found in patients with primary Sjögren's syndrome,

systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), RA, autoimmune hepatitis, and PBC.

Anti-SCL70 antibodies are primarily associated with diffuse skin disease but can also be detected in up to 30% of limited scleroderma patients. The degree of skin thickening is highly variable in these patients, but usually the severity of skin involvement becomes established within the 3 years from disease onset. RP is usually the first symptom and carries a high risk for recurrent digital ischemic ulcers. Anti-SCL70 positivity is associated with more significant organ involvement, more commonly severe ILD, arthritis, tendon friction rubs, SRC, and heart disease. The association between ILD and anti-SCL70 is independent of the degree of skin disease. The positivity of this autoantibody in African American patients carries an especially poor prognosis with higher scleroderma-related mortality. Rapid progression of skin changes is associated with more severe organ disease and an increased incidence of renal crisis, usually in the first few years from disease onset. Diffuse skin changes can lead to joint-tendon involvement with contractures affecting in particular fingers and elbows.

Anti-RNA polymerase III antibodies are associated with rapid and aggressive diffuse skin disease, increased risk of renal involvement, and GI bleeding from gastric antral vascular ectasia. These patients have the worst cutaneous involvement, with rapid widespread skin disease associated with signs and symptoms of deep tissue fibrosis involving joints, tendons, and muscles. Flexion contractures of the fingers, wrist, elbows, shoulders, hips, knees, and ankles are complications that can occur within a few months from the onset of disease activity. Development of friction rubs is common and associated with severe disease course and poor outcome. Approximately 25% to 40% of patents positive for this autoantibody develop scleroderma renal disease with hypertensive crisis and kidney failure. The risk is greatest in the early phases, when skin is rapidly progressing. Anti-RNA polymerase III subjects are less likely to develop lung involvement, but heart disease can be a late complication. Skin and deep tissue damage are the most worrisome long-term problems in this subtype of scleroderma. A "fibrosing" myopathy without evidence of the typical pathologic signs of inflammation (myositis), along with skin and joint

disease, leads to loss of strength and flexibility and is a major cause of long-term disability.

Studies conducted in different countries have consistently found an association between scleroderma and underlying malignancy in subjects that are anti-RNA polymerase III positive. 63-66 In one survey anti-RNA polymerase III positivity was associated with a significantly increased risk of cancer diagnosis within 2 years of scleroderma onset (OR 5.08). There was also an increased temporal clustering of cancer and scleroderma in the group of participants who were negative for anti-centromere, anti-topoisomerase I, and anti-RNA polymerase III antibodies. Patients with anti-RNA polymerase III antibodies and diffuse skin disease had a higher risk of breast cancer (SIR 5.14), prostate cancer (SIR 7.17), and tongue cancer (SIR 43.9), whereas patients with anti-RNA polymerase III antibodies and limited cutaneous disease had an increased risk of lung cancer (SIR 10.4). Similarly, within 3 years of scleroderma onset, CTP-negative patients with limited scleroderma had a higher risk of breast cancer (SIR 4.44) and melanoma (SIR 7.10), and CTP-negative patients with diffuse scleroderma had an increased risk of tongue cancer (SIR 40.5). Within the CTP-negative group a small subset has antibodies against the RNA binding region containing 3 (RNPC3), a component of the minor spliceosome complex. Compared with those with anti-centromere antibodies, individuals with anti-RNPC3 or anti-RNA polymerase III antibodies had a significantly higher risk of developing cancer, usually gynecologic tumors in women, within 2 years of scleroderma onset. As detection of cancer (most commonly breast and lung) often occurs in close temporal relationship with the onset of scleroderma, appropriate screening for underlying neoplastic disease in these patients is of paramount importance.

ANA testing by indirect immunofluorescence can detect autoantibodies exhibiting a typical nucleolar staining pattern in up to 40% of scleroderma patients in association with specific clinical phenotypes and outcomes. Of these, anti-Th/To antibodies and anti-PM/Scl antibodies are associated with limited skin disease, whereas anti-U3-RNP (fibrillarin) antibodies are associated with diffuse disease. Patients with anti-Th/To antibodies are at increased risk for development of severe ILD and PH. Anti-U3- RNP predict a less favorable prognosis with a higher frequency of internal organ involvement, including ILD, PAH, and renal crisis. This subset of autoantibodies is more frequently detected in African Americans with diffuse skin disease and poor prognosis. These patients commonly have hyperpigmented and hypopigmented skin changes and contractures of large joints associated with inflammatory or fibrotic muscle disease leading to significant morbidity. Cardiac disease is often subclinical until late-stage disease, when both right and left heart failure can occur.

Anti-PM/Scl, anti-Ku, and anti-U1-RNP antibodies are seen mainly in patients with overlap syndromes. The presence of anti- PM/Scl is associated with acute onset of weakness as a result of inflammatory muscle disease and a higher risk for ILD. Anti-Ku positivity is strongly associated with muscle and joint involvement. Anti-U1-RNP antibodies are seen in patients with mixed CTD, particularly among African Americans with limited scleroderma, manifesting commonly with polyarthritis, myositis, and lupus with skin or renal involvement. Diffuse skin disease and risk for late onset of PAH are increased overall. Less common autoantibody subtypes have been associated with unique clinical manifestations, including anti-B23 with PAH, anti-IFI-16 with digital ischemia, and anti-RNPC-3 with ILD and risk for can- 60, Several recent studies have also reported the detection in cer.

scleroderma patients of autoantibodies directed toward functional receptors. These include autoantibodies to angiotensin II type I receptor, endothelin-1 type A receptor, muscarinic-3 receptor, and platelet-derived growth factor receptor.71, Broader epidemiologic and mechanistic studies are needed to confirm their relevance and their role in the disease pathogenesis. Anti-SSA/Ro52 antibodies are found in 35.6% of scleroderma patients, although they are not associated with any specific clinical manifestations. Up to 11% of patients with scleroderma can test negative for ANAs.

### General Principles of Disease Evaluation .

### Natural History of Disease

The disease course and the ultimate clinical outcome vary a great deal among patients meeting diagnostic criteria for scleroderma. The clinical expression of the disease changes over time, with features of vascular disease such as RP presenting during early phases followed by an inflammatory process triggering varying degrees of skin fibrosis and internal organ involvement. Patients fall into very distinct subtypes of scleroderma for which the disease severity and type of internal organ involvement generally can be predicted by the extent and pace of affected skin, race, age of onset, and associated autoantibodies. Internal organ disease tends to be more severe in patients with the diffuse skin type than in those with limited scleroderma. A survey of 695 patients who had a baseline visit within 1 year after RP onset found that incident non-RP manifestations were skin sclerosis (75%), GI symptoms (71%), impaired diffusing capacity for monoxide less than 80% predicted (65%), digital ulcers (34%), cardiac involvement (32%), FVC less than 80% predicted (31%), increased pulmonary arterial systolic pressure more than 40 mm Hg (14%), and renal crisis (3%). Approximately half of these incident organ manifestations occurred within 2 years from presentation. While patients presenting with sclerodactyly alone have an overall better long-term prognosis, in a subset of them long-term complications such as severe GI dysfunction, ILD, or PH can develop. Subjects with diffuse skin disease are more likely to develop internal organ disease early in the course. A rapid rate of skin progression is associated with early internal organ involvement and increased mortality. Progression of skin thickening in most cases stops after several months reaching different degrees of severity and then gradually improves as skin recovers. In a subset of patients, severe skin and deep tissue involvement involving most of the body surface persist over years. (see "Skin Involvement" section).

### Measuring Disease Activity and Severity

One of the challenges in studying or caring for patients with scleroderma consists of determining and measuring disease activity, severity, and irreversible damage. These measures are not independent of each other and thus cannot be considered in isolation. Activity is a measure of ongoing disease that is dynamic and reversible; it is a direct reflection of ongoing biologic processes such as autoimmune-mediated inflammation or progressive tissue fibrosis. Severity is a measure of the impact of damage on the whole person or a specific organ at any given time. In the extreme, severity is a measure of irreversible end-stage damage. It is important to distinguish reversible disease activity from irreversible damage because, although both can cause clinical distress, intervention differs for the two. Patients with scleroderma can accumulate irreversible damage over time, and thus measuring disease

activity is more relevant early on, when disease has the potential of being reversed.

Serial bedside measurement of changes in skin thickness (modified Rodnan skin score [mRSS]) is used as a surrogate measure of disease activity. Active skin disease is associated with tissue edema, stiffness, and intense pruritus. Patients will report involvement of new areas of the body during the active phase. The overall degree of involvement is the level of severity, which is a predictor of the extent of organ involvement and overall prognosis (see "Skin Involvement" section). The Rodnan skin score is used as a quantifiable, easily obtainable, and valid score that changes over time. Thus the skin score has been used in clinical trials as a major outcome measure. In patients with diffuse skin disease, improvement of the skin score is associated with a better clinical outcome.

More detailed scales for specific organs are also in use, as well as other composite measures that include functional testing and selfreported clinical outcomes. For example, a skin assessment tool has been developed that combines the mRSS with a visual analogue scale (VAS) score of the patient's assessment of skin activity, a VAS score of the physician's assessment of skin activity, and measures obtained by a durometer. A validated questionnaire is in use to define mild to severe GI disease. Tools to assess severity and outcomes in PAH as related to scleroderma include pulmonary arterial pressures and cardiac function as measured by right heart catheterization (RHC) and echocardiography (ECHO), exercise testing as measured by the 6-minute walk and oxygen saturation, New York Heart Association functional class, severity of dyspnea on a VAS, and measures of quality of life and function obtained by the Short Form 36 and the Health Assessment Questionnaire and Disability Index (HAQ-DI) and physician global scale. Outcome measures considered valid in scleroderma patients include the Raynaud's condition score (RCS) for severity of RP, FVC, and Mahler's dyspnea index to monitor ILD, serum creatinine, blood pressure, and complete blood cell count during a SRC, and serum creatine phosphokinase (CPK) to monitor muscle disease.

A scleroderma severity scale has been developed by investigators to assess disease severity status in individual patients both at a given time and longitudinally. This scale is based on scoring that ranges from 0 (normal) to 4 (end stage) for each organ system involved in scleroderma, including a general measure, along with measures of the peripheral vascular system, skin, joints and tendons, GI tract, lung, heart, and kidney. This severity scale has the potential to measure disease activity if it is used in studies with serial observations, when individual organ scales can be combined into a composite score.

The HAQ-DI has been validated in patients with scleroderma with evidence of correlation with objective physical signs and the course of the disease. Higher degrees of impairment are found by HAQ scores in patients who have diffuse skin disease, higher skin scores, abnormal hand function, presence of myopathy or friction rubs, and joint pain. Change in the HAQ score occurs with changes in skin involvement and progressive organ disease. The HAQ is useful in evaluating patients with RP and correlates with the severity and presence of digital ulcers. VAS instruments that assess disease in various domains specific for scleroderma are added to the HAQ to focus on scleroderma-specific issues, including measures of RP and digital ulcers. The Short Form 36 survey, a simple self-report tool composed of 36 items in eight domains, is also used to assess health-related quality of life (HRQoL). A patient-reported outcome measure, the Cochin 17-scale, that includes measures of mobility and complex tasks execution and items related to cognitive function, has been evaluated in

scleroderma patients showing good reliability in capturing higher levels of global activity limitation in patients with more severe disease.

Developing reliable tools to assess disease activity and response to treatment in clinical care and clinical trials has been challenging. In 2001 the European Scleroderma Study Group (EscSG) has developed a preliminary activity index (AI) based on 1 1 core activity variables identified in a large multicenter cohort of scleroderma patients. This index provides more of an organ-specific assessment than a measure of global activity. The EscSG-AI has been subsequently revised and tested in a non-European scleroderma cohort, showing a moderate association with physician-rated disease activity. 83,

Using an expert-consensus approach, a combined response index for use in clinical trials in early diffuse scleroderma has been developed. The ACR Composite Response Index in Systemic Sclerosis (ACR-CRISS) uses a single weighted score to measure the likelihood of response to treatment integrating worsening or incident cases of cardiopulmonary-renal involvement with changes in five core set measures (mRSS, FVC percentage predicted, HAQ- DI, and patient and clinician global assessments). Analyses of ACR-CRISS scores in past clinical trials has raised some concern about its responsiveness to change due to evidence of both ceiling and floor effects. For this reason, a new "revised CRISS" has recently been proposed to assess the proportion of patients who achieve a predefined percentage of improvement in ≥1 of the core 86 set measures.

A significant body of research has been devoted to defining more precise measures of disease activity and prognosis, including quantification of serologic markers of inflammation, immune activation, and circulating cellular subsets, but none has developed into a widely accepted, clinically useful tool and currently no "gold standard" to measure disease activity in scleroderma exist.

### General Guidelines for Management

Several basic principles can be of help in managing patients with scleroderma. The first principle is that scleroderma encompasses different subsets of disease, each with a unique clinical phenotype; thus carefully determining the specific subtype of the patient sets the scene for deciding the most appropriate therapeutic approach. Even within a given subtype, the clinical manifestations and disease activity can be highly variable, likely reflecting different susceptibility to, or risk for, systemic complications and a dynamic biologic process that vary with time and that can shift in nature at different stages of the disease. The initial clinical presentation of RP suggests that vascular involvement targeting peripheral arteries and small tissue vessels is underlying the entire disease process. This vascular disease unique to scleroderma manifests as a multisystem fibrotic vasculopathy characterized by intimal fibrosis and occlusion of small peripheral arteries, arterioles, and capillaries, resulting in tissue hypoxia and injury. This generalized vasculopathy is associated with the second seemingly independent biologic process of tissue fibrosis, which results from injury and maladaptive repair and can lead to severe organ dysfunction. Early intervention is key to prevent irreversible tissue damage.

Signs of classic inflammation can often be present during the initial phases of the disease, particularly in the skin and soft tissues where features of edema or erythema may be visible, mimicking states of fluid overload. However, later on the fibrotic process becomes more dominant and, even if subclinical, it can gradually drive multiorgan damage. Although the skin may be the site

of the most dramatic physical findings, scleroderma is a multisystem disease, and the physician must always search for early organ-based complications. While a disease-modifying agent that controls overall the clinical manifestations of scleroderma would be ideal, most success in managing this condition has focused on an organ-specific approach. Occult organ disease should be identified early to allow a more customized and targeted therapy. Early intervention is most important for success; once irreversible tissue or organ damage is established, supportive care becomes the main and often only option. It is important to perform a full evaluation of every scleroderma patient, even in those with very early disease manifestations. Examination should include a baseline skin score and careful assessment of nail-fold capillaries in that these features can predict disease course. Autoantibodies, pulmonary function tests (PFTs), high-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) scan of the lungs, and echocardiogram should be included as well. Appreciation of age of onset, gender, and race also provides relevant insight. Careful assessment of comorbid conditions including standard screening for cancer is recommended. Scleroderma is a chronic disease that can be disfiguring, causes disabilities, and in some cases is life-threatening. It is important to educate the patient about the disease and the spectrum of its manifestations and provide continued effective emotional support.

Defining the subtype of scleroderma and the evidence for existing specific organ involvement determine the intervention needed. When a patient presents with rapidly progressive inflammatory skin disease without early signs of other vital organ involvement, it is reasonable to implement combination or sequential immunosuppression, followed by maintenance for an extended time. The anti-inflammatory program can then be coupled with necessary organ-specific therapeutic interventions based on the unfolding clinical phenotype. The missing component for a truly comprehensive approach is the availability of a uniformly effective direct anti-fibrotic agent that is able to prevent the progression of fibrosis once the inflammatory phase is under control. In addition, while scleroderma-related vascular manifestations are currently managed with effective vasoactive drugs (e.g., RP, PH, and SRC), no clear insight exists regarding the actual role of immunosuppression in preventing onset and progression of the systemic vasculopathy.

Although no one agent has been shown to control the disease, a variety of biologic drugs targeting specific inflammatory pathways and agents with some anti-fibrotic effects are used alone or in combination to attempt control of aggressive manifestations and prevent progressive organ disease (e.g., ILD). Patients with severe, nonresponsive disease can also be treated with myeloor immuneablative therapeutic approaches with or without autologous hematopoietic stem cell transplantation or alternatively entered into clinical trials testing novel therapies. 87-90

### Raynaud's Phenomenon

RP is an exaggerated vascular response of the digital arterial circulation triggered by cold ambient temperature and emotional stress. The diagnosis of RP is based on a history of excessive cold sensitivity and recurrent events of sharply demarcated pallor and/or cyanosis of the skin of the digits (see Fig. 85.2). Blanching reflects digital arterial vasospasm, and cyanosis occurs as a result of the deoxygenation of sluggish venous blood flow. Some skin blushing (redness) may follow due to reactive hyperemia after regular blood flow has been restored. Various surveys throughout the world estimate a prevalence of RP ranging from about 3% to 15% of the general population, more commonly among females (3 to 4:1).

During cold exposure (particularly during shifting temperatures and winter months), RP attacks increase in frequency and intensity. RP can be categorized clinically into primary and secondary forms (see Fig. 85.3). In primary RP, recurrent vasospastic events occur in the absence of an underlying disease process. Young age at onset (<20 years), symmetric manifestations of symptoms, mild to moderate severity, no association with digital ulceration or tissue gangrene, normal nail-fold capillary examination, and a negative ANA titer are all indicative of primary RP. Secondary RP occurs in a variety of settings, including autoimmune rheumatic diseases such as scleroderma, SLE, mixed CTD, Sjögren's syndrome, and dermatomyositis/polymyositis; occupational trauma (e.g., hypothenar hammer syndrome); the use of certain drugs (e.g., anti-migraine agents, ergotamine derivatives, amphetamines, and chemotherapeutic agents especially cisplatin and bleomycin); hematologic abnormalities such as cryoglobulinemia, cold agglutinin disease, paraproteinemia, POEMS (polyneuropathy, organomegaly, endocrinopathy, monoclonal gammopathy, and skin changes) syndrome, and cryofibrinogenemia; occupational and environmental causes including vascular trauma (e.g., injury to the distal ulnar artery in the hypothenar hammer syndrome, the use of vibrating tools, and frostbite); and compressive or obstructive vascular disease (e.g., thoracic outlet syndrome, and carpal tunnel syndrome). Hypothyroidism may predispose to RP. Vasculitis may cause ischemic digits, but the absence of preceding cold-induced and reversible color changes help distinguishing it from true RP.

Nail-fold capillaroscopy is the tool most commonly used at the bedside to distinguish patients with primary RP from those with scleroderma or another rheumatic disease. The utility of assessing patterns of nail-fold capillary abnormalities to monitor progression toward more severe disease manifestations has been reported. The simplest method of detection is to coat the skin of the nail fold with immersion oil and then view the area using a bifocal dissecting microscope or a handheld device such as an ophthalmoscope set at 20 or 40 diopters. Portable dermatoscopes can also be used to perform a rapid and effective examination of the nail-fold area. A computerized nail-fold video capillaroscopy technique is used in specialty centers. This technique provides enhanced digital images that can assess local blood flow and follow the disease course. Patients with primary RP have normal, thin, palisading nail-fold capillary loops (see Fig. 85.4), while in secondary RP, capillary loop dilation/enlargements and dropouts provide evidence for microvascular disease.

In scleroderma, the patterns of capillary abnormalities appear to correlate with the course of systemic disease manifestations. Capillary dilation (giant capillaries), microhemorrhages, and some disorganization of the capillary network are typical of early disease; dropouts, avascular areas, and signs of neoangiogenesis with bizarre architectural distortion manifest at later stages of scleroderma.96, Clinical features of scleroderma will develop in approximately 20% to 30% of patients who at presentation have RP and abnormal nail-fold capillary changes but do not meet established diagnostic criteria and do not have sclerodermarelated autoantibodies, usually within a 3to 4-year period. Patients with RP and nail-fold capillary changes and, in addition, a positive scleroderma-related autoantibody have a 70% to 80% chance of developing scleroderma within 2 to 3 years from presentation. Therefore capillaroscopy represents an important standard tool to examine patients presenting with RP and can help distinguish presence of primary RP or undifferentiated CTD from early scleroderma.

RP occurs in almost every patient with scleroderma and often is the first symptom of the disease. In scleroderma, RP and digital ischemia are clinical manifestations of both abnormal regulation of local vasomotor control and fixed structural vascular disease. Cold-induced vasoconstriction of peripheral blood vessels normally occurs via sympathetic stimulation. This is exaggerated and abnormal in scleroderma. Over time it becomes associated with a nonvasculitic vasculopathy characterized by endothelial dysfunction and vascular smooth muscle cell proliferation driving

increased collagen content in the intima of small and medium vessels, with loss of vessel flexibility and fibrotic obliteration of their lumina. Digital pitting with loss of fingertip tissue and small, painful, superficial ulcerations are very common (30% to 50%) and are usually noted as a consequence of disease affecting the small arteries and arterioles of the skin (see Fig. 85.5). Large, deep ulcerations of the distal portion of the fingers are a consequence of larger vessel (e.g., digital artery) occlusion associated with severe vasospasm. The latter event usually presents as a sharp demarcation of the distal digit with intense, localized pain resulting from ischemia. Failure to reverse these events may lead to loss of the entire digit or limb as a result of deep tissue infarction.

Although several methods may be used to objectively score attacks of RP, no test is considered practical or reproducible enough to replace the clinical criteria for diagnosis and management. Patients with an active RP attack will present with coolness of the involved distal fingertips and/or toes, which can be associated with a line of demarcation of skin pallor or cyanosis. In later stages of severe RP, if the condition is not treated, one may find signs of critical digital ischemia resulting in painful and unremitting digital ulcerations. Such findings warrant immediate medical treatment. Several methods may be used to assess the severity of RP. Traditionally, the patient is asked to use a diary to record the frequency and duration of attacks during days of usual activity. The RCS is a patient-based measure that considers the impact of RP on the patient, including pain, discomfort, and its effect on daily function. A composite index using six outcome measures

including the RCS, frequency and duration of attacks, attack symptoms, and patient and physician VAS of global assessment has been proposed in an effort to standardize outcome measures to assess therapeutic effect in clinical trials for RP. This composite score shows promise in reducing the high placebo response rate that is usually noted when only one outcome measure is used in clinical trial studies. Other laboratory-based measures, including laser Doppler, thermography, and plethysmography methods, are also used to obtain objective data and measurements of digital blood flow.

### Management of Raynaud's Phenomenon and Digital Ischemia

The primary goal in the management of RP is to improve quality of life and prevent secondary digital ischemia using nonpharmacologic and pharmacologic measures (see Fig. 85.6). In the setting of acute digital ischemia, rapid intervention using both treatment modalities are required. Management begins with educating the patient about the causes of RP and conveying a clear strategy to avoid triggers of RP events through lifestyle changes. The primary and most important prevention is avoidance of cold ambient temperatures, particularly rapid transitioning from a warm or hot environment to a cold one. A warm ambient temperature reduces the frequency and severity of both primary and secondary RP. Clothing should be layered and loose-fitting, with the goal of maintaining a warm core body temperature and not just warmth of affected extremities. Patients who have an acute ischemic event are best treated with rest in a warm environment

(at home or in the hospital), insulated from cold temperatures. Other potential therapies include minimizing emotional distress (reducing sympathetic tone) and avoiding aggravating factors such as smoking, sympathomimetic drugs (e.g., preparations for attention-deficit disorder), migraine headache medications (e.g., serotonin agonists), and nonselective beta blockers (e.g., propranolol). Although behavioral therapies (including biofeedback, autogenic training, and classical conditioning) are helpful, their benefit remains controversial, and they play no role in the management of acute ischemia related to scleroderma. Biofeedback alone is not helpful for primary RP.

Drug therapy for RP in scleroderma includes the use of a variety of oral or systemic vasodilators. Calcium channel blockers (CCBs) are considered to be first-line therapeutic agents. This class of medication works primarily by inducing arterial vasodilation through direct inhibition of vascular smooth muscle cell contraction; however, these agents provide additional benefits by reducing oxidative stress and inhibiting platelet activation. 100, Most published studies evaluating the efficacy of CCBs in RP have used dihydropyridines (e.g., nifedipine, amlodipine, nisoldipine, isradipine, and felodipine). CCBs appear to be more efficacious in primary than in secondary RP.102, A meta-analysis of 17 studies evaluating the efficacy of shortand long-acting formulations of CCBs reported a 33% reduction in attack severity and a near 50% reduction in the number of attacks per week. The current recommendation is to use an extended-release formulation of CCBs for treatment of nonurgent RP. The dose should be titrated to clinical efficacy, but common adverse effects (e.g., hypotension, headache, and pedal edema) should be monitored. For urgent

cases of RP, a short-acting formulation of the medication is preferred, but titration should be carefully implemented. Although CCBs are the agents most likely to be effective, a host of other vasodilators are used with evidence of efficacy, including nitrates, phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors (PDE5is) (e.g., sildenafil), and intravenous (IV) prostaglandins.

Topical nitrates applied to the base and dorsum of the fingers have shown significant efficacy in the treatment of both primary and secondary RP. Use of nitroglycerin gel on the fingers of patients with RP leads to a faster blood flow recovery after a cold challenge as assessed by laser Doppler imaging and to a significant improvement of the RCS. Use of nitroglycerin can be limited by adverse effects, including headache, dizziness, and local skin irritation. The PDE5is are thought to be effective in the treatment of RP by sustaining the vasodilatory effect of nitric oxide. 106, Studies using PDE5is have reported variable but generally beneficial effects in managing RP. A systematic review and meta-analysis of PDE5is (including sildenafil, tadalafil, and vardenafil) for treatment of secondary RP found statistically significant improvements in RCS, frequency of RP attacks, and daily duration of RP attacks favoring PDE5is. In patients with scleroderma who do not respond to a CCB alone, the addition of either, not both, a topical nitrate ointment or a PDE5i can be tried.

Among other agents used in the treatment of RP are drugs that enhance nitric oxide availability (e.g., cilostazol), serotonin uptake blockers (e.g., fluoxetine), Rho-kinase inhibitors, botulinum toxin

(Botox), antioxidants (acetylcysteine), angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs), and selective alpha2-adrenergic receptor antagonists. The evidence that these agents are effective alone or in combination is inconclusive. In uncontrolled case series, injections of botulinum toxin A to the hands and fingers showed favorable effects both in managing acute digital ischemia and in controlling chronic vasospastic activity. However, a placebo-controlled trial testing injection of botulinum toxin A into the digits of scleroderma patients found no benefit in terms of clinical symptoms or digital blood flow. Thus, the exact role of botulinum injection therapy needs further study. Despite the theoretical advantage of ACE inhibitors, a study of quinapril showed that these medications did not affect the occurrence of digital ulcers or the frequency or severity of RP episodes. Thus although ACEs are critical for the treatment of an SRC (see "Renal Involvement" section), they do not have a major role in the management of RP.

New emphasis is being placed on the prevention of scleroderma vascular disease with the use of vasoprotective drugs. IV infusions of vasodilating prostacyclins (e.g., alprostadil, epoprostenol, iloprost, and treprostinil) reduce the severity and frequency of RP attacks and are most helpful during periods of sustained critical ischemia. The effect of these agents in the treatment of RP include a strong vasodilating effect, inhibition of platelet aggregation, and enhancement of vascular function through other mechanisms. A prostacyclin delivered by IV infusion can be given intermittently to patients with scleroderma during the winter

months or throughout the year or can be used acutely during a vascular crisis. For example, iloprost (a prostacyclin analogue) is typically administered via a peripheral vein for a course of 3 to 5 consecutive days, at a (continuous) dose of 0.5 to 4 ng/kg per minute (titrated to the maximum dose tolerated by the patient). The infusion can be done over 8 hours if done in an outpatient setting or continuous if in an inpatient setting. IV iloprost has shown ability to decrease the frequency and severity of RP and, in some cases, increased digital ulcer healing. The use of oral prostacyclin analogues has been studied in primary and secondary RP, but there is insufficient evidence to support their use in clinical practice.

Endothelin-1 is strongly implicated in the pathogenesis of RP and the vascular disease of scleroderma. In a randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind multicenter study, bosentan, an endothelin-1 receptor blocker, showed efficacy in preventing new digital ulcers, along with improved hand function, but it did not improve Raynaud's events or healing of existing ulcers compared with placebo. In contrast to bosentan, another nonselective endothelin-1 antagonist, macitentan, failed in clinical trials to reduce the frequency of new ischemic digital ulcers. For patients with recurrent digital ulcers associated with SSc despite use of other therapies, including CCBs plus PDE inhibitors or a topical nitrate, the use of bosentan can be considered as an alternative to repeated IV prostacyclin.

HMG-CoA (3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-coenzyme A) reductase inhibitors (statins) can potentially modify progression of vascular injury and prevent vascular ischemia through different pleiotropic functions, such as by improvement of endothelial dysfunction, reduction of clotting, and introduction of mild anti-inflammatory effects. Data suggest that statins may increase the number of endothelial progenitor cells and improve vascular remodeling after injury. 116, While a randomized,

placebo-controlled study of statin use in scleroderma demonstrated a significant decrease in the number of digital ulcers, more studies are needed.

Sympathectomy is a viable option for patients with RP who do not respond to medical therapy and should be considered as an acute intervention during a critical ischemic event. Localized digital sympathectomy with lysis of fibrosis around the vessel is effective for acute ischemia and for the most part has replaced cervical sympathectomy. Responses to sympathectomy are not sustained over time, suggesting limited long-term benefit. In fact, RP attacks eventually recur, and medical therapy is needed to prevent new events. Careful assessment for correctable macrovascular disease should be performed when acute digital ischemia occurs, particularly when the entire finger is demarcated or when the event involves a lower extremity. In this setting, appropriate studies such as arterial Doppler ultrasound or angiographic imaging are warranted. If macrovascular disease is present, vascular surgery may help alleviate the occlusive process. Preferential involvement of the ulnar artery might occur in patients with scleroderma.

Patients with critical digital ischemia require immediate attention and, in some cases, hospitalization to reduce vasospastic activity, maintain warmth, and permit rapid initiation of vasodilator therapy. While no formal clinical trial has been conducted, there is agreement among experts that continuous IV prostaglandin infusion can effectively maximize vasodilation. Acute severe digital ischemia if prolonged can threaten deep tissue injury or loss of the involved digit(s). When oral and/or topical vasodilatory therapy does not quickly result in improvement in digital blood flow and/ or when IV prostaglandins are not readily available, a digital block with lidocaine or bupivacaine can provide rapid relief of pain. For refractory cases, a surgical approach to digital sympathectomy is used. Anti-platelet therapy with low-dose aspirin may be useful, but its benefit is unproven in the acute setting. Heparinization

may help during acute ischemic crises in the digits, but chronic anti-coagulation is not recommended in scleroderma. Fibrinolysis can be considered to manage acute occlusion of larger arterial vessels, but its utility has not been studied for routine use in scleroderma-related critical digital ischemia. Ischemic digital lesions should be treated with topical antibiotics and daily cleansing with soap and water. Debridement procedures should be performed very cautiously because tissue trauma may extend the local injury as a result of the avascular nature of involved digital tissue. Fingertip lesions that progress to dry gangrene should be permitted to undergo autoamputation. Surgical amputation is best offered only in cases of intractable pain or deep tissue infection.

Immunosuppressive therapy directed at RP and related digital vascular disease in scleroderma has not been formally studied. In the absence of other organ involvement (e.g., skin, lung), immunosuppression is not currently used to manage RP alone or its complications.

### Skin Involvement

The most overt clinical manifestation of scleroderma is skin disease. The extent, severity, and distribution of cutaneous

involvement can vary among patients and change over time in the same individual. Almost every patient with scleroderma presents with skin thickening and hardening due to increased collagen and extra-cellular matrix deposition in the dermis. The distribution of skin changes is characteristic, with more frequent and intense involvement of fingers, hands, forearms, distal legs, feet, and the face, and, to a lesser degree, the proximal limbs and anterior trunk. Sparing of the midback is typical. Scleroderma is classically subdivided into limited and diffuse cutaneous forms (see Fig. 85.7). Limited scleroderma is defined by skin thickening that is restricted to the face and limbs distal to the elbows and knees. Commonly, in this form of the disease, only the fingers and the face are involved. In contrast, diffuse cutaneous involvement is characterized by widespread skin thickening, including proximal limbs and truncal areas. Proximal skin involvement defines the diffuse cutaneous subset but may be absent in early stages of disease when signs of skin thickening are not prominent and other disease manifestations (e.g., RP and nail-fold capillary abnormalities) are more apparent.

Traditionally, patients are clustered into limited and diffuse skin subsets, but evidence suggests the existence of an "intermediate" group of patients. Each subset of disease defined by the

degree of skin thickening has a unique pattern of disease manifestation and risk for specific clinical outcomes. Therefore expression of skin disease can be used as a predictor of the disease course. While classification of disease by pattern of skin disease is simple to perform, popular, and traditional, it is recognized that autoantibody profile, organ composite scales, and genetic and molecular biomarkers may allow with better precision to define disease activity and to predict disease outcomes. The variable degree of skin involvement can be quantified by physical examination. The most widely accepted scoring system (the mRSS) is applied by pinching the skin in 17 different body areas and subjectively averaging the thickness of each specific site from 0 (normal) to 3 (very thick) (see Fig. 85.8). The skin score (maximum, 51) is a useful clinical measurement tool that can be used to quantify the severity of skin disease. Although the overall extent of skin involvement as measured by the skin score can predict certain clinical outcomes, it does not define the quality of the skin process nor the level of disease activity at any single point in time. Therefore it is important to follow up on the skin score over time and measure changes sequentially to monitor disease progression.

Cutaneous involvement in scleroderma begins with clinical signs of inflammation, which is called the edematous phase because it is characterized by edema of affected body areas. In patients with limited scleroderma, this event is mild and is restricted to the digits; however, in the diffuse form of the disease, cutaneous swelling and edema can be widespread and so impressive in the limbs that it mimics a fluid overload state such as congestive heart failure. Edema can also cause local tissue compression. For example, upon involvement of the wrist area, patients with scleroderma are not infrequently diagnosed with carpal tunnel syndrome (especially at disease onset) to explain hand and wrist discomfort. In association with edema, signs and symptoms of inflammation are common. Erythema of the skin, intense pruritus, and pain (see Fig. 85.7C) are characteristic of advancing active diffuse skin disease. This pain has a neuropathic quality with a reported "pins-and-needles" sensation. The disease process leads to loss of skin appendages and decreased hair growth and loss of sweat and exocrine glands; thus the skin surface becomes dry and uncomfortable. Small papules can be seen in areas of trauma as the result of scratching, giving the surface a cobblestone texture. The edematous phase continues for several weeks but eventually gives way to a fibrotic stage, with protracted activity that may last months or years.

During the fibrotic phase, acute inflammation is clinically less obvious, and excessive collagen deposition in the dermis thickens the skin, making it inflexible and causing further loss of skin appendages. Fibrosis extends beyond the dermis into the deeper layers with loss of subcutaneous adipose tissue (lipodystrophy).

In late stages of the disease, skin actually thins with atrophy and has a non-inflammatory bound-down appearance. Deeper tissue fibrosis causes permanent contractures around joints or may involve underlying muscle, causing myopathy (see Fig. 85.7D). Patients with diffuse cutaneous scleroderma experience the most dramatic widespread skin changes; those with limited skin disease may note only puffy fingers and digital thickening typical of sclerodactyly. A masked facies, small oral and orbital apertures, and vertical furrowing (rhytides) of the perioral skin are consequences of skin and soft tissue fibrosis. In some patients, gum atrophy and facial skin tightening make the front teeth appear more prominent. Flexion contractures of the fingers, wrists, and elbows often appear as a result of dermal sclerosis and fibrosis with atrophy of underlying tissues. Skin ulcers can develop as a complication of avascular fibrotic or damaged thinned skin and are very common at sites of trauma, such as over the digital MCP or proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joints or at the tip of the elbows, particularly when joint contractures are present at these sites (see Fig. 85.5A). Ulcerations may arise from underlying vascular disease and tissue ischemia (see "Treatment of Vascular Disease" section). Ankle or lower-extremity ulcers occur rarely as a result of macrovascular occlusive disease or comorbid conditions (venous disease). Areas of hypopigmentation (vitiligo-like) and/or patches of depigmentation with preserved perifollicular pigmentation (a "salt-and-pepper" appearance) can develop, typically on the face, arms, and trunk (see Fig. 85.9A). General tanning of the skin may be seen, even in the absence of sun exposure.

Although highly variable, active skin involvement might persist for the first 12 to 18 months of the disease, with no further clinical signs of inflammation or progressive skin fibrosis seen after this interval. During this later stage, the skin begins to repair and can return to normal texture or, in areas most severely affected (e.g., the fingers and hands), it can become thin and atrophic. During this recovery phase, new robust hair growth is seen, particularly on the forearms, and itching and pain disappear, consistent with spontaneous resolution of disease activity. After years from disease onset, the skin rarely relapses again into an active phase and gradually can recover normal texture and color. Patients who, over time, experience the establishment of a phenotype that is limited to the fingers (plus or minus facial changes) do not undergo conversion to the diffuse form of the disease.

Telangiectasias are erythematous matted skin lesions of vascular origin; for this reason, they blanch upon application of local pressure. Telangiectasias are composed of vasodilated post-capillary venules without evidence of inflammation and resemble the type of lesions seen in Osler-Weber-Rendu disease (hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia). Telangiectasias develop primarily on

the fingers, hands, face, and mucous membranes, but they may also be found on the limbs and trunk (see Fig. 85.9B). They tend to become more numerous over time in both limited and diffuse types of skin disease and are more obvious in White patients with limited scleroderma. The biologic mechanism leading to the development of telangiectasias in scleroderma is thought to be related to the underlying chronic tissue hypoxia that stimulates abnormal secretion of vascular growth factors (e.g., vascular endothelial growth factor [VEGF]). Thus the development of telangiectasias may indicate ongoing vascular injury and abnormal vascular repair or angiogenesis. The total burden of telangiectasias is associated with increased risk of PH, suggesting that they are clinical biomarkers of systemic vascular disease. Nail-fold capillary abnormalities can be observed at the base of the fingernails, and direct visualization is performed using an ophthalmoscope (after immersion oil is applied to the skin surface) or a dermatoscope or by video capillaroscopy. In early scleroderma, dilated capillary loops (giant capillaries) and microhemorrhages may be seen. At later stages, the nail-fold capillaries are attenuated and disorganized (see Fig. 85.4).

### Management of Skin Disease

Patients with only mild skin thickening (as is often the case in limited scleroderma) or those diagnosed at later stages (i.e., several

years into their disease course) typically do not require any immunosuppression for their skin disease (though this may be considered for other organ-specific manifestations, such as ILD or musculoskeletal inflammation, discussed below).

Telangiectasias can be shrunk with laser therapy (typically performed by a dermatologist) if they are cosmetically bothersome to the patient. However, they typically tend to redevelop over time on the same sites. There is currently no effective medication to treat calcinosis. Patients should be counseled to avoid repetitive local trauma and friction over affected areas as much as possible (e.g., wear soft elbow pads or silicone cushions on their fingertips) and to optimize tissue blood perfusion as hypoxia appears to be a significant trigger for calcinosis, particularly in the fingers.

Treatment of scleroderma skin involvement should be considered during the early active inflammatory phase, particularly in patients with evidence of diffuse and progressive cutaneous disease. It is important to recognize that while skin disease is the most clinically obvious, associated systemic manifestations and other organ involvement need to be addressed at the same time (see particular sections).

In the early active stage of diffuse scleroderma, pruritus can be one of the most distressing symptoms. Antihistamines, analgesics, or tricyclic anti-depressants (e.g., doxepin) are often used but usually provide only partial benefit. Phototherapy, low-dose naltrexone, and gabapentin can be helpful. Dryness of the skin surface results from damage to the exocrine structures caused by decreased or absent natural oil (sebum) production. This dryness can worsen pruritus, leading to skin trauma as a result of repetitive scratching. Ulceration and secondary tissue infection may also result. The best approach to treatment is characterized by frequent topical application of an emollient preparation, periodic cleansing with soap and water, and use of topical antibiotics for any traumatic skin ulceration. Physical therapy is important to prevent severe skin and joint contractures and to help patients with activities of daily living.

It is now recognized that the early edematous phase is secondary to an acute immune-mediated inflammatory process that triggers the fibrotic disease process. A variety of immunomodulatory drugs and newer agents with anti-fibrotic properties have been used to attempt control of skin disease. However, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) to date has not approved any therapy for cutaneous involvement in scleroderma as no randomized controlled clinical trial has showed clear superiority of one treatment over placebo. The use of the mRSS as the major outcome measure in these studies may have contributed in part to the failure of proving these treatments effective, as the identification of ideal cases with truly reversible disease has been challenging.

Nonselective immunosuppressive or anti-inflammatory treatments are used in early progressing skin disease. Corticosteroids can dampen inflammatory features such as associated arthritis or myositis, but they have not shown efficacy in stopping skin disease progression. In addition, there is evidence that steroids can increase the risk of SRC (see "Renal Involvement" section). Steroid use should be avoided or only used in low doses (less than 15 mg/day of prednisone).

Cyclophosphamide (CYC), methotrexate (MTX), and mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) are agents with anti-proliferative effects on inflammatory cells, in particular on activated T and B lymphocytes, that have been used for active skin disease. A prospective, observational cohort comparing use of MTX, CYC, MMF, or no immunosuppression therapy to treat early scleroderma skin disease found a modest trend favoring treatment with

the immunosuppressants in terms of mean change in skin score after 12 months, although the difference was not significant. MTX efficacy in treating skin disease and lung function has been investigated in two randomized placebo-controlled trials, showing only a small benefit on skin scores after 6 months (with weekly intramuscular injections) or after 12 months (with weekly oral therapy), respectively.123, Based on the findings of these studies, some experts use MTX for active scleroderma skin disease. Both MMF and CYC have shown evidence of benefit in the management of active scleroderma skin disease. MMF is typically preferred as the initial treatment based on the evidence gathered from uncontrolled case series and post-hoc analyses of ILD clinical trials showing favorable benefit on skin disease, good tolerance, and less toxicity compared with CYC. Further support for MMF comes from reports of flares occurring after dose reduction or discontinuation of MMF and the subsequent recovered disease control after restarting the medication. MMF is usually started at low doses such as 500 mg orally twice daily and titrated to up to 1500 mg twice daily. Benefit manifests with clinical evidence of reduced skin inflammation (e.g., decreased pruritis, less edema) and reduced or stable bedside mRSS score. Improvement generally begins within 6 to 8 weeks after reaching fully tolerated dosing.

If the patient does not stabilize or improve on MMF with evidence of further progression into the fibrotic phase of skin disease, then the use of other agents should be considered, although in many cases their benefit has been shown only in small studies or case series.

Intravenous immunoglobulins (IVIGs) exhibit immunomodulatory and anti-fibrotic properties. Administration of IVIG to patients with scleroderma has been evaluated in small open-label studies with some evidence that it can improve skin fibrosis, joint disease, muscle, and digestive tract symptoms. 127-131One trial in Japan found that repeated administration of IVIG was required for an improved outcome for diffuse skin disease. Some experts will add IVIG to MMF in cases that are not improving, particularly in the presence of associated musculoskeletal inflammatory manifestations.

The use of rituximab (anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody) has shown some promising results, with improvement of skin fibrosis and stabilization of lung function.133-137 A prospective study conducted within the EUSTAR network showed that treatment of scleroderma patients with rituximab compared with matched untreated subjects had a good safety profile and favorable changes on skin fibrosis.

Cell-based immunotherapy using autologous hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) preceded by myeloablative or nonmyeloablative conditioning regimens has also been studied to treat scleroderma patients with severe disease.88-90 In the Autologous Stem Cell Transplantation International Scleroderma (ASTIS) trial and the American Scleroderma Stem Cell versus Immune Suppression Trial (ASSIST), patients were randomized to receive HSCT or pulsed IV doses of CYC administered monthly for 12 or 6 months, respectively.8, Overall, these investigations confirmed previous observations that HSCT is effective in rapidly controlling skin disease, stabilizing lung function, and improving quality of life as assessed by patient-reported outcome .139-141 The ASTIS trial has also shown a better long-term measures. event-free and overall survival for HSCT compared with monthly IV CYC. A third study, the Scleroderma Cyclophosphamide Or Transplantation (SCOT) trial, randomly assigned patients to undergo myeloablative autologous stem cell transplantation (36 participants) or to receive CYC (39 participants). Unlike

ASTIS and ASSIST, the SCOT protocol added total body irradiation to the conditioning regimen and did not use CYC for stem cell mobilization. The primary end point was a global rank composite score (GRCS) comparing participants with each other based on a hierarchy of multiple disease features assessed: death, event-free survival (survival without respiratory, renal, or cardiac failure), FVC, the score on the HAQ-DI, and the mRSS. In the intention-to-treat population, the GRCS at 54 months showed that 67% of 1404 pairwise comparisons favored HSCT compared with 33% favoring CYC (p = 0.01). At 72 months, Kaplan-Meier estimates of event-free survival (74% vs. 47%) and overall survival (86% vs. 51%) also favored transplantation (p = 0.03 and 0.02, respectively). Treatment-related mortality in the transplantation group was 3% at 54 months and 6% at 72 months, compared with 0% in the CYC group. Nonmyeloablative (immunoablative) conditioning regimens without HSCT have demonstrated similar results.

Despite these positive findings, improvement of multiple organ function (i.e., skin, lungs), and sustained drug-free remission, this approach is not considered the standard of care for scleroderma, particularly for the risk of treatment-related morbidity and mortality (3% in SCOT; 10.1% in ASTIS) associated with high-dose immunosuppression and for the evidence that the disease can relapse in time. Myeloablation with or without autologous HSCT is an option for severe progressive scleroderma that should be performed in experienced centers with care to select patients who have failed low-dose immunosuppression or other novel investigative therapies and who have associated visceral organ disease that has not progressed to a stage of significant dysfunction.

Selective immunotherapy including T lymphocyte—directed treatments such as cyclosporin A, sirolimus (rapamycin), and anti-thymocyte globulin have some benefit.143, However, these studies were generally small and limited by drug toxicity. The use of extracorporeal photoimmunotherapy or photopheresis has been reported with modest improvement in skin disease but lacks any efficacy on internal organ manifestations. 145,

Several early-phase clinical trials (randomized and open label) have tested the efficacy of novel therapies to treat scleroderma skin disease, including agents directed against cytokines such as TNF (infliximab, etanercept), interleukin (IL)-6 (tocilizumab), IL-1 (rilonacept), transforming growth factor (TGF)-beta (fresolimumab, CAT-192), and IL-4/IL-13 (romilkimab); blocking costimulation between antigen-presenting cells and T lymphocytes (abatacept); or inhibiting Janus kinase (JAK) 1/3 singling (tofacitinib), soluble guanylate cyclase (sGC) (riociguat), LPA1 receptor (SAR100842), and B cell function by depletion (inebilizumab) or survival antagonism (belimumab). 147-160

In general, none of these early studies have provided significant evidence of benefit to control skin disease. IL-6 inhibition was further tested in a phase 3 double-blind study, again comparing tocilizumab to placebo. While no significant reduction of the skin tightness was observed, the favorable effect on the lung function with stabilization of the FVC over 48 weeks has led to the FDA approval of this treatment for ILD (see "Lung" section). JAK inhibitors have been shown to be efficacious in treating cutaneous thickening in both mouse models of scleroderma and in patients with refractory morphea. In a small unblinded randomized trial, tofacitinib 5 mg twice daily showed greater efficacy than MTX 10 mg orally weekly in reducing skin thickness and showed a satisfactory safety profile. .

Small uncontrolled trials testing use of the tyrosine kinase inhibitor imatinib showed no benefit and frequent adverse events

including fluid retention, nausea, fatigue, and elevation of creatine kinase. 164, While nintedanib was effective in slowing down the progression of ILD, no clear benefit for scleroderma skin disease was detected.

D-Penicillamine, a chelating agent that blocks collagen crosslinking, was a popular therapy focused on the idea that scleroderma was mainly secondary to progressive fibrosis. However, a double-blind, randomized clinical trial comparing the efficacy of low-dose versus high-dose D-penicillamine in early diffuse scleroderma found no significant difference between skin scores of the two groups at 24 months.

### Interstitial Lung Disease

Pulmonary involvement is found in most patients with scleroderma, but severe lung disease occurs in a relatively small subset of patients. ILD and PH are recognized as the most common lung complications and are now regarded as the major cause of death in scleroderma. A survey of the EUSTAR database, a cohort of over 5800 patients, found that 35% of all scleroderma-related deaths were directly attributable to ILD, with 26% of deaths due to PAH and 4% due to renal disease. In combination, it is estimated that lung disease is responsible for 60% of scleroderma-related deaths. While ILD and PH can both occur at the same time, one process usually dominates over the other. Lung disease can manifest without symptoms, or it can cause a significant limitation of quality of life or progress to respiratory failure. Chronic aspiration, pleural disease, spontaneous pneumothorax, neuromuscular weakness, drug-induced pneumonitis, and lung cancer need to be considered in the differential diagnosis of a patient with scleroderma who presents with respiratory symptoms.

ILD becomes clinically significant in up to 60% of patients with diffuse cutaneous scleroderma and in 20% of patients with limited skin disease. Higher risk of developing severe progressive ILD has been observed in patients with diffuse skin involvement, African Americans, Native Americans, and those positive for antitopoisomerase 1 (Scl-70), anti-U3-RNP, or anti-Th/To antibodies. Anti-topoisomerase positivity has been strongly linked to the carriage of the human leukocyte antigen (HLA)-DRB1*11 and HLA-DPB*1301 alleles, suggesting that a genetic predisposition to ILD exists. .168, Data from a study of patients with active lung disease show that those with limited and diffuse scleroderma were indistinguishable with regard to their baseline pulmonary functions, although patients with limited skin disease presented with more extensive pulmonary fibrosis, perhaps reflecting a delay in diagnosis and more advanced progression of lung involvement before study entry.

ILD typically manifests with declining lung volumes and increased parenchymal fibrosis with reticular interstitial thickening that is greatest at the lung bases. The most common histologic pattern of fibrosing alveolitis in scleroderma is nonspecific interstitial pneumonia (NSIP), as opposed to usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP), which is the typical presentation in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. A mixed pattern of NSIP and UIP can also be found. The histopathologic classification does not appear to predict outcome, but a greater degree of disease severity and functional respiratory measures at initial presentation are associated with poor prognosis. A surgical lung biopsy is not required in the setting of patients experiencing a typical disease course because the histopathology tends to be repetitive (NSIP) and not a useful predictor of subsequent disease course. ILD is usually characterized by a functional restrictive ventilatory defect with reduced gas

exchange. In patients with severe involvement, honeycombing of lung parenchyma and bronchiectasis and some modest degree of airway obstruction can be found. Pleural reactions are not common in scleroderma. Rare cases of spontaneous pneumothorax, adult respiratory distress syndrome, and pulmonary hemorrhage can occur. Aspiration resulting from oropharyngeal dysfunction or gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), a secondary infection, or heart failure can all complicate the course of scleroderma lung disease. Some investigators consider GERD associated with chronic aspiration to be a potential inciting factor for the development of ILD in scleroderma.

During earlier stages of ILD, the underlying active fibrosing alveolitis may be totally asymptomatic and may not be detected by conventional chest radiographs. The most common symptoms of scleroderma lung disease are dyspnea (initially upon exertion) and fatigue. Chest pain is not typical, and nonproductive cough is usually a late complication, particularly in association with the presence of traction bronchiectasis. Coughing in patients with scleroderma often is not the result of a primary lung problem but rather is a manifestation of GERD with associated laryngeal irritation. The most characteristic finding of ILD on physical examination is bilateral fine inspiratory crackles (i.e., "Velcro" rales) at the lung bases. The PFT is the method most used to detect ILD (see Fig. 85.10). The earliest functional abnormality is a reduction in the single breath diffusion capacity of carbon monoxide (DLCO). Although a decline in DLCO correlates with the severity of pulmonary fibrosis as measured by HRCT and predicts worse outcome, it is not a very specific measure and can also be abnormal in the context of pulmonary vascular disease and underlying chronic obstructive pulmonary disease/emphysema. Studies find that detection of ground-glass changes or fibrosis by HRCT scan may occur before a significant decline in lung function and thus may be a more sensitive test to diagnose early lung disease. A restrictive ventilatory defect is identified by a depression of the FVC and the total lung capacity. The most reliable tool for monitoring ILD over time is serial measurements of FVC. A decline in FVC of more than 10% from baseline is often indicative of disease activity and is associated with increased mortality. The course of lung disease may remain stable or exhibit worsening symptoms after variable intervals (months or years) of unchanged lung function. In some cases, progression is invariable and leading rapidly to end-stage lung disease. Longitudinal studies of large patient populations find that subgroups following a unique course of lung disease exist and are associated with specific serologic and clinical features. Patients with ACA and limited skin disease are less likely to have ILD, whereas patients with anti-topoisomerase have more commonly progressive disease. Patients presenting with a normal FVC during early stages of scleroderma have a better lung prognosis; in contrast, a reduced FVC at the initial encounter is associated with further progression of lung involvement, usually within the first 2 to 4 years from disease onset. The presence of ILD predicts increased mortality. One study found that patients with severe ILD have a 9-year survival rate of approximately 30%, whereas patients with no severe organ involvement have a 72% survival rate. The most rapid decline in FVC is thought to occur within the initial 3 years from disease onset, but progression of ILD can also occur later on, so it is recommended to monitor pulmonary function regularly at 6-month intervals in the early years and then on a yearly basis.

HRCT is more accurate than chest radiography in evaluating diffuse lung disease; it is a well-established, sensitive, and noninvasive method of detecting and characterizing ILD in scleroderma

patients. The extent of pulmonary fibrosis on HRCT correlates closely with PFT abnormalities and can be used to predict prognosis. Recent evidence shows that the degree of HRCT changes coupled with the level of lung function deficit can be used to generate a simple staging system (limited vs. extensive disease) with good prognostic value. An FVC of less than 70% or a disease extent greater than 20% according to HRCT predicts ILD progression and higher mortality. HRCT features of fibrosis are present in 55% to 65% of all patients with scleroderma and in almost every patient with abnormal PFTs. The earliest and most common abnormality on HRCT is usually found in the posterior and basilar portion of the lungs in the form of increased subpleural lung attenuations without distinct architectural distortion. With progression of the disease, increased "ground-glass" opacities are seen, but it has been well established that these changes alone are not always indicative of active inflammation, nor can they predict progression itself. Subsequent detection of a fine reticular pattern often precedes overt pulmonary fibrosis manifested by parenchymal distortion, reticular intralobular interstitial thickening, traction bronchiectasis and bronchiolectasis, and, in the late stages, honeycomb and cystic air spaces (see Fig. 85.11). When reticular interstitial abnormalities are present on HRCT, regression of disease rarely, if ever, occurs. Neither the clinical presentation nor the autoantibody profile alone is sufficient to select patients at higher risk of progressive ILD. Therefore at the initial visit, all patients should undergo evaluation with HRCT and PFTs to screen for ILD. Follow-up at 6to 12-month intervals is recommended with PFT and HRCT if respiratory symptoms worsen or lung function declines.

Pathologic studies of patients with scleroderma with early lung disease have shown that lung fibrosis is preceded by the presence of a mixed interstitial inflammatory infiltrate spilling into the alveolar spaces (alveolitis). It has been assumed that measuring abnormal levels of inflammatory cells in the bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) would allow identification of patients with active lung disease at risk for progression and who would potentially benefit from immunosuppressive therapy. The value of BAL cytology in predicting lung disease progression or response to treatment has not been uniformly confirmed and the routine clinical use of BAL cytology is not recommended. Other biomarkers have been investigated to monitor the activity and progression of ILD more accurately, but they are not yet available for routine clinical use. Markers of alveolar cell damage such as KL-6 or surfactant proteins A (SP-A) and D (SP-D) are increased in the serum of patients with scleroderma who have active ILD and predict survival. 175, Increased levels of matrix metalloproteinases (i.e., MMP-7) and proinflammatory molecules such as CCL-18 or IL-6 are also associated with declining lung function and worse 177-179 outcome.

### Management of Interstitial Lung Disease

Early detection and prompt therapeutic intervention remain essential in preventing progression of lung disease. Careful evaluation should help in stratifying patients by level of severity based on PFT and HRCT assessment and degree of activity by serial observation and establish presence of risk factors associated with progressive ILD (e.g., older age, active skin disease, African

American or Native American race, presence of anti-SCL70, elevated inflammatory markers). Mild ILD in low-risk patients (e.g., minimal changes on HRCT, limited skin disease, anti-centromere positivity) can be followed without intervention. Extrapulmonary disease may also dictate intervention.

Current treatment of scleroderma-related ILD is most often directed against the immune response and the inflammatory process driving lung injury and tissue fibrosis. Therapeutic protocols using CYC as a daily oral regimen or as monthly IV therapy have been used to achieve stable or improved lung function. A randomized placebo-controlled study comparing 1 year of oral CYC versus placebo suggests some modest benefit of the active drug. This benefit was completely lost at 2 years' follow-up, indicating that a sequential or maintenance immunosuppressive approach may be indicated to retain the clinical response. Other studies have shown

some benefit using azathioprine as maintenance therapy following IV monthly CYC. A study comparing oral CY to MMF showed equal (mild) improvement of the lung function in both treatment groups, with fewer adverse reactions in patients treated with MMF. Thus, MMF is considered safe and effective and is the preferred first-line immunosuppressive treatment of ILD in patients with scleroderma.

Several clinical trials (randomized and open label) have tested the efficacy of newer biologics to treat scleroderma. In a phase III randomized double-blind study, use of tocilizumab compared with placebo showed stabilization of lung function (FVC) and this was maintained in the placebo-treated patients who transitioned to tocilizumab. 148, Subjects in both arms showed similar risk factors for SSc-ILD progression, including disease duration, anti-SCL70 positivity, C-reactive protein (CRP) levels, baseline

FVC percentage, and extent of ILD. Assessment of quantitative ILD and fibrosis by computer software indicates that the stabilizing effects of tocilizumab was observed across all subgroups with different ILD severity. Toclizumab is now an FDA-approved treatment for ILD in scleroderma. Importantly, this tocilizumab trial enrolled patients with early active diffuse scleroderma and high inflammatory markers, which represent a unique subset. More studies will be needed to verify its efficacy in long-standing ILD or other subgroups. Some experts suggest using tocilizumab in patients with mild ILD who fall into a high-risk group for 183 progression.

Nintedanib is a small molecule that inhibits the tyrosine kinase activity of the abl-kinases and platelet-derived growth factor receptors, thus interfering with important profibrotic pathways activated in scleroderma. In a phase III randomized controlled trial (RCT), the efficacy of nintedanib was compared with placebo in scleroderma patients with ILD, regardless of the cutaneous subset. Patients were allowed to enter the study if receiving a stable dose of MMF or MTX. Nintedanib effectively slowed down the rate of progression of ILD, as the FVC dropped 52.4 mL per year in nintedanib-treated patients compared with 93.3 mL in the placebo group (difference 41.0 mL/year). As a result, nintedanib is now also approved by the FDA to treat scleroerma-ILD. A subgroup analysis to examine the efficacy of nintedanib by MMF use at baseline suggests that the combination of these two drugs may have a synergistic effect. Most experts begin therapy with MMF alone and add nintedanib if there is evidence of ILD progression by PFT or HRCT. Nintedanib use is frequently associated with GI side effects, especially diarrhea, that can significantly impact the patient's quality of life and limit its use. Pirfenidone (5-methyl-1-phenylpyridin-2[1H]-1) is another novel agent with anti-fibrotic and anti-inflammatory properties. In a phase III RCT, compared with placebo, pirfenidone has shown significant benefit (decreased disease progression) and a relatively mild adverse-effect profile in patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. A clinical trial is ongoing in scleroderma-related ILD.

Rituximab (anti-CD20 antibody) benefits ILD in a number of case reports and in a small open-label trial where it showed a modest benefit over IV CYC. A recent phase II RCT has been conducted in patients with CTD-associated ILD (38% with scleroderma) to assess efficacy of IV rituximab (1000 mg at weeks 0 and 2) compared with IV CYC (600 mg/m2 body surface area every 4 weeks for six doses). At 24 weeks, the FVC improved from baseline in both groups, confirming that rituximab can be a therapeutic alternative to CYC in individuals with CTD-ILD, including scleroderma.

Long-term management of patients with ILD can be challenging. While rapid progression of ILD usually happens in the first 3 to 5 years from disease onset, late progression can also occur. In patients who achieve stable lung function on immunosuppressive therapy, treatment reduction to a lower-dose maintenance level is recommended. Flares of disease do occur after immunosuppression is discontinued. Patients with advanced ILD (e.g., high score HRCT and FVC 50% or lower) would be treated more cautiously than patients with mild-to-moderate ILD (e.g., FVC 60%—70%). Presence of extrapulmonary disease and of features increasing the risk for worse outcome would indicate need for more assertive treatment.

Myeloablative or immunoablative conditioning regimens followed by autologous HSCT have been used to treat severe scleroderma. Despite the common incidence of early treatment-related adverse events including death, they have shown some benefit,

such as stability and improvement of lung function. However, their long-term outcomes and treatment toxicity need further assessment.89, Lung transplantation is an option in patients with severe ILD who are not responsive to medical therapy. Carefully selected patients with scleroderma have similar morbidity and mortality as patients undergoing transplantation for other lung diseases such as idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. A retrospective survey of 47 patients with scleroderma who underwent lung transplantation found that 1and 3-year survival rates were 68% and 46%, respectively. Another survey of 90 patients reported similar outcome, with survival at 1, 3, and 5 years of 81%, 68%, and 61%, respectively.

### Pulmonary Hypertension

Pulmonary arterial vascular disease represents a difficult clinical challenge with life-threatening consequences. It is now appreciated that smalland medium-sized arteries are a major target of the disease process in scleroderma. This affects the systemic vascular beds including the heart and lungs, causing defects in vascular reactivity with abnormal vasoconstriction, and also leading to abnormal vascular remodeling. An imbalance of local vascular mediators can be detected in the blood vessels affected by scleroderma. This includes enhanced secretion of endothelin, a vasoconstrictor and fibro-proliferative mediator, and defective synthesis of nitric oxide and loss of normal activity of prostacyclin, both potent vasodilator molecules.
