These changes lead to both vasoconstriction and progressive neointima formation, luminal narrowing, and obliteration of medium and pre-capillary arteries. Given the high capacitance of pulmonary arteries, these lesions impair blood flow, accounting for increased resistance and the eventual progression to PAH and its hemodynamic consequences. The injury to the pulmonary vascular system can be mainly "precapillary" in the setting of "pure" PAH or can unfold via either or both preand/or post-capillary mechanisms, manifesting as PH. Cardiac etiologies such as left-ventricular (LV) failure can lead to right heart dysfunction and should always be assessed carefully. RHC is required to confirm a diagnosis of PAH (see below).

The pulmonary vascular process is indolent and can remain clinically silent for a variable time. When it progresses to clinically significant PH or PAH it becomes a major cause of respiratory distress and mortality. Typical symptoms associated with clinically manifested PAH include dyspnea upon exertion, fatigue, and, less commonly, chest pain. Physical examination may be normal during the early stages of PAH, but as the disease progresses, a systolic murmur of tricuspid regurgitation; a loud pulmonic component, the S2; an S3 gallop; and signs of right heart failure (e.g., rightsided parasternal heave, prominent and elevated jugular venous pulse, hepatomegaly, and signs of fluid overload with peripheral edema) are appreciated. Later in the course of the disease, patients become dyspneic with mild physical activity, have a resting tachycardia, and demonstrate hypoxia with exercise. Sudden syncope or death can occur because of severe hypoxia and congestive heart failure.

PAH is usually a late complication of scleroderma, typically manifesting after 10 years from disease onset, particularly in patients with limited cutaneous involvement. However, every patient should be considered at risk for PH or PAH and yearly evaluation is indicated. It is becoming more evident that in some patients this condition may develop early and remain undetected. Bedside examination is not very sensitive in detecting PH, particularly during early stages, and thus it is recommended that every

patient with scleroderma be screened using objective testing such as electrocardiography (ECG), ECHO, and PFTs (see Fig. 85.12). Proper initial workup also should aim at excluding non-scleroderma-related complications such as chronic thromboembolic disease and underlying obstructive sleep apnea. The ECG can be normal but, as disease progresses, signs of right-sided heart strain with right-ventricular (RV) hypertrophy and right axis deviation can be observed. Detection by ECHO of increased right-ventricular systolic pressure (RVSP) is useful, but abnormal values need to be confirmed by RHC, given the possibility of false-positive or false-negative results. When the ECHO estimates an RVSP greater than 45 mm Hg, about 95% of the time this finding will be confirmed by RHC. Some clinicians use the tricuspid gradient as a measure of pulmonary artery pressure. Additional noninvasive screening includes PFTs. A low diffusing capacity (DLCO) without evidence of obstructive or restrictive lung disease (i.e., low FVC) suggests a defect in gas exchange that can result from pulmonary vascular disease. DLCO may progressively decline for years before the diagnosis of PAH is established. Increased serum N-terminal (NT)-pro hormone brain natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) may indicate presence of PAH and right heart strain, even when levels are modestly elevated (>395 pg/mL).195,

The diagnosis of PAH should always be confirmed by RHC, which provides direct measurement of pulmonary hemodynamics and helps define the cause of PH. Screening algorithms have been proposed to identify patients at risk for PAH who may be referred earlier to RHC. The DETECT algorithm follows a two-step approach that combines clinical, laboratory, electrocardiographic, and PFT parameters (step I) to select patients who should have ECHO (step II) and subsequent RHC if a threshold risk score is obtained. DETECT has been validated across many general scleroderma cohorts exhibiting a consistently high sensitivity and negative predictive value, but modest specificity and positive predictive value. While this may be appropriate for a screening tool, the high rates of false-positive results (indication to RHC) may lead to unnecessary referrals to an invasive and costly procedure. Other experts will refer patients to RHC in the presence of dyspnea on exertion with abnormal RVSP or dilated right ventricle on ECHO. RHC should also be considered for patients with dyspnea, a low DCLO with normal FVC, and/or elevated BNP or NT-proBNP, even if resting ECHO has normal or only mildly elevated RVSP. Patients with dyspnea without ILD and normal resting ECHO can be considered for dynamic testing, including cardiopulmonary exercise testing and exercise ECHO, which may

improve early diagnostic accuracy. 199, These testing strategies have not been standardized and/or validated to recommend their routine use in clinical practice.

The definition of PAH has been changed to allow early intervention. It is now defined as resting mean pulmonary arterial pressure equal to or greater than 20 mm Hg, with normal pulmonary capillary wedge pressure equal to or less than 15 mm Hg and pulmonary vascular resistance >3 wood units, although this threshold has been recently lowered to >2 wood units in the 2022 European Society of Cardiology/European Respiratory Society guidelines for the diagnosis and treatment of PH.201, In addition to confirming abnormal hemodynamic values, the RHC can help in differentiating PAH from pulmonary venous hypertension resulting from left heart dysfunction or pulmonary vascular occlusive disease. The 6-minute walk test can provide baseline functional information but does not accurately assess the severity of PAH. Because baseline hemodynamic parameters do not correlate well with the clinical course of PAH in patients with scleroderma, new cardiopulmonary dynamic testing such as exercise stress ECHO and exercise during RHC have been introduced, but their role in monitoring PAH has not yet been fully established. Exercise studies conducted in scleroderma patients have revealed that right heart disease can also be driven by underlying myocardial dysfunction. This defect can lead to dilation of the right heart under exercise conditions, with decreased capacity to compensate for elevated right heart pressures generated by progressing pulmonary vascular disease. Associated myocardial right heart disease accounts for the poor prognosis observed in scleroderma-related PAH compared with idiopathic PAH.

Estimates of the prevalence of PAH in patients with scleroderma vary. Using ECHO as a diagnostic tool, the prevalence of PAH has been estimated at between 30% and 50% of all studied patients, while investigations using confirmatory RHC have detected a prevalence of 8 to 12%.203, A meta-analysis reports an overall PAH prevalence in scleroderma of 6.4% (95% CI, 58.3) and PAH incidence of 18.2 cases per 1000 person-years (95% CI, 1227.4). Clinically, scleroderma-related pulmonary vascular disease can present and progress in some patients as severe isolated PAH; in others, it can be associated with mild or severe pulmonary fibrosis that is believed to contribute to lung injury and hypoxia causing vascular disease. Association of ILD and PAH usually entails a worse prognosis. Pulmonary vascular disease can also develop more slowly, manifesting with dyspnea upon exertion, isolated decline of the DLCO with no significant signs of ILD (i.e., low lung volumes), and a normal resting ECHO and/or RHC. These patients are considered to have microvascular lung disease and may be at high risk of developing overt PAH. Factors increasing the risk of developing PAH include limited skin disease, late age at onset of scleroderma, male sex, the presence of numerous telangiectasias, reduced capillary nail-fold density, low DLCO, increasing estimated RVSP on ECHO, or high serum NT-proBNP. PAH can occur in association with several scleroderma-related autoantibodies including anti-centromere, anti-U3 RNP, anti-Th/To, anti-Ku, anti-Ro52/TRIM21, and anti-U1 RNP. Patients with anti-centromere tend to develop PAH later in the course of the disease, although not all case-control studies have identified anti-centromere as an independent risk factor for PAH.194, Patients with anti-topoisomerase I rarely develop PAH but can manifest PH secondary to ILD and chronic hypoxia.

Pulmonary vascular disease has a major impact on quality of life and survival of affected patients. While there is no pharmacologic cure for PAH, early intervention aims to slow or prevent

### Management of Pulmonary Hypertension

All patients with PAH are encouraged to continue an active lifestyle as tolerated. Formal educational and exercise programs can improve their quality of life. Conventional therapy includes diuretic therapy (loop and potassium-sparing diuretics) and supplemental oxygen therapy, if needed. Anti-coagulation is not recommended in that studies suggest a worse outcome in scleroderma patients who are anti-coagulated. CCBs play no role in the treatment of scleroderma-related PAH. In recent years, several targeted agents have become available for the treatment of PAH. Many clinical trials testing these drugs in idiopathic PAH have included about 20% of patients with CTD, primarily scleroderma. Specific therapies include prostaglandin derivatives (e.g., epoprostenol, treprostinil, beraprost, and iloprost), endothelin receptor antagonists (ERAs) (e.g., bosentan, sitaxsentan, ambrisentan, and macitentan), PDE5is (e.g., sildenafil, tadalafil, and vardenafil), a selective prostacyclin receptor (IP receptor) agonist (selexipag), and a soluble guanylate-cyclase stimulator (riociguat). Riociguat is primarily indicated to treat inoperable and persistent/recurrent chronic thromboembolic PH and PAH. Inhaled prostaglandins can be an option in severe cases and have shown benefit in a large double-blind, placebo-controlled trial to treat PH associated with ILD. All these drugs can improve hemodynamics, exercise tolerance, and quality of life. Clinical trials do not suggest that any one of these agents is superior to another, but evidence indicates that prostacyclin therapy is the most effective and should be considered immediately in patients presenting with severe PAH.

Most clinicians believe that early intervention is most important because it leads to better outcomes (see Fig. 85.12). For patients with mild-to-moderate disease (functional class I or II), treatment with a single oral agent is usually considered (i.e., sildenafil, bosentan, or ambrisentan). However, data from recent clinical trials indicated a favorable survival benefit for ambrisentan and tadalafil upfront combination therapy compared with monotherapy in patients with newly diagnosed mild-to-moderate PAH.215-217 Sildenafil and bosentan can also be used in combination, even if their interaction and increased hepatotoxicity is of some concern. Patients presenting with more severe disease (functional class III or IV) and those who do not respond to initial therapy are usually treated with IV or inhaled prostaglandins in combination with oral agents. Several nonvasodilator drugs targeting inflammation, cell proliferation, hormones, growth factors, and vascular remodeling are under investigation for PAH. An RCT of B cell depletion with rituximab conducted in scleroderma PAH patients reported an adjusted mean change in 6-minute walk distance at 24 weeks favoring the treatment over placebo, although results did not reach statistical significance. New studies will investigate the impact of immunosuppressive therapy on pulmonary vascular disease. Mutations in the bone morphogenic protein receptor type 2 (BMPR2), a member of the TGF beta family, have been found in 70%80% of patients with familial PAH and 10%20% of patients with idiopathic PAH. Sotatercept is a fusion protein binding activins and growth differentiation factors and exhibiting the ability to promote pulmonary vascular remodeling by impacting BMPR2 activity. In phase 2 clinical trials conducted on patients receiving background therapy for PAH, sotatercep improved hemodynamic and functional outcome measures at 24 weeks compared with placebo.

Lung or heart-lung transplantation for PAH remains the treatment of last resort when medical therapy fails. Patients with scleroderma who are carefully selected for transplantation have an outcome that is similar to patients with other causes of lung disease. PAH in scleroderma is a progressive disease for which no specific or single therapy may suffice. Therefore careful longitudinal monitoring is important. Noninvasive testing with periodic clinical assessment with the 6-minute walk distance, repeat PFTs, and ECHO studies are helpful. When a major therapeutic decision is needed, such as switching to or adding a new therapy, a repeat RHC may be indicated. Further improvement in survival of patients with scleroderma who have PAH may result from future therapeutic interventions targeting the underlying inflammatory process and the dysregulated endothelial proliferation that mediates pulmonary vascular remodeling and consequent failure of the right heart.

### Renal Involvement

Renal involvement in scleroderma is classically characterized by the abrupt onset of very high blood pressure (malignant hypertension), elevated plasma renin, and rising serum creatinine reflective of acute renal failure, along with a constellation of symptoms and clinical manifestations such as headaches, malaise, hypertensive retinopathy, encephalopathy, and pulmonary edema, usually referred to as scleroderma renal crisis (SRC). Subclinical renal disease in scleroderma can also be present in the absence of symptoms. Despite the frequent detection of histopathologic renovascular lesions typical of scleroderma vasculopathy, clinically important renal impairment, independent of SRC, is seen in only a minority of patients. Although SRC is the most recognized

renal complication, abnormal renal function can be explained by factors other than intrinsic scleroderma renal disease such as medication adverse effects, comorbid conditions, or associated heart, GI, or lung disease. Cases of biopsy-proven oxalate nephropathy have been identified among scleroderma patients and are thought to be related to underlying GI dysfunction. One survey suggests that mild unexplained proteinuria without loss of renal function or evidence of glomerular disease is a common sign of renal disease in scleroderma. A superimposed inflammatory kidney disease can also occur. Several cases of pauci-immune necrotizing crescentic glomerulonephritis associated with myeloperoxidasespecific ANCAs have been reported in patients with scleroderma who have a presentation mimicking SRC.

SRC needs to be considered in patients with scleroderma who have sudden and severe elevation of blood pressure, with or without renal failure; in patients with sudden renal failure, with or without hypertension; and in patients with sudden-onset microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, with or without hypertension or renal failure. Nonmalignant hypertension alone without signs of renal dysfunction or mild urine abnormalities is unlikely to be due to SRC. SRC occurs in 5% to 10% of patients, mostly in those with diffuse scleroderma and in up to 20% to 25% anti-RNA pol III SSc patients. It is usually encountered within the first 2 to 4 years from disease onset. The estimated median duration of scleroderma at the time of SRC diagnosis is 8 months.226, Occurrence in later disease is uncommon. Patients at greatest risk of developing SRC are those with diffuse cutaneous scleroderma, particularly during phases of rapidly progressive skin disease. SRC is a rare complication in patients with limited scleroderma (approximately 1% to 2%). African Americans and patients with diffuse skin disease who are treated with a high dose of corticosteroid (>40 mg/ day of prednisone) or low-dose cyclosporine are at increased risk of developing SRC. A long-term use of low-dose prednisone may also increase the risk for SRC. For this reason, it is recommended to avoid corticosteroids or to use doses less than 15 mg daily, if necessary. Another survey has identified additional clinical features at the time of scleroderma diagnosis that are associated with future development of SRC: proteinuria, anemia, hypertension, chronic kidney disease, elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, thrombocytopenia, hypothyroidism, and anti-Ro antibody positivity. Antibodies to RNA polymerase III were found in about 60% of patients with SRC in one survey. Renal crisis is also associated with a positive ANA (speckled pattern) anti-U3-RNP and anti-topoisomerase I antibodies, but usually is not seen in patients with anti-centromere antibodies.

SRC presents with typical signs of malignant hypertension, including headache, altered vision, signs of congestive heart failure, florid pulmonary edema, confusion, or neurologic signs as a result of hypertensive encephalopathy in the setting of an abnormally high blood pressure, usually greater than 150/90 mm Hg. Hypertensive encephalopathy is characterized by acute or subacute onset of lethargy, fatigue, confusion, headaches, visual disturbances (including blindness from hypertensive retinopathy), seizures, or cerebral hemorrhage. In about 10% of cases, SRC occurs with normal blood pressure. New-onset anemia, asymptomatic pericardial effusion, and cardiac disease may precede an SRC. Laboratory testing at onset may show normal or high creatinine, modest to absent proteinuria, and/or microscopic hematuria. Renal insufficiency is usually not the presenting problem in an SRC but rather is a late complication of untreated disease. However, a rapid rise in serum creatinine can occur over several days with a benign urinalysis such as less than 2 g of protein excretion in 24 hours or mild

hematuria with some granular casts. Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia and thrombocytopenia can accompany or precede an SRC and may be the only finding in a normotensive patient. This presentation with normotensive SRC usually entails a worse prognosis. Distinguishing SRC-associated thrombotic microangiopathy from idiopathic thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura may be difficult but is important because treatments differ. Accurate assays for ADAMTS (a disintegrin and metalloproteinase [ADAM family] with thrombospondin-1 domains)-13 activity can be helpful because its level should be normal in scleroderma.

Poorer outcome is more frequent among males and among patients presenting with creatinine greater than 3 mg/dL (265 mmol/L). Approximately two-thirds of patients with SRC will require renal support with dialysis, but about half will recover function and discontinue therapy, usually within several weeks and most before 6 months. In some patients, dialysis may be required for longer periods up to 24 months before discontinuation, distinguishing SRC from other causes of renal failure. Patients with SRC may continue to recover renal function up to 3 years after the crisis, most often within 12 to 18 months. Interestingly, while patients with anti-RNA polymerase III antibodies are at higher risk of developing SRC and to require dialysis, they are also more likely to discontinue dialysis (53 vs. 26%, p= 0.01) after SRC and have better long-term survival (p = 0.003) than subjects who are anti-RNA polymerase III negative. The incidence of end-stage kidney disease from scleroderma appears to have declined in the United States since 1996. After initiating therapy for SRC, patients with scleroderma had a greater likelihood of kidney function recovery and a lower likelihood of transplantation than demography-matched patients without scleroderma.

The renal crisis truly mimics malignant hypertension, with rapidly progressive renal failure driven by microvascular disease, vasospasm, and tissue ischemia. The characteristic lesion of scleroderma vascular disease such as intimal hyperplasia or luminal narrowing, involving in particular the renal arcuate arteries, is detected even in patients without SRC. Although the histopathologic features of renal disease are well described, the pathogenesis of SRC remains poorly understood. It is assumed that intrinsic renal vessel disease is complicated by an intense vasospasm triggering high levels of plasma renin, which results in malignant hypertension. A study demonstrated that a significant decrease in complement hemolytic activity is present in SRC versus non-SRC patients, indicating that complement consumption does occur during a renal crisis. Vascular thrombosis, glomerular ischemic collapse, and peritubular capillary C4d deposits in patients with SRC are associated with a worse outcome (e.g., requiring dialysis or transplant or death) compared with normotensive controls and hypertensive non-SRC control subjects. Further evidence that complement dysregulation may play a role in SRC thrombotic microangiopathy comes from multiple case reports suggesting benefit from early administration of eculizumab, a monoclonal antibody directed against complement factor 5 (C5), yields favorable responses by blocking terminal complement activation and membrane attack complex formation.

Doppler ultrasound is a useful technique to evaluate morphologic changes in the kidneys, resistance to flow of renal arteries, and intrarenal perfusion, using the Doppler-derived renal resistance index (RRI). One survey found that the overall survival is lower in scleroderma patients with an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) <60 mL/min and RRI ≥0.70 than in scleroderma patients with eGFR ≥60 mL/min (p < 0.0001) and with RRI <0.70 (p < 0.01).

There is some evidence that serum levels of NT-proBNP may be useful to stratify risk when predicting renal outcome in SRC. Higher levels above a 360 pmol/L cutoff value (95% CI, 0.84 1.00, area under the curve, 0.94) selectively identify patients likely to require renal replacement therapy.

### Management of Scleroderma Renal Crisis

Before the discovery of ACE inhibitors, hypertensive renal crisis almost uniformly had a fatal outcome. In contrast, patients treated with ACE inhibitors have a good outcome 60% of the time, and death or irreversible end-stage renal disease is now much less common. The mortality rate at 1 year associated with SRC has decreased from 76% to less than 15%. However, despite aggressive anti-hypertensive therapy, the 5-year survival of patients with SRC remains only 65%. Although ACE inhibitors are standard therapy for SRC, it remains unclear whether other related drugs such as ARBs can be effective in treating or preventing a crisis. Endothelin and other mediators of vascular disease are implicated in the pathogenesis of SRC, and thus interference with endothelin function by a specific inhibitor may offer a novel therapeutic approach. A highly selective ERA showed some promise in scleroderma patients with scleroderma-related chronic kidney disease, but more studies are needed. However, bosentan, another selective ERA, did not improve renal outcome in SRC. A vasodilating prostaglandin (prostacyclin) may also provide rapid control of blood pressure while improving renal blood flow. While the use of eculizumab may be supported by the emerging evidence that complement activation plays a role in SRC thrombotic microangiopathy, the evidence of its usefulness is limited to case reports mostly conducted in patients with life-threatening and refractory SRC. More rigorous studies are needed to confirm its indication for routine use.

Any newly developed hypertension in a patient with scleroderma should be urgently evaluated because the key to successful therapy is early detection and rapid intervention (see Fig. 85.13). Patients with SRC should be hospitalized and should immediately be initiated on ACE inhibitors. Captopril, a rapid-acting ACE inhibitor, should be started to allow upward dose titration until systolic blood pressure is decreased by 20 mm Hg within 24 hours while avoiding hypotension. A long-acting ACE inhibitor agent can also be used with up-titration to a maximum dose, normally achieved by doubling the dose at 24-hour intervals. Treatment continues with an ACE inhibitor even if creatinine continues to rise. It is important to note that renal function can continue to deteriorate despite initiation of ACE inhibitors and correction of blood pressure may take several days. When an ACE inhibitor at full dose fails to control the blood pressure, other anti-hypertensive medications may be added, including CCBs, alpha-1-blockers, clonidine, endothelin inhibitors, or prostacyclin. Although ARBs are thought to be less effective, they can be used if ACE inhibitors are contraindicated or not tolerated. The use of beta blockers is discouraged in a SRC due to potential negative effects on cardiac output and peripheral vasoconstrictive effect. It is recommended that ACE inhibitor therapy should be continued lifelong in all patients experiencing SRC, regardless of whether they require renal replacement therapy. . Some experts recommend starting immunosuppressive therapy in the setting of SRC. During pregnancy, SRC can be a life-threatening complication to the mother and warrants use of an ACE inhibitor despite its teratogenic risk to the fetus. Some experts would recommend in women who have experienced SRC to continue an ACE inhibitor

throughout pregnancy despite its potential teratogenicity. In this case assertive pre-pregnancy counseling is critical.

Patients may continue to have progressive renal failure despite attaining control of blood pressure. When renal function declines other causes of renal disease should always be considered, especially in patients with limited scleroderma and in those with a high level of proteinuria or abnormal urinalysis such as red blood cell casts. A renal biopsy should be performed to confirm the diagnosis and to gain insight into the prognosis by determining the histologic degree of renal damage. Detection of other forms of glomerular inflammation via a kidney biopsy is important because it will dictate a different specific treatment approach.

In the absence of serious systemic disease or other extrarenal contraindications, scleroderma patients presenting with end-stage, irreversible renal failure should be considered for kidney transplantation, which may provide an overall survival benefit compared with long-term dialysis. An international survey from 1987 to 2013 documented outcome in 34 patients with scleroderma who had renal transplant for end-stage renal failure. Patient survival was 100%, 90.3%, and 82.5% at 1, 3, and 5 years post-transplant, respectively. Pulmonary involvement was an independent risk factor of death after transplantation. Recurrence of SRC is uncommon (5%) after a renal transplant. Renal allograft survival at 3 years is about 60%, which is comparable with the rate observed in SLE. It is recommended to defer renal transplantation until it is established that further recovery will not occur spontaneously.

The overall outcome in SRC remains unsatisfactory in terms of acute disease complications and long-term morbidity, need for renal transplantation, or long-term renal support with dialysis. Currently, there is no evidence to support the prophylactic use of ACE inhibitors in patients with scleroderma who are at risk for SRC. In fact, several studies have shown that use of an ACE inhibitor before the onset of SRC is associated with worse outcome, including higher mortality. 226, Therefore, it is recommended that a non-ACE

anti-hypertensive agent (e.g., ARB or CCB) is used for hypertension not due to SRC in patients with scleroderma.

### Gastrointestinal Involvement

Almost every patient with scleroderma has symptoms of GI involvement, ranging from mild GERD to severe bowel dysfunction, which can be life threatening. Virtually any segment of the GI tract can be affected (see Table 85.3). While there is some data to suggest IVIG can improve GI motility in a subset of patients, there is no clear evidence that immunosuppressive therapy is useful to prevent or treat GI dysfunction.

### Oropharynx

Patients may report that chewing is difficult because of decreased facial flexibility caused by skin and deeper tissue fibrosis. Perioral skin tightening can result in a decreased oral aperture, affect speech, and alter the ability to open the mouth wide enough for proper dental care or to bite into large solid foods such as an apple (see Fig. 85.14). There is a lack of evidence that progression to microstomia can be altered by immunomodulation or alternative drug therapy. A rehabilitation-directed program with mouth-stretching and oral augmentation exercises can improve oral function and mouth opening. Intervention with laser therapy, UVA1, Botox, or hyaluronidase have very limited evidence for benefit. Trials of autologous fat grafting with adipose-derived stem cells showed promise with improved oral opening and function. Dry membranes resulting from decreased saliva production can lead to difficult mastication. In some patients, periodontal disease, gum regression, and tooth ligament distention can cause loosening of teeth, which further affects chewing capacity. Bone resorption of mandibular structures (osteolysis) may complicate mobility and tooth health. Use of an electric toothbrush and general dental visits

every 3 months for cleanings, tooth care, and fluoride treatment are recommended. Specially formulated toothpaste, mouthwash, and saliva replacement/moisturizing gel for dry mouth are helpful (e.g., Biotene, OralBalance, and BioXtra). Cevimeline or pilocarpine can stimulate salivary glands and improve salivary flow.

Upper pharyngeal function is usually normal, but myopathy may develop in a subset of patients causing weakness of pharyngeal muscles, mimicking a neuromuscular disease. This manifestation is characterized by pharyngeal dysfunction with problems initiating swallowing and frequent coughing resulting from laryngeal penetration, and it can be associated with increased risk for aspiration of foods or liquids. Although few pathologic studies of the upper pharyngeal structures have examined scleroderma, both myositis and fibrosis are known to occur. It is important to formally evaluate issues of swallowing difficulties with an ear, nose, and throat evaluation. A video-fluoroscopic swallowing study with speech therapy assessment can help determine the causes of swallowing dysfunction, identify the risk for aspiration, and provide management options to prevent it. If there is evidence of myositis with elevated muscle enzymes and/or associated systemic weakness, then anti-inflammatory therapy may also improve pharyngeal weakness. Overlap with neuromuscular disease such as myasthenia gravis should be considered when pharyngeal dysfunction is severe.

### Esophagus

Dysphagia resulting from esophageal disease is the most common GI symptom, occurring in approximately 90% of patients.

Heartburn, regurgitation, and dysphagia for pills and solids (more than for liquids) are the most common symptoms, but atypical retrosternal pain (particularly at night), periodic cough, a sense of food "sticking" in the esophagus, and nausea can also result from esophageal dysfunction. Esophageal involvement in scleroderma is characterized by loss of normal smooth muscle function, especially in the lower two-thirds of the organ, and hypotonia of the lower esophageal sphincter (see Fig. 85.15A). Functional studies of esophageal motility suggest that neural dysfunction is common in patients with scleroderma and that this may precede myopathic dysfunction and histologic changes in smooth muscle layers. Manometric evaluation has identified the presence of esophageal hypomotility in areas that later did not show any histologic abnormality of the smooth muscle. Other studies have shown esophageal smooth muscle activity in response to pharmacologic stimulation (methacholine challenge) early in the disease, which is usually absent in patients with more advanced scleroderma. The cause of these abnormalities is unknown, but evidence suggests that autoantibodies directed to myenteric cholinergic neurons may play a role. There is clinical and laboratory evidence that neural dysfunction precedes esophageal muscle disease.

Tissue fibrosis has often been evoked as the cause of esophageal disease in scleroderma. However, pathologic studies demonstrate atrophy of the smooth muscle layers of the distal esophagus in the absence of significant fibrosis. Ischemia of the esophagus in scleroderma is suggested by functional studies showing impaired esophageal blood flow after exposure to cold temperatures and institution of rewarming protocols. Non-inflammatory

intimal layer hyperplasia in the arterioles of the GI tract has been described. Inflammatory infiltrates are usually not present in the smooth muscle unless severe transmural esophagitis is present, which suggests that inflammation is not a cardinal feature of the pathogenesis of esophageal smooth muscle lesions in scleroderma.

The severity of esophageal symptoms may not accurately reflect the seriousness of the underlying disease. Therefore every patient with scleroderma should be fully evaluated for esophageal involvement. New technology with multichannel intraluminal electrical impedance measurements, functional lumen imaging, or whole gut transit studies may provide sensitive measures of esophageal and gastric function. If untreated, GI reflux may lead to esophagitis, bleeding, esophageal strictures, or precancerous lesions such as Barrett's esophagus. Asymptomatic patients without abnormal laboratory test results (e.g., anemia or positive evidence of GI bleeding) do not require specific interventions. Patients with mild GERD can be treated empirically with agents to block gastric acid production (i.e., histamine H2-receptor antagonists or proton pump inhibitors [PPIs]). When more severe symptoms are present (e.g., daily GERD with dysphagia) or when treatment with H2-receptor antagonists or PPIs fails, an upper GI endoscopy is necessary to fully assess the anatomy of the esophagus and the extent of related disease. Direct endoscopy is appropriate to rule out Barrett's esophagus, stricture, or a site of uncontrolled esophagitis or bleeding. There may be an increased risk of candida infection if on immunosuppression and chronic acid suppression.

Barium swallow and cine-esophagography are sensitive tests for esophageal strictures. However, direct measurement of esophageal motility via esophageal manometry may be needed if the cause of symptoms such as atypical chest pain is unclear. Although complications from Barrett's esophagus (e.g., esophageal cancer) are uncommon, periodic repeat endoscopy to reassess status is recommended, even if symptoms are under therapeutic control.

It is critical that patients alter their eating behavior to complement medication therapy. Patients often experience better results by eating more frequent smaller meals, avoiding food intake for several hours before bedtime, moving the main meal toward midday, taking a walk after meals to help gastroesophageal emptying, and eliminating foods that aggravate symptoms (e.g., spicy sauces and caffeinated or carbonated beverages). Bedtime is often a time of severe reflux. This can be improved by avoiding filling the stomach at least 2 to 3 hours before bedtime and by sleeping at a 25-to- 30-degree angle by elevating the trunk during sleep.

Treatment of reflux by suppression of gastric acid with antacids or histamine H2-receptor antagonists is helpful but often disappointing in patients with scleroderma. Conversely, PPIs (e.g., omeprazole, pantoprazole) can be very effective, with no data indicating that one formulation of PPI is superior to another. Usually, long-term daily treatment is required. Higher doses of a PPI or combination with H2-receptor antagonists may be used periodically for breakthrough symptoms. If symptoms are not controlled with recommended medication dosages, then a formal 24-hour

ambulatory pH study may be necessary to determine whether persistent symptoms are due to uncontrolled acid reflux. A prokinetic drug (e.g., metoclopramide, domperidone) can be added when symptoms of dysphagia or endoscopic findings of esophagitis are present despite the use of effective acid suppression. These medications tend to be effective during early disease but are less likely to help later in the presence of advanced esophageal dysfunction. Many patients respond to relatively low doses, for example, at bedtime alone. Given the increased risk of neurologic complications with the long-term use of metoclopramide, many clinicians recommend domperidone as a relatively safer alternative when

long-term prokinetic treatment is needed. Domperidone should not be administered to subjects with pre-existing QT prolongation or in association with other drugs inhibiting CYP3A4 because of its arrhythmogenic potential. Erythromycin and other macrolides can benefit upper GI dysmotility and gastroparesis. However, lack of long-term efficacy due to tachyphylaxis, drug interactions with agents metabolized by CYP3A4, and risk for antibiotic resistance limit its use. A placebo-controlled trial evaluating the effectiveness of domperidone 10 mg three times daily or alginic acid (algycon) one chewing tablet three times daily as add-on therapy to omeprazole 20 mg twice daily in scleroderma patients partially

responsive to PPIs found that both domperidone and algycon are equally effective to improve frequency and severity of symptoms. Prucalopride, a selective high-affinity serotonin receptor agonist commonly used for constipation, can be beneficial in subjects with GERD. Buspirone, an oral 5-hydroxytryptamine 1A (5-HT1A) receptor agonist, can also improve symptomatic GERD in patients with scleroderma.

### Stomach

The degree of delayed gastric emptying (gastroparesis) is underappreciated in scleroderma, and gastroparesis often causes early satiety, aggravation of GERD symptoms, anorexia, abdominal pain, a sensation of bloating, or nausea. Frequently, weight loss in patients with scleroderma is a consequence of poor caloric intake as a result of lack of appetite from poor gastric function. Prokinetics (e.g., erythromycin, metoclopramide, domperidone) are used to improve gastric emptying and related symptoms, but results are generally disappointing and several small meals with good caloric content is often the most effective therapy. Gastritis or gastric ulcers can occur. Dilation of the microvasculature in the gastric mucosa is found in a subset of patients. This manifestation, also called gastric antral vascular ectasia (GAVE), is thought to be caused by an abnormal angiogenesis, leading to bizarre dilation of microvessels and arterial-venous (A-V) malformations similar to the telangiectasias seen in the skin, lips, and oral mucous membranes. One survey reports a prevalence of GAVE in 10.6% of patients, with an increased risk associated with older age of onset, diffuse disease subtype, and anti-RNA polymerase III positivity. In general, GAVE lesions are asymptomatic, but they can be responsible for occult GI bleeding. Extensive clusters of A-V malformations lead to the presence of longitudinal red stripes in the inner lining of the stomach, converging to the pylorus and described on endoscopy as "watermelon stomach" based on their appearance (see Fig. 85.15B). Endoscopic therapy with laser photocoagulation or cryotherapy can be used to ablate bleeding vessels. Rarely, bleeding associated with GAVE is refractory and requires multiple transfusions, repeated laser or cryotherapy, or even gastric surgery (e.g., antral or gastric resection). While small case series suggest CYC may improve GAVE, there is no solid evidence to show a benefit with immunosuppressive therapy. . While the beneficial use of thalidomide to treat refractory GI bleeding secondary to GI vascular malformations, including GAVE and GI angiodysplasia, has been suggested in a small case series and some anecdotal reports, formal use in scleroderma has not yet been properly investigated. 257

### Lower Gastrointestinal Tract

Bloating, abdominal distention, diarrhea, and constipation are common complaints caused by dysmotility of the small and large bowel in scleroderma patients. Functional and pathologic studies suggest that microvascular disease, neural dysfunction, smooth muscle atrophy, and later tissue fibrosis similar to that seen in the esophagus cause intestinal disease. Most cases present in similar fashion to irritable bowel syndrome. Constipation due to sluggish or atonic bowel function can be followed by repeated bouts of diarrhea with malabsorption, progressive loss of weight, and severe malnutrition. Delayed intestinal transit generates an environment conducive to small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO), which can manifest with abdominal discomfort, bloating, and recurrent bouts of diarrhea and eventually lead to malabsorption

and malnutrition if left untreated. SIBO is estimated to affect between 30% and 60% of scleroderma patients and can be associated with severe disruption of quality of life.

Recurrent episodes of pseudoobstruction constitute one of the most serious intestinal problems in scleroderma. These episodes are sometimes mistaken for surgical emergencies. Pseudoobstruction is a manifestation of profound loss of bowel smooth muscle function, causing severe dysmotility and segments of luminal dilation. Pneumatosis cystoides intestinalis sometimes complicates scleroderma of the bowel when gas leaks into the diseased intestinal wall and tracks into the mesentery of the gut or the peritoneal cavity, mimicking a bowel perforation (see Fig. 85.15C and D). Asymptomatic wide-mouthed diverticula, also resulting from fibrosis and atrophy of the bowel wall, are pathognomonic of scleroderma. Volvulus, stricture, and perforation are uncommon complications of severe bowel involvement. A scintigraphy-based whole gut transit study in scleroderma found there was no significant association between slow colonic transit and delayed transit in other regions of the GI tract.

Management of the lower GI tract includes preventing a constipationdiarrhea cycle through adequate fiber ingestion, use of stool softeners (docusate), or, if constipation is severe, periodic doses of osmotic laxatives (polyethylene glycol). The low fermentable, oligosaccharides, disaccharides, monosaccharides, and polyols diet is thought to benefit scleroderma patients with altered lower GI motility by decreasing the osmotic load and the rapid fermentation by colonic microbes. Fiber supplementation has been used but often causes bloating and may worsen gastroparesis and colonic emptying. Lubiprostone is helpful if chronic constipation predominates. Novel compounds are now available for chronic, refractory constipation such as prucalopride and linaclotide, with reports indicating benefit in scleroderma patients.260, Some experts also support the use of pyridostigmine and octreotide in the presence of severe, persistent lower GI hypomotility and pseudoobstruction. Intermittent-use antibiotics such as rifaximin, amoxicillin/clavulanic acid, ciprofloxacin, and metronidazole has shown efficacy in controlling cases with overt SIBO or with recurrent episodes of pseudoobstruction. In some cases of intractable diarrhea, the use of low doses of cholestyramine can be beneficial. Abnormal gut microbiota may be playing a role in GI dysfunction. While probiotics are often used, their role in managing symptoms of presumed GI dysbiosis is still under study. Novel therapeutic strategies with fecal microbiota transplantation are being explored but preliminary results need to be validated with larger trials. Total parenteral nutrition (TPN) may become necessary in patients with severe scleroderma-related bowel disease and malnutrition irresponsive to medical therapy. The presence of intestinal failure requiring TPN is associated with an overall poor prognosis.

Fecal incontinence can manifest in scleroderma caused by dysfunction of both internal (atrophy and fibrosis) and external (weakness) anal sphincters as demonstrated by endoanal ultrasound and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Treatment options for scleroderma-related anorectal dysfunction and fecal incontinence are mainly symptomatic, as surgical interventions are generally associated with unsatisfactory outcomes. Beneficial treatments include firming stool texture, performing exercises to strengthen the pelvic muscles, implementing biofeedback methods, and conducting surgical repair when aggravating factors such as rectal prolapse or severe hemorrhoids are present. Sacral neuromodulation, involving a direct, continuous, and low-voltage electrical stimulation of the sacral nerve roots, has been used with favorable results in a subgroup of patients, but more studies are needed. 262

### Primary Cardiac Involvement

The clinical manifestations of heart disease in scleroderma are highly variable, ranging from clinically silent cardiac involvement to frank heart failure. The reported prevalence of heart disease varies from 10% to more than 50%, depending on the diagnostic method used, but in general it tends to be occult and underestimated. Symptoms such as dyspnea, chest pain, or palpitations are commonly thought to be the result of more obvious organ involvement such as the lungs or the upper GI tract, and the contribution of heart disease often is not appreciated until the later stages. Cardiac disease can occur in both diffuse and limited subtypes of scleroderma and can manifest as a primary heart problem or in association with other organ failure. When clinically evident, heart disease entails an overall poor prognosis and predicts shortened survival.13, Along with pulmonary fibrosis and PAH, cardiac disease accounts for the majority of deaths in scleroderma. One study found that 25% of deaths could be directly related to heart disease (mostly heart failure and arrhythmias). A survey from Spain reports that mortality from heart disease has increased when comparing the 1990 to 1999 to the 2000 to 2009 decades. 13

While scleroderma is overall more common in women, severe cardiovascular involvement is found in men, in association with a poorer prognosis. In a large meta-analysis, cardiac involvement was associated with increased mortality (hazard ratio, 2.8; 95% CI, 2.13.8) after adjustments for age and sex. A study comparing 129 patients with scleroderma who had a left ventricle ejection fraction (LVEF) of less than 55% with 256 subjects who had a normal LVEF demonstrated that male sex, age, digital ulcerations, myositis, and no use of CCBs were independent factors associated with LV dysfunction. A survey of published data found evidence that cardiomyopathy in scleroderma patients is associated with several indicators of poor prognosis such as diffuse cutaneous disease, positive scleroderma-specific serology, Black race, older age at disease onset, tendon friction rubs, and worse quality-of-life 267 scores.

Scleroderma cardiac disease can be characterized by involvement of the endocardium, myocardium, and pericardium, separately or concomitantly. Pericardial effusion, auricular and/or ventricular arrhythmias, conduction disease, valvular regurgitation, myocardial ischemia, myocardial hypertrophy, and heart failure are all reported. Clinically overt pericarditis is uncommon, but asymptomatic and hemodynamically benign pericardial effusions are frequently detected by ECHO. In a controlled study, significant pericardial effusion was found in about 15% of patients compared with 4% of control subjects. Pathologic studies have shown that some degree of pericardial involvement is detectable in 33% to 77% of patients with scleroderma, usually with evidence of a fibrinous pericarditis with adhesions and chronic inflammatory cell infiltrates. Hemodynamic compromise resulting from tamponade physiology is rare but may require acute intervention with anti-inflammatory medication, pericardiocentesis, or creation of a pericardial window for slow decompression. The presence of a large pericardial effusion, even if it is asymptomatic, is a poor prognostic sign, particularly if it is associated with PAH or renal disease. Colchicine is recommended by experts as a first-line treatment for both acute and recurrent pericarditis; however, its role in scleroderma pericardial disease is not studied.

Focal myocardial fibrosis is the hallmark of established primary heart involvement in scleroderma. The fibrotic lesions are patchy, involve the myocardium of both ventricles, and are usually accompanied by evidence of microvascular disease with

concentric intimal hypertrophy associated with fibrinoid necrosis of the intramural coronary arteries and arterioles. This phenomenon results in reduced coronary flow reserve even with normal epicardial coronary arteries and in the absence of clinically manifested cardiac dysfunction. Vasospasm of coronary vessels and associated myocardial perfusion defects are demonstrated to occur at rest, with exercise, and after exposure to cold temperatures. These findings suggest that myocardial fibrosis may be associated with reversible vasospasm of the microvascular coronary circulation and that vasodilating agents such as CCBs may have the capacity to improve coronary flow and prevent further cardiac damage. Patients with angina-like chest pain may need to undergo angiographic studies because nuclear perfusion studies are likely to be abnormal as a result of microvascular disease. Studies have provided controversial data regarding increased risk for atherosclerotic coronary artery disease. Although pathologic studies and an analysis of coronary angiograms have found little involvement of coronary arteries in patients with scleroderma, epidemiologic surveys seem to indicate an increased risk of atherosclerosis in this disease, like in other rheumatic conditions such as RA or SLE.29, Therefore, typical angina symptoms should make one consider atherosclerosis of the coronary vessels or another process. Atypical chest pain can also be caused by musculoskeletal problems, esophageal reflux disease, or PAH mimicking cardiac disease. While microvascular disease and focal ischemia leading to myocardial fibrosis is considered a leading pathogenetic process in scleroderma primary cardiac disease, occurrence of myocardial inflammation (myocarditis) can also be detected. This is associated more frequently with heart failure and more extensive myocardial fibrosis compared with virus-negative myocarditis secondary to other systemic autoimmune disorders.

ECG and Holter monitoring often reveal some heart conduction defect or asymptomatic arrhythmia, which are thought to be consequences of myocardial fibrosis. Premature ventricular contractions are the most common abnormality, but sinus node dysfunction, first-degree heart block, supraventricular arrhythmias (supraventricular tachycardia and atrial fibrillation), and ventricular arrhythmias (ventricular tachycardia) are also observed. Complete heart block is uncommon. Scleroderma-related syncope is an ominous manifestation of late-stage PAH or an important arrhythmia. When an arrhythmia is suspected, prolonged assessment of the heart rhythm with Holter monitoring or loop recorders should be promptly pursued. More extensive evaluation with electrophysiologic studies is indicated in serious cases because a pacemaker or ablative therapy can help in the management of these life-threatening complications. In subjects with documented advanced cardiomyopathy and significant ejection fraction depression, placement of an automatic implantable cardioverter defibrillator device should be considered to prevent sudden cardiac death.

Transthoracic ECHO (TTE), a widely used type of noninvasive cardiac testing, is a sensitive tool to detect the presence of cardiac disease. TTE can provide estimates of elevated RV and pulmonary artery pressures, as well as evidence of right heart dysfunction such as atrial and ventricular dilation or septal wall motion abnormalities. A depressed LV contractility is not frequently detected in patients with scleroderma with the use of conventional TTE, but relaxation abnormalities can be found in up to 40% of cases. LV diastolic dysfunction is detected especially in patients with diffuse scleroderma, often occurring in the absence of systemic hypertension (independent of renal disease) and in association with pulmonary vascular disease. The presence of diastolic

dysfunction is related to a poor prognosis.276, Heart failure with preserved ejection function (HFpEF) is not infrequent in scleroderma. When present, HFpEF can pose a significant challenge with management and entails a poor prognosis, particularly when it becomes associated with significant diastolic dysfunction or secondary pulmonary hypertension (PH-HFpEF). Severe impairment of contractility and diastolic dysfunction is also found in the RV and this can result from primary heart disease or be secondary to pulmonary vascular disease and associated PH.

Although TTE is very helpful in monitoring underlying cardiac abnormalities later in the disease process, it lacks some sensitivity during pre-clinical stages of heart involvement. Novel diagnostic methods such as tissue Doppler ECHO, with or without strain imaging, are being used to detect subtle cardiac dysfunction. Analysis of speckled-derived strain of the RV by two-dimensional (2D)-ECHO has revealed a heterogeneous pattern of heart strain with significant regional myocardial dysfunction in scleroderma patients compared with controls. A recent study conducted by 2D speckle tracking echocardiology found early LV and RV regional impairment in 22% to 24% of patients with scleroderma, while only 2.1% showed reduced LVEF. Exercise testing during ECHO can also be used to detect underlying diastolic dysfunction and PH not previously recognized by resting studies. Exercise provocation in conjunction with RV longitudinal systolic strain identified differential regional contractile response to exercise in patients with scleroderma, suggesting subclinical impairments in RV reserve that may be missed by resting noninvasive 2D-ECHO assessments alone. Patients with regional and global LV longitudinal systolic strain (LVLSS) are more likely to have elevated CRP values, suggesting greater inflammation. LVLSS also appears to worsen in SSc patients over time.

Cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) is a noninvasive, nonradiation diagnostic imaging technique that can provide functional and structural characterization of scleroderma heart involvement earlier than conventional ECHO and with greater accuracy. 283, CMR detects subclinical myocardial fibrosis early in the disease course of patients with VEDOSS or in subjects with limited skin involvement and no significant internal organ involvement, a subset usually expected to have a more benign disease course. 285, One of these studies did not identify any association between focal or diffuse myocardial fibrosis and ventricular arrhythmias, making the exact prognostic implications of myocardial fibrosis by CMR in asymptomatic subjects unclear. While CMR has great sensitivity, its specificity remains suboptimal, and further studies are needed.

The systematic measurement of BNP or NT-proBNP is an integral part of cardiac evaluation in scleroderma patients. Blood levels of these molecules reflect both RV and LV volume/pressure overload and has proven to be a reliable prognostic marker for right or left heart failure in patients with scleroderma, independently predicting mortality. 213,287,288] Elevated serum levels of troponin I can also be detected in association with echocardiographic abnormalities such as low ejection fraction and regional hypokinesia and may represent a useful marker to identify ongoing myocardial injury in scleroderma patients.289, In one survey, patients with elevated troponin had a 2.16-fold (95% CI, 1.014.63, p = 0.046) increased risk of death compared with those without elevated troponin even after adjusting for age, sex, disease duration, and cardiopulmonary risk factors. . Thus persistently elevated troponin levels may warrant closer clinical investigation to assess for presence of scleroderma-related cardiac disease.

Early detection of scleroderma cardiac involvement is crucial to prevent life-threatening complications. All patients with

scleroderma should receive a routine screening ECHO, regardless of the presence or absence of arrhythmia. This should be performed with Doppler and STE when possible. Provocation with exercise should be considered when unexplained dyspnea is present without obvious findings at rest. Given the high prevalence of subclinical cardiac disease in scleroderma, it is reasonable to perform ECG, BNP, or NT-proBNP annually, as these are sensitive tests with low risk and relatively low cost.

An isolated cardiomyopathy without evidence of an inflammatory process is managed with conventional medications. Effective treatment of arrythmias, diuretic therapy for HFpEF, and appropriate management of comorbid conditions (e.g., hypertension, diabetes, hypercholesterolemia) that can affect heart function is key. Heart disease often manifests in the context of the multisystem manifestations of scleroderma (see sections), which require immunosuppressive or anti-fibrotic agents. There is no clear evidence that use of these drugs for asymptomatic findings of occult heart disease prevents subsequent complications. Novel therapeutic options to dampen early on in the inflammatory-fibrotic process in scleroderma heart disease (i.e., IL-1 inhibition) are under consideration. Patients with diffuse cutaneous scleroderma and skeletal muscle inflammation (polymyositis) are particularly prone to develop severe cardiomyopathy and tend to have a particularly poor prognosis. Acute myocarditis can in fact occur in association with inflammatory muscle disease and can present as sudden-onset heart failure. Prompt institution of immunosuppressive treatment is indicated in these cases. A CMR and/or an endomyocardial biopsy may be helpful tools to differentiate overt myocarditis from the myocardial fibrosis commonly present in patients with scleroderma. While therapy with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) or colchicine may be helpful to treat active pericarditis, it is not clear whether anti-inflammatory treatment is indicated for small, stable, and asymptomatic pericardial effusions. A predesigned approach involving a multidisciplinary team including a cardiologist, pulmonologist, and rheumatologist is recommended.

### Musculoskeletal Involvement

Musculoskeletal symptoms are often the earliest sign of the disease, with estimates of up to 20 to 30% of scleroderma patients presenting muscle or joint symptoms within the first year of diagnosis. Usually, these are nonspecific and include arthralgia, myalgias with diffuse muscular pain, and musculoskeletal stiffness and/or weakness that mimics a flulike syndrome, making a diagnosis of scleroderma challenging. It is common for patients to be diagnosed with carpal tunnel syndrome resulting from soft tissue swelling and inflammation in the hand and wrist area prior to recognizing the underlying diagnosis of scleroderma. The degree and type of musculoskeletal disease vary a great deal, influenced by the duration of disease, the level of overall disease activity, and the serologic and clinical subtype of scleroderma, for example, in early diffuse scleroderma, pain that is often widespread in areas of skin inflammation and advancing fibrosis. As the disease progresses, these patients can develop deep tissue disease with involvement of joint structures, tendons, subcutaneous tissues, and underlying muscles. Impaired hand function, with decreased hand mobility, reduced dexterity, and decreased grip force, is the most common musculoskeletal manifestation and is often a major cause of impairment to perform activities of daily living. In later stages, diffuse disease can result in irreversible joint contractures and a fibrosing myopathy, which are associated with pain, loss of

function, and significant disability. In patients with limited scleroderma, puffy fingers and loss of hand function and grip may be the only musculoskeletal symptoms throughout the disease course. Musculoskeletal involvement occurs in conjunction with active multisystem disease and is an independent cause of disability and impaired quality of life. Loss of muscle or sarcopenia is seen in about 20% of patients with scleroderma and is associated with physical impairment affecting everyday life activities and ability to participate in work. Although histologic evidence suggests that synovitis occurs, arthralgias, pain, and stiffness without signs of frank signs of synovitis constitute the usual clinical picture.

Erosive polyarthritis, seemingly specific for scleroderma, or seropositive RA can occur in patients with limited or diffuse skin disease. The prevalence of scleroderma and RA overlap is low (1% to 2%), with an estimated incidence of 5%.295-297 Anticitrullinated protein antibodies are rarely detected in patients with scleroderma and arthritis. Erosive arthritis is also commonly associated with periarticular calcinosis (see Fig. 85.16A) and can be seen with significant bone loss or osteolysis. A radiologic survey of 120 patients found abnormalities including erosion (21%), joint space narrowing (28%), arthritis (defined by concomitant erosion and joint space narrowing; 18%), radiologic demineralization (23%), acro-osteolysis (22%), flexion contracture (27%), and calcinosis (23%). Radiologic studies using ultrasonography and MRI confirm that hand involvement is usually advanced, with striking articular, bone, and soft tissue changes.298, Resorption of distal phalanges is significantly associated with digital ulcers and extraarticular calcification. While loss of bone in the fingers

with shortening of the digit (acro-osteolysis) and pseudoclubbing is the most common presentation, cases of osteolysis of the mandible and clavicle are also reported, suggesting a systemic defect.

Contractures of the PIP and MCP joints are most common and, rarely, contractures of the distal interphalangeal joint occur. Patients with diffuse skin disease can develop contractures of large joints, including wrists, elbows, shoulders, hips, knees, and ankles. These are the hallmark of severe scleroderma and are associated with fibrosis and ankylosis of the joint, resulting from disease in the overlying skin, fascia, joint capsule, and tendon structures.

Tendon friction rubs can be felt as a coarse crepitus over joints or over the forearm or lower leg with adjacent joint movement. These rubs are thought to be a result of low-grade tenosynovitis, local edema, and fibrosis of the tendon sheath, fascia, and joint structures. Friction rubs are seen primarily in patients with diffuse skin disease; when present, they are an indicator of a poor overall prognosis. They are found in about 15% to 30% of cases, more commonly in patients with diffuse skin disease and those with positive anti-topoisomerase, anti-RNA polymerase, or anti-U3- RNP antibodies.

A large multicenter survey reported the frequencies of synovitis, tendon friction rubs, and joint contractures to be 16, 11, and 31%, respectively. Synovitis, tendon friction rubs, and joint contractures are more likely to occur together and are more prevalent in patients with the diffuse cutaneous subset. These manifestations also associate with systemic disease including severe vascular, muscular, renal, and interstitial lung involvement. The presence of myopathy associates with cardiac disease and poor outcome.

Calcinosis is most often seen in patients with digital ulcers and is similarly observed in patients with the diffuse or limited cutaneous subtype. Calcium deposits often develop in the subcutaneous tissue of areas subjected to trauma such as the extensor surfaces of the forearms, elbows, or patellae. Unlike the more extensive calcinosis seen in patients with myositis, calcium deposits in scleroderma tend to be found in clusters around joints and sites of trauma. These deposits can restrict joint motion and can be associated with local acute inflammation similar to a gouty arthritis. They can also rupture through the skin, weeping a thick, white material. Once the skin is broken, secondary infection can occur. Calcinosis pathogenesis is not fully understood but it occurs in sites of poor blood flow and trauma, manifesting as a post-inflammatory defective repair process. The degree of calcinosis and some measure of activity help guide intervention. X-rays and ultrasound are considered sensitive modalities for assessing calcinosis.

Weakness in the muscles of the hands, arms, and legs is very common (80%); this can be subtle or profound. One study found measurable weakness in 30% of patients, with proximal more than distal strength being compromised. Myopathy in a person with scleroderma is often multifactorial, but patients with muscle involvement are at increased risk for poor outcome and decreased survival. A survey noted that the presence of muscle weakness is associated with several features of worse disease burden and independently predicts disability as measured by the HAQ-DI 300 Weakness is often caused by muscle atrophy as a result of score. the inflexibility due to joint disease and fibrotic skin with lack of usual mobility and exercise. It can also occur because of malnutrition resulting from scleroderma-related bowel disease. Frequently, muscle weakness in scleroderma can be a result of direct muscle disease. In a survey, 40.6% of scleroderma patients undergoing MRI showed evidence of skeletal muscle edema consistent with myopathy, even in subjects without symptoms or other signs of muscle involvement. A pathologic study of 42 subjects with muscle disease (79% female and 64% diffuse scleroderma) found multiple types, including muscle necrosis (67%), inflammatory myopathy (48%), acute neurogenic atrophy (48%), and fibrosis (33%).

In people with diffuse scleroderma, fibrosis can extend into the striated muscle, causing muscle atrophy and clinical weakness. This phenomenon called fibrosing myopathy presents in the setting of severe diffuse skin disease with joint contractures and mild elevation of CPK. Electromyography (EMG) demonstrates nonirritable myopathy, and a muscle biopsy shows little inflammation, fibrosis, and type 2 muscle atrophy. Fibrosing myopathy does not respond to traditional anti-inflammatory medications, including corticosteroids, and is associated with myocardial involvement, heart failure, and arrhythmias that can be severe and irreversible. This unique histologic subtype of myopathy carries a significantly higher mortality compared with scleroderma muscle disease characterized by inflammation and/or necrosis.

Approximately 5% to 10% of patients with scleroderma have a more defined inflammatory muscle involvement that can follow a disease course like in other forms of idiopathic inflammatory myopathy. These patients develop a more rapidly progressing proximal muscle weakness associated with high CPK levels, EMG significant for an irritable myopathy, and a muscle biopsy with typical inflammatory muscle infiltrates. In severe polymyositis cases, myocarditis can occur with heart failure. High levels of anti- PM/Scl-100 antibodies are found in about 4% of patients with scleroderma, often in association with acute inflammatory muscle disease. Patients with muscle weakness should be fully evaluated

for underlying causes with the use of laboratory measures of muscle enzymes, EMG studies, MRI, and muscle biopsy. These studies will help differentiate inflammatory muscle disease from other forms of myopathy.

### Management of Musculoskeletal Disease

Active symptoms and signs of musculoskeletal disease are frequently associated with overall disease activity, and these may improve as systemic treatment to manage other organ involvement is implemented. The management of muscle weakness begins with a careful evaluation to identify underlying causes. A myopathy due to disuse, malnutrition, medications, or late irreversible disease is best managed with direct intervention with improved dietary intake, discontinuation of toxic drugs (e.g., statins, steroids), and physical therapy-directed exercise. Muscle enzymes, EMG, and MRI of major muscle groups should help further define causes of underlying weakness. A muscle biopsy is recommended to characterize the disease process in that each histologic subtype can guide therapy and predict outcome. Inflammatory muscle disease is treated in the same manner as other cases of myositis. Steroids can be effective for musculoskeletal inflammation but should be used only at low doses (less than 15 mg/day) due to concerns of triggering an SRC. For severe myositis, IVIG can be initiated with steroids and MTX or MMF added for long-term control. Rituximab is also effective in a case series of scleroderma patients positive for anti-PM/Scl. The management of fibrosing myopathy is not established but again this can benefit from effective control of the systemic disease with immunosuppression and anti-fibrotic agents.

NSAIDs are helpful to control pain and joint inflammation but must be monitored and used with caution due to GI side effects and possible renal toxicity. Immunosuppressive agents may also dampen active joint and soft tissue inflammation. MMF used by most experts as the initial therapy for skin and ILD is not very effective for active joint disease but may treat an inflammatory muscle process. When inflammatory arthritis is present, traditional medications used in RA can be helpful. MTX is an effective agent to treat polyarthritis using the same approach as for RA. If MTX is not effective alone, then a biologic can be added or used as an alternative. One case series demonstrated that etanercept can be efficacious in improving active inflammatory joint disease in scleroderma patients and is generally safe and well tolerated. While tocilizumab did not show benefit to treat scleroderma skin disease, a case series reports benefit for inflammatory joint disease. Disappearance of tendon friction rubs is a sign of systemic and articular disease control.

Physical and occupational therapy should be started early to decrease the risk of contractures and support patients with conditioning and activities of daily living. Exercise and good nutrition while controlling the disease process are also important to prevent loss of muscle mass and strength even in the absence of inflammation.

Evidence of bone mineral deficit should always be assessed with baseline bone density scan, particularly in post-menopausal patients and those with significant nutritional difficulties. Presence of osteoporosis is treated in the same manner as nonscleroderma patients. As the pathogenesis of osteolysis is not fully understood, most experts approach this complication by optimizing control of RP with the idea that hypoxia and aberrant repair may be driving mechanisms.

Many agents exert some efficacy in treating calcinosis, but the medical management of this scleroderma complication is in general

very disappointing. Vasodilators (e.g., diltiazem), antiresorptive agents (e.g., bisphosphonates), calcium binding agents such as sodium thiosulfate (topical or systemic), vitamin K, colchicine, the IL-1 inhibitor anakinra, rituximab, and minocycline are among the agents that are helpful. Controlled studies of therapeutic agents for SSc-related calcinosis are needed, and outcome measures should be based on objective measures of disease activity. Reducing trauma, cushioning high-risk sites, and controlling the underlying inflammatory disease are the most effective strategies for treatment. Calcinosis accumulating around articular structures can drive events similar to acute crystal arthropathy (i.e., goutlike) and are best treated with NSAIDs and rest. Open wounds can occur at calcinosis sites that may get secondarily infected needing antibiotic therapy and/or debridement. Surgical removal of painful calcium deposits is an option but reoccurrence in the same area is very common and expected.

### Associated Disorders

The most common endocrine problem associated with scleroderma is thyroid disease, while the prevalence of other endocrinopathies is similar to that of the general population. Thyroid fibrosis, autoimmune thyroiditis resulting in hypothyroidism, and hyperthyroidism from Graves' disease are frequent and often unsuspected findings in scleroderma. Thyroid disease is reported in 10% to 15% of patients with scleroderma. .308,309An autoimmune basis for thyroid involvement is suggested by one series, which found Hashimoto's thyroiditis in 6% and Graves' disease in 3% of scleroderma-affected individuals. In a survey of 719 scleroderma patients, 273 (38%) subjects presented at least another autoimmune condition, most frequently autoimmune thyroid disease. Another cohort study reported an increased risk of thyroid disease among female scleroderma patients compared with controls, including subclinical hypothyroidism (OR, 3.2; 95% CI, 1.8, 5.7), clinical hypothyroidism (OR, 14.5; 95% CI, 2.3, 90.9), anti-thyroid peroxidase antibody positivity (OR, 2.7; 95% CI, 1.8, 4.1), and thyroid ultrasound hypoechoic pattern (OR, 3.2; 95% CI, 2.2, 4.7). Another survey found that presence of hyperthyroidism in scleroderma patients carries a 1.54fold increase of mortality rates during a mean follow-up of 17 313 Autoimmune thyroid disease should especially be sought years. in scleroderma patients with PBC, CREST features, and Sjögren's syndrome, as there are reports of overlap with all these conditions. Thyroid disease may not be recognized, as many symptoms of hypothyroidism or hyperthyroidism can overlap with the clinical manifestations of scleroderma and can be incorrectly attributed to the systemic disease. Treatments for thyroid disease are effective and should be implemented as persistent thyroid dysfunction may negatively impact the overall management of scleroderma.

Other disease-associated manifestations that often go unrecognized and yet cause significant morbidity include neurologic and audio-vestibular disease, oral complications, sicca syndrome, liver disease, bone disease (osteoporosis, osteolysis, avascular necrosis), lower-extremity skin lesions, and erectile dysfunction (ED). Awareness of these associated problems can improve quality of life and prevent undue distress. Involvement of the peripheral and autonomic nervous systems are the most commonly appreciated neurologic complications. Although the true prevalence has not been thoroughly investigated, a systematic review including reports on 182 cases indicates that myopathy (51.8%), trigeminal neuropathy (16.52%), peripheral sensorimotor polyneuropathy (14.25%), and carpal tunnel syndrome (6.56%) are

the most frequent manifestations affecting the peripheral nervous 314 Peripheral neuropathy in scleroderma patients can system. result from multiple causes, including nutritional deficiency from GI disease, entrapment neuropathy, vasculitis, or vasculopathy of small vessels typical of scleroderma vascular disease. A survey found a total of 17 in 60 (28%) patients with scleroderma had evidence of a peripheral neuropathy as defined by the presence of neuropathic symptoms and/or electrophysiologic evidence of neuropathy. However, the cause was attributed in 82.3% to a comorbid nonscleroderma-related condition. Autonomic neuropathy involving cardiovascular and GI systems is also reported.

Central nervous system (CNS) disease is generally clinically absent, but smoldering cerebrovascular disease is suggested by more frequent detection in scleroderma patients compared with controls of asymptomatic white-matter lesions by MRI. A survey found that CNS lesions correlate with presence of clinical headaches, depression, and peripheral vascular disease, and they are thought to be due to involvement of smaller arterial branches and perforating arteries. In a study, carotid artery Doppler ultrasound and brain MRI with brain fluid-attenuated inversion recovery and diffusion-weighted sequences were conducted on 72 patients with scleroderma and no CNS symptoms and 42 controls. Scleroderma patients had more common carotid artery intima-media thickness, higher CRP, and more brain MRI hyperintense lesions than controls (p < 0.05), suggesting an increased risk of vascular and CNS disease. Results from a study measuring carotid intima media thickness and pulse wave velocity showed that the presence of subclinical atherosclerosis is comparable between scleroderma and RA, a systemic disease with well-established high atherosclerotic burden. Subclinical atherosclerotic disease affecting the coronary arteries in asymptomatic scleroderma patients has also been confirmed by detection of increased cardiac calcium scores compared with matched healthy controls. Data also suggest that cardiovascular disease risk and atherosclerosis measured by macrovascular parameters correlate with the presence and severity of microvascular disease assessed by abnormalities on nail-fold video capillaroscopy. A cognitive function measurement study conducted in 20 scleroderma patients using Mini-Mental State Examination, Wechsler Adult Intelligence scale, and the P300 (P3) wave component of event-related potentials found that subclinical cognitive impairment is present in 65% of cases, suggesting that this is an unappreciated problem needing more dedicated investigation. A survey of anti-centromere-positive patients with limited scleroderma showed presence of subjective hearing loss 54% of the time compared with 0% in controls, with objective hearing loss detected by audiogram in 77% of patients compared with 26% of controls (p < 0.001). Hearing loss was bilateral in most cases and was attributed to sensory neural hearing loss.

In older patients with scleroderma, altered urinary tract function is a common comorbid condition. Evidence from urodynamic studies suggest that autonomic dysfunction can also affect bladder function in scleroderma patients presenting with increased urinary frequency, nocturia, hesitancy, and decreased stream.

Dry eyes (keratoconjunctivitis sicca) and/or oral mucous membranes (xerostomia) occur in about 25% of patients. Dryness in the eyes may result from associated Sjögren's syndrome or from severe facial periorbital skin fibrosis, which limits full closure of the eyelids. Topical artificial tears should be used frequently in these cases.

Although the liver is generally spared as a primary target organ in scleroderma, abnormal liver function tests are often encountered either due to a comorbid condition or associated

autoimmune disease. Both PBC and autoimmune hepatitis may develop in scleroderma. The prevalence of antimitochondrial antibody, antismooth muscle antibodies, and liver-kidney microsomal-1 autoantibody is increased in scleroderma patients compared with healthy controls. The prevalence of PBC among patients with scleroderma is about 2% to 2.5%, usually in patients with limited scleroderma who are anti-centromere positive.
