Bone disease can occur for a variety of reasons. Most patients with scleroderma are women who are near or in menopause and therefore are at risk for osteoporosis and its complications. This risk is increased by the chronic inflammatory nature of the disease, disuse, and several commonly used medications, such as corticosteroids or PPIs. Malabsorption and lack of sun exposure may lead to vitamin D deficiency, and bowel dysfunction can limit calcium intake. Avascular necrosis of the carpal bones of the wrist is reported and is thought to be a result of scleroderma peripheral vascular disease. In addition, osteolysis or bony resorption of the tips or tufts of the fingers, middle phalanges, distal radius, and ulna bones (less commonly, the distal clavicle, ribs, mandible, and distal toes) may occur (see Fig. 85.16B and C). Acro-osteolysis is common, presenting with shortening of the finger or pain of the fingertip. The pathogenesis of osteolysis is thought to be a manifestation of peripheral vascular disease and aberrant remodeling with increased osteoclast formation and higher VEGF levels affecting bones.

Lower-extremity cutaneous lesions can occur due to several causes, including skin fibrosis, stasis dermatitis, lipodermatosclerosis, panniculitis, subcutaneous calcinosis, and leg ulcers. Leg ulcers may result from traumatic breakdown of atrophic fibrotic skin, ischemic ulcers as a result of scleroderma vascular disease, vasculitis, and occlusive vascular events resulting from an associated hypercoagulable state. Livedoid vasculopathy is a rare complication causing skin ulcerations on the lower leg and foot as the result of small-vessel vasculitis or small-vessel thrombosis aggravated by venous insufficiency or states of fluid overload.

The presence of ED is often not investigated. However, studies find that ED and associated impotence are present in more than 80% of men with scleroderma due to local fibrosis of the corporeal smooth muscle and scleroderma microvascular disease. The management of ED is challenging and includes exclusion of comorbid conditions, the use of phosphodiesterase inhibitors, and consideration of the surgical placement of penile prostheses.

### Psychosocial Aspects

Scleroderma is a disease that can alter virtually every aspect of the patient's life. Although scleroderma can often be mild in its expression, a newly diagnosed patient is faced with a life crisis and must deal with a rare chronic disease that is complex and not completely understood by the medical community. A review of 26 studies identified major themes of psychosocial distress among patients with scleroderma, such as distressing appearance transformation, palpable physical limitations, social impairment, navigating uncertainty, and feeling alone and misunderstood. Patients learn that scleroderma is potentially a life-threatening disease that alters physical capacity and can be disfiguring. At its onset, patients are often confused, anxious, and frightened. Fear and misunderstanding become a major source of distress. Studies of psychosocial adjustment support the conclusion that a substantial proportion of patients with scleroderma have difficulty adapting to the disease and have reduced quality of life measures. In addition, several medications used to treat the disease and its

complications may also have some influence on mood and the sense of well-being. The presence of functional disability significantly impacts HRQoL assessed by physical function, physical role, bodily pain, general health, social functional, emotional role, and mental health domains. A high prevalence of sleep disturbance in patients with scleroderma was found to be associated with esophageal involvement, severity of disease, depression, and worse quality of life.

Psychosocial aspects of the disease do not appear to be consistently influenced by age, sex, race/ethnicity, education, or marital status. However, some data suggest that being disabled with low income leads to higher psychological distress. Depression in patients with scleroderma is common and is more related to the patient's personality, degree of pain, and level of social support than to actual disease severity. A large epidemiologic survey found that the proportion rate of depression among 2500 patients was significantly higher than healthy controls (16.2% vs. 10.9%) and that this proportion was even higher in females and subjects with low socioeconomic status. Pain and fatigue are common manifestations and, together with depressive symptoms, the most significant determinants of physical functioning and social adjustment—two important components of HRQoL—in patients with both limited and diffuse disease subtypes. Expert interviews with patients with scleroderma-ILD found that the disease manifestations have a profound impact on quality of life, working ability, psychological well-being, and social interactions of both patients and caregivers. Likewise, the severity of GI dysfunction has shown significant association with emotional distress and quality of life.

Personality traits influence the degree of psychological adjustment. Patients with scleroderma who describe themselves as anxious, worried, tense, or detail oriented are more likely to be depressed than are patients who describe themselves as agreeable or extraverted and outgoing. Disease unpredictability and lack of control cause increased distress. High self-reported uncertainty is related to poor adjustment. Thus improving the patient's understanding of the disease and defining expectations through education may reduce uncertainty and improve quality of life. Body image dissatisfaction is a significant concern. Patients are distressed by disease-related changes in visible parts of their body, especially of the face, fingers, and hands. A survey found that tight skin and facial changes were not as distressful as hand deformity with finger contractions and hand dysfunction. A scleroderma cohort study reported that concerns about appearance were very common in these patients, particularly in men across all age groups and in 329 younger women.

The impact of scleroderma on sexual function is not well studied and often not addressed by the caring physician. However, sexual dysfunction affects both men and women with scleroderma and has a major impact on their quality of life. Attention should be dedicated to this problem as part of a comprehensive patient evaluation and included in the delivery of care. While ED is the most common cause of sexual problems in males, genital tract and general physical changes are major contributors to sexual function disturbances in females. Women with scleroderma, particularly those with diffuse skin disease, have high levels of sexual impairment compared with women who have other chronic diseases for which sexual function has received greater attention. One study reported the prevalence of female sexual dysfunction to be 73% in scleroderma compared with 31% in healthy controls, showing that impaired sexual function was associated with higher disease activity, the presence of dyspnea and ILD, reduced physical

activity, functional disability, more severe depression, more pronounced fatigue, and impaired quality of life.

Psychological factors with demonstrated relevance to scleroderma include pain, depression, and distress about disfigurement, physical function, and social function. Although these dimensions of quality of life are interrelated, pain, depression, and distress about disfigurement are common and may respond to psychological intervention. Such intervention begins with providing compassionate support beyond just ordering medications. It is important to spend time in a comfortable setting educating patients about scleroderma, providing a clear understanding of the degree of their disease, and explaining to them what they need to do and what can be done for relief. Having insight into social support and life circumstances, including financial distress, work environment, and family structure, provides a framework for helping patients to decrease external distress. For example, a family conference held to explain the reality of a patient's health status or relevant needs can reduce home tension and can clarify the actual capacity in their family role. Support in obtaining adjustments to the work environment (e.g., permission to use a space heater) can make a difference. Follow-up visits that provide time to discuss issues of coping and social support are most important. Recognizing the personality of patients while addressing their specific concerns is helpful. Treating underlying depression and especially providing effective management of disease-related pain help improve quality of life and reduce social and psychological distress. Body image dissatisfaction is a significant concern in women with scleroderma and should be assessed routinely. Early identification and treatment of body image dissatisfaction may help prevent depression and psychosocial impairment in this population. Focus group interviews found that receiving emotional, informational, and instrumental support was important, with emotional support being the priority. To cope with the challenges of scleroderma, patients try to develop strategies to better manage the physical and emotional disease burden and improve their own quality of life. Easier access to disease-specific educational resources, to knowledgeable health care providers, to patients' groups and to supportive interventions, including tailored scleroderma self-management programs, can make a difference. The possibility of premature death from the disease is a major cause of fear and needs to be addressed with patients and their family. Most often, life expectancy is not influenced by the disease, yet patients fear death because they have scleroderma. When a patient is facing death from a severe disease, appropriate honest and sensitive support must be provided.

### Conclusion and Practical Recommendations

The first principle in managing scleroderma is recognizing that the disease expression is very heterogeneous. While the name "scleroderma" focuses attention to the skin, it is not just a fibrotic skin disorder, but rather a systemic disease with the potential of mild to severe multiorgan involvement. Defining the patient's specific clinical and serologic phenotype provides insight into risk for disease manifestations and guides intervention. Not all patients develop progressive or severe disease or develop specific organ involvement (see particular sections), yet the potential for scleroderma to become a life-threatening illness is present in every case. Despite the variable disease expression, there are common clinical features and biologic processes that link disease subtypes together. There is compelling evidence that scleroderma is driven by an autoimmune process and targeting the inflammatory/immune system early on makes sense. Autoantibodies are present years

before the onset of clinical symptoms, suggesting that a chronic indolent immune process underlies the disease at early stages. In fact, evidence has been provided that in very early scleroderma presenting with RP, puffy fingers, and evidence of microvascular changes, the earliest insult is a unique nonimmune complex process that leads to a systemic proliferative occlusive microvascular disease. This vascular insult triggers tissue injury via a cascade of secondary immune, inflammatory, and profibrotic mediators, yet a single pathway has not been identified as critical to the disease activity. This dynamic and uniquely complex biology can sometimes present with such subtle manifestations that a diagnosis is challenging. In contrast, it can unfold as an explosive disease with rapid progressive skin fibrosis and obvious systemic organ malfunction. Every patient with early clinical disease needs a comprehensive evaluation to define organ involvement, stage of disease activity, and level of severity of organ disease. It is recommended that every patient, in addition to standard examination, have a baseline PFT, ECG, ECHO, HRCT scan of lungs, assessment of nail-fold capillaries, and well-documented mRSS. In addition to standard laboratory testing, serologic studies (see "Autoantibodies" section), CPK, pro-BNP, thyroid-stimulating hormone, and inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP) are appropriate. These data along with the clinical assessment will help in defining the subtype of scleroderma, the expected risk, and the evidence of specific organ disease.

Progressive disease may not invariably occur in every patient, but early intervention may be appropriate if organ disease is detected in a high-risk individual. For example, evidence of early ILD may be treated promptly in a young African American woman who is anti-topoisomerase positive, especially in the presence of active skin disease and friction rubs. Serial evaluations and repeated assessments are key. In patients who are otherwise stable, these can be done every 6 months. Of course, more frequent studies should be considered based on the level of disease activity. The rheumatologist may not see patients in the early phase of the disease. Scoring the time from first onset of RP, which sometimes occurs years before the first non-RP clinical symptom, helps in appreciating the degree of occult disease progression before the diagnosis is made. It is common for scleroderma specialty centers to evaluate patients referred for consultation after 1 to 4 years from disease onset. This could imply that the pathobiology underlying the disease may have transitioned from an early active immunedriven process to a more dominant chronic profibrotic network associated with a decreased responsiveness to immunosuppression alone.

Recognizing the various expressions of the disease, the different stages and its variable course, and the degree of organ involvement is very helpful to define current management plans (see Table 85.4). Major advances have been made with interventions directed to specific organs or systems including RP, SRC, ILD, PAH, GI dysfunction, and musculoskeletal disease (see specific sections). However, no single drug has shown yet the ability to control the overall disease process. This is likely due in part to the challenges encountered by previous clinical trials, which have mostly focused on progressive skin disease and used the mRSS as their main outcome. Studies investigating novel therapies for scleroderma are now attempting to enroll patients with more homogeneous clinical phenotypes, who have early active and/or potentially reversible disease, and test composite scores of disease burden as primary outcome.

Attempts at disease modification have primarily focused on nonselective immunosuppression with the idea that this would

decrease inflammation, thus curtailing activation of downstream pathways known to propagate multiorgan fibrosis and widespread vascular injury. The results from this approach have yielded some evidence of organ-specific success but have been rather unsatisfactory with overall disease control. New understanding of the mediators and the molecular pathways playing a unique role in fibrosis is emerging that may soon provide new targets for treatment. While to date no drugs have convincingly showed the ability to directly block activated fibroblasts and to reverse the fibrotic disease process in scleroderma patients, several potential agents are being used off-label or are under investigation. Of note, nintedanib, a drug with anti-fibrotic properties, has shown benefit and is now FDA approved for treatment of scleroderma-related ILD. Increasing attention has also been placed on the fact that the underlying vascular injury typical of scleroderma is not only responsible for abnormal vascular reactivity (i.e., RP) but also drives the progressive obliteration and attenuation of small arteries, resulting in tissue hypoxia and chronic organ ischemia with all its consequences. Therefore drugs that improve vascular function and protect the endothelium are now being used more consistently. Ultimately, the key to current management of scleroderma is not to isolate treatment to one problem that seems to be dominant but to appreciate the complexity and dynamics of this multisystem disease and its overlapping pathogenetic mechanisms. Effective therapy should be implemented distinguishing manifestations of active reversible disease from those of irreversible tissue damage. In addition, appreciation for the unique sequence of events that includes a smoldering vascular injury, a more obvious early inflammatory phase, and then the progression toward a sustained

indolent fibrotic stage should guide the choice of the most appropriate therapy. Clearly, the use of one drug alone is not effective to control all these processes at once and to effectively manage the entire spectrum of all the scleroderma clinical manifestations. As long-term therapy is required, adjustments based on the unfolding of specific clinical and pathologic circumstances are needed. Early detection and intervention to dampen disease activity are most important. A combination therapy approach that attempts to treat the immune response, the vascular disease, and the underlying tissue fibrosis is recommended.

All patients need education, emotional, and physical support. Scleroderma is a painful disease, and managing pain is essential for reducing depression and improving quality of life. Optimization of nighttime rest may require the use of sleep aids (e.g., lorazepam or zolpidem). Anxiety and depression can be helped with anti-anxiety medications (e.g., selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors). Pain often needs a comprehensive approach that may require gabapentin or intermittent use of narcotics. Physical and occupational therapy are most important early in the course of the disease to reduce pain and improve activities of daily living. Family counseling helps the patient cope with the illness by providing a clear understanding of what may be needed at home. Adjustment of the work environment (e.g., limiting time at work, adjusting room temperature, granting flexibility, and changing work assignments) or helping patients to obtain disability support are also important. Open communication between the physician and the patient provides an essential element of care.

# Inflammatory Diseases of Muscle and Other Myopathies

### KEY POINTS

### Introduction

Idiopathic inflammatory myopathies (IIM), or myositis, are a heterogeneous group of systemic autoimmune rheumatic disorders characterized by chronic muscle weakness, muscle fatigue, and varying involvement of other organs. Most cases have varying degrees of mononuclear cell infiltration into skeletal muscle. These disorders were described in the literature more than a century ago as generalized muscle disorders affecting principally the trunk and proximal limb muscles, with or without skin involvement.1-5 It was also recognized that these diseases can range from acute and even fatal to slow, progressive, chronic, insidious conditions, with patterns of relapse and remission. Steiner's summary of myositis cases in 1905 made a clear distinction between idiopathic polymyositis (PM) and other forms of myositis caused by bacteria and parasites,6 and Stertz in 1916 first reported an association between dermatomyositis (DM) and internal malignancy. At about the same time, Batten8 described the first case of DM with classic histologic features in a child.

Since the 1940s, it has been recognized that IIM may occur in the absence of cutaneous lesions, muscle pain, or constitutional symptoms. It may present in an acute, subacute, or chronic

insidious form, with some fraction of cases showing systemic features or involvement of organs and tissues. The differential diagnosis has been described independently by several investigators, and the most chronic form was differentiated from an adult variety of muscular dystrophy. The first classification scheme and set of diagnostic criteria for myositis were proposed by Bohan and Peter in 1975.11, They include PM and DM but not inclusion body myositis (IBM). IBM was later defined by the presence of distinct histopathologic changes, including vacuoles and nuclear and cytoplasmic inclusions, as well as by distinct clinical features, including distal and asymmetric muscle involvement in contrast to proximal symmetric muscle involvement seen in PM and DM as well as nonresponsiveness to glucocorticoids. 13,

More recently we have recognized an evolving spectrum of the IIM including more systemic autoimmune disorders with frequent involvement of muscle, lungs, joints, skin, the gastrointestinal (GI) system, and the heart. The myositis disease spectrum has broadened from primary inflammatory muscle disorders including PM, DM, and IBM to encompass newer clinical subgroups such as immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy (IMNM), antisynthetase syndrome, amyopathic DM, and cancer-associated myositis.

This breakthrough is very much based on the identification of new autoantibodies that are highly specific for myositis spectrum disorder and are strongly associated with distinct clinical phenotypes.

### Epidemiology

The annual incidence of IIM may vary in different populations. A recent population-based registry study suggests an incidence rate for IIM, overall, of 11 (13 for women and 9.7 for men) per 1 million person-years in Sweden. Several retrospective studies have reported an annual incidence of less than 10 per million individuals17-21 (Table 86.1). This number may be an underestimate if a positive muscle biopsy was required for diagnosis. Data on prevalence are less. For the IIM all together, the prevalence was 12 to 14 per 100,000 in two recent population-based Scandinavian studies. 16,22

### Incidence of Inflammatory Myopathies

The prevalence of IBM as a separate entity was estimated to be 33 per million in Norway, 10.7 per million in the United States, 9.3 per million in Australia, and 4.9 per million in the Netherlands.23-26 The age-adjusted prevalence of IBM for those older than 50 years was reported as 16 to 35 per million.25, In some geographic areas, IBM appears to be the most common acquired progressive myopathy, representing 16% to 28% of all inflammatory myopathies. However, there may be referral biases in these studies. The incidence-prevalence studies need to be interpreted cautiously, given that most have not reported confidence intervals for their rates.

The incidence of the various IIM subgroups varies according to race, age, and sex. Some studies have reported that the incidence of PM is higher in Black patients than in White patients. IMs can occur in any age group, from early childhood to late in adult life. The onset of PM is usually in the late teens or older; the mean patient age at onset is 50 to 60 years. DM shows two peaks: 5 to 15 years and 45 to 65 years. IBM is commonly seen in individuals older than 50 years and is rare in younger adults. Some studies have reported sex-specific incidence rates. For example, in the case of PM and DM, females are more commonly affected than males (ratio >2:1), whereas in IBM, the converse is true (again, >2:1 ratio). Epidemiology data on the new IIM subgroups are lacking.

Inflammatory myopathies can occur in association with other autoimmune connective tissue diseases such as systemic sclerosis, systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), rheumatoid arthritis (RA), Sjögren's syndrome, mixed connective tissue disease, polyarteritis nodosa, and sarcoidosis. Significant proportions of all patients with myositis (1 1% to 40%) have an associated connective tissue disease.24, Several studies have also confirmed an association between malignancies and inflammatory myopathies. A retrospective study of myositis patients over a 20-year period revealed that myositis in approximately 12% (37/309) of the patients was associated with malignancy. A majority (81%, 30/37) of the patients studied had DM, and the remainder (19%) had PM. Overall, the frequency of malignancies has varied widely (4% to 42%) in different studies18,29 but, in general, the incidence of malignancy is higher in DM patients than in IBM or PM patients. It is difficult to determine the relative risks for a particular malignancy because a variety of malignancies are associated with myositis, and only small numbers of individual malignancies have been reported in any one study.

### Etiology of Myositis

### Genetic Risk Factors

An association with immune response genes and occasional reports of familial clustering of myositis support the role of

genetic factors in these diseases.31-36 Polymorphisms in class I and II human leukocyte antigen (HLA) genes are known genetic risk factors for several autoimmune diseases that include myositis, but the mechanisms for these associations remain unclear. One possibility is that because the gene products influence T cell repertoire development, tolerance, and immune responses to foreign agents, certain polymorphisms are selected on the basis of environmental triggers. It appears that the HLA- DRB1*0301 and HLA-DQA1*0501 alleles are the strongest known genetic risk factors for all forms of myositis in Whites. However, different phenotypes have additional HLA risk and protective factors.36, In Black/African American patients, neither DRB1*0301 nor DQA1*0501 is strongly associated with myositis. Instead, the HLA-DRB1*08 allele shows the highest general risk for myositis, whereas the HLA-DRB1*14 allele is strongly protective in Black/African American patients. The HLA-B8/DR3/DR52/DQ2 haplotype is found in a significant proportion of IBM patients. The risk and protection conferred by HLA associations differ significantly among different racialethnic and serologic groups. For example, in some populations (e.g., Koreans, Mesoamericans), there is no known association with HLA genes. Furthermore, HLA-DRB1*0301, which is a risk factor in Whites, is a protective factor in the Japanese population. The HLA-DRB1*0301, HLA-DQA1*0501, and HLA-DQB1*0201 alleles are strongly associated with myositisspecific antibodies in PM patients. Recent studies identified the HLA-DRB1*0101 and HLA-DRB1*1301 alleles as risk factors for IBM. Mechanistic data supporting the role of HLA molecules in disease pathogenesis are, unfortunately, lacking at present. Some studies reported that maternally derived chimeric cells are present in the peripheral blood and muscle tissues of juvenile dermatomyositis (JDM) patients, suggesting that HLA alleles control the occurrence of chimerism and explain the HLA association found in these disorders.42, Like other autoimmune disease conditions, myositis is a complex multigenic disorder involving other non-HLA immune response genes (e.g., cytokines and receptors, including tumor necrosis factor [TNF], interleukin [IL]-1, and TNF receptor-1); complement components (e.g., C4, C2); immunoglobulin (Ig) heavy-chain allotypes; and T cell receptors. Polymorphisms in other non- HLA genes, such as signal transducer and activator of transcription 4 and C8orf13BLK, appear to contribute prominently in Asian populations.45, Candidate and whole exome sequencing studies have identified that rare variants in VCP, SQSTM1, and FYCO1 genes are associated with IBM, suggesting impaired autophagy as a mechanism of IBM pathogenesis. 47,

A recent study investigating gene copy number (GCN) variations for complement C4 in myositis patients showed that low GCNs for C4T, C4A, and C4L played significant roles in increasing the risk of IIM.

The exact contribution of the genetic component in these disorders is currently unknown, in part because of their rarity, the small number of subjects in any single cohort, and the heterogeneity seen in the disease phenotype. Recent studies have confirmed the major histocompatibility complex (MHC) as the major genetic region associated with DM, JDM, PM, and IBM and some of the autoantibody-defined subgroups in large Caucasian popula- 50, Furthermore, DM also shares non-MHC genetic feations. tures with other autoimmune diseases, suggesting the presence of additional novel risk loci. International collaborative efforts are currently under way to identify novel genetic and environmental risk factors in myositis.

### Environmental Risk Factors

The temporal association of myositis onset and environmental agents in certain individuals suggests that specific exposures in the context of certain genetic backgrounds can initiate muscle inflammation. A number of different environmental agents have been implicated as risk factors in myositis and include infectious organisms, such as viruses and bacteria, and noninfectious agents, including ultraviolet light irradiation, cigarette smoking, drugs, and others (Table 86.2).

### Infections

Recent epidemiology data indicate that infections, in particular infections of the respiratory and GI tracts, are associated with an increased risk of IIM. For example, enteroviruses (influenza,

coxsackievirus, echoviruses) and retroviruses (human T-lymphotropic virus-I) are known to induce muscle inflammation. The myositis associated with enteroviruses usually occurs in children and is generally self-limited. A viral cause is strengthened by the presence of high-titer anti-viral antibodies and viral particles in patients' serum and tissue samples,54,55 as well as the induction of muscle inflammation by enteroviruses in animal models. A more recent association was observed between a previous cytomegalovirus infection and a subphenotype of PM and DM patients with a high frequency of so-called CD28-null T cells, possibly reflecting chronic stimulation (see later), indicating that some viral infections may influence the immune system and lead to chronic inflammation. Similarly, some microorganisms, such as staphylococci, clostridia, and mycobacteria, are known to affect skeletal muscle and cause acute muscle inflammation, but there is no evidence that these organisms actually cause chronic, self-sustaining muscle inflammation.

The recent emergence of myositis as a rare manifestation of COVID-19 has led to increased interest in the etiology, clinical presentation, and treatment challenges associated with this condition. COVID-19-induced myositis can vary widely in its presentation, from typical DM to rhabdomyolysis and back pain. The mechanism underlying virus-mediated muscle inflammation is attributed to angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 receptor—mediated viral entry and affliction of muscle fibers, which leads to innate and adaptive immune activation. Recent research has focused on the similarities between anti—melanoma differentiation-associated protein 5 (MDA5)positive myositis and COVID-19, with the aim of finding common etiopathogenic bases and therapeutic strategies. In addition, during the COVID-19 pandemic, there have been reports of patients developing myositis after receiving vaccination against COVID-19 including rare forms such as anti-MDA5-positive myositis. However, this is an association and the possibility of causation is unclear, especially in the setting of a global vaccination drive.

Parasites such as Toxoplasma gondii, Trypanosoma cruzi, and Borrelia burgdorferi have been implicated in the triggering of IIMs. The evidence in support of a parasitic cause includes the recovery of parasites from some myositis patients and their serologic response to the parasites; improvement in myositis symptoms after treatment with anti-parasitic drugs; a histologic picture of inflammation, including infiltration of macrophages and CD4+ T cells; and induction of myositis after parasitic infection in animal models.59-65

### Ultraviolet Light Irradiation

Ultraviolet (UV) light irradiation is likely to be a risk factor for DM because epidemiologic data have demonstrated a latitude gradient of PM and DM, with the latter more frequent closer to the equator and the former more frequent in northern countries. The ratio between PM and DM is associated with a latitude gradient and is directly correlated with UV light irradiation. This observed correlation is particularly strong in a subset of DM patients with anti-Mi-2 autoantibodies, indicating that UV light may be an environmental risk factor for its development. The association between UV light exposure and the subtype of myositis suggests that UV light is an exogenous modifier that can influence the clinical and serologic phenotype in myositis.66,67

### Cigarette Smoking and Other Inhalant Biohazards

Smoking is a risk factor for a subtype of myositis, the anti-Jo-1 positive (one of the anti-synthetase syndromes—see the section on autoantibodies), and has a possible interaction with the

HLA-DRB1*03 genotype. Environmental and occupational agents such as dust, gases, or fumes are also reported risk factors for patients' systemic autoimmune diseases, including PM or DM, as reported in rescue and recovery workers after 9/11 as well as in patients with anti-synthetase syndrome.69, These inhaled risk factors, together with the high frequency of interstitial lung disease (ILD) as a manifestation of the anti-synthetase syndromes, indicate a role for the lung as a target of the immune reaction in this subset of myositis.

### Drugs

Commonly used lipid-lowering drugs such as statins (e.g., atorvastatin, lovastatin) can cause an autoimmune myopathy. Statins inhibit 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-coenzyme A (HMG-CoA) reductase, a rate-limiting enzyme involved in the conversion of HMG-CoA to mevalonic acid, thereby preventing the synthesis of bioactive sterol and nonsterol metabolic intermediates in the cholesterol synthetic pathway. The mechanism by which these drugs cause an autoimmune myopathy is not yet clear.71-73 Patients with anti-3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA reductase (HMGCR) antibodies often have prominent myofiber necrosis with little or no muscle inflammation, also referred to as IMNM. It has been suggested that statins upregulate HMG- CoA autoantigen in regenerating muscle cells that, in turn, sustain an autoimmune response even after statin withdrawal, providing a mechanism for statin-induced IMNM. However, recent studies have indicated that some IMNM patients with anti-HMGCR antibody are statin-naive, indicating other potential triggers for this disorder75 (see details in "Immune- Mediated Necrotizing Myopathy"). The autoimmune form of statin myopathy requires immunosuppressive therapy as with other forms of IIM.

A more recent family of drugs that has been demonstrated to induce inflammatory myopathies is the new cancer therapies, immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs). ICIs enhance the immune system's ability to attack cancer cells by blocking inhibitory immune checkpoints. Although ICIs have shown remarkable efficacy in the treatment of several malignancies, they are also associated with immune-related adverse events that can affect various organs and tissues, including skeletal muscles (see Chapter 130). Cases with symptoms and signs indicating an inflammatory myopathy have been reported, ranging from myalgia to a severe course with pronounced muscle weakness with inflammation and muscle fiber necrosis evident in muscle biopsies. These patients rarely present with autoantibodies associated with myositis. The diagnosis of ICI-induced myositis requires a thorough evaluation of clinical, laboratory, and imaging findings and exclusion of other causes of myositis. A recent study using transcriptomic profiling identified three distinct types of ICI-induced myositis that the authors termed ICI-DM, ICI-MYO1, and ICI-MYO2: (1) the IL-6 pathway was overexpressed in all groups of myositis, (2) the type I interferon (IFN) pathway activation was specific for ICI- DM, and (3) the type 2 IFN pathway was overexpressed in both ICI-DM and ICI-MYO1.77 Treatment involves prompt cessation of the offending ICI and initiation of immunosuppressive therapy with glucocorticoids and other immunosuppressive agents. Overall, ICI-induced myositis is a rare but serious complication of cancer immunotherapy that requires a high index of suspicion and prompt management to minimize morbidity and mortality.

TNF inhibitors have been associated with the onset of autoimmune diseases such as vasculitis and a lupus-like syndrome. Recent reports have suggested that TNF inhibitors in inflammatory

arthritis patients may either induce or exacerbate DM or anti-Jo- 1-positive PM.78,79

### Malignancy

Malignancy is an additional risk factor for myositis, and there is a strong association between DM and malignancies. This early clinical observation has been confirmed in epidemiologic studies.29, With regard to PM and IBM, the association with malignancy is less convincing. The increased risk of malignancy associated with DM has been established both at the time of DM diagnosis and more than 10 years after diagnosis. A subgroup of DM has been named cancer-associated DM. Cancer-associated DM is often used to classify patients with DM with a detected cancer within 3 years before or after DM diagnosis, although the time span between the malignancy and DM varies between studies. No specific malignancy is associated with DM; rather, the most frequent malignancies are also the most common malignancies in the population.

The pathophysiologic mechanism for the association between malignancy and DM has not been clarified, but there could be several explanations. The strong association between malignancy and the onset of DM, the observation that removal of a tumor sometimes results in amelioration of muscle weakness, and the fact that tumor reappearance sometimes coincides with muscle weakness suggests that DM could be a paraneoplastic phenomenon. That is, the development of myositis is a consequence of the malignancy (related to autoantigens), or the malignancy and DM share disease mechanisms. The molecular mechanisms underlying this unique association are currently unclear, however. A recent report has shed some light on the connection between DM and malignancy by showing that myositis-specific antigens are highly expressed in cancer tissues and in regenerating muscle cells of myositis patients.81, It has been proposed that in cancer-associated myositis, an autoimmune response directed against cancer cross-reacts with regenerating muscle cells, enabling a feed-forward loop of tissue damage and antigen selection. This is further supported by the association between malignancy-associated DM and two newly identified myositis-specific autoantibodies (TIF1-γ and NXP2) in adult patients (see the paragraph on myositis autoantibodies). Moreover, a wider immune response with more than one autoantibody seemed to protect patients with anti-TIF1-γ from development of overt cancer. For malignancies that develop during established disease, the potential explanations include the presence of chronic inflammation or prolonged immunosuppressive treatment, which could contribute to the development of malignancy.

### Comorbidities

Associations of myositis with hypertension, diabetes, and ischemic heart disease have been reported. The prevalence of hypertension and diabetes in this population was 62% and 29%, respectively, considerably higher than the background prevalence of 9.4% and 4%. The authors of this report suggest that hypertension and ischemic heart disease are more likely to be present before the diagnosis of myositis, whereas hypertension and diabetes occur more frequently following the diagnosis of myositis in patients with DM than in patients with PM or IBM, suggesting that it is essential for the physician to perform a comprehensive assessment of possible comorbidity as these conditions may predispose to IIM risk. The same group also reported that patients with IIM are at a 75% increased risk for mortality, and cardiovascular diseases

followed by infection and malignancy account for the most common causes of death.

Cataloging genetic and environmental risk and protective factors in well-defined disease phenotypes is an important first step for discovering gene—environment interactions that could lead to preventive strategies.

### Pathogenesis

Significant advances have been made in our understanding of the pathogenesis of the human inflammatory myopathies.87-92 It is generally thought that IIMs are autoimmune in origin because they are frequently associated with other autoimmune diseases (e.g., Hashimoto's thyroiditis, scleroderma) and many patients exhibit an autoantibody response, including the presence of myositis-specific autoantibodies associated with specific clinical phenotypes. The development of extramuscular organ manifestations such as ILD, arthritis, or skin rash as the first clinical manifestations in many patients has also brought up the possibility that the immune reaction may actually start at sites other than the skeletal muscle. Although we can now identify clinical subgroups of myositis based on autoantibody profiles, most of the studies reflecting molecular pathogenesis have so far been performed in patients classified as having PM, DM, or IBM and these "older" subgroups are referred to in the paragraphs on pathogenesis.

### Humoral Immune Response

More than 50% of all IIM patients have uniquely defined autoantibodies, some of which are specific to myositis and some of which are merely associated with myositis. These are generally referred to as myositis-specific autoantibodies (MSAs) and myositis-associated autoantibodies (MAAs), respectively. MAAs include autoantibodies to various nuclear and cytoplasmic antigens. Anti-nuclear antibodies present in myositis are not particularly associated with any disease subgroup, whereas MSAs that are directed against antigens of the protein synthesis pathway (e.g., aminoacyltransfer RNA [tRNA] synthetases and signal recognition particles) and nuclear components (e.g., nuclear helicase [Mi-2]) are often associated with distinct clinical disease groups and subgroups (e.g., tRNA synthetases with ILD, Mi-2 with DM) (Table 86.3). These autoantibodies are sometimes present before the onset of clinical disease.

Anti-histidyl-tRNA synthetase (Jo-1) antibodies are the most frequent MSA seen and are present in approximately 16% to 20% of patients with IIM and in about 90% in patients with IIM and ILD.94-97 Antibodies against other aminoacyl- tRNA synthetases—such as threonyl-tRNA synthetase (PL-7), alanyl-tRNA synthetase (PL-12), isoleucyl-tRNA synthetase (OJ), glycyl-tRNA synthetase (EJ), asparaginyl-tRNA synthetase (KS), tyrosyl-tRNA synthetase (Ha), and phenylalanyl- tRNA synthetase (Zo)—are found less frequently (1% to 5%). Anti-Mi-2 antibodies are strongly associated with DM,98,99 with prominent features such as Gottron's papules, heliotrope rash, the V sign, and the shawl sign. Anti-TIF1-γ and anti- NXP2 are associated with cancer-related DM in adults and with JDM.100-102 Anti-MDA5 antibodies are associated with clinically amyopathic DM and rapidly progressive ILD in the Asian population, whereas the clinical phenotype is less specific in Caucasians.

An individual usually has only one MSA because they are often mutually exclusive. MSAs are infrequent or absent in IBM

patients. Recent studies have found that IBM patients have antibodies targeting muscle proteins, such as cytosolic 50-nucleotidase 1A, found in one-third of IBM patients.104, Another antibody reactivity found in patients with IBM targets desmin. Other recently described autoantibodies include anti-cortactin antibodies present in patients with PM, DM, and IMNM but not with IBM.

Another autoantibody targeting a muscle-specific antigen is anti-FHL1, which is present in up to 20% of patients with IIM but can also be detected in patients with systemic sclerosis. The anti-FHL1 autoantibody may be detected in patients who are negative for other MSAs, suggesting additional diagnostic value; however, an assay for autoantibody measurement is not yet commercially available.

MAAs such as anti-PM-Scl are frequently associated with a characteristic overlap syndrome that includes features of systemic sclerosis. This syndrome is characterized by muscle disease, prominent arthritis, and limited skin involvement; it frequently responds to immunomodulating therapy. Some myositis patients also have other MAAs, such as anti-snRNP, anti-Ro/ SSA, anti-Ku, and anti-PMS1. Some of the MSAs and MAAs show strong immunogenetic associations; for example, antibodies against aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases are associated with HLA- DQA1*0501, anti-Jo-1 with HLA-DRB1*03, anti-SRP with DR5, anti-Mi-2 with DR7, and anti-PM-Scl with DR3, suggesting a role of the adaptive immune system in the pathogenesis of these myositis subgroups, as a major role of the class II HLA molecules is to present antigens to T cells. Likewise, HLA-DRB1 alleles (DRB1*1101) have been found to be associated with an elevated risk for anti-HMGCR-positive statin-induced myopathy. These antibodies serve as excellent clinical markers and can help diagnose and categorize these heterogeneous disorders into homogeneous subgroups.

### Cell-Mediated Immune Response

The cellular immune response has mainly been investigated in muscle tissue and in peripheral blood of patients with IIM. T cells and macrophages generally predominate muscle infiltrates in myositis. Cytokines produced by these T cell subsets induce macrophages to polarize into pro-inflammatory M1 (classic) or proresolution M2 (alternative) phenotypes. M1 macrophages infiltrate the muscle in the early stages to help clear necrotic debris, whereas M2 macrophages arrive later to sustain tissue healing. The relative proportion of lymphocytes and macrophages in skeletal muscle seems to vary in different clinical entities; for example, in anti-HMGCR myopathy, M2 macrophages predominate over CD4+ and CD8+ T cells and CD123+ plasmacytoid dendritic cells (DCs). The presence of M2 macrophages is consistent with

the known role of macrophages in skeletal muscle regeneration. At the cellular level, there are distinct differences in the distribution and location of the various lymphocyte subsets in the muscle tissues in different IIMs. Two major patterns of inflammatory cell infiltrates are seen in muscle tissue. The first is a predominantly perivascular distribution, often in perimysial areas (Fig. 86.1Å and C), and is largely made up of CD4+ T cells, macrophages, and DCs. Occasionally, B cells are present in some patients. This pattern is seen mainly in patients with DM who have skin rash, but occasionally in patients without a rash. Recent studies also indicate that different autoantibody patterns seem to be associated with different histopathologic features in IIMs. The second pattern has a predominantly endomysial distribution (Fig. 86.1B), with mononuclear inflammatory cells often surrounding and sometimes invading nonnecrotic muscle fibers. These inflammatory cellular infiltrates are composed primarily of CD8+ T cells and macrophages, but CD4+ T cells and DCs are also present. This pattern is generally seen in patients without skin rashes and often in those with PM or IBM. In some patients, the two patterns of inflammation are seen in the same biopsy. The two distinct locations and the varying compositions of the inflammatory cell populations in the two areas suggest two different pathogenic mechanisms—one that targets the blood vessels and one that targets the muscle fibers.

The vascular involvement in patients with DM is also manifested in the skin and can be seen clinically in the form of nailfold changes and changes in the GI tract. The capillaries show clear hyperplasia, vacuolization, and necrosis, contributing to an ischemia that could cause fiber damage. 115, One of the earliest events in the pathogenesis of DM appears to be activation of the complement cascade. This activation leads to the subsequent deposition of complement components, which in turn results in the deposition of lytic membrane attack complexes in endothelial cells and the eventual loss of capillaries from complement-mediated damage. The capillaries are

abnormally thickened and enlarged and look like high endothelial venules, which are characteristics of vessels that facilitate lymphocyte trafficking (Fig. 86.2). The capillaries also show signs of neovascularization. This loss of capillaries results in some of the histopathologic features characteristic of this disease: capillary necrosis and loss, perivascular inflammation and ischemia (rarely seen), and perifascicular atrophy (a late feature; see Fig. 86.1C and D). Recent studies also point to a role for type I IFN-inducible genes in the pathogenesis of DM. Plasmacytoid DCs produce type I IFN and induce expression of IFN-inducible proteins such as MxA and IFN-inducible gene 15 in the perifascicular myofibers and capillaries of DM biopsies, suggesting that injury to muscle fibers and capillaries occurs as a result of the intra-cellular overproduction of one or more type I IFN-inducible proteins in DM.118, The factors that initiate complement activation in this disease are poorly understood. However, the consequences of complement-mediated damage are clearly visible in DM. Recent studies have provided evidence that type I IFN-mediated innate immunity is linked to the expression of innate immune receptors such as Toll-like receptors (TLRs) (e.g., TLR-3, TLR-7, and TLR- 9). Other studies have found that class I MHC-expressing immature muscle precursors can serve as a source of type I IFN, IFN-β, in myositis. In vitro experiments have indicated that TLR-3-induced IFN-β, in combination with IFN-γ, increases the expression of class I MHC molecules, suggesting a link between the innate and adaptive immune systems in myositis.

The endomysial inflammatory aggregates contain a high percentage of T cells, particularly activated CD8+ T cells, macrophages, and CD4+ T cells, and few natural killer cells. Immunoelectron microscopic studies have provided evidence of the invasion, replacement, and probable destruction of nonnecrotic muscle fibers by T cells and macrophages. Infiltrating cytolytic T lymphocyte cells (CTLs) express perforin-containing granules, which are characteristically oriented toward the target muscle fiber, indicating that muscle fiber injury may be partially mediated by perforin-dependent cytotoxic mechanisms (Fig. 86.3B and C). In PM and IBM, there is evidence of clonal proliferation of CD8+ T cells, both within the muscle and in the peripheral circulation. 124, T cell lines from patients demonstrate cytotoxicity against autologous myotubes, ,126 suggesting that the muscle fiber injury in PM and IBM is mediated by CTLs. CTLs are known to mediate target cell damage by both the perforin-granzyme B and Fas-FasL pathways. The overexpression of anti-apoptotic

molecules—such as Bcl-2, Fas-associated death domain-like IL-1 converting enzyme inhibitory protein, and human inhibitor of apoptosis protein—like protein—in the skeletal muscle of myositis patients suggests that perforin-granzyme B-mediated CTL damage may play a predominant role in muscle fiber injury and dysfunction in myositis.127-129

In contrast to previous findings, recent studies have also shown accumulation of B cells, plasma cells, myeloid DCs, late-activated macrophages expressing the 25F9 marker, and CD8+ CD28and CD4+ CD28- T cells (TCR V[β]-expanded T cells) in the skeletal muscle and peripheral circulation of patients with PM, DM, and IBM. These CD28cells and late-activated macrophages expressing 25F9 are thought to exhibit cytotoxic potential and produce pro-inflammatory cytokines in IIM skeletal muscle. 130, The role of FOXP3 expressing regulatory T (Treg) cells and the effect of these cells on inflamed muscle indicated these regulatory cells counterbalance muscle damage by cytotoxic T cells in IIM.132, Peripheral immune topography of IIM samples using a highdimensional flow cytometry approach suggests that DM samples display alterations of the B cell compartment, anti-synthetase syndrome samples show perturbations in CD4/T helper compartment, and CD8+ T cells alterations distinguishes IBM from other IIM.

On the basis of the data described, two different pathways have been proposed as major mediators of muscle damage and inflammation: one mediated through CTLs directed against muscle fibers, predominating in PM and IBM, and the other directed against vessels, predominating in DM and in anti-synthetase syndrome. However, the degree of inflammation is not consistently correlated with the severity of the structural changes in the muscle fibers or with the severity of the clinical disease, suggesting that nonimmune processes also play a role in disease pathogenesis. A role for nonimmune processes is supported by the following observations. First, marked structural changes in the muscle fibers occur in the absence of any inflammatory cells.135, Second, there is a lack of correlation between the degree of inflammation and the degree of muscle weakness.' 137 Third, some myositis patients do not respond even to powerful anti-inflammatory therapy. 138, Fourth, steroid treatment may eliminate inflammatory cells in myositis muscle tissue, but this removal alone may not substantially improve the clinical disease, suggesting that immunosuppressive therapies modulate disease activity but do not change other mediators of the disease pro- 140 0 Finally, the clinical disease may progress when identifiable cess. inflammation has subsided, 141 suggesting a role for nonimmune mechanisms in the pathogenesis of myositis. Thus the exact

contribution of immune-mediated pathways to muscle damage is currently unknown.

### Class I Major Histocompatibility Complex Expression

Normal skeletal muscle cells do not constitutively express or display class I MHC molecules, although they can be induced to do so by pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IFN-γ or TNF135,142- 144 or by the alarmin high-mobility group box 1 (HMGB1). In contrast, in IIMs, the early and widespread appearance of class I MHC in nonnecrotic muscle cells is a striking feature, even in muscle cells distant from areas of lymphocytic infiltra- .135, Class I MHC staining is usually observed on the tion. sarcolemma of muscle fibers, but some fibers also show staining in both the sarcolemma and the sarcoplasm (Fig. 86.3A and B). In some patients, expression is restricted to a few clusters (often early in the disease), whereas in others, almost every fiber is positively stained, particularly in late-phase and treatment-resistant cases. Researchers have explored the biologic significance of these observations by generating a conditional transgenic mouse model overexpressing syngeneic mouse class I MHC. The overexpression of class I MHC molecules in the skeletal muscle of mice results in the development of clinical, biochemical, histologic, and immunologic features that resemble human myositis and provides a close model of the human disease. The disease in these mice is inflammatory, limited to skeletal muscle, self-sustaining, more severe in females, and often accompanied by MSAs. Recent studies in this model further suggest that class I MHC overexpression leads to endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress, muscle atrophy, and a decrease in the force generation capacity of skeletal muscle, suggesting a role for class I MHC in the development of myositisassociated weakness.92,

A number of observations in human myositis patients and in the mouse model of myositis suggest that class I MHC molecules

mediate muscle fiber damage and dysfunction in the absence of lymphocytes. For instance, in human myositis, the induction of class I MHC antigen in muscle fibers occurs early, preceding inflammatory cell infiltration.149, Class I MHC staining of human myositis biopsies shows both a cell surface and a sarcoplasmic reticulum pattern of internal reactivity, demonstrating that some of the class I MHC molecules may be retained in the ER of these fibers.92, Persistent class I MHC overexpression in muscle fibers can exist in the absence of an inflammatory infiltrate. The controlled induction of class I MHC in the mouse model is followed by muscle weakness before mononuclear cell infiltration. Researchers have recently shown that in vivo gene transfer of class I MHC plasmids attenuates muscle regeneration and differentiation. Together, these observations, and particularly the obvious retention of class I MHC within the cell in both human and murine disease, indicate that the muscle fiber damage seen in myositis may not be solely mediated by immune attack (e.g., CTLs, autoantibodies) but may also be mediated through nonimmunologic mechanisms such as the ER stress response and hypoxia. Activation of ER stress in cells is linked to the induction of different forms of cell death such as autophagy and apoptosis. The expression of molecules that facilitate autophagy (TNF-related apoptosis-inducing ligand [TRAIL]) and apoptosis (TNF-like weak inducer of apoptosis) were increased in myositis patients, providing a molecular basis for progressive muscle damage in myositis. 153,

In myositis, it appears that overexpression of class I MHC in myofibers initiates a series of cell-autonomous changes that contribute to myofiber pathology. Recent investigations have indicated that overexpression of class I MHC on muscle fibers results in the activation of the nuclear factor-kB (NF-kB) and ER stress response pathways in human inflammatory myopathies and in the mouse model of myositis.92, NF-kB can be activated within minutes by a variety of stimuli, including inflammatory cytokines such as TNF and IL-1, T cell activation signals, and

stress inducers. It is likely that in human myositis, NF-kB activates both classic (pro-inflammatory cytokines) and nonclassic (ER stress response) pathways.92, Furthermore, there is evidence that downstream target genes (e.g., class I MHC, intercellular adhesion molecule, monocyte chemoattractant protein-1) regulated by the NF-kB pathway are highly upregulated in myo- .151, Studies have indicated that NF-kB p65 sitis patients. is activated both in human myositis biopsies and in the mouse model, 92,155,161,162 suggesting that this pathway may be directly involved in muscle fiber damage (Fig. 86.4).

### Cytokines and Hypoxia

A number of other effector molecules produced in muscle tissue by inflammatory cells, endothelial cells, and muscle fibers are thought to play a role in the pathogenesis of myositis. Most of the data assembled relate to cytokines, but some data related to chemokines are also available. The most consistently demonstrated cytokines in muscle tissue from patients with IIMs are cytokines with pro-inflammatory properties: IL-1α, IL-1β, TNF, and IFN- α. Recently IL-10, IL-13, IL-18, epidermal growth factor, vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), fibroblast growth factor, CCL3 (macrophage inflammatory protein [MIP-1α]), CCL4 (MIP-1β), CCL11 (eotaxin), IL-15, and IL-15Rα were also demonstrated to be significantly upregulated, and granulocyte colony-stimulating factor to be downregulated in patients with IIMs compared with unaffected individuals.163, Also, DNA-binding HMGB1 was found to exhibit both extranuclear and extra-cellular patterns in the muscle tissue of patients with PM and DM. Stimulation with IFN-γ showed an increased HMGB1 expression in muscle nuclei and myoplasm. Exposure to HMGB1 induced a reversible upregulation of class I MHC in the muscle fibers and an irreversible decrease in Ca2+ release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum during fatigue, suggesting a role for HMGB1 and class I MHC early in the pathogenesis of IIMs. In addition to inducing the upregulation of class I and II MHC molecules on muscle fibers, cytokines can have a direct effect on muscle fiber function, as has been demonstrated for TNF.

The relative importance of the various cytokines and chemokines in patients with myositis is still uncertain, but these molecules are potential biomarker candidates in this disease, as has been indicated by a recent study showing that serum IL-6

production and the type I IFN gene signature in the peripheral blood are correlated with disease activity in patients with DM. Studies provide evidence on how pro-inflammatory cytokines such as TNF decrease myogenic miRNAs (e.g., miR-1, miR-133a, miR-133b, and miR-206) and facilitate muscle degeneration in myositis. Furthermore, studies using experimental models show that inflammatory miRNAs (miR-146a, miR-142-3p, miR- 142-5p, miR-455-3p, and miR-455-5p) and dystrophin-targeting miRNAs (miR-146a, miR-146b, miR-31, and miR-223) decrease dystrophin protein on muscle fibers, suggesting an acquired dystrophin deficiency may occur through NF-kB-regulated miRNAs in myositis, thereby suggesting muscle injury, inflammation, and weakness are perpetuated in myositis.

Microvessel involvement was first observed in DM but has also become evident in PM. Endothelial cells in both subsets show increased expression of adhesion molecules and pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-1α. This phenotype can be induced by tissue hypoxia, which may result from capillary loss and local tissue inflammation. Muscle tissue hypoxia can contribute to clinical symptoms and muscle fatigue and may be associated with disease mechanisms in inflammatory myopathies. The expression of VEGF receptor in muscle fibers and hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF)-2α reactivity in the endothelial cells of patients with PM and IBM support a role for hypoxia in these conditions. Patients with DM showed HIF-1α and HIF-1β expression in endothelial cells, whereas expression of HIF-2α, erythropoietin receptor, VEGF, and VEGF-R were also observed on muscle fibers. These observations suggest that deprivation of blood supply by immunemediated mechanisms could trigger the upregulation of hypoxiarelated proteins as an adaptive response. In addition, magnetic resonance spectroscopic analysis, before and after a workload, has demonstrated reduced levels of energy substrates that are important for muscle contraction, such as adenosine triphosphate and phosphocreatine, compared with the levels in healthy individuals. This finding supports the hypothesis that an acquired metabolic disturbance occurs in chronic inflammatory myopathies and that this disturbance can contribute to impaired muscle performance.

Microarrays have provided considerable new insight into DM. Early on, mRNA profiling in DM showed a predominance of type I IFN-responsive pathways, suggesting the possible persistence of an anti-viral response. Particularly prevalent was the dramatic expression of the IFN-inducible MxA gene. This signature was

confirmed and extended,118 supporting an important role of the innate immune response, with prominent plasmacytoid DC infiltration in DM compared with the other inflammatory myopathies. Recent evidence has demonstrated high levels of type I IFN and genes induced by type I IFNs (IFN signature) not only in the skeletal muscle but also in the skin and blood of patients. 118, Some studies have shown that the levels of IFN signature genes observed correlated with disease activity. 171, The molecular mechanism associated with type 1 IFN-induced muscle weakness is not fully understood but there is some evidence that IFN-β can induce reactive oxygen species and mitochondrial damage in myositis muscle, suggesting a potential link to the cause of the functional impairment of muscle bioenergetics in these disorders.

### Summary of Proposed Mechanisms of Muscle Damage

Currently available data suggest that both immune (cell-mediated and humoral) and nonimmune (ER stress, hypoxia) mechanisms play a role in muscle fiber damage and dysfunction in myositis. Innate immune cell activation occurs as a result of injury to skeletal muscle, resulting in the release of damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs). TLR signaling activates various antigen-presenting cells (APCs) in the muscle. These APCs then activate CD4 T cells and initiate autoantigen-specific T cell responses and autoantibody responses. Class I MHC overexpression on muscle also leads to the activation of CD8+ T cell-mediated cytotoxicity. DAMPs bind to surface or endogenous TLRs expressed in muscle-infiltrating immune cells, capillaries, and fibroblasts. TLR signaling activates NF-kB and inflammasomes, resulting in the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines, chemokines, and adhesion molecules. Cytokines such as TNF can directly induce the death of muscle cells and also effectively inhibit myogenesis through microRNAs. TLR signaling also leads to inflammasome activation (leading to IL-1 secretion) and, potentially, to induction of pyroapoptosis in the affected muscle, whereas activation of TRAIL induces autophagy in the muscle. Recent studies using patient muscle samples and experimental models of myositis describe necroptosis, a caspase-independent form of cell death that can create pores in the plasma membrane that enable the influx of calcium or sodium ions, leading to the bursting of the cell, leakage of cellular contents and, eventually, necroptosis. Unknown cytokines reduce the expression of rate-limiting enzymes of the purine nucleotide cycle and of adenosine monophosphate deaminase (AMPD)1 in skeletal muscle. This acquired deficiency of

AMPD1 is likely to cause muscle weakness and fatigue in patients with myositis. In addition, class I MHC accumulation in the ER induces the ER stress response in muscle. Thus several immune, nonimmune, and metabolic pathways directly and indirectly contribute to muscle weakness and damage in myositis. The relative contribution of each of these pathways to muscle fiber damage is presently unclear (Fig. 86.5). Therefore the use of specific drugs to inhibit these pathways, either alone or in combination, would help define their roles in myositis and potentially show them to be effective therapeutic agents.

### Clinical Features

IIMs can be subgrouped based on differences in clinical, serologic and histopathological features into DM, clinically amyopathic DM, anti-synthetase syndrome, IMNM, IBM, and PM. The inflammatory myopathies most commonly occur as distinct disease entities as discussed below; however, myositis can sometimes coexist with other rheumatic conditions, and are then called overlap myositis. The rheumatic diseases most often associated with inflammatory myopathies are systemic sclerosis, Sjögren's syndrome, mixed connective tissue disease, and SLE; however, RA may also be associated with inflammatory myopathies. IBM may be associated with Sjögren's syndrome, SLE, and other autoimmune diseases. The clinical features of IIM are discussed in detail in the following section, and subsequently distinctive clinical features of the subsets of IIM are discussed, including DM, anti-synthetase syndrome, clinically amyopathic DM, IBM, and IMNM. Notably, with the identification of IMNM and anti-synthetase syndrome, the new PM subgroup has become less frequent, is often seronegative, and requires further clinical and histopathological characterization.

### Muscle Symptoms

The predominant symptoms in most patients with IIM are muscle weakness and low muscle endurance. The weakness is most pronounced in proximal muscle groups—typically in the neck, pelvic area, thigh, and shoulder muscles—with a symmetric distribution. Patients generally experience more problems with performing repetitive movements than with single-strength exercises, and they report difficulty walking uphill or upstairs, working with their arms above their shoulders, or rising from chairs. Also, in severe cases, distal muscles may be involved, affecting grip strength and more severely impacting health-related quality of life. The

onset of muscle weakness is often subacute, occurring during a few weeks, or it can be insidious, developing during several months. If untreated, the muscle weakness slowly progresses and, in the most severe cases, patients may become wheelchair-dependent. Problems with swallowing and nutrition can occur as a result of impaired contractility of the throat muscles (dysphagia), potentially leading to aspiration pneumonia. In rare cases, patients experience difficulty breathing because of weakness of the diaphragm or thoracic muscles and may require assisted ventilation.

### Skin

DM is characterized by the presence of certain types of characteristic rashes. The most specific skin manifestations are Gottron's papules and the heliotrope rash (Fig. 86.6). Gottron's papules are slightly elevated, violaceous, pink, or dusky red papules located over the dorsal side of the metacarpophalangeal or interphalangeal joints. These papules may also occur over the extensor side of the wrist, elbow, or knee joints. Gottron's papules are considered to be pathognomonic of DM. A macular rash (without papules) with the same distribution as Gottron's papules is called Gottron's sign (Fig. 86.6C and D). The heliotrope rash is a periorbital red or violaceous erythema of one or both eyelids, often with edema (Fig. 86.6B). Linear erythema overlying the extensor surfaces of joints is also relatively specific to DM (Fig. 86.7A). Many patients with DM have photosensitive rashes, typically found over the neck and upper chest (the so-called V sign) or the face or scalp, although this rash is not specific to DM (Fig. 86.7B and C). Another common rash in DM is located over the upper back and shoulders (shawl sign; Fig. 86.7D) or over the hips and thigh (holster sign). Pruritus is a common problem in DM and can sometimes be severe. Patients with DM often have skin lesions on their fingers, such as periungual erythema, nailfold telangiectasias, and cuticular overgrowth (Fig. 86.8), and this development can even lead to digital ulceration. Other less common skin manifestations are panniculitis, livedo reticularis, and nonscarring alopecia. Poikiloderma is characterized by hypoand hyperpigmentation and is often seen

in later phases of disease. Vasculitis may be seen in children with DM but only rarely in adults.

In general, skin rashes are mild to moderate in severity, with local erythema. In rare cases, a severe, diffuse erythema (erythroderma) can occur, occasionally with vesiculobullous lesions or ulcers. Skin rashes can precede the muscle symptoms by months or even years and, in some patients, the skin manifestations may be the only clinical sign of DM. This condition is often called clinically amyopathic DM or DM sine myositis (see the following text).

The pattern of the rash over the knuckles and dorsum of the hand is distinct in SLE and DM. The rash in DM generally spares the phalanges but affects the knuckles, whereas in SLE the rash is located over the phalanges but the knuckles are spared (Fig. 86.8A and B). However, no histopathologic skin features are specific for DM; most of the features are also seen in patients with SLE. Thus skin biopsy is rarely helpful in distinguishing between these two disorders. The cutaneous manifestations may fail to respond to immunosuppressive treatment, despite improvement in muscle symptoms. Thus it is possible that different molecular pathways or disease mechanisms cause the skin rash and the muscle inflammation.

Calcinosis, which can be severe, is found mainly in JDM but is occasionally seen in adults. Calcinosis occurs predominantly in sites that have been subject to friction or trauma, such as the elbows or knees. Sometimes calcinosis can be extensive and erupt, leading to ulcers. It is most often localized to the subcutaneous tissue but can also develop in the skin, fascia, or muscle and can be visualized by radiography, computed tomography (CT), or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Calcinosis seems to progress as long as there is active inflammatory disease. Also, once it has developed, it is often treatment resistant. Some data, however, suggest that calcinosis progression can be inhibited by effectively treating the inflammatory process in the skin and muscle.

Another type of skin pathology seen in inflammatory myopathies is called mechanic's hands. This rash is often associated with the presence of anti-synthetase autoantibodies and can be seen in

both PM and DM. The rash is a hyperkeratotic, scaling, fissuring of the fingers, particularly on the radial side of the index fingers (Fig. 86.9).

### Lungs

Lung involvement is frequent (30% to 40%) in PM and DM and is evident in up to 80% of patients with anti-synthetase syndrome, serving as a major cause of morbidity and mortality in these disorders. Clinical symptoms such as dyspnea and cough are common. Lung involvement can be caused by weakness of the respiratory muscles or inflammation of the lung tissue (ILD). Weakness of respiratory muscles may lead to restrictive lung disease, and involvement of the pharyngeal muscles is a risk factor for aspiration pneumonia. ILD, caused by inflammation at the alveolar level, is common in PM and DM and is more strongly associated with anti-synthetase (70% to 80% ILD) and anti-MDA5 (50% to 80% ILD) autoantibodies. ILD is diagnosed using sensitive techniques such as high-resolution CT of chest and measurement of pulmonary function and diffusion capacity. In most cases, the changes are present at the time of diagnosis of myositis, but ILD can precede development of clinical myositis and sometimes develop after immunosuppressive treatment has been started for myositis. In most cases, the ILD is mild to moderate and has a slowly progressive course. Anti-synthetase and anti-MDA5 autoantibodies are strongly associated with ILD, and thus serve as biomarkers for this extramuscular manifestation. ILD, especially in patients with anti- MDA5 and sometimes in anti-synthetase syndrome, can be rapidly progressive, leading to death, hospitalization, or supplemental oxygen requirement within a few months of disease onset.

In general, the clinical course and histopathology of ILD in myositis is similar to those in idiopathic ILD. However, response to immunosuppression and prognosis is generally more favorable compared with idiopathic forms of ILD such as idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. The most common histopathologic findings are nonspecific interstitial pneumonia (NSIP), usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP), cryptogenic organizing pneumonia (COP), and diffuse alveolar damage (DAD). Some studies suggest that NSIP and COP respond favorably to corticosteroids and immunosuppression, whereas histopathologic changes compatible with DAD or UIP show less robust responses and have a poor prognosis.

### Arthritis

Joint pain and arthritis are common in patients with PM, DM, and anti-synthetase syndrome, and can sometimes be a presenting feature. The most common form of arthritis is a symmetric arthritis of the small joints of the hands and feet, and therefore it can mimic RA. This arthritis is typically nonerosive but can sometimes be erosive and destructive. Most frequently, arthritis is seen in patients with anti-Jo-1 antibodies and other anti-synthetase autoantibodies, but it is also seen in patients with anti-MDA5 autoantibodies and in overlapping syndromes of other rheumatic diseases.

### Heart

Cardiovascular disease is a risk factor for death among patients with IIM. However, clinically evident heart involvement is rare, perhaps indicating that cardiac involvement may be overlooked in these conditions. Subclinical manifestations are frequently

discovered when patients with IIM are formally evaluated for an underlying cardiac disorder. The most frequently reported subclinical manifestations are conduction abnormalities and arrhythmias detected by electrocardiogram (ECG), and subclinical cardiomyopathies are common when cardiac MRI is performed, even in patients thought to be in remission. The underlying pathophysiologic mechanisms that can lead to cardiac manifestations in patients with IIM are myocarditis and coronary artery disease and involvement of the small vessels of the myocardium. Pulmonary hypertension may occasionally be seen, particularly in patients with anti-synthetase syndrome.

Examination with ECG is recommended in patients newly diagnosed with IIM. Serum tests such as creatine kinase—myocardial band (CK-MB) to detect cardiac involvement are unreliable in patients with inflammatory myopathies because CK-MB can be released from regenerating skeletal muscle fibers, a common feature in biopsies from patients with IIM. The CK-MB/total CK ratio may be greater than 3%, a threshold value that is used to define myocardial damage. A more specific marker for myocardial damage in myositis patients is increased serum levels of cardiac isoform troponin I. The other cardiac troponin isoforms, troponin C and troponin T, are less specific and are also expressed in adult skeletal muscle; increased serum levels have been reported in various muscle disorders.

### Gastrointestinal Tract

Difficulty swallowing is frequent in patients with inflammatory myopathies, particularly those with IBM and severe cases of DM, IMNM, and PM. Muscle weakness occasionally becomes severe and causes problems with nutrition and aspiration pneumonia. Pathophysiology is related to weakness in the tongue, pharyngeal muscles, and sometimes the lower esophagus. Reflux that requires special care is common, occurring in 15% to 50% of patients. Constipation, diarrhea, and stomach pain are less frequent symptoms and may result from disturbed motility of the gut or GI tract inflammation. Vasculitis in the blood vessels of the GI tract is rare but may be complicated by intestinal bleeding and is mostly seen in DM.

### Clinical Subsets of Idiopathic Inflammatory Myopathy Defined by Myositis-Specific Autoantibodies

### Anti-synthetase Syndrome

MSAs are highly specific for the myositis disease spectrum and are strongly associated with distinct clinical phenotypes and may thus be helpful to identify clinical subsets of myositis. The most common of the MSAs are the anti-synthetase autoantibodies directed against aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases (anti-Jo-1, anti-EJ, anti- PL-7, anti-PL-12, anti-KS, anti-OJ, anti-Ha, and anti-Zo). A clinically distinct subset of myositis, often called anti-synthetase syndrome, has been identified in patients with anti-synthetase autoantibodies. The most common of the anti-synthetase autoantibodies is anti-Jo-1, which is directed against histidyl-tRNA synthetase. This autoantibody is present in approximately 20% to 30% of patients with IIM. Anti-synthetase syndrome is characterized by the presence of anti-synthetase autoantibodies and a set of clinical features that includes ILD (most common), clinical myositis, Raynaud's phenomenon, fever, nonerosive symmetric polyarthritis of the small joints, and mechanic's hands (Fig. 86.9). Notably, some of the anti-synthetase autoantibodies are mainly associated with ILD (anti-PL12, anti-PL7), and these patients

with ILD may be missed as having an anti-synthetase syndrome in the absence of muscle and joint symptoms.

### Clinically Amyopathic Dermatomyositis

A subset of DM is clinically referred to as amyopathic DM. These patients have a skin rash, which is typical of DM, but no clinical signs of muscle involvement. The proposed definition is based on a skin biopsy consistent with DM and a duration of 6 months or longer in the absence of clinical or laboratory evidence of myositis. However, some patients do have subclinical myositis, based on muscle MRI, biopsy, or electromyogram findings at presentation, or have small muscle enzyme elevations but have no objective or subjective muscle weakness. These patients are referred to as hypomyopathic DM. Clinically, amyopathic and hypomyopathic forms of DM behave very similarly and are commonly referred to as clinically amyopathic DM (CADM).
