Some patients who initially appear to have CADM manifest clinically overt myositis at a later time point. Patients with CADM, however, can develop extramuscular manifestations such as ILD, which can be severe, especially when associated with anti-MDA5 antibody. Anti-MDA5 antibody in CADM and in typical DM is associated with characteristic skin rashes of palmar papules, cutaneous ulcerations, and ischemic digits (Fig. 86.10). Moreover, anti-MDA5, owing to its association with rapidly progressive ILD, portends a poor prognosis in CADM and DM patients. CADM may be associated with malignancies, as is the case for classic DM. The frequency of this subset is uncertain, but some recent studies suggest that this form of DM may be more common than previously thought.

### Inclusion Body Myositis

IBM is distinguished from the other subgroups of IIM on the basis of both clinical and histopathologic features. 185, Sporadic IBM is a distinct entity from familial hereditary inclusion body

myopathy, which shares some of the same clinical and histopathologic features but lacks signs of inflammation in muscle tissue. IBM was identified in the 1960s as a subset of inflammatory myopathies, distinct from PM, primarily on the basis of typical histopathologic features that include sarcoplasmic and nuclear inclusions and rimmed vacuoles.13, A characteristic clinical phenotype was later identified, characterized by a very insidious onset of asymmetric proximal and distal muscle weakness and atrophy (localized predominantly to the thigh muscles [quadriceps] and finger flexors) evolving over years and resistance to glucocorticoid treatment. Sporadic IBM cases are sometimes misdiagnosed as PM because the classic histopathologic changes (rimmed vacuoles and inclusions) may not be evident in early biopsies (Fig. 86.11).

In contrast to other subsets of IIM, IBM is more frequent in men than in women, and it is seen mostly in individuals older than 50 years. The onset is more insidious than that of the other subgroups of IIM. Patients with IBM rarely have pain. The most frequent initial symptoms are difficulty climbing stairs and walking uphill and frequent falls as a result of weakness in the knee extensor muscles and finger flexor weakness leading to difficulty in holding and grasping activities. Muscle weakness may become prominent, and even walking across a threshold may become a problem. Difficulty swallowing may also be an early clinical feature, reflecting the involvement of the pharyngeal muscles. The course is slowly progressive, leading to muscle atrophy that can be striking, particularly in the thigh and forearm muscles. Severe weakness may develop, and many patients become wheelchairdependent. Extramuscular organ involvement is rare, although a subgroup of patients with IBM has sicca symptoms and may develop a secondary Sjögren's syndrome. IBM is usually resistant to treatment with glucocorticoids and other immunosuppressive agents. Because of this resistance to treatment, some have questioned whether IBM is an autoimmune disease or a

degenerative muscle disease, the latter supported by the abnormal accumulation of proteins such as amyloid-β in muscle fibers. While this issue is still under debate among experts, discovery of new autoantibodies directed against cytosolic 5'-nucleotidase 1A in IBM has provided some more evidence for underlying autoimmune process.

### Immune-Mediated Necrotizing Myopathy

In the past decades, another subset of IIM has been identified that is defined by predominate muscle fiber necrosis without the classic lymphocytic infiltration in muscle biopsies seen in patients with other subtypes of IIM, called immune mediated necrotizing myopathy (IMNM) or necrotizing myopathy74,188,189 (Fig. 86.12). This subset is characterized by the presence of one of two autoantibodies in two-thirds of cases: anti-SRP antibodies or anti-3- HMGCR antibodies. One-third of the cases remain autoantibody negative, and some of them may be associated with underlying malignancy. Patients who have autoantibodies to HMGCR can be further divided into those who have a history of statin exposure and those who are statin-naive (non-statin-induced necrotizing myositis). Patients without statin exposure but anti-HMGCR antibody positive tend to be younger, have high CK levels, and respond less well to immunosuppressive therapy compared with statin-induced necrotizing myopathy.

The presence of anti-SRP or anti-HMGCR autoantibodies together with an upregulation of class I MHC in the muscle fibers and by deposition of complements (C5b-9) on sarcolemma are suggestive

of an autoimmune etiology of a necrotizing myopathy. The distribution of complement deposition is different from the capillary deposition that can be seen in anti-synthetase syndrome or DM.191, A necrotizing muscle biopsy can also be seen in other nonautoimmune etiologies, including hypothyroidism, heritable myopathies, and toxic myopathies or cancer-associated myopathies.

### Polymyositis

With the recognition of new clinical subgroups associated with myositis specific autoantibodies, IMNM, and anti-synthetase syndrome, the PM subgroup has diminished (see Table 86.5). It is now often referred to seronegative IIM with myositis, but its clinical phenotype needs to be defined.

### Myositis Associated With Malignancies

An association between DM and malignancies was observed in several early case reports and later confirmed by more systematic studies. The association of cancer is much stronger for DM (20% to 30%) than for PM (10% to 15%). The clinical implications of this association, irrespective of the pathophysiologic mechanisms involved, are that it is imperative to screen for tumors in patients with DM at the time of diagnosis and at relapse, particularly if the symptoms do not respond to conventional immunosuppressive treatment. The types of malignancies vary and include not only hematologic malignancies such as lymphoma but also solid tumors such as lung, ovarian, breast, and colon cancer. Generally, ageand sex-appropriate screening, including routine labs,

chest radiograph, colonoscopy, prostate examination, mammography, and a gynecologic examination, is recommended. If any abnormalities are found, physicians should guide a more thorough investigation for malignancies. However, the presence of certain MSA, anti-TIF1-γ and anti-NXP2, and disease subtypes such as DM may warrant more aggressive evaluation including CT scans of chest, abdomen, and pelvis to investigate for occult malig- 194, Racial-ethnic backgrounds should be considered in nancy. screening because cancer types vary according to race/ethnicity with lung and nasopharyngeal cancers being more frequent in Asians than in Caucasians.

### Classification and Diagnostic Criteria

At present, there are no prospectively validated diagnostic or classification criteria for myositis. Dividing diseases into homogeneous subsets serves several important functions, including allowing us to estimate disease incidence and prevalence, understand disease pathogenesis and natural history, and evaluate the patient's response to therapy and prognosis. More than four decades ago, Bohan and Peter11,12 proposed a set of five criteria to facilitate the diagnosis of patients with IIM. They classified IIMs into five groups: primary idiopathic PM, primary idiopathic DM, IIMs associated with malignancy, childhood IIMs associated with vasculitis, and IIMs associated with collagen vascular diseases. The exclusion criteria were several and included signs of central or peripheral neurologic disease, a family history of muscle disease, and symptoms and signs suggestive of muscular dystrophy, granulomatous myositis, infections, drug-induced myopathy, toxic myopathy, rhabdomyolysis, metabolic disorders, endocrinopathies, and myasthenia gravis.

IBM was later recognized as a separate disease entity. 185, Since Bohan and Peter proposed their classification criteria advances in clinical research have led to the identification of certain autoantibodies that are strikingly associated with some clinical phenotypes of myositis (Table 86.3).

A multidisciplinary collaboration has developed data-driven classification criteria for IIM, the 2017 European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology/American College of Rheumatology (EULAR/ACR) classification criteria for juvenile and adult IIM and their major subgroups (Table 86.4). Developed using cross-sectional data, two models were developed: one for patients with available muscle biopsy data and one for patients with typical DM skin rash without muscle biopsies. These models resulted in a high sensitivity and specificity, and they also performed well in classifying the subsets DM, JDM, PM, IBM, and CADM. The new criteria include anti-Jo-1 autoantibodies, emphasizing the need for standardized autoantibody tests to minimize the risk of false-positive or falsenegative results.

As a complement to the EULAR/ACR classification criteria, separate criteria based on expert consensus have been proposed for the classification of IMNM. These are based on presence of anti-SRP or anti-HMGCR autoantibodies in combination with proximal muscle weakness and elevated serum CK levels. There are also updated criteria for IBM that include both clinical and pathologic definitions.

### Clinical Evaluation

Clinical and laboratory characteristics of the different IIM subtypes are summarized in Table 86.5.

### Physical Examination Findings

Although most patients are first seen with muscle weakness or fatigue, the IIMs are systemic connective tissue diseases, and other organs are frequently involved; therefore the physician should conduct a full clinical examination when patients are seen with muscle symptoms. This examination could also be helpful in distinguishing IIMs from non-inflammatory myopathies.

The muscle problems reported by many patients consist of not only muscle weakness but also muscle fatigue or reduced muscle function and pain. Thus the evaluation must differentiate between strength and fatigue by evaluating muscle strength and testing repetitive movements for muscle fatigue. Symmetric proximal more than distal muscle weakness is seen in most patients with IIM, whereas both proximal and distal muscle involvement is seen in IBM and can be asymmetric as well. In the early phases, atrophy is usually not a pronounced phenomenon in IIM. In later phases, a moderate symmetric atrophy of proximal muscles may be present. More severe atrophy of the quadriceps muscles and the flexor muscles of the forearms, which may be asymmetric, often develop in patients with IBM, and deformities in the finger joints and difficulty making fists may also develop.

Muscle strength can be tested in various ways. The physician can quickly screen for weakness in proximal lower leg muscles by asking the patient to stand up from a sitting or squatting position without support. A more standardized test that is easy to perform in the clinic is the manual muscle test, with grading according to the Medical Research Council (MRC) scale. There are many variants of this test, but a short form, addressing eight muscles on the dominant side, is recommended as part of the disease activity score by the International Myositis Assessment and Clinical Studies. In many patients with IIM, muscle strength as assessed by the manual muscle test is good in most of the tested muscle groups, despite patient report of muscle weakness and fatigue. In these patients, testing that involves a number of repetitions is often a more sensitive method of detecting muscle impairment. The Functional Index in Myositis-2 (FI-2)—or the shorter version, FI-3—is a myositis-specific outcome measure that assesses a number of repetitions.201, With this test, proximal muscle groups are more involved than are distal muscles. This index is often used by physical therapists. In patients with IBM, knee extensors and finger flexors are often weak.

The physician should also examine the skin to detect changes, including those in nailfolds and the scalp. Joints can be affected by arthritis, and heart and lung changes should be carefully looked for.

### Laboratory Findings

Laboratory evaluations are critical components of both diagnosis and patient management. Combinations of laboratory tests are generally used during patient evaluations. Because no laboratory test is highly specific for IIMs, the results of these tests are usually interpreted in the clinical context.

### Biochemical Tests

Measuring serum levels of muscle enzymes is an important part of the evaluation of patients with myositis. Elevated levels of muscle-derived serum enzymes reflect ongoing damage to the muscle parenchyma. These measurements help differentiate IIMs from conditions such as steroid myopathy and denervation, in which

muscle-derived serum enzymes may be normal. Measurement of the serum CK level is traditionally the first step in the assessment of patients with IIM. CK exists as MM (skeletal muscle), MB (cardiac muscle), and BB (brain) isoforms in serum. In comparison with other serum muscle enzymes, CK appears to be a relatively specific and sensitive indicator of the degree of muscle fiber injury. However, ranges detected vary significantly among patients, with levels being normal in some patients and elevated by several hundred-fold in others.

Generally, 80% to 90% of adult myositis patients show an increase in CK during the initial evaluation. High levels are more often seen in patients within the IMNM subgroups. However, a certain proportion of patients, especially those in advanced stages

of the disease, show normal or relatively modest elevations in CK, in part because of a lack of muscle mass or the presence of inhibitors of CK activity.204, Normal CK is relatively more common in DM than in PM. In the absence of CK elevation, it is usually easier to diagnose DM than PM because of the presence of skin rashes in the former. It is also known that CK levels are generally lower in patients with IBM than in those with PM or DM. Therefore a normal CK level does not exclude a diagnosis of IIM, particularly IBM or DM.

Constantly elevated levels of CK are often a sign of inflammatory activity. A rise in CK level is generally correlated with overall disease activity but not with strength or functional measures of disease activity. 206, CK measurements are usually not useful for

monitoring disease exacerbations, and they should always be evaluated in the clinical context. CK levels may normalize without clinical improvement, or they may increase without clinical worsening; however, increasing levels point to a potential flare and warrant closer clinical evaluation. CK elevations are not specific for myositis because this enzyme is also elevated in other muscle diseases, including muscular dystrophies, rhabdomyolysis, hypothyroidism, and many drug-induced myopathies. The cardiac isoform troponin I has the highest specificity as an indicator of myocardial involvement and is the most reliable serum marker for detecting myocardial damage in patients with inflammatory muscle disease.

Measurement of other serum muscle enzymes, including aldolase, aspartate aminotransferase (AST), alanine transaminase (ALT), and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), significantly improves the chance of diagnosing myositis, especially in patients with active disease and normal CK levels. The main disadvantage of these enzymes is that they are also elevated in liver diseases; therefore the muscle source needs to be identified before interpreting the data.

The serum myoglobin level is a sensitive index of muscle fiber membrane integrity and can therefore be used to assess the degree of disease activity. The advantage of the myoglobin assay is that it involves a nonenzymatic immunologic reaction. The disadvantages are that a significant range of serum myoglobin levels occurs in myositis patients because of circadian variation, 210 and the test is less readily available than CK for routine use.

### Histopathology

Muscle biopsy is important for the diagnosis of inflammatory myopathies and a critical component to exclude other myopathies.211, For optimal biopsy results, it is important to select a muscle that is moderately weak. The histologic features can be grouped into general features that are common to all IIMs and specific features unique to a particular subgroup. The general features include fiber necrosis, regeneration, degeneration, variation in fiber diameter, increase in connective tissue, and inflammation.

Features specific to DM include loss of capillaries, alterations in the morphology of the capillaries, capillary necrosis with the deposition of complement products (e.g., membrane attack complex) on the vessel walls, and, rarely, muscle infarcts. Another specific histopathologic finding, albeit often a late sign, is perifascicular atrophy. Infiltrates in DM typically have a perivascular distribution and are dominated by a high percentage of CD4+ T cells and macrophages at the sites of inflammation, with B cells occasionally in evidence. Although perifascicular atrophy is the hallmark of the histologic changes seen in DM, it may not be visible if a biopsy is acquired early in the course of the disease. In early DM, the class I MHC expression is patchy, and the perifascicular areas are usually stained. Some of the biopsy features found in patients with DM, like the abnormalities of the microvasculature, have been reported in patients with anti-Jo-1 autoantibodies, whereas other muscle biopsy features are distinct from DM, namely necrosis of fibers in perifascicular areas with perimysial fragmentation. Moreover, perifascicular MHC II upregulation appears to be more specific for anti-synthetase syndrome.

The features of PM include the presence of macrophages and activated CD4+ and CD8+ T cells in muscle tissue and the expression of class I MHC molecules on muscle fibers. Mononuclear cell invasion of nonnecrotic muscle fibers in endomysial areas is a characteristic feature of PM and IBM. The histologic features of IBM resemble those of PM, but they also include unique features such as red-rimmed vacuoles and inclusions (cytoplasmic or nuclear) and amyloid deposits. An increased number of cytochrome-c oxidase-negative fibers can also be seen, but this change is not specific for IBM. In IBM, electron microscopy usually demonstrates 15 to 21 nm cytoplasmic and intranuclear tubulofilaments, which are not found in DM or PM. It is not uncommon to find biopsies that are negative for both rimmed vacuoles and tubulofilamentous inclusions. In this situation, the diagnosis may be based on typical clinical features. Nonresponsiveness to immunosuppressive treatment further supports the diagnosis of IBM in an otherwise typical patient. Inflammation surrounding necrotic fibers is a feature of some muscular dystrophies (e.g., facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy, limb-girdle muscular dystrophy type IIB, Duchenne's muscular dystrophy), in which it is secondary to muscle cell degeneration.

In patients with IMNM, the typical histopathological features of muscle fiber necrosis and inflammatory cell infiltrates are scarce or may be absent. The common and unique immunologic and histologic features of the various subgroups are listed in Tables 86.6 and 86.7, respectively.

### Imaging

### Muscles

Ultrasonography, CT, and MRI are the three general imaging techniques used to evaluate skeletal muscle. MRI has emerged as the method of choice for the examination of soft tissue muscle abnormalities because it efficiently visualizes and quantifies inflammation, fat infiltration, calcification, and alterations in muscle size and localizes pathologic changes to specific muscle groups (Fig. 86.13). MRI examinations can be helpful guides for muscle biopsy sampling, assessing active muscle disease versus damage as well as an aid in diagnosis given some distinctive MRI finding of DM, IBM, and IMNM. MRI is a potential outcome tool to be used in the longitudinal analysis of responses to therapy and in clinical trials, although its sensitivity to changes has not been determined. 215-217

Ultrasonography can be used to detect abnormal vascularization, and rates of blood flow can be monitored effectively with color Doppler imaging. The usefulness of ultrasound in diagnosis or as a tool to monitor treatment in patients with IIM still needs to be determined. CT is the modality of choice for identifying calcifications in soft tissues (e.g., JDM), but it is not useful for detecting inflammatory changes in muscle tissue. Cross-sectional CT images allow quantification of muscle atrophy and fat replacement in deep muscles that may not be generally accessible to ultrasonography. A combination of MRI and P-31 MR spectroscopy examinations produces the most comprehensive and accurate evaluation of patients but has not been evaluated for use in clinical practice.

### Lungs

High-resolution CT of the lungs is important for detecting ILD and should be considered at the time of myositis diagnosis because the prevalence of ILD is high. In contrast, conventional radiography may not always be sensitive enough to detect ILD. These are also important tests for assessing the effects of immunosuppressive treatment. Baseline high-resolution CT chest is recommended in patients with myositis even without any pulmonary symptoms, with the possible exception of IBM where ILD is rare.

### Electromyography

Changes on electromyography (EMG) are a useful indicator of muscle pathology, which are highly sensitive but usually nonspecific for myopathies. The major abnormalities include abnormal electrical irritability, a decrease in the mean duration and amplitude of motor unit potentials (short duration and low amplitude) or increase in the percentage of polyphasic motor unit potentials (increase polyphasia), and rapid firing of the motor unit potentials in relation to the level of activity (increased recruitment). Later in the course of the disease, fibers are lost from some motor units, and recruitment is reduced. Abnormal electrical irritability in DM and PM involves increased insertional activity, trains of positive sharp waves, and fibrillation potentials. Spontaneous electrical activity is a reasonable measure of disease activity in DM and PM. Earlier studies indicated that EMG abnormalities correlate with alterations in muscle strength and serum muscle enzymes; however, there is an agreement that EMG is not very sensitive to change in muscle strength. The inflammation in IIMs is often patchy, and EMG is useful in determining which muscle should be sampled for biopsy. Because EMG can cause histopathologic changes that complicate the interpretation of the biopsy, it is best to perform EMG on one side and obtain the muscle biopsy from the same muscle on the contralateral side. Even for IBM, in which the disease is often asymmetric, this technique is useful as long as the contralateral muscle is also weak.

### Differential Diagnosis/Mimics

The differential diagnosis of IIMs and other myopathies is important because the clinical associations and response to therapeutic interventions differ significantly. A variety of factors induce the clinical and pathologic spectrum that mimics myositis and a variety of myopathies closely mimic IIMs (Table 86.8).

### Dystrophic Myopathies

Dysferlinopathy. Genetic defects in the dysferlin gene result in limb-girdle muscular dystrophy type 2B and distal muscular dystrophy of the Miyoshi type. These diseases can appear in patients in their late teens or early 20s. The weakness in the limb-girdle type 2B phenotype first assumes a pelvifemoral distribution: the quadriceps muscle is affected first, followed by weakness in the arms in the later stages of the disease. A relatively acute onset with elevated levels of serum muscle enzymes points to PM as a differential diagnosis. The weakness in the Miyoshi phenotype occurs predominantly in the gastrocnemius and soleus muscles, thereby affecting the patient's ability to walk on the toes. The weakness is slowly progressive, with loss of ambulation generally occurring in the fourth decade, but earlier in some cases. Serum CK levels are

high during the active phase of the disease. In general, the muscle biopsy is dystrophic, with significant mononuclear cell infiltration and small sarcolemmal defects with thickened basal lamina structures over the defects.

Facioscapulohumeral Muscular Dystrophy. A partial deletion of the D4Z4 repeats near the chromosome 4q telomere at 4q35 leads to the facioscapulohumeral phenotype. The initial weakness usually affects the facial muscles, and the onset is insidious. Shoulder weakness is commonly seen because of the weakness of the scapular fixator muscles. The weakness is generally slowly progressive, with typical myopathic changes on the EMG such as brief, small-amplitude, polyphonic voluntary motor unit potentials. The presence of perivascular, endomysial, and perimysial inflammation is a common feature. Serum CK levels are elevated and vary with patient age and sex.

Dystrophinopathies. These X-linked recessive disorders are caused by mutations in the dystrophin gene. Milder forms of Becker's muscular dystrophy manifest as myalgias, muscle cramps, exercise intolerance, mild limb-girdle weakness, and quadriceps myopathy. The severe Becker's phenotype that is seen in patients

younger than age 8 years is indistinguishable from the Duchenne's phenotype. An elevation in serum CK levels is seen in asymptomatic patients. In Becker's dystrophy, the number of necrotic and regenerating fibers is decreased compared with the Duchenne phenotype, and the incidence of hypercontracted and central nuclei increases with age.

Proximal Myotonic Myopathy. CCTG expansion in intron 1 of the zinc finger transcription factor (ZNF9) gene results in type II myotonic dystrophy. The myotonia usually appears to be absent or minimal but is detectable by EMG. The weakness is mainly proximal, with minimal or no facial involvement. Smooth muscle, cardiac, and diaphragmatic involvement is common in this disease. First-degree heart block is the most common abnormality, and sudden death is well documented. Muscle biopsies show nonspecific features such as central nuclei, sarcoplasmic masses, and atrophy of type I fibers.

Sarcoglycanopathy. Mutations in sarcoglycans (α, β, γ, and δ) result in limb-girdle muscular dystrophy types IIC to IIF. Sarcoglycanopathies often start in childhood, with a median patient age of onset of 6 to 8 years. These diseases present initially as pelvic muscle weakness, including a waddling gait and difficulty performing common tasks such as getting up from the floor, climbing the stairs, and running. The trunk muscles are prominently affected, and upper-extremity involvement usually follows lower-extremity involvement. Distal muscles are generally spared until later in the disease process. Dilated cardiomyopathy is

often seen in these disorders, and muscle biopsies show marked regeneration and necrosis.

### Neuromuscular Disorders

Motoneuron Diseases. These diseases, including amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), are progressive, degenerative disorders of motor neurons in the spinal cord, brainstem, and cerebral motor cortex that manifest clinically as amyotrophy and exaggerated reflexes. These diseases are characterized by a selective loss of function of upper or lower motor neurons, finally leading to a progressive loss of both types of motor neurons over time. EMG shows fibrillation and fasciculation potentials in the muscles of the lower and upper limbs or in the bulbar muscles. Muscle biopsies show the presence of denervation atrophy and secondary myopathic changes in chronically denervated muscles. IBM is the primary muscle disorder most likely to be confused with ALS, and muscle biopsy helps differentiate the two. Serum CK levels are slightly elevated, particularly in the early stages of the disease and in men who are physically active.

Spinal Muscular Atrophy. Late-onset forms of spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) are characterized by progressive muscle weakness and atrophy and reduced tendon reflexes. EMG and muscle testing reveal neurogenic changes in the muscle. Typical muscle biopsy findings include small and large groups of atrophic fibers in the chronic and severe forms of SMA, respectively. Histochemical changes show fiber type grouping, indicating reinnervation.

Serum CK levels are slightly increased in juvenile-onset cases and normal in other forms of SMA. EMG shows abnormal spontaneous electrical activity (fibrillations, positive sharp waves, fasciculations), suggesting ongoing denervation.

Myasthenia Gravis. The clinical manifestations of myasthenia gravis include abnormal weakness that is worsened by repeated or sustained exertion and fatigability. Proximal muscles are usually more severely affected than distal muscles. This is a generalized disease that exhibits external ocular muscle involvement, positive anti-cholinesterase drug tests, and a decremental EMG response. Patients are often positive for anti-acetylcholine receptor antibodies.

### Metabolic Myopathies

Acid Maltase Deficiency. This autosomal recessive glycogen storage disease is caused by acid maltase gene mutations. The disease has infantile, childhood, and adult variants. The infantile form manifests in the first few months after birth as a rapidly progressive weakness and hypotonia, with death occurring as a result of cardiorespiratory failure. The childhood form manifests as a myopathy in which the weakness is usually greater in the proximal than in the distal muscles; the disease progresses relatively slowly, and patients die of respiratory failure. The adult form presents in the 20s as a progressive myopathy that resembles PM or limbgirdle muscular dystrophy, with additional respiratory symptoms. Serum muscle enzymes (e.g., CK, AST, and LDH) are increased in all three forms of the disease, and EMG indicates myopathy in all three cases.

McArdle's Disease. McArdle's disease is the most common of the nonlysosomal muscle glycogenoses. Exercise intolerance is the characteristic feature of this disease, and it often manifests as early fatigue, myalgia, and stiffness of exercising muscle that is relieved by resting. The EMG is normal in some patients and shows nonspecific myopathic changes in others. Forearm ischemic exercise testing shows virtually no increase in venous lactate in most patients. Serum CK levels, however, are variably elevated in these patients. Muscle biopsies show subsarcolemmal deposits of glycogen at the periphery of the fibers.

Mitochondrial Myopathies. Mitochondrial diseases are heterogeneous and often present a diagnostic challenge. It has been suggested that myopathy is the result of mutations in mitochondrial DNA in the skeletal muscle. The clinical course of the pure myopathy varies from rapidly progressive to almost reversible disease, with disease onset occurring from infancy through

adulthood. The weakness is facioscapulohumeral and more proximal than distal, with involvement of the orbicularis and extraocular muscles. Patients often complain of exercise intolerance and fatigue and have recurrent episodes of myoglobinuria. Muscle biopsy plays a critical role in the diagnosis of these conditions, especially the use of special mitochondrial stains that detect succinate dehydrogenase, Cox staining, and Gomori trichrome staining.

### Endocrine Myopathies

Cushing's Syndrome. Cushing's syndrome is an endogenous glucocorticoid excess disease that manifests as muscle weakness and wasting. Chronic corticosteroid treatment results in similar manifestations and significant loss of strength within a few weeks of treatment. Muscle biopsy shows increased vacuolations and glycogen accumulation in type II muscle. The onset of weakness is usually insidious. The weakness is primarily proximal, with more severe involvement in the legs than in the arms. These patients generally show normal serum muscle enzyme levels. Muscle wasting can often be reversed if the glucocorticoid levels are returned to the normal range.

Hyperthyroid and Hypothyroid Myopathy. Myopathy due to thyroid disease is characterized primarily by proximal muscle weakness and muscle wasting. When distal weakness occurs, it often follows proximal myopathy. Exercise intolerance, fatigue, and breathlessness are common complaints, and weakness of the respiratory muscles may result in respiratory insufficiency and the need for ventilatory support. Patients often have difficulty rising from a sitting position or lifting their arms above their heads. Serum muscle enzymes are often normal or low in hyperthyroidism and elevated in hypothyroidism. EMG findings are variable, with short-duration motor unit potentials and increased polyphasic potentials in proximal muscles; fibrillations and fasciculations are uncommon.

### Infectious s Myopathies

Human Immunodeficiency Virus Myopathy. Neuromuscular manifestations are common in HIV-induced myopathy (see Chapter 116). The clinical features typically include a myopathy of subacute onset that progresses slowly. The myopathy often starts as proximal symmetric muscle weakness with or without muscle wasting, similar to that in IIMs. EMG shows spontaneous activity, with fibrillation potentials, positive sharp waves, and brief, lowamplitude polyphasic motor unit potentials.

Human T-Lymphotropic Virus I Myopathy. Myositis associated with human T-lymphotropic virus I has been noted in certain areas of the world (e.g., Japan, Jamaica). In these patients, symptoms of PM and IBM occur either alone or in combination with tropical spastic paraparesis. Typical features include weakness and increases in serum CK levels. Histologic findings include interstitial inflammation, muscle fiber necrosis in PM and endomysial inflammation, vacuoles, amyloid deposits, and tubulofilaments in IBM.

Parasitic Myopathies. Diseases caused by various parasites— protozoa (e.g., toxoplasmosis, trypanosomiasis, sarcocystosis, malaria), cestodes (e.g., cysticercosis, echinococcosis, coenurosis sparganosis), and nematodes (trichinellosis, toxocariasis, dracunculiasis)—can cause myositis. The clinical features include nonspecific complaints such as myalgia and focal swelling and typical features of PM and DM. Each parasitic infection shows typical changes on muscle biopsy (e.g., the presence of tachyzoites and toxoplasma cysts along with perimysial and endomysial inflammation). A combination of muscle biopsy and serologic findings is useful in making a diagnosis.

### Drug-Induced Myopathies

A number of drugs are known to cause a myopathy that can closely mimic myositis. One of the most common class of

drugs that may cause a myopathy are statins (e.g., lovastatin, simvastatin). Most cases of statin myopathy resolve with cessation of therapy; therefore they are considered toxic statin myopathy. This is different from the above-described IMNM associated with anti-HMGCR antibodies. This antibody, however, is not found in patients with toxic statin myopathy, or most patients who are exposed to statins. Other agents that are known to cause toxic necrotizing myopathy include fibric acid derivatives (clofibrate, gemfibrozil), nicotinic acid, organophosphate poisoning, and ε-aminocaproic acid.

Other drugs that may cause a myopathy mimicking myositis include hydroxyurea, which can cause skin rashes that resemble DM. Agents such as IFN-α that are used to treat viral hepatitis and certain malignant tumors are also known to induce clinical features that resemble PM.

Amphiphilic drugs such as chloroquine, hydroxychloroquine, and amiodarone are also known to induce cytoplasmic vacuoles, necrosis, and longitudinal branching of muscle fibers. Drugs that affect microtubules, such as colchicine and vincristine, also induce myopathic changes, with the appearance of characteristic autophagic vacuoles in muscle fibers. Nucleoside analogues such as zidovudine are used to treat HIV because they act as false substrates for the viral reverse transcriptase. These drugs may also cause myalgias, proximal muscle weakness, and fatigue and are sometimes

associated with increased levels of serum CK. In these patients, zidovudine-induced mitochondrial myopathy may coexist along with HIV-induced T cell-mediated inflammatory myopathy. D-Penicillamine is known to induce clinical features reminiscent of DM. Recovery usually occurs after withdrawal of the drug.

### Management and Outcome

The recommended treatment for patients with IIM is based on a combination of pharmacologic therapy and physical exercise. The optimal pharmacologic treatment in patients with IIM is unclear. Few controlled trials have been undertaken, mostly involving the older subgroups, so recommendations are largely based on clinical observations from case series. With these limitations in mind, a suggested outline of treatment for patients with IIM excluding IBM is depicted in Fig. 86.14. In addition to providing treatment, it is important to give patients adequate information about their disease and its optimal management. This educational component is best provided by a rheumatology team and patient support groups.

### Pharmacologic Treatment

The initial pharmacologic treatment in patients with IIM is highdose glucocorticoids: 0.75 to 1 mg/kg body weight per day of prednisone (or equivalent) for 4 to 8 weeks, followed by slow taper to low-dose prednisone (5 to 10 mg) over 6 months, and subsequent attempt to taper and discontinue prednisone by 12 months. Most experts recommend that glucocorticoid treatment be combined with another immunosuppressive drug to reduce the side effects of the glucocorticoid and to boost the immunosuppressive effect. The most frequently used immunosuppressive agents are methotrexate and azathioprine. In the extension phase of one of the few double-blind, placebo-controlled trials that have been reported, the combination of azathioprine and glucocorticoids, compared with prednisone alone, was associated with better functional ability and a lower requirement for prednisone after 1 and 3 years.228, The recommended azathioprine dosage is 2 mg/kg per day. The dosing regimen for methotrexate is similar to that for RA—as much as 25 mg weekly, although there have been reports of higher doses used. Pulmonary involvement related to myositis is not necessarily a contraindication for methotrexate.

The combination of methotrexate and azathioprine has proven to be successful in a few patients with refractory myositis in a prospective, randomized, open-label crossover study comparing two aggressive approaches. There are several newer case reports and series that suggest that mycophenolate mofetil can be an effective second-line therapy in patients refractory to glucocorticoids, methotrexate, and/or azathioprine. Mycophenolate is increasingly being used for refractory DM rashes and ILD in myositis. Similarly, several beneficial reports of cyclosporine A or tacrolimus have been reported and is another potential alternative therapy, especially in patients with ILD. In patients with ILD, cyclophosphamide could be of value; however, rituximab is being used more commonly in patients refractory to traditional oral immunosuppressive drugs. Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) is a therapy that has been proven to be effective in several studies including a placebo-controlled randomized trial in DM. It can be used as an adjuvant to other treatments for myositis but is most often used for treatment-resistant DM, cancer-associated myositis, dysphagia, ILD, and in the setting of infection or pregnancy. In a placebo-controlled trial, IVIG was effective in treatmentresistant DM and is now approved by the U.S. Food and Drug

Administration for this subset of IIM. IVIG can also be effective in anti-HMGCR-positive necrotizing myopathy. However, IVIG use is limited as a result of its high cost, requirement of long and repetitive infusions, tolerance issues, and a therapeutic effect that may be transient. In patients with severe, rapidly progressive disease that might be life threatening and moderate to severe ILD, high-dose pulses of IV methylprednisolone are beneficial.

Pharmacologic treatment, including glucocorticoid tapering, should be guided by clinical outcome measures. As discussed earlier, the most appropriate outcome measures are muscle endurance and muscle strength and monitoring of organ-specific manifestations such as skin rashes or ILD. Side effects of high-dose glucocorticoids are frequently observed. Prophylaxis against osteoporosis is recommended with vitamin D and calcium and, when clinically indicated, bisphosphonates. Steroid myopathy is another possible consequence of glucocorticoid treatment that is particularly problematic in patients with inflammatory myopathies. There is no specific test to verify steroid myopathy but, in the absence of active clinical disease, steroid myopathy could contribute to muscle weakness. If steroid myopathy is suspected, tapering of the glucocorticoid dose with careful evaluation of the clinical response is recommended. Glucocorticoids may also cause hypokalemia and, if this is not corrected, it may be associated with muscle weakness and incorrectly interpreted as active myositis.

The depletion of B cells has emerged as a treatment strategy in autoimmune diseases. One approach is to use rituximab (monoclonal antibody against CD20). Although a large multicenter randomized clinical trial (RIM trial) in patients with refractory PM, DM, and JDM did not meet its endpoint, a post-hoc analysis indicated that patients positive for anti-Jo-1 or anti-Mi-2 autoantibodies may have a favorable response to rituximab. There are several favorable case series of rituximab use in patients with ILD, especially in anti-synthetase syndrome. Use of TNF inhibitors has produced mixed results but are not currently recommended for myositis, especially given cases of exacerbation of disease post anti- TNF. One trial examining the use of infliximab in patients with PM, DM, or IBM found that only 30% of patients experienced an improvement in disease symptoms, whereas the remaining participants suffered from adverse side effects or worsening of the dis- 234 In addition, a pilot study of etanercept showed worsening ease. of the rash associated with DM.

IBM is usually nonresponsive to glucocorticoids. There are occasional case reports of "stabilization" for a period of months, but this condition probably reflects the natural history of the disease. Prolonged administration of glucocorticoids to patients with IBM may actually lead to worsening of clinical aspects of the disease, despite the improvement in CK levels and reduced T cell numbers in biopsies. Prednisone treatment also increases the number of amyloid-containing fibers. A few small studies have shown some beneficial effect of IVIG, methotrexate, anti—T lymphocyte globulin, or mycophenolate. However, an open-label trial comparing methotrexate with methotrexate in combination with antiT lymphocyte globulin showed deterioration in those receiving methotrexate alone.

Anabolic steroids and oxandrolone may have some beneficial effects on muscle strength, although this benefit needs to be confirmed in larger studies. Most experts consider their use justified in combination with glucocorticoids for a limited period in patients who have inflammatory infiltrates on muscle biopsy, or in combination with a more aggressive immunosuppressive treatment (e.g., methotrexate, azathioprine) in patients with another connective tissue disease.

### Nonpharmacologic Treatment

With immunosuppressive treatment, approximately 75% of all patients improve, but few recover normal muscle function, even in the absence of muscle inflammation. In previous decades, patients with myositis were advised against exercise because of concerns over possible muscle damage and inflammation, but recent publications have demonstrated that combining exercise and immunosuppressive therapy is a safe approach and has clear beneficial effects on muscle strength and function. Chronic inflammation leads to loss of skeletal muscle because of low levels of physical activity, negative effects of glucocorticoids, and circulating cytokines. In addition, in late phases of disease, patients with PM and DM may still experience muscle weakness, despite the absence of muscle inflammation. Exercise has proven safe and able to improve muscle performance and health-related quality of life in both early and late phases of disease. Emerging evidence suggests that exercise can even decrease muscle and systemic inflammation. Similar to healthy individuals, exercise has a short-term benefit and needs to be implemented on a regular basis. 237,

In a pair of small studies of immunosuppressed myositis patients, personalized submaximal exercise programs improved muscle function without causing any increase in inflammation. This improvement was true for patients who had individually tailored exercise regimens243 and self-administered home exercise . Examinations of biopsies both before and after exerroutines. cise indicated that the patients showed improved muscle strength as the result of an increase in the proportion of slow-twitch (type I) muscle fibers and a reduction in inflammation and fibrosis.244, More evidence suggests that combining exercise and immunosuppressive therapy is a safe approach and can improve performance without disease exacerbation, and exercise can decrease muscle and systemic inflammation. The exercise regimen should be individualized and supervised by a physiotherapist to avoid the overuse of muscles, and it should combine aerobic and resistance exercise, starting as soon as the condition of the patient permits. Physical exercise is now recommended as a combination therapy with immunosuppressive treatment.

### Assessing Disease Activity and Outcome

The most important variable to measure in myositis patients is muscle strength or physical function. It is equally important to evaluate whether impaired muscle strength or function reflects active disease or irreversible muscle damage. In patients with dominating extramuscular manifestations, these should be evaluated and followed with relevant tests.

### Assessments of Muscle

Manual Muscle Test. There are several tools to measure muscle performance, but the method used most often in clinical practice and clinical trials is the manual muscle test with the MRC scale (see earlier). The drawback is that these tools measure muscle strength but not muscle endurance, which is often a major problem in PM or DM. Previously, the number of muscle groups tested using the manual muscle test varied, and different scales were used (5 or 10 grade). Recently a consensus was reached to assess eight muscle groups on the dominant side using a 0to 10-point scale, in which 0 indicates no muscle contraction; 5, the ability to hold the test position without any added pressure; and 10, the ability to hold the test position against strong pressure. The points between these scores are based on gradual increased resistance against the examiner's pressure. The eight muscle groups tested are

neck flexors, shoulder abduction (deltoid middle), biceps brachii, wrist extensors, knee extensors (quadriceps), dorsiflexion of ankle, gluteus maximus, and gluteus medius. The score achieved varies between 0 and 80.

Functional Index in Myositis. The Functional Index in Myositis and its revised form, the Functional Index in Myositis-2, were developed as outcome measures for patients with PM or DM. This test measures the number of repetitions that can be performed in defined muscle groups. 201, It is a more sensitive method of measuring impaired muscle function in patients with PM or DM. The drawback is that it takes long to perform, requires significant training, and therefore it is difficult to use in everyday clinical practice. Preferably, the Functional Index in Myositis-2 is administered by a physiotherapist and can be combined with the manual muscle test by a physician in the office. A shorter version, Functional Index in Myositis-3, has recently been validated and, with only three muscle groups tested, it will be more feasible to use regularly in the clinic.

Other Timed Tests. In addition, various timed tests are utilized to evaluate muscle function, endurance, and fatigability for therapeutic trials or observational studies. These tests comprise the 2-minute or 6-minute walking distance test, the timed 10-minute walk or run test, the timed up-and-go test, the 30-second chair stand test, and the Short Physical Performance Battery. However, these tests have not been fully validated in all subsets of adult patients with IIM. Validated functional measures can be important secondary endpoints in clinical trials or studies of patients with IIM, particularly in patients who have baseline muscle weakness. Standardization and normative data are of critical importance in the interpretation of these tests. On the other hand, questionnaires and scales that assess a patient's self-report of daily activities can be self-administered or administered by an interviewer. While functional questionnaires are feasible and easily administered, they do not directly evaluate physical activity.

Muscle Enzymes. There are five muscle enzymes that should be evaluated in any patient with myositis: CK, LDH, AST, ALT, and aldolase. While CK is most commonly used for initial diagnosis and assessments of subsequent treatment responses, in some individuals, AST, ALT, and LDH might be more commonly deranged. Therefore the most abnormal muscle enzyme at baseline (relative to its upper limit of normal) should be used for treatment responses or relapse assessment. Although muscle enzyme testing provides an objective assessment of active muscle disease, it is beneficial mainly to patients with PM and necrotizing autoimmune myopathy. In patients with DM or IBM, levels of muscle enzymes may not correlate well with disease activity. AST and ALT often cause confusion between active muscle disease versus hepatotoxicity associated with myositis therapies, which can be mitigated by the use of other liver-specific biomarkers such as gamma-glutamyl transferase, alkaline phosphatase, bilirubin, and, most importantly, glutamate dehydrogenase.

Imaging. MRI and muscle ultrasound could be valuable tools for muscle disease assessment and in quantifying longitudinal treatment responses in the future. However, standardization and validation are currently lacking, with only a few specialized centers able to perform longitudinal assessments of myositis with MRIs.

### Assessments of Extramuscular Involvement

In some patients, extramuscular symptoms predominate among the clinical features. These symptoms may require other assessment tools, such as those used to evaluate ILD. For monitoring the effects of treatment of ILD, PFTs and high-resolution CT

are recommended when there is worsening of pulmonary function of unclear explanation. Similarly, when rash or joint pain is the dominating clinical feature, frequent clinical examination of rash or arthritis is carried out to assess treatment responses, respectively. A clinical tool called the Cutaneous Dermatomyositis Disease Area and Severity Index, which is a physician-based scoring of DM rash, can be used for semiquantitative evaluation for treatment responses to rash. Similarly, disease activity tools for RA such as tender or swollen joint counts can be used clinically for articular assessments and treatment responses; however, these have not been validated for use in myositis.

### Patient-Reported Outcomes

The use of patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) is vital to standardize clinical trial outcomes and provide valuable data on both treatment efficacy and quality of life, which are immediately relevant to the management of disease activity. In patients with IIM, disease-specific PROMs are particularly relevant due to the heterogeneity in disease presentation and the variable effects of disease on patients. Currently there are many general PROMs that are being increasingly validated in myositis such as Short Form- 36, Health Assessment Questionnaire, visual analogue scale or numerical rating scale scores of pain, fatigue, Facit-fatigue, itch, skin quality-of-life indices, and Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System scores of pain, fatigue, and physical function. To assess the impact of IIM on the daily lives of patients, the Outcome Measures in Rheumatology Clinical Trials consortium is developing IM-specific PROMs and focus groups suggested the top five rated domains included muscle symptoms, fatigue, interaction with health-care providers and authorities, medication adverse effects, and pain.

### Measures of Physical Activity

Physical activity is one of the domains important to myositis patients as a treatment outcome. Fortunately, it can be monitored at home using wearable devices such as accelerometers, which have been pilot-tested in patients with IIM.249, Major advantages of this approach include practicality, objectivity, continuous longitudinal monitoring, and a lack of cognitive input from the patient or examiner. However, the interpretation of results must consider that completing physical activities depends on behavioral factors, not just motor capacity.

### Outcome Measures in Myositis Clinical Trials

The International Myositis Assessment & Clinical Studies Group (IMACS), a consortium of health professionals interested in myositis, made a consensus recommendation that outcome measures for patients with myositis include tools that measure disease activity, damage, and health-related quality of life. The IMACS network has developed one outcome measure to assess myositis disease activity and one to measure organ damage: the myositis disease activity assessment tool and the myositis damage index, respectively. Given that myositis is a complex and heterogeneous disorder, six different myositis core measures covering different aspects of the disease have been defined by expert consensus to be used in all future myositis clinical trials (Table 86.9). These outcome measures have been developed for clinical trials and research but can also be useful in clinical practice, although they require training. Furthermore, these six myositis core set measures were combined in a composite manner using data analysis and consensus methodology into a single response or outcome criteria for clinical trials.

# 87 Overlap Syndromes

### KEY POINTS

### Introduction

A common challenge in caring for patients with connective tissue diseases (CTDs) is how to approach the care of those whose signs and symptoms suggest an underlying autoimmune disease but whose clinical features do not fit neatly into a single, classically defined disease or syndrome. One reason for this diagnostic ambiguity is that rheumatic diseases are often defined descriptively using classification criteria that rely primarily on clinical and serologic pattern recognition rather than any single gold-standard test, and this leaves many patients without a precise name to call their disease. For example, a man who develops late-onset Raynaud's phenomenon and interstitial lung disease (ILD) in the setting of high-titer nucleolar-pattern anti-nuclear antibodies (ANAs) likely has an underlying CTD, but what to call it and how to predict whether it will ever evolve into a definable or clinically significant rheumatic disease is less clear. Developing a better understanding of overlap CTDs is critical to improving diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment of these patients.

### Historical Background

The concept of overlap CTDs is best understood in the historical context of how systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and mixed

connective tissue disease (MCTD), a prototypic overlap syndrome, came to be recognized and defined. In the 19th century, lupus erythematosus was originally described as a skin disease with distinctive clinical, anatomic, and histologic findings. By the beginning of the 20th century, a growing number of lupus patients had internal organ involvement, and from these observations emerged the concept of SLE as a single systemic disease with diverse clinical manifestations that for some included the skin. Further advances in serologic testing including fluorescent ANA testing and the identification of autoantibodies specific for human double-stranded DNA led to the more modern unifying concept of SLE as an immunologic rather than anatomic disease.

By the 1960s and early 1970s, investigators recognized a distinct subset of atypical SLE patients who exhibited overlapping features of SLE, dermatomyositis, and systemic sclerosis (SSc).2, Like many of those with SLE, these patients demonstrated autoantibodies to a macromolecular ribonuclear antigen derived from a saline nuclear extract, the extractable nuclear antigen. Further characterization of the antigen through enzymatic treatment with trypsin and ribonuclease revealed that patients with "atypical SLE" reacted to a different component of the macromolecule, the ribonuclear protein, than did the patients with classical SLE. Armed both with a clinical description and a matching serologic test, investigators named the newly described overlap syndrome "mixed connective tissue disease" and suggested classification criteria to help identify such patients for further study. Although this generally accepted classification has now been in use more than 40 years, there still remains some debate over whether MCTD is, in fact, a single disease or whether it may in fact be an intermediate stage of an eventually classifiable disease in evolution.5-9 Furthermore, the classification of MCTD fails to adequately describe many patients who have overlapping or incomplete features of one or more autoimmune diseases. Given our limited understanding of the molecular mechanisms that underlie such diseases, it remains unclear whether such patients have a unique, definable "undifferentiated connective tissue disease" (UCTD), an incomplete variant of a classically defined rheumatic disease, or two or more separate but coexistent autoimmune diseases.

### Immunogenetics of Overlap S Syndromes

Genetic susceptibility is thought to contribute significantly to the development of systemic autoimmunity. Because patients with MCTD and other overlap syndromes exhibit clinical and serologic features of multiple distinct autoimmune diseases, common genetic risk alleles shared by multiple autoimmune diseases might

also confer risk for these diseases too. While hundreds of genetic loci have been implicated in genome-wide array studies of autoimmunity, a few loci in particular increase the risk for multiple autoimmune diseases, and many of these loci cluster within genes that have common functional pathways that may play a role in disease pathogenesis10,11 (Table 87.1).

Polymorphisms in genes encoding the human leukocyte antigen (HLA) complex confer the most significant risk for developing systemic autoimmune diseases. It is believed that many of these HLA polymorphisms increase permissiveness of selfantigen presentation to cognate T cell receptors. Perhaps the best characterized of these is the rheumatoid arthritis (RA)- associated shared epitope, most commonly but not exclusively found within the HLA-DR4 molecule, whose presence confers a strong risk for citrullinated antibody positive, erosive RA.12, Conversely, the risk for developing SLE has most commonly been associated with HLA-DR3, whereas SSc has been linked to HLA-DR5.5,

Other HLA-DR polymorphisms have been shown to confer significant risk for developing MCTD and other overlap syndromes but not diseases like SLE or SSc that share many of the same overlapping clinical features.5, Indeed, these genetic associations provide some evidence of the uniqueness of MCTD as a disease. Specifically, HLA-DRB1*04:01 may identify those MCTD patients whose phenotype remains stable and distinguishable from SLE, SSc, or polymyositis. It may also identify a population of patients who develop an inflammatory and erosive polyarthritis indistinguishable from RA.5, In some MCTD patients, DRB1*15:01 and DRB1*09:01 may also confer significant risk for developing the disease. A separate study of Swedish patients not only implicates DRB1*04 as a susceptibility allele for MCTD but also homozygosity for a specific

polymorphism in major histocompatibility complex class I related gene A.

Protein tyrosine phosphatase N22 (PTPN22) is another gene for which functional polymorphisms have been shown to strongly associate with increased risk for multiple autoimmune disorders. Several studies have reported that polymorphisms such as the R620W minor allele correlate not only with development of SLE but also with SSc and polymyositis.20-28 Similarly, increased risk for multiple autoimmune diseases has been mapped to loci within genes involved with intra-cellular signaling and transcription. One such example is signal transducer and activator of transcription 4 (STAT4), which is activated through the Janus kinase signaling pathway. The rs757486 allele of STAT4 has been strongly linked to development of RA, SLE, and SSc—diseases whose clinical features overlap in patients with MCTD and undifferentiated CTD.29-33

Upregulation of interferon (IFN) inducible genes is a genomic hallmark of patients with active SLE, myositis, and SSc, whose clinical features overlap in many CTD patients. Not surprisingly, recent studies have identified single-nucleotide polymorphisms in both type I and type II IFN genes that appear to be associated with the risk for developing MCTD, suggesting that IFN pathways may play an important role in MCTD pathogenesis as with other CTDs. Another example is IFN regulatory factor 5 (IRF- 5), one of a series of transcription factors upregulated as part of the innate immune response to viral infections. Polymorphisms in IRF-5 have been linked in multiple studies across many different racial-ethnic backgrounds to development of SLE and possibly to some of its more specific clinical manifestations. Indeed, different polymorphisms confer increased SLE risk in different populations of patients, which may explain variations in the general clinical spectrum of disease between different racial-ethnic populations.35-40 Some of the same SNPs that confer increased risk for SLE have also been linked independently to other autoimmune diseases that include SSc, inflammatory myositis, juvenile idiopathic arthritis, RA, and Sjögren's syndrome. 31-33,41-50

### Autoantibodies in Overlap Syndromes

Autoantibody production is a prominent feature of patients who have overlap CTDs including MCTD.51-53 In many cases, the autoantibody response in patients with overlap CTD targets the same autoantigens as those described in patients with more classically defined rheumatic diseases such as SLE or SSc. ANAs are observed in practically all patients with MCTD by definition and are also reported in between 58% to 100% of patients with UCTD.54-58 Examples of specific ANAs found in UCTD include antibodies to the Ro (SSA) antigen, reported in 8% to 30% of patients, and topoisomerase 1 (Scl-70), particularly in those overlap patients with clinical features of limited scleroderma and SSc.54,

Often, this autoantibody response targets unique autoantigens or distinct epitopes on more ubiquitous autoantigens and may correlate with specific clinical features and/or prognosis. These target antigens are usually complex macromolecules consisting of polypeptides and nucleic acids that are involved with splicing, transcription, or other molecular machinery essential for cellular function.51, One particular subunit of the human spliceosome molecule, the U1 small nuclear ribonuclear protein (U1snRP), is a target of autoimmunity in patients with SLE, MCTD, and other CTDs51,53,62,63 (Fig. 87.1). It consists of a uridine-rich RNA molecule and a core of proteins that are

targeted by anti-Smith antibodies in patients with SLE. The U1snRP also contains a separate fragment, consisting of three proteins—A, C, and 70K—that is recognized by antibodies in patients with MCTD and to a lesser extent, SLE.52, These antibodies, known as "anti-RNP," are a requisite for the classification of patients with MCTD according to established criteria but are also present in 23% to 39% of patients with SLE.52, Some evidence suggests that the anti-RNP antibody response targets different epitopes in MCTD patients than in those with SLE.3,

The identification of additional autoantibodies and their targets has allowed for better characterization of patients with both classically defined and undifferentiated CTDs. Furthermore, the specificity of autoantibodies in patients with undifferentiated CTD provides both descriptive and prognostic information about the nature and severity of disease, including the presence or absence of specific internal organ involvement (Table 87.2).68-70 For example, among patients with inflammatory myositis overlap syndromes, those with antibodies to the PM/SCL antigen are more likely to exhibit clinical features of limited or SSc, ILD, and calcinosis52,54,71 (Fig. 87.2). Calcinosis is also a feature of another syndrome associated with the overlap of myositis, which can often be severe (including dysphagia and distal muscle involvement), joint contractures, and antibodies to the NXP-2 antigen. Another subpopulation of myositis patients with antibodies targeting the KU antigen often have overlapping autoimmune lung disease, including both pulmonary fibrosis and pulmonary hypertension. By contrast, antibodies to melanoma differentiation factor 5 (MDA 5) identify a more amyopathic subset of patients with an overlap of dermatomyositis and ILD. In these patients, the characteristic skin rash can be more ulcerative in nature than that which is typically seen in other forms of dermatomyositis, and the presence of anti-MDA 5 antibodies predicts a more progressive and refractory course of ILD72,73 (Fig. 87.3).

### Mixed Connective Tissue Disease

### The Controversy

Originally described in the early 1970s, the concept of MCTD as a unique disease remains a subject of controversy up to the present time. Experts on both sides of this debate have squared off against one another in special editions of scientific journals focusing on this very topic.74, The original description of MCTD was culled from a single cohort of SLE patients who appeared clinically to behave differently than the rest of their peers. This subgroup exhibited overlapping features of multiple CTDs, including SLE, inflammatory myositis, SSc, and RA. Anti-RNP antibodies were prevalent in but not exclusive to this subgroup and helped to differentiate MCTD from other diseases like SLE.

As a general rule, these patients were described as having namely a lower incidence of glomerulonephritis (GN), less severe internal organ damage, and a more benign prognosis with favorable survival rates compared with other CTDs. Some studies have cast doubt on these initial impressions and reported more severe outcomes and a worse prognosis than previously thought. Many of these studies also question the stability of the clinical phenotype of MCTD, reporting high rates of evolution from MCTD to more well-defined rheumatic diseases such as SLE or SSc with worse outcomes.5, As a result, some experts have suggested using the term undifferentiated autoimmune rheumatic disease to describe these patients rather than MCTD.

### Phenotypic Stability

The results from more recent, methodically sound studies have challenged earlier reports that question both the benign nature and phenotypic instability of MCTD. These include a

large population-based study conducted over three decades that not only reported a similar overall mortality rate in MCTD patients compared with the general population but also noted that only a minority of patients originally classified as having MCTD ever evolved into another rheumatic disease. Another report from a large observational cohort of 118 patients with MCTD found that only 12% evolved into another well-defined CTD over a mean disease duration of 17 years. Patients were defined as evolving from MCTD when new clinical features of a well-defined rheumatic disease developed in concert with a matching change in autoantibody profile. These findings corroborate those from other reports suggesting MCTD to be a distinct entity, not just an intermediate step in the evolution to other CTDs. Such conclusions are of more than just academic significance, as some believe that the diagnosis of MCTD carries prognostic significance, guides clinical care, and potentially improves patient outcomes.

### Epidemiology and Classification

MCTD is a rare disease with an incidence rate that varies between 0.2 and 1.9 per 100,000 patients per year.76, As in SLE, there is a striking imbalance in the prevalence of MCTD between sexes, with between 5 and 10 times as many women affected as men. 78,

There are few data describing racial-ethnic predisposition to the disease. After Sharp's original description of MCTD and subsequent publication of classification criteria, three other sets of criteria have been developed to classify patients with MCTD (Table 87.3). Each requires the presence of anti-RNP antibodies as a requisite criterion. While most other clinical features are similar between the different sets of criteria, each applies differential weighting resulting in the inconsistent classification of some patients who meet criteria for MCTD by one or more sets but not others. Two different studies of patients carrying a clinical diagnosis of MCTD found that the criteria proposed by Alarcon- Segovia and Kasukawa were most sensitive while those from Sharp the least.76,78

### Clinical Features

There are no distinctive features unique to MCTD, as it is by its nature an overlap syndrome. MCTD can begin with any of its overlapping features of SLE, SSc, inflammatory myositis, or RA, and these clinical features can appear at any time throughout the course of disease3 (Table 87.4). The most common reported clinical manifestations include Raynaud's phenomenon, sclerodactyly,

swollen hands, and polyarthritis/arthralgias.3, Less common are findings such as nephritis, lymphadenopathy, and alopecia, which are more distinctively associated with SLE.

### Joint Involvement

The spectrum of joint involvement in MCTD varies from a mild nonerosive and symmetric polyarthritis akin to what is observed in SLE to a more severe, erosive, and potentially destructive polyarthritis practically indistinguishable from RA.82, Polyarthralgias and arthritis are common and often present early in the disease, affecting between 60% and 95% of patients with MCTD.3, Many of these patients are rheumatoid factor positive and a few even demonstrate RA-specific autoantibodies to citrullinated proteins.84, When these seropositive patients present with erosive polyarthritis, it may be difficult to distinguish them from RA patients unless or until other overlapping features arise.

### Skin Involvement

Raynaud's phenomenon is one of the most prevalent findings in MCTD patients, occurring in as many as 75% to 90% during the course of their disease (Fig. 87.4A). Often, it is an early symptom for which a patient seeks medical attention or can be a sign picked

up by a practitioner evaluating the patient. It can even present months or years before the onset of other clinical findings typical of MCTD.2, Another frequent finding includes hand and finger swelling, often associated with Raynaud's phenomenon (Fig. 87.4B). The appearance of digital swelling and Raynaud's can mimic the appearance of SSc, particularly in its early sclerodermatous phase, and sclerodactyly, proximal scleroderma, digital ulceration, and calcinosis have all occurred as well. Nailfold capillaroscopy will frequently reveal dilated capillary loops, capillary dropout, and vascular malformations reminiscent of those seen in SSc or inflammatory myositis86 (Fig. 87.5). In fact, the presence of abnormal periungual capillaries is one of the most specific findings in patients whose MCTD phenotype remains stable over time. Less commonly, MCTD patients can experience SLE and dermatomyositis-like skin rashes, photosensitivity, and oral ulceration.

### Pulmonary Manifestations

Although generally thought of as a milder disease than other CTDs, MCTD nonetheless can cause serious and

life-threatening organ damage, particularly with respect to the lungs. Overall, pulmonary involvement is seen in up to 85% of MCTD patients.3, ILD accounts for the majority of pulmonary involvement and presents in a pattern similar to that seen in other CTDs such as SSc and inflammatory myositis. 88-91 On high-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) imaging, ground-glass opacities are the predominant characteristic, usually in a basilar and peripheral distribution with some subpleural sparing that most closely resembles a pattern of nonspecific interstitial pneumonitis87,88,91,92 (Fig. 87.6). Intralobular septal thickening, reticulation, and subpleural nodules are also frequently observed.91, A less common radiographic pattern closer to that of usual interstitial pneumonitis can also be seen and appears on HRCT as more severe fibrosis, with varying degrees of honeycombing, traction bronchiectasis, and a relative paucity of ground-glass opacities.90-92

Some MCTD patients with ILD are completely asymptomatic. Others present with symptoms that include cough and worsening dyspnea. The degree of fibrosis can range from mild to severe, with nearly one in five patients with ILD being graded as having severe fibrosis by HRCT, according to one study. Another suggested that most MCTD-associated pulmonary fibrosis is mild, although worsening of fibrosis can occur throughout the course of disease and result in a decline in pulmonary function and increased mortality. As ILD progresses, serial pulmonary function testing reveals worsening restrictive lung disease and declining carbon monoxide diffusing capacity, findings that are incorporated into the MCTD classification criteria proposed by Kasukawa.

Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) is arguably the most clinically consequential lung manifestation of MCTD. By report it affects between 3.4% and 23.8% of patients, depending on the study cited, the methods used to classify patients with MCTD and PAH, and the screening modality used to detect PAH.85, The etiology of PAH is similar in MCTD to other related conditions such as limited scleroderma and SSc and can present as a primary arteriopathy or secondary to underlying ILD and fibrosis.96, Histopathologically, the arteriopathy results from intimal proliferation and medial hypertrophy of the vessels (Fig. 87.7). Other causes of PAH, although less common, can also include

pulmonary thromboembolic disease and post-capillary left-ventricular dysfunction.

PAH is the leading cause of mortality for MCTD patients, even with recent advances in pharmacotherapy.81, One study followed 179 patients, 25 of whom had been diagnosed with PAH. The 25 patients with PAH had a significantly reduced 5-year mortality (73%) compared with the 154 without PAH (96%). Interestingly, these authors found a higher prevalence of anti-endothelial cell antibodies in those MCTD patients with than without PAH. Another study that followed 201 MCTD patients over a mean duration of 12 years found that one in six diagnosed with PAH died from their disease. Finally, a recent French national multicenter study examined 36 patients with MCTD and PAH and found a 56% 10-year survival rate, similar to the rate seen in patients with PAH associated with other CTDs such as SLE and SSc.

### Kidney

104 However, the spectrum of pathology can range from mild mesangial GN to more severe diffuse proliferative GN with subendothelial immune deposits, cellular crescents, and hypocomplementemia. 102, Children with MCTD have a relatively higher prevalence of proliferative GN than do adults, and this has significance for both diagnosis and treatment of their kidney disease. Rarely, MCTD patients can experience malignant hypertension, acute kidney injury, and microangiopathic hemolytic anemia akin to what is seen in SSc-associated renal crisis.3, Interstitial nephritis, thrombotic microangiopathy, and collapsing glomerulopathy have also been reported as well. The overall prognosis for adult MCTD patients with kidney disease is excellent, although several studies have shown that up to 14% of patients with kidney involvement, particularly those with proliferative GN, can progress to end-stage renal disease.

### Cardiovascular Manifestations

Cardiac involvement is common and can be detected in between 24% and 63% of MCTD patients, according to one systematic 109 This wide variation between studies is review of the literature. at least partly attributable to differences in how cardiac disease is defined and detected.3, The most common cardiac manifestation is pericarditis, which can affect between 30% and 43% of patients.81, Although often silent, as with SSc, the pericardial effusions associated with MCTD can rarely be significant enough to cause tamponade physiology and hemodynamic compromise. 112-115 In addition to pericarditis, MCTD can affect all of the other layers of the heart. Valvular heart disease is well reported, especially mitral valve proplapse. 110, Other studies report evidence of conduction system abnormalities ranging from asymptomatic interventricular conduction delay on electrocardiogram to complete heart block, myocardial dysfunction and myocarditis, and left-ventricular diastolic filling anomalies.116, Cardiomyopathy, leftand right-ventricular systolic dysfunction, and congestive heart failure can occur through several mechanisms, including as a result of PAH, intimal hyperplasia and arteriopathy of the coronary arteries, and frank myocarditis. 110,116-118

### Gastrointestinal Tract

Gastrointestinal (GI) complications of MCTD overlap prominently with those of SSc. Gastroesophageal reflux disease and dysphagia are by far the most common complications, reported in as many as 77% and 61%, respectively, of patients with SSc, MCTD, and UCTD. Those figures were somewhat lower, but still quite significant, in a study limited to MCTD patients, with 48% experiencing heartburn and 38% of patients, dysphagia. MCTD can involve both the upper third of the esophagus containing striated muscle and the lower two-thirds, consisting primarily of smooth muscle. Esophageal manometry will often reveal abnormalities in lower esophageal sphincter pressure, reduced amplitude and diminished

coordination of peristaltic waves throughout the esophageal body, and more uncommonly, reduced upper esophageal sphincter pressure.3, The esophageal dysfunction associated with MCTD appears to be less severe than what is observed in SSc, and many patients have only mild involvement or are asymptomatic.12i Interestingly, one study found a significantly higher prevalence of ILD on computed tomography (CT) imaging of patients who had either radiographic evidence of a dilated esophagus or clinical evidence of dysmotility, suggesting that chronic aspiration may in part contribute to pulmonary parenchymal disease.

MCTD can affect almost every other component of the GI tract as well.
