GI hemorrhage due to vasculitis can occur along almost its entire length, including the duodenum, small intestine, and colon. 123, Some of these cases have responded to immunosuppressive therapy, and other patients have experienced fatal complications. Mesenteric ischemia, colitis, GI hemorrhage, and bowel perforation with peritonitis can also ensue.

Pneumatosis intestinalis is a rare complication of both MCTD and SSc and can portend a poor prognosis, although it can also follow a more benign course in CTD patients who have evidence of intraabdominal air but not clinical peritonitis (Fig. 87.8). 125, The etiology of pneumatosis intestinalis is unknown, but one cause may be linked to bacterial overgrowth and excessive hydrogen production that can lead to leakage of luminal gas into the intestinal wall. Many of these patients can be managed conservatively with oxygen and supportive care. 125, Other GI manifestations include hemoperitoneum, hematobilia, pancreatitis, autoimmune hepatitis, primary biliary cirrhosis (PBC), and protein-losing enteropathy. 129-133

### Muscle Involvement

Inflammatory myositis is a hallmark overlap feature and part of the original description of MCTD. Approximately 80% to 90% of patients with MCTD have muscle involvement of one type or another. Myalgias are common, often without demonstrable

weakness or abnormal creatine kinase (CK) levels, imaging, or electromyography (EMG) testing. When present, inflammatory myositis can range from asymptomatic elevations in serum muscle enzymes to clinical features reminiscent of polymyositis, featuring symmetric proximal muscle weakness and CK elevation. Diagnostic evaluation can reveal nonspecific myopathic features on EMG and evidence of edema in proximal musculature on T1-weighted STIR and T2 fat-suppressed magnetic resonance imaging. Muscle biopsies can be indistinguishable from those seen in patients with polymyositis or dermatomyositis and can sometimes reflect histopathologic features of both diseases simultaneously, including endomysial infiltration of CD8+ cytotoxic T cells and concomitant perivascular infiltration of CD4+ T and B cells134 (Fig. 87.9). While some MCTD patients present with a subacute onset of their muscle disease, others more often present more acutely in the setting of systemic disease activity that can include fever.3,9

### Neurologic Disease

Involvement of the central and peripheral nervous system is relatively uncommon in MCTD compared with other CTDs such as SLE. Nonetheless, there are characteristic clinical manifestations that include trigeminal neuralgia, which can be an initial presenting symptom in MCTD patients and involves both sides of the head.135, Some of these patients may be corticosteroid responsive. Polyradiculopathy, mononeuritis multiplex, and peripheral neuropathy have also been reported. Headaches, often migraine-like, are a relatively common finding, but psychosis and seizure disorders are not. Central nervous system manifestations of MCTD include reports of aseptic meningitis, transverse myelitis, cerebral infarcts and hemorrhage, cauda equina syndrome, adhesive arachnoiditis, myasthenia gravis, retinal vasculitis, optic neuritis, and anti-aquaporin 4—positive neuromyelitis optica. 137-140

### Patients Presenting With Undifferentiated Rheumatic Disease

At disease onset, many patients present with signs and symptoms suggestive of a CTD but without a clear diagnosis. These patients are usually ANA positive and have at least one clinical feature of CTD but do not fulfill classification criteria for any defined CTD. For example, a patient with Raynaud's phenomenon, arthralgias, and puffy fingers may have a positive ANA but no other clinical features suggestive of SSc, SLE, or any other CTD. A subset of these patients likely has incomplete clinical features of

a disease that will, over time, evolve into a recognizable rheumatic syndrome. The majority of patients, however, who initially present with undifferentiated symptoms remain so over the entire course of their illness. Finally, some patients do not fit neatly into any one single disease diagnosis but, rather, have a true overlap of two or more distinct autoimmune diseases, each with their own clinical and serologic hallmarks.

### Early Undifferentiated Systemic Sclerosis

Limited and diffuse SSc often presents in patients who do not display all classical features of the disease at its onset. Indeed, isolated Raynaud's phenomenon is usually the presenting symptom in an ANA-positive patient, and a shorter time of progression from Raynaud's to other features of SSc portends a more aggressive disease course. However, the vast majority of patients with Raynaud's phenomenon will never progress to SSc or any other CTD. Those patients with higher-titer ANAs, those with antibodies for SSc-specific autoantigens such as topoisomerase-I, and those with nailfold capillary abnormalities are more likely to progress from an undifferentiated state to SSc.

### Undifferentiated Connective Disease: A Stable Phenotype

For those patients who present with clinical features suggestive but not diagnostic of a CTD, there remains considerable controversy over whether these patients each have their own distinct CTD as opposed to a clinical variant of a "named" rheumatic disease. One study of 91 patients examined the clinical and serologic profiles of UCTD patients over a mean duration of 5 years. Only 13% evolved over time into SLE while none evolved into either Ssc or idiopathic inflammatory myositis. Clinically, these UCTD patients experienced one or more of the following: arthralgias, Raynaud's phenomenon, arthritis, leukopenia, sicca symptoms, alopecia, and photosensitivity. These symptoms remained remarkably consistent over time. Those few patients who did evolve into SLE did so distinctively, with progression to nephritis, serositis, and hemolytic anemia as examples. Serologic profiles remained stable as well, with most patients exhibiting a single, definable ANA specificity, often against either the Ro(SSA) or RNP antigens.

Another cross-sectional, multicenter study of 184 patients found a similar frequency and constellation of signs and symptoms and overall milder clinical profile. A third study utilizing a large Hungarian cohort of more than 600 UCTD patients reported that two-thirds of the cohort remained undifferentiated after 5 years' follow-up, with Raynaud's, arthralgias, and arthritis representing the majority of reported complaints. Finally, a recent systematic literature review of 1118 UCTD patients published in six studies, followed for a duration ranging from 1 to 15 years, found that only 28% evolved to a clinically classifiable rheumatic disease. Thus, UCTD may represent a distinct and phenotypically stable group of CTDs that is often associated with a milder clinical course, particularly in those patients who, in the first few years, do not show evidence of transformation or evolution into other CTDs.57-59,79

### Overlap Syndromes With Dominant F Features of Scleroderma

Many patients with limited and diffuse SSc share overlapping clinical features with other autoimmune diseases. In some

instances, patients may actually have two or more separate, classifiable autoimmune diseases occurring simultaneously, such as those SSc patients who also display signs and symptoms of inflammatory myositis. Two separate studies found evidence of inflammatory myopathies in 14% to 17% of SSc patients, but this number has varied widely in other studies depending on how stringently myopathy is defined.145-147 A third study reported a 5.9% prevalence of a specific "scleroderma-polymyositis overlap syndrome" in an observational cohort of SSc patients from a single center.

SSc-myositis overlap is more common in diffuse rather than limited SSc and often lacks the characteristic autoantibody profile of either SSc or myositis alone. It is rarely seen in patients who have anti-centromere antibodies.146, Instead, patients with this and other SSc overlap syndromes frequently exhibit characteristic autoantibody profiles that correlate with their overlap phenotype. In the case of SSC-myositis overlap, some patients have nucleolar-pattern ANAs specific for the PM/SCL antigen. Patients with SSc-myositis overlap may have a higher prevalence of interstitial pulmonary fibrosis; more myocardial involvement, including congestive heart failure and cardiacrelated death; and an increased mortality compared with those with SSc alone. 147-149

Autoimmune hepatobiliary disease is another clinical entity long recognized to be associated with both SSc and primary Sjögren's syndrome. In one large registry consisting of 1572 SSc patients, 7.5% had evidence of hepatobiliary disease, more than 60% of whom had PBC. Of those patients with SSc-PBC

overlap, most had limited SSc, were anti-centromere antibody positive, and were positive (92%) for antimitochondrial antibodies similar to patients who have PBC without SSc.

### Overlap Syndromes With Dominant Features of Myositis

In addition to the clinical overlap with SSc already described earlier in this section, some patients with idiopathic inflammatory myositis experience extramuscular manifestations of their disease that include an RA-like inflammatory arthritis, ILD, and photosensitive rashes clinically and histologically similar to those seen in SLE. A recent retrospective multicenter study reported that patients with myositis overlap diseases were more likely to be younger and female than compared with those with inflammatory myositis without overlap features. As our understanding of idiopathic inflammatory myopathies has evolved, it has become clear that what was once thought of as one disease with or without skin involvement (polymyositis/dermatomyositis) per Bohan and Peter's 1975 classification, is actually myriad diseases, many with their own distinct muscle histopathology, autoantibody specificity, clinical presentation, and prognosis.152, As one example, many patients originally classified as having polymyositis with an overlap of Raynaud's phenomenon and RA actually have anti- Jo-1 (anti-synthetase) disease, a distinct syndrome associated with fevers, roughening of the skin on the fingers (mechanic's hands), Raynaud's, inflammatory polyarthritis, and ILD153 (Fig. 87.10).

### Sjögren's Syndrome and Autoimmune Thyroid Disease

Symptoms compatible with Sjögren's syndrome are prevalent in patients with autoimmune diseases that include SLE, RA, and others. These patients are more commonly seronegative than are patients with primary Sjogren's syndrome and have a lower risk of extraglandular involvement. Clinically, both primary and secondary Sjögren's patients experience similar symptoms of dryness of the eyes, mouth, or skin. On histopathologic examination, those with secondary disease will often have milder exocrine gland involvement with or without characteristic lymphoid aggregates. Autoimmune thyroid disease is also commonly seen in patients with RA, SLE, and other autoimmune conditions. In some cases, the thyroid disease may antedate the onset of other rheumatic diseases. Most patients with Hashimoto's thyroiditis make autoantibodies targeting thyroid peroxidase and/or thyroglobulin and those with Graves' disease make antibodies to the thyroid-stimulating hormone receptor. These patients may present across the spectrum of disease, from subclinical autoantibody positivity to overt signs and symptoms of thyroid hormone deficiency or excess, including thyrotoxicosis or myxedema.

### Treatment of Overlap Connective Tisue − Disease Syndromes

All patients with MCTD should be followed closely and managed according to their clinical and laboratory assessment and specific underlying internal organ involvement60 (Table 87.5). Because pulmonary involvement and PAH are significant morbidities that can begin asymptomatically, most MCTD patients should be screened at regular intervals with a combination of HRCT

chest imaging, pulmonary function testing, and echocardiography.3, No randomized prospective double-blinded clinical trials for MCTD or UCTD overlap diseases have been performed to guide approach to therapy for these diseases.96, In fact, a 2018 systematic review of clinical practice guidelines (CPG) for MCTD reviewed 124 different references and found none satisfactory upon which to guide CPG development. As a result, there is no standardized approach toward the treatment of patients with MCTD or overlap syndromes. MCTD and other overlap CTD patients have generally been thought to have a better overall prognosis than their counterparts with classically defined rheumatic diseases, including a better response to corticosteroid therapy. However, many observational studies refute this notion, especially for patients who develop PAH.9, Therefore, therapy is usually guided by major organ manifestation(s) and borrows from the approach to treating similar complications in other rheumatic diseases such as SLE, SSc, RA, and inflammatory myositis.

Corticosteroids offer a first-line approach to inflammatory complications such as myositis, alveolitis, arthritis, dermatitis, nephritis, and serositis.3, Low-dose corticosteroids are often beneficial for milder skin, pleuro-pericardial disease, and joint manifestations. Higher doses of corticosteroids are usually reserved for more severe internal organ involvement such as myositis, ILD, nephritis, myocarditis, and vasculitis. Interestingly, in addition to standard proton-pump inhibitor therapy, corticosteroids may also benefit MCTD patients with esophageal dysfunction, unlike those with SSc. Anti-malarial medications such as hydroxychloroquine can be used to treat skin rashes, arthritis, and other features that overlap closely with SLE.

Raynaud's phenomenon can be treated conservatively by keeping the extremities, head, and other body parts shielded from exposure to the cold and avoiding sympathomimetic agents. In

severe or refractory cases, vasodilators including calcium channel blockers, phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors (such as sildenafil), and prostacyclin analogs can be employed to control symptoms and ischemic complications. Intravenous immunoglobulin can be used for severe cases of inflammatory myositis as it is in patients with polymyositis and dermatomyositis, including those with esophageal involvement.156, Immunosuppressive and cytotoxic therapies are reserved for the most severe cases of internal organ involvement, both when additive therapy is required to control disease activity and when longer-term corticosteroid sparing effects are desired. These include the use of methotrexate, azathioprine, mycophenolate mofetil, and cyclophosphamide.

Low-dose methotrexate can be particularly useful in treating patients with more severe inflammatory a rthritis t hat i s not responsive to nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory m edications or low-dose corticosteroid therapy. Both methotrexate and azathioprine can also be effective to treat inflammatory myositis. Severe lung and renal involvement often necessitate treatment with azathioprine, mycophenolate mofetil, or cyclophosphamide. Newer targeted therapies such as the anti-interleukin-6 receptor antibody tocilizumab have demonstrated efficacy in stabilizing pulmonary function in patients with SSC-associated ILD, receiving U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approval in 2021.158, Similarly, the tyrosine kinase inhibitor nintedanib received FDA approval for demonstrating efficacy in slowing the progression of ILD in both idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and SSc-associated ILD patients with progressive fibrotic disease.160, Finally, the B cell depleting agent, rituximab, while failing to demonstrate superiority to cyclophosphamide, did improve forced vital capacity from baseline to 24 weeks similar to its active comparator while being associated with fewer adverse events.

Therapy for PAH has also advanced considerably in recent years and has improved exercise tolerance, quality of life, and symptoms. Right-heart catheterization can be useful to guide specific choice of therapy that includes calcium channel blockers, angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, prostacyclin analogs, and endothelin receptor antagonists.

As the immunobiology of CTDs becomes better defined, the treatment with MCTD will likely evolve in step with the development of new classes of targeted immunotherapies. For example, medications that block types I and II IFNs, their receptors, and the signaling pathways downstream from those receptors, such as Janus kinase inhibitors, are undergoing study for the treatment of CTDs whose features overlap closely with those of MCTD and UCTDs including SLE, SSc, and idiopathic inflammatory myopathies.

# Classification and Epidemiology of Systemic Vasculitis

88

### KEY POINTS

The incidence of vasculitis can vary across geographic regions, age, sex, and race, suggesting that genetic and environmental risk factors contribute to susceptibility to disease.

### Introduction

The vasculitides are a group of complex disorders characterized by inflammation of blood vessel walls that can lead to ischemia and organ damage. A vasculitis is considered primary when no underlying etiology such as infection, another rheumatic disease, drugs, or malignancy has been identified and secondary when the vasculitis is considered a consequence of one of these comorbidities or exposures. The heterogeneous and protean nature of the vasculitides' clinical courses and outcomes, as well as the lack of a single "gold standard" test for either diagnosis or classification, have resulted in great efforts to develop criteria useful in both clinical care and research. The first part of this chapter will review current classification criteria in vasculitis, and the second part will discuss current epidemiologic data on the vasculitides.

### Classification of Vasculitis

### Introduction to the Concept of Classification

The vasculitides are a diverse group of disorders, each with a distinct pathogenesis, natural history, and associated therapeutic

approach, which underscores the value of accurate categorizations. Due to the limited understanding of the pathophysiology of these complex diseases and their overlapping features, several categorization systems have been developed and revised by international collaborations to ensure consistency in disease definitions (i.e., nomenclature) and classification criteria.

There are important differences in the purposes of a nomenclature system, classification criteria, and diagnostic criteria, and therefore, they should not be used interchangeably. A nomenclature system is the name that should be used to define a specific disease process. A nomenclature system provides a framework upon which classification and diagnostic criteria can be developed. In 1994 the first International Chapel Hill Consensus Conference (CHCC) on the Nomenclature of Systemic Vasculitides convened to address the need for standardized terms and definitions; a revised version was developed in 2012.1, Prior to the CHCC, different names were being used for the same disease, and conversely, the same name was being used to refer to different diseases. For example, the term polyarteritis nodosa (PAN) was initially used to describe nearly any form of necrotizing arteritis; thereafter, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA)—associated vasculitides were noted to have a separate clinical presentation and course and were given distinct names to differentiate them from PAN. Over the past decade, academic medicine has shifted away from eponyms to descriptive or etiology-based nomenclature, and this movement has led to several changes in disease names within vasculitis (e.g., Wegener's granulomatosis was replaced by granulomatosis with polyangiitis, and HenochSchönlein purpura was replaced by IgA vasculitis).

Classification criteria are a set of standardized observations that are intended to create a relatively homogeneous cohort of patients for clinical research. Classification systems build upon the nomenclature system and include features of a disease that distinguish it from other similar diseases. The goal of classification criteria is to standardize patient populations by identifying patients who share key features of a condition and is less focused on capturing all possible patients with the condition. Classification criteria are less useful for individual patients and more important in the study of groups of patients, allowing comparison of

results across studies and ensuring appropriate enrollment into clinical trials. Classification criteria aim to have high specificity, while a lower priority is placed on sensitivity; therefore the falsenegative rates of most classification criteria make them less useful in routine clinical care (i.e., a given patient may have the correct diagnosis but may not meet classification criteria).

Unlike classification criteria, diagnostic criteria are a set of symptoms, signs, and tests that guide the care of individual patients and must be high in both sensitivity and specificity. Fewer attempts have been made in developing diagnostic criteria in vasculitis, owing to the challenges of forming criteria that can apply to the heterogeneous manifestations seen in vasculitis.

The first set of classification criteria for several forms of vasculitis was published in 1990 and endorsed by the American College of Rheumatology (ACR). As knowledge of vasculitis evolved, there was a need to revise the 1990 criteria and develop new criteria for microscopic polyangiitis (MPA), a distinct disease that was not included in the 1990 classification criteria. An international effort, the Diagnostic and Classification Criteria for Vasculitis (DCVAS) study was conducted to develop validated, data-driven sets of revised classification criteria for several vasculitides. Given the increased understanding of vasculitis, newer diagnostic tests, such as testing for ANCA, and advancements in vascular imaging, reappraising existing criteria was in order and signifies the substantial gains made in this field. It is important to note that the classification criteria were intended to be applied to patients

already diagnosed with vasculitis to differentiate among different forms of vasculitis; this would ensure standardized and homogenous populations for research studies. Therefore application of the criteria assumes a diagnosis of vasculitis has been established, including exclusion of potential mimics of vasculitis. Importantly, classification criteria should not be used as diagnostic criteria and do not perform well for that purpose.

### A Framework for Classification of Vasculitis: Vessel Size Versus Pathogenesis

The most widely used classification system used in vasculitis, which will be used in this chapter, begins with separating vasculitides based on the predominantly affected vessel size (Table 88.1 and Fig. 88.1). Large vessel refers to the aorta and its main branches and the corresponding veins; medium vessel includes the main visceral arteries and veins such as renal, mesenteric, and coronary arteries; and small vessel refers to intraparenchymal arteries, arterioles, capillaries, venules, and veins. However, there are limitations to this approach. The vessel-size category is based on the predominantly affected vessel size, but vasculitides in all the major categories can involve any size artery. Additionally, a subset of patients (such as in Behçet's disease) may lack any discernible vascular involvement, although there is still the potential for true vasculitis to occur. Most importantly, classification based on vessel size does not provide information on biologic processes. As

understanding of pathogenic mechanisms of disease grows, classification according to disease process (e.g., ANCA-associated vs. immune complex small-vessel vasculitis) is becoming increasingly popular, and molecular classification schemes may eventually complement or even replace current methods of discrimination.

### Small-Vessel Vasculitis

The small-vessel vasculitides can be further divided into ANCAassociated vasculitis and immune complex—mediated vasculitis.

### Anti-neutrophil Cytoplasmic Antibody-Associated Vasculitis

ANCA-associated vasculitis (AAV) is a group of small-vessel vasculitides characterized by necrotizing vasculitis predominantly

affecting small vessels, few or no immune deposits, and association with ANCA. AAV includes granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA), MPA, and eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA). The discovery of ANCA had a major impact on classification of vasculitis, particularly within the small-vessel vasculitides. For example, the inclusion of MPA within AAV rather than within PAN or IgA vasculitis was in part influenced by its association with ANCA.

While overlapping features exist among the three types of AAV, differences in predominant pathology, organ manifestations, and ANCA specificity help distinguish them. GPA is more commonly associated with granulomatous inflammation, upper and lower respiratory tract involvement, ANCA with a cytoplasmic pattern (C-ANCA), and specificity for antibodies to proteinase 3 (PR3). Patients with MPA commonly have glomerulonephritis

and perinuclear pattern (P-ANCA) with specificity for antibodies to myeloperoxidase (MPO). However, it is important to note there is a significant degree of overlap between GPA and MPA, and either ANCA type (PR3 and/or MPO) or negative testing for ANCA can be seen in both diseases. EGPA is distinguished by its association with asthma, blood eosinophilia, and eosinophilrich inflammation seen on tissue biopsy. ANCA is relatively less common in EGPA (38% to 73%) and, if positive, typically is MPO-ANCA.

In 2022, a revised ACR/European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology (EULAR)-endorsed classification criteria was developed and validated for GPA, MPA, and EGPA6-8 (see Table 88.1). Compared with the 1990 criteria, the 2022 criteria incorporated ANCA type, developed a separate set of criteria for MPA, and included more disease manifestations. The European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology/Pediatric Rheumatology International Trial Organization/Pediatric Rheumatology European Society (EULAR/PRINTO/PReS) task force developed classification criteria for pediatric GPA. Revised classification criteria for children are currently being developed to incorporate additional diseases (e.g., MPA) and newer diagnostic tests. Whether separate classification criteria for children are necessary is unclear and controversial, as many vasculitides often present similarly in adults and children, albeit with different prevalences.

### Classification by Anti-neutrophil Cytoplasmic Antibody Specificity

Within GPA and MPA, subclassification by antigenic specificity of ANCA (PR3 vs. MPO) is a common alternative to clinicopathologic classification. The ANCA-based approach is based on data from genomic studies and clinical trial data linking ANCA specificity to disease outcomes. Several studies have demonstrated that ANCA has a pathogenic role in AAV, although clinical observations suggest that ANCA alone is not sufficient to induce dis- 9-15 Two genome-wide association studies found that ease activity. genetic distinctions are more closely aligned with ANCA specificity than clinical presentations, further supporting that ANCA may indeed contribute to disease susceptibility and pathogenesis. 16, Furthermore, several studies have found that, compared with classification by disease type (GPA vs. MPA), ANCA specificity is more strongly associated with treatment response, relapse, and other long-term outcomes. 18-21 These clinical and genetic associations with ANCA specificity suggest that ANCA type may classify subsets of AAV better than the traditional GPA/MPA classification.

### Immune e Complex-Mediated Small-Vessel Vasculitis

The remaining primary vasculitides that predominantly affect small vessels have a common immunopathologic feature of immune complex-mediated inflammation that leads to tissue injury. This is in contrast to AAV, which is pauci-immune (i.e., few or no immune deposits). Among the immune complex—mediated small-vessel vasculitides, IgA vasculitis is the only disease to have a validated classification criteria available.7,

IgA Vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein). IgA vasculitis is characterized by IgA immune complexes and IgA deposition on tissue biopsy. Common features include rash (often purpura), arthritis/ arthralgias, abdominal pain, and renal disease (hematuria, proteinuria). The 1990 ACR criteria were developed to distinguish IgA vasculitis from other types of vasculitis seen in adults22 (see Table 88.1). In 2005 the EULAR/PReS developed criteria for children.

Cryoglobulinemic Vasculitis. Deposition of circulating cryoglobulins leading to organ damage is the hallmark feature of cryoglobulinemic vasculitis (CV). Importantly, it is possible to have asymptomatic cryoglobulinemia without a clinically apparent disorder of CV, and therefore, the detection of circulating cryoglobulins alone is insufficient to diagnose CV. CV is routinely classified further by the immunoglobulin composition of the cryoglobulins23:

Type I—Cryoglobulins are monoclonal immunoglobulins, typically IgG or IgM. Type I cryoglobulinemia develops in the setting of monoclonal gammopathies or B cell lineage malignancy (e.g., multiple myeloma, Waldenström's macroglobulinemia, or chronic lymphocytic leukemia).

Type II—Cryoglobulins are composed of monoclonal IgM (or IgG or IgA) with rheumatoid factor activity and polyclonal immunoglobulins. Type II cryoglobulinemia is most often associated with hepatitis C virus infection but can also be seen in infections with hepatitis B virus or HIV, malignancy, or autoimmune diseases such as systemic lupus erythematosus and Sjogren's syndrome.

Type III—Cryoglobulins are a mixture of polyclonal IgG and polyclonal IgM, and type III is often secondary to autoimmune disorders but also infections such as with hepatitis C virus.

Both type II and type III are referred to as mixed cryoglobulinemia and cause cutaneous vasculitis, peripheral neuropathy, and membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis, as well as nonspecific symptoms such as fatigue, arthralgias, and myalgias.

Hypocomplementemic Urticarial Vasculitis. Hypocomplementemic urticarial vasculitis (HUV) refers to an autoimmune disorder that involves urticarial vasculitis, which typically affects the skin and is associated with hypocomplementemia. When additional systemic features are present, such as arthritis, glomerulonephritis, uveitis, episcleritis, or recurrent abdominal pain, the disease is referred to as hypocomplementemic urticarial vasculitis syndrome (HUVS). HUV is commonly associated with low serum C1q levels and anti-C1q autoantibodies.

Anti-glomerular Basement Membrane Disease (Goodpasture's Syndrome). The presentation of anti-glomerular basement membrane (GBM) disease typically involves glomerulonephritis and pulmonary hemorrhage and is distinguished from other pulmonary—renal syndromes by the presence of anti-GBM antibodies, which have been implicated in the pathogenesis of disease. Between 10% and 50% of patients with anti-GBM disease also are positive for ANCA and can develop additional features of AAV both at the time of presentation with anti-GBM disease and later in the clinical course when the anti-GBM disease is quiescent. ANCA may also be detectable years prior to the onset of anti- GBM disease, further supporting theories that ANCA may be involved in disease pathogenesis.

### Medium-Vessel Vasculitis

### Polyarteritis Nodosa

The definition of PAN has evolved considerably since it was initially described in the 1800s. Early classifications of PAN included what was later referred to as microscopic polyangiitis and hypersensitivity vasculitis, but new insights led to recognition that these were separate diseases. PAN predominantly affects medium arteries such as main visceral arteries and their branches and commonly involves inflammatory aneurysms and arterial stenoses. To

distinguish PAN from MPA, the definition of PAN specifically excludes the presence of glomerulonephritis and ANCA. The 1990 ACR criteria for classification of PAN includes many of the common manifestations such as nonspecific constitutional symptoms, neuropathy, renal involvement, and testicular pain. PAN is strongly linked to hepatitis B virus infection and, to a lesser degree, is associated with hepatitis C virus and HIV. EULAR/PReS proposed separate criteria for childhood PAN, which removed the criteria for hepatitis B infection and modified the other criteria. It is also important to distinguish idiopathic PAN from deficiency of adenosine deaminase 227 (see section on Monogenic Vasculitides below).

### Kawasaki's Disease

Kawasaki's disease (KD) typically occurs in children under the age of 5 and predominantly affects medium and small arteries. Coronary arteritis is a common complication. The American Heart Association published diagnostic criteria and treatment guidelines for KD that were developed by a committee of experts and updated in 2017.28 Diagnosis of classic KD requires 5 or more days of fever plus at least four of the five principal clinical features. Patients with suspected KD who did not meet these diagnostic criteria are considered to have incomplete KD but may still benefit from therapy. Other groups from Japan and Europe have produced similar diagnostic criteria.7,29

### Large-Vessel Vasculitis

### Giant Cell Arteritis

Giant cell arteritis (GCA) is considered a disease exclusively seen in older adults and, by definition, onset occurs only in those aged 50 years or older. Early classification criteria, such as the 1990 ACR classification criteria of GCA, were focused on cranial symptoms of headache, temporal artery abnormalities, and an abnormal artery biopsy, typically a temporal artery biopsy; hence, in the past GCA was commonly referred to as temporal arteritis. However, replacement of the term temporal arteritis with GCA was motivated by an increased recognition that GCA can affect many other extracranial large arteries, including the aorta and its branches. Advancements in imaging of the vasculature now demonstrate that up to 30% of patients with GCA have extracranial large vessel involvement such as thoracic aortic aneurysms and subclavian artery involvement.30, The 2022 ACR/EULAR GCA Classification Criteria includes a wider spectrum of disease manifestations, including thoracoabdominal vessel involvement, polymyalgia rheumatica (present in about 50% of patients with GCA), and vision loss32 (Table 88.1). In addition, newer vascular imaging modalities, including ultrasound of the temporal artery and positron emission tomography (PET) of the aorta, were incorporated into the criteria, reflecting advances in imaging techniques for vasculitis. It is notable that GCA is a good example of a vasculitis that has the potential to have a range of arterial sizes affected, including large and medium arteries (e.g., aorta) and smaller arteries (e.g., central retinal artery).

### Takayasu's Arteritis

As opposed to GCA, Takayasu's arteritis (TAK) typically occurs in patients under the age of 50 to 60 years, and the classic presentation of TAK involves signs and symptoms related to its effects on the aorta and its major branches. In addition to expanding the inclusion of signs and symptoms of ischemia, imaging findings were a major

addition to the 2022 ACR/EULAR Classification Criteria for TAK33 (Table 88.1). Similarly to GCA, the inclusion of vascular imaging to the TAK criteria reflects the central role of imaging in clinical practice and enhances sensitivity to detect earlier-stage disease.

Giant Cell Arteritis and Takayasu's Arteritis: Two Different Diseases or a Spectrum of the Same Disease? With the growing awareness of large-vessel involvement in GCA, many similarities between GCA and TAK have been identified, raising the question as to whether these two separate diseases are varying expressions of the same disease.34, Similarities between GCA and TAK include overlapping signs and symptoms, similar patterns of large vessel involvement, similar histologic findings, and common genetic variants. However, studies have also suggested variations in vascular distribution and differences in the effectiveness of therapies. Additionally, GCA and TAK have different genetic associations, providing more evidence of a distinct pathogenesis. 42-44 The challenges in defining these overlapping groups of large-vessel vasculitides underscore the need for updated classification criteria and a deeper understanding of pathophysiology of these two entities.

### Other Classifications

### Variable-Vessel Vasculitis: Behçet's Disease and Cogan's Syndrome

Since Behçet's disease was first described in the 1930s, there have been over 15 classification criteria proposed for the disease. In an effort to develop a standardized criteria, the international study group (ISG) for Behçet's disease created a new set of criteria in 1990 that required at least three recurrences of oral ulcers over a 12-month period and at least two of the following: recurrent genital ulceration, eye lesions, skin lesions, or positive pathergy test. In several subsequent validation cohorts, specificity of the ISG criteria was high, but sensitivity was low. In 2014 an international team of 27 countries developed the new International Criteria for Behçet's Disease (ICBD) to improve sensitivity compared with the ISG criteria. The ICBD criteria no longer required the presence of oral aphthosis and included vascular lesions and neurologic manifestations. Despite the reported higher sensitivity of the ICBD criteria, ISG remains the preferred classification criteria for use in clinical trials of Behçet's disease.

There are currently no validated classification or diagnostic criteria for Cogan's syndrome, a disease characterized by ocular inflammatory lesions (notably interstitial keratitis), sensorineural hearing loss, vestibular dysfunction, aortitis, aortic aneurysms, and valvulitis.

### Single-Organ Vasculitis

Vasculitis can also occur in a single organ, such as the skin or the central nervous system (CNS). In these cases, comprehensive evaluation is needed to ensure the presentation is not an early or limited expression of a systemic vasculitis. Often, patients originally classified as having single-organ vasculitis will later develop other organ manifestations that require reclassification of disease. Primary angiitis of the CNS is the most clearly recognized singleorgan vasculitis and can involve both mediumand small-sized arteries.

### Secondary Causes of Vasculitis

Many other systemic autoimmune diseases are associated with vasculitis, including systemic lupus erythematosus, Sjogren's

syndrome, rheumatoid arthritis, and relapsing polychondritis. Vasculitis can also be attributed to a wide variety of medications, toxins, or infectious agents. The most common causes of druginduced severe systemic small vessel vasculitis include hydralazine and propylthiouracil, which are associated with MPO-ANCA and can potentially lead to alveolar hemorrhage and glomerulonephritis. Almost every class of medication has been associated with causing vasculitis, although true causality can be difficult to prove. With the advent of immunotherapy to treat cancer, there is recognition of vasculitis associated with immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs).47, Vasculitis has been observed in several ICIs and typically resolves with administration of glucocorticoids or withdrawing the ICI.

### Monogenic Vasculitides

Although vasculitis is generally considered a polygenic disease, the growing availability of whole-genome and exome sequencing has led to the discovery of single gene mutations in subsets of patients with vasculitis. Deficiency of adenosine deaminase 2 (DADA2) was the first monogenic vasculitis syndrome described and can present with features of PAN, especially ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke, often in younger the recognition that tumor necrosis factor inhibitors are effective in treating DADA2 but not used regularly in treatment of PAN, it is important to consider screening patients with suspected PAN for DADA2.51

VEXAS (vacuoles, E1 enzyme, X-linked, autoinflammatory, somatic) syndrome is caused by somatic mutations in

ubiquitin-activating enzyme 1 (UBA1) and was identified in men with a variety of inflammatory disorders (including relapsing polychondritis, PAN, and GCA) and hematologic abnormalities. Early data indicate that many cases of VEXAS occur among men with several forms of vasculitis, including GCA, PAN, and relapsing polychondritis, among other comorbidities.

COPA syndrome is caused by a mutation of the COPA gene encoding coatomer complex-I, which is involved in intracellular trafficking. Patients with COPA syndrome present with pulmonary hemorrhage, interstitial lung disease, and arthritis and can develop positive autoantibodies including ANCA. Patients with COPA respond well to several therapies used to treat AAV, including cyclophosphamide and rituximab. COPA syndrome is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern with variable penetrance. With the increasing availability of testing for these and other forms of monogenic disease, more patients with vasculitis or vasculitis-like disease will be more properly or additionally diagnosed with one of these syndromes.

### Epidemiology of Vasculitis

Ensuring the appropriate classification of each type of vasculitis is a critical first step to performing clinical research, including epidemiologic studies. Understanding the epidemiology of disease allows for identification of risk factors and patterns of disease. Such observations can inform studies on pathophysiology and clinical management. Table 88.2 presents the major epidemiologic features of several forms of systemic vasculitis. This section will

review common themes in the epidemiology of various types of vasculitis.54-102

### Geography

The incidences of various systemic vasculitides vary tremendously by geography. This variation may reflect differences in genetics, environmental exposures dictated by continent and latitude, and the prevalence of other risk factors for the disease. Although Behçet's disease is rare in North Americans (affecting only approximately 1 in 300,000), the condition is substantially more common among inhabitants of countries that border the ancient Silk Route.45, Similarly, although TAK is rare in the United States, the disease is reportedly the most common cause of renal artery stenosis in India. Several studies indicate that the prevalence of GCA in Olmsted County, Minnesota, is similar to that of Scandinavian countries, with an annual incidence rate of approximately 240 cases for every 1 million people older than 50 years. The similar prevalence calculations across these countries probably reflect shared genetic risk factors for this condition, because many of the current inhabitants of Olmsted County are descended from Scandinavian and Northern European immigrants. With the steady increase in worldwide migration and increasingly mobile societies, the prevalences of the vasculitides will continue to change in many countries, and clinicians need to avoid over-reliance on assumptions of the rarity of some diseases to avoid missing the diagnosis.

### Age, Sex, and Ethnicity

Age is an important consideration in the epidemiology of vasculitis. Among patients with KD, 80% are younger than 5 years. In contrast, GCA almost exclusively occurs in patients older than 50 years, and the mean age is approximately 70 years. Age also may affect disease severity and outcome. Most cases of IgA vasculitis occur in children and have self-limited courses that resolve within several weeks. In adults, IgA vasculitis has a higher likelihood of chronicity and a greater likelihood of a poor renal 106 outcome.

There are notable sex differences in the epidemiology of several types of vasculitis. TAK has an overwhelming tendency to occur in women (9:1 female-to-male ratio). Pauci-immune forms of vasculitis such as GPA occur in men and women with approximately equal frequencies, but some evidence exists for a female predominance in patients with the nonsevere form of the disease and a male predominance among patients with severe GPA. Behçet's disease tends to be more severe in younger male patients with a greater frequency of advanced ocular disease.

Some forms of vasculitis have striking variations in tendencies to affect specific ethnic groups. For example, GCA and GPA occur with a pronounced predominance in White people, whereas TAK and KD have higher incidences in people of Asian ances- 105, Additionally, the relative proportion of patients try. with AAV who have antibodies to anti—proteinase 3 (PR3-ANCA) versus antibodies to myeloperoxidase (MPO-ANCA) is quite different between Northern Europe (majority anti-PR3 ANCA) and Japan (vast majority anti-MPO ANCA).

### Genetics

Although genetic risk factors are undoubtedly important in the susceptibility to some forms of vasculitis, familial cases are rare (with the exception of GCA, as subsequently discussed). The

rarity of familial cases in vasculitis indicates that the genetics of these disorders, aside from monogenic causes (see section on Monogenic Vasculitides above), are polygenic and complex. For example, Behçet's disease is associated with human leukocyte antigen (HLA)-B51, which is found in about 80% of patients of Asian ancestry with the disease. The prevalence of HLA-B51 is significantly higher among patients with Behçet's disease in Japan than among control subjects without the disease (55% vs. <15%). However, among the sporadic cases of Behçet's disease involving White patients in the United States, HLA-B51 occurs in fewer than 15% of cases. In addition to increasing the risk of disease susceptibility in some patients, HLA-B51 increases disease severity. Patients with this gene are more likely to have posterior uveitis, CNS involvement, or other severe manifestations.

Reports of familial aggregation in GCA are common. Genetic studies have indicated roles for class II HLA alleles such as HLA- DRB1*0401 and HLA-DRB1*0101, although the specific associations have varied from study to study. 112, Other work indicates that certain TNF microsatellite polymorphisms may contribute to disease susceptibility.

Two genome-wide association studies confirmed a modest genetic component to the pathogenesis of AAV.16, These studies both demonstrated that the strongest genetic associations are with the type of ANCA (anti-PR3 vs. anti-MPO) rather than with the clinical diagnosis of GPA versus MPA. In particular, PRTN3, SERPINA1, and PTPN22 genes confer a higher risk of PR3-ANCA AAV, confirming the central role of anti—proteinase 3 autoreactivity in the disease process.

### Environment

Several environmental and occupational exposures have been linked to the development of vasculitis, although confirmatory data are frequently lacking. Medications and certain infections have well-known associations with vasculitides. As examples, antibiotics such as the penicillins and cephalosporins are common causes of drug-induced vasculitis, and virtually any medication can trigger vasculitis. Hepatitis B and C viruses have well-recognized links to PAN and mixed CV, respectively. Moreover, both medications and infections appear to possibly trigger IgA vasculitis.

Associations have been reported, but not confirmed, between exposure to inhaled silica dust and some types of pauci-immune vasculitis. Precise understanding of the relationships between exposures and vasculitis is complicated by difficulties in obtaining reliable measurements of the levels of such exposures, the likelihood of recall bias among patients who are diagnosed with vasculitis, and the choice of appropriate control groups.

The epidemiologic differences among individual types of vasculitis raise compelling questions about the etiologies of these diseases. Ultimately, better insights into the pathogenesis of these conditions should explain these differences and facilitate the development of new treatments and more refined classification schemes. In particular, elucidation of the cellular and molecular pathways, as well as genetic risk factors of vasculitis and other rheumatic diseases, will likely enhance current classification criteria. Most likely, criteria will move toward a hybrid of clinical, imaging, genetic, and molecular markers of disease, and the relative weights of these individual components will be determined by the degree of understanding of the pathogenesis of the disease and importance of the variables to clinical outcomes. Therefore disease classification is continually evolving and should be responsive to changes in understanding of the disease processes.

# Giant Cell Arteritis, Polymyalgia Rheumatica, and Takayasu's Arteritis

### KEY POINTS

### Introduction

Giant cell arteritis (GCA) and polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR) are discussed together because they affect similar epidemiologic subsets of patients and often occur together in the same individual. Although GCA is a disease of older people and Takayasu's arteritis (TAK) is a disease of younger people, their shared predilection for causing vasculitis of large arteries and their nearly identical histopathologic changes prompt their inclusion in the same chapter.

### Giant Cell Arteritis a and Polymyalgia Rheumatica

### American College of Rheumatology Classification Criteria

Classification criteria for the diagnosis of GCA have been proposed by the American College of Rheumatology (ACR) (Table 89.1). These criteria had limitations, which led to ACR/European

Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology (EULAR) updated classification criteria in 2022 to include highly specific features (e.g., sudden visual loss, jaw claudication) in addition to extracranial manifestations (e.g., large vessel involvement) (Table 89.1). Three classification schemes have been proposed for PMR (Table 89.2).3-5 The provisional criteria for 2012 were developed in part to incorporate information from ultrasound evaluation.

### Definitions

### Giant Cell Arteritis

GCA is the most common form of systemic vasculitis in adults. The disease affects primarily the thoracic aorta and its major branches, especially the extracranial segments of the carotid artery in patients older than 50 years. The most feared complication of GCA is irreversible loss of vision. Because the cause of GCA is unknown, various names—including temporal arteritis, cranial arteritis, and granulomatous arteritis—have been used to highlight different salient features. All the names for this disease have both merits and shortcomings. The designations temporal arteritis or cranial arteritis, for example, convey how frequently the temporal arteries or other cranial arteries are involved but fail to capture GCA's more widespread nature. Although the terms granulomatous arteritis and GCA recognize an important pathologic finding, this focus is undeserved because giant cells are absent in approximately half of the cases and may be present in other forms of vasculitis. With no perfect name available, this chapter bows to convention and refers to this disease as giant cell arteritis.

### Polymyalgia Rheumatica

Polymyalgia rheumatica, a term suggested by Dr. Stuart Barber in 1957, is a syndrome characterized by aching in the proximal portions of the extremities and torso. Because no specific diagnostic tests or pathologic findings exist, PMR is defined by its clinical features. The features included in most definitions of PMR are (1) aching and morning stiffness lasting half an hour or longer in the shoulder, hip girdle, neck, or a combination; (2) duration of these symptoms for 1 month or longer; (3) patient age older than 50 years; and (4) laboratory evidence of systemic inflammation such

as an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR). Some definitions also include a rapid response to small doses of glucocorticoids, such as prednisone 10 mg/day. The presence of another specific disease other than GCA, such as rheumatoid arthritis (RA), chronic infection, polymyositis, or malignancy, excludes the diagnosis of PMR.

### Epidemiology

The incidence of GCA varies widely in different populations, from less than 0.1 per 100,000 to 77 per 100,000 individuals age 50

years and older.6, The greatest risk factor for GCA is aging: the disease almost never occurs in individuals younger than 50 years, and its incidence rises steadily thereafter. The average age at diagnosis has risen during the past half-century, from 74.7 years in the 1950s to 79.2 years at present. Geography and race/ethnicity are also important risk factors. The highest incidence is found in Scandinavians and in Americans of Scandinavian descent. The lowest incidence of GCA is reported in Japanese, northern Indians, and African Americans. In western Europe, GCA is more common in the northern latitudes than the southern. The diagnosis of GCA has increased during the past 20 to 40 years, possibly because of greater physician awareness.6, Some studies have reported seasonal variations and clustering of cases, with peaks approximately 7 years apart.9, The prevalence of GCA in Olmsted County, Minnesota, home to many Scandinavian immigrants, is 200 per 100,000 population age 50 years or older. Autopsy studies suggest that GCA may be more common than is clinically apparent. Östberg16 found arteritis in 1.6% of 889 postmortem cases in which sections of the temporal artery and two transverse sections of the aorta were examined.

Genetic susceptibility to GCA was initially suggested by reports of it in families17 and, more recently, by studies demonstrating an association with genes in the class II human leukocyte antigen (HLA) region.18, Sixty percent of GCA patients have HLA- DRB1*04 haplotype variants, which have a common sequence motif in the second hypervariable region of the B1 molecule. This motif differs from the one associated with RA. The low prevalence of these alleles in African Americans might explain why GCA is uncommon in this population. To date, it is the form of systemic vasculitis most closely associated with class II HLA genes. Class I HLA genes, particularly HLA-B*15, might also augment susceptibility. Susceptibility to GCA and PMR has also been associated with polymorphisms of genes for TNF, intercellular adhesion molecules, and interleukin (IL)-18.6

The existence of environmental risk factors is suggested by the geographic clustering of GCA cases. Smoking increases the risk for GCA six-fold in women. Of the multiple infectious diseases potentially linked to GCA, varicella zoster has received the most attention.22-28 One study found varicella zoster viral antigens in the inflamed temporal arteries of 74% of patients with GCA compared with 8% of controls. Another study, however, identified varicella zoster viral antigen in only 3 of 25 affected temporal arteries. In addition, higher incidences of GCA have not been found in countries with increased incidence of herpes zoster. Retrospective studies described an increased risk of GCA after live varicella zoster vaccination (HR 2.70). A similar effect of the recombinant zoster vaccine on GCA incidence has not been described. Other studies have implicated Mycoplasma pneumoniae, parvovirus B19, and parainfluenza virus type I.12, The results of examining temporal artery biopsy specimens with polymerase chain reaction methods to detect parvovirus B19 DNA have been negative or inconsistent. The reported association between GCA and Chlamydia pneumoniae infection has not withstood close scrutiny. One study was unable to identify bacteria in temporal artery biopsies. Sex and health status also influence the development of GCA. Women are affected approximately twice as often as men. Having diabetes reduces the risk of GCA by 50% in women. Clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential (CHIP), a pre-malignant condition associated with increasing age and cardiovascular disease, occurs more frequently than expected in patients with GCA compared with ageand sex-matched controls. 33, All-cause mortality is increased in patients with GCA, particularly in the first year of diagnosis, though cardiovascular,
