infectious, endocrine, and gastrointestinal complications related to glucocorticoid use increase long-term risk.35-37

PMR is two to three times more common than GCA.6, In Olmsted County, Minnesota, 245 cases of PMR were diagnosed during the 22-year period from 1970 through 1991, providing an average annual incidence rate of 52.5 cases per 100,000 individuals age 50 years and older. The prevalence of PMR (active plus remitted cases) was approximately 600 per 100,000 individuals age 50 years and older. PMR is associated with the same HLA- DR4 genes as GCA.18,39

### Etiology, Pathology, and Pathogenesis

The causes of GCA and PMR are unknown. In GCA, inflammation is found most often in medium-sized muscular arteries that originate from the arch of the aorta.12, The inflammation tends to affect the arteries in a segmental fashion (possibly leading to "skip lesions" within arteries), but long portions of arteries may be involved. In patients who died during the active phase of GCA, the greatest frequency of severe involvement was noted

in the superficial temporal arteries, vertebral arteries, and ophthalmic and posterior ciliary arteries. The internal carotid, external carotid, and central retinal arteries were affected somewhat less frequently. In other postmortem studies, lesions were commonly found in the proximal and distal aorta and internal and external carotid, subclavian, brachial, and abdominal arteries. Because GCA affects vessels with an internal elastic lamina and vasa vasorum, and because intracranial arteries lose these structures after penetrating the dura, it is not surprising that GCA rarely involves intracranial arteries.44-46 In some patients with GCA, follow-up biopsy or autopsy surveys showed the persistence of mild chronic inflammation, even though symptoms had resolved.

Early in the disease, collections of lymphocytes are confined to the region of the internal or external elastic lamina or adventitia. The inflammation may be limited to the vasa vasorum in some cases. Intimal thickening with prominent cellular infiltration is a hallmark of more advanced cases. In heavily involved areas, all layers are affected (Fig. 89.1). Transmural inflammation of portions of the arterial wall (including the elastic laminae) and granulomas containing multinucleated histiocytic and foreign body giant cells,

histiocytes, lymphocytes (which are predominantly CD4+ T cells), and some plasma cells and fibroblasts are found.41, Eosinophils may be seen, but polymorphonuclear leukocytes are rare. Thrombosis may develop at sites of active inflammation; later, these areas may recanalize. The inflammatory process is usually most marked in the inner portion of the media adjacent to the internal elastic lamina. Fragmentation and disintegration of elastic fibers occur, closely associated with an accumulation of giant cells (Fig. 89.2; see supplemental eFig. 89.1 at Elsevier eBooks+). However, giant cells are seen in only approximately half of routinely examined specimens; therefore they are not required to make the diagnosis if other features are compatible. In contrast to some other forms of systemic vasculitis (e.g., polyarteritis nodosa, microscopic polyangiitis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis [GPA]), fibrinoid necrosis is rarely, if ever, observed in GCA and often indicates another diagnosis.

Immunohistochemical studiesdemonstrate inflammatory changes that are specific for each layer of the affected art 13, Dendritic cells, which can present antigen and ery. activate T cells, are found in the adventitia, along with two separate lineages of CD4+ T cells: (1) T helper (Th)1 cells that secrete interferon (IFN)-γ and IL-2 and (2) Th17 cells that secrete IL-17 family members including IL-17A.53-55 The adventitial T cells

show evidence of clonal expansion. The adventitia is also infiltrated with macrophages that secrete IL-1, IL-6, and transforming growth factor (TGF)-β. The media is populated mostly by macrophages that, in contrast to those in other layers, produce matrix metalloproteinases and oxygen-free radicals. Closer to the intima, the macrophages secrete nitric oxide and unite to form syncytia— the giant cells—which produce platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF) and substances that stimulate intimal proliferation. .41,

Although the gross appearance of arteries in patients with PMR is usually healthy, immunohistochemical studies of apparently uninvolved temporal arteries reveal increases of the same macrophage-related inflammatory cytokines found in GCA. The T cell cytokine IFN-γ is abundantly expressed in GCA and is absent in arteries from patients who have only PMR. Pathologically, relatively little else has been found in the arteries of patients with PMR. Granulomatous myocarditis and hepatitis have been noted. Muscle biopsies may be normal or show nonspecific type II muscle atrophy. However, a number of reports have shown the presence of lymphocytic synovitis in the knees, sternoclavicular joints, and shoulders and evidence of a similar reaction in the sacroiliac joints.58, Synovitis (mostly subclinical) was shown in bone scans demonstrating an increased uptake of technetium pertechnetate in the joints of 2 in 25 patients with PMR. More sensitive studies that used magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and ultrasonography have convincingly demonstrated that in PMR the principal foci of inflammation are the bursae surrounding the shoulder more than the glenohumeral joint itself. Sera from patients with GCA, PMR, or both demonstrate evidence of systemic inflammation, with increased levels of circulating immune complexes during active disease60 and elevated levels of IL-6 and IL-1.9

These observations, together with the results from experiments in which temporal arteries from patients with GCA have been implanted into mice with severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID), suggest that GCA results from an adaptive immune response in the wall of an artery.' .41,54,61,62In this model (Fig. 89.3), the key initiating event is activation of dendritic cells located in the adventitia, the only arterial layer normally penetrated by the vasa vasorum. In largeand medium-sized arteries, immunohistochemical studies reveal that the dendritic cells

in temporal arteries have a specific phenotype and express fascin and CD11c.41, Dendritic cells express Toll-like receptors (TLRs) that normally serve as sentinels, monitoring for any immunologic breach of the adventitia. In GCA, activation of TLRs on dendritic cells appears to be the initial triggering event.53, Of the many different types of TLRs, TLR-2 and TLR-4 might be the most important in GCA. Although the exact trigger of the adaptive immune response in GCA is not known, experiments in the GCA-SCID mouse model have shown that blood-borne lipopolysaccharide serves as an effective TLR ligand in temporal arteries. Other constituents of microorganisms or some self-antigens (e.g. oxidized lipids) might also be TLR ligands that activate the arterial dendritic cells. Dendritic cells in GCA patients are deficient in expressing programmed death ligand-1; deficiency of this immunohibitory checkpoint contributes to T cell activation in the vessel wall.65,

Once its TLRs have been engaged, dendritic cells differentiate from the resting to the active state and release cytokines such as IL-6 and IL-18, which recruit, activate, and retain CD4+ T cells in the blood vessel. The crucial role of dendritic cells in activating T cells and maintaining vasculitis has been demonstrated in the GCA-SCID mouse model. Depleting the dendritic cells markedly reduces the T cell infiltrate and suppresses the vasculitis. As noted, two separate populations of CD4+ T cells become activated and expand: IFN-γ producing Th1 cells and IL-17 producing Th17 cells. IFN-γ causes macrophages to migrate, differentiate, and form granulomas.55, Production of matrix metalloproteinases and lipid peroxidation agents by macrophages in the media results in the destruction of elastic laminae. The vessel attempts to counter the tissue destruction by elaborating a variety of growth factors, including PDGF, vascular endothelial growth factor, and

TGF-β, which prompt smooth muscle cells in the media to revert from a contractile phenotype to a secretory one and migrate to the intima. Proliferation of the intimal smooth muscle cells results in occlusion of the lumen. 41,

PMR appears to result from a similar but less intense adaptive immune response in blood vessels (as evidenced by the in situ production of many inflammatory cytokines). According to this model, both PMR and GCA begin with the activation of dendritic cells at the adventitia-media border.53, However, the distinguishing feature of PMR is the absence of T cells producing IFN-γ. Without IFN-γ to stimulate the recruitment and differentiation of macrophages, the level of arterial inflammation in PMR remains subclinical. Thus the development of GCA appears to require both vascular dendritic cell activation and a diseaseinducing repertoire of T cells.41, The constitutional symptoms of PMR and GCA are attributed to the high levels of inflammatory cytokines (e.g., IL-1 and IL-6) found in the sera. Whether these serum cytokine elevations result from blood vessel inflammation alone or from some other source of inflammation is not yet clear. The attractiveness of this model is increased by its ability to explain why subsets of clinical features occur together.

### Clinical Features

The mean age at onset of GCA and PMR is approximately 79 years, with a range of approximately 50 to 90 years of age.12, Younger patients with PMR have been described infrequently, though other diagnoses should be considered with younger age of onset. Women are affected approximately twice as often as men. Although the onset of the disease is usually insidious, typically evolving during weeks or months, in one-third of cases, the disease begins so abruptly that some patients recall the very day they became ill.12,57

### Giant Cell Arteritis

Classic Manifestations. The most common manifestations of GCA are constitutional symptoms, headache, visual symptoms, jaw claudication, and PMR12 (Table 89.3). Almost all patients experience one or more constitutional symptoms, including fatigue, weight loss, malaise, and fever.

Besides constitutional symptoms, headache is the most common symptom in GCA, being present in nearly three-quarters of patients. The pain is typically described as boring in quality, of moderate severity, and most commonly appreciated in the temporal area. However, the description of the headache varies enormously. It can be mild to so severe that the patient seeks immediate relief by going to the emergency department. The pain may localize to any part of the skull, including the occiput (because of involvement of the occipital artery).12, The most consistent characteristic is that the patient experiences the headache as something new and unusual. In untreated patients, the headache may subside over weeks, even though the disease activity continues. Often, the headache of GCA is not associated with any findings on physical examination. Abnormalities of the temporal artery—including enlargement, nodular swelling, tenderness, or loss of pulse—manifest in only approximately half of patients (Fig. 89.4). Some patients note tenderness of the scalp, which can be aggravated by brushing or combing the hair.

Visual symptoms are common in GCA, especially loss of vision and diplopia. Vision loss can be unilateral or (less commonly) bilateral, transient or permanent, and partial or complete.68, Vision loss that lasts more than a few hours usually does not reverse.

Loss of vision often reflects an anterior ischemic optic neuropathy caused by occlusive arteritis of the posterior ciliary artery, the chief blood supply to the head of the optic nerve. The posterior ciliary artery is a branch of the ophthalmic artery (which derives, in turn, from the internal carotid artery). Less frequently, vision loss in GCA stems from a retinal artery occlusion. Regardless of the site of the culprit lesion, the vision loss is usually profound, with more than 80% of patients unable to see hand waving. Vision loss is less likely to develop in GCA patients who are seen with fever or other systemic symptoms.70, One possible explanation of this protective effect of fever and other systemic manifestations is

that patients with prominent systemic inflammation demonstrate more extensive angiogenesis in temporal artery biopsies. The angiogenesis associated with increased inflammation may result in the development of collateral circulation that reduces the chance of ischemic events. Vision loss in the absence of other systemic symptoms occurs infrequently and is termed occult GCA.72,

The early funduscopic appearance in the setting of blindness caused by anterior ischemic optic neuropathy is that of ischemic optic neuritis: slight pallor and edema of the optic disc, with scattered cotton-wool patches and small hemorrhages68 (Fig. 89.5). Patients who experience blindness will demonstrate a relative afferent pupillary defect, characterized by differential pupillary responses to light. This relates to unilateral or asymmetric disease of the optic nerve or retina. Later, optic atrophy occurs. Rarely, blindness may be the initial symptom; however, it tends to follow other symptoms by several weeks or even months. Ophthalmoscopic examination in patients without eye involvement is generally normal, and, therefore, a normal ophthalmologic evaluation does not exclude the diagnosis. In most reports, the incidence of blindness is 20% or less.8, In a series of 245 patients from the modern era, 34 (14%) had some permanent loss of vision. In 32 of these patients, the deficit developed before glucocorticoid therapy was begun; in the other 2, vision loss occurred after therapy was started. Vision loss progressed in 3 of the 32 after therapy was initiated, and it improved in 5 patients. At 5 years' followup, among the patients who had visual deficits caused by GCA at the time glucocorticoids were started, the risk of additional loss of vision was 13% during the follow-up period. If no loss had occurred at the beginning of glucocorticoid therapy, there was only a 1% risk of new loss of vision during the subsequent 5 years.

Another potential ocular complication of GCA is ophthalmoplegia, occurring in around 5%. Diplopia usually results from ocular motor nerve palsies caused by ischemia and usually resolves after therapy is started. Oculomotor nerve involvement in GCA usually spares the pupil. Rarely, arterial lesions cause infarction of the occipital cortex and vision loss.

Intermittent claudication may occur in the muscles of mastication (jaw claudication), the extremities, and, occasionally, the muscles of the tongue or those involved in swallowing. In the jaw muscles, the discomfort is noted, especially when chewing meat, and may involve the muscles on one side of the mandible more than those on the other. Detection of jaw claudication may be increased by "the chewing gum test" in which jaw discomfort is provoked by the patient chewing gum at a rate of one chew per second for 2 to 3 minutes. Marked vascular narrowing from GCA may lead to gangrene of the scalp or tongue.

Atypical Manifestations. Approximately 40% of patients are seen with disease manifestations that are considered atypical54,77-79 (Table 89.4). In these patients, headache, jaw claudication, visual symptoms, and PMR do not occur or are less prominent.

Fever occurs in as many as 40% of patients with GCA, but it is usually low grade and overshadowed by other classic symptoms. However, 15% of GCA patients may present with fever of unknown origin (FUO) in which the temperature spikes are high, dominating the clinical picture.8, Although GCA causes only 2% of all cases of FUO, it is responsible for 16% of all such fevers in individuals older than 65 years. Approximately two-thirds of patients experience shaking, chills, and drenching sweats, features often attributed to infection or malignancy. The median temperature is 102.4° F (39.1° C), and the maximum is 103.6° F (39.8° C). The white blood cell count in GCA-induced FUO is usually normal or nearly so (at least before the initiation of prednisone).

Neurologic problems occur in approximately 30% of patients. 1, These are diverse, but most common are neuropathies and transient ischemic attack or stroke. Hemiparesis or brainstem events are the result of narrowing or occlusion of the carotid or

vertebrobasilar artery. GCA preferentially involves the posterior circulation: the 3:2 ratio of anterior to posterior stroke and transient ischemic attack seen in the normal population reaches nearly 1:1 in patients with GCA. Delirium, reversible dementia, and myelopathy have also been reported. However, the assignment of an exact cause of ischemic central nervous system (CNS) events is often challenging, given the older population in which GCA occurs. The neuropathies of GCA include mononeuropathies and peripheral polyneuropathies and may affect the upper or lower extremities. Presumably, they are secondary to the involvement of nutrient arteries, but little pathologic documentation is available. Among the vasculitides, GCA has a nearly unique propensity for involving the C5 nerve root, resulting in loss of shoulder abduction. Mononeuropathies affecting the hands and feet, so typical of polyarteritis and other forms of vasculitis, develop less often in patients with GCA.

Audiovestibular dysfunction can occur in the setting of GCA presenting as hearing loss, tinnitus, vertigo, dizziness, and disequilibrium; these nonspecific symptoms may be the initial manifestation of GCA.82-84 While these symptoms are more prevalent in an aging population at baseline, the prevalence is higher than matched patients with PMR, and symptoms often respond to prednisone.

Prominent respiratory tract symptoms occur in approximately 10% of patients. These include cough with or without sputum, sore throat, and hoarseness. When these symptoms are severe or an initial manifestation of GCA, they may direct the attention of the examining physician away from the underlying arteritis. Vasculitis may induce these symptoms by causing ischemia or hyperirritability of the affected tissues. Interstitial lung disease and bronchiectasis are rarely described in this setting. Otolaryngeal manifestations of GCA include throat pain, dental pain, tongue pain, glossitis, and ulceration or infarction of the tongue. 86,

Clinical evidence of large-artery involvement occurs in 10% to 15% of patients at presentation and in as many as 27% eventually.4, Prominent large-vessel vasculitis associated with GCA (LVV-GCA) tends to occur in younger patients and is less frequently associated with ischemic manifestations. One group found an association between LVV-GCA and prevalence of multinucleated giant cells on temporal artery biopsy, which suggests potential pathophysiologic differences in these subgroups. Positron emission tomography (PET) studies with fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) revealed that subclinical involvement of large arteries occurs in the vast majority of GCA patients. One PET study, for example, showed that 88% of 35 patients had increased FDG uptake in large arteries, with subclavian involvement in 7% and aortic involvement in 54%.

Clinically evident disease can be divided into early (within a year of diagnosis) and late (years after diagnosis) stages. Usually, early disease consists chiefly of large-artery stenosis resulting in upper-extremity claudication; bruits over the carotid, subclavian, axillary, and brachial arteries; absent or decreased pulses in the neck or arms; and Raynaud's phenomenon (Fig. 89.6). Angiographic features suggest GCA are smooth-walled arterial stenoses or occlusions alternating with areas of normal or increased caliber in the absence of irregular plaques and ulcerations, located especially in the carotid, subclavian, axillary, and brachial arteries. Late disease most frequently involves thoracic aortic aneurysm. . The tendency for aneurysms to develop late was confirmed in one series of 41 patients in which the average time between diagnosis of GCA and recognition of this complication was 7 years. Thoracic aortic aneurysm is 17 times more likely to develop in patients

with GCA than in people without the disease. To place this risk in context, thoracic aortic aneurysms are twice as likely to complicate GCA as lung cancer is to result from smoking. Abdominal aortic aneurysm is also 2.4 times more common in patients with GCA.4, In aggregate, nearly one out of five patients (18%) with GCA develops an aortic aneurysm or dissection.

One common approach is to screen with echocardiography at baseline and monitor pulses and manual blood pressure in bilateral upper extremities at each appointment, with further imaging if there is a clinical change. Manual blood pressure ascertainment is preferred, particularly as electronic recordings have been shown to underestimate systolic blood pressure and overestimate diastolic blood pressure compared with intraarterial recordings. A normal blood pressure assessed with an electronic cuff may miss a wide pulse pressure detectable by manual blood pressure measurement.

FDG-PET avidity decreases with initial therapy, though many patients have evidence of persistent subclinical inflammation by FDG-PET up to 5 years after initial diagnosis. Patients with large artery disease often do not have headache or other classic manifestations of GCA, and less than 50% have an abnormal temporal artery biopsy. Computed tomography (CT) angiography and magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) are the imaging modalities most commonly used to detect large artery disease in GCA.

In women, GCA can rarely present as a breast or ovarian mass.79, The mass lesions in these tissues result from granulomatous inflammation in and around the arteries. Angina pectoris, congestive heart failure, and myocardial infarction secondary to coronary arteritis occur rarely.

Clinical Subsets. Studies suggest that GCA is not just one disease but, rather, a number of clinical subsets that are the result of the differential expression of inflammatory cytokines.95, Ischemic events including blindness, stroke, and large-artery disease occur more commonly in patients who express high levels of IFN-γ and low levels of IL-6.96 In contrast, patients who produce high amounts of IL-6 are more likely to have strong inflammatory features (such as fever and

constitutional symptoms) and are less likely to develop vision loss or other ischemic events.96-98

### Polymyalgia Rheumatica

As in GCA, PMR patients are characteristically in good health before the onset of disease. Systemic manifestations such as malaise, low-grade fever, and weight loss are present in more than half of the patients and may be the initial symptoms of disease. High, spiking fevers are uncommon in PMR in the absence of GCA. Arthralgias and myalgias may develop abruptly or evolve insidiously during weeks or months. Malaise, fatigue, and depression, along with aching and stiffness, may be present for months before the diagnosis is made. In most patients, the shoulder girdle is the first to become symptomatic; in the remainder, the hip or neck is involved at the onset. The discomfort may begin in one shoulder or hip but usually becomes bilateral within weeks. Symptoms center on the proximal limb, axial musculature, and tendinous attachments. Morning stiffness resembling that of RA and "gelling" after inactivity are usually prominent. If the symptoms are severe, aching is more persistent. Although movement of the joints accentuates the pain, it is often felt in the proximal extremities rather than in the joints.3, Pain at night is common, and movement during sleep may awaken the patient. Muscle strength is generally unimpaired, although pain with movement makes the interpretation of strength-testing maneuvers difficult. Pain with movement also makes it difficult for patients to get out of bed or the bathtub. In the later stages of the syndrome, muscle atrophy may develop, and contracture of the shoulder capsule may result in limitation of passive and active motion.

As noted, the presence of bursal inflammation and synovitis in PMR has been described by many authors and is undoubtedly the cause of many of the findings in this condition. A careful examination may reveal transient synovitis of the knees, wrists, and sternoclavicular joints. The shoulders and hips are covered by heavy muscles, and minimal effusions of slight synovitis are not palpable on physical examination. Synovitis has been documented by biopsies, synovial analysis, joint scintiscans, ultrasonography, and MRI.57-59 Involvement of distal joints and prominent synovitis, rather than periarticular inflammation, should raise suspicion for other diseases such as elderly-onset RA. 100

### Diagnostic Evaluation

### Laboratory Studies

Except for the findings on arterial biopsy, laboratory results in PMR and GCA are similar (Table 89.5). A mild to moderate normochromic anemia is usually present in both diseases during their active phases. Leukocyte and differential counts are generally normal. A markedly elevated ESR and C-reactive protein (CRP) level are characteristic of both.101, In a study of 177 patients who had biopsy-proven GCA and measurement of both CRP and ESR, the CRP was minimally more sensitive than the ESR (86.4% vs. 84.2%). The odds ratio of concordantly elevated CRP and ESR was 3.06.102 Seven untreated patients (4%) had normal values for both ESR and CRP. The patients with normal inflammatory markers were more likely to have PMR and less likely to have constitutional symptoms or anemia. An ESR higher than 100 mm/ hr (Westergren method) is common, but untreated biopsy-proven cases of GCA may be associated with normal or nearly normal levels.101,102 2 Of the GCA patients, 10.8% presented with an ESR of less than 50 mm/hr, and 3.6% had a rate of less than 30 mm/hr. Rare individuals appear to be unable to develop an elevated ESR

or CRP during any inflammatory process, including active GCA. The ESR and CRP are also liable to be relatively low or normal in patients who have been receiving corticosteroids for another condition. Thus a normal ESR or CRP does not exclude the presence of GCA, especially in a patient with otherwise classic symptoms and findings. Platelet counts are often increased.

Nonspecific changes in plasma proteins are often present and include a decrease in the concentration of albumin and an increase in α2-globulins, fibrinogen, and other acute-phase reactant proteins. Slight increases in γ-globulins and complement may be present. Results of tests for anti-nuclear antibodies and rheumatoid factor are generally negative.

Liver function test results are mildly abnormal in approximately one-third of patients with GCA and in a slightly smaller number of those with PMR. An increased alkaline phosphatase level is the most common abnormality, but increases in aspartate transaminase and prolonged prothrombin time may also be found. Liver biopsy specimens are generally normal; granulomatous hepatitis has been observed. Renal function and urinalysis are usually normal. Red blood cell casts are found in some instances, but their presence does not correlate with clinical largeartery involvement.

Levels of serum creatine kinase and other enzymes reflecting muscle damage are normal. Electromyograms are usually normal, and muscle biopsy shows normal histologic features or only the mild atrophy characteristic of disuse.

Synovial fluid analyses reported in GCA or PMR show evidence of mild inflammation including increased synovial fluid leukocyte counts, with a mean of 2900 cells/mm3 but a range from 300 to 20,000 cells/mm3; 40% to 50% are polymorphonuclear leukocytes. Synovial fluid complement levels are usually normal. In some instances, synovial biopsy has shown lymphocytic synovitis. 58,

In the research setting, serum IL-6 levels are elevated in patients with PMR and GCA and appear to closely parallel the inflammaelevated in patients with GCA and PMR.

### Imaging

Patients who have signs of subclavian and axillary disease manifested by arm claudication, unequal arm blood pressures, and supraclavicular or axillary bruits may be diagnosed by angiogram, MRA, or CT scan.96, Typically, patients with extracranial GCA have smooth, tapered stenosis or occlusion of the subclavian, axillary, and proximal brachial arteries. In one series, temporal artery biopsy was positive in only 58% of patients with larger-artery involvement. MRI and CT are the best-established methods for detecting aortic involvement by GCA.

Other imaging techniques have been proposed to assist in the diagnosis of GCA. Color duplex ultrasonography showed abnormalities of the temporal artery in 28 of 30 patients with GCA (sensitivity of 93%). The most characteristic finding was a dark halo around the lumen of the temporal artery (Fig. 89.7). There is growing use of ultrasound, particularly in Europe, to aid in diagnosis and management of GCA. Novel ultrasound scoring systems based on the halo sign may also provide prognostic information, including identification of those with higher risk of ocular ischemia.107, Ultrasound may also help aid in assessment of exacerbations, with total number of halo segments and maximum temporal artery intima-media thickness correlating with inflammatory markers and Birmingham Vasculitis Activity score, though addition of imaging did not outperform standard clinical measures. However, the diagnostic value of ultrasonography is limited by the absence of expertise with this technique at most medical centers and conflicting estimates of its sensitivity and specificity. 110-114 One meta-analysis of 2036 patients in 23 studies estimated that the sensitivity and specificity of the halo sign were 69% and 82%, respectively. Another study found that ultrasonography did not improve the diagnostic accuracy of a carefully performed physical examination.

High-resolution MRI can demonstrate contrast enhancement and mural thickening of superficial cranial arteries in GCA. Small studies have found a sensitivity of 91% and a specificity of 73%, compared with temporal artery biopsy. 110-112Best results have been achieved with 3-T MRI scanners, and 7-T MRI scanners may be even more sensitive.8, PET has shown promise in detecting occult involvement of the aorta and great vessels by GCA; however, estimates of sensitivity have varied from 65% to 100% and specificity from 77% to 99%.110, PET scanning cannot image small arteries that are near highly metabolic tissues such as the brain, and thus cannot be used to study superficial extracranial arteries. Serial PET scans show active FDG uptake in times of clinical remission, though those with higher activity as described by the PET vascular activity score (PETVAS) were more likely to have exacerbations. However, other groups have questioned the utility of the PETVAS for prognostic purposes. There is suggestion that development of late vascular damage may be predicted by PET. For the rare patient who has a compelling story for GCA but negative bilateral temporal artery biopsies, one should reconsider conditions that mimic GCA described earlier (e.g., ask the pathologist to stain the biopsied arteries with Congo red to rule out systemic amyloidosis). If no other diagnosis becomes evident, then it is reasonable to search for occult large-vessel disease with an imaging test such as a PET scan or MRA to look for occult aortic disease. Rarely a patient's clinical picture strongly indicates GCA despite negative biopsies and imaging. In this case the physician can treat the patient for GCA while watching vigilantly for the emergence of another disease.

### Tissue Diagnosis

Temporal artery biopsy is the "gold standard" for diagnosing GCA.12, Because GCA does not involve the artery in a continuous fashion, temporal artery biopsy should be directed to the symptomatic side, if evident. Indurated arteries, tenderness, pulse abolition, and arterial dilation increase likelihood of a positive biopsy and can be used to optimize the sample. Removing a small (1 to 2 cm) section of temporal artery is usually adequate in patients who have palpable abnormalities of the vessel. Otherwise, the surgeon should try to excise a 4 to 6 cm sample, and the pathologist should examine multiple sections. In skilled hands, temporal artery biopsy is virtually free of morbidity or mortality. Scalp necrosis can rarely complicate active GCA but has not developed as a consequence of temporal artery biopsy.

Temporal artery biopsies performed at institutions experienced in treating GCA are sensitive and have a high negative predictive value. At the Mayo Clinic, the sensitivity of temporal artery biopsy is approximately 90% to 95%, meaning that only 5% to 10% of patients with negative biopsies will subsequently be proven (by additional biopsy, angiography, or autopsy) to have GCA and require corticosteroid therapy. The sensitivity figures noted previously include some patients who underwent bilateral temporal artery biopsy. Estimates of the value of bilateral biopsies vary.122-124Of 234 cases of biopsy-proven GCA, unilateral biopsy was positive in 86% and the second biopsy was positive in 14%. Other studies indicate that a second temporal artery biopsy improves the diagnostic yield by only 3% to 5%.

Management of a patient with a negative unilateral biopsy depends on how strongly the patient's clinical picture suggests GCA (Fig. 89.8). When GCA is still strongly suspected, a second biopsy or an imaging test (see subsequent discussion) should be considered. Opting for a second temporal artery biopsy makes the most sense in patients who have jaw claudication or diplopia.

Patients whose main symptom is occipital headache may be best diagnosed by biopsy of the occipital artery.

### Differential Diagnosis

Evidence that PMR and GCA are related and should be considered different manifestations of a common disease process is abundant.12, The associations with age, race/ethnicity, geographic region, and class II HLA alleles are the same in both disorders. Moreover, both disorders involve overproduction of many of the same inflammatory cytokines. Between 30% and 50% of patients with GCA develop PMR. Approximately 10% to 15% of patients who appear to have only PMR have positive temporal artery biopsies. In the absence of symptoms of GCA (e.g., headache, jaw claudication, visual symptoms, high fever), PMR by itself does not appear to cause vision loss and responds to low doses of glucocorticoids. However, in a study of 181 patients with PMR meeting the 2012 EULAR/ACR provisional classification criteria without GCA symptoms, about 20% had vascular changes by ultrasound

suggestive of LVV, mostly in an extracranial distribution. There was no difference in disease duration, inflammatory markers, or clinical manifestations in this subset with vascular change.

The diagnosis of GCA should be considered in any patient older than 50 years who experiences loss of vision, diplopia, new form of headache, jaw claudication, PMR, FUO, unexplained constitutional symptoms, anemia, and a high ESR. GCA can cause so many forms of cranial discomfort (e.g., headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, pain of the throat, gums, and tongue) that the disease should also be considered in any patient older than age 50 in whom new, unexplained "above-the-neck" pain develops. The protean manifestations of GCA mean that it should also be considered in the differential diagnosis of an older patient seen with dry cough, stroke, arm claudication, or acute C5 radiculopathy accompanied by other classic symptoms or findings of GCA.

Only a few individual symptoms or findings substantially increase or decrease the likelihood that a patient has this disease67 (Table 89.6). For example, jaw claudication, diplopia, abnormal temporal artery signs, scalp tenderness, and ESR greater than 50

mm/hr increase the likelihood that a patient has GCA. In one series of 373 patients, the presence of either jaw claudication or diplopia increased the likelihood of a positive biopsy by more than three-fold; the presence of both jaw claudication and double vision had a 100% positive predictive value for a diagnostic temporal artery biopsy. Conversely, the absence of headache or temporal artery abnormalities on physical examination, the presence of synovitis, and a normal ESR reduce the likelihood of GCA.

A large number of disorders can mimic GCA (Table 89.7). There are many causes of monocular vision loss besides vasculitis, including arteriosclerosis-induced thromboembolic disease. Patients with nonarteritic vision loss do not have other GCArelated symptoms, signs, or findings. The funduscopic examination may help by revealing Hollenhorst plaques in cases caused by cholesterol emboli. Anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, the most common cause of vision loss in GCA, can also be caused by arteriosclerosis. Nonarteritic optic neuropathy invariably produces a small optic disc and cup-to-disc ratio, whereas GCA-related optic neuropathy results in an optic disc of variable size. Thus a normal size or large cup in a patient with anterior ischemic optic neuropathy suggests GCA until proven otherwise.

Constitutional symptoms with anemia and an elevated ESR in an older patient may also be produced by occult infections (e.g., tuberculosis, bacterial endocarditis, HIV) or malignancy (especially lymphoma and multiple myeloma). These diagnoses highlight the value of selective serologic tests, imaging studies, and

immunoelectrophoresis in appropriate patients. Systemic amyloidosis can closely mimic GCA, which is one of the few disorders other than GCA that causes jaw claudication. The amyloid deposits in the temporal artery may not be detected unless the specimen is stained with Congo red. Polyarthritis in an older patient is much more likely to be caused by RA than by GCA. In one study of 520 GCA patients, fewer than 2% developed polyarthritis before GCA was diagnosed.

Criteria for the classification of GCA have been formulated and can help differentiate this arteritis from other forms of vasculitis122 (see Table 89.1). TAK, similar to GCA, can affect the aorta and the major arterial branches to the head and arms. TAK, however, is a disease of young women. Anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA)—associated granulomatous vasculitis (AGV) can affect the temporal artery and, along with systemic amyloidosis, is an exception to the rule that jaw claudication is pathognomonic for GCA. AGV, however, almost always produces telltale involvement of the respiratory tract or kidneys and is associated with ANCAs. Polyarteritis nodosa can also affect the temporal artery and should be considered if the biopsy does not contain giant cells and the patient has other features atypical for GCA such as mesenteric arteritis. Fibrinoid necrosis of the vasa vasorum is not associated with GCA but is seen in other forms of vasculitis, such a polyarteritis nodosa and ANCA-associated vasculitis. Primary angiitis of the CNS differs from GCA in that it affects the intracranial arteries.

The diagnosis of PMR is clinical and depends on eliciting the symptoms and findings noted earlier. Ultrasonography may improve the accuracy of diagnosis. Two sets of criteria for the diagnosis have been proposed3,4 (see Table 89.2). Several disorders can mimic PMR (see Table 89.7). Distinguishing early RA from PMR can be difficult, especially in the 15% of patients who are rheumatoid factor-negative and in those few patients with RA who have not yet developed prominent synovitis of the small joints of the hands and feet. Patients with polymyositis complain much more of weakness than of pain—the opposite symptom pattern reported by patients with PMR. In addition, in polymyositis, levels of muscle enzymes are elevated and electromyograms are abnormal. Although patients with neoplasms may have generalized musculoskeletal aching, no association exists between PMR and malignant neoplasia. Therefore a search for an underlying malignancy is not necessary unless some clinical evidence for a tumor is present or the patient has a RS3PE phenotype (described in the section on differential diagnosis) or an atypically poor response to low-dose prednisone.

While PMR is not caused by malignancy, PMR-like symptoms have been associated with use of checkpoint inhibitors in cancer. While arthralgia and myalgia are the most commonly reported rheumatic immune-related adverse events associated with immunotherapy, immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) has also been associated with risk of PMR. 129-131 Compared with patients with classical PMR, ICI-associated PMR was more likely to be related to with concurrent peripheral arthritis, and onset of symptoms often developed within the first 2 months of therapy. Cranial and LVV- GCA have also been described in this setting.

The COVID-19 pandemic also sheds lightly into the association between viral infection and PMR/GCA. Case series have reported an association between SARS-CoV-2 infection and development of PMR and GCA.133, Diagnosis can be particularly difficult as headache, fever, and elevated inflammatory markers are typical of both COVID-19 and GCA. In a study comparing symptoms in patients with GCA to patients with COVID

infection, jaw claudication and vision loss only occurred in GCA and cough and upper respiratory symptoms were more likely to be associated with SARS-CoV-2 infection. Thrombocytosis was more typical of GCA (47% vs. 4%) with lower prevalence of lymphopenia with GCA (2% vs. 53%).

Small case series (n = 10) have described PMR developing soon after COVID-19 vaccination, with median time from vaccination to symptoms of 10 days (range: 515). In this small study, all patients met 2012 ACR/EULAR classification criteria, and seven completed musculoskeletal ultrasounds that showed typical features of PMR. VigiBase, the World Health Organization global database of reported potential side effects of medicinal products, found that 290 PMR cases and 147 GCA cases were reported after roughly 1.29 million COVID-19 vaccinations; these rates were significantly higher than incident PMR (reporting odds ratio [ROR] 2.3; 95% CI, 2.02.6) and GCA (ROR 2.7; 95% CI, 2.3 3.2) when comparing to previous studies with influenza vaccination. While there is an association between COVID infection and/or vaccination and PMR, the vast majority of patients have PMR unrelated to COVID.

In the initial description of the vacuoles, E1 enzyme, X-linked, autoinflammatory, somatic (VEXAS) syndrome, one patient was found to have GCA. However, the UK GCA Consortium, which included 612 males with GCA, found no UBA1 mutations, suggesting that VEXAS was rarely associated with GCA. This is supported by other small studies (n = 44) which found not association between these conditions. While GCA was initially described in the seminal paper describing VEXAS, these cohorts show that this is relatively uncommon in the setting of GCA but should still be considered in the differential diagnosis for patients thought to have relapsing polychondritis, polyarteritis nodosa, and cutaneous vasculitis.

Some patients with chronic infections such as bacterial endocarditis may have findings that simulate PMR, and blood cultures should be obtained in patients with fever. Those with fibromyalgia usually do not have typical morning stiffness and have laboratory test results that are normal or nearly so. Rarely, the stiffness of early Parkinson's disease can be confused with PMR if the bradykinesia and tremor of Parkinson's disease are subtle or absent. Lumbar spinal stenosis sometimes causes patients to complain of pain and stiffness in the hip girdle area. The absence of symptoms above the waist helps differentiate it from PMR. Cholesterol-lowering statin drugs can produce myalgia with or without muscle enzyme elevations but rarely mimic PMR. Hypothyroidism in older adults can mimic many conditions, including PMR.

Remitting, seronegative synovitis with pitting edema (designated RS3PE syndrome) may be difficult to differentiate from PMR, and they may be related disorders. However, this association with RS3PE should raise suspicion for a paraneoplastic process. Acute symmetric polysynovitis of distal joints with pitting edema of the hands and feet develop in patients with RS3PE syndrome. RS3PE syndrome and PMR both respond to nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and low-dose prednisone. 12,122

### Treatment and Outcome

Most authorities recommend starting glucocorticoid therapy as soon as the diagnosis of GCA is strongly suspected. The main goal of treatment is to prevent loss of vision. Because vision loss is almost always permanent, it seems prudent to initiate corticosteroid therapy as early as possible, even before the biopsy is performed. Fortunately, the diagnostic yield of temporal artery

biopsy is not altered by corticosteroid therapy for at least 2 weeks, and perhaps longer.

### Glucocorticoid Therapy

Until recently, corticosteroids were considered the initial treatment of choice for GCA. Questions about the previously unchallenged role of corticosteroid therapy emerged in 2017 when tocilizumab (an inhibitor of IL-6) was approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration for treating GCA. Because of important unanswered questions about the long-term efficacy of tocilizumab (see later), corticosteroids currently retain their title as drug of first choice for the initial treatment of GCA (see Fig. 89.9 for treatment algorithm).

An initial dose of prednisone 40 to 60 mg/day or equivalent is adequate in nearly all cases. Dividing the dose for the first 1 to 2 weeks may accelerate the rate of improvement. If the patient does not respond promptly, the dose should be increased, no higher than 1 mg/kg/day. One double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomized trial involving 27 patients with GCA suggested that initiating treatment with intravenous (IV) methylprednisolone (15 mg/kg of ideal weight per day) for 3 days allowed more rapid tapering of oral corticosteroids and increased the likelihood of achieving a sustained remission. The small size of that study and the possible overreliance on laboratory tests to define relapse raise questions about the generalizability of these results. Indeed, a randomized, multicenter, controlled trial of IV pulses of a single dose of 240 mg of methylprednisolone in the initial treatment of 164 GCA patients showed no benefit. High-dose, IV-pulse methylprednisolone (1000 mg/day) for 3 days has also been tried in patients with recent loss of vision. Unfortunately, the loss remains permanent in the vast majority of patients. The occlusive nature of the vasculitis argues against any role of acute thrombolytic therapy in the treatment of blindness.

Because all patients with GCA require months of glucocorticoid therapy, measures to prevent osteoporosis should be started

early, as described in Chapter 103. In addition, because traditional risk factors for atherosclerosis (e.g., smoking, hypertension, diabetes, hypercholesterolemia) might increase the risk of vision loss or stroke in GCA,71 reducing or eliminating these risk factors is an important part of overall management.

When used as monotherapy, the initial effective dose of prednisone should be continued until all reversible symptoms, signs, and laboratory abnormalities have reverted to normal. This usually takes 2 to 4 weeks. After that, the dose can be gradually reduced by about 10% to 15% of the total dose each week or every 2 weeks. The decision to reduce prednisone should be based on a composite assessment of the patient's symptoms, signs, and laboratory markers of inflammation. The ESR and serum concentration of CRP are generally the most convenient and helpful laboratory markers of inflammation, though CRP is unreliable in patients concurrently receiving tocilizumab because that protein is regulated by IL-6. The ESR is reliable only if performed promptly after the blood sample is obtained. Serum levels of IL-6 appear to be the most sensitive marker of activity of GCA, but this test is not widely available. CRP may be slightly more sensitive than ESR in detecting flares. Our practice is to check labs on a monthly basis for the first 6 months of therapy, and then the frequency is decreased once the patient is clinically stable. At some point during drug tapering, the ESR or CRP may rise above normal again. While these are nonspecific tests, further reductions of prednisone should be temporarily interrupted in this setting. If, over the next week or so, the patient does not develop signs or symptoms of active GCA, reductions in prednisone (at smaller decrements and at longer intervals) can usually be resumed. Doses of 10 to 20 mg/ day or more are often required for several months before further reductions are possible. However, if the prednisone dose is dependent on the levels of inflammatory markers with no regard to the patient's overall clinical context, there is a risk of corticosteroidrelated side effects. Gradual reductions allow the identification of the minimal suppressive dose and help avoid exacerbations that result from too-rapid tapering. Even with a gradual reduction of prednisone, more than 50% of patients experience flares of disease activity during the first year. These exacerbations can usually be handled by increasing the prednisone by 10 mg above the last dose at which the disease was controlled.

Most patients with GCA have a chronic disease that requires prednisone treatment for at least 1 year and often for several years. In a prospective study in which 40 patients underwent follow-up temporal artery biopsy, four of nine patients biopsied 12 months after beginning corticosteroid therapy had persistent arterial inflammation. A minority of patients run a self-limited course of only several months. Glucocorticoids can eventually be reduced and discontinued in some patients. Many patients require low doses of prednisone for several years or more, often to control musculoskeletal symptoms.

### Tocilizumab

The search for a corticosteroid alternative finally achieved success in 2017 when tocilizumab, a humanized monoclonal anti- IL-6 receptor antibody, was approved for GCA in the United States. The door to treating GCA patients with tocilizumab had been opened by the discovery that IL-6 was highly expressed in affected arteries and in the circulation of patients with GCA.147- 150 Encouraging results in 24 patients with GCA described in case reports and small series prompted a phase 3 trial conducted in 251 patients with GCA randomly assigned in double-blind fashion to receive tocilizumab weekly or every other week, along with

prednisone (initially 20 to 60 mg daily) tapered over a period of either 26 weeks or 52 weeks. Sustained remission of GCA, the primary outcome measure, was achieved in 56% of those receiving weekly tocilizumab and in 53% of those on biweekly tocilizumab, compared with 14% and 18% of the two placebo groups. Patients treated with tocilizumab over 52 weeks registered higher quality of life scores and received nearly half the cumulative dose of prednisone as those in the placebo groups. Adverse events occurred at similar frequencies in the tocilizumaband placebotreated patients; serious adverse advents were more frequent in the placebo groups.

Long-term follow-up, extended to 3 years, have also shown good efficacy and safety with tocilizumab in patients with new and relapsing GCA. Based on these features, the 2021 ACR/ Vasculitis Foundation guidelines conditionally recommend addition of tocilizumab over glucocorticoid monotherapy. EULAR recommendations have suggested use as an adjunct for refractory or relapsing disease or due to glucocorticoid-associated adverse effects. Our practice has favored early addition of tocilizumab in favor of allowing a more rapid and successful glucocorticoid taper.

There is a black box warning associated with serious infection risk with tocilizumab. A history of diverticulitis is a relative contraindication as this can be associated with risk of bowel perforation in patients with inflammatory arthritis. Neutropenia, hepatitis, and hyperlipidemia are known complications of tocilizumab and should by monitored at baseline, 4 to 8 weeks after starting therapy, and then every 3 months afterward. Tuberculosis and hepatitis screening are necessary before starting therapy.

Optimal glucocorticoid tapering should limit cumulative glucocorticoid exposure while not increasing risk of ischemic complications. Glucocorticoid tapering in the tocilizumab studies, targeting discontinuation at 26 weeks and 52 weeks, is more rapid than traditionally used with glucocorticoid monotherapy. One regimen aims to decrease prednisone to 10 mg/day by week 11 and then another by week 13 with a plan to discontinue prednisone by 26 and 52 weeks, respectively. The treatment of each patient must be individualized; patients who were unable to adhere to the fixed glucocorticoid taper were switched to the open-label escape therapy during this study.

In a proof-of-concept study, 18 patients with newly diagnosed GCA were treated with IV methylprednisolone (500 mg daily for 3 days) in addition to IV tocilizumab (8 mg/kg) followed by weekly subcutaneous tocilizumab with no additional glucocorticoids. Remission at 24 weeks was high (14 of 18 patients) with low risk of relapse at 52 weeks (13 of 18). However, three patients had either persistent cranial or PMR symptoms and two discontinued tocilizumab due to adverse events. While this small study opens the possibility of accelerated glucocorticoid tapering, it is important to note that one patient developed new anterior ischemic optic neuropathy. Further study is needed to optimize glucocorticoid tapering.

While tocilizumab has advanced the therapy of GCA, its efficacy has important limitations. The possibility that IL-6 inhibitors may suppress the systemic symptoms and signs without eliminating the vasculitis was suggested by an autopsy in the one patient treated with tocilizumab who had appeared to respond and died of other causes, which showed persistent active arteritis. Other case reports have described active aortitis and dissection in patients on tocilizumab monotherapy. One hypothesis is that inflammatory markers are uninterpretable with tocilizumab, with one study showing that 92% of exacerbations had normal

inflammatory markers. Given these concerns, it is prudent to continue monitoring for progression of aortitis while on therapy.

### Other or Investigational

The nearly universal experience of serious side effects associated with daily corticosteroids has prompted the search for alternative steroid-sparing treatments, without much success until tocilizumab. The combination of weekly low-dose oral methotrexate and prednisone was steroid sparing in one placebo-controlled, double-blind treatment trial but not in another and was not associated with fewer adverse effects. Statins do not appear to modify the course of GCA or the need for corticosteroids.

Delineation of the cells and cytokines involved in the pathogenesis of GCA has invited trials of biologic agents. For example, the putative role of TNF in propagating a granulomatous vasculitic process suggested that TNF inhibitors might be effective in treating GCA. Unfortunately, neither infliximab nor etanercept is effective in GCA.161,

Other biologic agents might also be effective. Mavrilimumab, a granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor receptor antagonist, was recently studied in a phase 2 trial in addition to prednisone and showed high rates of sustained remission at 26 weeks (82% vs. 50%, p = 0.0038). Patients in this study who had exacerbations while on mavrilimumab had elevated inflammatory markers, an important clinical distinction from tocilizumab therapy, though further studies are needed to determine the efficacy and safety of this medication.

Abatacept, which inhibits T cell activation by blocking the engagement of CD28, when added to prednisone reduced the rate of relapse in one small, double-blind, controlled trial. Abatacept was less likely to induce partial or complete remission when compared head-to-head with tocilizumab, and patients were more likely to remain on higher doses of prednisone at 12 months.

In an open-label pilot study, the use of baricitinib, a Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitor, reduced the risk of GCA relapse (7% at 52 weeks) with most patients (13 of 15) able to discontinue glucocorticoids at the end of the study. Case reports have also suggested that other JAK inhibitors (e.g., upadacitinib) may also be efficacious.

A few case reports and small open-label studies have described apparent responses in GCA patients treated with the anti- CD20 monoclonal antibody rituximab to deplete B cells, with ustekinumab to block IL-12 and IL-23, or with anakinra to inhibit IL-1 receptors. Among nonbiologic agents, azathioprine was glucocorticoid sparing in one small trial. A retrospective study suggested that dapsone could also be steroid sparing. Small, uncontrolled studies have supported the belief that cyclophosphamide may be effective in GCA patients who cannot tolerate prednisone reduction.

No prospective, randomized, double-blind trials have tested the potential adjunctive role of aspirin or anti-coagulants in the treatment of GCA. However, aspirin is theoretically appealing because, in experimental models of GCA, it inhibits IFN-γ production more effectively than prednisone. In addition, three retrospective studies found that patients with GCA taking lowdose aspirin or anti-coagulant therapy had a threeto five-fold lower risk of an ischemic event such as vision loss.172-174 Together, these studies suggest that it is reasonable to administer low-dose aspirin to patients with GCA who do not have an excessive risk of gastrointestinal bleeding. Therefore the conditional recommendation for use of aspirin for critical or flow-limiting vertebral or carotid artery disease is reasonable and appropriate.

Arm claudication from GCA affecting the subclavian and axillary arteries usually improves or resolves with corticosteroid therapy. Rare patients with GCA who have severe upper-extremity claudication unresponsive to corticosteroid therapy may benefit from balloon angioplasty. In one series of 10 patients, all improved initially after angioplasty, but symptomatic restenosis developed in 50% during 2 months. In all cases, recurrent stenosis developed in vascular lesions that were greater than 3 cm long.

Thoracic aortic aneurysm is greatly increased in patients with GCA. Although it can be present at the outset, aneurysms are usually noted late in the disease course, an average of 7 years after onset. Some authorities have recommended annual chest radiographs or echocardiograms to detect thoracic aortic aneurysms.

### Treatment for Polymyalgia a Rheumatica

Patients with PMR without symptoms or signs or biopsy evidence of GCA are usually treated initially with prednisone 10 to 20 mg/day or equivalent.177, A systematic review of 30 studies recommended starting treatment with prednisone at 15 mg/day; lower initial doses were less effective and higher doses were more toxic. Salicylates and NSAIDs have been used but are less appealing; salicylates and NSAIDs adequately control symptoms in only a minority of patients with milder symptoms and add to overall adverse drug reactions when they are used with glucocorticoids.3, Prednisone therapy usually results in rapid (often overnight) and dramatic improvement of the musculoskeletal aching and stiffness and a more gradual return of the ESR and CRP levels to normal. A minority of patients with isolated PMR fail to respond to prednisone 20 mg/day after 1 week and may require as much as 30 mg/day as initial treatment. Studies suggest that these resistant cases are more likely to have ESRs greater than 50 mm/hr and high levels of IL-6. If a patient does not respond to prednisone 30 mg/ day for 1 week, this should prompt a search for an alternative diagnosis (Fig. 89.10). Lower doses of prednisone might not suppress an underlying arteritis if it is present. Thus the patient must be observed carefully even though the aching improves. In patients with PMR, the dose should be reduced gradually as soon as symptoms permit. Pre-treatment ESR, CRP, and IL-6 concentrations and initial responses to therapy appear to be helpful in dividing patients into subsets with different treatment requirements. If the laboratory test results become normal while the patient is receiving a smaller dose, the likelihood of an underlying active vasculitis seems to be much less, and the risk of vascular complications is smaller. However, this is not true in all instances because active arteritis has been observed even though the ESR improved.

Once the symptoms, signs, and laboratory abnormalities of PMR have resolved (usually after 2 to 3 weeks of therapy), the daily dose of prednisone can be slowly tapered. Some experts recommend tapering prednisone by 2.5 mg every week until 10 mg/ day is reached, at which point the decrements should be reduced by 1 mg each month. Flares are common, necessitating a dose increase to achieve remission before attempting a slower taper. The minority of patients with PMR succeed in tapering off prednisone in less than 1 year. Many require at least 2 years of low-dose prednisone.

Some, but not all, studies suggest that oral methotrexate (10 mg once a week for 48 weeks) can reduce the long-term need for corticosteroids in patients with PMR.179, It is not yet known whether the small but statistically significant reduction in

prednisone use achieved with methotrexate results in a clinically important reduction in prednisone-related side effects.

While tocilizumab has been approved for treating GCA, it has not been approved for treating PMR alone. A recent randomized trial in PMR showed that tocilizumab improved glucocorticoidfree remission and time-to-relapse and decreased cumulative glucocorticoid dose, though further study is needed to better understand its use in PMR.

In patients who had at least one disease flare during glucocorticoid tapering for PMR at a dose >7.5 mg/day, the addition of sarilumab allowed for significantly more patients to have a sustained remission at 52 weeks (28% vs. 10%, p = 0.02). Addition of sarilumab also significantly decreased the total glucocorticoid exposure. There were higher rates of neutropenia, arthralgia, and diarrhea in the sarilumab arm, which accounted for higher treatment-related discontinuation. This pivotal study led to the U.S. Food and Drug Administration approval of sarilumab for PMR in 2023. 182a

### Takayasu's s Arteritis

TAK, also known as pulseless disease or occlusive thromboaortopathy, is a form of granulomatous vasculitis of unknown cause that chiefly affects the aorta and its major branches, most frequently in 183, The disease is named for the Japanese ophyoung women. thalmologist who, in 1908, described a young woman with peculiar retinal arteriovenous anastomoses caused by retinal ischemia from LVV.

### American College of Rheumatology Classification Criteria

The ACR classification criteria for the diagnosis of TAK are listed in Table 89.8. However, these classification criteria were based on

data from only 63 North American patients and were never independently validated. ACR/EULAR updated criteria in 2022 to reflect a broader population of patients and to include advancements in imaging.

### Epidemiology

Although TAK has been described worldwide, it occurs most commonly in Japan, China, India, and Southeast Asia. Whereas the incidence of TAK in Japan is nearly 150 per million per year, it is only 8 to 25 per million in western Europe and North America. The prevalence has increased in other parts of the world, likely due to higher rates of immigration. TAK affects women eight times more frequently than men. The median patient age at onset is 25 years; however, approximately 25% of cases begin before age 20, and 10% to 20% of patients are seen after age 40 . Immunogenetic studies in Japanese patients suggest an years. association with several HLAs, especially HLA-Bw52, Dw12, DR2, and DQw1.188 Different HLA associations have been found in Koreans and Indians. No HLA association has been found in North American patients. Large genetic studies have identified several non-HLA loci that are associated with genetic susceptibility based on genome-wide associated level of significance (e.g., SVEP1, CFL2, VPS8, and chr13q21). In Mexican patients, TAK has been associated with previous exposure to Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

### Etiology and Pathogenesis

The cause of TAK is unknown. The nearly identical pathology in TAK and GCA has invited speculation that the model of immunopathogenesis of GCA described earlier (see Fig. 89.3) applies to TAK as well.41, Indeed, some have argued that TAK and

GCA represent a spectrum within the same disease. Similar to GCA, TAK is thought to result from an autoimmune process that targets large elastic-containing arteries. Both feature panarteritis involving infiltration of dendritic cells, T cells (including αβ, γδ, and cytotoxic), natural killer (NK) cells, and macrophages. In TAK, the majority of lymphocytes are perforin-secreting killer lymphocytes such as T cells and NK cells. The T cell receptors in TAK, as in GCA, are oligoclonal, suggesting that the vasculitis is driven in both diseases by a T cell response to a specific but unknown antigen. Chronic inflammation of the vessel wall leads to aneurysm formation, stenosis, or thrombosis more frequently in TAK than in GCA. Dissection occurs in TAK but is rare and less frequent than in syphilitic aortitis. The late phase of TAK, similar to that of GCA, is characterized by intima proliferation with superimposed atherosclerosis, medial necrosis with scarring, and adventitial fibrosis. As in GCA, the inflammatory involvement in TAK can be continuous or segmental, with

skip areas of normal vessel interposed between involved areas. It is possible that the humoral immune system may play some role in the pathogenesis of TAK. Most patients with TAK possess anti-endothelial cell antibodies that can damage vessels by inducing endothelial inflammatory cytokine production, adhesion molecules, and apoptosis.

The geographic clustering of cases has suggested that genetics and environmental factors participate in the pathogenesis of TAK. However, immunogenetic studies have not identified any other universally shared genetic risk factors. The young age of onset and the female predominance in TAK have invited speculation about the influence of female hormones in promoting an autoimmune disease process. In some countries, the apparent association of TAK with high rates of exposure to tuberculosis has suggested an infectious cause. An animal model of TAK has been produced in

mice by using a herpesvirus that infects the smooth muscle cells of the media. In that model, the media of large elastic arteries serves as an immunoprivileged site that allows the herpesvirus to propagate a chronic inflammatory response in the aorta and its major branches.

### Clinical Features

Although the presenting manifestations of TAK are protean, the vast majority of patients are seen with symptoms and signs of vascular insufficiency (from stenosis, occlusion, or aneurysm), systemic inflammation, or both115,183 (Table 89.9). In a North American series of 60 patients followed up at the National Institutes of Health, the most common presenting vascular symptoms were claudication (35%), reduced or absent pulse (25%), carotid bruit (20%), hypertension (20%), carotidynia (20%), lightheadedness (20%), and asymmetric arm blood pressures (15%). 183 Stroke, aortic regurgitation, and visual abnormalities were present at onset in less than 10% of patients. The extreme manifestations of retinal ischemia noted in Takayasu's original patient are rarely 183 Permanent loss of vision, the major concern in GCA, seen now. rarely develops in TAK.

Claudication affects the arms at least twice as frequently as the legs. Arm claudication first reveals itself as arm pain or fatigue experienced with use (e.g., while holding a hair dryer). Overall, bruit is the most common sign, eventually found in 80% of patients. Although bruit over the carotid artery is most frequent, it can also be found in the supraclavicular, infraclavicular, axillary, flank, chest, abdominal, and femoral areas. One-third of patients have multiple bruits. Unequal arm blood pressures eventually develop in half of all patients. As noted above for GCA, manual blood pressure ascertainment is preferred, particularly as electronic recordings have been shown to underestimate systolic blood pressure and overestimate diastolic blood pressure compared with intraarterial recordings. In the presence of bilateral subclavian stenoses, the only reliable measurement of systemic blood pressure may come from the lower extremities. Headache, which is common in TAK, does not correlate with carotid or vertebral disease, which develops in nearly 40% of patients. 183,

Constitutional, musculoskeletal, and other symptoms of systemic inflammation are also common presenting complaints. 115, About one in five TAK patients presents with fever and malaise, which can be accompanied by night sweats and weight loss. A few patients who have minimal or no signs of vascular insufficiency may appear to have FUO for weeks or months before the diagnosis of TAK becomes evident. A minority of patients present with myalgia or arthralgia (see Table 89.9). Some patients have striking midthoracic back pain, perhaps as a result of aortic inflammation irritating nociceptive nerve fibers.

Cardiac involvement occurs eventually in nearly one-third of patients (see Table 89.9). Aortic regurgitation develops in 20% to 30% of patients as a result of aortic root dilation, often within the first few years of diagnosis in patients with slow response to immunosuppression. Aortic regurgitation is important because it frequently progresses and may lead to left-ventricular dilation with secondary mitral regurgitation and congestive heart failure. Aortic valve replacement is often required eventually. Angina can develop as a result of coronary artery disease. TAK of the coronary arteries most often produces ostial lesions but can also produce either diffuse vasculitis of the coronary arteries or aneurysms. 195-197 Longitudinal evaluation of patients with TAK shows higher risk of ischemic heart disease, stroke, and peripheral vascular disease

(adjusted hazard ratio 1.9) compared with matched healthy controls. Myocarditis also occurs in TAK and causes potentially reversible congestive heart failure. Pericarditis is rare. TAK is, along with Behçet's disease, one of the few forms of vasculitis that can affect the large pulmonary arteries. Although TAK of the pulmonary arteries is rare (appearing in less than 3% of patients), affected patients can be seen with cough, chest wall pain, dyspnea, or hemoptysis.

Unlike polyarteritis or GPA, TAK rarely causes peripheral neuropathies. Cutaneous manifestations develop in less than 10% of patients with TAK. Erythema nodosum is most common, but purpura, livedo reticularis, and ulceration may rarely occur. As in GCA, a minority of patients with TAK who have active disease have a persistent, dry cough.

Pregnant patients with TAK are at higher risk of gestational hypertension, pre-eclampsia, and eclampsia. Low disease activity, tight blood pressure management, correction of renal artery stenosis, and anti-platelets are important to improve outcomes. Pregnancy appears to be relatively well tolerated in the presence of good medical care and in the absence of abdominal aortic involvement. 183,201,202

### Laboratory Studies

At presentation, the ESR is more frequently elevated (80%) than the CRP (~50%). Mild anemia and hypergammaglobulinemia are common. The white blood cell count is usually normal or

slightly elevated. The platelet count is elevated in one-third of patients, and may exceed 500,000/μL in those with active disease. The serum creatinine and urinalysis are usually normal. Any renal abnormalities are usually secondary to hypertension; unlike ANCA-associated vasculitis, TAK rarely causes glomerulonephritis.

### Imaging

Vascular abnormalities in TAK can be imaged by conventional angiography, MRI, MRA, CT angiography, or ultrasonography 44,110,112,183,203 (Figs. 89.11 to 89.13). Each imaging technique has advantages and disadvantages (Table 89.10). The earliest detectable abnormality in TAK is thickening of the vessel wall from inflammation. MRI, ultrasonography, and, to a lesser degree, CT can detect this early vessel wall thickening. The 2018 EULAR recommendations to prioritize MRI to evaluate for early mural inflammation and luminal changes provide a useful algorithm for evaluating patients. Conventional angiography is invasive and provides the least sensitive method for visualizing wall thickness. While considered the "gold standard" for delineating stenoses, occlusions, and aneurysms, conventional angiography is rarely used in clinic practice for TAK. However, only conventional angiography allows the direct measurement of central arterial blood pressure, which may be otherwise unobtainable in patients with stenotic lesions affecting all four extremities. Although MRA does not provide the same level of detail as conventional angiography, it comes close. Because MRA is not invasive and does not involve ionizing radiation, it has become the preferred imaging method for assessing the extent of vascular involvement and damage, both initially and during follow-up. The role of MRI in assessing disease activity is not clear because vessel wall edema and contrast enhancement have not correlated well with clinical measures of disease activity. Although PET scanning would be expected to be more sensitive than angiography in the early detection of vascular inflammation that precedes the development of stenoses, its sensitivity may be no greater than MRI. PET scanning has no established role in following disease activity in TAK. While PETVAS may have a role in GCA, longitudinal studies show that PETVAS does not reliably change with treatment in patients with TAK. This is not entirely explained by disease duration or therapy and is thought to reflect differences in vascular pathophysiology between these conditions. Indeed, one study of 28 TAK patients showed that PET scans did not correlate with clinical, biologic, or MRI assessment of disease activity. .

The most common sites of lesions in TAK are the aorta (65%) and the left subclavian arteries (93%)183 (Table 89.11). The left subclavian artery is affected slightly more frequently than the right. Carotid, renal, and vertebral arteries are also commonly affected. Lesions may be stenotic (93%), occluded (57%), dilated (16%), or aneurysmal (7%). Stenotic lesions are approximately four times more common than aneurysmal lesions. Stenotic segments often extend a few centimeters and may be followed by areas of dilation (see Fig. 89.11). The majority of patients (53%) have vascular lesions above and below the diaphragm. However, the frequency distribution of aortic lesions varies considerably from country to country, with a suggestion that abdominal aorta and renal involvement is more prevalent in patients of African descent. 183,207

### Diagnosis and Diagnostic Tests

The ACR has established classification criteria for the diagnosis of TAK (see Table 89.8). In clinical practice, its diagnosis is almost

always secured by an imaging procedure (see Table 89.10) that demonstrates the characteristic abnormalities of the aorta and its major branches (Fig. 89.14). Rarely, the diagnosis is first suggested when a pathologist finds granulomatous inflammation in a section of the aorta or other larger artery that was removed or biopsied during a vascular surgery procedure. Unfortunately, the diagnosis of TAK is often delayed; the delay averaged 44 months in one large

series. . The most frequent impediment to a speedy diagnosis is a physician's failure to consider TAK in the differential diagnosis. Although the rarity of TAK helps explain its omission from diagnostic consideration, another reason is that some patients have striking features of inflammation that camouflage or overshadow the somewhat more familiar vascular abnormalities. Indeed, a few patients with TAK present chiefly with FUO. Most of these patients have other, albeit subtle, manifestations of TAK such as bruits, diminished pulses, unequal arm blood pressures, or aortic regurgitation. In other patients with more striking vascular abnormalities, the physician might be lured into focusing on familiar and dramatic abnormalities such as anemia or thrombocytosis.

Thus instead of ordering an imaging test that would explain the patient's unequal and low blood pressure in the left arm, the physician mistakenly diverts the patient to a hematologist, gastroenterologist, or oncologist for additional blood tests and procedures that further delay the diagnosis.

Many of these delays can be prevented by remembering that TAK should be included in the differential diagnosis of any patient younger than 40 years who presents with FUO, aortic regurgitation, hypertension, or unequal or absent pulses. Delays in diagnosis can also be reduced by carefully searching for unequal or absent upper-extremity pulses and by listening for bruits not only over the carotid arteries but also above and below the clavicle (for subclavian artery bruits) and over the abdomen and flanks (for renal and other mesenteric artery bruits). Recognizing that anemia and thrombocytosis can be manifestations of active inflammatory
