disorders such as vasculitis can also help speed the diagnosis of TAK.

Once an imaging test demonstrates disease of the aorta or its major branches, the differential diagnosis narrows to a set of disorders that are usually easily differentiated (Table 89.12). Most rheumatic diseases that can affect the aorta are distinguished by their associated features. For example, Cogan's syndrome typically produces ocular inflammation (especially keratitis) and vestibuloauditory dysfunction. The one rheumatic disease that can be difficult to distinguish from TAK is GCA (Table 89.13). Usually, the patient's age and the distribution of lesions allow their rapid differentiation, but it can be difficult or even impossible to distinguish TAK from GCA in patients 50 years and older. The similarity of treatment (see subsequent discussion) diminishes the practical importance of solving this diagnostic dilemma.

Infections of the aorta are rare in most countries. Tertiary syphilis can be excluded by a negative fluorescent treponemal antibody test (the rapid plasma reagin test yields false-negative results in approximately one-quarter of patients with late-stage syphilis). Other diseases of the aorta (see Table 89.13) are usually readily separated from TAK by the history and physical examination. There has been growing appreciation for a small subset of patients who have noninfectious aortitis that is difficult to categorize. At one center, noninfectious aortitis was found in 8% of patients undergoing resection of the ascending aorta. Although nearly 70% had giant cells, only a minority neatly fit a diagnosis of TAK or GCA. A fraction of the cases of thoracic or abdominal aortitis are caused by IgG4-related disease, a systemic immune-mediated disease characterized by infiltration of IgG4-bearing plasma cells in the aorta or other affected organs. 210,211

### Treatment

### Medical Therapy

Corticosteroids are the cornerstone of treatment of active TAK. 183, Prednisone, at a dose of 0.5 to 1 mg/kg per day, is indicated for the treatment of active disease. Criteria for active

disease include new onset or worsening of two or more of the following: (1) fever or other systemic features (in the absence of other causes), (2) elevated ESR, (3) symptoms or signs of vascular ischemia or inflammation (e.g., claudication, absent pulse, and carotidynia), and (4) typical angiographic lesions. Although approximately 85% of patients with TAK present with active disease, approximately 15% do not. The initial dose of prednisone is continued for 4 to 12 weeks before commencing a gradual taper, as is done when treating patients with GCA (see previous discussion). Although nearly two-thirds of patients achieve remission, more than half later relapse. Relapses are especially common when the prednisone dose falls below 20 mg per day.

Relapses can be treated by increasing the prednisone dose or adding an immunosuppressive agent. No agent used for TAK has been evaluated in a double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. However, open trials have suggested that weekly oral methotrexate (started at 0.3 mg/kg per week, with the initial dose not to exceed 15 mg/wk) is a moderately effective corticosteroid-sparing drug. Methotrexate can be gradually increased to 25 mg/ wk. The emphasis is on lowering the corticosteroid dose because methotrexate seldom allows the elimination of prednisone completely; most patients continue to require at least 5 to 10 mg/ day of prednisone. Small open trials have provided even more encouraging results about the effectiveness of anti-TNF inhibitors (etanercept and infliximab) in treating patients with refractory TAK.215-217 These trials emphasize that although these agents can treat TAK, they rarely cure it: relapses are likely when the treatment is stopped. Tocilizumab, which blocks the IL-6 receptor, 147,148,218-220However, in has been effective in individual patients. a small cohort of patients (n = 18), tocilizumab has no effect on time-to-relapse compared with placebo. There are also reports of disease progression while on tocilizumab, masked by normal inflammatory markers.

TAK occasionally overlaps with inflammatory bowel disease, and when one patient with ulcerative colitis was treated with tofacitinib, there was evidence of vasculitis improvement by PET/CT. This led to studies comparing tofacitinib with methotrexate that showed that complete remission at 6 and 12 months was higher in the tofacitinib arm, and this was associated with lower relapse rates, longer relapse-free survival, and lower glucocorticoid doses at 3, 6, and 12 months. A similar study compared tofacitinib to leflunomide and also showed that the former was associated with high prevalence of remission and decreased cumulative steroid exposure.

Case reports and small series suggest that other corticosteroid-sparing drugs may include azathioprine (2 mg/kg per day), mycophenolate mofetil (2000 mg/day), cyclosporine, tacrolimus, leflunomide, and cyclophosphamide (2 mg/kg per day). 183, The toxicity of cyclophosphamide in young women is so high that it is rarely used in TAK. Although abatacept (CTLA-4Ig) might be effective in treating GCA, one randomized, double-blind, controlled trial suggested this agent is ineffective in TAK.

In a subset of patients, TAK will be identified years after the initial inflammatory phase. These patients may have pulse discrepancies or recall a history of FUO but will not have current fever, constitutional symptoms, anemia, or elevated inflammatory markers at time of evaluation. We recommend pursuing vascular imaging to confirm the diagnosis and to assess for active vascular disease. If quiescent at time of evaluation, these patients generally do not require corticosteroid or immunosuppressive therapy; however, longitudinal monitoring for recurrence and subclinical vascular progression is strongly recommended.

Efforts to prevent osteoporosis should be initiated e arly (as described in Chapter 107). Modifiable risk factors for atherosclerosis—especially hypertension, smoking, inactivity, diabetes, and hyperlipidemia—should be treated maximally.

### Surgical Therapy

TAK is the form of vasculitis most frequently requiring revascularization procedures. 183, A review of the experience with vascular interventions in TAK supports several general recommendations. Medical therapy rarely reduces or reverses stenotic lesions; however, it is critical to note that the mere presence of stenosis does not necessitate intervention. The gut, for example, has such rich collaterals that even critical stenoses of the celiac, superior, or inferior mesenteric arteries usually produce no symptoms and require no surgical intervention. Moreover, many patients with arm claudication will develop collateral circulation and improve substantially over time with medical therapy alone. For upper-extremity vascular insufficiency, patiently waiting for a response to medical therapy usually pays higher dividends than undertaking rapid surgical intervention. Second, whenever possible, surgical intervention should be deferred until TAK is in remission; procedures done during active disease often produce disappointing results. Third, b ypass s urgery y ields better results than angioplasty. With bypass graft procedures, autologous vessels give better results than synthetic grafts (restenosis rates of 9% vs. 36%). Patients who undergo aortic surgery are liable to develop anastomotic aneurysms; such aneurysms developed in nearly 14% of patients followed for 20 years. 229, Although angioplasty gives good short-term results, long-term results are often disappointing except for very short stenotic segments. The experience with conventional stents has been mostly disappointing.

### Outcome

Twenty percent of TAK patients have a self-limited disease. The rest have a relapsing-remitting or progressive course requiring chronic corticosteroid and/or immunosuppressive therapy. Nearly twothirds of patients experience new angiographic lesions. In one study from the National Institutes of Health, 74% of patients experienced some form of morbidity and 47% were permanently disabled. In a Japanese study of 120 patients, survival at 15 years was 83%. A study of 126 TAK patients in the United States reported 10-year survival of 97% and 15-year survival of 85%. Patients with TAK do have a higher mortality than the general population; the study estimated the standardized mortality ratio in TAK to be 3.0 (95% CI, 1.08.0). Age of onset older than 35 years; development of major complications (i.e., retinopathy, hypertension, aortic regurgitation, and aneurysm); or a progressive course was associated with decreased survival. Congestive heart failure and renal failure are the most common causes of death.

# Anti-neutrophil Cytoplasmic Antibody-Associated Vasculitis

### KEY POINTS

The anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA)—associated vasculitides are granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA), microscopic polyangiitis (MPA), and eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA). They affect smalland medium-sized vessels and share clinical, pathologic, and diagnostic features.

ANCA testing, especially by enzyme-linked immunoassay, is useful to diagnose ANCA-associated vasculitides in the appropriate clinical context, but its utility in assessing disease activity is unclear.

GPA is characterized histologically by necrotizing granulomatous inflammation in addition to vasculitis. Common clinical manifestations include destructive sinonasal lesions, pulmonary nodules, and pauci-immune glomerulonephritis (GN). GPA is most commonly associated with cytoplasmic-staining ANCA and antibodies to proteinase 3.

MPA is characterized histologically by vasculitis without granulomatous inflammation. Common clinical manifestations include rapidly progressive pauci-immune GN (which can be the only organ system affected clinically) and alveolar hemorrhage. MPA is most commonly associated with perinuclear staining ANCA and antibodies to myeloperoxidase.

EGPA is characterized histologically by eosinophilic tissue infiltration in addition to vasculitis. Common clinical manifestations include asthma and peripheral eosinophilia. Only 40% of patients produce detectable ANCA.

For patients with organor life-threatening disease, combination therapy (with either glucocorticoids and/or avacopan and either rituximab or cyclophosphamide) is needed to induce remission. Remission can often be maintained with less toxic medications such as methotrexate, azathioprine, and lower doses of rituximab. With current treatment regimens, disease remission is achieved in 75% to 93% of patients.

### Introduction

The anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA)associated vasculitides (AAV) target smallto medium-sized vessels in multiple organ systems, with sinonasal, pulmonary, and renal involvement being particularly common. Specific diseases included in this category are granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA), microscopic polyangiitis (MPA; including disease limited to the kidney), and

eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA; also known as Churg-Strauss syndrome). These diseases are categorized together, given their association with antibodies directed against antigens in the cytoplasm of neutrophils—proteinase 3 (PR3) and myeloperoxidase (MPO)—and many overlapping clinical manifestations, diagnostic testing, and treatment strategies.

### Classification Criteria and Nomenclature

To differentiate the various vasculitic syndromes, classification criteria and disease definitions have been proposed by multiple groups. The developers stress that classification criteria are not intended to be used as diagnostic criteria in a general population and that definitions serve as a consensus group of conditions for which classification (and ideally diagnostic) criteria could be developed. Revised classification criteria for GPA, MPA, and EGPA, developed in a collaboration between the American College of Rheumatology (ACR) and the European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology (EAAR; formerly EULAR) were published in 2022 and are expected to be the standard for enrolling patients in research studies.1-3 Previously, the most widely used criteria were ACR classification criteria endorsed in 1990, before there was widespread ANCA testing or a consensus definition of MPA. The ACR/EAAR classification criteria are shown in Table 90.1.

To better define the nomenclature of the systemic vasculitides, the Chapel Hill Consensus Conference (CHCC) was first convened in 1994 to reach consensus on the names for the most common forms of systemic vasculitis. Vasculitides were categorized into large-, medium-, and small-vessel groups. This conference formally defined MPA for the first time and differentiated it from classic polyarteritis nodosa (PAN) by defining MPA as a pauci-immune necrotizing vasculitis affecting small vessels, with or without medium-vessel involvement. PAN was defined as an arteritis of medium-sized and small vessels without involvement of the arterioles, venules, or capillaries (including glomerular capillaries). The CHCC nomenclature system was revised in 2012 and recommended a shift from using eponyms to noneponymous replacements. Other changes include the addition of variable vessel and single-organ vasculitis, as well as vasculitis associated with systemic disease and vasculitis associated with probable etiology (e.g., vasculitis associated with an infection, drug, or malignancy).

### 2022 American College of Rheumatology/European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology Classification Criteria for Granulomatosis With Polyangiitis

These classification criteria should be applied to classify a patient as having granulomatosis with polyangiitis when a diagnosis of smallor mediumvessel vasculitis has been made

These classification criteria should be applied to classify a patient as having eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangitis when a diagnosis of smallor medium-vessel vasculitis s has been made

The names and definitions of ANCA-associated vasculitis—GPA, MPA, and EGPA, as set forth by the CHCC 2012 conference— are presented in Table 90.2. The definitions for other small-vessel vasculitides are included for comparison.

It is important to note that the ACR classification criteria and CHCC definitions are not intended to serve as diagnostic criteria because they begin with the premise that a patient is known to have some form of vasculitis. Multiple previous studies showed that the 1990 ACR classification criteria and CHCC definitions had poor positive predictive value when applied to cohorts of patients referred for possible vasculitis, It would not be surprising if the new ACR/EAAR criteria have similar limitations, especially because GPA, MPA, and EGPA are all rare diseases. Other groups have developed diagnostic criteria for AAV, but these are not widely accepted.

### Epidemiology

Epidemiologic studies of AAV have been hampered by the evolving classification criteria and disease definitions, along with the rarity of these diseases. Most epidemiologic investigations of AAV

have studied populations of European descent. These studies suggest an overall incidence of approximately 10 to 30 individuals per million per year, with a slight male predominance (male to female, 1.5:1).10, These diseases are rare in childhood, and the incidence increases with age, with the peak incidence occurring in people between 65 and 74 years of age (6 cases per 100,000). Compared with adult-onset AAV, patients with childhood-onset AAV have a higher incidence of subglottic stenosis and a lower incidence of renal involvement.

AAVs appear to be more common in populations of European descent. In France, the overall prevalence of GPA, MPA, PAN, and EGPA was two times higher for subjects of European ancestry (104.7 cases/million) than for non-Europeans (52.5 cases/ million). GPA and MPA are thought to be rare in people of mostly African descent, but enough patients have been seen at expert centers for case series to be published.15, Additional study is needed regarding the epidemiology of AAV in non-European populations.

The numbers of patients diagnosed with AAV have increased since the 1990s. Between 1994 and 2006 in Germany, the prevalence of GPA increased from 58 to 98 cases per million; MPA,

from 9 to 28 cases per million; and EGPA, from 7 to 24 cases per million. In the United Kingdom (UK), the prevalence of GPA increased from 28.8 per million in 1990 to 64.8 per million in 2005.19 This increase likely reflects increased awareness and diagnosis after the development of the ACR classification criteria, CHCC definitions, and ANCA testing. In this setting, it is difficult to determine whether the incidence of a disease is changing. In addition, improved survival increases point prevalence.

In European populations, GPA is the most prevalent AAV. The incidence of GPA ranges from 4.9 to 10.5 cases per million per year. The reported prevalences have ranged from 24 to 157 per million, with the highest reported in Sweden and the UK.12, Variation in incidence and prevalence between countries has suggested that disease risk declines in a northsouth gradient in the Northern Hemisphere.

The incidence of MPA among European populations ranges from 0.5 to 11.6 cases per million per year. Unlike GPA, the highest incidence of MPA seems to occur in southern Europe, specifically in Greece and Spain. MPA is also more common in certain non-European populations, with an incidence of 14.8 cases per million per year in Japan and 24.0 cases in Kuwait, the highest reported incidence thus far.12, The prevalence of MPA ranges from 0 to 66 cases per million among European countries.

The overall prevalence and incidence of AAV appears to be similar between Japan (prevalence, 86 cases per million; incidence, 22.6 cases per million) and the UK (prevalence, 50 cases per million; incidence, 21.8 cases per million). However, more than 80% of patients in Japan are perinuclear-staining (p-ANCA) or MPO-ANCA positive, whereas two-thirds of patients in the UK are cytoplasmic-staining (c-ANCA) or PR3-ANCA positive. As suggested from the serologic differences, MPA is more common in Japan (occurring in 83% of patients with AAV), whereas GPA is more common in the UK (66%). Compared with patients in the UK who have GPA, renal involvement is less common in Japan.21, In China, population-based estimates of disease prevalence and incidence have not been defined, although a survey of 43.7 million inpatients reported that 0.25% were diagnosed with AAV. However, MPA comprises approximately 75% to 80% of the AAV cases, and MPO-ANCA is more prevalent than PR3- ANCA, even among patients with clinical symptoms suggestive of GPA.24, These findings suggest that among East Asian populations, the overall prevalence of AAV is at least as common as in the UK population, but GPA is far less common.

EGPA is the least prevalent of the AAV. Among European populations, the incidence of EGPA ranges from 0.5 to 6.8 cases per million individuals.12, Among patients with asthma, it ranges from 34.6 to 64.4 per million.26, The overall prevalence of EGPA in European populations has been estimated to range from 2 to 38 cases per million.12, A sex predominance has not been clearly demonstrated. In Japan, the prevalence of EGPA has been estimated to be 17.8 cases per million, with women more frequently affected than men.

### Triggering Factors

Environmental exposures, infections, and drugs have been hypothesized to be triggering factors for the development of AAV. Among environmental and occupational exposures, the most consistent associations have been observed with crystalline silica, with most studies showing an odds ratio (OR) of 2.5 to 5. Associations with other exposures such as heavy metals, farming, organic solvents, and pesticides have been studied, but results have not been

consistent. The influence of infection on GPA pathogenesis has been suggested by a cyclical pattern of occurrence observed in some studies. However, the only clear association is seen with Staphylococcus aureus, where nasal carriage of S. aureus has been associated with an increased risk of relapse in GPA. The role of S. aureus or other infectious agents in disease initiation has not been established. Initial studies are being conducted to investigate the role of the nasal microbiome on disease development and activity. Lastly, the most commonly reported drugs causing AAV include propothiouracil, hydralazine, minocycline, and levamisole-adulterated cocaine. Use of leukotriene antagonists and omalizumab has been linked to the development of EGPA. These agents may unmask underlying EGPA by allowing corticosteroid tapering or are prescribed to patients with undiagnosed and worsening EGPA, but a direct causal link cannot be excluded.34-36

### Genetics

GPA, MPA, and EGPA are complex genetic diseases, with multiple genetic variants with modest effects influencing disease risk. Thus, large cohorts of patients and controls are needed to identify genetic risk factors. GPA is the most thoroughly studied of these three diseases.

Familial studies of GPA have suggested a genetic influence on disease susceptibility. A nationwide registry-based study in Sweden showed that the relative risk of GPA in a first-degree relative of an individual with GPA was estimated to be 1.56 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.356.9). This familial risk is lower than in other autoimmune diseases such as systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and multiple sclerosis (MS) but is of similar magnitude as the familial risk in rheumatoid arthritis (RA). First-degree relatives of patients with GPA have an increased incidence of seropositive RA (hazard ratio [HR], 1.54; 95% CI, 1.092.19) and other autoimmune diseases, including MS (HR 1.92; 95% CI, 1.163.16). Children of individuals with GPA have an increased risk of RA (standardized incidence ratio, 1.34). In an independent cohort, a genetic risk score based on RA susceptibility genes was associated with GPA risk. These findings suggest that GPA and RA share genetic risk factors.

Initial candidate gene studies of GPA replicated associations with the class II human leukocyte antigen (HLA) region, CTLA4, PTPN22, and SERPINA1. The strongest associations with HLA region have been between GPA and the extended haplotype containing HLA-DPB1*0401, which has replicated in ANCApositive patients.42,43Some variants of cytotoxic T-lymphocyte associated antigen 4 (CTLA4) associated with GPA affect surface expression or messenger RNA stability.41, However, these associations were not identified in genome-wide association studies (GWAS). The R620W (rs2476601) variant of PTPN22 associated with GPA41,48,49 interrupts its binding with c-src tyrosine kinase, thus altering B and T cell receptor responsiveness. The rare Z and S alleles of SERPINA1 associated with GPA code for a deficiency of αl anti-trypsin, a serine protease inhibitor that is a major inhibitor of PR3.50 Additional meta-analyses have identified associations with eight genes outside of the HLA region.

Two GWAS have been published in GPA and MPA. The first study examined 2267 people with AAV and 6858 control subjects of northern European descent. The most statistically significant genetic associations in the combined (GPA and MPA) cohort were observed with HLA-DP(OR,3.67; p= 1.5 x 10-71), COL11A2(OR, 1.83; p = 6.4 x 10-24), and SERPINA1 (OR, 0.51; p = 2.4 x 10-9).

A second GWAS studied 1020 GPA cases and 2734 control subjects of European descent. This study confirmed the strong association with the HLA-DPB1*04 allele. An association with SEMA6A was observed but could not be replicated by a second group. A nominal association was also observed with SERPINA1.

A GWAS of 534 patients with EGPA found a strong association with HLA-DQ, but only in patients with MPO-ANCA, providing additional evidence that this HLA locus is associated with antigen-specific autoimmunity rather than other aspects of vasculitis. In contrast, the HLA region had little if any association with ANCA-negative EGPA. Seven of eight genes related to EGPA were also associated with eosinophil counts in unaffected controls. Alleles previously implicated by candidate gene studies were not replicated in this GWAS.

The genetic association studies conducted thus far have primarily examined people of European descent, and the epidemiology of GPA and MPA differs between European and Asian countries. Genetic studies of MPA in Japan have suggested associations between MPA and IRF5, the HLA-DRB1*09:01-DQB1*03:03 haplotype, and KIR2DS3.55, Studies in China have suggested association between MPA and HLA-DRB1*1101, GPA with HLA-DRB1*1202, and replicated with association with HLA- DPB1 and GPA.57, These associations, aside from HLA-DPB1 and HLA-DRB1*09:01-DQB1*03:03,59 need to be replicated. A study of African Americans with AAV showed that the odds of having HLA-DRB1 *15 were 73.3-fold higher in PR3-ANCA-positive people compared with healthy control subjects. In addition, a disproportionate number of people carried the HLA-DRB1 *1501 allele of European descent compared with the HLA-DRB1*1503 allele of African descent. Further studies in non-European populations are needed to determine whether the genetic risk factors identified in Europeans are broadly applicable to other ethnic groups.

### Clinical Manifestations

Although AAV can affect almost all organ systems, the frequency of organ involvement varies greatly. Data on organ system involvement come from a small number of cohorts of 30 to 400 patients.60-71 Some reports indicate that new organ system involvement occurs frequently over time, particularly in GPA.60, The diversity of presentations within a given organ system is apparent from case series and reviews focused on that organ system and reports of particularly unusual cases.60,

Not all clinical features of AAV are directly attributable to local vascular damage. This phenomenon is obvious with

regard to constitutional symptoms but, in addition, the risk of venous thromboembolic events is elevated in the absence of venous inflammation,76,77 and the pathophysiology of arthritis is unknown. The extent to which myalgia and gastrointestinal (GI) symptoms indicate vasculitis in these organ systems is not known.

As a rough approximation, the features of MPA can all be seen in GPA or EGPA, particularly in ANCA-positive patients. GPA, by definition, features perivascular necrotizing granulomatous inflammation, and EGPA features eosinophil-rich granulomatous inflammation and/or parenchymal infiltration by eosinophils. Unfortunately, many of the largest series and clinical trials do not allow comparison of organ system involvement in MPA, GPA, and EGPA, due to pooling some or all of the entities as ANCAassociated vasculitis.68,78-81

### Granulomatosis With Polyangiitis

Although the range of presentations and subsequent courses in GPA is extraordinarily broad, longitudinal analyses of larger cohorts generally agree on the frequency of involvement of different organ systems over time (Table 90.3).60, Frequencies in children appear to be similar to those in adults. Inflammation

Progression to glomerulonephritis (GN) or alveolar hemorrhage remains a common route to diagnosis, but ANCA testing has facilitated diagnosis at more "localized"82,83or "limited"84 stages or with unusual presentations. Constitutional symptoms and inflammation in the upper and/or lower airway may develop simultaneously with systemic vasculitis or may precede it by weeks, months, 83 or years.

Upper airway inflammation in GPA is notable for its destructive potential, but permanent damage does not always occur and is highly variable in its pace. Recurrent epistaxis, mucopurulent nasal discharge, and bloody nasal crusting are common. Inflammation of the paranasal sinuses causing pain (Fig. 90.1) is also common, which can be exacerbated by poor air flow over inflamed tissue. The nasal septum is particularly at risk, and septal perforation can progress to collapse and a characteristic "saddle-nose" deformity (Fig. 90.2). Bone erosion occurs elsewhere—for example, in the sinuses, hard palate, and orbit—but is much less common. Subglottic involvement occurs in approximately 15%60,73,74,85 and often causes obstruction (Fig. 90.3) due to either active inflammation or subsequent scarring, which can be life-threatening. It is observed particularly in children and young adults. .

Eye and orbital involvement are also striking in GPA, both in terms of frequency (30% to 60% over time and much higher than in MPA or EGPA) and diversity.60, Conjunctivitis and episcleritis occur frequently but are usually not painful and pose no danger to the patient. In contrast, scleritis is usually painful and can threaten vision if it is not treated aggressively. These conditions cannot be distinguished by simple inspection. Retinal vasculitis, uveitis, oculomotor nerve palsy, and optic neuropathy are less common but are well described.63, Inflammation of the lacrimal gland, sac, and/or duct, seen in about 10% of patients, leads to excessive tearing, and blockage of the lacrimal duct's entry into the nose can produce similar symptoms.60, Orbital pseudotumor (Fig. 90.4) is notable because it is relatively common (6% to 15%) and results in

blindness in 50% of affected individuals despite aggressive 60,63,72 treatment.

Other manifestations in the head include ear congestion and conductive hearing loss, which can result from inflammation of the middle ear or the auditory tube or by obstruction of the tube at its entry into the nose. Oral ulcers, gingivitis, and auricular chondritis are well described but less frequent. 60,

The lung is affected in several distinct ways. Pulmonary nodules, which are necrotizing and frequently cavitate (Fig. 90.5), often occur before or in the absence of systemic vasculitis and thus are a common feature of "localized"82,83 or "limited"84 GPA. Nodular disease is often asymptomatic or merely produces cough. Alveolar hemorrhage, characterized by mild to life-threatening dyspnea and hemoptysis, is also common but is clinically and radiographically distinct from nodular disease.87, Other well-described pulmonary manifestations include pleuritis60 and endobronchial lesions distal to the subglottis89; the frequency of the latter may be underestimated because they can only be definitively diagnosed by bronchoscopy. Clinically significant pulmonary fibrosis and bronchiectasis is relatively uncommon in GPA because parenchymal lung disease generally heals without scarring.

Musculoskeletal pain is common even in the early phases of disease. Monoarticular, oligoarticular, and polyarticular involvement are all seen. Arthralgia is more common than inflammatory arthritis, which can be detected on physical examination. Myalgia is usually not accompanied by abnormal exam findings or laboratory testing, and thus the musculoskeletal features of GPA can resemble polymyalgia rheumatica, spondyloarthritis, RA, crystal arthropathies, the full range of connective tissue diseases, or even fibromyalgia. One distinctive articular presentation is relatively common in GPA but uncommon in other diseases: migratory arthralgias or arthritis of large joints, in which patients experience severe pain in the wrist, elbow, shoulder, ankle, or knee for a few days before complete resolution, to be followed soon afterward by similar symptoms in one to two other joints.

Cutaneous small-vessel vasculitis and, less commonly, vasculitis of small arteries is observed in GPA. Purpura, papules, vesicles/ bullae, ulcers, digit ischemia, subcutaneous nodules, and livedo racemosa have been reported.90, A characteristic lesion is a superficial, nonerythematous cutaneous nodule with pathologic findings showing a necrotizing, palisading granuloma, but this lesion is also seen in EGPA and other systemic diseases.92,

Peripheral neuropathy can present either as a sensory polyneuropathy or a multifocal neuropathy (mononeuritis multiplex) with both sensory and motor deficits. Neuropathic pain is common but not universal in the setting of sensory loss. Cranial neuropathies are less frequent, with the exception of sensorineural hearing loss, which is an important source of morbidity. Although central nervous system (CNS) abnormalities such as stroke occur in patients with GPA,

vasculitis of intracerebral arteries is thought to be rare; pachymeningitis is another well-described but uncommon manifestation.

Patients with GPA will have cardiac problems and GI symptoms, but vasculitis of the heart muscle or the GI organs is very 96, Pericarditis, in contrast, is a more common uncommon. source of chest pain that is directly attributable to GPA.

GN is present in many patients at diagnosis and affects more than half at some point during their disease course.60, On biopsy, the GN is characterized as pauci-immune and is frequently necrotizing and crescentic (Fig. 90.6). Renal function may deteriorate significantly within a week or occur more slowly over months or years. Renal involvement is frequently asymptomatic until uremia or nephrotic syndrome develops, with the latter occurring in a minority of patients.

### Microscopic Polyangiitis

The clinical features of MPA consist of a subset of those seen in GPA (i.e., features that lack granulomatous inflammation).63, Reported frequencies of manifestations have varied much more than in GPA or EGPA (see Table 90.3), likely for multiple reasons: series from nephrology centers are expected to report very high rates of renal involvement65; series that include ANCA-negative patients without GN may include patients in whom the diagnosis might be debated63,64; confidence in defining involvement in some organ systems (e.g., cardiac, GI, and CNS) is challenging; and, most interestingly, there appear to be important differences in MPA between patients in Europe and East Asia, particularly in the type of lung involvement.

With those caveats, the following tentative statements can be made: GN is probably more common in MPA than in GPA, at least at diagnosis.60, Cutaneous vasculitis, neuropathy,99 constitutional and musculoskeletal symptoms, and risk of alveolar hemorrhage are probably similar. Involvement of the eye is distinctly less common. GI involvement has been reported at both low and relatively high frequencies in different series, so it is difficult to draw conclusions.63, As with GPA, it is also difficult

to determine the rate of true CNS or myocardial vasculitis; subclinical myocardial abnormalities have been detected. One manifestation that appears to be more common in MPA than GPA is pulmonary fibrosis.71,

The duration of symptoms before diagnosis of MPA is wide. The initial symptoms are often nonspecific constitutional and musculoskeletal complaints, which often develop over days or months but can be present for years. Patients who have MPA (or MPO-ANCA antibodies) typically present at a more advanced stage of renal failure with worse renal damage on histology than patients with GPA (or PR3-ANCA).105, However, it is not clear that GN in MPA is intrinsically worse than in GPA because the "granulomatous" manifestations of GPA may lead to earlier diag- C nosis. Severe pauci-immune GN associated with MPO-ANCA and without any evidence of vasculitis elsewhere is often referred to as renal-limited vasculitis or necrotizing crescentic GN rather than MPA.65,78

### Eosinophilic Granulomatosis With Polyangiitis (Churg-Strauss Syndrome)

While the hallmarks of EGPA are asthma and peripheral eosinophilia out of proportion to what might be seen in asthma or atopy, other symptoms and findings are needed to make the diagnosis. Constitutional and musculoskeletal symptoms are common and may be the first clue to a disease beyond asthma. Asthma is almost universal, but not always severe, and is variable in its onset relative to the onset of EGPA. Although EGPA is intimately linked to asthma, the conditions are distinct: Patients frequently have asthma exacerbations without exacerbations of other EGPA manifestations, and often asthma rather than EGPA-specific symptoms requires chronic glucocorticoid use for control.66,

The organ-specific manifestations of EGPA are attributable to vasculitis, parenchymal eosinophilic infiltration, or both. Reported frequencies of organ involvement are shown in Table 94.3.66, Upper-airway involvement is common in EGPA, but, in contrast to GPA, it is usually "allergic" in character and is seldom destructive. GN and alveolar hemorrhage are uncommon and are highly associated with positive ANCA (usually

MPO-ANCA), 66,70,108 which is detected in only 35% to 40% of patients with EGPA. 70,

Skin involvement is at least as common in EGPA as in GPA but again includes "allergic" lesions such as urticaria in addition to a wide range of cutaneous vasculitis manifestations. Nodules representing necrotizing granulomas can be seen, as in GPA. GI involvement, including eosinophilic infiltration of the GI tract, may be more common in EGPA than in GPA or MPA.

Neuropathy, which is thought to be due to vasculitis rather than the neurotoxins of eosinophils, is more common in EGPA than in GPA or MPA,63,66,69 and multifocal neuropathy can be used to distinguish EGPA from a hypereosinophilic syndrome (HES).70, Finally, clinically important cardiac involvement is clearly more common in EGPA than in MPA or GPA, with about 15% of patients having eosinophilic myocarditis severe enough to cause cardiomyopathy.63, Cardiac disease resembles that seen in HES and is usually seen in ANCA-negative patients. 66,70,108

### Diagnostic Testing

The roles of laboratory tests, other diagnostic tests, and biopsy in diagnosing GPA, MPA, or EGPA vary with the clinical setting.

ANCAs were initially discovered and established as a clinical test using immunofluorescence staining of neutrophils. Subsequently, the target antigen for the c-ANCA pattern was identified as PR3, and the antigen for the p-ANCA pattern was identified as MPO. Immunofluorescence staining (Fig. 90.7) was previously used as a screening test before testing for anti- PR3 and anti-MPO antibodies by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA). However, p-ANCA immunofluorescence has poor specificity for AAV, whereas MPOand PR3-ANCA antibodies have high specificity for AAV. Thus the most recent consensus statement proposes that ELISA methods be used as the primary screening method.

PR3or MPO-ANCA are sufficiently specific that they can be considered diagnostic in cases highly suggestive of vasculitis (Table 90.4). Examples include digital ischemia (diagnosed by physical examination), noncompressive neuropathy (diagnosed by nerve conduction studies), and alveolar hemorrhage (diagnosed by either bronchoalveolar lavage or witnessed hemoptysis plus computed tomography imaging consistent with diffuse bleeding). There is a difference of opinion in one key area. Some experts believe that a kidney biopsy should be performed whenever possible to confirm pauci-immune GN and give prognostic information derived from the degree of permanent damage, 106,112,113 whereas other experts

argue that red blood cell casts in the urine in the setting of PR3or MPO-ANCA is sufficient.

The poor specificity of p-ANCA alone (i.e., without positive testing for antibodies to MPO) is well known. However, anti- MPO or anti-PR3 antibodies have been documented in other conditions: endocarditis, SLE,115 inflammatory bowel disease (IBD),116 and use of cocaine adulterated with levamisole. These associations are important to remember because the clinical syndromes can overlap substantially with those of AAV. In endocarditis, lupus, and use of cocaine/levamisole, the presence of additional autoantibodies is the rule. In the case of cocaine/levamisole, there is often a disconnect between the observed ANCA pattern by immunofluorescence and testing for the specific antigen.

Other than the characteristic disease in the kidney, the disease of MPA in other organs is difficult to distinguish from that of other forms of small-vessel vasculitis by light microscopy. The AAV are more likely to involve small arteries and arterioles than are vasculitides associated with immune complexes, but involvement of capillaries and venules is the most common site in all forms of small-vessel vasculitis. The absence or paucity of immune complex deposition by immunofluorescence is helpful but not definitive because immune deposits may have been consumed by phagocytes in lesions more than 48 hours old. A biopsy definitive for GPA should include necrotizing extravascular granuloma in addition to small-vessel vasculitis, but this combination of features is seen in a minority of biopsy specimens. Similarly, the combination of small-vessel vasculitis and eosinophil-rich necrotizing granuloma is seen in a minority of biopsy specimens in EGPA. Nevertheless, it is often important simply to confirm, by biopsy, the presence of vasculitis in some organ system in a patient in whom MPA, GPA, or EGPA is likely, but nonvasculitic conditions are also considerations.

The presence of vasculitis, either proven by biopsy or strongly implied by documented multifocal neuropathy,70,110 is often essential to distinguish EGPA from the HES because only 40% of patients with EGPA test positive for ANCA, usually MPO- ANCA.70, In turn, a high circulating eosinophil count or eosinophilic infiltration on biopsy distinguishes EGPA from MPA, GPA, and other forms of vasculitis. A high circulating eosinophil count is also often the clue that a patient has EGPA or HES rather than merely asthma and nasal polyposis.

Biopsy proof of GPA is highly desirable in the ANCA-negative patient. Only 60% to 70% of patients with disease limited to the upper airway test positive for PR3or MPO-ANCA, in contrast to 90% or more with systemic vasculitis.60, Unfortunately,

only approximately 20% of nasal biopsies will show the triad of granulomatous inflammation, necrosis, and vasculitis. Malignancies, nasal cocaine use, other chronic trauma, and infections can also cause chronic inflammation, necrosis, and destruction of soft tissue and bone in the upper airway.73, In the lung, GPA is one of many conditions that can cause nodules as a result of granulomatous inflammation119; it is presumed that the key feature of vasculitis is much more likely to be seen in an excisional biopsy than in a transbronchial or transthoracic needle biopsy.

Determination of AAV disease activity is challenging. Patients are susceptible to both systemic and localized infection due to immune suppression and poor drainage of secretions from airway damage. Symptoms of these infections are similar to symptoms of AAV. Fluctuation in symptoms when patients have had significant organ damage—such as the airway in GPA, congestive heart failure in EGPA, or peripheral neuropathy in all forms of AAV—may occur with or without active disease. Musculoskeletal

and constitutional symptoms can occur in a wide range of acute and chronic conditions, and most patients with AAV report some degree of chronic fatigue regardless of their apparent disease status. Perhaps the greatest challenge is excluding active renal inflammation in a patient with prior kidney damage because proteinuria and hematuria can persist without evidence of additional renal damage over long periods,120 and gradual loss of remaining kidney function may be attributable to "grumbling" disease but also may occur without any evidence of active inflammation.

### Treatment

A retrospective study by Walton121 published in 1958 showed that, without treatment, the median survival of patients with GPA was approximately 5 months and that 81% of patients died within 1 year of diagnosis. Death was primarily due to progressive failure of multiple organ systems. The use of glucocorticoids

for treatment extended the median survival time to approximately 12.5 months. 122, The dismal prognosis for these diseases was not reversed until alkylating agents were used beginning in the 1960s. Current treatment regimens aim to induce remission and then maintain remission using less toxic agents. Treatment is tailored to disease severity, with organand life-threatening manifestations warranting the most aggressive therapy (summarized in Fig. 90.8). ACR/Vasculitis Foundation guidelines for the management of AAV (GPA, MPA, and EGPA) were published in 2021.124 EULAR last revised its guidelines for the management of primary smalland medium-vessel vasculitis in 2016.125,126

### Induction of Remission for Granulomatosis With Polyangiitis a and Microscopic Polyangiitis

Since the 1960s, oral cyclophosphamide (CYC), an alkylating agent derived from nitrogen mustard, has been used at a dose of 2 mg/kg/day, along with glucocorticoids, to induce remission for GPA and MPA. With oral CYC, remission rates for ANCA-associated vasculitis range from 75% to 93%60,123—a stark contrast to the very short median survival time before the use of this medication. In initial treatment regimens, CYC was used continuously for at least 1 year. However, prolonged use was associated with

significant adverse effects. In a study of 158 patients with ANCAassociated vasculitis treated with CYC for at least 6 months, 46% experienced a serious infection (including pneumonias, skin infections, and bacterial and fungal sepsis), 43% had CYC-induced cystitis, 2.8% experienced bladder cancer (a 33-fold increase), and 1.3% had lymphoma (an 1 1-fold increase). The risk of malignancy after CYC use is dose dependent. Among women between 18 and 35 years of age, 57% had cessation of menses for at least 1 year, were unable to become pregnant, or had laboratory evidence of ovarian failure. In part to minimize toxicity, some studies have adjusted CYC dosing based on renal dysfunction or advanced age. However, these adjustments have not been consistent across clinical trials. Given the toxicities observed with prolonged CYC use, alternate CYC regimens to minimize toxicities have been sought.

One alternative to daily oral CYC for remission induction is to use intravenous (IV) pulse CYC. In the CYCLOPS trial, 149 patients with either GPA or MPA received prednisolone and were randomized to receive pulse CYC (15 mg/kg IV every 2 weeks x 3 doses, then 15 mg/kg IV every 3 weeks until remission, and then continued for 3 more months) or oral CYC (2 mg/kg/day until remission, then 1.5 mg/kg/day x 3 more months). After receiving CYC, all patients received azathioprine. The mean cumulative dose of CYC in the IV pulse arm was approximately half of the

daily oral arm (8.2 g vs. 15.9 g) and, consequently, less leukopenia was observed in the pulse arm. The median time to remission was approximately 3 months for both groups, and there was no difference in improvement in renal function between both groups. Long-term follow-up (median duration 4.3 years) showed no difference in survival or renal function but a higher rate of relapse in the pulse arm compared with the daily oral arm (39.5% vs. 20.8%; HR for relapse in the daily oral arm, 0.50; 95% CI, 0.26 0.93; p = 0.029).

An increasingly used alternative to CYC for remission induction is rituximab, a monoclonal antibody directed against CD20, which is expressed on developing B cells from the immature B cell to the memory B cell stages. The mechanism of action for rituximab is not clearly known, but it can induce apoptosis of developing B cells and induce B cell depletion. Of note, B cell stem cells and plasma cells do not express CD20 and thus are not affected by rituximab. In the Rituximab in ANCA-Associated Vasculitis (RAVE) trial, a double-blinded, noninferiority study, 197 patients with GPA or MPA received glucocorticoid therapy and were randomized to receive either oral CYC (2 mg/kg/day) or IV rituximab (375 mg/m2 weekly x 4 doses). Patients in the oral CYC arm were switched to azathioprine (2 mg/kg/day) after achieving remission with 3 to 6 months of CYC therapy; patients in the rituximab arm were switched to oral placebo after the completion of four infusions. At the 6-month primary endpoint, rituximab was not inferior to CYC at inducing remission and was potentially superior to CYC for patients with relapsing disease. No difference was found in remission rates based on type of renal involvement, presence of alveolar hemorrhage, ANCA specificity or disease type, or whether patients became ANCA negative during the course of treatment. In the 18-month follow-up study, a single course of rituximab continued to be noninferior to oral CYC followed by azathioprine. No significant difference was found among duration of complete remission, severity of relapses, or rate of adverse 128 In the Rituximab versus CYC in ANCA-associated events. Vasculitis (RITUXVAS) trial, 44 patients newly diagnosed with AAV were randomized (3:1) to receive rituximab along with two infusions of CYC versus IV CYC for 3 to 6 months, followed by azathioprine. Rates of sustained remission and median increase in glomerular filtration rates (GFRs) at 12 months and severe adverse events and death were similar in both groups. Both studies indicate that rituximab and CYC have comparable efficacy for remission induction. A combination of rituximab and CYC, analogous to the RITUXVAS regimen, has never been compared with rituximab alone. Uncontrolled studies have shown patients on rituximab and CYC for remission induction are able to taper glucocorticoids rapidly, 130,131 but controlled trials are needed to confirm these findings.

Methotrexate (MTX) has also been studied in comparison with oral CYC for induction of remission of early systemic or localized disease. In the Nonrenal Wegener's Granulomatosis Treated Alternatively with Methotrexate (NORAM) trial, 100 patients with a new diagnosis of either MPA or GPA and without organor life-threatening manifestations such as severe hemoptysis, rapidly progressive neuropathy, or significant renal involvement (i.e., serum creatinine >1.7 mg/dL or 150 µmol/L, urinary red blood cell casts, or proteinuria >1 g/day) were randomized to receive either oral MTX up to 25 mg/week or CYC, 2 mg/kg/day. Both treatment groups received maintenance therapy for 10 months, and then therapy was tapered and discontinued by month 12. At 6 months, the remission rate was similar in both groups (89.8% in the MTX arm and 93.8% in the CYC arm; p = 0.041). In the

MTX arm, remission was delayed for patients with more extensive disease or pulmonary involvement, and the relapse rate was higher at 18 months (69.5% in the MTX arm vs. 46.5% in the CYC arm). Thus although MTX was able to induce remission in patients without organ or life-threatening involvement, it was less effective than CYC. Given the high relapse rate observed for both the MTX and CYC treatment arms, therapy for these diseases should be continued beyond 12 months.

More recently, abatacept has been studied as a remission induction agent for nonsevere, relapsing GPA. The addition of this agent to prednisone and remission maintenance therapy (e.g., MTX, azathioprine, or mycophenolate mofetil [MMF]) was associated with disease remission and reduction in glucocorticoid doses. The efficacy of this agent is being investigated in a larger trial (ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT02108860).

MMF has been studied as a remission agent as an alternative to CYC. In the Mycophenolate Mofetil versus CYC for Remission Induction of ANCA-associated Vasculitis (MYCYC) trial, 140 patients were randomized to receive either MMF (2000 to 3000 mg/day) versus IV-pulse CYC. MMF was noninferior to CYC in its ability to achieve remission by 6 months with a tapering glucocorticoid regimen (67% for MMF and 61% for CYC). However, relapse rates were higher in those receiving MMF than CYC during follow-up (33% vs. 19%, with incidence rate ratio [IRR] 1.97; 95% CI, 0.964.23; p = 0.049). Thus, interest in using MMF as a remission induction agent has waned.135,

The optimal glucocorticoid dosing regimen for remission induction and maintenance has not been established. Individuals presenting with lifeor organ-threatening disease are often treated with IV pulse glucocorticoids (e.g., methylprednisolone 1000 mg intravenously daily for 3 days) followed by high doses of oral glucocorticoids (e.g., prednisone 1 mg/kg/day) that are gradually tapered over many months (e.g., 6 to 18 months).81, However, glucocorticoid use is associated with significant morbid- 138, Therefore, the PEXIVAS study was conducted in part ity. to examine the efficacy of a reduced-dose glucocorticoid regimen (<60% of the standard regimen by 6 months) in patients with severe AAV. The reduced-dose regimen met its noninferiority endpoint for the efficacy outcome of death or end-stage renal disease, and patients in the lower-dose group had fewer infections (IRR 0.69; CI 0.520.93). Similar results were reported in the LOVAS trial, in which 140 patients with nonsevere AAV were randomized to a standard (beginning at 1 mg/kg) or lower (beginning at 0.5 mg/kg) prednisone taper, which met noninferiority criteria for the primary endpoint of remission at 6 months comparing reduced dose (71.0%) to standard dose (69.2%). Serious adverse events (18.8 vs. 36.9%; p = 0.02) and serious infections (7.2% vs. 20.0%; p = 0.04) were significantly less common in the reduced-dose group. Thus it is probable that standard glucocorticoid schedules developed over the past 50 years have used unnecessarily high doses.

A different approach to glucocorticoid sparing is to treat with avacopan, an oral inhibitor of the receptor for the complement degradation product C5a (C5aR), a potent chemotactic factor for neutrophils that had been shown to be essential for development of disease in a mouse model of MPO-ANCA-induced GN. In the placebo-controlled ADVOCATE trial, 331 patients were randomized to receive avacopan or a standard regimen of prednisone, along with either rituximab or CYC per the treating physician's preference. Patients could be receiving up to 20 mg prednisone at randomization, and 64% of patients were taking a mean of 14 mg daily. Patients randomized to prednisone then started a taper

at 45 or 60 mg, and those randomized to avacopan were tapered off prednisone per protocol within the next 4 weeks. The primary endpoint of remission at week 26 was met in 72.3% of patients in the avacopan group and 70.1% of patients in the prednisone group, achieving noninferiority. Glucocorticoid-related toxicities were lower in the avacopan group, but rates of infection and overall serious adverse events were similar in the two groups over the 52-week course of the trial. There was significantly greater average improvement in GFR in the avacopan group (7.3 vs. 4.1 mL/min per 1.73 m2), which was subsequently confirmed in the subset of patients with GFR (<20 mL/min per 1.73 m2)143 and was consistent with greater short-term improvement in proteinuria in a previous phase 2 trial. Important outstanding questions about avacopan include risk of infection or other toxicities and its potential role in remission maintenance.

### Maintenance Remission for Granulomatosis With Polyangiitis and Microscopic Polyangiitis

Given the toxicities associated with prolonged CYC use, a strategy was developed to "induce" remission using CYC and glucocorticoids and then "maintain" remission using a less toxic regimen. Medications studied as remission maintenance agents have included azathioprine, MTX, MMF, leflunomide, trimethoprim/ sulfamethoxazole, etanercept, and rituximab.

MTX was equally efficacious for remission maintenance compared with azathioprine in the WEGENT trial. In this study, 129 patients with GPA or MPA who achieved remission with CYC therapy were randomized to receive either azathioprine (2 mg/kg/ day) or MTX (up to 25 mg/week) for 12 months. The two medications had similar rates of remission maintenance and adverse events at 28 months of follow-up. Of note, 73% of patients relapsed after discontinuing the study medication at 12 months. Long-term follow-up of those in this trial (median duration 11.8 years) showed no difference in overall 10-year survival rates, adverse events, or relapses. PR3-ANCA positivity was significantly prognostic of long-term relapses.

MMF was investigated as a remission maintenance agent in the International Mycophenolate Mofetil Protocol to Reduce Outbreaks of Vasculitides (IMPROVE) trial. After remission induction with CYC, 156 patients were randomized to receive either azathioprine (2 mg/kg/day) or MMF (2000 mg/day) and were followed for a median of 39 months. Relapses were more common in the mycophenolate arm (HR for relapse in the mycophenolate arm, 1.65; 95% CI, 1.062.70; p = 0.03). Secondary outcomes such as renal function, proteinuria, and severe adverse event rates did not differ between groups. . Thus MMF is believed to be less effective than azathioprine in maintaining remission in AAV.

In a trial of 54 patients randomized to receive either leflunomide (30 mg/day) or MTX (starting at 7.5 mg/week and reaching

20 mg/week after 8 weeks), those in the leflunomide arm had a decreased rate of relapse at 6 months (6/26 in the leflunomide vs. 13/28 in the MTX arm). A higher rate of major relapses in the MTX arm led to an early termination of the study. However, adverse event rates were higher in the leflunomide arm. Thus additional studies are needed to determine the role of leflunomide for remission maintenance therapy and ideally would include a dose for which more data on safety are available (20 mg).

After reports of a beneficial effect of trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) for the treatment of GPA, a doubleblinded clinical trial randomized 81 patients with GPA who were in remission to receive either TMP-SMX (800 mg of sulfamethoxazole and 160 mg of trimethoprim) or placebo for 24 months. A higher proportion of patients receiving TMP-SMX remained in remission compared with placebo (82% vs. 60%). A subgroup analysis showed that patients with nasal or upper-airway lesions benefited the most from TMP-SMX use. Thus although TMP- SMX is not commonly used for remission maintenance in patients with AAV, it may be beneficial for patients with nasal or upperairway manifestations.

TNF inhibitors have had significant success as disease-modifying therapy for other autoimmune illnesses such as RA and IBD. Early case series suggested infliximab may be efficacious in controlling disease activity in GPA and MPA. The most rigorously studied TNF inhibitor in GPA and MPA is etanercept for remission maintenance. In the Wegener's Granulomatosis Etanercept Trial (WGET), 174 patients received standard remission induction therapy (CYC or MTX) and were randomized to receive concomitant etanercept or placebo, which was continued during the remission maintenance phase. There was no statistical difference in the rate of sustained remission between the etanercept and placebo arms (69.7% vs. 75.3%; p = 0.39) or in the time to remission. However, the incidence of solid cancers was significantly higher in the etanercept arm (six cancers vs. none; p = 0.01), suggesting that following CYC therapy with anti-TNF therapy can substantially increase one's risk of cancer. Based on these results, TNF inhibitors are generally not used to treat AAV.

Rituximab has also been investigated as a remission mainte- .151-153 In the Maintenance of Remission using Rituxnance agent. imab in Systemic ANCA-associated Vasculitis (MAINRITSAN) trial, 115 patients with either GPA, MPA, or renal-limited vasculitis, either new onset or relapsing, were randomized to receive either azathioprine (2 mg/kg/day x 12 months, followed by 1.5 mg/kg/day x 6 months, then 1 mg/kg/day x 4 months) or rituximab (500 mg IV x 2 doses at study entry and then every 6 months x 18 months), after having remission induced with CYC. At 28 months (the primary endpoint), the rate of severe relapses was significantly lower in the rituximab arm (5% in the rituximab arm vs. 29% in the azathioprine arm). The frequency of severe adverse events, including severe infections and malignancy, was similar in both arms. A difference in relapse rate has persisted at 60 months of follow-up off treatment since month 24 (for severe relapses, 28.1% in the rituximab arm and 50.6% in the azathioprine arm; HR for relapse in the azathioprine arm, 2.51; 95% CI, 1.344.69; p = 0.003), but the rates of relapse clearly accelerated in both groups after maintenance treatment was discontinued. Very similar results were seen in the RITAZAREM trial, which also compared rituximab to azathioprine for remission maintenance, but with differences from MAINRITSAN: The study was limited to patients with relapsing disease, remission induction had been with rituximab, and the remission-maintenance regimen for rituximab was more aggressive (1000 mg every 4 months). During

the treatment period of 24 months, relapses occurred in 13 of the 85 patients in the rituximab group and 32 of the 85 patients in the azathioprine group (HR, 0.35; 96% CI, 0.180.66); 6 and 17 of these relapses, respectively, were severe. Serious adverse events occurred in 22% (rituximab) and 36% (azathioprine) of patients during the treatment period. Fewer relapses were seen in the rituximab group (HR, 0.41; 95% CI, 0.270.61). Including a followup period off treatment (to 36 months since enrollment), fewer relapses were still seen in the rituximab group (HR, 0.41; 95% CI, 0.270.61).

In a trial that compared two different rituximab regimens for remission maintenance (MAINRITSAN-2), 162 individuals with newly diagnosed or relapsing GPA or MPA who achieved complete remission after induction therapy were randomized to receive IV rituximab 500 mg according to a fixed schedule (every 6 months) or in a tailored fashion based on laboratory parameters (when CD19+ B cells became detectable or ANCA titers doubled) until month 18. At month 28 (primary endpoint), 9.9% of the participants in the fixed-schedule group compared with 17.7% of individuals in the tailored-infusion group had suffered a relapse (p = 0.22). Those in the tailored-infusion arm received fewer infusions compared with the fixed-schedule arm (median three vs. five, respectively). This study suggests that CD19+ B cell counts and ANCA titers may be used to guide rituximab dosing for remission maintenance. The use of lowdose glucocorticoids (prednisone or prednisolone, 510 mg/day) as a standard component of maintenance therapy is a source of considerable controversy and varying practice. No randomized trial investigating this question has been completed. The studies previously described that compared rituximab to azathioprine for remission maintenance included prednis(ol)one, usually at 5 mg, in all patients in either group during the treatment period. Comparing relapse rates between trials is problematic because of different treatment regimens, different participant compositions, and different definitions of remission and relapse. With these caveats, a meta-analysis showed that trials that routinely continued glucocorticoids for 12 to 18 months reported markedly lower relapse rates than those in which they were discontinued earlier, usually by month 6.157

Although not all patients with AAV are destined to relapse, ongoing maintenance therapy has been shown to reduce relapse risk, relative to discontinuation, for both rituximab and the combination of azathioprine and low-dose glucocorticoids. 158,159

### Adjunctive and Alternative Agents

The role of plasma exchange (PLEX) in the treatment of AAV was investigated in two randomized trials. In the Methylprednisolone or Plasma Exchange for Severe Renal Vasculitis (MEPEX) trial, 137 patients with newly diagnosed GPA or MPA who had renal involvement confirmed by biopsy and serum creatinine greater than 5.8 mg/dL (500 µmol/L) were randomized to receive either seven PLEXs or 3000 mg of IV methylprednisolone, in addition to CYC and prednisone. Compared with IV methylprednisone, PLEX was associated with a 24% decrease in risk to progression to end-stage renal disease at 12 months. No difference in survival was observed. PLEX was subsequently examined in the PEXIVAS study, where 704 individuals with GPA or MPA with severe disease (eGFR <50 mL/min and/or lung hemorrhage) were randomized to receive PLEX (seven exchanges within 14 days) or no PLEX. The rate of death from any cause or end-stage renal disease was similar between the PLEX (28.4%) and no-PLEX (31.0%) groups

(HR 0.86; 95% CI, 0.65-1.13; p = 0.27). Whether some subgroup of patients still benefit from PLEX cannot be ruled out, and analyses of numerous subgroups did not identify a disease phenotype on which to focus further study. Meta-analysis of seven randomized trials continues to indicate reduced risk of end-stage kidney disease (ESKD) with PLEX,161 but since that outcome was not met in the single largest trial, use of PLEX is likely to drop and focus on patients at highest risk for ESKD.

Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) has been considered for patients who are unable to receive conventional immunosuppressive therapy. Case series using IVIG for remission induction have had conflicting results. In a randomized, placebo-controlled trial of 17 patients who received a single course of IVIG (2000 mg/ kg), 14 patients had significantly reduced disease activity, but this effect did not persist beyond 3 months.162, Larger controlled clinical trials are needed to fully understand the efficacy of this agent, but in light of the dubious feasibility of conducting such a trial, IVIG is included as a possible option for patients refractory to proven approaches in ACR treatment guidelines.

Other alternative therapies for AAV investigated in smaller studies include anti-thymocyte globulin, which causes T cell deple- 164; deoxyspergualin, which inhibits T cell maturation 165; and tion alemtuzumab (Campath, anti-CD52), which depletes both T cells and B cells.

### Treatment of Eosinophilic Granulomatosis With Polyangiitis

The optimal treatment of EGPA is less clearly defined compared with GPA and MPA. In part because of the differences in clinical manifestations, patients with EGPA are frequently excluded from the randomized clinical treatment trials of GPA and MPA. Even so, treatments found to be efficacious for GPA and MPA are used to treat EGPA, and the same general strategy of inducing remission with a more toxic medication and maintaining remission with a less toxic one is also applied.

The vasculitis and asthma manifestations of EGPA are usually managed separately. Asthma treatment generally follows recommended asthma treatment guidelines for patients without EGPA. However, many patients' asthma symptoms are corticosteroid dependent, and additional immunosuppression can be used for steroid-sparing effects. Initial management of systemic or vasculitic manifestations of EGPA relies on corticosteroids. Patients with EGPA who do not have poor prognostic factors as defined by the original Five Factor Score (serum creatinine >1.58 mg/dL, proteinuria >1 g/day, severe GI involvement, cardiomyopathy, or CNS involvement) can be treated with corticosteroids alone, but 35% of patients relapse when the drugs are tapered. Other immunosuppressive agents are indicated in addition to corticosteroids for patients with more severe disease. As with GPA and MPA before definitive study of rituximab, CYC is generally used to treat organor life-threatening manifestations. . The remission maintenance agents discussed in the previous section have not been widely studied in EGPA. One randomized, open-label study showed that azathioprine was efficacious for remission maintenance compared with CYC,167 but a more recent randomized trial showed no reduction in relapse rate. Approximately 80% of all patients require long-term use of glucocorticoids to manage manifestations such as asthma and sinonasal disease.167,

Current understanding of the efficacy of rituximab in EGPA is derived from case reports and case series. Most patients with

EGPA were treated with rituximab because of disease refractory to usual treatments (e.g., CYC) or medication intolerance. In the two largest case series to date, 69 and 41 patients with EGPA were treated with rituximab. In the first study, improvement was noted in 77% of patients at 6 months and in 83% at 12 months. Median prednisolone doses decreased modestly from 12.5 to 7.5 mg at 12 months, and rates of flares of asthma and sinonasal disease remained common. In the second study, 15 patients had been refractory to conventional therapy, 21 were relapsing, and 5 had new-onset disease. At 12 months, clinical improvement was seen in 88% of patients and prednisone was reduced in all patients. ANCA-positive patients were more likely to achieve or maintain remission in both studies. In an additional series, nine patients were all either in complete or partial remission within 3 months after rituximab treatment, with no flares observed in three patients retreated with rituximab for remission maintenance. Rates of remission and relapse were similar in 14 patients given rituximab for remission induction as in 14 patients given CYC. A randomized trial is needed to determine the efficacy of rituximab in EGPA.

Options for treating patients with EGPA changed dramatically after publication of a randomized, double-blind, placebocontrolled trial of mepolizumab,174 a monoclonal antibody directed against interleukin-5, a cytokine critical for activation of eosinophils. Among 136 participants, 28% of patients receiving mepolizumab achieved protocol-defined remission for at least 24 weeks during the 52-week trial, compared with 3% in the placebo group. The relapse rate was reduced by 50%, as was the average daily dose of prednisone. This trial (MIRRA) built on previous experience with mepolizumab in HES175 and in two uncontrolled pilot studies of mepolizumab in EGPA.176, The primary and several secondary outcomes in MIRRA were based on ability to reduce prednisone to 4 mg or need to increase the dose, for any reason. Therefore additional studies are needed to determine how effective mepolizumab and similar drugs are for asthma, parenchymal eosinophilic inflammation, and vasculitic manifestations. For now, mepolizumab should be regarded as a steroid-sparing drug used for remission maintenance and to control non-organthreatening flares, but not as therapy for active organ-threatening disease.

### Outcomes

Although the AAV are still sometimes fatal because of the severity of disease at onset or treatment resistance, most patients can be successfully treated, which has two important sequelae. First, the substantially increased risk of mortality in the first 6 months after diagnosis (approximately 10%) is mostly due to infection as a consequence of treatment, rather than vasculitis itself. Second, the moderately increased risk of long-term mortality is multifactorial, including infection, cardiovascular disease, and malignancy. In addition, permanent organ damage affects overall prognosis. Renal dysfunction is the only factor other than advancing age that is strongly associated with long-term mortality in MPA and GPA. Analogously, cardiomyopathy is by far the strongest risk factor for mortality in EGPA.

Although mortality has been greatly reduced, morbidity remains high because of permanent damage (particularly renal insufficiency, sinonasal symptoms, hearing loss, neuropathy, and dyspnea) and consequences of treatment (diabetes, hypertension, osteoporosis, weakness, and certain malignancies). Many patients report fatigue and reduced energy—symptoms that

cannot be assessed objectively—as the most important negative consequences of having vasculitis.

Previous studies have indicated an increased incidence of cancer in GPA. However, more recent studies have shown lower risks of bladder cancer, leukemia, and lymphoma than previously, reflecting that current approaches are likely associated with little increased risk.180-182 There remains an increased risk of nonmelanoma skin cancer, 180,181 and it is difficult to assess relative risks of uncommon cancers in rare diseases. Additional studies have shown an increased risk of cardiovascular disease. 182,

Relapse affects overall patient outcomes. The risk of relapse in GPA is about 60%,60,61,128,184,185 and that of MPA is about 30%.65, Whether this difference is due to the disease phenotype or ANCA specificity is uncertain.128, Not surprisingly, having relapsed in the past also increases the risk of subsequent relapses. Localized/limited GPA may have a higher rate of relapse than systemic/severe GPA, 83,84 and 30% to 55% of such patients may be ANCA-negative. 83,

Persistent and rising c-ANCA/PR3-ANCA titers were associated with increased risk of flare in some but not all studies. In a meta-analysis, the likelihood ratio was approximately 2, that is, below the level considered to be "diagnostic" for making treatment decisions with confidence.

Relapse of vasculitis or parenchymal eosinophilic disease beyond sinonasal disease and asthma is about as common in EGPA as in MPA and is somewhat more common in ANCApositive than in ANCA-negative patients. Relapses of sinonasal disease and asthma are common and often the main reason that more than 80% of patients with EGPA continue to take prednisone and often additional immune-suppressive drugs.

### Pathogenesis

MPA, GPA, and EGPA all feature leukocytoclastic vasculitis: fibrinoid necrosis of arterioles, capillaries, and venules by neutrophils, which infiltrate and die in the surrounding tissue and leave characteristic fragments of their nuclei visible under the microscope. Additional involvement of small arteries is sometimes seen, and that of small veins is rare. Although some deposition of immunoglobulins and complement can be seen (these diseases are "pauci-immune" rather than nonimmune), 118,188 immune complex deposition is thought to play little if any role in pathogenesis. Because ANCAs are highly associated with pauci-immune necrotizing vasculitis, much of the study of pathogenesis has focused on the generation and mode of action of ANCAs.

Although the bulk of MPO and PR3 is intra-cellular in neutrophil granules, these proteins may be translocated to the cell surface either constitutively or by inflammatory stimuli189 and serve as targets for ANCAs to activate neutrophils.190, In addition, MPO and PR3 may serve as targets extra-cellularly after degranulation, or particularly after release associated with neutrophil extra-cellular traps.

The best evidence that ANCAs are directly pathogenic comes from a mouse model in which anti-MPO antibodies (produced by immunizing Mpo-/- mice with mouse MPO) produce pauciimmune GN when transferred into normal mice. Neutrophils, and activation of the C5 component of complement with the C5a receptor, are required to produce GN.193-195 However, other features than GN are not seen, and GN itself is relatively mild.192, More severe GN and additional features of systemic

vasculitis are produced by transferring spleen cells into SCID mice, ,192 but whether all of this disease is attributable to anti- MPO antibodies or even to MPO-specific T cell immunity is unclear.

Efforts to produce a similarly simple model using PR3 have not been successful, and efforts to demonstrate pathogenicity of anti-PR3 autoimmunity require considerable experimental manipulation and produce limited disease. Whether this difficulty is due to the different structure and biology of PR3 in humans and rodents—or is evidence that anti-PR3 antibodies have limited pathogenicity in isolation—is not clear. Production of vasculitis using human anti-PR3 antibodies and mice with "humanized" immune systems supports the human-versus-mouse explanation and may provide the best evidence in favor of anti-PR3 antibodies causing vasculitis. 196, Mouse models of HES have been developed,198 but not the combination of eosinophilic and necrotizing vasculitis that would be a more specific model for EGPA.

T cell immunity is implicated in any process that results in high-affinity antibodies, but, in addition, CD4+ T cells are found in the necrotizing granulomatous lesions in GPA and are likely involved in macrophage activation and neutrophil recruitment locally. Multiple changes in the percentages of T cell subsets— Th1, Th2, Th17, and regulatory T cells—have been described in patients with different forms of AAV, in different tissue sites, and in different stages of disease activity.

The number of circulating proteins related to immunity inflammation, vascular injury, and tissue repair is so large in highly active GPA and MPA that it is difficult to obtain insight into pathophysiology from biomarker studies.200, In EGPA, circulating products of eosinophils are elevated in untreated disease. As expected, markers of Th2 responses are elevated, 203-205 but Th17 cells have been implicated as well.

Known genetic risk factors and environmental exposures explain only a small portion of the risk for GPA, MPA, or EGPA. Although it is possible that rare or unique (including somatic) genetic mutations or rare environmental exposures may contribute further to risk, it is also worth emphasizing that in many autoimmune diseases, random chance is likely to play an important role in determining whether tolerance to a particular autoantigen is broken.

### Conclusion

In the past 30 years, significant progress has been made in diagnosing and treating ANCA-associated vasculitis. Although this progress has dramatically reduced the mortality of AAV, patients continue to accumulate organ damage because of diagnostic delay and the tendency of these diseases to relapse. Thus many challenges remain. Clinicians and investigators alike would benefit from an improved understanding of the role of ANCAs in disease pathogenesis, identification of clinically actionable biomarkers of disease activity, and the development of more targeted therapies to reduce treatment toxicity. With this additional knowledge, the prognosis for patients with AAV may continue to improve.

### KEY POINTS

### Definition and Classification

Polyarteritis nodosa (PAN) is a multisystem disease characterized by necrotizing vasculitis predominantly in the medium-size arteries. Historically, the term periarteritis nodosa, first introduced by Kussmaul and Maier in 1866,1 has evolved over time into the more pathologically correct term: polyarteritis nodosa. In 1908 Dickson2 proposed the name polyarteritis nodosa as a definition for explaining destructive and proliferative changes of the vessel wall due to inflammation involving all the layers transmurally. PAN has been formally defined in the 2012 revised Chapel Hill initiative as necrotizing arteritis of medium and small-size arteries without glomerulonephritis or vasculitis in arterioles, capillaries, or venules and not associated with anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA).3, Herein, diseases involving small vessels like eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA), granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA), and microscopic polyangiitis (MPA) came out of the umbrella term polyarteritis nodosa. In addition, hepatitis Brelated PAN is clearly separated from PAN and classified as "vasculitis associated with the probable etiology." The lack of association with ANCA has also been emphasized.

Not only the definition but also the classification of vasculitides is a matter of issue for correctly placing the patient to proper diagnosis, especially when selecting the patients for clinical trials.
