The initial classification for PAN was introduced by the American College of Rheumatology (ACR) in 1990; this classification required the presence of at least 3 of the 10 following items: (1) granulocyte or mixed leukocyte infiltrate in an arterial wall on biopsy; (2) arteriographic abnormalities; (3) livedo reticularis; (4) myalgia; (5) diastolic blood pressure (BP) of >90 mm Hg; (6) monoor polyneuropathy; (7) elevated blood urea, nitrogen, or creatinine; (8) testicular pain/tenderness; (9) hepatitis B reactants; and (10) weight loss of >4 kg (sensitivity, 82.2%; specificity, 86.6%). No differentiation was made between PAN and MPA.

A European Medicines Agency (EMA) study group aimed to develop a consensus methodology for the classification of the ANCA-associated vasculitides and PAN. They proposed an algorithm based on exclusion of GPA (formerly known as Wegener's granulomatosis), EGPA, and MPA. The presence of histologically proven small-vessel vasculitis or glomerulonephritis and the presence of ANCA were considered to be features of MPA, not PAN.

In 2006 the European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology (EULAR)/Paediatric Rheumatology International Trials Organisation (PRINTO)/Paediatric Rheumatology European Society (PReS) endorsed the Ankara 2006 consensus criteria for the classification of childhood vasculitides including PAN. Classification of the patient as having cutaneous PAN (cPAN) requires the presence of necrotizing arteritis at histopathology or typical changes in angiographic abnormalities reflecting vasculitis in addition to the presence of one of the five following features: skin involvement, myalgia/muscle tenderness, hypertension, peripheral neuropathy, and renal involvement. It should be emphasized that the renal findings in PAN should be solely due to the involvement of the mediumand small-size arteries within the kidney tissue but not the glomeruli. Revised classification attempts may further address this issue.

In the past decade, we have become aware that necrotizing arteritis as defined for PAN may be due to other defined causes as well. A striking example was the monogenic disease caused by mutations in the ADA2 gene, formally the CECR1 (cat eye syndrome chromosome region candidate 1) gene mutations and deficiency of adenosine deaminase 2 (DADA2), described in 2014. DADA2 may present with classical features of PAN, both clinically and histologically.9, We were then introduced to another

autoinflammatory disease, VEXAS, which also may present with features of necrotizing vasculitis in certain organ systems. Last but not least, we observed PAN mimics during the COVID pandemic. These patients should now be classified under the category of "vasculitis associated with probable etiology" and not as PAN. Better understanding of the underlying pathogenetic mechanisms will surely enable us to better define and diagnose these patients.

### Epidemiology

We now know that with the evolving changes in its classification, by placing hepatitis B virus (HBV)—associated vasculitis in a group with vasculitis associated with probable etiology and placing MPA, GPA, and EGPA in a group with small vessel vasculitis, PAN has become a quite rare disease. However, it is very challenging to define the real frequency, as a satisfying classification system is not yet in use in clinical practice.

The estimated annual incidence of PAN according to ACR criteria was reported as 2.0 to 9.0 per million in adults in Europe and the United States. The prevalence was reported as 31 cases per million. While PAN is considered an adult disease with the highest incidence observed in the fourth to fifth decades of life, childhood-onset PAN is increasingly recognized with some variation in clinical manifestations compared with adult disease. Previously, it was confirmed that childhood PAN had better outcomes than adults, and the age at disease onset is around 9 to 10 years of age.14, Previous epidemiologic studies found that PAN is slightly more common among males, with the male-tofemale ratio of approximately 1.5:1.16 It may affect all ethnicities. A recent study investigated the inpatient prevalence of PAN from the Nationwide Inpatient Sample in the United States and found higher frequencies than what would be expected from the overall prevalence. The inpatient prevalence of PAN was 11.6 cases per 100,000 hospital discharges. The mortality rate was reported as 1% to 4% in children, while it was 14.5% to 24.6% in adult PAN patients.15,18,19

### Etiology and Pathogenesis

The etiology of PAN is still unknown; however, both innate and adaptive immunity are thought to play a role in the pathogenesis of necrotizing inflammation of the vessels. In the active phase of vasculitis, the main cells migrating to the vessel wall are neutrophils, but the T cellmediated immune mechanism is considered to play a significant role in the pathogenesis of the disease due to the subsequent predominant infiltration of T cells. The frequencies of T helper (Th) cells were studied in patients with PAN and compared with healthy controls and patients with GPA, and an imbalanced expression of excessive Th cells and defective regulatory T cells (Tregs) in PAN was demonstrated. Th cells were found to be significantly higher in number than in healthy controls, and in comparison with GPA, the expression of Th1 cells was higher but that of Th17 cells was lower in PAN. Additionally, a significant increase in Tregs was observed in PAN. However, defects in suppressive ability and CTLA-4 expression were observed as well.

The skin lesions of systemic vasculitis are predominantly CD8+ T cells that infiltrate the intima and that CD8+ T cells in the intima are activated in an antigen-independent manner. These cells cause vasculitis by inducing inflammation with neutrophil

infiltration. Activated CD8+ T cells produce interferon (IFN) γ that plays a critical role in activation of macrophages and perpetuating the secretion of proinflammatory cytokines. CD8+ T cells play a crucial role in both, leading to vessel wall injury and triggering inflammatory reactions. One study identified the expression of adhesion molecules on the luminal endothelium in the early lesions of PAN. They also concluded that initial luminal endothelium damage in the vasculitis process diminishes before the chronic phase.

### Clinical Features and Diagnostic Tests

The clinical spectrum of PAN is characterized by constitutional features and protean organ-specific manifestations overwhelmed by the extent of inflammation. The occlusion of the inflamed arteries may result in tissue ischemia and necrosis of the affected sites.

Constitutional symptoms like fever, weight loss, arthralgia, and myalgia are very common among patients. Purpura, nodules, and livedo reticularis are the main cutaneous findings; in a limited number of patients, digital necrosis may accompany the disease (Fig. 91.1). In 50% to 75% of the patients, the arteries of the peripheral nervous system are affected, presenting in the form of mononeuritis multiplex and rarely peripheral neuropathy. Central nervous system (CNS) involvement may occur due to vasculitis, but posterior leukoencephalopathy due to malignant hypertension may also be present and is usually associated with poor prognosis. Renal involvement is due to involvement of the intrarenal arteries without the presence of glomerulonephritis. Proteinuria, hematuria, and recent-onset hypertension have been reported due to this involvement. The gastrointestinal system is one of the major affected sites of PAN,

usually presenting with severe manifestations and poor outcome. There may be severe abdominal pain, gastrointestinal bleeding and perforation of the intestines. Although rare, cholecystitis, pancreatitis, and appendicitis may occur in patients with PAN. Cardiovascular involvement was reported in 22% of the patients, mainly as vasculitis-related cardiomyopathy. Albeit rare, testicular involvement is one of the significant features of PAN; patients may present with severe testicular pain and orchitis. Investigators have reported involvement of the gastrointestinal tract and skin at a rate of 50%, skeletal muscles and mesentery at a rate of 30%, and the CNS at a rate of 10%, as well as a high rate of involvement of the renal arteries.

Compared with adults, children and adolescents have higher frequency of cutaneous involvement and constitutional features, but lower frequency of neurologic manifestations. 15, In the retrospective study of the French Vasculitis Study Group, patients with HBV infection—related PAN have a more severe course but fewer relapses compared with patients with nonHBV-related PAN.

### Laboratory Tests

There is no single diagnostic laboratory test for PAN. However, due to the presence of inflammation, acute phase reactants including C-reactive proteins and erythrocyte sedimentation rate are elevated. Basic evaluation of the complete blood count may show anemia and thrombocytosis with accompanying mild to moderate neutrophilic leukocytosis.

Chest radiography should be obtained for differential diagnosis. Autoantibodies like ANCA and, if required, antinuclear antibody (ANA), complements, and cryoglobulin levels may help in the differential diagnosis of PAN as well.

### Histopathology and Imaging

PAN has been described for over 150 years. However, as there are no specific serologic tests, the diagnosis is still challenging. The EULAR/PReS/PRINTO-endorsed Ankara 2006 classification criteria require the demonstration of necrotizing arteritis either in a biopsy specimen or through the aneurysms in medium-size arteries that reflect the pathologic process (Fig. 91.2).

When a suitable biopsy site is present, histopathology-based diagnosis is a reliable method for differentiating PAN from other vasculitis syndromes. For imaging, a spectrum of angiographic findings have been defined to suggest the diagnosis of PAN.

The affected site should be chosen for biopsy, but skin, muscles, and sural nerves are common sites for the specimen. Renal biopsy is not the preferred method for the histopathological diagnosis since glomerulonephritis is not present and rupture of microaneurysms may lead to severe bleeding. In biopsy specimens from PAN patients, inflammatory lesions of medium-sized or small arteries are characteristically segmental and more pronounced in branching points. The propensity toward bifurcation sites had been justified by the influence of hydrostatic forces or the adhesion molecules secreted from the macrophages. However, arterioles, capillaries, and venules are generally not affected. The inflammation site in the vessel wall is rich in lymphocytes, neutrophils, and macrophages, and fibrinoid necrosis is present. At the chronic stages, lymphocyte and macrophage infiltration accompany the process of neoangiogenesis. With the initiation of remodeling, intimal proliferation and fibrosis ensue and then

lead to occurrence of stenotic lesions, thrombosis, microaneurysm formation, and rupture of the vessel walls.

One of the most important characteristics of PAN biopsy is coexistence of different stages of the inflammation such as active lesions, fibrosis, and healing lesions in the same specimen. 23, Microaneurysms or arterial stenoses of the visceral arteries have been reported in 40% to 90% of patients with PAN at presentation. 19,

Conventional angiography is the gold-standard technique for identifying vascular abnormalities with a sensitivity and specificity of ≈90%. However, with improving technology, now CT-angiography also has a high yield for demonstrating the aneurysms of PAN. The major angiographic finding is microaneurysms. Arterial steno-occlusive lesions are less common findings. Early diagnosis of PAN has been reported by a few investigators based on CT and MRI findings.34-36 One group reported positive CT-angiography findings in 15 of the 27 patients with PAN. The most common CT-angiography finding was aneurysm, followed by stenosis/occlusion. The most commonly involved arteries were the renal arteries, followed by the hepatic and splenic arteries. The most common visceral abnormality was splenic and renal infarct followed by bowel wall thickening and, rarely, perinephric hematoma. Although not assessed adequately, 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) positron emission tomography (PET) may show the increased uptake in the affected arteries.

### Differential Diagnosis

The differential diagnosis includes infectious diseases and lesions affecting smalland medium-sized arteries. Vasculitis has been associated with HBV, hepatitis C virus, human immunodeficiency virus, parvovirus B19, cytomegalovirus, Epstein—Barr virus, streptococcal infections, and finally COVID.38-40

The presence of eosinophilia may be a marker for ruling out EGPA (Churg—Strauss disease). The presence of ANCA suggests an ANCA-associated vasculitis such as MPA, GPA (Wegener granulomatosis), or EGPA.6, Kawasaki disease is the second most common vasculitis of childhood; it should be differentiated

from PAN, as it may occasionally involve medium arteries other than coronary arteries.

If there is a family history or atypical features, monogenic diseases should be sought. Many experts suggest that screening for mutations in the ADA2 gene should be done in all childhood onset patients since it is being increasingly recognized. DADA2 should be suspected, especially with the presence of early-onset strokes or hematologic or immunologic abnormalities.9, Researchers have suggested that DADA2 patients do not have the typical thrombocytosis seen in classic PAN.

### Treatment

PAN is a rare and life-threatening disease with heterogeneous clinical presentations. The major goal of therapy is suppressing inflammation and inducing long-term remission. In 2008 EULAR recommendations for the management of primary small and medium vessel vasculitis (in adults) were published. A combination of cyclophosphamide (intravenous [IV] or oral) and glucocorticoids for remission induction was recommended. High-dose glucocorticoids were advocated as an important part of induction therapy, and dose reduction to ≤10 mg/day was favored after 3 months of remission. This can be reduced gradually after 6 to 18 months according to patient response with the aim of discontinuing therapy. Cyclophosphamide doses of 2 mg/kg/day for oral use or 600 mg/m2 given at 2to 4-week intervals for IV pulse therapy were accepted as alternative regimens with similar effects, although IV application has fewer side effects.46, The authors strongly recommend lower doses in children, such as that used in the Euro-Lupus protocol.

For mild cases 1 mg/kg/day of prednisolone alone and tapering the dose after the control of manifestations is advised.48, For refractory or difficult to treat cases, there are rare reports suggesting the use of rituximab, anti-TNF agents, or tocilizumab.50-55

In 2021, the ACR/Vasculitis Foundation proposed guidelines for the management of PAN. Accordingly, for patients with newly diagnosed active, severe PAN, initiating treatment with IV pulse glucocorticoids over high-dose oral glucocorticoids were conditionally recommended. For pediatric patients, pulse glucocorticoid therapy seems to be safe with tolerable infection rate and morbidities compared with oral glucocorticoids. Initiating treatment with cyclophosphamide and high-dose glucocorticoids over high-dose glucocorticoids alone is recommended for patients with severe and active PAN. For patients with newly diagnosed active, severe PAN, initiating treatment with cyclophosphamide and glucocorticoids over rituximab and glucocorticoids was recommended. The efficacy of rituximab in PAN is uncertain as there is lack of large comparative studies in this disease. For patients unable to tolerate cyclophosphamide, agents like azathioprine or methotrexate are recommended over glucocorticoids alone. Although the benefit of plasmapheresis was not shown in PAN, it may be considered in catastrophic cases unresponsive to aggressive immunosuppressive therapies and may have a role in the management of HBV-related PAN. The duration of glucocorticoid therapy for PAN is not well entrenched, so in line with these recommendations, the duration of therapy should be guided with respect to the patient's clinical condition, values, and preferences. In the maintenance therapy of patients with newly diagnosed PAN, switching to another nonglucocorticoid immunosuppressive agent (azathioprine) is recommended.

In an international, open-label, randomized controlled trial to investigate the relative effectiveness of cyclophosphamide and mycophenolate mofetil for remission induction in childhood PAN, remission rates were similar with MMF treatment and CYC treatment. This study was conducted among a small group of pediatric PAN patients; however, it was the first randomized trial in childhood PAN.

### Outcome

If left untreated, PAN has a devastating course and a survival rate of 13% in 5 years.58-60 Patients with limited organ involvement and cutaneous disease have a better prognosis than patients with severe disease, but survival rates have increased with the use of cyclophosphamide in remission induction. Early diagnosis and prompt initiation of treatment have dramatically increased the 5-year survival rate. However, the relapse rate is about 20%.

The Paediatric Vasculitis Activity Score (PVAS) can be used to assess the activity of the disease. The French Vasculitis Study Group established a five-factor score (FFS) as a simple prognostic tool for evaluating patients with various forms of vasculitis, including PAN. Studies focusing on biomarkers for predicting disease activity in PAN have suggested that biomarkers such as D-dimer, anti-moesin antibody, and anti-endothelial antibodies are valuable markers, but none of these are currently used in routine clinical practice.63-65

### Cutaneous Polyarteritis Nodosa

cPAN is a rare subset of PAN confined to the skin and muscles in the absence of any systemic involvement. Differentiation of cPAN from systemic PAN may be challenging, especially in the presence of peripheral neuropathy and raised CRP. In cPAN livedo reticularis, painful subcutaneous nodules, or cutaneous ulcerations may be present. Rarely, petechia, purpura, and necrosis may occur during the course of the disease. Lesions are usually confined to extremities and then the trunk. Steroids are the mainstay of treatment, but their side effects limit their longer use.69-71 Patients may relapse when the steroid dose is reduced; therefore disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs like azathiopurine, hydroxychloroquine, methotrexate, mycophenolate, and tacrolimus may be preferred to maintain remission.69-73 cPAN has a more favorable disease course than systemic PAN, but nonspecific constitutional features still may accompany the disease.

### Monogenic Mimic of Polyarteritis Nodosa: Deficiency of Adenosine Deaminase 2

DADA2 is an autosomal recessive disease associated with lossof-function mutations in ADA2 gene.9, It is a monogenic autoinflammatory disease presenting with necrotizing vasculitis and displaying clinical features like livedo racemosa, neurologic involvement, lacunar infarcts and stroke, peripheral neuropathy, digital ischemia, cutaneous ulcerations, and target organ damage. .9, These patients may also have features of immune dysregulation or hematologic abnormalities.

ADA2 is a growth factor for leukocytes, is critical for endothelial stability, and has a role in immune development.9, Autoantibodies, particularly antinuclear antibodies, can be detected, and macrophages evolve to the proinflammatory

phenotype M1 rather than the M2 anti-inflammatory p henotype in patients with ADA2 deficiency.9, A recent study comparing the inflammatory m arkers in PAN w ith D ADA2 has shown that DADA2 patients with PAN-like presentation had higher concentrations of sRAGE and TNF, compared with classical PAN patients. .

After definition of DADA2 in 2014, awareness for this PANmimic disease has increased. According to the literature review with systematic evaluation of childhood PAN and DADA2, 613 childhood PAN and 207 pediatric DADA2 were compared: neurologic, gastrointestinal, and cardiac manifestations were frequently seen in DADA2 patients, while constitutional symptoms and testis involvement were more common among pediatric PAN patients. Cutaneous findings such as livedo, purpura, ulceration, subcutaneous nodule, necrosis, myalgia, and fatigue increased inflammatory markers during active disease, and vasculitis is frequently seen in both PAN and DADA2.77 During follow-up, the relapse rate was higher in PAN patients, while the mortality rate was higher among DADA2 patients. Anti-TNF drugs were the mainstay of DADA2 treatment; however, corticosteroids and immunosuppressive drugs were preferred in PAN. Diagnosis of DADA2 is made by analyzing the ADA2 gene mutations and measuring the levels of ADA2 enzyme. Patients carrying biallelic mutations and patients carrying heterozygote mutations with clinical manifestations have very low levels of ADA2 enzyme. Asymptomatic carriers may have low levels of ADA2, so knowing the enzyme levels is pivotal when planning the treatment. An increased risk of intracranial hemorrhage and lacunar infarction in DADA2 patients has often been confirmed, possibly due to endothelial involvement of cerebral vessels.10, Anti-TNF agents are the first choice in the treatment of DADA2 cases. Hematologic signs such as anemia, neutropenia, lymphopenia, thrombocytopenia, and low immunoglobulin levels may be demonstrated, and stem cell transplantation may be required in DADA2 patients.14,

In conclusion, the diagnosis and treatment of PAN continues to be a challenge for physicians. Better understanding of the pathogenetic pathways and multiomic studies will enable us to better manage these patients with precision medicine.

# Complex-Mediated Immune Small Vessel Vasculitis

### KEY POINTS

Vasculitis mediated by immune complexes (ICs) includes a heterogeneous group of disorders linked by excess IC production or by inefficient or dysregulated clearance of ICs.

Cryoglobulinemic vasculitis is most often associated with long-standing hepatitis C virus infection. The term mixed cryoglobulinemia is sometimes used for this disorder because the immunoreactants involved in the disease include both IgG and IgM.

### Introduction

The inflammation within blood vessel walls that characterizes vasculitis frequently leads to cellular destruction, damage to the vascular structures, compromised blood flow to organs, and organ

dysfunction. Immune complex (IC)mediated mechanisms play critical roles in many forms of systemic vasculitis, particularly those that involve primarily small blood vessels. The use of horse serum and sulfonamides as therapeutic agents for infectious diseases in the early 1900s frequently led to small vessel vasculitis on the basis of serum sickness or hypersensitivity phenomena. Hypersensitivity angiitis, often confused with the pauci-immune form of vasculitis now termed microscopic polyangiitis (see Chapter 90, Anti-neutrophil Cytoplasmic Antibody—Associated Vasculitis), 1,2 was one of five disorders included in the original classification of the vasculitides by Zeek in 1952.3

This chapter focuses on forms of small vessel vasculitis that are mediated by IC deposition. These disorders include hypersensitivity vasculitis, immunoglobulin (Ig)A vasculitis, mixed cryoglobulinemia, hypocomplementemic urticarial vasculitis (UV), and erythema elevatum diutinum (EED). IgG4-related disease can also be associated with an IC-mediated vasculitis of the skin and possibly other organs, but that disease is discussed primarily in its own chapter (see Chapter 126, IgG4-Related Disease). In addition, forms of vasculitis associated with connective tissue diseases (CTDs), particularly systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), Sjögren's syndrome, and rheumatoid vasculitis (RV), are discussed briefly. Antiglomerular basement membrane disease and the pauci-immune forms of vasculitis such as those associated with anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCAs) are discussed elsewhere. Throughout this chapter, the terms vasculitis and angiitis are used interchangeably when referring to inflammation involving small blood vessels (capillaries, venules, and arterioles).

All forms of IC-mediated vasculitis share certain elements of pathogenesis and have many cutaneous findings in common. The differential diagnoses for these conditions are also very similar, and it is therefore justifiable to consider many aspects of these diseases together. However, the epidemiology, etiology (to the extent that it is known), unique pathophysiologic mechanisms, distinctive clinical features, and approaches to treatment are discussed separately for each condition. Treatments are also summarized in Table 92.1.

### Pathogenesis

### Arthus Reaction

The Arthus reaction, described after the injection of horse serum into rabbits, forms the basis of our understanding of IC-mediated

diseases. The formation of ICs in the Arthus reaction initiates complement activation and an influx of inflammatory cells, followed by thrombus formation and hemorrhagic infarction in the areas of most intense inflammation. ICs, formed by the combination of antibody and antigen, are continuously created by the reticuloendothelial system as a means of neutralizing foreign antigens, but these are usually cleared swiftly and efficiently. Under some circumstances, however, ICs escape clearance and become deposited within the walls of blood vessels, joints, and other tissues, inciting inflammation and causing disease. ICs deposited in the blood vessel walls lead to vasculitis. Similarly, those deposited within small blood vessels of the kidney—the glomeruli—cause glomerulonephritis.

### Immunogenicity

The fate of ICs formed by the reticuloendothelial system is governed by several major factors. These include: (1) antigen load, (2) antibody response, (3) efficiency of the reticuloendothelial system, (4) the flow dynamics of blood vessels, (5) previous endothelial damage, and (6) the solubility of the ICs themselves. The ratio of antibody to antigen determines the solubility of ICs. Large ICs, formed when antibody and antigen are present in approximately equal proportions, are identified and removed easily by the reticuloendothelial system. Smaller ICs, formed in conditions of antibody excess, remain in the serum and do not elicit an immune response within tissues. In the setting of slight antigen excess, however, ICs precipitate from the serum and become trapped within certain vascular beds. Following the deposition of ICs in tissue, a cascade of pathologic events ensues: complement fixation, neutrophil recruitment, local inflammation, lysosomal release, oxygen free radical generation, and tissue injury.

### Cutaneous Manifestations

Small blood vessels generally include capillaries, postcapillary venules, and nonmuscular arterioles—vessels that are typically less than 50 µm in diameter. These are found principally within the superficial papillary dermis (Fig. 92.1). Medium-sized blood vessels, those between 50 and 150 µm in diameter, contain muscular walls and are located principally in the deep reticular dermis, near the junction of the dermis and subcutaneous tissues. Vessels larger than 150 µm in diameter are not commonly found in the skin.

Fig. 92.1, which demonstrates the location and size of blood vessels involved in various types of cutaneous vasculitis, illustrates the types of blood vessels affected by several forms of IC-mediated disease. A blood vessel's size correlates closely with its depth in the skin layers—the larger the vessel, the deeper its location. The pathologic findings in cutaneous vasculitides lie within the dermis and subcutaneous tissues. Although telltale signs of vasculitis are typically evident on the skin's surface, the epidermis itself is avascular.

Palpable purpura, synonymous with small vessel vasculitis, is the most common cutaneous finding in IC-mediated vasculitis (Fig. 92.2). Purpuric lesions result from the extravasation of erythrocytes through damaged blood vessel walls into tissue. Many other skin manifestations are possible in these conditions including vesicles, pustules, urticaria, superficial ulcerations, nonpalpable lesions (macules and patches), and splinter hemorrhages (Fig. 92.3). These lesions frequently occur in combination, and careful examination usually reveals a purpuric component. Purpuric lesions do not blanch when pressure is applied to the

skin. Moreover, following resolution, purpuric lesions may leave post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, particularly if repeated bouts occur (Fig. 92.3F).

In IC-mediated vasculitis, purpuric lesions are usually distributed in a symmetric fashion over dependent regions of the body, particularly the lower legs, because of the increased hydrostatic pressure in these areas. Purpuric lesions are not always palpable to the touch, and the existence of palpable purpura does not necessarily imply an IC-mediated pathophysiology; pauci-immune forms of vasculitis such as granulomatosis with polyangiitis

(GPA), microscopic polyangiitis, and eosinophilic GPA, for example, may present with similar findings in the skin (albeit distinctive histopathology; see Chapter 90), including either palpable or nonpalpable purpura. In contrast to pauci-immune forms of vasculitis, however, which usually lead to small, circumscribed areas of cutaneous vasculitis, cutaneous vasculitis associated with ICs often leads to diffuse, widespread lesions, usually occurring most densely on the distal lower extremities but extending up the thighs to the buttocks, abdomen, trunk, upper extremities, and occasionally even the face.

### Pathology

Full pathologic assessment of cutaneous vasculitis involves examination of a skin biopsy specimen by both light microscopy and direct immunofluorescence (DIF). DIF is a particularly critical procedure in the evaluation of small vessel vasculitides. DIF studies must be planned at the time the biopsy is performed because they require a fresh skin biopsy sample. It is sometimes possible to split a skin biopsy, sending one part for routine histopathological staining by light microscopy and the other portion for DIF.

### Light Microscopy

Fig. 92.4A displays the light microscopy findings of cutaneous vasculitis. The optimal time for skin biopsy is 24 to 48 hours after the appearance of a lesion. Biopsies should be obtained from a nonulcerated site. For ulcerated lesions—usually more typical of a medium vessel vasculitis—biopsies should be taken from the ulcer's edge. The cellular infiltrates in cutaneous vasculitis are usually composed of a combination of neutrophils and lymphocytes, but most cases demonstrate a predominance of one cell type or the other. Lymphocyte-rich infiltrates may be seen in specimens taken from either new (<12 hours) or old (>48 hours) lesions, regardless of the underlying type of vasculitis. Even in connective tissue disorders such as Sjögren's syndrome, the typical finding is a leukocytoclastic vasculitis rather than a lymphocytic vasculitis.

The essential histologic feature in any form of cutaneous vasculitis is the disruption of blood vessel architecture by an inflammatory infiltrate within and around the vessel walls. Leukocytoclasis refers to the degranulation of neutrophils (leading to the production of nuclear "dust"; see Fig. 92.4). Endothelial swelling and proliferation is also evident. Extravasation of erythrocytes may be evident in the biopsy but are not essential to the diagnosis.

### Direct Immunofluorescence

Although the diagnosis of cutaneous vasculitis rests on routine histology, the features revealed by hematoxylin and eosin stains do not distinguish between pauci-immune and IC-mediated disorders. DIF studies complement the histologic information and provide the only way of diagnosing with certainty some types of IC-mediated vasculitis (e.g., IgA vasculitis). The findings on DIF also often yield important clues regarding the nature of the underlying disease. The performance of separate biopsies for histologic and DIF analyses is recommended if sufficient numbers of lesions exist, as is usually the case with IC-mediated vasculitis.

To perform DIF studies, frozen sections are incubated with fluorescein-labeled anti-human IgG, IgM, IgA, and C3. Staining for other potential immunoreactants such as C1q and IgG subclasses (e.g., IgG4) is also available but may need to be requested based on clinical suspicion. The staining patterns of these

immunoreactants may provide insight into not only the diagnosis but also the pathophysiology of certain conditions. Fig. 92.4B displays the typical DIF findings in a skin lesion from a patient with IC-mediated vasculitis.

### Differential Diagnosis

The differential diagnosis of IC-mediated small vessel vasculitis is shown in Table 92.2. There are three main groups of disorders in the differential diagnosis of IC-mediated small vessel vasculitis: other forms of IC-mediated disorders, forms of small vessel vasculitis that are not mediated through ICs, and vasculitis mimickers that involve small blood vessels. A diagnostic algorithm that includes the critical laboratory and radiographic tests is shown in Fig. 92.5.

### Clinical Syndromes

### Hypersensitivity Vasculitis

The term hypersensitivity vasculitis (see Chapter 88, Classification and Epidemiology of Systemic Vasculitis) generally refers to an IC-mediated small vessel vasculitis of the skin that spares internal organs and usually follows drug exposures or infections. Consensus conference meetings on the nomenclature of the vasculitides have grappled with the most appropriate way to address the terminology for hypersensitivity vasculitis, a term first used by Zeek in 1952. The first Chapel Hill Consensus Conference in the early 1990s recommended eliminating the term bypersensitivity vasculitis in favor of cutaneous leukocytoclastic angitis because of the disorder's usual confinement to the skin and its predominant cell type, the neutrophil.

Twenty years later, the second Chapel Hill Consensus Conference retained the term cutaneous leukocytoclastic angiitis under a newly created category of single-organ vasculitis, consistent with the idea that hypersensitivity has a predilection for the skin. That same conference also added a new nomenclature term—drug-induced immune complex vasculitis—under a new category of vasculitis associated with probable etiology. The concept of hypersensitivity vasculitis, a condition characterized pathologically by IC deposition in capillaries, postcapillary venules, and arterioles, remains firmly embedded in the medical literature and clearly encompasses both cutaneous leukocytoclastic angiitis and drug-induced IC vasculitis. Because both the pathophysiologies and treatments of these hypersensitivity vasculitis subsets are similar, it makes sense to consider them together. An illness that is similar to hypersensitivity vasculitis——serum sickness—is a systemic illness that includes not only cutaneous involvement but also inflammation of joints, kidneys, and other organs.

In 1990 the American College of Rheumatology (ACR) performed a study designed to identify features that distinguished one form of vasculitis from others. The resulting ACR classification criteria for hypersensitivity vasculitis are shown in Table 92.3.8 The key historical element in evaluating a patient with possible hypersensitivity vasculitis is identifying exposures that may have triggered the reaction. However, in approximately half of all patients with presumed hypersensitivity vasculitis, no inciting agent can be identified. Under the agreements of second Chapel Hill Consensus Conference nomenclature, most patients with such a presentation would be diagnosed most precisely as having cutaneous leukocytoclastic angiitis.

A long list of medications, infections, and other exposures may lead to the syndrome of hypersensitivity vasculitis. The typical history for a drug-induced hypersensitivity vasculitis is the occurrence of clinical symptoms approximately 7 to 14 days after starting a new medication. Although virtually any medication can be associated with the induction of a hypersensitivity vasculitis, antibiotics (particularly penicillins and cephalosporins) are the most common offenders. Other common culprits are diuretics and anti-hypertensive agents. When confronted with a patient with a potential drug-induced vasculitis, however, it is critical to examine and potentially discontinue any medication added within a relevant time frame. Drug-induced hypersensitivity vasculitides begin to resolve within days of removal of the offending agent.

Thorough efforts are also required to exclude disease in organs other than the skin, the identification of which would implicate another form of vasculitis (see Fig. 92.5). For example, although

hypersensitivity vasculitis can mimic the skin features of microscopic polyangiitis, it does not involve the kidneys, lungs, peripheral nerves, or other internal organs and is not associated with ANCAs.

Removal of the inciting agent is the most critical therapy for hypersensitivity vasculitis when the likely agent can be identified. In patients who have been exposed to multiple medications, determining the inciting agent may be difficult and may require the

withdrawal of multiple agents simultaneously until the syndrome clears, typically in 1 to 2 weeks.

The prognosis for patients with hypersensitivity vasculitis depends on the inciting cause. Treatment with glucocorticoids is reserved for patients with extensive disease and can usually be discontinued within several weeks. Patients who experience repeated disease flares may need low-dose glucocorticoids to prevent recurrences.

### IgA Vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein Purpura) '

IgA vasculitis is an IC-mediated form of small vessel vasculitis that is strongly associated with IgA deposition within blood vessel walls. Many IgA vasculitis cases occur after upper respiratory tract infections. Multiple bacterial, viral, and other infectious agents have been suggested as the cause of IgA vasculitis, but the true cause remains unknown. The 1990 ACR criteria for the classification of IgA vasculitis are shown in Table 92.4.9

A major risk factor for HenochSchönlein purpura (HSP) (as well as IgA nephropathy, which has renal findings identical to those of HSP) is aberrant glycosylation of O-linked glycans in the hinge region of a fraction of IgA1 molecules. Rather than terminating with galactose, the aberrant galactose-deficient O-glycans end with N-acetylgalactosamine (GalNAc) or sialylated GalNAc. The terminal GalNAc moiety on the aberrantly glycosylated IgA1 may in turn be recognized by antiglycan antibodies, leading to the formation of circulating ICs that deposit in the skin, joints, kidneys, and other organs.

A high serum Ga-IgA1 level is not sufficient for the development of clinical symptoms. Rather, a "second hit" in the form of another environmental or inherited risk factor is required to produce IgA vasculitis. This probably explains why multiple types of infections and many different drugs (e.g., antibiotics) have been linked etiologically with IgA vasculitis.

The hallmarks of IgA vasculitis include an upper respiratory tract infection followed by a syndrome characterized by a purpuric rash (Fig. 92.6), arthralgias, abdominal pain, and renal disease. IgA vasculitis is usually viewed as a disease of childhood, and the majority of cases affect children younger than 5 years. Nevertheless, adults can also be affected by IgA vasculitis and have a greater tendency toward a prolonged disease course (with recurrent bouts of purpura) than do children. Colicky abdominal pain caused by gastrointestinal vasculitis is a common

characteristic of IgA vasculitis and frequently occurs within a week after the onset of rash. Sometimes, however, the gastrointestinal symptoms of IgA vasculitis precede the onset of purpura. This creates a diagnostic quandary, occasionally surrounding the possibility of an acute abdomen and leading to exploratory surgery. Endoscopy may demonstrate purpura in the upper or lower intestinal tract. Mild glomerulonephritis is common and generally self-limited, although some patients develop end-stage renal disease.

In children with mild manifestations, the clinical history alone may be sufficient to confirm the diagnosis. In more serious cases (e.g., in the presence of renal involvement) or when there is sufficient doubt about the diagnosis, biopsy of an involved organ is essential. Unlike other forms of IC-mediated disease, however, DIF reveals florid IgA deposition in IgA vasculitis. In the proper clinical setting, this finding is diagnostic of IgA vasculitis. Other forms of small vessel vasculitis may have small quantities of IgA within blood vessels, but IgA is not the predominant immunoreactant in such cases.

In mild cases of IgA vasculitis, no specific therapy is necessary. Even for patients with glomerulonephritis, it remains unclear that glucocorticoids or immunosuppressive agents significantly alter the outcome. Despite this, it is prudent to treat aggressive renal involvement with an immunosuppressive regimen that includes high-dose glucocorticoids. Mycophenolate mofetil is an excellent option in patients with severe renal disease for both additional immunosuppression and its potential glucocorticoid-sparing effects.

Recurrent skin disease, often consisting of multiple episodes occurring over many months, is not unusual. Nevertheless, even in patients with recurrent disease, the rule is for the disorder to subside and to resolve completely over a few months to a year. In a minority of patients, some evidence of permanent renal damage

persists in the form of proteinuria and hematuria. Less than 5% of patients develop renal failure as a result of IgA vasculitis.

### Cryoglobulinemic Vasculitis

Cryoglobulins are immunoglobulins characterized by a tendency to precipitate from serum under conditions of cold. Such proteins, detectable to various degrees in a wide array of inflammatory conditions, do not always cause disease. That is to say that a patient's serum may contain immunoglobulins that behave in the laboratory as a cryoglobulin—precipitating from serum once placed in a very cold refrigerator—but such immunoglobulins may not lead to the clinical syndrome of cryoglobulinemia in the patient possessing them. In some patients, however, cryoglobulins bind to circulating antigen (e.g., portions of the hepatitis C virion), are deposited in the walls of small and medium-sized blood vessels, and activate complement, leading to cryoglobulinemic vasculitis.

In contrast to most other forms of IC-mediated vasculitis, cryoglobulinemia tends to involve both smalland medium-sized blood vessels. Thus the syndrome of cryoglobulinemic vasculitis can be associated with the development of large cutaneous ulcers, digital ischemia, and livedo racemosa—findings characteristic of disturbances in medium-sized vessels—as well as palpable purpura and other hallmarks of small-vessel vasculitis. The first Chapel Hill Consensus Conference provided a consensus definition for mixed cryoglobulinemia (Table 92.5).

Three major types of cryoglobulinemia are recognized, defined by the specific kinds of immunoglobulins with which they are associated (Table 92.6). Type I, characterized by a monoclonal gammopathy (generally IgG or IgM), differs substantially from types II and III in its clinical presentation and disease associations. Type I cryoglobulinemia, associated with Waldenström's macroglobulinemia or, less frequently, multiple myeloma, is more likely

to cause syndromes related to hyperviscosity (dizziness, confusion, headache, and stroke) than necrotizing vasculitis.

In contrast to the monoclonal nature of type I cryoglobulinemia, types II and III are known as mixed cryoglobulinemias because they are composed of both IgG and IgM. In type II cryoglobulinemia, more than 90% of cases are caused by hepatitis C infection and the cryoproteins consist of monoclonal IgM and polyclonal IgG. Cases of type II cryoglobulinemia not associated with hepatitis C are sometimes termed essential mixed cryoglobulinemia because their cause is not known. Type III cryoglobulinemia, typically associated with polyclonal IgG and polyclonal IgM, is associated with many forms of chronic inflammation including infection and autoimmune disease.

Type II and III cryoglobulinemias often present with a triad of signs and symptoms: purpura, arthralgias, and myalgias. The purpura may be extensive and confluent (Fig. 92.7), sometimes involving the trunk, upper extremities, and even the face; in most cases, however, the rash is confined to the lower extremities. Other organ systems commonly involved in mixed cryoglobulinemia are the kidneys and peripheral nerves. Mixed cryoglobulinemia may cause membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis that resembles lupus nephritis histopathologically. It may also cause a vasculitic neuropathy, usually with sensory symptoms predominating over motor symptoms. Finally, in rare cases, cryoglobulinemia is associated with alveolar hemorrhage.

Skin biopsy is the most straightforward method of confirming the diagnosis. Light microscopy of purpuric lesions demonstrates leukocytoclastic vasculitis. In addition, DIF studies reveal various types of immunoglobulin and complement deposition, depending on the type. In type II cryoglobulinemia, for example, DIF reveals IgG and IgM deposition, as well as complement components.

Serologic testing may also yield clues to the presence of mixed cryoglobulinemia. To assay for serum cryoglobulins, the blood is collected in a prewarmed apparatus, allowed to clot at 37° C before processing, and then refrigerated at 4° C for several days. The percentage of the serum occupied by the cryoprecipitate is referred to as the cryocrit. The difficulties involved in performing cryoglobulin assays often lead to false-negative results. As noted, not all detectable cryoglobulins are associated with disease.

Nonspecific serologic testing may also implicate mixed cryoglobulinemia. A strong clue to the presence of

cryoglobulinemia is the presence of an extremely low level of C4, reduced out of proportion to C3. Two major entities in the differential diagnosis of C4 hypocomplementemia are SLE and IgG4-related disease, both of which can be associated with this finding.

The monoclonal component of type II cryoglobulins almost invariably has rheumatoid factor activity (i.e., binds to the Fc portion of IgG). Thus patients with type II cryoglobulinemia generally have high titers of rheumatoid factor but are anti-cyclic citrullinated protein antibody negative. As markers of clinical disease activity, C4 levels, rheumatoid factor titers, and cryocrits all fare poorly, often remaining abnormal in the face of clinically improved disease.

Treatment of cryoglobulinemia has seen substantial progress in recent years, both because of therapeutic advances in the treatment of hepatitis C and because of the efficacy of B cell depletion in treating many cases of truly essential mixed cryoglobulinemia. For hepatitis C-associated mixed cryoglobulinemic vasculitis, dual treatment strategies that combine anti-viral therapies and B

cell depletion approaches with rituximab are synergistic in treating this condition and often lead to long-term treatment responses.

The rationale behind rituximab use in cryoglobulinemia is that peripheral B lymphocyte depletion will lead to a reduction in plasma cells that produce cryoglobulins. Studies of these treatment modalities have suggested that disease relapses are associated with the absence of virologic control and peripheral B cell recovery, implying the need to combine the two treatment strategies. The optimal timing of anti-viral and B cell depletion strategies is not clear. Nevertheless, one reasonable approach is to initiate anti-viral strategies first and then to employ rituximab within several weeks.

Patients who present with overwhelming illness, such as the unusual patient with alveolar hemorrhage or with symptoms of hyperviscosity, are candidates for plasma exchange, with the goal of removing the pathogenic ICs as quickly as possible. One approach is to perform plasma exchange every other day with concomitant glucocorticoid therapy for a total of seven exchanges or until there is sufficient clinical improvement, followed by B cell depletion after plasma exchange is complete so that the B cell depletion agent is not removed by plasma exchange.

The prognosis of patients with cryoglobulinemia generally depends on the underlying cause. The outcome of type I cryoglobulinemia relates closely to the success in treating the cause. Type II or III cryoglobulinemia secondary to hepatitis C can be treated effectively if the viral infection is responsive to therapy. If patients do not tolerate anti-viral therapy well or if the treatment is ineffective, they may require low to moderate doses of prednisone to control the disease.

Patients with mixed cryoglobulinemia whose disease is not associated with either hepatitis C or a lymphoproliferative malignancy often respond well to rituximab plus glucocorticoids, with tapering of the glucocorticoids over several weeks. Such patients often require regular treatment with rituximab (e.g., every 6 months) to prevent disease return.

### IgG4-Related Vasculitis

IgG4-related disease (IgG4-RD; see Chapter 126) has long been known to be associated with a large-vessel vasculitis that is a cause of aortitis. More recently, it has been recognized that IgG4-RD in fact may be classified as a variable-vessel vasculitis. This is because it is capable of affecting blood vessels of any size, from the aorta through medium-sized arteries (e.g., the coronary vessels) to the small blood vessels of the skin. One of the histologic hallmarks of the disease—obliterative phlebitis—vividly illustrates the vascular tropism of this condition. ICs clearly participate in the small-vessel manifestations of the disease that present with cutaneous findings and have also been identified in the kidney and pancreas. Their specific contributions to obliterative phlebitis and to larger vessel involvement, if any, remain to be defined.

Cutaneous vasculitis in IgG4-RD is typically observed in the setting of extremely high serum IgG4 concentrations, elevations of other IgG subclasses (e.g., IgG1), C3 and C4 hypocomplementemia, and multiorgan IgG4-RD. The cutaneous findings in IgG4-related vasculitis, generally palpable purpura or confluent purpura, are indistinguishable from other types of cutaneous vasculitis but are typical of IC-mediated cutaneous vasculitides in being widespread in their distribution across the skin (Fig. 92.8).

### Hypocomplementemic Urticarial Vasculitis

Three different syndromes of UV are recognized: normocomplementemic UV, hypocomplementemic UV (HUV), and the hypocomplementemic urticarial vasculitis syndrome (HUVS). Normocomplementemic UV is typically a self-limited subset of hypersensitivity vasculitis. In chronic cases, normocomplementemic UV must be distinguished carefully from neutrophilic urticaria, a persistent form of urticaria not associated with vasculitis. In contrast, HUV is more likely to be a chronic disorder that has certain overlapping features with SLE: low serum complements, autoantibodies, and an interface dermatitis characterized by immunoreactant deposition (complement and immunoglobulins) at the dermalepidermal junction in a pattern essentially identical to the lupus band test. Finally, HUVS is a severe form of the disease associated with extracutaneous disease and an array of organ system findings atypical of SLE. For example, HUVS may be associated with uveitis, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), and angioedema.

Unlike common urticaria, UV lesions are frequently associated with moderate pain, burning, and tenderness in addition to pruritus. Whereas common urticaria typically resolve completely within 24 to 48 hours, UV lesions may take days to resolve

completely, often leaving residual hyperpigmentation; they may worsen without therapy. Patients with HUV or HUVS may present with purpuric lesions that are more dominant than urticarial lesions.

The skin lesions in UV tend to be centripetal, favoring the trunk and proximal extremities more than dependent regions. The lesions are painful and associated with a burning sensation rather than the pruritus of common urticaria. Biopsy of an urticarial wheal in UV demonstrates evidence of leukocytoclastic vasculitis, including injury to the endothelial cells of the postcapillary venules, erythrocyte extravasation, leukocytoclasis, fibrin deposition, and a perivascular neutrophilic (or, less commonly, lymphocytic) infiltrate. DIF demonstrates IC deposition around blood vessels in the superficial dermis and a striking deposition of immunoglobulins and complement along the dermal-epidermal junction. In the proper setting, these findings (interface dermatitis and immunoreactant deposition within blood vessels) are diagnostic of HUV. HUVS, in contrast, is a clinical diagnosis based on the presence of UV and the occurrence of typical features in extracutaneous organ systems.

Some cases of HUV respond to therapies commonly used for the treatment of SLE, including low-dose prednisone, hydroxychloroquine, dapsone, or other immunomodulatory agents. Serious cases of HUVS, particularly those presenting with glomerulonephritis or other forms of serious organ involvement, may require high doses of glucocorticoids or biologic agents such as tumor necrosis factor inhibitors or B cell depletion. Both COPD and cardiac valve abnormalities are associated with HUVS and may require specific treatment as well.

The prognosis of UV is often linked to the disorder with which it is associated. SLE, COPD, angioedema, and valvular abnormalities are all known to occur in association with this disorder and may strongly influence both quality and quantity of life. Some cases of HUV and HUVS resolve completely following courses of immunosuppression.

### Erythema Elevatum n Diutinum

EED is a rare, distinctive form of leukocytoclastic vasculitis limited to the skin. The disorder is distinctive because of the unusual distribution of skin lesions (found symmetrically over the extensor surfaces of joints) and the prompt response to sulfone medications. The cutaneous findings are typical of any small vessel vasculitis, with a predominance of papules, plaques, and nodules. Early lesions are often pink or yellowish and then become red or purple (Fig. 92.9). The natural history of untreated lesions is to persist for years, becoming doughy or hard with time. The lesions have a predilection for the skin overlying the small joints of the hands and the knees; they can also affect the buttocks. The trunk is generally spared.

The principal histopathologic findings of EED are leukocytoclastic vasculitis with fibrinoid necrosis. Although an IC basis is suspected in this disorder, DIF studies are not distinctive. EED has been associated with various CTDs, rheumatoid arthritis, other forms of vasculitis (such as GPA), HIV infections, and paraproteinemias (particularly IgA). EED typically responds promptly to dapsone or sulfapyridine, but chronic therapy may be required because skin lesions recur after cessation of treatment.

### Autoimmune Disease-Associated Vasculitis

Vasculitis rarely occurs in autoimmune diseases or CTDs without overt manifestations of the underlying disorder. The forms of CTD typically complicated by vasculitis include those related to SLE: lupus itself, mixed CTD, Sjögren's syndrome, and overlap CTD. Although vasculitis clearly occurs in some CTD settings, it is commonly overdiagnosed in attempts to explain perplexing disease features in patients with known rheumatic illnesses. For example, neuropsychiatric SLE is generally not caused by a true vasculitis but rather by other mechanisms that remain poorly defined. Whenever possible, the clinical hypothesis of vasculitis should be confirmed by biopsy before a label of "vasculitis" is given to poorly understood disease manifestations.

Cutaneous vasculitis in CTDs is associated almost invariably with hypocomplementemia and high titers of anti-nuclear antibodies (ANAs). DIF examination of skin lesions shows granular IgG and C3 deposition in and around dermal vessels, with or without IgM, reflecting the contribution of ICs to disease pathogenesis. The phenomenon of the "in vivo ANA" is also observed in keratinocytes and dermal cells in DIF studies (Fig. 92.10).

Vasculitis in patients with SLE-related disorders is more likely than other forms of vasculitis to be associated with a lymphocytic predominance. One variant of CTD-associated cutaneous vasculitis, the so-called benign hypergammaglobulinemia of Waldenström, is usually a true lymphocytic vasculitis. Patients with this disorder invariably have anti-Ro antibodies, and many have subclinical Sjögren's syndrome. Lymphocytic vasculitis typically demonstrates less disruption of blood vessel architecture than does leukocytoclastic vasculitis, perhaps because lymphocytes contain fewer of the destructive enzymes found within neutrophil granules. Fibrinoid necrosis, for example, is rare in lymphocytic vasculitis. True lymphocytic vasculitis is nearly always confined to the small blood vessels of the superficial papillary dermis. Even in Sjögren's syndrome, however, the histopathology encountered in most cases is that of leukocytoclastic vasculitis.

### Rheumatoid Vasculitis

RV must be distinguished from the isolated, periungual digital vasculitis that, in the absence of severe involvement, does not require intensive, vasculitis-specific therapy. Isolated digital vasculitis in patients with rheumatoid arthritis, characterized by splinter-like lesions in the periungual region (Bywaters lesions), is not necessarily associated with a poorer prognosis than rheumatoid arthritis without digital vasculitic lesions and does not require specific therapy for vasculitis. In contrast, RV is a potentially devastating complication that may involve both medium and small blood vessels and requires the most aggressive therapeutic interventions. Many clinical manifestations of RV are indistinguishable from polyarteritis nodosa, although microaneurysms are less common in RV. RV classically occurs in patients with nodular, rheumatoid factor-positive, joint-destructive disease who have few clinical indications of active synovitis at the time vasculitis begins. RV occasionally complicates early disease.

The most common presentation ofR V includes purpuric lesions with or without evidence of concomitant medium vessel vasculitis. DIF examination of the skin lesions shows granular IgM and C3 deposition in vessels, consistent with an IC-mediated pathophysiology in which rheumatoid factor, complement, and cryoglobulins may all participate.

Deep cutaneous ulcers near the malleoli are a hallmark of RV and require scrupulous local care, as well as judicious immunosuppression. Mononeuritis multiplex often complicates RV. Highdose glucocorticoids plus rituximab is an appropriate first-choice regimen for many patients with RV, with the addition of cyclophosphamide if there is evidence of advancing disease. Tumor necrosis factor inhibitors may also be reasonable options for patients with milder disease.

# Primary Central Nervous System Vasculitis

### KEY POINTS

### Introduction

Vasculitis affecting the central nervous system (CNS) most commonly occurs as a manifestation of a primary systemic vasculitis or as a secondary vasculitis in settings such as connective tissue diseases or infections. When the disease is confined only to the CNS (the brain, meninges, and spinal cord), it is referred to as CNS vasculitis (CNSV). Different nomenclatures have been used in the literature to describe CNSV including primary angiitis of the CNS (PACNS), granulomatous angiitis of the CNS (GACNS), and isolated CNSV. The 2012 revised International Chapel Hill Consensus Conference nomenclature of systemic vasculitides1 defined CNSV as isolated organ vasculitis when CNSV is not a component of a systemic inflammatory disease or an infectious process. For the purpose of this chapter, we will use the term CNSV to reflect primary CNSV.

CNSV is a rare disease that was first reported as a distinct clinical pathologic entity in 1959.2 The disease initially was described as fatal "noninfectious granulomatous angiitis with a predilection for the nervous system." Other reports of similar clinicopathologic phenotypes emerged in the literature, and "granulomatous angiitis of the central nervous system" was proposed to describe this

entity.3, Different terms subsequently surfaced in the literature, such as isolated angiitis of the CNS to encompass cases that were characterized by nongranulomatous pathologic findings. Currently, CNSV is a well-accepted term for this disease that emphasizes the sole involvement of the CNS.6, After the description of diagnostic criteria for CNSV proposed by Calabrese and Mallek in 19885 and the potential for effective treatment,8 published cases in the literature increased tremendously, and more than 500 cases have now been described worldwide.9,10

### Epidemiology

Because of its rarity and our evolving understanding of this disease, the true incidence of CNSV is difficult to calculate. In the recent era, the estimated annual incidence rate of CNSV is 2.4 cases/1 million person-years. Middle-aged men are predominantly affected by CNSV, with a median age at onset of approximately 50 years and a male-to-female ratio of approximately 2:1.6,7,10

### Genetics

The pathogenesis of CNSV is not well understood. To date, no evidence suggests a genetic predisposition, although this possibility remains under active investigation.

### Clinical Features

### KEY POINTS

Great progress has been made toward understanding the clinical features of CNSV despite the many challenges, which include the lack of highly specific diagnostic modalities, the sparse material for research, and the lack of controlled clinical trials. In the recent

era, specific clinical and pathologic subsets of CNSV have been identified that have prognostic implications. 11-14

The clinical presenting features in CNSV are varied but most commonly include a subacute onset of insidious headache, cognitive impairment, seizures, and diffuse and focal neurologic deficits.10-13 Due to the insidious nature of the symptoms, the diagnosis is often delayed,3 and low index of suspicion is needed to consider and evaluate for this condition in the acute setting. Less commonly, a subset of patients could present acutely with symptoms related to the mass effect in patient who have masslike (ML) presentation. Some of the less common presenting features include cranial neuropathies, new onset refractory epilepsy, and anterior visual pathway involvement.10, Because the disease is confined to the brain, meninges, or spinal cord, signs and symptoms of systemic inflammatory diseases are usually lacking. CNSV should be suspected in patients with typical clinical features including multiple CNS ischemic events in different vascular territories and vasculopathy without traditional risk factors.

### CNSV Subsets

### Pathologically Defined Central Nervous System Vasculitis

The original pathologic reports of CNSV as a granulomatous angiitis imposed a histologic-based nomenclature on the disease that led to the original name granulomatous angiitis of the CNS (GACNS). Until the 1980s, CNSV was largely considered a homogeneous entity with a uniform clinical picture and a grave prognosis. This paradigm was challenged with the introduction of direct vascular imaging as a diagnostic tool and the recognition that nongranulomatous pathologic findings occur in CNSV.

Initial attempts at subclassification of CNSV described three broad subsets: GACNS, benign angiopathy of the CNS (BACNS), and "atypical" CNSV. It has since become recognized that BACNS is part of the reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome (RCVS),12 with the other CNSV subsets now being defined by mode of diagnosis, by either pathologic or radiographic features. Further, other broad categories of CNSV have emerged in the literature that are based on the affected vessel size; these are referred to as the small vessel variant (SVV) and the large/medium vessel variant (LMVV). Imaging and histology play important roles in distinguishing these variants. In one study, LMVV had strong/concentric vessel wall enhancement on vessel wall MR imaging (VW-MR), while meningeal/parenchymal contrast enhancement was more frequently observed in the SVV group. In comparison, clinical symptoms and outcomes did not show significant differences between the LMVV and the SVV groups, and although relapse was relatively higher in the LMVV group than in the SVV group, this did not meet statistical significance. The majority of SVV was diagnosed by brain biopsy (SVV: 78.3% vs. LMVV: 30.8%, P = 0.022), with biopsy having a diagnostic accuracy of 100 % (18 of 18) in SVV and 57.1% (4 of 7) in LMVV, respectively (P = 0.015).

Three overarching patterns of destructive vasculitis can be observed in pathologic studies in CNSV17: (1) granulomatous vasculitis characterized by vasculocentric mononuclear inflammation associated with well-formed granulomas and multinucleated giant cells, with granuloma seen throughout the vascular wall, typical of GANCS; (2) purely lymphocytic pattern characterized by predominantly lymphocytic inflammation with occasional plasma cells, extending through the vascular wall with features of vascular distortion and destruction; and (3) necrotizing vasculitis, which is

the least frequently seen pattern, characterized by acute necrotizing vasculitis, similar to the pattern seen in polyarteritis nodosa, with transmural fibrinoid necrosis. Intracranial hemorrhage rarely occurred among these patients. Deposition of amyloid-β peptide can occur in granulomatous and necrotizing pathologic patterns, and when present, the diagnosis of amyloid-βrelated angiitis (ABRA) is confirmed. Granulomatous, necrotizing vasculitis pathologic patterns and ABRA carry a poor prognosis.

GACNS is diagnosed by the pathologic findings of granulomatous angitis (Fig. 93.1). Typically the CSF findings include those of an aseptic meningitis picture with negative staining for microorganisms. GACNS predominantly affects middle-aged men. The most common findings on neuroimaging include infarcts, most often bilateral, as well as high-intensity T2-weighted fluid attenuation inversion recovery (FLAIR) lesions on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) in the subcortical white matter and deep gray matter. A cerebral angiogram is not the diagnostic modality of choice, given its poor spatial resolution in the detection of small vessel vasculitis, which mainly occurs in GACNS.

ABRA is a rare form of CNSV with overlapping features of cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA) and granulomatous or necrotizing pattern vasculitis on the brain pathology. Amyloid-β peptide, a fragment of the amyloid precursor peptide, deposits in the brain, causing disease ranging from Alzheimer's disease to CAA, CAA-related inflammation, and ABRA. Patients with ABRA tend to be older and more prone to hallucinations and mental status changes than are other patients with CNSV. MRI cannot distinguish between ABRA and other forms of CNSV, although ABRA has a higher incidence of cerebral hemorrhage. ABRA carries a poor outcome, which could be related to older age, recurrent cerebral bleeding, and comorbidities.

Pathologic findings of lymphocytic infiltration rather than granulomatous features should prompt thorough evaluation for secondary causes of CNSV, such as infectious or lymphoproliferative diseases. Adequate staining and immunophenotyping should always be carefully carried out in this setting.

### Radiographically Defined Central Nervous System Vasculitis

Advances in neuroimaging and the ready availability of these techniques have led to their increased use and importance in the

diagnostic workup of CNSV. Cerebrovascular imaging techniques such as digital subtraction angiography (DSA), computed tomography angiography (CTA), or magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) are used to evaluate smallto large-/medium-sized vessel involvement.

Several pitfalls limit the use of cerebrovascular imaging as the sole means of diagnosis for CNSV. An abnormal cerebral arteriogram can be seen in a wide range of settings, and the poor specificity of the cerebral angiogram poses a major challenge in the diagnosis of CNSV. VW-MR concentric enhancement can be related to venous enhancement slow flow and vasa vasorum and can mimic the radiographic findings of CNSV. When the diagnosis of CNSV is based on cerebrovascular imaging, a thorough evaluation should be performed to rule out mimics, such as atherosclerosis, thromboembolic disease, radiation vasculopathy, and RCVS.20, The presence of an inflammatory pattern of the CSF may support a diagnosis of a vasculitic process, while normal CSF protein and white blood cells would argue against a diagnosis of vasculitis in this context.

### Diagnosis and Diagnostic Tests

### KEY POINTS

Spinal fluid, brain and vascular imaging, and brain biopsy are central to the diagnosis of CNSV and the process of ruling out other diseases. Abnormal spinal fluid is found in 80% to 90% of patients with CNSV. Abnormalities on a cerebral angiogram are not specific for CNSV and can be seen in a wide range of other settings. RCVS is an important mimic of CNSV that is characterized by thunderclap headaches, normal CSF, and abnormal findings of a cerebral angiogram in which the changes resolve within 12 weeks. Other important entities in the differential diagnosis of CNSV include infection, lymphoproliferative disease, primary systemic vasculitis, connective tissue disease, genetic diseases, and thromboembolic disease.

The diagnosis of CNSV is challenging because of the nonspecific clinical presentation, the lack of highly specific laboratory and radiologic tests, and the difficulty of obtaining pathologic material.

### Proposed Diagnostic Criteria for Central Nervous System Vasculitis

In 1988, Calabrese and Mallek5 proposed diagnostic criteria for CNSV that emphasized the importance of ruling out mimics when diagnosing CNSV. These criteria include (1) the presence of an unexplained neurologic deficit after thorough clinical and laboratory evaluation, (2) documentation by cerebral angiography and/or tissue examination of an arteritic process within the CNS, and (3) no evidence of systemic vasculitides or any other condition to which the angiographic or pathologic features could be secondary.

In 2009, other investigators13 proposed changes to the criteria described by one study, incorporating levels of diagnostic certainty in their assessment. They proposed use of the term definite diagnosis of CNSV when tissue biopsy findings provide confirmation of vasculitis and a probable diagnosis of CNSV when the diagnosis is based on high-probability findings on an angiogram in the absence of tissue confirmation but with consideration of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) profiles and neurologic symptoms to discriminate between CNSV and its mimics.

Although the original criteria by Calabrese and Mallek served as a platform of literature-based research, their interpretation has changed fundamentally as advancement of our diagnostic modalities has revealed many unexplained neurologic diseases. The importance of ruling out mimics of CNSV remains essential in the diagnostic approach of patients with suspected CNSV.

### Diagnostic Tests

### Laboratory Findings

Elevation of acute-phase reactants, anemia, and thrombocytosis are not typical of CNSV, and if present, they should raise the possibility of a primary systemic vasculitis or another underlying disease. Laboratory testing to rule out connective tissue diseases and thromboembolic abnormalities should be performed. Infectious workup with appropriate cultures, serologies, and polymerase chain reaction testing should be directed by clinical and diagnostic findings and host risk factors.

### Cerebrospinal Fluid Analysis

CSF is an important tool in the evaluation of CNSV. Although CSF findings are nonspecific in CNSV, their value lies in ruling out other entities. Obtaining appropriate CSF cultures, microbiologic stains, cytology, and flow cytometry is crucial in ruling out infectious and neoplastic disease. Elevated protein levels, modest lymphocytic pleocytosis, and occasionally oligoclonal bands and elevated IgG synthesis characterize the CSF in 80% to 90% of patients with pathologically documented CNSV.6, The median CSF white blood cell count is approximately 20 cells/μL, and the median CSF protein level is approximately 120 mg/dL.6, Advanced CSF molecular sequencing is being investigated as an unbiased approach to identify infectious etiologies in patients with "idiopathic" neurologic disease.

### Radiologic Evaluation

MRI is a sensitive modality for the diagnosis of CNSV, reaching 90% to 100%.9, Abnormalities include infarcts in 50% of patients, commonly affecting the cortex and the subcortex bilaterally. Affected areas include subcortical white matter, followed by deep gray matter, deep white matter, and the cerebral cortex. Hyperintense lesions on T2-weighted sequences are common but not specific for CNSV. Other abnormalities include spinal cord presentations, leptomeningeal enhancement in 8% of cases,10 and gadolinium-enhanced intracranial lesions in about one-third of patients.

Very rarely CNSV can present as an ML lesion occurring in less than 5% of cases. This presentation gained attention after the report of a series of 38 patients with histologically confirmed CNSV who presented with a solitary cerebral mass. Typically, the diagnosis is unanticipated and is confirmed after pathologic examination of either biopsy samples or surgical excision of the mass. Unfortunately, no specific features on clinical assessment, neuroimaging, cerebral angiography, or CSF examination can reliably distinguish ML-CNSV from other, more common causes of a solitary cerebral mass. Use of appropriate stains and cultures to rule out mycobacterial, fungal, or other infections and immunohistochemistry/gene rearrangement studies to exclude lymphoproliferative disease are essential to secure the diagnosis and exclude concomitant infectious or malignant processes.

Cerebral vasculature imaging, either by DSA or through MRA or CTA is an important modality in the diagnosis of CNSV. Alternating areas of dilation and stenosis characterize the angiographic

findings in CNSV and typically involve the vasculature on both sides but sometimes can involve single vessels. Other cerebrovascular features include smooth tapering of one or multiple vessels. Although cerebral angiograms may visualize abnormalities in medium-sized vessels, they have limited sensitivity to detect abnormalities in small vessels that are less than 500 µm in diameter. Although cerebral angiography is valuable, its specificity for the diagnosis of CNSV can be as low as 25%.25, The reported "typical" angiographic findings for vasculitis are not specific to CNSV and can be encountered in atherosclerosis, radiation vasculopathy, or vascular spasm. Moreover, a cerebral angiogram carries a poor positive predictive value in the diagnosis of CNSV in that the angiographic findings seen in RCVS can be consistent with those found in CNSV. VW-MR has additionally been used to obtain information regarding the radiographic patterns and appearance of the vessel wall in large-/medium-sized arteries. The VW-MR protocol includes black-blood contrast-enhanced T1-weighted sequences and a time-of-flight MRA of the circle of Willis using a 3-Tesla MR system for a better signal-to-noise ratio. Using VW-MR imaging, possible distinction could be made between atherosclerotic plaques (eccentric nonuniform vessel wall thickening and contrast enhancement) compared with infectious or inflammatory vasculitis (usually smooth concentric uniform vessel wall enhancement likely due to increased permeability of the endothelium or vasa vasorum27). In one study, using VW-MR features and concentric enhancement on VW-MR imaging, CNSV could be distinguished from other noninflammatory vasculopathies with a sensitivity of 90.5% and a specificity of 100%. This promising technique may have a role in following up with patients with CNSV. In a recent study of VW-MR, approximately 50% to 75% of patients will show changes in vessel wall contrast enhancement concordant with disease activity. Vascular studies thus should be interpreted with caution and should not be considered the diagnostic "gold standard" in CNSV.

### Brain Biopsy

Brain biopsy is thought to carry a low morbidity and mortality in patients with CNSV30 and is an important part of the evaluation to confirm the diagnosis and rule out mimics. When a brain biopsy is performed, an alternative diagnosis is identified in 30% to 40% of cases. The interpretation of the brain biopsy results should take into consideration the potential for false-negative results because of the patchy degree of involvement and the small amount of tissue that often is able to be obtained. The finding of vasculitis on pathologic examination does not exclude the diagnosis of infection or malignancy, and appropriate stains and markers should be pursued for accurate diagnosis. The leptomeningeal vessels are more often involved in comparison to parenchymal vessels, and including leptomeninges in the biopsy increases the diagnostic yield.

### Differential Diagnosis

The differential diagnosis algorithm of CNSV is large because of the lack of highly specific clinical features or laboratory or imaging findings (Table 93.1). Excluding other entities that can have similar findings is critical in confirming a diagnosis of CNSV. Certain disease categories in particular should be considered and warrant further detailed discussion.

### Reversible Cerebral Vasoconstriction Syndromes

Distinguishing RCVS, the leading mimic of CNSV, is important because it has different implications for treatment and outcome (Table 93.2). RCVS consists of a group of disorders characterized by acute-onset headaches and reversible cerebrovasoconstriction. These disorders include CallFleming syndrome, drug-induced angiopathy, migraine angiitis, BACNS, postpartum angiopathy, and drug-induced vasospasm. The clinical features of RCVS include acute onset of severe headaches, often thunderclap in nature, with or without neurologic deficit, with evidence of cerebral vasoconstriction that is reversible. The headaches are usually recurrent thunderclap headaches and can be precipitated by straining and coughing. RCVS can be associated with strokes (39%), generalized tonicclonic seizures (17%), convexity subarachnoid hemorrhage (34%), lobar hemorrhage (20%), and brain edema (38%). RCVS occurs more frequently in women than men. In contrast to CNSV, findings of CSF analysis are generally normal in people with RCVS except when a concomitant disorder or subarachnoid bleeding is present. The diagnosis of RCVS is usually considered when cerebral vascular imaging reveals multiple areas of smooth or tapered arterial narrowing followed by segments of normal-caliber or distended arteries.
