A monogenic disease in humans has not yet been described, but a role for NLRP6 in oral—gastrointestinal diseases, such as periodontitis, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH), and portal fibrosis, is suggested by increased expression of NLRP6 compared with patients without disease. 166, Beyond the gut, genome-wide association studies (GWAS) and single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) analysis have linked NLRP6 to platelet counts 168 and susceptibility to essential hypertension,169 suggesting a role for NLRP6 in cells outside the gastrointestinal tract. Consistently, ex vivo studies of synovial tissues from patients with RA showed reduced NLRP6 expression compared with patients with osteoarthritis.

### NLRP7

In vitro studies of human macrophages have demonstrated that NLRP7 forms an active inflammasome, triggered by acylated bacterial lipopeptides, 171,172 leading to the release of IL-1β and IL-18 in a caspase-1-dependent fashion, downstream of TLR2. It has been suggested that NLRP7 and TLR2 contribute to the host defense against intracellular gram-positive bacteria, inhibiting replication of Listeria monocytogenes and Staphylococcus aureus infection. In THP-1 cells, Mycobacterium bovis also activates the NLRP7 inflammasome, but this has not been demonstrated in primary human macrophages. NLRP7 colocalizes intracellularly with the Golgi complex and microtubule-organizing center, suggesting potential role in the negative regulation of inflammation. NLRP7-related diseases have been limited to the reproductive system n175 and specifically in patients with recurrent hydatidiform moles. NLRP7 is highly expressed in the placenta and throughout the first trimester of human pregnancy, with increased expression and activation in cases of fetal growth restriction. Studies suggest a role for NLRP7 in the generation and/or maintenance of the

maternal imprint, with cells expressing NLRP7 variants, resulting in autosomal dominant aberrant imprinting marks in the offspring. While further evaluation of this role for NLRP7 in epigenetics is needed, these findings suggest new sensor functions that have not previously been associated with NLRP family members and may have important implications for disease pathogenesis.178,179

### NLRP12

NLRP12 (Monarch-1, Pypaf7) was among the first NLRs identified, but much remains unknown about this sensor, and questions .180,181Studremain on whether it forms a complete inflammasome. ies demonstrate that it forms a six-helical bundle death domain fold, similar to the other NLRs182; however, gene-silencing studies suggest that NLRP12 acts as a negative regulator of TNF driven NF-κB signaling. Gain of function variants in NLRP12 have been linked to enhanced inflammation in cold-associated periodic fevers, similar to NLRP3.184-186 Other variants have been proposed as causes of noninfectious fevers in children with elevated serum acute phase reactants and buccal aphthous stomatitis. However, in many cases, healthy first-degree relatives have been described to carry NLRP12 mutations, suggesting that NLRP12related phenotypes may depend on additional genetic and environmental factors.

Thus much of our knowledge about NLRP12 function stems from murine knockout lines and investigations of colitis and colon tumorigenesis, similar to NLRP6, in that NLRP12 has a protective role in intestinal inflammation by suppression of NF-kB activation resulting in reduced colitis susceptibility. 183, Since microbial dysbiosis is associated with inflammatory bowel disease, it is proposed that NLRP12 plays an anti-inflammatory role by regulating gut microbial communities. In a meta-analysis of human 16S RNA data from twins affected by ulcerative colitis, NLRP12 expression was found to be significantly down-regulated in cohorts with active ulcerative colitis, compared with healthy controls and patients with inactive disease. Murine models have also suggested a role for NLRP12 in rapid myelopoiesis,190 as well as in reducing neuroinflammation in experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis, an experimental model of multiple sclerosis. It remains to be seen whether similar tissue-specific functions can be attributed to human NLRP12.

### PYHIN Proteins

AIM2 is perhaps the most well known non-NLR protein capable of forming an inflammasome. AIM2 forms an intracytoplasmic sensor that directly binds cytoplasmic bacterial or viral dsDNA or self-DNA.80, AIM2 is activated in two steps, with step 1 involving type 1 IFNs. Similar to NLRP3, AIM2 is important as a guardian of cellular integrity, as well as bacterial, viral, fungal, and parasitic pathogens, and has been associated with disease processes including cancer and autoimmunity. IFI16 is another DNA sensor that forms an inflammasome in the nucleus in response to specific DNA viruses. IFI16 has been proposed to play a role in cancer through regulating cellular senescence, as well as in aging-associated inflammation. More recently, autoantibodies to both AIM2 and anti-IFI16 were identified in patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), with the hypothesis that AIM-like receptors result in sustained IFN signaling, leading to promotion of autoantigens and worsening disease activity.

### Inflammasomes in Autoimmunity

A pathogenic role for inflammasomes in monogenic autoinflammatory disorders is clear based on Mendelian genetics and robust evidence from human and mouse immunologic studies. In contrast, the evidence supporting inflammasomes mediating autoimmune disorders is less direct and is limited to genetic association studies, altered mRNA gene expression, and human cell or mouse disease models that have generated conflicting data. The variety of inflammasome triggers (temperature, ion flux, crystals, metabolites, microbial products) suggests that the stimuli may determine the character of downstream inflammatory responses. However, the wide array of phenotypes associated with polymorphisms even within a single gene may indicate that the effects of these genetic variants ultimately lay at the transcriptional level, as different inflammasome proteins have unique expression patterns, or at the translational level, either through disruption of domain interactions or reducing the threshold for inflammasome activation. Nevertheless, a growing set of in vitro and ex vivo data implicates a role for inflammasome activation in a multitude of rheumatic diseases including SLE, celiac disease, crystal-induced arthropathies, and RA196 (Table 95.2).

### Genetic Variants in Inflammasome Genes and Autoimmunity

The association of polymorphisms with certain autoimmune diseases may indicate that specific combinations of genetic and environmental stimuli have disrupted the carefully orchestrated

inflammatory response. Single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in NLRP1 have been associated with autoimmune skin disorders such as vitiligo, autoimmune endocrine diseases, SLE, and RA, whereas SNPs in NLRP3, as well as its binding protein CARD8 are associated with susceptibility to RA and juvenile idiopathic arthritis in specific populations. Similarly, polymorphisms in IL1B and IL18 have been identified as susceptibility risk factors for RA in Caucasians and Asians198,199 and correlated to disease severity in SLE. However, validation of findings across multiple populations is necessary.

### Ex Vivo and Murine Studies of Inflammasomes and Autoimmunity

Baseline expression of inflammasome sensors has guided initial studies on the pathogenesis of these multifactorial diseases. For example, NLRP1 and AIM2 have long been known to be expressed in the skin, and recent studies have linked polymorphisms in these genes to susceptibility to several autoimmune skin disorders. Unsurprisingly, AIM2 expression is increased in keratinocytes in active psoriatic skin lesions. Studies of human keratinocytes have demonstrated, at least in vitro, that stimulation with dsDNA activates AIM2 in these cells, leading to IL-1β secretion. Similarly, the level of AIM2 expression in macrophages has been further associated with severity of disease in patients with SLE,203 suggesting a role for this DNA sensor in autoimmunity.

Adding further complexity, inflammasome molecule expression studies indicate the variability of gene expression based on tissue of origin and cell type and may be influenced by disease activity. In mononuclear cells from RA patients, the expression of common inflammasome components ASC and caspase-1 are increased,2 204 while the expression of NLRP3 and inflammasome activity are variable in mononuclear cells from RA patients depending on treatment.204, At the tissue level, NLRP3 expression is increased in studies of RA synovium compared with other forms of arthritis. 206 NLRP3 expression is similarly increased in several other autoimmune disease-associated tissues including skin in systemic sclerosis and kidneys in SLE,207,208 with increased IL-1β production from patients with SLE nephritis. However, despite the evidence for increased NLRP3 expression in RA synovium, NLRP3 knockout mice have generated variable results, suggesting a contributory role of other inflammatory pathways in disease pathogenesis.

Finally, recent work has suggested that effector and memory CD4+ T cells may instruct antigen-presenting myeloid cells to produce mature IL-1β independent of caspase-l and inflammasome activation. This activation was thought to parallel inflammasome-driven IL-1β release but acts through a TNFR- Fas—caspase-8 pathway. Mice deficient in these pathways were protected from developing T cellmediated autoimmunity in an experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis model. Despite these challenges, active targeting of the inflammasome or downstream cytokines may be a valuable therapeutic approach for these complex patients.

### Clinical Assays of Inflammasome Activity

For patients without a molecular genetic diagnosis, including those with autoimmunity or likely multifactorial disease processes, the contributory role of inflammasomes can be difficult to discern clinically. Most studies of the inflammasomes have been driven by primary cells and human and murine cell lines, investigating IL-1β/IL-18 release, ASC speck formation, and/or

cell death, limiting their use currently to research laboratories. More recently, PCRand bead-based immunoassays for the detection of cytokines have become more readily available to clinicians, but ageand sex-appropriate reference ranges accounting for diurnal cytokine variations and linking to disease specificity have yet to be established.213,214

### Inflammasome-Targeted d Therapies

The role of inflammasomes in multiple disease processes has prompted a concerted effort to identify therapies directly targeting the inflammasome215,216 rather than downstream cytokines as are currently available. Recently, the mechanism of several older anti-inflammatory drugs such as colchicine has been linked to inflammasomes. While a number of different approaches are underway which take advantage of the numerous regulatory steps of inflammasome biology, the most promising are drugs that appear to inhibit NLRP3 activation directly by either modifying the active conformation or preventing oligomerization in response to stimuli. Some of the most promising NLRP3targeted therapeutics are based on the drug known as CRID3 or MCC950, which has been used in numerous models and which binds NLRP3.219 Given what is currently known about structural changes and conformation in NLRP3, some drugs may benefit patients with certain genetic variants over others. Understanding the link between disease phenotype and pathogenesis remains the cornerstone of autoinflammatory syndromes and will inform future development of agents targeting inflammasome pathways.

### Conclusion

Over the last few decades, inflammasomes have been implicated in numerous diseases that are diagnosed and treated by rheumatologists. Inappropriate activation of these protein multimers in response to varying stimuli generates an inflammatory cascade with acute on chronic inflammation characteristic of many rheumatologic disorders. Given the known morbidity and mortality secondary to undiagnosed disease, evidence-based recommendations for diagnosis, treatment, and monitoring of patients with autoinflammatory diseases have been proposed to standardize their management worldwide. While significant progress has been made in understanding the molecular relationship between inflammasome regulation and activation, much remains to be unveiled. Questions related to downregulation of the inflammasome reaction, influences on the adaptive immune system, and maintenance of homeostasis remain. For autoimmunity disorders, increased clinical focus on next-generation sequencing and the modulation of symptoms with targeted biologics may reveal how the combination of genetic polymorphisms, time, inflammation, and epigenetic changes affect the inflammasomes and their interaction within the cellular microenvironment.

# Etiology and Pathogenesis of Hyperuricemia and Gout

### KEY POINTS

### Introduction

The ancient disease gout has a complex pathogenesis, and its modern relevance is underscored by the fact that gout is now the most common inflammatory arthritis in the United States. 1, Gout is a disease of both metabolism and inflammation, and its pathogenesis requires the intersection of two distinct processes: (1) the intrinsic accumulation of urate, at levels sufficient to drive the precipitation of monosodium urate (MSU) crystals, and (2) an inflammatory response to the crystals so formed. How these processes occur, and under what circumstances they cross from adaptive to pathologic responses, are the subject of this chapter.

### Evolutionary Considerations

### KEY POINT

High baseline levels of serum urate in humans may be the result of evolutionary pressures in an era when hyperuricemia provided survival benefits.

The metabolic production of uric acid is ubiquitous among mammals and many other forms of animal life, and it is important to recognize that urate generation is not a priori pathologic. Indeed, the production of uric acid may serve a variety of beneficial roles, an area of interest to molecular immunologists and molecular anthropologists alike.

### Uric Acid as a Danger Signal

Uric acid is a breakdown product of purine metabolism and was long considered nothing more than an excretable remnant. However, studies suggest that evolution has coopted urate to play a potentially critical role in organismal immunity. It has long been appreciated that the lysates of damaged mammalian cells can serve as adjuvants—that is, can promote immune responses to antigens— but the mediator of adjuvant action was not known. Using classical biochemical techniques, one group3 demonstrated that a major endogenous adjuvant found in damaged or dying cells is uric acid.

Thus uric acid may serve as a danger signal to promote immune responses. As first proposed by Matzinger, a danger signal is an intrinsically produced molecule, issued by an altered or damaged cell, that alerts the immune system to the need for an immunologic response. Viewed from this perspective, production of uric acid in a virally infected cell, for example, might serve as an upstream signal to promote activating antigen presentation (Fig. 96.1). Although damaged or dying cells tend to have limited ability to manufacture proteins, their output of uric acid characteristically increases during cellular breakdown. Uric acid danger signals

may also play an immunologic role in tumor rejection, as suggested by a mouse model. Although these observations require more study, they are consistent with a paradigm in which urate production at the local cellular level plays a central role in immunity and homeostasis.

### Uric Acid and Human Evolution

Most mammals have serum urate levels under 2 mg/dL. In contrast, humans and other primates, as well as some New World monkeys, demonstrate typical serum urate levels between 4 and 6 mg/dL (Fig. 96.2). The genetic and biochemical basis for these increases is well appreciated. During the Miocene era (approximately 10 to 25 million years ago), mutations in various primate species inactivated the uricase gene, which codes for the enzyme that degrades uric acid to allantoic acid (which, in contrast to uric acid, is a highly soluble and readily excreted substance). Genetic studies indicate that the uricase gene experienced inactivating mutations not once but multiple times, across multiple hominoid lineages (Fig. 96.3).6-8 Although uric acid transporters in the kidney (see below) co-evolved to keep urate levels within bounds, the net result was a rise in serum urate. Evolutionary biologists hypothesize that increases in urate generation, and mismatches in renal uric acid excretion, conferred a survival benefit for these

species. Several compelling and not necessarily mutually exclusive hypotheses have been proposed.

Primate species experienced a prior (during the Eocene era, 10 to 20 million years earlier) deletion of a gene permitting organisms to produce ascorbic acid. In mammals that produce it, ascorbic acid serves as their pre-eminent serum antioxidant. Thus loss of ascorbate production may have created an evolutionary liability, for which increases in urate provided antioxidant compensation, potentially as a protectant against aging and cancer. Others suggest that the effects of increased urate provided an evolutionary advantage by promoting hominoid intellectual function, either through its antioxidant effects or via activation of neurostimulatory adenosine receptors (in a manner similar to caffeine). Although the antioxidant theory would appear compelling, critics have pointed out that (1) the production of urate itself generates oxidant molecules, offsetting any possible urate benefit; (2) intra-cellular urate may have pro-oxidant effects11; and (3) the human/primate capacity for antioxidation may be large even in the absence of soluble serum antioxidants, limiting the potential need for urate as an antioxidant.

Specific evolutionary pressures exerted on primate species during the Miocene era. The Miocene was an important era in hominoid evolution and the hominoid diet during that time appears to have been extremely low in salt. Hominoids during the Miocene

may have experienced a "hypotensive crisis," which was particularly challenging in the face of the transition to bipedalism. An elevation in serum urate levels provided a mechanism for restoring normotension, through urate-induced renovascular injury. 13, To model this hypothesis, investigators exposed rats to a very lowsalt diet, resulting in hypotension. When treated with the uricase inhibitor oxonic acid (to mimic the primate uricase loss), the rats' urate levels rose, and their blood pressures normalized. The ability of uricase inhibition to restore blood pressure could then be reversed through the use of the urate-lowering agent allopurinol, confirming that the mechanism of oxonic acid's effect was through

serum urate elevation. Other studies have implicated elevated levels of urate as having a possible role in increased gluconeogenesis, which may have been beneficial in the calorie-poor Miocene era, but which may currently be contributing to the increased incidence of type 2 diabetes in our calorie-rich environment.7,

Although the loss of uricase promoted serum urate increases in humans and other hominoids, the levels of serum urate consequently achieved are usually insufficient to promote urate crystallization and gout. Rather, uricase inactivation created the circumstances under which additional increases in urate production, or impairments in urate excretion, can result in serum urate concentrations exceeding the solubility threshold. Accordingly, we next review the mechanisms of urate production and excretion, as well as the events that may tip the scales toward pathologic hyperuricemia.

### Determinants of Urate Levels

### Uric Acid Production and Excretion: Normal Levels and Hyperuricemia

Uric acid is a breakdown product of purines, and uric acid generation depends directly on both intrinsic purine production and purine intake. In humans, uric acid is an end-product metabolite; consequently, the depletion of uric acid depends directly on its excretion. The balance between uric acid production and excretion determines the serum urate level. Most individuals maintain a relatively stable serum urate concentration between 4 and 6.8 mg/dL and a total body uric acid pool of approximately 1000 mg. Individuals with serum urate levels >6.8 mg/dL (e.g., hyperuricemia), even without clinical gout, may deposit MSU crystals either occultly or in the form of appreciable masses (tophi), with the consequence that the total body uric acid pool may be significantly higher in individuals with asymptomatic hyperuricemia than in nonhyperuricemics.18, These occult deposits of uric acid (total body urate burden) may have implications for treatment

because they act as a "buffering reservoir" that resists initial treatment with urate-lowering agents.

### KEY POINTS

Uric acid is the end product of human purine metabolism. Uric acid production depends on both purine biosynthesis and the metabolic processes that convert purines into uric acid.

### Purine Biosynthesis

Purines are heterocyclic aromatic compounds consisting of conjoined pyrimidine and imidazole rings (Fig. 96.4). In mammals, the most common expression of purines comes in the form of deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) and ribonucleic acid (RNA) (containing the purines adenine and guanine), as well as singlemolecule nucleotides (adenosine triphosphate [ATP], adenosine diphosphate [ADP], adenosine monophosphate [AMP], and cyclic AMP and, to a lesser extent, guanosine triphosphate, guanosine diphosphate, guanosine monophosphate [GMP], and cyclic GMP). Purines are also critical elements of the energy metabolism molecules NADH, NADPH, and coenzyme Q. They additionally serve as direct neurotransmitters; for example, adenosine interacts with receptors to modulate cardiovascular and central nervous system function.

Purine biosynthesis is initiated on a backbone of ribose- 5-phosphate. The enzyme phosphoribosyl pyrophosphate (PRPP) synthetase catalyzes the addition of a pyrophosphate moiety to form the adduct PRPP (Fig. 96.5). Subsequently, the enzyme glutamine-PRPP amidotransferase catalyzes interaction of PRPP with glutamine to form 5-phosphoribosyl amine, the first committed step in purine biosynthesis (Fig. 96.6). 5-phosphoribosyl amine then serves as the backbone for a series of molecular additions, ending in the formation of the purine inosine monophosphate (IMP). IMP is converted into either AMP or GMP, which can then be phosphorylated into higher-energy compounds. Glutamine-PRPP amidotransferase and PRPP synthase are both subject to feedback inhibition by IMP, AMP, and GMP, providing a mechanism to slow purine biosynthesis in the setting of purine sufficiency. Collectively, the process of purine biosynthesis is highly energy dependent, requiring consumption of multiple molecules of ATP. Thus purine biosynthesis not only directly increases the substrate load for urate generation but also increases the turnover of already-formed purines that contribute to increased urate levels.

### Urate Formation and Purine Salvage

Purines generated by the previously described mechanisms are susceptible to enzymatic catabolism, presumably to maintain purine homeostasis (Fig. 96.7). Purines susceptible to degradation include the monophosphate nucleotides GMP and IMP, which are converted by nucleotidases (e.g., removal of the sugar phosphate moiety) to their purine base forms, guanosine and inosine. Additionally, AMP can be converted into IMP and adenosine into inosine by adenosine monophosphate dehydrogenase and adenosine deaminase, respectively, which can then undergo further

degradation via the inosine catabolic pathway. Further catabolism of both guanosine and inosine is mediated by the common enzyme purine nucleoside phosphorylase (PNP). Guanosine is converted to guanine, whereas inosine is converted to hypoxanthine. Both guanine and hypoxanthine are subsequently converted to xanthine by the enzymes guanine deaminase and xanthine oxidase (also known as xanthine dehydrogenase), respectively. Xanthine from either source is then converted directly to uric acid, again by the action of xanthine oxidase. Lacking the enzyme uricase, human and primate purine metabolism ceases with the production of uric acid.

Presumably because purine synthesis is energy expensive for the cell, evolution has dictated that mechanisms exist to recover purines before they irreversibly traverse the degradative pathway. These recovery pathways, collectively known as purine salvage, are intimately connected to the feedback regulation of purine synthesis. The major enzyme responsible for purine salvage, hypoxanthine/guanine phosphoribosyl transferase (HGPRT1, also known as HPRT1), catalyzes the transfer of phosphoribose to either hypoxanthine or guanine, to reform IMP or GMP, respectively (Fig. 96.8). These products are then available for reinclusion in the purine pool. A second salvage enzyme is adenine phosphoribosyl transferase (APRT), which restores adenine to AMP. However, as described earlier, most adenosine/adenine breakdown occurs via conversion to inosinic acid. Purine salvage regeneration of IMP, GMP, and AMP also drives feedback inhibition, slowing the de novo generation of urate.

Urate Overproduction: Primary and Secondary Causes

### KEY POINT

Hyperuricemia may result from urate overproduction owing to primary or secondary causes.

Primary Urate Overproduction. In rare patients, inborn errors of metabolism lead to urate overproduction and subsequent hyperuricemia. Several of these deserve mention. First, a small number of individuals possess PRPP synthetase enzymes that are hyperactive. The result is increased generation of PRPP, which can accelerate purine biosynthesis by Michaelis-Menton kinetics.

The second well-described class of abnormality leading to urate overproduction occurs within the purine salvage pathway. Deficiencies of HGPRT1 result in impaired purine salvage, and therefore increased substrate for uric acid generation. Additionally, because purine salvage normally results in nucleotide monophosphate generation, patients with purine salvage deficiencies accumulate lower levels of nucleotide monophosphates, resulting in loss of feedback inhibition of both PRPP synthase and glutamine- PRPP amidotransferase. Thus purine salvage failure resulting from HGPRT1 deficiency is compounded by secondary purine overproduction. In addition to mutations in HGPRT1 itself, mutations in ALDH16A1, a member of the aldehyde dehydrogenase superfamily, may promote hyperuricemia by impairing the function of HGPRT1.23

Two major variants of HGPRT1 deficiency have been described. Complete HGPRT1 deficiency, known as Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, is an X-linked recessive disorder manifesting in childhood as extremely high levels of serum urate, gout flares, nephrolithiasis, intellectual disability, and movement and behavioral disorders

including self-mutilation. The disorder can occasionally arise by de novo mutation; female carriers are asymptomatic but may have elevated serum urate levels. In contrast to the gout flares and nephrolithiasis, the neurologic findings in Lesch-Nyhan syndrome are independent of hyperuricemia and unresponsive to urate-lowering drugs. Life expectancy can be greatly reduced, and these patients rarely come to the attention of adult rheumatologists.

Individuals with Kelley-Seegmiller syndrome have a partial deficiency of HGPRT1.25 These patients present with early-onset hyperuricemia and gout but limited or no neurologic symptoms. Several variants of Kelley-Seegmiller syndrome have been described, based on the extent of HGPRT1 inactivity and the presence/absence of neurologic findings. Kelley-Seegmiller

mutations tend to occur in different regions of the HGPRT1 gene than those in Lesch-Nyhan patients (whose mutations typically localize to the PRPP-binding region).

Several hereditary defects of energy metabolism also promote elevated uric acid levels, mainly as a consequence of ATP turnover. Patients with glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency (type I glycogen storage, von Gierke's disease) demonstrate a high rate of both purine and ATP turnover. The lactic acidemia that secondarily occurs in patients with glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency may also contribute to hyperuricemia by promoting decreased renal uric acid excretion (see later). In fructose-1-phosphate aldolase deficiency, patients lack the capacity to metabolize fructose- 1-phosphate. Fructose-1-phosphate accumulation causes feedback

inhibition of fructokinase and fructose accumulation in the blood. As an apparent consequence of these changes, AMP accumulates and promotes hyperuricemia by the mechanisms described earlier. The role of fructose intake in patients without inborn errors of fructose metabolism is discussed later.

Secondary Urate Overproduction and Hyperuricemia. Several secondary causes can lead to urate overproduction. In most cases, these conditions induce increased cell turnover, with resultant purine generation and breakdown. Chief among these must be counted diseases of erythropoietic, lymphopoietic, and myelopoietic cell turnover, of both malignant and nonmalignant varieties. Among the erythropoietic diseases causing hyperuricemia, autoimmune, and other hemolytic anemias (red cell destruction with compensatory increased red cell generation), sickle cell disease, 31,32 polycythemia vera,33 and ineffective erythropoiesis (e.g., in pernicious and other forms of megaloblastic anemia, thalassemia, and other hemoglobinopathies) must be included. Patients with myeloproliferative and lymphoproliferative disorders including myelodysplastic syndrome, myeloid metaplasia, leukemias, lymphomas, and paraproteinemic diseases such as multiple myeloma and Waldenström's macroglobulinemia are also at increased risk for hyperuricemia.34-36 In some cases, hyperuricemia and concomitant renal failure may be the first presentation of these malignancies. Indeed, the extent of hyperuricemia may correlate with the degree of disease and cell turnover. Patients with essential thrombocytosis may also be at increased risk for hyperuricemia. An association between solid tumors and hyperuricemia has been reported39; given the slower turnover of solid tumor

cells, solid tumor hyperuricemia tends to be less common and less severe than in malignancies of bone marrow—derived cells.

Tumor lysis syndrome represents a unique form of tumorrelated hyperuricemia, in which cell death induced by chemotherapy causes not only hyperuricemia but also hyperphosphatemia, hyperkalemia, and hypocalcemia, often resulting in acute renal failure and arrhythmias. Although tumor lysis syndrome occurs most commonly during treatment for hematologic malignancies,40 it may also occur during treatment of solid tumors.41, Additionally, hyperuricemia has been reported subsequent to the use of granulocyte colony-stimulating factor, presumably through its ability to drive myeloid cell synthesis.43, Use of colony-stimulating factors may therefore contribute to the new onset of gout or the precipitation of flares with fluctuations in serum urate levels.

The increased cell turnover in patients with psoriasis has also been associated with elevated levels of serum urate.46, An association between sarcoidosis and hyperuricemia has been proposed, 36 again presumably relating to increased cell turnover and/or metabolic activity. However, the epidemiologic evidence supporting sarcoidosis as a cause of hyperuricemia is less than convincing.

Conditions leading directly to consumption/degradation of ATP also contribute to the potential for secondary purine turnover leading to hyperuricemia. Thus strenuous and prolonged exercise, particularly to levels driving anaerobic respiration, may induce transient serum urate elevations.49, Status epilepticus is likely to mimic these events. A number of acute illnesses including myocardial infarction (MI) and sepsis are also accompanied by ATP catabolism and can result in transient hyperuricemia.

Patients with hereditary myopathies including metabolic myopathies such as glycogen storage diseases, as well as mitochondrial myopathies, are susceptible to increases in serum urate levels after even moderate exercise.39, In these individuals, a limited ability to synthesize ATP on demand apparently results in a rapid turnover of established ATP pools during exercise, with resultant purine and uric acid formation. Patients with mediumchain acyl-coenzyme A dehydrogenase deficiency, a defect of fatty acid metabolism, have also been shown to have elevated levels of serum urate, although the mechanism for this effect is unclear.

Despite multiple potential mechanisms, abnormalities of urate overproduction account for only a minority of patients with hyperuricemia. Instead, failures of urate excretion appear to be primarily responsible for most cases of human hyperuricemia.

### KEY POINT

Urate excretion occurs via the gut and the kidneys. In the kidneys, a complex series of urate transport proteins mediates a net elimination of sodium urate.

In most humans, serum urate levels are maintained within a narrow range. Accordingly, mechanisms must exist to ensure disposal of urate. The gastrointestinal (GI) tract and the kidneys each participate in urate excretion.

### Gastrointestinal Excretion of Urate

Uric acid elimination via the GI tract has been recognized for more than 50 years but has been inadequately studied. On the basis of radiolabeled urate tracer studies, Sorensen estimated that in healthy individuals, the GI tract is responsible for the excretion of approximately 35% of the daily uric acid burden.54-56 GI uric acid excretion may increase in the setting of decreased renal uric acid excretion. Mechanisms of uric acid excretion into the gut appear to include both exocrine secretion (saliva, gastric, and pancreatic juices) and direct bowel secretory mechanisms and appear to involve a urate transporter known as ATP-binding cassette transporter G2 (ABCG2), which also plays a role in renal urate excretion (see below).39, The anion transporter NPT5 may also take part in in GI uric excetion. After excretion into the gut, uric acid undergoes degradation by intestinal flora. Studies suggest that alterations in the intestinal microbiome, potentially including reduced populations of the genus Coprococcus, may contribute to hyperuricemic states, both by decreasing the rate of intestinal urate degradation and through effects on molecules such as short-chain fatty acids that may regulate local inflammation.57,58

### Renal Handling of Uric Acid

In most circumstances the kidney is primarily responsible for uric acid excretion via complex multistep mechanisms. In the bloodstream, urate is completely or nearly completely unbound to plasma proteins, thus nearly 100% of bloodstream urate undergoes ultrafiltration in the renal glomerulus. As discussed later,

decreases in glomerular function therefore reduce urate filtration and promote rises in serum urate levels.

After ultrafiltration, urate (typically in the form of uric acid owing to low intraluminal pH) in the proximal tubule undergoes distinct but apparently simultaneous handling steps: (1) a resorption step, in which most of the filtered urate undergoes reclamation, and (2) a secretion step, in which resorbed urate is transferred back into the tubule lumen. The net result is excretion of only approximately 10% of the filtered load. In fully functioning nephrons, the amount of secretion is responsive to serum urate levels such that rises in serum urate induce increased renal excretion and restoration of total body urate homeostasis. Studies have emphasized the importance of organic anion transporters (OATs) and other active and passive transport molecules in the movements of urate in both directions across the proximal tubule.59,

Renal Tubule Uric Acid Resorption. Urate resorption in the proximal tubule depends on the action of several apical surface transporters and at least one resorption transporter at the basolateral surface (Fig. 96.9). Several genes and their associated renal tubular transporters are critical in the regulation of renal urate resorption in humans. SLC22A12 codes for urate transporter 1 (URAT1), a pharmacologically sensitive transporter on the apical surface of the proximal renal tubule. URAT1 acts as a urate/anion exchanger to move urate from the tubule lumen into the epithelial cytosol. The major inorganic counterion for URAT1 activity is Cl-. However, organic anions such as lactate, pyrazinoate, and nicotinate can substitute for chloride, with potential clinical consequences discussed later. The importance of URAT1 to renal urate resorption is indicated by the fact that patients with inactivating mutations of URAT1 excrete nearly 100% of their filtered urate and demonstrate extremely low serum urate levels (along with increased urinary uric acid levels and risk for uric acid kidney stones).61-66 Conversely, other mutations in the URAT1 gene appear to convey a risk for increased urate resorption and hyperuricemia, presumably through a gain-of-function mutation. Thus URAT1 appears to be the most important of the uric acid retaining transporters. Several well-established uricosuric drugs including probenecid, benzbromarone, lesinurad, losartan, and high-dose salicylates lower serum urate primarily by inhibiting URAT1.67,

OAT4 (gene, SLC22A11) and OAT10 (gene, SLC22A13) are two other apical anion transporters involved in renal uric acid resorption. Like URAT1, OAT10 is an anion exchange transporter; counterions that can inhibit urate transport by OAT10 include lactate, pyrazinoate, salicylate, cyclosporine, furosemide, thiazides, and nicotinate, a fact of clinical importance (see later). In contrast, although OAT4 also transports urate from the tubular lumen to the cytosol of renal epithelial cells, the counterions it employs tend to be dicarboxylates.59,

Urate transport by URAT1, OAT4, and OAT10 would lead to accumulation of urate intra-cellularly in renal tubule cells, and presumably to gradients that would eventually impair further uric acid uptake, if a mechanism did not exist to transport intra-cellular urate out of the cell across the basolateral surface. This function appears to be served primarily by GLUT9, which was first identified as a glucose transport family protein but has little or no glucose transport capacity. Instead, GLUT9 is an effective transporter of urate from the renal epithelial cell out into the renal interstitium.71, SLC2A9 encodes two variants of GLUT9 transporters (a and b), which have expression on both the apical membrane (SLC2A9v2) and basolateral membrane (SLC2A9v1) of the proximal renal tubule, both mediating urate reabsorption.

A number of different inactivating mutations of GLUT9 have been identified in both humans and mice; in each case the result is impaired urate resorption, increased urate excretion, and hypouricemia.71, GLUT9a and its splice variant GLUT9b are also expressed on other cells including chondrocytes, leukocytes, intestinal cells, hepatocytes, and vascular smooth muscle cells; the role of GLUT9 proteins (and the impact of probenecid, which inhibits GLUT9 and URAT1) on these cells is actively being explored. 80-82

Renal Tubule Uric Acid Secretion. Other transport proteins in the renal tubule epithelium regulate the secretion of urate from the peritubular interstitial fluid into the tubular lumen, contributing to the lowering of serum urate (see Fig. 96.9).

On the apical surface of tubular cells, ABCG2 (previously discussed in the context of gut urate excretion) may directly

mediate renal uric acid excretion, but its importance in the kidney may be less than in the gut.56, A genome-wide association study (GWAS) found that ABCG2 defects not only contributed to hyperuricemia but are also involved in the dysregulation of inflammation by augmenting interleukin-8 release in endothelial cells. Other studies have implicated two other anion transport proteins as playing a role in apical uric acid transport secretion from the cell, namely, NPT1 (gene, SCL17A1) and NPT4 (gene, SLC17A3).56, Additionally, the multidrug resistance protein MRP4 (gene, ABCC4) may mediate ATP-dependent uric acid transport. Whether conditions of metabolic energy failure promote hyperuricemia by impairing MRP4 has not been established but would seem plausible.

At the basolateral surface, OAT1, 2, and 3 may transport uric acid from the interstitium into the epithelial cell cytosol, promoting urate excretion. These transporters act via exchange with dicarboxylate anions and transport not only uric acid, but other organic anions and some drugs. Drugs such as didanosine, furosemide, torsemide thiazides, nicotinate, omeprazole, ticagrelor, and theophylline inhibit OAT1 and OAT3 secretion, and furosemide, pyrazinamide, and thiazides inhibit OAT2 (gene, SLC22A7) uric acid secretion, potentially contributing to elevated serum urate levels. Additional genetic studies have implicated nontransporter proteins as playing roles in urate excretion, including PDZK1, CARMIL, NHERF1, SMCT1, SLC5A8, SMCT2, and SLC2A12. It is thought that some of these proteins may contribute to a macromolecular complex regulating uric acid transport.

### Renal Causes of Hyperuricemia

### KEY POINT

Decreased renal excretion of urate, owing to intrinsic or secondary causes, results in elevated levels of serum urate.

Most patients with hyperuricemia underexcrete urate; that is, for any given serum urate level, their degree of renal uric acid excretion is inadequate to lower systemic concentrations (Fig. 96.10). The mechanisms of uric acid underexcretion are various and stem from either primary or secondary renal effects.

Primary Urate Underexcretion. In a subset of patients, hereditary defects of renal tubule uric acid excretion result in hyperuricemia. With the identification of the renal urate transporters, the underlying basis for some of these defects has become apparent. For example, ABCG2 loss-of-function mutations promote hyperuricemia, and up to 10% of gout cases in White Europeans may be attributable to hyperuricemia induced by defects in the uric acid exporter ABCG2.92, As noted previously, ABCG2 also appears to play an important role in GI uric acid excretion, and ABCG2 dysfunction may therefore also contribute to uric acid retention and hyperuricemia on a GI basis.94, Conversely, gain-of-function mutations in several transport-related proteins (e.g., PDZK1, CARMIL, NHERF1) may promote hyperuricemia by enhancing URAT1 (i.e., renal uric acid resorption) activity. Patients with hereditary tubular defects leading to net uric acid underexcretion typically display normal renal filtration and normal serum creatinine levels.

Familial juvenile hyperuricemic nephropathy (FJHN), also known as medullary cystic kidney disease (MCKD), constitutes a group of autosomal dominant disorders characterized by early hyperuricemia and progressive chronic kidney disease. This hyperuricemia typically precedes any glomerular insufficiency. Three variants are recognized, designated MCKD1, 2, and 3. In MCKD2, mutations in the uromodulin gene result in underproduction and/or mis-production of uromodulin (Tamm-Horsfall protein), the most prevalent protein secreted by the kidney.96-98 The probable importance of uromodulin deficiencies to FJHN has recently been underlined by the observation that although patients with the MCKD1 and MCKD3 subtypes of FJHN have mutations that are not in the uromodulin gene, they nevertheless display a phenotype of decreased uromodulin expression. The mechanisms through which uromodulin deficiencies predispose to hyperuricemia are not fully understood, but mice transgenic

for human uromodulin mutations develop renal tubular abnormalities and concentrating defects. A recent GWAS suggested a potential link between an SLC2A9 variant, fractional excretion of uric acid and sodium, albuminuria, and uromodulin.

Secondary Causes of Urate Underexcretion. Many secondary causes can result in nephrogenic retention of uric acid and subsequent hyperuricemia: age and gender, systemic illnesses, medications, and toxins.

Age and Gender. Classic studies103 documented that serum urate levels tend to be low in children. In males, urate levels increase precipitously at puberty, a time when females experience only a slight increase in serum urate. For women, a gradual increase over the subsequent years, followed by another rise at menopause, finally brings the serum urate near to that of men. Thus overall, men tend to have higher serum urate levels than women (Fig. 96.2), and the discrepancy between men and women in the period between puberty and menses underlines the role played by sex hormones in urate regulation. The ancient Greek physician Hippocrates appeared to recognize these phenomena in his aphorisms that "A young man does not take the gout until he indulges in coition" (i.e., achieves puberty) and "A woman does not take the gout, unless her menses be stopped."104 Studies suggest that in women, both estrogen (naturally occurring or pharmacologic) and progesterone may promote renal urate excretion. Estrogen also inhibits xanthine oxidase, reducing uric acid 105-107 Conversely, the rapid rise of serum urate in generation. male adolescence correlates with a sharp rise in testosterone and a decrease in sex-hormone binding globulin. Gender-specific sex hormones may also regulate ABCG2 transporter-mediated uric

acid excretion from the gut or kidney; several studies suggest that differences in ABCG2 variants correlate strongly with gout risk in men but not women. 108,

Systemic Illnesses (Table 96.1). Glomerular insufficiency (i.e., reduction in glomerular filtration rate [GFR]), whether acute or chronic and for whatever reason, promotes urate underexcretion and hyperuricemia. The mechanisms of hyperuricemia in patients with renal insufficiency are complex but depend first and foremost on decreased delivery of a filtered urate load to the renal tubule. In severe renal failure, hyperuricemia is practically universal. Lesser degrees of renal failure are more variably accompanied by hyperuricemia, as decreases in GFR trigger some compensatory increase in renal tubule uric acid secretion, and potentially because of GI compensation. Because glomerular insufficiency is a condition that accrues among older populations, it likely contributes to the higher rate of hyperuricemia and gout among older adults. An association between congestive heart failure and hyperuricemia has been reported, presumably because of the accompanying reduced renal perfusion seen in congestive heart failure.

Various forms of organic (metabolic) acidoses can promote renal underexcretion of urate. Thus patients suffering lactic acidosis (e.g., in hypoxia, sepsis, liver or kidney disease, post-surgery

or MI, during excessive anaerobic exercise, or in response to certain drugs such as metformin) may become hyperuricemic. Similarly, patients experiencing ketoacidosis (e.g., alcoholic or diabetic ketoacidosis, starvation ketosis) may also develop hyperuricemia. Although the mechanisms of these effects were previously considered to result from direct competition between the organic acids and urate for tubular excretion, they are probably better considered from the perspective of recent discoveries in renal urate transport (described earlier). Organic acids serve as exchange anions for the apical surface renal urate transporters URAT1 and OAT10. Such acids therefore provide a motivating force for increased urate resorption in the proximal tubule.

Dehydration (volume depletion) on any basis promotes hyperuricemia.11l Once again the mechanisms are complex but include decreased renal perfusion and subsequently decreased urate filtration and delivery to the proximal tubule. Compensatory sodium retention can reduce tubular uric acid secretion, probably at the Na+/urate cotransporters NPT1 and NPT4.

Patients who have undergone renal transplant experience increases in hyperuricemia and gout. It is likely that the hyperuricemia in renal transplant patients is not related to the transplant per se but to factors such as intrinsic renal insufficiency, diuretic use, and the use of certain anti-rejection regimens (see below). Reciprocally, some studies suggest that hyperuricemia in transplant patients may contribute to progressive renal dysfunction.

Medications (Table 96.2). Multiple drugs can affect serum urate levels, mainly through renal effects. Many diuretics, among the most commonly used agents to treat hypertension and congestive heart failure, can promote hyperuricemia. .114, The increase in gout risk owing to diuretic use is substantial and may range as high as 3to 20-fold. The mechanisms through which diuretics raise serum urate include induction of sodium wasting and volume depletion, resulting in a decrease in the fractional excretion of urate. However, individual diuretics may have more specific and direct effects on renal urate handling. For example, loop diuretics such as furosemide and bumetanide interact directly with the tubular urate transporter NPT4,90 and both thiazide and loop diuretics inhibit the renal urate exporter MRP4.118 Despite the volume-depleting effects of diuresis, not all diuretics promote

hyperuricemia. The potassium-sparing diuretics triamterene, amiloride, and spironolactone do not raise urate.

Drugs that are weak organic acids can raise serum urate by inhibiting tubular secretion similarly to the systemic acidoses. Included here is the lipid-lowering agent nicotinic acid. Lowdose salicylates, including doses of aspirin used for cardioprotection, also raise serum urate by impairing renal uric acid efflux. (At high doses salicylates become uricosuric through the inhibition of URAT1.119) The anti-tuberculous agent pyrazinamide is metabolized to pyrazinoate and 5-hydroxypyrazinoate; these organic acids act in a manner similar to nicotinate and low-dose salicylate. Another anti-tuberculous agent, ethambutol, also reduces renal tubular uric acid excretion and promotes hyperuricemia, albeit through unclear mechanisms.

Beta blockers modestly inhibit renal uric acid excretion by modulating renal perfusion. The calcineurin inhibitor cyclosporine is well known to promote decreased renal uric acid excretion and hyperuricemia. Cyclosporine induces tubulointerstitial injury and arteriolar hyalinosis; reciprocally, hyperuricemia may exacerbate cyclosporine's nephrotoxic effects.123, Most studies of cyclosporine's effects on urate have been performed in patients who have undergone renal transplant; cyclosporine's effects on urate in other settings are less well established. An alternative calcineurin inhibitor, tacrolimus, does not promote similar levels of uric acid retention.

Toxins. Several toxins affect the kidney to promote hyperuricemia. Chief among these is lead.125, Lead exposure is endemic to Western society, but at times, lead exposure has been excessive (e.g., during the Roman empire). In the 20th century, a large cohort of patients with lead-induced hyperuricemia (saturnine gout) was recognized during and after the era of Prohibition, predominantly in the southeastern United States and relating to the home brewing of moonshine using lead-lined distilling vessels (typically, automobile radiators). In the kidney, lead poisoning leads to interstitial and perivascular fibrosis and glomerular and tubular degeneration. Although patients with lead nephropathy initially experience only mild to moderate renal insufficiency, their clearance of urate is excessively limited, indicating a tubular defect in urate excretion. Suggestions that lead exposure may also promote purine turnover are provocative but less well supported. Epidemiologic data suggest that moonshine nephropathy may be more prevalent than commonly assumed. 131

Other toxic substances that have been potentially associated with hyperuricemia include cadmium and the polychlorinated biphenyls (PCB) PCB-138 and PCB-153, although it remains unclear if the mechanisms of hyperuricemia caused by these toxic substances operate via renal or metabolic (or both) path- .132, Patients with chronic beryllium poisoning, usually as ways. a result of occupational exposure, may also suffer diminished renal uric acid excretion and hyperuricemia.

### Diet and Uric Acid

### KEY POINTS

### Purine-Rich Foods

Purine-rich foods comprise a major source of daily purine load and hence a major source of generated urate. However, not all purine-rich foods convey equivalent risk: seafood and red meat, particularly organ meats, convey an increased risk for hyperuricemia, whereas consumption of purine-rich, leafy green vegetables apparently does not. Some research has emphasized that the effect of purine intake is modest, with studies suggesting that alterations in purine intake may result in, at most, changes in serum urate of about 1 mg/dL.102, However, such studies have rarely accounted for the role of renal urate excretion in the context of diet. Thus it is worth considering whether, for a patient who is intrinsically unable to excrete serum urate, an increased dietary purine load may produce more profound increases in serum urate levels than would be seen in a patient with normal excretory capacities. Lowering serum urate by reducing purine consumption, while recommended, may have unanticipated consequences. Too strict avoidance of purine-rich foods may lead to compensatory consumption of carbohydrates, thereby paradoxically promoting increases in serum urate (see later). Much research has suggested that promoting healthy dietary patterns, including the Mediterranean and Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension (DASH) diets, may holistically help lower both serum urate and diet-associated comorbidities. Not all healthy diets may be the same, however. Secondary analysis of one such study showed that a DASH-style diet lowered serum urate more than diets focused on carbohydrates or unsaturated fats.137, In contrast to purine ingestion, protein consumption does not increase the risk of hyperuricemia and/or gout, a point of occasional confusion for practitioners because many high-purine foods are also high in protein.

### Fructose

Osler recognized the ability of fructose to provoke gout flares as early as 1901.139 Little was made of this observation, however, until the 1960s and 1970s, when it was demonstrated that fructose loads, administered orally or intravenously, cause transient rises in serum urate levels, particularly in gout patients.140, These effects are reproduced with consumption of sucrose (which contains fructose), but not glucose or galactose. Fructose consumption does not provide purines directly but alters metabolism to promote purine and hence urate synthesis (Fig. 96.1 1). The first step in fructose metabolism is the donation of a phosphate (Pi) from ATP to form fructose-1-phosphate (enzyme phosphofructokinase), generating ADP. ADP is converted to AMP (enzyme adenylate kinase), which in turn is degraded via several steps to uric acid. Additionally, fructose-1-phosphate serves as a phosphate "sink" because the donated phosphate is no longer available for the regeneration of ATP from AMP and ADP. Because both Pi and ATP inhibit the purine degradation pathway (inhibition of AMP deaminase and 5' nucleotidase, respectively), depletion of these compounds contributes to the formation of uric acid. Depletion of ADP/AMP also impairs feedback inhibition of PRPP synthase and promotes purine biosynthesis. Epidemiologic studies confirm a role for fructose consumption in hyperuricemia; patients who consume excessive fructose in the form of fructose-sweetened soft drinks or fruit juices demonstrate both higher serum urate levels and increased incidence of gout, an effect not seen among consumers of sugar-free beverages.142, The importance of dietary fructose is underscored by the fact that the rise in gout prevalence over the past several decades has occurred in parallel

with an increased industrial use of high-fructose corn syrup as a sweetener in soft drinks and prepared foods.

### Alcoholic Beverages

Ingestion of alcoholic beverages is associated with increased incidence of gout and gout flares, and ample physiologic and epidemiologic data confirm that ethanol consumption promotes the development of hyperuricemia.151-155 Ethanol is a particularly effective agent for raising serum urate because it works through multiple mechanisms. Chief among these is the requirement for ATP degradation during ethanol metabolism, resulting in purine turnover and urate generation in a manner not dissimilar to that of fructose.156, The ability of binge alcohol consumption to induce lactic acidosis transiently contributes to hyperuricemia by decreasing renal urate excretion, as discussed earlier.158, Ketoacidosis may also ensue at high levels of acute-on-chronic alcohol consumption, particularly in the setting of transient starvation and/or vomiting 160; in such settings uric acid secretion may be inhibited, or uric acid resorption promoted by 3-hydroxybutyrate and acetoacetate, in much the same manner as lactic acid. Ethanol consumption also promotes a diuresis, probably via anti-diuretic hormone suppression162; dehydration and volume depletion can result in renal urate retention. Additionally, some alcoholic beverages, particularly beer, are intrinsically high in purines. Thus, consumption of even ethanol-free beer transiently raises serum urate levels, although not to the extent of alcoholic beer. In contrast to beer, consumption of one glass a day of wine, which is relatively low in purines, does not increase serum urate levels, although higher levels of wine consumption do.155, As noted earlier, saturnine gout contracted from lead-adulterated moonshine whiskey may also contribute to hyperuricemia in the setting of alcohol consumption.

### Dietary Components That May Lower Serum Urate

In contrast to purines, fructose, and alcoholic beverages, consumption of low-fat dairy products is independently associated with reduced serum urate levels. In physiologic studies, consumption of milk or milk proteins has a direct uricosuric effect

that results in serum urate lowering. Interestingly, dairy products may also have anti-inflammatory effects. Regular heavy coffee consumption (four to six cups daily) may have uratelowering properties that are independent of caffeine.167-169 In contrast, intermittent coffee consumption may be transiently prohyperuricemic, perhaps because of caffeine-induced diuresis and volume depletion. Increased intake of vitamin C has been epidemiologically associated with decreased serum urate levels, but this effect was not confirmed in a prospective study. 170, A limited number of small studies support the possibility that consumption of cherries, a long-standing complementary medicine treatment for gout, may inhibit xanthine oxidase, have uricosuric and anti-inflammatory effects, and reduce the risk of gout flares. 172,173

### Asymptomatic Hyperuricemia and the Biological Effects of Soluble Urate

### KEY POINT

Soluble urate is biologically active and, even in the absence of gout, adversely affects the cardiometabolic system.

The presence of an elevated serum urate without prior clinical gout flares is defined as asymptomatic hyperuricemia. Historically, the most commonly used values for hyperuricemia have been population based and set at >7 mg/dL for men and >6.0 mg/dL for women. However, the use of >6.8 mg/dL, the saturation point of urate for both men and women, has gained favor as a more physiologic marker.

### Soluble Urate and the Vasculature

Soluble urate, even in the absence of gout, has multiple potential biologic effects. As previously noted, extra-cellular urate acts as a

potent antioxidant. In contrast, urate inside cells may have prooxidant effects. Also noted earlier, there is evidence that rises in primate serum urate in the Miocene may have helped maintain normal blood pressure. In our current, salt-replete era, elevated levels of soluble urate may promote renal microdamage, contributing to hypertension and chronic kidney disease. Multiple population studies document a relationship between elevated urate and hypertension.

Commensurate with a role for soluble urate in hypertension, several studies indicate that urate lowering can alter blood pressure. Among adolescents with premature essential hypertension and hyperuricemia, treatment with the urate-lowering agent allopurinol normalized blood pressure, which reversed after allopurinol discontinuation. In adults with long-standing established hypertension, more potent urate-lowering approaches may be needed; in one study, the highly active urate-lowering agent pegloticase reduced mean, systolic, and diastolic blood 176 pressure.

### Soluble Urate and the Kidneys

The potential effects of soluble urate on the kidneys are numerous. In rats, elevated serum urate increases expression of renin/cyclooxygenase-2 in the juxtaglomerular apparatus, decreases nitric oxide synthase in the macula densa, and induces microvascular injury, macrophage infiltration, thickening of pre-glomerular arterioles, and tubulointerstitial fibrosis.177, In vitro, exposure of vascular smooth muscle cells to soluble urate increases smooth muscle proliferation and reduces capacity for regulatory vasodilation. Additionally, urate can affect the E-cadherin pathway and cause transformation of tubular epithelial cells to mesenchymal cells, which may promote renal fibrosis.

### Trained Innate Immunity

Landmark studies by Joosten and others have promoted the concept of trained, or learned, innate immunity. In contrast to the accepted paradigm that innate immunity is a fixed process, trained innate immunity suggests that chronic or intermittent exposure to bacterial molecules or internal phlogistons can induce epigenetic and/or metabolic changes that render innate immune responses persistently enhanced—in short, that the innate immune system can be "reset" to respond more rapidly and vigorously in the setting of chronic challenge. Chief among the internal phlogistons that have been identified is soluble urate. Consistent with this observation, patients with asymptomatic hyperuricemia have elevated baseline inflammatory markers, even in the absence of frank clinical inflammation (gout flares) (Fig. 96.12).

### Urate and the Regulation of AMP-Activated Protein Kinase

Additional studies have identified a role for intra-cellular noncrystalline urate in the promotion of multiple inflammatory and metabolic processes, through effects on the enzyme AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK). AMPK is a master regulator that acts in multiple cell types. In hepatocytes, AMPK activation inhibits gluconeogenesis 15 and triglyceride synthesis, and AMPK inhibition may promote fatty liver. In macrophages, AMPK activation downregulates inflammatory responses. In contrast, elevated levels of intra-cellular urate stimulate AMP deaminase, which

inhibits AMPK, leading to proglycemic, prolipidemic and proinflammatory profiles (Fig. 96.13).

# Crystal Formation: The Transition From Hyperuricemia a to Gout

### KEY POINT

MSU crystal formation involves physicochemical processes but may be regulated by synovial fluid proteins and immunoglobulins.

Soluble urate does not induce gouty flares; only crystallized MSU promotes acute inflammation. Urate crystallization is therefore a critical intermediate step in the progression from hyperuricemia to frank gout. 183,

Uric acid is a weak organic acid. At physiologic pH (7.4), approximately 98% of uric acid exists in the form of urate. At concentrations greater than 6.8 mg/dL, urate exceeds its apparent solubility limit in serum, potentiating the precipitation of needleshaped MSU crystals that can promote inflammatory responses.

In vitro models have shed light on the relationship between MSU crystallization and environmental factors such as pH, temperature, salt content, vibration, and large molecules.185-187 Urate may more readily precipitate at both lower pH and lower temperature, which may explain why gout flares are most commonly seen in the first metatarsophalangeal joint, a joint that is both circumferentially exposed (i.e., relatively low in temperature) and at the farthest outpost of the systemic circulation (i.e., most likely to be acidotic).

Crystal formation and gout flares most commonly occur within the confines of the joint. Some investigators have suggested that soluble urate is excreted more slowly from the joint than other serum elements, providing a possible mechanism for increased urate concentration within the joint space. Once MSU crystals are formed, the fenestrated endothelium of the synovium might permit the joint space to serve as a crystal "trap," preventing crystals from being dispersed and/or dissolved in the wider circulation. Other investigators have emphasized the possible role of cartilage itself in the precipitation of urate, particularly in the setting of aging and/or osteoarthritis (OA). Potential mechanisms through which aging cartilage might facilitate MSU nucleation/crystallization include changes in the proportions and/or chemical properties of cartilage glycosaminoglycans and proteoglycans, as well as increases in intra-cellular and extra-cellular lipid content of articular cartilage. 189-191 One recent report suggests that OA chondrocytes may actually secrete urate into the joint space, promoting local urate excesses in the synovial fluid. Most recently, one group reported that the synovial cell product lubricin may play an important role in preventing urate crystallization and that lubricin deficiencies may promote MSU crystallization, even among patients who are not hyperuricemic.

Interestingly, several investigators have suggested that urate crystallization may be an immune-assisted process. One group proposed that immunoglobulin (Ig) G antibody-binding to MSU monomers, previously assumed to be nonspecific, may promote the stacking of MSU crystals despite dispersion forces that exist in fluid and tissue. More recently, another group postulated a

direct role for urate crystalspecific IgM antibodies in the nucleation and formation of MSU crystals. If true, these observations would suggest one reason for the recognized fact that gout tends to get worse with time, since long-term exposure of the immune system to MSU crystals might lead to the increasing generation of crystal-promoting antibodies.

Although urate precipitation is the sine qua non of gout, not all urate precipitation may lead directly to acute gout flares. Imaging studies confirm that, in many patients with asymptomatic hyperuricemia, MSU crystals may already be deposited both on cartilage and in the synovium. These deposits are of consequence for their potential to directly damage tissue (see the section "Chronic Tophaceous Gout"), for their possible role in low-level systemic inflammation, and for their role as a reservoir of potentially inflammatory crystals. Thus local trauma, long recognized as a possible antecedent to acute gouty flares, may physically release cartilage-deposited crystals into the joint space, where they can initiate acute inflammation. In addition, acute lowering of serum and synovial fluid urate levels (e.g., during initiation of urate-lowering drugs) is well documented to precipitate gouty flares197 by a mechanism that is most likely akin to that in which glacial melting causes the sloughing off of icebergs and the exposure of previously hidden surfaces. These observations have led to a revision of the classical model of gout to suggest that urate crystal deposition likely precedes the first acute flare, with acute flares occurring as a result of crystal shedding into, rather than direct spontaneous precipitation within, the affected joint(s).198,199

### Acute Gout Flares: The Inflammatory Response to MSU Crystals

### Transition From Asymptomatic Hyperuricemia to Gout

For clinical purposes, the first acute flare defines the progression from asymptomatic hyperuricemia to gout. However, the basis for this transition remains incompletely understood. Although patients with higher serum urate levels are more likely to develop frank gout, as many as 50% of patients with the highest levels of serum urate may not develop gout over a 15-year period. And although MSU crystal tissue deposition is likely to precede rather than follow incident gout, patients with asymptomatic hyperuricemia and imaging-documented MSU crystal deposition do not necessarily progress to a first gout flare. Consequently, the transition from hyperuricemia to gout may depend on more than simply MSU crystal formation. Likely factors include the individual patient's intrinsic capacity to generate inflammatory responses to MSU crystals, whether due to heredity or environmental effects. As noted previously, soluble urate may drive persistent upregulation of (trained) innate immunity, which might contribute to a more ready response to MSU crystals. Similarly, recent studies have suggested a possible role for clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential (CHIP), defined as clonally expanded, somatically mutated cells in patients without hematologic malignancy. According to one group, the presence of CHIP is a risk factor for incident gout, and patients with CHIP are approximately 70% more likely to have gout than individuals without the condition. Patients with CHIP have elevated levels of IL-1β, suggesting that CHIP may function to amplify inflammatory (inflammasome) responses to MSU crystals, a phenomenon that was supported by a mouse model.

### Response to MSU Crystals

### KEY POINT

MSU crystals activate both complement and resident synovial macrophages, inciting neutrophil influx that itself promotes further inflammation.

MSU crystals are potent triggers of inflammation. The phlogistic potential of crystalline urate in human gout was established dramatically by Faires and McCarty, who self-injected MSU crystals into their knee joints and experienced iatrogenic inflammation. .203, In the clinic, the diagnosis of acute gout is definitively made when polarized light microscopy of synovial fluid from an inflamed joint reveals the presence of MSU crystals, neutrophils, and particularly intra-cellular MSU crystals (confirming crystaldirected neutrophil phagocytic activity). However, the inflammatory mechanisms of gout flares are complex and involve not only neutrophils but other cell types, inflammatory mediators, and well-organized sequences of events.

### MSU Crystals and Complement Activation

Complement activation by the alternative pathway is a continuous process in body fluids, in which C3 component activation in the fluid phase is followed by rapid C3b deposition onto nearby surfaces. On human cell surfaces C3b is routinely inactivated by

regulatory proteins. In contrast, the polyanionic surfaces of MSU crystals provide opportunities for unconstrained C3b deposition and activation of downstream complement components. Weissmann and Doherty208,209 independently demonstrated the ability of MSU crystals to activate complement from C2-depeleted serum, confirming activation of the alternative pathway.

Interestingly, MSU crystals also appear to activate complement by the classical pathway (i.e., via C1 activation). Crystal activation of the classical pathway may occur in two ways. First, MSU crystals may activate the classical pathway by an immunoglobulin-independent, C-reactive protein (CRP)-dependent path- 208, Second, formed MSU crystals possess the ability to way. bind antibodies, probably in a nonspecific manner, but sufficient to activate the classical complement cascade.208,

Either complement cascade will lead to the generation of C5a, a potent vasodilator and chemoattractant for inflammatory cells such as neutrophils.213, MSU crystal-mediated complement activation may also lead to generation of soluble complement membrane attack complexes, which may activate local cells to promote inflammation. Other pro-inflammatory proteins, including fibronectin and kininogen, may also adhere to urate crystals.

### Cellular Responses to MSU Crystals

The processes by which leukocytes respond to MSU and other crystals are multiple and complex and remain a focus of ongoing studies. In addition to classical cellular responses to immunoglobulins and complement, mechanisms appear to include crystal/ receptor interactions, crystal/membrane interactions, and effects driven when crystals gain access to the intra-cellular cytoplasmic space.

Cell-Surface Recognition of MSU Crystals. Several studies suggest that Toll-like receptors (TLRs), which are critical for innate immunity, respond to MSU crystals in much the same way as they do to pathogen-associated molecular patterns. In TLR2and TLR4-knockout mice, decreased cytokine production and neutrophil influx argue strongly for a role for TLRs in MSU crys- s. Impairment of MSU crystaldriven inflammatal responses. tion in CD14 knockout mice also supports a role for TLRs, since CD14 is essential for TLR2and TLR4-dependent signaling. However, other researchers observed no effect of multiple TLR knockouts on murine models of crystal-induced inflammation. Based on accumulating data, it would appear that TLR effects are more likely to prime rather than drive MSU-induced responses, for instance in the now-recognized role of "Signal 1" in activating the NLRP3 inflammasome (see below). Interestingly, MSU crystals may also interact with Clec 12a, a C-type lectin receptor, which drives inhibitory rather than inflammatory signals.

Other studies emphasize the ability of MSU crystals to electrostatically interact with cholesterol. Cholesterol-enhanced regions of plasma membranes (lipid rafts) are rich in signaling molecules and represent hot spots for cellular activation. Receptor-independent interactions between crystalline MSU and lipid rafts have been demonstrated in myeloid cells, resulting directly in cell activation: nonspecific aggregation of transmembrane receptors within the rafts activates immunoreceptor tyrosinebased activation motifs, followed by activation of the signaling molecule Syk.222, Syk activation can then induce cell activation including phosphoinositol-3 kinase signaling, cytoskeletal rearrangement, and crystal phagocytosis. Multiple other downstream signaling pathways may also be activated, including the extracellular signal-regulated kinase, c-Jun N-terminal kinase, and p38

mitogen-activated protein (MAP) kinase; phospholipases C and D; rho-family proteins; and nuclear factor-kB. Depending on the cell type in question, activation of these molecules will result in specific phenotypes including cytoskeletal alterations, production of cytokines and lipid mediators, and induction of phagocytosis and superoxide generation. 224-228

As noted earlier, MSU crystals may become coated by immunoglobulins and other serum proteins and may serve as a substrate for complement activation. Immunoglobulinand complementcoated urate crystals may also activate cells via their ability to engage immunoglobulin, complement, and possibly other cell-surface receptors. Consistent with this model, IgG-coated MSU crystals have been observed to incite greater inflammatory responses than those that are uncoated, and C5a receptor antagonists inhibit MSU crystalinduced peritonitis in a murine model. 229,

Phagocytosis and Activation of the NLRP3 Inflammasome. It has long been appreciated that MSU crystals can induce macrophages to produce IL-1β, and that IL-1β so produced is central to the process of gouty inflammation. It is now appreciated that this process is mediated by the NLRP3 (formerly NALP3, CIAS1, or cryopyrin) inflammasome, a multimolecular complex whose primary purpose is to convert pro-IL-1β (as well as pro-IL-18 and pro-IL-33) into its active form (see also Chapters 19 and 95). Pro-IL-1β is cleaved into activated IL-1β by the inflammasomeassociated enzyme caspase-1. Concurrently, capase-1-mediated

activation of a separate molecule, gasdermin-D, allows it to form pores in the membrane that facilitate both IL-1β secretion and an inflammatory form of cell death known as pyroptosis. In a seminal study, one group documented the ability of MSU crystals to activate the NLRP3 inflammasome and stimulate IL-1β activation and secretion (Fig. 96.14). The importance of the inflammasome in crystal inflammation has been well documented in mouse models: macrophages from mice lacking inflammasome components generate diminished levels of IL-1β on MSU crystal exposure, and intraperitoneal injection of MSU crystals into inflammasome-deficient mice, as well as mice deficient in IL-1β receptors, leads to significantly decreased neutrophil recruit- . Moreover, the ability of IL-1β-directed therapies to ment. abrogate both human gout and murine crystal-induced inflammation speaks to the centrality of inflammasome-generated IL-1β in the inflammatory response to MSU crystals.233-235 Before MSU crystals can stimulate the inflammasome to generate IL-1β, prior MSU-induced stimuli acting through TLR-2 and -4 (referred to as Signal 1; see above) must first drive the cell to generate pro- ILβ for the MSU crystal (Signal 2)driven NLRP3 inflammasome to act upon. Subsequent inflammatory responses (e.g., TNF production) appear to occur secondary to autocrine and paracrine engagement of cell surface IL-1β receptors.

To date, there is no single explanation as to how MSU crystals activate the NLRP3 inflammasome. Inflammasome activation by

MSU crystals appears to require, first and foremost, crystal phagocytosis. A recent study suggests that MSU crystal engagement of TLR-9, expressed intra-cellularly on the phagocytic vacuole membrane, can induce release of mitochondrial DNA, which then activates NLRP3 inflammasomes. However, most proposed mechanisms of MSU inflammasome activation require the ability of phagocytosed MSU crystals to induce phagolysosome membrane dissolution and crystal entry into the cytosol.237-239 Leading theories then center on the inflammasome as an internal sensor for cellular distress from oxidative stress or shifts in ion concentra- .238, In one proposed model, MSU effects on the plasma tions. membrane promotes cellular potassium efflux; the resultant hypokalemic state activates the inflammasome directly.240, In a murine model, MSU crystals induced increased expression of the potassium channel Kv1.5, providing another possible mechanism through which potassium efflux may occur to drive activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome.

Additionally, MSU crystal activation of the phagocyte NADPH oxidase leads to the generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS), which may be sensed by the inflammasome. Phagolysosome rupture also leads to cytosolic acidification and intra-cellular release of cathepsin B, both of which have been proposed as NLRP3 inflammasome activators. These various mechanisms

may not be mutually exclusive and may act synergistically (e.g. phagolysosomal disintegration and consequent cathepsin-B release may promote the production of ROS).

### Putting It Together: Initiation and Propagation of the e Acute Gouty Flare I
