The clinical picture of acute gout is one of a rapidly accelerating inflammatory response. Accordingly, cellular changes during the acute flare must reflect this acceleration (Fig. 96.15). Beginning with the appearance/release of MSU crystals, the initial phase of gouty inflammation must depend on already-available local mediators and cells that are both capable of urate crystal responses and already in place within the joint. Clearly, immunoglobulin binding and the activation of complement on the crystal surface must be one such early response. Interaction of the crystal with local tissue cells, facilitated in part by IgG and complement opsonization, is also likely to play an early role. Best studied among the early cell-type responses is that of the synovial macrophage, a resident cell in the synovial membrane. As noted above, macrophage activation in response to crystals results in synthesis and secretion of IL-1β, and secondarily secretion of TNF, IL-6, and the chemokine IL-8 (CXCL8), as well as release of potentially

tissue-destroying matrix metalloproteinases and toxic oxygen radicals. .224, Human synovial fibroblasts are also capable of responding to MSU crystals, leading to the generation of both inflammatory mediators and metalloproteinases. Finally, mast cells resident within the synovium also appear to be important in the early phases of acute gouty responses, as their depletion diminishes inflammation in murine models of crystal-induced inflammation. Mast cells increase in number and activity in the lining of experimental air pouches after MSU crystal injection, suggesting that additional mast cells may be secondarily attracted to the inflammatory site. In mice injected with MSU, mast cells contributed to the production of IL-1β, most prominently early in the inflammatory response to crystals.

Cytokines and other inflammatory mediators produced in the early phase of the crystal response act on the vascular endothelium to promote vasodilation and leakiness and to upregulate the expression of adhesion molecules such as selectins and ICAMs (intercellular adhesion molecules) on the vascular surface of the endothelial cell. These same cytokines promote neutrophil activation within the bloodstream, particularly the upregulation of the integrin adhesion molecule CD1 1b/CD18. A role for the crystal-generated complement component C5a in the activation of bloodstream neutrophils is also likely because C5a can potently stimulate CD11b/CD18 activation and neutrophil adhesiveness. The result is that neutrophils first adhere tightly to the endothelium and then exit the vasculature, followed by chemotaxis up the C5a complement gradient, leading to encounter with, and phagocytosis of, the provoking MSU crystals. The mechanisms of neutrophil activation by coated MSU crystals include those discussed earlier and additionally appear to include interactions with neutrophil CD11b/CD18 (which is also a complement receptor) and the IgG receptor

FcγRIIIB. Subsequent neutrophil intra-cellular signaling events include phosphorylation and/or activation of multiple kinases including Lyn, Syk, Tec, and Src; activation of PI-3 kinase; and activation of phospholipase C. Activation of MAP kinases is probably also involved because these kinases regulate neutrophil adhesion and superoxide generation.

Neutrophils encountering MSU crystals rapidly drive additional inflammation and neutrophil influx via several mechanisms (Fig. 96.16). First, neutrophils stimulated by MSU crystals generate a number of potent inflammatory mediators and neutrophil chemoattractants including IL-1β, IL-8, leukotriene B4 (LTB4), S100A8/A9 (also known as myeloid-related proteins 8 and 14), prostaglandin E2, CCL4, CXCL8, and crystal-induced chemotactic factor.251-253 IL-8 and LTB4 play a particularly important role in amplifying the chemoattractant gradient and promoting additional neutrophil influx. Second, neutrophils stimulated by MSU crystals release a wide range of products capable of directly damaging local tissues including oxygen radicals and metalloproteinases such as MMP-8. Although these mediators are intended for digestion of foreign particles within phagolysosomes, the large size of many urate crystals results in incomplete ("frustrated") phagocytosis of the crystals, so that lysosomal contents are released into the surrounding environment to promote extra-cellular tissue damage ("regurgitation during feeding"). This process appears to be facilitated when MSU crystals are coated with immunoglobulins. Alternatively, MSU crystals can induce neutrophil rupture and direct release of toxic neutrophil contents results, as well as the release of neutrophil extra-cellular traps (NETs), a web of chromatin and adherent enzymes that in the early stages of the gout attack may promote inflammation. In either case, the result is the potential for tissue damage and rapidly accelerating inflammation.

### Resolution of the Acute GoutyF Flare

One of the more interesting features of acute gouty arthritis is that, particularly in the early stages of the disease, most flares are self-limited. Multiple effects have been invoked to explain this phenomenon. MSU crystals may become coated with synovial fluid proteins (e.g., apolipoproteins B and E), inhibiting their ability to provoke inflammation. The stress of the gouty flare may promote adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) secretion; in addition to its ability to induce glucocorticoid release, ACTH can bind directly to melanocyte-stimulating hormone receptors to provoke anti-inflammatory effects and reduce phagocyte responses to MSU crystals.256-258

Other investigations have emphasized the local, active events through which inflammation may be resolved. For example, in vivo studies using the MSU crystal—induced mouse air pouch model suggest that local upregulation of expression of PGD2 and 15d-PGJ2 (a spontaneous dehydration product of PGD2) contributes to the resolution of crystal-mediated inflammation, probably through the ability of these molecules to activate the peroxisome proliferator activating receptor-γ (PPAR-γ) and, likely, the metabolic regulator AMPK. 259, MSU crystals also stimulate the expression of PPAR-γ itself, setting the stage for enhanced suppression of inflammation. 260 15d-PGJ2 inhibits secretion of IL-1β, IL-6, and IL-12 and TNF from macrophages and downregulates the expression of inducible nitric oxide synthase. Other targets of 15d-PJG2 include PGD receptors and the NF-kB pathway. 15d-PGJ2 also inhibits CXC chemokine production, alters cellular adhesion molecules, and stimulates apoptosis of endothelial cells. Other anti-inflammatory molecules (e.g., IL-10) are also upregulated, and the potent anti-inflammatory resolvins and lipoxins are almost certainly involved.

In considering the resolution of acute gouty inflammation, it is important to recognize the biologic programs that delay the production of anti-inflammatory molecules until the appropriate phase in the sequence. For example, PGD2 and 15d-PGJ2 production initially declines on exposure to MSU crystals, apparently facilitating the inflammatory response, but then rebounds to act during the resolution phase. Similarly, the generation of antiinflammatory lipoxins requires the accumulation of at least two active cell types (either neutrophils and activated endothelium or neutrophils and activated platelets), an evolutionary adaptation that creates an intrinsic delay before the anti-inflammatory effects are initiated, one that may be critical to allow initial inflammatory responses to infections.

Consistent with a "time-delayed" process of gout flare resolution, other studies emphasize the roles of the influxing leukocytes themselves in the resolution of the gouty flare. Several studies support the ability of late-influxing monocyte/macrophages to clear both MSU crystals and apoptotic neutrophils that have ingested crystals, resulting in decreased crystal burden. 264, Moreover, these influxing macrophages appear to differentiate into an antiinflammatory, M2 phenotype (in contrast with the inflammatory M1 phenotype of resident macrophages) and, upon phagocytosing crystals, to release TGF-β to provoke an anti-inflammatory effect. As noted previously, neutrophils that have phagocytosed crystals can release NETs that may initially play a proinflammatory role in the gouty flare. Subsequently, however, these NETs provide a stable scaffold on which extravasated neutrophil enzymes, particularly neutrophil elastase, encounter and degrade cytokines to promote inflammatory resolution (Fig.

96.17). Macrophages may then play an additional role in resolution of inflammation by the eventual clearance of NETs.

### Chronic Gouty Arthritis and Tophaceous Gout

The natural history of untreated gout frequently includes eventual progression to a state characterized by chronic inflammation and/or the establishment of macroscopic MSU deposits known as tophi (Video 96.1). Even during the asymptomatic, intercritical periods of gout, low-grade chronic inflammation can persist, with continuous phagocytosis of crystals by leukocytes. In patients with long-standing gout, intercritical inflammation can become frankly apparent, and the cytokines, chemokines, proteases, and oxidants that participate in acute inflammation can contribute to chronic synovitis, cartilage loss, and bone erosion, signaling the progression to chronic gouty arthritis.

Although tophi are composed first and foremost of MSU crystals, they are complex structures in which urate (1) is embedded in a matrix of lipids, proteins, and mucopolysaccharides and (2) drives a persistent inflammatory state. A tophus can alternatively be conceived of as a granuloma of mononucleated and multinucleated macrophages arranged in three distinguishable zones (Fig. 96.18). MSU crystals and debris constitute the central zone. Surrounding the central zone is the corona zone, consisting of macrophages, multinucleated macrophage-like cells, plasma cells, and mast cells. This biologically active corona is thought to account for the ultrasonographic finding of an anechoic rim that circumscribes a tophus.273-275 Eventually, the corona and central zones may become encased by a connective tissue layer, the fibrovascular zone. Within this zone, macrophages express surface markers of recent migration, maturation, apoptosis, continuous recruitment, and pro-inflammatory activation. T and B cells are scattered throughout both outer zones.276, Although classically a late feature of gout, tophi may occur early in the disease, particularly in patients with renal insufficiency and high serum urates. In some patients, tophi may develop even in the absence of any episodes of flares.

Tophi are important not only for their role as reservoirs of crystalline urate but also for their ability to damage the tissues in which they reside, including bone, cartilage, and tendons and other soft tissue structures. Mechanical factors, induction oflytic enzymes, and synthesis of pro-inflammatory cytokines all contribute to the tophus's ability to promote erosion and joint destruction. Tophus macrophages produce IL-1β, TNF, IL-6, IL-17, matrix metalloproteinases (MMP)-2, and MMP-9, and macrophage colonystimulating factor (M-CSF). These molecules promote further inflammation and tissue damage, as well as the maturation and activation of osteoclasts that actively resorb bone. For example, M-CSF interacts with M-CSF receptors on osteoclast progenitor cells to promote osteoclastogenesis. Tophus expression of IL-1β and other cytokines has additionally been shown to inhibit the viability and bone-maintaining effects of osteoblasts.276, Tophus T cells promote bone erosions through the elucidation of RANK ligand, the major promoter of osteoclastogenesis and osteoclast activation. Additionally, nontophaceous MSU crystals on the cartilage surface reduce chondrocyte viability, increase chondrocyte production of degenerative enzymes, and promote cartilage damage. Even in clinically asymptomatic patients, these inflammatory and erosive processes persist; damage may not be apparent until late in the process.

### Gout and Comorbidities

It is now appreciated that patients with gout suffer multiple comorbidities at a higher rate than the general population, including hypertension, kidney disease, diabetes mellitus, obesity, nonalcoholic fatty liver disease, cardiovascular disease, and OA, among others. 283, In fact, patients with gout suffer metabolic syndrome at rates approximately twice those of the general population.16, Several studies indicate that patients with gout suffer a higher mortality rate than the general population, which has remained elevated, even as mortality among patients with other rheumatic diseases has declined.286,

The direction of causality behind these associations remains incompletely elucidated, and there is no doubt that certain comorbidities—for example, renal disease—predispose to hyperuricemia and therefore gout. On the other hand, an accumulating number of physiologic and clinical studies suggest that gout may predispose to, and/or help drive, at least some of its associated comorbidities. For example, in separate population studies, the presence of gout was shown to be associated with a future risk of type 2 diabetes, whereas the presence of diabetes was not shown to be associated with a future risk of gout. 288,

The mechanisms through which gout might act to raise comorbid risk remain an area of intense study. It is likely that at least some effects of gout on comorbidities are mediated through hyperuricemia, given the biologic effects of soluble urate described earlier. For example, animal models have demonstrated the ability of hepatic urate production to drive nonalcoholic fatty liver disease, a phenomenon that can be abrogated by blocking urate production with allopurinol. Studies also suggest that elevated urate levels may inhibit insulin synthesis, increase insulin resistance, and induce hepatic glucose production, while others that have demonstrated elevated urate may directly promote atherosclerosis.291-293 However, in multiple studies gout has been shown to be associated with a higher prevalence of comorbidities than asymptomatic hyperuricemia, suggesting that additional mechanisms, unique to gout, may drive comorbidities. One possibility is that both the acute and chronic inflammatory states of gout "add on" to the risks invoked by hyperuricemia. From the point of view of chronic inflammation, it is interesting to note that treatment of gout with the anti-inflammatory drug colchicine may reduce both the incidence of MI among gout patients and the incidence of new-onset coronary artery disease.294-296 In one recent study colchicine also reduces the rate of kidney disease progression in patients with gout, again implying a potential pathophysiologic role for chronic gouty inflammation. In patients with gout, endothelial function (a recognized predictor of future cardiovascular events) is impaired to a degree proportional to elevations in both serum urate and CRP, implicating both hyperuricemia and systemic inflammation in the defect. Consistent with this notion, gout-related endothelial dysfunction can be partially reversed by guideline-concordant treatment with a combination of anti-inflammatory and urate-lowering therapy. Recent studies of gout flares (acute inflammation) suggest even more dramatic effects: In one study the risk of MI among gout patients with pre-existing coronary disease was roughly doubled for 120 days after a gout flare,300 a time period that correlates closely with a persistent post-flare rise in inflammation as measured by the neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (also an established marker of cardiovascular risk). In addition to effects on systemic inflammation, it is possible that the progression from hyperuricemia to gout drives other, more specific mechanisms that could promote

comorbid disease. For example, while controversial, recent studies using dual-energy computed tomography to image the vasculature suggest that patients with gout may deposit MSU crystals directly in the aorta and coronary arteries, which may drive local rather than systemic vascular changes.302, While gout may promote some or all of the aforementioned comorbidities, it is interesting to note that the presence of gout and/or higher uric acid levels has been associated with lower incidence and/or better outcomes in a number of neurodegenerative and/or neuroinflammatory diseases, including Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, and Huntington's diseases, and multiple sclerosis.304-309 Once again, the data is somewhat ambiguous, and the direction of causality and mechanisms of association remain uncertain. A better understanding of the mechanisms through which gout contributes to, or protects against, comorbidities could shed new light on the biologic mechanisms of gout and create new opportunities for its clinical management—a topic addressed in Chapter 97.

# Clinical Features and Treatment of Gout

### KEY POINTS

Gout is a chronic disease of monosodium urate (MSU) crystal deposition. Hyperuricemia is the central risk factor for development of gout, and this risk is concentration dependent.

MSU crystals trigger intermittent flares of extremely painful acute inflammatory arthritis, typically affecting the big toe, midfoot, and ankle.

Tophi lead to limitation of joint movement, superimposed infection, joint damage, and deformity and are associated with disability and poor health-related quality of life.

MSU crystal identification is the gold standard for gout diagnosis, but a clinical diagnostic rule has good accuracy.

Imaging methods such as ultrasound and dual-energy CT can assist in situations of diagnostic uncertainty.

Gout flares are managed with anti-inflammatory medications such as prednisolone, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), colchicine, or anti—interleukin (IL)-1β therapy (where available).

The central strategy for effective long-term gout management is dissolution of MsU crystals using urate-lowering therapy to achieve a serum urate target of less than 6 mg/dL for most patients and lower (5 mg/dL) for those with severe disease.

Gradual dose escalation of urate-lowering therapy and antiinflammatory prophylaxis with low-dose colchicine or other anti-inflammatory agents can reduce the risk of gout flares when initiating urate-lowering therapy.

Allopurinol, the first-line urate-lowering therapy for most patients, should be started at low dose and dose titrated until the serum urate target is achieved.

In the event that allopurinol is not tolerated or does not lead to achievement of the serum urate target, additional options are uricosuric agents or febuxostat.

In patients with severe disease who are unable to achieve serum urate target with available oral therapy, intravenous pegloticase every 2 weeks can improve outcomes. Careful monitoring of the serum urate response is required to reduce the risk of infusion reactions.

The high prevalence of comorbid conditions in people with gout necessitates active screening and management of concomitant cardiometabolic and kidney disease.

Dietary advice about the benefits of weight loss for patients with overweight/obesity, avoidance of sugary drinks, and reduction of alcohol intake for hazardous drinking is important for all people, including those with gout.

Compared with usual primary care, nurse-led care according to rheumatology society guidelines leads to greater adherence to urate-lowering therapy, lower serum urate concentrations, and major improvements in clinical outcomes including gout flares, tophi, and health-related quality of care and is cost-effective.

### Classification Criteria

The 2015 American College of Rheumatology (ACR)/European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology (EULAR) gout classification criteria (Table 97.1) are intended for identifying subjects who may be eligible for entry into a clinical study and should not be used for diagnosis. These criteria should only be scored if the subject has at least one episode of swelling, pain, or tenderness in a peripheral joint or bursa. If the subject has documented MSU crystals in a symptomatic joint or tophus, the subject may be classified as having gout without further scoring. The clinical criteria are used if MSU crystals are not documented. Each domain is scored for the highest category ever noted for the subject. A score of ≥8 classifies a subject as having gout. An online calculator is available to assist with scoring these criteria: http://goutclassificationcalculator.auckland. ac.nz/.

### Clinical Features of Gout

Gout is a chronic disease of monosodium urate (MSU) crystal deposition. MSU crystals form in the presence of high tissue urate levels and trigger intermittent flares of acute inflammatory arthritis,2 typically affecting the big toe, midfoot, and ankle. In some patients with hyperuricemia, tophi can also form; these lesions can lead to joint damage and deformity. Gout flares are managed with anti-inflammatory medications such as nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), colchicine, prednisone, or anti—interleukin (IL)-1β therapy. The central strategy for effective long-term gout management is dissolution of MSU crystals using urate-lowering therapy (see Chapter 66).

A consensus statement has been published regarding the labels and definitions for basic disease elements of gout (Gout, Hyperuricemia and Crystal-Associated Disease Network [G-CAN]). These labels describe eleven major elements of disease and are recommended for technical use by researchers and health care professionals (Table 97.2).

Hyperuricemia (elevated serum urate level) is almost universal in people with gout, but most people with hyperuricemia do not have gout. Various cut points are used by different laboratories to indicate hyperuricemia, based on both population distributions and pathophysiological definitions. Reporting serum urate according to population distributions does not reflect the pathophysiological basis of disease. Within the population, the risk

of developing incident gout is strongly dependent on the serum urate concentration; for example, in an analysis of 18,889 participants who were gout-free at baseline, the 15-year cumulative incidence ranged from 1.1% for people with baseline serum urate <6 mg/dL to 49% for ≥10 mg/dL, with a clear increase in incidence

according to baseline serum urate level4 (Fig. 97.1). ### Epidemiology

### Prevalence and Incidence of Gout

Gout is the most common inflammatory arthritis affecting adults. In the United Kingdom and North America, contemporary incidence of gout is estimated to be >2 per 1000 person years

(reviewed in ref. 9). For men, incident gout steadily increases with age, and for women, it increases after menopause. In the last three decades, prevalence has increased in both the United States and the United Kingdom. In the US National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) study, prevalent gout was observed in 2.9% participants in 1988 to 1994 and in 3.9% in 2007 to 200810 but remained stable between 2007 and 2016.11 In the United Kingdom Clinical Practice Research Database, prevalent gout was observed in 1.4% patients in 1999 and in 2.5% in 2012.12 This increasing prevalence is likely due to several factors including increasing longevity, longer survival with kidney disease and cardiovascular disease, use of medications that increase serum urate concentrations including diuretics, increasing obesity rates, and other changes in dietary exposures. There is substantially higher prevalence in some Indigenous populations including Taiwanese Aborigines, Mori in Aotearoa/New Zealand, and Polynesian Pacific Islanders; these populations have a prevalence that is at least 2-fold higher than other ethnicities.9,13

### Risk Factors for Developing Gout

Hyperuricemia is the central risk factor for development of incident gout, and many factors that are associated with incident gout in clinical practice are also associated with elevated serum urate concentrations (Table 97.3). Older age, male sex, post-menopausal status in women, and genetic factors are important biologic variables. Conditions associated with chronic high cell turnover such as psoriasis and myeloproliferative disease are frequently associated with hyperuricemia and may cause gout. Other medical comorbidities associated with development of gout include obesity, chronic kidney disease, obstructive sleep apnea, hypertension, heart failure, and other cardiovascular disease. Medications frequently used to treat these conditions, including diuretics,

### Factors Associated With Developing Gout

angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors, beta blockers, low-dose aspirin, and calcineurin inhibitors, are also associated with hyperuricemia and incident gout. Poor diabetes control is associated with reduced serum urate concentrations and incident gout, likely due to the uricosuric effect of hyperglycemia.

Gout typically presents in middle-aged men. Women have lower incidence and prevalence of gout, and the disease typically presents at an older age and after menopause. Compared with men, women with gout have higher rates of comorbidities, particularly chronic kidney disease and cardiovascular disease, and are more likely to be on diuretics.

Familial aggregation of gout does occur, and the risk for gout is almost two-fold higher when a first-degree relative has gout. Although genetic factors are strongly associated with serum urate concentrations and development of gout in the general population,18 testing for genetic variants is not routinely recommended in current clinical practice. The genetic variants associated most strongly with common gout are thought to exert influence through the effects on serum urate concentrations by influencing uric acid transport via the gut (in the case of ABCG2) or the renal tubule (in the case of SLC2A9, SLC17A11, SLC22A12, and others). ABCG2 variants are also associated with earlier onset of disease and higher risk of gout tophi.19, ABCG2 may also influence response to allopurinol. Monogenic syndromes such as partial hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase deficiency (Kelley-Seegmiller syndrome), phosphoribosyl pyrophosphate synthetase overactivity, or autosomal dominant tubulointerstitial kidney disease caused by UMOD pathogenic variants are rare but should be considered in people who present with severe hyperuricemia and gout at a young age (before the age of 30 years).

Dietary factors such as intake of high purine foods such as red meat, seafood, and beer and intake of sugar-sweetened beverages are also associated with elevated serum urate concentrations and development of incident gout in the general population (reviewed in ref. 22). Furthermore, intake of low-fat dairy, coffee, and vitamin C are associated with lower serum urate concentrations and reduced risk of developing gout. The Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension (DASH) diet (which emphasizes fruits, vegetables, and low-fat dairy foods and reduced consumption of saturated fat, total fat, and cholesterol) can reduce serum urate levels and is associated with reduced risk of incident gout.23, Overall, the effects of specific dietary components on serum urate concentrations are quite small in the general population.

Medications can also reduce the risk of developing incident gout; this includes anti-inflammatory medications such as canakinumab that do not change serum urate levels,26 and therapies that reduce serum urate concentrations such as fenofibrate and losartan.14, In people with obesity, intensive weight loss though bariatric surgery substantially reduces serum urate levels and risk of developing gout.

### Clinical Risk Factors for Flares in Patients With Gout

After the first flare, approximately one-third of people will experience at least one subsequent flare over the next 4 years. A number of factors are associated with gout flares in patients with established gout; these include higher serum urate levels, acute medical illness, surgical illness, use of diuretics, intake of purinerich foods or alcohol, dehydration, joint injury or overuse, use of low-dose aspirin, longer disease duration and presence of comorbidities. .29-32 Gout flares are also more common at times of high

ambient temperature and extremes of humidity. During the initiation period of urate-lowering therapy, gout flares occur more frequently, particularly if the serum urate is rapidly reduced or if anti-inflammatory prophylaxis is not co-administered. However, in the long-term, urate-lowering therapy prevents recurrent gout flares. Some other factors have been associated with reduced risk of recurrent gout flares, including lower serum urate levels and cherry intake.29,34

### Associated Comorbid Conditions

People presenting with gout frequently have concomitant medical conditions such as chronic kidney disease, obesity, cardiovascular disease, diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidemia, hypertriglyceridemia, kidney stones, cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, and heart failure (Table 97.4).35, Cluster analysis of comorbidities in a large cohort of patients with gout has identified five clusters (C1 to C5): cluster C1 (12%) includes patients with isolated gout and few comorbidities; cluster C2 (17%) includes those with obesity with high prevalence of hypertension; cluster C3 (24%) includes those with high proportion of type 2 diabetes; cluster C4 (28%) includes those with dyslipidemia; and cluster C5 (18%) includes those with a history of cardiovascular disease, renal failure, and diuretics. These comorbidities contribute to higher risk of poor outcomes for people with gout in the setting of COVID- 19 infection.

There is ongoing uncertainty about whether hyperuricemia or gout contributes to the development of cardiometabolic diseases associated with gout and whether pharmacologic lowering of serum urate levels influences the development or outcomes of these other conditions. However, in clinical practice, it is important to recognize that people presenting with gout are at high risk for cardiometabolic conditions and also mortality and to systematically screen and manage risk factors for kidney disease, diabetes, and cardiovascular disease.

### Clinical Presentations of Gout

Gout typically presents as an acute monoarthritis, although oligoor polyarticular presentations can occur. The first metatarsophalangeal joint (podagra) is a common site for the first presentation of gout (Fig. 97.2A). Other frequently affected sites are the midfoot, ankle, and knee joint. Gout flares have a stereotypic pattern, with rapid onset of maximal pain within 24 hours of onset and gradual resolution over 1 to 2 weeks. These episodes often start during the night. The cardinal features of inflammation are typically present, with severe joint pain ("the worst pain ever"), associated with joint swelling, warmth, erythema, and restricted movement. The joint may be exquisitely tender, and activities such as walking are limited. The overlying skin may desquamate during the resolution phase. In patients with severe joint inflammation, fever and other systemic symptoms may be present. Gout flares affecting the axial skeleton, hips, and shoulders can occur but are uncommon.

Gout flares are typically self-limiting over 1 to 2 weeks. The clinical features of joint inflammation completely disappear, and the patient remains asymptomatic (or back to baseline state) during this "intercritical period" until the next gout flare occurs. In the absence of treatment, gout flares occur more frequently over time, involving more joints including those in the upper limb, including the olecranon bursa, wrist, and small joints of the hands.

In the presence of persistent hyperuricemia, tophi and chronic gouty arthritis may develop. A tophus appears as a "draining or chalk-like subcutaneous nodule under transparent skin, often with overlying vascularity, located in typical locations: joints, ears, olecranon bursae, finger pads, tendons (e.g., Achilles)" )>1 (Figs. 97.2B and 97.3 to 97.6). Tophi are usually nontender but may become acutely inflamed with associated tenderness. These lesions may cause joint deformity and obstruction to joint movement. Foot tophi may lead to difficulty finding shoes. Participants with tophi experience high frequency of gout flares, pain, and activity limitation. Intraosseous tophi lead to bone erosion. Draining tophi may be complicated by superimposed infection. Chronic gouty arthritis manifests as nonresolving synovitis, often in patients with tophi. In the pre—urate-lowering therapy era, tophaceous gout typically occurred approximately a decade after presentation of the first gout flare. Some patients present with tophi as the first manifestation of disease, and others never develop tophi despite persistently high serum urate levels and recurrent gout flares. Older age, female sex, diuretic use, and chronic kidney disease are risk factors for presentation with early tophaceous disease. 44,

Complex clinical scenarios can occasionally present. These include rapidly progressive "eruptive" tophaceous gout, particularly in the renal transplant setting and in older patients who have chronic kidney disease and who are on diuretics. Although tophi are usually found in characteristic sites such as the first metatarsophalangeal joint, Achilles tendon, olecranon bursa, and ears, many atypical sites have been described including the head and neck; skin; eye; ear, nose, and throat (ENT) system; cardiac structures; breast; gut; nerves; and spine. Compressive neuropathies, particularly carpal tunnel syndrome, have been described.

Although the clinical features of gout have been well described in the medical literature for centuries, the SUGAR study, a large international case-control study using microscopically monosodium urate crystal proven disease as the gold standard, has allowed further quantification of the typical features of gout.

This analysis showed that the following clinical factors were most associated with microscopically proven gout: male sex, dietary trigger, involvement of the first metatarsophalangeal joint at the time of presentation or in past episodes, clinically evident tophus, joint redness, marked tenderness of the affected joint, two or more episodes that start abruptly and resolve within 2 weeks, resolution of symptoms by 14 days, and difficulty walking or using the joint.

### Investigations for Gout

### Microscopic Analysis for MSU Crystals

The gold standard for gout diagnosis is MSU crystal identification. On polarizing light microscopy of synovial fluid, MSU crystals appear as negatively birefingent needle-shaped crystals 1 to 20

µm in length (Fig. 97.2C). MSU crystals may be both intracellular and extracellular. Synovial fluid during a gout flare has an inflammatory pattern, with high numbers of neutrophils (sometimes >50,000 cells/mm3). MSU crystals may also be present in asymptomatic joints of hyperuricaemic patients with gout, particularly in joints that have presented with a gout flare.

Microscopic confirmation of MSU crystals can also be achieved through needle aspiration of a suspected tophus or swabbing a discharging tophus. These crystals can also be identified histologically in tophus tissue samples that are resected at the time of surgery, particularly if the tissue has been fixed in ethanol. The tophus has a characteristic, organized structure with bundles of MSU crystals (measuring up to 40 µm in length) within a central crystalline core, surrounded by a cellular corona zone of macrophages, giant

cells, and other immune cells, which is, in turn, surrounded by a fibrovascular zone of blood vessels, connective tissue, and scattered immune cells.

### Blood and Urine Testing

Serum urate testing can assist with clinical diagnosis of gout in symptomatic individuals, but hyperuricemia alone is not sufficient to make a diagnosis of gout, as most people with hyperuricemia do not have gout. The diagnosis of gout is unlikely in a patient with serum urate levels that are persistently low (less than 6 mg/ dL). Serum urate may drop acutely into the normal range in up to 40% during a gout flare,49 and if gout remains a possibility, serum urate should be retested after the episode of inflammatory arthritis has resolved.

Serum urate also plays an important role in monitoring treatment with urate-lowering therapy. Both the ACR and the EULAR50,51 recommend lowering serum urate to levels less than 6 mg/dL (0.36 mmol/L) in people with gout on urate-lowering therapy, and EULAR recommends a lower target (less than 5 mg/ dL) in those with a large MSU crystal burden (tophi). Serum urate monitoring can ensure appropriate dose titration of urate-lowering therapy. Periodic measurement of urate also allows assessment of adherence to urate-lowering therapy for patients who are on long-term therapy.

The C-reactive protein is usually elevated during a flare and may measure >100 mg/L in severe gout flares. During intercritical periods, the C-reactive protein is usually within the normal range. The complete blood count may also show elevated platelet and neutrophil count. These findings reflect the degree of systemic inflammation rather than the diagnosis of gout. Laboratory biochemistry tests may also indicate associated comorbidities in patients with gout, such as chronic kidney disease, dyslipidemia, and type 2 diabetes.

HLA-B*5801 is a major risk factor for allopurinol hypersensitivity. HLA-B*5801 is highest in people of Chinese, Thai, Korean, and African American ethnicity, and screening in these patients prior to commencing allopurinol is appropriate. In patients who are HLA-B*5801 carriers, a urate-lowering drug other than allopurinol should be prescribed.

### Plain Radiography

In patients presenting with the first gout flare, plain radiographs are usually normal, with the exception of nonspecific soft tissue swelling of the inflamed joint. Bone erosions on plain radiography appear as well-defined cortical breaks with a sclerotic rim and overhanging edge1; these radiographic features are usually present in patients with tophaceous gout, in whom the diagnosis is well established (Figs. 97.2D and 97.7). Plain radiographic joint space narrowing or widening is a late feature of advanced gout.

### Ultrasound

Some ultrasound-specific features of gout have been described, and this imaging test can assist with gout diagnosis. Primarily, these features reflect MSU crystal deposition within the joints and periarticular structures. The OMERACT gout ultrasound

working group has defined the elemental ultrasound lesions of gout as follows54: double contour is the "abnormal hyperechoic band over the superficial margin of the articular hyaline cartilage, independent of the angle of insonation and which may be either irregular or regular, continuous or intermittent and can be distinguished from the cartilage interface sign" (Fig. 97.2E); a tophus is "[a] circumscribed, inhomogeneous, hyperechoic and/or hypoechoic aggregation (which may or may not generate posterior acoustic shadow) which may be surrounded by a small anechoic rim" (Fig. 97.2F); aggregates are "[h]eterogeneous hyperechoic foci that maintain their high degree of reflectivity even when the gain setting is minimized or the insonation angle is changed and which occasionally may generate posterior acoustic shadow"; and an erosion is "[a]n intraand/or extraarticular discontinuity of the bone surface (visible in 2 perpendicular planes)." The double contour is thought to represent MSU crystals overlying articular cartilage. Aggregates may be present within the joint and also at tendon and ligament sites, whereas tophi can be observed at intra-articular, periarticular, and extra-articular sites. Inter-reader reproducibility is variable for depending on the ultrasound lesion, with a reproducibility exercise of ultrasound experts reporting interreader kappa values of 0.67 for tophus, 0.63 for double contour, and 0.61 for aggregates. Other ultrasound findings, including

synovitis, tendinitis, and joint effusion, may also be present in people with gout.

When the diagnosis of gout is suspected, ultrasound can identify sites for joint aspiration to allow microscopic identification of MSU crystals. In situations in which joint aspiration is not possible, ultrasound may also assist with the diagnosis. In the multicenter SUGAR study, the affected joints were scanned by ultrasound in 824 people presenting with joint swelling. This study showed high specificity for gout for double contour and tophus on ultrasound, compared with MSU crystal identification as the gold standard. In those with early disease (defined as the onset of the first episode within 2 years), the specificity for double contour sign was 92.3%, but the sensitivity was only 50.9%. High specificity was also observed in those with early disease for ultrasound tophus (95.4%), with a sensitivity of only 33.6%. These findings indicate that, when present, a positive ultrasound feature can provide valuable supportive evidence of gout, including in those with recent onset of disease. However, many patients with early disease do not have the characteristic ultrasound findings.

Although more frequent in those with symptomatic disease, some ultrasound features of MSU crystal deposition (including double contour and tophus) are also present in those with asymptomatic hyperuricemia who have no history of gout. These findings can be observed in more than one-quarter of people with hyperuricemia. The prognostic implications of these findings are unknown.

### Dual-Energy CT

Conventional CT allows excellent visualization of tophi and bone erosion. Dual-energy computed tomography (DECT) is a newer CT method that has utility for MSU crystal identification and gout diagnosis. DECT can determine the composition of different tissues by analyzing the difference in attenuation in a material exposed to two different x-ray spectra simultaneously. Different colors can be assigned to materials of different chemical composition, including urate and calcium in people with gout60 (Figs. 97.7 and 97.8). Inter-reader kappa values for DECT urate deposition range from 0.73 to 0.93. Automated software allows rapid volume measurement of urate crystal burden at scanned sites. This method of volume assessment has very high reproducibility (inter-reader intraclass correlation coefficients typically ≥0.95).

Meta-analysis of DECT studies has shown high sensitivity (87%) and specificity (84%) compared with the gold standard of microscopic MSU crystal confirmation. However, there are relatively few diagnostic accuracy studies, particularly in patients with very early onset of disease. Sensitivity of DECT in this situation is probably lower, with estimates as low as 50%. Lower sensitivity in early disease may be explained by pathologic observations that DECT can identify "dense" urate deposits (with at least 15 to 20 vol% urate) but that deposits with lower urate volumes may not be detected by DECT. The highest yield for DECT urate deposition is in the feet and knees, and these sites should be preferentially scanned for diagnostic purposes. Artefact, particularly in the nails and skin of the heels, is common, and scans should be interpreted by experienced readers with knowledge of common artefacts. As with ultrasound, DECT urate deposits are observed in approximately a quarter of people with asymptomatic hyperuricemia and no prior history of gout. The relevance of these findings to future outcomes, including development of symptomatic disease, is unknown.

DECT also has utility in assessment of severe disease, including tophi, bone erosion, and tendon involvement. In patients with tophaceous gout, DECT can detect much greater tophus burden than is clinically evident. Importantly, DECT measures the urate component within the tophus, but not the soft tissue component, so that tophi with similar physical size may have different urate crystal volumes on DECT. Bone erosion can be clearly viewed on the conventional CT images, which are acquired as part of the DECT scan, and MSU crystals can be seen associated with bone erosion in gout43 (Fig. 97.7). Tendon and ligament deposits, which may not be clinically evident, are easily visualized by DECT. Although this imaging method provides useful clinical information in many people with gout, DECT scanners are not universally available, and the cost and radiation exposure may further limit its use.

### MRI

With MRI, bone erosion, tophus, and synovitis may be present in people with gout. The tophus appears as a mass with intermediate signal intensity appearance on T1w images but more variability on T2w images. There is variable contrast enhancement at tophus border. MRI is not usually required for gout diagnosis but may have a useful role in assessing for complications of gout, such as tendon rupture, spinal involvement, or superimposed infection; MRI bone marrow edema is uncommon in gout, and the presence of high-grade bone marrow edema is strongly suggestive of concurrent osteomyelitis in patients with gout. MRI synovitis is common in people with gout, even early in disease, and urate-lowering therapy leads to reduction in MRI synovitis scores.

### Diagnosis

In a patient presenting with clinical features of gout (acute inflammatory arthritis, chronic synovitis, nodules), the gold standard for gout diagnosis is microscopic confirmation of MSU crystals. In the absence of microscopic analysis, the diagnosis of gout requires synthesis of available clinical and other laboratory information.

The differential diagnosis of the gout flare presentation includes other causes of acute monoarthritis, the most important of which is septic arthritis. Other important differential diagnoses are fracture, other acute crystal induced disease including "pseudogout" due to calcium pyrophosphate deposition (CPPD) or basic calcium phosphate arthritis or tendinitis, reactive arthritis, and psoriatic arthritis (Fig. 97.9). Osteoarthritis also affects the first metatarsophalangeal joint but can usually be differentiated from gout by the degree of joint inflammation and the temporal course of the disease. In most circumstances, gout can be readily distinguished from rheumatoid arthritis due to the temporal history and pattern of joint involvement. The differential diagnosis for tophi includes other causes of subcutaneous nodules, including rheumatoid nodules, tumoral calcinosis, lipid deposits, or osteophytes (Fig. 97.10).

It is important to note that gout can coexist with other forms of arthritis. For example, septic arthritis may occur in joints affected by gout, CPPD and MSU crystals may be identified concurrently in the synovial fluid of patients presenting with an acute monoarthritis, patients with psoriasis may have hyperuricemia and gout in addition to psoriatic arthritis, and gout flares and tophi more commonly affect joints affected by osteoarthritis. Gout can also develop in patients with rheumatoid arthritis,72 and differentiating rheumatoid arthritis flares from gout flares may be difficult in this setting. Alternative or concomitant diagnoses should be considered in patients who do not respond to gout therapy as expected.

Careful clinical assessment and laboratory tests, including serum urate testing and particularly microscopic analysis of affected synovial fluid or tissue, play key roles in differentiating between gout and other rheumatic diseases. A diagnostic rule developed in primary care has been published to assist with diagnosis of gout in patients with monoarthritis; this rule has also been validated in emergency department and secondary care settings (Table 97.5).

### Gout Management

### Guidelines

Gout management guidelines have been published by many rheumatology societies, including the ACR and the EULAR.50, All of these guidelines include recommendations regarding the key aspects of gout management, including treatment of gout flares, urate-lowering therapy (ULT), gout flare prevention with antiinflammatory drugs when commencing ULT, nonpharmacologic therapies, and management of comorbidities. Tables 97.6 and 97.7 summarize the key recommendations from the ACR and EULAR guidelines.

### Gout Flare Treatment

### Principles of Gout Flare Management

All patients with a diagnosis of gout should have an action plan for future flare management, and gout flares should be treated with anti-inflammatory drugs as soon as possible. Rest, elevation, hydration, and icing the acutely inflamed joint may also provide some pain relief. The main three drug classes used for gout flare management are corticosteroids, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, and colchicine. For a monoarticular presentation, intraarticular corticosteroid can be effective. Combinations of antiinflammatory agents may be needed for severe flares, particularly for polyarticular flares. Clinical trials have indicated similar efficacy for oral prednisolone, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, and colchicine but fewer side effects for prednisolone

compared with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs75 and for nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs compared with low-dose colchicine. The choice of these agents for an individual patient often depends on medical factors including kidney disease, diabetes, peptic ulcer disease, and concomitant medications, including strong P-glycoprotein and/or CYP3A4 inhibitors and anticoagulants.

In practice, a key consideration when choosing an agent for gout flare management is patient preference and prior experience of anti-inflammatory drugs for gout flare management. The duration of anti-inflammatory therapy should be individualized, and anti-inflammatory therapy should be continued until the flare has completely resolved. The IL-1 receptor antagonist anakinra has similar efficacy to standard gout flare treatments, 77,78 but may also be useful when other anti-inflammatory agents are contraindicated or not tolerated. Once established, urate-lowering therapy should not be discontinued at the time of a gout flare.

### Corticosteroids

For many patients, particularly those with multiple comorbidities, corticosteroids may be the most appropriate therapeutic option. A recent large multicenter randomized controlled trial has confirmed the results of prior smaller trials that oral prednisolone is as effective as oral NSAIDs for patients presenting to emergency departments for management of gout flare. In this study, oral prednisolone (30 mg daily for 5 days) and indomethacin (50 mg three times a day for 2 days, then 25 mg three times a day for 3 days) resulted in similar improvements in pain, and there were no differences between groups in joint redness and tenderness, additional intake of paracetamol, and mean patient satisfaction with analgesia. Although no serious adverse events were reported in either group, a greater proportion of patients in the indomethacin group had minor adverse events in the first 2 hours of treatment in the emergency department (including dizziness, sleepiness, and nausea) and over the 2-week period of follow-up after discharge from the emergency department (including nausea and vomiting). These findings provide further support for the use of oral corticosteroids for management of gout flares.

Adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) acts via melanocortin type 3 receptor to produce anti-inflammatory effects in gout. In hospitalized patients with multiple comorbidities where NSAIDs, colchicine and corticosteroids are contraindicated, a single dose may be effective. However, the availability and cost of ACTH can be barriers to the use of this agent in current clinical practice. For a detailed discussion of the pharmacology of corticosteroids, see Chapter 60.

### Nonsteroidal Anti-inflammatory Drugs

NSAIDs, both nonselective and cyclo-oxygenase-2 (COX-2) selective, have proven efficacy for treatment of gout flares. There is no clear evidence that any specific NSAID has greater efficacy for gout flare management. The selective COX-2 inhibitors are as effective as traditional NSAIDs but with fewer adverse effects, particularly gastrointestinal adverse effects. In general, NSAIDs should be used as early as possible after development of the flare, at full dose, and for the shortest possible period. Many patients with gout are elderly or have concomitant kidney disease and/or cardiovascular disease, and comorbid conditions may limit the use of NSAIDs for gout flare treatment. For a detailed discussion of the pharmacology of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, see Chapter 59 of this textbook.

### Colchicine

Colchicine modulates multiple pathways implicated in MSU crystal-induced inflammation by preventing microtubule assembly and thereby disrupting NLRP3 inflammasome activation, inflammatory cell chemotaxis, generation of leukotrienes and cytokines, and phagocytosis. Colchicine has a narrow therapeutic index and a high mortality with overdose. It is primarily eliminated via enterohepatic recirculation and biliary excretion, with 10% to 20% eliminated via the kidneys. Therefore dose reduction is required in patients with liver and/or kidney impairment. Colchicine is metabolized by cytochrome P450 3A4 (CYP3A4) and excreted via the P-glycoprotein (P-gp) transport system. Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors include protease inhibitors, imidazoles, and clarithromycin; moderate inhibitors include simvastatin and erythromycin. Inhibitors of P-gp include cyclosporine, tacrolimus, ketoconazole, and protease inhibitors. Co-administration of colchicine and CYP3A4 or P-gp inhibitors can result in accumulation of colchicine and toxicity. For patients with renal or hepatic impairment, concurrent administration of colchicine with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors or P-gp inhibitors is contraindicated. For patients with normal renal and hepatic function, a reduction in colchicine dose is recommended when concurrent treatment with a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor or a P-gp inhibitor is required.

Compared with placebo, colchicine can reduce pain and joint inflammation of a gout flare. Until the last decade, highdose colchicine was administered, with frequent gastrointestinal toxicity. This practice has changed substantially following publication of the Acute Gout Flare Receiving Colchicine Evaluation (AGREE) trial, in which patients with gout were randomized to receive low-dose colchicine (1.2 mg stat, then 0.6 mg at 1 hour), high-dose colchicine (1.2 mg stat, then 0.6 mg hourly for 6 hours), or placebo at the time of a gout flare. Both highand low-dose colchicine were significantly more effective than placebo, with similar improvements in pain scores. However, the low-dose strategy was much better tolerated than the high-dose strategy, with similar rates of adverse events to the placebo group.

Gastrointestinal side effects, particularly diarrhea, is the most common side effect from colchicine and is generally dose dependent. Bone marrow suppression and neuromyotoxicity are serious, but less common, side effects. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) currently recommends that colchicine should be prescribed for gout flare treatment at 1.2 mg stat followed by 0.6 mg 1 hour later. Further dose reduction may be required in patients with liver or kidney disease, the elderly, or those taking CYP3A4 or P-gp inhibitors. Patients should also be advised about safe storage of colchicine due to the risk of severe toxicity in the setting of overdose.

### AntiIL-1 Biologic Therapy

The recognition that IL-1β plays a central role in initiation of gout flare has led to testing of antiIL-1 agents for management of gout flares. Rilonacept, a fully human recombinant soluble decoy receptor protein that binds IL-1α and IL-1β, was less effective than indomethacin in reducing pain due to gout flares. Canakinumab, a fully human recombinant anti—IL-1β monoclonal antibody, has been tested in clinical trials of patients with gout flares who were unresponsive or had contraindications to NSAIDS and/or colchicine. A single subcutaneous injection of canakinumab 150 mg led to greater and more rapid reduction in pain and features of joint inflammation, compared with intramuscular triamcinolone (40 mg), in patients with gout flares. The cost of canakinumab is substantially greater than other anti-inflammatory medications for gout flares (https://www.nice.org.uk/advice/esnm23).

A small clinical trial comparing anakinra, the recombinant IL-1 receptor antagonist, with usual gout flare management (naproxen, colchicine, or prednisone) showed noninferiority between treatment groups, indicating that anakinra is an effective option for management of gout flares. In a phase 2 trial of 165 patients with gout flares, anakinra (100 or 200 mg/day for 5 days) had comparable efficacy to triamcinolone 40 mg intramuscularly (IM). For a detailed discussion of the pharmacology of anticytokine therapies, see Chapter 63 of this textbook.

### Urate-Lowering Therapy

### Principles of Urate-Lowering Therapy for Gout Management

In most countries throughout the world, urate-lowering therapy is not recommended for people with hyperuricemia but without gout. The 2020 ACR guidelines strongly recommended that pharmacologic urate-lowering therapy should be initiated in patients with gout who have subcutaneous tophi, frequent gout flares (≥2/ year), or radiographic damage attributable to gout. The 2016 EULAR update recommends that "urate-lowering therapy should be considered and discussed with every patient with a definite

diagnosis of gout from the first presentation" and that earlier urate-lowering therapy initiation should be considered in those who present with gout at a young age (<40 years), have very high serum urate levels (greater than 8 mg/dL, 0.48 mmol/L), or major comorbid conditions, such as heart failure, coronary artery disease, or kidney disease. A placebo-controlled trial of patients early in the disease course (serum urate ≥ 7 mg/dL, and only one or two prior flares) showed that urate-lowering therapy with febuxostat led to significant reduction in the proportion of patients experiencing gout flares over 2 years. However, less than half (41%) of participants in the placebo group experienced a further gout flare over the 2-year study period. These data can guide discussions and shared decision-making about long-term urate-lowering therapy for patients who have a recent gout diagnosis.

All rheumatology society guidelines recommend dose titration of urate-lowering drugs to achieve serum urate targets. Both the ACR and EULAR recommend a serum urate target less than 6 mg/dL (0.36 mmol/L) for all patients, with EULAR recommending a lower target less than 5 mg/dL (0.30 mmol/L) for patients with high burdens of MSU crystals, such as those with tophaceous gout. The goal of long-term urate-lowering therapy is to achieve MSU crystal dissolution and consequently prevent gout flares, disability, and joint damage due to gout. Both laboratory and imaging studies have demonstrated that reducing the serum urate below these targets leads to dissolution of MSU crystals, 88,89 and several clinical trials have also demonstrated the clinical benefits in flare prevention of long-term urate-lowering using a treat-to-serum urate target approach.71, For tophi, there is a linear relationship between the velocity of tophus regression and serum urate concentration, so that lower serum urate targets are advocated in this clinical situation. For patients who have achieved complete dissolution of MSU crystals and have had a prolonged asymptomatic period, dose reduction or stopping urate-lowering therapy may be considered, with periodic clinical and laboratory monitoring. A prospective study of patients has examined outcomes following withdrawal of urate—lowering therapy after 5 years if no tophus was present at baseline or 5

years after resolution of the last tophus. In this study, which followed patients for a mean duration of 33 months, recurrence of a gout flare was not observed in those with average follow-up serum urate of <7 mg/dL; however, recurrent gout flares were observed in patients with higher serum urate concentrations after stopping urate-lowering therapy.

Traditionally, it has been recommended that urate-lowering therapy be initiated after the gout flares have completely resolved (typically 2 weeks after flare resolution) because of concerns that urate-lowering therapy initiation may worsen or prolong the gout flare. Four clinical trials have now reported that initiation of uratelowering therapy (allopurinol or febuxostat) at the time of flare did not prolong the flare duration or worsen pain scores,94-97 and the 2020 ACR guidelines conditionally recommended starting urate-lowering therapy during a gout flare. The EULAR taskforce did not provide guidance on this issue.

There are three main pharmacologic approaches to urate lowering. First, xanthine oxidase inhibitors such as allopurinol or febuxostat prevent urate production. Second, uricosuric agents such as probenecid or benzbromarone) inhibit uric acid reabsorption in the proximal renal tubule and therefore increase renal uric acid excretion. Probenecid and benzbromarone can be used as monotherapy or coprescribed with a xanthine oxidase inhibitor. Finally, intravenous recombinant uricases such as pegloticase convert urate to the soluble metabolite allantoin and are used to treat patients with severe disease that has not responded to maximum doses of oral therapies. Pegloticase should not be coprescribed with other urate-lowering therapies, as these may suppress detection of serum urate elevations that are a marker of anti-drug antibodies and herald risk for infusion reaction.

For all patients commencing urate-lowering therapy, comorbidities and concomitant medications need to be considered. Prescribers should also be aware of the risk of severe bone marrow suppression when xanthine oxidase inhibitors such as allopurinol or febuxostat are coprescribed with azathioprine or 6-mercaptopurine, due to the risk of bone marrow suppression. Uricosuric agents should be avoided in patients with nephrolithiasis, in those with severe kidney disease, and in those with urate overproduction. Pegloticase should be avoided in patients with glucose- 6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency, due to the risk of hemolysis and methemoglobinemia. The key properties of the specific urate-lowering drugs are shown in Table 97.8. For a detailed discussion of the use of urate-lowering agents, see Chapter 66 of this textbook.

### Allopurinol

Xanthine oxidase inhibitors, particularly allopurinol, are the most widely used urate-lowering therapy. Allopurinol is recommended as the first-line therapy by the EULAR taskforce and the 2020 ACR gout management guidelines. When dose escalated to the serum urate target, allopurinol is an effective urate-lowering therapy. On average, doses of allopurinol 400 mg daily are needed to achieve a serum urate of <6 mg/dL.99,

Allopurinol is generally well tolerated and effective in reducing serum urate to target when dosed appropriately. However, adverse events may occur, with a mild rash occurring in 2% of patients prescribed allopurinol. Rarely (in <1/1000 patients), the potentially life-threatening allopurinol hypersensitivity syndrome (AHS) can develop, with rash (including Stevens-Johnson syndrome or toxic epidermal necrolysis), eosinophilia, fever, hepatitis, and acute kidney injury. HLA-B*5801 is a major risk factor for allopurinol hypersensitivity. Screening of HLA-B*5801 in high-risk

populations (Chinese, Korean, Thai) is recommended, and use of alternative urate-lowering drugs in HLA-B*5801 carriers can . Other clinical risk factors prevent this adverse drug reaction. for AHS are recent commencement (within 8 weeks), kidney disease, and diuretic use. For patients without other urate-lowering therapy options, allopurinol desensitization can be attempted for patients with mild skin reactions but should not be attempted for those who have had AHS.

Higher allopurinol doses, particularly in patients with kidney disease, have been associated with AHS in a number of reports, and these observations led to guidelines stating that allopurinol doses should be restricted according to creatinine clearance in patients with chronic kidney disease. Widespread adoption of these recommendations led to inadequate control of serum urate in the majority of patients prescribed allopurinol. Subsequent work has demonstrated that the starting dose of allopurinol is associated with AHS, and that starting dose should be reduced in patients with kidney disease, particularly if estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR < 60 mL/min/1.73 m2). However, once allopurinol has been tolerated at low dose, the dose can be safely increased until the serum urate target is achieved. This approach is effective in achieving serum urate target and is well tolerated. A general approach is for patients with eGFR ≥ 60 mL/min/1.73 m2 to start allopurinol 100 mg daily and for the dose to escalate by 100 mg every month until the serum urate is at target; for those with eGFR < 60 mL/min/1.73 m2, start allopurinol 50 mg daily and escalate the dose by 50 mg every month until the serum urate is at target. All patients commencing allopurinol should be advised of the risk of hypersensitivity and to stop allopurinol if they develop a rash.

### Febuxostat

Febuxostat potently and specifically inhibits xanthine oxidase and is an effective urate-lowering agent in people with gout. Febuxostat also leads to prevention of gout flares and tophus regression when prescribed long term. The original phase 3 trials reported higher frequency of gout flares soon after starting febuxostat at high doses, 108 and these initiation flares can be prevented by starting febuxostat at low dose and gradually titrating the dose. The most common side effects with febuxostat are diarrhea, nausea, and deranged liver function tests. For patients who have had allopurinol hypersensitivity, febuxostat is generally tolerated, although occasionally patients have developed rash or hypersensitivity with febuxostat. The 2018 CARES trial did report a higher risk of all-cause and cardiovascular mortality in patients receiving febuxostat, compared with allopurinol. However, the subsequent FAST trial and VA STOP-GOUT trial did not confirm this risk, with a trend to lower cardiovascular events in those treated with febuxostat, compared with allopurinol. 100,112

### Uricosuric Agents

Alternatively, in the event that allopurinol dose escalation is not tolerated or does not lead to achievement of the serum urate target, a number of uricosuric agents are available. If a lower dose of allopurinol is tolerated, allopurinol can be continued at this dose with the addition of a uricosuric agent, such as probenecid or benzbromarone (if available). Probenecid and benzbromarone can also be used as monotherapy. All patients receiving uricosuric agents should be advised to maintain a high fluid intake and avoid dehydration. Careful monitoring of liver function tests is also required for patients treated with benzbromarone, due to the risk of hepatotoxicity.

### Pegloticase

In patients with severe disease (high crystal burden, frequent flares, extensive tophi, joint damage) who are unable to achieve serum urate target with available oral therapy, intravenous pegloticase every 2 weeks can lead to a major reduction in MSU crystal burden, with improvements in flare frequency, tophus burden, and health-related quality of life. Infusion reactions can occur, primarily in patients who have developed anti-pegloticase antibodies. These antibodies occur in ~40% patients receiving pegloticase monotherapy and are associated with a loss of the serum uratelowering effect. Monitoring of the serum urate prior to each infusion and discontinuation of pegloticase if the serum urate levels are greater than 6 mg/dL (and especially if two consecutive levels exceed 6 mg/dL) are recommended. Concomitant immunosuppressive therapy with therapies such as methotrexate increases pegloticase response rates, reduces infusion reactions, and lowers anti-drug antibodies.

### Anti-inflammatory Prophylaxis When Initiating Urate- Lowering Therapy

Anti-inflammatory prophylaxis refers to the use of low-dose antiinflammatory drugs to prevent gout flares. This is particularly relevant for patients who are flaring frequently and at the time of commencing ULT. In the absence of prophylaxis, up to half of patients will have an acute flare following initiation of ULT. Generally, anti-inflammatory prophylaxis is recommended for at least 6 months after starting ULT and for longer duration if

patients have tophi. It is important to note that gout flares are more likely if patients are started on high doses of ULT, which leads to rapid reduction in the serum urate. The FORTUNE-1 study has shown that gout flares are substantially less frequent if urate-lowering therapy is gradually dose escalated rather than started at full dose.

Colchicine has been widely used as anti-inflammatory prophylaxis for decades. In a clinical trial of patients commencing allopurinol using a dose-escalation approach, patients receiving colchicine 0.6 mg twice daily had significantly fewer flares compared with those receiving placebo (0.52 vs. 2.91 over 6 months; P = .008) but also experienced more diarrhea (38% vs 5%, P = .009). The FORTUNE-1 clinical trial also demonstrated the efficacy of colchicine 0.5 mg daily in patients commencing febuxostat 40 mg daily; in this study, gout flares were experienced by 18.9% of patients receiving colchicine prophylaxis compared with 36.0% without prophylaxis, and there was no difference between the groups in adverse events. If used for anti-inflammatory prophylaxis, the dose of colchicine should be reduced in patients taking moderate to strong CYP3A4 and P-gp inhibitors and in those with kidney impairment. It is also recommended that a complete blood count and creatine kinase be checked every 6 months in patients with kidney disease who are receiving long-term colchicine anti-inflammatory prophylaxis. Advice about safe storage is again important when using colchicine as an anti-inflammatory prophylaxis due to the risks in the setting of overdose.

Although no randomized controlled trials have tested the use of low-dose NSAIDs, these agents are also used in clinical practice for anti-inflammatory prophylaxis. The presence of comorbidities such as kidney disease, hypertension, and cardiovascular disease may preclude the use of these agents. In many of the febuxostat phase 3 clinical trials, naproxen 250 mg twice daily was used as an alternative to colchicine 0.6 mg daily. Post hoc analysis of these clinical trials demonstrated that flare rates increased sharply (up to 40%) at the end of 8 weeks of prophylaxis, but flare rates were low (range, 3% to 5%) if anti-inflammatory prophylaxis was continued for 6 months. In the large CONFIRMS phase 3 trial of febuxostat,120 anti-inflammatory prophylaxis was given for 6 months, and there was no difference between naproxen and colchicine groups in overall rates of adverse events. Rates of diarrhea were similar between the groups, but those who received naproxen had higher rates of gastrointestinal and abdominal pain, and higher rates of dental and oral soft tissue infections compared with those who received colchicine. More liver function test adverse events were observed in patients receiving colchicine compared with those receiving naproxen.

Although not approved for this indication, the IL-1β inhibitor canakinumab is also an effective anti-inflammatory prophylaxis agent. In a dose-ranging study of canakinumab in patients with gout who were initiating allopurinol between 100 and 300 mg daily, a single dose of canakinumab between 50 to 300 mg provided superior prophylaxis against flares compared with daily colchicine 0.5 mg. Similar rates of serious adverse events (SAEs) were reported between the canakinumab and colchicine groups.

### Role of Dietary/Lifestyle Interventions

Dietary advice about benefits of weight loss for patients with overweight/obesity, avoidance of sugary drinks, and reduction of alcohol intake for hazardous drinking is important for all people, including those with gout. Both the ACR and EULAR guidelines recommend dietary modification as an adjunct to pharmacologic treatment in patients with gout, but note that the impact of dietary medications on serum urate is likely to be small. The 2020 ACR guidelines recommend limiting intake of alcohol, purine, and high fructose corn syrup and using a weight loss program if overweight/obese. Although dietary strategies have an effect on serum urate and incident gout risk in the general population, there is very little evidence for people with established gout that avoidance of specific dietary factors leads to sustainable or clinically meaningful reductions in serum urate concentrations. With the possible exception of bariatric surgery for patients with severe obesity, dietary/lifestyle modifications alone are generally insufficient to achieve target serum urate in people with established gout. Therefore lifestyle advice should be considered an adjunct, rather than an alternative, to urate-lowering medication.

There have been very few randomized controlled trials investigating the role of dietary interventions for patients with established gout, and none have shown benefit. A Cochrane review of dietary supplements, updated in 2021 noted "the absence of highquality evidence to either support or refute the value of dietary supplementation in people with gout.' ."123 Low-fat dairy or vitamin C, which have modest effects on serum urate in the general population, have not shown clinically meaningful serum urate-lowering or clinical benefit in people with gout.124, In addition, a placebo-randomized controlled trial of comprehensive dietary education in patients with gout who were treated with urate-lowering therapy did not

observe differences in serum urate concentrations after 6 months. These findings indicate that for people with gout who are treated with urate-lowering therapy, additional benefits on serum urate are unlikely with intensive dietary advice.

### Comorbidity Assessment and Management in Patients With Gout

The high prevalence of comorbid conditions in people with gout necessitates active screening and management of type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, hypertension, dyslipidemia, chronic kidney disease, obesity, and obstructive sleep apnea. Traditional cardiovascular risk factors should be intensively managed in people with gout, due to high risk of morbidity and mortality due to cardiovascular disease.

Some strategies for comorbidity management may also affect gout management. Observational studies have shown that very intensive weight loss with bariatric surgery can lead to clinically relevant reductions in serum urate in people with gout. Losartan, fenofibrate, and SGLT2 inhibitors have modest urate-lowering effects and may be preferentially selected to manage relevant comorbidities in patients with gout.50, Although low-dose aspirin can increase serum urate, this therapy should not be withheld in patients requiring aspirin to reduce cardiovascular risk.

Comorbidities may have a substantial impact on pharmacologic management of gout. In the context of gout flare management, highdose corticosteroids may lead to substantial disruption in glycemic and blood pressure control. In patients with severe chronic kidney disease, NSAIDs are contraindicated, and colchicine requires dose reduction. NSAIDs should be avoided in patients on anticoagulants for cardiovascular disease. Colchicine has clinical benefits in coronary artery disease and may be the preferred anti-inflammatory treatment in people with gout and cardiovascular disease. In terms of urate-lowering therapy, allopurinol starting doses should be reduced in patients with chronic kidney disease, and patients with chronic kidney disease typically require lower allopurinol doses to achieve serum urate target. Patients with chronic kidney disease are less likely to respond to uricosuric agents, and these agents should be avoided in patients with kidney stones.

A particularly challenging clinical situation is kidney transplantation, due to high prevalence, severity of disease, and potential for drug interactions. Gout occurs in up to a quarter of kidney transplant recipients. The calcineurin inhibitors contribute to hyperuricemia and gout risk and significantly interact with colchicine. Cyclosporine has a greater effect on colchicine concentrations than tacrolimus, due to its strong inhibition of CYP3A4 and P-gp. NSAIDs are usually contraindicated. The risk of myelosuppression with azathioprine is substantially increased by xanthine oxidase inhibitors such as allopurinol and febuxostat. Switching patients from azathioprine to mycophenolate may be required in order to optimize urate-lowering therapy and allow prescription of a xanthine oxidase inhibitor. In patients without kidney stones, probenecid or benzbromarone can be effective if xanthine oxidase inhibitor agents are not tolerated.

### Outcome

Patients with recurrent gout flares and tophi have high disability scores and poor health-related quality of life. Work productivity is also reduced in patients with severe gout, with an estimated . The incremental mean work day loss of 25.1 days per year.

direct cost of gout has been estimated to range from US$3165 to US$5515 (2004 and 2005 values, respectively) per annum, increasing to US$10,222 to US$21,467 (2008 values) per annum for patients with frequent gout flares or tophi.

Data from the US National Health and Wellness Survey has shown that people with uncontrolled gout (defined as serum urate >6 mg/dL or at least one gout flare in the past year) have higher presenteeism, overall work impairment, activity impairment, and more emergency department visits than those with controlled gout (defined as serum urate ≤6 mg/dL and no gout flares in the past year) or people without gout. Overall, patients with uncontrolled gout had both higher indirect and total costs compared with patients with controlled gout; importantly, there was no significant difference in total costs between patients with controlled gout and people without gout.

In patients with gout treated in primary care, physical function and health-related quality of life (HRQOL) are impaired by gout-specific factors and comorbidities. Gout-specific factors include recent gout flare, frequent gout flares, tophi, oligo/polyarticular flares, and body pain. Comorbid conditions that affect health-related quality of life in people with gout include diabetes mellitus, stroke, renal failure, myocardial infarction, and obesity. Several clinical trials have shown that urate-lowering therapy can significantly improve health-related quality of life, intensive urate-lowering with pegloticase led to improvement in SF-36 scores over 6 months,90 and nurse-led care according to British Society for Rheumatology (BSR) guidelines led to improvements in the SF-36 physical function scale and the gout impact scale.

### Strategies to Improve Gout Care

Despite the widespread availability of effective anti-inflammatory medications and many urate-lowering therapy options, gout continues to have a large impact on patients, their families, and their communities, due to painful flares, joint damage, disability, and loss of productivity.
