Numerous studies from many different countries have demonstrated low rates of urate-lowering therapy prescription, infrequent serum urate monitoring, suboptimal dosing of urate-lowering therapy when prescribed, and poor attainment of serum urate targets in those who do have serum urate testing. .138-140 Although urate-lowering therapy may not be required for those with infrequent flares and low MSU crystal load, many patients with recurrent flares or other indications for urate-lowering therapy are exposed to the risks of anti-inflammatory medications such as NSAIDs and high-dose corticosteroids without appropriate prescribing of long-term urate-lowering therapy. Unfortunately, even when urate-lowering therapy is prescribed, continuation rates are very low.

Perceptions of gout within the lay community and by health care professionals contribute to stigma and ineffective management strategies. Consistent with cultural representations about gout over many centuries, many patients describe that their friends, family members, and health care professionals view the disease with humor. Within contemporary depictions of gout, diet is widely portrayed as the cause and solution of the illness. 144 Interactions that promote the belief that gout is a self-inflicted disease caused by personal indiscretion can lead to embarrassment and prevent patients seeking medical care.

A key challenge to gout management is establishment and maintenance oflong-term urate-lowering therapy. The reasons for low rates of urate-lowering therapy initiation and continuation

are likely multifactorial and involve both health care provider and patient barriers, including beliefs that that gout is an intermittent flaring illness that only requires acute treatment, lack of knowledge about the role of urate-lowering therapy, perception of gout as self-inflicted due to personal indiscretion, and systems barriers to long-term therapy (time constraints, inconvenience, cost of long-term therapy). Patients may also intentionally stop their urate-lowering therapy because they are reluctant to take a medicine every day or are concerned about potential side effects. 145, E ducation s trategies t hat f ocus o n t he b iologic basis of disease, including the physiologic role of the kidney and gut in regulating serum urate concentrations, chronic deposition of MSU crystals, and the role of these crystals in triggering gout flares, p rovides a c lear r ationale for l ong-term u rate-lowering therapy.

Gout treatment, if it occurs at all, usually occurs in primary care, and new approaches for improved care have been described. Practice-based quality improvement approaches can lead to better care. A multifaceted primary care gout management improvement intervention has been described that includes engagement of intervention-site staff, s urveys o f p rovider p erformance improvement preferences, onsite live and enduring online education, electronic health record reminders, and monthly reports to providers comparing their measures against their peers. After 6 months, this intervention significantly improved gout quality performance indicators, including the percentage of patients with gout treated with urate-lowering therapy from 54.4% to 61.1%, the percentage with serum urate monitored from 56.1% to 79.2%, and the percentage at serum urate target increased from 26.7% to 43.3%. The numbers treated did not significantly improve at a control site, and all quality measures were higher with the intervention compared with the control site after 6 months.

Primary care models of care that include nurses or pharmacists have been described.148, A large randomized controlled trial within primary care has demonstrated that nurse-led care according to British Society for Rheumatology guidelines leads to major improvements in outcomes for patients with gout. In this study, nurses provided patients with holistic assessment, discussion of illness perceptions, and full information on gout (nature, causes, associations, consequences, and treatment options) and encouraged them to share in decision making. Follow-up assessments and measurement of serum urate concentrations were done as often as required by the nurse. Telephone contact (e.g., to review serum urate results) could be substituted for face-to-face visits, and home visits were permitted (e.g., for older patients). If the nurses had questions about gout management, they could seek advice from a rheumatologist. Compared with usual general practice care, nurseled care was associated with high uptake of and adherence to uratelowering therapy in more than 95% of study participants. More patients receiving nurse-led care had serum urate concentrations less than 6 mg/dL at 2 years than those receiving the usual care (95% vs 30%). At 2 years, greater improvements in gout flares, tophi, physical function, and the patient-reported gout impact questionnaires were observed with nurse-led care. The n urse-led intervention was cost-effective in the s hort-term a nd p otentially cost-saving in the long-term. This m odel r epresents a m ajor advance in improved care for the increasing numbers of people with gout; models such as these should be considered for adoption around the world.

# Calcium Crystal Disease: Calcium Pyrophosphate Deposition Disease and Basic Calcium Phosphate-Associated Syndromes

### KEY POINTS

### Introduction

Both calcium pyrophosphate (CPP) and basic calcium phosphate (BCP) crystals are highly inflammatory in some settings and can coexist in individual joints. They share some common mineralization pathways. No disease-remitting agents for either calcium pyrophosphate deposition (CPPD) disease or BCP-associated arthritis currently exist. Attention to the important clinical syndromes associated with calcium-containing crystals in rheumatology has lagged behind many less common rheumatic diseases. In this chapter, we discuss the clinical and epidemiologic features of CPPD and BCP-associated disease, explore pathogenic pathways, and summarize current diagnostic strategies and management paradigms.

### Calcium Pyrophosphate Deposition Disease

CPPD is a relatively new disease, first described in the early 1960s. It is defined by the presence of articular CPP crystals and includes a spectrum of both acute and chronic presentations of arthritis collectively known as CPPD. It remains considerably underdiagnosed and is quite common in elderly patients. The diagnosis is primarily based on CPP crystal identification using polarized light microscopy and characteristic radiographic findings. Treatment modalities remain largely symptomatic and are supported by few high-quality studies.

### Clinical Features

### KEY POINTS

### Acute Calcium Pyrophosphate Crystal Arthritis

Acute CPP crystal arthritis, formerly known as pseudogout, is by far the most commonly recognized clinical presentation of

CPPD disease. This type of arthritis produces acute onset of severe pain, swelling, erythema, and warmth of the involved joint. It typically causes a monoarticular or oligoarticular arthritis. The knee is most commonly involved, followed by the wrist. The ankles, shoulders, and elbows are also common sites of acute CPP crystal arthritis. Small joints in the feet and hands may also be involved and, in these cases, inflammation often spreads beyond the joint. Fever is common, and accompanying signs of inflammation, including circulating leukocytosis, and high inflammatory markers are typical. These features render acute CPP crystal arthritis indistinguishable from gout and septic arthritis in the absence of synovial analysis. Acute CPP crystal arthritis episodes are self-limited but typically last longer than gout attacks, with symptoms present for up to several weeks in the absence of treatment. The natural history of acute CPP crystal arthritis is not fully understood. A recent study showed that in 70 patients with acute CPP crystal arthritis, 25% had a second flare with a rate of 11.4 per 100 person-years.

Crowned dens syndrome is a variant of acute CPP crystal arthritis involving the cervical spine. It typically presents with acute or subacute onset of severe neck pain and limited range of motion. This is often accompanied by fever, and sometimes by delirium. Chondrocalcinosis seen on computed tomography (CT) scanning in the soft tissues around the dens helps confirm the diagnosis. Occasionally, aspiration is done, but this is a tricky area to access. As in all forms of acute CPP crystal arthritis, inflammatory markers are elevated and peripheral white blood cell counts may be high. Crowned dens syndrome is often mistaken for meningitis. Less commonly, the differential diagnosis includes giant cell arteritis, polymyalgia rheumatica, tumor, epidural abscess, or fever of unknown origin. Like all acute CPP crystal arthritis, crowned dens syndrome is self-limited, but attack length can vary from days to months.

### Chronic Inflammatory Calcium Pyrophosphate Crystal Arthritis

Chronic inflammatory CPPD is challenging to diagnosis and often falls under the umbrella terms of seronegative inflammatory arthritis or seronegative rheumatoid arthritis (RA). It is characterized by chronic inflammation in multiple joints. The joint involvement is less symmetric than RA. The joint distribution is similar to that of acute CPP crystal arthritis and typically involves the 2nd and 3rd metacarpophalangeal joints, wrists, elbows, shoulders, knees, and ankles. Accompanying symptoms and signs may include prolonged morning stiffness, fatigue, synovitis on physical examination, and high inflammatory markers. About 10% of patients will have low-titer positive rheumatoid factors (RFs), likely related to the increased prevalence of RF positivity with age.

### Calcium Pyrophosphate Deposition With Osteoarthritis

CPP crystals are present in 20% to 30% of patients diagnosed with knee osteoarthritis (OA). This rate is very consistent across different studies.7, CPPD limited to the knee accompanied by a history of prior meniscal surgery or injury may represent a unique limited form of CPPD. If CPPD involves multiple joints, the pattern of joint involvement differs from typical OA. CPPD with OA involves joints such as the shoulder, wrist, metacarpophalangeal joints, and ankles. Affected individuals may or may not have

attacks of acute CPP crystal arthritis. Interestingly, several studies have demonstrated higher pain scores in patients with calciumcontaining crystals in knee joints compared with those without evidence of crystals. 10,11

### Asymptomatic Calcium Pyrophosphate e Deposition

Chondrocalcinosis is often seen as an incidental finding on conventional radiographs in the absence of articular symptoms. This may be an early phase of CPPD disease, which precedes symptom onset. As such, it is analogous to asymptomatic hyperuricemia, which increases the risk for symptomatic disease but in and of itself does not warrant therapy.

### Less Common Clinical Manifestations of Calcium Pyrophosphate Deposition

Tophaceous CPPD. Tophaceous CPP crystal deposits are unusual and described almost exclusively in case reports. They are often tumor-like in that they invade bone and very frequently are diagnosed by biopsy. They are most frequently described in the periarticular areas around large joints such as hips and shoulders1 and can also occur in the temporomandibular joint.

Spinal Involvement in CPPD. Radiographic chondrocalcinosis is a common finding in the spine of older patients,15 yet the incidence of symptoms attributable to spinal CPPD is unknown. Radiographic CPPD in the spine typically involves annulus fibrosus calcifications, subchondral erosions, and vacuum phenomena of the sacroiliac joints. Crowned dens syndrome is the most commonly recognized form of spinal CPPD. However, other clinical presentations abound. In the largest study of spinal CPPD, 37 of 152 hospitalized patients with spinal CPPD had symptoms of inflammation. Peripheral joint involvement was common and the most frequent site of involvement was the cervical spine. The ligamentum flavum is a common site of crystal deposition. Presentations other than crowned dens syndrome varied from discitis to sacroiliitis to mass effects from tophaceous CPP crystal deposits in or near the spine. Facet joints can be involved. Severe degenerative changes were also noted.

Charcot-like Arthropathy. This is a very rare type of CPPD, characterized by a severe destructive arthritis similar to that seen with Charcot arthropathy, but in the absence of significant neuropathology. 17, It has been most frequently described in the foot and ankle.

Clinical Presentations of CPPD Associated With Genetic or Metabolic Causes. Age and injury are the major risk factors for CPPD. Indeed, the prevalence of chondrocalcinosis doubles with each decade over the age of 60 and is rare in younger people.19, Joint injury as a risk factor for CPPD has been best studied in the knee² but has also been observed in discs after spinal surgeries. 21 The onset of CPPD in patients under the age of 60 without injury warrants investigation for familial or metabolic causes.

Genetic Causes. Familial forms of CPPD were described in the early CPPD literature. Most kindreds show an autosomal dominant pattern of inheritance. Initial analysis of multiple kindreds showed two clusters of mutations in affected families. The cluster of mutations on chromosome 5P in the region known as CCAL2 were noted to be in a gene coding for a protein called progressive ankylosis protein homolog (ANKH) in 2002.23, The multipass transmembrane ANKH protein increases local levels of pyrophosphate in cartilage by regulating extra-cellular adenosine triphosphate (ATP) levels. Presumed gain of function mutations cause CPPD. The second cluster of mutations on 8q was termed

CCAL1.26 In 2014 a family with premature OA and CPPD was shown to have a mutation in the osteoprotegerin gene. Subsequently, other CPPD kindreds were described with this identical mutation. This mutation has recently been shown to produce a loss of function in this critical mineralization-regulating protein best known for its role in bone metabolism. The mechanism through which it contributes to CPPD remains to be determined.

### Epidemiology

### KEY POINTS

The prevalence of symptomatic CPPD disease is unknown. Prevalence of chondrocalcinosis on conventional radiographs underestimates CPP deposition given only moderate sensitivity for CPPD, but likely overestimates symptomatic arthritis. Billing codes may underestimate the prevalence of symptomatic CPPD due to underdiagnosis.

Radiographic chondrocalcinosis is more prevalent with older age. The relative frequency of different manifestations of CPPD disease has not been well characterized at a population level.

### Disease Prevalence

Historical estimates of CPPD prevalence were based on studies reporting the prevalence of chondrocalcinosis on conventional 19, These studies consisradiographs (CRs) of the knee. tently identified a greater prevalence of chondrocalcinosis with older age (up to 30% among adults age 85 and older) (Table 98.1). Radiographic studies were the basis for estimating that 8 to 10 million adults in the United States have CPPD. However, such studies likely underestimate the prevalence of CPPD given the limited sensitivity of CR for detecting CPP deposits. On the other hand, studies employing CR likely overestimate the prevalence of symptomatic CPPD disease since population-based surveys are generally not able to distinguish between and asymptomatic chondrocalcinosis and

symptomatic joint disease, including acute CPP crystal arthritis, chronic CPP crystal inflammatory arthritis, and OA with CPPD.

Prevalence estimates of the various manifestations of symptomatic CPPD disease are not well defined. Two 21st-century population-based studies in Europe provide estimates of symptomatic CPPD disease. A Swedish study reported the prevalence of "nongout crystal arthropathy" as 0.23% based on diagnosis codes, and the prevalence of codes for "pseudogout" in a UK study was 0.02% (Table 98.1).35, While these diagnosis codes provide a proxy for symptomatic CPPD disease, the sensitivity, specificity, and positive and negative predictive values of these codes have not been validated. It is likely that the true prevalence of symptomatic CPPD disease exceeds estimates based on diagnosis codes due to underdiagnosis of CPPD disease, including misdiagnosis as RA or seronegative inflammatory arthritis.5, There is no consistent association between chondrocalcinosis and biologic sex. A recent large case-control study identified male sex to be significantly associated with acute CPP crystal arthritis, but this association remains to be studied in other large cohorts with this phenotype of CPPD disease.

### Clinical Associations With Calcium Pyrophosphate Deposition Disease

Table 98.2 summarizes key clinical factors that have been associated with chondrocalcinosis and/or symptomatic CPPD disease. 1, Older age and joint trauma are consistently identified as positively associated with CPPD. CPPD is rare in persons younger than 60 years old, except in cases of familial CPPD disease characterized by ANKH or osteoprotegerin mutations.29, OA is strongly associated with CPPD disease, though it remains unclear whether CPP crystals are a cause or consequence of OA.41,

Several comorbidities and medications linked to CPPD pathophysiology deserve specific mention. Magnesium facilitates CPP crystal dissolution in vitro, and persistent hypomagnesemia such as in Gitelman syndrome has been associated with CPPD disease. Positive associations between proton pump inhibitors and chondrocalcinosis, and between loop diuretics and acute CPP crystal arthritis, may be due to hypomagnesemia. 36,

Hyperparathyroidism and hereditary hemochromatosis have consistently shown associations with chondrocalcinosis.9, Hypophosphatasia, characterized by deficiency of alkaline phosphatase—the enzyme responsible for breakdown of inorganic pyrophosphate—has been linked to CPPD disease in case reports and has not been carefully investigated in large-scale studies, perhaps because of the low prevalence of this metabolic disorder.40, Interestingly, arthritis rarely improves after appropriate management of the underlying cause in cases of metabolic diseases.

Many of the publications on CPPD disease before the 21st century were based on case reports and small clinic-based cohorts. Larger-scale epidemiologic studies in the 21st century evaluating associations between CPPD disease and other factors typically identified patients using diagnosis codes. Diagnosis codes for chondrocalcinosis and calcium metabolism disorders demonstrated high positive predictive value (PPV) of 91% for symptomatic CPPD disease in a nationwide Veterans Administration data set using other types of inflammatory arthritis as the comparator group but had a less robust PPV of 68% in an academic medical 47, Accurate identification of acute CPP crystal arthritis in center. electronic health record data was possible using machine learning approaches that integrate data from narrative notes and radiology reports with structured data, including synovial fluid crystal analysis laboratory results and diagnosis codes, achieving a PPV of 81%. Application of these methods to population-based data in the United States is challenging given the lack of a nationwide electronic health record system, though may be promising in contexts in which electronic health records are available for an entire population.

### Long-Term Outcomes in Calcium Pyrophosphate Deposition Disease

Approximately 25% of individuals with an initial episode of acute CPP crystal arthritis have recurrent episodes, as reported in two small cohort studies.49, Patients with a history of cancer or chemotherapy may be at greater risk for recurrent episodes of acute CPP crystal arthritis.49, Studies investigating the association between radiographic chondrocalcinosis and progression of OA have produced conflicting results, as summarized in Table 98.3. Two large cohort studies identified no association, one study identified an inverse association, and yet another study reported a positive association between chondrocalcinosis and progressive cartilage loss.43, Differences in study population demographics and modes of cartilage assessment might account for discrepant findings.

Extra-articular outcomes in CPPD disease remain understudied. Cardiovascular disease is a leading cause of morbidity and mortality in gout, RA, psoriatic arthritis, and systemic lupus erythematosus, but few studies have focused on cardiovascular disease in CPPD disease.53-57 Two recent cohort studies reported a significantly increased risk of nonfatal cardiovascular events (myocardial infarction, acute coronary syndrome, coronary revascularization, or stroke) in patients with CPPD disease versus matched compar- .39, Risk of cardiovascular events was 25% greater in U.S. ators. Veterans with CPPD disease versus matched controls. Individuals having had an episode of acute CPP crystal arthritis had an even higher two-fold increased risk for cardiovascular events in an academic medical center cohort study.

### Diagnosis

### KEY POINTS

Compensated polarized light microscopy is an imperfect gold standard but remains a critical test for confirming a diagnosis of CPPD disease. Ryan and McCarty's proposed diagnostic criteria were developed in an era preceding availability of advanced imaging modalities that have since demonstrated high accuracy for identifying CPP deposits. Ultrasound demonstrates greater sensitivity and only slightly lower specificity for CPP deposits compared with conventional radiography.

Diagnostic uncertainty and delay in diagnosing CPPD disease impact the patient experience of disease. Individuals with chronic CPP crystal inflammatory arthritis may be initially misdiagnosed with seronegative RA due to the clinical similarity and lack of recognition of chronic CPP crystal inflammatory arthritis as a disease entity, leading to unsuccessful courses of RA treatments.5, Methods to improve diagnostic accuracy for CPPD disease, as well as campaigns to increase provider awareness, have potential to facilitate earlier diagnosis, especially for patients with chronic CPP crystal inflammatory arthritis.

Ryan and McCarty's proposed diagnostic criteria for CPPD disease characterize three degrees of certainty based on the amount of evidence: definite, probable, and possible. In their schematic, a definite diagnosis of CPPD requires both synovial fluid crystal analysis demonstrating CPP crystals and chondrocalcinosis on CR in a symptomatic joint. A probable diagnosis of CPPD disease requires just one or the other of these, and possible CPPD disease is characterized by OA in unusual joints or a number of other features.

Synovial fluid analysis remains a critical diagnostic tool for CPPD. As shown in Fig. 98.1, CPP crystals are positively birefringent and rhomboid or rod shaped. They can be seen inside cells and are also significant when found extra-cellularly.

Compared with monosodium urate (MSU) crystals, they are less brightly birefringent and are often more sparse and smaller (Fig. 98.2). Up to 20% of CPP crystals may not demonstrate any birefringence. Accurate identification of CPP crystals requires some training. However, in one recent study, even experienced rheumatologists showed only a 39% accuracy in identifying CPP crystals. If a polarized light microscope is not immediately available, synovial fluid can be spun and dried on a microscope slide62 or mixed with heparin and refrigerated to preserve CPP crystals.

Imaging plays an increasingly important role in CPPD diagnosis, particularly for ultrasound. This concept is reflected in the European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology (EULAR) CPPD Working Group 2011 proposed updates to CPPD diagnosis, which recognize the limitations of CR and the favorable performance of advanced imaging modalities. While advanced imaging modalities hold promise for facilitating accurate diagnosis of CPPD disease, the EULAR definitions require presence of CPP crystals in synovial fluid or on histology for definite diagnosis. An international working group of rheumatologists and musculoskeletal radiologists recently developed definitions of imaging features characteristic of CPPD along with example images, including images of BCP deposits for contrast. The CR definitions have been tested in an independent cohort of patients scheduled for knee replacement and demonstrated moderate to high interreader reliability and high specificity (92%) with moderate sensitivity (54%) using tissue histology as the reference standard.

CR of joints affected by CPPD shows fine stippled radioopaque deposits referred to as chondrocalcinosis (Figs. 98.3, 98.4, and 98.5). Many other radiographic features, such as tendon calcifications, patterns of cartilage loss, and large subchondral cysts, have also been described in CPPD. CR is the most widely used radiographic test for joint assessment but its sensitivity for CPP deposition is only moderate. A recent meta-analysis of studies spanning three decades that used synovial fluid crystal analysis of the knee as the reference standard reported that CR

had a pooled sensitivity of only 0.59 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.530.65) for CPPD. Though CR demonstrates good specificity for CPPD 0.95 (CI 0.920.97) and high PPV 0.83 (CI 0.730.90), its low sensitivity and moderate negative predictive value (NPV) 0.76 (CI 0.710.80) suggest that CR does not optimally detect CPPD.

Ultrasound is increasingly recognized as a sensitive and specific modality for identifying CPP crystals, with a pooled sensitivity of 0.85 (CI 0.800.88) and pooled specificity of 0.91 (CI 0.880.94) using synovial fluid crystal analysis as the reference

standard. The high PPV 0.86 (CI 0.81-0.90) and high NPV 0.90 (CI 0.860.93) of ultrasound support its diagnostic accuracy. The Outcome Measures in Rheumatology (OMERACT) CPPD Ultrasound Subtask Force developed and validated definitions for ultrasound findings characteristic of CPPD.33, Key ultrasonographic features of CPPD include hyperechoic deposits of variable shape and size, localized within the fibrocartilage or hyaline cartilage, tendon, or synovial fluid, that remain within cartilage or tendon during dynamic assessment or that move within the synovial fluid during dynamic assessment (Fig. 98.6).

### Pathogenesis

### KEY POINTS

CPP crystal formation is essential to disease pathogenesis and yet is incompletely understood.

Once formed, CPP crystals can produce inflammation, have direct destructive effects on articular tissues, and disrupt joint biomechanics.

Although significant progress has been made over the 60-year period since CPPD was initially described, CPPD pathogenesis remains incompletely understood. CPPD begins with crystal deposition in the extra-cellular matrix of articular hyaline and

fibrocartilage. Once established, CPP crystals can cause joint damage and arthritis through several mechanisms. CPP crystals can induce inflammatory effects, mechanical effects, and directly damage cells in cartilage and bone.

### Crystal Formation

Many factors are involved in CPP crystal formation. This process most often takes place in cartilage matrix and is rare in other tissues. An overabundance of pyrophosphate (PPi) in the extracellular matrix of cartilage is an essential requirement for crystal formation. Thus PPi metabolism has been the focus of much of the work on CPP pathogenesis. PPi is generated constitutively by chondrocytes and regulated by factors such as transforming

growth factor-β and interleukin (IL)-1β. ATP transporters, notably the ANKH protein, also regulate chondrocyte PPi levels. Extra-cellular matrix also plays a role in crystal formation. More recently, bone abnormalities have been implicated in CPP crystal formation.

### Inflammation

CPP crystals induce inflammation through pathways similar to those of monosodium urate crystals, which involve the NLRP3 inflammasome,73 and neutrophil extra-cellular traps. Through activation of nuclear factor-kB and mitogen-activated protein kinases, CPP crystals promote the release of active IL-1β from inflammatory cells. While factors triggering an inflammatory response from crystals (an acute attack) have not been fully elucidated, it has been proposed that joint injury may dislodge crystals from their protected environment in cartilage. Similar to what occurs in gout, events that promote crystal dissolution may also initiate inflammation as small crystals are more inflammatory than large ones.

### Direct Effects on Cartilage and Synovium

CPP crystals exert direct effects on chondrocytes and synovial cells. They induce synovial fibroblast replication in synovial cells and protease production by chondrocytes.

### Treatment

### KEY POINTS

Management of CPPD disease is guided by the presenting manifestation(s). The EULAR 2011 CPPD management recommendations include pharmacologic and nonpharmacologic treatment for acute CPP crystal arthritis and chronic CPP crystal inflammatory arthritis; no specific therapies are recommended for OA with CPPD aside from typical OA treatments. Medical therapies to prevent CPP crystal formation or to remove CPP crystals from the joint do not currently exist.

Acute CPP crystal arthritis is usually treated with NSAIDs, colchicine, and/or glucocorticoids, and treatment selection is partly guided by comorbidities and avoidance of medication interactions.77, Rest and ice may help with symptoms but are unlikely to be adequate alone. Joint aspiration aids in diagnosis and ruling out gout or septic arthritis and can also provide therapeutic benefit. Intra-articular glucocorticoid injection is a good option for treating monoarthritis once septic arthritis has been ruled out. A short course of oral glucocorticoids (several days to several weeks) is often used, especially for patients with acute CPP

crystal arthritis in multiple joints. A short course (e.g., 3 to 9 days) of the IL-1 inhibitor anakinra showed benefit for treating acute CPP crystal arthritis in a number of case reports.78, A randomized controlled trial comparing a 3-day regimen of anakinra versus prednisone was terminated early due to recruitment challenges; among the 15 participants, changes in pain scores and C-reactive protein (CRP) showed a trend toward favoring anakinra without reaching statistical significance.

A recent large randomized controlled trial of treatment for acute CPP crystal arthritis merits specific mention. One group enrolled hospitalized adults age 65 and older with an estimated glomerular filtration rate greater than 30 mL/min/1.73 m2 and acute CPP crystal arthritis duration of 36 hours or less. One hundred and twelve participants were randomized a 2-day regimen of oral prednisone 30 mg daily (days 1 and 2) or oral colchicine (1.0 mg followed by 0.5 mg 1 hour later on day 1, plus 1 mg once on day 2). All participants received acetaminophen 1000 mg three times daily and tramadol 50 mg three times daily on day 1. Providers were permitted to prescribe prednisone, colchicine, or other treatments as needed on day 3 onward. The betweengroup difference in change in pain on the visual analog scale at 24 hours was -1.2 mm, which was not statistically significant. Notably, some patients continued to receive prednisone, colchicine, or other treatments after day 2 for pain relief. Diarrhea was the main adverse event in the colchicine group (26%), and hypertension was the most common adverse event in the prednisone group (13%). These results support the equivalence of a short course of colchicine or prednisone for patients with acute CPP crystal arthritis, in the context of other pain relief medications.

Chronic CPP crystal inflammatory arthritis can be challenging to treat. Methotrexate has been evaluated in several studies, including a randomized controlled trial among 26 participants that did not detect a difference in outcomes between methotrexate and placebo; however, it should be noted that the maximum methotrexate dose was only 15 mg per week and the study duration was only 3 months, which likely limited the ability to truly assess the potential impact of methotrexate on CPPD disease. Hydroxychloroquine 400 mg per day had a beneficial effect on swollen and tender joint counts and pain in patients with CPPD disease (phenotypes were not well described) versus placebo in a randomized trial among 36 participants. A small randomized controlled trial in 38 participants with "chronic pyrophosphate arthropathy" compared 6 months of oral magnesium 30 milliequivalents per day versus placebo and reported a nonsignificant trend toward improved joint stiffness with magnesium regardless of initial serum magnesium level. Oral colchicine demonstrated a reduced number of flares in a small trial of 10 patients with chronic CPP crystal arthritis, though the majority of patients were also using NSAIDs, which may have contributed to the observed reduction in flares. Synovial destruction via intra-articular irradiation produced reductions in pain, joint stiffness, and effusion among 15 patients with chronic CPP crystal arthritis of the knee, though this mechanism has not been well explored in recent decades.

IL-1 and IL-6 receptor inhibitors are promising for the treatment of chronic CPP inflammatory arthritis. A systematic literature review included pooled data from seven patients with chronic CPP crystal arthritis treated with anakinra for 139 days on average; tender and swollen counts and CRP levels decreased post-anakinra compared with pre-anakinra. A recent pilot study evaluating the use of tocilizumab in 1 1 patients with CPPD disease

(7 with chronic CPP crystal inflammatory arthritis and 4 with recurrent acute CPP crystal arthritis) reported improved patient global assessment at 3 months and ability to taper prednisone.

Classification criteria for CPPD disease, recently published and endorsed jointly by the American College of Rheumatology and EULAR, will facilitate identification of patients for enrollment in clinical trials to identify effective treatments for CPPD disease.86,86a,86b The OMERACT CPPD Working Group is establishing a set of core outcome domains to be measured in future clinical trials, which will facilitate comparisons across studies. .

### Basic Calcium Phosphate-Associated Arthritis

BCP crystals refer to submicron-sized calcium phosphate crystals including carbonate-substituted hydroxyapatite, octacalcium, tricalcium phosphates, and magnesium whitlockite. In the musculoskeletal system, BCP crystals are most commonly associated with two clinical syndromes; calcific periarthritis and BCP-associated arthritis. The detection of BCP crystals in the synovial fluid is fraught with challenges due to the submicroscopic size of BCP, the complex nature of the matrix in which they are found, and the fact that other crystals can coexist. Hence, diagnosis is based on radiographic detection of calcifications characteristic of BCP crystals or detection of BCP crystals confirmed by transmission electron microscopy or specialized crystal analytic approaches.

### Clinical Manifestations

### KEY POINTS

BCP deposition is often asymptomatic but can be associated with a wide spectrum of clinical manifestations. Although BCP crystals most frequently deposit in joint tissue, these deposits can also be found in the arteries, skin, breasts, and other tissues. In the musculoskeletal system, crystals are localized to cartilage, synovium, bursae, intervertebral discs, and tendon.90, Periarticular BCP crystal deposition can lead to calcific tendinitis, periarthritis, bursitis, and bone erosions. Intra-articular BCP crystal deposition is associated with a variety of degenerative manifestations, most notably Milwaukee shoulder syndrome (MSS), a form of apatiteassociated destructive arthropathy. It can also cause acute synovitis (albeit to a much lesser extent than CPP) and severe OA. Several secondary forms of BCP crystal-associated arthropathy have also been described (e.g., tumoral calcinosis, and calciphylaxis, which is a severe complication of renal failure characterized by nodular subcutaneous calcifications). Currently, there are no validated classification criteria for BCP arthritis. In CPPD arthritis, a dataand expert-driven process is currently underway and

is near completion to develop CPPD classification criteria. It is likely there will be similar work on establishing BCP classification in the future. Such criteria would facilitate clinical research and help address the major shortfalls in recognizing, understanding, and specifically treating the disorder (Table 98.4).

### Periarticular Basic Calcium Phosphate

Acute calcific periarthritis (ACP) is a self-limiting, monoarticular, periarticular process of dystrophic mineral deposition and adjacent inflammation. It is thought to be caused by the rupture of pre-existing calcific deposits and their transport into an adjacent soft tissue space, which in turn drives an acute inflammatory reaction. Patients present with a sudden onset of pain, localized swelling, erythema, tenderness, and restricted range of motion. Symptoms typically reduce in severity within 4 to 7 days and generally self-resolve in 3 to 4 weeks. As the name suggests, mineral deposition is most prevalent in a periarticular location; however, deposits within a bursa, at tendon insertions, or fascial attachments distant to the joint may also occur. Calcific periarthritis has a predilection for the shoulder but it can be found in any joint area of the body. Shoulder involvement is typically a painful disorder characterized by the presence of calcifications in either the midsubstance or insertion of the rotator cuff tendons and in the synovial tissues, including the subacromial bursa. The supraspinatus tendon (78%) is the most frequently involved, followed by the infraspinatus (16%), the subscapularis (6%), and the long biceps tendons.94, The calcific material is composed of clusters of calcium hydroxyapatite in crystalline or amorphous form. Clinical features include pain related to repetitive activities, tenderness, local edema, and varying degrees of movement impairment. Even without treatment, most patients report symptom resolution in 3 to 4 weeks. Outside the shoulder joint, the periarticular structures are more superficial, and clinical signs such as erythema, swelling, and local tenderness will therefore be more prominent in more superficial joints and may mimic an infective cause. Relapse of ACP is uncommon but a significant number of patients remain symptomatic, with no radiographic evidence of improvement. In these cases, the natural cycle of calcific deposition within tendons followed by resorption is somehow halted. Persistent calcification can lead to local complications of joint tenderness, tendon tears, adhesive capsulitis, and chronic pain.

### Intra-articular Basic Calcium Phosphate

BCP crystals like CPP crystals and urate crystals may induce selflimiting acute inflammatory attacks. Clinical symptoms include rapid onset of pain, soft tissue swelling, and joint mobility reduction. Fever may be present, and laboratory analysis may show increased inflammatory parameters and neutrophil count. An acute inflammatory attack related to BCP crystals can be challenging and is often misdiagnosed as cellulitis, gout, pseudogout, or septic arthritis. This situation can lead to inappropriate management with invasive diagnostic procedures and therapies, including unnecessary antibiotics and surgery.

Intra-articular BCP crystals are associated with a variety of degenerative manifestations, most notably MSS. MSS is the archetypical example of the structural consequences of apatiteassociated destructive arthropathy (Fig. 98.8). It is associated with rotator cuff defects, large joint effusions, and numerous aggregates of BCP crystals in the synovial fluid. There is subluxation of the humeral head from the glenoid fossa, often forming a pseudoarthrosis with the distal clavicle and acromion. In severe cases, destruction of the humeral head can occur. The original case series reported by one group demonstrated a mean age of onset of 73 years with a female preponderance of 4:1. Both shoulders were affected in 82% of cases. The shoulder on the dominant side is uniformly involved in unilateral disease and generally exhibits more advanced features in the case of bilateral joint involvement. Nearly all patients described pain during shoulder motion and at night while lying in bed. Bone-on-bone crepitus is also typical. Joint mobility is restricted or excessively mobile and unstable (when the joint is destroyed). The synovial fluid may be blood tinged as it contains high numbers of erythrocytes but low numbers of leukocytes.

Bony sclerosis and cyst formation in the humeral head are common, as well as cortical erosions of the greater tuberosity at the site of insertion of the rotator cuff. There has been debate as to the role of BCP crystals in the pathogenesis of MSS. It has been proposed that the presence of intra-articular BCP crystals is the consequence of advanced degeneration resulting from exposed bone and they may be present in varying degrees in all

OA joints. However, the scarcity of BCP crystals in advanced secondary degenerative arthropathies, such as those resulting from RA, argues against the concept of BCP as simply an epiphenomenon in MSS.

BCP crystals are common components of advanced large-joint OA. Patients with OA and intra-articular BCP crystals are generally clinically indistinguishable from those with typical OA, although the presence of BCP crystals is postulated to predict rapid progression to end-stage disease due to inflammation driven by a positive feedback loop. Knee joints are commonly affected by BCP deposition, and crystals are frequently found in OA cartilage, synovium, and synovial fluid. Apatite crystals were observed in 60% of synovial fluid samples from patients with knee joint OA in one study. Another small study showed that human knee and hip cartilage harvested at the time of joint replacement contained BCP crystals in 100% of cases and CPPD in 20%. The menisci can also be involved, and one group reported calcium deposition in 100% of OA menisci harvested at the time of joint replacement y105 In contrast to primary OA, lateral tibiofemoral comsurgery. partment involvement is common in BCP-associated destructive knee arthropathy. Concurrent CPPD, biomechanical abnormalities, chronic renal failure, and neuropathic factors appear to be predisposing factors. BCP in normal joints or those with early OA remains difficult to ascertain because BCP crystals are very small even when present in aggregates. Although most patients with BCP-induced arthropathy will present with a monoarticular disease, polyarthropathy can occur, making clinical differentiation from MSU and CPPD crystal-induced inflammation very difficult.

### Epidemiology

### KEY POINT

Much about the prevalence of BCP-associated clinical syndromes remains to be understood.

The epidemiology of BCP crystal deposition is poorly understood, and its true prevalence remains unknown. Prevalence of the various forms of articular BCP crystal deposition disease has been predominantly based on characteristic plain radiographic features of the disease in limited numbers of joints. Other studies have based prevalence on the results of synovial fluid analyses, but definitive studies based on pathologic findings on examination of articular cartilages, or imaging superior to plain radiography, are lacking. As such, the true prevalence of pathologic articular BCP crystal deposition is not known.

BCP crystal deposition was first described by Robert Adams, and later by Duplay, in the shoulder, which remains the most affected site. The best epidemiologic data on calcific periarthritis comes from a U.S. study of more than 12,000 shoulder radiographs undertaken as part of an insurance medical assessment. Calcific tendonitis occurred in 3% of this adult population. Calcifications were more common in women and, unlike other crystal deposition (urate, CPPD), the prevalence was highest in those younger than age 40.94 Calcific periarthritis occurring at sites other than the shoulder is uncommon but not rare. Cases have been reported in the hand, around the elbow, and in the knee, hip, ankle, and foot.108, Although a periarticular location is most common, deposits may be extra-articular and found in

bursae, tendon insertions of large muscles, or fascial attachments. Most calcifications, however, are asymptomatic, with just more than one-third of patients with shoulder involvement being symptomatic110 and one-third reporting antecedent trauma. Calcific shoulder periarthritis is three-fold more common in people with type 2 diabetes mellitus than in ageand sex-matched controls. It also has associations with hyperlipidemia, minor trauma, and hypomagnesemia.11, Diabetes of protracted duration treated with insulin for a long time was associated with a larger percentage of shoulder calcifications. Periarticular calcification is also seen in scleroderma patients and may result in acute calcific periarthritis. In contrast to idiopathic acute calcific periarthritis, resorption of periarticular calcifications after resolution of acute attacks occurs both less frequently and incompletely in scleroderma-associated ACP.

Intra-articular BCP crystal deposition is associated with increasing age and OA. The presence of BCP crystals in the synovial fluid of osteoarthritic knees correlates strongly with the severity of radiographic OA, compared with synovial fluids derived from OA patients without BCP crystals. In contrast to calcific periarthritis, apatite associated destructive arthropathy is more common in elderly women. It targets the shoulders, knees, hips, elbows, and ankles. Synovial fluid is often viscous, with low cell counts. In a comprehensive review using data from more than 72 patients with MSS, the mean (range) age of patients was 72 (5090) years, and there was a 4:1 female preponderance. The dominant shoulder is more commonly affected. Trauma, overuse, neurologic involvement, dialysis, and CPPD were the identifiable risk factors, however, no risk factors were apparent in a large proportion of patients.

### Diagnostic Tools

### KEY POINTS

Because BCP crystals are not consistently birefringent and typically too small to see on regular light microscopy, stains or advanced analytic techniques are necessary to confirm their presence.

The diagnosis of BCP arthritis is based on the presence of characteristic clinical features of joint swelling and pain, in association with synovial fluid analysis that excludes inflammation, infection, and other crystal arthropathies and radiographic imaging showing substantial joint injury. No simple test for BCP crystals is currently available and their detection is difficult due to their small size (nm) and the complexity of the synovial fluid samples in which they are found. Individual crystals are typically less than 1 mm (20100 nm) and aggregate in the synovial fluid to form amorphous-looking clumps. Light microscopy, which is readily available, has a limit of detection (>1 µm) insufficient for detecting most BCP crystals except when they are present in clumps. Microscopy with specific staining such as alizarin red staining of synovial fluid can identify the presence of calcium-containing crystals without distinguishing BCP from CPP crystals (Fig. 98.9). Although CPP crystals stain weaker than BCP crystals, this technique often leads to a false-positive interpretation of results. The preparation and dyeing of samples are laborious processes. As

a result of this, more specific methods have been used, including 14 C-ethane-1-hydroxy-1,1-diphosphonate binding assay, which is sensitive to within 2 µg of standard hydroxyapatite crystals/ mL, 102 and tetracycline staining, which binds to BCP crystals and appears fluorescent under ultraviolet light. 72

X-ray diffraction is used for the examination of BCP crystals and other crystalline materials. It involves a beam of x-rays passed through the specimen and scattered. The scattering of x-rays is observed with a detector that can determine the structural characteristics of the material. Raman spectroscopy is another technique that involves focusing a laser beam onto a sample through a confocal microscope. Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy involves making pellets of 1 to 2 mg of crushed samples mixed with potassium bromide, which are then pressed, and infrared absorption spectra by transmission are collected. Atomic force microscopy can measure microparticles in the order of nanometers and can measure force and topographic images. Transmission electron microscopy uses an accelerated beam of electrons, which passes through a very thin specimen to observe features such as the structure and morphology of electron-dense clumps of needlelike crystals that may be necessary to confirm BCP crystal deposition. Access to this imaging apparatus is limited and widespread availability in clinical practice is limited. Many centers rely on the clinical features of presentation and radiologic imaging for diagnosis. Thus a simple, reliable, and inexpensive method for BCP crystal identification is still needed.

X-ray is useful for identifying calcific tendonitis and MSS. Calcific tendonitis appears on x-ray with homogenous hyperdense calcifications with variable morphology but is typically globular with smooth or ill-defined margins. Milwaukee shoulder has a dramatic appearance on x-ray with bony erosions and destruction of the humeral head, joint space narrowing, large soft tissue swelling, and extensive amorphous calcification. Early radiographic changes consist of a high-riding humeral head due to rotator cuff tear, mild subchondral bone sclerosis, and narrowing of the glenohumeral joint space, with little or no osteophytosis. These changes may stabilize or show minimal cartilage erosions for several years, followed by sudden and dramatic deterioration. The bones on both sides of the joint are severely damaged, with extension into the undersurface of the acromion, the coracoid process, and the distal clavicle. Pseudoarthrosis between the humeral head, coracoid, and acromion is common.

High-resolution ultrasound imaging can detect aggregated BCP-related calcifications outside of joint cartilage including in the rotator cuff of the shoulder. Ultrasound is expedient, inexpensive, does not use irradiation, and can also assess for joint inflammation and alternative diagnoses and guide therapeutic joint aspiration. In BCP deposition, ultrasound has been used in most studies in calcific shoulder syndromes. BCP deposits near the insertion of the supraspinatus tendon can be readily assessed sonographically. They frequently affect the critical zone, which is a poorly vascularized area of the supraspinatus tendon 0.5 to 1 cm proximal to its insertion. Subacromial-subdeltoid bursa widening and positive power Doppler signal over calcifications are strongly associated with increased clinical activity and pain. However, ultrasound cannot differentiate between calcification of different etiology. Ultrasound has a role in guiding therapy in BCP crystal—associated arthropathies. A study reported that ultrasound-guided percutaneous needle aspiration and lavage in calcific tendinitis of the shoulder provides significant improvement in shoulder motion, pain, and disability. For those patients with calcific tendinitis of the shoulder requiring surgery, pre-operative marking of calcific

deposits using ultrasound significantly improves the clinical results of arthroscopic surgery.

Dual-energy computed tomography (DECT) holds the potential for better resolution of BCP crystals and distinguishing these crystals from CPPD. BCP and CPP crystals have specific chemical compositions as shown by the Raman spectroscopic analysis. Typical BCP calcifications are denser than CPP crystal deposits120 and, as materials act differently at different energies depending on their chemical composition, differences in composition can be shown and color-coded with DECT. A recent study has shown promising results with sensitivity of DECT to discriminate between BCP and CPP calcifications of over 90% compared with Raman spectroscopic analysis as the gold standard67 (Table 98.5).

### Pathogenesis

Both the avascular connective tissue of articular cartilage and the fibrocartilaginous meniscus are particularly susceptible to calcification. Crystals of BCP including partially carbonate-substituted hydroxyapatite (HA) may be deposited pathologically in articular cartilage, particularly in OA. Importantly, physiologic non-inflammatory deposition of HA is essential because HA is the principal mineral phase laid down during growth in cartilage and bone. Inflammatory conditions may also result from deposition of HA, as well as the closely related BCP crystals, octacalcium phosphate, and tricalcium phosphate or "whitlockite" in periarticular structures such as the rotator cuff (calcific tendinitis) and subacromial bursa of the shoulder.

The precise mechanisms through which BCP crystal-induced inflammation occurs are still being investigated. In mice, intraarticular injection of BCP crystals results in synovial inflammation, chondrocyte apoptosis and proteoglycan loss, and upregulation of inflammatory cytokines and cartilage-degrading enzymes. OA-associated BCP crystals are considered damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) and can exert an effect on articular cells including fibroblasts, macrophages, and chondrocytes.

In vitro, BCP crystals promote mitogenesis in osteoarthritic synovial fibroblasts and upregulate matrix metalloproteinase (MMP) expression in both porcine articular chondrocytes122 and human fibroblasts. . These crystals have been shown to promote prostaglandin E2, IL-1β, and cyclooxygenase production by human fibroblasts, TNF and IL-1 production by macrophages, 125,126 and IL-6 production by chondrocytes.

The direct binding of BCP crystals to the cell membrane of macrophages activates the membrane-proximal tyrosine-protein kinase SYK and downstream phosphoinositide 3-kinase, resulting in the upregulation of proinflammatory cytokines, MMPs, and DAMPs such as protein S100A8.92, Furthermore, the release of S100A8 can function in a feedback manner and bind to Tolllike receptor 4 and/or advanced glycosylation end product—specific receptor expressed on the cell surface to directly upregulate inflammatory mediators.

Although not a DAMP, IL-6 is a potential contributor to BCP crystal-induced inflammation and is an essential mediator of hypoxia-inducible factor 2α (HIFα)−induced cartilage destruction in mice. The catabolic effects of HIF2α on cartilage have been attributed to IL-6-induced MMP3 and MMP13 expression by chondrocytes. Furthermore, the addition of recombinant IL-6 to murine chondrocyte cultures resulted in increased calcium-containing crystal formation and the expression of genes encoding proteins involved in the calcification process including ANKH, the sodium/phosphate cotransporter pituitary-specific positive transcription factor and the calcium channel annexin A5.127

Osteopontin promotes MMP activation, macrophage recruitment, oxidative stress, and osteoclast activation. It also acts as a regulator of biomineralization and a potent inhibitor of vascular calcification and restrains BCP crystal deposition. It can be detected in fibroblast-like cells and multinucleated macrophages surrounding areas of calcification in calcific tendinitis. Osteopontin is highly enriched in regions of the bone surface where osteoclasts are anchored. There is also an expression of

osteopontin, cathepsin K, and tissue transglutaminase 2 (TTG2) messenger RNA in calcific periarthritis. The increased expression of osteopontin and TTG2 could be attributed to increased production in the calcific area, probably by osteoclast-like cells involved in the resorptive phase. This may suggest a mechanism for both resorption of BCP crystal deposits and tendon degeneration.

### Treatment

### KEY POINT

Treatment of BCP-related syndromes typically include anti-inflammatory strategies including NSAIDs and glucocorticoids.

NSAIDs and local glucocorticoid injection are effective treatment options for BCP crystal-associated calcific tendinitis and subacromial bursitis. BCP crystal—associated inflammation of the rotator cuff and subacromial bursa of the shoulder can be successfully treated by using needle aspiration, irrigation, and

steroid injections. Ultrasound-guided techniques, which promote the resorption of calcifications, can enhance the success of such approaches. Other treatment options include barbotage, high-energy extracorporeal shockwave therapy, and arthroscopic 136, Currently, patients with OA complicated by the surgery. presence of BCP crystal deposition are treated in the same manner as patients with usual OA because no additional treatments for this specific complication have been identified or approved. Current treatment options for destructive arthropathies such as MSS are generally unsatisfactory. A conservative approach that includes analgesics and NSAIDs, repeated shoulder aspirations, and joint rest can in some cases control symptoms satisfactorily. Tidal joint irrigation with methylprednisolone and tranexamic acid may be of benefit for symptoms and function in MSS. Surgical therapy is sometimes successful in relieving pain and restoring function but might be difficult to perform if a la rge extent of damage is already present in the joint and periarticular tissues. Joint replacement should be reserved for patients with refractory pain deemed appropriate for this procedure.

# Familial and Nonfamilial Autoinflammatory Syndromes

### KEYI POINTS

Autoinflammatory diseases are rare diseases characterized by recurrent or chronic inflammation.

Dysregulation of the interleukin (IL)-1β pathway is central to many autoinflammatory diseases.

A severe complication of long-standing IL-1β-driven autoinflammation is secondary AA amyloidosis, often leading to renal failure; the risk of this complication is greatly reduced when patients receive adequate treatment.

Because of the central role in many autoinflammatory diseases, a trial of IL-1 inhibiting therapy can be considered for diagnostic and therapeutic purposes.

### Introduction

The autoinflammatory diseases, often referred to as periodic fever syndromes, comprise rare, sometimes hereditary diseases characterized by inflammatory symptoms such as fever, abdominal pain, rash, or arthralgia. The term autoinflammation, coined in 1999,1 reflects that they are the innate counterpart of autoimmune diseases. Innate immunity is considered a first-line defense mechanism against infection and cellular damage. The diseases can be classified based on their pathophysiological mechanism and differences in phenotype into four main groups: interleukin (IL)-1 driven autoinflammatory diseases, interferonopathies, defects of ubiquitination, and nuclear factor kappa B (NF-kB)—associated autoinflammatory syndromes. Of these four, the IL-1-driven autoinflammatory diseases are the best characterized.

### Inflammasomopathies and IL-1-Driven Autoinflammatory Diseases

The term inflammasomopathy is reserved for diseases caused by defects affecting inflammasomes. Inflammasomes are protein complexes that are part of innate immunity. They function as a

danger sensor. Upon activation of the central component of the inflammasome by sensing pathogenor danger-associated molecular patterns, the formation of a multiprotein complex (the inflammasome) is triggered, leading to production of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-1β. Inflammasomes are named after their central sensing component. Multiple inflammasomes have been described, and these are named after their central sensing protein, including the NLRP3, pyrin, NLRP1, NLRP12, and NLRC4 inflammasome.

Chronic or episodical inflammation with fever (Fig. 99.1), abdominal pain, rash, chest pain, musculoskeletal symptoms, and a clear acute phase response with elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), C-reactive protein (CRP), and serum amyloid A (SAA) form the main phenotype in IL-1-driven autoinflammatory diseases.

These diseases include the four classic monogenic autoinflammatory diseases—cryopyrin-associated periodic syndrome, familial Mediterranean fever, TNF-receptor-associated periodic syndrome, and mevalonate kinase deficiency—and diseases without a (clear) genetic background, such as systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis/adult-onset Still's disease and Schnitzler syndrome.

### Cryopyrin-Associated Periodic Syndrome

In the past, three different autoinflammatory diseases were distinguished that are now known to be part of the cryopyrin-associated periodic syndrome (CAPS) spectrum: familial cold urticaria syndrome, Muckle-Wells syndrome, and neonatal-onset multisystem inflammatory disease (also known as the chronic infantile neurologic, cutaneous, articular syndrome). After the finding that all three of these syndromes are caused by variants in the NLRP3 gene, the division between the three phenotypes has largely been abandoned. The exact incidence of CAPS is unknown. Its prevalence is estimated at one to two cases per million.

CAPS is an autosomal dominant disease and is characterized by fever, urticarial skin rash, abdominal pain, myalgia, arthralgia or arthritis, and conjunctivitis (Fig. 99.2). Sterile meningitis, hepatosplenomegaly, or lymphadenopathy may be present. Possible neurologic symptoms are intellectual disability and papilledema.

Recurrent or chronic articular inflammation may lead to contractures with bony overgrowth (Figs. 99.3 and 99.4).

Typical dysmorphic features, such as frontal bossing and a saddle nose, may be present. In some cases, episodes may be triggered by exposure to cold. Patients may develop irreversible sensorineural hearing loss. The duration of attacks can vary between several hours in mildly affected individuals, to continuous inflammation in severely affected individuals. Disease onset is also variable: severe cases present during the neonatal period and, in milder cases, the first attack may not appear until adulthood. In untreated patients, the prevalence of secondary AA amyloidosis is approximately one in three.

### Etiology and Pathogenesis

In 2001, gain-of-function variants were identified in a previously unknown gene (NLRP3; also known as CIAS1 or cryopyrin) in CAPS patients.3-5 Most CAPS-causing variants are missense mutations located in exon 3, coding for the NOD domain of NLRP3.6 Upon stimulation with various ligands, NLRP3 forms interactions with adapter proteins ASC and caspase 1, which results in a multiprotein complex known as the NLRP3or

cryopyrin-inflammasome. Missense mutations in NLRP3 lead to overactivation of the cryopyrin inflammasome, resulting in an increased release of IL-1β [7]. Cells from CAPS patients show increased ASC speck formation, IL-1β release, caspase-1 cleavage, pyroptosis, and higher levels of reactive oxygen species (ROS).7, It has long been unknown which cell types mediated autoinflammation in CAPS, but in 2022 two studies independently showed that pathogenic variants in NLRP3 in macrophages or neutrophils alone is sufficient to trigger autoinflammation in mice.9, The autoinflammatory process is controlled by the leucine-rich repeats domain of NLRP3.11 A significant number of patients, originally described as "mutation-negative," were found to display somatic mosaicism with NLRP3 variants (only cells within the myeloid lineage displaying the mutation).12, Currently, over 100 (pathogenic) variants in NLRP3 have been reported, including some low-penetrance variants in persons that can be asymptomatic. 14,

The most recent diagnostic and classification criteria for CAPS were proposed in 201716 and 201917 (Tables 99.1 and 99.2).

With the exception of sequencing of the NLRP3 gene, there are no diagnostics tests that are able to distinguish CAPS from other

causes of inflammation. The ice cube test (i.e., holding an ice cube to a patch of skin to provoke urticaria) is negative in CAPS.

### Familial Mediterranean Fever

Familial Mediterranean fever (FMF) is the most prevalent autoinflammatory disease, with more than 10,000 patients affected worldwide. It occurs primarily in those originating from around the Mediterranean basin, including Turks, Arabs, Armenians, and non-Ashkenazi Jews. FMF is caused by pathogenic variants in the Mediterranean fever (MEFV) gene. FMF is an autosomal recessive hereditary disease because of pseudodominant inheritance due to consanguinity and a high carrier frequency of MEFV variants. The high carrier frequency is most likely a result of a survival benefit

in heterozygous carriers during plague outbreaks because of resistance against Yersinia pestis. 18

In 90% of patients with FMF, symptoms start before the age of 20 years. The inflammatory attacks usually last 1 to 3 days. Attack frequency varies widely; 2 to 4 weeks between attacks is the most common interval (Fig. 99.1). The main symptoms of FMF are serositis (peritonitis, pleuritis, or synovitis) and fever. Ninety-five percent of patients suffer from abdominal pain. This may be so severe that it mimics acute abdominal pathology, such as acute appendicitis. Arthritis is often confined to a single large joint (knee, wrist, ankle) and may lead to a more protracted course of the present episode. In approximately 30% of patients, the skin is affected, most often as erysipelas-like lesions on the shins or feet (Fig. 99.5).

The main long-term complication of FMF is AA amyloidosis. In historic cohorts, up to 75% of untreated FMF patients developed AA amyloidosis, which mainly affects the kidneys. Accurate treatment protects against amyloidosis. Recurrent attacks of peritonitis may lead to intraabdominal or pelvic adhesions, which may lead to bowel obstruction, or subfertility in women.

FMF remains a mainly clinical diagnosis. The 1997 Livneh criteria are still the most commonly used (Table 99.3).

Some patients fulfilling the Livneh criteria do not have genetic confirmation: in 30% of cases only a single or no pathogenic variant is detected after exome sequencing. Even in absence of genetic confirmation, treatment with colchicine is warranted in every symptomatic patient with fitting ancestry if the diagnostic criteria are fulfilled, to prevent against AA amyloidosis.

### Etiology and Pathogenesis

The discovery of the genetic background of FMF dates back to 1997, when two groups independently from each other discovered, until then, an unknown gene on the short arm of chromosome 6, consisting of 10 exons.21, FMF is predominantly an autosomal recessive disorder, caused by pathogenic variants in the MEFV gene, which encodes the protein pyrin. FMF is not the only disease associated with MEFV variants; pyrin-associated autoinflammation with neutrophilic dermatosis is an autosomal dominant hereditary autoinflammatory disease, and distinguishes itself from FMF by the presence of neutrophilic dermatosis.24, An autosomal dominant disease with pathogenic MEFV variants has also been described.

It is still not entirely clear whether pathogenic variants in MEFV result in gain or loss of function of the pyrin protein. Argument for the loss-of-function theory is the fact that pyrin is able to interact with caspase-1 and ASC, forming an inflammasome that regulates the cleavage of IL-1β. Most pathogenic variants are found in the C-terminal B30.2 domain in exon 10, result in a single amino acid change, and alter the binding of pyrin to caspase-1, causing a decreased inhibition of IL-1 cleavage. To support gain-of-function models, there are also studies that implicate that mutated pyrin is overexpressed in FMF patients and is able to interact with ASC and PSTPIP1 to directly cleave procaspase 1, leading to increased IL-1β release. 28,29

### TNF-Receptor-Associated Periodic Syndrome

TNF-receptor-associated periodic syndrome (TRAPS) is inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion. It is caused by variants in the TNF receptor subfamily 1A (TNFRSF1A) gene. Its phenotype is variable. Age of onset is between 2 weeks until far into adulthood.30-32 On average, inflammatory attacks last for 3 to 4 weeks, but longer and shorter episodes are also possible. During the inflammatory episodes fever is accompanied by skin lesions, myalgia and arthralgia, abdominal pain, and ocular symptoms.

The most common cutaneous symptom is a centrifugal, migratory, erythematous patch that may overlie an area of myalgia (Fig. 99.6).

Myalgia is often located primarily in the thigh muscles but may migrate during an episode, affecting all limbs and the torso, face, or neck. Arthralgia primarily affects large joints (hips, knees, ankles). Abdominal pain is often associated with gastrointestinal symptoms, like vomiting or constipation. The eyes may be involved as conjunctivitis, periorbital edema, or periorbital pain. As with the other IL-1-driven autoinflammatory diseases, AA amyloidosis is a complication of TRAPS, affecting 15 to 25% of untreated patients. 33,34

### Etiology and Pathogenesis

TRAPS is ultimately a genetic diagnosis confirmed by finding pathogenic variants in TNFRSF1A, which is located on the short arm of chromosome 12.1 Pathogenic variants are exclusively found in the extra-cellular domain of the protein. The R121Q and P75L (formerly R92Q and P46L) variants are the most commonly found variants of unknown significance, as they are also present in healthy persons, but may cause disease, which is often mild.

TRAPS-associated variants in the TNF receptor lead to a loss of TNF-signaling function, caused by accumulation of aberrant

receptors. The mutated TNF receptor is retained intra-cellularly, pooled in the endoplasmic reticulum.35-37 Mutant receptors cannot associate with the wild-type version but can form aggregates by self-interaction.36, This cytoplasmic receptor aggregation results in ligand-independent signaling, leading to uncontrolled pro-inflammatory cytokine production.38, Mitochondrialderived ROS appear to mediate this effect. Defective autophagy may also play an important role in the pathogenesis of TRAPS.

### Mevalonate Kinase Deficiency

Mevalonate kinase deficiency (MKD) has a spectrum ranging from mild to severe disease. On the mild end we find the hyperimmunoglobulin (Ig) D and periodic fever syndrome,42 characterized by early-onset febrile episodes of 5 to 7 days (Fig. 99.1), accompanied by rigors, lymphadenopathy, abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea, arthralgia, myalgia, and skin rash (Fig. 99.7). Hepatosplenomegaly may be present. Typically, the first episode is triggered by childhood vaccination. Other triggers are minor trauma, surgery, and physical or emotional stress. On the severe end are patients with mevalonic aciduria. These patients suffer from antenatal or neonatal inflammation, hydrops fetalis, psychomotor retardation, ataxia, failure to thrive, cataracts, and facial dysmorphia. Although the term hyperIgD syndrome implies elevated Ig D in all patients, IgD may be persistently normal44,45 and may be elevated in other autoinflammatory diseases, including FMF. IgA is elevated in 80% of MKD patients. 45,

MKD is confirmed by the finding of pathogenic variants on both alleles of the mevalonate kinase gene (MVK). In cases with a fitting phenotype and no or only heterozygous variants, or when genetic testing is unavailable, urinary mevalonic acid excretion may aid in the diagnosis. Elevated urinary mevalonic aciduria excretion during an inflammatory episode has a positive predictive value of 71%, and the negative predictive value is 98%.' 47 Measurement of mevalonate kinase activity requires cell culture and is only done for research purposes. Variants in MVK are not exclusive to MKD. Pathogenic variants have also been described in noninflammatory conditions, including retinitis pigmentosa and certain forms of porokeratosis. H

The exact prevalence of MKD is unknown. Over 100 patients have been reported in the literature. The majority of MKD patients is of White ancestry, possibly because of a founder effect. In the Netherlands, the carrier frequency of heterozygous mevalonate kinase mutations is 1 in 153.49

In patients with a mild MKD phenotype, prognosis is generally good. In some patients, fever episodes become less frequent and less severe after adolescence. Amyloidosis is rare in MKD.43, A potentially life-threatening complication of MKD is macrophage activation syndrome (MAS).

### Etiology and Pathogenesis

The pathogenic mechanism of MKD has not been fully elucidated. MKD-associated pathogenic variants in MVK lead to constantly decreased activity of the enzyme mevalonate kinase (MVK). MVK is part of the sterole and nonsterole isoprenoid pathway. It is located directly downstream from 3-hydroxy-3-methyl-glutarylcoenzyme A reductase. Its function is to phosphorylate mevalonic acid. Mutations in MKV lead to a shortage of isoprenoids and defects in prenylation.50, This effect increases upon elevations in core body temperature, which may explain why many patients with MKD experience their first attack after childhood vaccination, and (viral) infections are well-known triggers for MKD attacks. Defects in prenylation of GTPases, including those of the Rho/Rac/Rap families, lead to increased IL-1β secretion.53, In vitro studies of cells from MKD patients show that these cells are deficient in autophagy and have mitochondrial dysfunction and a reduced ability to clear antioxidant stress, leading to hypersecretion of IL-1β. Also, mevalonate can train the innate immune system, and cells of MKD patients showed a constitutive trained immunity phenotype56 that could contribute to the attacks of sterile inflammation in these patients.

### Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis and Adult-Onset Still's Disease

Systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis (sJIA) and adult-onset Still's disease (AOSD) are relative prevalent, nonhereditary, nonmonogenic, IL-1-driven autoinflammatory diseases. They are by some considered two forms of the same disease with the major distinguishing factor being age of onset: sJIA's onset is in childhood, and patients with AOSD are adults. sJIA/AOSD is characterized by chronic or episodic inflammation with fever, skin rash, arthralgia or arthritis, and

hepatosplenomegaly. Other frequent manifestations are pharyngitis, myalgia, pericarditis, pleuritis, and pulmonary infiltrates. Biochemically, an acute phase response is present, accompanied by increased serum ferritin. The disease's course may be fulminant; sJIA/AOSD is diagnosed on clinical criteria. The Yamaguchi criteria57 (Table 99.4) and Fautrel criteria58 (Table 99.5) are most commonly used.

sJIA/AOSD has three possible disease courses: monocyclic, polycyclic, or continuous disease. In monoand polycyclic disease the duration of an episode is highly variable. Inflammatory episodes may last for weeks to months. It is impossible to predict what the disease's course will be in the individual patient and, because of this, one should always be aware of possible relapse after an initial sJIA/AOSD episode. As the disease-free interval may also be long, tapering of immunosuppressive drugs could be considered when complete resolution of symptoms is achieved. Prognosis in general is good, except when complications arise. Possible life-threatening complications of sJIA/AOSD are myocarditis, acute respiratory distress syndrome, fulminant hepatitis, MAS, diffuse intravascular coagulation, and thrombotic microangiopathy. Prompt treatment with high-dose corticosteroids or IL-1 or IL-6 inhibitors is warranted in this case.

### Etiology and Pathogenesis

Most of the pathogenesis of AOSD still remains elusive. It is assumed that the multifactorial pathogenesis of sJIA/AOSD is a combination of infection, genetics, and environmental triggers. There may be a role for low-density granulocytes (LDGs) in disease activity. LDGs are a distinct subpopulation of neutrophils with pro-inflammatory features that co-sediment with the PBMC fraction after Ficoll gradient centrifugation and was initially only described in patients with systemic lupus erythematosus.62, LDGs in AOSD show increased IL-6 production and increased neutrophil extra-cellular trap formation,64,65 which induces IL-1β secretion.

Serum levels of N-terminal fragments of gasdermin D (GSDMD-N) have been found to be elevated in AOSD patients compared with healthy controls. GSDMD-N are, in an inflammatory setting, released for pore-forming and subsequent cytokine release. In MAS, an even further elevation of GSDMD-N was observed. GSDMD-N was positively correlated with levels of ferritin and IL-18,66 which are elevated in AOSD. Levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines, such as IL-10 and IL-37, may correlate with disease activity, although it still needs to be elucidated how they exactly contribute to the pathogenicity.

Disrupted autophagia may also be one of the defects in AOSD, as it was found that placenta-specific 8, a protein involved in regulating autophagy, correlated with the expression of IL-1β, IL-18, ferritin, and CRP in monocytes of AOSD patients.

### Other IL-1-Driven Autoinflammatory Diseases

Besides the five IL-1-driven autoinflammatory diseases described above, many other diseases with IL-1 overproduction as their main pathophysiologic mechanism exist. Details of some of the better-characterized syndromes are summarized in Table 99.6.

### Interferonopathies

The type-1 interferons (interferon [IFN] alpha and beta) have an important role in anti-viral defense under normal circumstances. Type-1 interferonopathies or, for short, interferonopathies, are conditions in which the type-1 IFN axis is activated.

Interferonopathies often result from aberrant nucleic acid sensing or via accumulation of host nucleic acid or other intra-cellular debris. They may also arise because of increased type-1 IFN receptor signaling. Type-1 IFNs are pyrogens and, because of this, patients often present with fever, which may be accompanied by rash and systemic inflammation. Contrary to IL-1-driven autoinflammatory diseases, vasculopathy or vasculitis is frequently present (Fig. 99.8). The interferonopathies are a phenotypically heterogenous group of diseases (Table 99.7). An overlap between autoinflammatory and autoimmune features is often present (Table 99.8). Onset is frequently within the first week of life, but late-onset disease in adolescence or adulthood has also been described. In some patients with interferonopathies, CRP and ESR may not be elevated. A peripheral blood IFN signature can be measured, including a 28-gene IFN scoring system, but this test is not widely available and may yield false-negative results, even in patients with genetic confirmation of an interferonopathy. Genetic evaluation is necessary in all patients with suspected interferonopathy.

### NF-κB-Related and/or Aberrant TNF Activity Autoinflammatory Syndromes

The NF-kB complex is an intricately regulated intracytoplasmatic signal complex that conducts signals from cell surface and intra-cellular danger sensors. After activation of NF-kB, transcription factors move from the complex to the nucleus, where expression of pro-inflammatory genes is promoted.
