Many proteins play a role in NF-kB-induced inflammation via sensing, inhibition, and ubiquitination. Prominent symptoms of NF-kB dysregulation are fever and systemic inflammation. Granuloma formation may be present, and these diseases may show signs that may also be seen in Behcet's disease. NF-kB and TNF are closely linked. TNF signaling can activate NF-kB, and activation of NF-κB induces transcription of TNF (Table 99.9).

### Ubiquitination Defects

Ubiquitination is a complex process in which small molecules called ubiquitins are coupled to target proteins. This is a three-step

process involving a few hundred enzymes in total. Ubiquitination changes a protein's destination in the cell. Ubiquitination is highly involved in proteasome-mediated degradation of proteins (Fig. 99.9).

In 2020 a new autoinflammatory disease was identified in older males. It was named the vacuoles, E1 enzyme, X-linked, autoinflammatory syndrome (VEXAS). VEXAS is caused by pathogenic variants in the X-linked E1 enzyme. The E1 enzyme is crucial for ubiquitination. Although VEXAS is monogenic, it does not have an early onset but presents around 40 to 50 years of age. This is because E1 variants appear in somatic mosaicism, in which some cells in the body carry a certain variant while others don't. VEXAS is caused when E1 mutations appear in myeloid cells. VEXAS may be one of the most prevalent autoinflammatory diseases, with an estimated prevalence of 1 in 13,59173 in a cohort of over 160,000 adults with a median age of 61 years. In this cohort 2 in 11 mutations were found in female patients without evidence of aneuploidy, and they were both symptomatic. The phenotype of VEXAS consists of autoinflammatory symptoms

associated with macrocytic anemia or myelodysplastic syndrome. Autoinflammation may be present before myelodysplasia becomes detectable. Inflammatory symptoms include, among others, fever, polychondritis, neutrophilic dermatosis, arthritis, medium-vessel vasculitis, colitis, and inflammatory eye disease. The diagnosis of VEXAS can be made by detection of somatic mutations in the UBA1 gene, which encodes the E1 enzyme. The finding of vacuoles in a bone-marrow sample in a patient with a suspicion of myelodysplastic syndrome should raise the suspicion of VEXAS and the initiation of genetic investigation.

The prognosis of VEXAS is unknown and largely depends on the nature and severity of the symptoms, the reaction to immunomodulatory drugs, the complications of treatment, and, if present, the severity and treatment of the underlying myelodysplastic syndrome.

### Diagnostic Approach to Autoinflammatory Diseases

The mainstay of the diagnosis of autoinflammatory diseases is clinical assessment, including a detailed medical and family history, and preferably at least one observation of the patient during an inflammatory episode. Especially physical examination (full body, with specific focus on ocular symptoms, skin rash, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, and arthritis) may show otherwise absent clinical clues during an inflammatory episode. In

most cases, and inevitably in IL-1-driven autoinflammatory diseases, a clear acute phase response including elevated ESR, CRP, and SAA are present during an inflammatory episode, while these are normal in between episodes. Leukocytosis with neutrophilia may be present. Specific laboratory tests—including serum ferritin, IgD and IgA, serum protein electrophoresis, or urine mevalonic acid excretion—may aid in the diagnosis in specific cases. Upregulation of type-1 IFNs can be measured with a type-1 IFN signature assay, but this test is nonexclusive and not widely available. It is important to keep in mind that more common causes of longstanding or recurrent inflammation, such as chronic infections and malignancy, should be excluded, especially in absence of genetic confirmation of an autoinflammatory disease. Bone marrow biopsy may be helpful when VEXAS is considered. Genetic testing may aid in the diagnosis. Whole-exome sequencing gene panels, which include multiple genes associated with autoinflammatory diseases, are becoming the standard for genetic testing, at least in the Western world. Upon suspicion of an IL-1-driven autoinflammatory disease, a therapeutic trial with short-acting specific IL-1 inhibiting drugs can be considered. If a quick and evident response appears after initiation of these drugs, the pivotal role of IL-1 in the pathophysiology is proven.

### Treatment of Autoinflammatory Diseases

Depending on the pathogenic mechanism of autoinflammatory diseases, several treatment options may be available.

### Nonsteroidal Anti-inflammatory Drugs

Patients with mild phenotypes of MKD, TRAPS, or AOSD may benefit from on-demand or chronic treatment with nonsteroidal

anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) such as ibuprofen, naproxen, or diclofenac. NSAIDs may also be used instead of acetaminophen as symptomatic treatment during painful episodes.

### Corticosteroids

Corticosteroids may be effective in many autoinflammatory syndromes, but the benefit may be only partial or patients may relapse during treatment. In most cases, high doses are needed to maintain a beneficial effect. With the major side effects of longterm high-dose steroid therapy, including infections, weight gain, Cushing syndrome, diabetes, osteoporosis, and neuropsychiatric symptoms, and after the introduction of IL-1 and IL-6 inhibitors, corticosteroids are used less and less for autoinflammatory syndromes. For VEXAS and interferonopathies, corticosteroids may be the initial choice of therapy.

### Colchicine

Colchicine remains the first-choice treatment for patients with FMF. It prevents inflammatory attacks completely in 60% to 75% of patients, and it significantly reduces the number of attacks in an additional 20% to 30%. Doses of colchicine may range between 0.5 and 3.0 mg per day,76 depending on effect and tolerance. The main side effects of colchicine are gastrointestinal complaints. Diarrhea and nausea often resolve with dose reduction. Severe side effects, including myopathy, neuropathy, and leukopenia, are rare and occur primarily in patients with renal or hepatic impairment or after combination with strong CYP3A4 or Pgp inhibitors, such as macrolides, azoles, or protease inhibitors. Long-term use of colchicine may be associated with vitamin B12 deficiency. In the past, the use of colchicine has been associated with infertility. In animal models a teratogenic effect has been reported. With increasing evidence, it is now known that the use of colchicine is not associated with a significant adverse effect on sperm production or function. Colchicine is considered safe to use during pregnancy (including the first trimester) and lactation. As cessation of therapy may lead to increased frequency of severity of FMF attacks, which may lead to decreased fertility because of intraabdominal adhesions and adverse pregnancy outcome (e.g., miscarriage or premature birth due to peritonitis), treatment should not be interrupted in fertile women.78, When colchicine resistance is present, IL-1 inhibition can be added to colchicine. We advise not to stop colchicine, as it still remains the only drug with proven protection against secondary AA amyloidosis.

### IL-1 Inhibition

Since the introduction of IL-1 inhibitors, these have become the mainstay of treatment for many patients with IL-1-driven autoinflammatory syndromes. Three different IL-1 inhibiting drugs are available: the IL-1 receptor antagonist anakinra, the monoclonal antibody against IL-1β canakinumab, and the IL-1 receptor fusion protein rilonacept. Availability and reimbursement of these three differ largely between countries. At the moment, there is evidence of effectivity for IL-1 inhibition in all IL-1-driven autoinflammatory diseases, including CAPS, colchicine-resistant FMF, TRAPS, MKD, and AOSD/sJIA.80-82 In many of these patients, IL-1 inhibition will be the treatment of first choice. In other autoinflammatory diseases, a therapeutic trial with IL-1 inhibition may be considered when there is evidence that the IL-1 pathway is involved in the pathogenesis based on clinical symptoms and biochemical markers such as elevated CRP or SAA. For anakinra, standard dose is 100 mg once daily, and for canakinumab the dose may range between 150 mg every 8 weeks or less to 300 mg every 4 weeks.

### IL-6 Inhibition

IL-6 inhibition is mostly used in patients with IL-1-driven autoinflammatory diseases that do not sufficiently respond to IL-1 inhibition. Tocilizumab, the IL-6 receptor antagonist, is the most commonly used IL-6 inhibitor. There is evidence for its effect in CAPS, FMF, TRAPS, MKD, and AOSD/sJIA, among others. Tocilizumab is available as subcutaneous injections and intravenous infusions. The main side effect is infection. It is important to note that IL-6 inhibition blocks the formation of CRP and SAA, rendering these unsuitable as markers for disease activity. Standard

dose for subcutaneous injection is 162 mg every week and 6 to 10 mg/kg every 4 weeks for intravenous infusion.

### TNFI Inhibition

Patients with TRAPS may benefit from treatment with etanercept. .80, In patients with increased NF-κB activity, TNF inhibition with adalimumab or infliximab can also be effective. TNF

inhibition is the treatment of first choice for patients with deficiency of adenosine deaminase 2, as it is the only drug that has shown full protection against ischemic stroke in these patients.

### JAK/STAT Inhibition

In autoinflammatory diseases, there is increasing interest in the effects of JAK/STAT inhibitors such as tofacitinub, ruxolitinib,

or baracitinib and their effects have been described in patients with FMF85 and AOSD/sJIA.86-89 For interferonopathies, JAK/ STAT inhibitors may be the first-choice treatment because of their mechanism in regard to the underlying pathophysiological mechanism.71,90,91

### Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplantation

Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation may be considered, especially in severe monogenic diseases.

### Conclusion

The autoinflammatory diseases comprise a wide spectrum of diseases, ranging from the classic monogenic IL-1-driven inflammasomopathies characterized by fever, serositis, and skin rash, to late-onset autoinflammatory diseases with genetic defects in recently discovered disease-causing genes and symptoms such as vasculopathy and cerebral calcifications. The workup of these diseases has mainly become one of clinical judgment and pattern recognition and genetic studies. The treatment of first choice for

the classic monogenic IL-1-driven autoinflammatory diseases and sJIA/AOSD remains IL-1 inhibition, with the exception of FMF in which colchicine remains the therapy of first choice to prevent against secondary amyloidosis. For interferonopathies, JAK/STAT inhibitors, especially baricitinib, seem promising. However, the optimal therapeutic strategy for the more complex autoinflammatory diseases remains one of the next major questions for clinical research.

# Etiology and Pathogenesis of Osteoarthritis

100

### KEY POINTS

### Introduction

Osteoarthritis (OA) is the most common joint disease in the world and yet one of the least well-understood forms of arthritis. It affects more than 500 million people worldwide and is one of the world's major causes of disability. According to the World Health Organization, OA causes a greater number of years lived with disability with a greater impact on disability than either heart

disease or tuberculosis. OA is one of the greatest unmet need in rheumatology and currently lacks any approved disease modifying therapy, largely due to a limited understanding of the pathophysiology of the disease.

The cardinal sign of OA is joint pain, especially pain that occurs or increases during physical activity. Other symptoms including joint stiffness, "gelling" phenomenon, aching, and other distressing experiences occur at different stages of the disease. Notably, the development of constant pain (the experience of pain that never goes away, even though it may fluctuate) is a sign of progression from early to later stages of OA. Underlying these symptoms is a complex pathophysiology within the joint environment, leading to derangements in homeostatic joint physiology and damage to essential joint tissues. OA pathogenesis progresses over years, fluctuates over time, and ultimately produces the clinically recognizable features of tissue damage, pain, and loss of joint and physical function, which is best described as joint failure.

Decades of important basic biomedical and clinical translational research have improved our understanding of the pathophysiologic mechanisms that occur during OA. However, it is increasingly recognized that it is the integration of these pathophysiologic processes through cross-talk mechanisms within and between joint tissues that ultimately leads to disease sequelae. Ongoing work aims to understand the full extent of integrated OA joint pathophysiology and marks an exciting new phase in the field, with opportunities to identify disease-modifying treatments.

### The Synovial Joint Is an Organ

Fundamental biologic mechanisms are required for maintaining the homeostasis of the synovial joint organ system. As a group of tissues with interdependent functions, the synovial joint is an organ like any other. The functional integration of the joint capsule, ligaments, synovium, synovial fat pads, articular cartilage, subchondral bone, and accessory tissues such as menisci (in some joints) permits movement while accommodating and normalizing mechanical loads. When synovial joints fail, movement is significantly impaired or completely lost. Maintaining joint

homeostasis is therefore critical to joint function. This simple concept relies on complex physiology at the local joint level and is modulated through systemic physiologic interactions with the rest of the body.

### Synovial I Joints Maintain Homeostasis by Interfacing With the Rest of the Body

All organs require perfusion, lymphatic drainage, and innervation to sustain tissue homeostasis. Synovial joints require the same inputs and egresses along with mechanical supports provided by bones and their ligament and musculotendinous junctions. Nearly all perfusion of the joint is handled by the vascular and lymphatic supply to/from the synovium and joint capsule. Oxygen and nutrients dissolved in blood plasma are perfused through these tissues and into the joint cavity to supply the avascular, alymphatic, and aneural cartilage and the inner fibrocartilaginous two-thirds of menisci when present,3 although the outer fibrous third of the meniscus has its own limited vascular-lymphatic and sensory nerve supply. Oxygen tension and glucose concentration are therefore highest at the surface of healthy articular cartilage (cartilage—synovial fluid interface) with declining gradients of each factor established between the surface and deeper zones. Conversely, inverted gradients are established due to blood flow in subchondral bone, which helps to supply oxygen and glucose to cartilage from below the cartilage—subchondral bone interface.

Although synovium-mediated perfusion is vital for cartilage and other tissue homeostasis, it has been demonstrated that additional inputs and egresses exist at the junction between articular cartilage and subchondral bone in both healthy and diseased states. The presence of small channels emanating from the subchondral bone and extending into the calcified articular cartilage zone6 provides additional sources for nutrient delivery,7 which are important for chondrocyte survival. This interface also provides opportunities for articular chondrocytes to communicate with osteocytes within the underlying supportive bony structure, for example through prostaglandin signaling,9,10 with osteoblasts, osteoclasts, and other bone marrow stromal cells. Although it is likely that the osteochondral junction plays an even more important role in joint diseases such as OA,11 'more detailed investigation is needed to understand the nature and mechanisms of molecular communication between cartilage and bone in homeostasis.

Due to the fundamental relationship between synovial joints and movement, sensory and sympathetic innervation to the joint is critical. Sensory fibers innervating the synovium and joint capsule, the outer third of the meniscus, subchondral bone, tendons, and ligaments provide real-time and constant proprioceptive and nociceptive feedback to the central nervous system for optimal control and protection of the joint during movement and rest. Underscoring the vital importance of joint sensory innervation, catastrophic joint failure can rapidly occur due to severe sensory nerve dysfunction, also known as a neuropathic joint. Impaired proprioceptive and nociceptive function in sensory nerves can occur due to primary (e.g., Charcot—Marie—Tooth disease13) or secondary (e.g. long-standing diabetes14) peripheral neuropathies. Additionally, sympathetic fibers accompanying the vascular supply to synovial joint tissues regulate blood flow to these structures, which is critical for joint homeostasis as described. Control of these sympathetic inputs is regulated both locally (e.g., due to release of purinergic signals by local joint tissues) and centrally by the autonomic nervous system.

### Joints Bear Mechanical Loads and Permit Movement

Synovial fluid starts out as blood perfusate, which synovial joints further modify to support normal joint functioning during movement. These modifications also support communication between peripheral joint tissues such as the capsule and synovium with articular cartilage. The synovium, and to a lesser extent the superficial layer of articular cartilage and menisci,16 secrete multiple factors including the lubricating protein lubricin, encoded by PRG4 in humans. Lubricin dramatically lowers the coefficient of friction of synovial fluid.18-20 This provides the healthy joint with easy, near-frictionless movement at the surfaces of cartilage and tendons, whereas loss of lubricin due to joint diseases likely plays a key role in loss of joint function. Lubricin has additional functions in joint homeostasis such as the prevention of synovial fibroblast hyperplasia. Synovium also secretes large amounts of hyaluronan into the healthy joint. At higher concentrations, hyaluronan can form a gel due to its physical properties as a polymer, which helps cartilage to resist compressive loads. In joint diseases when hyaluronan concentration is much lower, these properties are reduced or lost,22 which subjects the joint tissues to abnormal mechanical loading. However, hyaluronan on its own is a poor lubricant. By interacting with lubricin, the hyaluronan—lubricin complex provides the joint with excellent boundary lubrication (at tissue surfaces) and high load-carrying capacity, including during 24 movement.

Muscular contractions exert forces through tendinous insertions into bones to generate movement. Muscle-tendon functions are therefore closely related to synovial joints and have direct impacts on joint physiology. Through gravity and muscle-generated forces, the joint bears several different types and magnitudes of mechanical loading with wide ranging effects on synovial joint tissue physiology. Synovial joint structures have evolved accordingly in order to withstand and respond adaptively to these mechanical loads. Although historical medical advice about managing jointrelated problems often included limitations on movement and activity, important advances through arthritis and musculoskeletal research have transformed our understanding of the important clinical and physiologic benefits of nearly all forms of movement (sometimes meeting definitions of exercise).25-27 The cumulative effects of movement on synovial joint tissues provide an excellent model to understand how normal joint physiology is dependent on normal joint loading and movement.

Fibrous tissues such as the joint capsule provide mechanical stability to the joint during movement and prevents disarticulation. Strain forces on the joint capsule and synovium during acute exercise produce anti-inflammatory responses including the production of interleukin-10 (IL-10),28 which is a major cytokine involved in resolution of inflammation and tissue healing. Conversely, joint immobilization caused joint capsule atrophy and collagen bundle narrowing within 2 weeks in rats. In a similar experiment, immobilization of joint tissues caused increased expression of type I, II, and III collagen and matrix metalloproteinase (MMP)-1 and -13, with lower levels of tissue inhibitor of metalloproteinase (TIMP)-1, -2, and -3 expression in rabbit joint capsules. Although overloading any tissue can clearly cause traumatic injury, normal loading is required for normal joint tissue physiologic functions. Lack of normal tissue loading can quickly lead to the activation of catabolic mechanisms including the secretion of inflammatory cytokines and MMPs that can weaken tissues through enzymatic digestion.

### Osteoarthritis Causes Joint Organ Dysfunction

Due to the large number of risk factors and associations of OA with other diseases, OA cases result from a range of multidimensional processes that disrupt healthy joint physiology (Fig. 100.1). Regardless of the contributing factors, OA results from failure to restore and maintain joint homeostasis. As described above, synovial joints are designed to withstand normal environmental stresses and maintain joint homeostasis under these conditions. Therefore OA can develop when joints are subjected to abnormal environmental stresses that overwhelm endogenous repair and homeostatic mechanisms and/or when risk factors reduce the ability of the joint to withstand normal environmental stresses.

The abundance of evidence in the field currently suggests that pathogenic OA mechanisms probably initiate in structural joint tissues such as cartilage and bone, with emerging evidence that pathogenic mechanisms in synovium, tendons, ligaments, and meniscus propagate the disease. At the tissue level, it is often difficult to differentiate the pathophysiologic effects of risk factors on joint tissues from OA-specific mechanisms. Together, these mechanisms lead to the failure of joint tissues to withstand various normal and abnormal sources of physiologic stress. The resulting pathophysiology is analogous to organ failure in other diseases such as cardiac or renal failure.

### Endogenous Joint Tissue Repair Processes

Endogenous regenerative responses exist in all joint tissues to restore and maintain homeostasis under a range of physiologic conditions. Our understanding of these endogenous repair processes can be understood through the lens of acute tissue injury, usually a mechanical injury. Articular cartilage, subchondral bone, and synovium all have and contribute to the regenerative capabilities of the joint in response to injury. These processes

are often suppressed or overwhelmed by catabolic processes in OA. Nonetheless, there is future therapeutic potential if endogenous repair processes can be harnessed to overcome OA pathophysiology.

### Articular Cartilage

### Normal, Physiologic Mechanical Loading and Homeostasis

Articular cartilage is subjected to a wide range of mechanical loads during routine daily activities. For example, stair climbing can generate peak compressive forces between 10 to 20 Megapascals (MPa) that send signals to the articular chondrocytes embedded within the dense extra-cellular matrix (ECM). In the short term, this leads to small degree of cartilage compression but when sustained can lead to compression of up to 45% of the cartilage thickness.32, This unique ability of cartilage to withstand different degrees and durations of mechanical compressive, tensile, and shear forces makes it a specialized tissue that requires a unique set of homeostatic programs to maintain its integrity. The durability of articular cartilage over time is related to the chondrocytes and cartilage ECM components, especially the major proteoglycans (e.g., aggrecan) and collagens (type II collagen). Mechanical forces that are transmitted through the cartilage ECM are transduced by articular chondrocytes. Numerous mechanisms allow chondrocytes to detect and respond to the mechanical stimuli.

Normal mechanical loading of joint tissues produces protective and adaptive biologic responses that promote homeostasis and maintain the health of the joint. For example, running produces knee cartilage strains (compression) of 10% to 30%, varying by joint region, to which chondrocytes respond with increased synthesis of ECM components including collagens type II and IX,34 cartilage oligomeric protein (COMP),35 glycosaminoglycans, 36 and aggrecan. In contrast, both insufficient or excessive tissue

loading inhibits these anabolic effects. Too little activity (e.g., among sedentary populations) is therefore an important biomechanical risk factor for OA. Physically or metabolically injured joint tissues are also more susceptible to mechanical loads, such that loading magnitudes that approach the upper limit of normal might produce abnormal/injurious responses.

Normal loading of intact/healthy cartilage can provide counterbalancing effects including suppression of ECM disruption by MMPs and aggrecanases, which are produced by chondrocytes in response to stimulation with IL-1β. Mechanical loading in healthy and mouse models of OA (e.g., experimental OA induced in mouse knee joints by surgical joint destabilization) also decreases endoplasmic reticulum stress and increases autophagy in chondrocytes of noncalcified and calcified cartilage and in synovial cells. However, normal biomechanical loading is not well-defined, despite several decades of research into the effects of static and dynamic compression, shear forces, physiochemical stimuli, hydrostatic pressure, and even electric currents in articular chondrocytes and cartilage. In general, static compression is deleterious, whereas dynamic compression is generally protective within the range of normal (physiologic) loading. Static compression of articular cartilage and chondrocytes inhibits the synthesis of aggrecan and other proteoglycans and increases in cytokine and chemokine expression that paradigmatically lead to induction of MMPs and other degradative enzymes. 38, On the other hand, dynamic compression stimulates synthesis of aggrecans and matrix components and their assembly to restore tissue matrix.41, The frequency and amplitude of dynamic compression determines whether loading produces protective or deleterious physiologic effects, which has important considerations for clinicians and rehabilitation. For example, patients with hip or knee OA who must stand for long periods of time due to occupational requirements are at risk of OA exacerbation from prolonged static loading.

Responses to dynamic compression are conserved across mammalian species, although most studies have been completed in small and large nonhuman mammals. Human cartilage likely has the same properties, although experimental testing of live, healthy human cartilage in studies is uncommon, and most experimentation has been done in diseased samples with OA,43 usually at a late stage of disease. Dynamic compressive loading in chondrocytes also stimulates the production of chondrogenic growth factors and cytokines, including transforming growth factor β (TGF- β). It has also been shown that prolonged dynamic compression up to 12 hours per day in tissue culture is able to stimulate proteoglycan synthesis in mesenchymal stromal cells (MSCs) and can increase differentiation along a chondrogenic program, even in the absence of chondrogenic cytokines and growth factors. Therefore the combination of both physiologic dynamic compression and exposure to chondrogenic factors is likely most effective to induce chondrogenesis and/or maintain homeostasis under conditions of physiologic stress. Subsequent responses to normal loading include changes in chondrocyte gene expression including at the type II collagen promoter and synthesis and deposition of glycosaminoglycan (GAG) in the ECM over a period of days to a few weeks. Reflecting similar patterns in articular cartilage in vivo, the increased expression/synthesis is typically concentrated in the central region of the loaded area, with decreased expression/ synthesis in the annular region.37, Importantly, stimulation of aggrecan production by dynamic compression appears to be localized to regions with high interstitial fluid flow. Taken together, these in vitro and in vivo animal model studies indicate that

appropriate biomechanical loading of articular cartilage is essential for the maintenance of chondrocytes and cartilage homeostasis. This concept has bolstered the rehabilitation and orthopedics fields to prioritize correction and maintenance of normal biomechanical loading in patients, but it remains unclear how to define appropriate biomechanical loading in the clinical context, and work in this area is ongoing.

### Cartilage Responses to Acute I Injury

Responses to articular cartilage tissue injury have been well characterized. Articular cartilage has limited capacity for intrinsic repair due to its avascular nature and therefore the inability to mount a de facto wound-healing response. However, contrary to earlier descriptions of cartilage as having insufficient endogenous repair,54 articular cartilage does have the ability to autonomously repair superficial lesions, whereas deeper lesions may be repaired by fibrocartilaginous tissue that is different from healthy articular cartilage in both cellular and ECM composition, leading to altered mechanical properties of the repair tissue. As a result, it is commonly thought that this repair tissue is more susceptible to ongoing damage and disruption and therefore increases the risk of developing OA.

In response to injury, chondrocytes within the articular cartilage proliferate and synthesize ECM components such as collagen and proteoglycans to repair the damaged tissue. In addition, progenitor cells located in the bone marrow and synovium can migrate and differentiate into chondrocytes to help repair the damaged cartilage. In the setting of blunt or acute trauma, chondrocyte death leads to hypocellularity within the cartilage matrix. Interestingly, it has been shown that chondrogenic progenitor cells respond to this cartilage injury and repopulate the areas where mature chondrocytes have been lost within 7 to 14 days after the injury. These articular cartilage—derived chondrogenic progenitor cells (CPCs) migrate from the surrounding matrix and were first discovered in calf cartilage in 2004.57 CPCs reside mostly in the superficial zone of articular cartilage57,58 and are defined by their co-expression of CD105 and CD16659 or expression of CD9/ CD90/CD166,60 clonogenicity, multipotency, and expression of chondrogenic genes.61-64 There is no single marker that defines CPC cell type, but numerous studies have reported that NOTCH expression is key for the progenitor phenotype of CPCs in addition to the markers mentioned above.65, CPCs comprise up to ~5% of the total articular chondrocyte population but expand in number under OA conditions. Interestingly, additional sources of progenitor cells have also been reported, including cells originating in the bone marrow and migrating from below the tidemark and calcified cartilage. Articular cartilage-derived CPCs do not undergo hypertrophic chondrocyte differentiation, unlike bone marrow-derived MSCs with chondrogenic potential.68, Suppression of the osteogenic transcription factor RUNX2 in CPCs increases the expression of SOX9 (a key chondrogenic transcription factor) and enhance the capability of CPCs to produce and secrete ECM components that are key for articular cartilage repair. In vivo, CPCs migrate toward the site of injury to participate in endogenous repair of the cartilage lesion. CPCs respond to and migrate toward chemotactic signals including advanced glycation end products, damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs), and alarmins such as mitochondrial DNA and HMGB-1.70 Such factors are released after injury by chondrocytes undergoing necrotic cell death.

Taken together, these features underscore that articular cartilage possesses intrinsic repair capability. Further, these studies

highlight that OA can result from the failure of intrinsic cartilage repair mechanisms to meet increased demand on the joint organ system leading to joint failure. Clearly, the endogenous repair potential of articular cartilage is an effective contributor to maintaining joint homeostasis in the absence of other OA-precipitating risk factors. The last two decades of work to characterize and understand these repair mechanisms has led to excitement in the OA field that it may be possible to harness the intrinsic repair capability of cartilage for therapeutic benefit.

### Fibroblast Growth Factor Signaling and Acute Cartilage Injury

Although most of our early knowledge about the role of fibroblast growth factor (FGF) signaling came from developmental biology much has been learned about the role of FGF signaling in articular cartilage homeostasis and response to injury. In particular, FGF2 is produced endogenously in articular cartilage.71, It is sequestered within the ECM by proteoglycans, including perlecan and heparan sulfate proteoglycan. When articular cartilage is acutely injured, FGF2 is released from the ECM to activate FGF receptors (FGFRs) on the surface of articular chondrocytes. During OA, FGF2 expression is nearly twice as high as that of healthy normal joints in the synovial fluid. Because of the effects of FGF2 on driving vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) expression and neovascularization, a role for FGF2 in driving catabolism, impaired cartilage homeostasis, and hyperalgesia has been proposed.73,

An important dichotomy exists between humans and murine models of OA that confounded the field for some time. We now understand that human articular chondrocytes predominantly express FGFR1 and FGFR3, whereas mice and other murine species express FGFR2 and FGFR4.75 The dominant FGF receptor expression profile (with or without FGFR1) changes the role of FGF2 depending on the species context and has thereby limited the translatability of FGF treatments from pre-clinical OA models into patients. FGF2 activates both FGFR1 and FGFR3, so the expression profile of the receptor on chondrocytes determines the most likely biologic outcome. FGF2 in humans will activate FGFR1 signaling, which leads to Ras/Raf/MEK/ERK (mitogen-activated protein kinase [MAPK]) signaling, activation of RUNX2-mediated expression of matrix metalloprotease 13 (MMP-13), a disintegrin and metalloprotease with thrombospondin motif-4 and -5 (ADAMTS-4, ADAMTS-5), type X collagen, and VEGF, stimulating ECM degradation and inhibition of anabolic repair processes.73, In contrast, when FGFR3 expression is higher, FGF2 signaling leads to anabolic effects and maintenance of chondrocyte phenotype, which sustains homeostasis and cartilage repair. Overall, FGF2 (via FGFR1) leads to catabolic loss of ECM in human cartilage and thus is not a viable therapy. On the other hand, FGF18 is specific for FGFR3 signaling and does not bind to FGFR1. Thus FGF18 is an anabolic growth factor that is involved in chondrogenesis and endochondral development78 and is also important for maintenance of articular cartilage phenotype and repair. Although both FGFR1 and FGFR3 are capable of activating MAPK signaling, FGFR3 leads to suppression of the transcription factor noggin,79 which otherwise suppresses the protective effects of bone morphogenetic protein 7 (BMP7) signaling. Thus FGFR3 signals stimulate cartilage repair. It has been shown in acute cartilage impact injury models that FGFR3 signaling stimulated by recombinant human FGF18 (rhFGF-18; also known as sprifermin) leads to increased synthesis of aggrecan, increased type II collagen synthesis biomarkers

(CPII), and decreased type II collagen turnover biomarker C2C. Moreover, a large randomized, double-blind placebo-controlled trial of rhFGF-18 led to increases in articular cartilage thickness in patients with established radiographic knee OA. This study validated the chondrogenic potential of FGFR3 signaling that was seen in pre-clinical studies. These recent examples demonstrate the importance of pre-clinical research and underpin the enthusiasm of harnessing endogenous repair processes to sustain homeostasis and repair articular cartilage that has been damaged due to injury.

### Bone Marrow-Derived Mesenchymal Stem Cells and Endogenous Joint Tissue Repair

Endogenous joint tissue repair mechanisms also lead to the recruitment of MSCs from other tissues, which originate from a bone marrow lineage. Largely, these reach the joint through the synovium either by perfusion or expansion of synovial tissuederived MSCs82,83 or via the subchondral bone/bone marrow through the osteochondral junction. Surface marker expression of bone marrow—derived MSCs is similar to that of articular cartilage derived CPCs, with the main difference being the expression of hematopoietic markers.68,

Numerous chemoattractant—receptor pairs have been studied and have been implicated in the recruitment and/or differentiation of bone marrow-derived MSCs to synovial joints, such as SDF-1 (CXCL12) signaling through CXCR4; IL-8 via CXCR1 or CXCR2; MCP-1 (CCL2) via CCR2; MIP-3a via CCR6; SCM-1 via XCR1; TGF-β1 or TGF-β3 via TGF-βR; BMP-2, BMP-4, or BMP-7 via BMPRIs or BMPRIIs; platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF) via PDGF receptor alpha or beta (PDGFRα/β) (CD140a/b); insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1) via IGF-1R; FGF2 via FGFR-1, FGFR-2, FGFR-3, or FGFR-4; Nerve growth factor (NGF) via NGF receptor (NGFR); and HGF via HGFR, .87-98 These factors are induced and released among other factors. by injured chondrocytes and other joint tissues and contribute to the initial recruitment of a pool of MSCs to participate in joint healing responses.

The inflammatory joint environment in OA leads to breakdown of hyaluronic acid (HA), and low molecular weight HA will bind to TLR-4, thereby increasing MSC migration. Indeed, MSCs are found in high abundance in synovial fluid of patients with OA1 100 and may adhere to articular cartilage. However, it has been shown that this adherence is inhibited by HA through interactions with the CD44 hyaluronic acid receptor expressed on MSCs. Highermolecular-weight HA creates a pericellular HA coat that physically impairs MSC adherence to articular cartilage. 101-103 It is thought that the intrinsic repair mechanisms mediated by MSCs may be ineffective an OA because of the inhibitory effect of hyaluronic acid.104,

The synovium remains an important reservoir of adult MSCs with joint regenerative capability. Synovial-derived MSCs arise during joint patterning and formation of the joint interzone during embryonic development and can be defined as mesenchymal in origin by marker expression of growth and differentiation factor 5 (GDF5) and persist throughout adult life. The joint regenerative capability of these synovial-derived MSCs is dependent on Yes-associated protein (YAP). These cells contribute to synovial lining hyperplasia and migrate to sides of cartilage injury to participate in cartilage repair. Notwithstanding the discussion above on the inhibitory effects of HA and other factors that may interfere with MSC binding to articular cartilage, synovial-derived MSCs at least have the potential to participate directly in cartilage repair processes.

### Synovial Tissue

Synovium is a highly regenerative tissue that lines the inner surface of the joint capsule and produces synovial fluid. In response to injury, synovial cells can proliferate and produce ECM components such as hyaluronan and proteoglycans to help repair the damaged tissue. As a connective tissue, synovium has its own vasculature, lymphatic, and neural structures. As such, synovial tissue is able to undergo canonical wound-healing processes. With a simple mechanical injury, the synovial membrane does not undergo an extensive hypertrophic reaction but can demonstrate vasomotor changes with capillary dilatation and exudative effusion developing in the joint. A small cellular infiltrate will follow, and the synovial lining (intima) will increase from 3 to 10 cell layers thick. This morphologic change will resolve over days to weeks as long as the injury is not sustained. Accordingly, surgical models of OA that rely on joint arthrotomy will demonstrate complete healing of synovial tissue with minimal or no residual scar. This woundhealing property can be used as a "sham" or control condition, which is then compared with the experimental OA condition in which additional joint structures are transected, leading to joint destabilization.108' If synovial injury is repeated, post-traumatic synovitis will develop. This includes further thickening of the synovial intima, further infiltration of perivascular lymphocytes and monocytes, and infiltration of myeloid (mostly macrophages) and regenerative cells (MSCs) into the synovial fluid.109,

The synovial membrane also contains a population of progenitor cells that can differentiate into various cell types including synovial fibroblasts and macrophages. Synovial tissue—derived MSCs were first identified in human synovial tissue in 2001.82 Numerous subsequent studies have investigated the regenerative potential of these cells noting important properties including clonality, migration, and multipotency but also some important limitations. Several studies have demonstrated the ability of synovial tissue—derived MSCs to migrate first to synovial fluid104 and then to the damaged areas of the joint and differentiate into chondrocytes and osteoblasts, leading to regeneration of both articular cartilage and subchondral bone.87, One example of a study on synovial joint tissue regeneration involved the injection of MSCs into the joints of rabbits with induced OA. It was determined that the regenerative potential of synovial tissue— and bone marrow—derived MSCs is greater than that of MSCs derived from muscle or adipose tissues.

Although in vitro conditions may be ideal for chondrogenesis and maximize the regenerative potential of MSCs, the in vivo OA joint milieu is more complex and less amenable to sustaining chondrogenic programs. There are likely numerous inhibitory factors that reduce the ability and regenerative capacity of MSCs to participate in joint repair regardless of their site of origin. However, secreted anabolic factors from synovial cells also play a role in determining cell fates. Several researchers have found that synovial fluid contains high levels of growth factors such as TGF-β, which can promote the proliferation and differentiation of synovial cells to repair damaged tissue. For example, in a surgically induced rat model of OA, it was shown that synovial tissues stimulate a transient anabolic response in articular chondrocytes and that this effect was mediated at least partly by TGF-β.

### Subchondral Bone

Mechanobiological responses occur in subchondral bone, including early after acute traumatic or cyclic loading events.

Thinning of the subchondral plate within 1 to 2 weeks after joint injury is attributed to increased osteoclast activity causing early bone resorption and is associated with the onset and advancement of cartilage lesions. These observations from mouse OA models demonstrate the mechanical interrelationship between cartilage and bone, which may also be partially mediated by signaling at the bone—cartilage interface. The biologic interactions occurring between cartilage and synovium or between cartilage and bone underscore the importance of appropriate tissue loading to restore joint homeostasis when the joint experiences stressors such as injury. Bone remodeling in response to mechanical loading was also seen in a rabbit model of hindlimb loading. Increased osteoblast-mediated bone mineral deposition was rapidly followed by newly mineralized bone tissue formation. The sequential activation of bone resorption, followed by bone formation and remodeling, indicates the dynamic nature in early responses of subchondral bone to mechanical loads. Similar changes appear to occur in humans based on analogous imaging studies. 118-120 However, more work is needed to understand the importance and regional differences in subchondral bone microenvironment changes in response to acute and chronic injuries. Conflicting studies have shown that subchondral cortical plate and trabecular thickness will decrease shortly after injury such as in the medial femoral groove model of OA in dogs, 121 while thickness increased in rabbit and mouse OA models after medial meniscectomy. 122, Some differences in these observations may be explained by altered weight bearing on the affected limb after the induced injury.

Similar to the cartilage context, cyclic compressive loading also activates regenerative responses in subchondral bone including adaptive increases in subchondral cortical bone plate thickness in the posterior tibial plateau, corresponding to regions of increased load transfer. This tends to line up with the regions of cartilage pathology as well, underscoring the linkage between the osteochondral components. 125, In multiple studies, trabecular bone mass will decrease in opposition to the increasing subchondral plate cortical bone thickness.

The induction and resolution of bone marrow lesions (BMLs) under areas of articular cartilage impact also show signs of regenerative response to injury. Bone marrow edema is detected using water-sensitive sequences on MRI, revealing areas of microfracture. Histopathological studies of BML have demonstrated perivascular edema and features of tissue healing in humans and animal models of injury. Active bone remodeling is typically seen and osteocytes play a key role in mediating the bone remodeling process through the release of ATP, membrane-derived lipids such as sphingosine-1-phosphate, numerous chemokines, and VEGF species including VEGFA and RANKL (receptor activator of NF-κB ligand).131-134 RANKL contributes to the recruitment and activation of osteoclasts in the subchondral microenvironment to stimulate bone remodeling and repair of the microfractures associated with BMLs. Although it is clear that bone responds rapidly to normal and injurious mechanical loading, it is not clear whether the early changes affect longer-term clinical outcomes.

### Osteophyte Formation

Although osteophytes are clearly a radiographic hallmark of OA, they also occur in people with no history of active symptomatic OA. Further, osteophytes are formed through regenerative biologic processes in the joint environment. As such, osteophytes are considered an epiphenomenon associated with OA rather than a pathogenic driver of OA. Osteophytes may be formed as a compensatory attempt to improve joint stabilization, since surgical

removal of osteophytes increases joint instability. The size of osteophytes is not associated with an increased risk of progression in OÅ, 137-139 underscoring that osteophytes are mostly in keeping with a sign of active or prior joint tissue repair. The lack of association of osteophyte size with OA progression may be because some patients with fewer or smaller osteophytes have less severe disease, whereas others have more severe disease but mount a less robust anabolic response to OA ("atrophic OA"). Thus interpreting the presence, features, or changes in osteophytes in the clinic is contextual and challenging.

Osteophytes arise from cell populations at the intersecting cartilage and periosteal margins and at the entheses where they are known as enthesophytes. They arise due to recapitulation of the endochondral bone formation process. Multipotent periosteal cells are recruited to the joint margin and activated and proliferate in response to an inflammatory or mechanical stimulus. Periosteal cells will then differentiate along a chondrogenic lineage until hypertrophic chondrocyte formation occurs. This initially progresses centrally within the developing osteophyte and then expands outwardly as chondrocytes/cartilage undergo mineralization and eventual replacement by osseous tissues mediated by TGF-β and BMP2.95, The origin of osteophytes is also clearly linked to mechanobiological responses. It has been shown that osteophytes can be induced with a single mechanical impact applied to the periosteum in a rat model. Underscoring the concept that osteophytes develop in the absence of OA-related joint pathophysiology, this model confirmed that mechanical manipulation of the periosteum itself is sufficient to develop osteophytes in the absence of OA.

### Cross-Talk Mechanisms and Tissue Repair

### Cartilage-Bone Cross-Talk

Proper functioning of the osteochondral unit is essential for joint homeostasis. In the 1950s, it was believed that the calcified cartilage was an impermeable barrier and that transfer of molecules in solution was not possible between the subchondral bone and overlying cartilage. In 1962, it was shown that cationic dyes could permeate the subchondral bone to the calcified cartilage interface. Numerous studies have since demonstrated that crosstalk between subchondral bone and articular cartilage supports cartilage oxygenation, nutrient delivery, and the biomechanical properties of both tissues. Most of the interactions between chondrocytes and osteocytes in the osteochondral junction is indirect via soluble mediators. However, there may be some regions where cells are close enough to permit cell-cell contact. 147 Survival factors are made by subchondral bone cells including osteocytes and osteoblasts. These factors increase the viability of chondrocytes, which has been observed in explant co-culture models.148, Healthy osteoblasts can stimulate the expression of aggrecan, type II collagen, SOX9, and decrease the expression of MMP-3 and MMP-13 in chondrocytes. Cell culture of chondrocytes together with healthy osteoblasts can blunt the induction of inflammatory cytokines such as IL-1β and IL-6,150 whereas osteoblasts from diseased bone in OA abrogate most of these effects.151-153 Taken together, these studies indicate that interactions between subchondral bone and deep zone/calcified zone articular cartilage support joint homeostasis.

### Cartilage Cross-Talk With Synovium and Adipose Tissue

Cross-talk between synovium and other tissues in the joint is an emerging field. Co-culture of synovial tissue with articular

chondrocytes leads to induced anabolic responses in articular chondrocytes, mediated in part by TGF-β signaling. Similarly, co-culture of cartilage with synovium enhanced the effect of interleukin-1 receptor antagonist (IL-1Ra), including less GAG release and nitric oxide generation and induction of anti-catabolic factors including IL-14, matrilin-3, and carbonic anhydrase. On the other hand, single-cell RNA sequencing studies of human OA synovial and cartilage tissues have generated prediction models, suggesting that procatabolic cross-talk occurs between synovial cell subpopulations and articular chondrocytes. In particular, inflammatory synovial macrophages expressing high amounts of IL-1β and dendritic cells (DCs) may contribute to pro-inflammatory responses in chondrocytes. Supporting these findings, co-culture of bovine cartilage with synovium increases the activity of MMPs and aggrecanases to carry out cartilage degradation. This suggests that targeted depletion or inhibition of pathologic synovial cell subpopulations could be a therapeutic strategy in OA. Similarly, procatabolic signaling between adipose tissue and cartilage has been suggested by surgically inducing experimental OA in a lipodystrophy mouse model. The absence of adipose tissue protected against the development of joint damage and joint pain, whereas reconstitution of systemic adipose stores abrogated the protective effects on joint disease development.

Modeling experiments using whole transcriptome gene expression databases have demonstrated the potential for cross-talk signaling between all joint tissues including articular cartilage, synovium, subchondral bone, meniscus, and adipose tissues. . However, follow-up studies to confirm the biologic and clinical importance of these modeled ligandreceptor interactions are needed to better understand how their changes affect the joint milieu. Together, these studies provide important insights into the critical role played by regenerative and pathogenic cross-talk mechanisms between joint tissues on the maintenance of joint homeostasis (Fig. 100.2).

### Osteoarthritis Risk Factors and Their Effects on Joint Physiology

Classical OA risk factors exert their negative effects on OA risk by overwhelming and inhibiting joint regenerative responses and/ or promoting pro-inflammatory mechanisms, leading to pain and joint tissue damage.

### Aging

Aging is associated with loss of physiologic homeostasis, which leads to compromised tissue function and increased susceptibility to tissue injury and damage. OA is not an inevitable consequence of aging, but age is a major OA risk factor. Age-related changes are apparent in joint tissues. In cartilage, a loss of physiologically appropriate mechanical properties, decreased cellularity, and thinning (atrophy) are all features of natural aging. While these changes do not cause OA directly, aging processes increase the susceptibility to OA onset by reducing the capacity (organ reserve) of joint tissues to compensate and adapt to normal environmental stresses. Other age-related changes include increased infrapatellar fat pad size and secretion of adipokines into the b161 Many of the hallmarks of aging159 such as increased celjoint. lular senescence, mitochondrial dysfunction, telomere attrition, and altered cellcell communication have been described in joint tissues.

Senescent cells accumulate in cartilage162 and bone163,164 during aging. Senescence induces permanent cell-cycle arrest,165 resistance to cell death, metabolic reprogramming, and the senescence associated secretory phenotype166 (SASP). The SASP is characterized by secretion of pro-inflammatory cytokines including IL-1β, IL-6, IL-8, TNF, chemokines, growth factors, and ECM-degrading enzymes including MMP-3 and MMP-13.166 SASP factors induce stressful effects on neighboring cells and tissue structures in the local microenvironment, including impaired anabolic processes and activation of ECM digestion mechanisms. Interestingly, OA chondrocyte phenotypes exhibit SASP-like features. Further, injections of senescent cells into the knees of naïve mice caused OA-like changes,167 while depletion of senescent cells slows the development of age-associated OA in rats and creates a prochondrogenic environment. Together, these results suggest that senescent cells may drive OA pathogenesis.

Senescence is induced by intrinsic, replicative telomere shortening and extrinsic, cell stress-induced senescence factors. Adult chondrocytes do not divide in situ169 but will divide in vitro. Interestingly, telomere shortening has been shown in adult chon- ,162 but it is unlikely to occur from cell division given the drocytes, quiescent nature of chondrocytes. Extrinsic factors such as DNA damage, oxidative damage, inflammation, and abnormal loadingassociated cellular stress can damage telomeres. In addition to aging, these are likely additional inducers of OA-related senes- 171-175 Further, recent research has highlighted the presence cence. of senescent cells in bone. Bone remodeling, which relies on

both resorption by osteoclasts and formation by osteoblasts, is required for homeostasis. SASPs promote adipogenesis and bone resorption, compromising skeletal integrity and function and supporting the hypothesis that senescence deranges homeostatic joint physiology.

Age-related mitochondrial dysfunction causes impaired respiratory chain function, decreased ATP generation, and increased pro-inflammatory mediators177 similar to those released by SASP. Indeed, mitochondrial DNA haplogroups can increase risk and severity of OA or conversely protect against OA develop- 179,180 0 Interestingly, when one group compared proteomic ment. signatures in OA versus healthy cartilage, 25% of dysregulated signatures related to mitochondrial function. Redox homeostasis is maintained through the balance of oxidizing and reducing reactions. An inverse relationship between reactive oxygen species (ROS) and antioxidants can be seen in aging. While ROSs increase with age, ,183 decreases in antioxidants occur including glutathione and superoxide dismutase-2 (SOD2), rendering the cells more vulnerable to the effects of ROS.184, Increasing ROS concentrations can cause mitochondrial DNA damage186 and exacerbate respiratory chain dysfunction. Ultimately, alterations in redox homeostasis increase intra-cellular ROS and cause oxidative stress and production of inflammatory mediators, which can stimulate MMP-mediated tissue damage. 187-189

Oxidative stress190 and age-associated reductions in antioxidant protein function accelerates telomere shortening and cellular aging, promoting chondrocyte senescence and apoptosis.

During oxidative stress, excess ROS promote oxidative post-translational modification and cleavage of cartilage collagen and aggre- . These modifications ultimately result in disorganization of can. the collagen fibers and bundles compromising the biomechanical properties of the ECM, Oxidative stress can also promote the formation of advanced glycation end products, which in turn promote formation of new ROS by activation of receptor for advanced glycation end products (RAGE). Increased ROSs reduce chondrocyte responsiveness to the growth factor IGF-1, resulting in less activation of phosphoinositide (PI) 3-kinase—AKT signaling and suppressing matrix synthesis. In a mouse model of experimental OA, recurring administration of N-acetylcysteine (an antioxidant) prevented chondrocyte senescence and OA development,195 highlighting the importance of redox homeostasis in cartilage health.

Nuclear factor erythroid 2related factors 2 (Nrf2) is a major regulator of antioxidant and detoxifying enzymes including superoxide dismutases and heme-oxygenase 1 (HO-1) and is important in maintaining redox homeostasis. Aged chondrocytes show decreased levels of Nrf2196 and HO-1 protein. Interestingly, when researchers knocked out Bach1, an HO-1 transcriptional repressor, they were able to reduce the severity of age-related OA in a SOD2-dependent manner. Further, antioxidants such as ,198 licochalcone,199 diallyl disulfide,200 pterostibene, resveratrol, 201 202 prontandim,203and 6-gingerol203exert anti-inflamwogonin,2 matory and chondroprotective effects through Nrf2-dependent pathways. Finally, decreased Nrf2 indirectly increases NF-κB activity, causing inflammation 204 and perpetuating mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and senescence.

Adenosine monophosphate—activated protein kinase (AMPK) responsiveness is reduced in aged chondrocytes,205 compromising its ability to function as an energy sensor and regulate redox homeostasis. In addition, inflammatory cytokines including some SASPs hinder the phosphorylation of ÁMPK,206 reducing its function. Chondrocyte-specific deletion of AMPK resulted in accelerated age-related OA. Further, systemic administration of berberine chloride (an AMPK agonist) limited aging-associated OA development in mice through activation of AMPK-dependent antioxidant pathways. 207, Interestingly, AMPK activates sirtuin 1 (SIRT1), another energy-sensing molecule, which is required for chondrocyte expression of aggrecan and type II collagen alpha 1 chain. While less studied, AMPK may also play a role in limiting synovial inflammation. When one group stretched rabbit synovial fibroblast in vitro, AMPK was activated and led to reduced phosphorylation of NF-κB. Further, systemic administration of chitosan oligosaccharide, an AMPK activator, suppressed synovial inflammation in an experimental model of OA. Further, a reduction in AMPK activity in macrophages increases aerobic glycolysis, which is associated with pro-inflammatory activation and ROS generation. Taken together, these studies suggest that AMPK may suppress age-associated synovial inflammation and play a critical role in maintaining redox homeostasis in cartilage ECM.

Another consequence of aging is a reduction in autophagy. Autophagy maintains cell homeostasis by clearing expired and damaged intraand extra-cellular components to lysosomes for degradation and recycling. 213, Due to the limited rate of cell turnover in cartilage, autophagy is essential for maintaining normal function. Importantly, autophagy prevents accumulation of damaged organelles and misfolded proteins,216 preventing cellular stress and apoptosis. Age-related decreases in chondrocyte autophagy contribute to cell death and reduced anabolic capacity

of the tissue. Longevity factors including SIRT1, mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR), FOXO3, and NF-kB all regulate autophagy. Inflammation and stress repress autophagy through NF-kB and mTOR, while SIRT1 and FOXO3, another regulator of cell metabolism, enhance autophagy. Autophagy is required for the beneficial effects of calorie restriction on longevity,218 highlighting its intersection with cellular metabolism and mitochondrial function. Indeed, autophagy of mitochondria (mitophagy) is able to prevent accumulation of ROS by removing damaged mitochondria. Not surprisingly, stimulating mitophagy leads to improved joint structural damage outcomes in pre-clinical OA models,219 highlighting the importance of this pathway in OA risk and disease progression.

Aging cells exhibit an altered ability to respond to growth factors, independent of ROS accumulation. In aging chondrocytes, the relative expression of ALK1 to ALK5 (TGF-β receptors) is altered, resulting in decreased matrix synthesis and increased expression of MMP-13,220,221 further accentuating structural dysfunction of articular cartilage. Interestingly, with age both bone and bone marrow stromal cells show impaired IGF-1 responsiveness. IGF-1 is an anabolic factor that stimulates bone formation. Reduced bone formation can lead to alterations in mechanical force transmission increasing the risk of OA.

Collectively, these processes can be considered aspects of inflammaging. 223, Increases in cellular SASPs and adipokines drive inflammation, cellular stress, and mitochondrial dysfunction. Reduced autophagy and cellular homeostasis lead to decreased tissue cellularity and viability, anabolic capacity, and mechanical quality. These pathogenic mechanisms demonstrate how aging increases the risk of OA.

### Female Sex

Despite a lower prevalence of OA in women under 50, women are still two times more likely to develop OA. The dramatic increase in OA prevalence in post-menopausal women suggests that sex hormones participate in joint homeostasis.225, For instance, estrogen replacement therapy decreases risk of knee OA and reduces incidence of total knee arthroplasty. 227, While it was traditionally believed that joint tissue did not respond to estrogen, it is now clear that bone, cartilage, and synovial cells express estrogen receptors. 229-231

Estrogens and progesterone both appear to promote anabolic processes in articular chondrocytes, but systemic concentrations of estrogens and progesterone decline during menopause. Research has primarily focused on in vitro experiments to understand the role of estrogens and progesterone on chondrocytes. When adult female chondrocytes were treated with 17β-estradiol, anabolic processes including proliferation, production type II collagen and aggrecan, and increased proteoglycan sulfation were detected. Further 17β-estradiol treatment reduced production of MMP-1, -3, and -13 in female chondrocytes, stressing the role of estrogen in cartilage homeostasis. Interestingly, a dimorphic response to 17β-estradiol was seen, where two groups identified these effects only in female chondrocytes, suggesting that sex defines cellular responses in chondrocytes.232, Another group highlighted the role of 17β-estradiol in preventing telomere shortening where premenopausal concentrations prevented shortening but post-menopausal concentrations did not, suggesting that there is an overlap between estrogens and cellular senescence. Progesterone may play a role in maintenance of cartilage thickness by suppressing MMP activity. Indeed, serum progesterone concentration is

positively associated with cartilage volume in women. Progesterone and estrogen supplementation in a rat model of OA suppressed cartilage turnover and reduced signs of pathologic changes associated with OA; however, no clinical association between combined progesterone and estrogen supplementation and the need for total knee arthroplasty was seen. 228, Although less studied, estrogen is able to modulate bone turnover and remodeling by regulating osteoblast and osteoclast activity, with declining estrogen levels in post-menopausal women increasing the rate of bone remodeling in the subchondral plate.238, In the synovium, estrogen stimulates fibroblast-like synoviocyte production of MMPs, while progesterone inhibits production. In addition, progesterone appears to inhibit secretion of pro-inflammatory mediators by DC.

Women have more robust immune responses, and post-menopausal reductions in estrogens are associated with increased production of inflammatory cytokines such as IL-6.242, Further, low serum levels of estradiol and progesterone are associated with increased knee effusion synovitis in women. Estrogens appear to inhibit IL-6 production, and there is likely a synergistic relationship between reduced estrogens and IL-6 production. Metabolic syndrome is more prevalent in women, especially post-menopausal women,245 and the relationship with increased systemic inflammation associated with metabolic syndrome may drive OA risk. For example, a higher proportion of new knee OA cases were attributed to a body mass index of 27 or greater in women, further solidifying an interaction between female sex and MetS. On the other hand, it is thought that testosterone is protective against OA development, as the lack of testosterone in animal models and male patients with testosterone deficiency is associated with worse OA symptoms. Whether these effects are direct or indirect requires further investigation.

### Obesity and Metabolic Syndrome

Metabolic syndrome (MetS) is a group of metabolic derangements including central obesity, insulin resistance, dyslipidemia, and hypertension. An association between metabolic syndrome and low grade inflammation exists, ,248 and metabolic syndrome increases risk of OA.249, Knee OA is most strongly associated with MetS,250 in which increased joint load is hypothesized as the mechanism of action. However, one group also discovered that obesity increased the risk of OA in non—weight-bearing joints, 250 suggesting that mechanical load is not the only cause of MetSassociated OA. Interestingly, a direct role for adipose tissue was recently demonstrated in experimental models of OA. In a mouse model of lipodystrophy, the absence of adipose tissue protected animals from both spontaneous and post-traumatic OA, regardless of a lean or high-fat diet. Further, reintroduction of systemic adipose tissue restored the susceptibility to OA, highlighting a critical role for adipose tissue and adipose tissue—derived signaling molecules in OA risk and pathogenesis. .

Adipose tissue is the major producer of adipokines produced in the joint. Adiponectin, leptin, IL-6, and TNF are the best studied mediators in OA. Adipokine secretion changes with increasing adiposity, with which leptin, IL-6, and TNF increase and adiponectin tends to decrease. Interestingly, adiponectin appears to slow the progression of hand OA. Further, when chondrocytes are treated with adiponectin in vitro, they increase expression of TIMPs (specifically TIMP2), decrease expression of IL-1β, and are protected against ROS-induced apoptosis via AMPK/mTOR regulation of autophagy.252,253Outside of cartilage, adiponectin

is important for bone homeostasis. It promotes osteogenic differentiation and promotes osteoblast commitment but also inhibits osteoblast activity.254-256 In the synovial membrane, adiponectin has dual roles in macrophage activity. Adiponectin induced production of IL-10 in alternatively activated macrophages and induced expression of TNF, IL-6, and IL-12 in pro-inflammatory macrophages. Adiponectin also repolarizes pro-inflammatory macrophages toward a proresolving phenotype, suggesting a role .257,258With these benfor adiponectin in resolving inflammation. eficial effects of adiponectin in mind, MetS decreases the systemic concentration of adiponectin, increasing OA risk.

Models of leptin and leptin receptor deficiency have demonstrated the protective effects of removing leptin. In vitro, leptin induces chondrocyte production of IL-8, MMP-1, MMP- 3, MMP-9, MMP-13, and expression of Col10a1, with leptin deficiency reducing type X collage levels in growth plates. 261, Further, leptin may cause chondrocyte progenitor senescence, perpetuating chondrocyte inflammation and catabolic activity. Leptin also regulates bone remodeling through β-adrenergic signaling, inhibiting osteoblast proliferation and enhancing osteoclast resorption while simultaneously binding leptin receptors on MSCs and enhancing proliferation and osteoblast differentiation. 264-266

Resistin and chemerin are less studied in OA but represent an interesting avenue for future study. Resistin, produced by white adipose tissue, can increase chondrocyte expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines, chemokines, and MMP genes while also promoting osteoblast proliferation and osteoclast formation. 267, Chemerin was originally described as a leukocyte chemoattractant, but it is now recognized that chemerin receptors are also expressed by chondrocytes and bone cells. Interestingly, chemerin can promote chondrocyte production of MMPs and mediate bone metabolism through testosterone-mediated osteoblast and osteoclast formation. 270,

Interestingly, the adipokines IL-6 and TNF are both described as true SASPs, and IL-6 levels are associated with increased risk of knee OA. The infrapatellar fat pad produces IL-6 and TNF and secretes it directly into the synovial fluid contributing to the intraarticular milieu. As described earlier, IL-6 promotes cartilage 274-276while TNF and bone catabolism and suppresses anabolism, promotes catabolism, inhibits anabolism, induces ROS generation, and promotes osteoclast formation. 277-281

Altered cellular metabolism is a major consequence of metabolic disease. As discussed above, AMPK is a major regulator of metabolic reprograming via energy sensing and redox homeostasis. Interestingly, insulin resistance and hyperglycemia reduce AMPK activity causing inflammation and ROS generation, leading to oxidative stress. Further, glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase stimulates inflammation and oxidative stress and is found in higher quantities in obese patients. Interestingly, obesity and nutrient excess induces hyperactivation of mTOR complex 1 (mTORC1), a critical nutrient sensor responsible for anabolic processes. Increased mTORC1 activity impairs macrophage polarization toward proresolving phenotype. In addition, myeloid-specific deletion of tuberous sclerosis complex 1 led to hyperactivity of mTORC1, which also increased inflammatory factor production and worsening OA progression. Chronic nutrient excess overwhelms adipocytes' capacity to store fatty acids, resulting in excess circulating low-density-lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol (dyslipidemia) and free fatty acids. Mice fed diets consisting of lower ratios of omega-6 (pro-inflammatory) to omega-3 (anti-inflammatory) polyunsaturated fatty acids resulted in lower blood levels of IL-1B, TNF, leptin, and resistin. .286,

At the joint level, lower ratio omega-6 to omega-3 also reduced joint tissue ossification, synovial inflammation, and macrophage infiltration in this model.

Changes in lipid metabolism can also affect joint homeostasis through abnormal accumulation of lipids in chondrocytes. 288-290 Interestingly, chondrocyte cholesterol accumulation and highfat diet both aggravate disease in mouse models of OA.286, Further when researchers explored activation of nuclear receptors involved in lipid metabolism, activation of peroxisome-proliferated activated receptor δ, a fatty acid binding transcription factor, upregulated expression of Txnip. Txnip inhibits thioredoxin and causes endoplasmic reticulum stress, inflammation, and accumulation of ROS, suggesting a role for free fatty acids in ROS generation and oxidative stress. Further, when chondrocytes, bone cells, or macrophages are cultured with free fatty acids, they increase production of inflammatory cytokines, chemokines, and ROS.294-296 Finally, dyslipidemia also plays a role in activating synovial macrophages in OA joints via cholesterol. Binding of oxidized LDL to the LDL receptor stimulates the release of growth factors, MMPs, and pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-6 and IL-8, which promote OA changes in joint tissues. .297-299 Taken together, metabolic disease and derangements in nutrient profiles lead to reduced anabolic responses, and increased catabolism, inflammation, ROS generation and oxidative stress, all of which are deleterious for joint health.

### Abnormal Biomechanics (Alignment, Repetitive Microtrauma, and Joint Shape) and Injury

Mechanical loading is an important and well-known risk factor for OA. Historically, it was thought that mechanical load in OA resulted simply in "wear and tear"; however, research in the field has strongly demonstrated that mechanical load activates mechanosensitive signaling pathways that drive damaging pathophysiology leading to tissue damage. Biomechanical loads that are within the normal physiologic range (physiologic loading) stimulate restorative and homeostatic processes in the healthy tissue context. However, biomechanical loading can become abnormal (pathogenic) when the load magnitudes either exceed the range of physiologic loading for healthy tissues (e.g., with abnormal joint alignment, joint trauma, increased adiposity, and occupational risk) or when physiologically normal loads are transmitted through a joint that has reduced capacity for mechanoprotective mechanisms via loss of joint stability, altered articular cartilage or subchondral bone integrity and mechanical properties, and muscular atrophy. 300,

Joint biomechanics are pivotal to OA pathogenesis and can differ across stages of disease. Measures of knee joint loading during walking are associated with pain302-304a and measures of structural progression in OA.305-307 Additionally, less dynamic and sustained knee loading patterns are seen in patients with OA compared with controls. Further, alterations in muscle activation patterns during joint movement are associated with OA progression. 309, Most biomechanics studies have been conducted in large, weightbearing joints such as the knee or the hip; however, developments in the field are enabling more work to be conducted to understand the role of mechanics in hand OA.

Cartilage and bone are not the only joint tissues that experience mechanical load, nor are they the only joint tissues that are mechanoresponsive. Tensile strain loading of synovial cells in vitro induces changes in gene expression related to processes such as inflammation, ECM integrity, and oxidative stress, 312-315 all of

which can affect joint homeostasis. One group found that the tensile strain loading of fbroblasts resulted in oxidative stress-induced pro-inflammatory gene expression, which was suppressed by overexpression of HO-1 (a key mediator of redox homeostasis). This suggests that mechanical stresses may disrupt the homeostatic redox handling capacity of synovial fibroblasts. In line with this concept, OA pathogenesis may cause similar derangements in synovial tissue physiology and lower the tolerance to mechanical loads; this is similar to what has been described in cartilage and bone. A recent study found that physiologic responses to tensile loading in late-stage OA synovium included inflammatory signaling mechanisms, alterations in cell metabolism, and redox-related cell stress, all of which were frequency dependent. Similarly, in the temporomandibular joint, overloading shifted the homeostatic balance of anabolic and catabolic processes. 317, Together, these facts suggest that OA may disturb synovial homeostasis, lower tolerance to mechanical stress, and lead to aberrant responses to mechanical load such as mechanoinflammatory and oxidative stress processes, ultimately perpetuating OA pathogenesis.

Mechanoinflammation is defined as the inflammatory response to mechanical injury and/or stimulation, and it influences OA pathogenesis. Processes indicative of mechanoinflammation have been investigated in cartilage and synovial tissues in the context of OA. For instance, mechanical stresses on articular cartilage evoke inflammatory, redox, and metabolic changes in cellular physiology. Inflammatory responses to mechanical injury can activate TAK1, which drives aggrecan degradation in vitro and in vivo. 320, TAK1 also activates NGF, a key mediator of OA 301, In patients with late-stage knee OA, synovial peripain. vascular edema, a sign of tissue stress, was associated with aberrant knee loading patterns throughout gait, supporting the link between mechanical stress and synovial inflammation.

Interestingly, immobilization of the joint after OA induction prevents the development of OA and also inhibits inflammatory gene and protease regulation. Similarly, changes in the composition of synovial fluid biomarkers were observed after joint unloading with distraction surgery. In another study, suppression of mechanoinflammation in OA inhibited pain and matrix turnover and promoted intrinsic repair signaling.

It has been hypothesized that mechanoinflammation may be part of normal joint repair response; however, appropriate control of inflammatory signaling is required for proper homeostatic repair outcomes. Previous work suggests that the type of load can influence the balance between pro-degenerative and prorepair pathways. For example, shear stress at the articular surface activates mechanoinflammatory responses, while compressive load tends to drive chondroprotection, 301,324 as long as it is in the physiologic range.

### Genetics

Over the past decade, comprehensive analysis of genetics has given fundamental insights in disease pathophysiology and allowed identification of targets for therapeutic intervention. Genomewide association scans (GWAS), comparing OA patients to controls, has enabled the discovery of single nuclear polymorphisms (SNPs) associated with disease. These studies have focused on the most common form of OA, age-associated OA, and used multiple diagnostic tools such as joint space narrowing, pain or need for total joint replacement to select cases. Accounting for the effects of sex and genetic ancestry, researchers can rigorously interrogate disease-associated genetic variants using GWAS analysis. Numerous
