large GWAS studies in OA have determined that the vast majority of OA is caused by permutations of polygenic risks, most often through the additive effects of numerous SNPs that contribute to risk of developing pathophysiological changes to one or more joint tissues. One review indicates that 124 SNPs are significantly associated with OA risk. More recently, a meta-analysis on GWAS data encompassing 826,690 individuals identified 223 independent SNPs, with 84 of them previously unreported. Like other common diseases, OA-related SNPs are primarily located in noncoding regions of the genome, further solidifying OA as a polygenic disease. 327-329

As discussed earlier, endogenous regenerative mechanisms and tolerance to physiologic stresses are critical for the maintenance of homeostasis. SNPs in ECM proteins such as COL2A1, COL11A1, COL27A1, CHST11, and CHST3 are all associated with OA risk and may compromise the tissues ability to 328,330-332Further, dysregulation of withstand mechanical stress. growth factors including TGF-β, FGF18, and GDF5 are all associated with increased OA risk.330, As discussed earlier, TGF-β is a critical anabolic growth factor for chondrocytes. The OA risk variant rs6060369 is associated with a reduction in GDF5 expression, which results in changes in bone morphology and increased risk of spontaneous OA; this increased risk may be associated with altered biomechanics and increased mechanical stress. Further, GWAS has identified risk variants associated with fibrillin 2, LTBP1, and LTBP3, which function together to regulate availability of TGF-β in cartilage highlighting the connectedness of OA risk variants. Interestingly, FGF18 promotes an antiarthritic effect in a rat model of post-traumatic OA through anabolism and maintenance of redox homeostasis, suggesting a preventative role in oxidative damage.

Several OA risk variants colocalize with genes encoding histone modifying proteins, suggesting an epigenetic component of OA genetic risk factors. Inhibition of histone deacetylase enzymes reduced expression of MMPs and IL-1 in OA chondrocytes and OA mouse models.332, DNA methylation, another form of epigenetic regulation of gene expression, is also associated with OA risk variants. Specifically, researchers have identified a differentially methylated region upstream of RUNX2 that has reduced methylation in the OA risk variant and increased expression of RUNX2, a promotor of chondrocyte hypertrophy. b Age remains the strongest risk factor for OA. However, since polygenic risks may exert their effects on joint tissues slowly over time, advancing age may interact with genetic and epigenetic risk factors leading to the emergence of OA phenotypes in later life.

Individual cases of OA are not usually explained by a single genetic risk allele. However, there are rare, extreme cases of OA-like phenotypes with early-life onset that can be caused by major mutations in key risk-associated genes. Such conditions provide us with an important view of how the affected genes function and their importance to maintenance of joint homeostasis. For example, camptodactyly arthropathy-coxa vara-pericarditis syndrome (CACP) is caused by an autosomal recessive mutation in PRG4, encoding lubricin. Most synovial joints are affected, causing joint dysfunction due to loss of the lubricating, anti-inflammatory, and homeostatic effects of lubricin. Studies in animal models of OA have shown that intra-articular injection of lubricin protects against OA-related joint damage. Acromesomelic chondrodysplasias are a group of rare, heterogeneous skeletal conditions caused by mutations in GDF5, including in Hunter—Thompson and Grebe chondrodysplasia. 342,

Observation of the neonatal-onset limb-shortening effects of these conditions caused by autosomal recessive mutations has uncovered the pivotal role played by GDF5 in joint patterning and development. Pseudoachondroplasia is caused by an autosomal dominant mutation in cartilage oligomeric protein (COMP), which increases the risk of developing OA due to the critical role of COMP function in maintaining the biomechanical and physiologic properties of healthy articular cartilage. Autosomal dominant mutations in important components of cartilage ECM cause multiple epiphyseal dysplasia, including collagen type IX α-1 (COL9A1), collagen type IX α-2 (COL9A2), collagen type IX α-3 (COL9A3), COMP, and matrilin-3 (MATN3). Interestingly, an autosomal recessive mutation in the sulfate transporter gene SLC26A2 can also cause multiple epiphyseal dysplasia. Together, these mutations contribute to derangements in joint homeostasis due to ECM protein misfolding in the affected gene products. The accumulation of misfolded ECM proteins causes endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress. A similar phenomenon of protein-misfolding/ER stress occurs in metaphyseal chondrodysplasia type Schmid, which is caused by a mutation in type X collagen. Mutations that lead to the accumulation of calcium crystals also increase the risk of developing early-life onset of OA. These include autosomal dominant mutations in the osteoprotegrin gene TNFRSF11B (chondrocalcinosis 1) or the ANKH gene, controlling inorganic phosphate production and deposition in the ECM (chondrocalcinosis 2). The accumulation of CPP crystals in the ECM of cartilage, synovium, and other joint tissues leads to activation of the inflammasome (discussed below). Finally, alkaptonuria, caused by genetic deficiency of homogentisate 1,2-dioxygenase (HGD), causes accumulation of homogentisic acid in cartilage and blue-black discoloration (ochronosis). This leads to cartilage dysfunction and altered biomechanical properties of the tissue, increasing chondrocyte stress, and therefore increased risk of OA development.

### Interaction Between OA Risk Factors

Combinations of risk factors (stressors) such as tissue aging and metabolic derangements (e.g., hypertension, diabetes, and dyslipidemia) can produce aberrant biologic responses in joint tissues. Age-related changes in joint tissues include tissue atrophy (e.g. thinning of articular cartilage relative to younger ages), oxidative stresses resulting from mitochondrial dysfunction and the resulting release of ROS,348 and accumulation of senescent cells. Senescent cells are suspected to perpetuate local tissue damage due to SASP factors, including cytokines, chemokines, and MMPs associated with cartilage damage. Current research efforts are examining the potential efficacy of removing senescent cells using senolytic treatments in joints with OA. Age-related increases in myeloid cells and circulating pro-inflammatory cytokines351 are accompanied by increases in visceral and intra-articular adipose 352 Adipocytes are linked to OA through the production stores. of adipokines including adiponectin, leptin, resistin, and visfatin, which can increase the production of MMPs and aggrecanases by chondrocytes353 and induce senescence in joint-lining cells. Despite being independent OA risk factors, age and metabolic derangements frequently co-exist and are closely overlapping in pathophysiologic mechanisms. Aging and metabolic derangement likely act synergistically by contributing to aberrant innate immune activation in synovial joints. Overall, these processes

likely contribute to OA pathology in particular by reducing the joint's organ reserves and thus the ability to withstand both normal and abnormal biomechanical stresses that occur throughout the lifespan.

### Pain Experiences and Nociceptive Signaling in OA

OA-related pain originates due to pathophysiologic changes at the level of joint tissues and persists, progresses, spreads, and evolves due to failure of those early pathophysiologic changes to resolve. As such, OA is a major cause of chronic pain worldwide. OA pain pathophysiology is complex, and the experience of pain among patients is multifactorial and progresses over the course of disease. The most common type of OA pain is mechanical; patients experience pain when walking on a flat surface, stair climbing, and other activities of daily living. Although activity-induced pain is the most common pain experience, many other types of pain experiences have been described in OA such as inflammatory pain, 356 neuropathic-like pain, 357,358 and widespread pain.

There are key pain characteristics that align with OA disease stage. In early OA, patients describe pain as sharp and typically brought on by a predictable trigger. At the midpoint of disease, pain becomes more constant with a greater impact on daily activities and can be associated with other joint symptoms such as locking, some of which may be unpredictable. In the advanced stages of OA damage, the pain is described as a dull, achy constant pain that is accompanied by short, rather intense, and unpredictable intermittent pain. In advanced OA, the pain significantly affects daily activities and leads to avoidance behaviors and modification of activities. In addition to intermittent and constant type pain, people with OA show signs of both peripheral and central sensitization, which involves altered pain processing at the joint and at sites away from the affected joint, respectively. Due to the heterogeneous nature of OA pain over the course of disease, it is imperative to increase our understanding of pain in OA to provide better management for patients.

### Synovial Joint Innervation

OA is a disease of the whole joint361 and affects all joint tissues. Therefore understanding the relevant subsets of neurons and their innervation is key for the management of OA pain.

### Healthy Joint Innervation

In healthy joints, the synovium, capsule, menisci, ligaments, subchondral bone, and periosteum are all innervated by sensory and sympathetic neurons, 362-365 while the articular cartilage remains aneural and avascular. Normal processing of pain is a protective mechanism that involves the detection of stimuli that are harmful or potentially harmful to the tissue. There are specialized sensory and sympathetic neurons that innervate the joint and contribute to normal joint function.

Sensory nerves of the joint perform nociception and are either thinly myelinated, fast conducting Aδ-fibers or unmyelinated, slow conducting C-fibers. These innervate synovium, capsule, ligaments, menisci, subchondral bone, and periosteum and are polymodal, which means they can be activated by noxious mechanical, chemical, and thermal stimuli.366-368

Sympathetic nerve fibers of the joint are involved in vasomotor control, light touch, and proprioception and are thick myelinated

Aα and Aβ fibers. These innervate synovial membrane, joint capsule, periarticular bursae, fat pad, ligaments, menisci, and bone and are typically non-noxious and activated by joint movement. 366-368

### Osteoarthritis-Induced Changes in Joint Innervation

Over the disease course of OA, joint innervation changes. In human and rodent OA knee joints, there is nerve growth and vascular penetration into the subchondral bone, osteochondral junction, menisci, and osteophytes.369-371 Articular cartilage is aneural and avascular under normal physiologic conditions. However, sensory and sympathetic nerves can infiltrate the articular cartilage in both mild and severe OA via vascular channels. Several studies have shown increased PGP9.5+ nerves (pan-neuronal marker),369,372,373 increased presence of neuropeptide-immunoreactive nociceptors, 374 and an increased presence of Nay1.8+ nociceptors in OA joints, 371 all of which contribute to increases in pain.

The synovium has many homeostatic functions for the joint but is an important source of pain in OA. However, there is mixed evidence surrounding OA-induced changes in synovial innervation. One group found a decrease in nerve fibers in the synovial lining that was dependent on the degree of synovial inflammation. 375 In concordance, another study found there was decreased synovial lining innervation with more advanced cartilage degeneration in animals, Whereas other groups have identified increases in synovial sensory nerve fibers in human377,378 and animal models of experimental arthritis.379, Taken together, synovial innervation in OA is likely heterogeneous and context specific to the joint environment. Synovial neuroplasticity in OA should be investigated further.

Importantly, the plastic changes in joint innervation induced by OA may contribute to the recruitment of previously silent nociceptors. Studies assessing joint afferents at the level of the dorsal root ganglia (DRG), using Ca2+ imaging, showed increased signaling from a population of newly sensitized neurons in response to noxious joint stimulation.381-383 However, further characterization of this population of neurons is required.

The purpose of joint nociceptor remodeling in OA is unknown; however, it has been hypothesized that it may serve as a protective mechanism for preventing joint usage via enhanced pain signaling and therefore promoting healing. It has also been hypothesized that nociceptor remodeling may represent neurogenic repair of the joint to combat the progressive degeneration of cartilage and bone.

### Joint-Spine-Brain Connection

Pain signaling begins when joint nociceptors are activated by various stimuli and transmit pain signals via the DRG to the dorsal horn of the spinal cord, where they synapse with second order neurons. The signal crosses over and continues up the spinothalamic tract to the brain stem and thalamus, and signals get relayed to the hypothalamus, periaqueductal gray, amygdala, basal ganglia, limbic system, and somatosensory cortex. The descending pathway synapses in the dorsal horn to prevent release of neuropeptides and depolarization of neurons, thus dampening the pain signal. Loss of inhibition from the descending pathway along the neuroaxis can amplify central processing of pain.

Although there is much evidence to support that peripheral sources are the main driver of pain in OA, there is increasing literature suggesting the involvement of brain centers in OA pain. Remodeling of pain centers in the brain is seen in patients with

OA, and it has been hypothesized that there is a misinterpretation of peripheral source of pain by the central centers.

Functional imaging of patients with hip OA showed significantly greater brain stem activation compared with healthy patients in response to the same noxious stimuli. The magnitude of brain stem activation was positively correlated with neuropathic-like elements reported using the painDETECT score. The same group found that thalamic atrophy associated with painful hip OA was reversed at 9 months after total hip arthroplasty. Conversely, in a study of patients with knee OA, increased neural activity and connectivity between the cingulate cortex and rostral ventromedial medulla pre-operatively was associated with moderate to severe long-term pain after total knee arthroplasty. One study found that, relative to controls, functional connectivity between the secondary somatosensory cortex and left posterior insula was increased, while the functional connectivity between the bilateral posterior insula and motor cortices was decreased in patients with hip OA. Further, in response to painful physical activity, functional connectivity increased between the thalamus, periaqueductal gray matter, and brain stem, indicating that some connections are modulated by painful activity in OA. Changes in functional connectivity within the brain have also been shown in OA of the small joints. For instance, in patients with hand OA, functional MRI analysis showed increased activity in the thalamus, cingulate, frontal, and somatosensory cortex compared with controls. Interestingly, exercise interventions such as tai chi and stationary cycling reduce pain and functional connectivity in periaqueductal gray matter and ventral tegmental area for patients with knee OA over 12 weeks.

From the current literature, it appears there are distinct connectivity signatures and brain region activation that are dependent on the joints involved, stage of disease, and intervention applied (i.e., exercise versus surgery). This area of research in the OA field remains largely understudied, with small sample sizes, compared with other areas and requires further research to gain a complete understanding of brain circuitry in OA pain.

### Nociceptive Mechanisms in Osteoarthritis

### Types of Osteoarthritis Pain

Nociceptive, inflammatory, and neuropathic pain have all been described in OA, and each have distinct neurobiological mechanisms. Nociceptive pain is caused by tissue damage or stimuli that is potentially damaging to the tissue. This type of pain is what is classically associated with OA due to degenerative changes in the joint tissues. Aberrant joint biomechanics due to malalignment, osteophyte formation, subchondral bone sclerosis, muscle weakness or atrophy, or traumatic joint injury will open mechanogated ion channels on nociceptive nerves and generate nociceptive pain. 366,

Inflammatory pain arises from several sources within the OA joint. As structures within the joint degenerate, sensory nerves in the subchondral bone, menisci, and newly innervated articular cartilage become exposed to the intra-articular environment, which is concentrated with inflammatory mediators. In addition, sensory nerves in the synovium are also exposed to the intra-articular environment, and pathologic changes within the synovium such as increased immune cell infiltration and increased production of a localized source of proalgesic molecules contribute to inflammatory pain signaling. 393-398

Neuropathic pain is present in approximately 23% of people with hip and knee OA, is caused by damage to the nervous system

itself, and includes nerves at the level of the joint and in the dorsal root ganglia, spinal cord, and brain. The exact mediators of nerve damage in OA have not been fully elucidated to date; however, molecules such as lysophosphatidic acid,399 known to have demyelinating effects on peripheral nerves, have been found to be upregulated in OA synovial fluid. It stands to reason that other molecules concentrated within the intra-articular environment in OA could also contribute to demyelination of joint afferents; however, this remains to be explored.

### Pain Sensitization in Osteoarthritis

Increased and/or constant nociceptive mediator input from mechanical or chemical stimulation can alter the properties of nociceptive neurons at the level of the joint by activating intracellular signal transduction and increasing the production and transport of transducer channels and voltage-gated ion channels. The threshold for activation becomes reduced, and membrane excitability increases, making the nerves more likely to fire in response to normal and non-noxious stimuli,382-384 which is called peripheral sensitization.

Continuous nociceptor input locally at the joint can lead to increased excitability of second order neurons in the dorsal horn of the spinal cord. This is called central sensitization, a form of synaptic plasticity, and typically results in augmentation of the nociceptive signal and intensification of pain sensations.366, When there is long-term potentiation of nociceptive input to the spinal cord, lower-threshold afferents convert to pain drivers, and sensory input from outside the injury site is recruited. The expanded area of signaling allows second order neurons to receive input from tissues outside the affected joint and therefore leads to the phenomenon of referred pain.366, These synaptic changes have been observed in patients with established OA401 and are linked to high levels of pain and disability, 401,402 diffuse pain 4044and around the joint,403 increased pro-inflammatory cytokines, poor outcomes after joint replacement surgery. 405,

Recently the International Association for the Study of Pain (IASP) introduced the term "nociplastic pain," which is defined as "pain that arises from altered nociception despite no clear evi- CC dence of actual or threatened tissue damage causing activation of peripheral nociceptors or evidence for disease or lesion of the somatosensory system causing the pain. "407, Although sensitization is not included in the definition of nociplastic pain, it is a major underlying mechanism. Clinical criteria for nociplastic pain in patients with chronic musculoskeletal conditions has been released by the IASP407,408 and should be considered when assessing pain phenotypes of patients with OA.

### Neuroimmune Interactions in OA Pain

Interactions between the immune system and the nervous system play an important role in OA pain and have been characterized as bidirectional, meaning each can act on the other. Macrophages are the most abundant immune cell in the OA joint393 and can release inflammatory mediators such as TNF, IL-1, and NGF or other neurotrophins that signal via TrkA and increase .409-411 Macrophages also produce reactive nociceptor excitability. oxygen species that can activate nociceptors and can contribute to pain signaling in OA. Several studies have found that increased synovial fluid levels of macrophage markers' 412-414 and macrophage-associated chemokines415 are associated with worse pain in patients with OA. In synovial tissue, NGF expression 416 and an increase in activated macrophages417 were associated with

pain and other clinical symptoms. However, many studies to date use pan-macrophage makers for identification, which fails to convey the complex spectrum of macrophage activation and function within the OA joint.

Locally within the damaged joint, nociceptors can produce and respond to pro-inflammatory chemokines that lead to production of CCL2, a strong chemotactic signal for macrophages and mono- 409,418 cytes. Neuropeptides released by nociceptors modulate the macrophage phenotype. 419, Substance P released by activated nociceptors can result in increased NF-kBdependent production of pro-inflammatory cytokines by macrophages. Interestingly, in a pro-inflammatory environment, neuropeptides such as CGRP can act on TLR4-stimulated macrophages to increase production of IL-10,420 which is an important molecule for immune regulatory mechanisms within the joint.

In addition to acting locally within the joint, macrophages in the central nervous system, called microglia, are known to play an important role in chronic OA pain. Activation of microglia is associated with pain behaviors in both surgical421,422 and chemical 423,424 models of OA. Further, pain behavior was attenuated when microglia activation was inhibited in experimental OA, ,423 suggesting that spinal mechanisms are an important aspect of the pain experience in OA. The changes in microglia were also identi- 423,424indicating that these fied in the contralateral dorsal horn, effector cells may be important in complex pain states including widespread pain and referred pain.

Immune cells such as T cells and mast cells and nonimmune cells such as fibroblasts are also contributors to OA pain experiences. One study found that increased Th1 and Th2 cell infiltration in the synovial membrane was associated with higher pain scores on the numeric pain rating scale (NRS). Levels of circulating peripheral T helper and Th17 cells correlate with worse Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Arthritis Index (WOMAC) pain scores. In a rodent model of experimental OA, mast cells signaling via TrkA were involved in pain behavior outcomes and when exposed to NGF upregulated other pro-inflammatory mediators such as COX2 and PGD2.427 Synovial fibroblasts within painful joint regions from patients with earlyand late-stage OA were found to have different gene expression profiles that promoted signaling related to fibrosis, inflammation, and nerve growth. As pain is strongly associated with the degree of inflammation (synovitis) in OA, understanding the pathogenesis of pain requires further elucidation of the immune and nonimmune signaling networks within the OA joint.

### Cross-Talk Between Inflammation and Sensory Nerve Fibers in Osteoarthritis

DAMPs are molecules resulting from the degradation of joint tissues that can activate receptors expressed by nociceptors. Breakdown products from extra-cellular matrix proteins, leaking of plasma proteins from joint vasculature, and alarmins released from stressed or apoptotic cells are all sources of DAMPs in the OA joint.

DAMPs including TLR4 ligand, α2-macroglobulin, S100A8, and S100A9418,430 and for a 32-amino-acid aggrecan fragment431 have been detected in OA joints and can excite nociceptors via TLR signaling. Activation of TLRs by 32-mer increased production of CCL2 by cultured DRG neurons, s,356,431which is a proalgesic molecule and chemokine for immune cell recruitment.

The 32-mer aggrecan can activate nociceptors through TLR2 and produce hyperalgesia. Interestingly, TLR2 and TLR4 null mice developed OA-related joint degeneration and were protected from knee hyperalgesia after destabilization of the medial meniscus (DMM) surgery 31 but were not protected from developing

mechanical allodynia, suggesting that DAMPs may contribute to OA pain via mechanisms other than TLR signaling. Thus DAMPs are an important source of nociceptive activation within the degenerating OA joint and highlight cross-talk between nociceptive and non-nociceptive tissues in the joint.

### Nerve Growth Factor and Pain in Osteoarthritis

NGF was identified as a key molecule that regulates the growth and survival of sensory and sympathetic neurons 382,432 and plays a major role in producing pain. NGF has high affinity for the receptor TrkA on a subset of nociceptors, and this activation increases expression and activation of ion channels and receptors, voltage-gated sodium and calcium channels, mechanosensitive channels, and acid-sensing ion channels. NGF signaling also modifies nociceptor ion channels leading to sensitization.

In the OA joint, synovial fluid levels of NGF are significantly elevated compared with non-OA joints433 and are correlated with poorer knee joint function in OA patients. In human joints with advanced OA, NGF expression in synovial fibroblasts and macrophages was associated with pain. Additionally, NGF has increased expression in osteochondral channels in subchondral bone from patents undergoing total knee arthroplasty. In rodent models in which OA is surgically induced, NGF gene expression is upregulated in the joint at both early (mild OA) and later (chronic OA) time points in the model.322, Given the important role NGF plays in pain signaling and its identification within the OA joint, NGF has been explored as a potential target in the management of OA pain, and anti-NGF biologic therapies have shown efficacy in clinical trials. However, joint safety concerns have prevented the approval of anti-NGF therapies to date. Further research is needed to understand the role of NGF in joint homeostasis beyond its effects on pain.

### Joint t Tissue Damage

As outlined above, numerous mechanisms are activated in response to mechanical stimuli and other day-to-day physiologic stressors experienced by all joint tissues. Endogenous repair and homeostatic mechanisms aim to maintain tissue integrity, prevent the development of joint disease symptoms, and ultimately prevent the progressive loss and damage of joint tissues from leading to joint organ failure. Although OA is a single disease, it presents with remarkable phenotypic heterogeneity due to numerous permutations and interactions between extrinsic and intrinsic OA risk factors, which vary widely among patients. OA risk factors inhibit and reduce the effectiveness of endogenous repair and homeostatic mechanisms to protect the joint from OA pathogenesis. Further, when biomechanical and physiologic stressors experienced by joint tissues exceed the normal physiologic range (greater or lesser), OA pathogenic mechanisms are induced and overwhelm the joint's endogenous repair and homeostatic mechanisms, leading to the clinical manifestation of OA symptoms, functional loss, and structural damage.

### Cartilage e Damage

Cartilage health and damage is central to OA. The ECM that is synthesized by chondrocytes is made up of type II collagen fibers, which are formed during development and largely remain stable through life, along with a rich intercellular composition of GAGs, hyaluronan, aggrecan, and other proteoglycans. Distinction should be made between the interterritorial matrix that extends between chondrocytes and the territorial matrix immediately

surrounding chondrocytes (the pericellular matrix [PCM]). The chondrocyte interacts extensively with the territorial matrix and leverages this microenvironment to receive mechanical and other signals that are transmitted through the ECM. Early responses to mechanical injury in articular cartilage include changes to the PCM, which leads to weakening of the PCM. Breakdown and loss of key proteoglycans including decorin, perlecan, and heparan sulfate proteoglycan in the PCM result in increased exposure of chondrocytes to compressive and shear forces being experienced within their lacunae,4 437 thereby triggering exaggerated responses of the chondrocytes to increased biomechanical stresses. 438, These changes lead to the release and activation of matrix-bound factors such as FGF2 in the PCM, as discussed above.' 71

Damage to articular cartilage manifests initially as superficial zone erosion and loss of the superficial zone cells. This is particularly critical as vital regenerative cell populations (CPCs) reside in the superficial zone and upper cartilage layers. As the surface becomes more fibrillated, proteoglycan loss and altered proteoglycan distributions develop. Initially, proteoglycan loss occurs in the interterritorial matrix accompanied by increases in GAG production in the territorial matrix due to increased chondrocyte synthesis of proteoglycans as they attempt to repair the damaged ECM. Over time, proteoglycan losses lead to disruption of the interterritorial matrix as well. As cartilage damage progresses, deeper fissures form. Additional signs include proliferation of chondrocytes within lacunae, enlargement of the chondrocytes to take on more of a hypertrophic chondrocyte phenotype and eventually hypocellularity of large regions of the cartilage ECM (Fig. 100.3). In its worst state, superficial clefts extend down through the mid zone and into the calcified zone of cartilage, progressed to total cartilage erosion and exposure of the underlying subchondral bone plate (denudation).

### Extra-cellular Matrix-Degrading Proteases

Derangement in normal matrix turnover processes is a key feature of OA. Alterations in the ECM clearly modify the response of chondrocytes to soluble factors and matrix proteins that are in the

pericellular space. 440-442 Thereafter, increased levels and activity of MMPs and aggrecanases occur, including MMP-3, MMP-13, and MT1-MMP443-445 and ADAMTS-4 and ADAMTS-5446, leading to further disruption in digestion of the territorial matrix. MMP- 13 activity is specific for major cartilage components including aggrecan and type II collagen. It is also expressed by hypertrophic chondrocytes, leading investigators to speculate that recapitulation of chondrocyte hypertrophy such as is seen in endochondral ossification occurs in OA, leading to matrix digestion, calcification, and degradation. At a high level, cell stress—inducing factors (e.g., hypoxia, inflammation, mechanical stimulation, ER stress, etc.) in chondrocytes drive the expression of these matrix-degrading enzymes. In particular, hypoxia-inducible factor 2α (HIF-2α) and numerous inflammatory mediators have been implicated in the transcriptional and downstream regulation of MMPs and 447-449 9 It is clear that MMP-13 plays a key role in the aggrecanases. destruction of cartilage during OA pathogenesis through numerous studies. Perhaps the most notable of these studies demonstrated that mice overexpressing MMP-13 develop worse cartilage destruction and loss, whereas mice that are genetically deficient in MMP-13 are protected from cartilage damage. 450, Similarly, ADAMTS-5 has been strongly implicated in OA pathology and especially cartilage degradation. ADAMTS-4 and -5 in combination are more relevant in humans, whereas in mouse models of experimental OA are similarly protected from cartilage damage in dual ADAMTS-4 and -5 genetic knockout animals, compared with ADAMTS-5 knockout alone.452-454 Expression of ADAMTS aggrecanases are induced by inflammatory cytokines and other cell stress mechanisms, especially IL-1 and syndecan-4 (SDC4), which is also expressed by hypertrophic chondrocytes. Mice that are deficient in SDC4 are protected from cartilage damage.455-458 Further, SDC4 signaling leads to increased ADAMTS-5 activity.

### Loss of Chondrocyte Phenotype

The most recognizable hallmark feature of chondrocyte phenotype is the expression of SOX-9, a major transcription factor that drives the expression of a chondrogenic gene transcription

program including type II collagen, aggrecan, and other canonical cartilage ECM proteins. In addition to driving the synthetic properties of chondrocyte physiology, SOX-9 also stimulates proliferation and inhibits the transition to a hypertrophic chondrocyte or osteoblastic cellular phenotype.459, SOX-9 can also inhibit the expression of type X collagen, although in some studies it may participate in the induction of type X collagen gene expression.' 460 It is therefore not surprising that SOX-9 is highly expressed in normal articular cartilage and lost in OA cartilage, especially within cartilage lesions.461, The loss of chondrocyte phenotype is seen as an early manifestation of OA.462, Inhibition of SOX-9 expression in articular cartilage leads to early onset loss of aggrecan, other proteoglycans, increased expression in activity of aggrecanases including ADAMTS-5,464 and overexpression of SOX-9 in mice can sustain the joint architecture and protect against the development of OA-related cartilage damage. 465,

As described above, numerous chemokines and other growth factors are sequestered within the PCM and territorial cartilage matrix. Chemokines such as CXCL6, which signals via the chemokine receptor CXCR2, are normally sequestered by binding to heparan sulfate. CXCL6 is released from heparan sulfate sequestration in OA and is then free to signal to chondrocytes, which can help sustain the articular chondrocyte phenotype by induction of SOX-9 gene expression. However, negative regulation of CXCR2 leads to loss of SOX-9 expression and chondrocyte phenotype. This is particularly important in the context of injury. Overall, factors leading to suppression of SOX-9 tend to derange chondrocyte phenotype, making the articular cartilage more susceptible to subsequent damage.

### Recapitulation of Endochondral Ossification-like Processes

OA pathogenesis is not identical to endochondral ossification, but the two processes have overlapping features. Many molecules that are silenced in mature adult chondrocytes such as NOTCH-1, Jagged-1, SYND4, VEGF, and MMP-13 become reactivated in chondrocytes during OA development and progression. 468-470 Supporting the pathogenic role of each of these molecules, targeted deletion of each gene individually has led to protection against surgical induction of OA in most models. For example, cartilagespecific deletion of a NOTCH signaling factor (Jk recombination signal-binding protein) leads to impaired endochondral ossification at the latest stages and completely inhibits the development of OA in a mouse model. Similarly, genetic loss of SDC4 is also protective in surgical joint destabilization—induced mouse OA models. Recapitulation of aspects of endochondral ossification may also be mediated by HIF-2α, which is a potent transactivator of the type X collagen gene; MMP-13; and VEGF-A.

HIF-2α is also essential for endochondral ossification through mechanisms that are independent of oxygen levels or gradients. Heterozygous knockout of HIF-2α in mouse OA models confer protection against the development of OA. Together, these aspects implicate similar processes in OA as the ones occurring in the developmental context. Additional mechanisms for induction of chondrocyte hypertrophy have also been reported, including through the increase in expression of RUNX2. Although SOX-9 regulates the expression of RUNX2,459 loss of SOX-9 activity likely leads to increases in RUNX2 expression in chondrocytes in the early stages of OA development. RUNX2 leads to increased expression of chondrocyte hypertrophy-related genes such as MMP-13 and COL10A1. Heterozygous deletion of RUNX2 in mice confers protection against the development of OA-like

changes in mouse OA models. Furthermore, hedgehog signaling is a key regulator during endochondral bone developments but is increased in OA and exacerbates OA pathology in mouse models. In 2009 it was shown that inhibition of hedgehog signaling with pharmacologic or genetic knockdown strategies leads to protection against OA by inhibiting RUNX2-mediated regulation of ADAMTS-5.475 Taken together, several studies point to the release of adult mature articular chondrocytes from a stable synthetic phenotype during OA pathogenesis to a more hypertrophic and developmental-like chondrocyte phenotype that contributes to the development and progression of OA cartilage damage.

### Inflammatory Mechanisms Activated by Chondrocytes

One of the key differences between endochondral ossification during development and OA-specific chondrocyte phenotypic changes is the induction of inflammatory mechanisms in articular chondrocytes. Although the dichotomization of inflammatory versus noninflammatory arthritis has persisted in the clinical literature, it is well-established that inflammation is a key mediator of pathogenesis and disease progression in OA. OA does not demonstrate loss of immune tolerance and other facets of adaptive/autoimmune pathophysiology that are seen in rheumatoid arthritis and other forms of "inflammatory arthritis," but innate immune-driven inflammatory mechanisms have long been overlooked as a key aspect of OA, including for cartilage damage.

Secreted inflammatory factors contribute to all aspects of OA, including altered chondrocyte metabolism, amplification of catabolic cascades, shifts of chondrocytes toward hypertrophy, bone remodeling, and nociceptive signals released by chondrocytes to act on sensory nociceptors in the synovium and other tissues. Major cytokines including IL-1 and IL-6 promote cartilage damage. Chondrocytes become sensitized to inflammatory cytokine signaling when exposed to chondrocyte phenotype destabilizing factors such as SDC4.457 This results in exaggerated gene expression and other physiologic responses when OA-transformed chondrocytes are exposed to relatively small levels of inflammatory cytokines. Other aspects of innate immunity are also implicated in OA. Chondrocyte activation leads to triggering of the alternative pathway of complement activation and terminal complex formation. Blockade or genetic deletion of membrane attack complex components including C5a is protective against the development and progression of OA in mouse models of experimental knee OA. Similarly, TLR2 and TLR4 expression is increased in OA chondrocytes. Numerous TLR ligands are endogenously produced and increased in the OA joint environment, including low-molecular-weight HA, fibronectin, tenascin-C, and biglycan. These mediators can activate inflammatory mechanisms by binding to TLR2/4 and other DAMP receptors expressed on the surface of chondrocytes.478-482 These mechanisms lead to further shifts in chondrocyte phenotype, amplification of local inflammation by the release of chemokines from chondrocytes, and perpetuation of local matrix damage in the PCM and territorial matrix and microenvironment due to the induction of aggrecanases, MMPs, and other enzymatic factors in chondrocytes. This creates a vicious cycle of damage, begetting further cartilage damage and loss of chondrocyte phenotypic stability and viability.

### Synovitis and Fibrosis

Synovitis is the most obvious demonstration of chronic, nonresolving inflammation in the joints of people with OA (Fig. 100.4). The presence of synovitis is associated with worse OA

483-485 symptoms, greater joint dysfunction, higher risk for structural joint damage progression, and greater risk of requiring joint replacement. 490, Chronic synovitis plays a key role in mediating the pathogenesis of OA, largely driven by innate immune pathways including complement, DAMPS, and innate immune cell types.

As described above, numerous factors contribute to the induction and maintenance of chronic, nonresolving inflammation in OA, which is usually manifested by chronic synovitis. Several studies have characterized the synovial cell type composition of the synovitis that is seen in patients with OA. The predominant cell types include synovial fibroblasts and macrophages. Synovial fibroblasts express IL-6, the levels of which are associated with pain and structural joint damage measured by radiographs.' 492, However, numerous synovial fibroblast subsets have been identified, which may indicate different functions within the OA joint. For example, CD34+/CD90+ sublining fibroblasts may express a greater level of IL-6 than CD34-/CD90synovial lining fibroblasts. Synovial single-cell RNA sequencing data sets are beginning to shed light on the range of synovial cell subpopulations that exist in OA, with a wide range of fibroblast and synovial macrophage subsets emerging with divergent functions. Importantly, these cells are predicted to engage in bidirectional cross-talk

signaling between synovial cells and cells in other joint tissues through ligandreceptor interactions.

The most abundant immune cell types in inflamed OA synovium are macrophages, followed by T lymphocytes. Synovial macrophage activation is associated with symptoms and radiographic severity, which has been measured using single photon emission computed tomography (SPECT-CT) with folate receptor—targeted probes. Further, it has been shown that synovial lining macrophages are critical for maintenance of the synovial lining barrier. Early events in the development of OA pathogenesis include disruption and changes in the synovial lining barrier. The loss of synovial lining integrity likely has important implications for symptom and structure progression in OA, but further work is needed to understand the mechanisms in detail before treatments can be developed.

Infiltration of synovial macrophages is associated with worse pain, and blockade of macrophage recruiting cytokines such as CCL2 by pharmacologic or genetic inhibition of the CCL2 receptor (CCR2) decreases synovitis and cartilage destruction in pre-clinical OA models.496-498 However, depletion of synovial macrophages has been shown to be protective only in some studies but not others and in some cases has led to increased inflammation and synovitis. 499, These contrasting results underscore

the dual roles that macrophages play in synovial joint damage and in maintaining joint homeostasis. Therefore we require a better understanding of synovial macrophage subsets and their differential roles in the context of OA.

The presence of mast cells in synovial tissues is linked to the level of inflammation, pain, and cartilage damage in OA. Mast cellderived enzymes including tryptase can be found in synovial fluid, indicating degranulation events of synovial mast cells occur in OA. Mast cell depletion is protective against joint damage in a surgical joint destabilization mouse model of OA. Further, mast cells produce prostaglandins such as prostaglandin D2, which is potentiated by nociceptive factors such as NGF. A less clear role has emerged for neutrophils in OA, even though neutrophil-derived enzymes including elastase and neutrophil gelatinase-associated lipocalin are detectible in synovial joint fluid and associated with joint damage. Neutrophils are a rare cell type in OA synovial tissues, which helps to differentiate OA synovitis from autoimmune forms of inflammatory arthritis.

OA-related synovial T cell populations have been studied more recently in the OA field, and it has been determined that many different subtypes can be identified in OA, including at very early stages of OA pathogenesis.504, Th1, Th2, Th9, Th17, Th22, Treg, and cytotoxic T cells are all present in OA synovium, and differential T cell profiles are associated with disease activity and pain severity. However, the functional roles played by T cells in OA remains to be elucidated. Experiments need to be conducted to understand the function of each T cell subset in different OA contexts, as well as their relationship to OA risk factors.

Some of the earliest changes in OA pathogenesis include synovial lining hyperplasia and infiltration of hematopoietic cells in the synovial perivascular and subintimal compartments. As OA progresses, further thickening and hyperplasia of the synovial intima and subintima occurs and subintimal fibrosis is typically present in minor degrees, although in some cases they can be severe. Angiogenic changes are evident, usually seen with inflammatory infiltrates in the perivascular space. Inflammatory infiltrates typically co-exist with hyperplastic and fibrotic features during early to established stages of OA, whereas fibrosis and microvessel pathology tends to dominate as infiltrates become less prominent in late stages of disease. Excessive collagen deposition leads to further thickening and stiffening of the synovium. This fibrosis can impair joint mobility and function. The synovium continues to undergo hypertrophy, resulting in the formation of villous and nodular outgrowths. These outgrowths, known as synovial fronds, can invade the joint space, although their contribution to cartilage and bone destruction is not as well understood as it is in RA. In uncommon cases, the synovial lining may undergo metaplastic changes, transforming into a more fibrocartilaginous or osteocartilaginous tissue. This metaplastic transformation can further compromise joint health and function. Further, synovial cysts, fluid-filled sacs, can develop within the synovium in latestage OA. These cysts can cause localized swelling and may be associated with increased synovial inflammation.

The major mechanisms driving chronic, nonresolving inflammation in OA-related synovitis still require elucidation. However, it is likely that these mechanisms are similar to those described above and are clearly related to major OA risk factors and innate immunity. Not only are key innate immune cells such as macrophages and mast cells implicated in chronic OA synovitis, key components of the NLRP3 inflammasome are implicated in OA synovitis and lead to the propagation of IL-1β and IL-18.508 Activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome is likely driven by numerous DAMPs released by

cells experiencing high levels of cell stress. Inflammasome activation along with other mediators such as hypoxia, DAMP signaling through TLRs, and integrin signaling causes chronic inflammatory responses in synovial cells that are driven by key transcription factors such as ATS2, STAT3, and NF-kB1.510

### Crystal Formation and Dystrophic Tissue Calcification (Basic Calcium Phosphate, Calcium Pyrophosphate Dihydrate)

Dystrophic and pathologic calcification of cartilage and other joint tissues including synovium is a hallmark feature of OA. The most common crystal present in OA tissues is basic calcium phosphate (BCP), although calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate (CPP) crystals can also be present either instead of or co-existing with BCP (see Chapter 98). BCP crystals include hydroxyapatite, octacalcium phosphate, tricalcium phosphate, and carbonate apatite. Although the crystals can be detected in synovial fluid, they are commonly present in cartilage presenting as chondrocalcinosis on radiographs. Nearly all patients have BCP crystals in knee cartilage and approximately one in five have CPP crystals at the time of arthroplasty.511, Therefore cartilage calcification is common and strongly associated with aging although the degree of cartilage damage, and worse OA symptoms are also related to the presence of BCP and CPP crystals.513, Overall, BCP is more strongly associated than CPP with OA. Interestingly, vitamin K is an important regulator of bone and soft tissue mineralization. Vitamin K deficiency, including with the use of vitamin K antagonists such as warfarin, is associated with radiographic joint damage in OA.

It is thought that hypertrophic chondrocytes mediate much of the crystal nucleation and crystal formation for both BCP and CPP crystals. However, mitophagy and apoptosis are most strongly associated with BCP crystal formation. As described above in chondrocytes, high levels of RUNX2 and type X collagen underpin the hypertrophic chondrocyte phenotype and may also push chondrocyte transdifferentiation into osteoblast-like phenotypes capable of synthesizing and secreting different forms of crystals into cartilage ECM and the synovial joint environment. Therefore factors that promote chondrocyte hypertrophy-like states in the pathologic context of OA cartilage also engage the cellular machinery that is used by chondrocytes to calcify ECM in development and in the calcified zone of healthy articular cartilage. In chondrocytes and other cell types including synovial cells, mitochondrial autophagy is an important crystal nucleation mechanism. Inflammation, hypoxia, and other cells stress factors lead to calcium and inorganic phosphate sequestration in mitochondria, which causes the formation of amorphous calcium phosphate precursors (ACP). As autophagy progresses through sequential steps toward autophagosome formation, digested components of mitochondria containing ACP must be expelled by the cells, which leads to aggregation in the ECM and further calcification of the tissues.

Just as important as the mechanisms of formation, the effects of crystal precipitation and signaling in the ECM and in synovial joint environment contribute to the elaboration and propagation of innate immune dysregulation. The major effect of BCP and CPP crystal signaling through DAMP receptors is the stimulation of transcription, synthesis, and release of IL-6. Importantly, treatment of human cartilage explants with the tocilizumab to block IL-6 signaling-protected cartilage against BCP crystalinduced cartilage damage. Similarly, in a mouse model of OA, blocking IL-6 signaling or the downstream mediator STAT3

was protective against joint damage induced by BCP crystals. BCP crystals also activate chondrocyte hypertrophy by inducing type X collagen expression through canonical Wnt signaling and inhibition of SOX9 expression in cartilage.511, Key matrixdegrading enzymes including MMP-3, MMP-13, ADAMTS-4, and ADAMTS-5 are also stimulated downstream of BCP crystal signaling. Together, physiologic stresses in the joint environment contribute to the generation of BCP and CPP crystals, and reciprocally, the downstream effects of crystal-mediated innate immunity contributes to cartilage damage and progression of joint destruction pathways.

Adding further to crystalline complexity in OA, it should also be noted that a growing body of literature is demonstrating associations between worse patient and joint structural outcomes and the presence of hyperuricemia, gout, or intra-articular monosodium urate crystals; uric acid levels in the synovial fluid of OA patients without gout is associated with OA severity. The mechanism of action is not clear, but it is likely that increased innate immunity is one of the key components as uric acid is itself a danger signal (i.e., DAMP).

### Conclusion

The synovial joint is an organ system that is optimized for ambulation while responding restoratively to the normal biomechanical and physiologic stresses experienced by joints throughout the lifespan. However, when physiologic and biomechanical stresses exceed the intrinsic repair properties of joint tissues, cellular stress mechanisms are triggered. If sustained, pathogenic cell stress processes lead to suppression of endogenous repair mechanisms and the genesis of damaging and pro-inflammatory responses. In the clinical context, multiple stresses (OA risk factors) often co-exist in the same individual and coalesce to overwhelm joint homeostatic mechanisms and produce OA pathophysiology. These events underlie the clinical manifestations of joint pain experiences, nonresolving inflammation, and the progression of structural joint damage in patients with OA, which can ultimately lead to joint organ failure if left unaddressed.

Our understanding of the biologic mechanisms leading to the loss of joint regenerative capacity combined with cell stress is expanding rapidly. Ongoing research efforts will need to inform how these mechanisms are integrated and engage in cross-talk within and between joint tissues to identify treatment strategies to sustain joint health. Excitingly, tools are beginning to emerge that either restore necessary anabolic aspects of joint physiology and/or suppress pathogenic mechanisms of nonresolving innate immune inflammation. As clinicians, we should be targeting all modifiable sources of abnormal joint stresses while promoting the use of strategies aimed at improving the whole joint's and the individual tissues' ability to withstand normal stresses to reduce suffering, improve patient outcomes, and preserve the lifespan of the joint organ system.

# 101 Clinical Features of Osteoarthritis

### KEY POINTS

### Introduction

Osteoarthritis (OA), the most common form of arthritis, affects more than 300 million individuals worldwide1 and is strongly associated with aging (Fig. 101.1). Data from the 2010 to 2012 National Health Interview Survey provide an estimate of 50 million U.S. adults affected by arthritis, or nearly a quarter of the adult population, with more than 20 million reporting arthritis-attributable activity limitations2; even this is likely an underestimate. OA of the knee and hip has a significant functional impact because of effects on ambulation and mobility, is the cause of the majority of joint replacement procedures, and is associated with considerable medical costs. In the United States from 2000 to 2014, there was a dramatic increase in procedure volume for primary knee and hip arthroplasty, by 132% and 148%, respectively, to over 370,000 hip and 680,000 hip primary arthroplasties in 2014 (Fig. 101.2)4 Given the aging of society and the obesity epidemic, we can only expect the burden of OA to continue to increase.

OA affects all of the structures in and around a joint and should be considered a failure of the total joint, with the disease process affecting cartilage, subchondral bone, synovium, ligaments/tendons, meniscus, muscle, and nerve tissues. The clinically recognizable lateor end-stage joint with OA likely represents a final common pathway of many different factors, including genetics, environment, and biomechanical contributors.

### Epidemiology of Osteoarthritis

OA can be defined pathologically, radiographically, or clinically. The American College of Rheumatology (ACR) criteria for the

classification of OA of the hand, hip, and knee are shown in Table 101.1.6-8 For the hand, only clinical criteria are used, with a sensitivity of 92% and a specificity of 98%. For the hip, the sensitivity and specificity of the ACR criteria are estimated to be 91% and 89%, respectively, whereas for the knee they are 91% and 86%, respectively. Because of their high specificity, these criteria are most useful for differentiating OA from inflammatory arthropathy, but they are less so for differentiating individuals with early OA from healthy control subjects. Compared with radiographic definitions, the ACR criteria tend to underestimate the prevalence of OA. The European Alliance of Associations of Rheumatology and National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) have also proposed classification criteria; of the three, those from NICE are most sensitive for knee OA.10,

Radiographic demonstration of OA usually requires the presence of a definite osteophyte or joint space narrowing on plain radiographs, although magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)based definitions are under consideration. Clinical OA is usually defined by abnormalities on physical examination consistent with OA, such as nodal changes in the hands, limited and painful internal rotation of the hip, or crepitus with knee movement. Symptomatic OA is usually defined as pain, aching, or stiffness in a joint with radiographic OA. Definitions can vary according to the joint site, the frequency or intensity of symptoms, and the time span over which symptoms are assessed.

### Prevalence of Radiographic Osteoarthritis

Because of the multiple definitions of OA and different sources of study participants, prevalence estimates vary. Investigators13 have reviewed a few population-based studies that have estimated the prevalence of radiographic OA at the knee. Despite variations based on radiographic technique and participant age, these studies estimate that radiographic tibiofemoral knee OA is present in 14% to 37% of U.S. adults and is more frequent in women.14, Patellofemoral knee OA is also common (~25% prevalence) but less well studied. For radiographic hip OA, available estimates vary more widely, from less than 1% to 27%, depending on the population being studied. It is common for hand OA to be identified radiographically, especially in older individuals, but it may not be symptomatic or functionally limiting. For example, in the Framingham study, the age-standardized prevalence of radiographic hand OA was 44% in women and 38% in men, but only 16% and 8% of these, respectively, were symptomatic, with less than 10% having erosive

changes. A review of radiographic findings in foot OA reported a prevalence of 12% to 35% for first metatarsophalangeal OA,19 whereas another review reported a prevalence from 0.1% to 61% for radiographic midfoot and forefoot OA from 30 observational and case-control studies. Radiographic ankle OA, which is generally thought to be rare and usually the result of trauma, was identified in 7% of a large community-based U.S. cohort. The prevalence of spinal facet joint OA is also quite high; it is reported as affecting 60% of men and 67% of women by computed tomography in the Framingham Heart Study22 and 58% overall by radiography in the Johnston County OA Project. Disk space narrowing and osteophytosis of the lumbar spine are also frequently seen on radiographs.

### Prevalence of Symptomatic Osteoarthritis

A summary of prevalence estimates for symptomatic OA (i.e., symptoms in the presence of radiographic evidence of OA) of the hands, knees, and hips is presented in Table 101.2. On the basis of these findings, investigators13 estimated that more than 9 million U.S. adults are affected by symptomatic knee OA and that more than 13 million have symptomatic hand OA. One study24 used data from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) and the Framingham study to explore trends in the frequency of symptomatic knee OA and found a dramatic increase in self-reported knee pain over approximately 20 years but no

significant change in radiographic knee OA, resulting in an overall higher prevalence of symptomatic knee OA over time. Ankle pain and symptomatic OA were identified in 12% and 3%, respectively, of a community-based cohort. Few studies have assessed foot OA, but a large international consortium identified a high frequency of foot pain (13%36%), particularly in women and obese individuals. Another way to assess prevalence is by considering the lifetime risk of symptomatic OA by age 85, which has been reported as 45% for the knee, 25% for the hip, and 40% for the hand.

### Racial-Ethnic Differences in Osteoarthritis Prevalence

Racial-ethnic differences in the prevalence of OA are described at several different body sites. Radiographic and symptomatic knee OA were more common among Black compared with White individuals. In the Johnston County OA Project, radiographic knee OA was present in 32% of Black versus 27% of White participants, whereas symptomatic knee OA was present in 19% of Black and 16% of White participants. Compared with White women, Chinese women had a higher prevalence of radiographic knee OA, bilateral radiographic knee OA, and symptomatic knee OA, whereas Chinese and White men had similar frequencies of these outcomes. Black participants had similar28a to slightly higher29 frequencies compared with White participants of radiographic

and symptomatic hip OA, despite an apparently lower prevalence of hip OA among Black populations. Chinese people had overall lower frequencies of hip OA compared with White populations. Symptomatic hand OA was present at similar frequencies in White, Black, and Mexican American participants in NHANES III, although asymptomatic hand OA was more common in White people. Black individuals were much less likely to have radiographic or symptomatic hand OA phenotypes in a substudy of the Johnston County OA Project.33, Compared with Whites, Chinese people were also less likely to have radiographic or symptomatic hand OA. In the Johnston County OA Project, Black participants were 50% more likely to have radiographic foot OA than White participants, but symptomatic foot OA was similarly infrequent (~5%). Black participants were also more likely to have hallux valgus and hammer toes. In the spine, compared with White participants, Black individuals were less likely to have disk space narrowing, spinal osteophytes, or facet joint OA.

### Primary and Secondary Osteoarthritis

Historically, osteoarthritis was considered to be "primary" in the absence of an injury history or other joint disease and "secondary" if a predisposing disorder was present (Table 101.3). Nevertheless, as

Many individuals who experience secondary OA are likely predisposed to the condition with or without the identified inciting event. Others who have a disorder that is linked to secondary OA may not experience clinical OA. It may be most useful to think of OA as a common pathway through which a person's genetics, history of injury or other joint damage, mechanical factors, and psychosocial milieu act on the joint, in some cases leading to an "end-stage" or "failed" joint.

The fact that OA is a heterogeneous disease with a variety of risk factors, pathways, etiologies, presentations, and prognosis has become more widely recognized of late.38, This is true of individual joint

### Clinical Features

### General Signs and Symptoms

OA most commonly affects the knees, hands, feet, hips, and spine. These joints may be symptomatic, or signs of OA may be identified only on radiographs. People with OA generally describe pain in the joint(s) that is worse with activity, with limited morning stiffness (<30 minutes) and pain and stiffness with rest. This stiffness after inactivity, or the "gelling" phenomenon, is often a main feature, although morning stiffness is generally less severe and of shorter duration than that seen in individuals with systemic inflammatory arthropathies. Affected joints in OA often demonstrate bony enlargement and crepitus on examination, with concomitant reductions in range of motion. Soft tissue swelling or effusion may be present, although these symptoms tend to be much less dramatic than in inflammatory arthritis. Reports of pain may be more or less than expected on the basis of structural damage. The effects of depression, disturbed sleep, and other psychosocial factors on the pain experience in individuals with OA are increasingly being recognized.43-45 Awareness is also increasing of the contribution of central sensitization (i.e., enhanced neural signaling leading to hypersensitivity) to chronic pain in OA, which can result in pain remote to the affected joint site and loss of pain inhibitory mechanisms. A systematic review and meta-analysis of 39 studies with self-reported questionnaire data on neuropathiclike pain and/or pain sensitization found a frequency of these pain types of 20% to 40% among people with knee and 9% to 29% among people with hip OA, regardless of instrument used or clinical setting. Ongoing study is needed to determine optimal methods of identification and treatment of this issue.

### Joint-Specific Signs and Symptoms: Knee

Knee OA is characterized by the insidious onset of knee pain with gelling and limited range of motion. People with knee OA often describe pain and limitation with walking, transferring (as from seated to standing), and, especially, ascending or descending stairs. These reports of pain and limitation are often associated with a sensation of instability or "giving out" at the knee. A "locking" , sensation at the knee can be a consequence of stiffness, loose bodies in the joint space, or meniscal lesions and may be reproducible using the McMurray test. Knees with OA often have demonstrable crepitus (although this symptom is likely more indicative of patellofemoral than tibiofemoral disease47) and bony enlargement. Pain may be elicited by palpation of the medial or lateral joint line, or both. Effusions, when present, are often cool and generally without erythema. They can be associated with popliteal bursa enlargement (a Baker cyst) when large. Associated pain over the anserine bursa, or even the greater trochanter, often occurs in individuals with knee OA and may be related to altered biomechanics. Appreciation of such soft tissue symptoms is important because they may be amenable to corticosteroid injections with subsequent pain relief.

Malalignment, usually varus, is often seen in individuals with severe disease but can be present even in individuals with mild or early-stage disease. Clinically evident varus thrust is a risk factor for knee OA progression. Other signs of severe disease include flexion deformities or joint instability. Quadriceps weakness represents an early modifiable risk factor for knee OA progression, particularly in 50,51 and, in late stages of disease, it may be apparent as muswomen cle atrophy. Alterations in vibratory sense have been demonstrated in association with knee OA, although the relation of these factors to progression and pain is still unclear.53, Patellofemoral OA may be more common than tibiofemoral OA and can strongly contribute to pain and disability at the knee, but it is often overlooked. OA of the patellofemoral joint is characterized by crepitus and pain when ascending or descending stairs and is often located anteriorly. It can be seen in isolation or in association with tibiofemoral OA. The relation between patellofemoral OA and commonly seen patellofemoral pain disorders in younger individuals remains to be elucidated.55,56

### Joint-Specific Signs and Symptoms: Hip

OA of the hip can present with groin pain, which is fairly specific,56 but it may be described more vaguely as pain in the thigh, buttock, low back, and even in the ipsilateral knee. Therefore it is important to assess for other causes of pain in the "hip," including back pain (e.g., lumbar disk degeneration, spinal stenosis, facet joint OA, and sacroiliac pain); trochanteric bursitis; altered gait due to knee disease; meralgia paresthetica (i.e., lateral femoral cutaneous nerve entrapment); thigh claudication from vascular causes; or even intrapelvic causes. It is also important to consider other causes of hip and groin pain such as occult femoral neck fracture or avascular necrosis. People affected by hip OA have limitations in walking, bending, transferring, and stair climbing. Internal rotation of the affected hip is often limited and can be quite painful, even in early-stage disease; it is often evident to the patient through difficulty in putting on socks, tying shoes, or trimming toenails. Visible deformity, hip flexion contracture, or severe limitations of range of motion are indicators of more advanced disease, which may also be associated with shortening of the affected limb because of superior migration of the femoral head. In young individuals presenting with groin pain that is worsened by sitting and who have pain and limitation when

internally rotating and adducting the hip in the flexed position, femoroacetabular impingement syndrome is a consideration.

### Joint-Specific Signs and Symptoms: Hand

The hands often provide the first clue to a diagnosis of OA. As previously mentioned, evident bony enlargement of the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joints (Heberden's nodes) and proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joints (Bouchard's nodes) can be appreciated (Fig. 101.3). These nodes may be acutely inflamed with warmth and tenderness or may be bland, hard enlargements and are often more marked in the dominant hand. Some patients, most commonly older women, have erosive OA characterized by episodic inflammation, pain, and swelling. It remains a matter of debate whether this type of OA is part of the continuum or is a separate disease entity. OA involvement of the first carpometacarpal (CMC) joint is particularly problematic and can lead to significant pain, limitations in functionality of the hand, and reduced grip strength. CMC squaring, representing deformity of the joint due to osteophyte formation and joint space narrowing, can be seen on examination. Bilateral involvement of multiple joints

is frequent, both within (multiple PIPs) and across (both DIPs and PIPs) joint groups. Metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints are affected more commonly than previously recognized,60 although prominent involvement of these joints should prompt consideration of inflammatory/crystalline arthropathies or secondary causes of OA, such as hemochromatosis. Soft tissue conditions such as De Quervain's tenosynovitis should be considered because they are associated with hand OA, can mimic or aggravate symptoms, and are amenable to conservative management.

### Joint-Specific Signs and Symptoms: Spine

Facet joint OA is prevalent among older adults. In one study, cervical spine facet joint OA and lumbar spine facet joint OA were present in 57% and 89%, respectively, of community-living adults older than 65 years. The association between facet joint OA and back pain has been controversial,63 although a study using CT assessments of lumbar facet joint OA identified associations between severe facet joint OA and back pain, with an odds ratio greater than 2; individuals with multiple affected facet joints were also more likely to have back pain. Facet joint OA is associated with OA of other joint sites, including the knees and hands.

Osteophytosis of the spine is nearly ubiquitous in older individuals, although it is often asymptomatic. Lumbar disk degeneration (LDD), characterized by disk space narrowing, end-plate sclerosis, and herniation, is often seen in association with radiographic osteophytosis,66 although the relationship between LDD and OA of other joint sites remains controversial.23,

Symptomatically, these findings can be associated with radiculopathy, a pathologic process most commonly seen in older patients as a consequence of hypertrophied facet joints or uncovertebral joints, disk protrusion, osteophytosis of the vertebral body, or a combination of these features.68, Cervical radiculopathy most commonly involves the seventh cervical nerve root and is caused by degenerative changes at the C6C7 level. Patients may present with pain/numbness in the shoulders, triceps area, forearm, and dorsal long finger, and triceps weakness or loss of reflex may be present. Lumbosacral radiculopathy, frequently due to disk degeneration (particularly at lower lumbar levels), presents with radiating back pain that is usually exacerbated by leaning forward, sitting, or straining and is relieved by lying down. Specific clinical presentation varies by level, with the lower levels more commonly affected. L4 radiculopathy can result in medial lower leg sensory changes, weak knee extension and hip adduction, and potentially reduced knee jerk. At L5, foot drop and sensory symptoms of the anterolateral leg and dorsal foot may be seen, whereas S1 radiculopathy is characterized by weakness of plantar flexion, knee flexion, and hip extension with reduced ankle jerk. Cauda equina syndrome, a medical emergency, occurs as a result of compression of the lower lumbar and sacral nerve roots by a central disk herniation, commonly at L4L5. This syndrome results in bowel and bladder dysfunction, saddle anesthesia, and leg weakness.

Diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis, or DISH, is characterized by exuberant osteophytosis and calcification of spinal ligaments and entheses covering four or more spinal levels, leading to an appearance likened to flowing candle wax. Hyperostosis can also involve peripheral sites such as the elbows and pelvis. DISH is often asymptomatic and may be identified only by radiographic appearance or can present in a fashion similar to OA or LDD. Large anterior cervical spine osteophytes, which are more often seen in DISH but are possible in LDD, can cause dysphagia as a result of compression of the esophagus.

### Joint-Specific Signs and Symptoms: Shoulder

The shoulder is a common source of pain in people with OA, although the symptoms are more often due to osteophytosis and narrowing of the acromioclavicular and/or sternoclavicular joints than of the glenohumeral joint itself. Other maladies common in older adults, such as subacromial bursitis, rotator cuff disease, and adhesive capsulitis, should be assessed. Rotator cuff damage, in particular, can predispose to glenohumeral OA, which presents similarly to OA in other large joints with crepitus and reduced range of motion with pain. Disease at the cervical spine can present as pain in the shoulder region, and thus the shoulder evaluation should include an assessment of the cervical spine. Milwaukee shoulder syndrome is a rare destructive arthropathy of the glenohumeral joint associated with large effusions, which is bilateral in 60% of cases and also affects the knees in 50% of cases. Radiologically, periarticular calcifications and cuff rupture may be seen, and synovial fluid examination often reveals high red blood cell content and basic calcium crystals (particularly if Alizarin Red staining is used).

### Joint-Specific Signs and Symptoms: Other Joints

OA of the foot has been relatively neglected in the literature to date. The foot joints most commonly affected by OA include the talocalcaneal joint, talonavicular joint, calcaneocuboid joint, metatarsocuneiform joint, and first metatarsophalangeal (MTP) joint; these joints can be affected by erosive OA as well. OA of the first MTP joint is characterized by pain and hallux valgus (bunion) deformity and has radiographic features (e.g., joint space narrowing and osteophytosis) similar to OA at other joints. Loss of function at the first MTP joint as a result of ankylosis (hallux rigidus) can lead to altered gait. Ankle OA likely occurs more frequently than previously thought21 and may be due to biomechanical alterations from OA at other joints, in addition to accepted post-traumatic and injury-related etiologies. Elbow OA is rare74 and may be the result of trauma, vibration damage, or inflammatory entities such as gout or pseudogout. Temporomandibular joint OA is largely ignored in the orthopedic and rheumatologic literature but is well researched in the dental literature; it results in pain, clicking, locking, decreased range of motion, and crepitus of the joint, much like in other joints affected by OA.

### Polyarticular Osteoarthritis

Although the term generalized OA has been used to describe multiple joint involvement in OA, there is no universally understood or accepted definition of what constitutes multiple joint OA (MJOA; Fig. 101.4). It is clear that individuals with more than one joint involved have poorer functional status. In 1952 Kellgren and Moore provided the first clinical description of MJOA, involving primarily Heberden's nodes and the CMC joints, with the spine, knees, hips, and feet involved in descending frequency. Later studies defined MJOA in a variety of ways including numbers of affected joints (continuously or with thresholds) overall or in the hand, or summed semiquantitative radiographic scores. It remains unclear which joints should be included in such definitions, and particularly whether lumbar disk degeneration and hip OA are part of the same disease entity as other joints. Clinically, it is important to recognize that a patient with OA in one joint is likely to have disease at other sites and to assess the impact of that person's overall OA burden on their overall level of pain and functional status, rather than focusing on a single joint.

### Diagnostic Tests

OA is diagnosed clinically, and laboratory testing is rarely required. Similarly, if the diagnosis is clear based on history and clinical findings, radiographs are usually not required. The purpose of additional diagnostic testing in OA is primarily to exclude potentially treatable underlying conditions. Depending on the patient's presentation, the diagnosis may be straightforward, or the differential diagnosis may include inflammatory arthropathies, such as rheumatoid arthritis, crystalline arthropathies (particularly calcium pyrophosphate crystal deposition disease; see Chapter 98), spondyloarthropathies, or a variety of other inflammatory conditions. Particularly in the case of erosive/inflammatory OA, there may be significant clinical and radiographic overlap with psoriatic arthritis, requiring further evaluation. If the presentation is of a monoarthritis, evaluation for infectious causes should be performed. Finally, trauma and other mechanical disorders (e.g., tendon or ligament injury and meniscal tears) may be seen prior to, as a part of, or subsequent to the development of OA in a given joint.

### Laboratory Tests

There is rarely an indication for testing rheumatoid factor or antinuclear antibodies or for performing other serologic studies in the setting of clinically suspected OA; such tests should be reserved for patients with findings suggestive of a more inflammatory arthropathy. A complete blood cell count and chemistry panel, including glucose,

creatinine, and liver function tests, should be obtained before initiation of pharmacologic therapy for OA, especially in older individuals with comorbid medical conditions, because of an increased risk of adverse events in this population (see Chapter 102). In cases in which there is prominent involvement of the MCP joints, evaluation for hypothyroidism and hemochromatosis may be warranted.

### Synovial Fluid

The synovial fluid in people with OA is typically normal or mildly inflammatory, appearing clear and colorless to slightly yellowish. The leukocyte cell count is typically less than or equal to 2000 cells/mm3 (<2 cells seen across 10 high-power fields). Fluid is often obtained in the course of an intra-articular injection for a symptomatic joint, although diagnostic aspiration may also be performed in the setting of an effusion. Concomitant calcium pyrophosphate crystal disease can be identified, although other calcium crystals, or hydroxyapatite, are not seen on routine preparations (see also Chapter 53).

### Molecular Biomarkers

Quantitative determination of the products of cartilage, synovium, and bone metabolism has provided several putative biomarkers of OA pathophysiology.
