These biomarkers reflect processes such as cartilage turnover, bone resorption/remodeling, and synovial and other tissue inflammation. Such biomarkers, obtained from serum, urine, or synovial fluid, may eventually provide a method for early diagnosis, monitoring of treatment effects, and objective trial endpoints, although currently they are used primarily in research. Additional information is available in recent reviews 79,80 and in Chapter 100 in this book.

### Imaging: Conventional Radiography and General Considerations

Conventional radiography is widely available in clinical settings and is relatively inexpensive, making this modality useful to confirm the diagnosis of OA and exclude others, primarily when there is clinical uncertainty regarding the diagnosis, when the joint involved is atypical, or when evidence suggests other diagnoses such as inflammatory arthritis, fractures, Paget's disease, osteonecrosis, infection, or malignancy (see also Chapter 58). Radiographs of joints affected by OA typically show osteophytes, joint space narrowing, sclerosis, and cysts of subchondral bone, which will be described qualitatively on clinical radiographs.

For research purposes, semiquantitative and quantitative assessments are used. The semiquantitative Kellgren-Lawrence (KL) grading system remains the most commonly used for research space narrowing) to 4 (severe joint space narrowing with subchondral sclerosis); a grade of 2 is generally considered diagnostic of OA (Fig. 101.5). The KL grading system has several limitations, including variable definitions in the literature,83 the categorization of all "definite" joint space narrowing as KL grade 3, and the unclear applicability of this system developed in the 1950s to current and diverse populations. Additionally, identification of joint space narrowing on radiographs is not a specific finding indicative of cartilage loss but can also be reflective of meniscal disease. Other semiquantitative grading systems, such as the Osteoarthritis Research Society International (OARSI) grading system, 84 view osteophytes and joint space narrowing separately and assign grades for these specific OA features individually for various joint compartments. The choice of grading system depends on the goal

of the study and the joint site of interest. Quantitative joint space width, on the other hand, is a direct measure of the space between the femur and tibia that is performed either manually or in a semior fully automated manner. Quantitative joint space width is commonly assessed as the minimum joint space width, but it has also been explored at fixed locations; the latter method is comparable to MRI in the detection of OA progression.

### Imaging: Conventional Radiography of Specific Joints

Imaging of the knees should be bilateral while the patient is weight bearing and, for clinical purposes, it is generally anteroposterior (AP). Posteroanterior views in fixed flexion are commonly used for research,82 and sunrise views are needed to fully assess the

patellofemoral joint. Alignment, although best determined from full-limb views, can be estimated from routine knee films. An AP pelvis view should be obtained to assess hip OA and can be either supine or weight bearing. Additional views such as frog-leg, lateral, or Dunn views may be indicated for specific hip disease or to assess for femoroacetabular impingement or congenital abnormalities. For hand OA, a posteroanterior view of both hands, including the wrists, will reveal the characteristic features of OA. If there is an erosive component to hand OA, radiographs may demonstrate central erosions and "gull-wing" deformities of the interphalangeal joints (see Fig. 101.3). Marked destructive changes at the DIP joints may indicate another inflammatory disorder such as psoriatic arthritis or, rarely, multicentric reticulohistiocytosis. Prominent involvement of the MCP joints may indicate a metabolic process such as hemochromatosis or calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease.

Conventional radiography of the cervical and/or lumbar spine can show facet OA, disk space narrowing, and osteophytosis.

### Imaging: Advanced Modalities

Several advanced imaging modalities such as MRI, ultrasound, CT, and positron-emission tomography (PET) scans have been used in OA research, although with the exception of ultrasound, these specialized, expensive examinations are not indicated in routine clinical practice. A brief summary of these modalities in OA is provided in the following sections.

### Magnetic Resonance Imaging

MRI is the most well-studied advanced imaging modality in OA. Unlike radiography, it allows visualization of all joint tissues, including cartilage, menisci, ligament/tendon, synovium, effusions, and bone marrow simultaneously, although arthroscopy remains the gold standard for joint tissue assessment. An MRI-based definition of tibiofemoral OA has been proposed that requires either the presence of both definite osteophytes and fullthickness cartilage loss or one of these and one of the following features: a subchondral bone marrow lesion or cyst, meniscal disease (subluxation, maceration, or horizontal tear), partial-thickness cartilage loss, or bone attrition. There has been a push to use MRI as a clinical trial endpoint, rather than radiographic joint space loss, due to its greater responsiveness.

Semiquantitative scoring, which can be performed using conventional acquisition techniques, is frequently used to evaluate a number of OA features simultaneously, such as the articular cartilage, meniscus, ligaments, bone marrow, synovitis, and joint effusion. Several scoring systems are publicly available. Whole Organ Magnetic Resonance Imaging Score (WORMS), the oldest and most widely used semiquantitative system for MRI scoring in OA, utilizes a subregional approach to scoring of features, including cartilage, bone marrow lesions (BMLs), subchondral cysts, bone attrition, effusion, synovitis, osteophytes, meniscal tears, and cruciate and collateral ligaments. Other systems include the Knee Osteoarthritis Scoring System (KOSS), the Boston Leeds Osteoarthritis Knee Score (BLOKS), and the MRI Osteoarthritis Knee Score (MOAKS).

Overall, semiquantitative methods for knee OA are adequately responsive to change and are reliable. Potential structural phenotypes of knee OA based on MRI include meniscal/cartilage based, subchondral bone based, and those featuring inflammation. A 2014 study using MOAKS and data from the Osteoarthritis Initiative found that, among 849 individuals with no radiographic evidence of knee OA at baseline (bilateral KL grade = 0; one-third of whom had baseline frequent knee symptoms), the majority had cartilage damage (76%) and bone marrow lesions (61%) as identified by MRI, and these lesions were associated with prevalent and incident knee symptoms. Semiquantitative MRI scoring has also been utilized at the hip, hand, shoulder, and spine, although to a much lesser extent than for knee OA.

Quantitative assessment of MRI involves quantification of specific tissue characteristics such as thickness and volume of cartilage or size and volume of BMLs. These techniques require specific high-resolution sequences and are time and labor intensive but provide greater sensitivity to change compared with semiquantitative scoring. Quantitative MRI assessments can be used not only for cartilage and bone but also for menisci and for assessment of the infrapatellar fat pad.

Compositional imaging techniques, which allow visualization of anatomy and biochemical properties as well, have been used in

the setting of very early-stage disease prior to obvious structural alterations. Techniques include delayed gadolinium-enhanced MRI of cartilage and T1 rho, which can visualize changes in glycosaminoglycan concentrations, and T2 mapping, which reflects variation in collagen orientation and cartilage hydration status. Further study of these methods in human subjects, particularly related to changes in healthy knees over time, is needed to fully exploit their potential as outcome measures.

### Ultrasound

Ultrasound is a point-of-care modality that can be used directly by trained providers (e.g., rheumatologists, radiologists, and orthopedists) to assess joint disease in patients. Its relatively low cost, safety (because it does not entail use of radiation or contrast agents), short examination duration, convenience (it can be performed in the provider's office), and noninvasive nature make it an attractive OA assessment method (see also Chapter 41). It has several advantages compared with conventional radiography, including lack of radiation, ability to obtain numerous views of a given joint, and ability to assess soft tissues and inflammation. Limitations include the inability of sonography to penetrate the bony cortex, which prevents assessment of BMLs or deeper aspects of the joints. A study of 311 people age 61 to 63 years participating in the Newcastle Thousand Families birth cohort found a high prevalence of ultrasound osteophytosis at the DIP (70%), index PIP (23%), index MCP (10%), and thumb base CMC joints (41%), as well as the knees (30%) and hips (41%), whereas knee effusion was present in 20% to 24%. OA features at various sites, such as osteophytes, effusions, cartilage thickness, and synovitis, can be reliably assessed over time. Ultrasound-guided intra-articular injections can also be beneficial; a systematic review of 23 publications found that knee injections at the superomedial patellar, medial midpatellar, superolateral patellar, and lateral suprapatellar sites were more accurate with image guidance rather than without it. Ultrasound guidance also allows direct aspiration/injection of popliteal cysts for symptomatic relief.

### Computed Tomography

CT is the best modality for assessment of cortical bone and soft tissue mineralization. It is also the main technique used for assessment of facet joint OA. CT arthrography is the most accurate method for the evaluation of articular cartilage surface damage because of high contrast between cartilage, a contrast agent, and bone using this modality; newer weight-bearing assessments may further enhance these capabilities. CT can be used to define tissue calcification such as chondrocalcinosis, and even type of crystal deposition in the case of dual-energy CT. Expense, invasiveness, and radiation exposure are limitations to the use of CT in OA.

### Nuclear Medicine

Bone scans (technetium 99m hydroxymethane diphosphonate scintigraphy) provide a full-body image in one test, allowing location of the site of inflammation in patients with complex symptomatology. Bone scans have been used as a measure of whole-body OA burden for evaluation of systemic biomarkers. PET, most often using 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose, can detect synovitis, BMLs, and other sources of increased metabolic activity in aging and OA joints, and these findings have been associated with pain. Limitations include cost, limited availability, poor anatomic resolution, use of ionizing radiation, and invasiveness (because of the injection of the radiopharmaceutical agent). How these various modalities are utilized in OA imaging is evolving

with newer imaging techniques, as well as new application of artificial intelligence methodologies.

### Outcome

### Pain and Functional Status Assessment

Numerous validated tools for assessing functional status in OA are available and are widely used in research settings. As the focus on quality of care increases, these tools will likely be incorporated more frequently into clinical practice.

### Self-Reported Measures of Pain and Function

Questionnaire-based measures of pain and functional status provide rapid and repeatable patient-based assessments that can be monitored over time and for treatment response. Numerous well-studied, validated, and reliable measures are available for this purpose. For overall function, the Stanford Health Assessment Questionnaire (HAQ) disability index is often used, although it is not disease specific. For OA-specific lower-extremity pain and function, the Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Arthritis Index (WOMAC; Table 101.4) is the most frequently used

tool, although joint-specific measures such as the Hip Disability and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score (HOOS) and Knee Injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score (KOOS) are also validated and are often used in research. Measures are available for other joint sites as well, such as the Australian/Canadian Hand Osteoarthritis Index (AUSCAN) and Functional Index for Hand Osteoarthritis (FIHOA) for hand-specific function; Disabilities of the Arm, Shoulder, and Hand Questionnaire (DASH) for the upper extremity; and the Roland-Morris Disability Questionnaire and Oswestry Disability Index for low back disorders, among others. Various clinically important features of these measures have been established, such as responsiveness and minimal clinically important differences, all of which have been reviewed.

### Performance-Based Assessment

Performance-based measures (such as determination of walking speed or ability to stand from sitting) capture different constructs of physical function compared with self-reported assessments. The Osteoarthritis Research Society International has provided guidelines for appropriate performance-based tests for hip or knee OA, which include a 30-second chair-stand test, 40-meter fast-paced walk test, stair-climb test, timed up-and-go test, and 6-minute walk test, with the first three tests as a minimal core set of measures.

### Quality of Life

OA is a chronic, progressive, and often debilitating condition, and thus assessment of quality of life is an important outcome for monitoring and treatment. Generic measures of quality of life, such as the Medical Outcomes Study Short Forms (SF-36, SF-12, and SF-6D) and Assessment of Quality of Life (AQoL), are commonly used. The HOOS and KOOS previously discussed include quality-of-life domains specific to knee and hip OA. The Osteoarthritis Knee and Hip Quality of Life (OAKHQOL) has been validated for this purpose.

### Time to Total Joint Replacement

Total joint replacement is a "hard" endpoint in OA, but its use as an outcome measure is hampered by the prolonged time needed for assessment, the large number of patients and events required, and a variety of factors affecting an individual patient's decision to undergo this procedure, including health care system issues, procedure availability, comorbid conditions, ability to rehabilitate the joint, and patient/provider preference. To date, efforts have not been successful to identify a composite index that would consider pain, functional disability, and structural degradation; that would define the "need for total joint replacement"; and that could be used as an outcome measure.

### Responder Criteria

In some cases, it is more useful to categorize individuals as responders or nonresponders to treatments, given the shortcomings of outcomes based solely on imaging or self-report, particularly for clinical trials. The Outcome Measures in Rheumatology (OMERACT)-OARSI responder criteria provide a composite assessment, including threshold levels of percentage improvements in pain and function, and required thresholds of absolute change to define response and no response that are applicable in a variety of settings.

### Mortality in Osteoarthritis

The association between OA and increased mortality has received substantial attention in the last decade. A 2008 review indicated a modestly increased risk of mortality, primarily due to cardiovascular and gastrointestinal causes. A 2016 systematic review and meta-analysis of 7 studies and nearly 29,000 participants did not reveal excess mortality in OA overall but did find higher risk of cardiovascular death among participants with OA. Recent work has demonstrated that the association with excess mortality is primarily due to joint pain, rather than radiographic changes of OA. A large individual participant-level data analysis of more than 10,000 participants from six community-based cohorts showed 35% to 37% reduced time-to-mortality among participants with knee OA only when the OA was painful, regardless of radiographic findings. This remains an area of active study.

### Conclusion

OA is a highly prevalent and debilitating condition with increasing prevalence as a result of the aging of our society and the ongoing obesity epidemic. OA is readily recognized on clinical grounds, although further diagnostic testing and imaging are indicated in some cases to assess for potentially treatable underlying conditions. Pain is the most common reason for a person with OA to seek medical advice, and examination often reveals loss of function. Assessment of the patient's pain symptoms and functional limitations, in the framework of that person's goals, is necessary to formulate an appropriate plan of care in the absence of diseasemodifying medications. Current research in OA, in addition to ongoing efforts in both pharmacologic and nonpharmacologic therapeutic development, is focused on optimizing incident case and progression definitions a nd understanding t he whole-body burden of OA.

### KEY POINTS

### Introduction

Osteoarthritis (OA) is the most common form of arthritis, estimated to affect 528 million adults worldwide. Updated estimates of arthritis prevalence in the United States indicate that 91 million adults were affected by arthritis at any site in 2015.2 It is thus a substantial public health problem, compounded by the fact that musculoskeletal conditions are the second leading cause of years lived with disability. Increasing age, obesity, and knee injuries are among the common risk factors for knee OA, the most frequent joint affected by symptomatic OA.

Pain is the primary symptom of OA and the main contributor to functional limitations and disability. In the early stages of disease, the pain is primarily activity related, whereas later in the course of disease, the pain can become more constant, and this constant pain can be punctuated by episodes of often unpredictable pain. To date, there are no approved treatments proven to alter structural progression. Thus pain relief remains the main focus for OA management, in addition to maintenance of function.

### Therapeutic Pain Targets in Osteoarthritis

To develop a rational approach to pain management as a therapeutic goal, the contributions to pain in OA need to be better

understood to enable targeting appropriate pain mechanisms. Under normal circumstances, pain is a warning signal, such as when touching a hot stove or chest pain due to ischemia. In these instances, pain plays a protective role, signaling to the individual to withdraw from the threat, rest to allow tissue healing, or seek help. Once its warning role is over, persistence or continued pain (i.e., chronic pain) is considered maladaptive. However, unlike other conditions, OA does not heal or resolve and thus is often accompanied by chronic pain.

The definitive therapy for late-stage OA remains joint replacement, which is highly effective in improving both pain and function, providing evidence that structure does indeed contribute to symptoms in OA. In further support of the important contribution of articular structures to pain in OA, a randomized trial demonstrated intra-articular lidocaine to effectively decrease knee pain in comparison with placebo. These examples clearly suggest that structure must contribute to symptoms, and thus structural pathology is a reasonable target for OA therapy. However, a so-called structure—symptom discordance, in which some people experience pain despite minimal radiographic changes or others experience minimal symptoms despite advanced radiographic findings, also exists. This points to the importance of additional factors beyond structural pathology alone to the pain experience in OA.5,

While OA was traditionally characterized as a disease of cartilage and bone, it has been more recently recognized that OA is a disease of the whole joint. Contrary to the designation as a CC "non-inflammatory" arthritis, synovitis is present in a substantial proportion of knees. Further, the subchondral bone, periosteum, periarticular ligaments, periarticular muscle, outer third of the meniscus, and joint capsule including its inner synovial lining are innervated and are the likely sources of nociception in OA. MRI-based studies have demonstrated the importance of subchondral bone, including bone marrow lesions, and synovitis to the pain experience in OA, with inconsistent associations for other structural abnormalities (reviewed in refs. 7-9). In an arthroscopy study, an awake, unanesthetized evaluation of the knee identified the synovium, joint capsule, infrapatellar fat pad, and outer layers of the meniscus as being painful, whereas cartilage, which is aneural in healthy joints, was not painful (bone was not probed because it is known to be painful). However, as OA progresses, neurovascular invasion may disrupt the osteochondral junction. This is accompanied by growth of sensory nerves and increased expression of nerve growth factor, which can stimulate sensory nerve growth and facilitate sensitization, another pertinent mechanism for pain in OA.

Indeed, hyperalgesia, allodynia, radiating pain, and pain persistence post—knee replacement in ~20% to 30% of patients suggest

a role for neurophysiologic alterations such as sensitization in OArelated pain. Neurophysiologic data also support the presence of pain sensitization in OA, with individuals who have OA experiencing higher pain intensities compared with comparators free of OA to the same level of pressure stimuli, lower pressure pain thresholds, and increased temporal summation. 12-16

Patients with OA often have additional factors beyond structural pathology and sensitization that can contribute to their pain experience, including poor sleep, altered mood, and psychological factors. It is in the context of understanding the potential contributors to pain in OA (Fig. 102.1), including the structural pathology and other nonjoint-related factors that may be relevant for the clinical symptoms in this disease, that one can appreciate the rationale behind the various therapeutic strategies that are considered for the management of OA.

Beyond these recognized factors, the burden of OA pain and functional limitations is characterized by substantial racial/ethnic disparities, with minoritized racial groups including Black adults and Hispanic adults experiencing more severe pain and greater mobility restrictions than non-Hispanic white adults. These disparities in disease burden are multifactorial and likely related to racial/ethnic inequities in the management of symptoms and lifetime exposure to systemic racism that influence factors such as socioeconomic status, occupation, area of residence, etc.18-23 While addressing these inequities requires complex and multilevel approaches that cut across individual, interpersonal, community, and societal domains, it is critical to be mindful of these inequities when providing care to patients from minoritized racial/ethnic groups and attempt to address any barriers they may experience while seeking care.

### Approach to Management of Osteoarthritis

### General Considerations

The management of OA can be broadly grouped into education, physical interventions (i.e., physical activity, exercise, orthotics and assistive devices, manual therapy, physical agents including nerve ablation), mindbody interventions (psychological and complementary and integrative therapies), pharmacologic interventions, and surgical interventions (Fig. 102.2). While there are several treatment guidelines from various academic societies, there

is broad agreement on recommendations by the various organizations.24, However, there remains poor implementation of treatment guidelines.

Education and self-management approaches should be provided for all patients as a basis from which to build a comprehensive OA management plan that is appropriate for their stage of disease, with "refreshers" and new or additional relevant information provided as the disease progresses (Fig. 102.2). Because OA is a chronic disease, often present for decades in any given individual, patients with OA will likely need to be managed with a variety of different approaches over the course of their disease, often with combinations of interventions. Even after a surgical procedure, such as joint replacement, patients often need to have other interventions added or continued.

In addition to taking into consideration patient preferences and medical status or comorbidities, many of the interventions

also require consideration of accessibility, physical ability, and cost; many options may not be readily available within the context of traditional health care centers or, on the other hand, within the context of lowand middle-income countries. In general, when choosing among therapies, one may give preference to starting with treatments that offer the lowest systemic exposure or toxicity, such as exercise and local pharmacologic therapy directed at the affected joint. Referral to appropriate providers should be considered for individuals who may be experiencing negative psychological behaviors (e.g., depressed mood, catastrophizing, fear avoidance) or sleep difficulties. With disease progression, individuals with OA may have greater risk of falls, which can have detrimental downstream effects, including fracture. Also, stepped approaches may be considered where patients are initially provided low-cost, low-burden, and safer interventions (e.g., education and home exercise program) and individuals who may not respond are progressed to other interventions as needed (e.g., pharmacologic, cognitive behavioral therapy). However, research on such stepped approaches is still in its infancy. 27-29

### Education and Physical Interventions

All patients should be provided education related to the disease and self-management strategies, counseled about relevant physical interventions, with weight loss and physical activity (including structured exercise) being the most important aspects of managing all patients with lower extremity OA. Importantly, appropriate participatory language should be used to communicate about OA and management options rather than fatalistic language to encourage patients' engagement in their OA care.

### Patient Education and Self-Management

Patient education and self-management strategies are recommended as core intervention approaches by all clinical guidelines for management of OA. Patients can be educated using verbal and written information to improve their understanding of the disease, allay fears and misconceptions, and help them make informed decisions. Patients should be encouraged to seek information from reliable public sources on the Internet including the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), the Arthritis Foundation, and the Osteoarthritis Action Alliance. This should be an ongoing process rather than something that occurs once. It is also important to consider the language used during patient interactions. Use of biomedical language to explain health conditions can often instill fear, perpetuate maladaptive behaviors, and reduce active patient involvement in their care.31, Simple changes to words toward reduced usage of medical or precise terms, a healthrather than diseasefocused approach, and de-emphasizing structural pathology are some strategies that could be considered during patient 32,33 encounters.

Self-management strategies should be tailored to individuals and should focus on behavioral and lifestyle modifications that could help the patients improve their self-efficacy and reduce reliance on health care providers. These can include exercise and physical activity programs, weight-management strategies, use of assistive devices, and activity modifications. These programs can be delivered in-person for individuals or groups, via videos and self-management mobile health applications, or through telehealth approaches.34, Meta-analyses of published studies report moderate benefits of self-management programs for chronic musculoskeletal pain and for arthritis.36-38

### Weight Management

Obesity is both a risk factor and a consequence of lower-extremity OA. Hence, weight management strategies for overweight and obese patients with OA is extremely important. Being overweight or obese increases loading over the lower-extremity joints, leading to worsening OA; there may be a contribution of low-grade systemic inflammation related to adipose tissue to the symptomatic experience as well. Overweight and obese patients with knee OA should be provided personalized weight management strategies. In general, strategies that include both diet and exercise components to ensure that lean muscle mass is maintained and prevention of sarcopenia are more effective than diet alone. Ideally such interventions should be delivered using a team approach that includes nutritional counseling, an exercise program, and behavioral strategies. As for any chronic condition in which obesity is an important factor, achieving weight loss is challenging, and therefore a multimodal approach with professional support should be considered. Some patients may even require bariatric surgery. Significant improvements in pain and function have been reported with both dietand exercised-based weight-loss interventions and bariatric surgery for knee OA.40, There is a significant dose—response relationship between the magnitude of weight loss and the observed improvements in OA-related outcomes. While any amount of weight loss is likely to provide benefits, weight loss of 20% or more provides the most benefits. The 2019 American College of Rheumatology (ACR) OA guidelines strongly recommend weight loss for those who are obese or overweight.

### Physical Activity

Physical activity refers to any bodily movement produced by skeletal muscles that requires energy expenditure. Physical activity includes exercise as well as other activities that involve bodily movement and that are done as part of playing, working, active transportation, house chores, and recreational activities (Fig. 102.3). The 2019 ACR OA guidelines strongly recommend exercise and physical activity. Over 50% of men and up to 80% of women with knee OA fail to meet physical activity guidelines. Reduced walking activity could increase the risk of cardiovascular disease, depression, and early mortality in these patients. Hence, behavioral strategies for sustained improvements in physical activity are essential for patients with OA. Greater physical activity is associated with decreased pain and improved physical function in adults with hip or knee OA. Some patients may have a concern that increasing activity might make their OA worse; however, currently there is no evidence to suggest that increasing physical activity contributes to disease worsening. Furthermore, the overall benefits of increased physical activity far outweigh any potential risks. Any symptomatic exacerbation is typically short lived, with symptomatic improvement achieved over the longer term. Fatigue in OA can also be an issue, which may require counseling regarding activity pacing. Thus patients should be encouraged to engage and maintain engagement in physical activity as there is no risk of worsening their OA, and over the long term, they will have improved pain and function. As mentioned earlier, use of participatory language that focuses on what the individuals can do versus what they cannot do may encourage healthier behaviors. The physical activity recommendations published in 2018 (https://health.gov/paguidelines/second-edition/pdf/Physical_ Activity_Guidelines_2nd_edition.pdf) suggest a target of at least 150 minutes per week of moderate-to-vigorous intensity physical activity for people with OA (e.g., 3 to 5 times per week, for 30 to 60 minutes per episode). The type and amount of physical activity

should be matched to their preferences and abilities. During the shared decision-making process, health care professionals should counsel patients with osteoarthritis about the risks of disease worsening if there is a joint injury. Patients who are amenable to substituting lower-risk activities may be advised to consider walking (including walking outdoors or on the treadmill or use of an elliptical machine), biking, swimming, tai chi, and strengthening exercises. The 2019 ACR OA guidelines also emphasize that any increase in activity is beneficial and that replacing sedentary periods with light-intensity physical activity is also another way to improve health outcomes. Furthermore, bouts or episodes of any duration can be included in the accumulation of daily activity. Use of activity monitors, pedometers, and self-monitoring mobile health applications could also be a useful way to encourage greater physical activity in patients with OA.

### Exercise

Closely linked to physical activity is exercise, which is planned, structured, repetitive, and purposeful in the sense that the improvement or maintenance of one or more components of physical fitness is the objective. Exercises for OA can include strengthening or power, aerobic, neuromuscular, or range-of-motion and flexibility programs delivered on land or in aquatic environments (Fig. 102.3). In general, exercise programs are recommended as a core and first-line intervention for OA and have shown efficacy similar or better than pharmacologic therapies without the risk of adverse effects. Patients do best when provided with specific recommendations rather than simply being told to exercise. To date, no single type of exercise has been shown to be more beneficial for OA than other types, and thus the 2019 ACR OA guidelines do not recommend one type of exercise over another. Thus, providers should counsel every patient about various types of exercise options and provide them with an exercise program prescription that is tailored to their preferences, abilities, and comorbidities. Physical therapists are best suited to prescribe tailored exercise programs, and referral to physical therapy should be considered as part of the core treatment plan for patients with osteoarthritis.

The benefits of exercise are sustained as long as the patients continue to adhere to the intervention and can extend beyond OA to other comorbid conditions like cardiovascular disease, depression,

etc. Hence, a critical component of all these interventions is a home exercise program that the patient can implement on their own and strategies to ensure long-term adherence. In exercise trials, a substantial proportion of subjects stop their exercise program by 6 months. Pedometers and other devices have not yet yielded data to demonstrate long-term adherence. Reinforcement of exercise as a prescription may be helpful, as well as identifying barriers to ongoing exercise (see Table 102.1 for additional strategies to facilitate long-term adherence to physical activity and exercise).

Strength training refers to exercise programs that focus on improving the force generation or load-carrying ability of individual muscles or muscle groups. Muscle weakness is a ubiquitous finding in patients with OA. Muscle weakness can be multifactorial, resulting directly from muscle involvement in OA pathogenesis (e.g., fatty infiltration of the muscle, inflammation) and indirectly from reduced activity, injury, or muscle inhibition due to pain. Addressing reductions in muscle function, i.e., the ability of the muscles to generate force and power for daily activities, is extremely important in patients with OA. Strength gains can be achieved by individuals irrespective of their age. These exercises include high-resistance, low-repetition protocols with progressive increase in resistance over a period of time. Resistance can be provided by free weights, elastic resistance bands, or resistance machines. For patients with OA, strengthening programs should include both functional movements that target multiple muscle groups (e.g., stair or rowing exercises and movements that specifically target muscle groups around the affected joint and those immediately proximal and distal such as knee extensors and flexors, hip abductors, and calf muscles in people with knee OA). Progressive resistance-based strength training programs show significant improvements in pain and function for patients with OA.48-57 For hand OA, occupational therapists are best suited to provide specific hand exercises based upon the joints involved. Care should be taken to tailor the programs to individual's abilities, and the interventions should be delivered by expert professionals (e.g., physical therapists, strength and conditioning specialists, etc.).

Aerobic training refers to exercise that focus on improving cardiovascular fitness and aerobic capacity of the muscles. Patients with OA tend to be overweight and exhibit reduced fitness levels. Hence, improvement in aerobic capacity for pulmonary and

functional capacity is an important part of patient management. These usually include low-impact, low-intensity, high-repetition protocols and generally include walking and/or cycling as the activity for land-based programs. Aerobic exercise programs may also be delivered in a water-based setting (aquatic exercise). While aerobic exercise programs can be implemented in isolation, ideally they should be integrated with strengthening approaches.58-70

Range-of-motion and flexibility exercise refers to strategies to maintain or improve joint mobility. Patients with OA report joint stiffness and may exhibit some loss of end-range movement (e.g., loss of end-range knee extension due to OA). These exercises should always be included as part of the overall exercise protocol. They are insufficient for improvements in pain and function in isolation.

Neuromuscular training refers to exercise programs that are designed to improve control of functional movements. These

exercises rely on perturbing the ability of the body to maintain a position or perform a movement to train improved control. Patients with OA often exhibit alterations in neuromuscular control including reduced joint proprioception, reduced control of muscle activity during submaximal contractions, and abnormal movement and muscle activation patterns during daily activities like walking. The exercises commonly included in neuromuscular training protocols are balance and stability exercises, movement pattern retraining exercises, and aerobic and strengthening exercises. Neuromuscular training can lead to improved pain and function compared with usual care or pharmaceutical therapies.71-75 If delivered by an experienced professional, neuromuscular training is a valuable treatment option for people with OA since it could address multiple aspects of muscle impairments and neural control of movement.

The locations of exercise programs are generally land-based in settings like gyms, physical therapy clinics, or at home. However, water-based exercise programs are also an option for this patient population. Exercising in water can reduce the load over the joints, allowing patients to experience less pain and permit larger range of motion for the affected joints. Both strengthening and aerobic exercises can be delivered in water-based settings. Aquatic exercise leads to improvements in pain and function but to a lesser extent than land-based exercises.48, There are also challenges with accurately recording the dosage of the exercise in water-based programs, and not all patients have access to aquatic facilities for longer-term adherence. However, when available, water-based exercises offer a low-impact alternative to land-based exercise programs and should be considered for patients who are interested in these interventions. Making specific recommendations for hand OA exercises is difficult because of heterogeneity of types of exercises and types of hand OA studied to date in a limited number of studies.

### Therapies to Modulate Joint Loading

Patients with lower extremity OA, particularly knee OA, exhibit movement patterns that cause abnormal or increased loading over the joint during weight-bearing activities like walking. An example of an abnormal walking patterns that increases loading over the medial tibiofemoral compartment is called varus thrust. Patients who walk with a varus thrust have a transient lateral shift of the knee when they take a step. Being overweight or obese also increases the loading over the joints. Thus weight loss is recommended as an intervention strategy for these patients. To counter abnormal joint loading due to movement patterns, there are a number of intervention approaches that have been investigated or are being developed. These include gait-retraining strategies, orthotics (lateral heel wedge insoles, knee braces), aids/assistive devices (e.g., canes), and different types of footwear. For patients with predominantly patellofemoral OA, patellofemoral taping is commonly used in physical therapy clinics to improve the biomechanical function of the joint; patellofemoral bracing may also be beneficial. However, studies to date have used different techniques, making it difficult to discern true efficacy and clouding which approach to recommend.

Gait retraining refers to behavioral strategies to induce changes in walking patterns in an attempt to reduce loading over the medial tibiofemoral joint. Examples of gait-retraining strategies include walking with increased toe-out, walking with increased toe-in, and biofeedback to reduce knee loading in real time. While these intervention strategies appear to reduce knee loading and may have beneficial effects on pain, 87,88 widespread implementation

has been hampered by technological challenges and patient compliance. Most previous studies were conducted using expensive gait laboratories that require individual patients to make multiple visits to learn the new gait patterns. This approach is not scalable for wider dissemination. Furthermore, implementing the gait modification in free-living conditions requires use of technology that could monitor specific attributes of gait patterns (e.g., degree of toe-out) and provide feedback to the patient on when and how much to change their gait. While there have been a few promising advances in this area, more work is needed before these techniques are widely available and recommended.89,

Lateral wedge insoles are orthotics that can be worn inside the shoe to offload the medial tibiofemoral compartment during walking for patients with predominantly medial knee OA. These insoles include a heel wedge that is higher on the lateral side in an attempt to realign the leg by moving the lower extremity closer to the midline of the body. Similarly, medial wedge insoles could be used for patients with lateral knee OA. These insoles offer a potentially attractive option since they are extremely inexpensive and widely available. While lateral wedge insoles can lead to small reductions in medial knee loading,91 their effects on pain and function have not been encouraging in patients with medial knee OA. However, some recent work has suggested that when patients are screened for an initial response of reduced knee loading to lateral wedges, small but significant improvements in pain can be attained. Strategies to identify patients who show a response, i.e., a reduction in knee loading, need to be developed that do not require expensive and infeasible gait laboratory assessments. Results have been more promising with the use of medial wedge insoles for patients with lateral knee OA, but there also have been far fewer studies assessing the efficacy of medial wedge insoles. If these insoles are prescribed, it is important to ensure that the functional foot anatomy and any foot symptoms be taken into consideration and appropriate adjustments included. For example, patients who present with pronated feet should be provided an insole with medial arch support. However, long-term compliance with these devices is unclear. As such, the 2019 ACR OA guidelines conditionally recommended against lateral wedge insoles.

Footwear that could reduce knee loading has also been of significant interest for people with knee OA. Such footwear can include minimal shoes (flat, flexible, nonheeled), variable stiffness shoes (greater lateral stiffness than medial or a combination of lateral wedge and variable stiffness), unstable shoes, and biomechanical shoes (e.g., Apos Therapy, Apos US Management Inc, USA). Overall, the minimal shoes, variable stiffness shoes, and unstable shoes do not appear to reduce pain or improve function in people with knee OA.96-101 The biomechanical shoe combines a shoe with semicircular pods on the sole to modulate knee loading and induce neuromuscular training and thus reduces knee loading and pain, but further research is needed before making clinical recommendations. While the biomechanical shoe system can be relatively expensive, some of the other shoes, including minimal shoes and variable stiffness shoes, are commercially available at a fairly low cost. Hence, patients interested in trying such footwear should not be discouraged from doing so, although specific recommendations are difficult to make at present due to the paucity of data. Because of the lack of high-quality data, the 2019 ACR OA guidelines conditionally recommend against modified shoes.

Offloading knee braces are devices that are worn over the knee joint in an attempt to offload the medial knee compartment.

These braces attempt to realign the leg by applying pressure proximal and distal to the knee and at the knee. While offloading braces are effective at reducing medial knee loading compared with no brace, it is not clear whether they are effective compared with a regular brace. The changes in knee loading inconsistently translate to improvements in pain or function, with most studies being small with concerns for bias. Because they can be bulky and may be difficult to wear under trousers and/or are visible if wearing a skirt/dress, most patients do not prefer to use these devices long-term, leading to poor adherence and limiting their utility. Minor adverse events including slipping or skin irritation and blisters are possible. Hence, offloading knee braces could be an adjunctive therapy for patients who predominantly have medial knee OA and are willing to wear the devices. Patellofemoral braces are also available, and one trial has demonstrated a reduction in bone marrow lesion volume and pain over a short 6-week period, providing proof of concept of efficacy for patellofemoral OA bracing as well. The 2019 ACR OA guidelines strongly recommend tibiofemoral bracing and conditionally recommends patellofemoral bracing.

A walking cane used by the hand contralateral to the lower extremity joint with painful OA (e.g., holding in right hand for left knee or hip OA, Fig. 102.4) is a common prescription for people with advanced knee OA. Their use in individuals who are ambulatory in the community is limited, as these patients may not prefer to use a cane. The cane also works on the principal that it allows a reduction in the loading over the knee or hip joint. One unblinded clinical trial reported improved pain with the use of cane for 2 months in people with knee OA. The risks and costs of cane use are minimal and therefore can be reasonably considered when appropriate, often at later stages of disease; its use is strongly recommended by the 2019 ACR OA guidelines.

Further, in patients with comorbid conditions that necessitate aids for ambulation, a cane or other assistive devices can also help maintain balance and reduce the risk of falls. Therefore walking aids like a cane should be recommended for patients who may otherwise be at risk of walking disability or those who may be at risk of falls. Cane use may also be useful for patients who have symptoms and/or instability while navigating stairs.

For those with hand OA, joint loading is typically related to gripping activities that can contribute to pain, particularly at the first carpometacarpal (CMC) joint (Fig. 102.5). Modifications that can minimize joint loading include assistive devices that diminish the force required for gripping actions, such as cushioned utensils and/or assistive jar opening devices. Digital orthoses for first CMC OA are recommended; the data are less strong for digital orthoses for the other hand joints and therapeutic gloves, although given the low risk and low cost, these approaches can be tried. There are insufficient data to recommend rigid versus neoprene orthoses.

### Manual Therapy

Manual therapy includes a wide variety of techniques in which clinicians or patients use manual contact for a desired outcome like pain relief, regaining movement, or releasing adhesions. Examples of manual therapy techniques include joint manipulation and mobilization, muscle stretching, and soft tissue massage. These should be delivered by experienced professionals (e.g., physical therapists, osteopaths, chiropractors). However, the benefits of these therapies when used in isolation are unclear. Recent evidence also raises questions about their utility when provided in combination with exercise over exercise alone.

### Physical and Electrotherapeutic Modalities

The phrase physical agents and electrotherapeutic modalities refers to application of therapeutic heat (moist heat) or cold, electrical stimulation (e.g., transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation [TENS] and neuromuscular electrical stimulation [NMES]), radiofrequency ablation, or therapeutic ultrasound. These agents are applied locally to the involved joint and are meant to target pain and/or inflammation in OA. Heat can be applied using hot water or hot packs, electric diathermy, or therapeutic ultrasound. For hand OA, heat can also be applied with paraffin therapy. Some modalities are better suited for more superficial joints (e.g., knee, hand joints). In general, there does not appear to be any clear beneficial effects of heat application, including with the use of therapeutic ultrasound, for pain or functional improvement in

OA. One challenge with studies on therapeutic ultrasound has been the variation in protocols with no consensus on optimal dosage or protocol. Application of cold using cold compress, ice bags, or cold packs seems to have a positive effect on pain that occurs with movement but not overall self-reported pain. The 2019 ACR OA guidelines strongly recommend against the use of TENS due to reported lack of benefit in prior studies. NMES is the use of electrical stimulation to elicit muscle contraction and is used in physical therapy practice to overcome muscle activation deficits, maintain muscle strength in the absence of voluntary muscle activation, and strengthen muscles in combination with exercise. While the effects of NMES on pain in OA are unclear, it could be used in conjunction with a strengthening exercise program to elicit greater muscle contraction in presence of pain or activation deficits. While adverse events using these modalities are infrequent, any application of heat or cold needs to be accompanied with evaluation of integrity of skin sensation. These modalities should not be used in isolation but could be used as adjunct to primary treatment for patients who respond to these interventions or may believe in their efficacy.

Nerve ablation has recently been of significant clinical interest. It refers to focused application of a small current of thermal energy that generates heat (thermal radiofrequency ablation; cooled radiofrequency ablation, which includes a cooling component; or pulsed radiofrequency ablation) or cold (cryoneurolysis) to sensory nerves to impair their ability to transmit nociceptive signals. Evidence suggests that radiofrequency ablation may be effective at reducing pain and improving function, and cooled procedures may yield better outcomes than conventional or pulsed modalities with benefits persisting for up to 2 years.107- 110 In clinical practice, it is common to use a prognostic nerve block prior to ablation; however, the utility of the nerve block is unclear in OA. The superomedial, superolateral, and inferomedial branches of the genicular nerve are commonly targeted in radiofrequency ablation therapies for knee OA. Cryoneurolysis refers to percutaneous application of cold to peripheral nerves to disrupt nerve conduction. For knee OA, the infrapatellar branch of the saphenous nerve has been targeted. In a double-blind, sham-controlled trial, cryoneurolysis resulted in significant improvements in pain that lasted up to 5 months. Adverse events with these therapies seem to be infrequent and the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has recently approved a cooled radiofrequency ablation device (Coolief®, Avanos Medical, USA) and a cryoneurolysis device (Iovera®, Myoscience, USA) for use in patients with OA. The 2019 ACR OA guidelines conditionally recommended radiofrequency ablation due to heterogeneity of techniques and the lack of long-term safety data at that time. While more studies have been published since then with promising longer-term efficacy and safety results, there is still substantial heterogeneity in techniques and comparators.

### Psychological Interventions and Complementary and Integrative Therapies

Individuals with painful osteoarthritis may have comorbid depressive symptoms, sleep problems, and other psychological impairments like reduced self-efficacy, poor coping skills, pain catastrophizing, and fear-avoidance behaviors that may exacerbate the pain experience. These comorbidities can increase reliance on analgesics, interfere with adherence to treatment programs, and reduce efficacy of treatments. Interventions to address these impairments should be considered for relevant patients.

### Cognitive Behavioral Therapy

Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is a behavioral therapy intervention delivered by psychologists or other trained clinicians and is recommended as a first-line treatment for individuals with depressive symptoms. CBT is usually delivered via in-person sessions, but recently a number of internetand/or telephone-based CBT interventions have been developed for many chronic conditions. For people with knee OA, CBT by itself is not any better than usual care for pain management but could help with managing depressive symptoms and sleep and is helpful in other pain conditions. Hence, CBT could be considered as an adjunctive therapy for individuals with knee OA who present with depressive symptoms and/or sleep disturbances.

### Pain Coping Skills Training

Pain coping skills training refers to behavioral interventions that target catastrophizing, maladaptive coping strategies, etc., in patients with OA. Pain coping skills training alone or in combination with CBT can lead to improved self-management of pain in 116, Such interventions can be propeople with osteoarthritis. vided by trained physical therapists, or patients can be referred to online programs.

### Complementary and Integrative Therapies

Complementary and integrative therapies include a variety of approaches that are not considered part of Western medical practice and that could be used together with conventional approaches. Integrative therapies refer to using conventional and complementary approaches in a coordinated patient-focused way while addressing mental, emotional, functional, spiritual, social, and community aspects. Integrative health care approaches are growing, for example with the Veteran's Affairs (VA) health care system pioneering work in this area for chronic pain management in military and veteran personnel, as well as other health care systems providing integrative medicine services within the medical clinic setting.

Mindbody practices refers to a variety of complementary and alternative approaches delivered by a trained clinician or teacher and can include yoga, meditation, acupuncture, tai chi, relaxation techniques, etc. While acupuncture has been gaining popularity, the efficacy of acupuncture for pain management in OA remains unclear. Studies comparing acupuncture with usual care report improved pain and function, 118-124 but compared with sham acupuncture, the benefits are not consistently evident. 119, There are also different protocols for "sham" acupuncture, including penetrating versus nonpenetrating needles or non-needle sham and use of "true" acupuncture points versus other nonacupuncture points; generally, penetrating-needle sham-controlled studies have smaller effect sizes (e.g., 0.16) than nonpenetrating-needle sham-controlled studies (e.g., 0.50). It is also a possibility that the clinician's optimism and communication about positive outcomes could influence patient's perception of pain. While the evidence supporting acupuncture for OA is unclear, considering the relative safety of the intervention, it could be considered as adjunctive therapy for patients who have positive beliefs about acupuncture and is conditionally recommended by the 2019 ACR OA guidelines.

Tai chi is a Chinese mindbody practice that integrates meditation with breathing, relaxation, and slow, gentle movements. Tai chi improves pain and physical function in people with knee OA, including in a randomized controlled trial.84, As such, the 2019 ACR OA guidelines strongly recommend tai chi for knee

and hip OA. Yoga is an Indian mindbody practice that incorporates meditation, breathing, relaxation, and exercise. While there have not been many studies on yoga for OA, current research suggests beneficial effects with improvements in pain and physical function.66, Therefore for patients who are interested in tai chi or yoga and have access to an instructor, tai chi or yoga should be offered as a treatment intervention for people with OA, especially knee OA. However, yoga is likely not advisable for individuals with hip OA due to concerns about certain hip abduction movements that may be painful and/or harmful; the 2019 ACR OA guidelines conditionally recommend yoga for knee OA. To date, there are insufficient data to specifically recommend meditation for OA-related symptoms. However, mindfulness-based stress reduction (MBSR) has been demonstrated to be efficacious for chronic low back pain and is recommended by the American College of Physicians for management of chronic low back pain. It is likely the MBSR would have similar symptom benefits in OA, and given the lack of adverse effects and low cost, with several free smartphone apps, it is reasonable to recommend MBSR as an adjunct for patients' pain management strategies.

### Pharmacologic Management: Knee, Hip, Hand

Many patients will have tried acetaminophen and/or over-thecounter nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory therapy by the time they seek medical attention. Before escalating pharmacologic therapy, the first step should be to optimize patients' use of the physical modalities listed above and consider adjunctive mindbody approaches. Setting expectations is also important. While most patients expect and want a medication, they need to be counseled that much of OA symptom management requires their active engagement and participation through weight loss (where indicated) and physical activity. Further, a goal of "zero pain" is not realistic; setting reasonable expectations about "pain management" as focusing on making "pain manageable" so that they can carry out their activities with minimal limitations or restrictions from their symptoms is necessary to avoid disappointment.

Decisions regarding pharmacologic therapy should be guided by the severity and frequency of symptoms (Fig. 102.6). Mild and intermittent symptoms may be managed by the patient with asneeded analgesics. A single affected joint may be best managed by local therapy, such as topical therapy or intra-articular injection. More frequent and limiting pain may require multiple therapeutic options, including physical modalities and systemic as well as local therapies. When reasonable use of the various available and appropriate options have been tried without adequate symptom control, it is reasonable to consider referral to an orthopedic surgeon for consideration of joint replacement surgery.

### Local Therapies

Topical Therapies. Pharmacologic formulations that are able to penetrate the skin can help alleviate symptoms in superficial joints such as the hand or knee. The hip joint, being a deep joint, is not an appropriate site for topical therapy. The two types of medications that are available in topical formulations for use in OA are nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and capsaicin, and there are limited data to support the use of topical lidocaine. In general, for mild symptoms of knee or hand OA, particularly when only a single or few joints are affected, topical therapy may be a better option than prescribing an oral systemic therapy to minimize potential side effects from systemic exposure to an oral agent. Patients need to be mindful to ensure that the

topical gel or cream is not inadvertently wiped off the skin before the medication has penetrated the skin.

Topical NSAIDs likely produce their anti-inflammatory and analgesic and effects through inhibition of prostaglandin synthesis in peripheral tissue. The systemic absorption of topical NSAIDs is low, as demonstrated in a study comparing systemic bioavailability of oral versus topical diclofenac. NAIDs in topical formulations have demonstrated efficacy compared with placebo for knee and hand OA pain and function, although the effect is small. Nonetheless, their efficacy is generally similar to that of oral formulations. In meta-analyses of placebo-controlled trials, the diclofenac patch was found to have the greatest efficacy for pain and piroxicam gel for function. Data on deeper joints, including hip and shoulder OA, are lacking. Major local adverse reactions include dry skin, erythema, irritation, paresthesia and pruritus. Despite low systemic absorption, systemic adverse effects including gastrointestinal side effects and headaches have been reported, although the anemia and renal and hepatic abnormalities noted with oral NSAIDs are much less common with topical NSAIDs use. On balance, the adverse effects associated with topical NSAIDs are lower than that of oral formulations, and therefore topical NSAIDs may be considered the first line of treatment for knee and hand OA pain, particularly in elderly patients due to their safety and efficacy profile. Topical NSAIDs are strongly recommended for knee OA by the 2019 ACR OA guidelines.

Capsaicin is the active compound in chili peppers that makes them "hot." Capsaicin selectively stimulates the afferent C nerve fibers and produce substance P through activation of transient receptor potential vanilloid 1 (TRPV1) channels, resulting in reversible desensitization of the end terminals of these primary afferent pain fibers. This results in a period of enhanced neurostimulation (irritation, burning, vascular dilation) followed by decreased sensitivity due to exhaustion of substance P with regular use. Topical capsaicin thus provides analgesia through its effect on peripheral nerves around the joint tissue. Topical capsaicin has shown efficacy for a variety of painful conditions such as postherpetic pain, diabetic neuropathy, and musculoskeletal conditions, but only a few trials have been conducted in OA. Two older metaanalyses of trials of capsaicin versus placebo demonstrated pain

relief efficacy for musculoskeletal conditions overall, and in OA specifically.140, Although there have been no trials to date of topical capsaicin versus topical NSAIDs, a 2018 network metaanalysis suggested equivalence between topical NSAID preparations and capsaicin. Local adverse effects of topical capsaicin are much greater than for topical NSAIDs. In the meta-analysis noted above conducted in musculoskeletal conditions, the rate of local adverse events was higher with capsaicin compared with placebo (54% vs 15%), with burning, stinging, and erythema at the application site as among the cited adverse effects. Patients should be advised to use gloves, swabs, or tissue to avoid direct contact and to wash hands if applied using hands. In particular, patients must be cautioned about the burning pain they will experience if they touch their eyes prior to washing capsaicin off their hands. Systemic adverse effects are rare and mainly reported with higher concentrations (0.25% and 0.075%) rather than lower concentrations (0.025%). For example, a meta-analysis found coughing (due to inhaling capsaicin residue) in 8% of patients using capsaicin 0.075% and none using capsaicin 0.025%.

Lidocaine. Inflammatory joint tissue is hypothesized to induce increased afferent input from the surrounding peripheral nerves. Topical anesthetics are used to block sodium channels in sensory nerves surrounding the affected tissue. A 2-week open label study demonstrated significant improvement in pain and quality of life in OA patients who had suboptimal pain control with other analgesics. Post-hoc analysis of a trial of lidocaine 5% patch versus celecoxib 200 mg/day showed no difference in knee OA pain or skin reactions. Thus there are insufficient data to support the use of topical lidocaine for OA, although a lack of difference with celecoxib noted in that trial may suggest some potential for pain relief in OA.

In summary, topical agents are well tolerated and can be considered throughout the course of management for knee and hand OA. One particular type of topical agent cannot be clearly recommended above another, although topical NSAIDs have the most efficacy and safety data available in OA. The 2019 ACR OA guidelines provide a strong recommendation for topical NSAIDs for knee OA (conditional for hand OA) and conditional recommendations for capsaicin in knee OA while they conditionally recommend against capsaicin for hand OA.

### Intra-articular Agents

Certain formulations of pharmacologic agents can be delivered directly into the joint. This option is particularly attractive when a single joint is affected. There are data to support greater accuracy using ultrasound or other image guidance with joint injections. However, for the most part, hand and knee joints can be injected in the clinic without image guidance. The hip, being a deep joint, is recommended to be injected under image guidance. The agents that are injected intra-articularly for OA include glucocorticoids and viscosupplementation, although there is controversy about efficacy for the latter class of agents. Platelet-rich plasma, prolotherapy, mesenchymal stem cell therapy, and botulinum toxin have inadequate high quality data to support their use.

Glucocorticoids. Synovitis is a key pathologic entity in OA, and there is evidence implicating it in OA progression. Evidence from a Cochrane review of randomized or quasirandomized controlled trials of intra-articular steroid versus sham or no treatment suggested that pain relief from steroid injections was short term, i.e., moderate effect 1 to 2 weeks after end of treatment, small to moderate effect at 4 to 6 weeks, small effect at 13 weeks, and no clear evidence of an effect at 26 weeks. There is also evidence to support small improvement in function in OA patients receiving intra-articular corticosteroid therapy. While there has been some thought that joints with effusions, indicative of inflammation, may benefit more from intra-articular glucocorticoid injections, a randomized trial of triamcinolone versus saline intraarticular injections every 12 weeks over 2 years in a sample of individuals with knee OA who had evidence of effusion or synovitis on ultrasound demonstrated no difference in pain relief. Thus, this study has called into question the theory that knees with signs of inflammation benefit from steroid injections. A longer-acting formulation, triamcinolone acetonide extended release, has been approved by the FDA, although pain efficacy is not clearly of longer duration than conventional triamcinolone acetonide based on the primary endpoint of average daily pain. Nonetheless, this formulation has less systemic blood glucose effects.

Intra-articular glucocorticoids are generally considered safe. A Cochrane review found that those receiving intra-articular glucocorticoids were 27% less likely to experience any serious adverse event than other treatment arms, although results did not reach statistical significance. In the randomized trial of triamcinolone injections versus saline injections cited above, a nonsignificant greater risk of cartilage loss at 2 years in the triamcinolone group compared with the saline group. However, the clinical significance of the small differential change in cartilage over 2 years is not clear; indeed, the between-group difference of -0.11 mm over 2 years was less than the size of a voxel (0.3 x 0.3 x 1 mm). The 2019 ACR OA guidelines strongly recommended the use of intraarticular glucocorticoids for hip and knee OA, as did the 2019 Osteoarthritis Research Society International (OARSI) guidelines. 44, However, since then, controversy has arisen regarding the potential for rapidly progressive OA related to intra-articular glucocorticoid injections from a case series, although interpretation is difficult due to the observational nature of the report. Data from a large observational cohort also suggested increased risk of OA progression with intra-articular steroid use compared with no use; however, this association was not seen in another study using intra-articular hyaluronic acid as a comparator to better account for confounding by indication.151, Rare adverse effects have also been described.153,

Viscosupplementation. Hyaluronic acid is a polysaccharide present in synovial fluid that, together with other molecules, aids

joint lubrication. In OA, the concentration of hyaluronic acid is decreased due to depolymerization and increased clearance from the joint. Various hyaluronic acid preparations, known as viscosupplements, have been synthesized and injected intra-articularly to replete hyaluronic acid in the synovial fluid to improve lubrication, mainly for knee OA. The preponderance of data from published and unpublished trials of intra-articular viscosupplements overall have demonstrated either no efficacy or small and clinically irrelevant effects on pain and no effect on function in OA, and meta-analyses raise concerns about publication bias.155-157 There is stronger evidence regarding the lack of benefit in hip OA. Several society guidelines including the ACR, the American Academy of Orthopedic Surgeons (AAOS), and OARSI recommend against their use, either strongly or conditionally, or have weak recommendations for their use.

Platelet-Rich Plasma, Mesenchymal Stem Cell Therapy, Prolotherapy, Botulinum Toxin. Intra-articular autologous concentration of human platelets in a small volume of plasma in the knee is performed in an attempt to provide growth factors for anabolic effect in OA. However, heterogeneity and lack of standardization of formulations, as well as lack of long-term safety data, make it unsuitable for evidence-based OA management.158, Further, two recent randomized trials, one in knee OA and one in ankle OA, in which platelet-rich plasma preparations were compared with saline placebos, did not meet their primary endpoints for pain relief.160, As for platelet-rich plasma, mesenchymal stem cell studies are heterogeneous with lack of standardization in preparations and techniques used and thus cannot be recommended for OA management. For prolotherapy, only a limited number of small studies with variable regimens have been conducted to date, again making recommendations infeasible presently. Intra-articular botulinum toxin has efficacy in a small number of studies conducted to date. Due to the heterogeneity of study designs, the lack of high-quality evidence supporting efficacy, and inadequate long-term data, ACR and OARSI both recommend against the use of these agents.

In summary, intra-articular glucocorticoids remain the mainstay as the preferred therapy for local intra-articular joint injections. While the use of hyaluronic acid is not recommended by most society guidelines, clinicians may attempt a trial if other approaches, including intra-articular glucocorticoids, have failed, particularly as a trial to attempt to delay joint replacement surgery or provide some alternative symptom management while awaiting joint replacement surgery.

### Systemic Therapies

The vast majority of patients with OA will have tried over-thecounter oral medications before seeking medical attention for OA-related pain. The mainstays of oral therapy remain limited, with only minimal or moderate efficacy at best and often complicated by adverse events and/or contraindications. By the nature of their systemic exposure, therapies given orally or parenterally have greater concerns for adverse effects. A general guiding principle is to tailor the dose and frequency to the degree of symptoms, ideally choosing the lowest dose and shortest duration of therapy as possible, including use on an as-needed basis if appropriate rather than chronically.

Acetaminophen (paracetamol) is considered a weak analgesic through weak prostaglandin inhibition, with greater COX-2 inhibition than COX-1.165 It has traditionally been considered "first-line" therapy for pharmacologic OA management 25 but is no longer considered as such. A meta-analysis of trials of

acetaminophen showed a only small benefit for improving OA pain compared with placebo and less efficacy than oral NSAIDs. 166 A 2017 network meta-analysis demonstrated that acetaminophen had a nearly null effect on pain symptoms at various doses, with none of the doses reaching a minimum clinically important difference (effect size of -0.18, corresponding to a 4.5-mm difference on a 100-mm visual analogue scale). Thus, from an efficacy standpoint, acetaminophen is no longer considered appropriate as a single agent for managing OA pain. Despite its lower efficacy, some patients do use acetaminophen regularly or on a short-term basis, often due to contraindications for NSAID use. For regular users of acetaminophen, a total daily dose of 3 grams and under is considered the maximal safe dose, although hepatotoxicity needs to be monitored, particularly in older adults. For patients using long-term acetaminophen, monitoring should also be performed for gastrointestinal toxicity. Gastrointestinal blood loss/perforation can be associated with regular use of acetaminophen at doses greater than 2 gm/day. 168, The ongoing use of acetaminophen despite limited efficacy reflects in large part the lack of sufficient effective and safe alternatives.

Oral NSAIDs, Including COX-2 Inhibitors. Oral NSAIDs are the most commonly used and prescribed pharmacologic treatments for OA pain. Both selective and nonselective NSAIDs have shown moderate efficacy in improving pain in OA in randomized trials compared with acetaminophen. Risk stratification is needed for initiating and maintaining treatment with oral NSAIDs due to a multitude of adverse effects associated with them. Lower doses are considered safer and better tolerated, but higher doses are more efficacious. Thus the dose should be individualized for a particular patient based on their risk profile. While on NSAIDs, patients should be monitored for adverse effects, such as gastrointestinal bleed, renal insufficiency, and cardiovascular toxicity. In a large randomized trial of patients with OA or rheumatoid arthritis who had moderate or high cardiovascular risk (PRECISION), all of whom were on proton pump inhibitors, approximately 4% to 5% experienced a major NSAID toxicity (major adverse cardiovascular event, important gastrointestinal events, renal events, and all-cause mortality) over 1 to 2 years,170 highlighting the common occurrence of these adverse events. As much as is feasible, oral NSAIDs should be used for as short a time as possible and on an as-needed basis rather than long-term regular use.

Opioids (Tramadol, Nontramadol). Opioids provide analgesia through their action on M (predominantly), D, or K receptors in the central and peripheral nervous system. Since the primary presentation of OA is pain, opioids have been evaluated for the management of OA pain. However, neither traditional (nontramadol) opioids nor tramadol have shown benefit for OA pain, 171 and there is only a small benefit in pain and physical function demonstrated for the management of noncancer pain. The opioid epidemic in the United States and the rise in drug overdoses highlights the addiction potential of opioids. Osteoarthritis is among the most common conditions for which opioids are prescribed in the United States for people with obesity, which is a major risk factor for knee OA. There are also many other adverse consequences of nontramadol opioids and tramadol, such as sedation, increased fall risk, constipation, respiratory depression, altered cognitive status, etc. Overall, opioids should not play a role in the routine management of OA, but their limited use in certain circumstances may be appropriate when other approaches are ineffective or contraindicated. For example, for patients in whom NSAIDs are contraindicated, not tolerated, or ineffective or for patients in whom other approaches are ineffective, tramadol

may be an option to consider. Use of nontramadol opioids would be less advisable due to even higher risk of adverse events. Use of the lowest possible dose with the shortest duration possible should be implemented if tramadol (or nontramadol opioids) are being considered.

Duloxetine and Other Centrally Acting Agents. Duloxetine is a serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor (SNRI) with central effects that is purported to target central pain processing. A meta-analysis of three trials demonstrated improvement of pain and function in OA. Since that meta-analysis, two randomized trials of duloxetine for hip or knee OA have had conflicting results. In an open-label, cluster randomized trial of duloxetine delivered in a primary care setting, there was no difference compared with placebo on the primary outcome of pain at 3 months. However in a pragmatic, open-label randomized trial, duloxetine had significantly better change in pain scores compared with placebo. Nonetheless, for patients with widespread pain and/or pain hypersensitivity, duloxetine may be considered. A cost-effectiveness analysis demonstrated the benefit for adding duloxetine to usual care for knee OA, even in the absence of depressive symptoms. The 2019 ACR OA guidelines conditionally recommend the use of duloxetine. Adverse effects are more common in duloxetine users compared with placebo, including nausea, constipation, dry mouth, diarrhea, fatigue, dizziness, somnolence, and insomnia. Because of tolerability and side effect issues, the use of duloxetine may be limited. Other centrally acting agents, such as gabapentin, pregabalin, or other anti-depressants (other SNRIs, tricyclic antidepressants) have not been directly studied for symptoms of OA.

Immunomodulatory Agents. A number of other agents have been examined for efficacy in OA, without clear demonstration of benefit to date (Table 102.2). Thus 2019 ACR OA guidelines strongly recommend against their routine use in OA.
