Because synovitis and low-grade inflammation plays a role in OA pathogenesis, there has been interest in agents with anti-inflammatory

IL, Interleukin; NA, not available.

and/or immunomodulatory effects. Two randomized trials have studied the use of low-dose oral prednisolone for hand OA; in one, prednisolone 5 mg daily for 4 weeks did not perform better than placebo for change in pain scores among participants with hand OA. In the other trial enriched for an inflammatory phenotype of hand OA, prednisone 10 mg daily for 6 weeks demonstrated improvements in pain compared with placebo. Colchicine did not demonstrate symptomatic benefits in randomized trials compared with placebo for either knee or hand OA. 180, Hydroxychloroquine has been studied for hand OA in several well-conducted randomized controlled trials, demonstrating no efficacy. 182-184 Methotrexate has not been shown to have efficacy in OA to date, although preliminary results from the PROMOTE trial indicated a moderate benefit at 6 months that was reduced by 12 months. Despite the recognized role of proinflammatory cytokines in OA, biologics such as inhibitors of TNF and interleukin (IL)-6 have failed to demonstrate efficacy in randomized trials for knee and hand OA.186-189 In contrast, an exploratory analysis of a large trial of canakinumab, an IL-1β inhibitor, in individuals with cardiovascular disease and elevated high-sensitivity C-reactive protein levels found significant reductions in total joint replacements. Although prior randomized trials of IL-1β inhibitors in knee OA did not demonstrate benefit, 19 the canakinumab study had the benefit of a large sample size and longer follow-up. This finding supports the hypothesis of a subset of individuals with knee OA in whom directly targeting inflammation might be helpful.

Bisphosphonates and Vitamin D. The role of bone in OA pathogenesis is well established. However, trials of vitamin D have not demonstrated efficacy to date. Similarly, bisphosphonates have been studied for OA without clear benefit. While oral bisphosphonates have failed in trials, IV zoledronic acid showed promising results at 6 months, although longer-term efficacy was . Both ACR and OARSI guidelines recommend not present. against the use of bisphosphonates and vitamin D for the specific treatment of OA.

### Supplements/Nutraceuticals

Use of dietary supplements in the United States is on the rise. Approximately three-quarters of adults consumed dietary supplements in 2017. A number of supplements or nutraceuticals are purported to have benefits for OA, with controversies regarding actual efficacy, as will be outlined below. Unlike pharmacologic agents that are FDA-approved, supplements or nutraceuticals do not have the same level of oversight, with wide variation in the quantity and true ingredients present in a product.

Glucosamine and Chondroitin. Both glucosamine and chondroitin are glycosaminoglycans and constituents of the macromolecule aggrecan in cartilage. These molecules contribute to the healthy functioning of cartilage. However, it is not clear whether ingested glucosamine or chondroitin are actually incorporated into cartilage. There has been much controversy in the literature about the efficacy of these compounds, with some differentiation between glucosamine hydrochloride versus glucosamine sulfate. However, the dissociation of glucosamine from its salt when digested would argue against biologically meaningful differences between the two salts. The National Institutes of Health (NIH)—funded Glucosamine/Chondroitin Arthritis Intervention Trial (GAIT) study demonstrated no efficacy of glucosamine hydrochloride or chondroitin sulfate, alone or in combination, compared with placebo. However, in a prespecified subgroup of those with moderate to severe pain, the combination of glucosamine and chondroitin did have a higher rate of response than placebo. Further, meta-analyses have highlighted concerns regarding publication

bias and efficacy only being noted in industry-sponsored trials, with no efficacy demonstrated in nonindustry-sponsored trials (e.g., the NIH-funded GAIT trial). 197, Treatment guidelines do not recommend these agents.

Omega-3 Polyunsaturated Fatty Acids. The anti-inflammatory properties of fish oil, thought to be largely related to omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids, have been studied in relation to various types of arthritis, without clear evidence of efficacy to date. In a randomized trial of high-dose fish oil versus low-dose fish oil (a blend of fish oil with sunola oil), there was an unanticipated greater improvement in pain and function in the comparator lowdose fish oil arm than the intended treatment arm of high-dose fish oil; why this may be is not clear. More recently, a randomized trial of krill oil, which contains different concentrations of anti-inflammatory long-chain omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids than fish oil, demonstrated benefits in pain improvement but not structural benefit. At present, there are insufficient data to recommend fish oil or omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid supplements for OA.

Curcuminoid Formulations. Curcuma longa extract has antiinflammatory properties and has been investigated in multiple small trials for use in OA. In a 12-week, placebo-controlled trial for knee OA, C. longa extract showed benefits for pain but not 201 Currently OARSI provides a conditional recommenstructure. dation for its use.

### Surgical Management of OA

When physical modalities, pharmacologic approaches, and mind— body approaches in various combinations are insufficient for managing OA symptoms, patients and providers often consider surgical options. Arthroscopic meniscal surgeries are the most common orthopedic procedure, estimated to number 700,000/ year in the United States alone. Similarly, there are an estimated 790,000 knee arthroplasties and an estimated 450,000 hip arthroplasties performed annually in the United States, and these numbers are projected to rise to 3.5 million and almost 600,000, respectively, by 2030.

### Arthroscopic Procedures

Patients with knee OA often have meniscal lesions evident on MRI. The contributions of such meniscal lesions to OA symptoms is unclear. In a large study from the Framingham cohort, meniscal lesions were just as likely to be present in knees with OA as they were in knees without OA and in those with knee pain versus without, suggesting that many meniscal lesions are incidental findings and are therefore likely reflective of the underlying OA disease process affecting numerous articular tissues. Several randomized trials have been conducted to date demonstrating that arthroscopic partial meniscectomies offer no better symptom or function improvement than usual care or physical therapy, and in fact, no better than sham surgery. 203-209 This was true even among knees that have mechanical symptoms such as locking or buckling, symptoms that are traditionally thought to be appropriate for arthroscopic surgery. Thus, exercise therapy (physical therapy) and arthroscopic partial meniscectomy appear to offer similar benefits over the long-term (5-year follow-up in the large randomized trials),207,209 while there are also the risks of surgery to consider for arthroscopic procedures. Further, there are some concerns about the potential for greater OA progression and even risk of joint replacement from arthroscopic partial meniscectomy in longer-term follow-up from two trials to date.' 207, Thus,

physical therapy and analgesics as a first-line approach appear to be a reasonable initial strategy, with the decision to undergo subsequent arthroscopic partial meniscectomy to be undertaken in a shared decision-making process with full consideration of balancing risks and benefits, as well as patient preferences. There is a lack of sufficient data regarding hip arthroscopic procedures.

### Joint Arthroplasty

Knee and hip arthroplasties are considered definitive treatments for people with severe OA and difficult-to-manage symptoms as they are generally efficacious for pain relief and functional improvement. Clinically, hip arthroplasties have generally better overall outcomes than knee arthroplasties. At the knee, the joint replacement can be "total," meaning that all joint components are replacement, or "unicompartmental" (e.g., medial compartment only). Meta-analyses report that 82% of total knee replacements and 58% of total hip replacements last 25 years.212, While these surgeries have been clinically recognized to improve pain and function, a randomized trial of individuals with moderate-to-severe knee OA who were eligible for knee arthroplasty demonstrated that knee arthroplasty followed by nonsurgical care (i.e., exercise, education, orthotics, and analgesics) confirmed that knee arthroplasty results in meaningful symptom improvement compared with nonsurgical care alone. The number needed to treat was ~6, supporting the broad benefit of arthroplasty, although with a higher number of adverse events than conservative management. There are also well documented racial and ethnic disparities with patients from minoritized groups demonstrating lower utilization and worse outcomes with total joint replacement surgeries.

Nonetheless, despite the overall beneficial outcomes of knee arthroplasty, approximately 20% to 30% of individuals have persistent pain after knee replacement. Risk factors for poor pain outcomes are not fully understood but include pain due to factors other than knee OA and greater opioid use prior to joint replacement. There is variability among various providers regarding which patients should be referred for consideration of arthroplasty and at what point in the disease course. ### Other Surgical Approaches

Other joints affected by OA can also be considered for arthroplasty, including the shoulder and the ankle, and other surgical approaches for OA in the first CMC, first metatarsophalangeal joints, and ankle are also performed. The long-term outcomes of such procedures have not been studied to the same degree as they have been for knee and hip arthroplasties. For the knee, realignment surgery with high tibial osteotomy has been performed, often in younger patients as a means to defer knee arthroplasty to a later age. Joint distraction is a novel and experimental approach in which an external fixation device is affixed to the bones on either side of the joint, with the frame gradually adjusted to distract the joint, with an aim to unload the joint. The device is worn for a prolonged period of time, such as 2 months, before being removed, followed by extensive rehabilitation therapy. It has been used for ankle OA, and recently longitudinal data for knee OA were reported. However, more data in larger numbers and more follow-up is needed to understand the benefit:risk for such a procedure in knee OA.

### Experimental Osteoarthritis Therapies Under Development

Structural modification has been a major unmet need in OA. A recombinant form of fibroblast growth factor (FGF)-18 (sprifermin) has shown some promising results of increased cartilage thickness following intra-articular injection with benefit maintained

over 5-year follow-up, although symptom benefit did not occur concurrently with the structural improvement, and the degree of cartilage thickness attained is of unclear significance. 222, A posthoc analysis of a high risk subgroup did suggest symptom as well as structural benefit. A Wnt signaling inhibitor, lorecivivint, and a cathepsin K inhibitor both demonstrated structural but not symptomatic improvement in phase 2, placebo-controlled trials.225, However, subgroups with unilateral symptomatic knee OA had both symptom and structural benefit with one of the lorecivivint doses, suggesting possible benefit in this subgroup. ADAMTS-4 and -5 inhibition was studied in a phase 2 trial, although there was no benefit with any of the doses used in terms of structural changes.

A minimally invasive therapy called geniculate or genicular artery embolization (GAE), previously used for hemarthrosis, has received some attention as a potential therapy for OA. GAE is thought to disrupt angiogenesis and synovial nociceptive nerve fiber growth to provide improvements in pain and function, particularly in people who are refractory to conservative therapies.228, However, further work is needed to determine the long-term efficacy and to compare GAE to other available interventions.

While there is a much activity in these areas of drug development, these development efforts are occurring in the context of other promising therapies that were not successful in their development for OA, including BMP-7, inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) inhibition, and calcitonin, among others. Thus ongoing efforts are urgently needed to provide therapeutic options for the millions of people worldwide with OA who currently have limited therapeutic options.

# Metabolic Bone Disease

### KEY POINTS

Osteoporosis is a disease defined by low bone density and deterioration of microarchitecture, which reduces bone strength and increases fracture risk.

Major clinical risk factors for osteoporotic fractures include older age, low weight, family history of hip fracture, fracture occurring after age 50 years, glucocorticoid use, and inability to rise from a chair without assistance. More than 50% of osteoporosis in men results from secondary causes.

Post-menopausal and age-related bone loss results from an uncoupling of bone remodeling such that bone resorption is greater than bone formation, resulting in a net loss of bone.

Evaluation for risk of osteoporotic fractures with the Fracture Assessment Index for post-menopausal women and for men is critical to determine which people have a 10-year fracture risk (for the hip and major osteoporotic fracture sites) that is high enough to warrant treatment.

Treatment of high-turnover osteoporosis resulting from estrogen deficiency with anti-resorptive agents (e.g., estrogen, raloxifene, and bisphosphonates [alendronate, risedronate, zoledronic acid, ibandronate, and denosumab]) and anabolic agents (recombinant human parathyroid hormone 1-34, PTHrP analogue, and an antibody against sclerostin) can reduce incident vertebral fractures.

Treatment for osteoporosis with bisphosphonates should continue for 3 to 5 years, after which, if the bone mineral density T-score is greater than —2.5, the subject has not sustained a fracture, and the overall risk of fracture is low, the treatment can be discontinued and the patient can be reevaluated every 2 to 3 years.

Parathyroid hormone—related compounds (PTH and PTHrP) and an antibody to sclerostin (romosozumab) increase osteoblast maturation and lifespan, increase trabecular bone mass and cortical thickness, improve bone strength, and decrease fractures. Anti-resorptive therapy is necessary after a full course of PTH or anti-sclerostin antibody (romosozumab) to maintain newly formed bone mass.

Glucocorticoid-induced reduction in bone strength results from increased osteoclast activity and reduced osteoblast activity and the bone loss is most severe in the first 6 months of therapy. Bisphosphonate treatment can prevent fractures, and treatment with hPTH (1-34) can reverse glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis and reduce incident fractures.

Aromatase inhibitors reduce levels of serum estrogen and result in rapid bone loss in post-menopausal women undergoing adjuvant breast cancer therapy.

Gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonists decrease testosterone and estrogen levels and cause bone loss in men being treated for prostate cancer.

### Introduction

Osteoporosis is characterized by low bone density and a deterioration of bone microarchitecture that reduces bone strength and increases the risk of fracture. The hallmark of osteoporosis is the loss of both bone mineral and bone matrix. Bone consists of an organic matrix (collagen and noncollagenous proteins) and an inorganic mineral component (calcium and phosphate in hydroxyapatite crystals; see Chapter 4). Normally, bone turnover is tightly coupled with osteoclast-mediated bone resorption followed by osteoblast-stimulated bone formation. This delicate balance in bone remodeling results in no net change in skeletal mass. Osteoblasts synthesize osteoid-bone matrix that subsequently undergoes mineralization and becomes mature bone matrix. The skeleton contains approximately 80% cortical bone, which is concentrated in the appendicular skeleton and femoral neck, and 20% more metabolically active trabecular bone, which is located in the spine, epiphyses, and pelvis. Osteomalacia encompasses disorders in which there is decreased mineralization of bone matrix. Paget's disease is a skeletal disorder characterized by increased rates of bone turnover with the development of disorganized woven bone.

### Osteoporosis

### Epidemiology and Clinical Features

Osteoporosis is the most common metabolic bone disease worldwide. Osteoporosis is a "disease characterized by low bone mass and structural deterioration of bone tissue, leading to bone fragility and an increased susceptibility to fractures, especially of the hip, spine and wrist."1 Although usually asymptomatic, osteoporosis can produce loss of height, pain, dowager's hump, and increased risk of fracture. After 50 years of age, an exponential rise in fractures occurs, with 40% of women and nearly 15% of men experiencing one or more osteoporotic fractures in their lifetimes. Hip fractures are associated with a 12% to 24% mortality rate in women and a nearly 25% mortality rate in men within the first year of fracture; in addition, 50% of patients are unable to ambulate independently and require long-term nursing home care. These numbers will continue to grow exponentially as the elderly population of industrialized nations increases.

Bone accretion occurs during adolescence, when there is a large increment in bone mass. Peak bone density is normally achieved after puberty and into the third decade of life. Nevertheless, by age 22 years, most people have achieved nearly all of their peak bone mass. At menopause, an acceleration of bone loss usually occurs over approximately 5 to 8 years, with an annual 2% to 3%

loss of trabecular bone and a 1% to 2% loss of cortical bone. Both men and women lose bone with age. Over a lifetime, women lose approximately 50% of trabecular and 30% of cortical bone; men generally lose about two-thirds of these amounts.3, Osteoporosis was previously thought to be a silent disease that was part of the normal aging process. The advent of bone densitometry, however, has made it possible to accurately and reproducibly identify patients at risk for osteoporosis so that prevention and treatment strategies can be instituted to reduce the incidence of fractures.

### Pathophysiology of Menopausal and Age- Related Bone Loss

Bone is constantly undergoing remodeling, whereby areas of bone resorption produced by osteoclastic action are replaced by bone laid down by osteoblasts. Osteoporosis results from an imbalance between bone resorption and formation. The initiation of bone remodeling is still being debated; however, osteocytes, or terminally differentiated osteoblasts, located within the bone matrix and connected to one another and the bone surface may release chemical mediators that attract osteoclasts to the bone surface and initiate bone remodeling (Fig. 103.1). Osteoclasts originate from hematopoietic stem cells that differentiate into colony-forming unit granulocyte-monocytes that differentiate into osteoclasts, are attracted to the bone surface, attach to the bone matrix, and resorb bone tissue. Generally, bone resorption is rapid, and a resorption pit is formed within 10 to 14 days. After bone resorption is complete, osteoblasts, which are derived from the bone marrow mesenchymal stromal cells, attach to the resorbed bone surface and produce osteoid, which is then mineralized. Bone formation can take up to 3 or 4 months, and thus a normal bone remodeling cycle in adults can last 4 to 6 months (see Fig. 103.1A). A number of metabolic changes such as estrogen deficiency, immobilization, metabolic acidosis, hyperparathyroidism, and systemic and local inflammatory diseases can increase osteoclast number and activity, uncoupling bone turnover. This process results in greater bone resorption than bone formation and a net loss of bone tissue. New data show that a number of local factors in bone affect the regulation of bone formation and resorption and the coupling of these processes. These factors include insulin-like growth factors (IGFs), interleukins (IL-1, IL-6, and IL-11), TNF, receptor activator of nuclear factor-kB ligand (RANKL), and transforming growth factor-β. Animal studies have shown that IL-1, IL-6, and TNF knockout mice do not lose bone with estrogen deficiency. In addition, inflammatory arthritis animal models show that TNF, IL-1, and IL-6 are all strong stimulators of both osteoclast numbers, maturation, and activity. This link between the immune system and the maintenance of bone mass is intriguing, but additional work is required before we can understand its significance.

A number of mechanisms underlie primary osteoporosis, including a low peak bone mass as a young adult and rapid bone loss during menopause. Factors contributing to age-related bone loss include impaired calcium absorption with age, a compensatory rise in parathyroid hormone (PTH) levels, and greater resorption than formation of bone. Estrogen deficiency is associated with the release of cytokines including RANKL, IL-1, IL-6, and TNF, which leads to the recruitment and stimulation of osteoclasts in the bone marrow and increased production of bone-resorptive cytokines, which may contribute to menopauserelated bone loss. Estrogen therapy inhibits IL-1 release, and in oophorectomized rats and mice, an inhibitor of IL-1 (the IL-1 receptor antagonist) suppresses bone loss. IL-6 levels also increase

with age in human marrow cultures7 and in peripheral monocytes. IL-1 and TNF induce the production of IL-6 from osteoblasts and stromal cells. Further evidence supporting a role of IL-6 in bone turnover includes data showing that oophorectomized IL-6 knockout transgenic mice do not lose bone.

Two other proteins that influence osteoclast activity have been identified: osteoprotegerin (OPG) and RANKL, which are produced by osteoblasts. Estrogen deficiency increases osteoblast production of RANKL, which stimulates maturation and activity of osteoclasts by attaching to RANKL on the surface of immature and mature osteoclasts. Simultaneously, estrogen deficiency decreases osteoblast production of OPG, the decoy receptor that reduces RANKL production and activity. Adenoviral delivery of OPG ameliorates bone resorption in a mouse ovariectomy model of osteoporosis. Both pre-clinical animal models and clinical trials of women with low bone mass have been completed and demonstrate that inhibition of RANKL with an anti-RANKL monoclonal antibody prevents estrogen-deficiency bone loss.

In addition, a number of genetic, nutritional, and lifestyle risk factors predispose to the development of osteoporosis. Whites and Asians are at risk for low bone mass and osteoporosis, whereas African Americans have a higher bone density and one-third to one-half the number of fractures. 1, Some studies show that African Americans have lower vitamin D and urinary calcium levels, higher PTH levels, and more skeletal resistance to the effects of PTH on bone.10-12 Studies in twins and families show that up to 80% of the variance in bone mass is accounted for by genetic factors. Nevertheless, the contribution of individual polymorphisms of genes to the risk of osteoporosis at this time is very limited.14, Furthermore, genetically determined architectural features of bone such as a long hip axis length may contribute to increased fracture risk; conversely, a short hip axis length confers some protective effect.

Studies of families with high bone mass phenotypes have been identified, and this work was critical to understanding how the Wnt pathway activates bone formation and to the development of a novel anabolic agent, anti-sclerostin antibody, for the treatment of osteoporosis.17, Other risk factors for osteoporosis, as enumerated in Table 103.1, include low body weight and reduced gonadal steroid levels. According to some reports, lifestyle factors that may contribute to the development of osteoporosis include cigarette smoking, excessive alcohol intake, reduced physical activity, and inadequate calcium intake. Cigarette smokers have poorer health than nonsmokers, along with impaired calcium absorption, lower estrogen levels, earlier menopause, and more fractures, and they exercise less; smoking cessation reverses this risk of osteoporosis.

In a large, prospective study of 9516 women older than 65 years, the following lifestyle factors significantly increased the risk of hip fracture: no walking for exercise, intake of more than two cups of coffee daily, current use of long-acting benzodiazepines and anti-convulsant drugs, current weight less than weight at age 25 years, height greater than 5 feet 7 inches, age older than 80 years, fracture since age 50 years, inability to stand from a chair without using arms, poor depth perception, and self-evaluation of health as fair to poor. Low bone density in conjunction with a fall or trauma predisposed an individual to a fracture. Poor health and compromise of neuromuscular function increased the risk of osteoporosis and falls, which in turn increased the risk of hip fracture. Importantly, elderly white women with both a low bone mass and more than two risk factors had a nearly 20-fold increased risk for fracture.

Secondary causes of bone loss that can affect women and men of all ages and races are listed in Table 103.2. Glucocorticoid therapy is the most common secondary cause of bone loss. Osteoporotic fractures develop in an estimated 30% to 50% of patients treated with glucocorticoids. Glucocorticoid therapy causes bone loss through a number of different mechanisms such as producing a negative calcium balance through impaired intestinal calcium absorption; increasing urinary calcium excretion; decreasing bone formation; dose-dependent increasing apoptosis of osteocytes and

osteoblasts; increasing bone resorption by stimulating the maturation, activity, and lifespan of osteoclasts; and suppressing endogenous gonadal steroid production. Therapy with glucocorticoids leads to an early and, in some instances, dramatic loss of trabecular bone, with less effect on cortical bone. ### Osteoporosis in Men

Osteoporosis in men is now a major public health problem because of men's recently increased lifespan. The epidemiology of osteoporosis in men is just now being evaluated. Fracture risk occurs in adolescence and young adulthood and then increases after the age of 70 years. Long bone fractures occur more commonly in young men, whereas hip and spine fractures are more prevalent in men older than 70 years. The increase in fractures in older men is just as significant as it is in women, but it occurs about 10 years later in life, with an age-adjusted incidence of hip fractures in men of about one-third to one-half that of women. Elderly men who sustain hip fractures have a greater risk of dying within the first year or being permanently disabled compared with women. Recent data from the Study of Osteoporotic Fractures in Men determined that, after 15 years of follow-up, men of an older age (>75 years) who had low femoral neck bone mineral density (BMD), a history of a previous fracture, divorced marital status, greater height, use of tricyclic antidepressants, and a history of hyperthyroidism (Graves' disease) were independently related to an increased risk of hip fracture with low femoral neck BMD. In addition, in men with a low BMD (ranging from -1 to -2.5), the risk of hip fracture incidence increased from 4/1000 patient-years to 40.2/1000 patient-years.

### Osteoporosis in Rheumatic Diseases and Other Conditions

Individuals with systemic inflammatory diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis (RA), systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), and ankylosing spondylitis can have significant bone loss and osteoporosis. Patients with RA experience periarticular and generalized bone loss and an increased incidence of fractures compared with the general population. T lymphocytes, tissue macrophages, and synovial-like fibroblasts release inflammatory cytokines (IL-1, TNF, and IL-6) and inhibitory Wnt signaling proteins such as Dkk-1 and RANKL, which stimulate pre-osteoclasts in the bone marrow and synovium to actively resorb bone; in addition, osteoblast maturation is altered.29, In an animal model of inflammatory arthritis induced with collagen, animals pre-treated with OPG did not have bone loss within the periarticular bone or the presence of erosions.

Additional factors that might contribute to osteoporosis in patients with rheumatic diseases include decreased mobility, glucocorticoid therapy, and systemic inflammation. Some data, however, show that low-dose glucocorticoid therapy in women with RA does not have adverse skeletal effects, possibly because of a decrease in disease activity in association with the suppression of inflammatory cytokines and improved physical activity and function.33, Ankylosing spondylitis is also associated with fractures and reduced bone density in the spine and proximal femur, even early in the disease. Patients with SLE have a high rate of osteoporotic fractures in the presence of low to normal bone mass, suggesting that systemic inflammation alters bone turnover. Increased serum levels of TNF can reduce osteoblast maturation and increase osteoclast maturation and activity; in addition, other inflammatory factors such as oxidized low-density lipoproteins (LDLs) and inflammatory high-density lipoproteins (HDLs) can direct mesenchymal stem cells to differentiate into adipocytes instead of osteoblasts and impair bone mass. Infiltrative processes in the marrow such as multiple myeloma, mastocytosis, and Gaucher's disease may produce osteoporosis. Patients with Gaucher's disease show an accumulation of glucocerebrosides in macrophages in the spleen, liver, and bone marrow, which causes hepatosplenomegaly, anemia, thrombocytopenia, bone infarcts and infections, fractures, and osteonecrosis.

The immunosuppressant drug cyclophosphamide (Cytoxan) induces amenorrhea and hypogonadism, which may increase the risk ofbone loss. Women who undergo premature menopause from cyclophosphamide therapy can have estrogen-deficiency bone loss in their 30s. Young women with SLE who try to preserve ovarian function while undergoing cyclophosphamide therapy by taking gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonists may also experience estrogen-deficiency bone loss. In rodent models, the immunosuppressive drug cyclosporine produces a timeand dose-dependent bone loss38; in contrast, azathioprine (Imuran), rapamycin (Sirolimus), leflunomide (Arava), and low doses of methotrexate do not appear to adversely affect skeletal homeostasis. Therapy with both cyclosporine or tracolimus and/or prednisone in transplant recipients is associated with early accelerated bone loss after the initiation of treatment and the development of osteoporosis and fractures with continued exposure.

Vitamin D deficiency may also manifest as osteopenia and fractures, but this condition is both preventable and treatable. Vitamin D insufficiency is common in older patients and in people with SLE who do not get an adequate amount of sunlight or who use potent sunscreens. Also, patients with malabsorption syndromes and liver disease can have vitamin D deficiencies. Unlike the situation in osteoporosis, very low vitamin D levels are often characterized by a mineralization defect and osteomalacia. Vitamin D deficiency is present in up to 50% of women with hip fractures.

### Assessment of Bone Density and Osteoporotic Risk

Osteoporosis may first be diagnosed when a radiograph shows signs of demineralization or a spinal film shows evidence of compression fractures of vertebral bodies. Because an estimated 25% to 50% of bone mass must be lost to show osteopenia on radiographs, conventional radiography is an insensitive technique for diagnosing bone loss. Radiographs may demonstrate signs of secondary causes of osteoporosis such as the presence of subperiosteal resorption in people with hyperparathyroidism, characteristic lytic changes or bone infarcts in people with Gaucher's disease, local sites of lytic destruction in people with malignancy, and pseudofractures in people with osteomalacia. Bone densitometry makes it possible to measure the amount of bone in the relevant fracture sites of the spine, forearm, and proximal femur.

Techniques for evaluating bone mass include dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry (DEXA) and quantitative computed tomography (CT) scanning of the spine.1, Bone density evaluations using DEXA incorporate the attenuation of soft tissue and bone by radiographs to calculate the BMD. DEXA is both precise and safe, with a low degree of radiation exposure. With reproducibility errors of approximately 0.6% to 1.5%, this technique can detect small changes over time.2, Furthermore, newer DEXA techniques measure bone density rapidly, in 0.5 to 2.5 minutes. Quantitative CT (QCT) scanning allows for the direct measurement of trabecular bone in the central region of the spine, but the procedure entails a comparatively high radiation exposure, and time and precision errors are usually higher than those associated with DEXA. Recently QCT scans obtained for other reasons can be sent to an outside resource and analyzed for BMD and estimated bone strength. The correlation with DEXA measurements of BMD are greater than 95%, and this may be useful for some patients.

An inverse relationship exists between bone density and the gradient of risk for fracture.44, Prospective studies show that bone densitometry identifies patients with an increased gradient of risk for fracture. In 8134 women, a 1 standard deviation (SD) reduction in the bone density of the spine and the femoral neck compared with age-adjusted control subjects was associated with a 1.6and 2.6-fold increased risk of hip fracture, respectively. Measurement of bone density in the hip is more predictive of hip fracture than is measurement at another site. Studies show that in women older than 65 years, hip bone density is predictive of spine and hip fracture and that conventional spine

density does not add to the diagnostic utility of a single hip bone density test in assessing the risk of fracture.

FRAX also provides a 10-year risk of a hip fracture or a major osteoporotic fracture (i.e., hip, proximal humerus, and wrist). Lastly, the FRAX score is most accurate when used in untreated patients, and thus results should not be used to assess fracture risk for patients who are already receiving pharmacologic therapy.

### Markers of Bone Turnover

The development of sensitive biochemical markers of bone turnover makes it possible to analyze changes in bone formation and resorption at a given point in time and obtain additional information about a patient's risk of bone loss. Only three bone formation markers are currently available. Osteocalcin, a noncollagenous matrix protein in bone, is produced exclusively by osteoblasts; it correlates with histomorphometric bone measurements. In most conditions, bone resorption and formation are tightly coupled, and osteocalcin levels reflect bone turnover. The other markers of bone formation are bone-specific alkaline phosphatase (BSAP), an enzyme that is activated as osteoblasts mature, and amino-terminal propeptide of type I procollagen (PINP), a protein whose synthesis is high in maturing osteoblasts.48,

Sensitive indicators of bone resorption derived from the degradation of mature collagen include the urine and serum markers of type I collagen cross-links, including amino-terminal telopeptide of type I collagen (N telopeptides, or NTX) or carboxy-terminal telopeptide of type I collagen (C telopeptides, or CTX). In clinical practice today, however, only serum CTX-1 is widely used for an assessment of bone resorption, and this biomarker increases with estrogen deficiency at menopause and is high in patients with a variety of disorders characterized by accelerated bone turnover, including Paget's disease, osteoporosis, and RA.50-52 In clinical studies, anti-resorptive agents such as estrogen, bisphosphonates, and inhibitor of RANKL induce a significant decrease (30% to 80%) first in markers of resorption and then in bone formation markers, often within 3 to 6 months. Resorption markers decrease before formation markers and correlate with either maintenance of or an increase in BMD. A significant change in bone markers can be observed within a few months of anti-resorptive therapy, before changes in BMD occur.53, Both bone formation and resorption marker changes over 6 to 12 months have been found to predict future fracture risk. In a study of alendronate to reduce osteoporotic fractures, patients who had more than a 30% reduction in bone alkaline phosphatase had the greatest reduction in risk for new vertebral and nonvertebral fractures. Interestingly, studies have found that reductions in markers of bone turnover, either resorption or formation markers, are associated with a reduction in fracture risk.53, Nevertheless, long-term, prospective studies

of large numbers of women are necessary to determine whether selective biochemical markers of bone turnover can predict changes in BMD or fracture risk and whether these tests should be used in standard clinical practice.

Most bone turnover marker data are derived from large studies of anti-resorptive agents, but a bone-building anabolic agent, PTH, has been approved for the treatment of post-menopausal osteoporosis, osteoporosis in men, and glucocorticoid-induced bone loss. PTH stimulates osteoblast activity, and therefore PINP, osteocalcin, and other markers of bone formation increase rapidly, within a few weeks of the initiation of treatment. Activation of osteoblasts over time, however, results in RANKL production, which stimulates osteoclast activity. With continued PTH treatment, markers of osteoclast activity also increase, reaching levels equal to those of formation markers by 6 months of treatment. Because the overall result is an increase in bone mass, the bone turnover markers during PTH therapy reflect significant bone remodeling on both trabecular and cortical bone surfaces and within the cortex. A few small studies have found that increases in both bone formation and resorption markers predict an increase in bone mass with PTH treatment.55-57

### Evaluation for Secondary Bone Loss

The workup for osteoporosis is directed toward excluding secondary causes of bone loss and includes a determination of serum calcium, phosphorus, supersensitive thyroid-stimulating hormone, 25-hydroxyvitamin D (25-OHD), and intact PTH, as well as urine calcium and creatinine levels. Also, a complete blood cell count, alkaline phosphatase and liver function tests, erythrocyte sedimentation rate (in some cases), and serum and urine protein electrophoresis for patients older than 50 years may be necessary (Table 103.4). In men, additional testing for secondary causes of osteoporosis includes serum testosterone and luteinizing hormone.

Further tests to rule out neoplastic or endocrinologic disorders and a bone biopsy (a decalcified bone specimen is obtained after a double tetracycline label with two different fluorescent labels) should be considered in certain patients with progressive bone loss and in those in whom osteoporosis is unlikely. Identification and appropriate therapy for underlying secondary causes of osteoporosis are important. For example, treatment of vitamin D deficiency

Parathyroidectomy in patients with hyperparathyroidism characterized by hypercalcemia, hypercalciuria, nephrolithiasis, age younger than 50 years, or low cortical BMD (Z-score ≤2) was associated with a large (4% to 12.8%) increase in bone density over 4 years. However, bone density was stable for up to 6 years in patients with mild hyperparathyroidism. In addition, treatment of hyperthyroidism, hypercortisolism, and a variety of other disorders that may cause osteoporosis can produce increments in bone mass. Reduction in the systemic inflammation associated with rheumatic diseases such as TNF-blocking agents for RA or ankylosing spondylitis or glucocorticoid-sparing agents for SLE (e.g., azathioprine and mycophenolate mofetil) can also produce increments in bone mass.

### Treatment

### Calcium

The goals of therapy for osteoporosis are to reduce bone resorption and enhance bone formation, if possible. Bone loss occurs when the calcium intake and absorption are insufficient to balance the daily calcium losses. Prospective data show that calcium stabilizes bone mass.

Table 103.5 shows the current recommendations for optimal calcium intake for women and men from the 1997 report of the Institute of Medicine to the National Academy of Sciences. In the absence of kidney stones or an underlying disorder of calcium metabolism, these calcium intakes are safe. To prevent negative calcium balance, pre-menopausal women and men require 1000 mg and post-menopausal women and elderly men require 1200 mg of total elemental calcium daily. Children have increasing calcium requirements during adolescence, and data show increased

bone accretion with increased calcium intake in pre-pubescent and pubertal children. Calcium carbonate contains 40% elemental calcium and should be taken with meals because of poor absorption in achlorhydric patients in the absence of food. Calcium citrate, which contains 24% elemental calcium, has better bioavailability and is more readily absorbed. It is also absorbed well on an empty stomach in patients with achlorhydria. Recent studies underscore the fact that only recommended daily allowances of calcium and vitamin D are useful for bone health in post-menopausal women and elderly men. Additional supplementation over the recommended daily allowance has resulted in reports of increased cardiovascular disease.64-66

### Estrogen

Hormone replacement therapy (HRT) was once the mainstay of treatment in osteoporosis because estrogen inhibits bone resorption, produces a small rise in bone density, and reduces the risk of fracture by approximately 50% in retrospective observational studies. However, in 1998, data from the 4-year Heart and Estrogen/Progestin Replacement Study were published. In this study, post-menopausal women with a previous history of heart disease were randomized to receive estrogen (0.625 mg) plus progestin (2.5 mg) or placebo alone. Results showed no reduction in the overall rate of coronary heart disease or cardiac events in the treatment group; in fact, an early increase in risk for cardiac events was noted, possibly related to increased coagulability.

In addition, a large, multicenter, longitudinal study by the Women's Health Initiative (WHI)—in which 162,000 women aged 50 to 79 years were randomized into a placebo group, an HRT group (if the uterus was intact), or an estrogen-only group (if the uterus was absent)—was terminated early because of an increased risk of breast cancer and cardiovascular events. The research goals for the WHI study were to determine the effects of HRT, diet modification, and calcium and vitamin D supplements on heart disease, osteoporosis, and colorectal cancer risk. After a mean follow-up of 5.3 years in an 8.5-year study, the HRT group had an increased risk of seven more cardiac events per 10,000 women taking the drug for a year, eight more invasive breast cancers, eight more strokes, and eight more pulmonary emboli, but six fewer colorectal cancers and five fewer hip fractures.

At this time, the general recommendation is that HRT should be used only for vasomotor symptoms that occur at the time of menopause. When these symptoms abate, it is recommended that estrogen replacement (consisting of combined estrogen and progestin for women with an intact uterus) be stopped because the perceived cardiovascular benefits have not been substantiated and the cardiovascular disease and breast cancer risk make the benefit-to-risk ratio unacceptable for most women. It is important to acknowledge that the estrogen-only arm of the WHI study in women without a uterus did not show an increased risk of heart disease or breast cancer.

If a woman and her physician decide that she is going to take HRT or estrogen alone for vasomotor symptoms, in women with an increased risk of coagulation, transdermal estrogen replacement should be used.

### Selective Estrogen Receptor Modulators

The ideal estrogen replacement therapy would confer the beneficial effects of estrogen on bone and cardiovascular disease without increasing the risk of breast or uterine cancer. Selective estrogen receptor modulators (SERMs) are a nonsteroidal class of drugs

that bind to the estrogen receptor and differ from one another in their actions on estrogen-responsive tissues, acting selectively as agonists or antagonists. There are two SERMs used in clinical medicine today, tamoxifen and raloxifene. While tamoxifen was the first available SERM, studies of tamoxifen therapy in women with breast cancer produced a small increase in bone density of the spine over 2 years and reductions in both LDL and total cholesterol. In addition, a larger trial, the Breast Cancer Prevention Trial, studied 13,388 women at increased risk for breast cancer, comparing treatment with tamoxifen (20 mg daily) to placebo for 5 years. It found that tamoxifen reduced the risk of invasive and noninvasive breast cancer by 50%, and a decreased risk of fracture was observed as well: 45% reduction at the hip and 29% at the spine. An increased incidence of low-grade endometrial cancer was noted, but no change occurred in the risk of ischemic heart disease.

Raloxifene,72 which has been approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for the prevention and treatment of osteoporosis, is a SERM that acts as an estrogen agonist on bone, with antagonist effects on the breast and uterus. Raloxifene (60 mg/day over a 2-year study period) increased BMD in the lumbar spine by 2.4%, in the total hip by 2.4%, and in the total body by 2%, with a reduction in vertebral fracture risk at 2 years similar to that seen with estrogen or alendronate (5 mg) treatment. During the 2-year study period, raloxifene reduced the incidence of vertebral fractures by nearly 40% in the treated group compared with the placebo group, and fractures recurred in 7.6% of treated women with a previous fracture, compared with 14.3% of those in the placebo group. Endometrial thickness is not increased by raloxifene, but menopausal symptoms may be made worse. Raloxifene decreases LDL cholesterol by 12%, with a nonsignificant increase in HDL cholesterol, but it does not reduce C-reactive protein like estrogen does and was not found to provide cardiovascular protection.75-78 Raloxifene also decreased the incidence of breast cancer by 76% in patients enrolled in a clinical study of osteoporosis, with breast cancer incidence studied as a secondary endpoint. Another study compared tamoxifen and raloxifene, and yet another study evaluated raloxifene versus placebo, in the prevention of breast cancer. The first study reported that both tamoxifen and raloxifene reduced the risk of developing breast cancer, and the second study found that raloxifene reduced the risk of estrogen receptor—positive breast cancer compared with placebo in post-menopausal women.79, At this time, little information is available on the use of raloxifene in men, and thus it is not recommended for male patients.

### Testosterone

Men with osteoporosis, hypogonadism, and symptoms of low libido may benefit from testosterone replacement therapy. This therapy can be administered as testosterone cypionate or enanthate (50 to 400 mg intramuscularly every 2 to 4 weeks) or as a transdermal testosterone replacement patch that is applied to the scrotal area (Testoderm, 4 to 6 mg/day) or elsewhere (Androderm, 2.5 or 5 mg/day).81, Most studies find that bone mass increases with testosterone replacement when levels of testosterone were low at the initiation of therapy.

### Calcitonin

Calcitonin, a 32 amino acid peptide synthesized by the C cells of the thyroid gland, is a potent inhibitor of osteoclast-mediated bone

resorption. Although human and salmon calcitonin are commercially available, salmon calcitonin is most commonly used because of its greater potency. On the basis of data showing an increase in total body calcium, parenteral calcitonin was approved by the FDA for the treatment of osteoporosis in 1984, and calcitonin in a nasal spray was approved for the treatment of post-menopausal osteoporosis in 1995. Parenteral calcitonin (100 international units [IU] administered subcutaneously or intramuscularly three times a week or daily) can maintain bone density or produce a small increase in bone mass in the spine and, in some instances, the forearm, particularly in patients with a high bone turnover. Nasal spray calcitonin is absorbed through the nasal mucosa and is approximately 40% as potent as the parenterally administered drug (e.g., 50 to 100 IU of injectable calcitonin is comparable with 200 IU of nasal spray calcitonin). In osteoporotic women more than 5 years past menopause, nasal calcitonin (200 IU/day) increases spinal bone density by 2% to 3% compared with placebo, with no effect on proximal femur bone mass; higher doses are necessary in the early menopausal period.84, Nasal spray calcitonin therapy in patients with osteoporosis is associated with a 36% reduction in vertebral fractures over 5 years.

The adverse effects of parenteral calcitonin include nausea, flushing, and local irritation at the injection site. Calcitonin given intranasally is well tolerated, with the potential adverse effects of rhinitis and nasal symptoms such as dryness and crusting. Patients treated with parenteral or intranasal calcitonin may also obtain a beneficial analgesic response in the presence of osteoporotic fractures. Recently calcitonin nasal spray was removed from use in Europe because of a concern that it may increase the risk of prostate cancer in men, but at this time it is still on formularies in the United States.

### Vitamin D

Physiologic doses of vitamin D are important to ensure normal bone mineralization. People 50 years and older should take at least 600 to 1000 IU of vitamin D daily as a multivitamin or combined with a calcium supplement. Hypovitaminosis D is common in the elderly population, with one study demonstrating that 57% of patients in a general medical ward were deficient in vitamin D. Low vitamin D levels increase the risk of bone loss and fracture. Investigators41 found that 50% of patients admitted with acute femur fractures had vitamin D deficiency (25-OHD level <12 ng/ mL), and 36.7% had secondary hyperparathyroidism. Data show seasonal variations in vitamin D levels; low 25-OHD levels during the winter and spring are associated with decreases in bone density. The importance of vitamin D to skeletal health was shown when elderly women in a nursing home who were treated with only 800 IU/day of vitamin D had a 40% reduction in incident hip fractures over 18 months compared with placebo-controlled subjects. Although this dramatic effect on fractures in an elderly population may represent a correction of vitamin D insufficiency, this study underscores that adequate vitamin D replacement can effectively diminish fractures in older people. Insufficient calcium and low 25-OHD levels are common in ambulatory patients and should be identified and treated before anti-resorptive or other therapies for osteoporosis are initiated.

Therefore to maintain skeletal health, patients require a vitamin D intake that results in a serum 25-OHD level of at least 30 to 50 ng/mL and most patients will need 25-hydroxyvitamin D3 replacement of 1000 to 2000 IU per day. Replacement with 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (1,25[OH]2D) is not recommended

because hypercalcemia and hypercalciuria are common and require regular and costly monitoring.

### Anti-resorptive Drugs

### Bisphosphonates

Bisphosphonates are analogues of pyrophosphate, with a P-C-P rather than a P-O-P core; they are absorbed by the hydroxyapatite of bone and suppress bone resorption. Modification of the side chains can result in the development of a variety of compounds with differing abilities to inhibit bone resorption (Table 103.6). Some bisphosphonates are administered intermittently because of a long skeletal half-life and prolonged retention in bone. These compounds must be taken on an empty stomach because GI absorption is less than 10%.

Bisphosphonates have been used for the treatment of patients with Paget's disease of bone, hypercalcemia of malignancy, prevention and treatment of metastatic cancer to bone, and osteoporosis and for the prevention and treatment of glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis.

Alendronate has been approved by the FDA for the prevention and treatment of osteoporosis. Data in post-menopausal women with bone density at least 2.5 SD below peak bone mass show that alendronate (10 mg/day) compared with placebo produces an 8.8% and 7.8% increase in bone density in the spine and femoral trochanter, respectively, and a 5.9% increase in the femoral neck after 3 years of therapy88; smaller rises (2.3% to 4.4%) occur in bone density in the spine and proximal femur in women within 0.5 to 3 years of menopause. Fosamax treatment in women with osteoporosis (T-score <2.5) yields a significant reduction in spine and hip fractures compared with the patients treated with placebo. Alendronate did not reduce the incidence of clinical fractures in women who had low bone mass but not osteoporosis. .90, Alendronate treatment is also effective in increasing bone mass in the spine, hip, and total body and helps prevent vertebral fractures and loss of height in men with osteoporosis.

Adverse effects of bisphosphonates include GI symptoms such as stomach pain and esophagitis (caution is advised in patients

with active symptoms or a history of ulcer disease), myalgias and arthralgias, and, rarely, osteonecrosis of the jaw, along with subtrochanteric fractures with long-term use.93-97 A once-a-week preparation of alendronate (70 mg) is the most commonly used dose for the treatment of osteoporosis. This preparation increased spinal and hip bone mass similarly to alendronate, 10 mg/day, over a 2-year study period.

Risedronate, another oral bisphosphonate, administered at a dose of 5 mg/day, increased bone mass and reduced the risk of new vertebral fractures 50% better than did placebo.95-98 Another study performed to assess the effect of risedronate on hip fractures found that women with osteoporosis (defined by a femoral neck T-score of ≤-4.0) had a significant reduction in the risk of hip fracture. Risedronate has been approved for the prevention and treatment of osteoporosis (35 mg once a week and now 150 mg once a month)92 and for the treatment of Paget's disease (30 mg/day for 2 months, with retreatment if relapse occurs after 2 months). 99, Studies show that risedronate may be well tolerated even in patients with mild GI symptoms. Bisphosphonates may also reduce bone pain.

Ibandronate, another aminobisphosphonate, is approved for the treatment and prevention of post-menopausal osteoporosis. In phase III studies of ibandronate (2.5 mg/day) versus placebo in post-menopausal women with osteoporosis, incident vertebral fractures were reduced about 50%. Another study compared ibandronate, 150 mg once a month, with the daily 2.5-mg dose and found similar gains in lumbar spine and hip BMD. The FDA approved ibandronate, 150 mg/month, for the treatment of osteoporosis on the basis of this bridging study. Recently, intravenous (IV) ibandronate in a dose of 3 mg every 3 months was found to be similar to ibandronate, 2.5 mg/day, in terms of increasing lumbar spine and hip BMD. No data on hip fractures are available for this compound.

Zoledronic acid is approved for the treatment and prevention of post-menopausal osteoporosis. In phase III studies in post-menopausal women with osteoporosis treated with zoledronic acid, 5 mg once a year by IV infusion, the risk of incident vertebral fractures, hip fractures, and other major osteoporotic fractures were reduced by 68%, 40%, and 20%, respectively, compared with the placebo-treated subjects. In another phase III study of patients who had sustained a hip fracture, patients were randomized to either zoledronic acid, 5 mg once a year, or placebo, and after 3 years it was found that the incidence of osteoporotic fractures was significantly less in patients treated with zoledronic acid and that the mortality was lowered compared with the patients treated with placebo. Adverse effects of zoledronic acid include arthralgias and myalgias; however, these adverse events tend to be less frequent with subsequent infusions. In patients undergoing treatment with zoledronic acid, both serum calcium and 25-OHD levels should be monitored and deficiencies should be restored to normal levels before treatment. Zoledronic acid has been approved for the treatment and prevention of post-menopausal osteoporosis (5 mg once a year), osteoporosis in men (5 mg once a year), prevention and treatment of glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis (5 mg once a year), and Paget's disease. Zoledronic acid at a dose of 4 mg intravenously every 4 weeks is currently approved for the prevention and treatment of bone metastases in patients with breast cancer and multiple myeloma.

### RANK Ligand Inhibitor

Denosumab is a monoclonal antibody that is directed against RANKL and approved for the treatment of post-menopausal osteoporosis. In phase III studies in post-menopausal women with osteoporosis who were treated with denosumab (60 mg subcutaneously every 6 months) for 36 months or 3 years, the incidence of vertebral fractures, hip fractures, and major osteoporotic fractures was reduced by 68%, 40%, and 20%, respectively. The medication is well tolerated, but adverse events of skin infection requiring hospitalization were higher in subjects treated with denosumab than in those treated with placebo. Denosumab is a potent inhibitor of bone resorption with significant suppression of CTX-1, a marker of osteoclast activity.

CTX-1 is suppressed by nearly 90% a few weeks after each injection; however, the suppression of bone turnover is transient, and bone turnover and bone density return to baseline levels rapidly if the injections of denosumab are discontinued. Post-menopausal women with low bone mass who were treated with alendronate, 70 mg once a week, and then switched to denosumab, 60 mg every 6 months, had a significant gain of BMD compared with subjects who continued to take alendronate. Before treatment with denosumab, serum calcium and 25-OHD should be checked and replaced, if needed, to achieve normal levels.

### Adverse Events Associated With Potent Anti-resorptive Agents

All potent anti-resorptive agents (bisphosphonates and RANKL inhibitors) have been associated with osteonecrosis of the jaw, a rare disorder in which a small part of the jawbone dies; this occurrence is associated with exposure of the bone, with loss of the mucosal covering. Although osteonecrosis of the jaw is an adverse effect of all bisphosphonates and of the RANKL inhibitor denosumab, the incidence is rare (probably between 1/10,000 and 1/100,000 in people receiving osteoporosis medication doses); it is more common in patients with cancer who are treated with high doses and with a high frequency. Although the mechanism is still unclear, the American Dental Association recommends that the teeth be examined before the bisphosphonate or other anti-resorptive treatment is initiated and that those taking these medications should avoid dental procedures, if possible, but it is not necessary to stop the treatment if procedures are needed. In addition, the American Dental Association prefers to use the term anti-resorptive-associated osteonecrosis of the jaw.93,

Potent anti-resorptive agents (i.e., bisphosphonates and RANKL inhibitors) are also associated with atypical subtrochanteric fractures. These fractures are somewhat unusual in that

they occur below the lesser trochanter in the femur, the incidence is probably about 5 cases per 10,000 patient-years, they can be bilateral, and they may be related to the duration of the bisphosphonate treatment. At this time, if a patient treated with a potent anti-resorptive agent experiences midthigh pain, evaluation for a stress fracture should be performed because it appears that these fractures first appear as painful stress fractures that eventually evolve to a displaced fracture. The risk of a subtrochanteric fracture moves to nearly zero with discontinuation of the potent antiresorptive agents. 108,

The development of subtrochanteric fractures in patients taking potent anti-resorptive agents has led the FDA to make a recommendation regarding the duration of treatment of osteoporosis with these agents. The FDA rationalized that the registration trials for the bisphosphonates (alendronate, risedronate, and zoledronic acid) were 3 to 4 years in duration and that the extension trials for alendronate (FLEX), zoledronate acid (Horizon), and risedronate (VERT-MN) ranged from 3 to 10 years in length, and therefore sufficient long-term data existed from patients who were taking the drugs and had stopped taking them to determine the optimal duration of bisphosphonate use for the treatment of osteoporosis. The results of the three extension studies found consistent fracture rates and maintenance of BMD in both active and placebo groups. Based on these data, the FDA recommended that the decisions regarding the discontinuation of bisphosphonates should be based on the individual patient. Younger patients with a normal BMD (T-score of the hip greater than -2.5) after 3 to 5 years of bisphosphonate therapy may be candidates to stop treatment. Meanwhile, patients with an increased risk of fracture (e.g., patients of an older age, with prevalent fractures, high risk of falling, significant loss of height, or with BMD in the osteoporotic range [less than -2.0]) may benefit from continued bisphospho- 110-113 An additional analysis by FLEX investigators that nate use. evaluated the risk of fracture in subjects treated with alendronate, 10 mg a day for about 9 years, compared with alendronate for 4.5 years and then placebo for 5 years, concluded that subjects with a femoral neck BMD of greater than -2 were unlikely to benefit from additional treatment with a bisphosphonate after 4 years. Subjects with a femoral neck BMD of less than -2 with fractures or less than -2.5 without fractures, however, may benefit from continued bisphosphonate treatment. Currently, recommendations from most musculoskeletal societies recommend treatment with oral bisphosphonates for up to 5 years and IV bisphosphonate for 3 years and then to reevaluate BMD and fracture risk and, if the BMD is above -2.5 and the risk of fracture is low, then to allow the patients a drug holiday and to monitor BMD and bone turnover markers as appropriate to determine the length of the drug holiday.

### Parathyroid Hormone

Beginning in the 1980s, small, randomized studies determined that the 1-34 fragment of the PTH protein can significantly increase bone mass in the spine, with small losses or no gain at the skeletal sites rich in cortical bone.115, In 2001 a recombinant human PTH (rhythm) composed of the 34 amino acids from the amino-terminal end of the hormone, known as Forteo, was approved for the treatment of post-menopausal osteoporosis. In a large international, multicenter study, osteoporotic women who had sustained a fracture were randomized to receive rhPTH at a dose of 20 µg/day or 40 µg/day or placebo for an average of 21 months. Lumbar spine bone mass increased between 9% and 13%

in the subjects treated with rhPTH compared with the subjects treated with placebo; hip bone mass also increased slightly. Most importantly, the risk of new vertebral fractures was reduced nearly 70% in both sets of subjects treated with rhPTH, and nonvertebral low-trauma fractures were reduced nearly 50% compared with the subjects treated with placebo. Initially this study was supposed to continue for 3 years; however, it was stopped at approximately 21 months because of pre-clinical evidence of malignant bone tumors in animal models. Additional studies of osteoporosis in men treated with rhPTH 1-34 have reported significant gains in bone mass. Forteo is given as a daily injection. People using this medication may experience headache, nausea, and flushing with initiation of treatment, but these adverse effects generally become less severe after a few weeks.

A number of recent studies have evaluated whether rhPTH 1-34 or rhPTH 1-84 is more effective in combination with an anti-resorptive agent (either bisphosphonates or raloxifene) than rhPTH alone in increasing BMD and reducing fractures. 118, Interestingly, two studies found that the combination of PTH and alendronate was less effective in stimulating bone gain at the lumbar spine in both osteopenic women and men over 1 to 1.5 118, Nevertheless, in a recent study of post-menopausal years. women with osteoporosis who were treated with PTH alone, denosumab alone, or a combination of PTH and denosumab for 1 year, it was found that the combination treatment increased lumbar spine BMD by 9.1% and total hip BMD by 4.9%, which was significantly greater than either treatment alone. Continued treatments for an additional 12 months with PTH and denosumab further increased lumbar spine BMD to 12% and total hip BMD to 6%, and with 1 year of additional denosumab, bone mass at both the lumbar spine and total hip remained stable. 120

PTH stimulates new bone formation, increases bone mass, and reduces new vertebral and nonvertebral fractures, but when the medication is discontinued, the bone gained is rapidly lost. Investigators . performed a study in which patients were given PTH for 1 year, followed by 1 year of alendronate treatment. Interestingly, the BMD gain after 1 year of PTH was about 6%; when followed by alendronate, nearly an additional 6% BMD was gained at the spine. These data suggest that although PTH is an effective monotherapy for increasing bone mass, especially in the spine, the gain in BMD should be maintained with a potent anti-resorptive agent for a number of years.

### Abaloparatide

Abaloparatide is a synthetic agonist of the PTH type I receptor that was approved a few years ago for the treatment of postmenopausal women with osteoporosis and a high risk of fracture. Abaloparatide is a synthetic 34 amino acid peptide and an analogue of PTHrP 1-34 that shares about 76% homology and 41% homology with PTH (1-34). Although both abaloparatide and teriparatide bind to the same PTH type 1 receptor, abaloparatide appears to bind more efficiently to the RG over the RO conformation of the PTH receptor, and this may lead to a more transient effect of PTHrP and favorable anabolic action. Studies comparing biochemical markers of bone turnover with abaloparatide show less remodeling than with teriparatide.

Clinical studies with abaloparatide were performed in 2463 post-menopausal women with osteoporosis, 63% of whom had a history of fracture. Study subjects were randomized to either abaloparatide or teriparatide or placebo and the primary endpoint was the percentage of patients with new vertebral fractures, which occurred in 0.6% of patients taking abaloparatide and in

4.2% of subjects that received the placebo, making a 86% relative risk reduction in incident vertebral fractures and 43% relative risk reduction in nonvertebral fractures for abaloparatide. Abaloparatide had a greater increase in BMD at the lumbar spine, hip, and distal forearm than teriparatide; however, there was not a statistically significant difference in incident fractures at the vertebral and nonvertebral fractures between the two medications. Interestingly, there was a greater reduction in major osteoporotic fracture, defined as fractures of the wrist, upper arm, hip, and clinical fractures of the spine, in the abaloparatide compared with the teriparatide-treated subjects. Study subjects in the main study were eligible to enter an open extension trial after 18 months, and all were treated with alendronate 70 mg once a week for 24 months starting 1 month after completing the parent study. In this open extension trial, after 6 months, vertebral and nonvertebral fracture rates were significantly lower among patients previously treated with abaloparatide.

Adverse effects happen a bit more frequently with abaloparatide than the placebo group and included injection site reactions, dizziness, nausea, headache, palpitations, tachycardia, orthostatic hypotension, hypercalcemia, hypercalciuria, and increased serum uric acid levels.

### Romosozumab

Romosozumab is a monoclonal antibody that inhibits the Wnt signaling antagonist sclerostin and is currently in clinical development for the treatment of osteoporosis. Sclerostin is produced mainly by osteocytes within the bone and then is transported through the osteocyte canalicular network to the bone surface and inhibits both osteoblast and activates osteoclast maturation. Treatment with romosozumab in pre-clinical studies of estrogendeficient bone loss found restoration of bone mass to the baseline levels. A recent phase II clinical trial reported that in postmenopausal women with low bone mass, a monthly treatment with romosozumab for 12 months increased lumbar spine bone mass by 12%, femoral neck bone mass by 4%, and total hip bone mass by 4%; this increase was significantly greater than with treatment with either rhPTH (1-34) or alendronate.

Interestingly, the administration of romosozumab causes a rapid increase in PINP followed by a reduction in carboxy terminal collagen crosslinks (CTX). Two phase III clinical trials assessed the anti-fracture efficacy of romosozumab. The first trial was performed in post-menopausal women with osteoporosis defined by a T-score between. -2.5 and -3.5 at the total hip or femoral neck and compared romosozumab 210 mg once a month given subcutaneously with placebo for 12 months; both treatment groups were then treated for the next 12 months with denosumab 60 mg every 6 months. After the first 12 months, treatment with romosozumab decreased incident vertebral fractures and clinical fractures by 73% and 36%, respectively. At the 24-month point, which included 12 months of romosozumab and 12 months of denosumab, there was a significant reduction of 75% in incident vertebral fractures; however, there was not a significant reduction in nonvertebral fractures. Treatment with romosozumab significantly increased BMD at the lumbar spine, hip, and femoral neck. A second phase III study was performed in post-menopausal women with osteoporosis. Study subjects were randomized to romosozumab 210 mg monthly administered subcutaneously for 12 months or alendronate 70 mg weekly for 12 months, and then both study groups received open-label alendronate 70 mg weekly for 12 months. At the 24-month point, treatment with romosozumab followed by alendronate resulted in

a 48% reduction in incident vertebral fractures and a 19% reduction in nonvertebral fractures. In addition, the gains in BMD of the lumbar spine and hip were significantly greater in the romosozumab group followed by the alendronate group compared with the alendronate alone. There were very few adverse events reported with romosozumab treatment; however, an increased incidence of major cardiovascular events occurred in the romosozumab group compared with the alendronate treated group after 6 months, and this led to a black box warning by the FDA that patients within 12 months of a major cardiac event were not to be treated with romosozumab. 128,129

### Preventive Measures

Because bone loss is not completely reversible with existing therapies, prevention is essential for optimizing skeletal health. Strategies directed at increasing peak bone mass, reducing risk factors for bone loss (e.g., hypogonadism, decreased body fat, cigarette smoking, inactivity, and excessive alcohol intake), and reversing the secondary causes of osteoporosis may prevent bone loss. Patients should be advised to consume adequate vitamin D and calcium and participate in a regular weight-bearing exercise program. Weight-bearing exercise increases muscle strength and may stabilize or modestly increase bone density. Emerging data show that increased calcium intake and exercise can add to bone accretion during adolescence and that interventions such as vitamin D and calcium supplementation can reduce fractures in older patients. Thus it is highly recommended that preventive strategies or therapies be instituted at any age to diminish the risk of fractures, which rises exponentially with age.

### Glucocorticoid-Induced Osteoporosis

Bone loss is a common sequela of therapy with glucocorticoids, 130 and glucocorticoid use increases the risk of fractures in patients with rheumatic diseases. The severity of the bone loss in patients treated with glucocorticoids varies, with an approximately 3% to 20% decrease in bone density over 1 to 2 years. Glucocorticoid therapy is associated with increased fractures of the ribs and vertebrae, sites that contain predominantly trabecular bone, and it triples the risk of hip fracture in one-third of patients after 5 to 10 years of treatment.131, In adults, alternate-day glucocorticoid therapy does not prevent bone loss. In patients with rheumatic diseases, concerns over the development of glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis often limit the dose and duration of glucocorticoid therapy.

The lowest possible glucocorticoid dose should be used, along with general preventive strategies such as a regular weight-bearing exercise program, adequate calcium and vitamin D intake, and reduction of other risk factors that might contribute to the development of osteoporosis. Nevertheless, data show that even patients taking 5 mg/day of prednisone have accelerated bone loss compared with control subjects. General prophylactic measures to prevent glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis are shown in Table 103.7. Intestinal calcium absorption is impaired in patients treated with glucocorticoids, and early studies showed that this impairment could be offset with vitamin D (40 to 100 µg/day two to three times a week) or 25-OHD, which produced an increase in bone density of the forearm. The administration of supraphysiologic doses of vitamin D, however, requires careful monitoring of the serum and urinary calcium concentrations in patients at high risk for bone loss (with a normal urinary calcium level and no history of nephrolithiasis).
