Because of the enhanced bone resorption in patients treated with glucocorticoids, investigators have examined the effects of inhibitors of bone resorption. The use of bisphosphonates in patients receiving chronic glucocorticoid therapy is beneficial for both the prevention and treatment of osteoporosis. The use of alendronate, 5 or 10 mg/day for 1 year in patients receiving glucocorticoid therapy, increased lumbar spine BMD by 2.1% and 2.9%, respectively, and increased femoral neck BMD by 1.2% and 1%, respectively (p < 0.001). After 1 year of treatment, an insignificant reduction in new vertebral fractures occurred, but after 2 years of treatment, a nearly 40% reduction in new vertebral fracture risk occurred. Risedronate, 5 mg/day, was also effective in the prevention and treatment of glucocorticoid-induced bone loss. A study of zoledronic acid (5 mg IV/year) versus risedronate (5 mg/day) and teriparatide (20 µg/day) versus alendronate (10 mg/day) for 18 months indicated that both zoledronic acid and teriparatide improved bone mass more than the comparator, and subjects treated with teriparatide had a significant vertebral fracture risk reduction134 in glucocorticoid-treated patients. Also, treatment with denosumab 60 mg every 6 months for 18 months increased bone mass of the spine and hip more than risedronate 5 mg/day. Parathyroid hormone (hPTH 1-34) alone and in

combination studies of rhPTH 1-34 with HRT were both found to be more effective than alendronate or HRT alone in increasing lumbar spine and hip BMD in people with glucocorticoidinduced osteoporosis 134,

Men taking glucocorticoids may experience a lowering of testosterone levels. Men taking glucocorticoids are generally asymptomatic, but if they have evidence of low serum testosterone levels and symptoms of low libido, they can be safely treated with testosterone. Bone mass increases have been observed in men taking glucocorticoids who had low testosterone levels and were treated with testosterone. Nevertheless, because of the risks associated with testosterone treatment, it is more prudent to treat these patients with a bisphosphonate medication.

To prevent bone loss in patients with pulmonary diseases who require glucocorticoid therapy, treatment with inhaled glucocorticoids has been studied. Inhaled glucocorticoids appear to uncouple bone turnover and increase bone loss; however, this effect is dose dependent. Less than 800 µg/day of inhaled budesonide dipropionate does not increase the risk of osteoporosis, but more than 800 µg/day does increase the risk. New inhaled glucocorticoids are more potent than older ones; for instance, Advair, 200 μg/day, is equivalent to nearly 5 mg/day of prednisone. Therefore patients using steroid inhalers on a long-term basis should be screened for bone loss. Because patients who take glucocorticoids may lose a dramatic amount of bone, it is important to monitor the efficacy of a treatment intervention, assess the need for further diagnostic evaluation for other causes of bone loss, and consider alternative treatment strategies if a given therapy is ineffective in preventing bone loss or fractures. In patients at increased risk of fracture, therapy with a potent bisphosphonate, denosumab, or daily PTH or PTHrP injections are highly recommended to slow bone loss and the rate of new fractures. 142,

An unresolved question regarding the treatment and prevention of glucocorticoid-induced bone loss is how to evaluate and treat bone mass after the discontinuation of the glucocorticoid treatment. It is generally recommended that a BMD measure be obtained 3 to 6 months after the discontinuation of chronic glucocorticoid use and that a decision regarding additional treatment be made on the basis of the BMD measure and any recent history of a fragility fracture. Lastly, if pre-menopausal women of childbearing age treated with glucocorticoids need bone protection, treatment with denosumab or a PTH fragment is probably better than bisphosphonates, which have a long half-life in bone and could influence the health of the fetus.

### Osteomalacia

Osteomalacia is characterized by impaired mineralization of bone matrix. Calcium, phosphate, and vitamin D are necessary for the mineralization of bone. Normally, a steep inverse relationship exists between the serum calcium and PTH concentrations. A small decrease in the serum calcium concentration leads to a rise in PTH release, which promotes distal renal calcium reabsorption, proximal tubulorenal phosphorus excretion, and resorption of calcium from bone. Vitamin D is produced in the skin in the presence of ultraviolet light or is absorbed in the intestine from dietary or supplemental sources. Activation of vitamin D to 25-OHD occurs in the liver, and activation to 1,25(OH)2D occurs in the proximal tubules of the kidney. PTH, hypocalcemia, and hypophosphatemia stimulate the renal 1-hydroxylase enzyme that converts 25-OHD to 1,25(OH)2D, which in turn indirectly enhances intestinal calcium absorption. 144,

Osteomalacia results from reduced availability of calcium or phosphate for incorporation into the hydroxyapatite of bone or from deficient absorption or activation of vitamin D. The term rickets applies to the defective mineralization of bone and the cartilaginous growth plate in growing children. As shown in Table 103.8, osteomalacia or rickets may result from decreased availability of vitamin D as a consequence of insufficient ultraviolet light exposure, insufficient vitamin intake, or malabsorption in patients with GI or biliary disorders. Reduced levels of 25-OHD are caused by severe liver disease, increased renal excretion of vitamin D metabolites due to nephrotic syndrome, or accelerated metabolism of 25-OHD caused by anti-convulsant drugs. Decreased activation of 1,25(OH)2D is seen in patients with renal insufficiency as a result of increased phosphate levels; the resultant lower ionized calcium levels lead to secondary or tertiary hyperparathyroidism.

A careful history is important in the diagnosis of osteomalacia or vitamin D insufficiency. For example, a history of a malabsorptive process such as gastrectomy, intestinal resection, sprue, primary biliary cirrhosis, or pancreatic deficiency may lead to the identification of vitamin D deficiency and osteomalacia. Patients with osteomalacia may present with generalized pain involving the pelvis, spine, ribs, or lower extremities or with skeletal deformities

such as bowing of the long bones, kyphoscoliosis, or pelvic abnormalities. Another clinical sign of osteomalacia in adults is proximal muscle weakness, which may result in an antalgic or waddling gait and difficulty ambulating.

One of the radiographic signs of osteomalacia is the presence of pseudofractures, or Looser's zones, which are transverse lines of rarefaction through the cortices, with incomplete healing in the ribs, scapulae, long bones (Fig. 103.2), or pubic rami. Pseudofractures, however, may be indistinguishable from fractures associated with osteogenesis imperfecta or Paget's disease.

The biochemical parameters in patients with osteomalacia reflect the underlying pathophysiologic process and the compensatory biologic responses. In vitamin D deficiency states, the serum calcium levels are usually normal or slightly decreased because PTH levels rise rapidly as a compensatory response to impaired calcium absorption. 146, In renal insufficiency impaired renal production of 1,25(OH)2D, hypocalcemia, and skeletal resistance to PTH are thought to lead to the development of hyperparathyroidism and resultant renal osteodystrophy, mixed osteomalacia, and osteitis fibrosa cystica. In addition, aluminum intoxication may present with pure osteomalacia or adynamic bone disease.147, Chronic vitamin D deficiency may increase the secretory demands of the parathyroid glands, thereby producing secondary or, in some instances, tertiary hyperparathyroidism. In patients with osteomalacia who do not have hepatobiliary disease, alkaline phosphatase levels are often elevated.

X-linked hypophosphatasia (XLH) is a disease in which the PHEX gene is mutated, resulting in an elevation in FGF23 levels in the serum and hypophosphatemia due to renal phosphate wasting. The disease has X-linked inheritance as a result of this. The mother can pass the gene on to both her male and female offspring, and the father can only pass the gene on to his female offspring. The diagnosis of XLH is usually made in childhood from the development of osteomalacia and bone fractures. The treatment is based on oral phosphate replacement, vitamin D if needed, but usually not calcium supplementation as hypercalcemia can result. Recently an anti-FGF antibody, burosumab, was approved by the FDA for the treatment of individuals with XLH that do not respond to oral phosphate and vitamin D supplements. Tumorinduced osteomalacia can occur from a rare tumor that produces FGF23. Affected patients develop severe muscle weakness, fatigue,

and fractures. The tumors can be difficult to detect and can require advanced imaging. If the tumor can be removed, the symptoms and hypophosphatemia rapidly resolve. However, if the tumor is not able to be resected, then medical treatment to replace the phosphate is helpful and, if medical treatment is not sufficient to maintain normal phosphate levels and symptoms continue, treatment with buroamid is recommended.

The evaluation of a patient suspected of having osteomalacia is outlined in Table 103.9.

Osteomalacia is often a treatable disease, but the diagnosis may be overlooked. Vitamin D deficiency can be treated with physiologic doses of vitamin D, but higher doses (1000 to 2000 IU/ day) may hasten the healing of bone. In the presence of intestinal malabsorption, and until the underlying malabsorptive process is corrected, large doses of vitamin D (50, IU once a week to three or more times a week) or occasionally the active metabolite 25-OHD (Calderol) are often required. Careful monitoring of the serum and urinary calcium levels and 25-OHD concentrations is necessary to prevent vitamin D intoxication.

In patients with hypophosphatemia and disorders of renotubular phosphate reabsorption, mineralization of bone occurs with phosphate therapy and moderately high doses of 1,25(OH)2D, with the latter being necessary to prevent the secondary hyperparathyroidism associated with phosphate therapy. In patients affected by renal insufficiency or failure, a phosphate binder (calcium acetate or calcium carbonate) should be used after meals to decrease intestinal phosphate absorption. Calcium citrate therapy should not be used because it augments aluminum absorption. In people with renal failure, 1,25(OH)2D therapy administered orally147 (or intravenously in some patients undergoing dialysis) suppresses parathyroid cell secretion and proliferation; a three-fold elevation of the PTH level is advocated by some investigators to prevent adynamic bone disease. Analogues of 1,25(OH)2D that do not produce hypercalcemia but decrease levels of PTH are now available and may be useful in patients with renal insufficiency.

This biochemical hallmark reflects loss-of-function mutations within the gene that encodes the tissue-nonspecific isoenzyme of alkaline phosphatase (TNSALP) that is present on the surface of bones and developing teeth. ### Paget's Disease of Bone

Paget's disease of bone affects approximately 2% to 3% of the population older than 50 years and is uncommon in people younger than age 40.151 Paget's disease is characterized by enhanced resorption of bone by giant, multinucleated osteoclasts, followed by the formation of disorganized woven bone by osteoblasts. The resultant bone is expanded, weak, and vascular, and thus affected bones may become enlarged and deformed and the overlying skin may feel warm to the touch. The cause of Paget's disease is uncertain, although data showing the presence of viral inclusion particles in giant pagetic osteoclasts support a viral cause. Paget's disease tends to aggregate in families in an autosomal dominant pattern and, in 40% of patients, at least one other family member is affected.

### Clinical Features

Many patients with Paget's disease are asymptomatic, and the disease is detected by the incidental finding of an elevated alkaline phosphatase level or a characteristic radiographic abnormality. Other patients present with a range of symptoms that include bone pain, skeletal deformities (e.g., bowing of long bones, an enlarged skull, and pelvic alterations), pathologic fractures, increased cardiac output (with extensive disease), and nerve compression. Paget's disease typically includes a lytic phase, a combined lytic and blastic phase, and a sclerotic or "burned-out" phase occurring late in the disease process.

Radiographic signs of the three stages of Paget's disease may be present at different sites in the same patient. 152 The skeletal sites commonly involved in people with the disease include the skull (Fig. 103.3), vertebrae, pelvis, sacrum, and lower extremities. Degenerative joint disease may develop adjacent to the bones and cause pain that may obscure the symptoms associated with Paget's . Ten percent to 30% of patients with Paget's disease may disease. experience fractures that present initially as asymptomatic or painful short-fissure fractures traversing the bony cortex (Fig. 103.4). Healing of fractures in pagetic bone usually occurs normally, although cases of nonunion have occurred. A rare complication of Paget's disease of bone is sarcomatous degeneration in less than 1% of patients (with osteogenic sarcomas or, less commonly,

fibrosarcomas or chondrosarcomas); these patients generally have a poor prognosis. The development of a sarcoma may be heralded by the presence of a soft tissue mass, localized pain, and a rise in the alkaline phosphatase level.

Neurologic symptoms generally result from compression of the nerves by pagetic bone. Hearing loss is common and is caused by sensory loss and conduction abnormalities due to pagetic involvement of the bones of the inner ear. Paget's disease of the skull may also produce ocular and other cranial nerve palsies. Neurologic compromise of the thoracic or lumbar spine may lead to spinal cord compression or, in the latter instance, cauda equina syndrome.

### Laboratory Findings

Biochemical indices in patients with Paget's disease usually show normal serum calcium and phosphate levels. Secondary hyperparathyroidism may develop in approximately 10% to 15% of patients with the disease, presumably because of inadequate calcium intake to meet the skeletal demands of the heightened bone remodeling.

Alkaline phosphatase levels of bone origin (bone-specific alkaline phosphatase [BSAP]) are commonly elevated in patients with significant Paget's disease because of the increased osteoblastic activity combined with bone breakdown. In the absence of liver disease, the alkaline phosphatase level typically correlates with the extent of the pagetic involvement of bone, although it may be more elevated in Paget's disease of the skull (see Fig. 103.3).

Unexpectedly, circulating osteocalcin levels do not reflect disease activity in patients with Paget's disease as well as BSAP levels do. Markers of bone resorption such as urinary collagen crosslinks like N telopeptides and C telopeptides are also elevated in people with active Paget's disease. Other laboratory abnormalities in patients with the disease include hypercalciuria, hyperuricuria, and hyperuricemia, possibly related to the increased turnover of osteoclasts. Serum uric acid levels should be measured periodically because of the association of Paget's disease with gouty arthritis.

### Diagnosis

Radiographs show characteristic radiologic findings such as transverse lucent areas, osteoporosis circumscripta, enlargement of the bones, expanding lytic changes, the "blade-of-grass" lesion shown in Fig. 103.4, thickened cortices, a coarse trabecular pattern, or sclerotic changes.

### Treatment

The indications for treatment of Paget's disease (Table 103.10) include pain, hypercalcemia, fractures, high-output cardiac failure (a rare feature), and neurologic compromise.

Treatment of symptomatic Paget's disease is usually directed at suppression of the enhanced bone resorption and skeletal turnover with calcitonin or bisphosphonates. 151, Response to therapy is monitored by the reduction of symptoms and maintenance of the alkaline phosphatase level in a midnormal range, with retreatment once values rise 25% above normal.

### Bisphosphonates

Several bisphosphonates are currently approved by the FDA for the treatment of Paget's disease, including etidronate disodium, pamidronate, alendronate, tiludronate disodium, risedronate, and zoledronic acid.151153 The most frequently used bisphosphonate is zoledronic acid as it is available as a 5-mg IV infusion and a single dose of 5 mg over 15 minutes is sufficient for 2 years. Adverse effects can include fatigue, anemia, muscle aches, swelling of the feet, and flulike symptoms after the first infusion.

In addition to anti-resorptive therapies, nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs and aspirin are useful modalities to alleviate the joint pain and other symptoms that result from degenerative joint disease. Finally, surgical intervention may be needed in patients with Paget's disease and bony deformities, pathologic

fractures, nerve compression, or degenerative arthritis. Orthopedic procedures such as total joint replacement and osteotomies are associated with a reduced risk of intraoperative bleeding or other complications if patients are treated medically (e.g., with anti-resorptive agents or bisphosphonates) to reduce the disease activity and vascularity for at least 6 weeks before the procedure.

### Osteoporosis Induced by Other Medications

Aromatase inhibitors in women undergoing breast cancer treatment are associated with bone loss. Post-menopausal women maintain a low level of circulating estrogen because of aromatization of androgens to estrogen in tissues such as fat and muscle by the cytochrome P-450 enzyme. Inhibition of this enzyme is now used in post-menopausal women with breast cancer. There are two classes of aromatase inhibitors: nonsteroidal reversible inhibitors (anastrozole and letrozole) and steroidal reversible inhibitors (exemestane). These agents prevent the conversion of androgen to estrogen, resulting in low serum estrogen levels and increased bone remodeling. In clinical trials of aromatase inhibitors compared with either tamoxifen or placebo, fracture rates ranged from 3% to 7%. In a 2-year study, significantly higher markers of bone turnover and nearly twice the lumbar spine bone loss and fracture rates were observed with anastrozole compared with tamoxifen. In patients initiating aromatase inhibitor therapies, it is important to obtain a history of clinical risk factors for osteoporosis and a BMD measurement of the hip and spine. Preventive treatment should be initiated in women with normal or low bone mass and no history of fractures. Treatment of women with low bone mass (a T-score ≤-2) should be initiated with potent antiresorptive agents, and BMD should be monitored at least every 2 years. Recent studies with zoledronic acid and denosumab have been quite effective in this patient population.154, If a woman continues to lose bone mass while taking aromatase inhibitors despite compliance with potent anti-resorptive agents, and if the patient has not been treated with radiation to the skeleton as part of the breast cancer protocol, rhPTH 1-34 treatment can be used to build up bone mass.

Gonadotropin-releasing hormone antagonists are used to treat women with endometriosis and men with prostate cancer. These compounds induce bone loss by lowering estrogen levels, resulting in accelerated bone turnover. In a study of more than 50,000 men with prostate cancer treated with androgen-deprivation therapy consisting of either gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonists or orchiectomy, an increased risk of fracture or hospitalization due to fracture was found. Although the overall risk of fracture associated

with androgen-deprivation therapy was only modestly increased, the risk of fracture was significantly associated with the number of doses of gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonists.

Given the high incidence of prostate cancer and the increasing use of this treatment, assessment of bone mass and the prevention of additional bone mass loss are probably appropriate. Oncologists currently recommend that BMD be measured at the time of initiation of androgen-deprivation therapy and that clinical risk factors for osteoporosis be reviewed, including the history of fracture after age 30 years, the family history of hip fracture, smoking history, use of glucocorticoids, low testosterone level, and RA. If the patient has a low BMD (T-score <-2.5) or a T-score between -1 and -2.5 and other risk factors, treatment with calcium and vitamin D supplementation and a bisphosphonate (zoledronic acid, alendronate, risedronate, or denosumab) should be initiated. BMD of the lumbar spine and hip should be measured at least once a year while patients receive androgen-deprivation maintenance therapy. 156-159

### KEY POINTS

### Introduction

Proliferative bone diseases encompass a variety of conditions characterized by exuberant bone and entheseal ossifications and calcifications. New bone formation is the main feature in diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis (DISH) and hypertrophic osteoarthropathy (HOA) and is a common finding in osteoarthritis. New bone formation may also accompany some spondyloarthropathies such as ankylosing spondylitis (AS), psoriatic arthritis, and sternoclavicular syndrome, also known as SAPHO (synovitis, acne, pustulosis, hyperostosis, and osteomyelitis). New bone formation has also been described in endocrine diseases such as thyroid disorders, acromegaly, and hypoparathyroidism (Table 104.1).1-3 Osteoarthritis, spondyloarthropathies, and endocrine disorders are discussed elsewhere in this book (Fig. 104.1).

### Diffuse Idiopathic Skeletal Hyperostosis

DISH is a condition characterized by calcification and ossification of soft tissues, mainly ligaments and entheses. This condition was described by Forestier and Rotes-Querol in 19504 and was termed senile ankylosing byperostosis. It has a marked predilection for the axial skeleton, particularly the thoracic spine. Recognition that the condition is not limited to the spine and may involve peripheral joints led researchers to coin the name DISH, a term now widely used.

DISH is characterized by the production of coarse flowing osteophytes involving, in particular, the right side of the thoracic spine with preservation of the intervertebral disk space, as well as by ossification of the anterior longitudinal ligament. Calcification and ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament seem to be additional skeletal manifestations of DISH. Other entheseal regions may be affected, such as the peripatellar ligaments, Achilles tendon insertion, plantar fascia, olecranon, and others.6-8

Diagnosis is usually based on the definition suggested in 1976.5 This radiographic approach requires the presence of flowing, coarse osteophytes on the right side of the thoracic spine, connecting at least four contiguous vertebrae, or ossification of the anterior longitudinal ligament, preserved intervertebral disk height in the involved segment, and the absence of apophyseal joint ankylosis and sacroiliac joint involvement (Table 104.2). An MRI study suggested that degenerative disk changes are common in DISH. It is logical to consider that in the characteristic DISH age group, degenerative disk changes should not be a deterrent from diagnosing this entity. CT scans of the SIJs showed that bony ankylosis of the SIJs was also common. Taken together, these new data stress the need to update the classification criteria.

Another set of criteria, for epidemiologic purposes, was suggested. These criteria also consider peripheral enthesopathies. With these criteria, a definite diagnosis of DISH is established by criteria similar to those previously suggested. A probable diagnosis of DISH is possible, however, with continuous ossification or calcification, or both, of the anterolateral aspect of at least two contiguous vertebral bodies and bilateral well-corticated enthesopathies in the heel, olecranon, and patella. It has also been suggested that peripheral enthesopathies might represent early DISH, which may evolve, over time, to its full radiologic appearance.

### Etiology and Pathogenesis

The cause and pathogenesis of DISH are unknown. Several genetic, metabolic, and constitutional factors, as well as other bone formation-promoting peptides, are associated with this condition. They all might contribute to bone and entheseal new bone formation.

### Genetic Factors

Genetic factors might play a role in the pathogenesis of DISH. It is known that the prevalence of canine DISH in the Boxer breed is about 40%, whereas the overall prevalence of DISH in dogs is 3.8%, suggesting a genetic basis for the risk of developing canine DISH. Familial clustering of DISH or families with early presentation of DISH suggest a genetic background for this disorder in humans.23, Ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament is closely related to DISH, and the two conditions can coexist. COL6A1, which is the candidate gene for ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament, was significantly associated with DISH in Japanese patients but not in Czech patients25, Although the role played by COL6A1 has not been fully elucidated, it might be involved in ectopic bone formation in ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament (OPLL), as well as in DISH. Many other candidate genes for the promotion of OPLL have been reported, but their association with DISH has not been established yet. These findings would suggest that other factors might play an important role in the genetic predisposition for the development of DISH.

### Metabolic Factors

DISH has been linked to metabolic and constitutional factors such as obesity, a high waist circumference ratio, hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus (DM), hyperinsulinemia, dyslipidemia, elevated growth-promoting peptides, hyperuricemia, and use of retinoids (Table 104.3).28-36 The association of DISH with excess body weight has been well known since the early descriptions of the disease.11, This association was confirmed in a study in which patients with DISH were compared with healthy people and patients with spondylosis. The association of DISH with type 2 DM has been reported in several studies.33, It has been

assumed that the higher serum insulin levels in type 2 DM may contribute to the formation of DISH. No studies have been performed to address the issue of type 1 DM or the effect of exogenous insulin administration on new bone formation. However, in a recent study, the prevalence of DISH was no higher in diabetic patients than in nondiabetic subjects, suggesting re-evaluation of diabetes as a risk factor for the development of DISH. More often, DISH was associated with more complex metabolic and endocrine derangements, with or without overt type 2 DM, comprising glucose intolerance, hyperinsulinemia, dyslipidemia, hyperuricemia, and elevated levels of growth hormone and insulin-like growth factor (IGF)-I.29, Visceral adipose tissue has been linked to metabolic syndrome and an increase in cardiovascular morbidity. A recent study showed that the visceral adipose tissue in DISH patients is significantly larger than in control patients, supplying another support for the role of obesity in the pathogenesis of DISH.

Because of these metabolic abnormalities, patients with DISH have a higher likelihood of being affected by metabolic syndrome and are subjected to a higher coronary artery disease risk. DISH patients without cardiovascular disease were found to have a significantly higher risk for myocardial infarction (MI) over a 10-year period, suggesting that more scrutiny is warranted in evaluating cardiovascular (CV) risk in these patients. It has been shown that patients with DISH have not only significantly higher prevalence rates of hypertension, diabetes, and hyperlipidemia but also a higher prevalence of stroke. The significantly higher hazard ratio could be identified in both sexes whether hypertension existed or not. Hyperinsulinemia has a profound effect on ligaments and entheses that is independent of age and obesity. The differentiation of mesenchymal cells in ligaments into chondrocytes and the subsequent endochondral ossification is promoted by insulin.32, The enthesis provides the growth plate for tendons and ligaments in children and persists into adulthood. This particular structure is composed of collagen fibers, fibroblasts, chondrocytes, and calcified matrix, which is probably a target for the ossification process promoted by insulin.

### Other Bone Formation-Promoting Pathways

Bone morphogenetic protein (BMP)-2 is a potent osteogenic factor that promotes differentiation of mesenchymal stem cells into

fibroblasts and chondroblasts. It stimulates cell proliferation, alkaline phosphatase (ALP) activity, and collagen synthesis.44, Its ability to promote mineralization is inhibited by matrix Gla protein, which is highly expressed in bone and cartilage. Matrix Gla protein deficiency or its altered carboxylation may cause a high level of BMP-2 activity that leads to hyperostosis.36, Another possible explanation is the upregulation of BMP-2 and BMP-4 messenger RNA expression after tensile stress on ligaments in patients with OPLL.

The enthesis may also be under the influence of other growthpromoting peptides. Elevated growth hormone levels have occurred in DISH. Growth hormone is capable of inducing osteoblast cell proliferation and may promote local production of IGF-I, which mediates the action of growth hormone and can stimulate ALP activity in osteoblasts.29, ALP promotes the calcification process during bone formation and is considered a good indicator for the maturation stages of osteoblasts. It has not yet been determined why the new bone formation is localized mainly at the ligamentous and entheseal sites. In male patients with DISH, growth hormone serum levels are not elevated compared with patients with OA, but they are much higher in the synovial fluid.29, In the spine, vertebral blood supply could be a factor in the onset or progression of DISH. Intraerythrocyte growth hormone levels may exceed serum growth hormone levels and could be transported to the vertebral site.

The expression of various genes involved in cell division and growth is regulated by nuclear factor-kB (NF-kB), which is capable of regulating the differentiation of multipotential cells. Activation of environmental factors such as platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF)-BB and transforming growth factor (TGF)-β1 in ligament cells stimulates the activation of NF-kB, which influences the osteoblastic differentiation of mesenchymal cells. This event is accompanied by elevation of ALP activity in cells of patients with DISH and serves as an indicator of maturation stages of the osteoblast. Inflammatory cytokines such as PDGF-BB, TGF-β1, and others may be related to the onset of non—insulin-dependent DM and may be the link between this condition and the occurrence of DISH.54,

The Wnt-β-catenin pathway may induce bone formation. Wnt signaling can be inhibited by the endogenous secreted protein dickkopf-related protein 1 (DKK-1; also known as dickkopf-1). Low DKK-1 levels and thus reduced inhibition of the Wnt pathway might have a role in the development of extensive bony spinal bridges in a subset of patients with DISH.56-58 Vitamin A and its derivatives have been implicated in the pathogenesis of DISH because of their ability to promote new bone formation. Levels of vitamin A were higher in patients with DISH compared with control subjects, and some reports showed DISH-like manifestations in young patients treated with vitamin A or its deriva- 30, The role of vitamin A in the pathogenesis and clinical tives. manifestations in DISH is still controversial. Larger prospective studies are necessary to elucidate the role played by this vitamin in the pathogenesis of DISH.

Prostaglandin I2 (PGI2) is a potent inhibitor of bone resorption, and endothelin-1 might regulate ectopic calcification of the vasculature but may also regulate the proliferation of osteoblasts and osteoclasts. In vitro studies have suggested that endothelin-1 and PGI2 might play roles in the pathogenesis of DISH by induction, through various mechanisms, of ALP activity and osteogenic differentiation in spinal ligament cells.61-63

There are no convincing explanations for the predilection of the hyperostotic process to affect the anterolateral aspect of the

thoracic spine. The limited range of motion of the thoracic spine has been cited as a possible cause for the predilection to this site. This assumption cannot explain the involvement of the extremely mobile cervical spine or the lumbar spine, however. The less frequent involvement of the left side of the thoracic spine was ascribed to the pulsation of the aorta. This assumption was based on a few reports that described left-sided bridging osteophytes in cases with a right-sided aorta, suggesting that the aortic pulsations interfere with the production of the osteophytes. This hypothesis has been recently reiterated. Furthermore, a CT study suggested that the degree of thoracic spine new bone formation depends on the distance of the aorta from the spine. When the aorta is adjacent to the vertebra, little or no new bone formation was seen.65-67 The relationship between parathyroid hormone (PTH) and DISH has not been elucidated yet. However, in an animal model it promotes bony ankyloses.

Calcifications, ossification, and subsequent stiffening of ligaments and joint capsules have important pathogenetic implications. Recently patients with DISH have a significantly higher risk of developing aortic valve sclerosis. Whether this finding might share common pathogenetic mechanisms or only reflects the usual risk factors has yet to be determined (Fig. 104.2).

Osteoarthritis may have pathogenetic features in common with the peripheral joint manifestations of DISH. It was suggested that in the small non—weight-bearing joints in osteoarthritis, the process is caused by an increased intra-articular pressure and the subsequent development of "crash" forces. This development was attributed to thickening of the collateral ligaments of the joints that enforce a constraint movement not to primary damage to the cartilage. It seems reasonable that the joints affected by DISH may develop the same crash forces operating in small osteoarthritis joints as a result of this mechanism. This mechanism might explain the involvement of "atypical" joints that are not commonly affected by osteoarthritis and the hypertrophic osteoarthritic changes in the commonly affected joints.

### The Inflammatory Theory

It has been proposed that the initial event at the site of the enthesis might be a local inflammatory process that precedes the ossification process. The theory is supported by imaging findings in which it was shown that MRI studies of the spine in patients with DISH might detect early or late vertebral corner lesions compatible with the Assessment for Ankylosing Spondylitis (ASAS) definitions for axial spondyloarthritis. Furthermore, it seems that the rates of progression of DISH and AS are similar, which suggests possible similarities also in the initial pathogenetic mechanisms. A single ultrasonographic study of the peripheral entheses in patients with DISH found an increased tendency for inflammatory signs such as positive power Doppler and to some extent erosions supporting the theory of a local inflammatory process as the promotor of entheseal new bone formation. These and other findings suggest that this theory should be also pursued.

### Clinical Manifestations

The lack of specific symptoms and signs of DISH, as well as the radiographic diagnostic criteria, have raised doubts about DISH as a separate entity. Although the process may be asymptomatic, it is associated with morning stiffness, dorsolumbar pain, and reduced range of motion in some patients.7, Patients with DISH may have extremity pain involving peripheral large and

small joints and peripheral entheses such as the heel, Achilles tendon, shoulder, patella, and olecranon. Physical function in DISH patients is poorer compared with non-DISH patients. These findings were mitigated partially when adjusted for age, sex, and other parameters. Of particular interest was a reduced grip strength, most probably related to the stiffening of the small hand joints.

### Spinal Involvement

Pain in the axial skeleton may involve all three segments of the spine and the costosternal and sternoclavicular joints. The level of pain and disability is significantly higher compared with healthy subjects but is not different from patients with spondylosis. In some studies, up to two-thirds of the patients with DISH experience morning stiffness and spinal pain, and nearly half have a reduced range of motion.7, Reports of pain referable to the thoracic spine are common and are accompanied by a reduced chest expansion. However, other studies suggest that spinal DISH is not associated with increased pain, and at times patients reported less pain compared with patients who did not have DISH.76,

Although similar in some aspects to osteoarthritis of the spine, DISH is a distinct clinical entity with different characteristics. Classically, the portions of the spine that are involved in osteoarthritis are the lower portions of the cervical spine and the lumbar spine. Thoracic spine involvement is uncommon in osteoarthritis or occurs in late stages of the disease, as opposed to the common involvement of the thoracic spine in DISH. Thoracic spine involvement in DISH is characterized by preserved intervertebral height, whereas in spinal

osteoarthritis, reduced intervertebral disk height is common. These differences in the radiologic appearance and anatomic spinal distribution probably have to do with the different pathogenetic mechanisms described earlier. It is presumed that the primary target for the osteoarthritic process is the cartilage represented in the spine by the intervertebral disks and the cartilage of the facet joints.

The wear-and-tear forces operating in the extremely mobile lower cervical and lumbar portions of the spine might explain the frequent involvement of these segments in osteoarthritis, whereas the thoracic spine is the least mobile of the spinal segments. The main targets of the disease in DISH are the spinal ligaments and entheses (Fig. 104.3).5, These abnormalities are not limited to the thoracic spine and may involve the lumbar spine and the cervical spine (Fig. 104.4). In the lumbar spine, the large bridging osteophytes are not uniformly one-sided. These sites of ossification and subsequent production of large osteophytes may result in spinal stenosis.81, Orthopedic surgeons and their patients should be aware that the beneficial effect of surgery, in these patients, is shorter, and the reoperation rate is higher in these patients.

Severe complications may develop, especially when the cervical spine is affected; these complications include dysphagia, hoarseness, stridor, OPLL, myelopathy, aspiration pneumonia, sleep apnea, atlantoaxial complications, thoracic outlet syndrome, esophageal obstruction, endoscopic and intubation difficulties, and fractures (Table 104.4). The high prevalence of coexisting intervertebral disk damage in young patients with DISH suggests an important role for DISH in the pathogenesis of spondylosis

in this group of patients. At times, patients with DISH may assume the typical postural abnormalities of advanced AS such as accentuated kyphosis and reduced mobility of the spine. These two entities, although they may coexist, can usually be distinguished by the different age at onset, clinical presentation, radiographic appearance of the spine and sacroiliac joints, and HLA-B27 associations.86,

When the differentiation between AS and DISH is difficult on clinical and radiographic grounds, whole-body MRI can prove useful. In particular, the presence of ankyloses, facet joint ankylosis, SIJ ankylosis other than alterations of the SIJ such as edema and fat infiltration, and upper corner fat infiltration of the spine are supportive for AS.

### Extraspinal Involvement

Clinical manifestations similar or identical to those of osteoarthritis are prominent features of DISH in the peripheral joints. The peripheral joints affected by DISH have features that distinguish them from primary osteoarthritis, however. One is the more frequent involvement of joints that are not usually affected in osteoarthritis such as the metacarpophalangeal joints, elbows, and shoulders (Fig. 104.5).89-92 Other features are a more severe hypertrophic disease that may result in a reduced range of motion in the affected joints and calcified and/or ossified prominent enthesopathies. 92-94

As described previously, the primary event in DISH is thickening, calcification, or ossification of ligaments and entheses. In particular, enthesopathy affecting the peripheral joints has been described. The radiographic appearance of peripatellar, cruciate ligament insertion, and pericapsular osseous enthesopathies are some examples of the contribution of DISH to stiffening of the soft tissues surrounding a joint (Fig. 104.6). Entheseal ossification at various sites other than joints such as the heel, ribs, and pelvis is a common finding in DISH. The clinical implication of the peripheral involvement is not clear and is controversial. However, the enthesopathies may become symptomatic, exhibiting pain and swelling in the affected region. A high probability for the presence of spinal DISH was noted for ossification of the iliolumbar and sacrotuberous ligaments and with bony overgrowth of the inferior acetabular rim.95, A higher level of soft tissue tenderness and lower functional status have occurred recently in patients with DISH compared with patients who do not have DISH.

Patients with DISH often have higher body weight and body mass index, waist circumference, and systolic blood pressure. These factors and the metabolic abnormalities described earlier put patients at an increased risk for cardiovascular diseases. 35,

The diagnosis of DISH should be suspected in patients with osteoarthritis in atypical locations (e.g., the elbow), in patients with hypertrophic osteoarthritis, and in patients with large enthesopathies and entrapment neuropathies of uncertain origin. This is particularly true for patients with the associated diseases and metabolic abnormalities previously discussed. Chest radiographs may serve as a screening tool for the diagnosis of DISH with a sensitivity of 77% and a specificity of 97%.

### Fracture Risk and Heterotropic Ossification

The sites of ossification and the subsequent production of large osteophytes may result in spinal stenosis77 and spinal stiffening. Under these circumstances, force cannot be dissipated, and the spine behaves like a long bone with an increased risk of fracture. The increased spinal stiffness may play a more important role than the actual bone mineral density in the increased fracture risk and the fracture patterns observed in individuals with DISH. These fractures may be unrecognized, unstable, and associated with treatment delays and permanent neurologic deficits.

The tendency for new bone formation puts the patient at risk for the development of heterotopic ossification after joint surgery 105 and may jeopardize the outcome. Although it is not clear what causes these ossifications, it has been suggested that the surgical trauma—induced TGF-β release at the lesion site promotes recruitment of osteoblast precursor cells and determines the overexpression of BMP-2 in the surrounding skeletal muscle, inducing a further osteogenic differentiation. The use of irradiation or prophylactic nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) treatment has been suggested to prevent heterotropic ossifications for patients at risk.

progression; correct the associated metabolic disorders; and prevent spontaneous or induced complications (Table 104.5).

Specific therapeutic interventions in DISH have not been systematically explored, which is probably related to the inclusion of DISH in the spectrum of osteoarthritis and the assumption that the same therapeutic interventions for osteoarthritis are suitable for DISH. More recently it was suggested that serum levels of growth hormone and IGF-I might be a useful surrogate marker for assessing DISH progression and remission. It was estimated that a period of at least 10 years is necessary for the pathologic process to evolve completely. This notion has been recently corroborated by a CT study108 and implies that a long observation period is necessary to show that a therapeutic intervention prevents the development of the disease, arrests its progression, or, it is hoped, reverses the pathologic changes.

Few reports have been published about remedies to alleviate the symptoms of the disease, but some investigators have reported on the beneficial effects of light exercise, heat, analgesics, and NSAIDs. Exercise therapy failed to show a significant improvement in the spinal range of motion except for lumbosacral flexion. 0 More recently, the use of locally acting NSAIDs for the treatment of osteoarthritis was as effective as the same product by oral route, suggesting that locally acting NSAIDs also might be successfully used for the symptomatic relief of pain and stiffness that may be present in the peripheral joints of patients with DISH. Treatment of symptomatic enthesopathies might be necessary to alleviate local pain and swelling; this treatment can be achieved through use of local soft applications such as insoles for plantar spurs or protective bandages at other sites. Infiltration of a local anesthetic with long-acting corticosteroids may offer at least temporary relief in people with severe symptoms. When multiple sites are involved, the same therapeutic modalities mentioned for osteoarthritis may be used.

It seems appropriate to screen patients with DISH for known cardiovascular risk factors and to treat them when appropriate. General measures such as weight reduction, adequate physical activity, and a diet low in saturated fat and carbohydrates all might be important in preventing or arresting the progression of DISH. Some of these factors may have pathogenetic implications and may become therapeutic targets. On the basis of present understanding, therapeutic interventions should aim at a reduction of insulin secretion and insulin resistance. In patients with noninsulin-dependent DM, the use of biguanides, which decrease insulin resistance, may offer an advantage compared with the use of sulfonylureas, which increase insulin secretion.

When coexisting hypertension is treated, medications that might improve insulin resistance such as angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, calcium channel blockers, and α-blockers are preferred over medications that may worsen insulin resistance, such as thiazide diuretics and β-blockers. Some growth factors that might have a role in the development of DISH such as NF-kB, PDGF- BB, TGF-β1, growth hormone, and IGF-I may become targets for specific therapeutic interventions.

In some patients, several complications can be avoided if they are taken into consideration. Aspiration pneumonia can be partially avoided if instructions in proper deglutition and preservation of an upright position after meals are carefully explained to the patient. Physicians familiar with DISH can avoid or minimize damage to the cervical spine or to soft tissues in patients who might need certain diagnostic or therapeutic interventions such as upper gastrointestinal endoscopy or endotracheal intubation. It is reasonable to adopt common measures to prevent falls and trauma, especially in elderly patients. Heterotopic ossification after orthopedic surgeries, in particular hip arthroplasty, is common in patients with DISH. Several therapeutic interventions aimed at abolishing heterotopic ossification, such as administration of NSAIDs, anti—vitamin K, and irradiation, have been .113,114Patients at high risk of develreported with variable success. oping this complication, such as patients with DISH, should be considered candidates for one of these regimens. The therapeutic approach in patients with fractured ankylosed spine requires an aggressive intervention but with extreme caution due to the high risk of neurologic complications.

Therapeutic options are summarized in Fig. 104.7.116 Many tasks lay ahead to better define this disorder, understand the pathogenesis, and delineate effective interventions (Table 104.6). The research of DISH is hampered by its late diagnosis and the absence of information on the early changes that precede the ossification process.

### Surgery

C-spine large anterior osteophytes may cause a significant reduction in quality of life, in particular with dysphagia. Since there is no known medical therapy that can reverse the excessive bone formation, surgery might represent a feasible therapeutic option. Recurrence of the osteophytes is of concern, although the data are not clear about the time to recurrence due to different follow-up periods. It emerged, however, that a shorter time from the onset of symptoms and a milder severity of the symptoms may improve the final outcome.119, It has also been suggested that postoperative administration of indomethacin or irradiation might reduce recurrences in a similar way it might prevent postsurgical heterotropic ossifications.

### Hypertrophic Osteoarthropathy

HOA is a well-known entity characterized by skin proliferation, bone proliferation (periostosis), and large joint effusions. The hallmark and main visual manifestation is a bulbous deformity of the distal end of the digits, also known as clubbing or drumsticks (Fig. 104.8). Periostosis is a progressive process with predilection for the tubular bones, principally the tibia and fbula. Periostosis is bilateral and symmetric and spares the medullary cavity, axial skeleton, and skull. The prevalence of the condition is unknown, but it was found in skeletal human remains from thousands of years ago. It can be classified as primary or secondary HOA.

### Etiology

### Primary Hypertrophic Osteoarthropathy

Primary HOA is an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by periostosis, clubbing, thickening of the skin of the face and scalp, seborrhea, and hyperhidrosis. It is also termed pachydermoperiostosis. There is a male predominance, with a male-to-female ratio of 9:1; one peak of presentation occurs in the first year of life and the other in adolescence. Three clinical subtypes are defined as complete form, incomplete form involving solely the skin and bone, and a forme fruste with only skin thickening. Several genetic models were proposed, of which mainly an autosomal dominant form was found to be mostly associated with HOA. Two mutations are associated with the autosomal dominant forms. The most common one is the SLCO2A1 gene, which encodes the prostaglandins transmembrane transporter .124,125The and is responsible for most published familial cases. second gene is the HPGD gene, which encodes the enzymes

responsible for prostaglandin metabolism. Both cases results in primary HOA.

### Secondary Hypertrophic Osteoarthropathy

Secondary forms of HOA manifest as isolated clubbing or with the full spectrum of the disease. Clubbing may be unilateral or bilateral and has occurred in a variety of diseases, including pulmonary (most commonly cancers), cardiac, gastrointestinal, neurologic, infectious, vascular, and other diseases (Table 104.7). 127-135

### Pathogenesis

The pathogenesis of HOA is not fully scrutinized, yet three pathogenic processes have been suggested: pathologic vascularization, ongoing hypoxia, and connective tissue hyperplasia. Pathologic examination of distal digits found numerous platelet microthrombi with dilated capillaries in some biopsies. Another microcapillary photo examination study revealed dilated capillaries and arborized loops compared with controls, emphasizing the role of pathologic vascularization as part of this syndrome. Thickened skin reported in primary HOA found hyperkeratosis irregularities, acanthosis, hyperkeratotic plugs, and multiple pustules within the epidermis with sebaceous hyperplasia.

Various hypotheses have been generated in an attempt to explain the development of HOA. One group139suggested that megakaryocytes are fragmented into platelets during their passage in the lung capillaries. In severe lung diseases or right-to-left shunts, however, megakaryocytes or platelet aggregates bypass the pulmonary capillary bed and lodge in the peripheral vasculature of the digits.

Another group's study showed that locally released growth factors such as vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) and PDGF
