Factors associated with collapse speed included size and location of the necrotic lesion, but in each case a negative association was observed between APP angle and collapse speed.

### Treatment of Osteonecrosis

### Surgery

Most cases of osteonecrosis ultimately require surgical intervention. Sometimes surgical procedures can be used in conjunction with nonsurgical approaches. The more advanced the disease, the more extensive the surgery that is required.

The various surgical procedures used in the treatment of osteonecrosis include core decompression, structural bone grafting, vascularized fibula grafting, osteotomy, resurfacing arthroplasty, hemiarthroplasty, and total hip replacement. Table 105.6 shows the typical success rates for each of these procedures.

Arthroscopy is a valuable tool used in the treatment of osteonecrosis. It has been used to determine the position of the core decompression tract to the necrotic part of the femoral or humeral head,195 and arthroscopic debridement has been used in the treatment of osteonecrosis of the capitellum of the humerus in adolescents and in individuals with Kienböck's disease and osteonecrosis of the scaphoid.

Core decompression, which involves the removal of a core of bone from the femoral neck and head, is indicated in less advanced stages of osteonecrosis (Fig. 105.14). The core acts as a vent to reduce intraosseous pressure and intramedullary pressure, reversing ischemia and improving symptoms. Other benefits of core decompression include stimulation of angiogenesis, which leads to improved vascularization during the repair process. The effectiveness of core decompression in the treatment of nontraumatic osteonecrosis was demonstrated in a study of 34 patients with 54 affected hips. The mean age at presentation was 38 years. The patients were monitored for a mean duration of 10 years after surgery. Success was defined as absence of symptoms, no further progression of disease, and no further surgery. Clinical improvement was established in 26 hips (48%), and radiographic success was established in 20 hips (37%).

Computer-assisted core decompression has been used to provide greater precision in directing the core into the ischemic area and to minimize the duration of radiation. Because early diagnosis improves outcome and the incidence of developing osteonecrosis in a contralateral hip is high, core decompression is frequently performed on both hips simultaneously. This approach adds little risk compared with unilateral core decompression, with the benefit of better outcomes as a result of early surgical treatment of the contralateral hip.

In structural bone grafting, or bone impaction grafting, the bone graft is inserted into the necrotic segment through the core tract. The bone graft acts in similar fashion to a stent, providing support to overlying subchondral bone. The goal is to prevent collapse. This combination of procedures is frequently used in treating stage 1 or 2 osteonecrotic femoral heads. Allogeneic and autologous bone grafts, mostly harvested from the tibia or fibula, are used. When this technique was attempted in patients

with stage 3 and 4 lesions, the outcome was generally poor (100% failure after 2 to 4 years), with progression to collapse and further surgical procedures. Another study investigated outcomes after structural augmentation with autogenous bone grafts in stage 1 and 2 disease in 31 patients (33 hips). All patients had significantly reduced pain, along with an improvement in Harris hip scores from 76 before surgery to 91 after surgery.

Vascularized structural bone grafting also uses the core tract to insert a corticocancellous bone graft into the femoral neck and head along with its vascular pedicle. The vascular pedicle is anastomosed to a nearby vessel, adding a source of blood to the graft. The results of vascularized fibular grafting in the treatment of hips with osteonecrosis showed a survival of 61% of hips at 5-year followup and 42% at a median of 8 years. In another study, patients with 226 osteonecrotic hips were treated with a combination of autologous cancellous bone impaction and pedicled iliac bone block transfer. The anastomosis was to the ascending branch of the lateral femoral circumflex artery. Fourteen hips required conversion to total hip arthroplasty because of collapse, severe pain, or both. Of the remaining 212 hips, 92% were considered a clinical success and 76% were considered radiographically successful. The success rate declined from stage 2 to stage 4 hips (96% for stage 2 hips; 90%, stage 3; and 57%, stage 4). Free vascularized fibula

grafting has been compared favorably with other modes of surgical 202 treatment.

In the past decade injectable composite grafts—a combination of calcium sulfate (CaSO4) with calcium phosphate (CaPO4), a fully synthetic composite material enhanced with autologous bone marrow concentrate—designed to be mixed intraoperatively and injected into the space created by core decompression have been used with promising results. This treatment not only relieves hip pain but also prevents progression of osteonecrosis in most cases.

Osteotomy of the femur involves shifting the position of the osteonecrotic segment by making a cut in the proximal femur so that the osteonecrotic segment is rotated or flexed out of the weight-bearing region of the acetabulum and then replacing the weight-bearing region with viable bone. Healing of the necrotic region can proceed without the stress of weight bearing. Several different osteotomy techniques have been attempted to salvage hips with stage 2 or 3 osteonecrosis.

Resurfacing arthroplasty uses a metallic or ceramic shell placed over a femoral head that has been debrided of the necrotic area. The potential advantages of resurfacing arthroplasty include preservation of joint mechanics, bone conservation,203 more physiologic loading of the bone, a lower incidence of perioperative complications, and easier conversion to total hip arthroplasty in

case of failure. Complications of this procedure include femoral neck fractures, a secondary osteonecrosis when the procedure is performed for other reasons,205 and increased metal ion levels. Resurfacing arthroplasty has been recommended for patients with later-stage osteonecrosis, including those with femoral head collapse. A retrospective study compared the results of limited femoral head resurfacing and total hip arthroplasty in 30 consecutive patients with Steinberg stage 3 or 4 disease. The survival rate at a 7-year mean follow-up period for the resurfacing group was 90%, whereas the survival rate at a mean 8-year follow-up for the total hip arthroplasty group was 93%. A recent level 3 therapeutic study showed that hip resurfacing success rates at a 5-year

follow-up were comparable with those of total hip arthroplasty in patients with osteonecrosis who were younger than age 25.209

In hemiarthroplasty, only part of the hip joint is replaced. The original acetabulum is preserved, but the femoral head is replaced with a prosthesis. Two types of prostheses are used: unipolar and bipolar. In a unipolar prosthesis, the articulation is between the artificial femoral head and the acetabulum. In the bipolar prosthesis (presently the most frequently used), the articulation is within the prosthesis itself. Failure rates for hemiarthroplasties in individuals with osteonecrosis are 50% to 60% at 3 years for unipolar prostheses and 44% for bipolar prostheses. Another study evaluated the success rate of Charnley/ Bicentric hemiarthroplasty in the treatment of Ficat and Arlet stage

3 osteonecrosis of the femoral head. Failures included three hips that needed to be revised to cementless total hip replacement, two hips with radiographic changes of loosening and imminent failure, and one hip with progressive loss of joint space and secondary degenerative changes. The success rate was 84.2% after a mean of 56 months.

Total hip arthroplasty is complete replacement of the hip joint with a prosthesis, including the femoral head and the acetabulum. In a study of 55 consecutive hip arthroplasty procedures, cementless total hip arthroplasty provided favorable results in advanced-stage osteonecrosis of the femoral head. Although 10 of the 48 hips available for follow-up after a minimum of 5 years required revision, all of these patients had Ficat and Arlet stage 3 or 4 disease. A study of 53 hips in 41 patients treated with cemented total hip replacement

showed that at a minimum of 10 years of follow-up, 17.4% required revision. Compared with cemented total hip replacements performed for other conditions, osteonecrosis had a greater risk for loosening of acetabular and femoral components. A survivorship analysis of cemented total hip replacements in renal transplant patients with osteonecrosis of the femoral head showed excellent survival after 10 years (98.8%). After 20 years, the survival rate decreased to 63.8%. Along with the advancements in artificial intelligence, various computational and digital diagnostic models are also being developed for the surgical and nonsurgical treatment of osteonecrosis.

A more recent study of 300 consecutive primary total hip arthroplasty procedures for osteonecrosis and OA showed that surgery for osteonecrosis had better post-operative scores compared with

OA. The osteonecrosis patients were much younger than the OA patients. The authors concluded that conventional cementless total hip arthroplasty had satisfactory midterm results in osteonecrosis.

In individuals with ONJ, the most common surgical procedure is resection of the affected bone. Conservative treatment has also been used but has a higher recurrence rate. A larger extent of surgical excision and a higher number of surgical debridements were associated with a lower recurrence rate. Other modes of surgical therapy for ONJ include bone-contouring procedures, fluorescence-guided bone-contouring procedures, 213 and segmental osteotomies, but these procedures are generally reserved for more severe cases. Nonsurgical treatments, including hyperbaric oxygen therapy214 and low-intensity laser therapy, are controversial but have been used to treat ONJ.

### Nonsurgical I Approaches

The key to the successful treatment of osteonecrosis is early detection. Because many patients are relatively young, and because treatment of late-stage osteonecrosis is associated with high failure rates, earlier detection may be associated with a greater chance of preservation of the hip. The choice

of conservative nonsurgical versus more aggressive surgical options depends on the clinical and pathologic staging of the disease. Fig. 105.15 is an algorithm for the treatment of osteonecrosis.

Nonsurgical treatment of osteonecrosis of the femoral head includes refraining from weight bearing on the affected joint, use of analgesic and anti-inflammatory medications, and physiotherapy. Conservative medical treatment is effective only in the early stages for symptomatic relief. Nonsurgical management does not seem to alter the natural course of the disease. Electrical stimulation has been used in the treatment of osteonecrosis, in conjunction with core decompression. Electrical stimulation enhances osteogenesis and neovascularization. It also alters the balance between osteoblast and osteoclast activity, resulting in increased bone deposition and decreased bone resorption. Delivery of electrical stimulation can be performed by direct current (DC), pulsed electromagnetic field, and capacitance coupling. The success of electrical stimulation in the treatment of osteonecrosis has been rather mediocre. A study was performed on 11 hips in 8 patients with Ficat stage 2 osteonecrosis who underwent core decompression and placement of an electric stimulating coil within the core in

the anterosuperior segment of the femoral head. Of these 11 hips, 5 required a repeat operation and 6 had progressive deterioration 13 months after initial placement of the coil. In addition, there was little histologic evidence that the coil did indeed generate new bone deposition. The efficacy of this method of treatment is unproven.

On the other hand, another study compared the effectiveness of conservative nonsurgical treatment with core decompression with or without DC electrical stimulation. The clinical symptom scores and the rate of progression to arthroplasty were best in the group with core decompression and DC electrical stimulation and worst in the nonoperative group. Capacitive coupling

can be performed with or without core decompression and grafting. Forty patients with stage 1 to 3 osteonecrosis underwent core decompression and grafting; half of the patients wore active capacitive coupling units with electrodes over the femoral head for 6 months. The control group was 55 patients with osteonecrosis who were treated conservatively. Follow-ups at 2 and 4 years showed that core decompression with or without capacitive coupling provided a better clinical and radiologic outcome than did conservative treatment. Capacitive coupling did not improve the results further when used with core decompression and grafting.

Extracorporeal shock wave therapy has been used in the treatment of osteonecrosis of the femoral head. A study of 48 patients and 57 hips compared extracorporeal shock wave therapy with core decompression and bone grafting. Twenty-three patients with 29 affected hips were assigned to the shock wave group, and the remaining patients and hips were treated surgically. The patients in the shock wave group were given treatment of 6000 pulses of shock waves at 28 kV to the affected hip. The patients were evaluated radiographically and by their reports of symptoms (pain), Harris hip scores, and quality of life (daily work activity assessment). Shock wave therapy produced better results than did the nonvascularized bone grafting procedure, with comparatively less progression of disease. In 35 patients with 47 osteonecrotic hips, the use of shock wave therapy led to improvements in serum nitric oxide levels, angiogenic factors such as VEGF, and osteogenic

factors such as bone morphogenetic protein-2 and osteocalcin. Levels of inflammatory markers were reduced. It is interesting to note that although these changes did not persist beyond several months, the clinical and radiographic improvement, present in 83% of hips, was present after 12 months.

In a cohort of 153 patients who were on high-dose steroids, extracorporeal shock wave therapy was administered as a preventive measure in a randomized placebo-controlled trial and was found to reduce the risk of developing glucocorticoid-induced osteonecrosis of the femoral head, compared with a group that was not given shock wave therapy. This is impactful for its use as a preventive rather than a therapeutic measure. Further studies need to be done to confirm the findings and to establish risks and benefits to performing shock wave therapy before the appearance of osteonecrosis.

Conservative treatment of osteonecrosis of the talus is not promising, and the affected ankles generally continue to progress, requiring either core decompression or arthrodesis. Conservative treatment of bisphosphonate-induced ONJ includes cessation of bisphosphonate usage or surgical debridement. Good oral hygiene, regular dental assessment, and avoidance of dental procedures during bisphosphonate usage can prevent the onset of osteonecrosis.

The use of traditional Chinese medicine and other integrative forms of therapy have been studied but remain controversial. 220,221

### Prevention Versus Treatment

A recent study evaluated the role of antioxidants in the treatment of osteonecrosis. Japanese white rabbits were divided into two groups and fed either a normal diet or a normal diet supplemented with α-tocopherol. Osteonecrosis developed in 14 of 20 rabbits in the control group but in only 5 of 21 rabbits in the experimental group. This finding suggests that oxidative stress may play a role in the pathogenesis of osteonecrosis and that a role may exist for antioxidants such as vitamin E.

A group of researchers studied the use of adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) in rabbits to prevent corticosteroid-induced osteonecrosis and found that if ACTH is administered along with depot methylprednisolone acetate (Depo-Medrol), osteonecrosis is reduced. The authors of this study believe that ACTH enhances osteoblast support and stimulates the production of VEGF, which then stimulates the generation of new blood vessels. The result is an increase in blood flow to the vulnerable areas of bone, preventing cell death and reducing the likelihood of osteonecrosis.

### Stem Cell Transplantation

Corticosteroids interfere with the balance of adipogenesis and osteogenesis in the differentiation of mesenchymal stem cells. Corticosteroids shunt uncommitted osteoprogenitor cells in the bone marrow into the adipocytic pathway, leading to reduced osteoblast formation. Corticosteroids also reduce VEGF, which leads to a reduction in new blood vessel formation and potentially can lead to bone death. Alcohol has a similar effect on the differentiation of progenitor cells.

The balance between adipogenesis and osteogenesis has been targeted as a potential site for the treatment of osteonecrosis. Multipotential mesenchymal stem cells from femoral bone marrow near osteonecrosis sites are able to express messenger RNA aggrecan and type II collagen. Both are deposited into the bone matrix. These features are characteristic of chondrogenic differentiation. The mesenchymal stem cells can be differentiated into osteocytic lineage in vitro.

A pilot study evaluating the effectiveness of implantation of autologous bone marrow cells in the treatment of osteonecrosis used core decompression to implant stem cells into the necrotic lesions of the femoral head. The patients were divided into two groups: one that received core decompression alone as treatment for osteonecrosis (the control group) and one that received autologous bone marrow cell implantation along with core decompression (the treatment group). The patients were followed up for 24 months and, at that time, 5 of 8 hips in the control group, but only 1 of 10 in the treatment group, advanced to stage 3 osteonecrosis. In addition, greater improvement in pain and joint symptoms occurred in the treatment group, and the treatment seemed to be safe. Further studies are necessary to confirm these results.

Twenty-eight patients with 44 necrotic hips were treated with percutaneous decompression and autologous bone marrow mononuclear cell infusion. Patients were followed up for a minimum of 2 years and evaluated for clinical and radiographic progression of the disease. Overall slowing in the progression of the disease stage appeared to occur. The mean Harris hip score improved from 58 to 86.

In 2014, investigators reviewed the literature and published a report in which they concluded that using core decompression in conjunction with mesenchymal stem cell infusion in the form

of bone marrow leads to improved pain and functionality and halts progression of osteonecrosis of the femoral head, potentially obviating the need for future invasive procedures such as total hip replacement.

An increasing utilization of stem cell therapy for the treatment of osteonecrosis has demonstrated few safety issues, and the results of one study show that bone marrow mesenchymal stem cell transplantation with core decompression showed a lowering of total hip replacement arthroplasty conversion rate compared with core decompression alone, although there was no impact on ARCO 225 stage progression.

### Conclusion

Osteonecrosis is a potentially debilitating condition with significant morbidity despite medical interventions or surgery. Corticosteroid use is the most common cause of osteonecrosis, and corticosteroid-induced osteonecrosis can be reproduced in animal models. The pathogenesis of the disease is multifaceted and is not completely understood. Why is it that corticosteroid-induced osteonecrosis is more common in patients with certain underlying diseases and not in others? Does osteonecrosis have a genetic or epigenetic basis, and is there a familial predisposition? Common pathogenic mechanisms known to be involved in the disease include osteoblast/osteoclast survival and apoptosis, lipid metabolism, and coagulation abnormalities. However, it is still unclear how these mechanisms interrelate. To better appreciate the risk factors involved in osteonecrosis, a more complete understanding of the pathogenesis is necessary. Until then, the physician should always maintain a high index of suspicion for osteonecrosis whenever known risk factors are present, especially use of corticosteroids and alcohol.

Treatment of osteonecrosis can be nonsurgical or surgical. Results of hip replacement in these patients are generally poorer than in older patients with OA. Stem cell therapy is beginning to enter more into the conversation. Several studies on stem cell therapy to treat osteonecrosis have been published, and results appear to be favorable.

# Relapsing Polychondritis

### KEY POINTS

### Introduction

Relapsing polychondritis (RPC) is a rare autoimmune disease of unknown etiology, characterized by episodic inflammation of cartilaginous structures throughout the body (e.g., the ears, nose, upper respiratory tract, chest wall, and joints). Noncartilaginous tissues may become involved, particularly those with an abundance of proteoglycans, such as the eye, inner ear, heart, blood vessels, and kidney. Associated diseases such as vasculitis or myelodysplastic syndromes are present in as many as one-third of cases. The severity of the inflammatory process frequently requires the use of immunosuppressive agents. As its name suggests, RPC has an episodic pattern with periods of intense inflammation. Prognosis is variable, with a 5-year survival rate of 45% to 95%, depending on organ involvement and disease or treatment complications.

This disease was first described in 1923 by Rudolf Jaksch von Wartenhorst, an internal medicine physician, when he published the case of a young male with characteristic clinical features and named the disease polychondropathia.1, In 1960 investigators provided a more detailed description and renamed the disease relapsing polychondritis.

### Epidemiology

The worldwide incidence of RPC is unknown, but researchers from Rochester, Minnesota, suggest an annual incidence of 3.5

per million in that community. RPC occurs in all racial-ethnic groups and with similar frequency in men and women. Peak age of onset is 40 to 50 years, but it has been described in children5 and in people older than 80 years. No familial pattern of inheritance has been shown.

### Pathology

### Normal Cartilage

There are three types of cartilage tissue (hyaline, elastic, and fibrocartilage), which differ in the composition of the extracellular matrix. The cellular component of cartilage consists of chondrocytes, whereas the extra-cellular matrix is composed of interlinking fibrils of type II collagen, other collagens, hydrophilic proteoglycan aggregates, and a variety of matrix proteins. One such protein, matrilin-1, is exclusive to the respiratory tract, ears, and xiphisternum in adults and is only found in articular cartilage before skeletal maturity. Cartilage is an avascular structure that derives essential nutrients from adjacent tissue. The composition of cartilage confers resilience to external compressive forces. In healthy adults, turnover of cartilage components is slow, with incomplete repair processes. Degradation of collagen fibrils occurs with age, resulting from imbalances between naturally occurring proteolytic enzymes and their inhibitors.

### Relapsing Polychondritis Cartilage

There are limited data on the microscopic changes in tissue affected by RPC, partly because of the low disease incidence and also because the diagnosis is usually made on clinical grounds. In the initial stages, inflammatory cells infiltrate the perichondrium, with evidence of lymphocytes (CD4+ T cells), macrophages, neutrophils, eosinophils, and plasma cells on hematoxylin-eosin staining, whereas the structure of the cartilage appears unaffected.12, Immunofluorescence may reveal deposits of immunoglobulin and cartilage components at the cartilage— perichondrium junction. Later, the inflammatory cells invade the cartilage, releasing proteolytic enzymes such as matrix metalloproteinases and cathepsins.13, As the cartilage is destroyed, it loses its basophilic staining, and elastic and collagen fibers become disrupted.

Necrosis and a reduction in cartilage components may be observed. The cartilage is subsequently replaced by fibrotic tissue, with areas of calcification. Granulation tissue and gelatinous cysts may be observed within involved areas.

### Pathogenesis

Although the pathogenesis of RPC is unknown, evidence supports the concept of an autoimmune process. The presence of inflammatory cells and immune complexes in involved cartilage, the detection of autoantibodies in cartilage components, the association with human leukocyte antigen (HLA)-DR, the frequent concurrence with other autoimmune diseases, and the response to immunosuppressive treatment all support this hypothesis. Researchers have observed autoantibodies to types II, IX, and XI collagen in patients with this disease,9,16-18 and autoantibodies to matrilin-1 and cartilage oligomeric protein (COMP) have been detected in those with respiratory tract involvement.19-22 Type II collagen neoepitope can be found in the urine of patients with active disease. More recently, the serum level of soluble triggering receptor expressed on myeloid cells-1 has been cited as a potential biomarker of disease activity in RPC. Pro-inflammatory chemokines involved in the recruitment of monocytes and modulation of macrophage function, such as monocyte chemoattractant protein-1, macrophage inflammatory protein 1β, and interleukin (IL)-8, are significantly elevated in active RPC compared with controls. TNF expression is also higher in RPC. Furthermore, there is a class II HLA association with RPC. A two-fold increase in HLA-DR4 has been found in RPC, although a specific subtype has not been identified. There is a negative association between the extent of organ involvement in RPC and HLA-DR6.27

Several animal models have helped to elucidate some of the pathogenetic mechanisms underlying RPC. Chondritis can be induced in certain rat or mice species following injection of type II collagen.28, In addition, mice that express HLA-DQ6alphabeta/8alpha-beta transgenes develop a spontaneous form of polychondritis with auricular, nasal, and joint involvement. Experiments that used the matrilin-1-induced rodent model of RPC have demonstrated the importance of T cells, B cells, and complement components in the pathogenesis of this disease. 31 Deletion of IL-10 in this model resulted in increased disease severity, suggesting a role for this endogenous cytokine in suppressing episodic inflammation. The processes involved in the initiation of disease, escalation of the inflammatory response, and subsequent cartilage destruction are poorly understood. In a healthy individual, cartilage is an immunologically privileged site. However, in RPC, cartilage components are exposed and vulnerable to immunologic attack, resulting in a perpetuating process of systemic inflammation and local tissue damage. In genetically susceptible individuals, cartilage microtrauma or molecular mimicry between an infectious/inciting agent and cartilage structures might instigate a cycle of inflammation similar to other autoimmune disorders.13,33

### Clinical Features

Cartilaginous inflammation may initially result in a variety of nonspecific symptoms, including systemic features such as fever, night sweats, weight loss, and fatigue. RPC is more easily diagnosed when the characteristic clinical signs are present.

The diagnostic criteria for RPC are outlined in Table 106.1. Because of the relapsing nature and rarity of the disease, the diagnosis may not be established for some time. In one study, a mean delay of 2.9 years was noted between symptom onset and confirmation of diagnosis. Table 106.2 documents the frequency of clinical presentations in patients with RPC.

### Otorhinologic Disease

The most characteristic manifestation of RPC is auricular chondritis, in which the patient develops acute pain, redness, and swelling of the cartilaginous upper two-thirds of the outer ear, sparing the lobe35 (eFig. 106.1). It may be unilateral or bilateral and resolves spontaneously during a period of several weeks. Repeated episodes result in visible damage to the ear, which takes on a deformed, flaccid appearance, the so-called cauliflower ear (Figs. 106.1A and 106.2), and increased visibility of the underlying blood vessels can give rise to the "blue ear" sign. Although classic for RPC, this is the presenting feature in only 40% of patients, but eventually develops in as many as 85% of patients throughout their disease course. Such swelling of the outer ear causes temporary

conductive deafness. However, sensorineural deafness may result from an associated vasculitis of the internal auditory artery or its branches, leading to additional vertigo in some patients.34, Nasal chondritis develops in approximately 10% of patients at presentation and as many as 70% during the course of their disease.6, Repeated inflammatory episodes result in collapse of the nasal bridge and an alteration of the facial appearance—the so-called saddle-nose deformity (see Fig. 106.1B).

### Respiratory Disease

Involvement of the upper respiratory tract may be life-threatening and should be investigated at an early stage in the disease course. Although present in just 10% of patients at presentation, approximately 50% of those with RPC will ultimately develop pulmonary symptoms that are associated with a worse prognosis. Hoarseness, dysphonia, a persistent dry cough, or anterior neck stiffness could indicate upper-airway disease. Acute inflammation of the tracheobronchial tree may lead to tracheomalacia, dynamic obstruction, and acute respiratory failure, whereas repeated inflammatory episodes can cause subglottic stenosis, chronic dyspnea, and increased susceptibility to infection.22, In some patients, respiratory

symptoms can occur in the absence of the more typical clinical features of RPC, resulting in diagnoses of asthma or obstructive sleep apnea prior to confirmation of the RPC syndrome. 39,

Collapse of the upper airways may be precipitated by attempted intubation or bronchoscopy. Therefore a cautious approach to invasive investigations should be undertaken in patients with suspected RPC. Figures 106.1C and D demonstrate the computed tomographic (CT) and bronchoscopic appearances of a person with RPC. Furthermore, involvement of the rib cage and the development of costochondritis may result in chest pain in such patients.

### Cardiovascular Disease

RPC is most commonly associated with valvular heart disease and large vessel vasculitis and, more rarely with atherosclerosis, pericarditis, and myocarditis.41-49 Although more likely to occur in patients with long-standing disease, involvement of the heart and/or blood vessels may develop acutely with few prior symptoms.34, A review of 440 patients with RPC found a prevalence of aortic regurgitation in 7.7%, mitral regurgitation in 1.8%, and combined valvular disease in 1.6%, all more prevalent in males.' 44 Aortic valve disease is thought to be the result of progressive dilatation of the aortic ring rather than active local inflammation.

Mitral valve incompetence may result from valvitis or papillary muscle involvement. Myocarditis can lead to cardiac failure and conduction system abnormalities.34,

Vascular involvement in RPC ranges from 5% to 25% and affects blood vessels of any size. Aortic disease, including aortitis, aneurysm formation, and dissection, occurs in up to 10% of patients. RPC-associated vasculitis has been observed in a wide variety of locations, including the subclavian, carotid, iliac, renal, vertebral, axillary, femoral, inferior mesenteric, and brachiocephalic vessels, and in one small study was noted to be more common in young females.' 47 Small-vessel vasculitis has also been reported in RPC and may cause end organ damage to the skin, kidneys, testes, sclera, cochleovestibular system, or other areas. 50, Arterial and venous thromboses have been described in patients with RPC. There are also case reports of clinical findings similar to Takayasu's arteritis and the development of aneurysms in vessels smaller than the aorta.' 45

### Eye Disease

As many as 65% of patients with RPC will develop ocular disease, most commonly episcleritis and scleritis. Recurrent inflammation can lead to thinning of the sclera, giving a bluish appearance to the eye. Scleritis associated with RPC is more likely to be bilateral, necrotizing, recurrent, and linked to some visual loss compared with other autoimmune disorders. Keratoconjunctivitis sicca may occur with associated Sjögren's syndrome. Uveitis, retinal vasculitis, and optic neuritis are rare complications. Extraocular muscle palsy, periorbital edema, and proptosis may also occur as part of the RPC symptom complex.2,53

### Renal Disease

Proteinuria and/or hematuria may be observed on urinalysis in approximately 10% of patients with RPC. Renal pathology

shows mesangial proliferation and segmental or pauci-immune necrotizing crescentic glomerulonephritis.54, Electron microscopy may demonstrate immunoglobulin and complement deposits. Renal pathology may also occur in the context of co-existing diseases such as systemic lupus erythematosus or other rheumatic diseases. Patients with RPC and renal involvement have a greater incidence of associated vasculitis and a resultant worse prognosis.

### Neurologic Disease

Central and peripheral nervous system involvement is rare, affecting up to 10% of patients. Cranial neuropathy, particularly of the fifth and seventh cranial nerves, is the most common manifestation, but a wide variety of problems including headache, ataxia, hemiplegia, transverse myelitis, mononeuritis multiplex, aseptic meningitis, encephalopathy, and dementia have been described. Such lesions may be vasculitic or autoimmune in nature. 35,50,56,57

### Mucocutaneous Disease

Skin and mucous membrane changes develop in approximately 50% of patients with RPC. Rashes are present in as many as 35% of patients with primary RPC, whereas 90% of patients with associated myelodysplasia have mucocutaneous involvement. Oral aphthous ulcers are the most common symptom. Peripheral nodules, similar to erythema nodosum, can be noted in approximately 15% of patients. Rare skin lesions include peripheral limb ulcers, livedo reticularis, panniculitis, superficial thrombophlebitis, urticaria, and angioedema. Leukocytoclastic vasculitis, dermal vessel thrombosis, or septal panniculitis may be evident on biopsy. 58,59

### Joint Disease

Musculoskeletal manifestations are common and develop in 75% of patients during the course of the disease. Involvement of the joints may be oligoarticular or polyarticular, most commonly affecting the ankles, wrists, hands, and feet. Recurring pain in the sternoclavicular, costochondral, and manubriosternal joints has been described. However, other joints, including the sacroiliac joints, may also show evidence of inflammation, although it is possible that the presence of sacroilitis relates to the co-existence of a spondyloarthropathy. The arthritis associated with RPC is typically asymmetric, episodic, and nonerosive, and it does not correlate with RPC activity. Nevertheless, joint destruction in RPC has been described.61,62

### Associated Disorders

RPC has been described in association with a variety of other disorders, including rheumatic, vasculitic, and hematologic syndromes. Its co-existence with Behçet disease has led to the acronym MAGIC syndrome: mouth and genital ulcers with inflamed cartilage.63, A recent study outlined comparisons between Behçet disease, MAGIC syndrome, and RPC without additional features, suggesting that all patients who present with chondritis should be screened for associated pathology64 (Table 106.3). In older patients, particularly males, RPC may be linked with myelodysplasia and a worse prognosis.65,

VEXAS (vacuoles, E1 enzyme, x-linked, autoinflammatory, somatic) syndrome is a recently described and rare disease with some features of RPC, such as inflammation of the auricular or nasal cartilage and the multisystem nature of its organ

involvement. However, VEXAS is typically seen in middle-aged or older men and laboratory analysis consistently shows a significant macrocytosis in peripheral blood and cytoplasmic vacuolization of erythroid and myeloid precursors in the bone marrow, and genetic testing demonstrates characteristic mutations in the gene encoding for ubiquitin activating enzyme 167,68 (Table 106.4).

A retrospective study of 142 patients with RPC suggested three clinical phenotypes of this disease: (1) "hematologic," associated with blood-related malignancies and an increased incidence of skin disease and cardiac abnormalities; (2) "respiratory," with predominant tracheobronchial involvement; and (3) "mild" disease with good therapeutic responsiveness and improved prognosis.

### Differential Diagnosis

Auricular chondritis with sparing of the earlobe is characteristic of RPC. Redness and swelling of the whole ear, including the earlobe, may be the result of trauma or exposure to temperature extremes and should be distinguished from RPC. Pseudomonas aeruginosa or Staphylococcus aureus are potential causes of unilateral otitis externa, particularly in immunocompromised patients. Other infections associated with chondritis include leprosy and syphilis. Damage to the nose cartilage may be the result of trauma, local infections, or granulomatous lesions such as anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA)—associated granulomatosis vasculitis or lethal midline granuloma. Intranasal cocaine use should also be considered. A wide variety of inflammatory, rheumatic, and infectious conditions may mimic some features of RPC, particularly when multiple organs are involved. Cogan syndrome is

an inflammatory autoimmune condition that results in keratitis and vestibuloauditory symptoms and may be associated with vascular inflammation, although it is not linked with chondritis. Causes of systemic vasculitis (e.g., ANCA-associated vasculitis, polyarteritis nodosa, Behçet's disease, rheumatoid arthritis, or those associated with connective tissue disorders) should be taken into consideration, especially when the presentation is atypical. Valvular heart disease, particularly aortic incompetence and aortic root dilation, may occur in conditions such as Marfan's syndrome, syphilis, and idiopathic medial cystic necrosis and can also develop in relation to diseases that may coincide with RPC (e.g., ankylosing spondylitis).

### Diagnostic Tests

### Laboratory Tests

There are no specific blood tests for the diagnosis of RPC. Routine laboratory investigations may demonstrate nonspecific findings such as anemia or mild thrombocytosis. The acute phase response is typically elevated during periods of inflammation. Urinalysis should always be performed to determine the presence of subclinical renal disease or infection. Autoimmune tests are nonspecific, except when associated diseases are present concurrently.

### Tissue Sampling and Histopathology

In typical presentations of RPC, a biopsy is not necessary for diagnosis. However, when the diagnosis is unclear, a biopsy of inflamed cartilage may show evidence of perichondritis, as described earlier (Fig. 106.3).9, Areas of skin rash may demonstrate leukocytoclastic vasculitis; other frequent findings include panniculitis, neutrophilic dermatoses, or dermal vessel occlusion.

### Pulmonary Studies

Clinicians should conduct pulmonary function tests in all suspected cases of RPC, even in patients who are asymptomatic at presentation. These tests (including spirometry, lung volumes, and inspiratory/expiratory flow-volume loops) should be repeated in the event of new respiratory symptoms. If the test results are abnormal, CT of the chest is recommended to detect the presence of tracheal or bronchial stenoses or dynamic airway collapse, which may be evident only during the expiratory phase of the respiratory cycle.72-74 Extrapulmonary disease from costochondritis may cause a restrictive pattern on pulmonary function testing. Positron emission tomography/CT (PET/CT) scanning may have additional value because it can identify the presence of inflammation in areas where it is otherwise undetectable. PET/CT can also demonstrate treatment response with a reduction in inflammation after therapeutic intervention 46,75-78 (Fig. 106.4).

Bronchoscopy is warranted only if specifically indicated because the procedure may cause inadvertent damage to the upper airways, with the risk of precipitating respiratory failure. However, indirect laryngoscopy is helpful to monitor airway involvement. Bronchoscopic ultrasound can also be used to monitor disease.

### Cardiac Studies

Echocardiography is necessary to evaluate the aortic root and heart valves, not just at presentation but every few years after diagnosis, even in the absence of overt symptoms. Furthermore, many systemic inflammatory diseases are associated with accelerated atherosclerosis, and this may also be true for patients with

RPC, although because of small numbers of cases, this has not been widely described. Nevertheless, other cardiac disease risk factors should be ascertained.

### Ophthalmologic Studies

Routine retinoscopy should be performed at diagnosis. Referral to a specialist unit is recommended if abnormalities are detected and/ or if symptoms develop.

### Imaging

Plain radiographs of involved joints may show joint space narrowing or periarticular osteopenia. Erosions are not usually observed unless there is an associated rheumatic disorder. Dual radiograph absorptiometry may demonstrate osteopenia as a consequence of the underlying inflammation, prolonged corticosteroid use, or general debility.

### Additional Studies

At present, genetic testing offers little added benefit. Serum levels of cartilage biomarkers such as COMP or indications of an immune response to cartilage (e.g., antibodies to types II, IX, or XI collagen or matrilyin-1) are not routinely available, and their role in disease activity monitoring is unclear.20, Anti-glutamate receptor GluR ε2 autoantibodies have been detected in the cerebrospinal fluid and sera of a patient with RPC-associated limbic encephalitis. The potential use of other biomarkers, such as

urinary type II collagen neoepitope, has been highlighted in the literature. A disease activity index for RPC has been developed by international consensus in order to provide help in clinical assessment and to guide standardization of data for future clinical trials.82,83

### Treatment

Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and low-dose corticosteroids may successfully control minor inflammation of the nose, ear, or chest wall (Table 106.5). Dapsone can also be used for noncritical cartilaginous inflammation,1 and colchicine is of reported benefit in auricular chondritis. However, the presence of potentially life-threatening disease or severe chondritis requires highdose prednisone, typically at a dose of 1 mg/kg, reducing slowly as the inflammation recedes. 1, Although the RPC is usually steroid responsive, it can be difficult to withdraw these drugs completely without risking a flare in disease activity. Many patients require maintenance doses of prednisone and consideration of alternative immunosuppression. Disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drug (DMARD) treatment is indicated in patients who require a steroid-sparing agent and/or in whom life-threatening manifestations have developed.

Because of the rarity of this disease, there are no controlled trials of therapeutic interventions in RPC. However, methotrexate, cyclophosphamide, mycophenolate mofetil, azathioprine, chlorambucil, and cyclosporine have had successful results in some 34, Varied outcomes have been reported with leflupatients. Plasmapheresis has been used in resistant cases.34,95 nomide.93, Furthermore, intravenous immunoglobulin has been used successfully in recalcitrant RPC.

There are several case reports and small case series detailing the use of biologic agents in this disease.97-112 Such drugs are typically initiated in order to reduce corticosteroid use, particularly if oral disease-modifying agents, such as methotrexate, have not been successful in controlling inflammation. TNF inhibitors (TNFi) have been the most frequently studied, with further data available

in smaller numbers for anti-B-cell (rituximab), anti-IL-6 (tocilizumab), anti-IL-1 (anakinra), anti-T-cell (abatacept), and a Janus kinase inhibitor (tofacitinib). One study of 41 RPC patients with 105 biologic drug exposures found a response rate of 62.9% in the first 6 months of treatment, with a complete response rate of just 19%. Patients with an underlying myelodysplastic syndrome had a lower response rate, whereas those with nasal, auricular, or sternal chondritis and with concomitant oral DMARD use tended to have a better clinical outcome.

More recently, a systematic review of available evidence for treatment of RPC was performed. Overall, 177 patients with 247 treatment exposures were found, including TNF inhibitors (n = 92), methotrexate (n = 38), tocilizumab (n = 26), anakinra (n = 21), rituximab (n = 16), abatacept (n = 14), cyclophosphamide (n = 14), and azathioprine (n = 13), with smaller numbers of other drugs such as cyclosporin and dapsone making up the rest. The data suggested that abatacept, tocilizumab, and TNFi had the best outcomes with mean response rates of 72%, 66%, and 64%, respectively. Anakinra and rituximab had weaker response rates of 47% and 43%, respectively. However, for any given drug it should be noted that there was a variation in response between studies, indicating potential differences in disease severity and phenotype. Successful outcomes for autologous stem cell transplantation in treatment-resistant RPC have also been reported.114, It is not clear, however, if any of these treatments overtly influence the natural history of this disease.

A holistic approach to the management of RPC is essential. Knowledge of disease complications and recognition of early pathology may be lifesaving. Special consideration should be given to the management of upper-airway involvement, and the anesthesia team should be made aware of disease in this region before any surgical intervention. Symptomatic airway obstruction might require tracheostomy, tracheal stenting, or nighttime positive pressure ventilation to prevent airway collapse while the patient is asleep. There is limited experience with laryngotracheal reconstruction in patients with RPC, and such interventions should only take place during disease quiescence. 116, Heart surgery to

treat aortic root dilation, aneurysm formation, or valvular disease has a good outcome in most cases, although post-operative dehiscence is a complication in 12%.118, Most cases require postoperative immunosuppression. For patients with sensorineural deafness, cochlear implantation is usually beneficial with significant restoration of hearing. The successful use of bone grafting to correct saddle nose deformity has been reported.121, Neither hormonal activity nor pregnancy is thought to influence disease activity in RPC. However, several case reports have described the treatment of disease flares during pregnancy, typically with corticosteroids, with successful maternal and fetal outcomes. 123-125

### Outcome

RPC is an episodic, progressive disease that results in tissue destruction of target organs. Some patients have a mild course, complicated only by recurrent chondritis, whereas others develop potentially life-threatening problems. The most common cause of death is pulmonary infection, arising as a result of the disease or its immunosuppressive treatment. In young patients, adverse prognostic factors at presentation include anemia, hematuria, upper-airway disease, arthritis, and saddle nose deformity, whereas in older patients (more than 51 years of age), only anemia at presentation and/or myelodysplasia predicts increased mortality. The presence of vasculitis worsens prognosis, with a 5-year survival rate of 45%. In 1986, investigators reported the 10-year survival rate to be 55%, whereas in 1998, perhaps because of improvements in disease monitoring and treatment, another study described a 94% survival rate. 6,34

### Conclusion

RPC is a systemic autoimmune disorder, characterized by episodic inflammation of cartilaginous structures (e.g., the upper aspect of the ears, proximal airways, eyes, kidneys, heart valves, and blood vessels). It may occur in isolation or in association with other inflammatory diseases. Involvement of the trachea or cardiovascular system may have life-threatening consequences. Immunosuppressive treatment, including the use of biologic agents, abrogates disease features. A holistic approach is recommended to improve the morbidity and mortality of these patients. Above all, international collaboration to support clinical trials of therapeutic options in this rare condition is a process likely to yield much-needed data and more focused treatment approaches for the different phenotypes that constitute RPC.

# Heritable Diseases of Connective Tissues

### KEY POINTS

### Introduction

Heritable disorders of connective tissues are a heterogenous group of disorders characterized by abnormalities in skeletal tissues, which include cartilage, bone, tendon, ligament, and muscle. Disorders of connective tissues have been classified based on clinical features, radiographic findings, and molecular criteria. Historically, they are subclassified into those which primarily affect cartilage and bone, which are the skeletal dysplasias, and those that have a more profound effect on connective tissue, which include the EhlersDanlos syndrome group, Marfan syndrome, among others. The skeletal dysplasias are associated with abnormalities in the size and shape of the appendicular and axial skeleton and frequently result in disproportionately short stature. Until the early 1960s, most individuals with short stature were considered to have pituitary dwarfism, achondroplasia (short-limb dwarfism), or Morquio disease (short-trunked dwarfism). Presently, if genetic syndromes with significant skeletal findings and osteochondrodysplasias are considered together, there are more than 750 well-characterized disorders that are classified primarily on the basis of clinical, radiographic, and molecular criteria. With

advances in genomic technologies, including exome and genome analyses, newer findings have made classification of these disorders more complicated and nuanced. There are disorders that are genetically heterogenous, resulting from mutations in multiple genes and with differing modes of inheritance. Further, the same gene, (e.g., fibrillin-1), produces numerous conditions associated with both tall and short statures. This expansion in our understanding of the genetic basis of heritable disorders of the skeleton has led to a deeper appreciation of molecular mechanisms that underlie these disorders. Mutations in these genes encode extracellular matrix proteins, transcription factors, signal ligands and their respective cognate receptors, signal transducers, intracellular/ cytoskeletal adaptor molecules, enzymes, molecular chaperones, RNA processing molecules, ciliary proteins, and genes of lesserknown function.

### Skeletal Dysplasias: Overview

The skeletal dysplasias, or osteochondrodysplasias, are defined as disorders that are associated with a generalized skeletal abnormality. While each skeletal dysplasia is relatively rare, collectively the birth incidence of these disorders is almost 1 in 5000.3 These disorders range in severity from precocious arthropathy to perinatal lethality due to respiratory failure. Individuals with these disorders can have significant complications including orthopedic, neurologic, craniofacial, and psychologic effects. Many of these individuals seek medical attention for orthopedic complaints due to fractures, ongoing pain, arthritic complaints in large joints, and back pain due to ongoing abnormalities in bone, cartilage, tendons, and ligaments. Other organ systems can be affected, and in addition, as these patients age, addressing medical comorbidities is an important element of clinical care.

### Embryology

The human skeleton (from the Greek skeletos, meaning "dried up") is a complex organ consisting of 206 bones (126 appendicular bones, 74 axial bones, and 6 ossicles). The musculoskeletal system—including tendons, ligaments, and muscles in addition to cartilage and bone—has multiple embryonic origins and serves many key functions throughout life, including linear growth, mechanical support for movement, a blood and mineral reservoir, and protection of vital organs.

The patterning and architecture of the skeleton occurs during fetal development. During that period, the number, size, and the shape of the future skeletal elements are determined, and this process is under complex and exquisitely timed genetic control. Uncondensed mesenchyme undergoes cellular condensations (the cartilage anlagen) at sites of future bones, and this occurs by two mechanisms. In the process of endochondral ossification, mesenchyme first differentiates into a cartilage model (anlagen), and then the center of the anlagen degrades, mineralizes, and is removed by osteoclast-like cells. This process spreads up and down the bones and allows for vascular invasion and influx of osteoprogenitor cells. The periosteum in the midshaft region of the bone produces osteoblast progenitors, which then synthesize the cortex. This is known as the primary ossification center. At the ends of the cartilage anlagen, a similar process leading to the removal of cartilage occurs (secondary center of ossification), leaving a portion of the cartilage model "trapped" between the expanding primary and secondary ossification centers. This area is referred to as a cartilage growth plate or epiphysis.

There are four chondrocyte cell types in the growth plate: reserve, resting, proliferative, and hypertrophic. These growth plate chondrocytes undergo a tightly regulated program of proliferation, hypertrophy, degradation, and then replacement by bone leading to the primary spongiosa. The periosteum is a specialized cell layer that surrounds the cartilage growth plate and is a critical signaling center and source of progenitor cells to both cartilage growth and bone formation. This is the major mechanism underlying skeletogenesis and is how bones increase in length and how the articular surfaces increase in diameter. In contrast, the flat bones of the cranial vault and part of the clavicles and pubis form by intramembraneous ossification, during which fibrous tissue, derived from mesenchymal cells, differentiates directly into osteoblasts, which then directly lay down bone. These processes are under specific, temporal, and genetic control and abnormalities in the genes that encode these pathways frequently lead to skeletal dysplasias.

### Cartilage Structure

Collagens are the most abundant proteins in mammals. Collagen accounts for two-thirds of the adult weight attributed to articular cartilage and provides significant strength and structure to tissues. Collagens are a family of 29 proteins that consist of single molecules (monomers) that associate into three polypeptide chains to form a triple-helix structure. In the triple helix, every third amino acid is a glycine residue, and the general chain structure is denoted as Gly-X-Y, where the X and Y amino acids are commonly proline and hydroxyproline. The collagen helix can be compromised of identical chains (homotrimeric), as in type II collagen, or can consist of different collagen chains (heterotrimeric), as seen in collagen type I.

Collagens are widely distributed throughout the body, and 45 collagen gene products are expressed in a tissue-specific manner. Collagens are further classified by the structures they form in the extracellular matrix. The most abundant collagens are the fibrillar types (I, II, III, V, and XI), and their extensive cross-linking provides mechanical strength that is necessary for high-stress tissue such as cartilage, bone, and skin. Another collagen species is the fibril-associated collagens with interrupted triple helices (FACIT), which includes collagen types IX, XII, XIV, and XVI. These collagens interact with fibrillar collagens, as well as other extracellular molecules including aggrecan, cartilage oligomeric matrix protein (COMP), and other sulfated proteoglycans. Collagens types VIII

and X are nonfibrillar, short-chain collagens, and type X collagen is the most abundant extracellular matrix molecule expressed by hypertrophic chondrocytes during endochondral ossification. The major collagens of articular cartilage are fibrillar collagen including types II, IX, XI, and X. In developing cartilage, the core fibrillar network is a cross-linked copolymer of collagens II, IX, and XI10 and forms the backbone complex to which other structural proteins bind. Mutations in genes that encode these collagens result in varying skeletal dysplasias and highlight the importance of these molecules in skeletal development.

### Classification and Nomenclature

As mentioned above, in the 1970s, there was recognition of the genetic and clinical heterogeneity of these disorders, and there was a new awareness of the complexity of heritable conditions leading to skeletal dysplasia. As a result, there have been multiple attempts to classify these disorders in a manner that clinicians and scientists could effectively use to diagnose and determine their pathogenicity (International Nomenclature of Constitutional Diseases of Bone, 1970, 1977, 1983, 1992, 2001, 2005, 2010, 2019, and 2023).1, Initial categories were purely descriptive and clinically based. With recent advances in the ability to determine the genetic bases of these diseases, classification has evolved into one that combines the older clinical approach (including the eponyms and Greek terms) and incorporates these disorders into families that share a common molecular basis or pathway. The most widely used method for differentiating the skeletal disorders has been through the detection of skeletal radiographic abnormalities. Radiographic classifications are based on the different parts of the long bones that are abnormal (epiphyses, metaphyses, and diaphyses) (Fig. 107.1). These epiphyseal, metaphyseal, and diaphyseal disorders can be further differentiated depending on whether or not the spine is involved (spondyloepiphyseal, spondylometaphyseal, or spondyloepimetaphyseal dysplasias). Moreover, each of these classes of conditions can be further differentiated into distinct disorders based on other clinical and radiographic findings.

### Clinical Evaluation and Features

The skeletal dysplasias are generalized disorders of the skeleton and usually result in disproportionately short stature. As a general comment, most individuals with disproportionately short stature have skeletal dysplasias, and those with proportionate short stature are more likely to have an endocrine, nutritional, prenatal-onset growth deficiency, or another nonskeletal dysplasia genetic disorder. However, there are exceptions to the rule, such as congenital hypothyroidism, which is associated with disproportionately short stature. Disorders such as mild osteogenesis imperfecta and hypophosphatasia can be associated with relatively normal body proportions.

A disproportionate body habitus may not be immediately visible on physical examination. Therefore anthropometric measurements, such as the upper/lower segment (U/L) ratio, sitting height, and arm span must be measured when considering the possibility of a skeletal dysplasia, and should be measured in centimeters (Fig. 107.2). Sitting height is an accurate measure of head and trunk length, but it requires special equipment for precise measurements. Upper/lower ratios are easy to obtain and provide an accurate measurement of proportion. The lower segment is measured from the symphysis pubis to the floor at the inside of heel. The upper segment is measured by subtracting the lower segment measurement from the total height. For example,

a Caucasian child between the ages of 8 to 10 years has a U/L segment ratio of approximately 1.0 and an U/L segment ratio of 0.95 as an adult. Individuals presenting with disproportionately short stature will have altered ratios depending on whether they have short limbs, short trunk, or both. For example, an individual with short limbs and relatively normal trunk will have an increased U/L segment ratio, and an individual with relatively normal limbs but short trunk will have a diminished

U/L segment ratio (Fig. 107.2). Another means of determining whether there is disproportion is based on arm span measurements, which are measured from tip to tip of the third finger. Arm span length is typically very close to total height (one to one ratio) in an average-proportioned individual. A short-limbed individual will have an arm span considerably shorter than their height.

As in any disorder that has a genetic basis, it is critical to obtain an accurate family history, and this should include any history of previously affected children or parental consanguinity. The skeletal dysplasias are genetically heterogenous and can be inherited as autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X-linked recessive, X-dominant, or Y-linked. Less frequent genetic mechanisms of disease, including germline mosaicism, somatic mosaicism, uniparental disomy, microdeletion syndromes, and mutations in regulatory microRNAs (miRNAs) have been observed. For many patients and families, accurate diagnosis and recurrence risk can have significant impact on reproductive decisions. Another consideration for patients with short stature is that there is increased nonassortative mating, which leads to reproductive outcomes that have been previously unknown. For example, homozygous achondroplasia is usually lethal, and many newborns that inherit two dominant mutations (compound heterozygotes) are often more significantly affected due to the synergistic effects of two simultaneous conditions on the skeleton. It is also important to obtain accurate history relative to the onset of short stature and whether it developed immediately in the postnatal period or was noticed at age 2 or 3. Of the more than 750 skeletal dysplasias, many are prenatal in onset, but there are also many that do not result in disproportionately short stature and joint discomfort until childhood.

A detailed physical examination may reveal a diagnosis or help differentiate the most likely group of possible diagnoses. It is critical, once disproportion and short stature has been established and the limbs are involved, to determine which segment is involved:

upper segment (rhizomelic; humeri and femora), middle segment (mesomelic; radii, ulnae, tibiae and fibulae), and distal segment (acromelic; hands and feet). Numerous craniofacial features are seen in the skeletal disorders. Affected individuals frequently have disproportionately large heads or relative macrocephaly compared with their height percentile. Frontal bossing and a flattened nasal bridge is very characteristic of achondroplasia, one of the most common skeletal dysplasias. Cleft palate and micrognathia are commonly found in the type II and XI collagen abnormalities. 16, Abnormal flattening of the midface with a turned-up nose is frequently found in the chondrodysplasia punctata disorders, 18 and abnormal swollen pinnae are seen in diastrophic dysplasia. Individuals with skeletal dysplasias should be screened for ophthalmologic and hearing abnormalities since many of these disorders are associated with vision deficits and hearing loss.

Further evaluation of the hands and feet can further differentiate these disorders. Postaxial polydactyly is characteristically found in chondroectodermal dysplasia (EllisVan Creveld syndrome) and the short-rib polydactyly syndrome disorders. Short, hypermobile, radially displaced thumbs and medially deviated halluxes are seen in diastrophic dysplasia. Nails can be abnormally hypoplastic in chondroectodermal dysplasia, short and broad in cartilage hair hypoplasia, and almost absent in nail patella syndrome. Club feet or equinovarus can be seen in many disorders including Kneist dysplasia, spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia congenita, Larsen syndrome, and diastrophic dysplasia. Fractures may occur in several types of disorders including those that result from undermineralized bone (e.g., osteogenesis imperfecta, hypophosphatasia, achondrogenesis type 1A) or those that result from over mineralized bone (e.g., osteopetrosis syndromes and dysosteosclerosis). Other conditions with abnormal bone shape (e.g., gracile bone dysplasia) or genetic disorders with poor bone quality (e.g., Glass syndrome) may also be associated with fractures. 20,

Other organ systems can be involved, though not commonly. Congenital cardiac defects are seen in chondroectodermal dysplasia (e.g., atrial septal defects), the short-rib polydactyly syndrome disorders (complex outlet defects including isolated ventricular septal defects), and Larsen syndrome (ventricular septal defects). Gastrointestinal anomalies are rare among the skeletal disorders, but congenital megacolon can be seen in cartilage hair hypoplasia, malabsorption syndrome in SchwachmannDiamond syndrome, and omphaloceles in oto-palato-digital syndrome and atelosteogenesis I. Causes of respiratory dysfunction are multifactorial in etiology. Craniofacial abnormalities (e.g., cleft palate, midface hypoplasia, micrognathia) may lead to obstructive apnea. Cartilage defects can lead to laryngo-tracheo-broncho-malacia. Intrinsic lung disease may be present if the genetic mutation involved adversely effects connective tissues in the lung, resulting in abnormal alveolar structure. Abnormal chest wall compliance and deformity (e.g., kyphoscoliosis) can compromise tidal volumes.22,23

### Diagnosis s and Testing

After obtaining a thorough family history and physical examination, the next step is to obtain a full set of skeletal radiographs or genetic skeletal survey. A full series of skeletal views, including anterior, lateral, and Towne (angled anteroposterior) views of the skull, anterior and lateral views of the entire spine, and anteroposterior views of the pelvis and extremities, with separate views of the hands and feet, is optimal, especially after the newborn period. Most of the important clues to diagnosis are in skeletal radiographs that are obtained prior to puberty. Once the epiphyses have

fused to the metaphyses, determining the precise diagnosis can be exceedingly challenging. If an adult is evaluated, attempts should be made to obtain any available radiographs from childhood. There are many subtle clues in these skeletal radiographs that can lead to a precise diagnosis. For example, punctate calcifications in the areas of the epiphyses in the chondrodysplasia punctata disorders, which are not seen in adulthood, multiple ossification centers of the calcaneus in many disorders,24 and the pattern of hand shortening can aid in differentiating many disorders.

After obtaining radiographs, close attention should be paid to the specific parts of the skeleton (spine, limbs, pelvis, skull) involved and to the location of the lesions (epiphyses, metaphyses, and spondyl components) (Fig. 107.3). As mentioned above, these radiographic abnormalities can change with age, and if possible serial radiographs that span age periods should be reviewed. The presence of fractures is a clue to diagnosis, for example, in osteogenesis imperfecta and severe hypophosphatasia. In older individuals, fractures may be seen in disorders associated with increased mineralization, such as the osteopetrosis syndromes.

Morphologic studies of chondro-osseus tissue have revealed specific abnormalities in many of the skeletal dysplasias, 25 although with advances in genomic technologies, these studies are done with much less frequency. However, histologic evaluation of chondro-osseous morphology can be especially helpful in the research arena (Fig. 107.4). These studies are performed on cartilage growth plate and bone and have led to important insights into pathogenesis. On morphologic grounds, the chondrodysplasias can be broadly classified into disorders characterized by abnormalities in (1) endochondral ossification, (2) cellular morphology, (3) matrix morphology, and (4) in chondro-osseous transformation. For example, in thanatophoric dysplasia there is a defect in endochondral ossification with a very short if almost hypertrophic zone, a shortened proliferative zone, and overgrowth of the periosteum. In pseudoachondroplasia, there is a distinct lamellar pattern (alternating electron-dense and electron-lucent lamellae) in the rough endoplasmic reticulum of chondrocytes and a grossly

abnormal matrix in diastrophic dysplasia that causes a characteristic ring around the chondrocytes. These findings are diagnostic for these disorders, and overlapping histologic findings have been used to mechanistically tie disorders together with disorders across a phenotypic spectrum placed in bone families based on similar cartilage growth plate morphologic abnormalities.

There has been significant progress in the molecular diagnosis of these disorders. Molecular testing can be used to confirm a clinical and radiographic diagnosis, to predict carrier status in those families at risk for a recessive disorder, and for prenatal diagnosis of at-risk fetuses in some cases. With commercial availability of skeletal dysplasia panels, high and low bone mass gene panels, and exome sequence analysis for rare disorders not available on panels, molecular diagnosis can be achieved in most cases. If the clinical diagnosis is definitive or there is an established familial molecular variant, variant genes can be directly interrogated by testing, if needed.

### Management and Treatment

The optimal management of this diverse set of disorders requires an understanding of their natural history. This is often best accomplished by centers that have a multidisciplinary approach, including adult and pediatric physicians, as well as geneticists, orthopedists, rheumatologists, otolaryngologists, neurologists, neurosurgeons, and ophthamologists who are committed to the care of these patients.

Most medical complications in these disorders result from skeletal manifestations and vary depending on the specific disorder. For example, in disorders associated with significant odontoid hypoplasia such as Morquio disease, type II collagenopathies, metatropic dysplasia, and Larsen syndrome, flexion—extension films should be monitored at regular intervals to assess for C1-C2 subluxation. If there is evidence of significant subluxation, surgery

for C1-C2 fixation is indicated. Some providers support flexion and extension radiographic evaluation, including MRI of the neck in all cases of skeletal dysplasia, since so many of these disorders have cervical vertebral abnormalities. Genu varum, or bowed legs, can occur in many skeletal disorders. Causes are multifactorial and can include asymmetric growth within the physes and overgrowth of the fibula. This can lead to abnormal gait biomechanics and associated knee or ankle pain. Surgical correction of genu varum has traditionally been done via osteotomies. More recently, guided growth (eight-plate) techniques are being utilized. Children and adults with skeletal dysplasias should have regular eye and hearing exams since they may be at increased risk for myopia, retinal degeneration, glaucoma, and hearing loss depending on the disorder.

Frequently, patients with these disorders, which involve the epiphyseal structures, have significant joint pain and functional limitations. Since most of these disorders result from mutations in genes critical to cartilage function, joint cartilage may not provide adequate support and cushioning for function. Many of these patients seek attention for joint pain. Evaluation should include radiographs and MRI, when appropriate, to determine the etiology of the pain. In some disorders such as the type II collagenopathies, pseudoachondroplasia, multiple epiphyseal dysplasia (MED), and cartilage hair hypoplasia, by adulthood, so little cartilage remains at the knee or hips that joint replacement is indicated for pain relief. Lastly, weight control in adults with short stature is an ongoing issue with obesity contributing to inactivity, loss of function, and adult-onset diseases such as diabetes, hypertension, and coronary artery disease.

Achondroplasia is the most common of the nonlethal skeletal dysplasias (approximately 1 in 20,000) and serves as an example of how to approach these disorders, particularly because the incidence and type of medical complications evolve over the lifespan of the individual. People with achondroplasia have typical intelligence and typical lifespan and can lead independent and productive lives. The mean final height in achondroplasia is 130 cm for men and 125 cm for women. Diagnosis-specific growth and developmental charts have been developed for tracking linear growth, head circumference, weight, and gross-motor and development milestones. 28-31

In early infancy, there is a potential for serious compression of the cervico-medullary spinal cord secondary to a narrow foramen magnum, cervical canal, or both. Clinically, these infants show central apnea, sleep apnea, profound hypotonia, motor delay, excessive sweating, or neurologic abmormalities (e.g., clonus, unilateral strength differences, hyper-reflexia, or head preference). Flexion/extension MRI with flow studies is necessary to assess for stenosis or myelopathy. If present, decompression surgery is indicated. Other complications include upper airway obstruction, otitis media (serous or infectious), thoracolumbar kyphosis, and hydrocephalous in a small number of individuals. Recurrent ear infections can lead to chronic serous otitis media and hearing loss. Tympanic membrane tube placement is indicated in many of these patients. From early childhood, and as the child begins to walk, they can develop several orthopedic manifestations, including progressive genu vara, exaggerated lumbar lordosis, and hip flexion contractures. Craniofacial abnormalities lead to dental malocclusion, and appropriate treatment is necessary. As adults, the main potential medical complication is impingement of the spinal root canals, which can manifest with lower limb paresthesias, claudication, clonus, bladder, or bowel dysfunction. It

is critical that these complaints are addressed in a timely fashion since decompression surgery may prevent paralysis.

Growth hormone replacement has not been effective in increasing height in children with achondroplasia. Surgical limb lengthening has been employed successfully to increase limb length by up to 12 inches,34 but patients need to recognize that this technique needs to be done during the teen years, is performed over a 2-year period, and can be associated with complications. Since the discovery of the causal genetic defect in 1994,35 the molecular consequences of the activating mutation in fibroblast growth factor receptor 3 (FGFR3) have been elucidated. Most individuals with achondroplasia are heterozygous for the mutation, a G → A transition at nucleotide 1138, leading to the amino acid change Gly380Arg in mature protein. This amino acid change results in the constitutive activation of FGFR3, which results in decreased cell proliferation and differentiation mediated through increased activation of mitogenactivated protein kinase (MAPK).

Several means of pharmacologically decreasing the constitutive signaling above have been identified. Presently, there is one treatment that has been approved for use in children with achondroplasia: vosoritide or VOXZOGO™m 30 Vosoritide is a 39-amino acid analog of C-type natriuretic peptide (CNP). Vosoritide binds to the natriuretic peptide receptor 2 (NPR2), which reduces FGFR3 activity via inhibition of the FGFR3mediated MAPK signaling pathway. Clinical trials have shown that daily treatment with vosoritide, a subcutaneous injection, had persistent positive effects on growth with increases in annualized growth of ~1.57 cm/year over placebo. Ongoing studies are needed to determine whether earlier and longer treatment durations decrease the frequency of symptomatic spinal stenosis and foramen magnum stenosis or change the final adult stature of patients taking vosoritide.

Throughout their lives, individuals with achondroplasia and other skeletal dysplasias and their families experience various psychosocial challenges. This can be addressed by specialized medical and social support systems. Interactions with advocacy groups such as Little People of America (LPA) (http://www.lpaonline.org) can provide both emotional support and medical information.

### Biochemical and Molecular Abnormalities

Based on similarities in clinical, radiographic, and histomorphologic characteristics, heritable disorders of connective tissue have been placed into bone dysplasia "families."39 These families share common pathophysiologic or pathway mechanisms. In recent years, there have been substantial improvements in our understanding of the basic biology of these disorders. This has resulted from advances in the human genome project that improved various methodologies allowing for identification of the responsible genes. Genes associated with the osteochondrodysplasias can be organized into several categories to facilitate understanding of their pathogenesis: (1) defects in extracellular proteins; (2) defects in metabolic pathways (enzymes, ion channels, and transporters); (3) defects in folding and degradation of macromolecules; (4) defects in hormones and signal transduction; (5) defects in nuclear proteins; (6) defects in oncogenes and tumor suppressor genes; (7) defects in RNA and DNA processing molecules; (8) defects in intracellular structural proteins; (9) defects in chaperones; (10) defects in ciliary components; and (11) genes coding

proteins with functions that remain unknown. Examples of the molecular mechanisms involved in select skeletal dysplasias are provided below.

### Defects in Extracellular Structural Proteins

Type II Collagen and Type XI Collagen. Since type II collagen is found primarily in cartilage, the nucleus pulposus, and the vitreous of the eye, it has been hypothesized that skeletal disorders with significant spine and eye abnormalities would result from defects in type II collagen.
