Indeed, type II collagen defects have been identified in a spectrum of disorders ranging from lethal to mild arthropathy, including achondrogenesis II, hypochondrogenesis, spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia congenita, platyspondylic dysplasia Torrance type, spondlyoepimetaphyseal dysplasia (COL2A1-related), Kniest dysplasia, spondyloperipheral dysplasia (COL2A1-related), spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia with metatarsal shortening (COL2A1-related), Stickler syndrome (COL2A1-related), and dysplasia of the proximal femoral epiphyses (COL2A1-related). Together, these disorders are referred to as type II collagenopathies, and all result from heterozygosity for mutations in the gene COL2A1 that encodes type II collagen. 40,

Mutations that result in a substitution for a triple-helical glycine residue appear to be the most common type of mutation.' 42-44 There are some correlations between the location of the mutation and the disease phenotype. In spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia congenita (SEDC), glycine substitutions are scattered throughout the molecule. However, in Kniest dysplasia, mutations are more prominent in the amino-terminal end of the molecule.45-47 Stickler syndrome is genetically heterogenous and results from mutations in COL2A1, COL11A1, and COL11A2.48, In Stickler syndrome, the COL2A1 and COL1 1A1 mutations tend to be nonsense mutations resulting in premature translation stop codons. Patients with COL1 1A1 mutations, however, tend to demonstrate a more severe eye phenotype and hearing loss than patients with COL2A1 mutations.

Individuals heterozygous for various COL11A2 mutations have a nonocular form of Stickler syndrome, which is consistent with the absent expression of COL11A2 in the vitreous humor. COL11A2 is not expressed in the vitreous body and is replaced by COL5A2 in the ocular vitreous. Oto-spondylo-megaepiphyseal dysplasia (OSMED) is a rare disorder due to mutations in COL11A2 that can be inherited in both an autosomal recessive fashion and an autosomal dominant fashion. These disorders have radiographic similarities to Kniest dysplasia but are associated with profound sensorineural hearing loss and lack of ocular involvement. To add to the spectrum of type XI mutations, both dominantly and recessively inherited mutations in COL1 1A1 and COL1 1A2, respectively, can produce the very severe skeletal dysplasia, fibrochondrogenesis.52,

Cartilage Oligomeric Matrix Protein. Heteroyzgosity for mutations in COMP leads to both pseudoachondroplasia and MED. COMP is a member of the thrombospondin family of proteins and consists of an epidermal growth factor domain and a calcium-binding calmodulin domain. In both pseudoachondroplasia and MED, disease-producing mutations occur in the calmodulin domain, with a minority in the globular carboxyterminal domain. Both these disorders are associated with earlyonset osteoarthritis, particularly of the hips and knees, leading to chronic pain and joint replacement surgery in many individuals during early adulthood.

### Specific Heritable Disorders of Connective Tissue

### Osteogenesis Imperfecta

Osteogenesis imperfecta (OI) or brittle bone disease is a heritable disorder of bone and was one of the first genetic disorders hypothesized to result from a defect in collagen. While OI represents a form of osteochondrodysplasia, it will be discussed separately from the other chondrodysplasias delineated above. OI is a generalized disorder of connective tissue that predominantly affects the skeletal system and affects approximately 1 in 20,000 individuals. OI is a genetically and phenotypically heterogeneous disorder resulting from mutations in at least 22 different genes. More than 80% of OI cases result from dominantly inherited mutations in COL1A1 and COL1A2, which encode the α1 (I) and α2(I) chains of type I procollagen.59, The products of the remaining OI-associated genes are involved in type I procollagen biosynthesis, post-translational modifications, trafficking, cross-linking of telopeptide residues, osteoblast differentiation and function, and processes involved in bone mineralization. All forms of OI share the features of low bone mass, propensity to fracture, and short stature. While there is extensive genetic heterogeneity, many clinicians prefer the clinical categorizations of patient phenotypes into mild, moderate, severe, and very-severe/lethal groups. Since there is enormous clinical variability in these types, the subtypes will be discussed separately.

### Mild Osteogenesis Imperfecta (Type I)

Individuals with OI type I account for the majority of OI cases overall and demonstrate a relatively mild disease phenotype in terms of clinical course, the extent of skeletal deformity, and the radiologic appearance of the skeleton. Individuals usually have shortened stature for age or compared with unaffected family members, although reductions in stature are less than that observed in other forms of OI. In general, these patients experience an estimated 5 to 15 major fractures before puberty, as well as several minor traumatic fractures of the digits or involving small bones of the feet. Characteristically, the fracture rate falls dramatically after puberty only to increase during later life. Broadly speaking, prepubertal children average 1 fracture/year. In OI type I, long bone fractures usually heal without significant deformity, infrequently requiring the insertion of intramedullary rods and rarely resulting in fracture nonunion.

Although this form of OI is inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion, an individual may be the first affected in their family due to incomplete penetrance. Physical examination findings in type I OA include blue sclerae that can transition to gray to pale blue in adulthood. Arcus senilis, unrelated to lipid abnormalities, may occur in some patients. Other reported ocular defects include scleromalacia, keratoconus, and retinal hemorrhage. Teeth can show dentinogenesis imperfecta (DI) due to the effects of mutations on tooth dentin. Deciduous and permanent teeth (usually less affected) can have an opalescent and translucent appearance, which tends to darken with age. While tooth enamel is normal, the dentin is dysplastic, leading to chipping of enamel, erosion, and breakage. DI can be seen in all forms of OI. The prevalence of DI increases with OI severity.

During the second and third decades of life, a characteristic high-frequency sensorineural or mixed hearing loss can be detected. The incidence of mitral valve prolapse is not increased in these patients compared with the population at large, but

individual kindreds with increased diameter of the aortic root or subjects with aortic regurgitation have been reported. Many patients complain of easy bruising, and this may result from the effects of mutations on both the skin and the cutaneous blood vessels.

Mildly affected patients may not have fractures at birth, although clavicular fractures are occasionally detected post-delivery. Radiographically, affected newborns can have wormian bones seen on lateral views of the skull, and osteopenia is often detected through the skeleton, especially the spine (Fig. 107.5). Many cases of type I OI are so mild as to be missed on routine radiographic examination. Following birth, the frequency of fracture depends on the physical activity levels, the need for immobilization after lower extremity fractures, the attitude of the family toward independent activity, and genetic background. Mild scoliosis approximating 20 degrees is common.

Measurement of bone mineral density (BMD) by dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry (DEXA) at any age discloses a significant decrease associated with increased fracture risk. T scores (i.e., standard deviation from the young-adult mean BMD) are frequently in the range of -2.5 to -4.0 at the lumbar spine or proximal femur, consistent with the diagnosis of osteoporosis as defined by the World Health Organization (WHO). Z scores can be used in children to control for age, race, and sex in the analysis of BMD.

Molecular Pathology. OI type I results from mutations affecting the COL1A1(I) and COL1A2(I) polypeptide chains of type I collagen. Cultured fibroblasts from individuals with mild OI synthesize reduced quantities (approximately one-half) of the expected concentration of type I collagen. Most of the reported mutations in OI type I are nonsense and frameshift mutations and thus are predicted to lead to premature termination codons, although there are some exceptions.67,68

### Very Severe/Lethal Osteogenesis Imperfecta (Ol Type II)

Approximately 10% of OI patients have the very-severe/lethal neonatal form of the disease. Most cases result from sporadic mutations; however, recently recessively inherited forms of the disease have been documented.69-71 Infants with OI type II present with severe bone fragility, multiple intrauterine fractures at various stages of healing, deformed extremities, and occasionally hydrops fetalis. Radiographic features include wormian bones, multivertebral fractures, concertina-like compression fractures of the long bones and beading of the ribs due to healing callus formation.

Molecular Pathology. Most cases occur de novo, as new dominant mutations; however, autosomal recessive forms have been established, as has recurrence based on germline mosaicism. The biochemical abnormality in lethal OI is the inability to synthesize and secrete normal type I collagen. As a result, the amount of type I collagen in bone is low, much of the secreted collagen is abnormally overmodified, and the quantity of the minor collagens, types III and V, is relatively high. Bone collagen fibers are thinner then normal, and at the intracellular level, type I collagen is retained within dilated endoplasmic reticulum. Similar to most cases of OI, mutations in the genes encoding COL1A1 and COL1A2A lead to the dominant form or de novo form of lethal OI. Single glycine substitutions with the Gly-X-Y triplet of either COL1Aland COL1A2 lead to this form of OI, as do some small deletions, all producing severe effects on the triple helix. Recessive forms account for a small number of these cases. Some of these recessive forms result from mutations in the genes encoding either CRTAP (cartilage-associated protein), P3H1 (prolyl-3-hydroxylase 1), or Cyclophilin B (also known as peptidylpropyl

isomerase B or PPBI). These molecules form a complex that hydroxylates a third position residue at proline 986 (Pro986). This modification of a single residue is thought to stabilize the collagen helix, although the mechanism of disease production is probably much more complicated, and this protein may act as a chaperone complex.

### Progressively Deforming Osteogenesis Imperfecta (Type Ill)

The deforming variant represents the classic form of OI. Similar to very-severe/lethal OI (OI type II), most cases are autosomal dominant and form de novo, although there are some patients with inherited forms type III OI. Recurrent cases based on autosomal recessive inheritance due to mutations in numerous recessively inherited genes have been recently demonstrated. This variant of OI is characterized by progressive deformity of the limbs and kyphoscoliosis, thorax deformity, and a significantly short stature. The extent of growth retardation is remarkable, and in many adults the height may not surpass 3 feet (90 to 100 cm). Abnormal cranial molding occurs in utero and during infancy, producing frontal bossing and a characteristic triangular shaped facies. Radiographically, wormian bones and delayed closure of the fontanelles may be observed well into the first decade.

Pulmonary function can be diminished because of distortion of the spine and thorax and can progress over time and lead to restrictive lung disease and sleep apnea. In the neonatal and infant periods of life, in addition to the skeletal deformities, there is increased chest wall compliance that may require respiratory support. Over time, and with treatment, the increased chest wall compliance may resolve. Unfortunately because of diminished vital capacity, pulmonary insufficiency is a leading cause of death in subjects with OI type III. Many patients with scoliosis greater than 60 degrees develop respiratory compromise and require pulmonary support, including supplemental oxygen.

Platybasia due to soft bone at the base of the skull may cause the external ear canals to slant upward as the base of the skull settles on the cervical vertebrae. This distortion may lead to communicating

or obstructive hydrocephalus, cranial nerve palsies, and upper and lower motor neuron lesions. Headache, diplopia, nystagmus, cranial nerve neuralgia, decline in motor function, urinary dysfunction, and respiratory compromise are complications of basilar invagination. As opposed to OI type I, most affected OI type III patients have white sclera as adults. Approximately 75% of patients with type III OI have DI, necessitating constant dental care throughout childhood. Severe hearing impairment occurs in 20% of patients, although milder degrees of hearing loss are more common.

The skeleton in these patients has significant osteopenia, leading to multiple fractures in the upper and lower extremities and vertebral bodies, particularly prior to puberty. Unlike type I OI, in which fractures tend to heal without complication, fractures in type III OI frequently lead to skeletal deformity. In addition to marked osteopenia, radiographs demonstrate thinning of cortical bone, narrowing of the diaphysis, and widening of the metaphysis, which can merge into a dysplastic epiphyseal zone filled with whorls of partially calcified cartilage (i.e., popcorn deformity). Osteoporosis leads to collapse of vertebral end plates, contributing to worsening kyphoscoliosis. Pectus excavatum or pectus carinatum adds to thoracic deformity. In addition, lack of weightbearing increases the severity of osteoporosis and increases the risk of fracture. Many individuals with type III OI become wheelchair bound at an early age or walk with mechanical assistance.

Molecular Pathology. The molecular basis of OI type III is very similar to OI type II. Most of the cases result from heterozygosity for mutations in COL1A1 and COL1A2. These mutations are glycine substitutions scattered through the triple helix, as well as in-frame deletions. As in OI type II, familial recurrences result from recessively inherited mutations.

### Moderate Osteogenesis Imperfecta (Type IV)

Clinically, the phenotype of patients with moderately severe OI (OI type IV) falls between the milder OI type I and the more severe OI type III, and this diagnosis is somewhat subjective. In most cases, this type is usually inherited in an autosomal dominant

fashion. Fractures can be seen at birth, although some patients may not experience an initial fracture until beginning to bear weight or ambulate. The extent of skeletal deformity involving the spine, thorax, and extremities is usually intermediate between that of types I and III OI, and these patients also have short stature and frequently have scoliosis. Patients may have mild facial dysmorphisms, although typically not as severe as OI type III. Hearing loss occurs but is less frequent than in OI types I and III.

Most fractures occur during childhood and may recur during the postmenopausal period in women or in men older than age 50 years. Long-bone deformities tend to develop after fractures, which may lead to a difficulties with ambulation. Radiographs of the long bones and vertebral bodies demonstrate osteopenia with vertebral collapse. Although there is marked cortical thinning, bowing, and coarsening of trabeculae, the overall architecture of the bone is fairly typical.

Molecular Pathology. Molecular mechanisms underpinning OI type IV are similar to other forms of OI. Causal mutations are found in COL1A1 and COL1A2 and include glycine substitutions and in-frame deletions. At the present time, there is no evidence for an autosomal recessive form of OI type IV.

### Osteogenesis Imperfecta a Type V

This phenotype was first reported in 2000 as a variant within the heterogeneous group classified under OI type IV. In the initial report of seven OI patients, the phenotype was distinguished by the following criteria: moderate fracture history, hyperplastic callus formation, limitation in forearm pronation and supination due to progressive intramembraneous bone formation at the joint, normal sclera, and no DI. Radiographs can demonstrate a dense subphyseal sclerotic band, which is specific for this form of OI. Bone biopsy showed a meshlike appearance of irregularly spaced lamellae, different from the woven bone seen in OI types II, III, and IV.

Molecular Pathology. The etiology of this rare form has been established and results from heterozygosity for mutations in interferon-induced transmembrane protein 5 (IFITM5).

### Histopathology of Bone in Osteogenesis s Imperfecta

The range of histologic appearances of bone in the different OI phenotypes is as variable as the clinical phenotypes. Undermineralization and overmineralization of bone have been recognized within the same specimen. Bone histomorphology appears relatively normal in OI type I, but osteopenia due to thin lamellar plates and diminished cortical width is evident. Immature woven bone and lamellar disarray are characteristic of more severe OI phenotypes.

### Treatment

Over the years, there have been multiple attempts to treat OI with a variety of vitamins, hormones, and other agents, none of which has been successful. The list includes administration of mineral supplements, fluoride, androgenic steroids, ascorbic acid, and vitamin D. Since the mid-1990s, bisphosphonates administered parenterally to children has demonstrated favorable results. Intravenously administered pamidronate increases bone mass, decreases skeletal pain and decreases fracture incidence in children with severe OI. Dosage regimens in different series for children and adults have varied from 1 to 3 mg/kg, administered intravenously at 2to 4-month intervals, and lower-dose regimens also have been reported. Beneficial treatment effects are most marked in the spine, where vertebral remodeling may improve

vertebral height. Metabolic studies by have demonstrated transient decreases in serum ionized calcium and increases in serum parathyroid hormone (PTH) with treatment. Major side effects of intravenous bisphosphonate include an acute-phase response occurring most often during the first treatment cycle. In addition to the use of a bisphosphonate, current recommendations also include adequate calcium and vitamin D supplementation to maintain serum vitamin D levels within normal limits. Recently the use of anabolic treatment to build bone has been tested using teriparatide in adult patients in OI, and the study showed that patients with mild OI, but not severe OI, benefitted from treatment. Multiple other types of therapies are being developed or studied in OI and include antibodies targeting receptor activator of nuclear factor kappa-B ligand (RANKL), sclerostin, and transforming growth factor (TGF)β.

The use of surgery to correct deformities and to facilitate weight-bearing has been the subject of several reviews. Multiple osteotomies and realignment of deformed bone over intramedullary rods is an option for many children with severe bowing. Indications include frequent fractures at the apex of the bow, impaired standing, or limb-length inequality due to bowing. Expanding (telescoping) rods are best for growing children, for they require fewer revisions. Spinal deformities are common and usually progressive. Surgical stabilization is most advisable in the teen years or early adulthood when patients are best able to tolerate these complex reconstructions. Early basilar invagination may be halted with prophylactic posterior fusion of the occipital-cervical junction with plate fixation. Patients with severe brainstem compression may require anterior transoral decompression, as well as posterior instrumented fusion. Patients with various types of OI appear to be at increased risk of premature osteoarthritis, although the reasons for this are not clear. Total joint arthroplasty is usually successful in these patients; thus referral is appropriate.

Every child with OI benefits from appropriate rehabilitative therapy. Muscle strengthening exercises are esential as primary care and after immobilization for fracture. Perhaps the most beneficial programs have been developed around swimming, preferably in heated pools and as part of continuous rehabilitative medical care.

### Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome

The heterogenous group of conditions grouped together as Ehlers— Danlos syndrome (EDS) illustrates the genetic and clinical variability characteristic of the heritable disorders of connective tissue. Common features of these disorders include joint hypermobility, soft skin, often with increased elasticity, abnormal wound healing, and easy bruising. To date, 14 subtypes have been recognized, with the molecular causes identified in 20 genes for all subtypes except one: hypermobile EDS90 (Table 107.1). In the past, EDS subtypes were classified on a numerical basis; however, this has been revised recently to include descriptive terms, including classic, hypermobile, vascular, kyphoscoliotic, arthrochalasia, and dermatosparaxis types in addition to other rare forms. In spite of this classification and updated diagnostic criteria, it can be difficult to differentiate among the different subtypes clinically due to marked overlap of clinical features, as well as interand intrafamilial variability. Additionally, clinical features (particularly hypermobility) can be seen with other conditions, as well as in the general population. Beighton presented a clinically useful classification of joint laxity, which is most widely accepted system for assessing articular hypermobility (the Beighton score, Table 107.2). Generally speaking, joint laxity often decreases with age, and individuals with a Beighton score of

<5 may be addressed using the additional five-point questionnaire listed in Table 107.2.92

### Structural and Molecular Pathology of Classic and Vascular Ehlers-Danlos Syndromes

Abnormally large, small, or frayed dermal collagen fibrils and disordered elastic fibers have been observed in many forms of EDS

by electronmicroscopy,93 supporting that classic EDS results in part from a collagen abnormality. Type V collagen is a heterotrimeric collagen composed of the products of three genes: COL5A1, COL5A2, and COL5A3. Type V collagen stabilizes type I and III collagens by coassembling, thus supporting the overlapping phenotypes in classic and vascular EDS. Although vascular EDS was clinically recognized as a disorder distinct from the other forms of EDS, the finding that tissues from these individuals were deficient in type III collagen clearly distinguished this as a separate form of EDS. Type III collagen is a homotrimer [1 (III)3] found in skin, blood vessels, and the walls of hollow viscera. Heterozgyosity for mutations in the gene encoding COL3A1 leads to vascular EDS and affects both the synthesis and secretion of type III collagen.96-98 Various types of mutations have been identified including missense, nonsense, and deletions, and there is no correlation between the clinical phenotype and the type of type III collagen mutation. In this disorder, the biochemical abnormalities are decreased or absent production of a normal type III collagen homotrimer or production of an abnormal homotrimer that is retained in the endoplasmic reticulum and, if secreted, contributes to an abnormal matrix. Most cases now are determined by direct analysis of the COL3A1 gene, although in the past, biochemical studies were performed.

### Classic Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome

Classic EDS (cEDS) is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner. Cardinal features of cEDS are skin hyperextensibility, atrophic scarring, and generalized joint hypermobility. The skin tends to be soft and doughy to the touch, with increased fragility, manifesting as splitting of the dermis with relatively minor trauma. Wound healing is often poor. Recurrent joint dislocations occur frequently and usually resolve spontaneously or are easily managed by the affected individuals. However, over time, recurrent joint dislocations, periodic joint effusion related to trauma, and the eventual appearance of osteoarthritis pose significant management problems. Synovial thickening has been observed in EDS

accompanied by the accumulation of small masses of crystalline material in synovial villi. It has been observed that EDS patients constitute up to 5% of all patients in a pediatric arthritis clinic population. In children, other features include hypotonia with delayed motor milestones, easy fatigability, and easy bruising. Mitral valve prolapse is reported infrequently and is not usually clinically significant. Aortic root dilation has been reported and is rarely progressive.

In EDS, the skin has a characteristic soft or "velvety" feel that can be appreciated by stroking the forearms. Thin, atrophic corrugated, and hyperpigmented scars are often found on the forehead, under the chin, and on the lower extremities (known as cigarette paper or papyraceous scars), although this is not a uniform finding. Typically, skin lesions heal slowly after injury or surgery. Molluscoid pseudotumors (violaceous subcutaneous tumors ranging in size from 0.5 to 3 cm) may be palpated in tissue over pressure points on the forearms and lower extremities and may be seen on radiographs. Although many patients claim to bruise easily, ecchymoses distributed on the extremities are found only in patients with more severe forms of the disorder. Severe bilateral varicose veins are a common problem. Associated pulmonary complications of EDS include spontaneous pneumothorax, pneumomediastinum, and subpleural blebs.

### Hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome

Joint laxity with instability associated with subluxations and dislocations are common in Hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome (EDSHMB) and may occur spontaneously or with minimal impact, sometimes requiring surgical repair. The shoulders, patellae, and temporomandibular joints are frequent sites of dislocation. There is an increased risk for degenerative joint disease, and chronic pain is a major concern, sometimes disabling from a physical and psychological standpoint. The musculoskeletal pain may mimic conditions like fibromyalgia, amplified pain syndrome (AMPS) and chronic regional pain syndrome (CRPS). Affected individuals typically have normal skin without scarring, but skin may be soft and mildly hypertextensible with easy bruising. Multisystem complaints include headaches, functional bowel disorders, psychiatric diagnoses, and autonomic dysfunction manifesting as postural dizziness or postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS). Mild aortic dilation may be seen but is typically mild, with low risk for dissection.

The diagnosis of hypermobile EDS is based on clinical findings and family history with no known genetic or biochemical testing available to help confirm or rule it out. Diagnostic criteria were revised by the International EDS Consortium in 2017; the presence of three criteria is required: generalized joint hypermobility; evidence of syndrome features, musculoskeletal complication, and/or family history; and exclusion of alternative diagnoses. In light of decreasing joint range of motion with age, the Beighton scale described previously often leads to overdiagnosis in children and underdiagnosis in older adults.

Therapeutic interventions in hypermobile EDS, including the use of pain medications, muscle strengthening, individualized physical therapy, assistive devices, and other measures of joint protection, are mainstays of improving joint stability and alleviating pain. Calcium and vitamin D supplementation in addition to low-impact weight-bearing exercise helps to maximize bone density, which is often decreased. Regular dual x-ray absorptiometry (DEXA) is recommended for individuals with or at risk for bone loss. Many of these patients benefit from multidisciplinary care that includes relevant expertise in clinical genetics, cardiology,

rheumatology, orthopedic surgery, gastroenterology, neurology, and gynecology specialists.

### Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome, Vascular Type

Formerly referred to as EDS type IV, vascular EDS (vEDS) is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner and is considered to be one of the most severe types of EDS, because of its high mortality rate. Characteristic features include arterial, intestinal, and/or uterine fragility; thin, translucent skin; and bruising. Arterial rupture may be preceded by aneurysm, arteriovenous fistulae, or dissection; however, it may occur spontaneously. Common sites involved are the iliac, splenic, and renal arteries or the aorta, resulting in either massive hematomas or death. Patients are also susceptible to rupture of internal viscera and may experience repeated rupture of diverticula on the antimesenteric border of the large bowel. Problems with pregnancy vary from preterm delivery to uterine or vascular rupture, although delivery is uneventful in many instances. s.102, Typical causes of death in EDS families have included gastrointestinal rupture, peripartum uterine rupture, rupture of the hepatic artery, and vascular ruptures.

In contrast to the other forms of EDS, vEDS is not associated with hyperextensiblity of large joints, although small joints may be minimally hypermobile. These patients have thin, soft, transparent skin, through which a prominent venous pattern is seen, especially on their chest walls. In contrast to classic EDS, the skin is not "doughy" in vEDS, although excessive bruising may occur.

There is an increased risk for spontaneous hemopneumothorax in vEDS associated with hemoptysis and mitral valve prolapse. Surgical repair of ruptured vessels or internal viscera is extremely difficult because of friable tissues. Anesthetic and surgical difficulties related to intubation, spontaneous arterial bleeding during surgery, and the ligation of vessels that tear under pressure complicate surgical maneuvers. Similarly, arteriography may be dangerous in these subjects. Imaging studies may be reveal normal appearing aorta or other large vessels that rupture shortly after a cC 'normal study."

The diagnosis of vEDS is based on identification of a heterozygous pathogenic variant in COL3A1. Clinical diagnostic criteria are a useful guide and include both major and minor criteria. Major diagnostic criteria include arterial aneurysm, dissection, or rupture; intestinal rupture; uterine rupture during pregnancy; and family history of vEDS. Minor diagnostic criteria include thin, translucent skin (especially noticeable on the chest/abdomen), characteristic facial appearance (thin vermilion of the lips, micrognathia, narrow nose, prominent eyes), acrogeria, carotid-cavernous sinus arteriovenous fistula, hypermobility of small joints, tendon/muscle rupture, early-onset varicose veins, pneumothorax/hemopneumothorax, easy bruising (spontaneous or with minimal trauma), chronic joint subluxations/dislocations, congenital dislocation of the hips, and talipes equinovarus (clubfoot).

It is important to have a high index of suspicion for complications in vEDS, and it is recommended that affected individuals seek medical attention for any sudden, unexplained pain. Patients should carry documentation of their diagnosis such as a Medic- Alert device, emergency letter, and/or vEDS passport. Vascular surveillance may include ultrasound, magnetic resonance angiogram (MRA) or computed tomography angiogram (CTA) with and without venous contrast. Regular blood pressure monitoring should be undertaken to facilitate the early detection and treatment of hypertension. There is ongoing research investigating

medications that may decrease arterial complications and improve life expectancy.

### Arthrochalasia Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome (EDSARTH1 and EDSARTH2)

Formerly known as EDS VIIA and VIIB, arthrochalasia Ehlers— Danlos Syndrome (EDSARTH1 and EDSARTH2) represent autosomal dominant forms of EDS resulting from mutations in the COL1A1 and COL1A2 genes that cause faulty processing of type I collagen at the N terminus. 105, This type of EDS is characterized by pronounced and generalized joint hypermobility, skin hyperelasticity, moderate bruising, short stature, and subtle dysmorphic features including round facies with midface hypoplasia. The skin feels doughy and is usually fragile. Kyphoscoliosis and muscle hypotonia are frequently present. Affected individuals experience multiple dislocations, particularly involving large joints, including the hips, knees, and ankles, often presenting in the newborn period. Patients frequently require orthopedic surgery for joint dislocation with increased risk for complications due to tissue friability.

EDSARTH1 and EDSARTH2, collectively termed the arthrochalasia type, result from mutations involving the N-terminal propeptide cleavage site of type I collagen. The arthrochalasia type of EDS has provided insight into the process of normal type I collagen fiber formation. The initial observation was of an accumulation of unprocessed procollagen within the dermis of affected individuals. With subsequent recognition that procollagen had both Nand C-terminal extension propeptides and that separate enzymes were responsible for their removal, the syndrome became more sharply defined as an accumulation of procollagen with the N-terminal peptides still attached (pN collagen). Of the two distinctly different genetic abnormalities resulting in procollagen accumulation, the more frequent form is the mutational resistance of a procollagen cleavage site to the action of the N-terminal procollagen peptidase. The resistance results from an amino acid substitution or deletion in the proCOL1A1 or pro2COL2A1chain (type VIIA and VIIB, respectively), leading to a portion of the collagen chains containing an abnormal N-terminal extension. This results from mutations in COL1A1 or COL1A2 in exon 6 of the molecule that alter the proteinase cleavage site. Those individuals with mutations in exon 6 of COL1A1 are more severely affected than those with similar mutations in COL1A2.

### Dermatosparaxis Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome

Dermatosparaxis EDS (EDSDERMS), formerly known as EDS VIIC, unlike the aforementioned types, is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner. In this type, the skin is extremely fragile, soft, and doughy with easy bruising. Other features include blue sclerae, marked joint hypermobility, micrognathia, large umbilical hernia, epiphsyeal delay, and mild hirsutism. This type of EDS results from a deficiency of the procollagen N-propeptidase, in contrast to the arthrochalastic form, which involves the enzyme cleavage site; individuals have been identified who are homozygous for mutations in the gene. Interestingly, this defect is homologous to the defect in sheep and cattle with dermatosparaxis.

### Kyphoscoliotic Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome

Kyphoscoliotic EDS (EDSKSCL1 and EDSKSCL2) is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner. The findings in this disorder include severe kyphoscoliosis noted at birth, recurrent joint dislocations, hyperextensible skin and joints, poor tone, and reduced muscle mass. The skin is grossly abnormal and has been

described as pale, translucent, and velvety. Upon trauma, the skin shows gaping wounds that heal poorly. Kyphoscoliotic EDS is characterized by significant ocular involvement with microcornea, retinal detachment, and glaucoma, leading to blindness in some individuals. Severe kyphoscoliosis may lead to respiratory and cardiac compromise and ultimately cardiorespiratory failure.

Kyphoscoliotic EDS results from lysyl hydroxylase deficiency. A variety of mutations within the lysyl hydroxylase gene have been defined and include premature stop codons, amino acid substitutions, and internal deletions with compound heterozygosity reported. Defective lysyl hydroxylase impairs the conversion of lysyl residues to hydroxylysine on procollagen peptides. The consequence of deficient hydroxylysine content of collagen is the effect it has on cross-linking, which helps stabilize the mature collagen molecule.

### Other Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome Types

There are a number other rare forms of EDS listed in Table 107.1 that share some overlap with the other disorders or that have only been reported in a small cohorts of individuals.

### Marfan Syndrome

Marfan syndrome (MFS) is one of the most common hereditary diseases of connective tissue (Table 107.3). It is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner with an estimated prevalence of 1 in 3000 to 5000 individuals. There is a wide spectrum of clinical presentations from the severe infantile form to individuals who are only mildly affected. Although the most impressive findings are related to musculoskeletal, cardiac, and ocular manifestations, affected individuals may also have pulmonary, neurologic, and psychologic complications. MFS has become one of the genetic disorders for which there has been advocacy for treatment to slow disease progression and improve life expectancy. It is important for health care providers to recognize the condition early to prevent presentation with life-threatening emergencies.

### Clinical Features

MFS can be difficult to diagnose, with both underand overdiagnosis being an issue, especially when based solely on outward appearance. Stringent criteria for this diagnosis were proposed in 1996 and revised in 2010.113 In the absence of a known family history of MFS, the diagnosis is made for an individual with a pathogenic variant in the fibrillin-1 (FBN1) gene and either of the following: aortic root enlargement (Z score ≥ 2.0) or ectopic lentis and a systemic score ≥ 7.113 Features that lead to a systemic score are listed in Table 107.3 and were formulated in the revised Ghent nosology. Major morbidity and early mortality in MFS are related to cardiovascular complications including aortic dilation at the sinus of Valsalva with an increased risk for aortic tear and rupture, mitral and tricuspid valve prolapse, and pulmonary artery dilation. Aortic root dilation is found in approximately 50% of children with MFS and is progressive; it is also noted in >80% of affected adults. Dilation may be seen in the thoracic and/or abdominal aorta and less commonly in the carotid or intracranial arteries. Dissection usually begins above the coronary ostia and extends the entire length of the aorta. Severe and prolonged valvular regurgitation can lead to ventricular dysfunction and possible heart failure. Of all patients with MFS, 60% to 70% have mitral valve prolapse with regurgitation. Pregnant women are at particular risk for aortic dissection, particularly those who already have aortic root dilation, and this should be taken into consideration

Ectopia lentis occurs in 50% to 80% of patients with MFS. Subluxation of the lens is usually bilateral and appears by the age of 5 years. Although the lens is typically displaced upward, displacement into any quadrant may occur. Other ocular findings include myopia (>50% of affected individuals), increased risk for retinal detachment, glaucoma, and early cataracts.

Skeletal manifestations include bone overgrowth and joint laxity, disproportionately long extremities (dolichostenomelia), pectus/chest wall deformity, and arachnodactylty. Spinal abnormalities in MFS include increased interpedicle distance of nonrotated vertebrae, vertebral inversion (flattening of the normal kyphosis at the dorsal level and kyphosis or disappearance of the physiologic lordosis at the lumbar level), and vertebral dysplasia (dolichospondylia, elongated vertebral bodies with increased concavity). Scoliosis constitutes one of the major management problems in MFS. In one series, the average age of onset was 10.5

years (range of 3 to 15 years) with rapid progression during adolescence. If mechanical bracing or physical therapy fails to halt progression, spinal fusion should be considered, particularly when the curvature exceeds 45 to 50 degrees. 117, Thoracic kyphosis may be associated with reduced lung capacity and residual volume that may lead to pulmonary insufficiency. Diminished BMD leading to increased fracture risk has been reported in patients with MFS.

Dural ectasia, which may occur in as many as 40% of patients, results from enlargement of the spinal canal owing to progressive ectasia of the dura and neural foramina with vertebral bone erosion and nerve entrapment. This usually involves the lumbosacral spine. Large epidural venous plexuses in the lumbar and cervical regions can be visualized by MRI myelography, and leaking cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) from the dural sac can result in intracranial hypotension. Clinical signs of this are severe headache, low back and leg pain, weakness and numbness below the knees, and genital/rectal pain.

### Molecular Biology of Marfan Syndrome

Fibrillin-1 (FBN-1) protein is an important component of both elastic and nonelastic connective tissues throughout the body. It is the main protein of a group of connective tissue microfibrils that are essential for normal elastic fibrillogenesis. In nonelastic tissues, the Fibrillin-1-containing microfibril functions as an anchoring fiber.

FBN-1 mutations are associated with a wide range of phenotypes including acromicric dysplasia, ectopia lentis, geleophysic dysplasia type 2, MASS syndrome, stiff skin, and WeillMarchesani syndrome type 2.122-127 The majority of mutations in MFS and related syndromes are private mutations (occur genetically independent with no "hot spot" in the molecule). Exceptions include early-onset or rapidly progressive MFS, previously termed neonatal Marfan syndrome), with mutations clustering between exons 24 and 26 and exon 32,128 as well as acromicric and geleophysic dysplasias, which result from mutations in exons 41 and 42.129I Heterozgyosity for missense, frameshifts, deletions and insertions, splice site alterations, and nonsense mutations have all been reported.

### Treatment

In 1972, the life span of untreated patients with classic MFS was approximately 32 years. The early mortality in the MFS results primarily from complications associated with aortic dilation. This symmetric dilatation of the sinuses of Valsalva is progressive throughout life and is often detectable in infancy. In the early 1970s, it was suggested that surveillance and treatment could lessen the complications of aortic dissection in MFS. There have been many treatment trials with beta blockers. When compared against the control group, the treated individuals demonstated a significantly slower rate of dilation of the aortic root and improved survival, with fewer treated patients reaching a clinical end point (death, congestive heart failure, aortic regurgitation, aortic dissection, or cardiovascular surgery). 131,

Data generated from mouse models of MFS suggest that excessive signaling by the TGFβ family of cytokines plays a central pathogenic role. A large randomized controlled trial suggested that losartan (an antihypertensive and angiotensin II receptor blocker) attenuates TGFβ signaling and may have advantages over beta blockers. However, a randomized controlled study in MFS comparing atenolol to losartan failed to show any difference in efficacy between the two agents. Animal and human

data suggest that calcium channel blockers may negatively affect aortic complications. Affected mice treated with calcium channel blockers showed expansion of aneurysms and increased rupture risk with increased risk also noted in patients with MFS.

Regular echocardiography is the mainstay of surveillance for the aortic root complications of MFS. Elective repair of aortic root disease before enlargement to 4.5 cm is typically suggested and is preferable to emergency repair required for marked dilation or dissection. Mitral valve replacement is frequently accomplished during the same procedure. Most importantly, repeated trials have shown that patients who undergo elective repair, versus emergent repair, have a substantially better prognosis. Retrospective studies of patients with MFS undergoing thoracoabdominal CT or MRI as part of their clinical care showed that one-third had findings of peripheral vascular aneurysms, with approximately half requiring interventions.

Correction of scoliosis may be attempted with bracing; however, surgical repair, including fixation with rods, should be considered when the curvature exceeds 40 degrees. Arthropathy associated with excessive joint mobility may require orthopedic intervention. Dislocated lenses should not be removed surgically unless more conventional means of correcting vision are ineffective.

### Differential Diagnosis

Homocystinuria. Homocystinuria is an autosomal recessive inborn error of metabolism that shares several skeletal and ocular features with MFS and is therefore part of diagnostic consider- 138 Characteristic features include a marfanoid habitus with ation. joint laxity, scoliosis, lens dislocation, early-onset osteoporosis, mild intellectual disability, vascular thrombosis affecting arteries and veins due to increased clotting activity, and the cytotoxic effect of homocysteine on vascular endothelial cells. 138

Cystathionine β-synthase (CBS) deficiency is the most common cause of homocystinuria138 and leads to elevated levels of homocystine and methionine levels, whereas cystathionine and cysteine levels in blood are decreased. Importantly, this disorder is differentiated from MFS primarily because the direction of ectopia lentis is different, usually laterally or inferiorly, and progressive aortic root dilation is not seen.

Loeys-Dietz Syndrome. In 2005, individuals with a previously undescribed autosomal dominant aortic aneurysm syndrome were reported. This disorder, now referred to as Loeys-Dietz syndrome (LDS), is characterized by generalized arterial tortuosity with ascending aortic aneurysm and dissection, hypertelorism, bifid uvula, and/or cleft palate. Other findings include craniosynostosis, pectus deformity, joint laxity, talipes equinovarus, cervical spine instability, easy bruising, translucent skin, and abnormal wound healing. There is an increased risk for widespread and aggressive aneurysms, as well as uterine rupture and death during pregnancy. Of note, affected individuals have also been found to have a predisposition to allergic and inflammatory conditions such as food allergies and eosinophilic esophagitis. The phenotype has been considered to overlap with MFS and vEDS and similarly, there is marked interand intrafamilial variability.

Heterozygosity for mutations in TGFBR1, TGFBR2, TGFB2,TGFB3, SMAD2, and SMAD3 have been identified (Table 107.1). 139-141 From a management perspective, timely diagnosis is important because individuals with LDS are managed more aggressively than in MFS. Unlike with MFS, which is associated with slowly progressive arterial disease, in LDS the aneurysms tend to be particularly aggressive and rupture at an earlier stage and size. Diagnostic differentiation between LDS and

MFS is therefore very important. All individuals with LDS require frequent echocardiography to monitor the ascending aorta. MRA or CTA are also often deployed for surveillance in affected individuals, particularly if there are concerns of vascular involvement beyond the ascending aorta. Aortic aneurysms are corrected at smaller sizes (4 cm) than in MFS, and complaints such as abdominal pain and headache should be thoroughly investigated given the high risk for widespread vascular complications. The peripartum period can be dangerous for women with LDS and should be accompanied by an increased frequency of aortic imaging.

Congenital Contractural Arachnodactyly. Congenital contractural arachnodactyly (CCA) is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner and characteristic features include arachnodactyly, a marfanoid habitus, and multiple flexion contractures. . There is a characteristic "crumpled ear" deformity due to a flattened helix with partial obliteration of the concha. Marked deformity of the chest cage also occurs, and kyphoscoliosis is often progressive and severe. For unknown reasons, the contractures tend to become less severe with age. Radiographically, osteopenia can be seen. Aortopathies are less often seen. This disorder results from heterozygosity for mutations in Fibrillin-2 (FBN2).

### Conclusion

The h ereditary d isorders of c onnective tissue r epresent a h eterogenous group of conditions characterized by abnormalities in skeletal tissues, which include cartilage, bone, tendon, ligament, muscle, and skin. Clinical phenotypes vary across a broad clinical spectrum that ranges from extremely short stature to excessively tall individuals, and the types of altered genes span the genome and involve a diverse number of biologic pathways. Affected individuals usually require close medical surveillance and treatment across their lifespan. Greater understanding and appreciation of disease pathogenesis and the unique constellation of medical issues posed by each of these disorders will ultimately lead to improvements in quality of life and survival for those with heritable disorders of connective tissue.

# Etiology and Pathogenesis of Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis

108

### KEY POINTS

Juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) is a heterogeneous group of disorders consisting of seven subtypes, each with its own unique clinical presentation, genetic risk factors, and pathogenic mediators.

The JIA subtypes that mirror adult-onset diseases share similar genetic risk factors.

Macrophage activation syndrome, a deadly complication of systemic JIA, is associated with interleukin-18 and interferon-γ pathology.

The asymptomatic uveitis of oligoarticular JIA is associated with TNFmediated pathology exemplified by its responsiveness to TNF blockade.

Although each subtype has unique features, there are common genetic risk factors, common histopathologic appearances, and common responses to medications that unify JlA pathophysiology as a whole.

### Introduction

Juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) is generally defined by the presence of inflammatory arthritis with onset before age 16 years without another identifiable etiology. JIA is further subdivided into seven distinct subtypes, each of which likely reflects individual disease states, highlighting the massive heterogeneity that encompasses all of the phenotypes included by this nomenclature. In this chapter, we will consider the host and environmental factors that contribute to the common phenotype of chronic arthritis in JIA while also considering the pathogenic mediators of each of the specific subtypes separately. The ability of some therapeutic approaches to address the common features, such as treatment of arthritis with TNF blockade, does suggest that there are common nodes of pathophysiology within JIA. However, increasing sophistication of both basic and translational studies, as well as targeted therapeutic agents, has begun to highlight the differences between subtypes, making consideration of these differences from a pathoetiologic perspective critical.

The International League of Associations for Rheumatology (ILAR) has defined diagnostic criteria for JIA, which generally requires 6 weeks of arthritis with onset before 16 years of age. A complex set of inclusion and exclusion criteria further subset JIA into the following subtypes: oligoarticular (four or fewer involved joints), rheumatoid factor (RF) negative polyarticular (five or more involved joints with absent RF serology), RF+ polyarticular (five or

more involved joints with positive RF serology), systemic (extraarticular features of systemic inflammation), psoriatic (extra-articular features of psoriasis), enthesitis-related (axial arthritis and/or enthesial involvement), and undifferentiated (failing to meet criteria for the previous six categories). While these criteria have provided some utility in homogenizing populations for study, it is clear that certain features cross multiple subtypes (asymptomatic uveitis, antinuclear antibody [ANA] positivity), while other features are so distinct, it is harder to justify a nomenclature that implies a common link (for example, the autoinflammatory features of the systemic subtype). Among these, oligoarticular JIA appears to be a disease truly specific to the pediatric age group. Additionally, research on the pathophysiology of systemic JIA is far more abundant than that in its counterpart, adult-onset Still's disease (AOSD). As such, we have focused in this chapter on the pathoetiology of disease features more specific or prevalent in pediatric-onset disease.

Reclassification to try to better homogenize and define these different features is once again underway. For polyarticular (both RF+ and RF-), psoriatic, enthesitis-related, and systemic JIA, there is increasing momentum to merge classification with the adult criteria to remove the age distinction. Other attempts are ongoing to reclassify homogeneous populations of patients on the basis of biomarkers, demographics, and clinical features using machine learning techniques, although no formal results of these approaches have been published. Such alternate means to classify these diseases may ultimately define more biologically relevant populations of patients. However, until there is widespread use and agreement on these definitions, the ILAR criteria remain the gold standard for classification and will be the construct on which etiology and pathogenesis are discussed in this chapter.

### Epidemiology

JIA affects 1 in 1000 children, with 50% to 60% of cases being of the oligoarticular form and the remaining subtypes distributed approximately equally. While there is a female predominance in the oligoarticular, polyarticular, and psoriatic forms, there is more equal sex distribution in the systemic and enthesitis-related subtypes. The oligoarticular form is more often associated with young age of onset, with a peak between 1 and 2 years of age. This is in contrast to the enthesitis-related type, which has a mean

age of onset of 11.7 years. Other subtypes have broader peaks of age at onset or even bimodal distributions in the case of psoriatic arthritis.

JIA appears to be a worldwide phenomenon, although the distributions of the different subtypes do appear to be different depending on location. Like other autoimmune diseases, this is likely due to differences in both genetic ancestry (e.g., human leukocyte antigen [HLA] allele distribution) and local environmental/infectious exposures. Oligoarthritis is much more prevalent in European populations. Enthesitis-related arthritis demonstrated high pockets of prevalence in certain populations, such as the Haida people of Western Canada, likely reflective of the prevalence of the HLA-B27 allele in this population.

### Histopathology

### Synovium

The histopathology of the inflamed synovium of JIA is akin to that seen in adult-onset rheumatoid arthritis (RA) (Fig. 108.1). There is hyperplasia of synoviocytes, with increased vascularity that can be highlighted with endothelial stains. There may be more hypervascularity in the polyarticular subtype, more inflammatory cells in the oligoarticular subtype, and an increase in synovial lining hyperplasia in the enthesitis-related subtype, although in general there is a large overlap in histology among all of the different subtypes. Fibrin may be found layered on the synovial surface, consistent with an inflammatory process. A lymphocytic infiltrate is generally present consisting of mostly T cells, although B cells are also found, sometimes forming germinal centers. Macrophages and dendritic cells are also found throughout the inflammatory infiltrate.

### Skin

The rash associated with systemic JIA (Fig. 108.2) does not have any pathognomonic histologic features. It has traditionally been described as a mild mononuclear cell infiltrate of the subdermal capillaries and venules. As the rash is not often biopsied, large careful reviews of the histopathology are not readily available. A recent review of cases of the related AOSD rash demonstrates a wide range of neutrophilic, lymphocytic, or mixed inflammatory infiltrates. This same study did note a unique feature of apoptosis in the upper

epidermal layers but otherwise did not find a single histopathologic pattern that could be definitively suggestive of disease.

The histopathologic features of the rash of juvenile psoriatic arthritis are equivalent to those seen in psoriasis without arthritic features. While typically the rash is of the vulgaris form, guttate lesions may also be seen.

### Eye

The eye is a tissue not usually sampled in JIA patients, so data are limited on its histopathologic features. In a study of a single enucleated globe from a 12 year old with oligoarticular JIA, there

was lymphocytic inflammation in the ciliary processes and pars plana. These cells were mostly CD20+, suggestive that they were B-lymphocytes, with only occasional CD4+ and CD8+ T-lymphocytes present. The B-lymphocytes were mainly IgG+. No granulomas were seen. B cells also dominate in the vitreous of eyes with chronic idiopathic uveitis.

### Bone Marrow

The bone marrow is also not often sampled in JIA, with the exception of systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis (SJIA) in order to rule out malignancy. The bone marrow of SJIA can have activated macrophages and hemophagocytes present, even in the absence of overt macrophage activation syndrome (MAS), although these features are often more pronounced in the setting of associated florid MAS.8, Hemophagocytes are activated macrophages that have engulfed other hematopoietic elements (red blood cells, platelets, leukocytes) and can often contain multiple other cell types within them (Fig. 108.3). They are most easily identified in preparations where single cells are visible, for example, bone marrow aspirate smears and lymph node "touch preparations." When examining tissues in situ, for example, bone marrow, spleen, or lymph node biopsies, hemophagocytes may be less readily visible because it is often difficult to tell whether the hematopoietic cells are inside or simply adjacent to macrophages. Immunohistochemical staining with a macrophage cell surface marker, such as CD68 or CD163, can be helpful in distinguishing these two possibilities, with hemophagocytes demonstrating multiple cells contained within a single macrophage cell membrane (Fig. 108.4).

### Secondary Immune e Organs

As with the bone marrow, lymph nodes are typically only sampled in SJIA and not in patients with other JIA subtypes. The lymphadenopathy of SJIA is nonspecific, appearing as follicular hyperplasia, but it can sometimes resemble lymphoma. Further evaluation of cell surface markers should generally be able to distinguish this possibility. When overt MAS is present, hemophagocytes may also be found in the lymph nodes. Hepatitis can also be a prominent feature of SJIA, especially in MAS, and a limited examination of liver biopsies demonstrated CD68+ histiocytosis, as well as a preponderance of CD8 T cells.

### JIA Pathogenesis

### Environmental Triggers

While much of the focus on etiologic factors for JIA has been on genetic determinants, undoubtedly environmental triggers also play a role. It has been long observed that flares of arthritis are often preceded by typical childhood infections such as upper respiratory tract infections (URIs) or otitis media. More recently, attention has been given to alterations in the microbiome, often as a result of the use of antibiotics for infections, as an environmental risk factor for multiple subtypes of JIA. Other exposures have been ruled out as associated with the development of JIA, such as breastfeeding, secondary smoke, pets, or residential area. History of rubella vaccine does not appear to be associated with JIA,14 and measles/mumps/ rubella vaccination does not aggravate flare of disease. As the potential universe of exposures is virtually limitless, it is of course impossible to catalog all of the possibilities even without considering gene/environment interactions. Nonetheless, continued efforts to better characterize the environmental factors that lead to the development and flare of JIA continue to be undertaken.

### Host Contributors

### Genetic/Epigenetic

The relative paucity of described monogenic causes of JIA support the perception that, in general, the genetic contribution to

JIA is polygenic. Nevertheless, the few monogenic causes of juvenile arthritis may help illuminate specific mechanisms and such patients may have been classified as JIA in the era prior to widespread genetic testing. Pathogenic variants in several genes cause syndromes that can include chronic arthritis, including SYK, STING, TBK1, C2orf69, MAN2B2, LACC1/FAMIN,22- 24 MYD88,25and XIAP26,

The importance of polygenic causes of JIA is made apparent by the fact that there is 20% to 40% concordance in monozygotic twins28 and an increased risk of disease of the same subtype in the siblings of an affected proband. It should be noted that while this relative risk is increased, the absolute risk of JIA in sibling pairs remains extremely small, so that families with multiple affected children are rare.

As with many immune diseases, the major histocompatibility complex (MHC) locus has the largest number of genetic associations with JIA. The enthesitis-related arthritis subtype, which mirrors the adult spondyloarthropathies in its clinical presentation, has been associated with HLA-B27.30 Similarly, HLA- DRB1*0401 is associated with the RF+ polyarticular JIA,31 much as it is in adult RF+ RA. These findings suggest that the age cutoffs distinguishing the adult forms of these diseases are entirely arbitrary and that the juvenile forms can simply be considered early onset of the classical adult syndromes.

HLA-DRB1*0801 and *11 and DRB1*1301 have been associated with oligoarticular JIA. The DRB1*1301-DQA1*01- DQB1*06 haplotype in particular has been suggested to distinguish extended versus persistent endotypes of oligoarticular JIA. Just as the shared epitope hypothesis has been used to provide mechanistic meaning to the HLA-DR4 association with RF+ disease, it is tempting to suspect that the HLA association with oligoarticular JIA, which has a strong seropositive association with ANA, also relates to the presentation of some autoantigen. Numerous articles have been published cataloging HLA associations with multiple different subphenotypes of JIA, including age, sex, and other characteristics, and a catalog of these associations, both risk-conferring and protective, is beyond the scope of this discussion. The array of these class II MHC associations seems to implicate a role for CD4+ T-lymphocytes in JIA pathogenesis. It is noteworthy, however, that SJIA, which is classically seronegative and more autoinflammatory, is associated with a distinct group of MHCII haplotype associations: HLA-DRB1*11-HLA- DQA1*05-HLA-DQB1*03.34 This could suggest an unappreciated role for antigen in SJIA or that the mechanistic role of HLA association with JIA is more complex than simple antigen presentation, similar to what has been suggested for HLA-B27 and its linkage to increased unfolded protein response rather than presentation of an arthritogenic peptide. Alternatively, perhaps there is a role for antigen in SJIA despite its classification in the pantheon of autoinflammatory disorders. More recently, the complication of SJIA with interstitial lung disease (histologically pulmonary alveolar proteinosis/endogenous lipoid pneumonia) was strongly associated with the HLA-DRB1*15 haplotype previously associated with multiple sclerosis.

Non-HLA loci have also been associated with JIA. Broadly speaking, cytokines and their receptors, signaling molecules, and unfolded protein response genes have been the major themes of discovery in this area. While dozens of genes have been associated with JIA, few genes have stood up to replication in multiple candidate gene studies. Although not a risk factor for disease onset, variants in or near the gene encoding interleukin-1 receptor antagonist (ILRN, the endogenous version of the drug

anakinra) have been associated with response to IL-1 blockade in SJIA. As many single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) are not in coding regions, increasing interest in the effects of enhancer/promoter polymorphisms and other epigenetic effects has arisen as inheritable elements that might contribute to disease risk.

Given the large amount of heterogeneity in JIA, it is not surprising to find that many associated SNPs are not with JIA at large but rather with subtypes. For instance, the genetic loci of IL-23R and endoplasmic reticulum aminopeptidase-1 (ERAP) have been associated with ERA,37 consistent with these same associations in adult spondyloarthropathy. IL-23 signaling through its receptor may promote T helper (Th)17 cell survival, a CD4+ T cell fate associated with both JIA and adult spondyloarthropathy. ERAP is similarly associated with proper trimming and folding of proteins and the degree of unfolded protein response, another well recognized pathway in the pathogenesis of the spondyloarthropathies. In contrast, IL-6 polymorphisms have been associated with SJIA.38, Supporting the relevance of this association, IL-6 has been a successful therapeutic target in this subtype.

Studies evaluating the epigenetic changes associated with JIA are limited. The peripheral CD4 T cell methylation pattern observed in RA was not present in oligoarticular JIA. However, active JIA CD4 T cells showed differential chromatin accessibility that was not accompanied by changes in three-dimensional chromatin architecture. A role for epigenetic imprinting of monocytes is emerging as well. Studies in different JIA subtypes and using tissue-resident cells may further elucidate both JIA susceptibility and pathogenesis.

### Immune System

### Adaptive Immunity

T Cells. T cells and their cytokines have been associated with autoimmune arthritis and JIA in numerous reports. Given the HLA associations with JIA, it is tempting to speculate that there must exist arthrogenic peptides that are being presented to these T cells causing their activation. A model of antigenic T cell simulation leading to arthritis may also be suggested by the observation of restricted T cell receptor repertoires. .43, However, with the exception of citrullinated peptides, such autoantigens have largely eluded discovery. Other possibilities include altered T cell receptor or cytokine receptor signaling on T cells, supported by genetic associations with PTPN2245and IL-2RA.

CD4+ T cells adopt a number of different lineage fates, each of which have different functions, particularly with respect to the types of cytokines they secrete. Accordingly, aberrations in a number of functions of these CD4+ T cell lineages could result in pathology. Both Thl and Th17 CD4+ T cell lineages have been associated with JIA in the joint space and in the peripheral blood. Therapeutically, this has translated to successful use of IL-17 blockade in adult psoriatic arthritis and ankylosing spondylitis, with ongoing trials in pediatric disease. IL-17 promotes neutrophilic inflammation, which in turn can lead to bone and cartilage destruction, providing another rationale for blocking IL-17 as a therapeutic modality.

Regulatory T cells (Tregs) act to suppress immune responses and limit inflammation. Dysregulation of this suppressive effect may allow pathogenic inflammation. Indeed, it has been noted that expression of the master transcription factor required for their function and maintenance, Foxp3, is low to absent in the Tregs in the synovial fluid of JIA patient. Furthermore, perturbations in

Treg function that allow them to act in an inflammatory manner has also been noted in JIA.

B Cells. The effectiveness of B cell-depleting therapy in the form of the anti-CD20 monoclonal rituximab in RA provides striking empiric evidence for the role of B cells in disease pathogenesis. Additionally, many JIA subtypes are associated with autoantibodies: ANA, RF, and anti-citrullinated protein antibody (ACPA) among others, although a direct pathogenic link between these autoantibodies and disease has not been established. In the K/BxN animal model of inflammatory arthritis, the anti—glucose- 6-phosphate isomerase (anti-G6PI) autoantibodies fulfill Koch's postulates and are clearly pathogenic. However, anti-G6PI antibodies have not been found to be associated with human disease, and it therefore remains unclear whether antibodies themselves play any role in JIA or other autoimmune arthridities. Synovial B cells in JIA appeared activated, with increased levels of CD80 and CD8.51 Functionally, synovial B cells were better at activating T cells than their peripheral counterparts. Taken together, this suggests the JIA B cells may act as antigen presenting cells, and the effects of B cell depletion may correlate more with this function than with reduction of autoantibodies. In adult RA, this is further suggested by the fact that disease activity correlated better with CD4+ T cell numbers than B cell numbers after rituximab therapy.

### Innate Immunity

Antigen Presenting Cells. Data are scarce for cell autonomous defects in dendritic cells (DCs) in JIA. Both conventional DCs and plasmacytoid DCs can be found in the synovium, with the former found in the lining and the latter found within lymphoid aggregates. As described for B cells, JIA DCs express higher levels of CD80 and CD86. Plasmacytoid DCs may play a regulatory role in arthritis, through the release of granzyme B, which may suppress T cell proliferation.

Macrophages/Monocytes. Monocytes and monocyte-derived macrophages are capable of producing many of the cytokines targeted clinically in JIA including IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF. The cells are found in the synovial fluid and the synovial tissue itself, which produces large amounts of all of these cytokines. They also secrete the mediators of angiogenesis, VEGF and osteopontin (OPN), which may contribute to the hypervascularity of the inflamed synovium. More recently, increased activation and cytokine production by monocytes has been noted, specifically in the ERA subset of JIA, in particular by production of IL-23, which in turn induces Th17-directed responses.

Neutrophils. Neutrophils are the most abundant cells found in synovial fluid from JIA-inflamed joints. However, their role in disease pathogenesis remains poorly understood. It has been suggested that aberrant epigenetic modifications in neutrophils leads to altered mRNA transcription and function in JIA. Specific neutrophil effector functions have not been established in disease pathogenesis. Recent data have suggested an increase in low-density granulocytes in JIA, a neutrophil subset particularly associated with inflammatory responses.

In SJIA, well known for peripheral blood neutrophilia, elevated myeloid related protein 8/14 (MRP 8/14, also known as S100A8/9) is due in large part to excessive neutrophil function. Furthermore, IL-1β blockade reverses the many activated effector functions of neutrophils in SJIA,59 suggesting that this cell type may be one of the important targets of IL-1β that causes disease.

Stromal Cells. While the immune response is clearly important in the inflammation of JIA, stromal elements such as synovial fibroblasts are likely an important target of many of the

inflammatory mediators and therefore contribute to disease as well. Many of the aforementioned cytokines upregulate adhesion molecules on synovial fibroblasts, and synovial fibroblasts from JIA are more sensitive to this process. JIA synovial fibroblasts also appear more sensitive to the effects of TGFb signaling, altering their function. Thus, targeting not just the immune system, but also the fibroblasts being altered by immune effector functions, may be a future therapeutic strategy.

### Subtype-Specific Pathogenesis

### Systemic

Systemic JIA is clearly set apart from the other JIA subtypes both in its clinical presentation and in its pathogenesis. The lack of identifiable autoreactive serologies and the large degree of systemic inflammation suggest that this illness is better characterized as an autoinflammatory rather than autoimmune process. Accordingly, the dramatic response of many patients to IL-1 blockade conceptually fit with the inflammasome activation often seen in autoinflammatory disease. Unlike other JIA subtypes, several biomarkers are useful for diagnosis and/ or monitoring. The S100 proteins S100A8/S100A9 (also called MRP8/14 or calprotectin) and S100A12 (also called calgranulin) are highly abundant in activated monocytes and neutrophils and show diagnostic specificity for SJIA (as well as familial Mediterranean fever and a few other monogenic autoinflammatory diseases) among other potential causes of fever of unknown origin. 62, A soluble factor found in the serum of SJIA patients is sufficient to induce IL-1β production by mononuclear blood cells. This factor may well be S100A8/S100A9, as removal of this protein from the serum attenuates this effect. Treatment response to IL-6 antagonists suggests involvement of this pathway as well. IL-6 is elevated in the serum of SJIA patients and may be the direct explanation for growth failure and osteoporosis in the disease. IL-6 may also impair natural killer cell function, which has been implicated in the inflammation associated with SJIA. However, the role of the natural killer cell has been debated in SJIA, with conflicting reports about functional deficits in this cellular population. It is not clear whether the reported defects in natural killer cells are a cause or a consequence of the SJIA inflammatory milieu. The arthritis of SJIA may relate to excess IL-17, as peripheral blood CD4 Treg and γδ T cells show increased IL-17 transcription or stimulated production (respectively) that improves upon therapeutic blockade of IL-1 (a known inducer of IL-17).68,69

### Macrophage Activation Syndrome

MAS is an uncommon but potentially fatal cytokine storm syndrome that can complicate JIA—almost exclusively SJIA—and its immunophysiology may also hold clues to SJIA pathogenesis. Classification criteria for MAS complicating known or highly suspected SJIA were published in 2016 and require fever, high ferritin, and any two of transaminitis, hypertriglyceridemia, relative thrombocytopenia, or relative hypofibrinogenemia. These criteria overlap conspicuously with those of the related disease hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH), and MAS is often considered a form of secondary HLH occurring in rheumatic diseases. Despite the recent classification criteria, diagnosis of MAS remains challenging and requires recognizing the hyperinflammatory syndrome in the context of the level and dynamics of the biomarkers that define it.

"Full-blown" MAS complicates roughly 10% of SJIA and occurs most commonly at disease onset but can develop at any point. Given significant overlap in diagnostic features and biomarkers, active SJIA may represent a subclinical MAS state, implying a model that intimately relates the pathogenic factors of MAS to those of SJIA itself.8, Very high serum levels of IL-18 and detectable "free" IL-18 (that which is unbound by the natural antagonist IL-18binding protein) are quite specific for SJIA patients with active or "smoldering" MAS,73-76 s supporting IL-18 as the upstream driving cytokine of MAS-like inflammation in SJIA. It has been suggested that there is a high-risk group of SJIA patients that develop MAS, on either the basis of chronically elevated IL-18 levels74 or the presence of heterozygous or hypomorphic genetic lesions in cytotoxic granule function. Interferon-γ is a central pathogenic cytokine in animal models of MAS,78 as well as in human disease. Several biomarkers help distinguish MAS from active SJIA, and many overlap with biomarkers of disease activity in HLH. These include ferritin (particularly when normalized by erythrocyte sedimentation rate [ESR]),79 peripheral blood adenosine deaminase activity (ADA)80, the soluble IL-2 receptor α, and the IFN-γ-responsive chemokine CXCL9.81 Although total IL-18 levels are highly elevated in the SJIA patients most prone to MAS, they are even higher in active MAS and help distinguish MAS from other forms of HLH. Although there are no consensus guidelines, the treatment of MAS typically involves the use of agents common in SJIA, like glucocorticoids (often at pulse doses) and the IL-1 receptor antagonist anakinra). Treatment of severe or refractory disease often involves agents used in HLH like cyclosporine or low doses of the chemotherapeutic etoposide. IFN- γ and IL-18 blocking strategies are under investigation. The pathogenic mediators of MAS, as well as the reason for their dysregulation, continue to be an area of active study.

Multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children (MISC) is a newly recognized postinfectious syndrome caused by the severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) that shares some phenotypic and serologic overlap with MAS. MISC typically presents 3 to 4 weeks after infection with a constellation of symptoms including fever, abdominal pain, conjunctivitis, thrombocytopenia, lymphopenia, rash, and myocardial dysfunction. These patients often present with elevated CXCL9 as in MAS and often meet clinical criteria for MAS.83, On the other hand, MISC patients do not often develop the severe multiorgan failure picture of MAS; rather the cardiac and gastrointestinal (GI) limited manifestations are the major clinical features that require management. Further work on the pathophysiology of MISC, and how it may or may not related to MAS is likely to illuminate the origins of both entities.

### Oligoarticular

Oligoarticular disease is defined by having four or fewer joints affected at early stages of the disease course. Although synovial fluid is typically dominated by neutrophils, the T cells present show strong Th1 skewing. It is well recognized that some patients "extend" or develop a more polyarticular presentation later in the CC disease course, while others have "persistent" disease, meaning it remains oligoarticular. The etiologic factors that underlie this difference are of great interest because this might lead to our ability to predict outcome and therefore alter therapy earlier to intervene. Class I MHC polymorphisms, IL-10,86 and IFN-γ with activated macrophage signatures87 have all been associated with the

distinction between extension and persistence. Proteomic analysis of patients at a very early time point suggests that there may even be measurable serum biomarkers that would allow for the prediction of disease course88; however, these remain to be validated for clinical use.

### Uveitis

The strong association of asymptomatic, vision-threatening uveitis with oligoarticular JIA is a particular distinguishing feature of the disease. The causes of this uveitis remain unclear. It is associated with ANA positivity, but this may more likely be a useful biomarker epiphenomenon rather than a direct pathogenic link. Cytokines have been profiled from the tears of patients with JIA uveitis that can distinguish them from healthy controls and uveitis of other causes, with different sets of cytokines found to be predictive in different studies.89, More work is needed to validate these findings in larger cohorts.
