The remarkable efficacy of TNF blockade for many patients with this condition suggests a central role for this cytokine in uveitis pathogenesis. It is interesting to note that this is true for the monoclonal antibody-based TNF therapeutics but not for etanercept. The mechanistic reasons for this difference remain unknown. The studies of genetic associations with uveitis are completely mixed, especially for MHC allele associations, and the lack of reports of familial occurrence perhaps suggests only a weak genetic association. The major exception to this is the association of HLA-B27 with acute anterior uveitis, which is a distinct entity from the asymptomatic, chronic uveitis of oligoarticular JIA.

### Polyarticular

RF+ polyarticular arthritis shares a common genetic architecture92 and pathophysiology with adult RF+ disease. There is often a correlation with ACPAs, and the "shared epitope" hypothesis, in which MHC alleles more capable of present citrullinated peptides allow for T cell help B cells to produce these antibodies, holds as much for RF+ JIA as it does for adult disease. Thus the 16-yearsof-age cutoff is likely to be an artificial dichotomization. In RFpolyarticular JIA, SNPs in the TRAF1-C593 and PTPN2294 loci are associated with disease, although variants in these loci are also reported in other subtypes, perhaps suggesting that the pathogenic link to the RFpolyarticular is less specific. Regardless of RF status, peripheral T cells from treatment-naive poly-JIA patients showed enhanced IFN-γ signaling. Due to the more heterogeneous nature of the polyarticular JIA subtype, a specific pathophysiologic model may be more difficult to develop.

### Enthesitis-Related and Psoriatic

As in adult spondyloarthropathy, there is a strong association with HLA-B27 in the ERA subtype of JIA. There is a strong familial occurrence of ERA, as well as related conditions of inflammatory bowel disease and other HLA-B27-associated diseases. ERAP1 has also been associated with ERA. Because ERAP1 encodes a protein product that controls the unfolded protein response and because HLA-B27 has been noted to be prone to misfolding, the combinations of these genetic findings has suggested that an altered unfolded protein response may be in part the mechanistic cause for inflammation in ERA. Additionally, it has been suggested that in areas of microtrauma, normal inflammatory tissue repair becomes exaggerated, perhaps due to the aforementioned genetic predispositions. Th17-directed responses, perhaps arising from

aberrant resolution of microtrauma, may contribute to inflammation. Th17 responses have also been liked to psoriatic arthritis (PsA). IL-23R polymorphisms are associated with PsA,37 suggesting that the Th17 axis may be involved in pathogenesis, much as in adult disease.

### Conclusion

A unified model of JIA pathogenesis is unlikely to ever be defined. The heterogeneity of the different subtypes both in clinical presentation and in molecular defects suggests that the different subtypes each have their own unique origins. Nonetheless, there are also a number of similarities that can be leveraged for understanding. "Lumping" and "splitting" are each likely to reveal different aspects of disease pathogenesis, and future use of complex, multidimensional data sets coupled with advances in machine learning techniques are likely to illustrate the similarities and differences in novel and currently unpredictable ways. A combination of the systems biology approach paired with the traditional reductionist mechanistic validation of hypothesis is likely to continue to fuel the development of novel druggable targets. In combination with advances in biomarker discovery, the challenge will be to move beyond simple subtypes to a precise, individualized approach to therapy grounded in pathogenic models of disease.

# Clinical Features and Treatment of Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis

### KEY POINTS

### Introduction

Juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) is the most common rheumatic disease in childhood, but actual estimates of prevalence and incidence vary remarkably in different geographic regions, reflecting variations in disease reporting, classification, and racial/ethnic and environmental differences in disease expression. The reported incidence ranges from 0.83 per 100,000 children in Japan to 23 per 100,000 in Norway. Worldwide reports of JIA prevalence vary between 3.8 and 400 per 100,000 children, with a pooled estimate of 20.5 per 100,000, making JIA one of the most common chronic diseases of childhood. There are significant differences in the disease manifestations in children compared with adults. This chapter discusses the current understanding of the key clinical and diagnostic features of the various forms of JIA, treatment

approaches, and outcomes. The rapid growth in understanding the biologic basis for JIA coupled with the ongoing development of targeted therapies for rheumatic diseases are likely to lead to enhancements in these current recommendations. Data concerning long-term disease course and outcome in children with JIA in this modern treatment era remain limited, but there are international prospective inception cohorts of children with arthritis designed to address these gaps in knowledge.4, Research shows JIA treatment continues toward the era of personalized therapy.

### Classification Criteria for Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis and Differential Diagnosis

Previous nomenclature used to classify children with persistent arthritis (juvenile rheumatoid arthritis and juvenile chronic arthritis) was integrated under the umbrella term juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) by the International League of Associations for Rheumatology (ILAR). JIA is a heterogeneous group of disorders of unknown etiology characterized by arthritis lasting ≥6 weeks in children <16 years of age. The ILAR classification was formed by expert consensus in 1995, with revisions in 19977 and 2001,5 to identify subtypes of JIA for research purposes that are as homogeneous as possible and are mutually exclusive from each other. The ILAR classification criteria are based on predominant clinical and laboratory features, as well as the number of involved joints at disease onset, which are presented in Table 109.1.5 However, recent advances in genetics, gene expression, cytokine profiling, and biology have led to a better understanding of the etiology and pathogenesis of JIA,8 leading to other grouping schema that may be more homogeneous and data-driven than the ILAR classification criteria. In 2019 the Pediatric Rheumatology International Trials Organization (PRINTO) proposed an approach to developing a new classification based on evidence-based consensus. Instead of the seven ILAR JIA subgroups, they propose the following new subgroups: systemic JIA, rheumatoid factor (RF)-positive JIA, enthesitis/spondylitis—related JIA, early onset anti-nuclear antibody (ANA)-positive JIA, other JIA, and unclassified JIA. The PRINTO classification also proposes to extend the age of JIA to <18 years. PRINTO, as well as many others, also advocates

### ILAR Classification Criteria for Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis (JIA)

for the inclusion of anti-citrullinated protein antibody (ACPA) positivity into the definition of RF+ JIA.10, Comparison of the ILAR and PRINTO classification criteria ability to diagnose and identify categories of JIA by evaluating 1228 new-onset Canadian patients revealed that 63.3% of patients were not classifiable by the PRINTO criteria, while 12% of patients were not classifiable by the ILAR criteria. Furthermore, clinical and biologic data, when available from patients, aligned better with the ILAR categories than the PRINTO categories. Currently, the ILAR criteria continue to be used in both clinical practice and research.

The symptoms in children with rheumatic diseases can overlap with other concerning diagnoses, such as malignancies, infection, and trauma including nonaccidental trauma (abuse). Therefore it is crucial to evaluate these diagnostic possibilities before accepting the diagnosis of JIA, as JIA is a diagnosis of exclusion. The ILAR categories, while imperfect, are meant to simplify classification and are useful for typical presentations of disease. However, if a patient does not easily fit into the ILAR classification system, clinicians must carefully consider all other possibilities, rheumatologic and nonrheumatologic. For example, among patients with acute lymphocytic leukemia (ALL), 15% to 30% present with musculoskeletal symptoms without blasts in the peripheral smear and may be misdiagnosed with JIA. In addition, ANA status, rash, radiographic abnormalities, and objective signs of arthritis were not found to be helpful in distinguishing between ALL and JIA.

### Oligoarticular Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis

Oligoarticular JIA accounts for as many as 20% of all new rheumatic diagnoses in the general pediatric rheumatology clinic14 and has an annual incidence of 10 in 100,000 children. It is the most prevalent of all the JIA subcategories, comprising 50% of all patients with JIA in North America and Europe. The peak age of onset occurs in children ages 2 to 4 years, and the female to male ratio is 3:1.17 This subgroup is rare in African Americans, Native Americans,19 and southern Asians. There is a strong association with HLA-DRB1*11 and HLA-DRB1*08.1 There are two ILAR subgroups within oligoarticular JIA: (1) persistent oligoarticular JIA, in which the number of joints affected by arthritis remains fewer than five throughout the disease course, and (2) extended oligoarticular JIA, in which arthritis develops in additional joints 6 months after disease onset. Extension occurs in 30% to 50% of patients at 5 to 7 years after onset of disease. Symmetric disease, ankle and/or wrist involvement, and an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) in the first 6 months of disease have been associated with extension.

Oligoarticular JIA usually manifests as asymmetric arthritis of the lower extremities affecting one or two large joints, with the knee the most commonly affected, followed by the ankle, wrist, and elbow. Small joints of the hands can be involved. Hip and back complaints, especially in young children, are so unusual that extensive evaluation is warranted to rule out other conditions such as infection or malignancy. Significant constitutional and systemic symptoms are atypical in oligoarticular JIA and, if present, should raise concern regarding the accuracy of the initial diagnosis. Pain in an obviously inflamed joint is surprisingly minimal compared with septic arthritis, and in as many as 25% of cases, the symptoms may be subtle, with parents only noticing a limp and joint swelling. In a young child, there is reluctance to walk and bear weight, with a return to crawling after a period of immobility, such as in the morning or after a nap. There is a high risk for a relatively asymptomatic chronic uveitis, especially in ANA+

individuals, requiring regular ophthalmology examinations to detect early changes (see Uveitis).

Among children with oligoarticular JIA, a positive ANA in low to moderate titers (1:40 to 1:320) is seen in 70% to 80% of children with persistent oligoarticular JIA and 80% to 95% with extended oligoarticular JIA. The rate of ANA positivity is even higher in girls with early-onset disease. The typical child with oligoarticular JIA will have normal white blood cell counts, normal or mildly elevated acute phase reactants, and, in some cases, mild anemia.

The differential diagnosis of oligoarticular JIA includes other JIA subtypes (juvenile spondyloarthritis [JSpA] and juvenile psoriatic arthritis [JPsA]); other rheumatic diseases of childhood, or other inflammatory conditions such as inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). Nonrheumatic causes of joint pain and swelling should also be ruled out, such as septic arthritis, benign or malignant tumors, reactive arthritis, foreign body synovitis, pigmented villonodular synovitis, arterialvenous malformation, bleeding disorders (such as hemophilia), or bony fractures, including nonaccidental trauma. Mild trauma is rarely a cause of joint swelling in young children because serious sprains or orthopedic problems such as meniscal tears or ligamentous injury are exceedingly rare. In general, ligaments and tendons are stronger than growing bone in children, and the bone—ligament or bone—tendon junction is the weakest link. Therefore fractures are more common in children than adults. Transient joint effusions can develop in children with hypermobility after exercise. Lyme disease can cause recurrent monoarticular arthritis (typically involving the knee and often with popliteal cysts), usually for <6 weeks, and appropriate serology should be obtained if there is any exposure history.

### Rheumatoid Factor-Negative Polyarticular Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis

RFpolyarticular JIA is a heterogeneous subgroup that makes up 15% to 20% of all JIA cases, with a bimodal distribution of age of onset, with the first peak at 1 to 3 years of age and the second peak at 9 to 14 years. It has an approximate incidence of 0.3 to 6.5 per 100,000 children and a prevalence of 1.64 to 33.4 per 100,000 children, although there is significant variability in incidence and prevalence among different populations worldwide2, Girls are more commonly affected than boys, with a ratio of 2 to 4:1, even more so with onset in adolescence. Chronic anterior uveitis occurs in 15% to 20% of cases. Patients with RFpolyarticular JIA frequently have involvement of the small joints of the hands and feet, as well as the cervical spine and temporomandibular joints (TMJ). They can also have involvement of larger joints including hips, shoulders, knees, wrists, and ankles. RFpolyarticular JIA is quite heterogeneous, with at least three clinical phenotypes identified. One phenotype resembles oligoarticular JIA and is characterized by ANA+ girls aged 6 years or less, with an asymmetric arthritis in more than four joints, increased association with HLA DRB1*0801 (DRw8), and high risk of uveitis. The similarities between ANA+, RFpolyarticular JIA, and oligoarticular JIA have led to the hypothesis that these two entities are actually on the same disease spectrum. A second phenotype resembles adult-onset RFrheumatoid arthritis and is characterized by ANAolder patients, symmetric synovitis of large and small joints, a greater cumulative number of affected joints, elevated ESR, increased association with DPB1*0301, and less uveitis. A third phenotype with "dry synovitis" is characterized

by ANAschool-age patients with minimal palpable synovial fluid or thickening, notable joint stiffness and limitation, and normal to moderately elevated ESR. This phenotype is often refractory to treatment and can result in destructive joint disease.

RFpolyarticular JIA may be associated with low-grade fevers, fatigue, poor growth, weight loss, elevated acute phase reactants, mild anemia, and ANA positivity in as many as 50% of patients. ACPAs have been reported in ~6% to 7% of RFpolyarticular JIA patients25,26 and are correlated with more severe disease. In the future, these ACPA+ patients may be reclassified into the RF+ polyarticular JIA subgroup. The heterogeneity of patients with RFpolyarticular JIA has also been supported by gene expression studies showing multiple distinct gene expression signatures. .27,

The differential diagnosis of RFpolyarticular JIA includes the other JIA subtypes, such as enthesitis-related arthritis (ERA), which should be considered particularly in boys >6 years because sacroiliac (SI) involvement may not occur until adolescence. Other major considerations include other rheumatic conditions; malignancies such as lymphoma and leukemia; and infections such as Neisseria gonorrhoeae, rubella, parvovirus, and Lyme disease.

### Rheumatoid Factor-Positive Polyarticular − Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis

RF+ polyarticular JIA is a well-characterized JIA subcategory and is part of the same disease spectrum as adult RF+ RA, sharing immunogenetic, serologic, and clinical factors. RF+ polyarticular JIA has similar HLA associations as adult RF+ RA. RF+ polyarticular JIA makes up ≤5% of cases of JIA, with mean age of onset of 9 to 11 years and reported female-to-male ratios between 4 and 13:1.0.1 It has an incidence of approximately 0.1 to 0.72 per 100,000 children and a prevalence of 0.28 to 10.3 per 100,000 children. RF+ polyarticular JIA more frequently affects children of color.15, RF+ polyarticular JIA typically is a progressive, symmetric polyarthritis affecting the small and large joints of the upper and lower extremities, as well as the cervical spine and temporomandibular joints, while the sacroiliac joints and thoracolumbar spine are typically spared. Hip involvement is common and may be debilitating. The arthritis can be quite severe, often resulting in bony erosions and joint destruction. Radiologic changes tend to take place early, 30 especially in hands and feet. Rheumatoid nodules occur in as many as 30% of cases, most frequently around the elbow. 1 Other extraarticular manifestations are reported less often than in adults. Uveitis is unusual, seen in <5% of patients. 32,

Active polyarticular JIA may be associated with mild systemic symptoms, including fatigue and weight loss, as well as mild to moderate inflammation, such as elevated acute phase reactants and a normocytic, normochromic anemia. By definition, all patients have immunoglobulin (Ig)M—anti-IgG RF. The ANA test is positive in up to 55% of patients,34 and ACPAs have occurred in 57% to 73%.35, The prevalence of ACPAs varies in polyarticular JIA but usually coincides with RF status. Positive ACPAs are highly specific for this disease subgroup, which led to its inclusion in the new proposed JIA criteria.

### Juvenile Spondyloarthritis and Enthesitis- Related Arthritis

JSpA has been divided into two forms: undifferentiated and differentiated. The undifferentiated form is made up of seronegative

enthesopathy and arthropathy syndrome (SEA) and ERA (JIA subtype in the ILAR classification), whereas the differentiated form includes juvenile ankylosing spondylitis (AS), psoriatic arthritis, reactive arthritis, and arthritis associated with IBD. JSpA prevalence accounts for approximately 20% of all JIA cases but varies by geographic region and can comprise one-third of all JIA in parts of eastern and southern Asia. It has been recently reported that JSpA is the most common JIA subtype in some Asian countries such as Taiwan, where it makes up 40% of the JIA patients.

The clinical features of JSpA differ from adult spondyloarthritis, making adult classification criteria inaccurate for this pediatric group. Because of the significant heterogeneity of this disease phenotype, it has been difficult to propose a unified pediatric classification criterion. In fact, ILAR classification does not recognize JSpA as a distinct entity. Onset of JSpA is usually after age 6 years, and there is a higher prevalence in boys (male:female ratio 7:1), although girls may be under-recognized because of milder disease and less axial involvement. In many cases, JSpA is diagnosed initially as oligoarticular JIA in the younger ages. Patients rarely develop sacroiliitis until adolescence and instead usually are seen with lower-limb arthritis and enthesitis. Multiple studies have shown that disease onset before 16 years is associated with more peripheral arthritis and less axial symptoms. The articular manifestations of JSpA include hip and peripheral arthritis with an asymmetric oligoarthritis most commonly in the lower limb. As many as one-third of JSpA children will have the classic finding of tarsitis, which is inflammation of the subtalar joint and the surrounding tendon sheaths. Approximately 25% of JSpA patients have polyarthritis presentation at onset. Sacroiliitis is the most common presentation of axial involvement in JSpA despite children being less likely to have back pain and stiffness at presentation. Children instead may only report vague buttock pain, groin pain, heel pain, or excessive pain from enthesitis or tenosynovitis. A subgroup of children with ERA will progress to features more typical of adult AS, with SI joint and spinal inflammation during adolescence. This progression is more likely in boys who are human leukocyte antigen (HLA)- B27+ and have spinal or SI pain within 1 year of diagnosis. In addition, higher active joint and tender entheses count at diagnosis; hip arthritis; elevated C-reactive protein (CRP); and HLA-B27 positivity have associations with sacroiliitis. Compared with adults, in whom radiologic evidence of sacroiliitis is the diagnostic hallmark of AS, radiologic evaluation in children with JSpA is less often diagnostic because sacroiliitis is rare as a presenting symptom. Interestingly, the presence of hip disease in a patient with JSpA increases the likelihood of future sacroiliitis 11-fold, whereas the presence of dactylitis decreases it. Modified Schober's test can be used to evaluate lower lumbar flexibility, with a change <6 cm considered abnormal. Because thoracic excursion varies greatly in a growing child, only sequential measurements are helpful. In the adolescent, any thoracic excursion <5 cm should be regarded as abnormal. Enthesitis (inflammation of the tendon insertion site) is seen in 60% to 80% of JSpA patients. It is an early manifestation and occurs more frequently in children than in adult-onset AS. Children with enthesitis are more often older, male, and with polyarthritis and sacroiliac involvement. In a 2018 cohort study, the most frequent locations were the calcaneal plantar fascial insertion (39%), Achilles insertion (31%), tibial tuberosity (30%), and the inferior pole of the patella (27%). In addition, other enthesitis locations include the 2 o'clock and 10 o'clock positions on the

patella, greater trochanter, the iliac crest, metatarsal heads, and the base of the fifth metatarsal. Common features of enthesitis in JSpA include being symmetric, persistent, and multifocal with 25% exhibiting more than three sites. Enthesitis can also be seen in overuse or injury states; therefore caution must be taken to rule out those etiologies. Enthesitis can be visualized using ultrasound (US) or whole body MRI.

JSpA is associated with an acute anterior uveitis in 7% to 10% of children, which typically presents as an acutely red, painful, and photophobic eye that needs immediate medical attention because, if left untreated, it may lead to blindness. The HLA-B27 status is not statistically associated with development of uveitis or uveitis 48 symptoms.

Cardiovascular disease, although uncommon, can be severe in patients with juvenile AS, with inflammatory aortic regurgitation reported in as many as 10% of patients. Subclinical gastrointestinal inflammation has been known to be associated with JSpA, with findings of as many as two-thirds of patients observed to have changes similar to patients with Crohn's disease. Fecal stool calprotectin (fCAL) can be used to screen for gastrointestinal (GI) inflammation and is more elevated in children with ERA subtype compared with other JIA subtypes. In addition, fCAL was significantly higher in ERA patients with SI joint inflammation on MRI. Arthritis associated with IBD is also seen in children with two distinct patterns of joint involvement: (1) peripheral arthritis, which is more common than (2) sacroiliitis and spondylitis. Additional clinical manifestations unique to arthritis associated with IBD include erythema nodosum, pyoderma gangrenosum, chronic nonbacterial osteomyelitis (CNO), and rarely, hypertrophic osteoarthropathy. The peripheral arthritis activity correlates with gut disease activity, unlike the SI joint activity, which does not necessarily correlate.

Reactive arthritis, categorized under JSpA, occurs after infection with organisms from the gastrointestinal tract (i.e., Salmonella, Shigella, Yersinia, Campylobacter, Clostridium difficile) or the genitourinary tract (i.e., Chlamydia or Ureaplasma) without actual infection in the joint tissues. Usually self-limited, the arthritis can at times persist and transform into a more chronic arthropathy. In addition to the arthritis, urethritis and uveitis have been documented in children to complete the classic triad for reactive arthritis. The clinical infection usually precedes the arthritis, enthesitis, or extra-articular disease by 1 to 4 weeks.

HLA-B27 is present in 38% to 68% of patients with JSpA, depending on the ethnicity and cohorts evaluated. The ESR may be mildly or markedly raised, and there may be a mild anemia, but these should also raise the suspicion that the child may have subclinical IBD. RF is negative, and ANA may be positive.

The differential diagnosis of JSpA includes true infectious or postinfectious arthritides (viral, rheumatic fever, post-streptococcal, Lyme). More benign entities such as toxic synovitis and benign nocturnal limb pains of childhood (growing pains), as well as more concerning entities such as malignancies and solid tumors, should also be considered. Orthopedic diagnoses, such as Legg-Calvé—Perthes disease, slipped capital femoral epiphyses disease, and OsgoodSchlatter disease, and less common rheumatologic diseases, such as chronic nonbacterial/recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis (CNO/CRMO); synovitis, acne, pustulosis, hyperostosis, and osteomyelitis (SAPHO); Kawasaki's disease, and vasculitis, can share similar articular and extra-articular manifestations with JSpA. Both Behçet's disease and familial Mediterranean fever (FMF) can have sacroilitis features and therefore could be mistaken for JSpA.

### Juvenile Psoriatic Arthritis

Juvenile psoriatic arthritis (JPsA) was initially defined as juvenile-onset arthritis associated with psoriasis occurring at some point during the disease course. This definition has been further expanded to arthritis in the presence of psoriasis or at least two minor criteria—nail pits/onycholysis, dactylitis, or a first-degree family history of psoriasis—in the absence of specific exclusions.5, JPsA represents 2% to 5% of all JIA, with a slight female preponderance and a bimodal pattern of onset (2 to 4 years and 10 to 12 years). There are noted differences between the two age-onset groups, with the younger-onset cohort more likely to be ANA+, female, HLA-DR5-positive, with chronic uveitis and more autoimmune features, whereas the older-onset cohort more is likely to have HLA-B27 positivity, enthesitis, and axial disease. 50,

The psoriasis typically occurs within 2 years of the onset of arthritis, and for the majority of children, the skin symptoms follow the arthritis symptoms. In children, classic psoriatic vulgaris or plaque psoriasis characterized by well-demarcated, erythematous, scaly lesions occurring over extensor surfaces (elbows and knees), scalp, and trunk are the most common, followed by guttate or "drop-like" psoriasis. In children younger than 2 years, the most common finding is psoriatic diaper rash. Additional areas that should be evaluated include the hairline behind the ears, the navel, intertriginous, and anogenital regions (e.g., superior to the gluteal clef). Nail involvement (onycholysis) can be seen and is thought to reflect enthesitis of the distal insertion of the extensor tendons at the nailbed.

Because JPsA shares similar manifestations with multiple subtypes of juvenile arthritis, there is not one specific articular presentation. Patterns of joint involvement can be oligoarthritis or polyarthritis, with 55% to 70% of patients with JPsA having an oligoarthritis onset (fewer than five joints), although evolution to polyarthritis can occur in as many as 52%.57, Involvement of distal interphalangeal joints is rare at onset but highly suggestive of JPsA, and axial involvement is seen in 10% to 30% of patients. Dactylitis, swelling in the finger including tenosynovitis of the flexors, synovitis in the nearby joints, subperiosteal bone formation, and enthesitis at multiple insertions of tendons and ligaments resulting in the fusiform "sausage finger," is frequently seen in JPsA. In one study, as many as one-third of patients were diagnosed with another JIA subtype before the diagnosis of JPsA after a mean of 4.2 years. There were no differences in ANA status, HLA-B27 positivity, or uveitis frequency between oligoarticular JIA versus JPsA patients with fewer than five joints involved at onset. However, JPsA patients with fewer than five joints involved at onset did have more dactylitis, more small joint involvement, and less large joint involvement than oligoarticular JIA patients.53, Children with psoriatic arthritis may have mildly elevated acute phase reactants and mild anemia of chronic disease. However, as many as one-third have no laboratory evidence of inflammation.

### Systemic Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis

Systemic JIA (sJIA), which makes up 10% to 20% of all JIA, has unique characteristics that include fever, specific rash, and significantly elevated inflammatory markers in addition to arthritis. Recent research has identified biologic differences between sJIA and the other JIA subcategories, including prominent involvement of components of the innate immune system especially at

the onset of disease. However, aspects of the adaptive immune system such as autoimmune T cells can occur later in the chronic phase, suggesting that sJIA is on the spectrum between autoinflammatory and autoimmune disease.62,63

sJIA occurs at any age, with a tendency toward patients between 1 to 5 years, peaking around 2 years of age with no sex difference. Rarely, it occurs in adults and is called adult-onset Still's disease. The systemic features of sJIA are striking and are always present at onset, often predominating the clinical presentation. The arthritis may not be present for weeks up to months after onset, although arthralgias and myalgias are almost universally present. The fevers are typically spiking in character with a peak of 39° C daily, occurring once or twice a day, and can be subnormal between fevers. The child appears unwell and irritable during the fever but often recovers when afebrile. In 80% of patients, the fevers are accompanied by an evanescent, migratory, salmon pink, and sometimes urticarial macular rash (Fig. 109.1). The rash typically spares the face, can occur without specific distribution, can be subtle and scattered or diffuse, and can be difficult to identify in dark-skinned individuals. A helpful diagnostic feature is that the rash can be elicited by the Koebner phenomenon.

Other systemic features include lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, serositis (pleural/pericardial involvement/abdominal pain), and poor growth. Clinical and subclinical pericarditis and pericardial effusions are common, occurring in up to 36% of patients. Serious life-threatening complications of sJIA including macrophage activation syndrome (MAS) and the newly recognized sJIA-related lung disease (sJIA-LD) are discussed in the Special Considerations section. The arthritis in sJIA can vary from minimal to oligoarthritis to polyarthritis presentation64 and typically does not correlate with the severity of the systemic manifestations. Tenosynovitis and synovial cyst formation can also be seen. Although the systemic manifestations can be serious initially, the long-term morbidity is the result of severe articular damage with up to one-third having joint destruction, especially in the prebiologic era, and adverse effects of medications, especially chronic corticosteroids. There are no diagnostic tests for sJIA, but there are characteristic patterns of laboratory abnormalities, including high inflammatory markers, significant leukocytosis with neutrophilia and bandemia, thrombocytosis, and anemia. Liver transaminases, aldolase, ferritin, fibrin split products, and coagulation screen may be abnormal in severe cases and can be signs of early or impending MAS. ANA or other autoantibodies are rarely present.1,

Because of the nonspecific nature of sJIA, diagnosis should be approached as a diagnosis of exclusion. It is necessary to consider

infectious agents and malignancies, especially leukemia and neuroblastoma, with appropriate tests including cultures, bone marrow aspiration and biopsy, and other markers. The recurrent fever syndromes are often mistaken for sJIA, but the characteristic periodicity of the fevers and the other features should alert the clinician to a different diagnosis.66,67

### Special Considerations: Macrophage Activation Syndrome and sJIA-Related Lung Disease

Overt life-threatening MAS will develop in approximately 10% of patients with sJIA, and a milder form will develop in as many as 30%. If inadequately treated, the milder form could lead to full-blown MAS.68, MAS is a form of secondary or acquired hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis seen with rheumatic disease. The mortality rate can be 6% to 30% and accounted for the majority of the mortality in JIA prior to 2001.70 The main manifestations include unrelenting high fevers, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, severe cytopenias, liver dysfunction, CNS involvement (seizures/coma), and coagulopathy and bleeding. Ferritin often exceeds 10,000 ng/mL. Full-blown MAS is heralded by decreased leukocyte and platelet counts, falling ESR, liver dysfunction, hyperferritinemia, and elevated D-dimers. Histiophagocytosis by histopathology may not be diagnostically sensitive. New criteria for MAS in sJIA have been developed with good sensitivity and specificity to aid in diagnosis. There is no sex, age, or race predilection for MAS in sJIA. Half of MAS cases studied were associated with active disease; one-third of cases were associated with infectious triggers, most commonly Epstein-Barr virus; and a minority of cases were associated with medication exposures or unknown causes. Current understanding of pathophysiology includes excessive inflammatory cytokines, especially interferon γ, activation of T cells and macrophages and poor natural killer and CD8 cell cytolytic .73, Soluble IL-2RA, CXCL9 and CXCL10 levels, and activity. soluble CD163 are increased in MAS and may be helpful in monitoring response to therapy.

A serious chronic form of lung disease has emerged in the past 20 years and is recognized as a significant potentially lifethreatening complication of sJIA first described in 2013.75 A total of 89 children with sJIA-LD have been studied from two multicenter retrospective studies reported in 2019.76, Exposure to IL-1 and/or IL-6 inhibitors has increased the prevalence of this condition by up to fivefold since 2002, increasing significantly the recognition of this previously rare finding. Both cohorts identified onset of younger age (<2 years), mild pulmonary symptoms (no or mild hypoxia and chronic cough), and high incidence of erythematous clubbing at onset. Marked hyperferritinemia, MAS, elevated IL-18 levels, eosinophilia, and a prominent interferon-γ gene signature are frequent associations. Radiologic findings include patchy ground glass opacities and septal thickening without prominent fibrosis, and pathology suggests a unique inflammatory form of pulmonary alveolar proteinosis-like disease. There are no characteristic genetic associations identified including the lack of genetic associations with PAP, although patients with sJIA and Trisomy 21 were over-represented in the sJIA-LD cohort. There was over 30% mortality in patients with sJIA-LD. An additional observation is that some patients have a drug-related eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS)like reaction with association with the DRESS-associated allele HLA DRB1*15, suggesting a delayed hypersensitivity reaction. The relationship of

drug-related delayed hypersensitivity reactions and sJIA LD is not clear, and there are two hypotheses that are currently being evaluated internationally: whether IL-1 or IL-6 inhibitors act as antigens with direct effects on hypersensitization or whether the biologic effects of IL-1 and IL-6 inhibitors sets the stage for delayed hypersensitivity reactions through a cytokine plasticity hypothesis. Understanding a potential iatrogenic complication associated with cytokine inhibitors is critical for best determining how to manage children with sJIA. Patients need to be monitored closely for development of hypersensitivity and pulmonary symptoms.

### Treatment—Medical Therapy

With the development of increasingly more effective biologic and targeted synthetic disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs (DMARDs) for arthritis, pediatric rheumatologists now aim to achieve clinically inactive disease (on or off therapy). Several studies support the paradigm of treating aggressively to reach inactive disease as early as possible in the disease course or at least to minimize disease activity, which may ultimately lead to better outcomes, including quality of life, shorter periods of active disease, and less long-term joint damage.80,81* The evaluation of step-up therapy, combined early therapy, and treat-to-target are facilitated by rigorous disease activity measures including the JADAS, American College of Rheumatology (ACR) Pediatric 30/50/70, as well as well-validated definitions of clinical inactive disease and minimal disease activity. The treatment approaches discussed in this section are based on integration of the current understanding of best treatments including the ACR-published guidelines for treatment of JIA 85,86; comparative effectiveness studies based on consensus treatment plans developed by rigorous consensus methodology87; and randomized control trials (RCTs). In addition to treating active arthritis, several studies evaluate optimal strategies for de-escalation of therapy when clinical inactive disease has been achieved. In general, most studies in polyarticular-course JIA suggest that about half of the patients who have discontinued medications after reaching clinically inactive disease may flare by 6 to 12 months after discontinuation, with variations depending on multiple factors, such as time after onset of initiation of biologic or time in clinical inactive disease. Studies showed that approximately 50% of patients who flared after medication discontinuation could be recaptured within 6 months.

The pharmacology of individual drugs is discussed elsewhere. Special considerations for children are provided below. Table 109.2 shows medications, dosing, and routes of administration. For comprehensive safety and monitoring for biologics medications, please refer to the published 2021 ACR recommendations.

### Nonsteroidal Anti-inflammatory Drug Use in Children

Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and/or intraarticular steroid (IAS) injections are the first-line treatment in oligoarticular JIA to control symptoms of pain and stiffness. NSAIDs have both analgesic and anti-inflammatory properties by blocking prostaglandin formation via inhibition of cyclooxygenase-1 and cyclooxygenase-2. NSAIDs do not alter the natural history of JIA

but are frequently used as an adjunctive therapy to more definitive therapies. In general, NSAIDS should only be considered as monotherapy in initial therapy in patients with low disease activity. If control is not achieved in 1 to 2 months, additional therapy should be initiated.

### Intra-articular Steroid Injections

Early treatment with IAS is associated with better outcome,89 and IAS can bring about rapid sustained control of monoarthritis, especially of the knee. It remains to be seen whether IAS can be used as the sole therapy in persistent oligoarticular JIA, as arthritis in uninjected joints can develop, illustrating that IAS therapy does not prevent arthritis extension to previously uninvolved joints. An RCT of IAS treatment alone versus IAS with oral methotrexate (MTX) in oligoarticular JIA patients did not show significant differences in outcome between the two groups, but post-hoc analysis suggests that MTX use may help lengthen the effect of IAS therapy.

Intra-articular triamcinolone hexacetonide (TH) has been found to be superior to other preparations of intra-articular corticosteroids, such as triamcinolone acetonide (TA). Unfortunately, triamcinolone hexacetonide is no longer available in the United States. IAS injections with TA are expected to result in clinical improvement of arthritis for 1 to 2 months. If arthritis recurs, joint injections can be repeated as many as three times in a 12-month period. Difficult-to-reach joints, such as the hip, SI joint, TMJ, and subtalar joint, may be injected by using US or fluoroscopy. The effect of IAS injections on joint cartilage and subchondral bone remains unclear. Some research indicates that IASs can be a risk factor for development of subchondral bone lesions. IAS should be administered under sedation or general anesthesia for the young. The use of IAS for active arthritis has been recommended by the ACR guidelines for oligoarthritis but is considered adjunct therapy for polyarthritis.85,86

### Corticosteroid Use in Children

In general, systemic corticosteroids should be used sparingly in the treatment of any subgroup of JIA because of the severe morbidity associated with chronic use, even at low doses. Newer therapeutic modalities such as biologics may eliminate the need for any corticosteroids or limit the doses needed. This is especially true in sJIA, in which high-dose corticosteroids have been a mainstay of therapy for severe systemic manifestations. There is also a role for systemic corticosteroids in the treatment of systemic JIA with macrophage activation syndrome. Otherwise, the evidence for use of corticosteroids for the synovitis of JIA is controversial and conflicting. Systemic glucocorticoids are used only as a bridge to provide symptomatic relief as more definitive treatments are started; they are not routinely recommended for the treatment of polyarthritis per ACR recommendations. The Childhood Arthritis and Rheumatology Research Alliance (CARRA) consensus treatment protocols (CTPs) also include optional prednisone use at diagnosis in each treatment arm as an adjunctive treatment, with recommendations to taper by 3 months if possible. Both topical and systemic corticosteroids have a role in the treatment of JIA-associated uveitis. There are many adverse events associated with glucocorticoids, so they should be used with caution in the treatment of JIA.

### Conventional Synthetic DMARDs: Methotrexate and Others

MTX is effective, safe, and the most commonly used conventional synthetic disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drug (csD- MARD) in JIA.93, In a retrospective cohort study involving all JIA subtypes, the strongest predictor of response to MTX at 6 months of treatment was the time from diagnosis to start of MTX, suggesting that starting MTX early will lead to a better response. Recent evidence-based recommendations on methotrexate use were made by the Methotrexate Advice and Recommendations in Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis (MARAJIA) group. These include MTX being recommended as first line treatment in oligoarthritis that persists despite NSAID therapy and in systemic arthritis with predominant joint inflammation without active systemic features. In addition, MTX is recommended for the treatment of JIA-related uveitis refractory to topical treatment. The ACR guidelines support a dose of 0.6 mg/kg of parenteral MTX once weekly (equivalent to 15 mg/ m2/week, 25 mg/week). In a cohort study of MTX use in JIA, almost 40% discontinued MTX or added a biologic due to inefficacy after 3 years. Folic or folinic acid supplementation is recommended to prevent MTX side effects. Liver biopsies are not

indicated except in unusual circumstances. Sulfasalazine (SSZ) and leflunomide can be used before a TNF inhibitor (TNFi) in milder disease, although evidence suggests that leflunomide may be slightly less effective than MTX. SSZ is more typically used with HLA-B27—associated arthritis and JSpA.

The most common side effects of MTX are nausea, vomiting, and abnormal liver enzymes. Some children develop an intolerance to MTX because of the side effects, and leflunomide may be used as an alternative. The gastrointestinal side effects are more common in older patients but less likely seen in rheumatoid factor—positive polyarticular JIA patients. In a recent study more patients using parental experienced MTX intolerance, and patients experienced more anticipatory behavioral symptoms compared with the patients receiving oral MTX. MTX intolerance can be seen in up 50% of pediatric patients. Due to the frequency of this, many strategies have been tried to reduce these side effects including anti-emetic therapy, route and dose administration changes, pharmacologic conditioning, and psychological coping skills for anxiety associated with nausea. Lastly, it has been reported that adding methotrexate to a TNFi regimen reduces the development of antidrug antibodies, therefore potentially improving the efficacy of the biologic.

### Biologic DMARDS

### Tumor Necrosis Factor Inhibitors

TNFi agents are effective in many children with polyarticular course of any JIA subtype, although less in sJIA. In RCTs, etanercept and adalimumab have high efficacy and safety in patients with JIA with polyarthritis.107-115Combination MTX with etanercept or adalimumab appears to be more effective than TNF monotherapy. 114,

Infliximab did not reach statistical significance for efficacy in an RCT in polyarticular-course JIA patients117; however, there was a trend for a higher dose of 6 mg/kg/infusion to be more effective than the adult dose of 3 mg/kg/infusion. Higher doses of infliximab can be given if there is inadequate response and lack of efficacy occurs, but a loss of response may be due to development of neutralizing antibodies, which should lead to infliximab discontinuation. Proactive use of low-dose MTX may reduce the risk of neutralizing antibody development.

The TNFi golimumab resulted in clinically meaningful improvements in polyarticular-course JIA but did not meet the primary endpoint in a double-blind, randomized-withdrawal trial. However, in 2020, based on results from GO-VIVA, a multicenter, single-arm, open-label phase III trial evaluating the efficacy and safety of golimumab in children with active polyarticular JIA despite methotrexate, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved golimumab for active polyarticular JIA and PsA for patients ≥2 years of age120 (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02277444). This trial demonstrated that the pharmacokinetics and efficacy in the pediatric patients were consistent with results seen in patients with adult RA and PsA. A multicenter, open-label study of certolizumab pegol is currently in clinical trials for JIA with polyarticular course (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01550003).

In August 2009, the FDA issued a black box warning on the increased risk of cancer, particularly lymphoma, in children and adolescents receiving TNFi for arthritis or IBD. The other adverse events involved with TNFis are similar to those of adults and have occurred in children as well, including serious infections, demyelinating processes, optic neuritis, injection-site reactions or infusion reactions, and development of autoimmune conditions. In most of the recent epidemiologic studies to approximate malignancy risk, children with JIA appeared to have a twofold to fourfold increased risk of malignancy compared with children without JIA, which did not appear to be significantly associated with treatment, including TNFi. Efforts are underway in the United States and Europe to capture post-marketing serious adverse events (SAEs) with all biologics using disease registries or within the context of an established multicenter research network.

### Abatacept

Abatacept is FDA approved in children ≥2 years (subcutaneous)/≥6 years (intravenous) with moderate to severe polyarticular JIA. In its intravenous (IV) form, it was safe and efficacious in a RCT of polyarticular-course JIA patients who had inadequate response or intolerance to past csDMARD or TNFi. . IV abatacept continued to be clinically effective in the 3-year open-label extension study124 and the 7-year extension study. Some patients require longer periods for optimal response (>3 to 4 months) compared with TNFi. A phase III open-label, single-arm study of subcutaneous (SQ) abatacept in polyarticular-course JIA showed effectiveness and

improvement in symptoms over 24 months, including reaching inactive disease and decrease in CRP. The CARRA Preventing Extension of Oligoarticluar JIA (LIMIT-JIA) clinical trial is currently evaluating abatacept in oligoarticular JIA to prevent extension of disease and development of uveitis (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03841357).

### IL-1 Inhibitors

Anakinra was the first IL-1 inhibitor developed from the endogenous IL-1 receptor antagonist (IL-1Ra). Although anakinra has not been approved for use in JIA, a series of studies suggest that anakinra is effective in sJIA,127 leading to extensive use in this difficult-to-treat disease subtype. Two additional IL-1 inhibitors, canakinumab and rilonacept, have been developed and are highly effective and safe in RCTs of patients with sJIA.128, Canakinumab is a fully human monoclonal antibody against IL-1β that can be administered monthly and is the only IL-1 inhibitor approved for use in sJIA. Rilonacept, a fusion protein of the IL-1 receptor molecules and the Fc portion of IgG, is effective but not FDA approved for sJIA and is used infrequently. The safety profile of IL-1 inhibitors is less well understood compared with other agents because of the small number of patients in the phase III trials and the overall smaller number of patients with sJIA. In addition, patients with sJIA can have severe disease complications, making it difficult to attribute SAEs to a specific treatment versus underlying disease. Tuberculosis, opportunistic infection, demyelinating disease, or malignancy have not been noted, but clearly, more long-term studies and more patients are required to evaluate the actual safety concerns. An emerging concern regarding severe sJIA-related lung disease has been recently identified with both IL-1 and IL-6 inhibitors,76,77 but causality has not yet been confirmed. IL-1 inhibition has been effective in several monogenic autoinflammatory diseases involving the inflammasome and more recently effective in colchicineresistant FMF.

### IL-6 Inhibitors

Tocilizumab is highly effective in sJIA and polyarticular-course JIA patients and approved for use for both subtypes and uveitis.130-132 Similar to canakinumab and rilonacept, tocilizumab showed remarkable efficacy in sJIA. In an RCT, IV tocilizumab was safe and efficacious in biologic-naive and biologic-refractory patients, comparable to the efficacy of etanercept and adalimumab, in polyarticular-course JIA patients with sustained efficacy at 2-year follow-up. 107, Subcutaneous tocilizumab administration is equivalent to IV for systemic and polyarticular JIA. Concomitant MTX did not increase the efficacy of tocilizumab in polyarticular JIA. Infection, neutropenia, and reversible transaminitis were noted in both trials, with mild to moderate elevation of low-density lipoprotein and cholesterol levels in the trial with polyarticular-course JIA patients. A second IL-6 inhibitor, sarilumab, is currently in early-phase trials for approval in JIA (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02776735).

### IL-17 Inhibitors

The anti-IL-17A monoclonal antibody, secukinumab, is FDA approved for use in children for juvenile ERA and psoriatic arthritis. In addition, ixekizumab is being studied in juvenile spondyloarthropathies (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04527380). The recombinant human IL-18binding protein, tadekinig alfa, is currently in clinical trials in adult-onset Still's disease (ClinicalTrials. gov NCT02398435).

### Rituximab

Rituximab may be considered as a treatment option for patients who have not responded to other therapies and continue to have high refractory disease activity or used earlier in the disease course for aggressive treatment of severe polyarthritis.93,96,137,138

### IL-12/IL-23 Inhibitors

Phase III trials are actively recruiting for study of ustekimumab (IL-12/23 inhibitor) in juvenile psoriatic arthritis based on adult and pediatric studies (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT05252533) and guselkumab in JPsA (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT05083182 and NCT05083182) and pediatric Crohn's and ulcerative colitis (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04673357). The IL-23 inhibitors risankizumab and tildrakizumab are currently in active trials in adolescents with pediatric plaque psoriasis. 139,140

### Biosimilars

Biosimilars to etanercept, infliximab, adalimumab, and rituximab are now available on the market, with many others in development. According to the FDA, biosimilars have "no clinically meaningful differences" in safety or effectiveness compared with the originator drug. Biosimilars have shortened regulatory approval processes, and once one indication is approved through equivalence studies, then all other indications for the originator drug are approved as well. Thus, biosimilars of TNFis can be used in polyarticular JIA without any actual clinical comparison trials between biosimilars and originator drugs in JIA patients. Biosimilars are now beginning to be studied in children with JIA. The FDA has recommended studies in the pediatric population, which has different pharmacodynamics and pharmacokinetics than adults, usually metabolizing biologics more rapidly. Most descriptions of biosimilar use in JIA patients have been in prospective drug registries. There was a recently published prospective observational study on the use of etanercept biosimilars in children that showed similar responses.

### Synthetic Targeted DMARDS

### Janus s Kinase Inhibitors

Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitors are oral targeted synthetic DMARDs that have demonstrated efficacy in several autoimmune rheumatic diseases, including RA. In 2020 tofacitinib became the first and only JAK inhibitor approved by the FDA for treatment of active polyarticular-course JIA age ≥2 years in patients that have failed TNFi. The multicenter, double-blind, withdrawal phase III trial of JIA patients with polyarticular course demonstrated significantly lower flare rates in patients receiving tofacitinib compared with placebo (29% versus 53%), with similar frequency of adverse events. There are currently several clinical trials underway evaluating efficacy of tofacitinib, baricitinib, and upadacitinib in JIA and JIA-associated uveitis (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03000439, NCT01500551, NCT04088409, NCT04088396, NCT03773978, NCT03773965, NCT03725007, and NCT05609630). Based on adult data, JAK inhibitors carry a black box warning for malignancies and thromboembolic events.

### Potential New Therapies

The therapeutic armamentarium for JIA and all autoimmune diseases is expanding at a remarkable rate. Biologic DMARDS and most recently targeted synthetic DMARDS (JAK inhibitors) are

effective in JIA, and new clinical trials are ongoing in children with JIA as described above for each subgroup. These approaches will continue to be refined for targeting different aspects of JIA and related disease complications.

Entirely new approaches may be on the horizon. Recent studies of T cell therapies including chimeric antigen receptor T cells in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and approaches to developing engineered regulatory T (Treg) cells are two examples of potential future strategies1 s145, The mucosal origins hypothesis, proposing that mucosal sites of chronic inflammation resulting from environmental interactions may generalize over time to involve other tissues such as synovium, is increasingly of interest, with a recent study demonstrating autoantibodies from individuals at risk for RA against an arthritogenic gut bacteria.147, This mucosal origins hypothesis may yield an array of potential therapies that that could be preventative, therapeutic, or even curative when linked with the emerging sophisticated molecular and cellular approaches that are currently available or under development.

### Treatment of Juvenile e Idiopathic Arthritis Subtypes

### Oligoarticular Arthritis

Treatment of patients with arthritis in four or fewer joints is usually approached in a stepwise fashion starting with NSAIDs and/ or IAS for patients with low disease activity and quickly escalating up to MTX if not effective in 1 to 2 months.93, Poor prognostic features, including involvement of the hip or cervical spine or ankle or wrist involvement with high inflammatory markers, should prompt the use of MTX as first-line therapy. Radiographic changes, such as erosions and joint space narrowing warrant initiation of a biologic such as a TNFi. Children with ongoing arthritis and who fail anti-TNF agents may receive other biologics such as tocilizumab or abatacept.

### Polyarticular Arthritis

The CARRA developed CTPs for new-onset polyarticular JIA. The CTP include three treatment arms: (1) a "step-up" arm initiating csDMARD therapy, (2) an "early combination" arm starting both csDMARD and bDMARD together, and (3) a "biologic only" arm using any bDMARD as initial treatment. Oral prednisone and/or IAS are optional in all three arms. The CTP provide guidance for escalation of therapy if patients demonstrate inadequate response after 3 months of therapy. The Start Time Optimization of Biologics in Polyarticular JIA (STOP-JIA) study compared the effectiveness of the three CTPs in a prospective, observational study.84, While this study did not demonstrate a difference in the primary outcome measure of meeting the ACR criteria for clinically inactive disease without glucocorticoids at 12 months after starting treatment, more patients enrolled in the early combination CTP achieved inactive disease based on the clinical JADAS-10 and achieved ACR Pedi 70.84 A 3-year extension of this study demonstrates that patients in the early combination had significantly more time in clinically inactive disease compared with the other arms.

The ACR and the Arthritis Foundation (AF) published updated treatment guidelines for patients with nonsystemic polyarthritis in 2019.85 Initial treatment of children and adolescents with JIA and polyarthritis should include csDMARD therapy, with MTX

preferred over leflunomide or sulfasalazine and with NSAIDs and IAS as adjunct therapy. For patients with risk factors including positive RF or ACPAs or joint damage and high-risk joints such as cervical spine, wrist, or hips, bDMARDs may be considered as initial therapy. In patients with ongoing disease activity, escalation of therapy is recommended. For patients treated with TNFi who have moderate/high disease activity, switching to a non-TNFi bDMARD is recommended. However, with sequential use of biologics, the response rate is attenuated. Rituximab, tocilizumab, abatacept, or different combinations of various csDMARDs and bDMARDs have all have been used after failure of response to TNFis, with varying degrees of success.

Because children with RF+ polyarticular JIA are at higher risk of prolonged erosive arthritis compared with other subtypes of JIA, these children should be considered to be in the more severe disease category, requiring rapid escalation of treatment if even mild disease activity persists.

Three RCTs highlight the use of early aggressive treatment for polyarticular-course arthritis. In 2011 an open-label, multicenter RCT comparing combination csDMARDs (MTX, SSZ, and hydroxychloroquine) versus MTX and infliximab versus MTX alone in JIA patients with early, active polyarthritis, demonstrated that MTX and infliximab combination was the most effective arm. In 2012 an RCT called Trial of Early Aggressive Therapy (TREAT) compared two aggressive treatment arms (combination of corticosteroids, etanercept and MTX versus MTX alone) for patients with active polyarticular-course JIA within 1 year of diagnosis. There was a trend toward improvement in the MTX, etanercept, and prednisone arm, and it showed that clinical inactive disease (CID)155 at 6 months was attainable by using either of the two early aggressive treatment arms. This study also suggested a treatment window of opportunity: the shorter the disease duration before treatment, the higher the likelihood of reaching CID at 6 months (odds ratio [OR] per month, 1.3; P < .011).156, However, 65% of children were not able to sustain CID beyond 6 to 12 months, especially with medication taper, 158 suggesting that longer therapy may be helpful. In 2021 a multicenter doubleblind placebo-controlled randomized trial compared etanercept plus MTX with placebo plus MTX in active polyarticular JIA patients.1597 This study demonstrated that patients treated with etanercept plus methotrexate achieved inactive disease and remission more quickly than those treated with placebo plus methotrexate and had a more rapid decrease in JADAS-71.159

### Juvenile Spondyloarthritis

To date, there have been few studies or trials on JSpA.47, Primarily, treatment is based on arthritis activity and in particular the presence or absence of sacroilitis. For severe symptoms or evidence of potential joint damage (such as erosive sacroiliitis), the use of TNFis has been effective based on small pediatric studies and adult studies. 161-164 Adalimumab and etanercept have been evaluated in RCTs that show reduction in flare risk with the biologic and decreased disease activity and patient-reported pain. .43, The 2019 ACR treatment recommendations for JIA recommend TNFi over csDMARDs in the setting of active sacroiliitis or enthesitis despite NSAIDS. For patients with predominance of enthesitis symptoms, TNFis or bridging therapy with a short course of steroids is recommended over conventional DMARDS (csDMARDS), while patients presenting with predominantly peripheral arthritis could reasonably start with a trial of csDMARDs. Intra-articular steroid joint injections of the

sacroiliac joints improve symptoms 3 months after injection; however, within 2 years 47% of patients needed therapy escalation. Case reports of IL-12 and IL-23 targets (ustekinumab) showed improvement in children with ERA. IL-17 inhibitors are also now being used to treat adult spondyloarthritis with early promising results and studies with ixekizumab (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04527380) are ongoing in children. In addition to treatment with medications, physical activity has been part of the therapeutic program for patients with JPsA. The LEAP study showed improvement in fatigue with a 6-month home exercise program; however, adherence was low.

### Juvenile Psoriatic Arthritis

There have been only two open-label prospective studies examining the efficacy of biologics in JPsA, both of which showed improved response within 3 months.131, A study comparing treatment regimens of patients with JPsA versus oligoarticular JIÅ patients and polyarticular JIA patients found no difference in use of NSAIDs, MTX, and TNFis. In general, the treatment of JPsA should follow the treatment approaches for patients with oligoarticular- or polyarticular-course arthritis. MTX is of benefit for both skin psoriasis and arthritis in children. In children with more aggressive or axial disease, TNFis (which have also been successful in treating psoriasis) are indicated and may significantly limit bony destruction.56, Newer treatments include the targeted synthetic DMARDs (i.e., Janus kinase inhibitors) and IL-17 and IL-12/IL-23 blocking molecules, which show promising results in adults but have not been published in JPsA to date.

### Systemic Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis

Treatment for sJIA is an active area of research with evolving understanding of the autoinflammatory and autoimmune biology and the potential therapeutic roles for targeted biologics. Approaches to therapy of sJIA discussed in this chapter are informed by a variety of studies and publications including the 2021 ACR guidelines for sJIA, CTPs for sJIA,172,173 and published RCTs.128-130 Therapies such as MTX and TNFis are less helpful in controlling systemic symptoms of sJIA but may be helpful if the disease progresses to chronic arthritis with few systemic features.64, Since the onset and course of sJIA can vary from mild to severe in both the systemic manifestations and the synovitis, with few predictors of the course or severity, therapy should be tailored to the patient's status and response to treatment, escalating as necessary.

Mild sJIA, defined as mild systemic symptoms and synovitis without organ system involvement, can sometimes be successfully treated with anti-inflammatory doses of NSAIDs. Certain NSAIDs are helpful for different aspects of the disease (e.g., indomethacin can be used for fever control and serositis symptoms). In addition, if there are only a few large joints involved, IASs are an additional option. If symptoms do not respond or worsen, IL-1 or IL-6 inhibitors are increasingly being successfully used as the first line of disease-modifying therapy, 86,128,130,174,175 avoiding the use of high-dose corticosteroids in many cases.

With more severe intensive systemic symptoms and in the absence of MAS, corticosteroids may be a useful addition, either as daily high dose prednisone (60 mg/day) or IV methylprednisolone (30 mg/kg/dose, maximum 1 g/day) for up to 3 days, followed by tapering doses of oral prednisone. IL-1 and IL-6 inhibitors should be added if not already started to facilitate corticosteroid taper. Cyclosporine and monthly IV immunoglobulin

have shown some benefit for systemic symptoms in pre-biologic era studies for steroid-sparing effects. Tofacitinib, a member of the JAK/STAT inhibitors family, is the first targeted synthetic DMARD approved for polyarticular course JIA by the FDA in 2020.144 Tofacitinib and other JAK/STAT inhibitors appear to be effective in active systemic JIA and adult onset Still's disease, as well as interferon-γ (IFNγ)-mediated inflammatory monogenic or nongenetic disorders in children in small studies. Baricitinib is currently in clinical trials in sJIA for patients between 1 to 18 y (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04088396). The presence of high levels of IL-18 in sJIA have prompted studies of IL-18 inhibitors including the IL-18binding protein inhibitor tadekinig α, which is currently in a clinical trial (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02398435). For very severe refractory cases, stem cell transplantation (SCT) has been performed, and some cases have shown benefit.86,

The optimal treatment for MAS continues to evolve with understanding the underlying immunopathophysiology of the roles of IL-18 and IFNγ in sJIA-related MAS and cytokine storm syndromes including SARS-CoV-2 infection and related multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children and adults.74, Current therapy includes initiation with high-dose pulse corticosteroids (sometimes with cyclosporin A) and IL-1 inhibitor anakinra.86, Results of a current RCT (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02780583) studying high-dose anakinra to the treatment of MAS associated with sJIA are expected in 2023. The IL-6 inhibitor tocilizumab may be helpful, but both canakinumab (IL-1 inhibitor) and tocilizumab IL-1 and/or IL-6 inhibitors did not prevent MAS in RCTs.129, At the time of this writing, emapalumab, an anti-IFNy monoclonal antibody, has just been demonstrated to be effective and safe in a phase II trial of sJIA with MAS unresponsive to corticosteroids and suggests that targeting the significant IFNγmediated inflammatory response in MAS may be the most effective therapy. Emapalumab has been approved by the FDA for use in familial hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH), 183 and it is possible that its use will increase in sJIA-related MAS with the evolving research in this area.

Approaching management of the sJIA-LD is more challenging due to its complex immunopathophysiology with several potential pathways. At this time, the IL-1 and IL-6 inhibitors are first-line therapy for disease-modifying agents in sJIA and have been transformational in management of sJIA and prevention of long-term disability and corticosteroid dependence. Decisions about how to manage the rare occurrence of lung disease need to be evaluated on a case-by-case basis. Active multicenter international research efforts are focusing on potential drivers of lung disease including (1) immune dysregulation due to IL-1 or IL-6 inhibitor treatment leading to major shifts in levels of IL-18 and type I and II interferons, (2) the contribution of direct drug-related hypersensitivity reaction DRESS due to IL-1 or IL-6 inhibitors, or 3) a complex immunologic milieu of multiple interacting factors.76-79, Management strategies are not yet developed regarding when and if it is necessary to discontinue IL-1 and IL-6 inhibitors, whether to type patients for the DRESS susceptibility allele HLA DRB1*15, and most importantly, what other medications would be effective in sJIA that may help treat the lung disease and/or may not be associated with lung disease. The effectiveness of Jak/ Stat inhibitors in JIA 144 may be helpful in managing these patients with severe lung disease if IL-1 or IL-6 inhibitors are discontinued.179, As the research progresses in refining immune targets for these small molecule inhibitors and understanding the underlying drivers of lung disease, more definitive approaches will be developed.

### Clinical Features and Management of Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis-Associated Uveitis

Chronic anterior uveitis (CAU) is the most frequent extra-articular manifestation of JIA and can cause significant vision complications, including blindness. Diagnosis is often delayed since it is asymptomatic without conjunctival inflammation. In a large, prospective inception cohort of new onset JIA patients, the incidence of uveitis development was 2.8% per year in the first 5 years with the majority. Uveitis is most common in patients with oligoarticular JIA who have a positive ANA (17% to 26%), patients with RFpolyarticular JIÅ (4% to 25%), and patients with JPsA (10%). It is rare in patients with RF+ polyarticular JIA and sJIA.17, Uveitis incidence demonstrates geographic and racial/ ethnic variability, with higher rates in those of northern European descent and lower rates in those of African and Asian descent. Overall uveitis prevalence is considered to be approximately 20%, with some subgroups having much higher risk and prevalence. Risk factors for uveitis include ANA positivity, age at JIA onset 6 years or younger, disease duration 4 years or less, oligoarticular JIA subtype, JPsA subtype, and elevated ESRs at baseline or follow-up. 188, Use of MTX alone or combined with etanercept or adalimumab for arthritis treatment reduced the risk of uveitis development especially if started early in disease. 189-191

Chronic anterior uveitis is typically nongranulomatous, recurrent, usually bilateral, and asymptomatic. If unrecognized, uveitis can lead to serious visual deficits, which may worsen with time. Uncontrolled, long-standing inflammation can lead to posterior synechiae, band keratopathy, cataracts, secondary glaucoma, macular edema, hypotony, retinal detachment, and optic nerve edema, all of which may lead to irreversible vision loss. Because of its insidious onset, regularly scheduled screening by an experienced ophthalmologist with slit lamp examination is required for early diagnosis with specific screening guidelines as shown in Table 109.3.192 Treatment of uveitis requires close collaboration between the child's rheumatologist and ophthalmologist. Newly diagnosed patients are ideally screened within 6 weeks of diagnosis because approximately 30% of uveitis cases have been found at the onset of JIA,193 and 5% to 10% have occurred before diagnosis. In addition, 90% of uveitis cases are diagnosed in the first 4 years after JIA diagnosis, but uveitis has occurred even into adulthood.33, In contrast, children with JSpA have acute anterior uveitis, which is usually highly symptomatic (sudden onset of erythema, pain, and photophobia) and therefore requires only annual screening. The clinical course of the uveitis and arthritis may not parallel one another.

The differential diagnoses include infectious causes, such as tuberculosis, toxoplasmosis, cytomegalovirus, herpes simplex virus, syphilis, HIV, Lyme disease, cat scratch disease, and fungus. Uveitis can occur secondary to a systemic illness, such as in Behçet's disease, sarcoidosis, autoinflammatory syndromes, multiple sclerosis, tubulointerstitial nephritis and uveitis syndrome (TINU), and Vogt—Koyanagi—Harada syndrome. It is also important not to miss a malignancy such as lymphoma or retinoblastoma.

The goal of uveitis treatment is to diagnose early, control the acute inflammation and complications, treat the underlying systemic disease, minimize medication side effects, prevent recurrences, and preserve vision. Inflammation should be controlled to <0.5+ cells per eye without systemic steroids and on fewer than two topical. 194, Best practices for JIA-associated uveitis have been

reviewed by interdisciplinary uveitis and rheumatology experts to be used by physicians caring for patients with chronic anterior uveitis associated with JIA, including the CARRA CTP and the 2019 American College of Rheumatology guidelines.192, Initial treatment is to use high-potency topical corticosteroids (e.g., prednisolone), as well as mydriatics to dilate the eye in an attempt to prevent synechiae. If there is impending vision loss, severe inflammation, ocular hypotony, or macular edema, ocular steroid injections or systemic steroids can be used. In approximately 40% of patients, the uveitis remains active, and if topical or systemic corticosteroids cannot be weaned, alternative regimens need to be considered to prevent cataracts and glaucoma as well as ongoing inflammatory damage.194, MTX is usually the first choice,192,195 with an estimated response rate to MTX of 74%. In cases of refractory inflammation after 3 months of MTX, TNF inhibition using monoclonal antibodies is effective and is added to MTX therapy with synergistic effects.195, Besides patients who have failed MTX, the CARRA CTP also recommends TNF inhibition for patients who are intolerant of MTX. To date there have only been two RCTs on the use of TNF inhibition (adalimumab) versus placebo in MTX-refractory JIA uveitis, showing the benefit of adalimumab.200, TNF inhibition in the CARRA CTP consists of (1) weekly adalimumab; (2) every other week adalimumab; or (3) infliximab 6 to 10 mg/kg/dose (maximum 20 mg/kg/dose) every 4 weeks after loading. Infliximab and adalimumab appear to be equally effective, whereas etanercept is less effective. 196,

Alternative immunosuppression includes azathioprine 194,202 and mycophenolate mofetil (MMF).203, Cyclosporine has limited utility. Tocilizumab is effective in treating refractory .206, Rituximab, abatacept, and JAK inhibitors have also uveitis. shown positive results in controlling uveitis refractory to first line 20 agents.

Risk factors for uveitis complications and poor visual acuity include the presence of posterior synechiae (Fig. 109.2), band keratopathy, and glaucoma; oral steroid use; active uveitis, especially with 1+ or higher-grade anterior chamber cells; male sex; prior intraocular surgery; and onset before arthritis diag- .192, Since the use of more DMARDs and bionosed. logics, the occurrence of uveitis complications (such as cataracts, synechiae, and band keratopathy) have decreased. ### Imaging

Imaging is becoming increasingly important in JIA to confirm the diagnosis; to exclude other non-inflammatory diseases; to monitor therapy and disease activity; and to track evidence of joint damage. Imaging in children with inflammatory arthritis is challenging given the unique features of the anatomically changing joints during the normal growth process. Because children have a large amount of cartilage in their joints, a significant amount of destruction can occur before erosions are identified. Furthermore, physiologic features of normal bone growth can be misinterpreted as abnormal. Local growth disturbances can also be seen in children with JIA, including bony overgrowth, particularly

in the small joints of the hands and feet and in the knees, likely because of chronic hyperemia. In contrast, premature fusion of the epiphyses can lead to shortening of certain joints, most notably TMJ resulting in micrognathia. The articular cartilage of growing children has unique regenerative qualities, and studies have shown that children with JIA can have improvement in their radiographic joint damage. Joint protection is important in pediatric patients, and damage can be as frequent and as severe as in adult patients with RA, with a higher risk for bilateral hip damage in patients with JIA. The trend toward early aggressive treatment to prevent erosive disease shifts the imaging need away from plain radiographs and toward other imaging modalities that are more sensitive in detecting early disease activity, 223 such as MRI and US. Different radiographic modalities are now recognized to improve evaluation of certain aspects of disease.

Conventional radiography is good at ruling out trauma and orthopedic conditions, as well as evaluating late findings such as ankyloses, joint misalignment, enlarged epiphysis, premature physeal fusion, and spinal deformities. In early disease, radiographs only show soft tissue swelling, effusions, and periarticular ostoepenia. For lower extremities, weight bearing views are recommended to evaluate for joint space loss. In addition, standing scanograms can evaluate for leg-length discrepancies. In addition, pelvic radiographs can demonstrate axial disease involvement with joint space narrowing, sclerosis, erosions, and ankylosis. The iliac side of the sacroiliac (SI) joint tends to shows damage earlier than the thicker cartilage lined sacral side of the joint. In children, the contour of the maturing SI joint can be very irregular making evaluation more difficult and can lead to overinterpretation of erosions. US is being utilized more in children because it is noninvasive, safe, fast, and relatively inexpensive. Many pediatric rheumatology programs now are utilizing point-of-care US during the clinic visit for both diagnosis and to assist in therapeutic injections. The normal standards of joint cartilage thickness by

age and sex have now been established, and it is noted that JIA patients have reduced cartilage thickness compared with healthy controls.225, Patients with polyarticular JIA or sJIA appear to have thinner cartilage than patients with oligoarticular JIA. Recently, normal US standards in children for the hip, shoulder, and wrist joints have also been published. Ultrasound is more sensitive than plain radiography in the detection of effusions, synovial thickening, and synovial cysts especially in the smaller joints. It is an excellent tool to detect early inflammatory changes in synovitis, tenosynovitis, tendonitis, and enthesitis. In experienced hands, even cartilage thinning and bone erosions can also be seen. Furthermore, US evaluations of patients that were in clinical remission that demonstrated the presence of subclinical synovitis had a higher risk of disease flare, thus possibly predicting disease activity earlier. Another study showed that the risk of flare in US-positive patients versus US-negative patients was almost four times higher.
