Inflammatory involvement of the hip, shoulder, and elbow is more frequently accurately detected by US compared with a clinical examination.232, Color and power Doppler US can facilitate the evaluation of hyperemia and vascular abnormalities in affected joints and tendon involvement. It is still difficult to monitor disease activity with ultrasound due to lack of standard and validated scoring systems.

MRI is the most complete and sensitive imaging modality currently available for detecting enthesitis, synovitis, bone marrow edema, and bone erosions; however, its use is limited by expense and the need for anesthesia in younger children. The use of contrast can accurately differentiate between active and inactive states; however, new findings and implications of gadolinium deposition in the brain need to be further studied in children.

One study found subclinical synovitis present in >35% of presumed clinically inactive JIA patients. Certain joints are best evaluated using MRI in children, including the TMJ joint, SI joint, and cervical spine. The Adult Assessment of Spondyloarthritis International Society (ASAS) definition of radiologic sacroilitis was found to have low sensitivity in children. MRI is the imaging of choice for suspected SI joint involvement and is best visualized on fluid-sensitive sequences (STIR or T2-weighted fat saturation images). Interestingly, MRI is not the best modality to evaluate entheses due to cost, availability, and potential need for sedation. Recent work with diffusion-weighted MRI (DWI) that does not need contrast has shown promise by detecting arthritis with a sensitivity of 93% and a specificity of 81%. Because work to standardize normals in children is ongoing, caution must be taken when analyzing MRI imaging in children. A pilot study showed that contrast-enhanced MRI of the knee was useful for predicting flares in children with clinically inactive JIA. Regarding long-term outcomes, asymptomatic patients with a positive MRI and signs of inflammation on US are more likely to flare or show disease progression at 6-month follow-up. Furthermore, a longterm outcome study on radiographic damage showed restricted mobility in a joint at 15 years is the most important predictor of joint damage at 29 years of disease duration. Emerging imaging techniques for JIA evaluation include infrared thermal imaging of knee and ankle joints, three-dimensional imaging particularly of the TMJ, and motion detection with accelerometer and gyroscopes to quantify joint movement and gait analysis.

### Outcomes

With earlier, more aggressive, targeted therapies, the overall outcome of JIA is clearly improving. In a prospective inception cohort

(ReACCh-Out), within 2 years after diagnosis on contemporary treatments, the probability of zero active joints was >78% for all JIA patients, and the probability of inactive disease (no active joints, no extra-articular manifestations, and a physician global assessment of disease activity <10 mm) was >70% in all categories except for RF+ polyarticular JIA. Within 5 years, the probability of disease remission (inactive disease ≥12 months of no treatment) was 46% to 57% in all JIA subgroups with the exception of 0% in RF+ and 14% in RFpolyarticular JIA subtypes.

The STOP-JIA trial showed there were no significant differences in CID score between polyarticular JIA patients with three different treatment protocols (CTPs) (step up versus early combination versus biologic first) at the 3-year timepoint. However, the more important statistic is that the proportion of patients who achieved clinical remission at any time in the study was only 47% to 67%. 84,

Therefore even with new diagnostic and treatment approaches, JIA may persist through adulthood; flares are common off medicine and cause significant morbidity, functional disability, joint damage, growth impairment, decreased health-related qualityof-life (HRQoL),244chronic pain, 245 and economic hardship. Chronic pain in JIA patients persists despite absent clinical activ- HRQoL.248, While the majority of JIA patients can achieve inactive disease with treatment at some point, it is uncertain how long to treat and how to withdraw medication. More studies are needed to approach medication withdrawal in JIA. There is also substantial variation in disease remission frequencies depending on JIA subgroup, but only some patients are able to maintain remission of medications for long term.

### Oligoarticular Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis

The long-term outcome of oligoarticular JIA has improved steadily in the last 15 years. In the ReACCh-Out cohort, 96% of patients with oligoarticular JIA had inactive disease, and 57% were in remission off medication at 5 years. In general, patients with persistent oligoarticular JIA have the best prognosis of all JIA subtypes, with 66% to 80% of patients achieving clinical remission off medication.250, Extended oligoarticular JIA patients usually follow a similar chronic disease course as RFpolyarticu- lar JIÅ and have higher cumulative duration of active arthritis,252 more erosive disease, and a higher risk of chronic disability. Of children with extended oligoarticular JIA, 21% to 50% were in remission off medication. 250, Relapses occur, with disease flares occurring 2 years on or off medication in 41% to 45% of patients with persistent oligoarticular JIA and 47% to 56% with extended oligoarticular JIA.250, A large prospective inception cohort study showed a 42.5% risk of flares in the year after reaching clinically inactive disease while on stable treatment. Ongoing disease activity and extension of joint involvement in oligoarticular JIA patients are related to a poor outcome and radiographic damage,255 and therefore emphasis on control of disease activity is critical.

### Rheumatoid Factor-Negative Polyarticular Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis

RFpolyarticular JIA patients have variable outcomes, but the overall prognosis appears to be improving with new treatment strategies. Early response to treatment is an important predictor of long-term outcome, and patients who have at least one episode

of inactive disease within the first 5 years of disease may have less joint damage and a better functional outcome.256, Symmetric arthritis and early hand involvement predicts future disability and poorer overall well-being. Reported remission rates vary, depending on cohorts evaluated and remission definitions used. Earlier studies show remission rates of 14% at 5 years243 and up to 52% at 30 years. In a more recent study reporting outcomes of JIA patients treated during the biologic era with follow-up of 18 years, less than 20% of patients were in remission off medication, ~25% to 30% were in remission on medication, and ~50% continued to have active disease.

### Rheumatoid Factor-Positive Polyarticular Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis

Children with RF+ polyarticular JIA have the most severe articular outcome with the worst joint prognosis of all the JIA subtypes, especially in the era before biologic therapies but even now with contemporary treatments.30, This type of arthritis persists into adulthood, should be treated more aggressively, and can cause significant functional disability. In a recent cohort of patients on biologic treatments, there was a 93% probability of inactive disease, but there was 0% probability of disease remission off medications at 5 years. In a long-term outcome study of JIA patients from the pre-biologic era with 30 years follow-up, only 17% of patients with RF+ polyarticular JIA reached complete remission off medication. Children with RF+ polyarticular JIA in the ReACCh-Out cohort had a 33% probability of significant flare at 1 year and 52% probability at 2 years following inactive disease. A radiographic study published in 2003 reflecting the pre-biologic treatment era showed that 9 years after disease presentation, RF+ JIA polyarticular patients had more joint space narrowing and erosions (75%) compared with RFpolyarticular JIA (39%), sJIA (63%), and oligoarticular JIA patients (25%).

### Juvenile Spondyloarthritis

The long-term outcome of JSpA is not well studied, but as many as 40% of these children appear to progress to the adult form of AS. Compared with adult AS, juvenile AS had less severe axial involvement but worse hip involvement and worse functional impairment.260, Patients with earlier biologic treatment (<2 years) were twice as likely to be in remission off medication and had better functional outcomes than those starting biologic treatment >5 years out from diagnosis.

Children with ERA who were treated with TNFi in the first year after diagnosis had statistically significant improvement in joint count, patient-reported pain, and disease activity compared with patients only treated with csDMARDS. Children with ERA who were treated with TNFi in the first year after diagnosis had statistically significant improvement in joint count, patientreported pain, and disease activity compared with patients only treated with csDMARDS.

Predictors of failure to achieve remission include family history of AS in a first degree relative, HLA-DRB1*08 genotype, and ankle arthritis within 6 months of onset. Factors that are associated with poorer prognosis overall include: increased body mass index, ankle arthritis, hip arthritis, sacroiliitis, enthesitis, and HLA-B27.166, If the arthritis had persisted for >5 years, the chance of remission was only 17% in the pre-biologic era.' 263 Despite TNF inhibitors helping control inflammation, patients were not able to discontinue therapy without recurrence and may

not prevent ankylosis or the eventual fusion of the SI joints.41, Recent studies have also shown that patients with JSpA have poorer patient-reported outcomes of pain intensity, physical function, and health status.161, In addition, children with enthesitis regardless of juvenile arthritis subtype reported worse patient-reported outcomes (quality of life, function, and pain) than those without enthesitis.

### Juvenile Psoriatic Arthritis

Because of the heterogeneity in the patterns of arthritis in JPsA, the outcomes are variable and tend to track with the pattern of joint involvement. In one study, erosions were less common in JPsA compared with polyarticular JIA (23% versus 46%, respectively). Older reports note that JPsA patients have more persistent disease and worse functional outcomes than other subtypes of JIA. However, in more recent cohort studies, the outcomes appeared somewhat improved, with up to 60% of JPsA patients achieving inactive disease on therapy; however, much fewer achieve inactive disease off therapy.

### Systemic Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis

The advent of effective IL-1 and IL-6 blockade in sJIA has been transformational in effectively treating both systemic and articular disease and preventing long-term damage due to arthritis or corticosteroid dependence. The overall response rates for IL-1 or IL-6 inhibitor therapy in the RCTs demonstrated that 50% to 90% achieved pediatric ACR70 improvement and 30% to 50% achieved CID. In addition, 30% to 50% of patients discontinued corticosteroids.129, Participants in these clinical trials often had chronic active arthritis and corticosteroid dependence and were nonresponsive to other therapies. These results are especially remarkable in light of the natural history of sJIA before biologic therapies, where the course could be (1) continuous with persistent often destructive arthritis and disability, often more prominent after the regression of systemic symptoms in approximately 40% the patients; (2) relapsing, characterized by flares of systemic features with mild to moderate arthritis in 30%; or (3) monocyclic with remission within 2 years.268, Over 50% of patients received corticosteroids and multiple DMARDs. Patients with severe disease can have flares of extra-articular features at any time and may have active arthritis into adult life despite therapy. The severe growth delay seen before the use of IL-1 and IL-6 therapies is significantly decreased with biologic therapies in part due to decreased corticosteroid use, as well as growth delay due to systemic inflammatory features. Long-term articular damage has greatly decreased since the use of IL-1 and IL-6 inhibitors, although in many cases, long-term discontinuation is possible in only a minority of patients, and some level of cytokine blockade is needed for most. 271, Currently, there are several ongoing studies addressing whether there are predictors of which patients respond better to IL-1 versus IL-6 blockade. 273,

Systemic JIA accounts for the majority of the mortality seen in all JIA. The life-threatening complication of MAS occurs in approximately 10% of patients and does not appear to be prevented by ongoing treatment with IL-1 or IL-6 inhibitors. However, the initially high mortality rates of 22% have decreased significantly since 2001275 to around 5% to 8% with improved understanding and new therapeutic and management approaches to MAS.68, The new anti-INFγ monoclonal antibody, emapalumab, holds significant promise for patients with MAS associated with sJIA.

The emergence of severe lung disease (sJIA-LD) corresponds with the use of IL-1 and IL-6 inhibitors in the majority of patients76,77 with a mortality that may be as high as 30%. Multiple complex immune dysregulation interactions appear to contribute including cytokine imbalances and drug hypersensitivity reactions, 78,79,184 and dissecting the various potential factors and management strategies are under active study. Amyloidosis was previously a major cause of death in sJIA but is now much less common, most likely because of the use of more aggressive therapy to better control inflammation.

### Special Considerations in Children

Because most bone formation and growth occur in the first 20 years, arthritis in children can cause significant musculoskeletal abnormalities, both generalized and localized. Some joints, like the knee, may hypertrophy and cause leg-length discrepancy; other joints may shorten or have delayed growth, especially the TMJ and MTP joints.

TMJ arthritis is difficult to detect and diagnose since pain and physical exam findings may not be present early in disease. Once symptoms and exam findings are present, changes to the joint have already occurred. TMJ involvement may affect dentofacial development, resulting in retroor micrognathia, facial asymmetry, limitation in mouth opening, pain, and malocclusion. Gadolinium-enhanced MRI is the gold standard imaging study to detect active TMJ arthritis. Standardizing terminology and assessment for orofacial conditions in JIA: international, multidisciplinary consensus-based recommendations), and there is no single physical exam finding that accurately predicts TMJ arthritis identified on MRI. The prevalence of TMJ arthritis in JIA is reported between 40% to 96% depending on examination criteria and imaging modality used. Isolated TMJ arthritis can occur as the initial joint presentation of JIA280 or can occur in the face of inactive arthritis in other affected joints. TMJ arthritis can occur in all JIA subtypes. Recommendations for the orofacial examination of JIA patients to monitor for TMJ involvement have been published. These include a detailed assessment of orofacial symptoms and physical exam assessment of TMJ function, signs of TMJ arthritis, and facial morphology and symmetry.

In 2021, the ACR published guidelines for treatment of JIA, including TMJ arthritis. These guidelines provide seven specific recommendations for the treatment of TMJ arthritis, although six are conditional, and all have very low quality of supporting evidence. In patients with active TMJ arthritis, both NSAIDs and intra-articular corticosteroids (IACs) are conditionally recommended as part of the initial therapy. If response to NSAIDs and/ or IACs is incomplete, use of csDMARD or bDMARD is recommended. Despite short-term improvements in TMJ arthritis with IACs, long-term consequences include heterotopic bone formation284and impaired mandibular growth. Therefore, IACs should be used cautiously, especially in skeletally immature patients. The Temporomandibular Joint Juvenile Arthritis Working Group has also published consensus-based recommendations for the evaluation and management of TMJ arthritis and related orofacial manifestations in patients with JIA that include specific recommendations regarding IACs and intra-articular lavage to treat JIA patients with active arthritis or TMJ dysfunction depending on skeletal maturity.

Physiotherapy (PT) and occupational therapy (OT) are crucial for all children with JIA, for range of motion, strengthening, joint protection, and endurance. Children with hand involvement need

OT assessment and input regarding writing and school accommodations. Children who are seen later in their disease may already have flexion contractures that may require splinting and serial casting. Some children with marked leg-length discrepancies may require a shoe lift. Strict limitations from physical education at school and sports are generally not encouraged because physical activity plays an important role in rehabilitation and therapy; however, impact sports should be limited in the presence of joint effusions or when there is a concern for joint instability (i.e., C1/C2 atlantoaxial subluxation). A modified physical education program and sports activities to patients' own tolerance are recommended instead. Education is considered the child's main job, and trying to keep the child in school is of utmost importance for social and emotional growth. Children may be inconsistent in their report of pain; therefore the physical examination becomes important to understand the true extent of disease. Growth can also be affected in children with chronic inflammation; therefore one must be vigilant to watch for children falling off their growth curve as a sign of uncontrolled disease activity. Growth delay, a major issue for children with polyarticular JIA and sJIA, does improve with biologic therapy and good disease control without glucocorticoids (TNF inhibitors and IL-1 or IL-6 inhibitors for sJIA).270, Adolescents begin to think independently yet rely heavily on peer influences. This is a crucial time that can be extremely dangerous with impulsive decisions such as stopping medication or refusing medical care.

### Conclusion

The modern treatment of JIA has significantly decreased the longterm burden of disease but requires early recognition, diagnosis, aggressive treatment, and ongoing monitoring to extinguish disease activity. Pediatric rheumatologists have in their favor the remarkable capacity for childhood growth and development to allow repair and restoration of function. The advent of new biologic DMARD and targeted synthetic DMARD therapies and rapid translation of basic research into therapeutic strategies, as well as collaborative multicenter research networks, should continue to improve the outlook for children with arthritis.

### KEY POINTS

Compared with adult-onset systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), childhood-onset SLE (cSLE) is more severe, with more organ involvement and higher mortality.

Renal and CNS involvement causes significant morbidity and mortality and warrants aggressive therapy.

As survival has improved, it has become important to identify and prevent long-term complications of SLE and its therapy, including osteoporosis, infections, cardiovascular disease, and malignancy.

Neonatal lupus is a passive autoimmune condition distinct from SLE. Infants born to mothers with circulating anti-Ro/SS-A and anti-La/ SS-B antibodies are at risk for characteristic rash, hepatitis, cytopenias, cardiac conduction disease, and cardiomyopathy.

Drug-induced lupus affecting children and adolescents is treated by withdrawal of offending medication and immunosuppression if needed.

### Childhood-Onset Systemic Lupus Erythematosus

### Definition and Classification

Childhood-onset systemic lupus erythematosus (cSLE) is a chronic autoimmune disorder with potential to involve any organ, most commonly affecting the skin, joints, kidneys, lungs, cardiovascular (CV) system, hematopoietic cells, muscles, and central and peripheral nervous systems. The clinical presentation of SLE in both adults and children is heterogeneous, and disease manifestations range from mild to life-threatening. The disease is characterized by periods of disease quiescence and flare. Approximately 20% of SLE patients are diagnosed before age 18 years, and onset of SLE in childhood is associated with higher mortality and more widespread and severe organ involvement compared with adult SLE (aSLE).

Childhood-onset lupus is defined as onset at age younger than 18 years. Because no diagnostic criteria specific for cSLE

exist, classification criteria developed for use in adults participating in clinical trials are often used, albeit with limitations, in clinical practice. The 1997 American College of Rheumatology (ACR) Classification Criteria,3 the 2012 Systemic Lupus International Collaborating Clinics (SLICC) Classification Criteria,4 and the 2019 European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology (EULAR)/ACR Classification Criteria for SLE5 are discussed in Chapter 81 and have been validated in cSLE populations with varying sensitivities (69% to 98%) and specificities (67% to 100%).6-11

### Epidemiology

Childhood-onset lupus occurs worldwide, and disease prevalence is lower in children (2 to 34/100,000) compared with adults (20 to 150/100,000).1, Reported incidence ranges from 0.2 to 2.5/100,000 per year.1, As in adults, cSLE is more common in Hispanic and non-White populations.12-14, SLE is more likely to develop in females than males, and the ratio of female to male involvement varies across age groups. The female to male ratio is highest between puberty and menopause (ranging from 5:1 to 10:1), whereas before puberty the ratio is lower, estimated at 3:1 to 4:1.17 Diagnosis of SLE at an age younger than 5 years is unusual, whereas diagnosis in adolescence is most common with peak age of onset at 12.6 years.1,17

### Genetics and Pathogenesis

Adult and cSLE share complex pathophysiology (see Chapter 80) with genetic, epigenetic, sex, and environmental factors interacting to produce widespread immune system dysregulation (eFig. 10.1). The pathophysiology of cSLE is considered similar to that of adult SLE, although given the earlier and more severe phenotype, enhanced genetic susceptibility is suspected in cSLE.

SLE is principally a multigenic disorder in adults and children, and a higher genetic load is linked to younger onset. Genomewide association studies have identified more than 100 SLE risk loci, and greater than 40 gene variants were confirmed to be

associated with cSLE.18, These gene variants are associated with pathways involving oxidative stress, immune cell signaling, complement activation, and immune complex clearance. Copy number variation of certain genomic segments contribute to disease, including low C420 and high Toll-like receptor 7 (TLR7) gene copy numbers.18, More research is needed to assess the contributions of higher genetic load, ancestry and ethnicity on the presentation and disease course in cSLE.

Although the vast majority of SLE cases are multigenic, rare monogenic disorders cause SLE or lupus-like disorders, present in early childhood, and shed light on SLE pathogenesis (Table 110.1).18, Recurrent infections and severe cutaneous manifestations are common in monogenic lupus. In contrast to female predominance of multigenic SLE, males and females are equally affected in monogenic disease. Single gene mutations giving rise to a lupus phenotype involve abnormalities in proteins in the complement pathway, nucleic acid sensing and processing, apoptosis, and/or lymphocyte activation. Mutations affecting the early complement pathway (C1q, C1r, C1s, C2, C4A, and C4B) lead to SLE. Defective clearance of immune complexes results in their deposition in peripheral tissues, local inflammation, cytokine expression (including type I interferon [IFN]), and immune cell infiltration. Among complement disorders, C1q deficiency is the rarest but most strongly associated with SLE. Mutations in genes involved in nucleic acid metabolism represent primary type 1 interferonopathies that cause lupus-like disease. DNasel deficiency impairs removal of extracellular chromatin, which contributes to immune activation, type I IFN expression, autoantibody production, and early-onset lupus-like disease. Loss-of-function mutations in genes encoding the three prime repair exonuclease 1 (TREX1) also causes type I IFN expression leading to familial chilblain lupus. Gain-of-function variants in TLR7, a sensor of viral RNA, have been described in children with severe lupus. Disrupted apoptosis caused by gene mutations in FAS, FAS ligand, or protein kinase C delta (PKCD) leads to ineffective elimination

of T or B lymphocytes to cause lupus-like disease. Monogenic causes of lupus should be considered with young age at onset (<5 years of age), presence of severe or refractory skin disease, history of recurrent infections, and in the setting of consanguinity.

Increased expression of genes related to the type I IFN signaling pathway (IFN signature) is evident in cSLE. IFN-α, member of the type I IFN family, causes CD4+ T cell activation in addition to preventing B cell apoptosis and enhancing B cell proliferation and differentiation into antibody-secreting plasma cells, thereby promoting autoimmunity. Plasmacytoid dendritic cells (pDCs) stimulated by TLR7 and TLR9 play a central role in SLE as major producers of type I IFN. It has been demonstrated in cSLE that nucleic acidcontaining immune complexes, neutrophil extracellular traps, and oxidized mitochondrial DNA-protein complexes activate pDCs causing IFN production. 23-25 Erythrocytes carrying retained mitochondria that are internalized by macrophages also produce type I IFN in cSLE.

Genetic inheritance alone is insufficient to cause SLE, as suggested by 40% to 60% concordance rates for SLE in monozygotic twins. Thus other factors, including epigenetics and hormonal and environmental exposures, are important in SLE susceptibility. In both aSLE and cSLE, epigenetic changes, including methylation of DNA, post-translational histone modifications, and noncoding RNAs, regulate DNA compaction and accessibility, thereby modulating gene expression. DNA hypomethylation is common in SLE and has also been found to correlate with increased disease activity in cSLE. Variables that may induce epigenetic changes in lupus include exposure to ultraviolet (UV) radiation, particulate air pollution, silica, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, cigarette smoking, and infections including Epstein—Barr virus.

The risk of developing SLE is affected by sex and aneuploidy of the X chromosome. Several genes that regulate innate and adaptive immune responses are located on the X chromosome, including TLR7. Conditions with excess X chromosomes increase risk of developing SLE, including 46, XXY (Klinefelter's syndrome) and

46, XX male (de la Chapelle's syndrome). The prevalence of SLE is lower in females with 45, X0 (Turner's syndrome) compared with 46, XX (normal karyotype) females.

Evidence for a key role of reproductive hormones in SLE pathogenesis is reflected in the prevalence of disease in females of reproductive age and the frequency of flares during periods of hormonal change including pregnancy and the postpartum state. Estrogens exert effects via estrogen receptors α and β, both widely distributed in the immune system. Estrogens enhance humoral immunity and can affect DNA methylation. While exogenous estrogens appear to increase risk of developing SLE in postmenopausal women with SLE, oral contraceptive use has not increased SLE flare in the setting of stable disease.30, Although onset of SLE frequently occurs surrounding puberty in adolescents, the impact of puberty on the development of cSLE has not been extensively studied.

### Clinical Features

Childhood-onset SLE manifests with a vast array of clinical symptoms and findings. The most common presenting findings in cSLE include fever, malar rash, arthritis, glomerulonephritis, neuropsychiatric disease, and hematologic abnormalities. .17,32Several common clinical manifestations of cSLE are summarized in Table 1 10.2. Despite the similarities in SLE pathophysiology and genetics across the age spectrum, the clinical presentations of aSLE and cSLE differ. Compared with adults, children and adolescents have more widespread organ involvement (particularly renal, neurologic, and hematologic disease), have overall higher SLE disease activity scores, and are treated more frequently with moderateto high-dose corticosteroids (CSs) and cyclophosphamide.17,33-36

### Cutaneous Manifestations

Cutaneous lupus erythematosus (CLE) can occur in isolation or in the context of SLE. In children presenting with isolated CLE, evolution to cSLE can occur in up to 26% and is most likely to occur in the first year after diagnosis.37, As discussed more extensively in Chapter 81, subtypes of CLE include acute, subacute and chronic CLE. Acute CLE manifestations are photo-distributed on the face (malar rash) or more generally and can rarely include toxic epidermolysis. Subacute CLE rashes include annular, papulosquamous, and vesiculobullous lesions. Chronic CLE includes discoid lupus erythematosus (DLE; which can be localized, generalized, or hypertrophic), lupus panniculitis (also known as lupus profundus), chilblain lupus, hypertrophic lupus, lichenoid CLE, and tumid lupus. Of these, DLE is the most common, and characteristic histologic features include atrophy follicular plugging. DLE often leads to abnormal pigmentation and scarring. Individual patients may experience more than one form of CLE.39, Figs. 110.1 to 110.3 show common mucocutaneous findings in cSLE.

### Lupus Nephritis

Lupus nephritis (LN) is more common in cSLE compared with aSLE present in up 40% to 70%.17, As in aSLE, LN is suspected in the presence of unexplained proteinuria, hematuria, urinary casts, hypertension, abnormal renal function, and edema; renal biopsy is the gold standard for diagnosis. The distribution of histologic classes of LN is similar to adults (see Chapter 81).17, Proliferative LN (International Society of Nephrology/Renal Pathology Society [ISN/RPS] classes III and IV) often presents with nephritic urine (proteinuria, hematuria, casts), hypertension, and acute or chronic kidney injury. Membranous LN (ISN/RPS class V) as in

adults typically presents with proteinuria, nephrotic syndrome but preserved renal function. However, LN can be insidious, sometimes appearing with few or no symptoms, highlighting the importance of routine monitoring for renal involvement.

### Neuropsychiatric Systemic Lupus Erythematosus

Neuropsychiatric systemic lupus erythematosus (NPSLE) is challenging to diagnose, especially in developing children and adolescents who are at risk for mood disorders. The reported prevalence of NPSLE in children (cNPSLE) and adolescents ranges from 22% to 95% with more frequent occurrence in cSLE, typically early in the disease course. The ACR nomenclature and case definitions for NPSLE (see Chapter 81), primarily derived from adult data, are used in cSLE. Common presenting symptoms in cNPSLE include headache, mood disorder, seizures, cerebrovascular disease, and chorea. Cognitive dysfunction is evident in

approximately one-third of children and is diagnosed with formal cognitive testing.

### Antiphospholipid Antibody Syndrome

As in adults, antiphospholipid antibody syndrome (APS) can complicate cSLE. Adult classification criteria are used because pediatric versions do not exist. Although the incidence and prevalence are not established in children, in a large cohort of patients with APS, only 3% presented at 15 years old or younger. Manifestations of APS include thrombocytopenia, livedo reticularis, arterial and venous thrombosis, microangiopathic renal disease, chorea, cognitive dysfunction, and pregnancy loss. Catastrophic antiphospholipid antibody syndrome is a rare and life-threatening

complication characterized by simultaneous multiorgan microvascular thromboses with rapid onset of multiorgan failure in the setting of antiphospholipid antibodies. The mortality remains high, ranging between 24% and 33%.

### Macrophage Activation Syndrome

Macrophage activation syndrome (MAS), also known as secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH), can complicate SLE and incurs significant mortality. The underlying pathogenesis of MAS in SLE may differ from that of systemic onset juvenile idiopathic arthritis and Still's disease. Macrophage activation syndrome is likely to occur at onset of cSLE and without an infectious trigger.50,5i Typical clinical findings include high fevers, hepatosplenomegaly, cytopenias, liver dysfunction, coagulopathy, hyperferritinemia, and falling erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) despite evidence of systemic inflammation. Levels of soluble interleukin (IL)-2 receptor are often elevated.

### Diagnosis and Diagnostic Tests

Due to the heterogeneous and systemic nature of cSLE, the differential diagnosis is broad and often includes multiple infections (including EpsteinBarr virus, cytomegalovirus, histoplasmosis, coccidiomycosis, and tuberculosis), systemic-onset juvenile idiopathic arthritis, vasculitides, MAS, malignancies (especially leukemia and lymphoma), other systemic causes of glomerulonephritis, neurologic and cardiopulmonary disease, and drug-induced lupus.

The diagnosis of cSLE is clinical and made on the basis of a detailed history, meticulous physical examination, laboratory studies, and tissue biopsy when required. The diagnostic approach mirrors that used in aSLE (see Chapter 81) and includes assessment of complete blood count (CBC), hepatic and renal function, complement protein levels, direct Coombs's assay, and measurement of autoantibodies including antibodies to nuclear antibodies (ANA), double-stranded DNA (dsDNA), extractable nuclear antigens (Ro/SSA, La/SSB, Smith, and ribonucleoprotein [RNP]), and antiphospholipid antibodies. In cSLE, certain autoantibodies are detected more frequently than in adults, including anti-dsDNA, anti-cardiolipin, anti-histone, and anti-ribosomal P antibodies. As in adults, ANA-negative lupus is exceedingly rare in children and adolescents.

In the presence of abnormal or reduced renal function, prompt kidney biopsy to evaluate for the presence and class of LN is

recommended. Renal biopsy is an invasive procedure associated with risks of bleeding, infection, and other risks of general anesthesia required for biopsy in children. There is no clear consensus on optimal indications or timing of initial or repeat renal biopsy in cSLE.

While not yet used in clinical practice, several biomarkers show promise in diagnosing and monitoring cSLE. The IFN signature has been well described in cSLE but does not always correlate with disease activity.54, The presence of neutrophil extracellular traps correlates with disease activity, high anti-dsDNA antibody, and low C3 levels. Initial studies suggest that elevated levels of cellbound complement activation products, such as C4d deposition on B cells and erythrocytes, have high sensitivity and specificity in cSLE diagnosis and correlate with disease activity.

Urinary biomarker panels can detect active LN and predict renal flare in children. Several urinary biomarkers, alone or in combination panels, have been validated in LN in children, including neutrophil gelatinase-associated lipocalin (NGAL), monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 (MCP-1), α1-acid glycoprotein (AGP-1), ceruloplasmin (CP), lipocalin-type prostaglandin- D synthetase (L-PGDS), and transferrin. 22,

As in adults, neuroimaging to detect NPSLE includes standard and functional MRI and positron-emission tomography (PET) imaging with technetium. Abnormal findings on neuroimaging include white matter hyperintensities seen on T2-weighted images, cerebral atrophy, and small cortical infarcts. However, imaging may be normal in patients with diffuse manifestations such as headaches, cognitive dysfunction, and psychosis. While no serum or cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) serologic tests are diagnostic of NPSLE, CSF analysis may reveal nonspecific signs of intrathecal inflammation, including elevated protein levels and white blood cell counts. The association between anti-ribosomal P antibodies and psychosis in adult NPSLE has not been confirmed in pediatric studies. The developmentally appropriate neurocognitive test, pediatric automated neuropsychological assessment (peds ANAM), is used to detect and follow neuropsychological abnormalities, although limited by its length and requirement for special computer software.22,54,58,59

### Treatment and Management

Treatment decisions are often based upon adult clinical trial data as only one drug (belimumab) is approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration for cSLE. Although many aspects of adult and cSLE pathophysiology are similar, important differences exist and affect management, including pharmacokinetics, palatability of medications, ability to swallow pills, neurodevelopment, growth, puberty, and high-risk adolescent behaviors. Similar to aSLE, treatment of cSLE is tailored to the severity of specific manifestations. Some treatments are recommended for all children and adolescents with SLE, including hydroxychloroquine and photoprotection. Glucocorticoids are the mainstay for initial treatment of significant organ involvement; however, the substantial toxicity associated with long-term therapy mandates careful use, and steroid-sparing approaches are recommended to limit cumulative exposure.

### Hydroxychloroquine

Hydroxychloroquine (HCQ), an anti-malarial drug, is the firstline therapy for cSLE. Because HCQ use is linked to reduced risk of flare, clotting, CV disease, lupus-related organ damage, and improved survival, this medication is recommended for all

with cSLE if no contraindications exist. Based on adult studies, hydroxychloroquine has a favorable safety profile except for its dose-dependent risk for an irreversible retinopathy. In childhood, HCQ may be prescribed either in pill or suspension form with a recommended dose of ≤5 mg/kg/day; however, weight-based dosing may not correlate well with drug concentrations. Dosed appropriately, the rate of retinal toxicity after 10 years of exposure is <2%. As in aSLE, routine ophthalmology screening with visual fields and spectral-domain optical coherence tomography is recommended. Young children may not be able to cooperate with visual field testing, and involvement of a pediatric ophthalmologist is recommended.

### Glucocorticoids

Glucocorticoids prescribed in oral tablet, suspension, or intravenous (IV) preparations remain the mainstay for initial treatment of significant organ involvement in cSLE. For children, the typical dose of oral prednisone or prednisolone ranges from 0.5 to 2 mg/kg/day, depending on severity of illness. IV methylprednisolone "pulses" of 30 mg/kg/dose (maximum of 1 g/day) for 1 to 5 days are often used to treat severe disease. Although highly effective in suppressing lupus activity, side effects associated with glucocorticoid use including weight gain, growth failure, avascular necrosis, poor bone mineralization, pubertal delay, acne, striae, and mood fluctuations can be particularly problematic in children and adolescents; thus minimizing glucocorticoid exposure is critically important. Glucocorticoid tapering is tailored based on improvements in disease activity as measured by clinical and laboratory indices. If glucocorticoids cannot be reduced or eliminated due to continued disease activity, then a steroid-sparing, diseasemodifying anti-rheumatic drug (DMARD) or biologic therapy is recommended.

### Steroid-Sparing Agents: Disease-Modifying Anti-rheumatic Drugs −

Methotrexate is used to treat nonrenal manifestations of cSLE, including arthritis, serositis, and mucocutaneous manifestations. The side effect profile in children is similar to adults, although children may be more prone to CNS side effects. Methotrexate can be prescribed orally (tablets or suspension) or subcutaneously with weight-based dosing (up to 1 mg/kg or 15 to 20 mg/m2/ week; maximum of 25 mg/week). Leflunomide is an alternative to methotrexate that has not been specifically studied in cSLE.

Azathioprine is used for nonrenal manifestations of cSLE, for LN maintenance therapy when mycophenolate mofetil is not tolerated, during pregnancy, or when there is a high risk of pregnancy. Azathioprine given as a daily dose (1 to 2 mg/kg/day) can be appealing in the setting of nonadherence with twice-daily medications. Some rheumatologists assess thiopurine methyltransferase (TMPT) genetics and/or enzyme activity prior to initiating azathioprine in order to identify individuals at higher risk for azathioprine toxicity.

Mycophenolate mofetil and mycophenolic acid are used to treat renal and nonrenal cSLE. Dosing for mycophenolate mofetil is typically up to 600 mg/m2/dose bid (maximum 1500 mg bid). Levels of mycophenolate metabolites can be measured to assess adherence and guide personalized dosing. The side effect profile of mycophenolate is similar in adults and children with gastrointestinal intolerance, leukopenia, and infection being most common.60, Calcineurin inhibitors, including cyclosporine A, tacrolimus, and voclosporin, are used to treat refractory renal and nonrenal lupus manifestations.60,

Because of its potential toxicity, cyclophosphamide is reserved for severe or refractory cSLE. Appropriate hydration is needed to avoid bladder toxicity, and some rheumatologists use mesna for bladder protection. Gonadal toxicity is a concern for children treated with alkylating agents; fortunately, gonadal failure rates with cyclophosphamide are lower in children and adolescents compared with adults. The use of monthly triptorelin, a gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonist, provides ovarian protection for girls with cSLE who have entered puberty. In addition, cryopreservation of ovarian tissue or eggs is an option for females. Sperm banking can be offered to males. Fertility specialist involvement can help mitigate the risk of cyclophosphamide gonadal toxicity.

### Steroid-Sparing Agents: : Biologics

Monthly belimumab, 10 mg/kg/dose IV, is used to treat active cSLE and cLN.67, Contrary to children treated with aSLE, children treated with belimumab do not appear to experience increased rates of depression.

Clinical trials assessing the efficacy of rituximab in adults with renal and nonrenal SLE have been negative.70, Nonrandomized studies in children suggest efficacy in certain situations, including cSLE-associated cytopenias, refractory LN, NPSLE, and cutaneous disease. The recommended dose is either 750 mg/m2/ dose (maximum of 1 g/dose) at days 1 and 14 or 375 mg/m2/ dose weekly for four doses. Monitoring CBC, CD19 depletion, and immunoglobulin G (IgG) levels for hypogammaglobinemia is recommended.60,

Abatacept and tocilizumab are treatment options for refractory lupus arthritis. TNF inhibitors are generally avoided given their potential to induce drug-induced lupus. Anifrolumab is approved to treat aSLE,74 and clinical trials are underway to assess safety and efficacy in cSLE.

### Other Treatments

Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) are used judiciously in cSLE, primarily in treatment of musculoskeletal symptoms and pericarditis. It is not clear whether the CV toxicity associated with NSAID use in adults extends to the pediatric population. Plasma exchange may be used to manage severe and life-threatening cSLE manifestations.76, Nonpharmacologic interventions including aerobic exercise, dietary supplementation, psychotherapy, and patient education/support may be promising adjunctive therapies but require further study.

### Approach to Treating g Cutaneous Manifestations

Photoprotection is a cornerstone of prevention of cutaneous lupus lesions. UV radiation exposure can increase the risk of cutaneous flare and may contribute to systemic flare through delayed clearance of apoptotic keratinocytes. Routine, daily use of sunscreen is recommended, as are other photoprotective behaviors, including avoiding midday sun and wearing sun-protective clothing. When choosing a sunscreen, it is important to look for ingredients that provide both UVA and UVB protection, including physical agents such as titanium dioxide, zinc oxide, and chemical filters such as avobenzone. Sunblock with sun protection factor (SPF) 30 to 50 is recommended and must be applied in sufficient amounts at least 20 to 30 minutes before sun exposure and reapplied frequently. Children and adolescents may require school modifications to reduce sun exposure and allow application of sunscreen.

Topical corticosteroids can be effective for localized lesions but risk cutaneous atrophy with long-term use. Topical calcineurin

therapy can spare topical steroid exposure. Intralesional steroids can be effective for lesions refractory to topical steroids. Systemic therapy may be required for cutaneous disease and can include hydroxychloroquine, systemic glucocorticoids, DMARDs, and biologic agents. In addition, dapsone, quinacrine, oral retinoids, intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG), thalidomide, and lenalidomide are agents sometimes prescribed in treatment of refractory cutaneous disease. Randomized controlled trials for cutaneous lupus, particularly in the pediatric setting, are lacking.

### Approach to Treating Lupus Nephritis

Management of proliferative LN involves phases of induction to achieve disease control (usually the first 6 months of therapy) followed by maintenance therapy. Induction therapy typically includes oral and/or IV glucocorticoids and either cyclophosphamide or mycophenolate mofetil. In order to standardize approaches to treating LN in children and adolescents, consensus treatment plans (CTPs) were developed for induction therapy and are summarized in Fig. 110.4.82 The approach to maintenance therapy is similar to adults including use of mycophenolate mofetil, azathioprine, or every 2 to 3 month IV cyclophosphamide. Belimumab may also be used to treat active cLN. The use of the Euro-Lupus protocol using lower-dose cyclophosphamide every 2 weeks for six doses is increasing in cSLE but has not been rigorously studied.79, Calcineurin inhibitors and rituximab are considered in refractory cases. Additionally, renin angiotensin blockade is recommended for all with proteinuria unless contraindicated.

CTPs for membranous LN have not been developed, and no pediatric clinical trial data are available to guide treatment decisions. According to a national survey of pediatric rheumatologists, the most common medications used to manage membranous LN include glucocorticoids, renin angiotensin blockade, mycophenolate mofetil, rituximab, cyclophosphamide, and azathioprine. In the setting of end-stage renal disease (ESRD) due to cLN, hemodialysis is used more often than peritoneal dialysis, and renal transplant is recommended if feasible.41,84

### Approach to Treating Neuropsychiatric Lupus

No randomized controlled trial (RCT) or CTP is available to guide treatment decisions in cNPSLE, although some recommendations have been published through the Single Hub and Access Point for Pædiatric Rheumatology in Europe (SHARE) initiative. Treatment is tailored to the specific NPSLE manifestations and severity of disease. NPSLE manifestations clearly linked to ischemic events are treated with anti-coagulation unless contraindicated by comorbidities. For nonischemic, inflammatory NPSLE manifestations, the treatment approach is similar to that used in LN treatment. Induction approaches include use of high-dose glucocorticoids and cyclophosphamide, mycophenolate mofetil, or azathioprine. Rituximab, IVIG, and plasma exchange are options. With improved control of disease, maintenance therapy, often with mycophenolate mofetil or azathioprine, is prescribed. Adjunctive treatment with anxiolytics, anti-depressants, and antipsychotics may be required. Comanagement with neurology, psychiatry, and psychology is often needed.86,87

### Management of Antiphospholipid Syndrome

Evidence-based recommendations for diagnosis and treatment of pediatric APS have been published through SHARE. When cSLE is complicated by antiphospholipid antibody syndrome, long-term anti-coagulation is advised. In the setting of catastrophic antiphospholipid antibody syndrome, treatment includes

anti-coagulation, plasma exchange, and anti-inflammatory treatment with glucocorticoids, rituximab, and other immunosuppressive medications. Treatment approaches for children and adults with antiphospholipid antibody syndrome and catastrophic antiphospholipid antibody syndrome in SLE are similar (see Chapter 83).47,48

### Adherence to Treatment in Childhood-Onset Systemic Lupus Erythematosus

Adherence to complex treatment regimens is important for optimal outcomes in cSLE but can be challenging in adolescence. Nonadherence is common in lupus across the age spectrum and is associated with increased acute health care utilization and increased disease activity.89, Strategies to improve adherence include prescribing less complicated medication regimens, use of pill boxes and alarms, optimizing communication between the health care provider and the patient, educating patients on self-management, and involving psychologists and social workers to assist with overcoming psychosocial barriers. Unfortunately, evidence-based approaches to improving adherence in lupus have not been identified.91-95 Assessing and developing strategies to improve medication adherence are ideally addressed routinely in clinical settings.

### Opportunities for Prevention

As survival has improved for cSLE, long-term complications have emerged as significant challenges, prompting efforts focusing on reducing the risk of infection, optimizing bone health, and reducing CV risk.

Infection Prevention. Due to immunosuppression from SLE and its treatment, children and adolescents are at significant risk for severe and life-threatening infections.96, Vaccinations provide an important opportunity to prevent infections. Nonlive vaccinations, including those against pneumococcus, meningococcus, Haemophilus influenzae, influenza, and human papillomavirus are considered safe, with variable immunogenicity depending on immunosuppressive therapy in cSLE.98-102 The ACR developed recommendations supporting COVID vaccine administration for adult and pediatric patients with rheumatic disease, and adolescents with lupus and other rheumatic diseases develop immune responses to mRNA COVID-19 vaccine comparable to healthy controls.99,

The safety of live vaccines has not been established in immunocompromised populations. Thus live virus vaccines are withheld in setting of treatment with most DMARDs or biologics and with significant prednisone exposure, particularly when dose is ≥20 mg/day or 2 mg/kg/day for children <10 kg for >14 days.

Fortunately, Pneumocystis jiroveci pneumonia occurs infrequently in lupus, but the infection is associated with significant mortality. As with rheumatologists for adults, pediatric rheumatologists' thresholds for starting prophylactic trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole, dapsone, or pentamidine in immunosuppressed lupus patients varies. 105-107

Optimizing Bone Health. Glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis and failure to achieve peak bone mass are potential complications of cSLE. In cSLE, bone density loss occurs due to effects of chronic inflammation, vitamin D deficiency, decreased physical activity, and glucocorticoid therapy. 1 Dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry (DEXA) is the preferred approach for assessing changes in bone mineral density, although CT may be more accurate. Monitoring with DEXA is recommended in children prescribed glucocorticoid therapy ≥3 months. Lateral thoracolumbar spine imaging can detect asymptomatic vertebral compression fractures.

Ensuring adequate vitamin D and calcium intake, counseling regarding weight-bearing exercise, and avoiding risk factors, including smoking, are universally recommended. Bisphosphonates are not routinely prescribed for the treatment or prevention of osteoporosis in cSLE but may be considered in severe cases.

Cardiovascular Risk Reduction. Because atherosclerosis begins in childhood and is a major long-term source of morbidity and mortality in SLE, anticipatory counseling concerning CV risk reduction and screening for modifiable CV risk factors needs to start at a young age. Control of blood pressure and lipids with dietary and pharmacologic interventions is indicated. The Atherosclerosis Prevention in Pediatric Lupus Erythematosus (APPLE) trial results did not suggest that statins should be routinely offered to all children and adolescents with SLE, but post hoc analyses suggested that higher-risk subgroups may benefit. 108,

Reproductive Health. Most females with SLE have preserved fertility. While pregnancy can usually be safely accomplished, adverse outcomes including maternal flare, pre-eclampsia, pregnancy loss, prematurity, and intrauterine growth restriction are concerning potential complications, particularly in adolescents and young women. Pregnancy outcomes are optimal in the setting of well-controlled disease and when women are taking medications compatible with pregnancy. Adolescents are at risk for having unprotected intercourse, and many adolescents with lupus are taking teratogenic medications. Given the need to avoid pregnancy during times of active disease or when on teratogenic medication, assessment of intention to become pregnant and counseling regarding reproductive health concerns and contraception options are important in postmenarchal (usually ages ≥12 years) females. Due to estrogen's potential to incite disease activity and clotting, contraceptive medications containing significant doses of estrogen are often avoided. The results of the Safety of Exogenous Estrogens in Lupus Erythematosus National Assessment (SELENA) trial, which included adult women with low disease activity and excluded those with lupus anti-coagulant or moderate to high-titer anti-cardiolipin antibodies, suggested that oral contraceptives with low-dose estrogen do not increase the risk of clotting or flare in this limited population. Longer acting contraception such as intrauterine device, implanted etonogestrel, or intramuscular medroxyprogesterone is often recommended to adolescents given the risks associated with estrogen and nonadherence. Consultation with an adolescent medicine specialist can be very helpful in managing reproductive health concerns.

School Concerns. Children and adolescents with lupus have increased risk for lower school educational and vocational achievement compared with peers, despite similar neurocog- 112-114 Children and nitive function and demographic factors. adolescents with SLE may require school accommodations. In certain situations, formal personalized learning plans may be necessary to assist children with lupus achieve their educational goals. Examples of these plans in the United States include 504 plans and individualized education plans (IEPs). Neuropsychological testing can help identify deficits and potential interventions.

Mental Health Concerns. Mental health disorders are prevalent in cSLE, particularly depression (20% to 59%) and anxiety (17% to 37%). Remarkably, 14% of patients with cSLE report history of suicidal ideation.95, Untreated mental health disorders affect cSLE disease activity, management, and health care utilization. Disparities are evident in the mental health of children and adolescents with lupus. Non-White race is associated with increased risk of depression and suicidal ideation in cSLE but with lower likelihood of receiving pharmacologic treatment for mental health disorders.116, Depression severity is associated with poor medication adherence in cSLE, and treatment of mental health disorders improves adherence.95,121,121a Thus it is critically important to identify and treat mental health disorders in patients with cSLE.

Management of mental health disorders in cSLE is challenging, barriers such as stigma and limited mental health care access contribute to low utilization of mental health care.95, While not performed universally, routine mental health care screening can improve detection of anxiety, depression, and suicidal ideation and normalize mental health issues in patients with cSLE.95,

Transition to Adult Care. The transition from child-centered to adult-centered care is a vulnerable period during which adolescents and young adults with SLE are at risk for gaps in care and higher morbidity. Transition refers to the gradual process of preparing the adolescent and young adult for self-management in an adult care setting; transfer represents the time when care is handed off to an adult provider. While no SLE-specific guidelines exist for transition to adult care, disease agnostic approaches and interventions have shown promise. In general, it is recommended that pediatric rheumatologists develop a transition policy and share it with patients and families, provide developmentally appropriate self-management recommendations, assess readiness for transition to adult care beginning at age 14 years, and track progress and confirm ultimate transfer of care to adult rheumatologists. 122,124

### Outcomes in Childhood-Onset Systemic Lupus Erythematosus

### Outcomes and Health Disparities

The diagnosis of SLE during childhood increases risk of organ damage and premature death. Due to longer exposure to disease and treatment, cSLE is associated with more disease-related damage accrual compared with aSLE. In particular, development of cataracts, avascular necrosis, and renal damage are more likely to occur with cSLE versus aSLE. The risk of lupus-related damage is inversely related to age at onset, with prepubertal-onset SLE patients having higher risk of damage than peri-pubertal or postpubertal. Premature atherosclerosis is clearly linked to SLE, and increased carotid intimal medial thickness is evident even in

children and adolescents with SLE. Malignancies are more frequent in cSLE than in the age-matched population. Growth failure and delayed puberty are SLE-related morbidities unique to childhood and adolescence. Lower health-related quality of life in cSLE is associated with female sex, high disease activity, the presence of damage, non-White ethnicity, and the need for cyclophosphamide or rituximab therapy. In general, poor prognostic factors for cSLE include male sex, earlier age at diagnosis, Hispanic ethnicity or non-White race, lower socioeconomic status, and presence of renal or CNS disease. 15,

Fortunately, advances in understanding of SLE pathogenesis, diagnosis, treatment, and supportive care have improved, leading to longer survival. The 5and 10-year survival rates, which were lower than 40% in the 1960s, have increased to >90% in the 2000s, with higher survival rates in highversus low-income countries. Although there is no cure for SLE, most children and adolescents with SLE are now expected to survive into adulthood. Despite these improvements, mortality rates remain higher in cSLE versus aSLE, and survival rates have plateaued in recent decades. Mortality rates are higher in Hispanic and non-White adolescents and young adults. 16, In the United States SLE is the tenth leading overall cause of death, the number one cause of death from a chronic inflammatory disease in the 15 to 24 years age group, and the fifth leading cause of death in Black and Hispanic females aged 15 to 24 years. Across the age spectrum, early in the course of SLE, death most often occurs because of infection or severe SLE organ involvement (particularly renal and CNS disease). In the longer term, causes of mortality shift to infection, atherosclerosis, or malignancy. 15,

In parallel to overall survival, renal survival rates have improved; however, complete remission is achieved in only 40% to 60% of cLN despite aggressive therapy. Children who develop ESRD due to LN have a 5-year mortality of approximately 22%. Compared with other children on hemodialysis, those with cLN have double the mortality rate and are less likely to receive renal transplants despite the fact that, post-transplant, graft survival and infectious complications are comparable.41, Black and Hispanic youth with cLN are more likely to develop ESRD but are less likely than white youth to receive a renal transplant. Geographic disparities are also a concern in cLN, with those in the southern United States less likely to receive renal transplants and more at risk of death during hospitalizations. 16,134-136

### Quality of Care and Improvement Initiatives

Because achieving clinical remission in SLE is often unattainable, the concept of a lupus low disease activity state (LLDAS) has emerged as a goal for SLE treatment.137-139 Attaining LLDAS reduces the risk of severe flare and accumulating disease damage in cSLE. Provider and practice variation contribute to differences in the ability to attain LLDAS and clinical remission targets in cSLE. Attempts to reduce variation in care include international consensus efforts to standardize steroid dosing cLN,141 the SHARE initiative's evidence-based recommendations for diagnosis and treatment of cSLE,85 and a recommended set of 26 quality indicators for the care of patients with cSLE. Adherence to quality indicators in cSLE at pediatric rheumatology centers varies. 142, Approaches successfully used to enhance adherence to quality indicators include pre-visit planning and development of multispecialty lupus clinics.41,118,125-127

### Drug-Induced Lupus

### Definition and Classification

Drug-induced lupus erythematosus (DILE) is the presence of SLE manifestations occurring after exposure to specific medications in individuals with no prior history of SLE. Medications commonly implicated in DILE are listed in eTable 110.1. Specific classification criteria for DILE have not been published, and no published data address differences between adult and pediatric drug-induced lupus. Thus DILE is presumed not to differ across the age spectrum (see adult SLE; Chapter 81).

### Genetics and Pathogenesis

The pathogenesis of DILE is not well understood. Apart from an association with human leukocyte antigen, DR subregion (HLA- DR4), no specific genetic abnormalities have been associated with DILE, but acetylator status may be implicated. Hypotheses regarding pathogenesis include drugs serving as haptens prompting autoimmune response, direct cytotoxicity of drugs, and consequences of DNA hypomethylation. 128,144

### Clinical Manifestations

As in adults, DILE affects males and females equally and is unlikely to cause significant renal or CNS disease. It can be challenging to distinguish SLE and DILE; however, some clinical and serologic features and the resolution of symptoms after drug withdrawal can help arrive at the correct diagnosis. In general, DILE is milder than SLE. Hepatic involvement in drug-induced lupus is common.

Laboratory abnormalities can include circulating anti-histone antibodies (present in up to 95% of individuals with DILE), although these antibodies are not specific and can also be present in SLE unassociated with drug exposure. Anti-dsDNA and anti-Smith antibodies are unlikely to occur in DILE, and hypocomplementemia is less common in DILE than in SLE. Epigenetic abnormalities are important in drug-induced lupus, and hydralazine and procainamide, for example, can cause DNA hypomethylation.

### Treatment

Treatment of drug-induced lupus involves withdrawal of the offending medication and immunosuppressive therapy if indicated. Resolution of clinical findings may take months to years.

### Neonatal Lupus

### Definition and Classification

Neonatal lupus (NLE) is a separate entity from SLE and is one of the few rheumatic disorders presenting in the neonatal period or early infancy. NLE is a passive autoimmune condition caused by transfer of circulating maternal autoantibodies to the fetal circulation. No diagnostic criteria are available for NLE.

### Genetics and Pathogenesis

The maternal autoantibodies associated with the vast majority of NLE cases are anti-Ro/SS-A (or anti-SSA) and anti-LA/SS-B (or

anti-SSB); and anti-UA RNP antibodies. Because NLE develops in only 1% to 2% of children born to mothers with these circulating antibodies, these antibodies are not sufficient to cause NLE. Although the exact pathogenesis of NLE remains unknown, a popular hypothesis based upon in vivo studies postulates that Ro and La antigens are exposed on the surface of cardiac myositis during fetal cardiac development and become a target for maternal autoantibodies. The ensuing inflammatory cascade causes damages to the conduction system and, in some cases, leads to cardiomyopathy. While the cardiac sequelae of NLE are not reversible, the inflammatory changes related to NLE resolve when maternal autoantibodies are cleared from the infant's circulation, typically within 6 months.

### Clinical Features

The clinical manifestations of NLE include a nonscarring malar or annular rash commonly affecting the face, scalp, and trunk (Fig 1 10.5). The rash usually appears in the first 6 weeks of life and can be triggered by exposure to UV light. Histologically, the cutaneous findings are similar to those in subacute cutaneous lupus. Other findings can include immune-mediated cytopenias and hepatitis (transaminitis, hepatomegaly). The most frequent and serious complication of NLE is cardiac involvement. Cardiac conduction abnormalities can present in utero (starting at 16 weeks of gestation when maternal immunoglobulins can cross the placenta) or shortly after birth and range from prolongation of the PR interval to complete heart block (CHB). In addition, endocardial fibroelastosis and progressive cardiomyopathy can develop. Recurrence of NLE congenital heart block in future offspring is estimated at 17%.

### Treatment

Noncardiac NLE manifestations are reversible and usually do not require any treatment. Topical CS are sometimes used to treat the rash, and IVIG has been used for severe cytopenias. However, congenital heart block and cardiomyopathy are irreversible and can cause death and morbidity; thus therapies to prevent or delay the development of cardiac involvement are needed.

### Approaches to Detection and Prevention of Cardiac NLE

Given the risk for NLE, it is recommended that pregnant women with circulating anti-Ro/SSA or anti-La/SSB antibodies undergo monitoring of fetal PR interval and cardiac function during pregnancy beginning at 16 weeks. Several retrospective studies suggest that maternal HCQ use during pregnancy reduces the risk of cardiac NLE in offspring, and a prospective open-label, single-arm, two-stage study showed reduction of CHB to 50% of historical rates. Two prospective observational studies using IVIG (at replacement doses of 400 mg/kg every 3 weeks during second trimester) to prevent CHB anti-Ro-positive mothers with previously affected child showed unconvincing results. Treatment with anti-inflammatory doses of IVIG (1 to 2 g/kg) to prevent NLE has not been studied.

### Approaches to Treating the Fetus Affected With NLE

Evidence is scant and with mixed results for in utero treatment after cardiac NLE develops. Maternal treatment with fluorinated corticosteroids has some reported efficacy treating second-degree heart block. Treatment with IVIG is sometimes used in the setting of second-degree heart block; a clinical trial for this indication is underway. Anti-inflammatory therapy does not appear effective once third-degree heart block has developed. β-Agonists can be used to increase fetal heart rates in the setting of fetal bradycardia. Fluorinated CS and/or IVIG preand postnatal treatment improve survival in children with NLE cardiomyopathy/endocardial fibroelastosis. Cardiac pacing is required for some children with complete heart block. 147, Given their family histories, children with NLE may be at risk for autoimmune disease.

### Conclusion

Although the pathophysiology of cSLE is likely similar to adult SLE, clinical presentations, prognosis, and some aspects of management differ. Children and adolescents with SLE h ave higher disease activity at presentation; are at substantial risk for organ damage, including renal and CNS complications; and have overall higher mortality compared with adult counterparts. Especially because children and adolescents face a lifetime burden of disease and effects of therapy, early intervention is indicated to reduce the risk of long-term complications, including CV disease and bone loss. Randomized controlled clinical trials for pediatric SLE are lacking, and therefore therapeutic approaches are inferred from adult studies. However, children and adolescents require special attention to uniquely pediatric concerns, including impact of therapies on growth and body image, compliance concerns, and psychosocial and transition needs.

# Juvenile Dermatomyositis, Scleroderma, a and Vasculitis

### Juvenile Dermatomyositis

### KEY POINTS

Juvenile dermatomyositis (JDM) is a systemic immune-mediated vasculopathy affecting predominantly skin and muscle but can affect any organ system.

JDM is the most common inflammatory myopathy of children, and without appropriate immunomodulatory treatment, there is high potential for morbidity and potential for mortality.

there are differences in pathogenesis, presentation, and outcome. Malignancy is seldom associated with JDM, as opposed to adult DM. Children with JDM are at higher risk for calcinosis and lipodystrophy compared with adults with DM.

With treatment, children with JDM have a better long-term prognosis with improved survival compared with adults with DM.

### Introduction

Juvenile dermatomyositis (JDM) is the most common acquired idiopathic inflammatory myopathy (IIM) of children, accounting for over 80% of cases.1, Historically, the diagnosis of JDM was based on the criteria published in 1975,3,4 which included the pathognomic rashes of dermatomyositis (DM) (i.e., heliotrope rash and Gottron's sign), in addition to predominantly symmetric weakness of the limb girdle muscles, elevation of muscle enzymes, characteristic electromyographic findings, and muscle biopsy changes consistent with inflammatory myositis.

### Classification

Historically, the 1975 criteria were empirically derived to standardize how DM and polymyositis (PM) were diagnosed and to distinguish them from other inflammatory and noninflammatory conditions that can cause weakness. These standardized criteria also helped to identify more homogenous patient populations, which in turn helped to improve the research in this field.3,

Updated classification criteria for adult and pediatric IIM subtypes have been published by the International Myositis Classification Criteria Project (IMCCP) in 2017, referred to as the European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology (EULAR)/ American College of Rheumatology (ACR) classification criteria. These criteria were data driven, developed by consensus, and are

able to identify different subgroups of idiopathic inflammatory myopathies with greater sensitivity, specificity, and classification accuracy. These new classification criteria incorporate myositis antibodies, muscle enzymes, and specific histologic features, using a scoring system based on age of onset, muscle weakness, rashes, and other clinical and diagnostic results, including muscle biopsy if performed. Definite JDM corresponds to a 90% or greater probability of JDM, with scores of ≥8.7 and ≥7.5 with and without a muscle biopsy, respectively. Lower scores would be assigned to probable or possible JDM. There is a useful website calculator link to aid to use these improved classification criteria in clinical practice (http://www.imm.ki.se/biostatistics/calculators/iim/).

### Epidemiology

JDM is an inflammatory vasculopathy characterized by characteristic skin rashes and proximal muscle weakness and the most common IIM in children with an incidence of about 2 to 3 cases per million children annually in the United States and the United Kingdom.2, The mean age of onset is 7 years, with typically a female predominance (1.5:1 to 2:1). In the United States and United Kingdom, according to race and ethnicity, patients are most often white patients (65% and 83%, respectively), followed by Hispanic patients (14% in United States), Black patients (11% and 8%, respectively), and Asian patients (1% and 7%, respectively).

Although JDM has many clinical features that overlap with adult DM, JDM is not simply adult DM in pediatric age patients (Table 111.1). There are several features unique to JDM highlighting the differences based on the age of disease onset and disease pathogenesis. Myositis-specific antibodies (MSAs) and myositisassociated antibodies (MAAs) are found in both DM and JDM, in variable frequencies, and although malignancy is commonly associated DM, it is extremely rare in JDM, while calcinosis, cutaneous ulceration, and vasculitis are common in JDM compared with adult cohorts.

### Pathogenesis

As with DM, the pathogenesis of JDM is not entirely known and remains the topic of intensive research. As with other autoimmune conditions, JDM appears to occur in genetically susceptible individuals, and environmental factors also appear to play a role.

### Genetics

Human leukocyte antigens (HLA) have been associated with JDM, and the HLA DRB1*0301 allele has specifically been identified as the major risk factor for JDM in Caucasian patients. 8-11 The DQA1*0301 and DQA1*0501 alleles are additional risk factors for JDM in Caucasian patients, while the DRB1*15021 allele may be the predominant risk allele in Japanese patients. Protective alleles have also been identified in JDM including HLA DQA1*0202, DQA1*0101, and DQA1*0102.11, A new novel association with amino acid position 37 within HLA-DRB1 has been reported, which may differentiate the genetic basis of JDM from DM patients. Some genetic association studies have also found variations in interferon regulatory genes, and other inflammatory cytokines including polymorphisms in the tumor necrosis factor gene (TNF-308A allele),14 interferon regulatory factor 5, and interleukin 1 polymorphisms.15, Lower C4a gene copy numbers have been reported in JDM patients compared with controls.

### Immune Mechanisms

Both the adaptive and innate immune systems have been implicated in the pathogenesis of JDM. The interferon (IFN) pathway has been strongly implicated in the pathogenesis of jDM. Increased expression of type 1 IFN-regulated signature in JDM19 may serve as a longitudinal biomarker that may reflects changes in disease activity. Myogenic precursor cells (MPCs), derived from JDM muscles, characterized by strong vasculopathy, have been found to produce higher levels of type I IFN, which correlate with disease severity, supporting the role of MPCs as a source of type I IFN in JDM. Type 1 IFN induces several pro-inflammatory cytokines and chemokines, including Galectin-9 and CXCL10, which have been validated as biomarkers for disease activity in multiple JDM cohorts.21, B cell proliferation and associated autoantibody production increased expression of type 2 IFN, which was produced primarily by natural killer cells and activated T cells, and has also been implicated in JDM pathogenesis. Upregulated type 2 IFN and type 2 IFN-inducible genes have been

found to be higher in muscle biopsies of JDM patients compared with control patients including healthy and muscular dystrophy patients. Higher type I and type II IFN scores have also been found to be associated with muscle biopsy pathology and higher disease activity, while only type II IFN scores correlated with longer time to inactive disease. Plasmacytoid dendritic cells, which help recognize viruses in the peripheral circulation, are considered to be one of the major sources of IFN-producing cells and have also been implicated in JDM.

Immature transitional B cells and genes related to B cell survival have been implicated in JDM: they are expanded JDM peripheral blood and correlate with disease activity,25,26 and research that suggests a pathogenic role of MSAs in the development of inflammatory myopathies. Increased T regulatory cells in the peripheral blood have been found to be functionally impaired in JDM patients, and increased plasmablasts appear to correlate with T helper subsets and disease activity in JDM.27,

There is growing evidence for the role of discrete immune populations, including monocytes and macrophages in the pathogenesis of JDM, with changes in monocyte transcriptional signatures and interferon-inducible biomarkers such as Siglec-1 that appear to correlate with disease activity in JDM that can be found in the peripheral blood,29-31 as well as in imaging mass cytometry analysis on skin biopsy samples.

### Infectious and Environmental T Triggers

Ultraviolet light exposure is considered to be an environmental trigger for JDM,33,34 which is more common in patients with the MSA anti-TIF1-γ. In addition, higher UV index exposure in the month prior to JDM diagnosis has also been found to be associated with an increased odds of developing calcinosis in non-Black patients with JDM. Some prenatal environmental factors have been implicated in the development of JDM including birth seasonality particularly in patients of Hispanic descent, maternal exposures to silica, gasoline vapor, smoking, and carbon monoxide.

Reports of the temporal association of infections with the onset of JDM have also been described in retrospective analyses and parent interview: the most common associations were respiratory illnesses, gastrointestinal illnesses, and prescription of

antibiotics.39, Severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) is also associated with the onset of JDM. These associations with specific infectious processes raise the possibility of molecular mimicry as a mechanism in JDM, but no single agent has been identified.

### Maternal Microchimerism

Elevated levels of maternal microchimeric cells in the form of mononuclear cells and T lymphocytes have been reported in JDM,42 in both peripheral blood and muscle tissue. This has been described in patients with JDM compared with their siblings and healthy controls, which may suggest their role in the pathogenesis of JDM. However, in subsequent studies comparing children with JDM to children with muscular dystrophy (MD), microchimeric cells were not detected in B cells or dendritic cells, which are implicated in the pathogenesis of JDM. In addition, microchimeric cells of any given phenotype did not occur more frequently in JDM compared with MD muscle biopsies, suggesting that microchimeric cells might have a role in tissue repair and be recruited to sites of inflammation.

### Clinical Features

The classic presentation of a child with JDM includes pathognomic rashes and proximal muscle weakness. However, JDM is a systemic condition, and any organ system can be involved.

### Cutaneous s Manifestations

The characteristic rashes of JDM includes Gottron's sign and heliotrope rash, but the cutaneous manifestations may vary widely in JDM.
