Gottron's papules are papular lesions, often associated with erythema and scale and found over the dorsal aspect of the hands and feet (Fig. 111.1A and B) or classically overlying the metacarpophalangeal and interphalangeal joints, elbows, and knees. The heliotrope rash of JDM is periorbital, pink to violaceous, and may be associated with scaling and edema (Fig. 111.1C). The small-vessel vasculopathy associated with JDM is well demonstrated with the nail bed capillary changes commonly seen in this condition. These are abnormally large, dilated, shaped capillaries, best seen under magnification (Fig. 111.1D and E). Similar capillary changes can be seen in the upper eye lid and gingival margins (Fig. 111.1C). Nail bed erythema and cuticular overgrowth are also commonly seen (Fig. 111.1E).

Close monitoring of nailfold capillaries is recommended, since abnormal nailfold capillaries have been associated with longer disease duration of untreated disease. In addition, persistent changes in the nailbed capillary loops at 6 months and Gottron's sign at 3 months have been correlated with increased disease severity and longer time to remission.46, Similarly, lower nailfold capillary density has been correlated with smaller lung volumes, lower gas diffusion, and CT-detected airway disease.

Children with JDM are often extremely photosensitive, and other common cutaneous findings include malar rash,

erythroderma, V sign, Shawl sign, livedo reticularis, and oth- 44, The rashes found in JDM phenotypically similar to the ers. rashes found in adult DM. Interestingly, rashes including ulceration, calcinosis, and lipodystrophy are reported more commonly in JDM compared with adult DM, whereas mechanic's hands are uncommon in children. The ulcerative skin lesions (Fig. 111.2A to C) that can occur with JDM herald a more severe disease course, potentially life threatening systemic vasculopathy, and a more aggressive disease course that requires closer monitoring and more intensive therapy.

Calcinosis can be part of the acute inflammatory process of JDM and later in the disease represents disease chronicity and skin damage. Calcinosis is often found in the skin, subcutaneous tissue, or muscle of patients with JDM and can be localized or extensive (Fig. 111.3A to D). Calcinosis has a tendency to develop in areas of pressure or repeated trauma, is found in 40% or more of patients with JDM, can be cosmetically distressing, can cause pain, and can be associated with functional disability, joint contractures, ulceration, and infection. Increased rates of calcinosis tend to be associated with delays in treatment50,51 and improve with early and aggressive treatment of the inflammation associated with JDM.52,

Lipodystrophy, typically a late complication of JDM, is reported in up to 20% of patients or more in some cohorts; can be generalized, partial, or focal; and can be disfiguring.54-58 It is commonly associated with calcinosis and with more severe, chronic JDM. Interestingly, patients with lipodystrophy have features of metabolic syndrome and are at higher risk of insulin resistance and hypertriglyceridemia.

### Muscle Weakness

Classically the weakness of JDM affects the proximal muscles with symmetric involvement. The weakness of JDM can range from negligible to severe: it is not uncommon for the weakness of JDM to be insidious. Some patients may have no detectable weakness, while others may present with fatigue or myalgia alone. More severe weakness is also possible and can be severe enough that patients are unable to get up out of bed or a chair, walk up the stairs, or raise their arms above their head. The weakness of JDM can affect muscles of speech and deglutination and the muscles of the esophagus and diaphragm, causing trouble with swallowing, speaking, and/or breathing. Patients may present with muscular atrophy and contractures around joints due to muscle disuse that lead to irreversible, fixed contracture and physical disability if left untreated.

Head lag, Gower's sign, and Trendelenburg gait may be found in children with muscle inflammation and weakness due to JDM. Strength testing is often challenging, especially in children younger than 4 years of age due to many factors that may include fear of the examiner and the inability to follow directions during the assessment. Repeated standardized testing using manual muscle testing or the childhood myositis assessment scale is recommended to track changes in disease activity over time with a standardized approach.

In addition to blood muscle enzyme assessments, electromyography (EMG) and muscle biopsies can help support the diagnosis of JDM, but MRI is being used more broadly to assess for myositis in lieu of more invasive diagnostic modalities.68, Short tau inversion recovery (STIR) images or T2-fat suppressed MRI images

help identify areas of edema in the muscles of inflammation (Fig. 111.4).

### Systemic Manifestations

Virtually any organ system can be involved in JDM and may include the central and peripheral nervous systems gastrointestinal tract, joints, heart, and lungs. These manifestations can be a significant source of morbidity and mortality and should be monitored throughout the disease course. Systemic features can include cardiac conduction abnormalities, diminished respiratory and lung diffusion capacity, esophageal, gastric, and gastrointestinal dysmotility, ulcers, hemorrhage, and perforation. More than half of children with JDM have associated arthritis.

### Cardiopulmonary Disease

Cardiopulmonary disease is uncommon at disease onset in JDM, but when it occurs, it can carry high morbidity and mortality. Severe and acute cardiac involvement and cardiovascular complications are uncommon in JDM but pericarditis, myocarditis, conduction defects, and heart block have been reported. Abnormal electrocardiograms and echocardiograms were found in 9% and 48% of children at presentation from a Canadian cohort of patients, but findings tended to be mild and typically unrelated to JDM (i.e., prolonged heart-rate corrected QT interval [QTc], mild tricuspid regurgitation, or pulmonary insufficiency). A long-term follow-up of patients with JDM from Norway, for over a decade following disease presentation, suggests that there is decreased heart rate variability and long axis strain in JDM patients that correlated with skin disease activity at 1 year.71,

There also are significantly higher odds of cardiovascular and cerebrovascular morbidities including hypertension, obesity, diabetes, and other associated conditions, as assessed by the 2002 to 2012 National Inpatient Sample.

Fatal pulmonary complications rarely develop in JDM, but there appear to be regional differences, with increased rates of interstitial lung disease (ILD) and rapidly progressive ILD reported in Asia, including Japan, that is associated with anti- MDA5antibodies.74-78 Patients with anti-MDA5 antibodies commonly have less prominent skin involvement and may have features of amyopathic JDM.1, ILD has been described in 7% to 19% of children with JDM (see Table 111.1). From a single center, JDM patients were compared with age-matched controls and were found to have lower lung volumes and a restrictive ventilatory defect, with CT abnormalities found in 37% of patients including airway disease, calcinosis, and ILD, that were generally asymptomatic.

Due to the high morbidity that can be associated with undetected and untreated cardiopulmonary involvement, screening for disease is recommended and may include imaging such as radiography and CT,8 especially in patients with more severe presen- OZ tation. Earlier detection of cardiopulmonary disease would help guide treatment decisions and more aggressive treatment for these uncommon JDM manifestations.

### Amyopathic Juvenile Dermatomyositis

A small subset of patients with JDM are described as having amyopathic JDM (aJDM). These children present with the cutaneous manifestations of JDM but have no evidence of muscle weakness. This terminology is controversial, since patients may have undetected muscle disease, and comprehensive assessments for myositis, such as EMG, MRI, or muscle biopsies, are seldom performed when patients are not weak.83, Other terminology to define this subset of patients has also included clinically amyopathic, hypomyopathic, or skin-predominant JDM. Long-term follow-up and treatment of this patient subset is needed, since resistant skin disease is common, and almost 20% of children may ultimately develop weakness.

### Malignancy

Adult dermatomyositis has an association with malignancy, which typically presents as a paraneoplastic phenomenon within 2 years

of diagnosis, and most commonly includes adenocarcinomas of the cervix, lung, ovaries, pancreas, bladder, or stomach. The risk of malignancy is higher in DM in association with MSAs, especially antiTIF1-γ antibodies in up to 20% of adults. 85,

In children with JDM compared with adults with DM, the association with malignancy is uncommon (Table 111.1). However, leukemia and lymphoma are the most frequently reported malignancies in this context.62, Hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, and physical examination findings atypical for JDM should prompt additional work-up for malignancy.

### Diagnosis and Diagnostic Tests

Diagnostic tests for JDM should include a complete cell count with differential and a complete set of muscle enzymes including creatine kinase, aldolase, aspartate aminotransferase, alanine transaminase, and lactate dehydrogenase. With longer duration of untreated disease, muscle enzymes may become unreliable markers of disease activity. Other possible biomarkers of disease include neopterin and von Willebrand factor antigen, which are elevated in a subset of JDM patients. 89-92Interferon chemokine scores vary significantly with disease activity in JDM cohorts as assessed by the global visual analog scale (VAS),93 but these are not presently commercially available.

MSAs (see below) are becoming increasingly important in the assessment of JDM. MSAs can be found in up to 70% of JDM patients and appear to define specific subsets of JDM patients that may help predict disease severity, end organ involvement, prognosis, and help inform medication choices. Immunoprecipitation is generally considered to be the gold standard approach to testing and confirming MSAs, and research continues to optimize testing.94, Due to the growing importance of MSA and prognosis, more research is needed to determine the most sensitive and specific approaches to testing for MSAs.

### Myositis-Specific Antibodies

MSAs have been found to be specific for dermatomyositis subtypes96-98 and are thought to be found exclusively in patients with myositis. For JDM, the most commonly described include antitranscriptional intermediary factor 1 (anti-p155/140, also known as TIF1-γ), anti-nuclear matrix protein 2 (anti-NXP2, also known and MJ), and anti-melanoma differentiation—associated gene 5

(anti-MDA5, also known as CADM-140) and have been found to have distinct clinical features and outcomes.

Other common MSAs in adult DM include anti-synthetase antibodies, anti—signal recognition particle (anti-SRP) autoantibodies, and anti—Mi-2 autoantibodies. Anti-synthetase antibodies include anti-Jo-1, antiPL-7, antiPL-7, anti-PL-12, and other aminoacyl tRNA synthetases. These antibodies have been associated with anti-synthetase syndrome, consisting of mechanic's hands, Raynaud's syndrome, interstitial lung disease, arthritis, lipoatrophy, and fever; patients are typically older at age of 96,99,100 onset.

Patients with JDM and antiTIF1-γ antibodies, also known as anti-p155/140 antibodies, have been described in up to 35% of some patient cohorts and are associated with photosensitivity, Gottron's papules, malar rash, V-sign, and cuticular overgrowth. Patients may have a chronic or polycyclic disease course, and cutaneous ulceration is more common in JDM. 96,

Anti-MDA5 antibodies are reported in up to 20% of some cohorts and more commonly have amyopathic disease associated with oral and skin ulceration, fever, interstitial lung disease that can sometimes be rapidly progressing, arthralgia and arthritis, and older age of onset. Rapidly progressive lung disease has been reported more frequently in Japanese cohorts. In adults antiTIF1-γ antibodies and anti-MDA autoantibodies may be associated with malignancy, which is extremely uncommon in children.63,

Anti-MJ antibodies are also reported in up to 20% of some cohorts and are more commonly associated with muscle cramping and weakness requiring hospitalization, dysphonia, calcinosis, younger age of onset, and less frequent remission. Anti-MJ antibodies have been associated with markedly increased odds of calcinosis (odds ratio [0R], 7.0 [3.0 to 16.1]). 103

### Myositis-Associated Antibodies

Positive anti-nuclear antibody (ANA) testing is common in JDM, but the additional autoantibodies are typically negative. MAAs are autoantibodies that are also described with other autoimmune conditions. Notably, although the same autoantibodies are found in both adults and children, they are not always associated with the same clinical features.

A more recently described MAA, antibodies to cytosolic 5'-nucleotidase 1A (anti-NT5C1A) identified in adults with inclusion body myositis, has also been found more commonly in a subset of JDM to be associated with more pulmonary symptoms at diagnosis, requiring more hospitalizations and immunomodulatory therapy. However, these are not specific to JDM and are also found in juvenile arthritis patients and in healthy children (27%, 27%, and 12% respectively). Anti-Ro52 is another MAA reported in 14% of a North American cohort, is more frequent with anti-synthetase and anti-MDA5 MSA groups,106 and has been associated with ILD, chronic disease course, and more medications.

### Muscle Pathology

When children have atypical features and no rash, muscle biopsies are an essential part of the diagnostic work-up to confirm the diagnosis of JDM. Muscle biopsies from adult and juvenile DM are characterized by perifascicular atrophy, vasculopathy perivascular inflammation, fiber degeneration and regeneration, and swelling of the endothelial cells, and tubuloreticular inclusion bodies can be seen within endothelial cells with electron

microscopy. The inflammatory infiltrate is composed on B cells, CD4+ T cells, macrophages, and plasmcytoid dendritic cells. The vasculopathy of DM is characterized by deposition of complement and the membrane attack complex on capillaries, capillary thrombosis, and reduction in number of capillaries, which is typically perifascicular. Although there the pathology appears similar in both adult and juvenile DM, there appear to be differences in the molecular pathways between adult and juvenile DM. For example, increased expression of hypoxia-inducible factor 1α (HIF-1α) and macrophage migration inhibitory factor (MIF) genes has been described in JDM but not found in adult DM. In adult DM the perifascicular atrophy was more associated with IFN-associated genes, suggesting a greater role of innate immunity rather than the hypoxia-related mechanisms seen in JDM. Muscle biopsies from JDM appear to have more prominent vasculopathy compared with adult DM.

There is increased expression of MHC class I and myxovirus resistance A (MxA), which is an IFN-α/βinducible protein. Pathology scoring tools have been developed and validated to standardize histologic estimates of disease severity in JDM and also have good correlation with measures of disease activity. 108, Histopathologic severity and MSA subtype together are also able to predict duration of treatment in JDM.

### Imaging

Baseline chest radiographs should be performed in patients with JDM and can help screen for occult lung disease. Chest CT is essential in the assessment in any patient with suspected interstitial lung disease. MRI helps to identify areas of inflammation or edema and in some settings has replaced the need for invasive muscle biopsies, and should include either STIR images or T2-fat suppressed images (Fig. 111.4).69, Other imaging modalities are being studied for JDM, including ultrasound, which is not yet standardized to assess muscle inflammation.

### Differential Diagnosis

It is important to consider other diagnoses when considering JDM. Other autoimmune conditions that cause myositis include systemic lupus erythematosus, mixed connective tissue disease, scleroderma, and sarcoidosis.

Other primary IIMs are extremely rare in children, including polymyositis. Patients without rashes are typically not be diagnosed with JDM, and muscle biopsies should be strongly considered in those cases, since treatment and prognosis may vary based on the primary diagnosis.

Congenital myopathies and metabolic myopathies should be considered in any patient who presents with weakness, but typically features of the history, family history and exam help distinguish these from JDM. Working closely with neurology and considering other diagnostic testing such as genetic testing, EMG or muscle biopsy should be considered in atypical cases.

Infectious myositis can include rashes and can be associated with various infections including bacteria, viruses, and parasites and need to be considered based on the appropriate clinical circumstances, including exposure and travel history. Prominent eosinophilia may prompt a work-up for parasitic infections. Infections most often associated with myositis include influenza B, which can present with acute muscle pain, weakness, and elevated muscle enzyme levels that typically involve the gastrocnemius muscles. Other common viral infectious associations include

adenovirus, coxsackievirus, dengue virus, human immunodeficiency, and parvovirus B19. Myositis following COVID-19 infections has also been reported and could be due to viral myositis or induction of autoimmunity.

### Treatment

### Standard Initial Treatment Approaches

Prior to the use of corticosteroids for JDM in the 1960s, mortality was up to one of three children with JDM. A variety of immunomodulatory treatments have been used to treat JDM in addition to steroids and are essential for all patients with JDM due to the significant morbidity due to long-term steroid use, including cushingoid features, osteoporosis, glaucoma, cataracts, diabetes, avascular necrosis of bones, etc. Panels of experts worldwide have developed treatment approaches to help guide and standardize the treatment of JDM, and the mainstay of initial therapy includes steroids and methotrexate (MTX).

There are no U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA)- approved medications for JDM. Conventional, large-scale, blinded clinical trials are nearly impossible to perform for JDM, and only two randomized controlled trials have been performed.116, Thus, by necessity, current standard treatment recommendations are based on anecdotal experience, but more recently the treatment approaches for patients with JDM have become increasingly standardized by international panels of experts largely based on developed consensus. 75,

Specific consensus treatment plans have been developed for JDM patients with skin-predominant disease, moderately severe disease, and resistant skin disease and represent typical, reasonable treatment approaches for the initial treatment of JDM, with options to choose from based on the case severity and the experience of the treating clinician (Fig. 111.5).81,

Medications used for JDM typically include oral and parenteral corticosteroids in combination with steroid-sparing immunomodulatory treatment, most commonly methotrexate. To prevent the complications associated with long-term steroid use, it is imperative that steroid-sparing therapy is initiated promptly at the time of diagnosis.

Methotrexate is typically administered weekly, and recommended doses are 1 mg/kg/dose, typically not exceeding 25 mg/ dose. Oral steroid dosing is typically initiated 2 mg/kg/day, typically not exceeding 60 mg/day. High-pulse dose corticosteroids are often given at the start of therapy over 3 days (30 mg/kg/dose of methylprednisolone, typically not exceeding 1000 mg). Aggressive treatment of persistent disease activity improves outcome in JDM patients, so close monitoring and repeated assessments during the disease course is essential.

### Essential Components of Nonpharmacologic Treatment 2√

The basic treatment recommendations for JDM go beyond systemic medications and include a healthy diet with adequate calcium and vitamin D, vigilant photoprotection, exercise, physical therapy and rehabilitation, and mental health support (Fig. 1.6).

Photoprotection is essential as part of the treatment for JDM, as photosensitivity is so common. Photoprotection should include avoiding spending prolonged times outdoors during the sunniest parts of the day, seeking shade, wearing protective clothing including a hat, and applying broad spectrum sunscreen of at least SPF 30, even on cloudy days, with reapplication every 2 hours or more often with water exposure. Care should also be taken with time spent near windows.

Nutrition should focus on adequate and healthy caloric intake with sufficient calcium and vitamin D. Attention needs to be given to a diet that helps to limit the unhealthy weight gain that can be associated with steroid use.

Exercise should be encouraged, and a good physical therapy program is integral to the care of JDM patients. Historical concerns that physical activity could exacerbate myositis in JDM have been largely discredited. Exercise is important for muscle rehabilitation and recovery and to maintain normal range of motion in joints and also for the long-term cardiovascular benefits in children with JDM.

Mental health support is essential in the care of patient with any chronic condition, and its importance cannot be overemphasized.124, A multidisciplinary approach is essential, along with continuing to consider the addition of other steroid-sparing agents if necessary to optimize the outcome in JDM (Fig. 111.6A and B).

### Treatment for Refractory Disease

Several second-line agents are recommended for refractory JDM in treatment and consensus guidelines internationally 49,80,81,120,121 and include a variety of medications including intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG), rituximab, cyclophosphamide (CYC), cyclosporine, azathioprine, tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil (MMF), and more recently other biologic agents including abatacept and Janus kinase inhibitors.

Open-label studies and retrospective studies have supported the benefit of IVIG for patients with refractory skin and muscle disease. Placebo-controlled trials have not been completed in children, 81,126,127 but a recent double-blind placebo-controlled trial proved the efficacy in adult DM128,129 and allowed for the FDA approval for DM. Mycophenolate mofetil is another steroid-sparing agent that has shown benefit in patients with ongoing refractory disease. 130-132 Cyclosporine is beneficial in JDM, but recent studies suggest that methotrexate is the better option in the treatment of JDM due to its better safety profile and efficacy.

The efficacy and safety of using cyclosphosphamide in the treatment JDM is supported by retrospective studies, and

cyclosphosphamide is typically reserved for patients with more severe disease manifestations. 133-136 One study using marginal structural modeling (MSM) found improvements in global disease, skin disease, and muscle disease activity in CYC-treated patients versus those not treated with cyclophosphamide that was greatest at 1 year.

Biologic therapies are also being used broadly in the treatment of resistant JDM. These have included the B celldepleting therapy rituximab, in a trial of patients with refractory JDM and adult DM in a randomized double-blind, placebo-phase trial. Of the enrolled individuals, 83% met the definition of improvement, but there were no difference in the treatment groups. Post-hoc analysis from this trial suggests that those with JDM, positive myositis-specific autoantibody, and higher interferon gene expression signatures and chemokine scores were predictors of response to rituximab. 137,

Other therapies have been used with success in treatmentresistant JDM. 139, These include but are not limited to abata- 141, Janus kinase inhibitors, 143-146 cept, and tumor necrosis factor inhibitors. 147-149

### Outcomes

The long-term prognosis of children with JDM is improved with the use of immunomodulatory therapies. Prior to the use of immunosuppressive medications for JDM in the 1960s, nearly one-third of children succumbed to the disease. Presently, survival is greatly improved for JDM, and the survival rate is typically >95% in most regions of the world.

About 30% to 40% of patients have monocyclic disease, but the remaining patients tend to have polycyclic or chronic disease, so treatment may be necessary long-term, well into adulthood.

Undertreatment and/or delayed diagnosis and treatment are associated with increased long-term morbidities including calcinosis and lipodystropy, so aggressive treatment at the time of diagnosis is essential to limit these complications.

### Conclusions

Juvenile dermatomyositis is rare and has many features that distinguish it from adult DM. Aggressive treatment is needed for JDM compared with approaches more commonly used in adult DM, because of the impact of the disease on the growth and development of children, as well as the high risk of morbidity from features of disease more common in JDM including ulceration, lipodystrophy, and calcinosis. Early recognition and treatment of disease manifestations is essential to improve outcomes. Recent developments in JDM and DM research, including the prominent interferon signature associated with disease, as well as the contribution of MSAs and distinct disease subsets, have shed more light on the pathogenesis and possible changes to treatment approaches for this rare condition.

### Pediatric Scleroderma: Systemic a and Localized Forms

### KEY POINTS

### Introduction

The scleroderma disorders in children encompass both systemic sclerosis (SSc) and localized scleroderma (LS), also termed morphea. SSc is much less common than LS in childhood and comprises less than 10% of all cases.150, Both share the general features of an earlier inflammatory state, followed by collagen deposition and atrophy. Skin biopsies of these patients are typically indistinguishable, and they may share some common pathophysiology; however, their clinical manifestations are markedly different with unique morbidities and prognoses. LS is typically confined to the skin and underlying tissue, and although lacking fatal potential of SSc, as many as a one-half of the patients may have extracutaneous disease manifestations, such as joint

contractures and seizures. 152, Although any organ may be affected in SSc, vascular (relapsing polychondritis [RP]), cutaneous (skin thickening), gastrointestinal (GI), pulmonary, and musculoskeletal involvement are most commonly seen in children. A recent cohort study shows that interstitial lung disease (ILD) is just as prevalent in juvenile SSc (40%) compared with adult SSc, and ILD is the leading cause of SSc-associated death in adults. Both SSc and LS can be further classified by subtype (Table 111.2; see Table 111.4).

### Epidemiology

Both LS and SSc are uncommon in children; the estimated annual incidence of LS is 1 to 3.4 per 100,000 children,155,156 and that of SSc is 0.27 to 1 per million.155-157 Recent studies examining administrative claims data in the United States support a prevalence of 3 per 10,000 children for pediatric LS and 3 per 1,000,000 for pediatric SSc. The mean age of onset for pediatric LS is 6.5 to 8.5 years old and is slightly older for pediatric SSc at 8 to 10.5 years old. Unfortunately, there is significant delay in diagnosis, with an average of 0.7 to 2.8 years for SSc.152,155,158,159 and 0.9 to 1.6 years for LS.46, In rare cases of congenital LS, the mean time to diagnosis is longer, 2.9 to 3.9 years. .160, The approximate female to male ratio of pediatric SSc is 4:1,150,151 and for pediatric LS, it is 2:1. There is no clear evidence for racial predilection for either form of pediatric scleroderma, although Caucasian race is the most prevalent in published cohorts.

### Pathogenesis

### Genetics

HLA studies in pediatric-onset SSc and LS have shown unique HLA-DR and HLA-DQ findings compared with those found in adult-onset SSc. This includes a lack of association with adult SSc HLA findings of DRB1*11 or the specific alleles DRB*11:01 and *1 1:04. Although subanalyses showed an association of childhoodonset SSc to adult-onset SSc DRB1*01, it was only in children with older onset (>11 years old) with centromere antibody positivity. A novel association with DRB1*10 was observed in childhood-onset SSc (OR, 7.48; P = 0.002), which remained significant regardless of pediatric SSc subtype (limited or diffuse) or antibody positivity (topoisomerase, centromere antibody). HLA class I and II studies in the Morphea in Adults and Children Cohort, which includes about one-third childhood-onset morphea, or LS, showed only one common allele with adult SSc, DRB*04:04, and demonstrated the strongest associations of LS with DRB1*04:04 and HLA-B*37. These were more prevalent in those with linear scleroderma and generalized plaque morphea subtypes. Interestingly, more recent RNA sequencing analyses of LS skin demonstrate the significant upregulation of several HLA class II genes, including HLA-DQA1, HLA-DQB1, and HLA-DRB1, compared with healthy controls and in LS corresponded with higher inflammatory infiltrate and collagen deposition histologically and cutaneous disease activity scores. Familial history of autoimmune disease is not uncommon in either LS or SSc, with an approximate 20% positive family history of first-degree relative with conditions such as psoriasis, rheumatoid arthritis (RA), SLE, Sjögren's syndrome, thyroiditis and, less commonly, SSc and LS.151,152,160

### Immune Mechanisms

The skin histology of LS and SSc are indistinguishable.164-166 Mononuclear cell populations identified in both SSc and LS

skin specimens are predominantly T cells, both CD4 (T helper [Th]) and CD8+. Th cell—associated cytokines and chemokines, such as interleukin (IL)-2, -4, -6, -8, -13, and TNF, have been identified in the circulating sera and stimulated peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) from LS and SSc patients. 146, Chemokines associated with the IFN-γ pathway and Th1 profile—CXCL9, CXCL10, IFN-γ, IL-12p70 and MCP-1—have been associated with both LS and SSc, with sera CXCL9 and CXCL10 and cellular Th1 profiles associating with disease activity of clinical outcomes in pediatric and adult-onset LS. Furthermore, recent RNA sequencing studies of pediatric LS skin supports the IFN-γ related chemokines CXCL9 and CXCL10 to be in the top upregulated differentially expressed genes when comparing active LS lesions to healthy controls, with RNAscope fluorescent multiplex imaging demonstrating colocalization of T cells expressing CXCR3 (the receptor for CXCL9/10) and macrophages expressing CXCL9 and IFN-γ.154, These macrophage and T cellassociated chemokines and cytokines in turn further stimulate fibroblasts and endothelial cells to produce transforming growth factor (TGF)β and connective tissue growth factor (CTGF), which are thought to be the main stimulators of tissue fibrosis (via increased collagen production) and endothelial cell damage (via influence of adhesion molecules intercellular adhesion molecule-1 [ICAM-1] and vascular cell adhesion molecule-1 [VCAM-1]).174-176

The Th and regulatory T cell (Treg) immunophenotypes of patients with jSSc demonstrate decreases in functional Tregs compared with healthy controls, as well as association to more severe clinical phenotype and longer disease duration.173-175 A similar decrease of functional Treg population with a negative correlation with disease severity features is seen in LS. These together may

implicate a permissive state of immune regulation allowing progressive sclerosis in both pediatric LS and SSc.

Autoimmunity plays an important role in both jLS and jSSc with high prevalence of positive ANA and specific autoantibodies associated with disease severity in both conditions (see jSSc and jLS in the following sections), along with the increased incidence of concurrent autoimmune disorders, such as Hashimoto's thyroiditis, vitiligo, and type 1 diabetes mellitus in LS and thyroiditis and Sjogren's syndrome in SSc.

Nontraditional genetic factors, such as epigenetics and microchimerism, are other areas of interest under investigation. A recent DNA methylation study of jSSc and jLS patients determined that the majority of differentially methylated sites and genes represented were unique to either jSSc (STAT3, NF-κB, and IL-15 pathways) or jLS (HIPPO signaling pathway), suggesting a different underlying epigenetic pattern in both diseases, although there were some shared methylated gene expression, such as NOTCH3 and FGFR2.177-179 Clinically and histologically, LS and SSc share characteristics with chronic graft-versus-host disease (GVHD), also termed sclerodermatous GVHD, a condition in which microchimerism plays a role in pathogenesis. Chimeric cells have been identified in patients with LS and SSc by using real-time polymerase chain reaction (PCR) techniques.

### Systemic Sclerosis

### Classification

As with adult-onset SSc, there are three main subtypes of jSSc: diffuse cutaneous (dc), limited cutaneous (lc), and overlap syndrome. There are similar organ manifestations (see Table 111.2) but some

differences in the distribution of clinical subtype and associated antibodies between adult and pediatric patients (eTable 111.1).150, There are only a few large cohort studies evaluating jSSc,1 150,151,180,181 and overlap syndromes constitute approximately one-third of these patient cohorts. The antibodies associated with overlap syndrome, namely PM-Scl U1-RNP and Ku, and their associated clinical features of myositis and arthritis are more commonly observed in jSSc.150, In addition, musculoskeletal features, Gottron's papules, and lung disease are more frequently reported in those with overlap jSSc in an international cohort. Anti-centromere antibody-positive patients with jSSc are uncommon in jSSc compared with

adult SSc (≤15%)150,151,180,181,183 a and are <5% in children <10 30% to 50% of patients with jSSc classified as lcSSc180 (see eTable 111.1).

Because of some of these differences and the more indolent onset of symptoms in jSSc, provisional classification criteria were developed for jSSc to enable detection of early disease, such as the inclusion of positive ANAs, RP, and nailfold capillaroscopy changes. These criteria were developed through international efforts among the Paediatric Rheumatology European Society (PRES), EULAR, the ACR through the Delphi survey, and nominal group technique 183,185,186 and are displayed in Table 111.3. Some patients with undifferentiated or mixed connective tissue disease may have shiny or full-appearing skin of the distal fingers, but they must have the major criterion, "skin induration or sclerosis proximal to the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) or metatarsophalangeal (MTP)," in addition to two minor criteria, to be classified with jSSc (see Table 111.3). Despite this increased sensitivity, a need to define patients with early SSc, in both adult and pediatric onset, was recognized, and the 2013 ACR/EULAR criteria for the classification of SSc was developed (see Chapter 85; Table 85.1). This is a points-based metric in which a total score of ≥9 classifies the patient as having definite SSc, with skin thickening proximal to MCPs scoring an automatic 9 and meeting criteria but leaving room for earlier skin changes to account for some points, such as puffy fingers, sclerodactyly, and skin thickening of fingers (distal to MCPs), to be merged with other features, such as digital tip

ulcers, to gain cumulative points for classification. 187, This was validated in adult SSc, and validation is underway in jSSc, with preliminary data in both the CARRA jSSc and Padua jSSc cohorts showing 81% and 84% meeting 2013 ACR/EULAR criteria compared with 42% and 68% meeting the 2007 proposed pediatric criteria, respectively.

### Clinical Features

Please refer to Chapter 85 for details about organ manifestations in SSc. Here we will emphasize the similarities and differences between juvenile-onset SSc and adult-onset SSc.

In general, larger cohort studies of jSSc have been followed up into adulthood and compared with adult-onset SSc (aSSc) cohorts in that geographic region to compare disease course, organ complications, and outcome. The six largest studies are summarized in eTable 111.2,150,151,180-183 including updates from the North American Childhood Arthritis and Rheumatology (CARRA) jSSc (n = 64) and the international inception (n = 150) jSSc cohorts. These support similar frequency of the main adult SSc organ manifestations, such as ILD and pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH), but there are differences with increased musculoskeletal involvement (because of overlap prominence in jSSc) and less scleroderma renal crisis in juvenile-onset SSc.150, Despite this, jSSc was found to have significantly better survival rates compared with adult-onset SSc in these cohort studies.

Vascular Manifestations. Common features at the onset of jSSc are RP (70%) and skin changes of the hands (60%), including edema, sclerodactyly, and induration proximal to the MCPs (Fig. 111.7).132, In the largest cohort of pediatric SSc (153 patients) studied, 53% presented with both skin induration of hands and RP, and 10% of those presenting with RP also had digital infarcts. Throughout the course of the disease, almost all will have RP (97%) and skin changes of the hands (96%), and digital ulcers will develop in approximately up to a half (Fig. 111.8; see eTable 111.2).150, Nailfold capillaroscopy changes, including dilation with giant capillaries, tortuosity, hemorrhage, drop-off (avascularization) and, later, arborization of the capillaries, .161,189 are observed in children as they are in aSSc and, if identified in context with RP, should raise suspicion for diagnosis of jSSc. The prevalence of nailfold capillary changes in jSSc is 50% to 70%150,151,180,190 but is likely higher if standardized microscopy is performed.

Cutaneous Manifestations. Cutaneous manifestations are similar to adult-onset SSc, in which there is an edematous, sclerodactyly phase with an associated increase in skin thickness (see Fig. 11.7), followed by an atrophic phase. There is a distal tapering of fingers, with some jSSc having shortened middle and distal phalanges and loss of digital pads in adulthood. Joint contractures, especially of the hands, are common in jSSc due to overlying skin and deep tendon collagen deposition and tightening (Fig. 111.9; see Table 111.2). The typical scleroderma facies of tight atrophic skin produces a pinched nose, thin pursed lips, small mouth, and prominent teeth and occurs in children but may be less dramatic. Skin thickness is measured using the modified Rodnan Skin Score (mRSS)191 and in general mirrors that found in adult-onset SSc (see eTable 111.2). The mRSS was applied to jSSc subjects at an international scleroderma workshop recently, and an acceptable inter-rate reliability coefficient of 0.656 was determined between both pediatric and adult rheumatology providers. s. The mRSS is a practical tool in aSSc, correlating with disease severity, and its progression rate can predict survival in adults. Further study of the mRSS in this capacity in jSSc is underway in cohort studies and was recommended as one of the key assessments for the

management of jSSc determined from the consensus-based SHARE recommendations. Nearly all patients should have increased skin thickness; the only exception are the rare SSc sine scleroderma patients, which have only been presented as individual case reports in jSSc, usually with significant primary cardiomyopathy, pulmonary hypertension, and/or interstitial lung disease. Other skin findings in jSSc include those found in adult-onset SSc, such as subcutaneous calcium deposits (calcinosis cutis), hypoand hyper-pigmentation, and telangiectasias. Other organ manifestations in jSSc (in order of decreasing frequency) include GI, pulmonary, musculoskeletal, cardiac, renal, and neurologic symptoms (see Table 111.2).

Gastrointestinal Manifestations. GI symptoms occur in approximately half of children, although more detailed investigation often indicates the presence of abnormalities in a larger percentage. Esophageal dysmotility and gastroesophageal reflux (GER) often leads to dysphagia and esophagitis and also

increases the risk of aspiration, aspiration pneumonia, and potentially ILD. A main symptom, which may be overlooked as post-nasal drip or allergies in children, is night-time cough due to silent aspiration from GER. Gastroparesis with delayed gastric emptying, in addition to esophageal dysfunction, can lead to increased reflux symptoms. Evaluation of the GI tract using manometry and intraesophageal 24-hour pH monitoring have been reported as sensitive indicators of lowered esophageal tone and reflux. However, these modalities are used less often in pediatrics. Instead, a swallow study with speech therapy and radiology to evaluate for aspiration and dysmotility, followed by an upper GI study with small-bowel follow-through (SBFT), are typically used. A large, dilated esophagus is incidentally found quite commonly in jSSc when screening for ILD with chest CT and should be noted, given the association between this finding and ILD in two recent jSSc studies, with aspiration precautions and lifestyle modifications instructed.180, Screening for abnormal peristalsis, bolus clearance, and GER is recommended given the lower frequency of symptoms reported by children, despite abnormalities seen on these examinations. If the small bowel is involved, cramps, diarrhea, and constipation may result from peristaltic dysfunction. Episodes of pseudo-obstruction with post-prandial abdominal distension, pain, and nausea can occur because of a functional ileus. Bacterial overgrowth, steatorrhea, weight loss, volvulus, and even perforation can occur. Weight loss, low body mass index (BMI), and failure to thrive are relatively common at disease presentation in children with jSSc and may be the first non-Raynaud's symptom at onset. The importance of the child's BMI in jSSc is reflected by its inclusion as one of the severity markers for the jSSc Severity Score. Notably, 14% of the CARRA jSSc cohort and 15% of the International Inceptions cohort had age-specific BMI z scores less than -2 standard deviations, indicating moderate to severe malnutri- .181, When evaluating the association of different organ tion. manifestations in the CARRA jSSc cohort, it became apparent that those with GI involvement had more impact on quality-oflife measures, such as the Child Health Assessment Questionnaire (CHAQ), pain scale, and global well-being; therefore the

importance of GI manifestations in children with jSSc should not be overlooked.

Pulmonary Manifestations. Pulmonary involvement in jSSc ranges from 30% to 55% and includes ILD, PAH, and abnormal pulmonary function tests (PFT). PFT abnormalities especially of concern are decreased forced vital capacity (FVC) and diffusing capacity of the lungs for carbon monoxide (DLCO). The clinical presentation of ILD with slowly progressive dyspnea on exertion (DOE) with dry hacking cough, and that of PAH with a more rapid progression of DOE is similar between adults and children. ILD in children is often asymptomatic and only identified with PFT and/or chest imaging due to the child's response to selflimit more rigorous physical activities if experiencing DOE and to not verbalize or complain. A recent international cohort study of 150 jSSc patients identified ILD in 44%, with a surprising finding of 60% of those with ILD determined by chest CT to have normal PFT (FVC ≥80 and DLCO ≥80). This supports the SHARE recommendations and more recent guidelines of obtaining a baseline high resolution chest CT for all jSSc subjects in tandem with PFT.192, Similar to adult SSc, pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) is uncommon in jSSc with a recent international cohort study showing 6% (9 of 150) of patients with jSSc having PAH. Typically this is detected by echocardiogram in children, supported by serum pro—brain natriuretic peptide (pro-BNP) and the 6-minute walk test and verified by right heart catheterization (see "Evaluation" below).

Cardiac Manifestations. Cardiac involvement, although infrequent (see Table 111.2), is the major cause of scleroderma-related mortality in children, as evidenced by the deaths of 10 of 15 in one cohort151 and of 5 of 32 in another cohort. Cardiac manifestations result from the combination of myocardial fibrosis, vascular insufficiency, and inflammation and include heart block, bundle branch block, premature atrial and ventricular contractions, nonspecific T-wave changes, arrhythmia (supraventricular more common than ventricular), congestive heart failure, cardiomyopathy, and pericarditis. 199, Cardiomyopathy is the major cause of morbidity and mortality for the few jSSc patients with sine scleroderma. In contrast to pediatric SSc, scleroderma-related mortality in adults is primarily caused by pulmonary involvement (both ILD and PAH). 200,

Musculoskeletal Manifestations. Compared with adult-onset SSc, musculoskeletal involvement is more common in pediatric SSc. Approximately one-third of patients with jSSc experience inflammatory arthritis (joint effusions) in addition to the typical dry synovitis of scleroderma, reflected by the fibrosis of tendons traversing the joints, which limits their range of motion (ROM). 150, Early in the disease process, especially in those with dcSSc, tenosynovitis/bursitis causes palpable tendon friction rubs (a "leathery crepitus") when the joint is extended or flexed, demonstrated in approximately 10% of patients with jSSc.151, Myopathy typically results in symmetric proximal weakness and muscular atrophy and is typically described as bland, reflecting the relative lack of elevated muscle enzymes, despite weakness on examination and myositis on MRI. Muscle weakness ranged between 20% and 32% in jSSc cohorts (see Table 111.2)150,151,181 and was markedly higher than the adult comparison cohort in one of the studies. Myositis also occurs, more commonly in the overlap SSc subtype, and presents similarly to juvenile DM. Children with dcSSc and myositis are particularly at risk for severe cardiac involvement, including myocardial perfusion deficits and dilated cardiomyopathy. Often overlooked is the effect of myopathy on the respiratory muscles, intercostal muscles, truncal muscles,

and diaphragm, which can severely affect the respiratory reserve reflected by restrictive defects on FVC and total lung capacity, and in moderate to severe cases affecting the DLCO.

Renal Manifestations. Mild renal dysfunction is not uncommon in SSc and is secondary to vasculopathy rather than glomerulonephritis. It occurs with similar frequency in jSSc and SSc. In contrast, the more severe and morbid form of renal disease, scleroderma renal crisis (SRC), occurs in approximately 15% of adult patients with SSc but seldom in children (<5%, only five patients among the six cohorts).151, SRC is characterized by accelerated arterial hypertension, renal insufficiency, microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, and thrombocytopenia. SRC is most commonly seen early in the disease course of dcSSc in RNA polymerase IIIpositive patients, which is uncommon in jSSc (see eTable 111.2), and may account for the lower frequency of SRC in jSSc.

Neurologic Manifestations. Neurologic involvement in jSSc is rare (<5% in all studies) and can include CNS changes, such as seizure, abnormal brain MRI findings, and peripheral neuropathy. Peripheral neuropathy is typically secondary to nerve entrapment from bound down thick skin of the extremities, such as carpal tunnel syndrome.

### Diagnosis and Diagnostic Tests

The diagnosis of jSSc relies on distinctive clinical features (Table 111.4), and subtypes are further defined by both skin thickening distribution and scleroderma-related serum autoantibody profiles, which predict organ involvement in both adultand childhoodonset SSc (see eTable 111.1).150,151,204 (See eTable 111.2 for antibody relationship to clinical features and disease subtype.) Although many scleroderma-related autoantibodies have been identified in adult SSc, there is a high proportion of pediatric patients (20% to 23%) who have a positive ANA without a specific autoantibody identified.

### Disease Monitoring

For most children with SSc or suspected SSc, in addition to complete physical examination, including evaluation of skin thickness with the mRSS and nailfold capillary examination, initial cardiopulmonary assessment, especially evaluating for evidence of ILD and PAH, includes chest radiograph, PFTs with DLCO, ECG, echocardiogram, and more recently, high-resolution CT (HRCT) of the chest. 192, Expanding further, following the experience of adult SSc population in detecting subclinical cardiac disease, and given the high cardiac mortality potential in jSSc, additional cardiac screening is becoming more routine, including 24-hour Holter and loop recorder monitoring for arrhythmias, exercise stress echocardiogram to capture cardiopulmonary dynamic testing, cardiac MRI, and two-dimensional/three-dimensional speckle tracking echocardiograms.199, It is important to keep in mind normal parameters for pediatric patient testing, especially the lung function testing, including DLCO, which should be calculated using standardized prediction equations which account for weight, height, age, sex, and race. This will avoid the unwanted anxiety of a falsely low reading or false confidence in absent pathology if a "normal" reading is documented when unmatched norms are used. Additional cardiopulmonary testing is pursued if abnormalities are detected or the patient is too young to appropriately complete testing (i.e., PFTs). Abnormal PFTs typically prompt evaluation with HRCT of the chest, with many pediatric

centers including HRCT as first-line evaluation in jSSc given the variable effort and interpretation of PFTs, the relatively common observation of a normal chest radiograph despite the presence of . Rarely a ILD, and the updated SHARE recommendations. bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) is performed because inflammation (aveolitis) can be detected as ground glass opacities and subpleural micronodules on HRCT, and is utilized only in instances where evaluation of infection if needed before starting therapy. 198, PAH is typically screened by transthoracic echocardiogram with elevated right-heart pressures, providing evidence for PAH. The DLCO can also be used as an indirect measure to screen for PAH, especially if there is a decrease in the DLCO without evidence of obstructive or restrictive lung disease (FVC), suggesting a defect in gas exchange as a result of pulmonary vascular disease. More formal PAH evaluation with direct measurements is obtained by performing right-heart catheterization as in adults. A 6-minute walk (6MW) test may also be used to monitor lung disease (ILD and/ or PAH), but the standardized values in children are still being determined and depend on ethnicity, weight, height, and age, and nonpulmonary issues in jSSc, such as musculoskeletal involvement and fatigue, may contribute to decreased values. 192,

After initial organ assessment, ongoing cardiopulmonary screening with ECG and echocardiogram every 6 to 12 months and PFTs with DLCO every 3 to 6 months are recommended by most pediatric rheumatologists and recently endorsed by the SHARE guidelines, along with every 6 months mRSS and 192, There is a lack of consensus renal function assessment. regarding screening for GI involvement in jSSc. Most clinicians will screen at some point in time for evidence of silent aspiration and dysmotility with a swallow study and upper GI with SBFT; additional imaging is more dependent on symptoms (see previous discussion under "Gastrointestinal Manifestations"). A pediatric multidimensional severity score, the Juvenile Systemic Sclerosis Severity Score (J4S), encompasses several clinical variables, such as growth parameters and skin and internal organ assessment, developed under the framework of the Medsger Systemic Sclerosis Severity Score173,204 (see Chapter 85; Table 85.2), and could be useful to monitor disease severity over time; the J4S is being studied in clinical practice and is supported by the recent SHARE guidelines. 186,

General laboratory assessment is encouraged, including muscle enzymes, vitamin levels for GI absorption, pro-BNP for cardiac dysfunction, and urinalysis for proteinuria.192, There are no standardized biomarkers available, although a study has suggested serum KL-6, a mucin-like protein strongly expressed in type II pneumocytes, as a promising noninvasive pulmonary marker of fibrosis in jSSc.

### Treatment

Treatment of SSc is dependent on organ involvement, but general measures such as antacid medication for GI protection, prokinetic agents for dysmotility, rotating antibiotics for malabsorption, as well as vasodilators for RP and digital ulcers, nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), and physical therapy (PT) for arthritis or tendonitis are generally recommended. These pharmacologic and supportive measures are included in a recent review of SSc treatment applicability to pediatric scleroderma. Iloprost (not available in the United States) and bosentan were specifically recommended for the treatment of ischemic digital ulcerations in the jSSc SHARE statement. Corticosteroids (CSs) for myositis, arthritis, and other inflammatory clinical features are

more mainstream in jSSc and recommended in combination with DMARD therapy in early active disease,193 although they should be used with caution because they can prompt SRC. MTX and MMF are now used routinely at the time of diagnosis of SSc, especially for skin, subcutaneous, and articular involvement, and are part of the SHARE recommendations.193, More specific treatment recommendations, such as CYC and rituximab, for different organ manifestations have been agreed upon by a consensus conference of international scleroderma experts, should be considered for all patients with SSc (see Chapter 85 for additional information on treatment), and are supported by more recent jSSc SHARErecommendations. .193, Treatment for SSc-associated ILD is making advancements with two agents recently receiving FDA approval: tocilizumab for more inflammatory ground-glass ILD and nintedanib for more fibrotic (reticular) ILD. As in adult SSc, autologous stem cell transplant (ASCT) is an option and may be the best opportunity for survival in selected severe patients, with a number of successful outcomes reported.212, ASCT was also agreed on as a good treatment option for cases of jSSc with progressive disease refractory to immunosuppressive therapy by the SHARE committee.

### Outcomes

Despite all the potential organ involvement in pediatric SSc, it has a far more favorable prognosis at 5, 10, and 15 years compared with adult SSc. Investigators recently reported survival rates at 10 years of 98% in children compared with 75% in adults. In jSSc cohorts, the most common cause of death was cardiac (including PAH) and respiratory failure. 150, Death within a few years of onset of disease (majority ≤5 years) was reported in two jSSc cohorts. 150, One study proposed a model for prediction of poor outcome in jSSc that included fibrosis on chest radiograph, raised creatinine levels, and pericarditis. The research group at Padua University coordinated a study that developed and validated the J4S, to objectively establish the degree of jSSc severity in daily . This is not a mortality practice using a comprehensive score. predictor but a gauge to possibly use longitudinally to follow the patients' disease course and trajectory and will enable comparisons of patients across observational cohorts and assist in the stratification of patients for clinical trials. It is mirrored from the Medsger Severity Score,215 ranging from normal, mild, moderate, to severe involvement of different organ manifestations and general health parameters. The J4S is a promising measure and should be validated in prospective studies.

### Localized Scleroderma

### Classification

LS, also termed morphea, has a different pattern of skin involvement than SSc and encompasses several subtypes classified by depth and pattern of the lesion distribution. These disorders are characterized by inflammation-driven fibrosis and atrophy that are mainly confined to the skin and subcutaneous tissue in more superficial disease; however, deeper forms also involve the fascia, muscle, tendon, and joint capsule. Certain subtypes of LS have unique associated extracutaneous manifestations (ECMs). The Padua criteria are the most commonly used to identify LS subtype and have been recently validated to correctly classify 95% of a large adult and pediatric LS cohort (944 subjects). The criteria include a "mixed morphea" subtype, which includes more than one type, the prevalence of this category is 15% in juvenile

LS (jLS) (Table 111.4). The most common subtype in juvenile LS (jLS) is linear scleroderma (LiScl) (50% to 60%), which is characterized by a linear streak or band involving the dermis, subcutis, and often the underlying muscle, tendons, and bone. LiScl typically occurs as a single, linear, unilateral band on the extremities, trunk, or head.152, Linear lesions crossing the joint may cause joint contracture and limb dysfunction (Fig. 111.10A). Of particular concern in with LiScl is involvement of the underlying tissues, including muscle, bones, growth plates, and organs, which can lead to permanent shortening or atrophy of the limb in children (Fig. 111.10B). Orthopedic complications are reported in approximately 30% to 50% of patients with LiScl of the limb(s), causing mild to moderate disability. 153,

Linear lesions affecting the head affect approximately 25% of patients with jLS. Those with more obvious cutaneous findings sometimes have a dyspigmented linear streak or depression of the scalp and forehead termed en coup de sabre (ECDS), resembling a saber wound scar (Fig. 111.11). Those with more atrophy of the subcutis, with associated hemifacial atrophy of the mandible, maxilla, tongue, and muscle tissue of the face, are classified with Parry—Romberg syndrome (PRS) or progressive hemifacial atrophy. These disorders can occur together, either at the same location (side of face) or on opposing sides (Fig. 111.12), and are thought to be on a spectrum of the same process, collectively termed Craniofacial scleroderma (CfS).219, PRS and ECDS are associated with neurologic, ophthalmologic, and dental ECMs. Neurologic involvement is demonstrated in 8% to 20% of the patients with these conditions, including CNS involvement expressed as seizures, chronic headaches, optic neuritis, and, less frequently, neuropsychiatric changes or ischemic stroke. Brain MRI abnormalities associated with the CNS can be found in up to 34% of patients and include subcortical white matter lesions (typically ipsilateral to the cutaneous lesion), calcifications or blood products (areas of susceptibility), vascular malformations, and cysts. Orthodontic involvement in CfS includes malocclusion, atrophic roots, gingival recession, loss of alveolar bone, and tooth mobility. Ophthalmologic involvement in CfS includes episcleritis, optic neuritis, uveitis, enophthalmos, and fibrotic changes to the lacrimal gland or eyelid. 152, Guidelines for screening and monitoring these unique ECMs for CfS have been developed (see "Disease Monitoring" below).

The less common subtypes of jLS are superficial and deep circumscribed LS, generalized morphea, and pansclerotic morphea. Most superficial circumscribed lesions (epidermis and upper dermal involvement) affect the trunk, are more common in adults, and are usually treated topically. Deep circumscribed morphea affect the dermis and subcutis with variable penetration into the fascia and muscle. Typically, there are only subtle cutaneous changes, such as slight erythema and thinning of the dermis, but secondary to deep infiltrate causes a "scooped-out" appearance of the subcutis. Generalized morphea (GM) is more typical in the adult LS population, occurring in less than 10% of patients as myalgia, arthralgia, and fatigue.44, Lesions typically are widespread throughout the trunk and coalesce. This subtype is often associated with several autoimmune phenomena, including positive antibodies and concomitant and family history of autoimmune disorders. . Pansclerotic morphea is a rare subset of LS, affecting 1% to 2% of patients, and is the most disabling. It initially involves the trunk (chest and back) and then spreads toward the extremities but later may migrate to the trunk, only sparing the face and distal areas of fingers and toes (Fig. 111.13). There is a

rapidly progressive fibrosis of the deep dermis, subcutis, fascia, and muscles, with occasional bone involvement. This leads to significant contracture of joints, muscle atrophy, cutaneous ulcerations, and sometimes restrictive pattern of respiratory insufficiency if the trunk is involved. The development of squamous cell carcinoma is an additional complication in pansclerotic morphea, especially in areas of chronic wounds.

Eosinophilic fasciitis (EF), once considered a type of deep morphea by Peterson criteria, is not considered a subtype of jLS by the Padua criteria, although it often has features of deep morphea and

linear scleroderma, resulting in deep infiltration and joint contractures. The treatment approaches used for LS are also used for EF.

### Clinical Features

### Cutaneous Manifestations

Disease Activity and Damage Features: Clinical and Histologic Findings. Similar to SSc both clinically and histologically, LS exhibits an inflammatory phase early in the disease process and transitions to a more fibrotic phase later in the disease. Early

active lesions in LS are characterized by a violaceous inflammatory border or "lilac ring" and skin induration throughout the lesion that may appear waxy or ivory colored (Fig. 111.14). During this active state, lesions may also expand, and new lesions can accumulate.217, Histologic findings in the early stages of disease consist of a perivascular and perineural infiltrate of predominantly lymphocytes with rare plasma cells and eosinophils in the deep reticular dermis and subcutis, accompanied by thickened collagen bundles, decreased elastic fibers, and swollen endothelial cells.217, With time, disease damage accumulates and is represented by an increase in skin thickness, especially at the center of the lesion, combined with dermal and subcutaneous atrophy, appearing as visible veins, a "cliff drop" appearance of the dermis, and flattening or concavity of the subcutis, respectively. Histologic evaluation of the skin at this damaged stage reveals thickened hypocellular (homogenized) collagen that replaced the previous inflammatory infiltrate around the dermal appendages, leaving behind atrophic eccrine glands and hair follicles and loss of elastic fibers. In addition, capillaries may be decreased in number with a fibrotic wall and narrowed lumen. 217, Post-inflammatory

hyperpigmentation and hypopigmentation also are results of previous inflammation and are often the features that bring the lesion to the attention of a medical provider. Telangiectasias may develop in areas of damage in LS, sometimes giving the lesion an erythematous appearance, which should not be confused with erythema from active disease; dermatoscopic examination may help differentiate the two processes.

Extracutaneous Manifestations. ECMs are now recognized to occur in approximately half of LS patients in prospective cohort studies. According to a large international study of 750 children with LS, ECMs are more frequent in patients with LiScl and consist essentially of orthopedic complications (19% in the entire group, 50% in those with LiScl of the extremity) and neurologic or ocular findings (24 patients, 5% in the entire group, 60% in those with LiScl of the head).153, Musculoskeletal manifestations include arthralgia, arthritis, joint contractures, myositis, myalgia, muscle spasms, and hemiatrophy. Childhood-onset LS poses a major risk to undergrowth of limb and facial structures in the developing child, with studies reporting half the patients with LiScl of the head having hemifacial atrophy with deformity from tissue atrophy or muscle bulk reduction and one-quarter of

the LiScl limb patients having bone length difference with gait abnormalities.152, Less common ECMs are GI, respiratory, and renal, all of which occurred in less than 2% of the 750 patients examined. These estimates may be lower than the true percentage of ECMs because only symptomatic patients were included in the analysis. Interestingly, of the 168 patients with ECMs, 25% had articular, neurologic, and ocular manifestations unrelated to the site of skin lesions, further supporting the hypothesis that localized scleroderma is a systemic process. A recent study showed 20% (11 of 53 patients) of a jLS cohort had polyarthritis at sites distal from the lesion. This included patients with circumscribed superficial, generalized morphea and linear scleroderma of the head and limb.

### Diagnosis and Diagnostic Tests

LS remains a clinical diagnosis by physical examination features, and when there is uncertainty, a skin biopsy is supportive (findings described above). There are no diagnostic laboratory tests for LS, but there is a high prevalence of autoantibodies, including ANA, anti-histone antibody (AHA), and anti—single-stranded DNA antibody (ssDNA Ab). A positive ANA is found in 42% to 73% of patients with LS and has been associated with an increased risk for ECMs and disease recurrence. 234-236 The prevalence of ssDNA and AHA in LS is approximately 50%, and both are associated with disease severity features, such as deep muscle involvement, joint contractures, and increased number of lesions.234-236 In addition, rheumatoid factor (RF) is present in one-third of patients, particularly those who have GM, and also correlates to disease severity (greater number of lesions and deeper joint involvement).134, These antibodies (ssDNA and AHA) and RF may help in stratifying patients during the earlier stages of disease, suggesting the possible initiation of more aggressive therapy and increased surveillance.

General markers of inflammation, including erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and serum immunoglobulin levels (immunoglobulin [Ig]G and IgE), may be useful markers of disease activity in select patients with LS, particularly those with deep or eosinophilic-like variants. However, the majority of patients seen with active LS lesions do not have elevation of these markers. A recent review of the CARRA Registry data of 259 patients with jLS supports elevated creatine phosphokinase (CPK) or aldolase to reflect disease activity through their association with new lesions. CPK elevation was also associated with muscle atrophy and limb shortening and may predict muscle involvement.

### Disease Monitoring

Several tools have been used for the assessment of skin and subcutaneous involvement in LS, such as clinical skin scores, measurement tools, and imaging. The Localized Scleroderma Cutaneous Assessment Tool (LoSCAT) is a clinical skin scoring system that assesses disease activity and damage parameters and is the most widely validated and used cutaneous tool.237,238A A computerized skin score (CSS) can be used to determine the size of lesion in an objective manner. Measurement tools, including a durometer, which measures the degree of skin hardness, 201 and a cutometer, which measures skin elasticity. have also been proposed as useful. In addition, several types of imaging can be used for diagnostic or assessment and monitoring purposes, in tandem with the cutaneous examination such as thermography, laser Doppler flowmetry, ultrasound, and MRI.241-247 Musculoskeletal MRI to evaluate and monitor inflammation in the deeper structures (subcutis, fascia, muscle, tendon, bones and joints) has become more mainstream

in linear scleroderma and generalized morphea subtype assessment, with fascial thickening and enhancement and subcutaneous thickness being useful outcomes to monitor in regards to medication 239 response.

Recent recommendations regarding the evaluation and treatment of jLS have been published including SHARE consensus-based recommendations from PReS,248 an international collaboration of pediatric rheumatology and dermatology LS experts outlining minimal standards, CARRA LS experts' opinion, 250 and pediatric dermatology morphea expert opinion, 251 reaching several shared core recommendations. Some of tools included in the recommendations have been validated in LS, including the LoSCAT, ultrasound using higher frequencies (10 to 25 MHz), and MRI. Specific minimal standards of care for jLS evaluation mentioned across all recent recommendations include cutaneous monitoring for all patients with the LoSCAT and for those with linear scleroderma of the head, brain imaging with MRI, dental, and eye 248, In general, internal organ screening with echoscreening. cardiogram, PFTs, etc., for a patient with LS is not recommended because they tend not to have typical SSc features. 248-251

### Differential Diagnosis

Differential diagnosis is limited and includes lichen sclerosus et atrophicus and atrophoderma of Pasini and Pierini; superficial dermal and epidermal inflammatory conditions that are thought by some to be on the milder spectrum of LS; cutaneous T cell lymphoma, especially if there is a deeper purple skin discoloration; and collagenoma, usually presenting with induration of the skin and subcutis without pigmentary changes. Linear lesions of LS tend to follow the lines of Blaschko; therefore other childhood skin conditions following these lines need to be discerned, such as linear epidermal nevi, lichen striatus, and linear lichen planus, most of which will have more superficial changes, such as being raised, with slight scale or velvety/warty texture. Other possible conditions are associated with certain exposures and generally have more widespread lesions, such as GVHD (status, post-transplant), nephrogenic fibrosing dermatopathy (gadolinium administered in renal compromised state), and porphyria cutanea tarda (sun exposure).

### Treatment

The approach to the treatment of LS initially depends on the severity of the disease, which is characterized by the subtype of LS, potential involvement of deeper tissue and structures (such as joints), location of LS (crossing joints or involving the head), and disease activity state. The vast majority of jLS patients are treated with systemic therapy. The exceptions are very superficial circumscribed plaque morphea lesion(s), typically on the trunk, which have no progression for several years. jLS is a slow, smoldering disease, and the goal is to treat earlier in the disease to reduce inflammation, prevent damage, and preserve function.

There is growing consensus among both pediatric rheumatologists and dermatologists that systemic therapy is warranted for more moderate to severe jLS, which is defined as lesions with deep tissue involvement (subcutis, fascia, and muscle) that transverse a joint and potentially cause functional impairment, affect the face or scalp, are rapidly progressive or widespread active disease, and .248,249,251The for those who have failed topical or UV therapy. most commonly used systemic therapy is MTX in conjunction with CS. The only double-blind randomized control trial in jLS with objective measures comparing MTX and oral CS versus

placebo and oral CS found MTX to be effective and safe, and those treated with MTX significantly improved and had significantly fewer relapses compared with those on CS alone. An open-label extension (average follow-up, 40 months) supported continued MTX efficacy: 74% had a good response to methotrexate, and 73% of those responders remained in clinical remission for a mean of 25 or more months after stopping methotrexate. Relapses were documented during this longitudinal study, and the authors concluded that it is beneficial to continue MTX treatment for at least 24 months to ensure a prolonged and sustained disease remission. This was supported in two other cohort studies, reporting higher relapse rates in those with shorter MTX treatment duration and recent consensus recommendations. 234,

A subcommittee of CARRA derived four consensus treatment plans (CTPs) for the first 12 months of induction of therapy for those with moderate to severe jLS. Three protocols involve subcutaneous MTX (1 mg/kg, with a maximum dose of 25 mg/week), and the fourth was derived for those who either fail to respond to MTX or are intolerant to MTX. The protocols are divided into MTX alone, MTX with oral CS and taper, MTX with intravenous (IV) CS, and MMF in addition to either oral or IV CS. MMF was included as an alternative because it has been effective in severe MTX-resistant jLS (pansclerotic, GM, LiSCl subtypes). These regimens have been found to be equally effective and are also 248, Therapy in non-MTX endorsed through PRES consensus. responders typically involves the addition of monotherapy with MMF, followed by the use of various biologics that have been published in case reports with success in treating LS, including abatacept, tocilizumab, infliximab, and tofacitinib. 234,251,255,256,258,259

### Other Therapies

For a single superficial circumscribed lesion in a noncosmetic location, topical treatment with CS, calcineurin inhibitors, imiquimod, vitamin D, or recurrent phototherapy with UV light is acceptable.248, All modalities have had clinical success in case series or uncontrolled trials exhibited by lightening of hyperpigmentation and decreased skin thickness. UVA-1 was successful in two randomized control trials, especially in regard to early inflammatory and superficial dermal lesions.260, A meta-analysis of 19 studies including MTX or UVA therapy was conducted that included 193 children, 48 of whom were treated with UVA, and reported both MTX and UVA to have a positive effect in lesions of jLS; however, MTX appeared to be superior.

Intensive physical and occupational therapy in conjunction with systemic immunosuppressive therapy is recommended for those with linear or deep scleroderma of the extremity to help minimize joint contractures. Also, for those with ECDS and/or PRS, plastic surgery intervention is felt to be reasonable after the disease has been in remission without any signs of clinical activity. Augmentation includes fat transfer and grafting with microdroplets from the patient's abdominal subcutis to assist in filling in some of the subcutaneous atrophy to yield a more symmetric facial contour.' 263, For more severe disease, fasciocutaneous flaps and facial bone reconstruction are also options, although they are typically reserved for the late teenage years after the skeleton has matured.263,264

### Outcomes

The largest obstacle to good outcomes is awareness of LS among primary care physicians and timely referral to academic dermatology or rheumatology to enable correct diagnosis, evaluation, and treatment, especially while the disease is still in the active phase. When fibrosis and atrophy dominate, available therapies that target

inflammation are less effective. Two recent European studies demonstrated an average 11to 13-month delay from onset to correct diagnosis of LS.265, In one of the studies, all 50 cases were originally misdiagnosed or undiagnosed at first provider visit. The CARRA jLS cohort (n = 381) reported 17% of the patients having a 2-year or greater delay to their first pediatric rheumatology visit. North American dermatology and Italian pediatric rheumatology longitudinal LS cohort confirmed that a prolonged interval between onset and definitive diagnosis adversely affects the final outcome. 256,

Once systemic immunosuppressive therapy is initiated in patients with LS, the signs of disease activity typically resolve within months; damage features may improve but typically do not resolve.248, After this initial improvement, it is important not to discontinue immunosuppression too early, potentially resulting in relapse.234, In general, it is recommended to treat for 2 to 3 years with MTX with sustained remission before discontinuation of systemic therapy. After this initial course, it is not uncommon for the patient to relapse, and despite prior notions that LS "burns out," approximately 30% to 50% of patients will relapse, requiring reinitiation of systemic therapy. In the authors' opinion, these relapses typically occur in the same region as the original lesion, and most respond to reinitiation of systemic therapy.

### Conclusions: Localized Scleroderma and Systemic Sclerosis

Although the underlying pathogenesis of jLS and jSSc remains understudied and mostly relies on adult SSc studies, newer data are available suggesting a shared immunophenotype and associated cytokine profiles between juvenile and adult patients and between LS and SSc. Treatment is most effective during the active inflammatory state in both jLS and jSSc; therefore it is imperative to raise awareness in general providers for prompt referral, diagnosis, complete evaluation, and management. CARRA, PRES, the Pediatric Dermatology Research Alliance (PeDRA), and other international efforts are further refining disease activity, damage, and responsiveness measures of LS through CTPs to offer more defined guidelines for therapy management and to be used in future clinical trials of LS. The J4S is a promising tool for similar purposes in jSSc

### Pediatric Vasculitis

### KEY POINTS

For the rarer pediatric systemic vasculitides, treatment is largely based on data from adult trials; however, there are differences between adult-onset and childhood-onset disease that are being elucidated and require consideration when treating pediatric patients.

### Introduction

Childhood vasculitis encompasses a group of disorders characterized by the presence of inflammation in the blood vessel wall. Similar to adults, clinical symptoms vary depending on the types

and location of the vessels involved. Apart from Kawasaki's disease (KD) and immunoglobulin A vasculitis (IgAV), these diseases are relatively rare in childhood. KD and IgAV are usually acute and self-limited; however, the other forms can be organ or life-threatening, especially if not recognized and treated in a timely manner. Compared with adults, children may have a higher potential for significant morbidity due to the longer duration of disease or effects of treatment over the course of their lives. This section will focus on the types of vasculitis most commonly seen in the pediatric age group and highlight the unique features of childhood-onset disease.

### Classification

The framework for classification of childhood vasculitis is based upon the predominant size (large, medium, or small) of the involved vessels.
