Additional factors that have been incorporated into classification include clinical phenotype, histopathology, and the presumed underlying disease pathogenesis.268-271 The most widely used classification systems in adults are the ACR criteria that were proposed in 1990268 and the Chapel Hill Consensus Conference (CHCC) framework for nomenclature and disease definitions that were proposed in 1994 and updated in 2012 (CHCC 2012).269, The CCHC system provides comprehensive descriptions that can help define diseases, but it does not provide classification criteria. The CCHC framework and ACR classification criteria were based on adult data and have limitations for use in pediatrics. For example, the ACR criteria do not include IgAV and KD. In pediatrics, the most commonly used classification system is the European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology (formerly known as the EULAR)/Paediatric Rheumatology International Trials Organisation/Paediatric Rheumatology European Society (EULAR/PRINTO/PRES) classification scheme (Table 111.5).271, The EULAR/PRINTO/PRES classification is based on vessel size like the ACR and CCHC systems, but it also provides pediatric specific classification criteria for IgAV, polyarteritis nodosa (PAN), granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA), and Takayasu arteritis (TA). In 2022 new ACR/EULAR criteria for the classification of GPA,273 microscopic polyangiitis (MPA),274 and eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA)275 were proposed for adults. The utility of these criteria in the pediatric population has not been evaluated; however, they do provide the first-ever classification criteria for MPA.

### Immunoglobulin A Vasculitis

### Definition and Classification

IgAV, formerly known as HenochSchönlein purpura, .270is the most common vasculitis in childhood. It is a small vessel vasculitis that is characterized by IgA immune deposition and involvement of the skin, gastrointestinal, musculoskeletal, and renal systems. IgAV typically presents acutely with a self-limited disease course; however, a minority of patients will have a more chronic course.

The EULAR/PRINTO/PRES criteria for IgAV include a mandatory finding of purpura or petechiae (without thrombocytopenia) with lower limb predominance and one or more of the following.

Diffuse abdominal colicky pain (may include intussusception and gastrointestinal bleeding)

Arthritis or arthralgia

Histopathology showing leukocytoclastic vasculitis or proliferative glomerulonephritis with predominant IgA deposition

Kidney involvement (hematuria, red blood cell casts, or proteinuria)

### Epidemiology

IgAV has an incidence of 6 to 30 cases per 100,000 children,2 276,277 with a peak incidence between ages 4 to 6 years. Most studies suggest a slight male predominance at a ratio of 1.2 to 1.5:1. 276,

IgAV is much less common in adults, but adults may have worse renal outcomes.278-280 IgAV occurs throughout the year but less frequently in the summer months. 277, Infectious triggers have long been recognized, with more than half of affected children having a preceding upper respiratory infection. 277,282

### Etiology and Pathogenesis

The underlying cause of IgAV remains unknown; however, a combination of genetic, environmental, and immunologic factors likely plays a role.283, Associations with certain HLA alleles, as well as polymorphisms in other genes, have been reported. The presence of IgA deposits in vessel walls of affected organs is characteristic of IgAV, and both aberrant and increased levels of

IgA and IgA complexes are considered to play a central role in the pathogenesis of IgAV.

### Clinical Features

The classic tetrad of IgAV includes palpable purpura, joint pain, gastrointestinal complaints, and renal involvement. The signs and symptoms may develop over days to weeks. Nonthrombocytopenic purpuric skin lesions are the hallmark of IgAV, and their presence is required for the diagnosis. Palpable purpura usually appear in dependent areas; however, the trunk, arms, and face can also be affected. The rash typically appears in crops and may be preceded by a maculopapular or urticarial rash before evolving into the more classic purpura. Joint involvement is the second most common manifestation seen after rash, with arthritis or arthralgias 286,287The occurring in approximately three-quarters of children. arthritis is usually oligoarticular, with the knees and ankles most commonly affected. Joint involvement is the presenting manifestation in 15% of children. Subcutaneous edema, including periarticular swelling, is common. Gastrointestinal involvement occurs in up to two-thirds of children, usually manifesting as abdominal pain. 286, Other symptoms include nausea, vomiting, and gastrointestinal bleeding. Surgical complications occur in approximately 5% of children and include intussusception and bowel wall perforation. Renal disease is present in up to half of children and usually presents with hematuria and/or proteinuria and within 6 weeks of diagnosis. Renal involvement is usually mild and self-limited; however, a minority of children will develop nephritic or nephrotic syndrome, impaired renal function, or renal failure. 286, Less than 2% of children will develop long-term renal impairment. The risk is higher in older children and adults and in patients who have more severe renal disease at presentation , Other less common clinical manifestations of IgAV include pulmonary involvement, nervous system involvement, and urologic involvement (scrotal pain and swelling).

### Diagnosis and Diagnostic c Tests

The diagnosis of IgAV is based on clinical manifestations. Laboratory tests are helpful for identifying renal involvement and for excluding other diseases (for example, ruling out thrombocytopenia or coagulopathy as a cause for purpura). Markers of inflammation (ESR or C-reactive protein [CRP]) levels may be elevated but are nonspecific. Serum IgA levels are increased in approximately half of patients. If the diagnosis remains uncertain, a skin biopsy demonstrating leukocytoclastic vasculitis with deposition of IgA-containing immune complexes supports the diagnosis. In rare cases, renal biopsies are performed, particularly if the renal disease is severe and progressive. Imaging studies such as abdominal radiography and ultrasound are useful in patients with significant abdominal symptoms.

### Treatment

Most children with IgAV have self-limited disease that can be managed with supportive care, including hydration and pain management. For more severe disease, there may be a role for glucocorticoids and, in some cases, immunosuppressive treatment. In 2019 the European initiative SHARE (Single Hub and Access point for pediatric Rheumatology in Europe) published the firstever evidence-based consensus recommendations for the diagnosis and management of pediatric IgAV. SHARE recommends that in patients with severe gastrointestinal involvement, corticosteroid treatment could be considered based on some studies showing that corticosteroids shorten the intensity and duration of

abdominal pain. For the treatment of IgAV nephritis, SHARE recommends the use of corticosteroids (dosing dependent on severity) along with immunosuppressive treatment such as azathioprine, mycophenolate mofetil, or intravenous cyclophosphamide in some cases. Prophylactic corticosteroid treatment to prevent the development of IgAV nephritis is not recommended since controlled studies have shown that corticosteroids used in this way do not change renal outcome.292-294 Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors should be considered in IgAV nephritis to prevent/limit secondary glomerular injury for patients with persistent proteinuria.

### Outcomes

Overall, the majority of children with IgAV have a self-limited disease resolving within 4 to 6 weeks. Early morbidity is related to gastrointestinal involvement, and late morbidity is related to long-term renal impairment, which occurs in less than 2% of children. The risk of chronic renal disease is higher in older children and adults and those with more severe initial renal involvement.289, Recurrence of IgAV occurs in up to one-third of patients, typically within 4 months of initial presentation. 286,295

### Kawasaki's Disease

### Definition and Classification

KD is the second most prevalent form of pediatric vasculitis. It was first described in 1967 by the Japanese physician Dr. Kawasaki as a mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome. It is typically an acute and self-limited vasculitis that mainly affects mediumsized arteries. It predominately affects infants and young children and is rare in adults. Timely and appropriate treatment of KD is highly effective and significantly reduces the risk of coronary artery aneurysms, which is the most concerning complication of KD. 297,

Classification criteria for KD were proposed by EULAR/PRES in 2006; however, the criteria have never been validated. The criteria are almost identical to the diagnostic criteria set forth by the American Heart Association (AHA), which are the most widely used criteria for diagnosing KD.299,

The AHA criteria for diagnosing KD300 include a mandatory finding of fever for 5 or more days and at least four of the five following features:

Bilateral bulbar conjunctival injection without exudate

Erythema and cracking of lips, strawberry tongue, and/or erythema of oral and pharyngeal mucosa

Erythema and edema of the hands and feet in acute phase and/or periungual desquamation in subacute phase

Rash: maculopapular, diffuse erythroderma, or erythema multiforme-like

Cervical lymphadenopathy (≥1.5 cm diameter), usually unilateral

Patients with fever and fewer than four of the above criteria can also be diagnosed with KD if coronary artery abnormalities are detected either by two-dimensional echocardiography or coronary angiography.

### Epidemiology

KD has a worldwide distribution; however, the disease is significantly more prevalent in Asian countries, especially Japan. 300-302 Annual incidence rates as high as 260 per 100,000 children <5 years of age have been reported in Japan compared with 20 per 100,000 children <5 years of age in the continental United States. 301,

The majority of children are diagnosed before the age of 5 years, and boys are affected more commonly than girls.276,300,303

### Etiology and Pathogenesis

The etiology of KD remains unknown. The seasonality of KD, with peaks in the winter and spring and occurrences of epidemics, have suggested an infectious trigger; however, no specific infectious agent has been identified. In the absence of identifying a single infectious trigger, KD may result from an abnormal immunologic response to a more widely distributed infectious agent(s) in genetically susceptible individuals.304, The increased frequency of KD in Asian populations and in children of Asian descent residing in different countries, and the increased occurrence rates of KD among siblings and other family members of index cases supports a genetic component to KD susceptibility. 300,305,306

### Clinical Features

KD progresses through three phases: acute (as long as 14 days), subacute (2 to 4 weeks), and convalescent (4 to 8 weeks). The acute phase is characterized by high fever along with other clinical features that characterize KD: rash, bilateral limbic-sparing nonexudative conjunctivitis, unilateral cervical lymphadenopathy, mucous membrane changes (strawberry tongue, red cracked lips), and extremity changes (swelling and erythema of the hands and feet). The fever is often high spiking (above 102°F [39°C]) and minimally responsive to antipyretic agents. The subacute phase follows the acute febrile phase and is largely asymptomatic other than the desquamation of the hands and feet that is seen in some children. During this phase, coronary artery aneurysms may develop or become apparent as a result of the preceding acute phase. The final convalescent phase is asymptomatic.

Other clinical features are also commonly seen with KD even though they are not part of the diagnostic criteria. Extreme

irritability is frequently observed and is most likely due to aseptic meningitis. Cardiac involvement during the acute phase include myocarditis, pericarditis, valvulitis, congestive heart failure, and, rarely, shock. Gastrointestinal and musculoskeletal symptoms are also frequently seen.

The most concerning feature of KD is coronary artery disease, which causes the majority of the morbidity and mortality. Coronary artery dilations and aneurysms are detected most frequently in the subacute phase.

### Diagnosis and Diagnostic Testing

The diagnosis of KD is based on syndrome recognition and meeting sufficient clinical criteria as outlined by the AHA above. 300 For a child who has unexplained fever for 5 or more days and less than 4 of the principle clinical features at time of presentation, the diagnosis of incomplete KD should be considered. The AHA has proposed a diagnostic algorithm to help identify patients with possible incomplete KD who are at risk of developing coronary artery aneurysms and should receive treatment with IVIG (see Fig. 111.15).

Laboratory findings in KD are nonspecific but reflect systemic inflammation and help provide support for the diagnosis. Elevated ESR or CRP, an elevated white count with leukocytosis, and anemia are common. Thrombocytosis is characteristic, but not usually seen until the second week of illness. In some children, thrombocytopenia is seen, and this is a risk factor for developing coronary artery aneurysms. Thrombocytopenia can also be seen as part of disseminated intravascular coagulation or macrophage activation syndrome that are rare but serious complications of KD. Other laboratory abnormalities that support the diagnosis of KD are shown in Table 111.6 and include hypoalbuminemia, hyponatremia, elevations of serum transaminases, and sterile pyuria. An echocardiogram should be performed at diagnosis

and then repeated in 1 to 2 weeks and again 4 to 6 weeks after 300,312 treatment.

### Treatment

IVIG and acetylsalicylic acid (ASA) are considered first-line therapy for the treatment of KD. Studies have demonstrated that administering a single dose of 2 g/kg of IVIG within 10 days of fever onset decreases the risk of coronary artery aneurysm formation from 20% to 25% to 3% to 5%.313, Treatment beyond 10 days should still be considered if there is evidence of ongoing systemic inflammation. ASA should be used with IVIG at a moderate (30 to 50 mg/kg/day) to high dose (80 to 100 mg/kg/ day) until the patient is afebrile.300, Subsequently, ASA should continue at a low dose (3 to 5 mg/kg/day) until the child has had a follow-up echocardiogram at 4 to 6 weeks following diagnosis. 300

The role of corticosteroids as additional therapy in KD has been examined in numerous studies. The current evidence-based guidance from the AHA and SHARE is to give corticosteroids to patients who have severe KD, are IVIG-resistant, or are at high risk for IVIG resistance. 300, Severe KD features and factors felt to be predictors of IVIG resistance include, but are not limited to, age less than 1 year; features of shock or macrophage activation syndrome at presentation; early presence of coronary artery changes; and certain lab parameters including hyponatremia, significantly elevated CRP, low platelets, and low albumin.312, For cases refractory to treatment with IVIG, ASA, and corticosteroids, TNF blockade (e.g. infliximab) may be considered; however, there is no strong evidence that TNF inhibitors alter cardiac-related outcomes. 312,317-319

### Outcome

The majority of children recover from KD without any long-term sequelae. Morbidity and mortality in KD are primarily based on the extent and severity of coronary artery involvement. Despite treatment with IVIG, approximately 3% to 5% will develop coronary aneurysms, and this has implications for long-term cardiac morbidity and requirement for anticoagulation.300, Mortality from KD is less than 0.2% and usually results from myocardial infarction. 320,321

### Anti-neutrophil Cytoplasmic Antibody- Associated Vasculitis, Polyarteritis Nodosa, and Takayasu's s Arteritis

Other forms of pediatric vasculitis are rare and present with similar manifestations as adult-onset disease.276, Given the rarity of these vasculitides in childhood, much of the information on pathophysiology, clinical manifestations, and treatment is based on adult studies. This section will highlight some of the differences between adult and pediatric disease. Please refer to the individual chapters on each disease for more in-depth review.

### Anti-neutrophil Cytoplasmic Antibody-Associated Vasculitis

Definition, Classification, and Epidemiology. Anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA)—associated vasculitis (AAV) includes GPA, MPA, EGPA, and renal-limited pauci-immune glomerulonephritis. These diseases are collectively characterized by predominantly small vessel necrotizing vasculitis associated with the presence of proteinase 3 (PR3)-ANCA or myeloperoxidase (MPO)-ANCA. These diseases are often grouped together because the definitions and classification characteristics of each disorder are not mutually exclusive. AAV is rare in children, with an overall incidence that varies depending on geographic location, but ranges between 0.1 to 6.4 cases per million children per year. In contrast to adult-onset disease, pediatric-onset AAV is more common in girls. 323-325

EULAR/PRINTO/PRES proposed classification criteria for GPA, but not for MPA or EGPA. The criteria for GPA require three of the following six features272.

Renal involvement (hematuria, proteinuria, or necrotizing pauci-immune glomerulonephritis)

Upper airway involvement

Laryngo-tracheo-bronchial involvement

Pulmonary involvement

ANCA positivity

Granulomatous inflammation within the wall of an artery or in the perivascular or extravascular area on biopsy

There are no pediatric-specific classification criteria for MPA and EGPA; therefore classification of these diseases is largely based on the adult ACR and CHCC systems.268-270 The 2022 newly proposed adult ACR/EULAR criteria for the classification of AAV includes updated criteria for GPA and EGPA and the first-ever classification criteria for MPA274; however, the utility of these criteria in children has yet to be evaluated.

Clinical Features. The clinical features of the various AAV conditions overlap significantly and predominantly involve the kidneys, lungs, and upper airways. Constitutional symptoms such as fever, weight loss, and fatigue are seen in the majority of patients. 323,

Similar to adults, GPA is characterized by the triad of upper respiratory tract/ear-nose—throat (ENT) involvement, lower respiratory tract involvement, and renal disease. Cutaneous, musculoskeletal, gastrointestinal, and ocular manifestations are also 323,326 seen.

Compared with adults, children with GPA have higher frequencies of constitutional symptoms and respiratory involvement but a lower frequency of conductive hearing loss. 323, Some studies suggest a higher frequency of ENT involvement in children, especially over the longer term. 326,

MPA is characterized by renal disease (often rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis) that may be accompanied by cutaneous, musculoskeletal, renal, and/or gastrointestinal involvement. 323-325 EGPA is exceedingly rare in children but similar to adults is characterized by chronic rhinosinusitis, asthma, and peripheral blood eosinophilia. The vasculitis manifestations of EGPA are often not apparent until later in the disease course.

Diagnosis and Diagnostic Testing. Laboratory studies are similar to adults. ANCA positivity is common; however, the absence of ANCA does not preclude the diagnosis. The presence of PR3-ANCA is usually associated with GPA, whereas MPO- ANCA is more common in MPA.323,

Other laboratory findings are nonspecific and usually reflect systemic inflammation (anemia, high acute-phase reactants) or indicate other organ involvement (e.g., abnormal urinalysis, elevated liver enzymes). Other investigations such as imaging of the lungs or sinuses may help determine extent and severity of disease, and tissue biopsies (skin, kidney) may be necessary to confirm the diagnosis.

Treatment and Outcome. The rarity of pediatric AAV has limited the ability to obtain pediatric-specific data on drug efficacy and toxicity; hence, treatment recommendations are largely extrapolated from adult randomized trial data. Treatment of AAV is based on a remission-induction model followed by a remissionmaintenance model. Glucocorticoids continue to be a mainstay of initial treatment. Choice of primary immunosuppressive agent is dependent on disease severity and type of organ involvement. For severe organ or life-threatening disease, intravenous cyclophosphamide or B celldepleting agents are primarily used; whereas for milder disease, methotrexate and azathioprine are favored.328-331 Different from adults, current consensus-based guidance in children recommends the use of B celldepleting agents be reserved for children not responding to conventional treatments or those with relapsing disease. In an effort to obtain more pediatric-specific data regarding the effectiveness and safety of cyclophosphamide versus rituximab in childhood-onset disease, CTPs for severe pediatric AAV were published in 2022 with the goal of prospectively comparing patients treated with the different protocols. For remission maintenance, methotrexate, azathioprine, or rituximab are recommended.

Similar to adults, pediatric AAV is associated with a chronic relapsing disease course and high rates of damage.325, Direct comparisons between adults and children are difficult due to variability in how remission and relapse are defined, as well as duration of follow-up.

### Polyarteritis Nodosa

Definition, Classification, and Epidemiology. Polyarteritis nodosa (PAN) is a systemic necrotizing vasculitis affecting smalland/or medium-sized arteries. It frequently presents with systemic symptoms (e.g., fever, malaise, and weight loss) and involvement of the skin, musculoskeletal, and renal systems.

The EULAR/PRINTO/PRES classification criteria for childhood PAN include a mandatory finding of either necrotizing vasculitis on biopsy or angiographic abnormalities of smallor medium-sized arteries plus one of the following 335.

Skin involvement (livedo reticularis, subcutaneous nodules, skin infarctions)

Myalgia or muscle tenderness

Hypertension

Peripheral neuropathy

Kidney involvement (proteinuria, hematuria, or impaired renal function)

The estimated annual incidence of PAN in adults is 1 to 8 cases/million. It is rarer in childhood; however, epidemiologic data in the pediatric population is scarce. In children, the peak age of onset is ~9 to 10 years of age, and males and females are equally affected.334,

Clinical Features. PAN varies in its presentation from a relatively mild primarily cutaneous form to a more severe systemic form. The cutaneous form of the disease presents similarly in children and adults with rash, arthritis/arthralgias, and fever being the most common features. Children with the systemic form of the disease typically present with constitutional symptoms, rash, and other major organ involvement, primarily renal, gastrointestinal, and neurologic systems. Two studies comparing adultonset PAN to childhood-onset PAN had varying conclusions; both demonstrated less neurologic involvement in children; however, one study suggested that childhood PAN had a more benign 339 whereas the other study suggested that childhood-onset course, disease was more severe and carried a higher risk of relapse.

In childhood, the possibility of a more recently described monogenic vasculitis called deficiency of adenosine deaminase 2 (DADA2) should also be considered in any child being evaluated for PAN. Children with DADA2 have mutations in the CECR1 (cat eye syndrome chromosome region, candidate 1) gene encoding adenosine deaminase 2 (ADA2) and usually present at a young age with signs of systemic inflammation, prominent vasculitic rash (livedo racemosa, subcutaneous nodules), early onset stroke, musculoskeletal involvement and immunologic abnormalities.340, Stimulator of interferon genes (STING)—associated vasculopathy of infancy (SAVI) is another recently described condition that is characterized by severe vasculopathy and interstitial pulmonary disease.

Diagnosis and Diagnostic Testing. The diagnosis of PAN is based upon the presence of characteristic signs and symptoms and evidence of necrotizing vasculitis affecting small or medium vessels on biopsy or angiographic abnormalities of such vessels. Laboratory tests help identify the extent of other organ involvement and can aid in ruling out other secondary causes of vasculitis. Elevation of acute phase reactants is supportive but nonspecific. Biopsies and vascular imaging are guided by what organ systems are involved.

Treatment and Outcome. Treatment of PAN is mainly based on data from adults and is guided by the extent and severity of the disease. Corticosteroids are needed by most patients; however, more aggressive steroid-sparing treatments are usually required when the disease is not limited to the skin. As with other forms of chronic systemic vasculitis, the recommended approach is to start with induction treatment followed by less intense maintenance treatment for 12 to 36 months depending on the clinical course. The current adult-based guidance is to use intravenous cyclophosphamide and corticosteroids for remission induction of severe PAN, followed by maintenance with less toxic agents such as azathioprine or methotrexate.343, A recently published small pediatric randomized controlled study evaluated mycophenolate mofetil versus intravenous cyclophosphamide for remission induction in 11 children with PAN. Rates of remission were similar in both groups, but MMF was associated with a shorter time to remission and better health-related quality of life measures at follow-up.

Compared with adults, overall survival is better, and the relapse risk is lower in children. The overall mortality is about 1% to

4%, and relapse risk is about 10% to 35% in large pediatric PAN cohorts.

### Takayasu's Arteritis

Definition, Classification, and Epidemiology. TA is a granulomatous large-vessel vasculitis that affects the aorta and its major branches. Incidence in all ages is estimated to be between 0.8 and 2.6 per million persons/year. The incidence in children is not known; however, it is estimated that up to 30% of patients with TA present in childhood. Median age of onset is between 12 to 14 years, but it has also been reported in infancy. 350-352

The EULAR/PRINTO/PRES classification criteria for Takayasu's arteritis in childhood require a mandatory finding of angiographic abnormalities of the aorta or its main branches and pulmonary arteries (aneurysm/dilatation, narrowing, occlusion, or arterial wall thickening not due to fibromuscular dysplasia) and at least one of the following five features272.

Pulse deficit (lost/decreased/unequal peripheral artery pulse[s]) and/or claudication induced by activity

Systolic blood pressure difference >10 mm Hg between any limb

Bruits or thrills over the aorta and/or its major branches

Hypertension (systolic blood pressure greater than the 95th percentile for height)

Elevated acute-phase reactants

Angiographic confirmation may be performed by conventional radiography, computed tomography, or magnetic resonance imaging.

Clinical Features. The early symptoms of TA are nonspecific, and diagnostic delays are common. 337, Similar to adults, constitutional symptoms, hypertension, and headache are common at presentation. 337, Other symptoms include abdominal pain, vomiting, dyspnea, and musculoskeletal complaints. Claudication is more frequently observed in adults.337, Bruits, diminished pulses, and blood pressure discrepancies between limbs are signs seen on exam.

Diagnosis and Diagnostic Testing. The diagnosis of TA is based upon the presence of characteristic clinical findings and angiographic evidence of abnormalities (aneurysm, dilatation, narrowing, occlusion, or thickening) of the aorta, its main branches, or pulmonary arteries. Abnormalities may be demonstrated by conventional angiography, magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) or computed tomography angiography (CTA). Other vascular imaging modalities that may also be useful include Doppler ultrasound, as well as more specific vessel wall imaging modalities such as gadolinium-enhanced MRA and fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography (PET). Laboratory tests usually demonstrate nonspecific elevation of inflammatory markers. Additional investigations to rule out secondary causes of large vessel vasculitis, such as infections like tuberculosis, may also be required. 346,

Treatment and Outcome. The approach to treatment of childhood TA is similar to adults. The primary goal is to induce remission as promptly as possible to prevent irreversible vessel damage and resultant organ damage from vascular insufficiency. Corticosteroids are the mainstay of treatment but due to the chronic relapsing nature of the disease, the addition of a corticosteroid-sparing agent is recommended. The pediatric-based guidance from SHARE is to use cyclophosphamide or MTX as the preferred initial choices.47, Other agents that may be considered on a case-by-case basis are TNF inhibitors, anti-IL-6 therapy, and rituximab. For maintenance, MTX, azathioprine,

or mycophenolate mofetil is recommended. Treatment of TA also includes careful monitoring and management of hypertension along with endovascular and or revascularization procedures in some patients.

Recent advances in treatment and disease recognition in TA have resulted in decreased morbidity and mortality. Reported mortality rates in childhood-onset disease range between 0 and 27%. Some studies suggest a more systemic and widespread disease presentation in childhood-onset disease with lower rates of remission and increased need for biologic 353,355,356 treatments.

# Bacterial Arthritis

### KEY POINTS

### Epidemiology

Septic arthritis is a medical and surgical emergency associated with significant morbidity and mortality, especially in immunocompromised individuals. Delaying diagnosis and effective treatment can lead to irreversible joint damage, disseminated infection, or death. In children, the most affected joint is the hip, followed by the knee and the ankle. In adults, the knee, hip, and ankle are the most common sites of infection followed by the elbow, wrist, shoulder, sternoclavicular joint, sacroiliac joint, and foot joint. Polyarticular involvement may be seen in 10% to 20% of cases1 ,1-3 (see e-Fig. 112.1).

The overall incidence of septic arthritis varies depending on the country. In the United States the incidence is 4 to 10 per 100,000

individuals.4, In western Europe, it is 4 to 12 per 100,000 patientyears, and in Australia, it is as high as 29 cases per 100,000 in the aboriginal population. In children, bacterial joint infections have an incidence of 4 cases per 100,000 children per year, occurring more frequently in males under 5 years of age. The populations commonly affected include neonates, persons with hemophilia complicated with hemarthrosis, and persons with sickle cell disease, human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), and malignancy on active chemotherapy.

The incidence of bacterial arthritis in adults is 5 to 12 cases per 100,000 people and is more common among those with rheumatoid arthritis (RA) or a prosthetic joint, with up to 70 cases per 100,000 individuals. The incidence varies based on the presence of risk factors including older age, diabetes mellitus, HIV, osteoarthritis (OA), and immunosuppressive therapy.7, The incidence has increased likely due to the aging population, with OA requiring orthopedic procedures (i.e., intra-articular injections, joint replacements, etc.), increased use of potent immunosuppressant agents, and intravenous (IV) drug use in the opioid epidemic era. Other risk factors that increase the risk of septic arthritis include skin infection, history of septic arthritis, cirrhosis, hypogammaglobulinemia, end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis, crystal arthropathies, and low socioeconomic status6,9,10 (Table 112.1).

### Nongonococcal Arthritis

### Etiology

### Gram-Positive e Organisms

Staphylococcus aureus is the most common cause of native joint septic arthritis in all age groups and risk factors. Gram-positive cocci bind to connective tissue and extra-cellular matrix protein, increasing the likelihood of colonizing and infecting the joint space. Among neonates, Streptococcus agalactiae, S. aureus, and Streptococcus pyogenes are the most common organisms causing septic arthritis. Gram-negative bacteria cause up to 60% of musculoskeletal infections (osteomyelitis and septic arthritis) in children younger than 4 years, with Kingella kingae, a commensal organism in the oropharynx of young children, now recognized as an emerging pathogen causing up to 82% of these infections.12, Other pathogens capable of infecting the synovium include Salmonella spp., more commonly in sickle cell disease, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa in adolescents with active IV drug use, diabetes mellitus,

or puncture wounds. The incidence of Haemophilus influenzae and Streptococcus pneumoniae have significantly decreased with improved immunization coverage 13,14,14a (Table 112.2).

In adults, gram-positive cocci cause 75% to 80% of septic arthritis with S. aureus being responsible for 37% to 56% of cases. S. pyogenes and Streptococcus agalactiae are common among older adults and individuals with comorbidities that include diabetes mellitus. Methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA) is increasingly common. Risk factors for MRSA infections include IV drug use, HIV infection, and diabetes. Health care—associated infections play an important role, especially related to orthopedic procedures or catheter-associated bloodstream infections with seeding of the joint. Coagulase-negative staphylococci, such as Staphylococcus epidermidis, are rare causes of native septic arthritis but are commonly associated with prosthetic joint infections (PJIs). Staphylococcus lugdunensis, another coagulase-negative Staphylococcus spp., commonly causes suppurative skin infections with a similar spectrum of disease as S. aureus. It has been associated with arthroscopic procedures and is common in health care settings. Other coagulase-negative Staphylococcus spp. are rarely associated with native joint infections unless in immunocompromised individuals or in prosthetic joints.5,

S. pyogenes is the second most common cause of septic arthritis. It has been associated with IV drug use, autoimmune disorders, penetrating trauma, and contiguous spread from cellulitis in individuals with skin infections. S. agalactiae

(Group B streptococci) septic arthritis can be seen in chronically ill patients including older adults, and in individuals with chronic liver disease, diabetes mellitus, and neurologic disorders. Aggressive polyarthritis caused by Group B streptococci may result in serious functional damage and destruction of the joints. S. pneumoniae septic arthritis is less common since the introduction of pneumococcal vaccines. However, it can occur in individuals with impaired immunity including specific antibody deficiency or individuals following splenectomy or functional asplenia as occurs in sickle cell disease. Enterococci are a rare cause of native septic arthritis but can be seen in PJIs associated with RA, OA, steroid use, or polymicrobial infections, especially from gastrointestinal or urinary tract infections.

### Gram-Negative e Organisms

The Enterobacterales order——such as Escherichia coli, Citrobacter spp., Klebsiella spp., Proteus mirabilis, Enterobacter spp., and Serratia spp.—are less common, comprising approximately 20% of infections, generally in IV drug users, those experiencing trauma with direct inoculation, or people with chronic liver disease. 11, Enteric gram-negative bacilli account for 43% of communityacquired bacteremia from disruption of the gastrointestinal mucosa or from the urinary tract. However, only 10% develop septic arthritis as a complication from hematogenous seeding.

P. aeruginosa is common among gram-negative bacterial arthritis with IV drug use, diabetes mellitus, and orthopedic procedures being the most important risk factors. It has also been identified in polymicrobial infections associated with trauma.

Salmonella spp. can cause disease in patients with sickle cell anemia or thalassemia, HIV, systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia, and other malignancies. Most cases of Salmonella septic arthritis are monoarticular with the knee being the most common joint affected (57%) followed by the hip (23%) and shoulder (9%).

Haemophilus influenzae type b rarely causes infection since the introduction of the Hib-conjugated vaccine in 1985. H. influenzae has nearly disappeared as a pathogen of bacterial septic arthritis in young children, although unencapsulated or nontypeable strains can cause invasive disease and septic arthritis in all age groups with an incidence of <1%. Risk factors for Haemophilus influenzae septic arthritis include impaired antibody production, hypogammaglobulinemia, abnormalities in the complement cascade, alcohol abuse with chronic liver disease, and active malignancy. Other unusual gram-negative pathogens include Neisseria meningitidis, Pasteurella spp., and Brucella spp.

Brucella septic arthritis is uncommon in the United States but common in rural Arab populations and also in immigrants from Latin America and the Middle East with exposure to unpasteurized dairy products. The most common joint affected is the sacroiliac joint, with up to 54% of cases of septic arthritis in patients with brucellosis.

Tropheryma whipplei, a rare cause of arthritis, is a fastidious actinomycete that can cause migratory peripheral arthritis as part of the syndrome that includes malabsorption, lymphadenopathy, and hyperpigmentation neurologic involvement (oculomasticatory myorhythmia). Patients with Whipple disease often have a positive HLA-B27, commonly mistaken with other arthropathies. A high level of suspicion is needed to make a diagnosis, which can be obtained through a small intestine biopsy or polymerase chain reaction (PCR) from synovial fluid.

### Anaerobic c Organisms

Bacterial arthritis caused by anaerobes is unusual (5%7% of the cases) but may be seen in diabetic patients or individuals following penetrating trauma. Bacteroides spp., Cutibacterium acnes, Finegoldia magna, Clostridium spp., and Actinomyces spp. are among the anaerobes that can infect the joint as part of a systemic infection or direct inoculation. C. acnes (formerly Propionibacterium acnes) has low virulence and can take up to 14 days to grow. Because of the slow growth, it is recommended that cultures be held for 2 weeks if this organism is suspected. It has also been associated with PJIs because of its ability to form biofilm. Atypical organisms, such as Mycoplasma spp. and Ureaplasma spp., have a predilection for mucous membranes, the former for the respiratory tract and the latter for the genitourinary tract. Individuals with hypogammaglobulinemia have a higher colonization rate with these organisms and are, therefore, at higher risk of infection. The reduced number of antibodies in these patients enables the organisms to spread to the joints. Atypical organisms are difficult to grow on cultures and often require molecular or genetic sequencing testing to obtain a diagnosis21 (see "Diagnosis" section).

### Polymicrobial Infections

Polymicrobial septic arthritis is a rare clinical entity involving mostly large joints usually associated with bacteremia. Close to

10% of septic arthritis cases are polymicrobial. The most affected joints are the knee, hip, and shoulder, followed by the wrist and ankle. Polymicrobial polyarticular bacterial arthritis is usually associated with overwhelming sepsis or in the setting of systemic inflammatory disorders such as RA, SLE, spondyloarthropathies and other connective tissue disorders. In a case series comparing monoarticular and polyarticular septic arthritis, it was found that 15% of all cases of septic arthritis were polyarticular with a mean of three affected joints, most commonly the knee, elbow, shoulder, and hip. The most common organism isolated was S. aureus followed by Streptococcus spp. Fifty percent of the cases of polyarticular septic arthritis occurred in individuals with RA compared with 14% of monoarticular infections, making RA one of the most important risk factors for polyarticular septic arthritis.22-24

### Pathogenesis

Acute septic arthritis is usually monoarticular due to a contiguous source from skin or bursa infection, direct inoculation from trauma or animal bites, procedures (arthrocentesis, steroid injection), or hematogenous seeding from a bloodstream infection. Joint infections occur when microorganisms gain access to the highly vascularized synovium. The normal joint is resistant to invasion because of local and systemic host defenses. Nevertheless,

the synovium lacks a protective basement membrane, making it vulnerable to infection through hematogenous spread, the most common route of infection. Once bacteria reach the well-vascularized synovium, the low fluid shear conditions and the production of host matrix proteins allow bacteria to adhere to the tissue, causing infection. S. aureus is the most common cause of nongonococcal septic arthritis, and it has multiple virulence factors that are associated with its ability to bind the connective tissue and access the joint, evade the host defenses, and cause damage to the joint6 (Fig. 112.1). It has a thick peptidoglycan cell wall that acts as a protective barrier against the immune response from the host. Joint damage occurs from the combination of bacterial adhesion and toxins, the inflammatory cascade by the host immune response, and ischemia. S. aureus reaches the synovium with the assistance of microbial surface components recognizing adhesive matrix molecules (MSCRAMMs). These molecules are part of the cell wall peptidoglycan of S. aureus and bind to host matrix proteins including collagen, fibrinogen, elastin, vitronectin, laminin, and fibronectin. 25,

Among the most important S. aureus virulence factors are collagen-binding protein, clumping factor A and B, fibronectinbinding protein A and B, capsular polysaccharide, staphylococcal protein A (SpA), toxic shock syndrome toxin-1, and enterotoxins. Other virulence factors that help S. aureus evade the host immune response include Panton-Valentine leucocidin with LukS and LukF proteins, superoxide dismutase, staphyloxanthin, aureolysin, catalase, nuclease, and staphylokinase27,28 (see e-Fig. 112.2 and e-Table 112.1). When bacteria adhere to the synovium,

proteases break down the matrix components. Bacteria proliferate, precipitating an inflammation cascade activating T cells and producing interleukin (IL)-4 and IL-10, among other cytokines. Neutrophils are an important component protecting the joint from organisms; these are the first to migrate to the site of infection together with macrophages. Opsonization and phagocytosis are key defenses to eradicate the organism—mechanisms that are impaired by the presence of SpA and capsular polysaccharide. SpA interferes with the binding of complement by binding to the fragment crystallizable part of the immunoglobulin G. It has been also considered a superantigen for B cells, as 30% of human B cells show Fab-mediated binding of SpA.25,

Adherence receptors allow the intra-cellular movement of S. aureus into host cells (e.g., osteoblasts, endothelial cells, neutrophils). The ability of S. aureus to switch from a normal-colony phenotype to a slow-growing, antibiotic-tolerant, small-colony variant phenotype may partially explain why this organism causes persistent and recurrent infections. When internalized, the organism is protected from the host's immune system and from antimicrobial agents.

In response to bacterial infection of the joint space and tissues, the host releases a variety of cytokines and inflammatory mediators. Initially, IL-1β and IL-6 are released into the joint space, leading to an influx of inflammatory cells. These neutrophils and macrophages engulf invading bacteria and release additional cytokines, including TNF, IL-1, IL-6, interferon (IFN)-γ, and IL-8. In a mouse model of S. aureus septic arthritis, IFN-γ has been associated with a worsening of the severity of arthritis while protecting

the animals from septicemia. The host's early cytokine response may aid the clearance of organisms and limit infection in the host. A late cytokine response may amplify the destructiveness of an established infection. 31,32

### Clinical Features

The classic presentation of septic arthritis is new-onset pain, swelling, warmth, erythema, decreased range of motion of the affected joint, and occasionally fever. Bacterial arthritis of the large joints is more common, especially the knee and hip, the former in adults and the latter in children. People with septic arthritis often have underlying illnesses that increase the risk of joint infection, with RA being an important risk factor. Patients with RA and other inflammatory or crystal arthropathies that increase the risk of bacterial arthritis have baseline pain, swelling, and range-of-motion limitation of the joints which makes it sometimes difficult to differentiate an arthritis flare from a septic joint.

Most patients with bacterial arthritis are febrile and have decreased appetite, general malaise, weakness, and hesitancy to use the affected joint. In neonates or young children, septic arthritis is more difficult to identify as they usually do not present with typical signs and symptoms of infection. Some of the signs that can help and raise suspicion of a septic joint in this population are irritability, failure to thrive, decreased oral intake, tachycardia, and fever. On physical exam, the neonate may flex, abduct, or externally rotate the hip to relieve the intra-articular pressure. Children may be hesitant to extend or flex the other affected joints and may have weight-bearing limitations. In adults, the presentation is classic, although, in immunocompromised patients, typical signs may be absent. Thirty to 60% of cases of septic arthritis in healthy individuals present with fever; therefore the absence of fever does not rule out bacterial arthritis. The onset of symptoms can vary depending on the virulence of the organism causing the infection and the individual's immune status. More virulent organisms, such as S. aureus, will cause symptoms within 1 week. Monoarticular infection is present in 80% to 90% of the cases.

### Diagnosis

### Synovial Fluid and Blood Analysis

The diagnosis of bacterial arthritis starts with a high level of suspicion considering clinical features of a painful, swollen, erythematous joint in the absence of an alternative explanation for inflammation. Whenever bacterial arthritis is suspected, the most important diagnostic procedure is arthrocentesis with synovial fluid analysis. For joints that are deep and more difficult to aspirate, ultrasound-guided or fluoroscopy-guided needle aspiration should be performed. Delay in diagnosis or long duration of symptoms before seeking medical attention and the presence of bacteremia, leukocytosis at presentation, worsening renal function, and polyarticular infection are among the factors associated with poor outcome.

The synovial fluid analysis starts with the evaluation of the appearance of the fluid (see Fig. 112.2). A normal synovial fluid should look clear and viscous and will have few white blood cells (WBCs). Fluid from an infected joint may look purulent or turbid. Historically, leukocyte count in the synovial fluid has been used to differentiate between septic arthritis and other inflammatory arthropathies. The most common criterion for septic synovial fluid WBC is >50,000/mm3, with most cases close to 100,000/ mm³ with >90% polymorphonuclear (PMN) cells. Unfortunately,

this information alone is not enough to make a diagnosis, as atypical infections and immunosuppressed patients tend to have a lower WBC count, and other inflammatory arthropathies may have a higher WBC in synovial fluid.

Differential diagnoses of septic arthritis and pseudoseptic arthritis are listed in (Table 112.3).33a As there are multiple reasons for abnormal synovial fluid, culture continues to be the gold standard for the diagnosis of bacterial arthritis. When specimens are obtained for cultures, a Gram stain is performed (see Table 112.4 for sensitivity and specificity).34-37 The sensitivity of the cultures is improved by the inoculation of blood culture bottles with synovial fluid, and cultures are incubated for at least 4 days. If suspicious of an atypical organism, this might be extended to 14 days to allow slow-growers such as C. acnes to grow, although this organism is more commonly associated with PJIs.

Blood cultures should also be obtained prior to antibiotic therapy. They are positive in 30% to 50% of cases of bacterial arthritis; in 10% to 15% of cases, blood culture is the only method of identifying the pathogen. Extra-articular sites of infection such as pneumonia, urinary tract infection, or cellulitis may offer guidance regarding the possible pathogen causing septic arthritis. Synovial fluid glucose, protein, and lactate dehydrogenase offer limited diagnostic value for bacterial arthritis. Leukocyte esterase, released by leukocytes during inflammation, has been studied as a diagnostic marker for PJI and to differentiate between septic or aseptic body fluids such as cerebrospinal fluid, pleural fluid, and peritoneal fluid.

Other markers in the synovial fluid such as procalcitonin and presepsin have been recently studied for both native and PJIs. Procalcitonin is the peptide precursor of calcitonin, while presepsin is produced from CD14 after bacteria are phagocytosed by monocytes. These two biomarkers have been found to be elevated in the bloodstream in the presence of a bacterial infection. Synovial procalcitonin has been evaluated as a marker of septic arthritis including native and PJIs, and low synovial procalcitonin (<0.5 µg/L) had a negative predictive value of 90%, whereas a value above 4.5 μg/L had a positive predictive value of 82%. The utility of synovial fluid presepsin as a tool for early diagnosis of septic arthritis has been studied and is elevated in patients with native and PJIs compared with patients with OA. The sensitivity and specificity were higher than those of blood presepsin. 34,

Additional studies have been done comparing presepsin in synovial fluid and blood with other inflammation markers such as C-reactive protein (CRP) and procalcitonin in patients with native septic joint and crystal arthropathies. Synovial fluid presepsin has good sensitivity and specificity for joint infection, 85.7% and 85.2%, respectively. Synovial lactate and IL-6 are additional markers of septic arthritis, and lactate had the highest predictive value with a sensitivity of 75% and a specificity of 87%, especially with values >10 mmol/L. IL-6 had the highest sensitivity of 92% (with levels <7000 pg/mL) and a specificity of 64%. Even though these markers have been studied recently and their utility is promising, they have not yet all been incorporated into guidelines. There are multiple other markers that have been studied as predictors of infection, although with variable sensitivity and specificity when evaluated individually. Inflammatory markers such as erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and CRP are usually elevated in serum, but sensitivity is low.

### Genomic Testing

Additional diagnostic tools such as PCR, matrix-assisted laser desorption ionization-time of flight mass spectrometry

(MALDI-TOF), next-generation sequencing (NGS), and multiplex panels are available to aid in the diagnosis of septic arthritis, with rapid identification, especially on culture-negative septic arthritis using synovial fuid or tissue. Molecular diagnostics identify microbial genetic material, although the technology is unable to differentiate between live and nonviable organisms. This is particularly helpful in cases of prior exposure to antibiotics where cultures are negative. MALDI-TOF has the advantage of rapid identification, although sensitivity on synovial fluid

directly is low (6.3%). It can, however, identify organisms from synovial fluid that has been inoculated in blood culture bottles. Broad-range PCR and NGS are the most recent diagnostic resources to identify infectious pathogens by detecting genetic material in bacteria (16s rRNA) or fungal genetic material (18s and 28s rDNA). Targeted PCR is another tool that can aid in the detection of Kingella kingae (in children) and other fastidious organisms. This technology applies to viruses, bacteria, fungi, and parasites and uses nanopore sequencing to assemble short

fragments of genetic material into a complete sequence. This can be accomplished by mapping against a known reference genome for identification. The information on sequence and identification can be used to update the public database. The utility of this technique is mostly pathogen identification, identification of virulence factors, and detection of genes associated with anti-microbial resistance. Most of these methods have been better studied for PJIs and are further discussed in the "Diagnosis" section.5,40

### Imaging

Plain radiographs in septic arthritis are usually normal early in the course of the infection, but baseline films should be obtained to look for evidence of other diseases and contiguous osteomyelitis. Radiographs often show nonspecific changes in inflammatory arthritis, including periarticular osteopenia, joint effusion, soft tissue swelling, and joint space loss. In more advanced infections, periosteal reaction, marginal or central erosions, and destruction of subchondral bone may be seen. Bony ankylosis is a late sequela of septic arthritis. Dislocation or subluxation of the femoral head is unique to hip infection of neonates.

Ultrasound is the modality of choice to detect fluid collections in the hip and can serve as a guide in aspiration. It can be used in other joints, such as the popliteal cyst of the knee, shoulder, acromioclavicular, or sternoclavicular joints. Triple-phase bone scan using technetium 99m is often done in children to identify an associated metaphyseal osteomyelitis or avascular necrosis of the femoral head. Whole-body bone scan is preferred in young children because, despite focal symptoms, septic arthritis and osteomyelitis may be

multifocal in this age group. In septic arthritis of all age groups, the periarticular distribution of increased uptake is seen in the early "blood-pool" phase and the delayed images of the joint. Bone scans provide only nonspecific information, however, and cannot differentiate septic from noninfectious causes of joint inflammation. Bone scans are more sensitive than standard radiography in the diagnosis of arthritis because radionuclide uptake precedes morphologic bone changes that are seen on radiographs. A suggestive bone scan must be interpreted in the proper clinical context and supported by microbiologic data for a definitive diagnosis of joint or bone infection.

In joints that are difficult to evaluate otherwise or that have complex anatomic structures, computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) can provide useful images to delineate the extent of the infection. MRI is highly sensitive in the early detection of joint fluid and is superior to CT in the delineation of soft tissue structures and soft tissue abscesses. These images can show early bone erosion, revealing soft tissue extension, and facilitate arthrocentesis of the shoulders, hips, and acromioclavicular, sternoclavicular, sacroiliac, and facet joints of the spine. MRI findings such as reactive bone marrow can suggest the presence of secondary osteomyelitis, which can complicate septic arthritis. When multiple joint involvements are suspected, triplephase bone scintigraphy is the preferred modality of investigation.

### Treatment

Treatment of septic arthritis must begin immediately after the clinical evaluation is complete and all appropriate cultures are taken. A serious clinical suspicion of a joint infection warrants the initiation of empiric antibiotic therapy before culture confirmation is available. Delays in treatment allow the infection to become more established in the joint and permanently damage the articular cartilage. Untreated, there is the opportunity for the joint infection to spread to other body sites via the hematogenous route and become more widespread and more difficult to cure.

The principles of treatment of an infected joint, whether natural or prosthetic, follow those of treatment of an infected body cavity in which antibiotics must be used in conjunction with adequate drainage of the infected closed space. The clinical circumstances and the preliminary laboratory data aid the selection of antibiotic agents. Host factors, any extra-articular sites of infection, and the Gram-stained smear of the synovial fluid are the best early guides for the antibiotic agents with which to start. Table 1 12.5 lists current antibiotic agents for adults.

Narrow antibiotic coverage is indicated if gram-positive cocci are found in the synovial fluid and the clinician suspects a primary source of staphylococcal infection from the skin. Appropriate monotherapy in this case may be a penicillinase-resistant penicillin (e.g., nafcillin or oxacillin), or cefazolin, or vancomycin if MRSA is suspected. If gram-negative bacilli are noted in the synovial fluid, and the patient has a kidney infection, specific agents (e.g., ampicillin or a cephalosporin) against E. coli and other common urinary tract pathogens may be used. In healthy, young, sexually active individuals with community-acquired septic arthritis and a negative synovial fluid gram-stained smear, ceftriaxone is a reasonable option to cover N. gonorrhoeae. If synovial fluid Gram stain shows gram-positive cocci, vancomycin should be the empiric therapeutic option, considering the fact that a significant proportion of community-acquired S. aureus infections are now methicillin resistant. A reasonable initial empiric therapy to cover gonococci, S. aureus, and streptococci is ceftriaxone plus vancomycin, pending final culture results. In elderly debilitated

patients or adults with low risk for sexually transmitted disease and a negative gram-stained smear of synovial fluid, broad antibiotic coverage against a wide variety of organisms, including S. aureus, streptococci, and gram-negative bacilli, should be given initially. A typical regimen includes an anti-staphylococcal agent (e.g., vancomycin) plus a third-generation cephalosporin (e.g., ceftriaxone).

When the identity and the sensitivities of the organism are known, antibiotic therapy should continue with the most efficacious agent that has the best safety profile and narrowest spectrum. The parenteral route of antibiotic administration is the preferred initial treatment. Continued antibiotic therapy may be switched to oral agents if adequate blood levels can be achieved and maintained by this route. There is no evidence that the direct intraarticular instillation of drugs is necessary or preferable in septic arthritis because there is no barrier against the free diffusion of antibiotic agents from the blood to the synovial fluid.

Most penicillins, cephalosporins (excluding ceftriaxone), and carbapenems (excluding ertapenem) have short half-lives necessitating frequent dosing (i.e., every 4 to 8 hours). Extended or continuous infusion therapy maintains levels of the drug above the minimal inhibitory concentration for a longer period of time, thus improving clinical outcomes and providing for more convenience for patients and caregivers, particularly in the outpatient or home health setting. Selected extended and continuous infusion dosing is reflected in Table 112.5. Use of once-daily drugs, such as ceftriaxone and ertapenem, is increasingly used in the outpatient management of septic arthritis. These drugs, because of high protein binding, may not be appropriate for morbidly obese patients.

Most individuals with septic arthritis respond adequately to appropriate anti-microbial agents after initial joint aspiration for fluid analysis. In experimental infectious arthritis cases, early antibiotic therapy reduced the loss of collagen and erosion of articular surface, which minimizes the need for open surgical drainage.

It is generally accepted that prompt and adequate drainage of the septic joint is essential to decrease the risks of substantial loss of articular function; however, the best approach to drain the joint remains controversial.

From retrospective studies, daily aspiration of an infected joint showed better functional outcome than open surgical drainage, although the former had higher overall mortality.47, An explanation for higher mortality could be the higher comorbid conditions of patients who had daily aspirations than the ones who were more fit and underwent open surgical drainage. If the synovial fluid cell count and PMN percentage decrease with successive aspiration, the anti-microbial therapy is probably effective.49, If needle aspiration is technically difficult (as in the hip or the shoulder) or does not provide thorough drainage of the joint, the joint effusion does not resolve promptly, if sterilization of the joint fluid is delayed, the infected joint is already damaged by pre-existing rheumatoid disease, or infected synovial tissue or bone needs debridement, surgical drainage should be considered sooner rather than later.11, Arthroscopy is emerging as an alternative to arthrotomy with the advantage of reduced surgical morbidity. Wound healing is faster, and rehabilitation time is shortened. A retrospective analysis from the United Kingdom suggested that most patients can be treated medically (with repeated aspirations) and do not require surgical drainage (either by arthroscopy or arthrotomy). Although statistically not significant, medical therapy resulted in more complete cure and less deterioration of functional status at time of discharge. Another study, which included 20 adults with native hip joint septic arthritis, concluded that symptom duration, especially if it is longer than 3 weeks before presentation, was a statistically significant predictor of the need for excision arthroplasty. These results highlight the need for careful case selection for surgical intervention.

Durations of anti-microbial therapy ranging from 2 weeks to 6 weeks is recommended for nongonococcal septic arthritis, depending on the type, sensitivity of the microorganism, and presence of contiguous osteomyelitis. The duration of antibiotic administration can be 2 weeks for uncomplicated infection by susceptible microorganisms or 4 to 6 weeks for more extensive infection in an immunocompromised host or in the setting of abnormal joints (e.g., severe OA). Prospective data on the optimal duration of antibiotic treatment for native-joint septic arthritis is scant. A single-center, randomized, unblinded, noninferiority trial found that microbiological recurrences and antibiotic-associated adverse events were similar with 2 weeks of anti-microbial therapy post-surgical drainage in nonimmunocompromised adults with nongonococcal septic arthritis involving the hand and wrist compared with 4 weeks. Over 80% of the patients enrolled in this study had small joint involvement (of the hand, wrist, and metatarsal joints), arising most commonly through direct, traumatic inoculation; this contrasts with most cases of septic arthritis that involve large joints, arise from hematogenous seeding of the vascular synovial membrane during bacteremia, and affect patients that are older and have more comorbidities. These differences in the host and pathogenesis were noted in an earlier retrospective analysis of hand and wrist septic arthritis that also described high cure rates with a short duration of treatment (median total antibiotic treatment duration of 14 days). At present, generalization to most septic arthritis patients is difficult, but further studies are underway (SHASAR, NCT0371692) that may support the efficacy and safety of shorter courses of anti-microbial therapy in other groups of septic arthritis patients.

In terms of the route of antibiotic administration, one approach has been to switch from IV to oral antibiotics after 2 weeks, provided that there is clinical improvement, inflammatory markers are trending down, and oral antibiotics are available to which the microorganism is susceptible. In a review of 169 adults hospitalized with septic arthritis, IV antibiotic duration (821 days vs. ≤7 days) or even total antibiotic duration (longer durations vs. ≤14 days) were not associated with the risk of sequelae and recurrence. Immunosuppression, infection with gram-negative pathogens, and lack of surgical intervention were associated with recurrence of infection. The study's retrospective nature precludes definitive conclusions regarding anti-microbial duration but reinforces the potential for use of oral antibiotics and shorter overall durations of anti-microbial therapy in selected circumstances. The basis to support early switch to oral therapy for osteoarticular infections in adults gained high-quality data from the large, multicenter, openlabel, randomized OVIVA (Oral Versus Intravenous Antibiotics) trial, which enrolled patients with a variety of native and deviceassociated bone and joint infections (mainly PJIs). Following an initial week of IV antibiotic therapy, completion of treatment with oral antibiotics was noninferior to continuing IV antibiotics and was associated with shorter hospital stays and fewer IV catheterrelated complications. Of note, 92% of participants in OVIVA underwent surgical debridement, and extrapolation is difficult to cases in which adequate surgical management for source control is lacking. Antibiotic selection and dosing were left to the discretion of the treating clinician, which precludes direct comparison of specific oral regimens. During the first few days of management, immobilization of the infected joint by external splinting and adequate analgesic administration ensure patient comfort. Physical therapy, starting with passive then graduating to active motion, should be instituted as soon as the patient can tolerate mobilization of the inflamed joint because early active range-ofmotion exercises are beneficial for ultimate functional recovery. Involving the orthopedic surgeon and the physical therapist early on in the course of treatment facilitates the best choice of drainage procedure and results in the best functional outcome.

### Gonococcal Arthritis

With the increase in the incidence of sexually transmitted infections in the United States, Neisseria gonorrhoeae infections are increasing. There was a 63% increase in gonococcal infections in young individuals in 20142018.59 Women are typically asymptomatic with primary infection in contrast to men. N. gonorrhoeae is the most common cause of monoarticular septic arthritis in sexually active young adults, historically more common in women than in men. The spectrum of gonococcal disease includes genitourinary infection, proctitis, pharyngitis/tonsillitis, conjunctivitis, and bacteremia with disseminated infection causing dermatitis, tenosynovitis, septic arthritis, and rarely endocarditis and meningitis.3, If untreated, disseminated infection occurs. Risk factors such as pregnancy, intrauterine devices, pelvic surgeries, SLE, and other complement deficiencies have been associated with disseminated infection. According to the Surveillance for Disseminated Gonococcal Infection, Active Bacterial Core surveillance (ABCs) system in the United States from 2015 to 2019, additional risk factors were identified that might represent the initiation of a shift in epidemiology with increased numbers of male individuals infected, people with HIV, and drug or alcohol abuse.

The mechanism of infection in gonococcal arthritis is through hematogenous seeding. N. gonorrboeae colonizes the mucosal

membranes in the pharynx and urogenital tract and has multiple virulence factors that allow it to adhere to the cell membrane, invade the cells, and compete with the microbiota for nutrients to survive. These virulence factors interact with the host immune system, especially the complement system, through two important mechanisms: binding and inactivating the complement cascade avoiding opsonization and binding to the factor H through lipooligosaccharide and porin attempting to protect itself from identification as a pathogen by the complement system. Another mechanism of survival is modulating apoptosis and the inflammation cascade to survive inside the macrophages and polarizing macrophages to impair T cell production62,63 (see e-Table 112.2). Patients with terminal complement deficiencies, which affect the complement membrane attack complex (MAC), are at increased risk of Neisseria spp. infections. Up to 13% of patients with disseminated disease are diagnosed with a complement deficiency, according to a recent study from Canada. Certain drugs such as eculizumab and ravulizumab (indicated for hemolytic uremic syndrome, paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria, and myasthenia gravis) selectively bind to complement protein C5, inhibiting cleavage to C5a and C5b. They prevent terminal complex C5b-9 generation and MAC formation, hence increasing the risk of Neisseria spp. infections and dissemination (see e-Fig. 112.3). It is recommended that patients receiving eculizumab get routine testing for sexually transmitted infections and penicillin as prophylaxis for N. meningitidis given the life-threatening nature of this infection. Because of increasing anti-microbial resistance, prophylaxis for gonorrhea has not yet been established by guidelines; however, there are ongoing trials and increasing data regarding the potential benefits of using doxycycline for post-exposure prophylaxis in high-risk populations. The risk of dissemination persists for up to 3 months after discontinuation of the drug due to its long half-life.

Disseminated gonococcal infection (DGI) occurs after cellular invasion by bacteria, resulting in transcytosis of the epithelium. It can occur 3 weeks after a genitourinary or pharyngeal infection, with the site of infection playing a role in the risk of bacteremia. Pharyngeal gonococcal infection is usually asymptomatic; therefore patients may go untreated for weeks, increasing the risk of dissemination. The same concept is considered for asymptomatic women. Menstruation and the post-partum period also increase the risk of DGI due to changes in the vaginal pH and cervical mucus. The clinical presentation of DGI usually involves the skin and the joints (especially knees, elbows, and distal joints) and rarely presents with cardiovascular or neurologic complications (see e-Fig. 112.4). Recognizing clinical findings of DGI will aid with the diagnosis of a patient with Neisseria spp. infection presenting with fever, arthritis, tenosynovitis, vesiculo-papular or pustular rash, or migratory polyarthralgia. Gonococcal infections do not develop immunity; therefore individuals are at risk of recurrent infections with reexposure.

The two most common presentations observed are arthritisdermatitis syndrome and localized septic arthritis, with absent skin lesions on the latter. The diagnosis is based on clinical presentation and isolation or detection of the organism from sterile sites. It is important to obtain blood cultures, synovial fluid for analysis, and cultures or molecular testing (PCR or nucleic acid amplification test). It is also recommended to obtain samples from other nonsterile or mucosal sites (pharynx, urethra, cervix, and anorectum) for cultures and or molecular identification in cases of DGI. Cultures from the skin have an extremely low yield and are not recommended. The yield of blood cultures is higher in cases

of arthritis-dermatitis syndrome (positive in about 30%50% of the cases). Possible explanations for low sensitivity could be that patients may have a lower burden of bacteria in the bloodstream or the fastidious nature of this organism.

The appearance of N. gonorrboeae on Gram stain is unique, intra-cellular gram-negative diplococci (see e-Fig. 112.5). Gram stain cannot differentiate among species or pathogenic versus commensal species. When isolated from sterile sites, however, it is considered a pathogen. With molecular testing methods, identification is more likely, even if the organism does not grow on cultures. The main benefit of cultures relies on the ability to perform anti-microbial susceptibility testing. Synovial fluid evaluation is essential for the diagnosis of gonococcal arthritis. The appearance of the fluid tends to be less purulent compared with other bacterial infections, and the WBC count on synovial fluid ranges from 30,000 to 50,000/mm3. Synovial fluid cultures are positive in about 50% of cases of gonococcal arthritis. Molecular testing is an important aid for diagnosis in cases of culture-negative arthritis with high suspicion of gonococcal infection. Given the fastidious growth of this bacteria, it is recommended to inoculate aerobic and anaerobic blood culture bottles with synovial fluid (1015 mL) or to place the specimen on conventional broth and solid media to increase the yield of the cultures. Other serum markers such as CRP and ESR are usually elevated. In cases of negative cultures, NGS should be considered (see "Diagnosis" section).

### Treatment

The drug of choice for gonococcal arthritis in children and adults is ceftriaxone. IV antibiotic therapy is recommended for a total of 7 days with the option of transitioning to oral therapy if susceptibility testing is available. Anti-microbial susceptibility testing is important given the increase in anti-microbial resistance. Recently the Surveillance for Disseminated Gonococcal Infections, ABCs system evaluated, from 2015 to 2019, the anti-microbial susceptibility of N. gonorrhoeae isolated from cases in California and Georgia. Most isolates were susceptible to azithromycin, cefixime, and ceftriaxone. There is, however, an increase in resistance to ciprofloxacin (33%), penicillin (38%), and tetracycline (24%). The emergence of multidrug-resistant gonococci is a major concern, especially the FC428 clone. It is resistant to ceftriaxone and has decreased susceptibility to azithromycin. In England resistance of N. gonorrboeae to azithromycin increased from 4.7% to 8.7% between 2013 and 2020. Ceftriaxone resistance remained low, although did increase from 0.3% to 1.4%. Ciprofloxacin and tetracycline resistance had a high percentage of 44% and 65%, respectively. Cefixime remains highly effective. For patients with gonococcal arthritis with cardiovascular complications, such as endocarditis, the duration of therapy is 4 weeks (IV therapy) while for central nervous system (CNS) infection (meningitis), the duration of therapy is 2 weeks. With newer diagnostic techniques and the ability to detect genes associated with resistance, antibiotic therapy could be transitioned to the oral route to shorten the length of stay for hospitalized patients with DGI without cardiac or CNS complications.

### Injection Drug Use and Bacterial Arthritis

Injection drug use (IDU) has increased in importance as a risk factor for septic arthritis over recent decades and requires special consideration. More than 11 million people are estimated to inject drugs globally, with approximately half of all people who inject

drugs (PWID) residing in just four countries: China, India, Russian Federation, and the United States. Recently published studies from the United States over the course of the growing opioid epidemic are useful for examining trends in bacteriology, distinct clinical features, and management challenges of septic arthritis in IDU compared with the general population.

As in non-IDU cases, the knee is the joint most involved by septic arthritis in PWID, and a relationship was noted between inguinal injection site and ipsilateral knee involvement. However, IDU has also been described as a risk factor for septic arthritis involving atypical axial skeletal sites, such as the sacroiliac, acromioclavicular, sternoclavicular, and costochondral joints and pubic symphysis69 (see Fig. 112.3). One explanation for the predilection of the sternoclavicular and sacroiliac joints is contiguous spread from phlebitis of an adjacent vein arising after injection of contaminated drugs into an extremity. Along with blood cultures, CT imaging or MRI are valuable in the diagnosis of septic arthritis involving axial skeletal joints more commonly involved in IDU. These affected sites may not develop drainable joint effusions and have more difficult localization on examination or variable presenting features. These advanced imaging studies can also evaluate the presence of complications requiring surgical debridement, such as epidural or paraspinal abscess associated with septic arthritis of the spinal facet joints or chest wall abscess or mediastinitis associated with septic arthritis of the sternoclavicular joint.

S. aureus more frequently colonize PWID than the general population70 and can be introduced hematogenously during nonsterile injection events or through contiguous spread to a joint from an overlying infection of skin and soft tissue infection in IDU. S. aureus is the predominant pathogen in septic arthritis associated with IDU. Both MRSA and methicillin-sensitive S. aureus (MSSA) septic arthritis are more common in PWID than

in non-IDU cases. In a recent review, MRSA comprised nearly a quarter of all septic arthritis cases in PWID,69 although this is likely also influenced by local epidemiologic variation as the prevalence of MRSA varies worldwide.

Septic arthritis caused by Serratia or Pseudomonas species may be associated with the use of nonsterile solutions, and osteoarticular infections have also been described involving commensal oral bacterial flora (including Eikinella corrodens causing "needle licker's osteomyelitis" in PWID who lick their needles or skin prior to injection72 or fungal septic arthritis with Candida species (see chapter on fungal septic arthritis). P. aeruginosa causes around 10% to 15% of septic arthritis in IDU,73,74a accounting for fewer cases than in the 1970s and early 1980s in concert with changes in opioid use patterns. Serratia species are other opportunistic pathogens found in association with water, which are historically associated with osteoarticular infections and endocarditis in IDU. In a large series of septic arthritis spanning 1990 to 2018 in Boston, the frequency of infections with gram-negative bacilli was similar (6%) in both the non-IDU population and PWID, although septic arthritis caused by E. coli was more common in patients who did not inject drugs and Serratia species were the main gram-negative pathogens in those who did.
