Although the skin continues to be the major source of contamination and subsequent infection in IDU primarily with staphylococci, remaining vigilant regarding less common bacterial etiologies related to injection practices is essential.

Outcomes of hospitalization for PWID with lower-extremity septic arthritis are less favorable compared with patients without IDU, including higher mortality rates during hospitalization, greater resource utilization with increased health care costs and length of stay, and a higher probability of leaving against medical

advice.76, Among the management dilemmas that clinicians must confront in caring for PWID is the question of how best to deliver prolonged courses of anti-microbial therapy, for which IV administration has been the standard of care traditionally. Prolonged hospitalization can impose a substantial strain on both the patient and the health care system. Although a comprehensive review of published observational studies found that PWID successfully completed outpatient parenteral antibiotic therapy (OPAT) at high rates comparable to patients without IDU,78 whether an individual patient is an appropriate candidate to receive outpatient OPAT at home must be assessed carefully on a case-by-case basis.

Off-label use of long-acting, once-weekly IV lipoglycopeptides, such as dalbavancin or oritavancin, are also promising treatment options in PWID suffering from severe osteoarticular infections caused by gram-positive bacteria, including MRSA. These antibiotics are administered once weekly through a peripheral IV. A retrospective cohort study of dalbavancin use for treatment of complicated staphylococcal infections in PWID, including osteomyelitis, provides some real-world evidence to support the use of these agents in this challenging patient population. However, caution should be exercised given the high loss to follow-up described.

Interest has been increasing in the use of highly bioavailable oral antibiotic therapy for osteoarticular infections. The OVIVA study provides high-quality evidence that oral therapy appears to be as safe and effective as IV antibiotic therapy in patients with bone and joint infections,57 but some questions remain regarding how best to apply these findings to PWID. Access to oral antibiotic therapy and appropriate outpatient follow-up is uncertain for PWID in countries without a universal public provider system, such as the United States, in which more than a quarter of PWID are uninsured. MRSA infection only comprised 10% of bone and joint infections in OVIVA, in contrast to the higher rates seen in PWID in the United States. The number of patients with IDU included in OVIVA was not reported. Psychosocial factors may also lead PWID to have lower adherence to long courses of oral anti-microbial therapy. Additional research is required to optimize the delivery of antimicrobial therapy for this challenging and vulnerable patient group.

### Prosthetic Joint Infections

Total joint replacement for advanced arthritis is one of the major advances in medicine in the 20th century and continues to improve in the 21st century. Infection of prosthetic joints is an uncommon but devastating complication of joint replacement surgery. More than 800,000 total knee arthroplasties (TKAs) and 450,000 total hip arthroplasties (THAs) were done in the United States in 2020. Arthroplasties are increasing, and projections are that nearly 4 million arthroplasties (3.5 million TKAs and 572, THAs) will be done each year in the United States by 2030. In addition to hip and knee arthroplasties, shoulder, elbow, and ankle replacements are becoming more common, particularly in patients with RA. The U.S. infection rate of arthroplasties is about 1% for knees and hips. I U.S. infection rate is higher for elbow (3.3%) and lower for shoulder (1.3%) arthroplasties compared with hip and knee arthroplasties.82, Infection rates are much higher in patients undergoing revision of a prosthetic joint compared with primary arthroplasty (3% for hips and 6% for knees). The risk of infection is approximately twofold higher in patients with RA compared with those with OA.

The risk of PJI is related to many factors. The most important risks for infection include (1) a diagnosis of osteonecrosis (hazard ratio [HR] 3.65), (2) a diagnosis of post-traumatic arthritis (HR 3.23), (3) male sex (HR 1.89), (4) an American Society of

Anesthesiologists score of 3 or more (HR 1.65), (5) body mass index (BMI) of 35 or more (HR 1.47), and (6) diabetes mellitus (HR 1.28). Surgical risk factors included quadriceps-release exposure (HR 4.76) and the use of antibiotic-laden cement (HR 1.53). Certain patient populations are at increased risk of infection because of comorbid conditions (e.g., diabetes mellitus and RA). Other risk factors include long operative time, use of disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs, and smoking 85-88 (see Table 112.6).

Orthopedic implants adversely affect host defenses. Prosthetic devices impair opsonic activity and diminish the ability of neutrophils to kill bacteria. PMN leukocytes release lysosomal enzymes and superoxide into the area surrounding the prosthesis, resulting in tissue damage and local devascularization. Phagocytes may be focused on removal of the foreign body such that fewer cells are available to fight infection. Finally, polymethylmethacrylate bone cement can inhibit neutrophil and complement functions, and the heat produced by the polymerization of polymethylmethacrylate can damage adjacent cortical bone and result in a devascularized necrotic area, which is ideal for bacterial growth. After implantation, prosthetic joints are immediately coated by host proteins, including albumin, fibrinogen, and fibronectin. S. aureus, which possesses numerous host protein-binding receptors (MSCRAMMs), is a common pathogen in infection of prosthetic joints. Patients with a prosthetic joint in whom S. aureus bacteremia develops have about a one in three chance of experiencing an infection of the implant.

Another phenomenon crucial to development of infection is the ability of organisms to form biofilms on the surface of the prosthetic device. A biofilm is defined as an assemblage of microbial cells that is irreversibly associated with a surface and enclosed in a matrix of primarily polysaccharide material. Organisms grow on indwelling medical devices, potable water system pipes, and living tissues. S. epidermidis is particularly adept at attaching to and forming biofilms on foreign bodies such as prosthetic joints. Small numbers of these organisms from the patient's skin or mucous membranes, or from the hands of the surgeons or clinical staff, contaminate and colonize the orthopedic device at the time of implantation. Staphylococcal surface proteins (SSP)-1 and SSP-2 are fimbria-like polymers that facilitate adherence of S. epidermidis to polystyrene. S. epidermidis produces a polysaccharide/adhesin substance crucial to the formation of this extra-cellular matrix91 (see e-Fig. 112.6). Polysaccharide/adhesin mutants

PJIs are divided into early onset (<3 months after placement), delayed (324 months post-surgery), and late onset (>24 months after placement). Early and delayed infections are usually related to surgical contamination at the time of the implantation, whereas late infections usually result from hematogenous seeding of the joint. Most infections occur within the first 2 years of implantation. Because of its high virulence, S. aureus accounts for most early and late infections. Small-colony variants of S. aureus may be responsible for persistent and recurrent infections of prosthetic implants. These subspecies of S. aureus are difficult to treat because they grow slowly and are relatively resistant to cell wall-active anti-microbial agents, anti-folate drugs (trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole), and aminoglycosides. There is some concern that the practice of using gentamicinimpregnated polymethylmethacrylate beads to treat PJIs may select for the small-colony variant species. Delayed infections are usually caused by less virulent microorganisms such as coagulase-negative staphylococci and C. acnes. Because these low-virulence organisms are common skin contaminants, it is important to interpret culture results carefully.

Clinically, the most common symptom in patients with PJI is pain of the affected joint. Differentiating pain from mechanical loosening of the prosthesis from pain related to infection can be difficult. Typically, a patient with mechanical loosening but no infection has pain only with motion, whereas a patient with infection experiences pain at rest and with motion. Warmth at the implant site, effusion, erythema, and fever are frequently associated with early and late, but not delayed, infections. This difference in clinical presentation likely represents the virulence of the most common organisms associated with the three categories of infection.

### Diagnosis

The presence of a sinus tract with purulent discharge suggests involvement of the implant and is an indication for removal of the prosthesis. In the absence of a sinus tract communicating with the prosthesis, the diagnosis of PJI rests upon a constellation of clinical features, serum and synovial fluid laboratory parameters, microbiological identification, histologic interpretation, and intraoperative findings. Different organizations have developed criteria to aid in the diagnosis of PJI, including most recently the 2018 International Consensus Meeting (ICM) criteria (see e-Fig. 112.7),94 the 2019 American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons guidelines, and the 2021 European Bone and Joint Society (EBJIS) criteria. The EBJIS criteria for diagnosis of PJI have been revised and are shown in Fig. 112.4.95

These definitions were compared in a single-center retrospective study,96 which found that the EBJIS definition in the preoperative setting had better performance in predicting definitive diagnosis after surgery, with fewer patients having an inconclusive diagnosis, compared with the 2013 Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA)97 and 2018 ICM definitions. Although recommendations vary somewhat across different guidelines in the specific laboratory evidence supportive of PJI, generally serum ESR and CRP remain first-line tools in the pre-operative setting.

The diagnosis of PJI can be challenging, particularly if there was prior exposure to antibiotic therapy. Specimens that have been studied and are adequate for diagnosis include serum, synovial

fluid, sonicate fluid, and periprosthetic tissue. Swabs of the joint have low sensitivity and should be avoided.

### Serum

Biomarkers that are useful from serum are WBC count, ESR, CRP, IL-6, procalcitonin, TNF, and more recently, D-dimer. These markers have different sensitivity and specificity (see Table 112.4). Most recent studies have shown that even though these markers can be elevated after surgery, IL-6 returns to normal within a few days after the surgery compared with CRP and ESR, which may remain elevated for 3 weeks and months, respectively. Although ESR and CRP are often elevated in chronic inflammatory conditions, such as RA, limited evidence suggests that no difference exists in the thresholds of ESR, CRP, or synovial fluid WBC count with differential to diagnose PJI in patients with and without inflammatory arthropathies. Other challenges to the interpretation of systemic biomarkers in suspected PJI arise in the setting of prior anti-microbial use"9 and infection with low-virulence microorganisms that elicit less inflammation.

Serum procalcitonin can be a useful marker with a specificity of 90% shown in a recent meta-analysis using a cutoff of >0.5 ng/ mL, although sensitivity was low at 46%. Sensitivity was further improved when a cutoff of >0.2 ng/mL was used. D-dimer, which is a product of fibrin degradation, has been shown to be elevated in infectious processes and to be a predictor of poor outcomes. The first prospective study that reported high sensitivity (89%) and specificity (93%) of serum D-dimer in PJIs was published by one group. The serum D-dimer test has promise as a marker for the diagnosis of PJI, although its utility is limited in patients with coagulation disorders and inflammatory arthritis. In the absence of these conditions, it is one of the most effective serum markers for the detection of PJI, although it is difficult to determine the optimal cutoff. While D-dimer has been included as a minor criterion in the 2018 ICM definition of PJI, additional investigation is required to establish a threshold for its use in the acute setting and further refine its role in the diagnosis of PJI.

### Synovial Fluid

Synovial fluid WBC counts of >3000/mm3 is part of the Musculoskeletal Infection Society (MSIS) criteria for PJI. Leukocyte esterase is also included in those criteria, although the test strips have not been evaluated for synovial fluid. Other important markers in synovial fluid are IL-6 and alpha-defensin; the latter is an anti-microbial peptide produced by neutrophils, which has been studied as an important marker of PJI in synovial fluid. Intraoperative alpha defensin with values above 5.2 mg/mL had a sensitivity and specificity >95%,5,103,104 and CRP at values >9.5 mg/L has a sensitivity of 85% and a specificity of 95%.

The final diagnosis is made with the identification of a pathogen through cultures or molecular testing. For PJIs, five to six samples (tissue, not swabs) from periprosthetic tissue should be collected for cultures. Per MSIS criteria, at least two specimens with positive cultures, with the same organism, is sufficient evidence of PJI. Like the synovial fluid cultures in native joint infection, inoculating periprosthetic tissue homogenates into blood culture bottles increased the sensitivity from 63% to 92%. As biofilm forms in prosthetic material, explanted prosthetic material can be sonicated to extract bacteria. Sonicated fluid culture has better sensitivity over periprosthetic tissue culture, of 95% to 100% when inoculated into blood culture bottles and 87% from agar culture media. The most common cutoff value used for sonicated cultures is >5 colony-forming units. Even though this technique has better

Molecular diagnostics are becoming more popular as promising diagnostic tools for the detection of PJIs, especially in culture-negative PJI, as these techniques can detect microbial genetic material from pathogens that would not grow on cultures due to exposure to antibiotics or because of the fastidious nature of the microorganisms. In a meta-analysis about NGS, its diagnostic accuracy for PJI, the detection rate for culture-negative PJI, and the detection rate for PJI with a history of antibiotic exposure were evaluated. The study found that in terms of the diagnostic value of NGs, the PPV was 71% to 100% and NPV was 74% to 95%. For culture-negative PJI, the detection rate in six of the studies was 82% to 100%, whereas three studies had a low rate of 9% to 31%. Differences in the specimen used might explain the low numbers. In patients that had antibiotic exposure prior to testing, the detection rate was 74% to 92%.5, Multiplex PCR is more sensitive than periprosthetic tissue culture and sonicated fluid culture in the setting of antibiotic exposure, although it has the limitation that it can only detect specific targets and it cannot identify other pathogens that are not part of the panel.5, Metagenomic sequencing evaluates DNA fragments allowing

identification utilizing a reference database (see e-Fig. 112.8). The advantages of targeted NGS include improved sensitivity and shorter turnaround time compared with shotgun NGS (sNGS), even though it has the disadvantage of not being able to identify microorganisms such as viruses, parasites, and fungi. For the identification of bacterial PJI, this is considered a helpful technique, identifying novel or atypical organisms causing PJIs. In this study, targeted NGS (tNGS) on samples of sonicated fluid were analyzed and compared with sonicate fluid culture, with further comparison between tNGS and sNGS. tNGS had a 72% positive percentage agreement compared with sonicate fluid culture, which was 52%. administration. The limitation of this technique is that it cannot differentiate between contamination, colonization, or an actual infection. There is growing evidence of the benefits of using NGS to detect rare pathogens including fastidious bacteria such as Mycoplasma hominis, Finegoldia magna, and Parvimonas micra, among others. When comparing NGS-based targeted antibiotic therapy for culture-negative PJI to empirical antibiotic therapy, the former had a higher efficacy and resulted in a better infection control rate, lower complications, and shorter duration of therapy. These technologies are expensive, and their use needs to be restricted to patients in whom routine cultures do not yield a microbiologic diagnosis. It is important to have collaboration among the orthopedic surgeon, the infectious diseases consultant, and the clinical microbiologist to determine the appropriate patient population for these technologies.

Serial plain radiographs may be helpful; the presence of subperiosteal bone growth and transcortical sinus tracts is specific for infection. Bone scans with technetium 99m—labeled methylene diphosphonate are sensitive but lack specificity because the bone scan is typically positive for 6 to 12 months after the original implantation. Bone scans may be a useful screening test for patients with suspected late PJI. CT has limitations because of the imaging artifacts caused by the metal implant. MRI can be performed only in patients with titanium or tantalum implants. IDSA guidelines do not recommend bone scans, leukocyte scans, MRI scans, CT scans, or positron-emission tomography for the routine management of PJI.

Medical therapy of patients with PJIs is challenging. Organisms existing in biofilms are much more resistant to anti-microbial agents for several reasons. Most anti-microbial agents penetrate the biofilm layer adequately but do not inhibit growth of bacteria within the biofilm matrix. Biofilm-associated organisms, including the small-colony variants of S. aureus, grow much slower (i.e., are in stationary-phase growth) than organisms in suspension. As a result, anti-microbial agents such as vancomycin, penicillins, and cephalosporins, which act on rapidly dividing organisms, are not effective in treating device-related infections. Rifampin and fluoroquinolones (particularly moxifloxacin) may be more effective because they are active against organisms in the stationary phase of growth. IDSA guidelines recommend rifampin in combination with another agent for the treatment of rifampinsusceptible strains of S. aureus. There is evidence that clinical outcomes are improved in patients receiving rifampin, although the data are based on retrospective analysis.109, The role of newer anti-staphylococcal antibiotics—such as linezolid, daptomycin, telavancin, ceftaroline, dalbavancin, oritavancin, and tigecycline—is unclear at this time. There is some evidence that oritavancin may be active against biofilm-associated small-colony variants of S. aureus.

Treatment of late PJIs is complex. In most patients, effective therapy requires a combination of antibiotics with the removal of the orthopedic device. Failure to remove the infected prosthesis is frequently associated with a high rate of relapse, probably related to biofilm formation on the orthopedic implant. Removal of the joint prosthesis, debridement of infected bone, and placement of a new prosthesis during the same operation have been associated with a high rate of recurrence of infection, but studies indicate that single-stage revision and debridement with retention of the prosthesis may be effective in certain situations. 113, Patients who have had symptoms of pain and swelling of the joint for less than 8 days or less than 3 weeks115 and who have a stable prosthesis with little soft tissue damage and no sinus tract are candidates

for debridement, antibiotics, and implant retention (DAIR) if the pre-operative synovial fluid cultures are negative or if the cultures grow an easily treatable organism (see Fig. 112.5).97,

The treatment of choice for most patients is a two-stage process involving removal of the infected prosthesis and debridement of infected bone, stabilization of the joint by using an antibiotic-impregnated methyl-methacrylate spacer, and 6 weeks of IV antibiotics (first stage), followed by reimplantation of a second orthopedic implant (second stage). Using this approach, the success rate is approximately 72% to 95%; the success rate is slightly higher for hip versus knee arthroplasties. Risk factors for treatment failure include prior joint revision, presence of lymphedema with infection, RA, presence of a sinus tract, and infection with MRSA. Rarely, antibiotic treatment is continued indefinitely in a patient in whom the risk of removing the infected prosthesis is too great, the prosthesis is not loose, and the organism responsible for the infection can be reasonably suppressed by the use of an oral antibiotic agent.

### Prevention

There is consensus that pre-operative evaluation of a patient for occult infection, such as periodontal disease, is warranted, and corrective steps to eradicate any infection are essential before joint replacement. The role of antibiotic prophylaxis to prevent late PJI before diagnostic or therapeutic procedures that lead to transient bacteremia, especially dental treatment, has been controversial. Two case-controlled studies determined that there was no increased risk of infection of prosthetic joints following lowor high-risk dental procedures. A large case-crossover study including 9427 late- PJI hospital admissions in England, where anti-microbial prophylaxis has never been recommended, found no temporal relationship between invasive dental procedures and subsequent development of late PJI. A position paper from the American Dental Association and the American Academy of Orthopedic Surgeons published in

2013 stated that there was no convincing evidence to support the routine use of prophylactic antibiotics in patients with prosthetic joints who undergo dental procedures.

The incidence of late infection of a prosthetic joint as a result of procedure-related bacteremia is extremely low—10 to 100 cases per 100,000 patients with total joint replacement per year. The cost of providing antibiotic prophylaxis to all patients with prosthetic joints before all procedures that are associated with transient bacteremia is substantial. The efficacy of such antibiotic prophylaxis is not proven. Cost-effective analyses had mixed results. These discrepancies are due to the lack of reliable data and the different assumptions used in the calculations. In the patient with the greatest risk of infection, an invasive procedure that leads to bacteremia can sometimes result in an infected prosthetic joint. Counseling these patients on the risks and benefits of antibiotic prophylaxis would lead to an informed decision on which the patient and the physician can agree.

There is also consensus that perioperative antibiotic prophylaxis significantly reduces the rate of early post-operative infection, and this practice is routine. The use of extended oral antibiotic prophylaxis following primary or revision arthroplasty has been increasingly investigated as a means to minimize the risk of infection in high-risk patients. Compared with historical controls, a 7-day post-operative course of oral antibiotics aimed at staphylococci and streptococci was associated with a decrease in infection of primary TKAs or THAs at 1-year follow-up in patients with broadly defined high-risk host features, including autoimmune diseases, chronic kidney disease, diabetes, smoking, nasal colonization with MSSA or MRSA, and obesity with BMI ≥35 kg/ m2.123 In a multicenter, randomized controlled trial with at least 2 years of follow-up of patients undergoing two-stage THA or TKA revision for infection, patients who received microorganismdirected oral anti-microbial therapy for 3 months post-operatively were found to have fewer joint infections than those who did . While promising, further research is necessary before this not. practice becomes the standard of care.

### Conclusion

Bacterial arthritis is a serious condition in patients with native joints or prosthetic joints. The number of patients with prosthetic joints is expected to reach 4 million by 2030. As such, there will be an increase in the number of PJIs. The increasing use of biologic agents in the field of rheumatology and other internal medicine areas will inevitably result in an increase in the number of infections in patients with native joints. There are new molecular testing modalities that will likely improve the ability to make quick and timely diagnoses in patients with bacterial arthritis. It will be incumbent upon all specialties (internists, hospitalists, rheumatologists, orthopedic surgeons, infectious diseases, and microbiologists) to collaborate to make management of patients with bacterial arthritis a seamless process.

# VAIDEHI R. CHOWDHARY AND LINDA K. BOCKENSTEDT

# Lyme Disease

### KEY POINTS

### Introduction

Lyme disease is a complex multisystem disorder caused by the tick-borne spirochete Borrelia burgdorferi. The disease first came to medical attention in the United States in the late 1970s with the investigation of a clustering of cases of juvenile arthritis in the region of Lyme, Connecticut. A characteristic skin rash, described as single or multiple expanding red macules, often heralded the onset of arthritis. This rash, termed erythema migrans (EM), had been linked in Europe to the bite of Ixodes ticks and the subsequent development of neurologic abnormalities. Further investigation revealed that arthritis was one manifestation of a systemic disorder affecting the skin, heart, joints, and nervous system. In 1982 Burgdorfer isolated the causative agent, the spirochete B. burgdorferi, from Ixodes ticks. Demonstration that antibodies to this organism developed in patients with Lyme disease and its eventual culture from skin and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) confirmed the infectious etiology of the disorder. It is now the most common vector-borne disease in the United States and Europe.

### Ecology and Epidemiology of Lyme e Disease

Lyme disease has a worldwide distribution, with most cases reported in North America, Europe, and Asia. On each of these continents, hard-shelled ticks of the Ixodes family are the only known vectors for the disease. Other arthropods and bloodsucking insects such as mosquitos cannot transmit the infection, and person-to-person transmission has not been documented. The incidence of Lyme disease varies geographically and is determined by the prevalence of B. burgdorferiinfected ticks. In the United States cases of Lyme disease have been reported in all 50 states and the District of Columbia, but most are clustered in the Northeast and mid-Atlantic region from Virginia to Maine and westward through Pennsylvania, the upper Midwest (Wisconsin and Minnesota), and foci in northern California, Oregon, and Washington state. Cases of Lyme disease outside these regions are mostly acquired after travel to highly endemic areas. More than 90% of U.S. cases reported to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) are from Connecticut, Delaware, Maine, Maryland, Minnesota, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New York, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, Vermont, Virginia, West Virginia, and Wisconsin. The number of reported cases underestimates the actual case incidence, which is estimated to be about 476,000 annually.

The spirochetes associated with Lyme disease reside within the genus B. burgdorferi sensu lato (sl), and the vast majority of cases are caused by B. burgdorferi sensu stricto (ss), Borrelia garinii, and Borrelia afzeli. All three genospecies can be found in Europe, whereas B. burgdorferi ss and rarely B. mayonii, a recently emerging species found only in the upper Midwest, are the only species causing Lyme disease in North America.6, Variation among the genospecies may account for the differences in clinical expression of Lyme disease between the two continents: B. garinii and B. afzelii are more commonly associated with neurologic disease and late skin involvement, respectively, whereas B. burgdorferi ss is associated with arthritis. B. mayonii species gives rise to atypical disseminated EM lesions and high levels of bacteremia. Because of the prominence of musculoskeletal manifestations with B. burgdorferi ss infection, this chapter focuses mainly on Lyme disease in North America.

### Ticks and Lyme Disease

Lyme disease is found primarily in temperate climates where an enzootic cycle maintaining B. burgdorferi in Ixodes ticks is established. Ixodes ticks have a 2-year life span in which they pass

through three developmental stages—larva, nymph, and adult— feeding only once per stage. B. burgdorferi is not passed transovarially and is maintained by passage between reservoir hosts and ticks. Small rodents are the main reservoirs for B. burgdorferi ss and B. afzelii, whereas birds are the principal haven for B. garinii.

Larvae acquire B. burgdorferi after feeding on an infected mammal in late summer and then molt to nymphs, which lay dormant until the following late spring and summer. The peak incidence of Lyme disease is in the summer months, when humans come in contact with questing nymphs. Engorged nymphs molt into adult ticks, which feed mainly on deer but are capable of transmitting infection to humans. B. burgdorferi does not persist in deer, which serve to maintain and propagate the tick population.

### Pathogenesis

### Borrelia burgdorferi Invasion of the Mammalian Host

The onset of tick feeding signals B. burgdorferi residing in the tick midgut to undergo global changes in gene expression, multiply, and migrate to the salivary glands, where they pass with saliva into the blood meal host.11, Relatively few spirochetes—estimated in the hundreds—are deposited at the bite site, a process that takes at least 24 hours.13-15 From the skin, spirochetes can disseminate via the blood and lymphatics to establish foci of infection elsewhere in the body. Spirochete virulence, growth conditions that allow persistence at a particular site, and host factors that modulate the inflammatory response determine disease expression. Clinical disease mainly involves the skin, heart, nervous system, and joints.

B. burgdorferi has no known virulence factors common to other bacterial pathogens.16, Its genome encodes an abundant array of putative lipoproteins, some of which play critical roles in spirochete colonization of its different hosts. Outer surface protein (Osp) A is a midgut adhesin required for spirochete infection of ticks.18, Osp C is essential for initial infection of the mammal but is dispensable after spirochetes have disseminated and colonized other tissues. To do so, B. burgdorferi harnesses host plasmin to move through tissues21,22 and expresses adhesins, including decorin-binding proteins A and B, BBK32, and p66, which allow it to bind to extra-cellular matrix (ECM) proteins and integrins on cells.23, B. burgdorferi expresses a protease with aggrecanase activity and induces the host expression of matrix metalloproteinases, which degrade ECMs. Expression of VlsE, an Osp that undergoes antigenic variation, is required for infection to persist.

### Pathology of Lyme Disease

With the exception of B. mayonii, which can be associated with visible bacteremia on blood smears,8 few spirochetes can be seen in infected tissues of patients with Lyme disease. Because B. burgdorferi secretes no known toxins, the host inflammatory response is believed to underlie the pathology seen in Lyme disease. Innate immune cells responding to the tick bite site orchestrate the inflammatory response and can kill spirochetes. By the time patients present with symptoms of Lyme disease, however, adaptive immune cells dominate tissue pathology.27, Histopathologic studies of EM lesions, cardiac tissue, synovial biopsy specimens, and limited nervous system tissue (meninges, spinal cord, and nerve roots) reveal varying degrees of monocytic and lymphoplasmacytic infiltrates, especially perivascular, that include

macrophages, T cells, and B cells. The proportions of responding immune cells differ among EM, CSF, and synovial fluid samples, suggesting a tissue-specific immune response to B. burgdorferi infection. Although neutrophils are apparent in EM lesions of less than 24 hours' duration, these cells diminish in number as the lesion matures, giving way to lymphoplasmacytic infiltrates associated with macrophages and dendritic cells.27, A lymphocytic pleocytosis is seen in CSF of patients with central nervous system (CNS) involvement, whereas synovial fluid exhibits elevated leukocyte counts with a predominance of neutrophils. Lyme arthritis synovium resembles that of rheumatoid arthritis (RA), with chronic inflammation mediated by mononuclear cell infiltration and pseudolymphoid follicles formed by T cells, B cells, and plasma cells. In the synovium and, less commonly, the epineural area, perivascular infiltrates can be associated with endarteritis obliterans.

### Immune Response to Borrelia burgdorferi

Host cell recognition of B. burgdorferi occurs mainly through engagement of the Toll-like receptor (TLR) family of pattern recognition receptors, especially TLR2/TLR1 heterodimers (lipoproteins), TLR5 (flagellin), TLR7 and TLR8 (RNA), and TLR9 (spirochete DNA). Activation of TLRs on innate immune cells results in the secretion of proinflammatory cytokines, including interleukin (IL)-1β, TNF, IL-2, IL-6, and type I and type II interferons, that recruit inflammatory cells to the site of infection. .31-36 Both TLR-dependent and non-TLR-dependent pathways induce matrix metalloproteinases that promote tissue injury and spirochete dissemination in murine models.33-35 Other pattern recognition receptors may be engaged by B. burgdorferi after its ingestion by phagocytes, including the intra-cellular NOD2 receptors, which respond to peptidoglycan and potentiate the inflammatory response in vitro and ex vivo.

Humoral immunity is a key host defense against B. burgdorferi infection. B. burgdorferi lipoproteins are B cell mitogens, and antibodies that arise in the absence of T cell help are sufficient to resolve inflammation and prevent challenge infection in the mouse model of Lyme disease.38, With the induction of adaptive immunity, B. burgdorferi-specific immunoglobulin (Ig)G helps clear spirochetes from infected tissues. In humans, IgG1 and IgG3 subclasses are dominant. Recent single-cell immunophenotyping of the B cell response in EM lesions revealed infiltrating memory B cells and plasma cells, with features suggesting both local antigen-presenting cell function and local antibody production. Some of these cells had clonal relatives in the circulation. IgG-containing immune complexes are concentrated in the joints of patients in whom Lyme arthritis develops, and it is likely that B cells and plasma cells in the synovium also contribute to local antibody production. The B cellrecruiting chemokine CXCL13 can be found in the CSF of patients with neuroborreliosis43; B cells constitute approximately 15% of the nucleated cells, an order of magnitude higher than in other infectious and inflammatory neurologic diseases. Intrathecal production of B. burgdorferi— specific antibodies is found and some of these antibodies can also bind neural antigens. 44-46

B. burgdorferi infection primes CD4+ and CD8+ T cells, and the predominance of interferon (IFN)-γ producing T helper (Th) 1 response correlates with more severe arthritis and neuroborreliosis.47, Th17 cells are also involved. In the CSF, T cells represent more than 60% of the responding cells, with CD4+ Th1 cells a majority; approximately half of patients with neurologic

involvement have elevated levels of IL-17 as well.49-51 B. burgdorferi neutrophil-activating protein A is abundant in synovial fluid and can elicit IL-17 from synovial fluid T cells ex vivo.52, EM lesions and synovial fluid also contain other T cell subsets, including CD25+Foxp3+ T cells, CD8+ T cells, γδ T cells, and natural killer (NK) T cells, which may regulate the inflammatory .27, B. burgdorferi induces dendritic cell production response. of indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase, an enzyme necessary for tryptophan catabolism that is also capable of promoting the differentiation of tolerogenic T cells that produce IL-10.57 In both mice and humans, elevated IL-10 levels appear to correlate with less severe disease.1,11

### Mechanisms of Spirochete Persistence

When visualized in vivo, B. burgdorferi resides primarily in the ECM in connective tissue.28, Despite occasional sightings of spirochetes inside cells,59 an intra-cellular phase of the B. burgdorferi life cycle has not been shown. B. burgdorferi uses immune evasion strategies of an extra-cellular pathogen, which are directed toward deterring phagocyte ingestion and antibodyand complementmediated lysis. B. burgdorferi proteins inhibit multiple components of the complement pathway. These include OspC and BBK32, which bind complement component C4b61 and C1q, 62 respectively, to inhibit the formation of C3 convertase, and Erp and complement regulator—acquiring surface proteins that bind host factor H63 and FH-like factor 1 to prevent complement-mediated lysis.64-66 B. burgdorferi infection in mice, a reservoir host, is associated with a delay in germinal center formation, thereby deterring specific antibody-mediated killing and interfering with the development of long-lived plasma cells that provide protective immunity from reinfection.67, To impede antibody-mediated clearance, B. burgdorferi undergoes antigenic variation26,69 and reduces expression of lipoproteins as infection progresses.' 70 The VlsE gene undergoes random rearrangement of its expression locus, producing antigenically distinct variants of VlsE.26, In the chronic phase of B. burgdorferi infection in mice, spirochetes can be visualized in the ECM of connective tissue, especially in the skin, without an associated inflammatory response.

### Clinical Features of Lyme Disease

Lyme disease occurs in stages that reflect the immune response to spirochetes as they establish infection in the skin and later disseminate to distant organ sites (Table 113.1). Presenting clinical manifestations depend on the stage of the illness in which patients first seek medical attention. A characteristic feature of Lyme disease is that clinical signs can resolve without specific therapy, and patients may be seen in later stages of the illness without exhibiting signs of early disease.

### Early Localized Infection

The hallmark of Lyme disease is the skin lesion EM, which is present in up to 80% of patients (Fig. 113.1). The lesion arises within 1 month (median, 7 to 10 days) at the tick bite site, which is often in skin folds or where clothes bind. In children, the tick bite site can also be around the hairline. EM begins as a red macule that expands at the rate of 2 to 3 cm/day, enlarging to more than 70 cm in diameter. Characteristic lesions greater than 5 cm in diameter in an appropriate clinical setting are sufficient for establishing the diagnosis of Lyme disease. EM most often

manifests with uniform erythema, but central clearing can occur in larger lesions, producing a "bull's-eye" or target appearance (see Fig. 113.1B). Vesicular, necrotic centers or nodular appearances are rarer (see Fig. 113.1D, F), but even these EM lesions have relatively few symptoms other than a tingling or burning sensation. Intense pruritus or pain is unusual and should raise concern for alternative diagnoses.

EM may be accompanied by systemic flulike symptoms, including low-grade fever, malaise, neck pain or stiffness, arthralgias, and myalgias.74, Particularly severe systemic symptoms such as high or persistent fever should alert the physician to possible co-infection with another tick-borne pathogen such as Babesia microti or Anaplasma phagocytophilum (the agent of human granulocytic anaplasmosis, formerly known as human granulocytic ebrlichiosis). Lyme disease can also manifest with systemic symptoms alone.77, Absence of upper respiratory or prominence of gastrointestinal symptoms may help distinguish Lyme disease from common viral infections; nausea and vomiting, however, can be seen in Lyme disease caused by B. mayonii. Musculoskeletal complaints and debilitating fatigue associated with Lyme disease should be distinguished from fibromyalgia

and chronic fatigue syndrome, which are typically more insidious in onset and are not associated with objective findings or laboratory abnormalities.

Southern tick—associated rash illness (STARI) can produce a skin lesion similar to the bull's-eye form of EM. STARI is associated with the bite of the Lone Star tick, Amblyomma americanum, which is endemic to the southeastern and southcentral states but also can be found as far north as Maine or west as central Texas and Oklahoma. Systemic symptoms of fever, headache, myalgias, and arthralgias can accompany the STARI rash, but extracutaneous disease does not occur. The etiology of STARI is unknown; studies indicate it is not caused by B. burgdorferi. STARI is often treated with antibiotics, but their role is unclear. Both EM and STARI lesions resolve with antibiotics, but STARI patients recover more quickly than patients with Lyme disease from systemic symptoms.

In Europe, a sign of early Lyme disease is the skin lesion Borrelia lymphocytoma (Fig. 113.2). This rare lesion, most often resulting from a B. afzelii infection, presents as a firm nodule, most often on the areola in adults (Fig. 113.2A) or the earlobe in children (Fig. 113.2B). Pathology reveals a polyclonal lymphocytic infiltrate often referred to as pseudolymphoma.

### Early Disseminated Infection

Disseminated B. burgdorferi infection occurs within weeks of the tick bite. At this stage, clinically apparent disease is usually seen in the skin, heart, or nervous system. Patients with disseminated infection often have debilitating fatigue and can appear ill. Specific localizing signs and symptoms may fluctuate, but fatigue is usually a consistent complaint.

### Skin Disease

Fifty percent of patients with untreated Lyme disease experience multiple EM lesions, a sign of disseminated infection (see Fig. 113.1C). Secondary lesions are typically smaller and can occur anywhere on the body, but they are most noticeable on the trunk. The lesions usually appear as flat macules and can develop partial central clearing. EM lesions may be accompanied by migratory muscle, joint, and periarticular pain that

lasts hours to days, but arthritis does not appear until months after the initial infection.

### Cardiac Disease −

Cardiac involvement is clinically apparent in less than 1% of patients with Lyme disease.81, It most often occurs within the first 2 months of infection (average 21 days) and manifests as varying degrees of atrioventricular block, occasionally accompanied by mild myopericarditis. Both atrial and ventricular arrhythmias can occur, and sudden death has been reported. Electrophysiologic studies have mapped the conduction defect to the area above the bundle of His and involving the atrioventricular node, although multiple levels can be affected. Overt congestive heart failure is rare, and chronic cardiomyopathy, reported in Europe, has not been documented in the United States. Patients with Lyme carditis often have a history of EM and may have concomitant arthralgia and myalgia at the time of presentation. Absence of valvular heart disease helps distinguish Lyme carditis from acute rheumatic fever, and prominent myocardial dysfunction or pericardial involvement should suggest other infectious etiologies.

### Nervous System Involvement

Acute neurologic Lyme disease occurs in less than 10% of patients and most commonly manifests as cranial nerve palsy or meningitis. Although alterations in memory and cognitive function can occur in the setting of disseminated Lyme disease, such symptoms are most likely a consequence of systemic inflammation rather than actual CNS infection.76, Parenchymal CNS involvement (encephalomyelitis) is rare in the United States; the largest case series of U.S. patients with neurologic Lyme disease in whom brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was performed revealed that findings of scattered white-matter lesions occurred at a frequency similar to age-matched controls, suggesting that these are nonspecific. Other rare manifestations include ischemic stroke and cerebral vasculitis, which are primarily reported in Europe. 88,

Cranial palsy occurs in 9% of reported cases of Lyme disease and is the most common neurologic manifestation. The seventh nerve is most frequently affected, resulting in unilateral or bilateral facial palsy. Even in endemic areas, however, onset of seventh nerve palsy in the nonwinter months is caused by B. burgdorferi

infection in only 25% of cases. Bilateral facial palsy is seen in only a few other conditions—Guillain-Barré syndrome, HIV infection, sarcoidosis, and other causes of chronic meningitis—all of which are readily distinguishable from Lyme disease. Rarely, other cranial nerves (III, IV, V, VI, or VIII) may be involved. Lyme radiculopathy occurs in 4% of cases and typically manifests as pain, weakness, numbness, and reflex loss in a dermatomal distribution, resembling mechanical radiculopathies. Untreated Lyme radiculopathy can progress to become bilateral, which helps distinguish it from mechanical disease. When truncal involvement causes unilateral chest or abdominal pain, Lyme radiculopathy is often mistaken for visceral disease or early herpes zoster before the development of vesicular lesions.91, Lyme meningitis manifests with fever, headache, and stiff neck similar to viral meningitis, along with a CSF lymphocytosis and elevated protein. In children, Lyme meningitis can cause increased intracranial pressure (papilledema), which is rare in adults.94,95

### Other Organ System Involvement

A variety of other organs can exhibit pathology with disseminated B. burgdorferi infection, including the eye (keratitis, uveitis, papillitis), the ear (sensorineural hearing loss), the liver (hepatitis), the spleen (necrosis), skeletal muscle (myositis), and subcutaneous tissue (panniculitis). In general, more classic manifestations of Lyme disease are present concurrently or have been present in the recent past to suggest the diagnosis.

### Late Disease

Months after the onset of infection, untreated patients can develop late manifestations of Lyme disease, usually involving the joints (discussed separately later), nervous system, and the skin. At this stage of infection, two-tier serologic testing (enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay [EIA] and IgG immunoblot) for B. burgdorferi should be positive.

### Late Neurologic Disease −

Late neurologic Lyme disease is now rare; patients may be seen with encephalomyelitis, peripheral neuropathy, or encephalopathy. 97-99 Encephalomyelitis, seen predominantly in Europe with B. garinii infection, is a slowly progressive, unifocal, or multifocal inflammatory disease of the CNS, with increased T2 signals in the white matter on MRI. CSF examination often reveals a lymphocytic pleocytosis, elevated protein, and normal glucose; serum B. burgdorferi—specific IgG and intrathecal production of B. burgdorferi IgG can also be found. These findings help distinguish Lyme encephalomyelitis from multiple sclerosis, which may rarely be associated with positive IgG reactivity to B. burgdorferi in serum and CSF samples but without intrathecal antibody production.100, Multiple sclerosis patients with positive Lyme serologies do not respond to antibiotics used for neurologic Lyme disease, and routine testing for Lyme disease in patients who present with multiple sclerosis symptoms is not recommended.

Late peripheral nervous system involvement manifests as a mild sensorimotor neuropathy in a "stocking and glove" distribution, with evidence of a mild confluent mononeuritis multiplex on electrophysiologic studies.91, Patients may have intermittent limb paresthesias and occasionally radicular pain. The most common finding on physical examination is reduced vibratory sensation in the lower extremities. Serum IgG to B. burgdorferi should be present, but CSF examination is normal. Patients with this form of neuropathy should be evaluated for other infectious

B 12

Although late Lyme encephalopathy was reported in the 1980s, it is now rare. Patients complain of memory impairment and cognitive dysfunction that are best shown by formal neuropsychological testing.99, Occasionally, CSF examination can reveal elevated protein, lymphocytic pleocytosis, and intrathecal antibody to B. burgdorferi, but it can also be normal. Serum IgG to B. burgdorferi should be present, however, to consider the diagnosis. The mild cognitive dysfunction seen in patients with Lyme encephalopathy must be distinguished from neurocognitive deficits secondary to chronic stress, sleep deprivation, fibromyalgia, chronic fatigue syndrome, or aging. As for any chronic encephalopathy, toxic-metabolic causes should be excluded. Brain imaging studies are generally normal or show only nonspecific abnormalities and are not useful in establishing a diagnosis of encephalopathy associated with Lyme disease.

### Late Skin Disease

The late skin lesion acrodermatitis chronica atrophicans (ACA) is found mainly in Europe because of its association with B. afzelii infection, although any B. burgdorferi species can cause the lesion. ACA develops insidiously over years and is most often found on an extremity (Fig. 113.3). It begins as a unilateral bluish red discoloration and swelling (Fig. 113.3A), which evolves to atrophic, cellophane-like skin with prominent appearance of the blood vessels (Fig. 113.3B). Allodynia is considered a characteristic feature of the skin lesion. Approximately 60% of patients also have a peripheral sensory neuropathy affecting the involved extremity. A prominent lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate is shown on the skin biopsy specimen. Antibiotics can lead to improvement in pain and swelling, but atrophic skin remains.

### Lyme Arthritis and Other Musculoskeletal Manifestations s of Lyme Disease

Musculoskeletal symptoms are common in all stages of Lyme disease and include migratory pain in joints, tendons, bursae, and muscles.1, Typically, musculoskeletal pain affects one or two sites at a time, lasts only hours to a few days at any one location, and can be associated with significant fatigue. Although an early study reported that frank arthritis occurred in 60% of patients with untreated EM, the annual reported incidence has been around 30% for several decades.104, EIA and IgG immunoblot for B. burgdorferi are positive when arthritis appears, and B. burgdorferi DNA can be detected by polymerase chain reaction (PCR) in synovium and synovial fluid, even though cultures are negative. Although Lyme arthritis can resemble pauciarticular juvenile arthritis or reactive arthritis, patients generally test negative for anti-nuclear antigen (ANA), rheumatoid factor, and anti-citrullinated protein antibodies and do not have an increased frequency of human leukocyte antigen (HLA)-B27 alleles. Joint fluid analysis and synovial histopathology cannot distinguish these entities. Axial and sacroiliac joint involvement is not a feature of Lyme disease, but enthesitis can be seen.

Arthritis usually begins months or years after B. burgdorferi infection (average 6 months) and is pre-dated by migratory arthralgias in half of patients. b The most typical pattern is a monoarticular or oligoarticular arthritis involving one or a few large joints (≤5 total), with the knee affected in 80% of cases. Joints are warm

with large effusions, often greater than 100 mL in the knee, but there is comparatively little pain. Large effusions can lead to Baker's cyst formation and rupture. Other joints commonly affected include the shoulder, ankle, elbow, wrist, and temporomandibular joint. Synovial fluid is inflammatory with a predominance of neutrophils. Synovial fluid cell counts tend to be higher in children (range 46,000 to 60,000/mm3) and somewhat lower in adults (median ~25,000/mm3), although occasionally counts of ≥100,000/mm3 are seen.76,106Synovial histopathology resembles that seen in other inflammatory arthritis with marked synovial fibroblast proliferation, fibrosis, and mononuclear cell infiltration along the synovial lining and sublining. A unique feature of Lyme arthritis is an obliterative microvascular lesion reminiscent of the vasculopathy seen in tertiary syphilis. Children with Lyme arthritis may present more acutely with fever and a painful, swollen joint resembling septic arthritis. In areas endemic for Lyme disease, however, this presentation is more likely due to B. burgdorferi infection than to septic arthritis in the absence of other risk factors for the latter. The joints in Lyme arthritis are not as exquisitely tender as seen in septic arthritis. A clinical prediction rule (absolute neutrophil count of 10,000 cells/mm3 or greater and an ESR of 40 mm/h of greater) had a sensitivity of 100% and specificity of 68.1% to distinguish septic arthritis from Lyme arthritis in the pediatric emergency setting. Lyme arthritis is often intermittent, with episodes lasting a few weeks to months. Recurrent episodes are notable for smaller effusions and progressive synovial hypertrophy, bony erosion, and cartilage destruction. A small percentage (<10%) of patients with intermittent arthritis settle into a pattern of chronic arthritis, typically affecting only a single joint. Inflammation of a single joint that persists for more than 12 months or prominent involvement of small joints would be unusual presenting manifestations of Lyme arthritis.

The natural history of Lyme arthritis suggests that it is a selflimited disorder. In the late 1970s, before the use of antibiotics for Lyme disease, 21 patients who were seen with EM and later diagnosed with Lyme arthritis were followed for 1 to 8 years without anti-microbial therapy. Six patients had only a single

episode of arthritis, and the remaining 15 had recurrent episodes that decreased in frequency during the study period. On average, the number of patients who continued to experience episodes of arthritis decreased by 10% to 20% each year. Similar results were found in children in whom antibiotic treatment for arthritis was delayed 4 years.

### Post-infectious Lyme Arthritis

Approximately 10% of patients treated with standard antibiotic regimens for Lyme arthritis have persistent joint inflammation and proliferative synovitis that does not respond to further antimicrobial therapy. The pathogenesis of "post-infectious" Lyme arthritis (previously called "antibiotic-refractory" or "post-antibiotic" Lyme arthritis) is unknown, but persistent infection is considered unlikely. Current theories center on the development of a dysregulated inflammatory response, possibly related to initial virulence of the infecting spirochete strain, inefficient clearance of B. burgdorferi remnants and host inflammatory debris, and infection-induced autoimmunity. Spirochete strains that have a greater propensity to become blood-borne have been found at higher rates in patients with post-infectious Lyme arthritis. 113,

A single-nucleotide polymorphism in TLR1 (TLR1 1805 GG) was associated with heightened inflammatory responses to spirochete strains with greater disseminating potential; its greater prevalence among patients who develop post-antibiotic Lyme arthritis suggests that in certain people, high levels of IFN-γ accompanied by inadequate levels of IL-10 in infected joints could set the stage for persistent synovitis after infection is cleared. Although spirochete DNA can be detected in synovial fluid for months after treatment, its presence does not predict arthritis relapse rate or per- . Experiments in the mouse model of Lyme borreliosis sistence. revealed that spirochete debris, including B. burgdorferi DNA, can persist near cartilage and in the entheses for extended periods after infectious spirochetes have been killed with antibiotics, particularly when the initial pathogen burden was high. B. burgdorferi peptidoglycan has been proposed as a persistent bacterial antigen

that could perpetuate inflammation after bacterial killing. In addition, deficiency in the lysosomal enzyme β-glucuronidase (GusB) underlies the genetic susceptibility of the C3H mouse strain to more severe Lyme arthritis and also exacerbates arthritis in a serum transfer model of inflammatory arthritis. GusB functions to degrade glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) that are produced in higher abundance during inflammation. GAGs directly activate TLRs, and their accumulation could potentiate and prolong inflammation.

A genetic predisposition to post-infectious Lyme arthritis had been suggested in earlier studies that found an association with the RA-related alleles HLA-DRB1*0401, HLA-DRB1*0101, and HLA-DRB1*0404, raising the possibility that post-infectious Lyme arthritis resulted from infection-induced autoimmunity. Although an Osp A peptide that can be presented by these HLA molecules was initially thought to contribute to post-infectious Lyme arthritis through molecular mimicry with human leukocyte function—associated antigen 1, this theory has fallen out of favor.121-123 Linked T and B cell responses to four self-proteins—epidermal cell growth factor (ECGF), MMP10, apolipoprotein B100, and annexin A2—that have no homology to B. burgdorferi proteins have been found in patients with Lyme arthritis and are more abundant in those with post-infectious Lyme arthritis.41, IgG responses to these four autoantigens are mainly of the IgG2 and IgG4 subclasses, in contrast to those directed at B. burgdorferi, which are mainly IgG1 and IgG3.41,

Synovial fluid IgG4 levels of three autoantigens (ECGF, MMP10, and apolipoprotein B-100) correlated with the degree of synovial obliterative microvascular lesions and fibrosis.41, Alterations in regulation of the immune response have been reported. CD25+FoxP3+ T regulatory cells are reduced in number in the synovial fluid of patients with post-infectious Lyme arthritis. 54, Invariant NK T cells, which may have immunomodulatory properties, were notably absent in one study. Deficiencies in these regulatory cells could set the stage for synovial fibroblasts to evolve into an inflammatory phenotype, as has been found when fibroblast-like synoviocytes from patients with post-infectious Lyme arthritis are exposed to IFN-γ ex vivo. Elevated levels of microRNAs that post-transcriptionally modulate inflammatory gene expression, including miR-155, miR-223, and miR- 146a, were found in patients with post-infectious Lyme arthritis. If autoimmunity is responsible, it must eventually succumb to immune regulation because even this form of Lyme arthritis generally resolves within 4 to 5 years, or sooner with the use of disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs.1,104

### Diagnosis

The diagnosis of Lyme disease should be considered in individuals who are seen with an appropriate clinical history and who have a reasonable risk of exposure to B. burgdorferiinfected ticks (Fig. 113.4).76, Supporting serologic evidence is necessary to secure

the diagnosis at all stages of infection except when EM is present or, in the setting of immunosuppression, direct detection of B. burgdorferi by culture or detection of its DNA by PCR. Routine laboratory tests are nonspecific, with some patients exhibiting mildly elevated white blood cell (neutrophil) counts, erythrocyte sedimentation rates, and liver function tests. Findings of thrombocytopenia, leukopenia, neutropenia, anemia, and/or elevated indirect bilirubin levels should raise concern for co-infection with B. microti or A. phagocytophilum or an alternative diagnosis. Microscopic visualization of spirochetes in clinical samples is not sensitive enough for routine use in diagnosis.

### Culture

B. burgdorferi is difficult to culture from clinical specimens. 76, Culture of a skin biopsy specimen taken from the leading margin of an EM lesion is an exception, with B. burgdorferi detected in more than 40% of samples. The rate of positivity of culture of any other tissue or body fluid specimen is too low to recommend culture as a routine diagnostic test for Lyme disease. The validity of a novel serum culture assay for detecting B. burgdorferi in blood samples has been questioned and should not be used.

### Serologic Testing

Serologic assays that detect B. burgdorferi-specific antigens make up the only U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) cleared or approved diagnostic tests for Lyme disease.131, Presence of antibodies to B. burgdorferi at best indicates previous exposure to the organism, however, and should not be considered evidence of active infection. Earlier studies in endemic areas found that ~5% of people had asymptomatic IgG seroconversion to B. burgdorferi; this estimate may be higher now. 133-135 After antibiotic therapy, serum IgM and IgG titers to B. burgdorferi generally decrease slowly but can remain positive for years. 136-138 Repeat serologic testing is not recommended as a means for assessing response to treatment.

The CDC recommends a two-test approach to maximize clinical utility as no single serologic test is sensitive or specific on its 139, The standard two-tier serologic testing (sTTT) consists own. of an EIA or an indirect immunofluorescence antibody assay to detect IgM and IgG reactivity to B. burgdorferi as an initial screening test, followed by an immunoblot (Western blot) to confirm that positive or equivocal results are the result of antibodies that bind B. burgdorferi antigens. EIA and immunofluorescence assays are highly sensitive tests but lack specificity because of the cross-reactivity of antibodies induced by other bacterial pathogens with B. burgdorferi. A positive or equivocal EIA or immunofluorescence assay should be confirmed by IgM or IgG immunoblot analysis of B. burgdorferi proteins. Banding patterns characteristic of early infection include antibodies to the 41 kilodalton (kDa) flagellin protein and Osp C. With disseminated infection, and especially with late Lyme disease, IgG reactivity to an expanding array of B. burgdorferi proteins can be seen.136, A drawback to the sTTT is that the interpretation of Lyme immunoblots is subjective and weak bands, especially on the IgM immunoblot, can erroneously be scored, leading to a false-positive result. Many patients and healthy individuals have bands on immunoblots that do not meet criteria for a positive result but can create confusion for patients and health care providers. A positive IgM immunoblot alone (in the absence of a positive IgG immunoblot) should not be used as evidence of active disease in patients with illness greater than 1 month. The rationale for the "1-month rule"

is that most patients with active, untreated infection for >1 month should have a positive IgG response. Positive IgM serologies alone after 1 month of illness are most often false-positive tests, which occur in the setting of other infectious diseases (especially infectious mononucleosis and other spirochetal and tick-borne infections), RA (with or without rheumatoid factor), and conditions associated with a positive ANA (systemic lupus erythematosus). The sTTT has overall sensitivities of 25% in EM during the acute phase; 55% for EM in the convalescent phase; and greater than 95% in neurologic, arthritis, and other manifestations of late disease phase. 76,

In an effort to develop more sensitive and specific serologic assays for early Lyme disease, peptide-based assays have been developed, most often involving invariant regions of the OspC and VlsE proteins. The C6 (IR6) peptide-based EIA uses a highly conserved invariant region of the VlsE protein.131, As a single assay, the C6 peptide EIA has increased sensitivity but slightly lower specificity in early infection compared with the whole-cell lysate EIA.

To enhance specificity, a modified two-tiered serologic testing (mTTT) algorithm is now available as an alternative strategy to the sTTT.132, This approach utilizes two different EIA sequentially or concurrently and provides a categorical result (positive, negative, or equivocal) in each tier, thereby eliminating the need for immunoblot confirmation. The assay can also be performed more quickly than the sTTT. One limitation of the mTTT approach is that it does not provide the detailed information about antibody reactivity with the broad array of spirochete proteins that can be detected on immunoblot, although in practice, health care providers generally rely on laboratory reporting of immunoblot positivity to support a diagnosis of Lyme disease.

Some commercial laboratories have developed assays using recombinant antigens or use criteria for the interpretation of immunoblots that have not been validated. For this reason, the CDC advises using only validated tests cleared or approved by the FDA for serologic diagnosis of Lyme disease.

### Antibodies to Borrelia burgdorferi in Cerebrospinal Fluid

Serum antibody testing for Lyme disease by two-tier methodology is usually positive when patients present with Lyme neuroborreliosis and is the preferred testing method when considering that diagnosis.76, Intrathecal antibody production to B. burgdorferi is a highly specific test for CN Lyme disease.145, Positive tests are more commonly found in European neuroborreliosis than in North American Lyme disease, which may be the result of the higher association of B. garinii in CNS infection than B. burgdorferi ss. Intrathecal antibody production is measured by performing EIA using paired CSF and serum specimens to evaluate the ratio of B. burgdorferi—specific IgG in CSF and serum. A limitation to the use of this test is that methods have not been standardized across laboratories, and measurement of B. burgdorferi—reactive antibodies in the CSF without a concomitant serum sample or assessment of antibody production by immunoblot can be misleading. Furthermore, antibodies to B. burgdorferi may persist in CSF after treatment for Lyme disease and should not be used to assess efficacy of therapy. 76,146

### Polymerase Chain Reaction

PCR has been used to detect B. burgdorferi DNA in a variety of clinical specimens with variable success. The greatest utility

of PCR clinically is in Lyme arthritis, where its sensitivity for detection of B. burgdorferi DNA is 85% (range 40%96%). Although patients with Lyme arthritis have strong IgG responses to B. burgdorferi at the time of presentation, seropositivity at best indicates previous exposure to the organism and cannot distinguish past infection from current infection. In this situation, a positive synovial PCR test can be used to support a diagnosis of acute Lyme arthritis. Sensitivity of PCR is lower than serologic testing and synovial PCR is generally considered when there is a known history of Lyme disease in the past that has been treated with antibiotics or in the case of immunosuppression when patients may be unable to mount the appropriate antibody responses (see "Lyme Disease in the Immunosuppressed Host" section). Synovial PCR can remain positive for weeks to months after successful treatment and therefore even this test should not be equated with active infection in all instances. B. burgdorferi DNA can generally no longer be detected by PCR after 1 month of intravenous (IV) antibiotics or 2 months of oral antibiotics.

The sensitivity of PCR for detecting B. burgdorferi DNA in other body fluids (blood and CSF) is low.132, PCR of urine specimens is not recommended because of documented nonspecific amplification of nonB. burgdorferi DNA targets.

PCR testing is useful for establishing exposure to B. burgdorferi, but positive results are not necessarily a reflection of active infection because B. burgdorferi DNA can persist for months after spirochetes are killed with antibiotics in vitro and in vivo. There are currently no FDA-approved tests for PCR-based molecular techniques for detecting B. burgdorferi DNA in patient specimens.

### Other Laboratory Tests

A urine antigen test, immunofluorescent staining for cell wall— deficient forms of B. burgdorferi, lymphocyte transformation assays, or quantitative CD57 lymphocyte assays are offered by some commercial laboratories to aid in the diagnosis of Lyme disease. These tests have not been adequately validated for accuracy or clinical usefulness and should not be used.

### Imaging

Imaging studies have a limited role in the evaluation of patients with Lyme disease because no feature is sufficiently distinctive to confirm the diagnosis. Plain radiographs of arthritic joints show changes consistent with an inflammatory arthropathy, including joint effusions, synovial hypertrophy, and periarticular osteoporosis; with advanced duration of arthritis, cartilage loss, bony erosions, and calcified entheses can be seen. MRI of arthritic joints can confirm the radiographic findings and reveal associated myositis and adenopathy, which may be useful in distinguishing Lyme arthritis from septic arthritis in children. An ultrasound study found prominent hamstring involvement in patients with Lyme arthritis involving the knee.

Cranial and spinal MRI findings in neuroborreliosis can reveal focal nodular lesions or patchy white-matter lesions on T2-weighted images, consistent with inflammatory or demyelinating processes.87, These lesions typically resolve after treatment for Lyme disease, in some cases only after several years. Nonspecific findings of small white-matter lesions reported in Lyme neuroborreliosis are indistinguishable from those commonly seen in patients with risk factors for vascular disease and occur at the same frequency as in patients without Lyme disease.76, Positron-emission tomography and single-photon emission CT

studies are often normal or show only nonspecific changes with subcortical and cortical hypoperfusion. 156,157

### Treatment

Guidelines for the clinical assessment (Fig. 113.5) and treatment (Table 113.2) of Lyme disease have been updated. Because many of the manifestations of Lyme disease resolve without specific therapy, the goal of antibiotic treatment is to hasten resolution of signs and symptoms and to prevent later clinical manifestations. Generally, oral antibiotics are the recommended initial therapy for most manifestations of Lyme disease, except parenchymal involvement of the brain or spinal cord and Lyme carditis requiring hospitalization. Disseminated infection and late manifestations of Lyme disease may require longer courses of antibiotics, and there is often a greater lag time to symptom resolution compared with early disease. Optimal antibiotic choice and duration of treatment have not been determined for patients who have underlying disorders requiring B celldepleting therapies or chemotherapy.

Doxycycline is the antibiotic of choice in nonpregnant adults and children age 8 years and older because it is also effective against A. phagocytophilum, which may occur concomitantly with early Lyme disease. In European studies, doxycycline is the only oral antibiotic that is as equally effective as parenteral antibiotics in the treatment of acute neurologic disease without parenchymal CNS involvement.158, Amoxicillin and cefuroxime axetil are acceptable alternatives for the treatment of EM, facial palsy, and other nonneurologic manifestations of Lyme disease. Macrolide antibiotics are less effective than other anti-microbials and should be used only in individuals who cannot take doxycycline, amoxicillin, or cefuroxime axetil. First-generation cephalosporins are not effective therapy for Lyme disease.

Parenteral antibiotic therapy is an alternative choice over oral doxycycline for patients with acute neurologic disease manifesting as Lyme meningitis, cranial neuropathy, or radiculoneuropathy. The decision to use parenteral antibiotics should be based on individual factors because oral doxycycline is effective in this situation when patients are not on concomitant B celldepleting therapies. If parenteral antibiotics are administered initially, the course can be completed with oral doxycycline. Documented parenchymal brain or spinal cord disease should be treated with parenteral therapy. Ceftriaxone administered intravenously for 2 to 4 weeks is the preferred parenteral anti-microbial, 160 although parenteral cefotaxime and penicillin G are acceptable alternatives. Repeat treatment is not recommended for chronic neurologic abnormalities unless objective signs of relapse are present.

Patients with symptomatic cardiac involvement (chest pain, shortness of breath, syncope) or with significant conduction system disease (first-degree atrioventricular block with P-R intervals ≥ 0.3 msec or second-degree or third-degree block) should be hospitalized for cardiac monitoring and IV antibiotic therapy. Consultation with a cardiologist is recommended, and placement of a temporary pacemaker may be necessary. Oral antibiotics can be substituted for IV antibiotics when there is clinical improvement to complete the course of therapy.

For arthritis, a 28-day course of oral doxycycline or amoxicillin is recommended as initial therapy. The rate of arthritis resolution varies, with ~25% of patients exhibiting mild residual joint swelling after a first course of antibiotics. It is unclear whether an additional course of oral antibiotics for mild joint swelling is beneficial over observation alone or adjunctive therapy with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) or intra-articular

corticosteroids. Although intra-articular corticosteroids may be associated with a higher rate of persistent synovitis if instituted before antibiotic therapy, their use once antibiotic therapy has commenced can accelerate resolution of inflammation and reduce the incidence of post-infectious Lyme arthritis in children.76,

For patients with moderate-to-severe joint swelling after a 28-day course of oral antibiotics, IV ceftriaxone for 2 to 4 weeks

can be used. Alternatively, a second course of oral therapy can also be considered depending on other factors, including patient preferences. Longer courses of antibiotics for unresolved inflammation provide no additional benefit. In this situation, NSAIDs, intra-articular corticosteroids, and/or hydroxychloroquine are recommended for treatment of post-infectious Lyme arthritis. In patients who do not respond to this approach, other DMARDs

such as methotrexate and TNF inhibitors have been used with success. Arthroscopic synovectomy can be curative in two-thirds of patients who do not respond to medical management.

### Special Considerations

### Pregnancy and d Lyme Disease

Pregnant and lactating women with Lyme disease can be treated with the same antibiotic regimens recommended for nonpregnant patients except that doxycycline should be avoided. Maternalfetal transmission of B. burgdorferi can occur but, in contrast to syphilis in pregnancy, there is no evidence that the organism causes a congenital syndrome. Pregnant patients should be reassured that with recommended therapy for Lyme disease, B. burgdorferi infection in the mother causes no harm to the fetus.

### Lyme Disease in the Immunocompromised Host

Immunosuppressed individuals pose unique challenges to the diagnosis and management of Lyme disease. For individuals who reside or who have recently traveled to endemic areas, a history of tick bites and skin rashes suggestive of EM should raise suspicion for Lyme disease. Several case-control studies have been published from a single European center on the course and outcome of EM in individuals on TNF inhibitor therapy, chemotherapy for malignancies, or after solid organ transplantation. 165-168 Patients receiving TNF inhibitor therapy had a shorter time from tick bite to the onset of EM (median 7.5 vs. days), smaller diameter of lesions (median 10.5 cm vs. 15.5 cm), and more frequent signs of disseminated infection (18.8% vs. 0%). No differences were noted in presence of serum IgM and/or IgG antibodies against Borrelia in patients receiving TNF inhibitors compared with a control group (42.9% vs. 51.7%). Treatment failure, most often described as persistence of EM for more than 2 months after a first course of antibiotic therapy, was found more frequently in those on TNH inhibitor therapy (4/16, 25% vs. 0%), especially when immunosuppression was continued while antibiotics were administered, but resolved with a second course of therapy. Patients with EM and hematologic malignancies, especially those with lymphoid neoplasm, more often had signs of disseminated Lyme disease or treatment failure, especially in those receiving active chemotherapy. 167, Patients receiving rituximab had higher rates of disseminated Lyme disease (43% vs. 8%) and positive borrelial blood cultures (40% vs. <2%) compared with a historical cohort of immunocompetent patients presenting with EM from the same 166 Lower rates of B. burgdorferi antibodies were noted center. among patients receiving rituximab versus the historical controls (29% vs. 65%). Treatment failure was reported in one in seven patients whose EM lesion persisted for >2 months but responded to retreatment with another antibiotic. Nevertheless, the outcome of early Lyme disease after 1 year was excellent in all patients.

Patients with solid organ transplant and immunosuppression had a smooth course of illness and favorable outcome but remained seronegative at 1 year. In another case-control study, a heterogenous group of patients presenting with EM who had autoimmune diseases, chronic infection, or organ transplantation requiring immunosuppressive therapy was compared with immunocompetent individuals matched for age, sex, and antibiotic treatment. No differences in response to therapy, production of anti-B. burgdorferi antibodies, or clinical outcomes were found.

There are now several case reports of seronegative Lyme neuroborreliosis in patients receiving rituximab therapy alone or in combination with chemotherapy, most often in the context of lymphoid malignancies. Typical presentations involved the nervous system with meningoradiculitis or meningoencephalitis and exhibited CSF lymphocytic pleocytosis with negative serum and CSF borrelial antibodies. The diagnosis was often delayed because of initial suspicion for relapse of their underlying malignancy. Residence in a Lyme-endemic area and/or a history of prior tick bites raised suspicion for neuroborreliosis. The diagnosis can be supported by a positive PCR for B. burgdorferi sl DNA in CSF and resolution of signs and symptoms after empiric treatment with ceftriaxone. Although B. burgdorferi PCR on CSF samples from immunocompetent hosts with neuroborreliosis is insensitive (10%30%), these cases illustrate that this may not be true for patients receiving B celldepleting immunotherapies. It is also important to remember that co-infections that can be seen with Lyme disease, especially babesiosis, have significant morbidity and mortality in those with asplenia or functional B cell deficiency due to congenital immunodeficiency or anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody therapy.
