Judicious testing to exclude other tick-borne disease should be considered.

### Outcomes

Most patients treated for Lyme disease, including those who are on immunosuppressive therapies, resolve the disease with recommended courses of antibiotics. Some patients may experience a Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction, a self-limited worsening of symptoms within 24 to 48 hours of initiation of antibiotic therapy. Within the first week of treatment, patients may rarely show evolution of disease, such as the development of new EM lesions or facial nerve palsy, but these signs should improve as therapy progresses. In one study of immunocompetent hosts, EM that recurred after completion of antibiotic therapy for Lyme disease was found to be due to reinfection rather than relapse of a partially treated initial infection. The onset of noninfectious autoimmune arthritis (RA, psoriatic arthritis, or spondylitis) has been reported after an episode of Lyme disease diagnosed in an early stage of infection. Patients with Lyme arthritis most often resolve joint inflammation with antibiotic therapy, and the minority who experience post-infectious Lyme arthritis can be successfully treated with DMARDs or biologics. These medications can be discontinued without disease recurrence. Two reports from Europe evaluated the short-term (6 months) and long-term (median, 5 years) outcomes of children who had Lyme neuroborreliosis.178, Overall, complete clinical resolution was seen in the majority during the long term, although mild residual deficits occurred in some (incompletely resolved facial palsy or mild motor or sensory deficits). Importantly, nonspecific symptoms, such as fatigue, headache, and cognitive issues, were no more frequent in patients who had a history of neuroborreliosis than in age-matched controls, and residual deficits did not affect school performance.

Patients with Lyme disease may be co-infected with another tick-borne pathogen, most often with B. microti or A. phagocytophilum. Patients with co-infection tend to be more symptomatic at presentation and can have a delayed resolution of symptoms compared with patients with Lyme disease alone. Co-infection should be suspected when patients present with high fever or have laboratory abnormalities—such as leukopenia, anemia, elevated indirect bilirubin, or thrombocytopenia—that are not normally seen in Lyme disease. The impact of co-infection with the newly

emergent Ixodes tick-borne relapsing fever spirochete Borrelia miyamotoi on Lyme disease is not yet known.

### Post-treatment Lyme Disease Syndrome

A minority of patients treated for Lyme disease may have fatigue, musculoskeletal pain, and complaints of memory impairment despite conventional or prolonged courses of antibiotic therapy, a condition referred to as post-treatment Lyme disease syndrome. This entity should be distinguished from "chronic Lyme disease," which originally referred to patients who presented with latestage manifestations of untreated Lyme disease, months after the onset of infection. Use of the term "chronic Lyme disease" is discouraged because it now encompasses a broader group of people, including both those who may have post—Lyme disease syndrome and those for whom a diagnosis of Lyme disease cannot be established by clinical or laboratory criteria. Occasionally, patients may have other conditions such as RA or fibromyalgia, for which therapy has been delayed because of a misdiagnosis of Lyme disease. Latent autoimmunity also may be triggered by B. burgdorferi infection. RA, reactive arthritis or psoriatic arthritis, developing months after initial infection have been reported.

Musculoskeletal pain is common in the general population; the estimated prevalence of fatigue ranges from 7% to 45%. In the absence of a clinical history with objective manifestations of Lyme disease, supporting positive two-tiered serologic tests (or PCR or culture in the case of known immunodeficiency), definitive attribution of symptoms present for more than 1 to 2 months to B. burgdorferi infection should not be made.

In several controlled, population-based cohort studies that used validated standardized measures of outcomes (e.g., Short Form-36), patients with Lyme disease had more joint pain, symptoms of memory impairment, and worse functional status because of pain compared with controls.184, Follow-up studies suggest that quality-of-life measures improve with time. 186-192 Psychological factors and the presence of psychiatric comorbidity in patients with Lyme disease correlate with poor functional outcomes after treatment. A European study demonstrated that the frequency of nonspecific symptoms at 6 and 12 months after treatment for early Lyme disease was no greater than that of the control group, which included family members without a history of Lyme disease. Children are less likely than adults to have persistent complaints after treatment for Lyme disease.

Several controlled trials of antibiotics for persistent symptoms after Lyme disease failed to demonstrate sustained improvement. 195-198 In one study, the frequency of nonspecific symptoms was similar among patients treated for Lyme disease and a healthy control group, raising the possibility that in some cases attribution of symptoms to a previous diagnosis of Lyme disease may be anchoring bias. 76,

Prolonged antibiotic use is not without risk. Minor side effects are common, and serious adverse events such as biliary complications from ceftriaxone therapy or indwelling catheter—related infections occur at high enough rates to warrant only judicious use of antibiotics.195-197 Our evolving understanding of the role of intestinal dysbiosis, which can be a consequence of antibiotics, on human health and disease raises additional concerns over the use of long-term antibiotics. 200,201

### Prevention

The most effective way to prevent Lyme disease is to reduce exposure risk to B. burgdorferiinfected ticks through personal

protective measures and environmental controls. These measures include avoiding tick habitats such as wooded areas, stone fences, woodpiles, and tall grass; wearing protective clothing; and performing daily surveillance, including of pets, which can bring ticks into the home, and prompt removal of ticks (within 24 hours of feeding). Bathing within 2 hours of an outdoor activity with possible tick exposure is also effective. Other effective measures include use of insecticides that contain DEET, picaridin, IR3535, or oil of lemon eucalyptus applied directly to the skin, or permethrin applied to clothing. Yearly application of acaricides to property can kill ticks but should not be relied on as a means to prevent infection.

A single 200 mg dose of doxycycline (or 4.4 mg/kg to as much as 200 mg for children age 8 years and older) reduces the incidence of Lyme disease after a recognized tick bite but only when the patient presents within 72 hours of removal of an identified high-risk tick bite. High-risk bites are defined as the bite of an identified Ixodes tick from a highly endemic area where infection rates are more than 20% and the tick is engorged and attached for ≥36 hours. A recombinant Osp A-based vaccine to prevent Lyme disease was approved by the FDA in 1990 and later withdrawn because of low market demand and concern for potential vaccine-related side effects. A new OspA-based vaccine named VLA15 has been developed based on the six most common serotypes of B. burgdorferi sl species in North America and Europe. This vaccine has been modified to eliminate potential cross-reactivity with human proteins and a Phase III clinical trial is presently ongoing in endemic areas in the United States and Europe.

### Conclusion

Lyme disease is a localized or systemic infection that usually manifests with skin and musculoskeletal signs and symptoms, but it can involve other organ systems, especially the nervous system and more rarely the heart. The diagnosis should be based on objective clinical findings consistent with Lyme disease and supporting serologic tests. Patients receiving immunosuppressive therapy, especially B celldepleting therapies, for other conditions are more likely to present with disseminated infection and may not mount antibody responses. In these situations, direct measures such as PCR for B. burgdorferi DNA or culture may help support the diagnosis. Most patients are cured within 2 to 4 weeks of antibiotic therapy, although the time to disease resolution may be prolonged, especially for individuals in whom therapy was delayed; irreversible tissue damage may occur. A poor response to antibiotic therapy should raise concern for alternative diagnoses or co-infection with other tick-borne pathogens. Less than 10% of patients with Lyme arthritis develop persistent synovitis for which continued antibiotic therapy is of no benefit. Treatment with NSAIDs, hydroxychloroquine, or other DMARDs usually resolves arthritis and often these patients can discontinue DMARDs within a year. Some patients treated for Lyme disease experience a post—Lyme disease syndrome of fatigue, headaches, mild memory impairment, and musculoskeletal pain. Ongoing infection cannot be shown, and controlled treatment trials show no benefit of prolonged antibiotic therapy over placebo. Referral to an academic medical center with experience in the diagnosis and treatment of Lyme disease should be considered when patients do not respond as expected to therapy.

# Mycobacterial Infections of Bones and Joints

### KEY POINTS

### Introduction

The recognition of tuberculosis (TB) and other mycobacterial infections of the musculoskeletal system has become a major challenge for rheumatologists in the United States and other high income countries. Before 1999, most rheumatologists could easily go an entire year without seeing a single case of mycobacterial infection. Such cases were rare even at academic centers, where they would likely be presented as unusual teaching cases at clinical conferences.

The routine clinical use of TNF inhibitor therapy was introduced in 1999 in the United States, and with it came an unexpected increase in TB cases seen by rheumatologists. Fortunately, the initiation of routine screening with tuberculin skin test (TSTs)

and interferon (IFN)-γ release assays (IGRAs) has led to a sharp decline in the number of new cases, particularly those associated with reactivation of latent infection. Nevertheless, the risk of primary infection with new exposure mandates continued vigilance in these patients and potentially those on other biologic therapies. Moreover, for non-TB mycobacterial infections, there are no screening tests available, making vigilance on immunosuppressive therapy even more important.

Another major force driving the increase in mycobacterial infections is the HIV epidemic. In the pre-anti-retroviral therapy era, 21% of extrapulmonary TB cases in the United States were associated with underlying HIV infection. In low-middle income countries, the HIV epidemic has led to marked increases in osteoarticular TB co-infection. These cases are distinguished by disseminated disease suggestive of hematogenous spread, rapid progression, and more common co-existence with pulmonary infection.2, HIV testing should be a routine part of the workup of any patient presenting with a musculoskeletal infection secondary to Mycobacterium tuberculosis. The good news is that since the introduction of effective anti-retroviral therapy, the incidence ofTB and nontuberculous mycobacterial (NTM) infection in patients co-infected with HIV has declined sharply in the United States.

TB is an uncommon disease in high income countries. In the United States the incidence of TB has been steadily declining since 1990, and the majority of TB cases now may be considered imported (i.e., occurring in foreign-born individuals). Worldwide, TB remains one of the world's deadliest infectious diseases.4, In 2021, an estimated 10 million people developed TB, and 1.6 million people died from the disease. Worldwide, TB is the 13th leading cause of death and the leading cause of death from a single infectious agent, exceeding even HIV/AIDS. Tuberculosis cases and deaths increased during the COVID-19 pandemic, in part due to the disruption of TB services. More alarming is the increasing rate of multidrug-resistant TB (MDR- TB), which also increased during the COVID-19 pandemic, and the continued emergence of extensively drug-resistant TB (XDR- TB).5-7 MDR-TB is TB that is resistant to rifampin and any fluoroquinolone (a class of second-line anti-TB drug). XDR-TB is TB that is resistant to rifampin, plus any fluoroquinolone, plus at least one of the drugs bedaquiline and linezolid.

Approximately one-fourth of the world's population, 1.7 billion people, are latently infected with TB, providing a global reservoir that will continue to complicate its control. Globalization of the world economy promotes contact between populations of

the endemic and nonendemic regions. Immigrants to the United States from areas endemic for TB constitute an ongoing reservoir of patients with latent TB.

The challenge of diagnosing musculoskeletal mycobacterial infection reaches beyond the rarity of the disease. Such infections are often indolent and may lack the pain, fever, chills, and other prominent symptoms that typically accompany bacterial infections of the musculoskeletal system. In addition, routine culture techniques will not isolate the organism, so unless the diagnosis of mycobacterial infection is a consideration from the outset, the diagnosis may be missed. Delayed diagnosis of mycobacterial infections of the musculoskeletal system is common and will remain without a heightened index of suspicion.

For all these reasons, 21st-century rheumatologists need to be well informed about a group of diseases with which they may have had limited experience.

### Clinical Scenarios

To appreciate the entire spectrum of clinical problems a rheumatologist may encounter in dealing with mycobacterial infections, it is useful to think in terms of several distinct categories. Investigators° provide a clinically useful division of mycobacterial infections into four major categories.

### Direct Involvement of the Musculoskeletal System

Musculoskeletal infections caused by mycobacteria typically present as chronic, indolent, localized involvement of the bones, spine, peripheral joints, or soft tissues that produces a focus of nonspecific pain and, less often, swelling. Musculoskeletal TB infections almost always represent reactivation of infection acquired months, years, or decades earlier, which had hematogenously seeded bones and joints. Musculoskeletal NTM infections may occur as a result of hematogenous spread from the lungs or direct inoculation of environmental contaminants. In infections initiated by direct tissue inoculation, the traumatic event is often trivial or remote in time from the onset of clinical disease. Diagnosis may be delayed for months to years, in part because of minimal early symptoms and attribution of those symptoms to a noninfectious disorder until disease progression and disability prompt a more aggressive diagnostic investigation.

Constitutional symptoms are typically subtle or absent, and laboratory indicators of inflammation are often normal. Synovial effusion is frequently minimal, and the fluid, if it is obtainable, shows nonspecific inflammation. Radiographic abnormalities may be delayed, although newer imaging techniques have allowed the earlier detection of abnormalities and the distinction of TB from other infections and neoplasm.9, Characteristic pulmonary or extrapulmonary findings are not always present; for example, less than 50% of osteoarticular TB presents with evidence of active or past pulmonary disease. TSTs and IGRA testing may provide useful clues to the cause, but results are not invariably positive, especially in debilitated or immunosuppressed patients. HIV co-infection is common. Correct diagnosis is highly dependent, in most cases, on demonstration of the infectious agent by microscopic examination and culture of affected tissue.

In HIV-infected patients, mycobacterial infections are often diagnosed before the patients' HIV status is known, sometimes leading to its recognition. Atypical presentations of pulmonary

TB and extrapulmonary (often multifocal) infection are common; extrapulmonary infection occurs in 60% to 70% of such cases, compared with 16% of all patients with TB.

The clinical patterns of musculoskeletal TB include spondylitis, osteomyelitis, peripheral joint infection, and soft-tissue abscess. In a series of 230 consecutive cases of TB from the pre-antibiotic era, 5.2% had skeletal involvement; the spine was affected in 60% of these cases. TB of the bones and joints is seeded hematogenously from pulmonary infection. The sites most commonly affected are the spine and hips, followed by the knees and wrists; other joint involvement is uncommon. The typical symptoms of TB—fever, night sweats, and weight loss—are uncommon in musculoskeletal TB and, when present, suggest TB in other organs. Vertebral collapse because of spinal TB may initially be attributed to the more common osteoporosis-caused spinal compression fracture. TB only rarely involves skeletal muscle but must be considered in the differential diagnosis of an enlarging muscle lesion.13-15 Isolated cases involving tendons, trochanteric bursa, and fascia lata illustrate the variety of possibilities.16-19 Imaging studies do not reliably distinguish TB from neoplasm. Biopsy and culture are required for diagnosis.

In nonendemic areas, skeletal TB usually occurs in elderly, debilitated patients, most often in the form of solitary osteolytic lesions in the axial skeleton. The development of skeletal disease is often remote from the initial infection, which strongly implies reactivation of previous subclinical disease. Patients may have false-negative TSTs and IGRAs for several reasons, including long-term corticosteroid use or co-existing debilitating diseases, such as rheumatoid arthritis (RA) or chronic renal failure, that compromise resistance and produce anergy (Table 114.1).20, The occurrence of spinal disease in children in nonendemic regions has mostly been eliminated by effective medical therapy of pulmonary infection and identification and treatment of those with latent TB.

In contrast, in endemic areas with high infectivity rates, those infected are more commonly children and young to middle-age adults, and these individuals have a higher incidence of multifocal skeletal involvement. Bone seeding occurs through hematogenous spread, sometimes secondarily from another extrapulmonary site. When pulmonary findings are present, a miliary pattern is typical. Spread to bone may also occur from infected nodes, either by direct extension or through draining lymph channels.

### Spondylitis

The spine is the dominant site of involvement in skeletal TB, accounting for 50% to 60% of cases. Between 48% and 67% of lesions occur in the lower thoracic and thoracolumbar spine

in HIV-uninfected patients, whereas the lumbar spine is most commonly involved in HIV-infected patients. Infection usually begins in the anterior subchondral bone of a single vertebra adjacent to the intervertebral disk (Fig. 114.1 and Fig. 114.2). Progression occurs from 2 to 5 months and begins with extension from cancellous to cortical bone, and then across the disk space to adjacent vertebrae (Fig. 114.3). Bone destruction may lead to vertebral collapse, which typically occurs anteriorly, resulting in gibbus deformity. Isolated neural arch involvement and intraspinal abscess may also occur.

Paravertebral abscess begins with the extension of infection under the anterior longitudinal ligament. In the thoracic spine, this may extend into the pleural space and lung parenchyma. In the cervical region, it may spread to the posterior cervical triangle or retropharyngeal space. In the lumbar spine, a cold abscess characteristically produces lateral displacement of the psoas muscle and may dissect along its length to present as a mass in the inguinal triangle, gluteal muscle, or upper thigh. In isolated cases, a cold abscess occurs without apparent bone involvement.

A particular variant of this presentation is subligamentous TB, in which infection spreads up and down the spine beneath the longitudinal ligament, producing scalloping of multiple anterior vertebral bodies without disk involvement. This pattern is more common in the cervical spine. 24

The clinical presentation of spinal TB usually consists of localized pain, which may be accompanied by low-grade fever, weight loss, chills, and nonspecific constitutional symptoms. Paraparesis and paraplegia have occurred in 1% to 27% of patients in various series. In comparison with pyogenic vertebral osteomyelitis, patients with spinal TB more often are seen with a prolonged clinical course, thoracic segment involvement, spinal deformity, neurologic deficit, and paravertebral or epidural masses, and typically

without fever, chills, or constitutional symptoms. On occasion, patients with tuberculous spondylitis are seen with chronic inflammatory-type back pain more typical of a spondyloarthritis. The differential diagnosis, which is extensive, includes pyogenic and fungal osteomyelitis, primary and metastatic tumors, sarcoidosis, multiple myeloma, and eosinophilic granuloma.

Mycobacterial colony counts in bone biopsy specimens are relatively low. Only 40% of smears and cultures from psoas abscesses are positive. Among patients meeting strict clinical and radiographic criteria in one series, between 73% and 82% had compatible histologic features on biopsy; of these, 80% to 95% had positive culture results. Experience with direct amplification tests in spinal TB is encouraging. In a series of 319 cases of spinal TB from China, the GeneXpert nucleic acid amplification assay demonstrated a sensitivity of 85.2% and specificity of 100%. In a series of 69 patients with spinal TB from South Africa, the GeneXpert nucleic acid amplification assay demonstrated a sensitivity of 95.6% and specificity of 96.2% and reduced the time from biopsy to confirmation of the diagnosis from 35 days for culture to 48 hours.

Cervical spine involvement is relatively rare, accounting for only 0.4% to 1.2% of cases of extrapulmonary TB in the United States. The most common presenting symptoms are neck pain and stiffness, although hoarseness, dysphagia, torticollis, fever, anorexia, and neurologic disorders may also occur. Spinal involvement can progress to myelopathy because of delays in diagnosis. Radiographs may show characteristic osteolysis of the anterior vertebral body with sparing of the posterior portion, gibbus deformity, disk involvement, and a partially calcified paraspinous mass. Computed tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is useful for assessing compromise of the spinal canal. Retropharyngeal infection may extend into the craniocervical junction and, if not promptly recognized, may cause atlantoaxial dislocation and neurologic complications. 29,

The sacroiliac joint is involved in as many as 10% of cases of skeletal TB, often without other evidence of disease. Infection, and TB in particular, should be considered in all cases of unilateral sacroiliitis, particularly when other features of spondyloarthritis are absent. Emigration from an endemic area and a past history of TB increase the likelihood of this cause. Buttock pain on the involved side is the patient's presenting symptom and is often accompanied by proximal leg or radicular pain. Examination reveals sacroiliac tenderness to palpation and stress maneuvers. Sacroiliac films show joint widening and erosion. An elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate and anemia are common, and a positive tuberculin reaction or IGRA is typical. Biopsy of the sacroiliac joint shows granulomatous histologic features or nonspecific inflammation and a positive culture in most cases.

Atypical spinal lesions, which occur in approximately 10% of cases, may delay diagnosis and treatment. Atypical radiographic presentations in a single vertebra include concentric collapse, sclerotic foci, and selective involvement of the vertebral arches and costotransverse joints. Multiple vertebrae may be involved, either in continuity or as skipped lesions. Atypical clinical presentations may suggest a herniated intervertebral disk, failed back syndrome, spinal tumor, or a meningeal granuloma. 23,32

### Tuberculous Osteomyelitis

Bone lesions begin with hematogenous implantation of organisms in the medullary area. Metaphyseal involvement is most common, and lesions may spread through the growth plate to involve the adjacent joint, usually late in the disease course. Lesions are

typically destructive. Lytic lesions in unusual areas, such as the pubic symphysis, sacroiliac joint, and elbow, can be misdiagnosed as malignancy. Osteomyelitis may occur in a bone or joint that has been previously exposed to trauma.

Tuberculous osteomyelitis occurs in both children and adults. Although any bone can be involved, the femur and tibia are most commonly affected. In one large series from an endemic area, such cases represented 19% of bone and joint TB and 15% of cases of osteomyelitis of hematogenous origin. Bone pain was the most common presentation; a draining sinus, abscess formation, and

local swelling and tenderness were also common. The average delay before diagnosis was 28 months.

Multifocal osteoarticular TB is a less common variant of the disease,35,36 but TB should be considered in all patients from endemic areas who are seen with multiple destructive skeletal lesions. Skin testing and IFN-γ release assays may not be helpful in highly endemic areas because of the prevalence of asymptomatic, latent infection.

Radiographic findings include cavity formation with a thin adjacent layer of sclerosis in about 50% of cases, sometimes containing a sequestrum. The true extent of bone involvement may be difficult to detect because of clinically silent lesions. Bone imaging with technetium-99, although more sensitive than conventional radiographs, may provide false-negative results in early, indolent, or highly destructive disease. Tuberculin test reactions are positive in more than 80% of cases.

Soft-tissue lesions characteristically demonstrate rim enhancement on CT examination. CT may also facilitate percutaneous needle biopsy or abscess drainage. For a definitive diagnosis of osteoarticular TB, a biopsy specimen of an affected site must be obtained. Histologic examination generally reveals granulomatous inflammation. In one series of 121 cases, biopsy showed a positive culture in 33%, granulomatous histologic features in 46%, and both in 21%. Nucleic acid amplification might allow more rapid diagnosis. These tests do not rule out TB with certainty but have demonstrated good specificity and can provide early recognition of drug resistance. Treatment with anti-tuberculous therapy is generally effective. In a minority of cases, surgical debridement is required for healing. Initiation of therapy on the basis of histologic findings is appropriate pending culture results. Sinus cultures are commonly positive for pyogenic bacteria both before and after anti-tuberculous therapy, but these are presumed to be contaminants. Healing is associated with sclerosis at the margin of lesions. Misdiagnosis of the condition as pyogenic osteomyelitis may lead to unnecessary surgery or to delayed anti-tuberculous treatment, resulting in extension of infection into the joint and chronic disability.

### Septic Arthritis

The typical pattern of tuberculous joint involvement is a monoarticular arthritis involving the large joints, most commonly the hip and knee (Fig. 114.4 and Fig. 114.5).40, Other joints less commonly involved include the sacroiliac, shoulder, elbow, ankle, carpal, and tarsal joints. Infection begins in the synovium, with progression of destructive changes being slower than in pyogenic septic arthritis.

The diagnosis of tuberculous arthritis is often missed. A consecutive series spanning the years 1970 to 1984 emphasized typical features. Of 23 cases of musculoskeletal TB, 9 involved the spine, 1 the hip, and the remaining 13 the peripheral joints. Most patients were men older than 50 years. The history of TB or exposure was generally forgotten. In all cases, presenting symptoms were joint pain and swelling. Four patients had evidence of active pulmonary TB, and in two patients with sterile pyuria, M. tuberculosis grew from the urine. Only 5 of 10 patients tested had a positive TST. Radiographs showed changes of erosive arthritis in 7 and no changes in 4 of 11 joints studied. The median delay in diagnosis was 8 months.

Arriving at a correct diagnosis requires vigorous pursuit and usually a synovial biopsy and culture. Initial studies are often misleading and may contribute to delayed diagnosis or misdiagnosis. Synovial fluid findings are variable and do not distinguish this arthropathy from other inflammatory or septic arthritides. Cell counts more often suggest bland inflammatory, rather than septic, arthritis and may contain a preponderance of neutrophils. The diagnosis may be facilitated if the organism is observed on an acidfast smear of synovial fluid, but only 10% to 20% of reported cases are positive. In contrast, synovial fluid cultures are frequently positive. Radiographic changes are similar to those seen in other septic arthritides, beginning with juxta-articular bone demineralization and progressing to marginal bone erosion and articular cartilage destruction (seeFig. 114.4).

With the open-biopsy technique, granulomatous histologic features and positive cultures are present in more than 90% of cases. The histologic examination alone may be confusing because granulomatous synovitis can also be found in nontuberculous mycobacterial infection, sarcoidosis, erythema nodosum, brucellosis, Crohn's disease, and foreign-body reaction. As noted, synovial acid-fast smear is of limited value. Tuberculous arthritis is also reported in children, sometimes early in the disease course; synovial biopsy and culture are recommended in children with monoarthritis and a TST or IGRA.

TB must be considered among the possible causes of septic arthritis occurring in patients with pre-existing RA, although it is not widely seen in high income countries.45, Conversely, rheumatoid factor may be present in TB, leading to diagnostic confusion in the presence of chronic monarthritis.

Prosthetic joint infection with M. tuberculosis has occurred and may be caused by local reactivation of latent disease. In a series of 13 patients with TB prosthetic joint infection from France, infection complicated six hips, six knees, and one shoulder. Of note, PCR testing was positive in all five cases where it was utilized. In another case series of nine patients with prosthetic joint infection due to TB, all involved the hip; four of nine were diagnosed at the time of primary arthroplasty—a friable appearance suggested chronic infection or malignancy and prompted synovial biopsy and mycobacterial culture. Limited experience suggests the prosthesis can be retained if TB is an unexpected finding during arthroplasty.48,49

### Emergence of Tuberculosis During Treatment of Rheumatic Diseases

Many patients with systemic rheumatic disease have dysregulated immune systems that are treated with immunosuppressive drugs. Such an impaired immune response may permit the reactivation

of latent TB. TNF plays a key role in granuloma formation and stabilization, which promotes the containment of M. tuberculosis. The rate of TB among patients with RA before the widespread use of TNF inhibitors was approximately six cases per 100,000,50 although some studies have suggested that the rate in RA is higher than in the general population. In one large patient registry, the estimated incidence of TB associated with infliximab in RA patients was in excess of 1000 per 100,000 person-years of exposure during the years 2000 to 2001.52 In the United States, the rate was 52 per 100,000 person-years during the same time period. Etanercept may be associated with a lower risk for TB reactivation than infliximab: 10 cases per 100,000 person-years of exposure with etanercept, versus 41 per 100,000 person-years with infliximab, according to an analysis of U.S. Food and Drug Administration data. Similarly, British and French registries have identified a greater risk for TB associated with the use of adalimumab and infliximab than with etanercept.54, There are fewer data available for the newer TNF inhibitors, and comparisons are complicated by the widespread use of pre-treatment screening instituted after the first agents in this class were approved for use. Monoclonal antibodies to TNF may play a greater role in destabilizing granulomas than soluble TNF receptors. Nonetheless, similar precautions should be taken with any TNF inhibitor and all should be presumed to increase the risk of both new infection and reactivation of latent infection. The European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology published updated consensus recommendations that covered screening for tuberculosis and other chronic infections prior to the use of immunomodulatory therapy in 2022.55a

Non-TNF biologic agents have been associated with TB infection, although most of these cases occur in regions with endemic disease. Despite labeling recommendations for screening prior to therapy, cumulative clinical trial and post-marketing data suggest that the risk of reactivation is quite low. Biologics with mechanisms other than TNF inhibition may pose a lower risk for reactivation of TB because the mechanisms of action are not intimately involved with host defense related to intra-cellular organisms. Animal studies have suggested that abatacept does not impair the ability of mice to respond to M. tuberculosis, but this has not been confirmed in humans. Little or no evidence indicates that B cells play a major role in containing TB, and there does not appear to be an increased risk of TB after treatment with rituximab. Cases of tuberculosis have occurred with tofacitinib, although most occurred in regions with high background rates. The median time between drug start and diagnosis was 64 weeks, suggesting new infection rather than reactivation of latent disease.

Glucocorticoid use also poses a significant hazard for patients with latent TB. Many mechanisms account for this effect, including impairment of cellular immune responses and monocyte chemotaxis and function, including the monocyte's production of TNF. The use of glucocorticoids has been associated with a five-fold increased risk for TB in a case-control study involving a large general practice database in the United Kingdom. The risk appeared to be dose related but was seen even at the physiologic dose of prednisone, 7.5 mg/day. Just as with TNF inhibitors, the risk for TB was greatest early in the course of treatment. In a French study, prednisone at 10 mg/day or more but not lower doses was associated with an increased risk for TB.

Reactivation of TB in the face of TNF inhibitor therapy typically occurs within 6 months of treatment and often manifests as extrapulmonary disease. Institution of a protocol to screen and treat for latent TB infection (LTBI) in patients with RA before TNF inhibitor administration resulted in a 78% decrease in TB

disease. Treatment of LTBI can effectively and safely lessen the likelihood of TB disease in patients treated with TNF inhibitors. Indeed, it has been suggested that much of the blame for the development of TB disease in this situation can be attributed to incomplete compliance with screening protocols. Conversely, in a report of 84 patients at a single center who were treated with etanercept after demonstrating a positive TST, no cases of TB disease were seen during a mean of 2 years of follow-up despite the fact that 78 of 84 patients were prescribed treatment and only 52 completed the prescribed treatment regimen. Although screening for LTBI has reduced the incidence of TB disease, falsenegative TSTs and false-negative and indeterminate IGRAs can undermine such good intentions (see Table 114.1).

The approach to a patient with latent TB who needs a TNF inhibitor has not been standardized. Many authorities recommend that patients with positive TSTs or IGRAs and normal chest radiographs who have never been treated for TB receive at least 1 to 2 months of therapy before beginning a TNF inhibitor, if for no other reason than to be certain that they will be able to tolerate the full course of latent TB therapy. Appropriate regimens include 9 months of isoniazid, 4 months of rifampin, or 3 months of directly observed weekly isoniazid plus rifapentine. No reactivation was seen in patients with latent infection receiving concurrent therapy with tofacitinib and isoniazid. Patients discovered to have active TB should receive a complete course of standard antituberculous therapy before initiating a TNF inhibitor.

Although TNF inhibitors and steroids are predominant risk factors for TB, all patients with rheumatic disease treated with immunosuppressive therapy that impairs cellular immunity should be considered at risk. This is especially true in older adults, those who are malnourished, and immigrants from countries with high endemic rates of TB.

### Rheumatic Disorders Precipitated by the Treatment of Tuberculosis

A variety of rheumatic conditions may be precipitated by the drugs used in the treatment of TB. These include drug-induced lupus caused by isoniazid (INH) and rifampin. As with other cases of drug-induced lupus, they are associated with positive anti-nuclear antibodies and the presence of anti-histone antibodies. Typically, these patients follow a benign course, with resolution of disease after the drug is discontinued.

Arthropathy and tendinopathy have been described with the use of fluoroquinolones, especially ciprofloxacin and levofloxacin. The risk of tendon rupture (usually the Achilles tendon) is greatest in patients older than 50 years and increases with the concomitant use of corticosteroids.

Pyrazinamide interferes with the renal tubular excretion of uric acid and has been associated with the development of hyperuricemia and gout in adults.

Paradoxical reactions have been described in patients withdrawn from infliximab after the diagnosis and initiation of treatment for TB disease. These reactions present as a worsening of pre-existing TB lesions or the development of new lesions not attributable to the normal course of disease in a patient initially improving on treatment. The mechanism for such reactions is not completely understood but has been categorized within the spectrum of immune reconstitution inflammatory syndromes. Such reactions are more common in patients with HIV following the initiation of anti-retroviral therapy. After infliximab therapy is discontinued, its anti-inflammatory effects persist for 3 or 4 weeks,

which may explain the timing of this delayed reaction. No changes in anti-tuberculous therapy are necessary when a paradoxical reaction occurs; corticosteroids may ameliorate this response.

### Reactive Immunologic Phenomena in the Setting of Tuberculosis

A variety of reactive immunologic phenomena have been associated with M. tuberculosis infection. These are uncommonly seen in clinical practice.

Poncet's disease is an aseptic inflammatory polyarthritis that occurs in the presence of TB disease. Although any joints can be involved, the most commonly affected are the knees, ankles, and elbows. The mechanism is thought to be similar to other forms of reactive arthritis secondary to remote infection. Most cases resolve after satisfactory treatment of the TB. Reactive arthritis has been described following the intravesicular instillation of bacille Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccine for bladder cancer.

Other seldom-encountered immune reaction patterns described with M. tuberculosis include erythema nodosum, erythema induratum, and amyloidosis (AA type).

### Diagnosis

### Tuberculin Skin Test

The TST—also called the purified protein derivative (PPD)—has been in use for nearly a century and remains the most widely used screening test for TB worldwide. The test represents a crude mix of antigens from M. tuberculosis and is plagued by both false-positive and false-negative results. It is unable to distinguish latent infection from active disease and may be negative in the face of severe active TB. Corticosteroids (≥15 mg/day of prednisone) may render the TST negative in people with latent TB. Elderly and malnourished patients may not exhibit a positive TST. Table 114.1 provides a partial list of causes for a false-negative TST that are of special interest to rheumatologists.

False-positive results may likewise occur in the case of infection with nontuberculous mycobacteria or previous BCG vaccination. TST positivity degrades with time in BCG-vaccinated patients at a variable rate. The degree of positivity is influenced by a number of factors, including the number of BCG vaccinations and the number of subsequent TSTs performed. Some patients may retain a response as long as 15 years after BCG vaccination. Nevertheless, a TST result of 20 mm or greater is rarely the result of BCG. In addition, if faced with a high-risk situation, such as the initiation of TNF inhibitor therapy, one should probably make a presumption of LTBI even if the diameter of induration measures as little as 5 mm.

The important message for rheumatologists is that the TST is an important but imperfect screening tool for latent TB infection, with a sensitivity and specificity in the range of 70%. A negative TST should not eliminate the clinician's vigilance in monitoring patients treated with TNF inhibitors for reactivated or new-onset TB, especially in high-risk populations.

### Interferon-γ Release Assays

The limitations of the traditional PPD skin test in terms of specificity and sensitivity in identifying latent TB have led to the development of new T cellbased testing. These assays measure the production of IFN-γ by whole-blood mononuclear cells stimulated by specific M. tuberculosis antigens. The IGRAs, including

the QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus (QFT-Plus) (Qiagen; Venlo, Netherlands) and T-SPOT.TB (Oxford Immunotec, Inc.; Oxford, England) assays, appear to have equivalent or better sensitivity and improved specificity compared with TST.67, These assays contain specific M. tuberculosis antigens and are less likely to result in a positive test in people exposed to nontuberculous mycobacteria, including Mycobacterium avium complex or the attenuated Mycobacterium bovis strain in the BCG vaccine. They also offer the opportunity to circumvent operator error with TST administration and interpretation and do not require patients to return in 48 to 72 hours to have the test interpreted. IGRAs have replaced the TST in many centers for routine screening for LTBI. Studies of IGRAs in patients with RA and other inflammatory disorders have found them to have comparable or better accuracy than the TST, although a recent meta-analysis found that most of these studies have a high risk of bias.69-76 IGRA may be particularly useful in patients treated with steroids, which can reduce the sensitivity of the TST.

IGRAs are not without concerns. Indeterminate results from IGRAs in this setting have ranged from 1.2% to 28.6%, raising concerns about the performance of the assay from center to center.70, Within-subject result variability is an issue, especially when the TB antigen response is near the cutoff value.79, Factors that might contribute to IGRA result variability include reagent variability, blood volume, whether the blood tube is shaken gently or vigorously, delays in processing, and PPDinduced boosting of IFN-γ response. Positive IGRAs are more closely related to TB risk factors than are positive TSTs. Discordant IGRA-/TST+ results are associated with prior BCG vaccination, and discordant IGRA+/TSTresults are related to corticosteroid therapy, suggesting that the former represents a false-positive TST and the latter a false-negative TST. Nevertheless, the meaning of a discordant result is uncertain enough that patients with a positive test result with either IGRA or TST should be considered for therapy of possible LTBI. Additional experience will be required to provide confidence that a negative IGRA in the setting of a positive TST reliably excludes LTBI. If only one testing modality is used, one analysis found that use of an IGRA was more cost effective than the TST for patients screened before TNF inhibitor therapy.

IGRAs have also been studied in patients receiving a TNF inhibitor to identify newly acquired TB infection. Many authorities recommend ongoing annual monitoring for new TB infection in patients treated with TNF inhibitors, especially in highly endemic areas. Rates of TST conversion in patients on TNF inhibitor therapy are 33% and 37% from centers in Korea and Taiwan; corresponding rates of IGRA conversion were 14% and 11%, respectively, and appeared to better correlate with the risk of active TB.85, Pending formal guidelines, in regions where ongoing exposure to infectious TB may occur, routine monitoring for TB on therapy—perhaps annually—is wise and the use of an IGRA rather than a TST may limit the number of patients requiring preventive treatment.

### Imaging

Although imaging patterns suggestive of TB have been discussed, there are no pathognomonic skeletal radiographic features that can establish the diagnosis. Early features on radiographs may be equivocal or nonexistent. Chest radiographs are often normal or fail to show the posterior upper lobe cavitary infiltrates characteristic of reactivated pulmonary TB.

Conventional radiography is generally a useful approach for defining bone destruction, the extent of disease, and adjacent softtissue lesions. MRI is more effective in identifying early disease; it may help distinguish TB from other infections and neoplasm and can aid in evaluating the extent of disease.10, Scintiscans with technetium and gallium may also be helpful in localizing bone and soft-tissue lesions, but early false-negative findings are not uncommon. CT can be helpful in guiding diagnostic needle biopsy. Fine-needle biopsy is an acceptable alternative to core-needle biopsy and open biopsy for the diagnosis of osteoarticular TB in both the axial and peripheral skeleton, and it has the advantage of obviating general anesthesia.89, Both CT and MRI may also be helpful in monitoring therapy.

### Culture

Nearly all species of Mycobacteria are slow growing, with M. tuberculosis the slowest. Other bacteria may rapidly outgrow mycobacteria if the specimen is not inoculated on special isolation media. The small number of mycobacteria found in clinically infected areas further challenges the ability to confirm mycobacterial infection and accounts for the low yield of positive Ziehl-Neelsen staining (10% to 20%) in synovial fluid and other biologic fluids.

Synovial fluid and other body fluids are less likely than tissue to yield a positive culture. If a joint is suspected of harboring TB, a synovial biopsy should be obtained. Arthroscopically derived tissue yields higher positive cultures than needle biopsies. CT-guided needle aspiration and biopsy can provide invaluable information in the case of spinal involvement. Characteristic features on tissue pathology—caseating or noncaseating granulomas ± acid-fast bacilli on special stains—may allow an early presumptive diagnosis of TB pending culture results, which may take 4 to 6 weeks to be finalized.

### Polymerase Chain Reaction

Molecular diagnostics by using polymerase chain reaction (PCR) have proven very helpful in the rapid diagnosis of pulmonary TB, demonstrating a high yield even in patients with sputum smearnegative pulmonary TB, and are now endorsed for routine use by the World Health Organization (WHO). The role of molecular diagnostic assays in extrapulmonary TB is still being defined, but preliminary experience has demonstrated promise. In a small cohort of patients with vertebral osteomyelitis, multiplex PCR testing of bone biopsy specimens demonstrated 90% sensitivity and 100% specificity for TB infection, illustrating the potential for this technology to provide rapid and accurate diagnosis. Similarly, multiplex real-time PCR successfully distinguished TB from brucellosis as the cause of vertebral osteomyelitis, demonstrating a sensitivity of 87% and specificity of 100% in the diagnosis of TB. Nucleic acid amplification using the GeneXpert MTB/ RIF system has been proposed as a sensitive and specific method for identifying TB infection, although the cost and availability of the assay may limit its widespread use, particularly in resourcelimited nations. The WHO has been working to increase the availability of this test by underwriting its costs in highly endemic areas. The GeneXpert was evaluated in a series of 50 patients with bone and joint TB (75% with spinal TB) and demonstrated a sensitivity of 82% and specificity of 100%. The assay correctly identified 100% of MDR-TB isolates. Among 106 patients with suspected spinal tuberculosis, the Xpert MTB/RIF was 87% sensitive relative to histopathology.95a In a series of 67 patients with suspected bone and joint tuberculosis, the Xpert MTB/RIF assay

demonstrated a sensitivity of 93% and specificity of 62% relative to culture and sensitivity of 79% and specificity of 74% relative to histopathology.95b The positive rate of the Xpert MTB/RIF assay was significantly higher for granulation tissue specimens than for caseous necrotic tissue, sequestrum, and other necrotic connective tissues.

### Treatment

Patients with positive TSTs or IGRAs and no evidence of active tuberculous disease should be treated for LTBI. Regimens currently recommended for treatment of LTBI include 4 months of daily rifampin, 3 months of weekly isoniazid plus rifapentine, 3 months of daily isoniazid plus rifampin or, alternatively, 6 to 9 months of daily isoniazid.95c

Appropriate management of tuberculous infections of bones and joints is complex. Selection of appropriate anti-tuberculous agents and ongoing disease monitoring should involve co-management with an infectious disease consultant. Nonetheless, rheumatologists should be familiar with the basic treatment principles.

Treatment of M. tuberculosis infections that involve the musculoskeletal system consist of the same combination chemotherapy regimens that are effective in pulmonary TB. Treatment regimens for infections of the bone and spine are typically administered for longer durations than those recommended for lung disease and other extrapulmonary sites. These longer treatment courses for musculoskeletal disease have been recommended based on poor tissue penetration of anti-tuberculous agents into osseous tissues and the higher rates of relapse associated with these infections.

Current guidelines on the treatment of TB published jointly by the U.S. Centers for Disease Control, American Thoracic Society, and Infectious Diseases Society of America recommend a 6-month course of therapy for all sites except the bone (6 to 9 months) and the central nervous system (9 to 12 months). Rifampin is the critical component that allows shorter-course therapy.

The standard approach to TB therapy (both pulmonary and extrapulmonary) in the United States currently includes four drugs to start: isoniazid, rifampin, ethambutol, and pyrazinamide—also known as IREZ therapy. Once the isolate is confirmed to be sensitive to INH, the ethambutol can be discontinued. Pyrazinamide is administered for 2 months, and rifampin and INH are continued for the duration of therapy.

Longer courses of therapy are required for patients who are slow to respond. Radiographic features of mycobacterial disease may not change much after 6 months of treatment, and response to treatment is based mainly on clinical features, including reduction in pain, resolution of constitutional symptoms, and emergence of increased mobility. Longer courses are also advised for cases of relapse and resistant organisms.

Surgical intervention is seldom indicated for the initial management of osteoarticular TB. Possible exceptions at presentation include patients with advanced or progressive disease or existing or impending spinal deformity. MDR-TB, which refers to isolates that are resistant to isoniazid and rifampin, may also provide a relative indication for surgical debridement. Patients who have extensive joint destruction and immobility after an adequate course of chemotherapy may also be candidates for surgery.

After successful antibiotic therapy, arthroplasty of the hip and knee may be undertaken and is usually successful. Recurrence of disease in the prosthetic joint is less likely if the surgery is performed years after the infection, and the tissue obtained at surgery is culture negative. This may be impractical, however, when a

patient is unable to ambulate after an adequate course of therapy. In such cases, the TB therapy is continued through surgery and for at least 3 months post-operatively. If TB recurs in the prosthetic joint, it can sometimes be managed with antibiotic therapy alone. In some cases, however, removal of the prosthesis is necessary to cure the infection.

The increasing incidence of drug-resistant TB complicates the selection of appropriate drugs.97-99 Primary monoresistance to isoniazid occurs in approximately 8% of TB isolates in the United States. When identified, this does not substantially impact the treatment outcome. The U.S. MDR-TB rate has been relatively stable for the past decade, 1.6%. Worldwide, 3.6% of new TB cases were MDR-TB in 2021 and 18% in previously treated individuals. The treatment of MDR-TB is complex and often requires the use of multiple (often toxic) second-line agents for 18 to 24 months or longer. XDR-TB—that is, strains resistant to all firstline TB drugs and at least three second-line agents—was reported by 77 countries in 2016, with particularly high rates in India, the Russian Federation, South Africa, Belarus, and Ukraine.10o On average, an estimated 8.5% of individuals with MDR-TB have XDR-TB. Options for treatment of XDR-TB are very limited, and the risk of treatment failure and death is high.

Incomplete adherence with treatment is a particularly important risk factor for secondary drug resistance, and the likelihood of drug resistance increases following relapse after treatment. The WHO guidelines for treatment of drug-resistant tuberculosis were updated in 2021.

### Osteoarticular Infections Caused by Nontuberculous Mycobacteria

NTM are ubiquitous in the environment, including soil, water, and animal reservoirs. They are not typically spread from human to human, and infections with these organisms have been reported with increasing frequency. Although the majority of infections caused by these organisms are pulmonary, skin and softtissue infections may be seen in healthy individuals; a localized lymphadenitis may develop in children. Osteoarticular infections are usually caused by either direct inoculation of the organism or spread of contiguous infection. Blunt trauma has been implicated as a risk factor in cases of vertebral osteomyelitis due to NTM. NTM infections of the musculoskeletal system may develop in immunosuppressed individuals, but these infections are much less common than TB. In contrast to TB, nontuberculous infection is more likely to cause tenosynovitis, synovitis, or osteomyelitis and is less likely to cause spinal infection. A review identified only 31 cases of vertebral osteomyelitis due to NTM reported between 1965 and 2003.106 Although there are more than 120 species of NTM, the majority of musculoskeletal infections are caused by Mycobacterium marinum, Mycobacterium kansasii, and Mycobacterium avium-intracellulare (also called M. avium complex, or MAC), but cases of musculoskeletal infection with Mycobacterium haemophilum, Mycobacterium chelonae, Mycobacterium xenopi, and Mycobacterium conceptionense have also occurred. 107-111

Three distinct patterns of musculoskeletal involvement are reported: tenosynovitis, synovitis, and osteomyelitis. 112, Tenosynovitis is typically seen as chronic unilateral hand and wrist swelling (Fig. 114.6). Synovitis is frequently seen as chronic indolent asymmetric swelling in a knee, hand, or wrist. A number of species have been associated with these syndromes, and the

number isolated from immunosuppressed patients is growing. Predisposing factors, in addition to immunosuppression and direct inoculation, include environmental exposure and pre-existing joint disease.

In one recent case series of 32 cases of mycobacterial arthritis and tenosynovitis, M. tuberculosis was isolated exclusively from 11 patients with arthritis of large joints, whereas NTM were isolated primarily from 17 patients with tenosynovitis and only four patients with arthritis of large joints. Nevertheless, musculoskeletal infections with atypical mycobacteria may be indistinguishable from M. tuberculosis infections, so correct diagnosis usually requires tissue biopsy and culture. Synovial fluid, when obtainable, is typically inflammatory, and a culture may be helpful

only if specific mycobacterial cultures are requested. Identification of acid-fast bacilli on smear and granulomatous inflammation from a tissue biopsy specimen often provides direction for an appropriate microbiologic investigation, but histologic features do not consistently demonstrate granuloma formation. With a compatible clinical presentation and histologic findings, mycobacterial culture, including special techniques for M. marinum, should be requested. Direct amplification testing may be useful for more rapid identification of mycobacterial species in tissue specimens, but data from musculoskeletal cases are limited. In addition to mycobacteria, other causes of granulomatous synovitis include fungi, brucellosis, sarcoidosis, inflammatory bowel disease, and nonmetallic foreign bodies. Mycobacteria other than M. tuberculosis are responsible for a significant proportion of these cases.

MAC has become the most common mycobacterial infectious agent affecting patients with HIV/AIDS, in whom it has a tendency to cause disseminated disease. Osteomyelitis as a consequence of MAC infections has been seen, including in the spine (Fig. 114.7). Fortunately, there has been a sharp decline in the incidence of MAC following the introduction of highly active anti-retroviral therapy and MAC prophylaxis.

Isolation of M. tuberculosis is always clinically significant. In contrast, when dealing with a nontuberculous mycobacterial isolate, the clinician must judge whether it is a contaminant, represents insignificant colonization, or is the cause of disease. Certain guidelines have proven useful in this respect. 115,

The illness should be consistent with one or more syndromes associated with mycobacterial infection.

Other causes of disease, such as TB and fungi, should be excluded.

The mycobacterial species isolated is one associated with human disease. The most significant are those that are not common environmental contaminants (M. kansasii, M. marinum, M. simiae, M. szulgai, and M. ulcerans).

The site of isolation of the organism should favor true infection versus contamination or colonization. (Isolation from bone biopsy, synovial tissue, or synovial fluid strongly suggests infection; isolation from the respiratory tract may represent infection or colonization.)

Heavier growth suggests significant infection.

Repeatedly positive cultures suggest significant infection.

Because laboratory identification of the organism and sensitivity - testing may take weeks to months, initial therapy often includes multiple drugs to cover both TB and other mycobacteria. One common approach to initial empiric therapy is to link standard IREZ therapy for TB with clarithromycin or azithromycin until final culture results are available. The guidelines for the treatment of nontuberculous mycobacteria were published in 2007 and then updated in 2016 for pulmonary infection.121,121a a Surgical debridement of infected tissue may play an important role in the treatment of selected patients, especially for resistant organisms. The most efficacious drugs remain controversial, prolonged treatment is often necessary, and relapses are common. Therapy customized to the individual patient is crucial with nontuberculous mycobacteria infection. The key to effective therapy lies in the unique characteristics of the culture and sensitivity of the particular isolate.

### Emergence of Nontuberculous Mycobacterial Infections During the Treatment of Rheumatic Diseases

No published data exist on the risk of NTM infections in the setting of therapy with nonbiologic disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs, including methotrexate. The decision to interrupt or continue therapy in such instances should be made on a caseby-case basis and should involve an infectious disease specialist, recognizing that alternative treatments, such as steroids and biologics, may carry an even greater risk.

NTM are increasingly recognized as important pathogens in patients receiving a TNF inhibitor. Indeed, these infections now occur twice as frequently as TB in the United States, presumably because of the use of screening tests for the latter. The complexity of these infections was illustrated by a review of 239 cases of NTM infection reported to the MedWatch database, in which only 105 were established to be probable or confirmed according to established disease criteria. The most commonly reported presentation was in elderly women with RA, possibly because both NTM infections and RA are more common in this group; most patients were also taking concomitant steroids and/ or methotrexate. Infections with several different species within this group have occurred, with MAC the most common. As with TB, the risk appears to be associated with all drugs in the class, rather than a specific agent, although more infections have occurred with infliximab. Extrapulmonary disease is a common finding, which is unusual for these organisms. A paradoxical response to therapy, similar to that seen with TB, has been reported with treatment of MAC following infliximab. Not all patients with NTM lung disease will deteriorate on TNF inhibitor therapy, but some patients worsen despite administration of anti-NTM therapy. . Nevertheless, cessation of TNF inhibitor therapy should be strongly considered following the development of an atypical mycobacterial infection. Continuation or reintroduction of TNF inhibitors during treatment of NTM infections has occurred. 125,

Managing the risk of NTM infections in the setting of TNF inhibitor treatment can be challenging. Although screening has been helpful in reducing the risk of TB infection in this setting, there is no currently available method of screening for atypical mycobacteria. Because these infections are more common in individuals with pre-existing pulmonary disease, clinicians may wish to consider more extensive evaluation of RA patients with bronchiectasis about to initiate TNF inhibitor therapy. Although MAC prophylaxis is recommended for HIV-infected patients with CD4 counts of 50 or less, there is no experience with, and no guidelines for, such prophylaxis with TNF inhibitor therapy. The complex nature of these infections has been further demonstrated by a case of M. marinum mimicking RA, with synovitis and subcutaneous nodules developing during infliximab therapy.

### KEYI POINTS

Fungi are an infrequent but clinically important cause of bone and joint infections. These infections are often indolent in onset and may masquerade as other disorders. Travel and immigration have affected the geographic localization of several important fungal infections, which may be seen in nonendemic areas. Although diagnosis may be assisted by clinical presentation and serologic and antigen testing, histologic examination and culture of infected tissue are critical. Rheumatologists should be particularly careful when treating atypical cases of subacute arthritis or tenosynovitis with local and systemic corticosteroids when infection with atypical pathogens, including fungi, has not been ruled out. New antifungal therapies have broadened the effective options, but choice of drugs, duration of treatment, and combined surgical débridement must be carefully considered to achieve optimal outcomes. Immunocompromise, including anti-rheumatic biologic therapies, may predispose to fungal infections, often resulting in more acute and widely disseminated disease. Screening and/or prophylactic therapy have not proven useful for patients on immunosuppressive therapy, so a high index of suspicion should be maintained when such patients present with an acute illness.

### Introduction

Fungal infection is a relatively infrequent but important cause of osteomyelitis and arthritis. Fungal diseases that commonly cause osteomyelitis include blastomycosis, coccidioidomycosis, cryptococcosis, candidiasis, and sporotrichosis (Table 115.1). Fungal arthritis is less common and also most often associated with these same fungal pathogens but occasionally other species. The epidemiology of these fungal infections, their musculoskeletal presentations, and their treatment are considered in this chapter.

The epidemiology and clinical features of individual deep mycoses may suggest the diagnosis in some cases, but their indolent presentation, which often resembles that of other noninfectious diseases, may be misleading. Travel and immigration have blurred their geographic localization. Infection may be acute and overwhelming in immunocompromised patients, for whom

disseminated fungal infections are a major risk. Anti-cytokine and other immunosuppressive treatments for rheumatic diseases, particularly those targeting TNF, are associated with disseminated fungal infection,1,2 as are HIV infection, pregnancy, and treatments for transplantation and malignancies. Fungal arthritis has also occurred following intra-articular injection of contaminated preservative-free methylprednisolone. For rheumatologists, disseminated fungal infections are an important diagnostic consideration in some patients and must be considered before starting biologic treatments in those at risk; they may also complicate the clinical course of other arthritides. The presentation of fungal infections as a consequence of rheumatic disease therapy will also be considered in this chapter.

Fungal infections are typically diagnosed by histologic examination or culture of involved tissues. Improved molecular diagnostic techniques may facilitate the diagnosis, provided the possibility of fungal infection is considered and appropriate studies are requested. Synovial fluid leukocyte counts and culture results vary among fungal infections and in individual cases and may be misleading. Serologic testing may also assist in diagnosing and staging several fungal infections. Detecting fungal antigens and fungal RNA in blood, urine, other body fluids, and tissue may help with diagnosis in selected circumstances.

### Coccidioidomycosis

Coccidioidomycosis is endemic to the southwestern United States and areas of Central and South America, but cases are increasingly diagnosed in nonendemic areas because of travel and reactivation of remote infection. The soil fungi Coccidioides immitis and Coccidioides posadasii generally cause a primary respiratory illness following inhalation of the infectious fungal spores or arthroconidia from the environment. The risk of acquisition increases when soil is disturbed and in windy conditions. A self-limited acute pneumonia may result, associated with systemic manifestations such as arthralgia and erythema nodosum (valley fever), but infection is often inapparent and only infrequently becomes chronic or disseminated. Human-to-human transmission does not occur. Extrapulmonary infection is almost always caused by hematogenous spread from an initial pulmonary focus. The bones and joints are frequent sites of dissemination, particularly in immunocompromised hosts.

Septic arthritis of the knee is common, generally arising from direct infection of the synovium. Other joint infections are caused

by spread from a contiguous osteomyelitis involving the vertebrae, wrists, hands, ankles, feet, pelvis, and long bones. The onset is characterized by gradually increasing pain and joint stiffness with little swelling but early radiographic changes. In one series, arthritis was the only manifestation of disseminated coccidioidomycosis in 51 of 57 patients and was an aspect of more generalized disease in the remaining 6 patients.

Diagnostic confusion is common in osteoarticular coccidioidomycosis because of the delayed dissemination (months to years) after primary infection and because of atypical clinical presentations. The criteria for diagnosis include compatible clinical features, serologic studies, histologic examination, and culture. Enzyme-linked immunoassays (EIAs) for immunoglobulin M (IgM) and IgG are the most sensitive screening tests, and immunodiffusion assays are less sensitive but more specific. Quantitative complement fixation antibody levels are useful for monitoring the effect of treatment. Serologic testing for Coccidioides may have negative results early in the infection and in immunosuppressed patients. A specific EIA to Coccidioides galactomannan antigen in urine has shown promise in the diagnosis of severe coccidioidomycosis infection.9, The definitive diagnosis is most commonly made by the demonstration of granulomatous synovitis and typical spherules in a biopsy specimen, confirmed by positive culture. Synovial fluid, when obtainable, might not demonstrate septic leukocyte counts and could have a lymphocyte predominance. Synovial fluid is rarely culture positive; culture of synovial tissue may be more helpful. Radioisotope bone scans may be helpful to identify areas of infection.

With early diagnosis of effusive synovitis, antifungal treatment alone is appropriate. Treatment is usually initiated with oral azole antifungal agents, most commonly fluconazole or itraconazole. Amphotericin B is recommended if lesions are worsening rapidly or are in particularly critical locations, such as the vertebral osteomyelitis. Lipid formulations of amphotericin B have demonstrated less nephrotoxicity and infusion-related side effects than conventional deoxycholate amphotericin B and may be given at doses higher than those tolerated with conventional amphotericin. A recent meta-analysis showed similar efficacy with conventional and lipid-based amphotericin B formulations, with a better safety profile for the latter. With more widely disseminated infection or involvement of critical areas such as the spine and in highrisk hosts, the choice and duration of treatments are often complicated. Factors that favor surgical intervention are large-sized

abscesses, progressive enlargement of abscesses or destructive lesions, presence of bony sequestrations, instability of the spine, or impingement on critical organs or tissues (e.g., epidural abscess compressing the spinal cord).8, Newer antifungal agents such as voriconazole and posaconazole show promise as alternative therapy. 12, Long-term prophylaxis with fluconazole can limit the risk for reactivation in immunosuppressed patients.

Coccidioidal synovitis may also occur as a consequence of immune complex-mediated inflammation, a presentation that may complicate either primary pulmonary or disseminated disease and is typically polyarticular. It is accompanied by fever, erythema nodosum or erythema multiforme, eosinophilia, and hilar adenopathy. It abates in 2 to 4 weeks.6,19

### Blastomycosis

Blastomycosis, caused by Blastomyces dermatitidis, is endemic in the northern-central and southern United States. Infection is acquired by inhalation of conidia associated with decaying vegetation or decomposing wood and typically results in sporadic or less commonly clustered cases of acute or chronic pneumonia. Affected individuals do not appear to have any distinguishing or predisposing characteristics except for exposure to the organism during work or recreation. Clinical presentation includes pulmonary, skin, and bone involvement. About half of affected patients will present with fever; leukocytosis and an elevated sedimentation rate are frequently seen. Bone pain, swelling, and soft tissue abscesses are the most common manifestations of osteoarticular disease. Hematogenous dissemination is common; skin disease and osteoarticular disease occur most frequently. Bone involvement occurs in 25% to 60% of disseminated cases, and arthritis is estimated to occur in 3% to 5%. In a study of 45 patients with skeletal blastomycosis, 41 had osteomyelitis, while 12 presented with septic arthritis. In another series of 14 cases at a single institution, 12 presented as a bone mass; 3 of 4 cases of septic arthritis in this series developed due to direct extension of osteomyelitis. The skeletal areas most commonly affected are the long bones, vertebrae, and ribs (Fig. 115.1).23-26 Blastomycosis often mimics malignancy with subtle constitutional symptoms, nodular lung opacities, and lytic bone lesions.

Arthritis is usually monoarticular in the knee, ankle, or elbow but may rarely be polyarticular.21, Joint infection is an isolated skeletal disorder in only a few cases; joint radiographs more commonly show punched-out bone lesions (Fig. 115.2A). Synovial fluid is commonly purulent, but B. dermatitidis is not visualized with routine Gram stain and does not grow on routine culture media. Diagnosis is often delayed if specimens are not cultured on fungal media. The synovial histologic examination shows granulomas and abundant neutrophils—a so-called pyogranulomatous tissue response. Broad-based budding yeast forms may be seen (Fig. 115.2B). The yeast can be difficult to visualize with routine hematoxylin and eosin stains, but special stains, such as the Gomori methenamine silver (GMS) stain or periodic acidSchiff (PAS) stain, can be helpful. The diagnosis is also frequently made from involved nonarticular sites. Urinary antigen testing may be less sensitive than previously believed, particularly for nonpulmonary infection, but remains useful for monitoring response to therapy. For moderately severe or severe disease, treatment with amphotericin B for 1 to 2 weeks or until improvement is noted, followed by oral itraconazole for a total of at least 12 months, is recommended. For mild to moderate disease, oral itraconazole for 12 months is recommended. Serum levels of itraconazole should

be measured after the patient has been on treatment for at least 2 weeks, to ensure adequate drug exposure. 20,30-32

### Cryptococcosis

Cryptococcus neoformans, the fungus causing cryptococcosis, is geographically ubiquitous and is found in soil contaminated by pigeon feces; a related species, Cryptococcus gattii, is associated with certain types of eucalyptus trees in tropical climates and has been associated with an ongoing outbreak of disease in British Columbia, Canada, and the Pacific Northwest region of the United States. Risk of illness is increased in individuals with defects in cell-mediated immunity, including advanced HIV infection, organ and stem cell transplantation, lymphoreticular malignant neoplasms, TNF inhibitor treatment, and corticosteroid therapy. Concomitant corticosteroid use is a significant risk factor for cryptococcal and other fungal infections in patients receiving TNF inhibitor treatment.

Cryptococcosis is acquired by inhalation, and illness varies in acuity. It usually affects the lungs in its primary form, but it sometimes disseminates hematogenously to a wide variety of sites, including the CNS and skin. Bone infection is common, causing osteolytic lesions in 5% to 10% of cases, but articular involvement is reported rarely (Fig. 115.3).37, As seen in blastomycosis, bone lesions may mimic metastatic neoplasm (Fig. 115.4).

Cryptococcal arthritis presents as an indolent monoarticular arthritis in about 60% of reported cases and as polyarthritis in the remainder.39, The knee is most commonly involved. The majority of cases reported from the pre-AIDS era also demonstrated radiographic evidence of periarticular osteomyelitis. These patients were young adults, did not have debilitating disease or other evidence of dissemination, and had pulmonary involvement in only 50% of cases. Synovial tissue showed acute and chronic synovitis, multinucleate giant cells, prominent granuloma formation, and large numbers of budding yeast with special stains. Most recently reported cases are associated with immunosuppression and disseminated infection. Interestingly, osteoarticular cryptococcal infections have

been linked to sarcoidosis, although it is unclear whether this association relates to the immunologic impact of the sarcoidosis or to the immunosuppressive therapies used to treat it. Serum cryptococcal antigen testing appears to be very sensitive, in part because osteoarticular infection results from hematogenous dissemination. The choice of treatment for cryptococcal disease depends on both the anatomic sites of involvement and the host's immune status, with amphotericin B and fluconazole being considered most effective.40,42 5-Flucytosine is typically added to amphotericin B or fluconazole for the first 2 to 4 weeks (induction therapy) in cases of severe cryptococcal infection. .

### Candidiasis

Candida species are widely distributed in nature. Candida albicans is a normal commensal of humans, and other species can probably live in nonanimate environments such as soil. Since the advent of antibiotic therapy in the 1940s and related to the common use of immunosuppression and parenteral lines, candidiasis has been responsible for an increasing incidence of mucocutaneous and deep-organ infections. Osteomyelitis, although uncommon, is a potentially serious complication of hematogenous dissemination in both adults and children.45-47 A recent review identified a history of preceding candidemia in half of osteomyelitis cases, while it was the first proven site of infection in the other half. It may bone infection may emerge after successful treatment of infection at other sites. Bone infection is commonly located in two adjacent vertebrae or in a single long bone,50 although a few patients have had multiple sites of involvement. Candidal prosthetic joint infections may also occur as a late consequence of total joint replacement.

The usual clinical presentation is localized pain. Other symptoms and laboratory abnormalities vary. It can present months after an episode of fungemia, and clinical manifestations tend to be milder than bacterial infections at the same sites. This can lead to long delays in diagnosis. Bone changes of osteomyelitis are commonly demonstrated in radiographs of the symptomatic site. The diagnosis is established when a culture of involved bone obtained by either open or needle biopsy has identified a variety of Candida species. C. albicans causes the majority of infections, but the role of nonalbicans species has been increasing in recent years. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing

of blood may allow earlier diagnosis of disseminated Candida infection, although it is not yet widely available.
