Treatment with azoles (fluconazole, itraconazole, voriconazole, posaconazole, or isavuconazole), echinocandins (caspofungin, micafungin, or anidulafungin), or amphotericin B formulations can be effective.50, Species identification and susceptibility testing assist antifungal therapy selection (note that the nomenclature of some species has recently been updated). For example, Nakaseomyces glabrata (formerly Candida glabrata) frequently demonstrate dose-dependent susceptibility to azole antifungal agents (e.g., requiring higher doses of fluconazole for treatment) but remain susceptible to echinocandins; Pichia kudreiavzevii (formerly Candida krusei) are often resistant to fluconazole and may show reduced susceptibility to amphotericin but remain susceptible to newer azoles and the echinocandins; Clavispora lusitaniae (formerly Candida lusitaniae) are often resistant to amphotericin; and Candida parapsilosis may demonstrate reduced susceptibility to echinocandins (but they remain clinically active). Candida auris has emerged recently as a cause of outbreak of nosocomial infection. C. auris is notable because some strains are multidrug resistant and refractory to treatment. The use of surgical débridement must be individualized. With vertebral involvement but no neurologic complications, medical therapy alone has been effective.

Candidiasis is an uncommon cause of monoarticular arthritis. C. albicans is the most common pathogen, although septic arthritis due to other candidal species has occurred. Reported cases commonly involve a knee, occur in the context of multifocal extra-articular Candida infection, and are accompanied by constitutional symptoms. Both children and adults have been affected. Predisposing conditions include gastrointestinal and pulmonary disorders, narcotic addiction, intravenous catheters, leukopenia, immunosuppressive treatment (including TNF inhibitors), broad-spectrum antibiotics, and corticosteroids. Some involved joints were previously affected by arthritis, and infection has followed arthrocentesis in isolated cases. In most cases, radiographs reveal coincident osteomyelitis. Synovial fluid leukocyte counts may vary; Candida species have been cultured from synovial fluid in all cases but are not commonly identified on smear. Histologic studies of synovium show nonspecific chronic inflammation rather than granulomas. Mucocutaneous Candida infection has occurred in patients treated with the interleukin (IL)-17 inhibitors secukinumab and ixekizumab, but the risk of infection appears low and infections have been mild, resolving spontaneously or with standard therapy. 59-61

### Sporotrichosis

Sporotrichosis is caused by Sporothrix schenckii, a saprophyte found widely in soil and plants. Infection in humans occurs through inoculation of the skin or, rarely, inhalation into the respiratory tract; it is a source of infection among agricultural workers in tropical and subtropical areas. A zoonotic outbreak associated with Sporothrix brasiliensis transmitted by cats was recently reported in Brazil. It most commonly involves the skin and lymphatics but may disseminate from the lungs to the CNS, eyes, bones, and joints. In immunocompetent hosts, a single site is typically involved; in immunocompromised hosts, including patients on anticytokine therapy, multifocal disease may occur.

In contrast to the relatively common occurrence of skin infection, articular sporotrichosis is a rare disorder. 65, In 84% of patients in one series, there was no accompanying skin

involvement, suggesting entry through the lungs. Sporotrichosis most often occurs in individuals with a chronic illness that alters host defense, such as alcoholism or a myeloproliferative disorder. Sporothrix arthritis is most often indolent and infects a single joint or multiple joints in equal proportions. The knee, hand, wrist, elbow, and shoulder are most frequently involved; hand and wrist involvement distinguishes this from other fungal arthritides. Articular infection shows a propensity to spread to adjacent soft tissues, forming draining sinuses. Constitutional symptoms are unusual.

Radiographic changes vary from juxta-articular osteopenia to the commonly observed punched-out bone lesions. When it can be obtained, synovial fluid is inflammatory. Synovitis is characterized on gross evaluation by destructive pannus and on microscopic examination by granulomatous histologic features or, less frequently, by nonspecific inflammation. Organisms are difficult to identify in tissue, and the diagnosis is often made by positive culture of joint fluid or involved tissue. Incubation at room temperature facilitates growth of the mycelial phase of S. schenckii. Serologic testing is not useful in the diagnosis of sporotrichosis. In a small number of cases, sporotrichosis may disseminate to cause a potentially fatal infection characterized by low-grade fever, weight loss, anemia, osteolytic bone lesions, arthritis, skin lesions, and involvement of the eyes and CNS.67-70 These infections occur in immunosuppressed patients with either hematologic malignancies or HIV infection.

Amphotericin B and itraconazole have been effective in the therapy of systemic sporotrichosis, including osteoarticular disease. In contrast, fluconazole is only modestly successful in osteoarticular sporotrichosis.72,73

### Aspergillosis

Aspergillus species are ubiquitous, but infection occurs only rarely in immunocompetent individuals. In contrast, invasive infection is an important life-threatening complication in immunocompromised adults and children.74-78 It may spread directly from the lung to adjacent vertebrae, disk spaces, and ribs (more often in children) or through the bloodstream (Fig. 115.5).79-81 Rare cases of monoarthritis with adjacent osteomyelitis are also reported. The knee is the most commonly involved joint. The organism may be observed in infected tissue (Fig. 115.5B). The galactomannan EIA has been validated as a surrogate marker for invasive aspergillosis, and the (1→3)-β-D-glucan assay similarly may provide support for the diagnosis of invasive fungal infection. Treatment with combined surgical débridement and antifungal therapy is an ongoing challenge.75, Voriconazole has proven superior to amphotericin for the treatment of invasive aspergillosis and is now recommended for initial therapy. 78, Liposomal amphotericin B; alternative azoles including posaconazole and isavuconazole; and the echinocandins caspofungin, micafungin, and anidulafungin have demonstrated efficacy in salvage situations. Combination therapy has not demonstrated clear improvement in outcomes over monotherapy. In 2012 an outbreak of fungal infections, initially believed to be due to Aspergillus fumigatus but later attributed to the rarely pathogenic fungus Exserohilum rostratum, was traced to contaminated injectable methylprednisolone produced by a single compounding pharmacy in Massachusetts.4, The index case involved A. fumigatus meningitis following an epidural injection; subsequent cases included meningitis, stroke, and musculoskeletal infections, including vertebral osteomyelitis, diskitis, and facet joint infections. 86,87

### Histoplasmosis

Histoplasma capsulatum is a soil fungus that causes endemic disease in the Midwest and the southeastern United States. 39, Bone and joint involvement is rare but has been described in the knee, wrist, and ankle. Immunosuppression, including the use of TNF inhibitors, predisposes to disseminated histoplasmosis in adults and children, which may be confused clinically with sarcoidosis, tuberculosis, or reactive inflammatory conditions.89-92 Diagnosis depends on appropriate use of fungal staining and culture and antigen detection. A case report emphasizes the rare occurrence of fungal prosthetic joint arthritis. The more common osteoarticular involvement with histoplasmosis is a hypersensitivity syndrome accompanying acute pulmonary infection; it is characterized by self-limited polyarthritis, erythema nodosum, and erythema multiforme. Liposomal amphotericin B followed by itraconazole is the preferred treatment for severe infection and itraconazole for less severe cases. 88,95,96

### Scedosporiosis

Scedosporium species are environmental molds that have been identified as fungal pathogens in both immunocompetent and immunocompromised hosts. They may cause focally invasive and disseminated infection after cutaneous inoculation. Scedosporium prolificans has a predilection for bone and cartilage, leading to both septic arthritis and osteomyelitis. Infections are difficult to eradicate with surgery and antifungal agents, and the organism is resistant to amphotericin.97, Voriconazole or combination therapy is the currently recommended treatment approach.

### Treatment of Fungal Infection

Antifungal chemotherapy has improved over the past several decades, first with the introduction of amphotericin B and then with the oral antifungal agents flucytosine, ketoconazole, fluconazole, and itraconazole. More recent advances include the development of less toxic formulations of amphotericin B, liposomal amphotericin B, and amphotericin B lipid complex. Voriconazole, posaconazole, and isavuconazole are broad-spectrum azole antifungals; all have improved activity against aspergillosis, and posaconazole and isavuconazole have activity against mucormycosis. The echinocandin antifungal agents caspofungin, micafungin, and anidulafungin have emerged as alternative therapies for aspergillosis and as the treatments of choice for some Candida infections. For detailed treatment guidelines, several excellent reviews are available.100-110 In choosing an appropriate drug (Table 115.2) and course of treatment, the clinician must consider the infecting agent, clinical manifestations of the disease, immune status of the host, anti-microbial resistance, drug side effect profile, and direct and indirect costs of treatment. Treatment has become more complex because of immune system compromise in infected patients treated for transplant rejection, autoimmune disorders, malignant disease, and AIDS.

Itraconazole has become the first choice for treatment of the endemic mycoses—blastomycosis, histoplasmosis, and sporotrichosis. A loading dose of itraconazole of 200 mg three times a day for 3 days is recommended, followed by 200 to 400 mg daily. Absorption of itraconazole is unpredictable, and blood levels of itraconazole should be measured to ensure adequate drug exposure. Absorption of itraconazole requires stomach acid, so concurrent administration of drugs that reduce the acidity of the

stomach such as proton pump inhibitors and H2 blockers should be avoided. A liquid formulation of itraconazole has demonstrated improved absorption over the pill formulation. At least 6 months of treatment is required, and some patients may need up to a year of therapy. For cryptococcosis, fluconazole is the recommended azole.40, Amphotericin B is the preferred drug for meningeal and life-threatening infections, preferably given in combination with oral flucytosine. Specific treatment protocols and detailed side effect profiles are presented in reviews, Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA) guidelines, 12,32,43,54,84,96 and infection-specific references (see Table 115.2). Surgical débridement is critically important in the treatment of mucormycosis and may be of value as adjunctive treatment for other fungal infections, including selected patients with invasive aspergillosis and vertebral osteomyelitis caused by coccidioidomycosis—especially when there is evidence of spinal cord impingement or progression on repeat imaging on antifungal therapy. Surgery does not play a major role in the treatment of blastomycosis, histoplasmosis, or Pneumocystis jirovecii infection.

### Fungal Infection as a Consequence e of Antirheumatic Therapy

Many of the same fungal pathogens associated with osteoarticular infections may cause infection in patients treated with antirheumatic therapy, particularly biologic therapy. Animal models of infection point to an important role for TNF in host defense against many of these organisms, including Aspergillus, Candida, 114,115Coccidioides,116 113 Cryptococcus, and Sporothrix.

Coccidioidomycosis infection following TNF inhibitor therapy has occurred in endemic areas in the southwestern United States. In the largest published series, 12 of 13 cases followed therapy with infliximab, and 1 was associated with etanercept. All but two of these cases were believed to represent new infection rather than reactivation. In one medical center included in this series, the relative risk of coccidioidomycosis infection was 5.23 with infliximab therapy compared with other anti-rheumatic therapies. In all cases, coccidioidomycosis infection developed in the absence of other known risk factors, including diabetes, pregnancy, and HIV infection. Updated data from the same institutions, however, have suggested that biologic or nonbiologic disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drug (DMARD) treatment can potentially be

reinstituted during or after antifungal therapy. Coccidioidomycosis infection has also occurred in nonendemic areas, presumably as a consequence of fomite exposure.

Disseminated histoplasmosis infections have been reported following TNF inhibitor therapy in endemic areas in the Ohio— Mississippi River valley regions of the central United States; as with coccidioidomycosis infections, these occurred more frequently following infliximab therapy than with the other agents. The reason for the larger number of cases with infliximab is unclear; possibilities include a unique mechanism of action for infliximab, larger numbers of patients treated, patient selection, concomitant immunosuppressive therapy, or some combination of all of these. In most cases, patients developing disseminated histoplasmosis with TNF inhibitor therapy have been taking additional immunosuppressive therapy. In a series of 26 patients with histoplasmosis and rheumatoid arthritis (RA), TNF inhibitors (including adalimumab, etanercept, and infliximab), methotrexate, and corticosteroids were all implicated as potential contributing factors. 121 In a case-control series using commercial health claims data, corticosteroid use was a significant risk factor for the development of mycobacterial and fungal infections in patients treated with TNF inhibitors; the majority of these infections were tuberculosis and histoplasmosis. Patients with histoplasmosis typically present with cough, dyspnea, fever, and malaise and can rapidly become quite ill. Histoplasma antigen may be identified in the urine in 92% of cases with disseminated histoplasmosis, and this test may facilitate rapid diagnosis. Exposure to Histoplasma may result in asymptomatic latent infection; it has been difficult, however, to determine whether symptomatic infections following TNF inhibitor therapy represent reactivation or new infection. Both pulmonary and disseminated infections with cryptococcal infections have occurred with TNF inhibitors, as have infections with Aspergillus, Candida, Scedosporium, and Sporothrix.1,

P. jirovecii pneumonia (PJP) is caused by a fungus originally classified as a protozoan (Pneumocystis carinii). PJP, an opportunistic infection commonly seen in patients with advanced HIV infection, has occurred with a number of anti-rheumatic therapies, including cyclophosphamide and low-dose methotrexate, often in combination with corticosteroid therapy. 126, Interestingly, PJP as a consequence of low-dose methotrexate therapy is a particular concern in Japan, where one group identified the prevalence of asymptomatic carriage of Pneumocystis being as high as 18.8% in the elderly. These same authors have suggested that PCR testing may identify carriers at increased risk for PJP during therapy. The use of biologic therapy, including rituximab130 and TNF inhibitors,131 has been associated with the development of PJP. A recent analysis of data from the British Society of Rheumatology Biologics Register suggested that the rate of Pneumocystis infection was significantly higher with rituximab than with TNF inhibitor therapy, although the overall incidence of opportunistic infection did not differ among biologic therapies. PJP presents as fever, dry cough, and dyspnea. The clinical presentation in patients receiving immunosuppressive therapy is typically more acute than in HIV-associated cases. Organisms may be identified in sputum from HIV patients but are seen less commonly in rheumatologic patients; presumptive diagnosis may be made on the basis of PCR testing for P. jirovecii DNA. Elevated serum levels of β-D-glucan, a common component of fungal cell walls, may aid in the diagnosis. One series of 21 patients identified older age, pre-existing pulmonary disease, higher corticosteroid doses, and low serum albumin and IgG levels as potential risk factors for PJP in patients treated

with infliximab. Chest radiographs characteristically show bilateral diffuse infiltrates, while CT scans demonstrate groundglass opacities (Figs. 115.6 and 115.7); radiographic findings may be difficult to distinguish from methotrexate pneumonitis. Treatment includes supplemental oxygen and trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole (TMP/SMX) or pentamidine isethionate. Highdose corticosteroids are commonly used as adjunctive therapy in the treatment of HIV patients with severe PJP but are less well studied in patients taking immunosuppressive therapy.

PJP infection is also of concern with nonbiologic immunosuppressive therapy. In particular, the use of cyclophosphamide to treat systemic lupus, vasculitis, and other autoimmune diseases has been associated with a risk of developing PJP, although the overall risk appears to be low. In a review of published data on 76,156 cases of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) treated with cyclophosphamide, the risk of PJP was 15.88 per 10,000 patients, or 0.158%. Potential risk factors include high-dose

corticosteroid use, lymphopenia (especially low CD4 counts), 126,133Vasculitis renal disease, and overall high disease activity. patients with pulmonary involvement may be at increased risk, and diagnosis may be difficult in both these patients and lupus patients with pulmonary disease. Unfortunately, there are no published guidelines to address the use of PJP prophylaxis in autoimmune diseases, nor a clear consensus regarding the standard of care in this situation. Recent clinical trials in vasculitis have routinely employed PJP prophylaxis as part of the protocol, suggesting it may become a standard approach. Two recent surveys of U.S. rheumatologists, however, found that just 50.4% and 69.5%, respectively, routinely prescribed prophylactic antibiotics.126, Academic rheumatologists and more recent graduates are more likely to prescribe prophylactic therapy. TMP/ SMZ appears to be more effective than dapsone or aerosolized pentamidine, despite an apparent increased risk of sulfonamide allergy in the lupus population.136, There a re n o consistent standards or recommendations for the use of prophylaxis for fungal infection other than Pneumocystis.

Unlike mycobacterial infection, biologic therapy of rheumatic disease has not been definitively a ssociated w ith a n increased overall risk of fungal infection, although the lack of a statistically significant a ssociation w ith these rare infections cannot disprove a possible connection. . Indeed, fungal infections have occurred in a post-marketing biologic registry in France. In general, patients with a history of fungal infection or those with significant e xposure to these o rganisms should receive biologic therapy only when alternatives are not available or appropriate. Patients should be cautioned to minimize exposure to sources of infection during therapy (e.g., avoid exposure to histoplasmosis in old buildings [demolition, remodeling, cleaning], chicken coops, bird roosts, wood piles, or caves [spelunking]) and avoid exposure to outdoor dust in regions endemic for coccidioidomycosis. Patients receiving concomitant corticosteroid therapy may warrant closer observation during therapy.

In general, there remains little practical role for screening for latent fungal infection or for prophylactic therapy. Serologic tests and delayed-type hypersensitivity testing do not distinguish past, resolved infection from latent infection, although repeat coccidioidomycosis serologies have been proposed as part of an algorithm for determining the potential safety of reinstituting biologic therapy after treatment of an acute, nondisseminated infection. In regions where coccidiodomycosis is endemic, some have proposed screening and managing asymptomatic infections prior to prescribing TNF inhibitors, although there is, as yet, little data to demonstrate that this reduces the risk of symptomatic infections with therapy. Chest radiographs may identify calcified granulomas consistent with prior histoplasmosis infection, but this is a nonspecific fi nding. In Ja pan, it ha s be en su ggested th at TM P/ SMX therapy may normalize PCR testing in asymptomatic P jirovecii carriers treated with methotrexate and that this might reduce the risk of developing pneumonia, but this has not been studied in a U.S. population. 129 The lack of useful screening tests makes early recognition of infection and institution of therapy critical. Indeed, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has mandated a "black box" warning regarding the risk of fungal infections on the product labels of TNF inhibitors, reflecting the potentially fatal consequences of delayed recognition of such infections.

# Rheumatic Manifestations of Immunodeficiency Human Virus Infection

### KEY POINTS

### Introduction

In the years since acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS) was initially described in 1981, human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) has become one of the leading global health crises. According to new data in UNAIDS Global AIDS Update 2022, trends in HIV infections and AIDS-related deaths are driven by the availability of HIV services. In 2021 new infections fell globally at only 3.6% compared with 2020—the smallest annual reduction since 2016—demonstrating that global progress is slowing rather than accelerating. The rates of new HIV infections are still occurring at alarming rates in certain regions such as southern Africa, eastern Europe, and central and eastern Asia. An estimated 38.4 million people worldwide are living with HIV (Fig. 116.1). Approximately 1.5 million people became newly infected with HIV in 2021, and 650,000 people died. Worldwide, there were

0.84 males per female living with HIV in 2019, although the rate of new infections and deaths from HIV were approximately the same in both genders. One encouraging note was that the incidence of new cases and death fell more significantly in Sub- Saharan Africa (with a 28%52% decrease in incident cases and a 39%66% decrease in deaths), although the incidence remained stable or increased, whereas deaths generally decreased, elsewhere.

Progress in dealing with the HIV epidemic, including in education and in public health awareness, has undoubtedly influenced the decrease in new infections seen among young people in some countries in recent years. While availability of newer treatment strategies and better access to health care has resulted in increased life expectancy, HIV-1 infection will be managed increasingly as a chronic illness, and complications, such as musculoskeletal and rheumatic conditions associated with HIV infection and its treatment and illnesses associated with the later years of life, are expected to increase (Tables 116.1 and 116.2).

Among the rheumatologic disorders, clinicians face the challenge of treating potentially disabling inflammatory disorders with immunosuppressive therapy in the face of ongoing viral-induced immunocompromise. Diagnosing infection is especially important in an immunocompromised patient because the probability of a musculoskeletal complication of an opportunistic infection increases with advancing stages of the patient's HIV disease. At early stages (CD4+ count >200/μL), opportunistic infections are unlikely, although bacterial infections (especially tuberculosis) can still occur. Immunosuppressive drugs should be used with caution in this population.

### HIV-Associated Bone and Joint Disease

### HIV-Associated Arthralgia

As many as 25% of HIV-positive patients in recent series may have otherwise unexplained arthralgia.3, Arthralgias and myalgias also form a part of the constitutional symptoms of HIV-1 seroconversion. Whether arthralgia can be attributed to circulating viral

and host immune complexes caused by HIV infection per se or to other infections (e.g., hepatitis C) has not been determined. The pathogenesis is unclear but may involve circulating immune complexes, cytokines, or transient bone ischemia. However, patients presenting with arthralgia alone rarely progress to inflammatory

musculoskeletal disease. The most appropriate treatment consists of nonnarcotic analgesics and reassurance.

### Painful Articular Syndrome

Painful articular syndrome is self-limited and lasts less than 24 hours, is associated with few objective clinical findings, and is characterized by severe bone and joint pain.3, It occurs predominantly in the late stages of HIV infection. Its cause is unknown, and synovitis has not been described in these patients. The knee is most commonly affected, but elbows and shoulders can also be involved. Radiographic features are nonspecific; occasionally, periarticular osteopenia is seen. Treatment is symptomatic. Given the abrupt nature of this disorder's onset, these patients are more likely to be encountered in emergency departments and not in HIV clinics.

### HIV-Associated Arthritis

The first reports of a seronegative arthritis associated with HIV infection appeared in 1988,4 with frequencies up to 12%. HIVassociated arthritis is most common in Sub-Saharan Africa, where HIV-1 infection is pandemic. In the Congo, where the seroprevalence of HIV infection was previously 7% to 8%, AIDS had been the leading cause of aseptic arthritis (60% of cases). This is usually an oligoarthritis (Table 116.3), predominantly involving the lower extremities, and tends to be self-limited, lasting less than 6 weeks. The most commonly involved joints are the knees, ankles, and metatarsophalangeal joints, and secondarily the wrists, elbows, and metacarpophalangeal and interphalangeal joints, similar to other viral arthritides. Some patients have been reported as having a longer, more chronic course with joint damage.7,

The origin is unclear; no association has been noted with human leukocyte antigen (HLA)-B27 or any other known genetic factor. Synovial fluid cultures are typically sterile, although one report described the presence of tubuloreticular inclusions, suggesting a

viral origin, possibly HIV itself. Radiographs of affected joints are usually normal, except in uncommon cases with prolonged symptoms, in which joint space narrowing and destruction can occur. Treatment includes nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and, in more severe cases, low-dose glucocorticoids. Hydroxychloroquine and sulfasalazine have also been used. In more recent studies in children, combination anti-retroviral and immunomodulatory therapy was found to be effective.

### Reactive Arthritis Occurring in HIV Infection

Early reports in the United States suggested that reactive arthritis occurred more commonly in the setting of HIV infection;

however, later studies showed that this may be reflective of the sexually active nature of the population at highest risk for HIV infection. This contention is not borne out in studies from Sub-Saharan Africa, where HLA-B27 is rare, as were reports of spondyloarthritis before the HIV epidemic. With the arrival of AIDS, a dramatic upsurge in the prevalence of reactive arthritis and undifferentiated spondyloarthritis and, less often, psoriatic arthritis (PsA)8,12 has been reported, suggesting an influence of HIV infection,8,12 although in studies from Taiwan and Quebec, ankylosing spondylitis occurred less frequently than in HIV-negative individuals. 13,

The typical presentation is a seronegative lower-extremity peripheral arthritis, usually accompanied by enthesitis (dactylitis,

Achilles tendinitis, and plantar fasciitis). Mucocutaneous features are common, especially keratoderma blennorrhagicum (Fig. 116.2) and circinate balanitis. Extensive psoriasiform skin rashes can occur. The clinical overlap makes it difficult sometimes to distinguish HIV-associated reactive arthritis from PsA. Urethritis occurs in similar frequency as in HIV-negative reactive arthritis. Axial involvement and uveitis seem to be less common but do occur. Longitudinal studies from Africa have described an aggressive course with a poor prognosis.8,

HLA-B27 is found in 80% to 90% of patients with HIVassociated reactive arthritis, at least among Whites. Studies from Africa have found most patients to be HLA-B27 negative, however.8, It has been known for more than 27 years that the presence of HLA-B27 is associated with slower progression to AIDS. In asymptomatic HIV-infected, HLA-B27-positive individuals, cytotoxic T lymphocyte responses are dominated by recognition of a gag-encoded p24 protein epitope that is not seen in HIVpositive, HLA-B27-negative individuals.16, Other HLA alleles that have been associated with a better outcome in HIV infection have been implicated in psoriasis and PsA, including HLA-B13 and HLA-B57.16, Approximately half of Caucasian long-term nonprogressors have either HLÁ-B57 or HLA-B27.16 Other genetic and innate immune factors associated with nonprogression include delta32 CCR5 allelic associations and HLA-C/KIR interactions. HLA-B*57:03 was protective against HIV progression in a Zambian population but conferred susceptibility to spondyloarthritis. A recent study applying HLA imputation to genome-wide association study data for HIV-1 viral load in White European Americans, Africans, and Latinos pinpointed the MHC association to three amino acid positions (97, 67, and 156) marking three consecutive pockets (C, B, and D) within the HLA-B peptide-binding groove, explaining 12.9% of genetic susceptibility to HIV infection.

### Treatment

Treatment is similar to that for HIV-negative patients with reactive arthritis. NSAIDs are the mainstay, and in fact indomethacin has been shown to inhibit HIV replication in vitro, which seems to be unique to this NSAID. Patients frequently have an inadequate response to NSAIDs alone. Sulfasalazine was effective in some studies at doses of 1-3 g/day, and one study suggested that it ameliorated HIV infection. Methotrexate was initially believed to

be contraindicated because of its immunosuppressive effect, but with careful monitoring of HIV viral loads, CD4 counts, and the patient's clinical status, more recent studies have suggested a place for methotrexate in the treatment of reactive arthritis and PsA occurring in the setting of HIV-1 infection.

Hydroxychloroquine is efficacious not only in treating HIVassociated reactive arthritis but also in reducing HIV replication in vitro and in reducing HIV viral loads in vivo. Arthritis and the cutaneous lesions of HIV-associated reactive arthritis and PsA have been found to respond to etretinate (0.5 to 1 mg/kg/day), 25 although because of the side effects of this drug, its use should be reserved for patients unresponsive to or unable to use other treatments. Tumor necrosis factor (TNF) blockers have been used,26-29 although these agents should be used with caution and only in patients with CD4+ counts greater than 200/μL and HIV viral loads less than 60,000 copies/mm. .26-29 One prospective study of 17 HIV patients with spondyloarthritis, PsA, or rheumatoid arthritis (RÅ) found TNF blockers effective and safe for as long as 20 years when these precautions were followed at initiation of therapy. In this report, anti-interleukin (IL)-17A agents (secukinumab, ixekizumab) and Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitors were also well tolerated and effective.

More recent studies have reported that JAK inhibitors, specifically ruxolitinib and baricitinib, may not only be effective in treating HIV-associated inflammatory conditions but also HIV disease itself, especially inflammatory activation therefrom. 30,31

### Psoriasis and Psoriatic Arthritis

The extent of skin involvement with psoriasis can be extensive (Fig. 116.3) in HIV-infected individuals, especially in patients not on anti-retroviral treatment. Of note, cutaneous T cell lymphoma can resemble psoriasis and should be considered in the differential diagnosis of psoriasis in HIV-positive individuals. Psoriasis and PsA were infrequently reported in Sub-Saharan Africa before the HIV-1 pandemic, with the prevalence of psoriasis (in hospitalbased dermatology departments) ranging from 0.05% to 0.9% in West Africa and 2.8% to 3.5% in South Africa. However, this has increased significantly in the HIV-1 era, with more than 5% of HIV-positive individuals reported with psoriasis. Similarly, there were few data on PsA prevalence in Sub-Saharan Africa. PsA was reported before the beginning of the HIV pandemic (41.6%

among 61 patients with psoriasis) and many feel this to have increased with the growing HIV prevalence.32-34 More recently, the prevalence of HIV-associated psoriasis and PsA appears to be falling in the face of anti-retroviral therapy (ART),7 although recent data from Taiwan and Quebec suggest it is still more common than among the HIV-negative population.13,

In general, the arthritis in HIV-associated PsA is predominantly polyarticular, lower limb, and progressive. Psoriasis is commonly an extensive guttate-plaque admixture and, in contrast to the articular disease, was nonremittive with the onset of AIDS.32, Anti-retroviral treatment is effective in treating HIV-associated psoriasis and its associated arthritis.35, Phototherapy may improve the skin rash but also may enhance viral replication, worsen HIV disease, and increase the risk of skin cancer. Other agents that are efficacious include cyclosporine (although renal function must be monitored carefully) and etretinate. Methotrexate can also be used, albeit with caution. TNF blockers can be used in patients with refractory disease, and a number of patients have had dramatic improvements in skin lesions and in arthritis,26,29,37 although with the usual precautions (see preceding text) because frequent polymicrobial infections while on the drug resulted in its discontinuation in some patients. 37,38

### Undifferentiated Spondyloarthritis

Symptoms of reactive arthritis or PsA such as enthesopathy (plantar fasciitis, Achilles tendinitis) are observed in patients in whom full-blown disease does not otherwise develop. Treatment is symptomatic (e.g., NSAIDs, intralesional corticosteroid injections), although sulfasalazine should be considered in patients with more extensive disease.

### Osteoarthritis

With patients living longer and with the increased frequency of metabolic syndrome, the prevalence of osteoarthritis (OA), particularly of the hip and knee, is rising among patients living with HIV. Risk factors for knee OA in the setting of HIV infection are similar to the non-HIV population and have been described as including female gender, obesity, and Black or African American

40 Treatment is similar as in non-HIV patients, including race. physical therapy, intraarticular corticosteroid injections, and NSAIDs. Reduced levels of ghrelin has been associated with knee OA in HIV-positive individuals.

### Avascular Necrosis of Bone

Case-control studies have shown an association of osteonecrosis after the introduction of highly active anti-retroviral therapy (HAART), especially in those who have received corticosteroids.42, A meta-analysis revealed more than two-fold increased odds of avascular necrosis among HIV-infected patients exposed to protease inhibitors43; however, this association has recently been disputed in a large European cohort of 11,820 individuals followed 86,118 person-years. Other contributing factors include dyslipidemia (associated with protease inhibitor usage), alcohol abuse, use of megestrol acetate,45 the presence of antiphospholipid antibodies,46 intravenous drug abuse, 45,46 and HIV-1 itself. The most common presenting symptom of osteonecrosis is pain on weight bearing and activity, most commonly in the hips. Some patients may be asymptomatic, and the diagnosis may be based on incidental findings from radiologic studies. Most patients tend to present when subchondral collapse already has occurred. Radiographs, computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and nuclear medicine studies have been used successfully to diagnose osteonecrosis, as in HIVnegative patients.

### Hypertrophic Pulmonary Osteoarthropathy

Hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy (HPO) affects bones, joints, and soft tissues and can develop in HIV-infected patients with Pneumocystis jiroveci pneumonia. It is characterized by severe pain in the lower extremities; digital clubbing; arthralgia; nonpitting edema; and periarticular soft tissue involvement of the ankles, knees, and elbows. The skin over the affected areas is glistening, edematous, and warm. Radiography reveals extensive periosteal reaction and subperiosteal proliferative changes in the long bones of the lower extremities. A bone scan may show increased uptake along the cortical surfaces. In addition, treatment with voriconazole for chronic fungal infections seen in patients with advanced

HIV infection can be complicated by periostitis. When present, treatment of P. jiroveci pneumonia usually alleviates symptoms of HPO.

### Osteopenia and Osteoporosis

Osteopenia and osteoporosis occur more than three times as commonly in HIV-infected patients regardless of anti-retroviral treatment49 and can result in pathologic fractures. One metaanalysis found 15% of HIV-positive patients to have osteoporosis and 52% to have osteopenia. Risk factors for osteopenia include use of protease inhibitors, advanced stage of HIV infection, high viral load, low body mass, low bicarbonate levels, increased alkaline phosphatase levels, and especially, smoking and vitamin D deficiency.52, Clinicians should have a low threshold to screen for vitamin D deficiency, should provide adequate repletion as necessary, and (if not done already for many other reasons) counsel against smoking. Bisphosphonates and, in patients with HIV wasting syndrome, testosterone have been used to maintain bone density. Of particular note is a recent study that showed that bone mineral density in 481 Asians with well-controlled HIV infection did not differ from those without HIV infection, suggesting that effective control may prevent premature bone loss.

### HIV-Associated Muscle Disease

Muscle involvement in HIV infection varies from uncomplicated myalgias or asymptomatic creatine kinase (CK) elevation to severe, disabling, HIV-associated polymyositis or pyomyositis (Table 116.4). HIV-1 seroconversion can also coincide with myoglobinuria and acute myalgia, suggesting that myotropism for HIV may be present early in the infection.

### Myalgia and Fibromyalgia

One-third of HIV-positive outpatients may report myalgias, 3,56,57 and 11% were found to have fibromyalgia in one old series and the same in a more recent cohort.58, Fibromyalgia is associated with longer disease duration and a history of depression. Treatment is similar to that for fibromyalgia in the non-HIV setting, including anti-depressants, exercise, and continued reassurance and follow-up.

### Non-inflammatory Necrotizing Myopathy and HIV-Related Wasting Syndrome

Severe wasting from chronic infection, malignancy, malabsorption, and nutritional deficiency often accounts for weakness and disability in patients with AIDS. This wasting leads to loss of muscle mass. Cachexia and muscle wasting associated with HIV constitute "slim disease" in Africa. A non-inflammatory necrotizing myopathy of unclear pathogenesis has been described, accounting for 42% of patients diagnosed with myopathy. Even in patients without significant wasting, muscle biopsy specimens have shown diffuse atrophy, mild neurogenic atrophy, or thick filament loss without conspicuous inflammation. Whether this condition is immune mediated, as some have suggested,61 or whether it is the result of metabolic or nutritional factors remains unclear. Corticosteroids restore muscle strength and mass.

### Nemaline Myopathy

Nemaline myopathy is a rare disorder that has been described in some HIV-positive patients in addition to its occurrence as a congenital disorder. Nemaline myopathy represents a nonspecific myofibril alteration resulting from Z band disruption. Musclebiopsy specimens disclose prominent, randomly distributed, atrophic type 1 fibers with numerous intracytoplasmic rod bodies in the centers of the fibers, corresponding to nemaline rods on electron microscopy. Necrotic fibers and inflammatory infiltrates are usually not found. Some patients have been described to have associated monoclonal gammopathy. Although no inflammation is noted, corticosteroids may be useful. In addition, two cases of successful treatment with intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) have been reported.

### HIV-Associated Polymyositis

HIV-associated polymyositis most typically manifests early in the course of HIV infection and may be the presenting feature. In one large series of HIV-positive outpatients from a county clinic in Texas, the frequency was 2.2 per 1000.65 In another recent series from Taiwan, the prevalence was 5 per 20,444 patients compared with an expected frequency of 3.23 per 100,000.13

The pathogenesis of HIV-associated polymyositis is unclear— possibly stemming from direct viral invasion (leading to a

cytopathic effect and subsequent muscle necrosis), as suggested in one pathologic study,66 or from an autoimmune response of the HIV-positive host, as suggested by another study.

The most common manifestation is a subacute, progressive proximal muscle weakness occurring in the setting of an elevated CK. Myalgia is not a prominent presenting feature. Skin involvement is unusual, as is involvement of extraocular muscles and facial muscles. In a report from Africa, HIV-associated polymyositis cases were mostly female and, compared with the non-HIV polymyositis cases, were younger and with four-fold lower serum CK. On the other hand, only a handful of cases of dermatomyositis in HIV have been reported, usually in the setting of advanced immunodeficiency. CK levels may be less elevated or even normal in some HIV-associated polymyositis patients.65,

Treatment is similar to that provided for other inflammatory myopathies. CK elevation and muscle weakness respond to moderate-dose glucocorticoids.65, Refractory cases may require immunosuppressive agents, such as methotrexate, azathioprine, or mycophenolate mofetil. IVIG has been used with some success. These agents should be used with caution, however, with careful monitoring of the patient's clinical status, CD4 counts, and HIV-1 messenger RNA (mRNA) levels.

CK elevation is commonly encountered in outpatients with HIV infection, secondary to HIV per se, behaviors associated with higher risk for HIV infection (e.g., cocaine use), or HIV treatment. In most patients, these elevations are transient and are of little consequence, but they require careful follow-up for any sign of clinical deterioration before electrodiagnostic, advanced imaging, or biopsy studies are undertaken.

### Inclusion Body Myositis

Inclusion body myositis (IBM) has been recognized as a complication of HIV infection. This condition is clinically, histologically, and immunologically identical to sporadic IBM. Muscle biopsy specimens suggest two concurrently ongoing processes: an autoimmune process mediated by cytotoxic T cells and a degenerative process manifested by vacuolated muscle fibers and deposits of amyloid-related proteins. Of particular interest has been the finding of elevated mRNA levels and constitutive expression of Toll-like receptor 3, which is known to mediate inflammatory stimuli from pathogens and endogenous danger signals. Another is to link the innate and adaptive immune systems in muscle fibers of patients with HIV-associated IBM in close proximity with infiltrating mononuclear cells. One review of four cases of HIV-associated IBM found that involved CD8-positive T cells surrounding muscle fibers were virus specific and may cross-react with antigens on the surface of muscle fibers, suggesting that HIV may trigger a viral-specific inflammatory response that can lead to IBM. Another longitudinal study, which included patients with and without HIV infection and myositis, showed that those with HIV-associated polymyositis may present initially with features characteristic of typical polymyositis. However, in time nearly all eventually manifested symptoms more consistent with IBM, including hand and wrist flexor weakness, rimed vacuoles on biopsy, and anti-NT5C1A antibodies. This was not seen in a more recent study where only 50% of patients with HIV-associated myositis developed IBM over time.

### Myopathy Associated With Treatment

The three anti-retroviral treatment (ART) medications zidovudine, didanosine, and raltegravir are very well known to cause myopathy.75, Didanosine and zidovudine are in the family of nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs), and raltegravir is an integrase inhibitor. It is thought that the pathophysiology of the myopathy is dose related due to a mitochondrial dystrophy causing depletion of mitochondrial DNA. The mechanism is postulated to be multifactorial by inhibition of the bioenergetic machinery of the mitochondria, inhibition of DNA polymerase gamma, depletion of L-carnitine, and oxidative stress from zidovudine. Symptoms of myopathy include proximal muscle weakness, muscle tenderness, and myalgias. Should any of these symptoms occur while on these medications, they should be stopped for 4 weeks. If clinical improvement is not seen within the 4 weeks of cessation, electromyography and muscle biopsies should be performed next to further assess other etiologies of myopathy.

Increasingly the integrase inhibitor raltegravir is being added to ART regimens because of the limited side effect profile, albeit with an increased incidence of myalgias reported. This is, however, not associated with elevated CK levels nor is it doseor time-dependent. We suggest medication cessation and change to other ART should myalgias develop while on raltegravir.

### Rhabdomyolysis

Rhabdomyolysis can occur at all stages of HIV-1 infection and may be separated into three groups: (1) HIV-associated rhabdomyolysis, including rhabdomyolysis in primary HIV infection and recurrent or isolated rhabdomyolysis, (2) drug-induced rhabdomyolysis, and (3) rhabdomyolysis at the end stage of AIDS, possibly associated with opportunistic infections of muscle. Drugs implicated in rhabdomyolysis in HIV-positive patients include didanosine, lamivudine, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, ritonavir, indinavir, and raltegravir75,77a and, in conjunction with statin use, Genvoya ( (elvitegravir/cobicistat/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide).78,79

### Diffuse Infiltrative Lymphocytosis Syndrome

Diffuse infiltrative lymphocytosis syndrome (DILS), found exclusively in HIV-positive individuals, is characterized by salivary gland enlargement and peripheral CD8 lymphocytosis often accompanied by sicca symptoms and other extraglandular features. The prevalence of DILS is declining since the introduction of HAART. Using parotid enlargement as a criterion, the prevalence in Houston, Texas, was 4% in the pre-HAART era, 80 declining to 0.8% after the introduction of aggressive HIV therapy. In another study from Greece, using xerophthalmia and xerostomia as the defining criteria (and requiring confirmatory minor salivary gland biopsy and technetium scintigraphy),81 the prevalence of DILS was 7.8% and has decreased dramatically there and elsewhere after the introduction of HAART.

Minor salivary gland biopsy specimens show a focal sialadenitis, similar to that observed in Sjögren's syndrome, although destruction of the salivary glands tends to be lessened82 (Fig. 116.4). CD8-positive lymphocytes constitute most of the inflammatory infiltrate,83 in contrast to that seen in primary

(non-HIV-associated) Sjögren's syndrome. Lymphoepithelial cysts are seen frequently in the parotid glands of patients with DILS, leading to inspissated salivary secretions that may be painful. Diffuse cervical lymphadenopathy and elevated immunoglobulin (Ig) G4 levels may be seen with DILS; therefore IgG4-related diseases could be a potential mimic of DILS.

The characteristic, if not defining, presentation of DILS consists of painless parotid enlargement that is often massive (Fig. 116.5). This enlargement is accompanied by sicca symptoms in more than 60% of patients. Although parotid and submandibular enlargement is nearly universal in this disorder, certain extraglandular features are also prominent (Table 116.5). DILS and Sjögren's syndrome share some similarities and differences (Table 116.6).

Diagnostic criteria have been proposed for DILS as follows83.

HIV seropositivity by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay and Western blot analysis

Bilateral salivary gland enlargement or xerostomia persisting for longer than 6 months

Histologic confirmation of salivary or lacrimal gland lymphocytic infiltration in the absence of granulomatous or neoplastic enlargement

Minor salivary gland biopsy specimens are usually positive (Fig. 116.4) in ART-naive patients. Gallium-67 scintigraphy of the salivary glands was previously used when lip biopsy was not feasible or equivocal. Tc99m pertechnetate scanning offers little diagnostic help. Scintigraphy was used as a primary diagnostic aid in patients on protease inhibitors because minor salivary gland biopsy specimens are rarely positive in patients on combination ART. CT or MRI scans are useful to determine the extent of glandular swelling and to evaluate parotid cysts and possible salivary glandular malignancy.

Patients with asymptomatic glandular swelling and mild, if any, sicca symptoms can be observed over time. Anti-retroviral

treatment is effective in treating the glandular swelling and sicca symptoms associated with DILS and complications such as neuropathy. We have found also that a short course of moderate

doses of corticosteroids (30 to 40 mg/day of prednisone) are effective in treating the glandular swelling and sicca symptoms of DILS without adversely affecting the frequency of opportunistic infections, increasing the viral loads, or depressing the CD4+ counts. However, the effect is transient and the swelling may recur with tapering/discontinuation of steroids. Lymphocytic interstitial pneumonitis may require higher doses of corticosteroids (60 mg/day of prednisone), sometimes for extended periods. Radiation therapy to the parotid glands should be avoided. Cranial nerve VII palsy tends to respond poorly to any treatment. Combination ART is effective in resolving parotid epithelial cysts, although when refractory the cysts can be managed by aspiration and instillation of 1 mL (40 mg) of either methylprednisolone or triamcinolone suspension into the cyst. Frequent recurrence may necessitate surgical excision.

### Vasculitis Associated With HIV Infection

A wide spectrum of vasculitis has been described in patients with HIV-1 infection.85, Fever, malaise, weakness, rash, headaches, and neurologic symptoms are common in HIV-positive patients and triggers of vasculitis range from specific infectious agents and drugs to idiopathic causes. Among infectious causes, cytomegalovirus and tuberculosis are probably the most common.

One series found 34 (23%) of 148 "symptomatic" HIV-positive patients to have vasculitis. Of these patients, 11 met American College of Rheumatology criteria for a distinct category of vasculitis, including hypersensitivity vasculitis in six, polyarteritis nodosa in four, and Henoch-Schönlein purpura in one. Another series of 98 Chinese patients found that 20% had vasculitis, including 15 with Behçet's-like disease, two cases of Henoch- Schönlein purpura, two cases of digital gangrene, and one case of central nervous system (CNS) vasculitis. Granulomatosis with polyangiitis and pulmonary microscopic polyangiitis can occur in patients with high CD4+ counts and during immune reconstitution (see below). Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Churg-Strauss syndrome) has also been described. Behçet's disease and relapsing polychondritis occur in HIV infection90,91 and were reported as improving with HAART.

Rapidly progressive focal necrotizing vasculitis of the aorta and large arteries with occlusion and occasionally aneurysm formation and rupture have been described in Africans with HIV infection. In one recent study, 90% of HIV-positive patients, but no HIVnegative patients, had evidence of adventitial leukocytoclastic

vasculitis of the vasa vasorum of the femoral arteries. Giant cell arteritis likewise has been described in patients with HIV infection with aortic root dilation as well as Takayasu arteritis.93, Kawasaki's disease has been reported in HIV-positive children and adults. Cryoglobulinemic vasculitis with associated lymphocytic interstitial pneumonia occurs with and without hepatitis C coinfection. Patients with isolated CNS angiitis are usually seen with organic brain syndromes and neurologic deficits. In children and in one case report in an adult, HIV-associated cerebral aneurysmal arteriopathy was described as causing multiple fusiform aneurysms in the circle of Willis. CNS vasculitis may manifest as recurrent strokes. Although imaging studies (MRI, angiography) may be helpful, brain biopsy may be necessary to establish the diagnosis. Necrotizing granulomatous vasculitis not limited to the CNS has been reported in patients with low CD4 counts that respond to ART.

Diagnosis is based on a high degree of suspicion and on angiography and/or biopsy of specific organ beds. Similar to immunocompetent patients, perinuclear anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antigen (p-ANCA) and cytoplasmic ANCA (c-ANCA) may be useful with granulomatosis with polyangiitis or microscopic polyangiitis. However, biopsy with cultures is important to rule out infectious mimics.

Corticosteroids are the mainstay of treatment for HIV-associated vasculitis, although cytotoxic agents such as cyclophosphamide, IVIG, and plasmapheresis have been used in refractory cases. Painful neuropathy secondary to vasculitis responds well to high-dose glucocorticoids, in contrast to HIV-associated peripheral neuropathy.

### Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura

Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura is a thrombotic microangiopathy associated with thrombocytopenia and hemolytic anemias (accompanied by red cell fragments on peripheral blood smear), which is triggered by an excess of large von Willebrand factor secreted by the endothelium that results in vascular occlusion and critical organ ischemia, with a high mortality.99, It occurs much more commonly in the setting of HIV infection 101 and is caused by marked reduction of the metalloprotease enzyme, a-disintegrin-and-metalloproteinase-with-thrombospondin-motifs 13 (ADAMTS13) whose role is to cleave large multimers of von Willebrand factor into smaller monomers. Plasma infusion and plasma exchange are the key components of the treatment, but the overall mortality is around 40%.99,100

### Primary Pulmonary Hypertension

Pulmonary hypertension is a severe life-limiting disease that often affects younger patients. Patients with AIDS and primary pulmonary hypertension present with a higher degree of pulmonary hypertension than non-AIDS patients.102, The predominant histopathologic finding has been a plexogenic pulmonary arteriopathy, although thromboembolic changes have also been reported. Symptoms include progressive shortness of breath, pedal edema, nonproductive cough, fatigue, syncope or near-syncope, and chest pain. Pulmonary function tests show mild restrictive patterns with variably reduced diffusing capacities. Older studies suggested a very high mortality; however, with improving treatment of pulmonary hypertension, the prognosis has improved considerably. Treatment of HIV-associated pulmonary hypertension is similar to that in the non-HIV setting and includes

anti-coagulation, calcium channel blockers, prostanoids, endothelin receptor antagonists, and phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors, which have reduced the otherwise high mortality associated with this disease. 103,104

### HIV-Associated Musculoskeletal Infection

### Pyomyositis

Pyomyositis is a primary infection of skeletal muscle that does not arise from contiguous infection; it is presumably hematogenous in origin and is often associated with abscess formation. Rarely seen in developed countries, infectious myositis nonetheless is an important complication of HIV infection in areas most endemic for HIV, such as Africa and India,105 although recent data have shown pyomyositis to be significantly associated with HIV infection in the United States. It tends to occur in later stages of the infection, with CD4 counts less than 200/μL. Staphylococcus aureus is the most common pathogen. Other organisms that have been implicated include Streptococcus pyogenes, Cryptococcus neoformans, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Mycobacterium avium-intra-cellulare, Nocardia asteroides, Salmonella enteritidis, Escherichia coli, Citrobacter freundii, Morganella morganii, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and group A streptococci. Recently microsporidial species have also been reported as causing infectious myositis in HIV-1-infected patients with advanced immunosuppression.

The clinical course of pyomyositis can be roughly divided into three stages: invasive, suppurative, and late. The first stage, which typically lasts 1 to 3 weeks, is characterized by localized cramps and induration in conjunction with a low-grade fever. Large muscle groups, particularly those of the lower extremities, are most often affected. The degrees of pain and fever increase in the second stage, which is characterized further by the development of edema and purulence in the affected muscle. Untreated, the disease progresses to the third stage; within 3 weeks of onset, sepsis and death 108 The mortality rate associated with pyomyositis has can occur. been estimated to range from 1% to 20%. Ultrasound and MRI with contrast enhancement are effective in localizing infection, although sometimes tagged white blood cell scans may be needed. Oral and intravenous antibiotics in conjunction with surgical drainage are often required.

### Bacterial Arthritis and Osteomyelitis

Patients become more susceptible to bacterial infections of the bones and joints with advanced HIV infections. S. aureus is the most common infectious agent encountered, but parenteral drug use and not HIV infection per se may account for this. Osteomyelitis is associated with mortality rates of greater than 20% in HIV-infected patients. The most frequently involved bones are the wrist, tibia, femoral heads, and thoracic cage, but other rare sites, such as the patella and the mandible, have been reported.

Due to the fear of perioperative complications due to immunosuppression from HIV, some orthopedic surgeons are reluctant to perform joint replacement in HIV-infected individuals. In a nationwide database survey of HIV-infected patients undergoing total hip arthroplasty, there was only a slight increase in post-operative complications and length of hospital stay compared with non-HIV-infected individuals. In another study of patients with and without HIV infection undergoing total knee replacement, patients with HIV infection were at an increased risk for perioperative wound infections and a slight increase in average

length of hospital stay, although they were not at an increased risk for overall complications.

### Musculoskeletal Tuberculosis

Musculoskeletal involvement, the fourth most common extrapulmonary manifestation of tuberculosis, is found in approximately 1% to 5% of patients with tuberculosis. It can mimic many skeletal diseases and can manifest in various locations. Less than 50% of reported patients with musculoskeletal tuberculosis have radiographic evidence of pulmonary tuberculosis. M. tuberculosis disseminates hematogenously after an acute or reactivated pulmonary infection. Usually, skeletal tuberculosis lesions in immunocompetent patients are solitary, but in AIDS patients, they may have a multicentric distribution in approximately 30%. The vertebrae are the most common site involved, mostly the lower thoracic or upper lumbar segments. The frequency of tuberculous spondylitis is 50% to 66%; peripheral arthritis, 20% to 30%; osteomyelitis, 10% to 20%; and tenosynovitis and bursitis, approximately 1% to 3%. Treatment includes four-drug anti-tubercular therapy and, often, surgical intervention.

### Atypical Mycobacterial Infection

Musculoskeletal infection caused by atypical mycobacterial species is unusual in immunocompetent individuals. Atypical mycobacterial species most commonly implicated in causing septic arthritis or osteomyelitis in HIV include M. avium-intra-cellulare complex, Mycobacterium kansasii, Mycobacterium haemophilum, Mycobacterium terrae, and Mycobacterium fortuitum. M. haemophilum has been most frequently implicated in skeletal infection, accounting for more than half of cases, and M. kansasii is second, accounting for an additional 25% (Fig. 116.6). These are systemic infections that often involve several joints or skeletal sites. Cutaneous lesions, such as nodules, ulcers, and draining sinus tracts, occur in approximately 50% of patients. These infections tend to occur late in the course of HIV-1 infection, usually when the CD4+ T lymphocyte count is less than 100/μL. M. avium-intracellulare complex osteomyelitis has also been associated with immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome after initiation of HAART (see below). Along with standard anti-tuberculotic therapy, clarithromycin is effective.

### Bacillary Angiomatosis Osteomyelitis

Bacillary angiomatosis is a multisystem infectious disease caused by two closely related organisms: Bartonella henselae and Bartonella quintana. It seems to be a disease unique to HIV-infected patients and, to a lesser degree, to other immunocompromised patients. Clinical characteristics associated with bacillary angiomatosis and bacillary peliosis in patients with HIV infection include fever (temperature, >100° F [37.8° C]; 93%), cutaneous or subcutaneous vascular lesions, lymphadenopathy, osteomyelitis, and abdominal symptoms associated with profound depression of CD4 lymphocyte counts, anemia, and an elevated serum level of alkaline phosphatase.115-117 Osteomyelitis is found in approximately one-third of patients in association with skin disease. These lesions are usually characterized by extensive destruction of the cortical bone, periostitis, medullary invasion, and an overlying soft-tissue mass that might resemble cellulitis. Complete remission of bacillary angiomatosis after doxycycline or erythromycin therapy occurs, although bone lesions may need surgical drainage.

### Fungal Infections

In addition to bacterial infection, patients with advanced HIV infection (CD4 T lymphocyte count <100/μL) are at high risk for fungal musculoskeletal infections, particularly those caused by Candida albicans118 and Sporothrix schenckii. S. schenckii can manifest with oligoarticular or even polyarticular involvement and tenosynovitis (Fig. 116.7) and can be particularly difficult to eradicate, requiring long-term suppressive anti-fungal therapy. Various disseminated fungal infections, such as histoplasmosis, cryptococcosis, and blastomycosis, occur in HIV-1 infection and often cause osteomyelitis.

### Parasitic Infections

Muscle toxoplasmosis is found in profoundly immunosuppressed patients, typically manifesting with a painful subacute myopathy

and concurrent multivisceral toxoplasmosis. Toxoplasma cysts are observed mainly in muscle fibers in muscle biopsy specimens, and identification of cysts as Toxoplasma may be easier when specific antibodies or electron microscopy is used. Muscle weakness such as in polymyositis can occur in muscle toxoplasmosis. Treatment is based on a combination of drugs acting synergistically against T. gondii, including pyrimethamine and sulfadiazine or trisulfapyrimidines.

### Response of Other Rheumatic Diseases to HIV Infection

Before ART was introduced, many studies suggested that with declining CD4 T cell counts RA and systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) often went into remission. However, with ART making HIV now a chronic disease, rheumatic diseases are being

encountered more frequently in HIV-infected individuals. RA and SLE have been seen as a complication of the immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome. 121, The prevalence of RA that occurs in the setting of HIV infection appears to be rare based on results of a systematic literature review. HIV infection could in fact cause a false-positive rheumatoid factor (RF) and anti-citrullinated protein antibodies (ACPA). Nonetheless, RA has been seen to coexist with advanced HIV. One recent analysis from the Veterans Aging Cohort Study examining 2748 patients with a diagnosis of RA (of whom 21 had HIV) from 56,250 patients with HIV and 116,944 uninfected individuals followed over 2,384,541 person-years found that RA was less common in patients with HIV compared with uninfected individuals. RF and ACPA were lower in RA patients with HIV, and those with HIV were prescribed disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs less frequently than those without HIV.

Though the coexistence of HIV with RA and SLE has been seen to occur more often with well-controlled HIV infection, disease activity of RA and SLE appear to decline with concurrent HIV infection, though frequency of flares in SLE did not correlate with ART usage. 125, Three series of HIV-infected SLE patients from South Africa, Houston, Texas, and Porto Alegre, Brazil, including 13, 22, and 11 patients, respectively, have recently been reported.125-127 The first two showed a higher frequency of patients of African ancestry, overall lower disease activity, and seroreactivity125,126 (one compared with a simultaneously followed local non-HIV SLE cohort t127). However, in the Brazilian cohort, neuropsychiatric involvement, hemolytic anemia, and renal disease were more commonly encountered compared with local non-HIV SLE patients.

### HAART-Related Immune Reconstitution Syndrome

The immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) is an interesting paradox that occurs when the immune system restores itself after ART has been successfully started. It causes a rapidly declining clinical status despite increasing absolute CD4 counts and decreasing viral loads of HIV-1.128-131 It is thought that IRIS is due to dysregulation that occurs in the setting of rising CD4 T cells that are highly specific for a certain antigen or from the hyperresponsiveness of the innate immune system to helper T-cells. There is an inverse correlation between the absolute CD4 cell count and the probability of developing IRIS.

Although IRIS primarily occurs in the setting of infectious complications of HIV infection, autoinflammation leading to the development of autoimmune diseases can also occur. Diseases such as cerebral CD8 lymphocytosis, Guillain-Barré syndrome, alopecia universalis, and terminal ileitis as well as RA, polymyositis, SLE, autoimmune hepatitis, adult-onset Still's disease, and sarcoidosis have been shown to appear de novo after ART has been initiated. There are criteria that should be used to diagnose IRIS. One should have the diagnosis of AIDS, currently be on treatment with anti-retrovirals that result in an increase in CD4 cell count and decreased HIV viral load, exaggerated response to infection, and inflammatory symptoms appearing during therapy that cannot be explained by another cause. A meta-analysis found that the risk of IRIS is greatest in patients with a CD4 cell count of less than 50 cells/μL prior to ART initiation. Therefore, it is best if ART is administered before immunodeficiency is advanced. A recent clinical trial suggested

that JAK inhibitors may be effective in preventing inflammatory complications of ART.

### Laboratory Abnormalities Associated With HIV Infection

Humoral immunologic abnormalities are frequent in patients with HIV but are rarely associated with severe clinical signs. The most common laboratory abnormality is polyclonal hyperglobulinemia, found in 45% of HIV-positive individuals. RF and anti-nuclear antibodies, usually in low titer, have been described in 17% of patients with HIV infection in some series, 123,132 although antidouble-stranded DNA antibodies and hypocomplementemia are rare. Increased titers of ACPA and RF occur in advanced HIV infection. Although more specific than RF, before immune reconstitution, ACPA is an unreliable diagnostic marker for RA and does not necessarily predict future RA. In older series, IgG anti-cardiolipin antibodies are found in 95% of untreated patients with AIDS, particularly in patients with advanced disease, and overall in 20% to 30% of HIV-positive individuals. They were rarely associated with thrombotic events. However, in more recent series in the era of HAART, such high frequencies are no longer seen and, when anti-cardiolipin antibodies are present, they are more likely to be associated with thrombosis. C-ANCAs and p-ANCAs have been described in the serum of HIV-positive individuals, as have antiglomerular basement membrane antibodies. 135, Cryoglobulinemia is decreasing in this population since the introduction of HAART. Indeed, with HAART, many of these serologic abnormalities tend to decrease or resolve.134,137

### Conclusion

The impact of the global HIV pandemic continues to grow, and rheumatologists need to be aware of the wide spectrum of rheumatic diseases that occur in HIV-positive patients. HAART has changed the natural history of HIV infection. It has modified the frequency and expression of some HIV-related clinical syndromes and has been associated directly (toxicity) and indirectly (immune reconstitution) with the development of new ones. With longer survival and newer refinements in treatment, the spectrum of rheumatic disease seen in HIV-positive patients is very much a moving target for rheumatologists and is likely to continue to evolve.

# Viral Arthritis

### KEY POINTS

### Introduction

Many viruses are associated with arthritis that can be reminiscent of rheumatoid arthritis (RA): Old-World alphaviruses such as Chikungunya virus (CHIKV) and Ross River virus (RRV)1-5 and, more rarely, parvovirus B19, Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), rubella, and hepatitis B and C virus (HBV/HCV).6-11 Other viruses such as adenoviruses, coxsackie viruses, HIV, influenza, measles, mumps, and varicella zoster are more likely to be linked to autoimmune responses such as type 1 diabetes and may also affect the joints, leading to reactive arthritis. 1, Also associated with arthritis in some cases, Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) is discussed elsewhere in this text (see Ch. 119).

The phenotypes of these diseases may be distinct in terms of the primary cells and tissues initially targeted, the specific humoral and cellular immune responses elaborated, and the inflammatory effector pathways that predominate. Despite the different nature of each viral disease, however, they clearly share some common

pathogenic mechanisms involved in arthralgias including acute nocioception at nerve endings, macrophage activation and polarization, and fibroblast hyperplasia and invasion sustained by major angiogenesis in the synovial tissues as described in RA (Fig. 117.1).13-15

Early and robust systemic innate and adaptive immune antiviral responses are important events to protect the host, including the contribution of the epithelia, a major portal of entry for many of these viruses at the lung and skin levels. However, in the context of a major infection associated with high viremia and a failure to mount a robust anti-viral response, it has been proposed that the virus would escape from immune surveillance and find protective niches in tissues such as synovial tissues. Indeed, the acute viral infection might, in a genetically predisposed or otherwise susceptible host (e.g., association with human leukocyte antigen [HLA] or immune senescence in elderly patients), be able to recapitulate a polarized inflammatory response as described in RA and other autoimmune diseases. Viruses could also polarize host-cell defense mechanisms such as interferon (IFN) type I signaling pathways, apoptosis, and autophagy to its own advantage. 18, As a Trojan horse scenario, it has been shown that viruses (e.g., CHIKV) could hide in apoptotic cell remnants only to then be phagocytosed by tissue-resident macrophages and lead to viral persistence.

Synovial tissue is a sanctuary for many arthritogenic viruses, which can recruit reactive T cells and more rarely B cells to the joints to drive chronic inflammation and, ultimately, contribute to hyperplastic synovial pannus tissue formation and, finally, to the destruction of cartilage and bone as found in RA.15, Viruses could be brought into the synovial tissue by infected monocytes, fibrocytes, or lymphocytes before being transferred to resident cells such as synovial fibroblasts. 14,

Autoimmunity against self-antigens prominently expressed by infected synovial fibroblasts may be exceptionally engaged through bystander activation and the expression of cryptic antigens and more rarely through well-described molecular mimicry mechanisms.

Surprisingly, many of the self-antigens are nuclear or mitochondrial proteins released by dying cells as a consequence of the infection but are also critically involved as natural adjuvants (also called alarmins) to alert innate and adaptive immune cells.23, Chronic viral infection in the joint may contribute to the continuous release of several of these alarmins (e.g., high-mobility group box 1 [HMGB1], cardiolipin, adenosine triphosphate [ATP]), which could signal through pattern recognition receptors (PRRs) such as Toll-like receptors (TLRs) to activate nuclear factor kappa B (NF-kB) signaling and the synthesis of pro-inflammatory cytokines.25,

### Athritis

Paradoxically, the events mobilized by the innate immune system and involved in the clearance of viruses could also contribute to sustained chronic inflammation leading to arthralgia and ultimately the development of destructive arthritis. Regulatory mechanisms to control chronic inflammation have been recently emphasized, but little is known about their contributions in synovial tissues and whether or not they could favor viral persistence and chronic arthritis.

Preventive measures should include vaccinations whenever possible in endemic regions and particularly for vulnerable individuals such as older adults. Other treatment regimens include analgesics and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) for pain relief, and methotrexate (MTX) to control actual arthritis, although this may compromise patients' immune surveillance to prevent viral reactivation. 28-30

This chapter describes key examples of some of the major DNA and RNA viruses associated with arthritis and proposes common pathogenic mechanisms that may be the driving force of these chronic viral arthritic diseases. It should be emphasized that the mechanisms may involve exceptionally autoreactive T and B cells but more commonly involves a crosstalk between persistently infected synovial fibroblasts and macrophages, contributing to chronic inflammation as described in several chronic fibrotic disorders.

### Examples of Arthritogenic Viruses

### Parvovirus B19

Parvovirus B19 is well known for causing infection that has been linked to a number of conditions, such as fifth disease in children and arthralgias in adults (Table 117.1).32, This virus can mutate at high frequencies and as much as those typical of RNA viruses. . It has long been known to be also associated with arthritis.35, B19 is the smallest single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) virus of 6 kb and is 20 to 25 nanometers (nm) in diameter. The genome encodes for two structural proteins, VP1 (nucleotides 24444786) and VP2 (nucleotides 31254786), and for the major nonstructural protein NS1 (nucleotides 4362451).

Parvovirus B19 infection may be particularly deleterious during pregnancy because of the consequences on the fetus. The critical time of infection is during the first 20 weeks of gestation, when the fetal immune system is thought to be immature and red cell mass increases more rapidly, resulting in inhibition of erythropoiesis. B19 is the cause of erythema infectiosum (also known as fifth disease), a common childhood rash, and of various joint complications especially in adult women, although many B19 infections remain subclinical. The seroprevalence increases with age and more than 70% of adults are seropositive. Parvovirus B19 is mainly transmitted by respiratory aerosol spread from individuals with acute infection.

Parvovirus B19 replicates in human red blood cell precursors of the bone marrow. This leads to transient arrest of red cell formation. Hence, B19 infection can lead to transient aplastic crisis manifesting as severe anemia. B19 infection has, however, been shown to affect other hematopoietic cell lineages, causing various cytopenias. B19 DNA (DNA remnants) or antigen has furthermore been found in the fetal heart, liver, spleen, kidney, lung, muscle, and brain and in the heart, lung, liver, kidney, testes, cerebrospinal fluid, and synovium of children or adults. The main cellular receptor of B19 has been identified as the P-antigen of the blood group P system. P antigen, also known as globoside, is

present on erythrocytes, erythroblast, megakaryocytes, endothelial cells, fetal liver, and heart skeletal muscle cells. B19 also has two co-receptors: α5β1 integrin and KU80 nuclear autoantigen.

Immunity after infection with B19 is conferred by a B cell immune response with development of neutralizing antibodies. T cell-mediated responses are also involved and directed essentially against the capsid proteins VP1 and VP2.

B19 has been the object of intense investigation to clarify whether it is able to trigger autoimmune diseases. It has been suggested that it might be a major contributing factor or the precipitating agent of several autoimmune disorders including RA, systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), antiphospholipid syndrome, systemic sclerosis, and vasculitides. The joint manifestations sometimes mimic those of RA, and up to about 50% of patients with chronic B19 arthropathy meet the criteria of the American College of Rheumatology (ACR) for RA, suggesting that the persistence of the virus may be involved in the initiation and perpetuation of the disease.45, The involved joints—mainly the wrists, knees, and small joints of the hands—are painful, swollen, and often symmetrically affected.

The onset of arthralgias coincides with the detection of circulating immunoglobulin (Ig) M and IgG antibodies against the viral structural proteins, suggesting that the deposition of immune complexes in the synovial membranes may be responsible for the onset of the symptoms, as it happens for erythema infectiosum.
