Parvovirus B19 DNA can be detected in synovial fluid and cells, and synovial biopsy specimens of affected joints revealed infection of CD20-positive B cells or CD3-positive T cells by double immunostaining.47, In a subset of RA patients, parvovirus B19 DNA was detected in peripheral blood cells and synovial tissues, and VP1/ VP2 proteins were detected in peripheral T cells, macrophages, and synovial neutrophils. In a more recent study, the levels of circulating cytokines were measured in B19 DNA-positive or —negative RÅ patients. Plasma levels of interleukin (IL)-4 were higher in the former group while the level of pro-inflammatory cytokines was either not significantly different (e.g., for IL-12, IL-2, and tumor necrosis factor [TNF]) or was reduced (IFN-γ). A reduction in the level of key pro-inflammatory cytokines may contribute to an immunosuppressive environment and favoring viral persistence.

Molecular mimicry between host and viral proteins may contribute to the induction of autoimmunity. B19 infection has been associated with production of antibodies directed against a plethora of autoantigens, including nuclear antigens, rheumatoid factor (RF), neutrophils, cytoplasmic antigens (CAs), mitochondrial antigens (MAs; e.g., cardiolipin), smooth muscle actin (SMA), gastric parietal antigens, and phospholipid.51, For instance, one group reported that antibodies against B19 viral proteins reacted specifically with human keratin, collagen type II, ssDNA, and cardiolipin. More importantly, levels of reactivity against keratin and collagen type II were correlated with clinical hallmarks. Specifically, immunoglobulins from patients with arthritis reacted preferentially with collagen type II, whereas immunoglobulins affinity purified from patients with skin rashes reacted preferentially with keratin. To confirm a role of the virus in inducing an autoimmune response, BALB/c mice were immunized with the viral proteins and autoantibodies against keratin, collagen type II, cardiolipin, and ssDNA were subsequently detected in the majority of the mice that developed a strong anti-virus response.

In addition to RA, parvovirus B19 infection has been associated with a variety of other autoimmune diseases, including juvenile idiopathic arthritis, SLE, progressive systemic sclerosis, Sjögren's syndrome, primary biliary cirrhosis, polymyositis and

dermatomyositis.8, In patients with systemic sclerosis, the presence of parvovirus B19 in bone marrow and/or skin biopsy specimens has been reported from a significant number of subjects. Interestingly, the same authors found high levels of B19 DNA and of TNF expression in endothelium and fibroblasts of scleroderma patients. The degree of viral transcript expression correlated with active endothelial cell injury and perivascular inflammation—features considered to be important in the initial phases of the disease. In SLE patients, the presence of circulating B19 DNA is uncommon (less than 5%), but an association was found between a former B19 infection (as confirmed by high IgG and IgM levels to the virus) and the prevalence of autoantibodies against phospholipids.

It has been shown that B19 can induce in vitro an invasive phenotype in normal human synovial fibroblasts, given their robust ability to degrade reconstituted cartilage matrix, but the signaling mechanisms involved in cell infection and cell polarization remain largely ill-characterized. More recently, it has been shown that the viral NS1 protein of B19 can activate the NLRP3 inflammasome pathway involved in robust cytokine production by leukocytes. Additional experiments are warranted to better establish biologic links between the capacities of viruses to polarize resident joint cells into pro-inflammatory and aggressive phenotypes.

### Rubella Virus

Rubella virus is the sole member of the genus Rubivirus and belongs to the Togaviridae family together with alphaviruses (see next section). Rubella is an enveloped ssRNA virus composed of 9757 nucleotides and containing two long open reading frames, the 5' proximal (which encodes nonstructural proteins) and the 3' proximal (which encodes the structural proteins, Capsid, E1, and E2). The virion is spherical and measures 50 to 70 nm in diameter, with a 30 nm dense core.

Transmission is by nasopharyngeal secretions. Most cases of infection lead to a mild, self-limiting measles-like disease but major concerns arise when rubella infects the fetus, which can lead to miscarriage or congenital rubella syndrome (CRS). In CRS, rubella virus is able to infect the placenta and spread to the fetus, causing systemic inflammation and altering the function of many 60 organs.

Rubella E1 protein binds to myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein (MOG) and ectopic expression of MOG on nonpermissive cells can contribute to infection. Moreover, there is a high level of homology between rubella E2 protein and MOG, which could explain the ability of antibodies against rubella to cause demyelination at least in vitro.

Joint symptoms are a complication of naturally acquired rubella and occur in more than 50% of adult females with rubella but are rare among children and adult males with rubella. Symmetric or migratory arthralgias are more common than synovitis. Morning stiffness is prominent and symptoms usually resolve over a few days to 2 weeks. Proximal interphalangeal, metacarpophalangeal, wrist, elbow, ankle, and knee joints are most frequently affected. Periarthritis, tenosynovitis, and carpal tunnel syndrome may be seen. In some patients, symptoms may persist for months to years. Following vaccination, joint symptoms occur less frequently and are usually less severe and of shorter duration than those that occur following naturally acquired rubella. Live attenuated rubella vaccines have also caused a high frequency of postvaccination myalgia and paresthesia—symptoms similar to those in natural infection—beginning 2 weeks after inoculation and

lasting less than a week. However, in some patients, symptoms may persist for more than a year. RA27/3, the vaccine strain in current use, may cause post-vaccination joint symptoms in 15% or more of recipients.

Persistent rubella infection may be established in synovial cell cultures and as described in tissues. 65, Rubella-specific antibody titers in the synovial fluid of some patients with chronic arthritis are higher than those in serum, suggesting local synthesis of specific antibody. Persistence of rubella virus is also suggested by our previous studies, which demonstrated that virus-specific IgM may persist for up to 4 years following both natural infection and vaccination. The presence of rubella RNA in synovial tissues from patients may be due to reactivation and as a result of immunodeficiency or declining immunity in old age.

Rubella arthritis needs to be differentiated from other viral arthritides and from inflammatory arthritides, including RA. It may be clinically confused with parvovirus B19 infection, but serologies differentiate the two infections. NSAIDs are useful to control symptoms.

### Chikungunya a Alphavirus

CHIKV is an enveloped RNA positive-strand alphavirus of 12kb belonging to the Togaviridae family, transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes (Table 117.1). Aedes albopictus, the main competent vector of CHIKV, has become indigenous to many regions throughout the world. The Alphavirus group comprises 29 viruses, six of which can cause human joint disorders (arthralgias evolving into arthritis), namely CHIKV, O'Nyong-Nyong virus, Semliki forest virus (SFV) (in Africa, Asia, and Europe), RRV (in Australia and the islands of the Pacific), Sindbis virus (cosmopolitan), and Mayaro virus (in South America and French Guyana).

Several million CHIKV cases in humans have now been described in Africa, Southeast Asia, islands of the western and eastern Pacific and Indian oceans, and the Middle East (for a review, see ref. 69). Recent CHIKV outbreaks have been reported since November 2013 and have spread to several parts of the Americas.

CHIKV infection in humans results in a brief, usually 5to 7-day viremia, which is in principle controlled primarily by IFN type I and antibodies.71-73 However, CHIKV disease is often debilitating and associated with persistent arthralgias and arthritis that can last from weeks to months.14, Many patients developing chronic symptoms do not respond well to the usual analgesics, suggesting that the nature of chronic pain may be not only nociceptive but also neuropathic. Persistent symptoms, mainly joint and muscular pain, have been reported several months after CHIKV infection.76, Long-term CHIKV rheumatic manifestations are frequent underlying post-epidemic conditions. Predictors of nonrecovery include age >45 years, severe initial joint pain, and the presence of underlying osteoarthritis (OA).77, Rheumatic manifestations occur in up to 50% of adult patients and typically consist of a febrile arthritis mainly affecting the extremities (ankles, wrists, phalanges).77-83 Typically, joint symptoms occur in a fluctuating manner (often perceived as infectious relapses by the patients) but do not change anatomic location. Pain within or around tendons is also a common trait and may evolve into tenosynovitis. One group84 reported high levels of CHIKV IgM antibodies in a cohort of Indian patients with post-CHIKV RA-like illnesses. These patients were naive for musculoskeletal disorders prior to CHIKV infection. Surprisingly, few were positive for RF or anticyclic citrullinated peptide (CCP) antibodies, and these

findings were confirmed in several surveys of CHIKV patients with chronic arthralgias months post-infection.7, Tenosynovitis/enthesopathy rather than synovitis was evidenced by ultrasonography in several cases and these unique observations are in agreement with our x-ray imaging of enthesitis in post-CHIK RA patients in la Réunion.

In one study, patients with a diagnosis of RA following CHIKV infection were given classic disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drug therapy with MTX, salazopyrine, leflunomide, or hydroxychloroquine. In cases of inadequate response to MTX, treatment was successful with TNF inhibitors (e.g., etanercept, adalimumab). As the chronic disease progresses, more severe arthritis was reported 1 to 2 years post-CHIKV infection. Some patients with chronic rheumatic symptoms developed progressive erosive arthritis.79, In Manimunda's study, it was confirmed that the levels of RF and anti-CCP antibodies were not elevated in contrast to what is known in traditional RA. In the same study, one-third of the patients who had joint pain met the ACR classification criteria for RA. Magnetic resonance imaging findings included joint effusion, bony erosion, marrow edema, synovial thickening, tendonitis, and tenosynovitis.

CHIKV infection has been reported in multiple organs of the body and particularly the synovial tissues in humans and animal models.71, In vitro studies have been instrumental for the comprehension of CHIKV tissue tropisms and to provide insights into the causal pathogenic mechanisms. The main target cells for CHIKV infection and replication are fibroblasts. Recent studies corroborate this finding in addition to demonstrating that CHIKV readily infects human fetal lung fibroblasts (MRC-5 cells) and human synovial and skin fibroblasts. 18, Not all fibroblasts are equally susceptible to CHIKV infection. It has been shown that resting fibroblasts and a subpopulation of synovial fibroblasts (CD141+/CD90+) manifest some resistance through mechanisms still largely unknown.18, CHIKV can also infect epithelial cells (e.g., HeLa, HEK293, but not A549), endothelial cells, hepatocytes (carcinoma HuH7), neurons, astrocytes, neuroblastoma cell lines (e.g., SH-SY5Y), and muscle satellite cells.91, The cellular receptor that mediates virus entry has recently been characterized and identified as matrix remodeling associated 8 antigen (mxra8, also known as limitrin). Mutagenesis experiments have shown that mxra8 binds to a surface-exposed domain of CHIKV E2 protein. CD147 may also contribute to the binding to E2 and facilitate viral entry into host cells. Of note, the receptor to mediate SFV entry has recently been identified as the very low-density lipoprotein receptor. Evidence from biopsies of infected patients showed that CHIKV antigens were detected mostly in cells located in the skeletal muscle epimysium, of the joint capsule, and of the dermis. In contrast, immune cells, such as monocytes, lymphocytes, dendritic cells, natural killer (NK) cells, and their cell line counterparts (THP1, U937, H9) are not permissive to CHIKV infection.94, However, human monocyte and macrophage infection remains controversial and it is likely that they could be infected but with a poor capacity to replicate CHIKV.92,

There are very few studies to support the idea that alphaviruses will contribute to chronic RA-like diseases through the production of autoantibodies against self-antigens as it has been described for B19, EBV, or HCV. One study reported that Finnish patients with Pogosta disease following Sindbis infection had autoantibodies to NA, MA, and RF at a higher prevalence compared with healthy Finnish subjects at 3 years post-infection. Interestingly, anti-CCP antibodies were detected only in one patient out of 49,

who was also positive for RF. It remains to be determined whether this autoimmune profile is more prominent in recovered Pogosta patients versus those with long-term arthritis.

### Epstein-Barr Virus

EBV has been found in association with several common autoimmune diseases including SLE and multiple sclerosis (MS).7, The epidemiologic association with RA is more controversial. EBV belongs to the genus Lymphocryptovirus within the subfamily Gammaherpesvirus of the Herpesvirus family. It is the fourth member of this family. Herpesviruses are large DNA viruses with a linear double-stranded DNA (dsDNA) genome inside a membrane-coated icosaedrical capsid. The EBV genome has a length of 172 kilobases (kb). EBV has strong tissue tropism for B lymphocytes. The virus is associated with a wide variety of neoplasms including lymphoid tumors like Burkitt lymphoma, Hodgkin's disease, NK T cell lymphoma, epithelial malignancies, especially undifferentiated nasopharyngeal carcinoma, gastric carcinoma, and carcinomas of the salivary glands. The virus is shed into the saliva of persistently infected individuals who spread the virus to uninfected individuals. When transmitted orally, EBV initially infects either epithelial cells or resting tonsillar B lymphocytes. EBV binds through its viral envelope glycoprotein (gp)350 to the complement receptor type 2 (CR2/CD21) that is primarily expressed on B cells. This receptor can also interact with IFN- α, but the role of such molecular interactions in the IFN-mediated anti-viral response is unknown. B cellbound virions can also efficiently transfer to CD21-negative epithelial cells, which enhances the transfer of virus to others cells (possibly to fibroblasts) and establishes latency in B cells and other cells.107,

Both the latent and lytic EBV proteins are potent immunogens and elicit vigorous B and T cell responses. However, patients with RA have impaired control of EBV infection given that their peripheral blood T lymphocytes are less efficient at controlling the outgrowth of EBV-infected B cells. In immunosuppressed and immunodeficient patients, or in individuals with a functional defect of EBV-specific T cells, lytic EBV replication is regularly activated and an increased viral load can be detected in the blood. Enhanced lytic replication results in new infection events and EBV-associated transformation events and seems to be a risk factor both for malignant transformation and the development of autoimmune diseases. It is conceivable that an increased load or altered presentation of a limited set of lytic or latent EBV proteins that cross-react with cellular self-antigens triggers and perpetuates the pathogenic processes that result in arthritis, MS, and SLE.

Of critical note, patients with RA develop EBV-positive B cell lymphomas when MTX is used for immunosuppression, which is not the case for other immune-modulating drugs. It has been proposed that MTX could induce lytic EBV replication in latently infected EBV-positive cell lines in vitro. Thus MTX may promote the generation of lymphomas in RA and polymyositis patients by its immunosuppressive properties, combined with a specific reactivation of latent EBV genomes.

While a causal role of EBV in the generation of malignancies is established, a causal role in the generation of autoimmune diseases is circumstantial. However, cross-reactivity between viral antigens and self-antigens and the immortalization of pre-existing autoreactive B cells through infection with EBV with the consequent production of autoantibodies may be plausible viral mechanisms for triggering autoimmunity. Indeed, one group recently demonstrated high-affinity molecular mimicry between the EBV

transcription factor EBV nuclear antigen 1 and the central nervous system protein glial cell adhesion molecule (glial CAM on astrocytes and oligodendrocytes). Post-translational modification of glial-CAM may facilitate the molecular mimicry. A resulting abundance of cross-reactive antibodies may contribute to demyelination in MS patients. Strong genetic risk factors for developing RA are the alleles that contain peptide sequence homologies to EBV gp110 (BALF4). BALF4 is normally one of the most abundant EBV proteins in late lytic infection and also serves as a target of antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity against EBV-infected cells. The BALF4 open reading frame contains the sequence QKRAAQRAA, which is highly homologous to the RA susceptibility determinant (i.e., QKRAA found in certain HLA class II DRβ chains, such as DR4). Carriers of this shared epitope have a significantly higher risk of developing anti-CCPpositive RA, particularly among those with a history of cigarette smoking.

### Hepatitis C Virus and Other Flaviviruses

HCV is a positive-strand RNA virus of the family Flaviviridae. Studies of this virus have made huge leaps forward since the implementation of efficient cell culture systems. Worldwide, over 130 million people are chronically infected with HCV. The viral genome consists of a single open reading frame that is less than 10 kb long. The proteins of this virus are arranged along the genome in the following order: N terminal-core-envelope (E1)-E2- p7-nonstructural protein 2 (NS2)-NS3NS4A-NS4BNS5A- NS5B-C terminal.

Acute infection goes along with mild and generalized symptoms, and therefore mostly remains undiagnosed. In more than half of the patients, however, the infection persists and, over the years, can cause liver damage such as fibrosis, cirrhosis, or hepatocellular carcinoma. Viral antigen is detectable within the first weeks of exposure, accompanied by a rise in serum liver transaminases. Antibodies develop and clear HCV in some patients; however, in chronic HCV infection, viral anti-genemia and HCV RNA persist despite humoral and cellular immune responses. There is also evidence to suggest a possible pathogenic role for HCV-associated immunity in a broad spectrum of autoimmune diseases, including RA. Although this association may be sporadic or indicate an increased incidence of HCV infection in patients with autoimmune disease, case reports documenting the occurrence of acute and chronic HCV infection preceding autoimmune disease suggests a causal role in individuals who may be predisposed to the development of autoimmunity. Liver biopsy in HCV-infected patients is useful to establish disease severity and to exclude other causes of hepatitis such as alcoholism or hemochromatosis. A probable role for HCV infection in autoimmune hepatitis is emerging with the concurrent detection of autoantibodies such as anti-nuclear antibody (ANA) and anti-SMA.

Polyarthralgias and polyarthritis have been associated with HCV infection, and HCV RNA has been isolated from synovial fluid. Patients with chronic HCV associated with polyarthralgias/myalgias often have antibodies including RF and ANA without anti-dsDNA or anti-CCP antibodies.114, In one study, the prevalence of arthritis in chronic HCV patients was estimated to be 6.8%, and ANAs were more frequently positive in the subset of arthritic HCV patients. The optimal treatment for HCV-associated polyarthritis has not been determined, but MTX has been used with some success and minimal complications, although this agent should be avoided in those with cirrhosis. Discussed

further in Chapter 92 of this textbook, arthralgias/arthritis may also act as a manifestation of HCV-mediated mixed (type II) cryoglobulinemia.

Diverse receptors or factors are involved in HCV infection and include CD81, scavenger receptor class B type I and claudin-1. Occludin is also an essential HCV cell entry factor. It has been demonstrated that synovial fibroblasts from RA or OA patients were not able to support HCV replication despite the fact that they express CD81.

Arthralgia post-dengue infection has been reported but without translating into arthritis as described for the other arboviruses such as CHIKV. However, in the context of acute infection, articular inflammation may be more pronounced in patients already affected by RA. In a Brazilian retrospective cohort study including 69 SLE and 301 RA patients suffering from dengue infection, the morbidity and hospitalization rate were significantly increased compared with noninfected SLE and RA patients. Zika is another emerging RNA flavivirus. It has been detected in the synovial fluid of a RA patient and has been linked to disease exacerbation. The precise prevalence of arthralgia in Zika cases remains poorly defined, although a recent meta-analysis revealed no evidence of chronic rheumatic manifestations following Zika infection.

### Arthritogenic Viruses Hijack the Innate Interferon n Type Response to Favor Persistence

A major role of the immune system (innate and adaptive) is to rapidly control infection by viruses, for instance, at the major portals of entry (skin, nasopharynx) and before dissemination to other 123 To initiate an effective anti-viral immune response, all organs. cells should be capable of sensing and responding appropriately to pathogens. This coordinated response should in principle limit viral spreading and persistence through the mobilization of adaptive immune T and B cells.

A growing number of germ-line pattern recognition receptors (PRRs) have been characterized and are expressed on immune and nonimmune structural cells. These receptors are capable of recognizing a plethora of conserved pathogen-associated molecular patterns that do not occur under normal circumstances in the host. The PRRs sense specific viral structures and induce the production of type I IFN. Two types of PRRs exist: ubiquitously expressed cytoplasmic RNA sensing molecules and membranebound TLRs. The expression of TLR is more limited than that of the cytoplasmic receptors.

The retinoic-acid-inducible gene I (RIG-I)like RNA helicase receptors (RLRs), which include RIG-I and melanoma differentiation associated gene 5 (MDA-5), are a ubiquitously expressed group of cytosolic receptors that detect viral RNA structures and induce type I IFN-α and -β production. Binding of viral RNA enables interaction between the RLRs and downstream signaling molecules such as IPS-1 (IFN-β promoter stimulator-1; also known as MAVS, CARDIF, and VISA), which activate transcription factors (e.g., interferon regulatory factor [IRF] 3) and regulate the production of type I IFN. The expression of RLRs is low in the steady state but is highly induced by type I IFN, which enhances their capacity to recognize viruses and to propagate the anti-viral response. At least 10 TLRs have been identified in humans, of which three (TLR3, TRL7 and TLR9) recognize

nucleic acid viral components and stimulate type I IFN production. Interestingly, TLR expression is also regulated by IFN. TLR3 is triggered by dsRNA, whereas TLR7 recognizes guanosine-rich and uridine-rich ssRNA, and TLR9 senses unmethylated cytosine—phosphate—guanine motifs. TLR4, which is expressed on the cell surface, recognizes lipopolysaccharide from bacteria but also viral proteins and can stimulate type I IFN production.

Release of type I IFN from infected cells results in autocrine and paracrine stimulation of the IFN-α/β receptor, which through associated tyrosine and Janus (JAK) kinases leads to the phosphorylation of STAT (signal transducers and activators of transcription) 1 and 2. STAT1/2 heterodimers associate with IFN regulatory factor 9 and bind to IFN-stimulated response elements present in the promoter region of the IFN-stimulated genes (ISGs).

ISG-encoded proteins represent the anti-viral effector molecules that directly inhibit molecular and biochemical activities required for virus replication. Expectedly, type I IFN was shown to be essential for the anti-viral activities against many arthritogenic viruses as demonstrated in vitro and in vivo.71, However, many viruses (including CHIKV) block nearly all aspects of the IFN regulatory pathway. This includes the disruption of dsRNA and IFN receptor/JAK-STAT signaling events, the inhibition of IRF and NF-kB functions, and other mechanisms that target the anti-viral actions of specific ISG products.132-134

The anti-viral molecules induced by IFN include members of the apolipoprotein B mRNA-editing enzyme catalytic polypeptide (APOBEC) family and can mutate viral genomes, the Mx GTPase, an inhibitor of viral polymerases, and members of the tripartite motif family including the autoantigen Ro/SSA 52 kDa (Ro52, also known as TRIM21), which can inhibit viral replication at multiple stages in the life cycle. RNA-activated protein kinase (PKR) is yet another example of an anti-viral molecule.

Immune recognition is enhanced in cells exposed to type I IFN and controlling major histocompatibility complex class I expression and resulting in enhanced presentation of both viral and selfantigens for recognition by the immune system. Other changes include the induction of molecules (such as p53) that increase susceptibility to cell deathinducing stimuli, thus enhancing the killing of virally infected cells by the immune system. Type I IFN regulates pathways in target cells, antigen-presenting cells (such as dendritic cells [DCs] and macrophages), and effector cells (which mediate anti-viral effects and tissue damage).

Plasmacytoid dendritic cells (pDCs) have the unique capacity to rapidly secrete large quantities of type I IFN upon recognition of nucleic acid structures by TLR7 or TLR9.136 These cells are ideally suited to respond rapidly to viruses in the absence of prior IFN exposure. pDCs are, therefore, thought to have a central role in the self-amplifying nature of autoimmune diseases through the production of large quantities of type I IFN, which mediates numerous downstream functional effects on target cells and cells of the immune system.

Surprisingly, it was found that some parvoviruses do not appear to induce an IFN response in normal human fibroblasts, glia cells, or melanocytes. Furthermore, the authors found that parvovirus infectivity was unaffected by IFN treatment of human normal or tumor cells. The IFN-resistant phenotype of parvoviruses may give them an advantage, including the capacity to persist in tissue sanctuaries. In contrast, a great deal of information has been gathered over recent years about the innate and adaptive immune responses to clear CHIKV. Very high levels of circulating CHIKV can be reached in acute settings, ranging from 105 to 1012 virus RNA particles per milliliter of blood during the first

days of infection. CHIKV is efficiently cleared within a matter of days and the symptoms usually subside within a couple of weeks, suggesting a robust and efficient innate immune response that limits systemic viral replication. CHIKV is a ssRNA virus; therefore it may be detected by TLR7 and/or TLR8 (in mice). The helicase RIG-I and MDA-5 may also be involved in the recognition of CHIKV. Moreover, CHIKV can have a dsRNA intermediate during the replication cycle, which may be detected by TLR3. Recently one group showed that CHIKV infection leads to activation of the transcription factor IRF3 and subsequent transcription of IRF3-dependent anti-viral genes, including IFNβ. IRF3 activation occurred via the engagement of the adaptor molecule IFN promoter stimulator 1 (IPS-1). Recently investigators showed that CHIKV does not directly stimulate type I IFN production in immune cells such as DCs. Instead, infected nonhematopoietic cells sense viral RNA in an IPS-1-dependent manner and participate in the control of infection through their production of type I IFN. Although the IPS-1 signaling pathway contributes to the immune response, there is also evidence for a MyD88-dependent PRR that may be critical for preventing viral dissemination. CHIKV-induced type I IFN response seems to be protective in vitro and possibly induces the expression of restriction factors such as ISGs and oligoadenylate synthetase (OAS). 140,141OAS has been shown to be active against CHIKV replication in HeLa cells, and its role in other cell types needs to be further established.

In patients and in the nonhuman primate model, the secreted IFN-α response was transient and dropped to basal levels within 24 hours, while the peak of viremia persisted for several days. These data suggest that CHIKV may be capable of controlling the IFN response. Infection and replication of alphavirus usually cause a general host translational shutoff, leading to severe cytopathic activities in mammalian cells. One group confirmed this paradigm, demonstrating that translation of cellular (but not viral) genes is blocked during CHIKV infection. CHIKV was found to trigger inactivation of the translational molecule eukaryotic initiation factor subunit 2α (eiF2α) through a PKR-dependent pathway. Moreover, another group showed that CHIKV replication is resistant to inhibition by IFN once RNA replication has been initiated and that CHIKV actively suppresses the antiviral IFN response by preventing IFN-induced gene expression. Indeed, CHIKV infection efficiently blocked STAT1 phosphorylation and/or nuclear translocation in mammalian cells induced by either type I or type II IFN. Nonstructural protein 2 was a potent inhibitor of IFN-induced JAK-STAT signaling. Hence, CHIKV, like many viruses, has evolved to evade or counteract the anti-viral responses and, hence, favoring viral persistence.

An additional anti-viral molecular response is reported during CHIKV infection. Macroautophagy, referred herein as autophagy, is a fundamental homeostatic process that leads to the degradation and recycling of long-lived proteins and organelles. 142, Autophagy is first a fundamental cell-surviving process during starvation conditions but it also plays a role in both innate and adaptive immunity in response to pathogens. We have previously explored the role of the autophagy machinery in CHIKV infection and showed that cellular autophagy was promoted within CHIKV-infected cells and, furthermore, contributed to enhanced CHIKV replication.

A robust protective adaptive immune response develops after CHIKV infection,145 and this is also the case for all arthritogenic viruses listed previously. IgM antibodies against CHIKV can be detected in the sera of infected patients during the acute phase of

the infection and anti-CHIKV IgG antibodies, especially neutralizing, may prevent virus reinfection.145, Kinetics involved in the appearance of IgG, sometimes within the first days' post-infection, is in favor of a rapid development of a protective adaptive immune response. At the cellular level, a major immune response in the acute stage is characterized by a rapid mobilization of CD4+ and CD8+ T cells. Surprisingly, the level of TNF and IL-1β was rather weak during the acute phase and not significantly elevated com- .10,141Other Th1 cytokines were elepared with control groups. vated in acute settings (IFN-γ and IL-12), although the response seemed to be skewed toward a Th2/Th17 response as indicated with high levels of IL-4, IL-13, and IL-17.141 Another study demonstrated a production of IL-4, IL-10, and IFN-γ in the acute phase of CHIKV associated with a robust CD8+ T lymphocyte response in the early stages of the disease, and a CD4+ T lymphocyte—mediated response in the later stages. Of note, a specific CHIKV IgM response was shown to persist several months after infection87,148 in patients suffering from chronic arthralgias/ arthritis. This observation may be related to viral persistence.

### Arthritogenic Viruses Engage Trojan Horse Scenario to Avoid Adaptive Immunity

Many studies have searched for DNA or RNA of viruses in synovial tissues or fluid samples mostly of arthralgic patients. Many of the arthritogenic viruses aforementioned can be found in synovial tissue or fluid. The diagnostic significance of these findings depends both on the particular microbe and on the clinical context, whereby the findings should be interpreted with caution. Furthermore, for establishing the etiology of chronic arthropathy induced by latent viral infection, the concentration and the location of the pathogen—that is, in the synovial membrane, in synovial fluid, or in the cells of the latter—might be of importance. Even if the pathogen is found by polymerase chain reaction (PCR), or it can be cultured from the arthritic joint, its causal role is not easy to prove.

One of the emerging paradigms is that synovial tissue cells are infected and display an altered phenotype involved in tissue injuries.

Focusing on alphaviruses, it was found that persistent signs and symptoms such as joint pain (arthralgia) and arthritis (not necessarily associated with bone erosions) were reported several months after CHIKV or RRV infection.77, Indeed, rheumatic manifestations affect up to 50% of the adult patients 6 to 15 months post-CHIKV infection. There is a strong body of evidence that persistent joint damage is linked with the persistence of arthritogenic alphaviruses by mechanisms still poorly characterized.1, This hypothesis is now thoroughly tested for CHIKV; it is plausible that CHIKV hides in immune privileged niches and that those sanctuaries contribute directly to synovial tissue damage. The study of one group showed the presence of viral antigens and RNA 3 months post-infection in joints, muscles, lymphoid organs, and the liver. It is noteworthy that they found high levels of macrophage/mononuclear cell infiltration in lymphoid organs and large amounts of CHIKV antigen and viral RNA in spleen macrophages for prolonged periods (up to 3 months), demonstrating that macrophages act as the cellular reservoirs for CHIKV persistence. The same conclusions were drawn from a study in humans. Indeed, using a longitudinal study of hospitalized patients in la Réunion, we showed that CHIKV (RNA and protein) was found in perivascular synovial

macrophages in one chronic patient 18 months post-infection. One group confirmed this in a mouse model of acute infection. Indeed, rheumatic disease was associated with a prolific infiltrate of monocytes, macrophages, and NK cells and the production of MCP-1/CCL2, TNF, and IFN-γ.

As one plausible cytopathic mechanism, we found that CHIKV can induce apoptosis in vitro and in synovial tissues and that completion of the apoptotic process was important for viral propagation. Furthermore, CHIKV is able to hide in apoptotic blebs to enhance viral spreading to neighboring cells, especially macrophages that engulf the bleb. This "Trojan horse" scenario may take place in tissues, allowing CHIKV to escape the immune response and cause chronic pathologies, such as arthritis. These infected macrophages may recapitulate humoral and cellular inflammatory processes to drive arthritis (angiogenesis, tissue remodeling, and injuries). This Trojan horse scenario is a possible immune evasion strategy reported for many viruses (B19, HBV, Poxvirus, HIV, vaccinia). 153-156

### Other Mechanisms Favoring Viral Persistence Inside Synovial Tissues

Historically it has been thought that many viruses including B19 are, by the actions of the host immune system, fully removed from the body within a few weeks or months of infection. With highly sensitive detection tools, such as PCR and in situ hybridization, it is becoming increasingly obvious that eradication of a virus (if not all pathogens) from the human body is seldom complete. It is, however, critically important to also study healthy controls in order to avoid misinterpretations of disease causality.

Defective interfering (DI) particles may play a role in establishing or maintaining persistent infections. DI particles are replication-deficient deletion mutants that interfere with the growth of the homologous wild-type virus.

Another possible reason for viral persistence is that the synovial tissue cells constitute a good hiding place from the host's immune defense. The dominant local cell populations in joints are synovial and cartilage cells. Synovial cells can be divided into fibroblast-like and macrophage-like synoviocytes. These cells present several distinct phenotypical characteristics compared with classical fibroblasts and tissue macrophages. It may be that these cells have major immunoregulatory mechanisms to control tissue injuries but may also be mobilized during viral infection to favor viral persistence. A positive correlation was detected between CD4+CD25+ T regulatory (Treg) cell frequency and HCV chronic infection as detected by high levels of RNA titers in patient-derived liver tissues. It has been proposed that Treg cells may play a role in viral persistence by suppressing HCV-specific T cell responses in a cellcell contact manner. Chronic HCV infection may also be favored given the concomitant presence of virus-specific CCR7- CD8+ T cells. These CD8+ Treg cells are antigen specific, as they can be stimulated by HCV epitopes and suppress T cell responses through the production of considerable amounts of IL-10. It remains to be addressed whether these Tregs are mobilized by other arthritogenic viruses.

### Mechanisms Involved in Chronic Arthralgias

As a testament to the severity of joint pain encountered in many alphaviral arthritides in humans, the native African name for

CHIKV means "that which bends up." These arthralgias can be observed through the acute phase of the infection and persist over months to years in chronic patients. Joint pains are also clinical hallmarks associated with chronic B19 or HCV infections. 161-163

The joint is densely innervated, and its sensory innervation is geared predominantly toward nociception, indicating how vital positioning sense and awareness of potentially injurious movement are to proper joint function. Chronic pain pathways are subject to complex levels of control and modulation, both in the periphery and in the central nervous system. In humans, articular branches of the tibial nerve that innervate the posterior knee joint capsule contain 70% to 80% unmyelinated C-fibers and sympathetic nerves and have also been associated with pain. Nociceptors (nerve endings involved in pain) are abundant in the joint capsule, ligaments, periosteum, menisci, subchondral bone, and synovium. As cartilage is aneural, it is not involved in nociception of the joint.

Nociceptors express a broad range of receptors for ligands that will induce action potentials when the receptors are engaged and transmitting nociception to the brain. These ligands include cytokines, chemokines, neuropeptides, and prostaglandins, which can all form part of the biochemical milieu in the joint persistently infected by arthritogenic viruses. As a result of this peripheral sensitization, joint movement within the normal range becomes painful.

TNF, IL-17, and IL-6 are inflammatory cytokines abundantly expressed in response to infection by many of the arthritogenic viruses.5, Pro-inflammatory factors such as IFN-α, IL-6, and IP-10 were also found at higher levels in the serum of patients with CHIKV-induced polyarthritis than in noninfected healthy individuals, indicating their potential causative role in chronic 147, These molecules can cause projoint and muscle pain. longed mechanical hypersensitivity and sensitizing joint nociceptors to mechanical stimuli. The pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-1β and TNF can directly affect sensory neurons and can also trigger pain via downstream mediators such as other cytokines, chemokines, prostaglandins (PG), neurotrophins, nitric oxide, kinins, lipids, ATP, and complement anaphylatoxins. Interestingly, it has been reported that IFN produced by CHIKV-infected fibroblasts induced elevated expression of prostaglandins. HCV, and particularly the NS3 viral protein, is also known to modulate cyclooxygenase 2 activity and hence prostaglandin synthesis.170, All in all, PG may contribute to mechanisms of nociceptor activation and sensitization. In addition, the activation of complement system and the production of complement anaphylatoxins (C3a, C5a) in RRV-infected joints may contribute to arthralgia.

Inflammatory cytokines can also enhance local levels of nerve growth factor (NGF), a major contributor to peripheral hypersensitivity. The binding of NGF to its high-affinity receptor, TrkA, on peripheral nociceptors causes rapid potentiation of the thermosensitive ion channel TRPV1 (transient receptor potential cation channel, subfamily V, member 1), thus lowering the pain threshold and contributing to pain hypersensitivity. It remains unknown whether arthritogenic viruses directly affect NGF biology in the joint, although it has been shown that alphaviruses such as Sindbis can increase NGF production by glial cells.

Nociceptors express TLRs, which recognize a variety of alarmins released during tissue injury and contribute to pain generation. The primary function of these alarmins is to boost innate and adaptive immune cell anti-viral activities, but they could also contribute to chronic inflammation and joint pain. 23,24

### Mechanisms Involved in Chronic Inflammatory Viral Arthritis Resembling Rheumatoid Arthritis

RA is a heterogeneous systemic autoimmune disorder that is characterized by an antigen-driven immune response against selfantigens with the destruction of host tissue with a highly disabling impact that affects up to 1% of the world population. A hallmark of RA is its self-sustaining and auto-amplifying nature, in which immune-mediated tissue damage and tissue repair collaborate in a feed-forward loop to provide the destructive power and the fuel that sustain the inflammatory process.

In RA, CD4+ and CD8+ T cells, NK cells, and macrophages contribute to the local and chronic inflammation of the joints. Secretion of inflammatory cytokines like IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF15 play a pathogenic role in the disease process. Overproduction of pro-inflammatory cytokines is believed to be orchestrated predominantly by macrophage-like synoviocytes. Fibroblast-like synoviocytes invade the cartilage and contribute to joint destruction. The activation and differentiation of resident macrophages into osteoclasts is a key process leading to bone erosion.

While the pathogenesis of virally induced arthritis might be mediated through different routes, outcomes are remarkably similar with chronic forms of inflammatory arthritis such as RA. Available studies also suggest several overlapping features of disease pathogenesis. Similar to observations in RA, several studies have suggested that macrophage recruitment and subsequent secretion of pro-inflammatory cytokines and chemokines play a major role in the development of arthritis in alphavirus infection.10, Other cellular injuries occur that can mimic features in RA that include direct cellular lysis of virally infected cells, indirect effects mediated by the immune response, and/or enhancement of the invasiveness of synovial fibroblasts (acute or chronic arthritis) and production of immune complexes.

It has been demonstrated that osteoblasts and synovial fibroblasts infected by CHIKV drive osteoclastogenesis in vitro and in .178,179Osteoclasts are speessence may contribute to joint damage. cialized cells derived from the monocyte/macrophage hematopoietic lineage that develop and adhere to bone matrix, then secrete acid and lytic enzymes that degrade it in a specialized, extra-cellular compartment. Osteoprotegerin (OPG), receptor activator of NF-kB (RANK), and RANK ligand (RANKL) together regulate osteoclast function. Similar again to observations in RA, CHIKV and RRV patients presented high levels of RANKL and low levels of OPG, which would favor the appearance of macrophage-derived osteoclasts in the joints.5, Using a mouse model of CHIKV infection, one group demonstrated that blood monocytes were recruited to sites of infection through the action of chemokines such as CCL2 and differentiate into osteoclast-like cells leading to bone erosion. Furthermore, they observed that treatment with an IL-6 neutralizing antibody reduced bone loss and reduced RANKL/OPG ratios in sera of mice. Bindarit (a CCL2 inhibitor) was also able to control for the osteoclastogenic activity of CHIKV.

### Treatment and Prevention

Arthralgias and arthritis postviral infection are mainly treated with analgesics and NSAIDs, which may provide symptomatic relief but do not significantly modify the underlying disease process. For chronic arthritis lasting more than 3 months post-CHIKV

infection, treatment with MTX has yielded clinical benefit, possibly related to anti-proliferative effects on invasive fibroblasts or for its capacity to control the pro-inflammatory activities of alarmins such as HMGB1.182, Whether chloroquine may be useful as a prophylactic treatment or in the case of chronic infection needs further investigation. Several molecules are in development and have been tested in animal models. IFN-α treatment was able to prevent arthritis in mice but only if given before infection, suggesting that IFN-α may have a limited therapeutic role. High levels of MCP1/CCL2 are produced following alphaviral infection in humans10,141 and in mice suffering from polyarthralgia and polyarthritis post-alphavirus infection.73, Bindarit may hold promise by reducing the influx of inflammatory cells that mediate tissue damage post-infection.185, CTLA4-Ig (abatacept) showed promising results in CHIKV-infected mice, particularly when co-administered with a human monoclonal antibody directed against CHIKV. In treated mice, the authors observed significant decreases in joint swelling, synovial virus levels, inflammatory cell infiltrates, and chemokine/cytokine levels. In CHIKV-infected mice, intraperitoneal injections of suramin reduced viral loads, synovial inflammation, and cartilage lesions. Mefenamic acid associated with ribavirin, 189 phosphorodiamidate morpholino oligomers, 190 pentose polysulfate, 191 and favipiravir192 also improved arthritis and reduced the viral load in CHIKV-infected mice.

Vaccination remains the best strategy to prevent most vector-borne diseases. Ideally, vaccines should combine low cost, single-dose efficacy, and rapid and long-lived immunity with negligible risk of serious adverse reactions. For example, recombinant CHIKV vaccines are under development and have been tested in mouse or macaque models, using different technologies. .193-195 Some vaccines efficient against both CHIKV and Zika are also under evaluation in mouse models. CHIKV vaccines are currently being evaluated in phase II and III clinical trials and with promising outcomes. The most advanced CHIKV vaccine is a live-attenuated East/Central/South African strain (LR 2006- OPY1) isolated during the outbreak in la Réunion in 2006 and administered as a single-dose vaccine, VLA1553.197 VLA1553 has been granted PRIME (PRIority MEdicine) designation by the European Medicines Agency in 2020, and regulatory submissions are planned in Europe in 2023. In addition to live-attenuated viruses and virus-like particle vaccines, recombinant live-attenuated vaccines such as measles-CHIKV vaccine (also known as MV-CHIKV) have been developed and are under phase II clinical trial. 198

### Conclusion

Our understanding of the pathologic mechanisms involved in chronic arthralgias and arthritis developing postviral infection is still in its infancy given that several intricate humoral and cellular pathways are involved. Causal links will need to be verified in animal models and may be controlled for immune status, immune senescence, or any other comorbidities, such as chronic systemic inflammation. The development of animal models of chronic and flaring viral arthritis will be instrumental for screening new drug treatments and vaccines and to evaluate the shortand longterm effects of immunomodulation therapies of these arthritides. Addressing these knowledge gaps is critical and will require intensive investigations to improve animal models currently reported in the literature, which do not appear to develop chronic joint inflammation. Gene and protein profiling studies will be required

to address the phenotypic polarization of the synovial cells (fibroblasts and macrophages), which are chronically infected and contribute to progressive joint destruction. It is increasingly possible that viruses may control many of the inflammatory pathways, which may be of further interest to the pathogenesis of similar conditions such as RA and in the development of novel therapeutic avenues.

# Rheumatic Fever and Post-streptococcal Arthritis

### KEY POINTS

### Introduction

Rheumatic fever (RF) and rheumatic heart disease (RHD) occur in young, susceptible people who have not received treatment for group A streptococcal (GAS) infection. This chapter briefly describes the etiologic agent and reviews several genes involved in developing inflammatory and autoimmune lesions. Of note, the role of class II human leukocyte antigen (HLA) alleles is described in association with the disease and its function in antigen presentation to T cells, which activate the adaptive branch of the immune response. Mechanisms that underlie organ-specific lesions are also discussed. Both cellular and humoral immune responses are involved in the autoimmune reactions, and T helper (Th)1 and Th17 inflammatory cytokines mediate the development of rheumatic heart lesions. Clinical spectra and treatment are presented, along with perspectives regarding vaccine development targeting Streptococcus pyogenes infection.

Numerous barriers and gaps exist in implementing RHD prevention strategies and effective care of affected patients that fall short of recommendations. As a result, RHD continues to have a

devastating impact, with estimates of nearly 300,000 deaths globally each year and loss of > 10 million disability-adjusted life-years.

### Etiologic Agent (S. pyogenes)

RF is universally preceded by infection with group A streptococcus. Rebecca Lancefield classified the streptococci in 1941 and identified carbohydrates on the cell walls of the bacteria. She classified them as groups A, B, C, F, and G based on the types of cell wall polysaccharides present.

Group A is characterized by N-acetyl-β-D-glucosamine and rhamnose in the cell wall and is responsible for developing RF and RHD. These bacteria contain M, T, and R surface proteins and lipoteichoic acid, which are involved in bacterial adherence to epithelial cells of the throat. M protein, the major antigen, comprises approximately 450 amino acid residues extending from the cell wall. The N-terminal portion of this protein is highly variable and defines the emm type that is responsible for the antigenic diversity of the bacteria. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, more than 200 emm genotypes currently exist worldwide, with a variable distribution depending on the region.

The diversity of S. pyogenes is also influenced by social and economic conditions. Diversity is accentuated in low-income countries, likely because of the lack of treatment, resulting in the spread of bacteria and favoring genetic mutations. Similarities in the distribution of emm-type strains have been observed in highincome countries, Asia, the Middle East, and Latin America, in contrast to those found in Africa and the Pacific region. Interestingly, most of the streptococcal strains identified and described in this study were associated with the development of RF and RHD. The most frequent strain in a majority of countries was emml, accounting for approximately 20% of the strains compared with approximately 5% in Africa and the Pacific. Interestingly, the emml strain is also frequently associated with post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis and invasive disease.3,

In 2014, an analysis of 220 variants of the M protein revealed 48 emm clusters that contained closely related M proteins sharing binding and structural properties. Recently, complete genome sequences of S. pyogenes were defined using a PacBio Illumina sequencing platform that will provide more accurate identification

of the diverse strains of the bacteria, facilitating the diagnostics for infectious diseases. This advanced classification approach could further inform the development of new drugs and vaccine designs for treating and preventing diseases related to streptococcal infection.

The end of the C-terminal half, in contrast to the N-terminal portion, contains multiple repeat regions, presents a high degree of conservation of approximately 70%, and serves as the target of a vaccine development model.

### Epidemiology

The risk of RF after untreated S. pyogenes pharyngitis in susceptible people ranges from 0.3% to 3%.7, Susceptibility depends on the individual's genetic background and is influenced mainly by low socioeconomic conditions. Crowded households that facilitate the spread of bacteria, lack of access to antibiotics and medical facilities, and other factors associated with poverty are all wellrecognized risk factors for the development of RF. Likely, the higher diversity of S. pyogenes strains found in low-income countries plays a role in RF susceptibility due to a resulting increase in the risk of recurrent infections.

A high index of suspicion for acute rheumatic fever (ARF) is indicated, particularly when caring for patients originating from geographic settings where ARF is endemic. RHD affects more than 40.5 million people worldwide and results in 306,000 deaths annually. The incidence is highest among the world's most disadvantaged populations. Temporal trends in the health burden posed by RF and RHD, including incidence and related mortality, have not shown recent signs of improvement.

The incidence of ARF is 8 to 51 per 100,000 people worldwide. It most commonly affects children 5 to 15 years of age after a group A streptococcal infection. Since 1990, the prevalence of RHD has been rising steadily, reaching 40.5 million (95% confidence interval, 32.150.1 million) affected in 2019. The continuing increase in prevalence reflects increased global awareness, greater availability of echocardiography for case definition, improved survival in some places, and the chronic nature of RHD.

In high-income countries, tonsillitis is only a "throat infection." However, in developing countries, or even those of average income, in the case of Brazil, it may be a sign of RHD, which kills approximately 233,000 to 500,000 individuals per year globally.

RF/RHD continues to be a significant cause of morbidity and mortality in developing countries. This scenario is very different and diverse in high-income countries. RHD has mostly been eradicated in such countries, but a new disease burden is possible due to migration flow. Most ARF and RHD are in lowand middleincome countries where more than 80% of the world's ARF cases occur. Global estimates indicate that the burden of RHD is highest among people living in poor-quality housing, followed by rural areas, and lowest in urban areas.

### Clinical Manifestations

### Acute Rheumatic Fever

Manifestations of ARF result in a constellation of symptoms that may occur in isolation or any combination. In addition, as previously reported, the incidence of ARF manifestations varies in frequency and intensity among different age groups, individuals, and localities.

ARF is rare before age 3 and infrequent after age 15, with most cases occurring between ages 4 and 9. The inflammation tends to be more intense in younger children, who often exhibit greater prostration, fever, and carditis, whereas adults tend to show a greater incidence of arthritis. Symptoms begin approximately 2 to 3 weeks after GAS infection (average, 18.6 days), except for chorea, which usually begins after the fourth to eighth week. However, some patients appear to have a brief latency period due to clinically unapparent infection some weeks before the observed respiratory illness.

### Pharyngitis

Approximately half of preceding streptococcus pharyngeal infections can be asymptomatic. The proportion of patients in whom ARF will develop after a pharyngeal infection largely depends on the characteristics of the bacteria, population, and individual. Data obtained from RF outbreaks in U.S. military camps from 1949 to 1950 showed that ARF developed in 2.5% of patients infected with a rheumatogenic streptococcus strain. In a similar situation in 1987, the rate of ARF events per case of streptococcal pharyngitis was 1.6%.

### Arthritis

Arthritis is the most common and often the earliest major symptom of ARF, although rarely it may be preceded by carditis. The relative proportion of patients with ARF who have polyarthritis and the severity of this manifestation increases with age. In an early case series (1962), arthritis was present in nearly 100% of young adults, 82% of teenagers, and 66% of children. Tenderness is often disproportionate to the physical findings. A significant proportion of patients exhibit an additive rather than the classic migratory pattern of involvement, which occurs mainly in adults. A monoarticular presentation occurred in only 17% to 25% of the cases in the older case series. Still, it is currently much more common, attributed to the widespread use of antiinflammatory treatments. Untreated patients typically have 6 to 16 affected joints. Knees (76%), ankles (50%), and elbows and wrists (12% to 15%) are the most frequently involved sites. The shoulder (7% to 8%), phalangeal (7% to 8%), lumbosacral (2%), cervical (1%), sternoclavicular (0.5%), and temporomandibular (0.5%) joints are less frequently affected. Articular symptoms often last only a few days for each joint and uncommonly more than 1 week for each ARF attack. Arthritis typically responds well to nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). Other diagnoses should be considered if this pattern is not followed. Although arthritis is never radiographically destructive, Jaccoud's arthropathy (chronic post-RF arthropathy) has been described in RF and can occur after several recurrent articular episodes.

### Acute Carditis

Carditis occurs in 15% to 91% of the first ARF attacks, depending on the methods of patient selection and whether echocardiography is used for diagnosis.18, Carditis affects children more often and more severely than adults, but the latter are not spared. Inflammation may involve the pericardium, myocardium, and endocardium (pan-carditis), and it may be mild and silent (subclinical) or severe and lead to acute heart failure (HF) and death. In the acute phase, endocarditis is associated with edema of the valves and possibly vegetations (marantic vegetations) that do not produce emboli. The mitral valve is affected in almost all cases of carditis, which is attributed to the predominant migration of inflammatory cells through the papillary muscles. The tricuspid

valve is also frequently affected, but rarely in a meaningful manner. The aortic valve is involved in approximately 20% to 30% of cases. Valvular involvement may lead to a new or changing murmur used clinically to define carditis. Mitral regurgitation is the most common acute valvular lesion and may be isolated or concomitant with aortic regurgitation. Isolated aortic regurgitation is infrequent. Typical acute-phase murmurs consist of the high-pitched, blowing, holosystolic, apical murmur of mitral regurgitation; the low-pitched, apical, middiastolic, flow murmur (Carey-Coombs murmur); and a high-pitched, decrescendo, diastolic murmur of aortic regurgitation heard in the aortic area. Mitral regurgitation can be caused by valvular inflammation, deformity, and valve prolapse. The latter is caused by annular dilation and chordal elongation, and it typically involves the anterior leaflet with minimal leaflet redundancy. Rupture of the chordae tendineae is possible and often leads to acute HF and the need for emergent surgery. Aortic or mitral stenosis at presentation is atypical and may indicate previous undiagnosed RF.

HF is the most life-threatening feature of ARF and results from valvular damage and heart muscle dysfunction due to myocarditis and chamber dilation. HF occurs in 5% to 10% of people experiencing their first ARF episode and is more frequent during recurrences. Myocarditis in the absence of valvulitis should not be considered rheumatogenic in origin. Variable degrees of heart blockage may be present, and a temporary pacemaker may be required if HF occurs.

In approximately 10% of patients, pericarditis manifests clinically as pleuritic chest discomfort or pain and pericardial friction rub. Although effusion may be prominent, cardiac tamponade is rare.

### Transition From Acute to Chronic Heart Disease

RHD is a chronic condition resulting from poorly treated betahemolytic streptococci. If not diagnosed and managed appropriately in a timely fashion, RHD commonly leads to HF, thromboembolic events, and premature death in children, adolescents, and adults.

Inflammatory markers typically normalize within 3 months after the acute phase, but they may remain high for much longer in a subset of patients. The causes or prognostic implications of persistent inflammation are not known. According to the classic view, if the patient received appropriate prophylaxis and did not experience further GAS infections, then any deterioration observed after the acute attack would result from mechanical dysfunctions caused by valvular insufficiency (acute injury and scarification) or the slow progression of valve stenosis. However, it is recognized that local inflammation may persist in the myocardium and (mainly) the valves of some patients and may, to some extent, be responsible for observed deterioration over time. Samples from the valve and papillary muscles of patients with chronic RHD collected during valve replacement procedures often show variable degrees of mononuclear or lymphocytic infiltrates and sometimes Aschoff nodules, even in patients considered to be in remission clinically and based on laboratory results.22, Fig. 118.1 illustrates rheumatic valve lesions and infiltrating T lymphocytes.

In most cases, the fibrotic and neovascularization effects involved in healing processes do not affect valve function. Nevertheless, scarring may progress over the years and affect cusps, chordae tendineae, subendocardial tissue, and the annulus fibrosus, leading to valvular thickening, stiffening, incompetence, or stenosis. The speed of scarification and progression of mitral stenosis vary between geographic areas. In countries with a low

RF incidence, 20 to 40 years will pass until surgery is required, whereas in countries with a high incidence of RF, mitral stenosis is possible in patients younger than 5 years of age. Again, factors relating to this behavior are unknown but are believed to be linked to the degree of acute damage, recurrences, and the persistence of inflammation.

In the classic 1951 series,24 clinical signs of rheumatic valvular disease disappeared in 17% of the patients after 20 years. However, murmurs later developed in another 44% of the patients who initially did not have clinical carditis. In total, 70% of the patients eventually evolved to chronic RHD. More recently, Brazilian children with ARF were followed up prospectively, and 72% and 37% of them eventually experienced chronic valvular disease based on echocardiography and clinical assessment, respectively. Severe aortic and/or mitral disease occurred in 16% of the patients. Risk factors for progression to severe chronic valvular disease were moderate or severe acute carditis, ARF recurrences, and mother's low educational level.

### Indolent Carditis

Indolent carditis may be defined as carditis of insidious onset and slow progression (low acute-phase severity and absence of significant acute progression), especially in people presenting for a medical diagnosis months after the onset of RF. Recognition is usually delayed, and prophylaxis is not introduced; therefore multiple recurrences are likely to drive progression. Routine consultations typically lead to a diagnosis once symptoms of RHD are present. It is not rare, especially in the developing world, but the exact incidence of indolent RHD has not been ascertained.

### Subclinical Carditis

Subclinical carditis is defined as pathologic valvular regurgitation detected by echocardiography that is not clinically evident. Its clinical importance is discussed in the section on echocardiography.

### Rheumatic Heart Disease

RHD, the most common cause of acquired valvular disease in the world, is responsible for approximately one in four cases of HF in endemic countries. Chronic RHD is typically oligosymptomatic until HF is established. HF features include a third heart sound, tachycardia, dyspnea, rales, and edema. If the diagnosis is not established during the acute phase, RF often remains undetected for many people until the first symptoms of HF occur. In South Africa, 82.5% of affected children were previously undiagnosed. Sixty percent of the patients who are oligosymptomatic at diagnosis will not experience any progression of symptoms in 10 years, with survival rates exceeding 80%. In contrast, after developing New York Heart Association functional class III or IV disease, survival is estimated to be 0% to 15% over 10 years if surgery is not performed. In severe pulmonary hypertension, survival is expected to be no longer than 3 years without surgery. Typically, young patients exhibit pure mitral regurgitation, middle-age adults have mitral stenosis, and older patients present with mixed mitral valve disease. RHD usually remains asymptomatic for an extended period and frequently is not noticed if ARF does not manifest.

### Sydenham's Chorea

Another manifestation is Sydenham's chorea. Also known as St. Vitus' dance and chorea minor, Sydenham's chorea is a neurologic disorder characterized by emotional lability, personality changes, muscular weakness, reduced fine-motor skills, and uncoordinated abrupt, nonrhythmic, purposeless, jerky movements. In addition,

gait difficulties, headache, impaired cognition, dysarthric speech, and hypotonia are possible features. Motor symptoms disappear during sleep; may affect the hands, arms, shoulders, feet, legs, face, and trunk; and are frequently more marked on one side. Other classic signs of chorea include tongue fasciculation ("bag of worms") and a relapsing involuntary hand grip ("milkmaid's

sign"). Although movements may be partially repressed by will, they can impair important daily activities. Emotional changes may precede motor symptoms and manifest through outbursts of inappropriate behavior, including crying and restlessness. In rare cases, severe psychological manifestations may result in transient psychosis.

In contrast to the other manifestations of RF, chorea generally occurs 4 to 8 weeks after the streptococcal infection is sustained; however, a latent period of up to 8 months has been described. In the 1951 series of 1000 patients,24 51.8% had chorea. More recently, it occurs in 20% to 30% of patients with ARF. Females are affected more often than males, and a first episode of chorea in adulthood is rare, although recurrences are more common during this period of life.

Chorea may occur in isolation or along with other RF manifestations. A recent series showed that 71% and 42% of 69 patients with chorea also had carditis based on an echocardiogram and a clinical basis, respectively. In the series by Bland and Jones, 24 chorea was associated with less severe carditis, and this manifestation is believed to have a better overall prognosis. Most patients with chorea recover spontaneously within 2 to 6 months. However, cases have been reported where the condition persisted for up to 3 years.

### Pediatric Autoimmune Neuropsychiatric Disorders Associated With Streptococcal Infections

In pediatric autoimmune neuropsychiatric disorders associated with streptococcal infections (PANDAS), antibodies from the sera of patients with chorea can bind to neuronal cells and induce the release of dopamine. A subset of these patients experience behavioral disturbances such as tics and obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) years after the initial manifestation of chorea. Symptoms may abruptly worsen after a new streptococcus infection. These data led to the hypothesis that this spectrum of mental health disorders results from previous streptococcal infections in children. A strong association between OCD and the D8/17 antigen on B cells has been described. This antigen was believed to differentiate the clinical spectrum of patients who have RF with high specificity. The PANDAS hypothesis remains controversial, although it is broadly accepted that streptococcal infection can worsen symptoms of OCD in some patients.

### Fever

Most manifestations of ARF are accompanied by fever, except for chorea. Fever is seen in more than 90% of patients; a low-temperature cutoff of 100°F (38°C) has been suggested for diagnosing fever in endemic regions. In low-resource settings, a clear history of fever can be more important than the temperature at the time of examination. Fever may be absent, subtle, or high. Similar to subcutaneous nodules, erythema marginatum, and chorea, fever is extremely rare in adult-onset ARF. Malaise and myalgia are commonly associated with fever and may also be intense.

### Erythema Marginatum

While cutaneous manifestations including erythema marginatum (EM) are uncommon (0%-10%) and sometimes difficult to detect, these findings are highly specific and considered as major diagnostic criteria.14, EM presents as an evanescent, pink, nonpruritic, nontender rash that involves the trunk and sometimes the limbs but not the face. It is strongly associated with carditis. The lesion is also known as "erythema annulare" because its margins often assume the form of a ring. The border is irregular, serpiginous, and sharp on the outside but diffuses on the inside edge; it extends centrifugally while the center progressively clears. Lesions may appear, disappear, and reappear in hours and may be difficult to visualize on dark skin. A hot bath or shower may make them more evident. EM usually occurs early during ARF but may occur at any time, occasionally in the chronic heart disease phase.

### Subcutaneous Nodules

Subcutaneous nodules in RF resemble those of rheumatoid arthritis in terms of having a predilection for bony surfaces or areas near tendons (elbows, knees, ankles, Achilles tendon, and occiput); however, they are smaller and more fleeting (they rarely persist for more than a month and usually subside within 1 or 2 weeks). Lesions range from a few millimeters to 2 cm in size and are firm, painless, and loose in relation to adjacent surfaces. The skin over the lesions is not inflamed. The number of nodules present may vary from one to a few dozen (with an average of four). When abundant, the lesions tend to occur in crops and have a symmetric distribution. Subcutaneous nodules are virtually always associated with significant chronic active carditis and are uncommon in the early stages of the disease. Subcutaneous nodules were described in 8.8% of the patients in the series by Bland and Jones24 but only in 1.5% in a more recent series of 786 patients,38 representing the least common RF manifestation.

### Genetic Associations

In autoimmune diseases, the activation of innate and adaptive immune responses leads to tissue damage, possibly due to a previous infection caused mainly by viruses or bacteria. Controlling pathogens and triggering autoimmune reactions involve several genes (Tables 118.1 and 118.2).

Predisposition to develop RF and RHD is associated with some class II HLA alleles, and single-nucleotide polymorphisms in several genes related to activation of the immune response, initially driven against S. pyogenes and later against self-antigens. Results from genome-wide association studies from one group 39 suggested that some amino acid residue variations in HLA DQA1 and DQB1 may confer increased risk in indigenous people in Australia. A separate study40 showed that the IGHV4-61 *02 allele of the IGH (immunoglobulin heavy chain) gene segment was associated with RHD in the Aboriginal Australian population. .

The innate immune system detects pathogen-mediated injury and other bodily injuries and represents the first line of immune defense. Both immune and somatic cells present receptors that can recognize microbial molecules called pathogen-associated molecular patterns and tissue injury-induced molecules as a sign of damage-associated molecular patterns.

Most studies involve RF/RHD cohorts from diverse ethnicities and are representative of the genes involved in the development of the disease, as summarized in Table 118.2. In addition, genes associated with disease predisposition are described, considering their role in innate and adaptive immune responses.

### Innate Immunity

Toll-like receptors (TLRs) initiate host defense responses in multicellular organisms, acting as sensors of foreign microbial products. A polymorphism of TLR-2 at codon 753 leads to the replacement of arginine with glutamine. The genotype 753 Arg/Gln was more frequent in a Turkish ARF cohort compared with controls. This mutation likely interferes with the recognition of S. pyogenes and the innate immune response against the pathogen.

Mannan-binding lectin (MBL) is an acute-phase inflammatory protein that binds to a wide variety of sugars on the surface of pathogens to promote phagocytosis and complement cascade activation via the lectin pathway. Different variants of the promoter and exon one region of the MBL2 gene, which encodes MBL, have been reported in patients with RF/RHD. These studies have shown that the A allele, which encodes a high

level of MBL production, is associated with the development of mitral stenosis,4 whereas the O allele encoding a low production level is related to aortic regurgitation. Ficolins are proteins that bind to collectin cellular receptors and also initiate the complement lectin pathway. Three ficolin genes have been identified in humans with different functions, sequences, and specificities. Polymorphisms at ficolins are at positions within the promoter region of ficolin 2 (FCN2) encoding the ficolin-2 (L-ficolin) protein are associated with the serum levels of this protein. In Brazilian patients with chronic RHD, the haplotype G/G/A (-986/-602/-4) was shown to occur more frequently than in control subjects and was correlated with low levels of this protein and consequently prolonged infection duration or repeated streptococcal infections.

### Adaptive Immunity

The FCGR2A gene controls adaptive immune responses and plays a role in clearing immune complexes by macrophages, neutrophils, and platelets. In patients with ARF, a polymorphism that typically encodes the arginine (codon 131) instead yields histidine. This mutation encodes a protein with a low binding capacity to the immune complex, favoring the inflammatory response.

Susceptibility to the development of RF and Sydenham's chorea or RHD was first associated with diverse class II HLA alleles (DR and/or DQ) encoded by the DRB1 gene of the major histocompatibility complex, which is in the short arm of human chromosome 6. In addition, several HLA-DR alleles have been

described as associated with the development of the disease worldwide (Table 118.1).

Briefly, HLA-DR1 was found to be more frequent in patients with RF and RHD from South Africa48 and Martinique49 and in patients with Sydenham's chorea from Brazil. HLA-DR2 was detected more frequently in the Black or African American populations in the United States51 and Mexico,52 and DR3 and DR5 have been described as risk factors for susceptibility in northern Indian and Turkish patients with RF/RHD53-55 HLA- DR4 has been found in White patients with RHD in the United States51,55 and in patients in Saudi Arabia,56 whereas HLA-DR6 has been detected in South Africa57 and HLA-DR7 has been detected in the Brazilian White and Mulatto populations, 58,59 in Egyptians60 and Latvians,61 and in patients from some regions of Turkey.54, DR9 has been reported as a susceptibility risk factor in White Americans. These data are summarized in Table 118.1.

In Egyptian and Latvian patients with RHD, the association of HLA-DR7 along with some DQA or DQB alleles, both encoded by the HLA-DQ gene, was linked to the development of multiple valvular lesions.60, In Japanese patients with RHD, susceptibility to mitral stenosis seems to be partly controlled by the HLA- DQA gene or by genes in close linkage disequilibrium with some HLA-DQA and DQB1 alleles. An RHD cohort derived from a Mexican Mestizo population displayed an association between HLA-DR2 and some DQA and DQB alleles. As mentioned previously, some punctual amino acid variations on DQA1 and DQB1 alleles confer susceptibility to develop acute RF in Indigenous Australians.

CTLA-4 is a protein that plays a role in the adaptive immune response as a negative regulator of T cell proliferation.

A polymorphism (G/G) in exon 1 of the CTLA4 gene with an inhibitory function was found in higher frequency among patients with RHD.

Inflammatory and anti-inflammatory cytokines play a role in innate and adaptive immune responses and are also involved in developing RF tissue lesions. The IL1 gene cluster on chromosome 2 includes the genes expressing the pro-inflammatory cytokines interleukin (IL)-1a and IL-1b and their inhibitor IL-1 receptor antagonist. The absence or misrepresentation of two alleles of variable number of tandem repeats from the ILRA gene results in a robust inflammatory response. Patients with RHD with severe carditis display low frequencies of one of these alleles, suggesting an absence of inflammatory control.65, The TNF gene encodes the inflammatory cytokine tumor necrosis factor (TNF), contributing to the development of valvular lesions. Four independent studies have shown an association of TNF polymorphisms with RF and RHD.67,

The anti-inflammatory cytokines IL-10 and transforming growth factor (TGF)-β are produced by activated immune cells, especially monocytes/macrophages and T cell subsets, including regulatory T cells (Tr1 and Treg) and Th1 cells. RHD severity including the development of multivalvular lesions is associated with select polymorphisms in the promoter regions of the IL10 and TGFB1 genes.65,66

### Molecular Mimicry and Epitope Spreading
