The molecular mimicry mechanism considers the existence of similar or identical antigens in microbes (viruses, bacteria, and other pathogens) and their hosts and has been implicated in the pathogenesis of RF/RHD. This mechanism enables the microbe to evade the host immune response and facilitates self-antigen recognition after infection by cross-reactivity. T and B lymphocytes can recognize pathogens and self-antigens through molecular mimicry by four different types of mimicry, recognizing (1) identical amino acid sequences, (2) homologous but nonidentical sequences, (3) standard or similar amino acid sequences of different molecules (proteins and carbohydrates), and (4) structural similarities between the microbe or environmental agent and its host.

Diversification of the immune response against immunodominant epitopes from a pathogen, human tissue, or soluble protein leads to its amplification and has been defined as epitope spreading, 71 a process that favors recognition of several self-antigens and facilitates tissue damage in different organs. The major manifestations of the disease result from interactions between these mechanisms.

### Pathogenic Considerations of Specific Manifestations

### Arthritis

In the joints, anti-streptococcal antibodies likely against group A carbohydrates, components of the bacterial cell membrane, or the M protein precipitate to form immune complexes and activate the complement cascade to induce transitory arthritis.

### Sydenham's Chorea

The pathogenic mechanism leading to the development of Sydenham's chorea was clarified by one group.34, Briefly, these investigators showed that antibodies from the sera of patients with chorea could bind to neuronal cells. They also identified gangliosides as autoantigens that cross-react with N-acetyl-β-D-glucosamine, the

major cell wall streptococcal antigen. They also showed that autoantibodies mediate signal transduction by calcium/calmodulindependent protein kinase II, triggering dopamine release from neuronal cells. Sydenham's chorea involves involuntary, purposeless movements of the extremities and trunk; follows the index episode of acute rheumatic fever by 4 to 8 weeks; and may occur as an isolated manifestation. It is seen in 10% to 30% of cases of ARF and is considered a major manifestation for diagnosis.

### Rheumatic Heart Disease

Sera antibodies from patients with RF simultaneously recognize N-acetyl-glucosamine, a streptococcal carbohydrate antigen, and specific regions of cardiac myosin in the myocardium and tropomyosin and laminin in the valves. These cross-reactive antibodies may bind to the valvular endothelial and basement membrane, generating inflammatory signals that upregulate the expression of several adhesion molecules, facilitating lymphocyte extravasation into the valve. The expression of vascular cell adhesion molecule (VCAM)-1, an adhesion molecule in the vascular endothelium, is activated after initiating an inflammatory reaction by anti-myosin and N-acetyl-glucosamine antibodies. These molecules interact with very late activation antigen-4, another adhesion molecule expressed on CD4+ T lymphocytes, facilitating its infiltration into heart tissue. Recently, we verified that intercellular adhesion molecule, as well as the integrin P-selectin and several chemokines and their receptors, were upregulated in affected tissues. Among the chemokines, the gene expression of CCL3/MIP1α was upregulated in the myocardium, whereas CCL1/I-309 and CXCL9/ Mig were highly expressed in the valvular tissue of patients with RHD. An in vitro assay demonstrated that infiltrating T cells in valvular lesions migrated mainly toward a CXCL9/Mig gradient, suggesting that specific chemokines mediate both CD4+ and CD8+ T cell infiltration to the site of inflammation in the heart. Several cytokines contribute to the inflammatory process and cellular infiltration. These data are summarized in Table 118.3.

Cardiac myosin is the major antigen in the myocardium. Using affinity-purified anti-myosin antibodies, one group76 identified an epitope of the N-terminal M5 and M6 proteins consisting of a five-amino-acid residue (Gln-Lys-Ser-Lys-Gln) that cross-reacted with cardiac myosin. Human heart intralesional T cells obtained from valve tissue from patients with RHD who underwent surgery for valve correction allowed evaluation of in vitro reactivity against tococcal M5 peptides and mitral valve—derived proteins. The frequency of intralesional T cell clones that recognized LMM peptides was 63.2%. Thirty-four percent of the T cell clones presented different patterns of cross-reactivity: (1) myosin and valvederived proteins; (2) myosin and streptococcal M5 peptides; and (3) myosin, valve-derived proteins, and M5 peptides. In addition, it has been recognized that several LMM peptides simultaneously display multiple reactivity patterns in heart-infiltrating T cells and also against peripheral T cells of patients with ARF/RHD. The high percentage of reactivity against cardiac myosin strengthens its role as a significant autoantigen in rheumatic heart lesions. T cell reactivity toward myosin epitopes in patients with RHD may also trigger the broad recognition of valvular proteins with structural or functional similarities.

Valvulitis follows myocarditis; the mitral and aortic valves display the most damaged tissue. Similarities between N-acetyl- β-D-glucosamine, a polysaccharide present in both the streptococcal cell wall and heart valve tissue, are probably responsible for the autoimmune reactions, as suggested by the observation that

antibodies against N-acetyl-β-D-glucosamine display cross-reactivity with laminin, an extra-cellular matrix α-helical coiled-coil protein that surrounds heart cells and is also present in valves.

Vimentin, a structural protein that plays diverse roles, is vital for the binding and stabilization of collagen messenger RNAs. In vitro, this protein has been detected by a proliferation assay in both peripheral blood and heart tissue—infiltrating T cells from patients with RHD, reinforcing its role as a putative target antigen of autoimmune rheumatic lesions.77,

An evaluation of valvular tissues from patients with RHD, based on two-dimensional electrophoresis and mass spectrometry analyses, showed an imbalance of heart tissue protein expression, probably due to the autoimmune reactions that follow streptococcal infection. Briefly, several proteins displayed an elevated expression, including vimentin, lumican, and apolipoprotein- A1, whereas collagen-VI, haptoglobin-related protein, prolargin, biglycan, and cartilage oligomeric matrix protein had a reduced expression level.

The prediction of protein interactions in valve damage has also been evaluated by in silico analysis. Among the interactions, the potential roles of TNF, an inflammatory cytokine, and TGF- β (anti-inflammatory) and metalloproteinase (MMP)-25 were noteworthy. MMP-25 is involved in matrix degradation, as previously described,82 and probably also plays an essential role in mediating valve damage.

Table 118.4 summarizes the major events described herein leading to arthritis, Sydenham's chorea, and RHD.

### Cytokines and the Inflammatory Process

Cytokines are also key players in the inflammatory process during RF episodes and later in the development RHD. Four subsets of Th cells (Th1, Th2, Th17, and Tregs) are currently described. Cytokines are soluble mediators that regulate cell proliferation, differentiation, and survival. Antigen-activated CD4+ T cells polarize to these subsets, depending on the cytokine secreted.

Thl cells are involved in the cellular immune response and produce IL-2, interferon (IFN)-γ, and TNF. Th2 cells mediate humoral and allergic immune responses and produce IL-4, IL-10, IL-5, and IL-13. Th17 cells are essential for protecting against bacterial and fungal infections and developing autoimmunity. TGF-β, IL-6, and IL-23 induce this lineage and secrete IL-17 to mediate a pro-inflammatory response.

T regulatory cells (Tregs), a subset of cells that regulate the inflammatory and autoimmune process, are identified as CD4+CD25+CD127-CD45RO+FoxP3+ T cells and display immunosuppressive activity.

The roles of cytokines in RF and RHD have been evaluated in peripheral blood and heart tissues. Briefly, in patients with ARF and active RHD, increased production of IL-2 and elevated numbers of CD4+CD25+ cells have been observed, suggesting the expansion of activated CD4+ T cells in the peripheral blood85 and increased plasma levels of TNF. 86-88

The Th1/Th2 cytokine pattern of infiltrating mononuclear cells in the mitral valve and myocardial tissue in patients with ARF and chronic RHD reveal large numbers of IFN-γ and TNFsecreting mononuclear cells. Mononuclear cells secreting IL-10 and IL-4 (regulatory cytokines) were also found in myocardial tissues, whereas in valvular tissues only a few cells secreted IL-4. These low numbers of IL-4-producing cells may contribute to the progression of valvular lesions in RHD. Recently, we identified large numbers of IL-17and IL-23-producing cells in the valves. As previously mentioned, these cytokines belong to the Th17 subset of cytokines, frequently involved in the development of autoimmune diseases. In agreement with these data, a Turkish RHD cohort study recently reported increased numbers of Th17 cells in peripheral blood that correlated with IL-17A cytokine levels in the sera and decreased Tregs.

### Diagnostic Tests

ARF is diagnosed using the 2015 modified Jones criteria as no single laboratory test can be used to confirm the diagnosis. Thus it is mandatory that physicians need to be aware of the broad array of clinical signs and symptoms that can occur in ARF and conditions that are considered in the differential diagnosis. In a patient in whom ARF is suspected, the workup aims to detect evidence of recent streptococcal infection, document the presence or persistence of inflammation, and diagnose and follow the course of the disease.

### Throat t Cultures

A rayon-tipped throat culture swab obtained by sampling the tonsils and back of the throat is the current gold standard for diagnosing GAS pharyngitis. Nevertheless, approximately 75% of patients have negative throat culture findings when ARF symptoms occur. A positive throat culture finding may be due to a new infection or to the convalescent carriage of the rheumatogenic strain.

### Rapid Antigen Testing

Rapid streptococcal antigen testing (RSAT) has a high specificity (≥95%) but a moderate sensitivity (65% to 90%). A positive RSAT finding helps establish a diagnosis of GAS pharyngitis, but a negative RSAT finding does not exclude it. In high-risk ARF locations, where high-stakes decisions are being made, RSATs are not currently recommended. If an RSAT is used and is negative, additional costs are incurred because a follow-up throat swab is required.

### Streptococcal Antibody Tests

Antibody tests are directed against the extra-cellular products of streptococci and include anti-streptococcal lysine O (ASO), anti- DNAse B (ADB), anti-hyaluronidase, anti-nicotinamide adenine dinucleotidase, and anti-streptokinase antibodies. ASO and ADB are the most commonly available tests. ASO begins to rise at 1 week and peaks at 3 to 5 weeks after infection. It begins to decline after approximately 6 to 8 weeks, at a faster pace during the immediate subsequent months, and at a slower rate after 6 months. ADB begins to rise at 2 weeks and peaks at 6 to 8 weeks after infection. It begins to decline approximately 3 months after the precipitating infection. Antibody peaks typically coincide with the second or third week of ARF. Patients will have elevated ASO and ADB titers 80% and 85% of the time, respectively, when symptoms of ARF are present. When both ASO and ADB tests are conducted, 92% of patients will have abnormal test results. The antibody tests must be interpreted cautiously in areas with high rates of streptococcal infection and ARF because relatively high titers are commonly encountered in such populations. A second sample should be collected 2 weeks later to characterize a recent infection based on a significant rise in antibody titers. Asymptomatic pharyngeal streptococcus carriers usually have titers just above detectable; therefore a high titer indicates an actual infection. Increases in ASO occur in response to GAS infections and infections with groups C and G streptococci and other bacteria such as Bacillus, Clostridium tetani, and Listeria monocytogenes.

### Acute-Phase Reactants

Acute-phase reactants, the erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and C-reactive protein (CRP), rise during an ARF attack, except in circumstances characterized by chorea or erythema marginatum as a single manifestation. Acute-phase reactants aid in monitoring the evolution of inflammation and serve as minor manifestations based on the Jones criteria (detailed below). Salicylates or other NSAIDs may mask the results of these tests. ESR may stay elevated for up to 2 months after infection, whereas CRP normalizes within days.

### Other Laboratory Tests

Transient and asymptomatic abnormalities of liver function tests, bilirubin, and mild normochromic normocytic anemia are observed in many patients with ARF and usually normalize after cessation of inflammation. Blood cultures should be obtained to

help rule out infective endocarditis, bacteremia, and disseminated gonococci infection.

Depending on the clinical features, additional tests should be performed to rule out an alternative diagnosis, such as antinuclear antibody and brain magnetic resonance imaging.

### Chest Radiography

A chest radiograph may reveal an enlarged heart silhouette if myocardial dilation and/or pericardial effusion are significant. In addition, pulmonary edema may be observed in the presence of HF.

### Electrocardiography

Tachycardia and prolongation of the PR interval are the most common electrocardiographic findings of myocarditis. Rarely, third-degree heart block may be observed. Pericarditis can induce diffuse elevation of the ST segments. Electrocardiographic a abnormalities are present in approximately 21% of patients, 60% of whom have evidence of heart block.

### Echocardiography

Echocardiography is the primary clinical tool for RHD detection and diagnosis. Echocardiography may be used to estimate disease prevalence and potentially improve community awareness to facilitate better RHD control. With a sensitivity that is 10 times greater than auscultation in identifying valvular lesions, . the use of echocardiography results in a 16% to 47% increase in the identification of carditis in RHD. In addition to providing objective confirmation of valvular lesions, echocardiography provides an accurate means to detect progression during follow-up and helps to assess for the presence of nonrheumatic causes of valvular damage. Echocardiographic findings by Doppler in RHD are summarized in Table 118.5.

Long-term follow-up of subclinical carditis diagnosed in patients with a previous or current history of ARF is better characterized than subclinical carditis in asymptomatic populations. In the first group, valve lesions persist in 30% of patients after 5 years, and half of the patients diagnosed with subclinical carditis at the time of ARF show persistence or deterioration of their carditis during the ensuing 2 years. If not diagnosed in a timely manner and managed appropriately, including access to surgery when needed, RHD can lead to HF, thromboembolic events, and premature death in children, adolescents, and adults.

The World Heart Federation has developed a standardized, evidence-based guideline for the echocardiographic diagnosis of RHD to improve the reliability of screening, comparability, and reproducibility. Echocardiography should be used in followup for subclinical lesions to evaluate RHD progression and suspected ARF recurrence. It is envisioned that new guidelines may reduce the potential for the overdiagnosis of RHD in screening studies by excluding physiologic valve regurgitation and congenital valve anomalies that may be present in at least 1% of normal children.

Valvular injuries in RF lead to the fusion and thickening of the cusps and calcification of valves. The commissures also are compromised, leading to severe stenosis. Thus mixed valvular lesions are common. In that context, three-dimensional (3D) echocardiography can provide additional anatomic and morpho-functional information for patients presenting with possible rheumatic valvulopathies. Accordingly, 3D echocardiography is increasingly deployed for routine use in the assessment of patients with RHD presenting with valvular abnormalities.

### Diagnosis

No single clinical or laboratory finding is diagnostic of ARF, with the possible exception of Sydenham's chorea. Diagnostic challenges act as a major barrier to preventing RHD. The high frequency of patients presenting with mild disease and the recognized importance of detecting subclinical carditis prompted the revision of the Jones Criteria (the gold standard for RF diagnosis) in 2015 to better account for differences in population risk. Thus, the diagnosis of ARF remains a clinical decision.

The classic Jones criteria were first published in 1944.24 The latest 2015 revision distinguishes between moderate-to-high and low-risk populations and includes echocardiography to diagnose cardiac involvement97 (Table 118.6).

### Treatment

### Primary Prophylaxis

The primary prevention or primary prophylaxis of ARF aims to interrupt the link between Strep A infection and abnormal immune response to Strep A that causes ARF by early identification and treatment of Strep A infections.

Adequate treatment of streptococcus pharyngitis greatly reduces the likelihood of the subsequent development of ARF. Nevertheless, streptococcus cannot be differentiated from other pharyngeal pathogens on a clinical basis, important as cultures take days to provide results, and RSAT lacks adequate sensitivity and adds costs. Most sore throats are viral in origin. Fifteen to 30% of sore throats in children and 10% in adults are estimated to be due to GAS. Whether all pharyngeal infections should be treated a priori with antibiotics strongly depends on the incidence of ARF in the evaluated population. The case of Costa Rica is often used by those who advocate the use of antibiotics for all sore throat cases in locations with a high incidence of ARF. A policy of early empiric antibiotic use was instituted in Costa Rica in 1970, and the number of new cases of ARF fell from 94 new cases in that year to only four in 1991.98 A similar decrease in ARF incidence occurred in Europe and in the United States before the availability

of antibiotics, and critics attribute the decrease observed in Costa Rica, at least in part, to other socioeconomic improvements, including housing conditions, education, and health care access. New Zealand long ago introduced an efficient program of close surveillance and optimized treatment of pharyngitis for its highrisk populations, but to date these measures have not successfully reduced the incidence of ARF. This outcome could be related to the observation that approximately half of the streptococcus pharyngeal infections can be asymptomatic16 and that only a small portion of patients with a sore throat seek medical attention. New Zealand and Australian guidelines for sore throat management do not indicate throat swabs or antibiotics for low-risk people with mild symptoms, provided there is a low occupational risk of spreading GAS. People with a high risk of developing ARF should have a throat culture and be treated if positive results are obtained or should receive empiric antibiotics if follow-up is a concern.

In a recent study conducted in Ethiopia, Streptococcus pyogenes was responsible for 10.7% of acute pharyngitis cases among pediatric patients, and all isolates were sensitive to penicillin. Many patients showed reduced susceptibility to tetracycline and macrolides. Therefore prior to antibiotic prescription, screening children with acute pharyngitis for S. pyogenes and testing the antibiotic susceptibility are recommended.

### Acute Rheumatic Fever Treatment

Eradication of Streptococcus. Immediate eradication of streptococcus is standard practice for patients presenting with ARF, even before throat culture results are obtained. Although an improvement in 1-year outcomes was never demonstrated, antibiotic treatment is used to minimize prolonged exposure to the triggering factor and reduce the spread of rheumatogenic strains. Household contacts should also have throat cultures, and people with positive results should be treated even if they are asymptomatic. Penicillins are preferred, and the long-acting intramuscular penicillin G benzathine is the logical choice to facilitate adherence and initiate secondary prophylaxis.

Acute Carditis. The incidence of carditis in initial attacks of ARF varies widely across reports, based on populations studied and whether echocardiography was used. The extent of acute cardiac involvement is the most critical feature in determining the long-term morbidity and mortality of RF. Nevertheless, currently, no effective therapies have been demonstrated to alter the natural history of the disease. One group reviewed 170 articles and concluded that aspirin was not beneficial in treating acute carditis. This finding was reiterated by a United KingdomUnited States joint report in 1955.102

Studies of glucocorticoid therapy for the treatment of ARF were performed mainly in the 1950s and 1960s, before the availability of echocardiography. In 1995 a meta-analysis involving more than 130 studies concluded that glucocorticoids were not statistically superior to salicylates in preventing a pathologic murmur 1 year after treatment, and inflammation tended to recur once steroid therapy was withdrawn. However, given that the confidence intervals were wide and that there was significant heterogeneity in the results between these studies, the authors indicated that the precision of this meta-analysis was not high. Therefore marginal improvements may have been overlooked. Three Cochrane reviews have been published on the subject, and similar conclusions were drawn. Additionally, the clinical parameter used by the referenced studies does not allow accurate

inferences about the severity of heart damage. As a result, doubt persists, and glucocorticoids are still widely used to treat acute carditis worldwide.

The 2020 Australian guidelines indicate glucocorticoids as optional for very severe cases of carditis. Prednisone (1 to 2 mg/ kg per day up to a maximum of 80 mg/day, administered once daily or in divided doses) is usually the drug of choice. After 2 to 3 weeks of therapy, the dosage may decrease by 20% to 25% weekly. Two additional small, randomized clinical trials, 105,106 investigating intravenous (IV) methylprednisolone for the treatment of active rheumatic carditis have obtained inconsistent findings on the advantage of IV compared with oral glucocorticoid therapy for valvular outcomes. Nevertheless, the World Health Organization (WHO) and New Zealand/Australian guidelines recommend IV methylprednisolone in life-threatening circumstances. Salicylates or other NSAIDs may need to be resumed after discontinuation of glucocorticoids to avoid rebound joint symptoms or fever.

IV immunoglobulin (IVIG) was evaluated prospectively in a randomized clinical trial involving 59 patients with ARF (39 with carditis), and it was found that the treatment did not alter the natural history of the disease. No differences were observed in clinical, laboratory, or echocardiographic parameters during the 12 months of follow-up.

Bed rest is traditionally advised, although this recommendation is not based on clinical trial results. In the pre-penicillin era,

it was associated with a shorter duration of carditis, fewer relapses, and less cardiomegaly. Strict bed rest is no longer recommended for patients with carditis, and some clinicians use normalization of acute-phase response (ESR and CRP) as a guide to return to 14 exercise.

Heart Failure. Although HF is more frequent during recurrences, it occurs in 5% to 10% of initial ARF episodes. In addition to possible glucocorticoid use, other studies have evaluated treatment with beta blockers in people with HF due to acute carditis and, currently, these treatments are not recommended.

Valvular Interventions. Guidelines for the management of valvular heart disease recommend catheter-based interventions for severe or symptomatic valvular heart disease.109, In contrast, the guidelines describe little evidence supporting pharmacologic management to alter outcomes. Most of the global burden of symptomatic RHD occurs in regions where definitive surgical or catheter-based treatments may not be available. In that context, pharmacologic management may represent the only option for symptomatic improvement in such underserved regions.

Arthritis and Fever. Arthritis and fever often respond to NSAIDs within hours and almost always within 3 days. If not, the diagnosis of ARF should be reconsidered. Aspirin (80-100 mg/kg per day in children and 48 g/day in adults) is traditionally used and should be continued until all symptoms subside and inflammatory markers normalize. Most patients will need to take

NSAIDs for only 1 to 2 weeks; however, some may require them for up to 6 weeks and, in approximately 5% of cases, 6 months or more is required. Alternative NSAIDs can be used, and naproxen is effective and well tolerated. As NSAIDs alter the course of the articular disease, and since there is no evidence that the delay in its introduction worsens the prognosis, paracetamol or acetaminophen can be used initially if the diagnosis is uncertain. The recurrence of joint symptoms during NSAID withdrawal does not indicate ARF recurrence and can be treated with another brief course of anti-inflammatory/ full-dose NSAIDs.

Chorea. Chorea is often self-limited and does not require specific treatment aside from rest. Treatment decisions in Sydenham's chorea are currently based on the treating physician's clinical experience, the desire to avoid side effects, and the existence of only limited scientific evidence. Neuroleptics, diazepam, and anti-convulsant agents are effective in prolonged or incapacitating cases. Aspirin and glucocorticoid therapy do not influence this manifestation. A prospective comparison of carbamazepine, valproic acid, and haloperidol in 18 patients with chorea concluded that valproic acid was the most effective treatment. A reduction, but not eradication, of symptoms should be expected after 1 to 2 weeks of therapy. Medication should be continued for 2 to 4 weeks after the chorea has abated.

### Rheumatic Heart Disease Management

In 2022, RHD Australia published an update of previous guidelines focused on the prevention, early diagnosis, and management of patients with ARF and RHD.

Secondary Prophylaxis. Secondary prophylaxis involves the regular administration of antibiotics to people who have had ARF or RHD to prevent ARF recurrence. Patients with RF are at high risk for recurrence and progression of manifestations following a new GAS infection. Because streptococcal pharyngitis is often asymptomatic, prevention requires continuous anti-microbial prophylaxis rather than treatment of acute GAS pharyngitis episodes. Continuous administration of benzathine penicillin G (BPG) reduces the chances of new streptococcal pharyngitis in 71% to 91% of cases and the chances of a new episode of ARF in 87% to 96% of cases in addition to decreasing the severity of RHD114and its associated mortality.

Secondary prophylaxis is indicated for all patients with a documented history of ARF, Sydenham's chorea, or convincing evidence of RHD. BPG injections remain the cornerstone of secondary prevention; challenges with procurement and concern with adverse reactions remain important issues.

Intramuscular (IM) penicillin is more effective than oral penicillin in preventing recurrences. Monthly BPG is indicated at 1.2 million units by IM injection for people weighing more than 27 kg (60 lb) and 600,000 units for people weighing less than 27 kg30 (20 kg in New Zealand/Australian guidelines). Serum penicillin levels may be undetectable or low 28 days after a 1.2 million-unit BPG dose. IM BPG injections every 3 weeks should be considered for high-risk patients. Patients treated with this regimen exhibit fewer streptococcal infections and ARF recur- s101,117 and a greater resolution of mitral regurgitation over rences1 the long term. Prospective data from New Zealand showed that recurrences were rare (0.07 per 100 patient-years) among patients who were entirely adherent to a monthly BPG regimen, which is the current recommendation in the United States.

If an IM route is not possible or is refused, the second-line regimen is oral penicillin V, 250 mg twice daily. Patients with a documented allergy to penicillin should receive oral erythromycin 40 mg/kg (maximum of 1 g/day) daily, divided into two to four doses for children, and oral erythromycin 400 mg twice daily for adults and adolescents. 30,

Secondary prophylaxis should extend until the risk of ARF recurrence is irrelevant; thus the discontinuation time should be individualized. Guidelines from the WHO, New Zealand, and Australian guidelines were developed based on their respective data and differ slightly. In New Zealand, maintenance of prophylaxis up to 21 years of age is considered safe and effective in cases with absent or mild heart disease. In a review of data from the 1993 to 1999 Auckland (New Zealand) Acute Rheumatic Fever Register, only five recurrences occurred after the age of 30 years. Data from the Northern Aboriginal Territory of Australia showed that only approximately 1% of 259 ARF episodes recorded between 2005 and 2009 occurred after 40 years of age. Therefore 30 and 40 years of age were considered the most reasonable cutoffs to cease secondary prophylaxis for patients with severe carditis in New Zealand and Australia, respectively. In both countries, exceptions are made for individual circumstances warranting continuing prophylaxis (e.g., patients wanting to reduce an already remote chance of a recurrence).

It is unclear whether these prophylaxis regimens should be followed in sporadic cases in locations with a low incidence of ARF because these regimens have been developed mainly in regions where ARF remains a significant burden. In a prospective study in modern Chile, 59 patients with ARF judged to be at low risk for recurrences were permitted to receive no secondary prophylaxis. During the 3349 patient-months of follow-up, only two ARF attacks were observed, and the authors suggested that ARF prophylaxis could be discontinued safely in patients with a low risk of recurrence who undergo careful prospective surveillance. 119

The efficacy of secondary prophylaxis depends entirely on compliance. In a prospective international study involving 1790 patients, the prevalence of new ARF attacks was 0.45% in compliant patients compared with 11.5% in noncompliant patients. Only one in five patients with RF from Aborigine communities of Australia received 80% or more of the scheduled doses. Reasons for failed compliance were painfulness, a high frequency of injections, a long treatment period, and the patients' low socioeconomic and educational levels. In the GOAL trial, secondary antibiotic prophylaxis reduced the risk of latent RHD progression in children and adolescents.

Infective Endocarditis Prophylaxis. Infective endocarditis (IE) is a potentially lethal complication of RHD. Antibiotic prophylaxis prior to procedures has not been proven effective in preventing IE, but evidence supporting this practice comes primarily from animal models or empirical observations in addition to expert opinion. All patients with RHD or prosthetic valves should receive IE antibiotic prophylaxis before dental procedures and other procedures expected to produce bacteremia. People with a history of ARF but no valvular damage do not require endocarditis prophylaxis.

Transesophageal echocardiogram and esophagus-gastroduodenoscopy, colonoscopy, and cystoscopy are procedures that do not require IE prophylaxis in the absence of active infection. A different antibiotic should be offered for people receiving secondary prophylaxis for RF. Guidelines aimed at

the optimal diagnosis and management (including prophylaxis) of IE are offered and constantly updated by specialized 116 organizations.

### Vaccine Development

Although RHD control programs have been implemented worldwide, the disease remains a major health problem in several countries. In addition, the epidemiologic growth of streptococcal diseases in undeveloped and developing countries has encouraged many groups to study vaccine candidates to prevent GAS infections.

Strep A vaccines have been studied since the 1920s. As well as reducing pharyngitis, impetigo, ARF, and RHD, an effective Strep A vaccine given in early childhood would prevent other Strep A diseases, including post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, cellulitis, and severe and frequently fatal invasive disorders (i.e., bacteremia, toxic shock syndrome, necrotizing fasciitis, and infections in pregnant women and newborn babies).

Several vaccine development studies have been proposed previously without satisfactory results. In the past two decades, studies on vaccine development have improved with advances in genomics, proteomics, and immunomics; still, most vaccines remain in pre-clinical testing phases and few have reached phase I and II. 123

To date, the most promising vaccines under development incorporate C-terminal protective epitopes and differ concerning their mechanisms of action. One is based on a minimal protective epitope that induces protective antibodies124-126; the other is a long peptide (55 mers) identified as StreptInCor. The advantage of the StreptInCor vaccine model is the possibility of the vaccine epitope undergoing processing by antigen-presenting cells (monocytes and/or macrophages) to generate several peptides that induce both B and T immune responses, resulting in a safe and robust immune response. Experimental assays have demonstrated that the StreptInCor peptide induces high titers of opsonic and neutralizing antibodies in outbred immunized mice. 128, Using class II HLA transgenic mice, it was possible to evaluate the immunogenicity and safety of the StreptInCor vaccine epitope for 1 year. Specific and nonauto-reactive antibodies were produced. No autoimmune or other off-target pathologic reactions were observed in hearts or other organs of the mice.

Research has identified many potential vaccine targets (antigens) on the Strep A bacteria with promising results in laboratory and animal studies. Unfortunately, there have been scientific, regulatory, and commercial obstacles that have delayed the progress of a vaccine and, almost a century following initial vaccine development efforts, there is no safe and reliable human Strep A vaccine available. The development of a Strep A vaccine is the most attractive opportunity for a single medical intervention to meaningfully reduce the global burden of RHD.

### Post-streptococcal Arthritis

Although noncanonical pathogens are increasingly recognized to play a potential role in reactive arthritis, infections that affect the gastrointestinal or genitourinary tract are most frequently implicated in this diagnosis (see Chapter 77). However, the GAS and Chlamydia pneumoniae infections that affect the respiratory tract have also been implicated in reactive immune-mediated aseptic arthritis. A disputed question is whether post-streptococcal reactive arthritis (PSRA) should be considered an atypical and incomplete form of ARF or a separate disease. The small number of available

publications is predominantly based on small sample sizes and is hampered by the lack of a generally accepted definition of PSRA. These case series have suggested significant dissimilarities between the two conditions. Whereas ARF affects mainly children age 4 to 9 years, PSRA seems to have a bimodal age distribution with peaks between 8 and 14 years and between 21 and 37 years.131, Whereas RF symptoms typically commence 2 to 3 weeks after the streptococcal infection, the latency period in PSRA is approximately 10 days. Arthritis in PSRA is often additive and symmetric. Knee and ankle joints are usually involved, but small joint and axial involvement also occur. In PSRA, the mean duration of arthritis is approximately 2 months, but subsequent arthralgias may persist for 3 years. In up to 19% of patients, arthritis recurs after an interval of a few months. The response to salicylates and other NSAIDs is dramatic in people who have arthritis associated with ARF but less convincing in patients with PSRA. 133

A retrospective series involving 26 patients demonstrated that polytendonitis, tenosynovitis, and enthesitis are common presentations in PSRA and can be the only manifestation. This finding, and the possibility of axial involvement, raises suspicion that what is currently known as PSRA is genuinely a heterogeneous group of disorders, some sharing features of spondyloarthropathies, with others being more similar to ARF. An animal model of rheumatoid arthritis may facilitate our understanding of this heterogeneity. In this model, rats are treated via intraperitoneal injection of streptococcus cell wall fragments, which are highly resistant to biodegradation. Within 24 to 48 hours of administration, complement-dependent acute inflammation develops in the peripheral joints of the animal, together with the dissemination of cell wall fragments in the blood vessels of the synovia and subchondral bone marrow. In some rats, the initial inflammation subsides; in others, it persists or subsides and recurs. The chronic, T celldependent erosive polyarthritis that affects some rats is believed to be initiated by an inflammatory process promoted by macrophages struggling to degrade the cell wall fragments. Chronic joint inflammation develops only in susceptible rats but is not dependent on specific streptococcus strains. Remarkably, chronic arthritis will not develop in rats raised in a germ-free environment, suggesting that streptococcus cell wall fragments do not elicit a specific autoimmune reaction but instead function as an adjuvant, promoting other cross-reactive immune processes involving other bacteria, perhaps in the gastrointestinal or genitourinary tract. In PSRA, the streptococcus infection may have a similar adjuvant rule, promoting only latent autoimmunity (breach of immune tolerance). In such a case, the different clinical pictures of the PSRA spectrum would follow the different individual susceptibilities.

The most important practical question to be answered is whether patients with PSRA have an increased risk of RHD and require secondary prophylaxis. Three echocardiographybased studies in children with PSRA provided evidence of cardiac involvement in 6 of the combined 76 patients. Adults with PSRA were shown to be free of valvular abnormalities by echocardiographic screening in two case series and in one prospective study involving 75 patients who did not receive antibiotic prophylaxis and were followed up for almost 9 years. Because the present literature on PSRA is mainly based on American and western European populations, the conclusions may not apply to people in other parts of the world. The WHO ARF guidelines state that "patients with arthritis following a streptococcal upper respiratory infection should be considered to have RF if they fulfill the Jones criteria." The New Zealand and Australian guidelines state that the diagnosis of PSRA should rarely be made in

high-risk populations and with caution in low-risk populations. In those countries, patients diagnosed with PSRA at a high risk of developing ARF should receive secondary prophylaxis for at least 5 years. Low-risk patients should receive this treatment for at least 1 year. An absence of valve involvement should again be confirmed by echocardiography prior to the discontinuation of antibiotics.

### Conclusion

Acute rheumatic fever is triggered by S. pyogenes infection and is mediated by innate and adaptive immune responses influenced by environmental and genetic factors. The autoimmune reactivity that follows infection is due to molecular mimicry between human proteins and bacterial antigens. An imbalance between inflammatory/anti-inflammatory cytokines produced in response to the infection leads to acute and chronic inflammation. In addition, the low numbers of Treg cells facilitate increased inflammatory reactivity and chronic disease.

Although rare in most developed countries, rheumatic fever remains the most common cause of acquired valvular disease worldwide. Misdiagnosis can lead to severe consequences, so high levels of suspicion are recommended, especially for high-risk populations. The diagnosis is based on the 2015 Jones criteria, which uses clinical, laboratory, and echocardiographic findings and distinguishes lowand high-risk populations. Although adequate pharyngitis treatment can prevent most ARF cases, primary prevention policies have never been demonstrated to reduce the incidence of the disease effectively, and a vaccine against Streptococcus is eagerly awaited. Secondary prophylaxis prevents new attacks and minimizes sequelae in the long term but is dependent on adequate compliance.

### KEY POINTS

### Introduction

Considering the complete absence of data about the impact coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) had on patients with rheumatic disease in early 2020, one must consider the rapid acquisition of knowledge about this vulnerable population as remarkable. The creation of multiple global research consortiums early in the pandemic has generated numerous, important observations that helped guide the management of patients with rheumatic disease receiving immunosuppression. Later, focused industry efforts to develop mitigation strategies against COVID-19 such as vaccination and neutralizing monoclonal antibodies were critical for the global attenuation of poor COVID-19 clinical outcomes, although many of these studies either had no or very few participants on immunosuppression. Thus this led to another concerted effort by the academic research community to determine whether the benefits observed in the immunocompetent population were also observed in the immunosuppressed. Through these efforts, strategies have been identified for immunosuppressed patients to navigate through the challenges of the COVID-19 pandemic. Nevertheless, subsets of these patients continue to have

an elevated risk of poor COVID-19 outcomes such as those on B cell depletion therapies or mycophenolate mofetil. Here, we describe the risk of severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) infection, the impact of immunosuppression on COVID-19 outcomes, the development of de novo inflammatory conditions resembling systemic autoimmune diseases, and the current strategies to prevent and manage these patients with COVID-19.

### Risk of SARS-CoV-2 Infection

Potential differences in SARS-CoV-2 infection rates between individuals with rheumatic disease compared with the general population have been examined in multiple studies, including several population-based studies. In a Korean cohort study of 133,609 people tested for SARS-CoV-2 infection in early 2020, the risk of this infection in patients with rheumatic disease was slightly higher compared with matched individuals without rheumatic disease (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 1.19; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.031.40). Conversely, a population-based cohort from Italy did not demonstrate a higher risk of SARS-CoV-2 infection for people with rheumatic disease on anti-malarials compared with the general population (OR 0.94; 95% CI, 0.661.34) despite a slightly higher probability of being tested (OR 1.09; 95% CI, 0.941.28). A population-based matched cohort study from Ontario, Canada, analyzing data from January to December 2020 also found that the standardized cumulative incidence of SARS-CoV-2 infection was the same in those with immunemediated inflammatory diseases (IMIDs) compared with matched comparators (90 cases per 10,000 population in both groups), despite testing rates that were 20% higher in people with IMIDs. Yet a meta-analysis found an increased prevalence of SARS-CoV-2 infection in those with rheumatic diseases versus those without (relative risk [RR] 1.53; 95% CI, 1.162.01).

It appears that a more consistent increased risk of infection is observed when considering specific rheumatic diseases. For example, an Italian case-control study observed an increase in patients with rheumatoid arthritis (RA) (aOR 1.64; 95% CI, 1.322.05) but not in the whole connective tissue disease cohort (aOR 1.09; 95% CI, 0.721.66). A 34% increased risk of infection in patients with RA compared with those without was also observed in the UK Biobank, but not in patients with gout. Similarly, the

U.S. Veterans Affairs data set also found elevated infection risk (25%) in those with RA versus without. Likewise, in those with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), an elevated risk was observed compared with those without (adjusted hazard ratio [aHR] 1.28; 95% CI, 1.031.59),8 consistent with other studies that demonstrated an increased prevalence of COVID-19 in patients with SLE versus without SLE.9,

Overall, the interpretation of these data has been complicated by the heterogeneity of study design and confounders such as age, sex, and comorbid conditions. This is in addition to significant unmeasured confounding that could explain differences in infection rates, such as immunosuppressive use, circulating variants, rheumatic disease severity and activity, availability of testing and testing rates, case definition, local public health measures, and differences in individual behaviors related to COVID-19 risk mitigation.

### Impact of Immunosuppression on COvID-19 Outcomes

Systemic immunosuppression may affect COVID-19 risk and severity for people with systemic autoimmune rheumatic diseases who require these medications to control their underlying disease. This potential risk resulted in a relative increase in shielding behaviors such as social distancing and masking for people with rheumatic diseases, 13 particularly early in the pandemic. While glucocorticoids and disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs (DMARDs) have long been recognized to generally increase infection risk and severity, studies in the pandemic have provided more specific guidance about how this risk may vary by mechanism of action. Since glucocorticoids and several specific DMARDs have been repurposed to show efficacy in treating COVID-19, this adds to the complexity of how immunosuppression may affect COVID-19 risk during different phases of viral infection. Finally, immunosuppressants may blunt vaccine immunogenicity, which may result in less protection from COVID-19 infection and increased severity. An overview of the effects of immunosuppression on COVID-19 outcomes is shown in Table 119.1.

### Glucocorticoids

Several studies suggest that the use and higher dose of glucocorticoids may be associated with increased COVID-19 severity.

A study from the COVID-19 Global Rheumatology Alliance (GRA) showed that prednisone ≥10 mg/day was associated with two-fold increased risk of hospitalization from COVID-19 compared with no glucocorticoid use. Similarly, another GRA study also showed that glucocorticoid use was associated with COVID- 19-related death. However, dexamethasone is now the standard of care to treat hospitalized COVID-19 with high risk of progression to respiratory failure. This apparent discrepancy may be explained by biologic differences in the effects of glucocorticoids at different phases of viral infection. In early phases of viral infection, glucocorticoids may enhance viral replication and blunt clearance, resulting in worse outcomes. During the hyperinflammatory phase later in the course of infection, glucocorticoids may be helpful in dampening and preventing progression of inflammatory cascades and cytokine storms that may have otherwise resulted in more pronounced lung damage. It is also possible that the association of baseline glucocorticoids may be confounded by factors such as disease activity and severity. Regardless, patients requiring moderate doses of glucocorticoids are at higher risk of severe COVID-19, and therefore appropriate risk mitigation and early treatment should be encouraged.

### Conventional Synthetic DMARDs

Baseline use of conventional synthetic (csDMARDs) for rheumatic diseases has also been evaluated throughout the pandemic. Despite some early enthusiasm, 20,21 hydroxychloroquine is not effective in clinical trials to treat COVID-19,22 and patients with SLE on baseline hydroxychloroquine are not protected from being infected with COVID-19.23, Despite its common use in rheumatology, methotrexate has not emerged as a consistent risk factor for COVID-19 severity,25,26 although studies show it does blunt vaccine humoral responses. Mycophenolate mofetil has also emerged as one of the csDMARDs that may severely impact vaccine immunogenicity. Among patients with SLE, mycophenolate mofetil, along with cyclophosphamide and calcineurin inhibitors (e.g., cyclosporin), has also been associated with severe COVID-19 compared with hydroxychloroquine. While not traditionally viewed as a potent immunosuppressive, sulfasalazine While this may be explained by confounding factors, it is also plausible that sulfasalazine may impact COVID-19 severity by inhibiting type I interferon (IFN) production by plasmacytoid dendritic cells. There are relatively less data focusing on leflunomide and azathioprine.

### B Cell-Depleting Therapies

B celldepleting therapies such as rituximab have shown the most consistent association with severe COVID-19 outcomes across many immune-mediated inflammatory diseases. For example, an early study in a French cohort showed that rituximab-treated rheumatic patients had three-fold increased risk compared with those treated with other immunosuppressants. A GRA study focusing on patients with RA also found strong associations of rituximab use with severe COVID-19 compared with TNF inhibitor use. Rituximab severely reduces humoral response to vaccines, 33,34 although patients may still generate sufficient cellular responses. Thus rituximab-treated patients are at increased risk of breakthrough infection after vaccination and are the group within the rheumatic disease population still at highest risk for severe outcomes. Mitigation strategies should strongly be encouraged for

rheumatic patients on B celldepleting therapy (see the section "Strategies to Mitigate Poor COVID-19 Outcomes in Immunosuppressed Patients With Rheumatic Disease").

### Other Biologic DMARDS

Despite their widespread use, TNF inhibitors have not emerged as having a consistent signal for an association with COVID-19 severity. Using pooled data from three international registries of patients with COVID-19, TNF inhibition was associated with lower risk for severe COVID-19 compared with alternative therapies for immune-mediated inflammatory diseases,37 although this data should be interpreted with caution given the high risk of bias in this study such as reporting bias due to the use of registries, lack of a control group, and regional differences in hospitalization thresholds. Interleukin (IL)-6 inhibitors such as tocilizumab have proven efficacy in treating a subgroup of hospitalized patients with severe COVID-19,38 but baseline use of these medications has not been associated with COVID-19 severity. Similarly, IL-1 inhibitors such as anakinra may have efficacy to treat COVID-19,39 although less research has focused on baseline use in rheumatic patients. Abatacept has not shown any consistent association with COVID-19 severity. Despite its mechanism related to inhibiting B cell signaling, belimumab has not emerged as a risk factor for COVID-19 severity. There is currently a paucity of data related to COVID-19 risk of other biologic DMARD mechanisms of action, including IL-17A, IL-12/23, IL-23, type 1 IFN, and terminal C5 inhibitors.

### Targeted d Synthetic DMARDs

Baricitinib, a Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitor, has efficacy to treat hospitalized patients with severe COVID-19.40 However, a GRA study found that baseline JAK inhibitor use was associated with severe COVID-19 compared with TNF inhibitor use in RA. As noted with glucocorticoids, this apparent paradox may be explained by differential biologic effects of JAK inhibitors based on the timing of use in the different phases of viral infection (i.e., viral replication vs. hyperinflammatory phases). Also, baricitinib is less commonly used in RA, and there may be differences in infection risk based on JAK selectivity. Likewise, baracitinib has been identified using artificial intelligence algorithms for its potential to inhibit endocytosis of SARS-CoV-2 via inhibition of G-associated kinase and adaptor-associated kinase. Whether alternative JAK inhibitors such as tofacitinib or upadacitinib share this potential property is not well understood.41, Compared with many other DMARDs, the half-life of JAK inhibitors is short, so discontinuation of these medications may also impact associations in observational studies with COVID-19 outcomes. However, the association of baseline use of JAK inhibitors with worse COVID- 19 severity has not been consistent43 and may be explained by confounding factors such as line of therapy and rheumatic disease severity. There is currently a paucity of data related to COVID-19 risk of targeted synthetic DMARDs that include apremilast and avacopan.

### Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome e in Children and Adults

In the initial global wave of SARS-CoV-2 infection, pediatricians noted that in general COVID-19 led to much less severe

disease in children than seen in adults. However, in the spring of 2020 reports emerged of children hospitalized with critical illness including hyperinflammatory shock, heart failure, and features resembling Kawasaki disease (KD).45-49 The majority of these children had known prior COVID-19 or close contact with an individual with COVID-19 in the preceding weeks, or had antibodies detected against SARS-CoV-2. This disorder was initially termed pediatric multisystem inflammatory syndrome temporally associated with COVID-19 in the United Kingdom and multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children (MIS-C) by the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and the World Health Organization. By the end of 2022, more than 9000 children in the United States had been hospitalized with MIS-C and was estimated to occur in up to 3 per 10, SARS-CoV-2 infections in children.

### Clinical Characteristics and Diagnosis

The presentation of MIS-C can be highly variable, with common clinical signs, symptoms, and laboratory parameters shown in Table 119.2.45, Initially, MIS-C was notable for its similarity to KD49; however, children with MIS-C were much more likely to present in overt shock with moderate to severe myocardial dysfunction, as well as prominent gastrointestinal symptoms. In addition, along with history of exposure to SARS-CoV-2, children with MIS-C were generally older than those with KD and disproportionately Hispanic/Latino and/or Black.

It was recognized early that patients with MIS-C demonstrate significant variability in presentation. Two studies utilized latent class analysis in large cohorts of patients to define common disease phenotypes of MIS-C.48,56" Broadly this work highlights three groups of patients: one with the most severe disease including shock and myocardial dysfunction; one with moderate disease, numerous organ systems involved, and overlap with acute COVID-19; and one with more mild disease. The distribution of these phenotypes appeared to change over time, with fewer severe cases in more recent MIS-C waves.

There are no broadly accepted diagnostic criteria for MIS-C, and diagnosis is made by physician judgment. However, the MIS-C case definition generated by the CDC57 provides a framework for the evaluation of suspected cases as well as features consistent with its diagnosis (Table 119.3). Given the wide clinical spectrum of MIS-C and need to promptly diagnose and treat this condition while excluding other common mimics, a stepwise approach to evaluation is warranted. One approach endorsed by the American College of Rheumatology (ACR) suggests using routine laboratory tests to screen patients followed by a comprehensive evaluation for those with suggestive findings including lymphopenia, thrombocytopenia, hyponatremia, and hypoalbuminemia.

### Pathogenesis

The pathogenesis of MIS-C is incompletely understood. Initial immunologic investigations identified that children with MIS-C showed high circulating cytokine levels with low SARS-CoV-2 viral loads, supporting the notion of this as a post-infectious complication of COVID-19.59 This cytokine profile is distinct from acute COVID-19 and KD and is accompanied by activation of innate immune effector cells and lymphocytes.60-62 Notably, the elevation of IFN-gamma-induced pathways seen in severe MIS-C is a common feature of other cytokine storm syndromes including macrophage activation syndrome.63-65 This cytokine-rich environment is accompanied by production of autoreactive antibodies, which have strong specificity for proteins expressed in endothelial, cardiac, and intestinal tissue,60,62v which may relate to the unique clinical features of MIS-C.

An unresolved question is why MIS-C occurs in a small fraction of children after an otherwise unremarkable primary SARS- CoV-2 infection. Several studies have reported that some patients with MIS-C have mutations linked to autoinflammation, cytokine storm, or other inborn errors of immunity.66-69 Some reports have also found persistent leakage of SARS-CoV-2 viral proteins from the gut,70 although other work has failed to confirm this. More broadly, increasing evidence supports the existence of a superantigen effect in MIS-C, wherein an immunostimulatory molecule binds major histocompatibility complex class II outside the antigen-binding domain and stimulates large families of T cells in a Vbeta-specific manner. Patients with severe MIS-C have profound expansion of T cell receptor (TCR) beta variable gene 11-2 (TRBV11-2), which can represent up to 24% of clonal T cells.72-74 Modeling studies suggest that SARS-CoV-2 spike glycoprotein may resemble known superantigens and have a high-affinity interaction with TCR and specifically with TRBV11-2,72,75 further supporting this hypothesis (Fig. 119.1).

### Treatment

The initial treatment approach to MIS-C leaned heavily on therapeutics used in KD, including aspirin and intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG). However, as the initial series of patients were often refractory to these agents, treatment has evolved to include

early use of steroids or anti-cytokine biologics.45-48 Indeed, two large retrospective case series found that IVIG as monotherapy was associated with higher risk of progressing to cardiac dysfunction or requiring adjunctive treatment. In addition, one comparative study found that IVIG plus infliximab (vs. IVIG alone) led to lower requirements for additional therapy and a decreased length of intensive care unit stay. Currently, guidelines from the

National Institutes of Health (NIH) and the ACR support the use of IVIG plus steroids as first-line therapy; refractory patients were treated with pulse-dose steroids (30 mg/kg/day), anakinra, or infliximab (Table 119.4). Whether IVIG is an essential element of MIS-C treatment and optimal therapeutics for refractory MIS-C remain unknown.

### Prevention and Vaccination

A critical question related to the pathogenesis of MIS-C is whether it can be prevented. Since early 2022, the occurrence of MIS-C has dramatically reduced, including after the spread of new variants and periods of more substantial community transmission of SARS-CoV-2. This may be related to more widespread immunity to the virus, both through vaccination and prior infection. There is accumulating evidence to suggest that COVID-19 vaccination is highly protective (>90%) against the development of MIS-C.77, The reduction in MIS-C could also be linked to changes in viral pathogenicity, as a small study of unvaccinated Danish children found a substantially lower risk of MIS-C during the Omicron wave than from prior variants.

### Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome in Adults

While MIS-C is by definition a disorder of children, there is no biologic reason that such phenomenon would not occur in adults. Indeed, soon after the initial descriptions of MIS-C, reports emerged in several countries of clinically similar adult patients presenting with a multisystem inflammatory condition that has been termed MIS-A. A particular challenge is to discriminate

between MIS-A and the late phase of severe COVID-19, which can have similar, overlapping phenotypic appearances of hyperinflammatory multiorgan dysfunction. In MIS-A, patients have a true period of recovery from acute COVID-19 followed by a post-acute onset of new symptoms 2 to 6 weeks after the primary disease. In particular, new symptom onset in MIS-A includes cardiovascular dysfunction and mucocutaneous features that are rare in COVID- 1981 and a negative or low SARS-CoV-2 titer viral polymerase chain reaction. This is further distinguished from other post-acute sequelae of COVID-19 (PASC) or so-called "Long COVID", as the latter occurs in patients that are less acutely unwell and is notable for more general and constitutional symptoms and lack of severe cardiovascular compromise and shock seen in MIS-A.

Systematic reviews have examined clinical and laboratory features of patients with MIS-A and found that such patients were relatively young (mean age under 50), with a male predominance and a majority with other chronic health problems including diabetes, obesity, and cancer.82-84 Compared with MIS-C, patients with MIS-A more frequently presented with cardiac dysfunction and myocarditis, and less commonly with mucocutaneous features,85 although this may reflect a diagnostic bias toward more severe disease. A further review that also included adult patients 18 to 21 reported to the CDC under the MIS-C case definition found similar findings,86 further supporting MIS-C and MIS-A representing a continuum of disease across the lifespan. Treatment approaches to MIS-A are similar to MIS-C, with corticosteroids and IVIG typically leading to a favorable clinical response, but there are no comparative effectiveness studies in MIS-A to date.

### Autoantibodies and De Novo Autoimmune Disease in COVID-19

A concerning manifestation observed in some patients post-acute COVID-19 is the acquisition of new-onset autoimmune syndromes, as described through numerous case reports. 87-95 Two retrospective large database analyses have demonstrated increased risk in the development of an autoimmune disease following the acute phase of COVID-19. Using a test-negative design, data from the TriNetX U.S. Collaborative Network with propensitymatched patients with COVID-19 and controls, several systemic autoimmune and autoinflammatory diseases were found in higher rates in those with COVID-19, such as RA (aHR 2.98; 95% CI, 2.783.20), SLE (aHR 2.99; 95% CI, 2.683.34), and ankylosing spondylitis (aHR 3.21; 95% CI, 2.504.13) (Table 119.5). Similar findings were reported in a pre-print using routine data from German statutory health insurance organizations totaling over 640,000 people, where an incidence rate of an autoimmune disease 3 to 15 months post-C0VID-19 was 15.05% (95% CI, 14.6915.42) per 1000 person-years compared with 10.55% (95% CI, 10.2510.86) in those who never had COVID-19.97 It remains unclear currently, however, which risk factors are important, whether they are previously associated with autoimmune diseases (i.e., genetic predisposition, environmental triggers, hormonal milieu) or new risk factors specific for COVID-19-associated autoimmune disease.

A hallmark of robust immune activation, including the immune response to SARS-CoV-2 infection, is the generation of de novo autoantibodies. Autoantibodies against a broad range of protein classes, including immunomodulatory proteins and nuclear antigens classically associated with connective tissue diseases and other systemic autoimmune conditions, have been observed, particularly

in those with severe COVID-19.98-103 Many of these autoantibodies are functional, as autoantibodies to type I IFN are associated with the transition to severe COVID-19102 due to the central role of IFN in anti-viral immunity. Antiphospholipid autoantibodies have also been observed in up to half of hospitalized patients with COVID-19,107 and autoantibodies to neutrophil extra-cellular traps (NETs) impair the degradation of NETs, both of which may contribute to the coagulopathy observed in severe COVID-19.108 Interestingly, autoantibodies against certain chemokines are associated with differential clinical COVID-19 outcomes. While autoantibodies to chemokines were also found in those infected by HIV or possessed systemic autoimmune disease, distinct chemokine autoantibody signatures were identified in those who convalesced from COVID-19 (CCL19, CCL22, and CXCL17), required hospitalization (CXCL5, CXCL8, CCL25), or had long COVID at 6 months post-acute infection (CCL21, CXCL13, and CXCL16). It is critical to note that many viral infections have been associated with the production of autoantibodies, including Epstein-Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, and parvovirus B19.110 Indeed, over 50% of those who were critically ill for non-COVID-19-related diagnoses (including other respiratory viral infections and nonrespiratory bacterial infections) generated autoantibodies against cytokines and canonic antigens associated with connective tissue diseases. Importantly, no such autoantibody development has been observed following SARS-CoV-2 messenger (mRNA) vaccination, including those with mRNA vaccine-associated myocarditis,112 preserving this as a critical strategy to reduce the occurrence and severity of COVID-19.

The mechanism by which broadly reactive autoantibodies are generated in COVID-19 has been elucidated. Infection by SARS- CoV-2 drives a potent B cell response through the extrafollicular (EF) pathway, particularly in those with severe COVID-19.113- 117 As opposed to B cell responses generated through germinal centers (GCs), which may require weeks to fully manifest, EF responses occur early (within days) after pathogen infection or vaccination. EF responses serve to provide an initial source of antibodies, a response that is perpetuated in the absence of tolerance checkpoints present in the GCs to limit autoreactivity. In those with COVID-19, IgG1 antibody-secreting cells (ASCs) with autoreactivity to nuclear antigens, glomerular basement membrane, and carbamylated proteins were expanded from B cells possessing characteristics of EF pathway activation (i.e., double-negative B cells, little to no somatic hypermutation) within

2 weeks of infection. Patients who died from COVID-19 lacked GCs, also suggesting an EF-dominant response. Notably, this is the same mechanism by which autoreactive B cells drive autoantibody production in SLE.119,

Because EF responses are typically transient, this leads to the possibility that autoreactivity may also be transient in those recovering from COVID-19. Indeed, there was a rapid loss of these IgG1 ASCs (both autoreactive and SARS-CoV-2-specific) along with a slower contraction of autoantibody titers in those who recovered from COVID-19.100 In this same cohort, a subset of patients with persistently elevated autoantibody titers continued to exhibit symptoms following the acute phase of COVID-19, consistent with PASC. Similar observations have been reported, with persistently elevated ANA titers noted 12 months following the acute phase in those affected by PASC.121, It remains unclear currently whether those with COVID-19-induced autoimmune disease will also experience a resolution of B cell autoreactivity and regression of their disease or possess a more durable autoreactive response similar to those with SLE.

### Strategies to Mitigate Poor COVID-19 Outcomes in Immunosuppressed Patients With Rheumatic Disease

While vaccination remains the most durable strategy to effectively reduce the likelihood of poor clinical outcomes due to COVID-19 in patients with rheumatic disease, those on potent immunosuppressive regimens such as B celldepleting agents, anti-metabolites such as mycophenolate mofetil, and high-dose glucocorticoids remain at risk of breakthrough infections including severe COVID-19.12 Patients who are immunocompromised have prolonged shedding of SARS-CoV-2,123 which can contribute to prolonged infections that can contribute to the emergence of novel variants. 124-130 For these susceptible individuals, additional layers of protection are needed to overcome the poor immunogenicity generated following SARS-CoV-2 vaccination due to these immunosuppressive therapies (Table 119.6). Two main strategies have emerged as tools for these patients: (1) monoclonal antibodies against the spike protein of SARS-CoV-2, delivered either as preor post-exposure to SARS-CoV-2, and (2) anti-viral medications.

### Pre-exposure Prophylaxis Using Monoclonal Antibodies

Monoclonal antibody therapies have recently emerged as an important tool for patients on immunosuppression. Its use as either pre-exposure prophylaxis (i.e., tixagevimab-cilgavimab) or post-exposure therapy against asymptomatic or mild-to-moderate COVID-19 (i.e., bamlanivimab-etesevimab, casirivimabimdevimab, sotrovimab, bebtelovimab) have improved clinical outcomes in mostly immunocompetent recipients.131-134 These antibodies possess highly neutralizing properties to pre-Omicron variants of concern135,136 and, at least in the case of tixagevimab-cilgavimab, led to higher neutralizing antibody titer at day 270 post-administration compared with nonrecipients. Tixagevimab-cilgavimab uniquely harbor the YTE modification (M252Y/S254T/T256E)138 that increases neonatal Fc receptor antibody affinity by nearly nine-fold compared with wild-type IgG. This subsequently increases its half-life to nearly 90 days by protecting against endosomal degradation and thereby enhancing

antibody recycling. 137, This abrogates FcγR binding, eliminating any nonneutralizing effector functions that have been observed in mouse models of SARS-CoV-2 with sotrovimab.

Data later emerged from several observational studies in the immunosuppressed population, particularly for tixagevimabcilgavimab, where its administration associated with dramatic reductions in both breakthrough infection rates and severe COVID-19 outcomes compared with nonrecipients.141-146 The use of casirivimab-imdevimab as post-SARS-CoV-2 exposure in patients on B celldepleting therapies also led to substantially improved COVID-19 outcomes compared with nonrecipients. Both examples clearly demonstrate the efficacy of highly neutralizing antibodies against SARS-CoV-2 spike protein in clinical protection.

A major limitation of monoclonal antibody therapy is its static nature, the inability to adapt to new mutational threats the way infection can by triggering either new immune responses to novel variants or by vaccination that can generate long-lived germinal center responses that diversify antibody repertoires. This limitation already has been realized with monoclonal antibodies, which had previously received early use authorizations (EUAs) from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA), authorizations that were subsequently revoked following the emergence of highly immune evasive subvariants of Omicron harboring the R346X mutation (i.e., BA.4.6, BQ.1.1, XBB) in late 2022 that rendered these agents ineffective. Interestingly, in a small observational study, the emergence of mutations in the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein was associated with reductions in viral susceptibility to tixagevimab-cilgavimab or bebtelovimab, 150 although the clinical impact of such mutations remains unclear. Nevertheless, this highlights the need to continuously generate novel monoclonal antibodies that highly neutralize current SARS- CoV-2 variants, or possibly use high-titer COVID-19 convalescent plasma, although insufficient data existed at the time of this writing for the COVID-19 Treatment Guidelines Panel to provide recommendations (https://www.covid19treatmentguidelines.nih.gov/therapies/antivirals-including-antibody-products/ covid-19-convalescent-plasma/).

### Anti-viral Therapy

Ritonavir-boosted nirmatrelvir represents the only highly effective oral anti-viral medication for the treatment of COVID-19. Nirmatrelivir targets the SARS-CoV-2 3-chymotrypsin-like cysteine protease (Mpro), 151 an essential enzyme in cleavage of viral polyproteins into functional proteins, 152 and ritonavir is a CYP3A4 inhibitor that boosts nirmatrelvir pharmacokinetics.151, A reduction in the risk of hospitalization or death in unvaccinated adults with high risk of progressing to COVID-19 with laboratory-confirmed SARS- CoV-2 infection was observed in those taking ritonavir-boosted nirmatrelvir, although <1% of the participants in the treatment group were immunosuppressed. Data for patients with rheumatic disease emerged from the MassGenBrigham effort, where in a retrospective analysis, 1.3% of those who received ritonavir-boosted nirmatrelvir required hospitalization due to COVID-19 compared with 17.6% of those who received no outpatient treatment. After adjusting for age, estimated glomerular filtration rate, race/ethnicity, comorbidities, and zip code and median household income, the OR for severe COVID-19 in those who received anti-virals was 0.13 compared with no outpatient treatment (95% CI, 0.060.28). Notably, most of the study participants had been vaccinated against SARS-CoV-2, further supporting the use of anti-viral therapy in this population.

COVID-19 rebound (either return of positive SARS-CoV-2 test results or COVID-19 symptoms following anti-viral treatment) has been reported,155 including in patients with rheumatic disease where a conservative estimate of 7.9% was observed. The mechanisms of COVID-19 rebound remain unclear, although residual virus reservoirs may be present due to incomplete eradication. At the time of writing, no evidence exists supporting administering longer courses or a second course of ritonavir-boosted nirmatrelvir in those who experience rebound symptoms. Indeed, in patients with rheumatic disease with rebound COVID-19, none required subsequent hospitalization.

As ritonavir is a CYP3A4 inhibitor, important considerations need to be made regarding concomitant medications. Since colchicine and statins are CYP3A substrates, they are contraindicated with ritonavir-boosted nirmatrelvir, while calcineurin inhibitors (in particular tacrolimus)156 need to be dose adjusted. CYP3A inducers, such as carbamazepine, phenytoin, and rifampin, are also contraindicated and alternative COVID-19 therapies should be considered. Other immunosuppressives commonly used in rheumatic disease patients may interact with ritonavir. Mycophenolate mofetil and mycophenolic acid are metabolized by uridine 5'-diphospho-glucuronosyltransfeases (UGT), which is modestly induced by ritonavir. Additionally, glucocorticoids are metabolized by CYP3A4-mediated 6β-hydroxylation, suggesting that ritonavir will reduce glucocorticoid clearance and increase blood concentrations. Given the short duration of ritonavir-boosted nirmatrelvir therapy, no additional dose adjustments for mycophenolate nor glucocorticoids are recommended. In those where ritonavir-boosted nirmatrelvir is unavailable or inappropriate, intravenous remdesivir may be an option.

### Management of Patients With Rheumatic Disease Hospitalized Due to COvID-19

While certain immunosuppressive therapies are risk factors for COVID-19 disease severity, in later phases of COVID-19 where severe manifestations are present (e.g., hypoxia and raised

inflammatory markers), immunosuppression provides clinical benefit. This is largely due to the need for a robust immune response to SARS-CoV-2 early in infection to limit virus replication but a dominance of a hyperinflammatory milieu when COVID-19 has progressed to an advanced phase. Thus the treatment of hospitalized patients with COVID-19 is determined by disease severity (Table 119.7), with anti-virals key in the early viral replication phase and immunosuppressives in the late phase as currently outlined in the NIH OVID- 19 Treatment Guidelines Panel (https://www.covid19treatmentguidelines.nih.gov/management/clinical-management/ hospitalized-adults-therapeutic-management/).

Specific data for the use of anti-virals or immunosuppressives in immunocompromised patients who are hospitalized due to COVID-19 are not available because of the lack of representation in clinical trials. While clinical experience appears to support that treatment responses will be similar in the immunocompetent, customization is likely required. For example, those on high-risk immunosuppression (i.e., B celldepleting therapies) may experience a prolonged virus replication phase, leading to possible emergence of new variants. Thus use of anti-viral therapies may be needed for longer duration or later in the disease course in these individuals. Acknowledgment of traditional risk factors (i.e., age, comorbidities) associated with severe COVID-19 remain important in the immunosuppressed, 16,158,159 so these need to be considered in management decisions. Finally, the decision to hold or adjust baseline immunosuppressive therapies will require assessment of underlying disease activity, type of immunosuppressive used, possible drug interactions between immunosuppressives and COVID-19 therapies, and COVID-19 severity.

### Anti-viral Therapy

Anti-virals should be limited to use in the early virus replication phase of disease. In the immunocompetent population, discordant results with remdesivir were observed in two trials. In the ACTT-1 trial,160 a reduction in disease progression was
