observed in patients with COVID-19 on supplemental oxygen, and the SOLIDARITY trial showed no benefit. Nevertheless, current guidelines support the use of anti-viral therapy in the immunosuppressed (https://www.covid19treatmentguidelines.nih.gov/management/clinical-management/hospitalizedadults-therapeutic-management/). Importantly, no benefit was observed in those with more intensive oxygen requirements (i.e., high-flow nasal cannula or greater), thus supporting that those with minimal oxygen requirements likely represent patients in the early phase of COVID-19. Finally, treatment duration with anti-virals may require personalization as virus eradiation does not always occur in the immunocompromised population.162, Given the risk of prolonged viral replication, prolonged treatment with anti-virals beyond 5 to 10 days may be needed.

### Glucocorticoids

While specific data in the immunosuppressed are not available, there was a survival benefit in dexamethasone recipients (6 mg once daily for 10 days or until discharge if sooner) in hospitalized patients requiring supplemental oxygen (RECOVERY trial). The use of dexamethasone in the immunosuppressed requires clinical judgment, however: The clinician needs to weigh clinical severity along with risk of worsening of COVID-19, as glucocorticoids may delay or attenuate appropriate immune responses. For example, those on minimal oxygen requirements in the early phase of COVID-19 may benefit from anti-viral therapy alone, as the RECOVERY trial data suggested that this group may in fact incur harm with dexamethasone use. Furthermore, higher-dose steroids (dexamethasone 20 mg once daily for 5 days, followed by 10 mg dexamethasone once daily for 5 days or until discharge if sooner) are associated with increased risk of death in those with

hypoxia but who did not require noninvasive or invasive mechanical ventilation.

### Immunosuppressives

IL-6 inhibitors s165,166 and JAK inhibitors40,167,168 have shown clinical benefit in combination with dexamethasone in severe or critical COVID-19. Again, while the immunosuppressed were either excluded or present only in small numbers, benefit may be also appreciated in this population. The risk of secondary infections when these therapies are used in the immunosuppressed is not known, however. Safety data for baricitinib in acute COVID- 19 is reassuring, especially related to thrombotic events, probably owing to the limited treatment duration in patients with COVID-19 who are anti-coagulated.169, This finding differs from chronic JAK inhibitor dosing in RA studies, where safety signals were detected. Thus a personalized approach by the clinician is again warranted.

### COVID-19 Convalescent Plasma

The NIH COVID-19 Treatment Guidelines Panel currently has no recommendation for the use of COVID-19 convalescent plasma for immunosuppressed inpatients with COVID-19 (https://www.covid19treatmentguidelines.nih.gov/management/ clinical-management-of-adults/hospitalized-adults-therapeuticmanagement/). While no benefit was observed in three clinical trials where the study participants were hospitalized and largely immunocompetent, 76,172,173 subgroup analyses suggest possible benefit of COVID-19 convalescent plasma in the immunosuppressed without a chronic inflammatory disease 172,174,175 along with a meta-analysis. An FDA EUA has been issued for the use of high-titer COVID-19 convalescent plasma for treatment of COVID-19 in both nonhospitalized and hospitalized immunocompromised patients (https://www.fda.gov/media/141478/ download). Thus in those patients on substantial immunosuppression (i.e., B celldepleting therapies or combination immunosuppressive therapies) with either severe/critical COVID-19, who have risk factors for disease progression, or with prolonged SARS- CoV-2 infection despite anti-viral therapy, clinicians may consider administering high-titer COVID-19 convalescent plasma from a donor who has recently recovered from COVID-19 (to increase the likelihood of antibody coverage of a SARS-CoV-2 variant similar to one affecting the patient) and has been fully vaccinated.

### Conclusion

Taken together, the data generated thus far have provided reassuring results for most immunosuppressed patients with rheumatic disease. While there appears to be increased risk of SARS-CoV-2 infection, most patients requiring immunosuppression for their rheumatic disease appear to have acceptable clinical outcomes from COVID-19. Anti-virals continue to be an important mitigating strategy for those in the early phase of COVID-19, while monoclonal antibodies that can neutralize the circulating Omicron variants are under development.

Important questions remain, however. Will SARS-CoV-2 continue to evolve with more immune-evasive variants, requiring updated vaccines and monoclonal antibodies? If so, will those at the highest risk of both poor COVID-19 outcomes and immunogenicity responses both to SARS-CoV-2 infection or vaccination face a continuous threat that cannot be fully mitigated? Should we be withholding immunosuppressives following infection or prior to vaccination, and for how long? What will be the long-term fate

of those who have acquired new autoimmune syndromes following COVID-19? Finally, a formal discussion of PASC, outside of acquired de novo autoimmune disease described previously will require formal diagnostic or classification criteria, as over 200 symptoms have been attributed to this entity. We anticipate having a clearer idea of the impact PASC has on patients with rheumatic disease in the future.

# Vaccination in Rheumatic Disease

### KEY POINTS

Patients with rheumatic disease are at higher risk for serious and opportunistic infections, including those potentially preventable by vaccination.

DMARDs can negatively affect vaccine immunogenicity, most notably methotrexate and B-cell depletion therapy.

Some biologics (interleukin-6R [IL-6R], IL-12/IL-23, and IL-17 inhibitors) have little observed impact on vaccine immunogenicity.

Strategies for improving vaccine response include vaccinating prior to DMARD start and, in some cases, temporary hold of the DMARD after vaccination.

### Introduction

Patients with rheumatic diseases have an increased risk of contracting vaccine-preventable infections and suffer morbidity and mortality due to these infections.1-6 Vaccination of these patients can reduce the risk of infectious complications7,8; however, immune suppressing drugs used to treat rheumatic diseases can sometimes blunt vaccine-induced immune responses, making timing of vaccination in relation to immunosuppressive therapy sometimes critical. Further, despite their potential for providing protection, vaccines continue to be underused in practice.9, In this chapter we discuss the latest data and guidelines from the American College of Rheumatology (ACR), the European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology (EULAR), the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), and the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) on the effect on vaccine response in adult patients on disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs (DMARDs). Therapies considered include conventional synthetic DMARDs (csDMARDs), which include methotrexate, leflunomide, hydroxychloroquine, and sulfasalazine; targeted synthetic DMARDs (tsDMARDs), which include Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitors; and biologic DMARDs (bDMARDs, or biologics), which are targeted, usually antibody-based drugs that inhibit cytokine pathways (TNF, IL-17A and IL-17F, IL-23, IL-6, and IL-1), T cell costimulatory-signal of CTLA4 (abatacept), or targeted B-cell depletion via CD19 inhibition

(rituximab). For most studies evaluating DMARD effects upon vaccine responses, vaccine immunogenicity has been used as a primary outcome measure, as few studies are powered to detect clinical efficacy. Also, it should be noted that recommendations regarding severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) vaccination are changing rapidly at the time of this chapter's preparation. Lastly, outcome measures (definitions of response, how response is measured, and timing of response)11 and study designs are often inconsistent across studies, making it more difficult to compare the effects of different DMARDs upon different vaccines. This chapter focuses on the vaccines of most clinical relevance to the practicing adult rheumatologist, including the influenza, pneumococcal, herpes zoster, hepatitis B virus (HBV), tetanus diphtheria pertussis (Tdap), human papilloma virus (HPV), yellow fever (YF), and SARS-CoV-2 (COVID-19) vaccines.

### Influenza Vaccine

All influenza vaccines available in the United States this season are quadrivalent; they contain two influenza A and two influenza B virus antigens. s. The intranasal live attenuated influenza vaccine is contraindicated for those on immunosuppressive therapies. Influenza vaccine efficacy is estimated using a surrogate of hemagglutinin inhibition (HI) titers. An HI titer of 1:40 is considered "seroprotective" (defined as 50% vaccine efficacy).

### DMARD Effect on influenza Vaccine

Rituximab severely reduces influenza vaccine immune response. 13-20 Abatacept may impair influenza vaccine response, but data to support this are limited.21-24 Anti-TNF therapies10,25-27 and JAK inhibitors28 lead to lower fold increases in antibody titers; however, the proportion of patients achieving seroprotection appears to be similar to those not using these therapies. Data suggest that IL-6, IL-12/23, and IL-17 inhibitors do not affect influenza vaccine immunogenicity.29-33 Methotrexate (MTX) decreases humoral responses to influenza vaccine, and temporarily holding MTX at the time of vaccination is a recently recommended strategy for improving the proportion of patients that reach seroprotection. 34,35

### Influenza Vaccine Recommendations in Rheumatology Patients

Annual influenza vaccines are recommended for all who are ages 6 months and older.36, The ACR and EULAR recommend annual intramuscular vaccinations for all rheumatoid arthritis (RA) 1,38,39 patients.

The high-dose influenza vaccine is more effective in patients with rheumatic diseases. While high-dose influenza vaccine is recommended in the general population 65 years of age and older, the 2022 ACR guidelines have conditionally recommended this for those over age 18 who are on immunosuppressive medication.39-41 If high-dose or adjuvant vaccine is unavailable, then any influenza vaccine is preferred over no vaccine.

### Timing of Influenza Vaccine Relative to Immunosuppressive Therapy

Generally, influenza vaccination does not need to be delayed based on DMARD therapy schedule. However, there are data on optimized timing of methotrexate and rituximab dosing. Patients on methotrexate can improve their influenza vaccine immunogenicity by holding methotrexate for 1 to 2 weeks after vaccination especially in those on ≥15 mg/week. One study of RA patients showed that a temporary discontinuation of methotrexate for 2 weeks after vaccination improves immunogenicity of seasonal influenza vaccine without increasing RA activity. The latest EULAR guidelines acknowledge this fact1 but do not include this vaccine timing as a recommendation.

Those with planned rituximab initiation should receive the influenza vaccine prior to starting therapy. 1, Previous recommendations stated that for those already receiving rituximab, influenza vaccination should be administered 2 to 4 weeks prior to the next scheduled dose to maximize time since last dose. The 2022 ACR guidelines, however, recommend continuing rituximab as previously scheduled, although trying to maximize the time between last administration and vaccination while taking into account the need to vaccinate just prior to influenza season. Abatacept likely impairs influenza vaccine response, but data are limited. There are currently no guidelines for timing of the influenza vaccine when using this medication.

### Pneumococcal Vaccination

Pneumococcal conjugate vaccine 13 (PCV13) and pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine 23-valent (PPSV23) have been used together for the last decade to prevent pneumococcal disease. Recently the conjugate vaccine has been updated to include a greater number of serotypes, with both PCV15 and PCV20 being recently approved for use in adults.

### DMARD Effect on Pneumococcal Vaccine Response

Although studies conducted to evaluate DMARD influence upon pneumococcal vaccine immunogenicity have not been large, the results are similar to the influenza vaccine: rituximab13,17,42-44 and methotrexate11,45-48 reduce immune response to pneumococcal vaccines. Abatacept22,42,43 and Jak inhibitors28,49,50 modestly reduce immunogenicity, but other DMARDs do not. 13,

Please note, however, that almost all these data are for the PPSV23 vaccine specifically. There are several studies assessing effects of various JAK inhibitors on PCV13 immunogenicity, but these studies were uncontrolled.51, Additionally, we do not have any data available regarding PCV15 or PCV20 vaccine.

### Pneumococcal Vaccine Recommendations

Guidelines from the ACR, EULAR, CDC, and ACIP recommend pneumococcal vaccinations for patients with rheumatic disease taking DMARDs.1, For pneumococcal vaccine—naïve patients, a single dose of the PCV20 provides maximal benefit39 (CDC-ACIP recommendations, https://www. cdc.gov/vaccines/acip/recommendations.html). The CDC recommends that patients who have never received a pneumococcal vaccine should receive a single dose of PCV20 or start with one dose of PCV15 followed by a dose of PPSV23 at least 1 year later39 (CDC-ACIP recommendations, https://www.cdc.gov/ vaccines/acip/recommendations.html). A minimum of 8 weeks between PV15 and PPSV23 can be considered for patients on DMARDs39 (CDCACIP recommendations, https://www.cdc. gov/vaccines/acip/recommendations.html). If a patient has only received PPSV23, the CDC recommends administering one dose of PCV15 or PCV20 at least 1 year after PPSV23 was given 39 (CDC-ACIP recommendations, https://www.cdc.gov/vaccines/ acip/recommendations.html). In immunosuppressed patients who have received PCV13, the CDC recommends an additional two doses of PPSV23 before age 65 years and one dose of PPSV23 at age 65 years or older. This is with the caveat that the amount of benefit with the addition of PCV15 or PCV20 in those who have received PCV13 with prior PPSV23 had not been evaluated at the time of their recommendations39 (CDCACIP recommendations, https://www.cdc.gov/vaccines/acip/recommendations. html). Recent data, however, show improved immunogenicity with receipt of PCV20 after initial PCV13/PPSV23. .39,58

### Timing of Pneumococcal Vaccine Relative to Immunosuppressive eTherapy

Pneumococcal vaccination can be given irrespective of DMARD therapy timing with the exception of rituximab. Similar to influenza vaccination timing, those with planned rituximab initiation should receive the pneumococcal vaccine prior to the first infusion. If rituximab therapy is ongoing, the pneumococcal vaccine should be administered when the next rituximab dose is due, delaying rituximab infusion by 2 weeks if disease activity allows. Until further data are available with regard to methotrexate or other DMARDs and pneumococcal vaccine response, the ACR recommends other DMARDs including methotrexate can be continued without alteration to their dosing schedule.

### Herpes s Zoster Vaccination

### Background

Rheumatic patients on immunosuppressive therapy are at higher risk of developing herpes zoster infection compared with the general public especially those with inflammatory myositis and systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), as well as those using JAK inhibitors. There are two herpes zoster vaccines approved: the recombinant zoster vaccine (RZV) (Shingrix) and the live zoster

vaccine (ZVL) (Zostavax). The Shingrix vaccine appears more effective, and Zostavax is no longer marketed in the United States but is still available in many parts of the world. Zoster vaccine response is measured by humoral varicella zoster vaccine IgG or cell-mediated varicella zoster virus-specific T cell enumeration, which correlates more strongly with the risk of future shingles.

### Effect of DMARD Therapy on Vaccine Efficacy

There are limited data regarding whether DMARDs alter the immunogenicity of the herpes zoster vaccine. In one randomized trial of RA patients vaccinated with Zostavax and randomized to tofacitinib versus placebo, patients had similar responses in both groups. Patients on TNF inhibitors vaccinated with Zostavax had a 30% increase in humoral and cell-mediated responses compared with placebo. Rheumatology patients on rituximab have not been studied relative to their response to zoster vaccine; however, those with hematologic malignancies on anti-CD20 therapies (alone or with other chemotherapies) who received Zostavax mounted significant T cell responses (Agency EM. Shingrix 2020; available from: https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/medicines/ human/EPAR/shingrix, accessed 6/29/2021). Immunogenicity of zoster vaccine for those on other biologics, abatacept, and JAK inhibitors have not been reported. Currently there are no published data evaluating the influence of any DMARDs upon the immunogenicity of RZV.

Recent studies indicate that the zoster vaccine live (ZVL)/Zostavax may be safer in certain immunocompromised groups than previously thought. A cohort study of Medicare beneficiaries age 60 and older did not show increased incidence of herpes zoster infection 42 days after vaccination. ZVL was also safely administered to a small cohort of SLE patients without increased risk of infection 12 weeks post-vaccine.

A recent randomized control study of over 600 patients on TNF inhibitors receiving ZVL versus placebo did not have any confirmed varicella infections up to 1 year after vaccination with live vaccine. Another randomized control trial of 112 RA patients, 55 of whom received ZVL 2 to 3 weeks prior to initiation of tofacitinib versus placebo, only 1 patient of 55 (2%) developed cutaneous vaccine strain varicella infection, and later testing found that she lacked pre-vaccination immunity to varicella. Together, these data suggest that ZVL can be safely used in those actively using TNF inhibitors with or without concomitant methotrexate or low-dose steroids, but for those using JAK inhibitors, the data are less clear. One study evaluated the effect of ZVL in subset of RA patients who received the vaccine prior to initiation of tofacitinib (5 mg twice a day) or tofacitinib combined with MTX or adalimumab (40 mg every 14 days) plus MTX. The risk of herpes zoster infection was similar between the three treatment groups and similar to the nonvaccinated group as well. Notably, all patients on tofacitinib who developed zoster infection also received corticosteroids at baseline.

Currently just a few observational studies exist evaluating the reactogenicity and safety of the recombinant zoster vaccine in rheumatic disease populations. One study that assessed the risk of disease flare after receiving zoster recombinant adjuvanted vaccine found an incidence of 7% or less, and none required changes in

anti-rheumatic regimen. Another retrospective study of patients with immune-mediated inflammatory diseases who had received the recombinant zoster vaccine revealed that the vaccine was generally well tolerated, although a mild disease flare was not uncommon the first 12 weeks post-vaccination. A higher incidence of flares was seen in patients on glucocorticoids and thus higher disease activity.

### Recommendations

The 2022 ACR guidelines do not recommend live vaccines in patients actively receiving immunosuppressive therapy. This includes ZVL,39 and such therapy should be stopped for some time period before receipt of a live vaccine. In areas of the world where RZV is available, the ACR recommends giving this vaccine to those over 18 years old using immunosuppressive therapy.

The EULAR suggests that ZVL may be considered in highrisk immunosuppressed patients given the data stated above under "Safety of Zoster Vaccines in Immunocompromised Patients.' "1 Under limited circumstances, if ZVL is used over RZV, then similar to other live vaccines, this live vaccine should be administered 4 weeks prior to initiation of bDMARDs or tsDMARDs but not during treatment. Per EULAR recommendations, in those with uncertain varicella exposure, evaluation of serostatus can be considered before administration of live vaccine to prevent primary infection with the live vaccine.

### Timing of ZVL and RZV in Relation to DMARD Therapy

Direct evidence for optimal therapy hold time prior to live vaccines is missing, but the 2022 ACR guidelines recommends a pre-vaccination hold time of 4 weeks for csDMARDs, one dosing interval for bDMARDs, and post-vaccination hold time of 4 weeks for all DMARDs. No therapy schedule change is needed for immunosuppressive therapy except rituximab, which should be delayed by 2 weeks. For RZV, there is no published data evaluating whether DMARDs adversely affect vaccine response and whether holding might improve such response.

### SARS-CoV-2 Vaccination

### Background

A growing number of SARS-CoV-2 vaccines are in use worldwide, including mRNA, adenoviral vector, protein subunit, and inactivated virus vaccines. On August 31, 2022, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) also approved the bivalent mRNA COVID-19 vaccine booster, which contains the original SARS- CoV-2 strain used in the monovalent vaccines and the newer variants of SARS-CoV-2: Omicron BA. and BA.5.67

The BNT162b2 (Pfizer) mRNA vaccine was 95% effective (95% CI, 90.3 to 97.6), and the mRNA01273 (Moderna) vaccine was 94.1% effective (95% CI, 89.3 to 96.8) in preventing symptomatic COVID-19 infection following the second dose in phase III trials.68, The Ad26.COV2.S (Janssen/Johnson & Johnson) vaccine single-dose vaccine was 66.9% effective (95% CI, 59.0 to 73.4), and the ChAdOx1 nCoV-19/AZD1222 (University of Oxford, AstraZeneca, and the Serum Institute of India) vaccine was 70.4% effective

(95% CI, 54.8 to 80.6) following the second dose in phase III trials.70, SARS-CoV-2 vaccine immunogenicity can be measured by humoral IgG to spike protein or cellular T cell reactivity via interferon (IFN)-γ response to SARS-CoV-2 peptide.68, We still do not yet know how immunogenicity cutoffs correlate with efficacy, as no threshold of antibody or cell-mediated response has clearly been established as protective.

### Effect of DMARD Therapy on SARS CoV-2 Vaccine Efficacy

Early data in this setting are largely consistent with that from other vaccine studies. Data suggest that rituximab, glucocorticoids, MTX, abatacept, mycophenolate mofetil, and JAK inhibitors impair SARS-CoV-2 vaccine responses to varying extent in many patients. 72-77

The largest observational study to date evaluated the BNT162b2 (Pfizer) mRNA vaccine in 686 patients with rheumatic diseases. Compared with controls, in whom 100% seroconverted to vaccination (i.e., newly positive spike IgG), seroconversion was reduced among patients on rituximab (39%, P < .0001), mycophenolate mofetil (64%, P < .0001), abatacept (71%, P < .0001), JAK inhibitors (90%, P = .02), and MTX (92%, P = .02), while other DMARDs (leflunomide, hydroxychloroquine, TNF, IL-6, and IL-17 inhibitors) did not significantly affect seroconversion. Another prospective study of 133 patients with immune-mediated inflammatory diseases on various DMARD therapies and 53 controls vaccinated with mRNA vaccines found that rituximab significantly reduced mRNA vaccine immunogenicity, JAK inhibitors and MTX moderately reduced antibody titers, and other therapies (TNF, IL-12/23, and integrin inhibitors) had a modest impact on antibody formation.

Risk factors for a poor humoral response on rituximab include a shorter duration between rituximab dose and vaccine and lack of B-cell reconstitution.73, Rituximab-treated patients vaccinated 6 months after their last rituximab dose had seropositivity rates of only around 20%, and those vaccinated 1 year after the last rituximab dose had rates around 50%. Despite a reduced humoral response, early data suggest that at least a subset of rituximab-treated patients mount a cellular vaccine response similar to healthy controls, such that the net impact on clinical protection is not clear.

MTX appears to reduce some aspects of the SARS-CoV-2 vaccine response.74, One study found adequate humoral antibody titers (defined as IgG to spike protein >5000 units) compared with healthy controls. Patients on MTX, however, had reduced activated CD8+ T cells response but a preserved CD4+ T cell response. In another study, 84% of all MTXtreated patients and 92% of patients on MTX monotherapy seroconverted, compared with 100% of controls (P < .05). This is of increased significance in older individuals in whom MTX hold provides benefit in terms of improving immunogenicity to the COVID-19 vaccine.

TNF inhibitors appear to mildly reduce SARS-CoV-2 postvaccination titers but do not seem to significantly affect rates of seroconversion. Among 865 infliximab-treated inflammatory bowel disease patients, a single dose of the BNT162b2 mRNA vaccine or the ChAdOx1 nCoV-19 adenoviral vaccine was associated with lower antibody concentrations and seroconversion

rates compared with those on vedolizumab.74-76, There was no difference in the rate of seroconversion, however, in those studies after a second dose of the mRNA vaccine. Another study of patients on TNF inhibitors fully vaccinated with BNT162b2 mRNA vaccine showed no difference in seroconversion rates compared with healthy controls. Whether these reductions in quantitative humoral responses are of clinical significance is unknown.

JAK inhibitors likely reduce antibody titers and have a mild effect on seroconversion, although the clinical importance of these observations is unknown, and data are scant. Ten patients on JAK inhibitors in one study had a >6-fold reduction in titers compared with controls. However, in another study of 21 patients on JAK inhibitor monotherapy and 24 on JAK inhibitor combination therapy, 19 (90%) and 22 (92%), respectively, seroconverted, neither of which were significantly different from controls.

### Safety in Patients With Rheumatic Diseases

Because of its substantial immunogenicity, there is concern that the SARS-CoV-2 vaccine may induce flares in patients with inflammatory diseases. In a large multicenter study, there was no evidence of significant disease flare across different autoimmune inflammatory rheumatic diseases after receiving mRNA SARS-CoV-2 vaccine. Data from the EULAR Coronavirus Vaccine (COVAX) physician-reported registry also showed similar results with rare reports of disease flare after use of mRNA vaccines and AstraZeneca. Adverse effect concerns, however, have been supported by reports of thrombocytopenic purpura83-86 and myocarditis/pericarditis after vaccination.87-89 There have additionally been observational reports of new onset immune-mediated disease90 and/or disease flares after SARS-CoV-2 vaccination,90 which must be weighed against the risk of immune-mediated disease resulting from SARS-CoV-2 infection itself.76,

One study documented two fatalities post-vaccination: one ANCA-vasculitis patient developed cutaneous vasculitis with subsequent fatal sepsis 3 weeks after the second vaccine dose and the second had a history of cardiovascular disease and died of a myocardial infarction 2 months after the second vaccine dose. Other adverse events of note were two cases of uveitis, one case of pericarditis, six cases of herpes zoster, and one case of herpes labialis. Small prospective studies thus far have not found an increase in underlying inflammatory disease activity measures after SARS- CoV-2 vaccination.76,80' More prospective data are needed to understand the safety of these vaccines and risk of disease flare in patients with rheumatic diseases.

### Recommendations

The original ACR guidelines provided detailed recommendations for management of DMARD therapy in the setting of the SARS- CoV-2 vaccine. The 2022 updated ACR guidelines, however, excluded updated recommendations for COVID-19 due to the fast-growing pool of evidence and rapid changes in recommendations based on new data. With the latest bivalent COVID-19 booster, the CDC has updated the vaccine schedule for vaccine boosters in immunocompetent and immunosuppressed patients. These recommendations include that patients 12 years of age and older, after receiving the primary vaccine series, should receive one

bivalent mRNA booster. The new one-time bivalent booster dose replaces all prior monovalent mRNA booster vaccines for those 12 and older.

### Timing of COVID-19 Vaccine

The 2021 EULAR and ACR guidelines are in line regarding optimal timing of COVID-19 vaccine series, but the ACR offers much more detail. In general, for patients who have not initiated immunomodulatory therapy, COVID-19 vaccination should be given prior to initiation of therapy if possible due to impaired immune response with certain medications.

The following recommendations are based on the latest (version 5) ACR COVID-19 task force recommendations to help increase immune response to the COVID-19 vaccine primary series and boosters. Patients on intravenous (IV) abatacept should receive their vaccine 1 week prior to the next dose of IV treatment, while those on subcutaneous abatacept should hold their treatment (if disease activity allows) for one to two doses after receipt of a COVID-19 vaccine. Patients being treated with belimumab should hold therapy for 1 to 2 weeks after COVID-19 vaccination. IV cyclophosphamide should be timed a week after receipt of a COVID-19 vaccine when possible. Those on JAK inhibitors and mycophenolate should withhold therapy for 1 to 2 weeks after a COVID-19 vaccine if disease activity allows. No therapy interruption is needed in those on hydroxychloroquine and intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG). The task force failed to reach consensus on whether to temporarily disrupt the following therapies after receiving COVID-19 primary vaccination series and boosters: TNF inhibitors, IL-6 inhibitors, IL-1 inhibitors, IL-17 inhibitors, IL-12/23 inhibitors, and IL-23 inhibitors. The ACR task force also does not specify timing of COVID-19 vaccines for those on B cell-depleting therapy and recommends discussing optimal timing with their rheumatology provider.

An evidence-based vaccine guideline published in 2021 (nonsystematic review) recommended that any vaccine including COVID-19 vaccine be given at least 4 weeks before or 6 months after the administration of rituximab. If this is not achievable, then they recommend vaccination at time when immunoglobulin levels are normal. They also recommend COVID-19 vaccine during the inactive period of rheumatic diseases and while patient is on lower doses of corticosteroids. Based on data extrapolated from other vaccines, they recommend skipping 1 to 2 weekly doses of MTX after a COVID-19 vaccine to balance between effectiveness of the vaccine and avoiding disease exacerbation. Despite limited data showing that immunogenicity to the COVID-19 vaccine is not likely affected by TNF inhibitors, secukinumab, tocilizimab, IL-1 inhibitors, and abatacept, one group96 report that vaccination prior to the next scheduled dose with a plan to restart biologics after 14 days could allow time for antibody development. They also recommend holding tofacitinib prior to vaccination and resuming after 14 days.

### Hepatitis B Vaccination

### Background

There are three different single-antigen recombinant HBV vaccines available worldwide and several combination vaccines. However, the most common HBV vaccine is a yeast-derived single-antigen

vaccine. HBV vaccine immunogenicity is measured by anti-HBV surface antibody.

### Effect of DMARD Therapy on Vaccine Efficacy

TNF and IL-12/23 inhibitors reduce HBV vaccine immunogenicity, but most other immunosuppressive agents have not been extensively evaluated.98-100 TNF inhibitors decrease HBV vaccine immunogenicity, 98-100 but there may be differences between TNF inhibitors: lower antibody response rates for infliximab and higher response rates for etanercept. In a small study, ustekinumab was found to moderately reduce HBV response. In one trial, using high-dose HBV vaccine in DMARD-treated patients resulted in higher antibody response rates compared with a standard-dose vaccine, but this result did not reach statistical significance.

### Recommendations

In the United States HBV vaccination is recommended for adults at risk for HBV.101-104 Ideally patients who require HBV vaccination should be vaccinated prior to starting DMARD therapy, particularly for high-risk patients starting rituximab.

### Human Papilloma Virus Vaccination

### Background

Three HPV vaccines are approved; however, the 9-valent vaccine is the only HPV vaccine currently available in the United States. Women with rheumatic diseases on immunosuppressive therapies are at increased risk of HPV and cervical cancer, especially patients with SLE.106-111

### Effect of DMARD Therapy on Vaccine Efficacy

The effects of MTX and TNF inhibitors on HPV vaccine immunogenicity have been studied in patients with juvenile idiopathic arthritis, juvenile dermatomyositis, inflammatory bowel disease, and systemic lupus erythematosus. In these studies, MTX and TNF inhibitors did not affect vaccine sero- .112-115 SLE patients on mycophenolate mofetil conversion rates. combined with low-dose glucocorticoids moderately reduced seroconversion rates for HPV6 and HPV16 but not other subtypes of HPV vaccine. Other DMARDs have not been evaluated.

### Recommendations

The CDC recommends HPV vaccination for all patients (regardless of sex) at age 11 or 12 up through age 26.101 The ACIP recommends HPV vaccine for all ages 11 to 26 and in ages 26 to 45 based on shared decision making. The EULAR HPV vaccine recommendations align with those for the general population. The 2022 ACR guidelines conditionally recommend considering vaccination against HPV in those between ages 26 and 45 who are on immunosuppressive medications and not previously vaccinated. This recommendation was not specified to a certain sex, however.

### Tetanus Vaccination

### Background

The tetanus toxoid, reduced diphtheria toxoid, and acellular pertussis (Tdap) vaccine is a single-dose vaccine. Tetanus toxoid is a T celldependent antigen. Tetanus vaccine immunogenicity is typically measured by antitetanus toxoid IgG concentrations 4 weeks post-vaccination, where an antibody concentration of ≥0.10 IU/ mL is typically considered seroprotective; however, an endpoint of ≥4-fold increase in antibody concentration is also sometimes used.

### Effect of DMARD Therapy on Vaccine Efficacy

Rituximab reduces tetanus vaccine immunogenicity; however, the degree of effect differs in various studies.17, Studies of TNF inhibitors, JAK inhibitors, and abatacept suggest a modest impairment in immune response. .51, IL-6, IL-17, and IL-12/23 inhibitors have not been found to affect tetanus vaccine immunogenicity. 52,

Rituximab may have less of an effect on tetanus immunogenicity because of likely prior Tdap/DTaP vaccinations in most patients, leading to tetanus-specific memory B cells. In one study, RA patients on MTX monotherapy versus MTX + rituximab mounted similar humoral response. Another study, however, showed lower rates of protective antibody titers in patients on rituximab.

### Recommendations and Timing of Tdap Vaccine

Adults and adolescents should receive a Tdap followed by boosters of tetanus and diphtheria toxoids (Td) every 10 years or when indicated due to a wound, although a booster may be either Td or Tdap. Tetanus vaccination should ideally be done prior to starting rituximab therapy. The 2022 ACR guidelines recommend timing vaccination for when the next rituximab dose is due and then holding rituximab for 2 weeks after vaccination. No other changes in therapy schedule are recommended.

### Yellow Fever Vaccination

### Background

The YF vaccine is a live vaccine and recommended to immunocompetent persons who live or travel to endemic areas. 57, YF vaccine immunogenicity is measured by post-vaccination neutralizing antibody titers.

### Effect of DMARD Therapy on Vaccine Efficacy

Few studies have addressed yellow fever vaccine immunogenicity in immunocompromised patients given this is a live vaccine. In a Brazilian study involving 31 patients on biologics who were inadvertently revaccinated (patients had primary immunity from a prior vaccination), the patients had lower but adequate antibody titers. s. Another observational study of 17 patients on infliximab + MTX achieved satisfactory antibody levels in all but 1 patient.122a In another small study, all 15 patients on MTX achieved seroprotection. Patients on corticosteroids (mean, 7

mg/day; range, 5 to 20 mg/day), 18 of 34 of whom were vaccinenaive, had satisfactory vaccine titers.

### Yellow Fever Vaccine Safety in Patients With Rheumatic Diseases

Small studies suggest that the yellow fever vaccine may be safer than previously thought for patients on MTX, infliximab, and corticosteroids at <20 mg/day. 122,122a-124 A retrospective Swiss study of 92 patients on immunosuppressive medications who received the yellow fever vaccine (primary or booster) developed similar rates of side effects as healthy controls (controls had a similar proportion of patients with a primary YF vaccine history) and no serious adverse events. A prospective study of 15 patients on MTX (≤20 mg/week) receiving a primary YF vaccine found slightly increased rates of yellow fever RNA viremia in MTXtreated patients relative to controls (P > .39); however, these levels were never of clinical significance. In the earlier mentioned study from Brazil, patients revaccinated on biologics had no adverse events. In an observational study involving 17 RA patients who underwent yellow fever revaccination 1 month after infliximab, none developed yellow fever symptoms. 122a

### Recommendations

The 2022 ACR guidelines conditionally recommend against administration of live-attenuated virus vaccines to patients on csDMARDs, bDMARDs, and tsDMARDs. Exceptions are made for those on low-dose immunosuppression defined as methotrexate less than or equal to 0.4 mg/kg/week, azathioprine doses less than or equal to 3 mg/kg/day, prednisone less than 20 mg/day, or alternate-day glucocorticoids.

### Timing of Yellow Fever Vaccine

For travel considerations or for patients living in endemic areas at very high risk, patients and their providers may consider holding immunosuppressive therapy for vaccination. Direct evidence for optimal therapy hold time prior to live vaccines is missing, but the ACR guidelines recommend pre-vaccination hold time of 4 weeks for csDMARDs, one dosing interval for bDMARDs, and postvaccination hold time of 4 weeks for all DMARDs.

### Conclusions

Taken together, we note that for the majority of vaccine-preventable illnesses, DMARD dosing and vaccine schedules can proceed independent of one another. The notable exceptions are rituximab and methotrexate. To maximize immune response, patients should have as much time as possible since last rituximab dose (recommended to be given at next rituximab due date with delay of rituximab by 2 weeks) and methotrexate should be held 1 to 2 weeks after vaccination. Further research is necessary to clarify the benefits/risks of potentially holding other DMARDs for certain vaccinations. Specific evidence of Shingrix immunogenicity and efficacy in rheumatic diseases is currently missing, and understanding optimal ways of using this vaccine and others in the setting of various DMARD exposures continues to represent an unmet need in the field of rheumatology (Table 120.1).

### KEY POINTS

### Introduction

Amyloidosis is the term used to describe a heterogenous group of disorders characterized by protein misfolding and the extracellular deposition of previously soluble proteins as insoluble fibrils. In amyloid these fibrils associate with other components and accumulate, causing progressive disruption of tissue architecture and organ function. In all cases, the amyloid deposits have a remarkably uniform morphology of rigid elongated and nonbranching fibrils assembled on cross-β scaffolds, reinforced by steric zipper motifs that form a stable-β pleated-sheet configuration that can be visualized by near-atomic resolution studies. The diagnostic gold standard is Congo red staining of the tissues, with the classic finding of apple-green birefringence under cross-polarized light (see Fig. 121.1). There are also a number of nonfibrillary components shared by all types of amyloid deposits including glycoproteins of the heparin and dermatan sulfate groups, serum amyloid P (SAP) component,

apolipoprotein E and A4, laminin, and collagen IV. The formation of amyloid under favorable conditions in vitro appears to be an almost universal property of proteins, but there are only a limited number that form amyloid fibrils in vivo. All of these either contain areas of β-structure within their normal folded state (such as β-2 microglobulin, immunoglobulin light chains, and transthyretin) or are able to undergo α-helix conformation change to a β sheet formation (such as apolipoproteins including serum amyloid A [SAA] protein). The likelihood of these native proteins aggregating as amyloid is also influenced by the concentration of the protein (such as in chronic inflammatory conditions and AA amyloidosis and monoclonal gammopathy and AL amyloidosis), the protein's intrinsic tendency to assume a pathologic conformation (e.g., in wild type, or ATTR, amyloidosis), or the presence of a mutation that results in a pathologically less stable form of a protein (such as in hereditary systemic amyloidosis). More than 30 different precursor proteins form amyloid in humans, of which 13 can cause systemic amyloidosis. Amyloid fibrils deposit within the tissues and can be associated with a typical pattern of distribution within the organs, for example, fibrinogen A α chain predominately aggregates within the renal glomeruli6 and β2-microglobulin in the joints,7 although the molecular factors underlying this organ trophism remain poorly understood.

Amyloidosis can be classified in a variety of ways, based on the underlying precursor protein (the basis of internationally defined nomenclature°) or the underlying cause for protein production (hereditary or acquired), and also by the extent of amyloid deposition (localized or systemic) (see Table 121.1). Some types of amyloidosis appear to be diminishing, particularly AA amyloidosis and dialysis-related β2 microglobulin (Aβ2M) amyloidosis, which affects patients on renal replacement therapy. In both cases this reflects improvements in medical care.

This chapter focuses on reactive AA amyloidosis, a form of acquired systemic amyloidosis, given the close connection of this condition with underlying rheumatological disorders. Other types of amyloidosis are discussed as they are important differential diagnoses and can result in musculoskeletal complications of relevance to rheumatology.

### Diagnosis of Amyloidosis

A diagnosis of amyloidosis can be an unexpected finding on biopsy of an affected site, for example, laryngeal amyloid on biopsy of the larynx to investigate the cause of hoarseness, or due to clinical suspicion about underlying amyloidosis, for example, due to proteinuria in a patient without overt underling cause of renal dysfunction (see Fig. 121.2). In both scenarios, histology is the gold standard for the diagnosis of amyloidosis, with the demonstration of the presence of amyloid deposits by apple green birefringence when the tissue biopsy is stained with the aniline dye Congo red and viewed under cross-polarized light

(see Fig. 121.1). A negative result does not necessarily rule out amyloidosis, as amyloid deposits may be patchy. The sensitivity of Congo red staining is dependent on an adequate amount of amyloid, correct processing of the tissue, and adequate observer experience. A diagnosis of amyloidosis is not sufficient; the amyloid deposits must be subtyped to identify the underlying precursor protein and categorize the type of amyloidosis, which, in turn, influences treatment decisions (see Fig. 121.2). Tandem mass spectrometry may be required in cases where immunohistochemistry is nondiagnostic.

As AA amyloidosis commonly presents with proteinuria, the most commonly biopsied organ is the kidneys. Increased awareness and earlier suspicion about the possibility of amyloidosis may facilitate increased uptake of less invasive screening biopsies such as a rectal biopsy or fine needle aspiration of subcutaneous fat, an underutilized diagnostic test that carries a sensitivity of approximately 75%.

### AA Amyloidosis

AA amyloidosis occurs as a complication of chronic inflammation, and most patients present with proteinuric renal disease. In AA amyloidosis the amyloid precursor protein is the SAA protein, which is a normal serum component. SAA, like C-reactive protein (CRP), is both evolutionarily highly conserved and the most dynamic of the hepatic acute-phase response proteins, suggesting that it plays vital roles in inflammation and innate immunity. SAA is synthesized predominately by hepatocytes but also by macrophages, smooth muscle cells, adipocytes, and endothelial cells in response to pro-inflammatory cytokines, particularly TNF, interleukin (IL)-1, and IL-6. In healthy individuals, the median

plasma concentration of SAA is 3 mg/L with levels exceeding 2000 mg/L in an acute-phase response. In normal circumstances, SAA is taken up by macrophages, transported to the lysosomal compartment, and subsequently degraded. In patients with amyloidosis, this pathway is disrupted, and SAA monomers undergo proteolytic cleavage to form AA fibrils that deposit within the tissues. Glycosaminoglycans, SAP, and lipid components subsequently bind to the fibrils, conferring resistance to proteolysis and allowing the propagation of the characteristic β pleated-sheet 14 structure.

### Epidemiology of AA Amyloidosis

### Incidence

AA amyloidosis was the third most common type of systemic amyloidosis seen in the UK (after AL and Aβ2M) and was responsible for approximately 10% of new cases seen each year in the 20th century, with an estimated incidence of one to two cases per million person-years. This has decreased, most likely reflecting improved treatments for chronic infection and inflammation, particularly improved access to effective anti-inflammatory medications. In the UK, AA amyloidosis is now less than 2% of new diagnoses. A huge variety of underlying chronic inflammatory

diseases are complicated by AA amyloidosis (see Table 121.2). The distribution of underlying diseases varies with geographic region and has changed over time. For example, the incidence of AA amyloidosis in patients with familial Mediterranean fever (FMF) is largely dependent on colchicine usage but also varies depending on the geographic location of the patient and is more common in patients from Israel and Armenia and in those with Armenian ancestry,18 with evidence of more severe FMF disease in Turkey than in Germany.

The median latency between onset of inflammation and diagnosis of amyloid is approximately 17 years; however, the development of AA amyloidosis can occur as soon as 12 months, largely dependent on the degree of that inflammation. AA amyloidosis can occur at any age, and it is the major form of amyloidosis that can be seen in childhood.

### Risk Factors and d Underlying Conditions Associated With AA Amyloidosis

Any condition associated with sustained inflammation can be complicated by AA amyloidosis, including chronic infections (such as tuberculosis) and malignant neoplasms (see Table 121.1). The inflammatory arthritides were the most common cause of AA amyloidosis in the developed world, with up to 5% of patients developing the condition; however, the monogenic periodic fever syndromes,

such as FMF, carry the highest risk of AA amyloidosis; more than 60% of patients with untreated FMF develop AA amyloidosis, and amyloid complicates the TNF receptor-1 (TNFSF1A)—associated periodic syndrome (TRAPS) and the cryopyrin-associated periodic syndromes in 25% of untreated cases. As treatments for chronic inflammation are improving, the origin of AA amyloidosis has shifted away from the inflammatory arthritides toward other causes of chronic inflammation. Obesity is increasingly recognized as a potential cause. In approximately 28% of AA patients, no obvious underlying inflammatory cause can be found.15, In such patients, an undiagnosed periodic fever syndrome or cytokine-secreting Castleman's disease located in the mediastinum or gut mesentery should be considered, before the patient is labeled as having an unidentifiable cause for their AA amyloidosis.

In rheumatoid and idiopathic arthritis, the risk of developing AA amyloidosis is linked to the duration of disease activity, 24

but not all patients with long-standing inflammation go on to develop it. Likewise, in FMF, development of AA amyloidosis is related to severity of disease but not in all patients, suggesting that there are additional genetic, disease, and environmental related risk factors.

MMPs are present in AA amyloid deposits and degrade SAA and AA fibrils in vitro. Some inherited autoinflammatory conditions carry a very high risk of AA amyloidosis. FMF is predominately an autosomal recessively inherited condition, although heterozygotes can cause the condition. Homozygosity for the M694V genotype is well established as a risk for the development of FMF31; a total of 314 variants of the MEFV gene have been identified; however, five mutations— M680I, M694V, M694I, and V726A—on exon 10 and E148Q on exon two, account for more than 85% of cases. Mutations at position M680 and M694 are associated with earlier-onset FMF, more severe disease, and an increased likelihood of AA amyloidosis.

TRAPS is predominately inherited. Again, a large number of variants of the TNFRSF1 gene have been identified. Mutations affecting cysteine residues were accompanied by a higher risk for amyloid than noncystine mutations, although later papers did not reproduce this.35, In both monogenic periodic fever syndromes, country of origin is thought to confer a greater risk of AA amyloidosis suggesting that environmental factors and ethnicity also contribute.

### Clinical Features of AA Amyloidosis

The earliest clinical feature of AA amyloidosis is usually proteinuria (see Fig. 121.3). Peripheral edema frequently prompts investigation and more than 90% of patients have nonselective proteinuria due to glomerular amyloid deposition. Hematuria rarely occurs. Nephrotic syndrome is seen in more than 50% of patients. Renal impairment is common, with approximately 10%

of patients presenting with end-stage renal disease. The second most common presentation is organ enlargement, such as hepatosplenomegaly or thyromegaly. Splenic involvement is seen on SAP scintigraphy almost without exception, suggesting that the spleen is the first organ to be involved, although this is usually asymptomatic. Splenic rupture can occur but is extremely rare. Approximately 10% of patients have hepatomegaly evident on examination at presentation but on SAP scintigraphy up to 23% of patients have liver involvement. Elevation of serum alkaline phosphatase is seen in 5% of patients; however, this is nonspecific and may not necessarily indicate hepatic amyloid deposition. Elevation of bilirubin or serum transaminases is seldom reported and liver failure is exceptionally rare. Other, commonly involved organs include the gastrointestinal tract (GI) and adrenal glands. GI dysfunction is common in advanced disease, presenting predominately with diarrhea and occasional bleeding. Adrenal uptake is often seen on SAP scintigraphy, but few patients have adrenal insufficiency. Cardiac and neuropathic involvement are both extremely rare in AA and are features of very advanced disease.

### Other Important Types of Systemic Amyloidosis

This next section considers other types of amyloidosis of interest to the rheumatologist. Given the often similar and overlapping presentation (see Table 121.3), confident classification of patients clinically is often impossible, and immunohistochemistry should be performed on biopsy material to accurately subtype patients' amyloid.

### Systemic Light Chain Amyloidosis

Systemic light chain (AL) amyloidosis is the most serious and most commonly diagnosed form of amyloidosis, accounting for 60% of new referrals to the UK center, with an estimated incidence of 5 to 12 people per million person-years and with a median survival of only 12 months if left untreated. The condition is a complication of an

underlying B cell clone that produces immunoglobulin light chains. AL amyloidosis can therefore complicate any of the plasma cell dyscrasias including 15% of all cases of multiple myeloma, the lymphoplasmacytic lymphoproliferative disorders, and ~5% of all cases of monoclonal gammopathies. The light chains produced by the amyloidogenic clone may be affected by proteolytic cleavage, or mutations within the variable domain, affecting key structural sites resulting in the production of unstable light chains10; misfolding and aggregation of the unstable light chains subsequently results in amyloid fibril formation. The mechanism of how the amyloid fibrils cause organ dysfunction remains unclear, but disruption of the tissue architecture and direct toxicity of the pre-fibril oligomers are thought to contribute.

All organs, except for the central nervous system, can be affected by AL amyloid fibril deposition, and the clinical features of AL amyloidosis depend largely on the pattern of involvement. The most commonly affected organs are the heart (approximately 70% to 80%) and kidneys (approximately 60%). Cardiac involvement in AL amyloidosis is the critical determinant of prognosis and causes heart failure with preserved ejection fraction.42, Renal involvement manifests as in AA amyloidosis, with proteinuria that may evolve into nephrotic syndrome and renal failure. The pathognomonic signs of AL amyloidosis are soft tissue involvement, which includes macroglossia, periorbital purpura, and submandibular thickening. Peripheral nerve involvement is seen in approximately 15% of patients and is characterized by an initial painful length-dependent sensory polyneuropathy. Carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS) is seen in ~20% of patients. Involvement of the autonomic nervous system results in symptoms of postural hypotension, bowel disturbance, or erectile dysfunction. Motor deficits can occur as a consequence of progressive peripheral nerve involvement with AL amyloidosis or by direct amyloid infiltration of the muscles46; muscle involvement carries a median survival of 12 months, suggesting that myopathy in AL amyloidosis is both rare and a poor prognostic feature. Arthropathy can occur in AL amyloidosis due to amyloid deposits in the synovium. Patients present with a subacute but progressive, symmetric arthropathy that predominately affects the shoulders, knees, wrists, and small joints of the hands more than the elbows and hips. The lack of morning stiffness and only mild tenderness on examination of the joints helps distinguish amyloid-related arthropathy from rheumatoid arthritis, but amyloid nodules can confuse the diagnosis, which occur as whitish subcutaneous nodules. Amyloidosis should also be considered as a differential in patients presenting with jaw claudication,50 or sicca syndrome. Localized cutaneous and nodular pulmonary AL amyloidosis can complicate Sjögren's sydrome.

In more than 90% of cases of AL amyloidosis, a circulating monoclonal paraprotein or an excess of serum free light chains will be found in the serum or urine. Referral to a hematologist should be made at this stage for consideration of a bone marrow to identify and quantify any underlying B cell clone and referral to a specialist center is recommended to establish the extent and pattern of organ involvement (see Fig. 121.2). Treatment is chemotherapy targeted at this clonal B cell population, which in the majority of cases is an anti-myeloma-based regimen.

### β2 Microglobulin Amyloidosis

β2 microglobulin amyloidosis is a condition that occurs in patients with long-standing ESRF. Renal insufficiency results in high circulating plasma levels of β2 microglobulin, which are not sufficiently cleared by dialysis. Prolonged elevation of β2 microglobulin predisposes to deposition of β2 microglobulin amyloid deposits. After 3 years of commencing hemodialysis, it is estimated that 20% to

30% of patients will have developed β2 microglobulin amyloid deposits. The condition is diminishing in frequency,7,54 but the dominant osteoarticular deposition of the β2 microglobulin fibrils mean that this condition is important for a rheumatologist to be aware of. The condition manifests with CTS, pain and stiffness of the large joints, bone cysts, and pathologic fractures. Extra-articular amyloid deposition can occur, largely within the spleen. There is no treatment except restoration of normal renal tubular function by renal transplantation, but improved dialysis techniques have significantly reduced the incidence of this type of amyloidosis.7,55

### Wild-Type Transthyretin Amyloidosis

Wild-type transthyretin amyloidosis (ATTR), formerly termed "senile systemic amyloidosis," is an increasingly diagnosed cause (C of heart failure with preserved ejection fraction predominately in elderly men. Deposition of transthyretin can occur in the walls of the heart, smooth and striated muscle, fat tissue, renal papillae, and alveolar walls, but the spleen and renal glomeruli are rarely affected. The clinical manifestations of ATTR are predominately due to the cardiac deposition, but 48% of patients at our center have a history of carpal tunnel decompression,58 demonstrating that a significant proportion of ATTR patients also have CTS59 and spinal stenosis60 and so may present to the rheumatologist. Conversely, evidence of amyloidosis was found in the tenosynovium of 29% of men age 50 and older and women 60 years and older who underwent surgical carpal tunnel release, with 80% of cases deriving from wild-type TTR, highlighting the opportunity for rheumatologists to detect TTR amyloid early. As novel treatments become available, this may become an important opportunity for early intervention.

### Hereditary Amyloidosis

Hereditary systemic amyloidosis, in some types also known as familial amyloid polyneuropathy, is an autosomal dominant inherited condition characterized by features including progressive peripheral and autonomic neuropathy in addition to involvement of other visceral organs, which can include the heart and kidneys. Mutations in at least nine genes can cause the condition,63 but penetrance is variable and so it is often difficult to reliably predict the clinical phenotype based on the underlying mutation. The types of hereditary amyloidosis of interest to a rheumatologist include those that cause proteinuria (and so are a differential to AA amyloidosis), which includes fibrinogen α chain, AApoA1, AApoAIV, and gelsolin. Gelsolin amyloidosis is also of interest to the rheumatologist given the skin and connective tissue manifestations of this condition that could be mistaken for other rheumatological disorders. Gelsolin is a cytoplasmic protein that binds actin. The gelsolin variant is characterized by asparagine substituted for aspartic acid. Patients present with corneal lattice dystrophy, cranial neuropathy, and distal peripheral neuropathy.

Finally, other rare hereditary diseases that can cause amyloidosis that may present with a myopathy include mutations in dysferlin and anoctamin 5, which are both recessively inherited and result in limb girdle muscular dystrophy type 2B and 2L respectively. 56,67

### Diagnostic Tests for AA Amyloidosis

The diagnosis of AA amyloidosis, as with all types of amyloidosis, relies on histologic proof of the presence of amyloid deposits.

Once histology and immunohistochemistry have confirmed a diagnosis of AA amyloidosis, the next steps are to establish the extent of organ involvement.

### Imaging, Including SAP S Scintigraphy

SAP scintigraphy is a noninvasive method used to establish the presence, distribution, and extent of amyloid deposits within the visceral organs. SAP is a nonfibrillary component of all amyloid deposits, and so the scan is useful for all types. Radio-labeled SAP (123I-SAP) is intravenously injected and reversibly binds to amyloid deposits in proportion to the quantity present. The dose of radioactivity is small (8090 MBq for a 6-hour scan, 120190 MBq for a 24-hour scan), allowing serial scans to be performed that can monitor the progression or regression of amyloid deposits over time.

The scan is useful in detecting deposits within the liver, spleen, adrenal glands, bones, and kidneys (see Fig. 121.4) (except when patients reach ESRF when the lack of blood flow reduces the uptake of tracer). The resolution of SAP scintigraphy is insufficient to reliably identify deposits within the GI tract. Skin, nerves, and the heart and lungs are also not reliably evaluated due to the blood pool.

Cardiac amyloidosis is instead evaluated by a combination of electrocardiogram (ECG), imaging, and cardiac biomarkers. The ECG may be normal, but in advanced cardiac involvement small voltages are seen as well as pathologic Q waves (pseudoinfarct pattern) (see Fig. 121.5). A mean left-ventricular wall thickness of >12 mm on two-dimensional Doppler echocardiogram, in the absence of hypertension or other causes of left-ventricular hypertrophy, suggests cardiac involvement. Cardiac magnetic

resonance imaging (MRI) is recognized as a useful tool in detecting patients with early cardiac involvement with the finding of subendocardium late gadolinium enhancement70; however, AA patients often have renal impairment, and cardiac MRI is relatively contraindicated with an estimated glomerular filtration rate of <30 mls/min. In addition, the cardiac appearances associated with uremia are often difficult to distinguish from cardiac amyloidosis, even by cardiac MRI. The cardiac biomarkers, N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide and troponin T, are also not a reliable indicator of cardiac involvement in the setting of ESRD and so Mayo staging scoring systems, validated for AL amyloidosis patients, do not apply in the setting of AA amyloidosis. However, cardiac involvement in AA amyloidosis is rare.

### Treatment of AA Amyloidosis

### Principles of Treatment

The principle of treatment of all types of amyloidosis aims to halt, or slow, the production of new amyloid deposits to less than the rate of clearance of amyloid deposits while supporting organ function. In AL amyloidosis, this involves chemotherapy targeted at the underlying plasma cell clone, whereas in AA amyloidosis, treatment is targeted at the underlying inflammatory condition.

In the treatment of AA amyloidosis, disease activity and response to treatment is assessed by serial SAA measurements (where available), or CRP concentrations, given the strong correlation between both readings in most cases71; it is advised that simultaneous measurements of SAA and CRP are taken to establish if CRP can be reliably used as a surrogate marker for disease activity. The aim is biochemical normalization of SAA/CRP levels.

### General Supportive Management Including Renal Transplantation

The kidney is the major affected organ in AA amyloidosis, and so general measures should be directed at preserving renal function; this includes the avoidance of nephrotoxic drugs and hypoor hypertension (see Table 121.4). Patients are often nephrotic and, provided their blood pressure is maintained, a negative sodium balance should be aimed for; directing patients to restrict their fluid intake to 1.5 liters and limiting their sodium intake to 3 g per day. Loop diuretics may be required in high doses. Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors can help reduce proteinuria and have been found to reduce the risk of progression to ESRD. Anti-coagulation in nephrotic syndrome should be considered in heavy proteinuria given the risk of thrombosis. Approximately 40% of patients with AA amyloidosis will require renal replacement therapy (RRT), with a median time to dialysis of 78 months. Survival on dialysis is variable and may be related to the underlying disease and control of SAA levels. Peritoneal dialysis has a higher risk of infection and hypoalbuminemia, which is known to be predictive of mortality.

### Systemic Treatment

Systemic treatment needs to be targeted at the underlying inflammatory disorder (see Table 121.2). There are no agents that have specific benefit in AA amyloidosis. In all drugs, their effect is due to their efficacy in controlling the underlying chronic inflammation and suppressing SAA levels. Thus the choice of agent is
