In FMF, colchicine is widely used as prophylaxis against the development of AA amyloidosis at a dose of 0.6 to 1.2 mg/day. Long-term use of colchicine should be used for all FMF patients with AA amyloidosis; however, it has no role in an acute attack. The low doses required are generally well tolerated, aside from diarrhea, which is helped by a lactose-free diet. The drug is also safe to use throughout pregnancy and with breastfeeding. Colchicine treatment is sometimes trialed in AA amyloidosis patients with an unknown underlying etiology with monitoring of SAA levels. Cytotoxic agents, such as methotrexate and azathioprine, are useful in controlling the inflammation in rheumatic disorders, such as rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, and ankylosing spondylitis, reducing the risk of developing amyloidosis; however, the majority of published evidence has focused on the biologic agents with activity against the pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1, TNF, IL-6). There has been experience with use of the anti-IL-6 receptor antibody, tocilizumab, in the treatment of AA amyloidosis, with evidence for its efficacy over TNF antagonists in the reduction of SAA levels. There is limited available evidence for the use of other biologic agents, such as rituximab and abatacept; this may be in part due to their lack of direct anti-cytokine activity.76, Anti-cytokine therapy also has a role for the hereditary autoinflammatory conditions. Most experience to date has been with either recombinant IL-1 receptor antagonists or monoclonal antibodies against IL-1β, in both attenuating the underlying disease activity and the associated amyloidosis. There are reports of success with tocilizumab (IL-6 receptor blockade) for patients with amyloidosis complicating FMF and TRAPS,79 but the anti- TNF agents appear to be less effective in this setting.

### Renal Transplantation

Renal transplantation in AA amyloidosis offers improved quality of life and should be considered for patients whose underlying disease is controlled, reflected by sustained control of their SAA levels. Excellent 5and 10-year graft survival rates have been reported at 74% and 68%, respectively, which is comparable to control patients. Patient survival is, however, reduced in AA amyloidosis patients compared with controls at 5 years (82.5% vs. 94.2%) and 10 years (61.7% vs 83.4%), respectively. Although amyloid deposition in the graft is recognized,82 with a recurrence rate as high as 14%,81 most patients have a functioning graft until death, suggesting that factors other than graft failure or recurrence of renal amyloidosis are contributing to the increased mortality; such factors include sepsis and acute cardiovascular events, and so an in-depth cardiac assessment is advisable as part of the renal transplant workup process.

### Novel Treatments

Significant advances have been made in understanding the pathogenesis of amyloid deposition, which has facilitated the development of novel treatments that focus on the production of amyloid or clearance of amyloid deposits from the tissues. Eprodisate (1,3-propanedisulfonate), a drug developed to bind to the glycosaminoglycan binding sites on SAA and inhibit the formation of the glycosaminoglycan-amyloid fibril aggregate, offered potential as a targeted therapy in AA amyloidosis but unfortunately failed to reduce progression to ESRF or death compared with current active therapy in a phase 3 trial.

An alternative approach has been to deplete the plasma of SAP with small palindromic drugs such as R-1-[6-[R-2-carboxy-pyrrolidin-1-yl]-6-oxo-hexanoyl] pyrrolidine-2-carboxylic acid, 84 an effect that can be augmented by the use of anti-SAP antibodies to accelerate the clearance of amyloid deposits. .

In the future, silencing RNA and anti-sense oligonucleotides may be useful. There is proof of principal data from trials in data from ATTR,86,87 and clearly there is a possibility of using similar approaches to knock down hepatic production of SAA. This might be particularly beneficial in patients with AA amyloidosis of unknown cause, in those whose underlying inflammation has proved refractory to treatment, or those who cannot tolerate longterm immunosuppression due to infections.

### Outcomes

The overall outcome for patients with AA amyloidosis has improved largely due to better access to systemic anti-inflammatories and earlier detection. In 2007 a review of 373 cases of AA amyloidosis reported a median survival of 133 months from diagnosis (~11 years). Amyloid regression is seen in patients with well-controlled inflammatory levels, with evidence of amyloid regression on SAP scintigraphy with a corresponding improvement in both the degree of proteinuria and renal function. The recovery of organ function is associated with excellent long-term survival outcomes. Untreated AA amyloidosis is, however, still associated with significant mortality. Patients with persistently elevated SAA levels are at greater risk, with a reported ~18-fold increased risk of death.

### Conclusion

The amyloidoses that are of interest to rheumatologists are the AA type, which is a feared complication of diseases managed by the specialty, including chronic inflammatory arthritides, vasculitis, and the rare systemic autoinflammatory diseases. In addition, other types of amyloidosis can present to rheumatologists due to musculoskeletal complications, CTS, and spinal stenosis, which may lead to a diagnosis of amyloidosis and may require management by other specialties, such as hematology.

AA amyloidosis can complicate any chronic inflammatory condition. Patients present with proteinuria and a diagnosis relies on histologic confirmation of amyloid deposits within the affected tissue, usually with a renal biopsy. Imaging is useful to confirm the presence, distribution, and extent of amyloid deposits. Treatment is targeted at tight control of the underlying inflammatory disorder with systemic anti-inflammatory agents to reduce circulating SAA and CRP levels and reduce the risk of further amyloid deposition. Avoidance of further nephrotoxic insults during systemic treatment is crucial to preserve renal function and delay progression to ESRF. ESRF develops in up to 40% of patients with AA amyloidosis and hemodialysis may be a preferable mode of RRT given the lower risk of infection. Renal transplantation is an option but carries a ~14% risk of amyloid recurrence, although graft survival rates are good. Future therapies rely on reducing hepatic production of fibril precursors, targeting SAP, accelerating clearance, and preventing further amyloid fibril production, which hold promise for the future.

### KEY POINTS

### Introduction

Sarcoidosis is an orphan, systemic, and clinically heterogeneous disorder. Its cause has yet to be identified, but environmental, genetic, and infectious causes have been suggested. The hallmark of sarcoidosis is the development and accumulation of noncaseating granulomas in any organ system. Organ system involvement, which is unpredictable and varies between patients, is the primary determinant of morbidity and mortality in sarcoidosis. Any organ system can be involved, with the lungs affected in more than 90% of cases. Lymphatic, skin, and ocular findings are also common. Given the variability of sarcoidosis manifestations, diagnosing this disorder is often difficult. Patients may be asymptomatic or may present with a range of nonspecific symptoms. Occasionally, specific symptoms such as cough, dyspnea, burning of eyes, or a rash may suggest the diagnosis. When extrapulmonary symptoms develop, they sometimes result in rheumatologic manifestations, including but not limited to arthritis, skin lesions, or neuropathy. Rheumatologists frequently meet sarcoidosis patients when the presentation is atypical, when multiple organs are affected, or when a differential diagnosis must be clarified.

### Classification Criteria

No classification criteria for sarcoidosis have been prepared by the American College of Rheumatology or the European Alliance of

Associations for Rheumatology. However, the American Thoracic Society (ATS), the European Respiratory Society, and the World Association of Sarcoidosis and Other Granulomatous Disorders suggest a diagnosis of sarcoidosis with the following fulfilled criteria: (1) a compatible clinical picture, (2) histologic demonstration of noncaseating granulomas, and (3) exclusion of other diseases capable of producing a similar clinical picture. The ATS has published updated recommendations for diagnosing and detecting sarcoidosis.

### Epidemiology

Sarcoidosis is a global disease. The worldwide prevalence and incidence of sarcoidosis have been difficult to calculate because of its clinical heterogeneity and variable diagnostic criteria in different countries. In Northern Europe, up to 40 cases per 100,000 people have been reported,4,5 whereas in a study from Eastern Europe, only 3.68 cases of sarcoidosis per 100,000 people were found. The incidence of sarcoidosis in Japan is also low, with one study estimating it to be 3.7 cases per 100,000 individuals. Within countries, incidence rates may vary between races. In the United States the annual incidence of sarcoidosis is more than three times higher in black people (35.5 per 100,000) than in white people (10.9 per 100,000). Furthermore, the disease course is more progressive, with higher mortality in African Americans.9, Despite numerous epidemiologic studies of sarcoidosis, many clinicians and researchers believe that prevalence and incidence estimates are lower than actual disease rates because of inaccurate diagnoses or asymptomatic cases that are never diagnosed.

Although sarcoidosis affects men and women of all ages and from diverse ethnic backgrounds,5,12 some disparities have been noted. More women than men have been reported in studies worldwide; estimates indicate that 57% of patients with sarcoidosis are women. Relative to men, women with sarcoidosis have more ocular and neurologic manifestations. People of any age may develop the disease, but the median age of onset is around 40 years. A second peak of incidence occurs at around age 65 years, especially in women.9,13

### Etiology

The exact cause of sarcoidosis remains elusive. Multiple etiologic factors have been identified. The heterogeneity of the disease suggests that multiple causative agents may be responsible for the variable disease manifestations of sarcoidosis. Given the immunopathogenic mechanisms that underlie sarcoidosis, such a

disease trigger might be antigen-driven T cellmediated adaptive immunity that stimulates the cascade of events leading to granuloma formation. Because the lungs are affected in more than 90% of sarcoidosis cases, likely an environmental agent (including an infectious agent, potentially exposed via aerogenic routes) contributes to the onset of sarcoidosis.

Both inorganic and organic environmental factors with antigenic capabilities have been implicated in pathogenesis. Early studies on the causes of sarcoidosis suggested a link between sarcoidosis and agents associated with a rural lifestyle, such as the lumber industry and burning wood.14, A case-control etiologic study of sarcoidosis (ACCESS) found that burning agricultural debris and wood is mainly associated with pulmonary sarcoidosis but not systemic sarcoidosis. In a different analysis of the ACCESS trial, radiation, insecticides, mildew, and mold were environmental factors associated with the systemic sarcoidosis phenotype. More recently, a sarcoidosis-like phenotype presented in fire department rescue workers involved in the World Trade Center attack. These findings may indicate that each sarcoidosis subtype may have distinct inducing factors.

Because of clinical and histologic similarities, numerous methods have been used to look for an infectious agent as a cause of sarcoidosis, with most studies focusing on Mycobacterium tuberculosis or Propionibacterium acnes. When in situ hybridization was used, M. tuberculosis catalase-peroxidase protein (mKatG) was found in nearly 40% of tissue samples from patients with sarcoidosis. Recombinant mKatG protein was then used to study patients with sarcoidosis and measure mKatG antibodies, which were present in 50% of the patients studied. Other investigators have found evidence of an immunologic reaction to additional mycobacterial antigens such as ESAT-6.20, P. acnes has been found more frequently in granulomas from patients with sarcoidosis but also can be found in people without sarcoidosis. Thus its primary role in pathogenesis remains unclear.22-25 These studies suggest that sarcoidosis may represent overexposure of the patient to a commonly encountered microorganism associated with a dysregulated immune response. Because several types of bacteria have been associated with sarcoidosis, some clinicians have attempted to use antibiotics or antimycobacterial agents to manage the disease. Although skin sarcoidosis has occasionally responded to these ,26,27 their usefulness in treating other forms of sarcoidtreatments, osis appears minimal.22, In addition, serum amyloid A (SAA) accumulates in granulomas due to the hyperimmune T helper (Th) 1 cell response necessary for killing the infecting agent. This mechanism could explain the ongoing chronic granulomatous inflammation in many sarcoidosis patients. Furthermore, blood levels of SAA correlate with the disease stage and thus could serve as a biomarker or therapeutic target.

### Genetics

Compelling studies of familial clustering and the incidence of sarcoidosis among different racial groups indicate that genetic factors influence susceptibility. In the ACCESS study, first-degree relatives had a fivefold increased risk of developing the disease. Associations have been found between the risk of sarcoidosis and class I and II human leukocyte antigen (HLA) gene products, which have essential roles in antigen presentation. It is considered likely that a susceptibility locus for sarcoidosis exists within the HLA gene region, as is the case with other autoimmune diseases and cancers, such as Hodgkin's lymphoma. An intriguing analysis of data from the ACCESS study identified associations between

genetic factors (HLA alleles), environmental factors, and sarcoidosis phenotypes. A compelling argument can be made for a genetic factor predisposing individuals to disease and a subsequent environmental exposure that triggers the onset of sarcoidosis per se. Specifically, investigators found that HLA-DRB1*1101 and insecticide exposure at work are significantly associated with cardiac sarcoidosis and hypercalcemia. A similar relationship between HLA-DRB1*1101, mold and musty odors, and pulmonary sarcoidosis was described.

Specific HLA alleles are protective or associated with increased susceptibility or disease phenotypes. In Caucasian populations, HLA-DRB1*01 and HLA-DRB1*04 were protective against the disease, whereas HLA-DRB1*03, *11, *12, *14, and *15 were risk factors for sarcoidosis. Interestingly, HLA-DRB1*11 was found to be related to the presentation of the mycobacterial antigens ESAT-6 and mKatG, thus providing a possible mechanistic link between genetic background and reaction to a pathogen.

Moreover, HLA-DRB1*03 was associated with spontaneous resolution, whereas HLA-DRB1*14 and HLA-DRB1*15 were associated with a chronic course of the disease. In European patients with Löfgren's syndrome (LS), which is an acute form of sarcoidosis characterized by bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy (BHL), fever, erythema nodosum, and periarticular ankle inflammation, HLA-DRB1*03 is four times more common than in healthy individuals. It has been associated with a favorable prognosis. In one study, most DRB1*03+ patients experienced resolution of LS within 2 years after diagnosis. By contrast, nearly half of the patients without this allele had a chronic disease course. The mechanism underlying this difference in disease course remains unknown.

Genetic studies of non-HLA genes have been inconclusive. The two candidate genes most consistently associated with sarcoidosis are TNF and the interleukin (IL)-23 receptor (IL-23G). Other possible candidate genes have produced inconsistent results. The TNF G-308A polymorphism was found to be predictive of response to treatment with TNF inhibitors.

Analysis of gene-expression profiles to distinguish between tuberculosis and sarcoidosis has revealed similarities between the two diseases; however, matrix metallopeptidase 14 could be identified as the most distinctive marker for sarcoidosis. Ongoing genome-wide association studies seek to identify additional genes that may be linked to sarcoidosis onset and susceptibility. To date, these studies have identified several novel gene candidates. In particular, BTNL2, ANXA11, RAB23, OS9, CCDC88B, PRDX5, and NOTCH4 are potential loci for sarcoidosis susceptibility. Most of these genes play a role in the immune system, but their functional role has yet to be characterized.

More recently, epigenetic changes (such as DNA methylation) that influence gene expression without changing the primary nucleotide sequence have been identified as an essential mechanism in many diseases, such as cancer, kidney disease, and autoimmune diseases. Post-translational modification of gene expression by micro-RNAs (miRNAs) is different in sarcoidosis patients compared with controls. In this study, an miRNA profile identified by microarray analysis from patients and controls distinguished sarcoidosis from controls with a positive predictive value of 88%. In addition, the underexpression of specific miRNAs was associated with peripheral lymphopenia and airflow reductions, which are predictors of worse outcomes. Taken together, it is likely that sarcoidosis might be further subclassified in the future depending on the genetic backgrounds and their respective associations with distinct immunologic responses.

### Pathogenesis

Granuloma formation is a hallmark of sarcoidosis. The underlying immunologic events include (1) exposure to one or more (unknown) antigens, (2) activation of antigen-presenting cells (macrophages and dendritic cells), (3) a T cell response to eliminate the antigen, and (4) granuloma formation. Physiologically, granulomas act as shields, protecting tissues from pathogens and inflammatory reactions. Granulomas consist of a core of mononuclear phagocytes, such as epithelioid cells, multinucleated giant cells, and macrophages, which are encased by lymphocytes, including B cells, CD4+ T cells, and CD8+ T cells.

Granuloma formation occurs in stages: initiation, accumulation, effector phase, and resolution. After antigen exposure, macrophages detect antigens via pattern recognition receptors (e.g., Toll-like receptors [TLRs]) and internalize and process these antigens. In sarcoidosis, mainly TLR2 and TLR4 are involved. They then present these antigen(s) to the T cell receptor via HLA molecules. This step requires the presence of costimulatory molecules (such as CD80, CD83, and CD86) to determine the immune response (activation or inhibition). The butyrophilin-like 2 (BTNL2) gene may mediate one of these inhibitory signals. Locally activated naive CD4+ Th cells differentiate into activated CD4+ Th1-like cells during the accumulation phase, causing subsequent elevations in Thl-associated inflammatory mediators such as IL-2, interferon (IFN)-α, IFN-γ, monocyte chemotactic protein-1, macrophage inflammatory protein-1, and granulocytemacrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF). CD4+ Th cells also interact with antigen-presenting cells to initiate the development of granulomas and to preserve granulomas. Thus, T cells undergo oligoclonal proliferation in areas of immune system activity. At this point in the disease process, lymphocyte levels are typically increased at the sites of inflammation, but peripheral blood lymphopenia may occur due to sequestration. The ratio of CD4/CD8 cells becomes elevated in the lungs and other affected organs. During the effector phase, T cells and macrophages release mediators (IL-12, IL-15, IL-18, and TNF), which amplify the Th1-driven inflammatory response.

Macrophage-derived cytokines contribute to the external signaling milieu that favors the differentiation of CD4+ cells to Th1 cells.45, Ultimately, a feedback loop from a downstream-cytokine cascade induces macrophages to differentiate into epithelioid cells, which gain secretory capability, lose phagocytic capacity, and fuse to form multinucleated giant cells. These epithelioid cells form the cellular basis of granulomas. Th2 cells also contribute to granuloma formation. These cells synthesize fibronectin and C-C motif ligand 18 (CCL18). During resolution, the release of these mediators results in a positive feedback loop of CCL18-activated and macrophage-mediated collagen formation. Although granulomas spontaneously resolve without causing damage in most cases, this cycle leads to fibrosis in up to 25% of patients with sarcoidosis. As patients' fibrosis becomes more extensive, their prognosis worsens. Although the mechanisms responsible for granulomatous fibrosis have not been fully characterized, patterns of cytokine change (upregulation of transforming growth factor [TGF]-β) and Th2 cells may lead to an increased ratio of CD8 to CD4 cells. Fewer than 5% of patients die of sarcoidosis; fibrosis leading to respiratory failure contributes to many deaths. In recent years, other cell populations, such as regulatory T cells (Tregs) and Th17 cells that release IL-17A, have been detected to be upregulated in individuals with sarcoidosis.47-49 Interestingly, nicotine treatment improves TLR responsiveness and normalizes

the numbers of Tregs in individuals with sarcoidosis,50 supporting the anecdotal observation that the incidence of sarcoidosis is

Overall, there appear to be two possible immunologic scenarios in sarcoidosis: an intense immune reaction in patients with active disease, finally resulting in antigen clearance, or chronic disease with less inflammation but the inability to eradicate the inciting agent and subsequent chronic stimulation of the immune response, resulting in organ damage such as lung fibrosis. The interplay between T cells, B cells, and macrophages in sarcoidosis is not fully understood, and research is hindered by the lack of useful animal models mimicking all aspects present in patients with sarcoidosis.

### Clinical Features

Sarcoidosis can affect every organ system, with the lungs being the most commonly affected organ. Joint symptoms are common in sarcoidosis, affecting up to 25% of patients. The eyes (uveitis and retinal vasculitis), liver (abnormal liver function tests), lymph nodes (enlargement), and skin (lupus pernio, papules, nodules, plaques, and scar sarcoidosis [tattoos]) are the most frequent extrapulmonary organs affected (Table 122.1). According to newer data, renal sarcoidosis may be more frequent than previously reported when patients are specifically assessed for its presence.51a However, rheumatologists are more likely to be confronted with patients with systemic, atypical, primarily musculoskeletal manifestations or disease refractory to standard treatment. Additional possible symptoms are sarcoidosis-associated fatigue (present in 50% to 70% of patients)52; small-fiber neuropathy (44%), which is challenging to diagnose and treat53; and cognitive dysfunction. Musculoskeletal involvement can present as osseous sarcoidosis (axial manifestation or sacroiliitis) in up to 13% of patients5 or sarcoid myopathy, with a muscle biopsy demonstrating granulomas in up to 8%. The latter, however, is only rarely symptomatic, and a clinically overt myopathy is seen in only 1% to 2% of patients. Between 15% and 25% of patients with sarcoidosis may develop arthritis, the most frequently observed rheumatologic symptom of sarcoidosis. In patients with sarcoidosis, arthritis can be acute or chronic; the acute form is most common. Chronic arthritis is typically associated with multisystem sarcoidosis.

### Acute Sarcoid Arthritis

Febrile arthropathy is the most frequently observed joint involvement in sarcoidosis. Although any joint may be involved, the condition usually is symmetric, involving ankles, knees, wrists, and elbows, and co-occurs with BHL and erythema nodosum (EN). Of note, when assessed by ultrasound or MRI, ankle swelling in LS is most often due to periarthritis or tenosynovitis rather than true synovitis.57, Patients with acute sarcoid arthritis experience pain and stiffness, and their joints may be swollen or tender (see supplemental eFig. 122.1 on Elsevier eBooks+). Acute sarcoid arthritis sometimes resolves within weeks of onset, but occasionally symptoms last for several months. Once this condition resolves, it usually does not recur.

In a study of patients with acute sarcoid arthritis, investigators56 prospectively evaluated patients and published criteria to assist in diagnosis. Of 579 participants, 55 patients (9%) were diagnosed with sarcoid arthritis. Diagnoses were made after it was established that patients had a combination of arthritis and BHL,

as determined by chest radiography. From their study, the investigators derived criteria with 93% sensitivity and 99% specificity to guide physicians in differentiating between sarcoid arthritis and other causes of arthritis (Table 122.2).

In addition to the criteria of the above study of acute sarcoid arthritis, 56 most symptoms vary among patients. Patients with

sarcoid arthritis frequently have elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rates,56,59 but other symptoms, such as fever, are observed only in up to 66% of patients.56, Of note, in a small number of patients with acute sarcoid arthritis, abnormal alterations may develop in the bones that can be seen on radiographs of the hands or feet.

Of the following criteria, patients must have three of four characteristics to establish the diagnosis (sensitivity 93%, specificity 99%): Age <40 years Erythema nodosum Symmetric ankle arthritis Symptom duration <2 months

### Chronic Sarcoid Arthritis

The chronic form of sarcoid arthritis is less common than the acute form, and in the United States, it affects more African Americans than white people. It most often affects patients with systemic, multiorgan involvement and typically manifests as oligoarthritis or polyarthritis (Fig. 122.1). Sarcoid arthritis can have a varied presentation. In some patients, sarcoid dactylitis may be the presenting symptom (Fig. 122.2C and 2E), characterized by swollen soft tissues surrounding affected fingers, erythematous skin, or tenderness. Individuals with dactylitis also may have nail abnormalities, such as dystrophy. Therefore it is important to rule out other conditions that affect the nails, such as psoriatic arthritis, when making sarcoid arthritis diagnoses. The skin findings may be an essential clue in these patients since skin manifestations of psoriasis can usually be distinguished from cutaneous manifestations in sarcoidosis.

Other skeletal areas that may be affected by sarcoidosis include nasal bones, pelvic girdle structures, ribs, and the skull. One retrospective case-control study of bone sarcoidosis showed that patients with bone sarcoidosis had a higher incidence of liver, spleen, and extrathoracic lymph node involvement. The most commonly affected site was the spine (68.8%), followed by the pelvis (35.9%), and the hands (15.6%).

Patients with lupus pernio may be particularly at risk for developing abnormalities in their nasal bones. Because of the similarities between a patient with sarcoidosis with nasal bone involvement and a patient with granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA), physicians must distinguish between these conditions. Serology may be helpful because most patients with GPA will have a positive anti-neutrophil cytoplasm antibody (ANCA), but sarcoidosis does not usually lead to a positive ANCA. On the other hand, about 60% of patients with sarcoidosis will have an elevated angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) or soluble IL-2 receptor (sIL-2R) level at presentation, which is not seen in the presence of vasculitis. Lesions in the pelvic bones (Fig. 122.2D) or the spine (Fig. 122.2F) may at first lead one to suspect cancer metastases. Therefore a comprehensive assessment is warranted in patients with changes in their skeletal bones, even if they exhibit other typical symptoms of sarcoidosis.

Joint destruction (granulomatous erosions) or Jaccoud's deformity (i.e., deformity without apparent erosive destruction) can occur when inflammation persists, and phalangeal cysts or a trabecular pattern can be present on plain radiographs. In some patients, joint symptoms manifest early in the course of sarcoidosis, whereas other patients experience sarcoid arthritis several years after the onset of the disorder. Lupus pernio and chronic uveitis may manifest concomitantly with the chronic form of arthritis.

As with other organ system manifestations, several conditions may mimic sarcoid arthritis and should be excluded. For example,

symmetric oligoarthritis or polyarthritis and an elevated rheumatoid factor are common features of sarcoid arthritis, but they may also result from reactive arthritis (ReA) or rheumatoid arthritis (RA). Furthermore, a subset of patients with RA may develop interstitial lung disease (ILD), which can cause confusion in differentiating RA from sarcoidosis. In addition, coincident sarcoidosis eventually develops in some patients with RA, although it is rare for sarcoidosis to co-exist with other connective disease disorders. Therefore it is crucial for physicians to distinguish between the two conditions or to determine whether the two diseases are comorbid within the same patient.

Rheumatic fever may be suspected in patients with migratory polyarthritis, mainly when joint symptoms manifest before additional sarcoidosis-related symptoms are noted. A biopsy of the synovium or tendon sheaths may be helpful, with characteristic granulomas appearing upon pathologic examination. Differential diagnoses for patients with monoarthritis include gout, septic arthritis, and calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate—positive arthritis (see Tables 122.3 and 122.4, and supportive content for detailed considerations of the diagnostic approach).

### Diagnosis and Diagnostic Tests

The diagnosis of musculoskeletal disease related to sarcoidosis must be examined based on two different presentations. The first

is a patient with known sarcoidosis who presents with musculoskeletal symptoms. The other is a patient with musculoskeletal disease in whom sarcoidosis is a possible diagnosis. Although the evaluations may be similar, a patient with known sarcoidosis elsewhere with musculoskeletal manifestations consistent with sarcoidosis is usually assumed to have sarcoidosis in that area. However, in a patient with musculoskeletal involvement and no known sarcoidosis elsewhere, a biopsy usually will be required to confirm the diagnosis. The biopsy specimen may be from the lung or skin, but in some cases, it will be from muscle, lymph node, or other tissues.

Sarcoidosis is a diagnosis of exclusion. In clinical practice, other conditions are often suspected when considering only clinical symptoms (e.g., Hodgkin's lymphoma or tuberculosis with pulmonary findings or systemic symptoms). Therefore the workup's primary goal is to gather enough clinical clues and compatible features to diagnose sarcoidosis with sufficient certainty and exclude other diagnoses that warrant a different treatment approach. Fig. 122.2 presents some features consistent with the disease. Fig. 122.3 gives an overview of possible overlapping clinical features and differential diagnoses that more commonly need to be ruled out in potential sarcoidosis patients.

In many instances, the diagnosis will rely heavily on finding granulomas in a tissue biopsy. However, many other conditions can lead to a granulomatous reaction, as summarized in Table 122.5. Although sarcoidosis granulomas tend to be noncaseating and non-necrotizing, many patients with sarcoidosis exhibit some

necrosis in part of their granulomatous response. A biopsy is usually not required for some presentations such as LS, Heerfordt's syndrome (defined as fever, uveitis, parotitis, and cranial nerve palsy), BHL with uveitis, and asymptomatic BHL.

The heterogeneity of the disease may result in delayed diagnosis. One study of 189 patients with sarcoidosis found that only 15.3% of patients received a diagnosis during their first visit to a physician. Moreover, sarcoidosis can affect any organ, which may cause a patient to be referred to a specialist who may not commonly manage sarcoidosis. Patients with pulmonary symptoms are often misdiagnosed as having asthma. For individuals with musculoskeletal manifestations, the presentation of sarcoidosis may be similar to that of other conditions, most notably autoimmune disorders68 (see Fig. 122.369 and Table 122.4).

A vigilant approach is mandatory for the patient with musculoskeletal disease and possible sarcoidosis. A comprehensive multisystem evaluation, commonly performed in rheumatology practice, should prove informative. For example, about two-thirds of patients have hilar adenopathy on a chest radiograph. Scadding proposed a staging system of the chest roentgenogram70: stage 1 disease consists of hilar adenopathy alone (Fig. 122.2A); stage 2 disease is hilar adenopathy plus parenchymal infiltrates; stage 3 is parenchymal infiltrates alone; and stage 4 is fibrosis. Although this scoring is commonly used, differences may be noted in the staging of the radiographs, even among sarcoidosis experts. It has to be pointed out that the Scadding stages do not apply to chest CTs. Table 122.6 lists some of the features that, when present, support

Several tests (summarized in Table 122.3) have been proposed for patients with sarcoidosis to serve as a minimal evaluation. 2, The range of different tests arises because sarcoidosis is a multiorgan disease. One needs to look for evidence of specific organ involvement. Because serum ACE levels may or may not be elevated in patients with sarcoidosis and are therefore not accurate for the diagnosis,74 other biomarkers for the diagnosis (chitotrisodase75) or activity (sIL-2R, neopterin, chitotriosidase, lysozyme, KL-6, or amyloid A34) are being evaluated. MRI with gadolinium administration may identify the involvement of sarcoidosis in the brain78 or the heart. MRI findings also may support the localization of bone sarcoidosis or sarcoid arthritis and may identify asymptomatic lesions.

Several lines of evidence have indicated that 18F-FDG-PET may be helpful in the diagnosis and assessment of (extra)pulmonary sarcoidosis,81 but it usually is not recommended as a first

diagnostic tool. 18F-FDG-PET can be used to determine which organs are affected, particularly when no evidence of lung involvement is found; this includes cardiac sarcoidosis. A high-fat, highprotein, very low-carbohydrate diet in the preceding 72 hours before the study may suppress background physiologic cardiac uptake and increase sensitivity for detecting pathologic uptake. Furthermore, 18F-FDG-PET can point investigators to appropriate organs to biopsy when no distinct organ system involvement is apparent. For pulmonary sarcoidosis, endobronchial ultrasound is used to help the bronchoscopist select appropriate biopsy sites for transbronchial needle aspiration.

Criteria for specific organ involvement in patients with known sarcoidosis have been proposed and updated.2, Definitive organ involvement may be evident or can be established by

positive results of a granuloma biopsy from the affected tissue. For example, arthritis with no other cause may be attributed to underlying sarcoidosis. However, patients with phalangeal cystic changes almost definitely can consider their arthritis to be a manifestation of their sarcoidosis85 (Table 122.4).

Highly probable sarcoid arthritis with osseous involvement includes the typical features of the trabecular pattern, osteolysis, cyst formation, and punched-out lesions. Signs that sarcoidosis is at least probable include dactylitis, nodular tenosynovitis, and positive findings of PET, MRI, or gallium-67 bone imaging. Arthralgias are a sign of possible sarcoid arthritis, and patients who present with nonspecific arthritis are categorized under "no CC consensus." This classification has limitations and has not been validated in a prospective clinical setting. Overall, the diagnosis

of sarcoidosis and sarcoid arthritis may be difficult to establish. Table 122.4 gives an overview of clinical, laboratory, and imaging features of more frequently encountered autoimmune diseases that may present similarly to sarcoidosis.

### Treatment

### General Approach

Prednisone and adrenocorticotropic hormone have both been approved for treating pulmonary sarcoidosis. Still, no treatment for extrapulmonary sarcoidosis, including sarcoid arthritis, has been approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA). With the advent of 18F-FDG-PET scanning and other imaging modalities, more patients with asymptomatic but widespread disease will likely be diagnosed. Decisions to begin immunosuppressive therapy, however, depend on symptoms (e.g., persistent cough or dyspnea) and organ dysfunction (e.g., abnormal pulmonary function tests) and not on the mere number of organs affected (sometimes termed systemic sarcoidosis). Generally, treatment options are divided into first-, second-, and third-line therapies. The European Respiratory Society has recently published clinical practice guidelines for treating various disease manifestations. For further details, the reader is referred to this document. Other recommendations for more specific manifestations,

such as sarcoidosis-associated pulmonary hypertension, are also available.

The first-line therapy for most manifestations (except sarcoidosis-associated fatigue and small-fiber neuropathy) is corticosteroids. A dose of 20 to 40 mg/day should be maintained for 1 to 3 months and then tapered to a maintenance dose of 5 to 10 mg/ day, which, empirically, is usually maintained for 1 year. Secondline therapies include so-called disease-modifying antisarcoid drugs (DMASDs), including methotrexate (MTX), azathioprine (AZA), leflunomide (LEF), hydroxychloroquine (HCQ), chloroquine, mycophenolate mofetil (MMF), and cyclosporine A (CsA), which may also be indicated to avoid continued high-dose glucocorticoid therapy with its associated complications. For refractory cases, TNF inhibitors can be used as third-line therapy. The two beststudied agents of this class of drugs are infliximab (INF) and adalimumab (ADA). INF has been studied in two placebo-controlled trials and improved forced vital capacity (FVC) and dyspnea, especially in patients with longer disease duration and more dyspnea at baseline.91, ADA has shown some effectiveness in pulmonary sarcoidosis. Etanercept has proven to be ineffective for pulmonary and ocular sarcoidosis.94, In a randomized trial, the TNF inhibitor golimumab and ustekinumab, an antibody against IL-12/IL-23, were ineffective in treating pulmonary sarcoidosis. B cell inhibition by rituximab had mixed results in individuals with refractory sarcoidosis in a small clinical trial,97 but it has been

effective in singular cases. A definite recommendation for using rituximab to treat sarcoidosis cannot be made. Recently the Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitors have been successfully used in cutaneous and systemic sarcoidosis.99, One of these agents, tofacitinib, a pan-JAK inhibitor, resulted in marked improvement in skin sarcoidosis and stable pulmonary disease in one patient. Furthermore, tofacitinib also improved internal organ manifestations by suppressing type 1 immunity, including IFN-γ and IL-6, IL-12, IL-15, and GM-CSF. The therapeutic potential for novel members of the class with different JAK specificity is awaited.

A novel promising agent is efzofitimod, a 59-amino acid protein fused to the Fc region of human IgG1.101 Efzofitimod's amino acid sequence corresponds to the extracellularly active N-terminal region of the histidyl-tRNA-synthetase. The binding partner of this novel agent is neuropilin-2 (NRP-2), a cell surface receptor whose expression is upregulated following inflammatory insults. In a phase 1/2 clinical trial in pulmonary sarcoidosis, efzofitimod had a good safety profile and showed promising results for various secondary outcomes.

In addition, paradoxical reactions to biologic agents can occur, including positivity for anti-nuclear antibodies, drug-induced lupus erythematosus, demyelinating disorders, and sarcoid-like .103, A sarcoid-like reaction also has occurred granulomatosis. with ustekinumab,105 suggesting that mechanisms other than upregulation of interferon-α through TNF inhibition6might play a role. A genetic predisposition (possibly TNF polymorphisms) is likely, but it is impossible to predict which patients will experience this reaction. Therefore, a high index of suspicion is mandatory when using this type of drug. Tables 122.7 and 122.8 provide an overview of treatment recommendations for the various disease manifestations.

### Management of Sarcoid Arthritis

No randomized trials have been conducted that could guide clinical decision-making. To guide clinicians in management, we propose a treatment algorithm, shown in Fig. 122.4.3 Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAIDs), MTX, and local or low-dose systemic corticosteroids are our preferred firstline therapies. Alternatively, hydroxychloroquine and other DMASDs may be used. Using information obtained from the diagnostic evaluation, the clinician usually makes treatment decisions after carefully considering the disease's severity and probable clinical course, as revealed by its radiographic progression, and arthritis alone will only rarely be the main driver for treatment escalation.

The proposed algorithm requires regular patient visits to monitor disease activity, therapeutic efficacy, and tolerability. Responders continue to take first-line agents (usually prednisone or prednisolone) until disease resolution or treatment failure. Before nonresponders are prescribed second-line therapies, higher doses of corticosteroids may be used, or patients may be switched to methylprednisone, depending on tolerability and manifestations of toxicity. For patients who require second-line medications, two options are available: (1) MTX may be administered to MTXnaïve patients, or (2) non-MTX disease-modifying antisarcoid drugs (e.g., HCQ, LEF, and AZA) as monotherapy or combinations thereof may be prescribed to patients who have inadequate responses to first-line MTX.

For patients for whom this treatment approach fails, one can consider an alternative third-line biologic therapy or an aggressive course of systemic corticosteroids with careful toxicity monitoring.

Alternatively, participating in a clinical trial may be appropriate for some patients.

### Vitamin D

Vitamin D metabolism is more complex in sarcoidosis than other rheumatic diseases. Patients with sarcoidosis might be more sensitive to calcium and vitamin D substitution,108 with the associated risks of hypercalcemia and hypercalciuria, which are present in up to 10% of patients who do not receive vitamin D supplements. The mechanism usually attributed to hypercalcemia is increased production of 1,25-dihydroxy vitamin D (1,25-OH2D) by epithelioid cells in the granuloma (1α-hydroxylase activity). This risk must be balanced against the adverse effects of potential chronic vitamin D deficiency, and patients often require treatment for osteoporosis because of long-term glucocorticoid use. Bisphosphonates alone may be adequate to treat corticosteroid-induced osteoporosis. Patients who do not receive glucocorticoid therapy do not seem to have a lower bone mineral density per se because of sarcoidosis. Recently, higher levels of 25-hydroxyvitamin D (25-OHD) were associated with a higher frequency of fractures in patients with sarcoidosis. The authors found that levels between 10 and 20 ng/mL were associated with the lowest fracture risk. Because of the disassociation between 25-OHD and 1,25-OH2D in sarcoidosis, it seems reasonable to measure both levels to ascertain which patients should receive vitamin D supplements. 107, Fig. 122.5 depicts our approach to vitamin D testing and supplementation in sarcoidosis patients.

### Outcome and Prognosis

The overall mortality in sarcoidosis is low (about 5%),114 and many patients with spontaneous regression will never require treatment. In people who need treatment, important differences exist between African American and white patients. African American patients with sarcoidosis are known to experience a more severe and systemic disease; mortality is 12 times higher in this population.

### Conclusion

Much remains to be learned about sarcoidosis. The causes of this disease remain unclear, and no medications have been approved by the FDA for its treatment, except for prednisone and ACTH gel, which was approved in the 1950s based on a few case reports. Although increasing attention has been directed to the underlying mechanisms of granuloma formation and the cause (including an infectious cause), full details of sarcoidosis immunopathogenesis have yet to be determined. Appropriate animal models and candidate genes are needed to help advance our understanding of this disease. Developing and evaluating an appropriate primary outcome measure is required for clinical trial purposes to measure responses in this remarkably heterogeneous disease.

We have presented an algorithm that can be used in treating patients with an established diagnosis of sarcoidosis. However, treatment approaches vary by institution and individual clinicians because of a myriad of conflicting studies published about sarcoidosis management. The diversity of clinical presentations and the lack of large, well-designed, randomized, controlled clinical trials addressing the various clinical phenotypes make it impossible to provide more specific treatment recommendations. Furthermore, therapeutic choices will likely differ according to

the type and extent of organ system involvement observed in individual patients. Manifestations such as sarcoidosis-associated fatigue or small-fiber neuropathy are probably under-recognized because patients must be specifically assessed for their presence. The systemic nature of this disease, coupled with the complexity of phenotypic presentation among various ethnic groups and

within the same patient, makes it challenging to study this complex disease.

Steroid-sparing agents, including cytotoxic drugs and novel biologic therapies such as TNF inhibitors and B celldepleting therapy, have increasingly been used for relapsed and refractory disease. Several sarcoidosis studies have investigated TNF

# 123 Hemochromatosis

### KEY POINTS

### Introduction

Hemochromatosis refers to the presence of excess iron in body tissues because of increased iron absorption. Primary or hereditary hemochromatosis (HHC) is an autosomal recessive disease, whereas secondary hemochromatosis refers to iron overload as a result of increased iron availability, ineffective erythropoiesis, or inherited abnormalities of iron metabolism.

Hemochromatosis was first recognized in the 1880s in a series of case reports that described "bronze diabetes" and "pigmented cirrhosis," but von Recklinghausen1 is credited with the first use of the term in 1889. In 1935 the familial pattern of HHC was described by Sheldon,2 who suggested that the disease was due to an inborn error of metabolism. In 1955 Finch and Finch3 showed that HHC was caused by abnormal iron absorption in the presence of a normal diet. At that time, premorbid recognition of the problem was uncommon, and most cases were diagnosed at autopsy. In 1972 serum ferritin became available as a measure of iron stores. Three years later, investigators discovered that the HHC gene was present on chromosome 6, close to the human leukocyte antigen (HLA)-A locus. It took 21 more years for the mutated gene, HFE, to be described, and in the past decade, it has been recognized that other gene mutations also can cause iron overload. Genetic testing has revolutionized the diagnosis of HHC, although the phenotype of any given mutation may vary

greatly.6, Nevertheless, the detection of such genes has greatly enhanced the overall prognosis of this condition by allowing the disease to be diagnosed at a pre-clinical stage in high-risk individuals. This discovery, along with improved knowledge at a molecular level, has further aided our understanding of the pathogenesis and treatment of HHC and helped many patients achieve a normal life expectancy.

### Iron Metabolism in Health and Disease

Iron has an essential role in erythropoiesis and in normal cellular function. Along with anemia, chronic iron deficiency results in a variety of other clinical manifestations such as changes to the nails, tongue, esophagus, and muscles. In normal adults the average total body iron content is 3 to 4 g, mostly contained within hemoglobin but also present in myoglobin and cytochromes, in addition to the storage proteins, ferritin and hemosiderin (Table 123.1). Of a typical daily Western diet of 10 to 20 mg of iron, 1 to 2 mg is absorbed by duodenal enterocytes each day.9, Heme dietary sources from fish and meat have a higher bioavailability than nonheme sources, such as vegetables. The addition of ascorbic acid to the meal increases absorption of nonheme iron, whereas tannins, bran, and phytates inhibit iron absorption. 11,

Iron homeostasis, which is tightly controlled at cellular and molecular levels, is influenced by regulatory feedback between body iron requirements and intestinal iron absorption. Dietary iron enters the body in the duodenum, where, in the ferrous state, it gains access to the enterocyte via divalent metal transporter 1. It is then either stored intra-cellularly and eventually excreted through the feces or absorbed via ferroportin transfer out of the enterocyte, aided by ferroxidase activity of the ceruloplasmin homologue, hephaestin. Circulating iron is then either used (mainly by erythroid cells) or stored (in the liver or macrophages).

Communication between sites of iron uptake, utilization, and storage is tightly controlled. Ferroportin facilitates release of intracellular iron and is a major player in iron homeostasis, modulated by hepcidin, which plays a central role in the process. 13, Hepcidin is produced by the liver in response to changes in iron status and negatively regulates iron levels. It acts directly on ferroportin by binding to it and causing it to be internalized by the cell and destroyed. A signaling pathway for bone morphogenetic protein (BMP)-6 regulates hepcidin by binding to a specific receptor on hepatocytes. Hepcidin expression is normally induced by excess iron or inflammation and downregulated by iron deficiency, ineffective erythropoiesis, or hypoxia. 21 Persistently high levels of hepcidin are associated with the anemia of chronic inflammation;

iron is retained within the enterocytes and macrophages, leading to low transferrin saturation and reduced availability of iron for erythropoiesis. In contrast, inappropriately low hepcidin expression permits increased absorption of iron from the duodenum, high transferrin saturation, and iron overload in sites of tissue storage. Erythroferrone (ERFE) has been identified as a hormone produced by erythroid precursors acting directly on hepatocytes to decrease hepcidin production. 22,23

### Genetics

Four types of HHC have now been described, all of which are linked to gene mutations (Table 123.2). Classic HHC (type 1) is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations of the HFE gene located on chromosome 6.24 The most common mutation is a single amino acid substitution of tyrosine for cysteine at position 282 (C282Y), particularly in people originating from Northern Europe. Homozygosity for this mutation is a risk factor for organ damage as a result of iron overload, although phenotypic expression varies widely. Other mutations of the HFE gene include the replacement of histidine with aspartic acid at position 63 (H63D) and the substitution of serine for cysteine at position 65 (S65C). Clinical manifestations of the latter mutations are less significant, although compound heterozygosity may be associated with evidence of iron overload, particularly if comorbid conditions such as excess alcohol intake or steatosis are present. .25,

Unlike mutations of the HFE gene that may become clinically obvious in middle age, hemojuvelin (HJV-related HHC, type 2A) or hepcidin (HAMP-related HHC, type 2B) mutations result in juvenile HHC (type 2), with evidence of iron overload in the teens or twenties. The affected gene has been mapped to the long arm of chromosome 1 in type 2A and chromosome 19 for type 2B. In such cases, the rate of iron accumulation seems to be greater than in adult HHC and is associated with widespread organ involvement and early mortality. In these patients, cardiomyopathy, diabetes mellitus (DM), and hypogonadism are more common than severe liver disease.24, Affected individuals have been reported throughout the world. Transferrin receptor (TfR) mutations (TfR2related HHC, type 3) cause clinical disease similar to classic HFE-related HHC. Such mutations are very rare.30, Type 4 or ferroportin-related HHC is an autosomal dominant condition that is described in European and Australian families. 32, Two types of ferroportin mutations have been reported. In the first type, loss of surface localization of ferroportin results in a decreased ability of cells to export iron, causing iron to build up predominantly in macrophages. In the second type, hepcidin-induced ferroportin dysfunction leads to iron accumulation in parenchymal cells of the liver and other tissues. Phenotypic expression varies, with some patients manifesting the effects of iron overload in a similar manner to classic HHC and others showing minimal evidence of organ damage.

### Other Inherited Iron-Overload Syndromes

Several other inherited iron-overload syndromes have been described. In people of African descent, a common polymorphism in the ferroportin 1 gene is associated with mild microcytic anemia and a tendency to iron loading.35, Aceruloplasminemia is caused by homozygous mutation of the ceruloplasmin gene and results in anemia, evidence of iron excess, glucose intolerance, and neurologic symptoms. Familial atransferrinemia is an autosomal recessive condition associated with severe anemia in the presence of tissue iron deposition. A number of ferritin mutations have been described that result in hyperferritinemia, some with specific organ damage. Patients with hereditary hyperferritinemia-cataract syndrome have elevated ferritin levels and bilateral congenital cataracts. Neuroferritinopathy is an autosomal dominant movement disorder in which iron preferentially deposits in the brain despite variable serum ferritin levels. In contrast, the entity of benign hyperferritinemia has also been reported in which, despite a mutation in the coding region of L-ferritin, no clinical manifestations develop. A congenital form of iron overload is neonatal hemochromatosis, in which excess iron deposition results from immune-mediated liver injury and is ameliorated by administration of intravenous immunoglobulin during pregnancy. 42,43

### Epidemiology

Although HHC was previously thought to be a rare condition, genetic testing has revealed that it is one of the most common heritable disorders. Although 5 out of every 1000 individuals of Northern European origin are homozygous for the HFE mutation, phenotypic expression varies, and clinical cases are much fewer in number. In a study of nearly 100,000 individuals from primary care practices in the United States, the prevalence of C282Y homozygosity was as follows: white, 0.44%; Native American, 0.11%; Hispanic, 0.027%; African American, 0.014%; Pacific Islander, 0.012%; and Asian, 0.0004%. Peak age at the time of diagnosis is 40 to 60 years for classic HHC.

### Influence of Other Genes and Environment

Clinical manifestations of HHC vary greatly between people with similar mutations, suggesting that other factors or genes influence disease expression. One study demonstrated that among C282Y homozygotes, up to 82% have hyperferritinemia, whereas approximately 28% of homozygous males and 1% of homozygous females ultimately experience clinical manifestations of HHC—defined as the presence of liver disease, hepatocellular carcinoma, and arthritis of the second and third metacarpophalangeal joints—by age 65 years. In contrast, compound heterozygotes with C282Y/H63D mutations exhibit higher serum ferritin and transferrin saturation levels compared with normal control subjects but are at very low risk of clinical HHC. Studies have found that hyperferritinemic patients with relatives who have suffered the consequences of iron overload are at increased risk of organ damage compared with those with no family history of such clinical problems.

Other genes may play a role in modifying the phenotypic expression of iron overload. The presence of the gene CYBRD1, which encodes duodenal reductase DCYTB, is associated with lower serum ferritin levels than in C282Y homozygotes. Furthermore, mutations of other iron-related genes, such as hepcidin, hemojuvelin, haptoglobin, and BMP, may influence disease manifestations.49-53 In addition, increased expression of profibrotic genes (e.g., transforming growth factor) may accelerate the onset of cirrhosis in susceptible people.

The reason that HHC disease penetrance is more evident in C282Y homozygote males than females may be explained by recurrent menstrual blood loss and consequent slower accumulation of iron stores in women. Nevertheless, genetically determined sex differences in ferritin levels may occur because distinct HLA A*03B*07 and A*03B*14 haplotypes have been reported in men and women with clinical evidence of HHC.

Environmental factors, including diet, smoking, alcohol intake, and comorbid diseases, also influence clinical expression of HHC. Metabolic syndrome is associated with insulin resistance—associated iron overload, which, in the presence of HHC, may have a synergistic effect on liver damage. Concurrent liver disease due to hepatitis or steatosis may exacerbate the process

of fibrogenesis. In addition to the known toxic effect of alcohol on hepatocytes, it also downregulates hepcidin expression and increases iron absorption, contributing to end organ damage in patients with innate iron overload.57, Furthermore, meat consumption and high citrus fruit intake also contribute to increased iron loading. In addition, ingestion of noncitrus fruits may have a protective effect.

### Pathogenesis

The clinical expression of HHC may be influenced by several pathophysiologic mechanisms, including increased duodenal absorption of dietary iron; decreased expression of the key regulatory peptide, hepcidin; altered function of the HFE protein; and the direct and indirect toxic effects of iron deposition in target organs. Recent insight has been gained into the function of hepcidin. Human mutations and murine knockout models of genes for hepcidin, hemojuvelin, TfRs, or HFE result in reduced hepcidin levels and increased duodenal iron absorption. The HFE protein also plays a role as a hepatocyte membrane-based iron sensor, interacting with HFE and TfR-1 and -2, thereby influencing hepcidin expression.

Chronic iron overload is thought to cause tissue damage by several mechanisms, including impairment of mitochondrial function and weakening of lysosomal membranes with consequent discharge of enzymes into the cytoplasm. Increased free radical formation contributes to lipid peroxidation of cell membranes, and profibrogenic cytokines are released. The extent and duration of iron deposition correlate with the development of fibrosis, and it is thought that substantial hepatocyte and Kupffer cell iron accumulation precedes organ damage. In HHC, iron first accumulates in parenchymal cells, with reticuloendothelial (RE) involvement a late feature, in contrast to transfusional iron overload, in which RE cells are primarily targeted. Values of serum ferritin exceeding 1000 µg/L are associated with significantly increased risks of liver fibrosis and cirrhosis.7,19,63

### Clinical Features

### Extra-articular Manifestations

HHC presents more commonly in men than in women and typically manifests in middle-aged adults when iron stores gradually accumulate, often reaching 20 to 30 g.19, The classic findings of hepatic abnormalities, skin pigmentation, arthritis, DM, erectile dysfunction, heart enlargement, and/or conduction defects indicate late disease. Organ involvement varies and is unpredictable, although the liver, as the major site of iron storage, is usually affected. Not infrequently, abnormalities of liver enzymes, checked as part of a routine health review, identify the problem. With the recent availability of genetic testing, however, presentation by asymptomatic relatives of probands is now more common.

In the liver, increasing iron deposition results in eventual fibrosis and cirrhosis. It is worth noting that some patients with HHC and iron overload may progress to fibrosis even in the presence of normal levels of serum transaminases. Therapeutic phlebotomy can cause regression of some of these changes, particularly in early disease. Additional causes of significant liver disease are common in patients with HHC and may contribute to hepatocellular damage. In people with established cirrhosis, the risk of malignant hepatoma is 20-fold greater than the general population, with a higher risk in affected men than in women. 68,

Iron deposition in the heart can result in conduction system abnormalities and heart failure. Several large population studies of HHC and atherosclerosis have failed to find a link. Nevertheless, elevated ferritin levels, particularly in the setting of nonalcoholic fatty liver disease, may be associated with vascular damage via hepcidin upregulation.70-72 Glucose intolerance tends to be a late finding in HHC and is due to progressive iron accumulation in pancreatic β cells, causing low C-peptide and insulin levels. Usually α cell function is preserved, and serum glucagon levels are normal or increased. In patients with HHC who present symptomatically, DM has been noted in approximately 50%. For patients with HHC who have early insulin resistance and no evidence of cirrhosis, however, venesection may reverse iron deposition—induced β cell dysfunction.74, The risk of DM is higher in C282Y heterozygotes with no clinical evidence of HHC compared with control subjects. 76,

Pituitary involvement in HHC can result in reduced serum levels of secreted hormones, mainly from the anterior aspect of this gland, resulting in loss of libido and erectile dysfunction.78, Primary hypogonadism from testicular iron overload is much less common. Therapeutic phlebotomy may reduce these symptoms, particularly in younger men. Hypothyroidism in HHC is thought to be due to a direct toxic effect of iron on thyroid cells and is associated with low thyroxine and elevated thyroid-stimulating hormone. Such endocrine abnormalities may contribute to the development of osteoporosis in these individuals.

Skin discoloration occurs as a result of extra melanin and iron in the epidermis. It is a late finding, and the development of bronze diabetes represents the end stage of years of iron accumulation in the tissues.

Patients with HHC have increased susceptibility to certain infections. High serum iron concentrations may increase bacterial virulence, and excess iron in macrophages is thought to reduce phagocytosis. Particular caution is advised with uncooked seafood because of the risk of septicemia from Vibrio vulnificus. In addition, Yersinia enterocolitica, Listeria monocytogenes, Salmonella enteritidis serotype typhimurium, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Escherichia coli, Rhizopus arrhizus, and Mucor species all cause severe illness in patients with iron overload.

Apart from the increased risk of malignant hepatoma in patients with established cirrhosis, an independent association of nonhepatic cancers, particularly breast and colorectal tumors, in HFE C282Y homozygotes has been reported. In addition, H63D homozygosity increases susceptibility to colorectal cancer in people with pre-existing hereditary risks for this malignancy. Iron is potentially carcinogenic via several mechanisms, including its immunosuppressive properties and its role as an essential cofactor for tumor cell growth and in catalyzing the formation of hydroxyl radicals. Furthermore, cancer risk is lower with reduced iron stores.

### Articular Features

Arthralgia/arthritis is a common presentation in HHC, affecting 50% to 80% of patients and significantly interfering with quality of life.88-94 Although it tends to be a late feature, joint pain nevertheless may be the presenting symptom of HHC, alerting a diligent physician to the presence of an underlying metabolic disorder. Articular involvement may be widespread, but changes to the second and third metacarpophalangeal joints are most characteristic94 (Fig. 123.1). Arthritis may be present in the proximal interphalangeal joints, wrists, shoulders, hips, knees,

and ankles. Patients notice pain and stiffness of the involved joints, but clinical evidence of synovitis is usually absent. Hip damage develops in approximately 25% of people with HHC, and after hip arthroplasty, the risk of aseptic loosening of the prosthesis is increased compared with those without HHC.95, The differential diagnosis of HHC-related arthropathy includes severe osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, and other forms of inflammatory arthritis including crystalline arthritis. Rheumatoid factor is typically negative, however, and in established cases, radiographs show distinctive findings, such as joint space narrowing of the second and third metacarpophalangeal joints, hook-like osteophytes on the radial aspect of the metacarpal heads, and chondrocalcinosis, particularly of the triangular fibrocartilage adjacent to the ulnar styloid. Chondrocalcinosis may also be observed in other joints, particularly the knees (Fig. 123.1C), although this is a nonspecific finding. HHC-related arthritis is more common in male C282Y homozygotes than in other genotypes.

The pathogenetic mechanisms underlying HHC-related arthritis are unknown, and the prevalence of joint pain in this condition has not been found to correlate with body iron stores. Toxic effects from local iron deposition, acceleration of cartilage defects, and immunologic mechanisms have been implicated.90, Under light microscopy, the involved synovium demonstrates iron deposits, particularly in the lining cells, but inflammatory cell infiltration is not typical.98-100 Neutrophil infiltration of the synovial sublining layer has been described. Apatite and calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate crystals may be observed, but it is not known why they are preferentially expressed in HHC. In association with the increased incidence of calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate deposition disease in HHC, a putative role for a parathyroid hormone fragment (PTH 44 to 68) has been suggested. . In a study of more than 200 patients with evidence of liver iron overload, elevations of the serum PTH fragment 48 to 68 were noted in approximately one-third, with concentrations

positively associated with both serum ferritin and the number of clinically affected joints. Joint symptoms due to HHC tend not to improve after therapeutic phlebotomy.

### Differential Diagnosis

Because of the lack of a physiologic mechanism to enhance iron excretion, the inevitable result of increased iron absorption is iron overload, which may be due to inherited defects in iron metabolism, as previously described, or secondary to other causes (Table 123.3). A full history of medication use, including over-the-counter iron tablets, and a review of any blood transfusions should be elicited. Ineffective erythropoiesis in conditions such as the thalassemias or sideroblastic anemia can also result in the buildup of iron stores. Porphyria cutanea tarda is associated with hyperferritinemia, high transferrin saturation levels, and an increased incidence of HFE mutations. Nevertheless, the clinical findings, particularly dermatologic findings, distinguish this disease from HHC. Elevated ferritin levels may result from severe inflammation. Interleukin (IL)-6 is a potent stimulator of hepcidin via the STAT3 pathway, resulting in reduced iron absorption and elevation of tissue and serum ferritin levels, although these changes are accompanied by low transferrin satu- 104 Chronic liver disease resulting from hepatitis, alcohol ration. excess, or fatty infiltration is associated with hyperferritinemia and normal or elevated transferrin saturation values. Alcohol, independent of liver damage, induces ferritin synthesis and iron overload in people who consume more than two alcoholic drinks per day. 69,106

### Diagnostic Tests

A high index of suspicion is helpful when a patient presents with joint pain and abnormal liver enzymes. Although the differential diagnosis is wide, the presence of elevated ferritin and transferrin saturation levels (serum iron x 100/total iron-binding capacity) strongly points to the diagnosis of HHC. Serum iron should be measured with the patient fasting because concentrations may be increased after a meal. High ferritin levels also may be caused by systemic inflammation or malignancy, but these conditions tend to be associated with reduced transferrin saturation. Other reasons for elevated transferrin saturation include high serum iron as a result of hepatic cytolysis or low transferrin levels due to liver failure, and these possibilities should be excluded. If ferritin measures greater than 200 µg/L and transferrin saturation is greater than 45%, genetic screening is recommended. The finding of homozygosity for the C282Y mutation or compound heterozygosity for C282Y/H63D confirms the diagnosis. If these mutations are not present and evidence of iron overload exists, investigation for more rare genetic defects, such as alterations of the genes that encode hemojuvelin, hepcidin, TfR2, or ferroportin, can be considered in the context of the pertinent clinical features (Table 123.2). Although hepcidin levels may be helpful, they are currently not routinely available.

A liver biopsy may be considered for prognostic purposes in established cases. The patients most likely to show evidence of cirrhosis are those who have the combination of a ferritin level greater than 1000 µg/L, elevated transaminases, and thrombocytopenia.63, In contrast, patients with a serum ferritin level less than 1000 µg/L and no additional risk factors for liver disease are unlikely to have cirrhosis. A liver biopsy is therefore considered for those with advanced disease or if the diagnosis is in question, particularly in people with evidence of iron overload who are HFE negative. HHC can be distinguished histologically from alcoholic cirrhosis by the preferential distribution of iron in the hepatocytes in the former and in the Kupffer cells in the latter.

Other indications of liver damage include aspartate aminotransferase-to-platelet ratio index (APRI) and Fibrosis-4 Index (Fib4), which have been validated against liver biopsy for detecting advanced hepatic fibrosis in HFE-related HHC. However, ultrasound-based elastography underdiagnoses advanced fibrosis in these patients, particularly in those with ferritin levels <1000 . MRI of the abdomen also can be used to determine iron overload in the internal organs. Gradient T2-weighted sequences show decreased signal intensity and correlate highly with liver iron 110,111 concentrations. This imaging method also can identify other locations of iron deposition (e.g., in the spleen, pancreas, lymph nodes, and heart). Because HHC is a systemic condition, other investigations should include a search for diabetes, thyroid disease, hypogonadism, osteoporosis, and cardiomyopathy. Disease mimickers, such as porphyria cutanea tarda, ineffective erythropoiesis, chronic alcohol excess, and the metabolic syndrome, should be excluded. An algorithm summarizing a diagnostic approach to HHC is provided in Fig. 123.2.

### Screening

Greater disease awareness and the availability of genetic screening have meant that HHC is now likely to be diagnosed before the classic triad of cirrhosis, DM, and skin hyperpigmentation develops. Late presentation can occur, however, particularly in people with additional risk factors for iron overload or liver disease.

For individuals in whom genetic testing has identified a risk for HHC, but with no clinical evidence of disease, yearly biochemical screening is recommended, measuring serum ferritin, transferrin saturation, and liver enzymes. Such monitoring facilitates early detection of organ compromise and timely initiation of treatment.

### Population Screening

HHC is an attractive target for population screening because of its high prevalence, potential disease severity, availability of costeffective treatment, and impact of early diagnosis on the morbidity and mortality of affected patients. Nevertheless, the clinical penetrance of HHC is low, and the negative consequences (e.g., economical and psychological) of finding an associated gene mutation in an asymptomatic person without any evidence of disease can be considerable. General screening for HHC is therefore not recommended.19,110,112

### Screening People With a Positive Family History

Individuals with a first-degree relative who has been diagnosed with HHC should be tested for HFE mutations and evidence of iron overload. For children of a patient with HHC, it is recommended that the other parent be screened first, because offspring will be affected only if both parents carry a relevant mutation. In

first-degree relatives of C282Y homozygotes, the degree of iron overload is associated with disease severity in the proband. The risk of clinically relevant iron toxicity is extremely low for people who are found to have C282Y or H63D heterozygosity. Infrequently, H63D homozygosity is associated with mild iron 26 excess.

### Screening in Patients With Related Diseases

The European Association for the Study of Liver Diseases has recommended HFE testing in patients with unexplained chronic liver disease and raised transferrin saturation levels (Fig. 123.2). Furthermore, HFE testing should be considered in people with porphyria cutanea tarda, well-defined chondrocalcinosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma and those with late-onset type 1 DM because C282Y homozygosity has a higher prevalence in these conditions. HHC-related genotypes are a risk factor for the development of liver disease in the presence of significant comorbid illness, particularly chronic infectious hepatitis, porphyria cutanea tarda, or steatosis.19,114

### Treatment

Removal of iron from the body can be undertaken by phlebotomy, erythrocytapheresis, or the use of iron chelators. Treatment is divided into the "depletion" stage, which aims to reduce ferritin levels to normal, and the "maintenance" stage, in which the frequency of iron removal is decreased and ferritin levels are monitored. Some, but not all, consequences of iron deposition are reversed by removing iron. Most patients note an improvement in well-being and skin pigmentation; furthermore, amelioration of cardiac function and glucose control, in addition to hepatic fibrosis, has been documented.67, Nevertheless, symptoms of arthritis do not change, and established cirrhosis is irreversible.

Phlebotomy is the mainstay of treatment for iron overload in the setting of HHC. Every 500 mL of whole blood contains up to 250 mg of iron, and thus it can take more than 1 year for iron stores to normalize with weekly venesection. It is recommended that treatment be started when serum ferritin levels are consistently and progressively above normal local reference ranges. Weekly phlebotomy of 500 mL of blood should be guided by ferritin and hemoglobin/hematocrit levels, aiming for serum ferritin of 50 µg/L in the absence of anemia. Transferrin saturation levels are not an accurate measure of therapeutic efficacy because they are relatively resistant to change in iron stores in C282Y homozygotes. In the maintenance phase, the frequency of venesection depends on the response to treatment. Anemia should be avoided because it may trigger further lowering of hepcidin levels and encourage intestinal iron absorption. Although generally safe and well tolerated, adverse effects of blood removal in HHC include cardiac arrhythmias that may develop during rapid mobilization of iron stores. . Vitamin C supplementation may exacerbate such problems by facilitating iron release and increasing pro-oxidant and free radical activity. 19, In many countries, therapeutic phlebotomy from patients with HHC may contribute to the blood donation pool. 110,

Erythrocytapheresis removes more red blood cells per session than phlebotomy and preserves platelets, plasma proteins, and coagulation factors. The target of normal iron levels is achieved more rapidly with this technique in comparison with phlebotomy, but the financial costs are greater. The additional technical

expertise means that erythrocytapheresis is not commonly used to treat iron overload in individuals with HHC.

Iron chelators may be administered orally (e.g., deferasirox) or parenterally (e.g., deferoxamine); however, these drugs are associated with more adverse effects than phlebotomy and thus are reserved for patients who are intolerant of regular venesec- .115, Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) can potentially contion. tribute to reduced iron absorption because reduced gastric acid secretion lowers the solubility of inorganic iron, thereby decreasing its absorption. Furthermore, they may influence iron uptake into red blood cells, a process that requires proton cotransport. Currently, however, there is no evidence to show that chronic use of PPIs significantly affects iron levels in patients with HHC.

High doses of vitamin C facilitate iron release and increase prooxidant and free radical activity. 19, Therefore patients with HHC should not take supplemental vitamin C but can continue to eat fresh produce containing this substance. Other dietary recommendations include the reduction or avoidance of food containing high doses of iron, such as red meat and internal organs. Uncooked shellfish is a particular hazard because of the risk of contamination with V. vulnificus. Some alcoholic drinks contain iron, and all are potentially hepatotoxic. Alcohol should be consumed only occasionally because it seems to have a synergistic effect in the presence of iron overload on the development of cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma. Maintenance of normal body weight is important to avoid the hepatic damage associated with steatosis.

Just as the pathogenesis of joint pain in HHC is unclear, treatment of arthritis in this condition is unsatisfactory, and joint symptoms may progress despite effective phlebotomy. Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, colchicine, and intra-articular corticosteroids may be helpful in some cases. Osteoporosis is a potential disease complication, particularly in the setting of hypogonadism or reduced thyroid function.
