CARLOS J. LOZADA AND MARIA CARPINTERO

### KEY POINTS

### Introduction

Hemoglobin (Hb) has a tetrameric structure consisting of two α-globin and two nonα-globin polypeptide chains, each associated with a heme group. The interaction of these chains is responsible for the quaternary structure of the Hb molecule and its normal function. The fundamental role of Hb is oxygen transport.

Hemoglobinopathies are inherited diseases caused by mutations in globin genes resulting in varying defects in the synthesis and structure of hemoglobin. Abnormalities in hemoglobin can alter red cell shape, deformability, and viscosity. Approximately 1000 mutations have been described1; however, most are not associated with clinical disease. The gene mutations that result in sickle cell disease and thalassemia syndromes cause diseases that often involve the musculoskeletal system and will be discussed in this chapter.

### Thalassemia

The term thalassemia is derived from a Greek term that roughly means "the sea (Mediterranean) in the blood" and was used to describe anemias in people from Italy and Greece. The term is now used to refer to inherited defects in the synthesis of one or more of the αor β-hemoglobin subunits. Individual syndromes are named according to the globin chain of which the synthesis

is adversely affected. For example, α-globin chains are absent or reduced in patients with α-thalassemia; β-globin chains are absent or reduced in patients with β-thalassemia; δand β-globin chains are absent or reduced in patients with δβ-thalassemia; and so on. Thalassemias are inherited as pathologic alleles of one or more of the globin genes located on chromosomes 11 (β) and 16 (α) and range from total deletion or rearrangement of the loci to point mutations that impair transcription, processing, or translation of globin messenger RNA.

As a consequence of reduced globin chain production, a reduction of functioning Hb tetramers occurs. Impaired globin synthesis leads to an imbalance of the individual αand β-subunits. Free or "unpaired" α-, β-, and γ-globin chains are either highly insoluble or form homotetramers (Hb H and Hb Bart's) that cannot release oxygen normally or are relatively unstable and precipitate as the cell ages. Excess α-globin chains, for example, continue to accumulate and precipitate in individuals with β-thalassemia. Unpaired subunits are the major sources of morbidity and mortality (Tables 125.1 and 125.2). Several genotypes are associated with thalassemia. Hypochromia and microcytosis are found in all patients with thalassemia. In milder forms of the disease, these changes may be subclinical, causing few or no symptoms (thalassemia minor), while patients with severe disease typically present with transfusion-dependent anemia due to hemolysis (thalassemia major).

Thalassemias have been encountered in virtually every ethnic group and geographic location but are most common in the Mediterranean basin and tropical or subtropical regions of Asia and Africa. The "thalassemia belt" extends from the Mediterranean across the Arabian Peninsula, extending through Turkey, Iran, and India to southeastern Asia and southern China. The prevalence of thalassemia in these regions ranges from 2.5% to 15%. As with sickle cell anemia, thalassemia is most common in areas affected by endemic malaria. Malaria occurring in thalassemia heterozygotes results in milder infection and confers a selective advantage on reproductive fitness. The gene frequency of thalassemia has become fixed and remains highest in populations exposed to malaria over many centuries.

### Sickle Cell Anemia and Related Disorders

Sickle cell anemia is a single-gene disorder caused by homozygous inheritance for sickle Hb (Hb S). Hb S is the result of a single nucleotide substitution of valine for glutamic acid, the sixth

amino acid in the β-globin chain. Hb S is capable of carrying oxygen, but once the oxygen is released, the Hb joins with other Hb S molecules to form rigid rods that bend the normally flexible, diskshaped red blood cells into distorted narrow crescents. The sickled cells impede blood flow when they stick to the walls of blood vessels and to other blood cells. About 10% of black Americans are heterozygotes, inheriting a sickle globin gene from one parent and a normal gene from the other parent, and have sickle cell trait. Those with sickle trait generally demonstrate no significant clinical consequences unless they are subjected to marked dehydration or hypoxia. Rarely these individuals develop splenic infarction, stroke, or sudden death after strenuous physical activity, particularly at a high altitude. Individuals with sickle cell trait may have impaired ability to form concentrated urine (hyposthenuria), and a few have episodes of painless hematuria as a result of medullary infarction. Other internal organ damage is extremely uncommon, and heterozygotes overall experience a normal life expectancy.

One-fourth of the children of whose parents both have sickle trait are homozygotes and have red blood cells containing Hb

S (HB SS) without Hb A. These individuals suffer from severe hemolytic anemia and episodes of vaso-occlusion that cause acute bouts of pain and progressive organ damage. A similar clinical phenotype is encountered in individuals who are compound heterozygotes—that is, those who inherit the sickle gene from one parent and, from the other parent, either a β-thalassemia gene or a gene that encodes Hb C or another β-globin structural mutant. Patients with S/β° thalassemia1 are unable to make any Hb A and are as severely affected as those with Hb SS disease. In contrast, patients with Hb S/β+-thalassemia or with Hb SC disease have less morbidity and a longer life span.

The hallmark of sickle cell disease is the vaso-occlusive pain crisis,4 which is the most common clinical manifestation but can occur with varying frequency in different individuals. It results from the complex interplay between sickled red blood cells, neutrophils, endothelium, and plasma factors. The result is tissue hypoxia, leading to tissue death and associated pain. Episodes may be precipitated by dehydration, infection, and cold weather, although in half of the cases, no precipitating factor is found. Repeated splenic infarctions in childhood result in "autosplenectomy" and loss of splenic function by age 6 to 8 years in approximately one-half of patients.

### Epidemiology

Sickle cell disease is the most common hemoglobinopathy worldwide. The prevalence is higher in Sub-Saharan Africa, the Mediterranean basin, Middle East, and Asian/India, due to the protection the mutation provides against severe malaria. In Europe, it is estimated that 20,000 to 25,000 individuals are affected with sickle cell disease, although numbers are increasing due to immigration, particularly in Northern Europe. Sickle cell disease is also found in Greece and southern Italy, where β-thalassemia is also endemic.

It is estimated that 72,000 to 98,000 individuals in the United States have Hb SS, and around 300,000 babies are born with the disease worldwide each year; the numbers are expected to increase with gains in life expectancy related to systematic newborn screening and earlier intervention. Although life expectancy has improved with sickle cell disease, mortality remains high from both acute and chronic complications. 6,8

### Screening and Diagnosis

Preconception, antenatal, and neonatal screening have been implemented in the United States, Europe, India, and in some parts of the middle East and Africa. Preconception screening identifies asymptomatic parents whose newborn might be affected by sickle cell disease. Antenatal screening is performed with chorionic villus analysis, but new techniques have been in development to detect abnormal fetal DNA as early as week 4 of gestation. Universal newborn screening is mandatory in the United States and in most European countries for both sickle cell disease and thalassemia. Diagnosis is confirmed using DNA analysis to detect hemoglobin variants. Such screening tests vary in other areas of the world; some African counties, for example, have developed screening programs that are not universal and have encountered multiple challenges.

### Treatment

Optimal care for patients with sickle cell disease and thalassemia includes a multidisciplinary approach to treat the multiple manifestations and prevent end organ damage. In addition to supportive measures including red blood cell transfusion, a growing

number of medications have been demonstrated to provide therapeutic benefit.

Hydroxycarbamide (hydroxyurea) continues to be the first-line management to treat sickle cell disease. It reduces the number of painful episodes, transfusions, and hospitalizations, but only about two-thirds of adult patients have a response to this drug.

In recent years, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved three novel therapies for the treatment of sickle cell disease. L-Glutamine was approved in 2017 for patients 5 years or older with sickle cell disease. It decreases the frequency of painful episodes and hospitalizations. Crizanlizumab is a monoclonal antibody that binds to P-selectin. Triggered by inflammation, P-selectin expression is increased in endothelium and platelets and promotes vaso-occlusion in sickle cell disease. It was approved in 2019 to reduce the frequency of painful episodes in patients with or without concomitant hydroxyurea. Voxelotor is a polymerization inhibitor also approved in 2019 for the treatment of sickle cell disease in patients 12 years or older. Voxelotor increases oxygen affinity, thus decreasing hemolysis and improving hemoglobin levels without increasing the frequency of vaso-occlusive episodes.

Hematopoietic stem cell transplant with a fully matched donor represents a potential cure for sickle cell disease,13 although transplants are expensive, are not widely available, and have associated risks such as infections and life-threatening immune-system reactions with nonautologous donors.

Gene therapy is emerging as a potential treatment and possible cure for sickle cell disease. Conventional gene therapy, also known as gene addition, typically involves inserting new genes. Modification of harvested stem cells with a viral vector that is modified with the gene to be inserted. The virus then searches out the cells and inserts the gene into the cells' DNA, correcting the sickle cell mutation, after which the cells are transplanted into the patient. Gene editing is more specific when the faulty DNA sequence is removed and a piece of laboratory-created DNA is inserted. In both approaches, the modified DNA dictates the formation of a normal, working protein. A pilot study14 reported reduction or elimination of clinical manifestations using a viral vector in six patients with sickle-cell disease.

### Musculoskeletal Involvement: Sickle Cell Disease

### Vaso-occlusive e Crisis of Bone

Bone involvement in sickle cell patients is the most common clinical manifestation of the disease (Table 125.3), both as an acute process and as a chronic symptom. Painful osteo-articular crisis was the most common reason for emergency care of children with sickle cell disease in an African population (58.6%). Nearly all patients experience painful vaso-occlusive crises, which usually begin in late infancy and continue throughout life. Patients typically complain of pain; the episode can affect any area of the body, with the chest, low back, and extremities most commonly affected. Abdominal pain may mimic acute abdomen of other causes. Fever is often present, even in the absence of infection. Although microvascular occlusion can occur in any organ, it is common in tissues with low blood flow, such as the bone marrow, where deoxygenation and polymerization of Hb S leads to bone thrombosis, infarction, and necrosis. Spinal cord infarction can occur. The medullary cavity and epiphysis of long bones are frequently affected (Fig. 125.1). Patients have severe pain in one or

more areas of their bones, with tenderness, erythema, and swelling overlying areas of infarcted bone. Systemic symptoms including fever and leukocytosis may occur, and most patients generally recover without sequelae.

When infarction involves the vertebral body, collapse and a fish mouth deformity can result. Bone infarctions can occur in any bone, with a predilection for long bones. The most common sites are the tibia/fibula (30%), femur (25%), and the radius, ulna, or humerus (21%). Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is sensitive in detecting bone marrow infarction, but this technology is not useful in dDistinguishing acute infarction from osteomyelitis.

### Dactylitis

In children younger than 7 years of age, vaso-occlusion can manifest in the bone marrow of the small bones of the hands and feet, resulting in dactylitis21 (also called handfoot syndrome). Patients typically present with painful swelling of one or more digits (Fig. 125.2), as extensive infarction of the marrow, medullary trabeculae, and inner layer of cortical bone occur. Subperiosteal new bone formation follows, and as the episode resolves within 2 weeks, radiographs show a "moth-eaten" appearance of the involved digits (Fig. 125.3). Rarely, involvement of the epiphysis causes premature fusion of growth plates and shortened digits.

### Osteomyelitis

Patients with sickle cell disease have an increased risk of infections, including osteomyelitis,22 particularly from encapsulated organisms that are presumably secondary to loss of functional splenic tissue. The most common cause of osteomyelitis is Salmonella, followed by Staphylococcus aureus, and gram-negative enteric bacteria. One proposed explanation for the frequency of bowel organism—derived infections has been intravascular sickling leading to microinfarctions of the bowel. The diagnosis

of osteomyelitis in the context of sickle cell disease is an important management issue because the clinical symptoms of pain, swelling, tenderness, and fever are similar to those of bony vasoocclusive crises. Elevated markers of inflammation occur in both conditions. No single laboratory test or imaging modality reliably differentiates osteomyelitis from infarction. Until a definite diagnosis can be made, empiric treatment with anti-microbial therapy should be provided.

### Acute Synovitis and Septic Arthritis

When the epiphysis is involved by infarction during sickle cell crisis, a joint effusion may develop, presenting clinically as an

Synovial fluid should be examined and cultured to rule out infection. In a retrospective review of 2000 consecutive adult patients with sickle cell disease, 3% had septic arthritis.5, The majority of these patients (56 of 59) had Hb SS. Of the 59 infections, 36 involved the hip. The most common signs and symptoms included pain, swelling, and fevers higher than 38.2° C. Laboratory abnormalities among those with sickle cell disease and septic arthritis included a peripheral white blood cell count >15,000/ mm3, erythrocyte sedimentation rate >24 mm/hour, and C-reactive protein >20 mg/L. Cultures were positive in 96% of the joint aspirates, with staphylococcus and gram-negative infections the most common. Prior diagnoses of osteonecrosis, osteomyelitis, and comorbid medical conditions of diabetes mellitus and use of corticosteroids and hydoxyurea were associated with the risk of septic arthritis. Thus clinicians should have a high index of suspicion for septic arthritis in patients with sickle cell disease presenting with fever and joint pain. Distant osteomyelitis was more often the source of a joint infection than contiguous osteomyelitis.

Patients with sickle cell disease can present with arthritis, often polyarticular (80%) and symmetric (60%) involving the large joints of the lower extremity. Symptoms last less than 1 week, and radiographic changes are consistent with periarticular osteopenia, erosions of bone, and joint space narrowing.

### Growth Disturbance

A majority of children with sickle cell disease show declines in growth compared with normal peers. Puberty onset is delayed

on average by 12 to 24 months, as is skeletal age. Factors such as nutritional status and inactivity can potentially be optimized and to decrease the adverse effects on growth. Delayed skeletal maturation in children can also occur.

### Osteopenia and Osteoporosis

Osteopenia and osteoporosis are common in Hb SS disease, especially given the young age of disease onset in patients, overlapping with the critical period of bone development. The lumbar spine appears to be the site most often affected. Low body mass index is a consistent correlate of decreased bone density, as are low vitamin D levels.

### Osteonecrosis

Vaso-occlusion resulting in infarction of articular surfaces of long bones occurs most commonly in the femur, followed by the humerus, knees (distal femur or proximal tibia), and small joints of the hands and feet. Although previously thought to occur with increased frequency in Hb SC disease, its prevalence is greatest in patients with Hb SS disease. By the age of 33 years, 50% of patients experience avascular necrosis of the femoral head. The presence of concurrent deletional α-thalassemia and a history of frequent vaso-occlusive crises are classic risk factors for femoral avascular necrosis. Patients present with chronic joint pain with a progressive decrease in range of motion of affected joints. Multiple joints are commonly involved. The vast majority of untreated patients with avascular necrosis progress to femoral head collapse within 5 years. Symptoms nearly always precede hip collapse. The duration to collapse appears to be shorter with more advanced stages at study onset, with a majority of patients progressing to symptomatic avascular necrosis that requires intervention.

Avascular necrosis has been treated with a number of modalities including core decompression, osteotomy, bone grafting, surface arthroplasty, and joint replacement. The only randomized trial in avascular necrosis compared core decompression and physical therapy versus physical therapy alone and did not show a difference in outcome between the two arms; however, follow-up was short, and a significant number of stage III hips were included. Core decompression is a useful option in earlystage avascular necrosis. Several studies associate total hip replacement in individuals with sickle cell disease with a higher rate of orthopedic and medical complications36,37; however, other studies show a lower rate of orthopedic complications. Structural bone diseases in people with sickle cell disease make joint replacement technically challenging.

### Iron Metabolism

Red blood cell transfusion is a mainstay in the treatment of sickle cell disease complications. Most patients receive at least one transfusion in their lifetime, usually for acute complications. Blood transfusions increase arterial oxygen pressure and Hb oxygen affinity, thereby reducing red blood cell sickling and improving microvascular perfusion. Furthermore, regular blood transfusion regimens suppress endogenous erythropoiesis and therefore the production of red cells containing Hb S. Iron metabolism and consequently patterns of iron loading differ in sickle cell disease and thalassemia.

Erythropoiesis is variably increased in sickle cell disease, but it is not ineffective. Unlike patients with thalassemia, patients with nontransfused sickle cell disease do not develop systemic iron

overload because of increased iron absorption, and they may actually present with iron deficiency, possibly related to intravascular hemolysis and the resulting excessive urinary loss of iron. Inflammation, which is part of the pathophysiology of sickle cell disease, increases synthesis of hepcidin and consequently decreases iron absorption and enhances retention of iron within the reticuloendothelial system. As a result, tissues and organs are less commonly affected by iron overload in sickle cell disease than in thalassemia. When it does occur, musculoskeletal manifestations of iron overload include a symmetric, polyarticular arthropathy with bony enlargement. Notably, iron overload preferentially affects the second and third metacarpophalangeal joints in addition to the proximal interphalangeal joints, wrists, elbows, shoulders, and hips.

### Musculoskeletal Involvement: Thalassemia

### Decreased Bone Density and Osteoporosis

Skeletal changes in people with untreated thalassemia are related to bone marrow hyperplasia, cortical resorption, rarefaction of cancellous bone with coarsening of the trabeculae, and a generalized decrease in bone density (Table 125.4). In patients with thalassemia major, onset of the radiographic changes can be seen in their first year of life. Involvement of the spine, skull and facial bones, ribs, and metaphyses of long bones are typical. Osteoporosis is present in a substantial proportion of individuals with thalassemia intermedia (49% in one cohort), with higher bone density values in those never transfused, as well as in those who had not undergone splenectomy.

In the spine, osteoporosis and cortical thinning are associated with vertebral compression fractures (Fig. 125.4). After an initial increase in the height-to-width ratio of the vertebral body, thinning of the subchondral bone plates occurs and the bones become biconcave and wedge-shaped as multiple compression fractures occur. Patients can experience scoliosis and kyphosis. Lateral plain radiographs of the spine may show a "bone-within-a-bone" appearance as the end plate depression is evident (Fig. 125.5). MRI demonstrates a predominance of red marrow in the vertebrae and early degeneration of the intervertebral discs of the lower thoracic and lumbar spine. Abnormal intravertebral iron deposition can also be seen. One small clinical trial enrolled women with thalassemia major—related osteoporosis and demonstrated increased bone mass and decreased bone turnover with strontium ranelate therapy.' 45

### Extramedullary Hematopoiesis

Extramedullary hematopoiesis is seen as extraosseous extension of red marrow with symmetric lobulated confluent masses expanding

in the paravertebral and presacral spaces. These soft tissue masses have intermediate T1 signals, variable intensity of T2-weighted sequences, and mild gadolinium enhancement. Radionuclide imaging with technetium-labeled sulfur colloid may help define the hematopoetic nature of the masses. Spinal cord compression occasionally occurs as a result of epidural marrow extension. In

the skull, marrow expansion causes widening with thinning of the outer table and thickening of the inner table, with remodeling of the skull (tower skull; Fig. 125.6).

### Iron Metabolism

The anemia of thalassemia major typically becomes symptomatic between 6 months and 2 years of age, requiring the institution of a regular transfusion program. As a consequence of continuous anemia, erythropoiesis, although inefficient, can be intense; the bone marrow undergoes an marked expansion with consequent distortion of facial features, and the plasma volume increases. In addition, hepatosplenomegaly develops. A regimen maintaining a minimum Hb concentration of 9.5 to 10.5 g/ dL can prevent the aforementioned complications and fosters normal growth at least until puberty. Transfusion therapy, however, may result in iron overload in various tissues. Thus iron chelation therapy prevents accumulation of iron, promotes normal growth, and improves survival in patients with thalassemia requiring chronic transfusions. Deferoxamine chelation is effective but challenging to use because of its cost and the inconvenience of prolonged subcutaneous infusions. Deferiprone, an oral iron chelator, is more often used and offers improved compliance over deferoxamine. Mild arthralgias and/or arthritis involving the knees may occur in up to 38% of patients receiving deferiprone,48 which is usually self-limited or responsive to conservative management with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory agents. Some patients, however, can develop severe arthropathy related to deferiprone, requiring discontinuation of iron chelation therapy. Subchondral erosions can be seen on radiographs of the long bones of the hands in symptomatic children treated with deferiprone.

### Comorbid Rheumatic Disease

### Autoimmune Disorders

Autoimmune diseases, including rheumatoid arthritis (RA) and systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), have been reported in patients with hemoglobinopathies. Up to 50% of patients are positive for anti-nuclear antibodies. Several cases of mild recurrent arthritis have occurred in patients with thalassemia. RA is uncommonly diagnosed in patients with sickle cell disease. They can present with similar symptoms, although some authors have reported RA in younger patients with sickle cell disease. Patients carrying both diagnoses have more hospital admissions and more radiographic erosive changes. The prevalence and clinical features of RA in patients with thalassemia is unknown. One group reported that rheumatoid factor was detected in 23% of 90 patients, while anti-citrullinated protein antibodies were detected in only 2% in patients with thalassemia or sickle cell disease followed over a decade in Greece. Patients with RA had no other specific features that distinguished them from the patients with only hematologic disease. Patients with sickle cell disease and co-existing RA benefit from disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs), but data are lacking regarding the safety profile of the available therapies. Methotrexate has been used with improvement of the disease activity, pain, and quality of life. The safety of etanercept was preliminarily examined in a small study of eight patients with sickle cell disease and concomitant RA.

Autoimmune disease in patients with sickle cell disease may go undiagnosed, or diagnosis may be delayed as a result of shared clinical manifestations and multiorgan involvement. The presence of SLE and sickle cell disease, although uncommon, has been reported.57-59 Recognition of an autoimmune disease in patients with sickle cell disease may require the use of immunosuppressive medications including glucocorticoids that have been linked to exacerbations of sickle cell disease.

Autoimmune hepatitis (AIH) is rarely recognized in patients with sickle cell disease. One small study observed AIH in 13 of 77 patients, suggesting a higher prevalence than in the general population. Standard immunosuppressive therapy is used in patients with concomitant AIH and sickle cell disease with successful outcomes reported in patients undergoing liver transplantation.

### Gout

Increased red blood cell turnover in sickle cell disease leads to hyperuricemia, as can renal tubular involvement and a decrease in uric acid excretion. Hyperuricemia is a risk factor for declining renal function in patients with sickle cell. A retrospective review observed a 14% prevalence of gout in patients with sickle cell disease. In this study, gout was more common among those with Hb SS, hyperuricemia, and low hemoglobin. As with concomitant autoimmune disease, gout can be underdiagnosed due to low index of suspicion or confusion with other manifestations of sickle cell disease.

### Conclusion

Hemoglobinopathies, particularly sickle cell disease and the thalassemias, are often associated with significant and varied musculoskeletal manifestations, including osteonecrosis, osteomyelitis, arthropathies, and vertebral fractures. Perhaps under-recognized

in practice, awareness of the clinical presentations associated with these manifestations is essential to facilitate early recognition and effective management.

### KEY POINTS

Immunoglobulin G4-related disease (IgG4-RD) is an immune-mediated condition capable of affecting any organ of the body. The most commonly involved tissues are the major salivary glands, lacrimal gland, pancreas, orbits, biliary tree, and retroperitoneum.

Most patients have elevated serum IgG4 concentrations, often to extremely high levels, but there is a wide range of values across patients. When elevated at baseline, the serum IgG4 concentration is a useful biomarker of disease activity.

The hallmark pathology features of IgG4-RD are a lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate with a high percentage of plasma cells staining for IgG4, storiform fibrosis, obliterative phlebitis, and mild to moderate tissue eosinophilia. The foundation of the diagnosis rests upon solid clinicopathologic correlation.

Nearly all IgG4-RD patients respond to glucocorticoids, but most patients ultimately require long-term maintenance therapy or intermittent retreatment. Most patients' disease cannot be controlled sufficiently over the long term with tolerable doses of glucocorticoids.

B cell depletion strategies appear to be effective, perhaps in part through their interference with the antigen presentation by B cells to T cells. Other therapeutic strategies under investigation include B cell modulation efforts and depletion of cells of both the B and T cell lineages that bear SLAM-F7 on their surfaces.

### Introduction

Immunoglobulin G4-related disease (IgG4-RD) is a multiorgan immune-mediated condition that mimics many malignant, infectious, and inflammatory disorders.1-3 The diagnosis links numerous conditions once regarded as isolated single-organ diseases that existed outside of any known underlying systemic condition (Table 126.1). IgG4-RD has many similarities to sarcoidosis and certain forms of systemic vasculitis, being a remarkably protean condition in which the histopathologic findings are consistent across a wide range of organ systems. Classification criteria for IgG4-RD have been developed by the American College of Rheumatology (ACR) and the European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology (EULAR).

The growing awareness of IgG4-RD is critical, because this condition generally responds well to therapy, and the approaches to the treatment of IgG4-RD differ significantly from those of its mimics. IgG4-RD has a tendency to form mass lesions and is therefore often confused with cancer. Moreover, autoimmune disorders such as Sjögren's syndrome, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, systemic lupus erythematosus, and idiopathic membranous

nephropathy can be difficult to distinguish from IgG4-RD in many circumstances. Understanding the immune dysregulation associated with IgG4-RD has provided important insights into the processes of fibrosis, B and T lymphocyte cross-talk, and approaches to antigen identification.

### Epidemiology

Mapping the epidemiology of IgG4-RD has been hampered by insufficient awareness of this relatively newly recognized disease. IgG4-RD first crept into the medical literature as a unique entity only in 2003,5,6 and a reasonable picture of the disease's epidemiology is only now beginning to emerge. Epidemiologic studies are hampered by disease underrecognition, frequent difficulties in confirming the diagnosis even if it is suspected, and the absence of a unique International Classification of Diagnoses (ICD) code.

Much of the early understanding of the epidemiology of IgG4- RD was based on cohort studies from tertiary care centers. These reported consistently that the disease most often affects individuals in the fifth through the seventh decades of life but noted that cases are observed across the full spectrum of age, from toddlers to nonagenarians. Case series also suggested that IgG4-RD was characterized by a male predominance but that the sex distribution varies substantially, affecting different organs. The male predilection for most organ systems and for the disease overall contrasts with the classic autoimmune diseases. Nevertheless, women can clearly manifest the full panoply of organ system presentations.

Investigation of a large insurance claims database recently yielded important observations about the epidemiology of IgG4- RD in the United States. Two-thirds of the patients were white, consistent with the clinical observation that the disease occurs indiscriminately across the range of human races and ethnicities. The mean age was 56.5 years, and surprisingly, 58% were female. During the period of observation covered by the study (2015 to 2019), the incidence of IgG4-RD increased from 0.78 to 1.39 per 100,000 person-years, with an average annual incidence rate of IgG4-RD during that period of 1.20 per 100,000 person-years. This estimate is likely conservative, however, because the incidence of IgG4-RD appears to be growing substantially— nearly doubling over the 4-year period of the study. The increasing incidence is likely attributable to broader awareness in the medical community. The point prevalence on January 1, 2019, was 5.3/100,000 persons. The data from this study overall suggest that the incidence and prevalence of IgG4-RD are similar to those of anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody-associated vasculitis (AAV) and systemic sclerosis. 10,

IgG4-RD is associated with a significant increase in mortality rate. The adjusted hazard ratio for death among patients with IgG4-RD compared with ageand sex-matched controls was 2.51 (95% confidence interval [CI], 1.76 to 3.56), a figure that places it on par with AAV in terms of mortality rates. A substantial portion of this increased mortality risk in IgG4-RD appears to be related to the fact that glucocorticoids remain the first line of treatment.

Human leukocyte antigen (HLA) associations and other potential genetic links of IgG4-RD remain incompletely characterized. Detailed genetic studies with sufficient power have not yet been undertaken, but familial cases are rare.

### Classification Criteria

The ACR and EULAR classification criteria for IgG4-RD, published in 2020, have a sensitivity of 86% and a specificity of 99%. There are three steps to classification. First, a potential IgG4-RD case must fulfill initial entry criteria, requiring the disease involvement in at least one of eleven typical organs. These organs include the pancreas, bile ducts, orbits, lacrimal glands, major salivary glands, lungs, kidneys, aorta, retroperitoneum, pachymeninges, and thyroid gland (Riedel's thyroiditis).

Second, the potential case is evaluated for the presence of exclusion criteria (Table 126.2). The exclusion criteria consist of a total of 32 clinical, serologic, radiologic, and pathologic items that, if present, eliminate the patient from IgG4-RD classification.

Finally, eight weighted inclusion criteria domains are considered. The inclusion criteria address clinical findings, serologic results, radiology assessments, and pathology interpretations. Weights of the individual items of the inclusion criteria domains are shown in Tables 126.3 and 126.4. Potential cases that achieve a minimum of 20 inclusion criteria points may be classified as IgG4-RD, assuming they have involvement of a typical organ and do not fulfill any of the exclusion criteria.

### Pathology Features

### IgG4-RD as a Variable-Vessel Vasculitis

Substantial evidence now exists that IgG4-RD should be regarded as a primary form of vasculitis. IgG4-RD has a remarkable capability to affect blood vessels of nearly any type. In fact, IgG4-RD is among the most versatile forms of vasculitis known. IgG4-RD is a variable-vessel vasculitis that can affect blood vessels as large as the aorta and as small as post-capillary venules, if not the capillaries themselves. The most commonly described pathology manifestation of the vascular disease in IgG4-RD is obliterative phlebitis, a microscopic finding that is a widely recognized pathology hallmark of this condition (discussed further below). Furthermore, the well-known clinical features of small-vessel vasculitis, which typically present as cutaneous leukocytoclastic vasculitis, are also reported. 14-17

IgG4-RD can also affect the aorta in the manner of other largevessel vasculitides such as giant cell arteritis and Takayasu's arteritis. 18-23 In addition, IgG4-RD frequently leads to a "periaortitis," particularly in the abdominal aorta, which often accompanies retroperitoneal fibrosis. 24

IgG4-RD is capable of affecting medium-sized blood vessels, as well, particularly the coronary arteries. Coronary artery involvement in IgG4-RD can lead to wall thickening, periarterial soft tissue encasement, luminal stenosis, arterial wall calcification, and coronary aneurysms or ectasia. Coronary artery aneurysms, including focal fusiform aneurysms and diffuse vascular ectasia, occur commonly (Fig. 126.1). No other known form of vasculitis affects the coronary arteries of adults in this manner. The closest disease analogy is to IgG4-RD in this respect is Kawasaki's disease, which occurs essentially exclusively in children under the age of 5.

### Morphologic Change of Affected Organs

Transformations in the gross pathology of affected organs occur in IgG4-RD. The pancreas and kidneys become diffusely enlarged. In contrast, ductal organs (e.g., bile duct, bronchus) assume the appearance of a pipe stem, with diffuse wall thickening.

### Histologic Features

A defining feature of IgG4-RD is the similarity of the histologic appearance regardless of the organ affected. The hallmark morphologic findings include a dense lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate rich in IgG4+ plasma cells (Fig. 126.2Å and Fig. 126.2B). This lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate is enmeshed by an irregular, whorled fibrotic process that is termed "storiform" fibrosis (Fig. 126.2C). Obliterative phlebitis, resulting in destruction of the vascular wall and venous lumen, is another characteristic lesion observed in the majority of cases (Fig. 126.3). Obliterative arteritis is also observed in some organs, particularly the lung. Eosinophilic infiltration occurs in approximately 50% of cases, regardless of the organ involved.

### Immunostaining

The preponderance of plasma cells within tissue lesions stain for IgG4. An increase in the number of IgG4+ plasma cells/highpower field (hpf) and an elevated IgG4+/IgG+ plasma cell ratio can therefore support the diagnosis of IgG4-RD, but careful clinicopathologic correlation and sound clinical judgment must be exercised in rendering the diagnosis of IgG4-RD. An important issue pertains to the total number of IgG4+ plasma cells needed to regard a biopsy as being "diagnostic" of IgG4-RD. In fact, no number of IgG4+ plasma cells within a biopsy is sufficient to support the diagnosis of IgG4-RD on its own. Neither the number of IgG4+ plasma cells per high-power field nor the IgG4+/IgG+ plasma cell ratio is specific for the diagnosis of IgG4-RD. Rather, the finding of the characteristic histopathology in the right clinical context allows the pathologist and clinician to reach the diagnosis in collaboration. "Positive" IgG4 immunostaining lends additional support to the diagnosis of IgG4-RD but is not diagnostic in and of itself.

One may expect fewer IgG4+ plasma cells in biopsies from patients with fibrotic lesions such as retroperitoneal fibrosis (RPF) because of the overwhelmingly fibrotic nature of the pathology at the time of biopsy in most patients. In such patients, as few as 10 IgG4+ plasma cells/hpf may be regarded as supportive of the diagnosis of IgG4-RD, particularly if the remainder of the clinical and

pathology features are consistent with that diagnosis. In contrast, the number of IgG4+ plasma cells/hpf is generally much higher in biopsies of the major salivary glands, lacrimal glands, pancreas, lungs, kidneys, and many other organs.

The IgG4+/IgG+ plasma cell ratio can also be a useful metric to aid in diagnosis. Most cases of documented IgG4-RD have an

IgG4+/IgG+ plasma cell ratio of >40%. This value has been proposed as a criterion for diagnosis across all organs. The IgG4+/ IgG+ plasma cell ratio can be particularly helpful in the setting of advanced fibrosis (e.g., in RPF), when the paucity of cells makes large concentrations of IgG4+ plasma cells unlikely.

### Serum IgG4 Concentrations

Serum IgG4 measurements play an important role in the diagnosis and management of IgG4-RD, but the relevance of IgG4 levels must be considered from several angles.

### Dramatic IgG4 Elevations

A serum IgG4 level is often the first diagnostic test ordered when IgG4-RD is suspected. Large elevations of serum IgG4 concentrations (e.g., on the order of six to eight times the upper limit of normal for a given assay) strongly suggest the diagnosis. Nevertheless, a very high serum IgG4 concentration is not diagnostic of IgG4-RD. We queried the data warehouses at two large academic medical centers——Stanford University and Mass General Brigham—to examine the positive predictive value (PPV) of a serum IgG4 concentration ≥ 5 times the upper limit of normal. A diagnosis of IgG4-RD was determined using the ACR/EULAR Classification Criteria for IgG4-RD. The study reported a PPV of 73% for IgG4- RD among patients with elevations of serum IgG4 at least five times the upper limit of normal. Although these data support the significant weight placed on very elevated serum IgG4 in the classification criteria,4 it is notable that 27% of patients with such high IgG4 concentrations had either an alternative diagnosis to IgG4-RD or no identifiable cause of the serum IgG4 elevation. This underscores the importance of the classification criteria's entry and exclusion criteria when evaluating a patient with a very high IgG4 concentration for IgG4-RD.

Patients with multiorgan disease can have dramatic elevations in serum IgG4 concentrations, occasionally exceeding 4 or 5 g/dL. In such cases, the prozone effect may lead to spuriously low IgG4 measurements in nephelometry assays, requiring additional dilutions of a patient's sample. Patients with IgG4-RD also often have elevations of other IgG subclasses (particularly IgG1, IgG2,

and IgG3). The elevations of serum IgG4 concentrations, however, are usually disproportionate to those of the other subclasses.

### IgG4: The e Tissue/Serum Paradox

Despite the frequently striking serum IgG4 concentrations observed in patients with this disease, an important paradox exists. Among patients with active disease whose cases are identified on the basis of histopathology rather than by elevations in serum IgG4 concentrations, just over half of the patients have elevated serum IgG4 concentrations before treatment. In contrast, when cases were sought by querying a hospital laboratory database about the number of patients with abnormally high serum IgG4 measurements, the sensitivity of an elevated serum IgG4 concentration was 90%.

Two major points should be drawn from these studies. First, a large proportion of patients with biopsy-proven, clinically validated IgG4-RD have normal serum IgG4 concentrations, even before beginning treatment. Reliance upon serum IgG4 concentration elevations for diagnosis, therefore, leads to dangerous underdiagnosis. Second, among patients with elevated serum IgG4 levels, the range of values is extremely broad. The factors contributing to such variability in the IgG4 response remain poorly defined, but patients with the involvement of multiple organs tend to have the highest blood concentrations of IgG4.

### IgG4 as a Biomarker of Disease Activity

The relationship between serum IgG4 concentrations and disease activity in many patients—assuming that the serum IgG4 value is elevated at baseline—is strong enough in many patients to be a valuable disease biomarker. The relationship between serum IgG4 and disease activity is not, however, perfect. In a large retrospective study of type 1 autoimmune pancreatitis from 17 centers in Japan,30 serum IgG4 levels declined in all patients after treatment with glucocorticoids but remained above the upper limit of normal in 63% of the patients despite good clinical responses. Of the patients who relapsed, 30% had normal serum IgG4 levels at the time of relapse. Thus serum IgG4 concentrations should not be relied upon exclusively as an indicator of disease activity. Nevertheless, if a patient has a large serum IgG4 elevation at baseline, serial measurement is likely to be extremely useful as a biomarker of disease activity and a predictor of disease flare, particularly if patients are not continued on a remission maintenance regimen of glucocorticoids.

### Serum IgG4 in Other Conditions

Mild IgG4 elevations are common across a variety of conditions that can mimic IgG4-RD. Vasculitides such as granulomatosis with polyangiitis and eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis, bronchiectasis, biliary diseases such as primary sclerosing cholangitis, pancreatic cancer, and multiple others can have confoundingly high serum IgG4 concentrations, although they rarely, if ever, reach the highest values achieved by some patients with IgG4-RD. This imposes additional limitations on the diagnostic interpretation of an elevated serum IgG4; namely, false-positive elevations of serum IgG4 are common.

In summary, substantial elevations in serum IgG4 levels are useful in suggesting the diagnosis of IgG4-RD but are not diagnostic in and of themselves. A large minority of patients with histopathologically confirmed disease—on the order of 40%—have

normal serum IgG4 concentrations. The finding of normal serum IgG4 concentrations is particularly high within the subset of patients with primarily fibrotic disease. Patients with RPF, Riedel's thyroiditis, sclerosing mesenteritis, and fibrosing mesenteritis are emblematic of this subset.

### Pathophysiology

Most features of the current understanding of the pathophysiology of IgG4-RD remain highly theoretical, but the field is changing quickly. The theory that IgG4 itself is a crucial player in disease etiology, which held sway for many years after the first recognition of the elevated serum IgG4 concentrations in "sclerosing pancreatitis," has been debunked. Fig. 126.4 outlines current thinking regarding many of the different pathways contributing to the disease.

### Is the IgG4 Molecule Central to Disease?

Many patients with IgG4-RD have striking elevations of serum IgG4 concentrations, generally well out of proportion to those observed in other IgG subclasses. In addition, except for advanced cases characterized primarily by fibrotic lesions, IgG4+ plasma cells are nearly always present in abundance at sites of disease. The total number of IgG4+ plasma cells/hpf and the ratio of IgG4+ to total IgG+ plasma cells in tissue provide information that often bear heavily on the diagnosis. Substantial elevations of plasmablasts and other B cell subsets also occur in IgG4-RD. Consequently, the IgG4 antibody and humoral immunity have been emphasized most prominently in discussions of pathophysiology thus far.

Despite the tight link of "IgG4" to the name of this disease, IgG4 itself is unlikely to drive the pathogenesis of this condition. The subclasses of IgG, defined by the sequences of their heavy chain constant domains, differ from each other in important ways. IgG4, normally the least abundant of all of the IgG subclasses, accounts for approximately 4% of the total immunoglobulins among healthy individuals. The IgG4 molecule has unique chemical properties that render it unlikely to play a central inflammatory role. IgG4 demonstrates weak binding to C1q and to Fc-γ receptors because of a critical few amino acid differences in its CH2 domain.31, As a result, the ability of IgG4 to activate the classic complement pathway and participate in antibody-dependent cellmediated cytotoxicity is attenuated substantially in comparison with the capabilities of IgG1.32

Another unique feature of IgG4 is its ability to form "half antibodies" through the process of Fab arm exchange. Fab arm exchanges result in the formation of IgG molecules with two different binding specificities. Amino acid variation at the hinge region of IgG4 permits the reduction of the disulfide bonds that join the two halves of an IgG4 molecule. Recombination of the dissociated arms leads to the random formation of "asymmetric antibodies" composed of half-antibody fragments directed against different antigens. 31, The consequence is a reduced ability to cross-link antigens and form immune complexes.

In some circumstances, it is conceivable that the ability of IgG4 to activate complement is greater than expected, and the molecule is capable of participating in immune complex—associated tissue injury. IgG4 deposition has been found, in fact, within the kidneys of patients with IgG4-related tubulointerstitial nephritis. The tendency for IgG4-containing immune complexes may be particularly strong when serum IgG4 concentrations are dramatically elevated. Such immune complex—mediated injury, however,

is not considered to be the principal disease pathway underlying IgG4-RD. The role of complement in IgG4-RD requires further investigation. Approximately 40% of patients with this condition are hypocomplementemic before treatment. In these patients, the institution of effective treatment corresponds to rises in the concentrations of C3 and C4.

In summary, the properties of the IgG4 molecule appear to exert a suppressive effect on inflammation. Indeed, it has been demonstrated that the IgG4 response develops after chronic antigen exposure as a part of a tolerogenic response, as in the case of allergy desensitization therapies ("allergy shots").31, Therefore IgG4 may play the role of a noninflammatory "antigen sink," the purpose of which is to "mop up" antigen through its monovalent binding in a process that tends to downregulate inflammation.

### B Cell Lineage

Cells of that B lineage clearly play important roles in IgG4-RD. This is evident by, among other observations, the swift clinical responses of patients to B cell depletion.34, In addition, active, untreated IgG4-RD is characterized by high blood concentrations of plasmablasts and other types of B cell subsets. Somatic hypermutation is evident in the circulating plasmablasts in IgG4-RD, consistent with robust interactions of these cells and their precursors with T cells. B lymphocytes play multiple roles in IgG4-RD, including cytokine production and direct contributions to the processes of fibrosis in this disease.37, Most importantly, perhaps, B cell subsets play important roles in the presentation of antigen(s) to T cells. Antigen presentation by B cells to specific T cells, particularly a CD4+ cytotoxic T cell, represents one of the key cellular interactions central in this disease.

In the context of their antigen-presenting role, tissue-infiltrating B cells present disease-relevant antigens to naive T cells, promoting the expansion and differentiation of these T cell subsets into CD4+ or CD8+ cytotoxic T lymphocytes. It is possible that these cytotoxic T cells subsequently migrate to sites of disease, elaborating mediators such as interleukin-1 (IL-1), transforming growth factor β (TGF-β), and interferon-γ, thereby triggering apoptosis and fibrosis.39,41

### T Cells

Both T follicular helper cells (TfHc) and CD4+ cytotoxic T cells likely play critical roles in IgG4-RD. CD4+ T cells are dispersed throughout IgG4-RD lesions, constituting the most abundant cell within affected tissues. One appealing way to link the contributions of both the B and T cell lineages is through the hypothesis that CD4+ T cells (and possibly CD8+ T cells) are sustained by continuous antigen presentation by B cells. The TFHc response that is responsible for the development of germinal centers within lymph nodes and at extranodal sites of disease may be separate from the cytotoxic T lymphocyte pathways and their interactions with B cells.

### T Follicular Helper Cells

Germinal center reactions and collaboration between T and B lymphocytes drive the clonally expanded B cell responses observed in IgG4-RD. TfHc located on the periphery of germinal centers mediate the IgG4 class switch.41, Selected circulating subsets of TFHc—namely, the TFH2 and TFH17 subsets of TFHc—are demonstrated to have the capacity to help B cell responses in vitro. Circulating TfH cells that express PD-1 are

capable of B cell help. IgG4-secreting plasmablasts and longlived plasma cells are ultimately the products of the TfHC-driven class switch.

### CD4+ Cytotoxic T Lymphocytes

The presence of oligoclonal expansions of CD4+ cytotoxic T lymphocytes in both the peripheral blood and fibrotic lesions in IgG4-RD imply a central pathogenetic role for these cells. These cells upregulate granzymes, granulysin, perforin, and SLAM family proteins. They also elaborate interleukin-1, interferon-γ, and TGF-β, all of which may be important mediators of the fibrosis observed in this disease. Both plasmablasts and CD4+ cytotoxic T lymphocyte cells (CTLs) in the circulation decline following induction therapy with rituximab,39 confirming the important linkage of B cells with CD4+ CTLs in IgG4-RD. B cell depletion therefore has effects beyond B cells in tissue, reducing the number of infiltrating CD4+ CTLs, as well as the numbers of activated myofibroblasts.

### Identification of Potential Autoantigens

A plethora of autoantigens and autoantibodies are associated with IgG4-RD. Such putative autoantigens include carbonic anhydrase, plasminogen-binding protein, lactoferrin, pancreatic secretory trypsin inhibitor, amylase α-2A, trypsinogen, annexin-A11, prohibitin, and laminin-511.46-54 Most such findings, however, have suffered from lack of external validation.

Galectin-3 was identified recently as a major potential autoantigen in IgG4-RD. The approach involved the use of single-cell sequencing and cloning of paired heavy and light immunoglobulin chains. Anti—galectin-3 autoantibodies were found in approximately 30% of a cohort of 121 IgG4-RD patients with multiple organ involvement. The authors then demonstrated that the anti— galectin-3 autoantibodies were restricted to the IgG4 and IgE isotypes, consistent with the idea that plasmablasts from IgG4-RD patients can secrete either IgG4 or IgE. Moreover, the presence of these autoantibodies correlated strongly with elevated plasma levels of galectin-3, suggesting a breach of tolerance driven by the accumulation of this self-protein.

### Clinical Manifestations

IgG4-RD was recognized first in the pancreas, an organ in which the disease expression is termed type 1 IgG4-related autoimmune pancreatitis (AIP). The pancreas is only one of more than a dozen organs commonly affected by IgG4-RD. AIP, sialadenitis (particularly of the submandibular gland; Fig. 126.5), a variety of orbital and periorbital lesions (e.g., dacryoadenitis or inflammation of the extraocular muscles), lymphadenopathy, and IgG4-related retroperitoneal fibrosis (Fig. 126.6) are among the most common disease features. A variety of lesions in the lung (Fig. 126.7), the genitourinary tract (Fig. 126.8) including the kidney, and the aorta (Fig. 126.9) are also well described.

### Proliferative Versus Fibrotic Subsets of Disease Manifestations

Broadly speaking, it is reasonable to consider IgG4-RD to consist of two subsets, referred to as the proliferative and the fibrotic subsets (Table 126.5). The proliferative subset of disease manifestations tends to affect glandular and epithelial tissues, typically

including lymphadenopathy, dacryoadenitis, involvement of the major salivary glands, AIP, IgG-related sclerosing cholangitis, lung disease, tubulointerstitial nephritis, hypophysitis, and a variety of atopic features.

Proliferative manifestations of IgG4-RD are usually accompanied by substantial elevations in serum concentrations of IgG4, IgG1, and IgE; hypocomplementemia of C3 and C4; and a modest peripheral eosinophilia (on the order of 10%). Patients whose IgG4-RD is characterized by proliferative disease manifestations often have multiorgan disease.

In contrast, IgG4-RD patients whose disease is characterized by fibrotic disease manifestations often have disease at extraglandular sites. The focus of their disease may consist of a body region (e.g., the retroperitoneum) rather than a specific organ. The forms of disease expression that fit the fibrotic subtype include RPF, sclerosing mesenteritis, fibrosing mediastinitis, and Riedel's thyroiditis. Patients with fibrotic disease manifestations tend to have fewer organs involved and often have normal serum IgG4 concentrations or only mild elevations, as well as a comparatively lower degree of serologic activity. Nevertheless, the typical pathology hallmarks of IgG4-RD are readily discernible if adequate biopsy samples are obtained. Classic lymphoplasmacytic infiltrates with large numbers of IgG4+ plasma cells may not be evident in cases of RPF of longstanding duration, particularly if the sampling of tissue is small, but both storiform fibrosis and obliterative phlebitis can often still be identified. In patients with advanced fibrotic disease, the ratio of IgG4+ plasma cells to the total number of plasma cells in tissue may be more helpful diagnostically than the overall number of IgG4+ plasma cells/hpf.

This broad subset classification has limits, and overlaps exist between the categories of proliferative and fibrotic disease. Some patients with disease manifestations compatible with the fibrotic subtype (e.g., RPF) also have organ involvement that is typical of the proliferative subtype. A minority of patients with RPF, for example, also have IgG4-related sialoadenitis of the submandibular glands or IgG4-related autoimmune pancreatitis. In addition, some degree of fibrosis is inevitably found within the organs of patients with the proliferative subtype of disease, even if fibrosis is not the predominant feature.

It is probable that these two phenotypic subsets—proliferative as opposed fibrotic—are driven by specific pathophysiological determinants that remain undefined. Even though the biologic underpinnings of this separation require further elucidation, separation of the manifestations of IgG4-RD into these subsets appears to have some broad relevance to disease phenotype, treatment response, and prognosis.

### Constitutional and Musculoskeletal Symptoms

The presentation of IgG4-RD is typically subacute. Symptoms and signs of organ dysfunction can be evident for months or even years before the diagnosis. Although weight losses of 10 to 30 pounds can occur over months, fevers and hectic presentations are unusual. The weight loss associated with IgG4-RD may be an important clue to the presence of exocrine pancreatic insufficiency, the result of subacute injury to the pancreas caused by IgG4-related AIP. Fatigue commonly accompanies IgG4-RD, particularly when the disease affects multiple organ systems. Many

patients have arthralgias and other musculoskeletal symptoms, particularly enthesopathy, but frank arthritis is highly atypical and should signal other diagnoses.

### Orbits

Lacrimal gland enlargement (dacryoadenitis Fig. 126.10) is the most common feature of ophthalmic disease in IgG4-RD. Proptosis can result from combinations of orbital lesions. Inflammation and thickening of the extraocular muscles are the most common causes of proptosis in IgG4-RD, but orbital pseudotumors that do not affect the lacrimal gland can also contribute to this finding. Scleritis and nasolacrimal duct disease (obstruction) can also occur in IgG4-RD, thereby mimicking granulomatosis with polyangiitis.

### Nervous System n Disease

The brain parenchyma is involved only very rarely, but IgG4-RD is among the most common causes of "idiopathic" hypertrophic pachymeningitis. IgG4-RD can also lead to hypophysitis. IgG4related hypophysitis can lead to hormone deficiencies from both the anterior and posterior pituitary. MRI shows sellar enlargement and thickening of the pituitary stalk. MRI studies also often reveal

perineural inflammation of peripheral nerves in the area of the orbit, particularly the trigeminal and infraorbital nerves. Peripheral nerve lesions typically consist of perineural masses, often up to 3 cm in diameter. These are often observed on MRI in the absence of overt clinical manifestations but can lead to concern about the possibility of malignant growths.

### Salivary Glands

The triad of dacryoadenitis and enlargement of both the parotid and submandibular glands is a classic presentation of IgG4-RD that was known for more than 100 years as Mikulicz's disease.57, Isolated submandibular gland enlargement (Fig. 126.5) is also a common finding in IgG4-RD, but parotid and sublingual gland disease can also be prominent. Xerostomia often accompanies IgG4-RD, but this improves with immunosuppression (in contrast to Sjögren's syndrome). Biopsies of minor salivary glands can reveal IgG4-RD, although the sensitivity of this procedure is lower than that of a major salivary gland biopsy (e.g., the submandibular gland). Fine needle aspirates of major salivary glands are useful for excluding malignancy, but excisional biopsies are usually required for diagnostic confirmation.

### Ear, Nose, and Throat

Allergic rhinitis, nasal polyps, chronic sinusitis, nasal obstruction, and rhinorrhea are common in IgG4-RD. Mild to moderate

peripheral eosinophilia and serum IgE concentration elevations that sometimes exceed 10 times the upper limit of normal are common. The prevalence of atopy among IgG4-RD patients is similar to that of the general population, but a subset of nonatopic patients has peripheral blood eosinophilia and elevated IgE levels, 59 which suggests that processes inherent to IgG4-RD itself rather than atopy per se contribute to the eosinophilia and IgE elevation. Circulating Th2 memory cells are found only in IgG4- RD patients with pre-existing histories of atopy.

Mass lesions in the sinuses and destructive lesions in the middle ear and facial bones can occur in IgG4-RD, sometimes creating a challenging differential diagnosis with granulomatosis with polyangiitis, sarcoma, lymphoma, and other cancers. IgG4-RD can also lead to diffuse inflammation in the pharynx, hypopharynx, and Waldeyer's ring, frequently associated with mass lesion. Tracheal inflammation and vocal cord involvement have also been described. Riedel's thyroiditis has been linked convincingly to IgG4-RD. In short, IgG4-RD is in the differential diagnosis of any type of mass lesion in the head and neck region—and essentially anywhere else, for that matter.

### Lymphadenopathy

The lymphadenopathy associated with IgG4-RD is typically either a generalized lymphadenopathy or localized disease adjacent to an affected organ. The lymph nodes involved are generally 1 to 3 cm in diameter and nontender. Involvement of the cervical, supraclavicular, submandibular, axillary, hilar, mediastinal, para-aortic, retroperitoneal, and inguinal nodes is described. At least five histopathologic variants of IgG4-related lymphadenopathy have been described. One of these variants closely mimics Castleman's disease.

Establishing the diagnosis of IgG4-RD through lymph node biopsy is generally difficult because it is unusual for lymph nodes to undergo the degree of fibrosis observed in other organs, and increased concentrations of IgG4+ plasma cells are found commonly in lymph nodes in other diagnoses. As a rule, lymph node biopsy for the purpose of diagnosing IgG4-RD should be avoided in favor of sampling another organ, which is more likely to yield an IgG4-RD diagnosis. Often, however, lymph node biopsies are necessary to exclude such common IgG4-RD mimickers as lymphoma and sarcoidosis.

### Thoracic Aorta, Branches of the Aorta, and Coronary L Lesions

IgG4-related aortitis, which often is suspected on the basis of an incidental radiologic finding, is also sometimes an unexpected finding at surgery. IgG4-related aortitis can lead to aneurysms or dissections in the thoracic aorta.63-65 In contrast to giant cell and Takayasu's arteritis, which have a predilection for the primary aortic branches—particularly the subclavian arteries—IgG4-RD tends to spare these vessels, at least in terms of clinical manifestations. Small case series substantiate the concept that mediumsized blood vessels can also be affected by IgG4-RD, but definitive histopathologic investigations of primary aortic branch vessels have not been undertaken. As discussed earlier, however, coronary artery lesions in IgG4-RD, sometimes associated with aneurysm formation, are well-documented.

### Chronic Periaortitis and Retroperitoneal Fibrosis

Idiopathic RPF is now considered to belong to a larger disease spectrum now known as chronic periaortitis. The three major components of chronic periaortitis are IgG4-related RPF (Fig. 126.6), IgG4-related abdominal aortitis, and IgG4-related perianeurysmal fibrosis. IgG4-RD is responsible for up to twothirds of cases of idiopathic RPF66, Some cases of idiopathic RPF that do not appear to be part of the IgG4-RD spectrum can have similar presentations and can be distinguished from IgG4- RD through careful histopathologic and immunostaining studies.

Common presentations of IgG4-related RPF and chronic periaortitis are poorly localized pain in the back, flanks, lower abdomen, or thighs; lower extremity edema; and hydronephrosis from ureteral involvement. These presentations are generally subtle at first, subacute in onset, and nonspecific, leading to diagnostic delay. The disease targets three sites: (1) periaortic/arterial regions, involving connective tissue around the abdominal aorta or its first branches; (2) periureteral areas, leading to ureteral obstruction and hydronephrosis; and (3) a plaque-like mass that broadly involves the retroperitoneum. The classic radiologic presentation of IgG4-RD is a periaortic lesion beginning in the infrarenal region, extending inferiorly to involve the iliac arteries. The ureters course close to the lower aorta and iliac arteries on their way to the bladder and often become entrapped by the periaortic inflammation.

The classic lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate may no longer be evident in cases of RPF long-standing duration, but both storiform fibrosis and obliterative phlebitis can often still be identified. The ratio of IgG4+ plasma cells to the total number of plasma cells in tissue may be more helpful diagnostically than the overall number of IgG4+ plasma cells/hpf in patients with advanced fibrotic disease.

### Lung

The greatest diversity of clinical and radiologic presentations occurs in the lung. Thickening of the bronchovascular bundle, best appreciated on CT examination, underscores the tendency of IgG4-RD to track along bronchi and blood vessels, which course together. Other radiologic features of IgG4-RD include pulmonary nodules, ground-glass opacities, pleural thickening, and interstitial lung disease. The interstitial lung disease mimics nonspecific interstitial pneumonitis and other forms of interstitial fibrosis (Fig. 126.7). Another thoracic lesion extrinsic to the lungs—a paravertebral mass—is highly characteristic of IgG4-RD.

### Kidney

Tubulointerstitial nephritis (TIN) is the most characteristic form of IgG4-related kidney disease. IgG4-related TIN recapitulates the histopathology found in other organs. IgG4-related TIN is often distinguished from other organ manifestations of IgG4- RD by profound hypocomplementemia. The basis of this hypocomplementemia remains poorly understood, but one potential explanation involves the formation of immune complexes containing IgG1 or IgG3, as well as complement components. IgG1 and IgG3 generally bind complement more effectively than IgG4 does; however, it is possible that under some pathologic conditions, IgG4 is also able to bind complement. Immune complexes involving a variety of IgG subclasses (including IgG4) and different complement components have been identified by electron microscopy. The locations of these immune complexes within the renal tubules is particularly characteristic of IgG4-RD, but not diagnostic (they can also be present, for example, in lupus nephritis).

CT scanning in IgG4-related TIN can reveal substantial renal enlargement and hypodense lesions within the renal parenchyma. Advanced renal dysfunction and even end-stage renal disease can result. Proteinuria can develop, but the levels are usually subnephrotic. Kidneys affected by IgG4-RD can undergo atrophy, even in the setting of good clinical responses to therapy.

Membranous glomerulonephropathy also occurs in IgG4-RD, but the pathophysiology of this entity appears to have a pathophysiology different from that of IgG4-related TIN. The antiphospholipase A2 (PLA2) receptor antibody now known to cause idiopathic membranous glomerulonephropathy is not associated with IgG4-related membranous glomerulonephropathy. It is interesting to note, however, that the anti-PLA2 receptor antibody is primarily of the IgG4 subclass. IgG4-related membranous glomerulonephropathy is less common than TIN, but sometimes the lesions occur together.

### Pancreas

The pancreas was the first organ recognized to have an association with elevated serum IgG4 concentrations.5, Two AIP subtypes exist, only one of which (type 1) is associated with IgG4-RD. Type 1

AIP demonstrates the classic histopathologic findings of lymphoplasmacytic sclerosing pancreatitis. The histologic features of type 2 AIP, which is less common than type 1, include neutrophilic infiltration into the pancreatic duct epithelium.

The abdominal pain associated with IgG4-related AIP spans a broad range from a subtle, relatively asymptomatic presentation reminiscent of indigestion to substantial abdominal pain that mimics pancreatitis of other etiologies. In general, however, the abdominal pain of IgG4-related AIP is less severe than that associated, for example, with alcohol-induced pancreatitis. Perhaps because of the relatively mild abdominal symptoms accompanying IgG4-related AIP, a common clinical presentation is obstructive jaundice, which leads to concern for pancreatic adenocarcinoma. Unfortunately, many IgG4-RD patients have undergone modified Whipple procedures to resect what is presumed to be adenocarcinoma of the pancreas before the correct diagnosis is recognized.

Damage resulting from IgG4-related AIP is substantial. Secondary diabetes mellitus occurs in approximately half of all cases, and IgG4-RD clearly causes a subset of diabetes mellitus cases in individuals who have no overt risk factors for diabetes. Even more common than endocrine failure of the pancreas, however, is exocrine failure. Pancreatic atrophy and diminished ability of the organ to produce digestive enzymes lead to malabsorption, malnutrition, and often dramatic weight loss (e.g., up to 50 pounds). The degree of exocrine pancreatic dysfunction can be quantified through measurements of elastase in stool samples. Oral replacement of pancreatic enzymes with meals can reverse the weight loss caused by pancreatic damage. Pancreatic stones occur with increased frequency among patients with type 1 AIP.

The nearly diagnostic CT features of AIP include diffuse pancreatic enlargement with delayed enhancement and a capsule-like low-density rim (Fig. 126.11). Diffuse, irregular narrowing of the main pancreatic duct on endoscopic retrograde and magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) is also highly specific for AIP. Endoscopic ultrasonography-guided fine-needle aspiration is a useful diagnostic approach to excluding pancreatic cancer. Empiric glucocorticoid trials of 2 to 4 weeks' duration are also considered in some patients with pancreatic masses in whom AIP is considered because of the excellent response to glucocorticoids shown by most IgG4-RD patients.

### IgG4-Related Sclerosing Cholangitis and Cholecystitis

IgG4-related sclerosing cholangitis frequently occurs with type 1 AIP. The histology of IgG4-related sclerosing cholangitis includes obliterative phlebitis and transmural fibrosis with dense infiltration of IgG4+ plasma cells and T cells. IgG4-related sclerosing cholangitis must be differentiated from both primary sclerosing cholangitis and hilar cholangiocarcinoma. Neither serum IgG4 concentrations nor cholangiographic or cholangioscopic findings differentiate these diseases from each other with clarity. Thus an endoscopic transpapillary biopsy is usually required. Although cholangiocarcinoma can be excluded by endoscopic biopsy, the superficial nature of endoscopic biopsies limits their utility for diagnosing IgG4-related sclerosing cholangitis. In such cases, serum IgG4 concentration elevations (if particularly high) and searches for extrahepatic biliary disease can often lead to the correct diagnosis.

IgG4-related cholecystitis sometimes occurs with IgG4-related sclerosing cholangitis. Thickening of the gallbladder wall is detected on imaging, but it is usually asymptomatic.

### Other Manifestations

Sclerosing lesions of both the mesentery and mediastinum are described. Sclerosing mesenteritis often appears to originate at the mesenteric root. The ensuing process often merges imperceptibly with RPF and can evolve in a slow but devastating manner, encasing vital organs and blood vessels and obviating any attempt at surgical resection. Fibrosing mediastinitis can lead to the compression of vital mediastinal structures from proliferation of invasive fibrous tissue. The relationship between these fibrosing mediastinitis cases and antecedent histoplasmosis infections, if any, remains unclear.

Several clinical presentations of IgG4-related skin disease have occurred. The most common cutaneous manifestation is the presence of erythematous papules. These lesions typically affect the region of the head and neck but have also been described on the trunk and extremities. Among individuals with darkly pigmented skin, hyperpigmented lesions have been observed.

Biopsy-proven IgG4-related prostatic disease leading to prostatic enlargement has been reported. The diagnosis of IgG4related prostate disease is often made presumptively when the initiation of treatment for IgG4-RD in other organs mediates abrupt symptomatic relief of "benign prostatic hypertrophy."
