The differential diagnosis of IgG4-RD varies according to the sites of organ involvement. Table 126.6 shows the broad differential diagnosis of this condition, by organ.

### Treatment

### Philosophy of Treatment

Active treatment should be administered to patients with either active, symptomatic IgG4-RD.3, In addition, patients who have few clinical symptoms but demonstrate evidence of disease progression, particularly in vital organs, should be treated with the goal of completely suppressing disease

activity. Although IgG4-RD is most often an indolent disease; it is its subclinical nature that permits it to cause severe, organ-destructive and even life-threatening disease. Major organ involvement in IgG4-RD can remain subclinical for lengthy periods of time, leading all the while to irreversible organ injury. Thus, when the disease is diagnosed, the assertion and maintenance of effective disease control is essential to ensuring good outcomes.

Despite the normally indolent nature of the disease, a subset of patients requires treatment urgently. These include certain patients with AIP, who may suffer permanent damage to both exocrine and endocrine pancreatic function if the disease is not treated appropriately and a subset of those with IgG4-related kidney disease, some of which may develop rapidly progressive renal dysfunction. Retroperitoneal fibrosis may lead to severe postrenal injury, such as ureteral strictures and hydronephrosis. Patients with this disease complication may require ureteral stent placement acutely in order to prevent renal damage, even as systemic immunosuppression is initiated to control the underlying disease process. Patients with orbital disease are also prone to permanent extraocular muscle dysfunction if orbital myositis goes unchecked.

Some patients with IgG4-RD that involves only a single organ and are asymptomatic may be monitored without treatment. Patients with disease confined to the lacrimal or submandibular glands or with asymptomatic lymphadenopathy are good candidates for such a strategy of watchful waiting. However, it is important to bear in mind that certain organs such as the pituitary gland may not signal their involvement until after sustaining advanced damage, and such organ damage is a risk if a decision of watchful waiting is exercised. Leaving a patient untreated in the setting of rising indicators of active disease, e.g.,

serum IgG4 concentrations, is not recommended without close surveillance.

IgG4-RD occasionally recedes temporarily in patients with single-organ disease, but these patients may eventually present with disease manifestation in major organs such as the pancreas or kidney, leading to serious organ damage that could have been avoided with close follow-up. Laboratory surveillance in the setting of watchful waiting should include not only IgG subclasses but also a complete blood count with longitudinal tracking of the eosinophil count or percentage, serum chemistries, IgE, and C3 and C4. Intermittent imaging may also be important for some disease manifestations, e.g., RPF.

### Remission Induction

Glucocorticoids remain the cornerstone of treatment for most patients with IgG4-RD, and patients typically respond well to this intervention. The failure of a patient to respond to an appropriate course of glucocorticoid treatment urges reconsideration of the diagnosis. IgG4-RD usually demonstrates signs of improvement within days to several weeks of beginning treatment, depending on the type of organs involved. This is particularly true of the proliferative subset of the disease.

The goal of induction therapy often is to discontinue glucocorticoids within 2.5 to 4 months, but treatment strategies vary across countries. The tendency at some centers, particularly those in Asia, is to maintain patients on daily prednisone doses of 5 to 10 mg for several years once remission has been achieved. Shorter glucocorticoid courses are preferred at other centers, leading to complete cessation and the use of a CC 'steroid-sparing" therapy (e.g., mycophenolate mofetil) or a biologic agent (B cell depletion) if prednisone monotherapy fails. Anecdotal evidence supports the efficacy of conventional disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drug (DMARD) in certain settings, but in general B cell depletion is viewed as being more effective.

### Glucocorticoid Treatment

Patients with multiorgan disease and high serum IgG4 concentrations respond well to a starting dose of prednisone of 0.6 mg/ kg/day (30 to 40 mg/day), and this is often recommended for IgG4-RD. The starting dose of prednisone, usually maintained for 2 to 4 weeks, can be tapered thereafter through a variety of regimens designed to discontinue prednisone within 10 to 16 weeks, guided by the rapidity of clinical improvement on physical examination, improvement in laboratory biomarkers, and imaging changes.

Unfortunately, the impact of glucocorticoids in IgG4-RD is generally only temporary. Patients with multiorgan disease and high serum IgG4 concentrations at baseline are unlikely to achieve sustained remissions with limited courses of glucocorticoids. Once the failure of prednisone to induce long-term remission is evident, these patients require either lengthy glucocorticoid courses, placing them at risk for treatment-induced toxicity, or the early use of a biologic agent (preferably B cell depletion) or another treatment approach. The reality that IgG4-RD frequently leads to substantial pancreatic damage, placing patients at risk for glucose intolerance, combined with demographic profile of the typical patient with IgG4-RD—individuals who are middle-aged to elderly and often have comorbidities such as diabetes, obesity, osteoporosis, and hypertension—is a major contraindication to prolonged glucocorticoid therapy.

### Biologic Agents

Treatment strategies targeting cells of both the B and T lymphocyte lineages are logical approaches to the treatment of IgG4-RD. Given the multiple arms of the immune system involved in the disease, however, they are almost certainly not the only ones worthy of consideration.

Abatacept (antiCTLA4-Ig), which interferes with T cell co-stimulation, showed modest evidence of efficacy in an openlabel trial of 10 patients. This medication appears to be most effective in patients with mild disease but is probably not optimal in the absence of glucocorticoids, particularly for patients with multiorgan disease.

Most work to date has been done in B cell depletion.34, B cell depletion likely operates by interrupting antigen presentation to CD4+ CTLs, among other mechanisms. The concentration of CD4+ CTLs in both peripheral blood and disease-affected tissue declines following targeted B cell depletion.37, B cell depletion also reduces the number of infiltrating a ctivated myofibroblasts, thereby decreasing tissue fibrosis. IgG4-RD patients may be prone to tissue injury resulting from immune complex deposition. In theory, this may be ameliorated potentially by reducing immunoglobulin concentrations.

B cell depletion must be readministered at varying frequency in order to maintain efficacy. Re gular re treatment with B celldepleting agents such as anti-CD20 (rituximab) and anti-CD19 (inebilizumab) is likely not required to maintain disease remission, albeit retreatment at some interval—probably unique to each patient—is necessary for most. Signs of efficacy, often swift and substantial, were observed in 29 of 30 patients treated with a remission induction regimen of rituximab (two 1-gram doses administered 2 weeks apart). Of these patients, 77% achieved the primary outcome of disease remission off of prednisone at 6 months, but disease relapses had occurred in many individuals by 1 year. Longitudinal measurement of serum IgG4 concentrations is a useful gauge of when readministration of B cell depletion may be indicated.

### Investigational Treatment Approaches

A phase II trial of obexelimab, a monoclonal antibody directed against both CD19 and Fc-γRIIb, demonstrated positive treatment responses in 12 of 15 patients. Disease control was established without glucocorticoid use in most subjects. A phase III trial of obexelimab is now under way.

Inebilizumab, a monoclonal antibody directed against CD19 that has obtained regulatory approval in neuromyelitis optica, offers another potential B cell depletion strategy that is now at an advanced stage of testing in a worldwide, multicenter clinical trial. Finally, SLAM-F7 is a highly appealing drug target because it is present on both CD4+ CTLs and B cells. A proof-of-concept trial with the anti-SLAM7 monoclonal antibody elotuzumab, used to treat relapsed multiple myeloma, has begun.

# Arthritis Accompanying Endocrine and Metabolic Disorders

### KEY POINTS

Endocrine disorders can initially present or manifest with a multitude of musculoskeletal signs and symptoms. Additionally, endocrine manifestations of underlying autoimmune disorders are common and need to be recognized promptly.

### Introduction

Rheumatic manifestations are often the initial presentation of systemic illnesses. Each endocrine disorder has its own set of arthritic symptoms that can mimic or present as definitive rheumatic diatheses, requiring a high degree of vigilance and a thorough assessment of patients presenting with such varied symptoms. Both rheumatologists and general internists should be well versed in identifying the manner in which components of the musculoskeletal system are affected by diseases of the endocrine system. Additionally, recognition that endocrinopathies can arise in the course of treating rheumatic illnesses, such as with the use of corticosteroids, is critical in minimizing or reversing any potential adverse sequelae in these patients. This chapter will describe the common musculoskeletal manifestations of endocrine disease encountered in the clinical setting.

### Adrenal Gland Disorders

In 1932 Harvey Cushing described several rheumatic conditions, including osteoporosis, avascular necrosis, myopathy, and synovitis, later collectively termed Cushing's syndrome (CS). Primary CS is usually related to excessive endogenous production of cortisol and is either adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH)-dependent (pituitary adenomas) or ACTH-independent (adrenal tumor or adrenal hyperplasia), whereas exogenous CS is secondary to excessive exposure to exogenous glucocorticoids.

Steroid excess increases muscle protein catabolism and inhibits analog signaling, leading to atrophy, especially of type IIa muscle fibers. Myopathy presents as extreme muscle weakness and pain that is most often pronounced around the pelvic girdle and is reported in 70% of patients with active primary CS. This muscle weakness and pain may either occur suddenly or be insidious in onset. Muscle performance such as hand grip strength and performance on the chair rising test is impaired in patients with active CS. Although it is generally agreed that weakness gradually improves as corticosteroids are discontinued or with biochemical control of disease, some recent studies using body composition analysis with MRI and dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry (DXA) in patients with primary CS showed persistence of lower limb skeletal muscle mass decline even up to 13 years after achieving clinical remission.3,

Avascular necrosis generally occurs after prolonged use of highdose corticosteroids but can be observed months or even years after the discontinuation of corticosteroids.5, Less commonly, it can be associated with short courses of therapy or intermittent high-dose intravenous therapy; consequently, the risk for avascular necrosis should always be considered during clinical assessment.6, Although rare, case reports of avascular necrosis in patients with endogenous CS do exist.8,

Corticosteroids have inhibitory effects on replication and differentiation of osteoblasts, as well as intestinal and renal calcium reabsorption. Abnormalities of bone status are commonly seen in patients with CS, with osteopenia occurring in 40% to 78% of patients, osteoporosis occurring in 22% to 57%, and fractures occurring in 11% to 76%. The prevalence of osteoporosis is higher in individuals with adrenal CS than in those with pituitary CS. Male patients have a higher prevalence of osteoporosis and

vertebral fractures compared with females. 1, Several studies show improvement of bone mineral density (BMD) after biochemical remission, either through surgical or medical management; however, time to improvement is variable. Several studies show persistently low BMD and altered bone metabolic markers up to several years after achieving clinical remission. 12-16

### Acromegaly

### Clinical Features and Pathogenesis

Acromegaly is caused by hypersecretion of growth hormone (GH), usually as a result of a GH-secreting pituitary tumor. Other causes, such as increased GH-releasing hormone (GHRH) production from hypothalamic tumors, ectopic GHRH production, and ectopic GH secretion from nonendocrine tumors, are rare. Prevalence has been reported between 2.8 and 13.7 cases per 100,000 with an incidence range between 0.2 and 1.1 cases per 100,000 per year. Acromegaly occurs most commonly in middle-aged men and women, and there is a median diagnostic delay of 4.5 to 5 years. Hypersecretion of GH and insulin-like growth factor (IGF)-1, its primary mediator, have both somatic and metabolic effects.

GH and IGF-1 are important regulators of bone and cartilage homeostasis and have a central role in development of bone growth and bone mass. Musculoskeletal symptoms, including acromegalic arthropathy, are common complications of acromegaly and affect both weight-bearing and non—weight-bearing joints.18, At the time of diagnosis, arthropathy is one of the presenting symptoms in up to 50% to 70% of patients. Between 60% and 70% of patients experience involvement of large peripheral joints (i.e., the shoulder, knee, and hip). Back pain may be a particularly troubling feature of acromegaly. Approximately 50% of patients have axial arthropathy, mainly affecting the lumbar area. Carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS) occurs in approximately 60% of patients with acromegaly and is frequently bilateral.22,

GH secreted by the anterior pituitary acts on hepatocytes to secrete somatomedins, which have stimulatory effects on bone and cartilage, including chondrocyte replication, synthesis of proteoglycans, collagen, osteoblastic proliferation, and increased bone collagen (resulting in increased bone mass). Somatomedins also have insulin-like activity on muscle and fat. There are probably two phases in the pathogenesis of acromegalic arthropathy: an early and potentially reversible phase in which elevated GH and IGF-1 levels induce cartilage hypertrophy and laxity of periarticular ligaments and a late irreversible phase where GH excess persists, leading to degenerative joint disease with scarring, cysts, and osteophyte formation.25, Compared with patients with primary osteoarthritis (OA), MRI studies have shown that cartilage hypertrophy and composition differ significantly in patients with acromegalic arthropathy.

Arthropathy symptoms are significantly incapacitating and lead to a lower quality of life.28, Symptoms are chronic, and current evidence suggests that they can be persistent even after biochemical control of disease, with more than 70% of patients having progressive osteophytosis or joint space narrowing despite successful treatment.

### Bone Mass and Quality in Acromegaly

GH stimulates, either directly or indirectly through IGF-1, the proliferation of cells of the osteoblastic lineage and the differentiated function of mature osteoblast. It also stimulates the carboxylation of osteocalcin and the production of osteoprotegerin.

GH hypersecretion has different effects on cortical and trabecular bone; elevated levels have a deleterious effect on the former, whereas bone density tends to be increased in the latter because of periosteal ossification. These differences, associated with variations in DXA measurements because of bone enlargement in acromegaly patients, are a possible explanation as to why patients with acromegaly experience fractures even in the presence of normal BMD. 32-34

The increased risk of vertebral fractures in acromegaly has been confirmed by several studies, which describe its association with hypogonadism, higher IGF-1 levels, and longer duration of active disease. Incident vertebral fractures occurred in 42% of patients followed up for 3 years during the active phase of disease; however, progression of fractures was observed in up to 20% of patients with biochemical control of disease. 35,36

### Hypothalamic-Gonadal Axis

Many autoimmune disorders are more prevalent in women. Female-to-male ratios differ among connective tissue diseases. In rheumatoid arthritis (RA), the incidence is higher in post-menopausal as opposed to pre-menopausal women. Adult men have a significant delayed onset of disease. These findings may be due to gonadal hormones offering protection against RA in younger men (as a result of testosterone) and a predisposition to systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) in women (as a result of estrogens). 38,

Both sex hormones and genes expressed on sexual chromosomes have been proposed as potential explanations for sexand age-related effects on musculoskeletal disease presentations. This is exemplified in Klinefelter's patients, who have two XX chromosomes (XXY karyotype), reduced levels of androgens, and an increased risk for the development of autoimmune conditions. Besides their role in determining biologic sex, androgens also have specific effects on the immune system related to suppression of immune reactivity and inflammation, increasing the threshold for the development of autoimmunity. One prospective study reported a higher incidence of autoimmune disease in men with hypogonadism, whereas other studies have demonstrated low serum androgen levels in autoimmune disorders.42,43

### Androgens in Rheumatoid Arthritis

In a longitudinal study of the levels of total testosterone, sex hormonebinding globulin, and luteinizing hormone (LH) in 41 males with early RA (naive to disease-modifying anti-rheumatic agents [DMARDs] at study entry) over 2 years,37 it was only in male patients younger than 50 years that lower baseline levels of testosterone were found compared with control subjects. This has been documented in other studies, in which it was also noted that men who experience a dramatic loss of serum androgens with age may develop a more aggressive form of RA.44-46 The possibility of a causative effect between hypogonadism and the development of RA is contradicted, however, by studies that demonstrate that serum androgen levels are not lower before the onset of RA in all patients.4, The notion of low serum androgen levels as a consequence of RA is supported by increased levels of testosterone with response to treatment and decreased disease activity, as well as the inverse correlation with inflammatory markers.37, The role of androgens in RA susceptibility in women is less well understood, with some studies showing a protective effect and others suggesting that androgens may worsen disease severity.50-52 Women predisposed to higher androgen concentrations because of

a polymorphism in the CYB5A gene are protected from developing seropositive RA. Lower androgen levels have occurred in women with RA refractory to treatment; however, patients with higher serum androgen concentrations and a low number of CAG repeats in androgen receptors developed more aggressive RA.54, Low serum concentrations of androgens have occurred in women with RA, but no significant abnormalities have been noted before disease onset. Further prospective studies in the large emerging pre- RA cohorts will be informative of risk in both males and females.

### Ligamentous Injuries and Estrogen

Estrogen fulfills an important role in the development, maturation, and aging of bone, muscle, and connective tissue. Increased risk of musculoskeletal injury, accelerated bone wasting, and accelerated muscle wasting are well characterized in menopause.

In general, anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) ruptures occur two to eight times more often in female athletes than their male counterparts. One explanation may be the increase in knee laxity during pre-ovulatory and ovulatory phases of the menstrual cycle,57-61 because knee laxity is directly related to estrogen concentrations.62, Retrospective studies have shown that patients with ACL injuries were less likely to be on oral contraceptives.64, Interestingly, women suffer fewer muscle injuries than men; this is thought to be related to decreased muscle stiffness. Further research is needed regarding the possibility and timing of interventions.

### Diabetes Mellitus

Diabetes mellitus (DM) is one of the most common diseases worldwide, with increasing prevalence in most regions. Although much is known about the microvascular and macrovascular complications, the musculoskeletal complications of the disease are usually reported mainly as observational data (Table 127.1).66,

Diabetic muscle infarction (DMI) is observed exclusively in patients with DM, and other conditions such as adhesive capsulitis or limited joint mobility (LJM) are reported more frequently

in patients with diabetes. These last two, as well as other disorders such as CTS, flexor tenosynovitis, and Dupuytren's disease, are all part of a group of fibroproliferative soft tissue disorders in which increased levels of advanced glycosylation end products (AGEs) are thought to play a role. The deposition of connective tissue around joints, in tendon sheaths, and in fascia leads to the specific clinical manifestations, and this has been seen in histologic examination of the tissue.68, The extent of AGE formation depends on the concentration of sugars and the duration of exposure of macromolecules to these sugars. AGEs are implicated in the development of microvascular and macrovascular complications and in the accumulation of AGEs in the skin correlated with the presence of retinopathy, nephropathy, and LJM in type 1 DM. Patients with DM also more frequently report joint disorders, such as diabetic osteoarthropathy, and skeletal disorders, such as diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis (DISH). Finally, an increasing association between diabetes and bone mineral disease is being recognized, as are considerations in the treatment of such patients.

### Shoulder

Frozen shoulder, or adhesive capsulitis (AC), is frequently bilateral in patients with diabetes and is associated with severe pain and stiffness. Incidence has been reported in 10% to 20% and 3% to 32% of patients with type 1 and 2 DM, respectively, with a prevalence of 11% to 19% and 2% to 3% in DM versus agematched non-DM patients. A recent longitudinal study showed an increased risk for the development of AC in individuals with DM compared with non-DM individuals (hazard ratio [HR], 1.333; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.24 to 1.44). Symptoms are associated with poorer quality of life, depression, and higher diabetes-specific burden. DM seems to be an indicator of poor outcome for a conservative approach, but there seems to be no difference with respect to surgical management. 73,

Calcific shoulder tendinitis, which results from deposition of calcium hydroxyapatite crystals predominantly in rotator cuff tendons, is more prevalent in patients with DM. One study reported a three times higher prevalence of shoulder calcification in patients with DM compared with controls, but only a third of them experienced any symptoms. The cause of these tendon-related problems in the shoulder are unknown but may reflect altered matrix metalloproteinase (MMP)/tissue inhibitor of metalloproteinase (TIMP) expression. More work is required in this area.

### Hands

Limited joint mobility syndrome (diabetic cheiroarthropathy), also known as diabetic stiff hand syndrome, is not actually an arthropathy but rather a process that involves periarticular structures. It involves a fibrosing syndrome, resembling scleroderma, with thick, tight, and waxy skin predominantly over the dorsal aspect of the metacarpophalangeal (MCP), proximal (PIP), and distal interphalangeal (DIP) joints of the fingers. The "prayer sign' comes from the inability to oppose palmar surfaces of hands and fingers. Larger joints, such as wrists, elbows, knees, and ankles, can be involved. Prevalence between 30% to 58% and 45% to 76% of patients with type 1 and type 2 DM, respectively, have been reported, as well as an increase in frequency with age, disease duration, and poor glycemic control.76-78 Nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and steroid injections are not effective in management, and glycemic control, as well as physical therapy, is encouraged.

Flexor tenosynovitis, or "trigger finger," results from the occurrence of fbrosis and thickening of the tendon sheath, particularly when the tendon passes through the pulley, restricting the movement of the flexor tendon within its tendon sheath and later leading to inflammation, which causes pain and ultimately the locking of the involved fingers. Prevalence is higher in patients with type 1 and type 2 DM compared with the general population, and it is also higher in patients with poorly controlled disease than in well-controlled patients.80-82 Patients with DM are more likely to have multiple fingers involved simultaneously than non-DM patients.83-85 Management with steroid injections might not be as effective, and patients with multiple-digit involvement more often require surgical management.86,

Dupuytren's disease (DD) is classically described as the thickening of the palmar fascia and flexor tendons, as well as pretendinous bands, palmar or digital nodules, and flexion contractures of fingers, involving the ring and little finger. In patients with DM, DD is not only more prevalent, affecting 16% to 42% of individuals, but it also more often involves the middle and ring fingers.

CTS is an entrapment neuropathy caused by compression of the median nerve and, in patients with DM, it is thought to be related to fibroproliferative connective tissue. In patients with DM, the role of inflammation and neovascularization seems to be more prominent than in non-DM patients. Prevalence is higher in patients with DM, especially if co-existent with neuropathy; a recent systematic review and meta-analysis estimated an increased risk for patients with DM (odds ratio [OR], 1.69; 95% CI, 1.45 to 1.96). CTS in DM patients can co-exist with other pathologies, such as trigger fingers. Surgical management outcomes seem to be similar to non-DM patients.91,92

### Feet

Charcot's osteoarthropathy (COA), or diabetic osteoarthropathy, is associated with diabetic neuropathy and is a progressive, often rapid, and degenerative disease of the foot and ankle joints that leads to significant damage and deformity if left untreated. Incidence is about 0.1% to 5% in diabetic neuropathy, with prevalence ranging from 0.08% to 8.5%.93, COA incidence increases with duration of diabetes and diabetic neuropathy, and although it is more common unilaterally, it can involve both extremities in up to 39% of cases. Risk of amputation with COA is higher when associated with ulceration. Incidence of the latter in these patients is 17% per year.

There are two theories regarding the pathophysiology of COA: the neurotraumatic and neurovascular hypotheses. The first refers to cumulative trauma (in the context of loss of protective proprioception) as a causative factor, leading to the release of proinflammatory cytokines such as TNF, IL-1β, and IL-6, as well as upregulation of receptor activator of nuclear factor kB (NF-κB) ligand (RANKL), which leads to osteoclastogenesis and excessive bone turnover.96, The latter hypothesis proposes that because of autonomic dysfunction, patients with diabetes have increased blood flow to subchondral bone, resulting in increased osteoclastic activity and bone resorption. This phenomenon occurs even in the absence of peripheral vascular disease and creates bone fatigue and disorganization. Some studies have also shown that receptors for AGEs in chondrocytes can lead to upregulation of MMPs and increase inflammation. 99,

Initially, there is swelling, warmth, and erythema of the foot. Involvement of ankle, tarsal, and tarsometatarsal are most common, but rarely knees, wrists, shoulder, and intervertebral joints

can be affected. Progressive bone resorption, fractures, and dislocation lead to deformity and destabilization of the foot, giving the classic "rocker-bottom" appearance. In addition to plain radiography, MRI and bone scintigraphy can be useful studies for evaluating the extent of the disease. The initial approach involves joint stabilization and offloading. Other measures include antiresorptive therapy and surgery.

### Muscles

Diabetic muscle infarction, a rare condition marked by spontaneous infarction of muscle tissue with no preceding injury, occurs largely in patients who are considered "brittle diabetics. "101 Proposed mechanisms include microangiopathy and hypercoagulability, from alterations of the coagulation—fibrinolytic system and endothelial dysfunction. Characteristically, these patients will have accumulated numerous microvascular sequelae from their uncontrolled disease. Clinically, patients will present with abrupt onset of pain and swelling, usually involving the thigh or calf muscles, and creatine phosphokinase (CPK) levels may be normal or elevated. MRI using T2-weighted imaging may be useful in arriving at a diagnosis, with confirmatory testing involving an incisional muscle biopsy and demonstration of muscle edema and necrosis. Diabetic amyotrophy usually presents as weakness involving proximal muscles of the lower extremities and is also associated with pain. Treatment usually involves glycemic control and physical therapy.

### Diffuse Idiopathic Skeletal Hyperostosis

Diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis (DISH) is characterized by ossification of the anterior longitudinal ligament of the spine, can involve various other extraspinal ligaments, and is generally accompanied by osteophyte formation (Fig. 127.1). Intervertebral disk spaces and sacroiliac joints, however, are commonly spared. A high incidence of DISH has been demonstrated in a cohort of patients affected by both clinically active and subclinical DM (both type 1 and type 2), as well as smaller case series.104, A more recent study found that individuals in their fifth decade of life were more likely to be affected by DISH if they were obese, had a first-degree relative with either DM or hypertension, had lumbar or thoracic spinal pain, and were affected by enthesopathies or tendonitis. The likelihood of relatively young patients with three or more of these clinical parameters being affected by DISH was six times higher compared with ageand sex-matched control subjects (P = .004). It has been suggested that chronic elevation of serum insulin and IGF-1 leads to calcification and ossification in ligaments and enthesis regions exposed to mechanical stress.

### Bone Mineral Disease

Microarchitectural changes leading to a decrease in bone quality have been reported in both type 1 and type 2 diabetes. Although decreased bone mineral density has been commonly described in patients with type 1 diabetes, normal or high bone mineral density is most commonly associated with type 2 diabetes. Despite this, both forms of diabetes are associated with an increased risk of fragility fractures. An increased risk of hip fractures has been reported both in men and women with type 1 and type 2 diabetes, although this association seems

to be stronger in type 1 patients. Two different meta-analyses have reported an increased risk of hip fractures with type 2 diabetes, and a risk even five times higher in type 1 diabetes patients. 108,

Although the pathophysiology for bone metabolic disease in patients with diabetes is not clear, multiple factors play a potential role in this association. Peak bone mass is decreased in the young, possibly due to B cell failure resulting in decreased levels of IGF-1, leading to decrease in osteoblast function and collagen synthesis. Hyperglycemia can lead to increased proinflammatory cytokines such as IL-6 that can lead to increased osteoclast activity, and accumulation of AGEs lead to poor bone quality possibly through impairment of osteoblast activity. Other abnormalities associated with osteoprotegerin production and Wnt signaling pathway have been implicated.

Factors contributing to higher fragility fracture risk include duration of diabetes and microvascular complications such as concomitant retinopathy or nephropathy. Complications such as neuropathy, balance disturbances, sarcopenia, visual impairment, and hypoglycemia increase the risk for falls and fractures. . Compared with other diabetic complications, strict glycemic control may prevent the onset and or delay progression but will not reverse them. Medications also can decrease BMD. Thiazolidinediones can impair osteoblastogenesis, while sodium glucose transporter-2 inhibitors such as canagliflozin have been associated with hip bone loss and increased the hip fracture risk.

One can only conclude that measures to prevent fractures in high-risk diabetics are no different from those for high-risk postmenopausal diabetic women with low bone densities. Of concern is the type 2 diabetic who is at increased fracture risk even if the low BMD does increase with therapy. Measures such as healthy diet and physical exercises need to be reinforced given the important role in the prevention and treatment of both conditions.

### Thyroid Disease

### Hyperthyroidism

Patients with hyperthyroidism because of Graves' disease may present with pretibial myxedema and ophthalmopathy. The myxedema appears as nodules (usually 1 cm or larger) over the pretibial surface. They are composed of hyaluronic acid, are pink to purple in color, and are painless. 112, Patients with Graves' disease can also have proximal muscle weakness, associated shoulder adhesive capsulitis, loss of muscle mass, and weight loss. Most of these manifestations will correct with treatment. Nail changes, onycholysis, and clubbing (thyroid acropachy) may be associated with periostitis around the metacarpal joints, as well as soft tissue swelling of the digits. Unfortunately, this condition may not return to normal when the patient is treated.

A common and serious manifestation of hyperthyroidism is osteopenia/osteoporosis. Treating patients with thyroid hormone to achieve a normal level of thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), as well as adjusting the dose of thyroid replacement, is essential to achieving improvement in BMD (as measured by bone densitometry) in patients with hyperthyroid disease. 116,

Hyperthyroidism frequently overlaps with other autoimmune diseases. To evaluate for the prevalence of various non—organ-specific autoantibodies in patients with hyperthyroidism, 80 patients with SLE and RA and a control group of 34 healthy subjects were examined for serum FT3 and FT4, TSH, and antibodies against thyroglobulin and thyroperoxidase; in addition, an ultrasound of the thyroid gland was performed. Patients with hyperthyroidism had a significantly higher prevalence of anti-nuclear antibody (ANA) expression than control subjects (45% vs. 14.7%; P < .001). There were no significant differences in the prevalence of other antibodies between the groups. ANA+ patients were younger

than ANApatients and had significantly higher anti-thyroglobulin (anti-TG) values (P < .05). The prevalence of hyperthyroidism in people with RA and SLE was significantly higher than in control subjects (24% vs. 8%; P < .05). No significant differences in the prevalence of hyperthyroidism were detected between patients with SLE and RA. The investigators concluded that ANA is the most frequent non—organ-specific antibody associated with hyperthyroidism, whereas the other antibodies occur rarely. These results indicate that it is clinically important to screen patients with SLE and RA for the co-existence of thyroid autoimmune disease.

### Hypothyroidism

The most common cause of primary hypothyroidism in the United States is Hashimoto's thyroiditis (HT), also known as chronic immune thyroiditis, with an occurrence of 3.6/100 person-years in females and 0.8/1000 person-years in men.119, Other causes include pituitary adenoma or Sheehan's syndrome, surgical resection, iodine deficiency, deficiency in the iodothyronine synthetase pathway, or use of certain drugs (lithium or amiodarone). Hypothyroidism often presents with a characteristic symmetric arthropathy involving stiffness of the joints of the hands and knees. Upon palpation, the joints feel "gelatinous," and aspiration of fluid is usually non-inflammatory and viscous, with high levels of hyaluronic acid. Calcium pyrophosphate dehydrate (CPPD) crystals are often found, and hypothyroidism should be included in the differential diagnosis of joints that demonstrate CPPD crystals upon aspiration. Other conditions associated with CPPD crystal deposition include:

Hyperparathyroidism

Familial hypocalciuric hyperkalemia

Hemochromatosis

Hemosiderosis

Hypophosphatasia

Hypomagnesemia

Hypothyroidism

Gout

Neuropathic joints

Aging

Amyloidosis

Trauma, including surgery

In patients with hypothyroidism, a myopathy can occur and presents with pain, cramps, stiffness, proximal weakness, fatigue, elevated CPK levels, abnormal muscle disease on biopsy (atrophy of type II fibers and an increase in type I fibers), and hypercholesterolemia.122, Hoffman's syndrome is a rare disorder of hypothyroidism manifesting with increased muscle mass (pseudohypertrophy in addition to the other aforementioned manifestations). Kocher—Debré—Semelaigne syndrome is a disorder of infancy (cretinism) presenting with similar pseudohypertrophy toms of myopathy resolve upon treatment with thyroid hormone. Explanations for the effect of thyroid hormone on muscle include delayed contraction and relaxation (related to a change from fast to slow muscle fibers), alteration in myosin heavy chain gene forms, and impaired glycogenosis. A neuropathy such as CTS can also be the initial manifestation of hypothyroidism. The mechanism for compression is thought to be a result of the accumulation of glycosaminoglycans within the surrounding tissues. One systematic review of 4908 patients with CTS found a pooled odds ratio of 1.4 (95% CI, 1.0 to 2.0) for the prevalence

of concomitant hypothyroidism compared with healthy control subjects.

### Chronic Autoimmune Thyroiditis

Chronic autoimmune thyroiditis (ATD) is an inflammatory thyroiditis that is sometimes characterized by lymphocytic infiltration of the thyroid gland. The presence of arthritis in patients with ATD (even those with normal thyroid function tests) is increasingly observed. ATD encompasses a group of illnesses that include Graves' disease, chronic lymphocytic thyroiditis (CLT), and Hashimoto's disease. Graves' disease is characterized by production of antibodies against thyrotropin receptor, activation of thyroid follicular cells, modest infiltration of the thyroid gland by lymphocytes, and hyperthyroidism. In contrast, CLT can present with either hyperthyroidism or, more often, hypothyroidism. Both can have positive ANA autoantibody expression. Rheumatic complaints in patients with ATD include:

Carpal tunnel syndrome

Chondrocalcinosis

Shoulder capsulitis

Neck pain

Generalized stiffness

Myopathy

Fibromyalgia

Synovial effusions can occur and are non-inflammatory. Affected joints are knees, metacarpophalangeal joints, proximal interphalangeal joints, and metatarsophalangeal joints. Most patients are hypothyroid, and joint complaints resolve when treated with thyroid hormone suppression and decrease in TSH.

In a group of euthyroid patients with CLT and no well-defined connective tissue disease, 98% presented with arthralgia and 59% with fibromyalgia, 28% had Raynaud's disease, and 26% had sicca symptoms. Arthritis was radiographically present in 88% of these patients (arthritis of the spine accounted for 45%). TSH levels correlated with anti-thyroid peroxidase (anti-TPO) antibodies but neither erythrocyte sedimentation rate nor anti-TG antibody levels. The authors concluded that rheumatic manifestations frequently occur in patients with CLT in the absence of overt thyroid dysfunction.

### Thyroid Disorders in Patients With Rheumatic Musculoskelatal Diseases

In a recent prospective trial of 201 patients with rheumatic disease and 122 age-matched healthy control subjects, mean TSH values of the patients with rheumatic disease and the control subjects were 3.1 ± 2.7 and 1.9 ± 0.8 mIU/L, respectively (P = .004). The mean fT4 value of the patients with rheumatic disease was 1.43 ± 0.67 ng/dL, whereas that of the control subjects was 1.58 ± 0.68 ng/dL (P < .001), and thyroid autoantibodies were significantly higher in patients with rheumatic disease versus control subjects (P < .001). In another cohort of patients with and without RA, no difference was found in the incidence of hypothyroid disease between patients with RA and non-RA control subjects. Nevertheless, the presence of hypothyroidism in patients with RA was positively correlated with increased cardiovascular disease in the RA population even after adjustment for other traditional risk factors.

Medications used to treat various connective diseases, as well as the disease itself, can affect thyroid function. For example, glucocorticoids inhibit TSH secretion, thereby slightly lowering serum thyroid hormone concentrations. Aspirin and NSAIDs may lower serum thyroid hormone by interfering with the binding to their carrier proteins.

### Systemic Lupus Erythematosus

Anti-thyroid antibodies are present in 15% to 20% of patients with SLE. Concomitant hypothyroidism is estimated at 5.7% (five times greater than expected) as opposed to hyperthyroidism, occurring at 1.7% (similar to the normal population). In a large long-term study of patients with SLE, there was a twofold increase in HT. Anti-SM antibodies and antibody to double-stranded DNA favors this association, but disease activity and cumulative damage are not related to HT or the presence of autoantibodies. . This association may be genetic, as noted in a study of multiplex SLE families in which 35 of them who also had autoimmune thyroid disease demonstrated a linkage with 5q14.3-15 (the major susceptibility locus for SLE also found in autoimmune thyroid disease). This finding suggests that 5q14.3-15 harbors a susceptibility gene shared by patients with SLE and autoimmune thyroid disease.

A common reason for referral to a rheumatologist is a young female patient with arthralgias from whom the referring physician has obtained a blood sample testing positive for ANA autoantibody expression. Studies of patients with Graves' disease and chronic autoimmune thyroiditis have demonstrated more than 26% positivity for ANA and 34% for antisingle-stranded DNA antibodies. No patients in these studies had antibodies to doublestranded DNA or extractable nuclear antigens (anti-Ro/SS-A, anti-La/SS-B, anti-SM, or anti-RNP).

Polymyalgia Rheumatica and Vasculitis. Few studies are available, with some demonstrating a relationship but most 136-138 Nevertheless, the occurrence reporting no association. of polymyalgia rheumatica or giant cell arthritis may be more common in patients with autoimmune thyroid disease. A recent multicenter longitudinal study of patients with different forms of vasculitis also reported an association between hypothyroidism and myeloperoxidase—anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody—associated vasculitis.

Fibromyalgia. An attenuated response of TSH to thyrotropin-releasing hormone, as well as an increased prevalence of anti-thyroid antibodies compared with control subjects, has been described but is of uncertain clinical significance. 141,142

### Rheumatoid Arthritis and Psoriatic Arthritis

In both RA and psoriatic arthritis, an increase in subclinical and clinical disease and an increase in the frequency of anti-thyroid antibodies has been demonstrated compared with control subjects. .143-145 Even though these increases in anti-TPO and anti-TG antibodies and abnormal variation in TSH level were demonstrated, no significant alteration of hormone levels was found, nor was there any association with any particular RA phenotype.

In the Danbio registry of 1035 RA patients, 11.8% with thyroid disease and other comorbid diseases had significantly poorer initial response to RA treatment compared with patients with isolated RA. They concluded that RA patients are at increased risk of specific comorbidities with possible impact on treatment 147 A meta-analysis that included 35, RA patients outcome. reported an increased risk of developing thyroid dysfunction in RA patients, particularly hypothyroidism. 148, An association was also observed with subclinical hypothyroidism and subclinical hyperthyroidism. Although some studies have suggested that certain medications used for the treatment of RA (i.e., corticosteroids, leflunomide) could affect thyroid function, certain biologic DMARDs have shown a trend toward improvement in certain

markers of thyroid disease (e.g., anti-TPO and anti-TG antibodies). Given the high prevalence of thyroid dysfunction in RA patients, screening should be considered in patients with clinical suspicion as well as early treatment when indicated.

### Sjögren's Syndrome

The prevalence of thyroid disease in patients with Sjögren's syndrome runs from a low of 10% to a high of 70%; however, this phenomenon may be related to the demographics of Sjögren's syndrome, which usually affects older women. In one study, the occurrence of hypothyroidism was 14%, with the occurrence of thyrotoxicosis being 1.8%. Symptoms of Sjögren's syndrome, such as conjunctivitis sicca and xerostomia, have been reported in up to 32% of patients with autoimmune thyroiditis. In a large study of 479 patients with Sjögren's syndrome, the frequency of HT (6.26%) was found to be higher than in the normal population (1% to 2%); however, this increased frequency was not seen with Graves' disease. It was also observed that the presence of Graves' disease and HT could appear either before or after the occurrence of Sjögren's syndrome, making it difficult to ascertain whether primary Sjögren's syndrome was a predisposing factor for the development of autoimmune thyroiditis.

### Scleroderma and Overlap Syndromes

Fibrosis of the gland can lead to hypothyroidism, and in this group, only 50% of patients had positive tests for anti-thyroid antibodies. As with SLE, patients with scleroderma have a higher prevalence of thyroid autoantibodies with and without hypothyroidism. Unlike spondyloarthritis and RA, there was no link between thyroid autoantibody presence and disease activity or functional impairment.

Scarce data are available for overlap syndromes. Anti-thyroid antibodies were found in a quarter of the patients, and overt hypothyroidism was found in fewer than 20% of patients.

### Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis

The occurrence of anti-thyroid antibodies (anti-TG and anti- TPO), as well as thyroid function, was assessed in a small group of children with juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) compared with control subjects. The investigators concluded that children with JIA have a higher incidence of anti-thyroid antibodies and subclinical hypothyroidism than do normal children. The children who were positive for antibodies all had oligoarticular JIA.

In another study looking at the prevalence of other autoimmune diseases in 79 patients with JIA and their families (438 relatives), 15.2% had one or more autoimmune diseases, as did 13% of family members (more common in first-degree relatives). The most common was autoimmune thyroid disease.

### Spondyloarthritis

Associations extend beyond the psoriatic arthritis mentioned above to include the wider spondyloarthritis (SpA) spectrum. To evaluate the prevalence of HT in a group of patients (n = 357) with SpA and normal age-matched control subjects (n = 318), serum levels of TSH, free triiodothyronine, and free thyroxine, along with titers of anti-TG and anti-TPO antibodies, were assayed. Indices of thyroid autoimmunity were significantly more frequent in patients with SpA than in control subjects (24.1% vs. 10.7%, P < .05). In the SpA group, a higher prevalence of HT was found in patients with active disease than in those with low to moderate disease levels. Also in the SpA group, patients with disease

duration greater than 2 years had a higher prevalence of HT and anti-TPO antibody positivity than did patients with a disease duration less than 2 years. Ultrasonography of the thyroid gland was performed in all subjects, and rheumatic activity was evaluated. Ultrasonography detected a significantly higher frequency of thyroid nodules and hypoechoic pattern in patients with SpA than in control subjects. HT and anti-TPO antibodies were significantly more frequent in patients with SpA who had peripheral involvement (68.6%) than in patients with axial involvement (31.4%; P < .05). This study demonstrated a significantly higher prevalence of thyroid autoimmunity in patients with SpA compared with control subjects. Thyroiditis occurs more frequently in patients with longer disease duration and active rheumatic disease. The authors suggested that thyroid function tests be part of the clinical evaluation in patients with SpA.

### Parathyroid Disease

### Hypoparathyroidism

A disorder of parathyroid hormone (PTH), hypoparathyroidism is usually caused by either autoimmune destruction of the parathyroid glands (isolated endocrine deficiency syndrome or failure of other endocrine glands) or neck surgery with extensive removal of parathyroid tissue. Two other lesser causes are a congenital disorder with failure of derivatives of the third and fourth pharyngeal pouch (DiGeorge syndrome) and intra-cellular processing defects or mutations of the calcium sensing receptor. Bone structure and bone turnover is different from normal and may result in enthesopathy, as well as paravertebral and/or subcutaneous calcifications. The clinical manifestations (circumoral numbness, paresthesias, carpal and pedal muscle spasms, laryngeal spasm, tetany, and/or seizures), which are seen infrequently, are a result of hypocalcemia.

Albright's osteodystrophy or pseudohypoparathyroidism (pseudo-HoPT) results from end organ resistance (bone and kidney) to PTH and presents with elevated levels of PTH, hypocalcemia, and hyperphosphatemia. Type 1a HoPT (autosomal dominant) is inherited maternally and characterized by calcification of the paraspinal ligaments, short stature, and mental retardation. Patients clinically have shortened metatarsal and metacarpal bones and a defect in the genes encoding the α-subunit of the cell membrane—associated guanine nucleotide stimulating unit of adenyl cyclase. Type 1b HoPT also has resistance to PTH but has a normal phenotype and is inherited paternally.160, Soft tissue calcifications that are not clinically relevant (in basal ganglia, cataracts, shoulder joints, or subcutaneous tissues of the hands) have occurred in HoPT and infrequently in pseudo-HoPT. Surgically induced HoPT may also be accompanied by muscle weakness that is usually related to the degree of hypocalcemia and is responsive to treatment with vitamin D and calcium.

Renal disease can result in crystal deposition disease (sodium urate, calcium pyrophosphate, or basic calcium phosphate hydroxyapatite) as a result of hyperphosphatemia from reduced glomerular filtration and secondary hyperparathyroidism. Sodium urate deposition results in acute gout seen more commonly in people with renal insufficiency. Gout is rare in patients undergoing dialysis but can be seen after renal transplantation with decreased creatinine clearance and use of calcineurin inhibitors, such as cyclosporine. CPPD deposition is seen less often in renal disease than gout or hydroxyapatite and is rare in individuals undergoing dialysis. Hydroxyapatite deposition can cause acute

synovitis and periarticular inflammation. Painful subcutaneous nodules or chronic asymptomatic nodules (uremic humoral calcinosis) can occur. Prevention is achieved through phosphate restriction, adequate dialysis, and oral phosphate binding agents.

Renal osteodystrophy is a result of osteomalacia, osteitis fibrosa cystica, osteosclerosis, aluminum toxicity, osteoporosis, and β2microglobulin amyloid deposition and presents with bone pain, muscle wasting, and myalgias, as well as bone fractures. To define the abnormalities in skeletal microstructure and to establish the potential efficacy of PTH replacement in hypoparathyroidism, standard histomorphometric and microcomputed tomography analyses were performed on iliac crest bone biopsies obtained from patients with hypoparathyroidism. Participants were treated with teriparatide for 2 years and compared with ageand sex-matched control subjects with no abnormalities in parathyroid function. Initially bone density was increased and skeletal features reflected the low turnover state with greater bone volume/trabecular bone volume, trabecular width, and cortical width, as well as suppressed mineralizing surface and bone formation rate compared with control subjects. With teriparatide therapy, bone turnover and BMD increased in the lumbar spine. Requirements for calcium and vitamin D fell, whereas serum and urinary calcium concentrations did not change. The investigators concluded that the abnormal microstructure of the skeleton in hypoparathyroidism reflects the absence of PTH. Replacement therapy with PTH has the potential to correct these abnormalities and to reduce the requirements for calcium and vitamin D.

### Similarities to Other Rheumatic c Diseases

The skeletal abnormalities of hypoparathyroidism are caused by calcification, which can simulate ankylosing spondylitis with clinical signs, including morning stiffness, gait, and posture. Sacroiliitis is not expected, although it is the earliest manifestation in most patients with ankylosing spondylitis. The patterns of syndesmophytes in patients with hypoparathyroidism can resemble those of ankylosing spondylitis with an origin from the vertebral margin and preserved disk space, but more often there is also involvement of the posterior paraspinal ligament. Spinal changes in hypoparathyroidism have also been described to be similar to those in DISH, which is characterized by ossification of the anterior longitudinal ligament of the spine and of various extraspinal ligaments but is rarely reported before 50 years of age. The pain is not responsive to immunosuppressive agents and NSAIDs but may resolve completely upon treatment with calcitriol. Serum calcium may need to be included in the diagnostic workup of patients with inflammatory back pain, especially if they present with atypical features as previously described. It is important to differentiate hypoparathyroid-related spondylitis from ankylosing spondylitis because the management for the two disorders is different. In fact, some of the drugs used for ankylosing spondylitis, such as bisphosphonates, may worsen hypocalcemia. The mechanism underlying these skeletal changes in hypoparathyroidism is not well defined. Decreased intestinal calcium absorption caused by a defect in the action of 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D has been suggested to play a role in a controlled study of paravertebral ligamentous ossification. Investigators suggested that the ossifying diathesis of paravertebral ligaments, which is the origin of DISH, might be initiated or aggravated by hypoparathyroidism.

### Systemic Lupus Erythematosus

SLE is known to potentially affect any organ system, and hypoparathyroidism has been found to occur in 4.0% to 5.7% of

patients with SLE compared with 1.0% in the general population. Hypoparathyroidism is underestimated because it is poorly manifested clinically and can be precipitated by certain aggravating factors, such as corticosteroid treatment or vitamin D deficiency. Although acute hypocalcemia typically gives symptoms and signs of musculoskeletal irritability, chronic hypocalcemia usually gives mild symptoms and can even be asymptomatic. Despite the possible lack of outward manifestations, hypocalcemia may be a significant health risk as a result of QT interval prolongation and the consequent risk of sudden death. These cases raise the question of whether periodic calcium and phosphate screening should be routine care for patients with SLE.

### Hyperparathyroidism

PTH, along with vitamin D and calcitonin, controls calcium homeostasis. These hormones are responsible for bone metabolism and remodeling in addition to maintaining serum calcium in a very narrow range. In primary hyperparathyroidism (HPT), this balance is altered as a result of changes in the parathyroid gland, whereas changes in other organs of the body that result in calcium loss and vitamin D deficiency with increased secretion of PTH are called secondary HPT.

Approximately 1% to 2% of the population has hypercalcemia, with 10% to 20% of these individuals having HPT. Most patients with HPT have a single adenoma; carcinoma is rare, and in secondary HPT diffuse hyperplasia related to hypocalcemia or resistance to PTH is seen. Secondary HPT is most commonly the result of osteomalacia, vitamin D deficiency, and renal failure. Skeletal symptoms include arthralgias, as well as radiographic findings such as osteitis fibrosa cystica and subperiosteal resorption along the radial side of the phalanges. In addition, the distal tufts of the phalanges may also reveal subperiosteal resorption.

Arthritis associated with HPT involves the small joints of the hand (possibly becoming erosive) and spares the PIP joints. In this respect, it can mimic RA, but the presence of subperiosteal resorption is very distinctive. In contrast to RA, these patients

generally have low erythrocyte sedimentation rates, negative rheumatoid factors and anti-citrullinated protein antibodies, and laboratory values consistent with HPT. HPT more commonly involves the radiocarpal, inferior radioulnar, and MCP joints compared with RA. Lytic lesions resulting from HPT in the skeleton (Brown's tumors) are localized areas of fibrous tissue resulting from increased osteoclastic activity, giant cells, and decomposing blood. CPPD (pseudogout or chondrocalcinosis) is also associated with HPT. Attacks of gout also can be seen in HPT, and the concomitant occurrence of uric acid and CPPD crystals can be found in synovial fluid aspirated from acutely inflamed joints. In addition to the acute attacks of CPPD, chronic CPPD disease may result in erosive disease.

Early changes in bone such as sacroiliitis may occur in HPT. In one study with 49 MRI patients with asymptomatic HPT, 26 patients newly diagnosed axial spondyloarthropathy and 37 healthy controls were examined by MRI. Bone marrow edema (ASAS-Omeract active sacroileitis criteria) was seen in 16.3% of asymptomatic HPT patients, similar to controls but statistically lower than seen in axial SpA. Other acute inflammatory lesions, as well as chronic structural sacroiliac lesions, were also detected in asymptomatic HPT patients, similar to controls but also less than seen in axial SpA. These findings could not be attributed to excessive secretion of PTH hormone.

Muscle involvement can occur in HPT, presenting with proximal muscle weakness. Muscle enzymes are not elevated, and both electromyography (EMG) studies and muscle biopsy results demonstrate a picture of denervation.

### Lipid Disorders

Lipid-associated musculoskeletal syndromes are rare; however, symptoms in these patients can be incapacitating and difficult to recognize. The five major types of dyslipidemias/hyperlipoproteinemias are described in Table 127.2. One of the first reports described 10 of 18 patients homozygous for familial type II hyperlipidemia that presented with attacks of acute migratory polyarthritis lasting up to a month.

### Tendinopathy

Tendon xanthomas have been described in dyslipidemia types II and III, and type II has been associated with tendinopathy. Tendon xanthomata, which are collections of lipid-laden macrophages typically observed over the Achilles tendons, can be either symptomatic or asymptomatic. These develop during childhood in homozygote patients but can also be seen in heterozygous patients later in life. Association with tendinitis is variable but more common in homozygous patients. The presence of tendon xanthomata correlates with a 3.2-fold higher risk of cardiovascular disease. Type III patients present with tuberoeruptive xanthomata and plantar crease xanthomata, which are typically asymptomatic and do not involve tendons.

### Arthritis

Several other reports have been published of arthritis in patients with type II dyslipidemia. A case series of 41 patients followed up for 4 years described a transient migratory polyarthritis, which affected both large and small joints in 10 of the patients. Episodes lasted between 3 to 12 days, with moderate to severe pain. Non-inflammatory synovial fluid was obtained in some cases, supporting the hypothesis that symptoms arise secondary to periarthritis. This presentation is also supported by other reports in the literature. 183, Type IV patients have also developed episodes of arthritis, presenting as an acute or subacute pauciarthritis of large and small joints. Fluid from two of these patients was described as of a mildly inflammatory nature.185, Arthritis and musculoskeletal symptoms have responded to lipid-lowering therapy. 184,187,188

# Rheumatic Paraneoplastic Syndromes and Malignancies With Rheumatic Manifestations

### KEY POINTS

### Introduction

The relationship between cancer and rheumatic diseases is complex and bidirectional with many potential mechanisms linking the two entities. As discussed in Chapters 37, 129, and 130, a persistent inflammatory state and damage from rheumatic diseases or cytotoxic and biologic therapies employed to treat rheumatologic conditions may increase the risk of subsequent malignancy; similarly, malignancy or its treatment may induce autoimmunity or rheumatic manifestations. In this chapter, we describe salient features of rheumatic paraneoplastic syndromes that should alert clinicians to the possibility of an underlying malignancy. We also describe musculoskeletal and rheumatic symptoms that may be related to malignancy and/or its therapy.

Rheumatic paraneoplastic syndromes are rare but have characteristic features that can be of clinical importance for early detection and therapy of an occult malignancy (Table 128.1). They

are not directly caused by the tumor itself or its metastases but are mediated by soluble factors, such as hormones and cytokines, or humoral or cellular immune mechanisms against tumor cells. Therefore the clinical manifestation of paraneoplastic syndromes occurs distant from the underlying malignancy and can involve joints, fasciae, muscles, vessels, and bones. 1,

To classify a rheumatic disease as truly paraneoplastic, a causal relationship between the malignant disease and the musculoskeletal pathology has to be demonstrated. For the argument of causality over mere coincidence, a set of criteria was proposed more than 50 years ago, called the Bradford Hill Criteria. In the case of paraneoplastic syndromes, besides strength and specificity of an association between tumor diagnosis and rheumatic symptoms, their temporal relationship is the main critical issue. A syndrome is generally considered paraneoplastic when its manifestations appear either simultaneously or in some studies within 3 years of the detection of the malignancy. The best evidence for causation is established in retrospect, when it is possible to completely eliminate a tumor and the rheumatic symptoms undergo full remission.

In addition to these distinct paraneoplastic syndromes, certain cancers may more directly lead to symptoms that are similar to rheumatic diseases. Tumors can arise from mesenchymal cells in bone, cartilage, muscles, or connective tissues, or the musculoskeletal system can become invaded by metastatic spreading of tumors from other locations or infiltration by hematologic malignancies.5,

Finally, certain cancer therapies can induce rheumatic manifestations. Of particular interest to the rheumatologist are musculoskeletal symptoms caused by aromatase inhibitors,7 chemotherapy, radiation, and Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG)induced reactive arthritis,8 as detailed in this chapter. Most recently, various autoimmune phenomena have developed after treatment with immune checkpoint inhibitors, as discussed in Chapter 130.9

In this chapter we review the clinical characteristics and current pathophysiologic understanding of various forms of paraneoplastic polyarthritis, paraneoplastic vasculitis, hypertrophic

osteoarthropathy, eosinophilic fasciitis, tumor-induced osteomalacia, and cancer-associated myositis and scleroderma. We also discuss treatment of these paraneoplastic conditions beyond treating the associated malignancy. Rheumatic manifestations stemming more directly from malignancy and from the treatment of malignancy are also discussed.

### Paraneoplastic Arthritis

Numerous case reports and small case series have described a de novo manifestation of a highly inflammatory synovitis preceding or leading to the detection of an underlying malignant tumor. 10, The largest cohort of 65 patients with paraneoplastic arthritis (PA) detailed their clinical and demographic characteristics compared

with 50 patients with new-onset rheumatoid arthritis (RA). The mean age of onset in PA is 50, and a male preponderance of 65% stands in sharp contrast to RA. The synovitis usually starts as acute asymmetric (91%) and polyarthritis (34%), oligoarthritis (48%), or monoarthritis (18%), with highly elevated laboratory markers of inflammation. A diagnostic dilemma in PA arises by the fact that 23% of these patients test positive for rheumatoid factor and 1 1% for antibodies against anti-citrullinated proteins. Therefore in individual cases the diagnosis is difficult. Often the only clinical clue to search for an underlying malignancy remains an atypical pattern of joint involvement and a poor response to standard antirheumatic therapies, especially corticosteroids. So far, no consistent theory has explained the pathogenesis. In one case of renal cancer, T cell clones with identical receptor rearrangements were

identified in tumor and synovial tissues, suggesting a cross-reactivity of malignant cells and synovial antigens in PA. Recently citrullinated vimentin was recognized as an important tumor antigen in epithelial cancers. Also, T cellmediated immune responses against citrullinated vimentin expressing cancer cells have been defined, representing anti-tumor responses. Hence at least some forms of PA, especially those with antibody responses against citrullinated proteins, may be based on immune responses against citrullinated tumor antigens.

### Palmar Fasciitis and Polyarthritis Syndrome s

Recognizing a potential paraneoplastic syndrome in a patient presenting with arthritis is more straightforward when in addition to synovitis other characteristic features are present. This is the case in palmar fasciitis and polyarthritis syndrome (PFPAS), where inflammation of palmar and/or plantar fasciae leads to a very distinctive clinical presentation (Fig. 128.1A). PFPAS is characterized by a symmetric acute, diffuse, painful swelling of both hands caused by polyarthritis of fingers and wrists in combination with palmar fasciitis. This syndrome presents with marked thickening and induration of palmar tissues and rapidly progressive flexion contractures of the fingers. The findings upon palpation are described by the term "woody hands." Arthritis of other joints can be present but is usually milder; plantar involvement occurs in about 20%. Of reported cases of PFPAS, more than half of them occur in association with ovarian adenocarcinoma or other tumors of urogenital organs. Frequently, tumor markers such as CA125 or CA19-9 are positive and a diagnostic clue. 14, The pathogenetic mechanisms of PFPAS have not been resolved; however, a potential role of connective tissue growth factor has repeatedly been proposed. 16, In addition, there exists one anecdotal report about the induction of PFPAS by treatment with a metalloprotease inhibitor. In patients with suspected PFPAS, physicians should consider checking CA125, CA19-9, and/or prostate-specific antigen and performing imaging of the abdomen and pelvis if no known malignancy has been identified in the affected patient. Treating PFPAS proves difficult if no malignancy is found. Glucocorticoids and disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs have little effect; physical and occupational therapy may improve function. If no malignancy is found at the time of presentation, one should consider repeating screening in 6 to 12 months.

### Remitting Seronegative Symmetric Synovitis With Pitting Edema

In general, in any patient with RS3PE, a poor response to corticosteroids should be considered a red flag and prompt a search for an occult malignancy. Patients typically respond to lower doses of steroids over a 2to 3-month course; the average was 16 mg prednisone-equivalent daily in one systematic literature review. Rheumatologists can make sure patients' age-appropriate cancer screening is up to date upon diagnosis of RS3PE and consider further imaging based on any additional symptoms present.

### Pancreatic Panniculitis and Polyarthritis

Polyarthritis in association with a panniculitis resembling erythema nodosum occurs in patients with pancreatitis (hence the acronym PPP) and high levels of serum lipase. This syndrome is more common in men than in women. The same manifestations can be seen in acinar cell carcinoma, a subtype of pancreatic cancer, which also leads to high concentrations of lipase in the circulation. This causes extensive necrotic lesions of subcutaneous fat tissues with a surrounding inflammatory reaction. The polyarthritis is typically symmetric and most commonly affects the ankles, knees, wrists, and metacarpophalangeal joints. A review of 59 cases of PPP found pancreatic malignancy in 11.9%. In more than 130 publications, PPP is consistently associated with a dismal prognosis.23-25 There is generally a poor response to nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and corticosteroids; treatment should be focused on the underlying pancreatic disease.

### Erythromelalgia

Erythromelalgia is a syndrome characterized by attacks of severe burning, erythema, and warmth of the extremities. In most cases erythromelalgia involves the feet26 (Fig. 128.1C). Symptoms are exacerbated when the extremities are placed in a dependent position, during ambulation, or during exposure to increased temperatures. This disorder can be idiopathic or secondary to another disease like a malignancy. Myeloproliferative disorders, such as polycythemia vera and essential thrombocytosis, are the most common conditions associated with erythromelalgia and precede its diagnosis onset.28, In one retrospective study, however, only about 9% of patients with erythromelalgia had a concomitant myeloproliferative disorder. Because of the association with myeloproliferative syndrome, a thorough hematologic examination with complete blood cell counts with differential, peripheral blood smear and flow cytometry, and serum protein electrophoresis and immunofixation is recommended. If abnormal labs are present, consider bone marrow aspiration. The underlying pathophysiology of erythromelalgia remains unclear. Platelet breakdown products and platelet microthrombus formation may trigger inflammation, especially in the context of erythromelalgia associated with myeloproliferative disorders. In primary erythromelalgia, microvascular arteriovenous shunts have been proposed to cause this syndrome. In the largest published cohort, 168 patients were identified with erythromelalgia: 31.9% of patients reported worsening of disease, 26.6% reported no change, 30.9% reported improvement, and 10.6% reported complete resolution of symptoms. The most effective therapy seems to be the use of daily aspirin, leading to a significant relief of symptoms. A host of other therapies have been tried with varying success.32, Topical therapies include lidocaine, amitriptyline, and ketamine.34, Aspirin can be used if there is myeloproliferative disease and gabapentin and pregabalin have worked for symptom relief in some

patients. Intravenous iloprost showed benefit in the majority of patients treated in one study.

### Paraneoplastic Vasculitis

Although various vasculitides occur in temporal association with malignant diseases, the most prevalent manifestation is cutaneous leukocytoclastic vasculitis.36, Hematologic malignancies are identified as a cause in more than half of the paraneoplastic cases,

with myelodysplasia and non-Hodgkin's lymphoma being the most frequent diagnoses.38, Among solid tumors, lung, breast, and urogenital cancer are the most common causes of paraneoplastic vasculitis.37, In a retrospective analysis of 421 adult patients presenting with clinically unequivocal or biopsy-confirmed cutaneous vasculitis, 16 (3.8%) were paraneoplastic (9 hematologic, 7 solid malignancies). Four had additional joint symptoms and two each had gastrointestinal involvement or nephropathy. In this context it is of interest that in adult patients with histology-proven

Henoch-Schönlein purpura, malignancies have repeatedly been diagnosed; a deposition of immune complexes containing tumor antigens and immunoglobulin A is proposed as a possible pathogenetic mechanism. 42-44

### Hypertrophic (Pulmonary) Osteoarthropathy

Hypertrophic osteoarthropathy (HOA) or Marie-Bamberger syndrome is a classic musculoskeletal paraneoplastic syndrome and has frequently been described and reviewed in the rheumatologic literature. It is characterized by two distinctive symptoms: (1) the clubbing of distal phalanges of fingers and/or toes and (2) an inflammatory, proliferative periostitis causing bone and joint pain and occasionally synovitis and effusion.45, The predominant locations are tibia and fibula, knees, and ankles. This periosteal inflammation causes osteoblast activation, which is detectable by increased tracer uptake in bone scans and lamellar ossification of the periosteum along tubular bones in conventional radiography. In retrospective analyses, the frequency of HOA in primary lung cancer was close to 1%; however, HOA can also occur occasionally in other types of malignancies (mainly intrathoracic).47, Because of the characteristic acral fibroblast and periosteal osteoblast activation, this syndrome was initially thought to be a variant of acromegaly. Now it has become clear that platelet-derived growth factor or vascular endothelial growth factor produced by tumor cells can both contribute to the pathogenesis of HOA.49, Removing the tumor or other underlying cause often improves symptoms but is not always effective.48, In refractory disease, bisphosphonates like zolendronic acid and pamidronate have been shown to be effective in case reports.52-54 Upon a new diagnosis of HOA, physicians should consider obtaining high-resolution computed tomography of the chest to evaluate for thoracic malignancy.

### Eosinophilic Fasciitis

Eosinophilic fasciitis (EF) is a fibrosing disorder of the fascia and skin that can be associated with malignancy. It is often accompanied by peripheral eosinophilia, but peripheral eosinophilia or tissue eosinophilia are not necessary for the diagnosis. EF typically causes erythema and edema of the skin initially followed by woody induration.56, This can lead to a peau d'orange appearance to the skin55 (Fig. 128.1D). It primarily involves the limbs and trunk, sparing the hands and face. Patients may experience venous grooving due to induration of involved subcutaneous tissues (Fig. 128.1D). They often have myalgias and more rarely can have inflammatory arthritis. Evaluation of suspected EF can include checking muscle enzymes (CK, aldolase), complete blood count with differential, magnetic resonance imaging of an affected limb, and full-thickness biopsy down to fascia. As many as 10% of patients with EF have an associated hematologic disorder.56, The hematologic disorders associated with EF include lymphomas, leukemias, immune-mediated cytopenias, and myeloproliferative disorders. In evaluating patients with new EF, clinicians should ask about any associated symptoms such as night sweats, fevers, or significant weight loss and obtaining a complete blood count with differential on laboratory studies. Additionally, a serum protein electrophoresis and flow cytometry to evaluate for large granular lymphocyte leukemia can be performed. Treatment of EF usually starts with corticosteroids at doses of 0.5 to 1 mg/kg with a slow taper. In patients who are unable to taper steroids, methotrexate, mycophenolate, and intravenous immunoglobulin have been used.

### Tumor-Induced Osteomalacia

Tumor-induced osteomalacia (TIO) is clinically indistinguishable from other forms of osteomalacia, with progressive bone pain, spontaneous fractures, muscle weakness, and fatigue. The biochemical pattern consists of hypophosphatemia, hyperphosphaturia, normal calcium and parathyroid hormone, normal to low levels of calcitriol, and an increased alkaline phosphatase. The reason for the imbalance in phosphate-calcium metabolism is marked renal phosphate wasting, due to high concentrations of circulating fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF23, phosphatonin). FGF23 inhibits the reabsorption of phosphate in the proximal tubule and suppresses osteoblast differentiation and matrix mineralization in the bone. In the majority of cases, FGF23 is produced by a mesenchymal tumor (mixed connective tissue variant), with other histologies (hemangiopericytoma, giant cell tumor, osteosarcoma) being considerably less frequent. From over 300 cases of TIO, an intraosseous tumor was demonstrated in 40%, and in 55% the neoplasm was found in the soft tissue. Only 8% of the tumors were malignant. A successful localization and removal of the neoplasm usually results in a complete recovery from all symptoms. The majority of patients in one systematic review also required phosphate supplementation and administration of active vitamin D.

### Cancer-Associated Myositis and Scleroderma

Both myositis and scleroderma can present in the paraneoplastic setting, that is, with tight temporal association between diagnosis of the autoimmune disease and a malignancy. The clinical features of myositis and scleroderma are described in detail elsewhere in this book (Chapters 85 and 86).

In dermatomyositis, the temporal association of cancer and myositis onset has been known for decades.64, Dermatomyositis is more commonly associated with cancer than polymyositis or immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy. In paraneoplastic myositis, cancers are typically diagnosed within 3 years before or after myositis diagnosis.
