The autoantibodies most highly associated with paraneoplastic myositis are anti-transcriptional intermediary factor 1-γ (TIF1-γ) and anti-nuclear matrix protein-2; anti-3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-coenzyme A reductase or anti-small ubiquitin-like modifier 1-activating enzyme antibodies may have an association with cancer, but data are less clear.66, Patients with anti-TIF1-γ antibodies had higher rates of breast and ovarian cancer than the general population in one study.

In scleroderma, patients with anti-RNA-polymerase III antibodies and anti-RNPC3 antibodies are more likely to have shortinterval cancer, that is, a cancer diagnosis within 3 years before or after their onset of scleroderma.69-72 The types of tumors seen may vary based on scleroderma subtype. In anti-RNA Pol III-positive patients, those with diffuse skin disease had increased breast, prostate, and tongue cancer risk and those with limited skin disease had increased lung cancer risk compared with the general population.

For both of these diseases, a link between genetic alterations in the tumor and a concordant autoimmune response has been described. In scleroderma, patients with cancer and anti-RNA polymerase III antibodies were found to have mutations or loss of heterozygosity in the POLR3A gene in their tumors with the development of mutation and wild type peptide-specific CD4+ T cell immune responses and cross-reactive autoantibodies. In

dermatomyositis, genetic alterations in TIF1 genes sequenced from tumors were found in patients with anti-TIF1-γ antibodies and cancer.

### Malignancies With Musculoskeletal Manifestations

Some malignancies may present or be associated with joint, muscle, and soft tissue manifestations. A very common musculoskeletal symptom of malignancies is bone pain, which may be seen in many cancers if they metastasize to or originate in bone. Multiple myeloma in particular can commonly involve bone pain, and it may be a presenting symptom in patients. In one study, nearly half of patients presented with bone pain in the primary care setting months before their multiple myeloma diagnosis.

Patients with lymphoma may have articular symptoms for several reasons. Synovitis or joint effusions may occur due to associated gout, as a reaction of nearby lymphomatous spread, or due to infiltration of lymphoma into the synovium.77, Lymphomas may also have bony involvement and can be associated with pathologic fractures and bone pain. Finally, patients with certain types of lymphoma can also present similarly to Still's disease (angioimmunoblastic T cell lymphoma79) or granulomatosis with polyangiitis (extranodal diffuse large B cell lymphoma80).

Leukemia may present with either polyarthritis or arthralgia, though musculoskeletal symptoms tend to be more common in children than adults. Large granular lymphocyte leukemia is associated with RA and may even drive its development. Myelodysplastic syndromes can also present with a variety of autoimmune abnormalities such as inflammatory arthritis, vasculitis, neutrophilic dermatoses, and autoimmune cytopenias.

### Cancer Treatments and Rheumatic Manifestations

It is also important to be aware that certain medications and other treatments used for cancer therapy can trigger rheumatic manifestations. Aromatase inhibitors are used commonly in hormone receptor-positive breast cancer, often for several years of maintenance therapy. A common problem for patients on aromatase inhibitors is developing arthralgias. The arthralgias typically involve the wrists, hands, or knees and are symmetric. Trigger fingers and carpal tunnel syndrome have also been reported. As many as 20% of patients will discontinue aromatase inhibitors due to joint pain. A variety of chemotherapies have been associated with scleroderma-like disease, Raynaud's phenomenon, and digital ischemia. These include bleomycin, gemcitabine, carboplatin, and paclitaxel. Intravesical BCG therapy, used to treat bladder carcinoma, can trigger a reactive arthritis. For the most part, the reactive arthritis improves with cessation of the BCG therapy, though there are reports of some patients having chronic symptoms. Immune checkpoint inhibitors, one type of cancer immunotherapy, can cause a variety of rheumatic immune-related adverse events, as detailed in Chapter 130.

Finally, radiation therapy for cancer may cause several side effects similar to other rheumatic diseases. Head and neck radiation in particular can cause xerostomia that may be confused for Sjögren's syndrome. It can also trigger morphea or other fibrosing syndromes. Due to the association of fibrosing syndromes with radiation, there has been some concern about the safety of patients

with pre-existing scleroderma receiving radiation therapy for cancer. In one study of radiation therapy for breast cancer in scleroderma patients, about 50% developed localized skin thickening in the radiation port, but there were no generalized flares of the disease.

### Conclusion

Musculoskeletal paraneoplastic syndromes often precede other clinical manifestations of neoplasms and can facilitate timely diagnosis of a malignant disease. After successful elimination of all malignant cells, paraneoplastic symptoms usually subside, but some patients may have persistent symptoms. Paraneoplastic symptoms can also have significant impact on quality of life, morbidity, and mortality of patients with cancer. In recent years, some of the underlying mechanisms of paraneoplastic syndromes have been elucidated, improving our understanding of the pathogenesis of rheumatic as well as neoplastic diseases. Additionally, some malignancies may present with musculoskeletal symptoms that are more directly related to the cancer, especially lymphoproliferative disorders. Finally, certain treatments for malignancy can lead to rheumatic disorders.

# Tumors and Tumor-like Lesions of Joints and Related Structures

### KEY POINTS

### Introduction

Mass-forming lesions are often involved in synovial-lined joints and periarticular structures. Arthrosis, arthritis, trauma, crystal deposits, and structural derangements produce the most common lesions, which are nonneoplastic and include ganglion cysts, synovial cysts, tophaceous gout, and loose bodies. In contrast, it is uncommon for neoplasms, whether benign or malignant, to develop in joints and periarticular structures.

Joint neoplasms can be divided into tumors that are primary or arise de novo within the synovium and tumors that are secondary and access the joint by invading from neighboring bones and soft tissues or by spreading from distant sites via the vascular system. Primary joint neoplasms are more common and tend to recapitulate the phenotype of tissues that normally compose the joint and synovial sheath—synovium, fat, blood vessels, fibrous tissue, and cartilage. Regardless of the histologic type, benign variants greatly outnumber their malignant counterparts and, as a group, these tumors more frequently develop in the synovium in comparison with the other periarticular structures.

Tumors and tumor-like lesions of the joints and periarticular structures are biologically and morphologically diverse. They often pose significant challenges in diagnosis and treatment, and their clinicopathologic features are the focus of this chapter.

### Non-neoplastic Lesions

### Synovial and Ganglion Cysts

Cysts are defined as closed compartments or sacs that are lined by epithelium and are frequently filled with fluid. Neither the synovial cyst nor the ganglion cyst is considered a true cyst because each lacks an epithelial lining.

Synovial cysts are common and develop from the synovial lining of a joint, tendon, or bursa. They are nonneoplastic lesions and are caused by herniation of the synovium through the joint capsule or tendon sheath into neighboring tissues or by expansion of a pre-existing bursa. In adults, synovial cysts frequently develop in association with a variety of joint disorders, including trauma, osteoarthrosis (OA), crystal arthropathies, infection, and rheumatoid arthritis (RA) or one of its variants. Most synovial cysts have an anatomic attachment to a joint, and most originate in the posterior medial aspect of the knees of adults, where they are known as popliteal or Baker's cysts. Anatomically, this region of the knee is prone to the development of synovial cysts because the joint capsule can be structurally insufficient and in this age group there is co-existing joint disease.1, Synovial cysts of the posterior knee joint are purported to affect 2.4% of children, who, in contrast

to adults, are usually asymptomatic and have an otherwise normal knee joint. Other joints affected by synovial cysts in decreasing order of frequency are the shoulder, hip, and spine. In the spine they originate from the facet joints and are most commonly located in the lower lumbar region.

Synovial cysts can enlarge over time as they become further distended with increasing amounts of synovial fluid.1, Consequently, they may manifest as a periarticular mass, produce progressive joint pain and swelling, limit joint mobility, and compress adjacent neurovascular structures. An example of compression occurs in the spine, where synovial cysts that arise from facet joints may impinge or extend along spinal nerves, causing radicular pain.6-9 Other complications of synovial cysts, which sometimes can produce dramatic clinical findings, are rupture with extravasation of synovial fluid and secondary infection.

A variety of radiographic techniques have been used to image synovial cysts. Modalities that provide the greatest diagnostic information include arthrography, ultrasonography, computed tomography (CT), and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI).1, All of these techniques reveal synovial cysts to be simple or septated, thin-walled structures that are filled with fluid that has a density similar to that of water (Fig. 129.1).

Grossly, synovial cysts usually range in size from 1 to 10 cm. Their inner surface is smooth, glistening, and translucent; however, it can be distorted by attached blood clot, fibrin, inflammatory debris, or granulation tissue resulting from a prior hemorrhage or infection. The inner surface of the cyst wall is lined by flattened or plump cuboidal synoviocytes arranged in one or several cell layers and surrounded by an outer sheath of fibrous tissue (Fig. 129.2). Sometimes the synovial lining cells may be hyperplastic and form papillary fronds of varying size; other findings that may develop are scattered subsynovial collections of hemosiderin-laden macrophages from previous hemorrhage and aggregates of mononuclear cells and reactive fibrosis secondary to chronic irritation. Facet joint cysts often contain

abundant amorphous debris that may be focally calcified that is surrounded by macrophages and are associated with severe degenerative changes of the ligamentum flavum and its elastic fibers and the annulus fibrosus. Calcium pyrophosphate crystal deposition may be present (Fig. 129.3). Tumoral calcinosis-like crystal deposits and associated foreign-body giant cell reaction also may be present in approximately a third of cases.

The treatment of synovial cysts varies, depending on their location and associated symptoms. They can be managed successfully with conservative therapy; however, in certain clinical situations, surgical excision is required. 1,

Ganglion cysts have been recognized for centuries; Hippocrates described them as being composed of "mucoid flesh."9 They are more common than synovial cysts and arise from tendon sheaths, ligaments, menisci, joint capsules, and bursae. Occasionally, they develop de novo in the subchondral areas of bone (intraosseous ganglion) and, rarely, they arise within nerve or skeletal muscle and lack communication with a joint. Intraneural ganglia have been shown to develop from dissection of joint fluid along an articular branch of a nerve. Ganglion cysts are distinguished from

synovial cysts by virtue of the fact that they lack a surface lining of synoviocytes. A variety of hypotheses have been proposed to explain their pathogenesis, but none have been proven. The most accepted theory is that ganglia develop from mucoid cystic degeneration of periarticular structures and are lined by fibroblast and myofibroblast-like cells. They are commonly associated with repetitive motion activities, inflammatory arthritides, and trauma.

Most ganglia arise along the dorsal and volar aspects of the wrists and fingers and the dorsum of the feet.9, They are usually asymptomatic and typically manifest as a slowly growing, mobile, firm mass that moves with the structure from which it has arisen (Fig. 129.4). Ganglia may be painful if traumatized and can compress adjacent neurovascular structures, producing a variety of symptoms. The radiographic characteristics of ganglia are similar to those of synovial cysts, and they appear on imaging as small, fluid-filled cystic structures. 1, However, by ultrasound, ganglion cysts are generally more difficult to compress than synovial cysts, owing to the thicker, more viscous content and denser capsule of the ganglion cyst; this difference may allow the sonographer to distinguish these two entities through sonocompression characteristics.

Macroscopically, most ganglia are round, but they may form elongate cylindrical structures if they track along a tendon sheath. Ganglia are unior multiloculated, have thin walls, and are filled with translucent mucoid fluid rich in hyaluronic acid and other mucopolysaccharides (Fig. 129.5). The cyst lacks a distinct inner cell lining, and the bulk of the wall consists of dense fibrous tissue, which is usually surrounded by areolar connective tissue (Fig. 129.6). In many instances, the cyst wall is distorted by variable quantities of reactive myxoid tissue and muciphages, which result from small ruptures and extravasation of fluid (Fig. 129.7).

When ganglion cysts form, they may remain stable for years or may spontaneously resolve, and ganglia that disappear may subsequently redevelop. Treatment is frequently conservative because of their innocuous nature. Ganglia occasionally require aspiration or surgical excision, however, especially if they are symptomatic.

### Loose Bodies

Loose bodies and joint mice are generic terms for free-floating structures within a joint cavity. They are the most common tumor-like lesions of joints and may be exogenous, such as fragments of a bullet, or endogenous, such as pieces of articular cartilage, osteophytes, menisci, ligaments, or bone.13-15 When not otherwise specified, the term loose bodies refers to detached pieces of articular cartilage or subchondral bone (osteoarticular loose bodies) or both that lie free within the joint or that have become secondarily embedded in the synovium. Loose bodies can cause pain, crepitance, and locking, and they can limit the range of joint motion.

Osteoarticular loose bodies are a secondary complication of a variety of conditions, including trauma, osteochondritis dissecans, and arthritides of various causes. When dislodged, the sloughed articular cartilage remains viable because it receives its nourishment from the synovial fluid, but the subchondral bone dies because it derives its nutrition solely from blood vessels. Over time, as the loose body tumbles within the joint, its edges become rounded and smooth; however, it eventually becomes embedded within the synovium. Subsequently, the synovium may digest and resorb it, or adjacent subsynovial connective tissue cells may undergo a proliferative and metaplastic response. These cells produce layers of newly formed fibrocartilage and hyaline cartilage, which may undergo endochondral ossification and are

deposited on the surface of the loose body (Fig. 129.8). These layers of newly formed tissue surround the centrally located dislodged native structure, similar to the cambium layers of a tree (Figs. 129.9, 129.10, and 129.11), and provide a mechanism for the whole structure to increase gradually in size and become significantly larger than the initial osteochondral defect from which it originated. As the loose body enlarges, the innermost portion of original articular cartilage cannot be supported adequately by diffusion of synovial fluid, and it dies and calcifies. This combination of events causes the loose body to appear on x-rays as dense speckled and ringlike calcifications (Fig. 129.12). Radiographically and histologically, the differential diagnosis includes synovial chondromatosis. Histologically, the distinct laminar arrangement of cells and eosinophilic matrix and the more uniform cellularity separate loose bodies from synovial chondromatosis. Treatment is simple excision, which can be performed arthroscopically. 14, Recurrence depends on the underlying disease process but is less frequent than in synovial chondromatosis.

Intra-articular rice bodies represent an uncommon type of loose body formation where the joint space is filled with innumerable, free, polished ricelike bodies within the synovial fluid. The process may be idiopathic or a manifestation of a systemic disorder such as a rheumatologic disease (in particular, RA) or mycobacterial infection.17, These bodies begin as intrasynovial proliferative nodules and then become detached and free-floating in the joint

space (Fig. 129.13). Histologically, they are composed of necrotic cells and connective tissue surrounded by layers of abundant fibrin and collagen (Fig. 129.14). Most cases are treated by surgical excision, though spontaneous resolution of the process has occasionally been documented.

### Intra-articular Ossicles

Small bony nodules normally occur in the knees of some rodents and other mammals, and they rarely occur in humans.19-21 In rodents, small bony nodules are consistently found in the anterior portions of the joint and frequently in the posterior portions as well. In humans, nodules develop within the substance of the meniscus of the knee joint adjacent to its attachments to the tibia.

The exact origin of such structures is unknown, although they probably are true sesamoid bones, as seen in rodents. Alternatively, they may represent ossification secondary to local injury. This latter possibility is supported by the fact that previous knee trauma has been noted in numerous reported cases. The main symptom of meniscal ossicles is pain after exertion, such as walking or prolonged standing, with relief when the knee is at rest. Radiographs may reveal an intra-articular calcification that can

be confused with a loose body. MRI shows the ossicle to be a corticated marrow-containing structure that has increased signal intensity on T1-weighted images and decreased signal intensity on T2-weighted images.19, The ossicle is located within the lateral or the medial meniscus and appears as a small (≈1 cm in diameter), palpable bony nodule (Fig. 129.15). If the ossicle is symptomatic, it should be excised; however, if it is an incidental finding, it can be managed conservatively. 19,21

### Pseudotumors and Tumors in the Setting of Total Joint Arthroplasty

Joint arthroplasty is among the most common, cost-effective, and beneficial elective orthopedic procedures. While complications are infrequent, some degree of prosthetic loosening invariably occurs over time and with increased use. Loosening may be due to infection, wear debris reaction, delayed hypersensitivity reaction, or, rarely, the development of an associated sarcoma. A pseudotumor is one such category of complications, defined as a solid or cystic mass found in continuity with a prosthetic joint and not attributable to infection, malignancy, bursa, or scar tissue. The true incidence is unknown, but reported incidences range from approximately 1% to 10% or higher in populations undergoing systematic screening protocols. Pseudotumors occur in the setting of a range of articulations, including metal-on-metal, metalon-polyethylene, and metal-on-ceramic.

Examination of tissue removed at the time of pseudotumor removal or revision arthroplasty serves to characterize the disease process and (1) document the presence or absence of infection, (2) identify the spectrum of wear debris reactions, and (3) assess for histologic patterns associated with immunologic hypersensitivity reactions. As prostheses undergo wear and corrosion over time, fragmentation of their components leads to the microscopic and submicroscopic components being released into the periarticular tissues and phagocytized by synoviocytes and macrophages. This progressive accumulation of macrophages and particulate debris transforms the connective tissue sheath into an expanded synovial-like structure, also described under the terminology detritic synovitis. The different types of prosthesis-derived foreign material can be recognized by light microscopy and include barium-impregnated poly methyl methacrylate (bone cement), polyethylene fibers, and metal particles (Fig. 129.16).22, A very rare but nonetheless well-recognized potential late complication of joint implant is the development of an associated sarcoma. The patients are typically older adults with a mean latency of 6 to 11 years after arthroplasty. Histologically the sarcomas are high in

grade, most often osteosarcoma or undifferentiated sarcoma, and biologically aggressive, frequently being lethal.22,25,26

### Neoplasms

### Fatty Lesions of the Synovium

Although the subsynovial connective tissue of diarthrodial joints is rich in fat, a true lipoma of the synovium is rare. When lipomas develop, they most frequently affect the knee joint and the synovial tendon sheaths of the hands, ankles, and feet, where they are more common in the extensor than in the flexor synovial sheaths.27, Synovial lipomas can be sessile or pedunculated and, when pedunculated, they may produce pain if they twist on their stalks and become secondarily ischemic. Synovial lipoma, similar to its subcutaneous counterpart, is composed of lobules of mature white adipocytes that are delineated by a thin fibrous capsule (Fig. 129.17).

A more common but still unusual fatty lesion of the joint is lipoma arborescens, also known as villous lipomatous proliferation and lipomatosis of the synovium. This disorder is characterized by a diffuse increase in the quantity of subsynovial fat, which bulges into the overlying synovial lining, producing a villous architecture. It is uncertain whether the proliferating fat is neoplastic (lipomatosis) or is a manifestation of a hyperplastic or reactive process. Most cases occur in the context of degenerative or inflammatory arthritis, supporting the idea that the fatty proliferation may represent a secondary reactive process in most instances. Affected patients are usually adults, but the lesion sometimes develops in adolescents and rarely in children. In younger patients, lipoma arborescens may occur in the absence of an identifiable etiologic agent and affect joints other than the knee, raising the possibility of a distinct primary form of the disease. Lipoma arborescens causes chronic effusions, pain, and swelling and restricts joint motion. The duration of symptoms is often long, and symptoms can be present for as long as 30 years; however, acute onset has been documented.

Lipoma arborescens most commonly arises in the knee (Fig. 129.18), especially the suprapatellar portion, although it has also been observed in the hip, ankle, and wrist joints. Lipoma arborescens is typically localized to one joint, but several cases of bilateral knee involvement have been described. One study found that nearly a third of cases demonstrate an atypical presentation, with multifocality or disease outside of the knee. Laboratory studies

are unremarkable, and the joint fluid is clear and yellow. Plain films show joint fullness, and findings of OA are often present. Arthrography reveals multiple lobulated filling defects, which on CT represent a villonodular mass of low signal intensity that on MRI has the density of fat (Fig. 129.19). At surgery, the affected synovium has a prominent villous or villonodular architecture and is tan-yellow in color (Fig. 129.20). Histologically, the lesion is composed of sheets of mature adipocytes admixed with nutrient blood vessels, all of which are partially compartmentalized by fibrous septa and is covered on its intra-articular surface by several layers of synovial cells (Fig. 129.21). Synovectomy may relieve the symptoms and prevent effusions, but associated OA may be progressive.

The clinicopathologic differential diagnosis includes diffuse tenosynovial giant cell tumor, synovial chondromatosis, and synovial hemangioma. These lesions can be distinguished easily from lipoma arborescens by their distinct histologic features. Another disorder that should be included in the differential diagnosis is Hoffa's disease, which is a condition of irritation, inflammation, and hyperplasia of the synovial lining in regions where fat is normally present, such as adjacent to the patella or patellar ligament. .

### Vascular Lesions of the Synovium

Benign vascular tumors of the synovium are rare. Their growth pattern can be localized or diffuse. They tend to predominate in

adolescence and young adulthood, but symptoms frequently can be traced back to childhood. The joint most commonly involved is the knee, but hemangiomas have also been described in the elbow, the ankle, the tarsometatarsal and temporomandibular joints, and the tendon sheaths of the wrist and ankle.35, Unusual complications of synovial hemangiomas include a secondary destructive arthritis and Kasabach-Merritt syndrome.

Synovial hemangiomas produce a variety of symptoms, including unilateral, intermittent joint pain and enlargement, which may result in limitation of motion, locking, buckling, and hemarthrosis, especially after minimal trauma. Classically, the affected joint diminishes in size if sufficiently elevated to allow the blood to drain out of the lesion. On physical examination, the joint is swollen and doughy, and nearby cutaneous hemangiomas may be evident. Joint aspiration frequently yields bloody fluid. Pre-operative diagnosis of localized hemangioma is difficult; the differential diagnosis includes localized tenosynovial giant cell tumor, and in the knee includes discoid meniscus, meniscal tears, cysts, and ossicles. The diffuse hemangioma is more easily identified, but it can mimic diffuse tenosynovial giant cell tumor and hemophilic arthropathy.

Radiographic evaluation may show nothing more than a vague soft tissue shadow indicative of a swollen synovium and a distended joint capsule or regional osteoporosis in patients who have had long-term symptoms and recurrent hemarthrosis. Rarely, calcified phleboliths are apparent; however, they are associated more often with a soft tissue arteriovenous malformation with secondary joint involvement than with an isolated intra-articular hemangioma (Fig. 129.22). Arthrography may show an intra-articular filling defect, and arteriography may be negative in small, localized capillary hemangiomas, but contrast material may collect in the more diffuse lesions that contain cavernous or large ectatic vascular spaces (Fig. 129.23). CT reveals a lobulated soft tissue mass with mild enhancement after injection of contrast material. MRI may show that the tumor has a low to isointense signal on T1-weighted images and high signal intensity on T2-weighted images.

Macroscopically, the localized hemangioma tends to be small, but larger lesions (8 cm) have been documented. The hemangioma may be poorly defined or well circumscribed, sessile, or stalked, and ranges in color from red to dark blue-purple. Microscopically, the hemangioma is usually of the cavernous or venous type, with large dilated blood-filled vessels lined by cytologically benign endothelial cells. In arteriovenous hemangioma, which grows in a diffuse fashion, the entire synovium may be edematous and beefy red or stained brown by hemosiderin, and it consists of prominent tortuous, congested vessels that may penetrate the joint capsule and extend into neighboring soft tissues. Histologically, the vessels recapitulate architecturally abnormal arteries, veins, and capillaries; have abnormal interconnections; and are arranged in a disorganized tangle.

Therapy for a localized hemangioma is marginal surgical excision, which is usually curative. Diffuse lesions frequently are difficult to eradicate because of their extensive nature. Incomplete excision or debulking may be the only surgical option. Radiation therapy is not indicated.

Hemosiderotic synovitis is a chronic proliferative synovial disorder that develops as a consequence of repeated hemarthroses such as may be seen in synovial hemangioma, bleeding diatheses such as hemophilia, oral anti-coagulant use, trauma, and arthritis. Hemosiderotic synovitis most commonly involves the knee joint and presenting symptoms are those of pain and stiffness of the

involved joint, frequently attributable to joint effusions and secondary OA. The radiographic and clinical differential diagnoses are frequently nonspecific, and diagnosis relies on histopathologic

exam. Macroscopically, the synovium appears thickened and opaque and yellow with rusty brown regions and demonstrates thin villous projections. Microscopically, the synovium shows papillary hyperplasia, hemosiderin accumulation within the synoviocytes and adjacent macrophages, and scattered giant cells (Fig. 129.24). Hemosiderotic synovitis lacks the larger nodules and thickened fronds with sheets of mononuclear cells and giant cells that are characteristic of diffuse-type tenosynovial giant cell tumor (discussed in a subsequent section).16, Additionally, one study showed that while the giant cells in diffuse-type tenosynovial giant cell tumor demonstrate an osteoclastic phenotype (characterized by CD51 expression), the giant cells in hemosiderotic synovitis have a macrophage phenotype (characterized by CD14 and HLA- DR expression and negativity for CD51), and the Ki-67 proliferative index is lower in hemosiderotic synovitis. Treatment of hemosiderotic synovitis centers on addressing the primary cause of the hemarthrosis and surgical or conservative management of the frequently concomitant severe degenerative arthritis. 16,38

### Fibroma of Tendon Sheath

Fibroma of tendon sheath is an uncommon benign neoplasm that clinically mimics tenosynovial giant cell tumor but is morphologically distinct. Fibroma of tendon sheath was first identified as a clinicopathologic entity in 1936 and, since that time, more than several hundred cases have been reported.40, While classical examples are paucicellular with dense collagen, hypercellular variants have been described with areas reminiscent of nodular fasciitis, and these variants appear to have different molecular aberrations. A translocation t(2;11) (q31-32;q12) has been identified in classical fibroma of tendon sheath and is likely the driver of the neoplastic process. A t(9;11)(p24;q13-14) has also been documented as an alternative translocation involving 1 1q in a fibroma of tendon sheath; therefore different molecular aberrations are associated with this neoplasm. In contrast, cellular fibroma of tendon sheath has been shown to frequently harbor rearrangements of ubiquitin-specific peptidase 6 (USP6) on chromosome 17p13, suggesting that these variants may represent a tenosynovial variant of nodular fasciitis, a benign fibroblastic/myofibroblastic neoplasm characterized by USP6 rearrangement in >90% of cases;

however, the fusion partner in cellular fibroma of tendon sheath is thus far unknown and appears to be distinct from those in nodular fasciitis.

Fibroma of tendon sheath usually arises from the tendons and sheaths of the flexor surfaces of the distal extremities; approximately 70% of cases involve the fingers or hand. Of the fingers, the thumb is affected most frequently, followed in descending order by the index and middle fingers. Less commonly, large diarthrodial joints such as the knee and rarely the elbow, ankle, shoulder, and hip are sites of origin.40, Patients range in age from infants to elderly individuals, but the median age is the early fourth decade of life.40, The cellular variant of fibroma of tendon sheath appears to affect younger patients on average compared with the classic type. Most series report a male predominance, with the largest study of 138 cases having a male-to-female ratio of 3:1.40 Patients present with a slow-growing, painless mass that usually has been noted for several months to a year. In 6% to 10% of cases, a history of antecedent trauma is reported. Tumors developing in large joints can be painful, restrict range of motion, and may be palpable.46,

Plain radiographs show soft tissue fullness; rarely is there evidence of bone erosion. CT or MRI shows a solid, well-circumscribed mass of soft tissue density that usually has low signal intensity on T1-weighted images and variable intensity on T2-weighted images. At surgery, the tumors are often attached directly to the tendon or tendon sheath. They are rubbery, oblong, well circumscribed, or encapsulated; average 1.5 to 1.8 cm in greatest dimension; and have a tan-white cut surface (Fig. 129.25).40,

Microscopically, classical fibroma of tendon sheath is multilobular, with clefts interposed between adjacent lobules. The lobules are composed of spindle and stellate fibroblasts enmeshed in a collagenous and sometimes myxoid stroma (Fig. 129.26). Hypercellular regions reminiscent of nodular fasciitis may be seen and often blend with less cellular regions. Immunohistochemically, the tumor cells have the staining profile of myofibroblasts, and ultrastructurally, the cells have features of fibroblasts and myofibroblasts.

The natural history of fibroma of tendon sheath consists of slow growth that eventually ceases. The treatment of choice is surgical excision. Overall recurrence rate is 5% to 10%; however, a

higher (24%) recurrence rate occurred in the largest clinicopathologic series to date.

### Synovial Chondromatosis

Synovial chondromatosis is an uncommon condition characterized by the formation of multiple nodules of hyaline cartilage within the subsynovial connective tissue. If the cartilage nodules undergo endochondral ossification, the term synovial osteochondromatosis is appropriate. The presence of clonal karyotypic abnormalities in synovial chondromatosis supports a neoplastic process. Cytogenetic analysis has shown diploid or near-diploid complements with abnormalities involving chromosome 6, rearrangements of 1p22, and extra copies of chromosome 5.49 Approximately half of cases harbor FN1:ACVR2A or ACVR2A::FN1 fusions.50, Synovial chondromatosis is benign and does not metastasize.

Synovial chondromatosis most commonly affects middle-aged men, with an average age in the fifth decade of life. Middle-aged women are more likely to develop the disease in the temporomandibular joint. The genders are equally affected with regard to hand and foot involvement, and patients with hand and foot involvement are usually in their sixth decade.

Patients commonly describe joint pain, swelling, stiffness, crepitance, and limitation of motion with a locking or grating sensation on movement. Symptoms are usually long-standing, recurrent, and progressive.

Synovial chondromatosis typically arises in large diarthrodial joints. The knee is affected in more than 50% of cases, usually as a monoarticular condition. Other common sites include the hip, elbow, shoulder, and ankle. Infrequently, synovial chondromatosis arises in the small joints of the hands and feet and in the temporomandibular joint. When cartilage nodules develop in the synovial lining of bursae, tendons, and ligaments, this is known as extra-articular synovial chondromatosis. The extra-articular variant most commonly affects the fingers, followed by the toes, hand, wrist, foot, and ankle, and more than one synovial sheath may be involved.

Findings of plain radiographs largely depend on whether the cartilage nodules are calcified or ossified and whether they erode adjacent bony structures. Visible calcifications are absent in 5% to 33% of cases; however, most often, multiple oval intra-articular radiodensities are present and range in size from a few millimeters

to several centimeters (Fig. 129.27). The pattern of mineralization varies and may appear as irregular flecks that represent calcified cartilage or show a trabecular architecture, which is a manifestation of endochondral ossification. Lesions that are not mineralized can be seen on an arthrogram because they produce multiple filling defects. In approximately 11% of cases, nodules erode the neighboring skeleton, especially along the anterior aspect of the distal femur.

CT may show masslike nodules in the synovium that have a density similar to skeletal muscle. CT can also detect small calcifications and erosions before they are apparent on plain films. MRI shows that the nodules of cartilage have low signal intensity on T1-weighted sequences and high intensity on T2-weighted sequences, which reflects the high water content of the hyaline cartilage. Areas of calcification or mineralized bone have a low signal intensity on T1-weighted and T2-weighted sequences. CT and MRI scans are helpful in identifying the intra-articular source of the lesion and its anatomic extent. In long-standing disease, the bones adjacent to involved joints may be osteoporotic and may show changes of secondary OA.

The cartilage in extra-articular synovial chondromatosis has similar radiographic changes. Nodules of cartilage are frequently mineralized and may appear as a linear arrangement of small calcific densities that are aligned along the sheath and that can span many joints (Fig. 129.28).

The radiographic differential diagnosis of synovial chondromatosis includes osteochondritis dissecans, OA with loose bodies, tuberculosis, hemopathic arthropathies, pseudogout with extensive synovial calcification, and synovial tumors. In many instances, the clinical presentation and the radiographic picture should lead to the correct diagnosis. However, in a significant proportion of cases, radiographs and the clinical picture are vague, and thus only a biopsy specimen can remove all doubt about the diagnosis.

Characteristic of synovial chondromatosis is a thickened synovium containing numerous opalescent firm nodules of cartilage that bulge from the surface in a cobblestone pattern (Fig. 129.29). These nodules usually measure less than 5 cm and may lose their attachment to the synovium and form loose bodies, sometimes numbering in the hundreds. The calcified cartilage is white, and areas of ossification manifest as gritty tan trabeculae, which may house fatty marrow. The synovium adjacent to the cartilage may show reactive changes, such as edema, hyperemia, hyperplasia, and villous transformation. Infrequently, the disease manifests as a single, solitary nodule of cartilage, which may be very large and may undergo partial endochondral ossification (synovial osteochondroma). Intra-articular osteochondroma can severely limit joint motion and may be confused clinically with other types of neoplasms.

The cartilage nodules develop in the connective tissue of the subsynovial compartment (Fig. 129.30). Neoplastic chondrocytes produce the hyaline matrix that eventually forms individual nodules, which peripherally abut the surrounding tissues (Fig. 129.31). The cartilage varies in its cellularity, and chondrocytes range from small to large; some may be binucleate and hyperchromatic, similar to the chondrocytes in intraosseous chondrosarcoma (Fig. 129.32). Despite these histologic findings of concern, experience has shown that hypercellular variants with atypical chondrocytes usually behave in a benign fashion.

Over time, nodules of cartilage attached to the synovium can be invaded by blood vessels, which initiates the process of endochondral ossification, with woven and lamellar bone formation and the development of a medullary cavity with fatty marrow (Fig. 129.33). If these nodules lose their synovial attachments and become free-floating, they may continue to increase in size because the cartilage derives its nourishment from synovial fluid, although the osseous portion and the marrow die.

The treatment of choice for synovial chondromatosis consists of excision of the involved synovium and removal of all loose bodies. Open versus arthroscopic approach and the role of total synovectomy are currently matters of debate. The prognosis is good, although recurrences may develop if removal is incomplete. Most recurrences occur in the setting of diffuse involvement of the synovium.

Synovial chondromatosis rarely undergoes malignant transformation into chondrosarcoma, although in one series this phenomenon occurred in 6.4% of cases. However, a significant percentage of the reported cases of synovial chondrosarcomas have shown evidence of underlying synovial chondromatosis.59-61 The

chondrosarcomatous component exhibits marked hypercellularity, severe cytologic atypia, and prominent mitotic activity; the stroma is often myxoid. Synovial chondrosarcoma arising in synovial chondromatosis also frequently harbors FN1 and/or ACVRA2

gene rearrangements. Copy number alterations in CDKN2A also occur in synovial chondrosarcoma, similar to those in highgrade conventional chondrosarcoma.

### Chondroma of Tendon Sheath and Periarticular Structures

Solitary soft tissue chondroma is a benign neoplasm. It commonly arises in tendon sheaths and infrequently involves joint capsules or other periarticular structures. Alterations in FN1 have been documented with gene rearrangements involving FGFR1 or FGFR1.50 However, FN1 rearrangements are not diagnostically specific and have been identified in an increasing number of chondroid soft tissue tumors with variable matrix calcification. A recently proposed umbrella term, FN1-rearranged calcified chondroid mesenchymal neoplasms, includes a subset of lesions previously considered as chondroblastoma-like soft tissue chondroma.

Tendon sheath chondromas usually arise in the flexor tendon sheaths of the distal extremities and are about three times more common in the hands than in the feet.63-65 They affect the sexes equally and are detected in early to midadulthood, presenting as

a painless, slow-growing, firm mass. Radiographically, tendon sheath chondromas appear as an extraosseous, well-delineated soft tissue mass that contains calcifications, which are punctate or ringlike in 33% to 70% of cases.66, Grossly, the tumors are ovoid, firm, blue-white, well-circumscribed masses of hyaline cartilage that are usually 1 to 2 cm in dimension and, in contrast to synovial chondromatosis, are solitary. Histologically, the hyaline cartilage is well formed with occasional small foci of myxoid change. The cartilage can be cellular, and chondrocytes may show limited cytologic atypia, which sometimes causes confusion with chondrosarcoma. The treatment of choice is simple excision, which is infrequently associated with local recurrence. 64,

The intracapsular and periarticular regions are uncommon sites for soft tissue chondromas. When they occur, they usually originate in the anterior infrapatellar region of the knee (Fig. 129.34). In this location, chondromas can achieve a large size (8 cm) and may interfere with knee motion. Their structure and biologic behavior are similar to those of soft tissue chondromas that arise elsewhere. Intracapsular chondromas have occurred in the knees of three members of a family with familial dysplasia epiphysealis hemimelica. Two other cases have been described in which cartilaginous hamartomas of the volar plates of the proximal and distal interphalangeal joints of the hands and feet were associated with peculiar hypertrophic skin lesions of the hand and hemihypertrophy of the limb.

### Tenosynovial Giant Cell Tumor

Tenosynovial giant cell tumor comprises a group of benign tumors that affect the synovial lining of joints, tendon sheaths, and bursae. These lesions were previously known as giant cell tumor of tendon sheath or fibroxanthoma of tendon sheath, localized nodular synovitis or benign (giant cell) synovioma, and pigmented villonodular synovitis. Tenosynovial giant cell tumor may be localized or diffuse and intra-articular or extra-articular. It has the potential to be locally aggressive in that it may invade into bone, grow through joint capsules, extend along tendons, and infiltrate into adjacent

soft tissues. Despite its destructive potential, this lesion generally does not have the capacity to metastasize unless it undergoes malignant transformation.

The common histologic denominator of these lesions is the neoplastic proliferation of synovial-like cells that may form a localized mass or spread along the synovial surface and invade downward into subsynovial connective tissue. The growing cells expand the subsynovial compartment, producing finger-like extensions, villi, and redundant folds. These projections often fuse into nodules and form convoluted lobulated masses admixed with a tangle of hairlike villi. The process may be a local phenomenon involving only part of the synovial lining, or it may be extensive, with the whole synovial surface affected.

Previously considered a reactive process, possibly in response to repeated hemorrhage, tenosynovial giant cell tumor is now known to represent a neoplasm characterized by variable, relatively simple structural genetic changes, most commonly alterations involving CSF1, the gene encoding colony-stimulating factor 1 (CSF1). The first described and most common translocation is between chromosomes 1p13 and 2q35 in which CSF1 is fused to the collagen VI alpha-3 (COL6A3) gene.67, Other identified CSF1 fusion partners include COL3A1, S100A10, VCAM1, FN1, CDH1, CDH17, RBBP1, GSTM5, CD101, NOTCH2, PTGFRN, TGFBR3, NBPF20, and CENPF, as well as intergenic rearrangements.73-75 Despite the variability in fusion partners, current evidence suggests that loss of the regulatory 3' untranslated region of CFSl is the most consistent recurrent genetic driver in tenosynovial giant cell tumor. Consequently, overexpression of CSF1 occurs in the neoplastic cells, which account for only a minority (2% to 30%) of cells in the mass.71, The remaining cells largely represent nonneoplastic inflammatory cells that are recruited into the tumor because they contain the receptor for CSF1 (CSF1R).71, This phenomenon has been termed a landscape effect and is also observed in certain types of lymphomas and sarcomas. Recently novel somatic CBL missense mutations have been identified in approximately one-third of tenosynovial giant cell tumors, occurring with or without a concomitant CSF1 gene alteration, and may represent an alternative mechanism for increased CSF1/CSF1R signaling. 73,

Neither the presence of CSF1 rearrangement nor CSF1 messenger RNA overexpression in the absence of the classical translocation appear to correlate with the diffuse versus localized variant of tenosynovial giant cell tumor or with disease recurrence risk. Currently, the factors that determine whether a tenosynovial giant cell tumor will manifest as a localized or diffuse process—two clinically different diseases—are unknown, as these two tumor variants appear to have the same genetic underpinnings and histologic composition of cells.

### Tenosynovial Giant Cell Tumor of Joints and Tendon Sheaths: Diffuse Type

The diffuse type of tenosynovial giant cell tumor of the joint involves large areas of the synovial lining, although uninvolved areas are invariably present. Its incidence is approximately 1.8 per 1 million. Although it may occur in all age groups, spanning children to older adults, most of these tumors affect adults in the third to fourth decade of life. The sexes tend to be equally affected, although some series have reported a predominance of males or of females.77-79 Diffuse tenosynovial giant cell tumor of the joint usually manifests as monoarticular arthritis. Bilaterality or involvement of multiple separate sites has been infrequently reported.

Some patients with polyarticular disease also have had significant congenital anomalies. Primary complaints include pain and effusions that can be intermittent with repeated bouts over a long time, ranging from months to years.77, The involved area may be stiff, swollen, and warm, and a palpable mass can sometimes be appreciated. Point tenderness is detected in approximately 50% of patients. Anatomic instability of the involved joint is uncommon.

The knee joint is affected most commonly and is involved in about 80% of cases.77, The next most frequent sites are the hip, ankle, calcaneocuboid joints, elbow, and tendon sheaths of fingers and sometimes toes. Occasionally, the palm, the sole of the foot, and unusual locations such as the temporomandibular joint and posterior elements of the spine are involved. Bursal involvement is rare, but if it happens, it usually occurs in the popliteal and iliopectineal bursae and the bursa anserina. Infrequently, the disease affects large tendon sheaths proximal to the ankle and wrist and produces a periarticular soft tissue mass. 80, It is thought that some of these lesions dissect through a joint capsule or a tendon sheath and extend along fascial planes to produce a soft tissue 80 mass.

Invasion of bone on either side of a joint can be seen with intraarticular, bursal, or tendon sheath involvement. This phenomenon most frequently occurs when the tumor involves "tight" joints, such as the hip, elbow, wrist, and feet, or when tendon sheaths are closely apposed to neighboring bones (Fig. 129.35).82, Rarely, only one bone may be invaded by an intra-articular lesion and, in this situation, it may be difficult to distinguish this type of lesion from a primary bone tumor (Fig. 129.36).

Joint aspiration frequently yields blood-tinged brown fluid that lacks diagnostic abnormalities. Synovial fluid analysis may show a low glucose content, a minimally elevated protein level, and a fair mucin clot. The inflammatory cell count is usually low but may be elevated. Similar findings can be seen in trauma, Charcot's joint, bleeding disorders, sickle cell disease, and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.

In at least two-thirds of cases, a soft tissue density due to the tumor or effusion or both can be visualized on a plain film. 86-89

Joint narrowing or calcification is uncommon. Arthrography may show numerous nodular filling defects that extend into an expanded joint space. Arteriograms are unusually striking owing to the prominent vascularity of the tumor. An inverse correlation tends to exist between the degree of vascularity and the amount of fibrosis or scarring of the lesion.

CT and MRI are useful in delineating the extent of disease and can detect intralesional lipid and hemosiderin deposits, which are important diagnostic features. 86-88 The tumor has low signal intensity (equal to that of skeletal muscle) on T1-weighted images and is heterogeneous on T2-weighted images. Extension into the bone manifests radiographically as multiple, well-marginated, subchondral cyst—like lucencies or juxtacortical oval pressure erosions (Figs. 129.35 and 129.36).83, In the knee, the femoral area adjacent to the intercondylar region is the site most frequently invaded as the tumor grows along the cruciate ligamentous insertions. Periarticular osteopenia, periosteal reactions, and joint destruction are unusual because the joint space is preserved until late in the course of the disease.87, The radiographic differential diagnosis of a given case includes (1) tuberculosis, which generally involves more osteopenia and joint destruction; (2) hemophilia, which is also associated with more extensive joint destruction; (3) synovial chondromatosis, which frequently has calcified radiopaque bodies; and (4) RA, which shows more severe osteopenia and joint narrowing.

Grossly, the synovium in diffuse tenosynovial giant cell tumor is red-brown to mottled orange-yellow and looks like a plush angora rug (Fig. 129.37). Matted masses of villous projections and synovial folds are prominent and are admixed with rubbery-tosoft nodules (0.5 to 2 cm in diameter) that are sessile or pedunculated. The synovial membrane is thick and succulent and is often coated with a fibrinous exudate. Red-brown or golden brown tissue may extend deep into subsynovial structures or may invade the joint capsule. If a tendon sheath is involved, a sausage-shaped mass may be evident because the sheath is distended by the proliferating tumor. If the joint capsule is invaded, adjacent soft tissue structures, including nerves and vessels, may be covered by

wispy, red-brown tissue. If soft tissue invasion is extensive, the lesion may appear as a soft-to-rubbery, red-brown mass with foci of hemorrhagic cysts. Similar tissue may be present near the chondro-osseous junction or may be wrapped around vascular and ligamentous attachments to bone surfaces, which represent entrance points into the interior of the bone. Although other conditions, such as hemochromatosis and hemosiderosis, also may discolor the synovium brown, the nodular component is usually absent; in addition, microscopic features are definitive for separating these entities (discussed in a previous section).

Microscopic examination reveals marked synovial cell hyperplasia with surface proliferation and, more importantly, subsynovial invasion by masses of mitotically active polygonal or round tumor cells with moderate amounts of eosinophilic cytoplasm and round nuclei (Figs. 129.38 and 129.39). Included among the invading tumor cells are scattered lymphocytes, multinucleated giant cells (osteoclast, Touton, or foreign body type), hemosiderin-laden macrophages, and fibroblasts. Hemosiderin is usually present and can be located in the stroma or the cytoplasm of synovial lining cells, macrophages, and tumor cells (Fig. 129.40). Foci of hemorrhage are common and are surrounded peripherally by giant cells and macrophages. Scattered collections of foamy macrophages (xanthoma cells) filled with lipid are also a frequent finding. These different cell populations fill and distend the synovial villi, causing them to fuse with adjacent ones, forming nodules. In some nodules, abundant collagen deposition with hyalinization may cause confusion with neoplastic bone. Rarely, the tumor may contain focally calcified cartilaginous matrix.

Immunohistochemical studies have been interpreted to support a synovial cell or fibrohistiocytic phenotype of the neoplastic cells.48, The tumor cells express clusterin, D2-40, and CD90 and a minority of large cells stain with antibodies to desmin.91, It is important to note that the cells that harbor the translocation express CSF1, which can be detected by various methods including RNA in situ hybridization. Flow cytometric analyses have shown that some of these tumors, especially tumors that have large extra-articular soft tissue components, may be aneuploid and

have high proliferative indices. Although these flow cytometric findings may help predict which cases would be more locally aggressive, examples of diffuse tenosynovial cell tumors with these attributes have not metastasized.

Treatment of diffuse tenosynovial giant cell tumor of the joint is not standardized and has included radiation therapy, total synovectomy, isotopic synoviorthesis, arthrodesis, bone grafting, and primary arthroplasty.77, Although no single therapy has been consistently successful, wide synovectomy is currently the recommended treatment.77, It is difficult to perform an actual complete synovectomy, however; residual involved synovium frequently remains, causing a local recurrence rate of 16% to 48%.96, A macroscopically incomplete tumor resection is associated with a more than twofold increased risk for tumor recurrence compared with a macroscopically complete resection. Tumors arising in the knee have a higher rate of recurrence compared with tumors arising in other joints. Rarely, recurrent disease or tumors with large extra-articular components may require more radical surgery, such as ray resection or amputation. Studies have shown that moderate doses of radiation may control and even cure patients with such extensive disease, possibly obviating the need for radical surgery or amputation. A four-tier MRI severity classification has been proposed to define disease extent and stratify recurrence risk after surgical treatment, and this system appears useful to identify the most severe subgroup and therefore eligibility for systemic therapy or clinical trials of novel therapeutic agents.

Various drugs targeting the CSF1/CSF1R pathway are have been tested to determine their efficacy in clinically challenging 100, Initial studies focused on tyrosine kinase inhibitors cases. (TKIs) with activity against CSF1R, such as imatinib mesylate and nilotinib, with early studies showing success in the treatment of diffuse tumors involving the joint. Indeed, the first systemic therapy to gain approval by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration was pexidartinib (PLX3397), a novel small-molecule TKI with strong selective activity against CSF1R, in 2019. In the phase III study (ENLIVEN) of this agent for symptomatic tenosynovial giant cell tumor with severe mobility or functional limitations not amenable to surgery, patients treated with pexidartinib demonstrated an overall response rate of 39% (n = 61) at 25 weeks and 53% at 22 months with improvement in symptoms and function.102, Subsequent studies with long-term follow-up showed increased response rates than those seen in ENLIVEN. Side effects are generally manageable, with the most significant being mixed or cholestatic hepatotoxicity. Other TKIs with anti-CSF1R tested in phase I or phase I/II clinical trials include edicotinib (JNJ 4036527)and vimseltinib.

Most recently, clinically validated therapeutic approaches for targeting the CSF1/CSF1R pathway involve the development of antibodies that bind CSF1 or CSF1R. Targeted approaches are being tested with monoclonal antibodies such as lacnotuzumab (MCS110), a humanized monoclonal antibody directed against CSF1; emactuzumab (RG7115), a monoclonal antibody that inhibits the dimerization of CSF1R; and cabiralizumab (FPA008), a monoclonal antibody that directly binds the receptor ligand binding domain of CSF1R. These agents have been tested in phase I or phase II clinical trials and with ongoing studies.

### Malignant Diffuse Tenosynovial Giant Cell Tumor

Malignant tenosynovial giant cell tumor is rare and clinically aggressive. The joints of the lower extremity are most commonly affected, in particular the knee. Malignant tenosynovial giant cell tumor is considered primary when it arises in conjunction with co-existing, benign-appearing tenosynovial giant cell tumor and secondary when it presents as a sarcomatous recurrence at

a site of a previously documented benign tenosynovial giant cell tumor.94, The neoplastic cells appear cytologically malignant and may be spindle or polyhedral shaped. Rarely osteosarcomatous or chondrosarcomatous differentiation has been noted. Malignant tenosynovial giant cell tumors have the capacity to behave aggressively; approximately 33% of patients die of disease, 30% have pulmonary metastases, 20% have lymph node involvement, and 15% have distant metastases.94, A recent report of 10 cases showed that the malignant cells have an immunophenotype similar to that of normal synoviocytes and the mononuclear cells of benign tenosynovial giant cell tumor. The presence of CSF1 rearrangements and CSF1 overexpression in the absence of an identified rearrangement has also been documented in malignant diffuse tenosynovial giant cell tumor.105, Deletion of portions of 15q and trisomies involving chromosomes 5 and 7 have also occurred. 97, Conventional cytotoxic chemotherapy provides clinical benefit while targeted TKI therapy appears to be of limited utility.

### Localized Tenosynovial Giant Cell Tumor of the Joint

Localized tenosynovial giant cell tumor of the joint manifests as a solitary, well-circumscribed mass. It usually consists of a single sessile or pedunculated, sometimes lobulated, tumor that ranges from 1 to 8 cm in diameter (Fig. 129.41). Most commonly, it is unilateral, arises in the knee, and is equally distributed between the sexes.

Symptoms are similar to those of diffuse tenosynovial giant cell tumor, except that in the localized variant, a higher frequency of joint locking is reported because the mass interferes with motion. A few patients may present with acute severe joint pain caused by torsion and infarction of the tumor. Effusions are common, but the synovial fluid tends to be less bloody than in the diffuse variant, and it may be clear.

Imaging studies show a heterogeneous nodular mass that contains lipid and hemosiderin deposits (Fig. 129.42). In the knee joint, the tumor frequently arises in the suprapatellar notch, in the femoral notch, and between the meniscus and the joint capsule. Usually, no bone invasion occurs. Marginal excision is generally curative. Small lesions can be extirpated arthroscopically.

Histologically, localized tenosynovial giant cell tumor of the joint is identical to the nodules of the diffuse variant. The main difference is that the prominent synovial villi present in the diffuse variant are absent or sparse.

### Localized Tenosynovial Giant Cell Tumor of the Tendon Sheath

Localized tenosynovial giant cell tumor of the tendon sheath usually involves the hand or wrist, and less frequently the foot or ankle. It is the most common soft tissue tumor of the hand and usually arises from the flexor tendon sheaths of the finger; the index finger is affected most frequently, followed in descending order of frequency by the third, fourth, fifth, and first fingers.

Tumors of the digits predominate in females, with a male-tofemale ratio of at least 2:1,78,111 and tumors of the toes have an equal sex distribution. On average, patients are in the third to fifth decades of life and present with a painless, palpable, firm, mobile mass.

Clinically, the mass is usually solitary and is located on the flexor surface, but it may bulge into the extensor or lateral aspects

of the digits (Fig. 129.43). The tumors are slow growing, and the intervals between detection and surgical treatment have ranged from several weeks to longer than a decade, with an average interval of slightly longer than 2 years.78,

Radiographically, the tumors appear as well-circumscribed soft tissue masses and, in about 25% of cases, adjacent extrinsic excavation of the cortical bone has a sclerotic margin (Fig. 129.44).78, MRI reveals that the lesions have a hypointense signal on T1-weighted images and either a hypointense or a hyperintense signal on T2-weighted images. These findings are helpful in distinguishing giant cell tumor of tendon sheath from other soft tissue tumors. 7,

The gross pathology is that of a well-circumscribed, multinodular, round, rubbery, variegated red-brown-tan-yellow mass, generally not larger than 5 cm in diameter, which is firmly attached to but easily peeled off the involved tendon (Fig. 129.45). At surgery, the lesion sometimes may "pop out" of the incision. The cut surface reveals a solid mass that ranges from hues of yellow to orangered-brown, depending on the quantity of lipid and blood pigments present. Often bands or septa of white fibrous tissue subcompartmentalize (Fig. 129.46). The morphology and immunophenotype of the cell types present are identical to those in the diffuse variant (Fig. 129.47).91, Ultrastructurally, proliferating cells have features similar to type A and type B synovial lining cells. Flow cytometry has been performed on a few cases, and all have been diploid.

These tumors are benign and do not metastasize. Malignant giant cell tumors of tendon sheath have occurred.115, The treatment of choice is conservative surgical excision, which is usually curative. Local recurrence may be noted if excision is incomplete; average recurrence rates are <6%.76,78,111

### Malignant Tumors of the Joint

Malignant tumors of joints are uncommon and are classified into primary and secondary types. Primary malignancies are very rare and are virtually always sarcomas arising within the synovium of large diarthrodial joints, especially the knee. Patients are adults or adolescents who present with chronic symptoms of pain, swelling, and effusion, and most tumors are chondrosarcomas or synovial sarcomas. The largest reported series of primary de novo intraarticular sarcomas comprised 15 cases, all involving the knee joint; malignancies arising from pre-existing benign tumors were excluded. Patients showed a slight male predominance (3:2) with a mean age of 44 years (range 1684 years). Histologies included synovial sarcoma (five), extraskeletal myxoid chondrosarcoma (three), myxofibrosarcoma (two), undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma (two), myxoinflammatory fibroblastic sarcoma (one), conventional hyaline chondrosarcoma (one), and high-grade myofibroblastic sarcoma (one). Our experience has also included cases of intra-articular pleomorphic fibrosarcoma, malignant tenosynovial giant cell tumor, angiosarcoma (Fig. 129.48), and epithelioid sarcoma (Fig. 129.49). Secondary malignant tumors of joints, by definition, originate beyond the confines of the joint; most are sarcomas that extend from neighboring bone or surrounding soft tissue. Although synovial tissue is highly vascular, metastases or involvement of the synovium by carcinoma, melanoma, lymphoma, or leukemia is uncommon.

### Primary Sarcomas of Joints

### Conventional Chondrosarcoma

Conventional chondrosarcoma arising in the synovium is unusual; fewer than 100 cases have been reported in the English sarcoma arises in association with pre-existing synovial chondromatosis, and a large series of synovial chondromatosis reported malignant transformation into chondrosarcoma in 6.4% of 58, Patients are usually in the fifth to seventh cases. decade of life, and the disease is slightly more prevalent in males than in females (approximately 3:2).119, Typically, the tumor manifests as a progressively enlarging joint mass that may cause mechanical dysfunction, pain, and stiffness. In patients who have pre-existing synovial chondromatosis, the duration of symptoms is usually long (average 11.2 years), with repeated prior excisions of locally recurrent disease, and in some instances, symptoms may be present for 25 years.58,118- Approximately half of chondrosarcomas arise in the knee joint and one-third arise in the hip. The ankle, shoulder, elbow, temporomandibular joints, and spine are rarely involved.118, Clinically, rapid deterioration of longstanding synovial chondromatosis or rapid recurrence after synovectomy should raise concern for malignant transformation. 118,

Radiographic studies usually show a periarticular soft tissue mass that may have dense irregular or ringlike calcifications. Occasionally, invasion into the medullary cavity of adjacent bone is evident. The radiographic differential diagnosis varies according to the presence of calcification and includes synovial

chondromatosis, synovial sarcoma, diffuse tenosynovial giant cell tumor, and chronic synovitis.

Grossly, the involved joint is filled with synovium massively thickened by innumerable nodules of opalescent blue-white cartilage. The nodules of cartilage vary in size and may be free-floating in the joint cavity. In several cases, the tumor has extended into adjacent soft tissue and bone.

Microscopically, the tumor is composed of malignant hyaline and myxoid cartilage. Rarely, the matrix is entirely myxoid and has tic cartilage is cellular and contains cytologically atypical chondrocytes. The periphery of the lobules of cartilage is usually the most cellular and, in this region, some of the tumor cells can be spindled. Other findings include necrosis and permeation of invaded bone. Infiltration or destructive invasion of pre-existing bones

of the joint is the most reliable feature separating chondrosarcoma from synovial chondromatosis, as synovial chondromatosis demonstrates a "pushing" border when it infiltrates adjacent bone. However, a systematic review found this feature was present in a minority of cases. Co-existing synovial chondromatosis can be identified by its well-formed nodules of hyaline cartilage, which are less cellular, containing cytologically banal-appearing chondrocytes and a matrix that is frequently mineralized.

Treatment is usually surgical extirpation with consideration given for chemotherapy in high-grade lesions or lesions that have metastasized. Inadequate surgical removal virtually ensures local recurrence, which may necessitate subsequent radical excision. Metastases have occurred in approximately one-third of reported patients; the lung is the most common site for systemic spread.58, Synovial chondrosarcoma has a worse prognosis than conventional intraosseous chondrosarcoma, possibly due the difficult anatomic site (intra-articular) and the fact that overlapping clinical, radiographic, and pathologic features between secondary synovial chondrosarcoma and benign synovial chondromatosis frequently lead to a delay in a diagnosis of malignancy.

### Synovial Sarcoma

Synovial sarcoma is a common sarcoma that accounts for approximately 6% to 10% of soft tissue sarcomas. It usually develops in the deep soft tissues and rarely arises in joints (Fig. 129.50), but it may secondarily invade articular synovium from neighboring soft tissues. Earlier descriptions of this tumor attest to its wide spectrum of morphology because such names as adenosarcoma and synovial fibrosarcoma were used until the term synovial sarcoma, first introduced in 1936, became commonplace. The morphology of synovial sarcoma mimics a joint in its early stage of development in that it contains cleftlike spaces and glands delineated by large polygonal (epithelioid) cells surrounded by fascicles of spindle cells. The clefts and glands simulate a microscopic "joint space" that is bounded by synovial lining cells and is supported by subsynovial mesenchymal cells. Because epithelial or spindle cells may predominate, synovial sarcoma has been subtyped into biphasic and monophasic spindle cell and epithelial types, although the last type is exceptionally rare.

Synovial sarcoma commonly affects adolescents and young adults. In a series of 121 cases, the age range was 9 to 74 years, with a median age of 34 years; however, it occurs in children with significant frequency. 124-126

The term synovial sarcoma implies that the tumor originates from the synovium; however, fewer than 10% of cases are intraarticular or show continuity with a synovial lining. 127, The cell of origin is thought to be an immature mesenchymal progenitor cell or myoblast that is still thus far incompletely characterized.129,

Approximately 60% to 70% of synovial sarcomas arise in the extremities, especially the lower limb, in the vicinity of large joints, particularly the popliteal areas of the knee and foot.131, Regions of the thigh, hand, leg, and digits may be affected and, in the distal extremities, tumors are often adjacent to joint capsules or tendon sheaths or both. Tumors also have occurred in the neck, torso, craniofacial region, retropharyngeal space, retroperitoneum, spermatic cord, orbit, tongue, mediastinum, soft palate, heart, liver, kidney, lung, pleura, and prostate.

No clinical features specific to synovial sarcoma distinguish it from other sarcomas. The most common complaint is the development of a slowly enlarging, deep-seated, palpable mass that is

painful in about 50% of cases. 126, Symptoms may be present for an unusually long time, ranging from months to 25 years, with an average of about 6 months to 2.5 years, before medical evaluation is sought. 124, Delay in diagnosis is more frequent with tumors that are located in the deep soft tissues than in those that are based in the more superficial and clinically noticeable regions. In some cases involving the knee region, vague mild pain over several months may occur before a mass is appreciated and, if the tumor reaches a large size, limitation of motion finally may be noted. Head and neck lesions produce symptoms related to their specific sites, such as hoarseness and breathing or swallowing difficulties. Rarely, a patient may present with a symptom secondary to pulmonary metastasis, such as hemoptysis.

Classically, plain film findings of synovial sarcoma consist of a well-circumscribed, deep-seated soft tissue mass. Synovial sarcoma is one of the few primary soft tissue tumors that frequently calcify. Approximately 30% to 50% of cases reveal radiographically detectable calcifications that may have a fine, stippled, or dense appearance (Fig. 129.51). The calcification may be focal or may

present throughout most of the tumor. Periosteal reaction of adjacent bone is elicited in approximately 20% of cases, but bone is rarely invaded by the tumor.

CT is more sensitive than plain radiography in showing calcification or periosteal reaction. MRI is important in delineating the anatomic extent of the tumor and usually shows a large inhomogeneous mass with areas of hemorrhage. The radiographic differential diagnosis includes hemangioma, lipoma, synovial chondromatosis, soft tissue chondrosarcoma or osteosarcoma, myositis ossificans, aneurysm, and other sarcomas.

The gross pathology of synovial sarcoma reveals a well-demarcated, pink-tan, fleshy mass that easily detaches or "shells out" from its tumor bed (Fig. 129.50). The cut surface is usually uniform, gray-yellow, and rubbery. Calcified areas are gritty and hard. In larger tumors, areas of hemorrhage or necrosis or both with cystification and gelatinous breakdown of tissue may be seen. Synovial sarcoma sometimes grows between tendons, muscles, and fascial planes or wraps around neurovascular bundles.

Synovial sarcoma is subtyped into four patterns on the basis of predominant microscopic findings: monophasic spindle cell, monophasic epithelial, biphasic, and poorly differentiated variants. Use of such a classification system requires some subjectivity because many of these tumors have a variable histologic picture. A useful differential observation is that marked cellular pleomorphism and atypia are usually not present in synovial sarcoma and, when observed, tend to point to some other type of neoplasm, such as pleomorphic fibrosarcoma or undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma.

Microscopically, the hallmark of the classic biphasic synovial sarcoma is the two different populations of neoplastic cells consisting of epithelial and spindle cells (Fig. 129.52). Epithelial cells may be cuboidal or columnar and, similar to true epithelium, may have well-defined cytoplasmic borders. These cells may form glandular spaces, line papillae or cleftlike spaces, or grow in cohesive groups (Fig. 129.52). The epithelial cells are usually surrounded by fascicles of uniform, small, and plump spindle cells. Spindle cell fascicles are densely cellular and are frequently arranged in a "herringbone" pattern. In most biphasic synovial sarcomas, the spindle cell component predominates, and calcification of hyalinized stroma most frequently occurs in spindle cell regions. Some tumors may show bone formation, which may be present

in spindle or epithelial areas. In the monophasic variants, spindle or epithelial cells may be the only recognizable component. In the monophasic spindle cell variant, the tumor is composed purely of the spindle cell element that is arranged in hypercellular intersecting fascicles (Fig. 129.53). The monophasic epithelioid variant is the rarest and is composed predominantly of the epithelial cells—in most cases there is a minor spindle cell element. Poorly differentiated synovial sarcoma is composed of malignant round cells that may have rhabdoid morphology.

Immunohistochemistry has shown that epithelial and the spindle cell components frequently stain with antibodies to keratin and epithelial membrane antigen, markers usually associated with epithelial neoplasms.135, This pattern of reactivity has helped make it possible to separate synovial sarcoma from morphologically similar tumors, such as adult-type fibrosarcoma and malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor. It has also provided evidence that unlike tenosynovial giant cell tumor, synovial sarcoma does not arise from or recapitulate the synovium because normal synovial cells do not stain with these antibodies. Synovial sarcoma is also diffusely and strongly positive for TLE-1.138

Cytogenetic studies of synovial sarcomas have detected a consistent translocation t(X;18)(p11.2;q11.2) in almost all cases, resulting in SS18::SSX rearrangements, regardless of whether the tumor is biphasic or monophasic. 131, This finding provides insight into the genesis of synovial sarcoma, which is thought to be related to dysregulation of transcription and can be used as a diagnostic feature. This characteristic translocation leads to the fusion of the SWI/SNF chromatin remodeling complex subunit SS18 to the C-terminal repression domains of SSX1, SSX2, or rarely, SSX4, disrupting epigenetic control through SWI-SNFand histone deacetylase (HDAC)associated mechanisms and acting as the central genetic "driver" in this tumor.129, This genetic event is the only consistent cytogenetic abnormality in synovial sarcoma, which otherwise has demonstrated a relatively stable genome with few mutations. No relationship between the location of the translocation breakpoint and the prognosis has been discerned. 129 Recently, fusion-specific antibodies have been developed, making immunohistochemistry a tool that can replace molecular testing for SS18::SSX rearrangements in many instances.

The prognosis of synovial sarcoma is poor. In one study of 150 patients with nonmetastatic disease, 5-year, 10-year, and 15-year disease-free survival rates were 59%, 52%, and 52%, respectively. The presence of distant metastases has a great impact on prognosis; a recent systematic literature review found that patients with localized disease had a 5-year overall survival ranging from 40% to 90.7%, compared with 10% for patients with metastatic disease. Many factors influence prognosis; tumors that are small (<5 cm), arise in patients younger than 25 years of age, and lack poorly differentiated areas have a high rate of cure. In contrast, large tumors (≥5 cm) that arise in patients 25 years and older and that contain poorly differentiated areas have a dismal outcome. Pediatric patients (<16 years of age) have an improved prognosis compared with adults, despite similar clinical presentation in terms of tumor size, site, grade, and location. The impact of histologic subtype other than tumors containing a poorly differentiated component has been controversial.

The natural history of synovial sarcoma consists of local recurrence, which may be repetitive. Most recurrences manifest within 2 years after initial treatment, but intervals longer than 10 years are not exceptional. Ultimately, metastases occur in many patients (50%70%), with the lungs as the most common site (80%), followed by bone (10%) and liver (5%)142; regional lymph node

involvement has occurred in a few patients. About 10% of patients die within 1 year after diagnosis with metastatic disease, and 90% of these patients have massive pulmonary metastases.

Treatment must contend with issues involved with local and systemic therapy.
