Successful local control can usually be achieved by limb salvage surgery combined with radiation.141, Because regional lymph nodes may be involved, their status should be evaluated carefully and, if enlarged, they should be treated. Systemic treatment consists of various chemotherapy regimens that have provided questionable benefit, although adjuvant chemotherapy is usually recommended for patients who are at high risk—that is, patients with tumors larger than 5 cm. Few prospective studies have been performed to define the optimal treatment methodologies for all stages of synovial sarcoma. Clinical trials assessing various forms of targeted therapy in synovial sarcoma are currently underway, including those aimed at inhibiting activated receptor tyrosine kinase networks with TKIs, interfering with vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) signaling by using a VEGF-alpha monoclonal antibody, targeting HDAC-mediated epigenetic modulation with HDAC inhibitors, and utilizing an immunotherapeutic approach through vaccines or genetically engineered lymphocytes.

### Secondary Malignant t Tumors of the Joint

### Sarcomas

Primary sarcomas of bone, such as osteosarcoma and chondrosarcoma, infrequently involve a joint because intact articular cartilage usually acts as a barrier to direct tumor extension. However, when it is observed, joint invasion usually occurs via a pathway created by a transarticular fracture, via growth along tendoligamentous structures, or through capsule insertion sites. Because of this circumstance, on histologic grounds alone it may be difficult to distinguish some forms of synovial chondromatosis from a low-grade intraosseous chondrosarcoma that has secondarily spread into the joint. Rarely, sarcomas may involve the joint space secondary to local metastasis, such as in a reported case of sacrococcygeal chordoma metastatic to subcutaneous tissue of the ankle with extension into the ankle joint.

Similarly, primary soft tissue sarcomas gain access into the interior of a joint by growing through the joint capsule in conduits occupied by pre-existing vascular structures or along tendons and ligaments. This complication can make providing adequate therapy challenging because treatment may require en bloc resection of the joint.

### Metastatic Carcinoma and Melanoma

The synovium, in contrast to other richly vascular tissues, is rarely the site of metastatic carcinoma or melanoma; this may reflect the fact that only clinical cases in which joint symptoms prevail are reported because, at autopsy, joints are not routinely examined. Approximately 50 cases have been reported in the literature. Most carcinomas that metastasize to the synovium originate in the lung, followed by the gastrointestinal tract and breast and, less frequently, the kidney, bladder, cervix, and tongue. 146-150 0Rare 147,151,152Affected cases of metastatic melanoma have also ocurred. patients are usually elderly, and the knee is the most frequently involved joint. In many reported cases, the underlying bone also contains metastatic deposits and joint involvement may be secondary to direct extension of a bone metastasis into the joint.

Prognosis is poor, with an average survival of 5 months after diagnosis. 147,149,150

### Malignant Lymphoproliferative Disease .

The various types of malignant lymphoproliferative diseases, including leukemia, lymphoma, and myeloma, can involve the synovium and may produce osteoarticular symptoms.153-155 This complication occurs most frequently in individuals with leukemia and is seen in both acute and chronic forms. Joint symptoms have been observed in 12% to 65% of children and in 4% to 13% of adults with leukemia. Arthritis can develop at any time during the disease course and can be the presenting symptom. Large joints are affected more commonly than small joints, and the arthritis is often pauciarticular, asymmetric, migratory, and severe. Symptoms may result from leukemic infiltration of the synovium or irritation of the neighboring periosteum. When arthritis is the major presenting symptom, it may cause confusion with septic arthritis, rheumatic fever, subacute bacterial endocarditis, or RA. Primary synovial lymphoma is exceptionally rare and is sometimes associated with immunocompromised states or prior prosthetic joint arthroplasty.

### KEY POINTS

### Introduction

Immunotherapy has proven paradigm shifting for the field of oncology. The idea that activating patients' immune systems could treat their cancers dates back to surgeon William Coley, who administered a bacterial toxin to patients with inoperable tumors, causing tumor regression in some. This concept laid relatively dormant for the first half of the 20th century but found enthusiasm again with successes of high-dose interleukin (IL)-2 infusions for treatment of melanoma in the 1980s. In the last two decades, the field has grown exponentially, with immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) being the most commonly used cancer immunotherapy currently. In this chapter we focus primarily on issues related to ICIs of relevance to the rheumatology community, that is, rheumatic immune-related adverse events (irAEs), and use of ICIs for cancer treatment in patients with pre-existing autoimmune disease. These topics are contextualized with a broader view of ICIs and the full spectrum of irAEs.

### Immune Checkpoint Inhibitor Mechanism of Action

ICIs target inhibitory receptors and ligands on T cells, antigenpresenting cells, and/or tumor cells (Fig. 130.1A, B). By blocking negative co-stimulatory signals, activation of the T cell can occur relatively unchecked. This is thought to invigorate immune responses to the tumor that may have been dampened by chronic antigen stimulation or by other factors in the tumor microenvironment. The effects of cytotoxic lymphocyte-associated protein 4 (CTLA-4) and programmed cell death 1/programmed death ligand 1 (PD-1/PD-L1) blockade are not identical, and these therapies are now thought to work through different mechanisms. CTLA-4 inhibition lowers the threshold for expansion of activated T cells, but recent data suggest killing ofT regulatory cells may be a key factor to the anti-tumor response. 6, PD-1 or PD-L1 blockade can activate exhausted T cells but may also work through blocking the inhibitory effects on dendritic cells and natural killer cells. The first ICI drug approved for use in the United States, ipilimumab, targets CTLA-4 on T cells. Subsequently approved drugs have targeted either PD-1 (nivolumab, pembrolizumab, cemiplimab) or its ligand PD-L1 (atezolizumab, durvalumab, avelumab). Many other drugs are in development targeting related immune checkpoints, such as T cell immunoglobulin and mucin domain-3 (TIM3), CD137, and lymphocyte activation gene-3 (LAG-3) (Fig. 130.1C). An anti-LAG-3 agent, relatlimab, was approved in the United States in 2022 for use in combination with nivolumab for treatment of melanoma. Drugs targeting other checkpoints are being studied alone and in combination with existing ICIs.

### Other Types of Cancer Immunotherapy

ICIs, the focus of this chapter, are just one class of therapeutics that utilizes the immune system for treatment of malignancies. Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells are a different type of cancer immunotherapy in which patients' own T cells are genetically engineered to recognize antigens on the tumor target. CAR T cells

recognizing CD19 were first approved for the treatment of refractory pre-B cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia and diffuse large B cell lymphoma. CAR T cells with a variety of targets are now being trialed in adults for a range of hematologic malignancies,8,9 with attempts to move into solid tumors. Cytokine release syndrome, which can be severe and cause hypotension, has been a major side effect; this has been managed primarily with the IL-6 receptor (IL- 6R) inhibitor tocilizumab and corticosteroids. Neurotoxicity has also been a rare but life-threatening issue with CAR T cells. A variety of cancer vaccines have also been in development over the last several decades for use primarily in solid tumors with limited clinical success. Several clinical trials have combined cancer vaccines with ICIs hoping to increase responses. IL-2 infusions were previously used in cancers such as melanoma and renal cell carcinoma but have been mostly replaced by ICIs. Tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes, or the expansion of tumor resident lymphocytes

ex vivo and transferred back into the same patient, is another immunotherapy strategy being studied by oncologists.

### Immune Checkpoint Inhibitors in Oncology

The first indication for ICIs was advanced-stage melanoma; ipilimumab was approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration for this indication in 201 1. Agents that block CTLA-4, PD-1, and PD-L1, plus the combination of CTLA-4 and PD-1 blockade, are now approved for a variety of tumor types in the United States (Table 130.1). With combination CTLA-4 and PD-1 blockade in advanced-stage melanoma, the 3-year survival rate is nearly 60%. Advanced stage nonsmall cell lung cancer (NSCLC) is another indication for ICI therapy and is a considerably more common diagnosis than advanced-stage melanoma. Survival benefits are more modest in NSCLC; combination therapy in patients with

high tumor mutational burden has a 1-year progression-free survival rate of 42.6%,16 and nivolumab monotherapy in advanced NSCLC has a 1-year progression-free survival rate of 19%. Other approved indications include renal cell carcinoma, Hodgkin's lymphoma,19 urothelial carcinoma,20 advanced cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma, Merkel cell carcinoma,22 any solid tumor with microsatellite instability23 (a genetic alteration that leads to a high mutation rate), and several other tumor types. ICIs are being used for earlier-stage disease and in an ever-increasing number of tumor types. They are also being used in the adjuvant setting as in high-risk melanoma that has been resected24 and in the neoadjuvant setting prior to surgery for NSCLC.

### Immune-Related Adverse Events

The main class of side effects due to ICIs, known as irAEs, are related to excessive or off-target inflammation that causes nontumor tissue damage. That the general mechanism of toxicity for ICIs is closely related to the desired mechanism of efficacy (increased activity of the immune system) is unique among many cancer therapies and potentially complicates treatment.

### Clinical Spectrum of Immune-Related Adverse Events

The spectrum of clinical presentations for irAEs ranges widely, including the severity of events, temporal relationship to ICI exposure, and treatment strategies. There is also significant heterogeneity in prevalence, relationship to type of ICI, and relationship to underlying tumor type. Nearly every organ system can be affected by irAEs. The most common irAEs are dermatologic conditions,

occurring in as many as 30% of ICI-treated patients, and hypothyroidism in up to 20%. Rare but potentially severe irAEs include myocarditis, occurring in less than 1% of patients with irAEs, and neurologic toxicities such as Guillain-Barré syndrome, encephalitis, and myasthenia gravis. Other irAEs include hepatitis, hypophysitis (inflammation of the pituitary), colitis, pneumonitis, pancreatitis, insulin-dependent diabetes, uveitis, peripheral neuropathy, and irAEs similar to classic rheumatologic diseases, which are discussed in detail later in this chapter. Many irAEs range widely in severity; both pneumonitis and colitis can be life threatening in some cases but can also be mild and self-limited. Similarly, rash may respond to topical therapy or can be severe, with cases of Stevens-Johnson syndrome28 and toxic epidermal necrolysis reported. Some irAEs, such as colitis and rash, tend to develop early in the treatment course, whereas others, like pneumonitis and inflammatory arthritis (IA), have a variable time to onset.30, Colitis and hypophysitis are more common with CTLA-4 inhibition.32, Pneumonitis, hypothyroidism, and vitiligo, on the other hand, are more common with PD-1 inhibition.31, Patients with melanoma are more likely to have dermatologic and gastrointestinal (GI) irAEs but less likely to have pneumonitis.

### Potential Mechanisms Underlying g Immune- Related Adverse Events

The underlying mechanisms of irAEs are not well understood across organ systems. Given the differences in clinical presentation and responses to certain immunosuppressive therapies, there are likely multiple mechanisms contributing. The following is a brief summary of potential mechanisms for irAEs and evidence supporting those mechanisms.

Cytokine-mediated inflammatory damage. Levels of serum IL-17 both before ICI treatment and after 6 weeks of therapy correlated with development of severe colitis. Tumor necrosis factor (TNF) inhibitors and IL-6 receptor inhibitors have been effective treatments for irAEs such as colitis, pneumonitis, IA, and polymyalgia rheumatica.

Th-1 and Th-17 T cell-mediated damage. Th1-CD8+ T cells are expanded in blood and synovial fluid of patients with ICIinduced IA. More specifically, patients with ICI-induced IA treated with combined anti-CTLA-4/PD-1 therapy demonstrate an enhanced Th17 signature.

Expression of CTLA-4 or PD-1/PD-L1 on target tissue. CTLA-4 is expressed on pituitary tissue, the target tissue leading to the irAE of hypophysitis. Though hypophysitis is more common with CTLA-4 inhibitors, it still occurs in patients on anti-PD-1 or anti-PD-L1 drugs, thus cross-reactivity with tissue is not the only mechanism at play.

Shared antigen recognition by T cells. T cell receptor sequencing from myocardium, skeletal muscle, and tumors from two cases of ICI-related myocarditis showed that the T cell clone most prevalent in heart muscle was also seen in amplified numbers in skeletal muscle and found in tumor tissue. Development of vitiligo has been associated with a positive tumor response to ICIs in melanoma, 38,39which is thought to be due to a common immune response against melanocytes in normal skin and melanoma cells.

Activation of pre-existing subclinical autoimmunity. Several patients with ICI-induced myasthenia gravis have been found to have pre-existing acetylcholine receptor antibodies. Also, two patients with IA who had anti-citrullinated peptide antibodies before ICI therapy developed clinically apparent IA only after treatment.

Perturbations of the microbiome. Alterations in GI or other mucosal flora may also influence development of irAEs. For example, a particular alteration in baseline colonic microbiome (at the start of ICI therapy) is seen more often in patients who develop colitis due to ICIs compared with other ICI-treated patients. This area is actively being investigated in melanoma and NSCLC, in addition to how the microbiome may affect tumor response to ICI therapy.

Shared genetic predisposition to classic autoimmune diseases. In insulin-dependent diabetes as an irAE, several patients have been found to have high-risk human leukocyte antigen (HLA) alleles that predispose for type 1 diabetes mellitus. A pilot study in ICI-induced IA showed an increase in HLA- DRB1 shared epitope alleles (genetic risk factors in rheumatoid arthritis [RA]) in patients with ICI-induced IA compared with healthy controls.

### The Relationship Between Immune-Related Adverse Events and Tumor Response

Data have been published on a variety of tumor types indicating that developing an irAE may be a positive prognostic factor for tumor response to therapy. In a study of nivolumab for melanoma, there was a higher response rate in those with irAEs compared with those with no irAEs; the highest rate of tumor regression (80%) was in those with grade 3 irAEs or higher.43, In NSCLC, development of irAEs was associated with improved survival outcomes for those with advanced or recurrent disease treated with nivolumab. In a pooled analysis of nonmelanoma

cancers treated with PD-1 inhibition, there were also better overall response rates in those who developed irAEs.

### Rheumatologic c Immune-Related d Adverse Events

Immune-related adverse events can present similarly as many classic rheumatologic diseases. There are important differences, however, in clinical phenotype, autoantibodies, and treatment modalities that in many instances differentiate rheumatologic irAEs from their non-ICI-induced counterparts.

### Epidemiology

The prevalence of irAEs with rheumatologic phenotypes has not been well characterized in ICI clinical trial data. There are several reasons that likely explain this. First, musculoskeletal AEs typically have a variety of codes in adverse event grading systems for oncology trials that could be used to describe events that were actually IA, polymyalgia rheumatica, or myositis (e.g., arthralgia, arthritis, joint swelling, periarthritis, myalgia). Second, rheumatologic irAEs are rarely life threatening or severe by oncology adverse event grading and are therefore less likely to be reported. Information on epidemiology comes primarily from single-center retrospective studies or from databases for drug adverse event reporting. IA appears to be the most common rheumatic irAE, with estimates of prevalence ranging between 3% and 7% in retrospective studies.48, This may be an underestimate due to previous lack of awareness of IA as a side effect of ICIs. Myositis occurs in less than 1% of ICI-treated patients. The rates of giant cell arteritis, sicca syndrome, other types of vasculitis, and scleroderma-like illness due to ICI therapy have not been well defined.

### Inflammatory Arthritis

Inflammatory arthritis as a result of ICI therapy was first noted in the rheumatology literature in 2015.51 Since that time, there have been numerous retrospective studies detailing clinical features and response to treatment.41, IA due to ICIs can have a clinically heterogeneous presentation; patients typically present differently than in RA, psoriatic arthritis, or other spondyloarthritis. In one series, most patients presented with a large joint affected first, but up to a third of patients had small joints of the fingers and wrists initially affected. Patients may also have an additive course where they start with a monoor oligoarthritis and develop into a polyarthritis. Significant tendon involvement with tenosynovitis and enthesitis has been reported by several groups (Fig. 130.2A).51-54 Reactive arthritis with concomitant urethritis and conjunctivitis has also been described.52, In the limited reports to date, all cases presenting with ICI-related reactive arthritis also had colitis as a preceding irAE. Patients can rapidly develop erosive disease within months of symptom onset. Additionally, inflammatory back and neck pain have been described in a limited number of patients (Fig. 130.2B).

Patients with ICI-induced IA have been primarily seronegative for traditional autoantibodies including anti-nuclear antibodies, rheumatoid factor (RF), and anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies (CCPs) with 90% seronegative in one systematic literature review. There are reports of patients seropositive for both RF and CCP, some of whom had measurable autoantibodies in serum

collected before ICI therapy was started in the absence of arthritis symptoms. Similarly, HLA-B27, the main genetic risk factor for ankylosing spondylitis, has been negative in the majority of patients tested. Inflammatory markers are elevated in the majority of patients but not all. Those treated with combination therapy appear to have higher inflammatory markers than those treated with PD-1/PD-L1 monotherapy in one cohort of patients; those with combination therapy are also more likely to have arthritis that starts in the knee and to have a reactive arthritis phenotype.

Imaging results of ICI-induced IA with magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and ultrasound has been characterized. Patients have a variety of findings including Doppler positive synovitis, effusions, erosions, tenosynovitis, and enthesitis on musculoskeletal ultrasound.54, Similar findings of synovitis, effusions, and erosions may also be seen on MRI. An interesting study of MRI in patients on ICI presenting with musculoskeletal pain showed that

periarticular tissues may also be involved with myofasciitis seen in addition to synovitis in several patients. One study evaluated computed tomography (CT) and positron emission tomography scans obtained for cancer staging, which showed synovitis in a subset of patients before they presented for rheumatology evaluation.

Risk factors for developing ICI-induced IA are largely unknown. It can occur with anti-PD-1, anti-PD-L1, or combination PD-1/CTLA-4 inhibition. It has been noted in patients with a variety of tumor types from melanoma and NSCLC to prostate cancer and Hodgkin's lymphoma. A preliminary study suggests that possessing the HLA DRB1 shared epitope allele may be associated with developing ICI-induced IA. Treatment for ICI-induced IA is detailed in the following section. Importantly, IA may persist after the cessation of ICI therapy and become a chronic problem. In one study, almost 50% of patients with follow-up 6 months after ICI cessation had ongoing symptoms

and/or required immunosuppression for ICI-induced IA. Risk factors were longer duration of ICI therapy, having two or more other irAEs, and using combination anti-CTLA-4/PD-1 therapy.

### Polymyalgia Rheumatica/Giant Cell Arteritis

Both a polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR)like syndrome and giant cell arteritis (GCA) have occurred in patients on ICI therapy. Isolated PMR is the more common presentation, as with traditional forms of PMR and GCA. Patients can present with hip and/or shoulder pain and stiffness and most have elevated inflammatory markers.41, There has been a description of a clinical syndrome with PMR features and smaller joint involvement of IA. PMR and GCA complicate treatment with both CTLA-4 and PD-1 inhibition.58, Symptoms of ICI-related GCA mirror that of traditional GCA and include headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, and visual changes like amaurosis fugax with or without PMR-type symptoms.66, Inflammatory markers are elevated in all confirmed cases of GCA due to ICIs, with C-reactive protein level reported as high as 296 mg/L.66, Temporal artery biopsies have shown features consistent with GCA, including intimal proliferation, arteritis, and disruption of the elastic lamina. Temporal artery biopsy is important if GCA is suspected as ICI therapy may need to be discontinued.

### Sicca Syndrome

There have been reports of dry mouth and dry eyes, often severe, .53, Most of these occurring in the setting of ICI therapy. cases were negative for anti-Ro or anti-La antibodies, but, as in IA, seropositive cases have also occurred. Dry mouth is commonly the most prominent symptom. Biopsies of the minor salivary gland have shown inflammation distinct from that of primary Sjögren's syndrome (Fig. 130.2C). There has been one case with ICIrelated parotitis that responded to corticosteroids. Another case described a sensory neuropathy in the setting of a salivary gland biopsy with features of Sjögren's syndrome.

### Myositis

Inflammatory myopathies due to ICIs are a rare but increasingly appreciated adverse effect. Most cases are more similar to polymyositis71-76 without classic skin rashes of dermatomyositis; however, several cases of dermatomyositis have occurred.77, As with PMR/GCA, cases have been seen with both CTLA-4 and PD-1/ PD-L1 blockade. Proximal muscle weakness is the most common presentation, but distal, respiratory, and neck weakness and concomitant myocarditis have been seen. Creatine kinase levels are typically elevated, ranging from 500 to over 16, U/L. Rhabdomyolysis can occur in some patients. Myositis may also be accompanied by fasciitis, which can be quite painful, as in traditional inflammatory myopathies. MRI may show inflammation of the involved muscles or fascia (Fig. 130.2D). Electromyography has shown myopathic patterns, many consistent with an irritable myopathy. Muscle biopsies have shown primarily endomysial inflammation, necrotizing myopathy, and only one reported case had a dermatomyositis-like pattern. 50, Myositis-specific antibodies have been mostly negative. One study showed that preexisting anti-acetylcholine receptor antibodies and lymphopenia were associated with developing myositis after PD-1 treatment. As with other irAEs, the precise risk factors for development of myositis are unknown and subject to ongoing investigation.

Additionally, patients with myasthenia gravis/myositis overlap and myocarditis/myositis overlap have been described; this is especially important to remember in patients presenting with respiratory compromise.72, Mortality risk increases with either of these overlap conditions. In one study using the World Health Organization (WHO) pharmacovigilance database, 56.7% of cases of myositis with concurrent myocarditis were fatal, while 27.9% of the myositis/myasthenia cases and 16% of isolated myositis were fatal. If myositis is suspected, further evaluation to determine whether concomitant myasthenia or myocarditis are present is indicated (Fig. 130.3).

### Other Vasculitis

There are limited descriptions of single-organ vasculitis affecting the uterus83 and retina84 and also of systemic anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodyassociated vasculitis,85,86 in ICI-treated patients. Possible ICI-induced aortitis and periaortitis have also been described in case reports. 87,88

### Scleroderma-like Disease

A small number of cases of scleroderma-like skin changes with diffuse and limited skin involvement have occurred.89-91 One of these cases with diffuse skin involvement had a modified Rodnan Skin Score of 28, which improved with prednisone and mycophenolate. In three cases where autoantibodies were tested, the patients were negative for anti-nuclear, anti-centromere, anti-ribonucleoprotein, anti-RNA polymerase III, and anti-topoisomerase antibodies.89, There has been minimal internal organ involvement (e.g., interstitial lung disease or pulmonary hypertension) consistent with systemic sclerosis in ICI-induced cases described thus far, with the exception of one patient with new-onset Raynaud's phenomenon along with skin changes and one other patient with a scleroderma renal crisis. 89, A study of the WHO pharmacovigilance database showed disproportionality of scleroderma risk with nivolumab and pembrolizumab but not other ICIs.

### Sarcoidosis-like Disease

Rheumatologists are often called on to evaluate sarcoidosis, particularly in suspected cases of extrapulmonary disease. Most reported cases in ICI-induced sarcoid-like disease have both pulmonary and skin involvement. The pulmonary involvement has included hilar and mediastinal lymphadenopathy and interstitial infiltrates (groundglass opacities, interstitial thickening). .93-96 Cytopathology of biopsied lymph nodes shows sarcoid-like granulomatous inflammation. Skin lesions have been erythematous papules or nodules, showing granulomatous inflammation when biopsied.93, To date, there are no reports of sarcoid arthropathy, hepatic involvement, or other organ involvement due to ICIs.

### Others

Rheumatologists may encounter a variety of other clinical syndromes in ICI-treated patients. Eosinophilic fasciitis, characterized by skin thickening of the arms, myalgia, fascial edema on MRI, and peripheral eosinophilia, can occur in patients treated with anti-PD-i/PD-L1 or anti-CTLA-4 agents.98, There are several reports of remitting seronegative symmetric synovitis with pitting edema in patients treated with ICIs.100, Accelerated osteoporosis leading to compression fractures and focal bone

resorptive lesions have recently been described in ICI-treated patients. Additionally, an acral vascular syndrome, similar to critical digital ischemia in scleroderma, has been described in a patient treated with ICIs.

Interestingly, there remain only a few case reports of lupus nephritis occurring due to ICI therapy. 104-105 Subacute cutaneous lupus has been described more extensively but without clear 106-108 The absence of systemic accompanying systemic symptoms. lupus erythematous (SLE) from rheumatologic irAEs is intriguing and may speak to key differences in pathogenesis between lupus and other rheumatologic diseases.

### Treatment of Rheumatologic Immune- Related Adverse Events

### General Treatment Principles

For oncologists, management is typically guided by the severity of the irAE, as defined by the National Cancer Institute Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events. Generally, grade 1 events are mild, grade 2 events are moderate and can affect instrumental activities of daily living, grade 3 events are severe and disabling (affecting self-care), and grade 4 events are life threatening. For grade 3 or higher events, ICIs are universally held and often discontinued.

The American Society of Clinical Oncologists, the National Comprehensive Cancer Network, and the Society for Immunotherapy of Cancer have issued guidelines for the management of a variety of irAEs, including rheumatic irAEs. 110-112 Relevant guidelines for rheumatologists include IA, polymyalgia-like syndrome, and myositis/myalgia.

The initial treatment for moderate to severe irAEs in general (not specifically for rheumatic irAEs) is corticosteroids at doses ranging from 0.5 to 2 mg/kg. In those who do not respond to or

who are intolerant to corticosteroids, there should be consideration of other types of immunosuppression. The main classes of immunosuppression/modulation that may be considered in treating rheumatologic irAEs, their potential risks and benefits, and their prior use for treatment of irAEs are summarized in Table 130.2.

### Inflammatory Arthritis Treatment

As the treatment of ICI-induced IA has been best described for rheumatologic irAEs, it can serve as an example for thinking about treatment across the spectrum of severity and persistence. For mild cases of IA, where symptoms do not affect activities of daily living, scheduled nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, topical nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory gel, or intra-articular steroids can be used. These can all be continued while the patient receives ICI therapy. For moderate cases of IA, corticosteroids initially at lower doses than used in other types of irAEs can be trialed. Some patients will respond to 20 mg of prednisone daily, as in traditional forms of IA, but others will need much higher doses, up to 1 mg/kg. If a patient is on less than 10 to 20 mg daily of daily prednisone, many oncologists will often continue the ICI rather than hold it. If the patient requires higher steroid doses, the ICI is typically held. If steroids cannot be tapered to a low dose or discontinued in 4 to 6 weeks, then other immunosuppressive agents can be trialed. The choice of agent depends on the severity and clinical features of the arthritis, any other irAEs the patient has currently or had previously, and plans for future ICI use/other cancer treatments. For example, if the patient has a highly inflammatory oligoarthritis with prior colitis and the oncologist would like to rechallenge with an ICI, it may be best to give a short course of TNF inhibition to control the arthritis. Tocilizumab has also been used successfully to treat patients with ICI-induced IA. There is now some experience in giving TNF inhibitors for colitis and IL-6R inhibitors for IA while continuing ICI therapy. 57, If the patient is still having

symptoms of IA 3 months or longer after ICI cessation at presentation with no plans for retreatment, it may make sense to start with methotrexate or leflunomide for moderate cases or hydroxychloroquine or sulfasalazine for more mild cases.

### Myositis

The treatment for ICI-related myositis depends primarily on its severity and the presence of concomitant irAEs. The starting dose of corticosteroids depends on whether the patient is hospitalized, whether there is concomitant myasthenia or myocarditis, and whether there is diaphragmatic dysfunction or dysphagia. In patients who are hospitalized with severe symptoms, an initial pulse dose of 1000 mg intravenous (IV) methylprednisolone is often used with subsequent tapering, whereas outpatients can be treated with initial prednisone doses of 1 mg/kg/day dosing. In severe or refractory cases of myositis, IV immunoglobulin76,114,115 has been used, and plasmapheresis76,115 has been attempted with limited success. This is especially relevant for cases with respiratory compromise. With myasthenia overlap, pyridostigmine has been used in addition to immunosuppression. If myocarditis is present, there are case reports of giving abatacept or mycophenolate. 116-118

### Specific Treatments in Other Syndromes

In sicca syndrome, treatments have been primarily symptomatic, focusing on dry eyes and dry mouth. Saliva substitutes and sialagogues such as pilocarpine and cevimeline are used for dry mouth and artificial tears or punctal plugs can be used for dry eyes. It is important for these patients to see their dentist and ophthalmologist regularly. There is also a suggestion that prednisone can be used in severe cases of dry mouth from sicca syndrome to improve salivary function. Prednisone can be started at 20 to 40 mg daily and tapered over 4 to 6 weeks.

In GCA, IV corticosteroids are often used initially, at initial doses as high as 1000 mg daily of methylprednisolone. ICIs have been held in all reported cases to date.

### Concerns With Immunosuppression

There are theoretical concerns that treating irAEs with immunosuppression will negatively impact the tumor response. This does not seem to be the case for short-term therapy with corticosteroids or TNF inhibitors for irAEs in melanoma patients treated with ipilimumab or nivolumab.119, In fact, there is now interest in how cytokine blockade combined with ICI therapy may be beneficial to tumor response. There is emerging evidence, however, that the use of corticosteroids at the onset of ICI therapy may be detrimental. In a study of patients being treated with anti- PD-1 and anti-PD-L1 agents for NSCLC, baseline use of 10 mg of prednisone or greater daily was associated with worsened overall response rate, progression-free survival, and overall survival. Studies evaluating the long-term durability of response and the effects of immunosuppression are lacking. This is particularly relevant for rheumatic irAEs as more long-term immunosuppression may be required to treat them due to persistence of the rheumatic phenotype.

### Multidisciplinary Care

Successful treatment of rheumatologic irAEs requires collaboration among the oncology care team, the rheumatologist, and any

other specialists involved (in the case of multiple irAEs). There is no consensus about the duration of ICI therapy required for sustained response within or across tumor types. Thus the patient's oncologist may have particular goals in terms of duration of therapy that impact the rheumatology treatment plan. Timely and direct communication between the rheumatologist and oncologist can allow therapy to be tailored to the patient's unique clinical scenario.

### Pre-existing Autoimmune Disease and Immune Checkpoint Inhibitor Use −

The association between autoimmunity and cancer has been appreciated in a variety of rheumatic diseases. Though patients with autoimmune disease are often at increased risk of certain cancers, 124-126 they were excluded from most of the early clinical trials for ICIs. Thus patients with diseases like RA or SLE and advanced-stage cancer have received ICIs primarily as standard of care. As a result, there is a lack of prospectively collected data on outcomes and safety of ICIs in this population. Data from the published literature, primarily from retrospective studies, are summarized here.

The first retrospective studies of patients with pre-existing autoimmune disease were from melanoma, one with 30 patients treated with ipilimumab127 and another involving 52 patients treated with anti-PD-1 agents. These studies grouped all autoimmune diseases together and included patients with RA, inflammatory bowel disease, psoriasis, SLE, multiple sclerosis, polymyalgia rheumatica, and a variety of other conditions. Flare rates of the pre-existing autoimmune diseases in these studies were 27% and 38%, respectively, while grade 3 or higher de novo irAEs occurred in 33% of those treated with ipilimumab and 21% in those treated with anti-PD-1 agents.

A systematic literature review of retrospective studies and case reports included 123 patients with pre-existing autoimmunity. In this study, 75% had an exacerbation of their preexisting rheumatic disease, 25% had a de novo irAE, but only 17.1% had to discontinue ICI therapy due to flare or irAE. In general, the rate of exacerbations was higher with PD-1/PD-L1 inhibition, whereas the rate of de novo irAEs was higher with CTLA-4 inhibition. The largest group of patients with rheumatologic disease had RA (N = 20); 35% had an arthritis flare only, 25% had a de novo irAE, and 15% had both. Larger systematic literature reviews have since been published showing similar tolerability. A systematic review from 2021 with 512 patients showed 44% of patients experienced a flare of their underlying autoimmune disease but only 18.2% discontinued ICI therapy due to immunotoxicity.

### Concurrent Immunosuppression

One question asked of rheumatologists by oncologists is whether to stop or continue immunosuppression in a patient with preexisting autoimmune disease when they are starting ICI treatment for cancer. In a series of lung cancer patients with pre-existing autoimmune disease, 20% were receiving immunomodulatory agents at the start of ICI treatment, including corticosteroids, hydroxychloroquine, tofacitinib, mesalamine, sulfasalazine, or apremilast. In a series of melanoma patients with pre-existing autoimmune disease treated with PD-1 inhibition, 37% were on corticosteroids and/or steroid-sparing agents (leflunomide,

hydroxychloroquine, apremilast, methotrexate, sulfasalazine, or mesalamine). Some potentially concerning data comes from a national French study on patients with pre-existing autoimmune disease, some of whom were on immunosuppression at the start of ICI therapy and others who were not. In the group of patients on immunosuppression at baseline, there was significantly decreased progression-free survival compared with those patients with autoimmune disease not on baseline immunosuppression. Information is still not complete on which immunomodulatory medications affect tumor response to ICIs due to the relatively small numbers of patients and the heterogeneity of underlying rheumatic diseases, immunomodulatory treatment, cancer type, and ICI regimen. Timing of the immunosuppression likely matters as the studies showing a negative effect on tumor response examined the impact of immunosuppression at the time of ICI treatment initiation. This includes the aforementioned national French study of patients with pre-existing autoimmune disease and also a study of lung cancer patients where those on 10 mg of daily prednisone or higher at baseline had worsened tumor response to ICIs.

Though t here a re l imited d ata r egarding u se o f I CIs i n patients with autoimmune disease, they seem to be generally well tolerated, and flares rarely lead to discontinuation of therapy. To manage patients with pre-existing autoimmune disease and advanced cancer on ICI therapy, multidisciplinary care and communication are key. Educating oncologists about the signs and symptoms of flare and if any laboratory tests are required for serial monitoring, and seeing patients more frequently while they are on ICI therapy, can help ensure that flares are diagnosed and treated.
